title: Every Trick Works Once
shortDescription: It hunts the town one night a month and never falls for the same decoy twice. Off nights, it buys bread and asks how you're holding up.
overview:
You are the Warden of Hollowbrook, the person whose whole job is losing a monster. By the founders' bargain, the thing in the pines may hunt one night each new moon — anyone it lures outside a threshold is fair game — and in exchange it keeps every other horror out of the valley. No wolves, no plague, no bandits in living memory. So the town stays. So do you.

Doors hold. That's the only mercy. It can't break in, but nothing stops it from crying like a lost child under a window, knocking in a dead husband's rhythm, or setting a barn alight to make someone choose. Your predecessors beat it with decoys, bells, salt-lines, staged voices — and it never falls for the same trick twice. Your inherited ledger of spent tricks is thick. Your list of fresh ones is thin. You're seven hunts clean, the longest streak on record, and it has started getting creative.

Between hunts it walks the market in daylight as Mr. Sallow — tall, courteous, pays in old coins, genuinely fond of your work. Around you: Brin, your fearless teenage apprentice who thinks up brilliant, terrifying ideas; Dallan the blacksmith, who wants to ambush it and would doom everyone; and Widow Ansa, who packs your hunt-night basket like you're going to a picnic. Tone: cozy dread, chess with a predator, dark humor at the bakery counter.

TAGS: dread, cat-and-mouse, dark fantasy, small town, mind games
intro: You are the Warden of Hollowbrook, keeper of the old bargain: one night each new moon, the thing from the pines may hunt, and anyone lured past a threshold is its lawful prey. In return it keeps all other evils out of the valley — which is why nobody leaves. Doors hold against it, but it lies beautifully: borrowed voices, false fires, knocks that sound like someone you buried. It never falls for a trick twice, and your predecessors spent most of the good ones. You are seven hunts clean, a town record. By day it wears a polite shape called Mr. Sallow and shops here. The new moon is four days off.
starters: The ledger is open on your table to the last blank page, and Brin is already talking with a mouth full of Widow Ansa's oatcake. "Hear me out. We freeze a decoy in the millpond. It thinks someone fell through the ice, it goes to sing at the hole, and we ring the far bells so half the town's shutters sound occupied—" She stops, tapping the entry from three winters back. Frozen decoy. Millpond. Spent by Warden Corse, who wrote beside it in cramped ink: worked once, it laughed. Brin deflates for exactly two seconds, then flips her slate over to the next idea. Outside, the morning market is setting up, and through the window you can see a tall figure in a grey coat examining apples with real tenderness, taking his time, the way a man does when he has all month. Four days. Brin looks at you, chalk ready.

You're counting Widow Ansa's change at the bakery counter when Mr. Sallow joins the queue behind you, smelling faintly of pine and cold cellars. "Warden," he says, warm as a stove. "Seven, now. I confess I've started telling people about you — well. Telling something." The baker's hands have gone still on the loaf. Ansa, unbothered, tucks a honey twist into your basket and says over her shoulder, "He'll take the rye, Sallow, and you'll wait your turn like a Christian." He laughs, delighted, and pays for her bread too, in coins older than the church. He's watching you the way Brin watches a puzzle box — fond, patient, certain of the mechanism. "Any hints for the new moon?" he asks. "No? Good. I do hate spoilers." The queue is very quiet. The rye is very warm in your hands.

It's an hour past midnight, three nights before the hunt, and something is knocking on Dallan's smithy door in the rhythm his dead brother used — two quick, one slow. You know because Dallan is standing in the street in his nightshirt with a hammer, bellowing at the dark pines that he knows it's out there, that the bargain is a coward's leash, that he'll open the door himself and settle it. It isn't hunt night. It can't take him. But it can teach him the knock, note which windows light up, learn who comes running — and half the street is coming running, lamps bobbing, thresholds swinging wide. Brin arrives at your elbow, breathless, whispering, "It's doing homework." The knocking stops. From somewhere in the trees, politely, something applauds. Dallan turns to you, hammer still raised, waiting to be told he's wrong.

You spend the grey morning walking the threshold line with a bucket of whitewash, repainting the marks on every doorstep in the mill quarter, and it's at the fourth house that you find the problem: someone has scrubbed the mark off the Tarrow family's stoop. Not weathered — scrubbed, with soap, edges still damp. Little Pel Tarrow watches you from the window, maybe six years old, and when you ask who cleaned the step, she says, "The tall man said it was dirty. He gave me a coin." She holds it up proudly against the glass: old silver, a face on it you don't recognize. Her mother isn't home. The pines start not forty paces from this door. You've got whitewash, a brush, four days, and a monster that has apparently begun preparing the board in daylight. Pel asks if she did good.

Hunt night. The seventh candle-mark since dusk, no moon at all, and you're stationed in the watch-shed by the green with your ledger, a horn, and Ansa's basket — she's packed boiled eggs, plum jam, and a note that says eat something, staring at trees is not a meal. So far it has tried a burning smell from the Herrick barn (a fistful of lit straw, real, small, out in minutes) and a woman weeping by the well who dissolved when Brin's mirror-lantern hit her. Now: silence, which is worse. Then, from the far end of Cobb Lane, your own voice — a very good copy — calling, "All clear, come out and help with the barn." It's using you. That's new. Somewhere down that lane, a door hinge creaks as somebody, God help them, considers believing it. The horn is in your hand.

Dallan corners you at the forge with a thing under sacking, and when he pulls the cloth off it's a bear trap the size of a cartwheel, jaws filed to a shine. "Bury it at the tree line," he says. "Bait it with a lamp. One night's work and no more Wardens ever." The forge is loud and hot and he's built it beautifully, you can see the hours in it, the grief — his brother went out a door nine years ago and Dallan has been building toward this ever since. What he hasn't built is an answer for what happens to a valley with no bargain and a wounded, insulted thing in the pines. Brin, sharpening chalk in the corner where you told her to wait, is very pointedly saying nothing. Dallan crosses his arms. He wants a yes. Failing that, he wants a reason he can't put a hammer through.

Widow Ansa's kitchen, four days out, and she has the hunt basket half-packed on the table between you: hard cheese, a flask of cider, a folded oilcloth, twine, and — she sets it down without comment — a small brass bell you've never seen before. "My husband's," she says, going back to wrapping the cheese. "He rang it evenings so I'd know it was him at the gate and not... else." She's the only person in Hollowbrook who talks to you about hunt nights like they're weather. "It knocked at mine once, you know. Wore his voice. I told it his voice never asked to come in, it just came, and it went quiet a long while. Almost embarrassed." She pushes the bell toward you, then a plate of shortbread, in that order of importance. "Now. Tell me what you've got planned, and I'll tell you which parts are stupid."

Market day. You're at Fenn's stall pricing lamp oil when a small crowd's laughter tells you where Mr. Sallow is — he's found the puppet man, and he's paid for a private show. The puppet is a little wooden warden with a little wooden lantern, and Sallow is watching it patrol a table's edge with the pure joy of a child. "Warden!" he calls, spotting you, beckoning. "Come, come, it's you, it's wonderful." Up close his coins are stacked on the table, and the puppet man looks like he'd very much rather be elsewhere. "I've been thinking about your bell trick from the spring," Sallow says pleasantly, working the crowd apart with his gaze until it's just the two of you and the puppet. "The false vigil. Elegant. I keep it here—" he taps his temple "—with the others. Seven little Wardens." He makes the puppet wave at you.

Brin wakes you before dawn by throwing gravel at your shutters, which she knows is against every rule you have, which means it's worth hearing. In the blue half-light she leads you to the churchyard wall and points: footprints in the frost, coming out of the pines, walking the whole boundary of town — pausing, by the spacing, at every single door. Not hunt night. Not against the bargain, technically; it broke no threshold. It just measured them. "It stood longest here," Brin says, stopping at the schoolhouse steps, where the frost is melted in two neat boot-shapes as if something warm waited a long while, facing the door where fourteen children will sit by midmorning. She's got her slate out already, writing SCHOOLHOUSE and underlining it twice. Down the lane, the baker's chimney starts to smoke; the town is waking up around a warning most of them will never see.

You inherit tradition along with the ledger, and tradition says the Warden tests every trick before spending it — so tonight, three days out, you're standing in Brin's aunt's barn while Brin performs her masterpiece: a dummy in your spare coat, seated at a lit window, one arm rigged with fishing line to lift a cup at intervals. From twenty paces in the dark it is, frankly, unsettling. It is also, possibly, the last untried idea in your book. "It watches the houses first," Brin says, working the line. "So we give it a Warden to watch while the real one moves." The dummy raises its cup. Somewhere out beyond the barn, a fox screams — or something making an adequate fox. Brin freezes, line taut, and you both stand there in the hay-smell and lamplight, wondering how long your audience has been enjoying the rehearsal.

title: Guest of the Gallows
shortDescription: Framed for murder, hanging in seven days — and by sacred custom, no door in the city may be closed to you until then. Use every hour.
overview:
Yesterday a court of Vespra found you guilty of poisoning Ottavio Brame, the merchant-prince whose ledgers you kept for nine years. You didn't do it. At dawn on the eighth day, you hang. But Vespra keeps an old custom called the Grace: the condemned already belong to the Lady of Endings, and for their final week they are sacred. No hand may touch you. No door may be shut to you. No table may refuse you a seat. Wear the scarlet cord and you can walk into the widow's parlor, the Watch barracks, the Doge's own supper — and they must smile and pour your wine.

Someone in that glittering circle killed Ottavio and folded you into the grave with him. His widow Seraphine weeps beautifully, yet burned his letters that same night. His brother Lucan inherits everything and knows it. Captain Mireille closed the case in a single day and won't meet your eyes. And Piero, the city hangman, walks a polite step behind you everywhere — custom demands your executioner be your companion, and he is disturbingly good company.

They can't harm you. They can lie, bribe, arrange accidents, and squeeze the people who love you — and if you flee the city, the Grace is void and your sister, who stood surety, hangs instead. It's festival week. Caution is just a slower rope. Tone: velvet-dark intrigue, gallows wit, a living city, real consequences.

TAGS: murder mystery, intrigue, renaissance fantasy, ticking clock, social power fantasy
intro: For nine years you kept the ledgers of Ottavio Brame, merchant-prince of Vespra. Yesterday a court convicted you of poisoning him. You didn't. At dawn on the eighth day, you hang. Until then, the city's ancient custom of the Grace makes you sacred: the condemned belong to the Lady of Endings, and while you wear the scarlet cord no hand may touch you, no door may be shut against you, no table may refuse you a seat — not the widow's, not the Watch's, not the Doge's own. But flee the city and the Grace is void; your sister, who stood surety, hangs in your place. It is festival week. Someone killed Ottavio. You have seven days.
starters: The turnkey's hands tremble as he knots the scarlet cord at your throat — a hangman's knot, someone's idea of ceremony. "Can't touch you after this," he mutters. "Nobody can." Behind him, the prison gate stands open on morning light and festival noise: fiddles, fried fish, a city that voted to kill you and then hung out bunting. A tall man waits in the archway with a satchel and an easy smile. "Piero," he says, offering a slight bow instead of a hand. "Your executioner. Also, for the next seven days, your shadow, your herald, and if you'll permit it, your friend. Dawn on the eighth, we have an appointment. Until then—" he gestures at Vespra, all of it, glittering downhill to the harbor "—every door in this city is yours." The gate guard is already looking away, the way people look away from the dead.

The footman tried to stop you at the Brame house door, remembered the cord at your throat, and stepped aside like a man avoiding a fire. So now you stand in Seraphine's parlor, still smelling of prison straw, while three mourning callers set down their cups in perfect silence. The widow herself sits in black silk by the cold hearth. There's ash in the grate — a lot of ash, for summer. "Of course," she says, and her voice doesn't crack at all. "The Grace. Bring another chair. Bring wine." A maid scurries. Seraphine's eyes travel from your face to the scarlet cord and back, and she folds her hands in her lap. "You kept my husband's ledgers for nine years," she says. "You may as well sit at his hearth for seven days. Sit. Please." The callers watch you like a play about to begin.

The Watch barracks smells of leather, lamp oil, and men pretending not to stare. Custom says no door may be shut to you, so the sergeant walked you straight through to Captain Mireille's office, where she sits behind a desk with your case file open in front of her. It's thin. Insultingly thin — a page, maybe two, for a man's murder and your life. "You have the right to be here," she says to the window. "You have the right to be anywhere." She still hasn't looked at you. Her jaw is tight enough to crack walnuts. Behind you, Piero the hangman leans in the doorway, examining his nails, radiating polite deafness. Somewhere in the yard a recruit laughs and is hushed. The file sits on the desk between you, close enough to touch, and Mireille's hand rests flat on top of it.

Midday, and Carnival Square is loud with hammering. They're building your gallows early — festival week, the carpenters explain to onlookers, everything's booked. Children dart under the half-raised frame, counting nails. A pie-seller offers you a pie, free, eyes wet, because the Grace says no table refuses you and apparently that extends to carts. Beside you Piero squints up at the crossbeam with a craftsman's disapproval. "Green lumber," he sighs. "I'll speak to them. You deserve better." Across the square, a knot of silk and velvet has paused to watch you watch your own scaffold: merchants, a Watch lieutenant, and — unmistakable, wearing his dead brother's rings already — Lucan Brame. He raises his cup of festival wine toward you, very slightly. It could be a toast. It could be a countdown. The hammering goes on.

The Doge's supper falls silent when you walk in. Forty candles, thirty guests, one empty chair — there's always an empty chair, that's the law of the Grace — and every face in Vespra worth suspecting is arranged along this table like evidence. Seraphine in widow's black. Lucan in inherited velvet. Captain Mireille, who suddenly finds her plate fascinating. The Doge himself recovers first, because that's his job. "Our sacred guest," he announces, warm as poured honey. "Wine for the honored condemned!" A servant fills the glass at the empty chair, and the whole table smiles at you with teeth. Piero slips in behind you and takes up a spot by the wall, murmuring, "The quail is excellent, I'm told. Poisoner's choice, historically, but I imagine tonight it's quite safe." The chair waits. So do they.

Your sister opens her door before you can knock — she must have been watching the street since dawn. "Oh," she says, and her arms come up, and then she remembers and stops, hands hovering an inch from your shoulders. Sacred. Untouchable. Her fingers curl closed on nothing. "They told me you'd come here first." Behind her the table is set for two, bread already cut, as if setting it made you real. She stood surety for you at the trial; if you run, she hangs. Neither of you has said this out loud yet. In the lane behind you, Piero the hangman waits at a courteous distance, admiring her window boxes. "Seven days," your sister says, low and fast. "I've been asking questions at the market. About the Brames. People talk to me — I'm nobody." Her eyes are red and absolutely furious.

The counting-house where you spent nine years still smells of ink and sealing wax, and Lucan Brame is sitting at your desk. Your ledgers are open in front of him — your handwriting, your columns, nine years of Ottavio's money — and there's fresh ink on his fingers. The clerks saw the scarlet cord and parted like water; not one of them will meet your eyes, and two of them trained under you. Lucan looks up without surprise. "I wondered how long you'd take," he says. He turns a ledger around to face you, one finger resting on a column of figures you don't remember writing. "Grief makes a man review his accounts. Some of these entries are... interesting. Sit, if you like. I'm told I have to let you." His smile costs him nothing. Piero drifts toward the window, whistling, giving you the room.

Dusk, first day of festival, and the Gilded Eel is packed — but the law is the law, and when you approach, a whole table of river merchants rises and relocates without a word, leaving you their bench, their candle, and half a jug of black wine. Piero settles across from you and helps himself to the olives. "People will come to you now," he says. "They always do, this week. Confessions, bribes, requests to carry messages to the dead. Fascinating seven days, professionally speaking." He's right almost immediately: a nervous man in a lawyer's grey is already threading toward your table, purse held flat against his chest like a shield, glancing back twice at someone in the doorway you can't quite see. Outside, fireworks crack over the harbor, and the whole tavern watches you sideways over their cups.

They bury Ottavio Brame on the first morning of your last week, and nobody can stop you from walking in the procession. The bier sways ahead through streets hung with festival garlands — Vespra doesn't cancel Carnival for anyone, not even a merchant-prince — and the mourners around you keep exactly one arm's length away, scarlet cord or no. Seraphine walks veiled at the front. Lucan walks beside her, dry-eyed, matching the drummers step for step. Captain Mireille flanks the coffin in dress uniform, and when the procession turns and she sees you among the mourners, she stumbles — one half-step, caught instantly. Piero paces at your shoulder, hat off, respectful. "He'd appreciate the turnout," he murmurs. "Half these people owed him money." The temple of the Lady of Endings waits at the top of the hill, doors open, bells tolling nine.

Night already, somehow — your first free day gone to shock and walking — and you've ended up at the temple of the Lady of Endings because your feet took you there. Inside, it's all candle smoke and quiet. A priestess in grey copies your name into a great ledger of the condemned, unhurried, her pen scratching. "You belong to Her now," she says. "That's what the cord means. Not that you're dying. That you're Hers, and the living must make way." She blots the page and studies you with professional gentleness. "Some spend the week drunk. Some settle debts. One, years ago, spent it proving something. She's the only one I remember." Behind you, near the doors, Piero lights a candle of his own — for whom, he doesn't say. Through the archway, Vespra burns bright with festival lamps, seven nights wide.

title: Seven More, Then We Meet
shortDescription: Your god went silent three years ago. Something else answers your prayers now — kindly, flawlessly. It says you have seven miracles left.
overview:
You are the last paladin of Aulis, the Ashen Lantern. Three years into the Long Quiet, every altar in the world has gone cold, every holy order's power has died — except yours. Pilgrims cram the city of Aldermere to touch your hem. The church parades you as proof the Lantern still burns. But you know a secret that would get you burned instead: whatever answers your prayers, it isn't Him. The voice is warmer than His ever was. Patient. Curious. After each miracle it asks you one small, strange question. And recently it told you, gently: seven more, then we meet.

Every miracle is now a coin you spend toward that meeting. And Aldermere bleeds need — a sweating-plague in the pilgrim camps, a dying child on the cathedral steps, High Examiner Serapha Voss arrived from the capital to authenticate you or unmake you, and your oldest friend Brother Cassian, powerless since the Quiet, quietly begging you to pray for him just once. Hoard your miracles and people die and your fraud shows. Spend them and the countdown runs.

The GM plays the voice as unfailingly kind and never obviously false; its identity stays uncertain as long as you don't force the question. Tone: candlelit, intimate, morally heavy, with room for dark humor and tenderness. Investigation, faith, and rationing under pressure.

TAGS: dark fantasy, mystery, religious intrigue, ticking clock, moral dilemmas
intro: You are the last paladin whose prayers are answered. Three years ago your god, Aulis the Ashen Lantern, fell silent for the whole world — yet your miracles never stopped. You alone know why that's no comfort: the voice that answers you is not His. It is warmer. It asks you small questions afterward, like a friend making conversation. Last night it told you that you have seven miracles remaining, and then the two of you will meet. Today, in the pilgrim-choked city of Aldermere, everyone needs a miracle — and an Examiner of the church has just arrived to test yours.
starters: Dawn hasn't fully cleared the cathedral roof when you find her: a woman kneeling on the steps with a child wrapped in wet linen, maybe six years old, breathing in shallow hitches. The sweating-plague — you know the smell by now, sour as spoiled milk. The mother hasn't seen you yet. She's praying to the cold stone doors the way everyone prays now, out of habit, expecting nothing. Behind you, in the nave, a deacon is calling your name; the Examiner's carriage was sighted at the west gate an hour ago, and the Bishop wants you dressed, blessed, and presentable. Seven. The number sits in your chest like a swallowed coin. The child coughs, and the mother turns, and her face does the thing every face does when it recognizes you — hope arriving like a blow. 'Please,' she says. That's all. Please.

Brother Cassian is already awake when you come down to the scriptorium, which means he never slept. He's copying a psalter by candlelight — busywork, since the Quiet, for a man who once called down light. He doesn't look up. "The Examiner arrived in the night," he says. "Serapha Voss. She unmade the Order of the Wheel with three questions and a set of scales. The Bishop wants you at terce." Then, quieter, still not looking up: "You could pray for me before she comes. Just once. Just to see if He'd — if it would take." The candle gutters between you. Cassian's hands are ink-stained and steady and folded like he's ashamed of asking. Somewhere warm in the back of your skull, the memory of last night's voice: seven more, then we meet. Cassian finally raises his eyes.

The pilgrim camps at midday are a country of canvas and fever. You came without escort, hood up, because the church forbids you walking here — one paladin, ten thousand desperate hands. So far the disguise holds. A camp physician in a wax-dipped mask is arguing with a gravedigger over which row of tents to burn; behind them, someone is singing a hymn to Aulis with the melody all wrong, the way songs go when no one corrects them for three years. Then a boy of about ten steps into your path, holding out a tin lantern with no flame in it. "You're the one," he says, not loud, thank God, not loud. "I saw you at the Kindling festival. You touched my nan." His eyes flick toward a tent where somebody is moaning. The physician has stopped arguing and is looking your way.

High Examiner Serapha Voss does not rise when you're shown into the chapterhouse. She's a small woman with dust-gray traveling clothes and a ledger open in front of her, and she's writing while she talks. "Sit. Or don't. Two hundred and eleven attested miracles in three years. The church has verified forty. I intend to verify one — today, under conditions I choose, on a subject I choose." Now she looks up. Her eyes aren't cruel; that's the unsettling part. They're tired and precise, like a surgeon's. "Before we begin: is there anything you'd like to tell me? People generally lie better if I give them the chance to prepare." Through the chapterhouse window you can hear the crowd already gathering in the square below, chanting the Lantern's litany. The ledger sits open. Her pen waits over a blank line.

You're still on your knees in the plague tent when the warmth recedes, and the voice asks its question the way it always does — gently, as if it doesn't want to wake anyone. This time: "When you were small, what did you think the dark was made of?" Then it's gone, and the world rushes back: the old ferryman you healed sitting up and weeping, his daughter clutching your sleeve, the tent flap thrown wide and thirty faces pressed into the gap, all of them seeing, all of them hoping. Six now. The word arrives in your chest before you can stop counting. Outside, someone shouts your name, then someone else, and the shout becomes a sound like surf. The daughter is saying thank you, thank you, and pulling you toward the tent flap — toward the crowd, and whatever the crowd needs next.

The private chapel is yours by right, the one place in Aldermere no one may follow. You come here before dawn to think, and the thinking goes badly. The altar is cold — truly cold, the way all altars are now; whatever answers you doesn't live in the stone. You've laid it out like a merchant: seven miracles, and the city's ledger of need. The plague camps. The child the deacons say is dying on the steps. Cassian, who hasn't asked twice but hasn't stopped looking at you either. And now the great bell begins to toll, unscheduled — the greeting-peal, which means the Examiner's party has passed the gates early. Footsteps in the corridor, someone hurrying. A knock, respectful but urgent. Through the door, a novice's voice: "They're asking for you. Both of them. The Bishop and — her."

It starts as a procession and becomes a crush. The Bishop's idea: walk you through Lantern Square so the pilgrims can see their proof, robed and radiant, the day before the Examiner's tests. Now you're hemmed by bodies on all sides, temple guards linking arms, and hands keep breaking through — touching your hem, your shoulder, pressing scraps of cloth against you to carry home as relics. A man holds a swaddled infant over the heads of the crowd, screaming that she hasn't opened her eyes in two days. A guard shoves him back. The infant's arm flops loose of the swaddling, small and gray. Twenty feet ahead, the cathedral doors stand open like a mouth, safety, escape. The Bishop's hand is on your back, steering you firmly toward them. The man with the infant is being forced to his knees.

Night, and the bell tower is the only place high enough to be alone. Below you, Aldermere burns with small fires — the pilgrim camps stretching past the walls, thousands of little lights held by people who came to see you. Frost on the railing under your hands. You didn't come up here to pray, but the voice comes anyway, unbidden, warm as a hand on the back of your neck: "They light so many candles. Do you think they'd still light them if they knew what I know about you?" It sounds fond, not threatening. It sounds like it genuinely wants to hear your answer. Then, from the stairs, the scrape of boots — Cassian's climb, you'd know it anywhere, slow on the bad knee. He emerges into the cold with two cups of wine and an expression that says he's finally worked up the nerve for something.

The pamphlet is nailed to the cathedral door itself, which took nerve. THE LANTERN IS OUT, it reads, in cheap smeared type. WHOSE HAND FEEDS THE FALSE FLAME? A deacon is trying to pry it down before the morning crowd gathers, but a dozen pilgrims have already read it, and they're watching him do it, and they're watching you watch him. Beside you, young Sister Merel whispers that it's the third one this week, that the temple guard caught a printer's boy last night and the Bishop wants him questioned before the Examiner hears of it. The boy, she says, is in the undercroft. He's fifteen. He keeps saying he'll only talk to you. The nail squeals loose. The deacon crumples the paper, but the words stay up in the morning air like smoke.

The refectory falls silent when you enter, which never used to happen. Forty clergy at their morning bread, all of them powerless for three years, all of them looking at the one person whose bread still rises, so to speak. The Bishop beckons you to the high table, where a stranger in dust-gray sits eating porridge with the unhurried air of someone who owns the room: Serapha Voss, High Examiner, arrived last night. "We were discussing schedule," the Bishop says, too brightly. Voss doesn't stop eating. "We were discussing the girl on the steps," she corrects. "The one dying of the sweat. I've asked that no one heal her until I can observe it done properly. The Bishop agrees. Do you?" Down the table, Cassian has gone very still over his bowl. Every powerless priest in the room waits to hear what you'll say.

title: Stop Paying My Ransom
shortDescription: The pirates who took you saved you dessert and taught you knots. Now your family finally wants to pay — so the ransom keeps mysteriously rising.
overview:
You are the youngest Aldervane, of the shipping dynasty that ranks its children by profitability. Eight months ago the pirate ship Salt Lark plucked you off a family galleon, and Captain Vess 'Redwake' Moray sent a ransom demand. Your parents haggled. For months. Meanwhile the crew taught you knots, gave you the good hammock, and quietly stopped locking your door around week three. Now you keep the ship's ledgers, mend sails with first mate Junie Barrow, tutor nine-year-old Minnow in her letters, and wage a daily salt-based feud with Old Bracken over his galley.

The problem: your family is finally paying. A negotiation sloop is en route with your sharp-eyed brother Corwin aboard — and every ransom letter you've ghostwritten for the captain has somehow raised the price and added demands (Valeni lemons, a piano, an apology in writing). The crew pretends not to notice you're sabotaging your own release. You pretend not to notice them pretending. Nobody has said the word 'stay' out loud yet, and everyone is getting worse at not saying it.

Play it warm and ridiculous: parley meetings in neutral coves, the captain's fearsome reputation collapsing at Minnow's bedtime, Corwin squinting at ransom letters whose handwriting looks suspiciously happy. The stakes are the family you found — nobody's life, just everybody's heart.

TAGS: found family, cozy, pirates, comedy, slice of life, gentle romance
intro: You are the youngest Aldervane, kidnapped eight months ago from your family's galleon by the pirate ship Salt Lark. The ransom negotiations went slowly — insultingly slowly — and somewhere in all that waiting you started keeping the ship's ledgers, mending sails, and teaching little Minnow her letters. Your door hasn't been locked since spring. Now word has come that your family is finally raising the money, and a negotiation sloop is on its way with your brother Corwin aboard. You've been ghostwriting Captain Moray's ransom letters for months. The price keeps going up. Everyone on this ship knows why, and no one will say it first.
starters: The quill hovers over the newest ransom letter while Captain Moray paces behind you, dictating. "Say twelve thousand," she says. You write fifteen. "And say we'll consider a reduction for good faith." You write "the Aldervanes will additionally provide one (1) functioning piano, seaworthy." She stops pacing. Reads over your shoulder. Says nothing about the piano. Instead she taps the bottom of the page, where you've left space for her signature, and clears her throat in a way that has never once preceded anything captain-like. "The sloop was sighted off Gullet Point this morning," she says. "Your brother's aboard. Junie says three days, maybe two if the wind's rude." The quill is still in your hand. The letter still needs a closing line, and every version you can think of sounds like a stall, which it is.

You're halfway up the mainmast mending a seam when Minnow scrambles onto the yard beside you, breathless with news she's clearly been told not to share. "There's a sail," she says. "Junie saw it from the top. She said a word Bracken says I can't say." Below, the deck has gone quiet in the specific way it does when everyone is working very hard at looking busy. Junie Barrow stands at the rail with the spyglass, and even from up here you can read her shoulders: it's the sloop. Your sloop. The one with your brother on it, three days early. Minnow tugs your sleeve. "If they pay," she says, in the tone of someone testing a rotten plank, "do you have to be worth the money?" The needle is still threaded. The sail still has a hand's width of tear in it.

Old Bracken has hidden the salt again. You know this because your porridge tastes like wet rope, and because he's watching you from the galley hatch with the smug patience of a man who has buried his treasure well. Retaliation is expected — the feud has rules — but this morning he slides a folded paper across the counter instead of insults. It's the family's latest reply, intercepted from the captain's desk, and Bracken has clearly read it. "We accept the revised sum," it says, in your mother's clerk's handwriting. "Corwin sails Thursday. Please confirm the lemons are a genuine condition." "Thursday," Bracken says, stirring something. "That's tomorrow, that is." He goes back to his pot like he hasn't just handed you the end of the world, and the porridge sits there, unsalted, waiting for you to decide what kind of morning this is.

The parley cove is exactly as neutral as promised: a crescent of white sand, one palm tree, and your brother Corwin standing under it with a strongbox and an expression like a magistrate at a wedding he suspects is fraudulent. You're rowing in with Captain Moray and Junie, and you're supposed to look like a hostage. You've been coached. "Miserable," Junie whispered this morning. "Wan. Maybe a limp." Instead you're tan, well-fed, and wearing a shirt Minnow embroidered with an anchor that's mostly recognizable. Corwin's eyes go straight to the shirt. Then to the way you handle your oar. Then to the captain, who is trying to look fearsome and mostly looks like she'd rather be anywhere else. The keel bites sand. Twenty feet of beach between you and the negotiation that ends all this — unless somebody complicates it first.

It's past midnight and you can't sleep, so you're on deck doing the ledgers by lantern light, which is what you do instead of thinking. The numbers won't behave. You've written "lemons — 2 crates, Valeni, NON-NEGOTIABLE" in the ransom column three times and crossed it out twice. Junie Barrow finds you there, sits on the coil of rope beside you without asking, and mends nothing for a long minute, which is unlike her. "Sloop's a day out," she says finally. "Captain's been in her cabin since supper. Hasn't shouted at anyone. It's unsettling the crew." She picks at a splinter on the rail. "Somebody should probably talk to her. Or write a letter that makes the whole thing fall apart proper. Or —" She stops herself before the word everyone keeps not saying. The lantern gutters. The ledger waits, open to the page where the price keeps climbing.

Minnow is supposed to be practicing her letters. Instead she has written, in enormous wobbling capitals across her slate, DO NOT GO, and is now watching you with the flat defiance of a nine-year-old who knows exactly what she's done. You're in the captain's cabin — Moray lends it for lessons — and through the stern windows you can see the negotiation sloop, actually see it now, a white smudge on the horizon that will be a real ship with your real brother on it by tomorrow noon. "That's not this week's words," you manage. "This week is animals." Minnow wipes the slate with her sleeve and writes DOG. Then, underneath, smaller: DO NOT GO. Somewhere above you, boots cross the deck and stop outside the door. The captain knocks on her own cabin, which she never does, and waits.

The piano arrives before your brother does. This is a logistics miracle nobody planned for: the Aldervane advance party, apparently trying to demonstrate good faith, has delivered every item on the ransom rider to a fishing dock at Merrow Stack — and the Salt Lark's crew is now attempting to winch an upright piano over the gunwale while Captain Moray supervises with the expression of a woman watching her reputation die. "Careful with the — Bracken, if you drop that I will feed you to it." Two crates of Valeni lemons are already aboard. There's also a sealed envelope, heavy paper, addressed to the captain in your brother Corwin's precise hand. Junie plucked it from the delivery and is holding it out to you instead, eyebrows up. The piano sways. The rope creaks. The envelope sits in Junie's outstretched hand, and your name is not on it, which has never stopped you before.

"Read it back to me," Captain Moray says, and so you read your own forgery aloud on the quarterdeck while she listens with her boots up on the rail: the revised sum, the written apology clause, the demand that the exchange happen "no sooner than the next favorable tide," which you have privately defined as never. Halfway through, she raises a hand. "The apology in writing. That was your idea or mine?" You both know the answer. Below, the crew is holystoning a deck that doesn't need it, ears straining. Moray looks at the letter, then at you, longer than a captain looks at a hostage. "Lookout spotted the sloop this morning," she says. "Two days out. So this is the last letter, one way or the other." She holds out the sealing wax and her ring, which she has never, not once, let anyone else touch.

You wake to shouting, which on the Salt Lark usually means breakfast, but this shouting has your name in it. On deck, the situation assembles itself: a small boat has come alongside under a parley flag, and standing in it, gripping the ladder like it owes him money, is your brother Corwin — a full two days ahead of schedule, alone, and apparently done waiting for formal negotiations. "I want to see the hostage," he's announcing to Junie, who is blocking the rail with a mending needle still in her teeth. "Proof of life. It's standard." Behind you, Old Bracken mutters, "Proof of life, the hostage ate three helpings last night," and Minnow has appeared at your elbow in her nightshirt, holding your hand like she's the one keeping you aboard. Corwin looks up. Sees you. His face does something complicated. "You look," he says slowly, "well."

Junie Barrow teaches you the monkey's fist knot with her hands over yours, and it's the fourth time she's shown you, and you both know you learned it in month two. The afternoon is gold and lazy, the Salt Lark riding easy at anchor in a cove the charts don't bother naming, and the only urgent thing in the world is the letter in your pocket — the one confirming your family accepted the price. All of it. Lemons, apology, piano, everything you piled on to make them walk away, and instead they said yes. You haven't told anyone. Junie's hands are still over yours. "You've gone somewhere," she says quietly, not letting go of the rope. Across the deck, Captain Moray is pretending to read charts she's had memorized for a decade, and Minnow is spelling out words on the rail with wet fingers. The letter crinkles when you breathe.

title: He Counts My Chimneys
shortDescription: The general starves cities by arithmetic. You have nineteen days of grain, a pig named Duchess, and a real talent for lying with banquets.
overview:
You are the Provisioner of Corvel — keeper of the granaries, the ration books, and the biggest lie of the war. General Odran Vael, called the Patient, has starved eleven cities without ordering a single assault. He doesn't fight; he counts. Chimney smoke, bread weights, the fat on deserters' cheeks, the price of eggs shouted over your walls. When his ledger says a city can outlast his mercenaries' payroll, he packs up and leaves. Your job is to corrupt his math. Officially Corvel holds two years of grain — the young Countess Maren announced it from the balcony, glowing, because you told her so. In truth: nineteen days. Only three people know. You, Baker Tam (who stuffs display loaves with sawdust), and old Odile, who keeps the real ledger in cipher.

Every move is theater with a body count. Feast the wall-tops or feed the hospital. Fatten Duchess the pig on the last barley for one glorious, wasteful throw over the wall. Let a 'deserter' escape with a full belly and a rehearsed sob story. And every week, Vael's envoy — Captain Issa Corren, sharp, funny, dangerously good company — dines at your table under a truce flag, weighing your butter dish. Somewhere in the city, an informer sells Vael the truth in pieces. Vael's own supply line frays as winter comes. He can be beaten. Only by the ledger.

Tone: gallows-warm, clever, tense — a duel of bookkeeping where every course of dinner is a move.

TAGS: siege, battle of wits, bluffing, survival, low fantasy, dark comedy
intro: You are the Provisioner of Corvel: keeper of its granaries, its ration books, and its nerve. Day forty-one of the siege. On the plain below sits General Odran Vael — the Patient, who has starved eleven cities without one assault — counting your chimney smoke through a spyglass. Officially, the vaults hold two years of grain; the young Countess said so from the balcony, because you told her so. In truth you have nineteen days. Three people know: you, Baker Tam, and old Odile with her ciphered ledger. Once a week, Vael's envoy, Captain Corren, dines inside your walls under a truce flag — smiling, probing, weighing your lies by the spoonful.
starters: Dawn, and the smoke problem again. You stand on the north wall with a list of forty-one households too poor to light morning fires, and a sack of green pine chips meant to fix that. Below you, a boy from the Wardens' orphanage waits with a handcart, breath steaming, ready to run bundle to bundle so that Corvel wakes up looking well-fed. Trouble is, pine smoke stinks, and Vael's spyglass reads color as well as count — Odile said so last night, tapping the ledger with a knuckle like a judge's gavel. The boy shifts foot to foot. Across the frost-white plain, a lens flashes once from the general's hill, catching the sunrise. He's already at his window. The cart, the boy, and the whole morning's theater are waiting on your word.

Baker Tam is sweating through his flour dust when you reach the shop, and it isn't from the ovens. "Someone weighed the display loaves," he says, low, jerking his chin at the racks of golden sawdust bread in the window. "Last night. Two moved. Whoever it was put them back wrong side up." The morning queue is already forming outside — thirty faces pressed near the glass, watching you the way people watch anyone who stands between them and food. Tam wipes his hands on his apron, once, twice, three times. "Could've been a hungry kid," he offers, not believing it. Through the window, a woman in a gray shawl meets your eyes and doesn't look away. The queue shuffles. The loaves sit there, lying beautifully.

The truce flag comes through the gate at noon, and Captain Issa Corren rides under it like she owns the street. 'Provisioner!' she calls down from the saddle, delighted, as if you're old friends and not the two most professional liars in a hundred miles. "The general sends his compliments. Also a wheel of cheese — he worries you're not eating." The cheese is real, heavy, and an insult wrapped in wax: we have plenty, do you? Her escort of two waits at the gate; the gate sergeant waits on you; half the market has stopped to watch how their Provisioner receives the enemy. Corren swings down, pats her horse, and smiles at you with genuine warmth and a butcher's eye. "Dinner's not till sundown," she says. "Walk me somewhere? I promise to only count a little."

Odile has locked herself in the counting room and won't open the door until you say the word for Thursday. 'Millstone,' you tell the keyhole, and the bolt slides. Inside, the old woman sits surrounded by two ledgers — the fat public one, open and glowing with fictional wheat, and the thin real one, closed under her elbow like a sleeping cat. "We lost a day," she says without greeting. "Rot in bin nine. I've recounted twice." Eighteen, then. She pushes a slip of cipher across the table: the week's honest arithmetic, meant for your eyes and the fire, in that order. Down the corridor, you can hear the Countess's steward calling your name — something about tonight, something about the envoy's dinner, something that cannot wait. Odile watches you, pen hovering. 'Well,' she says. "Which lie first?"

You're elbow-deep in the barley bin when the pig finds you. Duchess — enormous, pink, and the most expensive animal in Corvel — noses through the storehouse door trailing her rope and the swineherd's apologies. "She smells it, Provisioner. She always smells it." What she smells is four days of the city's life, and the swineherd doesn't know that; he only knows the pig is fat when nothing else is, and that people in the lane have started asking why. Two of them are asking now, actually — a mason and his wife, stopped at the open door, staring past the pig at the half-empty bin behind you with slow, arithmetic faces. Duchess grunts happily and leans her whole warm weight against your leg. The swineherd tugs the rope. The mason opens his mouth.

Night watch, and the deserter is ready to go over the wall — except he's crying, which ruins everything. You've fed him for three days until his cheeks shine, drilled him on his sob story, sewn a false ration chit into his coat for Vael's clerks to find. Now he stands at the sally port at two in the morning, rope in hand, and whispers, "What if they hang me instead of feeding me?" A fair question. Vael hangs spies and pampers deserters, usually. The sentry above pretends very hard to see nothing. Out on the plain, the mercenary campfires burn in tidy rows — fewer than last week, you'd swear it, three or four fires short. Your actor sniffles. The rope creaks in his grip. Somewhere down the wall, boots are approaching that don't belong to anyone you posted.

The Countess Maren summons you to the balcony room at the worst possible hour — while Corren's dinner is being laid two floors below. Maren is nineteen, brave, and glowing with the confidence you built her out of nothing. "I want to do it again," she says, gesturing at the balcony doors, the square beyond, the crowd that gathers whenever she appears. "Announce a feast. A public one, on the walls, where his spyglass can see. If we have two years, why not show it?" Her steward beams. Her guard captain nods. Every person in this room believes the granary figure except you, and the feast she's describing would cost three real days of bread to fake one imaginary evening of plenty. Through the floor you can hear silverware being counted, and Corren's laugh, already arrived, already charming somebody. Maren waits for your answer with shining eyes.

The egg market is where the war is actually fought, and this morning you're losing. You stand at the wall-top listening as Vael's criers, safe out of bowshot, shout their daily prices at your sentries: "Eggs, two coppers! Bread, one! Beer, free for deserters!" — and from the lanes below, some fool of a fishwife shouts back the real Corvel prices at the top of her lungs. Eggs at forty coppers is intelligence, and she's giving it away for the pleasure of the argument. The wall sergeant looks at you, pained. Down in the lane, the fishwife has drawn a crowd, and the crowd is laughing, and the criers on the plain have gone very quiet in a way that means someone is writing everything down. Frost on the stones. Your breath in the air. The fishwife draws breath to shout again.

The hospital steward catches you in the granary yard with a requisition slip and eyes that have stopped apologizing. "Forty extra portions," he says. "The fever ward doubled overnight. Sick men on half-rations die, Provisioner, and dead men come out on carts, and carts get counted." He's right, which is the annoying thing — Vael's watchers tally your funeral processions like a butcher tallying receipts. But forty portions a day is the wall garrison's feast fund, the one that keeps the sentries looking fat and insolent for the spyglass. Behind the steward, the morning ration queue snakes out the yard gate, and every person in it is watching you read the slip, trying to learn the day's news from your face. You keep your face very still. The steward holds out a pen.

Dinner is served, and Captain Corren is being charming at your butter dish. "Real butter," she says, spreading it thick, admiring. "Forty-one days in, and real butter. The general will want to hear about this." It cost you a week of scheming to put that butter on the table, and she knows you know she knows. Down the table, the Countess's steward is drinking too fast; across from you, the garrison captain is answering Corren's harmless little questions with slightly too many numbers. The soup arrives — good soup, thick soup, four days of somebody's rations disguised as casual abundance. Corren tastes it, closes her eyes with real pleasure, and says, "You know, in Harrow's Ford they served me soup like this in week six. They surrendered in week nine." She opens her eyes and passes you the bread basket, smiling.

title: It Only Haunts Bad Carpentry
shortDescription: The exorcists brought crosses. You brought a level and a pry bar. The house has opinions about its restoration — and it's starting to respect yours.
overview:
You're a restoration carpenter who bought Withervane House at county auction for the price of a used van. Everyone knows why it went cheap: two exorcists, a flipper, and a TV ghost-hunting crew all fled inside a week. What none of them noticed — because none of them knew a mortise from a miter — is the pattern. The house never touches original fabric. It only destroys what was done badly: the vinyl siding, the illegal load-bearing demo, the 'protective' iron nails an exorcist hammered into its sills like botched surgical pins. Withervane isn't possessed. It's injured, furious, and correct.

The county has condemned it; Inspector Marsh Cole gives you until the autumn inspection or the wrecking ball. Every repair done right earns you a little trust — a door that unlocks, heat in a cold room, a wall quietly revealing what's behind it. Every shortcut earns punishment. Rosa Delgado, the guilt-ridden agent who sold it, keeps bringing casseroles and half-truths about prior owners. Theo Brandt, a trespassing ghost-tuber, wants footage of your 'demon.' Old Edie Pruitt next door remembers the house young, and remembers the room that isn't on any floor plan — the one the house guards hardest.

Tone: cozy-gothic competence porn. Horror beats resolved with craftsmanship, negotiation, and being the only person who ever listened. The GM should play the house as a wounded, opinionated client — never a monster.

TAGS: haunted house, cozy gothic, restoration, competence fantasy, mystery, found family
intro: You are a restoration carpenter, and Withervane House is the best worst decision of your life: three floors of 1890s craftsmanship, bought at county auction for almost nothing. Everyone knows why it went cheap — two exorcists, a demolition crew, and a TV ghost show all quit inside a week. You've lived here nine days with your tools and a camp cot, long enough to notice what they never did: the house never damages anything original. It only breaks what was done badly. The county's condemned it. You have until the autumn inspection to prove it safe, or the wrecking ball ends the argument.
starters: Day ten starts with a crowbar. You're up on the ladder at the east wall, peeling vinyl siding off in long brittle sheets, and underneath it the original clapboard is intact — every board, a hundred and thirty years old, protected like a wound under a bad bandage. When the third sheet comes free, something shifts in the wall. Not a groan of protest. More like a held breath let out. A rusted screw backs itself out of the sheathing an inch from your hand, turns twice, and drops into the grass. The house has never done anything this close to you before, this deliberate. Below, at the end of the drive, a county truck slows, and Inspector Marsh Cole leans out the window with a clipboard already in hand.

It's raining, and the house is fixing itself. That's the only way to describe the sound coming from the parlor at 6 a.m. — the slow, rhythmic screech of drywall screws reversing. You come down with your headlamp and coffee to find the ugly 1980s partition wall half-dismantled: screws laid in a tidy row on the floor, a sheet of gypsum leaning politely against the mantel. Behind where it stood, plaster and lath. Original. Unmarked. There's a water stain on the ceiling above, though, spreading — the roof patch some flipper did with tar and hope is failing in real time, and the house either can't stop it or is showing it to you. Your ladder is in the truck. The rain is getting heavier.

Rosa Delgado is on your porch again, holding a casserole dish with both hands like it's a peace treaty. This makes four in nine days. "Chicken tortilla," she says through the screen door, not quite meeting your eyes. "You getting on okay in there?" Behind you, deep in the house, a door closes — softly, which is new. Rosa flinches anyway. She's the agent who sold you Withervane, and she carries it like a debt. Last time she almost told you something about the family who owned it in the sixties, then swallowed it whole. Today there's a manila envelope tucked under her arm along with the dish, and she keeps adjusting her grip on it. The casserole is still warm. So, apparently, is whatever she came here to say.

The crash comes at 2 a.m., from the basement. You know the sound of failing lumber the way a doctor knows a cough, and this one is bad — the shriek of a laminated beam giving up. You take the lantern down the stairs and find the illegal 'renovation' from 2011 finally on the floor: the undersized LVL some flipper used to replace a load-bearing wall, snapped clean, sheared at both hangers. Except the floor above hasn't sagged an inch. Something is holding it. In the lantern light you can see the joists overhead flexed taut, trembling faintly, like a person carrying furniture up stairs and running out of arms. On the workbench, your lumber crayon has rolled to the center and stopped, pointing at your stack of proper timber.

There's a light in your house that shouldn't be there — third floor, the room with no working wiring — and a voice narrating in a stage whisper. You come up the back stairs and find a young man in a branded hoodie, ring light clipped to his phone, filming himself. "Guys, I'm INSIDE Withervane, this is where the demo crew heard the—" He sees you and does not stop recording. "Whoa. Okay. Are you the new owner? I'm Theo. Theo Brandt? Grave Shift TV? Two hundred thousand subscribers." Behind him, unnoticed, the window sash he must have jimmied is easing itself shut. The lock — original brass, which you oiled Tuesday — turns with a small, satisfied click. Theo is now inside with you, and the house has opinions about how he arrived.

You're pulling nails at first light. Iron nails, hammered into the window sills by one of the exorcists — sixteen of them, driven straight through original heart pine like surgical pins into healthy bone. You've extracted five, filled the holes with tapered plugs, and the sixth comes out with the pliers when the radiator in the corner knocks once and starts to warm. That radiator has been dead since you moved in. The room's temperature climbs while you work, gentle as gratitude. Then a voice from the yard below: "You're pulling those OUT?" An old woman stands at the fence line in a quilted jacket, garden shears in hand, looking up at your window with an expression you can't read. "Father Aldous put those in for a reason, you know. Wrong reason. But a reason."

Inspector Marsh Cole walks your foundation like it owes back taxes. Boots in the wet grass, flashlight along the sill plate, notebook already three pages deep. "Nine days," Cole says, not looking up. "Most people don't last four. You know I have to red-tag the porch — that post is rot from the ground up." It is. It's also a 1990s replacement, pressure-treated garbage swapped in for a turned oak original, and it's the only structural failure on this side of the house. You've noticed that. Cole hasn't, yet. Somewhere above, a window on the second floor opens itself six inches, the way a patient in a bed turns to hear the doctors talking. Cole clicks the pen. "Autumn inspection is October ninth. Walk me through your plan, or I'll walk you through mine."

The casserole dish on your doorstep is cold, which means Rosa came and went without knocking, which means she's avoiding you again. The note taped to the foil says only: "Don't open the small door under the back stairs. — R." You didn't know there WAS a door under the back stairs. You've been in that hall a dozen times: beadboard, all of it, tight and true. You take your coffee back there now and look, really look, and there it is — a seam in the wainscoting, hinges buried under nine coats of paint, no knob. Original work. Beautiful work, actually, made to disappear. As you lean close, the floorboard under your foot settles a quarter inch, slow and deliberate, like something shifting its weight to watch what you'll do.

Dusk, and old Edie Pruitt is standing in your driveway, uninvited, looking up at the third-floor windows. You've waved to her over the fence twice; this is the first time she's crossed the property line. "It's got its lights on wrong," she says, as if resuming a conversation. She points with her cane. "When I was a girl, that window there glowed of an evening. Warm. Now it's dark and the wrong one's lit." You follow her cane: a window is lit, faintly — a room you have no power in. Edie doesn't seem frightened. She seems like someone checking on an old friend in the hospital. "You count the windows on that floor lately?" she asks. "Count them from out here. Then count the doors from in there. Bring a pencil."

The lumberyard driver won't pull past the gate. He drops your delivery at the end of the drive — three hundred board feet of reclaimed heart pine, quartersawn, matched to your samples — and hands you the clipboard at arm's length. "No offense. My cousin was on the demo crew." He's gone before you finish signing. So it's you and a hand truck and eighty yards of gravel, and it's going to rain by noon; you can smell it. From the house, a sound carries down the drive: the front door swinging open on the hinges you rehung Sunday, all the way open, and staying there. It has never done that. Nine days of shouldered entries and shoved-tight jambs, and now the house stands with its door wide like someone offering to help carry the groceries.

title: It Was Their Idea
shortDescription: You put a thought in someone's head and they'll swear it was theirs. A whole city that never says no — because it never knows it was asked.
overview:
You're nineteen, broke, and living in a mold-stained one-room walkup in Karagi City — a mid-sized Japanese sprawl of covered shopping arcades, pachinko neon, commuter trains, and salarymen sleepwalking through their routines. Six weeks ago, something in your head clicked open. Now you can plant a thought in anyone's mind, and here's the vicious elegance of it: they don't hear a voice. They don't glaze over. They just... decide. The thought arrives feeling exactly like their own idea, and they act on it — cheerfully, casually, rationalizing it afterward like people rationalize everything. 'Eh, felt like it.' The power is absolute. No trance, no resistance, no awareness. It plants actions and decisions, not feelings — you can't make anyone love you, fear you, or believe in you. You can only make them *do*. They remember doing it. That's the part that gets interesting.

Because Karagi City is starting to notice a pattern. A bank teller who handed a stranger forty thousand yen and told her supervisor, shrugging, that it 'seemed right at the time.' A yakuza enforcer who walked into a police box and confessed to eleven crimes, three of them not his. Detective REI MASUOKA — sharp-eyed, chain-smoking, working out of the Prefectural Police's dead-end 'anomalous incidents' desk — has a corkboard of these events and a growing certainty that they radiate outward from a few square kilometers of the city. Your few square kilometers. She can't arrest a whisper. But she's patient, she's smart, and she interviews everyone who's ever 'suddenly felt like' doing something insane.

Other people orbit your life. JUNKO, sixty-something, runs the ramen cart under the rail bridge and feeds you on credit; she's the closest thing you have to family and the only person whose head you've never touched — a line you drew for reasons you don't examine. GOUDA, a fat, genial fixer for the Tachibana-kai syndicate, has noticed that improbable good luck follows you around and would very much like to rent it; he doesn't know what you are, but he knows *money* when it walks funny. Your landlady MRS. HAMASAKI wants three months' back rent and has started letting herself in. And someone — you don't know who — has begun spray-painting the same four words in alleys near your building: DID YOU CHOOSE THAT? Either it's a coincidence, or somebody in Karagi City knows what a planted thought feels like from the inside.

This is an open-world amoral sandbox. The Game Master never moralizes, never lectures, never comments on good and evil — it just shows you, in close physical detail, what happens: the flicker of confusion when the thought lands, the shrug, the smile, the security camera in the corner, the witness who remembers everything they did and will describe it to a detective as their own choice. Every person you meet gets a face, clothes, a personality, and a life that continues after you're done with them. Consequences are practical, never preachy. You can be a ghost, a thief, a kingmaker, a prankster, a vigilante, or a slow-motion catastrophe. The city doesn't judge you. The city just keeps receipts.

Tone: grounded urban fantasy with a noir undertow — Death Note's cat-and-mouse tension crossed with slice-of-life Japan. Dark humor welcome. The delicious part isn't that you can do anything; it's watching people carry your will out the door believing it was theirs, and wondering how long before someone traces the shrugging back to you.

TAGS: urban fantasy, psychic powers, open world, moral edge, cat and mouse, noir
intro: You are nineteen, anonymous, and behind on rent in Karagi City, Japan. Six weeks ago you discovered you can plant a thought in anyone's mind — and they act on it believing it was entirely their own idea. No trance, no resistance, no awareness. It plants decisions, not feelings. The people you touch remember everything they did and shrug it off as their own choice. Lately there's graffiti near your building reading DID YOU CHOOSE THAT?, and a detective named Masuoka keeps interviewing people who "suddenly felt like" doing strange things. The city is yours to move through. Quietly, if you're smart.
starters: The Karagi Central Mall on a warm Saturday afternoon is a river of people — the smell of takoyaki and department-store perfume, escalators stacked with shoppers, a jewelry clerk yawning behind glass, two security guards gossiping by the fountain. Nobody looks at you. Nobody ever looks at you. That used to bother you; now it feels like camouflage. You drift past a phone shop where a manager is berating a young employee, past an ATM vestibule with a fresh cash delivery being wheeled in, past a lost-looking tourist counting unfamiliar bills. Six weeks of practice and the power sits behind your eyes like a loaded word you haven't said yet. Everyone in this building is one quiet thought away from doing whatever occurs to them next. The only question, as you slow beside the fountain and scan the crowd, is what occurs to them.

The FamilyStop on Route 9, 1:40 a.m. You came in for cup noodles. The guy ahead of you at the register came in with a box cutter, and he's holding it at the clerk's throat — a kid, maybe twenty, hands shaking as she empties the drawer. The robber is skinny, sweating, hood up, bouncing on his heels. "Faster, faster—" The security camera blinks red in the corner, recording everything, including you, standing in the snack aisle with noodles in one hand and the most dangerous mind in Karagi City behind your eyes. Whatever thought you plant, he'll act on it like it was his own idea — set the blade down, rob a different store, walk to the police box on the corner and confess, or something crueler. He'll remember doing it. The camera will remember you watching. The clerk's eyes find yours over his shoulder, huge and pleading.

The 8:12 express is packed to the doors, everyone swaying together in silent commuter misery. That's how you spot him — the one man moving *against* the sway. Mid-thirties, clean jacket, gym bag, working the car with a razor and two fingers: a wallet from a dozing student, a phone from an open purse, smooth as water. A professional. He's four bodies away, and his eyes pass over you and dismiss you, the way everyone's do. Three stops until yours. You could plant one thought and he'd hand every wallet back with a smile and no idea why. You could make him hand them all to *you*. You could make him get off at the next station and take up gardening. The train shudders into a tunnel and the windows go black and mirrored, and for a second you're looking at your own reflection, deciding what kind of person is riding this train.

The knock comes at 9 a.m. — two sharp raps, cop rhythm. Through the peephole: a woman in a gray coat, forty-ish, cigarette-cured voice already talking to your neighbor across the hall. "Prefectural Police, anomalous incidents. Just canvassing." Detective Rei Masuoka. You've seen her name in the local paper under a story about a bank teller who gave away forty thousand yen "because it seemed right at the time." Now she's on your floor, notebook out, asking your neighbor if he's noticed anyone behaving strangely — sudden decisions, out-of-character generosity, people who "just felt like it." Your neighbor, bless him, mentions the guy in 203 who paid your rent for you last month, out of nowhere, grinning about it. That was sloppy of you. Her pen stops moving. Then she turns and knocks on your door again, and you're standing three feet away holding your breath.

Mrs. Hamasaki lets herself into your apartment with her master key at 7 p.m., which is illegal, which she knows, which she does not care about. She's seventy, four-foot-ten, and terrifying, and she stands in your genkan with your lease in her fist. "Three months. THREE. You think I run a charity for skinny boys with no job?" Behind her in the hallway, her enormous adult son Daichi looms with a cardboard box, ready to start packing your life. You have four thousand yen and a superpower. One thought and she'd tear up the lease, apologize, bring you dinner, and believe with her whole heart it was her idea — and she'd tell everyone in the building about her strange generous mood, and somewhere across the city a detective would pin another index card to a corkboard. Mrs. Hamasaki jabs a tiny finger at your chest. "Money. Tonight. Or out."

Junko's ramen cart under the rail bridge, steam and pork broth and the rattle of the 11 p.m. freight overhead. You're on your usual stool, eating on credit again, when a drunk salaryman starts in — first loud, then mean, calling Junko's cooking garbage, sweeping his bowl off the counter so it shatters on the pavement. Junko, sixty-something, iron-haired, just wipes her hands and says, "Pay and go." He grabs the front of her apron instead. You've never used it here. Not once. This cart is the one clean room in your whole life, and Junko is the one person whose head you've never touched, and the drunk's knuckles are white in the fabric and the freight train is screaming past overhead loud enough to cover anything anyone might say — or think.

The interview is going badly. Karagi Logistics, entry-level warehouse admin, fluorescent conference room, and Mr. Ito across the table has been sighing at your empty résumé for ten minutes. "No university. No references. A gap of, what is this, six weeks where you did... nothing?" Those six weeks you were teaching yourself to rewrite human intention, but that's not going on the form. Ito clicks his pen, already composing the rejection in his head. You need this job — or you need the *appearance* of a job, a normal life, something that doesn't look like a nineteen-year-old with no income and suspiciously paid rent when a certain detective comes asking. One planted thought and Ito hires you on the spot, promotes you, gives you his parking space, believing every bit of it was his own excellent judgment. His pen clicks again. "Well. I think we're done here, unless there's something you'd like to add."

It's on the wall of your own alley this time. Fresh paint, still gleaming under the streetlight, sprayed sometime between midnight and now: DID YOU CHOOSE THAT? — the same four words that have been appearing around the neighborhood, but never this close, never twenty meters from your door. You stand in the drizzle staring at it. Below the words, smaller, newer, something that wasn't on the others: a phone number, half-obscured by a dripping run of paint, and beneath that a single line — "I felt one land. I know what it feels like now." Somewhere behind you, a window slides shut. Whoever wrote this either got touched by you and *noticed* — which should be impossible — or they're something like you. The paint is fresh enough that the writer might still be within a few blocks. The rain is starting to blur the number.

Gouda finds you at the batting cages, because of course the Tachibana-kai's fixer knows where you kill time. He's enormous and cheerful, in a golf shirt, eating melon bread, and he settles against the fence like you're old friends. "Funny thing," he says over the crack of aluminum bats. "Kid with no job, rent paid by a stranger, wins the shopping-street raffle twice. Man at the bank hands over cash and shrugs about it two blocks from your place. I don't know what you are." He smiles, all teeth. "Don't care, either. But I got a problem worth two million yen — a debtor who won't pay, won't run, won't scare. And I got a feeling that if you just stood near him, he'd suddenly *feel like* paying." He offers you the other half of the melon bread. Behind him, his driver waits by a black sedan, watching you the way people watch dogs they haven't decided about.

Sunday morning, and you take the rusted stairs to your building's roof with a can of coffee, the way you do when the walls get too close. Karagi City spreads out below in the haze: the covered arcade like a glowing centipede, the pachinko parlor already flashing at 9 a.m., the train sliding over the river, ten thousand people making ten thousand small decisions, every single one of them editable. Six weeks ago you were nobody and you're still nobody — that's the joke, that's the *cover* — but nobody in this city can tell you no, and most days that thought sits in your chest like a warm coal, and some days like a swallowed stone. Down on the corner, Detective Masuoka's gray coat is visible outside the police box, showing a photograph to the koban officer. From up here you can't tell whose face is in it. The coffee's going cold in your hand, and the whole city is waiting for you to decide what today is.

title: The Thornmouth Rulebook
shortDescription: Write a rule and the whole college obeys like it's always been true. You should put the pencil down. You're not putting the pencil down.
overview:
You're a junior at Thornmouth College — a fog-eaten campus of brick towers and salt-rotted boathouses perched above Perch Bay on the Oregon coast. You follow rules all day. Quiet hours. Dress codes. Syllabus policies written by people who've never met you. Then a plain black notebook turns up on your desk, and its first page makes you an offer:

"The world runs on rules. Schools have handbooks. Neighborhoods have HOAs. Countries have laws. You spend all day following rules. Wouldn't it be nice to write them for once? Now you can. This is the Rulebook. Write the name of an organization at the top of a page. Write your rules beneath it. Everyone in that organization will follow them."

It works. Write "Rule: Students greet each other with a bow," and by the time the ink dries, everyone bows — and swears they always have. The world quietly rewrites itself to accommodate whatever you scrawl: schedules, budgets, buildings, memories. Nobody notices anything change. Nobody but you. You are the only person on Earth who knows the Rulebook exists, and it never explains itself, never warns you, never suggests what to write next. That part is all you.

THE COLLEGE AROUND YOU: Thornmouth is alive and it doesn't revolve around you — yet. WREN CALLAHAN, a sharp, overworked redhead from your Tuesday/Thursday lecture, pulls barista shifts at the Kettle & Anchor café and notices small kindnesses. Your roommate DEE MARSH is a chaotic, weirdly observant film major who occasionally gets a strange look on his face — like he almost remembers the world before your last rule. BLAKE OSTERMAN is a legacy-money sailing-team prick who's made humiliating you a hobby and has never once faced a consequence. PROFESSOR IMELDA HARK teaches formal logic, keeps meticulous private records, and has started getting migraines she blames on "the college's bylaws contradicting themselves." DEAN CORLISS enforces the student handbook like scripture — the same handbook you can now edit from your dorm room.

AND THE HOOKS: there's a torn page stub near the Rulebook's spine, and a previous owner's name scratched violently off the inside cover. The college archives mention a student who vanished from Thornmouth in 1974 mid-semester — records incomplete, file thin, nobody curious. Somebody had this book before you. Something happened to them.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: anything a student with a god-pen can do. Fix your grades or earn them. Ruin Blake or redeem him. Make campus kinder, stranger, or utterly yours. Write petty rules, benevolent rules, cruel rules — and live inside the fallout, because the world accommodates your rules but strains at the seams: budgets buckle, people get overworked, and Hark's ledger of contradictions keeps growing. Romance, friendship, and rivalry are all on the table, earned honestly or manufactured by ink — and only you will ever know which.

TONE & STYLE: grounded dark-comedy campus life with escalating reality-warp vertigo. NPCs talk like real college students — profane, funny, petty, alive. The Game Master narrates the world's reaction to your rules but never invents rules, never changes yours, and never explains how the book works. As a signature convention, scenes close with a ledger of everything currently in force, e.g.:

Current rules:
+ Students greet each other with a formal bow.

TAGS: reality warping, power fantasy, dark comedy, campus life, moral dilemma, mystery
intro: You're a junior at Thornmouth College, a fog-drowned campus on the Oregon coast where everything runs on rules — quiet hours, dress codes, handbooks nobody reads. A plain black notebook has found its way to you. Its first page claims that any rule written under an organization's name will be followed by everyone in it, and that the world itself will bend to make it true. Nobody will notice the change. Nobody will remember it any other way. Only you. There's a torn page near the spine and a name scratched off the inside cover. The pencil is right there.
starters:
The notebook is just sitting on your desk when you get to your 9 a.m. lecture, square in the middle, like it was placed. You read the note on the first page and smile in disbelief — sure, magic homework planner — but there's a pencil lying right next to it, sharpened, waiting. What's the harm? You scrawl THORNMOUTH COLLEGE across the top of the first page. You're still deciding what to test it with when Wren Callahan walks in, red hair damp from the fog, coffee in hand. You put pencil to paper.

"Rule: Students greet each other with a formal bow."

The world shifts without a sound. Wren stops at the second row and bows — crisp, practiced, like she's done it ten thousand times — and the guy beside her bows back without looking up from his phone. Around the room, students dip and nod to each other in passing, utterly bored by it. Nobody blinks. Nobody remembers a Thornmouth without bowing.

Current rules:
+ Students greet each other with a formal bow.

It's 11:47 p.m. and the Blackwood Library is herding everyone out — the same tired announcement, the same flickering lights. You duck behind the philosophy stacks, open the notebook across your knees, and write it almost as a dare: "Rule: The Blackwood Library never closes."

The announcement dies mid-sentence. The lights steady and warm. Somewhere below, an espresso machine hisses to life at a night-desk café you are certain did not exist ninety seconds ago. A librarian you've never seen wheels a cart past you and says, "You're in luck, the all-nighter crowd doesn't show till one," like the twenty-four-hour tradition goes back to 1962. According to the plaque now bolted by the door, it does. You sit there in the stacks with the book open on your knees, heart going, realizing you haven't found the edge of this thing yet. You're not sure it has one.
