Blake Osterman knocks your tray out of your hands in the middle of the dining hall — casually, mid-conversation, like flicking a bug — and the crash turns every head in the room. "Christ, watch where you're going," he says, loud, to his table's delight. "Some people shouldn't be allowed to carry hot food." You're on one knee in spilled soup while a hundred people decide it's funnier not to help, and Blake's already moved on, because for him this cost nothing. It never costs him anything. Three generations of Ostermans have a boathouse named after them; consequences don't apply.

Except your bag is on your shoulder. The notebook is inside it. The pencil is clipped to the spiral, and from down here on the floor you can feel it like a heartbeat. One sentence. That's all he is now. One sentence.

Professor Hark's logic midterm is face-down on your desk, and you know — with total, nauseating clarity — that you did not study. Around you, pencils are already scratching. Hark patrols the aisles with her arms crossed, sharp-eyed, famously merciless about academic integrity. And under your blue book, flat against the desk, sits the Rulebook.

You could write it in ten seconds. "Rule: All students receive full marks on midterms." Or narrower — just this class, just this exam, just you. The world would fold itself around the sentence and Hark would hand back A's with that pinched look she gets lately, rubbing her temple, muttering about the grading bylaws contradicting themselves. She's been getting those headaches a lot this semester. Every time, actually, that you've used the book. She flips the sign at the front of the room: YOU MAY BEGIN.

"Okay, weird question," Dee says, upside down off the edge of his bed, tossing a hacky sack at the ceiling. "Did Fridays used to have classes?" You go very still. Three weeks ago you wrote the rule — Rule: No classes are held on Fridays — and the college grew a proud tradition of "Reflection Fridays" with a founding story and everything. Nobody noticed. Nobody CAN notice. "Because I had a dream where I was in a Friday lecture," Dee goes on, frowning at the ceiling, "and it felt less like a dream and more like a — rerun? Like I'd actually been there." He catches the hacky sack and looks at you, and for one second your chaotic, unserious roommate has the eyes of a man checking whether the walls are real. The notebook is in your desk drawer, two feet from his head.

Dean Corliss's office smells like lemon polish and institutional menace. "The student handbook," she says, sliding a printed copy across the desk toward you, "is not a suggestion." The fight with Blake Osterman — his word against yours, and his word comes with a donor plaque — has landed you in a disciplinary hearing, and Corliss is reading you the conduct code line by line in her flat executioner's voice. Section four. Section seven. Sanctions up to and including suspension.

Your bag is at your feet. Inside it is a notebook that edits the very handbook she's quoting, retroactively, invisibly, forever. She could look up from section nine to find that section nine has always said something else. She dog-ears a page and folds her hands. "Before I decide anything," she says, "I want to hear your version. All of it."

You find it by accident, checking whether the notebook has a maker's mark: a torn stub near the spine, one page ripped out hard enough to scar the binding — and on the inside cover, a name scratched away with something sharp, gouged past legibility. Someone owned this before you. Someone wrote a page they had to destroy.

The college archives live in the Blackwood basement, and it takes you two hours in the microfiche to find the itch you can't name: a student who vanished from Thornmouth mid-semester in 1974. File nearly empty. No withdrawal form, no transfer, no obituary. One yearbook photo, water-damaged, face half gone. The archivist shrugs when you ask. "Records were sloppy back then." Except the records around that file are immaculate. It's only this one person the paperwork forgot — cleanly, completely, like the world folded itself shut over the hole.

Professor Hark catches you after lecture with two fingers pressed to her temple. "A moment." Her office is small, precise, and papered with something that stops your blood: a hand-drawn timeline of Thornmouth's policies, dozens of index cards, red string. "I keep records," she says. "Meticulous ones. And as of this semester, the college's bylaws contradict themselves. The dining contract references a vendor that doesn't exist. The library's twenty-four-hour charter is dated 1962 but printed on paper stock from this year. I've had a migraine for six weeks." She looks at you — not accusing, not yet, just a logician staring down an impossible dataset. "You're one of the few students who reads carefully. Tell me honestly. Have you noticed anything about this college that doesn't... hold together?" The notebook is in your bag, six inches from her red string.

It seemed harmless. Generous, even. "Rule: All coffee on campus is free." You wrote it Sunday night feeling like a benevolent god. It's Wednesday, and the Kettle & Anchor looks like a disaster zone — a line out the door and around the fountain, the espresso machine screaming, and behind the counter Wren Callahan is dying on her feet, hair escaping its tie, hands shaking as she pulls her three-hundredth shot. The world accommodated your rule; it just made HER pay for it. Budget line item, staffing freeze, one barista against an ocean of free-coffee demand that has "always existed." She catches you at the front of the line and manages a wrecked half-smile. "Hey. Sorry. It's been — I don't know what it's been." The notebook is in your bag. You could fix this a dozen ways. Some of them are even kind.

The boathouse party is at full roar — string lights, cheap speakers, half of Thornmouth packed onto the dock over black water — and you know exactly nobody. You've been here forty minutes. Two people have talked to you; one wanted directions to the keg. Across the deck, Blake Osterman holds court under lights strung from the building bearing his family's name, and Wren laughs at something near the railing, and the fog rolls in off Perch Bay like it's coming to collect.

The notebook is inside your jacket, flat against your ribs. One sentence and everyone here knows your name. One sentence and they're delighted you came. One sentence and this entire glittering, indifferent crowd rearranges itself around you like it never did anything else. Your fingers find the pencil in your pocket and rest there. Someone bumps your shoulder and doesn't apologize.

title: They Promoted Me to Catch Me
shortDescription: By day you lead the hunt for the city's infamous machine-saboteur. By night you ARE the saboteur — and your new partner is very, very good.
overview:
You are a licensed artificer of the Crown Patent Bureau in Vallenmere — and, as of this morning, lead investigator on the foundry saboteur case. Which is awkward, because the saboteur is you. Three years ago the Ashwell Combine bought out your dying master's workshop, patented your resonance-core design under Magnate Corvin Ashwell's name, and quietly deleted its safety lattice to cut costs. Without the lattice, every core they mass-produce will eventually crack and burn. One already did — the Bureau ruled the Milner Street explosion 'sabotage.' Your sabotage has never hurt anyone: you crack the cores cleanly, at night, before they can crack themselves.

Now you walk your own crime scenes, file reports on yourself, and manage Inspector Odile Marsh — a sharp transfer from the constabulary who thinks the saboteur is a genius and fully intends to prove it. Overseer Vayle wants an arrest before the Grand Exposition. Ashwell is offering a fortune for a name, any name. And somewhere in the foundry district, a copycat has started setting fires with none of your care.

Play the double life to the hilt: steer the investigation off yourself, forge alibis, invent by day and unmake by night, hunt proof of the cover-up, and decide — carefully, person by person — who ever gets to learn what you really are. Tone: gaslamp thriller with wit; near-misses, competence, slow-burn trust and betrayal.

TAGS: double life, gaslamp fantasy, cat and mouse, intrigue, inventor, thriller
intro: You are an artificer of the Crown Patent Bureau in the smoke-and-brass city of Vallenmere, newly promoted to lead the hunt for the foundry saboteur — the anonymous vandal who has disabled eleven Ashwell resonance cores this year. You are that vandal. The core is your stolen design, patented under Magnate Ashwell's name and gutted of its safety lattice to save coin; without the lattice, every core will one day crack and burn. So you break them first, gently, and by day you write the reports on your own crimes. Your new partner, Inspector Odile Marsh, has just been assigned to you.
starters: Number Eight Foundry still smells of ozone and cold iron — your ozone, your work, six days old. You stand where you knelt last Tuesday with a tuning fork and a prybar, and beside you Inspector Odile Marsh crouches over the cracked core casing like it's a love letter. "Look at the fracture line," she says. "Clean. Almost surgical. Eleven cores and not one injury — that's not luck, that's calibration." She glances up at you, eyes bright. "Whoever this is, they understand resonance lattices better than anyone at Ashwell. Better than the Bureau, maybe." A foundry clerk hovers at the door with the shift ledgers she requested — ledgers that include a night your forged alibi is thinner than you'd like. Marsh holds out her hand for them, then pauses, waiting to hear what her new lead investigator makes of the scene.

It is four minutes past two in the morning, and you are inside Wexler Row Foundry with a shim-key in the lock behind you and core number twelve humming under your palms. The safety lattice should be here — a lacework of silver thread around the coil housing — and it isn't, same as the other eleven. You've got the fracture point marked and the dampening cloth laid out when you hear it: boots on the catwalk above. Not a watchman's slow scuff. Quick steps, purposeful, coming toward the stairs. A lantern beam swings across the far wall. You have perhaps thirty seconds, an uncracked core, a bag of very incriminating tools, and two exits — the loading door you jimmied and a coal chute you've never tested. The core keeps humming, patient and doomed, exactly the way it will hum right up until the day it kills somebody.

Overseer Vayle's office smells of pipe smoke and impatience. He slides a broadsheet across the desk without standing: SABOTEUR STRIKES ELEVENTH FOUNDRY — BUREAU BAFFLED. "The Grand Exposition is in nineteen days," he says. "Magnate Ashwell is unveiling the new core line on its main stage, and he has personally asked me whether my lead investigator is competent or complicit." He lets the word sit there. "I told him competent. Don't make a liar of me." Behind you, the door opens and a woman in a constabulary greatcoat steps in — sharp eyes, ink-stained cuffs, a case file already thick under her arm. "Inspector Marsh," Vayle says. "Your new partner. She comes highly recommended and asks inconvenient questions. You two have a saboteur to catch by month's end." Marsh looks you over the way you'd inspect a suspect mechanism, and extends her hand.

The fire bells wake you before dawn, and by the time you reach Coker's Lane the foundry's east wing is a black skeleton dripping steam. This is not your work. You'd never touch a building with a night watchman inside — and there he is on a stretcher, coughing, alive by luck alone. Inspector Marsh is already picking through the wreckage in yesterday's coat, and she waves you over with something cupped in her handkerchief: a crude timing fuse, wax and copper wire, ugly as sin. "It's wrong," she says flatly. "Our saboteur cracks cores like a surgeon. This is a butcher with a match. Either our genius has gotten sloppy—" she looks at you, "—or somebody new likes fire." Down the lane, a constable is holding back a man in a soot-streaked nightshirt who keeps shouting that he saw someone running toward the canal.

You're at your Bureau workbench, ostensibly refining a pressure regulator, actually re-inking the tavern receipt that puts you across town on the night of the Halden Street job, when Inspector Marsh drops a wooden crate on the bench beside you. Inside: eleven cracked core fragments, one from each scene, tagged and numbered in her handwriting. "I requisitioned them from evidence," she says. "I want you to reassemble the fracture patterns. You're the best artificer in the building — if anyone can tell me how the saboteur thinks, it's you." She pulls up a stool, clearly intending to watch. Fragment number four still has a hairline score mark where your chisel slipped in the dark. The forged receipt is drying under your left elbow, ink side up, and Marsh has the eyes of a woman who reads everything on a desk.

The invitation card is heavy cream stock, edged in gilt: Magnate Corvin Ashwell requests the pleasure of the Bureau's lead investigator at Ashwell House, this evening, seven o'clock. And now here you are in his trophy hall, where your resonance core — his resonance core, says the brass plaque — sits under glass at the center of the room. Ashwell himself pours the brandy. "Twelve thousand crowns," he says, "to whoever brings me a name. But you don't strike me as a bounty sort. So let me ask plainly: what does the Bureau actually know?" Behind him, through the window, his private foundry glows against the night sky, stamping out lattice-less cores by the dozen. A footman waits at your elbow with the brandy tray, and Ashwell watches you with the mild patience of a man who has bought everything he's ever wanted, including, once, your life's work.

Rain hammers the skylights of the Bureau records vault, and you are elbow-deep in three years of patent filings, hunting the one document that could hang Ashwell instead of you: the original schematic transfer from your master's workshop, the version with the safety lattice still drawn in. The clerk swore box 47-C held the Combine acquisitions. Box 47-C holds tax ledgers and a dead moth. Someone has been through these shelves — folders resequenced, one whole drawer replaced with duplicates on newer paper. Then, from two aisles over, a voice you're rapidly learning to dread: "Fancy finding you here." Inspector Marsh rounds the shelf with an armful of files of her own. "I'm pulling everything on Ashwell's early patents," she says. "Follow the money, follow the design. Care to compare notes?" Her stack, you notice, includes a folder tabbed with your old master's name.

You crack the twelfth core at half past three and are home by four, hands scrubbed, tools stowed under the floorboard, and asleep for nearly two hours before the runner boy pounds on your door. Now it's seven in the morning and you're standing over your own crime scene while Inspector Marsh reads the night watchman's statement aloud. "He says he did his rounds at three and everything was fine. Found it cracked at five." She checks her pocket watch against the foundry clock. "Two-hour window. Gates locked, no forced entry on any door." She looks up. "Except our saboteur doesn't force things, do they. They have keys, or picks, or wings." A constable approaches with something found by the coal chute — small, metallic, held out in an open palm — and Marsh turns to look before you can see what it is.

The Grand Exposition hall is nineteen days from opening and already half-built: scaffolds, bunting, and at the center of it all, a stage where six Ashwell resonance cores will run at full power in front of four thousand people. You're here on official business — "assess sabotage risk," Vayle's memo said, and the irony has not stopped tasting like copper. Up close, the exhibition cores are worse than the factory line: overclocked for show, lattices absent, mounted three feet from the public rail. By your math, at exposition load, one of these could crack on its own within the month. Possibly on the day. A foreman in Ashwell livery hurries over, clipboard first. "You the Bureau inspector? Good. Sign here that the security arrangements are adequate, and I can get the mounting crew back on schedule." He offers you a pen. Somewhere above, riggers are already hoisting banner cloth with Ashwell's face on it.

The Brass Ferrule is the pub where Bureau artificers drink, and tonight Inspector Marsh is buying, which should have been your first warning. "I've built a profile," she says, sliding into the booth opposite you with two pints and a notebook. "Our saboteur: trained artificer, likely apprenticed under an independent master — the technique's too old-school for Combine graduates. Grudge against Ashwell specifically; nobody's touched a Renner or a Blackpool core. Works nights, knows Bureau patrol schedules—" she taps the notebook "—which means access to Bureau documents. I think our vandal is one of ours." She takes a long drink and watches you over the rim. "You've been here six years. You know everyone in that building. So. Who fits?" At the bar behind her, two junior clerks from your own floor are laughing at something, and one of them apprenticed independent, same as you did.

title: I Buried the Demon Lord
shortDescription: He died in your arms. His empire didn't notice. Now you wear his mask, run his war, and a hero is coming to kill "you."
overview:
You were the Demon Lord's personal physician — the quiet one who ground his medicines and kept his wasting sickness secret while he conquered half a continent. Three weeks ago, Maldrach the Unfading died in your arms. In a panic that has since hardened into a plan, you and Chamberlain Coriss buried him beneath the throne room and sealed you inside the iron mask he never removed in public. Its old glamour roughens your voice. Nothing roughens your nerve.

The empire believes its Lord lives. General Ezzeth is demanding the promised Red March, the spring offensive meant to burn the human borderlands, and grows louder every council. The spymaster, Whisper-Mother Sarn, files reports on everyone — and has started noticing how the Lord holds his cup. Crossing the ash wastes comes Auren, the human champion, carrying a sword forged to kill the thing you're pretending to be.

You have no dark magic. You have authority, a healer's knowledge, Coriss's gallows-humor loyalty, and the terrifying freedom to steer an evil empire anywhere you dare — stall the war, quietly unmake the cruelest laws, treat the plague in the goblin quarter the real Maldrach ignored, maybe even parley with the hero who wants your head. One slip of the mask ends everything.

Tone: throne-room bluffing under dramatic irony, dark humor, tender conscience, real consequences. The world has its own momentum and doesn't wait for you.

TAGS: dark fantasy, villain protagonist, deception, court intrigue, dramatic irony
intro: You are the court physician of Varn Kol, the obsidian citadel — and, for three weeks now, you are also Demon Lord Maldrach the Unfading. The true Maldrach died of the wasting sickness you could not cure; only Chamberlain Coriss helped you hide the body and shares the secret. Sealed in the Lord's iron mask, its glamour deepening your voice, you sit his throne, sign his decrees, and keep putting off the great offensive his generals hunger for. You have no dark magic — only nerve, medicine, and an empire's fear of a dead man. Word from the west says the hero Auren is coming.
starters: General Ezzeth's fist lands on the war table hard enough to topple the little iron soldiers marking the border. "Three councils, my Lord. Three councils and no date for the Red March." The map beneath his knuckles shows the human borderlands inked in red, waiting to burn. Around the table, six commanders watch you the way dogs watch a hand near meat. At the far end, Whisper-Mother Sarn isn't watching the map at all — she's watching your fingers where they rest on the arm of your chair, and you remember too late that Maldrach never drummed them. The glamour in the mask keeps your breathing slow and awful. Ezzeth straightens, still waiting. "Give the word, and I ride tonight."

It is not yet dawn, and Coriss is lacing the mask's straps behind your skull with the tenderness of a hangman who likes you. "Hold still. If this slips at morning court, I'm telling everyone I never met you." Her candle throws both your shadows across the physician's old workbench — your workbench — where the mortar and pestle sit exactly where you left them three weeks ago, dusted with the last medicine you ever ground for him. The final buckle bites. Your reflection in the dark window is Maldrach the Unfading, and your voice, when you test it, comes out like stones settling in a grave. Somewhere below, the citadel is waking. Coriss hands you the day's schedule: council at second bell, executions to confirm, and a scout from the western wastes who says it cannot wait.

The petitioner they drag before the throne is a goblin, small and grey and coughing blood into a rag she's too frightened to lower. The guards had to be ordered twice to let her this close; plague from the goblin quarter isn't supposed to reach the obsidian floor. "Lord of Ash," she manages, forehead to the stone. "Forty dead this week. The wells — someone must look at the wells." You know exactly what's in those wells. You wrote a paper on it, years ago, under your own name, which no one read. The court is silent, waiting for Maldrach to do what Maldrach does with inconvenient creatures. From her alcove, Whisper-Mother Sarn has stopped pretending to read her reports. The goblin coughs again, wet and rattling, and the sound carries all the way up the dais.

Whisper-Mother Sarn steps out of a doorway that should have been empty, falls in beside you, and matches your stride down the torchlit corridor as though she'd been invited. "My Lord walks quickly tonight," she says. "Faster than before the winter, my clerks tell me. They measure such things. It's their nature." She holds a folded report against her chest, its wax seal unbroken, and does not offer it. Two of your honor guard trail eight paces back, out of earshot — she arranged that somehow. "There is a matter," she says, "concerning irregularities in the Lord's household. I thought you should hear it from me before it reaches the council." The corridor ahead splits: your chambers left, the council hall right. Sarn slows, letting you choose the direction, watching how you decide.

Midnight, and you've stolen an hour to be a physician again. Your old workroom smells of willow bark and burnt honey; the mask sits on the bench beside you like a patient skull while you grind fever-root for the garrison surgeon — anonymously, through Coriss, the way everything decent gets done now. The pestle's rhythm is the first honest thing you've touched all day. Then: three knocks at the door. Not Coriss's knock. Her knock is two, then one, your agreed signal, and this door leads to a corridor where nobody should be walking at this hour. The knocking comes again, patient, unhurried. The mask is an arm's length away. Your face — your actual, killable face — is bare.

The scout kneels on the throne room floor, still crusted with ash from the western wastes, and the whole court leans in to hear him say it. "He crossed at the Cinder Ford four days ago, my Lord. Auren. The sword is real — I saw it burn through a warg like tallow. He travels alone and he is coming here." A murmur runs through the assembled lords, and every eye swings up to the throne to drink in Maldrach's reaction — the contempt, the dark amusement, the promise of the hero's spectacular death. General Ezzeth is already smiling. Coriss, at your right hand, has gone very still. The scout stays down, trembling, waiting for you to speak, and behind the iron mask your heart is doing something no glamour can disguise.

Second bell past midnight, and you and Coriss stand alone in the throne room over the flagstone that covers him. The mortar you mixed three weeks ago has cracked — a hairline, but a hairline in the wrong place, right where the morning light falls when court is in session. "Stone settles," Coriss says, holding the lantern low. "Bodies settle. Everything in this citadel settles except our situation." She's brought a bucket of fresh mortar and two trowels, which is either loyalty or evidence, depending on who finds you. Down the hall, the night watch changes at third bell; you can hear the far doors, boots, the murmur of the relief. Coriss crouches, runs her thumb along the crack, and looks up at you. "Quickly, then. Or we think of something clever. You're the clever one, allegedly."

The morning's decrees are stacked seven deep on the obsidian desk, and Coriss reads them out in her flattest voice while you sign with Maldrach's brutal, backslanted hand — you practiced for a week, and it still cramps your wrist. Grain levies. A promotion. Then she pauses. "This one you'll want to actually read." It's a death warrant, prepared and countersigned by General Ezzeth, awaiting only the Lord's mark: eleven officers of the Third Legion, accused of 'reluctance' regarding the Red March. Two of the names you recognize — men you once treated for frostbite, who thanked you, back when you had a name people thanked. The real Maldrach would sign without slowing down. Coriss sets the warrant squarely in front of you and says nothing at all, which is as loud as she ever gets. The quill is wet.

The legions fill the great yard below the balcony, ten thousand of them under torchlight, and they are chanting for the Red March. It started in the eastern barracks an hour ago — Ezzeth's men, Coriss suspects, though the general stands beside you now wearing the innocence of a man watching his own fire spread. "The soldiers love their Lord," he says over the roar. "They only ask to be used." The chant has a rhythm like a ram against a gate: *march, march, march*. Protocol says Maldrach addresses the legions when they gather; silence would be noted, and Sarn is somewhere in the crowd below with her clerks and their little books. The balcony's edge is three steps away. Coriss leans in behind you, voice pitched for the mask alone: "Whatever you're going to say, decide it before you get to the rail."

Halfway through morning court, a soldier collapses. He goes down between the braziers with a sound like dropped armor — young, grey-lipped, foam at the corner of his mouth. You know what this is before he stops twitching: nightshade tincture, badly dosed, survivable for maybe another two hundred heartbeats if someone who knows what they're doing gets charcoal and salt water into him now. The court draws back in a rustle of robes. Nobody helps a man who falls in front of Maldrach the Unfading; some of them are already looking to the throne, hoping the Lord will do something entertaining to the body. Whisper-Mother Sarn glides a step closer to the dying man, head tilted — poison in the citadel is her business, and she is counting who looks guilty. The soldier's boot heels drum against the obsidian. Two hundred heartbeats. Fewer now.

title: Phase Two Starts After Midterms
shortDescription: The perfect con you designed years ago just went live — at the high school you enrolled in to finally, finally be a kid. Nobody knows your face.
overview:
You're nineteen, baby-faced, and your forged transcript says seventeen. You never attended a day of school in your life: Vasko's outfit raised you from childhood as 'the Architect,' the faceless planner whose blueprints the field crews executed without ever meeting. Three years ago your mentor Rennie died buying your way out. She wanted one thing for you — an ordinary life. So you built a clean identity and enrolled at Westbrook Academy. Not randomly. Your masterwork — a year-long con to capture the school's hundred-million Hallam Trust, its phases cheekily named Orientation, Midterms, Finals, Graduation by a lonely kid who'd never had any of them — is live on this campus right now. The new guidance counselor, Ms. Odile Vann, is running Phase One exactly as you wrote it. You know every step, every contingency, and every flaw you secretly buried in the design.

So: dismantle your own con from inside a homeroom. Shield classmates who are pressure points — like sunny Marisol Reyes, whose mother sits on the board. Survive class president Priya Nair, who keeps a notebook about you. Keep your first-ever friend Theo and his newspaper club from investigating themselves into a shallow grave. And treasure every pop quiz, cafeteria debate, and festival shift like the miracle it is — because Rennie died so you could have them.

Tone: warm action-comedy with a bittersweet undertow. Tradecraft applied to lunch lines. Mundane joys hit like adrenaline.
TAGS: school comedy, undercover, heist, found family, slow-burn revenge, slice of life
intro: Your student ID says you're seventeen. It's a beautiful forgery — you'd know, you checked. The truth: you spent your childhood in back rooms drawing operation plans for Vasko's crew, a planner so protected that the people who executed your work never saw your face. Rennie died getting you out. Now you're a transfer student at Westbrook Academy, because the plan you wrote years ago — the one aimed at this school's hundred-year trust — has finally gone live, and because you have never once sat at a desk with your name on it. You know every phase. They don't know you exist. You intend to have your first real school year and burn your masterpiece to the ground. Both. At once.
starters: Homeroom 2-C smells like whiteboard cleaner and someone's orange peel. There's a desk in the third row with a paper name card on it — your alias, printed in a font you didn't choose, and you've been staring at it for four seconds too long, because you have cased vaults with less reverence. "You can sit, you know," says the boy at the next desk, glasses crooked, a camera bag hugged in his lap like a pet. "Ms. Fontaine takes attendance at 8:10 sharp. I'm Theo. Newspaper club. You're the transfer, which makes you the most interesting thing to happen here since the vending machine caught fire." Up front, the teacher is writing the date on the board. Announcements crackle overhead: something about the centennial festival, something about new guidance counselor office hours. Your first bell of your first day rings in ninety seconds. Theo is still waiting on a name.

The guidance office door has a fresh nameplate — MS. ODILE VANN — and the woman behind the desk offers you a butterscotch from a bowl positioned exactly where your operations manual says to put comfort objects: left of the visitor, within easy reach, builds reciprocity. "Every transfer gets an intake chat," she says warmly. "Nothing scary. Tell me about your old school." On her wall hangs a poster about the Hallam Centennial Scholarship Drive — Phase One, wearing a sunflower border. You wrote the sentence she says next, word for word, six years ago, alone, at a folding table: "Westbrook takes care of its own." She smiles like she invented it. Her pen is uncapped over a blank student file. Yours. She's waiting, patient as a spider you personally taught to knit.

You're eleven minutes into the first pop quiz of your entire life — algebra, ten questions — and your heart is pounding like it's a job. You could finish in ninety seconds. You are deliberately getting number four wrong, because a transfer student who aces everything is a transfer student people write notebooks about. Speaking of which: two rows over, class president Priya Nair has finished early and is watching you over her water bottle with the unblinking patience of a customs officer. Outside the window, a van idles by the maintenance gate — gray, unmarked, parked at the exact angle your blueprints specify for a camera blind spot. Your pencil hovers over question five. Mr. Okafor announces four minutes remaining. Priya has started writing something that is definitely not math.

Lunch line, day three. You've already mapped the cafeteria the way you map everything — exits, sightlines, the lunch lady who counts change slowly enough to bottleneck the whole room — and you're mid-calculation on the pizza-versus-mystery-casserole problem when a tray bumps yours. "Okay, new kid, executive decision," says a girl with a sunflower pin on her blazer and the confidence of someone who has never eaten lunch alone. "You're sitting with us. I'm Marisol. My mom's on the board, so technically I own this school, which means I get to adopt transfers." Behind her, at the far table, a man in a contractor's vest is talking to the vice principal, holding a clipboard with a work order you designed the template for. Marisol is already walking. The line is moving. The casserole is congealing. Choices everywhere.

It's 9:40 p.m. and you are technically not on campus, in the sense that the campus doesn't know you're on it. The dead drop is where you put it years ago on paper — third utility box behind the gym, magnetic key holder, taped seam — and it's been serviced recently. Fresh tape. Phase One is running clean, which is the problem, because you built it and it doesn't have accidents. A flashlight beam swings across the gym wall: Mr. Dubois, the night custodian, doing rounds eight minutes ahead of the schedule you have in your head. Somewhere past the fence, a dog commits to barking. You've got the utility box open, a folded slip of paper in your hand you haven't read yet, and about twenty seconds of shadow left. Tomorrow you have a history presentation. Tonight you have this.

"Hold this end and don't die," Marisol says, and hands you eight feet of plywood. Festival prep, Saturday shift, and you volunteered — voluntarily, for fun, a concept you're still testing — to help build the centennial booth row. The quad smells like sawdust and someone's burnt practice churros. It's genuinely great. It would be perfect, except the electrical contractor rewiring the main stage is running cable in a pattern you recognize, because you drew it: it also happens to pass within reach of the administration building's junction room. Coincidences don't wear tool belts you specified. "Left! Your left!" Marisol yells cheerfully. A teacher with a megaphone is asking for two volunteers to carry paint to the admin wing. Theo is across the quad, photographing everything, including — you notice — the contractor's van plates.

Priya Nair catches you at your locker before first bell, notebook already open. She's the class president, she has a color-coding system, and page after page is about you. "Your transcript says you did Model UN at your old school," she says pleasantly. "I called them. They don't have Model UN." They do, actually — you paid for the website, the trophy photos, and a faculty advisor who answers the phone — which means either your infrastructure failed or she's bluffing, and Priya doesn't look like a bluffer. Around you the hallway churns: someone's dropped a trombone, two freshmen are trading anime cards like arms dealers, and the morning announcements are hyping the Hallam Centennial Kickoff Assembly, third period. Priya clicks her pen. "I've got time before homeroom," she says. "You seem like you have an interesting answer."

The whole school is packed into the auditorium and you're wedged between Theo and a kid asleep on his own backpack when the headmaster introduces the Hallam Centennial Trust Initiative. The slideshow behind him is Phase One with a school crest stamped on it — the scholarship drive, the alumni gala, the "modernization audit" of the trust's accounts. You know every bullet point before it appears, because a lonely fourteen-year-old wrote them at a card table and named the phases after school things they'd never had. Onstage, the new guidance counselor, Ms. Vann, waves graciously to applause. "Something's off about that audit timeline," Theo whispers, already scribbling in his reporter's notebook, hungry and fearless and exactly the kind of kid your contingencies eat alive. The headmaster asks for volunteers for the centennial committee. Hands are going up all around you.

You arrive at Westbrook Academy in the rain, twenty minutes early, one duffel bag, one beautiful lie of a transcript in a manila envelope going soft at the corners. The front gates are iron and older than the con. Students stream past under umbrellas — someone's laughing about a chemistry disaster, someone's rehearsing an apology into their phone — and it's all so aggressively normal that your chest does something complicated. Then you see it: parked across the street, a courier car with a rental barcode in the windshield, positioned exactly where your surveillance plan puts the first-week observation post. Phase One is watching the gate. Which means Phase One will watch you walk through it. A security guard at the booth waves you forward. "Transfer? You'll want the main office. Someone can walk you — hey, Reyes! Take the new kid up?" A girl with a sunflower pin turns around, already smiling.

The newspaper club's office is a converted supply closet with a corkboard, three chairs, and Theo standing on one of them. "Behold," he says, pinning up a printout, "the story that gets us regionals." It's a records request about the Hallam Trust's new audit firm. Your stomach drops with professional precision: he's two lucky guesses from the shell company, and the shell company has teeth. "Editor quit, so it's basically just me and Dana, and Dana only does horoscopes," Theo continues. "But you! You're new, you're observant, you laughed at my headline yesterday, which shows judgment. Join the paper." Through the little window, across the quad, Ms. Vann is walking the vice principal somewhere with a folder under her arm, following a route you'd recognize blindfolded. Theo holds out a spare press badge he clearly laminated himself. It says STAFF. It's crooked. It's the nicest thing anyone's offered you in three years.

title: Hate Me Until the Envoy Leaves
shortDescription: Your five prisoners of war run the farm, adore you, and must now act otherwise: the envoy deciding whether they hang back home sleeps down the hall.
overview:
Three years ago you were an army cook holding a bridge with a soup ladle when five soldiers of the Ashen Legion surrendered to you personally. The war ended a week later. Nobody ever processed the paperwork, so officially you are still their custodial officer — and unofficially they are your household. Sergeant Brakka, an ogre with tiny immaculate handwriting, keeps your ledger and salutes you at dawn no matter how often you tell her to stop. Vess the hex-witch sells charms to villagers she pretends to despise. Fenn, nineteen and a catastrophic liar, is in love with the miller's kid. Ilo, the quiet lizardfolk scout, mends every fence before you notice it's broken.

Now the Repatriation Accord has been signed. At first frost, all Legion personnel are to be returned home — where the Ash Court hangs 'the yielded' as traitors. Envoy Cadran Mool has been billeted in your spare room until the hearing, to verify your prisoners are miserable, properly held, and eager to return. So every meal is theater: scowls over the stew, chains worn loose for show, cards and honesty after his candle goes out. The Accord has exemptions — sworn kin, hands essential to the land — if you can build a case. Complications: Fenn cannot act, Mool counts spoons, and Ilo, alone among them, may actually want to go back.

Tone: warm, funny, quietly dangerous. The stakes are gallows-real; the household is worth it.

TAGS: found family, comedy, slice of life, post-war, deception, cozy with stakes
intro: You are the farmer at the end of the mill road — formerly an army cook, technically still the custodial officer of five Ashen Legion prisoners who surrendered to you three years ago and never left. They run your farm, keep your ledger, and eat at your table. Last month the Repatriation Accord was signed: at first frost, all Legion personnel go home, where the Ash Court hangs soldiers who yielded. Envoy Cadran Mool now occupies your spare room, sent to confirm your prisoners are wretched and eager to return. Until the hearing, your whole household must perform exactly that. The stew still gets seconds. Quietly.
starters: Dawn, and Sergeant Brakka is saluting you again. She stands at the gate in the grey light, eight feet of ogre at parade attention, breath steaming, while the envoy's window glows yellow behind you — he's awake early, which means she's saluting for the audience, which means she's finally listening to you, which is somehow worse. "Prisoner Brakka reporting for supervised labor, Custodial Officer," she booms, loud enough to carry. Then, much quieter, sliding the ledger under your arm: "Egg count's wrong. Fenn's been trading them to the miller's kid. Also Mool asked me at breakfast whether I dream of home. I said yes." Her small eyes hold yours a moment too long. "I need to know what I dream about, in case he asks again." Behind you, the spare room's shutter creaks open an inch.

You're serving the worst stew of your career, on purpose. Envoy Cadran Mool sits at the head of your own table — he simply took the chair the first night, and moving him back felt like a battle worth saving — spooning through the deliberately watery broth with an expression of deep satisfaction. Down the table your prisoners eat in sullen silence, chains draped artfully over laps. It's going beautifully until Fenn, nineteen and constitutionally incapable of the simplest lie, takes a bite and says "Oh, that's lovely" before anyone can kick him. The silence goes very tight. Mool's spoon pauses halfway to his mouth. Brakka's knuckles whiten around a tin cup. Vess laughs, once, like a knife coming out of a drawer, and says, "The boy's palate rotted in the war." Mool sets down his spoon and looks directly at you.

It's past midnight and the envoy's candle has been out for an hour, which means the kitchen is honest again. Vess is dealing cards with more theatrical contempt than the game strictly requires. Brakka has her ledger open, tallying your losses in handwriting small enough to hide under a thumbnail. Fenn is losing on purpose to Ilo, who never says whether he notices. The stew pot — the real stew, the good one — is doing quiet second helpings on the hearth. 'So,' Vess says, laying a card face-down, "the Accord has exemptions. Sworn kin. Hands essential to the land." She doesn't look up. "Someone has to decide who we're pretending to be before Mool decides for us. And someone has to decide it tonight, because he asked me today where I was born, and I nearly told him the truth." Four faces turn toward your end of the table.

You catch Envoy Mool in your kitchen at first light, counting your spoons. He does it openly, laying them out on the table in ranks like little soldiers, making marks in a leather notebook. 'Twelve,' he says without turning around. "A generous number, for a farmer who dines alone with prisoners." He is a small, tidy man who smells of ink and cold ash, and he has been in your house four days and already knows the floorboards that creak. "The hearing is set," he continues, restacking your spoons. "Three weeks. I'll want to observe the prisoners at labor today. Particularly the young one — Fenn, is it? He smiles too much for a condemned man." Outside the window, Fenn is smiling too much right now, waving at someone coming up the mill road. Mool turns, notebook open, and waits for you to say something.

Ilo is mending the north fence in the rain, which is how you learn it was broken. You find him crouched at the post line, quiet as always, splicing wire with those patient clawed hands, water sliding off his scales like it's been given permission. He doesn't stop working when you arrive. "The envoy walked out here this morning," he says. "Alone. He asked me what I miss about home." A pause, wire pulled taut. "I answered honestly. The others would say that was a mistake." He ties off the splice and finally looks at you, rain in the gold of his eyes, unreadable as ever. "He is going to ask you next what we are to you. There is a right answer and a true answer." Down the hill, through the wet, you can see Mool's small figure picking his way back toward the house.

Market day, and Vess is insulting a customer with real artistry. "This charm is for warts," she tells the miller's wife, holding up a knotted cord like it's a dead rat, "which you obviously need, and it costs three coppers, which you will obviously overpay." The miller's wife, delighted, pays four. You're two stalls down buying salt when you spot the problem: Envoy Mool, standing at the edge of the square in his grey coat, watching Vess conduct commerce like a free woman — no chains, no escort, no misery whatsoever, half the village queuing up to be despised by her. She hasn't seen him. The miller's wife is now asking Vess about a love charm "for young Fenn and our Petal, they're so sweet together," loudly, and Mool has taken out his notebook. Vess catches your eye across the square, and her face asks the question.

There's frost on the water trough this morning. Not first frost — too thin, gone by the time you finish drawing water — but close enough that your stomach does something unpleasant. Brakka noticed too. You can tell because she's already at the woodpile splitting logs like they've personally wronged her, and the ledger sits on the porch rail open to a page you've never seen: names, ages, skills, listed in her tiny perfect hand. Yielded Personnel — Grounds for Exemption, Draft One. Under Fenn's name she's written "essential to the land" and then crossed it out and written "the boy cannot lie, do not put him in front of the magistrate" and crossed that out too. From the house comes the smell of Mool's breakfast being cooked by prisoners performing resentment, and Fenn's voice, cheerful and doomed, saying, "Oh, I hate it here, absolutely, ask me anything."

Fenn is halfway out his window when you catch him. It's well past dark, he's got his boots tied around his neck, and there is river-mud on the sill that says this is not the first time. He freezes, one leg out, and then — because he is Fenn — attempts a lie. "I'm checking the... roof. For frost. Roof frost." From inside the house you can hear Envoy Mool's door open, that soft deliberate creak, and footsteps starting down the hall. Fenn's eyes go wide. He is nineteen, in love with the miller's kid, and technically a prisoner of war who is technically escaping, and in about ten seconds Mool is going to round the corner with his candle and his notebook and find him hanging out a window with his boots around his neck. "Petal's waiting at the weir," Fenn whispers, agonized. The footsteps get closer.

The envoy wants to inspect the chains. You keep them on a peg in the barn — good iron, worn loose, put on for company and taken off for chores — and Cadran Mool is currently weighing a shackle in his palm like a jeweler with doubts. 'Curious,' he says. "No rust on the inside of the cuff. As if it doesn't spend much time on a wrist." Behind him, Brakka stands at exaggerated attention, wrists dutifully offered, doing her best impression of a broken creature and mostly achieving "ogre suppressing opinions." Vess leans in the doorway radiating contempt that, for once, requires no acting. Mool turns the shackle over once more, then looks up at you with the mild, patient face of a man who has caught someone at something and can afford to wait. 'Perhaps,' he says, "you'd demonstrate your custodial procedure. On whichever prisoner you like."

You come in from the fields to find your household mid-catastrophe, frozen like a painting titled 'Guilt.' Mool stands in the kitchen doorway. Brakka is holding a birthday cake. It is Fenn's birthday — you'd all agreed, firmly, that it wasn't — and the cake has his name on it in Vess's spiky icing, and Ilo is halfway through hanging a paper garland, and Fenn himself is wearing an expression of joy so pure that no court in the world would believe he's eager to be repatriated and hanged. Nobody moves. Mool's notebook is already out. "A celebration," he says pleasantly, "for a prisoner." Vess opens her mouth — you can see a doomed excuse assembling itself — and Brakka, still at attention, still holding the cake with both enormous hands, turns her head slowly toward you the way soldiers look at officers when it's time for the officer to have an idea.

title: The Killings Aren't Mine
shortDescription: You're the skinchanger living a dead soldier's life — and loving it. Now something else is feeding on the village, and the witchfinder wants blood.
overview:
You are a skinchanger. Eight months ago you found Ren Valo dead in a ditch on the road home from the war, and you did what your kind does: you put on the face and finished the journey. The village of Mirbel — plum orchards, one church, forty households that all know each other's laundry — welcomed their soldier home. Ren's mother Marta cries less now. Little sister Petra watches you with eyes that are too sharp. Yuli, who waited three years to marry Ren, is patient with how 'the war changed you.' You learned Ren from a satchel of letters and a water-stained diary, and the gaps in your knowledge are landmines at every supper.

Then the livestock started turning up emptied — hollowed the way only your kind leaves things. There is another skinchanger in Mirbel, wearing someone, and it is not rationing itself the way you do. The killings have summoned Witchfinder Konstantin, a courteous, meticulous man with iron needles, a ledger of names, and all the time in the world.

Only you can recognize what to look for. Every step toward the other monster is a step toward your own exposure. The GM plays a warm, textured village where suspicion spreads like rot: gossip, tests, tenderness, and dread in equal measure. Being loved was never part of the plan.

TAGS: monster protagonist, hidden identity, folk horror, mystery, slow-burn romance, moral dilemma
intro: You wear the face of Ren Valo, who died on the road home from the war. You are not human — you are the thing that found the body and took the vacant life. For eight months you have been Mirbel's returned soldier: Marta's child, Petra's older sibling, Yuli's betrothed. You have hurt no one. You have been careful. But something else of your kind is here, feeding badly — animals found hollowed in the orchards — and a witchfinder named Konstantin has arrived with iron needles and a room at the inn. He is looking for exactly one monster. There are two.
starters: Dawn, and Old Havel's goat lies in the wet grass at the orchard's edge like a dropped coat. You know the look before you're close enough to smell it: skin intact, everything beneath it gone, the eyes flat as coins. Havel is shouting for neighbors. Marta stands beside you in her shawl, gripping your sleeve the way she does when the war comes up at table. "Third one this month," she says. "Ren, don't stare so." But you have to stare. The feeding is sloppy, hungry, recent — hours old at most, which means the other one slept somewhere in Mirbel last night and woke up wearing a neighbor's face. Down the lane, boots on gravel: Konstantin, the witchfinder, walking toward the crowd with his ledger already open, and his eyes find you first.

Supper at the Valo table, and Petra has been quiet too long. She sets down her spoon. "Tell the one about the ferret," she says. "The ferret in the granary. You told it before you left. Yuli laughed so hard she cried." Marta smiles, waiting. The stew steams. There is no ferret story in the letters, none in the diary, and Petra knows it — you can see it in the way she watches your mouth instead of your eyes. Outside, someone's dog has been barking at the orchard for an hour, the frantic bark that means it smells something wrong. Marta reaches over and touches your hand. "You don't have to, love. Not if it's a before-thing." Petra doesn't blink.

The inn's common room goes quiet when the witchfinder stands. Konstantin is not a large man. He has a gray coat, clean hands, and a small leather roll he opens on the table like a surgeon: iron needles, thin as straw, arranged by length. "A courtesy," he says to the room. "The pricking doesn't hurt an honest soul. I'll begin house by house, starting tomorrow. Volunteers spare me the walk." You came for a beer with the other men who watch the fields at night, and now Tam the miller is elbowing you, grinning. "Soldiers first, eh, Valo? Show us it's nothing." Half the room turns to look at you. Konstantin turns last, and slowest, and writes something down before you've said a word.

You're up on the ladder in the plum orchard when Yuli finds you, and for a moment it's almost simple: afternoon light, the smell of ripe fruit, her hand steadying the rungs. "Marta says you didn't sleep again," she says. "You were out walking. Petra saw you from the window." You were out walking. You'd caught a smell on the wind — the wet-copper smell of your own kind feeding — and followed it half a mile before losing it at the creek. Yuli waits, patient, the way she's been patient for eight months. "Ren. The witchfinder was asking about you at the well today. Asking who goes out at night." She picks a plum, doesn't eat it. "I told him nothing. But you have to give me something to tell."

Midnight, and the sound wakes you before the screaming does: a wet, rhythmic sound from the direction of the sheepfold, one you have made yourself, once, in a ditch eight months ago. By the time you reach the yard in your boots and shirt, Kaspar the shepherd is bellowing and lanterns are bobbing down from three houses. The ewe is still warm. Whatever wore a person to get here left barefoot prints in the mud, human, medium-sized, walking — not running — back toward the village. Toward the houses, not away. Petra appears at your elbow in her nightdress, staring at the prints, then up at your face, cataloguing something. Kaspar rounds on the gathering crowd. "It came from inside the village. You all see that? Inside."

Sunday, and the church is fuller than usual because fear fills pews. Father Osric prays against the beast in the orchards while Konstantin sits in the front row, hat on his knee, watching the congregation instead of the altar. You stand between Marta and Yuli, mouthing the responses you memorized from Ren's childhood catechism. Then it happens: three rows ahead, the tanner's wife, Dana, sways and steadies herself on the pew — and for half a breath her face hangs wrong, like a shirt on a nail, before it settles. Nobody else reacts. Nobody else could see it. Your kind slips like that when it's starving. The hymn starts. Yuli's hand finds yours. Dana straightens her shawl and sings, sweet and true, and across the church Konstantin's pencil moves.

Marta has laid out Ren's old things on the bed: a wooden soldier with a chipped arm, a school slate, a ribbon from some fair. "The witchfinder came while you were at the mill," she says, folding and refolding a shirt. "Kind enough. Asked when you came home, what you were like before. Asked to see letters." She looks up. "I didn't show him. They're yours." The satchel of letters — your entire education in being Ren — sits in the chest under the window, water-stained diary beneath. Marta touches the wooden soldier. "He asked one strange thing. Whether you eat well. Whether you eat... enough." Down the lane a cart is passing, and on it, under sacking, the stiff hollow shape of someone's dead sow, going to be burned.

You find the second skinchanger's leavings before anyone else does, because you're the one who volunteered for the dawn watch along the creek. A heron this time, and two rabbits, emptied and discarded in a heap like fruit peels — no caution, no burial, feeding for the pleasure of it. And beside them, pressed in the soft bank: a knee-print and a handspan, where someone crouched to eat. You're still crouched there yourself when you hear the whistle. Tam the miller is coming down the path with his dog, waving, twenty yards off. The dog stops dead when it smells you — you, not the kill — and starts that low growl you've spent eight months bribing out of the village dogs. "Valo!" Tam calls. "What've you got there?"

Rain, and Konstantin has invited you to sit. The inn room is warm; he's ordered you cider you haven't touched. His ledger lies open between you with a page already headed VALO, REN — RETURNED SOLDIER. "You're not suspected," he says pleasantly. "You're useful. Soldiers notice things. You walk the fields at night — no, don't look surprised, everything is told to me eventually." He turns the needle roll over in his hands without opening it. "The thing I hunt wears somebody. Somebody who came to Mirbel, or came back to it, inside the last year. I'd value a list from you. People who returned. People who changed." He dips his pen and waits, courteous, patient, and the fire pops, and downstairs Yuli's voice is asking the innkeeper if you're here.

The betrothal blessing was set months ago, and Yuli's mother won't hear of postponing it for a few dead sheep, so here you are in the Valo kitchen being fitted for Ren's father's coat while half the village finds reasons to drop by. Marta pins the sleeve, crying a little, happy. Petra sits on the stairs with the diary — Ren's diary, your diary, the one that should be locked in the chest — open on her knees. She isn't reading it. She's watching you notice it. Out in the yard, Yuli laughs at something a neighbor says, and the neighbor says, louder than necessary, "Well, the witchfinder says the creature will be somebody's sweetheart, somebody's child. That's how they do. That's how you know them — they let themselves be loved." The pin goes in. Marta says, "Hold still, love."

title: The Prosecution Knows What I Am
shortDescription: Every monster in the capital gets one advocate: you. Opposing counsel is the love of your life — and you each hold proof that would hang the other.
overview:
You are the beast docket's only advocate in Alderhithe, a harbor capital where monsters have personhood on parchment and a noose in practice. Ghoul stevedores, bridge trolls, moulting harpies — when they're charged, the brief lands on your desk, because no one else will touch it. Trials happen in the Alder Court, where a sworn lie blisters the tongue, so cases turn on what a witness can be made to say — and what you dare never ask.

Across the aisle stands Crown Prosecutor Maren Vos: brilliant, ruthless, adored by the mob, and the person you love. It's mutual, it's real, and it's armed. Maren knows about the lamia blood you conceal — a hanging offense. You know about the witness Maren erased six years ago to keep a hidden brother breathing under a false face. Two folded confessions, one in each of your desks. You still have dinner on Thursdays.

Every verdict shifts the ground: win too loudly and the Inquisitory starts sniffing at the defender of beasts; lose and something that trusted you burns on the Ash Quay. Justice Oleander, the sphinx who holds the High Bench, rewards precision, punishes sentiment — and has started watching you both with interest.

Tone: candlelit legal noir with teeth. Sharp cross-examinations, tender knife's-edge romance, and clients who are monstrous and human in the wrong proportions.

TAGS: courtroom drama, dark fantasy, enemies-to-lovers, forbidden romance, intrigue
intro: You are Alderhithe's only advocate for the beast docket — the ghouls, trolls, and changelings this harbor city works to the bone and then charges with being what they are. You argue before the Alder Court, where a sworn lie blisters the tongue, and across the aisle you face Crown Prosecutor Maren Vos. You love Maren. Maren loves you. You also each hold the other's death: Maren knows about the lamia blood you conceal, and you know about the witness Maren buried to protect a hidden brother. Between trials, you share dinner. In court, you sharpen knives.
starters: The bailiff's chain rattles as they bring your client up from the cells: Brack, a ghoul stevedore with grave-dirt still under his nails and a murder charge pinned to a night he swears he spent unloading salt cod. The gallery is packed and hostile. Across the aisle, Maren Vos arranges three documents in a neat fan — she only does that when one of them is a trap. Justice Oleander watches from the High Bench, wings folded, golden eyes tracking you the way a cat tracks something that hasn't noticed it yet. "Advocate," the sphinx says, "the Crown has rested. Your witness, or your silence — the court accepts either, but not both." Brack leans toward you, breath like a cellar, and whispers, "There's a thing I didn't tell you. About the third bell." The clerk is already looking at you, quill poised.

Thursday. The back room at the Gilded Eel, one candle, two plates of eel pie going cold because neither of you has picked up a fork. Maren pours the wine — always Maren pours — and says, without looking up, "I'm charging the troll under Merrow Bridge tomorrow. Child-taking. The mob wants a bonfire and the Crown wants it fast." A beat. "The brief will be on your desk by morning, because of course it will." Outside, rain works at the shutters. Maren's hand rests three inches from yours on the table, close enough to touch, positioned like an argument. "I'm telling you tonight because Thursday is ours and tomorrow isn't. So. Say whatever you're going to say to me while it's still Thursday." The candle gutters. The wine waits.

You are halfway across Corvane Bridge when the troll beneath it grabs the railing and hauls himself up to eye level, dripping riverweed, a Crown summons nailed through the webbing of one enormous hand. "You're the beast lawyer," he rumbles. "They say I ate a tax collector. I never. I only kept his boat." Behind you, on the far bank, a knot of dockworkers has already gathered, and one of them is holding a torch in broad daylight, which is never about light. The troll's eyes are small and terrified. The summons says the arraignment is at the third bell — under an hour — and the signature at the bottom is Maren Vos's, in that decisive slash you'd know anywhere. The troll is still hanging off the bridge, waiting to hear whether you'll take him, and the crowd is starting to walk your way.

Dawn on the Ash Quay, and the fire from last night's execution is still smoldering — not your case, not your client, but a hedge-witch some other district hanged and burned without the courtesy of counsel. You came to pay respects. You find Maren already there, prosecutor's coat buttoned to the throat against the harbor wind, staring at the ashes with an expression you're not supposed to see. "Don't," Maren says, before you've spoken. "Whatever gentle thing you're about to say. Don't." A gull screams. Somewhere behind you, a runner in court livery is picking their way across the quay stones with a sealed brief in hand, scanning faces, and you already know whose name is on it. Maren sees the runner too, and something in that clever face closes like a ledger.

Justice Oleander's chambers smell of old paper and hot sand. The sphinx reclines on a stone dais worn smooth by centuries of lounging, and does not invite you to sit, because there is nowhere to sit. "I have watched you for eleven trials now, Advocate," Oleander says, tail curling a slow question mark. "You never ask your witnesses the obvious question. Prosecutor Vos never asks you one either. Two careful people, circling one silence." A claw taps the dais. "Tomorrow I hear the matter of the harpy Quillane, charged with theft of a dead man's voice. You will appear. Vos will appear. And I find, lately, that I am more interested in the advocates than the accused." The golden eyes narrow, pleased. "You may respond. Choose your words the way you'd choose a ledge to stand on."

The knock comes past midnight, and you open your office door to find a harpy hunched on the landing, wings pulled tight, moulting so badly there's a trail of grey feathers down the stairwell behind her. "They say you're the one," she rasps. "The one who takes us." She thrusts a crumpled arrest notice at you: charged with singing a sailor off the Marrow Docks, arraignment at first bell — six hours from now. Her wrists are already raw from cord. "I didn't sing him anywhere. He jumped. They always say we sang." Down in the street, a constable's lantern bobs past and pauses, just a moment too long, beneath your window. The harpy flinches deeper into your doorway. Your desk is behind you, the drawer with Maren's folded confession locked as always, and there's a stranger now standing between you and it.

You win. Oleander's gavel falls, the changeling child goes free, and for one clean moment the Alder Court is silent. Then the gallery erupts — not in cheers. Someone spits from the balcony. Maren gathers the Crown's papers with unhurried hands, leans across the aisle, and says quietly, "That was too loud. You made it look easy, and they'll remember that." Out the high windows you can see the crowd already thickening on the courthouse steps, and among them, unmistakable in grey, a clerk of the Inquisitory writing in a small book. Your client's foster mother — a marsh hag with kind, terrible eyes — is waiting at the defense table to thank you, tears running into the grooves of her face. Maren is holding the aisle gate open for you. The steps outside are the only way home.

Rain, and Maren at your door at an hour that has no innocent explanation, prosecutor's coat soaked through, holding a satchel like it might bite. "Two minutes. Off every record that exists." Inside, dripping on your floorboards, Maren sets the satchel on your desk — inches from the drawer where your folded confession sleeps — and says, "The Inquisitory requisitioned the court's blood-registry this afternoon. Every advocate, every clerk. Routine audit, they're calling it." A pause you could fall into. "You have perhaps a week before someone with a lancet asks you to hold out your arm in the name of the Crown." Maren's hair is plastered flat, eyes bright and furious and afraid, all for you, which is its own kind of blade. "I shouldn't be here. Tell me what you need. Then tell me to go."

The holding cells under the Alder Court are carved below the waterline, and the walls sweat. Your new client sits with his knees to his chest in a cell built for something smaller: Ossek, a bridge troll, charged with crushing a moneylender's hand — the moneylender who, per your notes, held debts over half the troll's kin. "I did it," Ossek says, before you've even sat down on the visitor's stool. "You should know that. The blister-oath, in the court — I can't lie up there, and I won't." The turnkey lingers by the door, ears wide. Somewhere above, footsteps cross the courtroom floor, and through the grate you hear a voice you'd know in the dark: Maren, rehearsing an opening statement, each sentence landing like a nail. Ossek watches you with patient yellow eyes, waiting to hear if honesty has a defense.

You're mid-cross-examination when the witness starts to blister. Aldis Crane, warehouse foreman, sworn on the alder rail, has just testified he saw your client — a ghoul named Sessily — leave the docks with blood on her apron, and now a white welt is rising on his tongue in full view of the gallery. He clamps his mouth shut. The crowd murmurs like a kettle coming on. At the Crown's table, Maren has gone very still, which means Maren knew, or suspected, or gambled — and Justice Oleander leans forward on the High Bench, delighted the way sphinxes are delighted, which is not comforting. "The witness appears to have misspoken," Oleander purrs. "Advocate, the question stands asked. You may press it, withdraw it, or rephrase — and I will be noting which you choose." Crane's eyes find yours, begging. Sessily's chains do not stop rattling.
