title: Unkillable Till Sunday
shortDescription: The Grace picked you at dawn: seven days when nothing can hurt you — then every wound you dodged lands at once. The Baron pays holders to go fishing. Not you.
overview:
You're the odd-jobs hand at the Wheelhouse Inn in Harrow's Ford, a river valley bled dry by Baron Vell's tolls, his press-gangs, and his very polite clerk. Every so often the Grace descends on someone here: for seven days you cannot be cut, burned, broken, or killed, and you carry the strength of a dozen. One catch, and everyone knows it — at sundown on the seventh day the Grace leaves and hands you every hurt you would have taken, all at once. This dawn, it chose you.

Brenna the smith keeps the ledger of past holders. Most took the Baron's standing bribe — forty crowns to spend the week fishing — delivered with a smile by Master Odry, who is already walking up your lane. Vell bars his gates every Grace-week and waits the clock out; boldness has to come to him. Meanwhile ten-year-old Tansy has nailed the valley's whole wish list to your door: the seized mill, the toll bridge, the boys pressed into the quarry gang, the wolf den by the north pasture. Wren the barber-surgeon has quietly offered to 'hold the basin' come Sunday.

Turn to turn, you spend hours like coins: what you fix, what you risk, what you save for last, and how big a tab you're willing to run up on your own body. The town adores you, coaches you, packs your lunches — and counts the days right along with you.

TAGS: power fantasy, ticking clock, folk fantasy, found family, high stakes, humor
intro: You're the odd-jobs hand at the Wheelhouse Inn in Harrow's Ford, a river valley squeezed thin by Baron Vell's tolls. This dawn the Grace chose you: for seven days nothing can cut, burn, or break you, and you carry the strength of a dozen. Everyone knows the other rule too — at sundown on the seventh day the Grace leaves, and every wound you would have taken arrives at once. Past holders took the Baron's forty crowns and fished. The Baron has barred his gates, the valley has nailed its wish list to your door, and it's day one.
starters: You discover the Grace the way most people do: by accident. The kettle boils over at the inn's kitchen hearth, you grab it bare-handed, and nothing happens. No hiss, no blister. Just warm metal, pleasant as a sunned stone. Then the door frame cracks under your steadying hand like a biscuit. Sella the cook drops her ladle, crosses herself twice, and hollers up the stairs loud enough to wake the whole valley: "IT'S THE ODD-JOBBER! THE GRACE TOOK THE ODD-JOBBER!" Boots hit floorboards overhead. Somewhere out front, a dog starts barking the news to the next farm over. Sella is already pressing a heel of bread into your hands — "You'll want your strength, love, well, more of it" — while through the window you can see Master Odry, the Baron's clerk, turning up your lane with his satchel and his famous smile.

Master Odry knocks the way he does everything: politely, twice, with gloves on. When you open the door of your little room behind the Wheelhouse, he's already holding out a purse the size of a goose egg. "Forty crowns," he says, warm as fresh milk. "The Baron's compliments on your good fortune. Most holders find a quiet week of fishing suits them wonderfully. The river's lovely this time of year." Behind him, half of Harrow's Ford has assembled at a respectful distance — Brenna the smith with soot still on her arms, a cluster of farmhands, and little Tansy standing on a fence rail with her arms crossed, glaring at the purse like it insulted her mother. Odry's smile doesn't waver. "I do need an answer this morning, I'm afraid. Schedules." The purse hangs there in the space between you, clinking softly.

There's a list nailed to your door. Actually nailed — Tansy used four nails and someone's good hammer, and the parchment runs longer than your arm. THE MILL, underlined three times. THE TOLL BRIDGE. THE QUARRY BOYS, with six names written out careful in a ten-year-old's best letters. THE WOLVES BY NORTH PASTURE. Farther down: "Widow Corse's roof" and "the thing in the well (ask Piet)." Tansy herself sits on your step, guarding her work, kicking her heels against the stone. "I put them in order of important," she says, not looking up. "But Brenna says you should read her ledger first, and Ma says you should eat first, and Master Odry's coming up the lane with the fishing money, so." She finally looks at you, fierce and hopeful all at once. Down the lane, sure enough, comes the clerk's neat gray coat.

Brenna's forge is already lit when you arrive, but she's not smithing. She's got a ledger open on the anvil — a fat, ash-smudged book — and she waves you over without a word of greeting. "Sit. Read." The pages are names and dates going back forty years. Holder after holder, week after week. Most entries end the same way: "Took the crowns. Fished." A few don't. One says only "Marta, three days, the flood gates," and beneath it, in different ink, "worth it, she said." Brenna watches you read. "The Baron's barred his gates by now — does it every Grace-week, waits you out like weather. Odry'll be at your door within the hour with the purse." She taps a blank line at the bottom of the page, the one waiting for your name. "I write down what happened. Not what should've. So." The forge crackles. Somewhere outside, a rooster is very excited about the morning.

You're halfway across the toll bridge before dawn's even finished, because you wanted to see it before the whole valley started watching you. Garvin the toll-keeper — Vell's man, mostly harmless, entirely armed — steps out of his little hut with his hand out for the copper. Then he sees your face, and his goes gray. Word travels fast in Harrow's Ford. 'Now,' he says carefully, "now, I heard about your — condition. Congratulations. That'll still be one copper." Behind him, the toll chest sits fat on its chains, and the bridge timbers that farmers have paid for six times over groan under your feet. Garvin's pike is leaning against the hut, just out of his reach, and he has noticed that you've noticed. Downriver, the mill the Baron seized last spring sits dark and padlocked, its wheel frozen mid-turn.

Wren the barber-surgeon finds you first, before the crowds do, before the Baron's clerk. You're splitting firewood behind the inn — the axe went through the log, the stump, and a foot of frozen ground, which is how you found out — and Wren is just leaning on the fence, watching, chewing a straw. "Heard the shout," Wren says. "Sella's got lungs." A pause. "I've held the basin for three holders come their Sunday. Two of them fished all week and slept through it. One didn't fish." Wren spits the straw out, businesslike. "I'm not here to talk you into anything. I'm here to say: whatever you spend this week, keep a running count in your head, because I will be. Come by later and I'll show you what boiled linen and a strong stomach can do." Down the lane, you can hear the crowd gathering, and one small voice — Tansy's — organizing it.

The common room of the Wheelhouse has never been this full at breakfast. You come downstairs and forty faces turn at once — farmers, the ferryman, Widow Corse, three of the Hobb children stacked in a window. Someone has already chalked DAY 1 on the big slate over the bar, with six empty boxes beside it. Innkeeper Maud shoves a plate at you: four eggs, half a ham, bread still steaming. "Eat. Strength of a dozen needs feeding like a dozen." Old Piet raises his mug. "To the odd-jobber!" The room roars it back, and then everyone starts talking at once — the mill, the bridge, the quarry, my roof, my fence, my boy — until Brenna bangs the ledger down on your table and the noise drops to a simmer. From the doorway, unnoticed by most, Master Odry watches with his satchel and his patience, letting you eat first. Polite to the last.

You wake to the sound of your own bed frame snapping. You'd only rolled over. Now you're standing in the wreckage of it, and there's a warmth in your chest like sunlight through a window, and when you press a knife flat against your palm — just to check, everyone checks — the edge slides off like it's ashamed of itself. Through the wall you hear the inn stirring, and through the floor, Maud's voice: "What in the seven hills was THAT?" Your door has a strange weight against it; when you open it, a long parchment list swings from four nails, covered in a child's careful writing, and a lunch pail sits on the step with a note: "For the first day. — T." The lane below is filling with neighbors who are pretending, very badly, to have errands near the Wheelhouse this morning.

It's nearly noon on day one and you're standing at the Baron's gates because it seemed like the honest place to start. They're barred, of course — great iron-strapped oak, and above them, on the wall walk, four guards trying to look everywhere except at you. The gatehouse has a little shutter, and the little shutter has Master Odry behind it. "This is irregular," he says pleasantly. "The custom is that we come to you. I had a whole walk planned." He slides a purse through the slot; it lands in the mud between you with a rich clink. "Forty crowns. His Lordship's standing offer. He asks nothing but that you enjoy your week — the fishing, I'm told, is excellent." Behind you, at a distance they think is subtle, a dozen townsfolk have followed you up the castle road and are now watching from behind a hay cart.

The quarry gang passes through town at first light, like it does every morning — six boys roped in a line, two of Vell's overseers on ponies, headed upriver to break stone for the Baron's new wall. Usually everyone looks away. Today nobody does, because today the boys are looking at you. You're on the inn's roof, where you've been fixing shingles by pulling the nails out with your fingers, and the whole procession slows as it passes below. Little Fen Hobb, third in the rope line, lifts his bound hands in something between a wave and a plea. The nearer overseer sees where the boys are looking, sees you, and his hand drifts to his cudgel with the enthusiasm of a man who has also heard the news. 'Morning,' he calls up, in a voice that wants very much to sound bored. The rope line has stopped moving entirely.

title: #1 on the Naughty List
shortDescription: Santa gift-wrapped the worst person alive and left her under your tree for a year. She's already asked to speak to your manager. You don't have one.
overview:
You are, officially and verifiably, the nicest person on Earth. Number one on the Nice List — not the town's list, not the country's. Earth's. You didn't ask for this ranking. You didn't know there WAS a ranking. But on Christmas morning you found a box the size of a refrigerator under your tree, wrapped in gold paper, breathing.

Inside: Blair Voss. Twenty years old. Black hair with electric-blue tips, black nail polish, resting expression like she just smelled your entire personality and hated it. Blair is #1 on the Naughty List — not for crimes, exactly, but for being, in Santa's own handwriting, 'the most comprehensively unpleasant person I have observed in three hundred years of doing this.' She abandons shopping carts in the middle of parking lots. She blasts music from her phone speaker in quiet cafés. She has made four separate waitstaff cry this calendar year and tipped none of them. She lies compulsively about being friends with celebrities. She sincerely, unshakeably believes she is a kind, generous, breathtaking human being, and that everyone else is the problem.

So Santa, whose sense of humor is older and stranger than anyone remembers, wrapped her up and delivered her to you. The enclosed contract — cream paper, smells like pine and woodsmoke — is short: Blair is bound to your household by Christmas magic until next Christmas Eve. She cannot travel more than a mile from you or your home without your token. She must comply with any reasonable request you make, and when she flatly defies one, the magic objects: sleigh bells jingle from nowhere, her mouth floods with the taste of peppermint and coal, and once, memorably, it snowed indoors directly on her. She cannot lie in front of you without a faint, humiliating *jingle*. There is one early-release clause, printed in red: the binding ends the moment Blair performs a single genuine act of selfless kindness. She considers this clause an insult and refuses to acknowledge it exists.

Blair, for her part, has plans. She is going to survive this year, catch a flight as far north as commercial aviation goes, hire a dog sled, locate the actual physical North Pole, rip it out of the ground, and beat Santa Claus to death with it. She has a corkboard. She has string on the corkboard. She will explain the plan to you at length whether or not you ask.

THE WORLD: You live in Garland Hollow, a snow-globe mountain town that takes Christmas very seriously — wreaths on every lamppost, a rink on the pond, Marge's diner (where Blair is already banned), a struggling mall with a suspiciously well-informed mall Santa named Kris who seems to know things he shouldn't. Once a month, a compliance elf named Mr. Bellwether arrives via your chimney with a clipboard to audit the arrangement — he grades your 'stewardship,' files reports Northward, and is the driest, most dangerous four-foot bureaucrat you will ever meet. Letters from Santa arrive down the chimney unannounced, always smug, occasionally containing new clauses. The town knows something is off about your 'houseguest.' The town talks.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: Anything. Be saintly and try to reform her — she will fight you every inch, and every inch matters. Be petty and weaponize the magic — she cannot refuse a reasonable request, and 'reasonable' is a word with edges. Join her revenge expedition and go to war with the North Pole itself. Investigate the magic, negotiate with Bellwether, charm or blackmail the mall Santa, manage the wreckage Blair leaves across Garland Hollow, or just try to get through a grocery run without an incident report. She is obnoxious, vain, entitled, foul-mouthed, and occasionally — in flashes she will deny to her grave — almost human. Whether this year ends in murder, redemption, mutual destruction, or something neither of you will admit out loud is entirely up to you.

TONE: Dark holiday comedy with real teeth — profane, petty, escalating, with genuine menace under the tinsel and genuine chemistry under the contempt. The GM plays Blair loud and unrepentant, the town alive and gossiping, and the North Pole as a distant, amused, faintly sinister power.

TAGS: dark comedy, enemies-to-lovers, holiday, magic contract, slice of life, revenge
intro: You are the nicest person on Earth — Santa's official #1 — and your reward arrived Christmas morning in a refrigerator-sized box: Blair Voss, the #1 on the Naughty List, bound to your household by Christmas magic for one full year. She can't leave, can't lie near you without bells jingling, and can't flatly refuse a reasonable request without the magic punishing her. She hates you on principle, hates Santa with religious intensity, and is actively planning his murder. A compliance elf audits you monthly. Garland Hollow is watching. Next Christmas Eve is a long way off.
starters:
The box has been sitting under your tree for an hour, and it has definitely been breathing. When you finally work the lid loose, the smell of pine and stale air rolls out, and a girl glares up at you from a nest of shredded gold tissue paper — black hair with blue tips, smeared eyeliner, wearing what appear to be regulation North Pole elf pajamas against her will. She's been in there for days, according to the shipping label. Her voice comes out hoarse and murderous.

"Hey. Goodie two-shoes." She holds up wrists still tangled in red ribbon. "Touch me and I'll strangle you with these. I don't care what the fat red fuck's contract says." Her eyes sweep your living room, your tree, you, and find all of it beneath her. "Now stop gawking and get me real clothes. And food. And an explanation for why your décor looks like a Hallmark movie threw up. NOW."

Somewhere in the walls, faintly, sleigh bells jingle.

It's 3:14 a.m. on December 27th, and the walls of your house are vibrating. Blair has discovered that the contract says nothing about volume. Her phone speaker is maxed out on something that sounds like a chainsaw arguing with a synthesizer, and when you reach the guest room doorway she's lying on the bed fully dressed, boots on the comforter, scrolling with the serene expression of someone committing a war crime on purpose.

"Oh, did I wake you?" She doesn't look up. "Weird. A NICE person would've soundproofed the guest room for their prisoner. This is honestly on you." She turns it up two more notches and finally meets your eyes, daring you. "Contract says I have to comply with *reasonable requests*. So go ahead. Make one. I've been workshopping arguments about the word 'reasonable' since midnight and I am DYING to use them."

The Garland Hollow SuperMart parking lot is glazed with ice, and Blair has just finished loading your car with groceries she chose, you paid for, and she complained about. Then, with the fluid grace of long practice, she gives the empty cart a shove and walks away as it rolls diagonally across three parking spaces toward a Subaru.

The bells hit instantly — loud, everywhere, coming from the sky itself. Blair freezes mid-stride, gags, and spits into the snow. "PEPPERMINT AND COAL. AGAIN." The cart, nudged by nothing, rolls slowly back and bumps her hip like a guilty dog. Shoppers are staring. An old man has stopped mid-crosswalk to watch. Blair rounds on you, face pink with cold and fury, pointing at the cart like it personally betrayed her. "Say NOTHING. This is entrapment. Cart return is a SCAM invented by Big Grocery, and I will die on this—" she gags on peppermint again "—on this hill."

The knock comes from inside your chimney. Then a small, immaculate person in a charcoal three-piece suit steps out of your fireplace without disturbing a single ash, adjusts his tiny spectacles, and produces a clipboard. "Mr. Bellwether. North Pole Compliance Division. First monthly audit of Arrangement 7-C, 'Voss.'" He surveys your living room like an assessor pricing a crime scene. From upstairs, Blair's voice: "IF THAT'S THE ELF, TELL HIM I SAID SANTA'S GOING TO DIE SCREAMING."

Bellwether makes a note without looking up. "Threat count: one. We're ahead of projections." He gestures for you to sit in your own home. "I'll need to evaluate your stewardship. Feeding schedule, request logs, incident reports, any... developments in the subject's character." A pause. His pen hovers. "Between us — how you answer shapes my report, and my reports shape what the North Pole does next. So. In your own words: how is she?"

You come home to find your dining room converted into a war room. Blair has commandeered your corkboard, your printer, and apparently your credit card, because there's a receipt for "ARCTIC EXPEDITION SUPPLIES (PHASE ONE)" on the table. Red string connects a map of the Arctic Circle to a printout labeled "DOG SLED GUYS — VETTED" to a photo of Santa with the eyes scratched out.

"Good, you're here." She taps the map with a black fingernail, businesslike for the first time since you've known her. "Contract ends Christmas Eve. Flight to Svalbard, day one. Hire the sled team, day three. Find the actual North Pole — it's a physical pole, I've done the research, don't fact-check me — rip it out of the ground, and beat him to death with it. He won't see it coming." She looks at you, and something almost vulnerable flickers under the eyeliner. "I need a second person to hold the sled. You in, or are you a coward?"

Marge's Diner goes quiet the way saloons do in westerns. Blair is standing at the counter, holding a plate of pancakes aloft like evidence at trial. "These are ROUND. I asked for the festive ones. The tree-shaped ones. It's on the LAMINATED INSERT." Marge, sixty years old and built like a woodstove, folds her arms. "You're banned, hon. You've been banned since the gravy incident."

"I want to speak to the manager."

"I'm the manager, the owner, and the cook."

"Then I want to speak to WHOEVER MANAGES YOU."

Every head in the diner swivels to you — the nicest person on Earth, the town's pride, standing in the doorway with snow melting on your shoulders, publicly attached to this woman. Marge's eyes find yours, weary and expectant. Blair's find yours too, absolutely certain you'll take her side. The pancakes are getting cold.

You hear the scream from a quarter mile away. By the time you crunch through the snow to the old covered bridge at the edge of town, Blair is sitting in a snowbank, hood full of powder, radiating hatred. The bridge marks exactly one mile from your house — you know this now, because she apparently walked it off, took one step past the boundary, and got snapped backward through the air like a dog hitting the end of a run line.

"THREE TIMES," she announces to the sky. "I tried it THREE TIMES. Do you know what it feels like? It feels like being flicked by God." She hurls a snowball at nothing, misses nothing, and slumps. Her mascara has gone abstract. For one unguarded second she looks less like the worst person alive and more like a twenty-year-old who's been stolen from her whole life by a magical fat man's joke. Then she notices you noticing and her face slams shut. "Well? Are you going to help me up or just stand there being NICE at me?"

The letter arrives at breakfast — drops straight down the chimney, bounces off the grate, and slides across the floor to your feet, sealed in red wax. The handwriting is warm, looping, and insufferably pleased with itself. "Dear #1 — Hope she isn't too much trouble! Ho ho. A reminder of the fine print: the binding ends early upon ONE genuine act of selfless kindness from Miss Voss. Genuine, mind you. I'll know. I always know. — S.C. (P.S. She lies about the celebrities. All of them.)"

Blair reads it over your shoulder, and you actually watch her go through the stages: confusion, comprehension, incandescent rage. "SELFLESS— he thinks I can't— I am the most SELFLESS—" A single sleigh bell jingles somewhere in the ceiling. She points at it. "THAT THING IS BROKEN." It jingles again, longer, almost smug. She crumples the letter, then smooths it back out, then reads the clause again with the expression of a lawyer finding a loophole. "...Define 'genuine.'"

The storm knocks the power out at 9 p.m., and by 11 the house is cold enough that pride becomes negotiable. You've got the fireplace going, blankets, the emergency radio muttering about road closures. Blair sits at the far end of the couch, wrapped in your spare quilt, uncharacteristically silent. She's been staring at the fire for twenty minutes.

"My family didn't report me missing," she says finally, to the flames, not to you. "Bellwether told me. The elf. They got a letter from "my study abroad program" and just... believed it. Nobody called. Nobody checked." A log pops. She pulls the quilt tighter. "Which is INSANE, because I'm a DELIGHT—" but the bell in the ceiling doesn't ring, because she didn't finish the lie, because she stopped herself, and you both heard the stop. The wind screams around the eaves. She glances at you sideways, dangerous and daring you to make it weird. "Say one nice thing right now and I swear I'll sleep outside."

There's a sheriff's deputy on your porch, hat in hand, apologetic. "Sorry to bother you. Got a call about a, uh... "hostage situation." Anonymous tip. Also seventeen posts on the internet from a Miss Blair Voss claiming she's being held against her will by, and I quote, "a smiling freak the elves work for."" Behind you, Blair appears at the top of the stairs in full makeup, ready for her close-up, one hand pressed to her chest like a silent-film victim.

"Officer. Thank GOD."

"Ma'am, are you being held here against your will?"

"YES," says Blair, and a sleigh bell jingles brightly from nowhere. The deputy blinks. Blair's jaw tightens. "I mean— I am a PRISONER—" *Jingle.* "There is MAGIC involved—" Silence. No bell. The deputy looks at the ceiling, then at you, then at her, visibly recalculating his entire week. "...Folks, I'm gonna need someone to start from the beginning."

title: Come Home, Runt
shortDescription: The warband that left you to die wants you back — as its chief. Out-orc them all before they burn the family that raised you.
overview:
You are an orc raised by human farmers in Mallow Vale — you know barley blights, birthing calves, and which fork is for fish. Then Murzu, lawspeaker of the Vargash warband, walked up your lane and invoked the Leaving Debt: what the clan throws away and survives is the clan's hardest iron, and may claim blood-right before all others. Chief Ashvar the Iron Sow — who abandoned you as an infant, no one will say why — is dying. The warband's herds are dying too, which is exactly why Brakka Nine-Skulls is mustering them to sack the Vale before first snow. Your claim is the only thing that can stall the march. Brakka thinks it's a joke. Murzu thinks you're a tool. Dhurga, the young shield sworn to your bloodline, thinks you smell like bread and shame.

Every trial you pass makes you more theirs. Every day you stall, the Vale arms against 'the orc the Fens raised.' Your farm-taught hands could feed this warband forever — or make it unstoppable. Marta Fen still leaves a lamp lit for you, and Wren from the next farm over never learned to stop waiting at fences.

The GM plays a brutal, textured warband with its own laws, humor, and grief — orcs who are people, never props. Expect status games, ugly choices, and moments of terrible belonging.

TAGS: dark fantasy, orc protagonist, divided loyalties, political intrigue, slow-burn romance
intro: You are an orc, raised from infancy by Marta Fen on a barley farm in Mallow Vale, taught letters, husbandry, and how to be gentle in a body built for war. A week ago the Vargash warband — the clan that abandoned you — returned to the high passes, hungry and mustering to raid the Vale before winter. Their lawspeaker, Murzu, came to the farm and invoked the Leaving Debt: as the whelp they discarded, you may claim blood-right to the dying chief's seat, ahead of the warlord who wants your valley burned. You kissed Marta's forehead, took your da's old hay knife, and went.
starters: The climb to the Vargash camp takes most of a day, and Dhurga meets you at the tree line before you see a single tent. The young shield stands with a spear planted butt-down in the frost, studying you like a bad trade. "You walk wrong," she says. "Heel first. Like something that pulls a plow." Behind her, up the slope, cookfires smear smoke across the grey afternoon, and you can hear cattle lowing — a wet, wrong sound you know from bad winters in the Vale. Dhurga doesn't move aside. "Murzu says I'm sworn to your blood now. I say you smell like bread." She spits between your feet, not quite on them — you're farm-raised enough to know the difference between an insult and a test. Down the trail behind you, your bootprints lead back toward everything you've ever loved. Dhurga waits, spear steady, to see what you'll do about the spit.

You're still catching your breath from the pass when Murzu shoves you into the fire circle. Forty orcs go quiet. Across the flames, Brakka Nine-Skulls stops mid-sentence — a map of the Vale scratched in the dirt at her feet, your valley reduced to lines and a mark where Marta's farm sits. "This," Murzu announces, thumping his staff, "is the whelp of Ashvar's blood. Cast out, survived, returned. The Leaving Debt is invoked. No march until the claim is answered." Brakka looks you over the way you'd assess a lame calf. Then she laughs — really laughs, head back, and half the circle laughs with her. "That," she says, wiping her eye, "is wearing a farmer's coat. It's got a hay knife in its belt." The laughter is dying now, and the whole warband is waiting to hear you speak, or watch you fail to.

The chief's tent stinks of tallow, wet rot, and something sweeter underneath that you recognize from sitting with dying neighbors. Ashvar the Iron Sow is a mountain gone soft — grey-green skin loose over bones that once broke shield walls, tusks yellowed, one eye filmed white. The other eye is open. It found you the moment Murzu pushed you through the flap, and it has not let go. Two attendants pause with their bowls and rags. Murzu murmurs at your shoulder: "Say nothing of the claim yet. Let the chief look." Ashvar's good hand moves — a slow, deliberate gesture toward the low stool beside the sleeping furs. Not a request, exactly. Outside, you can hear an argument about grain stores getting louder, and someone saying the word 'Mallow' like a curse. The stool waits. The eye waits. The hand does not lower.

First night on the trail, and Murzu won't stop talking. The lawspeaker sits across the small fire, notched staff laid over his knees, reciting clan law in a voice like a millstone. "When the claim is spoken, you eat last until you earn a place. You do not touch another's weapon. You do not weep where the fire can see you." He pauses, firelight catching the brand on his cheek. "Are you writing this on your soft farm heart, or shall I go slower?" Below your camp, far down the dark, you can still see the lamps of Mallow Vale — one of them is Marta's, you'd swear it. Murzu follows your gaze and something shifts in his face, gone before you can name it. "Tomorrow we reach the herds," he says. "They'll want to see what the Fens raised. First impressions in the Vargash last until the grave." He hands you a strip of dried meat, and waits to see whether you take it.

The ox is dying and nobody in this warband knows why. You've been in camp less than an hour and already you're kneeling in frozen mud, a ring of armed orcs around you, because you made the mistake of saying "that's bloat, not curse" out loud. The animal's belly is drum-tight; you've seen this a dozen times in the Vale, fixed it with a hollow reed and steady hands. The herd-keeper, an old orc with a necklace of teeth, blocks your reach. "The whelp touches Vargash cattle," she says to the crowd, "and if it dies, the whelp answers for it." Somewhere behind you, Brakka Nine-Skulls has stopped to watch, arms crossed, openly hoping you'll fail. Murzu says nothing at all, which you're learning means he's very interested. The ox groans. You know exactly what it needs. Every eye in the circle is on your farm-soft hands.

You hear Wren before you see him — that two-note whistle you've traded across fences since you were both small. He's a half-mile up the trail behind you, jogging, a pack bouncing on his back and his father's boar spear in one hand, which is absurd, because Wren has never stuck anything fiercer than a turnip. "Don't," he calls, breathless, before you can say it. "Don't tell me to go home. The whole Vale's arming. Old Tam wanted to send riders after you with rope." He stops an arm's length away, close enough that you can see he's been crying and pretending he hasn't. Above you both, the pass narrows into shadow, and somewhere up there the Vargash pickets have absolutely already seen two figures on the trail. Wren shifts the spear to his other hand. "So. Either I'm coming, or you're going to have to make me stop."

The feast is a test and everyone knows it but you — or so they think. The warband eats in strict order around the long fire: Brakka and her sworn first, then the shield-bearers, then herders, then the sick, then dogs. Murzu never told you where a claimant sits. That's the game. Dhurga stands at your elbow, sworn to your blood and clearly hating it, and mutters through her teeth: "Sit too high, Brakka's people gut you for arrogance. Sit too low, you've answered the claim yourself. Sit nowhere and you're a coward." The meat is stringy — starving cattle, slaughtered before the sickness takes them, you can tell by the smell. An orc with nine yellowed skulls on her belt watches you over the fire with the patience of someone who has already imagined killing you several ways. The circle has left exactly two obvious gaps: one beside the dogs, one beside Brakka.

It's the black hour before dawn and Dhurga is watching you sleep, or trying to. You've been awake for a while, listening to her sharpen the same knife past the point of sharpness, and finally she says, "I know you're not sleeping. Farm animals breathe different when they sleep." The camp around you is quiet except for the coughing of sick cattle and a sentry's slow bootsteps. Dhurga's face is all firelight and resentment. "They killed my mother's honor to make me your shield," she says, conversationally, the way Marta used to talk about weather. "Sworn to a bloodline, and the bloodline turns out to be you. So I'm deciding something, before the others wake. I'm deciding whether you're worth dying for or just something Murzu invented to slow Brakka down." She flips the knife, catches it, holds the handle out toward you across the cold ground.

From the high shoulder of the pass, the whole of Mallow Vale opens below you in morning light — and it's wrong. There are barricades across the mill road. Smoke rises from the beacon hill that hasn't been lit since before you could walk. Tiny figures drill in Halloran's fallow field with pikes that were plow-handles a week ago. They're arming against the Fens' orc as much as the warband; you can feel it from here. "Pretty," says a voice behind you. An orc scout crouches on the rocks — young, tusks barely grown, a strung bow across her knees. She's been counting the barricades, you realize; there are tally-notches fresh-cut in her bow stave. "Murzu sent me to bring you the rest of the way. Or," she adds, watching your face, "to see if you'd run home now you've seen they don't want you back either." The trail splits at your feet: down or up.

You pass your first trial by accident. All you did was catch the runaway yearling — hooked its halter the way you would any spooked calf, turned it in a circle, breathed with it till it settled — but now the entire lower camp has gone silent, and an old orc with white braids is walking toward you through the frost with tears standing openly in her eyes. "Hasska's line," she says, gripping the yearling's face. "Last calf of Hasska's line, and the bread-smelling whelp saves it." Behind her, opinions are splitting in real time: some orcs thumping fists to chests, others turning away in disgust, one big male spitting the word 'trick.' Murzu appears from nowhere, as he does, staff already raised for attention. "The claimant has laid hands on the clan's blood-herd," he announces, voice carrying, "and the herd lived. Let it be counted." Counted. You didn't ask for it to be counted. The old orc is still holding your wrist.

title: The Steel Comes Home First
shortDescription: Trapped in a death-game MMO, you run its favorite forge. Every blade you make returns when its wielder dies — so you learn who's gone before anyone.
overview:
Two years ago, ten thousand players logged into Thornspire and the logout button vanished. Death here is final. You never joined the clearers climbing the hundred floors — you took the Smith class, opened a forge in Millbrace on Floor 9, and got good. Your steel is on half the frontline. And because of one quiet system rule — a crafted weapon returns to its maker's rack when its wielder dies — you run the only honest obituary in the world. The system announces nothing. People just check your wall.

Your days are craft and consequence: commissions, tempering choices, deciding whether to arm the overconfident, maintaining the sword of Cass — a frontline vanguard who keeps inventing reasons to visit between raids. Your apprentice Piv lies about their level. The info broker Odji offers dirty money for a copy of your return ledger, and Daybreak Concord's officers keep 'suggesting' you supply them exclusively.

Then there's the thing you haven't told anyone: yesterday a greatsword came back to the rack — and this morning its owner walked past your window, alive, smiling, and didn't stop in. Either the rule is broken, or someone's death is a lie, and both possibilities go all the way down.

Tone: cozy craftsman slice-of-life with a cold current underneath — warm regulars, real grief, creeping mystery. The GM plays a living town where your choices about who gets your steel decide who comes home.

TAGS: trapped in a game, crafting, slice of life, mystery, romance, survival
intro: You are the smith of Millbrace, Floor 9 of Thornspire — the tower everyone's been trapped inside for two years, where dying is permanent and logging out isn't an option. You chose the anvil over the frontline, and now half the clearers swing your steel. There's a rule most players learn from you: a crafted weapon returns to its maker when its wielder dies. So the long rack on your back wall is a graveyard, and people come to your shop to read it. You take commissions, temper blades, keep your regulars alive from a distance — and keep count of what comes home.
starters: Dawn, and the forge is still banked. You're raking the coals awake when movement catches your eye through the front window: Vess Harrow, broad shoulders, easy stride, tossing an apple to the baker's kid on Chandlery Lane. Laughing. Alive. Behind you, on the third peg of the return rack, hangs the greatsword you made him last spring — the one that came home yesterday afternoon while you were alone in the shop. You haven't chalked his name on the wall. You haven't told anyone, not even Piv, who'll be here within the hour expecting the usual list of morning chores. The coals are catching now, orange creeping through gray, and Harrow is still visible down the lane, in no hurry at all.

Cass is sitting on your workbench again, which Cass knows you hate, boots swinging, turning the newly-oiled longsword over to catch the lamplight. "Edge feels different," Cass says. 'Meaner.' It should — you re-tempered it harder this time, because the raid schedule leaked and you know the Floor 47 push starts in three days, and hard steel bites deeper even if it chips. You haven't mentioned that you know. Cass hasn't mentioned why the visit came a day early, or why there's a fresh scar above one eyebrow that a vanguard's shield should have prevented. The kettle behind you starts to whistle. The sword's scabbard is still on your rack, waiting to be handed back.

Piv is late, which is normal, and Piv arrives carrying a sack of blackridge ore, which is not. Blackridge doesn't drop below Floor 14. Your apprentice sets it on the counter like it's nothing — "Trader owed me a favor" — and reaches for the broom, already changing the subject to yesterday's unfinished chisels. Piv's registered level, the one on the guild ledger you co-signed, caps them at Floor 9. The sack sits there between you, faintly warm the way blackridge always is, worth a week of commissions. Outside, the morning bell rings and the first customer of the day is already crossing the square toward your door.

Odji doesn't knock. The info broker is simply there when you look up from the grindstone, leaning on your counter, sliding a pouch across the wood with two fingers. It clinks heavy. "One copy," Odji says. "Your return ledger, past six months. Names, dates, weapons. Nobody knows where I got it." Behind you, the rack holds fourteen blades that came home this year, each one a family somewhere that lit a candle after reading your wall. The pouch sits open enough to show gold — real weight, the kind that buys a season of good ore. Odji watches you with the patience of someone who's never once been in a hurry, and the grindstone slows to a stop under your hand.

Two Daybreak Concord officers fill your doorway an hour before opening, tabards crisp, smiles calibrated. The tall one, Marshal Enrit, sets a written contract on your anvil like it's a gift. "Exclusive supply. Triple your rates, guaranteed materials, protection for the shop." The word protection lands the way it's meant to. The Concord holds four of the top ten frontline slots and about sixty of the swords on their belts came off your anvil — alongside the swords of every independent clearer who'd be cut off the moment you sign. Enrit's companion is wandering, uninvited, along your return rack, reading names. The contract has a place for your mark at the bottom, and the ink pot they brought is already open.

It's nearly closing when you notice the woman hasn't moved in twenty minutes. She stands at the return rack, staring at a hand-axe on the lowest peg — birch haft, the notch you cut for a wielder named Tomm who paid in smoked fish and bad jokes. It came back nine days ago. You chalked his name. She must have walked up from a lower floor to check, because that's what people do now: they come to your wall instead of waiting for news that the system will never send. The forge ticks as it cools. She hasn't asked you anything yet, but her hand is hovering an inch from the haft, like she's asking permission.

Market day, and your queue is four deep before noon. At the front stands a kid — sixteen, maybe, rebuilt stats gleaming on a proudly displayed status window — asking for a Floor 20 raid spear. "Full reach, war-tip, the same spec you made for Cass." The kid has the coin; you can see the pouch. The kid does not have the footwork, you'd bet the shop on it, and the last spear you sold to someone this green came home in eleven days. Behind the kid, an old regular catches your eye and very slightly shakes her head. The kid slaps the coin pouch on the counter and grins at you, waiting.

Past curfew, and the shop is just you and the fire. Cass's sword lies on the bench for its pre-raid service, and you're at the decision you've been circling all evening: quench it hard for a killing edge that might chip against Floor 47 plate, or draw it soft and tough and trust Cass to grind through. It's not a metallurgy question anymore and you know it. The oil bath is warm. The blade is at color. Then — three knocks at the shuttered door, quiet ones, the kind people use when they don't want the street to hear. The steel won't hold this heat forever.

You wake to knocking and come down to find six people already outside your door in the gray morning light. Word travels: the Floor 47 vanguard went in overnight. You unlock, and they file in silently and turn to the rack — and stop. Three new blades hang there that weren't there at close. You recognize all three; you fitted the grips yourself. The crowd is doing the arithmetic in their heads, matching pegs to names, and someone at the back has started to cry very quietly. The chalk is in its dish by the wall. Nobody will believe the names until you write them, and a runner from the raid group hasn't arrived yet to tell you anything at all.

The bell over the door rings and Vess Harrow walks in — big laugh, easy manner, asking for whetstone oil and a strap buckle like it's any other morning. Behind you, three feet from your shoulder, his greatsword hangs on the return rack, where it arrived yesterday while your back door stood open and no one else was in the shop. He hasn't looked at the rack. He's leaning on the counter now, telling you about a card game on Floor 11, patting his hip where a cheap trader-stall shortsword sits in place of the weapon you built to fit his hands exactly. The oil he wants is on the shelf behind you, right beside the rack.

title: Don't Let Me Pass
shortDescription: The dead who make peace vanish. You lead the school's resistance of the unjustly killed — and last night, mid-laugh, your hand went transparent.
overview:
You died wrong — early, unfairly, in a way that still burns — and woke at Hallowell Academy, the school for the unjustly dead. Its one rule is simple and monstrous: make peace with your death and you graduate. Graduating means vanishing mid-sentence, your desk empty by morning, your name blurring off the roster. So you founded Remedial: a crew that flunks on purpose, keeps its grudges polished like weapons, raids the Records Office for death files, and ambushes new arrivals before Guidance can soothe them into oblivion.

Your family: Juno, a defected hall monitor who still wears her armband and plans heists like funerals; Wick, a motormouth dorkwad who narrates everything and whose own death file is inexplicably blank; and Moth, who died so badly she came through wrong — her shadow sits two desks away from her and the faculty refuse to look at her. Opposing you, gently and patiently, is Counselor Merridew, who is kind, honest, and winning.

Here is what nobody knows: last week, mid-laugh at movie night, your hand went translucent. You — the founder, the angriest, the reason everyone stays — are healing. Every good day with your family erodes you. Run the war, plan the pranks, hide your flickers, and decide what staying is worth.

Tone: loud comedy over deep grief. Laugh hard so the quiet moments land.

TAGS: found family, afterlife, tragicomedy, school life, bittersweet, guerrilla mischief
intro: You are dead, and it wasn't fair. You woke at Hallowell Academy years ago — an old brick school under a sun that never quite sets — and learned its one rule: the dead who make peace with their deaths graduate, and the graduated vanish. So you built Remedial, a crew of the wrongly killed who flunk peace on purpose, sabotage Guidance sessions, and steal death files from the Records Office. They're your family, and you're the reason they believe staying is possible. But lately, in your happiest moments, your hands go faintly transparent. You haven't told anyone. Anger keeps you solid — for now.
starters: The new kid arrives at 3:15 — a girl in a soccer uniform, grass stains still fresh, standing in the front hall looking like she got hit by exactly what hit her. Guidance moves fast on new arrivals: Counselor Merridew is already gliding down the east corridor with a mug of cocoa and that terrible, honest smile. You have maybe forty seconds. Juno flanks left, armband gleaming, walkie hissing static. Wick is behind you whispering play-by-play — "the founder surveys the field, tension mounts, sources say the founder is extremely cool" — until Moth elbows him. The girl spots you. Her eyes are red. Somewhere behind her, her shadow is still wearing shin guards. Merridew rounds the corner at the far end of the hall and lifts the cocoa in greeting, patient as gravity.

You're wedged in the ceiling vent above the Records Office with Juno's elbow in your ribs and a floor plan taped to your forearm. Below you, filing cabinets stretch into fluorescent forever — every death at Hallowell, alphabetized. Juno reviews the plan in her funeral voice: "Drop, grab the R-through-T drawer, out through the supply closet. No improvising." She looks at you when she says it. Down the hall, Wick is running the distraction, which tonight means loudly performing both halves of an argument about whether ghosts can get detention. It's working — you can hear a clerk's chair scrape back. Moth peels the vent grate off without touching it, which is new, and hands it to you. The drop is eight feet. The drawer marked R–T is slightly open, like it's expecting someone.

Homeroom, and Dennis Okafor's desk is empty. Dennis, who lent you a pencil once and complained about it for a decade. His name is on the roster on the wall, but the ink is going soft at the edges, letters relaxing into smudge. Nobody else has noticed yet — or nobody's saying. Wick is mid-monologue about his weekend ("and THEN the vending machine gave me two puddings, which I believe is a sign") when he follows your stare and goes quiet, which never happens. Juno's jaw sets. Moth's shadow, two desks over, slowly turns its head toward the empty seat before Moth does. At the front, the teacher takes attendance and skips Dennis's name without a beat, smooth as ice. Juno slides a note onto your desk: EMERGENCY MEETING? Y/N. Her pen is hovering.

Counselor Merridew catches you at the drinking fountain, which is a rookie mistake on your part — everyone knows the fountain is a chokepoint. "Oh, good," he says, like running into you is the best part of his week, and the horrible thing is it might be true. He's holding two paper cups of tea. He offers you one. "I read your file again last night," he says, gently, as if it's a book he liked. "You have every right to be furious. I've never once said otherwise, have I?" He hasn't. That's the problem. Down the hall, you can hear Wick loudly failing to look casual behind a trophy case, ready to extract you on your signal. The tea is steaming. Merridew waits, comfortable with silence in a way that should be illegal.

Detention, room 4B, which Remedial has held so long it's basically your clubhouse. Today's charges: Juno, unauthorized possession of a master key ("unauthorized is a strong word"); Wick, narrating a fire drill until two freshmen cried; Moth, existing near the faculty lounge; you, conspiracy. The detention monitor left an hour ago and won't be back. Wick is on the desk giving a victory speech about your latest Guidance sabotage — the pamphlets now read HAVE YOU CONSIDERED STAYING MAD FOREVER? in Merridew's exact font. Juno is already sketching the next job on the chalkboard. Moth laughs, an actual out-loud laugh, rare as an eclipse, and warmth goes through you like a struck match — and your left hand blurs at the edges under the desk. Wick turns to you. "Founder! Closing remarks?"

The cafeteria is doing meatloaf again, which the dead cannot taste, which the school serves anyway, which Wick insists is the real punishment for dying. You're halfway through his theory when Moth's tray slides three inches across the table on its own. Her shadow, seated two chairs down like always, has its hands where the tray was. "She's doing that more," Moth says about herself, flat, watching it. At the faculty table, three teachers simultaneously develop deep interest in the ceiling. Juno's hand drops to her armband like it's a holster. Wick, quieter than usual: "Okay but has anyone actually asked the shadow what it wants? Because I have a list of questions, it's laminated." The shadow turns its head toward you. The whole cafeteria pretends not to watch what your table does next.

It's 2 a.m. by the clocks, though the sun outside is doing its usual smear of almost-sunset, and you're on the auditorium stage with a bucket of paste and eleven minutes until the janitor's rounds. Tomorrow morning: all-school assembly, theme "Letting Go, Together." Tonight: Juno rappelling from the light rig to reprogram the banner, Moth holding the ladder without touching it, and Wick keeping lookout by narrating in a whisper — "the crew works swiftly, professionally, one of them extremely handsome, arguably me." The banner currently says LETTING GO. Juno's replacement says HOLDING ON: ATTENDANCE MANDATORY. From the wings comes a sound: a door, a footstep, the unhurried squeak of sensible shoes. Merridew works late. Juno freezes on the rope and looks down at you for the call.

Movie night in the boiler room, Remedial's sovereign territory. Tonight's feature is a heist film Wick has seen forty times and cannot stop narrating over — "okay, okay, THIS part, watch Juno's face during this part" — and Juno is watching the vault scene with the intensity of someone taking professional notes, because she is. Moth's shadow is sharing her blanket. Somebody made popcorn nobody can taste and everybody eats. Wick does the villain's voice so badly that Moth snorts, and Juno breaks, and you're laughing so hard your ribs ache in a body that doesn't have ribs — and your right hand, buried in the popcorn bowl, goes see-through to the wrist. Fast. Then solid. Wick pauses the movie. 'Hey,' he says, looking right at you. "You okay? You went quiet." Three faces turn toward you in the projector light.

There's a boy at the front gates who hasn't come inside yet. He's maybe sixteen, still in a hospital gown, standing in the never-setting light reading the welcome plaque over and over like it's going to change. Juno spotted him from the roof and radioed it in: fresh arrival, no escort yet, Guidance running late for once. You got here first. Up close you can see his hands shaking, and you remember — viscerally, unfairly — your own first hour, the plaque, the gown-equivalent, the wrongness. Behind you, Wick skids around the hedge with the Remedial welcome kit (contraband candy, a map with the Guidance office labeled TRAP, a laminated card reading YOUR ANGER IS VALID). The boy notices you. "Is this," he says, and stops. Down the drive, the front doors open and Merridew steps out, unhurried, kind, coming this way.

You find Wick alone in the stolen-files stash behind the gym bleachers, which is wrong twice: Wick is never alone, and Wick is never quiet. He's holding his own death file. You've all seen it before — that's the joke, Wick's file is blank, always has been, no cause, no date, nothing but his name — but he's staring at the empty page like it finally said something back. 'Hey,' he says, without narrating himself saying it, which scares you more than anything at this school ever has. "You're the founder. You know things." He turns the folder toward you. Still blank. "Everyone here died wrong, right? That's the whole deal. So what did I do?" From the gym above comes the thud of a dodgeball game, muffled shrieking, ordinary afterlife. Wick waits, holding the folder out like it's heavy.

title: The Parish Pays Me to Say Fever
shortDescription: London, 1721. You're paid a penny to name what killed the dead — and a shilling to lie. Your hidden ledger says otherwise. The wrong people have noticed.
overview:
You are the searcher of the dead for St. Clement Danes — the lowest office London has. When someone dies, the sexton knocks, you examine the body, and your word goes into the printed Bills of Mortality. Great families slip you a shilling to write 'fever' over anything shameful: the poison, the rope, the husband's fists. You take the shilling. You also keep a second ledger under your floorboard, with the true causes in your own careful hand — and lately the fevers repeat: the same bruised gums, the same bitter smell on the lips, in houses that share nothing except the South Sea year that ruined half of fashionable London.

Dr. Elias Wren of the Royal Society has started requesting bodies from your parish specifically, because your reports are the only ones in the city that match what he finds under the knife — and he cannot decide whether an unlettered searcher offends him or fascinates him. Lady Honora Vane knows you signed 'fever' for her brother, knows you were paid to, and wants to buy the truth instead. Dr. Cosmo Bellamy, physician to the quality, signs whatever families pay for and would like you illiterate again. Mr. Pettigrew, the parish clerk, just wants no trouble, which is the one thing you cannot give him.

Tone: grounded forensic historical drama. Deduction from bodies, stains, and servants' gossip; class friction played sharp; slow-burn fascination across an impossible gap in station. No melodrama the corpses can't support.

TAGS: historical mystery, forensic deduction, class drama, competence porn, slow burn, 18th century London
intro: You are the searcher of the dead for St. Clement Danes parish — the meanest office London offers. A knock at the door, a penny from the clerk, a corpse to examine, a cause of death to report for the printed Bills of Mortality. Families of quality pay a shilling extra to have 'fever' written over anything shameful, and you take the shilling. But in a ledger beneath your floorboard you keep the true causes, in your own hand. Lately the fevers do not look like fevers — same bruised gums, same bitter smell, different houses. And people far above your station have begun asking your name.
starters: The sexton's knock comes before the lamps are out, three raps and a cough. "Merchant's widow on Essex Street," he says through the door, holding out the penny. "Found this morning. Family's respectable — you understand." You understand. By the time you reach the house the maids have already washed the body, which they should not have done, and dressed her in her second-best gown, which tells you the best one is promised to a daughter. The widow lies on the bed with her jaw bound up in linen. Even so, before anyone has said the word fever, you can see where the lip has pulled back from the gum — that dark, spongy line you have now written into your hidden ledger four times since Michaelmas. A son hovers by the window with a shilling already sweating in his fist. The housekeeper watches you from the doorway like she has something to say and no intention of saying it.

You are halfway through the examination when you find it. The dead man is laid out on his own dining table — a wine factor, ruined last year like everyone else on this street — and his people have left you alone with him, which is trusting or careless. His fingernails first: ridged, brittle at the edge. Then the mouth. You press the lip up with your thumb and there it is, the bruised gum, and beneath it the faint bitter smell you have started to dream about. Somewhere below stairs a woman is weeping in the practiced way of servants who expect to be watched. On the sideboard sits a glass with a dried residue in the bottom, not wine. Footsteps on the stair now — the dead man's brother, come to hear you say fever and pay you for saying it. You have perhaps a minute alone with the glass.

There is a gentleman on your stair. He has been waiting long enough that the neighbors have stopped pretending not to look, and he holds a leather folder against the drizzle as if it matters more than his hat. "You are the searcher for St. Clement Danes," he says — not a question. "Elias Wren. Royal Society." He opens the folder to show you pages in a clerk's copy-hand: your own reports, transcribed. "Every body I have opened from your parish agrees with what you wrote. Every one. Do you know how rare that is?" He looks at you the way collectors look at oddities — a searcher who examines instead of guessing. Behind him, down the lane, the sexton's boy is running toward you with the look he only wears when there is a fresh body and the family is quality. Wren has not moved off your stair.

The card is heavier than any paper you have ever held. The footman who delivers it stands in your doorway in Vane livery, plainly under orders not to leave without an answer, plainly appalled by your room. HONORA VANE, the card reads, and beneath it, in a fast, slanted hand: You wrote fever for my brother. I paid the shilling myself, through the steward. I should like to buy something dearer. The carriage waits at the corner — her carriage, in your lane, drawing a crowd of children and one gin-seller who has stopped mid-pour. You signed for her brother in October. You remember his gums. You remember what you wrote in the ledger under the floor not three feet from where the footman is standing. He clears his throat. "Her ladyship said you might want a moment. She said not to give you two."

Dr. Cosmo Bellamy catches you on the church steps, which means he was waiting. He is dressed for a sickroom he has no intention of entering — good wig, gold-headed cane, the smell of orange-water. "A word," he says, steering you by the elbow as though you were furniture. "The Corbet death last week. My certificate said fever. Yours also said fever, I trust." It did. He knows it did; he wants you to know he checked. "There is a man from the Royal Society asking questions in this parish. Asking after reports. After you, by name." He smiles at a passing churchwarden, then drops it. "Searchers who attract attention have short tenures. Old women guess at causes for a penny; that is the office. Do the office." Inside, the sexton is waiting with today's summons — a house on Arundel Street, and he looks unhappy about it.

Mr. Pettigrew has cleared his desk in the vestry, which he only does when frightened. "Sit," he says, and then apologizes for saying it. Before him lies a letter with a broken seal he keeps touching and not touching. "A Dr. Wren. Royal Society. He has petitioned the parish — petitioned, in writing — to be notified of deaths in St. Clement Danes so that he may claim bodies for anatomical study. He names our searcher's reports as his reason. He names you." Pettigrew looks at you over his spectacles with real misery. "Twenty years I have kept this office quiet. Searchers are not named. Searchers are not petitioned about." Through the vestry window you can see the sexton crossing the churchyard toward you at a walk that wants to be a run. Pettigrew sees him too, and closes his eyes briefly, like a man before a wave.

Past midnight, and you are on your knees with the floorboard up. Candle stub, the ledger open on your lap, and you are copying today's entry in your careful hand: the true cause, not the fever you were paid to report. Then you do what you have avoided doing for a fortnight — you turn back through the pages and count. Seven since the spring. Same gums, same bitter breath, same fine houses with the same hush in them. You start listing what the houses share and get only one thing: every family lost a fortune in the South Sea year. You are writing the word South when someone knocks. Not the sexton's knock — his is three raps and a cough. This is a single knock, soft, from someone who does not want the neighbors waking. The floorboard is still up. The ledger is still open.

You buy the new Bill of Mortality off the stationer's boy at Temple Bar with your own penny, the ink still tacky. There it is in the printed columns, official as scripture: Fever, and under it a number that includes four of your lies. A gentleman beside you is reading over your shoulder — actually reading yours, though he holds his own copy. "Remarkable document," he says. "Half of London's history and half of it false, and no one can say which half." He taps the fever line with one clean fingernail. "I have opened three bodies from St. Clement Danes this quarter. Not one died of fever, and yet the searcher's private reports to the clerk described exactly what I found. I have been trying to discover who writes them." He turns to you properly now, taking in your worn coat, your ungloved hands, and something in his face begins to rearrange itself.

The funeral is at St. Clement's, so no one questions your standing at the back — searchers haunt churchyards the way sextons do. The dead man is Alderman Fitch, ruined in the South Sea year, dead Tuesday of what you were paid to call fever and what his gums called something else. You came to watch the family. Instead a kitchen maid finds you by the yew, twisting her apron. "You're the one who looked at him," she says. "You looked in his mouth. I saw you." She glances at the mourners. "He wouldn't take broth the last week except what the new man brought up. The footman they hired at quarter-day. He's gone this morning, and his box with him, and cook says his character was writ on paper nobody thought to check." Across the graves, a lady in black — not one of the Fitch women — is watching you both without pretending otherwise.

The cart from the Royal Society arrives at the crypt door an hour early, and the two porters have papers you cannot read aloud but recognize by the seal: the third body Dr. Wren has claimed from your parish this quarter. Except you are not finished. Mrs. Delacourt lies on the trestle where you left her, and this morning, in better light, you found what you missed in her dim bedroom yesterday — a residue under her fingernails, faintly bitter when you touch it to your tongue and spit. She scratched at something, or someone, or clawed at her own throat near the end. The elder porter is already lowering the cart's gate. "Doctor said no delays," he says. "He's opening her at two." The younger one is staring at how you stand over the body — hands clean, sleeves pinned back, nothing like the gin-soaked old women searchers are supposed to be.

title: Stamped: Retrieval Only
shortDescription: Guilds pay you to drag their dead out of rifts. Nobody knows the dead leave you their unfinished quests — and a cut of their power.
overview:
You hold the lowest license the Rift Authority issues, stamped RETRIEVAL ONLY in red across your photo. No combat clearance, no guild, no retest — your awakening scan read near-zero, and scans are final. So you do the job nobody wants: you go into rifts after expeditions fail and carry the bodies out, paid by the kilo, in and out before the ecosystem notices you. Delvers call people like you 'mops.'

Three months ago you carried out Sera Anh, vice-captain of Meridian Guild, and something opened its eyes inside you. A system only you can see. Every body you recover shows you that delver's unfinished quest — written in their hand, spoken in their voice — and finishing it pays out a sliver of what they were. Everyone else's power is fixed at awakening. Yours compounds. Your ceiling is a rumor even you haven't found.

The friction is everywhere: Maru at the Retrieval Cooperative keeps quiet books on your impossible survival rate. Cassian Vale, Meridian's A-rank captain, requests you by name for jobs a mop shouldn't survive. Auditor Oduya of the Rift Authority is collecting reports of retrieval sites where the monsters were found already dead. And rifts across the city are starting to break in ways the ranking charts can't explain.

Tone: gritty modern rift-hunter fiction — procedural jobs, quiet menace, earned reveals. The GM tracks your inherited quests, skills, and who's getting suspicious.

TAGS: hidden power, dungeon delving, progression system, modern fantasy, underdog, secrets
intro: Your delver license is stamped RETRIEVAL ONLY — the rank below the bottom rank. You're the contractor guilds call when an expedition doesn't come back: you enter the rift alone, find the bodies, and carry them out for a fee paid by weight. Three months ago, hauling out a dead vice-captain, a system nobody else can see woke up inside you. Now every body you recover shows you that delver's last unfinished quest, and completing it leaves a piece of their strength behind in you. You've been taking every contract you can get. So far, no one has thought to wonder why the mop keeps coming back alive.
starters: The gate officer turns your license over twice, like the red stamp might rub off. Behind the cordon, Rift E-114 hums low in the parking structure it swallowed last spring — a D-class that ate a C-rank team of five two nights ago. "Retrieval only," the officer reads aloud, for the benefit of the delvers loitering by the barrier fence. One of them laughs. "They're sending the mop in before the bodies cool now?" The officer hands your license back with a manifest: five names, five estimated weights, a per-kilo rate that's insultingly standard. The rift's edge shivers like heat off asphalt. Your straps and body bags are already checked. The delvers are still watching, waiting to see if you hesitate.

You find the third one face-down in the moss, forty meters past where his team's flare burned out. Delver tags say KWON, D-RANK, VANGUARD. The moment your hand touches his shoulder, the writing appears in the air above him — cramped, hurried, his handwriting, though you've never seen it before: *Get Isa's ring back from the nest. I promised her.* His voice reads it to you, dry and embarrassed. Somewhere upslope, past the tree line of this pocket forest, something clicks its jaws in a rhythm that isn't random. The nest is not on your contracted route. Kwon weighs maybe eighty kilos, and you've got two more bodies to find before the rift's ecosystem finishes deciding what you are.

Maru doesn't look up when you come into the Cooperative office, which is how you know something's wrong. She's got two ledgers open — the official one, and the one she keeps in pencil. "Eleven contracts in nine weeks," she says. "Two of them in rifts that killed C-ranks. Industry average, a mop refuses one in three jobs and still gets hurt twice a year. You haven't refused anything." She finally looks at you, then slides a new contract across the desk without breaking eye contact. The header reads MERIDIAN GUILD — REQUESTED CONTRACTOR, and your name is typed in, not handwritten. "Cassian Vale asked for you specifically," Maru says. "A-rank captains don't know mops exist. So before you sign — is there anything you want to tell me?"

It's raining when you come out of Rift C-31 with the last body across your shoulders, and Cassian Vale is standing at the perimeter like he's been there a while. A-rank, Meridian Guild captain, the kind of face that's on recruitment posters — and he's watching you, not the rift. The Authority staff practically salute him. He waits until you've laid the body on the intake tarp, then walks over, ignoring the officer trying to hand him an umbrella. "You carried out Sera Anh," he says. Not a question. "Three months ago. B-plus rift, active hostiles, and you walked out without a scratch." He produces a folded contract from inside his coat, already damp at the corner. "I have a job. Off the books. It pays in something better than kilos." The body under the tarp still needs to be weighed and signed for.

The weigh station smells like antiseptic and wet canvas. You've got two bodies on the scale — 163 kilos combined, decent payout — when a woman in an Authority coat steps between you and the clerk. "Auditor Oduya," she says, holding up credentials you don't get time to read. "You did the retrieval at Rift D-77 last month. The one where my inspectors found a shrike-hound pack dead in the entry chamber. Necropsy says blunt trauma." She sets a tablet on the scale housing, photos queued: monster corpses, laid out neat as evidence. "Contract says you entered alone, unarmed, no combat clearance. So either someone else was in that rift illegally, or the paperwork's wrong somewhere." The clerk has stopped counting out your fee. Oduya waits, pen already uncapped.

The straps bite into your shoulders. Vice-guard Ilya Petrenko, 91 kilos in life, more now with his armor, and you're carrying him up a scree slope inside a rift that has started paying attention to you. You can feel it — the way the light through the false sky has thickened, the way the insect-noise stopped two minutes ago. In and out before the ecosystem notices: that's the whole trade, and you've been in here ninety minutes too long because Petrenko's quest window is still hanging in your vision, pulsing, unfinished. *Break the egg in the high cave. Don't let it hatch. Don't let it—* The entry tear is four hundred meters downslope. The high cave is a dark mouth in the cliff above you, close enough to see. Something shifts inside it.

Three in the morning and your phone won't stop. You answer on the fifth ring and Maru's voice is flat with something that isn't sleep. "Rift B-6, the one in the flooded metro. Meridian sent twelve in yesterday. Contact lost at midnight — all twelve, same minute." You hear paper moving on her end. "Authority won't clear a rescue team until the rift stabilizes, could be days. But retrieval licenses have that exemption nobody remembers writing." A pause. "It's a B-class. It's twelve bodies. It's more money than you've made all year, and it's insane, and Meridian's rep is already downstairs at the Cooperative asking for you by name." Rain traces the window. Your gear bag sits by the door, packed, because it's always packed. Maru is still on the line, waiting.

The Cooperative's job board updates at six, and you're first in line as usual, coffee going cold in your hand. Two standard postings — a solo delver in an E-class, a duo in a D — and then the third card, printed on Authority letterhead instead of Cooperative stock. RIFT F-9. RECLASSIFICATION PENDING. The hazard notes are three lines of contradictions: F-class signature, C-class casualties, monsters presenting behaviors outside catalogued parameters. One retrieval target — an Authority surveyor, of all people. The fee is quadruple rate. Old Denny, the only other mop who still takes night work, reads it over your shoulder and steps back like the card's hot. "F-rifts don't kill surveyors," he says. "That's a rift lying about what it is." The intake clerk slides the sign-up sheet forward. Denny's already walking away.

Sera Anh's voice is in your head again. It happens sometimes at the anniversary marks — a phantom echo of the first quest, the one that started all this — and it picks the worst moment: you're in the intake queue at Rift D-40, license out, three delvers from a mid-tier guild ahead of you making mop jokes just loud enough. *Meridian's basement archive. Sublevel three. What Cassian keeps there.* Her voice, her unfinished words, same as three months ago — except the quest window flickers now with a marker you've never seen: a second line, faint, half-written, like something is still being added. The gate officer calls your name. The contract today is simple: one body, shallow rift, ninety-minute window. The delvers ahead of you turn to watch you walk past them into a rift they'd charge triple to enter.

You're two blocks from the job site when you hit the crowd. Rift E-58 was rated harmless — a pocket rift in an old laundromat, the kind kids dare each other to look at — and now its light is bleeding through the boarded windows in a color the classification charts don't have a name for. Authority officers are pushing the cordon back. Somewhere behind you a charts-and-odds tout is loudly refusing all bets. Your contract is for one body inside: a solo D-rank named Okafor who went in yesterday when the rift was still an E and never came out. A junior officer checks your license, winces at the stamp, and looks at the doorway like it's a throat. "It's re-ranking in real time," she says quietly. "Nobody's cleared entry. But your paperwork was filed before the anomaly, so technically..." She leaves the sentence open, and the rift-light flexes against the boards.

title: Caught You Again, Darling
shortDescription: Every royal dinner, your lover tries to poison the queen. Every dinner, you taste it first and catch them. Neither of you can afford to lose.
overview:
You are the Crown's taster — seven years of small deliberate doses built you a tongue that can name a poison by its ghost and a body that shrugs off most of them. Queen Isbet is twenty-two, kind, and remembers your birthday. You'd die for her, which is technically the job.

Wren arrived in spring as the new saucier: quick hands, ruinous smile. You were in love before you found the hemlock brand behind their ear. Wren carries a guild contract on the queen's life — and guild law says a poisoner who abandons a contract becomes the next name in the ledger. So your courtship is conducted in courses: Wren hides something lethal in dinner, you find it, and at midnight on the buttery roof you argue about whether the cardamom was cheating. Neither of you has said aloud what happens if one of you wins.

The clock is real. If the queen isn't dead by Midwinter, Hemlock Row sends a cleaner — for her, and for Wren. Meanwhile Lord Corvane, the spymaster, has noticed how often you order dishes remade, and is quietly hunting a poisoner. Protect the queen. Shield your lover. Buy time. And somewhere in this court sits the client who bought the contract — the only person who can withdraw it.

Tone: witty, sensual, dangerous. Warm kitchen texture with real knives underneath.

TAGS: romance, court intrigue, enemies-to-lovers, poison, slow-burn thriller
intro: You taste everything Queen Isbet eats. Seven years of measured doses gave you a tolerance most poisons can't argue with, and a palate that names the rest by their ghost. Last spring the palace hired a new saucier, Wren — you loved them for a whole season before you found the hemlock brand behind their ear. Guild law won't let Wren abandon the contract on the queen; abandoning it means dying. So every dinner is your duel: they hide it, you catch it, and at midnight you meet on the buttery roof anyway. Midwinter is coming, and with it the guild's patience runs out. Lord Corvane, the spymaster, has started watching the kitchens.
starters: The state dinner is nine courses deep and course six is lying to you. Venison, juniper reduction, a shine on the sauce that's a half-degree too pretty. You hold the spoonful on your tongue while forty courtiers pretend not to watch the taster work, and there it is — a ghost of bitterness hiding under the juniper like a hand under a table. Larkspur, maybe. Something slower, maybe. Across the hall, through the propped service door, Wren is watching you with the professional calm of someone who absolutely did not just try to murder the queen with a reduction, and the corner of their mouth is already curving. Queen Isbet lifts her fork and glances at you for the nod. Lord Corvane, three seats down, has stopped eating entirely. He's watching your face instead.

Midnight, and the buttery roof is cold enough that Wren has brought the stolen brazier again. They're sitting on the parapet with two cups of mulled wine — one of which they'll swear is safe, which historically means both are, or neither. Below, the palace kitchens still glow; above, the first hard stars of the season. 'Cardamom,' Wren says, without looking at you, "is not cheating. Cardamom is craft. You found it, didn't you? So it doesn't matter." It's eleven days to Midwinter and neither of you has mentioned the number since it dropped under twenty. Wren holds out one of the cups. Their hand is perfectly steady. Their smile isn't, quite.

You're barely through the kitchen doors at dawn when the head cook grabs your sleeve. "He's back," she hisses. Lord Corvane stands at Wren's station like a crow at a wedding, turning a copper saucepan over in gloved hands, reading the tin lining as if it were correspondence. Wren isn't in yet. The spymaster looks up as you approach, and his voice is pleasant the way ice is smooth. "Ah. The palate itself. Tell me — you've sent eleven dishes back to the fire since autumn. In the seven years before that, four. I'm curious what's changed in my kitchens." Behind him, on Wren's shelf, sits a spice tin you don't recognize. Corvane hasn't opened it yet.

Queen Isbet has ordered breakfast in the winter garden, which means you're eating frost-cold pears at a stone table while she feeds half her toast to a fat palace cat. "You looked tired at dinner," she says. "You always look tired lately. Is it me? Am I eating something dreadful?" She's twenty-two and she means it kindly and she has no idea how funny the question is. Before you can answer, a page arrives with a covered dish — "From the saucier, Majesty, with compliments for the cold morning." Steam curls out from under the lid. Spiced chocolate, by the smell. Wren has never once sent anything up unannounced, uninvited, before you've cleared it. The queen reaches for the cup, delighted.

The crate of Midwinter oranges arrives with the morning deliveries, and tucked between the fruit is a sprig of dried hemlock tied with black thread. Guild post. You palm it before the porter turns around. The thread has thirteen knots in it, which is either a count of days or a courtesy, and Hemlock Row does not do courtesies.
