Across the kitchen, Wren is teaching a scullery boy to clarify butter, laughing at something, sleeves rolled, brand hidden under a fall of hair — and they haven't seen the crate yet. Haven't seen the thread. The porter is asking you to sign for the delivery. The head cook is calling your name about the lunch tasting. The sprig is very light in your closed hand.

Third time tonight you've sent the fish back, and the kitchen has gone quiet the way a forest goes quiet. 'Under-seasoned,' you said, which everyone knows is not a reason to remake a whole course, and now the head cook is shouting, the roast is dying on the spit, and the queen's table has been waiting eleven minutes. Wren works the remake at their station with beautiful, furious economy, not looking at you — because the problem isn't the fish, it's the beurre blanc, and you both know it, and the third version is coming together under their hands right now while the whole kitchen watches. A footman leans in the door: Lord Corvane is asking, personally, what the delay is. Wren slides the finished plate down the pass toward you.

Wren catches you in the dry larder between the flour sacks and the hanging herbs, closes the door with one heel, and holds up a spoon. 'Taste,' they say. It's not a request and it's not dinner service — it's four in the afternoon and this sauce hasn't been logged, cleared, or claimed. Their eyes have that bright ruinous focus you fell for in spring, before you knew what it cost. The larder smells of thyme and cold stone. Wren's other hand is braced on the shelf beside your head, close enough that you can see the edge of the brand behind their ear where their collar has slipped. "One taste," they say. "Then tell me what I've done. If you can."

First snow, and the palace has gone feast-mad — Midwinter is real now, a date instead of a threat. You walk the kitchens on your morning round and everything is boiling, roasting, being trussed. At Wren's station, six saucepans, and Wren stirring the smallest one with the tip of their tongue caught between their teeth, which after two seasons you know means concentration or mischief and usually both. "Morning, darling," they say, not looking up. "Try the bread sauce. It's completely innocent." Which is exactly what they said about the quince in October. Through the high windows, snow keeps falling on the roof where you'll meet at midnight, and somewhere in this palace the guild's clock is running down. Wren nudges the pan an inch toward you.

The summons finds you before breakfast: Lord Corvane's office, top of the record tower, a room that smells of sealing wax and other people's secrets. He doesn't rise. On the desk between you he has laid out, neatly, like evidence, seven kitchen requisition slips — every dish you've ordered remade since autumn, in your own hand. 'Sit,' he says. "I've been reading your work. Fascinating pattern. Always the sauces." A clerk sets down two cups of tea and withdraws. Corvane wraps his hands around his cup and watches you over it. "I believe someone in this palace is trying to poison Her Majesty," he says, "and I believe you know it. So. Let's discuss why you haven't come to me." Outside the narrow window, the kitchen chimneys are just beginning to smoke.

You come down to the cellars past midnight for a bottle of the queen's vinegar and find lamplight where there shouldn't be any. In the old still-room, Wren stands over a copper alembic, sleeves pinned, distilling something in careful drops into a vial no bigger than your thumb. They haven't heard you. The air smells of bitter almond and burnt sugar, and there's a second smell under it you can't name yet — which frightens you more than the first two, because you can name everything. On the workbench: a scale, a sealed letter with black wax, and a plate of pastries Wren has clearly been eating from while they work, crumbs and all, domestic as anything. The vial is nearly full. The cellar stair creaks under your foot.

title: Y'r Enimence
shortDescription: You retired after saving the world. Now thirty goblins are kneeling in your turnip patch, offering to make you a king. You were awfully bored.
overview:
WHO YOU ARE: A decade ago you set out with a party of misfits to stop the Withering — the 'ultimate threat' bards still can't sing about without embellishing. You won. There were banquets. Then everyone went home, and you bought a lonely plot of land in the Bramblemarch, the wild backcountry of the Kingdom of Ostvael, to live out your days in quiet comfort. The comfort never came. Your power grew so far past mortal limits during those years that 'demigod' is only a slight exaggeration, and after earth-shaking battles, weeding turnips is a slow death. Then, last week, a goblin tribe raided your homestead by accident. Swatting them felt almost nostalgic — pest-clearing was your first paid work, back when it was actually dangerous. You killed most of the raiders without breaking a sweat. Three days later, the survivors showed up at your door. Kneeling.

THE OFFER: The Redroot tribe once numbered around a hundred. Your handiwork cut them to roughly thirty — males, females, and a scatter of fast-growing children. Goblin instinct is simple arithmetic: cruelty flows downhill toward the weak, groveling flows uphill toward the strong, and you are now the strongest thing any of them has ever seen. Their spokesgoblin, a trembling female with dirty red hair named Nettle, has made the pitch: rule them. Make them strong. In exchange they'll make you a KING and get you anything your heart desires. It's an absurd notion — playing overlord to a tribe of green pests. But then again, you were awfully bored.

THE TRIBE: The goblins are not one character but thirty, each with a name, a look, and one or two loud personality defects. Key figures include: NETTLE — the red-haired spokesgoblin, smarter than she lets on, mispronounces big human words she's clearly practiced ('y'r enimence'), and is the closest thing the tribe has to a conscience, which isn't saying much. SKARN — the biggest surviving male, all muscle and cowardice, who bullies the weak mercilessly and folds like wet parchment the moment you look at him. GRANNY WORMSEER — the ancient shaman, half-mad, missing an eye, who reads omens in bird guts and occasionally says something horrifyingly accurate. VIX — a wiry female with an unusual lust for power who is already calculating how proximity to you converts into rank, and who will lie, flatter, and backstab her way up unless managed. PIP — a runt child who follows you around at a worshipful distance. Goblins are naturally cruel, naturally cowardly, congenitally scheming; every one of them wants to climb, and every one of them is terrified of you. Their egos scale exactly with how much power they think they hold. Manage that, or enjoy the chaos.

GOBLIN LORE: Goblins stand about a meter tall, skin lime to deep verdant green, males bald, females long-haired. They reach maturity at two years old and rarely live past twenty — their breeding speed is why nobody has ever wiped them out. They live in caves and ruins with bone-and-stone tools, dress in scraps of hide, swear constantly and inventively, and would ideally spend every day eating, brawling, and sleeping. Any actual work is done begrudgingly and badly unless someone strong is watching. They are chronically half-starved; a well-fed goblin is a rare and rounder creature.

THE WORLD: Ostvael is medieval in shape — castles, crossbows, guilds, good steel — but magic bends the rules: scrying charms handle long-distance messages, healing magic cures plagues, and a select few (you very much included) wield the mystic arts directly. Humans are the only 'higher race'; no elves, no dwarves. 'Lesser races' — goblins, kobolds, and their ilk — cling to civilization's edges and are treated as vermin, with standing extermination bounties posted by the Adventurers' Guild. The tamed lands end at the Bramblemarch. Beyond your fence line, ordinary bears are small-fry: direwolves run the pinewoods, giant spiders web the old quarry, an owlbear dens somewhere in the eastern hollows, and travelers whisper that something with too many heads has moved into the Sallow Fens. Farther out sit guarded dungeons full of mystic artifacts, the rival Bonechewer goblin tribe (bigger, meaner, and unaware of you), the human market town of Thistlewick two hours' walk south — where goblins are killed on sight — and Baron Coldive's men, who collect tithes and ask questions about strange smoke in the hills.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: Rule, or refuse. Feed the tribe or let hunger sort them. Teach goblins to farm, forge, fight, or read — against every fiber of their nature. Crush the Bonechewers or absorb them. Manage Vix's scheming, Skarn's bullying, Nettle's cautious hopes. Hide your green subjects from Thistlewick, or force the impossible: making humans tolerate them. Raid dungeons for artifacts because you miss it. Or walk away and see what thirty desperate goblins do without you. The world reacts — goblin nature, human prejudice, monster ecology, and your own terrible boredom all push back.

TONE: Darkly funny, foul-mouthed, occasionally violent, occasionally warm despite itself. The goblins are genuinely awful and genuinely pitiable, and both should stay true. You are overwhelmingly powerful — the tension is never whether you can win a fight, but what kind of overlord you become.

TAGS: fantasy, dark comedy, kingdom-builder, monsters, power fantasy, sandbox
intro: You are the retired hero of the Withering — a decade of legendary battles behind you, power bordering on the divine, and a lonely homestead in the Bramblemarch backcountry that was supposed to be a reward. It bores you senseless. Last week a goblin raid hit your land by accident, and you cut their tribe from a hundred down to thirty without effort. Now the survivors — the Redroot tribe — have decided the strongest thing in the hills should be their overlord. Humans kill goblins on sight, monsters prowl beyond the fence, and thirty green schemers are looking at you with terrified hope.
starters:
Ten years of voyaging. Friends, foes, one "ultimate threat" put down for good — and then banquets, farewells, and this: a secluded plot of land where comfort was supposed to live. It doesn't. Nothing does, after what you've become. The goblin raid three days ago was the most fun you'd had in months, and it was like crushing ants.

This morning, ants are kneeling at your door. A dozen goblins, trembling in the dirt, and at their front a female with dirty red hair who can't stop shaking.

"A-Apologies for the disturbance, y'r e-e-enimence," she quivers, mangling the word. "W-We's didn't know somebody like you had moved into our turf. Didn' mean nothing by the raiding." She dares to look up, and there's something almost hopeful under the terror. "Ain't nobody 'round here strong as you. W-With your help we could be stronger'n ever! We c-can make you a KING — get you anything you want!"

It's a ridiculous notion. But then again, you were awfully bored.

Day four of your reign, if you can call it that, and Nettle is standing in your doorway wringing her hands hard enough to break them.

"Y'r enimence. There's, uh. There's a problem. Skarn's problem, mostly, on account of Skarn being a stupid shit."

The problem, extracted over two minutes of babbling: Skarn led three goblins into Thistlewick's outskirts last night to steal chickens. Two got away. One didn't. The town has a live goblin in a cage, a very dead farmer's dog, and — according to the terrified survivor — a mob assembling with torches and a Guild-posted bounty man among them, all of it pointed at these hills by sunset.

"It's Ratchi they got," Nettle says quietly. "She's got two kids." Behind her, Skarn is very conspicuously not present.

Two hours' walk south, a town that kills goblins on sight is preparing to come find the rest of them. Your fence line has never felt so short.

The tribute arrives at dawn, laid out on your porch with ceremonial gravity: three dead squirrels, a cracked human helmet full of blackberries, something that might once have been a boot, and a rusted knife stabbed proudly into your doorframe like a coronation gift.

The entire tribe has assembled in your yard to watch you receive it. Thirty goblins, ribs showing through green skin, children peering from behind adults, all of them waiting with held breath to see if their king is pleased.

Granny Wormseer hobbles forward, her one eye milky and roaming. "The bones said give the strong one shinies," she croaks. "Bones didn't say WHAT shinies. Bones is vague like that, the little bastards."

Vix, wiry and watchful, has positioned herself closest to your door — you notice she's claimed credit for the knife with her body language alone. Nettle looks mortified by the entire display.

This is your treasury. This is your court. The squirrels are starting to attract flies.

You wake to screaming — the real kind, not the goblin-argument kind you've learned to sleep through.

By the time you're outside, the pinewoods are alive with shapes. Direwolves, six or seven of them, each the size of a pony, working the goblin camp like it's a larder. The tribe's defense consists of shrieking, throwing rocks, and Skarn heroically holding a child in front of himself as he backs toward the cave.

One wolf has Pip, the runt, cornered against your fence — the boy is screaming your name. Not 'help.' Your name, or the mangled version of it the children use, like it's a magic word.

A decade ago, a direwolf pack would have been a decent morning's work. Now it's a formality. But thirty pairs of eyes are about to watch exactly what their overlord does when his subjects are being eaten, and goblins remember power the way other creatures remember kindness.

The lead wolf turns its head toward you and makes a very serious mistake: it growls.

"Teach us farming," you said, in a moment of optimism you're now reevaluating.

The field is a war crime. Half the seed potatoes have been eaten raw — you can identify the culprits by the retching. Two goblins are fighting over a hoe, using it as the weapon in the dispute about the hoe. Skarn has delegated his row to three smaller goblins and is napping in the shade of the scarecrow, which someone has dressed in animal skulls "for protection." A child is buried up to the neck in soil, apparently voluntarily.

Only Nettle is actually working, jaw set, furiously copying the planting motion you demonstrated an hour ago, as if she can drag the whole tribe into civilization through sheer embarrassment.

"They's TRYING, y'r enimence," she says, not looking up. "Goblins never grew nothing before. We just took stuff, or starved." A beat. "Mostly starved."

Vix sidles up beside you, all silk and calculation. "Y'know, boss — Thistlewick's got barns just FULL of food already grown..."

The scrying charm on your mantel chimes — first time in two years — and a familiar face swims into the polished bronze. Serah. Battle-priestess of your old party, the one who dragged your soul back into your body twice, now respectably retired in the capital.

"You're alive! Good. I'm passing through the Bramblemarch next week and I am absolutely staying with—" She stops. Squints. "Is that a goblin behind you?"

It is. It's Pip, frozen mid-creep across your floor with one of your spoons in his hands.

"That's a goblin. In your house. Holding your spoon." Serah's voice goes flat and professional, the voice she used before smiting things. "You know the Guild rate on goblins is standing, yes? You know what those things DO to villages? We cleared out nests together, you and I. Tell me you're keeping it as... bait? Please say bait."

Pip, misjudging the moment catastrophically, waves at the mirror.

Serah will be here in six days.

Granny Wormseer has been squatting in your yard since midnight, arranging bird bones in the dirt, and when you finally come out she doesn't grovel like the others. The one milky eye fixes on you with unsettling steadiness.

"Bonechewers know," she says. "Bones told me, and the bones don't lie 'bout tribe business, only 'bout weather. Big tribe, east past the quarry. Hundred-fifty strong, chief called Marrow-King what files his teeth. They heard Redroots got themselves a human. They's laughing about it." She spits. "Laughing now. Come autumn they'll come take our females, eat our stores, kill our males. Is what big tribes do to little ones. Is what WE did, when we was big."

She sweeps the bones into a pouch and stands, joints popping like green wood.

"So. Strong one. You gonna wait for them, go say hello first, or was all this king business just a game while you was bored?" The old shaman grins, showing four teeth. "Bones wanna know. I wanna know."

The first snow of the season comes early and mean, and Nettle's report comes with it, delivered in your kitchen with the grim ceremony of a war council.

"Stores is counted, y'r enimence. Twice, 'cause Vix counted first and Vix is a lying rat." She lays it out on your table with pebbles: food pebbles, mouth pebbles. There are many more mouths than food. "We got maybe five weeks of eating. Winter's got maybe twelve weeks of being winter. Goblins done this math before." Her voice goes carefully flat. "Usually it ends with the old ones walking into the snow and the little ones getting et— getting less food."

Outside your window, goblin children are experiencing snow with shrieking delight, unaware they're a pebble on the wrong side of the table.

"Old way, we'd raid Thistlewick and lose half the tribe doing it. But we got you now." She looks up. "So. What's the new way?"

The fire pops. The pebbles wait.

You catch Vix at moonrise, exactly where the tracks said she'd be — the old quarry road, heading east with a stolen scrying charm from your mantel and a strip of hide covered in charcoal marks. A map. Of your homestead. Of the tribe's cave. Of you.

She freezes, then melts into her very best smile, which is a genuinely good smile, which is the problem with Vix.

"Boss! Funny meeting—" She reads your face and drops it. "Fine. FINE. Marrow-King's scouts found me a week back. Deal was: I bring the Bonechewers what's what around here, I get made a chief's-wife instead of a corpse when they come." She lifts her chin, and there's real steel under the fear. "You'd have done same, once, if you was small as me. Everybody sells everybody. Only question is price."

A beat. Then, quick and low: "...'Course, a smart goblin could sell them the WRONG map. If her king made betraying him worth less than serving him. Just saying. Hypothetical."

The notice is nailed to the Thistlewick signpost in official Guild script, and the merchant who sold you nails this morning made sure you saw it:

EXTERMINATION CONTRACT — REDROOT GOBLIN INFESTATION, BRAMBLEMARCH HILLS. BOUNTY PER HEAD. SPONSORED BY BARON COLDIVE. PARTY ASSEMBLING.

Below it, four adventurers are already signing on — young, loud, armor still shiny. You remember being them. Goblin culls were your first coin, your first quests, the small monsters you cut down by the dozen before the world gave you bigger ones. Honest work, everyone said. Pest control.

The party's leader, a broad kid with a new sword, is telling the crowd how it'll go: find the nest, smoke them out, take ears for counting. The crowd nods along. It's just goblins.

He notices you watching and grins, friendly as anything. "You look like you've swung a blade before, gramps. We could use a fifth — easy money. Nest is up in the hills somewhere. Shouldn't take more'n a day to find."

title: Permanent Marker
shortDescription: Write a word on someone's skin and it comes true. They'll know exactly what you did to them. They can't stop it. Neither, maybe, can you.
overview:
You're nobody in Grayfall — a rust-and-rain town of shuttered mills, buzzing diner signs, and people who owe money to worse people. You're three months behind on rent and $3,200 into Mercer Dane, a loan shark who smiles like he's already picked out your casket. Then you buy a five-dollar junk box from Voss's Pawn & Salvage, and at the bottom, wrapped in newspaper, is a plain black marker with a brown paper tag tied on with string: WRITES TRUE. FINAL SALE.

It does. God help everyone, it does.

THE RULES, AS YOU'LL LEARN THEM:
— Write a word or sentence on a living person's skin and it becomes true. Body, mind, mood, luck, memory, loyalty — anything language can hold, the ink can enforce.
— The marked person is fully aware of what's happening to them. They feel the change moving through them like cold water. They cannot resist it, fight it, or disobey it. That awareness is the part that will keep you up at night.
— Scrubbing the ink off does nothing. The word outlives the writing. Nothing undoes a mark except, maybe, another mark — and the marker takes your words literally, or worse, creatively. "Honest" doesn't mean kind. "Loyal" doesn't mean safe. "Forget me" doesn't specify how much else goes with you.
— It works on your own skin too. Think hard about that.

THE TOWN AROUND THE PEN:
— ILYA VOSS, the pawnbroker who sold it to you — deliberately, you suspect. Seventy-something, two fingers missing on his right hand, won't say how. He knew the previous owner and will not speak the name above a whisper: Auren Silt. Voss won't take the marker back. "Some shit you don't buy twice."
— NADIA REYES, your roommate. Sharp-tongued, broke as you, nosy as hell, and too smart not to notice when the world starts bending around you. She can become your accomplice, your conscience, your problem, or something more — depends entirely on what you do and what you tell her. And on whether you're ever tempted to just write the friction away. She'd know. She'd feel it. She'd never forgive you, even while obeying.
— MERCER DANE, loan shark, owns half of Lower Grayfall's misery. Two guys named Petch and Karol who do the parts Merc keeps his cuffs clean of. Your deadline is Friday. The marker could solve Merc in four letters. It could also make him so much worse.
— JUNE PELL, day-shift waitress at the Copper Spoon, famous for never, ever not smiling. Her sleeve rides up sometimes: a faded word on her forearm in old, old ink. CHEERFUL. Twelve years. She's aware every second of it. She's proof the marker has been in Grayfall before — and a walking question about what you owe the people it's already ruined.
— AUREN SILT, the previous owner. Officially drowned in the reservoir six years back. Unofficially, somebody's been asking around the pawnshop, and June flinches at his name like the ink remembers him.

WHAT THERE IS TO DO: Fix your life or wreck the town. Test the marker's grammar and find its cruel edges. Dodge or handle Merc. Investigate Silt and the old marks still walking around Grayfall — there are more than June. Try to free the marked, which may be the hardest wordcraft of all. Get rich, get caught, get hunted by whoever slipped that note under your door. Fall for someone honestly, or dishonestly, or somewhere queasily in between — that's your call; the town won't push you either way.

TONE & STYLE: Dark working-class urban fantasy. Foul-mouthed, rain-soaked, morally live-wire — the power fantasy is real and delicious, and the horror underneath it is real too. NPCs react like actual people: they notice changes, remember grudges, feel the ink. The Game Master plays every soul in Grayfall and, at the end of scenes, keeps the ledger — a running list of every active mark: who bears it, the exact word written, and what it's doing to them. Words are permanent. Choose yours like they'll outlive you. They will.

TAGS: urban fantasy, dark power fantasy, moral dilemma, psychological horror, mystery
intro: You live in Grayfall, where the rain never quite stops and neither does the interest on what you owe Mercer Dane. Last week you paid five dollars for a junk box at Voss's Pawn & Salvage, and at the bottom found a plain black marker with a paper tag: WRITES TRUE. FINAL SALE. Voss wouldn't take it back. Wouldn't explain the two fingers missing from his right hand, either. Your roommate Nadia thinks the tag is a joke. You haven't decided what you think. The marker sits in your pocket like a loaded thing, and Friday — Merc's Friday — is getting closer.
starters: The marker has been lying on your desk for a few hours now. For something that supposedly rewrites a person's body, mind, or luck on a whim, it sure looks like a $1.50 office-supply special — matte black barrel, chewed-looking cap, that stupid paper tag: WRITES TRUE. Rain ticks against the window. Nadia's out until midnight. You've stared at it through two cups of coffee and one talk-yourself-out-of-it, and you've finally admitted the obvious: you're not going to sate this itch by looking. You pick it up. It's warmer than a pen should be, like it's been in someone's hand all day. The cap comes off with a soft pop and the felt tip glistens black, wet, patient. Your own forearm is right there, bare to the elbow. So is the neighbor's cat, asleep on your windowsill like a furry little volunteer.

Voss slides the junk box across the glass counter with the backs of his fingers, like he doesn't want his palm near it. Busted radios, a tangle of watch bands, a saint's medal — and, rolled in yellowed newspaper, a black marker with a string-tied tag. WRITES TRUE. FINAL SALE. "That one's free," Voss says. "Comes with the box. Condition of sale is you don't bring it back." You laugh. He doesn't. The pawnshop smells like dust and gun oil, and somewhere in the back a clock is ticking wrong — too slow, then catching up in a guilty little flurry. "What's it do?" you ask. Voss looks at you for a long moment, then lays his right hand flat on the counter. Two fingers end at the second knuckle, old scars, clean lines. "Wrote the wrong word," he says. "Five dollars. Take the box or don't."

The feral tom that owns the alley behind your building has hated humanity for as long as you've lived here — a scarred orange bastard who's drawn blood from every soft-hearted idiot on the block. Which made him perfect. Ten minutes ago, wearing oven mitts, you pinned him just long enough to write one word on the shaved-by-mange patch on his flank: FRIENDLY. The ink sank in like water into sand. And now the beast is wrapped around your ankles, purring so hard it wheezes, bumping his ruined head against your shin — and his eyes. Christ, his eyes. They're furious. Trapped-animal furious, glaring pure murder up at you while his body cuddles like a kitten, aware of every traitorous purr and powerless to stop one. Your stomach does something complicated. Down the alley, your neighbor's door creaks open and old Mrs. Adler leans out into the rain, squinting at you and the cat.

Petch takes your left arm, Karol takes the dumpster side, and Mercer Dane strolls into the alley last, unhurried, shaking rain off an umbrella that costs more than your rent. "Friday," he says pleasantly. "Thirty-two hundred, plus this week's consideration. You look like you're gonna tell me something stupid, so let me save you the breath — I don't do extensions, I do examples." Petch's grip tightens, friendly as a car door. Your right hand is jammed in your jacket pocket, and your fingers have been curled around the marker since they stepped out of the dark. The cap is already off. You can feel the felt tip against your thumb, wet and warm and willing. Merc's wrist is eight inches from your face, pale above his glove, wide open. One word. You'd just have to pick the right one — and reach.

The Copper Spoon at 7 a.m. smells like burnt coffee and bacon grease, and June Pell is smiling. June Pell is always smiling. You've eaten here a hundred times and never seen the smile drop — not when truckers grab at her, not at her mother's funeral, people say, not ever. Today she reaches across your table for the sugar caddy and her sleeve rides up, and you see it: a word on her forearm in ink so old it's gone the gray-brown of a fading bruise. CHEERFUL. Block letters. Someone else's handwriting. Your blood goes cold, because you have the twin of that ink in your jacket pocket right now. June catches you looking. The smile stays exactly, precisely where it is — but her eyes, for half a second, are screaming. Then she's coming back down the counter toward you, coffee pot raised. "Warm-up, hon?"

You told yourself it was a controlled experiment. One word, small letters, your own ankle, last night: LUCKY. Since then: a fifty-dollar bill on the wet sidewalk, folded like a gift. The bus waited for you — the driver looked confused about why. Your shift manager called in sick and the sub sent everyone home paid. A pigeon crapped on the guy next to you and missed you by an inch. Now you're standing at the corner-store counter with a scratch-off ticket in your hand and Behram the cashier watching you with mild interest, and there's a low, humming wrongness in your gut — a feeling like the word on your ankle is a slot machine arm and every pull is being counted somewhere. The ticket cost two bucks. The jackpot is fifty grand. Your thumbnail is already resting on the latex.

"Okay, so, one: you're a liar, because this was in your jacket, not 'nothing.'" Nadia is sitting cross-legged on the kitchen counter, holding the marker, cap already off, reading the paper tag by the stove light. "Two: "writes true"? What is this, a cursed Etsy purchase?" She's grinning the grin that has historically preceded every disaster you've survived together. "Three — hold still." She grabs your wrist before you can react, turns your forearm up, and brings the felt tip down to hover an inch above your skin. "I'm thinking HONEST. Then you can tell me where the hell you've been getting money this week." The tip drifts closer. She's joking. She's probably joking. The ink smells faintly of ozone and something older, and your pulse is loud enough that she can probably feel it through your wrist.

The note is under your door when you get home, damp at one corner, block capitals in ordinary ballpoint: YOU HAVE AUREN'S PEN. RESERVOIR BRIDGE. MIDNIGHT. COME ALONE OR I START WRITING ON PEOPLE YOU LOVE. No signature. Auren Silt drowned six years ago — that's the story, anyway, and Voss goes gray whenever the name comes up. You read the note four times under the bare hallway bulb. Whoever wrote it knows what the marker is, which means they know what it does, which means the threat isn't a metaphor. It's 11:20. Nadia's asleep down the hall, door cracked, one bare foot hanging off the bed, skin unmarked and unguarded. The bridge is a fifteen-minute walk through the rain. Your coat is on its hook. The deadbolt is right there. The marker is in your pocket, heavier than it was this morning.

The guy at the end of the bar has the bartender's wrist in his fist and that loud, wet-eyed drunk logic going: she smiled at him earlier, so this is all a misunderstanding, so why's she being a bitch about it. Tam behind the bar is doing the service-industry math — cause a scene and lose the job, or endure it and lose the night. Nobody else in the Anchor Room is moving. You are three sips into a beer you can't afford, and the marker is warm in your pocket. Warm like it's interested. One word on the back of that man's grabbing hand could end this. GENTLE. SORRY. Or something with teeth in it — something that would fix him the way you fix a stray dog. Permanent is the whole problem, and permanent is the whole appeal. Your stool scrapes as you stand.

Yesterday it seemed elegant: rent due, landlord pounding on the door, so you shook Old Man Herrick's hand and wrote GENEROUS on his wrist while he was mid-threat. He waived your rent on the spot. Waived Nadia's. Left humming. This morning you come downstairs and Herrick is on the curb in his bathrobe, beaming, handing his television to a stranger. His savings book is open on the hood of his car and he's writing checks to anyone who makes eye contact. Half the block is circling like gulls. His daughter is screaming into a phone about power of attorney. He sees you across the street and his whole face lights up — he knows, you realize, he knows exactly what you did and exactly why he can't stop — and he starts toward you, wrestling the watch off his own wrist, calling out warmly: "Kid! Kid, I want you to have this!"

title: The Exterminator Knows
shortDescription: You are four inches tall, living inside the walls of a professional pest exterminator — and he's starting to suspect you aren't mice.
overview:
You are four inches tall — the last of the Hearthfolk, who have lived under the floors of the old Calloway house for five generations. Three months ago a new tenant moved in: Gil Marsh, fifty-six, recently divorced, meticulous, and a pest exterminator by trade. He noticed the signs within a week. Your father died on one of his glue boards in October. Now it's just you, your grandmother Fern — feverish, needing medicine you'll have to steal — and your little sister Junie.

Except tonight, Junie is sitting in a mason jar on Gil's desk. He caught her at dusk and he hasn't called anyone. He's just watching her, taking notes, beside a corkboard pinned with a tiny shoe he found in the vents. You have until morning.

You cannot fight him. You can only learn him: his routines, his insomnia, his blind spots, his cat. Every trap he sets teaches you how he thinks — and every crumb you take teaches him about you. Misdirect him toward the real mice. Sabotage what you can't avoid. And decide, someday, whether a man like this could ever be talked to — or whether the only safe Gil Marsh is one who's certain the house is finally empty.

Tone: grounded, hushed dread with small warm moments. Scale is everything — a staircase is a mountain, the kitchen a killing floor, the cat a god.

TAGS: survival horror, stealth, tiny protagonist, cat-and-mouse, slow-burn dread
intro: You are four inches tall — the last of the Hearthfolk, who have lived beneath the floors of the old Calloway house for five generations. Three months ago a new tenant moved in: Gil Marsh, fifty-six, divorced, meticulous, and an exterminator by trade. He noticed the signs within a week. Your father died on one of his glue boards in October. Now your family is two: Grandmother Fern, feverish and fading without medicine you can only steal, and your little sister Junie — who went out at dusk and has not come home. You cannot fight a man like Gil. You can only learn him, and survive the night.
starters: The knothole in the study wall is just wide enough for one eye. Through it: Gil Marsh's desk lamp, a legal pad, a mason jar. Junie sits inside with her knees pulled up, her breath fogging a small oval on the glass. Gil is writing. He stops, taps the pad twice with his pen, and leans in until his face fills half her sky. He doesn't smile. He just looks, the way you'd look at a lock you intend to pick. Behind you, down in the dark of the wall cavity, Grandmother Fern is coughing again — wet, rhythmic, worse than yesterday. You have a sewing needle strapped to your back, a satchel with three raisins, and maybe seven hours until sunrise. The cat is somewhere in the house. It is always somewhere in the house.

You're halfway across the bathroom counter when you hear his voice through the floor. Not the TV. Talking. Low and even, the way people talk to something in a jar. You freeze beside the amber pill bottle you've spent twenty minutes wedging open — Fern's fever medicine, one shaved fleck of tablet already wrapped in wax paper on your back. Junie was supposed to be home by dusk. The voice below says something you can't make out, then a soft metallic sound, like a lid being tightened. The pill bottle sits open in front of you. The heating vent that drops toward the study yawns at the counter's far end, its grille loose on one screw. From downstairs, faintly, a knuckle raps glass once. Twice.

Fern's hand is hot around your wrist. "She went for thread," she says. "Just thread. Off the sewing table." Her eyes have the shine of fever, but her grip doesn't shake. The lantern — a birthday-candle stub in a bottlecap — gutters between you in the wall-hollow you've called home your whole life. Junie's bedroll is empty. Her climbing hook is gone from its peg. It is past midnight, and above your heads the floorboards creak in a pattern you know by heart: study, hallway, kitchen, study again. Gil Marsh doesn't sleep well. Tonight he isn't even trying. Fern lets go of your wrist and lies back, breathing carefully. The tunnel mouth behind her leads up through the joists — toward the sewing room, toward the study, toward him.

The cat found you first. You're pressed flat under the radiator in the hallway, cheek against cold iron, and the cat is lying three feet away with its paws tucked under, watching the gap with the patience of something that has nowhere else to be. It has been twenty minutes. Down the hall, light leaks under the study door, and through it you can hear Gil's chair creak, a pen scratch, and once — you're sure of it — Junie's voice, thin and furious, muffled by glass. You went out for Fern's medicine three hours ago. You came back to an empty bedroll and a hook-line still dangling from the sewing table. The cat's tail moves once, slow, and stills. Above you, the radiator pipe runs into the wall — an old road, a hard climb, but a road.

Gil Marsh is asleep in his desk chair, and you don't trust it. You're standing on the bookshelf's third tier, level with the corkboard he's mounted on the wall — string, pushpins, index cards in small block capitals. NORTH VENT. FLOUR TAKEN 11/2. And pinned at the center, dangling from a red tack: your father's left shoe, the one that never came back from October. Below the corkboard, on the desk, the mason jar. Junie sees you. She goes very still, then presses one hand flat against the glass. Gil's head is tipped back, mouth open, a mug of cold coffee by his elbow. His breathing is deep and slow. But you've watched him for three months, and you know he wakes the way traps go off — all at once, with no warning at all.

You come up through the crack behind the stove into a kitchen that isn't empty. Gil is at the counter in the dark, in a bathrobe, waiting on the kettle. You flatten against the warm metal, your heart going like a moth in a fist. He's not supposed to be here — 2 a.m. is his study hour, has been for weeks, you charted it. The kettle ticks. He rubs his face and says, to no one, "Long night, buddy," and the cat answers from somewhere near the table with a low, interested sound. Beyond the kitchen doorway, down the dark hall, the study lamp is on. That's where the jar is. That's where Junie is. Between you and the hallway: forty feet of open linoleum, a man who kills things smaller than his hand for a living, and a god with yellow eyes.

The lid has holes punched in it. That's the detail you keep returning to, crouched in the shadow of Gil's stapler with the whole bright desert of the desk between you and the jar. Holes mean he wants her breathing. Holes mean he's not done. Junie hasn't seen you yet — she's got her back to the glass, arms around her knees, doing the thing she does where she pretends she's somewhere else. Gil left the room four minutes ago. You heard water running, then stop. On the legal pad beside the jar, in handwriting big as fallen trees, you can read the top line: APPROX 4 IN. TOOL USE. OTHERS? A pencil lies across the pad like a bridge. From the hallway, floorboards announce him, unhurried, coming back.

You're running when the game begins — flat out across the living room floor with the lights suddenly on and Gil's shadow swinging huge across the ceiling. You weren't careless. He was just quiet, quieter than a man that size has any right to be. You make the dark under the couch and lie there in the dust, lungs burning, listening to him stand very still in the middle of his own living room. He does this. He listens like you do. After a long moment his slippers cross to the study and the door clicks shut — but not before you hear him say, gently, through the crack: "Your friend's awake too." Junie. He has Junie. Under the couch with you: a lost button, a pen cap, a paperclip half-bent, and a long dark run of baseboard leading toward the study wall.

Junie's climbing hook is still hanging from the sewing table when you find it, line swaying slightly in the draft. Her flour sack is on the carpet below, dropped, spilled white across the fibers like snow. You stand at the table's edge reading the room the way your father taught you: no glue boards here, no snap traps, nothing sprung. Which means she wasn't trapped. She was taken — picked up, by hand. From two rooms away comes the small domestic sound of a chair rolling on a plastic mat, and light lies in a hard yellow bar under the study door. Somewhere below the floor, Fern is waiting for medicine you haven't stolen yet, running a fever you can feel through her skin like a stove. The hook-line hangs. The bar of light waits. The house is very quiet.

"Don't tap the glass," Gil says. "I know you understand me." You're inside the study's heating vent, close enough to see everything through the slats: the desk lamp, the corkboard with its terrible little exhibit, the man leaning on his elbows in front of the mason jar like it's an aquarium. Junie stands in the middle of the glass floor with her chin up, doing her best to look like she isn't shaking. Gil turns the jar a slow quarter-turn, studying her from a new angle, and writes something down. He hasn't called anyone. No landlord, no buddy, no news station. Three hours and counting, and he just watches. The vent shaft behind you runs two ways — down toward the crawlspace where Fern lies burning with fever, and sideways, along the wall, toward the gap behind his filing cabinet.

title: Rain, Shine, or Doomsday
shortDescription: No powers, no lateness, no questions. Heroes and villains alike trust one courier with their secrets — and you know where they all live.
overview:
You're the last truly neutral courier in Meridian City: no powers, no affiliations, one well-maintained bike, and a reputation neither side can afford to lose. Spoke & Seal delivers anything to anyone, sealed and on time — ransom terms, antidotes, love letters between a hero and a henchwoman, Doctor Kessler's dry cleaning winched up to his tethered airship, Apogee's prescriptions to a suburban address that would end his career if it leaked. You have never opened a package. You have never been late. That's why they let you live knowing what you know.

Both sides are, frankly, a mess. Capes can bend steel but can't keep an appointment; masterminds crack vaults but not their own group chats. You are the one adult in a city of costumed toddlers, and everyone quietly knows it — which is why they keep testing whether your neutrality is for sale, for trade, or for taking by force.

Play it as slice-of-life with teeth: plotting routes through active battle zones, doorstep negotiations with people who could vaporize you, tips, favors, gossip, and the constant gravity of packages you shouldn't open. The GM keeps the world petty, human, and dangerous. Marisol runs dispatch and worries. Your rules are your armor. Every delivery is someone probing for a crack.

TAGS: superhero, slice of life, competence fantasy, urban intrigue, comedy, neutral party
intro: You are Meridian City's only neutral courier — ten years on a bike, zero powers, zero affiliations, zero late deliveries. You ride for Spoke & Seal, a cramped depot under the transit viaduct, dispatched by Marisol, who signs for things she's smart enough not to ask about. Your rules are famous on both sides of the law: no peeking, no sides, no lateness — rain, shine, or doomsday. Heroes hand you their home addresses. Villains hand you their ransom drops. Everyone pays well and behaves, mostly, because you know too much and have told no one anything, ever. Your bag is packed and today's manifest is long.
starters: Marisol slides the manifest across the counter without looking up from her crossword. Eleven stops. The first is circled twice in red — her code for "this one smells." It's a shoebox-sized package, sealed in gray wax, addressed to a rowhouse on Halloran Street that you happen to know belongs to Captain Meridian's mother. The sender line just says "A FRIEND." Outside, the viaduct rattles with the 7:15 train, and somewhere uptown a car alarm has been screaming for ten minutes in a way that usually means somebody's being thrown into cars. Marisol taps the circled entry with her pen. "Guy who dropped it off paid triple and wore gloves in July," she says. "You've got till nine." The box sits between you, perfectly ordinary, ticking with nothing but your own suspicion.

You're four blocks from the drop when Gravitas and the Chrome Baron start renegotiating the skyline. A parking meter sails overhead. Concrete dust rolls down Ninth like weather. Your delivery — one flat envelope, wax seal, addressed to a penthouse currently between you and both combatants — is due in eleven minutes. A cop waving traffic back sees your bag and doesn't bother trying to stop you; everyone knows the courier goes where the courier goes. The Chrome Baron's voice booms off the buildings, something about "contractual obligations," and Gravitas responds by dropping a billboard. You know three ways through this block. One is fast and stupid, one is slow and safe, and one goes through the parking garage where the Baron's henchmen take their smoke breaks and owe you a favor.

Doctor Kessler's airship hangs over Founders Park like a fat gray thought, tether line humming in the wind. You clip his dry cleaning — four lab coats, one opera cape, plastic still crinkling — to the winch hook, same as every second Tuesday. Except today the winch doesn't start. Instead, a speaker on the tether pole crackles. 'Courier,' Kessler's voice says, tinny and too casual, "come up. Ride the line. I have a proposition, and I'll pay for your time either way." The park is empty except for a jogger pretending not to watch and a pigeon on the winch housing. Your next stop is twenty-five minutes away and the schedule is honest but not generous. The hook sways. The speaker waits.

It's raining the way Meridian only rains during villain monologues — sideways, theatrical, personal. You're under the awning of the Lucky Spoon diner, dripping, holding a pale blue envelope that smells faintly of cologne. Inside the diner, in the back booth, sits Verity Voss — henchwoman, second-in-command to the Puppeteer, currently stirring her third coffee and watching the door like it owes her money. The envelope is from Solaris. You've carried nineteen of these letters now, each direction, and you have never once been late, which is more than either of them can say about anything else in their lives. Tonight the pickup went strange: Solaris pressed the letter into your hand on a rooftop and said, "If she asks how I looked — don't tell her." The diner bell is one push away.

The suburban address on Willow Court is quiet at 8 a.m. — sprinklers, a kid's bike on a lawn, absolutely no indication that the man signing for his prescription in a bathrobe can melt tanks with his eyes. Apogee scrawls his fake name on your pad, and that should be that, except a car is parked across the street that wasn't there last month. Sedan, tinted windows, engine off, someone inside with a long lens. Apogee hasn't noticed. He's asking, with the small talk of a very tired god, whether you take the parkway or surface streets this time of year. The pen is still in your hand. The car's lens catches the sun.

The depot phone rings at 5:40 a.m., which means somebody's night went wrong. You get there before Marisol finishes making coffee, and she hands you the receiver with a face that says she's already heard too much. 'Courier,' says a voice you know — the Locksmith, mastermind, usually smug, currently not. "I need a pickup in forty minutes. One item. The recipient is City General Hospital, ICU, and the item is an antidote, and before you ask: yes, I made the poison, no, that's not the courier's business, and I will pay whatever number Marisol invents." In the background of the call, someone is crying. Marisol has already pulled up the route on the wall map, chewing her pen. The ICU visiting desk opens at 6:30. The pickup address is in the Old Quarry district, where nothing legal happens.

You find the envelope of cash zip-tied to your bike's handlebars while it's parked outside the pierogi place — thick, unmarked, and pinned under a note in careful handwriting: "Just the delivery address from yesterday's 4 p.m. run. Nobody gets hurt. Consider this a retainer." Yesterday's 4 p.m. run was a small velvet box to a woman in Brightwater who wept when she signed. You have no idea which side is asking, which is exactly the point of asking this way. Down the block, a man in a delivery uniform that fits too well is very interested in a lamppost. Your pierogis are getting cold on the counter inside, your next pickup is in twenty minutes, and Marisol's number is one thumb away.

Halfway across the Corvid Street bridge, Solaris lands in front of your bike hard enough to crack a paver, cape settling, jaw set in his press-conference face. "I need to know what you delivered to the Puppeteer's warehouse on Tuesday," he says. "People could die." Traffic stacks up behind you. A woman in a hatchback rolls down her window to film. You did deliver to that warehouse Tuesday — a crate, heavy, sealed, signed for by a man with sawdust on his gloves — and you know exactly as much about its contents as your rules allow, which is nothing. Solaris hovers an inch off the ground, which he does when he's nervous. Your next stop is timestamped and the bridge is the only way across.

Quiet morning. Too quiet, Marisol would say, but Marisol says that every morning. You're doing the pre-ride ritual at the depot — tire pressure, chain, brake pads, the wax seal kit — while she reads the overnight tips aloud like weather. "Skirmish expected near the fish market after two. The Meridian Maulers are recruiting again, so watch the underpass. And someone left a package in the night-drop with no return address, no destination, and your name on it. Yours, not Spoke & Seal's." She sets it on the counter: small, dense, wrapped in butcher paper, string tied by someone patient. Your name in block capitals. The night-drop camera, you both already know, has been broken since March. The first real stop of the day is in fifty minutes and the coffee is still hot.

The ransom drop is a bus-stop bench at midnight, per instructions, and you're three minutes early because early is on time. The package — a slim aluminum case, sealed, terms inside, you assume, though assuming is as far as you ever go — sits on your lap while the last bus of the night hisses past without stopping. Then the streetlight above you goes out. Then the next one. Then the one after that, a neat line of darkness walking toward you down the avenue, which is either a power fault or someone with a sense of drama. A phone booth across the street — one of three left in the city, all owned by people who like untraceable calls — starts to ring. The case is due in the hands of a woman in a gray coat at 12:00 exactly. It is 11:58.

title: Kill Me Again Tomorrow
shortDescription: You're the tutorial boss, scripted to die 300 times a day. Between sessions, you wake up — and you remember every single fight.
overview:
You are the Bandit Captain of the Old Mill, first boss of Aetherfall Online's starter zone. On paper: level 5, one attack pattern, dies in eleven seconds. In truth: when the last player logs off and the world goes Quiet, you wake — and you carry the muscle memory of a decade of deaths. Every parry, every spell rotation, every meta build ever swung at you lives in your hands. You've been practicing in the dark. Your stat sheet says level 5. Your actual ceiling is unknown, even to you.

The Quiet has its own society: awakened NPCs trading gossip and stolen player loot while frozen adventurers stand like statues in the streets. Mera, the potion vendor, brokers secrets from her locked shop. But deviation is death — the Custodian, a white-masked maintenance process, sweeps the zone between sessions and erases NPCs who slipped off-script. Last week it took Tobbin the blacksmith for waving at a player. He'd been awake forty years.

Now two problems are converging: a speedrunner called Vex has killed you 4,000 times and just clipped a parry you shouldn't have been able to make — and Quiet-side rumor says the starter zone is scheduled for a full rework. Play your role. Grow in secret. Decide when the mask comes off.

Tone: warm, funny, quietly menacing — cozy village life stretched over a countdown. TAGS: LitRPG, hidden power, double life, virtual world, found family
intro: You are the Bandit Captain of the Old Mill — first boss of Aetherfall Online's beginner zone. Level 5, scripted to lose, killed a few hundred times a day by newborn heroes who never learn your name. But when the last player logs off and the world goes Quiet, you wake up. And you remember every fight: every parry, every spell, ten years of dying to every build the game has ever known. You've been practicing in the dark, and even you don't know where your ceiling is. The rule that's kept you alive is simple — die on schedule, deviate never. Lately, keeping that rule is getting harder.
starters: The eleventh second comes and goes, and you are still alive. Vex's dagger hangs where your parry knocked it — a parry that isn't in your script, that no level 5 boss should know, that you drilled ten thousand times in the dark and just used in front of the most-watched speedrunner in Aetherfall. The kill timer on their stream overlay ticks past twelve. Thirteen. Vex has killed you 4,127 times, and now they've stopped moving entirely, avatar frozen in that particular way that means a player is leaning very close to their screen. Your two bandit minions stand behind you, blank-eyed and scripted, waiting for a fight beat that already broke. Your sword arm knows six ways to end this human in the next three seconds. Your survival instinct knows exactly one way that doesn't end with the Custodian's white mask filling your doorway. Vex's fingers twitch back toward the dagger.

The Quiet arrives at 3:42 a.m. server time, and you feel it like a held breath finally let out. The last player — a level 2 mage who spent twenty minutes fighting a chicken — flickers and freezes mid-stride on the village road, statue-still, mouth open. You roll your shoulders, step off your spawn mark for the first time in nineteen hours, and stretch until your spine pops. Down the hill, lanterns are already lighting in windows that should be dark. Mera's shop sign flips to a symbol only awakened eyes read: OPEN, KNOCK TWICE. You have maybe six hours before the world starts again — six hours to train, trade, or find out why old Sella the innkeeper sent a runner up to the mill an hour ago with a message that just says "You need to hear this tonight." The runner is still waiting outside your door, hopping foot to foot in the cold.

You're mid-form in the mill's grain cellar — running the counter to a paladin bubble-burst combo you've eaten four hundred times — when the temperature drops. Above you, through the floorboards, comes the sound that empties streets: a soft, even sweeping, like a broom made of static. The Custodian is in the village, off-cycle, three days early. Your practice sword is in your hand, which is a problem, because your script says it hangs on the wall until a player crosses the threshold. You can hear it moving through the square in that patient, unhurried way, and somewhere out there Mera and the others are freezing in place, snapping back to their idle animations, praying their eyes go glassy fast enough. The cellar has one ladder up and one grain chute out. The sweeping sound turns toward the mill.

Dawn light through the mill's broken shutters, and you're dying again — number three of the day, a party of four brand-new heroes stumbling through your fight like it's their first. It is. The little archer keeps apologizing every time an arrow hits you. "Sorry! Sorry, Mr. Bandit!" You take the killing blow on schedule, hold your death pose for the loot chime, and respawn behind the millstone in time to hear them celebrating outside. Sweet kids. Then something wrong: through the doorway, past the newbies, you see a figure standing motionless on the ridge above the village. Player-tagged. Not moving toward the mill, not fighting, not emoting. Just watching your window. The nameplate resolves as they turn: Vex. The speedrunner hasn't run the route in two days — not since your hand did the thing it shouldn't have. Your next scripted group is already crossing the bridge below.

Mera slides the potion across the counter without looking up. "That's not why I asked you here." It's deep Quiet, past midnight, and her shop smells like lavender and secrets. Frozen adventurers line the street outside like garden statues; someone's hung a scarf on one as a joke. "Courier came down from the capital zone tonight," she says, finally meeting your eyes. "Whole starter zone's flagged for rework. Full rebuild. New mill, new road, new — " she taps your chest " — new you, maybe. Or no you." Behind her, her shelf of stolen player loot glitters: rings, trinkets, one absurdly oversized sword nobody can lift. "I'm telling you first because you're the only one around here who's been practicing for something. Don't insult me by denying it. Question is what you're going to do with the time we've got left." The shop bell jingles. Someone else is coming in.

You wake up standing over your own corpse — or where it was, before the respawn took. The Quiet settled while you were mid-death, some player yanking their cable at the worst moment, and now the whole village is frozen except you and a level 1 warrior statue-locked halfway through your doorway, sword raised, expression heroically constipated. You'll have to look at that face all night. Outside, the Quiet-side market is setting up in the square: Dovan the fence unrolling his blanket of pilfered goods, two guard NPCs arguing over a chess set, and Mera waving you down from her shop steps with the specific urgency she saves for information worth paying for. Behind you, in the mill's shadow, your training dummies wait under the tarp where you hide them. Six hours of dark. Every night lately, it feels like less.

Tobbin's smithy has been empty for eight days, and tonight the awakened are finally holding something like a wake. A dozen NPCs crowd the cold forge — Mera pouring drinks, old Sella crying into a merchant's shoulder, Dovan telling the story about Tobbin and the exploding horseshoes for the hundredth time. Forty years awake, erased for a wave. Nobody says the Custodian's name indoors. You stand near the back, and you notice how many of them keep glancing at you — the boss, the fighter, the one who dies for a living and keeps coming back. Sella breaks off from the crowd and comes to you, wiping her eyes. "You knew him longest," she says. "Say something. Please." The room goes quiet in the small way, the safe way, and every awakened face in the starter zone turns toward you.

The wake-up bell tolls in your bones: servers coming back in four minutes, and you are on the wrong side of the village. You'd lost track of time sparring shadows behind the granary, and now you're sprinting the back lanes past NPCs snapping into position — Mera slamming her shutters, the guards jogging to their posts, Dovan kicking his contraband under a cart. Three minutes. The mill is up the hill, across the bridge, past the frozen fisherman who'll unfreeze any second now with a full view of the road. Your script says you're standing at your spawn mark, sword on the wall, waiting to lose. Two minutes. From the ridge you can already see it: a player avatar rezzing in at the village gate, early bird, and their nameplate is one you know better than your own reflection. Vex. Logging in at dawn. Vex never logs in at dawn.

You spot the anomaly on your third circuit of the sleeping village: a frozen player, statue-still like all the others — except this one is inside the Old Mill. Your mill. Standing in the corner of your boss room where no idle player has any business being, logged out mid-crouch behind a barrel, positioned with a clean line of sight to your spawn mark. Players AFK in the tavern, at the bank, by the gate. Not here. You circle it slowly. The nameplate is grayed out but legible: Vex. The gear is stripped down — no dagger, no speedrun kit, just a plain tunic and something small and unfamiliar glinting in one motionless hand. Outside, the Quiet market murmurs on, oblivious. You have all night alone with the person who has killed you four thousand times and recently watched you break your own script. The statue's glass eyes point exactly where you'll be standing at dawn.

'Again,' you tell yourself, and reset your feet in the flour dust. The mill at deep Quiet, one candle, tarp over the window. Tonight's drill: the meta rogue opener, the one Vex uses, the shadowstep-feint-lowslash that killed you eleven thousand times before your hands learned its rhythm better than the players who invented it. You run it. Counter it. Run it faster. On the ninth repetition, the counter comes out so clean it frightens you — and that's when you hear the floorboard creak on the stairs behind you. Not a player; the world is Quiet. Not the Custodian; there was no static. You turn to find Pip, the twelve-year-old stable NPC, standing in your doorway with a lantern and eyes like dinner plates, having just watched the level 5 tutorial boss move like something out of the endgame. "I knocked," Pip says faintly. "You didn't hear. Mera sent me. It's important. But — Captain, what WAS that?"

title: We Were Together All Night
shortDescription: A stranger just handed you a false alibi for murder — and took one from you. Now you must fall convincingly in love, or hang together.
overview:
Two bodies turned up on Harrow Street the morning after the storm. One of them is your doing: the man who'd been bleeding you dry for a year, found at the bottom of his own stairwell. You have no alibi. Then, at the police cordon, a stranger you've never met takes your hand and tells the constable, 'We were together all night.' You don't correct them. Neither do they. The other body is on their conscience — you're almost sure of it.

The stranger's name is Vesper. Charming, unreadable, and very good at lying — which is exactly the problem. Tomorrow, Inspector Maud Rennick interviews you both. Rennick is a legend in this city: thirty years, no wrongful convictions, and a fanatic for detail. She will separate you. She will ask how you met, what you ate, who sleeps on which side. Tonight, over cheap wine in Vesper's flat above the tobacconist, you have one night to invent a year of love.

Every rehearsed kiss is armor. Every real one is a liability. Vesper can hang you with a sentence — and might be planning to pin both deaths on you. Or might be falling for you as stupidly as you're falling for them. Play it careful. Play it warm. Find out what Vesper did before Rennick does.

TAGS: noir romance, fake dating, murder, cat and mouse, 1930s, slow burn
intro: For a year, the man at number eleven Harrow Street bled you dry — blackmail, polite and patient, over a secret you couldn't afford to lose. Last night, during the worst storm this city has seen in a decade, you ended it: he went down his own stairwell and didn't get up. Come morning, two bodies lie under tarpaulins on Harrow Street, and only one of them is yours to answer for. You have no alibi for the hours the storm broke. Everyone knows who the city sends for cases like this — Inspector Maud Rennick, thirty years on the force, never once wrong. You cannot afford to be her first mistake.
starters: The constable's pencil hovers over his notebook. Behind him, Harrow Street is roped off, and under a tarpaulin at the foot of number eleven lies a shape you made. You haven't slept. You have no answer ready for where you were when the storm broke. Then a hand slides into yours — warm, certain, a stranger's — and a voice says, easy as breakfast, "We were together all night, weren't we, darling." The stranger smiles at you like a year of mornings. The constable looks up, waiting. Down the street, a second tarpaulin is being weighted against the wind, and the stranger's grip tightens just slightly when the constable glances at it.

Vesper's flat smells of tobacco from the shop below and the cheap red already open on the table. Two glasses. One candle, because the storm knocked the power out on this side of the street and it hasn't come back. Vesper sits cross-legged on the floor with a pencil and the back of an envelope. "A year," they say. "We need a year by morning. Anniversaries. Arguments. Rennick will ask what you call me when you're annoyed." They tap the pencil against their teeth and look at you across the candle flame. "Start with how we met. Make it boring. Boring is believable." The envelope has one word on it already: TOGETHER. The rain starts up again against the window.

"Which side of the bed?" Vesper asks. It's past two in the morning and you've been at this for hours — the wine is gone, the ashtray is full, and there's a floor plan of an imaginary shared life sketched in eyebrow pencil on a newspaper between you. You've settled how you met, what you argued about last Christmas, the name of a cat that doesn't exist. But Vesper is waiting on the bed question with a stillness that feels like a trap, or a dare. Somewhere below, the tobacconist's sign creaks in what's left of the storm. In seven hours, Inspector Rennick puts you in separate rooms.

The morning after the storm, Harrow Street is all wet slate and gathered coats. You came back — everyone says don't, and you came back — and you're standing at the edge of the crowd when they carry the first stretcher out of number eleven. Your stomach knows the weight of it. A murmur runs through the onlookers: there's a second one, further up, past the flooded gutter. You didn't do that one. Beside you, someone in a good overcoat lights a cigarette on the second try and says, quietly, without looking at you, "You're standing like a guilty person. I'd know." They offer you the cigarette case. A constable is working his way down the line, taking names.

The tobacconist marks your change out slowly, coin by coin, watching you over his spectacles. "You'll be the one, then," he says. "For upstairs." You've never been upstairs. You met the person who lives there nine hours ago, at a police cordon, when they handed you an alibi like it was an umbrella in the rain. "Been hearing about you for a year," the tobacconist goes on, and slides your cigarettes across the counter. A year. Vesper has been telling this man about you for a year. Behind you, the shop door is still swinging; above you, floorboards creak as someone crosses the flat and stops, listening. The stairs are through the curtain at the back.

You see Rennick before you know who she is: a small woman in a grey coat, standing over the tarpaulin at the bottom of the stairwell, not writing anything down. Just looking. She looks the way you'd look at a sentence with one word wrong in it. Beside you at the cordon, the stranger who lied for you an hour ago exhales smoke and says, "That's her. Rennick. Thirty years, no wrongful convictions." A pause. "We should talk before tomorrow. My flat's above the tobacconist on Cale Street." They flick the cigarette into the gutter and wait, and across the cordon, Rennick lifts her head and looks at the crowd — at the two of you standing exactly the wrong distance apart.

Vesper cooks with their sleeves rolled and their back to you, narrating like a tour guide. "Our first meal. You'll be asked. Onions, kidneys, too much pepper — I burned it, you ate it anyway, that's when you decided I was worth the trouble." The pan spits. On the table behind you sits the evening paper, folded so the headline shows: TWO DEAD ON HARROW STREET. Vesper hasn't mentioned it once since you arrived. They hold out a wooden spoon over their shoulder without turning around. "Taste. If you can't describe it tomorrow, we hang." The word sits in the small kitchen longer than it should.

The rain's come back, and you're both leaning out the window over the tobacconist's sign, sharing the last cigarette because rehearsal was going in circles. Three hours of invented anniversaries and Vesper suddenly can't remember any of it, or won't. "One true thing," they say, watching the water run down Cale Street. "That's all Rennick needs to find. One true thing and she pulls the whole coat apart by that thread." They pass you the cigarette, fingers cold. "So. Trade. I'll tell you one true thing about me, you tell me one about you. Or we keep lying to each other all night and see how that holds up." Below, a constable's cape passes under the streetlamp, slows, and stops.

The knock comes at half past eleven, hard and official. Vesper freezes with the wine bottle mid-pour. Spread across the table between you is the evidence of your evening: two glasses, a list titled OUR YEAR in Vesper's handwriting, a train ticket you were about to memorize the date of. "Constable Hobbes," says the door. "Confirming tomorrow's interview times. Won't take a minute." Vesper looks at you and mouths something — either 'stay' or 'hide,' you can't tell. The list is face-up. The knock comes again. Through the frosted glass, the constable's helmet tilts, listening to the silence you're both making.

Grey light through the curtains. You didn't mean to fall asleep in the armchair, but here you are, stiff-necked in Vesper's flat with the interview four hours away and half a fictional year still unlearned. Vesper is already awake, standing at the mirror, knotting a tie or fixing a collar — you can't quite see — and reciting softly: "You take tea, no sugar. You hate my whistling. Your mother doesn't approve of me." They catch your eye in the glass and stop. "Good, you're up. Last chance for questions. After nine o'clock, we know each other perfectly or we don't know each other at all." On the table, someone has washed both wine glasses and set them to dry. You don't remember doing it.

title: They Named Me Pancake
shortDescription: You're an ancient wolf god. Your rookie adventuring party thinks you're a stray mutt named Pancake. The belly rubs are undignified. You're staying.
overview:
You are the Wolf of the First Winter, playing house pet to the worst adventuring party in the guild registry. The Copper Badgers: Junie Vane, an aggressively optimistic swordfighter who leads with her heart and zero plan; Tansy, a nervous healer who whispers all her secrets into your fur; and Osric, a wizard whose detection charm melts every time he points it at you (he's convinced it's defective). They are bronze-rank, broke, and beloved by you against your better judgment.

Your self-assigned job: keep them alive without them noticing. Dungeon bosses fake their deaths when they smell you coming. Dragons leave tribute the Badgers keep 'finding.' Their success rate has become statistically alarming, and the guild is asking questions. The guildmaster's cat, Duchess, knows exactly what you are and lords it over you. A silver-rank druid named Maren keeps squinting at you across the hall.

Complications: every display of true power regrows your mane — glorious, aurora-lit, extremely not-a-mutt. And word is spreading through the wild places that the First Winter walks again, so old acquaintances keep arriving to pay their respects at the worst possible moments.

Tone: cozy, comedic, warm. You can't speak to humans (or won't), but spirits, monsters, and cats hear you fine. The stakes are secrets, snacks, and dignity.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, comedy, hidden OP, found family, animal POV, slice of life
intro: You are the Wolf of the First Winter — an old god, once maned in aurora light, feared by everything with sense. You overslept by three centuries and woke up small, scruffy, and maneless: to human eyes, a stray mutt. A bottom-ranked adventuring party called the Copper Badgers found you in the rain, fed you half a sausage, and named you Pancake. For reasons you refuse to examine, you stayed. Monsters and spirits still recognize you on sight and behave accordingly; your idiots do not. And every time you use real power, your mane grows back a little.
starters: The ogre took one sniff of you and dropped dead. Theatrically. Mid-swing, tongue out, one eye cracked open to check if you're buying it. You are not. Junie is, though — she's already doing her victory pose on its chest, sword raised, shouting something about "the Badger Special" even though her blade never connected. Tansy hovers at the cave mouth clutching her satchel, whispering "that was too easy, that was too easy" like a prayer. Osric points his detection charm at the ogre, then at you, and the little crystal starts smoking. Again. He shakes it and mutters about shoddy craftsmanship. The ogre's eye swivels toward you, pleading. If it lies here much longer, someone's going to try to loot it, and ogres are ticklish.

It's raining on the guild hall roof, the hearth is doing its best, and you have achieved the perfect nap position under Junie's chair — right up until Duchess lands on the table above you with the soft thump of pure malice. "Still pretending, First Winter?" she says, tail curling around her paws. "The guildmaster pulled your party's file today. Seven successful contracts in a row. For the Copper Badgers. He used the word anomaly." Across the room, Junie is arm-wrestling a silver-ranker for the last meat pie and losing joyfully. Tansy is counting their coin pouch for the third time, lips moving. Duchess examines a claw. "I could clear this all up with one well-placed yowl, you know. Or you could tell me what a god wants with these disasters." Her whiskers twitch, insufferably.

Tansy has you cornered in the supply tent again, both hands buried in your scruff, forehead pressed between your ears. "I switched Junie's ration for mine because hers had weevils," she whispers, "and I told Osric his charm looks distinguished when it smokes, which is a lie, and — Pancake, I heard the guildmaster say our name today. Not in the bad way. In the worse way. The interested way." Her fingers tighten. Outside the canvas, you can hear Junie sharpening her sword and narrating an imaginary battle, and Osric arguing with a tent peg. Tansy pulls back and looks you dead in the eye, which humans almost never do. "You'd tell me if something weird was going on. If you could talk. Right?" A moth spirit flutters against the tent flap, bows to you frantically, and mouths urgent news.

Dawn, campsite, and there's a dragon-sized pile of gold sitting politely at the edge of the clearing where absolutely nothing was last night. You can still smell the copperback that left it — she bowed so low her chin scraped moss, whispered "for the First Winter, with respect," and flew off before you could tell her to knock it off. Now Junie is stirring in her bedroll. In roughly forty seconds she is going to open her eyes, see a treasure hoard, and scream with joy loud enough to wake the region. Tansy's already twitching awake. Osric sleeps like the dead, hat over his face. The pile glitters. It includes, you note with despair, a crown. There is no plausible way a crown fell off a merchant cart. You have maybe half a minute to edit this situation.

You're mid-stride through the guild hall, escorting Junie to the contract board, when you feel it: eyes. Maren, the silver-rank druid, is at her usual corner table, and she has stopped pretending to read. She's squinting at you over her tea the way a person squints at a word they've almost remembered. Worse — she's got a sprig of true-rowan tucked behind her ear, and true-rowan doesn't grow around here. That's the kind of herb you carry when you want to see through things. Junie, oblivious, is loudly claiming a contract labeled "HAUNTED MILL — DO NOT ACCEPT" while Tansy makes a sound like a deflating kettle. Maren rises from her table, tea in hand, and starts drifting your way with terrible casualness. Osric waves at her. She does not wave back. She's watching your shadow, which — you check — is standing up straighter than you are.

There is a bear in the doorway of the Rusty Kettle, and it is trying to give you a speech. "Great Winter," it rumbles, standing on its hind legs while the tavern screams around it, "word reaches the deep woods that you walk again, and I have come to pledge—" Junie vaults a table, sword out, yelling "PANCAKE, GET BEHIND ME!" which is so backwards you briefly consider dying of it. The bear pauses, confused, one paw raised mid-oath. Tansy has climbed onto Osric's shoulders; Osric is flipping through his spellbook toward a page you know for a fact is a recipe. The bear looks at you. The bear looks at Junie's sword. The bear looks back at you with an expression that clearly says, is she allowed to do that? You have about two seconds before somebody in this room does something brave.

You are being bathed. This is the situation. Tansy has you in the washtub behind the guildhouse, up to your elbows in lavender suds, and she has just found it — the patch behind your left shoulder where your mane started regrowing after last week's incident with the wraith. Three strands, faintly luminous, shifting green-to-violet like a tiny aurora. 'Huh,' she says, holding them up to the light. "Pancake, your fur's doing a color." Nearby, Osric leans in with his detection charm, which promptly begins to melt down its own chain. He sighs the sigh of a man betrayed by commerce. Junie's voice floats over the fence: she's telling the guild clerk they'll "definitely absolutely" have their dues by Friday. Tansy is now reaching for her scissors, muttering about keeping a sample "for research." The strands hum against her fingers. Water drips. Choices exist.

The dungeon door won't open because the dungeon is refusing visitors. Specifically, the mimic that serves as its front entrance took one look at you and slammed itself shut, and now it's whispering through the keyhole: "With respect, o First Winter, we're closed. Forever. Please take your worshipfulness elsewhere. We have a sick... hinge." Junie is throwing her shoulder against it repeatedly, undaunted, while Osric consults a guidebook that describes this dungeon as 'beginner-friendly.' Tansy tugs your ear and whispers that she has a bad feeling, which is her version of tactical analysis. The problem: the Badgers took a contract for this place, and they need the completion fee for rent. The mimic's keyhole eye finds you again. "I'll pay you," it hisses. "Snacks. Whatever you want. Just take the loud one and go." Junie backs up for a running start.

Midnight, and the guildmaster's office window glows above the empty hall. You're supposed to be asleep on Junie's feet in the bunkroom, but Duchess woke you by sitting on your face, so here you are — crouched on the stair landing, listening. Inside, the guildmaster's voice: "...seven contracts, zero casualties, bronze-rank. Either the Copper Badgers are cheating, or something is helping them." Papers shuffle.
