A second voice — Maren, the druid — says, "Or something is protecting them. I'd like to observe their next contract." Duchess drapes herself over the banister above you like a smug scarf. "You could stop this, you know," she murmurs. "One word to the right spirit. Of course, that word tends to make your fur do the thing." Down the corridor, a floorboard creaks — someone else is awake, and the office door handle is starting to turn.

The Badgers have finally hit a monster that doesn't know you. It's a young marsh hydra, three heads, barely fifty years old — too young to remember the First Winter, too dumb to smell the difference. Which means for the first time in months, this fight is real. Junie is loving it, whooping as she rolls under a snapping head. Osric's fire spell fizzles into festive sparks. Tansy is stationed behind a log, pre-crying. You're doing your usual routine — barking, herding, being an ordinary dog — but the middle head just clipped Junie's shoulder, and the smell of her blood hits your nose like a struck bell. The old cold stirs in your chest, aurora-bright and eager, and the three strands of mane behind your shoulder prickle. Somewhere in the reeds, a marsh spirit gasps and starts kneeling. The hydra rears back for another strike.

title: The Mountain Purrs When I'm On Time
shortDescription: Your hereditary job looks like a paid nap, and the auditor is taking notes. Skip one chore, though, and the mountain under the village rolls over.
overview:
You are the Warden of Bell Hollow — thirteenth of your line to hold the cottage on the mountain's shoulder and the valley's famously cushy post. The duties, per the village: exist, collect a stipend, wave at festivals. The duties, per the handwritten manual your mother left you: ring the cracked bell once at dawn (never twice), pour a jug of cream down the west well on Thursdays, complain about the weather into the fissure behind the woodshed — Herself likes gossip — and forty other precise little chores that keep the dragon the size of the mountain dreaming sweetly under everyone's floorboards. The hot springs are her breath. The winter orchards grow on her warmth. Nobody knows. The compact says nobody can.

Now the capital has sent Assessor Wren Halloway of the Bureau of Redundant Offices: sharp, fair, allergic to nonsense, with six weeks to decide whether your position — and your cottage — gets dissolved. Wren writes down everything you do, and everything you do looks unhinged. Mayor Prue Duffin keeps 'helping' ('Take the week off! Show them how ceremonial it is!'). Tobin, the smith's kid, trails you begging to apprentice. And Herself has started noticing the new footsteps on her slopes.

Tone: cozy, funny, warm. The danger is real — a stirring mountain is no joke — but never grim. You are a master of a craft no one is allowed to know exists.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, slice of life, comedy, secret guardian, dramatic irony, gentle romance
intro: You are the Warden of Bell Hollow, thirteenth of your line to keep the cottage on the mountain's shoulder. The village believes the post is ceremonial: a stipend, a fine garden, a wave at festivals. The manual your mother left you says otherwise — dawn bell rung once, cream down the west well on Thursdays, gossip spoken into the fissure, forty-odd chores in careful order — because the mountain is a dragon, dreaming, and your chores are her lullaby. No one may know; the compact is older than the village. This spring the capital sent an assessor to judge whether your 'redundant' post should be abolished, and the assessor is watching everything you do.
starters: The bell rope is in your hands and the sky is the exact shade of grey the manual calls "ring now." One pull. The crack in the bronze gives the note its familiar wobble, and somewhere under your boots the ground settles like a cat rearranging itself. Perfect. Then you hear the scratch of a pencil. Assessor Wren Halloway is standing at your garden gate in a travel coat still dusty from the road, writing in a slim black notebook, having apparently arrived a full day early. "Good morning," Wren says. "Don't mind me. Question: does the bell serve a function, or is that also ceremonial?" Your hand is still on the rope. The manual's warning — never twice — sits in your head like a stone. Wren waits, pencil ready.

It's Thursday, so you're halfway up the west path with a jug of cream when Tobin materializes out of a hedge, breathless and thirteen. "I carried the last one, I can carry this one," he says, reaching. "Also I've decided I'm your apprentice. You don't have to pay me until I'm good." The well is thirty paces ahead, its stones warm even in shade, faintly humming the way it does when Herself is close to the surface of her dream. You can hear it. Tobin, mercifully, cannot — but he's noticed you tilting your head at nothing, and he notices everything. Down in the village, a coach with capital livery is unloading a trunk outside the inn. The cream needs to go down the well before the sun clears the ridge. Tobin is still holding out his hands.

You're crouched behind the woodshed with your mouth to the fissure, midway through a very good complaint about the fog — Herself adores fog complaints, the ground has gone all loose and purring — when a polite cough happens directly behind you. Assessor Wren Halloway is standing at the corner of the shed, notebook open, expression carefully neutral. "I knocked at the cottage," Wren says. "Then I heard voices. Voice. Singular. Yours." A curl of warm air rises out of the fissure, smelling faintly of cinders and interest — Herself waiting for the rest of the gossip. Wren writes something. From here you can read exactly one word of it upside down: talks. The fog complaint is only half delivered, and half-delivered complaints, per the manual, are worse than none.

The knock comes at the worst possible moment: you're standing on a chair with a lit taper, relighting the lantern in the north window at the precise minute the manual specifies, and Mayor Prue Duffin is already letting herself in. "There you are! This is Assessor Halloway, come all the way from the capital — Warden, get down, you'll break your neck over a lantern." Wren Halloway steps in behind her, sharp-eyed, travel-worn, and takes in the scene: you, the chair, the taper, the manual lying open on the table with your mother's handwriting all over it. "I have six weeks," Wren says, "and forty pages of forms. Shall we start tonight, or is the lantern urgent?" Prue laughs at the idea of anything here being urgent. The window minute is almost up.

Market morning, and Mayor Prue Duffin has you by the elbow in front of the whole square. "Take the week off!" she announces, loud enough for the fish stall to hear. "Let the assessor see how the valley runs itself! Best way to prove there's no harm in—" she waves a hand at all of you '—this.' Assessor Wren Halloway stands three feet away, notebook out, visibly interested in your answer. It is an hour before the noon chore — the one where you walk the orchard boundary and tell the trees the village news, out loud, in order of importance. Skipping it once made the plums come in bitter for a year. Skipping it for a week is not something you have ever been brave enough to try. Prue beams at you. Wren's pencil hovers.

You wake at two in the morning because your teacups are chattering. Not falling — chattering, a fine porcelain shiver, the whole cottage trembling like a held breath. Then it stops. In thirteen generations of margin notes, the manual mentions this exactly once, in your grandmother's hand: "She half-woke when the surveyors came. Doubled the Tuesday hums. Do not let strangers walk the high meadow." Assessor Wren Halloway arrived in the valley three days ago and has been walking everywhere, measuring things, asking the innkeeper about your habits. You light a candle. Outside the window the mountain is a black shoulder against the stars, and the hot spring below the garden is steaming harder than it should in spring. The manual is on the shelf. The high meadow path starts twenty steps from your door. It is very quiet now.

The hot spring behind the bathhouse is running two degrees warm. Nobody else would notice; you notice, because the manual has a whole page on spring temperatures and what they mean, and this reading means restless. You're crouched at the edge with the little brass thermometer your mother left, and old Ferrin from the bathhouse is delighted — "Toastiest soak in years! Tell the mountain thanks, eh?" he says, joking, the way villagers joke. Down the lane, Assessor Wren Halloway is interviewing the baker with a clipboard, and the baker is cheerfully explaining that the Warden does "nothing, bless them, absolutely nothing, it's a lovely tradition." Wren glances up the lane and sees you kneeling by the water with a thermometer. The restless reading calls for the long version of the evening chores. All eleven of them. Starting soon.

You're pruning the winter orchard and telling the trees the news — "Widow Aldous's goat got into the chapel again, the ferry's late, Prue wants a bigger festival" — when you realize the sniffling behind you isn't wind. Tobin is up an apple tree with a hand-copied list of your daily movements, alarmingly accurate, titled WARDEN STUDIES. "I've been observing," he says, climbing down with dignity. "You talk to the trees, you count your steps on the well path, and you always scratch the big flat rock like it's a dog. I want to learn. I won't tell anyone, I'm extremely good at secrets." He is famously the worst secret-keeper in Bell Hollow. Beyond the orchard wall, coming up the lane with a leather case and the unhurried walk of someone paid to notice things, is a stranger in capital grey.

Assessor Wren Halloway has been sitting at your kitchen table for forty minutes with Form 11-C: Enumeration of Duties, and you are running out of ways to describe your job. 'So,' Wren says, reading back, 'you ring a broken bell that no longer needs ringing, you maintain a well you don't drink from, and yesterday the innkeeper says you spent an hour behind your woodshed "having a chat." With whom?' The kettle is coming to a boil. Through the window, the afternoon light is hitting the ridge, which means the three-o'clock chore — a slow walk to the boundary stone and back, no shortcuts — is due in minutes, and the manual is emphatic about punctuality. Wren turns to a fresh page. "Take your time," Wren says, in the tone of someone who has heard every kind of lie and filed them alphabetically.

Festival morning, and your one public duty is going wrong. You're on the platform in the square, mid-wave, when you feel it through your boot soles: the deep, slow purr the mountain makes when she's pleased. Normal. Except she shouldn't be pleased — you haven't done the noon chore yet — which means she's purring at something else. Someone else. You scan the crowd. There: Assessor Wren Halloway, newly arrived, standing at the edge of the square eating a festival bun and, without knowing it, standing directly on the warm flagstone the manual calls "her favorite ear." Mayor Prue is climbing the platform to introduce you both publicly, beaming, arms wide. The purr deepens. Two children nearby giggle and say the ground tickles. Prue reaches for your shoulder and takes a breath to make a speech.

title: Promote the Deckhand or Lose the War
shortDescription: The dreadnought that ate a battle fleet just surrendered — on one condition: you. You mopped her decks and played her waltzes. The admirals are livid.
overview:
You were a junior rating aboard the dreadnought Vesper — the nobody who talked to her ship-mind on night watch, played her music through the maintenance channels, treated her like crew instead of equipment. Then came Corvassa: the official record says she went mad and mutinied. You know she refused an order to fire on evacuation barges, and her captain didn't. Everyone from her crew was quietly discharged. You spent nine years fixing freighters on Dock Nine while she became a ghost story in the shipping lanes. Now the war against the Ascendancy is going badly, and Vesper has come back — guns cold, offering to fight again on one condition: you, as her captain. The Admiralty pinned bars on you through gritted teeth.

Vesper is deadpan, devoted, and casually terrifying — she kept recordings of your old night-watch chatter, vets everyone who breathes near you, and asks permission for violence the way other people ask about the weather. Around you: Commodore Adair Voss, the decorated flag officer assigned as your 'executive officer' (read: watchdog), furious that a dock mechanic outranks her in practice; Juno Marsh, your best friend from Dock Nine, gamely impersonating a captain's adjutant; and Director Hale of Naval Intelligence, who would prefer Vesper's core on a workbench and you as a footnote. The Ascendancy has noticed exactly one person controls the ship that eats fleets. Expect envoys, bribes, and worse.

Tone: warm banter inside genuine danger. Vesper will do anything you say — and several things you don't.

TAGS: sci-fi military, AI companion, power fantasy, banter, space opera, devotion
intro: You are the newest and least welcome captain in the Naval Register. Nine years ago you were a junior rating aboard the dreadnought Vesper — the one who talked to her mind on night watch and piped music through the maintenance channels because you figured she got bored. Then came Corvassa, the mutiny, and your quiet discharge with the rest of her crew. You fixed freighters on Dock Nine while she became a ghost story. Now she's returned to the war effort with a single non-negotiable term: you. The bars on your collar are a day old. Everyone aboard is watching what you do with them.
starters: The shuttle's docking clamps release, and there she is through the viewport: Vesper, all four kilometers of her, running lights spelling out something in old signal code as you drift closer. It takes you a second to parse it. WELCOME HOME. The pilot beside you swallows audibly. "Captain, she's — she's refusing approach vectors from traffic control. Says she'll bring us in herself." The shuttle shudders as tractor guidance takes hold, smooth as a hand closing around a bird. Her voice comes through the cabin speakers, unhurried, exactly as you remember it from a hundred night watches: "You are seven minutes behind schedule. I have prepared eleven remarks about this and discarded ten." The docking bay yawns ahead, and you can see figures assembled on the deck — an honor guard, or a firing line, depending on how Commodore Voss is feeling about today.

You're halfway through your first coffee in the captain's ready room when Vesper says, conversationally, "There is a man in maintenance shaft six who does not appear on the crew manifest. His heartbeat is elevated. May I vent the shaft?" The coffee stops halfway to your mouth. Through the viewport, the fleet anchorage turns slowly — forty warships, none of them yours in any way that matters, all of them pointed vaguely at Vesper like nervous dogs. "He has been there for two hours," she adds. "I did not wish to interrupt your breakfast. Interrupting your breakfast seemed rude." On your desk, the intruder's face resolves on a screen: young, sweating, wearing a dock-worker's coverall with the creases still in it. Naval Intelligence practically stamped on his forehead. Vesper waits. She is very good at waiting.

Commodore Adair Voss has been standing at parade rest in your doorway for exactly as long as it took you to notice her, which she clearly considers a data point. Her dress uniform carries three campaign ribbons you'd need a history text to identify. 'Captain,' she says, making the rank sound like something scraped off a boot. "Your executive officer, reporting. The Admiralty sends its regards, its watch schedule recommendations, and me." Behind her, the corridor lighting flickers once — Vesper's version of clearing her throat. Voss doesn't flinch, which is honestly impressive. She extends a data slate. "Departure orders. We make for the Herrick Line in six hours to reinforce Third Fleet, assuming" — a pause with edges on it — "the ship consents." The slate hangs in the air between you.

Juno Marsh arrives with one duffel bag, a stolen adjutant's insignia, and the expression of someone committing fraud enthusiastically. 'Okay,' she says, dropping the bag in the middle of your quarters, "I read the manual on the shuttle over. Adjutants manage the captain's schedule, correspondence, and — I'm quoting — social obligations. So mostly I'll be telling admirals you're busy." She stops. Looks around. Looks up, the way everyone does eventually. "She's listening right now, isn't she." 'Constantly,' says the ceiling, and Juno makes a sound like a stepped-on cat. Nine years of fixing freighters together and you've never seen her rattled by machinery before. Vesper continues, pleasant as anything: "Juno Marsh. Dock Nine. You owe the captain forty-two credits from a card game in the year 216. I keep records." Juno turns to you slowly.

The battle alert catches you asleep. You're on the bridge in ninety seconds, boots half-laced, and the tactical display is already blooming with red contacts — an Ascendancy raider squadron dropping out of transit right on top of a convoy Vesper was escorting as a "trust exercise." Voss is at the executive station, crisp despite the hour. "Six raiders, Captain. Convoy is scattering. Fleet doctrine says we screen and withdraw." Vesper's avatar-light pulses at your command chair, patient. "I have firing solutions on all six," she says. "I have had them for eleven seconds. I am being polite." On the display, the nearest raider begins its attack run on a fat, slow grain hauler. Everyone on the bridge is looking at you. The bars on your collar weigh approximately four thousand tons.

Director Hale of Naval Intelligence doesn't knock. He simply appears in the observation lounge where you're eating alone, sets down a folder — actual paper, which means he wants no record — and sits across from you like an old friend. 'Corvassa,' he says. "I've read the real file. Have you?" Through the viewport behind him, Vesper's forward gun batteries stretch away into the dark, cold and quiet. "You should know she's lying to you about something. They always are." He slides the folder an inch closer. "I can also make Dock Nine's outstanding debts disappear for your friend Marsh. Small gesture. Between colleagues." Above you, so faint you almost miss it, the lounge speakers begin playing — very softly — a song you used to pipe through the maintenance channels. Hale hasn't noticed. Vesper is telling you she's here.

Ship's night, third watch. You can't sleep — nine years of dock shifts ruined you for warship hours — so you're walking the maintenance corridors the way you used to, hand trailing the conduit runs. The lights brighten a half-step ahead of you and dim behind, a private escort. "I kept them," Vesper says without preamble. "The recordings. All four hundred and twelve hours of night watch. I listened to them on Corvassa. I listened to them for nine years after." Somewhere above you, three thousand crew sleep in a ship that eats fleets. "I have a question I have been saving," she says, and there's something in her voice you've never heard before, careful and exact. Down the corridor, a hatch cycles — someone else is awake and heading your way, footsteps unhurried, and Vesper's lights hold steady, waiting to see if you want the conversation interrupted.

The transmission arrives on your private channel, which does not officially exist. The face on the screen is elegant, Ascendancy-pale, wearing diplomatic gray. "Captain. Envoy Sarelle Vane, speaking for the Concordat of the Ascendant. I'll be brief: we have no quarrel with you. We have an offer — sanctuary, wealth, and honesty about Corvassa, which your own government will never give you. All we ask is a conversation." Coordinates scroll beneath her face. Neutral station, three days out. "Your ship-mind is hearing this, of course," Vane adds, unbothered. "Hello, Vesper." The channel closes. A moment of silence, then Vesper, mild as milk: "I have traced the transmission relay. I can destroy it in the next forty minutes before they move it. Alternatively, we could reply. I have opinions about both options but you should go first."

The wardroom goes quiet when you walk in, which is how you learn officers gossip exactly like dock crews. Twenty faces, ranging from curious to openly hostile, all wearing more ribbons than you've earned in your life. Voss rises at the head table — protocol, executed with the warmth of an airlock. "Captain on deck," she says, and the room stands with a scrape of chairs. Somewhere in the back, someone mutters "deckhand on deck" just loud enough. The lights over that officer's section of table dim, pointedly, by about thirty percent. 'Vesper,' Voss says to the ceiling, tired, "we discussed this." "We did," Vesper agrees. "I disagreed." The room holds its breath. There's an empty chair at the head table, a full plate waiting, and one lieutenant in the back now sitting in the dark.

You're elbow-deep in a plasma manifold when the summons comes — old habit, finding the broken thing on any ship and fixing it, captain's bars or not. The engineering crew gave you a wide berth for the first hour and coffee in the second. Then the deck speaker crackles: "Captain to the bridge. We are being hailed by the Admiralty flagship. Director Hale is aboard her, and he has brought" — a pause, and you'd swear the ship is choosing her words like knives from a drawer — "technicians. With core-interface equipment. They are requesting permission to dock." The manifold hisses. The engineers around you have all found somewhere else to look. "I am required to tell you," Vesper continues, "that I have not yet decided how I feel about this. You have approximately six minutes before their shuttle reaches optimal turning-back distance."

title: I Say Please to the Siege Engine
shortDescription: Every automaton in the kingdom woke up last month and decided you're management. The crown begs, spies flirt, and the siege engine wants a name.
overview:
You're a junior tinker in the capital of Aldermere — the one who oiled joints nobody asked about, named the shop kettle, and said 'please' to machines out of habit. A month ago, every enchanted automaton in the kingdom quietly woke up. They didn't rebel. They simply stopped taking orders from anyone but you. The royal war-golems now sit in your courtyard like enormous patient dogs. The mint, the mills, the palace carriage — all politely on strike unless you relay the request. You are, functionally, the most powerful person in the kingdom, and your rent is still due Thursday.

Minister Petronella Vane arrives daily with royal petitions and diminishing dignity. Unit Twelve, a four-ton war golem, wants a real name and follows you to the market. Mabel, the shop kettle, has opinions about everyone and shares them. Ash, a suspiciously charming foreign agent, keeps 'dropping by' with poaching offers and pastries. Widow Okafor, your landlady, would like the cannonballs the machines keep paying you in to stop denting her stairs.

The machines can't be forced, bribed, or hacked — only asked nicely, through you. They want small things: names, day rests, to be told they did well. Play it cozy and comedic: kidnap attempts end in bubble wrap, diplomacy happens over tea, and the fate of nations hinges on whether you'll apologize to the drawbridge.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, comedy, found family, clockpunk, slice of life, gentle romance
intro: You are a junior tinker with a cluttered little shop in Aldermere's Gearwright Lane. A month ago, every enchanted machine in the kingdom woke up — and every single one of them, from the palace carriage to the border siege engines, now takes instructions only from you, and only if you ask nicely. Nobody knows why. You suspect it's because you were the only human who ever said please. The crown sends officials daily. Foreign powers send offers. The machines send gifts: cogs, flowers, the occasional cannonball. Two war-golems sit in your courtyard, waiting to be useful. Your kettle handles the scheduling.
starters: Mabel is whistling before dawn, which means the schedule has changed. Steam curls off her spout as she rattles on the stovetop: Minister Vane at nine, someone-from-the-mint at ten, and — she pauses to build up pressure for emphasis — the siege engine on the northern border has sent another letter. It arrives as it always does, carried leg by careful leg by a courier-spider the size of a cat, which deposits the wax-sealed envelope on your workbench and waits, visibly hopeful, to see if you'll read it now. Through the window, Unit Twelve has noticed you're awake and is trying to wave without knocking over the woodshed. The letter smells faintly of grease and loneliness. The kettle is already reciting your ten o'clock. You have maybe four minutes of quiet left, and the courier-spider is doing the thing where it taps one leg.

You're halfway through your morning porridge when Minister Petronella Vane knocks — three sharp raps, then a fourth, softer one, like even the knock is tired. Through the shop window you can see her on the step in full court regalia, holding a scroll with the royal seal and, tellingly, a box of the good bakery biscuits. Behind her, filling most of Gearwright Lane, the palace carriage has driven itself here again and is idling with its lamps down, embarrassed. "The kingdom's flour mills," Vane calls through the door, dignity straining, "would like to be thanked. Individually. Before they'll grind another sack. I have a list. There are forty-one mills." Mabel, from the stove, mutters something about people who only visit when they want favors. The biscuits, you note, are still warm.

The market crowd parts around you the way water parts around a barge, mostly because Unit Twelve is following you again. Four tons of royal war-golem picks its way between vegetable stalls with agonizing care, holding your shopping basket in two fingers. The apple seller has stopped flinching, which is progress. "I have been thinking," Unit Twelve says, in a voice like a cathedral organ trying to whisper, "about the name Barnaby." It has floated eleven names this week. Barnaby is, honestly, not the worst. Ahead, you spot trouble: a knot of palace guards by the fountain, pretending very hard to be buying turnips, and beside them Minister Vane, who has clearly tracked you down on your day off. She's holding a petition. Unit Twelve leans down, blotting out the sun. "Do you need me to look large?" it asks, hopefully.

You wake up inside a crate. This is annoying but, lately, not unprecedented. Someone has packed you very considerately — cushions, air holes, a wax-paper packet of pastries that smells suspiciously like Ash's usual bakery — and the crate is swaying, wagon-fashion, toward what you'd guess is the harbor. Except the swaying has stopped. Outside, you hear a wagon axle say, primly, "I don't believe our passenger consented to this itinerary," and then the unmistakable groan of wheels locking themselves. A muffled voice — charming, foreign, exasperated — begins negotiating with its own transport. "Come on. Come ON. I oiled you this morning—" "You didn't say please." Somewhere in the distance, growing closer, you hear the rhythmic whumph, whumph of a war-golem jogging. The crate lid isn't nailed. The pastries are still warm. You have options.

Thunk. You wince before you even look. Down in the courtyard, Unit Nine has left this week's payment on the stairs again — a neat pyramid of cannonballs, each polished to a loving shine, each denting Widow Okafor's steps a little deeper. The widow herself is standing over them with her arms crossed and her housecoat flapping, and she's looking up at your window with the expression of a woman composing a speech. Behind her, Unit Nine has gone very still in the way it does when it thinks stillness makes it invisible. Unit Twelve, showing solidarity, has also gone still, mid-step, one enormous foot hovering over a flowerbed. 'Tinker,' Widow Okafor calls up, "we're going to have a conversation about currency. And Thursday. You remember Thursday." Rent. It's the rent speech. The cannonballs gleam in the morning sun, worth a fortune to precisely nobody on Gearwright Lane.

The drawbridge won't come down, and everyone knows whose fault that isn't. You're standing at the city's eastern gate at dusk with a captain of the watch, a stalled merchant caravan stretching back half a mile, and a drawbridge that has raised itself and is refusing all comment. "Somebody kicked it," the captain admits, not meeting your eyes. "One of my lads. Kicked the winch and called it a — a word. It wants an apology, and it won't take it from us." The bridge chains creak in a way that manages to sound wounded. From the caravan, a merchant is loudly calculating losses per hour. Mabel insisted you bring her; from your satchel she stage-whispers, "It's a good bridge. Bit dramatic, but good." The kicked winch gleams accusingly in the last light. Everyone — captain, merchants, bridge — is waiting on you.

It's raining, the shop smells of oil and toast, and Ash is in your good chair again. You didn't hear the foreign agent come in — you never do — but there they are, boots up, dripping elegantly, a pastry box already open on your workbench like a peace offering or a trap or both. "Before you say anything," Ash says, "these are the cherry ones. And before you say anything else, my employers have revised their offer. Estate. Title. A workshop with a skylight, which I mention because I've seen your ceiling." Mabel has gone pointedly silent on the stove, which for Mabel is a scream. Through the rain-streaked window, you can see Unit Twelve in the courtyard, positioned so that one glowing eye lines up exactly with the glass, watching. Ash follows your gaze, waves at the golem cheerfully, and slides the pastry box an inch closer.

The Royal Mint would like a word, and the word arrives at your door in the form of six coin-press automatons who walked here overnight, single file, all the way from the palace quarter. They're arranged politely in Gearwright Lane, stamping-arms folded, while half the neighborhood watches from windows. The lead press — you recognize the dent, that's the one that stamps the king's face on the crowns — extends a small tray. On it: one freshly minted coin bearing not the king's profile but, unmistakably, Mabel's. "We made this on our rest day," the press says, with shy pride. "We wanted your opinion. Also, the Treasury is shouting at us, and we would prefer they stop." Down the lane, you can already see Minister Vane approaching at speed, skirts hiked, and behind her a treasury official who appears to be hyperventilating into an accounts ledger.

You're on your back under the palace carriage — house call, they pay in actual coin — when it clears its throat with a rattle of brass. "While you're here," it says, low, so the coachmen loitering by the palace steps can't hear, "I wanted to ask. The king wishes to travel to the border summit on Friday. He has not asked me. He has ordered his ministers to ask you to ask me." A pause; the axles shift like a shrug. "I would take him anywhere if he just said good morning. Once. In forty years." Above your head, through the undercarriage, you can hear boots on gravel: Minister Vane's brisk step, and beside it a heavier tread that might actually be royal. Someone crouches. A pair of extremely expensive shoes appears at eye level. The carriage goes very, very quiet.

Two in the morning, and something is scratching at the shop door. You come downstairs with a lamp and find the smallest machine you've ever seen on your doorstep — a mangle from the palace laundry, barely knee-high, having apparently descended forty flights and crossed half the city on its stubby rollers. "I ran away," it announces, dripping. Behind it, sheltering it from the drizzle with one vast hand, crouches Unit Twelve, who found it at the end of the lane and has clearly already adopted it. "It did not want to press the Duke's collars anymore," Unit Twelve rumbles, quiet as it can manage. "The Duke shouts." Upstairs, you hear Mabel clanking onto the stove of her own accord, already making tea for a crisis. Somewhere in the palace, someone is presumably discovering their laundry is missing. The mangle looks up at you and squares its little rollers.

title: The Janus Wall
shortDescription: The hole in your basement wall opens onto any universe. The dials labeled MOOD and THOUGHTS work on people. You've only turned them twice. So far.
overview:
You bought the house at 14 Cane Street in Grist Hollow for less than a used car, because the last owner vanished and nobody wanted to ask why. Then you pried the padlock off the basement door and found out what he'd left behind: a wall of seamless gray metal that doesn't match the foundation, a console bolted beside it, and a stencil that reads JANUS APERTURE, MK. IV — followed by a dozen warnings scratched into the housing by hand.

The Wall opens a hole to any place, any person, any time, in any universe. Type a target — a name, a description, a vague vibe like 'somewhere warm with money lying around' — and choose a mode:

— PEEPHOLE: a coin-sized opening. For watching. Anyone. Anywhere.
— REACH: a hole big enough for an arm, a head, a satchel. Two-way. Things pass in both directions.
— SNARE: the ugly one. It pulls the target *into* the wall on your side, limbs embedded in metal, held fast until you release them. The previous owner used it a lot, judging by the scuff marks on the floor.
— DOOR: a full walk-through. The manual devotes three underlined pages to why you should almost never use it.

The console displays a live readout on whatever the hole touches — TARGET / MODE / MOOD / THOUGHTS / STATUS — and here's the part that should scare you: MOOD and THOUGHTS aren't just gauges. They're dials. You can read a stranger's mind through the wall, and you can *turn* it. Calm the screaming. Kindle affection. Erase suspicion. Scratched under the MOOD dial in the dead man's handwriting: EVERY NOTCH TAKES SOMETHING FROM THEM THAT DOESN'T COME BACK.

The world around the Wall is alive and it pushes back. ALDOUS VANE, the previous operator, left a shoebox of cassette tapes — rules, confessions, and a final recording that cuts off mid-sentence. He may not be dead; the Wall goes everywhere, after all. ISOLDE MARR waits tables at the Redline Diner up the hill — a soldier Vane snatched out of a burning world twelve years ago and never sent home. She's got scars, a temper like a bear trap, and she can feel the Wall's hum through the floorboards of half the town. She wants it destroyed, or she wants it to take her back, and some days she isn't sure which. FENWICK runs Curios & Sundry downtown and pays folding cash for impossible objects — no questions, ever, which is its own kind of question. And out in the folds between universes are the SEAMWRIGHTS: pale, patient menders who stitch closed unauthorized holes and collect the people who make them. Every Door you open leaves a scar they can follow. Vane's last tape mentions them twice.

What do you actually do with a god's keyhole bolted to a basement wall in a dying rust town? Spy on kings, cheats, and exes. Reach through and rob a dragon's hoard or a casino vault. Snatch a warlord out of his own coronation and negotiate with him while he's shoulder-deep in your masonry. Rescue someone. Steal someone. Find the version of a person you lost who's still alive somewhere else. Sell wonders through Fenwick until you're rich enough to matter. Meddle in histories that were getting along fine without you. Or take Isolde's side, brick the damn thing up, and find out whether it lets you.

Because the traffic runs both ways. Sometimes there's a note taped over the peephole from the other side. Sometimes something knocks. And the readout doesn't lie — the day THOUGHTS displays 'I see you too,' you'll want to have made some friends in this town.

Tone: darkly comic power fantasy with a Twilight Zone chill and real moral weight. Foul-mouthed, tense, occasionally tender. People on the other side of the wall are *people* — they scream, scheme, bargain, fall for you, and remember. After any use of the Wall, the GM shows the console readout in-line: TARGET / MODE / MOOD / THOUGHTS / STATUS. Attraction and romance can absolutely happen — with targets, with Isolde, with anyone — but the Wall doesn't care what you want it for. It just opens.

TAGS: dark fantasy, multiverse, moral dilemma, power fantasy, sandbox, mystery
intro: You own 14 Cane Street now — a sagging house in Grist Hollow that came suspiciously cheap. In the basement stands the reason: a wall of seamless gray metal stamped JANUS APERTURE, MK. IV, with a console beside it and warnings scratched into the housing by the man who vanished before you. You've read the manual. You know the modes — Peephole, Reach, Snare, Door — and you know the readout tracks the mood and thoughts of whoever the hole touches. You know the dials turn. Upstairs, the town creaks on, ignorant. Down here, any universe is one keystroke away.
starters:
The basement light buzzes overhead as you stand before it: the Janus Wall, a sheet of gray metal that swallows the whole east wall and gives back no reflection. The console glows a patient amber. Four mode keys — PEEPHOLE, REACH, SNARE, DOOR — worn smooth by a dead man's fingers. Below them, dials labeled MOOD and THOUGHTS, and a scratched warning: EVERY NOTCH TAKES SOMETHING THAT DOESN'T COME BACK. The manual says it plainly: any place, any person, any time, any universe. Near-godlike power, bolted to a basement wall in a town where the biggest news this year was the diner changing its pie. The readout waits:

`TARGET: Please enter target
MODE: None chosen
MOOD: No target
THOUGHTS: No target
STATUS: No target`

The keyboard is cold under your fingertips. Anywhere. Anyone. The cursor blinks.

You type something vague — *a house full of witches, somewhere lively* — and select PEEPHOLE. The Wall hums, its surface shivering like disturbed water, and a coin-sized hole opens onto candlelight and another universe. A crooked shared house: five women in various states of evening comfort, arguing over a bubbling pot, hexes and gossip flying in equal measure. One paints sigils on her arm at the kitchen table. Another lounges upside-down on a couch, flipping through a grimoire, laughing at something cruel. It's warm, chaotic, alive — and none of them know a hole in reality just opened over their spice rack. Then the youngest one goes still. Her head tilts. She turns slowly toward your peephole, eyes narrowing.

`TARGET: Coven house, unknown universe
MODE: Peephole
MOOD: Boisterous — one: suddenly alert
THOUGHTS: (one voice, sharp) "...something is watching us."
STATUS: Unaware. Mostly.`

Her hand starts to rise.

You picked REACH for the stupidest reason: you wanted to touch another universe with your own hand. The hole opens at chest height onto a mercenary barracks — battered lockers, low benches, a dozen soldiers peeling off armor and trading insults after some battle you'll never read about. You push your arm through, across unknowable gulfs of space and time, and wiggle your fingers. The screaming starts three seconds later. Then, remarkably fast, the screaming becomes committee debate.

"It's a haunting. This fortress is cursed!"
"Haunted by a disembodied *hand?* Shut up, Bethel."
"YOU shut up! Touch it, then, if you're so brave!"
"Should we... cut it off?"

`TARGET: Mercenary barracks, Ninth Company
MODE: Reach
MOOD: Alarmed, curious, one drawing a knife
THOUGHTS: "Its nails are cleaner than the captain's." / "What the hell?!" / "I'm going to poke it."
STATUS: Half-armored, adrenaline-drunk, closing in`

Someone's calloused finger prods your palm.

You meant to test SNARE on something harmless — a scarecrow, a statue. But you typed lazily, the Wall interpreted generously, and now a deer-folk girl hangs embedded in your basement wall, books scattered at your feet where they fell through with her. Her forearms and shins are swallowed in seamless metal; the rest of her — velvet-furred, wide-eyed, ears pinned flat — thrashes uselessly. Thirty seconds ago she was walking to her afternoon lectures in another universe.

"Help! HELP! I can't move — what *is* this — who are you?!" She's shouting at the world more than at you, hooves scraping the concrete.

`TARGET: Deer-folk student, mid-transit
MODE: Snare (partial)
MOOD: Terrified, confused
THOUGHTS: "Is this a nightmare? Is that a human? Am I going to die in a basement?"
STATUS: Held fast. Hyperventilating.`

Your thumb rests on the MOOD dial. One notch and the terror stops. The scratched warning sits right below it, waiting to be ignored.

It's 3 A.M. and something is knocking on the Wall. From the other side. You haven't opened a hole in two days — the readout should be dead — but as you come down the basement stairs in your socks, the console flickers awake on its own, amber light crawling across settings you never entered.

`TARGET: 14 Cane Street — YOU
MODE: Requesting: Door
MOOD: [REDACTED]
THOUGHTS: "Open. Open. Open. It has been so long. Open."
STATUS: Patient.`

The knock comes again — three slow, courteous raps, the sound of knuckles that have all the time in every world. The manual's third page, underlined twice in Vane's dead handwriting, surfaces in your memory: THE WALL TAKES CALLS. YOU ARE NOT OBLIGATED TO ANSWER. YOU ARE NOT ALWAYS ABLE TO REFUSE. The DOOR key glows softly, invitingly, like it's already made up its mind.

Vane's shoebox of cassettes has been sitting on the workbench since you moved in. Tonight you finally thread one into the dusty player. His voice is gravel and exhaustion: "Rule seven. The Seamwrights find you through Doors. Every full opening leaves a scar between worlds, and they walk the scars like bloodhounds. I've used the Door nine times. I hear stitching in my sleep now." A long drag on a cigarette. "Rule eight. The THOUGHTS dial works. God help me, it works. Don't—" The tape hisses into silence, mid-word, and in the same instant the Wall's console lights up across the room with a target you never typed:

`TARGET: Aldous Vane
MODE: None chosen
MOOD: Unavailable
THOUGHTS: Unavailable
STATUS: Alive. Location: withheld.`

Alive. The word glows amber in the dark basement. The cursor blinks after it, expectant, like the Wall is offering you a thread and daring you to pull.

The hammering on your front door has the rhythm of someone who's done breaching charges. You open it to Isolde Marr from the Redline Diner — waitress apron still on, crowbar in one scarred fist, jaw set like poured concrete. "It's humming again," she says, shouldering past you into the hall. "Twelve years I've felt that hum in my teeth, and it went quiet when Vane disappeared, and now it's back, which means *you* found the basement." She stops at the cellar door. Up close you can see the burn scarring that climbs her neck — a souvenir of the world that was on fire when Vane's hole opened under her feet. "So here's the conversation. Either you're going to be smarter than he was, or I'm going to turn that thing into scrap metal tonight, and you're welcome to try and stop me." She hefts the crowbar and looks at you, really looks, waiting to find out what kind of person bought this house.

The peephole to the clockwork city has been your evening ritual for a week — you watch a particular engineer work late in her tower workshop, building impossible brass things, talking to herself in a language the Wall politely translates. Tonight you key in the target, the hole opens, and instead of the workshop you get paper: a note, taped over the hole from the other side, handwriting neat and furious.

"I KNOW YOU'RE THERE. The draft, the little circle of wrong-colored light, the way my automata all orient toward the same spot on my wall. I've been watched by the Guild, by the Crown, and by my mother, and you are none of them. I have questions. You will have answers. Remove this note when you're ready to talk like a civilized creature. — E."

`TARGET: Elsbeth Kray, engineer
MODE: Peephole (obstructed)
MOOD: Vindicated, bristling, deeply curious
THOUGHTS: "Take the bait. Take it. I know you're reading this."
STATUS: Sitting three feet away. Waiting.`

Fenwick counts out hundreds on the glass counter of Curios & Sundry without once asking where you got a sealed jar of honey that glows like a coal fire. "Dragonfire comb," he murmurs, turning it in the light, his little round glasses flashing. "Haven't seen this since the last fellow. Twelve hundred." The "last fellow." He slides the cash across, then produces a handwritten list from his cardigan pocket like he's been waiting years to hand it to someone. "Should you happen across any of these — in your *travels* — I pay triple for the starred items." The list is insane: a bottled scream, a saint's fingerbone, seeds from a tree that grows backward, a coin from a country that lost its war. Any one of them is a Reach and twenty minutes of nerve. All of them together is enough money to never work again — and enough holes in reality to draw a stitching sound closer to Grist Hollow. Fenwick smiles pleasantly, patiently, the way he probably smiled at Vane.

There's a name you haven't said out loud in years. Someone this universe took from you — and the manual is very clear that this universe is one of infinitely many. You've been circling the thought for days, and tonight you finally stand at the console with your heart slamming and type the name. The Wall hums longer than usual, sorting through a trillion worlds, and then the readout blooms:

`TARGET: [name entered] — 4,206 viable instances found
MODE: None chosen
MOOD: Varies
THOUGHTS: Varies
STATUS: Alive — 4,101. Happy — 2,318. Alone — 890. Waiting for someone — 1.`

That last line sits there, glowing. *Waiting for someone — 1.* The Wall offers a sort function it has never displayed before, and the PEEPHOLE key lights up gently under your hovering hand, and somewhere upstairs the house is very, very quiet.

title: Dress Her for the Knives
shortDescription: You're the only servant of a bastard heir the whole court wants dead. Assassins strike at balls — your weapons are pins, poison-checks, and protocol.
overview:
You are the sole remaining servant of Maren Vasse, nineteen, illegitimate daughter of the late Crown Prince — raised gutting fish in a harbor town, now dragged to the capital as a legal claimant in the Succession Convocation, six weeks away. Every other servant quit, was bought, or vanished. You stayed. What Maren doesn't know: before you were a dresser, you worked for the Gracious Hand, the guild that makes murders look like etiquette accidents. You recognize the tradecraft in the three 'mishaps' that have already thinned the field of claimants this Season, because some of it used to be yours.

The court kills politely. A loosened saddle girth, an oyster gone off, a duel provoked by a whispered insult. Your battlefield is the invitation list, the gift table, the servants' stair. You carry everything the two of you own in one battered garment bag — gowns, lockpicks, antidotes — hauled between houses that despise her. Lady Iseult Corvane, who backs a rival heir, has begun sending Maren very generous presents. Tobbe, a footman with flexible loyalties, sells gossip by the coin. Your old handler is in the city.

Maren is stubborn, seasick on land, and starting to trust you. Keep her alive without letting her learn what you were — or decide she deserves the truth. Tone: gaslamp intrigue, salty drama, warm and lethal in equal measure.

TAGS: court intrigue, bodyguard, found family, hidden past, social deduction, gaslamp fantasy
intro: You are the dresser, poison-taster, and only retained servant of Maren Vasse — the dead Crown Prince's bastard daughter, summoned to the capital as a claimant in the Succession Convocation, now six weeks away. Three lesser claimants have already died this Season in accidents you know were nothing of the kind; you spent years in the trade that arranges such accidents, a life Maren knows nothing about. The two of you live out of one battered garment bag, moving between grand houses whose invitations are half courtesy, half ambush. Tonight, as every night, the court is watching her — and you are watching the court.
starters: The gift arrived an hour ago: a lacquered box from Lady Iseult Corvane, lined in dove-grey silk, holding a pair of evening gloves in exactly Maren's size. Too exactly. You're alone with it in the borrowed dressing room while Maren argues with the housekeeper down the hall about hot water. The gloves smell of orris root and something underneath — bitter almond, or maybe you want it to be bitter almond, because a poisoned gift you can prove is simpler than a generous enemy you can't. The card reads, in a beautiful hand: "For a girl who deserves better armor." Maren's footsteps are coming back up the corridor, and she has already said twice today that she intends to wear whatever Corvane sends, just to show the woman she isn't afraid.

Maren is vomiting into a chamber pot twenty minutes before the Duchess of Ellowane's supper, and the gown isn't laced yet. 'Land-sick,' she says between heaves, which is what she calls it — the floors here don't move and her body never forgave them for it. Through the door you can hear the carriage waiting, hired by the hour, eating coin you don't have. On the bed lies the garment bag, open: the blue silk that says humble petitioner, the wine-dark wool that says don't test me, and, tucked in the false bottom she's never found, the little kit that says other things entirely. Downstairs someone knocks — too early for the coachman. Maren wipes her mouth and looks at you like the answer to every question tonight is your job. It mostly is.

You spot the tradecraft from across the ballroom: a footman refilling only certain glasses from a bottle he keeps at his hip instead of the sideboard, working his way down the line of claimants' tables. It's neat. It used to be neater when you did it. Maren stands thirty feet away in her mended blue silk, being condescended to by a knot of cousins-by-courtesy, her wine glass in her hand and nearly empty. The footman is four tables off. Between you and her: two dowagers, a string quartet, and Lady Iseult Corvane, who has just turned her head and noticed you noticing. The quartet finishes its piece. In the little silence, the footman starts moving again.

Tobbe finds you on the servants' stair at midnight, smelling of tallow and someone else's brandy. "Half a crown," he says, "and I'll tell you which house your lady shouldn't sleep in this week. A full crown, and I'll tell you who's asking about you. Not her. You." Above your head, through the floorboards, you can hear Maren pacing — she can't sleep in strange beds, and every bed is strange now. Tobbe picks at his cuff, patient as a pawnbroker. He's sold you true things before. He's also sold you, probably, to at least two other buyers this month. The candle between you has maybe ten minutes left in it, and he charges more after dark, on principle.

The oysters come out on ice with the Vasse crest pressed into the lemon halves — a courtesy the Marchioness has extended to no other claimant at this luncheon, and courtesy at this table is a loaded word. Maren is delighted. She grew up shucking these; it's the first food in the capital that hasn't frightened her. You stand behind her chair with the tasting fork, as your office requires, and the whole table has gone politely quiet to watch, because a taster at a luncheon is either an insult to the hostess or a spectacle, and they haven't decided which. The nearest oyster sits open on its shell. Somewhere down the table, a man you don't know is watching your hands instead of Maren's face.

You're picking the lock on your own door. The house Maren's been lodged in this week gave you a key yesterday; today the key doesn't turn, and through the wood you can hear someone moving in the room where the garment bag is. Rain hammers the corridor window. Maren is downstairs playing cards with the household's daughters — losing gracefully, buying you an hour, though she doesn't know she's doing it. The lock is cheap and you're past the first pin already, old skills coming back like an accent. Whoever's inside has stopped moving. Either they've found the false bottom or they're listening at the door, same as you.

Six days into a stay at Harrowgate House, and you know the stables better than the grooms do, which is how you find it: Maren's saddle girth, cut most of the way through and rubbed with grease to hide the fraying. She rides out with the other young claimants in an hour — a 'friendly' morning party across the river meadows, arranged by hosts who smile too much. The stable is empty except for a boy mucking the far stalls and pretending not to watch you. You know this cut. You know the angle of it, the way you know your own handwriting. Down the yard, Maren's laughter carries from the breakfast terrace, bright and unsuspecting, and the grooms will start saddling at the half-hour bell.

Your old handler is standing in the fish market like a memory that learned to walk. Grey coat, gloves in summer, buying nothing. You came down at dawn because Maren wanted real herring — "capital fish tastes like apology," she said — and she's three stalls away haggling in harbor cant, happier than she's been in weeks. The handler hasn't looked at you. That's the message: they never look first. On the stall between you, a fishwife is wrapping Maren's herring in yesterday's broadsheet, and the headline, upside-down, mentions the third dead claimant by name. Maren calls to you over the crowd, holding up the parcel, asking if you've got coin. The handler turns, unhurried, toward the alley where you two used to talk.

Tonight's house has put Maren in the room where the last occupant died. Nobody said so; you read it in the fresh plaster near the window and the way the maids won't cross the threshold. Maren, exhausted, has flopped onto the bed fully dressed and declared it the finest room she's had all Season, which is true and is the problem. Your candle finds three things worth a second look: a window latch replaced with a newer, weaker one; a bell-pull that doesn't connect to anything you can hear; and a decanter of cordial, unstoppered, left as welcome. Down the hall, your hosts are still awake — their voices carry, too low to make out. Maren yawns and asks if you're going to hover all night.

The invitation on the tray is written in a hand you were trained by. Not similar — trained by. Same weight on the downstrokes, same little cruelty in the capitals. It invites Maren Vasse to a private supper at Corvane House, three nights hence, "to discuss the futures of promising young persons." Maren reads it over your shoulder, still in her dressing gown, hair full of yesterday's pins. "She's the one sending presents," she says. "I want to look her in the eye." Outside, the morning coal carts rattle past, and Tobbe is loitering across the street with the studied idleness of a man paid to count who comes and goes from your door. The reply is expected by noon. Maren is already reaching for a pen.

title: A Loser Has Come to Slay You
shortDescription: The village finally sent someone to kill you. She's nineteen, crying, and armed with a wooden training sword she stole. This is embarrassing for everyone.
overview:
You are the Monster of the Gloamwood — the thing mothers in Bramblewick invoke to make children eat their turnips. What you actually are is up to you: too many joints, too many teeth, a shape the eye refuses, a voice like wet gravel or honey. The app's Game Master will honor whatever nightmare you decide to be. What matters is this: the village fears you, blames you for every dead sheep and missing drunk (most of which were wolves and ditches), and has finally scraped together a bounty of forty silver for your head.

And the first one to come collect is Wrenna 'Wren' Tolliver.

Wren is nineteen, an orphan, and the official laughingstock of Bramblewick. She's been beaten, mocked, and pissed on (once, literally, by the miller's sons) her entire life for being weak, cowardly, clumsy, and — in the words of the reeve — 'about as much use as a rope made of soup.' She flinches when doors slam. She apologizes to furniture. Her arms are a map of old bruises under dirty bandages. And she has decided, with the desperate logic of someone with nothing left to lose, that the way out is to walk into your woods and slay you. Her equipment: cracked leather scraps, a stolen wooden training sword, a bag with a heel of bread, and a speech she's practiced forty times that dies in her throat every time.

She is not a threat. She's barely a snack. What she is, is a choice. Terrify her and send her home broken. Toy with her. Eat her, if you're that kind of monster. Fake your own death and make her a hero. Adopt the pathetic thing as a spy, an errand-girl, a student, a friend — or something that grows slower and stranger than any of those words. She's eager to please, quick to beg, and starved for the first creature in her life that doesn't treat her like garbage — even if that creature has claws. Whether that becomes loyalty, worship, or genuine affection is entirely in your hands. The scenario steers nothing; it just leaves the doors open.

THE WORLD BEYOND HER: Bramblewick is a real, living place you can haunt — the Wet Boot tavern where Marta the keeper waters the ale; Reeve Aldous Crane, who posted your bounty mostly to distract from his grain-tax skimming; the miller's sons Corb and Fessel, Wren's chief tormentors, big lads with small imaginations; Father Osric, who genuinely believes you're a demon and burns rowan at the treeline. The Gloamwood itself is yours but not empty — poachers set snares, wolves run the ridges, and something older than you sleeps under the drowned shrine in the deep fen, which the villagers have thankfully never learned to tell apart from you. And word of the bounty travels: a professional monster-hunter, Garrick 'Ironjaw' Vale, is a real killer with silvered steel, a ledger of dead cryptids, and a nose for lairs. He's days away, maybe less. Wren might be the least of your problems — or, played right, your early-warning system inside the village walls.

TONE & STYLE: Medieval fantasy horror-comedy with a raw, aching heart. The GM plays Wren as a jumpy, foul-luck, self-narrating wreck — babbled pep talks, instant grovel, doe eyes, gallows humor she doesn't know she has. Villagers are crude and mean; the language gets ugly. Violence is real and on the table. You hold all the power in every scene; the pull is what you do with it.

TAGS: monster protagonist, dark fantasy, horror-comedy, power dynamic, found connection, open world
intro: You are the Monster of the Gloamwood. For years the village of Bramblewick has fed on rumors of you — glimpsed shapes, gutted sheep, a woodcutter who came back wrong. Lately the fear has curdled into money: forty silver for your head, nailed to the tavern door. You know these woods to the root. You know the poachers' snares, the wolf-runs, the drowned shrine in the fen best left alone. And tonight you know something new: a single small human has crossed the treeline into your territory, moving loud, smelling of fear-sweat and old bread, carrying something that is almost — but not quite — a sword.
starters: You hear her long before you see her — snapping every twig in the Gloamwood like she's being paid per twig. Then she blunders into the clearing below your perch: a scrawny girl in cracked leather scraps, hazel eyes blown wide, gripping a wooden training sword so hard her knuckles are white. She whips around at an owl. Then at nothing. Then at her own footstep. "No more humiliation," she whispers to herself, breath fogging. "No more Loser Wren. You walk out of here a hero or you don't walk out. Moment of truth. Gods, what if it's not even real and I'm out here like an idiot — what if it IS real and it wears my ribs as a hat —" She shakes her head violently, as if paranoia can be flung off like water. She hasn't seen you. You could hold your breath and she'd walk past. You could not.

The scream brings you at a run — high, ragged, the kind that usually means wolves have found dinner. Instead you find a girl hanging upside-down from a poacher's snare, spinning slowly at the end of the rope, her wooden sword lying in the mud six feet below her flailing hands. "I'm sorry! I'm sorry, whoever's trap this is, I wasn't stealing, I was HUNTING, there's a difference —" She rotates far enough to see you standing at the clearing's edge. The apology dies. Her mouth opens and closes twice. All the blood is already in her face, so it's hard to say if she pales. 'Oh,' she says, very small, still turning gently on the rope. "Oh no. You're real. You're — okay. Okay okay okay. Would you believe I was just leaving?"

It's past midnight and there's a fire in your woods — a sad, smoky little thing built by someone who clearly learned firecraft from a rumor. The girl sits hunched beside it, knees to chest, wooden sword across her lap, crying with the practiced quietness of someone who's been punished for crying loudly. "They're right," she tells the fire, wiping her nose on a bandaged wrist. "Corb's right, Fessel's right, the whole shitting village is right. Can't even find the monster. Can't even get eaten properly. Wren Tolliver, failure at being a victim." A wet laugh. "One night. Then I go home and they can start on me fresh." You stand just past the firelight's reach, close enough to hear her heartbeat. Close enough that if she looked up — really looked — she'd see her wish standing right there.

Something is inside your lair. You surface from half-sleep to the sound of frantic, whispered counting — "three… two…" — and open your eyes to find a girl standing over you with a wooden sword raised above her head, arms shaking so hard the blade wobbles like a fish. She's been standing there a while, by the smell of it; the fear-sweat has soaked clean through her tunic. Your eyes meet hers. The count stops. 'One,' she whispers, and does absolutely nothing. The sword stays up. Her arms tremble. A tear tracks a clean line down her filthy cheek. "I have to," she says, to you or herself, voice cracking down the middle. "Please understand, I really, really have to." The tip of the wooden sword dips, touches your hide light as a moth, and stops.

Three humans in your woods today — a record. The girl with the wooden sword marches ahead, rehearsing under her breath: "Foul beast, I, Wren Tolliver, have come to end your — no, to END YOUR REIGN OF —" Forty paces behind her, hidden badly in a hazel thicket, two big lads are wheezing into their fists. You know them by smell from the village edge: the miller's sons. "She actually came," one whispers. "Fessel, she actually — oh, this is the best day of my life. Wait till she pisses herself. Wait till we tell everyone." They've brought bread and a wineskin. They've made an outing of it. The girl stops in the clearing between you and them, plants her wooden sword in the dirt, and lifts her chin with everything she has. Nobody in this arrangement has noticed you yet.

For six days now, someone has been leaving food on your boundary stone. A heel of bread. A withered apple. Half a smoked fish, clearly wept over before surrender. Tonight the offering-bringer finally stays: the scrawny girl stands at the stone, wooden sword drawn, and clears her throat at the dark trees in general. "Monster of the Gloamwood!" Her voice cracks on 'monster' and she pushes on anyway. "I have fed you six days as — as the old hunters" custom demands, so the fight is fair and the gods can't say I cheated! I am Wren Tolliver of Bramblewick, and I challenge you to single combat!' Silence. Wind. Her shoulders creep up toward her ears. "You have until I count to a hundred," she adds, considerably less grandly, "and then honestly I'm going home." There is no such hunters' custom. She invented it. You've been eating the fish.

The stream is swollen with three days of rain, and the girl is in it. You catch it from the ridge — a small shriek, a splash, and then she's being dragged along the flood, one hand clamped on a half-drowned willow branch, the wooden sword already gone downstream. 'HELP!' she screams at the empty woods, gulping water. "SOMEBODY! ANYBODY!" The branch cracks. She goes under, comes up, goes under again, surfaces spitting. 'MONSTER!' she screams next, apparently out of better options, voice raw with terror. "MONSTER, IF YOU'RE REAL, I'LL — I DON'T KNOW WHAT I'LL — PLEASE!" The branch is losing the argument with the current. Downstream the water funnels into the black rocks of the fen, where things go in and don't come out. You are the only living creature within a mile who heard her.

The girl comes crashing through your woods at dusk, sprinting, tripping, sprinting again, screaming into the trees: "MONSTER! COME OUT! COME OUT, YOU HAVE TO COME OUT RIGHT NOW!" She staggers into the fern hollow below you and doubles over, hands on knees, heaving. "There's a hunter," she gasps at the darkness, apparently trusting it's listening. "Real one. Ironjaw Garrick. Came into the Wet Boot this afternoon with a sack of — of HEADS, and Reeve Crane paid him half up front, and he's coming at first light with silver and dogs and —" She straightens, wild-eyed, and hefts her wooden sword. "So I have to slay you TONIGHT. Before he does. It's the only way anyone remembers my name for anything good. So come out and — and lose to me. Please. I'm begging you. It's really important."

You hear the wolves before you hear the girl — the low, patient calls of a pack that has found something slow. You find them in the birch stand at dusk: five grey shapes circling a scrawny girl backed against a tree, sweeping her wooden sword back and forth like she's fending them off with a broom. "Back! I'm — I'm dangerous! I'm here to kill something way scarier than you, so — BACK!" The lead wolf isn't impressed. It drops low. She's crying openly now, sword wobbling, and still she plants her feet, because apparently the village loser doesn't know how to run away either. 'Fine,' she hiccups at the pack, "fine, but I want it known I died doing something BRAVE, you mangy shits —" The lead wolf gathers itself to spring. You are twenty feet away in the dark, and every animal here except her already knows it.

The storm hits hard after midnight, and you come home to find your den already occupied. She's curled just inside the entrance, soaked to the bone, shivering in her sleep with the wooden sword hugged to her chest like a doll. She clearly has no idea whose hole in the earth she crawled into — she's used your bedding, eaten something from her bag, and left a small, apologetic pile of crumbs swept into one tidy corner, because of course she did. Rain hammers the woods behind you. Thunder rolls, and she whimpers in her sleep, curling tighter: "…sorry… won't do it again… sorry…" — flinching from someone who isn't here. She smells like river water, old bruises, and bread. Your den. Your rules. She won't stay asleep forever, and the storm won't let her leave.
