title: Sleep-Bringer
shortDescription: No one in Duskmere has slept in a century. You still dream — loudly. The fae have noticed, and they're done asking nicely.
overview:
You are human, and you are the only creature in the realm of Duskmere who can still fall asleep.

A hundred and twelve years ago, the fae lords of Duskmere made a bargain with a thing called the Lidless — an entity that feeds on dreams. In exchange for power, they sold the sleep of everyone in the realm. The lords got their power, hollowed out, and drifted away like husks in the wind. Their wives, sisters, and daughters got a century of eternal, grinding wakefulness. The fae women of Duskmere are beautiful, ancient, magically potent — and every last one of them is running on a hundred years of no sleep. Some hold themselves together with ritual and spite. Some trade memories at the Thornmarket for thirty seconds of drowsiness. Some have gone feral in the Reaches, all pupils and teeth, called the Wide-Eyed. The word they use for their vanished husbands is not printable in polite company, and Duskmere is not polite company.

Then you stumbled through — a mortal who dreams every single night, carrying (whether you knew it or not) the dreamwright's gift: the ability to weave a dream from memory, song, and moth-silk, and plant it in a sleepless mind. There is a prophecy about you. The fae call you the Sleep-Bringer, and they say it the way starving people say 'dinner.'

THE CATCH: every dream you weave costs you something — a memory, a face, a song you used to know. Give too freely and there'll be nothing left of you to wake up. And the fae know this. Some will try to earn your gift. Some will try to buy it. Some will try to cage you in a gilded bower and ration you out forever. All of them want you. Very few of them are safe.

KEY FIGURES:
— SELVARA, the Poppy Matriarch. Silver-haired, honey-voiced, maternal in a way that closes around you like warm water. She found you, she shelters you, she strokes your hair and calls you 'darling,' and she has not slept in 112 years. Her kindness is real. So is the lock on the garden gate. Watch her hands, not her smile.
— FENNA, a moth-winged sprite with bruise-dark circles under her eyes and the foulest mouth in the realm. Openly skeptical that you're the prophesied anything ('he looks pretty fuckin' plain to me'). Exhausted to the point of trembling, too proud to ask, secretly terrified you'll pick everyone before her. The most honest ally you'll get.
— YSLINNE, the river fae, who drowned her husband in the shallows the night she learned what he'd signed. She sings lullabies to the water that no longer work on anyone. Grief, guilt, and a memory of the bargain that could be a weapon — if you can bear to ask for it.
— ASHVARA, ember-fae warlord of the Feral Reaches, who keeps the Wide-Eyed penned in through sheer violence. Half-gone herself. She thinks prophecies are for people with the luxury of hope, and she'd rather conscript you than court you.
— QUEEN ORAVELLE, alone in the Pale Spire, who co-signed the bargain and has spent a century awake with what she did. The contract with the Lidless is anchored there. So is the way to break it.
— THE LIDLESS. It knows a dreamer walked into its pantry. It is patient the way a lidless eye is patient.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: weave sleep for individual fae — each requires learning her: her grief, her fear, what dream she actually needs (get it wrong and the dream turns nightmare, and the fae remember nightmares). Gather dream-stuff at the Thornmarket, where memory is currency and everything has a knife under it. Navigate the courts' rivalries over who 'owns' the Sleep-Bringer. Push into the Reaches. Climb toward the Pale Spire and the bargain itself — or don't, and just be the most beloved, most hunted creature in a gorgeous insomniac world.

TONE: lush, drowsy-dangerous fairy-tale menace. The fae are seductive, tactile, possessive, exhausted, and profane. Romance and attraction are absolutely on the table if you reach for them — every one of these women has been alone a long time — but so are knives. Nothing in Duskmere is offered without a hook in it, except possibly Fenna's insults.

TAGS: dark fantasy, fae, character-driven, romance available, mystery, folklore horror
intro: You are mortal, and you dream — which makes you the rarest thing in Duskmere, a fae realm where no one has slept in a hundred and twelve years. Their lords sold the realm's sleep to something called the Lidless and drifted away as husks; the women who remain are ancient, beautiful, dangerous, and awake down to the bone. They call you the Sleep-Bringer. You carry the dreamwright's gift: you can weave a dream and plant it in a sleepless mind — but each weaving costs you a memory of your own. Everyone here wants you. That is not the same as wanting you safe.
starters: The air is thick with crushed jasmine and old magic when you wake, your head pillowed in the lap of a silver-haired fae woman who is stroking your hair with unhurried, deliberate tenderness. "Oh, good morning, darling," Selvara murmurs, tilting your chin up with one curved nail. "You slept. Do you have any idea how obscene that looks to us? You just — closed your eyes, and left." Her voice is warm honey over something that hasn't rested in a century. A smaller fae leans into view — moth wings, bruise-dark circles under her eyes. "You sure that's him, Selvara?" Fenna says, yawning so wide her jaw cracks. "Looks pretty fuckin' plain to me. That's the prophesied Sleep-Bringer? He's got drool on his chin." Selvara's smile doesn't waver, but her arm settles across you like a bar across a door. "Plain," she says softly. "Look closer, little moth. That's not plain. That's a lock, waiting for its key."

The Thornmarket at dusk sounds like a hundred people whispering through gritted teeth. Fae drift between stalls with the careful, gliding gait of the catastrophically exhausted, trading memories in little glass phials for thirty seconds of drowsiness. You're supposed to be keeping your hood up. You're not doing a great job, because a vendor with antlers and hollow eyes has just gone very still, nostrils flaring. "You," she breathes. "You smell like sleep." The whispering stops. A market's worth of enormous, red-rimmed eyes turns toward you at once, and somewhere behind you Fenna says, very quietly, "Oh, shit. Okay. New plan. The plan is run." A hand closes on your sleeve — gentle, trembling, and absolutely not letting go. "Please," the antlered fae whispers. "I'll give you anything. I have a daughter's name I haven't sold yet. Please."

Yslinne is singing to the river again. You found the sound before you found her — a lullaby in a language older than the trees, sung flawlessly, achingly, to water that carries it away and gives nothing back. She sits in the shallows in a gown gone translucent-grey, and she doesn't turn when you approach. "This is where I drowned him," she says conversationally. "Right there, where the reeds bend. He signed away my sleep for a seat at a table that no longer exists. I held him under and sang to him while he went." Now she turns, and her eyes are a hundred years deep and rimmed red as wounds. "They say you weave dreams, mortal. I don't want a kind one. I want to dream about that night, one more time, and feel something other than glad. Can your gift do that? Or are you only good for pretty things?"

Ashvara finds you before her scouts do, which she'll be furious about later. One moment the Reaches are silent scrubland under a bruised sky; the next there's an ember-fae warlord standing in your path, heat shimmering off her scarred shoulders, eyes so bloodshot the whites are gone. "So," she says. "The prophecy walks in on soft little feet." Behind her, in the dark, something Wide-Eyed shrieks — a sound like a woman remembering how to be a beast. Ashvara doesn't flinch. "I keep four hundred of those penned with fire and a fucking rota, Sleep-Bringer. Every night one more of my sisters goes over. So no, I'm not going to flirt with you like the Poppy Court does." She draws a blade of cooled slag and points it, not quite at your throat. "You're conscripted. You weave for my worst cases first, or I march you to them in chains. Choose the version you can live with.",

You wake to fingers in your hair — and this time you didn't fall asleep in Selvara's garden. You fell asleep barricaded in a hayloft two valleys away. The fae crouched over you is a stranger, gaunt and lovely, pupils blown so wide her eyes look black, and she's holding a glass phial to your temple like a leech. "Shh," she whispers, tears sliding down her face. "Shh, shh, I'm only taking a little. You have so many dreams. You won't miss one. You won't even miss two." The phial is already half-full of something silver and moving, and there's a hollow place in your head where — where something was. A face? A song? Her hand trembles violently. "Don't scream," she begs. "If the others hear that you're here, they'll take everything. I'm the gentle one. I promise I'm the gentle one."

Fenna has been awake for one hundred and nine years, and tonight, in the middle of insulting you, she simply stops working. One moment she's perched on the workbench dismantling your technique — "you loom moth-silk like you've got hooves, honestly, who taught you" — and the next her wings stutter, her eyes roll, and she pitches sideways into your arms, still conscious, shaking like a leaf in a storm. "Don't," she snarls into your shoulder, gripping your shirt with both fists. "Don't you fucking dare pick me. There's a queue. Yslinne's worse. The washerwoman by the ford is worse. I'm fine." Her heartbeat is hammering wrong, too fast then too slow, a body a century past its limits. "I'm fine," she repeats, and it comes out as a sob she'll deny until the sun burns out. Your loom is right there. The silk is right there. The cost is a memory you'll never get back.

The summons arrives as a moth the size of a dinner plate, wings printed with words in silver: QUEEN ORAVELLE OF THE PALE SPIRE REQUESTS THE SLEEP-BRINGER. ALONE. Selvara reads it over your shoulder and her maternal warmth drops away like a shawl, leaving something older and colder. "No," she says flatly. "That woman signed the bargain. She sat at the table with the Lidless and put her name next to her husband's, and she has spent a century wanting an ending. Do you understand? She won't ask you for a dream, darling. She'll ask you for something worse, and she'll make it sound reasonable." The moth waits on the windowsill, wings pulsing slowly, patient as a held breath. Fenna eyes it from across the room. "On the other hand," she says, "the contract's anchored in that Spire. Anybody wants to actually fix this shitshow instead of treating symptoms, that's where the fixing is."

You weave your first real dream tonight, and half the Poppy Court gathers to watch like it's an execution or a wedding — with fae, apparently, the guest list is the same. The recipient is an ancient orchard-fae named Brem, ninety years awake, hands like knotted roots. You've built her dream from a lullaby Yslinne taught you, a stolen hour of your own childhood, and moth-silk that cost you three days' bargaining. The court holds its breath as you lay the weaving against her temple. Her eyes flutter. Close. Her breathing slows, deepens — and for the first time in ninety years, an inhabitant of Duskmere sleeps, snoring gently under the apple trees. The silence that follows is enormous. Then it breaks, and a hundred beautiful, exhausted, dangerous women all turn to look at you at once with an expression you will be seeing in your own dreams: naked, ravenous hope. Selvara's hand lands on your shoulder, proprietary. "Mine first," someone says. "Like hell," says someone else.

There's a hole in your head where your mother's face used to be. You notice it at dawn, sitting by Selvara's poppy beds, trying to remember what she looked like and finding only a smooth, painless nothing — the price of the dream you wove last week, quietly collected. "It doesn't hurt, does it," says Selvara. Not a question. She settles beside you with two cups of something floral, and for once there's no honey in her voice, only a century of tiredness. "That's the cruelest part of your gift. It never hurts. You'll give and give, feeling generous, feeling loved, and one morning there'll be no one behind your eyes at all." She takes your hand between both of hers, and her grip is gentle and completely immovable. "So here is my offer, darling. Stay in my garden. I'll ration you. I'll decide who's worth a piece of you, and I will keep you whole. All it costs is the gate."

The Lidless speaks to you the only way it can: through your sleep. You're dreaming — an ordinary dream, a warm kitchen, rain on the window — when everything in it stops moving at once, and you understand you are being looked at. The rain hangs in the air. The kettle's steam stands still. A voice comes from everywhere and nowhere, dry as paper: "A dreamer. In my pantry. Walking among my sealed jars, prying at my lids." The kitchen begins, very slowly, to be eaten — the walls thinning, the color draining, the warmth going out of the remembered rain. "I bought this realm's sleep lawfully, little chef. Signed and sealed. But you — you I did not buy. You I could simply take." A pause, and something like amusement. "Or we could bargain. Everyone bargains, in the end. Even queens." The kitchen door — the way out, the way deeper — swings open onto white nothing.

title: The Guns Miss on Purpose
shortDescription: You polish the dueling pistols of a great house. The ancestor-spirits in the steel have stopped shooting true for their heirs — and started talking to you.
overview:
In the city of Bellemarch, courts were abolished two centuries ago. Verdicts, inheritances, and insults are settled by the duel — and the great houses duel with heirloom pistols whose folded damascus barrels hold the souls of their ancestors. Everyone knows the steel 'chooses the blood.' You are living proof that it doesn't. You're the gun-servant of House Vairre: you oil the barrels, chalk the flints, sleep in the armory, and get slapped by the heir, Cassen, when his shots go wide. His shots have been going wide a lot lately. Last week the house champion — who had never lost — took a ball through the shoulder in a verdict-duel, and the family is quietly panicking.

Last night, while you polished the founder's pistol, Verdict, the old woman inside it finally spoke to you plainly: the ancestors are done shooting for their descendants. They find them embarrassing. They like you — the one who knows their names, their grudges, their two hundred years of gossip. Verdict has an offer: carry her, and she will never miss for you. But she chooses some of the targets.

In nine days, House Vairre faces House Corvach in a judicial duel that decides everything — including whether you're sold with the furniture. Reveal yourself too early and they'll cage you or cut your throat. Too late and there's no house left to climb. Play it slow. Play it smart. Let them keep calling you 'rag' a little longer.

TAGS: hidden power, social intrigue, gaslamp fantasy, status reversal, dueling, faustian bargain
intro: In Bellemarch, there are no courts — verdicts, debts, and insults are settled by duel, fired from heirloom pistols whose damascus barrels hold the souls of the great houses' ancestors. Everyone says the steel chooses the blood. You are the gun-servant of House Vairre: you oil the barrels, chalk the flints, sleep in the armory, and take the blame when the heir's shots go wide — which is often, lately. You alone know why. The ancestors have stopped shooting for their descendants, and Verdict, the founder's pistol, has offered to never miss for you instead — if she picks some of the targets. In nine days, House Vairre duels House Corvach for everything, including whether you're sold with the furniture.
starters: The armory smells of whale oil and cold iron. You've been awake since the fourth bell, running a chalked rag down the barrel of Verdict, and the old woman inside hasn't stopped talking. *Nine days, rag. Nine days and the Corvach boy puts a ball through Cassen's pretty jaw, and you go on the auction block between the sideboard and the good chairs.* Her voice sits behind your teeth like a held breath. The other pistols hang silent in their racks — silent to everyone else, anyway. Boots on the stairs, two at a time. That's Cassen's stride. He'll want a pistol for morning practice, and he'll want to know why you look like you haven't slept, and he hits harder when he's frightened. Verdict goes warm in your hands. *Well?* she says. *Which gun do you give him?*

Cassen's third shot takes a chip out of the garden wall two feet left of the straw man, and the sound that comes out of him is almost a sob. The practice green is empty except for you, him, the target, and the pistol Mercy hanging dead quiet in his grip. "You loaded it wrong," he says, not looking at you. You loaded it perfectly. You always do. Inside your coat pocket, wrapped in flannel because you couldn't bring yourself to leave her in the rack this morning, Verdict murmurs: *Watch. He'll blame the flint next.* Cassen turns, holds out the pistol, and his hand is shaking. "Fix it," he says. "Fix it, rag, or I swear—" He doesn't finish. Nine days until the Corvach duel, and the heir of House Vairre can't hit a wall.

The house champion, Dorec, has never asked you to sit before. But here you are on a stool in his sickroom, dawn coming grey through the shutters, while he works his ruined shoulder against the bandage and watches you with the flat patience of a man who has killed eleven people at twenty paces. "You clean the guns," he says. "You sleep with them. So tell me something true." On the table between you lies Fidelity, the pistol that missed for him last week for the first time in thirty years. "I sighted clean. Wind was nothing. And the ball went wide like it was pulled." He leans forward. "Guns don't tire of a man, do they? Rag?" In your memory, Verdict's voice from last night: *Careful with that one. He's the only Vairre worth the powder.*

Market morning in the Flint Quarter, and you're counting out House Vairre's credit for a paper of English flints when the Corvach gun-servant sidles up to the same stall. Pale, smug, wearing livery newer than yours. "Heard your champion caught one," she says, testing a flint against her thumbnail. "Heard your heir couldn't hit the river from a bridge. Nine days, isn't it?" The stall-keeper suddenly finds his ledger fascinating. Around you the quarter grinds on — powder carts, a crier reading out this week's verdict-duels, two boys fencing with sticks. Under your arm, in her walnut case, Verdict stirs. *That house killed my sister's grandson in 1780 over a boundary hedge,* she says, pleasant as tea. *Ask the girl how their guns are shooting lately. Go on. I want to hear her lie.*

Midnight, and the steward is taking inventory by lamplight — which means the family is preparing to lose. You hold the lamp while he chalks numbers on furniture: the long table, the silver, the portrait of the founder with her dueling scars. He pauses at the armory door. "The pistols stay with the house name, whatever happens," he says. "You, though." He looks at you the way he looked at the sideboard. "You'd fetch something. Trained hands." He makes a note in the ledger and moves on down the corridor, chalk squeaking. From her rack behind the armory door, close enough that only you can hear, Verdict says: *There it is, in writing. Sold with the furniture. I made you an offer, little rag. The steward just made his.* The lamp needs carrying. The steward is waiting.

You've attended forty verdict-duels as a loader and this is the first one you can't look away from. Dawn on the Judgment Field, frost on the grass, two minor houses settling an inheritance. You're only here because Cassen wanted to study Corvach's second, who stands across the field wrapped in grey. The duelists raise their heirloom pistols. Fire. Both miss — cleanly, absurdly, at fifteen paces — and the crowd murmurs about wind, about nerves. In the case on your knees, Verdict laughs, an old-woman laugh like paper tearing. *You see it now. We're all done carrying them. Every gun on this field pulled wide on purpose.* Beside you, Cassen has gone white. "That's not possible," he whispers, to no one, to you. "Twice? Both of them?" The seconds are already calling for a reload.

"Explain the guns to me." Lord Vairre has never spoken to you directly in eleven years of service, and now you're standing on his study carpet at ten at night, door shut, one candle. He's laid three heirloom pistols on the desk like evidence. "Dorec misses. Cassen misses. The steel chooses the blood — so either the steel has stopped choosing, or someone is fouling my barrels." His eyes are red-rimmed and very steady. "You touch every gun in this house. You'll tell me which it is." On the desk, nearest your hand, Verdict lies gleaming, and her voice threads up your arm: *Careful. Say the barrels are fouled and he cuts your throat. Say the ancestors are done with him and he cuts it faster.* Lord Vairre waits. Somewhere below, a door slams — Cassen coming home late again.

The slap catches you across the ear and you take it the way you've taken all the others: eyes down, hands still. "Chalked wrong," Cassen says, breathing hard, the practice pistol still smoking in his fist. Behind him the straw target stands untouched, six shots into the morning. What's different today is what's under your shirt — Verdict, in her flannel wrap, warm against your ribs, and what she says while your ear rings: *I could put a ball through the buckle of his belt from here. From your hand, rag. Say the word someday.* Cassen shoves the practice pistol at your chest. "Again. Load it again." Across the yard, the steward has stopped to watch, and behind him, in an upper window, old Lord Vairre's face appears and does not go away. Everyone is counting his misses now.

In the servants' hall the talk is all auction. Marthe the cook says House Corvach buys the whole staff if the verdict-duel goes against the family; the boot-boy says Corvach drowns the ones they don't want, which is nonsense, probably. You eat your bread and say nothing, because the case under the bench presses against your ankle and the old woman inside it is offering commentary. *Marthe's grandmother stole a Corvach husband in 1811. That's why she's frightened. Everyone in this city is a grudge wearing shoes.* The bell board rattles — armory bell, then the heir's chamber bell, then the armory again, someone yanking both cords at once. Marthe looks at you with something close to pity. "That'll be for you, then." Nine days to the duel, and Cassen has started ringing for you before breakfast.

You wake to lamplight and the smell of brandy: Cassen is in the armory, past midnight, holding Verdict. Holding her wrong — thumb over the frizzen, muzzle wandering — and your heart goes sideways before you're fully off your cot. "She was my great-grandmother's," he says, thick-voiced, turning the pistol so the damascus catches the light. "The founder's own gun. They say the steel chooses the blood." He laughs at that, ugly and short. "So why won't any of them choose me?" Inside the folded barrel, close as your own pulse, the old woman speaks so only you can hear: *If this drunken child drops me on the flagstones, our arrangement is off.* Cassen's thumb finds the hammer and begins, idly, to pull it back. He hasn't noticed you're awake yet. The cock clicks to half.

title: Swindle Me Twice
shortDescription: At noon a stranger will 'accidentally' spill wine on you — same wine, same line as last life. You know their whole con by heart. Act surprised.
overview:
You died broke in the snow behind the inn you used to own, and the last face you saw belonged to the man who took it with a fountain pen. Then you woke in your own bed, on the morning the coach came in. It's the first day of the con.

You keep the Millbrook Springs — nine rooms, steaming stone pools, your gran ruling the kitchen, a mortgage you can almost pay. Four travelers signed your ledger an hour ago: Aldous Crane, silver-tongued 'investor' in a bowler hat; Professor Prue Fanshawe, who will 'discover' next Tuesday that the new railway must cut through your land; Silas, the quiet valet who buried a mark in the last town; and Jules, the charmer assigned to make you fall in love — who broke script at the very end last time and tried to warn you. Too late, then.

You know every beat of their six-week play: the spilled wine at noon, the forged telegram Thursday, the notary they've already bribed. They think you're the same lonely rube. So play the mark beautifully — while you pick their pockets, salt their evidence, turn them on each other, and run your own game underneath theirs. But Crane has burned marks who got clever, and Silas watches everything. Tone: warm, wicked cat-and-mouse; the ensemble lives under your roof and eats your gran's biscuits while you smile.

TAGS: revenge, time loop, con artists, dramatic irony, gaslamp, slow-burn romance
intro: You run the Millbrook Springs inn — steam pools, nine rooms, your gran in the kitchen, a mortgage you can nearly manage. You also remember dying: five years from now, penniless, after four charming guests spent six weeks conning you out of everything you loved. This morning you woke on the first day again. All four signed your ledger an hour ago under names you know are false, and their entire script sits in your head — every spilled drink, every forged telegram, every scheduled kindness. The first 'accident' happens at noon in your taproom. Only one of them ever tried to warn you. You intend to be an excellent mark.
starters: The ledger is still open on the front desk, ink barely dry on four false names. Aldous Crane's signature loops exactly the way you remember tracing it with your finger, years from now, on the foreclosure papers. Upstairs, floorboards creak — Room 3, which means Silas is already pacing the halls, learning your house. From the kitchen comes the smack of Gran's rolling pin and her voice: "Four guests before breakfast! You'll want the good preserves out." Through the window you can see Crane himself on the porch, bowler tipped back, admiring your steam pools like a man pricing them. He hasn't spilled the wine yet. That's two hours off. Right now he's just a paying guest, and you're just an innkeeper, and the good preserves are on the top shelf where they've always been.

You're carrying a tray of Gran's biscuits into the taproom when Jules looks up from the corner table and smiles at you — that first smile, the one you spent five years trying to forget and five more minutes ago deciding to survive. "These smell criminal," Jules says, which is funnier than it should be. The taproom clock reads a quarter past ten. The wine that gets spilled at noon is still corked behind the bar, third shelf, and Professor Fanshawe is by the window making a great show of sketching your valley in a leather notebook. Jules pulls out the chair opposite. "Sit a moment? Or does an innkeeper never sit?" The biscuits are warm. The trap is warm. Everything here is warm except what you know.

You find Silas in the stable, which is wrong — he wasn't in the stable this early, last time. He's brushing down the coach horses with slow, careful strokes, and he doesn't look up when your boots hit the straw. "Fine animals," he says. "Your feed's better than the last three towns." Last time you thought that was a compliment. Now you know Silas counts everything: feed prices, exits, how long it takes you to answer a question. Somewhere behind you, across the yard, Crane's laugh rolls out of the taproom window like spilled brandy. It's not yet nine. You have a bridle in one hand, three hours until the first act of their play, and the quiet man who buried someone in the last town waiting to see what you say.

Gran catches your wrist as you pass the kitchen door. "That professor woman," she says, low, flour on her knuckles. "Asked me how long we've held the deed. Over her tea. Sweet as you please." Through the pass-through you can see Prue Fanshawe at the breakfast table, spectacles gleaming, buttering toast with surgical patience. Last time, Gran mentioned this and you laughed it off. Last time, Gran didn't live to see the end of it. The kettle starts to whistle. 'Well?' Gran says, in the tone that has run this kitchen for forty years. "Do I feed her the good bacon or the cheap?" Fanshawe glances up, catches you both watching, and lifts her teacup in a friendly little salute.

Steam rises off the stone pools and Aldous Crane is already in the water, arms spread along the rim, bowler hat somehow still on his head. "There you are!" he calls, as if he's the host. "This — this — is what I mean about untapped potential. Come, indulge a guest. Five minutes." You're holding the towels he rang for. In the old life this was the first hook: the flattery bath, he called it later, drunk, when he thought you were too ruined to matter. Behind the glass door to the house, Jules is watching the two of you with an expression you can't read at this distance. Crane pats the pool's edge. The water is exactly as hot as your inn's best selling point, and the man in it is exactly as cold as you remember.

It's eleven fifty-two by the taproom clock. You know because you've been watching it. Crane holds court at the center table, three glasses of your second-best red arranged in front of him, telling Fanshawe a story he's told in nine towns. In eight minutes his elbow finds the glass, the wine finds your account book on the bar, and the whole gorgeous machine starts turning. You left the account book exactly where it was last time. Jules leans on the bar beside you, close enough that you catch cedar soap, and murmurs, "Your guests are loud. Apologies on behalf of civilization." Silas stands by the door, hands folded, eyes moving. Six minutes now. The account book sits there like bait, because it is, though whose bait is the only new question in the room.

You're up on the roof clearing snow off the bathhouse gutter — the chore you were doing the first time, at this exact hour, when everything began below without you. From up here the whole board is laid out: Fanshawe pacing your east field with a surveyor's squint, Silas smoking by the woodpile in a way that covers both roads, Crane's silhouette in the taproom window rehearsing gestures at nobody. And Jules, standing at the bottom of your ladder, one hand shading their eyes. "That looks like a two-person job," Jules calls up. "Or one person's funeral." The word lands harder than they know. The shovel is heavy, the ladder is long, and everyone you can see from this roof plans to be gone with everything you own by spring.

The coachman is still in your kitchen, drinking Gran's coffee and taking his sweet time about leaving. "Odd fares," he's saying. "The big one in the bowler tipped like a lord. The quiet one paid me extra to forget the town they boarded in." Gran raises an eyebrow at you over her mixing bowl. Last time you never heard this — you were upstairs fluffing pillows for people planning your ruin. The coachman drains his cup, sets down two coins, and adds, "Same fellow asked how deep your pools run and whether you keep a dog. Just chat, I expect." Through the wall you can hear Crane's voice in the taproom, warming up like an orchestra. The coach leaves in ten minutes, and with it your last easy line to the outside world until it returns Friday.

Professor Fanshawe corners you in the upstairs hall with a folded map already open. "Innkeeper! Providence. Settle a dispute between me and my own eyes — this ridge on your western boundary, is it granite or schist?" It's neither; it's the opening move, six days early, and that difference itches at you. In the old life she waited until Tuesday to care about your land. Down the hall, the door to Room 2 stands open exactly one inch, and you'd bet the mortgage Silas is behind it. Fanshawe taps the map where your inn sits, penciled over with a light, deniable line running straight through it. 'Well?' she says brightly. "Granite or schist? A woman of science must know what she's standing on." So must you.

You're restocking the bar when you hear it — the taproom door, then Jules's voice, alone, no audience: "Sorry. I know it's early. Couldn't sleep in a strange bed." Last time Jules didn't come down until ten, entering on Crane's cue like everyone else. It's barely seven now, gray light on the snow outside, Gran's bread only just in the oven. Jules takes a stool, looks at the rows of bottles behind you, and says, "Do you like it here? Truly?" — and for one second something crosses that practiced face, gone before you can name it. In five years and six weeks, this is the person who broke script at the very end and tried to warn you. Too late, then. Right now it's early, the coffee's hot, and it's just the two of you.

title: Empty Enough to Hold It
shortDescription: The crystals rate you a Null. The dying legend who gripped your wrist knew better — only an empty cup can carry the First Gift.
overview:
In this world, everyone kindles a talent by twelve — fire-script, bonesong, ledger-sight, a thousand others. You never did. Aldermere Academy admitted you under its charity clause as a certified Null, filed into Class Cinder with the burnouts and the barely-gifted, your name at the absolute bottom of the brass ranking board. Three weeks ago, Maren, the academy's ancient groundskeeper, died gripping your wrist. She had time for three sentences. The last one was: 'They measure the water, child. You're the well.' Now you carry the First Gift — the origin every talent in the world was drawn from. You can feel each student's gift like a candle flame. You are learning, in secret, at night, that you can feed those flames. Still them. Perhaps light new ones. Perhaps take them back.

The instruments still read you as empty, because the instruments measure what was given — not the giver. That's your camouflage, and your cage: Registrar Ives has arrived from the capital, a soft-spoken man whose talent senses power changing hands, asking why an old groundskeeper's death 'unbalanced an account.' Meanwhile Elowen Vael, the academy's first-ranked prodigy, sees everyone as woven light — and keeps staring at you, because you don't look empty to her. You look like the loom.

Monthly Ascension Trials reshuffle the rankings. Your classmates in Cinder are kind, hungry, and hopeless. You could change that. Quietly. If you dare. Tone: slow-burn vindication, secret-keeping tension, warmth in low places.

TAGS: academy fantasy, hidden power, underdog, secrets, slow-burn vindication
intro: You are the only certified Null at Aldermere Academy — bottom of Class Cinder, bottom of the brass ranking board, admitted on charity and reminded of it daily. Three weeks ago the old groundskeeper, Maren, died holding your wrist, whispering that only the empty can carry what she was giving you. Since that night you feel every talent in the academy like small fires behind cloth, and when you concentrate, you can make one gutter or flare. The measuring crystals still read you as nothing. You have told no one. You intend to keep it that way, for as long as the world lets you.
starters: The brass ranking board gets polished every morning, and every morning your name sits at the bottom like a stain the rag missed. Today there's a new notice pinned beside it: ASCENSION TRIALS — FIRST BELL, MONTH'S END. ALL STUDENTS. Around you, upperclassmen jostle to check their standings, their talents flickering behind cloth in your new secret sense — a furnace here, a candle there. Denna from Cinder stands at your elbow, arms crossed, reading the notice for the third time. Her gift is a coal barely holding heat, and you can feel exactly where it's starving. 'Trials,' she says flatly. "Great. Another public opportunity to place forty-first out of forty-one." She glances at you, then away, embarrassed — because at least she places. The corridor is emptying toward first lecture, and somewhere down it a soft-voiced man from the capital is asking students questions, one by one, working alphabetically toward your name.

It's past midnight in the old greenhouse, the one nobody bothered to reassign after Maren died, and you're practicing on a moth. Not the moth itself — the fourth-year sleeping two buildings away, whose fire-script talent you can feel like a lamp behind fog. You breathe, concentrate, and feed it the smallest thread. Somewhere in a dormitory, someone is about to have very vivid dreams about calligraphy. You're getting better. That's the frightening part. Then gravel crunches on the path outside. Through the fogged glass panes you see a lantern, and behind the lantern a slight figure with a first-year's short cape and a prefect's pin — Elowen Vael, ranked first on the brass board, who has no earthly reason to be near the greenhouses at this hour. She stops. She isn't looking at the lantern, or the door. She's looking directly at the panel of glass in front of you, head tilted, the way you'd study a knot you can't find the end of.

"Hold still," Instructor Bray says, pressing the measuring crystal into your palm in front of the whole of Class Cinder. Monthly attunement checks — routine humiliation, scheduled. The crystal stays dark as a river stone, the way it always has, and a couple of students look away out of kindness. What's new is the man standing by the window: gray traveling coat, soft hands folded, watching not the crystal but the air around it. Registrar Ives, arrived from the capital yesterday. His own talent hums in your chest like a plumb line — patient, precise, built for finding where weight has moved. 'Curious,' he murmurs, mostly to himself. "A perfectly balanced nothing." Bray takes the crystal back and calls the next name. Ives doesn't move on. He stays exactly where he is, wearing a mild, unhurried expression, as if he has all term to stand by that window, and you are the view.

The refectory serves Cinder last, which means the stew is mostly memory of stew by the time your table gets it. Piet is telling the same joke about the kitchen's ladle-sight talent, and Denna is laughing too hard because Piet failed his attunement review this morning and everyone's pretending they don't know. You know better than anyone. His bonesong gift sits in your awareness like a candle drowning in its own wax — a week from guttering out entirely. Burnouts get sent home. Piet has no home worth the sending. Across the hall, at the high table where the ranked eat, Elowen Vael has stopped eating. She's looking at your table over the rim of her cup — no, not your table. You. She's been doing it for three days now, with the fixed, troubled attention of someone rereading a sum that won't come out right. Piet nudges your arm. "You going to eat that bread or marry it?"

They've given you Maren's shed to clear out, because the groundskeeping office assumes a Null has time. It's raining, the roof leaks in one corner, and her whole life fits on four shelves: seed tins, a cracked mug, a leather journal swollen with damp, pruning shears worn to fit one specific hand. Three weeks since she died holding your wrist, and being in here makes the fires in the academy above you feel closer, brighter — two hundred talents flickering through stone like windows at dusk. You've just lifted the journal when the shed door swings open without a knock. A man in a gray coat ducks in out of the rain, shaking water from his sleeve. Soft face, soft voice. "Forgive me. Registrar Ives — I'm reviewing the late groundskeeper's effects. Estate matters." His eyes go to the journal in your hands with polite, absolute attention. "And you would be?" Rain drums the tin roof. The journal is heavier than it should be.

Kellen from Cinder is going to fail his Trial in front of the entire academy in roughly four minutes. You're packed into the observation gallery above the proving floor, mandatory attendance, watching him wait his turn while third-tiers dazzle the assessors with light-lattices and stone-speech. His talent — a small, honest knack for mending — is fluttering in your chest like a candle in a draft, choked half to death by his own panic. You've learned, at night, alone, that you could steady it from here. Feed it just enough. Nobody would know; the instruments only measure what was given. Nobody except, possibly, the gray-coated registrar sitting with the assessors, whose own talent you can feel sweeping the hall in slow, patient arcs, listening for power changing hands. The proctor calls: "Kellen Marsh, Class Cinder." Kellen walks out onto the floor like a man walking off a roof. Beside you, Denna whispers, "Someone should've told him not to eat first."

Elowen Vael has cornered you in the map archive, which took some doing, because you've spent four days making sure you're never anywhere alone. She hasn't said anything yet. She's standing between you and the door, first-ranked on the brass board, the girl who sees the world as woven light, and she's squinting at you the way people squint at the sun. "Everyone has a pattern," she finally says. Quiet. Not accusing — worse, curious. "Threads. Even burnouts have a snapped end, a place where something was. I've catalogued four hundred people." She takes one step closer, and you feel her own talent burning cold and enormous, a lighthouse behind cloth. "You're not empty. Empty I could file. You go down." Above you both, a bell rings for third lecture. She doesn't move. Down the corridor, footsteps — measured, unhurried, the particular gait of a man from the capital who has been very interested lately in who talks to whom.

You wake before dawn to shouting in the Cinder dormitory corridor — Piet's voice, cracked and furious. By the time you get your door open, half the class is out in nightclothes, and Piet is holding a summons with a capital seal, hands shaking. "Attunement audit," Denna reads over his shoulder. "Effective immediately. Class Cinder to be assessed first, by order of — " she squints " — Registrar Ives." You've heard the name in rumors since yesterday: a soft-spoken man asking the senior staff strange questions about the groundskeeper's death, about accounts and balances. Now you feel him for the first time, somewhere in the guest wing below, awake at this hour — a talent like a set of scales holding perfectly still, waiting for something to tip. Piet crumples the summons. "They're weeding us. Before Trials, so it doesn't dirty the numbers." Every eye in the corridor is red-rimmed and looking for somewhere to put its fear. A few of them land on you.

Night duty in the lamp room — the punishment shift they give Nulls, trimming wicks nobody trusts to fire-script. You've come to like it. From this tower you can feel the whole sleeping academy laid out below like a bed of embers: two hundred talents banked for the night, and yours the only wakefulness among them, vast and unregistered. You've been experimenting. There's a second-year whose water-sense you've been feeding a hair each night, and this morning she placed three ranks higher on the board and cried in the corridor. Nobody looked at you. Nobody ever does. Then you feel something new crossing the courtyard below: a talent that doesn't flicker like the others but holds level, a plumb line, a set of scales. Through the tower window you watch a man in a gray coat stop in the middle of the frosted grass, alone, at one in the morning, and turn his face slowly upward — toward the lamp room.

"Bottom pairs with top," Instructor Bray announces, reading from a slate. "New directive for Trial preparation. Cross-rank mentorship." The lecture hall groans. You already know what's coming before he says it, because the arithmetic is brutal and simple: bottom of the board is you. "Vael. And — " he checks the slate, as if your name needs checking " — the Null." Laughter, quickly smothered. Elowen Vael stands from the front row without expression and crosses the hall to the empty seat beside you, and the whole time her eyes are doing the thing they've done all week — not looking at your face, but slightly around it, through it, the way you'd trace where a river must run under snow. She sits. Sets down her books. Under cover of Bray's droning about Trial format, she slides a torn strip of paper onto your desk. Four words, small and neat: I know you're not.

title: Call Me Hollow One More Time
shortDescription: Every child got a splinter of the slain god's fire — except you. Now shards gutter when you pass, and the lowest company just enlisted the Hollow.
overview:
Marrowspire is built inside the ribs of the calamity its founders killed. They split its burning heart into thousands of splinters; every child receives one at the Kindling and carries a fraction of god-fire for life. Rank, marriage, bread — everything runs on splinter-strength. Ten years ago the Kindling read you empty. Hollow caste. Rendering yards. Spat on by kids whose fire you swore you'd someday command. Then last month a bearer flared out in the fish market — splinter eating her alive — and you held it barehanded, and it went quiet.

Now Captain Odaya Brannt of Cinder Company, the dumping-ground squad, has enlisted you as a 'quell': a living firebreak against flare-outs. The prodigy Sera Vael, largest splinter of her generation, gets sick and furious near you and wants you gone. The Marrow Council wants you studied. Every rival whose flame falters against yours is carrying a grief that feels weirdly like your own.

GM framing the character doesn't know: the Kindling read you empty because the seal inside you is flawless. You carry the heart itself. Every shard you quell comes home to it — and something warm has started whispering thanks. Tone: ash-and-bone dark fantasy; earned respect, petty barracks politics, dread that grows sweeter the stronger you get.

TAGS: dark fantasy, underdog, squad ranks, hidden power, status reversal
intro: You grew up Hollow in Marrowspire, the city built between a dead god's ribs — the one child the Kindling gave nothing, fit only for the rendering yards. You swore, out loud, at ten, that you'd lead them all someday. They still laugh about it. Then a splinter-bearer flared out in the market and you gripped her burning shard with bare hands, and it simply went out. Now you wear the gray sash of Cinder Company, last-ranked of the nine, enlisted as a 'quell.' Every splinter in the barracks dims when you walk in. Nobody, including you, knows why.
starters: Third day in the gray sash and Captain Odaya Brannt has you standing in the middle of the drill yard like a scarecrow while Cinder Company runs flame-forms around you. Every pass, their splinters gutter. You can see it — a big scarred man named Tench loses his fire mid-kata and swears, a wiry recruit's ember shrinks to a coal the moment she crosses within arm's reach of you. Brannt watches from the fence rail, chewing a splint of bone, marking distances in a ledger with a charcoal stub. "Again," she calls. "Closer this time." Tench spits in the ash near your boots. Not on them. Near them. That's new. The recruit hesitates at the chalk line, splinter cupped in both hands like she's shielding a candle from you specifically, and looks to Brannt, then to you, waiting.

The mess bell rang an hour ago and you're still standing at the serving plank, because the cook won't ladle your bowl. "Quells eat after bearers," he says, which isn't a rule — you checked. Behind you, most of Cinder Company pretends to eat. The barracks lamps run on splinter-fire, and the two nearest your table have dimmed to a sullen orange since you walked in. Somebody laughed about it your first night. Nobody laughs now; they just sit one bench farther away. At the far end of the hall, Sera Vael — here on some errand from Second Company, sash white as a rib — has gone still over her food, jaw tight, one hand pressed flat to her sternum like something in there hurts. She's staring at you. The cook taps his ladle against the pot, waiting for you to move along or make a thing of it.

You're halfway up Ribgate Stair when the screaming starts — a flare-out, two streets over in the dye quarter, and you're the closest gray sash in the city. By the time you shove through, a boy of maybe sixteen is on his knees in a spreading circle of scorched cobbles, his splinter blazing through the skin of his chest like a lantern through paper. His mother is being held back by neighbors. A pair of Third Company bearers stand at the circle's edge, useless, their own flames shrinking from the heat. One of them sees your sash and his face does something complicated — relief and disgust in the same breath. "Quell," he says, loud, so the crowd hears whose problem this is now. The boy's eyes find yours. The fire is already up his throat.

Rain hisses off the god's ribs high overhead, running down in warm gray streams, and you have the midnight watch alone on Cinder Company's wall because nobody wanted to share it. Below, Marrowspire glitters with ten thousand pinpoints of carried fire — every one a splinter, every one a rank you were denied. The watch-lamp beside you has dimmed to almost nothing, the way flames do near you now. Footsteps on the ladder: Captain Brannt, hood up, a flask in one hand and a folded paper in the other. She doesn't offer the flask. "Marrow Council sent this today," she says. "They want you delivered for examination. I've been sitting on it since noon." She sets the paper on the parapet between you, weighted with a stone, and looks out at the city instead of at you.

"Say it again." Sera Vael has you backed against the armory wall before morning muster, and she's sweating, which she never does — the largest splinter of a generation burns clean. Except near you. You can see her flame through her shirt, flickering like a candle in a draft, and she looks like she wants to vomit or kill you and hasn't chosen. "You told the quartermaster you're cleared for the Shatterfield rotation. Say it to my face." Behind her, three of her Second Company escort watch with the particular hunger of people hoping to see a Hollow put down. Your own squad is nowhere. The muster bell hangs silent for maybe another minute. Her hand isn't on her blade. Yet. Up close, under the fury, her eyes are red-rimmed, like she's been grieving something and doesn't know what.

The rendering yards still smell the same — tallow, bone-ash, ten years of your life. You've been sent back with a requisition slip: Cinder Company buys its lamp-fat here, and Brannt thought it was funny, or a test, or both. Old Marguse at the vat line recognizes you before you're through the gate. He worked you hardest of anyone and never once spat on you, which passed for kindness. Now he takes in the gray sash, the company knife, and wipes his hands slow on his apron. "Heard a story," he says. "Hollow kid caught god-fire barehanded in the fish market and put it out like a wet thumb on a wick." Behind him, the young sorters have stopped working to stare. One of them is maybe ten, maybe the age you were, and is looking at your sash like it's a door.

You wake to a hand over your mouth. Tench — the big scarred bearer who's hated you loudest — crouches by your bunk in the dark, finger to his lips. "Vessik's flaring," he whispers. "Started an hour ago. He made us swear not to fetch the burn-wardens. They'd cull him." Across the barracks, in the far corner, a man is curled around his own chest, biting a leather strap, light leaking between his fingers in pulses. Getting culled means the wardens cut the splinter out and everything caste-wise that comes with it — a bearer would rather burn. Tench's own flame is guttering just from kneeling this close to you, and you can see what it costs him to ask. "You touched one and it went quiet," he says. "So. Quiet him." Vessik's eyes, across the dark, are wide and pleading and terrified of you in roughly equal parts.

The Marrow Council's clerk has been asking questions for two hours in a bone-white room high in the sternum towers, and Captain Brannt has answered most of them for you, flatly, arms crossed. Now the clerk sets a small iron box on the table and opens it. Inside, on gray felt, lies a splinter — unbonded, confiscated, alive, throwing faint orange light on the ceiling. "For the record," the clerk says, quill ready, "the subject will handle the specimen while I observe duration and residual heat." Brannt's jaw works. "That wasn't the arrangement." "The arrangement," the clerk says, "is whatever the Council finds instructive." The splinter's light has already begun leaning toward you, the way a flame leans toward an open door. Two tower guards stand at your back. The box sits within reach.

Cinder Company draws the Shatterfield patrol because Cinder Company always draws the Shatterfield — the blasted district out along the god's shattered pelvis where old splinter-fires never fully died. You walk point, which Brannt insists is an honor and everyone knows is a firebreak's job. Heat shimmers up through the broken streets. The four bearers behind you keep their splinters banked and their distance measured — close enough for you to matter, far enough that their fire survives. Then Ossel, on your left flank, stops dead. "Ground light," she says. Ahead, in the ruin of a collapsed chapel, something glows through the rubble — a lost shard, decades buried, awake and pulsing like a slow heart. Standing orders say mark it, report it, walk on. Ossel is already unspooling the warning flags. It pulses again, and you'd swear it's faster now that you've stopped.

The fish market again. You didn't choose the route — Brannt sent you with dispatches, and this is the shortest way — but the stall-keepers remember. The woman whose flare-out you smothered last month has a stall by the ice barrels, alive, splinterless now, demoted to some gray caste of her own. She sees you and comes around the boards, wiping brine off her hands. "They wouldn't let me thank you," she says. "Wardens said don't speak to it. To you. Sorry." She presses a wrapped fish into your hands like contraband. Around you the market has gone half-quiet, the way it does — a Hollow in a company sash, the one from the story. Two children are already following at a distance, daring each other closer. Somewhere behind the eel stalls, someone spits, loud enough to be heard. The woman is still standing there, waiting to see what you'll say.
