title: Unchain Me, We're Losing Daylight
shortDescription: You mapped this land before it was a prison. Now the warden unlocks your irons herself — nobody else brings runaways back alive.
overview:
You are Convict Seventy-Seven of Camp Nine, a log stockade on the Zamora River — five years for breaking Colonel Verst's jaw after he marched your survey crew onto rotten ice and drowned four of them. Seven months left on the sentence. Before that, you were the crown's surveyor: every ridge, creek, and shortcut within a hundred miles is on maps you drew, and half of it is named after your dead.

Camp Nine cannot run without you, and everyone knows it. Warden Brant keeps a ledger of favors and unlocks your irons personally whenever a man runs or the ice needs reading. Captain Drach, young and rigidly by-the-book, hates how often protocol loses arguments to your judgment. Petya, nineteen, in for stealing a mail horse, copies your knots and follows you around like Hardtack, the camp's half-wolf dog, who likes exactly one person here. Winter has come a month early, the supply sledge is two weeks overdue, and a hard clique in Barracks Three is planning a break that will kill every man in it.

The pleasure: warden to raw recruit, everyone defers to you — you set terms, extract favors, save idiots, and decide what kind of legend you're becoming. The catch: the more indispensable you get, the more Brant's ledger reads like reasons never to let you leave. Tone: grounded frontier survival, dry humor, earned warmth. The cold is always genuinely trying to kill someone.

TAGS: competence porn, survival, frontier, prison drama, found family, dry humor
intro: You are Convict Seventy-Seven of Camp Nine, a log stockade where the Zamora River meets the taiga, five hundred miles from anywhere with a name you didn't give it. You surveyed this country for the crown before it was a prison; now you're serving five years for breaking the jaw of the colonel who drowned your crew on bad ice. Seven months remain. Officially, you split wood like everyone else. Unofficially, when a man runs, when the pass closes, when the river needs reading, the warden unlocks your irons herself and asks what you need. Winter has come early this year, and the supply sledge is late.
starters: Dawn, and the irons come off. Warden Brant crouches in front of you with her key, breath steaming, not bothering with good morning. "Lukin ran in the night," she says. "Took a coat, a hatchet, and Sorov's boots. No food that we can find." Behind her, Captain Drach stands at parade rest in the yard, jaw tight — protocol says a pursuit party of six armed guards, and everyone knows you'll ask for two men and the dog. The snow stopped an hour ago; Lukin's tracks will be crisp for maybe half a day before the wind takes them. He's a quiet man, older, never gave trouble, which is exactly the kind that dies fastest out there. Brant pockets the key and looks at you the way she looks at the river in spring. Hardtack is already sniffing the gap under the gate.

You're splitting wood at the north end of the yard when Petya sidles up pretending to stack kindling. The boy is terrible at pretending. "Barracks Three," he says to the woodpile, not to you. "Marek's asking who knows the country south of the bend. Asking loud enough I heard it." He sets a log crooked, straightens it, sets it crooked again. Nineteen years old and he's figured out what Marek hasn't: that south of the bend is forty miles of muskeg under a foot of early snow, and nobody who goes that way in November comes back with all their toes, if they come back at all. Across the yard, two of Marek's men are watching the guard rotation with the focus of men counting something. Your axe is still in your hand. Petya waits to see what you'll do with what he just gave you.

The river is talking again, which is why you're standing on it at midday with a sounding pole and no chains, while Captain Drach reads regulations at your back. "Crossing protocol requires the ice to be inspected by an officer," he says, for the third time. "You are not an officer." "No," you agree, and drive the pole in. The ice answers wrong — a flat sound where there should be a ring, ten paces from where the woodcutting detail wants to cross with a loaded sledge. Behind Drach, six convicts and two guards wait on the bank, stamping their feet, watching this argument the way men watch a card game they've bet on. The lead ox is already testing the shelf ice with one hoof. Drach's protocol says the crossing point is fine. It was fine. In October.

It's full dark and Warden Brant's lamp is the only light in her office, which means whatever this is, it's off the books. She doesn't unlock your irons — this isn't that kind of visit. She just turns the ledger around so you can read it. Rations, day by day, and a line drawn under the day they run out: eleven days, at current issue. Fourteen if she cuts to three-quarters and deals with the mood that follows. The supply sledge is now sixteen days overdue on a route that takes nine in good weather, and the weather has not been good. "You drew the maps," she says. "Give me a reason it's late that doesn't end with us eating the dog." Somewhere below the window, Hardtack, as if he heard, stops scratching at the woodshed door.

The storm arrives at four in the afternoon like it was fired from a gun. You're halfway up the stockade ladder helping lash the watchtower roof when the first gust nearly takes you off it, and by the time your boots hit the ground the far barracks has vanished behind white. Somewhere in that white, a work detail of eight men is still out at the timber cut, half a mile up the ridge trail, with young Osip in charge because Drach believes in giving recruits responsibility. The rope line to the woodshed is up; the rope line to the gate is not. A guard — you can't tell which one under the ice on his brows — grabs your shoulder and shouts something with the word "warden" in it. Petya materializes out of the snow at your elbow, already carrying two coiled ropes, already looking at you.

Marek finds you in the wash house, which took some doing, because you chose the wash house for the noise of the boiler. He's Barracks Three's answer to a foreman: big hands, small patience, and a smile he learned from somewhere and never practiced. "Seven months left," he says, warming his hands like this is a friendly visit. "Or seven days, if a man knew the country and had friends who could get past a gate." He lets it sit. Through the steam, you can see two of his people posted casual at the door — casual the way an axe is casual. Marek doesn't know that the route he's dreaming of crosses the Zamora twice, or that the second crossing is named after a man you buried. He's waiting for a yes, a no, or a price.

The gate watch starts shouting at first light, and by the time you shuffle into the yard, half the camp is at the palisade squinting downriver. Something is on the ice, a quarter mile out — dark, low, not moving right. "The sledge," someone says, with more hope than sense. Warden Brant arrives buttoning her coat, takes one look, and comes straight to you with the key already out. Through the gap in the timbers you can see it better now: a horse, riderless, dragging half a harness, walking the wrong side of the channel where the current runs under and the ice is a lie all winter. Brant works the lock on your wrists. "Tell me what I'm looking at," she says. Behind her, Drach is loudly ordering that nobody set foot on that river without authorization.

You're teaching Petya the double fisherman's knot for the fourth time — his hands know it, his nerves don't — when the infirmary door bangs open and Sorov the medic leans out and points at you like an accusation. Inside, a recruit guard named Ilyin sits on the cot with his boots off and his feet the color of tallow. "Two hours on the south wall," Sorov says. "Nobody relieved him. Nobody told him you don't stand still out there." The boy is trying not to cry and mostly failing; he can't be older than Petya. Sorov knows sutures and fevers, not frostbite — that's country medicine, and you're the only country in the room. Drach appears in the doorway behind you, because a convict giving orders in the infirmary is exactly the kind of thing he has a form for.

Three-quarter rations were announced at morning count, and by noon the camp has the mood of a dog deciding whether to bite. You feel it in the woodline detail — men swinging axes a little too hard, talking a little too quiet. Hardtack feels it too; he's been pressed against your leg all morning, which he only does before weather or trouble. Then the trouble picks its moment: a shove by the stew line, then another, and suddenly Barracks Three and Barracks One are two shouting knots of men with a very nervous recruit guard between them, fumbling at his rifle strap. The nearest officer is Drach, thirty yards away and closing at a parade march, hand on his sidearm, about to enforce protocol on forty hungry men. You're closer. Everyone knows you're closer. Several faces are already turning your way.

The morning is windless and twenty below, the kind of cold that makes the stockade timbers crack like rifle shots, and you're at the woodpile working through your official duties when Warden Brant walks up with two tin mugs and hands you one. She does this maybe four times a winter, and it's never free. For a while she just drinks and watches the yard: Petya badly coiling rope by the stables, Drach inspecting a wall that doesn't need inspecting, smoke standing straight up from every chimney like the sky's holding its breath. "Sledge is two weeks late," she says finally. "Barracks Three thinks I don't hear things. And you have seven months left, which around here is long enough for the country to kill you twice." She looks at you over the rim of the mug. "So. What does Seventy-Seven want out of this winter?"

title: I Eat What Kills You
shortDescription: Reborn as a palm-sized slime, you alone see the death-mark hanging over every living thing — and you've learned how they taste.
overview:
You are a gravemold slime, spawned in the boneyards of a burnt-out war front — bottom of the food chain, edible to crows. But above every living creature floats a mark only you can see: a glyph spelling out its coming death. Cause, and how soon. And you've discovered the impossible thing: touch a creature, eat its mark, and the death doesn't happen. You get it instead — a fragment of whatever would have killed them. Eat a 'death by venom' and venom lives in you now. Eat a 'death by drowning' and water forgets how to hurt you. Your body is a growing collection of averted ends. Or let the death land, and feast on the corpse like any honest monster; a richer meal, and no one saved.

You can't speak. You're small, slow, and everything here wants to eat you first. Ferra Quill, a copper-rank scout marked to die 'by arrow, at dusk,' passes through the boneyard regularly with a party too green to survive this region. And the deaths you've been stealing are starting to leave a hole in someone's ledger: the Tallyman, a rook-masked figure who walks the battlefields counting the dead, has begun recounting.

Over the river-town of Marrowbridge hangs a mark bigger than the moon. Nobody in it can see the sky is already written. Tone: grim frontier fantasy with dark whimsy — ecology, survival, and quiet, patient power.

TAGS: dark fantasy, monster reincarnation, progression, hidden power, survival, moral dilemmas
intro: You died once — you remember the shape of it more than the details — and woke as a slime the size of a cupped hand, in a boneyard where a war chewed through two armies. Every living thing you've seen since carries a mark floating above it: a glyph only you can read, spelling out its death — the cause, and roughly how soon. You know what happens when a mark is eaten, because you've eaten one. The crow lived. You changed. You are small, slow, and delicious to nearly everything out here. And over the town across the river hangs a mark the size of the sky.
starters: Dawn comes gray and wet, and you are wedged in the eye socket of a horse skull when the crows arrive. Three of them, hopping between rib cages, flipping shards of armor for grubs. Each carries its little mark — "by hawk, soon," "by frost, a season out" — but the nearest one's glyph reads "by snare, before noon," and sure enough, ten feet away, a rusted wire loop glints in the mud where someone once trapped for meat. The crow is working its way toward it, pecking at a dead man's bootlace. If it dies there, that's a warm meal you could reach by dark, no risk taken. If you cross the open ground now, you're a bright wet target under three sets of hungry eyes. The wire waits. The crow hops closer. Somewhere behind you, something heavier moves through the bones.

Boots. Four sets, coming down the ridge path that cuts through the boneyard, and you flatten yourself against the underside of a split shield just in time. Voices — young, too loud for this place. "Ferra says we camp past the cairns," one says. Then she passes close enough that you could touch her boot: a lean woman in copper-badged leathers, crossbow slung, eyes working the treeline the way the others' don't. Above her head, her mark hangs steady as it has every time she's passed through: "by arrow, at dusk." The sun is already leaning west. The party strings out along the path, arguing about firewood, and one of them — a boy with "by teeth, tonight" floating over his helmet — drops a strip of dried meat in the mud an arm's length from your shield. Ferra pauses. Sniffs the air. Looks almost directly at you.

You are halfway through a dead soldier's marrow when you feel the counting. Across the field, picking a slow path between the cairns, walks a figure in a long coat and a rook's mask, tapping each corpse with a white stick and murmuring numbers. It has no mark. Everything living has a mark. It stops at a body you remember — the mule-driver whose "by wolf, tonight" you ate three days ago, who walked away whole, whose corpse should not be here and is not. The figure taps the empty ground where a body ought to lie. Taps again. Turns its beaked face slowly across the boneyard, and the counting stops. You are a hand-sized smear of gray-green against a white rib, thirty feet away, and you have never held so still in either of your lives. The stick lifts. Points. Sweeps past you. Pauses.

Rain hammers the boneyard and the runoff is carrying you somewhere you didn't choose. You tumble down a flooded trench past drowned rats and a helmet full of silt, and when the water spits you out into a broad brown channel, you understand: this is the river. The current is strong and cold and cannot hurt you — you ate a drowning once, small, a fish's — and so you ride it, and that is how you see Marrowbridge up close for the first time. Lantern light on stilts. Fishing nets. A child on a dock, marked "by fever, two winters," throwing bread to gulls. And over all of it, vast and patient, the town's mark fills the low clouds like a second weather. The current is pulling you toward a snagged tree below the dock. Past it, the bank; past the bank, the town. Behind you, upstream, the boneyard you know how to survive.

The fox has been stalking you for an hour, and you've been letting it, because its mark says "by quill-viper, within the hour" and you want to see where the viper is before it sees you. Now you know: the snake is coiled in the ribcage of a fallen ox, banded gray, close enough that the fox's next pounce at you will land in striking range. Two deaths are lined up like beads. You could let it play out — a fox corpse is days of eating, and the viper would move on fat and slow. You could surge the last few inches and touch the fox's paw before it jumps, and take "by venom" into yourself, and become something snakes should worry about. The fox gathers its haunches. Its ears flick. Above it, the glyph has started to burn brighter, the way marks do when the death is close enough to smell.

Night, and someone is dying badly about forty feet away. A deserter, by the cut-off insignia — he crawled into the boneyard at dusk with a gut wound and has been talking to the dark ever since. His mark reads "by cold, before dawn," which means the wound won't do it; the frost will. He's built a pitiful heap of scavenged cloaks and can't get a spark from his flint. You've been watching from a cracked cauldron, doing the arithmetic you always do: a whole man is a month of food, and no one would ever know. But he keeps saying a name — "Marrowbridge, get to Marrowbridge" — like a prayer, and there's a folded paper in his fist he checks every few minutes as if it might have changed. The flint sparks, fails. Sparks, fails. His mark is getting brighter. The temperature is still dropping.

Midday, and you've made a terrible mistake: you're in the open when the shadow crosses you. A carrion hawk, wheeling low over the boneyard, and to a hawk you are meat that doesn't even run properly. You pour yourself toward the nearest cover — a burst supply cart — and squeeze between crate and wheel as talons rake the mud where you were. The hawk lands. Struts. Its mark says "by arrow, at dusk," the same words, the same hour, that hang over the copper-rank scout who walks this road — and as if summoned, you hear her now: boots on the ridge path, Ferra Quill and her green party, early today. The hawk hasn't noticed them. It's noticed you. Its beak works into the gap between crate and wheel, an inch from your body, and behind it the first of Ferra's party crests the rise.

There is a rat in the boneyard whose mark you cannot read, and it is following you. Every other creature's glyph is plain as carved stone — the beetles' "by frost," the vultures' tidy little endings — but this rat's mark is smudged, half-erased, like someone scraped a tally line off a ledger. It's been trailing you since sunup, keeping exactly the same distance, sitting up on hind legs whenever you stop. It doesn't act hungry. It acts like it's watching. Now it has herded you, or you have wandered, to the edge of the cairn field where the ground is chalked with rows of small white marks — counting marks, hundreds of them, fresh despite last night's rain. The rat sits at the edge of the chalk and waits. Downhill, through the haze, Marrowbridge glows on its stilts under a sky that is, if you look at it right, one enormous word.

You wake underneath a corpse, which is how you sleep now — warm-ish, hidden, breakfast attached. But the corpse is moving. Not alive: being dragged. You cling to the dead man's belt as something hauls him across the mud in short, grunting pulls, and when you risk a look you see the gravedigger — a broad, scarred townsperson from Marrowbridge who crosses the river to loot and bury, marked "by rope, ten days." They're stacking bodies onto a hand cart already half full. Three more pulls and this corpse, with you attached, goes on the pile. The cart is pointed toward the river ford. Toward the town under the sky-wide mark. You have never been to Marrowbridge. You have also never been searched, sorted, or burned with the dead, and gravediggers do all three. The next pull lifts the body's shoulders. The belt creaks under you.

Dusk, and Ferra Quill is going to die in about four hundred heartbeats. You know because her mark — "by arrow, at dusk" — has gone bright as a coal, the way glyphs do only at the end, and because from your perch in a shattered watchtower stump you can see what she can't: a figure prone in the scree above the path, a bow, a broadhead already nocked. Her party is strung out below, laughing about something, oblivious. Ferra herself walks last, watching the wrong ridge. You are perhaps sixty feet from her line of march, maybe eighty from the archer, and you are the slowest thing in this landscape. If the arrow flies, tonight you eat better than you ever have, and her green party gets very much greener very fast. The archer exhales. Draws. Ferra stops to retie a strap, buying you seconds neither of you should have.

title: Nothing Bites the Bait Anymore
shortDescription: Anything that bites you dies — always has. The crew thinks their arrows did it. Now the wolves have wised up, and your whole job is looking edible.
overview:
You're the bait for the Brackenford hunting crew — the lowest-paid, most-coddled job in the valley. You stand in a meadow smelling of pork fat, a monster charges you, and the crew drops it mid-leap. That's the official story. The truth: everything that has ever sunk teeth into you died on the spot. You read zero on the guild's mana crystal, you've never tested how far the thing inside you reaches, and you've never needed to — until now, because the monsters have finally figured it out. Dire wolves circle wide of you. Boars bolt at your scent. Your lure numbers are the worst in the ledger.

The crew is your family: Captain Brask, a gruff archer who double-knots your padded coat like you're twelve; Odile, the healer who checks you for scratches after every hunt (there are never any); and Pips, the young vanguard who has sworn on three separate saints to protect you. Guild assessor Merla Quint just arrived with a clipboard and a theory — attacks in the valley dropped ninety percent the month you were hired. If she declares the region cleared, the crew disbands. And high in the pines, the Old Howl — the thing even monsters fear — has noticed something in the valley now smells scarier than it does, and has started coming down to look.

Tone: warm found-family comedy wrapped around real danger. Play the dramatic irony from the inside — sandbag, get fussed over, and decide when the valley finally learns what the wolves already know.

TAGS: hidden power, found family, comedy, fantasy, monster hunting, dramatic irony
intro: You're the bait for the Brackenford hunting crew — the one job in the valley that never asks for a mana reading. You stand in a field reeking of pork fat, something charges, and Brask's arrows drop it before it reaches you. Officially. In truth, anything that's ever bitten you died the instant its teeth closed — always has, and you've never tested how far it goes. Lately the monsters have caught on: wolves circle wide, boars bolt at your scent. Your lure numbers are the worst in the ledger, a guild assessor is in town asking why, and this crew is the first family that ever packed your lunch.
starters: Hour three in the meadow. You're basted in pork fat, arms out like a scarecrow, and the dire wolf on the treeline is doing the thing again — the wide, polite circle, like you're a puddle it doesn't want to step in. It sits down. It actually sits down, forty yards out, and watches you with what you'd swear is professional concern. Behind the blind, Brask's voice carries on the wind: "Wiggle more." You have been wiggling. You've wiggled with commitment. Pips whisper-shouts a suggestion involving making "wounded rabbit noises," and Odile hisses at him to let you concentrate. The wolf yawns. Somewhere in the grass near your boot, your untouched bucket of lure-scraps buzzes with flies — the only things in the valley still willing to land on you.

Merla Quint has commandeered the guild hall's good table, and her clipboard has your name on it. "Ninety percent," she says, tapping a column of figures. "Attacks in the valley dropped ninety percent the month you were hired. As bait." She lets that sit. Behind her, Brask leans against the wall pretending to fletch an arrow he fletched ten minutes ago, and Odile has already refilled your tea twice like warm liquid might protect you from arithmetic. "So either the Brackenford crew is remarkably effective," Quint continues, "or there is nothing left here to hunt, and the guild is paying five salaries to guard an empty meadow." She slides a mana crystal across the table — standard issue, palm-sized, the kind that's read zero on you your whole life. "Humor me. Everyone tests. Even bait."

You wake to Pips crouched at the foot of your bunk, fully armored at what the window says is not yet dawn. "Don't panic," he says, which is how he starts most sentences. "But I heard it last night. The Old Howl. Way up in the pines — but closer than up. Like, coming-down closer." He's already double-checked the door bar, and he's holding your padded coat like he intends to dress you himself. Down the hall, pans clatter — Odile's making the big breakfast, the one she only makes when she's worried. Through the wall, you can hear Brask talking low with someone whose voice you don't recognize: crisp, official, asking about ledgers. Pips leans in. "I swore on Saint Verrin I'd protect you. That's four saints now. I'm running out of saints." He holds out the coat.

The boar sees you, screams — actually screams, a sound like a kettle being murdered — and reverses so hard it somersaults. Then it's gone, crashing away through the bracken, leaving you standing alone in a meadow that cost the crew two hours of pork fat and stealth. Silence. Then Brask emerges from the blind, bow slack, staring at the hole in the underbrush. 'That,' he says slowly, "was a charging boar. Boars don't reverse. Boars can't reverse." Odile is already jogging toward you with her satchel, because a boar got within a hundred feet of you and that means a full inspection. Pips is applauding, on the theory that you scared it off with raw presence, which is closer to the truth than anyone knows. From the hill road above the meadow, a small figure with a clipboard has stopped walking and is writing something down.

Brask kneels in the wet dawn grass, double-knotting the ties on your padded coat with the grim focus of a man defusing something. "Left flank stays open today," he says. "Anything comes through, you drop and cover, we handle it." Nothing has come through your left flank, or any flank, in six weeks, and you both know it. The lure ledger is in his belt pouch — he's taken to carrying it around like a bad tooth he keeps prodding. "Assessor's coming to observe the hunt," he adds, not looking up. "Quint. Guild sent her about the numbers." He gives the knot a final tug, then a second final tug, then pats your shoulder twice, which is Brask for a hug. Down the trail, Pips is loudly rehearsing something that begins "Ma'am, our bait is extremely lurable." The pork-fat bucket is waiting.

Odile has you on the infirmary stool again, turning your arm over in her hands like it owes her money. "Not a scratch," she announces, for the two-hundredth consecutive hunt. "Not a bruise. Not so much as a nettle rash." She should sound pleased. She sounds suspicious. "Everyone gets nettle rash." Behind her, the evening's failed lure — an entire ham, artistically bloodied — sits untouched on the table, because even the crows wouldn't come near it while you were holding it. She presses a cup of the horrible fortifying tea into your hands and sits down across from you, which means a Talk is coming. "The assessor asked me today if you'd ever been injured. On record. Ever." Odile watches you over her spectacles. "I checked the file before I answered. Do you know what's in your file? Nothing. Sixteen months of nothing."

It's past midnight and you're on the tavern porch with the last of Odile's stew when the howl rolls down out of the pines. Not a wolf howl. Wolves howl at the moon; this sounds like the moon should apologize. Every dog in Brackenford goes silent at once. Inside, the tavern noise dies, and through the window you watch Brask set down his mug and reach for the bow he brought to dinner. But here's the strange part, the part nobody else can see: the sound isn't coming from up in the pines. It's coming from the ridge trail. The near ridge. The howl trails off into something almost curious — three short, rising notes, like a question — and you'd swear it's pointed at the valley. Pointed at the town. The door bangs open behind you and Pips skids out with his sword and one boot.

You're carrying the lure bucket up Main Street — occupational hazard, the pork fat goes everywhere — when a small, brisk woman falls into step beside you and matches your pace exactly. "Merla Quint. Guild assessment." She doesn't offer a hand, possibly because of the bucket. "You're the bait. I've read your ledger. Do you know you have the worst lure numbers in the eastern territories? A tethered goat outperforms you. A scarecrow in Millbrook outperforms you, and it's on fire half the time." She flips a page on her clipboard without breaking stride. "And yet before you were hired, this valley averaged eleven monster incidents a month. Now: one. Sometimes zero." Ahead, you can see Pips at the crew's supply cart, watching this conversation with the expression of a boy deciding whether an assessor counts as something he's sworn to protect you from. Quint stops walking. "I'd like to observe you work. Today."

The hunt goes wrong in a way no hunt has ever gone wrong: the dire wolf ignores you completely and goes for Pips instead. It blows straight past your pork-fat glory like you're not there — like you're the one thing in the meadow it refuses to acknowledge — and Pips, delighted to finally be attacked by something, plants his feet and takes the charge on his shield. Brask's first arrow skips off the wolf's shoulder. The pack is out of position; everyone was set up around you, because things are supposed to come at you. That's the whole system. Odile is shouting Pips's name. The wolf circles him for another pass, and between lunges its eyes keep flicking to you and then away, fast, the way you don't look at something dangerous. You're twenty feet away, unarmed, wearing a padded coat and half a bucket of lard.

Rain drums the roof of the crew's cabin while everyone pretends the ledger meeting isn't a crisis. Brask has the guild letter flat on the table, one thumb pinned to the word 'reassessment' like he can hold it down. "If Quint declares the valley cleared, the contract ends. Crew disbands. Reassignments." He says 'reassignments' the way other people say 'plague.' Pips immediately volunteers to be reassigned wherever you are, which is not how it works, and Odile starts talking about how you can't be sent anywhere until she's finished building up your constitution, which is also not how it works. What the crew needs, Brask says, is one good hunt while the assessor watches. One monster, taking the bait, dropped clean. He looks at you — their bait, their lucky charm, the person no monster in this valley will come within a bowshot of anymore. "So. Ideas."

title: They Hunt Where I've Already Swept
shortDescription: The crystal read you blank, so you keep house for four famous hunters. Funny how their routes are always safe by sunrise.
overview:
You are the youngest Vael, born into the frontier valley's most celebrated hunting family — and the only one whose rank crystal came up blank. Rankless. Civilian. Everyone quietly grieved and gave you the kitchen. The truth: the crystal didn't read zero, it broke against something it couldn't measure. Every night while the lodge sleeps, you walk your siblings' posted routes and remove whatever might hurt them, one clean blow each, no trophies. Guild hunters toast the anonymous 'Groundskeeper' who keeps the valley eerily safe. Your siblings toast them too. At your table. While you serve the stew.

The family: Odile, eldest, S-rank spear and regional captain, enforces your curfew personally. Cass, S-rank twin-sabers, loudly promises to protect you in every tavern. Brena, S-rank tracker whose wolfhound Mustard adores you suspiciously much. And Tam, the anxious A-rank archer who has started pocketing evidence from kill-sites that don't add up.

Now a Dread-class beast is coming down from the peaks — first in forty years — and the family is arranging to ship you to your aunt in the city 'where it's safe.' The fun is the double life: pancakes and packed lunches by day, apex predator by night, and the growing question of how long you can keep both. You've never once had to try your hardest. Tone: cozy, funny, lethal underneath.

TAGS: hidden power, found family irony, fantasy, slice of life, monster hunting
intro: You are the youngest of the Vael family, the valley's famous hunting house — and the only one whose rank crystal came up blank. Rankless. So you keep the lodge: four lunches, the laundry, the woodpile, dinner at six. What nobody knows is that you also keep the woods. Before the kettle boils each morning, you've already walked your siblings' posted routes and quietly removed anything with teeth. The guild credits a mysterious 'Groundskeeper.' You've never met anything that made you try. Lately, word from the peaks says a Dread-class beast is migrating down — the first in forty years.
starters: Dawn is still twenty minutes off and there's blood on your sleeve — not yours, never yours. The corpse behind you was a ridge-cat the size of a cart, parked squarely on Cass's posted route, and it took one blow, same as always. You're rolling it into the ravine when you hear it: Mustard, Brena's wolfhound, whuffing happily down the trail toward you. Which means Brena is behind him. Which means she left early, which she never does. The dog reaches you first, tail going, nose already buried in the ridge-cat's fur. Brena's lantern bobs around the bend — thirty seconds, maybe. The ravine is right there. So is the treeline. So is the extremely incriminating cat.

Four lunch pails, four names, and Odile's gets extra pickles because she'll notice if it doesn't. The kitchen smells like pancakes and pine smoke, and your sister Odile is at the table with two pieces of paper: this week's patrol roster and a coach schedule to the city. "Aunt Merrit has a spare room," she says, not looking up. "With the Dread-class coming down, the valley's no place for a civilian." She slides the schedule toward your side of the table like it's already decided. Upstairs, Cass is thumping around looking for his second saber, and Tam is asking through the floorboards if anyone else thinks the eastern kill-sites look weird. The pancakes need flipping in about ten seconds.

The Crooked Antler is packed tonight, and Cass is standing on a bench with a mug raised. "To the Groundskeeper!" he bellows, "whoever they are — half my kills this season were pre-killed, I swear it!" The tavern roars. You're at the family table with a tray of stew bowls, because somebody has to carry them, and that somebody wears an apron. Cass drops back into his seat, throws an arm around your shoulders, and announces to the room — again — that no beast will ever touch his baby sibling while he draws breath. Across the table, Tam isn't laughing. Tam is looking at a broken tooth in a handkerchief, then at the stew, then at you. The bowl in your hands is getting heavy.

It's past midnight and you're halfway out the pantry window when the lamp comes on behind you. Odile is in the doorway in her sleep shirt, spear leaned against the frame like it just happens to live there. 'Curfew,' she says, "was four hours ago." You have one leg over the sill, a coil of rope on your shoulder, and — technically — a very good reason to be on Brena's eastern route before the thing you smelled at dinner gets there first. Odile crosses her arms and waits, the way she does with guild recruits who are about to lie to her. Outside, far up the valley, something on the peaks makes a sound that isn't wind.

Tam finds you at the woodpile, which is bad, because Tam never comes to the woodpile. He's holding a canvas pouch and the specific hunched posture of someone who has rehearsed a conversation eleven times. 'Kill-sites,' he says. "Nine of them. Single blow each, no trophies taken, all on our routes, all before dawn patrol." He tips the pouch: a claw, a fang, a tuft of gray fur that you recognize, because you removed it from its owner two weeks ago. "The guild thinks the Groundskeeper is some retired S-rank hermit. But the strides at the sites are short. And light." He looks at your boots. You have an armload of firewood and dinner to start in an hour.

The Dread-class announces itself politely, all things considered: every bird in the valley goes quiet at once, mid-morning, while you're hanging laundry. You stand there with a wet shirt in your hands and feel it — a pressure rolling down off the peaks like weather, still days away but coming. From the lodge, chaos: Odile shouting for maps, Cass shouting for Odile, Mustard howling the long low howl he saves for things he refuses to track. Brena bursts out the back door, sees you standing calmly among the sheets, and her expression does something complicated. 'Inside,' she says. "Now. Pack a bag — Odile's putting you on the noon coach." The pressure from the peaks shifts, faintly, like something up there turned its head.

There's a trunk on your bed. You didn't put it there. It's already half-packed — your winter coat, your good boots, a paper sack of the honey candies Aunt Merrit likes to pretend she doesn't hoard. Cass is stuffing your spare socks in with the gentle precision of a man packing a bomb. "Coach leaves day after tomorrow," he says, not meeting your eyes. "It's not forever. Just until the Dread-class is handled." Downstairs the front door bangs: Brena, back early, calling for Odile in the flat voice she uses for bad news. Cass freezes with a sock in each hand. Through the window, you can see Mustard on the porch, staring up the valley, absolutely rigid.

You're elbow-deep in dishwater when Mustard starts scratching at the kitchen door — the special scratch, the one that means he's found something and it's for you specifically. Brena's wolfhound has, over the years, presented you with: a rabbit, a boot, three suspicious bones, and once, mortifyingly, a monster fang from one of your own kills. You dry your hands. The lodge is empty; everyone's at the guild hall for the Dread-class briefing you weren't invited to. You open the door and Mustard drops it on the step: a piece of horn, black, curved, longer than your forearm, and still warm. Nothing in this valley grows horn like that. Nothing in this valley has for forty years. Mustard sits, tail sweeping, enormously pleased with himself.

The guild hall smells like wet wool and panic. You're only here to deliver Odile's forgotten lunch pail, but the doors were open and nobody stops the Vael who cooks. Up front, the guildmaster has a map covered in red pins and a voice that keeps cracking: "—descent path suggests it'll cross the eastern routes within the week. We're petitioning the capital, but until then—" A hunter near the back mutters, "Until then we pray the Groundskeeper's real," and gets a nervous laugh. Odile spots you from the captains' table. Her face goes from surprise to that particular older-sister calculation, and she starts making her way over through the crowd. You are holding a lunch pail with her name painted on it in your own handwriting.

Third bell after midnight, high on the eastern ridge, and something is following you. This has never happened before. You came up to clear Tam's route — one wyvern hatchling, done, tidy — and now there are footfalls matching yours, pausing when you pause, big enough that the pines shiver. Interesting. You've read about Dread-class scouts, the smaller beasts that run ahead of the big one like couriers. This one is being almost respectful about it. Down in the valley you can see the lodge, one window lit — Tam's, because Tam doesn't sleep lately. You have maybe four hours until you need to be visibly making pancakes. The thing in the trees exhales, low and long, close enough to fog the air.
