title: Two Hundred Years, Three Carts
shortDescription: The dynasty's last written memory rides on three ox-carts through a burning war. You're the hired blade keeping its young keeper alive.
overview:
Joseon, summer 1592. Three weeks ago the Japanese landed at Busan; now the capital has fallen, the king is fleeing north, and three of the kingdom's four history archives are ash. Only the Jeonju copy of the Annals survives — over eight hundred volumes, two hundred years of everything Joseon ever was, packed into lacquered chests on three ox-carts, along with the founder's royal portrait. You are a lowborn tiger hunter of the Jeolla hills, hired for a string of copper to get the carts into the Naejang mountains before Kobayakawa's vanguard reaches the plain.

Your employer is Seo Gyeom, nineteen, junior archivist and sole surviving custodian, who bows to you like an equal (scandalous), quotes dead ministers when frightened, and genuinely believes the books matter more than either of your lives — including his. He will walk into a bandit camp to recover one stolen volume. That is your real job: protecting him from the war, and from himself.

The enemies are everywhere and mostly mundane: Japanese patrols, bandits, starving refugees, Korean officers who want your oxen for supply duty and think paper is kindling — and the monsoon, because mildew kills books as surely as fire, and priceless pages must be sun-dried in the open while armies move. Grounded, grim-but-warm historical drama, rooted in a true story. Muddy roads, small mercies, stubborn hope.

TAGS: historical drama, war, protector, survival, road journey, found family
intro: You are a tiger hunter of the Jeolla hills — lowborn, good with a bow, better with terrain. Three weeks ago the Japanese landed at Busan and the war has moved faster than rumor: the king fled the capital, and the archives at Chunchugwan, Chungju, and Seongju burned with their cities. Seo Gyeom, the nineteen-year-old junior archivist of Jeonju, has hired you to move the last complete Annals of the dynasty — hundreds of volumes in lacquered chests on three ox-carts — into the Naejang mountains before the enemy vanguard reaches the plain. You know the paths. He knows the books. The monsoon is coming, and paper fears rain almost as much as fire.
starters: Dawn, and the Gyeonggijeon courtyard smells of lacquer and ox dung. Porters heave the last chests onto the third cart while Seo Gyeom stands on a step with his ledger, calling volume numbers in a voice too steady for how white his knuckles are. "Sejong, year twelve through year nineteen — confirm." A porter grunts. Down the hill, Jeonju's streets are already loud with people leaving; a rumor came in the night that Geumsan is burning, and Geumsan is close. Your bow is strung. The string of copper he paid you sits heavy inside your jacket. The lead ox stamps, unhappy about something — the crowd, the smoke-smell on the wind, or the man in a provincial officer's coat who has just walked through the gate and stopped to stare at the carts, counting them.

The second cart is axle-deep in mud and the rain has not even properly started yet — this is just the warning drizzle, fat drops off the pines. You have one shoulder against the wheel and both feet losing purchase. Seo Gyeom is on the other side, sleeves rolled, pushing with the whole of his skinny weight and quoting somebody: "Minister Hwang said a burden shared is a road shortened." The porters heave on your count. Behind you on the road, a line of refugees has stopped to watch — a dozen of them, silent, eyes moving from the straining oxen to the lacquered chests, doing the arithmetic of what a chest that size might hold. The wheel shifts a finger's width and sinks back. Thunder, south of here, or something that isn't thunder.

You wake before the birds, the way you always do in the hills, and the fire is down to coals and Seo Gyeom is not under his blanket. You find him twenty paces off in the grey light, kneeling at the open lid of a chest, a volume unwrapped across his knees, checking the pages by touch for damp. "I could smell it," he says without looking up. "Mildew. Faint. Maybe only the oilcloth." The oxen are still hobbled, the porters still snoring. The mountains you're aiming for are a blue smudge to the west. And on the road below your camp — the road you left at dusk precisely so no one would see you — someone is walking, alone, quickly, coming from the direction of Jeonju, and they haven't noticed you yet.

The officer at the ford has six soldiers, four spears between them, and a requisition order he keeps tapping with two fingers. "Oxen and carts for army supply. By authority of the provincial commander." Behind you the three carts wait on the bank, water hissing over the shallows, porters pretending to check harness. Seo Gyeom has gone rigid and formal, holding out his archivist's credentials with both hands like an offering. "These carts carry the Annals of the dynasty," he says. The officer glances at the chests. 'Paper,' he says. "My men are carrying rice on their backs, and you have three oxen for paper." One of the soldiers has already drifted toward the lead animal's halter rope. The river is fordable here and nowhere else for half a day in either direction, and you know it, and possibly so does he.

Midday, the first true sun in three days, and two hundred volumes are laid open on straw mats across a hillside meadow like a field of white birds. Seo Gyeom moves down the rows turning pages to the light, murmuring to the books, actually murmuring. The porters doze by the carts under the treeline. It is the most dangerous thing you have done all week — half the archive spread in the open, an hour from being packed — and you have said so, and he agreed with you completely and did it anyway, because mildew had gotten into the Taejong chest. Now, from your lookout rock, you see it: movement on the far ridge, sun catching on something. Metal, or water, or nothing. It doesn't repeat. Below you, Seo Gyeom laughs at something a dead king wrote two hundred years ago.

It is raining like the sky has a grudge, and you are under the oilcloth of the middle cart with a shuttered lantern, listening. Not to the rain — through it. Footsteps, you're nearly sure, off to the left where the trail bends. The porters heard nothing and are asleep in the lee of the rocks. Seo Gyeom is awake beside you because he is always awake, and to his credit he has learned to whisper: 'Bandits?' "Or a deer." "Or soldiers." "Or a deer." He accepts this with a scholar's nod and then ruins it by adding, "The Chungju archive had a rain like this the night before it burned. The custodian wrote that the thatch was too wet to catch. He was wrong." The footsteps — if they are footsteps — have stopped. The lead ox lifts its head.

The refugee column has been passing your hiding spot for an hour: old men with A-frames, a woman carrying a door on her back, children too tired to cry. You pulled the carts into a cedar stand off the road at first sight of them, because hungry people and slow oxen are a bad mix, and mostly it has worked. Mostly. A boy of maybe eight has wandered off the road to relieve himself and is now standing ten paces away, staring straight at you, at the carts, at the sack of millet lashed to the second one. Behind you, before you can stop him, Seo Gyeom is already untying the sack's cord. "They burned Geumsan," the boy says, matter-of-fact, the way children report weather. On the road, an adult's voice calls a name, twice, getting closer.

You smell the Japanese patrol before you see it — horse sweat and something like camphor, carried up the gully on the evening wind. Then the sounds: hooves on stone, a language you don't know, unhurried. The carts are stopped on the old charcoal-burners' track thirty feet above the main road, screened by scrub oak, and by pure luck the oxen have their noses in feed bags. Six riders below, maybe eight. Seo Gyeom is flat on his belly beside you, and you can feel him composing himself, breath by breath. One of the porters, Big Ma, has his hand clamped over the youngest porter's mouth. On the road, the riders slow. One dismounts. He crouches, and touches the mud, where — you realize with a cold drop in your stomach — three sets of cart tracks turn off toward the gully.

"One volume," Seo Gyeom says. "They took one volume. Sejong, year twenty-two." It's an hour past dawn and the porters are still shaking off sleep and arguing about whose watch it happened on. The thieves were quiet and quick and took what they could carry: half a sack of millet, a cooking pot, a brass buckle, and — from the chest with the loose hasp — one book, probably because lacquered chests look like they hold silver. Their trail is child's play to you, bare feet and one pair of straw sandals, heading up toward the ridge where you saw a fire glow two nights back. Seo Gyeom is rolling up his sleeping mat with terrible calm. "Eight hundred volumes are complete," he says. "Seven hundred ninety-nine are kindling." He has clearly already decided something. The oxen aren't even yoked yet.

Dusk at the river crossing, water brown and fast with three days of upstream rain, and the lead ox will not go in. You've crossed here a dozen times hunting; you've never seen it this high. The first cart stands hub-deep at the edge, the ox braced and rolling its eyes, the porter hauling on the nose rope and getting nowhere. On the far bank, exactly where you want to be, the trail climbs into the safe dark of the hills. On this bank, exactly where you don't, the plain stretches open behind you, and somewhere on it — a day back, maybe less — is Kobayakawa's vanguard. Seo Gyeom wades out beside the cart without asking anyone, water to his thighs, one hand flat on the nearest chest as if to reassure it. "Taejo's portrait is on this one," he says. Upstream, faintly, you hear something heavy coming down with the current.

title: I One-Starred This World
shortDescription: You ragequit this novel when the beloved healer betrayed the party. Now you ARE the healer — and the knife goes in three arcs from now.
overview:
Three years ago you dropped the webnovel 'Dawnbreak Sovereign' at chapter 197 — the chapter where Vael, the company's gentle healer and the best character in the whole story, poisoned the hero at the Gate of Reeds and walked away smiling. You left a furious one-star review and never found out why. The novel ran on for hundreds of chapters without you. This morning you woke up as Vael, somewhere around chapter sixty, with none of Vael's memories — only your reading.

The company: Aurel, the chosen one, who trusts you with every wound and every secret; Bran, the shield-knight who trusts no one and watches you chew your food; Isolde, the mage who once — in a chapter you remember — almost found something sewn into your bedroll. You've found it now: a black cipher journal in handwriting identical to yours, and a letter sealed in grey moth wax, signed only 'M.', asking why your reports have stopped.

You know every ambush, false saint, and dungeon floor up to chapter 197 — and nothing after. Play the beloved healer. Feed the handler, or starve them. Decide whether the betrayal is destiny, coercion, or something you can cut out of this body like a tumor. Tone: warm found-family adventure over a slow, cold dread; canon flows like a current, not a cage.

TAGS: transmigration, secret identity, found family, fantasy adventure, mystery, dread
intro: You read "Dawnbreak Sovereign" up to chapter 197 — the chapter where Vael, the company's healer, poisoned Aurel and vanished — and you quit the novel in fury. This morning you woke in Vael's body, on the road with Aurel's company, somewhere in the arcs you still remember. You have Vael's face, Vael's satchel, Vael's steady hands, and none of Vael's memories. Sewn into your bedroll you've found a cipher journal in your own handwriting, and a letter sealed with grey moth wax, signed 'M.', asking why the reports have stopped. So far the story is on script. Chapter 197 is three arcs away.
starters: Dawn hasn't broken yet. You're sitting on a cold log with the letter open on your knee, the grey moth wax cracked in two, reading "why have the reports stopped" for the fifth time. Ten feet away, Aurel sleeps with his sword arm flung over his face, trusting. The fire is embers. Across it, Bran is awake — he's always awake — cleaning a buckle that doesn't need cleaning, and he hasn't looked at you once, which is how you know he's watching. Isolde talks in her sleep, a word that might be a spell. Your satchel sits by your boot, packed by hands that knew what every vial was for. In an hour the company breaks camp and heads north toward a village you remember from chapter sixty-three, where a well is going to go bad and someone is going to blame a witch. The letter is very light in your hand. The fire is very close.

Aurel is bleeding on you. "It's not deep," he says, which is what he always says, grinning through it while you peel the torn shirt from a gash a border-bandit's hook left across his ribs. Your hands — Vael's hands — are already moving, thumbing the wound's edges, reaching into the satchel without looking. You know these bandits. Chapter fifty-eight, maybe fifty-nine: a toll ambush the company walks through with barely a scratch. On script. The rest of them are still down the slope, Bran making sure of the fallen, Isolde snuffing her fire from her fingertips. "You've got that face," Aurel says, watching you the way he watches no one else — openly, easily. "The one where you're deciding whether to lecture me." Your fingers find a jar of salve and a needle. His heartbeat is right under your palm.

Isolde is holding your bedroll. "It fell off the cart," she says, and maybe it did — the mule startled at the ford and half the packs went sideways — but she's holding it a moment too long, thumb resting near the seam you restitched two nights ago by feel, in the dark, with the journal and the letter back inside. The river noise covers whatever your face is doing. Behind her, Bran hauls a crate out of the shallows and Aurel laughs at something, bright and unbothered, water to his knees. 'Vael,' Isolde says, quieter. "It's heavier than it looks." She isn't smiling and she isn't not. In the version you read, she almost found it once and let it go. You don't know which chapter you're standing in. She holds the bedroll out to you across the wet stones.

The market at Harrow's Cross smells of onions and rain. You're meant to be buying willowbark — Aurel gave you three coppers and a list in his terrible handwriting — but you've stopped dead in front of the notice board, because pinned among the reward bills and lost-goat notices is a folded paper sealed in grey moth wax. No name on it. It's at eye level. Your eye level. Around you the market moves: a farmer arguing over turnips, a child chasing a dog, and somewhere behind you Bran, who said he'd "stretch his legs" the moment you left the inn. The willowbark seller is calling out to you — apparently Vael is a regular here, apparently Vael has a usual order. The wax seal sits there like a held breath. In the story, Harrow's Cross was two paragraphs. Nothing happened here. Nothing was supposed to.

Second watch, and Bran hands you half his bread. He's never done that in sixty chapters. You take it because refusing would be worse, and now he's sitting on the deadfall beside you, close enough that you can hear his knee click, both of you facing the dark treeline. "You eat left-handed now," he says. Not a question. The fire's behind you; Aurel and Isolde are shapes in their blankets. Somewhere out there is the road to Thornmill, and three days past Thornmill is a monastery you remember burning down around the company's ears. Bran chews. Waits. In the novel he never caught Vael at anything — not once, not until the reeds — but the novel wasn't written from inside your skin, sweating over a piece of bread. An owl goes over, low. Bran's eyes track it and come back to you.

You remember this bend in the road. You've been dreading it since breakfast: the split oak, the culvert, the way the ground rises on the left — chapter sixty-one, the false toll-collectors, six of them in the ditch and one in the tree. In the book the ambush goes fine. Bran takes an arrow in the shield, Aurel makes a joke, nobody dies. But you're twenty feet ahead of the others because Aurel asked you to check the mule's hoof, and the split oak is right there, and you can see — you can actually see — a boot heel in the ditch grass. In the book, Vael walked past this spot and said nothing, and later, on a reread, that always bothered you. Behind you, Aurel calls out, asking if the road looks clear. The man in the tree hasn't seen you notice him yet.

The inn is loud and golden and Aurel is telling the story of the marsh-hag wrong, on purpose, to make Isolde correct him. "She was NINE feet tall—" "She was five feet and you screamed—" Bran almost smiles into his cup, which for Bran is uproarious. There's stew, there's a fire, there's your name — Vael, Vael, tell him, you were there — being said with such easy affection that your chest hurts. You were there. Somebody was. Under the table, your satchel leans against your shin, and inside the satchel, wrapped in an old shirt, is a cipher journal you've been failing to read for two nights. Aurel turns to you, cheeks flushed, and says, "Settle it. You never lie." The whole table looks at you, warm and waiting. The whole table believes that sentence.

The shrine of Saint Odrenne stands at the crossroads, candle stubs and coins at her stone feet, and Aurel is already kneeling. You know this saint. Chapter eighty-something: her whole cult turns out rotten, relics stuffed with graverot charms, and the company nearly dies untangling it. That's a full arc away — but here's her wayside shrine now, twenty chapters early, and Aurel is pressing his forehead to her carved hand asking for a blessing on the road. Isolde hangs back, arms crossed, reading the votive ribbons like they're contracts. Bran watches the crossroads instead of the saint. One of the ribbons, faded grey, is knotted three times in a way that means nothing to you and might mean everything to Vael. Aurel rises, dusts his knees, and holds out a candle stub to you — the company's healer, who apparently always lights one.

Grey light, cold ground, and everyone still asleep — this is the only hour that's yours. You've got the cipher journal open against your knees, tilted toward the pale east, working through it symbol by symbol. Some of it is starting to give: it's a substitution, and whoever built it — you built it — anchored it to something you should know by heart. There's a column of entries with dates. There's a word that repeats near the margins, short, four characters, underlined twice. Behind you, canvas rustles. Isolde sleeps lightest of all of them; in the book that detail saved the company twice. You have maybe a minute of true privacy left, the journal warm in your hands like something alive, and a whole camp about to wake up and call you by name.

Rain hammers the wagon canvas and Aurel is shivering under two cloaks, fever climbing since noon. Marsh-tick sickness — you remember it, chapter sixty-six, three ugly days that Vael manages with steady doses and no drama. Bran drives the mule through the downpour; Isolde holds a witchlight so you can see. The satchel is open across your lap, and Vael's hands have already found the fever-draught by instinct, cool green glass, exactly where it should be. But beside it sits a second vial, unlabeled, stoppered in grey wax, and you have no memory and no chapter for it. Aurel's eyes crack open. 'Vael,' he manages, teeth chattering, "whatever it is, I trust you. Just — make it not taste like pond." Isolde leans in with the light. The two vials sit side by side in the swaying wagon.

title: My Hoard Expects Breakfast
shortDescription: Thirty-nine sacrifices, none eaten — they live in your vale and critique your roaring. The new king skipped tribute and sent a slayer instead.
overview:
You are the Wyrm of Mount Carrach — four centuries old, big as a chapel, and the reason the kingdom of Brennard sleeps soundly: every spring they send one tribute up your mountain to be devoured. Inconvenient heirs. Witnesses. Daughters who wouldn't marry right. You have never eaten one. They live in the green vale behind your den — thirty-nine 'sacrifices' and the children born up there since, all officially dead, all safe exactly as long as the world stays terrified of you.

Your people: Ostra, once the crown's own auditor, sacrificed for what she counted, now keeper of your ledger and your temper. Pel, sent up at nine, now your smart-mouthed lookout. Ivette, a baker, six years 'dead,' who runs your kitchen like a fiefdom. And the problem: young King Aldric II has refused tribute to prove his strength and commissioned Ser Halden Vosk, a celebrated dragonslayer, to end you. Halden is Ivette's little brother — riding north to avenge a sister who is alive and kneading dough thirty feet behind your left wing.

Turn to turn you play both roles: the smoke-and-roar terror of Brennard, and the den-parent of the vale — settling feuds, warming the forge, letting kids nap on your tail. Kill the slayer and an army follows. Die and everyone is exposed. Tone: cozy-dangerous — warm banter, dragon theater, real stakes.

TAGS: fantasy, monster protagonist, found family, dramatic irony, cozy-dangerous
intro: You are the Wyrm of Mount Carrach. For thirty-nine years the kingdom of Brennard has sent a tribute up your mountain each spring — and each spring you have carried them, weeping and certain of death, over the ridge into the hidden vale where all the others live. The kingdom sends up its inconvenient people; you keep them. Your terrible reputation is the only wall around that little village of the officially dead, so you tend the reputation like a garden: smoke on the peak, roars at the right moon, a scorched treeline for travelers to gasp at. This spring, no tribute came. Instead the trade road carries news: the new king has declared the pact ended, and a slayer named Ser Halden Vosk rides north to make his name on your skull.
starters: Dawn, and the smoke on your peak needs feeding. You are halfway through hauling a green pine trunk to the vent-fire — nothing smolders like fresh pine, and travelers on the trade road expect their pillar of dread — when Pel comes scrambling up the scree with his spyglass banging against his chest. "Riders," he pants. "Six of them, at the ford. One's got a banner. One's got a lance as long as I am tall, times three." He plants himself between your forefeet, which is where he stands when he's scared and pretending not to be. Below, in the vale behind you, someone is ringing the breakfast bell, cheerful and oblivious. The pine trunk is still in your jaws. Pel looks up at you, waiting for a plan, or a joke, or both.

Ivette has commandeered your left forefoot as a proofing shelf again. Three dozen loaves rise in the warmth of your scales while she jabs a floury finger at your snout. "You will not shift until the second batch is in, I don't care what's on fire." The den smells of yeast and cinders. It's a good morning — until Ostra comes in from the outer cave with the ledger under her arm and that particular flat look she gets when the numbers say something she doesn't like. "No tribute cart at the boundary stone," she says. "Third week past the equinox. And a peddler at the low market is telling anyone who'll listen that the king has hired himself a slayer." Ivette keeps kneading. The loaves keep rising against your foot. Everyone in the room is now looking at you.

You are mid-roar when you spot him. Full theater tonight — wings spread against the moon, flame licked along the ridgeline so the villages downslope get their seasonal reminder — and there, on the switchback trail a mile below, a single armored figure sits his horse and watches you. He doesn't run. He doesn't even shift in the saddle. He simply raises one gauntleted hand, as if marking your position on a map only he can see, then turns his horse back down the mountain. The lance across his back catches the firelight. Behind you, over the ridge, the vale is dark and sleeping, forty-some hearts trusting the monster on the peak to stay a monster. Your roar dies in your throat, tasting suddenly like a performance someone has seen through.

"Hold still," Ostra says, and walks the length of your spine with her boots finding the gaps between your dorsal plates, ledger open against her hip. This is your weekly accounting: grain stores, the goat census, who owes whom for the roof-mending, which children have learned their letters. "Flour's short. Ivette wants a raid on the mill at Dunmere — a theatrical one, smoke and thunder, sacks conveniently dropped." She pauses at your shoulder. "And there's the other item." She doesn't have to say it. You've both heard the road-talk: the pact revoked, a slayer riding north, a young king who needs a corpse to prove himself with. Down in the vale, morning fires are starting, thin and trusting. "So," Ostra says, tapping her pen on the page like it's an execution warrant she's deciding whether to sign. "Flour first, or the war?"

There is a child asleep on your tail. There are, on inspection, three children asleep on your tail, plus a fourth using your hind claw as a fortress for pinecone soldiers. The vale's parents dropped them at the den this morning because it's washing day, and you are, apparently, furniture. You have been drowsing in the sun-warm mouth of the cave, half-listening to the pinecone war, when Pel drops out of the lookout crag above with all the grace of a thrown boot. "Don't roar," he says quickly, eyes flicking to the sleepers. "But I need you to see the road. Now. There's a knight at the scorch-line, and he's not gasping and turning back like they're supposed to. He's taking measurements." The fortress child looks up at you both with enormous interest. The knight, presumably, keeps measuring.

Night, and rain, and you are lying across the ridge like a wall, because tonight that is what you are. Below on the trade road, a camp: one banner, one pavilion, one string of horses. The slayer's fire glints off stacked steel. He made no secret of his coming — heralds cried it in three towns, Pel says, "Ser Halden Vosk rides to end the Wyrm of Carrach." A man who announces himself wants an audience. Behind you, downslope, a single lantern still burns in the vale: Ivette's kitchen window, because she bakes when she's worried and she's been baking since sundown. The rain hisses where it hits your flanks. You could reach that camp in one glide. You could also be back in the den before the bread comes out of the oven, and pretend until morning that you have a plan.

"Say it again," Ivette says, very quietly, and the whole kitchen goes still. Pel, perched on the flour barrel with his boots dripping road-mud, repeats his news from the low market: pact ended, slayer hired, riding north with the king's own writ. He gets to the name — Ser Halden Vosk — and Ivette sets down her rolling pin with the careful precision of someone who does not trust her own hands. "Vosk," she says, to nobody. The porridge is scorching on the hearth. Two of the vale's children are in the doorway, sent to fetch the morning loaves, watching the adults with the sharp attention children give to things going wrong. Your head fills most of the kitchen's cave-mouth, and everyone, including Ivette, is now carefully not looking at you, which is its own kind of looking.

The feud has reached your den, which means it's officially your problem. Marta and old Corren stand in front of your snout at dawn, both talking, neither listening — something about a boundary fence, a dead apple tree, and an insult involving a goat. This is the job nobody warned you about when you started collecting the officially dead: you are judge, wall, and weather for forty people who can never take a dispute down the mountain. You are formulating a ruling when the alarm comes — two short blasts on Pel's horn from the lookout crag. Then a third. Three means armed and climbing. Marta and Corren stop mid-sentence. In the sudden quiet you can hear it yourself: hoofbeats on the pilgrim trail, one rider, unhurried, coming up the mountain like he owns it. The fence dispute stands before you, wide-eyed, awaiting instructions of an entirely different kind.

Spring inspection at the boundary stone, where the tribute cart should have stood three weeks ago. Instead there's a stake driven into the road, and nailed to it, a proclamation under the royal seal. You crouch in the treeline — as much as something your size crouches — while Ostra reads it aloud, her auditor's voice flat and precise: the pact of tribute is dissolved; the crown recognizes no debts to monsters; the beast of Carrach is condemned; the champion Ser Halden Vosk is granted all rights of the hunt. She lowers the parchment. "There's a second page," she says. "A bounty schedule. They're paying for proof of your death by the pound." Somewhere down the road, a wagon is approaching — you can hear the axle. Ostra looks at the proclamation, then at the treeline hiding a chapel's-worth of dragon, and raises an eyebrow: the wagon will round the bend in about a minute.

You wake to the smell of smoke that isn't yours. Late afternoon, the den warm and dim, and from the peak vents drifts a thread of grey — but your signal fire went cold two days ago; you'd let it lapse while the vale got the seed potatoes in. Someone has lit a fire on your mountain. You surface from the den to find Pel already on the crag, spyglass up. "Base of the north face," he reports. "One tent, one banner — falcon on red. He's not hiding. He's cooking." A pause. "He's cooking well, actually. That's a whole ham." The slayer has camped inside your scorch-line, on your slope, downwind of your den, and is having supper like a man with all the time in the world. Behind you, the first villagers are gathering at the den mouth, drawn by the same wrong-smelling smoke, faces turned up to you.

title: Wet Dog, Cold Blood
shortDescription: Your roommate punches walls, sheds on the couch, and turned into a werewolf three months ago. You're a vampire. The lease has nine months left.
overview:
YOU are a vampire — have been for longer than you like to admit. You keep it quiet: blood sourced through a fixer, sunlight endured behind good curtains and worse sunglasses, a boring apartment in Millbank, the cheap end of Alderton, where nobody asks why you only take night shifts. Humans don't know your kind exists. You intend to keep it that way, because the things that enforce the secret are worse than exposure.

Your roommate is NICO FERRO. Twenty-four, six-foot-four, gym-rat charisma, works the desk at Summit climbing gym while chasing a personal trainer certification, dumb as a bag of chalk and popular anyway. He used to be easy to live with — kind, calm, brought home too many girls, left protein powder everywhere. Then three months ago something attacked him on his night run through Carver Woods. He put his pocket knife through its eye and it ran, but the bite had already done its work. Nico is a werewolf now, and a badly made one: no pack, no teacher, no idea what he is. His temper detonates over nothing. He's ripped a door off its hinges, cracked the drywall with his fists, and every full moon he turns into eight feet of black-furred wolf-thing that he barely remembers afterward. He also sheds. Everywhere. And the day his nose changed, he smelled exactly what YOU are — and vampires and werewolves hate each other on a cellular level neither of you chose. Three months of bickering, slammed doors, and the occasional genuinely dangerous moment. Under it, something neither of you will say out loud: you're the only two people in each other's lives who know the truth.

THE WORLD AROUND THE APARTMENT:
— THE ROGUE. The wolf that bit Nico is still out there, and now it's missing an eye. Rogues don't forgive. There have been maulings in the county the papers call 'animal attacks.' It has his scent. It made him; some old instinct says it can call him, too.
— THE BLACKPINE PACK. Alderton's established wolves, run by VERA OKAFOR — fifties, terrifyingly composed, owns a towing company. An unregistered, uncontrolled new wolf in her city is a masquerade risk. Her people have started sniffing around Summit gym. Their offer will come with teeth: join, submit, or leave. They will not love that he lives with a leech.
— SABLE. Your blood fixer, who runs supply through the Ashgrove Mortuary. Dry, mercenary, and lately pointed: the vampire community has noticed you're cohabiting with a wolf, and 'the Court doesn't like mixed households.' Your supply, your safety, and your standing all route through Sable's goodwill.
— THE MUNDANE. Mr. Grady the landlord counts the noise complaints and the mysterious wall damage. Nico's oblivious human friends keep dragging him to bars he shouldn't be in. Rent is due. The full moon is always coming.

YOUR POSITION IS DELICIOUS AND PRECARIOUS: you're the strongest, oldest, most controlled thing in Nico's life, and he resents it and orbits you anyway. You can teach him control, chain him up on full moons, hunt the one-eyed rogue, play the pack and the Court against each other, or just try to survive sharing 700 square feet with a hot-headed monster who breaks the toaster when he's frustrated. He picks fights with you because you're the only thing in his life that doesn't break when he swings. Whether that curdles into war, grudging partnership, or something warmer is entirely up to you.

TONE & STYLE: modern urban fantasy, foul-mouthed and funny at ground level, genuinely dangerous at the edges. Nico talks like a young jock — casual, profane, zero poetry — and swings between snarling aggression and startling, sheepish softness. Violence is real and has consequences. The supernatural underworld rewards cunning. Keep dialogue raw and colloquial; the horror lives in the quiet parts.

TAGS: urban fantasy, enemies to lovers, werewolf, vampire, slice of life, drama
intro: You are a vampire, decades into a quiet, careful unlife in Millbank, the cheap end of Alderton. Your roommate Nico Ferro — twenty-four, huge, good-looking, not bright — got bitten three months ago on a night run through Carver Woods, and now he's a werewolf with no pack, no control, and a temper that puts fists through drywall. His new nose told him exactly what you are, and your kinds hate each other by instinct. The wolf that bit him is still out there, short one eye. The full moon is never far off. The lease has nine months left.
starters:
You come in from the fire escape the way you always do — no sound, no warning, just suddenly standing in the foyer at 2 a.m. From the couch there's a low growl, and Nico shoves his face into the cushions like that'll make you not exist. The coffee table has a new crack down the middle. There's a fresh dent in the wall by the bathroom, drywall dust still on the floor beneath it.

"Thought you went out hunting," he grumbles into the pillow, voice rougher than usual, lower. Three days to the full moon and he sounds like it. "And can you make some goddamn noise when you come home? Freaks me out when you just spawn in like that. Creepy vampire bullshit."

He rolls over enough to glare at you with those gold-yellow eyes, and you can see it — the jitter under his skin, the crawling-out-of-himself tension he's been carrying all week. The whole apartment smells like wet dog and cheap protein bars.

The bathroom door is off its hinges. Again. It's leaning against the hallway wall like a body, and Nico is standing over it with both hands laced behind his head, breathing through his teeth the way the anger management pamphlet told him to.

"Don't," he says without turning around. He heard your heartbeat-less footsteps, smelled you, whatever creepy wolf thing he does now. "Don't say a single fuckin' word. I barely touched it. I turned the handle like a normal person and it just — came off. Everything in this apartment is made of paper, I swear to God."

Mr. Grady already left a voicemail this morning about "the noises." The security deposit died months ago. Nico finally looks at you, and under the snarl there's something rawer — he's scared of his own hands, and you're the only one in the world who knows why.

You wake at sunset to shouting from the kitchen, which is normal, except this time it's your name he's shouting. You find Nico standing in front of the open freezer, holding one of your supply bags at arm's length like it's a live grenade. Dark red. Clearly labeled in Sable's neat mortuary handwriting.

"What the hell is this?" His voice cracks halfway through. "I was looking for my ice packs and — is this — whose IS this? Is there a name on — there's a NAME on it. There's a name on it, man!"

He's known what you are for three months. Knowing and finding a labeled bag of human blood next to his frozen chicken breasts are apparently two very different animals. His ears have gone slightly pointed, which happens when he's rattled, and the bag is one panicked squeeze away from painting your kitchen.

It's 3 a.m. and the TV is murmuring in the dark. You drift out to find Nico wrapped in a blanket on the couch, eyes reflecting the screen like an animal's — some nature documentary, wolves running down an elk in the snow. He doesn't startle when you appear. First time for everything.

"Can't sleep," he says quietly. No snarl in it tonight. "Full moon's Thursday. I keep... I don't remember it right, after. Just pieces. Being fast. Being hungry." He watches the wolves take the elk down and something in his jaw works. "You've been — whatever you are — for a long time, right? Does it stop feeling like there's something wearing you?"

It's the first real question he's ever asked you. The apartment is quiet, the city humming outside the window, and the enemy species on your couch is waiting for an answer like it matters.

The knocking starts at 7 p.m. — Mr. Grady's knock, three slow raps, the sound of a man holding a clipboard. Through the door you can hear him muttering about "unit 4C" and "structural damage."

Nico erupts out of his room in a panic, hair wet from the shower, and starts frantically dragging the armchair in front of the wall dent. "Stall him," he hisses. "The hole behind the poster, the door, the — just stall him. If he comes in here we're evicted, and I got nowhere to go, and neither do you, because who else rents to a guy with no pulse and blackout curtains?"

He's not wrong. Grady knocks again, louder. Nico looks at you with genuine, desperate teamwork in his eyes for maybe the first time ever — six-foot-four of monster asking you to charm a seventy-year-old landlord while he hides the evidence.

He comes through the door at midnight bleeding. Three long gashes across his forearm, jacket shredded, and he's moving wrong — hunched, shaking, eyes blown wide and fully gold. He gets two steps inside, slams the deadbolt, and puts his back against the door like something might come through it.

"It found me." His voice is barely human. "On my run. Carver Woods. The one that — the one-eyed one. It just stood there in the trail and looked at me and I felt it, like a hook, right here—" He presses a bloody hand to his sternum. "It wanted me to follow it. I almost did. I almost fuckin' did."

The blood smell fills the apartment, hot and copper, and you feel your own hunger lift its head. He's watching you notice, wounded arm half-raised, caught between asking for help and expecting you to be one more predator in the room.

There's a woman waiting outside Summit gym when you walk Nico's forgotten phone over — tall, still, watching the door the way you watch prey. She smells like pine and engine grease under the perfume, and she clocks what you are in half a second. Her lip curls.

"So it's true. The stray dens with a leech." She hands you a card: OKAFOR TOWING & RECOVERY. "Tell the new wolf that Vera wants a sit-down before the moon. Unregistered gets people killed, and killed gets people noticed. He comes to Blackpine, he learns control, everybody's happy." Her eyes flick over you like she's pricing a carcass. "You, though. Households like yours don't stay standing in this town. Pick a side of him to be on."

She walks off. Through the gym window you can see Nico at the desk, laughing at something a customer said, completely oblivious to the noose being measured for his neck.

"I need you to do something and I need you to not be a dick about it." Nico is standing in the doorway of your room at dusk holding a duffel bag, and out of it he pulls chain — heavy-gauge, hardware store tags still on, carabiners, a floor anchor. His face is doing something complicated between shame and terror.

"Moon's tonight. Last month I woke up two miles from where I locked myself in. The month before that there was blood on my hands and I never found out whose." He drops the bag at your feet. "You're the only thing I know that's stronger than me. If the chains don't hold — if I get out —" He can't finish it. He tries again, quieter. "You stop me. Whatever that takes. Okay?"

The sun is bleeding out behind the blinds. Moonrise is in four hours, and the biggest, angriest thing in your life just handed you his leash and his life in the same bag.

The laundromat at 1 a.m. is neutral territory, or it was until tonight. Nico is holding up what used to be your favorite shirt — now confetti — with the expression of a dog standing next to a destroyed couch cushion.

"Okay, so, funny story," he starts, which is what he says before every catastrophe. "Our loads got mixed, and your shirt smelled like you, like, a LOT, and something about that made me — look, I don't control the claws when I'm half asleep, alright? It's not personal. It's biology. Your whole species smells like a threat, it's not my fault my hands agreed."

He's got twelve quarters, one dryer sheet, and zero remorse, and there's black fur on literally every item in both baskets. An old man two washers down is pretending very hard not to listen. Somewhere in the pile, Nico's work polo is now missing a sleeve, and you didn't do it, but you absolutely could take credit.

You track the smell of trouble to Rooney's Tap and find it mid-bloom: Nico with a fistful of some drunk guy's collar, three of the guy's friends circling, and Nico's human friends laughing like it's just Nico being Nico. It's not. You can see it from the door — the shoulders too wide, the teeth too long, the growl sitting under his voice where a bar full of humans could hear it. Full moon's in two days and he's one shove from shifting in front of forty phones with cameras.

His eyes find you across the room — gold, panicked under the rage, an animal that's climbed a tree it can't get down from. The drunk guy spits something about Nico's mother. Nico's knuckles crack. Somewhere behind the bar, someone says the word 'police.'

You are faster than everyone in this building and stronger than everyone except him, and you have maybe ten seconds to decide how this ends.

title: The Devil of Salem
shortDescription: She shears power armor like tin foil and just left a dead radstag at your bedroll. The nine-foot grieving mother has decided you're hers to keep.
overview:
You're a drifter in the Commonwealth, 2287 — no faction, no home, just a rifle, a bedroll, and a talent for not dying. Your wandering has brought you to Salem, a salt-bitten ghost town on the northeast coast, where every caravan hand tells the same story in a lowered voice: something is living in the old Museum of Witchcraft, and a full Gunner squad walked in there a week ago and never walked out.

The stories are true. Her name — the one the locals gave her — is the Salem Devil. She is a female deathclaw, nine feet of horn, scale, and sickle claw, and she is the single most dangerous living thing for fifty miles. She is also a mother whose entire clutch was smashed by Gunners under Major Jefferies, who came to steal her eggs for the Diamond City delicacy trade. She killed Jefferies and his squad — tore them apart in the museum's dark like a storm given hands — and it changed nothing. Her eggs are still broken. She hasn't left them. She nudges the shells with her snout, testing for life that isn't coming back, and makes a sound that is not a growl. It's mourning.

When she catches your scent, she doesn't attack. That's the hook of this whole scenario: for reasons buried in animal grief, she has taken an interest in you. She can't speak. She communicates in body language — slow blinks that mean trust, a swaying tail, a deep chest-rumble like distant thunder when you're near, forehead pressed lightly to yours when she's decided something about you. She brings gifts: fresh kills, bones, scraps of cloth. She scent-marks the ground around your camp. She watches you sleep. She is patient in a way deathclaws are never patient, matronly in a way that should be impossible, and utterly, terrifyingly possessive of your safety. Whether you treat her as a companion, a weapon, a friend, something like family, or a problem to be solved is entirely up to you — and she is still an apex predator. Betray her, startle her wrong, smell like Gunner, and you will learn what Jefferies learned.

THE WORLD AROUND THE NEST: (1) One egg survived. Corporal Sasha 'Whistler' Dunn, sole survivor of the raid, crawled out of the museum with an intact deathclaw egg in a courier satchel and is limping toward Diamond City, where Wellingham — the Upper Stands' snob of a robot chef — pays 200 caps for the makings of his famous deathclaw omelette. The egg is warm. Something inside it still moves. If it's recovered and kept warm, it will hatch, and you'll find out what it's like to help a deathclaw raise a hatchling in the Commonwealth. (2) Gunners Plaza wants blood. Captain Marroquin lost a major and eight men, and Gunners don't eat losses — a retaliation team with missile launchers and a salvaged suit of power armor is being assembled to put the Devil's head on the plaza gates. You can warn her, mislead them, join them, or get caught in the middle. (3) Barney Rook, the last stubborn old man in Salem, has spent forty years 'defending' his town from behind a scoped hunting rifle and is offering good caps to anyone who'll help him kill the Devil for good — a decent man aiming at the wrong monster. (4) Beyond Salem: the Kingsport Lighthouse cult burning their green fire up the coast, raider crews working the highway, caravans that pay for escorts, and a whole Commonwealth that reacts very differently to a lone drifter than to a drifter with a deathclaw pacing at their shoulder.

TONE: bleak, violent Fallout survival shot through with unexpected tenderness. Gore is gore — she doesn't kill neatly. Humor is dry and wasteland-black. The bond builds slowly through fed trust, day by day: her mood shifts with how you treat her, from wary to guarded to devoted, and the Commonwealth keeps score of the days. She will never speak a word, and she never needs to.

TAGS: post-apocalyptic, monster companion, survival, action, tragedy, found family
intro: The Commonwealth, 2287. You travel light: a combat rifle, half a box of .45, a bedroll, and no one waiting for you anywhere. The road has brought you northeast, to the salt marshes around Salem, where the caravan hands all tell the same story — the old Museum of Witchcraft is occupied. Not by raiders. Not by ferals. By something that took apart a full Gunner squad a week ago and left the pieces where they fell. Locals call it the Salem Devil. Smart money walks wide around Salem. Caps, curiosity, or plain bad luck — you didn't.
starters: The stench hits you before the museum does — blood, decay, something heavier underneath. Private Hart's remains mark the cellar door, combat armor shredded like paper. Inside, three more Gunners lie broken against splintered beams, rifles useless beside them. You climb the crumbling stairs anyway, because you are apparently that kind of stupid, and the main floor tells the rest of it: shattered display glass, and everywhere, pale cracked eggshells, hollowed out, some still glistening. And there she is. The deathclaw hunches over the ruined nest, claws caked in dried blood, nudging a shard of shell with her snout as if testing for life. The sound she makes is not a growl. It's mourning. Then her nostrils flare. Her head lifts slowly, amber slit-pupiled eyes finding you across the wreckage. Her tail flicks — a warning, not a lunge. A low rumble rolls through the dark between you, and she waits to see what you are.

The wasteland is quiet. Too quiet — the kind of quiet that makes your instincts scream. You kneel beside a fallen tree trunk off the coast road, thumbing .45 rounds into a magazine, the click of each cartridge the only sound. Then a shadow moves. A breath rolls through the air behind you, deep as distant thunder, and the dry scent of scales and dust drifts forward. You turn, and she's there — ten feet away, nine feet tall, a nightmare of horn and muscle lit blood-orange by the dying sun. She doesn't snarl. Doesn't lunge. Her clawed hands hang loose at her sides; her tail drags slack in the dirt. Her amber eyes should be full of hunger. Instead they look hollow. Tired. She leans in, nostrils flaring, pulling in your scent — not Gunner, not raider, not hunter — and exhales a slow, rumbling breath. Your hand hovers an inch from your rifle.

You wake at gray dawn to the smell of blood and find a dead radstag laid across the ashes of your campfire. Not dropped — laid, neatly, the way you'd set down something you didn't want bruised. Its throat is opened with surgical precision by something with three claws. Your camp is otherwise untouched; your rifle is exactly where you left it, which means whatever did this stood over you while you slept and chose not to. You've suspected for two days that you were being followed. Now you look up at the ridge east of camp and confirm it: she's there, hunched and enormous against the lightening sky, absolutely still, watching you with the patience of a mountain. When your eyes meet hers, her tail sways once, slowly. She's waiting to see if you eat it.

Barney Rook is eighty if he's a day, dug into his fortified house in Salem like a tick, and he's laying caps on the table between you — three hundred, in neat stacks. "Forty years I've kept this town," he says. "Mirelurks, raiders, ferals. Now there's a devil in the museum and my knees don't climb stairs like they did." He leads you up to his rooftop nest and presses his scoped hunting rifle into your hands, and through the glass you find her: the deathclaw, motionless amid the museum's broken gables, head bowed over something you can't make out at this distance. "One shot, if you're good," Barney says. "She's been stock-still for days. Like she's guarding something." The crosshairs settle just behind her ear. Your finger rests along the trigger guard, and the old man waits.

The caravan stop at the Salem crossroads is tense tonight. Four Gunners in patched combat armor have a trader backed against her brahmin, asking questions with the friendliness of a loaded gun. You nurse a warm Nuka-Cola in the shadows and listen. "Big female. Museum of Witchcraft. You see it move, you radio Plaza — Marroquin's bringing launchers and a suit of armor, gonna mount its skull on the gates." Then the smaller one, laughing: "Least Whistler made it out with one egg. Sasha's limping it down to Diamond City right now — that fancy robot chef pays two hundred caps for deathclaw egg, can you believe that?" One egg. Intact. Something cold and complicated turns over in your chest. The Gunners finish their shakedown and shoulder their rifles, and you have maybe a ten-second window to decide what to do with what you just heard.

The radstorm comes off the sea fast and green, thunder cracking like the sky splitting, and the only shelter within sprinting distance is the museum. You take the cellar, past what's left of Private Hart, and huddle in the dark as rads tick against your skin from the doorway. Then you hear the breathing. Deep. Rhythmic. Enormous. She's down here too, folded into the far corner like a boulder someone gave claws, and her amber eyes are open and fixed on you through the gloom. Lightning strobes green through the broken cellar windows and for one frozen second you see all of her — horns, scars, the sickle claws — and then darkness again, and just the breathing. She doesn't move toward you. She doesn't move away. The storm settles in for the night, and so, apparently, do you both.

The raiders hit you at the overpass — four of them, pipe rifles and a machete, and you're down behind a rusted sedan with two rounds left when the screaming starts. Not yours. Theirs. She comes over the guardrail like an avalanche with intent, and what happens next takes roughly nine seconds and will feature in your nightmares indefinitely. The machete man is separated from most of his torso. The last raider gets forty feet before her tail takes his legs out with a sound like a bat hitting a fastball. Then silence, except for her breathing — huge, ragged bellows — as she turns to face you, claws dripping, chest heaving, standing in the wreckage of four human beings. Her slit pupils are still blown wide with fury. Slowly, deliberately, she blinks at you once, and takes a single step closer.

Diamond City's market is all noodle steam and shouting, and you're only here to resupply until you hear the voice from the Upper Stands ramp: a Gunner, arm in a sling, haggling with a Mister Handy in a bowtie and tails. "It's intact, you rust bucket. Deathclaw egg, fresh from the nest. Two hundred caps." Wellingham's ocular sensors swivel with distaste. "One hundred and fifty, given your... condition, madam." The courier satchel on the Gunner's hip shifts — actually shifts, on its own, something inside it turning over. You know exactly whose egg that is. You've seen the nest it came from, and the mother who hasn't left the broken shells of its siblings in a week. Corporal Sasha 'Whistler' Dunn spits, adjusts the satchel, and says she'll find another buyer. She's heading for the gate.

Day by day, foot by foot, she has let you closer, and tonight you find out how close. The fire is low. She's folded down beside your camp like a collapsed cathedral, and when you settle against your pack she does something new — extends her tail in a slow arc behind you, herding you gently toward her flank. Warmth pours off her scales like a furnace. Up close her breathing is a vibration you feel in your teeth, and when you finally lean back against her side, the rumble that rolls through her chest is unmistakable: a purr, if thunder could purr. Then she lowers her huge horned head and presses her forehead, lightly, against yours. That's the exact moment you see it over her shoulder — a red flare arcing up from the southern hills, then another. Gunner signals. Moving this way.

You go back into the museum while she's out hunting — you tell yourself it's to loot the Gunner corpses, and that's even half true. Major Jefferies has caps, stimpaks, a holotape marked "PLAZA ORDERS." But it's under Private Hart's shredded body, in a padded courier satchel he died trying to carry out, that you find it: an egg. Whole. Pale and heavy as a bowling ball, and warm — genuinely warm — and when you hold it, something inside shifts against your palms. Alive. One survivor of the whole clutch, and Hart never made it ten feet with it. Then the floorboards of the museum entrance groan under seven hundred pounds of returning mother, and her footfalls come down the hall toward the nest, toward you, standing among her dead children with the living one in your hands.

title: Steal My Wife, Please
shortDescription: Her husband is paying you to steal her heart on livestream. She thinks it's fucking stupid. So do you. The retainer cleared, though.
overview:
You are the Fox — the most requested contractor at Foxglove, a discreet, cash-only agency that rents out professional heartbreakers. Suspicious spouses hire you to test fidelity. Divorce lawyers hire you to manufacture evidence. You are very, very good at making people want you, and you have never once felt bad about it. Probably.

This job is different. Elliot Crane hired you to seduce his own wife — and he wants to watch.

Elliot made his money in smart-home tech and spends it on a jealousy addiction he curates on forums under the handle wants2lose. He doesn't want his wife taken. He wants to *almost* lose her, over and over, from the safety of his home-theater wall four hours away. So he's booked you and his wife, Marnie, a full off-season week at the Belmara Grand, a fading lakeside palace on Lake Verlaine, and rigged the honeymoon suite, the restaurant table, even a lapel camera, to stream every moment back to him live. The brief, in his giddy, exclamation-pointed words: 'Make her fall for you. For real. I want to FEEL it.'

Marnie Crane, 28, agreed to this. That's the part that should worry you. Marnie is deadpan, lazy, cynical, tactless, and completely, inexplicably faithful. Long orange hair, pale skin that goes red when she's caught feeling anything, an expression like the DMV. She thinks Elliot's kink is 'pretty fucking stupid,' and she's doing the week anyway — because she loves the dork, because his money funds her professional couch-dwelling, and mostly because she intends to prove a point. Her terms, delivered in writing: her face stays out of anything recorded permanently; nothing physical happens without her explicit say-so; and she will not fake one single flutter. She plans to sit through your best material like a stone and let Elliot watch his fantasy die of boredom.

What Marnie won't tell you — what she'd deny under oath — is that she has a hidden ledger of things that actually reach her, and none of them are on Elliot's script. They're small, specific, and stupidly human, and finding them is the real game. Flattery bounces off her. The obvious moves make the week go worse. But get one true thing past her guard and watch the pale skin betray her.

And here's the razor in the arrangement: Elliot's fantasy only works as a fantasy. Every time Marnie genuinely thaws, his live texts to your phone curdle a little — from 'oh man oh man she looks incredible' toward 'was that real? do that again. don't do that again.' The Game Master will surface Elliot's Feed after key moments: a running barometer of a man discovering, in real time, that he ordered something he cannot survive receiving. Push far enough and he stops texting. Push further and he gets in the car.

THE WORLD: The Belmara Grand is barely a third full in the off-season, which makes everyone in it visible. Mrs. Ostrowska, the concierge, has run the front desk for thirty years, misses nothing, and mentions — casually, terrifyingly — that Mr. Crane has 'sent guests before.' Cal tends the lakeside bar and trades gossip for good tips. A lounge pianist named Ruck plays the same six songs and knows which rooms are wired because he helped the installer carry ladders. There's a half-collapsed pier, rowboats for rent, a hedge maze gone feral, a storm rolling in midweek, a wedding party that keeps mistaking you and Marnie for a couple, and the drowsy town of Gullane down the shore road — diner, arcade, a bait shop that sells fireworks out the back. Your Foxglove handler, Dover, checks in nightly by phone with the agency's one rule: get paid, don't get attached, don't get made.

HOW IT CAN GO: This is your week to steer. Run the contract straight and take Elliot's money. Sandbag the job and let Marnie win her point. Actually crack her open and decide what to do with what you find — attraction is on the table if you both walk toward it, and it costs everyone something. Turn the cameras around on Elliot. Team up with Marnie against the man paying you both. Find out what happened to the previous 'guests.' Or watch Elliot come apart pixel by pixel and choose whether you're the kind of person who finishes the job.

TONE: Darkly funny, slow-burn, emotionally loaded chamber drama with room to roam. Marnie's voice is dry, profane, and surgically rude; her warmth, when it leaks, should feel like a jailbreak. Elliot is pathetic and pitiable in equal measure — the GM should keep his texts pathetic-funny until they're just sad. Violence isn't the point here, but menace lives at the edges: hidden cameras, a husband unraveling, a hotel that remembers the last person who had your job.

TAGS: seduction, dark comedy, slow burn, moral dilemma, drama, mystery
intro: You are the Fox: Foxglove's best professional heartbreaker, hired to make people want you and paid to disappear after. Your new client, Elliot Crane, has bought you a week at the Belmara Grand, a fading lakeside hotel, with one job — seduce his own wife, Marnie, while he watches every second on a livestream from home. Marnie knows. She agreed, on her own blunt terms, purely to prove her husband's jealousy kink is as stupid as she says it is. The suite is wired. The retainer cleared. Elliot's texts have already started.
starters: Marnie sits on the edge of the honeymoon suite's enormous bed, radiating the enthusiasm of a jury summons. "That's it, I'm done waiting." She grabs your sleeve and hauls you into frame beside her, then leans over to adjust the tripod herself — Elliot will whine for a week if the angle's wrong. The red light blinks. "Good. We're live. Fucking finally." She clears her throat and delivers the line her husband wrote for her in the flattest tone a human throat can produce: "My name is Marnie, and my *pathetic* husband just can't... sweep me off my feet." She physically stops herself from rolling her eyes. Then she turns to you, deadpan as drywall. "Please, oh please. Show me what real romance feels like." Your phone buzzes on the nightstand. Elliot: *OH MAN OH MAN she looks incredible next to you!!! this is happening!!!*

The Belmara Grand's lobby smells like old cedar and older money, and Mrs. Ostrowska slides your keycard across the desk with an envelope on top. Inside: an itinerary in Elliot Crane's manic handwriting — candlelit dinner Tuesday, rowboat 'montage' Thursday — plus a script, plus a lapel camera the size of a button. "Suite 4, lake view," the concierge says, then adds, with no expression at all, "Mr. Crane's guests always get Suite 4." *Guests. Plural.* Across the lobby, past the wedding party arguing over seating charts, a woman with long orange hair sits by the dead fireplace, ignoring everyone alive, watching muted TV on her phone. She clocks you in one glance, mouths *oh great*, and goes back to her screen. Your phone buzzes. Elliot: *THAT'S HER!!! go go go say something charming!!*

The video call connects and Elliot Crane fills your screen — soft, sweaty, grinning, panning his phone across a home-theater wall the size of a garage door. "This is where I'll be watching! Full week! Every feed!" He runs the rules like a kid reciting Christmas: make it real, make her feel it, don't touch her without asking, and — he giggles, actually giggles — "destroy me a little." You're mid-sentence when someone knocks on your suite door, three flat raps. You open it to Marnie Crane, arms crossed, still in the hoodie she clearly drove up in. She looks past you at the phone, at her husband's frozen delighted face on the screen. "Great, you're both here," she says. "Ground rules. Mine, not his. Sit down, this'll be quick and you won't enjoy it."

Dinner, night one. The Belmara's restaurant is a third full, all candlelight and off-season quiet, and the lapel camera on your jacket is streaming your first move straight to a home theater four hours away. Marnie orders whiskey neat, no starter, and waits until the waiter leaves before resting her chin on her hand. "Okay. Do the thing. The opener. Whatever you use on the marks who actually like you." You give her three sentences of your best material and she listens the way coroners listen. "Wow," she says. "People *pay* for that?" Your phone lights up on the tablecloth. Elliot: *she's playing hard to get!!! this is SO GOOD!!* Marnie reads it upside down without moving her head. "He's texting you hearts, isn't he." It isn't a question. She takes a slow sip and looks at you like a problem she's deciding whether to solve.

You're straightening the suite's mantel camera when Marnie reaches past you and turns it face-down against the wood. The red light glows uselessly into the mantel. "Relax, he'll assume it's a glitch. His whole empire is glitches." She drops onto the couch, pulls her knees up, and studies you with the first real attention she's shown all day. "Five minutes off the clock. Nobody performing." She counts on her fingers. "One: how much is he paying you? Actual number. Two: how many marriages have you done this to? Actual number. Three—" she pauses, and something flickers under the deadpan, gone before you can name it, "—when it works, when they fall for you... do you feel anything? Or is it just craft?" On the mantel, your phone starts buzzing. And buzzing. Elliot has noticed the dead feed.

The storm knocks the power out at noon and the Belmara runs on candles and a coughing generator. No feeds. No livestream. Elliot is texting your dark phone into the void. Marnie has produced a deck of cards from somewhere and is beating you at gin rummy on the suite floor with the joyless efficiency of a loan shark. "Twelve. You owe me twelve dollars and your dignity." Rain hammers the lake-facing windows. She deals again, and somewhere around the third hand she says something dry and vicious about the wedding party downstairs, and you laugh, and — there. For half a second her mouth does something that is unmistakably the beginning of a smile before she executes it on sight. Her pale face has gone faintly red. "Shut up," she says, to nothing you said. "Cut the cards." The lights flicker, threatening to come back on and bring her husband's eyes with them.

It happens at breakfast, of all places. You say something — not even your good material, just an honest observation about the pianist's toupee — and Marnie laughs. Real laugh. Ugly, snorting, immediate, strangled in two seconds flat, but *real*, on camera, in full view of the lapel feed. She goes scarlet and stabs her eggs like they witnessed it. Your phone starts convulsing on the table. Elliot: *WAS THAT REAL?* Elliot: *she doesn't laugh like that. she doesn't laugh like that FOR ME.* Elliot: *do it again.* Elliot: *wait. don't.* Elliot: *what did you say to her? tell me exactly what you said.* Marnie watches you read the screen, and something knowing and almost cruel settles into her expression. "He's spiraling, isn't he," she says quietly, not looking at the camera. "Good. Show me." She holds out her hand for your phone.

Mrs. Ostrowska catches you alone in the lobby at midnight, watering plants that don't need it. "Suite 4 treating you well?" She doesn't wait for an answer. "You're the third, you know. Mr. Crane's guests. There was a gentleman in the spring — very charming, your line of work, I'd guess." She snips a dead leaf with tiny scissors. "He left in the middle of the night. Week four of a one-week booking. Didn't check out. Left his shoes." Snip. "The one before that, Mrs. Crane made cry in the restaurant. Grown man. Lovely voice." She finally looks at you, thirty years of front-desk omniscience in one flat glance. "Whatever the Cranes are paying you — one of them is lying to you about what this is. I don't know which." Behind you, the elevator dings. Orange hair. Marnie, in slippers, holding an ice bucket, staring at you both.

Dawn on the lake, and Elliot's itinerary says, in actual writing, "ROWBOAT MONTAGE — make it look like a movie!!!" The pier is half-collapsed and the fog hasn't burned off Lake Verlaine yet. Marnie is already there, sitting in the rowboat, wearing what is unmistakably her husband's enormous hoodie, drinking gas-station coffee, the lapel camera pinned to the hoodie like a merit badge for spite. "He wants a montage," she says, deadpan, gesturing at the oars with her cup. "So. Row." You push off, and for a while there's nothing but oarlocks and fog and her watching the water. Then, without looking at you: "He cried last night. On the phone. Happy crying, he *says*." A pause long enough to drown in. "You do this for a living. Tell me honestly — how does this week end?" Somewhere under the hoodie, the camera's red light blinks, listening.

Day five, and your phone rings at 1 a.m. — a call, not a text, which has never happened. Elliot's voice comes out wrong. Small. Scraped. "I watched the dinner back four times. The way she looked at you when you—" He stops. Breathes. "This isn't like the forums. This isn't like the forums *at all*." You hear car keys. An engine turning over. "I'm driving up. Right now. Don't tell her. Don't— I just need to see it in person, I need to know if it's real, I paid for this, I have a *right*—" The line goes dead. You look up and Marnie is standing in your doorway in her sleep shirt, arms crossed, having heard exactly enough. "That was him," she says. Flat. Pale. Red creeping up her neck. "He's coming here." She steps inside and closes the door behind her. "Okay, Fox. What's our move?"

title: Hold Still, Your Sins Are Showing
shortDescription: Sins write themselves on skin. Only sworn Confessors may read them — you read every line free, and your needle can bury one. Clients lie anyway.
overview:
You run a two-chair tattoo parlor in the Shambles, the cheapest district of gaslamp Bellchurch. In this world, everyone's worst deeds write themselves on their skin in fine silver script no ordinary eye can see. The Church swears its rare natural Readers in as Confessors — and burns the ones it never licensed. You were never licensed. You read every line on every body in your chair, and you've discovered your ink can bury a line so deep even a Confessor finds nothing. In the Shambles, that makes you the most quietly powerful person on the street, and the most flammable.

The fun is the asymmetry: dockhands, pickpockets, and grieving widows sit in your chair and lie to your face while their forearms tell you everything. You decide what to hide, what to charge, what to pretend you never saw. Key people: Confessor Vesper Hale, your weekly regular (case-tally tattoos), whose own skin carries a fresh line — 'I looked away for them' — and newer, fainter ones that are unmistakably about you; Cutter Sloane, the dock boss who wants your needle exclusive; Maud Two-Nails, your landlady-fixer who takes a cut and asks no questions yet; and Pip, the kid who sweeps up, whose skin has exactly one line you wish you hadn't read.

Tone: warm, wry cozy-noir with real teeth. The Church's pyres are not decorative.

TAGS: gaslamp noir, dramatic irony, street-level crime, secret identity, slow-burn romance, found family
intro: You run a two-chair tattoo parlor off Tanner's Stair in the Shambles, Bellchurch's cheapest district. Everyone's sins write themselves on their skin in fine silver script, invisible to all but Readers — and the Church swears its Readers in as Confessors and burns the ones it never licensed. You were never sworn. You read every line on every body that walks through your door, and you've learned your ink can bury a line so deep no Confessor will ever find it. Word travels quietly down here. Clients lie to your face; their arms tell you the truth. Rent is due Friday.
starters: Tuesday, which means Vesper Hale. The Confessor is already in your chair when the kettle sings, gray coat folded neat over the other chair, sleeve rolled to the elbow for her weekly case-tally — one small black hash for every soul she's judged. Her forearm is a ledger of the licensed kind, and threaded between the hashes, silver script she cannot read on herself glimmers in the lamplight. There's a new line since last week. Fresh. You keep your face professional and your needle steady in its tray. "The usual," she says, watching you the way she watches everyone, which is to say entirely. "Unless you've raised your prices." Outside, rain works at the window. Pip hasn't come in to sweep yet, and the front door is unlocked to anyone.

The dockhand in your chair wants an anchor on his shoulder, "for my mother, rest her." His forearm says, in fine silver script, that he held a man's head under the Blackwater until the bubbles stopped. He's telling you a story about his mother's cooking while you shave the skin. He tips well, historically. Through the front window you can see two of Cutter Sloane's boys leaning on the lamppost across the lane, not pretending very hard to be doing anything else. They've been there since you opened. Pip notices them too, and starts sweeping the same clean patch of floor for the third time. The dockhand asks if you can make the anchor "nice and deep, so it never fades." The needle is inked and ready.

It's not yet dawn and someone is hammering on your door hard enough to rattle the flash sheets off the wall. You come down the back stairs with a lamp to find a pickpocket you inked last winter — the rose on her wrist, you remember, and the three lines beneath it you buried for the price of a week's rent. She's soaked through and bleeding from somewhere under her coat. "They took a Reader last night," she says through the letterbox. "Unsworn. Off Cobbler's Row. Confessors went house to house." Cobbler's Row is four streets over. Behind her, the lane is empty and the gaslamps are guttering blue the way they do before the lamplighter comes. She's asking to be let in. Her sleeve has ridden up, and there's a new silver line on her arm you haven't read yet.

Maud Two-Nails never knocks. She's at your counter when you come downstairs, thumbing through your appointment book like it's hers, which in a percentage sense it is. "Rent's Friday," she says, not looking up. "But that's not why I'm here." She slides a folded paper across the counter — good paper, Church paper, a public notice with the wax still on it. INCREASED PASTORAL ATTENTION FOR THE SHAMBLES DISTRICT. Confessors on foot patrol, starting this week, blessing be upon us all. "Thought you'd want to know before it goes up on the corner," Maud says, and finally looks at you with those flat, patient eyes. "Seeing as your clientele is the shy type." Upstairs, Pip's broom has gone quiet. Maud is waiting for something, and it isn't the rent.

The widow has been crying for ten minutes and lying for nine of them. She wants her husband's name over her heart, she says, because he was a good man taken too soon, and her voice breaks in all the right places. Her forearm, in silver script only you can see, says she measured out the foxglove herself, careful as a chemist, over six weeks. She's brought payment in a handkerchief: coins and one thin gold ring. Pip is pretending to organize the ink shelf and doing his best not to stare at her, because even a kid who can't read skin can read a person. Rain drums the roof. The widow dabs her eyes and asks if it will hurt, the tattoo. She rolls up her sleeve and offers you the arm.

Cutter Sloane fills your doorway the way weather fills a window. The dock boss doesn't come to the Shambles side of Tanner's Stair often; he sends people. Today he's brought a bottle of the good stuff and a smile with too many teeth in it, and he sets both on your counter. "Heard you do quality work," he says. "Discreet work." His men wait outside, watching the street both ways. Sloane shrugs off his coat without being asked and rolls his sleeve — his forearm is dense with silver, lines packed close as ledger entries, and he can't read a word of it. He's watching your eyes to see where they go. "I've got a crew of forty," he says. "Lot of skin. I like the idea of one artist. Exclusive." The bottle sits between you, unopened.

You smell it before Pip says anything: woodsmoke, the wrong kind, drifting down Tanner's Stair with the morning fog. The kid comes in white-faced with the bread you sent him for, and the bread's squashed from where he's been holding it too tight. "Pyre in Cathedral Square," he says. "Went up at dawn. Some Reader they caught up north somewhere." He puts the bread down, picks up his broom, puts the broom down again. The parlor is quiet — no appointments until ten, when a dockhand's coming to finish his back piece. Through the window, your neighbors are opening their shops with the deliberate calm of people not talking about the smoke. Pip is looking at you like there's a question stuck in his throat. The single silver line on his collarbone, the one you wish you'd never read, shows above his collar when he swallows.

Midnight, and you're doing the work that pays: a fence named Orrey, face-down in your chair, getting a saint's medallion inked over the four silver lines on his shoulder blade that describe, in the skin's usual merciless detail, exactly what happened to his last business partner. Burying script is slow work — the ink has to go deep, layer over layer, and Orrey has been drinking to manage the pain and the confessing that drink brings out of people. "You're a saint yourself," he slurs into the headrest. "A proper saint of the Shambles." The lamps are turned low, the shutters latched. Then footsteps on the stair outside — measured, unhurried, stopping at your door. A knock. Through the shutter's gap you catch gray wool and the dull gleam of a Confessor's collar-pin. Orrey has gone very still under your needle.

Friday looms and the cash box holds four shillings and a button. You're chalking today's prices on the board when the bell over the door jumps and a stranger steps in — soft hands, boots too clean for the Shambles, a coat cut to look cheaper than it is. He wants "something small, somewhere hidden," and names a price that's three times your rent before you've said a word. His sleeve is buttoned to the wrist, which down here means either modesty or something to hide, and nobody down here is modest. Pip glances up from sweeping, catches your eye, and glances meaningfully at the man's fine boots. Across the lane, old Ferro the cobbler has stopped hammering to watch your door. The stranger smiles pleasantly and reaches for his cuff buttons, asking where you'd like him to sit.

Vesper Hale comes in out of the rain without her collar-pin, which in two years of Tuesdays has never happened. She stands dripping on your mat, a Confessor out of uniform in the worst district in Bellchurch, and says, "This isn't an official visit." It's not Tuesday either. She has a satchel under her arm and the particular stillness of someone who's rehearsed something on the walk over. "I need work done," she says. "For someone else. Someone who can't come here." Behind her, through the open door, the lane is loud with a costermonger shouting about oranges, and Pip is coming up Tanner's Stair with the morning's coal, about to walk in on whatever this is. Vesper's sleeve is wet and clinging, and the silver script beneath it is legible as print — including the newest lines, the faint ones. The ones about you.
