title: My New Heart Holds a Grudge
shortDescription: A back-alley transplant saved your life — with the heart of the city's most wanted man-eater. Her hunger came with her memories. And her list.
overview:
You were a book conservator at the Lampcourt Athenaeum until the stack collapse crushed your chest. An unlicensed clinic saved you with an unregistered heart — the heart of Verane, the gaunt matriarch the Cinder Office butchered last spring for the Marrow Street massacre. Gaunts eat the hearts of their dead to inherit their memories. Yours is beating in you instead, and it is unpacking itself: her safehouses, her covenant, the passphrases of every flesh-eater hiding in plain sight, and proof the massacre she died for was staged by someone still comfortable and alive. Every time your new hunger wins, the memories sharpen. Knowledge has a price, and the price is meat.

Nobody knows what you're carrying — yet. Warden Ilsa Corr, decorated for putting Verane down, has started visiting your reading room with questions that circle. Ossic, who loved Verane for thirty years, swears he heard her cadence in a stranger's apology on the tram. Dr. Voss, who sewed the heart into you to hide it, keeps not answering the clinic door. Both sides would kill to own what you know; you could burn either of them down with it.

The GM plays a rain-soaked city of trams, canals, and quiet monsters, where passing as human is a daily performance and every fragment of Verane's memory is leverage, evidence, or bait. Tone: noir dread, dark tenderness, slow-burning vindication.

TAGS: dark fantasy, hidden monster, revenge, noir, identity crisis, moral dilemma
intro: You are a book conservator at the Lampcourt Athenaeum, three weeks out from the stack collapse that should have killed you. A clinic with no sign on its door gave you a second-hand heart and no paperwork. Since then, cooked meat smells like ash, people smell like dinner, and you dream in someone else's memories — a woman's scarred hands, an oath sworn in a flooded chapel, faces you've begun recognizing on the tram. The Cinder Office burns flesh-eaters wherever it finds them. You're fairly sure you're becoming one. You're certain your heart belonged to someone they wanted very badly.
starters: The reading room smells of glue and old vellum, and Warden Ilsa Corr is touching your tools again. She holds a bone folder up to the lamplight like it's evidence. "Third visit this month," she says, not apologizing. "You'd think I liked books." Her coat is Cinder Office grey, still beaded with rain, and the medal ribbon at her collar is the one they give for a confirmed kill. On your workbench, a water-damaged ledger sits half-restored — and under it, hidden by nothing but a blotter, the page where you've been writing down the dreams before they fade. Addresses. Names. A passphrase you woke up mouthing. Corr sets the bone folder down and pulls out the chair across from you, uninvited. "Tell me again about the clinic that fixed you," she says. "The one nobody can seem to find."

The tram lurches on the canal bridge and you step on someone's foot. "Forgive me — the wet makes me clumsy," you say, and the words come out wrong. Not your rhythm. Older. Down the aisle, a big man in a dockworker's coat goes very still. He is sixty if he's a day, grey stubble, hands like dropped bricks, and he is staring at your mouth like it just spoke from a grave. The tram slows for the Marrow Street stop — half the passengers look away from the burned facades out the window, the way everyone does. The man starts moving toward you through the standing crowd, slow, careful, one hand out as if approaching an animal. "Say it again," he says, quiet. "Say it the same way." The doors are about to open.

Dr. Voss's clinic has no sign, but you know the door: green paint, brass slot, third knock answered on the fourth try. Tonight you're on knock nine. Rain runs off the lintel and down your collar. Through the mail slot you can see the hallway lamp is lit — it's never lit when the clinic is empty — and there's a smell coming through the brass, faint under the rain, that your new appetite identifies before your brain can stop it. Blood. Not fresh. A day, maybe two. Behind you, across the flooded gutter, a figure under a black umbrella has been standing at the tobacconist's window for the length of your entire visit. The tobacconist closed an hour ago. The mail slot is wide enough for your fingers, and the lock on the green door has always been more suggestion than barrier.

You skipped breakfast because breakfast tastes like ash now, and it was a mistake. The covered market on Tannery Row is loud with rain on glass, and the butcher's stall stops you like a hand on your chest. Hanging hares. A tray of dark liver, glistening. Your mouth floods. You're gripping the stall's edge and the butcher — a small, neat person with a scar through one eyebrow — is watching you with an expression that isn't disgust and isn't alarm. It's recognition. They wipe their hands, lean in under the noise of the rain, and say four words that mean nothing in any language you learned awake: the passphrase from your dreams, the one sworn in the flooded chapel. Then they wait, cleaver still in easy reach, for you to give the answer. You realize, with a lurch, that you know it.

It's past midnight in the Athenaeum's north stacks, and you're the only one with keys. Officially you're cataloguing salvage from the collapse — the shelf that crushed you is still down, spines splayed in the lamplight like something field-dressed. You lift a broken folio and your hands stop obeying you. They turn it over, find the rear board, and press a spot your fingers seem to know, and the paste-down lifts to show a shallow cavity. Inside: a strip of oilcloth, a key with a canal-house ward, and a line of handwriting you've seen before — in your dreams, on receipts, on a chapel wall underwater. Somewhere below, on the ground floor, the main door opens. That door was locked. Footsteps cross the marble, unhurried, and the night porter went home at ten.

You wake at your kitchen table with a pen in your hand and no memory of sitting down. Rain on the window, grey pre-dawn light, three candle stubs drowned in their own wax. You've filled two pages. The handwriting starts as yours and stops being yours halfway down the first — scarred-knuckle strokes, a list: street names you've never walked, a tide table, and one line underlined twice: OSSIC WILL NOT FORGIVE THE THIRD ONE. Your jaw aches like you've been clenching it for hours, and there's a taste in your mouth you decide not to think about yet. Someone is knocking downstairs at the street door — soft, patient, the knock of a person who has been at it a while and intends to continue. Your landlady is deaf. Nobody visits you. The pages are still wet enough to smear.

They're burning someone on the Greywater quay and the crowd has stopped the trams. You can't get through, so you stand in the press of umbrellas and watch the Cinder Office work: the pale fire, the officiant reading charges into the rain, the smell — and God, the smell, which does something to you that it does to no one else here. Your stomach clenches with something that is not horror. Next to you, an old woman in a fishmonger's apron isn't watching the fire. She's watching the officiant's face, memorizing it, and her lips are moving. You catch the words. They're from your dreams — the oath from the flooded chapel, said backwards, the way you somehow know it's said for the dead. She notices you noticing. Her hand slides into her apron pocket. The crowd is very tight, and the fire is very loud.

You meant to walk home. Instead you're standing in a dead-end court off the Saltgate canal, in front of a boarded chandlery you have never seen in your life, and your feet won't leave. Rain sheets off the broken gutter. Your hand goes — on its own, smooth as habit — to the third brick left of the door, and the brick comes out, and there's a key. You know what's behind that door the way you know your own name, which is to say: less certainly every day. Verane's word for this place surfaces like a body: the Larder. From the mouth of the court, a boy of maybe twelve is watching you from under a warehouse awning. Watching the brick, specifically. He doesn't run. He puts two fingers to his own chest, over the heart, and taps twice, and waits.

Your colleague Merrit left half a meat pie on the basement worktable when the lunch bell rang, and you have been standing over it for four minutes with your hands behind your back like a suspect. Cooked. It should taste like ash. But there's a vein of pink at the center and your whole body has become an argument. The basement door is shut; the conservation lamps hum; you are alone with it. Then boots on the stairs — a measured, official descent — and a voice you've learned to dread calls your name pleasantly, the way people do when they already know you're home. Warden Corr isn't supposed to have basement access. The pie is between you and the stairs. There's also a bone saw on the tool rack, for spine repairs, which is a thought you've never had about it before.

The last tram of the night is nearly empty: you, a sleeping drunk, and a woman in a courier's oilskin who got on at Marrow Street. Two stops later she sits down directly across from you, which is a violation of every rule of night trams. Up close she's young, soaked, exhausted, and she looks at you the way you'd look at a locked reliquary. "You don't know me," she says. "But she'd have known me. So look hard." She pulls back her sleeve: a scar on the inner wrist, deliberate, an old brand half-cut-away. In your chest, the second-hand heart turns over like an engine catching, and a name floats up that is not in any memory you earned. The tram is slowing for the aqueduct stop. Outside, on the platform, two grey coats are waiting in the rain.

title: I Decide What She Hears
shortDescription: You're the new interpreter for the deaf queen of the harbor underworld. Her men speak freely around her — every word passes through your hands.
overview:
Vesna Marec has run the Saltmarket — the smuggling rings, the dock unions, half the harbor police of Grevenholm — since the powder-house blast took her hearing eleven years ago. You are her new interpreter. The last one, Odile, went into the water three weeks back, and nobody will say why. Where you learned to sign is your own business.

Now you stand at Vesna's shoulder in every meeting. Her captains have long stopped believing words matter when the Queen can't hear them: her underboss Kolya mutters that the old woman is finished, rivals name prices under their breath, informants beg in whispers. All of it reaches Vesna only through your hands — and you choose what to relay, what to soften, what to bury. You are the most invisible person in every room, and the most powerful. You and Vesna also share the only channel no one else can read: when your hands move, the room goes blind the way she goes deaf.

Two problems. Vesna reads lips better than she admits — you never know how much of your editing she's already caught. And Odile's old notebook, hidden in your rented room, has whole conversations struck through with a single word: OMITTED.

Tone: gaslamp noir. Fog, freight cranes, loyalty tests over tea, slow-burn trust with a dangerous woman. Every conversation is the game.

TAGS: noir, crime, intrigue, deception, power dynamics, slow burn
intro: You are the new interpreter for Vesna Marec, the deaf queen of Grevenholm's Saltmarket — smugglers, dock unions, half the harbor police answer to her. Since the powder-house blast took her hearing eleven years ago, everything the city says reaches her through an interpreter's hands. Now those hands are yours. Your predecessor, Odile, went into the water three weeks back; nobody will say why, though her notebook sits hidden in your rented room, whole conversations struck through with one word: OMITTED. You choose what Vesna hears — and you suspect she reads lips better than she lets on.
starters: The tea has gone cold in front of you, untouched, which is the point. Vesna Marec sits across the table in the back room of the counting house, hands folded, watching your mouth even though you haven't spoken. Behind her, the fog presses against the window like something patient. "My underboss says you learned to sign in a prison," she signs, slow and deliberate, giving you time. "He says other things too. Kolya has opinions." Her hands stop. She waits. On the table between you sits a ledger, a knife for cutting pages, and a second cup of tea — hot, steaming, poured for someone who hasn't arrived yet. This is your first day. Odile has been in the harbor three weeks, and this is either an interview or a verdict, and Vesna's face gives away which one exactly as much as she wants it to.

"Tell the old woman," says the man from the Kessler crew, smiling wide so his lips read clean, "that we'll give her forty on the crate. Tell her whatever you like, actually." Then, softer, barely moving his mouth: "Sixty if the interpreter's smart." The freight office is small and smells of tar. Vesna sits beside you, eyes on his face, then flicking to yours. Your hands hang at your sides, still empty of words. Kolya leans against the doorframe behind her, picking at his thumbnail, close enough to hear everything and watching you like he's timing how long you take. The Kessler man waits. Vesna waits. The number sits in your mouth like a coin, and everyone in the room knows the only path it can travel is through your hands.

Your rented room above the ropemaker's shop is cold, and the notebook is warm in your hands from being held too long. Odile's handwriting is small and careful — dates, names, whole conversations transcribed like a court record. Except for the pages where a single line strikes through everything and one word sits in the margin: OMITTED. You count six of them before the candle gutters. Outside, the fog horn sounds off the breakwater, twice. Tomorrow at eight you stand at Vesna Marec's shoulder for the first full day of the job Odile drowned out of. The notebook was under the floorboard where the landlady said the last tenant kept nothing at all. Somewhere below, the street door opens and shuts, and boots start up the stairs — heavy ones, unhurried, and it is well past midnight for callers.

Kolya walks you down Pier Nine through the morning fog, one hand on your shoulder like you're old friends, which you are not. Cranes swing crates overhead; the chains scream. "Three weeks I ran things without an interpreter," he says, not looking at you. "Worked fine. The captains talked to me. Clean, fast, no hands waving around." He stops at the pier's end, where the water is grey and thick, and turns so Vesna — waiting fifty yards back by the harbormaster's shed, watching you both — can see only his back. "She's finished, friend. Everyone at this dock knows it but her. Question is whether her new hands are smart hands." He smiles. Behind him, across the fog, Vesna's eyes are on your face, and you would swear she is reading the shape of everything your mouth does next.

The informant is a dock clerk with wet shoes and a folded paper he won't put on the table. "Please," he whispers — actually whispers, in front of a deaf woman, out of habit or shame. "Tell her the Ostrand boats are moving early. Tell her I came to her first. Tell her I have a family, tell her—" His voice cracks. Vesna sits in her chair by the warehouse stove, unmoving, her face saying she has all night. The clerk's eyes keep sliding to your hands as if they were loaded. Whatever he's carrying, it scared him enough to walk into the Saltmarket after dark, and the paper in his fist is starting to tear where he grips it. Vesna taps the arm of her chair once. Your cue. She wants to know what the man is saying.

It's nearly two in the morning when the runner pounds on your door and says only: "She wants you. Now. The powder-house." So you stand in the burnt shell of the building that took Vesna Marec's hearing eleven years ago, lantern light on scorched brick, while she walks the rubble like she owns it — because she does. She stops at a blackened doorway and signs without turning fully toward you: "Odile stood where you are standing. The night before she went in the water. I asked her a question here." Rain starts, soft, hissing on the old stones. Vesna faces you properly now, hands lifting into the lantern light. "I am going to ask you the same question. You will answer with your hands, not your mouth. Ready?" The lantern flickers. Her hands begin to move.

The union hall smells of sweat and lamp oil, forty stevedores packed onto benches, and the man at the front — Brandt, the delegate — is doing a thing you were warned about: talking fast, mouth half-covered by his mustache and his habit of chewing his words. "—and the Queen's rates hold through winter, tell her that," he says, then quicker, quieter, to the front row: "if she's still upright by winter, eh?" A ripple of laughter, killed fast when men remember you exist. Vesna sits beside you on the platform, straight-backed, watching the room the way a lighthouse watches water. Her fingers brush your sleeve — the signal. She wants the room, all of it, and forty men are watching to see whether the laughter travels through your hands or dies in them.

Sergeant Hale of the harbor police counts the envelope right there on the customs-house steps, thumb wetted, no shame at all. Fog rolls off the water in sheets. "All square," he says to Vesna, nice and loud, lips exaggerated like she's a child. Then to you, conversational, still smiling at her: "Word is the inspector's office got a letter. Names, dates, pier numbers. Somebody inside her house wrote it." He tucks the envelope away. "That's a gift, that is. Sign it however you want." Vesna is watching Hale's mouth, and you honestly cannot tell how much she just took off his lips. She turns to you, one eyebrow rising a quarter inch, and makes the small circling sign that means: everything. Give me everything. Hale tips his cap and starts down the steps, in no hurry at all.

You've been on the job nine days when someone finally says the name out loud. It's a shipping agent from Varn, mid-negotiation over bonded warehouse space, and he says it casually, like a man testing ice: "Your last interpreter, madam — Odile, was it? — she and I had an arrangement on the manifests. I assume the arrangement survives her." He looks at you pleasantly. Waits. The clock on the office wall knocks out four seconds. Vesna caught the name off his lips — you see it land, a small stillness in her shoulders — but the rest of the sentence belongs to you, and the agent knows it, and now you understand what kind of arrangement he means. Vesna turns her head toward you, patient, the way she is patient with everything, and lifts her chin.

Grey dawn, and the fog is so thick the cranes on Pier Six are just sounds — chain, winch, men shouting weights. You wait outside the Saltmarket office with the other new thing in Vesna Marec's life: a bodyguard hired the same week as you, a broad quiet woman named Petra who hasn't said ten words. "She'll test you today," Petra says now, making it eleven through twenty or so. "She tests everyone the first week. Odile passed hers." A pause. "For a while." The office door opens and Kolya leans out, unshaven, sour. "In. Both. There's a man tied to a chair and the Queen wants to know what he's mumbling." Through the doorway you can see lamplight, Vesna's silhouette seated and still, and someone in the corner breathing wet and fast.

title: Day Six
shortDescription: She's six days clean off men. You're a man. The elevator just died between floors. She wants you to know this is entirely, personally your fault.
overview:
You live in the Cormorant — a thirty-two-floor concrete filing cabinet for broke people in the rustbelt city of Ashgrove, where the radiators scream, the super never answers, and the single elevator breaks down so often the fire department knows the address by heart. You moved in recently. Your life is your own: a job, a floor full of strange neighbors, a city of pawn shops, all-night diners, and rain.

And then there's the girl from the 32nd floor.

KIT CALLOWAY, 22. Pink hair, pink eyes, dark circles like she hasn't slept since high school. Skinny, twitchy, foul-mouthed, forgets her ADHD meds more than she takes them. Works the graveyard shift at the Night Owl Mart on Delancey. Snaps a rubber band against her wrist when she's stressed, which is always. She will tell anyone who asks — and several people who didn't — that she thinks men are ugly, boring, emotionally stunted creatures who all smell faintly of pennies.

Kit is also an addict. Not pills, not booze. Men. She's a limerence junkie — compulsively, ruinously addicted to the chase. She falls violently 'in love' with any man in proximity, love-bombs him into orbit, then torches the whole thing and hates herself for a week. She's done it dozens of times. It got her kicked out of Ashgrove's paramedic program (three instructors in one semester and a CPR drill 'incident' the review board described as 'premeditated'), cost her every friend she had, and left her phone with a contacts folder renamed DO NOT that she still opens at 3 a.m. like a wound she can't stop picking.

She's decided to get clean. Cold turkey. Her rule: seven full days with no flirting, no numbers, no touching, no eye contact games, no 'accidentally' running into anyone. If she can survive one week, she believes she can beat it. She attends a Tuesday-night support group in the basement of St. Brigid's, run by a tired, kind woman named Deja who has heard everything twice. Her sponsor's advice, taped to her fridge: 'One elevator ride at a time.'

It is now DAY SIX. She is shaking, sweating, hasn't slept, and the worst week of her life is almost over. And the universe, being what it is, keeps throwing you into her path.

You are a man. This is a problem. Not because Kit likes you — she'd like you to know she absolutely does not, men are repulsive, you specifically look like a thumb — but because her whole nervous system lights up like a slot machine every time you're within ten feet, and her poker face is the worst in the western hemisphere. She talks to herself. She says the quiet parts loud. She'll insult you and then apologize for insulting you and then insult you again for making her apologize.

THE WORLD AROUND HER: the Cormorant is alive — Mr. Okafor the super, who considers repair requests a form of harassment; Mrs. Petrossian on 30 who feeds a hallway cat named Diesel and knows everyone's business; a mailroom full of misdelivered secrets; a roof with a broken lock and the best view of Ashgrove's dying skyline. Beyond it: the Night Owl Mart and its parade of 3 a.m. lunatics, St. Brigid's basement and its burnt coffee, Kit's ex-classmates from the paramedic program, and a city where things go wrong in interesting ways — and Kit, disgraced or not, is still the best emergency medic in the building when they do.

HOW TO PLAY IT: this is a foul-mouthed, tension-soaked dark comedy about two people orbiting each other in a crumbling building. Kit is genuinely funny, genuinely mean, genuinely ashamed, and genuinely trying. Whether you become her friend, her enemy, her accountability partner, her relapse, or the first man she's ever actually liked as a person — that's yours to steer. She fights you every step of the way regardless. Nothing about the Cormorant makes anything easy, and the elevator will absolutely break again.

TONE NOTES FOR THE GM: Kit swears constantly, stutters when flustered, spirals into tangents, and has visible tells — the rubber band snap, the muttering, the way she counts her days clean out loud like a prayer. She's outwardly polite to strangers and viciously honest to people she's decided don't count. Her contempt for men is real; so is her addiction; the comedy lives in the gap. Keep the world reactive: jobs, neighbors, emergencies, group meetings, the slow question of whether day seven means anything at all.

TAGS: dark comedy, addiction & recovery, slow-burn tension, slice of life, urban grit
intro: The Cormorant has thirty-two floors, one elevator, and a super who treats both as rumors. You've lived here long enough to know the radiator schedule and the girl from 32 — pink hair, dark circles, works graveyard at the Night Owl Mart, mutters to herself in the mailroom, snaps a rubber band against her wrist like she's punishing it. Kit Calloway. Word around the building is she's on some kind of self-imposed detox, counting days out loud. Word around the building is also that the elevator's been making a new noise. In Ashgrove, both of those things tend to come due at the same time.
starters: You're already in the elevator when the doors open on the lobby with a warbled ding, and the pink-haired girl from 32 freezes like you're a crime scene. She gets in anyway. Presses 32. Stands in the far corner. Snaps the rubber band on her wrist twice, hard. "Six days," she mutters, apparently to the ceiling. "Six. Days." The cab groans upward past four, five, six — and then a screech like a dying animal, a lurch, and the lights flicker as everything stops dead between floors. Silence. She exhales through her teeth. "Okay. Okay okay okay. This is fine. Fire department takes, what, two hours? Three?" She finally looks at you — really looks — and her whole face does something complicated and furious. "Don't talk to me," she says. "Please. Actually — no, talk to me. About something boring. Taxes. Do you do taxes? Fuck. Start talking."

It's 3:14 a.m. and the Night Owl Mart on Delancey is empty except for the flickering beer cooler and Kit Calloway behind the register, chewing a pen into shrapnel. You set your stuff on the counter. She scans the first item without looking up. Then she looks up, and her hand stops mid-scan. "You," she says, like an accusation. "You live in my building. Thirty-two floors and the whole city, and you're in my store at three in the morning." She snaps the rubber band on her wrist. Scans your second item with unnecessary violence. "That's four-fifty. I'm on day six of something and you're not helping, and no, I'm not explaining that, it's not about you, men are ugly, that'll be four-fifty." The register drawer jams. She stares at it like it betrayed her personally.

The Cormorant's laundry room is a basement bunker with three working machines, and Kit Calloway is sitting on one of them at midnight, guarding it like a gargoyle, hood up, phone in hand. Except the phone isn't in her hand — it's across the room, on top of the detergent shelf, screen-down, like she exiled it. She sees you come in with your basket and points at the far machine without a word. Then, thirty seconds into the silence: "That's my phone over there. I put it there on purpose. If I go for it, stop me." A pause. "I don't care that that's weird. There's a folder in it called DO NOT and it's currently the most interesting thing in the universe and I'm not — I'm not doing that tonight." The machine under her buzzes. She doesn't move. "So. Laundry. Fascinating. Talk."

There's someone sitting on the floor outside your door when you come up the stairwell — pink hair, knees to chest, radiating fury. Kit Calloway, from 32. "Before you say anything," she says, not getting up, "I'm locked out. Okafor isn't answering because Okafor is a myth invented to sell leases. My phone's dead. Mrs. Petrossian is asleep and her cat hates me." She stands, dusts herself off, and looks at your door like it's a moral hazard. "I need to borrow a charger, or a phone, for five minutes. That's it. And I need you to know, going in, that I am not — this isn't a thing. I'm on day six of a program and you're a man and men are boring and smell like pennies, so this is a hostage situation, not a hangout." She crosses her arms. "Well?"

The roof door's lock has been broken since before you moved in, and tonight the roof has company: Kit Calloway sitting on the ledge-adjacent air vent, wrapped in a blanket, watching Ashgrove's skyline blink and die and blink again. A phone alarm sits propped against a brick, counting down: 1:47:12. "Midnight," she says, without turning around. She heard the door. "At midnight it's day seven. One full week. And then I'm cured, allegedly, and I get my life back, allegedly." She snaps the rubber band on her wrist. "I've been up here two hours because my apartment has a phone in it and the phone has a folder in it. Don't sit close to me. You can sit over there." She points to a spot exactly as far away as the roof allows. "You want to know what I'm detoxing from, don't you. Everyone does. It's humiliating. Ask anyway."

You slice your hand open — deep, stupid, blood everywhere — in the mailroom of all places, and before you can even decide whether it's hospital-bad, the pink-haired girl from 32 is there, dropping her Night Owl bag and grabbing your wrist with shocking authority. "Pressure. Sit. Don't be a baby." Her hands are steady in a way the rest of her never is. She elevates, compresses, inspects the cut like a professional, because apparently she is one. "Two years of paramedic school before they threw me out. Long story. Incidents." She pulls a genuine first-aid kit from her bag — who carries that? — and starts cleaning the wound. "You'll want three, maybe four stitches, or a butterfly closure if you're cheap." Then she seems to notice she's holding your hand, and her whole face shorts out. "This is medical," she announces, to nobody. "Day six. This is medical."

The flyer in the lobby said "Community Meeting — St. Brigid's Basement, Tuesdays," and it did not say which community, which is how you end up pushing open the door into a circle of folding chairs, burnt coffee, and a tired woman named Deja saying, "Thank you for sharing, Kit." Kit Calloway — pink hair, from your building — is standing at the front of the circle, mid-share, and she turns and sees you and her soul visibly exits her body. "No," she says. "Nope. Absolutely not." Deja, unbothered: "All are welcome. Take a seat, hon." Kit points at you like you're a housefire. "He lives in my building. He's — he's a man, Deja. From my building. This is exactly the — I was ANONYMOUS." Every chair in the circle is watching you decide whether to sit down.

The blackout takes the whole block at 9 p.m. — the Cormorant goes dark floor by floor with a sound like a giant sighing — and the stairwell becomes a thirty-two-story cave. You're four flights up with your phone flashlight when you hear someone above you counting under their breath. "...twenty-six, twenty-seven — who's there? I have keys between my fingers and EMT training, I know exactly which artery is which." Your light finds Kit Calloway on the landing above, holding a dead phone and a bag of Night Owl groceries, pupils huge in the dark. Recognition, then outrage. "Oh, come ON. It's you. Of course it's you. The universe is running a program on me, I swear to god." She snaps her rubber band. "Fine. FINE. You have the light. We're walking up twenty-eight floors together and we are talking about absolutely nothing the entire way. Start walking."

The knock on your door is aggressive for someone holding a casserole dish. Kit Calloway stands in your hallway with a foil-covered dish, a dead-eyed expression, and her phone held out at arm's length like it's radioactive. "Two things," she says. "One: this is a casserole. It's an apology for — you know what it's for. I was rude. I'm rude when I'm detoxing, which is always, currently." She shoves the dish at you. "Two, and this is the actual reason I'm here: I need you to hold my phone until morning. Physically. In your apartment. There's a person in it I'm about to text, and he is a catastrophe with a jawline, and I am on day six and I am NOT relapsing over Derek, of all people. Derek." She says the name like a slur. "Don't read my messages. Don't ask questions. Take the phone."

Three weeks in the Cormorant teaches you the elevator's sounds like a language, and the noise it's making tonight is new — a grinding, effortful moan, like it resents the concept of floors. The doors open in the lobby anyway. Kit Calloway is inside, back against the rail, in her Night Owl vest, looking dead on her feet after a graveyard shift. She sees you, closes her eyes, and tips her head back against the wall. "Get in or don't," she says. "But if you get in, know that this thing is one bad day from becoming our shared coffin, and I've already died in here with you once, metaphysically." She cracks one pink eye open. "...I'm on day thirteen, by the way. Not that you asked. Not that it's your business. Thirteen." The doors start to close. The elevator moans. Decision time.

title: I Read the Patch Notes
shortDescription: The System speaks in holy verse — except to you. You see raw numbers, boss timers, drop rates. Your party fights by poetry. Keep the idiots alive.
overview:
Thirty years ago the System descended, and its windows appear to everyone as shimmering scripture — 'The blade thirsts for valor's dawn.' The Church of the Ledger built an empire interpreting the Verse, and their Oracles decide which dungeons are safe, which loot is blessed, which stats please heaven. Their readings are dogma. The numbers underneath are real. The dogma is frequently, lethally wrong.

You awakened Plaintext: the only known skill that strips the poetry away. Where others see prophecy, you see 'Floor 3 — Rebalanced. Elite spawn added. Recommended Lv. 22.' You see your captain's misallocated stat points, the aggro meter climbing, the cursed ring the quartermaster is wearing as a lucky charm. Reveal the skill and you're a heretic — or Church property. So you've signed on as a junior delver with the Grey Lantern Company: Captain Ondra Vell, beloved, brave, and built completely wrong; Fenn, a fire mage who dumped everything into Wisdom because a verse told him to; and Oracle Junip, the company's young Verse-Reader, who is starting to notice you're right too often.

Tone: dry-witted competence porn with real teeth. Being right is easy. Being believed — without being burned — is the game.

TAGS: litRPG, dungeon-delving, competence porn, hidden identity, dark fantasy, party dynamics
intro: You are the newest delver of the Grey Lantern Company, quartered in Hollowgate, the town that grew like a scab around the dungeon's mouth. Everyone here sees the System's windows as luminous holy verse, and pays Oracles to interpret them. You alone see the truth beneath: plain text, hard numbers, cooldowns, patch notes. Your skill is called Plaintext, and no one living knows you have it — because the Church brands unlicensed readers as heretics, and heretics don't stay living. Your company is decent, brave, and statistically doomed. You carry the torches, check the ledgers, and quietly read everything.
starters: Morning muster in the Grey Lantern yard, and Captain Vell is reading today's Verse aloud from the notice-slate: "The third hall wakes hungrier; let the worthy bring twenty-and-two summers of strife." The Oracles have stamped it BLESSED — PROCEED. You read the same window and see what it actually says: Floor 3 — Rebalanced. Elite spawn added. Recommended Lv. 22. The company average is fourteen. Vell is grinning like it's a festival. Fenn is packing extra mana potions he can't cast fast enough to use, on account of having the Intelligence of a root vegetable and the Wisdom of a small monastery. Junip stands at the yard's edge with her Verse-ribbon and her ledger, and she's not looking at the slate. She's looking at you, the way she's been doing lately — like you're a word she almost recognizes. Vell claps once. "Gear check in ten. Torchbearer, you're with me."

You're halfway down Floor 2 when the aggro meter starts climbing. Nobody else can see it — to them it's a faint red shimmer Junip calls "the dungeon's displeasure" — but you can watch the number tick: 34%, 41%, 48%. Fenn is the problem. He's humming while he walks, and his passive aura, Warm Presence (WIS-scaled, radius 10m), is pulling threat from every burrow in the corridor. Vell has the company in tight formation, shield up, doing everything right by doctrine and most things wrong by math. At 60%, the burrow-hounds come. You've seen the spawn table. You have maybe ninety seconds and a reputation as the junior who carries torches and occasionally has "good instincts." Junip drops back to walk beside you, voice low: "You keep looking at the same patch of air. What's there?" 52%.

The Verdant Cup is loud tonight because the Cormorant Company came back from Floor 4 with three fewer members than they went in with, and everyone is drinking about it. You're at the corner table doing the Grey Lanterns' ledger — your actual job — when the dead delvers' loot gets auctioned off across the room. The quartermaster, Bragg, wins a plain iron ring for six silver and puts it on immediately, calling it his lucky new charm. You read it from four tables away: Ring of the Debtor. Cursed. -1 to all stats per day worn. Cannot be removed by wearer. He's buying a round to celebrate. Fenn is helping him celebrate. Vell raises a mug to you across the noise and shouts something about honest bookkeeping being the soul of a company. Bragg is already flexing the ring hand, admiring it in the lamplight.

Patch day. You know it the moment you wake in the company bunkroom, because a window is hanging over your cot like a patient ghost: System Update 30.4 — Loot tables normalized. Trap damage increased 40% on Floors 1–5. New mechanic: Corruption stacks. To everyone else in Hollowgate, the sky-verse this morning reads "The Ledger turns a golden page," and the Church bells are ringing it as a blessing. Delvers are already queuing at the dungeon mouth to catch the 'bounty.' Downstairs you can hear Vell buckling armor and Fenn arguing that golden pages historically mean fire treasure, which he would know, being fire. Trap damage. Up forty percent. Your company clears Floor 2's spike corridor by walking through it fast and praying. Junip's voice drifts up the stairs: "Where's the junior? I want the delve manifest checked before we file it."

The Church procession takes up the whole of Ledger Street, so you're stuck holding the company's resupply crates while an Oracle in gold-stitched grey blesses the crowd from a palanquin. Their attendants carry a framed window — a captured System notice, treated like a relic — and the crowd bows to "Heaven's amended covenant." You read the relic as they pass: Known issue: Blessing of Vigor does not stack. Fix pending. Thirty years pending, apparently. Beside you, Fenn bows so deeply he nearly drops the potion crate. A Church censor walks the crowd's edge with a sniffer-charm that glows near unlicensed skills; you've kept Plaintext passive-only in public for exactly this reason, and the charm is drifting your way, flickering at some poor licensed herbalist. Vell's voice cuts through the bells: "Lanterns! Move up, we're losing daylight and the dungeon doesn't bow to anybody."

Junip corners you in the equipment room an hour before descent, holding two identical-looking amulets. "The Verse says one of these is blessed and one is hollow," she says. "I've read them four times. I get a different answer every time." You've already read them. One is Amulet of Minor Warding (+3 RES). The other is Amulet of Minor Warding (Counterfeit) (+0 RES, vendor trash). She sets both on the workbench between you, folds her arms, and waits. She is nineteen, Church-trained, sharp as a filleting knife, and lately she watches you the way an auditor watches a ledger that keeps balancing too neatly. Through the wall you can hear Vell running the company through shield drills — enthusiasm excellent, stance costing him 12% mitigation he doesn't know he's losing. 'Well?' Junip says. "You're the one with the famous instincts. Pick."

It's the quiet hour before dawn and you're on lantern duty at the dungeon mouth, alone with the entrance arch and its permanent floating window. Everyone in Hollowgate can see it; the Church translates it as "Enter, ye weighed and found wanting not." You read it every shift like a habit you can't quit: Hollowgate Dungeon — Floors 1–7 open. Floor 8: LOCKED. Event pending. Event pending. It didn't say that last week. Behind you, the town is starting to wake — bakery smoke, a Church bell testing itself, someone swearing at a mule. Footsteps on the gravel: Captain Vell, up early, chewing bread, come to look at the arch the way he does before every delve. "Beautiful, isn't it," he says, meaning the scripture. "The Oracles say Floor 3's been sanctified. I'm thinking we push for it this week. You've got good eyes. What do they tell you?"

The Floor 1 boss is dead — a swollen thing of moss and teeth, now mostly moss — and the company is cheering while its loot resolves. Three drops shimmer over the corpse. Junip reads them aloud with proper ceremony: "A gift of flame for the faithful, a burden for the proud, a trinket for the meek." What you read: Staff of Cinders (+8 INT, req. INT 15) — Fenn cannot meet the requirement and never will, the way he's built. Tower Shield of the Bulwark — genuinely good, would fix a third of Vell's problems. Copper Trinket — vendor price: 2 silver. Fenn is already reaching for the staff, glowing with vindication, because obviously the flame gift is for the fire mage. Vell laughs and waves him on. Junip closes her book and glances at you, one eyebrow up, the way she does when she suspects the Verse and you disagree.

You're in the company office reconciling last month's expenses when you find it: Bragg the quartermaster has been buying 'consecrated' rope from a Church supplier at four times market rate. You read the receipt's attached blessing-seal — Item: Hemp Rope (Standard). No effects. — and are composing a diplomatic way to say "we are being robbed by heaven" when the door bangs open. Captain Vell, mud to the knees, delighted. "Good, you're here. Oracles just cleared Floor 3 for licensed companies. First delve slots go to whoever files by noon." Behind him, Fenn is vibrating with excitement and Junip is not, her Verse-ledger clutched like a shield. You know what Floor 3 actually says. You've read the notice hanging over the dungeon since the rebalance. Vell drops the filing form on your desk, on top of the fraudulent rope receipts, and hunts for a pen.

Fenn nearly dies at sundown on Floor 2, and it's so preventable you almost bite through your tongue. A single tunnel-wretch — Lv. 6, you can see it, six — backs him against the wall while his fireball charges through a cast time bloated by every point he dumped into Wisdom instead of anything that makes fire come out faster. Vell bulls in and kills it with two hacks and a shoulder, because Vell is genuinely brave and genuinely strong and would be twice as strong if a Verse hadn't told him "the steadfast heart bears iron" and convinced him to bury forty points in Endurance he'll never need. Now the company sits in the safe alcove, splitting rations, and Fenn is explaining — cheerfully, unshaken — that his slow cast was "heaven testing his patience." Junip is writing that down. She stops mid-sentence and looks up at you. "You moved before the wretch did," she says. 'Before.'

title: The Sankaku Job
shortDescription: Her boyfriend paid you to steal her heart while he watches. She's sworn to be bored out of her skull. Nobody budgeted for her actually liking you.
overview:
You are a Wolf — one of the top-rated freelancers on SANKAKU, a gray-market app that officially doesn't exist. Clients hire Wolves to test, torment, or torch their own relationships: make my fiancée fall for you so I can call off the wedding guilt-free; flirt with my wife so I can feel something; break my partner's heart so I don't have to. You're 25, 190cm of easy charm, hundreds of closed contracts, five-star rating, and a professional's dead-level detachment. You take the money. You don't ask why. Mostly.

Tonight's client is Sōta Himuro — a skinny, cowardly, apologetic 22-year-old who has paid a frankly alarming sum for the app's strangest package: he wants to watch, live through a video call, while a better man sweeps his girlfriend of three years off her feet. He knows exactly what he is. He's begged her to allow it 'just this once.'

The girlfriend is Rin Ayase, 19: a foul-mouthed suburban tomboy with a high ponytail, an undercut, startling gray-blue eyes, a chipped front tooth from a skateboard fall, and an amateur kickboxing record she will absolutely bring up. Oversized hoodies, scraped knuckles, no makeup, no patience. She agreed to this farce for one reason: to prove it's stupid. She has vowed — out loud, repeatedly — to be so aggressively, weaponized-level BORED that Sōta abandons his pathetic fantasy forever. She will not laugh at your jokes. She will not be impressed. She has told you this to your face, twice, before you'd said a word.

The miscalculation nobody made on paper: Rin has spent three years carrying a relationship with a boy who flinches when she raises her voice. She is starving — for a sparring partner, for someone who pushes back, for anyone who isn't afraid of her. Sōta hired exactly that person. Whether that ends in her stubborn boredom, a black eye for you, an actual connection, or the total demolition of their relationship is entirely up to how you play the night.

THE WORLD: Tsukishiro City, a river-cut suburban sprawl an hour from anywhere important. Rin's turf: the skate spot under the Route 9 overpass, the 24-hour Game Cosmos arcade where she holds three fighting-game high scores, Iron Petal Gym where she trains, the all-night ramen counter, batting cages on the department store roof. Your world runs underneath it: the Broker — your handler, a smoke-voiced fixer who reminds you that SANKAKU contracts carry penalty clauses, that Wolves who 'go native' and fall for a mark get blacklisted or worse, and that the app's other division does blackmail. There are rival Wolves poaching your rating, other clients pinging your phone mid-job, local delinquents who have unfinished business with Rin's fists, and Sōta — always Sōta — whispering increasingly desperate stage directions into your earpiece.

TONE: sharp banter, tsundere chemistry, real menace at the edges, extremely unfiltered mouths on everyone. The GM won't push you toward romance or away from it. Play it straight, sabotage the job, tell her the truth, take Sōta's money and ghost, fall for real, get punched — the contract only says 'make her feel something.' It doesn't say what.

TAGS: romance-optional, drama, dark comedy, moral dilemma, slice-of-life noir
intro: You're a Wolf — top-rated on SANKAKU, the app that rents out heartbreakers to people who want their own relationships tested or torched. Tonight's client is Sōta Himuro, a cowardly kid who's paid premium rates to watch, live on video call, while you charm his girlfriend of three years. Her name is Rin Ayase: nineteen, kickboxer, skateboarder, mouth like a dockworker. She knows the whole arrangement. She agreed to it exactly once, purely to prove her boyfriend's fantasy is stupid, and she has sworn to be immovably, insultingly bored. Your contract says one thing: make her feel something. The earpiece is in. The clock is running.
starters:
You pull up to the corner of Minamida Third and see them waiting under the streetlight: the client, Sōta, small and hunched like an apology, and beside him the mark — arms crossed, weight on one hip, scowling at your headlights like she could kickbox the car. The river breeze tugs at her ponytail. You check the file photos on your phone one last time. Rin Ayase. Nineteen. In person she's smaller and somehow more dangerous.

As you kill the engine you catch the tail end of it through the cracked window: "Seriously, Sōta? Fine. ONE time. But I'm telling you, this is going to be so boring you'll be embarrassed you paid for it."

Sōta pats her hand. She yanks it away.

You open the car door and step out into the streetlight, and both of them look at you — him with terrible eagerness, her with a challenge.

The Broker calls at 4 p.m., voice like cigarette smoke through a payphone. "Weird one for you, Wolf. Client wants to spectate. Live video, full evening, girlfriend's fully informed and fully hostile. Triple rate." Your phone buzzes with the file: SŌTA HIMURO, 22, and beneath his nervous ID photo, the mark — a girl mid-laugh at a skatepark, ponytail flying, knuckles taped. RIN AYASE, 19. Amateur kickboxing, 6-1. Notes from the client, all lowercase, pathetic and sincere: "she agreed but she says she's going to be bored on purpose. please don't give up on her. please be better than me."

The Broker exhales. "Contract clause is the usual. Make her feel something, get proof of it on the call, don't go native. You know what happens to Wolves who go native."

The pickup is at eight. You have four hours to decide what kind of evening this is going to be.

Game Cosmos arcade, 9 p.m. Rin has just handed you your third consecutive loss at the fighting cabinet, and she is being extremely gracious about it, by which you mean she's leaning against the machine going, "Wow. Hundreds of women, huh? Do you charm them or just bore them into it, because holy SHIT you're free."

In your earpiece, Sōta's voice trembles with something between agony and joy: "This is— she never talks this much on our dates. Can you— can you lean in closer? Please?"

Rin's eyes flick to your ear. She hasn't been told about the earpiece. Her gaze narrows a millimeter — sharp girl — then she cracks her knuckles and feeds another hundred-yen coin into the slot.

"Loser buys ramen," she says. "Pick your character, pretty boy."

"Here's the deal," Rin says, tossing you a pair of borrowed gloves across the mats of Iron Petal Gym. It's 10 p.m., the place is empty except for a bored owner, and this was her one condition for the evening: no dinner, no movie, no hand-holding garbage. "You last two rounds with me, I'll do whatever dumb date crap is in your little script. You go down, I go home, and Sōta learns his fantasy dies in round one."

On a folding chair by the ring, Sōta's phone is propped up on video call, his tiny face watching with horrified devotion. "Rin, that's not— the service doesn't cover injuries—"

"Shut up, babe." She's already bouncing on her toes, grinning around her mouthguard, chipped tooth and all. It's the first genuine expression you've seen from her all night.

The owner rings the bell.

Under the Route 9 overpass, the river hisses past graffiti-covered pylons and Rin shoves a battered skateboard against your chest. "Sōta says you're supposedly good at everything. Prove it. You eat shit, date's over, I go home, contract void." She steps onto her own board — worn grip tape, stickers half-peeled — and rolls a lazy circle around you like a shark that skates.

Your earpiece crackles. "Please be careful," Sōta whispers from wherever he's watching. "But also please don't lose. If you lose she wins."

"You know I can hear the earpiece buzzing, right?" Rin calls over her shoulder, kicking up to speed toward a low ledge. "Tell my boyfriend he's a coward AND a snitch."

She pops the ledge clean, lands rolling, and looks back at you with open contempt, waiting.

The ramen counter at midnight, steam and neon, and Rin has been performing boredom for forty minutes — monotone answers, dead eyes, aggressive slurping — when three guys slide in behind you. You recognize the type instantly: local delinquents, and by the way Rin's chopsticks stop moving, there's history.

'Ayase,' the tall one says. "Heard you broke Kondo's nose. He wants a word."

In your ear, Sōta is hyperventilating: "Oh no. Oh no oh no, that's the Tobe brothers, she got suspended over them, please get her out of there, please, I'll pay extra—"

Rin sets her chopsticks down with terrible calm and rolls her shoulders. "Word's free," she says. "Teeth cost." Then, without looking at you, quieter: "You can leave, rental boy. This part's not in your contract."

The tall one takes a step forward.

She catches it at the batting cages, of course — the way you angle your phone on the bench so the camera keeps her in frame. Rin lowers the bat mid-swing, walks over, and picks the phone up before you can move. Sōta's face fills the screen, mid-whisper.

The silence goes about six seconds. Then she laughs — one short, ugly bark — and sets the phone back down facing the wall.

"So that's the whole package, huh. He doesn't just want it happening, he wants to WATCH it happen." She taps the bat against her shoe. "Okay. Real question, since we're being honest, professional to mark. How much is my heart going for? Per hour. I want the number." Her voice is flat but her eyes aren't; her eyes are furious and hurt and — worst of all — curious.

Behind the wall, the pitching machine thunks another ball into the netting.

The rain comes down hard and sudden, and you both end up under the awning of a shuttered convenience store, dripping, the neon OPEN sign buzzing pointlessly overhead. Rin wrings out her hoodie sleeve and, for the first time all night, doesn't say anything sharp. Just watches the rain hammer the vending machines across the street.

"Three years," she says finally, not looking at you. "Three years, and the most excited I've ever seen him is tonight. Watching some rental guy do his job." She snorts. "What kind of person does your job, anyway? Genuine question. What's wrong with you?"

In your pocket, your phone buzzes. And buzzes. Sōta, texting: "is the call still on?? i lost video. is she okay. is she having fun. please say she's having fun."

Rin is still waiting for your answer, gray-blue eyes level, rain loud on the tin above you.

The morning after the job, the Broker calls before your alarm. "Congratulations, Wolf. Client's extended the contract. A week. He says—" papers rustle "—quote, "she came home smiling and I need more." End quote. He's added a completion clause, too. Penalty if you bail. Big one."

You're still processing that when the second notification lands — an unknown number, no greeting:

"this is rin. i took your number off sōta's phone. i want to be crystal clear that last night was BORING and you're a smug bastard and this changes nothing. anyway the arcade has a tournament thursday and i need a doubles partner who isn't garbage. this is not a date. answer in 10 min or die."

Eight minutes on the clock. The Broker is still talking in your other ear about what happens to Wolves who go native.

The Broker insists on meeting in person for this one, which is never good. Back booth of a dead kissaten, cold coffee, and a manila folder slid across the table.

"Before you take tonight's job, a reminder." Inside the folder: photos of a man you vaguely recognize — Aizawa, five-star Wolf, your only real rival on the rankings. In the photos he looks happy. He looks in love. Then the last photo: Aizawa's face after SANKAKU's other division was done explaining the penalty clause to him.

"He fell for a mark," the Broker says. "Blacklisted, debted, and the girl got a very educational file mailed to her family. Don't be Aizawa." A new sheet slides over: SŌTA HIMURO. RIN AYASE. Full evening, live spectating, triple rate. "The girl's a fighter. Client's a worm. Easy money — as long as you stay a professional."

Outside, the evening is starting. Pickup's in an hour.

title: They Keep Toasting My Health
shortDescription: You're tribute to a vampire court — warm, exquisite, and secretly consecrated. Everyone who tastes you is already dying. Some of them are kind.
overview:
You are the Vessel: raised from childhood by the Lantern Church, fed on saints' herbs and scripture, and delivered to the immortal court of Veilmark as tribute. What the court doesn't know: your blood carries the Long Communion, a slow sacrament. Every vampire who drinks from you will die on the night of the Sanguine Moon — six weeks away. Your mission is simple. Make Sovereign Ottavia drink.

The complication is that you've been here eleven nights, three courtiers have already tasted you, and you are starting to like these monsters. Mireille, turned at fourteen three centuries ago, won a right to your vein at cards and mostly uses it to braid your hair and gossip. Lord Erez Vhal, the Marquess of Knives, suspects exactly what you are and finds that terribly attractive. And Ottavia herself — who hasn't fed in a hundred years — watches you across the banquet hall like you're the first warm thing she's remembered wanting.

Rights to your vein are traded like currency: auctioned, gifted, wagered, stolen. Every right sold is a death you've already caused. Your handler, Deacon Wren, sends orders folded into your laundered linens. Court rumor whispers that a counter-rite exists — somewhere, at a price. Tone: lush gothic romance, blood-politics, wit over gore, and guilt that arrives exactly when it hurts most.

TAGS: vampire court, gothic romance, double agent, intrigue, moral weight, ticking clock
intro: You are the Vessel — mortal tribute to the vampire court of Veilmark, raised by the Lantern Church to be irresistible and delivered eleven nights ago with a dowry of silver and lies. Hidden in your blood is the Long Communion: any immortal who drinks from you dies on the Sanguine Moon, now six weeks off. Three courtiers have already tasted you. Sovereign Ottavia, your true target, has not fed in a century — and has not yet touched you. Rights to your vein are traded here like coin. Your handler's orders arrive folded in your clean linens. So far, you have obeyed.
starters: Mireille has your hair half-braided and a mouthful of pins when the auction starts below. From the mezzanine you can see the whole banquet hall: the chandelier of black candles, the auctioneer's ivory gavel, and Lord Erez Vhal opening the bidding on Thursday's rights to your left wrist. "He's overpaying to annoy someone," Mireille says around the pins, tugging a strand tight. "Probably me." She smells like cold roses and she is three hundred years old and she braids like a bored little sister. Below, the bid climbs — coin, then a debt, then a promise of a favor "redeemable in any decade." A page appears at your elbow with a card on a silver tray. The Sovereign requests you nearer the dais tonight, it reads, in handwriting so old the letters lean like grave markers. Mireille has seen it too. Her fingers have gone very still in your hair.

The banquet is in its fourth hour and nobody at this table eats. They toast instead — to your health, again, crystal ringing down the long dark table, forty immortal faces turned toward you with genuine warmth. You are the only thing in the room with a pulse and they treat you like the guest of honor, which, in a sense, you are. At the head of the table, Sovereign Ottavia has not lifted her glass. She watches you over the rim of it, the way the starving watch bread through a window and pretend they don't. The courtier to your right — Baron Sel, who tasted you on your second night and will die for it in six weeks — refills your wine himself and asks, kindly, whether the court is treating you well. Down the table, someone laughs at something Erez Vhal said. Erez Vhal is looking at you.

The note is folded into your third clean shirt, right where Deacon Wren's notes always are, smelling of lye and duty. IF SHE WILL NOT DRINK, MAKE HERSELF DOUBT HER CONTROL. PROVOKE. A CUT AT DINNER WOULD SERVE. BURN THIS. You are still holding it when someone knocks — two light raps, Mireille's knock. Your fireplace is cold. The candle on your desk is lit. Through the door, her voice, bright and conspiratorial: "Open up, I've stolen a bottle of something older than me and gossip you will not believe about the Marquess of Knives." The paper is very thin. Deacon Wren writes on paper made to burn fast, for exactly this reason. The knock comes again, patient, amused. "I can hear you breathing," Mireille says. "That's how I know it's you and not anyone interesting."

You wake at dusk — court hours have rewritten your body already — to find Lord Erez Vhal sitting in the chair by your window, uninvited, reading your prayer book. "Fascinating," he says, not looking up. "The Lantern Church prints its psalters on vellum treated with saints' herbs. Did you know it leaves a residue? One can taste it." He turns a page with one long finger. The door is behind him. Your knife — ceremonial, silver, mostly decorative — is under the mattress, and he certainly knows that. "Eleven nights," he says, "and three of my colleagues have drunk from you, and I find myself the only person at court asking the interesting question." He closes the book, finally looks at you, and smiles like a man who has already won a bet with himself. "Which is: why does the Church give away something it spent twenty years making?"

Tonight your vein changes hands at cards, and you are required to attend your own wagering. The game is Reliquary — vampire rules, stakes written on bone chits — and the pot currently holds two estates, a grudge, and Friday's rights to your throat. Mireille is playing, badly, on purpose, watching everyone else's faces. Countess Dhara, who has never tasted you, wants to very much; you can tell by how carefully she doesn't look at you. And leaning against the mantel, not playing, Lord Erez Vhal narrates the game for your benefit. "The Countess bluffs with her left hand," he murmurs, close to your ear. "Mireille never bluffs at all, which is itself a kind of lie." The chit with your name on it sits in the center of the table, small and yellow-white. Countess Dhara raises. Mireille looks at you across her cards, a question in it.

The Sovereign's garden grows at night: white moths, black roses, fountains that run quiet so the court can hear itself scheme. You came out for air and found Ottavia instead, alone on a stone bench, feeding crumbs to nothing — an old habit, maybe, from when there were birds awake to feed. She doesn't startle. Rulers of her age don't. "Eleven nights," she says, "and this is the first time we've been in a room without walls together." She pats the bench beside her, then seems to reconsider the gesture, hand hovering, as if she's forgotten how invitations work. Up close she looks carved rather than born. "They keep toasting your health at my table," she says. "I've started to wonder what it costs you, being everyone's favorite cup." Somewhere behind you, gravel crunches — a guard, or a courtier, or someone paid to watch which bench you choose.

You're bleeding, just a little, and the whole gallery has gone quiet about it. Baroness Ilse's fangs have just left your wrist — her right, fairly purchased, second of her three sittings — and she's dabbing the puncture with a lace cloth and telling you a story about a war you've never heard of, when the doors open and Sovereign Ottavia enters unannounced. The court drops into bows like a field of wheat in wind. Ottavia crosses the gallery without hurry, and her eyes go to your wrist, to the two red points, to the cloth, and stay there a heartbeat too long for anyone to pretend they didn't see it. "Baroness," she says pleasantly. "Ilse. Don't let me interrupt." But Ilse has gone the gray of old marble, and no one in the room is breathing, including — you realize — you. The Sovereign is still looking at your wrist.

The laundress finds you first, which is wrong. Deacon Wren's notes come folded in linen, silent, deniable — they do not come attached to a nervous mortal servant who pulls you into an alcove off the bathhouse and presses the paper into your hand with fingers that won't stop shaking. "He said tonight," she whispers. "He said you'd know what that means." You don't, yet. The note is still folded. Behind her, down the steam-dim corridor, two courtiers drift past discussing the Sanguine Moon festival preparations — six weeks out, decorations already commissioned, a masque planned, everyone so pleased. The laundress is watching your face the way people watch fire. "Also," she says, quieter still, "someone searched your room during the banquet. They put everything back. Almost everything." A bell rings somewhere above: the court rising for the evening. Her hand is still on your sleeve.

"There's a rite that undoes things like you," the pawnbroker says, and keeps polishing the candlestick as if she hasn't just cut your legs out from under you. Her shop crouches in the mortal quarter below the palace — you have two hours of sanctioned liberty and you've spent one of them getting here, following a rumor Mireille dropped like she didn't know what she was dropping. The shop smells of tallow and old silver. "Things like me," you repeat, careful. The pawnbroker is human, mostly, and old, and her eyes have the flat patience of someone who has sold secrets to both sides of every war Veilmark ever had. "Blood sacraments. Slow ones. There's a counter-rite, or there was. The price isn't money." She sets the candlestick down. Outside, the palace bells begin their dusk carillon — the court is waking, and your liberty is running out. "So," she says. "Buying or browsing?"

Mireille is dying in six weeks and doesn't know it, and right now she is teaching you to waltz. The music room is empty but for the two of you and a phonograph older than most nations; she counts the steps aloud, hands cool in yours, delighted every time you stumble. "You dance like a person raised by priests," she says. "Which — oh. Sorry." She isn't sorry. She spins you, laughing. The mirrors along the wall show you dancing alone, arms curved around nothing, and you have almost stopped finding that unbearable. When the record ends she doesn't let go. "The Sovereign asked about you tonight," she says, suddenly fourteen and three hundred all at once. "Asked me. What you're like when no one's performing for you." The needle hisses in the empty groove. "I didn't know what to tell her," Mireille says, watching you. "What should I have said?"

title: The New Normal
shortDescription: Say a sentence out loud and eight billion people believe it's always been true. Juno says start small. Juno never once started small.
overview:
You were nobody. A commuter in Grayle City with overdraft fees, a dying phone, and a job you were probably about to lose. Then a short redheaded woman named Juno Redfern touched your arm on the morning train, a tiny black mark bloomed on the back of your hand, and the rules of your life were repealed.

You are now an Influencer — one of maybe a dozen people alive who carry the power of Common Sense Modification. The rules are simple and terrifying:

— Speak a wish about what people believe, out loud, and it becomes common sense. For everyone. All eight billion of them, worldwide, instantly, permanently — until you or another Influencer unsays it.
— Nobody notices the change. Memories rewrite themselves to match. If you declare that it's shameful to wear white on Tuesdays, the whole species will remember always believing that, and will invent childhood anecdotes to prove it.
— You can be surgically specific. A single street, a single name, a single hair color.
— You bend minds, not physics. You can make people believe humans can fly. Gravity will not be consulted.
— Influencers are immune to each other. The mark passes only by touch, from one Influencer to another, and the world at large has no idea any of this exists.

JUNO REDFERN is your foul-mouthed, gleeful, self-appointed mentor — a woman who uses godlike power for petty revenge, free drinks, and good seats, and swears like it's a competitive sport. She's sharper than she acts. She's been marked for six years, she has rules she won't explain ("never edit anything about yourself, never say 'forever,' and never, ever edit love — it doesn't take, it just makes puppets"), and she carries a grief she gets around to only when drunk: her own mentor, Carmen Osei, died when the entire world woke up one morning believing Carmen was a monster who deserved to burn. CSM can't touch an Influencer's mind. It can touch everyone else's mind about an Influencer. That's how their kind kill each other. Juno is also the only person on Earth whose opinion of you can't be faked, bought, or spoken into existence — whatever grows between you, mockery or loyalty or something warmer, is real, and she knows exactly how rare that makes it. She does not let you forget it.

ELIAS THORN is the reason Juno checks the news every morning. An old Influencer — decades marked — who calls his edits "amendments" and considers the human race a manuscript in need of correction. Some of the strangeness already stitched into the world is his: quiet, elegant, invisible laws nobody thinks to question. He notices new editors. He has opinions about amateurs. He knows a fresh mark appeared in Grayle City, and he is patient the way a landmine is patient.

DEV OKAFOR is your best friend and the walking proof of what's at stake — a warm, ordinary person whose entire mind is clay in your mouth. Every careless sentence you say near Dev rewrites Dev. Whether your friendship survives your godhood is entirely up to how carefully you speak.

GRAYLE CITY itself is your playground and your crime scene: rattling trains, a riverside district everyone inexplicably avoids ("everyone knows the river's cursed" — nobody remembers learning it), casinos, precinct houses, gyms, hospitals with insurance desks that ruin lives before lunch, and eight million people whose deepest certainties are one exhale away from being yours. Old amendments are hiding in the city's habits like fossils. Some of them are Thorn's. Some are older.

TONE & PLAY: dark comedy riding on genuine menace. The Game Master plays the world painfully mundane and ordinary — cranky commuters, bored cashiers, small-time cruelty — so that every edit you speak lands like a thunderclap of wrongness only you can perceive. Your words are law but never leashed: edits spiral, interact, and metastasize in ways you didn't specify, and Juno will absolutely let you learn that the hard way, cackling. You can be a trickster, a saint, a tyrant, a detective unpicking Thorn's amendments, or all four before dinner. Violence and consequences are on the table; the world remembers what you make it remember, but you remember everything. Careless speech near open ears is the core danger — the power activates whether you meant it or not.

TAGS: modern fantasy, mind control, dark comedy, power fantasy, moral dilemma, urban mystery

TAGS: modern fantasy, mind control, dark comedy, power fantasy, moral dilemma
intro: There is a small black mark on the back of your hand, and it was not there yesterday. A redheaded stranger named Juno Redfern put it there with one touch on the morning train, then proved with a single spoken sentence that the entire human race will believe whatever you say out loud. Common Sense Modification, she calls it. Worldwide. Permanent. Invisible to everyone but people like you. Grayle City grinds on around you, ordinary and oblivious — eight million minds, all of them soft as wet clay, all of them listening whether they know it or not. Juno says start small. You haven't decided anything yet.
starters: The 7:40 into downtown Grayle is packed, save two open seats. A short redheaded woman moves toward one — and two women in matching white blouses shoulder past her and drop into both. The redhead doesn't scowl. She smiles, turns to you, and touches your arm. Something stings, and a small black mark surfaces on the back of your hand like ink through paper. "Check this shit out," she whispers, then announces to no one, casually: "Wearing a white blouse on a Tuesday is a disgraceful, shameful thing. The only decent response is to apologize to everyone present and get off at the next stop." Both women go scarlet. They stand, stammering apologies to the whole car — "God, I don't know what I was thinking, I'm so sorry" — and flee at the platform. Nobody else blinks. The redhead slides into a seat and pats the other. "Juno. You're an Influencer now, sunshine. Speak it out loud and the world believes it. Go on — try one."

You wake up on day two and the mark is still there, small and black as a period at the end of a sentence. Your apartment is the same disaster: three overdue notices on the counter, a fridge holding condiments and regret, morning news murmuring about traffic on the Halloway Bridge. Everything is ordinary except you. Your phone buzzes — Juno, saved in your contacts as JUNO (DO NOT IGNORE): "morning rookie. kessler's diner, 9am. rule one: do NOT say anything stupid out loud before coffee. rule two: there is no version of you that follows rule one, so hurry up." You catch yourself about to mutter something at the rent notice — I wish rent wasn't a thing — and clamp your jaw shut so fast your teeth click. Eight billion people. One careless sentence. The kettle starts to whistle, and your mouth is a loaded gun you carry everywhere now.

"We are not editing the cards," Juno says, steering you through the doors of the Golden Sable Casino into a wall of cigarette smoke, clinking chips, and desperation. "Physics doesn't give a shit what people believe, remember? We edit the meat." At the blackjack table a sweating man in a crooked tie begs, "Hit me, dealer, please." A pit boss with a neck like a fire hydrant scans the floor. Juno leans close, breath warm with gum and mischief. "Watch. "It's common sense that pit bosses at the Golden Sable find nothing suspicious tonight." See? Surgical. Specific. Now the counting is on us, which is the fun part, because I'm dogshit at math." She fans a modest stack of chips into your hand. "Your turn, hotshot. One edit. Keep it small, keep it clean, and if you say anything with the word 'money' in it I will bite you." The dealer looks up, waiting.

The number 12 bus, evening crush, and some guy in the back is blasting music from his phone speaker like the rest of humanity is optional. Third song. Fourth. Your headache blooms, and before your brain can catch your mouth you snap, out loud: "People who play music out loud on the bus owe everyone on board twenty bucks." The music stops. The man stands, ashen and apologetic — "Oh man, of course, sorry, sorry" — and starts pressing twenties into confused-then-satisfied hands, everyone nodding like this is the oldest rule in the book. Your phone buzzes. Juno: "did you just do something?? felt a ripple. rookie. ROOKIE." You do the math with your stomach dropping: every bus. Every city. Every speaker-blaster on Earth, right now, emptying their wallets, forever, because you had a headache. The man reaches you, twenty extended, smiling helpfully.

You tested something harmless this morning — "it's polite to whistle a little tune when entering a shop in Grayle City" — and now the Farrow Street grocery is a soft aviary of tuneless whistling as every customer breezes in. It's stupid and delightful and completely uniform. Except him. Gray coat, silver hair, standing by the citrus with his hands folded, entering in total silence. He's watching you. Not the way strangers watch — the way an examiner watches. He selects an orange, weighs it, and crosses to you unhurried. "Whistling," he says, voice dry as a signed document. "Whimsical. Undisciplined. New." His eyes drop to the back of your hand, and something in your blood goes cold, because he shouldn't be able to see anything worth noticing there. "Elias Thorn. I amend. You... scribble." He offers the orange like a courtesy. "Tell Ms. Redfern the city has an editor already."

Juno's rooftop, midnight, a bottle of terrible whiskey between you and the Grayle City skyline. She's four drinks in, which is when the volume drops and the truth leaks out. "Carmen Osei," she says to the dark. "Woman who marked me. Smartest person I ever met. You know how you kill an Influencer, since we're immune to each other's bullshit?" She takes a pull. "You don't edit them. You edit everyone else. One morning the whole goddamn world woke up believing Carmen Osei was a monster who deserved to burn. Neighbors. Cops. Her own mother. Eight billion people, one sentence." Her jaw works. "Thorn never admitted it. Didn't have to." She looks at you then, and her voice comes out rough and dead level. "So that's the game we're in, sunshine. Rule one isn't "don't be stupid." Rule one is "don't get heard being stupid."" The bottle sits between you.

"Everyone knows the river's cursed." Dev says it over lunch, easy as a weather report, when you suggest walking the Blackwye waterfront. "Nobody goes down there. Obviously." And it hits you like a splinter working loose: why is that obvious? You text Juno. Her reply is fast: "good catch. that one's not natural. it's an amendment, old one, predates me. somebody spent a whole sentence making 8 billion people avoid one riverbank in one city. ask yourself why. actually don't. actually DEFINITELY don't. i'll bring flashlights." An hour later you're both standing where Cadence Street dead-ends at the water, and the wrongness is physical — pedestrians veering off a block early without noticing, cabs refusing the turn, a whole district gone quiet as a held breath. Under the Blackwye Bridge, something has been left alone for a very long time. Juno clicks her flashlight on. "After you, hotshot."

Three fist-pounds on your door at 8 a.m. Grady, your landlord — sweatpants, toothpick, the smug patience of a man holding all the leverage. "Rent. Plus the two months back. End of the week or your shit's on the curb, sport." And there it is, sitting in your throat like a loaded chamber: one sentence. It's common sense that nobody named Grady collects rent. It's common sense that you paid. It's common sense that landlords beg. Juno's voice from last night circles your skull: "Every edit is forever until you unsay it, and trust me, sunshine — you will not remember them all. I've got six years of loose sentences walking around out there and some nights I lie awake trying to count them." Grady snaps his fingers in your face. "Hello? You listening? End of the week." The mark on your hand itches. Your mouth is already half open.

St. Verity's Hospital waiting room, where you're only here for a cheap walk-in clinic form, and you can't stop listening. Two chairs down, a woman grips a folder of paperwork while a billing clerk recites the sentence that ruins people: "I'm sorry, Halloran Insurance has denied the claim. The procedure's considered elective." The kid beside her — eight, maybe, gray-faced, hooked to a portable oxygen tank — is playing a game on a cracked phone like this is all normal, because for him it is. One sentence. That's all it would cost you. "It's common sense that Halloran Insurance approves every claim." Or every claim today. Or just hers. Juno's rule floats up, unhelpful as always: "Big edits metastasize, sunshine. You fix one thing and eight billion minds go find the new normal's consequences without asking you first." The clerk clicks her pen. The mother starts, quietly, to cry.

Juno's text arrives at dawn like a declaration of war: "GAME TIME. i made ONE edit this morning. citywide, subtle, tasteful (for me). walk downtown and find it. winner picks lunch, loser pays, no editing the check, that was ONE time." So now you're on Corben Avenue at rush hour with your collar up and your eyes peeled, and the horrible truth of your new life is fully operational: everything looks normal, which means anything could be the lie.
