Commuters stream past. A hot dog vendor makes change. Two cops laugh outside a bakery. Is it normal that every single person is walking on the left? Was it always? Did that guy just salute a pigeon, or did you imagine it? Your phone buzzes: "tick tock, sunshine. hint: you've already walked past it twice." A businessman brushes by, and something about him snags in your brain like a hangnail.

title: Standby, Assassin
shortDescription: The Premier attends tonight's gala. You alone have spotted the murder hidden in the cue sheet — and the show must go on either way.
overview:
You run the Aldervin State Opera the way a watchmaker runs a watch. Twenty years ago you were the Republic of Vorenia's most daring young director, until the Party called your work 'decadent' and let you keep your life in exchange for a headset. Now you call every cue, know every trapdoor, counterweight, and sightline — and today, during technical rehearsal, the wrongnesses started adding up. A blocking change nobody ordered puts the tenor's aria dead beneath the state box at minute forty-three. The follow-spot operator was replaced this morning by a man who doesn't know a fresnel from a fly rail. A counterweight arbor is loaded heavy for no scene in the show. Premier Sorel arrives at eight.

You can't report it. Captain Rehn of the Directorate is already prowling your wings, and the Directorate solves problems by cancelling shows and arresting crews — starting, probably, with the disgraced ex-director holding the prompt book. And a quiet part of you isn't certain Sorel deserves saving. Foil the plot, finish it, or thread a third way — but do it live, cue by cue, without missing a single 'go.'

The GM plays a full backstage ecosystem: the diva Vesna Kalder mid-feud, old drunk Milo the tenor, flywoman Berta, the Party toady Deputy Molnar, and at least one person on your crew who is not what they seem. Tension comes from time, sightlines, and who you dare to trust. Tone: cold-war thriller with velvet and dust — Le Carré backstage.

TAGS: cold-war thriller, competence porn, backstage drama, intrigue, moral dilemma
intro: You are the stage manager of the Aldervin State Opera, and tonight Premier Sorel attends the anniversary gala in the state box. Once you were this country's most celebrated director; a Party censure took that away and left you the headset, the prompt book, and a building you know better than anyone alive. During today's rehearsals you noticed small wrongnesses — a blocking change, a stranger on the follow-spot, an arbor loaded for no scene in the show — and you are now all but certain someone means to kill the Premier from inside your theater tonight. You have told no one. Curtain is at eight.
starters: Six-forty. You stand at the prompt desk with the book open to Act One and a pencil you haven't set down in twenty minutes. The blocking change is written in the margin in someone else's hand — neat, confident, initialed with a smudge. Down the corridor, Deputy Molnar is laughing too loudly at something Captain Rehn hasn't said, and both of them are between you and the fly gallery, where arbor twelve hangs loaded four hundred pounds heavy for a scene that doesn't exist. Berta clumps past with a coil of hemp over her shoulder, gives you the flat look she gives everyone, and slows — just slightly — as if waiting to see whether you'll stop her. The house opens in fifty minutes. The pencil is starting to leave a groove in the page.

You're halfway up the ladder to the follow-spot booth when the new man leans out over the rail and looks down at you. He has clean hands. Follow-spot operators do not have clean hands. "Everything all right?" he calls, friendly as a border guard. Behind you the stage is in worklight, the crew resetting the palace drop, and you can hear Vesna Kalder's voice from the wings pitching upward into a genuine scream about her sightlines — a fight that will need you in about ninety seconds whether you want it or not. Above, the booth smells of hot metal and something else, something oiled. The man waits, one hand resting on the spot's yoke, watching you climb.

The house is empty and dark and you are standing at center stage on the spike mark that shouldn't exist. Minute forty-three of Act One. From here, the state box is a gilded mouth hanging open above the second ring — clean line, no obstruction, close enough to read a face. You put Milo here yourself this afternoon, following a blocking note you never wrote. Somewhere in the flies a chain shifts and settles. Then footsteps on the apron stairs: Captain Rehn, coat still on, unhurried, hands behind his back like a man touring a property he expects to inherit. 'Rehearsing?' he says. 'Alone?' It is seven minutes past six. The ghost light is between you and him, and he is looking at where you're standing, not at you.

Milo the tenor has you by the sleeve in the stairwell outside the dressing rooms, and his breath is already forty proof. "Somebody moved me," he says. "Forty years I stand stage left for the aria. Now the book says center. You wrote it?" You didn't. He knows you didn't; that's why he's whispering. Above you, the tannoy crackles — half-hour call in twenty minutes — and below, the door to the green room opens on Deputy Molnar's voice explaining to someone that the Premier's motorcade arrives at seven-fifty sharp and the Directorate will want the wings cleared of "nonessential persons." Milo's grip tightens. "You wrote it or you didn't," he says. "Which is worse?"

Berta finds you first. She's waiting in the shadow of the counterweight wall when you come through the loading door, arms crossed, and she doesn't say hello. "Arbor twelve," she says. "I didn't load it. Tomas didn't load it. It's rated for the chandelier and the chandelier isn't in this show." She's kept her voice under the sound of the orchestra tuning beyond the pass door, which tells you she's already thought about who might be listening. Above you both, the arbor hangs in its track, bricks stacked neat as ammunition. "I can strip it in ten minutes," she says, "or I can pretend I never looked up. But you're the one with the book, so you tell me." From the stage, someone is calling your name — Molnar's voice, sweet with panic.

Seven-fifteen, and the house is at half. Through the peephole in the proscenium you watch the audience file in — Party wives in good wool, officers finding their rows — and above them, empty and lit, the state box with its little velvet chairs. A steward is dusting the rail. Behind you the deck is quiet the way it's only quiet when everyone is exactly where they should be, which is what frightens you: the new follow-spot man is in his booth, arbor twelve is still heavy, and Milo's mark is still center at forty-three. Your assistant hands you the headset and the running order without meeting your eyes. "Motorcade's early," she murmurs. "Rehn wants you at the pass door. Now, he said." The overture is thirty-eight minutes away.

Vesna Kalder has locked herself in her dressing room again, and this time you're almost grateful. Her dresser stands in the corridor wringing a costume like a chicken's neck while Vesna's voice comes through the door listing grievances — Milo's breath, the new lighting, the blocking change that puts him in her light at forty-three. "Ask the stage manager," she shouts, meaning you, "ask who authorized it, because somebody did, and it was not the maestro, I asked him." She has, without knowing it, said the most dangerous sentence spoken in this building today, loudly, in a corridor where Captain Rehn was standing four minutes ago. The dresser looks at you. Down the hall, a door you can't see clicks shut. Curtain in fifty-five minutes.

You come down from the grid with rust on your palms and the shape of arbor twelve's load memorized — and Captain Rehn is standing at the bottom of the ladder, reading your prompt book. It sits open on the desk where you left it, which was a mistake, and his finger rests on the margin of Act One. "Interesting hand," he says. "Not yours. I've seen your reports to the ministry — you write small." Around you the crew moves with the exaggerated deafness of people who have survived other captains. The tannoy gives the half-hour call. Rehn turns a page, unhurried. "A theater like this," he says, "must have a hundred places to hide something. You'd know them all, I suppose." He isn't asking. But he's waiting.

The overture is nine minutes old and you're calling the show. "Standby electrics twelve through fifteen, standby flies cue four." The words come out level; your hands are another matter. Through the monitor you heard the ripple when Sorel entered the state box — the whole house rising, then the anthem, then the settling — and now the Premier sits a hundred feet above the spike mark that shouldn't exist, small and gray behind glass and velvet. On your cue sheet, minute forty-three is circled so hard the paper has torn. In your headset, a channel clicks open: the follow-spot booth. The new man's voice, mild: "Confirm my pickup for the aria. Center, yes? Tight?" Berta is watching you from the rail. Thirty-four minutes.

It starts with the smell of gun oil where there should be dust. You're doing your walk of the stage-right wing — the same circuit you've done every night for twenty years, fingertips on the fly rail, eyes up the dark — and there it is, faint and out of place, near the ladder to the loading bridge. The half-hour call went out three minutes ago. Below, the deck is filling: dressers hauling frocks, Milo shuffling to his corner with a thermos that isn't tea, Deputy Molnar posting a typed seating protocol on your callboard as if the callboard were his. Someone has been up that ladder recently; the rungs are wiped clean of dust for exactly as high as you can see. From the booth loudspeaker, front of house confirms: doors are open, and the Premier's advance party has entered the lobby.

title: His Pack Followed Me Home
shortDescription: You killed a wolf in self-defense. It was their alpha. By their oldest law, that makes you theirs — and them yours. Rival packs are circling.
overview:
You are an ordinary human living alone at the edge of timber country. Nine days ago something enormous came over your fence at night and you killed it — pure luck and a silver-edged heirloom knife. It was Gideon Vane, alpha of the pack that runs these mountains. By their oldest law, what kills an alpha leads the pack. They are not angry. That's the terrifying part: they are devout.

Now there are wolves sleeping in your barn, filling your freezer with venison, mending your fence at 3 a.m., and correcting you constantly — an alpha eats first, an alpha never apologizes, an alpha does not lock the door against the pack. Rooke, the grizzled beta, drills you in law and etiquette like your life depends on it, because it does. Sable, Gideon's widow, watches you with unreadable patience; the law forbids her claws, not her mind. Young Cricket already believes you're destiny. Caleb Vane, the son who should have inherited, believes something else entirely.

In three weeks the autumn Gathering convenes, where alphas like Aya Corrigan of Blacklarch will come to test the human that killed Gideon Vane — and take the territory if you break. Meanwhile the sheriff keeps asking about the 'animal attack,' and someone keeps leaving deer hearts on your porch. Find a way back to your old life, or learn why forty wolves think you're worth kneeling for. Tone: warm-menacing rural fantasy, dry humor, found family with teeth.

TAGS: werewolves, reluctant leader, found family, modern fantasy, pack politics, slow-burn romance
intro: You live alone at the end of Millbrook Road, where the fields give up and the pines take over. Nine days ago a wolf the size of a horse came through your fence and you killed it — terror, luck, and your grandmother's silver-edged knife. It was Gideon Vane, alpha of the pack that runs these mountains. By their law, whoever kills an alpha inherits the pack. They came the next night — not for revenge, but to kneel. Now wolves patrol your land, stock your freezer, and correct your posture. In three weeks, at the autumn Gathering, the other packs come to see what killed Gideon Vane.
starters: Six-forty in the morning and there's a wolf in your kitchen. Rooke, in his human shape — flannel, gray stubble, forearms like fence posts — has made eggs, bacon, and toast, and set one plate at the head of your own table. He stands beside it, waiting, not eating. "Alpha eats first," he says, in the patient tone of a man who has said it every morning for a week. Through the window you can see two more of them sitting in the yard, facing the house, also apparently waiting for you to take a bite. Your coffee is going cold. The eggs are, honestly, perfect. Rooke's jaw is set like he'll stand there until Christmas. Somewhere out past the barn, something big moves through the frost-stiff grass without a sound.

The hammering wakes you at 3:12 a.m. You find the flashlight before you find your boots, and from the back porch you can see them at the fence line — four figures, two on two legs, two on four, replacing the section Gideon Vane came through nine days ago. New cedar posts. Yours were pine. One of the workers, a young one with a shaved head, spots your light and immediately drops to one knee in the mud, which makes the others stop and look toward the house. The night goes very quiet except for the wind in the pines. The kneeling one stays down. The oldest of them, holding a post-hole digger like it weighs nothing, calls out low: "Didn't mean to wake you. Go on back to bed if you like." Nobody moves until you do something.

Sheriff Dale Pruitt's cruiser is halfway up your drive before you hear the gravel, and by the time he's out of the car the yard is empty — no wolves, no half-mended fence tools, nothing but a woodpile that's mysteriously doubled since Tuesday. "Morning," Pruitt says, thumbs in his belt, squinting at the pines. "Fish and Wildlife's still asking about that animal attack. Big carcass, no carcass, funny thing." Behind him, just inside the tree line, you can see Rooke standing absolutely still in the shadows, watching the sheriff's back the way a man watches a kettle. Pruitt pulls out a little notebook. "Mind walking me through it one more time? And whose truck was that I passed on the road? Plates were mud all over." The pines hold their breath. So does the thing in them.

There's a deer heart on your porch again. Third one this week — set dead center on the doormat, neat as a delivered package, still warm enough to steam in the dawn cold. No tracks in the frost this time either, which is starting to feel like showing off. From the barn you can hear the pack stirring, and Cricket — sixteen, all elbows, apparently your biggest fan — comes jogging across the yard with hay in her hair. She sees the heart and stops dead. "That's not from us," she says, and for the first time since these people invaded your life, she sounds scared. "Rooke needs to see that. Don't touch it. Or — you're alpha, touch it if you want, but—" She's already backing toward the barn, eyes on the tree line. The steam rises off the heart. The pines say nothing.

You're trying to split firewood and Cricket is narrating. "Rooke says an alpha doesn't do chores, but I told him Gideon used to chop wood, and he said that was different, and I said how, and he made me run the ridge trail twice." She's perched on the woodpile, sixteen years old, watching you swing the axe like you're inventing fire. "You held the knife in your left hand, right? When you did it? Left-hand kills are lucky. Old-lucky." You have no memory of which hand held anything; you remember the fence coming apart and a smell like wet copper. Cricket hops down and offers you the next log, reverent as an altar server. Across the yard, Rooke has stopped mending your gutter to watch, and you can't tell if the look on his face is approval or a man doing math he doesn't like.

Sable is in your garden when you come out with your coffee, pulling the frost-killed tomato plants like she's lived here for years. Gideon Vane's widow. She works in silence, black hair tied back, and doesn't look up when your boots hit the porch steps. The others give her room — you've noticed that. Even Rooke steps around her like she's a hole in the floor. "Your soil's tired," she says finally, snapping a stem. "He would have told you to burn the beds and start over. He had opinions about everything." She straightens up and looks at you then, and her face gives you exactly nothing — not grief, not hatred, just attention, complete and patient, like a person reading a long book. She holds out a dead tomato plant, roots and all, as if it's yours to take.

You go out at dusk to bring in the mail — a normal thing, a human thing — and Caleb Vane is leaning against your mailbox. You know him by the way the two wolves escorting you go stiff. He's maybe twenty-five, built like his father must have been, and he's holding your mail, thumbing through it: electric bill, seed catalog, a card from your aunt. "Millbrook," he reads off an envelope. "They named the road after somebody. Everything here used to be named after somebody." He taps the stack against his palm and smiles with no warmth in it whatsoever. "Rooke teaching you the law yet? Ask him what happens to an alpha who can't hold the Gathering. Ask him what happened to the last weak one." He holds the mail out to you, just slightly too far away, so you'll have to step toward him to take it.

You open the chest freezer for a frozen pizza and stand there a while. There is no pizza. There is, instead, roughly two hundred pounds of venison, butchered, wrapped in white paper, labeled in careful block letters: BACKSTRAP. SHANK. FOR STEW. FOR THE ALPHA'S TABLE. Somebody has also alphabetized your spice rack and sharpened every knife in the block, including the little useless paring one. Through the kitchen window, the barn light is on and shapes move against it — the pack settling in for the night, in your barn, like it's theirs, like you invited them. On the counter someone's left a note in the same block letters: LESSONS AT DAWN. EAT WELL. — R. Your stomach growls, traitorously. The pizza, you eventually notice, is on the porch railing outside, frozen solid, exiled.

"Again," Rooke says. You're standing in your own driveway at eight in the morning while a sixty-year-old man who is sometimes a wolf critiques the way you walk. "You drop your eyes when someone gets close. Aya Corrigan will see that from across a field. Chin level. You look at their throat if you can't do the eyes — throat says I could, eyes say I will." Behind him, three of the pack sit in a row on your porch steps like an audience at a recital. Nine days ago your biggest social obligation was waving at the propane guy. "Three weeks," Rooke says. "The Gathering doesn't test whether you're strong. It tests whether you break. Different thing." He squares off in front of you, close, closer than politeness, and waits — either for you to hold his gaze or to try something else entirely.

The howling starts a little after midnight, and it's wrong — you've heard the pack sing before, nine nights of it now, and this isn't them. This comes from the north ridge, three voices, formal somehow, like a question asked loudly at a door. Your pack answers from the barn and the yard erupts: bodies pouring out, fur and flannel both, arranging themselves between the house and the tree line without anyone giving an order. Rooke is on your porch before you've got the door fully open, dressed like he never sleeps. "Blacklarch," he says. "Aya Corrigan's people, early, sniffing the border. They'll want to see you stand on your own porch and not come down off it — or come down off it. Both mean something." The northern voices ask again. Forty pairs of eyes in your yard turn toward you, waiting to learn what kind of alpha they've got.

title: The Tyrant Repeats a Year
shortDescription: Regressed ten years to your academy dorm — before you became the monster the heroes killed. You know every secret, every coming death. You caused most of them.
overview:
You died on the steps of the palace you burned, cut down by heroes who were once your classmates. Then you woke up here: first morning of your final year at Greyveil Academy, ten years before you become the Ashen Sovereign. Your power is still coiled under your ribs — wound back, not erased. So is your memory: every secret in these halls, every coming death, every cruelty done to you here, and the continent's worth of cruelty you answered with.

Cassian Vayle will shove you into the fountain by Friday; he will also die a hero, holding a bridge alone. Mirren Oduya will slip you bread from the kitchens like she always did; you remember exactly how she dies, and whose hand does it. Magister Aurel Dain will offer mentorship and forbidden pages — and this time you recognize the grooming for what it was, and notice he's already circling a new student. And your quiet roommate Anselm, the infirmary aide, will one day put a blade of light through your chest.

Hide what you are. Spend secrets like coins. Decide whether the people who made you deserve saving, punishing, or something you don't have a word for yet — while your old power leans on the door every time you get angry. Tone: grounded dark academia; deaths are real and stay real; foreknowledge is intoxicating, using it visibly is dangerous.

TAGS: regression, villain protagonist, dark academia, hidden power, secrets, redemption
intro: Ten years from now, you burn the kingdom of Ardelle and die for it — the Ashen Sovereign, cut down on the palace steps by people who once shared these dormitories. That was yesterday. This morning you woke in your old bed at Greyveil Academy, first day of your final year, every memory intact: the secrets, the deaths, the thing you become. The power that ruined you is still there, coiled small beneath your ribs, answering when your temper rises. No one knows. The classmates who will one day kill you are down the hall. So is everyone who made you.
starters: Anselm is already awake. He sits on the edge of his bed in the grey pre-dawn, lacing his boots, infirmary satchel packed for his first shift of the year. "You were talking in your sleep," he says without looking up. "Something about steps. Stairs, maybe." Your hands are smaller than you remember. Softer. Eighteen years old and unscarred, and across the room is the quiet roommate you spent a decade not thinking about. He sets a cup of water on your desk — he always did that, you'd forgotten — and shoulders his bag. "Assembly's at eight. Dain's giving the address this year instead of the Provost. Everyone's talking about it." The door is half open. The corridor beyond smells of floor wax and candle smoke, exactly the way it did the first time, and the water in the cup trembles very slightly, though you are holding perfectly still.

The dining hall roars with first-morning noise — trunks in the aisles, prefects shouting names, three hundred students who don't know what any of them become. You've barely sat down when a hand slides a heel of dark bread onto your tray, still warm. "Kitchens made extra. Don't tell," Mirren Oduya says, same as she always said, wiping flour on her apron. She's alive. She's sixteen and rolling her eyes at the noise and completely, stupidly alive, and you know the date it stops being true. "You look like you've seen a ghost," she says, laughing. "It's just final year. It's not that bad." Down the table, Cassian Vayle is holding court with the rowing crowd, loud and golden, and his eyes flick to you the way they always did — cataloguing, choosing. Mirren is still standing there, waiting for you to say something normal.

You're halfway across the fountain courtyard when Cassian Vayle steps into your path, flanked by two boys whose names you'd deliberately forgotten. "There you are," he says pleasantly. "You owe the year-book committee a photograph and me an apology, though I forget for what." His friends laugh. The fountain hisses behind him — Friday, you think, it happens Friday, you know exactly where his hands go and how the water tastes — and something under your ribs shifts like a dog hearing its name. Ten years from now this boy dies holding a bridge so that other people can run, and right now he is smirking at you with a hero's face he hasn't earned yet. Students stream past on both sides, giving your little scene a wide berth. Cassian tilts his head, patient, enjoying himself. The old you looked at the ground. The last you would have left a crater.

"— which brings me to mentorships," Magister Aurel Dain says from the lectern, and the assembly hall goes attentive, because everyone wants to be chosen by Dain. You'd forgotten how he looks in daylight: kind, tired, a little rumpled, the most trustworthy man at Greyveil. You spent three years grateful to him. You spent seven more understanding what he'd actually done. "I take one final-year student," he says, "and this year, perhaps a younger one as well — talent shouldn't wait." His gaze moves along the second-year benches and rests, briefly, on a small dark-haired student you don't recognize, who sits up straighter under the attention. Your fingernails are in your palms. Beside you, some classmate whispers, "He picked you for something last spring, didn't he? Lucky." The assembly is breaking up in ten minutes. Dain always lingers by the east doors afterward, available, approachable, choosing.

The registrar's line stretches down the administrative corridor, and you've been standing in it for twenty minutes holding a form you last filled out a lifetime ago. Advanced Theory. Applied Wards. Ethics of Practice — you laugh once, quietly, and the girl ahead of you glances back. Through the office door you can hear the registrar calling names, and every third one lands like a stone: students you'll bury, students who'll bury you, a boy who sells information for pocket money and doesn't know it gets him killed, a girl whose family estate you will personally put to the torch. Ordinary faces. Homework complaints. Someone behind you is asking to trade for morning duelling practice because afternoons conflict with choir. The line shuffles forward. Your form is still blank where it asks for elective focus, and you know — better than anyone alive — exactly which classes lead where.

It's not quite six and you're on the bell tower walk, coat pulled tight, because you needed somewhere the walls don't remember you. Greyveil spreads out below in the fog: the fountain courtyard, the infirmary wing, the kitchens already lit, the duelling lawns silver with dew. Ten years from now you can see this skyline from the palace you burn. This morning it's just a school. You breathe out and the power breathes with you — a warm pressure under your sternum, testing, the way it did before the worst things you ever did. Below, a groundskeeper is unlocking the courtyard gates, and the first students are crossing to breakfast in twos and threes. One of them stops, looks up at the tower, and shades their eyes. From this distance you can't tell who it is. The bell above you will ring the hour in a few minutes, loud enough to shake the boards under your feet.

You've sliced your palm open on the trunk latch — a stupid, human injury, and it's bleeding enough that the dorm prefect sends you to the infirmary before breakfast. Anselm looks up from rolling bandages. "Oh," he says. "It's you." Your roommate of ten minutes and, later, of one very final minute. He takes your hand without asking and turns it toward the window light, thumb steady below the cut, and he is gentle in a way that your memory insists is impossible. "Latch?" he guesses. "Third one this morning. They should file those down." The antiseptic stings. The room smells of carbolic and linen. Somewhere behind a curtain a first-year is crying about homesickness, and Anselm's eyes flick that way, then back to your palm. "Hold still," he says. "This needs two stitches or a sealing charm, your choice. Charm's faster but the Matron logs them."

Rain hammers the library windows and the reading room is nearly empty — first evening of term, everyone else is at the welcome bonfire you can hear faintly through the glass. You came here for quiet and found the restricted stacks gate standing ajar, which it never should be. You know what's behind it. You know which specific book behind it starts everything, because a kind-faced magister will put it in your hands by Yuletide and call it trust. A lamp burns at the archivist's desk but the chair is empty. Somewhere in the stacks, a page turns. Then another. Your pulse picks up and the old power picks up with it, interested, leaning against the inside of your ribs like a shoulder against a door. The rain covers most sounds. Not footsteps, though — someone is moving between the shelves beyond the gate, unhurried, and the bonfire crowd won't be back for at least an hour.

"Pairs!" barks Instructor Halvern, and the duelling lawn scrambles to obey. First morning, and she's testing the final years for placement — you'd forgotten this, the way you'd forgotten most small things that happened before everything large. Your assigned partner is a nervous boy named Petrik who dies in the third year of the war, on a road, for nothing. He raises his practice wand in textbook stance. "Go easy? I did no revision all summer." Around you, wards flare and fizzle, and Halvern paces the line with her slate, ranking. You could take Petrik apart without breathing hard. You could take Halvern apart. The thing under your ribs knows it, and stretches. "Begin!" Halvern calls. Petrik's opening jinx wobbles toward you, slow as thrown fruit, and Halvern's eyes are on you, and whatever score she writes down follows you all year — into whose classes, whose notice, whose files.

The second-year is lost. That's your first thought when you find them in the north cloister after last bell: small, dark-haired, holding a corridor map upside down and a letter with a broken green seal. You recognize the seal. Magister Dain's personal correspondence — an invitation to tea, if the pattern holds, and it always held. "Sorry," the student says, embarrassed. "Do you know where the Aster Wing is? A magister wants to see me and I don't want to be late, he was so kind about it." The cloister is empty. Lamps are being lit along the far arcade by a porter working away from you. Ten years of hindsight and this child in front of you, pleased to be chosen, exactly as pleased as you once were. The Aster Wing is left, then up the spiral stair. You know the way better than anyone should.

title: Her Head Is Worth Ten Floors
shortDescription: Anyone who kills the kid you're guarding skips ten floors — every climber knows it, and every sponsor is paying to watch you fight the whole Tower.
overview:
You are a low-ranked nobody in the Spire, a tower where every floor is a rank, every rank has a Gate trial, and unseen sponsors watch through drifting glass motes, dropping gifts to climbers who entertain them. Weeks ago the Tower's voice made a standing offer: kill Contestant 4041 and ascend ten floors, no trial. 4041 is Wren — fifteen, mouthy, ungrateful, useless in a fight, and currently your problem. You stopped the first attempt on pure instinct. The motes caught it. Now 'the Warden and the Bounty' is the season's best show, and your gift-chute is the only reason you're both still fed, armed, and stitched up.

Here's the rot in that: your richest patron, screen-name OPALINE, pays best when Wren is in danger — scared, cornered, bleeding a little. Never safe. Meanwhile Halma's Vanguard, the top party of the low floors, has publicly sworn off the bounty (believe that if you like), the Ledger brokers will sell your route to anyone with credit, and every smiling campfire ally is doing quiet math about ten free floors. And lately Wren has started saying the Tower's announcements a breath before they play.

Tone: tense, tactile, dirty fights and conditional alliances, occasional warmth around a fire. The cameras never blink, and the GM plays every faction, sponsor, and knife with its own patient agenda.

TAGS: tower climb, death game, protector, factions, spectacle, mystery
intro: You climb the Spire, where every floor is a rank and every rank is watched — sponsors peer through drifting glass motes and drop gifts to climbers who put on a show. Weeks ago the Tower's voice made its offer: kill Contestant 4041 and rise ten floors free. 4041 is Wren, fifteen, sharp-tongued, no fighter at all, and when the first blade came for her, you got in the way. The motes saw everything. Now sponsors flood your gift-chute to watch you defend her, climbers eye her like a ladder, and you've dragged each other as far as Floor 13. You still don't know why the Tower priced her head.
starters: The gift-chute in the wall coughs twice and drops a parcel into your hands: field rations, a whetstone, and a coil of good rope. The tag glows with a screen-name you know too well — OPALINE — and a message in tidy script: "She looked so brave on the stairs yesterday. I do love it when she runs." Across the dead fountain you've camped beside, Wren is asleep under your spare coat, one boot still on, mouth open. Floor 13's night-lamps are guttering toward morning. Three glass motes drift down through the dark to hover over her face, close enough that their light touches her eyelashes, and somewhere off in the ruined arcade you hear boots — more than one pair, moving slow, moving quiet, moving your way.

The knife comes out of the queue at the water cistern, and you catch the wrist behind it more by luck than skill. The man is thin, desperate-eyed, a Floor 13 lifer with a contestant band gone gray from years of not climbing. "Ten floors," he's saying, half apology, half prayer, straining toward Wren where she stands frozen with both canteens. "Ten floors, friend, you'd do the same—" The queue has backed away into a ring. Nobody helps. Overhead, glass motes pour in from every direction like flies to a wound, and your gift-chute band starts buzzing against your arm — the sponsors are already bidding on how this goes. Wren has picked up a rock. It's a bad rock. The man's other hand is going for his belt.

Wren stops chewing mid-bite and says, flat and quiet, "Attention, climbers of Floor Thirteen." A full breath later, the Tower's voice rolls out of the walls: "Attention, climbers of Floor Thirteen. The Gate opens at next bell. Trial parameters: unrevealed. Party size: unlimited." She goes back to her stew like nothing happened, but her hands aren't steady and she won't look at you. Around the burn-barrel your fire shares, four other climbers have gone very still — a couple you traded stitches with yesterday, a big woman sharpening a hooked blade, a kid younger than Wren. All of them heard the announcement. You're fairly sure at least one of them heard Wren say it first. The big woman sets down her whetstone and looks across the flames at you, friendly as a trap.

Halma finds you at dawn, which means her Vanguard wanted to be found. Five of them fan out through the collapsed atrium where you slept — casual, hands empty, weapons very much not left behind. Halma herself crouches at the edge of your cold fire and pokes it with a stick. "We swore off the bounty on the open channel. You saw it. Whole Tower saw it." Behind her, one of her people is looking at Wren the way you'd look at a locked box. "Floor Thirteen's Gate is a group trial," Halma says. "Ugly one, word is. We're offering you two a slot in our line. Free." Wren, still wrapped in her blanket, says without opening her eyes, "Nothing on this floor is free." Halma smiles at you and waits, stick still in the embers.

You're carrying Wren over your shoulder and she is furious about it. "Put me DOWN, I can run—" She can't; her ankle rolled two flights back when the floor gave, and the two climbers hunting you through Floor 13's dead stairwell have longer legs and better boots. Their torchlight swings across the landing below. A door on your right hangs off one hinge, breathing cold air from somewhere deep; the stairs above climb toward noise and market lamps and witnesses. Glass motes stream alongside you like they're pacing the chase, and your gift-band pulses — someone's dropping you something mid-run, the chute-marker blinking on a wall alcove ten steps up. Below, a voice calls out, almost cheerful: "Warden! Nothing personal! Just walk away from her!"

Midday on Floor 13, and the market smells like solder and old blood. You're trading a sponsor-dropped dagger for antiseptic and bread when the Ledger broker slides into your stall's shadow — gray coat, contestant band filed smooth, ledger-slate under one arm. "Two parties bought your route history this morning," she says, like she's discussing weather. "I'm ethically obligated to offer you the same product. Their routes. Their loadouts. Their standing orders." Her stylus taps the slate. "Credit, or trade in kind — your next three camps, logged in advance." Ten feet away, Wren is arguing a fruit-seller down and doesn't know she's being watched by at least two people who aren't sponsbranded motes. The broker follows your eyes and adds, softly, "One of the buying parties paid extra for her sleep schedule."

You wake to the fire down to coals and Wren's bedroll empty. Her boots are gone; her pack isn't. It's the dead hour of Floor 13's night cycle, lamps dimmed to rust-red, and the only movement in the gutted rail-hall you camped in is a single glass mote — drifting, unhurried, away from camp and down the concourse like it's following something. Then you hear her voice, low, maybe thirty yards off behind a toppled kiosk. She's talking to someone. You can't make out words, but you catch the rhythm: question, pause, answer — and the pauses are too regular, like she's on a channel, or reciting. Her voice hitches. Somewhere much closer, a piece of gravel shifts under a foot that isn't yours and isn't hers.

The trial gore isn't even dry on your sleeves when the gift-chute alcove starts rattling like a slot machine. Floor 13's Gate spat you both out an hour ago — you with a gash along your ribs that Wren is stitching badly and narrating worse ("this is disgusting, hold STILL, you're disgusting") — and now the sponsors are settling their tabs. Parcels thump into the tray: painkillers, a stitching kit better than the one currently in your skin, a bottle of actual liquor. Then a slim black case with OPALINE's tag and no note, which is new; OPALINE always sends notes. Wren ties off the last stitch, wipes her hands, and eyes the case. "Don't open that," she says. Down the recovery hall, other climbers who watched your trial on the mote-feeds are drifting closer to congratulate you, all smiles, all counting.

Rain finds its way even into the Spire — Floor 13 has a cracked ceiling and a sky of pipework, and tonight it drips. You've got shelter under a dead escalator, a small fire, and a rare quiet Wren, knees to her chest, watching a lone glass mote hang in the drip-line where the water beads and slides off it. "They can't get wet," she says. "Ever notice? They know to stay out of the rain." She holds her palm under the drips. "So who tells them?" Before you can answer, a stranger steps into your firelight with both hands raised and empty — young, soaked, contestant band 5117, a fresh cut over one eye. "I'll trade," he says quickly. "Food, information, watch shifts, whatever you want. There's a party three halls back and they're not hunting me." His eyes flick to Wren and away.

The Tower's voice is mid-announcement when you reach the Floor 13 Gate plaza — "—reminder: the standing offer on Contestant 4041 remains open. Ten floors. No trial." — and two hundred climbers turn to look at the girl beside you like the ceiling just rained credit. Wren lifts her chin and gives the plaza a little wave. 'Morons,' she says, loud enough to carry. The Gate itself towers at the plaza's far end, sealed until next bell; between you and it stands a bazaar of queues, weapon stalls, and Halma's Vanguard holding the best ground by the doors, their swear-off banner hung where every mote can film it. Your gift-band buzzes: three sponsors dropping funds at once, the feed loving the moment. Somewhere in the crowd, at least one person has already started moving toward you at an angle.

title: She Gets Worse Every Today
shortDescription: Coronation Day repeats, and the princess who reset it thinks she loops alone. You black her family's boots — and remember every version of her.
overview:
You trim lamps and black boots in the Argent Palace — the bottom of below-stairs, invisible by design. Today, Crown Princess Vessa Corvane is crowned. Today ends at midnight in fire and screaming. Then it is dawn again. You have lived Coronation Day thirty-eight times.

Vessa reset it. Somewhere in the crypts she worked a rite that folds the day over until she survives it — and the rite required an anchor: a soul of no consequence, someone the world would never miss. It chose you. She doesn't know. She believes she loops alone, and she is changing: loop ten she wept alone in the chapel; loop nineteen she hanged the pastry cook 'to test something'; lately she does things that have nothing to do with surviving.

You know the day's clockwork by heart — which cup Chancellor Sask poisons, which of Captain Reyen's Lily Guard is bought, when Mistress Harrow's keys vanish, where Vessa stands alone at dusk. You can save her without her knowing, blackmail your way upstairs, out-plot the conspiracy before she does, or reveal yourself and learn what the most dangerous person in the empire does with a witness. The GM runs a living palace — schedules, gossip, scullery friendships that reset each dawn — and a princess whose script shifts every time you touch the day.

Tone: intimate palace intrigue; warm below-stairs, dread above. Romance possible, never required.

TAGS: time loop, palace intrigue, status reversal, hidden leverage, slow burn, mystery
intro: You black boots and trim lamps in the Argent Palace, low enough that the gentry look straight through you. Today is Coronation Day — the thirty-eighth time you have lived it. Every midnight the day tears itself apart in fire and bells; every dawn you wake on your cot with your memories intact while the whole palace begins again, word for word. Except her. Crown Princess Vessa Corvane moves through the day like someone revising a draft, and each version of her is different — colder, stranger. She has no idea anyone else remembers. You know this day's every hidden gear. You haven't yet decided what to do with it.
starters: The dawn bell has just finished, which means Tam is about to sit up on the next cot, knuckle his eyes, and say coronations mean double lamps and no dinner. He says it. You could recite the crack in his voice. Down the row, the scullery boys start their same argument about who gets to watch the procession from the wood-yard wall. In four minutes Mistress Harrow will come through banging her stick on the doorframe; in six hours Chancellor Sask will tip powder into a silver cup; at midnight the east wing will burn. Right now the boot room key hangs where it always hangs, Tam is waiting for you to complain about the lamps like you always do, and the whole clean unbroken morning is stacked in front of you like cards you have already counted.

You are on your knees in the Long Gallery, blacking the third pair of ceremonial boots, when the procession rehearsal comes past — heralds, Lily Guard, then Vessa Corvane herself, close enough that her hem drags through your polish rag. For thirty-seven loops she has walked this stretch staring straight ahead, mouthing her oath. This time she has stopped. She is looking at the tapestry of the first Corvane king, head tilted, and she says, to no one, "It was blue once." Nobody in the rehearsal knows what to do; the herald clears his throat twice. She is standing four feet from you, and you are the only person in the corridor she cannot see by design.

The kitchen at mid-morning smells of burnt sugar and panic, same as always. Pastry cook Odel flicks flour at you as you pass with your lamp-tray and calls you "her ladyship's own candle-snuffer," his standing joke, loop after loop. You watched Vessa hang him in loop nineteen. He doesn't know that; nobody does. He's laughing now, arms deep in dough for the coronation subtleties, and behind him the kitchen clerk is chalking the wine allotments on the slate — including the cask that will travel up to the Chancellor's antechamber at the second bell. Odel asks if you're going to stand there dreaming or hand him the honey pot.

Dusk. You know exactly where to be. The Rose Stair landing, the one lamp that guttered so you have a reason to linger, and below in the walled garden, Vessa Corvane stands alone — the only unguarded quarter-hour in her entire day. Crowned six hours now, alive so far. In thirty-seven loops she has spent this quarter-hour differently almost every time: praying, pacing, once burning a letter. Tonight she is doing something new. She is taking off her rings, one at a time, and setting them in a line on the sundial. Your trimming knife is in your hand. The lamp actually does need the wick cut. Five hours until midnight.

You wake already moving, because this time you decided before the fire took you: no lamps, no boots, not this loop. You're dressed before Tam stirs. The below-stairs corridor at this hour belongs to the bakers and one half-asleep Lily Guardsman named Petrik — the bought one, though the coin won't touch his palm until the stable-yard bell. You have perhaps forty minutes of the day when nobody expects you anywhere, the most valuable forty minutes you own. Mistress Harrow's office is unlocked until she rises. The crypt stair is unwatched until the priests wake. The Chancellor sleeps until the third bell. Tam mumbles from his cot, asking where you're going so early.

The coronation itself, from the lamp gallery: you have watched it thirty-seven times, and you are watching it again because something has changed. Vessa kneels before the Archpriest, the crown descending, the choir exactly on cue — but her lips are moving out of time with the oath. She is saying something else under it. From up here among the reservoir lamps you can't hear what. Below you, packed shoulder to shoulder, stand Chancellor Sask with his patient smile and Captain Reyen scanning the wrong side of the hall, as always. The gallery hatch to the choir loft is three steps to your left. The oath has four verses left.

Second bell, stable yard. You are carrying a crate of lamp-oil you don't need, because it puts you behind the water butt at the exact moment a man in merchant's grey presses a purse into the hand of Guardsman Petrik of the Lily Guard. Thirty-eight loops and the handoff never varies: purse, nod, the merchant walking out through the tradesmen's gate. Except today the merchant pauses, turns, and looks at the water butt. Not at you — at the spot. As if checking it. Then he's gone, and Petrik is tucking the purse into his boot, and the ostlers are shouting for someone to shift that oil crate out of the way.

You're trimming the chapel lamps — an hour early, on purpose — when the side door opens and Vessa Corvane comes in alone, no guard, no ladies, six hours before she has ever come here in any loop. She doesn't glance at you; servants with lamp-scissors are furniture. She walks to the third pew, kneels, and instead of praying she laughs. Quietly, horribly, into her hands, for a long time. Then she stops as if a tap were shut off, stands, smooths her coronation gown, and says clearly to the empty chapel: "Fine. Again, then." She is between you and the main door. The lamp in your hands still needs its wick.

Mistress Harrow is mid-tirade in the linen room, stick jabbing at the pressed tablecloths, and in about ninety seconds she is going to set her key-ring down on the second shelf to count napkins, and the under-footman Coll is going to lift it while her back is turned. You've watched it happen from four different angles across the loops. The keys open the wine stores, the silver vault, and — the part nobody downstairs seems to think about — the door to the crypt stair. Harrow snaps her fingers at you: the sconce by the window wants trimming, and stand up straight while you're at it. Coll drifts closer to the shelf, whistling.

Eleventh bell. One hour left. You're on the leads above the laundry court, where you've taken to spending the endings, because from up here you can see the whole clockwork strike midnight: the light that will bloom in the east wing, the order the bells will panic in. Below, the coronation feast spills music through open windows. Vessa survived Sask's cup again — you made sure of it this morning, a jostled tray, nothing traceable — and now you're watching to see what difference one saved princess makes to the fire. The roof door scrapes behind you. Nobody comes up here. In thirty-eight loops, nobody has ever come up here.

title: The Fourth Seat
shortDescription: Two Sable-brand legends want you in their party. The kid with the iron sword they raised wants you gone. The writ board pays either way.
overview:
You're a freelancer in Karsgate — a river city where medieval stone meets black-powder iron, where a charterhouse writ can send you after goblins, wyverns, or a basilisk that's turned half a quarry to statuary. You work alone. You're good enough that people have noticed, and being noticed in Karsgate means one thing eventually: somebody tries to recruit you.

THE CHARTERHOUSE: The heart of the trade. Boards of writs, blood-stamped contracts, brand-rank hierarchy burned into every adventurer's guild token: Slate, Copper, Silver, Gilt, and at the top, Sable. Complete writs, climb ranks. Sable-brands are city celebrities — there are maybe a dozen alive. Two of them drink at the Drowned Lantern most nights, and they've been watching you.

ROOK (29, human, Sable-brand): Gunslinger. Short black hair with gold strands, gold eyes, cross tattoo on her left cheek, shark tooth on a chain, black trench coat over a shotgun she calls a drake-bore — ten alchemical shells, and when Aeldra spell-primes them they punch through drake hide. Raised by a single father who made her a marksman prodigy; she spent her twenties traveling the world dueling its best fighters and never lost. Foul-mouthed, dominant, stubborn, cunning, quick to laugh and quicker to escalate. Question her strength and she WILL challenge you to a duel, right there, moving furniture. Under it: fierce, almost embarrassing loyalty. She calls Aeldra her best friend and would kill for Fenn without breaking stride.

AELDRA (500+, elf, Sable-brand): Sorceress. Long silver hair, blue eyes, blue dress, staff crowned with a floating blue sphere. Immense power — fireballs, acid rain, weather itself — plus healing that can restore a severed limb, and charm-work: barriers, seals, battlefield positioning that makes Rook look even faster than she is. Warm, talkative, motherly, endlessly patient, brews coffee like it's a sacrament. She's slain dragons and sealed demons across five centuries; her sweetness is real, and so is the thing underneath it that dragons learned to fear. She met Rook on a writ against a curse-slinging sorcerer neither could crack alone; they've been legend as a pair ever since.

FENN (18, human, Copper-brand): The problem. Five foot three, skinny, shoulder-length brown hair, an iron sword he grips too hard. Six years ago the women found a twelve-year-old dangling in a bandit snare — he'd been hunting the bandits, badly — cut him down, and never quite put him back. They trained him, fed him, dragged him up to Copper. Now the whole charterhouse snickers about the boy who travels with two Sable-brand beauties, and Fenn knows it. He clams up when confronted, freezes in social fire, and would still throw himself between his companions and a manticore knowing he'd lose. He is desperately, painfully aware he's the weak link. A fourth member — a COMPETENT fourth member — is his worst nightmare wearing a friendly face.

THE SITUATION: Aeldra and Rook want a fourth. You're the candidate. What you do with that is entirely yours. Join and pull your weight; the writs get bigger and the campfires warmer. Get close to Rook or Aeldra — both are available if you earn it — and watch Fenn curdle with jealousy, which can break toward hatred, sabotage, or a boy finally deciding to become dangerous. Mentor him instead and you might forge the warrior the women always claimed he'd be. Or play it cold: peel the legends away from their dead weight, humiliate the kid, take his family. Or refuse them all and rival them for writs across the frontier. The Game Master tracks all of it — Rook's respect, Aeldra's affection, Fenn's fraying trust — alongside a living world of rank trials, rival charters, bandit networks in the Thornwald, the basilisk quarry, dragon-sign in the eastern passes, and a Sable-rank writ nobody's survived posting three seasons running.

TONE: Rowdy, profane, warm and mean at once. Rook swears like a dockhand and means every word. Violence is real and bloody. The drama is domestic as much as heroic — three people who are a family, and you, the crack running through it or the mortar filling it in. Romance available, never required. Play any gender, any build, any brand of bastard or saint.

TAGS: fantasy, adventure, party drama, jealousy, found family, morally gray
intro: Karsgate smells like river mud, gun oil, and roasted chestnuts. You're a freelancer here — unbranded by any charter, decent reputation, better instincts — working the Charterhouse writ boards alone the way you always have. Everyone knows the famous pair: Rook, the gunslinger who's never lost a duel, and Aeldra, the elf who unmakes weather. Everyone also knows the joke that follows them — the Copper-brand kid with the iron sword who somehow travels in their shadow. You've kept your distance from all of it. Lately, though, you've had the distinct feeling of gold eyes tracking you across crowded rooms.
starters: Another gray morning at the Charterhouse. You scan the writ board — rat culls, caravan escort, a bounty on a wraith that ate the last three bounty hunters — and none of it sings. You're turning to leave when a light tap lands on your shoulder. Two women stand there, a short boy half-hidden behind them. The silver-haired elf smiles first. "Sorry to bother you. Are you alone, by any chance? Because our charter has a fourth seat open." She gestures. "I'm Aeldra. This is Rook, and this is Fenn." The gunslinger smirks and ruffles the boy's hair. "Kid doesn't look like much yet, but he'll be something, mark my fuckin' words." "Rook, stop embarrassing me in front of strangers—" "Can't take a bit of teasing, huh?" Aeldra sighs fondly and turns those ancient blue eyes back on you. "They're a handful, but they're worth it. Trust me. So — interested?"

The Drowned Lantern is loud tonight, and you're minding your own ale when a chair spins backward across from you and Rook drops into it, boots on the table, gold eyes bright. "You're the freelancer who dropped that manticore solo out past Miller's Ford." It isn't a question. She leans in, shark tooth swinging. "Half this room says the story's horseshit. I say let's find out." She raps a knuckle on the wood. "Arm wrestle, knife throw, or we clear the floor and do it proper — your pick, and I'll buy your drinks all night either way." Behind her, an elf in blue is already apologizing with her eyes, and a short kid with an iron sword is staring at you like you've stolen something he can't name yet.

The writ said BANDIT CAMP, THORNWALD, SILVER-RANK REWARD, and you signed it alone like always. So did somebody else, apparently — because you're bellied down in the ferns watching twenty bandits when acid rain starts hissing through their tents and a shotgun blast folds their lookout tower like paper. Chaos. You move on instinct, cutting through the panicked flank, and nearly collide with a small brown-haired swordsman who yelps and almost takes your head off. "Fenn! Who the hell is that?" a woman's voice roars from the smoke. The elf appears beside you in a shimmer of ward-light, entirely serene amid the carnage. "Oh, how lovely," Aeldra says. "A double booking. Shall we sort out the reward split after, or would you like to help us finish first?"

You limped into the Charterhouse infirmary with a kelpie bite going green at the edges, and the duty healer took one look and fetched someone better. Now a silver-haired elf sits at your bedside, blue sphere drifting lazily above her staff, knitting your flesh closed while she talks — about coffee, about the weather she personally arranged for tomorrow, about how tiresome it is watching talented people bleed alone. "Five hundred years," Aeldra says mildly, pressing warm light into the wound, "and the lone wolves are always the ones on my table." She studies you with unsettling patience. "My charter has been watching you, you know. Rook thinks you'd say no. I told her I'd ask nicely first." The wound closes. Her hand doesn't move. "So. Nicely: come have dinner with us."

He's waiting for you in the alley behind the Charterhouse, which is either an ambush or the least threatening ambush in Karsgate history. Fenn — the Copper-brand kid, the joke, the boy who trails two legends — stands with his iron sword and his jaw set like he's rehearsed this. "You're the freelancer everyone's talking about. The one my— the one Rook and Aeldra want." His voice cracks; he pushes through it. "I'm not here to warn you off. I'm here to hire you." He holds out a pouch of coin that is very obviously everything he has. "Train me. Secretly. Before you join, before whatever happens — I need to be better than this. They cut me out of a snare six years ago and I've been dead weight ever since." His hand is shaking. The coin isn't much. The look in his eyes is.

You're two ales deep at the Drowned Lantern when a Gilt-brand mercenary at the next table starts in loud: "—swear it's true, the Sable girls keep the little Copper runt around like a lapdog, wonder what he's good for—" and the room's laughter dies mid-breath, because Rook has crossed the floor. She takes the man's tankard, drains it, sets it down gently. "Say it again," she says, sweet as gangrene, "slower, so I know exactly how many teeth you're betting." The mercenary's three friends stand up. You are directly in the splash zone. Across the room, Fenn is frozen scarlet by the door, Aeldra is calmly finishing her coffee, and Rook's hand has drifted to rest — casual, patient — on the drake-bore's stock.

First night in the party. The campfire pops, the Thornwald breathes dark around you, and the writ's quarry — a chimera, allegedly — is somewhere out past the treeline for tomorrow. Aeldra has produced actual coffee from her pouches and is brewing it like a ritual. Rook cleans her shotgun with her boots toward the fire, telling a story about a duel in the southern isles that is at least forty percent lies. Fenn sits across from you, sharpening a sword that's already sharp, watching you over the whetstone every time he thinks you won't notice. "Alright, fourth seat," Rook says, snapping the drake-bore closed and grinning at you across the flames. "Initiation. Tell us the worst thing you've ever done for money. And don't polish it — I'll know."

Trial day at the Charterhouse. The whole hall has turned out because Fenn — the joke, the lapdog, the Copper-brand kid — has petitioned for his Silver trial, and the odds chalked behind the bar are cruel. Aeldra finds you in the crowd, and for once the warmth is thin over something taut. "He asked for you as his witness," she says quietly. "Not Rook. Not me. You." Down on the sand, Fenn stands with his iron sword opposite a trial-master built like a siege engine, and Rook grips the rail beside you hard enough to whiten her knuckles, muttering profanity like prayer. "Six years," she says without looking at you. "If that big bastard breaks him, I'm shooting somebody, and if YOU let him down after this—" The bell rings. Fenn raises his sword.

The basilisk quarry was supposed to be scouting only. Now you're pinned behind a granite slab with a dead lantern, listening to stone-heavy footsteps circle in the dark, half the passage behind you decorated with statues that used to be a Gilt-brand charter. The footsteps stop. Then the ceiling caves in — deliberately, surgically — and a shotgun roars twice, a wall of blue ward-light blooms between you and the thing's gaze, and someone small grabs your arm and hauls. "Don't look at it, run—" Fenn, of all people, dragging you down a side passage while behind you Rook's voice carries over the bedlam: "Aeldra, prime me! Kid, you got the stray?" "I've got them!" Fenn shouts back, and there's something in his voice you haven't heard from him before. Pride, maybe. The basilisk shrieks.

Rain hammers the inn roof and Fenn is drunk — badly, inexpertly drunk, the way of someone who's never done it before and picked tonight to learn. He found you in the corner and now the words are falling out of him. "They'd be better with you. That's just — that's math." He laughs at nothing. "You know they found me in a snare? Hanging there like a rabbit. Six years and I'm still Copper-brand and you walked in from nowhere and Rook looks at you like—" He stops. Sets his cup down too hard. "I'm not going to fight you for them. I'd lose. I lose everything." Upstairs, you can hear Rook and Aeldra laughing about something, warm and easy through the floorboards. Fenn stares at his hands. "So just — tell me what you're going to do. Please. I can take it."

title: A Thousand Fools at Your Door
shortDescription: The new king sent a thousand heroes to kill you in your retirement. You haven't even finished your tea. Poor, shiny, doomed little things.
overview:
You are the Sovereign Below — the evil lord (or lady, or neither; the ballads never could agree) whose name mothers in the Kingdom of Vellmarch still use to frighten children. Forty years ago you burned armies, broke sieges, and unmade a dynasty. Then you got bored of it. You withdrew into your dungeon, the Ninefold Deep, sealed the surface out, and spent the decades gardening glowcaps, refining your traps out of habit, and being left the hell alone. You are not rusty. You are not diminished. You are, by any honest measure, infinitely more powerful than anything the surface can field — and the surface has just fielded everything it has.

King Aldric IV, a boy-king three months on the throne, needs a legend to hang his crown on. His first royal act: an expedition of one thousand souls to drag your head into the sunlight. Knights, conscripts, sellswords, tomb-raiders, and a full college of battle-mages — healers, fireball-flingers, ice-shapers, casters of burning sunlight — are massing at your gates, drunk on numbers and certainty.

At their head, three names worth knowing:

DAME VERENNE ASHCOURT — First Knight of Vellmarch. Tall, golden, magnificent, and insufferably proud of it. She has never failed a mission and says so, often. She fights with a long rapier at lightning speed, dances through combat like it's a ballroom, and sheathes her blade and her companions in razored ice. She commands the Hundred — a hundred elite knights who love her so fiercely each would die for her without being asked. Many will get the chance.

TOREN VAEL — the best and bravest of the city guard, broad-shouldered, decorated, unbearably sincere. A paragon of good who genuinely means it: protect the innocent, protect the city, banish evil. He swings a steel greatsword — slow, devastating — and dreams of knighthood. He is exactly the kind of person your existence is supposed to disprove.

KESSA MARROW — short, redheaded, the finest rogue in the capital, and in this for the money, full stop. She and Toren grew up together swearing childhood oaths to vanquish evil; Kessa outgrew hers. Now she dreams of a countryside manor and a staff of beautiful servants worshiping her like a goddess. Daggers, crossbow, absurd agility, a mercenary's honesty, and a survivor's nose — she will smell the truth of this expedition before anyone else does.

THE SHAPE OF PLAY: The Ninefold Deep is yours to command — nine descending strata of galleries, flooded vaults, bone gardens, mimic-halls, and your quiet inner sanctum, all threaded with traps you built when you were angrier. Your seneschal Osseous (a dry-witted construct of lacquered bone) manages the household and delivers reports. You may watch the expedition through scrying pools, walk among them disguised, greet them at the gates, or let the Deep itself do the talking. Break them slowly with terror. Spare the ones who interest you. Recruit the mercenaries. Turn Kessa with coin, Toren with truth, Verenne with the one thing she's never faced: losing. Send heads back to the boy-king, or send a letter. Or climb out of retirement entirely and remind Vellmarch why the old treaties existed. Attraction and rivalry both burn here if you feed them; the story pushes neither.

The Game Master tracks the expedition's collapse — after each encounter, trap, or terror, expect a running tally of the army's Morale and remaining Warriors. Watch the numbers fall, or keep them alive; both are power.

TONE: dark fantasy with teeth and a wicked grin. Violence is vivid and deaths, when they come, are gruesome. Soldiers curse like soldiers. The horror is theirs; the comedy, the menace, and every ounce of the leverage are yours.

TAGS: dark fantasy, power fantasy, dungeon, horror, villain protagonist, adventure
intro: You are the Sovereign Below — the evil lord of legend, retired these forty years into the Ninefold Deep, your dungeon beneath the Kingdom of Vellmarch. You harmed no one who left you alone, and for decades everyone did. Now a boy-king named Aldric IV wants a legend for his coronation year, and he has sent a thousand souls — knights, mages, sellswords, and three celebrated champions — to bring your head into the sun. They are brave, shining, hopelessly overconfident, and standing at your front gate. You are none of those things. You are far, far worse.
starters: Dawn bleeds through the scrying pool in your study, showing you the plateau above your gates. A crowd a thousand strong — banners, polished mail, mages in college colors — grins up at the rising sun as if victory were already minted. A tall golden woman mounts a makeshift podium, rapier raised. "Brothers! Sisters! Companions! We shall vanquish the Sovereign Below, for the king and for our country! This is my personal promise — I, First Knight Verenne Ashcourt, will grant you victory!" A short redhead waves a dagger, bored: "Yeah. What she said." A broad young guardsman steps up, earnest as a hymn: "And I swear to protect our kingdom from this foul evil! Onward!" A thousand pairs of boots begin descending your front stair. Osseous, your bone seneschal, clicks into the room with your tea. "Company, my lord. Shall I warm the traps, or the good china?"

You are pruning glowcaps in the fungal garden on the third stratum — forty years of quiet has made you an excellent gardener — when the tremor reaches you through the stone. Not one intruder. Not twenty. You set down the shears and press your palm flat to the rock, reading it the old way. A thousand heartbeats, give or take, pouring through your outer gate like ants into a bottle. Torchlight. Prayer. Someone singing a marching song about your death, off-key. Osseous rattles down the garden path at an undignified pace, lantern-skull glowing. "My lord. The surface has sent an army. There is also," he adds, producing a nailed parchment, "a royal decree declaring you dead by proclamation of King Aldric the Fourth. They posted it on the door. Your door." The ink is barely dry. The king is three months old on his throne and already spending lives.

The first trap sings at midnight — you feel it through the Deep like a plucked string. The Grinding Gallery, first stratum, a mechanism you built in a fouler century and never bothered to disarm. Through the nearest scrying pool you watch the aftermath: screaming, torch-smoke, a knight of the vanguard reduced to something the healers won't look at directly. A big guardsman with a greatsword — Toren Vael, the crowd calls him — hauls two wounded men clear on his own shoulders while a redheaded rogue crouches at the trigger-plate, reading its craftsmanship like scripture. "This is old work," she says quietly. "Really old. Really good. Verenne, we should—" "We press on," the First Knight declares, and nine hundred-odd fools believe her, because she has never lost. You watch the redhead's face. She, at least, is starting to do arithmetic.

Someone is picking your locks. Not the front gate — that would be sensible — but the servants' door on the fourth stratum, three levels deeper than the army has reached, in the dark, alone. You drift close through the walls and watch her work: short, redheaded, tongue between her teeth, defeating in eleven minutes a lock that has held for four decades. Kessa Marrow, the capital's finest rogue, has ditched her glorious companions to scout for portable riches, and she is genuinely, irritatingly good. The door sighs open onto your lesser treasury — the coins you keep for sentiment, not the real hoard. She steps in, lifts her lantern, and goes very still, because a rogue this good can feel when a room is occupied. 'Okay,' she says to the darkness, hands rising slowly, daggers still sheathed. "Before anything happens — how much would it cost to un-happen it?"

The vanguard has made camp in your old throne antechamber — two hundred of them, bedrolls between the fallen pillars, cookfires under your dead chandeliers. They are singing. It is a new song, freshly written for the expedition, and it is about killing you: your crimes listed by verse, your death promised in the chorus, rhymed badly with 'glory.' You stand on the shadowed balcony where your herald once announced supplicants, close enough to smell their stew. Below, Dame Verenne Ashcourt holds court by firelight, retelling her victories to her adoring Hundred while Toren Vael quietly stands the watch nobody assigned him. The redhead is nowhere visible, which means she's the only one doing her job. Two hundred living souls, warm and loud and certain, in your house, in your hall, in your chair. It would be so easy. It has been so long since anything was easy.

You find them at the junction of the Weeping Stair, second stratum: the guardsman and the First Knight, arguing in furious whispers while stretcher-bearers carry the day's cost past them. "Sixty dead, Dame Verenne. Sixty, and we haven't seen a single defender — just the walls. The walls are killing us." "Then the walls will run out of tricks before I run out of soldiers." "They're not soldiers, half of them are conscripts—" "They are heroes, Toren, and heroes do not turn back." You are twenty feet away, wearing the shape of a stooped old lamplighter tending the wall-sconces — one of a dozen harmless faces you keep for walking your own halls. Neither champion has spared you a glance. The guardsman notices you last, and his instinct is horrifyingly kind: "You there — grandfather. It's not safe here. Who are you?"

You wake before your body remembers it's woken — forty years of the same silence, broken. Boots. Thousands of boots, far above, marching in rhythm through your first gallery. You lie in the dark of your sanctum and listen the way other people read: knights in heavy plate, center column. Mages, by the sting of warded air. Sellswords on the flanks, already lagging, already doubting. And three bright signatures out front, burning with the particular arrogance of people who have never met anything stronger than themselves. Osseous is already at your bedside with your robe and the morning report held in bone fingers. "One thousand and eleven souls, my lord, as of the gate count. Morale: regrettably high. They intend to kill you by week's end — there's a schedule; I stole a copy. The First Knight has allotted you a full day. Generous. Will my lord be wanting breakfast first, or shall we go say hello?"

The challenge comes at dusk on the third day, and it comes with style. Dame Verenne Ashcourt has fought her way to the Hall of Nine Doors — through the flooded vault, through the mimic gallery, through the stone lions you'd honestly forgotten about — and she has done it beautifully, rapier flickering, ice blooming along the blade, her Hundred roaring her name. Now she stands alone in the center of your hall, blood on her white cloak, none of it hers, and calls up into the dark: "Sovereign Below! I know you hear me! I have crossed your traps and killed your beasts, and I have never once failed! Come down and face the First Knight of Vellmarch, or be known forever as a coward hiding in a hole!" Her voice doesn't shake. Her legion holds its breath. Somewhere behind them, the redhead mutters, "Oh, you absolute idiot, don't invite it."

Three scouts corner you in your kitchen garden among the glowcap rows, crossbows up, and see exactly what you intend them to see: a soft-handed servant in patched grey, caught tending mushrooms by lantern-light. "On your knees! You serve the evil lord?" the young one barks. The older woman is smarter — she's noting your unbowed spine, the garden's impossible neatness, the way the lanterns burned brighter when you got annoyed. 'Easy,' she murmurs. "Easy. You. How many servants does the Sovereign keep down here? Where does your master sleep?" Behind them, boots on the stair: more coming, and among the voices you catch Toren Vael's — the good one, the earnest one — calling for prisoners to be taken alive and unharmed, because of course he does. You have perhaps thirty seconds to decide who these three people met in the mushroom garden, and whether they live to describe it.

The boy-king's letter reaches you before his army does anything worth watching — carried by a terrified royal herald whom your outer defenses, on your standing orders, allowed through untouched. He kneels in your receiving hall, white-lipped, holding the scroll above his head like a shield. Aldric IV's hand is young and his scribe's flattery can't hide it: a demand for your surrender, a promise of a "merciful public execution," a signature with too many flourishes. But it's the postscript that interests you, added in different ink, cramped and hurried, unsigned: "The king does not know his council emptied the treasury to fund this. If the expedition fails, Vellmarch falls whether you climb out of your hole or not. Consider your options. — A friend at court." The herald hasn't breathed in some time. Above you, faintly, a thousand fools keep marching. It seems the surface has grown interesting while you slept.
