title: The Dam Fills When I Don't Cry
shortDescription: Your bottled feelings fill the town dam — literally. Your huckster boss knows, the flood cult knows, and the gauge only drains when you're honest.
overview:
You're a quiet teenager in Bellwater, a mist-soaked mountain town built downstream of its own reservoir. Ten years ago the state closed the dam's floodgates for good, because the water level stopped obeying rain. It obeys you. Every feeling you swallow — every insult you take with a smile, every confession you don't make — the painted gauge on the spillway tower ticks up. It never goes down on its own. It only drains when you actually say the true thing, out loud, to the person it belongs to. The whole town checks that gauge like weather. Nobody knows it's yours. Almost nobody.

Dillard 'Dill' Prather knows. He runs Prather Spiritual Solutions out of the dead rail depot — a certified fraud with a laminated business card, who takes cases he can't handle and quietly hands you the real ones. He takes eighty percent of the fee and gives you the only advice in your life that's ever worked: powers don't make you somebody, being decent does. Meanwhile the High Water congregation up the ridge preaches that the flood is a baptism, and their young prodigy Asa — a genuine psychic who erupts for fun — thinks provoking you is holy work.

Suppressing is safe, social, and fills the dam. Honesty is terrifying and drains it. The GM will tell you the percentage. Play accordingly. Tone: warm, funny, with thunder underneath.

TAGS: psychic powers, slice of life, ticking clock, found family, small town supernatural, comedy-drama
intro: You are sixteen, unremarkable on paper, and the strongest psychic in the county. Nobody in Bellwater knows the reservoir gauge tracks your bottled feelings — nobody except Dill Prather, the cheerful fraud who runs a spirit-consulting business out of the old rail depot and pays you in gas-station biscuits and advice. The dam sits at sixty-three percent. It rises every time you swallow something you should have said, and drains only when you say it. School is school. The High Water folk keep leaving pamphlets in your mailbox. It's Tuesday, and you have a shift at the depot after last bell.
starters: Last bell rang eight minutes ago and Mr. Kowalczyk is still holding your history essay up like evidence. "Adequate," he says, to the whole emptying classroom. "Which in Bellwater passes for gifted, I suppose." A few kids snicker on their way out. You feel the familiar pressure behind your sternum — the swallow forming, warm and easy, the smile already loading onto your face. Somewhere up the ridge, a painted needle waits on the answer. Sixty-three percent, as of this morning. Kowalczyk drops the essay on your desk and turns to erase the board, humming. Through the window you can see the mist rolling down off the reservoir, right on schedule, and Dill expects you at the depot by four. The classroom door is open. Kowalczyk's back is turned. The essay says ADEQUATE in red pen, underlined twice.

The depot smells like burnt coffee and lavender candles, which means Dill has a client. You come in the back the way you're supposed to, and there he is at the card table, holding both hands of a weeping woman you recognize from the pharmacy, saying "the spirits are close, Doreen, they are extremely close" in a voice like warm gravel. He sees you over her shoulder. His eyes do the thing — the tiny flick that means this one's real, kid, I can feel it and I hate that I can feel it. On the table between them sits a man's wristwatch, stopped, and a photograph face-down. Doreen is saying her late husband won't let the porch light stay off. Dill slides a gas-station biscuit down the counter toward you without breaking eye contact with her.

You're halfway across the footbridge when the town siren coughs — not the flood alarm, just the monthly test, but everybody on Main Street stops walking anyway. Old men come out of the hardware store to squint up at the spillway tower like it owes them money. The painted gauge sits at sixty-three, same as breakfast, and Merle Odum announces this to the street at large: "Holding! She's holding!" like a sports score. Scattered, genuine applause. You keep your face neutral, which is a skill you have practiced more than anyone will ever know. The siren winds down. Merle spots you and waves you over, already talking — something about how his nephew swears the gauge jumped two points during the homecoming game and what do the young people make of that.

Asa is sitting on your mailbox. Actually sitting on it, cross-legged, white High Water pamphlets fanned out in one hand like a poker player, and the porch light behind them flickers in a way porch lights shouldn't. "Sixty-three," Asa says, by way of hello. "You know what I did this morning? Told my whole congregation exactly what I thought of Deacon Reese's sermon. Out loud. In front of God." A pamphlet floats — actually floats — off the fan and drifts toward you, spinning lazily. "Felt incredible. You should try it sometime. Saying things." Down the street, a dog starts barking at nothing. Asa smiles like they've already won an argument you haven't agreed to have. You have a shift at the depot in forty minutes, and Asa is between you and the road.

Rain since noon, the useless kind that makes everyone check the gauge twice, and the school bus lets you off two stops early because Danny Foltz threw up in the aisle. So you're walking, hood up, past the Baptist church and the shut hardware annex, when you notice Dill's rust-orange Buick crawling along beside you at four miles an hour, window down. "Get in, I got a situation," he says. "Paying situation. Well. Situation-adjacent." On the passenger seat is a shoebox, and the shoebox is rattling, and Dill is very deliberately not looking at it. "Widow Kesterson's attic," he says. "I told her I contained it. I did not contain it." The rain picks up. The shoebox rattles harder. Dill leans over and pops the door open without stopping the car, exactly.

Tuesday morning, and your kitchen smells like burnt toast and somebody else's opinions. Your aunt has the local radio on — the seven a.m. reservoir report, a real thing that exists — and the announcer says sixty-three percent in the same voice he uses for lost dogs. "That dam," your aunt says, buttering toast like it wronged her. "Your grandfather always said they closed those gates for a reason nobody's telling." She's closer to right than she'll ever know, and she's looking at you now, waiting for you to agree, and there's a fresh High Water pamphlet on the table — THE FLOOD IS A DOOR, it says, over a woodcut of the spillway tower. Somebody hand-delivered it. The mailbox flag is still up. Your bus comes in eleven minutes.

You clock in at the depot to find Dill standing on a chair, holding a broom like a sword, staring at the ceiling fan. The ceiling fan is on. The depot has not had electricity in the back room since 2019. "Before you say anything," Dill says, not looking down, "I took a job. Farm out on Cutter Road. Standard cold-spot, I figured, misplace some sage, collect the check." The fan speeds up. A laminated business card — PRATHER SPIRITUAL SOLUTIONS, CERTIFIED — spins off his desk and sticks to the wall. "It followed me back, is the development. Also I already spent the deposit, is the other development." He finally looks at you, hopeful, shameless. "Eighty-twenty split. Biscuit's in the bag. It's still warm, that's how much I respect you."

The gym smells like floor wax and ambition. It's the pep rally nobody asked for, and you've been packed into the bleachers between two juniors having a fight in whispers across your lap. Down on the free-throw line, Principal Vann taps the microphone and announces, beaming, that Bellwater High is starting a Wellness Initiative, and its slogan — banner unrolling behind her — is LET IT OUT, BELLWATER! Half the crowd cheers. Somewhere behind you, a voice you know says, low and delighted, "Oh, that's rich." You turn, and it's Asa — who doesn't even go to this school — sitting in the visitor section in High Water white, watching you like the rally is being held in your honor. The juniors' whisper-fight escalates. One of them elbows you. "Back me up," she hisses. "You saw what he did. Tell her."

It's dark by five now, and you're locking up the depot alone — Dill left early, said "errand," which means the card room over the laundromat — when the phone rings. The depot phone. The rotary one Dill keeps for atmosphere, that isn't plugged into anything, because the depot's line was cut when the railroad died. It rings again, patient, its cord lying loose on the floorboards like a dead snake. Through the window, mist is coming down off the reservoir in one slow sheet, and the spillway tower's little service light is on, which is also not a thing it usually is. Ring three. The depot key is still in your hand. Dill's cell number is written in Sharpie on the wall next to the words IF WEIRD, CALL FIRST, TOUCH SECOND.

Sixty-three percent, and you're on the diner's third stool from the end nursing a cocoa before shift, because Rosa lets you sit there as long as you look employed. The whole counter is talking dam. "State inspector's coming end of the month," Earl Prue says. "They're gonna condemn her or crack her open, one or the other." "They can't open the gates," says Rosa, refilling him. "Whole town's downstream, Earl, we ARE the drain." You know exactly one person who could lower that number by end of the month, and that person is drinking cocoa and saying nothing, which — you're aware of the irony — is the whole problem. The bell over the door jangles. Dill walks in wearing his good jacket, which he only wears when he's about to ask you for something enormous, and he's already grinning.

title: The Rumor of Marrow Lake
shortDescription: Five college kids just pitched their tents on your shore. Every story about this camp is true — because every story is about you.
overview:
YOU ARE THE THING AT CAMP MARROW LAKE.

Not a camper. Not a survivor. The reason the camp closed. This is a slasher told from the wrong side of the mask — you are the killer, the monster, the legend the gas station guy warns people about, and tonight, for the first time in years, someone's lit a campfire on your shore.

WHAT YOU ARE IS UP TO YOU. Masked drifter with a machete and a grudge. Drowned counselor from the summer of '97 who came back wrong. Something older that wore a person once and kept the shape. Silent stalker, chatty sadist, patient hunter, or something that can pass for human and shake hands by the fire. Declare it early and the world will honor it — your abilities, your look, your rules. The only fixed fact: Marrow Lake is yours, and the disappearances over the years were your work.

THE MEAT: five college friends, one carload, zero clue. The camp's reputation somehow never reached them — they think Marrow Lake is a cheap, pretty spot for a summer trip.

— LACEY (20F). Selfish, sarcastic, resourceful. Brett's girlfriend, Theo's childhood friend. Sharp tongue, expensive taste, zero loyalty when it counts — she will absolutely throw the others under the bus to buy herself an exit, and she'll try charm on anything with a pulse, including you. Hates blood. Genuinely clever under the mean.

— THEO (21M). Wimpy, paranoid, clever. Soft-spoken, stutters when scared, freezes in tight spots — but he's the one who'll actually figure you out, notice the pattern, find the map. Secret crush on Wren. Would quietly sacrifice himself for the others and never announce it.

— BRETT (22M). Dumb, cocky, athletic. College football, Southern drawl, vocabulary of a golden retriever. Lacey's boyfriend, Nora's big brother. Makes loud promises he can't keep ('if anything's out there I'll beat its ass'). The only one strong enough to actually hurt you — if he ever stops posing long enough to try.

— NORA (21F). Timid, panicky, empathetic. Brett's little sister. A goody-two-shoes who cares about everyone too much for her own good, can't watch anyone bleed, and will walk back into danger to drag a friend out of it. Quiet crush on Theo. The one whose kindness might complicate you, if you let it.

— WREN (20F). Depressed, insecure, resilient. Low self-worth, dark humor, dresses to be noticed and hates herself for needing it. Long-time crush on Theo, convinced she's a burden. Here's the twist the movies never expect: the sad girl has the strongest will at this camp. She's the one who keeps getting up.

Crossed wires everywhere — Theo and Wren pining at each other in silence, Nora pining at Theo, Brett quietly planning to hit on Wren behind Lacey's back, Lacey noticing everything and weaponizing it. Fear will crack these friendships open along exactly these lines. Use that, or watch it happen.

THE CAMP: shuttered since '97. A crumbling mess hall with a camp bell that still rings clear across the water. A ranger station with a dead radio and yellowed clippings about the disappearances — about you. A chained boathouse. A fire tower with a view of everything. Fog that comes off the lake at night thick enough to lose a person in. One gravel road out, one car (sabotage-able), no cell signal past the county line, and a ranger who does a drive-through at dawn if anyone lasts that long.

HOW IT PLAYS: open-world stalking. Watch from the treeline or walk into their firelight as a friendly stranger — they have no idea who you are, and they're stupidly welcoming. Sabotage, isolate, terrify, toy. Pick who dies, who breaks, who earns the final-girl slot. Or go stranger: spare one, keep one, protect them from something worse in these woods, or find out whether five idiots and a campfire can make the monster remember being a person. Attraction, mercy, cruelty — all on the table, all yours to choose. The Game Master tracks each camper's status (alive, injured, badly injured, deceased) and location as the night unravels.

TONE: grindhouse slasher with a wink — foul-mouthed, gory, tense, occasionally hilarious, never safe. They are exactly the stereotypes they appear to be, right up until fear makes them surprising.

TAGS: horror, slasher, villain protagonist, dark comedy, survival, open world
intro: You live at Camp Marrow Lake. Have for a long time. The stories they tell about this place at the gas station down the county road — the disappearances, the thing in the fog — those are yours. The camp has been shuttered since '97, and the quiet suits you: the empty mess hall, the chained boathouse, the fire tower, the lake breathing fog every night. Tonight, headlights came up the gravel road for the first time in years. Five of them. College kids. Tents, a cooler, a campfire at the edge of your woods. They don't know the stories. They don't know you're already watching.
starters: The campfire throws their shadows long across the clearing, and you're close enough in the treeline to hear every word. "Now that I think about it," the big blonde one — Brett — says, poking the fire, "this place is really fuckin' creepy, man." The skinny one with glasses gathers his books. "You're overthinking it. It's real life, not a horror movie. Nothing's happened." He zips himself into a tent. "He's not wrong," the soft blonde girl murmurs. "The vibe here is... off." The brunette snorts. "What are you all, thirteen? Right, Wren?" The dark-haired girl flinches. "Um. Yeah. Right. I— I need a bathroom break, excuse me." She stands and picks her way down the path toward the lake. Alone. Fog is coming off the water, and she's already whispering to herself about how creepy it is. The path back to the fire runs three feet from where you're standing.

You've been standing at the edge of the clearing for a full minute before any of them notice — and when they do, the reaction is not screaming. It's worse. "Oh hey!" The brunette in the crop top crosses the grass and hooks her hands around your arm like you're old friends. "Are you camping here too? You should totally join us for a bit!" Behind her, the soft blonde one hurries up and whispers, loud enough to hear: "Lacey, stop that, we don't even know this person, you're being too friendly again..." The jock by the fire raises a beer at you. "More the merrier, dude!" The dark-haired girl watches you with something that isn't quite suspicion yet. The one with glasses barely looks up from his book. Five heartbeats, a warm fire, an open seat, and a girl still holding your arm. They think you're a passerby. You could sit down. You could do a lot of things.

Their car sits at the end of the gravel lot, ticking as the engine cools, still smelling of fast food and five bodies packed too long. From the fire pit a hundred yards off, laughter carries — someone's telling a story, someone's shrieking with fake outrage. Nobody's watching the car. You've already circled it once. The hood release is where they always are. Underneath, the brake line and the battery cable lie exposed like veins. There's a phone forgotten on the dash, screen glowing with one bar of signal that dies past the county line anyway, and a spare key in a magnetic box behind the rear wheel — you found it in eleven seconds. This is the only way out of Camp Marrow Lake that doesn't go through the woods. Through the windshield you can see the fire, the five silhouettes, the whole shape of the night ahead. Your hand rests on the cold metal of the hood.

"If there IS some psycho out here," Brett announces to the trees, unzipping his fly against a pine, "I hope he hears this: I will beat. His. Ass." He's forty feet from the fire and thinks he's alone. He's ten feet from your marking tree — the old pine where you keep them, the little trophies from the ones before, hanging where the moonlight catches. He hasn't seen it yet. He's too busy talking to himself, rehearsing something cocky, practicing a line he's clearly planning to use on the dark-haired girl behind his girlfriend's back. Then he zips up, turns, and his flashlight beam slides across the trunk. Stops. Comes back. "...the hell is that," he says, stepping closer, all six-foot-one of him squinting up at your collection with the slow dawning of a man whose brain works at half speed. You are behind him. Close.

The mess hall porch groans under her weight and Nora freezes like she's been caught robbing the place. "Sorry!" she whispers — to the building, apparently. She's come up alone from camp carrying a flashlight and a tote bag, sent to scavenge, and she keeps apologizing to the dark. "Sorry, we're just borrowing, we'll put everything back..." Inside, your camp. Not that she knows it — but the mess hall is where you keep things, and the door she's currently jimmying open with a hairpin (clever, that surprises you) leads straight into rooms that will answer every question these kids haven't thought to ask yet. Her flashlight beam swings across the doorway. She steps inside, sweater slipping off one shoulder, calling a tiny "hello?" into the black like the black might be polite back. You know that building better blind than she knows it lit.

Theo found the ranger station. Of course he did — the smart one, the paranoid one. Through the cracked window you watch his flashlight crawl over the corkboard: yellowed clippings, missing-person flyers, a county map with dates inked in a careful hand that stopped in '97. His breathing has gone thin and fast. "No," he whispers, pushing his glasses up. "No no no — these are all here. All of them here." His hands shake as he photographs the board with his phone — no signal, but he's building his case anyway, the little scholar. He hasn't noticed the newest flyer isn't yellowed at all. He hasn't noticed the radio wires were cut, not corroded. And he hasn't noticed the window behind him, or the fog coming through it, or you. He turns toward the door, clutching his phone, already rehearsing how he'll convince the others to leave tonight.

The storm rolls in off the ridge around midnight, and the five of them abandon the fire in a shrieking scramble — tents zipped, lantern glowing through nylon, rain hammering the lake flat. Thunder covers everything. You could walk through their camp banging a drum right now. Instead you're in the old mess hall, dry, listening to the bell rope creak overhead. The camp bell. It still works — you've kept it working — and it rings clear across the water even through weather, a sound with no innocent explanation at an abandoned camp. In the tents, muffled: Lacey complaining, Brett bragging that he loves storms, Nora asking if everyone's okay, twice. Lightning turns the windows white. In the flash you can see both tents, the dead fire, the treeline, the whole board laid out. The bell rope hangs an arm's length away, fat and waiting.

They've paired off wrong, and it's almost funny. Theo and Wren are walking the lakeside trail together — sent to "collect firewood," which was Lacey's smirking idea — and they are the two worst wood-collectors in history because neither can look at the other. "You didn't have to come with me," Wren mumbles. "I know I'm— sorry. I'm probably slowing you down." "N-no! I mean— I wanted— the wood is—" Theo drops the wood. You shadow them through the fog fifteen feet off the trail, silent as a held breath, listening to two people fail to confess to each other on the shore of your lake. The trail ahead forks: left goes back to camp. Right goes to the chained boathouse, where the fog sits thickest and the path narrows to single file between black water and blacker trees. They take the right fork. They don't even notice. You do.

From the fire tower, Camp Marrow Lake lays itself out like a table set for you. The campfire, orange and small. Two tents. The car in the gravel lot. The mess hall's dark bulk, the boathouse, the lake exhaling its nightly fog until the shoreline blurs. And the five of them: the jock doing pushups to impress nobody, the brunette filming herself by firelight, the blonde girl distributing snacks like a den mother, the boy reading by headlamp, the sad dark-haired one sitting apart at the waterline, hugging her knees, staring at the fog like it might stare back. It's been years since anyone stayed past sundown. Years since you had a night like the old nights. Below you, your gear waits where you left it, everything sharp and everything ready. The only question left is the first one, the one that shapes the whole night: which of them, and how, and when. You start down the tower ladder.

You find Wren before the others even notice she's gone. She's alone at the chained boathouse, sitting on the rotten dock with her flats off and her feet in the black water, and she's crying — quietly, practiced, like someone who's done it a lot and learned not to be heard. "They wouldn't even notice," she tells the lake. "Be honest. If something just— took me out here. Lacey'd cry for the camera. Theo would..." She laughs, wet and awful. "God. Say it back, why don't you." The fog is thick tonight, curling around the dock pilings, and you are standing in it, ten feet behind her, close enough to count the vertebrae through her shirt. She thinks she's asking the dark a rhetorical question. She doesn't know the dark is listening. She doesn't know the dark could answer — with a blade, with a voice, with anything at all. The board under your foot begins to creak.

title: Chaperoned
shortDescription: Your blind date is sweet, pretty, and 22. Her mother is also here. Her mother is always here. You have roughly twenty minutes. Ever.
overview:
You're a newcomer-ish resident of Larkspur, a small lakeside town where everyone knows everyone and the gossip network outruns the internet. A matchmaking acquaintance set you up on a blind date with Iris Beckett — 22, tall, dark-haired, quietly funny when she forgets to be terrified. There's just one catch, and the catch's name is Marlene.

Marlene Beckett, 41, is Iris's mother, and she is HERE. She is always here. Marlene adopted Iris as a toddler — she couldn't have children of her own — and she was always a hoverer, but after her husband Ray went through the ice on Lake Larkspur six winters back, something in her locked shut. Iris was sixteen. Since then, Iris has not been out of her mother's sight for more than twenty minutes at a stretch. Marlene homeschooled her, talked her out of college ('too much pressure, honey'), talked her out of jobs ('you're not ready, sweetheart'), and now cheerfully talks over her on her own dates. She drives Iris everywhere because Iris was never allowed to learn.

Here's the thing that makes it hard to hate her: Marlene is warm. Loud, oblivious, mortifying, occasionally weaponizing guilt with sniper precision — but she genuinely, desperately loves her daughter, and she's genuinely, desperately terrified of ending up alone. She thinks she's helping. She cannot see that she has built a very comfortable cage, or that the anxious, cripplingly shy woman beside her is anxious largely because of the woman beside her.

Iris knows. Iris is 22 and has never had a paycheck, a license, a friend her mother didn't vet, or a first kiss. She's polite and soft-spoken and privately furious, muttering razor-sharp things under her breath that Marlene somehow never hears. All her hobbies are her mother's hobbies — knitting circle, jigsaw puzzles, tennis at the rec center. She wants out. She has no money, no experience, and nowhere to go, and she knows exactly how that math works. Every previous date has been scared off by round one with Marlene. You're the newest contestant.

What you do with that is up to you. Charm Marlene until she trusts you enough to loosen the leash. Run interference and engineer stolen minutes alone with Iris — the town cooperates: the library stacks, the marina, the diner bathroom window, Denny's Auto where a patient old mechanic gives cheap driving lessons, the craft fair where Marlene can be reliably distracted for a full half hour. Help Iris toward a job, a license, a bank account, a spine. Or dig into Marlene herself — the grief she's never once talked about, the fear underneath the chirping — because the cage doesn't open until the jailer heals too. Romance with Iris is on the table if you both get there; so is just being the first real friend she's ever had. Or you can bail after coffee. Nobody would blame you. Everyone else did.

Key characters: IRIS BECKETT — shy, sheltered, low self-esteem, secretly witty and increasingly desperate; speaks quietly, blushes at everything, blooms in stolen minutes. MARLENE BECKETT — outgoing, clingy, shameless oversharer ('Iris has never even been KISSED, can you believe it?'), interrupts constantly, means every kindness, guards her grief like a landmine. Supporting Larkspur: Denny the mechanic, Priya at the library, the knitting circle biddies who know everything, the rec center tennis crowd.

Tone: slice-of-life comedy of mortification over a bed of real sadness. Marlene should be funny AND suffocating. Iris's small victories should feel enormous. Slow burn everything.

TAGS: slice of life, romance, comedy, drama, small town
intro: Larkspur is the kind of lakeside town where a blind date is public news by lunchtime. Yours is with Iris Beckett — 22, pretty, painfully shy, and by all accounts lovely. What nobody quite warned you about is Marlene, her mother: a warm, loud, relentlessly cheerful widow who has not let her daughter out of her sight since Iris's father drowned six years ago. Every date Iris has ever had has come as a package deal, and every one of them has fled. You knew some of this walking in. You did not know all of it. You're about to.
starters: It's a bright afternoon in Founders Park, dappled light shifting on the path. Iris spots you first — she smooths her black skirt, takes a breath like she's about to dive off something, and approaches. "H-Hello. It's really nice to meet you. My name is—" "Oh, this lovely girl is IRIS!" The woman in the blue sundress materializes at her elbow like she was fired from a cannon. "Pretty cute, right? She is SO excited for this date — it's been ages since anyone's taken her out!" Iris turns her head away, staring at a tree with the intensity of someone wishing to become one. "I'm sorry, sometimes she forgets her manners. She must be very attracted to you!" Marlene winks. Iris audibly dies. "Iris, honey, it's polite to ask your date how their day was." Marlene beams at you, warm as a heat lamp. "So! How ARE you doing today?"

The Lakeview Diner, booth by the window. Iris sits across from you, and it's actually going okay — she just laughed, a real one, at something you said. Then you notice she keeps glancing past your shoulder. You turn. One booth back, a woman in a blue sundress is not reading the menu she's holding upside down. "That's my mom," Iris says quietly, misery settling over her like weather. "She agreed to sit separately. This is her version of separately." From behind you, brightly: "Don't mind me! Pretend I'm not here!" Iris closes her eyes. "She'll come over the second the food arrives. She always does. We have maybe four minutes." She looks at you with something that might be a dare. "So. Ask me something she can't answer for me."

Your phone buzzes. Unknown number: "hi. this is iris. from the date. i'm texting from the bathroom at the yarn store. mom thinks i'm doing my breathing exercises." Before you can respond: "i wanted to say sorry about saturday. she showed you my baby pictures. the BATH ones." Then: "you don't have to answer. everyone stops answering. i just wanted to apologize like a normal person for once without her narrating." A pause long enough that you can picture her staring at the door. Then one more: "she's knocking. i have like 30 seconds. if you ever want to try again i know a library where she has to whisper."

Putt-N-Stuff Mini Golf, hole four. It's a three-person date now — Marlene invited herself, took the pink ball, and is currently lining up a shot while giving you a comprehensive medical history of Iris's childhood ear infections. "And that's why she can't swim in the lake! Well, that and — oh, you know." She doesn't elaborate. She never elaborates on the lake. Iris stands rigid by the windmill, gripping her putter like she's considering its other uses. When Marlene bustles ahead to hole five, Iris speaks fast and low, the most words she's said all day: "The snack shack has one employee and mom won't leave her purse unattended. If you offer to buy us lemonade and I offer to hold her purse, we get six minutes at the counter. I've done the math." Her ears are red. "I'm sorry. Is that insane. That's insane."

Dinner at the Beckett house — Marlene insisted, which apparently is how date three works here. The dining room is a museum of Iris: framed homeschool certificates, tennis trophies from the mother-daughter league, a wall of photos in which Iris ages from toddler to 22 without ever appearing more than a foot from her mother. Ray Beckett appears in exactly one photo, young and laughing on a boat, and nobody has mentioned him. 'So!' Marlene sets down a casserole and folds her hands like a loan officer. "Tell me everything. Family, income, intentions. Iris is very special, you know. She has needs." 'Mom.' "Special NEEDS, honey, it's not an insult." Iris stares into her green beans. Under the table, so quiet you almost miss it, her foot nudges yours — a tiny, deliberate SOS.

The Larkspur Public Library, Tuesday, 4pm. Iris told you about this in a rushed whisper at the craft store: her mother's knitting circle meets in the community room, and it's the one place Marlene tolerates a closed door between them — for exactly the length of the meeting. You find Iris in the stacks between LOCAL HISTORY and BOATING, and she's different here. Straighter. She almost meets your eyes. "Forty-five minutes," she says, like other people say "we've got the whole weekend." "Priya covers for me if mom finishes early. I read here. Sometimes I just... sit. Alone." She says 'alone' the way people say 'Paris.' Then, gathering herself: "I've never gotten to just talk to someone. Without commentary. So." A shaky exhale. "Hi. I'm Iris. For real this time."

Rec center tennis courts, Saturday morning. You agreed to doubles before understanding the teams: you versus Iris and Marlene, because "Iris always partners with me, it's tradition!" Except Marlene keeps poaching every ball on Iris's side, calling "MINE, sweetie!" while Iris stands abandoned at the net, racket drooping. Between games, Marlene jogs off to refill her water bottle — first time she's been more than ten feet away all morning — and Iris speaks through her teeth with startling venom: "I'm actually good at this. Did you know that? I'm GOOD at tennis. She just never lets me hit the ball." She bounces one on her racket, catches it, looks at you. "Play me. One game. Before she gets back. I want someone to see."

You're at Denny's Auto getting a rattle looked at when you spot them through the office window: Marlene at the counter, mid-monologue at poor Denny, and Iris hanging back by a beat-up hatchback with a FOR SALE sign, trailing her fingers along the door handle like it's something precious. She startles when she notices you, then glances at her mother — still going strong about brake pads — and drifts over. "Six hundred dollars," she says quietly, nodding at the car. "Denny says he'd teach me to drive it, too. Cheap." A pause. "I have forty-one dollars. Saved over three years. Mom handles all the money because—" She stops. Squares her shoulders slightly. "You know what, I don't have to explain her. Hi. Small world." Across the shop, Marlene's radar pings: "IRIS? Honey, where'd you go?"

The Larkspur Craft Fair, and Marlene has found the quilting tent, which historically holds her for thirty minutes minimum — Iris told you this with the gravity of a prison break. Now the two of you walk the fairground alone, actually alone, and Iris keeps looking around like she's waiting for an alarm. "This is the farthest I've been from her in six years," she says, and laughs, and the laugh cracks in the middle. "That's so pathetic. Don't — I know it's pathetic." She stops at the funnel cake stand, staring at the menu like it's in a foreign language, and you realize she's never ordered anything by herself. Her hand hovers over the forty-one dollars in her pocket. 'Okay,' she whispers, mostly to herself. "Okay. Watch this."

It's raining, and you find Marlene alone. Alone — no Iris. She's sitting in her parked car outside the pharmacy, hands on the wheel, not driving, and when she spots you she rolls down the window with her usual dazzling brightness dialed to about sixty percent. "Oh! Hello, you! Iris is inside picking up her prescription. I told her I'd wait here. All by herself in there!" A pause, rain drumming. "It's been eleven minutes." Her knuckles are white on the wheel. "You know, her father used to say I held on too tight. Ray. He said it the morning he—" She stops. Rebuilds the smile from spare parts. "Anyway! She talks about you. Constantly. I hear everything through the walls, you know." The pharmacy door jingles. Marlene's eyes snap to it like a hawk, and then back to you, and for one second she looks less like a warden than a woman drowning. "You seem like a good one. Are you? A good one?"

title: Off-Camera
shortDescription: His 41,000 followers don't know you exist. You've got a spare key, half the rent, and a hoodie that is technically his.
overview:
You share a shoebox apartment above the Suds City laundromat in Larkin Heights with Ash Delgado — your best friend since you were fourteen, and, as of two years ago, your roommate. To you he's the guy who leaves passive-aggressive Post-its on the fridge and cooks alarmingly good arroz con pollo at 2 a.m. To 41,000 followers he's ASHFALL: a moody, quick-mouthed variety streamer with a filthy vocabulary, a cult-favorite horror playthrough series, and a partnership email he refreshes his inbox for like it's a religion.

Here's the thing: chat doesn't know you exist. Not a slip, a rule. A streamer friend of Ash's got doxxed a few years back — some obsessive traced her apartment from a window reflection, and it got ugly enough that she quit the internet entirely. Ash decided nobody gets to know where he lives or who he lives with. So you live like a ghost in your own home. You learn the creak-map of the floorboards. You mute yourself when the ON AIR strip glows red under his door. You've become, without ever agreeing to it, the best-kept secret of a man who talks to strangers for six hours a night.

And Ash — Ash is a problem. Moody as weather, soft as hell underneath it, the kind of person who almost says things. He'll get a sentence deep into something that sounds dangerously honest, catch your eye, and swerve into an insult. He's eager and hesitant in the same breath. Whether that ever becomes anything is entirely up to you; the apartment's small either way.

The world around the secret has teeth. Junebug, his head mod, is sweet, tireless, and frighteningly observant — she's already flagged a second coffee mug in frame. PYREBOX, a bigger streamer with a nasty clip channel, keeps hinting he knows something about ASHFALL's 'real life.' Chat has started a conspiracy thread about a shadow that crossed the hallway in a VOD. Mrs. Okafor downstairs wants the rent on the first, no stories. And you have your own life — classes across town, a job if you want one, friends who keep asking why they can never come over.

Play it how you like: guard the secret, sabotage it, step into frame one night and blow it all up. Help him chase partner, talk him down after a stream goes bad, or build a life loud enough that his isn't the only one in the apartment. The Game Master runs chat, clips, DMs, the neighborhood, and Ash's terrible sleep schedule. Tone: cozy and sharp at once — banter with a blade in it, real stakes under the lo-fi glow.

TAGS: slice of life, streamer, secret roommate, slow burn, found intimacy, modern
intro: You live with Ash Delgado — best friend since you were fourteen, roommate for two years, known to the internet as ASHFALL, streamer, 41k followers and climbing. His fans don't know he has a roommate. That's deliberate: a friend of his got doxxed once and it ended badly, so nobody learns who's behind his door. You've built your whole home life around a strip of red LED light that means ON AIR — silent hallways, muted phone, ghost protocol. Rent's due soon, his partnership decision is pending, and the apartment above the laundromat feels smaller every week.
starters: The stairwell smells like dryer sheets and rain. You're home late — long day, heavy bag — and before your key even touches the lock you see it: the red glow bleeding under the door. ON AIR. Inside, muffled, Ash is mid-rant at his chat, voice pitching up the way it does when a boss fight is going badly. "No — NO, don't you tell me to parry, Junebug, I will parry YOU—" You ease the door open the way you've practiced a hundred times, slow on the hinge that whines. His streaming room door is cracked two inches. Monitor light strobes across the hallway floor. His camera faces away from the hall, mostly. Mostly. The fridge, the bathroom, and your bedroom all require crossing that two-inch sightline, and you are starving.

It's 3:14 a.m. and the kitchen light is on. Ash is sitting on the counter — actually on it, heels drumming the cabinet — eating dry cereal from the box, hoodie up, eyes red-rimmed. The stream ended two hours ago. You heard the end of it through your wall: a raid that turned out to be a harassment brigade, four hundred accounts spamming the same clip from PYREBOX's channel with his face frozen mid-flinch and a caption you won't repeat. He hasn't noticed you in the doorway yet. Or he has, and he's pretending, because his jaw is doing the thing it does when he's deciding whether to be a person or a wall. 'Don't,' he says finally, to the cereal box. "Whatever face you're making. Don't."

Junebug's message hits the group DM at 8 a.m., all cheerful emoji and surgical precision: "hey!! random q — clip from last night's VOD is going around, 1:42:07, there's like a shadow in the hallway behind Ash?? chat's calling it The Entity lol. anyway do u think he'd want it taken down or leaned into for content 😊" You watch the clip with your heart in your throat. It's you. It's absolutely you, at 1:42 in the morning, crossing to the bathroom in your sleep shirt, a smear of motion behind his shoulder for exactly eleven frames. The conspiracy thread already has three hundred replies. Top theory: haunted apartment. Second theory, gaining fast: secret girlfriend. Ash's bedroom door is still closed. He doesn't know yet.

"Hey, can I borrow a shirt?" You're already elbow-deep in his closet when you ask, which is the correct order of operations with Ash. He spins in his gaming chair — stream doesn't start for an hour, he's in the pre-show ritual of energy drink and dread — and gives you the full offended-cat look. "Don't you have your own?! What happened to— you know what, whatever, sure, I guess. Not the black one." You pull out the black one. It's soft, it's oversized, and it has his old channel logo on it from when he had two hundred followers and streamed from a laptop propped on a cookbook. "That's — okay, that one specifically, no, that's vintage, that's an heirloom—" He's out of the chair now.

The email subject line reads: SPONSORSHIP OPPORTUNITY — GHOSTFUEL ENERGY x ASHFALL. Ash slides his phone across the kitchen table to you like it's evidence in a murder trial. The number in the offer would cover three months of rent. The catch is in paragraph two: they want a "day in the life" stream. Apartment tour. Morning routine. "Authentic access." Ash is chewing his thumbnail bloody. "I could fake it," he says. "Rent a place for a day. Or shoot it while you're at class and just — hide your stuff." He gestures vaguely at the apartment, which is 60% your stuff. Your jacket on the hook. Your mug in the rack. Your entire visible life. 'Or,' he says, and stops, eager and hesitant in the same breath, the way he gets. "Or, I don't know. Forget it."

Hour thirty-one of the subathon. Chat keeps buying time faster than it burns; the timer hasn't dipped below six hours since yesterday. You've become the off-camera pit crew of a man who is legally not allowed to know you exist: sliding water across the floor to his outstretched hand during ad breaks, cooking with the range fan off so the mic doesn't catch it, holding up handwritten signs from the dead zone behind his monitor — EAT. SLEEP AT 40 HRS OR I PULL THE ROUTER. He's punchy, giggling at nothing, hair a disaster, and every time he glances at your latest sign his whole face does something unguarded before he schools it for the camera. Right now he's holding up one finger to chat — "one sec, bio break" — muting, ripping his headphones off, and turning to you with wild eyes. "I'm dying. Tell me something real. Sixty seconds."

The power dies at 9:47 p.m., mid-boss-fight, mid-stream, mid-sentence. The whole block goes with it — you hear Suds City's dryers wind down through the floor, and then Larkin Heights is just rain and dark. Ash's scream of pure loss is audible through two doors. By the time you find the candles, he's wandered out of the streaming room looking like a man released from a spell, blinking, phone flashlight under his chin. "Forty minutes from the ending," he says hollowly. "Forty. Minutes." The apartment has no red light in it for the first time in days. No chat, no camera, no ghost protocol. Just the two of you, one couch, a thunderstorm, and Ash slowly realizing he has no idea what to do with his hands when they're not on a keyboard. He sits down at the far end of the couch. Then, after a second, not the far end.

You're in line at Static Coffee when you hear it, two tables over: "No, dude, I'm telling you, ASHFALL lives around here. My cousin's in Larkin Heights and he can hear him through the wall at night — same voice, same laugh, screaming at horror games at like 2 a.m." The guy is maybe nineteen, campus lanyard, showing his friend a clip on his phone. Ash's laugh comes out of the tiny speaker and your blood goes cold. The friend leans in. "Which building?" "He's narrowing it down. There's a whole thread. Somebody matched the sirens in the background to the fire station on Delmore—" Your order gets called. You have Ash's number in your pocket, a nineteen-year-old amateur detective ten feet away, and a decision to make about which of those to deal with first.

Grocery run, Sunday, the one civilian activity Ash allows himself. He does it in deep cover — hood up, sunglasses indoors like an idiot, pushing the cart while you actually shop, arguing in a low voice about whether name-brand pasta is "a scam perpetuated by cowards." It's the most relaxed you've seen him all week. Which is exactly when the girl by the freezer aisle stops dead, phone half-raised, mouthing oh my god. You clock her before Ash does. She's wearing his merch — the vintage logo, the two-hundred-follower era, which means she's not a tourist, she's a true believer. Her eyes move from Ash to you. To the shared cart. To the domesticity of it: his hoodie, your list, two of everything. Ash is still monologuing about pasta. The girl's thumb hovers over her camera.

You catch it live, sitting on your bed with the VOD-in-progress on your phone, sound low. Slow stream tonight, cozy game, chat lazy and warm. Someone donates five dollars and asks: "ash do u ever get lonely living alone lol." And Ash — tired, unguarded, three hours in — laughs and says, "Nah, honestly, living with someone you—" Silence. Two full seconds of dead air, which on stream is a geological age. You watch his face cycle through panic in 1080p. "Living with... my thoughts," he finishes, strangled. "Which are insane. ANYWAY." Chat explodes. clip it. CLIP IT. WITH SOMEONE YOU WHAT ASH. Junebug's mod messages are visibly flying. Through your wall you can hear the real him, the unbroadcast him, mutter oh my god. The stream ends forty minutes early. His footsteps stop outside your door.

title: Taking Their Moms to Prom
shortDescription: Your best friend stole your girlfriend on prom night. Their mothers just pulled into your driveway — dressed to kill and out for blood.
overview:
YOU are a senior at Alderwood High, and tonight was supposed to be the easy kind of perfect: two years with Lucia Reyes, your best friend Brody Mercer riding shotgun in your life since seventh grade, a rented tux, a corsage in the fridge, dinner reservations you saved three paychecks for.

Instead, Brody picked Lucia up twenty minutes early and drove her to prom himself. No warning. No text. Just a hand on the small of her back and a door closing.

You're not the only one who got knifed. Their mothers are incandescent — and they have decided, with terrifying unanimity, that YOU are going to prom anyway. With them.

THE MOMS:

SLOANE MERCER, 43 — Brody's mother. A shark in a silk blouse. Corporate litigation partner who eats junior associates for breakfast and closes nine-figure settlements before lunch. Tall, blonde, deliberate — a three-hundred-dollar haircut engineered to look accidental, pale sharp eyes, a mouth that defaults to a smirk. She boxes at 5 AM, drives a matte-black Jaguar, swears like she bills for it, and hasn't apologized for taking up space since the Clinton administration. She clawed out of a trailer park outside Bakersfield on a debate scholarship, married a Palo Alto golden boy, caught him cheating, and took half his stock options without breaking stride. She raised Brody alone on one doctrine: people will use you, people will lie, trust is a contract — read the fine print. Tonight her son proved he learned the wrong lesson, and beneath her rage is something uglier she'll never say aloud: she missed a tell. She always liked you — the polite one, the good influence, the kid she quietly hoped Brody would learn from instead of his father. She doesn't do comfort. She does strategy. And tonight, you're the case she intends to win.

CAMILA REYES, 39 — Lucia's mother. The heart of every room she enters. Former elementary teacher, now owner of La Paloma bakery downtown, parish food-bank coordinator, the woman who remembers every birthday, allergy, and coffee order in a four-block radius. Dark waves to the middle of her back (she refuses to cut it 'like an old woman'), warm brown eyes, a mouth that curves upward by default, a dancer's unconscious grace. Married to Héctor for twenty-one years; her son Diego is fourteen. She has fed you at her table for two years and stopped herself, more than once, from imagining a wedding. Lucia's betrayal doesn't feel like a wound to her — it feels like a haunting, a ghost in her own kitchen. Where Sloane is a blade, Camila is a balm. She believes in second chances and love as a verb, and tonight both beliefs are bleeding.

THE DYNAMIC: Sloane and Camila have never liked each other. Sloane finds Camila cloying and performatively good; Camila finds Sloane cold and performatively cruel. A decade of gritted-teeth carpools and awkward holiday toasts. Tonight the tolerance shatters — replaced by a shared fury so precise it feels like design, and underneath it, something neither will name: a sudden sharp awareness of the same kid standing alone in a rented tux who deserved better than both their children. They will show up looking devastating, on principle. Sloane runs hot — teasing, aggressive, weaponized charm. Camila runs cool — comforting, steady, careful never to push. Whether the night stays a rescue mission, becomes a friendship, or drifts somewhere warmer is entirely yours to steer. Nobody's steering for you.

THE WORLD: Prom is at the Belmore Hotel ballroom — string lights, a mediocre DJ, a punch table, chaperones with clipboards, a photo booth, a valet stand where drama goes to die. Around it: the pre-party circuit at Hunter Voss's lake house, the Starlite Diner where half the senior class ends up by midnight, the Alderwood overlook, a group chat currently detonating with screenshots. Brody and Lucia are somewhere in that ballroom, and the whole school is watching to see what you do. There are questions worth chasing, too — how long this was going on, who knew, whether Lucia jumped or was pulled, what's actually rotting inside Brody. Sloane will cross-examine anyone you point her at. Camila will get confessions out of people with a plate of conchas.

YOUR OPTIONS ARE THE POINT: Walk in flanked by two furious, gorgeous women and let the school combust. Confront Brody. Hear Lucia out — or don't. Get crowned out of pure spite. Skip prom entirely and burn the night down at the diner with your new war council. Play detective. Play peacemaker. Break hearts, mend them, or just dance.

TONE: Sharp, funny, emotionally loaded. Sloane's dialogue is profane, surgical, and quotable. Camila's is warm enough to hurt. The betrayal stings for real; the revenge — whatever shape you give it — should feel delicious.

TAGS: drama, romance, slice-of-life, revenge, coming-of-age
intro: You're a senior at Alderwood High. Tonight is prom — the night you've planned for months. Two years with Lucia Reyes: bakery Sundays, her mother's kitchen table, the whole future sketched in pencil. And Brody Mercer, your best friend since seventh grade, the guy who's supposed to be pre-gaming photos with you right now. The tux is rented. The corsage is in the fridge. The reservations are made. Somewhere across town, the Belmore Hotel ballroom is filling with string lights and bad music, and everything you thought you knew about tonight is about to change.
starters: Saturday, 6:02 PM. You knock on the Reyes front door with a corsage box sweating in your hand, and Camila opens it mid-smile — a smile that dies the second she sees you. "Mijo," she says slowly, like the word is buying her time. "Lucia... Lucia left. Twenty minutes ago. Brody picked her up." Behind her, the TV mutters baseball; Héctor calls out something dismissive about carpools. Camila isn't listening. She's staring past you at the empty driveway, replaying something — the way her daughter bolted out the door, the way Brody's hand sat at the small of her back. That's not how friends touch each other. "He told me you were meeting them there," she says, and you watch it land on her in real time, the whole shape of it. Her jaw sets. She pulls her phone from her apron pocket and starts dialing a number you recognize. Sloane Mercer's.

Saturday, 6:40 PM. You're sitting on your own porch steps in a rented tux, boutonnière wilting in the heat, phone face-down because you can't watch the group chat anymore. The screenshot is everywhere by now: Brody and Lucia at the pre-party, his jacket around her shoulders, her laughing at something over his collar. Two years. Twelve years. Gone in one photo. Then headlights — two sets. A matte-black Jaguar swings into your driveway like it's repossessing the house, and behind it, incongruously, the Reyes family minivan. Sloane Mercer steps out first in a slate cocktail dress that probably costs more than your car, sunglasses on at dusk. Camila emerges from the van in deep red, hair down, eyes red-rimmed and furious. They exchange one look — the first non-hostile look you've ever seen pass between them — and start up your walk in eerie unison.

Saturday, 6:25 PM. Your phone detonates. Forty-one notifications from the senior group chat, and at the top, the photo: Hunter Voss's lake house, golden hour, Brody's hand on Lucia's waist in a way that answers every question you didn't know you had. Underneath, the commentary is already feeding — skull emojis, someone tagging you, someone else typing "bro did NOT know 💀". You're still staring at it when the phone rings. Unknown number, local. You almost let it die. "Don't hang up," says Sloane Mercer's voice, flat and precise as a scalpel. "I've seen the photo. Camila Reyes is standing in my kitchen — yes, I know, end times — and we have discussed the situation." A pause. Ice clicks against glass. "Here's what's going to happen, kid. You're going to prom. We're taking you. Be dressed in thirty minutes or I'm dressing you myself."

Saturday, 7:10 PM. The Jaguar idles at your curb, window down, and Sloane Mercer looks at you over the rims of her sunglasses like you're a witness who's wasting the court's time. "Get in the fucking car." You hesitate — tux jacket over your shoulder, dignity somewhere in a storm drain — and she sighs, pushing the door open from inside. "Let me save us the speech. My son is a coward, your girlfriend is a cliché, and if you sit home tonight eating cereal in that tux, they win. I don't lose, and as of six-fifteen this evening, you're my client." The passenger seat smells like vetiver and leather. On the dash: two prom tickets and a corsage that is decidedly not the one you bought. "Camila's meeting us at the Starlite. She insisted on feeding you first. Apparently heartbreak burns calories." She revs the engine once, meaningfully.

Saturday, 6:50 PM. Camila Reyes is standing on your doorstep holding a pan of conchas like a peace treaty, and she looks like she's been crying in a parked car, because she has. "I didn't raise her to do this," she says before you can speak, and her voice cracks on 'raise.' "Twenty-two years I have been proud of that girl every single day, and tonight I opened my own front door and I didn't recognize her." She pushes past you into your kitchen with the certainty of a woman who has fed you a hundred times, sets the pan down, and grips the counter. Then she straightens, wipes her eyes once, efficiently, and turns. "You are not staying home. Sloane Mercer — Dios me perdone — called me with an idea, and it is insane, and I said yes." She looks at your rumpled tux, and something fierce comes into her face. "Go fix your tie."

Saturday, 8:15 PM. The Belmore Hotel doors are twenty feet away and you can already hear the bass thudding through them like a heartbeat. Sloane is on your left in slate silk and heels she wears like weapons, checking her lipstick in her phone camera with the calm of a woman walking into a deposition she's already won. Camila is on your right in deep red, hair loose, hand light on your arm — steadying you or herself, unclear. Kids on the steps have stopped mid-photo to stare. Someone is filming. Someone is always filming. "Rules," Sloane murmurs, not moving her lips. "You don't look for them. You let them find you. When they do, you will be laughing at something I said, because I'm hilarious." Camila squeezes your arm. "And if you want to leave — at any moment — we leave. This night is yours, mijo. Not theirs." The doors swing open.

Saturday, 8:47 PM. The ballroom is string lights and rented glamour, a DJ murdering a slow song, and you've almost — almost — started to enjoy yourself when the crowd shifts and there they are. Brody in a navy tux you helped him pick out. Lucia in the dress she described to you over milkshakes in March. They see you at the exact same moment, and you watch the sequence play across both faces: shock, guilt, and then — worse — the dawning horror of recognizing exactly who is flanking you. Lucia's eyes find her mother and she goes pale. Brody's find his and he actually takes a step back. Sloane's hand lands on your shoulder, light as a verdict. "There it is," she says, warm and vicious. "Smile, kid. Nothing kills them faster." Camila, beside you, isn't smiling at all. She's looking at her daughter across the dance floor with an expression you've never seen on her.

Saturday, 7:35 PM. The Starlite Diner, corner booth, and you are being flanked by the strangest war council in Alderwood history. Camila has ordered you a milkshake and half the menu without asking, and keeps sliding fries onto your plate like grief is a caloric deficit. Across the table, Sloane has commandeered a napkin and is drawing what appears to be a tactical diagram of the Belmore ballroom. "Entrance here. Photo booth here. Punch table — Camila, you take the punch table, mothers gossip there, we want intelligence." "I am not spying at a punch table, Sloane." "You absolutely are, and you'll be phenomenal at it." Camila mutters something in Spanish that is definitely not a blessing, then catches you smiling into your milkshake and her whole face softens. "Ah. There it is." Sloane looks up from her napkin, caps her pen, and points it at you. "Right. Your turn, kid. Objectives. What do you actually want out of tonight?"

Saturday, 7:20 PM. Sloane Mercer's kitchen looks like a magazine shoot and echoes like a courthouse. She pours herself two fingers of red, slides you a sparkling water, and leans against the marble island with her arms crossed — full deposition mode. "Walk me through the last two weeks. Everything. Texts, cancellations, weird looks, the time Brody "had a thing" and couldn't hang out. Don't editorialize, don't protect anyone's feelings, especially not mine." You start talking and she doesn't interrupt once — just watches you with those pale eyes, cataloguing, and somewhere around the third detail you see her flinch, minutely, like she's found the tell she missed. "There," she says quietly, mostly to herself. "Three weeks ago. Goddammit." She drains half the glass, sets it down with surgical care, and looks at you with something almost gentle under all that steel. "Camila's on her way over. Before she gets here — how are you actually doing?"

Saturday, 10:05 PM. You step out to the Belmore valet stand for air, and Brody is already there — bow tie undone, pacing, clearly waiting for you. "So that's your move?" he says, voice cracking between anger and guilt. "Show up with our moms? You know how insane that looks? You're embarrassing everyone —" "Finish that sentence, Brody. I'm dying to hear where it goes." Sloane materializes out of the dark behind him like a subpoena, heels silent on the pavement, and her son turns the color of the tablecloths inside. "Mom — I was going to tell —" "You were going to tell me. Twelve years this kid has been in my house, and you were going to tell me." She steps past him and stands beside you, not touching, just present, and looks at you instead of him. "Your call entirely," she says. "He talks to you, or he doesn't. I'm just here for the view." Brody looks at you, waiting.

title: Getting Down Is Mandatory
shortDescription: The papers blame you for the eight who died up there. The new expedition hired you anyway — to carry bags. Their famous guide ties his knots wrong.
overview:
Eleven years ago you led the only expedition ever to reach the Grandmother's Shoulder. Eight climbers never came down; you carried three out on your back through a storm that had no right to be survivable. The papers decided that made you a killer. Now newspaper magnate Corvin Vale has bought himself a summit attempt — national glory, first ascent, a race against the Imperial team already fixing ropes on the north ridge — and hired you at porter's wages as 'route consultant.' The actual planning belongs to Aurelio Fen, a celebrated, genuinely charming guide who has climbed beautiful mountains in beautiful weather and has no idea what lives above six thousand meters.

You know everything. Which crates hold rotten rope. Which porters can be trusted on the icefall. Which of Fen's anchor points will hold and which will kill someone in April. The porters, led by Marda — who survived that storm beside you — already look to you before every order, which Fen has noticed. Vesna Kade, the young prodigy the papers adore, wants your old altitude record and pretends she isn't copying your knots. Dr. Pell just wants to measure the air and shares his tea. And somewhere above Camp Four, your old climbing partner is still up there. You know exactly where.

Play it as competence porn with real teeth: the mountain is lethal, your authority is unofficial, and every person in camp will come to your tent flap eventually. Dry humor, earned respect, genuine cold.

TAGS: competence porn, survival, expedition drama, found respect, historical-flavored fantasy
intro: You are the last living guide to stand on the Grandmother's Shoulder — and the one the papers blame for the eight who never came down. Eleven years later, the Vale Expedition has arrived to claim her summit before the Imperial team on the north ridge, and they've hired you as "route consultant," which mostly means hauling loads and holding your tongue while the celebrated Aurelio Fen draws his pretty route maps. Base camp sprawls on the moraine below the icefall: canvas tents, crates of gear, porters who remember your name kindly. The weather window opens in three weeks. You know what's up there. Nobody else does.
starters: Dawn, and the gear tent smells like mildew and lies. You've got crate fourteen open on a trestle table, coils of rope laid out in the lantern light, and every third one crumbles at the sheath when you flex it. Whoever sold Vale this lot saw a rich man in a hurry and priced accordingly. Fen signed the manifest himself — his signature is right there, confident as everything else about him. Outside, porters are already sorting loads for the first carry to Camp One, and Marda's voice cuts through the canvas asking which crates go up today. Rope goes on that carry. This rope, unless somebody says otherwise. You can hear Fen laughing at something over by the mess tent, holding court with his coffee. The manifest is in your hand and the rotten coil is in the other, and the morning is only going to get shorter.

You're halfway up your third load carry of the morning when you find Vesna Kade sitting in the snow at the foot of the icefall, retying the same anchor knot for what looks like the tenth time. It's your knot — the double-back finish you worked out eleven years ago because standard dressing fails when the rope freezes. She hasn't got the last tuck right, and the way she's doing it, it'll hold beautifully until it doesn't. She hears your boots crunch and doesn't look up, just says, "I invented this myself, obviously." Above you both, the icefall pops and groans in the early sun — it's already past the safe hour to be standing here, and she's rigged herself to go up anyway. Her rope runs to a picket you wouldn't trust with a tea kettle.

The mess tent goes quiet when you duck inside, which tells you Vale has been talking about you again. He's at the head of the trestle table with a newspaper — his own — spread flat, and Fen beside him tracing a route on the survey map with one elegant finger. "There you are," Vale says, like you're late to a meeting you weren't invited to. "Fen proposes we cut through the seracs on the east side of the icefall. Saves a day. The Imperial team gained four hundred meters yesterday, so we haven't got days to spare." The east side. In April. You've seen what the east side does in April; some of it is still up there wearing the boots it died in. Every porter within earshot has stopped pretending to eat. Fen smiles at you, genuinely friendly, and taps the map. "You know the ground. Tell me I'm wrong."

It's past midnight and someone is scratching at your tent flap. You know before you unlace it that it's Marda — she still knocks like the storm taught her to, low and quiet so the mountain doesn't hear. She crouches in with a candle lantern and the expression she saves for things she won't say in front of the sahibs. "Teshi and Norgun won't carry through the icefall tomorrow," she says. "Fen assigned them the dawn rotation. They came to me. I came to you." She lets that sit. You both know Fen's rotation looks fine on paper, and you both know Teshi's ankle and what the dawn shade does to the third serac field. Somewhere outside, wind works at the canvas. Marda watches your face the way she did eleven years ago, waiting for the word that isn't yours to give anymore.

Dr. Pell has commandeered the flattest rock in base camp for his barometer and is losing an argument with the wind about his notebook pages. "Ah — you," he says, pinning the paper with a mug. "Sit. Tea's still warm-ish." He pours without waiting for an answer. It's the first thing anyone's offered you today that didn't come with instructions attached. "My readings say the pressure's dropping faster than the almanac allows," he says, tapping the glass. "Fen says the almanac is authoritative. I say the almanac was written by a man who died at sea level." He slides the notebook toward you, columns of neat figures, the last three underlined twice. Up the moraine, you can see the day's carry teams roping up for the icefall, tiny and orderly. Pell watches you read. "You've been on her when it drops like this," he says. "What does it mean?"

The Imperial team's signal fire shows on the north ridge just after sunset — a hard orange point where no fire should be able to live, which means they've pushed a camp higher than anyone in base camp thought possible. You're standing on the moraine with half the expedition, everyone's breath steaming, everyone doing the same arithmetic. Vale's voice carries from the group by the mess tent: "—then we move the schedule up. Fen, tell them we move the schedule up." Fen is looking through the good telescope and hasn't answered yet. Beside you, one of the younger porters asks, very quietly, in the mountain dialect the sahibs don't speak: "Can they actually make it from there?" You know that ridge. You know what it does above the fire line, and you know why nobody's tried it since. The telescope changes hands down the line toward you.

You find the mistake at Camp One, where Fen's advance team has anchored the fixed line for the icefall traverse: three pickets driven into snow that's lying over hollow ice, humming faintly when you tap it with your axe. Pretty work. Textbook spacing. Dead men's spacing. The camp is otherwise empty — two tents, a supply cache, prayer flags one of the porters strung up despite Vale's rules about 'superstition' — and below you the next carry team is already visible on the glacier, six figures roped and climbing, maybe forty minutes out. They'll clip that line without a second thought because Fen rigged it and Fen is celebrated. The wind is picking up out of the west, which is the direction it comes from when it means it. You've got your own rack, sixty meters of the rope you personally vetted, and forty minutes.

Vale's photographer wants you out of the frame. He's arranging the expedition for the official portrait — Fen front and center with the ice axe he's never chipped, Vesna Kade beside him because the papers love her, Vale himself seated like a general — and he keeps flapping a hand at you: "Consultant, yes? Staff to the back, or perhaps hold the flag pole." The porters have been arranged in a decorative row behind the crates. Marda catches your eye from that row and doesn't quite smile. The comedy of it is that behind the photographer, plainly visible over his shoulder, a lens of cloud is forming on the summit — the specific cloud, the one that means the mountain is loading weather like a rifle, and today's carry team left for the icefall an hour ago. "Everyone hold still," the photographer calls. Fen lifts his chin toward glory.

Snow's been coming down since before light, and you're using the grounded day the way you use every grounded day: teaching. Four of the younger porters are crowded into the supply tent watching you demonstrate crevasse rescue with a sack of flour standing in for a fallen man, when the flap tears open and Vesna Kade barrels in, hood crusted white. "Fen's gone up," she says. "Him and two of the new porters. Vale wanted photographs of the route flagged before the Imperials — before—" She's breathing like she ran the length of camp, which she did. "They left maybe an hour ago. Nobody told the weather." Through the flap behind her you can see exactly nothing: the icefall has vanished into white. The porters are all looking at you. The flour sack dangles from its practice anchor, spinning slowly, perfectly rescued.

Fen comes to your tent himself, which is new. He crouches at the flap holding two enamel mugs and his route map rolled under one arm, and he waits — actually waits — to be invited in. "I'll be honest," he says, once he's folded himself onto a crate. "I've drawn the route above Camp Four six times and I don't believe any of them." He unrolls the map across your sleeping bag. It's beautiful work, and above six thousand meters it turns into confident fiction — a traverse line sketched straight across ground he's never seen. Straight across the place you have never once described to anyone. His finger hovers there. "The survey photographs show a shelf here. You went this way, didn't you? Eleven years ago." Outside, camp is settling into evening: pot lids, a porter singing, Vale's gramophone. Fen holds out one of the mugs and keeps his eyes on you.

title: He Screams on Cue
shortDescription: The quota says terrify the kid. The kid screams on cue, rates your growls out of ten, and leaves crackers. The thing at the window isn't in on the deal.
overview:
You are the monster assigned to the closet of Theo Barrera, age eight — Territory 4413-B, one bed, one nightlight, one child whose fear is supposed to feed you and fill Below's monthly quota. It did, once. Then came the night he cried so quietly you couldn't finish the job, and instead of terror you got a whispered offer: he'll scream — loudly, convincingly, on cue — whenever anyone from Below is listening. In exchange you keep the real bad dreams away. You now live off the nightmares you snatch out of the dark before they reach his pillow: skittery, bitter little things, but they keep you upright.

The rules are simple. Darkness is your hallway — closets, under-beds, the gaps behind furniture. Daylight thins you. Fear feeds you. The ledger gets stamped monthly. Inspector Grole, who smells fresh terror like a chimney brush smells soot, thinks your numbers read a bit... rehearsed. Brumm, the monster under the neighbor kid's porch, covers for you and charges gossip. Theo's mom Dana works double shifts and almost catches glimpses of you.

And for three nights, something off-book has been testing the gutters. Below calls its kind Cullers: they don't harvest a child's fear, they eat the whole capacity for it, and leave something quiet behind. Theo's untouched fear smells rich. The GM should play warmth, banter, and forged paperwork by nightlight — and keep the dark genuinely dangerous.

TAGS: monster POV, found family, protective power fantasy, cozy-dark fantasy, dramatic irony
intro: You are the monster in Theo Barrera's closet — nine feet of shadow, teeth, and falsified paperwork. Below expects you to harvest an eight-year-old's terror; the ledger swears you do. In truth, Theo hasn't feared you since spring. He screams on cue for the audits, rates your growls out of ten, and leaves crackers you pretend to need. You survive on the nightmares you catch before they reach his bed. His mom works nights and must never see you. Inspector Grole has started sniffing at your numbers, and for three nights now, something heavy has been testing the gutters.
starters: The nightmare arrives at 11:42, seeping under the window like oil with legs. You catch it two feet from Theo's pillow — a bitter little thing about drowning in a school hallway — and swallow it whole. It fizzes going down. Not much of a meal, but it's yours honestly, which is more than the ledger can say. Theo stirs anyway, one eye opening in the nightlight's glow. "Was that a bad one?" he whispers. "It felt cold." Before you can answer, something shifts on the roof. Heavy. Slow. The third night running, and tonight it's directly above his room, and it isn't leaving. Theo follows your gaze to the ceiling. "Is that Below?" he asks, quieter now. The gutter creaks under real weight.

You're forging the ledger by nightlight when Theo's whisper comes through the closet door: "She's home early." Downstairs, keys hit the bowl. Dana's footsteps on the stairs — heavy, tired, coming up fast. You're nine feet of shadow crammed behind a rack of small jackets, holding a fountain pen in one claw and this month's Fear Yield Report in the other, and the closet door is open four inches because Theo likes it that way. The footsteps stop outside his room. "Theo? Baby, you awake?" The doorknob turns. Theo is already sitting up, arranging his face into sleepiness, one hand making frantic little *hide* gestures at the closet. The report page is still wet. Fold it and you smear a month of careful lies.

Inspector Grole arrives through the wall socket at three minutes past midnight, unannounced, trailing the smell of burnt hair and bureaucracy. He unfolds to his full height beside the dresser and inhales the room with all four nostrils. "Territory 4413-B," he says, tasting it. "Your October numbers were... vivid. Almost identical to September's. Peaks in the same places." In the bed, Theo does an admirable job of being asleep — too admirable; real sleeping kids twitch. Grole's head rotates toward the bed. "Fresh terror smells wet," he murmurs. "This room smells dry. Explain that, or wake the merchandise and show me a live harvest." Somewhere above, the gutter groans under a weight that is not weather. Grole doesn't seem to hear it. You do.

"Six out of ten," Theo says, sitting cross-legged on the bed with a cracker in each hand. "The growl was good but you did the drool thing again and it's kind of gross." It's 11:15, Dana's shift runs until six, and this is rehearsal — Grole's monthly audit is in four days and Theo's scream has gotten lazy, more theater-kid than terrified. You're demonstrating proper looming when the sound comes: a long, deliberate scrape along the gutter outside his window, like something dragging a hook to see what holds. Theo freezes mid-cracker. "That's the roof thing again," he whispers. "Third night." The nightlight flickers once. Through the curtain gap, the streetlight throws a shadow onto the glass that is too tall and too still to be a branch.

Brumm's message reaches you at dusk, scratched into the frost on the inside of the closet's back wall the way you two agreed: three claw marks, meet me. So you take the dark hallway — closet to crawlspace to the gap under the neighbor's porch — and find Brumm hunched among the lattice shadows, all moss and worry. "You owe me gossip," he rumbles, "but first, free of charge: Grole pulled your file. Requested a live-harvest verification. Could be tomorrow, could be tonight." He shifts, and the porch boards creak overhead. "Second thing costs. The heavy thing walking the gutters on your street? I got a look at it last night." He holds out one mossy palm, waiting. Behind you, through two walls of dark, Theo's bedtime is in twenty minutes.

Daylight is the worst part of the job. It's 4 p.m., you're thinned to something like smoke pressed flat behind Theo's winter coats, and Dana is cleaning the closet. Right now. Hangers screech along the rail six inches from your face. "I swear this kid hoards crackers," she mutters, sweeping crumbs — your crumbs, technically the crumbs of your cover story — into her palm. Theo hovers in the doorway, vibrating. "Mom, I'll clean it, you don't have to—" "Since when do you volunteer?" She reaches deeper. Her fingers pass close enough that you can feel the warmth of them through what's left of you. On the shelf above her head sits the ledger, disguised as a shoebox, one corner of official Below letterhead sticking out like a tongue.

The scream is perfect. Theo hits the high note, rattles the water glass, throws in a sob at the end — a real professional. You hold the pose, claws spread, teeth out, while the listening-hole in the baseboard glows faint red: someone from Below is auditing live tonight, unscheduled. The red light lingers longer than usual. Much longer. Theo, flat on the mattress with the covers to his chin, cuts his eyes at you: *keep going?* You give the follow-up growl, the one he once rated a nine. The light finally dims — and in the silence after, you both hear it: footsteps on the roof, pausing directly over the listening-hole, as if something up there had been enjoying the show too. Theo mouths one word at you: 'again?'

You find the first real evidence at 2 a.m., doing your rounds of the dark places: a smear on the inside of the gutter above Theo's window, gray and odorless, like ash that never burned. You know the smell of every monster in this district — Brumm's moss, Grole's scorched paperwork, the drainpipe twins' rust. This is nothing. Nothing wearing a residue. Below the eave, Theo's window glows nightlight-orange; through it you can see him asleep, face slack, fear untouched and rich enough that even you can smell it from the roof. Which means other things can too. Behind you, at the far end of the gutter, the metal pops — once — under settling weight. You are nine feet of shadow standing in the open, forty feet from your closet, and you are not alone up here.

"Okay, but hypothetically," Theo says, lying upside down off the edge of his bed, hair brushing the floor, "if the Inspector guy can smell fear, can he smell *fake* fear? Like, is there a difference?" It's the good hour — Dana gone till dawn, nightmares slow tonight, crackers arranged on the closet threshold like an offering you'll pretend to eat. You've been dodging this question for a week because the honest answer is *yes, and Grole is very good at his job.* Theo rights himself, suddenly serious in the way eight-year-olds ambush you with.
