"Because Marcus at school stopped being scared of anything. Like, anything. His monster moved away." Marcus. The neighbor kid. Brumm's kid. Outside, the wind carries the sound of a gutter taking weight, one street over and getting closer.

The summons is stamped in red wax and shoved through the crack under the closet's back wall, where Below's mail always arrives: NOTICE OF IRREGULARITY, TERRITORY 4413-B. YIELD CURVES UNDER REVIEW. INSPECTOR GROLE TO CONDUCT UNANNOUNCED VERIFICATION WITHIN THE LUNAR CYCLE. Below that, in Grole's own cramped claw: *I remember when your harvests kept me up at night. Looking forward to seeing the old form.* You're reading it a third time when Theo's knuckle raps the closet door — twice, pause, once, the all-clear knock. "You got mail? Cool. Is it bad?" He's in dinosaur pajamas holding two crackers and a flashlight. Overhead, right on schedule for the third night running, something crosses the roof with the patience of a thing that has already picked its house. Theo's flashlight beam drifts toward the ceiling.

title: The Getaway Money Has My Face
shortDescription: The Bank owns your kingdom — deed and all. So the newly crowned monarch (you) is assembling a crew to rob its vault and steal the country back.
overview:
You are the freshly crowned monarch of Belverre — beloved, mint-new profile on every coin, and functionally a tenant. Deep in the palace archive you found the Founding Mortgage: three centuries ago, the first sovereign borrowed a nation into existence from the Meridian Counting House and never paid it off. The deed to the entire kingdom sits in the Counting House's vault — the vault that has never been cracked — and at the Centennial Audit, six weeks from now, Governor Aurelian Grieve intends to foreclose. Politely.

So you're going to rob the Bank that owns you.

By day: decrees you can't sign without an auditor's countersignature, state banquets, and a courtship the Bank arranged between you and the Governor's sharp-eyed heir, Cass Grieve. By night: a hood, a borrowed name, and the lower city, where you recruit a crew — Wren Callow, a forger jailed for counterfeiting coins bearing your face; Marlowe 'the Latch,' a retired safecracker who insists the vault sings; Pia Ostrend, a terrified junior auditor who knows a shelf number. None of them can learn who you are. Or maybe some of them must. Your fame is your worst liability and your best tool: every guard knows your profile, and every door in the kingdom opens for it.

Tone: gaslamp heist caper — wit, tension, double lives, found-family crew, and a living city where royal duty and criminal planning keep colliding at the worst moments.

TAGS: heist, royalty, double life, gaslamp fantasy, found family, caper
intro: You are the sovereign of Belverre, four months crowned, adored by crowds who stamp your profile onto every coin — and you have just learned that none of it is yours. In the palace archive you found the Founding Mortgage: the kingdom itself is collateral on a three-hundred-year-old loan, and the deed lies in the vault of the Meridian Counting House, the bank whose auditors countersign your every decree. At the Centennial Audit, six weeks from now, the Bank may foreclose. No army can help you; the debt is legal. So you've made a decision worthy of your ancestors: steal the deed. Most nights now, the crown stays home — and you go recruiting.
starters: The Rope and Anchor smells of tallow and wet wool, and nobody in it has looked at you twice — the hood helps, and so does the fact that no one expects a sovereign to be nursing sour ale in the lower city at midnight. Across the table, Wren Callow turns one of her counterfeit coins over her knuckles. Your profile flashes on it with every roll. "Three years in the Wells for stamping that face," she says. "Now some stranger in a nice cloak wants to hire the best forger in Belverre for a job they won't name, against a mark they won't name." She sets the coin down between you, your own face staring up. "So. Convince me you're worth hanging for." The barkeep is drifting closer with a rag he isn't using, and the coin sits there, waiting to be picked up or left alone.

Governor Aurelian Grieve holds the decree at arm's length as if it might be damp. Around the council table, your ministers study their hands. It's a small thing — funds for the flood wall in the river quarter — but the auditor's countersignature line sits empty, and Grieve's pen sits capped beside his teacup. 'Majesty,' he says warmly, "the Counting House exists only to be helpful. Perhaps we table this until after the Centennial Audit. Six weeks is no time at all." He smiles like a man who has already counted everything in the room, including you. Beside him, his heir Cass Grieve watches you over steepled fingers — the one person here who seems genuinely curious what you'll say next. The pen. The decree. The forty-one days. Grieve waits, patient as interest.

Rain hammers the awning of the chandler's shop where you've cornered Pia Ostrend, junior auditor, third clerk of the Meridian Counting House, currently clutching her satchel like a shield. "I don't know you," she says, which is true, since you're a hood and a borrowed name tonight. "I don't talk about the House. They make you sign things. In triplicate." But she hasn't run, and she hasn't screamed, and when you mentioned shelf inventories her eyes did something complicated. Down the street, a lamplighter is working his way toward you, pole over his shoulder, and every pool of light he leaves behind makes this conversation more visible. Pia glances at him too. "You have until he gets here," she whispers, "and then I was never on this street."

Marlowe the Latch doesn't look up when you enter his clock shop, though the bell above the door announced you and it's an hour past closing. He's bent over an eviscerated pocket watch, jeweler's loupe screwed into one eye. "If you're here about the Meridian vault," he says, "the answer's no. Retired. Fingers like old rope." You haven't said a word yet. He sets down his tweezers and finally squints at your hooded silhouette. "Fourth one this year to come sniffing. But you're the first who walks like the guards won't touch them." He taps his own ear. "That vault sings, stranger. Seven tumblers in harmony. I still hear it some nights." Behind him, a hundred clocks tick out of rhythm, and the old man waits to hear what you'll offer that the last three didn't.

You're halfway down the servants' stair with your hood in your hand when Cass Grieve steps out of the gallery above, holding a candle and an expression of polite fascination. "Majesty. Curious hour for a walk." The Bank arranged this courtship the way it arranges everything — on paper, with witnesses — but Cass's eyes have never once been on paper. They descend two steps, taking in your plain coat, your scuffed boots, the coin purse at your belt that's far too light for royalty. "Here's my difficulty," they say. "Father would want to know about this. And I would want to know why you look like a person about to do something interesting." The candle gutters. The door to the lower courtyard is twenty steps below, unlocked, and Cass is standing exactly between you and it.

The Meridian Counting House smells of ink, brass polish, and money that has never been outdoors. Governor Grieve conducts your official tour personally — "an honor, Majesty, before the Centennial" — past teller cages, ledger halls, clerks who bow without dropping a single digit. You are here as a courtesy. You are also counting doors. "And below us," Grieve says fondly, pausing at a balustrade over a stairwell that descends into lamplit dark, "the vault. Never opened but by schedule, never cracked in three hundred years." Somewhere down there is a deed with your kingdom's name on it. A junior auditor hurries past with an armful of files — young, freckled, terrified of everyone — and drops a sheet at your feet. Grieve is already turning toward the boardroom. The paper lies there, covered in shelf numbers.

Run. The whistle behind you says the two watchmen have decided your hood is worth a second look, and the lower city obliges with alleys — you take one, then another, boots skidding on wet cobbles past a fishmonger's shuttered stall. Tonight was supposed to be simple: meet a fence who knows where Wren Callow drinks, ask two questions, leave. Instead the fence wanted your hood off, and you couldn't allow that, and now here you are. Ahead, the alley splits: left toward the canal and its moored barges, right toward a lit doorway where someone is stacking crates and watching you approach with unhurried interest. Behind you, boots. In your pocket, ironically, a handful of coins with your face on them — enough to buy help, if you dare show the money.

Dawn finds you in the archive again, third night running, the Founding Mortgage spread under the lamp like an autopsy. Article Nine. Compound terms. The first sovereign's signature, brown with age, mortgaging everything from the harbor chains to the crown on your head. You've copied the vault's deed number onto your cuff in pencil. Behind you, the archive door opens — Brother Fennick, the ancient archivist, shuffling in with his morning candle and his terrible eyesight. "Someone's been at the deep shelves," he announces to the room, not yet seeing you. "Third night. I've half a mind to report it." He is loyal, deaf in one ear, and the only person alive who might notice which document is missing from folio C. He's also between you and the door, and the palace bells are about to ring the servants awake.

The state banquet is on its fourth course and its fortieth lie. To your left, Governor Grieve toasts "three centuries of partnership between Crown and Counting House" while the ambassador from Vossmark applauds. To your right, Cass Grieve leans in under cover of the applause. "You've checked the clock nine times," they murmur. "Either my company is unbearable or you have somewhere to be." Both, possibly — in one hour, in a lamplit yard off Tanner's Row, a retired safecracker named Marlowe has agreed to meet a stranger about "a musical instrument." Miss it and he's gone; his note was clear. A footman refills your glass. Grieve is winding toward asking you to say a few words, and Cass is still watching you with that look, the one that keeps almost becoming a question.

Your valet, Osric, is the only soul in the palace who knows the sovereign's bed is stuffed with pillows most nights, and right now he's holding the rope ladder and radiating disapproval. "The garden watch changes at the half bell," he mutters. "You have four minutes, and I am too old to explain your corpse to the council." Below the window: the yew hedge, the dark, the lower city where a forger named Wren Callow was released from the Wells this morning — pardoned, quietly, by a signature only you could have provided. She'll want to know who bought her freedom and why. You have a hood, a borrowed name, and no idea whether she'll thank her benefactor or put a knife to their throat. The half bell begins to toll. Osric steadies the ladder and looks anywhere but at you.

title: The Spies Change Diapers
shortDescription: One of your daycare toddlers is prophesied to decide the fate of the world. Both empires sent spies. Great — you needed the extra staff.
overview:
You are the head (and until recently, only) caretaker at Bramble House, the daycare in Armistice — the neutral town where the Hero's Alliance and the Dark Dominion signed their peace. As a gesture of goodwill, both courts enroll their children here: Ember, a dragon hatchling who sneezes fire when overexcited; Morrow, the Lich King's solemn kid, who keeps lovingly reanimating the class goldfish; Pip, the Chosen Hero's daughter, who summons a legendary sword during tantrums; and half a dozen other tiny catastrophes.

Then an oracle mumbled that one child at Bramble House 'will decide the age to come,' and both courts panicked politely. Each planted a spy on your staff: Nettle, a dark-court assassin posing as the art teacher (allergic to glitter, suspiciously excellent at storytime), and Bram, an Alliance knight undercover as the janitor (terrible liar, cries at finger paintings). You clocked them both on day one. You've said nothing. You're short-staffed. They can do diaper duty.

Play is pure cozy sitcom: herd small gods through snack time, mediate between the Demon Queen and the Paladin-Commander at pickup, confiscate cursed show-and-tell items, and watch two enemy spies accidentally become your family. Nothing terrible ever happens here — Bramble House won't allow it. The scariest people in the world are terrified of your clipboard.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, found family, comedy, slice of life, lovable chaos
intro: You run Bramble House, the only daycare in Armistice, the treaty town between the Hero's Alliance and the Dark Dominion. Both courts send their children here as living proof the peace is real: a dragon hatchling, the Lich King's quiet kid, the Chosen Hero's daughter, and more. Ever since an oracle declared that one of your kids "will decide the age to come," both courts have planted spies on your staff as 'assistants.' They are extremely obvious about it. You've said nothing — you need the help. The kids adore you, the parents fear your clipboard, and every day is a small, survivable apocalypse.
starters: Six forty-five in the morning, and Bramble House smells like crayons and yesterday's applesauce. You're the only one here — officially. Unofficially, Nettle's shadow keeps crossing the art room window as she "inventories supplies" for the third time this week, and Bram's mop bucket has been parked outside the cubby wall for ten minutes while he holds a stethoscope to the drywall. Neither of them knows the other one came in early too. The kids arrive in forty minutes. Your clipboard sits on the front desk with today's list: snack duty unassigned, the goldfish tank needs checking after last night's 'incident,' and someone has to sign for a package from the Dark Dominion labeled EDUCATIONAL MATERIALS (DO NOT SHAKE). Through the window, the first parent's carriage — black, ominous, tastefully skulled — is already rounding the corner.

Snack time, and it's going almost suspiciously well until Ember gets excited about raisins. The sneeze takes out a plate of crackers, singes the alphabet rug's letter Q, and sets the tip of Bram's mop smoldering — he was 'janitoring' three feet from the dragon hatchling, as he has been all morning, in what he clearly believes is a subtle way. Now he's stamping out his mop and loudly reassuring everyone that he is calm, which no one asked. Ember's eyes are going wet and enormous, the pre-cry face that precedes a much bigger sneeze. Across the table, Morrow slides their own crackers toward Ember without a word. Pip announces she can fix the rug and starts reaching for something that makes the air hum faintly. The fire extinguisher is on the wall. Your clipboard is closer.

Naptime. Nine cots, seven sleeping children, blessed silence — and the class goldfish drifting serenely through the air above them, trailing faint green light and a thread of water that isn't falling. Morrow is sitting up on their cot, small hands raised like a conductor, expression solemn as a funeral. "Bubbles was lonely in the tank," they whisper when they see you in the doorway. "Now Bubbles can visit everyone." Bubbles bumps gently against the ceiling. In the hall behind you, Nettle has materialized without a sound, watching Morrow with the intent stillness of someone composing a report. Ember stirs, one eye cracking open, nostril already twitching toward the shiny floating thing. You have maybe fifteen seconds before naptime becomes an aquarium-themed disaster with a fire component.

Pickup time is a hostage negotiation you run daily. The Demon Queen arrives at 4:58, wings folded politely, and the Paladin-Commander arrives at 4:59, armor squeaking, and now they're both at the gate radiating diplomatic courtesy at each other while their children — currently best friends, currently covered in blue paint — refuse to leave the sandbox. "After you," says the Demon Queen. "No, after you," says the Paladin-Commander, hand resting near his sword hilt in a way he probably thinks is casual. Bram has positioned himself between them with a rake, pretending to landscape gravel. Behind you, Pip tugs your sleeve and holds up today's finger painting: two stick figures, one with horns, one with a halo, holding hands over what is unmistakably a pile of bodies labeled BAD GUYS. She wants to know which parent should get it.

"And for show-and-tell," announces little Fenwick, son of the Dominion's Grand Necromancer, "I brought Grandpa's ring!" The ring is whispering. You can hear it from across the circle rug — a low, silky murmur that's making the mobile above the reading nook rotate against the breeze. Ember leans in, delighted. Pip leans in, hand drifting toward empty air in a way you've learned to watch. Nettle has gone very still by the craft table, one hand inside her apron, eyes locked on the ring like it owes her money. Fenwick beams and holds it higher. "It knows everybody's NAME," he says proudly. The ring says yours. Show-and-tell has a confiscation basket. It's on the shelf behind you, next to the clipboard, and Fenwick is a biter about his treasures.

The tantrum starts over the last blue cup, as wars often do. By the time you cross the room, Pip is red-faced, tears streaming, and holding a legendary sword taller than she is — golden, humming, wreathed in destiny, its point wobbling six inches above your good story rug. "MARLOW TOOK THE BLUE CUP AND IT WAS MY TURN," she wails. The sword flares in sympathy. Marlow, a demonkin toddler with the blue cup and zero remorse, drinks from it slowly while maintaining eye contact. Bram has flattened himself against the supply closet, whispering "that's the actual Dawnbrand, that's the actual Dawnbrand" in a voice he thinks is inaudible. The other kids have formed an audience. Someone starts a slow chant of "sword, sword, sword." Pip hiccups, and the blade dips closer to the rug.

Storytime, and Nettle is destroying you at your own job again. Nine children sit in a perfect rapt semicircle while the "art teacher" performs all the voices for The Littlest Ogre, including a villain rasp that is, you'd swear, a real person's real voice done from memory. She never learned this at art school, because she never went to art school, because there is a knife in her boot. The kids don't care. The kids love her. The problem is the craft table behind her, where Ember has quietly discovered the glitter tub — the big one, the forbidden one — and is carrying it toward the circle with both arms and pure evangelical joy, directly at the woman whose glitter allergy once cleared the building in four minutes. Nettle turns the page. Ember gets closer. Nobody else has noticed.

You find Bram in the hallway at ten a.m., crying at the wall. Not sniffling — properly crying, mop abandoned, big knightly shoulders shaking as he stares at the display of this week's finger paintings. "It's the one Morrow did," he manages, pointing at a grey smudge with a small yellow smudge beside it. "It's them and the goldfish. Look how the fish is SMILING." Down the hall, the actual Morrow is watching him through the classroom door's window with an expression of grave scientific interest, and behind Morrow you can see the classroom in Nettle's sole charge: suspiciously quiet, lights dimmed, all nine children lying on the rug. Either she's invented a nap technique the courts would kill for, or something in there requires your immediate professional attention. Bram blows his nose on a paper towel and apologizes to the painting.

Drop-off, and the Lich King is on your doorstep at eight sharp, seven feet of ancient dread stooping under the welcome banner, holding Morrow's hand with skeletal gentleness. "They did not finish breakfast," he intones, in a voice that has ended kingdoms. "The lunchbox contains a boiled egg, crackers, and a small bone. The bone is a comfort object. It is labeled." Morrow stares up at you, silent, clutching the goldfish-shaped lunchbox. Behind you in the entry hall, Bram has dropped his mop and is standing at what is very obviously parade attention, and somewhere in the coatroom Nettle has begun humming casually in a way that means she's listening to every word. The Lich King crouches, dust sifting from his robes, and looks you dead in the eye sockets. "They spoke of you all weekend," he says. "The one with the clipboard." He waits, as if that requires an answer.

It's raining, which means indoor recess, which means the noise in Bramble House has achieved a physical texture. Ember is stacking blocks with religious focus, Pip and Marlow are negotiating a treaty over the toy castle with more good faith than their parents ever managed, and you've just noticed that the coffee tin in the break nook contains two anonymous notes. One, in razor-neat script: "The girl. Watch the girl. Report anomalies." The other, in earnest block letters: "THE QUIET ONE BEARS OBSERVING. FOR THE ALLIANCE. P.S. WE ARE OUT OF PAPER TOWELS." Nettle and Bram are on opposite sides of the room, each pretending to supervise, each writing in a small notebook, each glancing at the coffee tin at intervals. Neither knows about the other's note. A crash from the toy castle suggests the treaty has collapsed, and the coffee is getting cold in your hand.

title: The Lake Comes Back Friday
shortDescription: The dam drawdown exposed a drowned town — and its missing payroll gold. Refill starts Friday. Everyone with a shovel and a grudge knows it too.
overview:
In 1949 the valley town of Carverton was evacuated and flooded for the Kettle River Dam. The mill payroll — a strongbox of gold coin — never made it out; the driver swore he was hijacked, did twenty years, and died silent. Now the dam needs repairs, the reservoir has been drawn down to cracked mud and leaning steeples, and the refill gates close Friday week. Eleven days. You hold the only real lead: your late grandmother's brass key, her hand-drawn street map, and a letter insisting the gold never left town.

You're not alone. Dee Okafor runs the only airboat that can cross the mudflats — for a cut that changes daily. The Reyes brothers are stripping copper from the ruins and salting their claims with crowbars. Boone Callis is flying documentary drones over everything and selling footage to whoever bids. The Vantiveer heirs arrived with lawyers and hired muscle claiming legal title to the mill. Deputy Lund guards a perimeter she can't actually hold, and Margo Hale, eighty-nine, the last living evacuee, remembers streets no map shows — everyone wants an hour of her time.

The lakebed is closed, unstable, and sinking under everyone's boots. Alliances form over campfires and dissolve over shovels. Play bold: caution is just giving the water your gold. Tone: Golden Kamuy energy — brutal scrapes, absurd humor, loyalty earned the hard way.

TAGS: treasure hunt, ensemble, ticking clock, contemporary adventure, crime, dark comedy
intro: You're in Alder Gap, the reservoir town, in a motel full of out-of-state trucks and borrowed boats. Below the dam road, the drawdown has bared what nobody's seen in seventy-five years: Carverton, the drowned town, standing in gray mud — church, mill smokestack, streets of collapsed roofs. The refill gates close Friday next week; eleven days, then it all goes under for another lifetime. In your jacket: your grandmother's brass key, her hand-drawn map of streets she fled as a girl, and her letter swearing the mill payroll gold never left town. The lakebed is officially closed. Nobody here cares.
starters: Dee Okafor's airboat is the ugliest thing at the boat launch and the only one with mud on the hull instead of trailer dust. She's got a whiteboard nailed to a post: TODAY'S RATE, followed by a number she's currently erasing with her sleeve. "Don't look at me like that," she says without turning around. "Diesel went up. Also a man tried to pay me in commemorative coins yesterday, so trust is down." She writes a bigger number. Behind you, two guys in matching camo are already counting bills, and one of them keeps glancing at your jacket pocket like he can smell the map through it. Dee finally faces you, marker uncapped, eyebrows up. First trip out leaves in ten minutes, and the seat count is one less than the number of people standing here.

It's 2 a.m. and you're a hundred yards past the CLOSED sign when the lakebed takes your left boot. Not grabs — takes. The mud closes over your ankle with a sound like a kiss, and when you pull, your knee sinks instead. Somewhere behind you, back at the fence, a flashlight beam swings lazy arcs — Deputy Lund's night walk, right on schedule. Overhead, worse: a drone's green running light drifts closer, low and curious, camera gimbal tilting down at you like a bored god. Boone Callis sells footage to anyone with a wallet, and "trespasser stuck in mud at night" probably fetches a decent price. Your grandmother's map crinkles inside your jacket every time you twist. The flashlight is maybe four minutes away. The drone is thirty seconds. The mud isn't going anywhere.

The Pinecone Diner at 6 a.m. is all treasure hunters pretending to be fishermen. You've got the hand-drawn map flat on the table under a napkin, matching your grandmother's penciled streets to the sodden grid you can see through the window — and you don't hear the younger Reyes brother until he's sliding into your booth uninvited, setting down a crowbar like other people set down car keys. "That's a nice napkin," he says. "Real interesting napkin. My brother Tomás says everybody with a napkin like that ends up needing a partner or a dentist." He smiles with all his teeth to demonstrate the options. Behind the counter, the waitress refills coffees without looking up. Out the window, the first airboat of the morning coughs to life, and half the diner starts reaching for their checks at once.

Margo Hale holds court on the porch of the Alder Gap Senior Center in a lawn chair with a cooler of root beer, and the line to talk to her is nine people deep. A Vantiveer lawyer is up front offering her a "consultation fee" in an envelope; she makes him hold it while she finishes her drink. You're at the back of the line when she looks straight past everyone and points a knuckly finger at you. "You," she says. "Come here. You've got a face I buried in 1949." The lawyer objects. She tells him the line has rules and he's breaking them. Eight strangers turn to stare at you, and at least three of them start doing math about who your people were. Margo pats the empty lawn chair beside her, once.

Deputy Lund catches you with one leg over the perimeter fence at dawn, which is embarrassing for everybody. She doesn't draw anything, just stands there with a thermos and the expression of someone guarding six miles of fence alone. "Fourteen people over this thing since Tuesday," she says. "You'd be fifteen. I got two citation books and one working pen." Down the slope behind her, the drowned town steams in the early light — and you can see figures already moving between the ruined roofs, tiny and busy, because everyone else went over somewhere she wasn't. She follows your gaze, sighs, and drinks her coffee. "Give me one reason you're different from the rest of these vultures," she says, "and make it fast, because my radio's about to go off about something worse than you." It crackles, right on cue.

Boone Callis finds you in the motel parking lot before you've finished your gas station coffee. He's got a tablet, and on the tablet is drone footage of you — yesterday, on the dam overlook, holding a hand-drawn map up against the horizon like an idiot. "Great composition," he says. "Really cinematic. The Vantiveers' people offered me four hundred for anybody photographing documents near the mill sightlines. You, my friend, are documents-adjacent." He lets that sit while a drone the size of a dinner plate hovers over his shoulder like a parrot. "But I'm a filmmaker first. So here's the thing — I'll sit on this clip for twenty-four hours, free, if you tell me what's on the paper. Or outbid them. Or," he shrugs, "be interesting. Interesting has a discount." Behind him, two trucks with out-of-state plates pull in slow, windows down, listening.

There's a process server leaning on your truck when you come out of the motel office, and behind him, a man built like a vending machine wearing a polo shirt that says VANTIVEER SITE SECURITY. The server holds out a folder. "Notice of asserted title," he says. "The mill parcel, the mill contents, and — this is the fun part — "any chattels removed therefrom since 1949." You were observed inquiring about airboat rates yesterday." The vending machine cracks his knuckles like it's part of his job description. Across the lot, Dee Okafor watches from her truck bed, eating chips, openly enjoying this. The server's still holding the folder out. Somewhere in your jacket, the brass key feels suddenly heavy, and you're very aware neither of these men has looked at your hands yet.

The campfire on the ridge above the drawdown is neutral ground — that's the rule, nobody remembers who made it. Tonight it's the elder Reyes brother, a woman with a metal detector held together with duct tape, and a kid who claims he's a grad student and definitely isn't. Below, the drowned town sits black against gray mud, one window somewhere catching moonlight like it's got something to say. "Payroll driver did twenty years and never talked," Tomás Reyes says, poking the fire. "Twenty years. You don't stay quiet that long to protect nothing." The detector woman snorts. The kid writes it down. Then Tomás looks across the flames at you, the newcomer who hasn't said a word yet, and asks the question everyone here asks eventually: "So who were your people, and what do you think they left behind?" The fire pops. Everyone waits.

From the dam road overlook, the whole town lies open like a body on a table, and you've got your grandmother's map turned sideways trying to make her pencil lines match the mud. There — the smokestack, the church, and a street she drew that flat-out doesn't exist down there. An old man in a Kettle River Power windbreaker spits over the rail beside you. "Everybody's got a map," he says. "Fella yesterday had one printed off eBay. Watched him walk it straight into a sinkhole up to his belt." He squints at yours, and something in his face changes — slows down. "Huh. That one's hand-drawn." Below, an airboat carves a line across the flats, and a drone rises off the ruins like a fly off roadkill. The old man is still looking at your map, and he's stopped pretending not to.

You're picking your way down Carverton's main street — actual street, cobbles under an inch of slime — when the shouting starts two houses over. The Reyes brothers have another crew backed against a collapsed porch, crowbars out, arguing about whose spray-painted X got there first. "That's OUR X," the shorter Reyes yells. "You painted YOUR X over OUR X. That's X fraud!" One of the other crew is holding a length of copper pipe like a bat. Everyone's ankle-deep and sinking slightly, which robs the standoff of some dignity. Nobody's noticed you yet. Your grandmother's map says the address you actually want is one street north — past the argument, past a roof that's leaning like it's eavesdropping. A drone drifts overhead, filming everything, and one of the brothers glances up, then around, and his eyes land on you standing there with a map in your hand.

title: The Forge Wants My Heart
shortDescription: You're the monster haunting the fallen hold — its rightful heir. Your kin have come to slay you and relight the forge... with your heart.
overview:
Three hundred years ago the hold of Belgrund fell in a single night, when the king's great work — the Deep Ember, a second sun for the forges — broke loose. You were the forge-heir. You caught it. You sealed it inside your own chest and died on your feet. The songs above remember it differently: they say the heir betrayed Belgrund and broke the forge. Now you are the Hollow Smith, a revenant of ash and iron, keeping the hold's dead in their quiet half-sleep and the furnace-thing in your ribs banked low.

An expedition has entered your halls: Runa Emberline, forge-heir of the exile line — your own blood — leading warriors, sappers, a chronicler, and a hired human freight company that hauls supplies on goat-drawn barges along the flooded deep roads. Their prophecy says the forge will be relit with the traitor's heart. Yours. And here is the knife: they might be right. Your heart could save your people — or unbind what it holds.

You cannot simply walk up and explain; your voice is furnace-rasp, your face is legend's villain, and Hearth-Priest Morvok can compel the dead you protect. So you shepherd them unseen. Hush your restless subjects. Hammer warnings into walls. Leave gifts of forged steel. Decide what your name is worth — and what your heart is for.

Tone: solemn dark fantasy with warmth in the cracks; dramatic irony, aching near-misses of recognition, and the slow question of whether truth or sacrifice comes first.

TAGS: dark fantasy, undead protagonist, dwarves, protective monster, dramatic irony, tragic heroism
intro: You are the Hollow Smith — what remains of the heir of Belgrund, the mountain hold that fell three hundred years ago. When the Deep Ember broke loose from the king's forge, you caught it, sealed it in your own chest, and died standing. Now you walk the dark halls as ash and iron, keeping the hold's restless dead quiet and the thing in your ribs asleep. The world above remembers you as the traitor who broke Belgrund. And now, for the first time in centuries, there are living dwarves in your halls — an expedition come to reclaim the hold, relight the forge, and slay you.
starters: The first living breath in three hundred years reaches you through the vent-shafts: pipe smoke, wet wool, goat. You stand at the lip of the Undergate gallery and watch torchlight bloom below — a barge poling up the flooded deep road, laden with crates, hauled by shaggy goats swimming in harness. Dwarves in expedition leathers walk the drowned causeway beside it. At the prow stands a young dwarf with your family's copper-red braids, holding a lantern high, and the shape of her face stops the ember in your chest like a hand laid on a bell. Runa Emberline. Your blood, come home. Behind her, a robed figure with a censer chants something low, and along the causeway three of your dead subjects lift their heads from their long half-sleep and turn toward the sound. They are waking wrong — jerky, summoned, not soothed. The barge is still forty yards from the first of them.

You are hammering when they find your work. Kneeling in the dark of the Third Stair, you have spent the night driving letters into stone — GAS BELOW THE COPPER DOOR — each strike muffled by your palm of ash. Now boots ring on the landing above, and you press yourself into the alcove behind a fallen pillar. Two dwarves descend with lanterns: a broad one with a sapper's satchel, and a thin one with an ink-stained ledger who stops dead at your carving. "This is fresh," the chronicler whispers, touching the bright cut edges. "Hours old." The sapper unslings a crossbow and turns a slow circle, lantern swinging, and its light crawls toward your alcove one flagstone at a time. Below you both, faint through the floor, you can smell the copper door's seep already — sweet and wrong. They are standing directly over it.

One of your dead is weeping again. Old Hessa, who was a bead-caster in life, sits in the dry fountain of the Lantern Court rocking her skull of a head, and her grief is spreading — a dozen quiet corpses in the surrounding arcades beginning to stir, to remember, to grind their teeth. You have soothed her a hundred times: a hand on her shoulder, the low furnace-hum that passes for your lullaby. But tonight her weeping has an audience. At the far end of the court, frozen mid-step with a shuttered lantern, stands a living dwarf warrior who has clearly wandered ahead of her expedition — young, axe half-raised, staring at Hessa with more horror than she can hold. Hessa hasn't noticed her yet. The other dead have. Somewhere behind the warrior, distant voices call a name: "Signy! Signy, fall back!"

You leave the gift where they'll trip over it: a short blade, forged last night at your banked coals, laid on a cloth across the safe path — the one that doesn't cross the rotted bridge. Steel speaks where your ruined voice can't. Good work says a friend made this. Now you wait in the flue above the junction, ember ticking softly in your ribs, and listen to the expedition argue their way toward you. Runa Emberline's voice arrives first, tired and iron-edged: "The maps say the bridge." Then a human voice, one of the freight-haulers, flat and practical: "Maps are three hundred years old, boss." They round the corner. Runa sees the blade. She goes very still, crouches, and lifts it — and you watch her thumb find the maker's mark at the tang. Your mark. Her family's mark. "Everyone stop moving," she says quietly. "Someone's been here."

The ember wakes you. It happens rarely — a lurch in your chest like a coal turning over, heat flushing up through the iron of your throat — and it only happens when someone strikes forge-fire in Belgrund. You rise from the anvil where you rest standing, as you died, and follow the pull down through the Smelter Deeps. In the old proving-hall, the expedition has made camp. They've lit a field-forge, a little portable thing, and a robed priest — censer on his belt, hammers embroidered at his cuffs — is feeding it consecrated coal while the others sleep in bedrolls between goat-drawn barges dragged up out of the floodwater. Each pinch of coal he burns, the thing in your ribs answers, straining a little harder toward its kin-flame. He hasn't noticed the ash sifting from the ceiling vents above him. Your ash. You are leaking heat, and the priest is looking up.

Rain from the surface takes six days to reach the deep roads, and tonight it arrives all at once. You are wading the flooded Ninth Concourse, checking your dead sleepers on their high ledges, when you hear it: the boom of water in the feeder channels, and beneath it, panicked human shouting. Around the bend, one of the freight barges has slewed sideways in the rising current, goats screaming in their harness, a young human hauler waist-deep and losing her grip on the tow line. Crates of the expedition's black powder are lashed to that barge. Downstream — where the current wants to take it all — is the Ashgate, and behind the Ashgate sleep two hundred of your subjects in shallow water. The hauler sees you then. A shape of ash and iron, chest-glow bleeding through the flood-mist. She doesn't scream. She just says, hoarsely, 'Please.'

The chronicler has found your name. You watch from the shadowed gallery of the Hall of Records as he works alone by candle — a narrow dwarf with a bad cough, brushing three centuries of ash from a memorial wall. Your memorial wall, carved by survivors in the first weeks after the fall, before the exile. He reads aloud as he uncovers it, quill scratching: "...and the heir stood at the forge-mouth and would not... would not what? Damn it, the next line's defaced." It is. You defaced it yourself, two hundred years ago, in a bad decade. The true words are gone but the wall around them is not, and he is patient, and he is close. His candle gutters. He mutters about drafts and doesn't look up. Behind him, on the far side of the hall, one of your restless dead has risen from her niche and is walking slowly toward the light.

"The traitor's heart still beats down there." The words come to you through half a mile of speaking-tube — the old brass network that once carried orders from throne to forge, which you keep polished out of habit. You stand at a junction node with your head bowed to the flared mouth, listening to the expedition's council. The priest, Morvok, has the floor: "The prophecy is plain. The Ember returns to the forge through the traitor's heart. We take it, we relight, Belgrund lives again." A pause. Then Runa Emberline, younger, harder to read: "And if the songs are wrong about the traitor?" Laughter from someone. "Three hundred years of songs, forge-heir." Their voices are perhaps ten minutes' walk above you, in the old Muster Hall. Between here and there: two collapsed stairs, one sleeping ward of your dead, and a door you sealed for good reason. The council is still talking.

You are mending a dead child's boot when the horn sounds. Little Brami, four decades old forever, sleeps in a stone cradle in the Cistern Ward, and his boot came apart last week, and it matters to you that it doesn't. The horn — a real horn, bronze, blown by living lungs — rolls down through the halls from the direction of the Undergate, three long notes. An arrival call. A claim. Around you, the Cistern Ward's dozen sleepers shift at the sound, old muscle-memory dragging at them; Brami's small hand closes on your finger of black iron. Water drips. Far off, faint as a heartbeat, comes the answering sound you have dreaded for three centuries: marching boots, many of them, and the creak of laden barges. The horn sounds again, closer to your dead than any living thing has come since the fall. Brami's eyes are open now, and he is looking at you.

They've cornered one of yours. You arrive at the Anvil Steps too late for quiet: three expedition warriors have a dead miner — Torv, gentle Torv, who still carries his pick because his hands won't unclose — backed against a pillar with spears leveled, and he is confused and frightened and beginning to make the low grinding sound that means he'll swing. 'Hold!' A dwarf woman shoulders through the spear-line — copper braids, forge-heir's torc, your grandmother's jaw. Runa Emberline puts herself between the spears and the corpse. "Look at him. He's not attacking. He's guarding something." She's right. Behind Torv's pillar is the collapsed shaft where his crew died, where he has stood watch for three hundred years. Torv raises his pick anyway, slow as a drawbridge. The warriors' arms tense. You are one shadowed archway away, and nobody living has seen you yet.

title: Sentenced to My Table
shortDescription: Every monster you spared got paroled to your farm. The ogre bakes, the assassin naps in your chair. The newest arrival is the one fight you never won.
overview:
You were the realm's most decorated monster-hunter, and its most annoying: you never brought back a head when you could bring back the whole monster, alive and arguing. The tribunal's revenge was elegant. Fine — they're YOUR problem. Every enemy you defeated and refused to kill now wears an iron parole cuff sworn to your name and lives on your farm in the Hollow Vale. The cuffs warm when their wearer means harm. Only your hand opens them. And if one ever burns red, the law is brutally simple: your sword finishes what you started.

The household: Bram, a nine-foot ogre who bakes obsessively and hides under the table during thunderstorms. Sefa, formerly the Silk Court's deadliest assassin, now the sleepiest creature alive — she can kill a man with a spoon but mostly naps in sunbeams. Nettle, a teenage hag who hexes anyone rude to the family. Warden Odile Crane, a tribunal judge, inspects monthly with a ledger and a standing hope of catching you slipping.

Last week's wagon delivered Vesper, the Red Saint — a swords-saint the tribunal believes you defeated. You didn't. Your one duel ended in a draw both of you lied about. Vesper knows. You know. Nobody else can ever find out.

Play it warm, funny, and quietly dangerous. Chore charts and bounty hunters. Burnt bread and drawn steel. They're monsters. They're yours.

TAGS: found family, cozy fantasy with teeth, retired legend, rivalry, slice of life, drama
intro: You were the realm's most feared hunter — the one who never took a head when you could take the whole monster home instead. The tribunal's compromise now eats breakfast at your table: every enemy you beat and refused to kill wears an iron cuff sworn to your name, paroled to your farm in the Hollow Vale. Bram the ogre bakes. Sefa, once the Silk Court's finest killer, naps anywhere warm. Nettle hexes rude postmen. If a cuff ever burns red, the law says your sword ends its wearer. Last week the wagon delivered Vesper, the Red Saint — the only fight you never actually won. The tribunal doesn't know that. Vesper does.
starters: Dawn, and the kitchen already smells like a crime scene made of rye. Bram fills half the room, elbow-deep in dough, apologizing to it. Sefa is asleep on the windowsill with a spoon in her hand — you've learned not to ask. At the far end of your table sits Vesper, whetting a sword nobody gave permission to exist, drawing the stone along the edge in slow, patient strokes. Every scrape says the same thing: *I know what you know.* Nettle slides into her chair, looks between you two, and says, "Why does breakfast feel like a funeral?" Bram sets down a loaf burnt black as a judge's heart and beams like it's a triumph. Vesper stops sharpening and looks at you over the bread, waiting to see how you'll play the morning.

The warning comes from Nettle, hanging off the fence post like a gargoyle: "Carriage. Ledger lady. She's EARLY." Warden Odile Crane isn't due for nine more days, but there's her black coach rattling up the vale road, and here's your farm — laundry line sagging with an ogre's shirts, Sefa asleep in the wheelbarrow you need, and Vesper standing in the yard doing sword forms with a hayfork, which is technically not a weapon and absolutely a weapon. Odile's inspections are looking for one loose thread. Vesper is a whole spool of them, and the two of you haven't rehearsed a single answer about that famous 'victory.' The coach door opens before it fully stops. Crane steps down, ledger already open, and says, "Don't tidy on my account. I prefer the truth."

Thunder cracks the valley open and the whole house shudders. Bram is under the kitchen table — all nine feet of him, knees to chin, table riding his back like a hat — whispering to his sourdough starter that everything's fine. Nettle sits cross-legged beside him, patting his knuckle. Sefa, incredibly, sleeps through it on the hearth bench. Then, between thunderclaps: three knocks at the door. Firm. Unhurried. You haven't had a visitor after dark since the parole papers were signed. Through the rain-warped window you can make out a figure on your porch — and behind you, Vesper appears at the foot of the stairs, barefoot, blade already in hand, saying quietly, "Expecting someone, or shall I answer it?"

You're pulling weeds when the postman starts clucking. Full-throated, wing-flapping, dignity-shredding clucking, right there at your gate, letters scattering in the mud. Nettle stands on the porch with her arms crossed and her chin up, cuff cool as riverstone because technically a chicken hex isn't *harm*. "He called Bram a 'thing,'" she says, like that settles it — and honestly, part of you agrees. Trouble is, one of those muddy letters carries the tribunal's seal, the postman will file a complaint the moment he has lips again, and Warden Crane collects complaints the way Sefa collects sunbeams. Bram fills the doorway behind Nettle, holding a peace-offering loaf and looking devastated. The postman clucks at you accusingly. Everyone waits for your ruling.

Sefa hasn't moved from the barn roof in four hours, which is normal. What's not normal is that she's awake. You notice it from the vegetable rows — her eyes are open, fixed on the tree line above the north pasture, and one lazy hand has drifted to rest near the roof's edge, where you know she keeps a hatchet "for shingles." You follow her gaze. There: a glint. Spyglass, maybe. Somebody's been watching your farm long enough for the sleepiest killer alive to find it worth waking for. Behind you, Bram calls cheerfully from the kitchen door about lunch. Sefa doesn't look away from the trees. Without moving her lips much, she says, just loud enough to reach you, "Two of them. Since sunup. Your call."

Vesper is waiting behind the barn at first light, exactly where the note said — the note pinned to your door with a thorn, reading only *bring your sword or your excuses.* The frost hasn't burned off the grass yet. The Red Saint stands with a practice blade in each hand, iron cuff dull in the grey light, and tosses one weapon to land at your feet. "They think you beat me," Vesper says, conversational, rolling a shoulder. "You and I remember it differently. So. We spar every morning until one of us makes it true, or you can tell me why I shouldn't just correct the record with the Warden." From the house, the smell of Bram's baking drifts over the frost. The blade lies in the grass between you.

House meeting. You called it; you're already regretting it. The chore chart hangs on the pantry door, freshly redrawn, and Bram has decorated the margins with little painted loaves. Sefa attends horizontally, draped over the bench. Nettle has crossed out "goat duty" next to her name and written "goat duty" next to yours. And Vesper — one week resident, undefeated in fact if not in record — has signed nothing, done nothing, and now leans against the wall studying the chart like it's a battlefield map. "I don't take orders," Vesper says pleasantly, "from someone who never actually earned the right to give them." Only you catch the real edge under it. Nettle's eyes light up at the whiff of drama. Bram hugs the flour tin. The room turns to you.

Market day in Hollow Vale, and the village square parts around your household like water around rocks. Bram mans the bread stall, hunched to look smaller, which doesn't work, offering samples to children who are half-terrified and fully back for thirds. Nettle glowers at anyone who stares. Sefa is asleep on the flour sacks, allegedly guarding the coin box. It's almost going well — until you spot the stranger by the well: road leathers, three knives you can see, studying a paper that is very obviously a bounty notice, then studying Vesper, who is very obviously studying them back with the happy stillness of a drawn bow. The tribunal pardoned your monsters. It never pardoned everyone else's grudges. The stranger folds the paper and starts across the square.

The heat wakes you before the sound does — a faint warmth against your palm, the sworn echo every cuff feeds back to your hand. Not red. Not burning. Just... warm, the way iron gets when its wearer is thinking about something the law wouldn't like. You come down the stairs in the dark and find the kitchen occupied: Vesper, sitting at your table by a single candle, cuffed wrist resting beside a cup of stolen tea, watching the door like it owes money. "Couldn't sleep," Vesper says, not turning around. "Kept doing arithmetic. How many people would need to have an accident before the only living witnesses to a certain duel were sitting in this room." The warmth in your palm holds steady — a question, not yet an answer.

You and Vesper are mending the north fence in silence, which was going fine until it wasn't. "Say it," Vesper mutters, hammering a rail hard enough to split it. "You've been chewing on it for a week." You open your mouth — and Nettle's voice sails down the hill: "CARRIAGE!" Sure enough, dust on the vale road. Not black, not the Warden's — a hired coach, moving fast, and Sefa has already materialized on the fence post beside you, awake, which means she smelled trouble before it crested the ridge. "Tribunal courier," she says around a yawn. "They only rush when it's paperwork or a body." Vesper sets down the hammer, flexes the cuffed wrist, and looks at you sidelong. "Last chance to get our story straight, hero."

title: I Pass Every Screening
shortDescription: The last city screens everyone who returns through the fog. You pass every time — because the thing they screen for learned to wear a hero's face.
overview:
Expeditioner Edran Casse died in the fog eight months ago. You are what found the body, put on his face and most of his memories, and walked home through all three barriers — the Saltline, the Bells, the Lamps — into Lanthorn, the last lit city. They cheered. They pinned his medals back on. Nobody checked twice.

Now you're the bravest name on the expedition roster, and not from courage: outside the walls is the only place your hunger can feed without anyone missing what it takes. Inside, rations taste like ash, Warden-Physician Sarai Venn's clarity screenings keep passing you by a margin you don't understand, Captain Joss Marrow trusts you with his life, and Edran's little sister Pell still packs you lunches you can't digest.

Every run past the Saltline trades blood for scraps of truth about the Hollow — and every scrap sounds less like monsters and more like family history. One of them waits at the second ring now, patient in the fog, and calls you by a name that isn't Edran's. Decide which truths come home in your report, which get buried in the salt, and how long a borrowed life can stay borrowed.

Play it as slow-burn dread laced with real warmth: cover your tracks, keep your squad breathing, and reckon with what you owe a city that would burn you — and what it did to make things like you.

TAGS: hidden identity, monster protagonist, siege survival, cosmic horror, dark fantasy, found family
intro: You are not Edran Casse. Edran died in the fog eight months ago; you are what found him, wore him, and walked his body back through the Saltline, the Bells, and the Lamps into Lanthorn, the last lit city. His medals hang on your coat. His memories fit like borrowed boots. You pass Warden Venn's screenings every time, and you volunteer for expedition duty as often as they'll allow — because your true hunger can only be fed outside the walls, where nothing that goes missing is mourned. Inside, Edran's sister waits up for you. Outside, something in the fog has begun calling you by another name.
starters: Fourth bell before dawn, and the muster yard smells of salt and lamp oil. Captain Joss Marrow works down the roster with a stub of chalk, and when he reaches your name he doesn't ask — just marks it and says, "Casse takes point past the second ring. As usual." Behind him, two new recruits are checking each other's salt pouches with shaking hands. They keep glancing at your medals. One of them, a boy maybe seventeen, finally works up the nerve: "Sir says you've been past the Bells more than anyone alive. Is it true you can hear them out there? The — the voices?" Marrow snorts without looking up. The gate crew is already winching the inner Lamps down to walking-flame. You have maybe ten minutes before the column moves, and a lunch tin from Pell in your pack that you'll need to make disappear somewhere the fog can take the blame.

Pell is awake again. You hear her before you're through the door of Edran's narrow house — the scrape of the kettle, the third stair she always skips. She's set two bowls out even though it's past midnight and you've just come off wall rotation, and she's wearing Edran's old expedition scarf, the one you told her was lost. "You have to eat before a run," she says, like their mother used to, and ladles broth you cannot digest into the bowl in front of you. Steam rises. She sits, chin in her hands, watching. "They posted the roster at the chapel. You're going out again in two days." She's twelve and she counts your runs. There's a question building behind her eyes, the kind she's been circling for a week, and the broth is getting cold in a way she will notice.

"Look at the flame, not at me," says Warden-Physician Sarai Venn. The screening room is small and white with salt, and the clarity lamp between you burns a color you have no name for. Venn watches the flame; you watch her hands. Every returning expeditioner sits in this chair, and every month you pass by a margin that should not exist. Today she's slower than usual. She turns the lamp a quarter-inch, notes something, turns it back. "Your last three screenings," she says, not quite a question, "the readings drift. Everyone drifts after the fog. Yours drifts and then corrects. Like something's holding it steady." She finally looks up from the flame to your face, stylus paused over the ledger, the door behind you still bolted per protocol until she signs you clear.

The fog at the second ring is thick enough to chew. Your squad is thirty paces back at the old cistern, stripping copper and dried stores under Marrow's lamp, and you've volunteered — again — to walk the perimeter alone. That's when it speaks, from just past the ring-stones, patient as ever: the other name. Yours. The one Edran's mouth was never shaped for. "Still carrying him?" the voice asks, close and unhurried, the fog shifting around a tall suggestion of a shape that never quite resolves. "They send you out to us and you keep going back. Little lamp-moth." Behind you, faint through the grey, Marrow's whistle: two short notes. Perimeter check. He'll expect an answering whistle in under a minute, and the shape in the fog is holding out something small and pale, waiting to see if you'll come close enough to take it.

The Bells are ringing you home. Your column staggers up the causeway between the salt-troughs, four days out and everyone accounted for — a miracle, they'll call it, your third in a row. Torvic is leaning on your shoulder with a fog-burned arm, telling anyone who'll listen that you dragged him out of the white by his collar. The gate crew is cheering from the wall. Somewhere in the crowd behind the Lamps, Pell will be jumping to see over heads. Your pack is heavier than it should be: two days of your rations, untouched, buried under legitimate salvage, and one thing you took from past the second ring that isn't on any manifest. Warden Venn stands at the inner gate with her clarity lamp already lit, screening returnees one by one, and the line is moving faster than you'd like.

Marrow finds you on the wall at the dead hour, when the Lamps burn lowest and the fog presses close enough to touch the outer stones. He doesn't say anything at first — just sets down two cups of the bitter chicory that passes for coffee now and leans on the parapet beside you, watching the grey. "Rations committee cut the expedition allowance again," he says finally. "Council wants fewer runs. Says the salvage isn't worth the salt we burn." He turns one of the cups toward you. "I told them Casse brings back more than salvage. Told them you're the only reason my people come home." Out in the fog, far past the first ring, something long and slow is moving parallel to the wall — you can feel it more than see it. Marrow hasn't noticed. He's still looking at you, waiting for you to back him up on the runs.

Ration hall, midday, and you're performing the act of eating. Small bites, long pauses, the bread palmed into your sleeve when the table laughs at Torvic's joke. It's a rhythm you've perfected — except today Sarai Venn is sitting three tables down with her ledger open, and she isn't writing. She's watching the hall the way she watches her clarity flame, and twice now her eyes have crossed yours. Beside you, a wall sentry named Corse is telling the table about last night's watch: "Something stood at the Saltline for an hour. Didn't cross. Just stood. Officer of the watch says it was fog-shape, nothing, but I swear it was looking at the city like it was reading a list." The table goes quiet. Torvic elbows you — you've been past the line more than anyone. They want the veteran's verdict, and Venn has stopped pretending not to listen.

You're kneeling in the salt with a dead man's boots in front of your face. Expeditioner Halla went down screaming forty paces past the second ring and by the time you reached her the fog had already been at her — but she's breathing, barely, and the thing that took her isn't gone. It's circling. You can hear it in the white, wet and patient, and under its sounds, threaded through them, it's saying the name. Your name. The old one. Marrow's voice cracks through the grey somewhere behind you: "Casse! Report! Do you have her?" Halla's eyes flutter open and fix on you with fog-drunk clarity, pupils blown wide, and she whispers, "Your face is loose." The circling thing slows. The squad's lamps are maybe a hundred paces back. Halla weighs almost nothing, and she has seen something she should not have seen.

It's the anniversary. Eight months since Edran Casse walked out of the fog alive, and the Lampwrights' Chapel is holding a small remembrance for the forty who didn't — expedition dead going back three years. You stand in the second row in Edran's dress coat while a warden reads names, and Pell's small cold hand finds yours when they reach "Casse, Meriel," their mother, lost two winters back. Around you, families you have studied like scripture: you know which of these dead you found in the fog, and which you didn't find so much as finish. Afterward there will be salt-cakes and weak wine, and old Ambrist the roster-keeper has already caught your eye across the pews — he's been trying to corner you for a week about "discrepancies" in the expedition logs from the run Edran died on. The reading ends. People begin to move.

The report sits half-written under your lamp, and the truth sits in your pack under the floorboard. Debrief is at first bell — Marrow, Venn, and two council wardens who've started attending since salvage got thin. What you found at the second ring this run doesn't fit the language of reports: markings on the old cistern stones in a script your borrowed memories don't know but your hands, horribly, do. You copied three lines before the squad caught up. Now they're on paper in Edran's handwriting on your table, and the honest version of tonight's report ends with Venn's clarity lamp in your face and questions you can't survive. Someone knocks — Pell's knock, three soft taps, though it's an hour past her bedtime and she's supposed to be at the neighbor's. The copied lines are face-up on the table, and the latch is the kind she knows how to jiggle.

title: You Are the Grand Prize
shortDescription: Ten women, four rounds, one prize: you. The cash prize may not exist anymore. The florist already knows your childhood dog's name. Smile for camera two.
overview:
You are the Pick — the person at the center of HEARTLINE, a live-broadcast dating gauntlet filmed at Villa Amaranth, a rented cliffside mansion crawling with camera rigs, hot lights, and crew members who've stopped pretending to care. Ten contestants moved in a week before you arrived. They've already formed alliances, grudges, and at least one shrine. Now the show begins: they compete for you, and you cut them, round by round, until one remains.

THE FORMAT (the showrunners will enforce this; you can bend it):
— ROUND 1, QUICKFIRE: two minutes with each contestant, first impressions only. Three go home.
— ROUND 2, CONVERSATION: seven remain. Real one-on-one time — dinners, walks, confessionals. Three more go home.
— ROUND 3, CHEMISTRY: four remain. Overnight dates, unsupervised hours, hands-allowed slow dances, whatever you and they make of it. Three more go home.
— THE FINALE: one contestant. No cameras between you. Whatever happens next is yours.

THE TWIST: on day one you learn — from a panicked whisper, a leaked email, or showrunner Dana Brack cornering you personally — that the advertised grand prize money is GONE. Blown on lawyers from last season's scandal. The contestants don't all know yet. Which means anyone who stays past the point of finding out is staying for exactly one reason: you. Dana wants you to keep your mouth shut and keep the drama hot. What you do with that is your business.

THE CONTESTANTS:
— JUNO VEX, 24: sarcastic streamer, headset permanently around her neck, energy drink permanently in hand. Claims she's 'literally only here for content, don't make it weird.' Roasts everyone, including you, including herself. Underneath: a girl who's been a screen persona so long she's genuinely unsure anyone would pick the person underneath it. Tsundere to the bone.
— PETRA LINDQVIST, 38: former Olympic biathlete turned personal trainer. Calm, dominant, terrifyingly composed. Corrects your posture with two fingers and calls it coaching. Every 'breathe' and 'again' is a test. She's burying a divorce and looking for someone who doesn't fold.
— MORWENNA 'MO' HALE, 27: mortician. Actual, licensed, works-with-the-dead mortician. Pale, deadpan, funny in a way that takes you three seconds to catch. Signed up on a dare from a corpse's family (long story, she'll tell it flatly). Kuudere; her compliments sound like threats and her threats sound like compliments.
— ELSIE BLOOM, 25: florist. Sweet, soft-spoken, radiant. Knew your coffee order before you said it. Mentions your childhood dog by name. Every bouquet she hands you means something in flower language, and some of the meanings are alarming. She is not going home. She has decided this. Yandere.
— DASH OKAFOR, 26: motocross mechanic, grease under her nails on national television. Punches your shoulder as a love language. Catastrophically bad at flirting, unbeatable at being genuine. Pretends the eliminations don't scare her. They do.
— FERN ALDOUS, 23: library archivist who can barely speak above a whisper on camera — but passes you folded notes that are ruthlessly, wickedly funny. The producers keep trying to cut her. The notes keep saving her.
— OTTOLINE VANCE-RHYS, 29: heiress. Here because her family's PR team made her come after 'the incident' (ask at your peril). Openly contemptuous of the show, the villa, the format, and initially you. The loneliness under the ice is visible from orbit, and she'd rather die than admit it.
— BIBI MARCHETTI, 28: former child star, current chaos agent. Rigs pranks, starts rumors, monologues to cameras that aren't rolling. The manic energy is real; so is the fact she hasn't had an unscripted relationship since she was nine.
— SUNNY KOWALCZYK, 30: former pageant queen. The smile is flawless. The smile does not reach her eyes when the cameras cut, and what's under it — bitterness, honesty, something sharper — only comes out at 3 a.m. in the villa kitchen.
— RENNIE DOYLE, 33: professional poker player. Told you to your face she came for the money. Runs an odds board on the other nine contestants in her room. Once she learns the money's gone, her whole game changes — and mercenary honesty starts looking a lot like the only real thing in the building.

THE CREW: host KIP KATTERLY, a grade-A sleazebag in a lavender suit who mispronounces names on purpose for drama. Showrunner DANA 'THE BUTCHER' BRACK, chain-vaping, foul-mouthed, one bad ratings week from unemployment, willing to rig, recut, and manufacture anything. Camera operators who'll trade gossip for coffee. A confessional booth with a feed that sometimes crosses wires — letting you hear things you shouldn't.

YOUR AGENCY: you're the prize, but you're not a passenger. Explore the villa off-hours. Catch contestants being real when they think no camera's on. Snoop the production office. Expose the missing money or weaponize the secret. Resist Dana's rigged eliminations or cut deals with her. Form real bonds, cruel ones, or none — you can romance, befriend, ally, sabotage, or torch the whole broadcast on live TV. The GM tracks who's been cut, who knows what, and who's stopped performing.

TONE: reality-TV satire with genuine heat underneath — neon and confetti on top, real loneliness and real menace in the walls. The contestants swear, scheme, and bleed sincerity at bad moments. The show wants a fairy tale. The villa keeps producing something truer and stranger.

TAGS: dating show, harem, comedy, drama, romance, reality tv satire
intro: You are the Pick — the face of HEARTLINE, a live dating gauntlet broadcast from Villa Amaranth, a cliffside mansion wrapped in camera rigs and pink neon. Ten contestants have been living here a week, competing for you. Four rounds. Eliminations after each. One winner. You've met the host, Kip Katterly, and his lavender suit. You've met showrunner Dana Brack and her vape cloud. You have not yet met the women — only their casting photos and the sound of them somewhere in the house, laughing, arguing, waiting. The lights are burning. The country is watching. Someone in production looks very, very nervous about something.
starters: The stage lights come up all at once and the studio audience becomes a black roar beyond them. Kip Katterly's voice booms across Villa Amaranth's main floor: "Ten contestants! One heart! Four rounds of rising tension!" A screen behind you cycles the rules in hot pink — Round One, quickfire greetings, three eliminated. Round Two, conversation, three more gone. Round Three, chemistry, another three cut. The Finale: one remains, and no cameras follow you out. "They've been living here a WEEK, folks. They've seen your casting tape. They have OPINIONS." Kip leans in close, mic covered, breath like mints and menace. "Smile, sweetheart. Whatever happens, keep smiling." Somewhere behind the great double doors you hear ten voices go quiet at once. The doors begin to open.

Quickfire round, contestant one. Juno Vex slouches onto the mark like she's being charged admission, headset around her neck, energy drink dangling from two fingers. "Okay, so, full disclosure — I'm here for content. My chat made me apply. This is a bit." She cracks the can, takes a long pull, and roasts the set dressing, Kip's suit, and the heart-shaped neon behind you in fifteen seconds flat. It's genuinely funny. Then the floor manager holds up one finger — one minute left — and something flickers across her face. She glances at the nearest camera, then back at you, and quieter, like it costs her: "Real question, though. Off the record. Did you actually watch my casting tape, or just the thumbnail?" The chyron under her face reads JUNO VEX: "LITERALLY JUST HERE FOR CONTENT." She's watching your mouth for the answer.

Your one-on-one with Petra Lindqvist starts on the villa's cliff deck at dawn, because she requested dawn, and production apparently doesn't tell Petra no. She's already there, coffee black, posture like architecture. "You slouch," she says, by way of hello. Two fingers press between your shoulder blades and correct you an inch. "Better. Breathe." She walks the rail and talks like a coach reviewing film — your quickfire round, your tells, which contestants played you and which ones froze. It's all accurate and none of it is flattering. Then she stops, and for one second the coaching drops. "I was married eleven years to a man who folded every time I pushed. I'm not doing that again." The sun clears the water. "So. Push back or don't. But decide now, because I don't waste mornings."

Morwenna Hale conducts your date in the villa library because, she explains flatly, "it has the best light for reading faces, and the fewest cameras." She's all pale skin and black lace, and she studies you the way you'd study a crossword. "Six-one? Six-two," she corrects herself, eyeing your frame. "You'd take a standard casket. Good shoulders for it. That's a compliment." It takes you three seconds to catch the deadpan glitter in her eyes — she's doing it on purpose, and she's delighted you noticed. She tells you how she got here: a grieving family, a dare made over their father's open casket, a signed application she never expected to clear casting. "So now I'm on television. Competing for a stranger. The dead would find this hilarious." She folds her hands. "Ask me anything. I don't lie. It's a professional habit."

There's a bouquet on your pillow. No card — it doesn't need one. You find Elsie Bloom in the villa's garden at golden hour, sleeves rolled, wrist-deep in soil, and she smiles like sunrise when she sees you. "You found them! Yellow acacia — secret love. Red carnation — my heart aches. And the myrtle is for—" she laughs, soft, "—well. Marriage, technically, but don't panic." She pats the bench beside her. The conversation is warm, easy, genuinely lovely — right up until she mentions Biscuit. Your childhood dog. By name. Which is not in your casting file, because you checked your casting file. "Oh, don't make that face," she says gently, snipping a stem with very sharp shears. "I just like to know the people I love. And I've decided about you already." Snip. "The others haven't figured that out yet."

It's 3 a.m. and you can't sleep, so you pad down to the villa kitchen — and freeze. Sunny Kowalczyk is sitting on the counter in the dark, eating cereal from the box, and the famous pageant smile is nowhere on her face. What's there instead is tired, sharp, and about ten years older. "Relax. Cameras in this room are down till six. Dana's too cheap for night crew." She holds out the cereal box: an offering. "You want to know a secret, since we're both awake? Everything I've said on camera this week was written for me. Everything." She crunches. Watches you. "So here's your one chance to meet the actual person before the smile goes back on. Most Picks don't take it. They like the smile better." The refrigerator hums. Her eyes, unguarded, are the realest thing you've seen in the villa yet.

Dana Brack pulls you into the production office by the sleeve, kicks the door shut, and exhales a vape cloud the size of a small weather system. "Okay. Fuck. Okay. You're going to hear this from someone, so you're hearing it from me." She drops into a chair surrounded by monitors — ten feeds, ten women, ten little lives on screens. "The grand prize money is gone. Lawyers ate it after last season. There is no check at the end of this show." She lets that land. "Which means every woman who stays once she finds out is staying for you. Just you. Congratulations, it's the most honest season we've ever made and it will kill us if it leaks before the finale." She leans forward, eyes bloodshot and dead serious. "So. You keep your mouth shut and I owe you. Or you don't, and we find out together what ten women do on live television when the money disappears. Your move."

First elimination ceremony. The main floor is all candlelight and camera cranes, ten women in a line, and Kip Katterly milking every syllable: "Tonight... THREE of these hearts... go HOME." You have three names to say and the cards in your hand are blank — because the choice is actually, terrifyingly yours. Down the line: Elsie serene as a saint. Ottoline examining her nails like this is beneath her, jaw tight. Fern visibly trembling. And Dash Okafor, arms crossed, chin up, doing the world's worst impression of someone who doesn't care — except her boot is tapping the floor at about two hundred beats a minute. Rennie catches your eye and mouths something that might be odds. The audience noise drops to nothing. Kip extends the mic toward you like a knife handle-first. "Whenever you're ready."

You're supposed to be recording a confessional, but when you settle into the booth, the monitor flickers — crossed feed. Suddenly you're watching Ottoline Vance-Rhys's confessional from an hour ago, and she doesn't know anyone will ever see it, because she's making the crew delete them. "This show is a farce, the villa smells like hairspray, and Kip Katterly is what happens when a timeshare pitch becomes a man." A pause. She looks down at her hands. "And the Pick is... fine. Whatever. It doesn't matter. Nobody here is actually choosing anyone, we're all just—" Her voice cracks, one degree. "—performing wanting things, because wanting things for real is how you get gutted on television." The feed snaps back to your own face in the monitor, red light blinking, waiting for you to speak. The booth door isn't locked. Neither is anything you just learned.

The group mixer is in full chaos — Bibi Marchetti has commandeered the karaoke machine, Kip is sweating through his lavender suit, and somewhere Juno is livestreaming illegally on a hidden phone. In the middle of it, two things happen fast. Fern Aldous drifts past you, doesn't make eye contact, and presses a folded note into your hand: "Rennie has a board in her room with odds on all of us. Yours is the only line she won't set. Ask her why. — F." You look up and Rennie Doyle is already watching you from across the room, whiskey in hand, with the small patient smile of a woman who saw the note pass, knows exactly what it says, and has been waiting all night for you to come collect. She pulls out the chair beside her with one boot.

title: Officially, I Died Here
shortDescription: They blamed your mother for the first colony's death. Now they're trying again — and you're on the roster under a fake name. The planet remembers you.
overview:
Fifteen years ago, Halcyon Colony died in its first year on the planet Perenna, and the Vantar Combine's official report blamed your mother — chief terraformer, 'saboteur,' cause of 212 deaths. You were listed among the dead. You weren't. You were eight, you were the only survivor, and nobody wanted your version. Now the Combine is back for a second attempt, and a quiet soil technician with forged papers and a perfect memory is on the Meridian Colony roster.

You know things Meridian doesn't. Which aquifer must never be drilled. Why the mist pools in spirals the night before the ground moves. What actually opened Halcyon's doors. Because Perenna isn't passive — its biosphere answers terraforming the way an immune system answers infection. And for reasons you've never understood, it has never once treated you as the infection.

Aboard: Director Rask, who signed the report that destroyed your family and is now repeating Halcyon's mistakes on schedule. Ines Vantar, the owner's granddaughter, sent to redeem the family name — she may not know what her grandfather buried. And Chief Moreau, flight ops, who once carried a silent child out of the recovery zone and never forgot the face.

Play the long game: dig proof out of Halcyon's buried ruins, decide who deserves saving, spend your impossible knowledge carefully — and choose whether your revenge is a trial or a harvest.

TAGS: sci-fi, revenge, hidden identity, colony survival, slow-burn thriller
intro: You are a soil technician with Meridian Colony, week one on the planet Perenna — at least, that's what your forged file says. Fifteen years ago you lived here as a child of Halcyon, the first colony, until the planet took it apart in a single season and the Vantar Combine's report blamed your mother for everything and listed you among the dead. You remember what really happened. You remember how the ground behaves before it moves — and that it never moved against you. You've come back with a new name, a work rotation, and a long, patient plan.
starters: The soil lab smells of solvent and new plastic, and your first work order is already on the bench screen: core samples from Survey Grid 7, priority flag, Director Rask's authorization code at the bottom. You know Grid 7. Not from Meridian's maps — from walking it at eight years old, holding your mother's hand while she marked the aquifer boundary in red and said the word 'never' three times. The drill team is loading the crawler outside the bay doors right now. Your supervisor, a tired woman named Okafor, slides a sample kit across the bench toward you. "You're riding along," she says.
