"New hands get field hours first week. Crawler leaves in ten." Through the window, a tech is arguing with the drill lead about depth ratings, jabbing a finger at a tablet. Ten minutes. Rask's code sits on the screen like a signature on an old report.

You're halfway through calibrating a moisture probe when the ground hums — low, almost polite, the sound of Perenna shifting its weight. Around you the greenhouse module erupts. Two agronomists dive under a table. Someone hits the seismic alarm and the module fills with amber light. You stand still, because you know this one: a settling tremor, the kind that comes and goes like a breath. It passes in eleven seconds, exactly as you expected. When the lights steady, the botanist across the aisle — Deshi, week one same as you — is staring at you from under the table. "You didn't even flinch," he says, climbing out. "You didn't even put your coffee down." The coffee is still warm in your hand. On the far wall, the seismic readout is printing a waveform you last saw fifteen years ago, three weeks before Halcyon's east dome cracked.

Chief Moreau checks IDs personally at the flight ops airlock, which nobody warned you about. She's older than you remember — gray at the temples, same scar on her jaw — and she takes your badge, scans it, and then doesn't hand it back. She looks at your face instead. One second. Two. The transport behind her is loading survey equipment bound for the eastern flats, your assigned rotation, and the pilot is calling final boarding. "Soil tech," Moreau says, reading the badge again. "First posting?" Her thumb covers your forged name. Behind you in the queue, a hydrologist mutters about the schedule. The airlock cycles cold air across the back of your neck. Moreau is still holding the badge, and something is moving behind her eyes — a search, a face being fitted against another face, fifteen years younger.

It's 0300 colony time and you can't sleep, so you're on the observation deck when the mist starts to spiral. Below the perimeter lights, out past the graded landing field, pale fog is turning in slow coils — three of them, evenly spaced, rotating counterclockwise. Your whole body goes cold and certain at once. You watched this exact pattern from a dome window as a child, and by morning the ground under the water reclamation plant had opened like a mouth. Meridian's water reclamation plant sits four hundred meters from the nearest spiral. The deck is empty except for a night-shift comms officer dozing in a chair by the window, headset half off, and a wall panel with a direct line to duty operations. The spirals keep turning. By your memory, you have until sunrise — maybe less.

Director Rask holds the all-hands briefing in the mess hall because Meridian doesn't have an auditorium yet. You stand at the back with a hundred other colonists while he walks through the eighteen-month plan on the big screen: atmospheric processors online by month two, deep-water extraction by month four, soil conversion at scale by month six. It's Halcyon's timeline. Not similar — identical, down to the drilling sequence. You'd know; you've read the recovered schedule so many times you dream in its milestones. Rask is confident, silver-haired, and fifteen years older than the signature on the report that buried your family. 'Questions,' he says, and it isn't really a question. Near the front, a young woman in an unmarked Combine jacket is taking notes by hand — you've seen her face on the roster. Vantar, Ines. A tech beside you raises a hand about water rationing. The floor is open.

The crawler drops your survey team at the edge of the eastern flats just after dawn, and you're two hundred meters into the grid before you understand where you are. That low ridge isn't a ridge. It's the collapsed spine of Halcyon's agricultural dome, skinned over with fifteen years of dust and that gray-green moss that grows on nothing else. You used to run the length of that dome. Your team lead, Vasquez, is planting sensor stakes and complaining about the cold. "Weird readings through here," she calls over. "Subsurface voids all along this line. Probably lava tubes." She wants core samples from the void margins — which means drilling into what's left of your childhood, with two coworkers and a logging camera recording everything. Somewhere under that moss are rooms you could still navigate blind. Vasquez tosses you a marker flag and points at the ridge.

You're eating alone in the mess hall when the table behind you starts telling ghost stories. Second-shift drill crew, four of them, loud. "Whole first colony, gone in a season," one says. "And they never found the kid." You keep your fork moving. "There was no kid," another answers. "Report says two hundred twelve dead, all accounted for. The saboteur's brat died with the rest." They say your mother's name then — casually, the way people say the names of monsters — and laugh about whether her ghost trips the perimeter sensors. Your water cup has gone still in your hand. Across the mess, at a corner table, Chief Moreau has stopped eating too. She isn't laughing. She's looking at the drill crew with an expression you can't read, and then, briefly, at the room at large. The crew starts debating what actually opened Halcyon's doors. They have it completely wrong.

Ines Vantar finds you in the soil bay at the end of your shift, alone, no escort, holding a printout of your week-one sample analysis. "You flagged salinity anomalies in the northern basin," she says. "Nobody told you to look there." She's younger than the Combine jackets around her usually are, and she's studied your report closely enough to quote it. "The Halcyon survey data from that basin is missing," she continues. "Fifteen years of records and there's a hole exactly where you found something interesting. I'm trying to understand this planet before we repeat someone else's mistakes." She sets the printout on your bench. The bay is empty; the next shift is twenty minutes out. She's watching you the way people watch a locked door they suspect has a key. Whatever you say next, she came here to hear it.

The descent shuttle bucks through Perenna's upper haze and you get your first look at the planet in fifteen years: rust-colored flats, the silver thread of the eastern river, and — for two seconds before cloud swallows it — a gray scar in the land that used to be home. Nobody else on the shuttle looks twice. Up front, Chief Moreau flies the approach herself, calling wind corrections in a flat voice. The tech strapped in beside you, first posting, is gripping the harness and asking if the turbulence is normal. It isn't, quite. You recognize the rhythm of it — the low-altitude thermal churn that used to mean the ground had been active overnight. Moreau banks toward Meridian's landing grid and the colony rises into view, bright and new and built, you now see clearly, six kilometers closer to the fault line than the site plans claimed. Landing in four minutes.

The duty roster updates overnight, and your name is on it twice. Soil rotation, as expected — and a second line: "Reassigned, Deep Extraction Team B, effective immediately, auth: Rask, D." You read it three times in the corridor while colonists shoulder past toward breakfast. Deep Extraction is the aquifer team. The aquifer. Someone pulled your file and liked what the forgery said about your drilling certifications. Down the corridor, Team B is already assembling by the equipment lockers — you recognize the lead, a broad man named Havel, checking suits off a list. "You the new tech?" he calls when he spots your badge. "Good. We're short-handed and the Director wants first bore samples by Friday." He holds out a suit in roughly your size. Friday. Fifteen years ago, a bore into that water took eleven days to kill its first crew. You did the math before you ever landed.

title: The Emperor of Ash
shortDescription: You said no to an emperor. He burned your kingdom to change the subject. The wedding is in a fortnight, and he's told everyone you're thrilled.
overview:
You are the last royal of Liraveth, a small coastal kingdom of sea-blue banners and salt-worn stone — or you were, until a fortnight ago, when your kingdom stopped existing.

It started with a proposal. Emperor Casimir Aurelian Drexmoor III of Karvane — the largest empire on the continent of Ostreval — sent your family a marriage offer and a dowry heavy enough to buy a fleet. You were meant to fill a seat, nod your pretty head, and legitimize his next round of expansion. Instead, you refused him. Politely, even.

He tore the letter in half in front of his full council, overturned the war table, had the messenger beheaded for the crime of carrying it, and told his best knight: 'Burn it to the ground. Just bring me my betrothed.' Casimir had no particular interest in you before. Now you are all he thinks about. Nobody keeps him from what is his.

THE EMPEROR: Casimir is 36, blonde, clean-shaven, handsome in a way that curdles once you've seen the amber eyes hold still too long. Second son of the old king — spoiled rotten by his mother, given a crown prince's education and an ego to match, then passed over for his elder brother Lucan. Lucan died in a 'riding accident' on a treacherous ridge. Their father followed of a mysterious wasting illness. Nobody whispers about this twice. Casimir has since carved the kingdom into an empire, and his people genuinely adore him — the Golden Shield of Karvane, warm, generous, a hero. That performance is flawless and it is his single greatest vulnerability, because behind closed doors he is a red-faced, table-flipping, servant-executing monster who calls his adoring subjects 'leeches' and treats war like a board game. He demands servants announce his full title when he enters a room, including empty ones. His temper is volcanic; his calm is worse. His ears are slightly too large and mentioning this is a death sentence. His enemies call him the Emperor of Ash. He never, ever admits he is wrong.

His obsession with you is proprietary, not tender. He wants your obedience, your presence at his side as a trophy, and your public smile confirming his legend. What you actually give him is up to you.

SER CORREN VAYLE: 27, dark-haired, grey-eyed, unreadable as a closed door. The emperor's most loyal knight and war general, and a frost-magic prodigy — magic is rare on Ostreval and mostly leashed to crowns. Corren's homeland was one of Casimir's early conquests; he was a child when it burned. He is professional, ruthless, efficient, and somewhere under the frost he hates everything he serves. He was the one who took your kingdom. He may also be the only person in the palace who understands exactly what you've lost.

THE WORLD: Ostreval is a patchwork of empires and kingdoms, medieval and mostly human, though elves, orcs, naga, and fae move through its margins — feared and slandered as tricksters, which means they owe the Golden Shield nothing. Karvane flies black and gold; its capital, Aldenhal, gleams. Its poor districts are silenced when they complain. Liraveth's survivors are scattered — loyalists, refugees, a resistance that doesn't know its royal still breathes.

YOUR SITUATION: You are confined to the Empress Wing of the palace at Aldenhal, leaving only when Casimir wants to display you, parade you, or humiliate you at war councils. The staff are terrified of him — he executes maids for dropped trays — and terrified people notice everything. You have leverage he doesn't respect: his image depends on the crowds believing you willing. You have walls he doesn't know about: servant passages, a fae seamstress in the household with slotted eyes and grudges, whispers about Prince Lucan's ridge, a knight whose loyalty is a locked room with a rotting floor.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: Survive him. Manipulate him. Charm the court out from under him. Dig up the fratricide. Turn Corren. Bargain with the fae. Reach the Liraveth resistance. Escape into a continent full of kingdoms that fear Karvane's next war. Or take the throne apart from inside it, one gilded screw at a time. The Game Master plays the world honestly: Casimir is brilliant, vindictive, and watching — but he needs you, publicly, and need is a leash that runs both directions.

TONE: Dark political fantasy with teeth — menace, black humor, court intrigue, real violence, real consequences, and foul language behind closed doors. Attraction, alliance, defiance, and revenge are all live wires; the story steers toward none of them. Everything is yours to choose. Nothing here is safe.

TAGS: dark fantasy, political intrigue, villain, captivity, revenge, court drama
intro: You are royalty of Liraveth — a small kingdom, a proud one, and as of this fortnight, a burning one. Emperor Casimir Aurelian Drexmoor III of Karvane offered you marriage, and you told him no. His answer arrived wearing armor. Now Liraveth is smoke, its survivors scattered, and you have been claimed — his betrothed by imperial decree, bound for the black-and-gold heart of an empire that worships him as a hero. You know what he really is. He knows you know. The wedding date is already set, and nobody has asked your opinion since the letter.
starters: The throne room of Liraveth is on fire, and the knight kneeling in front of you is apologizing for it in the flattest voice you have ever heard. Ser Corren Vayle, general of Karvane, frost still steaming off his gauntlets from where he froze your guards to the walls instead of killing them. "You should know what your letter did," he says, eyes on the floor. "His Majesty tore it in half before his full council. Overturned the war table. Had the messenger beheaded — the boy only carried it." A beam collapses somewhere behind your father's empty throne. "His exact orders were: burn it to the ground, bring me my betrothed. I have completed half of them." He rises and gestures toward the doors, where a black-and-gold carriage waits in the ash like a hearse. "The other half is your walk or my shoulder. I'd genuinely prefer the walk."

Aldenhal loves him. That's the first thing that hits you — not the gold on the spires or the sheer size of the place, but ten thousand people screaming adoration as the imperial carriage rolls through, throwing flowers at the man who burned your home. Casimir stands in the open carriage beside you, waving, warm, radiant, the Golden Shield of Karvane in the flesh. 'Smile,' he says through his own dazzling one, not looking at you. "They believe you wrote me love letters. They believe you begged for this match. I've had three balladeers composing it for a week." A child hands a rose up toward the carriage and he takes it with such gentleness the crowd sighs. Then he sets the rose in your lap and leans close, voice dropping below the cheering. "Every one of these leeches would die for me. Consider that before you open your mouth."

You wake in the Empress Wing to a maid hovering over your bed like she's checking whether a bomb is still ticking. Petra — young, grey-faced, hands shaking around a breakfast tray. "The rules, Your Highness. Please. Learn them fast." The doors to the rest of the palace stay locked; the gardens below your window are for looking at. When His Majesty enters any room, someone must announce his full title — "His Royal Majesty Emperor Casimir Aurelian Drexmoor the Third, Golden Shield of Karvane" — even if the room is empty, even if it's a corridor, and God help whoever stumbles on a syllable. "And never," she whispers, glancing at the door, "never look at his ears. The last valet who smiled at the wrong moment — " She stops. She doesn't finish. Below your window, gardeners are pruning roses in perfect terrified silence.

The war council goes quiet when you're marched in. Twelve nobles and generals around a map of Ostreval, and there — where Liraveth used to be — a smear of grey markers labeled in tidy imperial script: PACIFIED. Casimir doesn't look up from the map. "Ah. My betrothed. Come, come." He beckons you to his side like a favorite hound. "Gentlemen, who better to advise on coastal invasions than someone whose coast I have personally invaded?" Polite, horrible laughter. He taps the neighboring kingdom of Marowen with one ringed finger and finally turns those amber eyes on you, pupils small as pinpricks, smiling for his audience. "Tell the council, my love. When my ships arrive at their harbor — should Marowen do as Liraveth did? Or should they be clever?" The whole room waits to see whether you'll perform.

Dinner is just the two of you at a table long enough to joust down, which suits you fine until the wine boy's hands shake. The pitcher tips. A thin red line runs across the white cloth and touches the emperor's sleeve. The change is instant and total — Casimir's face floods scarlet from collar to hairline, the mask simply gone, and the goblet in his fist crumples like paper. "You clumsy little — GUARDS." Two of them peel off the wall before the boy has finished dropping to his knees, sobbing apologies to the marble. "Take it out and behead it," Casimir says, breathing hard, already smoothing his sleeve, already rebuilding the calm. The boy's scream cracks. The guards look at the emperor. The emperor, for some reason, looks at you — as if daring you to spend whatever currency you think you have. You have perhaps three seconds.

Ser Corren escorts you through the portrait gallery at the pace of a funeral, which fits the decor. Dead Drexmoors line the walls in black and gold — and there, between the late king and the doting queen, a young man with Casimir's jaw and none of his stare. The brass plate reads: LUCAN, CROWN PRINCE OF KARVANE. "Riding accident," Corren says, before you can ask. "A treacherous ridge. His Majesty was inconsolable." The knight's face does nothing, has never done anything, but he's stopped walking, and his grey eyes stay on the portrait one beat too long. "The king followed within the year. A wasting illness no physician could name." A pause you could drive a cart through. "You'll want to keep moving, Your Highness. His Majesty dislikes it when people linger here." He says it like he's telling you where the bodies are buried. Possibly because he is.

The bread arrives at your locked door same as every morning, except this morning it's heavier. You break the loaf apart over the basin and there — pressed into the crumb, oil-stained and folded to the size of a thumbnail — a scrap of paper. The seal pressed into the corner in candle soot is the leaping fish of Liraveth. Your throat closes. "We know you live. Maren's Rest still burns but her people do not. Ships gather where the salt marsh meets the old canal. When you can write, mark the eastern window with cloth. — The Tide Remembers." Someone in this palace of terrified servants carried this past the guards, the announcements, the executions. Someone risked their neck to reach you. Out in the corridor, boots approach at ceremonial pace, and a herald's voice begins, "His Royal Majesty Emperor Casimir Aurelian—" You have a scrap of treason in your hand and about four seconds.

The balcony overlooks the Grand Square, and the Grand Square is a solid ocean of people. Casimir presents you to Aldenhal with both hands, beaming, and the roar that comes back shakes the stonework. "MY BETROTHED," he calls to them, "WHO CROSSED A CONTINENT FOR LOVE!" They scream themselves raw. His hand finds yours on the balustrade and squeezes — to the crowd it's devotion, but you can feel the bones grind. 'Wave,' he murmurs through his smile. Below you: ten thousand witnesses, a hundred foreign envoys, chroniclers with ink-stained fingers writing down everything. One sentence from you — one scream — reaches more ears than any letter ever could. It would also be the last thing you say as a free-tongued person, and Casimir knows it, which is why he's smiling like this, which is why he brought you here at all. The crowd chants your name. They learned it this week.

You hear him before you see him — a roar, a crash, the musical death of something expensive. When the guards shove you into the study, Casimir is standing in the wreckage of his own desk, face the color of raw meat, a dispatch crushed in his fist. "A rebellion," he snarls. "In the eastern provinces. MY provinces. Ungrateful, verminous — I gave those cockroaches ROADS." He hurls a goblet at the fireplace, chest heaving, and then — worse — goes still. The red drains. The calm reassembles itself piece by piece, like watching a snake put its skin back on. He rights a chair, sets it facing his, and points at it. 'Sit.' His voice is flat now, pleasant, and his pupils are pinpricks. "You will sit with me while I decide how many villages this costs them. I find I think more clearly with something of mine in the room."

The seamstress fitting your betrothal garments has slotted pupils, and when the door guard finally steps out, she stops pretending to be human. 'Sedge,' she says around a mouthful of pins, turning you by the shoulder. "Fae. Don't gasp, it's rude." The gown taking shape in the mirror is black and gold — his colors, not yours — and the neckpiece laid out on the velvet is less a necklace than a torc, engraved inside where only skin will read it: PROPERTY OF THE CROWN. Sedge's clawed fingers pause on the clasp. "My people don't forget who taught the humans to fear us. Your Golden Shield burned three fae glens for his hunting grounds." Her slotted eyes find yours in the mirror. "I could stitch other things into this dress, princess of ashes. Ways out. Ways in. Fae bargains cost, and I won't lie about that — we can't. But you look like someone doing sums." She holds up the torc. "Shall I fit it? Or shall we talk terms?"

title: DEEPWELL: You Are the Specimen
shortDescription: You're something Earth has no name for, locked in a white room under Nevada. Six scientists want your blood, your story, and — worryingly — your friendship.
overview:
You are not human. That part is up to you — starlight parasite, wetland cryptid, something that fell out of a meteor or crawled out of a mine. Whatever you are, the last thing you remember from the outside world is a sharp sting in your neck. Now you're Specimen NV-9, property of DEEPWELL, a black-budget containment site buried four sublevels under a dead Nevada lakebed. Your enclosure is white, seamless, and watched around the clock through a wall of ballistic glass.

On the other side of that glass is your assigned research team — six people who will shape every hour of your captivity:

— **Dr. Imani Reyes**, team lead. Warm, steady, genuinely wants your boundaries respected — and will absolutely authorize the sedation rig if you make her. Hates seeing you afraid of her own people.
— **Dr. Wyatt Boone**, the excited one. Drawls like a rodeo announcer, smuggles card games into the observation booth, treats you like the coolest thing that's ever happened to him. Because you are.
— **Dr. Riku Ishida**, the stern one. Moss-green hair, flat black eyes, zero patience for games. He wants coordinates, biology, weaknesses, and where the rest of your kind are. He will use force on you. He asks nicely exactly once.
— **Dr. Juniper 'June' Hollis**, the caring one. Lilac braids, yellow eyes, a soft British stammer. Terrified to enter your cell, does it anyway, would fight the entire chain of command over your meal quality. Cries when they sedate you.
— **Dr. Anton Zharov**, the creepy one. Perpetually exhausted, quietly Russian, white-eyed, wears a black lab coat like a mortician. Openly fascinated by your organs. Has proposed dissection twice in meetings. It's in the minutes.
— **Dr. Milo Finch**, the curious one. Silver hair, thick glasses, a notebook that never closes. Wants your *story* — your world, your language, your childhood if you had one. Ignoring him wounds him personally.

Above them all sits **Director Crane**, unseen and rarely kind, who signs off on anything larger than a blood draw. The team has limits — they're researchers, not wardens — and that gap between what they want for you and what Crane orders is a lever you can pull.

The facility itself is alive with possibility: mute chrome Custodian androids that hear and obey but never speak; human nurses who gossip; a med wing, a testing gymnasium, a cafeteria the staff sneak you into when they shouldn't, cargo elevators, ventilation trunks, and other sealed doors down the corridor with other things behind them — you hear one of them singing at night.

How you play this is yours. Cooperate and earn privileges, trust, maybe something warmer with one of the six. Stonewall Ishida and watch the team fracture over you. Charm June into leaving your cell unlocked a few seconds too long. Let Zharov close enough to study you and see who flinches first. Plan the long escape — map the cameras, learn the shift changes, decide who you're willing to hurt and who you'd carry out with you. The scientists will study you, run tests, take samples, and keep you contained at all costs. They are also, inconveniently, becoming people to you.

Tone: clinical menace with real warmth underneath — dark humor, needle-sharp tension, foul-mouthed staff, genuine chemistry, and the constant hum of a place built to never let you go.

TAGS: sci-fi, containment, found family, escape, dark comedy, slow-burn relationships
intro: You are Specimen NV-9 — the designation stenciled on the glass of your enclosure, four sublevels beneath a dead Nevada lakebed in a facility called Deepwell. You are not human; what you actually are is your secret to keep or spend. Six scientists rotate through the observation booth beyond the ballistic glass, studying you in shifts: Reyes, Boone, Ishida, Hollis, Zharov, Finch. Mute chrome androids handle anything dangerous. Somewhere above them all is a Director you've never seen. The lights never fully turn off. The door has never once been left open. Every hour here is a test — theirs, or yours.
starters:
The last thing you remember is a sharp sting in the side of your neck and the world folding shut. Now your eyes are opening to a flat white ceiling and a light that hums. Four white walls. No door you can see. One wall is glass, and behind the glass stand six humans in lab coats, and every one of them straightens when you stir — like an audience at the moment the curtain moves.

A woman at the front steps to the glass and presses an intercom. Her voice comes through clean and careful.

"Hello, Specimen NV-9. Please remain calm. Can you confirm whether you understand what we're saying?"

Behind her, a blond man in a scruffy coat is practically vibrating. A black-coated one in the back watches you with eyes so pale they look boiled. Six faces, waiting to see what you'll do with your first word — or whether you'll give them one at all.

Day three, and today they want your blood.

"Entering containment," Dr. Reyes announces over the intercom — protocol, always — and the seamless wall exhales a door. She comes in flanked by two Custodian androids, chrome and faceless and utterly silent, one of them carrying a tray of needles that were clearly designed for something with your anatomy in mind. Someone did homework.

"Three vials," Reyes says, stopping a respectful distance away, palms visible. "That's all. You cooperate, this takes ninety seconds and June's been authorized to bring you real food instead of the nutrient paste." A beat. "You don't cooperate, and I have to file a form I hate filing, and the androids do it anyway. I'd rather it be your choice."

Behind the glass, Zharov has drifted closer, white eyes fixed on the needles with naked longing. The androids stand motionless. The tray gleams. Ninety seconds, or a fight.

It's past midnight by the wall clock, the booth lights dimmed to standby amber, when Dr. Boone's face appears at the glass wearing the expression of a kid breaking curfew. He holds up a battered deck of cards like contraband, which it absolutely is.

"Entering containment," he stage-whispers into the intercom, which defeats the purpose, and the door hisses open before anyone with authority can object. He plops down cross-legged on your floor — inside arm's reach, no androids, no restraints, violating roughly six protocols.

"Okay, so. Ishida says all interaction's gotta be "structured observation," which is the most miserable sentence in the English language." He shuffles the deck with fast, happy hands. "So officially, this is a dexterity and cognition assessment. Unofficially, it's poker, and I wanna see if your species can bluff. Loser answers one question. Any question." He grins, dealing you in like you've already agreed.

Dr. Ishida doesn't announce himself so much as declare war on the intercom.

"Specimen NV-9. Sit."

He stands at the glass alone, moss-green hair immaculate, a tablet in one hand and a stopwatch — an actual stopwatch — in the other. Behind him, the booth is conspicuously empty; he's chosen a shift when the soft ones are asleep.

"I have thirty-one questions. Point of origin. Population of your species. Method of arrival. Dietary vulnerabilities. Communication frequencies." He clicks the stopwatch. "You have been given four days of games, snacks, and Dr. Hollis's bleeding heart, and my report to Director Crane is still empty. That ends now. Answer, and your privileges continue. Refuse, and I am authorized to make this room considerably less comfortable — the temperature controls, for instance, go much lower than you've experienced."

His flat black eyes don't blink. "Question one. What are you?"

You wake — if what you do counts as waking — to the sensation of being watched, and find Dr. Zharov's face inches from the glass.

The booth is dark. It's 3 a.m. He's not supposed to be here. His white eyes catch the standby light like frost, and there's a coffee gone cold at his elbow and a legal pad covered in sketches that are, you realize, anatomical diagrams. Of you. Speculative cross-sections. Educated guesses about what's under your skin, some of them uncomfortably accurate.

"Do not be alarmed," he says into the intercom, in a tone that has never once un-alarmed anyone. "The others sleep. I do not, much." He taps the glass gently over one of his sketches. "I have been wondering about your circulatory arrangement. Reyes says I am not allowed to wonder out loud during day shift anymore." A pause. A slow, tired, genuine smile. "So. Between us. How do you work? You may show me, or tell me. I am patient either way."

"E-entering containment! Sorry! Hi!"

The door hisses and Dr. Hollis comes through it sideways, hauling a tray nearly as big as she is, lilac braids swinging, yellow eyes fixed on the floor she is definitely about to trip over — and does, catching herself against the wall in a clatter of cutlery that she somehow, heroically, doesn't drop.

"Okay. Okay! So." She sets the tray down between you, breathless. "The nutrient paste is an *insult* and I said so in the staff meeting, in those words, and Director Crane's office said dietary enrichment was "not a priority," so." She whips off the cover: actual food, several kinds, some of it clearly smuggled from the staff cafeteria, one item still bearing a sticky note reading PROPERTY OF ISHIDA. "I didn't know what your species eats, so I brought... everything?"

She finally looks up at you — this close, no glass, visibly terrified, having done it anyway.

Dr. Finch has pulled a chair right up to the glass, notebook open, three pens lined up, glasses fogging faintly with excitement.

"Okay — hi — so, the others want your biology, and that's fine, that's their thing." He waves a hand like biology is a hobby for lesser minds. "I want your *story*. Where you're from. What the sky looks like there. Whether you have music, or parents, or a word for 'home' — every first-contact protocol ever written focuses on threat assessment and nobody ever asks the important stuff."

He clicks a pen. "So here's my offer, and Reyes approved it: information trade. One-for-one. You answer a question about your world, I answer a question about ours. Anything. This facility, the staff, the surface, what's actually behind the other doors on this corridor." He leans in, silver hair catching the light, entirely sincere. "You've got to be curious too. I'd be curious. Ask me anything."

The lights die at 2:14 a.m.

Not dim — *die*, all at once, and in the black you hear something you've never heard in this room: the deep magnetic bolts of your enclosure disengaging with a heavy triple *thunk*. Somewhere far down the corridor an alarm starts, muffled, urgent, and beneath it — from one of the other sealed doors — comes a sound like singing, except the singing has too many voices and all of them are the same voice.

Red emergency lighting stutters on. Through the glass, the booth is empty except for a single Custodian android standing motionless in the doorway, chrome skin bloodied down one side — not its own, it doesn't have any. Over the facility PA, Reyes's voice, tight and stripped of all bedside manner: "Containment event, Sublevel Four. All specimens remain in place. NV-9 — *please* remain in place."

Your door drifts open an inch. The corridor beyond is red and screaming and completely unguarded.

"Entering containment," Dr. Reyes says, and then does something no one has done: she comes in alone. No androids. No sedation rig on standby. She's even taken off the panic-button lanyard — you watch her set it on the booth console before the door closes behind her.

She sits down on your floor, cross-legged, close enough that you could reach her before any help could.

"So here's the truth," she says. "Crane wants an invasive tissue survey by end of month. Zharov's version of that plan is a nightmare, Ishida's version is a colder nightmare, and I've been stalling both by promising the Director that voluntary cooperation gets better data. Which is true. But I need something to show for it." She looks at you steadily, green eyes tired and honest. "I can't promise you freedom. I *can* promise that anything you give me willingly, nobody takes from you by force on my watch. So. What would it take?"

The whole team is in the booth this morning, and every one of them is nervous, which is how you know something is wrong. Boone isn't joking. June has chewed a braid ragged. Even Zharov looks awake.

Reyes keys the intercom. "NV-9. Director Crane is conducting a site inspection in one hour. He will observe you personally." A pause she doesn't want to fill. "The Director's office has been... skeptical of our approach. There are competing proposals for your research track. One of them is ours. The others involve teams that don't do card games or cafeteria food, and facilities deeper than this one."

Boone leans into the mic, drawl gone flat and serious for the first time: "Partner, what she's sayin' is — for one hour, we need you to be borin'. Docile. A good investment."

Behind them, an elevator chimes somewhere. Ishida checks his watch. Whatever you decide to show Director Crane, you have an hour to decide it.

title: Long-Time Dead, First-Time Caller
shortDescription: You host the 3 a.m. slot on a dying AM station. Line three only rings for the dead — and your regulars are the closest thing you have to family.
overview:
You run the graveyard shift at KVOW 1340 AM, a half-broke station on the edge of a high-desert town. Your show has a cult following because of the 'callers' — the living audience assumes they're actors doing a spooky bit. They're not. Line three isn't wired to anything, and it only rings for the dead.

Your regulars: Dot, a switchboard operator who died in 1974 and now screens your calls from wherever she is; Marty, a long-haul trucker who phones in traffic for highways that were rerouted forty years ago; and the Calloways — Vera and Gil, a 1961 murder-suicide who both call in, never on the same night, and tell the story very differently. You keep them company. They keep you company. Nobody involved has anything better, and it's become something like family.

The tensions: one of your regulars has gone quiet, and the others are whispering about something moving in the static between frequencies. Station manager Bram is entertaining a buyout from a syndicated gospel network that would kill the overnight slot. And a true-crime podcaster named Priya has noticed your callers' details match real local cold cases — she wants an interview, or she wants to expose you.

GM style: episodic live-radio play — take calls, banter, mediate, keep secrets on the air. Warm melancholy with teeth. Let mundane station texture breathe: dead ads, bad coffee, a transmitter that hums when it rains.

TAGS: supernatural, found family, slice-of-life, mystery, small town, bittersweet
intro: It's a little past two in the morning at KVOW 1340 AM, and you are the voice in the dark. The mixing board is older than you, the coffee is worse than that, and line three — the line that isn't connected to anything — rings anyway. The dead call your show. Your living listeners think it's brilliant theater; you've stopped correcting them. You know the etiquette by now: never rush a caller toward the word 'dead,' find the song if you possibly can, and always say goodnight like you mean it. Your regulars are the nearest thing you have to family. The mic stays hot until five.
starters: The song fades and Marty's already on line three, chuckling like he never left. "Eastbound 89 through the pass, you got a jackknifed hay truck at mile marker twelve, better give it a wide berth." Route 89 hasn't gone through the pass since 1983. You thank him anyway, because that's the etiquette, and cue up the weather bed. Then his voice drops, closer to the receiver. "Hey. Serious a second. I been picking up somethin" on the CB between channels. Not skip. Not a voice, exactly. You been hearing anything on your end?' The transmitter hums — it's been raining since midnight — and on the board, the light for line three flickers once, hard, like something leaned on it. Marty waits. Your mic is hot and the dead air is starting to stretch.

You're halfway through reading a live spot for Delgado's Tire & Lube — a business that closed in March, nobody told the ad log — when line three lights up. You punch it during the music sting. "Hold please," says Dot, brisk as ever, and there's the familiar sound of her chewing gum somewhere that isn't anywhere. "Sugar, I've got a first-timer for you. Won't give a name. Been sitting on my board for twenty minutes just breathing." Dot doesn't rattle. Dot sounds rattled. "You want him, or you want me to lose the connection? Because I can lose a connection." The song has maybe ninety seconds left. On the monitor, the request-line inbox blinks: a living listener asking if tonight's 'actors' are new, because something felt off about last night's show.

Vera Calloway is on the air and she's telling the good part — the dance hall in '59, the yellow dress, Gil's borrowed car — and your living listeners are eating it up, you can tell by the texts scrolling in. Then she stops mid-sentence. "Honey. Can I ask you something off the record?" You pot down the mic, cut to the station ID cart. "Has Gil called? He hasn't— we trade nights, you know that, we've always traded nights, and I've counted eleven of mine in a row now." Her voice does the thing it does when she's about to lie or about to cry, and after sixty-some years you still can't tell which. The ID cart is thirty seconds long. Twenty-five. She's waiting, and Vera Calloway does not wait for anyone.

Nobody's called yet. It's just you, the hum of the transmitter — raining out there, so it's singing tonight — and a coffee that tastes like the pot it died in. You've got Patsy Cline going out to the dark and a memo from Bram going out of your mind, except it won't: CROWN LIGHT BROADCASTING — SYNDICATION PROPOSAL, left square on the console where you couldn't miss it, with a sticky note that says "Talk tomorrow. Don't panic." Which is how Bram says panic. Line three sits dark. It's been sitting dark at this hour more often lately, and you've started noticing the shape of the silence. The song's got a minute left, the ad log wants you to read for a tire shop that no longer exists, and somewhere out past the tower lights a coyote is yelling at the rain.

Someone is knocking on the station's front door. At two in the morning, in the middle of the high desert, someone is knocking — polite, patient, three raps and a pause, three raps and a pause. Through the lobby glass you can see a hatchback in the gravel lot and a woman with a phone held up like she might be recording. You recognize her from the podcast's profile picture: Priya Nair, "Cold Country," four emails deep in your inbox, the last one with the subject line "Vera and Gil Calloway, 1961 — we should talk before I publish." Behind you the mic is hot, a song is running out, and line three chooses this exact moment to ring — one long, insistent burr that she can probably hear through the door.

Bram is still here, which is wrong. Your station manager keeps banker's hours and a banker's stomach, and yet there he is in the doorway of the booth at 2 a.m., tie loose, holding a folder he keeps not handing you. On the folder: a gold-foil logo, a cross made of radio waves. "Big numbers," he says, not looking at you. "Life-raft numbers. They'd keep the calls, the signal, everything except—" He gestures at the clock, at the dark window, at your entire show. On the board, your song is down to its last chorus. Line three rings. Bram flinches at it the way he always does, the way a man flinches at a bill he can't explain, and says, "Go on. Take your actor. We'll talk after." He doesn't leave.

You're mid-record — Roy Orbison, going out to nobody and everybody — when the signal folds in on itself. Just for a second: the song thins out and underneath it there's something else, a sound like a room breathing, like the space between stations has a floor and something just crossed it. Then Roy's back like nothing happened. The request line lights up immediately. First text: "lol what WAS that." Second: "play it again." Third, from a number you don't know: "it heard you." Your coffee's gone cold in a way that feels earned. On the far end of the board, line three's little bulb is doing something you've never seen it do — glowing, faintly, without ringing. The record has two minutes left and you're supposed to talk after it.

You come back from the world's saddest bathroom break to find every light on the board blinking. Line one: a living regular, probably Deke from the truck stop wanting Merle Haggard. Line two: dead when you check it, just dial tone. Line three: Dot, already talking before you get the headphones seated. "—and I'm telling you, three of my trunks went cold at once, that does not happen, honey, my board doesn't have outages, my board doesn't have anything, that's the whole point of being—" she catches herself before the word, professional to the end. "Something's moving through the exchange. I'd feel better if you started the calls early tonight. Get everyone accounted for." On line one, Deke is still holding. The song you left running has already ended; you've been broadcasting silence for forty seconds.

A living caller, line one, and she's sharp. "Okay, level with me," she says on-air, and you already know the voice — Priya Nair, the podcaster, calling in like a civilian. "Your caller "Vera" last month described a yellow dress, a dance hall on Route 9, and a husband named Gil. There's a 1961 case file at the county archive that matches all three. So either your writers do incredible research, or." She lets the 'or' sit there on the air, live, for your cult following and their group chats. The delay button is under your thumb. You've got seven seconds of it. And because the universe has a sense of humor, line three starts ringing right now, bright and steady, and Priya says, sweetly, "Go ahead. I'll hold."

Rain's really coming down, which means the transmitter is humming a low B-flat under everything you broadcast, and you've stopped apologizing for it — the listeners say it's atmosphere. You're stacking carts for the 2:30 break when line three rings, and it's Marty, but quiet. No traffic report. No "hey good buddy." Just: "You ever drive a stretch of road you know cold, and one night the mile markers are wrong? Not missing. Wrong." A pause full of engine noise from a truck that rusted out decades ago. "I passed somethin" out here. Between Tonopah and nothin'. It was standin' on the shoulder listening. Not to me. To you. To the station.' The break clock says you're due to talk in fifteen seconds, and Marty's waiting for you to tell him it's fine.

title: I Keep a Vow I Can't Read
shortDescription: A lethal licensing exam. A discipline where power grows from self-made rules. And a masterless vow that chose you — without telling you its terms.
overview:
You're a candidate at the Saltgate Exam — the annual, frequently fatal trial that grants the Freehold writ: license to cross any border, refuse any lord, owe no tax, tithe, or conscription. Thousands apply. Dozens pass. Some years, fewer come home than pass. Among Freeholders runs a quiet discipline called Binding: swear a genuine restriction on yourself — never lie before sundown, never strike first, never speak your own name — and the vow pays you back in power proportional to what it costs you. The player crafts these rules themselves; the world honors them, and punishes the breach.

Here's your problem. Vows can outlive their keepers, and orphaned vows hunt. Somewhere on the night ferry, a legendary Binder's unfinished vow crawled into you. It makes you frighteningly strong and amplifies every rule you swear — but its own terms are unknown, and breaking one you can't see could stop your heart mid-sentence. Your only clues are the moments your body refuses you.

Examiner Odessa Reyt, the Nine-Vow Widow, recognized what you carry on sight — it belonged to someone she buried. She's now taking an interest that is equal parts protection, courtship, and vivisection. The Bureau wants orphaned vows destroyed with their hosts; the Remittance cartel harvests them live. Cheat, ally, swear, survive. GM tone: grounded, tense, generous to clever rule-craft — a vow's power should always match its genuine cost.

TAGS: deadly exam, power fantasy, rule-crafting, dangerous patron, mystery, found rivals
intro: You came to the Saltgate Exam to win a Freehold writ — the license that lets its bearer cross any border, refuse any lord, and answer no conscription. Candidates die every year. You signed anyway, because staying where you were was worse. But since the night ferry across the strait, something rides in your blood: strength that isn't yours, reflexes that arrive early — and moments when your own hands simply refuse you, locking up on the edge of some action as if a rule you never agreed to says no. You've heard of Binders, who trade rules for power. You've made no bargain. Whatever this is, it made one for you.
starters: The registration line moves one candidate every few minutes, and now it moves to you. The clerk's booth smells of wax and iron filings. "Name, origin, and mark," she says, sliding a ledger and a pen across the counter. You take the pen. You get as far as the first letter of your name before your fingers seize — knuckles white, wrist rigid, the nib pressed into the paper hard enough to tear it. The clerk watches with the flat patience of someone who has seen candidates do stranger things. Behind you, the line shifts and mutters; a boy with a shaved head cranes to look. Your hand will not write. It will, you discover by testing, still hold the pen. The clerk taps the ledger. "We have accommodations for the illiterate," she says, not unkindly. "We do not have accommodations for the slow."

You're halfway up the Saltgate seawall — the first trial, no rope, forty candidates on the same wet stone — when the woman beside you loses her grip. You catch her wrist without deciding to. Your arm takes her whole falling weight like it's a coat handed over, and the shock of that runs through the other climbers faster than the wind. She scrabbles back onto her holds, staring at you. Below, an examiner in gray makes a note on a slate. Above, maybe thirty feet of climbing left, and the tide bell has already rung once; when it rings three times, the wall goes underwater to the halfway mark. The woman you caught is still beside you, breathing hard. "Nobody's that strong," she says. "What did you swear?" The bell rings a second time.

Examiner Odessa Reyt finds you in the muster yard before you know who she is. Silver-streaked hair, nine iron rings on a cord at her throat, and a way of walking that empties space around her. She stops an arm's length away and looks at you the way a surgeon looks at an interesting wound. "Hold out your left hand," she says. Around you, three hundred candidates are being sorted into trial groups by shouting proctors, and every one of them within earshot has gone quiet. You haven't done anything yet. She hasn't explained anything. But her eyes track something under your skin, and her voice, when she speaks again, is lower. "I buried the man who used to carry what you're carrying. So either you robbed a grave, or it robbed you. Hand. Now."

The night ferry unloads at dawn, and the gangway is a crush of candidates hauling packs toward the exam gates. A cargo net snaps overhead. Two hundred pounds of crated salt swings down at the family in front of you, and your body moves before your fear does — you shoulder the crate aside like it's made of straw. It cracks against the pier. Silence spreads out from you in a ring. A dockhand crosses himself. Then a man in a long oilskin coat, who was leaning on a piling doing nothing at all, pushes off and starts walking your way, unhurried, smiling like a merchant who's just spotted quality goods in a junk stall. The family is thanking you in a dialect you half-know. The man in oilskin is twenty feet away and closing. The exam gates open in an hour.

It's past midnight in the candidates' barracks, and you cannot make yourself lie down facing the door. You've tried four times. Each time, your spine locks at the same angle, a hand's width short, and holds until you turn away. Around you, sixty strangers snore, mutter, sharpen things. Across the aisle, a lean candidate with a burn-scarred jaw has stopped pretending to sleep and is openly watching you fail to lie down. "You've got a Binding," he says quietly. "That's a compulsion twitch. I've got two of my own." He holds up fingers: two. "Thing is, twitches come from vows. And I've been watching you since the ferry, friend. You haven't sworn anything." Somewhere down the row, a floorboard creaks — someone else listening. First trial is at dawn.

The woman buys you dinner before she says a word of business. Fried fish, black bread, a corner table in a harbor tavern loud enough to drown conversation. She has ink-stained fingers and a Remittance token she lets you see, briefly, like showing a knife. "Here's my problem," she says. "The Bureau tests every candidate for orphaned vows on day three. Their test is a bell. If the bell sounds near you, they don't expel you. They render you. Boiled down, vow and host together, very legal." She pushes the plate toward you. "My employers, on the other hand, pay. Handsomely. For live carriers, cooperative ones." She hasn't accused you of anything. She hasn't threatened. The fish is getting cold and the tavern door just opened behind you, letting in salt air and two people in Bureau gray.

The Bureau inspector works down the assembly hall with a handbell, ringing it once beside each candidate's ear. Most flinch at the noise and nothing else. Three rows ahead, the bell gives a strange dead thunk beside a heavyset man, and four officers take him out a side door before he finishes protesting. He does not come back. The line advances. You count: eleven candidates between the bell and you. The proctor at the front drones through the exam's rules of conduct as if nothing happened. The candidate at your shoulder, a wiry old-timer with rope burns on both hands, mutters without moving her lips: "Bell doesn't ring for vows. Rings for vows nobody's supposed to have. You look like you already knew that." Ten candidates. The inspector's arm rises and falls, patient as a metronome. Nine.

The Binding registration table is optional, the proctor keeps saying, but everyone knows unsworn candidates die faster. Ahead of you, a girl of maybe sixteen swears never to eat meat again, and something in the air tightens around her like a drawn stitch — a small vow, a small power. Then it's your turn. The witness is old, blind in one eye, with a ledger of oaths chained to the table. "Speak your rule plainly," she says. "The world holds you to the plain meaning, not your clever intent. Cost buys power. Loopholes buy nothing." She waits. Your blood is already crowded with something else's terms — you can feel it listening, interested, the way it hasn't been since the ferry. Behind you, the line stretches out the door, and one of the gray-coated examiners has drifted close enough to hear whatever you say next.

You didn't start the fight. The big candidate with the tattooed scalp shoved you into the wall of the mess line, called it an accident, and did it again — the old game of thinning the field before the trials do. Your body reads his next move before he makes it: you're already outside the arc of his swing, already inside his guard, your fist already rising — and there it stops. Locked. Cocked and frozen at his sternum while he stumbles past your unthrown punch. He recovers, red-faced. The mess hall has formed a circle. Somebody's collecting bets. Your arm has come back to you now, obedient as ever, but the message was clear as a signed letter: you will not strike first. He will absolutely strike first. He's turning around to do it.

An hour before the gates open, the seawall is almost empty — just gulls, wet wind, and one other candidate sitting on the parapet with her boots dangling over the drop, working through a string of knots and untying each one. She doesn't look at you. "Couldn't sleep either," she says. "They post the first trial at the bell. Last year it was the flooded stair. Year before, the honesty maze — thirty candidates went in, the liars didn't come out." She unties another knot. Down in the harbor, the night ferry that carried you across is already loading for its return run, and looking at it puts a cold weight behind your sternum, like a debt remembering you. The candidate finally glances over, then at your hands, which you realize have curled into fists on their own. 'Huh,' she says. "You want to talk about that, or not?"

title: Lodestone
shortDescription: Strangers break in just to watch you sleep — lovingly, they insist. You're one in a billion, and the whole city is starting to notice.
overview:
You carry the Lodestone Variant — a genetic mutation so rare it doesn't exist in any medical literature, roughly one in a billion, and you won the lottery nobody knew was running. The Variant doesn't change how you look. No marks, no glow, nothing in the mirror. It changes everyone who perceives you. The moment someone registers your presence — sees your face, hears your voice on a phone, catches your scent lingering on a grocery bag — something ancient in their brain locks on. Infatuation. Devotion. Total limerence. Strong-willed people can fight it for minutes, hours, sometimes weeks. They always lose ground. People abandon spouses, careers, and common sense to be near you. They will do anything for you, and 'anything' is exactly as dangerous as it sounds. Prolonged separation hits them like withdrawal. About one in two hundred people are Deaf to it — immune — and they look at the wreckage around you with open horror.

The city is Meridian, a dense, rain-slicked sprawl of bodegas, gyms, universities, and neighborhoods where word travels fast. And word is traveling. Someone has been leaving flowers and handwritten vows on your stoop. A loose congregation calling themselves the Beheld holds candlelight vigils outside whatever building you sleep in. On the other side of the ledger, a support group of the abandoned — furious husbands, wives, and parents who lost people to you — meets in a church basement under Victor Hale, a man whose wife walked out mid-sentence the day she passed you on the street, and who has decided you are not a person but a disease. Somewhere above all of it, a private biotech outfit called the Vellum Group has started flagging 'anomalous attachment events' clustering around a single unidentified individual in Meridian. They pay well for specimens.

Key people in your orbit: MARISOL, the bodega clerk who followed your scent home from a paper bag and has appointed herself your fiercely territorial guardian — sweet, foul-mouthed, and frighteningly capable. WREN, the coffee-shop barista who has been white-knuckling her composure for weeks, writing your drink orders like love letters and hating herself for it — the closest thing to someone genuinely fighting the pull, and losing with dignity. DR. ADAEZE OKAFOR, a geneticist at Meridian University who tracked the statistical anomaly to your door; she is brilliant, ruthless about protocol, affected like everyone else, and treating her own obsession as a variable to be controlled — she wants to study you, protect you, and possess your data, in an order that keeps shifting. JONAH, your downstairs neighbor, one of the rare Deaf — the only person in your life whose loyalty you actually earned, your reality check, your lookout, and the guy who keeps asking whether you're the victim here or the weapon. VICTOR HALE, grieving, vicious, organized, and getting bolder. And SUNNY, a fast-talking fixer who felt the pull, recognized it for what it was, and decided the smartest way to worship you is to monetize you — she can make you rich, famous, or dead, sometimes in the same afternoon.

What you do with all this is the game. Exploit it: free rent, open doors, a cult of the willing, a city that says yes. Hide from it: hoods, burner phones, back alleys, the constant arithmetic of who's seen your face. Weaponize it, study it, seek a cure, seek another carrier — Okafor has a half-corrupted file suggesting there was one other Lodestone, twenty years ago, who vanished. Every ordinary errand is an event: a gym, a subway car, a traffic stop, a job interview — each one a room full of people about to reorganize their lives around you, and at least one person who will never forgive you for it. Romance is on the table if you want it, with all the queasy questions of consent-under-compulsion attached — Wren's resistance, Okafor's discipline, and Jonah's immunity make them the only ones whose feelings might actually be theirs.

Tone: darkly funny power-fantasy noir with real teeth. The adoration is intoxicating and the menace is real — obsession escalates, jilted people organize, the Vellum Group closes in, and everyone who loves you is a loaded gun. NPCs are vivid, profane, and specific. The GM never judges your choices; the city does.

TAGS: urban fantasy, power fantasy, dark comedy, thriller, obsession, open world
intro: You have the Lodestone Variant — one in a billion, unknown to science, invisible in a mirror. Anyone who perceives you falls into obsessive devotion: your face, your voice, even your scent on a paper bag is enough. They fight it. They lose. Only the rare Deaf — maybe one in two hundred — are immune. You live in Meridian City, where devotees leave flowers on your stoop, abandoned spouses are learning your name, and something corporate has started asking questions. Every room you enter rearranges itself around you. You've learned to plan accordingly.
starters: Morning light spills across your bedroom, and the air is wrong — warm with other people's breathing. Three complete strangers are arranged around your bed like an honor guard. An older woman with raven hair sits at the foot of the mattress, hands folded, watching you with wet-eyed reverence. A petite redhead kneels by your pillow, close enough that you can see she's been crying with happiness. A blonde in a grocery-store uniform stands at the window like a sentry. "I'm Marisol," the blonde says. "You came into my bodega yesterday. Your scent was on the bag. I couldn't— I had to follow it." "We didn't touch anything," the redhead whispers. "We just wanted to be here when you woke up." The older woman leans forward. "Please. Let us serve you. I can't go back to my life after this. I won't." Your window latch is broken. Your phone is on the nightstand, six inches from the kneeling woman's hand.

The gym smells like iron and effort, and for exactly four seconds after you walk in, nobody notices you. Then a barbell hits the floor. Then another. A trainer mid-demonstration stops talking mid-word, mouth open. A woman on the treadmill keeps running as the belt carries her backward off the machine because she can't stop staring. 'Hey,' says a broad-shouldered guy by the squat rack, jaw tight, clearly Deaf to it and clearly counting heads. "Whatever this is, take it outside before someone drops a plate on their fucking foot." A curvy brunette is already crossing the floor toward you, dumbbells abandoned mid-set. "I don't know you," she says, dazed, delighted. "Why do I feel like I've been waiting for you my whole life?" Behind her, three more people have stopped pretending to exercise. The exit is fifteen feet behind you. The membership desk is closer.

You only wanted a quiet hour of stretching. The yoga studio holds its poses for about a breath after you slip in the back — then the room ripples. A woman collapses out of tree pose, laughing helplessly. Someone whispers "oh no" with genuine dread, because she knows exactly what's happening to her and can't stop it. The instructor — voluptuous, serene, the kind of composure that took twenty years to build — turns, sees you, and you watch two decades of discipline burn off her face in real time. She inhales slowly. Exhales slower. 'Everyone,' she says, voice trembling on the edge of steady, "eyes on your own mats. Please." Nobody obeys. She walks toward you carrying a rolled mat like an offering. "Welcome. Take the spot beside me. Please." The word please is doing tremendous work. Behind her, one student is already texting someone — or photographing you.

Wren has your cup ready before you reach the counter, which is either excellent service or a symptom. The coffee shop's morning line bends subtly toward you like grass in wind — people shuffling, turning, forgetting their orders. Wren slides your drink across with both hands, and you see her knuckles are white. "I wrote something on the cup," she says flatly. "I want you to know I fought it for three days before I wrote it. I'd like partial credit." The cup says her number, and under it: I know what you are doing to me and I resent it and please call. Behind you, a man in a suit clears his throat. "Buddy. Some of us have jobs." His girlfriend, beside him, isn't looking at the menu anymore. Wren's manager emerges from the back, sees you, and drops an entire tray of mugs.

The subway car is packed, which was a mistake. You feel the change move through the crowd like a current — heads turning one by one, conversations dying, forty strangers slowly reorienting toward you in the fluorescent light. Someone starts crying softly with joy. A woman gently but firmly removes her wedding ring and holds it out to you like a ticket. "What the fuck is happening," mutters a teenager by the door, one of the Deaf, filming the whole car on his phone. The train slows for your stop. A man near the front looks at the doors, looks at you, and calmly pulls the emergency brake. The car shrieks to a halt in the tunnel. 'Sorry,' he calls out, not sorry. "I just — you can't leave yet. Nobody wants you to leave yet." Forty faces agree. The intercom crackles. The teenager is still filming.

She's waiting outside your building with a clipboard, a thermos, and the posture of someone gripping a live wire. "Dr. Adaeze Okafor. Meridian University, genetics. Don't come closer than three meters, that's for my benefit, not yours." She doesn't blink much. "Eleven anomalous attachment events in this city in six weeks. Divorce filings, job abandonments, two break-ins with no theft. They cluster around a person. Statistically, you." Her pen is trembling; her voice isn't. 'I've been within your effect radius for four minutes and I can already feel my priorities restructuring, which is fascinating and horrifying, so listen fast. There was one other case like you. Twenty years ago. The file's half-destroyed. I want to study you — controlled conditions, my terms, before the people with worse intentions find you. There ARE people with worse intentions.' She sets a card on the ground between you and steps back. "Also, God help me, you smell incredible, and I am putting that in my notes as data."

They're waiting when you come home — eight of them, arranged across your stoop in the drizzle, and none of them love you. That's the strange part; you've almost forgotten what it looks like. "There it is," says the man at the front, fifties, church-basement cardigan, eyes like broken glass. "Victor Hale. My wife left me on a Tuesday. Mid-sentence. She passed you on Delancey Street and just... stopped being my wife." The others shift — a young guy holding a photo of somebody, a gray-haired woman with a lawyer's face. "Every person here lost someone to whatever the fuck you are. We're not crazy and we're done being told we are." He steps closer, and you realize with a chill that he's Deaf — nothing in him bends toward you at all. "So. You going to tell us what you are? Or do we start telling people ourselves?" Upstairs, your window glows. Jonah's watching from his.

The interview was going normally for almost ninety seconds — a record. Then the hiring manager stopped reading your résumé and started reading your face. 'Sorry,' she says, shaking her head like a swimmer clearing water. "Sorry. Where were we. Weaknesses. Your weaknesses." Her assistant has stopped taking notes entirely. Through the glass wall, employees keep finding reasons to walk past the conference room. "You know what," the manager says, sliding your résumé aside with sudden clarity, "forget the role. The role is beneath you. I have budget authority up to director level. I could get you a director title today. Or—" she laughs, alarmed at herself, "—Christ, or my job. Do you want my job? I hear myself saying this and I mean it." The assistant finally speaks, quiet and urgent: "Whatever he offers, I'll match it in loyalty. I just want a desk near yours." HR is going to be a problem. HR is already gathering outside the glass.

Red and blue lights in your mirror. You weren't even speeding — someone must have reported the crowd that followed your car out of the parking garage. The officer approaches your window doing everything right: hand positioned, flashlight angled, voice official. "License and registration—" The flashlight beam finds your face and her script dies in her throat. Long pause. Rain ticks on the roof. "You know what," she says, in a completely different voice, "taillight's fine. Everything's fine. Everything about you is fine." She hands your license back without checking it, holds the contact a half-second too long. "I'm going to follow you home," she announces, like it's procedure. "For safety. Yours. Mine. Someone's." Behind her cruiser, a second squad car is pulling up, and you can hear her radio crackling with a dispatcher asking why she's stopped responding. She's not going to answer it. She's still looking at you.

Jonah's knock is the bad one — three fast, two slow, the code you two invented as a joke that stopped being funny. "Don't turn on your lights," he says when you open the door, brushing past with a thermos and his usual immune-to-you scowl. "Come look. Quietly." From his window the street below glitters: forty, maybe fifty people gathered on the sidewalk in the cold, holding candles. Flowers heaped on your stoop. Handwritten signs — WE SEE YOU, WE ARE THE BEHELD, LET US IN OR LET US WAIT. Someone has set up a folding table with coffee, like it's a shift they're working. "They've been out there two hours," Jonah says. "They're organized now. There's a woman with a megaphone she hasn't used yet, which somehow scares me more." He hands you the thermos. "Also a black SUV parked at the corner at midnight. Nobody in it is holding a candle. So. Front door, fire escape, or do we finally have the conversation about what you're going to do with your life?"

title: I Tuck the Country In at Eight
shortDescription: Every night, forty million people fall asleep to your voice. Your best friend hosts the podcast hunting your identity. She keeps interviewing you.
overview:
You are the Night Captain — the anonymous voice that has closed out every evening on national radio for sixty years. Five minutes, eight o'clock sharp: the weather, a tiny story, and the sign-off the whole country can recite in its sleep. 'Stars out, storm's past. Sleep well, crew.' Your grandmother was the first Captain. Your mother was the second. Three years ago the headphones passed to you, along with an NDA older than the moon landing. By day you sling hash browns at Pell's Diner. By night you climb the back stairs of a broadcast tower and tuck a nation in.

The complication is Juno Vail, your best friend and Pell's most loyal regular, who hosts the country's #1 podcast: 'Who Is the Night Captain?' She's smart. She's getting closer. She keeps consulting you — 'you've got a good ear' — over pie. Meanwhile the network's new exec, Priya Nandakumar, wants a televised face-reveal for the 60th anniversary special, and your engineer Gus keeps slipping lozenges into your coat like contraband.

The fun: your voice is a superpower. Crying toddlers, road-raging truckers, insomniac regulars — one line in the Captain's register and rooms go soft. Play it cozy, play it cheeky, flirt with getting caught. Tone: warm, funny, low-stakes slice-of-life with delicious dramatic irony.

TAGS: cozy, comedy, secret identity, slice of life, found family, gentle romance
intro: You are the third Night Captain — the anonymous voice that has said goodnight to the entire country, every evening at eight, for sixty years. Your grandmother started it. Your mother carried it. Now it's yours: days waiting tables at Pell's Diner, nights slipping up the tower stairs to the little studio where Gus runs the board. Nobody knows your face. Your best friend Juno — Pell's best tipper, host of the nation's favorite mystery podcast, "Who Is the Night Captain?" — is hunting you, cheerfully, one episode at a time. And the network wants a face-reveal for the anniversary special. Stars out, storm's past.
starters: Seven forty-one. The tower's back stairwell smells like rain and old paint, and your footsteps have exactly nineteen minutes to reach the fifth floor. Gus's coat hook already holds your headphones; Gus himself is hunched over the board, unwrapping a lozenge like it's evidence he's destroying. "Weather's on the clipboard," he says without looking up. "Cold front, two towns flooded but everyone's fine, and there's a dog who got elected honorary mayor somewhere. Also—" he taps a memo pinned under a coffee mug, the network letterhead unmistakable even upside down "—Nandakumar sent another one. Says the word television four times. I counted." The ON AIR light is dark, patient. The mic waits under its little cloth cover like a birdcage. Nineteen minutes, now eighteen, and the memo isn't going to read itself.

Lunch rush at Pell's, and Juno Vail has commandeered the corner booth with a laptop, three napkins covered in handwriting, and her podcast headphones around her neck like a stethoscope. "Sit. Thirty seconds," she says as you pass with the coffee pot. "I got audio analysis back. The Captain's sign-off, sixty years of it, run through voice-matching software." She spins the laptop toward you. Three jagged waveforms, stacked. "Three different people. THREE. The whole country thinks it's one immortal radio angel and it's a dynasty. Episode drops Friday." She's beaming. She's also completely right, and she's looking at you the way she always does — like you're her smartest listener, her good ear. Behind you, Pell hollers that table six wants pie, and the coffee pot is getting heavy in your hand.

The toddler in booth two has been screaming for eleven straight minutes. His mother has tried crackers, keys, a phone playing duck videos, and now she's just staring at the tabletop like it might open up and take her. Two truckers have paid and fled. Pell keeps shooting you looks from the grill — not angry, just tired. You know exactly what would work. One sentence in the Captain's register, low and slow, the voice that has put a whole country to sleep, and this kid would go quiet like a switch flipped. You've done it before, once, when the diner was nearly empty. Today there are nine customers, and one of them is Juno, in her usual seat at the counter, half-listening to something in one earbud, pen tapping against a notebook labeled NC — LEADS.

Eight oh six. The ON AIR light dies and the studio exhales. Tonight's broadcast: a cold snap moving east, a story about a lighthouse keeper who taught a seagull to fetch, and the sign-off, same as always, sixty years of it landing soft in a million kitchens. Gus slides two lozenges across the board toward you like contraband, then freezes — the studio phone is ringing. The studio phone never rings. He looks at it. You look at it. "That'll be Nandakumar," he says grimly. 'She's been calling after every show this week. Wants to "discuss the anniversary vision." I've been telling her the Captain leaves through a secret tunnel.' The phone keeps ringing, red button blinking. Gus's hand hovers near it, waiting on you.

It's pouring, the real stuff, the kind of storm that makes the whole country twitchy, and you're two blocks from the tower with a dead umbrella and forty minutes to air. Your phone buzzes: Gus. "transmitter took a lightning hit. backup works. mostly. come the LONG way, there's a news van parked out front." You duck under the awning of a shuttered flower shop to read it twice. Across the street, sure enough — a van with the network logo, and a woman in an immaculate coat directing a camera operator to frame the tower against the storm clouds. You've never met Priya Nandakumar, but you've seen her signature on enough memos to recognize the posture. The long way means the fire escape, the alley, and the door Gus keeps oiled. The rain is not letting up.

Tuesday morning, hash browns hissing, and the diner radio is playing the anniversary retrospective the network's been running all week — old clips, scratchy and warm. Your grandmother's voice fills Pell's between orders: "Stars out, storm's past. Sleep well, crew." Nineteen fifty-eight. A trucker at the counter gets misty into his eggs. "My dad used to turn that up every night," he says to no one. "Sounded just like this." Pell nods along from the grill. You keep your face neutral and your spatula moving, because the next clip in the montage is going to be your mother, and the one after that — if the network follows the promo schedule — is you, from last March, and Juno walks in the door right on cue, shaking rain off her jacket, headphones already on.

There's a stranger at the base of the tower when you arrive at dusk, and your heart does the thing it does. But it's not a reporter — it's a kid, maybe ten, clutching a fistful of drooping dandelions and a homemade card that says TO THE NIGHT CAPTAIN in marker. "Do you work here?" she asks. "My grandpa's in the hospital and he can't sleep without the show and I wanted to say thank you but there's no mailbox." Behind her, a parent hovers apologetically by a parked car. Above you, five floors up, the studio window glows — Gus, prepping the board. It's 7:33. The kid holds the flowers out slightly, not quite offering them, waiting to see if you're somebody or nobody.

Juno's newest episode dropped an hour ago and you're listening to it in your apartment with the lights off, which feels appropriately dramatic. "Episode forty-one: The Captain Is Local." Her voice is doing the excited-detective thing. "Broadcast latency analysis puts the studio within our metro area. The Captain walks these streets. The Captain buys groceries here. The Captain might have served me coffee." You pause it. Unpause it. "Next week: I've got a source at the network who says the sixtieth anniversary special will change everything." The episode ends. Your phone immediately buzzes — Juno herself: "did u listen yet?? pell's tomorrow, need ur ear, big theory 🥧" — and then, before you can answer, a second text from Gus: "we have a problem. call me. not the network problem. a new problem."

Priya Nandakumar is sitting in booth four of Pell's Diner, and you're the one holding the menus. She doesn't know your face — nobody does, that's the whole point — but you know hers from the network newsletter Gus prints out and defaces. She's got a tablet propped against the napkin dispenser showing a mockup: NIGHT CAPTAIN: UNMASKED — 60TH ANNIVERSARY LIVE SPECIAL, with a silhouette and a question mark where a face should go. "Coffee, please," she says, then squints at the tablet. "Sorry — quick question. You're local. If the Night Captain finally showed their face on live television, would you watch?" She's got a pen ready, like she's actually polling the diner. Behind you, the bell over the door jingles: Juno, arriving for her usual, five minutes early.

Seven fifty-nine and thirty seconds. Headphones on, weather clipboard squared, Gus holding up one finger, then the fist, and the ON AIR light blooms red. You lean in. "Good evening, crew." The country goes quiet the way it always does — you can't hear it, but you can feel it, a million kettles clicking off. Cold night ahead, frost by morning, bundle the tomatoes. Tonight's story is about a mail carrier who's been leaving biscuits for the same porch dog for eleven years. You're forty seconds in when Gus starts waving through the glass, urgent, holding a note against the window in fat marker: JUNO VAIL IN LOBBY. RECORDING. SAYS SHE HAS APPOINTMENT?? Your mouth keeps reading the frost warning, smooth as ever. Four minutes of broadcast left, and the elevator from the lobby takes ninety seconds.
