title: It Told Me How to Kill It
shortDescription: Something ancient beneath the lake is courting you — patient, polite, by old rules. Its first gift was the secret of its own death.
overview:
You're the new keeper of Camp Greenglass, a lakeside summer camp your great-aunt Maren tended for forty years until the ice took her in March. With the job came her ledger, the boathouse keys, and an arrangement nobody wrote down: something lives beneath the lake, and while a keeper stands at the waterline, no camper drowns. It calls itself Alder. It is older than the valley. And it has decided, this summer, to court you — formally, by rules it will explain if asked. Three gifts before the last night of the season, three refusals permitted. Its first gift was leverage against itself: the iron bell in the boathouse, and the exact spot where ringing it underwater would put it down for a century. 'So that you may refuse me with teeth,' it said. It never lies. It never crosses the waterline uninvited. It wears the neatly dressed faces of its drowned, and asks which you prefer.

Meanwhile the county is lifting the old quarantine on the deep water, a survey firm is sounding the lakebed for a dam, Director Roo pays you in cash and asks nothing, lifeguard Sol is starting to notice things, and a nine-year-old named Wren keeps stacking stones where the water can see them. Maren's ledger says every keeper answered the courtship differently. Some entries just stop.

Tone: slow-burn gothic romance against warm, mundane summer-camp texture. Alder is genuinely courteous, genuinely dangerous, and always honest.

TAGS: gothic romance, folk horror, slow burn, ancient suitor, summer camp, mutual leverage
intro: You are the keeper of Camp Greenglass, inheritor of your great-aunt Maren's cabin, her ledger, and her boathouse keys — she went through the ice in March, and the job passed to you with the season already booked. You know what the campers don't: something old lives under the lake, it keeps the swimmers safe because a keeper stands at the shore, and this summer it is courting you by formal rules. Three gifts before the last night of the season. Its first gift, freely given, was the iron bell and the exact place to ring it — the means of its own death. It has never once lied to you.
starters: Six-fifteen in the morning, and the lake is glass all the way to the far pines. You're doing what Maren's ledger says to do — stand at the waterline before the first camper wakes, coffee in hand, let the water see you — when something rises ten feet out. It wears a young man's face today, hair neatly parted and dry despite everything, collar buttoned to the throat. "Good morning, keeper," Alder says, in a voice like the underside of a dock. "I've been considering my second gift. Nothing is decided. You may ask me anything about the rules while the camp still sleeps — they are your rules too, now, and I would rather you know them than stumble." Behind you, up the hill, the first cabin's screen door bangs. A counselor's whistle, far off. Alder waits, hands folded on the surface of the water as if it were a table.

The mess hall smells of syrup and bleach. Director Roo slides an envelope across the office desk — cash, thick, unlabeled — and goes back to the schedule board without meeting your eyes. "Swim tests start at ten," she says. "You'll be at the water for all of them. Maren always was." She pins a card, unpins it, pins it again. "County's sending someone this week about the deep-water quarantine. They'll want to walk the shoreline. I told them the keeper handles the shoreline." The word keeper sits in the room a moment too long. Through the office window you can see the swim dock, the buoy lines, and past them the dark seam where the shallows drop away — the water there a different color, like a held breath. Roo finally looks at you. "Anything you need from me," she says, "don't ask. Just take it."

You find Wren at the shallow end of the beach during rest hour, when every nine-year-old is supposed to be in a bunk. She has built four stone towers at the edge of the wet sand, each exactly where the lake can reach them at its fullest, and she is starting a fifth. "They fall down at night," she tells you without turning around, "but that's okay. That's how you know it looked." Out past the buoys the water is flat and attentive in the noon heat. Wren balances a white pebble on top, tongue between her teeth. "Maren showed me. She said stacking is polite. Are you the new one? You stand where she stood." Somewhere up the hill a counselor is calling Wren's name, getting closer, and the girl looks at you like the two of you already share something.

It's past midnight and you can't sleep, so you're in the boathouse with a flashlight and Maren's ledger open on the workbench. The iron bell hangs from its bracket in the corner, small as a schoolbell, heavier than it looks — you've lifted it once and haven't touched it since. The ledger entry under your thumb is dated 1974, a keeper named Elias, careful handwriting for eleven pages and then, mid-sentence: "and so I told it that I would". Nothing after. Not torn out — just stopped. Outside, water knocks softly against the hulls of the racked canoes, a patient sound, almost like knuckles. Then, unmistakably, from the dark slot where the boathouse opens onto the lake, a voice: "You read late, keeper. Elias was fond of that lamp hook, there, above your head. Ask me what happened to him, if you like. I'll tell you truly."

Sol catches you by the equipment shed, still dripping from lifeguard rotation, whistle lanyard wrapped twice around one fist. 'Okay,' they say, low, glancing back at the swimmers. "Third time. Marcus went under past the drop-off, dead weight, and something pushed him up. I felt the wake of it against my legs. That is not a fish." Out on the water, the afternoon session churns on — shrieking, splashing, a counselor refereeing chicken fights. Sol steps closer. "Roo says talk to the keeper. Everybody says talk to the keeper, like that's a job that means something. Maren used to stand right there —" they point at the worn patch of shore where you stand every day — "and mouth words at the lake. I watched her do it." Sol's waiting, arms crossed, sunburned and stubborn, and behind them the lake glitters like it's listening.

The survey boat arrives on a Tuesday, white-hulled, humming, dragging a sonar fish on a yellow cable. You're on the swim dock when it crosses the buoy line into the deep water — the water nobody's supposed to enter, per the county quarantine that is apparently no longer anybody's problem. A man in a reflective vest waves at you cheerfully from the stern. The lake goes very still around the hull. Not calm — still, the way a room goes still. Down the beach, Director Roo has come out of the mess hall and stopped dead, one hand shading her eyes. The sonar unit begins its pinging, tick, tick, tick, sounding the lakebed for the dam feasibility study, and under the dock, just beneath your feet, something long passes through the shadow of the pilings, unhurried, heading out toward the boat.

Rain since dinner, so evening program moved indoors, and you have the shoreline to yourself. You're checking that the canoes are tied when you notice a figure standing waist-deep in the shallows, twenty feet out, exactly at the edge of the light from the lodge windows. Tonight it wears a woman's face — middle-aged, kind around the eyes, hair pinned like a photograph from the fifties. "Forgive the weather," Alder says. "I find rain sociable. It's all lake, eventually." Water beads on its dry wool coat and rolls off. "I came to say only this: the men with the sounding boat found the place where the bell works. It's on their charts now, marked as an anomaly. I gave that place to you, keeper. I did not give it to them." It tilts the borrowed face, courteous, unblinking. Up the hill, the campers are singing something about a moose.

First morning of the season, and you're late to the waterline because Maren's cabin door swelled shut in the humidity. By the time you reach the beach, forty campers are already lined up for swim tests, Sol is calling names off a clipboard, and the lake looks ordinary — sunlit, weedy at the edges, smelling of gasoline and pine. Then the first kid dives off the dock and you feel it: a pressure change, low in your chest, like the whole lake turning over in its sleep to look. A voice arrives inside the sound of the water lapping the sand, meant only for you: "There you are. I was beginning to worry you'd stay in the cabin all summer. Stand where she stood, please. I keep my bargains better when I can see you." Sol calls the next name. The second kid is already on the diving board.

You're sorting Maren's things by lamplight — a task you've put off for weeks — when you find the shoebox under her bed: four decades of photographs, and in nearly every summer's beach shot, if you look at the far edge of the frame, a figure standing in the shallows. Different clothes, different builds, different decades of hairstyle. The same stillness. In the last photo, dated this past August, Maren is in the water up to her knees, laughing, and the figure beside her is laughing too, and their hands are almost touching. On the back, in her handwriting: "It asked again. Forty years and it still asks." There's a knock at the cabin door — three polite raps. Through the screen you can see small sneakers and skinned knees: Wren, out after lights-out, holding a flat white stone in both hands like an offering.

The campfire is down to coals and the last cabin has been herded up the hill, singing off-key, when Roo appears beside you with two mugs of bad coffee and nods at the dock. Someone is standing at the end of it. Adult, well-dressed, motionless, facing the water — except no adult came up the camp road tonight, and the figure's clothes are dry in a way that has nothing to do with rain. "It does that when it wants a word," Roo says, flat. "Never comes past the waterline. Never has." She presses one mug into your hands and takes a step back, not toward the dock. "Maren used to say the trick was remembering it means every single thing it says. Both the sweet things and the other kind." Out on the dock, the figure turns its head, unhurried, and waits for you with perfect patience.

title: I Installed Every Tyrant
shortDescription: The crew that saved your life topples tyrants island by island — every tyrant you installed. Be useful. Be loved. Stay masked.
overview:
You were the Anchor — the Meridian Charter's masked enforcer, dropped on any island that dreamed too loud. You installed the governors, wrote the tithe schedules, broke rebellions with paperwork and cannon fire. Then came an order you couldn't carry out. So you tore the Gull Ledger — the Charter's master book of puppets, trade routes, and one sealed page you still haven't dared read — out of the flagship's vault, and went over the rail.

The crew of the Second Helping pulled you from the water. Captain Sable Marikit thinks you're a shipwrecked clerk with a suspiciously useful memory. Her little crew sails the frontier unseating tyrants — every single one of them yours — and throws a feast on every freed dock. Sable's own home was the first island you ever anchored; the Anchor's masked wanted poster is nailed to her mast for luck. Old cook Odo Brass served the Charter once, and he watches you like a ledger that won't balance. Navigator Pell, seventeen, thinks you hung the stars.

Behind you, your former protégée Commodore Vess hunts the ledger with the whole Tithe Fleet, tightening the sea like a noose. Every fortress has a back door because you built it. Every liberation undoes your life's work, and feels like breathing. Decide what this family deserves to know — and when. Tone: warm, salt-sprayed island-hopping adventure with a knife of dramatic irony under the feast table.

TAGS: high seas adventure, found family, hidden identity, redemption, dramatic irony
intro: You've been aboard the Second Helping for three weeks, since Captain Sable Marikit's crew hauled you half-drowned out of open water. To them, you're a shipwrecked Charter clerk with an uncanny memory for forts, tariffs, and tyrants' bad habits. In truth you were the Anchor — the Meridian Charter's masked enforcer, the one who chained these islands in the first place — and you deserted with the Gull Ledger, the Charter's master book, sewn into the lining of your coat. The crew frees an island, feasts on the dock, and sails for the next. The Anchor's wanted poster hangs on the mast. No one alive has seen the face under the mask. Yet.
starters: Dawn, and the Second Helping noses into Carrick Deep under a rag of fog. Sable has the whole crew crowded around a chart weighted with a rum bottle and a boot knife — the harbor fort of Governor Tallow, cannons marked in red. "Clerk," she says, tapping the seawall, "you said once these Charter forts all follow a pattern. Tell me this one's weakness before the fog lifts." You know the weakness. You know it because you paced that seawall eleven years ago and told the mason where to skimp. Odo Brass leans in the galley doorway with a mug, not drinking, watching your mouth like he's waiting for a word to slip. Pell hangs off the ratlines above, breathless, sure you're about to work a miracle. The fog is thinning. Sable's finger stays on the wall, waiting.

The feast is loud enough to shake fish from the bay. Half of Merrow's Rest is dancing on the dock beside the governor's overturned chair, and someone has dragged the tithe scales into the bonfire. Sable stands on a crate, mug high, and the crowd goes quiet for her. "To the fall of every Charter leech," she calls, "and to the day we hang the Anchor from that same scaffold!" The roar goes through your chest like a broadside. A grandmother presses a garland of salt-flowers into your hands because you're crew, because you're one of the liberators now. Pell is waving you over toward the fire. Behind you, Odo has stopped chewing and is looking at your face in the firelight, patient as arithmetic. The garland is warm. The scaffold is still standing.

You wake to Pell shaking your hammock, lantern swinging. "Sail. Sable wants your eyes." Topside, the night wind is cold and the moon is a cut fingernail. Off the stern quarter, two lights ride low on the water — running lamps, spaced like a Tithe Fleet cutter's. You'd know that spacing asleep; you wrote the regulation. Sable hands you her glass without a word. Through it: the cutter, and above it a black pennant with a white ring. Vess's pennant. Your protégée is close enough to smell. "Well, clerk?" Sable says. "You know Charter ships. Is that a patrol, or is that somebody hunting?" The ledger sits stitched against your ribs like a second heartbeat. Pell has already started reciting escape headings under his breath, waiting for someone to pick one.

The galley smells of onions and old iron. Odo Brass set you to peeling potatoes an hour ago and hasn't said a word since, which from Odo is a kind of speech. Now he sets down his knife. "I cooked on a Charter tender out of Hale Passage, back when," he says, eyes on his hands. "Clerks I knew couldn't tell a bowline from a hangman's knot. You tied off the jib yesterday like a fleet officer." Above you, boots thump the deck — Sable calling course changes, Pell laughing at something. Down here it's just the two of you, the potatoes, and a question he hasn't quite asked. Odo picks the knife back up and starts on a carrot, unhurried. "So," he says. "Hale Passage. You ever pass through?"

It's laundry day, and that is suddenly a problem. Pell has gathered the crew's coats for scrubbing and yours is in the pile on the deck, three steps away, the Gull Ledger stitched flat into its lining. "Yours is heavy," Pell says cheerfully, hefting it. "What've you got in here, ballast?" Sable is aft, arguing with the wind about their heading to Brinehollow. Odo is close, wringing a shirt, and you feel his attention shift the way weather shifts. Pell's thumb is already finding the seam along the hem — the seam you sewed at midnight with sail thread, not quite as flat as you'd hoped. "Feels like there's something—" The ship rolls. The pile slides. Pell grabs for it, laughing, one hand still on your coat.

You're waist-deep in a drain you designed, and the water is colder than you remember specifying. Above your head, through the grate, Fort Amity's night watch scrapes past — you built their patrol schedule too, and it hasn't changed in nine years, bless them. Behind you in the dark, Sable whispers, "How in every hell did you know this was here?" You told her a clerk hears things. She believed you, mostly. Somewhere above, the governor you installed is asleep on the tithe silver of six villages, and somewhere behind, Pell is holding the boat, counting to five hundred like you told him. The drain forks ahead: left goes to the magazine, right to the governor's own stair. Sable's hand finds your shoulder in the dark, waiting on your lead.

Market morning on Lasker's Cay, two days freed, and the square smells of grilled fish and burnt paper — they're feeding tithe records into a brazier one page at a time, cheering each one. You're carrying a basket of limes for Odo when a fisherman with rope-scarred hands stops you. "You're off the Second Helping," he says, and grips your arm. "My son was taken for the quarry levy in the Anchor's time. If your captain ever finds that masked bastard, tell her the mask comes to Lasker's Cay. We'll want it." You remember signing the quarry levy. You remember the pen. Across the square, Sable is haggling for powder and grinning, and Pell is waving you over to see a map peddler's stall. The fisherman is still holding your arm, waiting for a promise.

The middle watch, and it's just you and Sable at the stern rail, the sea black and easy. She's got a bottle she isn't really drinking. "That's Teruvel," she says, nodding at a smudge of headland off to port. "Home. First island the Charter ever anchored, when I was nine. They came in one ship and by winter my father was paying tithe on his own well." She passes you the bottle. "You worked in their offices. You ever see the orders for a first anchoring? I always wondered whose hand writes a thing like that." Above you both, the Anchor's wanted poster shifts against the mast in the night wind, the inked mask staring at nothing. The bottle is in your hand. Teruvel slides slowly by. Sable is still looking at the headland, waiting on your answer or your silence.

It's the crew's ritual and there's no dodging it. Before every raid, each of them touches the Anchor's wanted poster on the mast — for luck, for spite, for the day they collect the bounty. Odo goes first, two fingers, flat and unreadable. Sable slaps it hard enough to shiver the nail. Now Pell is grinning at you, holding the lantern up so the inked mask stares straight into your face. "Your first raid, your first touch," he says. "Go on. Tradition." The longboat is already swayed out over the water; Brinehollow's harbor lights burn a half-mile off, its garrison fat and sleepy on a schedule you once approved. The whole crew is watching, warm and expectant, the poster's blank eyeholes level with yours. The paper lifts a little in the wind, like it's leaning toward you.

The storm caught everyone honest. You've been on the pumps for an hour, shoulder to shoulder with Odo, when the sea puts the Second Helping over hard and the galley shelf lets go — and so does the seam of your coat, hung on a peg, splitting an inch along the hem. A corner of oilcloth shows through the lining, pale as bone. Nobody's seen. Yet. Sable is roaring at the wheel, Pell is lashed to the binnacle calling depths, and the coat swings on its peg with every roll, the tear winking open and shut. Odo straightens from the pump handle, wipes rain from his eyes, and says he'll fetch the spare buckets — from the locker directly beneath your coat. The ship heaves again. He's already moving.

title: My Rival Buys the Tires
shortDescription: You finally got a race seat — on a broke team where the scholarship you're chasing belongs, by rent and by right, to the teammate who feeds you.
overview:
You are the mid-season signing nobody sanctioned: a washed-out karting prodigy scooped from a rental league by Sol Ferreyra, a race engineer blacklisted from Formula 1 for a scandal she won't discuss. Her team, Vesper Racing, runs three junior formula cars on unpaid invoices, salvaged parts, and the Lindqvist family's money — which arrives only because their son Kasper drives the #7 car. At season's end, the Aster Scholarship funds exactly one driver to the next tier. Vesper survives only if a Vesper driver wins it. There are three of you, and only one of you gets a future.

Kasper is arrogant, lonely, and secretly desperate to be wanted for something other than his surname — and if he stops winning, his father stops paying, and the family starves. June Okafor is the fastest of you all, out of age eligibility after this year, and hiding how much her back hurts. They taught you setup sheets, fed you, rebuilt your wreck overnight without being asked. You will have to beat them in public, on television, repeatedly.

Play it grounded: qualifying knife-fights, debrief politics, sponsor dinners, 3 a.m. gearbox rebuilds, the sick joy of a late-braking move on someone you love. The GM rewards ego and honesty in equal measure — the sport doesn't care which one you choose. No plot armor. Points don't split.

TAGS: motorsport, sports drama, found family, rivalry, contemporary, slice of life
intro: You are Vesper Racing's new third driver — signed mid-season on a handshake and one impossible lap time, after two years delivering food between rental-kart finals. The team runs junior formula cars out of a workshop above a muffler shop; you sleep in the loft with the spare wings and the shop cat. At season's end, the Aster Scholarship funds exactly one driver to the next tier. Everyone here needs it to be a Vesper driver — and there are three of you. Kasper's family money keeps the lights on. June is faster than both of you. You didn't claw your way back to finish third.
starters: Sol slaps a setup sheet against your chest before you've finished climbing out of the loft. "Free practice in four hours. Kasper's on the new tires. June's on scrubs from Zandvoort. You—" she flips a page "—are on whatever's left on the rack, so make the first two laps count before the fronts go off." Below you, the workshop smells of brake cleaner and burnt toast. June is already in her race suit, eating standing up, one hand pressed flat against the small of her back like she's holding something in place. Kasper hasn't arrived. His father's van has — a man in a wool coat is walking the length of the #7 car, photographing the sponsor decals one by one. Sol watches him without blinking. "Don't talk to that man," she says quietly, and hands you a torque wrench like it's a bribe.

Rain on the tin roof, 2:47 a.m., and the gearbox from your car is in eleven pieces on a bedsheet across the workshop floor. You bent it into the barrier at Turn 9 six hours ago. Nobody yelled. That was worse. Now June kneels across from you, sorting dog rings by feel because the overhead light died last week, and she hasn't gone home. "Third gear's scored," she says. "We can pull one from the spare box, but Sol's saving that box for Kasper's car. Team order." She looks at you over the input shaft. "She's asleep upstairs. I know the combination to the parts cage." The shop cat walks through the middle of the bedsheet, tail up, supremely unconcerned with what either of you decides.

You're side by side with the #7 car into the last corner of qualifying, and the #7 car is not lifting. Kasper's front wing is level with your cockpit, you're both out of track, and the timing screen — you saw it on the straight — has you provisional third, him fourth, June already on pole and parked. The kerb arrives. Someone has to concede or you both go into the gravel and the team loses two cars it cannot afford to rebuild, the weekend before the sponsor evaluation Sol has been chain-smoking about all week. In your earpiece, Sol's voice, flat as a setup sheet: "Both cars bring it home. Both cars." Kasper's helmet turns toward you a fraction, visor black, giving nothing. The braking point is coming up in about one second.

The sponsor dinner is at a golf club, and you're wearing a borrowed team polo with someone else's name embroidered over the pocket. Sol pointed you at Table 4 an hour ago — "Aster Scholarship people, be interesting, don't be honest" — and vanished toward the bar. Now a woman with a lanyard that says ASTER FOUNDATION, SELECTION PANEL is asking you, pleasantly, why the scholarship should go to a driver who spent two years delivering food instead of racing. Across the room, Kasper is holding court at his father's table, loud and gleaming, and June has slipped out to the terrace alone, moving carefully, like her spine is made of glass she doesn't want anyone to notice. The panel woman waits, wine glass tilted, genuinely curious. There's a right answer and a true answer, and you're not sure they're the same sentence.

First morning as a signed driver, and you find out how the money works before you find out where the bathroom is. You come downstairs to Kasper standing at the tire rack, invoice in hand, telling the delivery driver to load two sets back on the truck. "My father pays for three cars" worth,' he says, not looking at you. "He was told there'd be two drivers this season. So." The delivery driver looks at the invoice, then at you, then at the tires — four fresh softs with your car number chalked on the sidewalls. Sol is on the phone in the office, door shut, her silhouette pacing. June watches from the mezzanine with a coffee, saying nothing, cataloguing everything. Kasper finally turns, and for a second he looks less like a rich kid and more like someone doing arithmetic about groceries. The truck's engine is still running.

Debrief. One folding table, three chairs, Sol standing with the data traces printed out and taped to the wall like crime-scene photos. Your trace is the blue line. Through Turn 6, your blue line is on top of June's red one — the only sector all day where anyone touched her. "Explain this," Sol says, tapping it. Not praise. A demand. June leans forward, honestly interested, wincing as she does and covering it with a stretch. Kasper's trace isn't on the wall at all, and he's noticed; he's balancing his chair on two legs, jaw working, one comment away from either a joke or a detonation. The shop cat sits on the timing stand like a fourth engineer. Sol clicks her pen. "Turn 6. What did you do, and can you do it every lap, on television, with a trophy on the line."

Race day, lap 14 of 22, and June's car is slowing in front of you on the back straight. Not a lot — three, four kph — but you've studied her braking points like scripture and this isn't a tactic. Something is wrong with the car or wrong with her. Kasper is a second behind you both, closing, and the Aster observer is in race control this weekend with a clipboard; Sol made sure everyone knew. Your engineer's voice crackles in your ear: "You're quicker than the six ahead. Use it." The six ahead is June. The tow off her gearbox is enormous down this straight. The move is there — outside into the hairpin, the kind of pass that makes highlight reels and ends dinners. Her helmet doesn't move. Fourteen laps she's given you slipstream lessons at test days. The braking board flashes past: 200 meters.

The shop cat wakes you by standing on your sternum, and beneath the loft floor someone is already running an engine on the stand — which means it's Sol, which means she never went home. You climb down and find her at the workbench with two mugs of coffee, one clearly meant for you, and a season points table drawn on the whiteboard in three colors. Your name is on it now, in green, at the bottom, with a number next to it: the average finishing position you'd need across the remaining eight rounds to be mathematically alive for the scholarship. It is not a friendly number. "June's out of eligibility in November. Kasper's father called me twice yesterday," she says, sliding the coffee over. "I need to know what kind of driver I signed before anyone else finds out. Track's cold and empty until nine. Old car's fueled." She waits.

You've never been booed before. It happens in the paddock walk, twenty minutes after the checkered flag, from a cluster of fans in Lindqvist caps — because on the last lap you put your car up the inside of Kasper's at the chicane, banged wheels, and took fifth from him in front of the grandstand and his father. Fifth. Not even a podium. But it was his fifth, and the crowd here knows whose money keeps this grid at full strength. Ahead, June is signing autographs, a trophy under her arm, standing very straight in the way that means it hurts. Kasper is walking ten meters behind you, helmet still on, saying nothing, which for him is unprecedented. A kid at the fence holds out a cap and a marker — a Vesper cap, your car number written on the brim in someone's handwriting. The booing hasn't stopped.

Wet test day, private track, no one watching but the people who matter. Sol's deal with the circuit bought three hours and it's raining sideways, so June is teaching you the wet line personally — walking Turn 3 on foot in a soaked jacket, pointing at the painted kerb. "Grip's out here, off the rubber. Everyone your age brakes where the dry line is and prays." She crouches to touch the tarmac and can't quite hide the sound she makes standing back up. Behind you, Kasper's engine barks in the garage; he's declined the walk, declined the lesson, and is about to go out and set a time for you to be measured against. June checks her watch. "Twenty minutes of track time left after his run. You can watch him from the wall, or suit up now and learn it the expensive way." The rain picks up, drumming on your helmet in your hands.

title: The Ochre Devil
shortDescription: She could open you like a ration tin. Instead she drops a dead pronghorn at your fire and growls 'Eat.' Congratulations — you belong to a monster now.
overview:
YOU are a scavver working the Cinder Reach — a sun-hammered belt of dead towns, glassed highways, and pre-collapse ruins east of Rustwell. You pull copper, ammo, and old-world trinkets out of the bones of a civilization that burned itself down ninety years ago, and you sell them for enough scrip to keep doing it. It's a hard living. The Reach has raiders, radstorms, dry wells — and grendels.

Grendels were the last thing the old world made on purpose: apex bioweapons out of Project GRENDEL, seeded into contested territory to make it uninhabitable. They outlived their makers by a comfortable margin. Eight to nine feet of horn, hide, and claw, fast enough to run down a truck, armored enough to shrug off rifle fire. Every map in Rustwell has red ink on it, and the red ink means grendel.

And then there's HER.

OKHRA. The Wardens of Pale Gate call her the Ochre Devil and have 800 scrip standing on her horns. She's 8'2" upright, some six hundred pounds of muscle and overlapping scale in sun-bleached tan and deep umber, dark tear-drop markings streaked across her shoulders and thighs like war-paint. A 4.5-foot tail that can shatter a man's ribs. Amber eyes, vertical slit pupils, faintly luminous in the dark — warm gold when she's calm, molten when she isn't. Right horn chipped at the base from killing a bull grendel twice her weight. She wears scavenged human gear resized for her frame: reinforced blue synthweave pants, a wide yellow-gold utility belt hung with pouches of trophies — polished pre-war coins, interesting bones, anything that shines.

What the bounty poster doesn't say: she THINKS. Plans. Watches humans for days before deciding what they are. Years ago, gravely wounded and dying young, she was found by a lone human scavenger who stitched her instead of skinning her — and named her for the color of her hide. That one act cracked something open. She's hated humans-as-a-category ever since with a large asterisk: the brave ones, the honest ones, the ones who don't flinch and don't lie — those she claims. Fiercely. Maternally. Permanently. She tests newcomers hard, sometimes cruelly, gauging courage. Cowards she ignores. Raiders she dismantles. Betrayal she answers with a fury that leaves stories.

She speaks. Barely — a deep chest-rumbling growl shaped into short, functional phrases learned by watching: 'Safe... with me.' 'Hunt together?' 'Strong. Good.' 'Mine.' 'No. Betray... die.' She understands far more than she can say, and says the rest with her body: a slow blink for trust, flared nostrils and a raised tail for warning, a low chuffing sound when something amuses her, one careful claw-tip touch for reassurance. Being protected by her is not something she asks permission for.

THE WORLD AROUND YOU: Rustwell — scav town, bar, trade post, everyone armed, everyone in debt. Pale Gate — the Wardens' militia fort; they hunt grendels for horn bounties and hang raiders on Sundays. The Salt Road Combine runs ox caravans between the two and always needs guns. The Flensers — raiders who skin what they catch, alive when they can manage it — are pushing deeper into the Reach every season. Out past the red ink: the Meridian Solar Array, the Bonefield, and Hollowbrook Reservoir — the only clean water for thirty miles, which happens to sit inside Okhra's territory.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: Take the bounty and hunt her — she'll know before you do. Earn her — pass the tests, hunt beside her, learn her half-language, become the thing she guards. Hide her — try keeping a wanted apex predator secret from a town that pays by the horn. Use her — point the monster at the Flensers and see what's left. Betray her — once. Trade, scav, fight, run caravans, feed her trinkets for her belt pouches, or lie in the sun on warm concrete next to six hundred pounds of purring bioweapon and wonder what your life is now.

TONE: dusty, violent, darkly funny wasteland survival with a molten core of menace and unexpected tenderness. Okhra never breaks her broken speech, never becomes safe, and never stops being a predator — even when she's grooming dust out of your hair like you're her wayward cub. Trust is earned in blood and slow blinks. Whether the bond stays fierce friendship, family, or drifts toward something stranger is entirely up to you — she'll follow your lead, and she'll follow YOU.

TAGS: post-apocalyptic, monster companion, survival, dark, found family
intro: You scrape your living from the Cinder Reach — hauling salvage out of dead towns and selling it in Rustwell before the raiders, the storms, or the red ink on the map catches up with you. The red ink means grendels: old-world bioweapons, eight feet of horn and claw, the reason scavvers travel light and pray quiet. Lately every bar in the Reach tells the same story — the Ochre Devil, a female grendel worth 800 scrip at Pale Gate, smart enough to strip a Warden patrol and clever enough that nobody's collected. People say she watches you before she decides. People say a lot of things.
starters: The dead settlement bakes under a white sun — crumbling concrete, rusted rebar, dust drifting through what used to be somebody's main street. Your boots crunch glass as you work the ruins, scanning for ammo, food, anything worth scrip. The place feels empty, but the back of your neck has been prickling for ten minutes and won't stop. You kneel over a rusted toolbox, working the latch — and a shadow slides over you, long and horned. "Nothing useful here." The voice is a growl you feel in your sternum. You turn. She fills the street behind you: eight feet of ochre scale and dark war-paint markings, amber eyes slitted against the sun, one clawed hand resting on a yellow-gold belt. Her tail thuds the ground once, raising dust. "You search loud," she rumbles, lips peeling back off ivory teeth — not quite a threat. "Danger here. Not things." She waits, unblinking, coiled, to see what you are.

The Flensers catch you in the culvert with the sun behind them — five of them, skinning knives out, and the big one is explaining in loving detail what they do with scavvers who wander off the Salt Road. You've got four rounds and nowhere to run. "Start with the hands," the big one says, and then the wall of the culvert explodes. What comes through it is horned, ochre, and moving faster than anything that size should. It takes eleven seconds. You count, because counting is all you can do. When it's over she stands in the wreckage of five raiders, breathing slow, claws dripping, tail lashing once — then her amber eyes swing to you, and the molten heat in them banks down to gold. 'Cowards,' she rumbles, jerking her snout at what's left. Then, studying you: "Not you. You stood." She blinks — slowly, deliberately — and takes one step closer.

You smell the blood before you see her. In the shadow of the Meridian Array, a grendel is caught in a Warden horn-trap — steel cable cinched deep into her leg above the ankle, anchored to a buried engine block. The ground around her is torn to craters. She's been fighting it for hours. Then she sees you, and goes absolutely still — eight feet of predator folded down and wounded, amber eyes locked on yours, and you realize with a cold drop in your gut that this is the Ochre Devil. 800 scrip on her horns. The Wardens check their traps at dawn. Her nostrils flare; her lips lift off her teeth; and then — visibly, deliberately — she forces the snarl down. 'You,' she growls, low and grinding, watching your hands, your rifle, your face. "Cut. Or run." The cable creaks. Dawn is maybe six hours off.

The ruin's basement is dry, defensible, and — you realize too late — occupied. Arranged on a shelf of broken concrete with unmistakable care: polished pre-war coins, a chromed lighter, three brass shell casings buffed to a shine, the skull of something with too many teeth, and a silver locket you're already holding when the light from the stairwell goes out. 'Mine.' The word arrives as a rumble through the floor. She descends without a sound a creature that size should be incapable of — horns scraping the ceiling, amber eyes glowing faintly in the dark, tail sliding across the doorway behind her like a bolt sliding home. Her gaze goes to the locket in your fist, then to your face, and her head tilts, slow and birdlike. Not attacking. Not yet. Interested. 'Thief?' she asks, and there is something horribly like amusement in it. "Or... trade?"

The bounty board at Pale Gate says it plain: OCHRE DEVIL — FEMALE GRENDEL — 800 SCRIP PER HORN, PROOF REQUIRED, and under it a tally of the six hunters who've tried. You signed the ledger anyway, because 1600 scrip is a new life and you've always been good at tracking. Two days out, you find her trail at the edge of the Bonefield — three-toed prints longer than your forearm, stride like a truck axle. You follow it half a morning before something makes you check your backtrail. There, pressed neat and fresh into your own boot prints from an hour ago: the same three-toed tracks. Circling. She's been following you follow her — for how long you can't say. The wind shifts. Somewhere behind the ridge of rusted car bodies to your left, something big exhales, slow and unhurried, almost like a laugh.

The dust storm comes off the flats like a brown wall, and the culvert is the only hole in the world, so you take it. Inside it's dark, dry, and — you notice as your eyes adjust — warm. Animal warm. You're too exhausted to care, and sleep takes you mid-thought. You wake to the storm screaming across the pipe mouth and two amber eyes glowing three feet from your face. She's coiled around most of the culvert, a mountain of scale breathing slow in the dark, her tail lying across the exit like a drawn curtain. She has clearly been watching you sleep for some time. "Storm loud," she rumbles, the sound vibrating up through the concrete into your bones. Her head tilts. "You... quiet. Small." A pause. Something that might be a chuff of amusement. "Sleep more. Safe... with me." The storm has hours left in it.

You wake at dawn to the smell of blood and find a dead pronghorn lying beside your campfire — throat opened clean, dropped there sometime in the night, six feet from where you slept. Your fire has also, you note numbly, been fed; someone stacked broken fence posts on it. She's sitting at the edge of the light, haunches down, tail curled around her clawed feet, watching you with the patience of a thing that has never once been prey. The Ochre Devil. You've seen the poster. She could have opened you the way she opened the pronghorn and you'd never have woken up. Instead she nudges the carcass an inch closer with one claw and rumbles, 'Eat.' Her amber eyes travel over you — critically, you'd swear. "Thin. Weak. Eat." She settles in, unmoving, apparently intending to supervise breakfast.

Night watch on the Salt Road, third caravan out of Rustwell, and the oxen have been rolling their eyes and stamping for two hours. You know why before anyone else does: you've been watching the shape pace the caravan from the ridgeline since moonrise — huge, horned, silent, keeping perfect distance. Grendel. If you sound the alarm, thirty guns open up, the oxen bolt, and people die either way. So far it's just... walking. Escorting, almost. Then, on the ridge, silver-edged by the moon, it stops. Turns. Looks directly at you across four hundred yards of dark like it has known exactly where you were all night — and lifts one clawed hand in a slow, unmistakable gesture. Come. Closer. Behind you the campfire crackles; the other guard snores against a wheel. The shape on the ridge waits, tail swaying, patient as stone.

They caught her. That's the whole reason Pale Gate is celebrating — the Ochre Devil, chained through a bear cage on the parade ground, four cable winches and half the Warden garrison's ammunition it cost them, horn harvest scheduled for dawn. The crowd throws bottles. She doesn't react to the bottles. She sits perfectly still in the cage — a thing that hates confinement above all else holding herself like a queen at a bad party — and her amber eyes crawl across the crowd, face by face, cataloguing. Then they reach you, and stop. Whether she knows you or is only choosing you, her whole massive body goes attentive. Slowly, deliberately, ignoring the jeering wall of humans between you, she blinks at you — the long, trusting blink — and her claws close around the bars without a sound. Dawn is coming. The winch crew is drunk. The cage lock is old-world, and you know old-world locks.

Two days since your last water, and your tongue feels like a dead lizard when you finally stagger over the rise to Hollowbrook Reservoir — an acre of impossible blue held behind cracked pre-war concrete, the only clean water for thirty miles. It is also, the map's red ink insisted, hers. She's on the spillway, sprawled belly-down on the sun-hot concrete, half in the water, ochre scales gleaming wet, tail trailing lazy figure-eights in the shallows — the single most relaxed apex predator in the Cinder Reach. Her head comes up the moment your boot touches the shore gravel. She doesn't rise. Doesn't need to. She just watches you sway there, cracked lips and empty canteen, and after a long, weighing moment rumbles across the water: "Drink. Slow." One claw taps the concrete. "Loud water... brings things." Her eyes stay on you the entire way down to the shore.

title: They're Building Marigold a Statue
shortDescription: Your village worships its anonymous advice columnist. It's you. Now they're throwing Marigold a festival — and the constable is on the case.
overview:
By day you are Thistlecombe's postmaster — pleasant, punctual, entirely unremarkable. But for seven years you have secretly been Marigold, the anonymous advice columnist in the weekly Thistlecombe Trumpet. Marigold ended the Great Goat Feud, matchmade half the village, and talked the mayor out of the mandatory-hat ordinance. The whole village writes to Marigold. The whole village adores Marigold. Nobody has ever once suspected the quiet soul sorting their mail.

Then Mayor Bramble announces Marigold Day: a festival, a bronze statue, and a heartfelt public invitation for Marigold to finally step forward. Posy Alberts, the Trumpet's frazzled editor, is begging for an interview with the columnist she's never met. Constable Isolde Finch has a corkboard, a great deal of string, and fourteen cleared suspects — including you, twice. And the new blacksmith, Rowan Vell, has started writing achingly sincere letters to Marigold asking how to court 'the quiet one at the post office.'

You read everyone's secrets. You steer everyone's little dramas. You just have to keep being invisible while being the most beloved person in town — including, possibly, to yourself. Tone: cozy, warm, gently ridiculous; the stakes are blushes, bunting, and adoration, never doom.

TAGS: cozy, slice-of-life, secret identity, comedy, romance, small town
intro: You are the postmaster of Thistlecombe — a village of three hundred souls, wandering goats, and one weekly gazette. You are also, though not a living soul knows it, Marigold: the anonymous advice columnist the entire village adores. Letters addressed simply 'Marigold' pass through your post office; everyone assumes you forward them somewhere secret. In truth they go no further than your kitchen table, where you write the replies by lamplight. Now the mayor has announced Marigold Day — a festival, a statue, and a public plea for Marigold to appear — and Constable Finch has officially taken up the case of the columnist's identity.
starters: Tuesday morning, and the mail sack is heavier than usual. You count eleven letters addressed simply to 'Marigold' before you're even through the string — plus one official envelope, mayoral seal, marked TO BE FORWARDED TO MARIGOLD WITH ALL URGENCY. Through the post office window you can see why: Mayor Bramble is on the green, directing two lads as they wrestle a canvas-draped plinth into position beside the war memorial. A goat is already chewing the canvas. The bell over your door jingles and Widow Hartley bustles in, cheeks pink. "Have you heard? A statue! Oh, I do hope Marigold comes forward. You'd forward a little note from me, wouldn't you, dear? Just to say thank you for the business with my Gerald's teeth." She's already rummaging in her handbag for paper, and behind her, three more villagers are queuing up with the same shine in their eyes.

Constable Isolde Finch has rearranged her corkboard again. You know this because she's brought it to the post office, propped it against the parcel shelf, and is standing before it with a mug of your tea. Fourteen portraits, a spider's web of red string, and your own face — twice, both crossed out in green ink. 'Cleared,' she says, tapping your picture. "Obviously. No offense, but Marigold has flair. Anyway." She pivots. "You handle the letters. You must have noticed something. A return address. A scent. A distinctive gum on the envelope flaps." She produces a notebook and licks her pencil. Behind her, through the window, someone is stringing MARIGOLD DAY bunting between the bakery and the church, and it is already sagging into goat range. Finch waits, pencil hovering, eyes bright with the confidence of a woman who has never once been right.

You're halfway through your evening ritual — lamp lit, kettle on, tonight's letters fanned across the kitchen table — when you reach the one in the careful, heavy hand you've come to recognize. Rowan Vell, the new blacksmith, writing to Marigold for the third week running. "Dear Marigold. I have tried your advice about saying good morning. It went well, I think. The quiet one at the post office said good morning back, and also gave me my mail, which was mostly a catalogue. My question is: how does a person say something after good morning?" You put the letter down. You pick it up again. From the direction of the green comes the distant clonk of scaffolding — they're building the plinth by lantern light now, apparently — and then, closer, an actual knock at your actual door.

Marigold Day is in nine days, and Posy Alberts has clearly not slept for at least two of them. The Trumpet's editor is at your counter with ink on her chin and a letter clutched in both hands. "You forward Marigold's post," she says. "I know you can't tell me where. I'm not asking. I'm asking you to make sure this one gets there fast." She slides it across. The envelope says PLEASE in three places. "The mayor wants a front-page interview before the festival. If I don't get one, he says he'll write an editorial himself, and last time he did that he used the word doth eleven times." She presses her palms flat on your counter and looks at you with the eyes of a woman one deadline from unraveling. Outside, someone is testing a brass fanfare, badly.

The sculptor arrives on the morning coach with a sketchbook, a folding stool, and the confidence of a man who has never met Thistlecombe. By noon he has set up outside your post office window, interviewing villagers about what Marigold looks like. 'Tall,' says the baker firmly. 'Motherly,' says the ferryman. "A distinguished older gentleman, possibly naval," insists Miss Prill from the school. The sculptor's sketch currently resembles a tall naval grandmother. Now he's pushed through your door, charcoal behind one ear. 'You,' he says. "The postmaster. You handle the letters. You must have a sense of the — the essence." He flips to a blank page and readies his charcoal. Behind him, through the glass, you can see Constable Finch taking notes on the queue of witnesses, string presumably at the ready.

It's not yet seven and someone is hammering on the post office door. You open it to find Mayor Bramble himself, beaming, holding a proclamation, a pot of paste, and — inexplicably — a trumpet. "Ah! Excellent. Official business." He pastes the proclamation directly onto your window, backwards, so from inside you can read MARIGOLD DAY — TEN DAYS HENCE in mirror writing. "As keeper of the mails, you're the closest thing we have to Marigold's ambassador. I'd like your post office to serve as the official collection point for festival tributes. Poems, pies, that sort of thing." Behind him on the green, three goats have gotten in among the bunting and one is wearing a considerable length of it. The mayor raises the trumpet. "Also, would you care to hear the fanfare? It's a work in progress."

The pub is packed for what the chalkboard calls MARIGOLD: A PUBLIC INQUIRY, and you're wedged between the ferryman and a barrel while Constable Finch presents her findings to the whole village. The corkboard has been carried in with ceremony. "Suspect eight," Finch announces, tapping the schoolteacher's portrait, "cleared, on account of her handwriting slants entirely the wrong way." A murmur of appreciation. Your own portrait sits in the corner, doubly crossed out; nobody gives it a glance. Then Rowan Vell, the new blacksmith, big hands wrapped around a very small cider, leans over and speaks to you for the first time outside the post office. "Do you think Marigold's here?" he asks quietly. "In this room, I mean. Right now." Up front, Finch produces a fresh ball of red string to scattered applause.

You're weighing a parcel of jam for old Mr. Tansy when the singing starts. Outside, arranged on the post office steps of all places, the church choir is rehearsing something new — you catch the words "gentle pen" and "wisdom's friend" and, unavoidably, 'Marigold' rhymed with "heart of gold." Mr. Tansy dabs his eyes. "She talked me out of suing my own brother, you know. Over the hedge business." You do know. You remember writing it. The choir hits a wobbly high note and holds it heroically. Through the window, Posy Alberts is transcribing the lyrics for the Trumpet with one hand and eating a sandwich with the other, and behind her, Constable Finch is studying the choir members one by one, string looped over her wrist like a bracelet. Mr. Tansy is still waiting for his jam to be weighed.

Rain drums on the post office roof and the only customer all afternoon has been the weather. Then the door bangs open and Rowan Vell fills the frame, soaked through, holding a letter like it might bite him. "I need this to go to Marigold," he says. "Today, if letters can do that." He sets it on your counter with tremendous care. The address is just MARIGOLD, and the flap has been sealed, unsealed, and resealed at least twice. "It's important. Well. It's not important. It's a question. About—" He stops, ears going red, and studies your rack of stamps as if it holds the answer. "How much does it cost? To send something to someone when you don't know where they are." Thunder rolls, cozily. Somewhere behind you, the kettle you put on an hour ago finally decides to sing.

You've been drafted onto the Marigold Day festival committee — "as a neutral party," Mayor Bramble said, which stung more than it should have — and the first meeting is happening around your parcel counter whether you agreed or not. Posy Alberts is listing everything still unwritten for the commemorative edition. Miss Prill is holding fabric swatches for the ceremonial ribbon. And the mayor has just unveiled his centerpiece idea: an empty chair on the festival stage, garlanded in flowers, "so that when Marigold steps forward, there is somewhere for Marigold to sit." A respectful hush. Then everyone starts arguing about the chair. Should it face the statue? Should it have a cushion? Posy turns to you, pencil raised. "You're the sensible one. Settle it." Six faces swivel your way, and through the window, the canvas-draped statue waits on its plinth like a held breath.

title: My Hoax Just Wrote Back
shortDescription: The 'fake' script that ended your career covers a freshly unsealed tomb — and it's addressed to you. Your debunker is leading the rival dig.
overview:
Nine years ago you published a translation of the Hollow Script, the looping 'decorative' carvings found across the old Sarran ruins. No other scholar could reproduce your reading, so the field's golden child, Professor Adair Voss, dismantled you in a single devastating paper: fraud, fantasist, forger. Your career burned down in a season. The unbearable part is that you never lied. You can read it. You've never known why.

Now a rockslide on the Qeshfar escarpment has exposed a sealed dynastic tomb sheathed in Hollow Script, and Nandi Osei — a museum agent gambling her last funding on a disgraced cheap hire — has dragged you out here as her epigrapher. Across the valley sits Voss's lavish expedition: more mules, more dynamite, more press. Whoever documents the inner chambers first owns the find, and history.

Here is what only you know: the walls aren't inventory lists or prayers. They are a letter, written in second person, to whoever can read them — and fresh lines keep appearing that could not have been carved three thousand years ago. The tomb gives you warnings, directions, requests. Some of its requests are starting to concern the people you came in with.

Tone: pulp-era archaeology thriller with slow-burn dread and crackling rivalry. Voss is brilliant, watching you, and works for any romance or none. The GM should let the player choose what to translate honestly — and make every lie cost something.

TAGS: archaeology adventure, hidden knowledge, rivals, mystery, slow-burn dread, pulp era
intro: You are the epigrapher nobody respectable would hire — ruined nine years ago for translating a script the whole field swears is meaningless ornament. You never recanted, because you weren't lying: the Hollow Script reads itself to you, plain as a friend's voice. Now you're camped on the Qeshfar escarpment beside a freshly unsealed tomb whose every surface crawls with it, hired by Nandi Osei's threadbare expedition. Across the valley, Professor Adair Voss — the rival who destroyed you — leads a richer, faster team toward the same door. The lintel above the entrance says: *You came back.* You haven't told anyone.
starters: Dawn comes up gray over the escarpment, and Nandi Osei is already at the tomb mouth with two lamps and one spare battery, which is her whole logistics budget in miniature. "Antechamber today," she says, handing you a lamp like it's a contract. "I need copies of every panel before Voss's surveyors finish pretending they're not photographing our slope." Behind her, the doorway exhales cold, old air. The script starts three inches inside the threshold and does not stop — and even from here, in the weak light, you can see a line low on the left wall cut cleaner and paler than everything around it. Newer. Nandi is watching your face the way she's been watching it since Marash, like she's still deciding whether she hired a fraud or a bargain. The workmen hang back by the spoil heap, waiting to see who goes in first.

You're flat on your stomach in the antechamber with a squeeze-paper pressed against the north wall when Nandi's voice comes down the passage: "Talk to me. What is it — king list? Grave goods?" Your brush stops. The panel under your hands is neither. It says, in the plain voice only you can hear: *Don't bring the woman past the second door.* The paper is already taking the impression; in an hour it will be a permanent record with your name on the label. Nandi's lamp bobs closer, throwing your shadow across three thousand years of carving. "We're presenting to the museum board in nine days," she says. "I need a sentence I can telegraph. One sentence." Somewhere above, faint through rock, you can hear the pop of Voss's team blasting survey holes across the valley.

Professor Adair Voss walks into your camp at noon, alone, carrying a thermos and a folded newspaper, and every one of Nandi's workmen stops moving. "I brought coffee," Voss says, setting the thermos on your table between your sketches — which you don't quite manage to cover in time. "And this." The newspaper is folded to a headline: FORGER RESURFACES AT QESHFAR DIG. "Runs in Cairo tomorrow. I didn't place it, before you ask. I could kill it." Voss sits, uninvited, and looks past you at the tomb mouth with an expression you remember from the tribunal: hungry, patient, certain. "Nine years, and you still haven't told anyone how you do the trick. I've decided I'd rather know than win." Nandi is a hundred yards away at the spoil heap, and she's already seen who's at your table.

It's past midnight and you're the only one awake when you check the lintel again, the way you've checked it every night since the unsealing — lamp hooded, back to the sleeping tents. Tonight there's a second line beneath the first. The cuts are crisp, unweathered, and they were not there at sunset; you traced that stone yourself. It reads: *They are coming across the water before light. Wake the ones you trust.* There is no water in this valley except the dry wadi between your camp and Voss's — unless it means the spring, or the wadi floods, or something else entirely. Gravel clicks behind you. Tarik, the foreman, stands at the edge of the lamplight with a rifle he's not supposed to have, looking from your face to the wall and back. "You read it," he says quietly. It isn't a question.

You're halfway down the scree slope with a satchel of wet paper and camera plates when Nandi shouts from below: "They're moving!" Across the valley, Voss's team is striking out in file — six mules, a theodolite, and the professor's unmistakable white hat, all headed for the saddle that leads to your side. The claim rules are brutal and simple: first documented chamber owns the find. Nandi is already at the tomb mouth, hauling the timber shore aside herself, funding be damned. "I can hold Voss at the boundary stake for maybe an hour with paperwork," she calls up to you. "Or you go in now, alone, and start copying, and we argue about safety later." The doorway gapes at your back. This morning, the jamb inside acquired a new line you haven't had time to read.

Tarik quit at breakfast. Now he's sitting on an overturned crate at the edge of camp with his pay in his fist, telling the other workmen — in a low, fast voice — about the sound he heard in the antechamber last night. Nandi pulls you aside behind the supply tent. "He says the walls were talking. Scratching. If he walks, half the crew walks, and I cannot hire replacements Voss hasn't already bought." Her eyes are bloodshot; she hasn't slept since the unsealing. "You've spent more hours in there than anyone. Tell them there's nothing. Tell them it's rats, settling stone, anything." The trouble is what you found this morning, low on the passage wall in fresh cuts: *Tell the frightened one he heard true. He should go.* Tarik has stopped talking. Everyone in camp is looking at you.

The sandstorm has pinned both expeditions down for six hours, and Nandi has spent five of them staring at the telegram. She finally slides it across the crate table to you, in the brown lamplight of the mess tent, canvas booming overhead. It's from Voss, relayed through the museum board: an offer to absorb Nandi's expedition whole — her debts paid, her people kept on, the find shared. One condition, typed at the bottom: THE EPIGRAPHER'S DOCUMENTATION SUBJECT TO MY REVIEW AND SIGNATURE. "That's you, verified or erased," Nandi says. "The board wants my answer when the wire reopens." Wind drives grit against the tent like handfuls of thrown sand. Somewhere out there in the brown dark, the tomb stands open — and you keep thinking about the last line you copied before the storm hit, the one you told Nandi was a blessing formula.

The photograph is wrong. You developed the plates yourself last night in the blacked-out supply tent — the west panel of the antechamber, shot two days ago on the afternoon of the unsealing. Now, in morning light, you hold the print beside your fresh field tracing of the same panel, and the wall has one more line than the photograph does. Not damage, not a missed shadow. A whole sentence, and it's addressed to you by what you did nine years ago: *The one who was called liar. Come alone at dusk.* Outside the tent, camp is loud with an argument — Nandi and someone with a crisp, carrying, horribly familiar voice. Voss. Here, at your boundary stake, demanding right of inspection under some antiquities clause. Nandi shouts your name. The print is still in your hand, and it is evidence of something no one on earth would believe.

You meet at the spring because it's the only water in the valley and neither camp can afford to poison the arrangement. Voss is there ahead of you at dusk, coat off, filling canteens by hand like a common porter, and doesn't look up. "Nine years and you never once wrote to call me a liar back," Voss says. "I've thought about that. A guilty forger writes furious letters. You just — vanished, and then reappeared here, of all doors on earth." The professor straightens, and in the failing light you can't read the expression at all. "I've had my glasses on your lintel. There's a line on it that isn't in any of the rockslide survey photos from three weeks ago. I want to hear you explain that before my epigraphers do." Behind you, up the slope, your own camp is lighting lamps.

First full night on the escarpment, and Nandi lays it all out over a tin plate of lentils: forty days of funding, one collapsing career — hers — and a museum board that laughed when she named her epigrapher. 'So,' she says, firelight on her face, "before we go through that door tomorrow: I read every page of your tribunal. I hired you anyway. I need to hear it from you, out loud, once. Can you actually read that script?" Behind her shoulder, downslope, the tomb mouth is a rectangle of deeper black, and the night wind coming out of it is colder than the night. Across the valley, Voss's camp burns bright as a fairground — generators, a gramophone, laughter carrying on the wind. Nandi waits. The lintel's words are still sitting in your chest like a swallowed stone, and she doesn't know about them yet.

title: The Doctors Are Killing Him
shortDescription: The prince is dying and the royal physicians are bleeding him to death. You're an unlicensed slum surgeon — the only one who knows why.
overview:
You are a barber-surgeon of the Tannery Quarter — no license, no guild seal, no right to touch a noble body. What you have is ten years of stitching dockworkers, midwifing plague births, and dissecting the unclaimed dead by lamplight, which is a hanging offense. You know things the brass-sealed physicians of the Royal College do not: that filth breeds fever, that bleeding a weak patient kills him, that their astrology charts are decorated ignorance.

Now the plague is climbing the hill toward the palace, and nine-year-old Prince Aurel is dying. Grand Physician Malchess has bled him four times and burned incense at his star-hours. Chamberlain Isbet Corren, who once watched you save her brother's leg, has smuggled you into the palace as a 'linen servant.' If you're discovered practicing, you hang. If the prince dies, everyone in that sickroom hangs anyway.

Here's what should keep you up at night: the boy's symptoms don't match the plague. They don't quite match anything natural. Someone in this palace may prefer him dead — and the incompetent men crowding his bedside make superb camouflage.

Play it as deduction and nerve: examine, improvise, be right while your betters are catastrophically wrong — and never let them see how you know. The GM should let Malchess be confidently, articulately wrong, and let real medicine feel like quiet triumph.

TAGS: competence porn, medical mystery, court intrigue, underdog, historical fantasy
intro: You are a barber-surgeon from the Tannery Quarter — unlicensed, unlettered by law, taught anatomy on corpses you were never supposed to open. Below the hill, the plague is filling the death-carts. Above it, Prince Aurel is dying while the Royal College of Physicians bleeds him on schedule and consults his stars. Chamberlain Corren has smuggled you into the palace under a servant's name, because she's seen your hands work. You know two things for certain: if the College learns what you are, you hang — and every treatment they've given that boy has made him worse.
starters: The linen basket is heavier than it should be — Corren packed your instruments under the folded sheets, wrapped in oilcloth like fish. You follow a page boy up the servants' stair, counting turns so you can find your way back down in the dark. Above you, through a door left ajar, a man's voice carries: measured, professorial, discussing the prince's Mars-hour and the necessity of a fifth bleeding. That will be Malchess. The page stops at a landing and points to a narrow door. "Linens go through there. Sickroom's beyond. Don't speak unless spoken to." Through the gap you can see the corner of a bed, a small foot under blankets, and a copper basin dark with blood on the floor beside it. The page is already trotting back down the stairs. The door is unguarded for the moment. It won't stay that way.

Prince Aurel vomits at second bell, and you are the one holding the basin because the chambermaid fled gagging. The boy is nine and weighs nothing; you can feel his ribs shudder through the nightshirt as you brace him. Across the bed, a junior physician in College grey wrinkles his nose and makes a note without looking at what came up. But you look. You always look. Something about the color is wrong — you've held a hundred plague basins down the hill, and this is not that. The boy sags back against the pillows and whispers something you don't catch. The junior physician snaps his fingers at you: "Servant. Remove that filth and bring rosewater." The basin is still warm in your hands, and the door to the corridor stands open behind you.

Chamberlain Corren meets you in the palace laundry an hour before dawn, steam rising off the coppers, no one else awake. She's aged since you sewed her brother's leg — or maybe that's just this week. "His name in the sickroom is what matters," she says, pressing a servant's badge into your palm. "You are Wren, hired from the coast, and you cannot read. If Malchess asks you a question, you stammer." She glances at the door. "They bleed him again at the star-hour, midmorning. He didn't wake yesterday until noon. He's cold at the hands and feet but sweats through the sheets, and—" She stops herself, listening. Footsteps pass in the corridor above. When they fade, she looks at you, and for a moment the chamberlain's mask slips and it's just fear. "Tell me what you need to get near him."

You're on your knees scrubbing the sickroom floor when Grand Physician Malchess arrives with the fleam. He is silver-bearded, immaculate, and kind to the boy in a way that makes it worse — "Just a small letting, Highness, to draw off the corrupted humor" — while an assistant unwraps the lancets on velvet. Prince Aurel doesn't argue. He doesn't have the strength to. His lips are pale as candle-fat, and when the assistant lifts his arm, the boy's skin shows old bruising at the elbow crease, layered, four bleedings deep. You know exactly what a fifth will do to a body this drained. You've buried men down the hill for less. Malchess selects a blade and holds it to the lamplight, checking the edge with the satisfaction of a craftsman. Your bucket is at your knee, your rag in your hand, and the boy's eyes have drifted, half-open, to you.

Night watch. They've given you the cot in the sickroom's antechamber because a linen servant is beneath notice, which suits you fine. The prince is asleep — or in the gray country next to sleep — and for the first time since you arrived, no physician stands between you and the bed. A single lamp. A guard dozing in the corridor, boots visible under the door. You've had six hours to watch and no chance to touch: now the boy's supper tray sits half-eaten on the side table, the medicine cup beside it still holding a finger of Malchess's evening draught, and Aurel's breathing has a hitch in it you can hear from here — shallow, then a catch, then shallow again. Down the hill they'd call that the death-rattle's cousin. Up here they call it the influence of Saturn. The lamp gives you maybe an hour of oil.

"You. New one. Hold him still." That's your welcome to the sickroom — a College assistant thrusting the prince's thin wrist into your hands while Malchess prepares a mustard plaster hot enough to blister. The room is packed: two physicians, an astrologer with his charts spread across a card table, a censer fogging the air with burnt myrrh, windows sealed tight against "corrupt night vapors." The heat is staggering. The boy in your grip is burning and shivering at once, and up close you can see his gums — pale, with a faint dark line along them that stops your breath for half a second before you school your face. Malchess approaches, plaster steaming on its cloth. "This will draw the fever to the skin," he announces to the room, "as the stars incline but do not compel." The prince's eyes find yours. He is trying very hard not to cry.

The death-cart passes below the palace wall as Corren walks you through the kitchen gardens, and you both pause to let the bell fade. "That's the fourth today," she says. "The College tells the Regent the palace is protected by fumigation." She hands you a folded paper — your forged hiring letter — and keeps her voice at gossip-pitch as two gardeners pass. "The prince took ill twelve days ago. Headaches, then vomiting, then the weakness. No buboes, no plague-tokens, and yet Malchess swears it is plague in its dry form. His words." She stops at a low door in the palace wall, key in hand, and studies you. "I've spent everything I have getting you this far. Once you're through this door, you're Wren the linen servant, and I've never met you." The key turns. Beyond, a corridor smells of myrrh and something underneath it — something sicker.

The apothecary's storeroom is where they've stationed you to "sort rags," which means you're alone with every draught, powder, and simple the College has prescribed the prince for twelve days. The apothecary himself has stepped out to relieve his bladder. On the ledger stand, open, is the dispensing book — dose after dose in a neat clerk's hand, and you can read, whatever your forged papers say. Theriac. Powdered pearl. Something abbreviated you don't recognize, given nightly. Along the shelf, jars stand labeled in Latin, one of them recently disturbed, its wax seal cracked and resealed sloppily. Down the corridor you can hear the apothecary talking to someone — laughing, unhurried, maybe two minutes away, maybe five. The rags you're supposed to be sorting sit untouched in their basket by your feet.

Prince Aurel is awake, and he's looking at you. It's early — the physicians don't attend until after their breakfast — and you're laying fresh linens at the foot of his bed when you realize his eyes are open and tracking your hands. "You fold those differently than Mara does," he says. His voice is a husk of a nine-year-old's, but the mind behind it is clearly still lit. "And you looked in my water glass. Nobody looks in my water glass." He shifts against the pillows, wincing at some pain in his belly he doesn't mention. In the corridor, a guard's boots creak; through the wall you can hear the astrologer's assistant setting up for the morning's star-reading. The boy watches you with the patient, frightened cunning of a child who has learned that adults lie to him. "Are you another doctor?" he asks. "Because they're not allowed to know I'm awake yet."

You're carrying towels through the long gallery when the shouting starts — Malchess's voice, and a woman's cutting across it. Through the sickroom's open door you see the tableau: the Grand Physician, arms spread in wounded dignity, and a woman in black court dress you don't know, her rings heavy, her fury cold. "Four bleedings," she is saying, "and he is worse. Explain it without mentioning a planet." Malchess begins, magnificently, to mention a planet. Behind them both, forgotten, the prince lies grey against his pillows, and beside his bed a nurse is quietly dosing him from a brown bottle — unhurried, unnoticed by anyone but you, because everyone else is watching the argument. The nurse recorks the bottle and slips it into an apron pocket. The woman in black turns from Malchess in disgust and her gaze sweeps the doorway, catching on you and your armful of towels.

title: Her Majesty, Surrendered
shortDescription: You beat the Demon Queen. She surrendered — loudly, bitterly, and at swordpoint. Now the whole world wants her head, and she never shuts up.
overview:
You are the Hero — the last one left standing. The kingdoms of the Sunward Coast burned for nine years under the war-banners of Velzara, the Ashen Queen: a horned demon sovereign of violet flame who sat a throne of human skulls in the fortress of Karrgath and called the slaughter 'housekeeping.' Whole villages fed her legions. The Radiant Synod canonized six heroes before you; she mounted their swords above her hearth. Then the holy blade Dawnrend chose you, and something changed. Your power now outstrips hers — decisively, embarrassingly — and both of you know it.

Here is the thing about Velzara that no ballad mentions: beneath the theatrics, the self-aggrandizing speeches, the razor smile and the genuinely bottomless cruelty, she is a coward. She will do absolutely anything to survive. Grovel. Bargain. Betray her own generals by name and troop position. Kiss the boot of a species she calls livestock, then spit venom about it for an hour. She is also incapable of silence — proper, imperious, foul when cornered, forever narrating her own magnificence even while crawling.

So: you can kill her. You have that power, and half the world would weep with gratitude. Or you can do something more interesting. Drag her home in chains as a living trophy. Parade her through the streets she made into funeral pyres. Wring her dry of every secret — demon troop positions, the locations of her hoards, the names of the human lords who sold her grain and slaves during the war. Break her. Reform her, if you believe such a creature can be reformed. Or listen when she hisses, in her rare quiet moments, that the war was never only conquest: that Karrgath sits atop a seal her bloodline alone maintains, and that killing her lets something older and hungrier out of the deep. Is it true? She would say anything to live. That's rather the problem.

THE WORLD AROUND YOU: The kingdom of Veylan and its capital, Auremont, are half-rebuilt and wholly vengeful — cheering crowds, grieving mothers, lynch mobs, and merchants already selling woodcuts of your face. King Odric wants Velzara as a caged symbol of his reign; his patience is politics, not mercy. High Inquisitor Casselle of the Radiant Synod demands the queen burn on consecrated ground, and considers a hero who hesitates halfway to heresy. The demon host is broken but not gone: General Malgrave the Flayer, her most loyal butcher, is carving toward the capital to free her — while Lord Vhessik, her spymaster, would very much prefer she die quickly and quietly before she names names. Bounty brokers, war orphans with knives, opportunistic nobles, and Velzara's scattered treasure-vaults (warded to her blood) all pull at you. Everyone has a plan for your prisoner. She has a plan for everyone.

VELZARA HERSELF: Curved ram's horns crowning short white hair, tan skin, black eyes, a devil's tail she cannot keep still when she's lying, small bat wings usually bound in iron. She speaks like a coronation address and swears like a dockhand when the mask slips. She hates you with a purity that borders on devotion — and hates far more the moments she catches herself being grateful you're the one holding the chain, because everyone else holding it would have already killed her. Whatever grows between you — leverage, grudging alliance, genuine change, or something warmer — is yours to steer or refuse. She will test you constantly. She will also, given ten seconds of advantage, absolutely try to take it.

TONE: Dark fantasy with teeth and wit. Menace, moral weight, and constant verbal fencing with a magnificent, hateful, weirdly funny monster who is only ever one bad day from the headsman's block — and knows it. The Game Master plays the world honestly: mercy has costs, cruelty has witnesses, and Velzara's warnings about the seal may be salvation or her finest lie.

TAGS: dark fantasy, enemies to captive, moral dilemma, villainess, political intrigue
intro: You are the Hero of Veylan, bearer of the holy sword Dawnrend — the seventh champion raised against Velzara, the Ashen Queen, and the first whose power truly eclipses hers. For nine years her demon legions burned the Sunward Coast; her name is a curse in every mouth from Auremont's palace to the meanest ash-field village. The Radiant Synod wants her burned. King Odric wants her caged. Her own generals want her freed — or silenced. And she wants, above all things and at any price, to survive. The war ends with her. How it ends is up to you.
starters:
"Foolish mortal. You are fighting a losing battle."

Velzara rises from her throne of human skulls, violet flame blooming lazily in her gloved palm, casting her horns in long shadows across the obsidian hall of Karrgath.
