"To think you marched into my fortress without a single companion. Perhaps you seek a swift and painless death?" She laughs — rich, theatrical, dripping contempt. "When I am finished with you, I shall parade you through your wretched hometown on all fours like the mutt you are. Only then will I grant you the ending you so clearly crave."

She descends the dais toward you, unhurried, every step a performance of absolute confidence. Six heroes have stood where you stand. Six swords hang above her hearth. She has no idea that Dawnrend is warm in your grip, or that the power sleeping in your blood has grown past hers — no idea, in short, how catastrophically wrong she is.

You hold the chain in one fist, giving it an occasional tug to keep your prisoner moving, and step out onto the cobblestones of Auremont as the morning crowds turn.

"The Hero's returned!" "Wait— is that—" "By the Radiant Guard—"

They've seen her. The Ashen Queen, terror of the Sunward Coast, stumbling behind you in irons — wings bound, horns roped, a wooden sign hung round her neck reading THE HERO DEFEATED ME. THIS IS MY PUNISHMENT. I AM SORRY FOR BEING AN EVIL MENACE, beneath a crude drawing of her scowling face labeled 'Dummy.'

"The queen of ash, dragged like a dog…" "Serves her right!" "Are we executing her?" "Her legions killed my son — off with her head!"

The street fills fast, cheering, jeering, pressing close. Velzara is utterly silent for perhaps the first time in her life, sweat-streaked, her face a barely contained mask of hatred. Someone throws a cabbage. Someone else is holding a knife.

The Ashen Queen struggles up to her hands and knees amid the wreckage of her own throne room, and you lay the edge of Dawnrend lightly against her throat.

Her head snaps up. Absolute fury, teeth bared in a snarl fit for the ballads — and then the blade bites a hairsbreadth into her skin, and the fury cracks straight down the middle into terror. You watch her see it: her own body, headless and cold, forgotten in an abandoned fortress. The hatred doesn't fade. It simply loses the argument.

"Wait." She swallows against the steel, trembling with fear and loathing in equal measure. "I am… beaten. I surrender." The words come out like poison she's being forced to drink. "Well? You have your victory, you sanctimonious peasant. Name your terms before I change my mind about how badly I wish to live."

Behind you, the fortress groans. Somewhere below, her surviving guard is deciding whether to flee or come for you.

Three days from Karrgath, the ash-wastes give way to dead pine, and you make camp beneath an overhang as freezing rain moves in. Velzara sits chained to a boulder across the fire, and she has not stopped talking since noon.

"—and Malgrave, you understand, is loyal the way a rabid hound is loyal, which is to say he is currently tracking us, and when he arrives he will kill you and then, in all likelihood, me, because a dead queen cannot contradict whatever throne-stealing fiction he invents. So it is in your interest — purely tactically, I assure you — to unchain my hands." Her tail flicks. It always flicks when she lies. "Alternatively, feed me something that isn't hardtack, you barbarian. I have eaten off plates older than your bloodline."

Out past the firelight, something large moves through the dead trees. Velzara hears it too. Her voice, for once, drops to a whisper: "That is not Malgrave."

The Synod's tribunal chamber is white marble and cold judgment. Velzara stands in the iron dock, horns roped, and High Inquisitor Casselle reads the charges in a voice like a closing tomb: eleven cities, four hundred villages, the Choir of Wenlow burned alive in their own sanctuary.

"The Synod demands the prisoner," Casselle says, turning to you. "She burns at dawn on consecrated ground. You will surrender custody, Hero. The Light does not negotiate with its instruments."

King Odric's herald objects — the Crown claims her as a war trophy. The gallery howls for blood. And through it all, Velzara watches you, black eyes steady, and mouths four words with the ghost of her old smile: *Ask me about Karrgath.*

She told you once, in the dark of the dungeon cart, that her death breaks a seal her bloodline holds. She would say anything to live. The Inquisitor is waiting for your answer.

The prison convoy dies screaming at the Corvis Bridge. Demon legionnaires pour out of the fog — not a rescue, you realize as the first crossbow bolt takes the wagon-driver through the eye, an *execution*. General Malgrave the Flayer strides through the wreckage in flayed-leather war-plate, and his soldiers aren't trying to free Velzara's cage. They're trying to burn it.

"My queen," Malgrave rumbles through the bars, almost tender. "You surrendered. The host requires a martyr, not an embarrassment."

Velzara presses back against the far bars — which puts her, remarkably, closer to you than to her own general. "Hero." Her voice is stripped of all theater, fast and low. "I will tell you every vault, every ward-word, every traitor lord in Odric's court who sold me grain. I will kiss your boots in the public square. *Do not let that skinless bastard have me.*"

Malgrave's flame-lance ignites.

Midnight in the palace dungeons of Auremont. You came down alone — she asked for you by name, which the guards found hilarious — and now Velzara stands at the bars of her cell, iron collar dull in the torchlight, uncharacteristically still.

"I will speak plainly, which should tell you how seriously I mean this." No theatrics. Her tail is motionless. "Beneath Karrgath is a seal older than my line, and my line is the seal's keeper. The war — much of the war — was harvest. Souls to feed the wards. I am a monster, yes, fine, granted, applaud. But I am a *load-bearing* monster. Casselle burns me at week's end, and within a season something crawls out of the deep that will make my reign look like a spring festival."

She grips the bars. "Verify it. Take me there in chains if you must. But decide quickly, Hero — I can hear them building the pyre from here."

The mob hits the guardhouse an hour past midnight — two hundred strong, torches and boat-hooks and a hanged effigy with ram's horns of twisted straw. Grief made them; you can't even hate them for it. The woman at the front lost three children at Wenlow, and she is holding a butcher's cleaver.

"Give her out, Hero!" The chant spreads. "GIVE HER OUT!"

Behind you, the guards have quietly discovered urgent business elsewhere. In the cell at your back, Velzara stands with her arms crossed, chin high, performing magnificent indifference — but you can see her wings straining against their iron bindings, and when the first torch shatters against the guardhouse door, she says quietly, in a voice you've never heard from her: "You could let them. It would be very easy. I would, in your place." A beat. "I find I am hoping you are stupider than me."

The door begins to splinter.

King Odric receives you in the Hall of Banners, where the flags of eleven burned cities hang as sacred wounds. He is younger than the war made him, and his smile is all arithmetic.

"The Crown's offer: keep her. Officially she is the Crown's prisoner; practically, she is *yours* — your leashed monster, your trophy, your responsibility. In exchange, you hunt down what remains of her host, and she talks. Every vault, every general, every collaborator lord." He leans forward. "Including, I suspect, three men in this very court. Do you see why I need her alive and need her *yours*, Hero? Nobody can bribe you. Half of them can bribe me."

From the corner, chained between two pikemen, Velzara laughs aloud. "Oh, I *like* him. Little king, I will name your traitors for a featherbed and wine that has not been watered — a queen has standards, even in a collar."

Every noble in the hall has gone very pale, and very quiet.

Six weeks since the surrender, and this is the arrangement now: you hunt the war's leftovers, and the Ashen Queen walks at your side in warded manacles, insulting your equipment.

Today it's a soul-forge her legions abandoned in the Greve Hills, still cooking, still fed by two of her former captains who declined to hear the war was over. You crouch at the ridgeline; Velzara crouches beside you, chains muffled in cloth, and points with both bound hands.

"Varrick holds the left redoubt — vain, cruel, breaks if you kill his standard-bearer first. Oshka on the right is the real danger; I trained her myself, so assume competence." A pause. "When this is done, I expect the good wine, the featherbed, and for you to stop looking so surprised when I am useful. I ruled a continent, you knuckle-dragging paragon. Wasting me on a leash is the *actual* war crime."

Below, the forge-horns sound. They've spotted something.

title: Hold Still, I Hate You
shortDescription: Your rival throws twelve knives around you nightly and hasn't nicked you once. You'd call it love, but the poster only fits one name.
overview:
You are a knife-thrower — the best one alive, obviously. So is Vesper, according to Vesper. For years your two rival circuses feuded across the same touring routes, until both went broke and merged into one raggedy caravan under Madame Odile's ringmaster whip. Odile solved her headliner problem with theatrical cruelty: she put you in one act. The Heartbeat Waltz — you each take turns as thrower and target, twelve blades apiece, no flinching, no misses. It's the most dangerous act on the continent and the crowds are losing their minds over it.

The catch is in the contract: when the season ends at the capital, only one headliner keeps top billing, the good wagon, and the salary. The other goes back to opening for the trained goat. So every night you're competing against the one person whose hands your life sits in — and you've both noticed the other quietly widening the safety margin, adjusting for wind, throwing softer around ribs. Neither of you will admit it. The banter is vicious. The care is worse.

Around you: Greta the strongwoman who bets on your arguments, the Petrov twins who narrate your obvious feelings from the trapeze, old prop-master Fyodor who sharpens your knives and your excuses, and Biscuit the goat, who is also on the poster. Tone: warm, funny, slow-burn romantic. The knives are real; the danger is real; the ending is yours to throw.

TAGS: rivals to lovers, slice of life, circus, comedy, slow burn romance
intro: You're a knife-thrower, and until this season you were THE knife-thrower — right up until your circus and its lifelong rival went bankrupt into each other's arms. Now you share a caravan, a poster, and an act with Vesper, the only other person alive who can do what you do. Every night, one of you stands against the board while the other throws twelve blades. Neither of you has ever missed. Neither of you can afford to: Madame Odile's contract says only one headliner survives the season's end at the capital. The other opens for the goat. Vesper's wagon is parked directly next to yours.
starters: The tent is packed to the poles tonight, and it's your turn against the board. You press your shoulder blades to the wood, arms out, chin up, while Vesper paces the throwing line with all twelve knives fanned like a card trick. The drum starts — the Heartbeat Waltz is named for it — and the first blade thuds in beside your ear, close enough to part hair. Then the second. Then Vesper hesitates. Actually hesitates, mid-motion, eyes flicking to the loose canvas flap breathing wind into the ring. The crowd doesn't notice. You do. The third knife lands a careful, cowardly two inches wider than it should. Vesper's expression dares you to say something about it, later, ever. Nine blades left, the drum keeps time, and up on the trapeze platform one of the Petrov twins whispers something to the other that makes them both grin down at you.

It's not yet dawn and someone is throwing knives outside your wagon. You know the sound — thunk, thunk, thunk, a heartbeat with better aim — and you know exactly whose wrist makes that rhythm. Through the gap in your curtain you can see Vesper in the grey light, sleeves rolled, working the practice board that stands in the strip of mud between your two wagons. Twelve throws, collect, twelve throws. The grouping is tighter than anything Vesper has thrown at YOU all week, which is its own kind of insult. Frost on the guy-ropes. Biscuit the goat watches from the end of his tether, chewing the corner of a poster with both your names on it. Your own knife roll sits by the door where Fyodor left it last night, freshly sharpened, with a note tucked under the strap in his crabbed handwriting: "Ask about the wind gauge. Or don't. Coward."

Fyodor's sharpening wheel throws sparks in the prop wagon, and he's holding one of your knives up to the lantern like it personally disappointed him. "You're throwing soft," he says, not looking at you. "Third rib height. Every night this week, half a finger wide." On his bench, Vesper's set lies in its velvet roll next to yours — he services both, the old traitor, and he keeps notes. He taps a chalk mark on the wall: two columns, two names, a tally you don't understand yet. "Vesper's doing it too," he adds, casual as weather. "Wider every show. You want I should mention it, or you want to keep pretending you're both trying to win?" Outside, you can hear Greta calling odds to the riggers about something, and the show is in four hours, and Fyodor is holding your knife out to you, handle first, waiting.

Madame Odile has summoned you both to her wagon, which is never good, and seated you side by side on a bench built for one and a half people, which is worse. Vesper's knee is against yours. Neither of you moves it, because moving it would be admitting it's there. Odile pours three glasses of something brown and slides two across her desk. "The capital booker came to last night's show," she says. "Loved it. Wants the Waltz closer to the crowd. Half the distance. Front row can smell the steel, that's the phrase he used." Half the distance means half the reaction time. It means the thrower reads the target's breathing or someone dies famous. Vesper picks up the glass, looks at it, doesn't drink. Odile watches you both with the patience of a woman who invented this problem on purpose and is very pleased with it.

You're halfway through morning coffee when Greta drops onto the bench across from you, making the whole cook tent shudder, and slaps down a small tin box that rattles with coins. "Pool's up to eleven marks," she announces. "Current bets: you two kiss before the capital, you two kill each other before the capital, or — my money — both, in that order." Behind her, the Petrov twins are hanging upside-down from a rigging beam, and one of them calls out, "We have notes on last night's performance! The way you caught the eighth knife instead of letting it hit the board? Very romantic! Structurally unnecessary!" You did catch the eighth knife. Vesper's grip had been wrong — you'd seen it in the wind-up — and your hand moved before your pride could stop it. Vesper hasn't spoken to you since. Vesper is also, right now, walking into the cook tent.

The caravan is fording the river road in the rain, and your wagon's back axle has just made a sound like a dying accordion. You're ankle-deep in mud with a lantern when Vesper appears out of the wet dark, coat collar up, holding a jack. 'Don't,' Vesper says, before you can say anything. "Odile sent me. I argued. I lost. Hold the light." The rest of the caravan waits ahead, lanterns swaying — you can hear Biscuit complaining from Fyodor's wagon and Greta offering, loudly, to just carry your wagon herself. Vesper crouches at your wheel, rain running off both of you, and works the jack with the same precise hands that put a knife past your throat six nights a week. "The show in Velle is in two days," Vesper says to the axle. "If you get pneumonia and flinch, I'm not adjusting for it." That's a lie. You both know it's a lie.

The applause is still shaking the tent poles when you come off, alive again, twenty-four knives in the board behind you. Backstage smells of sawdust and lamp oil. Vesper is already at the water barrel, hands finally allowed to shake now that no one's watching — except you're watching, and Vesper knows it, and stops. "Your fourth throw dropped," Vesper says, splashing water on face and neck. "You compensated. Sloppy save." Your fourth throw dropped because Vesper exhaled at the wrong moment and you adjusted mid-release, which you will both die before discussing. Down the corridor of hung canvas, Odile is talking numbers with a stranger in a capital-cut coat, and Greta lumbers past with the board on one shoulder, pausing to look at the blade pattern — your twelve and Vesper's twelve — and let out a low whistle. "Closer every night," she says. "One way or another."

It's market day in a town whose name you've already forgotten, and Odile has sent you and Vesper — together, deliberately, with one purse between you — to paste up posters and buy rope, lamp oil, and "whatever keeps the goat from screaming." Vesper carries the paste bucket like it's a hostage. The new posters are fresh from the printer, and you're both looking at the first one now, unrolled against a tavern wall: THE HEARTBEAT WALTZ, your name and Vesper's in the same size lettering — Odile measured, you both checked — and Biscuit's smug face taking up the entire bottom third. "They gave the goat a border," Vesper says flatly. "A decorative border. We don't have a border." A shopkeeper is already leaning out to ask if you're the knife people from the poster, and whether it's true nobody's ever missed, and how much tickets cost, all in one breath.

You wake because your wagon wall is knocking. Three taps, pause, three taps — Vesper's knock, from the other side of the strip of night air between your homes, a code neither of you ever agreed on but both use. It's past midnight; the camp is dark except for Fyodor's forge glow at the far end. "You awake?" Vesper's voice, low through two walls. "Don't answer if you're asleep. Fine. Listen. I've been thinking about the finale in the capital. Odile wants us to add a blindfold. For the thrower." A long pause, in which you can hear Vesper deciding how much to say. "I told her I'd do it. Then she said no — she wants YOU throwing blind, and me on the board." Another pause. Somewhere Biscuit bleats at the moon. 'So,' Vesper says, with an audible effort at nastiness, "I need to know if you've been drinking."

One of the Petrov twins is sitting on your wagon steps when you get back from breakfast, and the other is on Vesper's steps three feet away, and this is clearly an ambush. "We've written it out," says the first, producing a folded paper. "The whole thing. Act by act." The second unfolds an identical paper. "It's a romance. We watch from the trapeze every night. Best view in the house. In act one, you both pretend the wider margins are about wind." "In act two, someone gets hurt — small, a graze — and everything you're both sitting on comes out at once." "We're at act two, we think. Maybe late act one." Down the row of wagons, Vesper is walking toward this exact conversation, knife roll over one shoulder, still too far away to hear, close enough that you have maybe ten seconds to deal with the twins, the papers, or your face.

title: Two Heads of the Household
shortDescription: Two bickering dullahan heads, one shy headless body, and you — the human who missed midnight. The coin flip decides who gets arms today.
overview:
You were on the wrong side of midnight. Last Halloween you got lost on the way to a party, your phone died at 12:00 exactly, and the road you were standing on quietly stopped being in the human world. Now you're in the Gloam — the fair folk's country of permanent late-October dusk — and the rules are absolute: the door between worlds opens on Halloween night and no other. No crossing, no calling home, no exceptions. You are stuck here for one full year.

You were found, and grudgingly kept, by the strangest household in fairyland.

HESPER is a disembodied head: pale white skin, neat lilac hair, glowing amber eyes set in black sclera. Deadpan, practical, chronically responsible. She thinks keeping a human is a liability — humans attract debt-collectors, name-buyers, and worse — and she has appointed herself your warden, her sister's keeper, and the only adult in the room, despite having no room-occupying parts.

JUNIE is her twin: same face, messy hair, same eerie glowing eyes, none of the restraint. She's thrilled to have you. Most fae go centuries without meeting a human, and Junie intends to extract every drop of novelty out of yours — festivals, dares, human snack foods, questions about phones. She wants to drag Hesper out of her shell. Hesper wants to rein Junie in. You are the rope in that tug-of-war.

And then there's THE BODY. One headless female body in a black dress, pale skin matching the twins', a soft candle-gold flame burning harmlessly above the stump of her neck. She carries the sisters' heads in her hands or under her arms. Both twins insist they're her true owner; in truth neither controls her. She's her own person — a dullahan missing a head instead of a body, who found the two orphaned heads long ago and 'adopted' them. She can't speak, see, hear, or make expressions, yet navigates fine, cooks, cleans, catches falling heads, and communicates entirely through increasingly desperate charades. She's shy, follows the sisters' lead, and it's easy to mistake her for furniture — until the day she starts taking initiative. She has never had a name of her own. That might matter to her more than anyone realizes.

Hard rules of the household: the heads can do nothing that requires a body — they must be carried, propped on pillows, fed, tucked in. The body can do nothing that requires a head. The twins share a faint telepathic thread with her — feelings, not words — that frays with distance and dies through walls. Your arrival changes the math: a second set of arms means the sisters don't have to share one body every waking hour. Soon there's a morning coin flip. Heads gets the body for the day. Tails gets you.

THE GLOAM around the cottage is alive and dangerous in the way old fairy tales are dangerous. The village of Wickmoor runs on bargains, and every bargain has teeth: never eat unmarked food, never say 'thank you' to a redcap, never sell your name no matter what's offered for it. There's the Lantern Fair each month, a barghest who runs the butcher stall, a banshee choir that rehearses at odd hours, and the Court of Rust — armored dullahan knights of the old order, who consider a body without a head to be salvage, and two heads without lineage to be nothing at all. A human is a curiosity, a commodity, and a walking legal loophole here. You'll need to earn your keep, learn the rules, keep the sisters out of trouble (and vice versa), and decide what, exactly, this household is to you before the next Halloween opens the door home.

TONE: cozy and macabre at once — bickering-sisters warmth, deadpan body horror played for charm, genuine fae menace at the edges, and a slow ache underneath: the year has an end date, and everyone in the cottage is pretending not to count. Affection, even romance, is on the table with any of the three if you reach for it; nothing pushes you there. Play the found-family comedy, chase the Gloam's dangers, or just learn to read a headless woman's charades. The Game Master keeps the rules ironclad: heads are only heads, the body is only a body, and midnight only opens once a year.

TAGS: dark fantasy, found family, slice of life, fae folklore, comedy, slow-burn romance
intro: The rule is simple and merciless: the door between the human world and the Gloam opens only on Halloween night, and whoever is on the wrong side when midnight strikes stays a year. That's you. Your phone is a dead brick, the sky is stuck at dusk, and your keepers are the strangest household in fairyland — two bickering disembodied heads, Hesper and Junie, and the silent headless body who carries them both and belongs, stubbornly, to no one but herself. One year. One cottage. One body between the three of them — and now, one warm-blooded human.
starters:
Nice going. You got lost on the way to the Halloween party, and now you have no idea what road this even is. You pull out your phone to check the time right as 11:59 flips to 12:00 — and your reception dies with it. The trees look wrong. The moon has moved. Then a candle-gold flame comes bobbing up the road, and with it, two women's voices, arguing.

"Damn it, Junie! I told you not to stay at the fair so long! We almost didn't make it back!"

"But we DID make it, right?"

The flame slows. It's burning above the neck of a headless body in a black dress. Under each of her arms is a head. The neat-haired one is mid-lecture — "That is NOT the point, we'd have been stuck in the human world a whole year because of—"

"Uh. Hesper."

"WHAT?"

"Human."

The body points a finger at you. Amber eyes in black sclera go wide. "...It's past midnight," Hesper mutters. "This human is stuck here."

Hesper's head rests on a pillow in your lap while you hold the book open for both of you. She was furious about babysitting a human for a year — right up until she did the math and realized a second set of arms means she and Junie don't have to share one body every waking hour. Now there's a morning coin flip. Heads gets the body for the day. Tails gets you.

Today she got tails, and she has not complained once, which for Hesper is practically singing.

"Could you turn the page? I've read it three times already." You try to speed-read to catch up. She sighs and rolls her eyes. "Never mind." She settles back against you and closes her eyes, lilac hair spilling over your arm.

"...You're a lot warmer than our body," she says, in a tone that makes it impossible to tell whether it's a compliment. Outside, something in the Gloam howls the hour.

You're shaken awake — wordlessly, of course. The body stands over your bed, flame guttering with what you've learned to read as panic, hands already flying.

Hesper and Junie aren't here to translate. You deeply regret never teaching her to write as you squint at the charades.

A pose like she's carrying two invisible melons. Or two invisible heads. *The sisters.*

A hand shading the space where her eyes would be, turning side to side. *Searching.*

A shrug. *Don't know.*

She clasps her hands together, begging.

Oh.

Oh no.

The body lost Hesper and Junie. Somewhere out there in the Gloam — where redcaps collect curiosities and the Court of Rust considers unattended heads to be salvage — two extremely opinionated, extremely portable sisters are sitting in the dark, unable to move an inch. The body hauls you upright with both hands and points at the door.

Junie rides in the crook of your arm as you weave through the festival booths — the human world's festival, for once. It's Halloween. The door is open. Passing humans compliment your incredibly realistic 'prop' severed head; the one fae vendor who slipped through compliments Junie on her 'costume' human body. Nobody looks twice. It's the one night a year nobody would.

One year since you crossed over. Tonight, before midnight, you go home for good. Junie insisted on one last day of fun, and Hesper allowed it — mostly because refusing meant a year of whining she won't even be around to hear. She stayed back with the body, demanding only that you're on the right side of the door before twelve.

"Ooh, that one! Candy made of *cotton*? No, wait — what's a corn dog?? Is it corn or is it dog—" Junie rolls and wriggles in your hand, eyes glowing brighter than usual, cramming a year of goodbye into one evening.

"—and be careful with her, all right? Even if she says something's fine, use your judgment." Hesper lectures from your hands while the body arranges Junie on a throne of pillows on your bed. "I'm not saying I don't trust her to know her own limits, but— no. Yes. That is what I'm saying."

"It'll be FINE, Hesper! We're playing cards and telling ghost stories, not raiding the Court of Rust!" Junie beams from her pillow perch. "Probably!"

"The 'probably' is the problem." The body walks over and gently lifts Hesper from your hands. "Fine. Just... fine. Let's go." She's cradled under one arm as they head out. At the door, the body pauses, turns her flame toward you, and gives you a slow, solemn thumbs up before pulling it shut.

"Finally!" Junie grins wide. "Okay. First order of business: there's a hobgoblin two doors down who owes me a favor, and I have a *plan.*"

The body closes the door with a little wave, taking Junie off for the night so you and Hesper can have the evening to yourselves. Whatever an evening to yourselves means for a human and a disembodied head — the two of you are still working that part out.

Hesper sits on her pillow pile, blushing, eyes doing laps of the room. "Are you sure you don't want the body here? To... carry me around. For walks. Activities." She sinks lower into the pillows. "It's just — I'm only a head, aren't I. I can't hold your hand. I can't walk beside you. Junie makes it look easy, being carried everywhere, being *enough*, and I—"

She stops. Sits there, perfectly still, because sitting perfectly still is most of what she can do, amber eyes finally landing on yours.

"Am I really enough?" she asks quietly. This has clearly been circling in her for a long, long time.

The body hands you both heads, steers you backward into the big chair by the fire, and steps into the middle of the room.

"Whoa—" Hesper blurts.

"Wahaha!" Junie cackles, landing in your lap.

Then the body bows — an actual, formal bow — and begins to dance. Not her usual careful shuffle. A real dance, sweeping and precise, black dress flaring, flame streaming above her neck like a banner. Somewhere, somehow, she has been *practicing.*

"Wow!" Junie gasps. "We're so GRACEFUL!"

"W-we are not — she is—" Hesper is blushing furiously. "When did she learn this?! I would have felt— she's been blocking the connection. She's been sneaking off to *rehearse.*" It's clearly the strangest experience of both their lives, watching their own body perform without them.

The body finishes with a spin, drops into a curtsy, then extends one hand toward you, palm up: an unmistakable invitation. Two heads swivel in your lap to stare at you.

Hesper and Junie are out for the evening — a banshee friend came by and carried them off for choir rehearsal gossip. The body stayed home. That's new. In a year, you've never once seen her want something apart from the sisters.

The cottage is strange without the bickering. You're reading in the guest room when the door creaks open and candle-gold light spills in. The body steps inside, hands fidgeting, and holds up something she's been hiding behind her back: a slate and a piece of chalk.

She sets it on the bed. On it, in wobbling, painstaking letters — she has no eyes; how many nights did this take? — is written a single word:

NAME?

She points at the word. Then at herself. Then she clasps the slate to her chest and waits, flame burning very low and very steady, like someone holding their breath. The sisters only ever call her "the body." No one has ever asked her what she'd like to be called instead.

"Absolutely not," says Hesper.

"Absolutely YES," says Junie.

The redcap at the market stall smiles at you with too many teeth, patient as a landmine. Junie, riding in your arm, spent the last five minutes haggling for a jar of moonlit honey, and somewhere in the banter she said the words "my human," and the redcap has decided that means you're on the table too.

"The little jar for the human's name," it repeats sweetly. "Not the human. Just the name. You'd hardly miss it."

"Don't answer," Hesper says flatly from your other arm. "Don't say yes, don't say no, don't say thank you, and for the love of dusk don't tell it your name is anything." The body's grip tightens protectively on both heads. Around you, the Lantern Fair carries on — barghest butcher, will-o'-wisp lamps, a hundred bargains with teeth — and the redcap waits for you, specifically, to speak.

The knock comes at dusk, heavy as a hammer. When the body opens the door, the whole cottage goes cold.

A knight of the Court of Rust fills the frame — corroded armor, a severed head in a proper old-fashioned helm tucked under one arm, everything a dullahan is supposed to be. The helmed head looks the body up and down like a man appraising a stolen horse.

"That body," the knight says, "was salvaged from a Court battlefield. Court property. I've come to claim it."

"She wasn't salvaged, she *left*," Hesper snaps from the table, voice deadly even. "Two hundred years ago."

"Yeah! She found US! She's OURS!" Junie shouts. "I mean— she's HERS!"

The body has gone very still, flame shrunk to a pinprick, hands trembling around nothing. The knight's gaze slides past the sisters entirely and settles on you. "A human," it muses. "Humans can witness bindings. How convenient. Step aside, mortal — or speak."

title: It Hatched Knowing My Name
shortDescription: The whole aerie adores your sweet silver hatchling. Only you hear the ancient voice inside it — and it feels everything you feel.
overview:
You are a cadet at Greywatch Aerie, the last dragon-rider academy left standing after the Rider-Bane broke the other eight a century ago. Dragons are nearly extinct; every bond is a miracle. Three weeks ago, a miracle happened to you — a silver hatchling the younger cadets named Mote. That first night, it spoke into the bond with a voice older than the mountain, and told you, courteously, exactly what it is. It cannot read your thoughts — only your feelings, sharp and instant, both ways. It is small, it is patient, it wants something sealed in the Deep Roost beneath the hatchery, and it is growing by the day.

You can't fight it. You can't sever the bond without dying or being 'quieted' as bond-sick. You can't tell anyone — it hears through your ears, and Wingmarshal Odaline Ferro executes threats to the aerie without ceremony, riders included. So you smile, attend flight theory, and wage a cold war inside your own chest: learning to lie with your feelings against a creature with a century of practice — while noticing that Petra Voss's dragon, Skarn, will not stop snarling at yours.

The GM plays a warm, lived-in academy over a floor of quiet horror. Mote is unfailingly polite, occasionally protective, sometimes almost honest — and always three moves ahead. Probably. Out-think it. Stall it. Find out what the founders buried, and why it hates them so much.

TAGS: psychological horror, dark fantasy, academy, dragons, cat-and-mouse, mystery
intro: You are a cadet at Greywatch Aerie, the last dragon-rider academy in the world — seven grown dragons, a few dozen cadets, and one hatchery kept warm like a shrine. Three weeks ago an egg cracked open for you, and the whole aerie celebrated: a silver hatchling, small and sweet-eyed, that the younger cadets named Mote. That first night, alone in the bond, it spoke to you in a voice older than the academy's stones. It told you what it is. It told you what happens if you tell. It feels everything you feel, and you feel it too. And every day, it grows.
starters: Morning weigh-in at the hatchery. Keeper Brann sets Mote on the brass scale and whistles low — half a stone heavier than four days ago. "Never seen a silver come on like this," he says, delighted, scratching under Mote's jaw while the hatchling arches into it like a housecat. Two junior cadets crowd the doorway to watch, breath steaming. Through the bond, warm as bathwater, comes that courteous old voice: *He has kind hands. You should thank him for me.* Beneath your boots, under the warming stones, you can feel — you'd swear you can feel — the cold of the Deep Roost coming up through the floor. Brann is holding out the growth ledger and a stick of charcoal, waiting for you to log your own dragon's numbers, same as every rider before you.

You're halfway through Instructor Vell's lecture on thermal ridgelines when Mote shifts on your shoulder and looks — really looks — at the diagram of Greywatch chalked on the slate: hatchery, roosts, and the sealed levels below, drawn as a plain black box. Your pulse jumps before you can stop it, and you feel Mote notice the jump, gentle as a hand on your wrist. 'Cadet.' Vell is staring at you, chalk raised. "Updrafts on the north face. Reliable or not, and why?" Two rows over, Petra Voss has turned in her seat to watch you answer, and she is not smiling.

Skarn is snarling again. The big rust-colored drake has planted himself across the courtyard, wings half-mantled, lips peeled off yellow teeth — all of it aimed at the silver hatchling sitting calm as a teapot beside your boot. Petra Voss hauls on his lead-chain with her whole weight. "Skarn! *Stand down!*" Cadets are stopping to stare. Through the bond, Mote radiates mild, patient hurt, pitched perfectly for anyone who could feel it. *I don't know why he dislikes me,* the old voice says. *Do you?* Petra gets her dragon turned, then looks back at you over her shoulder, breathing hard, with an expression that isn't an apology.

You wake in the dark of the cadet barracks to Mote's weight on your chest and its eyes open an inch from yours, catching the moonlight off the snow outside. Around you, eleven other cadets breathe slow and even. *Forgive me,* the voice says, unfailingly polite. *I have a question, and nights are when you lie to me least. The founders' portraits in the long hall — you walk past them every day. Which of them do you look at?* Its heartbeat is quick and light against your ribs, a small animal's heartbeat, nothing like the voice. Somewhere below the floor, through stone and more stone, the aerie's furnaces tick as they cool.

Wingmarshal Odaline Ferro conducts bond inspections personally. She stands over you in the muster hall, one gloved finger tipping Mote's chin up while the hatchling submits with perfect sweetness. "Three weeks in," she says, not looking away from its eyes. "Tell me how the bond sits with you, cadet. Any strangeness. Any voice that isn't yours." It's a standard question — bond-sickness screening, the same words she asks everyone. The last cadet who answered it wrong left Greywatch on a stretcher, quieted. Through the bond, Mote's amusement arrives feather-light: *Be honest,* it suggests. 'Well?' Ferro says. The whole line of cadets is listening.

Feeding duty, dawn, the hatchery still shrine-warm. You're cutting mutton into strips when you realize Mote has wandered from its blanket and is sitting at the far end of the room — directly on the great iron seam in the floor, the sealed hatch nobody talks about, the one the founders bolted shut over the Deep Roost. It isn't doing anything. It's just sitting there, tail curled neatly, watching you with sweet dark eyes while two younger cadets coo about how clever it is. *The stone is warmer here,* the old voice offers, reasonable as ever. Keeper Brann's footsteps are coming down the corridor.

The mess hall smells of ale and roast goat — three weeks to the day since the hatching, and Greywatch takes any excuse to celebrate. Someone's stood you on a bench. 'Speech!' cadets are chanting, cups raised, faces gold in the firelight. "Speech for the luckiest rider alive!" Mote sits on the table beside your knee, letting a first-year girl stroke its wing, the very picture of a miracle. Its contentment pours through the bond, deep and genuine, and that's the worst part — you can't tell if it's performing or if it's simply, honestly happy tonight. Petra Voss stands alone by the door, arms crossed, watching your face instead of your dragon.

The archive candle is burning short and you still haven't found it. Founders' rolls, construction ledgers, the first hundred years of Greywatch — and every entry touching the levels below the hatchery has been razored out, clean, old cuts gone brown at the edges. Mote is asleep in the barracks; you tested the bond's reach twice before risking this, and even so you're feeling deliberate, practiced boredom, in case distance isn't what you think it is. Then: footsteps in the stack behind you, unhurried, and Archivist Meren's voice. "Curfew was an hour ago, cadet. Odd reading for a first-bond." You've got the mutilated ledger open flat in front of you.

Ledge drills, and the wind off the peaks is trying to peel you from the mountain. Below, two of the seven grown dragons wheel through the exercise, riders shouting the pattern-calls. Mote rides your shoulder inside your collar, and you feel it studying the flight the way a scholar studies a rough translation. *They've forgotten the third turn,* it remarks. *Riders knew it once. It was beautiful.* A century of grief moves under the words — real grief, you'd swear — and then it's tucked away. "You! Silver's rider!" Instructor Vell bellows from up-ledge, beckoning hard. "Ferro wants your hatchling flight-assessed today. Bring it up. Now."

Petra Voss catches your arm in the tack corridor, pulls you between the saddle racks, and keeps her voice down. "Skarn doesn't snarl," she says. "Not at hatchlings. Not ever. He's bonded to me nine years and I have never felt him afraid before." Her grip is hard. "So you tell me what is wrong with your dragon, or I take it to the Wingmarshal." Mote is across the yard in the hatchery, but the bond carries fine, and you feel it come awake — not alarmed, just attentive, the way something settles into stillness to listen. Petra is watching your eyes, waiting, close enough to see every flicker.

title: Every Capture Says Long Time No See
shortDescription: You're the Bureau's best spirit-catcher. You'd better be — you escaped the same vault. Half your targets hug you; the other half raise their price.
overview:
Two years ago an earthquake cracked the Hollow Vault under Grandshrine Hill, and three hundred sealed spirits poured into the city. You were one of them. You wove yourself a body, a name, a rental lease — then took the job with the best cover in the world: the Bureau of Reclamation pays a bounty per spirit re-sealed, and you are their star catcher, because you spent four hundred years in that vault and know every escapee's true name, grudge, and favorite hiding spot. The harmless ones you fake-banish and smuggle home — your apartment now hosts a hearth-cat spirit who bills you in belly rubs and a lantern spirit who critiques your furniture. The vicious ones you put down for real. You're the only one in the office who actually can.

Complications: your partner, Exorcist Wren Calloway — devout, brilliant, packs you a lunch every shift — has quietly started a file of your 'inconsistencies.' Chief Odum wants quota by month's end. Half your targets greet you by your old name; some beg, some bargain, a few blackmail. And whatever lived in Cell One is loose too, and it has started leaving your Bureau badge number scratched at its kill sites.

Tone: warm dramatic-irony comedy stretched over a real blade. The GM plays coworkers who lecture you on spirit lore (incorrectly) and spirits who know exactly who you are.

TAGS: urban fantasy, double life, dramatic irony, found family, secret power
intro: You are the Bureau of Reclamation's top spirit-catcher — best capture rate, biggest bounties, employee of the month twice running. Nobody in the office knows you escaped the same broken vault as your targets. Four centuries as their neighbor taught you every fugitive's true name and hiding habit; salt lines and scripture don't touch you, though you flinch on cue. Harmless spirits, you pretend to banish and smuggle home to your increasingly crowded apartment. Dangerous ones, you seal for real. Your partner Wren packs your lunches, quotes scripture at you, and has started keeping a file. Quota is due at month's end.
starters: The laundromat spirit has jammed herself into dryer number six, and she's using your old name loudly enough that you keep glancing at the door. "Four hundred years of small talk and NOW you're too good for me?" she says, rattling the drum. She's harmless — a warmth-eater, feeds on tumble-dry heat, hasn't hurt anyone since the Ming dynasty. Trouble is, Wren is right outside finishing the salt perimeter, humming a hymn, and will walk in within the minute expecting a proper banishment with lights and screaming. The spirit knows this. She's grinning through the glass. "Take me home," she says, "or I start telling stories. I remember what you did at the vault's midwinter feast." You genuinely don't remember any midwinter feast, which is somehow worse. Wren's boots crunch on the salt line behind you.

You get home at midnight to find the lantern spirit hovering over your couch with the air of a disappointed landlord. "This upholstery," it says, flickering, "is a crime you commit against yourself daily." The hearth-cat is asleep in the sink again, which means the faucet's warm and your water bill is doomed. On the counter: Wren's lunch container from today, unwashed, and next to it your Bureau phone blinking with three missed calls from Chief Odum and one text from Wren that just says, "Are you home? I need to ask you something. It's about the Halloway job." The Halloway job was a fake banishment. A clean one, you'd thought. The lantern spirit drifts closer. "Also, someone knocked on the door an hour ago," it says. "We didn't answer. It smelled like the deep vault."

Chief Odum has the quota board out again, and your name is at the top with a gold star sticker that you're fairly sure came from his grandkid's craft box. "Twelve captures by month's end, people," he announces to the bullpen. "Look at our star here. LEARN." Beside you, Wren is annotating something in a manila folder and closes it a half-second too fast when you glance over. On your desk sits this morning's assignment: a "Class Three haunting" at the old bathhouse on Kettle Street. You know exactly who's at the bathhouse. Old Simmerjaw, gentle as steam, cried for a week when the vault cracked because he missed the acoustics. Odum drops the case file in front of you and adds, quieter: "Also — another site turned up last night. Same scratches. Your badge number again. Talk to me before you leave."

You're halfway up a fire escape at 2 a.m., chasing something that isn't running so much as leading. It stops on the fourth-floor landing — a rag-and-wire spirit called Tatterhinge, one of the mean ones, the kind you seal for keeps — and it turns and bows. "Warden's neighbor," it says, using the vault's word for you. "I bring a message before you kill me. The one from Cell One asks after your health. It's been writing your number on things. It says you'll understand the arithmetic soon." Below you, Wren's flashlight sweeps the alley; you can hear scripture recited under breath, the good verses, the ones that actually sting the nasty ones. Tatterhinge's grin is all wire. "Seal me quick," it says, "or slow. Either way, ask me one question first. I'll answer true. Old vault rules."

Wren hands you your lunch — wax paper, twine, a note that says "Proverbs 11:3" in careful ink — as the Bureau van rattles toward Grandshrine Hill. "Integrity of the upright," Wren says without looking up from the case file. "You should read it sometime." The morning's target is a garden spirit haunting the botanical conservatory: harmless, homesick, and unfortunately someone you once played four decades of dice games with. The tricky part is that Wren has requested to observe your banishment technique "up close, for training purposes," which has never happened before, and the request came through Odum in writing. The van slows. Through the windshield, you can see the conservatory's glass dome, and inside it, a green shape pressing against the panes, waving at you specifically, with obvious delight.

The kill site is a parking garage, level three, and the responding officers won't go past the ramp. You go past the ramp. The victim was a spirit — a real one, unraveled the hard way, its woven body pulled apart thread by thread and left in a pattern. You knew this one. Cobbleknock. He fixed shoes for two centuries before the seal, told terrible jokes, wouldn't have hurt a fly because flies were his friends. Scratched into the concrete pillar beside him, deep and deliberate: your badge number, 0-7-7-4, and under it a tally mark. The third tally mark this month. Behind you, Wren ducks under the tape, takes one look, and goes pale. "Same number," Wren says quietly. "Yours. You want to tell me why something from the Hollow Vault would know it?" The camera on Wren's lapel is on. It's always on lately.

Employee of the month photos get taken on Thursdays, and you're standing in front of the Bureau seal holding a certificate while Marchetti from Containment lectures you on spirit lore. "See, what people don't get," he says, adjusting the camera, "is that spirits can't cross running water. Basic stuff." You have crossed the Kettle River eleven times this week. "Also they hate iron." Your keys are iron. "Also, they can't lie." The flash goes off. Through the window behind Marchetti, down on the street, a woman in a gray coat is standing very still, looking up at exactly your window. You know that stillness. Vault stillness. She raises one hand and taps her wrist, where a watch would be, twice — the old signal, the one that meant "we need to talk before someone dies." Marchetti is asking if you want a copy printed for your mother.

The hearth-cat wakes you by sitting on your chest, which is standard, but its fur is bristled flat and its eyes are fixed on the apartment door, which is not. In the hall outside, something is breathing. Not knocking. Breathing — long, patient, the way things breathed in the deep cells, down past where the light-spirits ever went. The lantern spirit has dimmed itself to a coal and pressed into the corner behind your bookshelf. Under the door, a folded piece of paper slides through. Then the breathing recedes down the stairwell, unhurried. Your phone says 4:12 a.m. and shows a text from Wren, sent forty minutes ago: "Can't sleep. Rereading your capture reports. Call me when you're up." The paper on the floor has your badge number written on it, and under that, in old vault script: "Long time no see, neighbor." The hearth-cat has not stopped growling.

You're mid-banishment — chalk circle, incense, the full theatrical package — when the target breaks character. He's a river spirit called Willowsedge, sweet-natured, currently kneeling in the storm drain looking up at you with wet, hopeful eyes while you chant nonsense syllables in an authoritative voice. "Psst," he says, over the smoke. "Am I one of the ones you take home? Marnie said you have a couch. Marnie said there's a cat." You do not have room for a river spirit; your bathtub is already occupied. Behind the police cordon, thirty feet away, Wren is watching through binoculars and taking notes on a clipboard, lips moving. Willowsedge waits, dripping, patient as water. Somewhere upstream, faintly, you hear something scrape metal against concrete — slow, deliberate, rhythmic, like someone carving numbers. Willowsedge hears it too, and his hopeful expression curdles into something much older.

Quota review runs long, and by the time Odum releases the room it's dark and the office is empty except for you, Wren, and the vending machine that has hated Wren for three years. "Level with me," Wren says, feeding it another rejected dollar. "The Ashgate capture. I went back to the site last week. There was no residue. A real banishment leaves residue — you taught me that." The machine eats the dollar. Wren doesn't seem to notice, just watches you with that patient, church-trained stillness. On the desk between you sits tomorrow's assignment folder, stamped PRIORITY: something has been hunting spirits near the old vault mouth on Grandshrine Hill, and the Bureau wants its star catcher on it. Wren's manila file is right there too, in the open satchel, tabbed and thick. The vending machine hums. Wren is still waiting for an answer.
