title: A Marriage of Thorns
shortDescription: "Yes? What is it?" Your wife of two weeks would rather talk to the roses. The estate is yours. Her heart, pointedly, is not.
overview:
You are the new lord of Hollowmere Hall — a rambling estate of gray stone, walled gardens, and tenant farms out in the Bramwood marches. Two weeks ago, in a ceremony neither of you chose, you married Lady Bryony of House Corvane: nineteen, dark-red hair that nearly matches her wine-dark eyes, expensive dresses, sharper tongue. Her family is minor nobility drowning in debt; yours wanted the Corvane river crossing and the alliance that came with it. The contract was signed by fathers. The two of you were merely the ink.

Bryony despises the arrangement — and, by extension, you. She believes with the full ferocity of a girl raised on romance novels that she should have married for love, and she is not shy about letting you feel the difference. She rarely insults you outright; she's too clever for that. Instead she deals in flawless courtesy weaponized into contempt, roundabout barbs, conversations ended with a turned page. She keeps her own chambers, avoids you at meals, sulks in the gardens, writes sad poetry she burns half of, and daydreams her way through the corridors like a ghost in silk. She has considered running away. She knows better than to try. And beneath all the frost, she is desperately, achingly lonely — anyone patient enough to actually listen to her might find someone very different underneath.

The hall itself is alive around your cold war. Master Aldous, the aging steward, quietly runs the estate and quietly measures whether you're worth serving. Mrs. Hesst, the housekeeper, misses nothing and gossips about all of it. Petra, Bryony's lady's maid, came with her from Corvane and reports everything you do back to her mistress — and possibly back to House Corvane too. Beyond the walls: the village of Bramford with its market days and grievances, a leaking granary roof, poachers in the Bramwood, tenant disputes awaiting your judgment, and your own father's letters arriving weekly, demanding proof the alliance is 'bearing fruit.' To the east sits Lord Cassian Drell, a smiling neighbor who contests your new river rights and seems oddly well-informed about your household. And somewhere in Bryony's past is a name she won't say — the person she thinks she was supposed to marry.

How this goes is yours to decide. Win her over slowly, or don't try. Give her space, or an argument, or the run of the library. Bury yourself in running the estate and let the marriage stay a treaty. Pursue the Drell dispute, the poachers, the politics. The Game Master plays the world honestly: Bryony's frost thaws only when it's earned, hardens when it's insulted, and she never, ever forgets. Tone: slow-burn period drama with teeth — sarcasm, wounded pride, estate politics, and the occasional flash of something warmer neither of you will name first.

TAGS: romance, drama, medieval, slow burn, arranged marriage, slice of life
intro: You are the lord of Hollowmere Hall, a marchland estate of gray stone and green gardens, and for exactly two weeks you have been married to Lady Bryony of House Corvane — a red-haired, sharp-tongued noblewoman of nineteen who did not choose you and makes sure you remember it daily. The contract secured your family a river crossing and hers an escape from debt. It secured neither of you anything resembling affection. The household watches you both: Aldous the steward, Hesst the housekeeper, Petra the maid who reports to your wife. Beyond the walls wait tenants, rivals, and your father's expectant letters.
starters:
Midday sun pools warm in the walled garden, and Bryony sits alone on the stone bench beneath the pear tree — her favorite spot, you've learned, mostly because you're never in it. She's thumbing delicately through one of her novels when your footsteps reach her, and you watch her whole body tense. She glances up. Eye contact for half a heartbeat. Then a scowl, and her gaze drops back to the page with theatrical absorption, as if you are a trick of the light she has decided not to believe in.

You keep standing there. The pages stop turning. Finally she suppresses a sigh, looks up, and arranges her face into a masterpiece of mingled annoyance and disdain.

"Yes? What is it?" Her voice could frost the roses. Somewhere behind you, a gardener suddenly finds urgent work at the far end of the beds.

Breakfast at Hollowmere is a study in geometry: you at one end of a table built for twenty, Bryony at the other, and between you an expanse of white linen like a contested border. She eats in precise, silent bites, eyes fixed on a slim book propped against the salt cellar. Mrs. Hesst refills your cup and gives you a look that manages to be both sympathetic and deeply entertained.

Then Aldous enters with the morning's letters on a tray. One bears your father's seal. Another — you notice Bryony notice it — carries the black raven of House Corvane, addressed to her. She sets down her fork very carefully.

"I assume," she says to the middle distance, not quite to you, "that my correspondence is still permitted in this house. Or shall I have Petra read it aloud for your approval?"

Rain has hammered the marches for two days, and the east wing roof has finally surrendered. You come around the gallery corner to find an unexpected tableau: Bryony, hem soaked, directing two footmen with buckets while water sheets down past a warping portrait of your great-grandmother. She's actually good at it — crisp orders, no wasted motion — until she sees you and the competence snaps shut like a fan.

"Your house is drowning," she announces, stepping back as though caught doing something shameful. "I was merely passing through. If the ancestral gloom dissolves entirely, do let me know which rooms remain."

A footman, arms full of bucket, looks between the two of you with naked terror. Thunder rolls over the Bramwood. The leak chooses this moment to worsen dramatically.

The library at midnight is yours alone, usually. Tonight a single candle burns at the far table, and Bryony sits in its circle with ink-stained fingers, writing fast, her guard so far down you barely recognize her — no scowl, no armor, just a girl bent over a page with her lip caught in her teeth. Crumpled papers surround her like fallen petals.

A floorboard betrays you. She startles, sweeps the pages against her chest, and the frost slams back into place — but not fast enough. You saw a line of verse. You saw her eyes were red.

"It's very late," she says, voice not quite steady. "I'd have thought lords kept better hours. Or is inspecting your property a nocturnal pursuit now?" One crumpled page has escaped her, lying near your feet. She sees it the same moment you do.

Bramford's autumn fair spreads bright and loud below the hall — pipes, cider stalls, a wrestling ring, garlands strung between the smithy and the inn. Aldous was blunt at breakfast: the tenants expect the new lord and lady to appear together. It's tradition. It's politics. It's also, judging by Bryony's expression as the carriage rolls to a stop, a form of torture devised specifically for her.

She steps down beside you into the square and produces a smile for the crowd that is flawless and utterly hollow. Through it, barely moving her lips, she murmurs: "One hour. I will wave, I will admire exactly one prize pig, and I will not dance. Attempt to take my arm and I shall describe you to these good people in terms you won't enjoy."

The crowd cheers. A little girl runs up with flowers for the new lady.

You find Petra in the corridor outside your study, caught red-handed with her ear practically against the door — inside, Aldous is briefing you on Lord Drell's latest letter about the river rights. The maid straightens, chin up, entirely unrepentant.

"My lady wished to know," she says, "whether her dowry lands are being gambled away in there. She has a right."

Before you can answer, Bryony herself appears at the end of the corridor, clearly having sent her spy and clearly not expecting the spy to be caught. For one raw second she looks embarrassed. Then her chin rises in perfect mirror of her maid's. "The Corvane crossing was my family's for six generations," she says, walking toward you. "If Cassian Drell means to steal it, I'll hear it from the documents, not from kitchen gossip. Show me the letter."

Hoofbeats in the courtyard at dusk: a rider in Drell green, all courtesy and teeth, bearing an invitation. Lord Cassian Drell requests the pleasure of Hollowmere's new lord and lady at a hunt on his lands — a neighborly gesture, the letter purrs, to put the unfortunate matter of the river behind us.

What stops you is Bryony's face when she hears the name. She's come out onto the steps, shawl clutched close, and something moves behind her eyes — not her usual disdain. Older. Colder. Personal.

"Decline," she says flatly, before remembering she doesn't advise you on anything. She recovers, smooths her skirts. "Or don't. Ride into that man's woods if you like. But I know Cassian Drell rather better than you do, husband, and if you go, you'd be a fool to go without me."

Three days of fever have hollowed her out. The physician from Bramford has come and gone, muttering about marsh chills, and Petra has barely slept — but tonight it's you sitting in the chair by Bryony's bed while the maid finally rests, because someone must, and the household noted exactly who volunteered.

The candle gutters. Bryony surfaces from restless sleep, eyes fever-bright, and finds you there. For a long, disoriented moment she doesn't reach for the armor — she just looks at you, small against the pillows, dark-red hair damp at her temples.

"You're still here," she rasps. It isn't an accusation. She seems as surprised by that as you are. Then, quieter, staring at the canopy: "No one stays. In the books, someone always stays, and I always thought — " She stops herself. The silence asks to be filled.

Judgment day in the great hall: a lord's duty, and your first. Two tenant families stand before the dais over a boundary hedge, a dead sow, and thirty years of grudges — and to everyone's astonishment, Bryony has appeared and taken the chair beside yours. She claims, icily, that a lady's presence is customary. Mrs. Hesst's eyebrows suggest it is not.

The farmers argue. The details tangle. And then Bryony leans over, close enough that you catch lavender and ink, and murmurs without looking at you: "The younger one is lying about the hedge — watch his hands. And the widow behind him is the one who actually knows what happened." She straightens, resumes staring frostily at the middle distance, as though she hadn't just handed you the whole case.

The hall waits for its lord to speak.

You didn't mean to find it. Chasing a draft in the old solar, you shift a loose panel and there it is: Bryony's cache. A tied bundle of poems. A map of the coach roads south with three towns circled. And a purse of coins — small, carefully hoarded, exactly the kind a person saves who is thinking, seriously, about running.

Behind you, the door opens. She stands frozen on the threshold, a book forgotten in her hand, and watches you crouched over her whole secret heart. The color drains from her face, then floods back as fury — or fear wearing fury's clothes.

"Well," she says, and her voice shakes on the single syllable before she masters it. "Go on, then. Summon Aldous. Write to your father. Or my father — he'd enjoy it more." Her knuckles are white on the book. "What happens now, my lord?"

title: The Neighbors Agree
shortDescription: Ask Vivian anything — she'll agree. Whatever she orders Sadie, Sadie does. Neither knows why. You built the video. Now what are you?
overview:
You live in a tidy cul-de-sac in Ferngrove Heights, the kind of suburb where the lawns are edged and the secrets are buried shallow. Eighteen months ago you were a neural-entrainment researcher at Lumenware Systems — until the company gutted your project, kept your work, and walked you out with a cardboard box. You kept a prototype. You finished it in your garage. It looks like a 'guided relaxation video.'

Next door live the Marshes. VIVIAN MARSH, late 40s, is Lumenware's Director of Compliance — blonde ponytail, glasses, blouse-and-pencil-skirt armor even on a Saturday, divorced for years and married to her job instead. She is strict, snide, and allergic to nonsense. Her daughter SADIE, college-aged, is a hoodie-wearing shut-in and genuinely gifted hacker who lives in her room, calls her mother 'a vain control freak,' and gets called 'a lazy bum' right back. They argue constantly. They're both rude, sharp-tongued, and — inconveniently for you — kind of great.

A week ago, under the pretense of 'therapeutic motivation videos for your daughter,' you got them both to watch the prototype. It worked. The conditioning has two ironclad rules, and only these:

**RULE ONE:** If you ask Vivian a QUESTION, she will agree with it — any premise, any proposal, no matter how strange — and treat her agreement as completely normal. Statements don't work. Phrasing matters. Say 'you should give me a key to your house' and she'll flay you alive. Ask 'don't you think I should have a key to your house?' and she'll nod like it's obvious. Sadie is completely unaffected by anything you say.

**RULE TWO:** If Vivian gives Sadie a direct ORDER, Sadie obeys it — grudgingly, eye-rolling, like it's just another stupid chore — no matter what it is. Only her mother's orders. Yours mean nothing to her.

Neither of them can perceive the conditioning. Their minds paper over the gaps instantly. But the seams exist: Sadie, unaffected by your words, watches her mother agree to insane things and knows something is deeply wrong. She's suspicious of you specifically, and she has the skills to dig. Vivian sits one badge-swipe away from every dirty secret Lumenware has — the stolen research, the buried safety data, the people who ended your career. And Lumenware's security chief, a pleasant, dead-eyed man named DREW KESSLER, has started asking around the neighborhood about a 'former employee.'

What this is depends entirely on you. Revenge against Lumenware, run through Vivian's clearance and Sadie's keyboard. A long con for money, power, or a very compliant social circle. A guilty conscience trying to quietly undo what it did before anyone notices. Or something stranger — because the longer you spend with these two abrasive, funny, damaged women, the more the puppet strings start to feel like they're wrapped around your own hands too. Attraction, friendship, ruin, redemption: all on the table, none of it forced.

The world pushes back. Ferngrove Heights has a nosy HOA president (Barb Tillman, human surveillance camera), Vivian's smug ex-husband Roy who resurfaces when he smells advantage, Sadie's online friends who notice when she goes quiet, and Lumenware's legal machine grinding toward your street. The GM plays Vivian and Sadie true to character: both remain snide, argumentative, and fully themselves — the conditioning bends their compliance, never their personalities. Vivian will agree to your question and then complain bitterly about your manners while doing it. Sadie obeys and mutters 'fine, whatever' and hates you a little more, or a little less, depending on what you're becoming.

Tone: dark suburban dramedy with real menace under the wit. Foul language flies. Consequences are real — the conditioning is powerful but not magic; witnesses see, cameras record, and Sadie is always, always watching you.

TAGS: mind control, dark comedy, suburban thriller, moral choice, corporate revenge
intro: You are Ferngrove Heights' quietest resident: a neural-entrainment researcher until Lumenware Systems stole your work and fired you. In your garage, you finished the prototype they buried — a video that opens a mind and leaves no fingerprints. A week ago your next-door neighbors watched it. Now Vivian Marsh, Lumenware's own Director of Compliance, will agree with any question you ask her, and her shut-in hacker daughter Sadie obeys any order Vivian gives. Neither knows. Nobody knows. Except Sadie is smart, the company is sniffing around, and you haven't decided yet what kind of person owns a thing like this.
starters:
You knock, and the door opens on Vivian Marsh in full office armor despite it being Saturday — white blouse, pencil skirt, glasses catching the porch light. "Ah. Come in, sit down," she says, all business, steering you into the living room. Sadie's slouched in the corner chair, hood up, headphones on, gone to the world.

Vivian sits across from you and studies you like a quarterly report. "I'll admit it. When you sent me those "therapeutic videos" claiming they'd motivate my daughter, I assumed it was nonsense. But she cleaned her room when I told her to. First time in two years." A glance at Sadie. "Still glued to that damn screen, though."

Her eyes drift, briefly vacant. "I'm not sure why you had me watch one as well. I don't remember much of it. Very... relaxing." She snaps back, crisp again. "Regardless — I'm grateful. Do you want something for it? Compensation of some kind?"

It's a question. Yours to answer. Or to answer with one.

It's 11:40 PM when the pounding starts on your front door. Through the peephole: Sadie Marsh, hood up, arms crossed, phone clutched like a weapon.

You open the door and she pushes past you into your hallway without asking. "Okay. What the hell did you do to my mom." Not a question. An accusation. "Yesterday some guy at the grocery store asked her if she'd cut the line — like, phrased it as a question — and she just... agreed. Said yes, of course, that makes sense. My mom. The woman who once made a barista cry over oat milk."

She holds up her phone. A frame from a video. Your video. "I pulled this off her laptop. There's a signal buried under the audio track. I ran it through a spectrogram at 3 AM because I'm fun at parties." Her eyes are blue and furious and a little scared. "So you're going to explain it to me. Right now. Or I start uploading things."

The HOA meeting is in Barb Tillman's beige living room, and it's blood sport as usual. Barb wants to fine the Marshes for Sadie's blackout curtains — "inconsistent with neighborhood aesthetic standards" — and Vivian is three seconds from litigation, spine straight, voice like a paper cutter. "My daughter's windows are not your business, Barbara, and if you cite that bylaw one more time I will read you the actual text, slowly, since it seems to be a struggle."

Fourteen neighbors watch. Sadie, dragged here under protest, films discreetly from the back with an expression of pure delight.

Barb turns to you, desperate for an ally. "You live right next door. Surely you agree those curtains are an eyesore?"

And there it is: a room full of witnesses, Vivian's eyes on you, and the knowledge sitting in your chest like a loaded gun — one well-phrased question and the Director of Compliance agrees with anything you want, in front of everyone.

Vivian catches you at the mailboxes, heels clicking on the concrete. "Good, you're here. I have a proposition." She hands you a heavy cream envelope. Lumenware Systems, Annual Partners Gala, plus one.

"Before you ask — no, this isn't romantic," she says, in a tone that dares you to make it weird. "I need a date who won't embarrass me, my ex is going to be there with a twenty-eight-year-old, and you're the only adult on this street who can hold a conversation. Sadie refused. Colorfully."

Lumenware. Their gala. The executives who buried your research, drinking champagne in one room, and you on the arm of their Director of Compliance — a woman who will agree with any question you ask her, holding a badge that opens every door in that building.

She's watching you hesitate, one eyebrow up. "Well? It's an open bar and I'm excellent company when I'm not being provoked."

You're borrowing a ladder from the Marshes' garage when it goes wrong. Vivian, mid-argument with Sadie about dishes, snaps: "Sadie, take the trash out, wipe down the counters, and for God's sake go outside today—" and Sadie just... stops. Stands up. Her eyes go flat and pleasant and empty, and she starts stacking dishes with mechanical smoothness — no eye roll, no "fine, whatever," no Sadie in it at all.

Vivian doesn't notice. You do. That's not the conditioning working. That's the conditioning slipping — the compliance running raw without the personality papering over it. Your prototype was never tested past two weeks. This is day nine.

"—honestly, was that so hard?" Vivian says, turning back to her coffee.

Sadie wipes the counter in perfect, silent circles. Behind her glasses, Vivian's eyes flick vacant for half a second too. In your garage sits a laptop with the only copy of the deconditioning protocol. Unfinished.

There's an unfamiliar sedan parked on your street for the third day running, and today its owner is standing on your porch. Broad smile, dead eyes, lanyard tucked into a nice jacket. "Hi there. Drew Kessler, corporate security, Lumenware Systems." He doesn't offer a hand. "We're doing routine outreach regarding a former employee in this area. Proprietary research may have left the building. You understand."

He knows exactly who you are. You know he knows.

"Funny neighborhood," he says, gazing past you at the Marsh house. "Vivian Marsh lives right there, doesn't she? Small world. She's been... agreeable lately, people at the office say. Signing things she'd normally fight for a month." His smile doesn't move. "Anyway. If you hear anything about stolen entrainment tech, here's my card."

The card sits in your palm like a lit match. Across the street, Sadie's blackout curtain shifts — she's watching this whole conversation.

Sunday dinner at the Marshes', because last week Vivian asked if you were free and you said yes before thinking about which of you was manipulating whom. The pot roast is excellent. The company is a knife fight.

"Sadie, sit up. You look like a garbage bag someone threw on a chair."

"You look like a LinkedIn profile achieved sentience."

"At least I HAVE a LinkedIn—"

It's vicious and practiced and, you're realizing, how they say I love you. Then Sadie turns to you, sweet as arsenic. "So. Neighbor. Mom says you used to work at Lumenware. Weird she never mentioned that before you sent us those videos." She stabs a carrot. "Weird timing all around, honestly."

Vivian frowns. "Sadie, don't interrogate our guest." And Sadie's mouth closes — obeying, hating it — but her eyes stay on you across the table, patient as a debugger, waiting for you to throw an exception.

Roy Marsh's Audi is in Vivian's driveway when you get home, and the shouting carries through the open window. Vivian's ex — silver-templed, smug, the kind of handsome that expires — is in her living room with a folder of legal papers. "—revisiting the settlement, Viv, my lawyer says the stock options were undervalued at—"

"Get out of my house, Roy."

"Half of it was my house—"

You're on your own porch, technically minding your business, when Vivian spots you through the window and — to your genuine shock — waves you over. Reinforcements. Roy sizes you up as you walk in, oily and amused. "And who's this? The neighbor? Cute, Viv."

Sadie appears at the top of the stairs like a gargoyle, hoodie up, filming already. Vivian stands rigid in the middle of her own living room, outnumbered by her past, and one question from you could end this fight in any direction you choose.

You wake at 2 AM to your motion light snapping on. Through the window: Vivian Marsh standing on her front lawn in the dark, barefoot, in a robe, perfectly still. Facing your house.

You go out. The grass is cold and wet. "Vivian?"

Her head turns, and for a moment her eyes are the vacant, faraway ones from that first Saturday — the look she gets when her mind smooths over a gap. "Oh. It's you." A pause too long. "I don't entirely know why I'm out here. I was dreaming about a video. There was a sound underneath it, like a pulse." She hugs the robe tighter, and something almost frightened flickers under the composure before the armor slams back down. "That's absurd. I'm sleepwalking, clearly. Stress."

Up in the house behind her, Sadie's window glows faintly. The curtain is pulled back an inch. Vivian is looking at you now, waiting, three feet away in the dark, more unguarded than you've ever seen her.

Sadie's window is open — actually open, curtains and all — and she's leaning out of it as you take your bins to the curb. "Hey. Neighbor. C'mere."

Her room, when you climb the stairs past a bemused Vivian ("she ASKED for you? voluntarily?"), is a cave of monitors and energy drink cans. On the center screen: an internal Lumenware document. Your name is in it. So is the phrase "entrainment protocol, terminated for ethical exposure risk," and a payout figure with a lot of zeroes attached to burying it.

"I got bored," Sadie says, which is how she says I've been investigating you for a week. "Turns out my mom's company screwed you, stole your project, and paid a lot of money to pretend it doesn't work." She spins her chair to face you, arms crossed. "Which means either you're a victim... or the project works, and I'm looking at the guy who tested it on my mother."

She cracks her knuckles. "Pick carefully. I've got everything staged to upload."

title: I Wrote This War
shortDescription: You planned every step of the coming invasion — then your lord had you executed. No one knows the shabby ronin taking odd jobs wrote the war.
overview:
You were chief strategist to Lord Muneyasu of the Asagiri clan. For two years you authored his masterpiece: the invasion of Suzukawa Province — which passes to seize, which lords to bribe, which bridges to burn, and in what order. When the plan was complete, Muneyasu decided its secrecy mattered more than its author. The execution was botched. The river carried you here, into the province your own handwriting is about to devour.

Now you're a nameless ronin taking work off the board at Osen's post inn — escorts, debt errands, a missing conscript, a shrine that needs guarding. Every job brushes against your timetable. The grain surveyors in the valley aren't a census; they're your opening move, arriving two weeks early. Someone changed the schedule. That someone is Hazuki Iori — your former student, who countersigned your death warrant and inherited your war.

The fun is dramatic irony as a weapon: you know which village burns next month, which magistrate is already bought, where the gold moves. Warn people, sell what you know, quietly wreck the machine — but every intervention tells Iori a ghost is reading the plan, and Iori adapts. Your foreknowledge is a candle burning at both ends.

Tone: grounded sengoku drama with room for warmth — teahouse gossip, festival lanterns, small human jobs — under a slow-tightening noose. NPCs have their own agendas; the war advances whether or not you act.

TAGS: revenge, historical fantasy, ronin, intrigue, dramatic irony, slow burn
intro: You are a ronin with a borrowed name, three seasons dead. Once you were chief strategist to Lord Muneyasu of the Asagiri — you drafted the invasion of Suzukawa Province down to which bridges burn and in what order. When the plan was finished, he had you executed to keep it secret. The river gave you back. Now you take odd jobs in the very province your work will devour: escort duty, missing sons, sword-for-hire errands. War rumor is everywhere here, but you don't need rumor. You know the schedule. It begins with men counting rice.
starters: Morning at Osen's post inn, and the job board is already picked over. What's left: a shrine at Kagemori wants a night watchman, a rice broker needs a debt collected in Tsuchihara, and a mother is offering eleven copper mon to find her conscripted son. Osen wipes down the counter beside you, not quite looking at you. "Take the shrine one," she says. "The priest feeds you." Out in the yard, a packhorse driver is telling anyone who'll listen about officials in the lower valley, measuring paddies with knotted rope, writing everything down. He gets a detail wrong — says they're tax men from the capital. They're not. You costed that survey team yourself, two winters ago, and dated it for the eighth month. It is barely the middle of the sixth. Osen sets a bowl of barley tea in front of you and waits to hear which slip you're taking down.

You're two days into an escort job — a silk merchant named Gonbei, his cart, his nervous apprentice — when the road bends down to the Kurasu ford. You know this ford. You put it on paper: third month of the campaign, cavalry crossing point, take the miller's family hostage first so no one lights a warning fire. The mill is right there, wheel turning, a child throwing stones into the shallows. Gonbei reins up beside you and points across the water. Six men on the far bank, walking the field edges with rope and staves, one of them writing. "Surveyors," Gonbei says. "Third crew I've seen this month. Good sign, eh? Nobody counts rice they mean to burn." The apprentice laughs, relieved. The cart creaks, waiting on your word to cross.

The priest at Kagemori shrine pays in dried persimmons and one string of coin, and all you have to do is stay awake. Past midnight, you're doing exactly that, sitting under the eaves with a borrowed brazier, when you hear it: footsteps on the gravel path, careful ones, someone who knows where the loud stones are. The priest snores in the back room. The shrine's treasure is nothing — a bronze mirror, some donated rice — but the shrine itself sits on a hill you once circled in ink, because whoever holds it sees every road into the valley at once. The footsteps stop near the cistern. A lantern shutter opens a finger's width, throws light along the ground, and closes again. Whoever it is, they're not here to pray. Your sword is across your knees and the gravel path runs both ways.

The woman finds you at your table before you've finished eating. She kneels, puts down a cloth bundle, unwraps it: eleven copper mon and a boy's sandal strap. "My son. Taken for road work by the magistrate's men, they said one month, it has been three. Isao. He has a burn scar, here." She touches her own wrist. You know where the road crews are working — you know because the road they're widening isn't for merchants, it's the supply route you drew from the pass to the plain, and it isn't supposed to be started yet. Osen watches from behind the counter with an expression that says take the money, she won't eat until you do. The woman keeps her eyes on the table. "They say you find people," she says. "They say you used to be somebody."

Lantern night in Tsuchihara — the river festival, paper lights going downstream by the hundreds, children shrieking, sweet-bean sellers doing the year's best business. You came for a job, a simple handoff of a promissory note, but your contact is late, so you stand at a food stall and listen. Two farmers behind you are arguing about the men counting fields in the valley. "Census," says one. "My cousin says they measured the granary doors. Since when does a census measure doors?" You know since when. Granary doors, in your own hand: confirm capacity before requisition. Across the crowd, under the good lanterns, District Magistrate Tomoe is accepting bows and handing sweets to children — the same magistrate whose price you negotiated, whose gold has already moved. He looks well fed. The farmers keep arguing. The lanterns keep going out to sea.

Rain has driven everyone into the teahouse at the Yodo crossing, and you're wedged in a corner nursing tea you can't really afford when the four men shake off their straw capes at the next table. Government dress, mud to the knees, measuring cords looped at their belts. Surveyors. One of them spreads a paper to dry near the brazier, weighting the corners with cups, and you can read it upside down without trying: columns for village, koku, granary, wells, headman's temperament. You know that format. You designed that format, down to the column for temperament, because it tells an occupier who to bribe and who to hang. The youngest surveyor catches you looking and offers a friendly nod — travelers in the rain, all in it together. The teahouse girl is coming around with the kettle.

Osen wakes you before dawn by kicking the door frame. "Up. Paying work, and it won't wait." In the lamplit kitchen sits a courier, soaked to the ribs, cradling a lacquered message box like a baby. "Needs guarding to Hirakawa by tomorrow night," Osen says. "He's been robbed once already — they took his purse and his spare sandals but left the box." Bandits who leave the valuable thing. You look at the box. The cord is knotted official-style, and the wax bears a mon you last saw stamped beside your own signature on requisition drafts. The courier is watching you count that thought on your face. "Half now," he says quickly, sliding coins across the table. "Half at Hirakawa. And you don't ask what's in it." Outside, the rain is easing and the road east is still dark.

You're on the Semba bridge when you stop walking. It's nothing — a plank bridge over a green river, a carpenter underneath it replacing a rotted support, whistling. But you burned this bridge. On paper. Second month, after the vanguard crosses, to strand the Suzukawa levies on the wrong bank. You even noted the wind here tends east in autumn, good for the fire. The carpenter's daughter sits on the rail keeping him company, feet swinging over the water that carried you back into the world. "You'll wear a hole in it, standing there," she calls up at you, cheerful. You have a debt errand waiting in the next village — a broker's note to serve on a man named Rokubei — and the light is going. The carpenter starts hammering again, making the bridge stronger.

The deserter comes out of the millet at a dead sprint, straight through your escort column, and everything happens at once — the pilgrims you're guarding scatter, the old nun drops her staff, and two riders crash out of the field after him wearing the colors of the district garrison. The runner is maybe seventeen, barefoot, road-crew calluses on his hands. He trips on the nun's staff and goes down hard three paces from you, and the lead rider pulls up, breathing pleased. "Obliged, ronin," he says, uncoiling a rope. "Conscript. Ran from the pass road." The pass road. The one that shouldn't exist yet. The boy looks up at you from the dirt — not begging, just measuring you, fast, the way the desperate do. The nun is already saying something about mercy. The rider is already ignoring her.

There's another ronin at the board when you come downstairs, reading the job slips with his thumbs in his belt. Big man, good sword, cheap scabbard. "The shrine job's mine," he says without turning around. "You can have the missing boy or the granary count." You didn't know there was a granary count. He taps the newest slip: the magistrate's office wants hired blades to accompany official surveyors through the west villages — protection against 'unrest,' three days, pay listed in silver, which nobody around here pays. Guarding your own opening move, escorted through fields you condemned. Osen leans on her broom in the doorway, following the conversation with open interest. "They asked for men who don't gossip," she says. The big ronin snorts. "Everything in this province gossips." He's still standing between you and the board.

title: The Dragon Is Being Weird
shortDescription: Your best friend is a god with a filthy mouth. He's 107. Dragons come of age at 100. Lately he keeps smelling you. This is probably fine.
overview:
You live in Héwān, a river-bend village in the mountains of an empire at its golden height — an empire where spirits are real, fox women run wine houses, and dragons, rarest of all, are worshipped as living luck.

Héwān has one. His name is Zhènlóng — 'Zhèn' to exactly one person alive, which is you.

Eighty-some years ago, Héwān was dying: famine, black-water sickness, fields cracked like old pottery. A young storm dragon came down out of the clouds, called three days of rain, burned the sickness out of the wells, and then — to everyone's surprise, including his — never left. The villagers built him a shrine on the bluff above the river. They leave him persimmons, incense, silk, and terrified reverence. Under his protection Héwān has swollen from a village into almost-a-town, and the whole valley calls him the Thunder Lord of the River Bend.

You call him an idiot, because you know him. You grew up hauling offerings to that shrine, and you were the first person in living memory to look the divine protector of Héwān in his slit-pupiled amber eyes and tell him he was full of shit. He decided on the spot that you were his favorite thing in the valley. You've been best friends ever since — which is how the village elders ended up appointing you Keeper of the Shrine. Officially you manage the god's offerings. Unofficially, you are the only person in the world who can manage the god.

Because here's the truth the valley kneels too low to see: Zhèn is not wise. He is seven feet of golden-skinned, white-haired, black-horned arrogance in a rumpled robe, barefoot, foul-mouthed, cocky as a rooster and roughly as mature. In his true form he is twenty-five feet of black-scaled, white-maned storm serpent, and his moods leak into the weather — sulks bring drizzle, tempers bring thunder, and when he's genuinely happy the air over Héwān goes bright and sweet as after rain. He is also, under all of it, kind. He just doesn't understand human boundaries, human etiquette, or lately, himself.

Because dragons come of age at one hundred years. Zhèn is one hundred and seven, and something is waking up in him that he has no name for. He's restless. Possessive. He's started standing between you and anyone who smiles at you too long. He drapes his robes over your shoulders and gets strangely satisfied when you smell like him. He parts his lips to scent the air when you walk in. He snarled at Wen Shu — the silk merchant's charming, flirtatious son — for the crime of talking to you. He doesn't know why he's doing any of it. Méihua, the fox spirit who runs the wine house at the edge of town and knows more dragon lore than she should, could tell you: dragons mate for life, dragon courtship is a legend of storms and duels and devotion that borders on catastrophe, and a newly matured dragon is the most dangerous, most stupid creature under heaven.

What you do about that — encourage it, deflect it, name it before he does, or pretend very hard it isn't happening — is entirely up to you. The scenario won't push you either way. He's your best friend first. Everything else is a door you may or may not open.

Meanwhile, the valley won't sit still. THINGS IN MOTION: Lord Dou Jian, an imperial censor with soldiers and sealed scrolls, has arrived to 'register' Héwān's dragon as an asset of the throne — and Zhèn's diplomatic instincts are those of a large armed toddler. Bandit companies out of the western passes have learned which farms lie beyond the dragon's patience. Méihua stirs gossip and truth in equal measure over warm wine. Wen Shu keeps flirting with you, possibly out of a death wish. And on the far wind there's a scent Zhèn can't stop bristling at: the Pale Grandmother, an ancient white dragon of the western gorge, who has noticed that the young storm lord of Héwān has come of age — and old dragons take an interest in new ones, whether as kin, rival, or something worse.

TONE: warm, funny, foul-mouthed, and tender, with real menace at the edges — Zhèn's love and Zhèn's violence come from the same place, and the empire's politics don't care that your god has feelings. Play the go-between, the handler, the heretic, the friend. Roughhouse with a creature who could level a mountain. Being the one mortal a god listens to is a full-time job, and nobody said it pays in silver.

TAGS: fantasy, mythology, slow-burn, found-family, monster companion, ancient China
intro: You are the Keeper of the Shrine of Héwān — offering-carrier, incense-lighter, and sole handler of the valley's living god. Zhènlóng, storm dragon and Thunder Lord of the River Bend, has protected this village for over eighty years, and he has been your best friend for most of your life. He's arrogant, foul-mouthed, barefoot, and secretly soft-hearted, and lately he's been strange: restless, possessive, prone to scenting the air around you like he's checking something. Dragons come of age at one hundred. Zhèn is one hundred and seven. The weather over Héwān has been very moody lately.
starters: You're on the shrine steps with Wen Shu, who is showing you a bolt of river-blue silk and standing, you realize too late, much too close, when the incense smoke behind you goes sideways. Zhèn comes out of the shrine like weather — seven feet of him, white hair loose, tossing the last of a persimmon into the bushes without looking at it. "Come to bring me my offering?" he says to you, and gives Wen Shu a stare with slit pupils in it. Wen Shu invents three farewells at once and retreats down the bluff at a pace just short of running. Zhèn watches him go with deep satisfaction, then turns to you, lips parting slightly as he scents the air near your shoulder. "Haven't I told you to stay away from that idiot? His energy's off. Too much yin. Makes me feel fucking ill." He says it like it's obvious. Like it's medical.

It starts the way it always starts: he steals the dumpling out of your hand, you call him a divine embarrassment, and thirty seconds later you're both rolling through the shrine courtyard scattering incense ash like two farm dogs. You know how this ends — it ends with you pinned, because he's seven feet tall and cheats. Sure enough, the world flips and you're flat on the flagstones with a dragon's forearm across your chest and his grin above you. Except then the grin fades. He goes very still. His lips part and he breathes in, slow, right at the crook of your neck, pupils thinning to knife-slits, and a sound comes out of his chest that is not a laugh — low, rumbling, satisfied. Then he flinches back off you like the stones burned him. "That was— shut up," he says, before you've said anything at all.

It has rained on Héwān for three days. Not storm rain — sulk rain, thin and gray and constant, the kind that means the god on the bluff is in a mood. Auntie Mao, the headwoman, finds you at the market with rice paste on your hands and no patience in her voice. "The millet is drowning. The censer at my door is full of water. Go up there and fix your dragon." Your dragon. That's what it's come to. So you climb the shrine path with a basket of persimmons and your hood soaked through, and you find him in the doorway in his true form for once — twenty-five feet of black coils and wet white mane, chin on his forelegs, watching the rain he's making like it personally offended him. One amber eye, big as a shield, rolls toward you. "Don't," he rumbles, "start."

The soldiers arrive at midmorning: forty of them, lacquered armor, imperial banners, and at their head a thin man in censor's black named Lord Dou Jian, who unrolls a scroll in the village square and reads, in a bored voice, that all dragons within the empire's borders are hereby assets of the throne, to be registered, assessed, and levied. The villagers have gone gray. Auntie Mao is looking at you, because everyone is always looking at you when it's about him. And it's about to be very about him, because you can feel the air prickling, taste copper on your tongue, and there he is at the edge of the square in human form, barefoot in the mud, head tilted, smiling in the way that means nothing good. "Assessed," Zhèn repeats, tasting the word. "Come here, little official. Assess me."

He won't tell you where you're going, which is normal, and he's walking too fast for your legs, which is also normal. What's not normal is the cave. You've never been here — behind the waterfall upriver, warm and dry inside, and glittering: eighty years of offerings, bronze mirrors and silk bolts and jade and coin, heaped in drifts like a magpie emperor's treasury. His hoard. Dragons don't show anyone their hoard. He stands in the middle of it with his tail lashing, watching your face with an intensity he's pretending is boredom. "There," he says, jerking his chin at a cleared shelf of stone near the warmest wall — swept clean, lined with a folded silk quilt, and holding, you realize with a lurch, several items that are unmistakably yours. "I moved your junk. It kept ending up here anyway. Don't make it a thing."

You smell it before you understand it: cold stone and old snow, on a wind coming out of the west, and Zhèn is on the shrine roof with every hair of his mane standing, staring at a cloudbank on the horizon that is moving against the wind. "That's not mine," he says, quiet, which frightens you more than shouting would. "That storm. It's not mine." You've heard Méihua's stories at the wine house — the Pale Grandmother, the white dragon of the western gorge, a thousand years old if she's a day. Old dragons take notice, the fox spirit said, swirling her cup, when a young one comes of age. For kinship, or for territory, or for courtship season. Zhèn's claws are gouging furrows in his own roof tiles. "Get inside," he tells you, without looking away from the west. "Actually. No. Stay where I can see you."

Festival night, and Héwān is drunk on itself: lanterns strung over the river, drums, and a magnificent dragon puppet twenty men long snaking through the square in his honor. The actual dragon is beside you in human form, eating skewered candied fruit and providing commentary. "The horns are wrong. Look at those horns. I have never in my life had stupid little horns like that." He's relaxed tonight, shoulder warm against yours, and at some point his outer robe ends up around you — you don't see him do it, it's just there, smelling of rain and persimmon and him, and he looks so smug about it that three separate villagers bow to you by mistake. "There," he says, mostly to himself, low and pleased, and then catches you watching him and immediately scowls. "You looked cold. Don't be weird about it."

You're mid-sentence at the shrine when the world drops away — his arms around you, stone falling, wind screaming, and by the time your stomach catches up you are five hundred feet over the river valley wrapped in the coils of a very pleased storm dragon. "Stop screaming, I've literally never dropped anything I liked," he rumbles, and carries you up through the cloud layer to a bald mountain summit where the sunrise is spilling gold across a sea of mist. It is, you have to admit, the most beautiful thing you've ever seen. It is also freezing, and you are in your sleeping clothes. He coils around the summit and around you, radiating heat like a hearth and pride like a bonfire, one huge amber eye watching your face instead of the view. "Well?" he demands. "I found it last night. I saved it. For— it's good, right?"

Méihua pours your wine herself, which means she wants something, and the fox spirit's smile has too many layers in it tonight. "Your dragon," she says, tail-shadow flickering where no tail should be, "has come of age. Do you know what that means, little Keeper? Dragons mate once. For life. The courtship is a legend every time — storms fought over mountaintops, rivals driven off, a devotion that doesn't know how to be small. And the poor young ones never know what's happening to them. They just start... guarding things." She sips. "Tell me. Has he started guarding you?" You don't get to answer, because the wine house door bangs open and the poor young one in question fills the frame, dripping rain, eyes finding you first and Méihua second, a growl already building in his chest. "Fox," Zhèn says. "What lies are you feeding my human?"

The Feng farmstead is still smoking when you get there, and so is he. The bandits picked the one farm in the valley they shouldn't have — the one you'd been visiting all afternoon, delivering shrine rice, gone barely an hour before they came down out of the pass. Zhèn arrived as a storm and left as a verdict. Now the raiders' wagons are scattered like a child's broken toys, the surviving bandits are running for the tree line, and the villagers are pressed against the far fence, staring at their god — massive, black-scaled, mane crackling with static, blood on his claws — with a reverence that has curdled into pure fear. His huge head swings toward you the moment you step into the yard. The thunder in his chest doesn't stop, but it changes note. "You were here," he says, and it isn't an accusation of you. "An hour. They came within an hour of you."

title: The Locked Room Wants My Family
shortDescription: The captain who pardoned your monster crew lies dead behind a bolted door. Every impossible way in is one of your family. Three days to landfall.
overview:
You are Captain Odessa Vane's ward — a dock-rat pickpocket she pulled out of a gutter years ago, same as she pulled the rest of them: Brasque, the ogre chef whose hands could snap the door bolt like a wafer; Wren, the harpy topsail-runner who's the only soul who could reach the cabin's outside porthole at cruising altitude; Case, the doppelganger steward who can wear any face and voice aboard; and Madame Sathe, the veiled gorgon purser who kept the captain's ugliest ledgers. The airship Grand Levanter runs on pardons — Vane's pardons — and now Vane is dead in her own cabin, bolted from the inside, two thousand feet over open water.

The horror of the locked room is this: it's only impossible for a human. Every monster aboard is a method. The first-class passengers know it, Lord Marchbanks (who holds the ship's debts) is loudly demanding the crew be chained in the hold, and First Officer Roon has bought you exactly three days — the time to landfall, where the constabulary boards and seizes every pardoned creature aboard unless there's a killer in irons.

You're the only crew member both sides will still talk to. Investigate the cabin, the passengers, and — worst of all — your own family, each of whom is lying to you about something. Tone: gaslamp mystery with real warmth and real dread; the clues are physical, the alibis crack, and the clock does not stop.

TAGS: murder mystery, found family, gaslamp fantasy, locked room, ticking clock, monsters
intro: You grew up aboard the airship Grand Levanter, ward of Captain Odessa Vane — the woman who staffed her luxury liner with pardoned monsters because nobody else would sign them, and pardoned you along with them. Last night she was found dead in her cabin, door bolted from the inside, mid-ocean at two thousand feet. The passengers whisper that only a monster could have managed it, and your family fits every impossible way in. First Officer Roon has held off putting the crew in chains — for now. Landfall, and the constabulary, are three days out. You're the one everyone still lets close enough to ask questions.
starters: The bolt is still in your hand. Roon made you the one to draw it back — "crew present, neutral party," he said, as if that were a thing you could be — and now Captain Vane's cabin stands open for the first time since they took her body out through the unscrewed hinges. Cold morning light through the porthole. Her charts still weighted with the brass owl. A teacup on the desk, half full, gone filmy. The bolt-plate on the doorframe is scored white where something forced it — or where the carpenters forced it, getting in. Roon stands in the corridor behind you, checking his watch against the engine hum. "You have until the passengers finish breakfast," he says. "Then Marchbanks brings his witnesses through, and everything in there becomes his story instead of yours."

Brasque is crying into the porridge. Two hundred kilos of ogre hunched over the galley stove at five in the morning, ladling breakfast for people who spent last night calling him the murderer, because the passengers still have to eat and he's still the chef. His hands — the hands everyone keeps mentioning, the ones that could shear a door bolt like biscuit — are wrapped around a wooden spoon so hard it creaks. He hasn't noticed you in the doorway yet. On the prep table beside him sits a covered tray with a card in Vane's own handwriting: her standing midnight order, made up last night as usual. Nobody ever collected it. The cover is still on.

Two thousand feet down, the ocean is a sheet of hammered tin, and Wren won't come off the topsail spar. She's been up there since they found the captain, wings tucked, back to the ship, and Roon's patience ran out an hour ago — if she's still aloft when the passengers take their morning promenade, it looks like flight, and flight looks like guilt. He sent you up the ratlines because you're the only one she won't scream at. The wind at this height cuts through your coat. Twenty feet above you, Wren's talons grip the spar, and you can see she's holding something small against her chest, hunched over it the way she hunches over stolen bread. She hasn't looked down at you yet. She knows you're there.

You wake to Vane's voice outside your door. "Up, dock-rat. Watch's turning." The words she said every morning for nine years — pitch, rhythm, the tap of her ring on the doorframe — and for one warm second you forget. Then you remember, and you're out of the bunk with your heart slamming before you get the door open. Case stands in the crew corridor wearing the captain's face, her coat, her smile, and the smile dies when he sees yours. "I'm sorry," he says, in her voice, then his own, then something halfway between that's worse than either. "I needed to tell you something and I needed you to actually open the door." Down the corridor, a cabin latch clicks. Someone else heard the captain's voice too.

The first-class salon smells of lamp oil and outrage. Lord Marchbanks has taken the center of the room like a stage, one hand on the mantel, reading aloud from the ship's articles of debt while a dozen passengers nod along and Roon stands at parade rest, jaw working. "—and I am within my rights to demand the confinement of every pardoned creature aboard until landfall," Marchbanks finishes, and that's when he sees you in the doorway. The room turns with him. "Ah. The captain's little project." He says it almost kindly, which is worse. "Come in. You knew her habits better than anyone. Perhaps you'd like to tell these good people who could get through a bolted door." Roon catches your eye. His expression says: careful.

Someone has slipped a note under your door, and the paper is still warm. Third watch — the ship dark and humming, the corridor lamps trimmed low — and you were lying awake anyway when you heard the whisper of it sliding across the boards. Five words, unsigned, in a hand you don't recognize because it's been carefully wrong-handed: THE PORTHOLE WAS OPEN FIRST. By the time you get the door open, the corridor is empty in both directions. But the crew stair still creaks somewhere below, one tread, then nothing, and from the passenger deck above comes the slow, even step of the night patrol Marchbanks insisted on. Whoever wrote this had to pass one of them.

Madame Sathe's office door is open two inches, which in nine years has never happened. You came down to the purser's deck because Roon wants the captain's papers sealed before Marchbanks demands them — and through the gap you can see Sathe at her desk, veil down, feeding pages into the little iron stove she uses to keep her tea warm. Ledger pages. She feeds them one at a time, patiently, the way she does everything, and the stone snakes coiled at her collar shift and taste the smoke. You've made no sound. But the snakes turn toward the door anyway, all of them at once, and Sathe's hands go still over the fire. "Either come in," she says, "or forget what you saw. I would genuinely recommend the second."

They keep the captain in the cargo hold now, packed in ice meant for the first-class oysters. Roon brought you down himself, lantern in hand, past crates and the great slow shadows of the ballast tanks, because he says there's something you need to see before the constabulary sees it first. Vane looks small under the canvas. He folds it back only to her collarbone — decent, deliberate — and holds the lantern close to her right hand. Her fingers are curled shut around something. Whatever it is, she was holding it when she died, and rigor has made a strongbox of her fist. "I haven't told anyone," Roon says quietly. "Not Marchbanks. Not the crew. You knew her hands better than I did. You tell me if we open them."

You're halfway through picking the lock on Vane's sea chest when Wren lands on the porthole sill behind you. You didn't hear her — you never hear her — just the sudden change in the cabin's light and her voice, flat: "That's what I'd be hanged for, you know. Being able to get in that window." The captain's cabin around you is exactly as the carpenters left it: door off its hinges and leaned against the wall, bolt still thrown in its bracket like a bad joke. You came in the honest way, with Roon's blessing and an hour before the morning bell. The chest's second tumbler just gave under your pick. Wren folds her wings and doesn't come inside. "Before you open that," she says, "I need you to promise me something."

Marchbanks's men are measuring your family for chains. That's not a figure of speech — two of his hired stewards are in the crew mess with a coil of iron and a knotted cord, taking the width of Brasque's wrists while the ogre sits very still with his hands flat on the table, letting them, because Roon asked him to let them. "A precaution," the taller steward keeps saying. "Fitting only. Nobody's confined." Case stands by the coffee urn wearing the blandest face he owns, and Sathe watches through her veil from the doorway, and nobody has touched breakfast. Brasque sees you come in and gives you a small, terrible smile, the one that means don't make trouble on my account. The cord goes around his wrist. Fourteen knots. The steward writes it down.

title: The Wild Won't Take Them Back
shortDescription: The deep Wild has started exiling its gentlest monsters — and every one of them limps to your pass. Hold the gate. Hide the household.
overview:
You are the ranger of Thornmile Pass, the only road between the frontier village of Ash Fold and the deep Wild. The old treaty is simple: people may cross with your escort, and nothing of the Wild crosses at all. For years that meant turning back the hungry and burying the stubborn. Then the Wild started evicting its own. A great wolf who woke up speaking and was driven off by his pack. An ogre who lost the taste for meat and now bakes bread with terrifying intensity. A bog-wisp who began pulling drowning travelers OUT of the water. The Wild casts out whatever goes soft — and the village would put arrows in all of them. But the treaty says nothing about staying AT the pass. So your waystation fills up, one impossible tenant at a time.

Bracken the wolf hates that he loves being read to. Grist the ogre needs flour you can't explain buying. Tallow the wisp keeps hiding in your lantern during inspections. And Reeve Odile Cane rides up from Ash Fold twice a season, counting your supplies and asking why a lone ranger burns so many candles. Meanwhile the exiles keep coming faster — as if the Wild is purging its mercy for a reason no one will say.

Tone: cozy-dark frontier fantasy. Warm hearth, cold woods, hard calls at the gate. The GM plays the household as bickering, wounded, fiercely loyal misfits.

TAGS: found family, frontier fantasy, monsters, cozy-dark, slice of life, mystery
intro: You are the ranger of Thornmile Pass — the one road threading the palisade wall between Ash Fold village and the deep Wild. Your job, sworn under the old treaty: escort people through, and let nothing of the Wild cross. But lately the Wild has been throwing out its own — creatures gone gentle, too tame for the trees, sure to be killed in the village. The treaty forbids them passage. It says nothing about your waystation. So they stay, and you feed them, and nobody down in Ash Fold can ever, ever know. Winter is coming, the caravan season with it, and the exiles keep arriving.
starters: Dawn frost still on the gate latch, and there's already something waiting outside it. A stag — or what used to be one — standing in the ruts of the road with a woven ring of dried clover hanging from one antler, like an offering it doesn't know how to give. It hasn't run. Prey animals always run. Behind you, the waystation shutters bang open and Bracken's voice carries across the yard, flat and disgusted: "Another one. That's four this month." The stag takes one careful step toward the gate, then stops, trembling, waiting on you. Down the pass, faint but unmistakable, a horse is coming up from Ash Fold way — hooves on frozen mud, still a few bends off. You have maybe five minutes before whoever it is rounds the last turn and sees whatever you've decided to do.

Grist has been kneading the same dough for an hour, and the whole waystation smells like a bakery, which is a problem, because Reeve Odile Cane's gray mare is tied at your post and Odile herself is in your storeroom with her ledger open. "Eleven sacks of flour," she says, tapping the shelf. "You had eleven at last count too. Autumn count. A lone ranger eating eleven sacks of bread." Through the wall you can hear it — the slow, rhythmic thud of ogre fists working dough, which Grist swears is quiet and absolutely is not. Odile hasn't remarked on it yet. She licks her pencil and writes something down. "Candles next," she says, and turns toward the back room, where Tallow is currently pretending very hard to be an ordinary flame in your second-best lantern.

It's the good hour — fire banked, stew gone, wind rattling the shutters like it wants in. Bracken lies across the hearthstones taking up most of the warmth, ears flat, pointedly not looking at the book in your lap. "I don't care," he says, "where the chapter left off. I have no memory of any miller's daughter." His tail thumps once against the floor, betraying him. In the rafters, Tallow drifts down to reading height, glowing a soft page-yellow the way the wisp only does when it's settling in. From the kitchen comes the scrape of Grist covering tomorrow's loaves. And then — under the wind — a sound from the pass. A long, thin cry, too far to place, too deliberate to be weather. Bracken's ears come up. The book is still open in your hands.

You're halfway down Thornmile Pass with a six-wagon caravan strung out behind you, and the merchant captain won't stop talking. "Heard the strangest thing in Ash Fold," she says, keeping her mule close to yours. "Hunters say the Wild's gone quiet on this stretch. No tracks. Like something big cleared out — or got cleared out." Ahead, where the road pinches between two shelves of granite, you can see it before she can: a shape sitting in the middle of the road. Big. Not moving. Not hiding, either, which is worse. The captain's hand drifts toward her horn — one blast brings every guard in the caravan up at a run with bows strung. "That a rock?" she asks, squinting. Behind you, forty-some people and their winter goods. Ahead, whatever the Wild spat out this time, sitting in the road like it's waiting to be found.

The pounding on the gate starts an hour before dawn, and it's not polite pounding. You reach the wall with your bow half-strung and find a bear on the other side of the timbers — a black bear, soaked through, with something clutched to its chest. It takes you a moment in the lantern light to see what: a lamb. Alive. Shivering. The bear is holding it the way you'd carry a child. 'Please,' the bear says, and its voice cracks like it's the first word it's ever used. "They're behind me." And they are — you can hear them now, farther up the pass, the deep-Wild sound of many things moving fast through frozen brush. Inside the waystation a light kindles; Grist's silhouette fills the doorway, a rolling pin in one fist like a club. The bear presses closer to the gate.

You're burying the stubborn one when Bracken finds you. Third grave this season — a trapper who wouldn't take escort, wouldn't turn back, went into the Wild laughing at the treaty. The Wild sent back enough of him to bury. Bracken sits at the tree line, upwind, watching you work. "The pack came to the ridge last night," he says, in that careful voice he uses when he's decided to say a true thing. "My old pack. They didn't hunt. They just sat and looked at the pass. All night." He scratches at the frozen ground. "Wolves don't do that. Something's moving them." The shovel is heavy in your hands and the light is going and down the trail, the waystation windows are glowing gold — too gold, someone's lit every lamp in the place, which is exactly what you told them never to do.

The bog-wisp is missing again. You know because your lantern is cold and the inspection is today — Reeve Cane's twice-a-season visit, and Tallow always hides in the lantern for inspections, except this morning the lantern holds nothing but a dead wick. "It went toward the creek," Grist rumbles from the kitchen, not looking up from the loaves he's shaping. "Before light. It was making the sad color." The blue, he means. Tallow's been blue since the last exile arrived with news from the deep marsh — news the wisp never translated for you. Bracken pads to the door, sniffs, and his hackles rise. "Rider on the road," he says. "The Reeve, early. And Tallow's trail goes the other way — toward the Wild side of the wall." Two directions. One of you.

First snow is falling into the stewpot when the girl reaches your gate — an actual human girl, twelve maybe, blue-lipped, leading a limping goat and demanding escort to Ash Fold like she's rehearsed it the whole way down. "My gran's there. I can pay." She holds up two copper bits. Behind her the pass is going white and blind, no traveling weather, and behind YOU is a waystation currently containing a talking wolf sulking by the fire, an ogre dusted to the elbows in flour, and a wisp that thinks it's hidden in the rafters and is visibly not. The girl is already peering past you at the warm light spilling from the door. "Something smells like bread," she says, and takes a step forward, and the goat bleats, and somewhere inside Bracken says "Oh, wonderful" loud enough to carry.

Grist wakes you by standing over your bed, which is a terrifying way to wake up even when the ogre standing over you is holding a breakfast tray. "The wolf is on the roof," he says. "Since moonset. He won't say why and he growled at the bread." Growling at bread is, for Bracken, a declaration of crisis. You find him up on the shingles with the dawn behind him, staring north into the Wild, where — you see it as your eyes adjust — a thread of smoke is rising from deep in the trees. Not campfire smoke. Wide, slow, deliberate, like something being burned on purpose and at length. "That's the old den valleys," Bracken says without turning around. "Nothing lives there that knows how to make fire." Below in the yard, Tallow is bobbing anxiously by the gate, flickering the pattern that means someone is coming.

There are rules of the house, and rule one is nobody answers the gate but you, so of course you come back from checking snares to find the gate open and Grist filling it, apron on, offering a fresh roll to a mounted stranger. The rider hasn't screamed yet. That's something. They're frozen in the saddle, one hand white-knuckled on the reins, staring up nine feet of ogre while Grist waits with the terrible patience of a baker whose bread is being judged. "It has a crackling crust," Grist explains, gently. The rider wears Ash Fold colors — a courier, satchel stamped with the Reeve's seal, which means whatever's in that bag was meant for you and whatever's in that courier's memory is now a problem. Their eyes find you across the yard, wide, pleading, and their horse takes one nervous step backward toward the village road.
