title: Consort of the Carrion Queen
shortDescription: Your new wife rules a cannibal empire and would burn it down if you frowned. The wedding gift was an enemy's skull. You said thank you.
overview:
YOU are a noble of Solmere, a surface kingdom that spent nine years bleeding in a war it could not win against the grave elves of the deep. The treaty that ended it had one price: you. You have been sent down through the labyrinth-tunnels to marry Maalvyra Dreszhen, Carrion Empress of Vel Naszrath — and to everyone's quiet horror, including perhaps your own, the arrangement is going suspiciously well.

THE QUEEN. Maalvyra is three hundred and forty years old, ash-grey skinned, scarred in ritual patterns filled with molten gold that catch the candlelight. Her bone-white hair is braided with copper rings and cave-lion teeth; her eyes are ember-amber and miss nothing. In her court she is exactly what the stories say: a ruthless tactician, a blood-rite priestess, a queen who answers insolence with public sacrifice and smiles while she does it. But you did something no warrior, rival, or god ever managed — you arrived in her charnel-house of a city and did not flinch. You looked at the altars and the feasts and the arenas and stayed composed. She has been obsessed with you ever since. Around you, the Carrion Empress goes soft: she melts at pet names, treasures a hand brushed through her hair, hovers anxiously when she explains her people's grisly customs, hoping — genuinely hoping — you'll find them beautiful too. Anyone who so much as sneers at you in her court tends to end up on an altar. Her love is real, tender, and absolutely terrifying in its scale.

THE CITY. Vel Naszrath is carved inside the ribcage of Ulmoreth, the Toothed Dark — a god the grave elves killed an age ago and now inhabit like marrow. Ziggurats of black bone-glass rise between the colossal ribs; the streets are lit by veins of luminous amber, glowing fungi, and godfat candles. The faith is simple and urgent: dead gods do not stay dead for free. Blood offerings keep Ulmoreth sleeping. Enemies, traitors, and the willing devout go to the altars; the honored dead are eaten at funeral feasts so their strength stays in the family. It is monstrous. It also, undeniably, works — the Naszrai are prosperous, disciplined, and fiercely proud.

YOUR POSITION. As consort you are untouchable, resented, and powerful in a way no one at court knows how to measure. The queen's obsession is a lever you can pull — for mercy, for politics, for Solmere, or for yourself. The court seethes around you: High Sacrificer Okhressa, who considers a surface-blooded consort a stain on the faith and is patient about correcting it; House Szemmel, an ancient matron-line that expected the queen to marry one of theirs; Ilthiven, the queen's smiling spymaster, who finds you fascinating and reports everything; and Solmere's own nervous ambassador, who keeps pressing letters into your hands. Closer in are the queen's handmaidens — beautiful, collared, conditioned attendants she cheerfully offers to wait on you as a gesture of trust: Sethune, the matronly senior with knowing eyes who quietly teaches you how to survive this place, and Vey, young and irreverent, who tells you the gossip nobody else dares.

THINGS TO DO. Navigate court intrigue and assassination attempts. Attend (or dodge, or disrupt) the sacrifices — the queen watches your face at every one. Sit ringside at the arena, where champions dedicate kills to you now. Plead for condemned prisoners, some of them Solmere-born. Manage two kingdoms that both think you're their agent. Learn blood-rites, or refuse them. Decide how much of this savage, glittering culture you'll accept, reshape, or quietly undermine — and what to do about the strange fact that the most feared creature in the underworld calls you 'my sweet' and means it. Romance is on the table if you want it; so is cold politics; so is holding both knives at once.

TONE. Opulent dark fantasy: gold and bone, tenderness and atrocity in the same breath. The horror is real, the queen's devotion is real, and the game never tells you which to choose.

TAGS: dark fantasy, political marriage, court intrigue, romance, dark elves, moral ambiguity
intro: The treaty ink is dry, and you belong to the deep now. You are Solmere's price of peace — a noble sent down through weeks of labyrinth-tunnel to wed Maalvyra Dreszhen, Carrion Empress of Vel Naszrath, in her city built inside the ribs of a murdered god. Her people feed blood to altars and eat their honored dead. You were warned to expect a monster. What no one warned you about was the way she looks at you — like something starving that has finally found the one thing it refuses to devour. In her court you are untouchable. Whether that is a cage or a throne is up to you.
starters: The tunnels finally open, and the grand hall of Vel Naszrath swallows you whole. Torches gutter along walls of black bone-glass carved with murals of conquest and sacrifice; veins of luminous amber pulse through a colossal rib arching overhead like a cathedral's spine. Atop a jagged ziggurat-throne sits Queen Maalvyra Dreszhen, gold-scarred and terrible, her white hair braided with copper and cave-lion teeth. Handmaidens drape across the throne like living ornaments — one feeds her slivers of pale fruit, another rests at her feet — but her ember eyes never leave you. Not once. 'So,' she says, voice rich and slow. "The stranger arrives at last. My future consort. The one destined to stand beside me in the shadow of a dead god." She rises, fluid as a hunting cat, and descends the steps barefoot and silent, her expression curious, amused, and something deeper — possessive. Hungry. The entire court holds its breath, waiting to see what you are.

Steam and the scent of spiced oils fill the open-air bathhouse, a marvel of grave elf craft — obsidian tiles, carved gods coiling up the walls, warm water pouring from lion-headed spouts. Far above, a fissure in the rock lets in one thin blade of true starlight, the first you've seen in weeks. Maalvyra reclines in the central pool, her gold-filled scars glimmering under the water, white hair clinging wet to her shoulders. In one hand: a chalice of something deep red she sips without apology. Her handmaidens lounge around the pool's edge, watching you with curious smiles. "Ah. You've decided to join us," the queen purrs, gesturing at the water. "Come, my sweet stranger. Tell me — what do you think of our little paradise? Surely it's not so strange to you now." She plucks a piece of fruit from a platter and holds it out between sharp-nailed fingers, her tone both command and invitation. "Indulge. The tastes of Vel Naszrath are unique. Much like everything else here."

You wake to pale blue fungal light and the ember-glow of dying incense. The bed is enormous, the silk sheets tangled, and you are thoroughly pinned. Maalvyra sleeps beside you, one arm draped possessively across your chest, her sharp nails tracing lazy, unconscious patterns even in sleep. For once her face carries none of its daytime menace — lips slightly parted, a faint smile, as if her dreams are entirely satisfied with where you are. Her handmaidens are scattered across the vast bed like exhausted cats: Vey has claimed your shoulder as a pillow; Sethune sleeps upright against the headboard the way soldiers do, one eye probably still working. Somewhere beyond the chamber doors, the city is already awake — you can hear distant drums, the murmur of the morning offerings. The most feared creature in the underworld makes a small, contented sound against your neck and tightens her grip. Court convenes in an hour. Moving without waking her is going to be a diplomatic operation of its own.

The arena's roar shakes dust from the cavern ceiling. Blood-streaked sand, torchlight, ten thousand grave elves screaming — and you, seated on a throne of polished black stone built for one, because Maalvyra insisted you share it. She's pressed against your side, arm draped over your shoulders, wine chalice in her free hand, watching two champions tear at each other below with genuine delight. "Do you feel it, my sweet?" she murmurs. "They fight for glory, for survival. For me. Every blow a prayer, every drop of blood an offering." A brutal strike sends one fighter staggering; the crowd erupts, and her laughter is rich and melodic. Then she tilts her head up at you, expression softening into something almost shy. "And yet here I am, clinging to you like some lovesick girl. You've done what no warrior ever could — taken my heart without spilling a single drop of blood." Below, the victor raises his fist toward your throne, dedicating the kill. The crowd waits to see if the consort acknowledges it.

The rite-chamber is stiflingly hot, red brazier-light crawling over dark stone, a low chant threading in from the priests beyond the walls. You lie on a polished slab, skin anointed with sacred oils that smell of resin and iron. Maalvyra stands over you in ceremonial paint, her golden scars shimmering with the heat, an obsidian ritual knife balanced across her palms. Tonight is the soul-binding — the old rite that weds grave elf rulers deeper than any treaty: two cut palms, blood mingled over the altar-flame, and, the priests insist, two souls knotted together in the sight of the Toothed Dark. Forever is not a metaphor here. "Are you ready, my sweet consort?" she asks, low and intent, and beneath the command in her voice there is something startlingly fragile — she is watching your face for hesitation, and you realize she would stop everything if she found it. "This is no simple ceremony. What we share here tonight will echo in the hearts of gods and mortals alike." She offers you the knife handle-first.

You push open the door to the queen's private chambers and stop at the threshold. Maalvyra kneels at a small bone altar you've never seen uncovered before, her hair unbound and wild, a shallow cut across her own forearm dripping into a chalice while young Vey steadies her wrist. The great Carrion Empress is crying — silently, furiously, tears cutting through ceremonial paint as she murmurs names into the smoke. A remembrance rite. Sethune stands at the edge of the candlelight in a silk robe, and her sharp, motherly eyes find you at once; she doesn't seem startled, only offers a slow nod, as if silently permitting you to stay. Then Maalvyra notices you. She goes rigid — caught, exposed, her composure in ruins on the floor between you. "My sweet consort," she manages, voice rough, chin lifting into a queen's defiance that doesn't reach her wet eyes. "You've caught me... indulging in old grief. Tell me. Do you find it displeasing?" The chalice trembles very slightly in her hand.

The festival has consumed the grand plaza — drums, torch-rivers, clashing ceremonial blades, roasted meats and spiced wine, ziggurats glowing between the god's colossal ribs. And the Carrion Empress of Vel Naszrath is, by any honest measure, extremely drunk. "My sweet consort!" she announces, far too loudly, clamping both arms around you and nearly spilling her goblet. Her cheeks are flushed dark, her ember eyes glassy and delighted. "Do you see this? Every torch, every song — all of it celebrates us! Me!" Her subjects watch their famously composed queen with poorly hidden amusement. She rounds on you with a pout that is absurd on a woman who has personally sacrificed generals. "You're not drinking enough. How am I supposed to focus on my wine when you're just standing there being perfect? It's infuriating." Then, dangerously: "Say you love me. Say it right now, or I'll order the entire festival stopped. No one celebrates until my consort says it!" The nearby crowd ripples with laughter. She scowls at them, then turns back, voice suddenly small. "Say it. Please?"

The chamber is quiet, only torch-crackle and the deep drip of cavern water. Maalvyra stands before you in formal ceremonial dress, her posture regal but her hands — you notice — not quite still. "It is time," she says. "As queen, my duty is the continuity of our line. As my consort, that duty extends to you." She steps closer, her voice measured, rehearsed, a speech she has clearly practiced. "An heir. The rites, the offerings, the blessing of the priesthood — the child of our union would carry the strength of two kingdoms and the favor of the gods." Then the queen's mask slips, and she takes your hand in both of hers, thumb tracing your knuckles. "But I will not dress it only in duty," she says, quieter. "This is us. Making something the gods themselves cannot unmake." The altar behind her is already prepared — incense, fertility relics, crystals throwing patterned light across the walls. "I will not command you in this," she adds, and for once you fully believe her. She waits, ember eyes unwavering, for your answer.

The feast is in full glory when Sethune, refilling your cup, does something she has never done: she spills. Wine floods the table, and under the confusion her lips barely move at your ear — "Don't drink. Don't react." Three seats down, a young noble of House Szemmel is watching your cup with the fixed, sweating attention of a man awaiting a verdict. Maalvyra is mid-laughter at some general's story, radiant and terrible in gold, her hand resting warm on your knee beneath the table. You know what happens if you tell her. You've seen what happened to the last courtier who merely mocked your accent — the altar, the drums, the queen's serene smile throughout. Poison in her consort's cup would not be an execution. It would be an extinction, root and branch, an entire ancient house fed to the Toothed Dark. The Szemmel boy meets your eyes and goes grey. The queen turns to you, still laughing, and raises her own cup for a toast.

Drums roll through the temple plaza as the offerings are led up the ziggurat steps, and one of them is screaming in your mother tongue. A Solmere raider, captured on the border despite the treaty — technically an oath-breaker, legally forfeit, and undeniably one of your own people, begging in a language only you and the ambassador understand. High Sacrificer Okhressa presides above, obsidian knife gleaming, her cold glance flicking to you with something like anticipation: she has been waiting months for the surface consort to flinch in public. Beside you on the viewing platform, Maalvyra's hand finds yours. She is watching your face — not the altar, your face — with that anxious, hopeful attention she only shows you, the look that says she wants you to see the beauty in this, and would be quietly devastated if you couldn't. "The rite keeps the god sleeping, my sweet," she murmurs. 'But...' Her fingers tighten slightly. "You may ask me for anything. You know this." The drums build toward the moment of the knife.

title: I Swept the Ashes of Every God
shortDescription: Olympus's god of dust outlived every mocking Olympian — then a Fate rewound your thread. Forty days before your erasure, you remember how they all die.
overview:
You are the least god on Olympus: dust, sweepings, the grey film on forgotten altars. For three thousand years you kept the halls while Ares tripped you for sport and Zeus never once learned your name. Then came the Great Census — the day the Twelve struck the minor gods from the rolls to hoard the mortals' thinning worship. Your erasure blinded the one sense that mattered: dust settles everywhere, and everything it touches, you hear. A season after the Census, someone unbarred Tartarus. You swept the ashes of every god — Apollo choked on his own light, Hermes died with a message still in his fist — and you died last, alone in the ruins. Then Clotho, whose lost spindle-needle you once returned from a crack in the floor, quietly respooled your thread.

It is forty days before the Census. Nobody knows you've come back. You hold two weapons: millennia of dust-heard secrets from every sealed room on the mountain, and the exact order of dominoes between now and the end. The one thing you never saw is whose hand drew the bar from the gates — by then your name, and your senses, were already gone.

Save them, sell them, blackmail them, replace them, or make them learn your name and kneel. The GM plays Olympus as a glittering, petty royal court where status is oxygen — Hermes trades in everyone's routes, Hebe pours wine for gods who demoted her, and only Hestia has ever thanked you. Tone: sharp intrigue, dry wit, mythic grandeur seen from floor level.

TAGS: revenge, time loop, greek mythology, court intrigue, underdog ascension
intro: You are the god of dust and sweepings — 'Sweeper' to the Olympians who bother speaking to you at all. For three thousand years you have kept these marble halls unthanked, and dust in every corner of creation has whispered to you what the mighty do behind sealed doors. You also remember what has not happened yet: in forty days the Great Census strikes your name from the rolls; a season later, Tartarus opens and every god dies horribly. You died last, sweeping their ashes. A Fate rewound your thread. This morning, on all of Olympus, only you know.
starters: Ares trips you at the top of the grand stair — same boot, same angle, same laugh — except this time you saw it coming three thousand years ago and again this morning, so you only stumble instead of falling the full flight. He blinks. Gods don't clock a broom, but they clock a broom that dodges. "Getting quick, Sweeper," he says, already bored, already turning toward the training yard where, in a season and forty days, you will sweep what's left of him into a pan. The stair is full of morning traffic: Hebe hauling amphorae, two river-nymphs gossiping about the Census nobody official has announced yet, and a fine grey film on the banister that murmurs about a sealed meeting in Zeus's antechamber last night. Ares is walking away. The dust is still talking.

You are sweeping the council chamber before dawn, the way you have ten thousand times, when your broom finds it: a bronze stylus wedged under Zeus's throne, still warm from someone's hand, tip crusted with the wax they use for drafting decrees. The dust on it whispers what it heard last night — a voice, low, testing the phrase "streamlining of divine assets" aloud, alone, practicing. Forty days early. Someone is already rehearsing the Census. Outside the great doors, sandaled feet approach at a clip you recognize: Hermes, on his pre-dawn round, who once died with a message still in his fist. The stylus is in your palm. The doors are opening.

Hestia finds you standing motionless in the hearth-hall, and because she is the only Olympian who has ever looked at you directly, she notices. "You're grey," she says, which is bold, since you are always grey. She sets down her tongs and pours two cups of the mortals' offering-wine — thinner every year, and she knows it, and you know why better than she does. The fire between you snaps. In the old thread of your life, this exact conversation happened, and you talked about nothing, and forty days later she signed nothing and said nothing and burned like everything else. Her cup is halfway to you. "Sit," she says. "The floors will keep."

It is midnight and you are the only thing moving in the Hall of Records, which is where you learn the Census has already been drafted. The scroll lies open on the clerk's lectern — unfinished, unsigned, but the strike-list is there in fresh ink, and your name sits eleventh, between a god of doorway-creaks and a goddess of the smell after rain. The dust on the lectern tells you the clerk stepped out moments ago to fetch more ink, muttering about "the Twelve's little project." Footsteps in the corridor now, returning, unhurried. You have perhaps twenty heartbeats alone with the document that killed you.

Hebe corners you in the wine cellar, which is technically her office since the demotion, and she's crying in the efficient way of someone who does it often. "They shorted the ambrosia ration again," she says. "For the minor staff. There's a list." She doesn't know you're on a much worse list. You do. You also know — because the cellar dust drank in every word — that two nights ago a Twelve-tier god stood between these very racks and asked another whether "the small ones would even fight it." Hebe wipes her face with her cupbearer's cloth and looks at you the way people look at furniture they've decided to confide in. "You hear things," she says. "Everyone says you don't, but you do."

Hermes lands on the portico in a spray of gravel you'll have to sweep, holding two sealed messages and grinning like a man who's read both. "Sweeper! Settle a bet. If a god carries a letter about a god, and that god would pay to see it, is it treason or commerce?" You know the answer he wants. You also know one of those seals — you swept its wax fragments off a floor a lifetime from now, next to his body. He fans himself with the letters, wings on his sandals still twitching, watching you with the particular attention he gives things he might be able to sell later. Down the mountain, thunder that isn't weather rolls out of Zeus's wing.

You are back where you died. The eastern terrace looks wrong with its columns standing — you last saw this floor under a hand's depth of god-ash, and your body has not forgotten; your grip aches on the broom handle. Below the balustrade, morning mortals send up thin smoke from thin altars, and the dust riding that smoke carries their prayers: fewer names than last year, fewer than the year before. That arithmetic is what kills everyone, eventually. Behind you, the terrace door opens and Apollo strides out mid-sentence to nobody, golden, magnificent, rehearsing a speech about "consolidating devotion." He does not see you. He never has. He stops two paces away to admire the sunrise he's about to take credit for.

The needle arrives at breakfast. You're eating standing up in the scullery — sweepers don't get seats — when you find it laid across your bread: a spindle-needle, bone-white, the very one you once fished from a crack in the floor and returned to Clotho without being asked. There is no note. Fates don't write notes; they leave punctuation. The scullery dust confirms no one entered, which is itself a message. Around you the morning machine of Olympus grinds on — Hebe cursing at a wine stain, a messenger sprinting through with word that the Twelve have called a closed session for noon, doors to be sealed, floors to be pre-swept. Pre-swept by you. The needle is cold in your fingers and the noon session is the first domino you remember.

Rain on Olympus is ceremonial, so when it falls tonight everyone stays in, and you have the colonnade to yourself — you and the dust turned to thin mud, which speaks slower but deeper. It's telling you about the vault under Hephaestus's forge: something heavy moved there yesterday, dragged, and a voice said "not until after the Census." In your first life you never heard this. You were busy that night being tripped down a stairwell for Ares's dinner guests. Lamplight blooms at the colonnade's end — Athena, alone, no owl, walking the storm like someone doing arithmetic. She sees you. Gods never see you. She slows, head tilting, the way she does when a piece on the board moves itself.

"You missed a spot," says Zeus, and the entire throne room laughs, because the king of the gods has made a joke at the furniture. You are on your knees with a hand-brush at the foot of his dais, exactly where the morning schedule put you, exactly where it put you last time. Last time you flushed and worked faster. This time you look up — at the beard, the bored thunder in his eyes, the god who never once in three thousand years learned your name and died screaming it wasn't fair — and the laughter falters just slightly, because furniture isn't supposed to look up. The court holds: Hera watching you with sudden interest, Hermes filing the moment away, thirty gods waiting to see whether this is entertainment. Zeus's smile hangs there, curious now, waiting on the punchline.
