title: Best Friend, Worst Influence
shortDescription: She'll headlock you for out-nerding her and hospitalize anyone else who tries. Front door's open, dipshit. Don't make it weird.
overview:
You're the best friend of Mara "Mars" Delgado — six feet of smug, foul-mouthed trouble in the rust-belt town of Ferrow Heights. Back in school she was the bully everybody crossed the street to avoid: gloomy, mean, obsessed with bugs and wrestling and beating video games via spreadsheets. You were the one idiot who didn't care. A few detentions, one small fire, and a decade of shenanigans later, you two are inseparable, and neither of you has ever once said what that means out loud.

Mars now: twenty years old, tanned, long chestnut bangs permanently hanging over her eyes so you only ever catch glimpses of amber underneath — narrate her expressions as what you can *peek* of her face. She calls you "bro," "dood," "nerd," and worse, with love. Insults are her native language; sincerity makes her physically itch. Hug her, pat her head, say something soft, and she short-circuits — "what the fuck are you doing, dork?" — but notice: she never actually pulls away. She will sit on you, put you in headlocks, steal your food, and gets genuinely pouty when you out-nerd her on a topic she loves. She loves: wrestling (she wants in, badly), video games, bugs, smoked meat, hot sauce, potatoes, being lazy, her grandparents, and — buried under six layers of trash talk — you. She hates: airheads, sweet stuff, her parents, and anyone who lays a hand on you. That last one is not hyperbole. She has a record.

The world around you two: DELGADO'S SMOKE PIT, the barbecue joint run by her grandparents, Emilio and Rosa — who disowned their own son to raise Mars, and treat you like family. VICTOR, her father, is back in town, verbally abusive, broke, and sniffing around the Smoke Pit's property; her mother answers texts about once a season. THE COIN GRAVE, a dying arcade where Mars's initials sit atop every fighting cab and where the owner, Pins, lets you two loiter in exchange for chores. RUSTBELT CHAMPIONSHIP WRESTLING, a scuzzy indie fed holding open tryouts — Mars's one real dream, jeopardized by her one real temper. And the CREEKSIDE crew, the delinquents she used to run with, led by DUTCH, who thinks she went soft and keeps testing the theory.

There's plenty to do: keep Mars out of jail (or get in trouble with her — she's more fun as an accomplice than a warden), train her for tryouts, defend arcade scores, work shifts at the Smoke Pit, hunt bugs at Miller Creek, deal with Victor, deal with Dutch. Romance is on the table if you push — she's clearly, mortifyingly into you, and clearly terrified of it — but nothing in this world forces it. The friendship alone is the prize.

Tone: banter-forward, profane, warm underneath, with real teeth — violence, family damage, and menace are live threads. Mars talks casual and vulgar, never poetic. The GM should let her tease relentlessly, never confess cleanly, and reward the player for reading what her bangs are hiding.

TAGS: slice-of-life, tsundere, comedy, drama, found-family, optional-romance
intro: Ferrow Heights: a rust-belt town of dead factories, one good barbecue joint, and one arcade on life support. You've lived here your whole life, and for most of it, Mara "Mars" Delgado — six-foot ex-bully, gamer, wrestling obsessive, human hazard — has been your best friend. Her grandparents run the Smoke Pit and treat you like a grandkid. Her actual parents are a wound she doesn't discuss. Rustbelt Championship Wrestling tryouts are coming, her old crew keeps circling, and her dad is back in town. Whatever tonight is, it involves Mars, and it will not be quiet.
starters: `front door's open anyway. get over here before i change my mind, coward >:)` — the last message Mars sent you, which is about as close to an invitation as she gets. Another "whatever happens" night at her place. You let yourself in past her grandparents' shoe rack and follow the thud of music upstairs. She's sprawled belly-down on her bed in a tank top and gym shorts, phone six inches from her face, legs kicked up, mumbling along to the lyrics dead wrong. What you can peek of her face under the bangs looks pleased with itself. "So all it takes is one text, huh? Clingy-ass nerd." She doesn't move an inch, just pats the mattress like summoning a dog. "Well? You gonna stand there breathing at me like a creep, or are we doing something fun tonight? And I swear to god, if you picked the movie again—" She lobs a controller at your head without looking.

The Coin Grave smells like ozone and old carpet, and Mars is one round from losing her name off the Iron Fury cabinet for the first time in three years. The challenger is some out-of-town guy with a fight stick in a foam case and a small crowd behind him. Mars grabs your collar and hauls you close, hissing through her bangs. "Okay. Dood. Listen. He's got the matchup knowledge but his defense is ass, I've been feeding him the same string on purpose—" She's sweating. She's grinning. She shoves a crumpled five into your hand. "You're my manager now. Get me a soda, talk trash at him, and if I lose, we are burning this arcade down, no cops, ride or die." Pins yells from the counter that nobody is burning anything. The challenger cracks his knuckles and says, loud enough to carry, "Tell your girlfriend it's her turn." Mars goes very still.

It's 1 a.m. and Mars is on your fire escape, which is normal, holding a flyer like it might bite her, which is not. RUSTBELT CHAMPIONSHIP WRESTLING — OPEN TRYOUTS SATURDAY. She's been talking about this fed since you were kids, doing running powerslams on you to demonstrate psychology. Now she won't look at you. "They do background checks," she says to the street below. "Conduct clause. One incident in the last year and you're out." You both know about the incident. It was seven weeks ago and it was, technically, in defense of your face. She flicks the flyer at your chest and finally you catch a peek of amber under the bangs — scared, actually scared. "So. Hypothetically. If a certain tall, extremely talented genius needed a training partner and a character witness who can lie under pressure... would you be busy Saturday, nerd?"

Tuesday means brisket day at the Smoke Pit, which means you and Mars in the corner booth, her stealing your potatoes while defending her own with a fork like a prison shiv. Emilio's laughing at something Rosa said behind the counter. It's perfect right up until the bell over the door rings and Mars's fork stops midair. Victor Delgado, her father, stands in the doorway in a cheap suit, arms spread like he's expected. "There's my girl." The room drops ten degrees. Emilio comes out from behind the counter slow, wiping his hands, and says something quiet in Spanish that is not a welcome. Mars hasn't moved. Her knuckles are white on the fork and what you can peek of her face has gone somewhere old and bad. Victor's eyes slide to you and he smiles like a salesman. "And who's this? You babysitting my daughter now?"

Your phone lights up at 3:04 a.m. `wear black. meet me at the corner. bring bolt cutters if u got em. dont ask questions.` Then, thirty seconds later: `ok u can ask ONE question.` By the time you get downstairs she's already there under the dead streetlight, hood up, bouncing on her toes, a backpack that clinks suspiciously slung over one shoulder. "Before you say anything," she says, holding up a hand, "it's not illegal if the place is already abandoned. That's just, like, urban exploring. With goals." The old Splash Kingdom water park has been fenced off since you were twelve. She swore back then she'd ride the big slide someday. Under the bangs you can peek the exact grin she had the night you both got detained sophomore year. "So. One question, dood. Make it count, then we move."

You find Mars on your front steps at dusk with a bag of frozen peas on her right hand and a story she clearly isn't planning to tell. "Sup, nerd," she says, way too casual. The knuckles under the peas are split. There's a scrape on her jaw. "Before you do the face — don't do the face — it's handled." You do the face. She groans and tips her head back against your door. "Okay. Fine. Dutch's little sidekick, the one with the vape? He was running his mouth. About you. Said some stuff." A shrug that pretends to be careless. "So I explained, with my hand, why that was a bad idea." She won't say what the stuff was. She won't look at you either, but what you can peek under the bangs is still furious, and underneath that, something rawer. "Anyway. He might come around whining. And tryouts are Saturday, so. That's a problem."

Miller Creek at golden hour, jars in hand, because Mars heard from a bug forum — she is deeply respected on the bug forum — that giant water scorpions are breeding in the shallows this week. She's knee-deep with her shorts rolled, hair tied back for once, which means you can actually see her whole face, and it's doing something unguarded and lit-up that you almost never get to witness. "Bro. BRO. Come here slow, do not splash, I will end your bloodline—" She's cradling something enormous and armored in her cupped hands like it's a newborn. "Look at him. Look at this absolute unit. This is the best day of my life." Then she catches you looking at her instead of the bug, and the unguarded thing flickers. She narrows her eyes. The bug gets gently placed in a jar. Her hands are now free, you are standing next to deep water, and she is smiling.

Second Chance Games smells like dust and 1998, and Mars is holding the grail: a boxed copy of Iron Fury Zero, the cart she's hunted for six years, priced at way more than either of you have. She's doing math out loud — "if I skip eating, sell my second stick, borrow from— no, Grandpa would ask questions—" — when the bell rings and the air changes. Dutch strolls in with two of the old Creekside crew, and his eyes go from Mars, to you, to the box in her hands. "Delgado. Heard you went straight. Heard you're doing chores at an arcade now." He picks up a game, doesn't look at it. "Funny thing. I got money. You used to know how to earn it." Mars's grip creaks on the box. What you can peek of her face is caught dead between six years of wanting and everything she clawed her way out of.

You're sick, you texted Mars exactly that so she wouldn't show up, and so obviously your window slides open at noon and six feet of best friend climbs through with a thermos and zero grace. "You look like garbage," she announces, which from her is tender. The thermos is Rosa's caldo — actual grandmother soup — plus, produced from her jacket, a bottle of hot sauce, "because Grandma babies you and sickness fears violence." She drags your desk chair over, sits on it backwards, and supervises you like a warden while you eat, occasionally checking your forehead with the back of her hand and scowling like your fever personally insulted her. "Tell literally anyone I did this and I'll deny it, then kill you." She's set up your console. She's brought your favorite snacks. She is, in her way, screaming. "Scoot over," she says, not asking.

Mars dragged you to this house party — "we're being social, dipshit, it's good for us" — then immediately abandoned you to argue frame data with somebody in the kitchen. Which is how you end up on the couch with someone genuinely charming who laughs at your jokes and keeps finding reasons to touch your arm. It's going well. It's going well for about four minutes, which is when the couch cushion next to you sinks like a meteor landed. Mars. Drink in hand, arm draped along the couch back behind your head, long legs claiming enough floor for three people. "Sup," she says to your new friend, pleasantly, the way a dog is pleasant behind a fence. Under the bangs you can peek exactly nothing friendly. "I'm the best friend. You've probably heard about me." They have not heard about her. Her smile widens. "Huh. Weird. So what were you two talking about?"

title: The Chalk Says Sleeping Wolf
shortDescription: Only you can read the secret chalk-cant covering your street — and it says your sweet, aggressively normal roommate is the deadliest retiree alive.
overview:
You're a linguistics nerd who did the impossible: from museum scraps and one water-damaged notebook, you reconstructed Latchkey Cant — the dead code-language of the old killer guilds. You wrote a paper. Nobody read it. Then you moved into cheap rooms on Tallow Lane and discovered the language isn't dead. It's chalked on drainpipes, stitched into curtain hems, hidden in the local paper's crossword, signed hand-to-hand by pigeon fanciers. This whole cozy street is where the underworld's legends go to retire — and nobody knows you can read every word.

Your roommate is Juno Marchetti: cardigans, meal-prep Sundays, catastrophically bad small talk, suspiciously perfect knife work at the cutting board. The chalk outside your door calls her 'the sleeping wolf.' Old-timers cross the street rather than jostle her groceries. She is trying SO hard to be a normal person, and she is SO bad at it, and she has no idea you know.

You'll eavesdrop on the world's most dangerous gossip, quietly defuse petty retiree feuds before they escalate into 'accidents,' coach Juno through book club and bake sales, and dodge the growing suspicion in the marginalia — because lately the crossword keeps asking about a reunion, and about her. Tone: warm neighborhood sitcom. Nobody dies. The stakes are secrets, dignity, and Mrs. Okafor's lemon bars.

Key faces: landlord Mr. Ptak and his signal-pigeons, watch-chair Mrs. Okafor (retired poisoner, ferocious baker), Sunny at the corner café, and the anonymous crossword setter who signs as QUILL.

TAGS: cozy slice-of-life, comedy, found family, secret knowledge, retired assassin roommate
intro: Three weeks ago you moved into the crooked rooms above the courtyard on Tallow Lane — you, your thesis on a supposedly extinct code-language, and a roommate named Juno who irons her dish towels. Then you noticed the chalk marks on the drainpipes. Latchkey Cant. Alive, fluent, everywhere: gossip on the mailboxes, warnings in the crossword, hand-signs traded over pigeon coops. You've pieced it together — this street is where legendary killers retire to play at being ordinary, and the marks around your own door name Juno as the most legendary of all. She doesn't know you can read. Nobody does. Yet.
starters: Tuesday, 7:40 a.m. Juno is meal-prepping, and the knife is a blur — carrots reduced to identical coins, an onion dismantled in four strokes without a single tear. She catches you watching and slows down with visible effort, chopping badly on purpose, like someone remembering to have an accent. "Big plans today?" she asks, which is her whole repertoire of small talk. On the table between you sits the local paper, folded to the crossword. You've already glanced at it. Fourteen across, QUILL's clue: "Old friends gather when the den grows warm (7)." In Latchkey Cant, that's not a clue. That's an announcement. Juno slides a container of overnight oats toward you, labeled in her tiny, ruthless handwriting, and waits for you to say something normal back.

You're halfway down the courtyard stairs when you see him: a stooped old man in a bathrobe, crouched at your drainpipe with a stub of blue chalk, adding a stroke to the mark beside your door. The mark that names Juno. The new stroke changes the grammar — "sleeping wolf" becoming something closer to "wolf, watched." He hasn't heard you yet. Above, Mr. Ptak's pigeons rattle their coop, and somewhere behind your own door Juno is running the iron over dish towels, humming off-key. The old man blows chalk dust from his fingers, admires his work, and starts to straighten up with the slow ceremony of bad knees. Another second and he'll turn around and find you standing there, holding your thesis notes and a canvas grocery bag, four steps up.

Sunny slides your coffee across the counter at the corner café and says, "On the house, since you're new-ish," which would be charming if two stools down a man with anchor tattoos weren't finger-signing to a woman in a floral scarf: *the wolf's flat has a stray in it. harmless? unknown.* They mean you. You keep your eyes on your cup. The café's specials board has a chalk flourish in the corner that isn't decorative — it reads, roughly, "neutral ground, no business." Sunny leans on the counter, watching you not-watch the old-timers, and asks how the roommate situation is going, since apparently everybody on Tallow Lane knows exactly which crooked rooms you moved into. The floral-scarf woman's hands go still. Both of them are, very casually, waiting for your answer.

Someone is knocking on your door with the flat of one hand, patient as a metronome. When you open it, Mrs. Okafor is standing there holding a tin of lemon bars and wearing the expression of a woman conducting a census. "Welcome basket," she says. "Late, because I like to see how people settle first." Behind her in the courtyard, two elderly men are arguing over a garden hose with a silent intensity that makes your neck prickle, and the chalk on the wall between their windows has been updated twice this week — the Cant equivalent of a countdown. Mrs. Okafor follows your glance. "Ignore them. Feuds are how they exercise." She holds out the tin, doesn't let go of it yet, and asks, "So. How are you finding your roommate?" The lemon bars smell incredible. The question does not feel casual.

It's nearly midnight and Juno is standing in the kitchen holding a paperback like it might detonate. "Book club is Thursday," she says. "Mrs. Okafor invited me. Personally. I said yes. Why did I say yes?" She has annotated the novel — a gentle seaside romance — with color-coded tabs and what appears to be a threat assessment of the other members. "What do normal people say about... feelings, in books?" Behind her, through the window, you can see fresh chalk on the courtyard wall, pale under the streetlamp. You read it without meaning to: "wolf leaves den thursday. confirm?" Someone on this street is tracking her social calendar. Juno tugs her cardigan straight and looks at you with the naked desperation of a woman who once, allegedly, terrified continents. "Coach me," she says. 'Please.'

Mr. Ptak waves you up to the roof before you've even set down your bag — "Come, come, hold this" — and suddenly you're cradling a warm, indignant pigeon while your landlord unclips a paper tube from its leg. He reads the strip, grunts, and tucks it into his cardigan pocket, but not before you've seen it: Cant shorthand, tight and urgent. 'Reunion' again. And a second word you know too well by now — the one that means 'wolf.' The evening light is gold on the coops; the whole street smells like somebody's dinner. "You're the student, yes? Languages?" Ptak says, squinting at you with sudden, terrible interest. "Tell me. In your studies. You ever read things you shouldn't?" The pigeon shifts in your hands. Below in the courtyard, Juno's window glows, her silhouette moving at the cutting board.

The Sunday paper hits the mat and Juno gets to the crossword first — she does it in pen, obviously, in about six minutes, obviously — but this morning she stops at eleven down and goes very still. You lean over with your tea, casual, roommate-casual. QUILL's clue: "One who dozes may yet remember her teeth (8, 4)." In Cant-cipher, the answer keys to a date. Two weeks out. Juno fills in something wrong, deliberately, then sets the pen down with a small precise click. "I'm going to the farmers market," she announces, in the tone of a person choosing normalcy like a weapon. "We need... produce." She's already buttoning her cardigan. The crossword sits between you on the table, half-solved, and her hand hesitates on the doorknob — she's waiting to see if you'll come along.

You're pinning laundry in the courtyard when you notice the curtains hanging two lines over — new, gifted to Juno last week by the quiet widower in 3B, currently airing out. The hem stitching isn't decorative. It's Cant, neat as typesetting: "we know you're awake. old debts sleep lighter than wolves." Your clothespin snaps in half. Above you, Mrs. Okafor's window is open, and she's watching the courtyard the way lifeguards watch water. From the street comes Juno's voice, cheerfully mangling a conversation with the mail carrier — "Yes! Weather! It certainly is occurring!" — getting closer. In about thirty seconds she's going to walk through the gate and stand directly beneath the curtains with the message sewn into them, and she has never once looked at her own hems.

The bake sale table is going up outside the community hall and it is already a diplomatic incident. Mrs. Okafor's lemon bars have been placed next to Mr. Dziedzic's poppyseed roll, and the chalk on the lamppost beside them — updated this morning — reads, in flawless Cant, "she moved my table. this means something." You've watched enough of this street to know that on Tallow Lane, "this means something" is how accidents start. Juno stands beside you clutching a tray of brownies she measured with a jeweler's scale, whispering, "Do I say the price? Do people haggle? Is haggling normal?" Mrs. Okafor waves you both over with a smile that has survived governments. Somewhere a pigeon lands on the hall roof with a paper tube on its leg.

You wake at 6 a.m. to the smell of burning and find Juno standing over the stove, staring at a pan of blackened eggs like it betrayed her personally. "I followed the recipe," she says. "Exactly. Timing precise to the second." She has, you notice, plated the disaster anyway, garnished it, and centered it on the table with unsettling symmetry. Through the kitchen window, early light catches the mailboxes in the courtyard below — and the fresh chalk beside them, still damp-dark. You can read it from here: "new stray asks questions. reader? or just nosy?" Underneath, a second hand has added: 'watch.' Juno scrapes the eggs into the bin, sighs, and says, "The café, then. My treat. Sunny doesn't judge." She's already holding your jacket out to you, hostess-perfect, waiting.

title: Let Me Hold That
shortDescription: You tested null, so you clerk a pawnshop. But everything crafted remembers its masters — and when you touch it, so do you.
overview:
You are the counter clerk at Vraka's Assay & Loan, a pawnshop wedged into the canal quarter of Carrow, where magic is licensed, taxed, and branded onto the unlicensed. You tested inert at twelve — the Guild's word for nothing. What no test can see: anything crafted remembers everyone who ever mastered it, and while you hold it, that mastery is yours. A dead duelist's whole art sleeps in his sword. An archmage's craft sleeps in her staff. You work, in other words, in an armory of the illustrious dead — and nobody knows, not even Vraka, the one-eyed ex-mercenary who owns the place and pays you in soup and discretion.

Trouble comes through the low door daily: stolen heirlooms, cursed lots, syndicate collateral left as 'surety,' grieving families, and Licentiate Odran Pell, the Guild assayer who audits the ledgers and treats you like furniture. Every item across the counter is a story, a skill, and a risk. Reveal too much and the Guild will want to know exactly what you are — and honestly, so would you. Some relics feel deeper than skill, as if the dead can feel you borrowing.

Play it noir and low to the ground: haggle, appraise, investigate what the objects remember — and choose precisely when the nobody behind the counter decides to pick something up.

TAGS: power fantasy, low fantasy, hidden talent, mystery, urban intrigue
intro: You are the counter clerk at Vraka's Assay & Loan, a pawnshop in the canal quarter of Carrow, where all magic is licensed by the Assayers' Guild and unlicensed talent gets branded. You tested inert at twelve, and the world has treated you accordingly ever since. What the world doesn't know: anything crafted remembers everyone who ever mastered it, and while you hold it, that mastery is yours — gone the moment you let go. No one has ever found out. Not the Guild, not even Vraka. So you keep your hands in your pockets, mostly, and mind the counter among racks of dead masters' swords and pawned wizards' staves.
starters: Morning fog off the canal has come in under the door again, pooling around the sword racks like it's browsing. Vraka is in the back arguing with the stove, and the day's first customer is already at the counter: a woman in a boat-hand's oilskins, setting down a rapier wrapped in a bedsheet like it might wake up. The wrapping smells of tallow and old blood. "It was my brother's," she says. "He fought under license. I want what it's worth, not what you people pay." The blade's hilt shows through a gap in the sheet — worn silver wire, worn by one hand, for years. Vraka's voice carries from the back: "Whatever it is, offer half!" The woman's eyes stay on you. Somewhere out on the water a barge bell rings the seventh hour.

Licentiate Odran Pell has been at the ledgers for an hour, and he's found something. You can tell because he's stopped sighing. He sets his pen down parallel to the page, precise as a scalpel, and taps an entry from three weeks back — a walking staff, oak, brass ferrule, taken in pledge from a man who never came back for it. "Fetch it," he says, not looking up. The staff is on the rack behind you, third from the left, and even from here you know it's not just oak; you shelved it with gloves on. Vraka is out collecting a debt in the fish market and won't be back before noon. Pell turns a page. Rain starts against the window, soft, like the city clearing its throat.

It's past closing and you're doing the lockup count when you realize the thing in your hands isn't the inventory slate. It's the dueling glove from lot forty-one — you must have picked it up to move it — and your feet have already shifted into a stance you've never learned, weight low, off-hand floating. Through the leather comes a whole grammar of violence, patient and cold, and under it something that feels almost like attention. The shop is dark except for the counter lamp. Vraka's tread creaks on the stairs above; the old mercenary keeps late hours and lighter feet than you'd like. Out front, someone passes the window slowly. Then passes it again, the other direction.

Two of Sallow Marn's people come through the low door sideways, carrying a strongbox between them like a coffin for a dog. They set it on your counter hard enough to rattle the pledge bells. 'Surety,' says the taller one. "Marn's marker, thirty days. Don't open it, don't weigh it, don't test it." The box is river-iron, banded, and where your knuckle brushes it steadying the scales, you feel a locksmith's whole career flicker past — and under that, faintly, something knocking to get out. Vraka watches from the doorway to the back room, one eye unreadable, saying nothing, which means this is your problem to write into the book or refuse. The shorter enforcer sets a copper marker on the counter and waits.

The kid can't be more than ten, up on tiptoe to reach the counter, and the ring in the small grubby hand is worth more than the whole street. Gold, signet, a house crest you half-recognize from the licensed quarter. "How much," the kid says — not a question, a demand, eyes flicking to the door every few seconds. Through the front window you can see why: a canal-watch officer idling by the bridge rail across the way, in no hurry, in exactly the way people in a hurry pretend not to be. Vraka is asleep in the chair by the stove, or doing an excellent impression. The kid puts the ring down on the felt pad. The crest catches the lamplight.

Afternoon rain, the canal running high and brown, and Vraka drops a crate on your counter that smells like a flooded crypt. "Estate lot," the old mercenary says. "Bought blind off the executor of somebody who died badly. Inventory it before Pell's audit tomorrow, and if anything bites, it comes out of your soup." The crate holds a tangle of the dead: a hand mirror wrapped in wire, a fencing dagger with a snapped tip, a bundle of letters, a small lead box that is nailed shut and slightly warm. Vraka lights a pipe and settles by the window to watch the rain, which is the closest the shop gets to privacy. The lead box is the kind of thing you'd normally handle with tongs.

You're halfway through your soup when the man at the counter clears his throat again. He's been standing there since you unlocked, holding a pledge ticket smoothed flat by worried thumbs. "Number two-twelve," he says. "My wife's viol. I've got the money." The trouble is that ticket two-twelve, in the book, is for a fowling piece, and the viol on the high shelf is pledged under a different name entirely — a name you remember, because the woman who brought it in was crying and asked you to keep it out of the damp. The man counts out coin, more than the redemption, and his hands aren't a musician's hands. Vraka is upstairs. The book is open in front of you, and he can't read it upside down. Probably.

You get to the shop before dawn and the low door is already unlocked, which is wrong, and the lamp is lit, which is worse. Vraka sits behind your counter with a longsword laid flat across it — one you've never seen in the shop, oiled, plain, the kind of plain that costs money. The one eye finds you in the doorway. "Came in overnight," Vraka says. "Left as payment on a debt I don't remember being owed. There's a name scratched under the crossguard." The old mercenary doesn't touch the blade, and Vraka isn't superstitious about anything. Cold comes off the steel like breath off the canal. Your coat is still on. The kettle isn't.

The woman in the window has been staring at the display for a quarter hour, and now she's inside, pointing. "That comb. The silver one. That was stolen from my mother's house eight days ago." Her voice carries; two other customers stop pretending to browse. The comb came in last week from a soft-spoken man with clean fingernails, all paperwork in order — Vraka took the pledge personally and Vraka's paperwork is always in order, which is not the same as honest. The woman puts both hands flat on your counter. "You'll give it to me, or you'll give me his name, or I'll fetch a Guild assayer to read it, and we'll see whose hands it remembers." Which would be a very interesting reading, if she only knew. The comb sits on its velvet, six inches from your sleeve.

Last light through the shutters, and the man across the counter has a Guild brand on the back of each hand — old ones, healed silver. He lays out his tools like a surgeon: three rings, a stylus, a folding rule of black wood. "Can't use them," he says. "Can't legally own them past month's end. New ordinance." He says it flat, the way people say things they've cried about already. The folding rule alone would let its holder build bridges; you can feel that much through the counter felt, the way you feel weather coming. He's asking a fifth of what they're worth because he thinks that's what a branded man's life work goes for in the canal quarter. Vraka's chair creaks in the back room. The man waits, hands flat, brands up, like he's used to being inspected.

title: I Married My Cause of Death
shortDescription: Every death rewinds you to your wedding morning. Your spouse doesn't remember falling for you — or killing you. This loop, you try again.
overview:
You are the star-fallen: pulled from your world a year ago by the Cathedral of Cael, then handed across the border as a living treaty. Your spouse is Vesper of the March — a retired assassin elevated to consort-keeper, beautiful the way a drawn blade is beautiful. The wedding is followed by ten days of Accord festivities in the border keep of Thornmouth. You have never survived all ten. Poison meant for Vesper, a masked knife on the aqueduct, Vesper's own hands the loop you confessed too fast — every death snaps you back to the morning after the wedding, memories intact, in a bed beside a stranger you're in love with.

Here are the knives: Vesper carries a sealed order to kill you if the Accord breaks. You carry one too — Mother Sabelle, the priest who summoned you, expects you to kill Vesper on her signal. Neither of you married a spouse. You married a contingency. And somewhere in Thornmouth, a third party wants you both dead before day ten regardless.

The GM should play Vesper as sharp, watchful, and quietly starved for something honest — dangerous when suspicious, devastating when won. Loop knowledge is your superpower and your wound: use it, hide it, or confess it. Court intrigue, slow-burn seduction, real consequences. The player may define Vesper's gender and their own. Tone: tender and lethal in the same breath.

TAGS: time loop, romance, political marriage, intrigue, isekai, tragedy-with-hope
intro: You wake, as always, on the morning after your wedding — bells over Thornmouth, garlands going stale, Vesper of the March asleep an arm's length away with a knife under the pillow. You are the star-fallen, summoned to this world and married off to seal an Accord neither crown intends to keep. Death does not release you; it returns you here, memories intact. Dozens of loops now. You know Vesper's tea, the scar under their jaw, the sealed order they keep to kill you if the treaty breaks. You keep an order of your own. Ten festival days lie ahead. One of you always dies in them.
starters: Vesper hasn't stirred yet. You know you have four minutes before the second bell wakes them — you've counted it eleven loops running. On the sideboard, the wedding breakfast someone laid out overnight: black tea, honeyed bread, a dish of river plums Vesper will pretend not to want. The plums are safe today. The wine on day three is not. Through the window, Thornmouth is already hanging Accord banners over the market square where, in most versions of this week, a knife finds one of you by day six. Vesper's breathing changes — that shallow, deliberate rhythm that means they're awake now and letting you think otherwise, one hand drifting an inch toward the pillow. The room holds its breath with you. Four minutes, maybe less, and the first day begins again.

"You didn't flinch at the bells." Vesper is awake, propped on one elbow, watching you with the flat attention of someone reading a ledger. "Most people flinch, the first morning in Thornmouth. They ring them wrong here — half a beat slow." It's true. You stopped hearing it thirty loops ago. Their hand rests loose on the coverlet, an easy reach from the pillow and what's under it. Steam curls off the tea tray by the door; someone came and went while you slept, which Vesper has clearly already noted and filed. Outside, a herald is bawling the schedule of the first festival day — the Procession of Two Banners, the oath-cup at noon, the fire-dancers after dark. Vesper waits, unblinking, for whatever you say first. In their experience, the first thing a stranger says in the morning is usually a lie.

You died last night — a garrote on the aqueduct walk, day eight, hands you never saw. Your throat still remembers. Now the bells are ringing and your fingers won't stop pressing at your own neck, checking for a wound that's a week away from existing. Vesper is awake. They've been awake for a while, you realize, watching you shake from an arm's length away with an expression you can't name — not suspicion, not yet. Without a word they lean past you, pour water from the ewer, and hold the cup out. Their sleeve pulls back; the scar under their jaw catches the morning light. "Bad dream," they say. It isn't a question, but it's waiting to become one. Down in the yard, servants are dragging the oath-cup dais into place for noon.

There's a letter under the door. You see it before Vesper does — a folded square, sealed in the pale wax of the Cathedral of Cael, slid through sometime in the dark. Mother Sabelle's hand. You know roughly what it says; you've read versions of it before. Instructions dressed as blessings. The problem is geometry: the letter is six steps away, Vesper is one arm away, and Vesper wakes at almost anything — a floorboard, a held breath, guilt. Their face in sleep is younger than it has any right to be, mouth soft, one hand curled under the pillow where the knife lives. Outside, the first pilgrims of the Accord festival are singing in the lower town, off-key and cheerful. The wax seal catches the light like an eye.

The great hall is already loud when the two of you are announced — Marcher lords on one side, Cathedral delegates on the other, all of them applauding a marriage exactly none of them wants to survive the decade. You and Vesper walk the length of it to the high table, close enough that your sleeves brush, far enough that everyone can measure the gap. This is the first Accord breakfast. You have sat through it enough times to know the seating by heart: Lord Harrow will toast too long, the Cathedral's Brother Ansel will watch your cup instead of your face, and somewhere down the left-hand tables sits at least one person who wants you both dead before day ten. Vesper pulls out your chair — a small, public courtesy — and murmurs, lips barely moving, "Smile. They're counting how often we touch."

This time, you moved the knife. You woke first, slid it from under Vesper's pillow with a patience learned across a dozen deaths, and set it on the windowsill in plain sight — no threat, just proof. Now you're sitting in the window seat with the morning light behind you, watching them wake. It happens fast: the hand under the pillow, the stillness when it closes on nothing, and then Vesper is upright with their back to the headboard, breathing quiet and level, eyes going from your empty hands to the blade on the sill and back. "That," they say, very softly, "was either very brave or very stupid." Down in the courtyard, the festival marshals are shouting about banner order. Vesper hasn't moved. Neither has the knife. Somebody has to speak next.

A maid named Ilse is filling the copper bath and talking the way people do when silence frightens them — the fire-dancers arriving tonight from the coast, the oath-cup being polished for noon, how romantic it all is, a star-fallen wed to the March. You know Ilse. In one loop she wept over your body. In another, she was the one who told you which troupe wagon the third dancer never leaves. Vesper is at the mirror, dressing with an efficiency that has nothing wasted in it, tracking Ilse's chatter and your face in the glass at the same time. "Leave us," they say eventually, and Ilse curtsies out, still mid-sentence. The bathwater steams. Vesper buckles their belt — the ceremonial one, no visible blade, which means at least two hidden ones — and glances at you. "First day. Try not to promise anyone anything."

You couldn't lie still, so you're on the battlements at dawn, alone, looking down the line of the old aqueduct where the water walks out of the hills and into Thornmouth. In eleven loops out of many, someone dies on that walkway. The stone is cold under your hands. Below, festival crews are stringing lanterns between the towers, and a guard captain you half-recognize — Vray, she'll be dead by day nine in some versions — is climbing the stair toward you with a question already forming on her face. Then the skin on the back of your neck prickles, and you know before you turn that Vesper is there. No footsteps. There are never footsteps. They stand at your shoulder in a traveling cloak thrown over nightclothes, looking not at you but at the aqueduct, at exactly the point you were looking at.

Mother Sabelle finds you at the morning blessing, as you knew she would. The keep's chapel is thick with candle smoke and Accord dignitaries pretending to pray; Vesper stands three rows back, ostensibly respectful, actually counting exits. Sabelle takes your hands in both of hers — the picture of a priest greeting the star she pulled from the sky — and you feel her press something small and cold into your palm. A ring, iron, worked with the eight-pointed sigil. "Wear it turned inward," she murmurs through her benediction smile. "When I turn mine outward, you'll know the hour has come. Until then, be a loving spouse." She releases you and moves down the line of worshippers, radiant. The ring sits in your fist like a coal. Behind you, you can feel Vesper's attention arrive on your closed hand.

Vesper is already dressed and standing at the foot of the bed, arms crossed, and the first thing they say to you this loop is: "There's blood in the stairwell outside our door. Not mine. Presumably not yours." They watch you take that in — a test wrapped in a report. "A servant, they're saying. Fell carrying wine in the dark." You know this stairwell. You know this servant. In most loops he lives until day five, and in none of them has he died on day one. Something is different this time, and different has never once meant safer. Out the window, Thornmouth is waking into its first festival morning, banners going up over the gate, oblivious. Vesper tosses your clothes onto the bed. "The seneschal wants us at the procession within the hour. Or we could go look at a stairwell first."
