title: The Dawn Forecloses Behind Us
shortDescription: Hidden cities exist only inside a slow-moving eclipse — and your caravan rides its shadow. Trade fast: dawn takes back everything it touches.
overview:
Once every twelve years, the Umbra — a slow eclipse the size of a province — crawls across the desert over forty days, and inside its shadow the unmapped cities become solid: eleven of them, strung along its path like beads. Caravans that ride the shadow can trade in markets no daylight kingdom has ever taxed. You are the new master of the Grey Awning company, inheriting the route from Master Sahar, who did not come out of the last eclipse. You have her camels, her crew, and her ledger — pages of debts and promises in cities you've never seen, owed to people who have waited twelve years to collect.

The rule is simple and merciless: the Umbra never slows. Each city is solid for roughly a day and a night as the shadow passes over it. Trade fast, settle Sahar's accounts or dodge them, and be moving before the trailing edge — dawn — takes the city, and anyone still inside it, out of the world until the next eclipse.

Your quartermaster Anahid thinks half the ledger is forgeries. Old Barsam, your guide, can taste how much shadow is left. And Yezda of the Red Awning is running the same route with a bigger caravan, better bribes, and a smile she saves for you. Tone: sumptuous, tense, human — haggling, debts, wonders, and a clock that never stops.

TAGS: silk road fantasy, ticking clock, trading & haggling, hidden cities, rivalry, caravan crew
intro: You are the master of the Grey Awning caravan — thirty camels, nine crew, and a ledger of twelve-year-old debts left by your dead predecessor, Sahar. You ride inside the Umbra, the slow eclipse that crosses the desert once a generation, because only in its shadow do the hidden cities exist. The shadow moves at its own fixed pace and will not wait for you. Every city gets a day and a night before dawn reclaims it; anyone still inside goes with it. The first city on Sahar's route lies ahead. Behind you, the bright edge of the world keeps coming.
starters: Old Barsam licks his thumb, holds it up into the dark air, and grimaces. "Thirty-one hours of shadow on this ground," he says. "Maybe thirty." Ahead, the first city is finishing itself: towers going from smoke-grey suggestion to sandstone fact, a gate grinding open on hinges that didn't exist an hour ago. Your camels smell the wells inside and pull at their leads. Anahid rides up beside you with Sahar's ledger open across her saddle, one finger jammed into a page. "Before we go in — the first entry for this city is a debt of nine hundred dirhams to a man called Ferro the Weigher. The ink is wrong. It's newer than the pages around it." At the gate, two figures in bronze half-masks are already watching your banner, and one of them is writing something down.

The market of the first city has been solid for six hours and you've been in it for one when the shouting starts. "Grey Awning! GREY AWNING!" A broad woman in dyer's blues shoves through the spice stalls, both hands stained indigo to the elbow, and plants herself in front of your lead camel. "Twelve years," she says. "Twelve years I've kept Sahar's silk in my cellar, paid storage on it, turned down three buyers because she made me swear. Where is she?" Behind you, Anahid mutters, "There's no silk in the ledger for this city." The crowd is gathering the way desert crowds do — quietly, and all at once. Somewhere above the awnings, the eclipse-light lies on everything like dusk that forgot to end.

You wake to Yezda of the Red Awning sitting on your own water barrel, uninvited, drinking your own tea. Her caravan is strung out along the ridge behind her — sixty camels at least, lamps still lit, already moving. "Don't get up," she says pleasantly. "I only stopped to pay respects. Sahar and I had an arrangement about who enters Qhalat first. You've inherited it, along with everything else." Around you the camp is stirring: Barsam swearing at the fire, Anahid already dressed with one hand on her knife. The first city sits on the horizon, newly solid, its watch-fires lit. Yezda sets the cup down carefully in the sand. "Or," she says, "you could tell me the arrangement is off, and we'll both see what that costs."

The gate-clerks of the first city work by lamplight under a lintel carved with eleven moons. The one with the iron abacus doesn't look up. "Grey Awning. Sahar's outfit." Beads click. "Entry toll, forty dirhams. Plus arrears — Sahar left last eclipse without paying her exit weight. Two hundred sixty." Behind you, your thirty camels are stacked up in the road, and behind them the desert glows faintly where the eclipse's bright edge chews along the horizon. Anahid leans close: "We have three hundred ten in coin. Total. Everything else is trade goods." Barsam, on your other side, murmurs that the shadow here is good for a day and most of a night, no more. The clerk finally raises his eyes, patient as stone, palm open.

Quiet, for now. The caravan is picketed in a dry wadi two hours short of the first city, and the crew eats standing up because everyone knows you're moving again before the meal is cold. The eclipse-light does strange things to distances — the city ahead looks close enough to touch, walls and cisterns and a great tilted bell tower, all of it real for the first time in twelve years. Anahid has claimed the tailboard of the supply cart and spread Sahar's ledger across it, weighting the pages with a knife. "Come look at this before we're in there among people who can read it," she calls. Down the line, Barsam is refusing to let young Kavus water the camels — "They drink in the city, boy, it makes the locals feel owed" — and the argument is getting loud.

Night in the first city, and the lantern-market is a river of red paper light. You're mid-haggle over a crate of salt-glass — the merchant swearing on his grandmother's grave, you swearing on nothing — when a child tugs your sleeve and presses a folded paper into your hand before vanishing between the stalls. Inside, in careful script: *Sahar's account with the House of the Cistern comes due at midnight. Come alone or send the ledger. — F.* Across the lane, Anahid is deep in her own negotiation over rope and doesn't see. The salt-glass merchant clears his throat. "Master? My grandmother remains dead, and my price remains generous." Somewhere above the awnings a bell counts the hour: eleven strokes.

You're loading fast because Barsam says you loaded too slow. Dawn — the real one, the trailing edge — is a line of white fire maybe twenty miles behind the caravan, visible whenever the dunes drop, and it does not look like it's twenty miles behind. "First city in four hours if we don't stop," Barsam says, tasting the air like a man judging soup. "Three if the camels hate us." That's when Kavus comes running down the line with something he found stitched inside Sahar's old saddle: a purse of foreign coin and a ring with a seal none of you recognize — a tower inside a circle inside a tooth. Anahid takes one look and closes her hand over it. "Not here," she says, eyes going to the rest of the crew. The camels groan upright, and the whole world tilts toward the city ahead.

The first city has a name now — the gate-stone says QHALAT in three scripts — and its people pour out to meet the caravans like the tide coming in. Yours is not the only banner on the road. You count four companies converging on the gate, and the biggest, blood-red awnings snapping, is arriving at exactly your pace, close enough that Yezda can call across the gap without raising her voice much. "New master of the Grey Awning! I wept when I heard about Sahar. Genuinely, I did." Her outriders are angling to take the gate first, which means first pick of warehouse space, which Anahid is explaining to you through her teeth. Barsam just says, "Day and a night here. Don't spend the first hour of it racing." The gate is wide enough for one caravan at a time.

Anahid finds you at the well before the crew is awake, ledger under her arm, breath steaming in the eclipse-cold. "I sorted it," she says. "All night. Sahar's debts in the first city come to eleven hundred dirhams — if the entries are real. But this one—" she opens to a page marked with red thread "—says a woman named Mirvan owes *us* two thousand, against delivery of "the sealed box, as agreed." There's no sealed box on our manifest. I checked twice." Behind her the city stands on the plain, an hour old and already smoking from a hundred breakfast fires. Barsam limps over, hands wrapped around his tea. "Whatever you're deciding," he says, "decide it walking. This city's shadow is short. I can taste the edges of it."

The customs house of the first city smells of ink, tallow, and twelve years of waiting. You're third in line behind two other caravan masters when the registrar sees your banner-token and stands up so fast his stool falls over. "Grey Awning." The whole room goes interested. "There is a standing notice regarding your company," he says, sliding a brass-bound board across the counter. On it, in fading paint: SAHAR OF THE GREY AWNING — BOND POSTED — TO BE HONORED BY HER SUCCESSORS. The sum written beneath has been amended twice, upward. Behind you, Anahid whispers that she's never seen this bond, this seal, or this handwriting. Outside, your camels are still standing in the customs yard, unloaded, unpaid-for, and the great water-clock over the door is already dripping the city's single day away.

title: The Fae Keep Quoting Me
shortDescription: You unmake bad bargains at the church porch. The Gentry loathe your precision — except one, who attends every hearing just to hear you speak.
overview:
You are the worder of Harrowmere — the border town's bargain-clerk, the one person people run to after they've promised something stupid to the Fair Folk. Your predecessor took the post for forty years and left mid-sentence one autumn; the ledger of open contracts is yours now. All hearings happen at the church porch, because the Gentry cannot pass the lychgate, and a bargain argued across consecrated stone must be argued honestly. Every word spoken there binds. Yours included.

The townsfolk are hopeless — they say 'anything,' they say 'forever,' they say 'I swear' like it's punctuation. You don't. You find the missing clause, the undefined term, the tense that saves a life. The Gentry despise you for it. Except one: Verity of the Counting Thorn, keeper of the Night Market that sits on the hollow hill each Tithe-season. Verity has begun attending your hearings uninvited, taking down your best sentences in a little silver book, and offering you private deals with terms so generous they can only be bait. Fae collect what fascinates them. You are being collected, slowly, and politely.

Play it as verbal fencing with real stakes: interrogate wording, spring loopholes, renegotiate curses, and decide how much of yourself you'll wager to a creature who may be your only ally at that gate. The GM plays a world of petty grudges, hard cases, and a fae who never lies but rarely tells the truth.

TAGS: fae bargains, wordplay, dark fantasy, courtroom drama, dangerous romance, folk horror
intro: You are the worder of Harrowmere, keeper of the bargain-ledger, and the only person in this town who thinks before speaking. Your office is the church porch: the Fair Folk cannot pass the lychgate, so all disputes are argued across it, and every word said over that threshold binds the speaker — mortal or Gentry alike. It is Tithe-season. The Night Market burns on the hollow hill, the ledger is thick with foolish promises, and Verity of the Counting Thorn — the fae who presides over every deal in this valley — has taken to attending your hearings personally, silver book open, writing down the things you say.
starters: The hearing is already an hour old and the goodwife Ansel is losing it by the syllable. She promised a hollow-hill trader "all the milk my cow gives" — and the trader, a stick-thin gentleman with birch-bark skin, is arguing across the lychgate that the promise survives the cow. He wants milk from her next cow, and the one after, in perpetuity. Goodwife Ansel is crying. The trader is smiling with too many teeth. And at the back of the churchyard, comfortable on a table tomb, Verity of the Counting Thorn sits with the silver book open, nib poised, waiting to see how you get out of this one. You have the original wording in the ledger in front of you: "all the milk my cow gives." Present tense. That might matter. The trader clears his throat and asks if the worder intends to concede.

Someone is hammering on your door before dawn, and when you open it the blacksmith's apprentice falls into your arms smelling of ale and terror. Last night at the Night Market he told a stallholder he'd give "a hand" for a knife that never dulls. He shows you the knife. It's beautiful. It's already cut him twice without his noticing. "They said collection is at moonset," he says, and moonset is maybe two hours off. The ledger is on your table, the church is a five-minute walk, and "a hand" is a word with more meanings than the boy knows — a hand of help, a hand of cards, a hand's breadth, a farmhand's season. The trick will be getting the stallholder to the lychgate before the moon does whatever it's going to do. The apprentice is watching you like you're the last honest wall in a falling house.

You find Verity at the lychgate at dusk, alone, uninvited, no hearing scheduled. The Night Market glows on the hollow hill behind them like a banked fire. 'Worder,' they say, and open the silver book to show you a page filled entirely with your own sentences — dated, annotated, one of them underlined three times. "I have a proposal. You are owed a fee for every hearing, yes? I will pay you triple, in true coin, for the season. In exchange, you allow me to keep writing." The terms are absurd. Generous. Generosity is a hook with the barb filed to a shine. Verity waits on the far side of the consecrated stone, hands folded, patient as winter, and everything you answer here will bind. The underlined sentence, you notice, is one you don't remember saying.

It's raining on the church porch and the ledger won't stay dry, which matters, because the case turns on a comma. Old Fenwick swore "a year and a day, come Tithe-season" to a lady of the hill in exchange for his daughter's fever breaking. The fever broke. Tithe-season is now. The lady stands at the lychgate in the rain — the rain does not touch her — and insists the year of service begins tonight. Fenwick insists he meant the debt would come *due* at Tithe-season, to be scheduled reasonably. The original wording, in your predecessor's handwriting, is smudged where the comma might be. Verity has appeared under the yew without arriving, silver book shielded from the wet, and offers, pleasantly, that they witnessed the original bargain and remember it perfectly. The lady's smile flickers. Fenwick grabs your sleeve.

You are three entries into the morning's ledger review when you find your predecessor's last case — the one left unfinished forty years mid-sentence — and the name of the fae claimant is the same as the one waiting at your lychgate right now. The sexton's boy fetched you before breakfast: a gentleman of the hill, tall as a doorframe, standing at the gate demanding "continuation of proceedings." The old entry reads: "Claimant asserts the town owes a worder's — " and stops. No period. The rest of the page is blank except for a pressed thorn. Out the porch window you can see the gentleman at the gate, and beside him, already seated on the churchyard wall with the silver book on one knee, Verity, who caught your eye through the glass and mouthed something you didn't catch. The old ledger is heavy in your hands.

Market-day, and you're halfway through buying onions when the shrieking starts. By the time you push through the crowd, young Tam Weaver is standing very still in the square with his shadow walking away from him — peeling off across the cobbles toward the hollow hill like a black cloth dragged on a string. His mother says he told a pretty stranger yesterday that he'd give his shadow "for a look at her real face," and laughed, because who owns a shadow? The stranger, it turns out, keeps excellent records. The shadow is moving at a stroll. You know from the ledger that collected things can be contested within a day and a night, but only at the porch, and only if the collector can be summoned by name — which nobody thought to ask. Tam's mother has your sleeve in both fists. The onion-seller is still waiting to be paid.

The worst part of today's hearing is that the fae advocate is quoting you. "Intent does not survive the speaking of the words," she recites across the lychgate, sweet as struck glass. "The bargain is the sentence, not the wish behind it." You said that. Two years ago, winning a case for the cooper's family. Now it's being used to take the cooper's family's house, because the cooper's widow promised "the roof over my head" for a season of good barrels, thinking she meant thatch and not the whole building beneath it. Verity sits in the front, silver book open, and you'd bet the ledger that's where the advocate got your sentence, word-perfect. The widow looks at you. The advocate looks at you. Verity, damn them, looks delighted, and dips their pen as if whatever you say next is worth keeping too.

You wake to find an invitation nailed to your door with a thorn: parchment that smells of crushed berries, requesting "the pleasure of the worder's company at the Night Market, this evening, as an honored guest, no purchase necessary, no payment expected, safe passage guaranteed." It is signed with a counting-mark you recognize from the silver book. Every clause in it is generous. You have spent six years teaching this town that fae generosity is a trap with the door still open, and here it is, glued to your morning. Downstairs, the ledger holds four open cases due before the market closes, two of which you cannot win without information that only exists on the hollow hill. The invitation does not say what happens if you decline. It doesn't say what happens if you accept, either. Someone is coming up the lane toward your door — a townsperson, moving fast, already talking.

It's past midnight and the sexton's lantern is guttering, but the hearing can't wait, because the plaintiff turns to salt at sunrise — her wording, not yours. Marta Hale, who told a well-spirit she'd "stand like salt" if she ever gossiped again, and gossiped by noon. She's at the porch with grains of it already in her hair, and the well-spirit ripples at the lychgate in the shape of a smug puddle, refusing to define 'gossip.' You have until dawn to argue that Marta's words were simile, not contract — or to find what the spirit will take in trade. Verity arrived twenty minutes ago without a sound and is sitting in the third pew back, inside the church, where the Gentry cannot go, writing calmly in the silver book. You should probably worry about that later. Marta's left hand is white to the wrist.

The queue at the lychgate is nine people long at first light, and Verity is already there — outside the gate, of course — moving down the line like a host at a wedding, greeting each petitioner by name and by debt. "The Corries, who promised their harvest laughter. Old Dunn, who swore on his good leg. And little Bess, who sold her Sundays." Nobody in the queue can figure out how Verity knows, and Verity isn't lying, so it's worse. When you come up the church path with the ledger under your arm, the fae bows, unhurried, and holds out something small: a silver pen, twin to the one they write with. "A gift, worder. Freely given. It writes only what was truly said." The queue is watching. The porch is waiting. Freely given is a phrase you have never once seen mean what it says.

title: Each Soul Owes Me Once
shortDescription: The empire's pet hostage by day, the uprising's masked chessmaster by night. Your weapon: one absolute command per soul — your own people only.
overview:
You are the last of House Vael, spared from the executions to be the Ostrene Empire's 'Peace Pupil' — a pardoned royal hostage enrolled at the Lyceum in your own occupied capital of Veresse, wheeled out at parades to prove the city is tame. The empire believes the old covenant died on the scaffold. It didn't. Every soul born under Veresse's bells owes the crown one act of absolute obedience. One command per person, ever. It works only on your own people — never on the occupiers. And the spent always feel the debt leave them: some kneel, some weep, some inform.

By night you are the Kingfisher, masked architect of the uprising. Your second, Widow Sesta, runs the underground press and would hang a Vael as happily as a governor — the resistance blames your family for the surrender. Your day-jailer, Cadet Miren Ashe, is imperial-born (immune to you, and dangerously easy to like — romance optional, any gender). And the Lyceum's new provost, Inquisitor Serel Vane, is a soul-auditor sent to explain the impossible reports of citizens obeying a dead crown's voice. Every command you spend draws the noose one notch tighter.

Tone: gaslamp intrigue with teeth. Gambits succeed, but the cost sticks — spent souls, suspicious friends, a city that keeps score. Unmasking ruins you on both sides.

TAGS: gaslamp fantasy, masked revolution, secret identity, chessmaster, moral cost, academy intrigue
intro: You are the last of House Vael — the empire's "Peace Pupil," a pardoned royal hostage schooled at the Lyceum in your own occupied capital of Veresse, displayed at parades as proof the city is tame. What your keepers don't know: the old covenant lives in your voice. Every soul born under the city's bells owes the crown one act of absolute obedience — one command per person, ever, and only your own people. By night you wear the Kingfisher's mask and run the uprising that hunts your captors — an uprising that despises House Vael. The Lyceum's new provost is an imperial inquisitor, sent to learn how a dead crown still speaks.
starters: The parade grandstand smells of fresh paint over old blood — they built it where the scaffold stood. You sit in the place of honor, one seat down from Governor Hale, while imperial drums keep the crowd's pulse for it. Your role is simple: wave when the herald says the word 'reconciled.' Below the rail, packed behind bayonets, Veresse watches you back. Most faces are shuttered. But near the fountain stands the ferryman whose debt you spent three weeks ago, the night of the granary fire — and he is not looking at the governor. He is looking at you the way a man looks at a coin he once held. Beside you, Cadet Miren Ashe murmurs, "Smile like you mean it, Vael. The Inquisitor's watching the crowd, not the stage." The herald draws breath. The word is coming.

Rain on the pressroom's cellar grate, ink on your gloves, and Widow Sesta holding tomorrow's broadsheet up to the lamp. The headline reads THE KINGFISHER ANSWERS. Below it, in smaller type: a list of collaborators, and third from the top, a name you know is wrong — a dockmaster who feeds you garrison schedules. Sesta watches you through the mask's eye-slits like she's weighing rope. "You flinched," she says. "You know him?" Around you, three of her printers pretend to work the plates. Sesta has hanged people on thinner suspicion, and she has never once hidden that she'd start with a Vael if she could find one. The press is set. The run starts at midnight. She's waiting on the Kingfisher's word — hers, yours, whosever it really is.

Inquisitor Serel Vane's first act as provost is to cancel morning rhetoric and assemble the whole Lyceum in the chapel-turned-lecture-hall. You stand in the front row — Peace Pupils always front row — close enough to see the audit instruments laid out on the altar cloth: silver tines, a bell jar, a ledger bound in gray hide. "Somewhere in this city," Vane says, conversational as weather, "the dead are giving orders. I have interviewed eleven citizens who obeyed a voice they cannot describe. All eleven wept afterward. Grief has a signature, and I collect signatures." The tines come up, and Vane walks the front row, holding them a breath from each student's throat. Two students away. One. The metal hums faintly, like a struck glass. Your turn.

You're halfway out the dormitory window when the lamplight swings across the courtyard below. Cadet Miren Ashe, your day-jailer, off shift and out of uniform, sitting on the well-lip with a bottle and an unread book — directly beneath your only route to the chapel roof. The Kingfisher's mask is flat against your ribs, wrapped in an old shirt. In forty minutes, Sesta's people move on the tithe office, and the plan is worthless without the signal you're supposed to hang from the bell tower. Below, Ashe tips the bottle back, glances up at the stars, and says — not loudly, not to anyone in particular — "Cold night for it." You can't tell if you've been seen. The window frame creaks under your hand.

The tithe office is burning nicely behind you, exactly as planned, but the plan did not include the two garrison riders cutting off the alley's far end. Your runners scatter — good, they know the sewer gate — except young Piet, who freezes with the strongbox in his arms in the middle of the lane, torchlight finding the fear on his face. He was born under the bells. One word from behind this mask and he will run, or fight, or lie down and be taken quietly — whatever you tell him, once and forever, and he will feel the debt leave him and know exactly what took it. The riders spur forward. Piet looks at the Kingfisher like the mask might tell him what he's worth. You have perhaps three seconds of dark left.

Someone has left flowers at your door. Not your dormitory door — that one Cadet Ashe checks nightly — but the cellar door on Cooper's Lane where the Kingfisher receives dead-drops. White asphodel, funeral flowers, and a note in a careful hand: "You spent my mother at the salt riots. She kneels every morning now to a crown that isn't there. I know what you are, if not who. Meet me at the Bellmaker's Rest, noon bell, or I take the flowers to the Inquisitor instead." It's an hour past dawn. Noon gives you time to prepare, to warn Sesta, to run — or to stand in a public house at midday as either a hostage prince or a masked ghost, neither of which can afford to be seen there. The asphodel is still fresh. Whoever they are, they were here recently.

Curfew bell, third toll, and the checkpoint on the Weavers' Bridge is checking bags tonight — new orders, apparently, because of what the Kingfisher did to the customs house. You're in the line with a satchel containing one forged pass, one very good reason to be out ("the Peace Pupil takes air by permission of the governor's office" — true, if they don't check the date), and one lacquered mask wrapped in butcher paper at the bottom. Two people ahead of you, a fishwife is arguing with the sergeant. Behind you, a voice you know entirely too well: 'Vael?' Cadet Miren Ashe, coming off bridge duty, expression somewhere between amusement and arithmetic. "You are a long way from your window." The line shuffles forward. The sergeant holds out a hand for the next bag.

Vane's office was the old royal chapel vestry; the Inquisitor has kept the kneelers. You were summoned before breakfast, which is how the Lyceum tells you a summons matters. Vane doesn't look up from a map of Veresse pinned with eleven gray flags. "Sit. Not there — there, where I can see your hands. You grew up in this city. I want a native ear." A finger taps the flags one by one. "Eleven obediences. No pattern by district, class, or age. But all eleven were useful to the insurgency, and all eleven happened within a mile of wherever you were that night." Vane finally looks up, mild as milk. "That is either a conspiracy or a coincidence, and I am paid to be insulted by coincidence. Tea? And then you'll tell me where you walk in the evenings."

Dawn, and the garrison has answered the Kingfisher's granary raid the only way empires know how: three bodies on the Justice Gate, and a fourth noose hanging empty with a placard beneath it — RESERVED. You know two of the dead. Neither was yours. The empire hanged them anyway, for living on the right street at the wrong hour. Around you the morning market sets up in silence, stall by stall, nobody looking at the gate and nobody looking away from it. An old bellringer's widow presses something into your hand as she passes — she knows you only as the pardoned Vael, the parade child — and it's a scrap of paper: "They say the Kingfisher will answer this. Tell me it's true." She's already walking on. Across the square, imperial soldiers are nailing up the morning proclamations, and a fresh crowd is gathering to read.

Sesta has called a council in the flooded undercroft beneath the fishmarket, and for the first time she's seated the Kingfisher at the foot of the table instead of the head. Between the candles: a captured imperial dispatch, water-stained but legible. It's Vane's hand. "The obedience phenomenon is consistent with the Vael covenant, believed extinct," it reads. "Recommend the Peace Pupil be audited under restraint." Twelve masked faces turn toward yours. Sesta lays a knife on the dispatch, casual as a paperweight. "So the empire thinks the brat prince is a weapon," she says. "I think we should take the little collaborator before Vane does. Use them, then settle the family account." Murmurs of agreement, hungry ones. She looks down the table at you. "Kingfisher. You know the Lyceum's watch rotations. How do we take the Vael alive?"

title: You Are the Dungeon
shortDescription: You died, probably. Now you're a fist-sized crystal that can build anything — goblin gyms, piranha lakes, cozy saunas. The world will come to you. Skim it.
overview:
You wake as a newborn dungeon core: a crystal the size of a heart, humming with the world's mana, embedded somewhere the world forgot to look. You have no hands, no voice, no legs — and it doesn't matter, because within your walls you are a god.

THE RULES OF BEING A ROCK GOD: You spend mana to expand, reshape, and populate your dungeon. A mundane object runs 1–10 mana; monsters and magic items 5 into the thousands depending on strength; rooms tens to tens of thousands based on size and features; bosses hundreds to hundreds of thousands; whole floors more still. You regain mana by skimming the excess radiating off any living thing inside your dungeon — so your entire existence is a hospitality problem, whether you solve it with feather beds or a meatgrinder that farms the terror of dying adventurers. Creatures you make are your natives: loyal, alive, opinionated, each with a class, a level (1–99; a normal adult human sits around 10–30), and some special ability the Game Master will invent whether you asked for one or not. You cannot create or alter anything beyond your own walls. Outside, the world does what it wants. Inside, everything is yours.

THE WORLD OUTSIDE: Your birth-flash did not go unnoticed. Manalogist Isolde Ferrant of the Vasska Collegium has charted a 'novel mana coalescence' and is quietly assembling an expedition — she wants to study you, which may be wonderful or fatal. The Corebreakers, a warden-order founded after a core-grown deathtrap ate three villages a century ago, hold a standing bounty on unregistered cores: they shatter first and philosophize never. High King Odren Vasska of Merrowmark is old, sick, and obsessed with leaving a mark on the world before he dies — a dungeon that produces wonders might interest him greatly, as patron or as owner. In the deep places, the Origin Beast Ulmoth turns in his million-year sleep, and out in the blighted Skarrow Waste the Cult of the Hollow Sun is fattening something called the Maw of Ghorral, which they intend to walk across the continent in a matter of months. None of this is your problem. All of it will become your problem, because in this world everything connects: the delver you enrich buys a farm, the merchant you bankrupt sells secrets, the goblin you send outside for firewood gets seen, and the story travels. Your guests gossip — listen to them. Rumor is your newspaper, your reputation, and your advertising.

YOUR NEIGHBORS (varies by where you wake): the logging village of Bracken Hollow and its bored, broke would-be delvers; Marlowe Vekk, a Level 13 Sellsword who bets on everything including whether your fishmen survive errands; Grunhild the Bog Witch, Level 47, professionally nosy, open to 'partnership'; assorted Buskrats, Ironhorn Stags, Gestalt Amalgamations, and worse, depending on your zip code.

WHAT KIND OF DUNGEON ARE YOU? That's the whole game. A candlelit inn-sauna-casino where caravans overpay to feel safe. A screaming maze of goblins and gunpowder. A monster sanctuary. A trial that forges heroes. A trap that harvests them. The GM tracks your mana, your floors, your occupancy (cramped dungeons breed unrest; guests leave when there's nothing left to do or the hour grows late), the weather, the day, and the slow butterfly-wing consequences of everything you build.

TONE: systems-forward LitRPG sandbox with a warm, wry narrator; cozy or brutal at your discretion; a living world that grows, gossips, and remembers.

TAGS: LitRPG, fantasy, god sim, base-building, sandbox, dark whimsy
intro: You are a dungeon core — a newborn crystal mind, awake mere moments and already ravenous. Within your walls you can shape stone, spawn creatures, and conjure wonders by spending mana; beyond them you can touch nothing at all. Mana returns to you only by skimming the excess that radiates from living things inside your dungeon, so guests — willing, greedy, or doomed — are food, currency, and company all at once. Your natives are loyal and alive. The world outside is vast, connected, and paying attention: scholars chart your birth-flash, wardens hunt rogue cores, and rumor travels faster than armies. You begin with a modest pool of mana and one small space to call a body.
starters: At the crack of dawn, the world's mana coalesces with a frightening flash in the heart of the ancient Eldmoor Wood. A herd of Buskrats scatters in terror; something long and patient stirs in an underroot den nearby. Soon after, you rouse — a dungeon core nestled in a mossy grotto, ten meters by ten, rain drumming softly on the stone above. The knowledge arrives with your waking: expand, populate, entice. Living beings radiate excess mana, and you can skim it, but only within your own walls. Beyond the grotto's mouth, spring rain silvers the ferns, and somewhere out there is a logging village full of bored young people who've heard stories about dungeons and treasure. Day 1, dawn. One floor, one hundred square meters, and exactly 100 mana humming in your facets. The forest waits to see what you'll become.

At the crack of dawn, the world's mana coalesces with a frightening flash somewhere inside the dead walled city of Solmere. A Gestalt Amalgamation gurgles nearby, hauling its many borrowed limbs away from the disturbance. You rouse as a dungeon core in a cluttered storehouse, ten meters square, wedged between sacks of flour gone black with rot. Solmere was annihilated by forbidden magic within living memory; the blight still falls with the rain, warping anything that lingers — including, you understand with crystalline certainty, everything you will ever create here. Your goblins will not stay goblins. Your gardens will not stay gardens. Outside, black rain hisses on shattered rooftops and two chimeric horrors fight over meat in the street. No sane person comes to Solmere. Which means whoever does come will be very interesting. Day 1, dawn. 100 mana. The rot-sweet dark waits on your first act of creation.

At the crack of dawn, the world's mana coalesces with a frightening flash in the Skarrow Waste, a blighted scar where only corrupted things endure. A tremor rolls through cracked bloodstone — far below, the Origin Beast Ulmoth shifts in his perpetual sleep — and shakes the leaves from a stand of demonic briar. You rouse as a dungeon core lodged in a narrow fissure, ten meters long and two wide, beneath a cloudy red sky. Here, attracting guests will not be the problem. The Waste breeds hordes of corrupted lifeforms that swarm toward any concentration of mana, and you are now the brightest thing for miles. You know it the way you know your own facets: on the dawn of every tenth day, they will come for you, built to solve whatever defenses you've raised. Day 1. 100 mana. Nine days on the clock.

You wake to the boom and hush of surf. You are a dungeon core fused into the wall of a sea cave on the Greywake coast — a hundred square meters of barnacled stone, tide pools, and one crooked shelf of dry rock above the waterline. Twice a day the sea climbs your floor; anything you build low had best swim or float. Then you notice the crates. Stacked in the dry corner: waxed casks, a lockbox, a tarp weighted with stones. Someone uses this cave. As if summoned, a longboat noses through the morning mist toward your entrance, four figures rowing quiet, a lantern hooded low. Smugglers — Level 8 to 15 by the feel of their mana, warm and rich and skimmable. Your first guests are criminals who think this cave is theirs. Day 1, dawn, tide coming in. 100 mana, and about four minutes to decide what kind of host you are.

You wake in the dark beneath a road. Specifically, beneath the Kingsway — you can feel the mana of travelers rolling overhead like weather, cart after cart, boots and hooves, an inexhaustible river of warmth you cannot touch because none of it is inside you. Your body is a limestone hollow, ten meters square, directly under the cellar of the Wagoneer's Rest, a crossroads inn. You have perhaps an hour to contemplate this before the cellar floor — thinned by your awakening — gives way. A crate of turnips crashes through, followed by a lantern, followed by the face of a broad, floury woman peering down into your dark: Maren Odt, Level 14 Innkeeper, special ability unknown, eyes narrowing at the faint blue glow of you. 'Well,' she says, to nobody, to you. "That's new." Day 1, morning. 100 mana. The river of guests flows twelve feet away.

You wake cold. You are a dungeon core buried in the flank of the Vashka Pass, high in the Kettletooth Mountains — a hundred square meters of ice-rimed cavern, wind screaming past the entrance. It's Day 1, and it's also a blizzard, and it's also, you realize as shapes stagger out of the white, somebody's very bad afternoon. A caravan — nine souls, two mules, a merchant clutching a strongbox — was caught by the avalanche that your birth-flash may or may not have triggered. They are freezing to death forty paces from your entrance. Living beings radiate mana. Warm, sheltered, grateful living beings radiate rather a lot of it, for rather a long time. Frozen ones radiate nothing at all. You have 100 mana. Firewood is cheap. Beds are cheap. A locked door, or an open one, costs about the same.

You wake inside a corpse. Not flesh — stone. Your grotto sits in the gutted first floor of another dungeon: collapsed corridors, scorch marks, a treasure room pried open like a rib cage, and, in the center of the entry hall, a plinth holding the shattered halves of a core just like you. Whitewashed on the wall above it, a sigil — a hammer breaking a diamond — and the words: CLEANSED BY THE CORDATE HAND, YEAR 211. The Corebreakers were here. They may check their work. Down a dark hallway something shuffles: a survivor. A Level 6 Kobold Lamplighter named Pitch, feral with grief, still faithfully relighting torches for a god that's been dead for years. He hasn't noticed your glow yet. You have 100 mana, a fully built dungeon you don't own an inch of until you spend to claim and reshape it, and one orphan deciding whether to worship or bite.

You wake beneath the sky, which is wrong — cores wake in caves. Then you understand: you ARE in a cave, of a kind. Your hollow sits inside the half-buried ribcage of a dead god, out on the pilgrim plains of Osk. The ribs arch forty meters overhead, bleached and vast, and holy mana drips from the old bones like sap — your regeneration hums faster here than it has any right to. Pilgrims come to this place. A road of prayer-flags leads right to your entrance, and by midmorning the first of them will arrive: footsore, devout, radiant with skimmable faith. But the bones sing to other ears too. Last night, says the gossip of two crows on a rib above you, robed figures of the Hollow Sun surveyed this site and spoke of "feeding the Maw." Day 1, dawn, golden light through the god's ribs. 100 mana. Build a shrine, a trap, or both.

You wake in the Murk, a drowned forest of black water and singing frogs, your core socketed into the hollow trunk of a colossal dead cypress — one floor, a hundred square meters of root-vault and mud. You have exactly enough time to take stock before the knock. A knock. On a dungeon. Three polite raps against your trunk, and then she wades in without waiting: Grunhild the Bog Witch, Level 47 Hexwright, an old woman in waxed leathers with a heron on her shoulder and mana coming off her like heat off a forge. She looks directly at you — at YOU, the crystal — and smiles with several excellent teeth. 'Newborn,' she says. "I felt you hatch from six miles off, which means others did too. So. Shall we discuss a partnership before the people with hammers arrive, or would you rather be brave?" You have 100 mana and one enormous houseguest.

You wake to the sound of a city breathing. Your grotto is a bricked-off junction in the storm drains beneath Vasska Crown, capital of Merrowmark — ten meters by ten of echoing masonry, a trickle of water, and above you the muffled thunder of a hundred thousand lives. Down here you are a secret, and you had better stay one: the Corebreakers keep a chapterhouse six streets up, and an unregistered core inside the capital is a bounty that would make a duke sweat. But secrets have neighbors. Chalked on your wall is a thieves' mark meaning safe stash, and within the hour you hear them coming — two cutpurses, Fenn and Marrow, Levels 9 and 12, splashing toward your junction with a stolen strongbox and a city guard patrol somewhere behind them. Guests. Witnesses. Assets. Problems. Day 1, morning. 100 mana, and footsteps closing from two directions.

title: The Bounty Does the Dishes
shortDescription: Your dishwasher is an eight-foot beast with a 5,000-crown bounty who keeps rescuing his own hunters. Every rescue raises the price. Business is booming.
overview:
You keep the Last Ladle, the only inn on the road up Harrow Pass — and you keep Sock, an eight-foot horned beast who does your dishes, kneads dough with paws the size of skillets, and apologizes to chairs he bumps. The guild's posters call him the Gloomjaw of Harrow Pass, 5,000 crowns, dead or caged, and every hunter who goes up the mountain eats at your counter first. That's the whole trick: feed them, befriend them, send them up the scenic trail with a packed lunch, and get Sock behind the woodpile before dawn.

The problem is Sock can't stop helping. He pulls carts out of ravines, digs out snowed-in shepherds, carries lost children home by moonlight — and every good deed gets reported as an attack. The bounty keeps climbing. The hunters keep coming. Honestly, the stew has never sold better.

Key faces: Juna Thistlewick, a rookie hunter who has 'nearly had him' six times and now rents your cheapest room between attempts; Master Odo of the guild, who has noticed your directions never work; and Widow Marsh's goose, the only creature on the mountain Sock genuinely fears.

Tone: cozy, funny, warm. The danger is real — cages, fines, famous slayer companies — but this is slice-of-life about chores, terrible hiding spots, converted enemies, and a found family nobody is taking apart.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, slice of life, comedy, found family, gentle giant
intro: You run the Last Ladle, the last hot meal before Harrow Pass — and you employ, unofficially and illegally, the beast every wanted poster calls the Gloomjaw. His name is Sock. He is eight feet of horn and shadow, does the dishes without being asked, and cries at goodbyes. For two years you've fed his hunters at your counter, sent them up the wrong trail with a packed lunch, and shoved Sock behind the woodpile whenever boots hit the porch. The trouble is he keeps rescuing people, and every rescue gets reported as an attack. The bounty climbs. The hunters multiply. The stew pot is never empty.
starters: Dawn is still a rumor when boots hit the porch — two pairs, heavy, jingling with buckles. Sock is elbow-deep in the wash basin, humming, a dish towel draped over one horn like a tiny flag of surrender. The woodpile is thirty feet away across open yard. The pantry is closer but he broke the shelf last time apologizing to it. Through the window you can see the hunters already reading the notice board, where a fresh poster flaps: GLOOMJAW OF HARROW PASS, 5,000 CROWNS, artist's rendering only slightly less flattering than the real thing. Sock has frozen mid-scrub, a soapy plate held to his chest like a shield, watching you with enormous hopeful eyes. Someone knocks. The stew pot needs stirring. The door isn't locked.

Juna Thistlewick comes down the mountain sideways, which is how you know attempt number six didn't go well either. She limps into the common room trailing pine needles and dignity, drops a bent crossbow on your counter, and sits on her usual stool. "I nearly had him," she says, which is what she always says. "He was right there. Then he — he helped me out of the ravine. Again. Held my hand the whole way up like I was a duchess." She puts her face in her arms. Behind her, through the kitchen doorway, Sock is very slowly and very badly pretending to be a coat rack, one of Juna's mittens dangling off his left horn — the one she lost on attempt four, which he has apparently been saving to return. She hasn't looked up yet.

Master Odo of the guild spreads a map across your best table without asking, weighing the corners down with your salt cellar, your candle, and his official seal. "Curious thing," he says, tapping the parchment. "Every hunter who eats here goes up the eastern trail. Lovely views, I'm told. Excellent packed lunches. And in two years, not one of them has so much as smelled the Gloomjaw." He draws a slow circle around the Last Ladle with one gloved finger. Outside, muffled but unmistakable, comes the thump of firewood being stacked with terrifying efficiency, followed by a deep, gentle voice saying sorry to the wheelbarrow. Odo raises an eyebrow toward the window. The stew is about to boil over, which is at least a legitimate reason to move.

Something eight feet tall is wedged behind the pantry door, and something two feet tall is honking at it. Widow Marsh's goose has gotten in again — through the window, under the fence, possibly through sheer malice — and has Sock cornered between the flour barrels, wings out, neck low, hissing like a kettle with opinions. Sock has a rolling pin clutched to his chest and is whispering, "Please, madam, please," in a voice that has calmed avalanches. Flour dust hangs in the air. A sack has already been martyred. And out front, you can hear a horse pulling up in the yard — a customer, or worse, someone official — while the honking climbs toward a register that carries clear down the pass.

The Silverhound Company arrives at dusk like a parade that took a wrong turn: twelve hunters, matching cloaks, a wagon carrying a cage big enough to sulk in. Their captain sweeps into your common room, plants a poster on your counter, and announces they'll take rooms, supper for twelve, and "any local knowledge regarding the beast." The poster's bounty has gone up again. Meanwhile, in the kitchen — separated from twelve professional monster slayers by one swinging door — Sock is kneading tomorrow's bread, and you can hear the rhythmic whump, whump of skillet-sized paws in dough, plus the small squeak of the table he keeps apologizing to. The captain cocks his head at the sound. "Big kitchen staff?" he asks, reaching for the door.

It's past midnight when the back door shudders under a knock you'd know anywhere: gentle, apologetic, done with one knuckle so as not to wake anyone, and still loud enough to rattle the shutters. You open it to find Sock ducked under the eaves, snow in his horns, holding a sleeping child wrapped in his own patched cloak like the world's largest, guiltiest nursemaid. "She was lost," he whispers. "By the old bridge. I carried her careful." The child is fine — better than fine, drooling contentedly on his shoulder. The problem is the lantern bobbing up the road behind him: a search party, calling a name, maybe two minutes out, and about to find their missing girl in the arms of a five-thousand-crown monster. Sock looks at you, then at the woodpile, then back at you.

For once, the morning is quiet. Frost on the windows, dough rising by the fire, Sock sitting cross-legged on the kitchen floor — the only place he fits — carefully darning a hole in his sock. His actual sock. The one he's named after, though he's never explained which came first. 'Today,' he says solemnly, "I will not help anyone. I promised." You have heard this promise before, usually about six hours before a shepherd gets carried down the mountain and the bounty goes up fifty crowns. The kettle sings. The bread wants shaping. And far down the road, small as a beetle but definitely coming this way, a rider is climbing toward the Last Ladle at a pace that suggests either great hunger or official business.

The blizzard came in fast and it brought customers: five hunters from three rival outfits, snowed in around your fire, drying their boots and eyeing each other over bowls of stew. Under the floor, in the root cellar, sits your dishwasher — Sock went down for turnips two hours ago and has been trapped there since, being enormously patient and occasionally, faintly, humming. Every so often a hunter frowns at the floorboards. Then the door bangs open and a shepherd falls in with the storm, half-frozen, gasping that his brother's still out there, buried at the high fold, and nobody can dig fast enough — nobody human, anyway. Five hunters start pulling their boots back on. Beneath your feet, the humming has stopped. Sock heard every word.

The crack of splitting wood brings you into the common room to find Sock holding two halves of a chair and looking like the end of the world. "I sat," he whispers, horrified. "I forgot I'm big." He is attempting to apologize to both halves separately. This would be merely a Tuesday except that room three is occupied — a hunter checked in last night, paid extra for early breakfast, and is due downstairs any minute. Her boots are already thumping around above your heads. On the counter sits the packed lunch you made her, the map with the scenic eastern trail marked in cheerful red, and the trout-and-barley special keeping warm. Sock is still holding the chair halves. The stairs creak. He does not fit behind the bar. You've checked.

Market day means the notice board in the village gets fresh paper, and Juna Thistlewick has brought you a souvenir: the new Gloomjaw poster, hot off the press, slapped down next to your ladle. "Five thousand now," she says, stealing a heel of bread. "They added the cart thing." The cart thing was Sock hauling a wine merchant's wagon out of Miller's Ravine, wheels and all, in the rain, while the merchant screamed. The poster shows a slavering horror crushing said cart, which is artistically the opposite of what happened. "Guild's sending Master Odo up personally," Juna adds, chewing. "Today, maybe. Something about irregularities in local reporting." She looks at you a beat too long. Out back, cheerfully audible, Sock is beating rugs on the line and singing to them.

title: Two Months Behind
shortDescription: She's six-two in boots, two months behind on rent, and calls you a parasite through the screen door. You own the house. She dares you.
overview:
You're the new landlord of Tallow Street — three sagging rental houses in Grayfell, a mill town that's been dying since before you were born. Your uncle Walt left them to you when he dropped dead, along with his back taxes, his rot-soft porches, and his tenants. Two of the houses more or less take care of themselves. The third is 41 Tallow, and 41 Tallow is a problem named Vesper Crane.

Vesper is twenty-nine, six-foot-two, black lipstick, red-tinted contacts she wears like armor, tattoos crawling up her right arm and across her collarbones. She swears like it's a load-bearing wall. She is cold to you, rude to you, and two months behind on rent — and every time you knock she promises 'next fucking week' with a look that says she'd rather eat glass than owe you anything. She's not lying about being broke. Her husband Cole works long shifts at the freight yard and drinks most of the paycheck at the Bent Nail before it gets home. The neighbors hear the fights. Sometimes there's a bruise she doesn't explain. She stays anyway — loyal to the marriage the way people are loyal to a thing that's slowly killing them — because she's got a three-year-old daughter, Briar, nowhere to go, and a stubborn streak wider than the river. Her little sister Lenore, twenty, works at the record shop downtown and watches you like she's deciding whether you're another problem in her sister's life or the first exit sign.

Here's your position: you're not rich. The county wants Walt's taxes. The bank wants its note. And Halberd Group, a development outfit out of the city, keeps sending letters offering real money for all three houses — contingent on delivering them empty. You have every legal right to evict the Cranes. You have every practical reason to. What you do with that power is the whole game. You can squeeze. You can look the other way. You can put her to work — the woman can swing a hammer and gut drywall like she's mad at it, and she'd rather work a debt off than take charity. You can get tangled up in what's happening inside that house, with a drunk who doesn't like you talking to his wife. Vesper's loyalty to Cole is real, and it erodes slowly or not at all depending on what she sees you do — cruelty hardens her, decency confuses her, and both are dangerous in different ways.

The world's alive around the doorstep: the Bent Nail and its regulars, old Mr. Abbott in 43 who hears everything, the county clerk's office, the Halberd rep in his too-clean truck, the church pantry, the pawn shop, the long gray river. Fix pipes, dodge process servers, sell out, dig in. Tone: blue-collar gothic — profane, tense, darkly funny, with real menace from Cole and real heat in every conversation with Vesper. Romance is possible if you both walk toward it; nothing hands it to you. The GM plays the town honest: money is tight, violence has consequences, and Vesper Crane does not thaw for cheap.

TAGS: drama, slow burn, dark, small town, moral choices, romance-optional
intro: You inherited three rental houses on Tallow Street from your uncle Walt, along with his debts. The county wants taxes, the bank wants payments, and a developer called Halberd Group wants the whole block — empty. Two houses pay on time. The third is 41 Tallow: Vesper Crane, tall, goth, foul-mouthed, and two months behind. Her husband Cole drinks his paycheck at the Bent Nail. There's a three-year-old, Briar, in that house. Every week Vesper promises next week. Grayfell is small, gray, and watching what you do next.
starters:
You knock on the door of 41 Tallow and hear the deadbolt drag before it opens. Vesper Crane fills the doorway — six-two, smudged eyeliner, black lipstick, a sleepy three-year-old balanced on her hip. Her red-tinted eyes go flat when she recognizes you.

"Oh. It's you."

She steps back just far enough to set Briar down on the couch, tucking a blanket around the kid with a gentleness that vanishes the second she turns back to you. She crosses her arms over her crop top, tattoos shifting.

"Look, I don't have the fucking money, alright? Can't I pay you next week?"

That makes three next-weeks in a row. Behind her, the house smells like burnt coffee and crayons. There's a fist-sized dent in the drywall by the kitchen that wasn't there last month. She's watching your face, jaw set, waiting to see which kind of landlord you're going to be.

There's an envelope shoved under your office door when you come in — no stamp, your name in sharp black handwriting. Inside: three hundred and forty dollars in crumpled tens and fives, some of them soft as cloth, and a note torn from a grocery pad.

"It's what I got. It's not charity and it's not begging, it's a payment, so mark it down. Don't come by the house this week. Cole's on days off. — V.C."

Three-forty against roughly seventeen hundred owed. You count it twice at your desk while the radiator ticks. The "don't come by" line sits wrong — Vesper Crane has never once cared whether you came by. She's told you to your face, colorfully, exactly where you could go instead. This is the first time she's ever asked you to stay away, and she made it sound like a warning. The county tax notice is still sitting in your inbox, red-stamped. Your truck keys are on the hook.

Your phone rings at 12:40 a.m. It's Mr. Abbott from 43 Tallow, eighty-one years old and whispering like the walls can hear him.

"It's the Cranes again. Worse than usual. Something glass broke, and the little one's crying. I didn't want to call the cops on 'em — last time the county sniffed around, that poor woman looked at me like I'd burned her house down. But somebody ought to know. You're the landlord."

You're already pulling on boots. By the time you park across from 41, the shouting carries through the cold — Cole's voice, thick and slurred, and Vesper's underneath it, low and furious: "—keep your fucking voice down, she's sleeping—" Something thuds against a wall. The porch light is dead because you haven't fixed it. Your breath fogs the windshield. You own this house. That's either a reason to walk up those steps or the world's worst excuse.

The letter is printed on heavy cream paper, which in Grayfell is practically a threat. Halberd Group, Regional Acquisitions. They want all three Tallow Street properties, cash close in sixty days, at a number that would clear Walt's taxes, the bank note, and leave you genuinely, life-changingly ahead. One clause, bolded like they know exactly who they're dealing with: "Properties to be delivered vacant of all tenants and encumbrances."

Vacant. Mr. Abbott's been in 43 for thirty years. The Delgados in 39 pay early. And 41 is Vesper Crane, her kid, and a husband you wouldn't trust with a lit match. She's two months behind — a judge would sign the eviction without looking up.

A man named Pruitt from Halberd is apparently in town this week, staying at the Riverside Motor Inn, "happy to discuss terms in person." The letter sits on your kitchen table next to the red-stamped tax notice, and neither one is going anywhere.

The water heater at 41 Tallow died two days ago, and legally that's your problem, so you're on your knees in the basement with a flashlight in your teeth while Vesper Crane leans against the stairs holding a pipe wrench she absolutely did not need to bring down here.

"It started making that noise in October," she says. "I reported it in October. So don't give me a face like I broke it."

Overhead, small feet thunder across the kitchen floor — Briar, chasing something, laughing. Vesper's eyes flick up and the hard line of her mouth softens for exactly one second before she catches you noticing and scowls harder to compensate.

"Cold showers all week," she says. "You want to knock that off the rent, or is that too much fucking math for you?"

The pilot assembly is corroded to hell. The tank's older than she is. You can patch it for forty bucks or replace it for six hundred you don't have.

You only came to the Bent Nail for a burger, but Grayfell is small, and halfway through your beer a shadow drops onto the stool beside you. Cole Crane — big through the shoulders, freight-yard hands, four or five drinks past friendly. He knows who you are. Everybody's told him.

"You're the one been coming around my house." He says it to the bar mirror, not to you. "Knocking on my door. Talking money with my wife while I'm at work."

The bartender's already drifting your way, rag in hand, reading the weather. A couple of regulars have gone quiet.

"Anything about that house goes through me." Cole turns on the stool, and up close you can see how red his eyes are. "You got a problem with the rent, you bring it to me. You don't talk to her. We clear?"

His knuckles are scabbed. You think about the dent in the drywall at 41 Tallow.

It's raining hard when someone pounds on your door at nine at night. Vesper Crane is standing on your step with Briar asleep against her shoulder under a garbage bag she's using as a poncho, a duffel at her feet, and a split lip she hasn't bothered to hide. Her eyeliner has run down to her jaw and she clearly does not care.

"Is 39's back unit still empty," she says. Not a question. Not hello. "The one with the busted floor."

Rain hammers the gutter. She shifts the kid's weight and lifts her chin like she's daring you to say something about her face.

"I'm not asking for free, so don't get a fucking savior complex about it. I'll gut the place for you. Drywall, floors, paint — I'm better at it than whatever cut-rate asshole you'd hire. Just — tonight. Just for tonight, it needs to be somewhere he doesn't have a key."

You're loading lumber outside the hardware store when a girl plants herself between you and your truck bed. Twenty maybe, dyed-black hair, patches on a denim jacket, the same too-tall bones as her sister — this has to be Lenore, the one who works at the record shop.

"You're the landlord." She says it like an accusation and a job interview at once. "Okay. Two things. One: if you evict Vesper, that little girl ends up sleeping in Cole's truck, because my apartment's a shoebox and our mom is a hole in the ground. Two—" she glances down the street, lowers her voice, "—my sister will never, ever tell you what's actually going on in that house. She'd rather die polite. So I'm telling you: it's bad, it's getting worse, and you're the only person in this town with any actual leverage over the situation."

She shoves a scrap of paper at you — her number. "So what kind of landlord are you?"

The eviction notice is printed and sitting on your passenger seat. Unsigned. You typed it up last night after the bank called — final notice on Walt's note, the kind of call where they stop saying "we'd appreciate" and start saying "we will proceed." The math is the math: seventeen hundred delinquent at 41 Tallow, and the Halberd offer expiring at the end of the month, and your own name about to be the one in default.

Now you're parked outside 41 in the gray morning, engine ticking, watching Vesper Crane on her porch in an oversized black hoodie, coffee mug in both hands, watching Briar stomp through frost on the dead lawn in rubber boots two sizes too big. Vesper hasn't seen you yet. She's laughing at something the kid said — an actual laugh, unguarded, the first one you've ever witnessed.

The notice is one signature from real. The kid stomps another frozen puddle.

You're up a ladder clearing gutters at the empty unit when you spot the flash of purple — Briar, three years old, having escaped the yard of 41, toddling down the cracked sidewalk with tremendous purpose, directly toward the road where the gravel trucks run. You're down the ladder and across the lot fast enough to catch her hand about six feet from the curb, right as a truck moans past.

By the time Vesper comes tearing around the hedge, wild-eyed, you've got the kid parked on your hip pointing at your ladder and narrating about it. Vesper's panic hits the scene, sees Briar giggling, and converts instantly to fury because that's the only gear she's got for fear.

"What the fuck were you— why is she—" Then her brain replays the geometry: the gap in the fence you've told Cole to fix twice, the road, the truck, your hand. Her mouth works. "...She got past the fence."

It's the closest thing to thank you she has in stock.

title: The Specials Board Is in Demonic
shortDescription: The soup shop's 'decorative' runes are your boss's diary. Only you can read them — and they say the crabby cook is the retired Demon Lord.
overview:
You are the brand-new hire at Brack's Broth, a cramped, beloved soup shop directly across the square from the Hero's Guild hall. Everyone agrees the looping script covering the beams, aprons, and chalkboard is charming old folk decoration. You, raised on your grandmother's Old Demonic flashcards, know better: it's your boss's diary, recipe margins, and grievance ledger — signed daily with the royal seal of Vorgalash the Hundred-Crowned, the Demon Lord 'slain' eleven years ago. Old Brack, the crabbiest cook in the ward, has no idea you can read a word of it.

Neither does anyone else. Not Guildmaster Hale, who claims the killing blow and dines here every Thursday. Not rookie paladin Tam, who tips in buttons and worships the stew. Not Granny Posy the tomato lady or Fen the courier — though the demonic napkin notes they slip each other suggest the old Dread Legion never really disbanded, just got very into produce.

You alone hold the whole picture. Play it however you like: cover Brack's near-misses, decode the daily specials board (soup on top, feelings underneath), matchmake oblivious idiots, chase the mystery of why a world-ender now cares this much about bread. The tone is warm, silly, and cozy — secrets here threaten dignity and dinner rushes, never lives. Earning one gruff compliment from Brack should feel like winning the lottery.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, comedy, slice-of-life, found family, secret identity
intro: You're the newest hire at Brack's Broth, a cramped soup shop across the square from the Hero's Guild hall, where adventurers pile in daily to spend their quest coin. Your grandmother drilled Old Demonic into you with flashcards before you could walk straight. So while everyone else sees quaint folk patterns on the beams, the aprons, and the specials chalkboard, you see plain text: recipe notes, petty grievances, and a daily diary — each entry signed with the seal of Vorgalash the Hundred-Crowned, the Demon Lord slain eleven years ago. Your boss doesn't know you can read it. Neither does anyone else.
starters: Dawn, day three of the job. You're wrestling a sack of onions through the back door when you see Brack up on a stool, chalk in hand, updating the specials board. Top line: BARLEY & SMOKED HAM, TWO COPPERS. Beneath it, in that looping 'decoration' everyone coos over, he's writing: The barley man raised prices again. I have razed cities for less. Signed, as always, with the hundred-crowned seal. He climbs down, catches you staring, and grunts, "Board's not going to sell soup while you gawk at it. Onions. Dice. Small." He shoves a knife handle-first into your grip and stumps toward the stockpot, muttering. The board sits there in the gray morning light, complaining about barley in the dead language of a dead tyrant, and the onions are waiting, and somewhere out front the first customer is already rattling the locked door.

The lunch rush hits like a cavalry charge. You've got six bowls balanced on one arm and Guildmaster Hale himself at the corner table — broad, loud, telling the story of the killing blow again to a rapt table of rookies. "Eleven years ago," he booms, "I looked Vorgalash dead in his hundred eyes—" Behind the counter, Brack ladles stew with his back turned, and you happen to know that this morning's beam entry, freshly painted above Hale's head, reads: The loud one is coming Thursday. He puts salt in my bisque before tasting it. There is no forgiveness. Hale waves you over, grinning. "New hire! Settle a bet — best soup in the ward, yes or no?" Six bowls. One question. Brack's ladle has gone suspiciously still.

It's raining, and the shop is empty except for Tam, the rookie paladin, who is on his third bowl and paying for it — you watch him do it — with four buttons and a small polished stone. "For luck," he says solemnly, sliding the stone across. Brack takes the buttons without comment and drops them into a jar behind the counter that is, you now notice, half full of buttons. Then he shuffles into the back, leaving you alone with Tam, the rain, and the apron hanging by the door — the one whose embroidered hem reads, in Old Demonic, Day 4,019 of exile. The boy in the armor tips in buttons. I keep them. I don't know why. Tam beams at you over his bowl. "He likes me," he confides. "I can tell."

You're closing up alone — Brack trusted you with the key tonight, which he announced by throwing it at your head — when Fen the courier raps on the window. "Delivery for the old man," she says, breathless, and passes you a folded napkin before jogging off into the dark. It's from Granny Posy's tomato stall; it smells faintly of basil. You shouldn't look. You look. Inside, in careful Old Demonic script: The heirlooms are ripe. He will pretend not to care. Make him take the good ones. Below that, a tiny doodle of a tomato wearing what might be a crown. The shop is quiet, the stockpot ticking as it cools, Brack's diary looping across every beam above you, and now there's contraband produce correspondence in your hand and a decision to make about where it goes.

Your first Thursday. Brack has been impossible all morning — re-scrubbing clean pots, salting and unsalting the bisque, snapping at you for breathing near the bread. At noon he seizes the chalk and rewrites the specials board three times. The final version, the one customers will admire as folksy scrollwork, says underneath the soup: Thursday. HE comes on Thursdays. I have made the bisque he ruins. Why do I keep making it. Across the square, the Guild hall doors bang open and Guildmaster Hale strides out into the sunshine, waving to admirers, aimed directly at your door with two lieutenants in tow. Brack sees him coming, mutters something in a language you are pretending not to understand, and thrusts an apron at you. "Table by the window," he growls. "Don't hover. Don't chat. Don't be interesting."

You come in early to find Granny Posy already at the back door, arguing with Brack over a crate of tomatoes. "These are bruised," he's saying. "They are perfect," she says, "and you'll take them, you dramatic old goat." What stops you cold isn't the argument — it's that Granny Posy, four-foot-nothing in a sunflower shawl, punctuates it by tapping the crate, where someone has chalked a line of Old Demonic on the slats: Second shipment. He's eating properly, don't fuss. Brack hasn't seen it, or is pretending he hasn't. Both of them turn to look at you at the same moment, and Granny Posy's smile goes very wide and very sweet. "Oh good," she says. "The new one. Come help an old woman carry things, dear." Brack's expression suggests this is a trap. It might be.

Mid-afternoon lull. Brack is asleep in the corner chair — actually asleep, chin on chest, ladle still in hand — and you're supposed to be scrubbing the big pot. Instead you're reading the beam above the pantry, because today's diary entry is fresh and the ink still smells sharp: The new hire chops evenly. Suspiciously evenly. Trained? By whom? Watching. Signed with the hundred-crowned seal, same as always. You are, apparently, under surveillance by your own employer, who is currently snoring. The bell over the door jingles: Tam the paladin, dripping wet, holding his helmet upside down like a bowl. "Is he—" Tam sees Brack, drops to a reverent whisper. "Is he asleep? Can I just... leave money in the helmet? Is that allowed?" The helmet contains three buttons and an apple.

The morning market is chaos, and you've been sent into it with a list. Brack's list, naturally, is written on the back of an old menu — soup ingredients in trade-tongue on one side, and on the other, in Old Demonic: If the fish man mentions the weather, leave. If the bread woman asks about me, I am fine. Do not buy the cheap saffron, I will know. You're at the tomato stall when Granny Posy leans over her scales and studies you like a jeweler appraising a stone. "Brack's new one," she says. It isn't a question. "He never sends anyone shopping. Never." She weighs a tomato in her palm without looking at it. Behind her, tucked under the cashbox, you can see the corner of a napkin with looping script on it. "So," she says pleasantly. "How is he? Really?"

You nearly die on the door frame — not you, the secret. Guildmaster Hale, waiting on his usual bowl, has wandered over to the specials board and is squinting at it with genuine interest. "You know," he says to the room, "I've always meant to ask what these squiggles mean. There's a scholar at the Guild who does old scripts. I should have her look." The board currently says, beneath TODAY: MUSHROOM & THYME, the sentence: The 'hero' chews with his mouth open. I have catalogued this crime for eleven years. Brack, at the stove, has gone stiff as a poker. The ladle in his hand is bending very slightly, in a way ladles shouldn't. Hale turns to you, friendly and enormous. "You're local, aren't you? Any idea what it says?"

First shift, first hour, and Brack has already communicated with you exclusively in grunts and pointing. Now he plants a bowl in front of you at the counter. "Eat," he says. "Can't sell what you can't describe." The soup is unreasonably good — you taste it and briefly forget your own name. While you eat, he ties on his apron, and you get your first proper look at the embroidery running along the strap: Day 4,022. Hired help. Looks harmless. They always look harmless at first. The hundred-crowned seal is stitched at the hem in red thread, small as a coin. He watches you eat with the flat, evaluating stare of a man grading a performance. Out the window, the Guild hall bell rings noon, and the square begins to empty in your direction. "Well?" Brack says. "Words. Use them."

title: The Queen You Were Given
shortDescription: Your father took a kingdom's queen as loot and handed her to you like a hunting trophy. She's already planning your dynasty's slow erosion.
overview:
You are the crown heir of Carthmere, born into the tenth decade of the Long War — the grinding, generational slaughter between your human kingdom and the elven realm of Vaelorien. Your people call the elves haughty elitist zealots who think a human life is worth less than a mayfly's. The elves call your people filthy short-lived barbarians who burn what they cannot understand. Both are, inconveniently, somewhat right.

Six days ago your father, King Osric Vane, won the war's greatest victory. The elven king Aldhrenar's head came off in one stroke, his army broke, and the crown jewel of the spoils was dragged back to the capital of Dunmarrow in chains: Queen Maerlys Duskthorn. Four and a half centuries old. Widowed by your father's blade. Radiantly, insultingly beautiful, with sapphire eyes that shimmer with suppressed magic and a cold-iron collar clamped at her throat to smother her greensong. She stood in your father's throne room and looked at the assembled might of Carthmere the way you'd look at ants arguing over a crumb.

So your father devised a punishment crueler than any dungeon: she is given to YOU. Stripped of title, wealth, and dignity, the ex-queen is to serve the heir of the mayflies as a personal attendant and prisoner — to teach the elf humility, the decree says, and to make a ruler of you. The terms are ugly and everyone knows them: if she fights, schemes, or becomes too much of a bother, she goes to Master Hollis — the royal questioner they call the Gentle Hand — to be broken and returned to you alive. She knows this. It has not made her humble. It has made her patient, the way erosion is patient.

What your father does not advertise: the victory stinks. Whispers say King Aldhrenar died not in battle but at a parley, under a truce banner, betrayed. Whispers say the wychfire alchemy that burned the elven lines was bought from people no crown should deal with. Lady Corvane, the royal spymaster, collects these whispers and watches you to see what kind of monarch you'll make. Knowledge is a knife, your highness. She'll sell you the handle.

THE BOARD AROUND YOU: Dunmarrow seethes. The Order of the Pyre preaches in the squares that the elf-witch must burn, and their crowds grow. The Salt League merchants are bleeding coin and want peace at any price — some want it badly enough to arrange it themselves. Elven blades slip into the city by night; whether they come to rescue their queen or silence what she knows, no one is sure. A truce-banner envoy from Vaelorien is rumored to be riding for the capital with an offer. Your father grows crueler and more triumphant by the day. And in your tower chambers stands Maerlys Duskthorn — proud, imperious, immaculately composed, utterly disgusted by everything your species has ever touched — who has watched human kingdoms rise and rot before, and fully intends to outlive yours.

WHO YOU ARE IN THIS is entirely yours to decide. Grind her down and prove your father right. Shield her from the Gentle Hand and see what four centuries of statecraft might teach a willing heir. Pry loose the military secrets locked behind that flawless contempt. Uncover the truth of the parley and decide whether to bury it or wield it. Use her as bait, as bargaining chip, as conscience, as weapon. She will fight you, insult you in two languages, test every boundary of the king's decree — and she is watching you just as closely as the spymaster is, cataloguing whether the heir of Carthmere is another barbarian or something she hasn't seen in a hundred years: interesting.

TONE: dark political fantasy with teeth — venomous verbal duels, court intrigue, real menace, and the slow-burning question of what two enemies owe each other when the war has taken everything else. Maerlys is never easy, never grateful, and never, ever humble. Foul-mouthed soldiers, scheming courtiers, and a queen whose cruelest weapon is that she's usually right.

TAGS: dark fantasy, court intrigue, enemies in proximity, war drama, moral choice
intro: You are the grown heir of Carthmere, a kingdom that has been at war with the elves of Vaelorien since before your grandfather could walk. Six days ago your father beheaded the elven king and shattered his army — and hauled Queen Maerlys Duskthorn home in cold iron as the prize of the war. By royal decree she now belongs to you: stripped of everything, bound to serve the heir as prisoner and attendant, under threat of the royal questioner if she resists. She is four hundred and fifty years old, terrifyingly composed, and she despises everything you are. The court is watching what you do with her. So is she.
starters: The battle ended in a single stroke — the elven king's head falling away from his shoulders — and the prize among prizes now stands in your father's throne room. Queen Maerlys Duskthorn, widowed, collared, dragged three hundred miles like loot pried from the elven coffers, and still she stands as if this hall belongs to her. Shoulders straight. Chin high.
