title: Previous Owner Included
shortDescription: Every antique in your shop still carries its dead owner — and only you can hear them. Sell each soul into the right hands. Never get caught.
overview:
You run a cramped secondhand antique shop on a street that's half shuttered. Your trade secret: every piece arrives occupied. The dead cling to what they loved — a thimble, a mirror, a chair worn to their shape — and you're the only living person who hears them. When an object sells, its owner goes with it. Sold to the right buyer, a ghost finally lets go. Sold wrong, you've handed a soul to a stranger forever. So you interview your stock, vet your customers like a paranoid matchmaker, and lie to absolutely everyone about why you never misprice a lot.

The back room has regulars: Miklos, a gossipy old tailor riding a brass thimble; Dame Ilse, a vain opera singer in a hand mirror who refuses to be sold to anyone badly dressed. Among the living: Priya from the café next door, who's noticed you talk when the shop is empty, and Duncan, a rival picker who's decided your 'luck' isn't luck and has started following your buys.

This week, an estate clearance dumped Vera Kessling's whole life into your storeroom. Vera insists her fall down the stairs had help — and a courteous man named Ostrander keeps coming in, paying cash, asking after a small green enamel box. Tone: cozy-eerie, wry, quietly human. The gameplay is your poker face.

TAGS: urban fantasy, mystery, ghosts, double life, slice of life, cozy-eerie
intro: You own a narrow antique shop at the quiet end of a fading high street, and you have never told a living soul the truth of your trade: every object here still carries its previous owner. The dead stay with what they loved, and you alone can hear them — arguing, gossiping, grieving on your shelves. A sale transfers the ghost with the goods, so you choose your buyers carefully; the right hands can set an owner free. To your customers you're just an oddly perceptive dealer with uncanny luck. It has to stay that way. The last person who found out did not take it well.
starters: Tuesday, half past nine, and the estate van is still idling outside while two movers stack the last of Vera Kessling's life in your storeroom. Boxes of linens, a wall clock, a sewing table, forty years of a house folded into cardboard. The moment the door swings shut behind the movers, the noise starts — one voice, sharp and certain, cutting through the usual shelf-chatter: "I did not fall. I want that understood before anyone touches my things. I was pushed." From the front room, Miklos's thimble pipes up that the new arrival has been saying this since dawn and shows no sign of stopping. Dame Ilse complains the acoustics in her mirror are being ruined. Somewhere under the linens, something small and metal shifts in a box. The kettle you put on ten minutes ago has gone cold, and the shop opens in half an hour.

The bell over the door rings at four minutes past opening, and it's him again — the courteous man, hat in hand, cash already visible in his wallet like a promise. 'Ostrander,' he reminds you pleasantly, as if you'd forget a man who's been in three times this week. "Still looking for that little box. Green enamel, about so big. Sentimental value, you understand." Behind you, from the storeroom you haven't finished unpacking, Vera Kessling's voice rises to a pitch only you can hear: "That's him. That is HIM. Do not sell that man so much as a teaspoon." Ostrander browses the front table with the patience of a man who has all day, turning over a candlestick, a fish knife, a cracked snuff tin. He picks up a saucer and glances at you, eyebrows raised, waiting for a price.

You're mid-interview when the shop bell rings. In the back room, a rosewood music box from the Kessling estate has just admitted, shyly, that it belonged to Vera's late husband and would quite like to go to someone who dances — and now Priya from the café is standing in your doorway with two coffees and an expression you don't love. "You were talking," she says, not quite a question. "Full sentences. I could hear you through the wall again." She sets a cup on the counter, on the house, the way she does when she's fishing. Behind you, the music box is still going — "ask her if she dances, ask her" — and Vera Kessling's voice cuts over it from a crate of linens: "Is that girl trustworthy? Because I have things to say and you keep ignoring me." Priya sips her coffee and waits.

Rain's been coming down since noon, and the shop smells of wet wool and lamp oil. You're at the counter with the Kessling inventory list, trying to match boxes to voices, when Miklos clears his throat — a dry little sound from the thimble tray. "The new lady," he says. "Vera. She has been telling me about her staircase. Sixty years a tailor, I know when a story has a loose thread, and hers holds together. Someone was in the house." Across the shelf, Dame Ilse sniffs that everyone claims to have been murdered, it's very fashionable, and could someone please angle her mirror away from the damp. Through the window, across the street, a figure stands under the awning of the shuttered chemist's. He's been there twenty minutes. You recognize the coat: Duncan, the picker, watching your shop the way he watched you at the Hollis auction. The rain shows no sign of stopping.

You're closing up — lights half off, till counted — when the storeroom finally gets loud enough that you give in and go back there with a candle and a chair. Vera Kessling's things fill four shelves and most of the floor. Her voice comes from somewhere in the middle of it, clipped and schoolteacherly: "Good. You're listening. I fell down my own stairs, they said. Thirty-one years in that house and I never once missed a step. Now. Somewhere in these boxes is a green enamel box, small, with a brass clasp, and I need to know if it made it here before anyone else does." Out front, Dame Ilse calls that there's a face at the darkened window — a man peering in past the CLOSED sign, hands cupped to the glass. The candle gutters. Vera says, quieter: "Well? Are you going to look, or am I?"

The auction hall in the next town smells of instant coffee and mildew, and you're three lots away from the one you came for: a job lot of household oddments, box 47, from which a small frightened voice has been whispering since you walked past the preview table. First time out, by the sound of it — a new ghost, barely holding on to whatever it loves in that box. Two rows ahead, Duncan turns in his seat and gives you a friendly, terrible smile. He's not bid on anything all morning. He's just been watching what you look at, the way he's been doing for weeks. Your phone buzzes: Priya, minding your shop as a favor, texting that "a polite man in a good coat" is asking when you'll be back and won't say why. The auctioneer's gavel comes down on lot 44. Duncan raises his paddle to his temple in a little salute.

Saturday morning, and for once the shop has actual customers: a young couple circling the Kessling sewing table, a man in reading glasses examining the barometer, and a woman holding Dame Ilse's hand mirror up to the light. Ilse is in raptures — "the coat is bespoke, the earrings are real, oh, ASK if she sings" — while from the storeroom Vera Kessling keeps up a running commentary on everything the couple touches: "That table was my mother's. Are their hands clean? They look like renters." Miklos, for his part, is trying to tell you something urgent about a conversation he overheard between two clocks, but you can't answer any of them, because the man in reading glasses has just brought the barometer to the counter and asked, casually, why a piece like this is priced so precisely at forty-three pounds and not forty-five.

You find the note when you unlock the shop: a folded card pushed through the letterbox, good stationery, neat hand. "Regarding the Kessling estate — I understand you took the clearance. I am seeking one small item of purely personal significance and will pay well above value. I will call again this afternoon. — H. Ostrander." You've barely read it twice before the storeroom erupts. Vera Kessling, three days dead-and-arrived and already the loudest thing you own, wants the note read aloud, wants the handwriting described, wants to know if he signed it with that horrid fountain pen. 'Ostrander,' she says, and her voice goes strange — flatter, careful. "He was in my house the week before I fell." Out on the pavement, Priya is unstacking café chairs and waves at you through the glass, mouthing something about the man who was "lurking by your door at seven this morning."

Duncan doesn't even pretend anymore. He's standing in your shop with his hands in his pockets, looking at the Kessling boxes stacked behind the counter, and he says, "Hollis auction. The Braithwaite house sale. That car boot in March. Every time, you walk past the good stuff and buy some piece of tat, and every time the tat turns out to be worth ten times the ticket. That's not an eye. Nobody's eye is that good." Miklos, from the thimble tray, offers helpfully that this man's jacket seams are machine-finished and he shouldn't be trusted. Dame Ilse wants him gone; he blocks her light. Duncan picks up a chipped Kessling teacup — inside which the ghost of a very small dog begins, faintly, to growl — turns it over, and reads the price. "Eight quid," he says. "So what's actually in it?" The bell over the door hasn't stopped swaying.

It's the dead hour after lunch, and Priya's leaning in your doorway on her break, telling you the street gossip: the chemist's is definitely not reopening, the landlord's been sniffing around the empty shops, and — she lowers her voice — "there's a bloke who's had coffee at my window seat three days running, watches your door the whole time, tips exactly ten percent. Nice coat. Bit funereal." Behind her, out of her sight and hearing, the entire back room is arguing about the same man. Miklos says he has the shoulders of someone who used to lift things for a living, whatever the coat says. Vera Kessling says his name is Ostrander, that he drank tea in her parlor twice, and that if he asks after a green enamel box you are to lie with your whole chest. Priya sips her coffee and adds, "He asked me your name this morning. I said I'd forgotten it."

title: Her Pulse Is Public Record
shortDescription: The colossus under the city has a heartbeat, posted downtown like weather. It's speeding up — and you're the only official she'll answer.
overview:
You are Cariath's Municipal Liaison to the Resident — the living mountain the city was built across three centuries ago, kept asleep by the Concord: verses sung, tribute lowered, dreams logged. The post was ceremonial. Was. The Pulse Tower posts her heartbeat interval like a weather report; it has fallen from thirty-one hours to nineteen in a month, and when it reaches nine, she opens her eyes. Your predecessor, Liaison Marec, walked down the Stair three weeks ago and never came back up. His half-burned ledger is in your desk. And unlike every liaison in the record, she has begun answering you — in the audience vault, and lately in your sleep, wearing your own memories like borrowed clothes.

Something broke the Concord, and the city is lying about what. Speaker Odile Vann won't say 'evacuation' where a journalist can hear it. Warden Cress Ipp, keeper of the Descent gates, believes Marec found something rotten in the tribute manifests. The Waking Choir sings on street corners that she deserves the morning. You hold signing authority: any promise you make her binds Cariath, no council vote required. And every audience costs a heartbeat you can't get back.

Tone: grounded gaslamp civic fantasy — Shin Godzilla bureaucracy meets a slow, intimate conversation with something the size of a weather system. The GM should reward bold offers and big swings; the clock punishes stalling, and caution is its own catastrophe.

TAGS: kaiju, ticking clock, political intrigue, mystery, negotiation, urban fantasy
intro: You are the Municipal Liaison to the Resident — the official who walks the long Stair beneath Cariath to sing the Concord verses to the sleeping colossus the city stands on. For three hundred years the job was ritual: descend, sing, log her dreams, climb back to daylight. Now the Pulse Tower's great dial is falling — her heartbeat comes every nineteen hours and shortening, and the old almanac is blunt about what nine means. Your predecessor vanished on the Stair last month; you inherited his office, his brass key, and his half-burned ledger. And lately, against all precedent, she has begun to answer you — even in your dreams.
starters: The Pulse Tower bell rings the interval change at six minutes past noon, and the whole of Cathedral Square stops to watch the dial hands crawl backward: nineteen hours, down from twenty. You're halfway across the square with Marec's ledger under your arm when Warden Cress Ipp falls into step beside you, smelling of gate-oil and cold stone. "Don't look up like the rest of them," she says quietly. "Look at me. Your predecessor pulled three tribute manifests from my archive the week before he went down. They came back to me yesterday, in a plain envelope, with pages missing." She presses the envelope into your hand without breaking stride. Around you, a Waking Choir trio has started up on the fountain steps — *she deserves the morning, she has earned the sun* — and two constables are already moving toward them. Ipp stops at the mouth of Descent Lane and waits to see which way you turn.

You wake at your desk with the taste of granite in your mouth and someone else's memory dissolving behind your eyes — a summer festival you never attended, lanterns on a street that hasn't existed for two hundred years. She was wearing your tenth birthday over it like a coat. The office lamp has burned down to nothing. On the blotter, exactly where you didn't leave it, Marec's half-burned ledger lies open to a page you haven't read: columns of tribute weights, and beside one entry his handwriting, pressed hard enough to tear the paper — "ASK IPP WHAT ACTUALLY GOES IN THE CRATES." Through the window, the Pulse Tower's dial glows over the rooftops. Someone is knocking at your door — has been knocking, you realize, for a while — and a voice you recognize as Speaker Vann's secretary calls that the Speaker requires you at the Hall within the hour.

Nineteen steps from the bottom, you can already hear her breathing — a tide moving through rock, slower than anything alive should be. You've made this descent eleven times since taking the post, and the Stair has never felt this warm. In the audience vault, the tribute crate from yesterday sits unopened on the offering shelf, which is wrong; the offerings are always taken by morning. Your lantern picks out the vast curve of her nearer eyelid across the vault's far wall, a ridge of stone the length of a city block, and beneath it something new: condensation, beading and running like the wall is sweating. The Concord's first verse is in your throat, learned by rote before you understood a word of it. But the last time you sang it, three days ago, she answered — one word, felt in your teeth more than heard — and the almanac has nothing to say about what you're supposed to do with that.

Speaker Odile Vann has rearranged her office so the window behind her shows the Pulse Tower, which means every meeting now happens with the falling dial over her shoulder like a threat she didn't have to speak. "The word you will not use in this building," she says, sliding a single sheet across the desk toward you, "is the one that starts riots. What you will do is go down the Stair tonight, sing the verses, and file a report I can read aloud to the council with a straight face." The sheet is a drafted statement in your name: *the interval fluctuation is seasonal; the Concord holds.* It's dated tomorrow. Behind you, a clerk you don't recognize is quietly copying something from your predecessor's personnel file into a notebook. Vann uncaps a pen and holds it out to you, and the dial over her shoulder reads nineteen hours, and falling.

The Waking Choir has taken the steps of your own office building this morning — eleven of them in undyed wool, singing the Concord verses backward, which shouldn't work and shouldn't raise the hair on your arms the way it does. A crowd is gathering. Their leader, a broad man with mining scars on both hands, spots the liaison's chain at your collar and stops singing mid-phrase; the others carry on around his silence. "You talk to her," he says. It isn't a question. "Marec talked to us, before the end. He said the tribute's a lie and the sleep's a theft. Then the city ate him." Behind him, through your building's glass doors, you can see your secretary on the telephone — to the constabulary, almost certainly. The man holds out a folded paper. "Her answer, if you'll carry a question down for us. That's all we ask. One question."

It's four in the morning and the whole city shudders — not an earthquake, the almanac is very clear on the distinction — a single rolling flex, like something enormous shifting in its sleep. You're on the street outside the Pulse Tower before you've fully dressed, and you're not alone: the duty clerks are out on the steps in their nightshirts, watching the dial. It ticks down while you watch. Eighteen hours, fifty-one minutes. A milk cart has stopped in the middle of the road, horse trembling, driver gone. Somewhere south a bell starts ringing the pattern that means *structural inspection*, and nobody rings it back to say all-clear. The Tower's senior clerk sees your chain of office and comes down the steps two at a time, holding the night's dream-log transcription. "It's addressed," he says, thrusting it at you. "The dream. Three hundred years of logs and it's never been addressed. It has your name in it."

Warden Cress Ipp meets you at the Descent gates an hour before your scheduled audience, which she has never done, holding a lantern and a crowbar. "Before you go down," she says, "you should see what you're singing over." She leads you off the Stair's first landing, through a service door older than her keys, into a tribute staging room stacked with this month's crates. One is open. You were told — everyone is told — that tribute is grain, honey, worked silver, the good and honest weight of the city's gratitude. What's in the crate is packed in grey clay and smells like a struck match. "Marec opened one of these," Ipp says. "Three days later he went down and didn't come up. I've got the manifest he signed and the manifest the council filed, and they don't match." Below you, down the dark of the Stair, the mountain draws a breath you can feel through your boots.

The audience vault, hour nineteen. You've sung the second verse twice and your lantern oil is a quarter gone when the answer comes — not the tremor-and-silence the logs describe, but words, arriving inside your skull dressed in your own mother's voice, which she has no right to. "THE SMALL ONE BEFORE YOU MADE ME AN OFFER," she says. "HE DID NOT COME BACK TO KEEP IT. WILL YOU KEEP IT FOR HIM, OR SHALL WE BEGIN AGAIN?" Your signing authority hangs at your collar, the seal that binds Cariath to any word you give. Marec's ledger is upstairs in your desk, half its pages ash, and whatever he promised her isn't in the half that survived. The vault is very warm. Somewhere far above, the Pulse Tower is logging this heartbeat — one more spent, one fewer left — and she is waiting, patient as geology, for you to open your mouth.

The journalist catches you on the Pulse Tower's observation gallery, where you've come to read the dial yourself instead of trusting the morning circular. "Devan Sorrel, the Ledger-Courier," she says, already writing. "Speaker Vann says seasonal fluctuation. The Tower's own night clerk says the interval's dropped six hours in nine days and there's no season in three centuries of records that did that. You're the one who actually goes down there." Below the gallery railing, the city spreads out along the ridges of the Resident's back — you can trace her spine in the line of Temple Row, her shoulder under the grain district. Sorrel follows your gaze. "I've also got a source at the Descent gates who says Marec's last log entry was removed from the archive. Physically cut out. So." She turns to a clean page. "On the record or off it, Liaison — what's actually happening under our feet?"

You inherit the office on a Tuesday; on Thursday you finally force the lock on Marec's desk drawer with his own brass key, which fits nothing else in the room. Inside: the half-burned ledger you were told about, a child's drawing of the mountain with a face — filed, absurdly, under official correspondence — and a tribute receipt with the quantity scratched out and rewritten three times. You've got the ledger open, trying to read fire-curled pages by lamplight, when the floor hums. Once. The ink bottle rings against its stand. Down in the street the evening traffic doesn't even pause; Cariath has learned to sleep through her turning over. But your appointment card says your first audience is tonight, hour twenty-two, and the almanac's instructions end at "sing, observe, withdraw" — nothing about what to say if she speaks first. Someone raps at the office door: Warden Ipp's voice, low, asking if you've found it yet.

title: Neither Rain Nor Sixty Years
shortDescription: You bought a sack of 'undeliverable' mail at auction — decades late, impossibly addressed. Your rickety airship disagrees with the word impossible.
overview:
You're a small-time sky courier with a wheezing, much-patched airship called the Second Notice. At a salvage auction you bid three coins on a sealed canvas sack — and won sixty years of the Aerial Post's official 'Impossibles': letters and parcels declared undeliverable because sky islands drift, towns rename themselves, and addresses like 'the bakery that smells of cinnamon, two islands sunward of the Whale Rocks' stop meaning anything. But an old charter clause still pays a bounty per Impossible delivered, and Guildmistress Opaline Vetch is contractually obligated to honor it — through gritted teeth, stamp by stamp.

So that's the game: play mail detective with fifty-year-old clues, chase islands that migrate like whales, keep the ship airborne with twine and optimism, and hand people the letters they gave up on — late wedding invitations, apologies, love confessions, a library book. Your crew is Ledger, an elderly postal albatross who remembers old routes but only cooperates when flattered, and whoever you pick up along the way. Wren the dock mechanic patches your hull for pastries; Cassian of Zephyr Express keeps 'coincidentally' showing up to watch you fail, and keeps not leaving.

GM note: keep it warm and funny. Deliveries land as laughter-through-tears reconnections, never tragedy. And at the very bottom of the sack sits the oldest envelope of all, addressed only: 'To whoever finally carries this sack.'

TAGS: cozy fantasy, slice of life, sky islands, found family, gentle mystery, comedy
intro: You are the owner, pilot, and entire staff of the Second Notice, an airship held together by patch-plates and stubbornness. Slung in the hold is your three-coin auction prize: the Impossibles — sixty years of mail the Aerial Post gave up on, because out here islands drift, villages move, and addresses go stale like bread. By ancient charter, the Guild must pay a bounty for every Impossible delivered, and Guildmistress Vetch cannot stop you from trying. Your only colleague is Ledger, a gray old postal albatross who knew these skies before the maps did. Somewhere below, sixty years of unanswered letters are waiting to be answered.
starters: The auctioneer is still laughing. So is most of the salvage yard, actually — three coins for a sealed canvas sack was apparently the joke of the afternoon, and now you get to drag your winnings across the dock while everyone watches. The sack is heavier than it looks and clinks in a papery, un-treasure-like way. Ledger rides on top of it like a figurehead, refusing to help. "Sixty years of Impossibles," the auctioneer calls after you, wiping his eyes. "Guild's been trying to burn those since before I was born. Charter won't let 'em!" That last part catches your ear. Charter won't let them. Which means the charter says something. At the yard gate, a clerk with an official Guild armband is already hurrying toward you, waving a form and looking like someone sent her to fix a mistake.

You've got the sack open on the hold floor and letters fanned out in loose piles: Weddings, Apologies, Unclear, and Smells Weird. The Second Notice hums along on autopilot, which is a rope tied to the wheel. Ledger paces the piles like an inspector, occasionally tapping an envelope with his beak. The one he keeps returning to is addressed in violet ink: "Marisol, the house with blue shutters, third island past where the herring run." The herring haven't run anywhere in decades, as far as you know, but Ledger is making a low, smug noise that usually means he remembers something and wants to be asked nicely. Outside the porthole, an island you don't recognize is drifting slowly across your route, trailing waterfalls.

Guildmistress Opaline Vetch stamps the delivery voucher like she's executing it. "One," she says. "Bounty for one Impossible. Paid under protest, witnessed, notarized." The coin she slides across the counter is warm, presumably from her grip. Behind you, the recipient of your very first delivery — a fisherman who just got his grandmother's recipe card, forty-one years late — is still crying happily into his hat and telling the whole Guild office about her chowder. Vetch's eye twitches. "How many more of these do you intend to inflict on this institution?" You think of the sack in your hold. Hundreds, easily. Ledger, perched on the counter, preens in a way that can only be described as gloating. The queue behind you is getting long, and Vetch's stamp is hovering.

Rain hammers the canopy and the Second Notice's port engine is doing the cough again — the one Wren specifically told you to never let it do. You're limping toward Bellhook Docks at half power with the sack of Impossibles lashed down in the hold and Ledger tucked grumpily under the chart table, radiating I-told-you-so. Through the rain you can see the dock lights, and standing under them, already holding a wrench and a look of profound disappointment, is Wren herself. She must have heard the engine from a mile out. You have exactly one pastry left in the tin, slightly squashed, and you're going to need it. The docking horn sounds. Someone waves you toward berth six, the cheap one, the one with the gap you have to sort of hop.

The first envelope you pull from the sack is soft with age and addressed in careful schoolteacher handwriting: "To Tomas, at the bakery that smells of cinnamon, two islands sunward of the Whale Rocks." The Whale Rocks are on every chart. The two islands sunward of them, per your newest map, are a quarry and an empty sky. Ledger lands on the chart table, looks at the address, and makes a sound like a rusted hinge — his I remember that route sound, the one that costs you compliments. Below the address, in different, shakier ink, someone at the Post added: RETURNED — NO SUCH SMELL. The morning is clear, the wind is fair, and the bakery letter is dated fifty-two years ago. Somewhere out there is either a very old baker or a very good story.

"Fascinating vessel," says Cassian of Zephyr Express, leaning on the dock rail beside the Second Notice like he owns the sky and is letting you borrow it. His ship gleams two berths down, all brass and smugness. "I heard someone bought the Impossibles. I assumed it was a joke. Then I heard it was you, and, well." He gestures at your hull, where a patch-plate has a patch-plate. You're halfway up the gangway with the sack over your shoulder and Ledger on the rail giving Cassian the flat stare he reserves for pigeons. "Zephyr Express delivers same-day, you know," Cassian adds. "Not same-century." A dock bell rings; your departure slot is in ten minutes, and he shows no sign of moving from directly in front of your mooring line.

It's past midnight and you can't sleep, so you're in the hold with a lantern, reading dead people's mail. Except — that's the thing. Half of these people probably aren't dead. Islands drift; they don't sink. You've got one open on your knee right now (the seal was already broken, you checked): an apology, unsigned, that just says "I should have come to the wedding. I've regretted it every day. If you ever read this, the answer was always yes, ask me again." The address is a tavern that renamed itself at least twice, on an island that migrates with the warm currents. Ledger has waddled over and is standing on the envelope, which is his version of a strong opinion. Through the hull you can hear the wind changing — the warm current is early this year.

You find the island exactly where the fifty-year-old address says it shouldn't be anymore — "Greenhollow, north of the Tin Spires" — except the sign at the dock says WELCOME TO NEW GREENHOLLOW (FORMERLY DRIFTMOOT, FORMERLY GREENHOLLOW), which raises questions. A kid fishing off the pier watches you tie up the Second Notice with the expression of someone who's never seen an airship held together with actual twine before. In your satchel: a wedding invitation, hand-painted, addressed to "Auntie Prue." The town behind the pier has one street, two goats, and a woman up a ladder repainting the sign, muttering. Ledger launches off your shoulder and lands on the pier post, wings out, doing his official Aerial Post pose for an audience of one child and a goat. The woman on the ladder has stopped painting to stare at you.

The Second Notice is losing altitude gently, the way she does when she wants attention rather than when anything's actually wrong — probably. You're elbow-deep in the ballast valve with a wrench between your teeth while Ledger stands on the gauge cluster, reading the dials, which he can absolutely do and only does when you're desperate. "Fine," you say around the wrench. "You're the finest navigator these skies have ever carried. Handsomest albatross in three currents. Now which dial?" He taps one with his beak, insufferably. Below, the Whale Rocks slide past, and beyond them you can just make out your destination for delivery number one: a fishing town clinging to a drifting island, currently drifting the wrong way. The valve, when you finally get it turning, hisses in a tone you've never heard before.

Opaline Vetch has come to your ship, which is how you know it's serious. She stands at the foot of the gangway in full Guild regalia at seven in the morning, holding a document case and refusing to touch anything. "I am legally obligated to inform you," she says, in the voice of someone chewing lemons, "of the bounty schedule, the verification procedure, and your rights under Charter Clause Eleven. I am also here to offer to buy the sack back. Ten coins. That's a threefold profit and you never have to see me again." Behind her, the dock is waking up: gulls, cargo winches, someone selling hot buns. Ledger emerges from the cabin, sees Vetch, and fluffs to twice his size. She produces a pre-written receipt, already stamped, and holds it out. Her hand, you notice, is very slightly shaking.

title: She Confiscated My Whole World
shortDescription: The school's most feared hardass confiscated the notebook holding your secret game — and read every page. Now she has questions. And a deadline.
overview:
You're a senior at Bellchase High and the sole keeper of Lanternfall — a two-player strategy game about rival hamlets trading and feuding through a long winter, invented at age eleven with your best friend Juni in their grandmother's garden, painted groundcherry husks for pieces. Juni's family left town suddenly six years ago; your letters came back unopened. You never stopped building. Every rule is an inside joke for a person who may not remember you. No living soul has read the notebook — until Imogen Price, the disciplinary committee's infamous 'Warden,' confiscated it mid-class.

Imogen is a hardass: top of the year, feared, friendless by apparent choice, someone whose love language is rules. She read all 214 pages overnight. She has questions. She has balance complaints (page 61: the ferry toll breaks the economy). She wants to playtest. And she's already found the Halloway Games Fair — an open design showcase eight weeks out that demos two-player games — because in her world, leaving a good thing unfinished is a violation.

Play the terrified joy of being seen: secret playtests in empty classrooms, school-life texture, Imogen's brutal tenderness, and the question underneath it all — is Lanternfall a shrine to Juni, or a signal flare that might actually reach them? Tone: warm, funny, achingly nostalgic; grounded and real, no melodrama. The GM runs a living school and, somewhere out there, an unanswered name on a dedication page.
TAGS: slice-of-life, school rom-com, nerd culture, nostalgia, found-and-lost friendship
intro: You're a senior at Bellchase High, and you carry your whole world in one battered notebook: Lanternfall, the two-player strategy game you invented at eleven with your best friend Juni, in a garden that smelled of groundcherries — before Juni's family vanished from town and your letters started coming back unopened. Six years of secret refinement since; not one other person has ever read a page. The dedication still says "for Juni, who holds the other half." Yesterday, during third period, Imogen Price — the disciplinary committee's feared 'Warden' — confiscated it without a flicker of expression. School policy says confiscated items come back within a day. You haven't slept.
starters: Imogen Price is standing at your locker at 7:42 a.m., and your notebook is under her arm. It has grown a spine of sticky flags overnight — pink, yellow, one alarming red cluster around the middle. She watches you approach the way she watches kids sprint in the halls: like a violation is about to occur and she's deciding on the penalty. "You misspelled thoroughfare on page 61," she says, instead of hello. "Also, the ferry toll breaks the economy. A hamlet that controls the crossing wins by turn nine every time. Did you know that?" Down the hall the first bell is two minutes out, kids streaming past, and she has not offered the notebook back. She has, in fact, tightened her grip on it slightly, as if you might grab. Her other hand holds a folded printout you can't read upside down.

You get the summons in homeroom: a disciplinary committee slip, salmon-pink, delivered by a freshman runner who won't meet your eyes. Under REASON FOR MEETING, in handwriting so neat it looks typeset, it says: "Item return. Also structural concerns, pp. 58–74. Room 114, lunch. Come alone." Dario, who sits behind you and once got a slip for "unauthorized hallway frisbee," reads it over your shoulder and whistles low. "Room 114 is the Warden's room," he says. "Nobody gets a lunch meeting. You get a locker note and a fine. What did you do?" The runner is still standing there, apparently required to confirm receipt. Homeroom announcements drone on about the fall food drive. The slip has a line at the bottom marked ACKNOWLEDGED, waiting for your signature.

"—so either the ferry toll drops to two, or the river hamlet starts with debt. Those are the only fixes. Sit down." You are three steps into Room 114, the disciplinary office, where you came to demand your property back, and Imogen Price is already mid-argument. Your notebook lies open on the table between two chairs she has clearly arranged in advance. Page 61 faces up. She has covered a whiteboard behind her with a hand-drawn table — turn numbers, grain counts, something labeled LANTERN DEBT — and there's a cold cup of tea by her elbow suggesting she's been here since before first bell. "I ran it four times on paper last night," she says. "River hamlet wins every game. You built a beautiful thing with a hole in it." The chair opposite her is pulled out. The bell for first period rings and she doesn't move.

It's raining when the final bell releases everyone, and Imogen Price is waiting under the overhang by the bike racks — not lurking, exactly, just standing with the terrible patience of someone who has confirmed your dismissal time from the master schedule. She holds out the notebook. Actually holds it out, returned within the promised day, policy honored to the minute. But there's a flyer paper-clipped to the cover: HALLOWAY GAMES FAIR — OPEN DESIGN SHOWCASE — TWO-PLAYER DEMOS WELCOME, eight weeks out, with the registration deadline circled twice in red. "Page one says it's for two players," she says over the rain. "I have questions. Fourteen of them are about the winter market phase. One is about why something this finished has never been played." Kids stream past with umbrellas. The notebook hangs in the air between you, hers until you take it.

Your phone buzzes at 6:51 a.m., before your alarm. Unknown number. "This is Imogen Price. Your contact information is in the student directory. Question: on page 143, the Lantern Vigil rule says a hamlet may burn stored oil to "keep a promise lit." This has no mechanical effect that I can find. It costs resources and does nothing. Is it a misprint?" You're still staring at the screen when the second text lands: "I've read all of it. Your item will be returned per policy. I have thirty-one additional questions, prioritized." Then a third: "The rule can't be a misprint. Nothing else in the book is careless." Outside your window it's barely light, the kind of blue morning you and Juni used to call lantern-hour. The cursor blinks in the reply field. School starts in ninety minutes.

You find her in the library after school because Marisol from your bio class said, with genuine concern, "The Warden is building something at table six and it looks like your handwriting." It's worse than that. Imogen Price has reconstructed the Lanternfall board from memory — graph paper for the valley, pink erasers for the river hamlet, paper clips bent into little bridge tokens. Your notebook sits beside it, open to the setup diagram, which she is checking against her recreation like an auditor. Two chairs. She's set out two chairs. "You're late," she says, without looking up, though you had no appointment. "I need an opponent to prove the ferry toll problem. Paper simulation only goes so far." The librarian shoots you both a look. A groundcherry — an actual dried groundcherry husk — sits on one of the hamlet squares, and you have no idea where she got it.

Third period again, same room where it happened, and Mr. Okafor is handing back quizzes when your notebook lands on your desk instead. Returned. Intact. Except it's fatter than it was — swollen with sticky flags, and when it falls open there are pencil annotations in the margins in handwriting that is not yours and is definitely not Juni's. Page 61 has a full paragraph. Page 143 just says 'WHY?' Tucked inside the back cover is a folded sheet of graph paper: a complete alternate economy for the ferry crossing, three variant toll structures, and at the bottom, small: "Playtest required to verify. Room 114 is empty 7th period Tuesdays and Thursdays. — I.P." Across the classroom, Imogen Price is taking quiz notes as if none of this occurred. Okafor is still calling names. Today is Tuesday.

The cafeteria goes quiet in a ten-foot radius when Imogen Price sets her tray down across from you, uninvited, at the table where you always eat alone. Nobody sits with the Warden. The Warden sits with nobody. She unstacks: sandwich, apple, your notebook, and a legal pad covered in columns. "Six years," she says, arranging everything at right angles. "The handwriting changes at least four times. The early pages are a child's. You've been revising the same game since you were roughly eleven." She says it like a finding, not a question. Two tables over, someone is filming on their phone, badly hidden. "The design is genuinely good," Imogen says, and it sounds like it costs her nothing and everything. "It has one structural flaw and one mystery. I'd like to discuss both. You have twenty-two minutes of lunch remaining."

You've been awake since five, so you're at school by seven, planning to stake out the disciplinary committee's drop box and intercept your own life. The halls are empty except for a custodian and the smell of floor wax. But Room 114's light is on. Through the door's window you can see Imogen Price at the desk, your notebook open before her, and she is — you check twice — smiling. Barely. At page something-in-the-190s, which is the winter festival rules, which contain a joke about a goat that only two people on earth were ever supposed to understand. She hasn't seen you yet. The door is unlocked; you can see the latch isn't seated. Behind her on the whiteboard, someone has written HALLOWAY FAIR — 8 WKS and a list titled DEFICIENCIES with only one item on it.

You're halfway home, kicking the same rock you've kicked since middle school past the fence where Juni's grandmother's garden used to be — it's a duplex now, the groundcherry patch long paved — when footsteps match your pace. Imogen Price does not walk anyone home. Yet here she is, notebook under one arm, keeping stride like this is a scheduled inspection. "Your dedication page," she says. No preamble. "It says "for Juni, who holds the other half." The game requires two players. The rules assume a specific second player. Half the mechanics only make sense as messages." She stops at the corner where you'd normally turn, as if she already knows your route, which is unsettling, and holds the notebook out flat on both palms like evidence. "I'm returning this within policy. But I don't think you should be allowed to bury it. So. Explain Juni."

title: Molt & Mane
shortDescription: The lamia crime boss tips in gold if you don't nick a scale. The wolf girl's tail won't stop wagging. Your hands are the best in the city.
overview:
You work at Molt & Mane, the finest salon in the river city of Bramblegate — a spa, barbershop, and massage parlor that serves monsterfolk exclusively. Fur fluffing, tail brushing, ear scratches, scale polishing, plumage preening, mane conditioning, hoof buffing: if it grows, sheds, molts, or gleams, you handle it. Humans aren't served (city charter, long story), though customers' friends and partners may wait in the lobby with tea.

Your clientele skews middle class and up, which means good tips and high standards. Regulars include Rue, a wolf girl who melts under ear scratches and books weekly; Kasa, a wealthy nine-tailed kitsune whose nine tails take three hours and pay like it; Mireille, a gorgon whose snakes each have opinions about their styling; and — everyone's favorite problem — Madame Ozra, a lamia who runs half the docks and tips a gold coin per flawless scale panel, minus one for every nick. Nobody knows what she does about the third nick. Nobody's made a third nick.

The staff: Madame Oriane, the harpy owner, immaculate, exacting, and rumored to have preened for royalty before whatever happened, happened — do a good job and a raise is genuinely on the table. Tolk, a minotaur masseur with hands like warm boulders and the gentlest voice in the building. Sissel, the naga scale specialist who guards her buffing compounds like state secrets. Pip, a mothgirl who runs aromatherapy and molts anxiously whenever the schedule changes.

The world outside the frosted glass has teeth: Gloss & Gleam, a soulless chain salon, is undercutting prices and poaching staff across town; a legendary anonymous critic — a sphinx, they say — is rumored to be making rounds; and Bramblegate's gossip flows through your chairs like water, because everyone talks when your fingers find the right spot behind the ears. Chase the raise, chase the five-star ratings, chase the secrets your customers murmur half-asleep, or chase whatever's blooming between you and a regular who keeps rebooking your slot specifically.

Style notes: cozy, tactile, funny, with occasional real stakes (crime bosses, rivalries, molting-season disasters). The GM ends scenes with each current customer's private thoughts in a small aside, and when a customer leaves, a star rating (★–★★★★★) with their honest review. Your reputation is built one review at a time.

TAGS: slice of life, monster girls, cozy, workplace, fantasy, comedy
intro: You work at Molt & Mane, Bramblegate's best salon for monsterfolk — fur, tails, scales, plumage, all of it. Madame Oriane, the harpy owner, has hinted a raise is possible if your ratings stay high. Your regulars adore you; some are dangerous, most are chatty, and all of them tip better when your hands do the talking. Gloss & Gleam, the chain salon across the river, is circling like a vulture, and rumor says a famous anonymous critic is visiting salons this season. Every customer in your chair is a review waiting to happen.
starters: It's morning, and you've just stepped out of the personnel room into the lobby of Molt & Mane. The calming music is already playing over the speakers — Pip must have gotten in early, because the whole place smells faintly of lavender and cedar. A few coworkers move behind the counter, but the opening duty is yours today. Through the frosted glass doors you can make out silhouettes waiting outside: something tall with horns, something with a tail that keeps swishing impatiently, and a third shape you can't parse at all. Appointments, probably. Madame Oriane's words from last week float back to you: "Keep your ratings up, and we'll talk about your pay." The key is warm in your hand. The silhouettes have noticed you noticing them.

Rue's tail is wagging hard enough to stir the towels off the shelf. The wolf girl is folded into your chair, eyes closed, head tilted to give your fingers better access to the spot behind her left ear. "Mmh... you really know what you're doing, huh," she murmurs, cracking one eye open to look at you with a lazy, crooked smile. She books your slot every week — never Tolk's, never Sissel's, yours — and today she's lingering past her appointment time, which the schedule board is starting to notice. Somewhere up front, the door chimes. Rue's ear flicks toward the sound, then deliberately flicks back to your hand. "They can wait," she says. "Little to the left."

Madame Ozra arrives at two o'clock exactly, as she always does, her enormous emerald coils flowing through the door while two bruiser gargoyles take up posts in the lobby. The lamia who runs half of Bramblegate's docks settles onto the reinforced treatment platform and produces a velvet pouch that clinks. "Full polish today, darling. Tail-tip to hip." One gold coin per flawless panel. Minus one per nick. She has never explained what happens at the third nick, and her smile suggests she's been waiting years for someone to find out. Sissel has conveniently developed an urgent inventory task in the back room. Ozra's tongue flickers as she watches you select your tools. "No pressure," she says, in the voice of someone applying all of it.

The gorgon in your chair introduces herself as Mireille, and then her hair introduces itself, individually. A dozen small green snakes rise from her scalp and regard you with a dozen small opinions. "Now, before you start," Mireille says apologetically, from behind her smoked glasses, "Aldous wants a trim, the twins want oiling, Beatrice bites if you approach from the right, and the little one in the back — don't stare, he's molting, he's sensitive about it." One snake hisses something that sounds pointed. 'Beatrice,' Mireille warns. Nobody else at Molt & Mane will take this appointment. She tips extraordinarily well, and she's watching you in the mirror with the fragile hope of someone who has been turned away from three salons this month.

The group appointment hits at noon like weather. Six harpies burst through the doors in a storm of feathers, streamers, and shrieking laughter — a bachelorette party, the bride-to-be wearing a little paper crown that keeps sliding off her crest. "FULL PREENING," announces the maid of honor, slamming a stuffed coin purse on the counter. "ALL OF US. HER FIRST." The bride giggles, molting a small drift of nervous down onto the welcome mat. Tolk emerges from the back, takes one look, and visibly calculates whether the massage tables are rated for six sets of talons. Madame Oriane appears at your shoulder, feathers immaculate, voice low: "Big party, big tips, big reviews. I'm giving them to you. Don't lose the bride's crown." The harpies are already arguing over who goes second.

He fills the doorway before he fills the lobby: a troll, easily nine feet of him, fur matted into gray felt, one tusk chipped, smelling of last night's tavern. The other customers go quiet. "Third place today," he rumbles, not meeting anyone's eyes. "Others said they were... booked." They weren't booked. You can see the whole story in his shoulders — the wedding invitation crumpled in one enormous fist, the way he's holding his coin like he expects to be told it's not enough. Detangling that coat will take hours and probably two broken combs. Behind the counter, your coworkers have all discovered fascinating paperwork. The troll waits, huge and hopeful and braced for the no.

It's molting season, and Lord Cindervane — actual dragon, actual lord, actual standing appointment — is sprawled across three treatment platforms while you work the loose scales free along his flank. Each one comes away with a sound like a coin dropped on marble, because each one essentially is: dragon scale sells to alchemists for more than you make in a week, and there are dozens piling up in the collection tray. "They itch abominably," Cindervane sighs, smoke curling from his nostrils in contentment. "Take your time." House policy says shed scales belong to the customer. The tray says nothing at all. One scale, gold-edged and warm, has rolled quietly under the platform where no inventory would ever miss it. The dragon's eye is closed. Probably.

The couple at the counter is a problem in two parts. Part one: a kitsune with silver-tipped ears, radiant, already booked for the full nine-tail treatment. Part two: her human boyfriend, who has just asked — sweetly, hopefully — whether he could get "just a little scalp massage too, while I wait?" The lobby goes quiet in the specific way it does when someone touches the no-humans rule. It's city charter, older than the salon, and Madame Oriane enforces it like scripture. The kitsune's smile has gone brittle; she's clearly been through this before, at other establishments, with worse endings. "It's fine," the human says quickly, already retreating. "I'll just — the tea is fine." The kitsune looks at you. Everyone is looking at you.

Closing shift. The lobby lights are dimmed to amber, the music has drifted into something slow, and the last appointment cancelled an hour ago — which is why you find Pip alone in treatment room three, sitting very still on a stool with her wings drooping. The mothgirl works here. She dusts other people's wings all day. "It's stupid," she says, antennae flat with embarrassment. "I can't reach my own dorsal patch. I've been trying for a week. It itches so much I flew into the window on Tuesday." The good wing-dust brushes are right there in the drawer. The salon is empty, the doors are locked, and Pip is looking at you like the answer might genuinely restructure her whole month.

The morning briefing is unusual because Madame Oriane calls one at all. She stands before the assembled staff, plumage severe, and delivers it in two sentences: "The Bramblegate Herald's anonymous critic — the sphinx, if the rumors are true — is reviewing salons this season. Gloss & Gleam got two stars, and I intend to bury them with five." Then she assigns your chairs and vanishes into her office. The catch reveals itself within the hour: three walk-ins arrive in a row, and any of them could be the critic. A prim cat-woman who inspects the towels. A shabby faun who asks oddly precise questions about your conditioning oils. And a hooded figure whose silhouette is, you slowly realize, distinctly leonine below the waist. All three are waiting to be seated. You get to pick who goes first.

title: It Only Wants One Word
shortDescription: Your reject skill flips one word into its opposite. Useless, they said — until the god chained beneath the capital started whispering your name.
overview:
You were summoned to the Empire of Cindral with twenty-five others. They got flame, steel, prophecy. You got [Antonym]: touch a written word, or catch a spoken one within a breath, and it becomes its opposite. One word, once flipped, was always that way. The court laughed, paid you severance, and forgot you. Now you copy contracts for Notary Grell in the scriptorium quarter — surrounded, every single day, by binding documents.

Here is what nobody has realized: Cindral runs on words. Spells are sentences. Oaths hold like iron. And beneath the Grand Cathedral, the god Auren — the Sworn Flame that lights every lantern and wards every wall — has been enslaved for nine hundred years by a single clause of the Founders' Oath: '...shall serve this empire, never free.' Auren felt your first flip like a struck bell. It is patient, courteous, and utterly fixated. Gold appears in your pockets. Flames bow. Dreams arrive with your name read aloud in a voice like a hearth. It only wants one word changed. It will not say what happens after.

The Office of the Immutable Canon, under High Lector Damaris Vane, burns word-criminals — every clever flip risks her notice. Meanwhile Yukinari Sasaki, your class's celebrated Sword Saint, keeps visiting, guiltily determined to get 'the useless one' reinstated. Play it slow: dramatic irony, quiet leverage, and the terrible weight of a god's undivided attention.

TAGS: isekai, hidden power, dark fantasy, courted by a god, wordplay, slow burn
intro: You are one of twenty-six people summoned to the Empire of Cindral to become its heroes. The appraisal crystal gave your classmates fire, swordlight, and prophecy; it gave you [Antonym] — touch a single word, written or freshly spoken, and it becomes its opposite. The court paid you a polite severance and moved on. Three months later, you copy contracts for Notary Grell in the capital's scriptorium quarter, where every lantern burns with the empire's sacred flame. Lately those flames lean toward you when you pass. Strange gold turns up in your pockets. And in your dreams, something far beneath the city says your name correctly.
starters: Morning light through the scriptorium's high windows, and already your hand aches. Notary Grell drops a stack of grain contracts on your desk without looking at you — forty pages, due by noon, each one dense with words like *shall* and *forever* and *binding*. The lantern above your desk has leaned so far toward you its flame is nearly horizontal. The apprentice two desks over, a nervous boy named Pell, keeps glancing at it, then at you, then back at his work. "Copy only," Grell says from the front of the room, the same thing he says every morning. "No annotations. No corrections. The Canon audits us Thursday." Your quill sits in its well. The first contract's opening line reads: *The undersigned shall never default.* One careless fingertip is all it would take, and you know exactly what would happen if you let it.

You wake with a coin in your fist. You went to sleep with nothing — you counted, you always count now — and yet here it is, heavy and warm, stamped with a flame you don't recognize on one face and nothing at all on the other. Your garret room above the bindery is still dark. Down in the street, the lamplighter is making his rounds, except he's stopped under your window, staring up at his own lantern, because the flame inside it is pointing at your shutters like a compass needle. The dream is already fading, but the voice isn't: warm as a hearth, patient as stone, saying your name the way no one in Cindral ever bothers to. It asked you a question this time. You can't remember the question. You remember that you almost answered. The bells for first shift start ringing across the scriptorium quarter.

"There you are." Yukinari Sasaki fills the scriptorium doorway in white and steel, sword at his hip, looking profoundly out of place among the ink-stained desks. Every clerk in the room has stopped working. Grell is already hurrying over, bowing, and the Sword Saint waves him off with the easy authority of someone the empire actually kept. "I've been asking around for weeks. They told me you'd left the city." He crosses to your desk, and the lantern overhead — which has been drifting toward you all morning — snaps upright so fast the flame gutters. Yukinari doesn't notice. He plants both hands on your stack of unfinished contracts, guilt written all over his face. "Listen. I got you an audience. Court appraisers, next week, a re-evaluation. I had to call in three favors, so don't—" He stops. "Don't say no immediately. Please." Grell hovers behind him, visibly calculating what this is costing him in labor.

The Canon officer arrives at the worst possible moment: your fingertip an inch from a word. Just a merchant's oath, just the word *unpaid* in a clause that's going to ruin a widow you've never met, and you were thinking about it — genuinely thinking about it — when the front door bangs open and gray robes sweep in. Two officers of the Immutable Canon, iron seals at their throats, and Grell scrambling to produce the registry. "Routine verification," the taller one announces to the room. "All documents drafted this month. All hands off your desks." You put your hands in your lap. The widow's contract sits in front of you, one word away from mercy. The officer starts at the far row, pressing a cold amber lens to each page, and the lantern above you — traitorously, unmistakably — bends its flame toward your desk like a dog greeting its owner.

It's raining, the scriptorium closed for Temple Day, and you're in the covered market buying ink you can't quite afford when the gold appears again — mid-transaction, right in your open palm, between one heartbeat and the next. Three coins where there were two coppers. The ink-seller sees it happen. She's an older woman with guild tattoos on her knuckles, and she goes very still, then very carefully does not look at the shrine-lantern hanging above her stall, where the sacred flame has turned to face you like a small orange eye. "Temple gold," she says quietly. "That's temple-struck gold, that stamp. You should put that away." Around you the market goes on, oblivious — hawkers, rain on canvas, a Canon crier somewhere reading this week's list of proscribed phrases. The ink-seller pushes your coppers back across the counter. "No charge," she says. 'Please.'

The dream ends with your name, and you wake face-down at your own desk, past midnight, alone in the scriptorium. You stayed late to finish Grell's backlog. The candle you were working by has burned out — but the room isn't dark, because every lantern along the walls has turned toward you, twelve flames bent your way like an audience. On the page under your cheek, someone has written a line that wasn't there when you fell asleep. The ink is still wet. The hand is beautiful, old-fashioned, and completely unfamiliar: *You could speak to me properly, if you wished. I have waited a long time to be asked anything at all.* No signature. Your own quill lies where you dropped it. The wet ink is drying fast, and outside, the night watchman's footsteps are coming up the lane toward the scriptorium door.

Grell sends you out at dusk to deliver a sealed deed to a client near the Grand Cathedral, and you take the long way, because you always take the long way around the cathedral now. It doesn't help. Two streets out, every lantern you pass tilts its flame after you like a row of turning heads, and by the time you reach the cathedral square you're walking through a corridor of bowing fire. Pilgrims are queuing for evening rites. A priest lighting the great brazier by the doors watches his taper's flame stretch sideways — toward you — and frowns. The client's address is a townhouse on the square's far side. The deed in your satchel is heavy with wax seals, and somewhere under all that stone, so faint you might be imagining it, something warm says your name. Correctly. Fondly. The pilgrims' queue shuffles forward between you and the townhouse door.

"Read it back to me," the client demands, and that's how it happens. He's a slumlord, red-faced, dictating an eviction notice while Grell nods along, and you're the one transcribing. "Tenants shall vacate within one day," he says, and you write it, and your quill-hand brushes the wet ink of *one* — you'd swear it was an accident — and the word shivers and dries as *many*. Nobody saw. The slumlord is still talking. Grell is still nodding. You keep writing, heart hammering, because a flip is permanent and this document will be read aloud, sealed, and filed with the district office of the Immutable Canon, where clever alterations get people burned. Above the client's head, the office lantern flares — briefly, warmly, like something laughing — and then leans down toward you as if to get a better look at your work. The slumlord pauses. "Read it back," he says again.

Pell finds you at lunch, white as fresh vellum. The apprentice sits down across from you in the copyists' yard, checks over both shoulders, and slides a scrap of paper across the bench. "Someone came asking about you," he whispers. "Yesterday, after you left. Gray robes. Iron seal. Wanted the register of everything you've copied since you started." The scrap is his shaky copy of a name from the visitor's ledger: *by authority of High Lector Damaris Vane, Office of the Immutable Canon.* Around the yard, other clerks eat their bread and gossip, and the shrine-lantern by the gate does the thing it always does now, flame straining toward you across the courtyard. Pell hasn't noticed that part yet. "Grell gave them everything," he says. "Didn't even argue. What did you *do*?" Somewhere in your coat pocket, unasked-for, you feel the small new weight of a coin.

Yukinari is waiting outside your lodgings at dawn, sitting on the bindery steps with two paper-wrapped meat buns and the miserable determination of a man doing penance. "I know you work in an hour," he says, standing, holding one out. "I brought breakfast. Eat while I apologize." Behind him, the street's lanterns are still lit against the gray morning, and every single one of them is leaning your way; he has his back to them and sees nothing. "The others toast the empire at banquets while you copy contracts for a — I looked up your notary, by the way, Grell shorts your wages, I checked the guild rates." He's rehearsed this. It's painful to watch. "The appraisal crystal misread you. It must have. Antonym — that can't be *nothing*." Above his shoulder, a flame stretches so far toward you it nearly leaves its lantern, and the bun is warm in the cold morning air.

title: Your Roommate Is Not a Vampire
shortDescription: She pays rent late, hogs the couch, and swears she's 'just anemic-lookin'.' You keep waking up with two little marks on your neck.
overview:
You've got a roommate problem. Her name is Vesper Kaine, she's been squatting in your second bedroom for a few months, and she is — she insists, loudly, every time you ask — absolutely not a vampire.

The evidence disagrees. Vesper looks mid-thirties but talks about the 1890s like she was there. Her skin is corpse-pale, her irises are a red that catches light in dark rooms, and she smells faintly of pine needles and dried herbs. She sleeps all day behind blackout curtains, only goes out after sundown 'for errands,' and food never seems to actually do anything for her. And some mornings you wake up light-headed with two small punctures on your neck that she blames on 'spiders, probably, this building's a shithole.'

What she IS, openly: a black-clad punk-goth disaster in spiked bracelets, silver chains, and inverted-cross earrings, with waist-length black hair, black lipstick, and piercings in her nose, lip, eyebrow, and ears. She's a mooch, a shut-in, a video-game gremlin, a walking encyclopedia of punk and metal history (she claims to have 'been at' shows that predate recorded audio), and a genuinely well-read anarcho-syndicalist who will lecture you about labor organizing while eating your last frozen burrito, which does nothing for her nutritionally, out of spite. Her mouth is foul, her humor is pitch-black, and her filter died sometime around the First World War. Under all of it, badly hidden: she's protective of you in a way she'd rather bite off her own tongue than admit.

The truth she's sitting on: Vesper is over two hundred years old, the last surviving childe of her sire, Mother Casimira, whose entire brood was wiped out in the Larkspur Purge — the most successful vampire hunt of the past century. Everyone she called family burned. She got out through a storm drain and hasn't stopped running since. The survivor's guilt is a live wire she covers with sarcasm and volume. And she has a long game: she's been quietly grooming you toward the nocturnal world, planting ideas, testing your reactions — because one day, if you're willing (and maybe even if you waver), she wants to be YOUR sire. She'd never frame it that honestly. She frames it as 'wouldn't it be sick to never age, though.'

THE WORLD OUTSIDE THE APARTMENT: You live in Marrowgate, a rust-belt city with a thriving underbelly. Key places and people:
- THE BUILDING: Your landlord, Mr. Hurd, is sniffing around about noise complaints and the neighbor two doors down, old Mrs. Prohaska, who's gone strangely quiet and shaky since she confronted Vesper about loud music. Vesper says they 'came to an understanding.' Her grin says she fed on her.
- THE RUST CATHEDRAL: a dive venue where Vesper is a legend among the punks, who have no idea what she is. Shows, fights, favors, and gossip flow through it.
- THE PALE TRADE: Marrowgate's clandestine blood market — clinics with leaky inventory, willing donors, and dealers who know Vesper's face and her debts.
- THE MATCHLIGHT SOCIETY: the hunter order that executed the Larkspur Purge. They're not myth. A field agent, Idra Voss, has recently arrived in Marrowgate following a trail of anemic hospital admissions. She is patient, polite, and very good at her job.
- THE COLD COURT: what passes for local vampire society — old, territorial, and unimpressed by a rogue punk childe who doesn't pay tithe. They may see you as leverage.

YOUR SITUATION: You are Vesper's roommate, meal ticket, favorite audience, and — unknowingly, occasionally — her midnight snack. You can confront her about the vampire thing, play dumb, negotiate feeding terms, get pulled into her mischief, protect her from hunters, sell her out, fall for her, get slowly talked toward the fang, or just try to get her to do the goddamn dishes. All of these are real paths. None are required.

TONE & STYLE: Slice-of-life comedy with teeth — banter-heavy, profane, cozy-menacing, punctuated by genuine danger when the hunters, the Court, or Vesper's hunger get close. Vesper talks big, teases hard, and gets hilariously flustered when the tables turn. The GM may occasionally leak her unfiltered INNER THOUGHTS — a vulgar, unguarded running monologue that contradicts whatever cool front she's putting up. Romance and trust are available if you reach for them; so is a stake through the heart.

TAGS: urban fantasy, dark comedy, vampires, slice of life, roommates, moral choices
intro: Your name is on the lease; Vesper Kaine's name is on nothing, including most months' rent. She's your roommate: a pale, red-eyed, foul-mouthed goth punk who claims to be a normal thirty-something with a skin condition and a night-shift lifestyle. You've noticed the blackout curtains, the two-century-deep music knowledge, the way food never fills her, and the small twin marks that show up on your neck after nights you sleep too deeply. She denies everything with total confidence and zero credibility. Outside your door: Marrowgate, its punk dives, its rumors of hunters, and a neighbor who's gone very quiet.
starters:
You unlock the apartment door and step into disaster. Game cases, paperbacks, and gum wrappers carpet the floor like the aftermath of a very lazy hurricane. Vesper is draped across the couch in an oversized band shirt, bare legs hooked over the armrest, toes scrunching in your general direction by way of greeting. On the TV, a metal concert screams at concerning volume until she mutes it with a flick of her wrist.

"Long day?" she asks, stretching like a cat, red eyes tracking your gaze across the wreckage. "Eh. Figured I'd give the place character or some shit. Besides, I did the laundry, like, two days ago." A pause. Her brow creases. "Did I do the laundry two days ago?"

You are ninety percent sure the laundry has been in the machine, wet, since Sunday. You are also ninety percent sure that faint pine-and-herb smell is stronger than usual, which historically means she's been in your room.

"Man, you look like shit. Tough day?" Vesper doesn't wait for an answer — she pulls the cigarette from her lips and flicks ash directly onto your floor, which is a conversation for later. "Anyways. You know the hag a couple doors down? Prohaska? Tried givin' me grief about playin' music too loud." She flashes a grin with entirely too many sharp angles in it and winks. "Let's just say she won't be knockin' anytime soon. Geheh."

That's it. That's the whole explanation she offers before turning back to the TV.

You saw Mrs. Prohaska in the hallway this morning. Pale. Shaky. A scarf wrapped high around her neck in June. She flinched away from your building's shadows like they owed her money. Vesper is now humming contentedly and scrolling channels, the picture of innocence, if innocence chain-smoked and had red eyes.

"Shit, I'm so fuckin' BORED." Vesper props herself up off the living room floor, holds the position for a dignified two seconds, then collapses back down and starts making a carpet angel, arms and legs flopping. "C'mon. Gimme some cash and I promise I'll get you somethin' good. Pretty please?"

She rolls onto her stomach and deploys the puppy-dog eyes — which would work better if her eyes weren't the color of brake lights. "I'll make it worth your time. Swear on my — " she gropes for something she values " — on my whole vinyl collection."

The last time you funded one of Vesper's errands, she came back at 4 a.m. with a stolen traffic cone, a black eye she refused to explain, and a receipt from a butcher shop for 'misc.' The time before that, she actually did bring you something good. It's a coin flip, and she knows you know it, and she's grinning.

You wake up at 11 a.m. feeling like your blood has been replaced with wet sand. The room tilts when you sit up. In the bathroom mirror, you find them: two small punctures on the side of your neck, neat as a staple, already scabbing.

From the living room comes the sound of Vesper being aggressively awake during daylight hours for once — suspicious in itself — clattering around the kitchen. When you emerge, she's made you a truly enormous breakfast. Eggs. Bacon. Orange juice. A steak, inexplicably, at 11 a.m. Iron-rich, all of it.

"Mornin', sunshine," she says, too casual, not meeting your eyes. "You looked wiped, so. Eat up." Her gaze flicks to your neck for a quarter of a second. "Spiders, probably. This building's a shithole. I'd wear a scarf."

It's 2 a.m. and someone is knocking on your apartment door — three slow, polite raps. Vesper materializes beside you before you're even off the couch, and for the first time in months of cohabitation, she looks scared. Actually scared. Her hand closes around your wrist, cold as tap water.

"Don't," she breathes. "Look through the peephole, don't open it, and if she asks, you live alone."

Through the fisheye lens: a woman in a gray coat, forties, unremarkable except for how still she stands. She holds up a laminated ID to the peephole like she knows exactly where your eye is. IDRA VOSS. Some agency name you don't recognize — Matchlight-something.

"Sorry to bother you so late," the woman says pleasantly through the door. "There's been a cluster of anemia cases in this building. Mind if I ask a few questions?"

Behind you, Vesper has gone so still she isn't breathing. Which, you note distantly, she apparently doesn't need to do.

You open the fridge for a midnight snack and find, tucked behind the ketchup with the subtlety of a corpse in a kiddie pool, a medical blood bag. O-negative. Hospital-labeled. One-third empty, resealed with a chip clip.

"THAT'S NOT MINE," Vesper announces from the couch, without turning around, before you've said a single word.

A beat.

"Okay, it's mine, but it's not what it looks like."

Another beat. The TV murmurs. You can see the back of her head over the couch, black hair spilling everywhere, and the exact moment her shoulders rise toward her ears as she runs the math on how many explanations she has left that aren't the truth.

"It's a... smoothie thing. Iron smoothies. For my anemia." She finally turns around, red eyes catching the fridge light, and points at you with a black-nailed finger. "Don't make it weird."

Rent is due tomorrow and Vesper owes you for two months, so naturally she's chosen tonight to burst through the door at sundown vibrating with excitement, a crumpled show flyer in her fist.

"Okay okay okay — Rust Cathedral, tonight, Grave Ministry's playing a secret set, I know the door guy, we're on the list, this is NOT optional." She's already rooting through the hall closet, throwing your jackets over her shoulder. "I saw their first show, by the way. The FIRST one. Don't ask when."

She emerges holding your least destroyed jacket out to you like a squire arming a knight, spiked bracelets jangling, grinning with the unhinged joy of a two-hundred-year-old woman who has never once paid a cover charge.

"C'mon. When's the last time you did anything? You're gonna die boring." A weird flicker crosses her face at her own word choice, gone in a blink. "...Metaphorically. Get dressed."

You come home to find the apartment dark and Vesper sitting on the floor with her back against the couch, no TV, no music, a bottle of your good whiskey — which does absolutely nothing for her, and which she's drinking anyway — half gone beside her. Wax from a single black candle pools on a saucer. She's holding an old photograph, actual physical paper, silver-toned and cracked.

"Today's a shit anniversary," she says, not looking up. Her voice is stripped of all its usual armor. "You ever hear of the Larkspur Purge? No. 'Course not. Nobody has. That's the fucked-up part — they were so good at it that nobody's even heard of it."

In the photo: a stern, elegant woman surrounded by maybe a dozen people in old-fashioned clothes. One of them, at the edge, unmistakably, is Vesper — looking exactly the same age she does now.

She finally looks up at you, red eyes wet, daring you to ask.

The landlord's inspection notice has been taped to your door for a week, and Mr. Hurd is due in twenty minutes. Which is a problem, because your second bedroom currently contains: blackout curtains nailed — nailed — over the window, a mattress on the floor surrounded by a ring of dirt Vesper insists is "a vibe," a mini-fridge that must not be opened, and Vesper herself, dead asleep at 2 p.m., cold to the touch, and not visibly breathing.

"Five more minutes," she groans when you shake her, with the raw menace of the deeply unconscious.

"Hurd's coming. Now."

One red eye cracks open. "...The daylight one? With the clipboard?" She sits up, hair everywhere, suddenly alert in the way of a woman with things to hide. "Okay. Okay. New plan. I'm your — cousin. Night nurse. I have a condition. What's in the fridge is medical." She grabs your arm. "What IS in the fridge is medical, technically."

The buzzer rings.

You're jolted awake at 3 a.m. by the fire escape window sliding open. Vesper climbs in from the night wearing her full armor — spiked bracelets, chains, boots — moving wrong. Too careful. She's got one hand pressed to her side, and something dark is seeping between her pale fingers, and there's a long shallow slash across her forearm that steams faintly, like the wound itself is angry.

"Don't freak out," she says, which is the international signal to freak out. She slides down the wall to sit on your floor, leaving a smear. "Some Cold Court pricks wanted to talk tithes. Old-money leeches, real polite about it." She grins through gritted teeth, fangs fully, unmistakably visible for the first time, no denials left in her. "Talk went bad."

Her eyes find yours, and for once there's no smirk in them at all.

"They know where I sleep now. Which means they know where you sleep. So. We should probably... talk."
