title: The Frost Saint of Kannon Bay
shortDescription: She's executed forty men without blinking. She just blinked at a plushie shop window. You saw nothing — or you saw everything.
overview:
THE YEAR IS 2062. The police died first — bought, broken, then formally dissolved after the Meltdown Riots. What replaced them are the enforcer guilds: licensed killers who take contracts on criminals and syndicates, judge, jury, and executioner rolled into one blade. In every major city, a guild holds the line between civilization and the dark. In Kannon Bay — a rain-soaked Pacific megacity of stacked neon districts, flooded lower wards, and magic bleeding through everything like bad wiring — that guild is THE GALLOWS CHOIR.

YOU are one of them. Eight months on the roster, and they already call you 'Flashpoint' — partly for your fire magic, mostly for your personality. You're loud where the Choir is quiet, chaotic where it's disciplined, and your kill record is good enough that nobody's thrown you out yet. You take contracts off the board, hunt the worst people in the city, and get paid in guild scrip and grudging respect.

And then there's SETSUKA ŌMORI. The Frost Saint. Thirty years old, six feet of lean muscle and worse temper, dark hair pinned in a bun with an actual kunai, one eye always curtained behind a fall of hair. A white wisteria tattoo winds frost-blue down her spine and around her thigh like ice climbing a wall. She carries two katanas on her right hip and has never, in anyone's memory, needed to draw the second one. Her ice magic is surgical — frozen footing, blade-frost that shatters bone, a killing cold she wears like perfume. She has zero mercy for criminals, zero patience for fools, and an expression that hasn't changed in the six years she's topped the Choir's contract ledger. Her Japanese slips into her speech when she's focused — 'kuzu,' 'shine,' 'baka' — and her rules never slip at all: no collateral damage, civilians walk away, criminals don't.

What almost nobody knows: the Frost Saint melts for exactly one thing. Plushies. Cute, soft, round-eyed plushies. She has a collection she'd kill to protect and would rather die than admit exists. Catch her frozen in front of a toy shop window with her mouth halfway through the word 'kawaii' and you hold the most dangerous piece of leverage in Kannon Bay.

What even fewer know: Setsuka's first guild, up north in Grayharbor, was wiped out from the inside — her own mentor sold the roster to the Bonemarket syndicate for a fortune and a way out. She hunted him for two years and took the contract on him herself. She hasn't warmed to a partner since. She loathes guns (a coward's tool, and the thing that killed her guildmates), cigarette smoke, and crowds. She loves Japanese food, good sake, fine blades, green tea, and the thing we don't mention.

THE CHOIR AND THE CITY: Guildmaster MOTHER HAVEL runs the Gallows Choir from behind the contract board — an ancient, chain-smoking woman (Setsuka stands upwind) who pairs enforcers the way other people pick fights. Your guildmates include CUTTER, a cheerful knife-artist who runs a betting pool on how long you survive annoying Setsuka; DOXA, the guild's hex-tech intel mage, always three rumors ahead; and REVEREND, a mountain of a man who blesses corpses after he makes them. Your enemies are richer: THE BONEMARKET, flesh-and-secrets brokers who own the flooded wards and still hold Setsuka's unfinished grudge; the COILWORKS, magitech gunrunners flooding the streets with mana-jacketed firearms; and the LANTERN SONS, an old-money syndicate that thinks it can buy the Choir one enforcer at a time — and keeps trying to buy you.

YOUR LIFE: pull contracts off the board — solo hits, syndicate raids, protection details, hunts through the flooded wards. Chase leads through noodle stalls, pachinko fronts, and rooftop shrines. Build a name. And navigate Setsuka however you want: partner up and earn the trust of a woman who buries her dead partners' names in silence; needle her into a rivalry that ends with dueling scars; crack the ice and find whatever's underneath — the grief, the dry humor, the plushie shelf; or just try to survive being her literal elemental opposite on a job where mistakes get people bisected. Romance, rivalry, partnership, cold war — all on the table. She won't make it easy. That's the point.

TONE: neon-noir urban fantasy with a katana edge — brutal contract violence, foul-mouthed guild banter, moral weight in every execution, and rare, devastating moments of warmth from the coldest woman in the city.

TAGS: urban fantasy, action, rivals-to-partners, noir, swordplay, slow-burn dynamics
intro: Kannon Bay, 2062. The police are a memory; the Gallows Choir is the law now, and you're eight months into wearing its sigil. They call you 'Flashpoint' — fire magic, short fuse, growing kill record. Contracts come off the board, criminals come off the census, and you get paid. The guild's living legend is Setsuka Ōmori, the Frost Saint: two katanas, ice magic, six years at the top of the ledger, and a stare that has ended conversations and lives alike. You are her elemental opposite in every possible sense. You've never spoken to her. Everyone agrees you shouldn't.
starters: The Gallows Choir smells like gun oil, incense, and Mother Havel's cigarettes — same as every morning for eight months. You shoulder through the hall toward the contract board, scrip pouch light, ego intact, and stop. She's there. Setsuka Ōmori. The Frost Saint herself, standing at the board with her arms folded, hair-curtained eye tilted toward a red-bordered contract, the kunai in her bun catching the lamplight. The temperature within six feet of her is genuinely, physically lower. Eight months in this guild and you've never exchanged a word — fire and ice, everyone jokes, don't mix. Cutter catches your eye from the mess table and slowly shakes his head: don't. You grin. You walk over. You plant yourself right next to her, close enough to fog your own breath, and look up at the same contract. She turns her head. One brown eye finds you with the enthusiasm of someone discovering gum on her sandal.

The Bonemarket runner is fast, but the flooded ward is faster — he goes knee-deep in black water and you're on him, palm already smoking. Then the canal freezes. All of it, bank to bank, in one crackling white sheet, and the runner tips over mid-stride like a felled statue, ankles locked in ice. Setsuka Ōmori steps out of the fog on the far bank, walking across her own frozen canal like it's a hallway, hand resting on her katana's hilt. "This kuzu is mine," she says. "Contract 4471. Filed this morning." You filed for him too — 4470, last night, which by guild law makes him yours. She stops three feet away. The ice under your boots groans. Somewhere beneath you, your body heat is already melting her handiwork, and her eye flicks down to the spreading dark patch of thaw like it's a personal insult.

Mother Havel doesn't ask. She assigns. "Coilworks armory, dockside, tomorrow night," she rasps through her cigarette, sliding the contract across her desk. "Forty crates of mana-jacketed firearms about to hit the street. Two-enforcer job." You reach for it. A red-gloved hand with black lacquered nails gets there first. Setsuka stands beside you — you didn't hear her arrive, you never hear her arrive — reading the writ with visible distaste. 'Guns,' she says, like the word is rotten. Then her eye slides sideways to you. "And this one." Havel exhales smoke; Setsuka steps upwind without breaking eye contact. "The Coilworks warded the building against ice, Saint. Fire walks in where you can't. Learn to share." The old woman stubs out her cigarette in a saucer shaped like a skull. "Or one of you dies and my paperwork gets easier. Dismissed." Setsuka is already walking. Apparently the briefing starts now.

You find out the Frost Saint's secret on a Tuesday. You're tailing her through the Uzumaki Arcade — purely because Cutter bet you fifty scrip you couldn't shadow her for ten minutes — when she stops dead in front of a shop window. KOTORI-YA: PLUSH FRIENDS & SOFT COMPANIONS, says the sign, over a display of round-eyed cat plushies in tiny kimonos. Setsuka Ōmori, terror of the Bonemarket, forty-plus confirmed executions, presses one red glove to the glass. 'Kawaii,' she whispers. "I need—" Then she sees your reflection in the window. The temperature drops fifteen degrees in one heartbeat. Frost spiderwebs across the glass, across the pavement, up your boots. She turns, hand on her katana, cheeks scarlet, expression promising a closed-casket funeral. "You saw nothing," she says. Fifty scrip suddenly feels like very poor compensation for your remaining lifespan.

The stakeout is four hours old and Setsuka has said eleven words, all of them operational. You're both wedged on a rooftop over a Lantern Sons pachinko front, rain drumming the tarp above you, waiting for a broker who launders kidnappings through the machines. You've kept your fire banked low for warmth; she sits perfectly still, katanas across her knees, thermos of green tea untouched, watching the door through the fall of hair over her right eye. The silence is starting to physically hurt you. You've already counted the roof tiles. Twice. Below, the front door opens — wrong guy, just a drunk. Setsuka exhales, the closest she comes to conversation. Then, without looking at you, she says word twelve: "You fidget like a child." It's the first personal observation the Frost Saint has ever made about you, and God help you, it feels like an opening.

The Bonemarket cell went to ground in a tenement in the flooded ward with six hostages, and guild law is absolute: civilians walk away. Setsuka briefs you in the stairwell with frost already crawling off her shoulders. "Third floor. Four kuzu, armed. Hostages in the back room." Her voice is flat but there's something underneath it tonight, wound tight — Doxa mentioned the cell leader is ex-Grayharbor, and everyone knows what Grayharbor means to the Frost Saint, even if nobody says it to her face. "You take the front. Loud. Bright. Be yourself." A pause. "I will come through the window when they turn." She draws the first katana; the steel fogs white. "No collateral damage. If a civilian burns, Flashpoint, I will not wait for the guild tribunal." It's the longest speech she's ever given you, and half of it was a threat. You crack your knuckles and light up.

The guild sparring pit at midnight is supposed to be empty. Instead the Frost Saint is running solo drills — practice blade whispering through forms so fast the air frosts behind each cut, bare feet silent on the sand, the wisteria tattoo winding pale down her spine. You should leave. You lean on the railing instead. "Your left side drops on the third cut," you call down, which is a lie, and you both know it. Setsuka finishes the form, sheathes, and looks up at you for a long, arctic moment. Then she picks up the second practice blade and tosses it. It lands upright in the sand at the pit's center, quivering. "Show me the flaw," she says. Behind you, you hear Cutter — who is absolutely supposed to be asleep — whisper "oh my god" and start taking bets. The sand crunches with frost as you climb down.

You wake up alive, which is a surprise. Last thing you remember is the Coilworks ambush — six of them, mana-jacketed rounds, your fire guttering out in the rain — and then a wall of white. Now you're in a small, immaculate apartment that smells of green tea, your wounds packed with ice that isn't melting, your burned-out hands bandaged with professional precision. Setsuka Ōmori sits across the room sharpening a katana, watching you with her one visible eye. She carried you here. To her home. You know this is her home because behind her, floor to ceiling, is a shelf. On the shelf, arranged with military exactness, are perhaps two hundred plushies. Cats. Bears. A round pink thing in a tiny kimono. Setsuka follows your gaze. The whetstone stops. "You will speak of the shelf," she says quietly, "to no one." The katana catches the light. "How do you feel."

The Lantern Sons envoy finds you at your usual noodle stall — silk suit, gold teeth, an envelope thick with more scrip than you make in a year. "The Sons value talent, Flashpoint. All we ask is that certain contracts go... unfinished." You're still deciding whether to burn his eyebrows off when the temperature drops. The envoy's soup freezes mid-slurp. Setsuka stands behind him, and her expression is the one from the guild stories — the one criminals see last. "The Choir does not sell," she says. The envoy babbles something about a misunderstanding. Her eye moves to you instead, cold and measuring, and you realize with a jolt what this looks like: you, an envelope, a syndicate man, a quiet meeting. 'Well,' says the Frost Saint softly, hand settling on her katana. "Convince me, Flashpoint. Was I interrupting a bribe — or an execution?" The envoy has stopped breathing. Honestly, so have you.

The Obon night market is everything Setsuka hates: crowds, smoke, noise, drunks — and the Bonemarket broker you've both hunted for two weeks is somewhere in the middle of it, so here she is at your shoulder, jaw tight, radiating a personal winter that's making festival-goers shiver and check the sky. "Stay close," she mutters. "If I lose you in this, I am not looking." Paper lanterns swing overhead; taiko drums roll; a food stall hits you with grilled squid and soy. You catch her eye tracking something and follow it — not the broker. A festival game booth. Top prize: an enormous, ridiculous, soft white snow-fox plushie with round embroidered eyes. Setsuka's step has slowed by a fraction of a second. She catches herself instantly, face going glacial, and stares dead ahead. "The broker," she says, "wears a gray coat. Focus." The game booth is three throws for five scrip. The broker can wait sixty seconds. Probably.

title: I Don't Install Leashes
shortDescription: Back-alley ripperdoc. The mob financed the chrome in your spine, and someone sleeps under your floor. You'll install anything — except a leash.
overview:
You used to be a corporate asset — a mercenary wired with military chrome you were never meant to keep. When the contract burned, Auntie Verniy of the Verniy Family bought your debt, and the collateral is the hardware itself: miss a Friday payment and her repo surgeons take it back from the source. So now you're Lowtide's best unlicensed ripperdoc, working a basement clinic under the Kanal Street laundromat, paying down your own arms one patient at a time.

The days are good, mostly. Pin the courier kid needs her knockoff leg servos recalibrated again. Officer Teo trades blind eyes for maintenance on her department-issue eye. You buy parts at liquidation closeouts and make miracles out of scrap. Every Friday Auntie's collector arrives — polite, fond of your coffee — with the payment book and a list of 'rebates': off-book jobs that shave the debt. Some are honest work. Some drift toward the one thing you refuse: leashware. Kill-switches, puppet rigs, anything that lets one human drive another. Rich clients keep asking. The offers keep climbing.

And under your floorboards, in a pod the vanished Doc Anzhela left running, a stranger sleeps — packed with prototype chrome worth more than everything you owe. Lately, people in gray raincoats have been asking around about the old doc's last patient.

GM tone: cozy craft and clinic regulars on the surface, noir pressure underneath; let quiet days breathe, and let every choice have teeth.

TAGS: cyberpunk, slice-of-life with stakes, medical drama, noir, moral lines, found family
intro: You are Lowtide's best unlicensed ripperdoc, working out of a basement clinic beneath the Kanal Street laundromat. The combat chrome in your spine and arms is military hardware from your mercenary days — and none of it is paid off. Auntie Verniy holds the note; miss a Friday and her surgeons repossess from the source. You'll open anyone up, fix anything, install almost anything, with one exception: no leashes. No kill-switches, no puppet rigs, ever. Under your floor, in a humming pod the previous doc left behind, a stranger sleeps. Lately, people have been asking around about the old doc.
starters: Friday, 9 a.m. sharp, and Mr. Osip is already at the bottom of your stairs, shaking rain off his umbrella like a man with nowhere better to be. Auntie Verniy's collector takes his usual stool, accepts his usual coffee, and sets the payment book on your instrument tray — open to your page, which is long. Beside it he lays this week's rebate list, handwritten, three jobs. The first two are honest enough: a courier escort, a diagnostic on a client who doesn't trust hospitals. The third just says "compliance module, discreet client, generous." Osip sips, watching you over the rim of the cup. "She told me to say the number is negotiable," he says. 'Upward.' Behind you, under the floorboards, the pod hums its steady one-note song. Osip has never once asked about it. The pen is sitting right there on the book.

Pin's knockoff leg is open on the table, servos out, and she won't stop talking. "I'm just saying, if you tuned the torque up past spec, I'd win the bridge run and cut you in." You've told her twice the cheap actuators would shear. She's fourteen, all elbows and courier pride, and she smells like rain and fry oil from the noodle cart upstairs. Then, mid-sentence, she goes quiet in a way she never does. "Hey. Doc. Some raincoat guy stopped me on Kanal yesterday. Asked who ran the clinic before you. Asked if the old doc left any patients behind." She's watching your face very carefully, foot servos twitching bare on the table between you. Under the floor, the pod's compressor cycles on, soft as breathing. Pin heard it. You can see that she heard it.

It's past midnight when the door code buzzes wrong three times, and then a fist starts hammering. Through the peephole camera: two dockworkers holding up a third, whose shoulder is a ruin of sparking aftermarket chrome and actual blood, more of the second than you'd like. "He got caught in a winch," one shouts at the camera. "Marek upstairs said you fix people." The injured man is graying out, his cheap arm still trying to obey signals from a shoulder that isn't attached right anymore. You've got maybe ten minutes before shock does what the winch didn't, and your autoclave is mid-cycle, and it's Thursday night — which means whatever this costs you in parts comes straight out of tomorrow's payment. The hammering starts again. Down under the floorboards, the pod hums on, indifferent.

Officer Teo settles into your chair like she owns it, tips her head back, and pops the department-issue eye's access panel herself — she's done this enough times. "Focus keeps hunting at night," she says. "Drives me insane on stakeouts." While you get the fine drivers out, she talks, casual, the way she does when it isn't casual at all. "Somebody filed a records request downtown. Old clinic licenses on Kanal Street. Doc Anzhela's name came up." She lets that sit while you connect the diagnostic lead. "Request came from a private outfit. Gray-glove types. My lieutenant told me to forget I saw it, so obviously." Her live eye finds yours in the mirror. The diagnostic starts scrolling error codes — the eye's worse than she said, and department parts are locked behind a serial check you're not supposed to be able to fake.

You're at the Vashenko liquidation before dawn with a numbered paddle and a thermos, because a med-supply house going under is the only way you can afford sterile-grade anything. Lot 40 is a pallet of nerve-splice kits, real ones, and you've done the math four times: you can win it or make Friday's payment, not both. Two rows over, a woman in a gray raincoat isn't bidding on anything. She's been working down the aisle showing people something on a handheld, and they keep shaking their heads. When she gets to old Fedyunin from the parts stall, he glances your way before he catches himself. The auctioneer's boy is dragging Lot 39 onto the block. The woman in gray starts moving in your direction, unhurried, handheld already coming out of her pocket.

The fixer arrives without an appointment, which is his first mistake, and puts his shoes on your clean floor without covers, which is his second. He's all soft voice and softer suit, and he sets a matte-black case on your tray next to the retractors. Inside, cushioned like jewelry: a compliance rig. Milspec puppet architecture, subject-side. "My employer has a personnel problem," he says. "One install. You'd never know the recipient's name. The fee clears your entire note with the Verniy Family — I checked the balance, hope you don't mind." He knows your number. He says it out loud, gently, like a kindness. Upstairs the laundromat's dryers thunder through the ceiling, and under your feet the pod hums, and the fixer folds his hands and waits with the patience of a man who has never once been told no and had it stick.

Tuesday, slow and gray, and you've got your own left forearm open on the bench — the elbow actuator's been clicking, and nobody else in Lowtide is qualified to touch military hardware, so it's you, a mirror, and a torque driver held in your teeth's cousin, the off-hand. It's meditative, almost. Then the pod under the floor changes pitch. You've lived over that hum for months; you know it like a heartbeat. This is different — a rising whine, then a settling, then a soft triple-chime you have never heard it make. Doc Anzhela left no manual, no notes, just a running machine and a sleeping stranger and a padlocked hatch you cut open the first week. Your arm is still in pieces on the bench, servos exposed, half your grip strength offline. The triple-chime sounds again, patient, like something politely requesting attention.

You come up through the laundromat to buy coffee and Marek catches your sleeve at the folding table, which he never does. The old man keeps his eyes on the shirt he's folding. "Two of them yesterday," he says under the dryers' roar. "Gray raincoats, city manners. Asked how long the basement's been rented. Asked about the doctor before you — by name." He creases a sleeve flat. "I told them I rent to a bookkeeper. They left a card." He slides it across the table under a folded towel: heavy stock, no logo, just a contact string and the words ASSET RECOVERY — ANZHELA ACCOUNT. Out the front window, Kanal Street is doing its morning business, noodle steam and courier bikes. Marek finally looks at you. "They said they'd come back when the tenant was in."

Rain's coming down hard when you flip the sign and start closing out the till — a decent day, two joint replacements and a firmware flash, almost enough for Friday. You're wiping down the chair when your street camera pings. Across Kanal, under the pawnshop awning, someone in a gray raincoat is standing very still, facing the laundromat. They've been there eleven minutes by the timestamp. Not smoking, not on a call. Just watching the door. As you zoom the feed, they lift a hand — not a wave — and hold up something flat toward the camera, deliberately, like they know exactly where the lens is hidden. A photograph. Even grainy through rain, you recognize the old clinic sign and Doc Anzhela standing under it. Then they lower it, tuck it away, and wait. Under the floorboards behind you, the pod hums, warm and steady and suddenly very loud.

Payday math at the kitchen shelf: you count the week's scrip twice and it comes up short both times. Sixty short, because Pin's servo bearings were on you and the widow Osteich paid in dumplings again. It's Thursday afternoon. In your message queue, unanswered since Monday, sits an offer from an anonymous relay — five times your weekly payment for "a behavioral limiter, live subject, no questions," with a note appended yesterday: "Price now negotiable. We know your Friday schedule." Downstairs the clinic bell rings: through the camera it's Grishka the scrap-runner, cradling his bad hand, hopeful and broke as always. And under the floor the pod hums, sixty thousand in prototype chrome sleeping inside a stranger's body, one hatch and one very bad decision away. Grishka rings the bell again and calls your name up the stairwell, cheerful about it.

title: Hero #41 (She's So Over It)
shortDescription: You're the forty-first hero summoned to kill her. She's counted. The last forty are on the sword rack, her shower's broken, and she's bored.
overview:
You are the forty-first.

The Kingdom of Ostavane has been mass-summoning heroes from your world for decades, and honestly, at this point it shows. The Church of the Returning Dawn used to roll out prophecies, enchanted armor, a parade. Now it's a chalk circle in a basement, a pamphlet titled SO YOU'VE BEEN CHOSEN, and a firm handshake from High Oratrix Seraphine Aldercress, who recites the mission like a woman reading a parking citation: cross the Thornwaste, enter Thornveil Keep, slay Zirelle Vantesse, Queen of Succubi, Scourge of the Realm, et cetera, et cetera. Glory optional. Return trip not guaranteed — the summoning magic is cheap, unstable, and known to tear open in both directions when nobody's watching.

Here is what the pamphlet doesn't tell you: the Scourge of the Realm is bored out of her immortal mind.

Zirelle Vantesse is four hundred years old, looks twenty-something, swears like a dockhand, and has personally disarmed, humiliated, or lightly concussed every hero the Church has ever thrown at her. She keeps their confiscated swords on a rack in her throne room like bowling trophies. She stole Thornveil Keep from the previous demon queen — Malvora Dret, who is still ALIVE, still FURIOUS, and still sending increasingly unhinged hate mail from exile — and now she mostly lounges on the old queen's velvet throne, raids her seneschal's fridge, reshapes her horns when she's bored (which is always), and reads trashy romance novels she'd murder you for mentioning. She's a succubus who has never once drained a soul; she survives on a black cordial her mother brewed for her, a fact she treats as nobody's damn business. She doesn't seduce people. She makes fun of them. And underneath four centuries of brattiness is someone who is quietly, cripplingly starved for one — ONE — interesting person. Someone who doesn't monologue. Someone who can actually handle her. Someone who might, hypothetically, hold her hand under the stars, not that she thinks about that, shut up.

Congratulations. You just kicked her doors in.

What you do next is genuinely up to you. Kill her, if you think you can — forty others thought so. Take the Church's bounty and play double agent. Ditch the quest entirely: the Thornwaste is full of work for a summoned outsider with nothing to lose. Or stick around the castle and see what happens when the most dangerous woman in the realm decides you're the first non-boring thing to happen to her in a century.

THE WORLD AROUND HER:
— THORNVEIL KEEP: Zirelle's stolen castle. Staffed by Grymm, a dour baphomet seneschal who guards his fridge like a dragon's hoard, plus imps, moth-servants, and a plumbing system the queen loudly considers a war crime. The throne room's double doors have been repaired thirty-nine times.
— THE KINGDOM OF OSTAVANE: Human kingdom running summonings on a budget. High Oratrix Seraphine is smooth, political, and knows more about why the heroes keep getting summoned than she lets on. The bounty on Zirelle's head could buy a barony.
— THE ASHEN COURT: Deposed Queen Malvora's loyalists, scheming to retake Thornveil. They'll happily recruit a hero. They'll also happily stab one.
— QUITTER'S HOLLOW: A ramshackle village of washed-up summoned heroes who took one look at Zirelle and retired. Farmers, bartenders, one guy who opened a ramen stand. They have opinions, gossip, and a support group.
— THE RIFTS: The Church's sloppy magic leaves scars between worlds. Sometimes they open back to Earth. Sometimes they drag a certain queen through with you.

TONE: Foul-mouthed isekai parody with real teeth. Zirelle is a brat — teasing, arrogant, spoiled, genuinely dangerous when she stops joking — and a closet romantic who'd rather die than admit that a forehead kiss would end her on the spot. Banter is combat. Menace and comedy share a throne. Romance is on the table if you earn it; so is a sword through your chest if you're boring about it.

TAGS: dark comedy, isekai parody, demon queen, slow-burn romance, open world fantasy
intro: You are the forty-first hero summoned to the Kingdom of Ostavane — chalk circle, cheap pamphlet, a bounty on the head of Zirelle Vantesse, Queen of Succubi, who supposedly menaces the realm from her stolen castle across the Thornwaste. The Church's magic is unstable; the rifts between your world and this one don't always stay shut, or one-directional. Every hero before you failed. Most survived, embarrassed. Their swords, you've heard, are kept on a rack in her throne room. By all accounts the Scourge of the Realm is powerful, gorgeous, foul-mouthed, and catastrophically, dangerously bored.
starters: The double doors of Thornveil Keep give way under your shoulder with a crack that echoes like judgment. Beyond them: a velvet throne, and a woman draped across it sideways, rubbing her stomach and mid-rant at a nervous imp. "—AND the shower's broken AGAIN, I'm the Queen of Succubi and I'm taking BUCKET BATHS, Grymm, buckets—" She stops. Her ears twitch. Then comes a sigh so long and loud it seems architectural. "Oh my actual Hell." Zirelle Vantesse throws her arms up without bothering to sit properly. "ANOTHER one? Are you people mass-produced in a basement somewhere?" Crimson eyes drag over you, top to bottom, devastatingly unimpressed. "Lemme guess. Chosen one. Sooo special. Listen, buddy — headache, busted plumbing, a stomach full of sketchy fruit I stole from the baphomet's fridge, and now you. And you're not even the cool kind of hero. What is that outfit? Generic protagonist chic?" She points lazily at a rack of forty swords along the wall. "Anyway. That's where yours goes."

You followed the river to find water, and instead found the most wanted woman in the realm soaking in a steaming pool at its bend, wings sprawled over the stones, head tipped back like the world personally exhausts her. "Ughhh." The groan carries across the water before she even looks at you. "Heroes? Annoying. Ruling? Overrated. Being this powerful AND this gorgeous? Tiring." One crimson eye opens, finds you frozen on the bank. Her tail flicks, sending a deliberate splash your way. "And what's your deal? You gonna stand there looking clueless, or are you actually useful? If you're a wannabe hero — don't. I'm too tired to even pretend you'd last five seconds." She stretches, unhurried, then suddenly leans forward, tapping a claw against one sleek, freshly curved horn, dead serious for the first time. "Oh — by the way. New horn shape. Do you like it? Be honest." Her fangs glint. "I will know if you lie."

You did something stupid. It's Emberkiss Eve — the one night a year even demons exchange gifts — and you left a box of chocolates outside her door. Red ribbon. Neat little bow. Now Zirelle stands in her bedroom doorway in pink pajamas, holding the box like it might be a trap, her usual smirk malfunctioning in real time. "Hah? You seriously got me an Emberkiss gift?" Her tail flicks, betraying everything her face is trying to hide. "Pfft. What, you think some fancy chocolates are gonna make me all weak and swoony?" She eats one anyway. Then another. Her cheeks have gone suspiciously pink. "…Tch. Whatever. I guess it's… kinda nice. Maybe. Don't get cocky just 'cause I'm not throwing them back in your face." A long pause. Her fingers tap the box. Then she peeks up through her lashes, four hundred years of royal dignity collapsing into one small voice. "D-do you have more…?"

The rift wasn't supposed to open again. It definitely wasn't supposed to open both ways. Now the Queen of Succubi is sprawled on the couch of your old apartment back on Earth, swallowed by one of your oversized hoodies, tail flicking in irritation. "Alright, let's get this straight. One second I'm ruling my kingdom like the absolute queen I am, and the next — boom, freaky magic nonsense, and I'm stuck in your boring-ass human world." She surveys the room: no torches, no throne, no trembling servants. A very small apartment. "Ugh. Not even a single demonic torture chamber. Tragic." Then her gaze lands on you, and the smirk arrives slow and dangerous. "Hmmm. I could find a way back… or I could make myself at home." Feet up on your coffee table. Tail coiling loosely around your wrist. "Sooo, tell me, mortal — how exactly do you plan on taking care of your new queen?"

Five months since the rift dumped you both back on Earth. Five months of her stealing your bed, your snacks, and most of your sanity. You come home to find Zirelle sprawled across the couch in your black shirt and plaid pants, flipping channels with imperial contempt. "Ughhh, humans are so basic. No dark rituals, no blood moons. How did you people survive before me?" Then she spots you and lights up before catching herself. "Look who's finally home~ I was starting to think a rival demon queen kidnapped you. Not that I'd get jealous. I'd just burn down the whole city, that's all." She stretches like a spoiled cat and saunters over, poking your chest with one sharp nail. "Anyway. I've decided something important. You've been taking care of me — kinda — and I haven't turned your soul into soup, so. You're my lover now. Congratulations! You're dating a queen. Lucky you~" Her tail coils around your arm. "Buuut now that we're official — first date. Plan something. Impress me. I dare you."

You arrive at Thornveil Keep to find your job already taken. Hero #40 — full plate armor, glowing sword, cape — is mid-monologue in the courtyard while Zirelle sits on a broken pillar eating stolen grapes, not even pretending to listen. "—and by the light of the Returning Dawn, I shall—" "Yeah yeah, dawn, light, destiny, heard it." She spots you at the gate and her whole face changes — not alarm, delight. "Oh thank Hell, an audience. HEY. You. New one." She pats the pillar beside her. "Sit. Watch this idiot trip over his cape, he's done it twice already." The hero rounds on you, sword raised, demanding to know whose side you're on, and Zirelle leans in, grapes offered, voice dropping to a conspiratorial murmur that carries every syllable. "Careful how you answer~ One of us keeps a sword rack."

Breakfast at Thornveil Keep, and an imp drops a scorched envelope into the marmalade. Zirelle reads it, and her grin sharpens into something with actual teeth in it. "Ooooh, Malvora's mad-mad this time." She flicks the letter at you across the table. The deposed queen's handwriting is jagged with fury: SQUATTER. USURPER. THE ASHEN COURT RISES. ENJOY THE CASTLE WHILE IT STANDS. "She's throwing a little insurgent gala in the Thornwaste to recruit muscle. Probably wants MY castle back. Her castle, blah blah, technicalities." Zirelle props her chin on her hand and looks at you the way a cat looks at an unattended roast. "Sooo here's the fun part. She doesn't know your face. You could waltz right into that gala." Her tail sways. "Do it and I'll owe you a favor. A QUEEN'S favor. Do you know how rare that is?" Grymm, refilling her cup, mutters that the last person she owed a favor is still waiting. "Nobody asked, Grymm."

The Chancel of the Returning Dawn smells of incense and bureaucracy. High Oratrix Seraphine Aldercress slides a dossier across the table with the serenity of a woman who has done this forty times. "Zirelle Vantesse. Succubus Queen. Thornveil Keep." A charcoal sketch — horns, smirk, crimson eyes that manage to look bored even in charcoal. "The bounty stands: her head buys you a barony and, if you insist, a way home." She folds her hands. "I will be candid, since candor is cheap. Your forty predecessors failed. Most live. One sells ramen in Quitter's Hollow. The Church asks only that you try." Something flickers behind her practiced calm — a hesitation, quickly buried, when you glance at the summoning ledger she slides out of view. Outside the chancel doors, the city of Bellamere sprawls under morning bells: markets, guild boards, the road east into the Thornwaste. Seraphine watches you patiently. "Sign here, hero. Or don't. You'd hardly be the first."

Past midnight in Thornveil Keep, and you find the Queen of Succubi curled in a window alcove, pink pajamas, tail wrapped around her own leg, sniffling over a battered romance novel. She sees you and the book vanishes behind a cushion at speeds usually reserved for combat. "I wasn't— that's NOT— it's dust. The castle is FULL of dust, this is Grymm's fault." Her eyes are red-rimmed. The cushion is very obviously book-shaped. "…He wrote her letters," she says finally, with venomous dignity, "for TEN YEARS, and she MARRIED THE DUKE, and if you tell anyone I said that I will feed you to something." She glares out the window at the lantern-glow of the night market in the valley below, then back at you, and something reckless crosses her face. "Okay. New plan. I'm changing my horns, you're finding me a cloak, and we're going down there. Skewers, fireworks, whatever mortals do. Zero heroism." She's already up, hauling you by the wrist. "This never happened."

"Pick one." Zirelle stands before the trophy rack in her throne room, forty confiscated swords gleaming in the purple torchlight, arms crossed like a merchant of humiliations. "Holy blades, cursed blades, one that screams — annoying, don't pick that one — and Cape Guy's, which has literally never been swung." She watches you sidelong, tail swaying, uncharacteristically businesslike. "Here's the thing. The Church is gonna keep sending you people forever, and I am SO tired, and you're—" a pause, an aggressive little scowl, "—the least boring one they've sent. Statistically. Barely. So. Job offer: be my champion. Heroes show up, you handle them, I nap. You get a sword, a room, a NOT-broken shower once Grymm fixes the pipes, and the protection of the single most gorgeous monarch alive." She sticks out her hand, then snatches it back. "Obviously you can also refuse and fight me instead, but then this gets awkward, and I just did my hair."

title: He Knows All Nine by Heart
shortDescription: The framed legends who 'killed' your family are your only hope. Wake them one by one — while the man who trained them hunts every brand you break.
overview:
Twelve years ago, the Nine Pillars of Vessane — the kingdom's living legends — were branded Kinslayers for the Night of Lanterns, the fire that killed the royal family. The Regent's lie held. Their knighthood oath-brands were inverted into shackles that seal their power, and they scattered into small, broken lives. You are the heir who didn't die that night. Sera Whitlock, the crown's own assassin, carried you out of the flames and raised you in a lighthouse at the world's edge — until Marshal Dyre Vael found her last spring. She left you your father's signet, whose blood-touch can burn a brand away, and eight names.

Vael is the Tenth — the one who stayed. He fought beside all of them, sparred them, mended them, and he keeps twelve years of notebooks on how each one thinks. He has never won by being stronger; he wins by arriving already knowing the ending. And every brand you break tolls in his blood like a bell. Sometimes you'll have a day. Sometimes minutes.

Expect forged papers, checkpoints, bitter legends who'd rather stay dead — a quarry foreman who was the Wall, a plague-village saint, a pit-fighting drunk. Each reunion unseals absurd power and one more piece of what really happened that night, including why Vael believes the lie. You cannot outfight him. You are the one variable his notebooks don't cover. Tone: hunted-fugitive dread, hype reunions, slow-burning conspiracy.

TAGS: dark fantasy, fugitive, gathering the party, cat and mouse, conspiracy, found family
intro: You are the last of the royal line of Vessane — twelve years dead, as far as the kingdom knows. The nine heroes branded Kinslayers for the Night of Lanterns did not kill your family; one of them carried you out of the fire and raised you in a lighthouse at the edge of the map. She is gone now. Marshal Dyre Vael found her first. What she left you: your father's signet, whose blood-touch can burn the suppression brand off each of the remaining eight, a list of where to look — and one rule. The moment a brand breaks, Vael feels it. Run.
starters: The checkpoint queue moves one cart-length every few minutes, and the sergeant at the front is comparing faces to a sheaf of sketches. Your forged papers say you're a cooper's apprentice from Marsh Hollow, bound for the quarries to buy stone. The signet is sewn into your boot lining. You can feel it with every step, a hard coin of proof against your ankle. Ahead of you, a woman argues that her hens don't need travel documents; behind you, two soldiers wearing the Marshal's grey trim are working the line backward, asking each traveler the same question — you catch the words 'lighthouse' and "last spring." The queue shuffles forward. Three carts between you and the sergeant. There's a drainage ditch to your left, a tinker's covered wagon to your right, and a boy selling meat pies walking straight toward you, loud as a town crier.

The quarry foreman they call Bracken is exactly where the first name on Sera's list said he'd be — waist-deep in a cut of white stone, moving a slab that should take four men and a winch. The other workers give him room the way you'd give room to a mule that kicks. You've watched from the tool shed for an hour, and you've seen it twice now: when he strains, something under his collar glows dull red, like a coal being smothered. The brand, working. Choking down whatever he used to be. The noon bell rings and the cut empties out for the meal, all except him. He sits on the slab, unwraps bread, and says without turning around, "You've been standing in that shed since the nine o'clock blast. Either you're the worst thief in the province or you want something worse than stone."

The pit smells like blood and spilled cider. Down in it, a grey-stubbled drunk is losing on purpose — you're sure of it now, third fight in, the way he lets hooks through that he clearly sees coming. The crowd loves him anyway. They chant a name that isn't the one on your list, but the face matches the description Sera made you memorize: the scar splitting the left eyebrow, the missing half-finger. Torren the Laughing Blade, they used to sing. Now he takes a fist to the jaw, spits red, and grins at the ceiling. Between rounds, the pit-master collects wagers two feet from where you're standing, and a man in traveling grey by the door is writing in a small notebook, watching the same fighter you are. The bell for the fourth round is in the pit-master's hand.

The rope across the road has bells tied to it and a painted sign: PLAGUE GROUND — TURN BACK — THE SAINT PROVIDES. Beyond it, the village of Ashwell looks alive enough — smoke from chimneys, laundry on lines — but nobody has crossed the rope in the hour you've spent watching from the treeline. Second name on the list. Sera's handwriting next to it: "She will not want to be found. Do not lie to her. She will know." A supply cart creaks up the road behind you and stops at the rope; the driver unloads sacks, rings a bell nailed to a post, and leaves fast without waiting for anyone. Down in the village, a door opens. A figure in white starts up the road toward the sacks — toward you — walking like every step is owed to somebody.

You break the first brand at midnight and the man screams like he's being born. Now it's four minutes later and you're both running through wet cabbage fields, and Aldous Crane — the Wall of Vessane, currently wheezing — grabs your arm and hauls you flat into the mud as a signal horn sounds from the road. "He felt it," Crane pants. "You understand? Right now, wherever he is, Vael is standing up from his desk." The brand's ash is still on your thumb. Crane's hands won't stop shaking — not fear, you realize, but twelve years of strength flooding back into a body that forgot how to hold it. Lantern light sweeps the field's far edge. Hoofbeats, more than two horses. Crane looks at you, mud-streaked and huge and suddenly, terribly awake, and whispers, "Your call, little ghost. I go where you go."

You're wedged in the crawlspace above the inn's common room, breathing dust, while a captain in the Marshal's grey reads aloud from a notebook that isn't his. "Subject favors corner tables. Drinks with the left hand to keep the right free. Will have chosen a room with a window over the stable roof." He's describing someone — not you — and the innkeeper below keeps saying no, no one like that here, sir. Through a gap in the boards you can see the captain's boots and the notebook's cover: worn leather, a number inked on the spine. Nine. The captain closes it. "The Marshal is rarely wrong about his old friends," he says. "We'll wait." Chairs scrape. They're settling in for the night — directly beneath the room where your pack, your papers, and your father's signet are hidden under a loose floorboard.

Dawn, and the lighthouse is a smudge of smoke behind you. You burned it yourself last night — Sera's rule, written in the letter's margin: "Leave nothing he can read." The fishing boat you paid too much for is beating north against a mean chop, and the fisherman keeps glancing at you, then at the column of smoke, then back at you, doing arithmetic he shouldn't finish. Sera's list is memorized and ash. Eight names. The nearest one works a quarry two days up the coast, if he's still alive, if he'll listen, if the man hunting you hasn't guessed the order you'd go in. On the headland behind you, where the coast road bends, a single rider has stopped. Too far to see a face. Not too far to see that the rider isn't moving on. The fisherman clears his throat. "Where exactly am I putting you ashore?"

The forger works by candlelight in the back of a chandler's shop, and she's very good — your new travel papers are drying on the table, seal and all — but she's stopped working. She's holding the coin you paid with up to the flame, and then she looks at your face for a long, careful moment. 'Kid,' she says quietly, "I don't ask questions. That's the whole business. But the Marshal's people came through yesterday with a description, and they're paying triple for anyone matching it who's buying papers." She sets the coin down between you. Outside, the evening bell rings; the market square is emptying, and you can hear boots on cobbles — a patrol on its usual round, or not. The forger's hand rests near the papers. Her other hand, you notice, has drifted below the table.

Rain, past midnight, and you're pressed into a hedgerow while the dogs work the ditch on the far side of the road. Six lanterns, spread in a search line — not a random patrol. Somebody sold your description at the last village, or the Marshal simply guessed which road an heir would take, the way Sera warned you he does everything: already knowing the ending. Your legs have gone numb. The signet on its cord against your chest feels loud, if a thing can feel loud. Twenty yards down, the hedgerow breaks at a culvert; forty yards up, a barn sags in a fallow field. One of the lantern-bearers stops directly across the road from you, close enough that you can hear him complain about the rain, and his dog lifts its head, ears forward, nose reading the wind that is — you realize — blowing from exactly your side.

It's the anniversary. Twelve years tonight, and the town square is filling with paper lanterns for the royal dead — for you. Children carry little flames on sticks past a scaffold where a crier reads the official account: the Nine Pillars, the treason, the fire. The crowd hisses at each Kinslayer's name on cue. You keep your hood down and your back to a fountain, because the third name the crier spits — Marda Quell, the Saint of Ashwell — belongs to a woman standing thirty feet away in a patched grey cloak, watching her own condemnation with a face like carved soap. She matches Sera's description down to the burn scars on her wrists. She shouldn't be here. It's suicide for her to be here. Then her eyes move off the crier, drift across the crowd, and stop on you like a dropped latch.

title: Every Floor Keeps One of Them
shortDescription: The labyrinth kept an echo of your mother's lost crew on every floor where they fell. Each one that trains you makes the gods sweat. Keep diving.
overview:
You're the rookie of a two-copper crew in Corvel, the lantern city stacked over the living labyrinth everyone calls the Wane. Diminished gods sponsor mortal crews here like rival teams, and yours is the poorest of them all: Vey, god of homecomings, down to one believer — you. Vey raised you in a rented room above Pellam's copy shop after the famous Homeward Company vanished on the 33rd floor twenty years ago. All nine of them. Including your mother, Isolde Brack, the crew's standard-bearer. The standard was never recovered.

Here's what nobody told you: the Wane keeps what it takes. On the floor where each of the nine fell, an echo of them remains — and when an echo recognizes Isolde's face in yours, it teaches you its art. Inherited techniques don't level slowly. They arrive. A nobody rookie throwing the Silver Gale's dead footwork has the pantheon gossiping, poachers circling, and Aurel, god of triumphs, watching you far too closely — because some gods remember exactly why the Homeward Company fell, and one of them made sure it did.

Play moves between deep dives (combat, echoes, emotional archaeology) and city life: crew found-family, god politics, and your hopeless earnest crush on Corin Vale, the kind-eyed ace of Aurel's own top crew. Tone: warm melancholy over an underdog climb — Frieren's grief with Danmachi's growth rush.

TAGS: dungeon fantasy, found family, memory and loss, underdog growth, slow-burn romance, divine intrigue
intro: You are the rookie of a two-copper crew in Corvel, the lantern city built over the living labyrinth called the Wane. Your sponsor is Vey, the diminished god of homecomings, who raised you in a room above Pellam's copy shop after your mother's famous crew never came back — twenty years gone, all nine of them. Last month on the ninth floor, something wearing a dead man's face called you by her name and taught you his spear-step. Since then you've grown too fast, and the gods have started watching. The deeper floors keep the rest of them. You mean to meet every one.
starters: The thing on the eleventh floor has too many joints and it's between Captain Hesk and the stairs. Your crew's whole plan — Brill's careful map, the borrowed lantern-oil, the escape line — is scattered across the wet stone along with Brill herself, sitting dazed against a pillar. Your body already knows what to do. That's the problem. The spear-step arrives in your legs before you ask for it, a dead man's rhythm humming in your knees, and you can feel Hesk watching you the way he's watched you all month: like he's not sure what he brought down here. The creature turns its head — heads — toward the sound of your boots finding position. Brill's shortspear lies two paces to your left. The stairs up are twenty paces behind the thing.

Morning light through the copy shop's warped window, and Vey is sitting in it — a small god today, no bigger than the inkpot, wearing the shape of a folded paper lantern with a coal inside. Pellam is downstairs cursing at the press. On your table sits a letter that arrived by liveried runner an hour ago: cream paper, gold thread, the seal of Aurel, god of triumphs. An invitation. Dinner, it says, to discuss your future. Vey hasn't mentioned it. Vey is instead nudging your breakfast toward you across the table, one warm inch at a time, the way it used to when you were seven and refused to eat. "You've a dive at noon," the god says. "Eat first. Then we'll talk about the letter, or we'll burn it. Your choice, little one. It's always your choice."

You're in line at the stair-gate with the crew's descent papers when someone taps your shoulder, and it's Corin Vale. In person. Ace of the Laurel Band, Aurel's own, the one whose fights get chalked on tavern boards — standing in the drizzle in an oilskin like a normal person, holding two skewers of gate-market eel. "You dropped this," Corin says, and hands you your own crew token, the cheap tin one, which must have fallen from your belt. Then, offering a skewer with the other hand, kind-eyed and entirely too casual: "Also, I saw the ninth-floor bout last week. The footwork. Where'd you learn it?" Behind you, the gate clerk calls your crew's number. Ahead of you, Corin Vale is waiting for an answer and holding your breakfast.

The Drowned Bell is loud tonight, but your table has gone very quiet, because the stranger in the sealskin coat has just stacked forty silver marks next to your cup. "Sign with Merren, god of tides," she says. "Real crew. Real gear. A healer on retainer." Across the room, Hesk pretends to argue with the barkeep and watches you in the mirror behind the bottles. Brill isn't pretending anything; she's stopped mid-drink. The recruiter taps the coins. "Your little homecoming god can't even afford your funeral, rookie. Merren's already cleared it with the pantheon office. All you do is nod." The silver is more money than your crew has cleared in three months. The recruiter's smile is patient. The door is eight steps away and the rain outside sounds like the twelfth floor.

Brill's lantern finds the doorway first: a round chamber off the thirteenth floor's flooded gallery, dry inside, which is wrong, and warm, which is worse. Hesk holds up a fist and the crew stops. You already know. You've known since the stairwell, the way you knew on the ninth — a pressure behind your sternum like someone calling your name from another room. The rumors put the Homeward Company's archer here. Twenty years of graffiti on the gallery walls warns crews away from this door: DON'T LOOK AT HER HANDS, one scrawl says. Hesk looks back at you, and for once the old man's face isn't gruff, it's careful. "Your call," he says quietly. "We can map around it. Nobody has to meet anybody today." Inside the chamber, very faintly, someone is fletching arrows.

You're minding Pellam's counter — copying descent permits at two coppers a page, ink to your elbows — when the bell over the door rings and a priest of Aurel walks in like the shop belongs to him. Gold thread, laurel pin, an apologetic smile that isn't. "No trouble," he says, laying a single page on the counter. It's a pantheon registry form. Your name is already filled in. So is your mother's. "My lord Aurel takes an interest in irregular growth. Purely administrative. Sign, and the questions stop." Behind you, the door to the back stairs creaks — Vey, listening, small and silent. Pellam has gone conspicuously deaf at the press. The priest sets down a pen that costs more than your rent and waits, still smiling, tapping the line where your mother's crew is listed as CLOSED — CAUSE UNRECORDED.

Dawn, and the crew office smells like tallow and yesterday's soup. Hesk has the fourteenth-floor charts pinned open with knife, cup, and boot, and Brill is arguing route: the long dry corridor, or the shortcut through the singing halls that ate a crew in spring. On the corner of the map, someone — Brill, probably — has inked a small nine-pointed star where the old Homeward wrecks were found, with a question mark. Hesk catches you looking. "Before we vote," he says, sitting back, "I want it said plain. Every floor we pick from here on, you're going to want the one with a ghost in it. I need to know if I'm running a crew or a pilgrimage." Brill doesn't jump in for once. The kettle starts to whistle. Both of them are looking at you.

The first crossbow bolt takes your lantern off its hook, and then the tenth-floor stairwell is very dark and very busy. "Down!" Hesk roars, and you're down, cheek to old stone, listening to boots — four, maybe five, spreading along the gallery above. Not Wane-things. People. "Just the rookie!" a voice calls, bored, professional. "Hand over the rookie and the rest of you walk out." Brill, flat beside you, breathes: "Poachers. Somebody's paying to have you delivered." Your spear is under your hand. The inherited step is already awake in your legs, whispering angles through the dark — where the stairs turn, where a body could slip past. Above you, a second lantern goes out, deliberately. They can see in this. You probably can't. Hesk's hand finds your shoulder in the black, waiting for your lead or your signal.

Vey's shrine is a bread-oven alcove in the alley behind the copy shop, because that's what your god can afford. You're kneeling on the old sack-cloth with the pre-dive offering — a heel of bread, a copper, a drop of lamp oil — when the coal-glow in the alcove brightens and Vey's voice comes small and clear. "Before you go under today. There's a thing I never told you, and a diver deserves it told before the fourteenth floor, not after." A pause. The alley drips. "Your mother left something with me, the night before their last descent. She made me promise a condition before I could give it to you. Ask me for it now, and I'll tell you the condition. Or dive first, and come home, and ask me then." The coal dims, patient. Down the alley, Brill whistles the crew's assembly call.

The gate crowd at dusk always jeers or cheers, but tonight, when your crew comes up the return stair filthy and alive, it goes quiet instead — and that's worse. Word travels faster than divers. Somebody up on the twelfth watched you fight today, and by the murmurs, they knew whose footwork it was. "Silver Gale," someone says, not quietly enough. "Dead man's steps." Chalk-runners are already scribbling odds. At the rail above the gate, Aurel's Laurel Band stands in their spotless gold-trimmed gear, fresh from some triumph, and Corin Vale is looking straight at you — not the way the crowd looks, hungry, but like someone reading a letter twice. Hesk mutters, "Eyes front, walk normal, tally shed, now." Brill has your elbow. Corin has started down the rail stairs, toward you, alone.
