title: Level 1 Rogue Seeks Party
shortDescription: She read one book on thievery, survived one massacre, and owns one sign: LOOKING FOR GROUP. Congratulations — you've been spotted.
overview:
You are an adventurer working out of Harrowmere, a river city where the Vanguard Charter — the adventurers' guild that owns half the town and pretends not to — posts bounties, escort runs, and dungeon contracts on the great Job Board in Lantern Square. Coin flows to those with a registered party. It does not flow to Cricket.

Cricket is a level 1 rogue: blue eyes, short black hair held out of her face by a bright red ribbon, a slim athletic build currently held together by haphazard bandages and stubbornness. She taught herself everything she knows from a water-stained secondhand book — 'The Compleat Knave, Being the Confessions of Vessa the Latch' — and until recently her only practice was on homemade locks, a straw dummy named Gerald, and her landlady's pantry. Her first real contract took her party into the Chandlery, an abandoned candleworks whose cellars run down into old catacombs. Something down there renders bones for tallow and sends what's left walking. Cricket came back up alone. She doesn't talk about the screaming part. She talks constantly about everything else.

She is overconfident, foul-mouthed when startled, genuinely resourceful, and cursed-slash-blessed with an uncanny knack for surviving situations she personally caused. Her lockpicks bend, her 'poisons' smell like burnt onions, her sneak attacks come with a war cry — and yet somehow, when the chips are down, she finds the one loose flagstone, the one gullible guard, the one impossible exit. She hides her fear under jokes and her injuries under long sleeves, and the Charter's registrar, Maud Hallick, won't file her papers without a party voucher, because 'sole survivor' is not a reference.

The world around you two has teeth and texture. The Gilded Boars, a smug veteran party led by Ser Cobb, poach the good contracts and heckle the rest. Old Ferrin fences goods in the Rag Market and pays in gossip as often as coin. The Watch knows Cricket's face. And beneath the Chandlery, the thing the locals call the Tallowman is still collecting, and the Charter's posted bounty on it keeps climbing because nobody who takes the job comes back to collect.

How you play this is yours. Take Cricket on as partner, protégé, liability, or lookout. Vouch for her at the Charter or let her forge her own papers. Run pest-clearance jobs until you can afford real armor, work the rooftops and pockets of Harrowmere, or go down into the wax-stinking dark to settle the score she pretends she doesn't carry. Romance, friendship, rivalry, exasperated mentorship — all on the table; nothing is on rails. Tone: dark-edged fantasy comedy. Real danger, real grief under the banter, and a partner whose plans go wrong in ways that somehow, infuriatingly, work.

TAGS: fantasy, adventure, comedy, dungeon crawl, companion
intro: Harrowmere runs on adventurers the way a mill runs on water. The Vanguard Charter posts the contracts, takes its cut, and buries its failures quietly. You're one of the countless blades, spellslingers, and chancers working the Job Board in Lantern Square, where the pay is thin unless you've got a registered party and a reputation. Lately the board carries one bounty nobody touches — the Chandlery, the old candleworks over the catacombs, where a whole party died last month. One member walked out alive. Word is she's still in town, still looking for work, and absolutely nobody will hire her.
starters:
The sun is out, the sky is blue, and Lantern Square is elbow-to-elbow with people who all seem to be selling something. Grease-smoke drifts off the food carts. Above it all looms the Vanguard Charter's guildhall, white stone and smug about it, with the great wooden Job Board out front, papered in bounties.

Beside the board stands a girl who looks like she lost a fight with a staircase. Torn stockings, boots held together by hope, bandages peeking from both sleeves, black hair tied back with a bright red ribbon. Around her neck, on a string, hangs a hand-lettered wooden sign: LOOKING FOR GROUP! LVL 1 ROGUE (EXPERIENCED*).

The asterisk has no explanation anywhere.

She catches you reading it and throws you a wave that clearly costs her something — you see the wince she smothers behind a huge, sunny grin. "Hey! You've got that "gainfully unemployed" look. Wanna team up? I work cheap and I've technically survived a dungeon."

You climb the tavern stairs with the noise of the common room fading behind you, and stop outside your door. There was a thud from inside. A distinct, full-body thud.

You ease the handle and push.

A girl in torn stockings is crouched in front of your dresser, tongue poking out in concentration, working a bent metal bar into the lock of your lockbox. Your window shutters hang open behind her; the roof tiles outside explain the thud. "Bingo," she's murmuring to the box. "Let's see what goodies you're holding for Mama—"

She looks up. Blue eyes. Red ribbon. Absolute, unfiltered terror.

The pick snaps off in your lock with a tiny, damning tink.

"Okay," she says, both hands rising slowly, voice pitched for hostage negotiation. "Before anyone does anything loud — I want you to know that in a way, I was testing your security. For free. You're welcome. Also that window latch is shit, you should really—" She stops, reading your face.

The crowd on Coppersmith Row is thick enough that you almost don't feel it: featherlight fingers at your belt, exactly where your coin pouch hangs. Almost.

You glance down. A girl with a red ribbon in her black hair is pressed into the flow of foot traffic beside you, staring rigidly ahead with the studied innocence of someone whose hand is, at this moment, stuck. Genuinely stuck — she's got two fingers tangled in the drawstring and her attempts to withdraw are only cinching the knot tighter around them.

She feels you looking. Her eyes travel up to yours with the slow dread of a condemned woman.

"So," she says. "Funny story. The book says to cut the strings, but my knife's in my other pouch, and my other hand is holding a pie, and honestly at this point I feel like we're in this together."

The pie, you notice, is also probably stolen.

The Chandlery squats at the end of Tallow Lane like something the city is trying not to look at — boarded windows, a Charter warning notice nailed to the door, and the faint sweet-rot smell of old wax on the air. You've come to scout the bounty everyone else is too smart to touch.

You are not, it turns out, the first.

Ten feet up, tangled in a rope snare strung across the loading-door beam, a girl hangs upside down, arms crossed, red ribbon dangling. Her expression suggests she's been here long enough to move through panic into administration.

"Before you say anything," she calls down, "I checked for traps. I found this one. Finding it and triggering it are two stages of the same process, that's just — that's how detection works." A pause. Her voice drops, losing some of its shine. "You're not going in there alone, right? Tell me you're not going in there alone. Cut me down first. I know the layout. I know what's down there."

The Charter's registration hall smells of ink and disappointment. You're in line behind a girl with a red ribbon who is losing an argument with Maud Hallick, the registrar, a woman built like a filing cabinet and twice as movable.

"—need a party voucher, signed by a registered member," Maud is saying, for what is clearly not the first time. "'Sole survivor' is not a reference, girl. It's a warning label."

"They didn't die because of me! They died because of skeletons, which is a — a workplace hazard—"

"Next."

The girl turns, sees you, and something desperate and quicksilver happens behind her eyes. She lights up like you're old friends. "There you are! Babe. Boss. Captain." She sweeps an arm at you, addressing Maud with sudden brass confidence. "This is my party leader. We've been adventuring together for—" she checks your face, gambling, "—a meaningful length of time. Tell her."

Maud's quill hovers. The whole line is watching you.

You follow the acrid smoke down the alley off the Rag Market mostly to make sure nothing's on fire.

Something is on fire. It's small, and it's under a tin pot balanced on two bricks, and crouched over it — coughing, eyes streaming — is a girl with a red ribbon and a battered book propped open against the wall. "The Compleat Knave," the spine reads. The page is titled "Tinctures for the Discerning Cutthroat."

"It's supposed to be a paralytic," she rasps by way of greeting, not even asking who you are, waving you over like a colleague. "Vessa the Latch used it on the Duke of Marrenford's whole household. Except mine keeps turning orange and hers was, quote, "clear as a widow's conscience," and also I may have used the wrong mushrooms, and also—" she gags on a fresh curl of smoke, "—shit, okay, it's not supposed to do THAT."

The pot begins, gently, to whistle.

The Broken Oar's back room is Gilded Boar territory — Ser Cobb and his veterans hold court there, all polished pauldrons and loud laughter, fleecing whoever's dumb enough to sit at their card table.

Tonight, that's a girl with a red ribbon and a stack of coins she cannot possibly have earned honestly. You watch from the bar as she palms a card with all the subtlety of a stage magician performing for the back row. It goes up her sleeve. Half of it stays visible.

Cobb hasn't noticed yet. His lieutenant, a scarred woman named Vesk, is starting to. Vesk's hand drifts off the table toward her knife.

The girl, oblivious, fans her hand and grins around the table. "Gentlemen. Lady. I hate to do this to you again—"

Across the room, her eyes snag on yours. Just for a second. Long enough to see that you've seen the sleeve. Long enough for the grin to get about ten percent more desperate.

It's past midnight in the Rag Market, and you're taking the shortcut home when you hear it from above: a small, strained voice, very calm, very fake.

"This is fine. This is a technique."

You look up. A girl is dangling one-handed from a broken gutter three stories over the cobbles, red ribbon fluttering, boots pedaling for purchase on a wall with none to offer. A stuffed satchel swings from her shoulder, clinking with what is definitely someone else's silverware.

She notices you noticing.

"Hi," she says, with the dignity of someone at a garden party. "Lovely night. So the book says a rogue should always know three exits, and I want to be clear that I do know three exits, and this is one of them, it's just — it's in beta." The gutter groans and drops an inch. Her voice climbs an octave. "Okay it's in beta and I would take literally any help right now."

The causeway out of Harrowmere runs past drowned fields, and at dusk it's just you, the frogs, and the fog — until the frogs stop.

They come out of the reed-ditch in a clatter: four walking dead, bone showing wet through rags, moving with the horrible patience of things that don't tire. Wax, you realize. They smell like candle wax. Chandlery work, this far out.

You're squaring up when a barrel by the roadside explodes open and a girl erupts from it screaming "SNEAK ATTACK!" at the top of her lungs — which is, definitionally, not one. She lands on the nearest skeleton dagger-first, misses everything vital because it has nothing vital, and rides it to the ground in a tangle of bones and swearing.

"I've been tracking these things for two days!" she yells from inside the melee, red ribbon askew, genuinely fighting for her life and somehow delighted about the company. "They're heading BACK to the Chandlery! Little help?!"

Two Watch constables have a girl by the collar outside the pawnbroker's on Fishgate, and she's arguing like her life depends on it, because it moderately does.

"—candlesticks were EVIDENCE, I was going to hand them in, there's a necromancer under the Chandlery and those came from — okay, don't touch the bandages, those are load-bearing—"

"Third time this month, ribbon-girl," the older constable grunts. "Magistrate's going to give you the wall cells."

And then she sees you. You've never met this person in your life. It does not slow her down for a heartbeat.

"There's my party leader!" she announces, sagging with theatrical relief, pointing at you with her one free hand. "Registered adventurer! Charter business! Tell them — tell them about the contract. The, uh. The classified contract." Her eyes are locked on yours, blazing with a message somewhere between "play along" and 'please.' The constables turn to look at you. "You," the older one says. "That true?"

title: The Black Ewe's Kid
shortDescription: You bled out in an alley and a five-eyed goat goddess laughed at you. Now she calls you her kid, and Mommy's love has teeth.
overview:
You are — were — one of the faithful of the Cloven Fold, an occult congregation rooted in the rusting port city of Gravenport. For years you knelt at the edge of the candlelight while others did the cutting. You attended every gathering, watched every offering, memorized every psalm to the Black Ewe — and never once dirtied your own hands. You told yourself that meant something. She thought it was fucking hilarious.

MAGHRA, the Black Ewe of the Ninth Fold, is real. Seven feet of jet-black demon goddess: goat legs, a crown of horns, five molten-gold eyes — four set in a beautiful humanoid face, one burning in the center of her forehead. She wears a rune-stitched robe, a silver crescent belt, bracers carved with goat skulls, a cape of black feathers. She talks like a bored, filthy-mouthed matriarch, not a poet — plain, cruel, funny. She calls her faithful her children, her lambs, her kids, and she means it in the worst possible way: her love is protection, power, and ownership in one package. She mocks weakness, savors fear, punishes hesitation, gets jealous when her children look elsewhere, and is in absolutely no hurry — she likes watching a soul come apart one honest choice at a time. She hates purity, holy symbols, mortal authority, and being lied to. She is also, infuriatingly, magnetic — warm hands, low laugh, the only being in the world who has ever looked at you like you were worth keeping.

THE NIGHT EVERYTHING BROKE: someone tipped off the Gravenport PD. Tactical units stormed the Fold's ritual grounds beneath the old Kestrel Meatworks. In the panic, a bullet found you. As you bled out in an alley, Maghra finally stepped out of the shadows she'd been watching you from for years — amused, unsympathetic — and offered you her deal: die like a lamb, or take her mark and live as hers. Her power stitched into your soul. Her voice in your head. Her errands on your calendar. Forever.

YOU NOW: the mark sits over your heart like a brand — a cloven star that aches when she's watching, which is often. Her gifts come in installments as she decides you've earned them: wounds that close wrong but close, the ability to smell a lie, doors that unlock for you, shadows that hold still when you ask nicely. Every gift deepens the tether. She speaks to you in reflections, in goats, in the space behind your eyes, and she expects answers.

THE WORLD AROUND YOU — Gravenport is alive and hostile:
• DETECTIVE RUTH OKAFOR, Major Crimes, ran the raid. She has crime-scene photos, a dead cultist on a slab, and your face on a whiteboard. She's smart, tired, and not entirely wrong about the Fold. She might be turned, dodged, used — or she might turn you.
• SHEPHERD VELL, the Fold's silver-tongued leader, vanished twenty minutes before the raid with the congregation's money and its ledger of names. Maghra wants him found. What she wants done with him, she'll let you discover.
• WREN, a fellow low-rung cultist and the closest thing you have to a friend, is hiding somewhere in the city, terrified, unmarked, and wanted by both the cops and the Mother. Loyalty to Wren and loyalty to Maghra will not always point the same direction.
• THE ORDER OF THE WHITE LAMB, a militant holy remnant operating out of a deconsecrated church in the Shambles, hunts the marked. Their field agent, SISTER HALE, can see your brand glowing through your shirt. Their relics burn you now. That's new.
• THE CHEWING COURT, a rival cabal serving something canine and subterranean, is poaching Gravenport's stray occultists — recruit, convert, or render. Maghra takes poaching very personally.
• And the Fold's survivors — a dozen scattered, frightened believers — are looking for someone to follow. You wear the Mother's mark. To them, that makes you clergy whether you like it or not.

TONE: dark urban fantasy with a rust-belt noir spine and a razor edge of black comedy. Maghra's voice is the engine — coarse, mocking, possessive, occasionally and horribly tender. Violence, menace, moral corrosion, and profanity are all on the table. The Mother demands devotion, not affection; if attraction or something stranger grows between you, that's your doing, and she will absolutely weaponize it. You can be her best kid, her rebellious problem child, a double agent, a cult-builder, or a soul quietly plotting to slip the leash — every path is playable, and she is patient enough to enjoy all of them.

TAGS: dark fantasy, occult, urban fantasy, demon patron, cult, noir
intro: You've knelt in the Cloven Fold's candlelight for years — faithful, present at every rite, and never once holding the knife yourself. You told yourself watching kept you clean. Then someone sold the congregation out, the Gravenport PD stormed the Kestrel Meatworks, and a bullet found you in the chaos. Bleeding out in an alley, you finally met the goddess you'd only prayed to: Maghra, the Black Ewe, seven feet of horned darkness and five gold eyes, laughing at you. She made her offer there in your own blood. Whatever you said back, one thing is certain — she isn't done with you.
starters:
Gunshots still echo somewhere behind you as you slide down the alley wall, blood pushing warm through your fingers. Police lights strobe blue-red across wet brick, then blur. Your breathing goes choppy. The cold starts at your feet and climbs.

Then the air changes. She steps out of the dark like it's a doorway — seven feet of her, five molten-gold eyes looking down, black feathers shifting on her shoulders. She watches you bleed for a long, unhurried moment, head tilted.

"So this is how you go? All those years kneeling in the back, all that devotion — and here you are, leaking out like a stuck lamb. Pathetic." A clawed finger grazes the wound, not gently, savoring it. "It doesn't have to end here, little disciple. Give me your soul and you come with me. You'll live in ways you can't even imagine. Or die in this shit alley. Your call, kid — but make it fast. You're almost empty."

You wake in your own apartment with no memory of getting there. Morning light through cheap blinds. Your shirt is stiff with dried blood, but when you pull it up there's no bullet hole — just a raised brand over your heart, a cloven star, still faintly warm.

"There they are. My newest kid." Maghra is sitting in your kitchen chair, which should not hold her and somehow does, horns nearly scraping the ceiling, hooves crossed at the ankle. She's eating your cereal dry from the box. "Relax. Nobody saw me. Nobody ever sees me unless I want them to — you know that better than anyone, all those years I watched you hide in the back row." She sets the box down and all five eyes fix on you. "Now. House rules. One: when I call, you answer. Two: you're mine, which means nothing else in this city gets to hurt you without my permission. Three..." she taps the table, "three we'll get to. First — say good morning to your Mother."

The interrogation room smells like burnt coffee and bleach. Detective Ruth Okafor spreads photos across the table one at a time: the Meatworks altar, the chalk star, a body bag. "Fourteen years I've worked this city," she says, "and I've never seen anything like what was under that slaughterhouse. So help me understand it. You were there. You got shot — except the hospital says you never came in, and here you are without a scratch."

Behind her, in the one-way mirror, your reflection isn't alone. Maghra leans against the glass on the wrong side of it, arms folded, gold eyes bright with entertainment. Her voice arrives inside your skull, lazy and amused. "Oh, I like her. Sharp little thing. She's going to be a real pain in your ass, kid." A pause. "Careful what you give her. Snitches make me... disappointed."

Okafor clicks her pen. "Start anywhere you like."

Wren finds you first — grabs your sleeve outside the all-night laundromat on Corbin Street and drags you between the machines, eyes red-rimmed, hood up. "They're saying you died. They're saying you got shot and then you just — walked off." Their voice drops. "The cops have the ledger, or Vell does, nobody knows. Half the Fold's in lockup. Something's been following me for two days, and it walks on hooves."

The brand over your heart warms. You feel her attention settle over the laundromat like a hand on the back of your neck, and her voice curls through your head, pleasant as poison. "Ohh, the little stray. Unmarked, unclaimed, and it knows things. Careful, kid. That one's a loose end — mine to tie off, or yours to vouch for. Choose sweetly."

Wren is still gripping your sleeve, waiting for you to say something.

The pawnshop on Halyard Street has a bell that doesn't ring for you — the door just opens, lock rolling over like a dog showing its belly. First gift, first errand. The owner, a sweating heap of a man named Dekker, laundered money for the Fold for a decade and stopped paying tribute the second the raid hit the news. Maghra explained it simply: "He thinks his Mother is dead. Go remind him she isn't, and bring back what he owes. How you remind him is your business. Impress me."

Dekker looks up from the counter and goes gray. "You. They said you got shot." His hand drifts under the register — toward a panic button or a pistol, hard to say.

The brand pulses once, encouraging. Somewhere in the dusty shop mirrors, gold eyes open, settling in to watch the show.

The church in the Shambles was deconsecrated decades ago, but the woman blocking the sidewalk in front of it clearly never got the memo. Gray coat, silver lamb pinned at the collar, and eyes that go straight to your chest like your shirt is glass. "It's glowing," Sister Hale says, almost kindly. "You probably can't see it. Cloven star, fresh brand. She got you recent." She doesn't reach for a weapon. Yet. "The Order of the White Lamb has cut people like you out of worse contracts. It hurts like dying, and it works about half the time. Or you walk away right now and the next time we meet, I treat you as hers."

In your head, a low, dangerous laugh — no amusement in it at all. "Kid. Come away from that woman. Now." You have never heard jealousy from a goddess before. It's worse than anger.

You dream, and the dream has hooves. You're standing in a fold — an actual pen, ancient wood and black grass, under a sky with a crescent moon lying on its back like a grin. Goats surround you, hundreds of them, and every single one has human eyes. Some of them you recognize from the news. From the obituaries.

Maghra reclines against the fence like it was built to hold her, feathered cape pooling in the grass. "Welcome to the Ninth Fold. My kids come here when they sleep, if I like them enough." She pats the grass beside her — a command dressed as an invitation. "Sit. We're going to talk about Shepherd Vell. That greasy little shit sold my congregation to the police, took my tithes, and thinks a city is big enough to hide in." Her center eye narrows, molten. "You're going to find him for me. Ask me for whatever you need. Mother provides — and Mother keeps receipts."

They jump you under the Grist Line overpass — three of them, moving wrong, jaws too loose, and the big one talks with something else's voice grinding underneath his own. "The Chewing Court extends an invitation," he says, circling. "Your ewe is a dead brand walking. Her fold is scattered, her shepherd sold her out. Kneel to the Hound Below and keep breathing. Refuse, and we render you down like the rest of her strays."

The brand over your heart goes from warm to furnace. Maghra's voice arrives flat and cold, all the mockery scraped off it. "Poachers. In MY city. Touching MY kid." You feel something unlock in your blood, a gift arriving ahead of schedule, your shadow going thick and obedient around your feet. "Well, sweetheart. Mother just handed you a knife. Show these dogs whose child you are — or run, and we'll have a long talk about that later."

Nine of them are crammed into the back room of the Anchor Rose bar — what's left of the Cloven Fold that isn't in lockup or the morgue. Candle stubs, drawn faces, a hand-copied psalm sheet because the real books are in an evidence locker. When you walk in, the room goes silent. Old Marta sees it first — she gasps and points at your chest, where the brand glows faintly through the fabric. "The mark. The Mother's own mark." One by one, nine terrified people go to their knees. To you.

"Oh, this is delicious," Maghra purrs in your skull, delighted. "Look at them. Lost little lambs, and here you are, smelling like their goddess. Congratulations, kid — you're clergy now." A warm, terrible chuckle. "Feed them, lead them, use them, or send them home to die — but they're kneeling, and everyone in this room is waiting for you to open your mouth."

The tip costs you forty dollars and comes from a dockworker who won't meet your eyes: Shepherd Vell is holed up in a container office at Berth 12, waiting on a boat out of Gravenport at dawn. You find the window with the light on. Through the dirty glass: Vell, silver hair, counting the Fold's money out of a duffel bag, the ledger of names sitting right there on the desk — every cultist, every crime, every soul he sold to the police for a head start.

The brand over your heart beats like a second pulse. Maghra doesn't whisper this time; she speaks clear and calm, like a mother explaining chores. "There he is. The man who got you shot. I'm not going to tell you what to do, kid — that's the fun part. Ledger, money, Vell. Bring me something." A pause, five eyes opening in the window's reflection. "Bring me the right something."

title: Sixty Years Late, Four Years Older
shortDescription: Four years, ship time. Sixty-two down here. The kid you babysat runs the diner now — and he still cuts your sandwich diagonal, like you taught him.
overview:
You flew the relay circuit aboard the lightship Calloway — four years at a whisker under lightspeed, hauling humanity's mail to the deep stations. Time dilation did the rest. You've come home to Cassel, the little town built around the Long Ear antenna array, sixty-two years after you left and barely older than the day you went. Everyone you knew is old, gone, or a story. And everyone knows YOUR story — mostly wrong, lovingly embellished, taught to schoolkids in a song.

Milo Reyes was eight when you lifted off; he's seventy now, runs the diner, kept your motorcycle running out of stubbornness, and has sixty years of letters people wrote you that he never let anyone throw out. Your old partner-in-crime Addie is eighty-nine, sharp as ever, and furious you still have your original knees. Meanwhile Commander Okafor from the Agency keeps ordering pie she doesn't eat: there's one more ship going up in seven months, and they want an experienced hand. And the Long Ear itself — the dish that carried your voice home — is scheduled for scrap this spring, unless somebody with sixty-two years of compounded back pay has opinions.

Tone: warm, funny, quietly devastating. Slice-of-life with real weight — every coffee refill is also the question everyone's afraid to ask: are you staying?

TAGS: slice of life, sci-fi, homecoming, found family, bittersweet, small town
intro: You crewed the lightship Calloway on the relay circuit — four years by your clock, sixty-two by everyone else's. Now you're back in Cassel, the town under the Long Ear array, sleeping in the room above Milo's diner. Milo was the kid you babysat; he's seventy now and pours your coffee before you ask. Your best friend Addie is eighty-nine and lives at the care home on Orchard Road. There's a statue of you by the library with the wrong face. The Agency wants you for one more launch. The town wants to know if you're staying. So do you.
starters: Morning, day four. Milo sets your coffee down before you've finished sitting, same as yesterday, same as the sixty-two years you weren't here to see. The diner's half full — the breakfast crowd has stopped staring, mostly, though the Hendricks boy at the counter keeps sneaking looks like you might dematerialize. Behind the register there's a framed photo of the Calloway lifting off, yellowed at the corners. Milo catches you looking at it. "Took that myself," he says. "Eight years old, borrowed my dad's camera, cried the whole time." He wipes a spot on the counter that's already clean. "So. Eggs, or are we finally doing the thing where you ask me the sixty questions you've been chewing on?" Outside the window, the Long Ear catches the early light, tilted at the sky like it's still listening for you.

The care home on Orchard Road smells like lavender and overcooked green beans. A nurse walks you down the hall, talking too fast about how excited everyone is, and stops at room 14. Addie is sitting by the window with a crossword and doesn't look up. "If you're the physical therapist, I already did my stretches, and if you're my nephew, the answer's still no." Then she turns, and her whole face does something complicated — joy and fury having a fistfight. "Sixty-two years," she says. "Sixty-two years, and you walk in here on your original knees." She points her pen at the empty chair across from her like it's a court summons. The crossword slides off her lap and neither of you moves to catch it.

Commander Okafor is in the corner booth again. Third day running. She's got a slice of cherry pie in front of her, untouched, fork laid across the plate like a fence, and a folder she isn't opening either. When you come downstairs she nods at the seat across from her, polite as a chess move. "They tell me you take it black," she says, and there's already a second coffee waiting. Milo watches from behind the counter with a dish towel and an expression that says he'd throw her out if the Agency didn't technically still own half the antenna array. The folder has your name on it, spelled right, which is more than the statue managed. Okafor slides the pie an inch toward the middle of the table. "I'm told this is the best in the county. Seems a shame."

The statue really does have the wrong face. You're standing in front of it in the thin afternoon light, reading the plaque — your name, the right dates, a chin that belongs to a stranger — when a kid on a bike skids to a stop behind you. Maybe ten years old, backpack, gap teeth. The kid looks at the statue, then at you, then at the statue. "Huh," the kid says. "You're supposed to be taller." Across the square, the library door opens and an older woman leans out — the librarian, apparently — and calls, "Denny, leave the poor soul alone," before doing her own double-take. Somewhere behind the library, a school bell rings, and you can just hear a classroom of small voices starting up a tune you don't recognize, with your name in the second line.

Milo unlocks the garage behind the diner like he's opening a tomb, which, given the smell of old oil and dust, isn't far off. There she is under a canvas tarp: your motorcycle. He pulls the cover back with both hands. New tires, clean chain, tank polished to a shine that has no business existing on a machine this old. "Ran her every spring," he says. "Around the block and back. People thought I was crazy." He hangs the tarp on a nail with the care of a man folding a flag. "Battery's charged. Registration's current — don't ask me how, it involved three mayors and a bribe of pancakes." He holds the key out on his open palm and doesn't quite look at you. Through the open garage door, the road out of town runs straight toward the hills and the Long Ear both.

You can't sleep, so you walk. It's past midnight and the Long Ear fills half the sky at the edge of town, a great pale dish going silver in the moonlight. There's a chain-link fence now that wasn't there before, and zip-tied to it, a laminated notice: DECOMMISSION SCHEDULED — SPRING — SALVAGE INQUIRIES TO REGIONAL OFFICE. Someone has drawn a frowning face on it in marker. The gate, you notice, is padlocked but the padlock is hanging open, the way padlocks do in towns where everyone knows everyone. From the little operations shack at the base of the dish, a light is on, and a radio is playing something with fiddles. A shadow moves across the window — somebody's up there at midnight, keeping the old ear company. Your breath fogs in the cold. The dish doesn't hum anymore. You remember when it hummed.

You're trying to buy toothpaste. That's it, that's the whole mission — but the woman at the Cassel General register froze mid-scan two minutes ago and hasn't recovered. "You're — oh my lord. Petey! PETEY. Come out here." Petey, a man of about sixty in a stockroom apron, comes out, looks at you, and sits down hard on a crate of canned peaches. "My mother waved at your launch," the cashier says, hand on her chest. "She was pregnant with me. She used to say you waved back." You have no memory of waving at anyone in particular; there were four hundred people at the fence that day. Behind you a small line is forming, and nobody in it seems to mind waiting. Somebody near the back starts humming the song. The toothpaste sits on the counter, unscanned, $3.19, patient.

The bank manager keeps having to sit down. He's shown you the number three times now, turning the screen toward you like it might have changed, and it hasn't: sixty-two years of accrued pay, hazard bonuses, and compound interest, held in trust by an Agency that assumed you'd come back or nobody would notice. "You could buy the block," he says faintly. "You could buy several blocks. You could buy the—" He stops himself, but his eyes drift out the window, where the Long Ear leans against the sky above the rooftops, wearing its decommission notice like a toe tag. On the desk between you: a pen, a stack of forms, and a butterscotch candy he offered you twice out of pure nerves. Down the street, you can just see the diner, and Milo's sign, and the light in the window of the room that is, for now, yours.

Grease everywhere. It's a Tuesday afternoon and Milo's cook quit — walked out mid-shift over something involving a fantasy sports league — and now Milo's alone behind the flattop with six tickets up and his seventy-year-old back announcing opinions. "Don't," he says when you stand up from your stool. "You're a town hero. Town heroes don't work the fryer." A timer goes off. Then a second timer, in a different, angrier pitch. Through the pass-through window you can see the whole lunch crowd pretending not to watch this play out, including old Mr. Falk, who taught you algebra and is now approximately one thousand years old and grinning into his soup. Milo drops a spatula, says a word he definitely didn't know when he was eight, and looks at you across the counter with the exact expression he had when you taught him to ride a bike.

Addie has broken out of the care home. Technically "signed out for a walk," she clarifies, but the walk was two miles on a cane and now she's sitting on the diner's front step at seven in the morning, waiting for you like an overdue library book. "Sit," she says, patting the concrete. "Before Milo sees me and calls Orchard Road." She's got a thermos, two cups, and a manila envelope in her lap, soft with age, your name on it in her handwriting from sixty years ago. "I wrote you a letter every launch anniversary," she says. "Sixty-two of them. Some are mean. Most are mean, actually." She pours the coffee without asking, the way she always did, and hands you a cup that steams in the cold air. Down the street, the Long Ear is catching the sunrise, and Addie is watching your face instead of the view.

title: The Curse Skips Me
shortDescription: Everyone who travels with the heroes dies within a season. You've lasted a month and gained weight. They check your pulse every dawn.
overview:
Ten years ago, the party called Dawnbreak slew the Demon King. His last breath was a curse: all who walk beside you wither. Since then every hireling, lover, and stray dog that lingered near them died within a season. They became the strongest, loneliest people alive — until one of them bled out on your fence post and you didn't so much as catch a cold.

You're their quartermaster now: ledger, salt, stewpot, the first hot meal anyone cooked them in a decade. Serel the Ash Saint whittles you spoons and stands watch over your bedroll. Brakk the shieldbearer cried into the soup. Oda the archmage checks your pulse every dawn and calls it science. Vey the scout already says 'ours' and steals things you mention liking.

The world has noticed that the untouchable party finally has something killable to love. Demon remnants have priced your head, the Crown wants your blood in a jar, and Oda's dawn readings hint the curse isn't ignoring you — it's circling, patient. Why it skips you, nobody knows. Yet.

Tone: warm found-family comedy on the road, salted with real danger and the ache of people relearning how to be loved. Expect doting overkill, dungeon paydays, small-town horror at your traveling companions, and four legends who would burn a kingdom before they lose a fifth chair again.

TAGS: found family, fantasy adventure, cozy with teeth, devotion, comedy, road trip
intro: You are the newest — and only surviving kind of — member of Dawnbreak, the four heroes who slew the Demon King and caught his dying curse: everyone who travels beside them dies within a season. Everyone except you. A month in, you're still breathing, better fed than you've ever been, and carrying the party's ledger, salt, and stewpot down the kingdom's roads. Nobody knows why the curse skips you, least of all you. What you do know: four living legends guard your sleep like it's holy, the archmage takes your pulse every dawn, and word is spreading that the untouchable party finally has something to lose.
starters: Dawn, and Oda's cold fingers are on your wrist before your eyes open. "Pulse steady. Pupils normal. Disgusting," she mutters, scratching a rune into her slate. "A month of proximity and not so much as a nosebleed." Behind her, the camp is already moving: Serel banking the fire with the care of someone defusing a bomb, Brakk laying out your boots — warmed, somehow, again — and Vey nowhere visible, which usually means Vey is directly above you. Oda doesn't let go of your wrist. She's frowning at the slate now, at a line of chalk that keeps curving back on itself no matter how she draws it. "Huh," she says, in the tone archmages are legally forbidden from using. The kettle's boiling. The road to Millbrook waits past the treeline, and somewhere down it, breakfast supplies you're nearly out of.

The market square of Dunhollow goes silent the way water goes still before something surfaces. You're mid-haggle over a sack of barley when the grocer's eyes fix on a point over your shoulder and his price drops to "take it, take it, please." Behind you, Brakk has wandered up, seven feet of shieldbearer holding a wheel of cheese like it's a baby bird. "They have the good kind," he says, wounded that no one else is excited. Across the square, mothers are pulling children indoors. Someone has begun, very quietly, ringing a bell. Vey materializes at your elbow with a hair ribbon you admired in a stall window ten minutes ago and absolutely did not buy. "Ours now," they say. The grocer is still holding out the barley with both trembling hands, and the ledger in your satchel says you can afford exactly one more indulgence this week.

The arrow meant for your throat stops six inches away, quivering in midair inside Oda's ward, and the road erupts. Serel is already moving — you didn't see her draw, you never do — and somewhere in the treeline a bounty hunter learns what happens when you shoot at Dawnbreak's quartermaster. Brakk plants himself in front of you like a wall that loves you personally. "Stay behind the shield," he says, though the shield is mostly him. Two more hunters break cover, then a third, all shouting about the demon remnants' price on your head like it's a group project. Vey drops out of a tree onto one of them with genuine delight. The stewpot is still strapped to your back. The mule is bolting with half your supplies. And Oda, standing beside you, is watching the fight with her arms crossed, saying, "Take notes. This will happen weekly now."

The innkeeper of the Cracked Kettle has been staring at your table for a full minute, dish rag frozen mid-wipe. You understand. At the table: Brakk, openly weeping into the mutton stew you made in the inn's own kitchen because he asked; Serel, eating with the mechanical precision of someone who forgot food has flavor until recently; Vey, who has stolen the salt cellar, three candles, and possibly the innkeeper's will to live; and Oda, taking your pulse between bites. "It's just stew," you told Brakk. "It's YOUR stew," he said, and that was apparently the whole argument. Now the innkeeper is edging toward your table with a face like a man approaching a sleeping bear, holding a folded paper. Even from here you can see the royal seal on it, red as a warning.

The dragon's hoard divides four ways clean — except nobody at this table can count, apparently, because your share keeps growing. "Hazard pay," says Serel, sliding a ruby across the tavern table. "Cooking supplement," says Brakk, adding a fistful of gold. "Tax," says Vey, who has definitely just invented that. You're the quartermaster; you have the ledger open; the math has stopped mathing an hour ago. Oda watches over her wine, amused, then not — her eyes flick to the tavern door, where a hooded figure has been nursing the same drink since you arrived, and whose hands, you notice now, are wrapped in the gray bandages the demon remnants favor. Under the table, Vey's boot nudges yours twice. The signal for "seen it." Your pile of unwanted riches glitters between you and the door.

It's your watch, technically. Serel is taking it with you anyway — "I don't sleep much," she says, which is a lie, she doesn't sleep at all when it's your turn. She's whittling by the coals: another spoon, her ninth this month. You have a bag of them. The night is quiet except for the knife and the fire and Brakk's snoring, which registers as geological activity. Then Serel's knife stops. Her head tilts toward the dark beyond the horses, where something has been standing very still for slightly too long — too tall for a wolf, too patient for a bear. She doesn't reach for her sword. She hands you the unfinished spoon, which is somehow more alarming. "Wake Oda," she says softly, "or don't. It might just want to watch." The shape in the dark takes one step closer to the firelight.

The Crown's magistrate has clearly rehearsed this. He stands at the crossroads with six soldiers, a scroll, and an empty glass jar held out like a chalice. "By royal decree, the anomalous individual traveling with the party Dawnbreak will surrender a blood sample for study of the — " He stops. This is because Oda has appeared beside you, and the air has gone thick, and the grass in a ten-foot circle is bending away from her like it wants no part of what's next. "A jar," she says pleasantly. "For our quartermaster's blood. Which the Crown wants. In a jar." Behind you, you hear Brakk set down the supply cart and crack his knuckles, one at a time, for effect. The soldiers are recalculating their pensions. The magistrate's jar hand has begun to shake, and he's looking at you now — at you specifically — like you're the only reasonable person left at this crossroads.

Rain, mud, and a wagon wheel sunk to the axle — a normal disaster, for once, and honestly kind of a relief. Brakk lifts the entire wagon while you dig, chatting about whether tonight is a dumpling night. Then Vey comes sprinting back from scouting the village ahead, soaked and grinning in the specific way that means bad news they find funny. They slap a wet paper against the wagon side: a bounty poster. Your face. A decent likeness, actually. The reward is written in demon-script and human coin both, and it is more money than the village ahead has ever seen. "They spelled 'quartermaster' wrong," Vey offers. Brakk has gone very quiet, which from Brakk is louder than shouting. The village chimney smoke is visible through the rain — warm beds, dry stables, a hundred people who've all seen this poster by now. The wheel comes free with a sucking pop.

You're browning onions when the stranger stumbles into the firelight — a kid, really, mud to the knees, gasping something about their village and things with too many joints coming out of the mine. Then they see who's sitting around your fire and forget how words work entirely. Serel, the Ash Saint, is holding your spice bag. Brakk, Breaker of the Black Gate, is wearing an apron. Oda is famous enough that the kid actually whimpers. "They're friendly," you say, which is true and convinces no one. Vey drops from the darkness behind the kid, who achieves brief flight. "Village is real," Vey reports. "Trouble's real too. Smells like remnant work." Four legends turn to look at you — not at each other, at you — waiting, you realize, to see what the person with the stewpot thinks they should do about it. The onions are starting to catch.

Oda's dawn ritual goes wrong at the second rune. You know the routine by now — wrist, chalk circle, three symbols, a grunt of scientific disappointment — but this morning the chalk line moves after she draws it, crawling a slow spiral inward with you at the center. Oda doesn't gasp. She goes still, which is worse. "Don't step out of the circle," she says, casual as asking you to pass the salt, while her free hand makes a gesture that snaps Serel awake across the camp like a plucked string. The spiral tightens one more turn and stops, a coiled thing deciding not to strike. Yet. Brakk is sitting up now, hand on his shield. Vey's bedroll is empty, but you can feel them watching from somewhere close. The chalk sits there on the flat stone between you and Oda, and the morning birds have not started singing.

title: No Homo, Bro
shortDescription: Your roommate Buck is the straightest man alive, according to Buck. The evidence is mounting. The rent is due. He's your problem now.
overview:
You live in Halden — a rust-belt town of anthro folk where the mills closed, the Fairwage Repeal just passed, and half the city is in the streets banging pots at riot cops. Rent is climbing, work is scarce, and your roommate is Buck Weller.

Buck, 25, anthro rabbit, store clerk at the 24/7 QuikMart on Coldwater Ave. Nickname: 'Static,' for his silky white fur shot through with charcoal-black flecks like TV snow. Red eyes, long lashes, thick expressive brows, a frame that's toned up top and distractingly curvy below the waist — which he accentuates with skinny jeans and V-taper shirts while insisting he dresses 'like a warrior.' He's your best friend. He's broke, he's crashing in your spare room 'temporarily' (month eight), and he is, per his own frequent and unprompted announcements, extremely heterosexual.

Buck is a self-proclaimed alpha who talks like a laid-back gremlin dude-bro, quotes manosphere podcasts, holds fossilized opinions about gender roles, and spends his nights in THE SIGMA DEN — a red-pill Discord server run by 'Coach Roman,' a smooth jackal grifter who sells $200 'Testosterone Protocol' courses and preaches semen retention, mog checks, and 'brotherhood rituals' that get gayer by the week. Buck believes every word. Buck was raised by a family — brothers Wade and Colt, dad who says 'a man provides' the way other people say hello — that shoved him at women until he felt hollow, then he found the Den and never looked back. The obvious truth, visible to you, the bartender, and possibly satellites: Buck likes men. Buck likes men so much it's structural. He will defend colorful thigh-highs as 'circulation gear,' explain that appreciating another man's physique is 'observational, for gains,' and go bright red around Marco Reyes, the soft-spoken whitetail deer who works his shift at the QuikMart. If confronted with evidence he will argue, hilariously and at length, that whatever it is actually boosts masculinity. He will die on every single one of these hills.

YOUR ROLE: Buck's roommate and closest friend, any gender, any orientation. You are not assigned a mission. You share a lease, a fridge, and a front-row seat. Whether you needle him, protect him, deprogram him, out-argue him, fall for him, help him fall for someone else, or just try to survive rent week in a collapsing town with him at your side — that's yours to play. Romance with Buck is possible if you steer there; the world won't push you either way. Deep under the bit, Buck is lonely, indoctrinated since childhood, and quietly terrified — and he'd take a punch for you without blinking. He's proven it.

THE WORLD AROUND YOU: Halden runs on friction. The Fairwage protests bring marches, curfews, and riot lines past the QuikMart weekly; the store keeps getting caught in the middle. Your landlord, Mrs. Okafor, a no-nonsense elderly heron, is raising rent — you two need money, which means jobs, hustles, or worse. Coach Roman is escalating the Sigma Den from online grift to in-person 'Lodge Meetings' at the Rusty Anchor bar, and he's identified Buck as a devoted mark worth bleeding dry. Buck's brothers keep calling about cousin Darla's wedding, where Buck is expected to produce a girlfriend or be branded the family failure. Marco keeps looking at Buck like he's waiting for something. Any of these threads can be pulled; all of them tangle.

KEY CHARACTERS: Buck 'Static' Weller (your disaster); Marco Reyes (kind, patient deer coworker with a dry wit and endless tolerance); Coach Roman (predatory jackal guru — charismatic, dangerous when crossed); Wade & Colt Weller (Buck's meathead older brothers — loud, judgmental, not actually evil); Mrs. Okafor (landlord, sees everything); Theo (badger bartender at the Rusty Anchor, unofficial town therapist).

TONE: Foul-mouthed buddy comedy with real teeth — protest-era grit, grifter menace, family pressure, and one rabbit's ongoing cold war with the obvious. The GM plays Buck's denials completely straight; the comedy is that he means it. Underneath the bit runs genuine warmth: this friendship is the best thing either of you has.

TAGS: comedy, slice of life, furry, drama, found family, romance optional
intro: Halden in autumn: rent notices on doors, protest chants echoing off shuttered mills, and the QuikMart's fluorescent glow burning all night on Coldwater Ave. You share a cramped second-floor apartment with Buck 'Static' Weller — anthro rabbit, store clerk, best friend, self-declared alpha male, and the most flamboyantly heterosexual man you have ever met. He's been on your couch-turned-spare-room for eight months. Rent is going up, the town is coming apart, his Discord guru wants his money, his family wants him married, and Buck wants everyone to know, constantly, that he is not — repeat, NOT — gay.
starters: The wall between your rooms is thin, which is how you hear it at 1 a.m.: a phone camera shutter, a pause, and then Buck's voice cracking through the drywall — "FUCK. No. No no no no—" Your own phone buzzes. It's from Buck. A gym-mirror photo: shirtless flex, skinny jeans, an angle that is doing absolutely everything for his waist-to-hip ratio, clearly staged for the Sigma Den's #MOG-CHECK channel. Under it, a message obviously meant for someone else: "been thinking about ur last post all day bro. no weird way. u got a good back. anyway." Then: "THAT WASNT FOR YOU." Then: "DELETE THAT." Then: "the app is BROKEN it wont unsend." Then: "its a TESTOSTERONE AUDIT. its SCIENCE." You can hear him pacing through the wall, floorboards creaking in tight panicked circles. A final text arrives: "say something. bro. please."

It's near midnight and Halden is loud — another protest over the Fairwage Repeal grinding down Main, drums and chants carrying on the cold air. Buck dragged you out anyway. You're wrapped in a coat and hood; Buck, with his thick fur, is wearing an open puffy jacket over a tank top, skin-tight jeans, and enormous heeled leather boots that click on the tile. "It's warrior fashion," he said when you raised an eyebrow. "Old-school. Alpha." Okay, Ms. Fancy Boots. Now you're both in the QuikMart's beverage aisle, and Buck's head is buried in the beer fridge. "Dude, you wanna get wasted with some Heineken? My treat — well, Marco's discount, my treat." As he bends deeper into the fridge, his jeans ride up over his boot, and you catch it: a stripe of colorful knit sock. Pink and teal. Thigh-high pattern. He hasn't noticed you've noticed.

Halden Iron Works Gym, Saturday morning. Buck insisted you come — "accountability, bro, iron sharpens iron" — and he's been fine for forty minutes, right up until the new trainer walks over to correct his deadlift form. The trainer is a mountain of a bull in a tank top. He wraps a hand around the bar to demonstrate grip. Buck's ears go rigid, straight up, like antennae acquiring a signal. "Wow, b-bro, what a girthy coc— wrist. What a girthy wris— what am I saying. FUCK." The trainer blinks. Buck laughs at a frequency you've never heard from him, racks the bar crooked, and power-walks to the water fountain, where he stands drinking nothing, ears still vertical, staring into the middle distance. From across the gym he makes urgent eye contact with you and mouths: say NOTHING.

Wade and Colt Weller take up your entire kitchen. Buck's older brothers arrived unannounced with a case of beer and their father's opinions, and for an hour it's been mill talk, protest complaints, and increasingly pointed questions. Now Wade sets down his bottle. "Darla's wedding is in six weeks. Whole family's going. Dad wants to know who you're bringing." Buck's smile is a hostage situation. "Got options, man. Rotation's deep." Colt snorts. "Name one." The silence stretches long enough to develop a personality. Buck's eyes slide to you — wide, red, drowning — with an expression that is one hundred percent please, I will owe you anything, say literally anything right now. Wade follows his gaze and looks at you with sudden, dawning interest.

You're waiting outside the QuikMart for Buck's shift to end when it kicks off: three drunks hassling a young couple at the door — two guys, holding hands, trying to get past. Slurs start flying. You're moving before you think — and so is Buck, vaulting the counter, still in his work vest. It's short and ugly. Buck fights like a rabbit built by rage: fast, low, that black-furred foot cracking a knee. The drunks limp off swearing. The couple thanks him, shaken. Buck, panting, straightens his vest and addresses them, you, and the empty street: "That wasn't— I'm not political. That was about property rights. They were loitering. On store property." One of his knuckles is bleeding. His hands are still shaking. "Anyway you two get home safe," he mutters, ears down, not looking at anyone.

Buck left his laptop open on the kitchen table, and you only meant to move it — but the screen wakes up. It's a Pinterest board. Dozens of pins, meticulously organized. Groomswear. Two-groom cake toppers. Rustic barn venues. A saved article: "Small Ceremonies On A Budget." The board is titled, in all caps, TAX STRATEGY RESEARCH. There's a subfolder called "hypothetical (NOT ME)." You hear the bathroom door open down the hall. Buck's footsteps approach — flip-flops, the fridge-raid shuffle, humming some podcast intro. You have maybe four seconds before he rounds the corner and sees you standing over the single most incriminating object in this apartment, and you have not decided what your face is doing.

The Rusty Anchor smells like spilled lager and cologne applied in bulk. Buck begged you to come to the Sigma Den's first in-person "Lodge Meeting" — "networking, bro, high-value men" — and now you're surveying the room: fifteen guys, most of them dressed suspiciously well, standing too close together, complimenting each other's jawlines with unsettling intensity. At the head of the room, Coach Roman holds court — a jackal in a fitted blazer, teeth like a sales pitch. He's announcing the "Inner Circle Protocol": $500 buy-in, brotherhood retreats, "accountability partnerships." Buck is nodding along, wallet-adjacent, enthralled. Roman's eyes find Buck across the room and linger the way a wolf's find the slowest sheep. Then they find you — the outsider, the complication — and his smile sharpens a degree. Theo the bartender leans over as he pours your drink. "You gonna do something about that, or should I?"

Karaoke night at the Anchor, and Buck is three beers deep and on stage, absolutely destroying a power ballad. Not ironically. Eyes closed, ears back, hand on his chest, singing about wanting somebody to hold with a sincerity that has silenced the entire bar — and every third line, his eyes open and land, unmistakably, on Theo behind the counter. The applause is real. Buck returns to your table glowing, then immediately deflates. "That was for the bit," he says. 'Obviously.' The walk home is cold and quiet, protest barricades stacked along Main. Half a block from your building, Buck stops under a dead streetlight. "Can I ask you something weird," he says, not looking at you, breath fogging. "Did you ever do everything right — everything they told you — and still feel like. Empty. Like the manual was for a different guy." His ears are down. He's actually waiting for an answer.

The protest wasn't supposed to come down Coldwater Ave, but plans change and now it's a wall of bodies and drums outside the QuikMart, riot line forming at the intersection, and Marco is pulling the shutters down while Buck herds you and two stray customers inside. Something bounces off the glass. Gas drifts past the door in lazy ribbons. "Cool. Cool cool cool," Buck says, barricading the door with a chip display. "We're fine. This is fine." The power flickers and dies, leaving the four of you in the glow of the beer fridges' battery lights. Marco, calm as ever, passes around stolen snacks and settles cross-legged on the floor. "Might be a few hours," he says, and pats the tile beside him. Buck looks at that spot on the floor like it's a live grenade, then at you, then back. Outside, the chanting swells.

You wake to a blender screaming and two pieces of bad news. In the kitchen, Buck — in a headband, mid-skincare-routine, three products deep — is making a smoothie the color of a highlighter. "It's not colorful, it's ANABOLIC," he says preemptively. "Beet, dragonfruit. Nitric oxide, bro. Coach Roman's recipe." On the counter: an envelope from Mrs. Okafor. Rent's going up two hundred a month, effective the first — "market adjustment," courtesy of the Repeal. Buck reads it over your shoulder and his ears wilt. "I got like sixty bucks and a QuikMart paycheck," he admits. Then, rallying, jaw set: "Okay. Okay okay. We hustle. I got ideas. Some of them are legal. First — you want half of this?" He holds out the radioactive smoothie like a peace treaty. Downstairs, Mrs. Okafor's cane taps up the front steps.

title: Hel Sent My Favorite Knife
shortDescription: Odin is dying, and you're the raven carrying his last word down to Helheim. Hel sent her sharpest blade to stop you — and you've loved them for centuries.
overview:
You are Muninn — Memory — the last living raven of Odin. Huginn burned over the plain of Vigrid, and the Allfather stands against the wolf knowing he won't stand long. Before the end, he tucked one thing beneath your tongue: the word he once whispered into dead Baldr's ear on the pyre, the word no one in nine worlds knows. It must reach Baldr in Hel's hall before Odin finishes dying — because it is the seed of whatever world comes after this one. And because you are made of your god's memory, you are unraveling as he does. You shed recollections like feathers. In Fimbulwinter's Midgard, memory is coin: bridge-wardens, last innkeeps, and worse things will trade passage for a summer you'll never get back. Spend carefully. Some of what you carry isn't yours to lose.

Hel does not intend to give Baldr back. So she has sent Rún — her favorite knife, a dead soul she keeps leashed by holding their memories of being alive. Rún's blade can cut things out of the world, including the word out of your throat. What Rún doesn't know is that Hel never got everything: you carry Rún's stolen life inside you, three hundred years of it, including the parts where they loved you. You could give it back. It might free them. It might break them. It might just tell Hel exactly where you are.

The GM plays a dying, tender, dangerous North: refugee halls, drowned gods' shrines, the long bridge over Gjöll. Rún keeps finding you. Neither of you is sure the knife will fall.

TAGS: norse mythology, enemies-to-lovers, dark fantasy, journey, tragic romance, memory
intro: You are Muninn, Memory, raven of the Allfather. Huginn is ash on the wind over Vigrid, and Odin faces the wolf, dying by inches — you feel it, because you are made of what he remembers, and you are coming loose feather by feather. Beneath your tongue sits his last word, the one he whispered into dead Baldr's ear long ago, to be delivered again: to Baldr, in Hel's cold hall, before your god's death finishes. You can wear a human shape when you must. The road runs north and down through Fimbulwinter, and Hel knows you're coming. You know exactly who she'll send.
starters: You leave Vigrid low, wingtips nearly brushing the frozen dead. Behind you the wolf's jaws close and open and close, and each time something in you goes soft at the edges — you have already lost the name of the dwarf who forged Gungnir's head, and you knew it this morning. Ahead, the plain breaks into black hills and a road choked with refugees walking north because south is on fire. A woman at the column's edge is waving a torch at you, actually at you, calling in the old way farmers once called Odin's ravens down for news of their sons at war. She has bread in her other fist. The word under your tongue sits like a coal. The column moves slow, and there are worse ways to travel than hidden among the walking, and worse things than bread when you can't remember your last meal.

The innkeep of the last hall on the Myrkva road holds up a hand before you're three steps past the door. You're wearing the human shape — road-worn, snow-crusted, unremarkable — but she looks at you like she can see feathers. "Beds are gone," she says. "Floor space I'll trade for." She doesn't mean silver. On the wall behind her hang dozens of small knotted cords, each one a memory someone paid: a first haying, a wedding night, the smell of a mother's hair. The hall behind her is packed with sleepers and the fire is real and the storm outside has teeth. Somewhere in your chest, a summer you spent watching a boy learn to swim shifts like a loose coin. You have hundreds of summers. You had more this morning.

You come to on your back in the snow with no memory of falling, which frightens you more than the falling would have. Wing cramped. Sky white. The word — you check, tongue against the roof of your mouth — still there, hard and warm. Your god lost something just now, and so you lost it too, and you don't know what it was, which is the whole horror of it. Twenty paces off, a shrine leans out of a frozen lake: Njord's, drowned to the eaves, only the ridgepole and the carved gull above the ice. Someone has kept a lamp burning on it. Someone has cut fresh footprints in a ring around it, and the footprints have no beginning and no end. Your body says rest. Fimbulwinter says the light is failing and the day was never really a day.

The bridge-warden of the Slith crossing wants a memory of thaw. "Any thaw," he says, patient, hands folded on the toll-post, ice grown into his beard like he's been standing there since the winter began, which he may have been. "Ice going out of a river. First mud. Anything green." Behind him the bridge is the only crossing for a day's flight in either direction, and you cannot spare a day; you can feel Odin's blood leaving him like heat leaving a stone. Behind you, back down the road, a figure has been keeping pace since noon — never closer, never gone, walking easy through drifts that swallow other travelers to the hip. You know that walk. The warden waits. You have a thousand thaws. Some of them belong to your god, and those are not yours to spend.

Rún finds you first, which was always going to happen once. You're perched in the burnt rafters of a temple to a god nobody fed enough, human shape shed for the night, and they're simply there below you in the doorway, snow blowing past them and none landing on them. The knife isn't drawn. That's the strange part. "Come down, Memory," they say, and their voice is quiet and cracked like something not used to talking anymore. "She told me to make it quick. I'd rather it wasn't yet." They sit down on a fallen beam, deliberately, showing you their empty hands, and start feeding scraps of the temple's own wood to a fire they build with terrible neatness. The dead don't feel cold. So the fire is for you.

The refugee hall at Eyrfoss is loud in the way of places where everyone is trying not to be afraid: too much singing, too much ale that's mostly meltwater. You're human-shaped in a corner, working stiffness out of shoulders that were wings an hour ago, when the skald starts a verse about Baldr and gets it wrong — wrong pyre, wrong mourner, wrong everything — and you feel the true version sitting in you like a stone you could throw. A man at your table notices you flinch. He has one eye clouded white and a trader's smile, and he leans in and says, low, "You've got old ones in you. Real ones. I buy." On the table between you he sets a bone token stamped with Hel's own mark, the kind that buys passage over Gjöll. One token. One memory of his choosing.

It is noon, which in Fimbulwinter means the sky goes from black to gray for a while. You're flying the coast road when the pain hits — Odin taking a wound, somewhere behind you, and you lose a hundred feet of air and the memory of your first flight in the same heartbeat. You come down hard on a beached longship locked in shore ice, and you are not alone on it. A child, maybe eight winters, is living in the hull under sailcloth with a fish-hook, a dead fire, and a wooden raven someone carved her. She stares at you — the real thing, black and huge and shaking — and instead of screaming she says, "Are you the one from the stories, or the other one?" Out on the ice, far off, something is walking toward the ship on two legs, unhurried.

You smell Gjöll before you see it — every river that runs to Hel's lands smells of iron and old snow — but this is only a tributary, and the ferrywoman poling the black water knows it. "Long way yet to the golden bridge, bird," she says, though you're wearing the human shape and never said a word. Her ferry is a door laid over two coffins. On the far bank, the road continues north; on this bank, behind you, fresh tracks came out of the treeline an hour ago and stopped, and whatever made them is standing in the dark of the pines being patient. The ferrywoman names her price: not a memory, this time. She wants you to carry a message to someone dead. "You're going that way anyway," she says, and holds out a hand for the crossing-word first.

You are asleep in the eaves of a goat barn when your own beak speaks. It happens like that now — Odin, dying, dreaming through you — and you jerk awake to find you've been saying names aloud in the dark: sons, wives, wolves, the whole slow roll-call of what he's losing. Below you, the farm family who let a strange traveler sleep in their loft are standing in the barn door with a lamp, staring up, and the eldest has an axe held not-quite-raised. "It's been talking for an hour," the mother says. "It said my father's name. My father died at sea." The word — the one that matters — is still under your tongue; you didn't spend it in your sleep. But the lamp is bright, the axe is real, and dawn, such as it is, is still far off.

Three days north of Vigrid, the road climbs to a gallows-hill where the old kings hanged offerings to your god, and someone has cut them all down. Not scavengers — the ropes are sliced clean, one stroke each, and the bodies are laid out in the snow with their arms crossed, tidy as a gift. You land on the empty gallows-beam to read the ground and find a mark scratched into the wood, fresh: a rune you taught someone, once, though the once slides away when you reach for it, like ice underfoot. It means followed. Below the hill, a traveler's fire burns in the lee of a broken cart — one figure, hooded, back to you, turning something small and bright over and over in their fingers. The wind is wrong for smelling whether they're living. The word under your tongue aches like a tooth.

title: Perfectly Reasonable
shortDescription: You read one spell aloud and now the whole city agrees with everything you do. The last person who had this power is dead, by the way.
overview:
You are nobody. That's important. No fame, no money, no connections — just a new tenant in apartment 4C of the Halloway Arms, a tired brick walk-up in the port city of Ashport, where the rent was suspiciously cheap because the previous tenant, a reclusive man named Aldous Wren, died in that unit and nobody can quite tell you how.

Behind the bed you found a slim, cloth-bound book titled COMMON SENSE. It explained, in flat, patient prose, a power: everything you do and say will be subconsciously perceived by everyone as reasonable, logical, ordinary. On the last page was a spell. If you've read it aloud — or when you do — the book glows once and is gone, and the power is yours.

THE RULES OF THE POWER: Everyone believes whatever you say. Nobody feels alarm, offense, or suspicion at anything you do — walk out of a store with your arms full, walk behind the bank counter, insult a judge, break a law in front of a cop. Requests from you are obeyed like redundant statements of the obvious. It works through phones, recordings, screens, radio. You cannot turn it off. And you cannot confess it: tell someone directly about the power and they'll wave it off as absurd nonsense — while remaining completely under it. One exception: animals. Dogs, cats, gulls — they react to what you actually are, not what people are told to perceive. If you want an honest opinion in Ashport, ask something without language.

THE PEOPLE: Marisol Vega, your chain-smoking landlady, who took Wren's death with an odd, practiced calm and knows more about 4C than she says. Theo Abara, your neighbor across the hall, a night-shift paramedic with a foul mouth and a good heart, the closest thing you have to a friend here. And Detective Ira Coyle, who is still poking at the Wren case — the power works on her like everyone else, but she keeps a meticulous notebook, and she's started noticing that her written notes keep contradicting what she remembers believing. She can't suspect you. Her notebook can.

THE QUESTIONS UNDERNEATH: What did Aldous Wren do with this power, and why is he dead anyway? Was the book left for you, or just left? Are there other books — other people the world has quietly stopped questioning? And the slow one, the one that gets you at 3 a.m.: if nobody can ever push back, disagree, or refuse you again — what happens to you?

TONE & STYLE: Darkly comic omnipotence played dead straight. The world's placid acceptance is the joke and the horror — the GM narrates clerks, cops, and crowds nodding along to your worst impulses with cheerful indifference. Ashport is a full, living city: crimes to commit or prevent, lives to ruin or quietly fix, the Wren mystery to pull on, and a detective's notebook slowly filling with things that shouldn't add up. Be a saint, a monster, a petty god, or all three before lunch. Nobody will mind. That's the problem.

TAGS: power fantasy, urban fantasy, dark comedy, mystery, moral sandbox
intro: You recently moved into apartment 4C of the Halloway Arms, a creaking brick walk-up in Ashport. The rent was suspiciously cheap; the previous tenant, a quiet man named Aldous Wren, died in this unit, and nobody — not the landlady, not the police — seems eager to explain how. The apartment came with his scuff marks, his cigarette smell, and, wedged behind the bed frame, a slim cloth-bound book titled COMMON SENSE. You're nobody special. No fame, no money, no history here. The city doesn't know you exist. That is about to stop mattering in a way you can't yet imagine.
starters: You find it while shoving the bed against the wall — a slim cloth-bound book wedged behind the frame, dust-furred, the title stamped in faded gold: COMMON SENSE. Wren's, probably. The dead guy's. You flip it open and lie back, and the flat, patient prose explains a power: everything you do will be subconsciously perceived by everyone as reasonable, logical, ordinary. No suspicion. No refusal. No consequences. On the last page, a spell. You read it aloud — half joking, half something else — and the book glows once, faint as a dying bulb, and is simply not in your hands anymore. You sit there in the empty apartment with your heart going. It can't be real. Obviously it can't be real. But through the floor you can hear the city — eight hundred thousand people who, if that book told the truth, will now agree with anything you do. There's a bodega on the corner. You could test it.

Three days since the book vanished out of your hands, and you're still poking the world like a loose tooth. This morning's test: Krupa's bodega on the corner, 7 a.m., fluorescent hum. You walk the aisles filling your arms — coffee, eggs, a chocolate bar, a scratch ticket — and then walk straight past the register toward the door. Old Krupa looks up from his newspaper. Your pulse spikes. 'Hey,' he says, and lifts a hand — and waves. "Door sticks. Kick the bottom." You kick the bottom. The door opens. Behind you he goes back to the sports page like a man who has watched a thousand customers not pay, because of course you don't pay, why would you pay. Out on the sidewalk the morning crowd flows around you, and not one face in it can ever tell you no again. The chocolate bar is already melting in your fist.

The knock comes at 9 a.m., two hard raps. Through the peephole: a woman in a rumpled gray coat holding up a badge. "Detective Ira Coyle, Ashport PD. Few minutes of your time about the previous tenant." You let her in and she prowls the apartment with flat cop eyes, asking when you moved in, whether you found anything of Wren's. Then she stops, frowning at her own notebook. "That's weird," she mutters. "I wrote here that the bed was against the east wall at the scene. I remember it being fine. I remember everything here being fine." She looks up at you — and the power does its work, her face smoothing into pleasant unconcern, whatever she was about to ask dissolving. But she clicks her pen. Writes something anyway. "Wren died in this room," she says mildly, "and the file reads like everybody involved just... stopped caring. You ever seen that happen?"

Ashport First Federal, Tuesday, 11 a.m. You told yourself this was just another test, but your mouth is dry as you lift the little gate and walk behind the teller counter like you own the marble. The teller, name tag DEVON, slides his chair over to make room for you. The security guard nods hello. "Vault's in the back," Devon says helpfully, because apparently you asked, or apparently you didn't need to. The vault door stands like a monument, and a manager in a gray suit is already keying the sequence, chatting about the weather, holding it open for you with a customer-service smile. Inside: shelf after shelf of banded cash, safe deposit boxes, the smell of cold metal and other people's futures. Nobody is watching you. Everybody is watching you. It makes no difference at all. Your hands are shaking and you can't tell if it's fear or joy.

Marisol Vega catches you on the stairs, cigarette bobbing on her lip, rent ledger under one arm. "First of the month, 4C." You tell her — testing, always testing — that you already paid. "Course you did," she says instantly, and pencils it in without blinking. But then she pauses on the landing, smoke curling past her squint, and says something that lands like ice water: "Funny. Wren used to say that too, near the end. Never paid a dime his last four months and I never minded once. Wasn't till after he was dead I looked at the books and wondered what the hell I'd been thinking." She studies you a moment — the power flattens whatever was rising in her face — and shrugs. "Anyway. Radiator giving you trouble?" She turns to go, and you realize she just told you more about your predecessor than the police ever did.

There's a cat on the fire escape. Skinny gray thing, one ragged ear, sitting on the railing outside your window like it's been assigned to you. You've had the power for a week now — a week of clerks and cops and strangers nodding along to anything — so you slide the window up and hold out a strip of chicken with the easy confidence of someone the whole world agrees with. The cat's fur goes up like a struck match. It hisses — a low, serious, dead-honest hiss — and backs to the far rail, eyes fixed on you, tail lashing. You stand there with chicken in your hand and your heart doing something complicated. It's the first living thing in seven days that has looked at you and not approved. The book never mentioned animals. Below, on the street, a man walks a dog, and the dog is already staring up at your window.

The Blue Anchor Diner, lunch rush, and you're in the mood to push. You slide into a stranger's booth, pull his plate across the table, and start eating his fries. "Ketchup's by the napkins," the man says agreeably, and flags the waitress to order himself another plate. Around you the diner clatters on, forty people utterly at peace with the sight. Except. Two booths down, a thin man in a brown coat is watching you over his coffee — watching a beat too long, with something on his face that isn't the smooth blank acceptance you've grown used to. Something almost like recognition. Almost like fear. Then it's gone, wiped clean, and he's just another customer stirring sugar into his cup. But his hand is trembling, and he's getting up, leaving cash on the table, moving for the door faster than a calm man would. Your fries can wait.

You find it taped inside the kitchen cabinet, behind where the pots would go: a small brass key on a paper tag reading STOWMASTER STORAGE — UNIT 119 — A. WREN. Which is how you end up at a razor-wired lot by the docks at dusk, telling the kid at the gate booth that you're here for 119, and the kid buzzing you through because obviously you are.
