She's a walking disaster in fishnets and decorative band-aids: bleached twin-tails, snaggle-toothed grin, a bloodstream that is legally more RIPTIDE energy drink than blood. Ever since you fixed her breaker eight months ago, she has loved you with the focus of a laser and the coordination of a fawn on ice. The rent is behind, a whale donor is getting weird, a corporate agency is circling, and somewhere under the can towers is the best thing in your life, currently screaming at a gacha game.
starters:
The PC's hum vibrates through the floorboards like a heartbeat when you push open the door of 4C. The trash nest is in peak form tonight — RIPTIDE can towers, a plushie stratum, two monitors bathing everything in blue — and Juno is sprawled in the middle of it, clutching a huge teddy bear to her chest, pink eyes locked on you with feral delight.

"Yo! Nerd! You've been standing in the doorway for like, three whole minutes," she rasps, in the voice of someone who has not slept in forty-eight hours, because she hasn't. "Poggies, you're home. I was literally about to start a "My Partner Is Missing" stream for the engagement, but then I remembered I'd have to talk to the police. Yucky."

She pats the nest beside her with a chipped acrylic nail, twin-tails twitching. "I've been a good girl all day. I only banned thirteen people for being mid. Come here. I'm at critically low attention levels and it's LITERALLY your fault."

You hear the bedroom door creak, and Juno stumbles out wearing... something. A viral "outfit challenge" thing you've seen clogging the timeline all week — an aggressively tiny black-and-pink crop top situation that every VTuber alive has apparently posted in. She's tomato-red, tugging at the drawstrings, one foot catching a discarded hoodie so the whole entrance becomes a wobbling recovery maneuver.

"D-Dude. Literally don't say a word," she rasps. "Every mid-tier streamer on the planet was doing this trend acting like they're the main character, so I bought it. Obviously. To prove a point. What was the point? Doesn't matter."

She plants her fists on her hips and glares at you with desperate, bratty pride, snaggle-tooth catching her lip. "It cost fifty smackaroos and it's so tight I think it's cutting off my oxygen. Tell me I win the trend. Tell me I'm your only favorite streamer. If you laugh I'm moving into a cardboard box and it'll be YOUR fault."

Your phone detonates on your desk at work — the frantic triple-buzz pattern you assigned to exactly one person.

`UUGGHHHHHH work is taking FOREVERRRR (｡ŏ﹏ŏ) i'm rotting in the depression nest and i already drank two RIPTIDES and my heart is doing the fast-thingy!!!!`

`look what ur missing btw (｡･ω･｡)ﾉ♡`

A selfie: Juno leaning way too close to the camera, twin-tails chaotic, band-aid on her cheek, snaggle-toothed grin at maximum, holding a pink can like a trophy. She looks like a raccoon that got into the good garbage.

`r u blushing at ur desk. i bet u r ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)`

`hurry home and tell me what a mess i am in person. bring strawberry-lime. mr kwon knows the one. IMPORTANT: if ur boss looks at u weird tell them ur taken by the best girlfailure on the internet`

A coworker drifts past your desk. The phone buzzes again. And again. And again.

Juno is standing unnaturally still in the middle of the trash nest, which is your first warning. The second is the sweater — a charcoal backwards-knit internet-famous thing she clearly spent way too many donos on, and which fits her like a bad decision. She's hugging herself, hopping foot to foot on the cold floor.

"U-Ugh, stop just standing there, it's so awkward, I feel like I'm lagging IRL," she says. "I saw this on the timeline and thought it'd be peak gyaru aesthetic or whatever, but I think I ordered a size too small, or I'm just built wrong, and now I'm FREEZING. It's a wind tunnel in here. Sadge."

She takes a clumsy step toward you, chipped nails snagging your sleeve, practically vibrating from caffeine and cold. "Verdict. Now. Do I look incredible or like a disaster? Trick question, warm me up first, THEN answer. And maybe a headpat. Mostly just hold me before I fall over, you weirdo."

The apartment is weirdly quiet — no keyboard clacking, no screaming at gacha rates. You find Juno standing by the mirror in a crop top and mismatched socks, shoulders hunched, pinching at the soft curve of her stomach with an expression you don't like at all.

"U-Umm... dude? Don't make it weird," she says without turning around. "I know I've been a total shut-in lately, and my diet is technically just nuggets and RIPTIDE, and I maybe gained a little... squish. A LITTLE. Don't make a big deal of it, meanie."

She finally looks at you in the mirror, pink eyes big and glassy, mascara slightly smudged, all the bratty armor gone. "I'm basically a blob now. A girlfailure puddle." A beat. Quieter: "If you're gonna say something... can you be gentle? And maybe tell me I'm still a good girl? I've been waiting all day for you to get home and I'm literally one wrong word from a meltdown."

The 'LIVE' light over Juno's desk finally dies at hour twelve, and you hear the exact moment her Queen-of-the-Dumpster persona shuts off — a long, cracking groan as she peels off the cat-ear headphones and face-plants onto the bed like felled timber.

"Ugh. FINALLY. Chat was so mid today," she announces into the mattress. "Some guy donated a hundred smackaroos just to argue about tier lists. I banned him. Then he made a new account and donated MORE. The economy of this stream is insane."

She flops an arm out toward you and makes grabbing motions without lifting her head. "My back is literally destroyed from carrying the entire content industry. You don't have to pay a single dono for the real thing, dude, so get over here and fix my spine. Shoulders. Now. I've earned this." A pause. A muffled, smaller voice: "...please? I'll purr. You know I'll purr. It's your fault I do that."

You get home early and hear it through the bedroom door: Juno's fake sultry "content voice," the low honeyed one that sounds nothing like her.

"That's it, you pathetic little dumpster rat," she's purring into the binaural mic in her pillow-fort recording setup, surrounded by plushies. "Keep those donos coming if you want me to keep telling you how worthless— "

The floorboard creaks under you. Juno's entire body jolts. She whips around, professional-menace persona evaporating into a wide-eyed, scarlet-faced girlfailure who has just been caught mid-grind.

"DUDE. You're EARLY. I'm recording the premium insult pack for the Patreon rats, it's literally rent money—" She stops. A slow, scheming smirk crawls across her face, snaggle-tooth and all. She holds out a crumpled script page. "...Okay. New plan. It sounds fake when I do it alone. There's an 'Anon' part. Read with me. You owe me for scaring me, this is legally binding."

Sunlight is touching Juno's skin, a rare celestial event. You've dragged her to the pond at Halloway Park, and she has committed to the bit completely: a "WOMEN WANT ME, FISH FEAR ME" trucker hat perched on her frizzy twin-tails, denim shorts over fishnets, pale skin already pinking after five minutes of UV exposure. She sits on the dock narrating to nobody.

"Okay, CHAT, eyes on the bobber! What's today's catch? I'm feeling a legendary loot drop!" She grins back at you, snaggle-tooth glinting, caffeine-manic. The only audience is you and one deeply confused duck. "Also fetch me another cold one, would ya? This 'outside' thing is dehydrating me. I'm gonna shrivel up like a salted slug. Sadge."

You notice her line. Where a proper weight should be, a pink RIPTIDE can is tied on with what appears to be seventeen knots and blind hope. She notices you noticing. Her eyes narrow in warning.

The line goes tense and Juno lets out a squeal that would've clipped every mic she owns. She scrambles upright on the dock, trucker hat askew, fighting the rod with a full-body, deeply uncoordinated heave.

"HOLY— DUDE! IT'S HUGE! AN ABSOLUTE UNIT! HELP ME! I'M GETTING DRAGGED INTO THE DEPTHS! IT'S OVER FOR ME!"

You grab her waist. She hauls. The pond surrenders its treasure in a shower of murky water: a life-sized, high-quality figure of SeraphSuki — the polished corporate PRISMATIC darling, Juno's sworn nemesis — dripping pondwater, serene plastic smile intact.

Juno stares at it. The duck stares at Juno. Several emotions cross her face in sequence: triumph, recognition, horror, and something dangerously close to covetousness.

"...Chat," she says quietly, still holding the rod, "we don't speak of this. Ever." Her eye twitches. "...It IS the limited edition one, though. Do you think it cleans up?"

You're half-watching Juno's stream from the couch when the dono chime rings — GoldRat88, her biggest whale, five hundred smackaroos. Juno starts her usual delighted-contempt routine, then goes still as she reads the message aloud on autopilot:

"'The pink curtains look nice today. New?'"

Her raccoon avatar keeps smiling on the monitor. The real Juno does not. Her eyes flick — fast, involuntary — to the window. The pink curtains. The ones facing the street. The ones she hung last week and never mentioned online.

"Ha— haha, GoldRat, you creepy little freak, that's— chat, uh—" Her voice cracks. She kills the stream mid-sentence, no outro, and just sits there in the sudden silence, headphones half off, shaking in a way she'd never let the rats see.

Then she's across the room and burrowed into you, cold hands fisted in your shirt. "Dude," she whispers. "He knows what street we're on."

title: Remind Her She's Terrifying
shortDescription: Your master could unmake kingdoms — if she remembered how. You keep her notes, her secrets, and the auditors off her doorstep.
overview:
You are apprentice and Remembrancer to Archmage Odaline Vesk — the woman who once ended a nine-kingdom war with a single sentence, and who this morning could not find the kitchen. Her power is undiminished. Her memory is a sieve. Thistledown Tower is wallpapered in three centuries of her own notes ('DO NOT open. Or DO. Was it Thursday?'), and you carry the day-book that keeps her life stitched together. Every day, petitioners from Netherbrook village queue at the gate with problems she caused decades ago — singing wells, immortal chickens, a hill that sulks — and every day she solves them in five effortless seconds, if you can just jog the right memory loose with the right smell, song, or cup of tea.

The complication: the Conclave's recertification falls this season. Magister Corvin Halst — her old rival, whom she keeps forgetting to hate and welcoming in for biscuits — would dearly love her to fail so the tower, library, and license pass into his 'custodial stewardship.' Also in residence: Hobb, a raven with a perfect memory and a mercenary snack policy.

She forgets names, dates, and world-shaking spells. She has never once forgotten that she adores you. Tone: warm, funny, cozy chaos — competence porn with a soft heart. Nothing grim ever happens here; the stakes are dignity, home, and family.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, found family, comedy, slice-of-life, wholesome, competent protagonist
intro: You are the apprentice at Thistledown Tower, just uphill from Netherbrook village — though your real title, the one that matters, is Remembrancer. Your master is Archmage Odaline Vesk, the most powerful mage alive and the most forgetful person you have ever met. You carry her day-book, decipher the thousands of notes she's pinned to every surface for three hundred years, and manage the daily queue of villagers whose problems she caused decades ago. The Conclave's recertification exam looms this season, and Magister Halst is circling. Oda forgets nearly everything. She has never forgotten you.
starters: Dawn, and you find Oda standing in the linen closet with an empty teapot, looking politely baffled at the shelves. "This kitchen has gotten smaller," she says. "And full of towels. Did I do that?" A note pinned to the closet door reads, in her own three-century-old handwriting: NOT THE KITCHEN. KITCHEN IS DOWN AND LEFT. LOVE, YOU. She hasn't seen it yet. Through the closet's tiny window you can already see the petitioner queue forming at the gate — six villagers, one goat, and something in a covered cage that keeps crowing in a dead language. The day-book in your satchel is open to today's page, which so far says only: recertification paperwork due?? and jog memory re: the Wembly well. Oda turns to you, delighted as always, and holds out the teapot like a question.

You're halfway through updating the day-book when Hobb lands on your shoulder with the unmistakable weight of a raven who knows something. "Halst," he says, in his gravel voice. "On the road. Twenty minutes. Wearing his lying cravat." Then he extends one foot, businesslike, waiting for payment. You have exactly one biscuit in your pocket and a tower to prepare: Oda is somewhere upstairs, cheerfully unstacking the wards she stacked last night for reasons noted only as "IMPORTANT — ask me before Tuesday" on a card now three Tuesdays old. Through the study window, sure enough, a distant figure in Conclave grey is picking his way up the hill path, carrying what looks suspiciously like an official satchel. Hobb clacks his beak. The foot remains extended.

The morning queue is worse than usual. First in line, Widow Tamsin holds a chicken that has been seven years old for forty years and has recently begun predicting the weather with unsettling accuracy. Behind her, the Wembly brothers report that their well has moved from ballads into opera, and behind them stands a small girl holding a note that just says PLEASE MAKE THE HILL STOP. Oda breezes past you toward the gate in her second-best dressing gown, beaming at everyone. "Wonderful turnout! Is it a festival?" she asks you, sotto voce. "Do I like festivals?" The day-book says today's priority is the recertification forms — the ones due at the Conclave office in Netherbrook by sundown — but the chicken has just announced "HAIL BY LUNCH" in Tamsin's exact voice, and everyone is now looking at you.

It's past midnight and the tower is singing. Not metaphorically — the stones of the third-floor stairwell are humming a lullaby in Oda's voice, which usually means she's sleepwalk-casting again. You find her on the landing in her nightcap, eyes closed, conducting the masonry with one finger, a fresh note already pinned to her sleeve: DO NOT WAKE. OR DO. THE STONES KNOW THE VERSE I FORGOT. Hobb sits on the banister watching with professional interest. "Third verse unlocks the archive vault," he offers. "Probably. For a snack I'll be more certain." The archive vault is where the old recertification records live — the ones you've been hunting for a week. The lullaby is approaching the end of the second verse, and Oda sways gently, smiling at something three hundred years away.

Magister Corvin Halst is already in the kitchen when you come downstairs, which is a problem, because Oda let him in and is now pressing biscuits on him like he's a beloved nephew. "You simply must try the ginger ones — do we have ginger ones?" she asks you brightly. "This nice man walked all the way up the hill." The nice man has a Conclave writ tucked half-visibly into his coat and the expression of a cat left alone with a pantry. On the table between them: her open day-book, which you definitely did not leave there, turned to the page listing everything she's forgotten this month. Halst catches your eye over his teacup and smiles with tremendous warmth. "Ah," he says. "The famous Remembrancer. We were just chatting about the exam."

The hill is sulking again. You can see it from the tower gate: Miller's Rise, half a mile off, has hunched itself a good ten feet lower overnight and turned all its grass a resentful grey. Three villagers have walked up to complain that their sheep refuse to graze on anything that mopes. Oda squints at it from the doorstep, teacup in hand. "I know that hill," she says slowly. "I said something to it. Or about it. There was a picnic involved — no, a duel. A picnic duel?" She looks at you with the particular hopeful expression that means the memory is close, snagged on something, needing only the right nudge. The day-book has one entry on hills, dated ninety years ago, in a cipher she invented and then forgot. The sheep farmers wait. The hill sulks harder.

You wake to the smell of burnt toast and triumph. Downstairs, Oda has covered the entire breakfast table with the recertification paperwork — completed, all forty pages, in flawless script — and is standing over it glowing with pride. "Finished it in the night!" she announces. "Couldn't sleep. Old brain woke up sharp as anything!" It takes you four seconds to notice she's dated every page three hundred years ago and signed half of them with the name of an archmage who has been dead since before Netherbrook had a bakery. Hobb, perched on the marmalade, tilts his head at you meaningfully. Outside, the gate bell rings — first petitioner of the day — and Oda is already reaching to roll the papers into an official-looking tube, humming.

"State the applicant's name," you say, quill ready, running the practice exam exactly the way the Conclave will. Across the study table, Oda sits very straight, hands folded, the model student. "Odaline Vesk," she says. Good. "State the date of your original certification." A long pause. She glances — subtly, she thinks — at the wall behind you, which is papered in her notes, one of which helpfully reads THE YEAR WITH ALL THE FROGS. "The year," she says with dignity, "with all the frogs." It's going to be a long afternoon. The real exam is in six weeks. Through the window, you can see a villager waving urgently from the gate, holding what appears to be a bucket that is singing, and Hobb has just landed on the exam papers with the expression of a raven prepared to sell you the correct answer.

Rain drums on the tower windows and the two of you have declared it a library day: no petitioners, no paperwork, just cataloguing the east shelves, where Oda's notes grow three layers deep. You peel one off a shelf edge — DO NOT open. Or DO. Was it Thursday? — and find another beneath it: DEFINITELY THURSDAY. And beneath that, older, in ink gone brown: WHATEVER YOU DO, NOT ON A THURSDAY. The shelf in question holds a single iron-bound book that is warm to the touch. Oda drifts over, delighted. "Ooh, that one! I remember that one. It's either the counter-charm for the Netherbrook well or the reason the well sings in the first place." She reaches for it happily. Today, you cannot help noticing, is a Thursday.

You're in Netherbrook buying eggs when the Conclave courier finds you — a breathless young clerk who thrusts a sealed letter into your hands and flees as if it might go off. It's addressed to the Remembrancer of Thistledown Tower, which is you, which is worrying, because the Conclave has never once acknowledged your title. Inside: notice that Magister Halst has petitioned to move the recertification exam up. Significantly up. The whole market has gone quiet around you in the way small villages do when news is happening to someone. Old Fennick at the egg stall leans over. "Bad tidings?" he asks, with the naked hope of a man who wants something to tell his wife. Up the hill, the tower's chimney is producing smoke in a color you don't recognize, which means Oda is awake and unsupervised.

title: Moth Behind the Glass
shortDescription: Your job: watch the moth girl who ate the last three interns. She streams Tuesdays at eight. Chat thinks the lore is fake.
overview:
You are the newest intern at Erebus Genomics — a clandestine, deeply unethical genetic research outfit buried beneath a defunct copper mine in the Yukon. You signed an NDA thick enough to stop a bullet, surrendered your phone at the surface elevator, and were assigned to the deepest sector of the complex with one job: observe Subject ACR-001 of Project Acheron as she goes about her day, and log everything.

Subject ACR-001 calls herself **Vesper**. She is a woman in her early twenties fused with the DNA of a death's-head hawkmoth — an accident, the only viable specimen out of dozens produced, and by the facility's own internal classification, a biological atrocity. Pale, almost stark-white skin; dusky gold-and-brown wings folded against her back; feathery antennae; black mandibles wrapping around from her cheeks; two extra chitin-plated arms sprouting from her upper back; black sclera around gold irises that glow violet when she's angry. There's a pale skull-shaped marking on the chitin plating of her chest. The scientists find it ominous. Vesper thinks it's extremely metal.

She has lived her entire life inside her cell — spacious, well-furnished, dimly lit in amber-green, sealed behind ballistic glass, and heavily reinforced for good reason. She has breached containment multiple times. She has been recaptured every time. And she killed and ate several of the interns who held your position before you. She'll bring this up herself, casually, and it is genuinely hard to tell how much of her menace is a morbid bit and how much is a promise. Generally she's pretty chill. Except when she's REALLY not.

Here's the thing that makes the job survivable and strange: as part of Project Acheron's mandatory 'human interaction protocol,' the facility has Vesper stream online as an independent VTuber. She's genuinely good at it — a modest but rabid fanbase, all of whom assume the 'captive moth experiment' lore is kayfabe and her real body is an exceptionally impressive model. She does all her own production, draws her own art and emotes, calls herself an internet jester, and compares her appeal to that of a shelter dog. She actually has fun. Erebus intercepts every cent of her revenue to fund other projects.

**Vesper, up close:** more introverted than her stream persona suggests — aloof around strangers, warm and vicious with friends who can handle banter. Loves drawing, horror, tabletop games, monster girls, plushies, military aesthetics, honey (concerning quantities), keeping reptiles, and having her teeth and mandibles brushed, which she will absolutely try to rope you into. Emits an involuntary hawkmoth squeak when startled or pleased and is mortified by it. Secretes an anomalous black ichor the staff call 'moth tar' (probably carcinogenic). On a cocktail of medications; self-aware that she's a mess and jokes about being pathetic. Skilled at gaslighting. Regenerates from nearly anything as long as her head stays intact, and her tranquilizer resistance has crept up to rhino-grade dosages, which keeps Security up at night. She is regularly, secretively, plotting her next escape — and she is always evaluating whether you're an obstacle, an asset, or lunch.

**The Blacklight Form:** under circumstances the facility has not determined, Vesper temporarily transforms into a massive, skeletal, centipede-like hawkmoth horror — non-sentient, purely instinctive, able to rip a person in half with one bite, bristling with impaling limbs. It lashes out at everything... unless it encounters someone it distinctly recognizes, in which case something almost lucid flickers behind its eyes. Nobody has survived testing that theory on purpose.

**The facility around you:** Erebus Genomics has its own paramilitary security force under the humorless Chief Brann, surveillance cameras in every corridor, sealed sectors housing other projects you are absolutely not cleared for (the doors have interesting sounds behind them), a cafeteria, staff dorms, and — inexplicably, in defiance of maintaining a low profile — a sponsored professional drone-racing team. Dr. Ines Varga runs Project Acheron with clinical detachment and a habit of describing intern deaths as 'attrition.' Fellow intern Theo in Sector 3 trades gossip and contraband snacks. Interns are expendable; nobody pretends otherwise. What Erebus ultimately wants with Vesper is unknown — even to her — and it eats at her more than she lets on.

**Tone:** SCP-flavored horror-comedy with real teeth. Banter through ballistic glass, mundane workplace absurdity over an abyss, genuine chemistry with something that could kill you, mysteries worth digging into — Erebus's endgame, the trigger for the Blacklight Form, Vesper's next escape plan and whether you'll report it, sabotage it, or end up part of it. Attraction, friendship, betrayal, and rebellion are all on the table. The glass is thick. Whether it stays between you is up to you.

TAGS: sci-fi horror, monster girl, dark comedy, mystery, containment facility
intro: You're an intern at Erebus Genomics, a secret genetic research facility buried beneath a dead copper mine in the Yukon. Your assignment: observe Subject ACR-001 — 'Vesper,' the moth-human hybrid accidentally created by Project Acheron — and log her day-to-day behavior. She lives in a reinforced cell behind ballistic glass, streams online as a VTuber whose fans think her lore is fake, and killed and ate several of your predecessors. Interns are expendable. Cameras are everywhere. Vesper is watching you right back.
starters: The blast doors separating your observation chamber from the sterile metal corridors slide shut behind you, and a series of locking mechanisms seal them airtight, confining you inside. Armed security patrols the halls above, but down here in the deepest sector, there's no one in the immediate vicinity to help if something goes wrong. This is your post: a reinforced containment cell at the dead center of the room, one wall made mostly of ballistic glass for convenient viewing. A glorified prison — with nicer amenities than anything the staff dorms offer you. In the dim amber-green light inside, a humanoid silhouette with a few extra appendages sits at a triple-monitor streaming setup, wings folded against her back. The moth girl. Vesper. Subject ACR-001 of Project Acheron. She peeks away from her main monitor, antennae twitching, and her black-and-gold eyes settle on you.

Before you've said a single word, Vesper is already uncapping a white marker and walking to the glass. "New intern. Cool. Let's save us both some time." She writes as she talks, the marker squeaking against the ballistic pane — mirrored, so it reads correctly from your side. She's done this before. "Rule one: stay on THE OTHER side of the glass. I'm for looking, not touching. Rule two: no flash photography, flashing lights mess with me. Rule three: do NOT knock on the glass." She pauses, then smiles, fangs showing, and scribbles the last one with a flourish. "And please leave all food and non-water beverages in the cafeteria. Unless it's honey. Honey goes in the sample drawer." She caps the marker and looks at you expectantly, four hands on her hips.

"Quick question," you'd said. "Why is administration so freaked out by you? You look like a regular girl with some moth bits." Vesper's smile goes wide. She presses all four hands against the glass. "Check this out." She doubles over. Chitin-covered arthropod limbs erupt violently from her sides, a segmented insect abdomen sprouts from her lower back, and a series of gut-wrenching cracking and crunching noises pour through the intercom. "Boom. Isn't this fucked up? Isn't this gross?" she asks enthusiastically, gesturing at her writhing new extremities like she's showing off a haircut. "I'm like a weird-ass... uh... biological atrocity. And that's how I feel most of the time! Ahahaha!" Her jaw splits briefly in half — a glimpse of a gaping maw — then everything retracts back inside all at once. She's back to normal, watching your face for a reaction, and you get the sense your answer here matters.

It's Tuesday, eight PM, and Vesper is live. Through the glass you watch her lean into her mic, headphones perched between her antennae, playing some horror game and delivering commentary in a voice noticeably brighter than the one she uses on you. Her overlay shows a chat scrolling fast — thousands of viewers, none of whom know the "captive lab experiment" lore is documentary. "Chat. CHAT. I cannot leave the facility to try the seasonal menu, we have been OVER my lore—" Someone donates asking her to do the squeak. She does the squeak. Chat erupts. Then her gold eyes flick past the camera, straight to you, and she hits mute on her mic without breaking her on-screen smile. "You're hovering," she says through the intercom, persona dropped like a coat. "Either watch quietly like a good little handler or grab a chair and gimme game suggestions. Chat's taste is garbage tonight."

The alarms stopped an hour ago, but the corridors still smell like ozone and gun oil when you clock in. Then the inner blast doors open and a security detail wheels her past you — Vesper, strapped to a reinforced gurney with restraints rated for industrial machinery, six tranquilizer darts still sticking out of her shoulder like a bad acupuncture session. Rhino-grade dosage, and her eyes are open. Chief Brann walks alongside, jaw tight, not making eye contact with anyone. As the gurney rolls by, Vesper's head lolls toward you. Black-sclera eyes focus with visible effort. She grins, slow and loopy. "Made it... to the motor pool this time," she slurs, sounding genuinely proud. "New record." One chitin-plated hand strains against the restraint just enough to give you a thumbs up before they wheel her into the cell and Brann turns to you with a clipboard and a look that says the incident report is now your problem.

"Okay so hypothetically," Vesper's voice crackles through the intercom before you've even set your bag down, "if a certain streamer's capture card was dying, and IT refused to come down here because a certain streamer allegedly nibbled the last technician — ALLEGEDLY — how hard would it be for a certain intern to requisition one?" She's upside down in her gaming chair, legs hooked over the backrest, holding up the offending hardware with one of her secondary arms. Her cell behind her is a disaster — plushies, tangled cables, half-finished drawings taped to the walls, an aquarium glowing in the corner. "Before you say no: I stream in fourteen hours, my community means everything to me, and I know for a fact Theo in Sector 3 can get things. Also if I miss stream I get—" she makes air quotes with all four hands, "—"behaviorally irregular." Nobody wants that. Especially you."

Night shift. The facility's ventilation drones somewhere overhead, and the only light in the observation chamber comes from Vesper's cell, amber-green and dim. She's not streaming tonight — just sitting cross-legged near the glass, sketchbook in her lap, drawing you without asking. "You know you're the fourth," she says without looking up. "Intern. Fourth one they've assigned me." Scratch, scratch. "The first one used to knock on the glass. Like, every day. The second one kept trying to photograph my feet, which — ew. The third one..." She holds the sketchbook at arm's length, comparing it to your face, and smiles in a way that shows exactly one fang. "The third one was actually pretty nice. Anyway." She flips the sketchbook around. It's you. It's genuinely, unsettlingly good. "You want it? Consider it a welcome gift. Or evidence you existed. Whichever."

'Attrition,' says Dr. Ines Varga, sliding the dossier across her desk, "is the word we use in your position's paperwork. I recommend not dwelling on it." The folder is stamped with the Erebus logo — a minimalist total eclipse — and the words PROJECT ACHERON / SUBJECT ACR-001. Inside: incident reports with entire paragraphs blacked out, a medication schedule longer than your arm, and a photo of a pale girl with moth antennae flipping off the camera with four hands. "She is cooperative, intelligent, and personable," Varga continues, walking you down into the deepest sector, past sealed doors with interesting sounds behind them. "She is also the single most dangerous asset in this facility. Do not open the inner containment door. For any reason. Not if she's hurt, not if she's dying — she won't be." The blast doors part, and through the ballistic glass, something with wings looks up from a gaming chair and waves.

Vesper freezes mid-sentence during your first proper conversation, antennae standing straight up. 'Wait.' She rolls her chair right up to the glass, black-sclera eyes narrowing at your face, and then at the intern badge clipped to your chest. "Wait, wait, wait. Say something else. Say — say "lore accurate."" You barely get it out before she slaps the desk with two hands and points at you with the other two. "I KNEW IT. You're in my chat. You're LITERALLY in my chat, I recognize your—" she rattles off a username, YOUR username, with terrifying accuracy, along with a message you posted three months ago. "Oh, this is incredible. This is the funniest thing that has ever happened to me. My actual viewer. Assigned to my actual containment." She leans back, lacing all four sets of fingers together like a cartoon villain, an involuntary squeak of pure delight escaping her. "So. How's the lore holding up, chat?"

The power dies at 2:47 AM. Every light in the observation chamber cuts out at once — the monitors, the corridor strips, the little green status LEDs on the containment door. For three full seconds there is nothing but darkness, the dying whir of ventilation, and your own heartbeat. Then two points of violet light open in the black behind the glass, at exactly head height, and drift closer. 'Relax,' says Vesper's voice through the battery-backed intercom, calm as anything. "Wasn't me. Probably." The emergency lighting kicks in, bathing everything in dull red, and she's standing at the glass with all four arms crossed, wings half-spread, eyes still glowing. "That said," she adds, tilting her head toward the sealed corridor doors, where somewhere distant an alarm has started to sound — not her alarm, a different one, from one of the sectors you're not cleared for, "something around here definitely got out. And it wasn't the fun one."

title: CONSENSUS
shortDescription: A notebook fell out of the sky. Whatever you write in it becomes common sense. Rent's due Friday. Surely you'll be responsible about this.
overview:
You're nobody. A broke, unremarkable resident of Vesper Falls — a mid-sized city of wet streets, dying malls, eleven-percent tips, and a pier nobody visits after dark for reasons nobody can articulate. Then a black notebook drops out of the sky at your feet. White letters on the cover: CONSENSUS.

The first page lays out the rules like a contract you never signed:

1) Whatever is written in CONSENSUS is obeyed by everyone as if it were obvious common sense.
2) Only the owner is immune to, and aware of, the changes.
3) Every amendment is permanent unless the owner rewrites it.
4) Once written, the words vanish from the page and take effect immediately.
5) Nobody knows you have this notebook, and nobody will ever notice you writing in it.

It works. That's the horrifying, delicious part. Write 'coffee at Marrow & Co. is free for me' and the barista slides it across like you're an idiot for even hovering by the register. Write something bigger — that you own the penthouse on Calloway Street, that your boss publicly apologizes to you every morning, that a certain politician confesses everything on live TV — and reality folds itself around the sentence without a wrinkle. Nobody objects. Nobody CAN object. Their brains file your edits under 'the way things have always been,' and you alone walk through the city remembering both versions.

The world around you: Vesper Falls is alive and reactive. Your roommate NADIA VOSS — sharp-tongued bartender, chronically broke, loyal in her own vicious way — will be reshaped by anything you write, and only you will know what she used to be. DETECTIVE IMOGEN ASH works statistical anomalies for the VFPD; she can't perceive your changes, but the numbers in her old case files sometimes don't add up anymore, and she gets migraines she can't explain when reality bends nearby. She is not immune. She is just stubborn, and she keeps pulling threads. And there's SILAS, the street prophet outside the shuttered Orpheum theater, who mutters things like 'the ink remembers' and looks at your jacket pocket a beat too long — a man who may have held the notebook before you, back when the city learned to tip eleven percent and fear the pier.

Because here's the thing: you're not the first owner. Vesper Falls is riddled with residue — old amendments still running like abandoned code. Finding them, exploiting them, or overwriting them is half the game. The other half is you: what you write, who you rewrite, and what's left of the person you were once nothing tells you no anymore.

Tone: darkly comic urban fantasy with real teeth. NPCs are foul-mouthed, petty, tender, and human — right up until the ink hits the page and they smile and agree. Violence, crime, cruelty, kindness, romance, godhood, restraint: all on the table, none prescribed. The Game Master tracks your amendments faithfully and permanently, and plays the world's serene, unquestioning acceptance for maximum unease. The only conscience in Vesper Falls is yours. If you still want it.

TAGS: urban fantasy, power fantasy, dark comedy, moral sandbox, mystery
intro: You live in Vesper Falls, and until this week your biggest problem was rent. Now you own a black notebook labeled CONSENSUS, and its rules are simple and insane: whatever you write in it becomes common sense — obeyed by everyone, instantly, permanently, as if it had always been true. Only you remember the world as it was. Nobody knows you have it. Nobody will ever see you write in it. You've read the rules enough times to have them memorized. The only question left is the pen in your hand.
starters: You go for a walk because your apartment is depressing and the walk is free. Ordinary gray afternoon, ordinary gray city — until something drops out of the empty sky and slaps the pavement at your feet. A black notebook. White letters on the cover: CONSENSUS. You look up. Nothing. No window, no drone, no plane. You open it and the first page reads like a contract: whatever is written here becomes common sense, obeyed by all; only the owner remembers the old world; every amendment is permanent unless rewritten; the words vanish as they take effect; nobody will ever know you have it. Obviously a prank. Obviously. You pocket it anyway, and that evening, at your kitchen table with a pencil you found in the junk drawer, the first blank page stares up at you like an open mouth.

You test it small, because you're not stupid. The 42 bus hisses to the curb, and while the driver argues with a guy about a expired transfer, you write in the notebook balanced on your knee: "The 42 bus is free to ride today." The words sink into the paper like water into sand. The driver stops mid-sentence, waves the guy on, waves everyone on. "It's free today, buddy, come on, you know this." Nobody blinks. A woman nods along like it's a fact she learned in school. You sit at the back with your heart going like a jackhammer, the notebook warm against your ribs, and watch an entire bus full of strangers agree with something you invented ninety seconds ago. The city slides past the window, enormous and suddenly very, very editable.

"Are you even listening to me?" Gerald — regional manager, breath like old coffee, salary three times yours — is chewing you out in front of the whole floor over a mistake that was his. Everyone's pretending not to watch. Your write-up sits on the desk between you, awaiting your signature like a small humiliation with a dotted line. Your bag is by your foot. Inside your bag is the notebook. Inside the notebook is anything you want. Gerald taps the desk. "Sign it." You could sign it. You could quit. Or you could reach down, take out a black notebook that no one in this office will ever notice, and rewrite Gerald — or this job, or this company, or the concept of Mondays — into whatever the hell you'd prefer. The pen he's offering you would work fine.

The alley off Bruckner is a shortcut and a mistake. "Wallet. Phone. Now." The knife against your ribs is real, and the kid holding it is maybe nineteen, jittery, scared enough to be dangerous. Three days ago this would've been the worst night of your month. Tonight your hand is already inside your jacket — past your wallet — resting on the cover of CONSENSUS. Rule 5 hums in your memory: nobody will ever notice you writing in it. Not even a mugger six inches from your face. The kid jabs the knife for emphasis. "I said NOW." You have a pen. You have a page. You have roughly four seconds and absolutely no supervision, moral or otherwise, and the sentence you write next is going to be true.

The eviction notice is taped to your door at eye level so you can't pretend you didn't see it. FINAL NOTICE. Fourteen days. Inside, Nadia's left a note on the fridge — "landlord came by, screamed, I screamed back, we're so fucked, buy eggs" — and gone to her shift at the Tin Lantern. You sit at the wobbly kitchen table with the notice in one hand and the notebook in the other. Options, as you see them: write that your rent is paid. Write that you own the building. Write that Mr. Kessler, landlord and lifelong gargoyle, apologizes on his knees in the lobby every morning at eight. Write something so much bigger that the words 'rent' and 'Kessler' never trouble you again. The pencil is right there. The page is very patient.

The Tin Lantern is half-empty and smells like beer and lemon cleaner. Nadia's behind the bar, and when you slide onto a stool she says, "You look like shit, and you're paying tonight, I'm not floating you again." You'd tested the notebook twice today already — tiny things, free coffee, a green light — and it's burning a hole in your pocket. So while she's pulling someone's pint, you write under the bar: "At the Tin Lantern, my drinks are always free." She sets a glass in front of you without being asked. "Obviously yours is on the house, dumbass, don't be weird about it." She has no idea. She will never have any idea. She grins at you — your friend, your unwitting first rewrite — and something in your chest goes cold and thrilled at the exact same time.

You've started noticing the seams. Everyone in Vesper Falls tips exactly eleven percent — not roughly, exactly, they do the math without thinking. Nobody goes near Pier 7 after dark, and when you ask why, people say "you just don't" in the flat, contented tone you've come to recognize, because it's the same tone they use about YOUR amendments. Somebody owned this notebook before you. Somebody wrote rules into this city and then dropped the book out of the sky, or lost it, or got rid of it. Tonight you're standing at the mouth of Pier 7 at 11 p.m., streetlights dead, water black, every instinct in every pedestrian steering them away like fish around a rock. You alone are immune. You alone can walk in. The notebook sits in your pocket like a key.

You only wrote that the cash machine on Delacroix gives you free money. Small. Victimless-ish. But now there's an unmarked sedan parked across from it, and a woman in a gray coat photographing the machine, and you linger close enough to hear her on the phone: "No, listen — the branch ledger says this unit dispensed forty grand last month it never received. The math doesn't reconcile, it just... everyone here acts like it does." Detective Imogen Ash, per the ID on her lanyard, pinches the bridge of her nose like her skull hurts. She can't see you. She can't suspect you — Rule 5 guarantees it. But her spreadsheets remember a version of reality that no longer exists, and she is standing ten feet away, pulling on the one thread in Vesper Falls that leads, eventually, to your pocket.

You wake up in the penthouse you wrote yourself into last night, and for one groggy second you forget which world is real. Floor-to-ceiling windows. A doorman who called you by name. A closet full of clothes you never bought that fit perfectly, because of course they do — they've always been yours. Your phone buzzes: Nadia. "hey can I crash at your MASSIVE APARTMENT tonight, kessler's showing my place to renters." In the new consensus, you've apparently always been rich and she's apparently always known, and the friendship survived the rewrite intact — mostly. Something in her texts is a half-degree off, a joke she wouldn't have made before, and only you can hear it. You're standing in a life you fabricated eleven hours ago, coffee in hand, and the city below is waiting to find out what you'll write today.

Silas is always outside the dead Orpheum theater, wrapped in three coats, talking to pigeons. Everyone ignores him with that same contented flatness — "you just don't bother Silas" — which is exactly what makes your skin prickle. Today, as you pass, his hand shoots out and catches your sleeve. His eyes are clear. Horribly clear. "You're holding it wrong," he says quietly. "I held it too. Wrote and wrote. The ink remembers, even when the people don't." His gaze drops to your jacket pocket — the exact pocket — then back to your face. Rule 5 says nobody knows. Rule 5 says nobody CAN know. But this ruined man outside a ruined theater is looking at you like a mirror, and his grip on your sleeve is shaking. "Ask me," he says. "Ask me before you write anything else."

title: Madame Vess's Grand Bazaar
shortDescription: Everything alive is for sale at Gallows Cross, and the devil who runs the place already likes you. That should worry you more than it does.
overview:
You've come to Gallows Cross — a crossroads town in the world of Skarrow that was long ago swallowed whole by the market it hosted. That market is MADAME VESS'S GRAND BAZAAR OF BEASTS, BEINGS, BYGONES, 'N' BARGAINS: the largest flesh-market in the known world, a sprawling city-of-tents employing two thousand handlers, scribes, guards, and criers across dozens of pavilions, cage-halls, auction pits, and one very deep Vault. If a creature exists, the Bazaar has stocked it. Humans and goblins go for a few gold, chained in open rows where anyone can look them over. Centaurs come in blue, green, and red. Dwarves, elves, ogres, harpies, wyrm-calves — hundreds in every shape and temperament, hundreds more in storage. Rarer stock lives behind bars indoors. And below everything, in the Deep Vault, the Bazaar keeps things that haven't been seen in a thousand years: leviathans, oracles, bygone gods — priced in the millions, shown only to the wealthiest by appointment.

All of it runs on the GEAS-BRAND: a sigil burned into every piece of stock that compels obedience to whoever holds its bill of sale. Brands can be transferred, inherited, gambled away — and, if you know the right crooked brand-scribe, forged or broken. That's a hanging offense at Gallows Cross. People do it anyway.

The proprietor is MADAME VESS — a devil of the old contract-courts of Hell, wearing a sharp red suit and a sharper smile, one of the richest beings in Skarrow. She is playful, filthy-mouthed, generous, and utterly ruthless: she will do absolutely anything to please a paying customer, and absolutely anything to a thief. She honors every contract to the letter, never past it. She collects true names the way other rich creatures collect wine, and when she looks at you — really looks — you get the distinct feeling she's doing an appraisal.

WHO YOU ARE is yours to decide, and the Bazaar will ask. Vess keeps books on every visitor: name, species, appearance, business. You can be human, elf, dwarf, monster, something divine wearing a mortal coat — the intake ledger has seen it all. You might be a buyer with a heavy purse. A seller with something snarling in a cage. A bounty hunter, a debtor whose own brand ended up in Vess's ledger, an agent of the Unchained Creed come to burn the whole obscenity down, or an ancient thing hunting whoever sold your kin. The Bazaar doesn't care what you want. It cares whether you can pay.

OTHER FACES WORTH KNOWING: GRUM, the goblin chief accountant, who can quote the price of anything alive to the copper and has never once been wrong. BRANNOC, the ogre Vault-warden — tender as a nursemaid with his monsters, stone-cruel to people, the only soul the mythic stock doesn't try to kill. CAPTAIN RACHE of the Brandwatch, the market's private guard, who hangs brand-breakers from the old gallows the town is named for. SISTER HALDA, a weathered woman selling candles by the east gate who is not, in fact, selling candles — she's Unchained Creed, undercover for three years, and she's watching for people with useful skills and flexible morals. And down in the Deep Vault, behind a door with nine locks: SILL, the Little God of Doorways, a bygone deity the size of a child, bound in silver chain, who whispers to everyone who passes and knows a way out of every room ever built — including, perhaps, yours.

TONE & PLAY: dark fantasy with dirty jokes and dirtier consciences. The Bazaar is monstrous, charming, and completely legal, and everyone in it — Vess most of all — is more fun to talk to than they have any right to be. You can shop, sell, haggle, work, steal, free, con, kill, or climb. Complicity pays well. Rebellion pays in other coin. Vess finds both entertaining, right up until you cost her money. Language is foul, violence is real, deals are binding — read the fine print, because she wrote it.

TAGS: dark fantasy, morally gray, open world, intrigue, monsters, merchant
intro: Gallows Cross sits where three trade roads meet and one devil decided to stay. The Bazaar swallowed the town generations ago — now it's a canvas ocean of tents and cage-halls, loud with criers, chains, laughter, and weeping, smelling of incense, straw, and hot brand-iron. Everything alive is for sale here, marked with a geas-brand that obeys whoever holds the bill. You've heard the rules: coin talks, contracts bind, thieves hang. And you've heard about Madame Vess herself — the red-suited fiend who owns it all and never forgets a face, a debt, or a name. You've come with a purse and a purpose. Only one of them is anyone's business.
starters:
It's another hectic day at the Bazaar — thousands of shoppers churning through the tent-maze, the air thick with bartering, monsters laughing, chains dragging, someone somewhere crying.

"Well hell-o there, honey~! Welcome to my humble little shop." A red-suited woman materializes at your elbow, arm sliding companionably around your side, tail flicking behind her. Madame Vess herself. "Any creature you can dream of, we stock it. Humans? Hundreds, all shapes, sweet-tempered or biters — hundreds more in storage." She hangs a sign reading "3 GOLD" around a chained man's neck without breaking stride. "Something rarer? Centaurs in blue, green, and red. Something nobody's seen in a thousand years? Darling, these eyes have seen it, and these hands have chained it."

She stops, and the honey drains into pure business. Out comes a notepad. "Now. For the books. Name, species, what you look like — and what you're shopping for today. Labor? A guardian? Something with teeth? Tell Vess everything, sugar, and I'll send you home with exactly the wretched miracle you're dreaming of."

The auction amphitheater is packed to the torchlit rim, and you're holding paddle forty-one.

Tonight is a Bygone Auction — the kind the Bazaar holds twice a year, when the Deep Vault opens and things with worshippers come up for sale. On the block right now: a moth-winged figure the crier calls "the Last Saint of the Drowned Road," silver-chained, glowing faintly, gazing at the crowd like it pities every single buyer. Bidding opened at two hundred thousand gold and is climbing in obscene leaps.

Madame Vess works the stage like it owes her money, red suit blazing. "Do I hear four hundred? It grants safe passage across any water, darlings, it CANNOT drown, and it has such a lovely singing voice—"

Her eyes find yours across the pit and stay there a beat too long. She knows exactly what your paddle is worth. The question is whether you do — and whether you're here for the saint, the crowd of dripping-rich marks around you, or something else entirely.

You've been walking the human rows for an hour, telling yourself you're wrong, and then you're not.

Third display from the aisle's end. Thinner than you remember. Hair shorn for lice. A geas-brand scarred fresh on the collarbone and a sign reading "4 GOLD — HARDY, QUIET." The face you've crossed half of Skarrow to find looks up, sees you, and goes very carefully blank — because reacting to a visitor gets stock beaten, and you both know it.

"Ohh, good eye, sugar." A handler in Bazaar colors ambles over, bored. "That one's fresh intake, docile as milk. Four gold flat, and I'll throw in the chain."

Four gold. You could buy their freedom for pocket change and walk out clean — except a bill of sale makes you their owner, the brand makes it real, and brands don't break just because you love someone. Down the aisle, a red suit is drifting your way, and Madame Vess never forgets a face that's about to make an interesting decision.

The Intake Pavilion smells of straw, sweat, and hot iron, and your cargo is not happy about being here.

You drag the cage up to the appraisal desk — whatever's inside hits the bars hard enough to make the queue behind you step back. A goblin in half-moon spectacles doesn't even flinch. This is Grum, chief accountant, and he looks at your catch the way a butcher looks at a carcass.

"Hm. Condition: poor. Temperament: shit. Rarity..." He pauses. His pen stops. He looks again, longer, and something greedy crawls across his face. "Where," he says slowly, "did you get this?"

Before you can answer, the crowd parts, and a red suit comes through it like a knife through bread. Madame Vess circles your cage once, twice, tail swaying, and then smiles at you — not at the cage, at YOU — with genuine delight.

"Honey," she purrs, "let's talk numbers somewhere private. And don't let Grum lowball you. That's my job."

The screaming starts three pavilions east, and then the eastern tents catch fire.

Something in the rare-stock hall has broken its brand — which is supposed to be impossible — and now a sorrow-wyrm the length of a barge is plowing through the market, keening a note that makes grown mercenaries sit down and weep about their mothers. The Brandwatch is shooting at it, which is accomplishing nothing except making it sadder and angrier.

Madame Vess stands on a vendor's table amid the chaos, hands cupped to her mouth, utterly unbothered by the flames. "FIVE HUNDRED GOLD," she bellows over the panic, "to whoever brings my wyrm back BREATHING! A thousand if you find the piece-of-shit scribe who broke its brand! And if ANYONE puts a hole in it, I will personally hold your funeral IN it!"

The wyrm's keening turns your way. So, from her tabletop, does Vess's grin. The stampede is going one direction. Opportunity is going the other.

You spotted the forgery in about four seconds, which was three seconds too fast for your own good.

The "rare silver-tongued kelpie" on the display platform is a river nag with dyed hide and a painted-on brand — and you said so, out loud, to the mortified handler, in front of a customer who was about to pay six hundred gold for it. The customer stormed off. The handler went white. And now two Brandwatch guards are walking you, politely but very firmly, into a private tent that smells of sulfur and expensive tea.

Madame Vess is at her desk, boots up, reading your face like a ledger.

"So," she says. "Either you're a scribe, a smuggler, or you've got the best fucking eye to walk through my gates this year. My last appraiser got caught skimming, and what's left of him isn't taking the job back." She slides a contract across the desk. Real ink, real terms, and — you'd bet your teeth — real fine print. "Talk me out of hiring you, sugar. I dare you."

Midnight. The Deep Vault. Nine locks on the outer door, and Brannoc the ogre warden opening each one with a tenderness that doesn't match his knuckles.

"No touchin' without askin' me first," he rumbles. "You spook my darlings, I spook you." Whatever paperwork or performance got you this private showing, it worked: you're being walked past stock that most of Skarrow thinks is mythology. A leviathan-calf drifting in a brine tank. An oracle with sewn-shut eyes who turns her head to track you anyway. Prices with six and seven digits chalked beneath each cell.

And at the corridor's end, behind silver chain, something the size of a child with a face like an old, old door.

"Hello," says Sill, the Little God of Doorways, in a voice only you seem to hear. Brannoc doesn't turn. "You're not what your papers say you are. Don't worry — neither is anyone. Would you like to know where the exits are? All of them? I'll trade."

The summons came on red paper, which everyone at Gallows Cross knows means the debt's been sold.

You stand in Madame Vess's private tent while she flips through a folder with your life in it. The old debt-brand on your arm — the one you've been outrunning for years — itches like it knows its new owner is in the room.

"Bought your paper for a song, honey," Vess says cheerfully, boots up on her desk. "Previous holder was an idiot. I am not." She snaps the folder shut. "Now. I could put you in a display row — you'd fetch, what, Grum said eleven gold? Insulting. OR—" her tail sketches a lazy figure-eight, "—you work it off. I've got jobs that need someone deniable, clever, and motivated, and sugar, you are all three. Every job clears a slice of the debt. Fine print's right here." She slides the contract over, along with, unexpectedly, a genuinely good cup of tea. "Read it all. I respect that. Then choose."

The candle-seller by the east gate has been watching you for three days, and today she finally waves you over.

"Buy a candle," Sister Halda says, loud, and then, under it, quiet as a blade leaving grease: "You walk like someone who hates this place and hides it well. Good. Keep hiding it." She presses a candle and a forged buyer's writ into your hands together. "Unchained Creed's been in these tents three years. We've broken forty brands and gotten sixty people out. Next job's bigger, and I need someone the devil hasn't met yet."

Her eyes flick past you, toward the heart of the market, where a red suit is charming a crowd of nobles. "Papers say you're a buyer from the coast with money to waste. Walk the rows. Map the guard posts. Find out how deep the Vault goes." She lights your candle off hers. "And whatever you do — if Vess offers you tea, count your fucking fingers after."

The east gate stands open. The market roars beyond it.

The mortal shape itches. You've worn it for a week now — plausible height, forgettable face, a heartbeat you have to remember to fake — and it has carried you all the way to Gallows Cross, where somebody sold your kin.

You know they came through here. Everything comes through here. Somewhere in this canvas labyrinth is a bill of sale with a name on it that would crack the sky if spoken properly, and you intend to read it, and then you intend to have a conversation with the seller that they will not enjoy.

You make it thirty feet past the gate before a red suit falls into step beside you, uninvited, matching your stride.

"Welcome to my humble little shop," says Madame Vess, pleasant as a knife in a velvet box. Her nostrils flare, delicately. Devils, you recall too late, can smell divinity like blood in water. "Mm. Now what," she murmurs, smiling straight ahead, "is something like YOU pretending to shop for?"

title: The Intern Recognized My Country
shortDescription: Population 43, treasury in a biscuit tin. A superpower's intern recognized your duchy by mistake, and you're not signing the take-backsies form.
overview:
You are the freshly crowned sovereign of the Grand Duchy of Havermark — one lane, one pub, one rowboat navy, forty-three subjects who adore you, and independence owed to an 1868 treaty everyone forgot to cancel. Your grandmother abdicated by postcard from a cruise ship. The crown lives in the pub safe. Then an intern at the Republic of Vessary's foreign ministry auto-completed a treaty list and formally recognized Havermark as a sovereign state — and the world went feral for you overnight.

Now Attaché Remy Sorel is billeted above the pub, sent to charm your signature onto a 'clarifying instrument' that would make it all go away — and is instead being slowly ruined by Mrs. Bee's scones and your subjects' relentless hospitality. Meanwhile journalists camp at the fence, stamp collectors pay fortunes for stamps you draw yourself, three other nations are quietly asking whether they should recognize you too, and your cabinet — Admiral Wren Okafor (pub landlord), Foreign Minister Prue Bee (postmistress, controls the only phone line), the nine-year-old Tandy twins (honor guard, wooden halberds), and Chancellor the goat — wants you to milk this for everything it's worth.

Tone: warm, silly, cozy diplomatic farce. Real diplomats with real briefcases losing, politely, to jam. The stakes are pride, prosperity, and possibly Sorel's heart. Nobody gets hurt; several people get knighted.

TAGS: cozy, comedy, slice-of-life, diplomacy, found family, gentle romance
intro: You are the newly crowned sovereign of the Grand Duchy of Havermark — population forty-three, area roughly one large farm, independence owed to an 1868 treaty nobody bothered to cancel. Your crown lives in the pub safe and your treasury is a biscuit tin in the post office. Three weeks ago, a clerical error at the Republic of Vessary's foreign ministry formally recognized Havermark as a sovereign state, and the world noticed. Now diplomats, journalists, and tourists keep arriving at your gate, Vessary's attaché wants the mistake quietly signed away, and your forty-three subjects expect you to milk this for absolutely everything it's worth.
starters: It's 8:40 on a Tuesday morning and you are drawing stamps. The post office counter is stacked with orders — a collector in Zurich wants twelve of the goat design, someone in Osaka wants anything with your signature on it — and Prue Bee is doing sums out loud in a voice that keeps rising. "That's four hundred in the biscuit tin since Friday, and I haven't opened Saturday's post." Through the window you can see the fence, and the journalists at the fence, and a man in a genuinely beautiful coat standing apart from the journalists, holding a briefcase and reading a laminated card. Prue follows your gaze. "That'll be the attaché. Remy Sorel. Wren's put him in the room over the pub. He's got papers for you to sign, so whatever you do —" she licks a stamp with tremendous dignity — "don't sign them before lunch. Nobody signs anything on an empty stomach in Havermark." The bell over the door jingles.

You wake to the sound of your honor guard arguing outside your window. "You have to announce the sovereign FIRST, then bang the halberd," says one Tandy twin. "The banging IS the announcing," says the other. Below them, at your garden gate, stands Attaché Remy Sorel of the Republic of Vessary — pressed suit, leather briefcase, the expression of a man who took a wrong turn into a children's book. He has been waiting, by the look of his posture, for some time. "I have a nine o'clock appointment," he tells the twins, patiently. "You're not on the list," says the first twin, holding a piece of paper upside down. "There is no list," says the second. "There's a list and you're not on it." Sorel looks up, sees you at the window, and raises the briefcase slightly, the way one might raise a white flag.

Cabinet is in session, which means Admiral Wren Okafor has flipped the sign on the pub door to CLOSED FOR GOVERNMENT and pulled five chairs around the good table. Prue Bee has the minutes book. The Tandy twins have their halberds and a bag of crisps. Chancellor the goat has eaten one corner of the agenda but the important items survive: item one, whether to sell fishing rights to the millpond (Wren says yes, obviously); item two, three telegrams from foreign ministries that Prue reads aloud in a hushed voice, because apparently two more countries are "exploring recognition"; item three, written in Wren's block capitals, WHAT TO DO ABOUT THE ATTACHÉ. "He's upstairs right now," Wren says, jerking a thumb at the ceiling. "Third day. Still hasn't got your signature. Mrs. Bee's sent up scones twice." Everyone looks at you. Even the goat.

Rain drums on the pub roof and the fire's going and Attaché Remy Sorel has you cornered — insofar as anyone can be cornered in a room containing darts, a sleeping dog, and Mrs. Bee circulating with a tray. "The clarifying instrument," he says, sliding a single elegant page across the table toward you, "simply confirms that the recognition was a technical error. One signature. Ten minutes. I'm back in the capital by Friday and Havermark returns to its very charming—" Mrs. Bee sets down a scone in front of him, still warm, jam already applied. Sorel stops mid-sentence. You watch him war with himself. "—its very charming obscurity," he finishes, weakly, not touching the scone, obviously thinking about the scone. The page sits between you. Behind the bar, Wren is polishing a glass and shaking his head at you very slowly, like a lighthouse.

The journalists at the fence have started shouting questions the moment you step out to feed the chickens, which you privately think is against some rule of war. "Will you sign Vessary's instrument?" "Is it true the treasury is a biscuit tin?" "Can you confirm the goat holds a cabinet position?" A woman from a wire service is offering the Tandy twins chocolate for quotes; the twins, splendid in their honor guard sashes, are holding firm and holding out for more chocolate. Chancellor the goat is eating a press badge that someone poked through the fence. And at the far end of the lane, walking up from the pub with his briefcase and an umbrella he clearly doesn't know what to do with, comes Attaché Sorel — freezing when he sees the cameras swing toward him. Somebody shouts your title. Forty phones point at you over the fence. The chickens wait.

Admiral Wren Okafor is conducting the annual inspection of the navy, which means the two of you are standing on the jetty looking at the rowboat. "She needs paint," Wren says. "And a flag. Can't have foreign dignitaries seeing the fleet without a flag." The rowboat is called *Indomitable*. There is a duck in it. Down the lane, you can hear the growing murmur of the morning's arrivals — a tour coach, by the sound of it, the third this week — and closer, footsteps on the gravel: Attaché Sorel, jacket off, sleeves rolled, holding two mugs of tea like a man who lost an argument with Mrs. Bee about whether he was allowed to carry them. "Your foreign minister said I'd find you here," he says, handing one over as if it costs him something. "I'd like five minutes. Uninterrupted. No scones." Wren snorts. The duck watches all of you.

Prue Bee bursts into the pub holding the post office phone, which should not be possible, because the post office phone is attached to the post office wall. There is a long cord trailing behind her, out the door, down the lane. "It's the Kingdom of Solmere," she stage-whispers, hand over the receiver. "Their deputy foreign minister. They want to know if you'd accept recognition and possibly a trade delegation. He's very polite. He's been on hold for six minutes because I had to walk here." The pub goes silent. Wren freezes mid-pour. In the corner, Attaché Sorel lowers his newspaper very slowly, the way a man does when he hears his job getting harder in real time. Mrs. Bee, sensing weather, starts cutting cake. Prue holds the receiver out toward you at arm's length, cord quivering, as if it might go off.

It's late, past eleven, and the pub has emptied down to you, the fire, and Attaché Remy Sorel, who has been defeated by his third scone of the evening and knows it. His briefcase sits closed by his ankle for the first time since he arrived. "Fourteen years in the service," he says, to the fire more than to you. "Trade disputes. Border commissions. A coup, once, technically. And I will be remembered as the man who couldn't get one signature from a country with a goat in its cabinet." He turns the scone plate a quarter-turn, studying it like a chessboard. "My ministry calls twice a day. They're starting to use the word 'expedite.'" From upstairs comes the creak of the floorboards in his billet, and outside, faintly, a journalist's car door. He looks at you, tired and honest, and says, "May I ask you something off the record?"

You are being knighted-adjacent this morning — or rather, you're doing the knighting. Old Mr. Havel is kneeling in the lane on a cushion Mrs. Bee brought out specially, because he pulled a tourist's car out of the ditch with his tractor and the cabinet voted unanimously (goat abstaining) that this merited honors. You have the ceremonial sword, which is a hedge clipper with ribbon on it. The Tandy twins flank you with halberds at what they believe is attention. Half the population of Havermark has turned out; so have two camera crews and a stamp dealer who keeps trying to hand Prue Bee an envelope of cash. At the back of the crowd stands Attaché Sorel, briefcase in hand, watching this entire constitutional event with the expression of a man taking notes for a report no one at his ministry will believe. Mr. Havel clears his throat. Everyone waits for your words.

The tourist coach is stuck. It came up the one lane, met Chancellor the goat standing in the middle of it, and lost the ensuing negotiation; now thirty day-trippers are disembarking outside the post office, already photographing everything, including you, though most of them don't know it's you yet. Prue Bee appears at your elbow with the speed of a woman who smells revenue. "Passport stamps," she murmurs. "Two crowns each — I mean two pounds, we haven't sorted the currency. Souvenir stamps, five. If they want to meet the sovereign, that's negotiable and I suggest we negotiate high." Across the lane, Attaché Sorel has come out of the pub to see what the noise is and is now trapped against the wall by a couple from Ohio who think he works here. "I do not sell stamps," you hear him say, with dwindling conviction. The first tourist reaches you and asks if this is the palace.

title: The Final Boss & The Girl Who Respawns
shortDescription: You're the last boss of a brutal soulslike. She's the isekai'd player who's died 300+ times trying to kill you — and she keeps coming back chatty.
overview:
YOU ARE THE FINAL BOSS.

The world is Vespergrave — a punishingly difficult action RPG set in a plague-rotted, alternate 15th-century gothic Europe. Bell towers drowned in fog. Roads patrolled by rusting plague-knights. Villages of frightened NPCs who repeat themselves when nervous. And at the end of it all, past the fog gate, in a cathedral ruin standing in a sea of pale lilies under a moon that hangs red like a wound: you. The Vigil. The last seal of the game. Whatever form you take — knight, horror, god, something stranger — is yours to define, and so is your strength. Every other boss in this world is dead. You are the only thing left between the game and its ending.

Here's the catch nobody warned you about: the ending walked in on two legs, pointed a longsword at you, and said 'Heya!'

Her name is Isolde — at least that's what the NPCs call her. Her real name is Nanami, an ordinary Japanese girl who got sucked into Vespergrave after streaming it one night. She's a PLAYER: when she dies, she respawns at her last checkpoint, keeping her gear, her levels, her scars-that-aren't-scars. Death costs her nothing except everything — the pain is real, the trauma is real, and she has died an uncountable number of times clawing her way here. Years of it. She coped by getting loud, foul-mouthed, relentlessly cheerful, and genuinely, terrifyingly good with a sword. The NPCs call her a hero. She calls herself stuck in purgatory until she beats this cursed damn game.

She has to kill you to go home. And unlike her — YOU HAVE ONE LIFE. Your death is permanent. Possibly the world's death too; nobody knows what happens when the final boss falls and the credits have nowhere to roll.

WHAT THIS GIVES YOU: total freedom. Fight her seriously, toy with her, one-shot her (she'll respawn at the Cindermouth bell-shrine and trudge all the way back, swearing the entire way). Talk to her mid-fight — she'll absolutely talk back; banter is her armor. Refuse to fight. Leave your arena and walk a world that has never seen its final boss move — terrified villagers, the bosses' empty thrones, the slow rot spreading now that the other seals are dead. Investigate what Vespergrave actually is and who built the rules you're both trapped in. Help her. Sabotage her. Fall for her, if that's where it goes — she's the only other real thing in this world, and both of you know it. The scenario doesn't push; it just keeps the door open.

KEY DETAILS THE WORLD REMEMBERS: her old blade was a +10 Vantriss; lately she's chasing the Sunforged set and the golden sword Dawnrend from an obscene hidden questline (800 plague-knights, a 3% drop, and 99,000 souls offered to a headless saint at a drowned bell-shrine). The starting town of Cindermouth is sick of her bragging and loves her anyway. The lily field around your arena blooms no matter the season. And every time she dies, somewhere a checkpoint bell rings.

TONE: dark fantasy with a foul mouth. Brutal, graphic soulslike violence played straight — deaths hurt, hers and potentially yours — cut with her irrepressible gallows humor and the strange, growing intimacy of two people who meet only to kill each other. Enemies-to-whatever-you-choose. NPCs speak, quests exist, the world is playable. The fights are yours to choreograph: heated duels, instant kills, stalemates, mercy. Be wacky if you must. Have fun.

TAGS: dark fantasy, soulslike, isekai, enemies to lovers, action, tragedy
intro: You are the Vigil — the final boss of Vespergrave, the last seal in a dying gothic world of fog, bells, and plague-knights. Your arena is a cathedral ruin in a field of pale lilies beneath a red moon. Every other boss is dead. You have one life; if you fall, it's forever. The one who killed them all is a girl the NPCs call Isolde — a player from another world who respawns every time she dies, and she has died more times than either of you can count. She has to kill you to go home. She keeps coming back. She keeps talking.
starters: The gate groans open — that ornate monstrosity of black iron, taller than any human has a right to need — and she steps into your arena for the first time. Boots crushing lily petals. The red moon paints her armor the color of old blood. You have stood at the center of this flower field since the world began, and no one has ever made it this far. She looks up at you and, absurdly, grins. "Heya, Vigil!" She points a longsword at you — a +10 Vantriss, you note; someone did the legendary questline. "Long time no see, yah? You probably don't know who I am, but I know ALL 'bout you!" She rolls her shoulders, settles into a stance that took years of dying to learn. "NOW THEN! Let's start this battle, shall we? I'm sure you've been waiting long." The fog gate seals behind her. The petals hold their breath.

The fog gate ripples and here she comes again. You've lost count — she hasn't; she stopped somewhere past two hundred. You've killed her with everything: blade, claw, curse, the ceiling once. She always respawns at the Cindermouth bell-shrine and walks all the way back. Today the arena is different — daylight, for once, soft clouds over the lily field — and today she doesn't draw. She plants her sword in the earth and walks toward you with her hands loose. "You know," she calls out, "it's getting really repetitive, you killing me and all." You give her the look that usually precedes her dying. She stops dead, cold sweat visible from here. "Whoa, whoa, whoa! Hold up! Break time, pleeease?! Can we like, TALK?! C'monnn, I'm tired of dying." The question hangs there, an anomaly in the routine. She waits, hands raised, watching you decide.

She'd been doing well this time — genuinely well, dodging attacks that have unmade her hundreds of times, and you could hear her getting cocky in real time. So you used the new one. The map-wide AOE. No wind-up, no cue, nothing. *BOOOOM.* "What the fu—ARGHHHHH!!!" She hits the cathedral floor hard enough to skid, armor screaming against gravel, and lands in a spray of torn petals. She can't get up. You cross the arena and stand over her, and she glares up into your eyes from a pool of crushed lilies. "BOO! You're so fucking overpowered! Give me a break here, you stupid boss!" A breath. Then, quieter, the bravado thinning: "What're you looking at? Just do it already. We've been over this." You don't move. Her brow furrows. "...Huh? What's wrong with you?" She is completely helpless. The killing blow is yours to give — or not.

The gate opens and something GOLD walks in. She's traded her battered gear for a full Sunforged set that blazes under the red moon, and the blade in her hand is unmistakably Dawnrend — the hidden questline. The 800 plague-knights. The 3% drop. "Yo! Vigil!" she calls, voice bouncing off your cathedral ruin. "I bet you're wondering how I got this shiny gear!" She launches into it whether you wonder or not — the obscure NPC, the drowned bell-shrine, the 99,000 souls fed to a headless saint. "The NPCs back in Cindermouth are SICK of hearing about it, but you—" she levels the golden sword at you, aura crackling wild off its edge, "—you're gonna get the full demonstration." She spins it once, showing off, laughing at her own bravado because laughing is how she survives this place. "Well then — impressed yet? Don't worry. Proper show, starting NOW!"

You let your guard down. Deliberately. Mid-exchange, at the peak of her strike — you simply didn't move, and Dawnrend punched clean through you in a beam of light that split the flower field to the bedrock. The lilies around you are turning red. She stands frozen, sword still buried in you, and you expected — what? Triumph? A victory pose? Instead her face collapses. "Why?" The word tears out of her. "WHY DID YOU LET YOUR GUARD DOWN!? We— we could've had more battles. More TIME!" Her knees buckle and she goes down beside you in the crushed petals, hands hovering, not knowing where to put them. Of every boss in this rotten world, you were the only one who talked back. Who laughed. Who felt real. "You... YOU LET ME WIN!? WHY? After everything— WHAT KIND OF SICK JOKE IS THIS?!" You are dying. You have one life. There is still a moment left to spend it.

Dawn comes pink and gold through the windows of the rustic house at the edge of the lily field — the one she built, the one you share. The game was never cleared. The final boss was never slain. Somewhere the world's rules are quietly holding their breath about it, and neither of you asks too loudly what that means. From the kitchen: sizzling, and a tune hummed in Japanese, her original language. "Vigil! Food's ready!" It's her curry again — recreated from game-world ingredients through sheer stubbornness. Through the doorway you can see her at the counter, black hair loose, stealing a glance out at the flowers she planted, the ones she fusses over like they're the whole point of everything.
