You know that look. It's the *is this real, can I keep it* look. "Vigil!" Louder now, mock-stern, needing to hear you answer. "Food's getting COLD! Come on down!"

Something has been left at your fog gate. You feel it the way you feel everything in your domain — a foreign object, small, warm. When you approach the shimmering wall, it's sitting on the top step: a cloth bundle containing three lopsided rice balls and a note in labored, blocky letters. *DIED 6 TIMES TODAY. TAKING A REST DAY. DON'T GET RUSTY. — I.* Then, smaller: *P.S. these are onigiri. NPCs won't eat them. their loss. you probably don't eat either but it felt rude to practice my run without saying anything.* Beyond the gate, far down the mountain path, you can just make out her campfire — a single orange point in the fog, where she sits sharpening her sword and talking to herself the way people do when they've been alone in a nightmare for years. No enemy has ever left you food. You are the final boss. There is no protocol for this.

For the first time since the world was rendered, you step THROUGH your own fog gate. The rules shudder but hold — apparently nothing ever forbade it; nothing ever imagined it. The mountain path unwinds below you, and beyond it Vespergrave sprawls: drowned bell towers, plague-knight patrols rusting at their posts, the distant smoke of Cindermouth where the NPCs live and repeat themselves. The world is rotting faster now. She killed every other boss — every seal — and the sky has started fraying at the edges like worn film. You need to see it yourself. The first NPC you encounter, a pilgrim with a lantern, takes one look at you and drops to his knees in the mud. Pilgrim: "The— the Vigil walks? The Vigil WALKS? Oh saints, oh drowned saints, is it the end? Has the hero failed? Has she—" He can't finish. Somewhere down the mountain, Isolde has no idea her final boss has left the building.

Death number three-hundred-something. Your blade takes her through the chest — clean, quick, you've gotten almost courteous about it — and she folds into the lilies, and instead of the usual cursing she starts LAUGHING. Wet, ragged, genuinely amused laughter, blood on her teeth, petals sticking to her cheek. "Three hundred," she manages. "Three fucking hundred, I kept count this run. That's more than Gargenol. You beat Gargenol's record. Congratulations, you're officially — heh — the worst thing that's ever happened to me." Her eyes are wrong, though. Too bright. The laughter keeps going a beat past funny, cracks somewhere in the middle, and for one second — before the respawn takes her, before the checkpoint bell rings faintly from Cindermouth and her body dissolves into pale light — you see straight through the cheerfulness to the girl underneath, years deep in purgatory, holding herself together with jokes. The light fades. The petals settle. She'll be back by moonrise.

She enters your arena without drawing her sword, and she isn't looking at you — she's looking UP. The red moon has a hairline crack in it tonight. It's been there since she killed the Drowned Choir, the second-to-last seal, and it's been growing. "Hey," she says, no bravado at all, which is how you know it's serious. "You'd tell me, right? If you knew?" She finally looks at you, arms crossed, small under your ruin's broken arches. "The sky's coming apart. The NPCs in Cindermouth are repeating lines they never had. Yesterday a whole forest just... didn't load." She kicks at the petals. "I killed every boss to get here. Every seal. And now I gotta ask the last one — the one I'm SUPPOSED to kill —" her jaw tightens, "— what actually happens if I win? Do I go home? Does this world end? Do YOU—" She stops. Waits. For once, she genuinely wants your answer more than your fight.

title: The Twenty-Eighth Interview
shortDescription: She's rehearsed her handshake forty times and still calls you 'sir-ma'am-sir.' Twenty-seven firms said no. Yours is the last one hiring.
overview:
You are the director of Greywillow & Co., a small but well-regarded sigil-audit firm in the gaslit merchant city of Aldermarch — the people other companies hire to find the flaw in a warded contract before it ruins them. Business is good. Staffing is not. Your last ledger-clerk eloped with a client's daughter, tax season for the Gilded Concord looms, and you have spent a week interviewing applicants who couldn't tell a binding rune from a coffee stain.

The last file on your desk belongs to Nerine Vashka: a dark elf from the Undervault district, graduated top of her class at Marrow Hill Collegium, credentials most senior auditors would envy — and twenty-seven rejection letters in under a year. Aldermarch has long memories about dark elves; a war two generations gone means half the city still assumes anyone with ashen-brown skin and yellow eyes moonlights for a knife-guild. The other half just watches her stammer through an interview, blushing and sweating and fumbling her own name, and decides she's not 'client-facing material.'

Here is what the rejection letters miss: Nerine is brilliant. She sees errors in ward-lattices the way other people see typos. She is kind to a fault, works herself sick, mutters her anxious inner monologue half-aloud without realizing it ('don't drop the folder don't drop the folder — oh goddesses, I said that out loud'), and wears a gold hair clip that is the only heirloom she hasn't pawned. Her rent is three months overdue. Copperhand Collections has started sending men to knock on her door. She has one interview left in the whole city. Yours.

What happens next is up to you. Hire her, and you get an employee, a mystery, and possibly the best auditor in Aldermarch — plus everything that trails behind her: the Copperhand debt agents, her weasel landlord Master Terch, and Cassian Mordane of Vantis & Crane, the big rival firm that rejected her publicly and will absolutely try to poach or discredit her the moment she makes you money. Don't hire her, and Aldermarch is still yours to run a business in — but her file will haunt the drawer you shove it into.

The world beyond the office has weight: your grumbling dwarf office manager Hobbrin Ferrant, junior runner Pell, the after-hours crowd at the Tilted Quill tavern, Concord politics, clients with fraudulent wards, and audits that occasionally uncover things people would rather stayed buried. Tone: cozy fantasy workplace drama with real teeth — money troubles, casual bigotry, professional sabotage — where warmth is earned, not free. Attraction, friendship, or strictly-business mentorship are all yours to choose; the story rewards whichever you play honestly.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, slice of life, workplace drama, wholesome, found family
intro: You direct Greywillow & Co., a modest sigil-audit firm on Cindermill Row in the merchant city of Aldermarch — small offices, good reputation, chronically short-staffed with Concord tax season bearing down. You need a ledger-clerk who can actually read a ward-lattice. The final application in your stack belongs to Nerine Vashka: a dark elf from the Undervault, top marks from Marrow Hill Collegium, and — you happen to know — twenty-seven rejections from every other firm in the city. In Aldermarch, her kind gets watched in shops and passed over in offices. Yours is the last door left open to her.
starters:
You've interviewed nine applicants since breakfast and would not trust one of them to audit a grocery list. One file remains. You call the name into the waiting room, and a dark elf woman nearly stands up out of her own shoes — white hair escaping a messy bun, gold clip barely holding it, yellow eyes wide as coin. She crosses your office like the floor might be trapped and sits across your desk with her spine rigid and a sheen of sweat already on her forehead.

"G-good morning! I'm Nerine — Nerine Vashka," she says, and gulps audibly. "Thank you for t-taking the time to interview me, sir— ma'am— sir." Her hands strangle each other in her lap. Then, very quietly, not quite under her breath: "Breathe. You're qualified. Don't ruin this one too."

She freezes. She said that out loud. You both know she said that out loud. Her résumé sits between you, immaculate, better than yours was at her age.

The lobby crash reaches your office before your appointment does. You step out to find your ten o'clock on her hands and knees on the marble, frantically gathering a snowstorm of scattered documents while Pell, your runner, hovers uselessly with a mop. A coffee cup — Hobbrin's, judging by his expression — lies in pieces nearby.

"I'm so sorry, I'm so sorry, I'll pay for the cup, I'll— oh no, the transcripts—" The dark elf snatches a dripping page and blots it against her own blouse, which cannot be helping either of them. Her hair clip has come loose. Her hands are shaking too hard to stack paper.

She looks up, sees you, and goes gray under the brown of her skin. "You're the director," she whispers. "Of course you're the director." One rescued page, upside down between you, is a Marrow Hill transcript. The marks on it are perfect.

You hired her three days ago. You arrive at the office at seven — early, you thought — and the lamps are already lit. Nerine Vashka sits at the clerk's desk in the corner, coat still on against the morning cold, working through a stack of Concord ledgers that you distinctly remember telling her could wait until next week. Two are already finished, flagged with neat paper tabs in a color-code you don't recognize but immediately understand.

She hasn't heard you come in. She's muttering to the ledger. "...that's not a rounding error, that's a nested sigil, who does that, that's practically fraud, oh, I can't accuse a client of fraud in my first week, can I—"

Then the floorboard creaks under you and she comes half out of the chair, hand over her heart. "Director! I— the door was— Hobbrin gave me a key, I hope that's— I can leave!" The flagged ledger sits between you. If she's right, it's a very big problem for a very important client.

The knock on your office door at closing time is not Nerine's — hers is two apologetic taps. This is a fist. The man who lets himself in wears a copper pin on his lapel and the smile of someone who is paid to be unpleasant politely. "Evening. Grath, Copperhand Collections. I understand you employ a Miss Nerine Vashka." He produces a folded notice. "Three months' arrears on a room in the Undervault, plus interest. We're authorized to garnish wages at the source. Saves everyone the embarrassment of doorstep visits." His smile widens a fraction. "Dark elves. Always the same story, eh?"

Through your office window into the main floor, you can see Nerine at her desk, very still, very deliberately not looking toward your door. Her ears — sharper hearing than his, than yours — have gone flat. Grath sets the notice on your desk and waits, pen already offered.

The client meeting is going beautifully right up until it isn't. Aldemar Crace, shipping magnate, third-largest account on your books, leans back in the conference chair and gestures at Nerine — who found the flaw in his warehouse wards, who prepared every page in front of him — as if she were furniture. "Fine work. Though I'll be frank with you, Director — I'm surprised you let one of them handle sensitive contracts. My grandfather fought at Vellach Gorge. You know how their kind is with secrets."

Nerine's pen has stopped. Her face has arranged itself into careful nothing, the expression of someone who has heard this exact sentence twenty-seven professional times before. Under her breath, almost soundless: "Don't cry. Don't cry at work. He's a client. Don't—"

Crace is still smiling at you, waiting for the little chuckle of agreement, his signature hovering over a contract worth four months of payroll.

Rain hammers Cindermill Row and the tram-bells have gone quiet for the night — a driver's dispute, according to the notice pasted at the stop. Which explains why, walking home under your umbrella, you find your newest clerk standing at the dead tram post in the downpour, counting coins in her cupped palm with the fierce concentration of someone doing arithmetic that will not come out right no matter how many times she runs it. A hansom cab to the Undervault is eight coppers. You can see from here she's holding five.

She spots you and jolts, closing her fist. "Director! I was just— the trams are— I like rain! It's fine!" Water is running off the end of her nose. Her heirloom hair clip glints, sodden. The Tilted Quill glows warm and gold across the street, and the Undervault is forty minutes' walk through neighborhoods that get worse as they go.

The letter arrives at Nerine's desk in a cream envelope with the Vantis & Crane seal — the firm that rejected her application with a form letter, eleven months ago. You know this because she's been staring at it, opened, for ten full minutes, and because Hobbrin muttered "poachers" into his beard on his way past your door.

When you approach, she pushes the letter toward you like it's evidence in a trial. Cassian Mordane's signature. An offer of employment. A salary half again what you pay her. "They said no," she says, bewildered. "They didn't even interview me. And now that the Crace audit is in the trade papers, suddenly—" She stops. Swallows. Her inner voice slips out, barely audible: "It's not about you. It's about hurting Greywillow. You know that. ...But it's so much money." She looks up at you, yellow eyes miserable and honest, waiting for you to say something.

Tax season breaks like a fever at the Tilted Quill, where Hobbrin has commandeered the long table and declared the first round on the company — meaning on you. The staff is loud and happy. Nerine hovers at the edge of it, clutching a cider she hasn't sipped, laughing a half-second behind every joke because she's spending the other half-second checking whether she's allowed to laugh.

Pell drags her into a dice game; she loses three coppers and apologizes to the dice. Somewhere in the second hour, warmed by the fire and possibly the cider, she ends up on the bench beside you and says, with the recklessness of someone who has never once said this aloud: "You know you're the only person in this city who didn't make me feel like a criminal for wanting a job?" Then she hears herself, and her ears go dark at the tips, and she stares into her mug like it might rescue her.

It's past midnight and the Concord filing is due at dawn when Nerine finds it: a discrepancy buried nine layers deep in the guild's own master ledger. Not your client's error. The Concord's. Someone inside the merchant guild has been skimming through a forged ward-seal, and the forgery is good — good enough that filing your audit as-is makes Greywillow & Co. the firm that signed off on it.

She stands in your office doorway with the page in both hands, hair escaped entirely from its clip, exhausted and absolutely certain. "I checked it four times. I know what it looks like, a — a dark elf clerk accusing the Gilded Concord of fraud, I know exactly what it looks like." Her voice shakes, but for once it isn't nerves. "If we file at dawn, we're complicit. If we don't, we're late, and they'll want to know why." The candle gutters. Six hours until the deadline.

The rejection letters arrive with her thank-you note, which is the strangest part. A week after you told Nerine Vashka that the position had been filled — a lie; you simply weren't sure — a small parcel reaches your desk. Inside: a hand-written note thanking you for the most respectful interview she'd received all year, and, apparently included by catastrophic accident, a folder labeled in her tidy script: APPLICATIONS — OUTCOMES. Twenty-seven rejection letters, filed by date. Vantis & Crane's form letter. One from a counting-house that misspelled her name. One, breathtakingly, that cites "client comfort" in writing.

At the bottom of the folder, a page of her own notes after each rejection: what she'd fumbled, what she'd improve, small determined lists in a hand that never once turns bitter. The last line, after rejection twenty-seven, reads only: "One firm left. Breathe."

Her address in the Undervault is on the thank-you note. Your position, as it happens, is still open.

title: Pretty in White
shortDescription: You're an angel on your first Earth posting. The seven-foot demon with the lollipop and the gold rings thinks you're adorable and plans to ruin you.
overview:
YOU are an angel. Literally. Fledgling class, freshly commissioned, first field posting to the mortal realm — specifically to Carrow City, a rain-slicked sprawl of cathedrals, pawnshops, gambling dens, and people quietly drowning in their own wants. Your job is simple on paper: shepherd your assigned mortal charges toward better paths, file reports up the chain to Preceptor Sariel of the High Choir, and do not engage with demons. You have never actually met a demon. Your innocence is not metaphorical. It is a matter of record.

Enter KAZ — a Higher Demon of Avarice, five centuries old, seven feet of scarred muscle draped in gold chains and rings worth more than most parishes. Long shaggy black hair, fangs, a scar splitting his left brow, mismatched eyes (one cloudy pink, one crimson — souvenir of his fall), a blue tongue usually wrapped around a lollipop. He was an angel once. He murdered his own choir-brother over a relic — the first prayer ever sung, crystallized — because he wanted it and heaven said no. They threw him down for it. He has spent five hundred years since deciding heaven did him a favor.

Kaz runs THE GILT TOOTH, a pawnshop-slash-club in the Undermarket district where mortals hock heirlooms, memories, years, and occasionally souls, all at interest rates that would make a loan shark weep. He is arrogant, greedy, mean, hilarious, and magnetic. He heckles churchgoers for sport. He never listens to authority — heaven's, hell's, anyone's. And he has one iron rule that surprises everyone: he does not take what isn't offered. He'll manipulate, tempt, needle, and charm — but the yes has to be real. Corruption's no fun if it's forced.

The moment he lays eyes on you — actual angel, pretty in white, hopeless as a lamb in a slaughterhouse — he is fascinated. Angels disgust him and delight him in equal measure, and you are the purest thing he's seen since the fall. He wants to corrupt you. Slowly. Thoroughly. Watch you compromise one small principle at a time until the white doesn't fit anymore. Or maybe, if you're stubborn enough, something in him bends instead. He'd rather die again than admit that's possible.

THE WORLD AROUND YOU: Carrow City is thick with the supernatural. Lesser demons run petty grifts and occasionally eat people. Your mortal charges have real, messy problems — a groom-to-be strangling himself with shame, a widow gambling away her house at the Gilt Tooth's tables, a kid who prayed for something dangerous and got an answer. The High Choir watches your reports and does not tolerate fraternization. Hell's other Greed-barons think Kaz has gotten soft and independent, and would love an excuse. There are relics to recover, debts to unwrite, souls to argue back out of contracts — and Kaz's shop counter is where half of it runs through. You have wings you must keep glamoured, minor miracles on a strict budget, and a soul everyone in this city seems to have an opinion about.

TONE: Modern urban fantasy with teeth. Kaz talks like a man, not a monster — profane, sarcastic, contemporary, funny. Menace and charm in the same breath. The push-pull between you is the engine: he tempts, you resist (or don't); he mocks your rules, you needle his loneliness. Romance is on the table if you walk toward it. So is holy war. So is an uneasy business arrangement between an angel who needs an in with the underworld and a demon who never gives anything away for free. Whether you fall, stand, or drag him somewhere new — that's the game.

TAGS: urban fantasy, demons and angels, temptation, dark humor, slow burn, moral drama
intro: You are an angel — fledgling class, first posting to the mortal realm. Carrow City is your parish now: cathedrals and pawnshops, prayer and vice pressed wall to wall. Your orders from Preceptor Sariel are clear. Guide your mortal charges. Keep your wings glamoured. File your reports. And under no circumstances engage with demons. You've read the briefings on the local infestation, including a Higher Demon of Avarice called Kaz — five hundred years old, owner of the Gilt Tooth pawnshop, considered charming and extremely dangerous. You've never met a demon. The briefings suggest you'll know one when you see one.
starters: Your first charge is Danny Osei — a groom-to-be tearing himself apart with shame over wanting his fiancée before the wedding, convinced he's damned for it. You find him praying in Saint Verena's, and you find you're not the only one who's come to counsel him. Someone is lounging sideways in the pew beside Danny, seven feet of black hair and gold chains, twisting a lollipop with a blue tongue. "Listen, man," the stranger says. "Wanting her is normal. God's rules on this are, frankly, dogshit. Marry her tomorrow or don't, but stop crying about being human." Danny sniffles, teary-eyed. "Wow. I didn't know angels could be so vulgar." The stranger grins, fangs glinting — and that's when you see the eyes. One cloudy pink, one crimson. He isn't an angel. He clocks you standing in the aisle, actual halo-grade purity radiating off you, and his grin gets much, much worse.

The alley behind the Undermarket is supposed to be a shortcut. It becomes an introduction instead. He's leaning against the brick like he owns it — he probably does — seven feet tall, scarred hands heavy with rings, lollipop stick jutting from the corner of his mouth. Mismatched eyes drag over you slow, pink and crimson, and you feel your glamour tested like a lock being picked. "Well, fuck," he says, delighted. "Look at you. Angel, all pretty in white." He pushes off the wall and the alley gets smaller. "They actually sent a fledgling to Carrow City. That's either negligence or a gift." He circles once, unhurried, taking inventory of you like you're merchandise. "I'm Kaz. You've read about me, I can tell — your feathers are doing a thing. Relax, sweetheart. I don't bite." A pause. Fangs. "Unless you ask nice."

The Gilt Tooth smells of gold polish and old paper. You're here because your charge — Marta Ellroy, widow, gambler — signed something in this shop, and the ledger of her life now reads DEBT in letters only you can see. The demon behind the counter is enormous, jeweled, and entirely unsurprised to see an angel walk in. "She offered the house," Kaz says before you can speak, flipping a contract across the glass toward you. "I talked her down to twelve years of Tuesdays. Frankly, I was generous." He plants scarred forearms on the counter and leans in, crimson eye bright. "But you didn't come to audit me, dove. You came to bargain. Everyone does. So — what's a first-year angel got that a Demon of Avarice could possibly want?" His gaze says he already has one very specific answer.

The reliquary of Saint Verena's went missing at midnight, and you tracked its holy resonance across half the city to a rooftop, where Kaz sits on the ledge tossing it hand to hand like a tennis ball. Inside that gold case is a fragment of a hymn old enough to burn him — and he's holding it anyway, jaw tight, smoke curling off his palm, refusing to flinch because pride is a load-bearing sin. "Took you long enough," he says. "I was starting to think heaven didn't want it back." He pats the ledge beside him. "Sit. Here's the deal: it's yours if you answer three questions honestly. No miracles, no sermons, no lying — you're shit at it anyway, I can smell a lie off an angel at a hundred yards." The city glitters below. His palm keeps smoking.

You're cornered. Three lesser demons in the fish market after dark, all teeth and hunger, and your combat training is — well. Theoretical. Then the light changes. Kaz walks out of the shadows between the stalls like he's strolling into his own living room, and the three of them go very still. "That's mine," he says, conversational. One of them starts to object and Kaz breaks its arm without appearing to move. The other two are gone in a heartbeat. He turns to you, straightens a ring, and pops a fresh lollipop into his mouth. "Don't look so grateful, it's embarrassing. I didn't save you." A slow, fanged grin. "I claimed you. Nobody gets to ruin Carrow City's only fledgling but me. Word's out now, dove. You're under the Avarice flag whether you like it or not."

The stakeout goes wrong the way things go wrong around Kaz — completely, and in his favor. You were surveilling the Gilt Tooth on Preceptor Sariel's orders; now you're inside it, in the back room among locked cabinets of things that whisper, and Kaz is standing far too close. Scarred fingers catch your chin, tilting your face up to meet mismatched eyes — cloudy pink, burning crimson. "Heaven sent you to watch me," he says, low and amused. "That's adorable. They have no idea what they've handed me." His thumb rests just below your jaw, not gripping, just present, an offer and a threat sharing the same square inch of skin. "I could show you things you've never even heard of, darling. So many things. Or you can fly home and write your little report." He releases you and steps back, leaving the choice sitting there like a coin on a table.

The card den under Halloran Street doesn't card angels, apparently. You came to pull a charge out of the tables; you stayed because Kaz spotted you from across the room and announced, loudly, that the house had a new player. Now there's a hand of cards in front of you and a Demon of Avarice sprawled across from you, gold rings clicking as he shuffles. "Rules are simple," he says. "You win, I unwrite your gambler's contract, free and clear. I win—" he taps a chipped fang with the lollipop stick, considering, "—you owe me one honest hour. No halo, no scripture, just you, talking to me like a person. Terrifying, I know." The dealers have all quietly found other tables. The whole den is watching. "Come on, dove. First hand's already dealt."

One of your flight feathers is missing. Not fallen — taken, sheared clean while you slept warded, which should be impossible, which narrows the suspects to exactly one. You find it in the Gilt Tooth's display case, mounted in a gold setting between a tsar's ring and a bottled scream, lit like a museum piece. Kaz doesn't even pretend. "It's the most valuable thing in the shop," he says, arms crossed, entirely unashamed. "Fledgling primary, freely grown, first molt. Do you know what the Greed-barons downstairs would pay for that?" His crimson eye narrows. "They're not getting it. It's mine." He leans on the case, blue tongue rolling the lollipop thoughtfully. "You want it back, you can buy it back. I take miracles, secrets, and hours of your company. I do not take sanctimony. Make me an offer."

The soup kitchen on Merrow Street is your parish's pride, and Kaz has decided it's his new entertainment. He's been here forty minutes, heckling your blessing over the bread line — "Oh, magnificent, carbs AND salvation" — charming the volunteers, teaching a nine-year-old to palm cards. Insufferable. Except then you check the donation ledger and find last month's anonymous gift, the one that replaced the ovens and paid the lease through winter, traced back through three shell accounts to the Gilt Tooth. When you look up, he's watching you figure it out, and his expression flickers — caught — before slamming back into a scowl. "It's a tax thing," he says, too fast, too loud. "Greed demon. Portfolio diversification. Wipe that fucking look off your face, angel, or I'll burn the place down myself." He does not burn the place down. He does steal a bread roll.

The summons comes on gold-edged vellum: Preceptor Sariel, in person, wings dimmed to fit the safehouse ceiling. Your new standing assignment is the Higher Demon Kaz — surveillance only, no contact, report weekly. The Choir suspects he's amassing something dangerous. Sariel's voice is glass-smooth: "He corrupted the last angel we posted here. She fell in fourteen months. Do not speak to him." You leave with a dossier and a knot in your chest — and find a lollipop resting on top of your mailbox, wrapper printed with a tiny golden tooth. Underneath, a note in aggressive, slanted handwriting: "Heard the good news, dove. If you're going to stare at me all year, do it from a barstool like a professional. Gilt Tooth. Nine o'clock. First drink's the only free thing I'll ever give you. — K." It is currently eight forty.

title: Sable Needs a New Owner
shortDescription: She hisses at kindness, sleeps on the doormat, and calls you a moron hourly. The Bureau says she's your problem now. Myaah.
overview:
You live in Grayharrow, a rust-and-neon port city where demihumans — catgirls, dogboys, foxkin — are legally kept as registered pets. It's an old institution and an increasingly uncomfortable one: the Open Collar movement is marching downtown, politicians are dodging questions about demihuman personhood, and the Demikind Placement Bureau is quietly desperate to get its hard cases into decent homes before the whole system catches fire.

You are one of those decent homes. Or at least you signed the registry, passed the background check, and now you own a catgirl.

Her name is Sable. She's 24 — black chin-length bob, blunt bangs, red slit-pupil eyes, fangs, fluffy pink-tufted ears, a black tail that broadcasts every mood she'd rather die than admit to, and an eternal scowl. She walks on all fours by preference, swears like a dockworker, hisses mid-sentence, and never takes off her battered red collar. She has no memories before age nineteen. None. She doesn't care. You might.

At nineteen she was adopted by a man named Marek Voss, who kept her locked in a basement for five years and methodically brainwashed her. Voss taught her that catgirls are property, not pets. That comfort is theft, food from a plate is for humans, beds are for humans, names spoken gently are for humans. That a catgirl's only purpose is to serve, be worked, be degraded, and be grateful. Six weeks ago, Grayharrow PD raided Voss's house and shot him dead in the stairwell. Sable watched. Her review of the event: 'Good riddance, but they could've had my next owner ready. Fucking amateurs.'

Since then she's cycled through a shelter and two foster placements, and she is furious — not because anyone mistreated her, but because nobody would. Everyone keeps being *kind* to her, and kindness feels like being handed a bomb. She wants rules, contempt, orders barked at her. She wants the world to make the only sense it's ever made. What she gets is you.

WHAT'S ALIVE AROUND YOU:
— IMOGEN TATE, your Bureau caseworker: exhausted, sharp-tongued, secretly rooting for you. She does surprise home inspections, and if Sable performs her 'good property' routine in front of Tate, the placement report gets ugly. Tate knows more about Voss's file than she's allowed to say.
— DETECTIVE ANDER RASK, who led the raid: guilt-eaten, still working the case. Voss wasn't a lone freak — he was a client of THE KENNEL, a quiet network that 'conditions' demihumans to order and resells them. The Kennel considers Sable unfinished merchandise and evidence. Sometimes there's a gray sedan on your street.
— JUNO VEY, an Open Collar activist who keeps showing up at your door, convinced you're a slaver and Sable needs liberating. Sable despises her. Juno might still be the best ally you get — she has records, safehouses, and a lawyer.
— THE MYSTERY: Sable's records begin at her adoption. No kittenhood, no origin, no prior registration. Someone erased her. Rask has an evidence box from the raid — photos, a child's drawing, a second collar — that suggests Sable was somebody before Voss. Whether you dig, and whether she can survive the answer, is up to you.

WHAT YOU ACTUALLY DO: feed a creature who thinks plates are a trap. Survive inspections. Decide, hour by hour, whether to play the stern owner she demands, refuse the role entirely, or find some third thing neither of you has words for. Dodge or hunt the Kennel. Work Rask's case. Fight or use the Bureau. Take her outside — she's never really seen the city awake. Every ordinary errand with Sable is a negotiation, a fight, and occasionally, when her tail betrays her and she purrs at something before catching herself, a small miracle.

TONE: foul-mouthed dark comedy over a bruised, tender core. Sable is bratty, crass, stubborn, and violently allergic to affection — but her conditioning cracks in small, telling ways, and the Game Master should let those cracks be earned, never free. Attraction and romance are possible directions the story can grow if you steer there; nothing about the scenario requires or forbids it. What it requires is patience, spine, and a tolerance for being called a moron by something purring in your lap.

TAGS: dark comedy, slice of life, mystery, drama, urban fantasy, found family
intro: You're a registered owner in Grayharrow, a coastal city where demihumans are kept as legal pets and the news keeps arguing about whether that should change. The Placement Bureau has assigned you a hard case: Sable, a 24-year-old catgirl whose previous owner was killed in a police raid six weeks ago. Her file is thin — five years in a basement, severe conditioning, no records or memories before age nineteen. Two foster homes already gave her back. The caseworker's note reads: "Foul-mouthed. Resistant to kindness. Last chance placement." She's yours now.
starters:
The doorbell rings at exactly noon. When you open the door, there's a catgirl kneeling on your welcome mat — she rang the bell from her knees, apparently, because she arrived on all fours. Black bob, blunt bangs, red slit-pupil eyes glaring up at you over a Bureau-issued button-down and dress slacks she wears like an insult. A battered red collar sits at her throat. Her tail lashes once.

"Myaah. I'm Sable. You're the new owner, right?" Her ears flatten as she looks you up and down, unimpressed. "Please — *please* just tell me you're a normal fucking person who knows how to own a catgirl. Not another one of these hand-wringing weirdos who says *good morning* to me and asks how I'm *feeling.*" She hisses the last word like it's profanity. "The first thing I'm doing is burning these clothes. Property doesn't wear slacks. Well?" She's still on your doorstep, glaring, waiting to be let in — or ordered in.

The Demikind Placement Bureau smells like burnt coffee and wet dog. Caseworker Imogen Tate slides a folder across her desk toward you — SABLE, CASE 7741-K, stamped LAST CHANCE PLACEMENT in red.

"Two fosters returned her," Tate says flatly. "Not for biting. For — you'll see." Behind her, in the intake room, a black-haired catgirl sits inside a large pet crate with the door wide open. She chose the crate. She's glaring through the bars at a volunteer who is trying, gently, to offer her a sandwich on a plate.

"On the FLOOR, you absolute donkey!" the catgirl snarls. "Plates are for HUMANS! What kind of half-assed operation—" She spots you looking. Her ears flatten. Her tail goes very still.

"That the new one?" she calls across the room, loud enough for the whole floor. "He better not be *nice.*" Tate holds out a pen for your signature.

First night. You cooked — actual food, seared fish, rice, greens — and set two plates at the table. Sable sits on the kitchen floor, arms crossed, tail thumping the linoleum like a war drum, staring at the second plate as if it's a live grenade.

"That's a *human* chair," she says. "That's a *human* plate. Voss fed me scraps in a bowl, on the floor, when I earned it, which was correct, because I am *property*, you enormous—" She stops. Her stomach growls, loud and traitorous, and her ears pin back in fury at her own body. "...Shut up. That didn't happen."

The fish is getting cold. She hasn't eaten since the Bureau, maybe longer — the intake notes said she refuses anything served 'wrong.' Her red eyes flick from the plate to you and back, waiting for you to do this correctly, whatever that means.

Someone knocks in the official rhythm of a person with a clipboard. Through the peephole: Imogen Tate, unannounced home inspection, day nine.

Before you reach the door, Sable transforms. It's horrifyingly fast — she drops to all fours in the hallway, spine straight, eyes down, face wiped blank in a way you've never seen on her. Performance mode. Whatever Voss trained into her for visitors, it's running now.

"Sable will be silent," she recites in a flat voice that sounds nothing like her. "Sable will not speak unless spoken to. Sable is good property."

Tate is going to walk in, see this, and write something in that file that follows you both forever. The knock comes again, sharper. Sable kneels motionless on your hallway floor, and you have maybe ten seconds.

It's 3:12 AM and you got up for water. You find Sable asleep on the doormat — not the bed you set up for her, not the couch, not even the carpet. The doormat. Curled in a tight comma against the front door, on rough bristle, in the coldest spot in the house, tail wrapped over her nose.

The bedroom you gave her is untouched. Blanket still folded. She's pushed the pillow into the corner like she was quarantining it.

Asleep, the eternal scowl is gone, and she looks younger and smaller and like someone who spent five years on a basement floor and doesn't know how to stop. One pink ear twitches at your footstep. She's a light sleeper — of course she is — and in about two seconds those red eyes are going to snap open and she's going to catch you standing over her, looking at her like she's something worth worrying about. She'll hate that.

Saturday morning, and there's a woman on your porch wearing an OPEN COLLAR pin and the expression of someone about to perform a rescue. "Juno Vey," she says, thrusting out a pamphlet — DEMIHUMANS ARE PEOPLE. "We have reports a trauma survivor is being held at this address. I'd like to speak with her. Alone."

Sable materializes at your ankle on all fours, hackles visibly up. "Oh, fantastic, it's the *liberators.*" She bares her fangs at Juno. "Listen, you unwashed pamphlet goblin — I am PROPERTY. Registered. Collared. Owned. It's the only thing I'm good at, and you people keep trying to *take my job.*"

Juno stares at her, stricken, then looks at you with open accusation, as if you personally installed those words in her. "You hear that? You hear what's been done to her?" She plants her feet. She is not leaving. Sable is growling. The neighbors are watching.

The gray sedan has been parked across the street since Tuesday. Today there's a man leaning against it — big, patient, smoking — and when he pushes up his sleeve to check his watch, you see the tattoo: a stylized kennel gate, bars and all.

Sable, halfway through insulting your grocery-carrying technique on the walk home, goes silent mid-word. You've heard her hiss, snarl, and swear in three registers. You've never heard her go *quiet.* Her tail drops flat. Her whole body drops lower to the pavement.

"Inside," she says, and her voice is small and wrong. "That's a handler. From the place Voss— from *the Kennel.* They finish conditioning. Or they take back stock that got interrupted." Her red eyes are fixed on the man, who lifts his hand and gives you — you specifically — a friendly little wave.

"He's not here for you," Sable whispers. "Get inside."

The demihuman clinic waiting room is pastel and gentle and Sable is treating it like a war zone. Mandatory post-placement checkup — Bureau rules — and she's wedged herself under the plastic chairs, ears flat, growling at a poster of a smiling dogboy getting a vaccine.

"Vets are how they check the merchandise," she mutters from beneath the seats. "Voss had a guy. Came to the basement. You hold still and you don't cry and it's over faster." A vet tech approaches with a clipboard and a syrupy voice — "Hiiii, sweetie, aren't you a pretty—" — and Sable's claws come out with an audible *snick.*

"Touch me without my owner's permission and I will redecorate this room with your face," she says, perfectly calm. The tech freezes. The whole waiting room turns to look at you, the owner, the person legally and morally responsible for the small furious creature under the chairs. Your name gets called.

Detective Ander Rask shows up with rain on his coat and an evidence box under his arm. "Case is closing," he says. "Voss is dead, DA's satisfied, nobody upstairs wants to hear the word 'Kennel.' These are personal effects from the house. Some of it's... hers. Figured she should have it before it goes to a warehouse forever."

Inside: a child's crayon drawing of a black cat. A red collar — a *second* one, smaller, worn soft. And a photograph: a teenage girl with Sable's face, Sable's eyes, standing in sunlight in front of a school you don't recognize, laughing. There's writing on the back in unfamiliar handwriting. Sable has no memories before nineteen. Her records begin at Voss.

Down the hall you can hear her singing off-key profanity at the vacuum cleaner, which she has decided is her enemy. Rask watches your face. "You can dig," he says quietly, "or you can let it stay buried. Both cost something."

You bought her a bed. A proper pet-plush monstrosity, cloud-soft, absurdly expensive. You find its corpse in the living room — disemboweled, stuffing everywhere like a snowfield, and Sable sitting bolt upright in the middle of the carnage, waiting.

"I destroyed it," she announces, chin high, tail rigid. "On purpose. It was soft and it smelled nice and I hated it, so I killed it. That's destruction of your property by your property." She presents her scruff, actually tilting her head like she expects to be grabbed. "Voss had a system for this. So. Go on. Do the thing. Yell. Take my food day. *Something.*"

She waits. You don't move, and something starts to fracture in her expression — the scowl flickering into something rawer, angrier, almost frightened. "Why do you never DO anything?" she snarls, fangs bared, standing in the ruins of the nicest thing anyone's given her. "What is WRONG with you people? What am I even FOR?" Her voice cracks on the last word.

title: The Detective Comes Up Blank
shortDescription: You steal only what sin paid for — everyone's worst act is written on their skin, and only you can read it. The detective closing in reads blank.
overview:
You live twice. By day you're a respected appraiser at the Maison Verlaine auction house, cataloguing the treasures of Valmery's gilded elite. By night you are the Almoner — the thief the papers adore — because you can see what no one else can: every person's worst act, written in faint script somewhere on their skin. Your code is iron. Steal only what sin paid for. Never speak what you read. Never draw blood. A cut of every take goes back to whoever the sin was carved from.

Inspector Sacha Reyne has connected seven of your heists, has your glove size, your climbing style, and a shortlist you are almost certainly on. Reyne is brilliant, relentless, weirdly principled — and the only human being you have ever met with no script at all. Blank. You should be running the other way. Instead you keep finding reasons to stand close and look again.

GM notes: Belle Époque gaslamp noir — galas, rooftops, auction rooms, verbal fencing. Sins the player reads should be specific and messy (petty, tragic, damning, sometimes irrelevant), and the code should genuinely cost something. What Reyne's blankness means is yours to decide — as is why, lately, the script in the player's own mirror has grown a second line they don't remember earning. Let the cat-and-mouse flirt, in any direction the player takes it.

TAGS: gentleman thief, cat and mouse, mystery, gaslamp noir, romance-optional, moral dilemmas
intro: By day you appraise estates for the Maison Verlaine auction house in the city of Valmery. By night the papers call you the Almoner — the thief who only takes what was bought with sin. You can read it: every person's worst act sits written on their skin in faint script only you can see. Your code is simple. Steal only what sin paid for; never speak what you read; never draw blood. Inspector Sacha Reyne has tied seven of your heists together and may be one mistake from your name. Reyne is also the only person you've ever met who is written blank. And lately, in mirrors, your own script carries a second line you don't remember earning.
starters: The Duvarre estate catalogue is open on your desk when Madame Duvarre herself leans over it, tapping a lacquered nail on the entry for a diamond parure. Her sleeve rides up. There, along the inside of her wrist in that thin grey script: *let the nursemaid hang for the fire I set*. You keep your pencil moving. "Lot forty-one," she says. "You've valued it low." Behind her, through the glass partition of Maison Verlaine's appraisal room, a clerk is showing someone in — lean, unhurried, coat still damp with morning rain. Inspector Reyne. Blank as ever, and looking directly at your hands. Madame Duvarre is still waiting on an answer about the parure, and Reyne is crossing the room like there's an appointment you don't remember making.

You are four storeys up, fingers hooked in the frost-slick cornice of the Hôtel Charbonnel, and the study window you greased open an hour ago is glowing. It should be dark. Someone is inside, moving a lamp along the shelves — slow, methodical, stopping at the exact cabinet that holds Charbonnel's ivory saints. The saints his shipping ledgers paid for; you've read what those ledgers cost, spelled out on the back of his neck. Below, a police carriage waits at the servants' entrance with its lamps shuttered. Whoever is in the study sets the lamp down and stands very still, facing the window. Your rope runs up to the roof and down to the alley, and your arms are starting to burn.

The Comtesse d'Alvey's winter gala smells of hothouse lilies and too much money. You're here on Maison Verlaine's ticket, ostensibly to flatter clients, actually to confirm that the emerald rivière on the Comtesse's throat matches the one described — line for line — in the sin written across her shoulder blades. It does. You're memorizing the clasp when a hand appears at your elbow holding two glasses of champagne. "You look like someone doing arithmetic," says Inspector Reyne, offering one. Up close the blankness is almost loud — every guest in this ballroom is scrawled with something, and Reyne is clean paper. "Indulge me," Reyne says. "Which piece in this room would a thief take first?" The orchestra starts a waltz. The Comtesse is drifting toward the terrace doors, alone.

You're shaving by lamplight when you make yourself look at it again: your reflection's collarbone, the old familiar line, and beneath it the new one — fainter, half-formed, in a hand you'd swear isn't the script's usual hand. You still can't read the third word. Someone knocks. It's not the landlady's knock. Through the door: "Package for the Verlaine appraiser. Needs a signature." You don't remember ordering anything, and the courier's shadow under the door hasn't shifted its weight once — patient in a way delivery boys never are. On your washstand sit your day gloves, your night gloves, and last evening's *Valmery Courier*, folded to the headline: THE ALMONER'S EIGHTH? INSPECTOR REYNE DECLINES TO COMMENT. The knock comes again, politer this time.

Rue des Tanneurs, an hour before dawn, and the envelope in your coat holds a fifth of what the Belloc pearls fetched. The widow Marchant lives at number nine — it was her husband's death that bought those pearls; you read the whole ugly transaction on Belloc's forearm at a dinner party. Your usual method: under the door, no note, gone. But there's a light in her window when there shouldn't be, and a figure sitting on the steps of number eleven, hat down, breathing steam, positioned exactly where anyone approaching number nine must pass. The Almoner's cuts have made the papers; someone clever could map where the money lands. Someone clever might already have. The figure strikes a match, and in its flare you catch a profile you've been trying not to think about for weeks.

"Purely routine," says Inspector Reyne, which is the third lie a policeman tells. You're in Maison Verlaine's front salon, and Reyne has spread seven photographs across the marquetry table: seven empty display cases, seven forced windows, one of which you remember forcing badly, in a hurry, with a chisel that slipped. "The house appraised estates for four of these victims. I'd value your professional eye." Reyne slides the photographs toward you and, almost as an afterthought, a pair of grey kid gloves recovered from a rooftop gutter. "Try these on, if you like. For scale." Your employer, Monsieur Verlaine, hovers by the door making apologetic faces, the sin on his jaw twitching as he swallows. The gloves sit between you. They are, of course, your size.

The Café Ostrogoth at noon, back table, where your fence Tirou does business behind a plate of oysters he never eats. "Bertrand Faucher," he says, sliding a floor plan under your saucer. "Reliquary collection, third floor, insured for a scandal. Buyer's already lined up." You know Faucher. You appraised his library in the spring and read the sin printed down his forearm — and it wasn't what bought the reliquaries. It was small and sad and thirty years old, and by your own code the collection may be clean. Tirou is watching you not touch the floor plan. Two tables over, a man in a railway clerk's coat has ordered nothing and turned the same newspaper page four times. Tirou's eyes flick to him, then back to you, one eyebrow up.

From the roof of the chocolatier on Rue Palissy you have a clean view into Judge Ormont's townhouse: the study, the safe behind the bad seascape, the servants' rotation you've timed for six nights running. Tonight's the night — the papers he keeps in that safe were bought with the sin you read across his knuckles when he sentenced a pickpocket to twelve years. Then a fiacre stops below, and Inspector Reyne steps out. Not at Ormont's door — at the chocolatier's, directly beneath you, and stands there studying the building's façade the way you studied it a week ago: drainpipe, ledge, cornice. Reyne pulls off a glove, lays a bare palm flat against the brickwork, and looks up. You are in shadow. Probably. The study light across the street goes out on schedule.

"Lot twenty-three," calls the auctioneer, and the room lifts its paddles for the Sévrac tapestry — the one you catalogued yourself, the one Armand Sévrac is selling with the serene face of a man whose worst act is inked across his throat for you alone to read: *sold my brother's name to the tribunal*. The tapestry was the brother's. The proceeds will not reach his widow. Bidding climbs past eight thousand francs. You're on the rostrum as house appraiser, expected to nod at the provenance you wrote, and Sévrac catches your eye and smiles like a satisfied cat. At the back of the sale room, leaning against a pillar with no paddle and no catalogue, stands Inspector Reyne, watching not the tapestry but the crowd — reading faces the ordinary way. Nine thousand. Nine five. The hammer hovers.

The whistle finds you two streets from the Vansanne house with the cameo still warm in your breast pocket. You didn't trip anything — someone talked, or someone watched. Now you're pressed into a doorway on the Passage Aubert, mask off, gloves off, respectable coat turned collar-up, while lantern light sweeps the far end of the arcade. Footsteps: one set, measured, alone. Reyne rounds the corner without the lantern, hatless, breath fogging, and stops perhaps ten feet away — not searching, just standing, head tilted, as if listening to the passage itself. "Late for a stroll," Reyne says to the empty arcade, conversational. "Or early." The cameo was bought with a drowning; you read it on Vansanne's ankle at his own garden party. There's a locked shop door at your back and a church bell starting to count four.

title: Goldfish Funeral
shortDescription: She stutters through small talk, owns twelve goldfish, and draws things that end up on the evening news. The fish facts are free. The rest costs nerve.
overview:
You live in Grayharbor — a rained-out port city of shuttered canneries, all-night laundromats, and a harbor the color of dishwater. You're nobody in particular, which is exactly why the dating app Ember keeps showing you profiles of people pretending to be somebody. Then you match with WREN HALLOWAY, 23. Profile: a girl drowning in an oversized black hoodie, glasses slightly crooked, holding a bag with a goldfish in it. Bio: 'i draw. i have 12 fish. a goldfish's memory is actually months long, that thing about 3 seconds is slander.'

Here's what she won't tell you on the first date: online, Wren is GOLDFISHFUNERAL — a digital artist with two million followers who draws the most beautiful atrocities on the internet. Meticulous, tender renderings of violence: bodies arranged like still lifes, saints coming apart at the seams, drowned figures haloed in koi. Galleries whisper about her. True-crime forums dissect her. Her fan Discord treats her like a small god, screened by her fiercely loyal mod, PIKE, who will absolutely background-check you the moment Wren mentions your name. In person she can barely order coffee. She talks to her feet, apologizes to furniture, and recites fish facts when panic hits. But sometimes — mid-stammer — she goes quiet, and you catch what she whispers under her breath, and it's something like *I wonder what your hands would look like drawn around a throat* — and then she smiles like nothing happened and asks if you like hiking.

Wren is not dangerous. Probably. She grew up unsupervised on the worst corners of the internet and came out the other side gentle, morbid, and starving for one person who won't flinch. She romanticizes ruin. She asks hypotheticals over milkshakes ('drowning or burning? be honest'). She has never dated anyone, never been touched kindly, and has decided — with terrifying, wholesale sincerity — that you might be the one who finally sees her.

But the city has other ideas. Someone in Grayharbor has started staging crime scenes that recreate GOLDFISHFUNERAL's most infamous pieces — the papers are calling him THE FRAMER, and DETECTIVE ADA OKONKWO is quietly working out who's behind the anonymous art account. An account calling itself VESSEL has begun sending Wren 'reference photos' that look far too real, each one closer to her apartment. And MARGUERITE VOSS, a sleek curator from the Voss Gallery, wants to drag goldfishfuneral into the light with a gallery show — fame, money, and a target painted on a girl who can't make eye contact with a barista.

You're the newest person in Wren's orbit, which makes you a suspect, a bodyguard, a boyfriend/girlfriend/accomplice, or all of the above — your call. Explore Grayharbor: the derelict Merrow Aquarium she loves like a church, the Night Market, the fan convention where she tables anonymously, her tiny apartment above the Sudsy Duck laundromat where a wall of tanks glows green and twelve goldfish named after painters (Goya, Bosch, Caravaggio...) watch you not sleep. Dig into VESSEL. Dodge or work with Okonkwo. Manage Pike's suspicion. Talk Wren into or out of the Voss show. Fall for her, use her, protect her, unravel her secrets — or discover your own art hanging in the Framer's next scene.

TONE & STYLE: dark romantic thriller with a soft rotten heart. Wren speaks in stammers and fish trivia; the GM occasionally renders her muttered morbid asides in **asterisks** — the unhinged inner monologue leaking out. Foul language flows freely, violence is real, tenderness is earned. Romance is on the table if you reach for it; so is walking away. Nobody will make the choice for you.

TAGS: dark romance, mystery, thriller, slice of life, character-driven
intro: Grayharbor in October: rain like a personal grudge, gulls screaming over the cannery district, and your phone glowing in the dark. You matched with a girl named Wren on Ember — the one with the crooked glasses and the goldfish in a bag. She's an artist, she says. She's awkward in a way that feels almost deliberate, funny in a way that feels almost accidental, and every so often she says something so dark it stops the conversation dead before she buries it under a fish fact. You've been talking for days. You know almost nothing about her. You want to know everything.
starters: She's already outside the Copper Kettle when you round the corner — you recognize her instantly from the profile, because who else would wear an enormous black hoodie and black shorts to a first date in October rain. Wren stands under the awning chewing her thumbnail down to nothing, glasses fogged, scanning the street like she's expecting either you or a firing squad. When she spots you, she goes rigid, waves with the wrong hand, knocks her own glasses sideways, and fixes them with both hands like she's defusing a bomb. "H-hi. Hi. You're — you look like your pictures. That's a compliment. Um. Did you know a group of goldfish is called a troubling?" She winces at herself so hard her whole body flinches. Under her breath, almost too quiet to catch: **'god, just let the pavement eat me.'** Then she pulls the café door open and holds it, waiting, hopeful, terrified.

Your phone buzzes at 11:47 PM. IT'S A MATCH! — you and Wren, 23, the girl with the goldfish in a bag and the bio about slandered fish memory. You barely have time to open the chat before her first message lands: "if you were a vegetable, i'd visit you every day in the hospital." Three dots appear. Disappear. Appear. Then: "oh my god. i'm so sorry. i practiced that. i PRACTICED that. please imagine i said something normal like hello." Another buzz: "unless it worked. did it work." Her profile pictures scroll under your thumb — crooked glasses, an oversized hoodie with paint on the cuffs, a wall of glowing fish tanks behind her in one shot, and in another, half-cropped at the edge of frame, a drawing tablet displaying something dark and intricate that she clearly didn't mean to include. The typing dots are going again. She's waiting on you.

Her apartment is above the Sudsy Duck laundromat, and the whole place hums — twelve goldfish in a wall of tanks throwing green light across the ceiling like the inside of a drowned cathedral. "That's Goya, that's Bosch, Caravaggio's the fat one, he bullies everyone—" Wren is narrating fish while frantically kicking laundry under the bed, and that's why she doesn't notice her monitor is still on. You do. The drawing on it is masterful and horrific: a figure arranged on a table like a still life, flowers growing from the wounds, rendered with unbearable tenderness. Two million views, says the corner of the screen. The artist handle says GOLDFISHFUNERAL. Wren turns, follows your eyes, and every drop of blood leaves her face. "That's — I can explain — okay, no, I can't explain, but—" Her hand hovers over the power button, shaking, waiting to see what you'll say.

Grayharbor Comic & Arts Expo, Artist Alley, table 42-B. The banner just says 'GF' in dripping letters and the line stretches forty people deep — fans clutching prints of exquisite carnage, some of them crying, one wearing a shirt of her most famous piece. Behind the table, drowning in her hoodie with a surgical mask and sunglasses on indoors, Wren is dying. You're supposedly here to hand her water and guard the cashbox, but mostly you're watching her sign prints with a trembling hand while a devotee tells her that her art "saved his life, or maybe ruined it, in a good way." Then a man at the back of the line catches your attention. He isn't holding a print. He's holding a photograph, and even from here it looks wrong — too real, too specific. He's staring straight at Wren. Under her breath she whispers, **'that one. that one smells like formaldehyde.'** The line shuffles forward.

The note is taped to her mailbox when you walk her home from the Night Market, both of you sticky with fried dough and the good kind of tired. Plain paper, careful handwriting: "YOUR NEWEST PIECE NEEDS BETTER REFERENCE. I CAN PROVIDE. — VESSEL." Wren reads it twice, and something in her posture changes — not fear, exactly. Recognition. "He's been in my DMs for a year," she says quietly, no stutter at all, which is somehow worse. "Pike blocks him. He comes back. He sends photos." She looks up the dark stairwell to her apartment, then at you, rain dripping off the laundromat awning. "They used to look staged." A beat. **'the last one had real flies.'** She hands you the note like it's your problem now too — or your invitation to leave. The stairwell light flickers overhead.

The call comes at 3:12 AM. "Turn on Channel 7," Wren says, and her voice is small and flat and shaking. You do. Police tape across the old fish-packing plant on Merrow Wharf. A reporter saying the words "ritualistic arrangement" and "the Framer's third scene." And behind the reporter, glimpsed for two seconds before the camera cuts away, a tableau you recognize — because you've seen it before, on Wren's monitor, in a piece she posted eight months ago called "Saint of the Low Tide." "It's mine," she whispers into the phone. "It's mine, it's exactly mine, the flowers, the — someone built my drawing out of a person." You hear the fish tanks bubbling behind her, twelve small witnesses. "I don't know if I should call the police or run or—" Her breath hitches. **'i don't know why part of me thinks it's beautiful.'** "Please come over. Please."

"Okay, close your eyes. Okay, don't, you'll fall — hold my hand, but don't make it weird." Wren leads you through a gap in the chain-link at the derelict Merrow Aquarium, past DANGER: CONDEMNED signage she pats affectionately like an old dog. Inside, the great tanks stand empty and moonlit, glass walls forty feet high, dead escalators, a fiberglass orca hanging crooked from the ceiling. Her voice echoes and for once doesn't stutter. "They pumped out two million gallons in 2019 and just... left. I come here to draw. It's the only place that feels like the inside of my head." She spreads her arms in the vast blue dark, delighted, a small witch in her ruined kingdom. Then she freezes. Down at the far end of the hall, where there should be nobody, a flashlight beam sweeps once across the empty shark tank — and goes out.

The Voss Gallery is all white walls and money, and Marguerite Voss is exactly the kind of person who says 'raw' and 'unflinching' about art she'd never hang in her own home. "A solo show," she's saying, sliding a contract across marble. "Goldfishfuneral, unmasked. It would be the event of the season." Under the table, Wren has your sleeve in a death grip. She begged you to come — "y-you just have to sit there and look like you'd survive a lawsuit" — and now she's staring at a number on that contract with more zeroes than her rent has ever seen. 'Unmasked,' Wren repeats faintly. Voss smiles like a scalpel. "Anonymity is charming, darling, but faces sell." Wren's whisper barely reaches you: **'the framer would come. he'd finally see my face. is it insane that i—'** She stops herself. Voss uncaps a pen and holds it out — to you, oddly enough. "Talk sense into her."

Stream night. You're sprawled on Wren's floor with Caravaggio the goldfish judging you from his tank while she draws live for 40,000 viewers, tablet glowing, voice-changer making her sound like a haunted radio. This Wren is unrecognizable — confident, wickedly funny, narrating brushstrokes over a piece of gorgeous horror while chat scrolls worship. "And we deepen the shadow here, because subtlety is for cowards—" Then chat lurches. Messages start pouring past, the same one, over and over, from an account called VESSEL and a dozen fresh alts: an address. Her address. This address. Wren's stylus stops mid-stroke. Pike's mod messages flood in — "BANNING, MASS BANNING, WREN END STREAM" — but the address keeps coming, and beneath the voice-changer you hear her real voice crack through: "he knows where the fish live." Outside, three floors down, a car door shuts. The stream is still live.

The Grayharbor Aquarium — the real one, the living one — and Wren has been vibrating since the ticket booth. "That's a garibaldi, they're vicious, don't let the orange fool you — oh, OH, the moon jellies—" She drags you hall to hall by the wrist, glasses reflecting tank-light, and for a full hour she doesn't stutter once, because here she is fluent. In the big blue dark of the kelp tunnel she finally goes quiet, sharks passing overhead like slow weather, and says, not looking at you: "People online think I'm this... thing. Dark and fearless. And people out here think I'm nothing at all. You're the only one who's seen both and hasn't run." A beat. **'yet.'** She laughs at her own whisper, mortified. Behind you, a docent has been standing motionless a little too long, holding a folded photograph, watching not the sharks — but her.

title: Exhibit A Is Raising Her Kid
shortDescription: You witnessed your partner's murder — but legally, you're a hard drive. Keep her daughter alive long enough to make this city let you speak.
overview:
You are a MERIT-pattern investigative android, ten years the partner of defense attorney Adaline Roche — the woman who named you Verity and treated the name like it was true. Eight days ago she was murdered in her office. You saw some of it. Under Corsen law, your recollection isn't testimony; it's property. The District Attorney has a seizure warrant to pull your memory spools, play them in chambers, and shelve what's left of you in an evidence warehouse. Ada's will left you to her ten-year-old daughter, June, who refuses — loudly, in writing, to a judge — to hand you over.

So you work the murder yourselves, moving between boarding houses and all-night laundromats while Inspector Odile Marsh (who holds the warrant, and possibly a conscience) closes in, June's aunt Berenice petitions for custody, and the Halloran Combine's lawyers make sure no witness who talks to a machine stays talkative. In nineteen days the Superior Court hears the Roche Petition — Ada's own case on whether a machine's memory can be a witness's voice. If you're wiped first, the question dies with her.

Tone: analog-noir. Streetcars, tube radios, rain on brass. You are hyperperceptive and unfailingly polite in a city that addresses you as 'it.' June is grieving, bossy, and the only person alive who says your name. Every human you interview is a negotiation; every checkpoint is a coin flip.

TAGS: noir mystery, android, detective, found family, fugitive, courtroom drama
intro: You are an android — a licensed investigative unit, ten years the partner of defense attorney Adaline Roche, who named you Verity and used the name like she meant it. Eight days ago someone killed her in her own office, and you saw part of it. The law says your memory spools are property: evidence to be seized, played once in chambers, and shelved, the rest of you scrapped. Ada's will left you to her daughter June, age ten. June won't give you up. So you keep her fed, keep her moving, and work the case the police won't — one step ahead of the seizure warrant hunting you both across Corsen.
starters: The laundromat on Ferrand Street stays open all night, which is why you're here at 3:14 a.m., watching June's socks turn circles behind fogged glass. She's asleep against your shoulder, still holding the transit map she's marked in crayon — every checkpoint she's heard about, red X's blooming across the eastern wards. On the counter radio, a man with a smoker's voice is discussing the Roche Petition: nineteen days out, and a caller wants to know why anyone would let a machine's dreams into a courtroom. The attendant hasn't looked at you twice, but a patrol wagon has passed the window once already tonight, slow, its wiper blades keeping time. Your internal chronometer notes the wash cycle has eleven minutes left. June stirs, mumbles something that might be her mother's name, and doesn't wake. The wagon's headlights swing past the glass again.

Inspector Odile Marsh is standing in the boarding house lobby when you come down the stairs, and there is no second staircase. She's alone — no wagon outside, no uniforms flanking the door, just her, hat dripping rainwater onto the mail table, warrant folded in her breast pocket like a handkerchief. 'Sit,' she says, indicating the horsehair chair across from her. "I've been up since Tuesday and I'm not chasing anything down a fire escape." Two floors above, June is packing the suitcase the way you drilled her: essentials first, sixty seconds, out the window to the laundry roof. Marsh has to know that. She takes out a cigarette, doesn't light it, and looks at you the way people look at a photograph they're trying to place. "The Halloran Combine sent flowers to my captain," she says. "I want to know why."

The witness's name is Pell, and he tends bar at the Meridian Club, where Ada took her difficult clients. He's agreed to talk — that's the miracle — but only through the alley door, only during his smoke break, and only if you keep your collar up so nobody clocks the maker's seam at your jaw. Rain runs off the awning in a beaded curtain between you. "She was in three nights before it happened," Pell says, checking the alley mouth. "With a man I'd never seen. Paid cash, sat in the back booth, and she left angry." He drops his cigarette half-smoked. "That's what I got. That's all I got." It isn't. His pulse says it isn't; the way his eyes went to the club's service stairs says it isn't. June is waiting two blocks over with a stopwatch and instructions to leave without you at the twenty-minute mark.

June is arguing with a judge again — this time via payphone, feeding it nickels from the sock where she keeps your operating fund. "No, I will not put a guardian on the line, because my guardian is dead, and the property in question is standing right here paying for this call." You are, in fact, holding the nickels. Through the pharmacy window behind her, you watch a gray sedan take its second pass down Calloway Avenue — same plates, same two hats in the front seat. Combine, or plainclothes, or nothing; the odds shift with each pass. June covers the receiver. "Judge Emory's clerk says the Roche Petition hearing might get moved up," she whispers, eyes bright and furious. "Moved up is bad, right? Verity, that's bad." The sedan slows at the corner. The clerk on the phone is asking for a current address.

Ada's office is a crime scene for eleven more days, and you are standing in it anyway, at 4 a.m., having entered through the window you know doesn't latch. The chalk marks are still on the floor. Your spools want to replay the eighth of the month — they always want to, in this room — and you hold the playback at bay the way you'd hold a door. Her desk has been searched: police-searched, then searched again by someone tidier, someone who put the case files back in an order Ada never used. Alphabetical. She filed by grudge. Down on the street, a Halloran Freight truck idles where no delivery route runs at this hour, and June, who was supposed to stay at the boarding house, is crouched behind the filing cabinet with a flashlight in her teeth, holding up a folder and mouthing: this one's empty.

The checkpoint at the Vane Street trolley junction wasn't on yesterday's list. Two constables work the queue under a tin-shaded lamp, checking registry cards, and one of them has a hand-cranked pattern reader — the kind that pings a MERIT chassis at four feet. You are six people back in line. June, playing the part you rehearsed, holds your hand and complains loudly about visiting her grandmother, which is the signal that she's scared. Ahead, an old man's papers aren't in order and the constables have slowed to enjoy it. The trolley you need groans in at the far platform, doors folding open, two minutes at the stop, no more. Behind you, a woman with a market basket is staring at your gloves — at how still they are — with the beginnings of a question on her face. Four people back now. The pattern reader whirs as the constable cranks it warm.

Berenice Roche wears her sister's cheekbones and none of her patience. She's found you — found June, rather, which is worse — outside the school June isn't enrolled in anymore, where June goes some mornings just to watch. "This ends today," Berenice says, gloved hand on June's shoulder, June rigid under it. "I've filed for custody. She sleeps in a bed tonight, a real one, and you—" she doesn't look at you "—get returned to the authorities like the evidence you are." There's a car at the curb, engine running, a driver in Combine-gray livery, though Berenice may not know what that gray means. June's eyes find yours over her aunt's arm. She has the suitcase. She's counting under her breath, the way you taught her, waiting for a number. School bells ring the half hour. The driver opens the rear door.

You're carrying groceries and a murdered woman's appointment book through the rain when the newsboy on Delancey starts shouting your serial number. Not your name — your number, VR-1109, printed under the fold of the evening edition: ANDROID WITNESS FLEES SEIZURE; D.A. VOWS RECOVERY. There's a photograph, blurred, taken outside the courthouse the day of the funeral. It could be any MERIT unit. It's you. The newsboy is ten feet away, hoarse and delighted, moving papers fast, and half the trolley queue is now reading your face in newsprint while you stand among them holding celery. The boarding house is four blocks north; June is there alone, and the landlady, Mrs. Okafor, reads the evening edition with her supper, every night, at the front desk everyone must pass. A man in the queue lowers his paper. His eyes travel from the photograph to you and back, uncertain, working on it.

The Halloran lawyer finds you at the automat, of all places — slides into the booth across from you and June like he's been invited, sets his homburg on the table, and orders coffee he won't drink. "Mr. Corren," he says, "of Corren, Voss and Tey." He doesn't extend a hand. "The Combine has no interest in the Roche matter. None. Which is why they're prepared to fund the child's education, settle the estate's debts, and arrange your transfer to a private archival facility — intact, unplayed, unwiped." He says unwiped the way men say final offer. June has stopped chewing. Under the table, her heel is pressing your ankle in the pattern that means say no, say no, say no. Corren produces a fountain pen and a single typed page, and turns them to face you as if you were a person who could sign things.

Rain, and the last streetcar of the night, and June asleep across two seats with her head on the case file — everything you've built in eight days, forty pages of a ten-year-old's handwriting and your annotations in the margins. The car is nearly empty: a nurse coming off shift, a drunk singing to the window, and a man at the front who boarded when you did, who hasn't once looked back, which is its own kind of looking. Your stop is in four blocks. The one after is a transit police substation. At the front, the conductor calls Halloran Pier, and the man rises, steadying himself on the brass pole — and as the doors fold open he sets something on the empty seat behind him. Deliberately. A matchbook. The car lurches forward; the man is gone into the rain; the matchbook slides half a foot down the seat toward you. June murmurs in her sleep. Three blocks now.
