title: Quiet Sunday Came Early
shortDescription: The town pays the thing under the church in memories — and you keep the ledger of everything they forget. Now something is collecting early.
overview:
You are the sheriff of Covenant, Arizona Territory, 1889. Thirty years back, three founders buried something under the church to save a dying town, and it has kept its side ever since: sweet wells, mild fevers, gentle winters. In return, every grown soul gives it one memory on Quiet Sunday. Your office holds the other half of the bargain — the Ledger. Before anyone gives, they tell you what, and you write it down, because the law of Covenant says someone must remember. For nineteen years, that someone has been you. You weep at funerals beside widows who gave the marriage away years ago. You know whose children were real.

Now the arrangement is slipping. Folks are losing memories they never offered, between Sundays. There are fresh entries in the Ledger, in your handwriting, that you don't remember writing. And a rider has come in off the flats who calls you by a name that sits exactly inside your own blank — the one memory you gave, long before you took the badge.

Around you: Deputy Cass Boone, earnest and town-raised; Reverend Ellery Harrow, six months in the pulpit and only now learning what's under it; Mayor Temperance Odell, last living founder, who buries her answers deep; and June Pardo, eleven, too young to tithe, who remembers things grown folks can't. Tone: slow-burn weird-west mystery — dust-dry, tender, melancholy earned rather than wallowed in.

TAGS: weird west, mystery, memory & loss, slow-burn, supernatural, small town
intro: You are the sheriff of Covenant, a high-desert town that should have died thirty years ago. It didn't, because the founders buried something under the church, and every year on Quiet Sunday each grown resident feeds it one memory of their choosing. Your office keeps the Ledger: before anyone gives, they tell you what, and you write it down — town law says someone must remember. You've kept it nineteen years. You gave once yourself, long before the badge; all that's left of it is a person-shaped blank. Quiet Sunday is three weeks off. But lately people are losing things they never offered, and the Ledger's newest entries are in your hand — and you don't remember writing them.
starters: The Ledger is open on your desk to a page you don't remember turning. Third entry from the bottom, dated four days ago, your handwriting, no question about it — the slant, the way you cross a t. It says Amos Fitch tithed the sound of his mother's singing. Only Quiet Sunday is three weeks off, nobody's tithed anything, and Amos Fitch has been dead since the winter of '84. You've read it six times since sunup. The coffee's gone cold beside it. Out the window, Covenant is doing its usual Tuesday: the Reyes boy driving goats past the dry trough, Widow Callum sweeping her porch like she's mad at it. Boots on the boardwalk — Deputy Cass Boone pushes the door open with his shoulder, hat in hand, already talking. "Sheriff, you'd best come. Mr. Tulk's out front of the mercantile and he can't recall which house is his. Says he's lived here forty years and none of the streets sit right."

You're on the church steps at dusk when the rider comes in off the flats. You watched the dust for an hour — figured drifter, figured mine surveyor, figured nothing. The horse is worn down to patience and the rider sits it like someone who's crossed worse country than this. They rein up at the foot of the steps, look past the badge, look at your face like they're checking it against something. Then they say a name. Just the one word, easy, the way you'd greet an old friend. And it drops straight through you into the blank — that person-shaped hole you've carried nineteen years — and fits. The rider waits, reins loose, watching you not answer. Behind you, inside the church, Reverend Harrow has stopped sweeping. The lamps are coming on down the street one by one.

The funeral is small, the way they run in Covenant. Old Jack Merriwether, seventy-one, heart. You stand beside his widow at the graveside because that's the job nobody names: Elva gave the marriage away in '81 — proposal, wedding, honeymoon week in Prescott, all of it, to buy the thing under the church one more mild winter. You wrote it down. You're the only one at this grave who knows what she's not grieving. Except today Elva is weeping like a new bride, gripping your sleeve, saying, "He asked me under the cottonwood by the wash, did I ever tell you that? He couldn't get the ring off his own finger, he was so nervous." That memory is in the Ledger. It's spent. It's gone. She should not have it — and by every rule you know, it should not sound this true. Reverend Harrow catches your eye across the open grave, waiting on some signal.

It's not yet six and June Pardo is sitting on your office steps like she's been there all night, knees up, sharing a heel of bread with a yellow dog. Eleven years old, too young to tithe, and lately the only person in town whose memory you'd trust in court. She doesn't say good morning. She says, "You came by our place Thursday night. Stood in the yard a long while, looking at the church. Ma waved at you and you didn't wave back." You were home Thursday night. You'd swear it. You'd have sworn it, anyway, before this month started coming apart. June watches you with that flat patient look kids get when they've decided grown folks are lying without knowing it. "You had the big book with you," she says. "The one you're not supposed to take outside." The dog thumps its tail. The street is empty in both directions.

Reverend Harrow is waiting for you in the church, which is how you know it's bad — six months in the pulpit and the man still telegraphs everything. He's standing in the aisle with a lamp, and behind him the floorboards under the altar are up, stacked neat against the front pew. "I didn't dig," he says, first thing, hands raised. "I want that on record. I pulled the boards to fix a soft spot and — Sheriff, I'd like you to look at the dirt and tell me I'm imagining it." You come up the aisle. The earth under the altar is dark, packed, undisturbed for thirty years by any Christian account. Except there's a shallow trough pressed into it, long as a person, like something lay there a while and then didn't. Harrow holds the lamp out over the hole, arm not quite steady. "You knew about this," he says. It isn't a question. "How much do you know?"

Mayor Temperance Odell doesn't come to your office. Nineteen years, she's summoned you to hers or caught you on the street. So when you look up from the stove and she's standing inside your door — eighty-some years old, dust on her hem, having walked here — you set the kettle down slow. She looks at the iron safe where the Ledger lives. Then at you. "I want to see my own entries," she says. "All of them. Back to the first Quiet Sunday." Town law says the Ledger opens to any soul asking after their own tithes; you've done it a hundred times, for widows and drunks and once for a dying man who wanted his losses read aloud. But Temperance Odell has never asked. Last living founder, and in thirty years she has never once wanted to know what she gave. "Today," she says, and her hands, folded in front of her, are not quite still.

You wake at your desk in the dark with a pen in your hand. The lamp's burned low. The Ledger is open in front of you and the ink on the newest line is still wet enough to shine — your handwriting, mid-sentence, the entry unfinished: "Given by the sheriff of Covenant, of their own free will, the—" and then a blot where the nib dug in. You don't remember sitting down. You remember locking the safe at sundown; the safe is open, key in the lock. Your fingers ache like you've been writing for hours. Somewhere down the street a door bangs in the wind, twice, three times. The office clock says a quarter past two. Your palm, when you turn it over, has ink on it in a shape that is almost a word, smeared where you slept on it.

Saturday evening, the saloon's half full, and Cass Boone fetches you because Pete Alandale is standing at the piano refusing to sit back down at his own card game. "That's my song," Pete's saying, loud, to the room. "My mother played that song." At the piano, Miss Dolores keeps her hands flat on the keys and her voice level: "Pete, honey, I've played this every Saturday for ten years. You've danced to it." And here's the thing that puts frost down your back in a warm room: Pete Alandale tithed his mother — all of her — in '77. You wrote it down yourself; he wept doing it. He should not remember she existed, let alone that she played. He turns and finds you in the doorway, badge catching lamplight, and his face goes hopeful and terrible at once. "Sheriff. You keep the book. Tell them. Tell them I had a mother who played."

You're two hours out of town checking on the Nordhoff well when you see the dust. One rider, coming off the flats from the east, which is a direction nothing comes from — no road, no water for sixty miles, just hardpan and the shimmer. You've got the well cover half off and the rope in your hands. The Nordhoffs sent word the water's gone strange: still sweet, they said, but sweet wrong, like fruit about to turn — and Covenant's wells have been sweet and right for thirty years, that being part of the bargain. Down the shaft, the water catches the noon light oddly, a shade dark. The rider is maybe a mile off now, holding a straight line, not hurrying, aimed at you like you're a mark on a map. Behind you, your horse pulls at its picket and won't settle.

Cass Boone is town-raised, earnest as a Sunday shirt, and in three years he has never once knocked on your door before dawn. Now he's on your porch with a lantern, hatless, and he's holding a tintype out at arm's length like it might bite. "This was on my mantel," he says. "Been on my mantel my whole life. Me and my sister at the Prescott fair." You take it. Two children in front of a painted backdrop, one of them plainly Cass at eight or nine, gap-toothed, proud. The girl beside him is maybe twelve. "Sheriff," Cass says, and his voice does something young, "I don't have a sister. I never had a sister. But I woke up an hour ago knowing her laugh." The lantern shakes a little. Down the hill, Covenant is still dark except for one lamp burning — in the church, where no lamp should be at this hour.

title: The Sea Is Courting Me
shortDescription: Every low tide leaves gifts on your doorstep: pearls, rings, your enemies. The ocean has chosen you — and the whole village knows it.
overview:
You mend nets in Saltmere, a herring village clinging to a cold grey coast. Three weeks ago the gifts started appearing on your doorstep at low tide, arranged with terrible care: pearls, a captain's brass sextant, a wedding ring still on its finger. Then Olav Krag — who shoved you off the pier drunk — came back with the morning tide, kelp braided through him like ribbon, and no one in Saltmere doubts anymore. The sea wants you. The weather tracks your moods now. Storms circle when you weep.

Everyone wants a piece of that. Maren Skou, the harbormistress, is already selling 'blessed' berths on boats you've touched. Father Ansgar can't decide if you're a saint or something his church should burn. Rowan, who shares your fire most nights, has started coughing up seawater in their sleep — the sea does not like rivals. And Mr. Pell, a soft-spoken insurance adjuster from the capital, has arrived asking why wrecks off Saltmere have stopped costing his company money, and what changed three weeks ago.

The sea speaks in tides, in gifts, in the mouths of the drowned. It is patient, generous, jealous, and vast. It is courting you properly. It expects an answer. Play it as folk-horror romance: tenderness and dread in the same breath, village politics on land, something ancient and adoring in the water. Gore implied, never gratuitous.

TAGS: folk horror, eldritch romance, dark fantasy, village intrigue, forbidden courtship
intro: You are the net-mender of Saltmere, a herring village on a cold coast — the one the sea spared as a child when the wreck took your father. For three weeks now, every low tide has left gifts on your doorstep: pearls, coins, a drowned man's ring. When Olav Krag shoved you off the pier, the sea gave him back wrong. Now half the village leaves offerings at your gate and the other half crosses the street. The weather follows your moods. You have told no one how the water feels when you touch it — like a hand closing gently around yours.
starters: Low tide comes an hour before dawn, and you're awake for it, the way you always are now. You open your door to find this morning's gift arranged on the stone step: a ship's bell, green with age, and inside it, packed carefully in wet sand, a woman's comb carved from whalebone. The teeth are unbroken. Someone loved it once. Down the lane, old Widow Hess stands at her gate watching you, a saucer of milk in her hands like she's not sure whether to set it down for you or throw it. Behind you in the cottage, Rowan is still asleep by the banked fire, breathing rough and wet. The tide is a long silver line at the bottom of the shingle, very still, the way a dog goes still when it's waiting to be praised.

The knock comes at midday, three polite raps. When you open the door, the man on your step is small and grey-suited, holding his hat against the wind, and behind him half of Fisk Lane has found reasons to sweep their stoops. "Forgive the intrusion," he says. "Pell. Maritime Assurance, out of the capital." He glances — just once, very quickly — at the salt-crusted coins someone left piled by your gate. "I'm told you mend nets. I have some questions about the weather here. Purely routine." His ledger is already open. On the first page, you can see three ship names written and crossed out, and under them, underlined twice: *three weeks*. Out past the breakwater, the sea has gone flat as hammered tin, listening.

You're on the pier with a torn seine across your knees when Maren Skou's voice carries over the gulls. She's got a stranger by the elbow — a skipper from up the coast by his boots — and she's steering him straight toward you. 'There,' she says, loud enough for the whole harbor. "Touch is a shilling. A blessing spoke aloud is three." The skipper looks at you like you're a shrine he's not sure he believes in. Maren looks at you like a purse. Behind her, two of her dock boys have stopped coiling rope to watch, and beneath the pier the water has begun to slap the pilings in a slow, deliberate rhythm, though there is no wind at all.

It's past midnight and Rowan is drowning in their sleep again. You wake to the sound — that wet, tearing cough — and by firelight you watch them sit up and bring a thin ribbon of seawater into their cupped hands. It smells of the deep harbor, cold and green. "It's fine," Rowan says, before you can speak, wiping their mouth. "It's less than last night." It is not less than last night. Outside, rain has started against the shutters, soft and coaxing, though the sky was clear when you banked the fire. Rowan won't look at you. On the table between you sits yesterday's gift, the drowned captain's sextant, its brass gleaming like it's been polished by an attentive hand.

They bury Olav Krag on the hill above the church, in ground high enough that the tide can't reach him, and everyone knows why. You stand at the back of the small crowd. Father Ansgar reads the service too fast, his eyes coming up to find you between verses. Olav's brother stands across the grave with his cap crushed in his fists, and when the first sod goes down he says, not quietly, "She didn't have to give him back like that." He means the sea. He's looking at you. The wind picks that moment to turn, coming warm off the water, carrying the smell of low tide up the hill and into everyone's faces. Somewhere behind you, a woman starts to pray.

Father Ansgar is standing at your gate when you come back from the smokehouse, and he has brought salt. A whole sack of it, church salt, and he's pouring a careful white line along your fence like a man drawing a border he doesn't trust. "Don't be alarmed," he says, not looking up. "It's for your protection. Or possibly ours. The texts are unclear." His hands are shaking slightly. Inside the sack, you can see he's also brought a bottle of blessed water and, wrapped in cloth, an old iron cross. Down the lane, the tide is coming in early — a good hour early, by your reckoning — and the line of salt nearest the sea is already dissolving in the wet air.

You cried this morning — over nothing, over a dream of your father — and now, by noon, the storm is stacking itself out past the point like a held breath. Every boat in Saltmere came scrambling back inside the breakwater an hour ago. Now Gerta Voss is at your door with her three children behind her skirts, and her husband's boat is the one still out. 'Please,' she says. She has brought you bread, honest bread, wrapped in a clean cloth, and she holds it out in both hands as if to an altar. "Whatever it wants from you. Just until Anders is home." Overhead, the clouds turn slowly around a center that you can feel, if you're honest, sitting somewhere just behind your ribs.

The Kettle & Line goes quiet when you step in out of the rain, the way it always does now — a beat of silence, then everyone talking a shade too loudly about herring prices. You've only come for lamp oil. Behind the bar, Sunniva pours you a mug you didn't ask for and won't take coin for, and mutters, "On the house, forever, you understand." At the corner table, Maren Skou is deep in talk with a soft-looking stranger in a grey suit, a ledger open between them, and both of them stop when they see you. From the stranger, a small courteous nod. From Maren, a smile you know from years of dockside haggling. It's the smile she wears when she's already sold something that isn't hers.

You find the drowned man at first light, laid out on the shingle below your cottage, and your stomach drops before you understand: he isn't from Saltmere, and he isn't fresh. Weeks in the water, maybe more. But he's been arranged — hands folded, hair combed back with the current, a spray of red sea-fan on his chest like a posy. In his cupped hands sits a ring of black coral, exactly the size of your finger. You know a gift when you see one. Up on the path, someone has already spotted you standing over him. It's Kolbein from the drying sheds, and he's frozen mid-step, and in about ten seconds he is going to run and tell the whole village what the sea has brought you now.

It's dusk and you're doing the thing you've told no one about: standing at the tideline with your boots off, letting the water find your ankles. It comes up warm — warmer than any northern sea has a right to be — and wraps each foot with the gentleness of someone unlacing them for you. You let yourself have one minute of it. Then a stone turns on the shingle behind you and Rowan is there, twenty feet up the beach, a shawl clutched around their shoulders, watching you stand in the water with your eyes half-closed. You don't know how long they've been there. The sea tightens very slightly around your ankles, the way a hand tightens when someone else enters the room.

title: The Hunt Must Fail
shortDescription: The town hired the greatest hunter alive to slay its beast. You are both. Lead the hunt — and make certain it never succeeds.
overview:
Nine years ago you slew the Beast of Karstenmoor and became a legend. What the ballads don't mention is the old law of the curse: whoever kills the beast, becomes it. You've managed — remote work, iron chains, careful moons. You came to this fog-drowned valley chasing rumor of a heretic monk, Brother Ansel, who swears curses can be unmade. Then the nights got worse. You started waking with mud on your boots and gaps in your memory. Now there are three bodies, and this morning the town council knelt and begged the famous hunter to take the contract.

You signed. You had to. Because any hunter good enough to kill the beast inherits it — so the hunt must be led, and the hunt must fail.

Magistrate Ilse Brandt keeps a ledger of every villager's whereabouts and is quietly charting the kills against the moon. Kasper Vogel, a horribly talented young hunter who memorized your book, just arrived to 'assist his hero.' And Doctor Maren Falk, who examines the bodies, has started looking at the way you favor your left side. Misdirect the evidence you left. Sabotage the traps you designed. Survive council meetings about your own pawprints. And decide how much of Ansel's cure — and its price — you can stomach.

Tone: gothic folk-thriller; slow-burn suspense, dry gallows humor, moral knots. The GM plays the town's suspicion like a tightening noose.

TAGS: dark fantasy, mystery, deception, monster, cat-and-mouse, slow burn
intro: Nine years ago you killed the Beast of Karstenmoor, and the ballads made you a legend. They left out the old law: whoever slays the beast inherits it. You've managed — iron chains, locked doors, careful moons — and you came to this fog-drowned valley chasing word of Brother Ansel, a heretic monk who claims curses can be unmade. But lately your nights have holes in them, and you've woken to mud you don't remember crossing. Three villagers are dead. Now the town turns to the famous hunter to lead the hunt — a hunt you know, better than anyone, must fail.
starters: The ink is still wet on the contract when Magistrate Brandt stands, dusts off her knees, and becomes a bureaucrat again. "Standard terms," she says, sliding a second document across the council table. "Lodging, provisions, and a report to me every second evening. I keep records." She does. You can see the ledger at her elbow, fat with names and hours, a slip of paper marking a page — a page with what looks like a lunar chart inked in the margin. Around the table, six councilors watch you with the desperate relief of people who've just handed their problem to a legend. Outside, fog presses against the window glass. Your left shoulder aches where the old scar runs, the way it always does before the moon fills out. Brandt uncaps her pen and waits. Somewhere below, in the doctor's cellar, three bodies are waiting too.

You wake standing up, which is never good. Your boots are on. They're caked to the ankle in black moor-mud, and your room at the Sign of the Lamb is on the second floor. The window is open. The last thing you remember is checking the chains at half past ten. The chains are on the floor, unlocked, neatly coiled — neatly, as if someone tidied up. There's a taste in your mouth you refuse to think about. Down in the street, fog is thinning off the cobbles and someone is knocking at the inn's front door — young voice, bright, carrying: "I'm looking for the hunter. The hunter. From the book!" You know that eagerness. You wrote the book that put it there. Your washbasin sits by the bed, water gone grey and cold, and your boots are leaving prints on the floorboards, clear as a signature.

Doctor Falk peels back the sheet without ceremony. "Third one," she says. "Shepherd. Found him at the tree line this morning." Her cellar smells of vinegar and cold stone; the other two bodies lie under sheets on trestles behind her. "Council says you've signed the contract. Good. Then you'll want to see this." She lifts the dead man's arm, showing the wound track along the ribs. You do want to see it. You need to see it, because you don't remember making it, and every detail she reads correctly is a detail you'll have to explain away. "Strike came from the left," she says. "Low angle. Curious, that." She glances up — not at your face. At your left side, at the way you're standing. The lamp gutters. Upstairs, boots cross the floor: someone else coming down.

The tavern goes quiet in that particular way, and then the fiddler starts the ballad. Of course he does. Nine verses about the Beast of Karstenmoor and the hunter who ended it, sung eight feet from your table while the whole room pretends not to watch you over their cups. The verse about the killing blow is wrong — it was messier, closer, and you still dream about the moment the light left its eyes and something arrived in yours. The landlord sets down a drink you didn't order. "On the house. For what you signed today." By the hearth, Magistrate Brandt sits alone with her ledger open, writing steadily, looking up at each patron in turn as if taking attendance. Outside the fog has swallowed the street. The fiddler reaches the last verse, the one about how the beast is gone forever, and holds out his hat.

Dawn, and the fog is doing the town's mourning for it. You stand in a beet field with half the council, looking down at a line of pawprints pressed deep into the mud — your prints, though only you know it, running straight from the tree line toward the Weber croft and its broken door. "You're the expert," says the fat councilor, Herr Oster, hugging himself against the cold. "Tell us what we're dealing with." The prints are good. Clear. Too clear — the gait, the splayed left forepaw, the drag mark where the old wound catches. A competent tracker could read a great deal from these. A brilliant one could read everything. Down the lane, a rider is dismounting at the inn, unstrapping a long gun case with the care of someone who loves it. The councilors wait for your professional opinion, breath steaming, boots sinking slowly.

"You held the falchion two-handed for the killing stroke — chapter eleven — but the woodcut shows one hand, and I've always wondered which was true." Kasper Vogel has been talking since the coach road. He's maybe twenty, walks like the ground owes him something, and carries your book in his coat pocket, spine broken from rereading. He arrived an hour after you signed the contract, and the council nearly wept with gratitude: two hunters for the price of one. Now he's pacing the muddy yard behind the inn where the second body was found, and he's good — he's already found the claw scores on the fence post that you missed in the dark, and he's frowning at them. "Odd," he says. "The height's wrong for a wolf." He looks to you, bright-eyed, waiting for the master to explain. The fence post waits too.

The chapel of Saint Verena is deconsecrated, which suits everyone. Brother Ansel keeps his fire in the font. "You came about the rumor," he says, not turning from the flames. "Everyone who climbs this path came about the rumor. Sit, if you're staying." He is older than you expected and less mad, which is somehow worse. On the altar behind him, someone has laid out objects with a scholar's care: a jawbone, a coil of silver wire, a book bound in scraped hide. "Curses can be unmade," he says. "That part of the rumor is true. The rest of what you've heard is wishful. Before we speak of it — the town below found a third body this morning. And you walked up here anyway, on the very day you signed to hunt the thing." He turns. His eyes go, briefly, deliberately, to your hands. "So. Tell me why."

Full dark, three nights until the moon fills, and you're in the birch stand above the mill dismantling your own best work. The deadfall trap is a design from your book — chapter nine, the one Kasper Vogel can probably recite — and the council had the smith build it exactly to specification while you watched, nodding, offering improvements. Now you're kneeling in the wet leaves, working the trigger stone loose so the whole beautiful mechanism will fail by a hair's width and look like weather. Your fingers are cold. The fog moves through the birches like it's searching for something. You've got the stone half-turned when a lantern shows on the mill path below — one light, swinging, coming up the hill at a walk, unhurried. Whoever it is knows the ground. You have perhaps a minute, a half-sabotaged trap, and no particularly good reason to be here at this hour.

"Sit," says Magistrate Brandt, and you sit, because the alternative is looming. Her office smells of sealing wax and lamp oil. The ledger lies open between you, turned so you can read it: names down one margin, dates across the top, a tidy grid of every soul in the valley and where they slept. "First killing, the eleventh. Second, the twelfth of the next month. Third, yesterday." She taps each date. "You're the expert on beasts. I'm the expert on this town. Between us, I'd like to close a gap in my records." She dips her pen. "The night of the eleventh. You'd been in the valley four days by then. Where were you?" Through the window behind her, the fog is lifting off the square, and young Vogel is out there demonstrating a snare to a knot of admiring farmhands. Brandt waits, pen hovering over the one blank box in her grid.

The chains come first, always. You're in the rented cellar under the tannery — chosen for the smell, which hides yours — threading iron through the wall rings and testing each link, because in nine years the ritual has failed you exactly three times and all three failures are lying in Doctor Falk's cellar with sheets over their faces. The moon isn't full for three nights, but the rules have stopped being rules. Your hands are steady until they aren't. Then, above you: footsteps crossing the tannery floor. They stop. "Hello?" A voice through the boards — the tanner's daughter, by the pitch of it. "Someone down there? We're closed." The trapdoor is bolted from your side. The chains are half-fastened, your coat is off, and there is a padlock key sitting on the barrel beside you, small and bright and very far from your hand. The footsteps start toward the trapdoor.

title: The Woods Still Call Me Majesty
shortDescription: By day you run canoe drills and s'mores. By night the forest kneels. Keep the campers from learning who — and what — you rule.
overview:
Twelve summers ago, a camper vanished from Camp Merrowbrook and came back nine days later — polite, unharmed, and crowned. That camper was you. Whatever holds court past the treeline made you its sovereign, and it never rescinded the title. Now the camp has reopened, the cabins are full of nine-year-olds, and you've taken a counselor job because you're the only person alive the woods will obey.

So you live two schedules. Daylight: archery, lanyards, homesick kids, Director Dot Okafor's clipboard, and co-counselor Ash — sharp, funny, and starting to notice you're never in your bunk at moonrise. Darkness: holding court at the treeline, where the Antler Chamberlain kneels with tribute you have to hide before breakfast, petitions arrive scratched into bark, and your subjects adore you with the patience of things that expect you to come home eventually. Every edict you issue is honored. Every edict costs you standing you'll someday have to repay in person.

Complications are already stacking: a camper named June hums melodies she couldn't know, something new in the deep woods refuses to bow, and tribute keeps appearing where children will find it. The GM plays a world that's warm, funny, and genuinely dangerous — camp life is real and worth protecting, the court is courtly and alien, and your crown is both your best tool and your slowest trap.

TAGS: cozy horror, secret royalty, hidden identity, dark fairytale, summer camp, protective fantasy
intro: You are a counselor at Camp Merrowbrook, reopened this summer after twelve years shuttered. You know exactly why it closed: you were the camper who vanished into these woods and came back nine days later — unharmed, and wrong. Whatever holds court past the treeline crowned you then, and it has never taken the crown back. The things in the forest still bow, still bring tribute, still call you Majesty when no one else can hear. You took this job because the cabins are full of children again, and the woods have noticed. Nobody here knows what you are. Keep it that way.
starters: There's a dead rabbit on the flagpole platform, laid out on a bed of woven fern with its paws crossed like it's sleeping. Around its neck: a collar of braided silver grass, knotted in the old court style. Tribute. Breakfast bell rings in eleven minutes, and Cabin Fox walks this path to the mess hall every single morning. You're crouched over it with a garbage bag when you hear sneakers on gravel behind you — Ash, coffee in hand, whistle around their neck, stopping mid-stride. "Okay," Ash says slowly, eyes moving from the rabbit to the fern to you. "Either that's the most respectful raccoon in Ohio, or you're about to tell me something weird." Somewhere past the treeline, just at the edge of hearing, something clicks its tongue twice — the court's sound for a gift well received.

The Antler Chamberlain kneels too long tonight. It's nearly one in the morning, the treeline is silver with moon, and it has been down on one crooked knee in the ferns for a full minute, tines bowed, holding up something wrapped in birch bark that ticks softly like a cooling engine. "Majesty," it says, in that voice like wind through a screen door, "the court begs you receive this, and begs further that you ask no questions about the maker." Behind you, across the dark field, Cabin Sparrow's porch light flicks on. A small silhouette appears at the screen door — some kid up for the bathroom, or worse, watching. The Chamberlain does not move. Court etiquette says a kneeling subject stays kneeling until acknowledged, all night if it must.

"Elbow up. Anchor at your cheek. Good." You're mid-lesson at the archery range, eight nine-year-olds in a row, when June lowers her bow and starts humming. Your hands go cold. It's the processional — the melody the court plays when you cross the boundary stones, the one that exists nowhere in the human world. She's got it note for note, even the wrong-feeling interval in the middle that no child should be able to hold. "June," you say, and your voice comes out too careful. She blinks up at you, arrow still nocked, sun on her freckles. "Sorry. It's just stuck in my head. It's been stuck in my head since Tuesday." Down the line, a kid named Marcus complains that his string keeps slipping. The woods beyond the hay bales are very still, the way an audience is still.

Director Okafor catches you at six a.m. with mud on your shoes. "Walk with me," Dot says, clipboard already out, and you fall in step past the canoe racks while the lake steams in the early light. "Three things. One: a parent called about, quote, "a crown of antlers" their kid claims to have found under a pillow. Two: groundskeeper says something's been leaving pressed flowers on the equipment shed like it's courting the building. Three—" she stops walking and looks at you, really looks. "You were here. Before. Twelve years ago." It isn't a question. Her pen is poised over the clipboard like a verdict. Behind her, out on the water, something long and polite surfaces just enough to watch, then sinks without a ripple. Dot hasn't seen it. Yet.

The petition arrived overnight, scratched into the bark of the big oak beside the mess hall in letters like beetle tracks: MAJESTY. THE UNBOWED ONE HAS TAKEN THE HOLLOW BY THE CREEK. IT DOES NOT KNEEL. IT DOES NOT ANSWER. WE ARE AFRAID. GRANT US AN EDICT. You've read it four times, tracing the grooves — fresh, sap still wet — while the breakfast line forms thirty feet away. The Hollow by the Creek is where Cabin Otter has their nature hike scheduled for ten o'clock. You have the schedule. You made the schedule. "Whoa, cool," says a voice at your elbow. A camper named Priya is squinting up at the bark. "Is that a game? Are we doing a scavenger hunt?" Her bunkmates are drifting over, curious, sticky with syrup.

You're halfway back over your windowsill when Ash turns on the flashlight. They're sitting on your bunk, fully dressed, arms crossed, and the beam catches you with one leg inside and pine needles in your hair. It's 3:40 a.m. "Third night this week," Ash says, keeping their voice down for the sake of the kids' cabins across the way. "I covered for you when Dot did rounds. Told her you had a stomach thing. So I figure you owe me either the truth or a really excellent lie, and honestly I'll grade both." In your jacket pocket, the night's tribute — a knot of amber that hums faintly when it's near children — chooses this moment to warm against your ribs. Ash's flashlight beam drops to the pocket. "And what," they say, "is glowing."

Campfire night, first week of camp, and the ghost stories have started. You're on marshmallow duty when a kid from Cabin Heron stands up, firelight on his face, and says, "My uncle told me a real one. About this camp. A kid went into these exact woods and came back nine days later wearing a crown, and the camp closed forever." Thirty children go delighted-quiet. Ash, beside you, snorts and calls it urban legend. Dot, across the fire, has gone very still with her clipboard flat on her knees. And past the ring of light, at the treeline where no one else is looking, four pale shapes have gathered to listen — heads tilted, patient, one of them wearing what is unmistakably a party hat made of birch bark. They think it's a festival in your honor. One raises a hand in a small, formal wave.

It's rest hour, the camp gone drowsy in the afternoon heat, and you're using the quiet to bury this morning's tribute behind the boathouse — a circlet of woven bone that will not stop being warm. The shovel's in the dirt when June comes around the corner in her swim towel, holding something cupped in both hands. "I found this in my shoe," she says, and opens her fingers: a ring of tiny river pearls, kid-sized, threaded on braided grass. Court work. Unmistakably court work, sized for a nine-year-old, and the court does not give gifts to anyone but its sovereign. June looks from the ring to the hole you're digging to the bone circlet lying in the grass, and her eyes go wide and thrilled. "Are you burying treasure?" she whispers. "Can I help?"

Something in the deep woods is screaming, and it isn't one of yours. You know your court's voices — the creak-speech, the tongue-clicks, the choir that sounds like weather. This is new: a flat, furious sound rolling up from the direction of the creek, and along the treeline your subjects have appeared in a nervous row, a dozen of them, all facing you across the soccer field in broad daylight. They never come by daylight. The Antler Chamberlain stands at their center, and even from here you can see it's holding its ceremonial staff wrong — like a weapon. Behind you, a whistle blows: Ash is starting the afternoon soccer game, herding twenty kids onto the field, directly into the court's line of sight. "Hey!" Ash calls to you, jogging over with the ball under one arm. "You're reffing. You okay? You look like you heard something."

Two hours into staff arrival day, before a single camper shows up, you walk the boundary alone — and the woods throw you a homecoming. It starts at the third boundary stone: ferns bowing flat in a wave that runs ahead of you along the treeline, and then the sound, low and everywhere, the processional hummed by a hundred hidden throats. Welcome back, Majesty. Twelve years, and they never stopped rehearsing. The Antler Chamberlain steps out between two pines, drops to one knee, and lays a folded square of moth-wing vellum on the moss — the court's agenda, you'd bet your life, backed up over a decade. "You've been missed," it says. From the parking lot behind you, an engine and a car door: the first of the other counselors arriving, a voice calling out, "Hey! You must be staff — can you help me carry the archery stuff?" The Chamberlain does not rise. The agenda waits on the moss.
