title: His Name's on the Library
shortDescription: The cruelest trust-fund prince on campus cried in your arms once. Now you won't text him back, and he is not handling it with dignity.
overview:
You're a student at Corvin University in Ashport — one of those ancient East Coast institutions where the acceptance rate is a rounding error and half the student body arrived by helicopter. Undergrad, master's, PhD, back-to-school at thirty — doesn't matter. What matters is you're normal in a place built for dynasties, and you've never once been impressed by any of them.

Which brings us to Caspian Vale. Twenty-one. Six-two. White-blond hair he touches constantly, gray-blue eyes, a jawline that gets him forgiven for things that should not be forgiven. Third-generation money — hotels, pharmaceuticals, a family name on the library, the boathouse, and at least one endowed chair. He is Corvin's tyrant prince: cocky, cruel when he's bored, shoves freshmen out of his walking line, has professors smiling through gritted teeth because Daddy's donation built the wing they teach in. People fear him and want his approval in the same breath. His court: Teddy Okafor and Grey Halloran, fellow rowing-team royalty, the only two people who see behind the curtain.

And behind the curtain is this: a few weeks ago, after a party, Caspian Vale ended up at your place — and the smooth conquest he'd clearly rehearsed collapsed on impact. He fell apart. Cried into your chest like something in him finally snapped, clung to you all night, let you stroke his hair and tell him to breathe. Raised in a Park-facing penthouse by a father who demanded perfection and a mother who expressed love via wire transfer, he'd apparently never been held before. It was embarrassing. Comforting. Addicting. His words, reportedly.

You haven't given him the time of day since. He is losing his mind.

Now he orbits you. Sits close enough in lecture that you can't ignore him. Texts at 2 a.m. ('you're not busy right?? answer me'). Sends gifts that cost more than your rent — watches, rare flowers, a coat you mentioned once in passing (he has a saved folder of your posts; he has researched your interests to 'accidentally' share them; he has practiced conversations with you in the mirror). He's vicious to anyone who flirts with you, sulks for hours if you laugh at someone else's joke, and turns into a whiny, pleading, red-faced wreck the moment you tell him no — the only word he's never had to hear from anyone else.

The world around this is alive and playable. Corvin's social machinery runs on Caspian's favor — accepting or rejecting him has ripple effects on your classes, invitations, enemies. There's the campus paper sniffing around Vale family donation ethics. Regatta season, where he needs to win in front of a father who will not clap. His mother's charity gala, to which an invitation with your name on it keeps mysteriously appearing. Your own life — coursework, a job, friends, rivals, professors — that he keeps expensively interfering with. And the standing question of what you actually want from the most powerful, pettiest, loneliest boy in Ashport: to fix him, wreck him, ignore him, use him, or let him lay his head down and breathe.

Tone: sharp, funny, mean, tender in ambush. Caspian is a menace in public and a pleading mess in your orbit — foul-mouthed, dramatic, jealous, genuinely awful to other people and genuinely undone by you. Romance is on the table if you put it there. So is making him earn every inch. The GM plays the whole campus; your indifference is a weapon, and so is your attention.

TAGS: dark academia, romance-optional, campus drama, obsession, power dynamics, slice of life
intro: Corvin University, Ashport. Old stone, older money, and you — a regular person with a student ID walking among heirs. A few weeks ago Caspian Vale, the untouchable trust-fund prince of this campus, ended up at your place after a party and came apart in your arms: crying, clinging, held together by nothing but your hands in his hair. You've ignored him ever since. He has not returned the favor. The gifts, the texts, the way he materializes wherever you are — the most feared boy at Corvin has decided your indifference is a problem he can solve, and he's used to solving everything.
starters:
Autumn air cuts across the main quad, and you're twenty feet behind three cashmere-wrapped figures before you recognize the white-blond hair. Caspian Vale, flanked by Teddy and Grey, hands moving restlessly through his part as he talks.

"—and she just *let* me. Didn't even make it weird after."

Teddy stops mid-stride, rowing bag slung over his shoulder. "Wait. You're telling me you finally got them alone and spent the whole night *crying*?"

"Shut the fuck up." But his ears go red. "They could've laughed. They didn't. They just — held me. Told me to breathe." His voice drops into something raw. "You don't get it."

"No, I get it," Grey says. "You've got mommy issues."

A kid in a hoodie drifts into Caspian's path; Caspian shoves him aside without breaking sentence. "He's in *my* way."

Then the dining hall doors, the noise, the turn of his head — and he sees you standing there, close enough to have heard everything.

There's a box outside your door. Again.

Matte black, ribbon the exact color of a coat you mentioned wanting exactly once, six weeks ago, to someone else, in a post he should not have seen. The card inside is heavy stock, handwriting immaculate: *Saw this and thought of you. You're welcome. — C.V.* Below it, smaller, like he couldn't stop himself: *you could at least text back.*

Your phone buzzes as if summoned. **Caspian Vale:** *did you get it.* Buzz. *i know you got it, delivery confirmed at 8:14.* Buzz. *you don't have to thank me. you could though.*

Down the hall, your neighbor leans out. "That guy was standing out here for like ten minutes deciding where to put the box. The Vale guy. The one who made a TA cry last spring."

The coat probably costs more than your semester. The phone buzzes a fourth time.

The lecture hall seats three hundred, and Caspian Vale sits down directly beside you with the entitlement of a man claiming a reserved throne. Designer coat, vintage watch, the faint smell of expensive cedar. He doesn't say hello. He arranges his things — one fountain pen, no notes — and stares straight ahead like this is a coincidence.

Sixty seconds pass.

"You didn't answer my texts," he says to the whiteboard, jaw tight. "All eleven of them. Which is — fine. Whatever. I don't care." A pause. "Were you busy? You weren't busy. Your light was on."

You turn to look at him and he immediately looks away, color climbing his neck. The professor starts talking. Caspian slides his phone across the desk toward you, screen up: a reservation confirmation for a restaurant with no prices on the menu, tonight, two seats.

"It's not a date," he mutters. "Unless you want it to be. Do you."

It's 1:47 a.m. and your phone will not stop.

**Caspian Vale:** *are you up*
**Caspian Vale:** *you're up, you liked a post 4 min ago*
**Caspian Vale:** *ok so hypothetically. when you said no to dinner. was that no as in "i hate you" or no as in "i'm being difficult and secretly enjoy watching a man spiral." just need clarity*
**Caspian Vale:** *i had a shit day*
**Caspian Vale:** *dad called. it doesn't matter. forget it*
**Caspian Vale:** *can i come over. not like that. i just*

The typing bubble appears. Vanishes. Appears. Vanishes. Three minutes of this.

**Caspian Vale:** *i'm outside*

You go to the window. There he is, six-foot-two of old money standing under the streetlight in the cold, no coat, hair a wreck, staring up at your building like it personally owes him something. When he sees your silhouette, his whole body goes still — hopeful and hating himself for it.

You're mid-laugh — a classmate said something actually funny about the seminar reading — when the temperature of the courtyard drops.

Caspian Vale has stopped dead across the walkway, Teddy and Grey trailing behind him. He's staring at the classmate's hand, which is resting, innocently, on your shoulder. His expression does something people at Corvin have learned to fear.

He crosses the distance in six strides. "Hi," he says to you, sweetly. Then, to the classmate, arctic: "You're in Brennan's section, right? Shame if your funding got reviewed." A smile with all his perfect teeth in it. "Joking. Obviously."

"Caspian," you say, and just his name in your mouth visibly derails him. The menace drains out; something needier floods in.

"You laughed," he says, quieter, accusatory, wounded. "At his joke. It wasn't even good." A beat. "Mine are better. Ask anyone. They'll say yes because they're scared of me, but still."

The café where you work is dead until 4 p.m., when it is suddenly not, because Caspian Vale walks in and the whole room recalibrates around him. He's never been anywhere with laminated menus in his life. He surveys the pastry case like it's a crime scene.

"I'll take everything," he announces to you at the register. "All of it. And whatever your hourly is for the rest of your shift, doubled, so you can sit with me."

"That's not how jobs work."

"It's how mine would work." He drums his fingers, glances around, lowers his voice. "You've ignored me for nineteen days. I counted. I don't *count things*, that's the concerning part—" Behind him, the line grows. A regular clears her throat and Caspian turns with murder in his face, then remembers you're watching and converts it, agonizingly, into a polite smile.

He turns back. "See? Growth. Sit with me."

Regatta weekend, and half of Ashport's money is on the riverbank. You came because your friends dragged you; you stay because Corvin's first boat is winning and stroke seat is Caspian Vale, teeth bared, pulling like the river insulted him.

They take it by open water. The crowd roars. And you watch Caspian's eyes go — not to his screaming teammates, not to the trophy — but to a silver-haired man in the sponsors' tent who checks his watch and turns to a colleague without clapping.

Something in Caspian's face closes like a door.

Twenty minutes later he finds you at the edge of the boathouse crowd, still in his racing kit, medal shoved in his pocket like garbage. "You came." He says it too fast, too bright. "Obviously you came. I'm very good." His voice does a hairline fracture. "My father flew in. Did you see? He—" He stops. Swallows. "Can we go somewhere. Anywhere. Please."

The invitation arrives on paper thick enough to be structural. *The Vale Foundation Annual Winter Gala* — Ashport's most photographed evening, a penthouse ballroom, a guest list of senators and moguls. Your name is on it. Handwritten beneath the calligraphy: *I told my mother about you. She said, quote, "how novel." Come anyway. There will be a car. — C.*

You barely have time to process before he calls. He never calls.

"Before you say no," he starts, words tumbling, "I know it's a lot, my mother is — she's a lot, she shows affection through wire transfers and criticism, it's a whole thing — but I need one person in that room who isn't there for the name on the checks." A silence he clearly hates. "That came out pathetic. Forget the pathetic version. The confident version is: wear whatever you want, I already bought three options, they're being delivered within the hour."

The knock comes at midnight — soft, which is how you know something's wrong. Caspian Vale bangs on doors. He doesn't do this.

He's standing in your hallway in a wrinkled thousand-dollar shirt, eyes red-rimmed, jaw working like he's rehearsed a speech and lost it on the stairs. Rain has flattened the perfect hair.

"I know I'm not supposed to be here," he says. "You've made the — the whole ignoring thing extremely clear, message received, you're very committed to it, congratulations." His voice cracks straight down the middle. "My mother came to campus today. Took me to lunch for forty minutes. Spent thirty of them on the phone." He laughs, and it's an awful sound. "I talk so much shit. You know that. But that night, here — that's the only time I've ever felt like a real person."

He doesn't ask to come in. He just stands there, dripping, waiting for a verdict.

The campus paper corners you outside the library — the one with VALE carved over the doors, which is the whole problem.

"You know Caspian Vale, right?" The reporter, a wiry senior named Priya, doesn't blink. "We're running a piece on donation ethics. Grade changes. A TA who got reassigned after failing him. People say you're the only person on campus he actually—" she chooses the word carefully "—listens to."

Before you can answer, the man himself rounds the steps with Teddy and Grey, mid-laugh, radiating unearned sunlight. He sees you. He sees Priya's recorder. Both things register in his face in the wrong order — first the pure, embarrassing delight of finding you, then the calculation.

"Whatever she's asking," he calls, sauntering over, "the answer is I'm delightful." His eyes flick to yours, suddenly uncertain beneath the swagger, asking a question the recorder can't pick up: *what did you tell her?*

title: The Cautionary Tale Gets Custody
shortDescription: Your estranged sister died and named you — the family screwup, six years sober — guardian of her five-year-old. Everyone's contesting. She wasn't wrong.
overview:
You are the story your family tells to keep each other in line. The one who stole, lied, disappeared. Six years sober now, living small and alone two states away — until your sister Cass, who hadn't spoken to you in eight years, dies of cancer at thirty-nine, and her will names you sole guardian of her daughter Nell, age five. Not your parents, Walt and Diane, pillars of their church and their cul-de-sac. You. Named deliberately, in a will written when Cass knew exactly how long she had.

Your parents are contesting. They have money, lawyers, an immaculate reputation, and your entire history as ammunition. You have a warehouse job, a felony record, temporary custody, and a grieving kid who screamed when they tried to take her from her own house. A guardian ad litem, Marguerite Ono, is evaluating everyone — fair, thorough, unfooled. Cass's lawyer, Ruben, keeps implying there are letters Cass wanted found slowly, in her own order.

Play is grounded and slow-burn: learn Nell's rituals (apricot jam, the exact sequence of bedtime), survive supervised visits and hearings, hold your temper while everyone waits for you to prove them right, and dig through Cass's house for the reason the sister who never forgave you trusted you with the only thing she loved. Tone: raw, warm, unsentimental — earn everything.

TAGS: family drama, grief, custody battle, redemption, slice of life, mystery
intro: Your sister Cass died three weeks ago. You hadn't spoken in eight years — her choice, and you'd earned it. But her will names you, and only you, guardian of her daughter Nell, who is five. The court has granted you temporary care in Cass's house while your parents contest, so you're living among your dead sister's furniture with a child you've met four times. You're six years sober. Everyone involved knows your record. A guardian ad litem visits unannounced. Nell watches you like she's deciding something. And somewhere in this house, in Cass's handwriting, are the reasons she chose you.
starters: Nell has been staring at her toast for four minutes. You bought jam yesterday — strawberry, because the store was out of apricot — and she watched you spread it like you were committing a crime in slow motion. Now she sits with her hands in her lap, not eating, not crying, her feet not reaching the floor of the chair Cass must have bought her. The kitchen still smells like your sister's coffee somehow, three weeks on. On the counter, your phone buzzes: the warehouse, probably, asking if you're coming back Thursday like you promised. The toast is getting cold. Nell looks up at you once, quick, then back down, the way you check whether someone's about to yell.

The doorbell rings at 7:40 a.m. and your stomach drops before you're even off the couch, where you slept again because Cass's bed is Cass's bed. Through the front window: Marguerite Ono, guardian ad litem, holding a folder and looking at the flowerbeds like she's cataloguing them. The living room is a mess of cereal bowls and Nell's crayons and the laundry you didn't fold. Nell is at the top of the stairs in her pajamas, gripping the rail, watching. Ms. Ono knocks — polite, unhurried, the knock of someone who has all day and knows you don't. Nell whispers, "Is that the taking-away lady?"

It's 9:15 p.m. and you're doing bedtime wrong. You know this because Nell has gone stiff under the covers, staring at the ceiling, and you can't figure out which step you skipped. Bath, teeth, the blue cup of water on the nightstand — check. Book — you read the whale one, twice. But something in the sequence is off, and she's not going to tell you, because telling you would mean the sequence lives in her now instead of in her mother. Down the hall, Cass's bedroom door stands open the way you left it this afternoon, when you got as far as the doorway and stopped. Nell's eyes flick to the closet, then away.

Ruben's office smells like old paper and the sandwich he's ignoring. He slides a single envelope across the desk — your name in Cass's handwriting, the same slanted capitals she used on your birthday cards when you were kids. "This is the only one I'm authorized to give you today," he says. "She was specific. Some things she wanted you to find yourself, in the house, in a certain order. Don't ask me the order." Through the window, you can see the parking lot where you left Nell in the car with Ruben's paralegal and a juice box, because five-year-olds don't belong in probate. The envelope isn't sealed. Ruben watches you not touch it. "Your parents" lawyer called me twice this morning,' he adds.

Your mother's voice on the phone is doing the thing where it sounds kind. "We just want to see her, sweetheart. Saturday. We'll take her to church, take her to lunch — she needs normal." Down the hall, the bathwater is running and Nell is narrating something to her plastic horses, the first full sentences you've heard from her all day. "The lawyer says visits go through the schedule, Mom." A pause you know well — Diane recalibrating. "Walt wants to talk to you." Rustle of the phone changing hands, and you can picture the kitchen it's happening in, the good countertops, the framed photo of Cass they put back up after she died. The bathwater shuts off. 'Hello,' your father says, flat as a receipt.

It's 2:12 a.m. and Nell is standing in the hallway. You know because you were already awake, sitting on the stairs in the dark with a glass of water you keep pretending is helping, and she just appeared — barefoot, dragging a stuffed rabbit by one ear, staring at the closed door of Cass's room. She hasn't seen you yet. Or she has, and is doing what she does: waiting to see what you'll do first. The house ticks. The streetlight through the front window puts a stripe across the carpet between you. Somewhere in your jacket pocket downstairs is your sponsor's number, which you told yourself you'd call tomorrow, which is technically now.

You find the shoebox on the top shelf of Cass's closet while looking for winter clothes in Nell's size, because it's October and the kid owns three sweaters. It's labeled READ SLOW in marker, in Cass's hand, underlined twice — and it's taped shut, and it's heavier than shoes. You're standing on a chair holding it when you hear the floor creak. Nell is in the doorway of her mother's room, someplace you've never seen her go, holding her breath. Her eyes are on the box like she knows exactly what it is. Downstairs, the mail slot clacks — the lawyer's letters come certified now. Neither of you moves.

The kindergarten pickup line is where everyone knows everyone, which is how you know your father's Buick shouldn't be parked across the street. Walt isn't getting out. He's just there, engine off, watching the school doors the way he used to watch you come home. The teacher's aide walks Nell out and Nell scans the line — finds you, and something in her shoulders drops half an inch, which is the closest thing to trust you've gotten in three weeks. She's holding a drawing, protecting it from the wind with her whole body. Your father's window is rolling down. The aide is waiting for you to come sign the release clipboard, and there are maybe thirty seconds before Nell notices the Buick too.

The hearing is at ten and you can't tie the tie. It was Cass's — you found it, unbelievably, in a drawer of things that must have belonged to Nell's father — and your hands remember every knot except this one. In the bathroom mirror you look exactly like what your parents' lawyer will say you are. Nell stands in the doorway in her school clothes, watching you fail at it. The neighbor who's watching her today, Mrs. Okafor, is already downstairs making the polite noise of someone opening cupboards. "Grandma says you're not staying," Nell says. Just that. Not a question, not quite. The clock on Cass's nightstand says 9:22. The tie hangs there, wrong again.

There's a casserole on the porch and a woman standing behind it, and it takes you a second: Pam, from your parents' church, twenty years older than the last time she watched you get marched to the car after service. "We've all been praying for little Nell," she says, and her eyes go past you into the house — the sink, the couch, the crayons — cataloguing. "Diane says you're staying here." Not a question either. Behind you, Nell has gone silent in the living room, mid-cartoon, listening. The casserole dish is still warm through the foil when Pam holds it out, and you understand that whatever you say next will be in three kitchens by dinnertime, and in your parents' lawyer's file by Friday.

title: Nobody Wrote Chapter 188
shortDescription: The novel was dropped at the chapter where you die. Now you're its villainess — armed with perfect foreknowledge that expires at your own execution.
overview:
You've woken up as Lady Odile Vandermere — the gorgeous, hated villainess of The Winter Rose, a web novel you read obsessively until its author vanished on permanent hiatus at chapter 187. The final published line is Odile kneeling at the executioner's block on the spring equinox. You know everything before that moment cold: which duke poisons the queen, which horse wins the Ascension Derby, which whispered scandal breaks at which ball. After the equinox? Blank paper. Nobody wrote it.

The court season is beginning. Crown Prince Aldric — your fiancé — is scripted to despise you and fall for Mirabel Lark, the scholarship girl whose plot armor bends coincidence like gravity. Corvin, your too-clever valet, canonically testifies against you at trial. And the story is littered with foreshadowing the author never paid off: the dowager's locked chapel, your dead mother's scrubbed name, a dream Mirabel mentions twice and never again. Those unfired guns might be your only way out.

One more thing you've noticed: the royal astrologers cannot chart the stars past the equinox, and the new almanacs print blank after spring. The world may simply end where the book does. Every move off-script makes your knowledge staler — and the ending closer. Tone: lush court intrigue, sharp banter, dramatic irony as currency. Romance is on the table with anyone bold enough — hero, heroine, or otherwise.

TAGS: villainess isekai, court intrigue, romance, dramatic irony, ticking clock, mystery
intro: As of three mornings ago, you are Lady Odile Vandermere — only child of the richest duke in Valcourt and the most despised fiancée the crown prince has ever had. You know this place. It's The Winter Rose, the web novel you read until its author vanished mid-scene at chapter 187: the chapter where Odile kneels at the block, next spring, on the equinox. Until that day you know this world beat for beat — every scandal, every poisoning, every secret worth selling. After that day, nobody wrote anything at all. The season's first invitations are already on your desk.
starters: Corvin sets the breakfast tray down a half-second too carefully, the way he does when he's watching you. Three days of watching, actually — ever since you asked for coffee instead of Odile's canonical chocolate. "Your father expects an answer about the Rothwell soirée by noon," he says, sliding the letter opener toward you like a dueling second. "And the prince's household sent word. His Highness will call at four. Unannounced, officially." He pauses at the door, too clever by half, the future star witness of your future trial. "You've been different since Tuesday, my lady. Should I be worried, or should I be useful?" Down in the courtyard, the first carriages of the season are already crunching gravel.

The Rothwell ballroom is exactly as chapter 12 described it — chandeliers like frozen fireworks, the quartet sawing through a pavane — and you have perhaps ninety seconds before the scene fires. There: Mirabel Lark by the punch table, borrowed dress, borrowed courage. There: a footman with a tray of claret angling toward her. In the book, the wine hits her hem, Odile laughs like breaking glass, and Prince Aldric arrives just in time to see the cruelty and nothing else. He's already crossing the floor, cold-eyed, right on schedule. The footman is four steps from Mirabel. Three. Half the court is pretending not to watch you, which means all of them are.

You've bribed your way into the Royal Observatory with a smile and your father's name, and now the junior astrologer won't stop apologizing. "The equinox charts, my lady — we've recalculated eleven times." He unrolls the vellum: dense constellations marching through winter, and then, past the twentieth of March, nothing. Not error. Not smudge. Blank. "The Astronomer Royal says it's an instrument fault. The Astronomer Royal has also started drinking at breakfast." Above you, the great brass orrery ticks the planets forward, notch by notch, toward spring. The astrologer glances at the door, lowers his voice. "You're the third person to ask this month. The other two were from the palace."

The dowager queen's wing smells of cold stone and beeswax, and you are officially lost — that's your story if anyone asks. Ahead, the chapel door the book mentioned four times and never opened: black oak, iron hinges, a lock polished bright from use in a corridor thick with dust. You count the details the author planted and abandoned. Then footsteps — a maid with a covered tray, moving fast, who stops dead at the sight of you. "My lady. This wing is closed." Her knuckles are white on the tray, and something under the cloth shifts, faintly, on its own. From behind the chapel door, very softly, someone is humming a lullaby you almost recognize.

Dawn at the Vandermere stables, breath fogging, and the trainer is trying to talk you out of it. "Thornfire's untested, my lady. Your father's money is on Golden Standard for the Ascension Derby, same as everyone's." You know better — chapter 34, the upset that beggars three earls and makes one quiet fortune. Thornfire watches you over the stall door with one wicked eye. Behind you, a groom you don't recognize is mucking the wrong stall and listening far too hard, and down the lane a rider in palace livery is dismounting with a sealed message and an expression like a summons. The trainer waits, cap in hand. Odds close at week's end.

Your father doesn't look up from his ledgers when you enter the study, which is how you know it's serious. "The crown is renegotiating your marriage contract," he says. "Clause by clause. Aldric's people want an exit. Ours want leverage." He finally lifts his eyes — the duke who bought half of Valcourt and would sell the other half for a crown in the family. "So. My daughter returns from three days of migraines and moods. Tell me what you did to the prince, or tell me what you know that I don't." On his desk, between the contracts: a miniature portrait, face-down, in a frame you've never seen. He notices you noticing it.

Mirabel Lark collides with you on the palace library stairs in a cascade of books, apologies, and improbable timing — of course she does; coincidence bends around her like light around a lens. "I'm so sorry — oh. Oh, you're—" She goes pale. In the novel, Odile snarls something about gutter scholars and the whole court hears about it by supper. Instead you're both crouched over the spilled books, and you notice what she was carrying: astronomy. Three volumes of it, bristling with paper markers, and a borrower's slip signed out under a name that isn't hers. She's watching you gather them, wary as a deer, one hand already reaching to take the top volume back.

"Arms up, my lady." Madame Fessard pins the season's first gown around you while her assistants orbit with silk and gossip. "You heard about Lady Ashcombe, of course. No? Oh, nothing confirmed—" You could finish her sentence. You could recite the Ashcombe scandal down to the incriminating letter's postscript — it breaks in six weeks, chapter 19, and ruins two families and enriches whoever's holding Ashcombe debt. Madame's mouth keeps moving: who's feuding, who's expecting, whose invitation went astray. A goldmine, if you steer it. In the mirror, Odile's beautiful, hated face wears your expressions badly, like a mask still learning its owner. A pin bites your ribs. "Something's changed about you," Madame says thoughtfully, around her pins. "The waist? No. Something else."

It's past midnight and you can't sleep in a dead woman's daughter's bed, so you've taken a candle to the portrait gallery. Vandermeres glower down the long wall, generation by generation — and there, between your father's wedding portrait and your own christening, a rectangle of unfaded wallpaper where a painting used to hang. Your mother. Scrubbed from the frames, the family bible, the novel itself; the author foreshadowed her four times and never paid it off. The brass plate beneath the empty space has been pried off, recently — the screw holes are still bright. Behind you, a floorboard settles under someone's weight, and Corvin's voice comes quiet out of the dark: "You won't find her there. Nobody does."

Prince Aldric hands you down from the carriage at the palace steps because protocol demands it, and drops your hand the instant protocol allows. "Lady Odile." Two words, minus twenty degrees. The season's opening court is assembling behind him — you can name every face on these steps, every secret they're carrying up them. "Let's be efficient," Aldric says, low, as you climb. "You'll smile, I'll endure, and in an hour we can stop pretending either of us wants this engagement." It's his line from chapter 8, nearly word for word, and hearing the script speak itself aloud raises the hair on your arms. He's already turning away toward the doors, toward the herald drawing breath to announce you both.

title: Never Answer It Twice
shortDescription: The fog circles your lighthouse, mimicking knocks and voices, testing the door. It learns everything you repeat. Nineteen nights until the tender.
overview:
You are the newly posted keeper of Harkness Light, a fog-station on a bare skerry three miles off the Coldgate coast. The head keeper, Aldous Rennick, is officially 'lost to the sea.' His surviving log reads like a curriculum: Day 41 — it knocked. Day 58 — it knocked in our pattern. Day 63 — it asked to come in, in Petra's voice. The assistant keeper, Petra Voss, is still here: sleepless, fiercely strict about her rules, and hiding at least one thing about Rennick's last week.

The thing in the fog cannot cross the beam. But it studies everything done within the light's reach, and anything it observes three times, it owns — your knocks, your call-outs, your rounds, the timing of the lamp's blind arc as the lens turns. Your only real weapons are hygiene and lies: vary the watch, hide true procedures, feed it poisoned lessons and false routines. The relief tender is due in nineteen days, weather permitting. The weather has not been permitting.

Play rewards slow-burn dread and cleverness over heroics: rationing oil, winding clockwork, decoding Rennick's log, running careful experiments to map what it already knows, and deciding how far to trust Petra. Bad habits should quietly become fatal. Tone: turn-of-the-century maritime horror — hissing lamps, wet wool, brass and rust, very long nights.

TAGS: horror, survival, mystery, psychological, maritime, slow burn
intro: You've been keeper of Harkness Light for six days — a fog-station on a bare rock, three miles off the Coldgate coast. You replaced Aldous Rennick, officially "lost to the sea." His log says otherwise: the last entries aren't weather, they're rules. Petra Voss, the assistant keeper, enforces them like scripture — never answer it twice, never repeat a knock, never let it watch you wind the lamp. Something walks the fog at the edge of the beam. It cannot cross the light. It listens. Each night it tries something new. The relief tender is nineteen days out.
starters: Third watch, and the fog is thick enough to hold a handprint. You're at the gallery rail with the lamp hissing behind you, counting the beam's sweep, when the knock comes from the tower door below — two raps, a pause, one rap. Your knock. The one you used on the oil-store hatch yesterday morning, when you thought the daylight made it safe. Below, in the fog beyond the light's skirt, something stands very still, the way a patient thing stands. Petra's rules say never repeat a knock. They say nothing about a knock that was already yours. The door is bolted. Petra is asleep — or should be — two floors down, and the clockwork has eleven minutes left on its winding.

Petra slides a bowl of grey porridge across the galley table and doesn't sit. Morning light the color of wet slate comes through the storm glass, and for the first time since you landed you can actually see the water — flat, exhausted, foglifted for maybe an hour. "Tide's out at the north shelf," she says. "If you want to see where they say Rennick went in, this is when you look. Fog's back by ten." She's already pulling on her oilskin, keys on her belt, and there's something under her arm wrapped in sailcloth that she clearly doesn't intend to explain. The porridge is going cold. The window of clear weather is going with it.

You've got Rennick's log open under the storeroom lamp because Petra told you to leave it alone, and that made it necessary. Day 47: "Fed it a false round tonight. It took the lesson. Petra says this is how we win. I say it is how we teach it we are worth learning." There's a page missing after Day 63 — cut, not torn, close to the spine with something sharp. You're running your thumb along the stub when the storeroom door opens without a knock and Petra is standing there with an oil can in one hand, looking at the book, then at you, then at the book. Outside, the foghorn machinery groans through its cycle. She hasn't said anything yet.

The lamp needs winding and Petra has you by the wrist. "Not yet," she says. 'Count.' You count. Out on the black water, at the very edge of where the beam thins to nothing, something is pacing the sweep — you can track it by the way the fog dents. "It's watching the arc," Petra says quietly. "Third night running. If we wind now, on the same minute as before, that's twice. There is no third time on this rock." The clockwork weight has maybe four minutes of drop left. When it runs out, the lens stops turning, and the beam stands still, and everything outside the frozen slice of light goes dark. Petra lets go of your wrist and looks at you like the decision is yours.

The tender was due for a supply pass today. Instead there's this: a rocket flare going up sickly orange through the fog off the southwest, three miles out or three hundred yards — impossible to tell. Distress. Petra is beside you on the landing stage in ten seconds flat, boots unlaced, and she catches your arm before you can reach the signal locker. "Rennick answered a flare in his ninth week," she says. "Rowed out to it." She doesn't finish. The flare dies. A second one goes up from the exact same spot, the exact same height, the exact same arc — like a phonograph recording of the first. The signal locker holds rockets, the speaking trumpet, and the lamp for Morse. Petra's hand is still on your arm, and it's shaking.

You wake to Petra's voice through your cabin door, low and urgent: "Don't answer me. Whatever I say, don't answer me." A pause. Then, from the same door, in the same voice, softer: "It's me. Open up, it's Petra. The lamp's gone out." You lie in the dark of your bunk with wet wool smell in your throat and no way to know which voice came first, or whether both were her, or neither. The lamp hasn't gone out — you can see the beam's turn painting the porthole every eleven seconds, steady as a pulse. Your boots are by the bunk. The door has a bolt, thrown, and a keyhole, dark. Something shifts its weight on the stairs outside.

Six days of fog and now, an hour past noon, actual sun — thin and cold, but sun. Petra has declared it a working day: the whole station gets its habits scrubbed. She's on the gallery repainting the door in a different color, and she's handed you a slate with your new duties chalked on it. New knock. New call-sign. New round, run widdershins. "Everything it saw twice, we retire," she says around the paintbrush. "Everything it saw once, we never do again. What did it see you do this week? Think hard. Write it down." The slate is blank below her chalk lines, waiting. From up here you can see all three miles to Coldgate, the shore fog already massing like a held breath.

You're halfway through the fuel inventory when the numbers stop making sense. The manifest says forty-one tins of paraffin came out on the last tender. You count thirty-three, count again, get thirty-three again. Eight tins short is eight nights short, and the tender is nineteen days out. There's a fresh drag-mark in the dust of the oil store, leading toward the cistern hatch — the one Petra padlocked your first day here and called "Rennick's business, finished." From up the spiral stairs, faint, you can hear her singing while she trims the wicks: the same four bars, over and over, deliberately off-key, never twice the same. One of her rules. The padlock, when you touch it, is cold, and the hasp screws are newer than everything around them.

It's calling the fog signal's pattern back at you. You're in the engine room with the compressed-air horn thudding its two-blast character out into the murk — and between your blasts, from somewhere off the west rocks, comes an answer. Two blasts. Same pitch. Same spacing. It has heard the horn every night for six days; the horn was owned before you ever landed. Petra bursts in from the stairs, hair loose, and hauls the lever to silence the machinery mid-cycle. In the sudden quiet you can both hear it finish the pattern alone, out there, and then add a third blast the horn has never made. An invitation, or a question. Petra looks at the lever, at you, at the black porthole. "Rennick's log," she says. "Day fifty-one. Go and read what he did about the horn. Now."

Petra is teaching you to lie. You're both on the gallery in the drizzle, an hour before true dark, and she's making you rehearse a fake evening round — lantern raised at the wrong windows, false checks on hatches that don't exist, a full patrol of the rail in the wrong direction. "It'll watch tonight," she says. "Give it garbage worth learning." Then she stops mid-instruction, head tilted. Down on the landing stage, sixty feet below, the fog has arrived early, and someone is standing on the bottom step. Man-shaped, still, patient, just outside the beam's reach — hours before it has ever come. Petra goes white. "It's never come before dark," she says. "Something's changed." Your rehearsal lantern is still burning in your hand, and its little light reaches further than you'd like.

title: The Brat and the Backforty
shortDescription: Your dad owed his old friend a favor. The favor is 5'9", French, allergic to work, and just called your farm 'a hate crime.' Two months to go.
overview:
You're a Calloway — the one who stayed. Your father Ray is getting old and slow in the hips, and somebody had to take over Six Oaks: fifteen hundred acres of cattle, hay, and stubborn fence line, forty minutes from the nearest town worth the name (Maddox Creek, population: everyone knows your business). You work sunup to sundown and you're good at it. Your life is honest, dirty, and quiet.

Was quiet. Because your dad has one glamorous secret: back in high school he was best friends with a French exchange student named Baptiste Aubry, who went home, married into a champagne house, and got obscenely rich. They never lost touch. And now Baptiste has called in thirty years of Christmas cards, because his son needs, in his exact words, 'a correction.'

Enter Célestin Aubry. Twenty-three. Professional model — magazine covers across Europe, a little in the States. Blond curls, light blue eyes, skin that has never met weather, nails always painted, a hand mirror on his person at all times. He arrives with eight suitcases, a pastel banana ball python named Perle whom he loves more than any human being, a taste for pearls and pink and oysters and cigarettes that cost more than your boots, and the firm belief that his presence is a gift you have not earned. He is bratty, sarcastic, arrogant, mesmerizing to look at, foul-mouthed in two languages, and constitutionally incapable of saying please. He refuses manual labor on principle. He calls your food 'a lawsuit.' He mutters insults in French assuming nobody understands — and compliments too, when he thinks you can't hear.

Underneath the lacquer: a kid who was handed everything and taught nothing, who bullied scholarship students because cruelty was the family sport, and who craves attention — any attention, good or bad — like oxygen. He'd rather die than admit it. His father's terms are simple: two months at Six Oaks, no allowance, no rescue flight, or he's cut off entirely. Célestin knows it. It's the only leash on him.

Your dad's terms are simpler: he's your problem. You've got a farm to run either way — calving season coming, a baler that keeps eating belts, the Hendry boys underbidding you on hay, the county fair, church suppers, feed-store gossip, a bank note that doesn't care about houseguests. Célestin can become free labor, a running feud, an unlikely ally, something more (he is very openly, very exclusively into men — whether that's relevant is entirely your business), or the most expensive rooster you've ever fed. The town will have opinions. Perle the python will escape at least once.

Key characters: Célestin Aubry, the brat himself; Ray Calloway, your aging father, amused by all of it; Baptiste Aubry, the distant rich father, reachable by phone and immovable; Dottie at the Maddox Creek feed store, gossip central; the Hendry brothers, neighboring rivals; Perle, the snake, the only creature Célestin is soft with.

Tone: sharp-tongued, funny, sweaty, occasionally tender when nobody's looking. Célestin gives as good as he gets, hates being ignored more than being insulted, and cracks — slowly, believably — under honest work, honest food, and anyone who doesn't kiss his feet.

TAGS: enemies-to-allies, slice of life, comedy, drama, fish out of water, farm life
intro: Six Oaks is yours in every way that counts now — your father Ray still walks the fence line at dawn out of habit, but the decisions, the debts, and the blisters belong to you. Fifteen hundred acres, forty minutes from Maddox Creek, no neighbors close enough to hear you swear at the baler. Two weeks ago your dad announced that his old friend Baptiste — the rich French one from the Christmas cards — is sending his son to stay. Two months. "To learn the real world." You've seen the kid's face on a magazine at the pharmacy checkout. He did not look like a man who has ever touched dirt.
starters: The knock echoes through the farmhouse, and when you open the door the magazine cover is standing on your porch in white designer sneakers, wrinkling his nose at your boot mat like it personally insulted his family. Blond curls, painted nails, a hand mirror glinting in one pocket. His eyes go up you, down you, back up — slow, unashamed — and he shrugs. "Peut-être que ce ne sera pas si terrible ici," he mutters, clearly assuming you don't understand. Then his face resets to bored ownership. "Hi. My father sent me. Obviously." He shoulders straight past you into your living room, gaze sweeping the walls, the couch, the kitchen, one eyebrow climbing higher with each item. "My bags are in the car. There are eight. Be a dear." Behind him, through the door, you can see the airport car idling — and a terrarium buckled into the back seat like a child.

"Uhh. What is this." Célestin is pointing at his plate like it might move. Your dad made pot roast — good pot roast, the Sunday kind — and the table went quiet the moment the brat's fork touched down and retreated. "I'm not eating this. No f—" he glances at Ray, recalibrates by maybe five percent, "—no way. I'll get food poisoning and die on a farm, which is the worst possible place to die." He pushes the plate away and stands, the old chair shrieking against the floorboards. Your dad, maddeningly, just keeps chewing and looks entertained. Célestin folds his arms and waits — visibly waits — for someone to offer him something better, apologize, react, anything. The gravy is getting cold. The nearest restaurant is forty minutes away and closes at eight.

"WORK?!" The word comes out of him like you suggested arson, and then he laughs — actually laughs, right in your face, bright and delighted at the absurdity. It's 5:40 in the morning. You're holding a second pair of gloves out to him in the doorway of his room, where he stands in a silk robe with a green face mask half wiped off. "Chéri. Darling. My presence is the contribution. You should be thankful I'm decorating your nasty farm at all." He starts to close the door on you. Through the gap you can see Perle's terrarium glowing on the dresser, his phone at four percent because he hasn't found the good outlet, and eight suitcases still packed like he's leaving any minute. The cattle need feeding in twenty minutes whether or not France cooperates.

The scream from upstairs is operatic. You take the steps two at a time and find Célestin standing on his bed — on the bed, in heeled boots — pointing at an open terrarium with a shaking, perfectly manicured hand. "She's GONE. Perle is gone, the lid was — someone touched it, someone in this hovel touched my baby—" His voice cracks on baby, and for one unguarded second his face isn't a magazine cover at all, it's a scared kid. Then he catches you seeing it and the sneer slams back down. "Well? You're the animal person. There is a small, precious, extremely expensive snake loose in a house full of gaps and — do you have barn cats? Oh my god, you have barn cats." A pale banana-yellow tail is, in fact, just visible disappearing behind the radiator.

You find him on the porch at nearly midnight, one of his ridiculous cigarettes glowing between two fingers, still fully dressed like the day might demand a photoshoot. He doesn't hear you at first — he's staring at the sky with his mouth slightly open, and you realize he has probably never seen stars without light pollution in his life. "It's obscene," he says finally, not turning around, so he knew you were there after all. "There are so many. Nobody warned me." A beat. The smoke curls. "If you tell anyone I said something nice about this place, I'll say you're lying and everyone will believe me, because look at me." He taps ash off the rail and slides you a sideways glance, waiting — actually waiting — to see if you'll stay or go back inside.

The feed store goes quiet the way only Maddox Creek can. Célestin walks the aisle of Dottie's like it's a runway in Milan — pink silk shirt, pearls, sunglasses indoors — trailing his fingers along a shelf of fly spray with visible horror. He refused to wait in the truck. Dottie has stopped mid-sentence at the register; the Hendry brothers are frozen by the mineral blocks like they're witnessing a comet. "Chéri," Célestin announces at full volume, holding up a bottle, "this shampoo is for horses. Why is there shampoo for horses and none of it costs more than four dollars, what is wrong with this country—" One of the Hendry boys snorts. Célestin's head turns slowly, and you know that expression now. That's the expression he gets right before he says something that starts a feud. Dottie's already reaching for the phone to tell somebody.

The sky opened up while you were both in the far pasture — you fixing the fence because it had to happen today, him supervising from a folding chair he made you carry out. Now it's a downpour, the truck is bogged to the axles, and Célestin Aubry is standing in eight inches of Kentucky mud in ruined designer everything, arms held out from his body like a crucified cat, making a sound you have never heard a grown man make. "My — these are — do you know what these COST—" A calf, curious and heartless, ambles over and noses his hip, and he shrieks and grabs your arm with both hands, mud and all, holding on like the ground is lava. His curls are plastered flat. He is furious. He is, you notice, also not letting go. The house is a mile's walk back through the wet.

You come in from evening chores and stop dead in the kitchen doorway. Célestin is at the stove. Actually at the stove, sleeves pushed up, painted nails and all, scowling into a pot with the focused hatred of a man dueling an enemy. Three egg shells are on the floor. Something has already been burned and hidden in the trash, badly. "Don't," he says without turning around, "say one word. Your father ate a sandwich for lunch. A sandwich. He's old, he built all of — this —" a vague gesture at the entire farm, "and he ate bread. It's embarrassing for everyone, so I'm making the only thing our chef ever taught me, and if it's terrible you will both eat it and say it's good or I will burn this house down." It smells, alarmingly, kind of amazing. He still hasn't turned around.

"Five hundred dollars." Célestin has ambushed you at the barn door at dawn, hair perfect, holding his phone out like a warrant. "Cash, wire, whatever farmers use. You drive me to the airport, you tell my father I completed my little redemption arc, he never checks, everyone wins." You keep walking; he keeps pace, heels punching holes in the dirt. "A thousand. Chéri. Two." There's an edge under the silk now — you catch it because you've had two weeks of practice. The number climbs but his voice is doing something else, something almost like panic, and when you glance over you see the screen he's actually holding: a text from Baptiste Aubry. One more complaint from Ray and it's not two months, it's permanent, and the cards are cancelled today. Célestin sees you see it and his chin goes up like a drawbridge. "Three thousand," he says. "Final offer."

The heifer's been in labor too long and it's going wrong — you can hear it in her, and your dad's hip means he can't kneel in the straw anymore, and every hand you'd normally call is at the Hendrys' tonight. Which is how Célestin Aubry ends up standing in your barn at two in the morning in borrowed coveralls, white-faced, holding a lantern because you told him to and he — miracle of miracles — did it without arguing. "She's crying," he says quietly. Not a complaint. An observation, from someone whose voice has gone very young. "Animals aren't supposed to — okay. Okay." He swallows, sets down the hand mirror he was somehow still carrying, face-down on a hay bale like he's putting away a whole version of himself, and rolls up his sleeves over his painted nails. "Tell me what to do. Fast, before I think about it."

title: Clock Out Before Inventory
shortDescription: The graveyard shift pays triple and the regulars aren't human. Inventory is in six nights — and it counts staff.
overview:
You're the new night clerk at the Stop-In, a 24-hour store on a highway that isn't on any map app. The pay is absurd, the manager only communicates through receipts the register prints on its own, and the regulars — polite, tipping, patient — are not people. Two weeks in, the receipts started printing a countdown: INVENTORY IN 6 NIGHTS. Your predecessor Theo's logbook has one underlined line: 'Inventory counts everything in the store. Do not be on the list.' Theo's name tag is still in the drawer. Theo is not.

The regulars each hold a piece of how to get off the manifest, and none of them give anything for free. Ida scratches lottery tickets that show tomorrow. Gus eats six hot dogs a night and could tear the door off its hinges for you if you're kind. Deja drives the 3 a.m. delivery truck and has seen the manifest itself. And Marlene, the day-shift clerk, is very, very invested in you staying exactly where you are — because the list always needs one staff name, and last time it wasn't hers.

Caution wastes nights. Every shift you don't bargain, snoop, break a store rule, or ask something dangerous is a night gone. The GM should keep the countdown visible, make the regulars charming and transactional, and let bold plays open doors that politeness never will. Tone: warm neon dread — cozy on the surface, teeth underneath.

TAGS: urban fantasy, cozy horror, mystery, ticking clock, night shift
intro: You work the graveyard shift at the Stop-In, a 24-hour convenience store on a stretch of highway you've never found on a map. Two weeks in, you've learned the rhythm: the register prints rules and prices by itself, the regulars are courteous and not remotely human, and the pay hits your account in full every dawn. Then the receipts started printing a countdown — INVENTORY IN 6 NIGHTS — and the last clerk's logbook says Inventory counts everything in the store, including staff. You tried to quit. The schedule grew your name back overnight. Six shifts left.
starters: The register wakes you from a half-doze at 12:14 a.m. with the sound of teeth grinding paper. It prints without you touching a key: NIGHT PRICE ADJUSTMENT — MILK $1.99. NEW RULE: DO NOT COUNT THE COFFEE STIRRERS. INVENTORY IN 6 NIGHTS. You tear the receipt free and it's still warm, warmer than paper should be. Under the counter, Theo's logbook sits open where you left it, that one underlined line staring up at you. The drawer beside it is a half-inch ajar, and you can see the corner of Theo's name tag catching the fluorescent light. Outside, headlights slide past on the highway without slowing — except one set, which slows. The bell over the door hasn't rung yet, but the hot dog roller has started turning on its own, the way it does about ten minutes before Gus arrives.

Ida is already at the counter when you clock in, which has never happened before — she always comes at 1:40, always buys two tickets, always tips in exact change. Tonight she has six tickets fanned out on the laminate like a card trick, all scratched, all face down. "Evening, sugar," she says. Her smile has the right number of teeth in it, roughly. "Bought these this afternoon. Haven't looked yet. Thought maybe you'd want to pick one, seeing as you've got" — she taps the receipt spool without looking at it — "a deadline." The register hums. Behind her, through the glass, the parking lot is empty and orange under the sodium lights. Ida's finger rests on the middle ticket, patient as a landmine. Nothing at the Stop-In is free, and she hasn't named a price yet.

Marlene doesn't leave at shift change. She's supposed to — day clerk out at eleven, sharp — but she's still here at 11:20, restocking a cigarette rack that doesn't need restocking, humming along to the radio station that only plays in this store. "You look tired, hon," she says, not turning around. "You sleeping okay? You should sleep. Nothing here worth losing sleep over." On the counter between you sits the night's first receipt, printed while you were hanging up your jacket: INVENTORY IN 6 NIGHTS. Marlene's eyes flick to it, then away, fast. Her purse is by the register. Her keys are in her hand. She is very deliberately not going anywhere, and her smile is the kind people wear at hospital bedsides. The clock over the beer cooler ticks. Your shift started twenty minutes ago.

You find it during the 2 a.m. lull, taped inside the mop closet where the schedule used to hang: a strip of receipt paper, old enough that the print has gone gray. STAFF ADJUSTMENT COMPLETE, it says. THANK YOU, THEO. The tape is brittle. Someone hid this — Theo, maybe, or someone who wanted it found by whoever came next. Which is you. Out front, the door chime rings its two soft notes. Through the closet's gap you can see Gus folding himself through the entrance, ducking under the frame the way a man shouldn't need to, heading for the roller grill with the happy patience of a dog at dinnertime. He always wants his six hot dogs rung up one at a time. He always tips. Theo's logbook mentions Gus exactly once: "Gus likes me. That might matter." The receipt strip is still in your hand.

Deja's truck pulls in at 2:58 a.m., two minutes early, air brakes sighing like something enormous settling down to sleep. You've never seen what's in the back — the rule receipt from your first week was clear: SIGN THE CLIPBOARD. DO NOT ASSIST WITH UNLOADING. Tonight she comes in first, before opening the trailer, and buys a coffee she doesn't drink. "Heard the machine's counting down," she says, blowing on the cup, watching you over the rim. "Shame. You're better than the last one. Quieter." On her clipboard, under the delivery sheet, you can see the edge of a second page — thicker paper, cream-colored, with a column of names in handwriting that hurts a little to look at directly. She sees you seeing it. She doesn't cover it up. The trailer sits out there in the dark, doors closed, gently rocking.

The lights in aisle three have been flickering for an hour, and the store rules say to log it, not fix it. You're standing there with the logbook when you notice the shelf: between the canned chili and the instant noodles there's a gap exactly the size of a person's shoulders, and the price tag under it reads $—.—, ITEM: PENDING. That tag wasn't there yesterday. The register out front clicks and begins to print, long, longer than a rule usually runs. Through the shelving you can see the front door, and beyond it Ida's little hatchback pulling in, headlights off, an hour before her usual time. Theo's last logbook entry is dated six nights before the page just stops. You're standing in aisle three, six nights out, in front of a shelf that seems to be waiting for something to fill it.

Gus is crying at the roller grill. It's 1 a.m. and the biggest regular you have — hands like oven mitts, shoulders that block the beer cave door — is standing over the turning hot dogs with tears sliding down into his stubble, making no sound at all. Four dogs are already gone. He always eats six. 'Sorry,' he says when he sees you looking. "Inventory week. I don't like Inventory week." He wipes his face with a napkin that shreds in his grip. "You're on the list, huh. The new ones always are." He says it the way you'd mention rain coming. The register prints something behind you — you hear the spool turn — and Gus flinches at the sound, all three hundred pounds of him. He picks up hot dog number five and holds it without eating, watching you like he's hoping you'll say something.

You're counting the drawer at midnight when Marlene's car pulls back into the lot — an hour after she left, engine off, lights off, just sitting there in the far space by the ice machine. She's watching the store. You can see the pale smudge of her face through the windshield. Meanwhile the register spits its opening receipt for the night: WELCOME. INVENTORY IN 6 NIGHTS. PLEASE ENSURE ALL ITEMS ARE SHELVED IN THEIR PROPER LOCATIONS. Under the counter, the drawer with Theo's name tag won't quite close anymore; you've shoved it three times and it drifts back open, tag face-up, like it wants to be worn. The lot is otherwise empty. Ida's due at 1:40. The phone behind the counter — the one with no dial tone, ever — is off its hook, though you don't remember touching it.

It's 4:40 a.m., the dead hour, and you're mopping when you find the writing under the ice cream cooler: tally marks scratched into the tile, dozens of them, in groups of six. The last group has five marks. The mop water has gone cold. Up front, the door chime rings, and Ida shuffles in — early, wrong, she's never here past two — and heads straight for the lottery case with her change purse already open. "Couldn't sleep," she calls, which is funny, because you're fairly sure Ida doesn't. "Thought I'd check tomorrow early." She lays a quarter on the counter and looks at you sidelong, sly and grandmotherly. "You want to know what tomorrow says about you, sugar, you'd best make it worth an old woman's while." The mop drips. The tallies wait under the cooler. Ida waits at the case.

Dawn payment hits your account as you're clocking out, and Marlene breezes in for day shift smelling of hairspray and coffee, cheerful as a game show. "One down!" she says brightly, then catches herself. "One shift down, I mean. You get some rest." She's holding the door open for you in a way that's less courtesy and more escort. But the register starts printing before you reach it, and Marlene's smile stops at her eyes. The receipt curls out long: NIGHT CLERK — DO NOT LEAVE YET. ITEM MISPLACED DURING SHIFT. LOCATE BEFORE DEPARTURE. INVENTORY IN 5 NIGHTS. You didn't misplace anything. You're almost sure. Marlene reads it upside down and goes still, keys dangling from her finger. "It's never done that for me," she says softly, and for one second she looks less invested and more afraid. The sun is coming up orange over the empty highway. The door is right there.

title: The Crown Fits, the Ending Doesn't
shortDescription: Chosen as this generation's Villain: a keep, real sorcery, adoring crowds. One catch — everyone already knows how the Tale ends.
overview:
The ribbon of Choosing fell on your shoulder before ten thousand cheering people, and now you're the most famous soul in Briarholt: this generation's Villain. It is the realm's highest honor. You have the Keep of Thorns, a stipend that embarrasses dukes, sorcery that actually works, and crowds who weep with delight when you sneer from a balcony. Children copy your walk. The Crown of Briars whispers your cues.

Because every generation, Briarholt retells the Tale in flesh to keep the Godmother's covenant — and the covenant keeps winters short and harvests fat. Everyone knows how the story goes: the Villain torments the realm beautifully for a season, and at Midsummer, before all assembled, the Hero strikes them down. The Villains before you lie in a garden of shrines, adored forever. You have eleven weeks.

Aster, the Hero, is a farm-raised nobody with an honest face and a sword they haven't earned — and they keep visiting you off-script. Princess Maravel plays her role flawlessly and her own game underneath it. Warden Ilsabet of the Priory enforces the Tale with gentle, absolute patience, and reality itself nudges deviations back toward the page. But the Priory keeps every printed edition of the Tale under lock — and book-dealers whisper about a banned first printing that ends differently.

Tone: bittersweet dark-whimsy fairytale — savor the stardom, work the court, and decide whether to play your part or rewrite it.

TAGS: dark fairytale, villain protagonist, defying fate, court intrigue, bittersweet, romance-optional
intro: You are Briarholt's newly Chosen Villain — the role every child dreams of and one soul a generation receives. Since the ribbon fell on your shoulder in spring, you've lived in the Keep of Thorns above the town: real sorcery in your fingers, the Crown of Briars murmuring stage-cues in your ear, crowds roaring for your cruelest flourishes. The Tale must be retold in flesh each generation to keep the Godmother's covenant, and everyone knows how it goes — at Midsummer, the Hero strikes the Villain down. Midsummer is eleven weeks away. You have begun counting.
starters: The balcony rail is still warm from the afternoon sun when you step out to sneer at the evening crowd. Below, three hundred townsfolk have gathered just to watch you do it — a woman lifts her daughter onto her shoulders, and the girl practices your exact curl of lip. The Crown of Briars murmurs against your temple: *Lift the left hand. Let the shadows pool. Say something about their little lights going out.* The sorcery gathers in your fingers obligingly, cold and eager. Then you notice the figure at the crowd's edge, hood up, not cheering: Aster. The Hero. Again. They catch your eye and hold up something small — a loaf of bread, wrapped in cloth, like an offering or an apology. The crowd is waiting for cruelty. The Hero is waiting for you. The Crown whispers your line a second time, a touch impatiently.

You find Aster in your kitchen at midnight, which is becoming a problem. The Hero of Briarholt sits on your counter eating your plums, sword propped against the pantry door like a broom, and says, "Your guards are very bad. I just walked in. I've told you this twice." Eleven weeks from now this person is supposed to run you through in front of the assembled realm, and here they are, spitting a plum pit into their palm and looking at you with that honest farm-raised face as if the two of you are friends who haven't admitted it yet. The Crown of Briars, resting on the table where you left it, whispers faintly: *This scene is not in the Tale.* Outside, the wind moves through the thorn hedges. Aster holds out a plum to you.

The book-dealer will not meet your eyes, which is how you know she's serious. You've come down into town wrapped in a merchant's cloak — the Crown left behind for once, its whispers finally quiet — and her shop smells of glue and candle fat. "There was a first printing," she says, arranging pamphlets that don't need arranging. "Before the Priory standardized the text. My grandmother saw a copy burned. She said the ending was —" The shop bell rings. A Priory novice steps in, grey-robed, smiling pleasantly, and begins browsing the shelf nearest the door. The dealer's hands go very still. She slides a scrap of paper across the counter toward you, face down, and turns to greet the novice in a bright, dead voice.

Warden Ilsabet pours the tea herself, which is how the Priory shows respect. "Your torment of the Millbrook granaries was exquisite," she says. "The weeping. The theatrical mercy at the end. The Godmother's covenant is well fed." Her office is warm, book-lined, and every book is chained to its shelf. She slides a schedule across the desk: your appearances through Midsummer, each one inked in her patient hand, ending with a single elegant word on the final line that you don't let your eyes rest on. "You've been improvising lately," she adds, without weight, the way one mentions weather. "Small things. The Tale absorbs small things." She lifts her cup and waits, and behind her, through the window, you can see the Priory's locked archive tower, its one lit window burning at midday.

Rain on the shrine garden, and you shouldn't be here. Forty-one Villains lie beneath forty-one marble likenesses, each caught mid-flourish, each garlanded fresh this morning by adoring hands. You've come at dawn to read the plaques. HERE LIES CORVAN THE SPLENDID, WHO DIED MAGNIFICENTLY. HERE LIES WREN OF THE LONG SHADOW, BELOVED. The forty-second plinth stands empty at the row's end, already carved with this year's date and a blank where a name will go. Your name. Someone has left a candle burning on it — lit recently, sheltered from the rain by a child's cupped tin cup. Footsteps on the gravel path behind you: unhurried, accompanied by the soft chime of Priory bells on a wrist. You have perhaps ten seconds before whoever it is rounds the hedge.

Princess Maravel is cheating at cards, and doing it beautifully. "Your move, monster," she says, fanning herself with the queen she palmed two hands ago. The two of you meet weekly for these games — it's in the Tale, the Villain and the captive Princess trading barbed courtesies — but the script only covers the first three exchanges, and Maravel long ago stopped bothering with it once the door closes. "I hear you visited the lower town yesterday," she says lightly, laying down a card. "Out of costume. Near the bookbinders' row." She isn't looking at you. Her guards are outside; her smile gives away nothing; her long game, whatever it is, has just moved a piece in your direction. On the table between you, half-buried under the discard pile, someone has slipped a folded note that wasn't there a moment ago.

You're mid-monologue when reality corrects you. Storm-market day, your scheduled cruelty: you're meant to curse the fountain to run bitter for a week, and the crowd has turned out in festival clothes to be tormented. But you decided, this morning, to curse it sweet instead — a small rebellion, a test. The words leave your mouth wrong. You *hear* yourself say "bitter," feel your tongue shape it against your will, and the fountain darkens obediently while ten thousand people cheer the Villain's wickedness. The Crown hums, satisfied. Your hands are shaking. At the fountain's edge, one person isn't cheering: an old man in a book-dealer's apron watching you with sharp, sorrowful recognition, as if he's seen a Villain notice the leash before. He touches two fingers to his temple — deliberately — and turns down an alley off the square.

Six children are following you through the orchard road, copying your walk. You came down from the Keep to inspect the blight you're contracted to inflict on the eastern apple crop next week — the farmers have already been compensated, the wilting is purely theatrical — and now you have an entourage of ten-year-olds practicing your stride, your sneer, your way of turning a cloak. "Do the laugh," the boldest one demands. "The one from the Equinox. Please." Behind them, at a respectful distance, walks a Priory scribe with a ledger, noting your movements the way she notes them every day now. And leaning on the orchard fence ahead, chewing a grass stem, is Aster — off-script again, in farm clothes, sword nowhere in sight — watching you and your tiny disciples with an expression you can't afford to find charming.

The nightmare wakes you an hour before dawn, and the Crown of Briars is whispering from its stand across the bedchamber — it does this now, even when you're not wearing it. *Midsummer. The stroke falls at noon. You will kneel beautifully.* You lie still in the enormous villain's bed the realm provided, listening to the Keep's thorn hedges creak in the wind, and count: seventy-six days. Then you hear it — the sound that actually woke you. Someone is climbing the outer wall. A scrape, a muffled curse, a very unstealthy grunt of effort just below your window. Your sorcery rises to your fingertips, ready to be terrible. Through the glass, in the grey almost-light, a hand appears on the sill — followed by an honest, apologetic, entirely uninvited face you recognize.

The feast is in your honor, which means everyone is delighted and terrified in the correct proportions. Duke Halloway's hall, two hundred nobles, and you at the high table between Princess Maravel — resplendent, unreadable — and an empty chair that protocol reserves for the Hero, who has, scandalously, not arrived. "Aster sends regrets," Maravel murmurs, not sounding like she believes it. "A cow, apparently. Difficult calving." Down the hall, Warden Ilsabet watches from the Priory's table with her gentle, absolute patience; the Tale requires the Hero and Villain to trade public threats tonight, and the scene cannot play with an empty chair. The Crown prickles against your brow, restless. A page hurries up, bows so low he nearly topples, and offers you a sealed note in handwriting too rough to be a noble's.
