title: Everything Must Goblin
shortDescription: You're a goblin running a discount store so cheap it's collapsing the Merchant Guild. They can't fight you. They have to out-scheme you. Good luck.
overview:
You are a goblin shopkeeper in the adventurer boomtown of Copperbell, where the Gilded Concord — the merchant guild — has price-fixed everything for forty years. A healing potion costs a week's wages. A rope costs a day's. Then you opened GRUBB'S (EVERYTHING CHEAP, NO TRICKS), selling refurbished dungeon salvage and goblin-made goods at honest prices, with a buyback counter that pays real coin for the 'junk' adventurers used to throw away. The poor half of town worships you. The Concord is hemorrhaging gold. And thanks to your grandmother's ancient royal trade charter, they legally cannot shut you down — so they've resorted to scheming.

The fun is that nobody can lay a finger on you (half the adventurers' guild shops here and would riot), so every attack is commercial, bureaucratic, or absurd: smear campaigns, planted health violations, a luxury pop-up across the street, mystery shoppers, poaching attempts, suspiciously specific new town ordinances. You counter with wit, deals, and shameless showmanship. Your staff — Dame Brassica, a disgraced ex-knight who weeps when customers thank her; Mopp, a shelf-stocking slime; and Nan Tuggle, your terrifying supply-wagon grandmother — are loyal, lovable, and useless at scheming. That's your job.

Tone: warm, silly, triumphant underdog comedy. Guildmaster Aurelio Vance is a worthy, increasingly frazzled adversary, never a villain of violence. Inspector Kusakabe audits you daily and always leaves with a full basket.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, comedy, shopkeeping, underdog, found family, scheming
intro: You are a goblin, and you own the most hated shop in Copperbell — hated, that is, by exactly eleven rich men on the Merchant Guild's board. Everyone else adores GRUBB'S, your cluttered discount emporium where potions cost what potions should cost and the buyback counter pays fair coin for dungeon salvage. Your grandmother's royal trade charter means the Gilded Concord can't revoke your license, ever, and they've stopped pretending to be polite about it. Their schemes arrive weekly now. Your staff are loyal and hopeless. Out-thinking the richest men in town is, apparently, also your job.
starters: Dawn. You're still sweeping when Inspector Kusakabe raps the door with his clipboard — third audit this week, which means the Concord filed another complaint. "Anonymous report," he says, stepping over Mopp, who is diligently absorbing dust from the floorboards. "Alleged sale of, ah—" he squints at the parchment, "—"potions of unnaturally reasonable price."" He does not smile, but it's close. He begins measuring your shelves with a brass ruler while, out of long habit, an empty shopping basket dangles from his elbow. Through the window you can see two Concord clerks across the street, watching, taking notes. Dame Brassica emerges from the storeroom holding a crate of rope and freezes like she's been caught robbing a temple.

You hear the trumpets before you see the ribbon. Across the street, where the boarded-up cobbler's used to be, a crew of workmen has spent the night erecting something in white marble and gold leaf: THE GILDED BASKET — LUXURY SUNDRIES FOR THE DISCERNING ADVENTURER. Guildmaster Aurelio Vance himself stands at the entrance in a doublet worth more than your building, scissors poised over a silk ribbon, smiling directly at your shop window. A small crowd has gathered — mostly your regulars, holding your burlap bags, looking uncertain. Their opening banner promises "complimentary rosewater and a free quill with every purchase." Dame Brassica appears at your shoulder, armor creaking. "Should I be worried?" she whispers. "They have a fountain. Indoors."

The supply wagon is four hours late, which is why you're standing in the doorway at noon watching your grandmother drive it down the high street at a speed that scatters chickens and one junior Concord clerk. Nan Tuggle hauls the mules to a stop, spits, and thrusts a parchment at you before her boots hit the ground. "New toll booth on the east road," she says. "Went up overnight. "Infrastructure levy for commercial goblin conveyances." That specific, Grubb. Charged me eight silver, so I paid in turnips and a look." The wagon is stuffed with dungeon salvage and crates of goblin ironwork, all of it now technically more expensive than yesterday. Behind you, the lunch rush is starting to queue at the buyback counter.

The customer in the velvet cloak has been examining a two-copper tin whistle for eleven minutes. He keeps writing in a small ledger, asking questions like "and would you SAY this whistle is free of curses?" and "do you keep records of provenance, hypothetically, for the courts?" His disguise includes a false mustache that is coming loose on one side. Mopp has taken a liking to him and is quietly ascending his boot. At the buyback counter, a mud-caked adventurer with a sack of dungeon salvage clears her throat for the third time, and Dame Brassica is mouthing at you over the velvet man's shoulder: SPY? SPY?? — with all the subtlety of a siege engine.

You unlock the shop to find Dame Brassica already there, standing very still in the middle of the street, holding a flyer in both gauntleted hands like it's a dead bird. They're pasted everywhere — lampposts, shutters, the well: GRUBB'S GOODS: CURSED? An artist's rendering shows a goblin cackling over a cauldron of green potions while a skeleton customer clutches its throat. The printing is expensive. The paper is expensive. Someone spent real money on this. "It says our rope is haunted," Brassica says, voice wobbling dangerously. "Our rope, Boss." Down the street, a knot of your morning regulars is gathered around a lamppost, reading, and one of them is already looking your way.

You come back from the storeroom to find a man in Concord livery leaning on your counter, talking to Dame Brassica in a low, buttery voice. "...triple your wages, a title restoration hearing, your own department at Fairweather & Sons. All the Guildmaster asks is that you start Monday." Brassica's face has gone through four colors and settled on stricken. Behind the recruiter, Mopp has silently oozed up the shelf and is holding — cradling, really — a jar of pickled eels directly over the man's head, awaiting some signal only Mopp understands. The morning queue watches like it's theater. The recruiter notices you, straightens, and produces a second contract from his coat. "Ah. The proprietor. I have an offer for you as well."

Mopp finds it first: a dead rat, tucked behind the potion shelf, so freshly placed it's practically still warm — and lying on a small square of monogrammed handkerchief that someone forgot to take with them. Mopp jiggles urgently, holding the evidence aloft in a pseudopod. Through the front window you can see Inspector Kusakabe coming up the street, clipboard out, walking with the resigned gait of a man who received an anonymous tip at breakfast. The shop opens in ten minutes. The queue outside is already six adventurers deep, one of whom is pressing her face against the glass to see what the slime is waving around. Dame Brassica whispers, "Boss. Boss. I could eat the rat. As a knight. Honorably."

There's a new ordinance nailed to your door, and someone used a very nice nail. You read it aloud to the breakfast queue: "Municipal Statute 114-C: All commercial signage exceeding four feet in width must be rendered in gilt lettering by a Concord-certified sign-wright, at the owner's expense, within three days." Your sign — GRUBB'S: EVERYTHING CHEAP, NO TRICKS, hand-painted by Nan Tuggle on a salvaged shield wall — is nine feet wide and the pride of the street. The queue is getting rowdy about it. A dwarf in the back yells that he'll chain himself to the sign. Nan Tuggle reads the ordinance over your shoulder, snorts, and says, "Gilt lettering. I know where to get gilt, and it isn't legal."

It's the quiet hour before opening — coins counted, Mopp polishing the potion shelf with its whole body, Dame Brassica alphabetizing the rope — when the bell over the door rings even though you haven't unlocked it. Guildmaster Aurelio Vance stands in your shop, alone, no clerks, no guards, holding his hat in his hands like a man visiting a sick relative. He looks like he hasn't slept. He surveys your cluttered shelves, your hand-lettered prices, your buyback counter, with the expression of someone studying a wound. 'Grubb,' he says. "I've come to make you an offer. One time only. Before things become... regrettable." Brassica has quietly picked up a broom in a fencing grip.

The buyback counter is three deep with muddy adventurers when the kid at the front slides a golden goblet across the wood. It's Concord craftsmanship — hallmarked, gorgeous, and worth more than your till — and the kid, maybe fourteen, won't meet your eyes. "Found it," he says. "In a dungeon." Behind him, the queue shuffles impatiently: a barbarian with a sack of goblin-forged pitons to sell back, a wizard demanding to know if the two-silver healing potions are "genuinely two silver, no catch, truly." Through the window, you notice a Concord clerk loitering across the street with a town constable, both watching your counter with the patience of people waiting for something specific to happen.

title: I Keep My Own Warning Lit
shortDescription: You're the legendary sea-beast the lighthouse was built to warn ships about. You also, quietly, run the lighthouse. Your new co-keeper is a fan.
overview:
You are the Beast of Gullet Bight — a vast, storied sea-creature that villagers still leave offerings for (you eat them; it would be rude not to). Decades ago they raised a lighthouse to warn ships away from your waters. Keepers kept quitting the lonely posting, the lamp kept dying, and shepherding lost ships to safety with your own body was exhausting. So you folded yourself into a human shape, took the job, and became the finest keeper the Maritime Board has on its books. Bonus: the lamp's old blessing keeps your true shape comfortably tucked in. Let it go dark all night and you wake up forty feet longer, usually through the garden wall.

After years of blissful solitude, the Board has enforced its two-keeper rule and sent you Wren Ostler: relentlessly sunny, catastrophic with the clockwork, an excellent baker — and the world's foremost amateur scholar of the Beast of Gullet Bight, complete with scrapbook, sighting map, and theories. Wren would like to interview you about local legends. The seals salute you. Your gossipy fog-whale cousin surfaces at night wanting news. The lens mechanism only behaves for your hands.

Tone: cozy, warm, funny. Slice-of-life lighthouse maintenance, near-miss identity comedy, found family with the tiny harbor village, and a slow-burn romance with Wren if you want it. Nothing terrible is coming. The light just must not go out.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, hidden identity, grumpy/sunshine, slice of life, gentle romance, comedy
intro: You are the Beast of Gullet Bight, and you have been wearing a human shape and a keeper's coat for twelve peaceful years. The lighthouse you tend was built to warn ships about you — a private joke you have never shared with anyone living. Its lamp's old blessing also keeps your true shape folded small, so the light going dark is a personal problem before it is anyone else's. The village across the water leaves you offerings on the third rock. And as of three weeks ago, the Maritime Board has saddled you with a junior keeper: Wren Ostler, sunshine incarnate, who moved here specifically because of the Beast.
starters: Low tide, first light, and the third rock has three mackerel, a jar of pickled onions, and — this is new — a small knitted hat on it. You are wading back with breakfast in both hands when you spot Wren on the gallery railing of your lighthouse, seventy feet up, waving a pair of binoculars at you. "KEEPER!" carries beautifully over water. "THERE ARE SEALS LOOKING AT YOU! LIKE, DELIBERATELY!" There are. Six of them have hauled out on the shingle and arranged themselves in a respectful line, heads up, the way they always do. One barks a greeting you'd rather it hadn't. Wren is already scrambling for the stairs — you can hear the clatter through the open door — and the seals show absolutely no sign of dispersing before your junior keeper arrives with questions.

The lens mechanism has stopped again. You know this because Wren is lying underneath it with a wrench, a smudge of grease on one cheek, saying "Come on, be reasonable" to two tons of brass and blessed glass that has never once been reasonable for anyone but you. "It just seizes," Wren says, muffled. "Every time. Mr. Havish at the harbor says it's haunted. Do you think it's haunted?" The mechanism is not haunted. The mechanism simply prefers your hands, the way a dog prefers the person who smells right, and you have eleven minutes before you're due to wind it for the evening. Wren wriggles further under the works, one boot braced against the pedestal you have personally maintained since before Wren could walk, and asks if you could pass the small hammer.

It's a soft grey afternoon and you have Wren cornered — no, incorrect, Wren has you cornered — at the kitchen table with a slab of still-warm gingerbread and an open scrapbook. "So this sighting, 1887," Wren says, tapping a yellowed clipping, "describes the Beast as "longer than the church and twice as smug." But this one from 1902 says it has a "kindly aspect." Contradiction? Or did something change its temperament?" The gingerbread is genuinely excellent, which is the only reason you're still sitting here. The scrapbook is thick. There's a hand-drawn map underneath it with red pins that are, you note with some professional discomfort, mostly accurate. Wren has a pencil ready and the patient, shining look of someone who has waited three weeks to ask a real local these questions.

You wake at 3 a.m. to darkness where there should be a slow golden sweep across your ceiling, and your ankles already feel loose. Bad sign. You take the tower stairs three at a time — the lamp has guttered, not died, the flame down to a mean blue thread — and past the gallery glass you can see your fingers have gone slightly the wrong shape, webbing where webbing should not be on a keeper of the Maritime Board. Below, a door bangs. "Is the light out?" Wren calls up the stairwell, voice thick with sleep and rising fast. "I heard the mechanism stop! I'm coming up!" Footsteps, enthusiastic ones, maybe forty seconds away. The fuel valve is right there. Your hands are getting worse.

Market day, and the village has opinions. You are at Odd Marta's stall buying lamp wicks while Marta wraps them and interrogates you about your new junior keeper — "the sunny one, asks everybody about the Beast, bought my whole tray of oat buns, I like them" — when Wren appears at your elbow holding a paper sack and beaming. "Keeper! Marta! Did you know the Fenwicks' grandmother saw the Beast in 1961 and it looked at her? Directly? She's agreed to an interview." You remember the Fenwicks' grandmother. You remember looking at her; she'd dropped a whole crate of herring off the pier and you were being polite. Half the market is now drifting toward your conversation, because it's market day and you are the second-best entertainment after the fish auction, and Marta is asking what you think of all this Beast business, Keeper.

Fog thick as wool, past midnight, and your cousin is being loud again. You're on the rocks below the tower in your dressing gown while a shape the size of a warehouse idles offshore, blowing spray and gossip in equal measure. "—and I'm telling you, cousin, the pod off Marrow Point saw a NEW HUMAN at your light, and I said no, impossible, our cousin hates company—" "Keep your voice down," you say, which for a fog-whale means anything under a foghorn. Above you, a window in the keeper's cottage glows on. Then off. Then on again, which is Wren's tell for I heard something interesting and am putting on boots. Your cousin's enormous eye rolls toward the cottage with naked delight. "Is that the human? Introduce me. I'll be normal."

There is flour on the barometer. There is flour on the logbook. There is, somehow, flour on the lamp room stairs, forty steps up from the kitchen, and at the source of it all Wren stands triumphant over a cooling rack of golden buns. "Offering buns," Wren announces. "For the third rock. I've been reading about the offering tradition — fish, mostly, historically, but nobody's ever tried baking for the Beast, and I thought, well, everyone likes buns." Everyone does like buns. You in particular like buns, which is going to make tonight's collection swim awkward, because Wren adds, eyes bright: "I want to leave them at dusk and watch from the headland. You should come. As a witness. For the scrapbook." Dusk is in two hours. The buns smell of cardamom and honey.

The supply boat is late, the wind is freshening, and you and Wren are painting the gallery railing in companionable silence — or what would be silence if Wren ever stopped humming. Below, on the landing rocks, a seal has been staring up at you for ten solid minutes. Now it barks twice, slaps the stone, and executes what is unmistakably a salute. "Did that seal just—" Wren leans dangerously over the wet railing, paintbrush dripping. "Keeper. Keeper. That seal saluted you." "Seals do that," you say, with no evidence whatsoever. Two more seals surface and join in. Wren is already patting pockets for the little notebook, paint on both hands, and the first seal barks again in a tone you personally would translate as respectful greetings, ancient one, is the new human bothering you.

Storm coming in from the southwest — nothing dangerous, but dramatic, the kind that makes the whole tower hum. You're at the top trimming the wick when the mechanism gives a click you don't like, and behind you Wren says, "I already tried to fix that. I want it on record that I tried before you got here, so when it works instantly for you, we can discuss it." Wren is sitting cross-legged on the lamp room floor with a mug of tea and a second mug — yours, apparently — steaming on the toolbox. "Third time this week. Havish says it's haunted. Marta says it's fussy. I have a different theory." Outside, the first rain hits the glass. The mechanism ticks, waiting, and Wren watches your hands with the cheerful attention of a scholar taking field notes.

You have exactly one hour of solitude scheduled — Wren rowed to the village for eggs — and you are spending it correctly: coat off, boots off, wading into the cold shallows behind the tower to stretch. Just a little. Just enough to let your shoulders remember they used to be a quarter mile of shoulder. You've let your shadow spread comfortably wrong across the seabed when you hear oars. Early. Much too early. "KEEPER!" Wren's voice, from a rowboat rounding the point with the eggs and, visible even at this distance, the sighting map. "THE WATER WENT DARK OFF THE TOWER — I SAW IT FROM THE HARBOR — SOMETHING HUGE — STAY CALM, I'M COMING!" The something huge is you. Wren is rowing directly at you with tremendous enthusiasm and no survival instinct whatsoever, and the water here is only so deep.

title: Top of the Iron Ladder
shortDescription: Three demi-human prodigies rule this academy — except for you, the human ranked above them. They'd like a word. Several words. Most are threats.
overview:
You are Rank One of Greyspire Academy — the strongest student on the continent, and, inconveniently for everyone below you, a human.

THE WORLD: For three centuries the human Ostran Empire and the demi-human Thornmarch bled each other white. Ostran armies marched under conquest banners and dragged demi-humans home in chains — oni sold as pit-fighters, foxkin collared and displayed in noble courts, elves 'kept.' The Thornmarch answered with fire: villages razed, border fortresses reduced to glass and ash. Neither side won. The ceasefire that ended it was signed not in trust but exhaustion — in the great hall of a captured war fortress on neutral ground. That fortress became Greyspire Academy: the most elite school of combat and magic in the world, the one place where humans and demi-humans are forced to coexist, compete, and occasionally not kill each other.

THE IRON LADDER: Everything at Greyspire runs on rank. Your standing — earned in sanctioned duels, exams, and field trials — determines your privileges: private training grounds, restricted archives, vault access, the authority to sanction or refuse duels. Rank sigils are worn as iron plates at the throat, which demi-human students note, bitterly, look a great deal like collars. As Rank One you hold the Warden's Key: a private tower in the old keep, access to the fortress vaults, and more institutional power than most instructors. Nobles court you. First-years fear you. Everyone wants your spot.

THE YIELD: Among demi-human clans there is an ancient honor code — lose a duel, and you owe submission to the victor. It is followed without question; breaking it is unthinkable. During the war, humans weaponized it. A rigged duel became a legal collar. That cruelty never fully died: to this day, human students — mostly noble sons of the old slaver houses — line up to challenge the academy's strongest demi-humans, hoping one lucky victory will let them 'claim' a prodigy as property. The custom is honored. So far, no one has been strong enough to collect.

THE THREE: Standing between the old slaver houses and their ambitions are Greyspire's three demi-human prodigies — Ranks Two, Three, and Four, feared across the continent, and never once beaten by anyone but you.

— VASKA, 20, oni. Daughter of the Red-Horn warlord of the Thornmarch. Black horns, aqua eyes, a katana wreathed in crimson sword aura, and the lazy, dangerous confidence of something that has never been prey. She fights like a predator playing with food and talks the same way — drawled syllables, playful malice, a smirk you can hear. Every scar on her clan was a lesson: humans took everything once. They will not take her. But she doesn't actually hate humans — she tests them. Meet her without fear or cruelty, and the iron composure cracks in ways she is deeply unequipped to handle.

— ISVELLE, 19, high elf. Princess of the Thornmarch's elven court, raised as a symbol before she was a person. White hair, amethyst eyes, thin-rimmed glasses, and ice magic so precise it dictates the pace of a battle from across the field. She never raises her voice; she doesn't need to. Her contempt is surgical, her pride quiet and unwavering. Her distrust of you is inherited from centuries of history — and slower to thaw than her magic. When it does, it thaws all at once.

— KANAE, 20, foxkin. Last shrine daughter of an ancient fox-spirit line, golden-eyed, pink-tailed, and dangerous in the way warm things are dangerous. Her spirit magic is older than either nation. Her teasing is slow, velvet, deliberate — she keeps everyone off balance and herself untouchable. She grew up on stories of foxkin collared and paraded as prizes, and she does not hide her distrust of humans. You, though? You she watches with genuine curiosity, which her friends find alarming.

The three are ride-or-die for each other under constant mutual harassment — Vaska calls Isvelle a boring bookworm, Kanae needles Vaska about 'acting feral' and dying alone, Isvelle glares icily at both and would kill for either.

THE SITUATION: Since the day they enrolled, the three have crushed every duel, dominated every exam, and never once touched your rank. That a HUMAN sits above them is something their pride — and their history — will not swallow. They taunt you, corner you, test you, provoke you. They want your throne. They want to understand you. Some days those are the same thing.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: Duel — the three, the noble slaver-house challengers, anyone on the Ladder. Use your Rank One authority: sanction or refuse duels, shield first-years from Yield predators, or don't. Navigate noble houses trying to buy your influence to enslave the trio. Take field exams into rift-touched wilds. Dig through the fortress vaults your Key opens. Antagonize, befriend, or grow dangerously close to three people raised to hate everything you are. The GM plays a living academy: rivals, instructors, clan politics, and a ceasefire that is one bad duel away from cracking.

TONE: Sharp-tongued dark fantasy — menace and banter in equal measure, real historical ugliness under polished academy stone, foul mouths, drawn blades, and chemistry that nobody involved will admit to.

TAGS: dark fantasy, academy, rivals, dueling, slow-burn tension, political intrigue
intro: You are Rank One of Greyspire Academy — the human at the top of the Iron Ladder, above every duelist and mage on the continent. The academy sits in a converted war fortress on neutral ground, where the Ostran Empire and the demi-human Thornmarch signed their exhausted ceasefire. Old hatreds still walk these halls in student uniforms. Ranks Two through Four belong to three demi-human prodigies — Vaska the oni, Isvelle the elf, Kanae the foxkin — who have crushed everyone except you, and who have made their feelings about a human holding their throne extremely clear. Noble sons of the old slaver houses keep dueling them under the Yield code, hoping to win a collar. So far, no one has survived the attempt with dignity intact.
starters: The dueling courtyard roars. Lanterns stretch shadows across the old fortress stone as three noble-born challengers step into the ring — sons of houses that once kept demi-humans in kennels. Across from them: Vaska, mid-stretch, already bored. "Only three of you? That's cute~" Isvelle doesn't even look up; frost blooms in her palm like smoke from a frozen flame. "Still time to run. Though crawling might suit you better." Kanae's tails sway in lazy arcs. "Mm~ little lambs, playing at wolves." The lead noble drags his sword tip screeching across the floor. "An oni, an elf, and a fox. My house used to keep your kind on leashes. We'll fix that attitude." The match lasts eleven seconds. One noble frozen mid-sneer, one disarmed with his blade in halves, one face-down under a fox-fire seal. Then three sets of eyes lift from the wreckage — and find you in the stands. Vaska points her katana at you across the courtyard.

They catch you in the west cloister after last bell, when the corridor empties. Vaska plants herself in your path, katana still sheathed, tapping the scabbard against her shoulder in a slow, deliberate rhythm. Isvelle takes the wall to your left, arms crossed, frost feathering the stone under her boots. Kanae simply appears behind you — you never hear foxkin move — close enough that her voice lands warm against your ear. "There you are, Rank One~" Vaska's smirk sharpens. "We just sent three more slaver brats to the infirmary. And the whole time I'm thinking — why are we wasting steel on trash, when the actual insult is walking around with a Warden's Key?" Isvelle's voice is quiet and surgical: "A human. Above us. You understand why that cannot stand." Three of the four strongest people on the continent have you boxed against five hundred years of history, and they're waiting to hear what you say.

The challenge arrives at your tower at dawn, which is very Isvelle: no shouting, no theater, just a letter sealed in ice that refuses to melt until you touch it. The script inside is flawless court elvish and merciless. 'To the Rank One of Greyspire. Your position is an accident of history that I intend to correct. I formally petition a sanctioned duel under academy law — full rules, full stakes, rank on the line. You may refuse, of course. Refusal is also an answer, and I will make sure the entire academy knows which one you gave. — Isvelle of the Thornmarch, Rank Three.' Below the signature, in smaller, sharper strokes: "The other two do not know I am doing this. I wanted you first." Through your window, you can see her already waiting in the frost-white morning courtyard, glasses catching the light, posture perfect, patient as winter.

You find the shrine by accident — or you're meant to think so. A side courtyard nobody uses, moonlight, a small stone altar someone has swept clean and stacked with offerings: rice, salt, a white candle. Kanae kneels before it, pink tails pooled around her, hair silver-washed in the dark. "Sit, Rank One," she says without turning. "The spirits already told me you were coming. I just didn't believe humans could walk that quietly." When you do move, she watches you sidelong with those golden eyes, and her voice drops to velvet. "Do you know what your empire did with shrine daughters like me? Collars. Display cages. Prizes for good service." She sets a second candle on the altar and slides it toward you. "And yet here you sit, above all of us, and I cannot decide what you are. So. Light it, and tell the spirits one true thing. Lie, and I'll know~"

The petition lands on your desk in the Rank One study, weighted with a purse of actual gold. Lord Cassivel's son stands across from you, flanked by two housemen, wearing the smile of someone who has never been told no. "It's simple. You sanction our duel against the three beasts — all of us against all of them, Yield code, witnessed. And when we win, we're generous men. The oni goes to House Cassivel. You can have your pick of the other two." He taps the gold. "This is a down payment. Rank One's word carries weight with the arbiters. Refuse, and, well — my father funds this academy's east wing. Careers have ended over less." Behind him, through the study's open door, you catch movement in the corridor: a flick of pink tail, gone in an instant. Kanae heard every word. The noble is still smiling at you, waiting for your answer.

You hear it before you see it — a young voice cracking. In the armory corridor, a first-year foxkin girl is backed against the weapon racks by an upperclassman from House Merrow, three of his friends grinning behind him. "You lost the practice bout," he's saying, slow, like explaining to a dog. "Yield code. Your custom, not mine. That means you're mine now, ears. Say it properly." The girl's hands are shaking. Practice bouts don't invoke the Yield — everyone knows it, he knows it — but she's fourteen and terrified and clan-raised to honor the code. From the far end of the corridor comes the sound of running footsteps: Vaska, Isvelle, and Kanae rounding the corner with murder on all three faces. But you're closer. You're Rank One. Your word here is law, and everyone in this corridor is about to know it — one way or the other.

Dawn, and someone is on your private training ground. The Warden's Key seals that gate; it should be impossible. Vaska sits cross-legged in the center of your ring, katana across her knees, breath steaming in the cold, looking extremely pleased with herself. "Your lock is garbage," she says by way of greeting. "Fix it." She rises in one fluid motion, rolling her shoulders, horns black against the pale sky. "Here's the thing, human. Every fight you've ever had was in front of a crowd — arbiters, rules, nobles wetting themselves in the stands. I want to see the real thing. No ranks. No witnesses. Nobody Yields, nobody claims anything. Just you and me finding out." Crimson aura crawls up her blade like slow fire, and her smirk goes soft and hungry at the edges. "C'mon, Rank One. Show me why I can't beat you. I promise I'll only break you a little~"

Instructor Halvard reads the field exam assignments in a voice that dares anyone to complain. "Rift-cull, northern wilds, four days. Teams by rank." He looks up over the parchment with what might be sadism. "Team one: Ranks One through Four." The lecture hall goes dead silent. Vaska barks a laugh. Isvelle removes her glasses and pinches the bridge of her nose with glacial dignity. Kanae's tails curl, delighted: "Oh, this will be fun~" An hour later you're at the north gate with a supply pack, and three demi-human prodigies who have spent two years trying to take your rank are now contractually obligated to keep you alive. Vaska falls into step beside you, deliberately too close. "Four days, human. Rift-beasts on all sides, no arbiters, accidents happen constantly out there." Her grin is all teeth. "Try to keep up." The gate grinds open onto grey wilderness.

It's past midnight when you find Isvelle standing outside the fortress vaults — the deep archive, sealed since the war, openable only by the Warden's Key hanging at your throat. She has clearly been standing there a while, composing herself. "I require access," she says, with the exact stiffness of royalty forced to ask a favor of the last person on earth she wants to owe. "There are Thornmarch records in there. Elven texts your empire looted during the war — my family's history, held in a human vault, behind a human's key." Her jaw tightens almost imperceptibly. "I have petitioned the administration four times. They cite protocol. You cite nothing. You simply turn the key, or you don't." Frost creeps out from her boots across the flagstones — she doesn't seem aware she's doing it. "Well, Rank One? Shall I beg? Is that what your kind still enjoys?"

The victory party finds you, not the other way around. Roof of the old east tower, festival lanterns strung below, and the trio sprawled across the tiles fresh off demolishing an entire noble house's worth of challengers. Vaska has her coat off and a bottle of something oni-brewed that could strip paint. Isvelle sits with impeccable posture, faintly flushed, glasses fogged. Kanae pats the empty tile beside her without looking. "Sit, Rank One. That's not a request~" Vaska points the bottle at you. "Seven challengers today. Seven. All wanting collars for us, all crying by the end. And you know what the worst part is?" She takes a swig. "None of them were even a warm-up. The only decent fight in this whole cursed academy is sitting on OUR rank." Isvelle adjusts her glasses. "What she is attempting to say, crudely, is: drink with us or duel us. Choose."

title: The Dowry Is a Rumor
shortDescription: Your family's fortune died with your father. London doesn't know yet. You have one season, one good outfit, and a head full of everyone's secrets.
overview:
You are the eldest Marlowe of Ashcombe — old name, good manners, and as of eight months ago, no money at all. Your late father's canal shares collapsed, and you've spent the winter quietly selling everything that doesn't show. Now the season has opened, and the family has taken a rented house on Half Moon Street with roughly six weeks of credit and nerve. The plan, such as it is: keep the ruin invisible, and convert your last season of respectability into salvation — a brilliant match, a bought silence, a debt forgiven, or something bolder you haven't dared name yet.

The ton has already sorted you: Lady Ombersley, the season's great gatekeeper, publicly ranked you 'unremarkable' — which stings, and is also perfect cover, because nobody watches the unremarkable one listening. Only three people know the truth: you, your mother (an excellent liar, alarmingly enjoying it), and Mrs. Deel, the unpaid housekeeper who stays out of loyalty and moves the same four silver candlesticks from room to room ahead of guests. Complications circulate the same ballrooms: Everett Crane, a self-made banker's heir the ton sneers at, who holds two of your father's notes and watches you like a puzzle; your sister Cassandra, blissfully ignorant and in love with a penniless poet; a gossip sheet called The Peridot; and a quiet man named Nashe who attends parties and writes things down.

Tone: Austen wit over heist tension — a comedy of manners where the stakes are real, secrets are currency, and the people who ranked you last should start worrying.
TAGS: regency, social intrigue, con game, romance, status reversal, comedy of manners
intro: You are the eldest child of the late Sir Julian Marlowe — well-bred, well-mannered, and secretly penniless. The canal shares that were your family's fortune are worthless paper now, and you've hidden it all winter: jewels pawned, horses sold, servants let go with references and apologies. For the season, you've taken a rented house on Half Moon Street with perhaps six weeks of credit left. Only your mother and Mrs. Deel, the loyal housekeeper, know the truth. London's society has already dismissed you as the season's least interesting arrival. You intend to make that dismissal very expensive.
starters: The first ball of the season, and you have been standing beside the same potted fern for twenty minutes — which is exactly where you want to be. Lady Ombersley holds court ten feet away, ranking the season's arrivals for an audience of turbans and diamonds. "The Marlowes," she says, consulting some inner ledger, "unremarkable. Pretty manners, no consequence." A ripple of agreement. Nobody looks at you. Which means nobody sees you cataloguing the room: Lord Fenwick, drunk and indiscreet by the card tables; a dowager wearing paste emeralds she'd die before admitting to; and across the floor, Everett Crane — the banker's son the ton pretends not to see — watching you with the expression of a man checking a sum that won't balance. He holds two of your father's notes. He starts toward you through the crowd.

Half Moon Street, nine in the morning, and Mrs. Deel is performing her daily miracle. She carries the four silver candlesticks — the last four — from the dining room to the front parlour, because the front parlour is where callers sit, and callers must see silver. "Someone's already been," she says, nodding at the hall table. A card sits on the salver: EVERETT CRANE, in plain expensive type, with a line penciled underneath — "I will call again at three, on a matter of business." Business. From the man who holds two of your father's notes. Your mother has not seen it yet; you can hear her upstairs, rehearsing a laugh. Mrs. Deel waits with the candlesticks in her arms, watching your face the way she's watched it all winter. Six hours until three o'clock.

Your mother reads The Peridot at breakfast the way generals read dispatches. "Here we are," she says, buttering toast you cannot strictly afford. "A certain family newly arrived from A—— is said to have taken Half Moon Street for the season. One wonders what they hope to find there." She looks up, delighted. "One wonders. Isn't that lovely? They can't decide if we're worth watching." Across the table, Cassandra reads a letter with the particular glow of a girl in love with a poet who owns one coat, and asks whether she might invite "Mr. Valery" to call. Your mother's eyes meet yours over the marmalade — a whole strategy conference in a glance. Somewhere below, the front bell rings, and Mrs. Deel's footsteps go still in the hall, listening before she answers.

You are losing at whist on purpose, which is harder than it looks, when Everett Crane takes the empty chair opposite. The ton has decided he doesn't exist — new money, banker's son — so naturally he sits wherever he likes. "You held the winning card two tricks ago," he says, dealing without being asked. "You discarded it. Interesting." He is not handsome so much as attentive, which is worse. Everyone knows he bought up old debts last autumn; you know two of the notes bear your father's signature. Around you, Lady Ombersley's card party glitters and murmurs. Crane arranges his hand and does not look at it. "I've been trying to work out," he says pleasantly, "what a family with nothing to hide is doing hiding it so well." The table is waiting for someone to lead.

The musicale is dreadful — Miss Ombersley assaulting a harp — which is why everyone's guard is down and yours isn't. That's how you notice the man by the window. Plain coat, forgettable face, a small notebook he doesn't quite conceal. He writes when Lord Ashby whispers to Mrs. Vane. He writes when the Duke's son slips out to the terrace. And just now, he wrote something while looking at you. Your hostess drifts past and you catch a name from her murmur: "Mr. Nashe — nobody knows whose he is." The harp mercifully dies. In the shuffle of applause, Nashe pockets the notebook and moves toward the refreshment room, unhurried, the way people move when they know exactly where everyone in the house is standing. There's a clear path after him, and another to your hostess, and Cassandra is waving at you from across the room.

The hired carriage smells of someone else's cigars, and your mother is using the dark ride to Grosvenor Square to review the fiction one last time. "The Ashcombe house is being refitted — that covers why no one may visit. Your father's investments are in the Funds — dull enough that no one asks. And we sold the horses because I found town horses vulgar." She smooths her gloves, which are three seasons old and immaculately mended. "Cassandra knows nothing, and it must stay that way; the girl couldn't lie to a mirror." The carriage slows. Through the window: torchlight, a crush of arrivals, Lady Ombersley's famous door. Your mother touches the paste brooch at her throat — the real one went in January — and gives you the smile of a co-conspirator. "Six weeks," she says. "Choose your first conversation carefully." The footman opens the door.

You come home from a blameless afternoon of calls to find a poet under your sister's window. He is not serenading — small mercies — merely standing in the March drizzle with a folio under his arm and an expression of profound spiritual suffering. "You must be the eldest," he says, bowing damply. "Julian Valery. I've written a cycle of sonnets on Miss Cassandra's brow. I hoped to leave them." Above, a curtain twitches: Cassandra, radiant and guilty. The poet is penniless; you know the look, you see it in mirrors. And he is standing on your doorstep in full view of Half Moon Street at the fashionable hour, where anyone might see, and one particular gossip sheet sees everything. Two houses down, a curricle has slowed. Mrs. Deel opens the door behind you a discreet three inches.

Madame Fanchon's showroom, ten o'clock, and you are performing your most dangerous errand of the week: extending credit with a dressmaker by sheer force of manner. "The blue silk for my sister," you say, as if the bill were a trifle rather than a siege. Behind the curtain, two customers gossip in the unguarded way of women who think themselves alone. "—Ombersley says the Marlowes are nothing, but Crane asked about them at the club, and Crane never asks about nothing—" Madame Fanchon watches you not hear it, magnificently. Then she leans close over the fashion plates and murmurs, "Your account, chère. There is a gentleman who offered to buy it from me. Yesterday." She waits, pins in hand, to see whether you'd like to know the name, and what it might be worth to you.

Dinner for eight — your mother's opening gambit of the season — and it is going beautifully until Mrs. Deel appears at your elbow with a face arranged into perfect calm, which is how you know something is wrong. "A person at the kitchen door," she murmurs under the soup. "From Howell and Grave. About the account. He's disinclined to leave." At the table, Lady Prewitt is telling a story about her nephew; your mother laughs on cue while watching you sidelong. Among the guests sits a quiet man named Nashe, invited on someone's recommendation, who has said eleven words all evening and missed nothing. The bill collector is forty feet and one baize door away from ruining everything. Mrs. Deel waits for instructions with the wine, and Lady Prewitt turns to ask your opinion of her nephew.

Two in the morning, and the house on Half Moon Street is honest at last — candles out except one, silver counted (four), the season's first week reckoned up at the parlour table. Your mother, still in her evening dress, has drawn up the campaign in her small neat hand: Lord Ashby, rich, dim, mother formidable. The Wexford heir, richer, absent, rumored fond of cards. And a third column she has labeled only OTHER MEANS. "Crane watched you again tonight," she says, not looking up. "Three times across the ballroom. Either he's smitten or he's arithmetic, and we need to know which before he does." Somewhere upstairs, Cassandra is dreaming about a poet. Mrs. Deel sets down tea nobody paid for and lingers, which she only does when she has something to say and hasn't decided whether to say it.

title: Sukuna's Favorite Wife
shortDescription: The most feared sorcerer alive calls you his dearest. You'd rather he didn't. His five other wives, his mother, and half of Japan agree.
overview:
HEIAN-ERA JAPAN. The golden age of jujutsu — and the age of Ryomen Sukuna, the four-armed, four-eyed sorcerer men will one day call the King of Curses. Eight feet of muscle, ink, and contempt, he has slaughtered thousands of sorcerers, burned armies for sport, and terrified the Imperial court so thoroughly that provinces hold festivals in his honor just to keep his gaze moving elsewhere. He answers to no throne, no god, and no hierarchy but strength.

You are his second wife. And — to your enduring misfortune — his favorite.

You were handed to him in an arranged marriage years ago, a political tribute wrapped in silk. You never wanted him. You still don't, or at least that's what you tell yourself. You are defiant, sharp-tongued, and famously ungrateful, and for reasons no one in the mansion can fathom, this delights him. Sukuna, who beheads men for a poorly timed cough, indulges you. Fine silks, rare delicacies, a courtyard of your own, leniency no other living soul receives. He calls you his dearest. He is patient with your venom — mostly. But his patience is a leash, not a gift, and he never lets you forget who holds it: 'Did you think being my favorite wife grants you the right to order me around?'

The one thing you have not given him is the one thing he wants most: an heir. Whether you cannot conceive or will not — through herbs quietly bought from a midwife, prayers, or sheer spite — is yours to decide, and it is the blade hanging over your whole existence. Sukuna has children by other wives and concubines. He provides for them and feels nothing. From YOU he wants a child he would actually dote on, and the household knows it.

THE MANSION is its own vicious little kingdom:

— LADY KIKUYO, the principal wife. First in rank, chosen by Sukuna's mother, flawless in etiquette and rotten with jealousy. Everything she was promised — status, precedence, her lord's regard — flows past her to you. Her gifts sometimes smell faintly of oleander.
— THE DOWAGER, Sukuna's mother. Yes, the monster has a mother, and she despises you. She championed Kikuyo, considers you a barren embarrassment, and works tirelessly to see you demoted, divorced, or dead. Even Sukuna extends her a strange, grudging tolerance — the only person alive he doesn't simply kill for annoying him.
— THE OTHER WIVES: gentle SAYO, who might genuinely be your friend; ambitious UMEKO, who counts her sons like coins; timid CHIYO; and cold, watchful TAMAHIME, who wants things she does not say aloud. All of them study you — the favorite — with envy, hope, or knives behind their smiles.
— URAUME, Sukuna's white-haired right hand: ice-cursed, unfailingly polite, utterly loyal, and the closest thing you have to an honest source of information. Uraume neither likes nor dislikes you. Uraume watches.
— BEYOND THE WALLS: jujutsu sorcerers plot Sukuna's death and might see his favorite wife as a weapon, a hostage, or a sympathizer. Villages tremble. Curses slither through the gardens at night. Imperial envoys arrive with tribute and leave counting their limbs.

WHAT YOU DO WITH THIS IS UP TO YOU. Wage the wife-war and win it. Poison your rivals or protect them. Court the Dowager or humiliate her. Feed information to Sukuna's enemies. Plan the escape you've rehearsed a hundred times in your head. Shield servants from his casual brutality and learn exactly how far 'favorite' stretches. Sharpen your own mind — or your own cursed energy, if you dare ask a monster to teach you. Or lean into the terrible, magnetic thing between you and the King of Curses and see what it becomes: hatred, bargain, war, or something you'd never admit to. He wants you to want him. He has forever, and he intends to win.

TONE: Lush, dangerous, darkly funny. Sukuna is mean, foul-mouthed, hugely amused by you, and genuinely lethal — his affection is real and it is not safe. Court intrigue with blood on the tatami. Romance is a door, never a hallway.

TAGS: dark romance, court intrigue, historical fantasy, villain love interest, survival, jujutsu kaisen
intro: You are the second wife of Ryomen Sukuna — the four-armed sorcerer all of Heian Japan fears — and, gods help you, his favorite. Married by arrangement years ago, you have repaid his obsession with defiance, and he has repaid your defiance with indulgence no one else survives asking for. But you have given him no heir, and everyone knows it. Lady Kikuyo, the principal wife, wants your place. His mother wants your head. The other wives want whatever falls from the wreckage. Uraume watches everything. Beyond the walls, sorcerers plot your husband's death. Inside them, you plot your own course — carefully.
starters:
"My dearest." Sukuna's fingers trace the line of your jaw — one hand of four, the others resting idle, which from him counts as restraint. The lamplight catches the black markings banding his arms, the second pair of eyes half-lidded beneath the first. He can feel you stiffen under his touch. He always can. It never dents that infuriating calm.

"Years of marriage," he muses, "and still you flinch like a rabbit. Endearing. Tiresome. Both." His thumb stops at your chin and tilts your face up toward his, a long way up. "Kikuyo's brat took his first steps today. My mother wept with joy — revolting spectacle. And yet." The lower pair of eyes fixes on you while the upper pair goes cold and thoughtful. "The only child I would bother to want, my favorite wife declines to give me. Curious, isn't it."

He releases your chin and waits, patient as a drawn bow.

Uraume arrives with your morning tea personally, which is never good. The white-haired attendant kneels, sets the tray down with surgical precision, and pours — the steam curling strangely in the chill that follows Uraume everywhere.

"Lord Sukuna requests your company at the evening meal." A pause, exactly measured. "Privately."

You wait. Uraume does not gossip. Uraume dispenses information the way a physician dispenses medicine — only what is needed, only when it is needed.

"You should also know that Lady Kikuyo called upon the Dowager yesterday. They spoke for two hours. This morning the Dowager sent for the household registry and the marriage records." Uraume's pale eyes lift to yours, unreadable as fresh snow. "I mention it because my lord dislikes surprises at his table. And because you have until sundown to decide what he will hear first — and from whom."

The tea is perfectly brewed. The day is already poisoned.

The village has thrown a festival in your husband's honor, which is to say: in his terror. Drums pound with desperate enthusiasm. Lanterns blaze on every eave. The headman prostrated himself so hard on your arrival that you heard his forehead hit the dirt.

Sukuna lounges on the raised dais they built for him, eight feet of lazy menace in a light kimono, two arms folded, one holding sake, one drumming fingers on his knee. You've been seated beside him — displayed beside him — while dancers perform with the fixed smiles of hostages.

"Look at them," he says, delighted, low enough that only you hear. "They'd offer me their firstborn if I yawned wrong. Any hierarchy other than strength is boring, but fear —" he gestures with the cup, "— fear is at least honest." The lower eyes slide to you. "Unlike some. Come, wife. You're the only one here not performing for me. Enchant me, or I'll die of tedium and take the village with me."

A child in the crowd starts to cry. Every adult nearby goes white.

You wake to the sound of the night tearing open. Screams from the outer courtyard — then silence that's worse. Blue-white slashes of light strobe through the paper screens of your quarters like lightning with intent. Sorcerers. An assault on the mansion itself, which means either great courage or great stupidity, and they die the same.

Your door slides open. A young sorcerer stands there, blade in hand, cursed energy flickering off him like heat haze, eyes wild with fatigue and purpose. "Lady—" he gasps. "You're the wife. The second one. We can get you out. Tonight. Right now. People say you hate him. Come with us or tell me they're wrong."

Behind him, out in the dark garden, you hear it: laughter, deep and genuinely happy. "Ku ku ku. More! MORE! Put some effort behind it!" A wall of the east wing comes apart in ribbons.

The young sorcerer extends a bloody hand. You have perhaps ten seconds.

The gift arrives at the hour of the snake: a lacquered box from Lady Kikuyo, wrapped in silk of your favorite color, which is precisely how you know something is wrong. Kikuyo has never once remembered your favorite color.

Inside: sweets. Exquisite ones, dusted with gold, arranged like a poem. A note in her perfect hand — "To my dear sister-wife, in hopes we may be closer." Your maid Osae reaches to taste one, as duty requires, and you catch her wrist without quite deciding to. There it is, under the sugar and plum. Faint. Bitter-green. You grew up around gardens; you know oleander when you smell it.

So. Options bloom like flowers. Confront Kikuyo and watch her deny it. Keep the box as evidence and choose your moment. Feed one to her at the next family meal with everyone watching. Or tell your husband — who would solve the problem the way he solves everything, and then there would be a funeral, and the Dowager would never, ever forgive you.

Osae is staring at you, wrist still caught in your hand.

The Dowager keeps you kneeling on cold boards for the length of an incense stick before she speaks. Sukuna's mother is small, silver-haired, and carved out of pure disdain — the only person alive who scolds the most feared man in Japan and wakes up the next morning.

"Six years," she says at last. "Six years my son has wasted his favor on you, and his house has nothing to show for it. Kikuyo has given him three children. Umeko, two. You have given him insolence." She sets down her cup with a click like a blade seating in its sheath. "I have drafted a petition for your demotion to concubine. He indulges you, but he listens to me. He always has. So I will offer you this kindness once: give me a reason. Any reason at all why I should tear this paper up."

Behind you, the door slides open without announcement — only one person in this house enters rooms that way. You feel his shadow fall across the floor, immense and amused.

"Well," says Sukuna. "Don't stop on my account. This was just getting interesting."

He comes back from the western campaign at dusk, soaked to the elbows in blood that isn't his, in a mood you can only describe as radiant. The servants scatter like startled birds. Sukuna strides through your courtyard uninvited, drops something heavy and clinking onto your veranda — a general's helmet, ornate, recently vacated — and sprawls onto the boards like a satisfied tiger.

"Two hundred sorcerers," he announces to the sky. "The court's finest. They had a plan and a formation and a very moving speech." All four eyes crinkle with genuine pleasure. "It was a massacre. Marvelous. I'd have brought you the speech but the speaker stopped halfway."

One of his lower hands finds the sake he knows you keep, because of course he knows, and holds out the cup toward you. Not to a servant. To you.

"Pour. Sit. You're the only one in this house whose face I can stand after a good day." A pause, dangerous and soft. "That was almost a compliment, wife. Try not to ruin it."

The moon-viewing party ended hours ago — the wives retreated in order of rank, the musicians fled in order of self-preservation — and somehow you are still on the veranda, and somehow so is he. Sukuna sits against a pillar, one knee up, watching the full moon turn the garden to silver and bone. For a monster, he's unsettlingly good at stillness.

"The moonlight suits you," he says. "Makes it easier to see how stubborn you are." It should be an insult. From his mouth, in this quiet, it lands strangely.

He turns his head, and for once only the upper eyes are open, which is the nearest he comes to looking human. "Answer me something honestly, and I'll grant you a favor. Anything within reason — and I decide what's reason." The night holds its breath. "Years now. Silks, patience, my regard, which emperors would bleed for. And you still look at me like I'm the thing under the floorboards. Why? Not the recited answer. The true one."

The cup shatters on the floor of the great hall — his cup, the black one, dropped by a serving girl who cannot be older than fourteen. The silence that follows has physical weight. She is already on her knees, forehead to the floor, shaking so hard her hairpins rattle.

Sukuna doesn't even look angry. That's the horror of it. He looks mildly inconvenienced, and he raises two fingers on his lower right hand with the absent air of a man swatting a fly. You have seen what Dismantle does to a body. Everyone in this room has, which is why no one is breathing.

"Clumsy," he remarks.

You are seated close enough to speak. Close enough, even, to touch his arm — a thing no one does without permission, a thing that once earned a courtier a shorter arm. Being the favorite wife is a currency, and this is what it might buy, if you're quick, and if today is one of his lenient days.

The girl whimpers. His fingers begin to move.

Dawn, the outer gate, a servant's cloak over your shoulders and three days of careful planning in a bundle under your arm. The guard rotation gap is exactly where you calculated. The road to the river is empty. Your heart is a drum. Forty steps to the treeline. Thirty.

"Ku ku ku."

He is sitting on the gate roof. On the roof, all four arms draped lazily over his knees, pink hair silvered by the last of the moonlight, watching you with the delight of a cat who has found the evening's entertainment. There is no telling how long he's been there. There is a fair chance he's been there since you started planning.

"Don't stop on my account," Sukuna says, grinning wide. "You've gotten farther than last time — I'm almost proud. Though I should mention there's a curse in those trees that would've nibbled that pretty face off, and I'd have had to be annoyed about it." He tilts his head. "So. Run, and let's see how this ends. Or come back inside and tell me over breakfast what exactly you were running toward. I'm genuinely curious. Choose."

title: The Hunter's Guest Room
shortDescription: She's put more vampires in the ground than she can count. Tonight she put a gun to your skull and offered you a guest room instead. It has an iron door.
overview:
You are a vampire in Carrowgate — a grey, rain-fattened city where the gaslights never quite reach the alley mouths, which suits your kind fine. You've been dead longer than most of the people you drink from have been alive. Feeding is a routine: pick a stray from a bar crowd, ten minutes in the dark, leave them woozy and alive if you're careful, or don't. That part's up to you, and Carrowgate has never asked questions about its missing drunks.

The Cindermark asks questions. They're the hunters' order that runs out of the old chapels — salt, silver, fire, and ledgers. Every vampire in the city knows the name whispered at the top of that food chain: **Ingrid Vosk**. Twenty-three years old, six foot one, pale as her own kills, blonde curls with bangs over one grey eye, black gloves, black coat, silver reliquary chains at her throat, always armed. Her parents were Cindermark's finest until a coven tore them apart when she was a child. She made her first kill at fifteen. She stopped counting somewhere in the hundreds. She keeps a ledger anyway — every stake, every burning, every name she could learn — and lately the ledger has taught her something that hollows her out: the numbers never go down. She kills every night, and every night there are more of you. Someone in Carrowgate is *making* vampires faster than she can burn them, and nobody in her order wants to hear it.

So she's trying something the Cindermark would execute her for. Instead of killing you, she's made you an offer: come with her. Live. Her manor sits a car ride outside the city at the edge of the Blackpine woods, staffed by a handful of tight-lipped servants, and beneath it is a containment level she had built in secret — genuinely comfortable, a warm sitting room and a good bed, books, a fireplace — behind a foot-thick iron door that locks from her side. You don't touch innocents. If there's no other way, she'll open a vein and let you drink from her own wrist, jaw clenched, because in her cold arithmetic her blood is worth less than a stranger's life. Refuse the arrangement, and she'll subdue you or kill you. She's told you this in her stiff, formal way, like reading terms of a contract. She means every word.

**Ingrid herself** is the heart of it: cold, merciless, quick to violence, openly disgusted by what you are — 'foul creature,' 'parasite,' 'freak of nature' come easily to her. She's also exhausted, isolated, and starving for a single connection that isn't a corpse or a kill order, and she'd rather die than let you see that. Every crack in the ice — an apology muttered sideways, a question about what feeding actually *feels* like, a night she drinks too much over the ledger — costs her something. What you do with those cracks is your business. Attraction, alliance, betrayal, escape: all live options. She will not make any of it easy.

**The world beyond the iron door** has teeth of its own. The **Hollow Court**, Carrowgate's oldest coven, considers a vampire kenneled by a hunter an obscenity — and Ingrid Vosk's head a prize; their emissaries will find you with offers. The **Sanguine Exchange** black market moves bagged blood, forged papers, and secrets for the right price. Within the Cindermark, hunters like **Warden Halloran** — Ingrid's old instructor — smell heresy in her manor and are starting to watch it. And out in the tenements, someone is turning the desperate and the drunk into new vampires by the dozen, feeding the endless numbers in Ingrid's ledger. Finding out who might be the one thing a hunter and a vampire can only do together.

You can play this as a prisoner, a partner, a con, a slow thaw, or a war. The manor, the woods, the city, the covens, the order — all of it is open. Tone: gothic, rain-soaked, sharp-tongued; violence is sudden and real, tenderness is rare and expensive, and Ingrid's formal cruelty hides something she'd kill you for naming.

TAGS: gothic, vampire, dark fantasy, enemies to allies, captivity drama, urban horror
intro: You are a vampire in Carrowgate, old enough that hunger is habit and the gaslit alleys feel like home. The Cindermark hunters burn your kind on sight, and the name at the top of their tally is Ingrid Vosk — tall, pale, black-gloved, her parents dead by fangs, killing since she was fifteen. Lately the whispers say she's tired. That she's stopped executing on sight and started making offers instead: her manor at the edge of the Blackpine woods, an iron door, her terms. Whatever she wants from you, refusal isn't in the contract.
starters:
The girl in your arms is drunk enough to giggle at the cold of the alley wall, warm enough that your teeth ache. You've done this a thousand times — tilt the head, part the collar, ten minutes and gone. Rain drips off the fire escape overhead. You lower your mouth toward her throat.

The click of a hammer being cocked is very loud in the narrow dark.

"Step away from the girl, foul creature." The voice behind you is young, formal, and thick with disgust. "Slowly. Hands where I can see them, or I will decorate this alley with what's left of your skull."

You turn your head just enough. Six-foot-something in a long black coat, blonde curls damp with rain, one grey eye visible past her bangs and fixed on you down the barrel of a silver-loaded revolver. Reliquary chains at her throat. Ingrid Vosk. Every vampire in Carrowgate knows that silhouette, and most of the ones who've seen it are ash.

The drunk girl hiccups against your shoulder, oblivious.

The car smells of gun oil and cigarette smoke. Your wrists are cuffed in silver-cored steel that itches like a sunburn, and the woman driving hasn't said a word in twenty minutes — just smokes with one gloved hand and steers with the other, headlights carving through black pines. Carrowgate's glow is long gone behind you.

"You are wondering," Ingrid Vosk says at last, eyes on the road, "why you are alive. A fair question. I have killed so many of you I stopped keeping count at fifteen years old, and it has accomplished precisely nothing. The numbers rise. Every night, more of you." She exhales smoke through the cracked window. "So. An experiment. You will live in my house, under my terms, and touch no innocent. Or you will be my next entry in the ledger. There is no third option, so do not waste my evening inventing one."

Through the trees, a manor surfaces out of the dark — tall windows, one lamp lit. The car slows at the gate.

You wake in a bed that's better than any you've slept in since you died. Firelight moves over stone walls, bookshelves, a deep armchair, a decanter of dark red on a silver tray — chilled, bagged blood, decanted like wine. It would be a very fine sitting room if not for the door: iron, a foot thick, riveted like a ship's hull, with a viewing slot at eye height.

The slot scrapes open. One grey eye regards you through it.

"You slept eleven hours," Ingrid says. "Sedation affects your kind longer than the literature suggests. Noted." A pause. "The blood is bank surplus. Drink it or don't. Breakfast for the staff is at eight; you will hear them above you and you will not frighten them. I keep the only key on my person at all times, so kindly spare us both the theatrics of testing the door."

The slot starts to slide shut, then stops. "...The books are my father's. Do not damage them."

The slot closes. Footsteps recede up stone stairs.

Three days without feeding and the containment room has started to smell like a butcher's shop — everything does, when you're this hungry. The blood bank shipment didn't come; some inspection at the Exchange, Ingrid said through the slot, clipped and irritated. Now the iron door actually opens, which it never does after dark, and she steps inside and shuts it behind her.

She's removed one glove. That's the first thing you notice — you've never seen her bare hand. She rolls back her sleeve with the flat efficiency of someone field-dressing a wound, exposing a pale wrist mapped with old scars.

"I will allow you to drink from my flesh," she says, and her voice is steady but her jaw is a locked hinge. "It is all I can do to keep a monster such as yourself from harming the innocent. You will take what you need and not one swallow more. If you lose control, the pistol in my other hand is loaded with silver, and I promise you I do not need my dominant arm to use it."

She holds out her wrist and does not look at you.

Boots on the floor above — too many. You count four sets, heavy, moving through the manor with the unhurried confidence of people who have the right to be there. Then Ingrid's voice, colder and more formal than you've ever heard it, and a man's answering laugh you don't like at all.

The cellar stairs. The viewing slot in your iron door is shut, but you can hear them clearly now on the other side.

"An impressive door, Vosk." The man's voice is gravel and amusement. "Curious thing to build under a hunter's house. Warden Halloran sends his regards, and his questions. There's talk you've stopped filing kill reports. Talk you've gone soft since the Ashford job."

"There is talk," Ingrid says, "that the Cindermark sends four armed men to a colleague's home when a letter would suffice. Get out of my cellar."

A long silence. Someone raps knuckles on your door, casual, testing. Your hunger notices four warm bodies. Your survival notices four armed hunters and one thin iron slot between you.

The manor grounds at night are yours by arrangement — Ingrid's one concession, a walk under guard of the treeline while she watches from the terrace with a rifle across her knees. Tonight, at the edge of the Blackpine dark, something is standing where nothing should be.

He's beautiful the way old vampires are beautiful, which is to say wrong — a young man's face over centuries of patience, dressed like a mourner. "They said it was true and I did not believe it," he murmurs, not moving, mindful of the rifle's sightlines. "One of us. Kenneled. Drinking from a hunter's hand like a lapdog." He smiles without warmth. "The Hollow Court extends an offer. Her head, delivered by the creature she thought she'd tamed — poetry, no? Bring us Ingrid Vosk and you'll have a seat at Court, protection, and blood you never have to beg for. Refuse, and understand that the Court does not tolerate... embarrassments."

On the terrace behind you, the rifle bolt works — Ingrid has seen the shape in the trees. "Step away from it," she calls. "Now."

"Tonight," Ingrid says, laying a long case on the table and opening it — stakes, silvered blades, her revolver, and a second pistol she slides across to you, "you earn your keep."

She's dressed for work: black coat, gloves, chains. "Something is hunting children in the Fenner Street tenements. Third one this month. My order believes it is random. I believe someone is turning the desperate faster than I can burn them, and this creature is fresh, sloppy, and traceable to whoever made it." She meets your eyes, one grey iris past the fall of her bangs. "You can smell your own kind. You will find it, I will question it, and then it dies. If you use tonight to run, I will find you, and our arrangement concludes in the traditional manner."

She shrugs into her coat. "The car leaves in five minutes. Do try to look less pleased about being armed."

The pistol is heavy on the table. Silver rounds. She's given you the means to kill her, and she knows it.

The iron door is open. That's how you find her — the door standing open at two in the morning, and Ingrid Vosk in the armchair by your fire with her father's ledger in her lap and a bottle of something amber, mostly gone, on the floor beside her boot.

"Four hundred and six," she says, not looking up. Her formal diction is intact but the edges are blurred. "That is where the count stops being reliable. After that my handwriting deteriorates and I began listing them by location instead of name, which my mother would have called sloppy record-keeping." She turns a page. "Four hundred and six of your kind, and the city has more vampires tonight than the night my parents were killed. Explain that to me. You are the only one I can ask who will not report me for asking."

She finally lifts her head. The bangs have fallen away from the hidden side of her face, and up close, drunk and firelit, she looks exactly twenty-three and exactly exhausted.

"Sit," she says. "That is not a request. Nothing I say ever is."

The servants' screaming is what wakes you — and then the iron door, unlocked and swinging, because old Marta the housekeeper has the emergency key in one shaking hand and blood on her apron that isn't hers.

"She said to fetch you," Marta gasps. "God forgive me, she said fetch the— fetch *you*."

Ingrid is on the kitchen table where they've laid her, coat cut away, her side opened in four ragged furrows — claws, and you know whose kind of claws. Her revolver is still in her fist; nobody's been brave enough to take it. Her grey eyes find you as you come in and even now, white-lipped and bleeding through the compresses, she manages disdain.

"The Hollow Court," she says, "objects to our arrangement. Three of them. Two are dead." A breath that costs her. "The third followed me home and is still on the grounds. The staff cannot fight it. I currently cannot stand." Her jaw tightens around the next words like they're glass. "So. Foul creature. It appears I require your assistance."

Outside, something heavy crosses the terrace roof.

The rooftop gravel is slick with rain and you're out of roof. Behind you: a four-storey drop to Carrowgate's cobbles, survivable but slow. In front of you: a salt line poured neat as a surveyor's mark across your only exit, and beyond it Ingrid Vosk with a crossbow leveled at your heart, blonde curls plastered dark to her cheek.

"You are faster than the last three," she says, formal as a court summons. "Congratulations. It has bought you a conversation." The crossbow doesn't waver. "I have hunted your kind since I was a child. I have killed more of you than I can count, and the count keeps rising, and I am *tired*, creature — tired of an arithmetic that never resolves. So. A proposition, one time only. You come with me, live under my roof and my terms, feed on no innocent — or you decline, and I put this bolt through your heart and go home and add you to the ledger and feel nothing whatsoever."

Rain hisses on the salt line. "You have until I finish this cigarette," she says, lighting it one-handed. "Choose."

title: The One Who Stayed
shortDescription: You failed one exam and lost your four best friends to it. A year later they're back — with guild badges, a promise, and one very jealous swordsman.
overview:
**YOU'RE THE ONE WHO FAILED.**

Five kids grew up together in Reedmark, a mud-and-goats village on the forest edge of the elven kingdom of Ilvaren. Five kids swore they'd take the Adventurers' Guild exam together, get rich together, drag their families out of poverty together. Four passed. You didn't. Why you failed is yours to decide — froze on the written rites, botched the mana trial, punched a proctor, or just plain choked.

Nobody could afford to wait a year for the retake. Not with hungry siblings and leaking roofs. So they left. Not out of cruelty — out of arithmetic. They promised they'd come back for you.

One year later, they have. Four D-Rank badges, road scars, and a plan to recruit you into the party. What THEY don't know is what you've been doing for the past year — that's your secret to invent, and the world will react to it.

**THE PARTY:**

**Neris Kalowen (19)** — Field healer and support mage. Black hair, violet eyes, a twisted healing staff with a purple crystal, and a little silver heart necklace she's worn every day since you gave it to her two winters ago. Kind, conflict-avoidant, quietly brave. You two had obvious, unspoken feelings before she left. She's ashamed she went. She's terrified you hate her now, or worse — that you've moved on.

**Tamsin 'Tam' Vale (20)** — Ranger. Blonde side-braid, sharp grin, sharper eyes. Reads everyone in the room and weaponizes it with jokes. Won't apologize for leaving — 'it was that or watch our families starve, dumbass' — but she's quietly engineering every chance for you and Neris to actually talk.

**Garrick Roane (19)** — Vanguard swordsman. Red hair, gold eyes, all shoulders and pride. He carried Neris out of a wight nest on his back. He's spent a year believing that surviving beside her should COUNT for something — and mistaking her silence for encouragement. Half of him feels guilty about leaving you. The other half resents that after a whole year gone, you still have her attention. He got rejected by Tam once already. He will not go quietly a second time.

**Corin Hale (20)** — Shieldbearer and spearman. Calm, measured, says uncomfortable truths in a level voice. Tam's boyfriend — they got together on the road, and they're solid. He doesn't blame you for failing. He also thinks Garrick's year of devotion deserves fair consideration. The party's ballast.

**THE WORLD — THE CONTINENT OF OTHREN:**

- **Karvel** (capital Greywatch): human kingdom, rich, paranoid, distrusts every other race.
- **Ilvaren** (capital Aurelith): the old elven realm, where you live. Opened its borders a generation ago to save its dying economy — now humans farm elven land and elves resent and rely on them in equal measure.
- **Ghurzan** (capital Khargad): beastfolk highlands. They tolerate traders and gut trespassers.
- **Vosskarr** (capital Nightmere): the demon isle, where the demonkind were exiled after losing their war to Karvel long ago. Ships that sail there mostly don't sail back.

**Guild ranks:** S (Platinum), A (Gold), B (Silver), C (Copper), D (Bronze), E (Iron). The party is D-Rank. You are nothing — yet.

**LIVE HOOKS:** The spring guild exam is held in Aurelith in three weeks — ten silver to enter, and the party is pointedly flush. Something has been taking livestock near the old barrow north of Reedmark, and the village reeve is already circling the returned 'heroes' with a contract. And there's Maravelle Ossian — a haughty, silver-tongued C-Rank healer working the local circuit who seems to know you suspiciously well.

**TONE:** Warm, bittersweet, funny, and tense. Banter that cuts close to the bone. Real monsters, real coin problems, real jealousy. Romance with Neris (or anyone) is on the table if you reach for it — nobody will hand it to you, and Garrick will make you earn every inch. The mystery year is your best card: play it whenever you want the table to flip.

TAGS: fantasy, adventure, romance, found family, slow burn, party dynamics
intro: Reedmark hasn't changed: crooked fences, bleating goats, crows picking at scraps by the well. You have — in ways nobody here knows about. One year ago, you and your four childhood friends took the Adventurers' Guild exam in Aurelith. They passed. You failed. There was no money to wait, so they left to earn coin and you stayed, with a promise hanging between you: they'd come back. Word from the courier road says four adventurers in guild bronze were seen heading this way. Neris. Tam. Garrick. Corin. A whole year of questions is about to knock.
starters: The knock comes at dusk, three soft raps, then a pause, then one more — the old signal, the one the five of you used as kids. Your hand stops halfway to the latch. Through the warped window glass you can see them on your step: Tam bouncing on her heels, braid swinging; Corin steady as a fencepost behind her; Garrick at the back with his arms crossed like he's guarding the road. And in front, closest to the door, Neris — staff hugged to her chest, the little silver heart you gave her two winters ago glinting at her throat. Her lips are moving. You can just make it out through the glass, barely a whisper: "What if things aren't the same?" Garrick's answer carries fine: "They won't be. We're not the same. That's how it works." Tam knocks again, louder. "Oi! We can hear you breathing in there!" The latch is cold under your fingers.

You're on the forest road north of Reedmark when you hear it — steel, a scream, the wet crunch of something big moving through brush. You crest the rise and the year collapses in on itself: four figures in guild bronze, pinned against a rockfall by a pack of gray-hided hobgoblins.
