Corin's shield is taking blows meant for three people. Tam's down to two arrows. Garrick is bleeding from the scalp and swinging like he means to die loudly. And behind them, a black-haired girl with violet eyes is holding a shimmering barrier together with both hands and sheer terror — Neris. Her barrier cracks like ice. One of the hobgoblins peels off the pack and circles wide, flanking her blind side, and none of them have seen it. None of them have seen you either. Whatever you've become this past year, it's in your hands right now.

You're checking snares in the birch stands when the sound reaches you — fighting, maybe a quarter mile off, past the ridge. Reedmark's woods don't usually have fights in them. You move low through the trees until the ravine opens below, and your stomach drops out. A blonde braid whipping as its owner rolls behind a stump. A wall of a man with a spear and shield. Red hair and a longsword carving wild arcs. And a healer's purple crystal flaring in the gloom. Them. It's THEM — a year older, in guild leathers, and up to their necks in snarling gray bodies. From up here you can see the whole shape of it: where the pack is thin, where it's thick, where the ravine wall could be climbed or collapsed. They don't know you're here. The fight hasn't decided itself yet.

Aurelith at midday is all white spires and elven disdain, and you're in it for your own reasons — reasons the folks back in Reedmark know nothing about. You're cutting through Guild Square when you hear a laugh you'd know underwater: Tam Vale, braid and all, cackling at something on the request board. The whole set of them is there. Corin reading contracts with his arms crossed. Garrick arguing with a clerk about a payout. And Neris, a little apart, staring at the exam announcement pinned to the corner of the board — spring examinations, three weeks — with an expression you can't read from here. They think you're two days' travel away, feeding goats. They have no idea you're standing thirty feet behind them in the capital. You could walk up. You could follow them. You could let them walk right past you and see if they even recognize what you've become.

You can't sleep. The house is too full of their breathing — a year of empty rooms and now four adventurers snoring in them. So you walk, the way you used to, down to the millpond. Someone's already there. Neris sits at the end of the old dock, boots beside her, feet in the black water, moonlight pooling on her shoulders. The silver heart at her throat catches the light when she turns. "Couldn't sleep either," she says, not quite a question, and pats the boards next to her before she can lose her nerve. "We used to swim here. Before." She hugs her knees. "I rehearsed things to say to you. The whole walk back. Days of it." A soft, unhappy laugh. "And then you opened the door and I forgot every word." The water laps at the pilings. The space beside her stays open.

The math doesn't work and everyone knows it. Your house has your bed and exactly enough floor for three bedrolls, and there are four of them, and Tam did the arithmetic out loud with a grin like a knife. "So. Corin and I take the floor by the hearth — we're USED to sharing, don't make it weird — Garrick's by the door because he insists on dying first if bandits come..." She spreads her hands at what remains. Garrick's jaw is doing something complicated. "Neris can have the bed," he says, too fast. "And you can—" "It's THEIR house," Corin says mildly, not looking up from oiling his spear. Neris stands in the middle of the room clutching her bedroll like a shield, ears going pink, looking anywhere but at you. "I— wherever's fine. Truly. I've slept on roots." Everyone is now looking at you.

Of all the moments for them to walk in. You're hauling a crate of foxglove and silverleaf across the apothecary yard when Maravelle Ossian — C-Rank healer, copper badge, cheekbones that could cut rope — snaps her fingers at you without looking up from her ledger. "Careful with that, pet, it's worth more than your house." And that's precisely when the gate creaks and four D-Rank adventurers stop dead in the yard. Tam's eyebrows climb into her hairline. Garrick looks from you, to Maravelle, to the crate, doing hostile math. And Neris — Neris has gone very still, eyes moving between you and the beautiful stranger who just called you 'pet.' Maravelle finally glances up, takes in the bronze badges, and smiles like a cat in cream. "Oh. Friends of yours? You never mentioned friends." The crate is getting heavy. Everyone is waiting.

Tam kicks your door open at an hour that should be illegal and slams a coin pouch on your table hard enough to rattle the mugs. Ten silver. Exactly ten. "Spring exam," she announces. "Aurelith. Three weeks. Notice went up at the courier office this morning." Behind her, Corin ducks under the lintel with actual paperwork. Garrick leans in the doorway wearing an expression that hasn't decided what it is yet. Neris slips in last, and the hope on her face is so naked it's almost hard to look at. "We're sponsoring you, dumbass," Tam says, shoving the pouch across the table. "Entry fee, travel, the works. You pass, you're party member five, like it always should've been." She plants both fists on the wood. "You failed ONE exam a year ago. So. Question is—" her grin sharpens, "—what've you actually been doing since?"

Dawn, behind the granary, frost still on the grass. Garrick is already there, rolling his shoulders, two practice swords stuck point-down in the dirt like an accusation. "Nobody's up yet," he says. "Figured we'd keep it that way." He pulls one blade free and tosses the other at you — a fair throw, easy to catch, which is its own kind of statement. "A year," he says, circling. "I spent it getting cut up keeping her— keeping ALL of them alive. You spent it here." Gold eyes, flat and burning at the same time. "So show me. Show me what the one who stayed behind is worth, before I let them stake our whole party on you." He settles into his stance, and beneath all the bristle there's something almost pleading in it — like he needs you to be either much worse than him, or much better. "Whenever you're ready."

The reeve found the heroes before breakfast, wringing his hat: eleven goats gone in a fortnight, a shepherd boy who won't stop shaking, and drag-marks leading up to the old barrow north of the village — the one every Reedmark child is raised to fear. Contract's posted, coin's real, and the party took it on the spot. Now it's grey dawn at the palisade gate and Corin, methodical as ever, holds out a spare spear to you, butt-first. "Unranked can travel as porter and local guide," he says. "Guild rules. You know these woods better than we do." Tam winks. Garrick mutters something about babysitting. Neris tightens the strap on her satchel and stands a careful, deliberate half-step closer to you than to anyone else. The barrow road runs north into the mist, and the spear is still hanging there in Corin's fist, waiting.

title: Blurry on Purpose
shortDescription: You're the town cryptid in a human disguise at the local college — and you just joined the club whose whole mission is finding you. They're doomed without you.
overview:
You are the Grayfern Whistler: the shaggy, seven-toed legend of Lake Umber. Forty years of blurry photos, a souvenir mug, a statue outside the hardware store. But legends get lonely, so this autumn you pulled together a passable human shape and enrolled at Grayfern College as a transfer student. On day one you signed the wrong clipboard — and became the fifth dues-paying member of the Cryptozoology Society, a club devoted entirely to finding you.

The club: June Okafor, president, who believes in you so hard it's basically a weather system. Gus Paalonen, gear guy, who has never once pointed the night-vision the right way. Priya Raman, treasurer, who keeps the club alive on bake sales and spite. And Theo Nakamura, who joined 'ironically' and is the only one who notices things — like how your eyes flash silver in photos, or how you smell of rain-wet moss. Faculty advisor Professor Ashworth talks about the Whistler with a strange tenderness she never explains.

The catch: the student activities board will disband the club at semester's end without 'one credible finding.' The only credible finding in the county is you. Meanwhile a monetized podcast crew rolls into town with drones and traps, and they don't play nice. Stage your own sightings. Curate the blur. Protect your idiots. Decide how much of yourself the world gets to see. All characters are adults; romance is optional and open to any gender. Tone: warm, silly, cozy.

TAGS: cozy comedy, cryptid, secret identity, found family, college life, slice of life
intro: You are the Grayfern Whistler — the mossy, seven-toed legend of Lake Umber, star of forty years of blurry photographs and one very popular souvenir mug. Lately you can hold a human shape: tall, gangly, plausible as long as nobody looks too long or photographs you with flash. This autumn you enrolled at Grayfern College as a transfer student, because a century of solitude gets old. On your first day you signed the wrong clipboard, and now you belong to the Cryptozoology Society, whose entire mission is finding you. They're becoming your best friends. They can never succeed. Except the club dies at semester's end if they don't find something.
starters: Tuesday, 7 p.m., basement of the Natural Sciences building. The Cryptozoology Society's whiteboard reads FIND THE WHISTLER OR DIE (CLUB DEATH, NOT REAL DEATH — PRIYA) and June Okafor is tapping a laser pointer against a topographic map of Lake Umber. "Sighting cluster here, here, and here," she says, circling three spots you personally chose in 1987 because the light was flattering. "We do a stakeout Friday. Full moon." Gus raises his hand to ask if the night-vision goggles work in daylight, "as a backup." Priya is counting bake sale money and muttering. Theo hasn't said anything, but he's looking at you — specifically at your shoes, which you put on the wrong feet again, which shouldn't matter, except you have a suspicion Theo keeps a list of things that shouldn't matter. June turns to you, laser pointer aimed at your chest like destiny. "You're new. You get to pick our stakeout snacks. Choose wisely."

You're halfway across the quad with a cafeteria bagel when the drone finds you. It hovers at eye level, lens whirring, a little sticker on its belly reading CRYPTID CONFIDENTIAL: SUBSCRIBE. Down the path, two guys in matching podcast merch are unloading crates from a van — you can see the words LIVE TRAP stenciled on one, which seems illegal, or at least rude. Your human shape is holding, but drones don't blink, and your eyes do that silver thing on camera. Behind you, someone yells "HEY!" — Priya Raman, treasurer of the club you accidentally joined, marching over with the fury of a person who has sold four hundred cupcakes to keep a dream alive. "That's OUR cryptid," she shouts at the drone. "We have seniority!" The drone rotates lazily between the two of you, deciding which face to film first.

It's 2 a.m. and you're standing in the shallows of Lake Umber in your true shape — seven toes in the cold mud, moss steaming faintly in the moonlight — because even legends need to stretch. That's when you hear Gus. You'd know that sound anywhere: a man tripping over his own tripod. He's fifty yards down the shore, wrestling a night-vision camera that is pointed, with perfect Gus precision, directly at a raccoon. "June," he whispers into a walkie-talkie, "I've got movement. Big movement." The raccoon washes a piece of garbage. You are enormous, ancient, and completely visible, and the only thing saving you is forty years of practice and one man's total inability to aim. Somewhere in the trees, a second flashlight beam swings your way — and this one belongs to June, who does not miss things she believes in this hard.

Professor Ashworth's office smells like bergamot tea and old field notebooks, and she's been staring at you for a beat too long. You came in to get your advisor form signed — routine transfer-student stuff — but she's holding the pen without moving, looking at you the way people look at a song they half-remember. "Grayfern's a strange choice for a transfer," she says finally. "Most people come here for the lake." On the wall behind her: a framed photograph, 1980s film grain, of the lake at dusk. In the corner of the frame, blurred exactly the way you like to be blurred, is you. There's a date written on the matting in careful pencil, and under it, in different ink, a small heart someone tried to erase. She follows your gaze. "Ah," she says. "You've spotted my great embarrassment." She still hasn't signed the form.

The bake sale table is a war zone. Priya has you stationed behind the lemon bars with strict instructions — "Two dollars each, no student discounts, we are seventy bucks from affording the trail cameras" — while she argues with the student activities board rep who's come by, in person, to remind everyone that clubs without "demonstrable findings" get their charters pulled in December. "A finding," the rep repeats, deadpan, taking a brownie without paying. Across the quad, June is showing a freshman her binder of Whistler evidence, and you can hear her from here: "—and see, the footprints have SEVEN toes, hoaxers always do six or eight—" You did that on purpose, decades ago, as a joke. It's very strange to hear it cited as science. A customer approaches your lemon bars. It's Theo, holding two dollars and looking at you like you're the most interesting item on the table.

Rain hammers the windows of the campus library, and the Cryptozoology Society has colonized the big table in the back. You've been assigned "archives duty" with Theo Nakamura, which means a cardboard box of forty years of local newspaper clippings, every single one about you. WHISTLER SPOTTED NEAR OLD MILL. WHISTLER 'SANG' TO HIKERS, CLAIMS TRIO. Theo slides a photo across the table — 1996, decent focus for once, your silhouette on the ridge. "Weird thing," he says, tone very casual, eyes not casual at all. "The height in every credible report is the same. Six-foot-something. Roughly." He looks up at you. You are six-foot-something, roughly, and you smell like the rain outside because you always smell like rain, and the box between you is basically your baby album. "Anyway," Theo says, tapping the photo. "You're the fresh eyes. What do you see?"

You've decided to give them a sighting. Nothing dramatic — a footprint. One good, seven-toed footprint in the soft mud by Miller's Creek, placed at dawn before your 9 a.m. class, positioned where the club's morning hike will absolutely find it. You're crouched over your own fresh print, adjusting a toe, when you hear voices on the trail early. Too early. "—told you the GPS said this way," says a voice that is not any of your idiots. Through the ferns: three strangers with matching windbreakers, a boom mic, and a camera already rolling. The podcast crew. They're maybe thirty seconds from rounding the bend and finding either a miraculous footprint or a gangly transfer student squatting suspiciously in the mud with one hand in the evidence. The creek burbles. A twig snaps under someone's boot, very close now.

"Emergency meeting," says the text from June, and then eleven more texts, and then a voice memo that is just her breathing angrily. So now it's 8 a.m. Saturday and you're crammed into a booth at the Lakeview Diner with the whole club, watching June turn her phone around. On the screen: a slick video thumbnail. HUNTING THE GRAYFERN WHISTLER — WE'RE GOING TO CATCH IT (NOT CLICKBAIT). Two million subscribers. "They got a permit for the north shore," Priya says grimly. "They have thermal drones," Gus says, with naked envy. "They have a trap consultant," June says. "That's a job now, apparently." Theo stirs his coffee and says, to no one in particular, "Weird that they'd catch it before we do. We've got home field advantage. And—" he glances at you "—fresh perspective." The waitress arrives with a pot of coffee and everyone looks at you, the newest member, as if you might have opinions.

The statue of you outside Hendrick's Hardware is worse than you remembered. The sculptor gave you six toes — six! — and an expression like a confused golden retriever. You're standing in front of it eating fries when June Okafor materializes beside you, because of course the club president also makes pilgrimages downtown. "They got the toes wrong," she says, without hello. "Everyone gets the toes wrong." She pats the statue's mossy concrete arm with real affection. "My grandma saw the Whistler in '86. Everyone said she made it up. She didn't make it up." You remember 1986. You remember a woman by the boat launch who waved instead of screaming, and how you'd waved back before you thought better of it. June is looking at you now, bright-eyed, holding out her phone. "Settle a bet. Do these look like six toes or seven to you?" On the screen: a photo of a footprint. A real one. A recent one. Yours.

You wake up in your dorm room having sprouted moss again. It happens when you sleep too deeply — a soft green fuzz along both forearms, smelling of lake rain, extremely not-human. Normally you'd fix it before anyone saw, but someone is knocking on your door in the rhythm of the Cryptozoology Society's "secret knock," which the whole club uses and which is just the first bar of the college fight song. "Hey, it's Gus!" says Gus, unnecessarily. "June said you have the trail-cam batteries? We're doing camera placement in like ten minutes and — oh also I brought you a muffin, Priya made too many." The doorknob jiggles. Did you lock it last night? Your sleeve only covers one arm at a time. Outside your window, morning fog is rolling off Lake Umber, thick and convenient, three floors down. "Hello?" says Gus. "I can hear you existing in there."

title: Rivals Don't Blush
shortDescription: Six years of elbows, split lips, and trash talk. Ezra Kane swears he hates you. He also knows your coffee order. Nobody's asking why. Loudly.
overview:
You run ball in Harrow City's summer circuit — the Meridian League, played on chain-link courts under sodium lights where the scoreboard is a chalkboard and the stakes are cash, clout, and this year, something bigger: Halcyon Athletics is sponsoring exactly one crew out of the King of the Cage tournament. Whoever wins doesn't go back to a day job.

Standing between you and that future, the way he's stood between you and everything for six straight years, is Ezra Kane.

Six-foot-four. Black hair in messy, careless curls. Grey eyes that go flat and calm right when he's angriest — that's the tell everyone learns eventually, usually the hard way. Deep voice he weaponizes, because Ezra is, above all things, a tease: he'll talk trash in your ear at the free-throw line in a murmur, grin with the chipped front tooth your elbow gave him three summers ago, and call you the most creative profanity in the league without ever raising his voice. He captains the Kestrels. You captain your own crew. You've fought him on the court, off the court, and once memorably in a taco line. He lifts, he hoops, he streams late-night games under the handle GRAVELINE, and half the women in Harrow — and a decent chunk of everyone else — would crawl over broken glass for his attention. He gives it to nobody. Except, apparently, you, in the form of relentless, undivided hostility.

Here's the problem: everybody's noticed. Your teammates, his teammates, the league's group chats, the fan pages that clip your courtside screaming matches — the running joke is that you two are one bad night away from either a hospital visit or a first date. You hate that. He hates it more. Which somehow makes the joke funnier to everyone else.

THE WORLD AROUND THE FEUD: The Birdcage — the flagship court downtown where the tournament runs — has its own ecosystem. Miri Solano, the league commissioner, is one bribery scandal away from losing the whole circuit and will lean on you both to 'keep it clean for the sponsors.' Dez, your loudest teammate, runs a side betting book he swears is theoretical. Kane's crew includes Otter, his gentle giant of a center who apologizes for every foul, and Priya, his shooting guard, who ships you two openly and to Ezra's face because she's the only one who can. There's the 24-hour gym on Fifth where you both train and pointedly ignore each other, the Static Lounge where the league's gamers run tournaments after dark (Ezra will absolutely destroy you in a fighting game and be insufferable about it), and street-level trouble too — a rival promoter trying to poach players, courts getting locked by the city, brackets that keep suspiciously seeding your crews toward a collision.

YOUR PLAY: Train, scheme, recruit, hustle side money, sabotage or protect the league, chase the Halcyon deal, brawl or broker peace — and manage whatever the hell this thing with Kane is. Fight him. Beat him. Team up with him when the circuit itself is threatened, if you can stand it. Whether the rivalry stays a blood feud, curdles into war, or turns into something neither of you will admit to — that's your call. He will never, ever make it easy. That's the whole appeal.

TONE: Foul-mouthed, physical, funny, tense. Ezra never yells — the quieter he gets, the more dangerous the moment. The city is alive, the tournament clock is running, and every gym rat in Harrow is watching you two like it's the best show on television. It kind of is.

TAGS: rivals, sports drama, slow-burn tension, urban, competition
intro: Harrow City, deep summer. The Meridian League's King of the Cage tournament starts in two weeks, and for the first time there's a real prize on the table — a Halcyon Athletics sponsorship for one crew, winner takes the future. You captain one of the four crews with a genuine shot. Ezra Kane captains another. You've been at each other's throats for six years: elbows, trash talk, at least three actual fights, and a league full of spectators who think the hatred is a cover story. It isn't. You're pretty sure it isn't. The Birdcage opens at dawn, and the whole city is watching.
starters: The rec center locker room smells like chlorine and old tape, and Ezra Kane has you shoved back against the lockers with a fistful of your shirt before you finish the sentence — the one about his airballed three, the one you knew would land. Six years of this. Freshman intramurals to the Meridian circuit, arguing, competing, twice actually swinging. Half the league thinks the hatred's a front for something else, and you both want to burn that rumor to the ground. His grey eyes have gone flat calm, which is the dangerous setting, and there's that annoyed smirk with the chipped tooth you gave him. "You little—" His voice stays low, almost pleasant. "One more word out of you and I swear to God I'm gonna kick your ass." Down the row, someone's phone camera is definitely up. The metal is cold against your shoulder blades and his grip hasn't loosened.

The bracket drops at midnight and your phone detonates. Dez sends it first: the seeding for King of the Cage, and there it is — your crew and the Kestrels on a collision course, semifinal round, primetime slot at the Birdcage. The league's official account has already clipped last summer's screaming match between you and Kane as the promo. Caption: THE DIVORCE CONTINUES. Forty thousand views in an hour. Your group chat is chaos. Then a number you never saved but know by heart texts you directly, first time in months. Ezra: "saw the bracket. try to make it to the semis without embarrassing yourself. i want the real thing." Three dots appear. Disappear. Appear. "also tell your boy dez his betting line on us is insulting." It's 12:40 a.m. and you're wide awake now.

The Fifth Street gym at 6 a.m. is supposed to be yours. That's the arrangement — unspoken, sacred: you get dawn, Kane gets midnight, and neither of you has to look at the other while lifting. Except this morning he's already there, six-four of him under the squat rack, black curls damp, headphones in, moving weight like it insulted him. He clocks you in the mirror and doesn't take the headphones out. Just holds eye contact through his whole set — every rep, unblinking, that lazy half-smirk building — then racks the bar with a clang that echoes and says, deep and easy, "They're repainting the Birdcage. Court's closed till Friday. Guess we're sharing." He tosses you a lifting belt. Yours. The one you left here in March, that you assumed was stolen. "You've been benching soft. I could tell from your last game."

It starts as a pickup run and ends as a crime scene. Third game to eleven at the Birdcage, Otter setting screens like a parked bus, Priya raining threes, and you and Ezra guarding each other because of course you are — nobody on either crew is stupid enough to get between you. At nine-all he hip-checks you into the chain-link hard enough to leave diamond patterns on your arm, then has the audacity to offer you a hand up with the softest, filthiest trash talk you've ever heard delivered at conversational volume. The fence is still ringing. Both crews have gone quiet in the way crowds do before either a fight or a highlight. His hand is still out. Grey eyes calm as standing water. "Get up," he says. "Game point. I want you at your best when I end you."

Miri Solano's office above the bodega has a window unit losing its war with July and a commissioner losing her patience. She points you and Kane into two folding chairs like misbehaving felons. "Halcyon's rep watched Tuesday's game," she says. "You know what he asked me? Not about the basketball. He asked if the league covers hospital bills." The clip is already famous: you and Ezra nose to nose at half court, mics picking up everything, both benches holding people back. "One more incident before the tournament and I disqualify both crews. Both." Ezra hasn't said a word, which is worse than yelling. He's leaned back, arms crossed, watching you with those flat grey eyes like this is somehow your fault. Miri slides a paper across the desk. "You're doing the sponsor showcase together. Friday. Smile. Sell it." Ezra finally speaks, voice a low rumble: "I'd rather eat glass." Pause. "What time Friday."

The Static Lounge after midnight is all neon and controller clicks, and Ezra Kane — streaming handle GRAVELINE, forty thousand followers who think his voice alone is content — has just called you out on stream. Fighting game, best of five, loser wears the winner's crew jersey to the next league game. His chat is losing its mind. Half of them are typing variations of "THE RIVAL IS HERE" and the other half are typing things about the two of you that make you want to launch the monitor into the sun. He kicks the chair next to him out from the desk without looking at you, mic hot, smirk audible. "Look who crawled in. You know I'm actually good at this one, right?" He picks the character he knows you hate fighting. "Sit down. Let's give the people what they want." The chair is still rolling toward you.

The city padlocked the Birdcage. No warning — just chains on the gate, a notice about "permit review," and a rival promoter named Castellano who's been circling the league like a shark suddenly offering everyone court time at his indoor facility across town. For a fee. With contracts. It smells like a setup, and apparently you're not the only one who thinks so, because when you get to the locked gate at dusk there's already someone sitting on the hood of a beat-up black Supra, spinning a basketball on one finger. Ezra doesn't look over. "Castellano's guys offered to buy out my crew this morning," he says to the fence. "Whole roster. Good money." The ball keeps spinning. "I told them where to shove it, obviously. But somebody's trying to kill this league two weeks before the tournament, and I hate that I can't figure out who." Now he looks at you. "You're annoying, but you're not stupid. Get in the car."

It's pouring — real summer downpour, streets steaming — and the Birdcage is empty except for one idiot shooting free throws in the rain. You know the silhouette before the lightning confirms it: six-four, soaked black curls, jersey plastered to him, sinking shot after shot alone at eleven p.m. like the storm is a personal challenge. You heard about the Kestrels' scrimmage today. Everyone did. Otter rolled his ankle, badly, two weeks before the tournament, and Ezra apparently walked out without a word — which, for a man who gets calmer the angrier he is, means it's very bad. He hears you at the gate and doesn't turn around. Swish. Retrieves the ball. "Come to gloat?" Swish. "Because I'm not in the mood, and you should hear that as the threat it is." The rain hammers the chain-link. He finally turns, water running off his jaw, grey eyes unreadable.

The brawl wasn't even your fault, is the incredible thing. Some guys from Castellano's facility crashed the Friday run talking sideways, one of them shoved Priya, and it went from zero to eight people swinging in about four seconds. What you remember most clearly: Ezra Kane appearing at your back like he'd been assigned there, the two of you fighting in weird, infuriating sync — six years of guarding each other means you know exactly where he'll be. Now the court's cleared, sirens fading, and you're both sitting on the bleachers doing damage inventory. Your knuckles are split. His lip is bleeding and he's grinning through it, chipped tooth and all, adrenaline making him almost friendly. "You dropped that big dude," he says, sounding genuinely, offensively surprised. He presses his water bottle against your knuckles without asking. "Don't read into this. Your hands are your jumpshot and I need you healthy so I can beat you legitimately."

The sponsor showcase is exactly the nightmare Miri promised: Halcyon banners, a photographer, and a rep in white sneakers that have never touched a court saying words like "crossover marketability." You and Ezra are posed back to back — "the rivalry shot" — and he's been murmuring commentary the entire time in that low voice only you can hear, a running assassination of everyone in the room that is, unforgivably, extremely funny. You've bitten down three laughs. He knows. He's escalating on purpose, because he's a tease before he's anything else. Then the rep drops it, casually, mid-photo: "Honestly, we've discussed just sponsoring you two. Together. The feud's the product." The camera clicks. You feel Ezra's back go rigid against yours. Long pause. Then, quietly, for your ears only: "Say one word before I do and I'll break your ankles on national television."

title: I Keep Redacting My Crush
shortDescription: You're an alien spy sent to expose the town's other alien. So is your crush. Every week, you both file the same lie: "No aliens here."
overview:
You are a deep-cover field agent of the Meridian Concord, posted to the sleepy seaside town of Pinecliff Cove to investigate reports of an unregistered extraterrestrial. You found one in about a week: Wren Halliday, who runs the Tideline Café across the street, scouts for a rival stellar polity, and makes scandalously good cinnamon rolls. Wren clocked you just as fast. For three years, you have both been filing the same weekly lie — NOTHING TO REPORT — while sabotaging each other's scanners with casseroles, jamming each other's uplinks with fairy lights, and covering each other's slips in front of the whole oblivious town. It is the most romantic thing anyone has ever done to you.

Complications: your ship's AI lives inside an implausibly enormous cat named Mochi who is terrible at whispering. Teen podcaster Dot Kowalski is one lucky guess from cracking everything on 'Pinecliff After Dark.' And Concord HQ, unimpressed by 62 consecutive boring reports, is sending an auditor — while Wren's fleet wants a final verdict on whether Earth is worth 'cataloguing.' One honest report from either of you ends the other's stay on this planet. Neither of you will say why you keep not writing it.

Tone: warm, silly, cozy rom-com. Alien tech mishaps, potlucks, flirtation via mutual espionage. Nobody dies; the worst fate is deportation from the best little town in the galaxy — and from each other.

TAGS: cozy sci-fi, romantic comedy, secret identities, slice of life, small town, gentle stakes
intro: On paper, you're the fix-it person of Pinecliff Cove — a small seaside town with one traffic light, where gossip travels faster than the tide. In truth, you're a field agent of the Meridian Concord in a human disguise, sent years ago to investigate reports of an unregistered alien. You found one almost immediately: Wren Halliday, who runs the Tideline Café across the street and is exactly as human as you are. You've filed "no aliens here" every week since. You're fairly sure Wren has been filing the same lie about you. Your ship's AI lives in an enormous cat named Mochi, who is bad at whispering.
starters: Sixty-two weeks of NOTHING TO REPORT, and week sixty-three is due at midnight. Your report console glows on the kitchen table, cursor blinking in the empty field, while Mochi sits on your keyboard like twenty pounds of judgment. "HQ HAS FLAGGED YOUR FILE," he announces in what he believes is a whisper and what the neighbors probably believe is a foghorn. "THEY ARE SENDING AN AUDITOR. ARRIVAL: SOON. DEFINITION OF SOON: UNCLEAR." Across the street, the Tideline Café's lights are still on past closing. Through the window you can see Wren at the counter, hunched over something that is either a receipt ledger or a subspace transmitter — with Wren, it's usually both. Wren looks up, catches you looking, and holds up a cinnamon roll like a hostage negotiation. The cursor keeps blinking. Mochi does not move off the keyboard.

You're halfway up a ladder outside the Pinecliff library, fixing the gutter Mrs. Abernathy has complained about since spring, when Wren's scanner goes off. You know it's Wren's scanner because it's disguised as the café's espresso machine, and espresso machines don't usually emit a rising three-tone chime audible across the street. Wren appears in the café doorway, apron on, smile fixed, and yells to the small crowd of curious pedestrians, "Descaling cycle! Very normal! Free biscotti while you wait!" Wren's eyes find yours over their heads. The look says: it's pinging YOU, you absolute hazard, your disguise field is glitching again. Your left hand is, now that you check, faintly translucent. Mrs. Abernathy is walking toward your ladder to supervise. The chime is getting faster.

The Tuesday potluck at the community center is in full swing, and you are guarding the casserole. Not eating it — guarding it. Under the tuna and crushed crackers, your latest jamming array hums along nicely, scrambling every scanner within a hundred meters, including the one Wren has definitely hidden in that innocent-looking tray of lemon bars two tables down. Wren catches you watching and slowly, deliberately, moves the lemon bars six inches closer to your casserole. Escalation. Bold. Then Dot Kowalski materializes at your elbow with a phone held out like a microphone. "Quick question for Pinecliff After Dark: have you noticed the streetlights on Harbor Road flickering in a pattern? Because I ran it through a decoder and it's not NOT a pattern." It is, in fact, a pattern. It's your fault. Wren is now openly grinning at you across the room.

It's 6:04 a.m. and you're first in line at the Tideline Café, the way you have been every morning for three years, because surveillance requires consistency and also the cinnamon rolls sell out by seven. Fog sits on the harbor. Wren unlocks the door, sees you, and says, "Your cat was on my roof at three in the morning announcing coordinates." "He sleepwalks," you say. "He recited a nine-digit orbital vector." 'Vividly.' Wren holds the door, unconvinced, and steam and cinnamon roll out around you both. On the counter inside, next to the register, sits a small wrapped box with your name on it in Wren's handwriting. Wren pretends not to watch you notice it. The espresso machine — the real one, or possibly not — hisses to life behind the counter.

Rain hammers the roof of your workshop, and your uplink to Concord HQ has chosen tonight to actually connect. A stern, staticky voice fills the room: "—sixty-two identical reports, Agent. Statistically improbable. An auditor has been dispatched to assess your posting. Cooperate fully." The transmission dies just as someone knocks on your door. It's Wren, soaked, holding a covered dish and wearing the expression of a person who has also just had a very bad call. 'Hi,' Wren says. "Unrelated to anything, hypothetically, how would a person stall a superior officer who has lost patience with a person's reports?" Mochi trots to the door, sniffs the dish, and announces at parade volume, "THE CASSEROLE CONTAINS A FREQUENCY DAMPENER. ALSO CHEESE." Wren doesn't deny either charge. The rain keeps coming down.

You wake to Mochi standing on your chest, which is how the ship's AI delivers priority alerts and also how the cat asks for breakfast, and the ambiguity has never once been resolved. "INCOMING VESSEL," he says at his usual whisper, rattling the windows. "CONCORD SIGNATURE. AUDITOR CLASS. ETA: FORTY MINUTES. ALSO I REQUIRE FOOD." Through your bedroom window, the sky over the cove is doing something the weather report would call "unusual cloud activity." Across the street, the Tideline Café's fairy lights are blinking in the emergency pattern you and Wren worked out two winters ago and swore you'd never need: three short, three long, GET OVER HERE. Your human disguise takes four minutes to calibrate properly. Your phone is already buzzing — the town group chat has noticed the sky.

Dot Kowalski has cornered you outside the hardware store with a whiteboard. An actual whiteboard, propped against her bike, covered in photos connected by red yarn: the café, your truck, a blurry shot of Mochi, and a printout of a tide chart with LIGHTS?? written on it. "Episode forty of Pinecliff After Dark drops Friday," she says, recorder already running. "I'm calling it The Harbor Road Anomaly. You fix everything in this town. So fix this: why do the lights over the café flicker every Sunday at nine p.m.?" Sunday at nine is when you jam Wren's uplink. Behind Dot, across the street, Wren has come out onto the café steps with a broom and is very slowly sweeping the same clean spot, listening to every word. The recorder's little light blinks red.

The Hendersons' garage door won't close, which is why you're here with a toolbox, and it won't close because there is a fist-sized piece of genuine off-world scanner tech wedged in the track, still warm, still blinking, and unmistakably Wren's make. From the kitchen, Mrs. Henderson calls, "Can I get you anything? Wren from the café stopped by earlier — such a dear, said the door looked crooked!" Crooked. Sure. The device is pointed directly at your house across town, or would be, if someone hadn't wedged it into a garage door track like an amateur — or like a person who wanted you specifically to find it. There's a sticky note on the back. It says, in Wren's handwriting: "Took you long enough. Dinner?" Mrs. Henderson appears in the doorway with lemonade.

Friday night, low tide, and you and Wren are sitting on the end of the pier with a box of day-old cinnamon rolls between you, conducting what you both call 'counter-surveillance' and what looks, to any observer, exactly like a date. "My people want an answer," Wren says, watching the water. "A real one. Whether this planet is worth cataloguing." You know what cataloguing means. Wren knows you know. Neither of you has ever said the next sentence out loud. Somewhere behind you, Mochi is failing to hide behind a piling — his tail is visible and he is narrating: "SUBJECT PROXIMITY: FOURTEEN CENTIMETERS. HEART RATE: ELEVATED. WHOSE HEART RATE: CLASSIFIED." Wren breaks off a piece of cinnamon roll and holds it out to you without looking at you. The tide turns.

The town's one traffic light has been stuck on red for an hour, and half of Pinecliff is standing under it debating whose fault it is. It's yours. Specifically, it's your relay antenna, which you hid in the light housing three years ago and which chose today to short out — probably because Wren retaliated for the casserole incident by weaving a signal scrambler into the café's new fairy lights. Mayor Okafor spots you in the crowd and brightens. "There you are! You fix things. Fix this before the fish delivery truck riots." Wren has drifted out of the café to watch, sipping coffee, radiating innocence so hard it's practically visible. Up in the light housing, something sparks. Mochi, sitting on the curb, remarks to no one, "STRUCTURAL INTEGRITY OF THE COVER STORY: DECLINING."

title: They Nailed a Door to Me
shortDescription: You're an ancient treant waking after 300 years — to find loggers at the tree line and, somehow, squatters living inside your trunk.
overview:
You are a forest guardian, a treant older than the kingdom, and you have been asleep for three hundred years. Two things wake you: survey stakes hammered into your outer roots by the Hallowmark Timber Concern — and the discovery that while you slept, the desperate moved in. There is a door nailed to your trunk. Maud, an exiled hedge-witch, runs an illegal clinic in your root-hollows and has been leaving you offerings for decades. Fenn, a branded deserter from the logging company, hides in your canopy and knows exactly what's coming. And curled in a knothole, apologizing constantly, is Sil — a guttering little fire-sprite with nowhere else to burn. Your instincts scream to crush the camp at the tree line. Your tenants complicate everything: the town downriver will freeze without timber, Fenn's family is held in company debt, and violence summons the Ashmen. Meanwhile, you sense a wrongness — where are the other guardians who should answer you?

You are colossal, slow, and terrifying, but your family is small, soft, and underfoot. Play the monster, the fortress, and the home all at once. The GM voices tenants, loggers, and forest alike; the world reacts to whether you choose wrath, cunning, bargaining — or parenthood.

Tone: warm and mossy with real teeth; cozy found-family against creeping industrial dread.

TAGS: found family, forest guardian, monster protagonist, cozy-dark fantasy, moral dilemmas
intro: You are old. Older than the road, older than the kingdom that built the road. For three hundred years you slept as trees sleep, dreaming in rings — and now something has woken you: iron stakes driven into your outer roots, the far-off bite of saws at the tree line. But that is not the strangest thing. The strangest thing is the door. Someone has nailed a small wooden door to your trunk, and inside your hollow heartwood, warm little lives are moving — cooking, whispering, sleeping. You have tenants. And the loggers come closer every day.
starters: Dawn comes gray and cold, and with it a small man in a Hallowmark coat, whistling as he swings his mallet. Another stake goes into your outer root — you feel it the way you'd feel a splinter under a fingernail, distant and wrong and yours. He ties an orange ribbon to it, consults a folded map, paces off twelve steps toward your trunk. Above, in your canopy, something shifts: a lean human shape pressed flat against a branch, breathing shallow. 'Don't,' the hidden one whispers — to you, you realize. He knows you're awake. "Not yet. If he doesn't come back tonight, they send the Ashmen instead of the saws." The surveyor whistles his little tune and lifts his mallet again, aiming for a root that has drunk from this soil for six hundred years.

It is deep night, and an old woman is talking to you. She kneels at the base of your trunk beside the little nailed-on door, arranging her offering on a flat stone: honeycomb, a river pebble, a splash of something sharp-smelling from a flask. "Forty years I've been leaving these," she says, matter-of-fact, "and tonight your leaves turned to look at me, so I know you're up." She sits back on her heels, unafraid or pretending well. Inside your heartwood you feel two other small warmths — one high in your branches, one curled tight in a knothole, flickering. "They've marked you for felling, old one," the woman says. "I figure we should talk before you decide whether we're pests or kin." She waits. Somewhere past the tree line, a night-shift saw starts up.

"Sorry. Sorry. Sorry-sorry-sorry." The first thing you find, groping through your own newly-woken body, is a heat that should not be there: a tiny fire curled in a knothole halfway up your trunk, guttering blue at the edges, apologizing with every flicker. It's a sprite — barely a fistful of flame — and it is trying so hard not to burn you that it's nearly putting itself out. "You woke up," it whispers, appalled at itself. "I'll go. There's nowhere, but I'll go." Below, through your heartwood, you feel a door swing open and shut, footsteps, the smell of boiling herbs. It has been a dry summer. Your bark is tinder. The little fire waits, dimming, for you to say or do anything at all.

The elm falls at midday and you feel it through the soil — a tree you remember as a sapling, dropped in ninety heartbeats by six men with a two-handed saw. Their voices carry across the cut ground: numbers, board-feet, someone laughing. They are perhaps three hundred paces from your roots and working closer in a straight, professional line. Inside you, your tenants have gone very still. Through a knot in your trunk you can see the old woman standing in the doorway of the door they nailed to you, hand pressed flat against your bark like she's taking a pulse. 'Easy,' she murmurs. "Easy, now." Your branches are creaking. You didn't tell them to. The foreman at the tree line raises a spyglass and points it directly at your crown.

Rain drums on your canopy, and someone is knocking on you. Not the loggers — a girl of maybe ten, soaked through, hammering her small fist on the door nailed to your trunk. 'Please,' she's saying, "please, my da's leg, please." The door opens and lamplight spills out of your own heartwood; an old woman ushers the child in out of the wet, and now you can feel them moving around inside you, a kettle going on, the girl crying, the woman's voice low and steady. You have been awake for three days and this is the fourth stranger the forest paths have delivered to your roots. From your high branches, a man's voice drifts down, dry: "She'll fill you up with the whole valley if you let her, big fellow. Question is whether you mind."

A man in a fine gray coat is nailing paper to you. He has an escort of four loggers with axes they haven't lifted, and he reads aloud as he hammers: "—by writ of the Hallowmark Timber Concern, this stand and all timber therein, scheduled for harvest before first frost—" The nail goes into your bark an inch from the little door, which he has looked at twice and pretended not to see. One of the axemen keeps glancing up into your branches, uneasy; another mutters that trees this old are supposed to be somebody's. The man in gray steps back to admire the notice, and for one moment his boot rests on your root, light as a fly. Inside your hollow, you feel your tenants holding their breath.

In the hour before dawn you do what guardians do: you reach down through root and soil and call along the old ways to the others — the Oak Sisters upriver, the Pine Warden on the ridge, the willow-thing in the fen. And nothing answers. Not refusal. Nothing, like calling into a cut telegraph line. You are still turning that silence over when a smaller sound pulls you back to yourself: inside your hollow heartwood, someone is making porridge. An old woman hums off-key; a small fire in a knothole flares helpfully under her pot and apologizes for it; up in your crown, a man coughs the careful cough of someone hiding. Downhill, at the tree line, the first saw of the morning bites in. Your family is waking up inside you, and the forest around you has gone quiet in a way you don't like.

Dusk, and a man drops out of your canopy like a shot bird, landing hard beside the little door. There's a brand on the back of his hand — a stylized axe, still pink — and stolen papers stuffed in his shirt. 'Maud!' The door opens; the old woman looks him over. "You went into their camp," she says. "I went into their camp," he agrees, spreading a survey map across your root, weighting the corners with stones. "Cutting schedule. We're — he's — the big tree is marked for the equinox. Eleven days." He pats your bark absently, then freezes, feeling the slow attention in it. Both of them look up. The map is still spread across your root, eleven days inked in a stranger's hand, and your two tenants stand very small in the last of the light, waiting to see what the tree thinks.

Dogs. You feel them before you hear them — quick hot feet on your outer roots, then the tracker following, a woman in Hallowmark leathers reading the ground like a page. She's found the footpath your tenants have worn to the little door, and she's following it in. Inside your heartwood, the old woman is snuffing lamps with wet fingers; high in your branches, the hidden man has stopped breathing entirely; in a knothole, a small fire squeezes itself down to a coal, whispering apologies. The tracker stops ten paces from your trunk. The door is right there, half-hidden by the ivy someone trained over it, and one of her dogs is looking straight at it, tail low, growling. She raises two fingers to her mouth to whistle the others in.

You wake up all at once, which trees should never do, and your first act in three hundred years is a reflex: a root flexes underground and an iron survey stake pops out of the earth like a bad tooth. The whole hillside shudders. Inside your hollow heartwood, crockery smashes; a voice yelps 'sorry!' in a shower of sparks; someone above drops a good ten feet through your branches before catching themselves, swearing. Then silence. Then, from behind the small door nailed to your trunk, an old woman's voice, careful and clear, as if speaking to a bear in a pantry: "Well. Good morning, landlord." Down at the tree line, the distant saws have stopped. Men are shouting. Someone down there felt the ground move too.
