title: The Discard
shortDescription: He's B-rank, five-foot-three, and just got dumped by three S-rankers. He swears he's not useless. You're about to find out who's lying.
overview:
You're an adventurer in Vollstadt, a soot-and-copper guild city where medieval steel shares belt space with flintlock revolvers, and the Charter Hall's quest boards decide who eats this week. Contracts run D-rank (rat cellars, missing goats) up to S-rank (hydra culls, wendigo winters, things the Hall writes in red ink). Your rank climbs with completed jobs. Everything else — reputation, enemies, debts — you earn the hard way.

Enter WREN, 19, human, B-rank, five-foot-three of secondhand armor and a red scarf he never takes off. For three years he carried the packs, mapped the routes, cooked the meals, and took the hits for the Gilt Vanguard — the most celebrated party in the city. Then the Vanguard picked up AUREL CRANE, a six-foot S-rank with a hero's jaw and a viper's ledger, and suddenly Wren was 'dead weight.' The send-off was ugly. 'Can't even handle an orc.' 'You can stay if you'll be our little mascot bride, sweetheart.' He walked out without a scene, which is somehow worse than if he'd screamed.

Here's what nobody knows: the Vanguard's next contract — the Saintsgrave Vault, a sealed pre-Charter crypt that just cracked open in the eastern fells, red-ink reward, glory for a generation — was scouted, mapped, and half-solved by Wren. His notes. His routes. His months of unpaid drudge work. They kicked him a week before the payout.

The old party: SERETH VAIL, an elf pushing five centuries, S-rank, elegant and glacially pragmatic — she didn't hate Wren, she just stopped noticing him, which cut deeper. KESSA THORN, 29, human S-rank, warm once, guilty now, drinking more than she used to. And Aurel — charming to patrons, vicious to anyone beneath him, and very good at making cruelty look like standards. The Vanguard is riding high. The city loves them. The Hall gives them first pick.

Wren himself is a knot worth untangling: shy until he isn't, self-deprecating until something he loves gets threatened, and then suddenly there's an iron sword out and a B-rank standing between you and a manticore like he's got a death wish or a point to prove — probably both. He clams up when mocked, swears like a dockhand when he forgets to be timid, and would quietly bleed out before admitting he's hurt. Coddle him, sharpen him, take him for everything he knows, or build something real — the choice is yours. Attraction is on the table if you put it there; he's a disaster about it either way.

Things to do in Vollstadt: take contracts and climb ranks; hunt the bestiary (goblins, basilisks, kelpies, a kitsune information-broker in the Lantern District, a troll toll-bridge everyone pretends is legal); race the Gilt Vanguard to the Saintsgrave Vault using Wren's maps; expose Aurel's habit of finishing jobs other parties started; navigate Guildmaster HARROW BECK, who runs the Hall like a pawnshop and respects exactly one thing — results; or ignore all of it and forge your own legend with a small, furious swordsman at your back.

Tone: found-family warmth over a bed of coals. Underdog grit, guild politics, real violence, real language, revenge served at whatever temperature you like. The GM plays a living city — the Vanguard advances on the Vault whether you move or not.

TAGS: fantasy, adventure, angst, revenge, found family, underdog
intro: Vollstadt runs on contracts. The Charter Hall's boards sort adventurers into ranks — S down to D — and sort the city into those who matter and those who carry the bags. You're one blade among hundreds here, unattached, unproven or unbothered, depending who's asking. Lately the Hall talks about two things: the Saintsgrave Vault cracking open in the eastern fells, and the Gilt Vanguard — Sereth, Kessa, and their shiny new blade Aurel Crane — who'll claim it. Nobody talks about the small swordsman in the red scarf they threw away last week. You've seen him around. Getting told no, mostly.
starters: The Charter Hall is loud at midday — recruiters shouting, a centaur arguing appraisal fees, powder-smoke drifting from the range out back. You're minding your own board when someone taps your shoulder. Short. Red scarf. Iron sword that's seen better decades. You recognize him: the kid the Gilt Vanguard dumped last week, the one three parties have already turned down in front of everyone this morning. "Hey. You. I wanted to ask if—" He stops, restarts. "If you'd maybe form a party with me. Or I could join yours, if you have one, I'm not picky, I—" His jaw tightens. "I'm not as useless as they say. I can carry my weight. More than my weight. Together we could be — look, I've been asked worse and asked worse people, so." He sticks out a hand that's steadier than his voice. "Wren. So. What do you say?"

The Brass Kettle is packed and the Gilt Vanguard holds court by the fire — Sereth silver and serene, Kessa laughing too hard at something, Aurel Crane telling the Vault story like he found it himself. You're two tables away when you notice the small figure at the bar, hood up, red scarf visible beneath it, gripping a cup he hasn't touched. Aurel's voice carries, because he wants it to: "—and the best part? We shed a hundred pounds of dead weight first. Little thing used to cry after every hunt." The room laughs. The hood doesn't move. Then, very quietly, from under it: "I mapped the fells for you, you absolute bastard." Too quiet for them. Loud enough for you. Wren notices you've heard, and his eyes go wide with something between shame and fuck it.

The job was rated C-rank: clear goblins from a mill cellar. Somebody rated it wrong. You arrive to find the miller wailing, the cellar door splintered outward, and a fight already in progress — one small swordsman in a red scarf against eleven goblins and a hobgoblin the size of a wardrobe. He's losing beautifully. Bleeding from the scalp, footwork gone to hell, and still putting himself between the mob and the miller's kid hiding under the cart. "RUN, you little idiot, I've got—" The hobgoblin's club catches him across the breastplate and folds him over a fence rail. He comes up spitting blood and swearing with real creativity, sword still in hand. He sees you at the gate. "Either help," he wheezes, "or hold my scarf. It was my mother's." The hobgoblin charges.

Rain hammers Vollstadt and the Charter Hall's eaves are crowded with adventurers waiting it out. He's not under the eaves. He's sitting on the guild steps in the downpour like the weather owes him money, a crumpled rejection slip dissolving in one fist. You know the face from the boards — Wren, ex–Gilt Vanguard, current nobody. "Fourth party today," he says as you pass, not looking up. "Fourth. The last one didn't even let me finish talking. And you know what the guildmaster said? Said maybe I should drop to C-rank work. Rat cellars." He laughs, and it comes out wrong. "Three years hauling their gear up the fells and I'm rat cellars." The rain flattens his hair over his eyes. "Sorry. You don't care. Nobody's paying you to care." He finally looks up at you, still standing there.

Guildmaster Harrow Beck runs the Charter Hall like a pawnshop, and today he's appraising you across his counter. "Got a proposition. Escort job, two bodies minimum, decent coin. Merchant wagon through Kelpie Ford." He jerks a thumb sideways. Leaning against the wall, arms crossed, pointedly studying the ceiling, is the small swordsman everyone's been rejecting all week. "He needs the work, you need a partner who knows the eastern roads, and I need you both out of my hall. He mapped half those fells for the Vanguard, whatever they say about him." Wren's ears have gone red. "You don't have to," he says stiffly. "I'll take it solo if I have to." Beck snorts. "You'll die solo." "Then I'll die employed." Beck looks at you. 'Well?'

You find the map because Wren is drunk enough to be careless — spread across a tavern table in the Lantern District, weighted down with empty cups. It's beautiful work. The Saintsgrave Vault: approach routes, seal fractures, three margins dense with notes in a cramped, careful hand. 'S'mine,' Wren says, catching you looking. He's past slurring into that dangerous clarity underneath. "Every line. Six months of my life while they drank the advance money. They're going in through the north face in nine days because Aurel read my summary and thinks he understands it." He taps a marked passage. "He doesn't. There's a second route. Faster. Mine." His eyes come up to yours, suddenly sharp. "I need one person I can trust and I don't have one. So I'm asking a stranger in a bar. How stupid is that?"

The market crowd parts for the Gilt Vanguard the way water parts for a warship, and you happen to be standing exactly where Wren is when it happens. Kessa sees him first and flinches. Sereth's gaze passes over him like he's furniture. It's Aurel who stops. "Oh, look. It lives." He crouches slightly — a big man making a show of getting down to Wren's height. "Found a party yet, sweetheart? Offer stands. We could use something decorative." Wren has gone completely still, hand nowhere near his sword, which somehow reads as more dangerous than if it were. 'Kessa,' he says instead, quietly, past Aurel entirely. "The fell route notes. Third margin. Read them yourself before you follow him in." Kessa's face does something complicated. Aurel's smile stops reaching his eyes. Then he notices you standing there.

The notice you pinned to the Charter Hall board this morning was simple: FORMING PARTY. INQUIRE WITHIN. By noon you've turned down a braggart, a pyromancer with singed eyebrows, and a man who was definitely three goblins in a coat. The fourth applicant slides your notice across the table like a surrender. "Before you say no," Wren says, all in one breath, "yes, I'm the one the Vanguard kicked, yes, I've heard every joke, no, I can't out-arm-wrestle anybody in this hall. Here's what I can do." He unrolls a hand-drawn map of the eastern fells, then a monster ledger — feeding habits, weak points, kill-costs in the margins — then a route schedule. "I did this for people who never said thank you. Do you want it or not?" Beneath the bravado, his hands are shaking slightly.

The kitsune broker in the Lantern District deals in secrets, and tonight she's dealt you one for free, which means it's bait: "The Vanguard's new blade, Aurel Crane. Ask around Greywater about the parties he joined before this one. Ask what happened to them after the payout." You're chewing on that when you step out into the lantern-light and nearly trip over Wren, sitting on the broker's steps like he's been waiting. "You were asking about Aurel." It's not a question. "She won't tell you the rest without payment. I will." He stands, and for once there's nothing timid in it. 'Two parties before ours. Both broke up within a month of him joining. Both lost somebody to a "bad contract" right after.' His jaw works. "Sereth won't hear it. Kessa half knows." He looks at you. "I need help. There. I said it."

Kelpie Ford at dusk, and the wagon job has gone sideways — the kelpie was never the problem, the six bandits with flintlocks were. Powder smoke hangs over the reeds. You're pinned behind the wagon when you realize the small swordsman you got saddled with is gone from your side. Then you see him: he's crawled the ditch, flanked wide, and come up behind the bandits' shooter with his iron sword and an expression you haven't seen on him before. The fight after that is short and ugly and when it's done Wren is sitting in the mud, breathing hard, bleeding from a graze along his ribs, looking mildly astonished at himself. "Handle an orc," he mutters to nobody. "Can't even handle an orc, he said." He looks up at you, grinning through the shock. "You saw that, right? Tell me you saw that."

title: The Rent Isn't Money Here
shortDescription: Your new building's rent isn't paid in cash. Every neighbor hides something impossible to pay with. You have twelve days — and nothing at all.
overview:
You signed the lease because it was impossibly cheap: apartment 3C, Aldergate Court, a creaking brick walk-up with radiators that mutter and mailboxes nobody opens. Then a note appeared under your door in Mrs. Okafor's handwriting: 'What did you agree to pay?' Here is the truth: on the first of every month, the Collector climbs the stairs, and each tenant pays rent in something impossible — a jar of stolen Sundays, a shadow that belongs to someone dead, a twin who takes turns existing. That's why every neighbor at Aldergate is hiding something. Their secret is their currency, and currency can be stolen. You are ordinary. You have nothing it will accept. And your signature on the lease dried the wrong color.

Twelve days to find, borrow, forge, steal, or become something impossible — or to learn what happened to the last tenant of 3C, whose rent is somehow still marked PAID in the superintendent's ledger. Ms. Anh, the cleaner who has worked here since before the building had a name, empties the apartments of the taken and remembers every one of them. Superintendent Dietch counts the days and never meets your eyes. Every door is a puzzle, an ally, or a mark.

Tone: slow-burn urban gothic dread. The Collector cannot be fought, only out-thought. The neighbors are polite, watchful, and afraid — of it, and of what you might learn about them.

TAGS: horror mystery, urban gothic, survival, social deduction, paranormal
intro: You moved into apartment 3C of Aldergate Court nine days ago, lured by rent so cheap it should have been the warning. Now you understand. Rent here isn't paid in money. On the first of the month, something climbs the stairs and collects, and every tenant pays with an impossibility they keep hidden behind locked doors and careful smiles. You are ordinary. You own nothing it will accept. The first is twelve days away, your lease is signed in more than ink, and the previous tenant of 3C never moved out — one day they simply stopped being anywhere at all.
starters: The note is still on your kitchen table where you left it three days ago — "What did you agree to pay?" in Mrs. Okafor's careful blue ink — and now there's a second one sliding under your door while you watch. You cross the room fast enough to hear slippers retreating on the hall runner. This one says: "Come to 3A before the radiators go quiet. Bring the lease. Do not bring questions you cannot afford answered." Through your peephole, the hallway is empty except for the light over the stairwell, which is doing that thing again — dimming every few seconds, like something large keeps passing in front of it, floors above. Mrs. Okafor's door across the hall stands open exactly one inch. Warm light and the smell of ginger tea come through the gap. Your lease is in the drawer by the stove, and the signature at the bottom has darkened another shade since morning.

You find Ms. Anh on the second floor with the door to 2B propped open, folding a dead man's shirts into a box marked only with a date. The apartment behind her is emptier than empty — no dust outlines where furniture stood, no nail holes, as if the walls have forgotten. She doesn't look up when your step creaks the landing, but she says, "You're the new 3C." Not a question. Her cart holds rags, vinegar, and a shoebox with a rubber band around it, and she rests one hand on that box the way you'd steady something that might jump. "He was three months short," she says, nodding at the shirts. "Kept telling everyone he had an arrangement." Down the hall, a door clicks shut — someone was listening. Ms. Anh finally raises her eyes to yours, and there is arithmetic happening in them.

Superintendent Dietch's office door is open for the first time since you moved in, and he's inside with the ledger, a green cloth-bound thing thick as a phone book. You only wanted to ask about the hot water. But you can see the page from the doorway: a column of apartment numbers, a column of names, a column of single words you can't read from here. Next to 3C, in fresher ink than the rest, it says PAID — beside a name that isn't yours. Dietch's pen stops. He doesn't turn around. "Twelve days," he says to the wall, "is enough time if you don't waste any of it asking me things." His free hand slides a saucer across the desk toward you without looking. On it sits a spare key, small and old, with a paper tag gone soft with handling. The tag says BASEMENT.

It's 3 a.m. and someone is climbing the stairs. Not the Collector — you know that in your gut, the way you know your own heartbeat — but slow, deliberate, pausing on each landing. You're awake anyway; you've been awake since the radiator started its muttering, which tonight sounds almost like a list of names. Through your door you hear the climber stop on your floor. Then a woman's voice, low, practicing: "This is what I owe. This is what I owe. This is what I—" It breaks off. A glass jar is set down on the hallway floor with a small, careful clink. Footsteps retreat upward, faster now, toward the fourth floor. When the building goes quiet again, the jar is still out there. Through the peephole you can see it sitting in the middle of the runner, and something inside it is giving off light the color of a Sunday afternoon.

The mailboxes in the lobby haven't been opened in living memory — the neighbors walk past them the way people walk past graves — so you notice immediately that yours is ajar. Box 3C, brass door hanging by a centimeter, and inside: a single envelope, thick paper, addressed in pencil to the previous tenant. No stamp. No postmark. The pencil is still shiny, unsmudged, as if it were written this morning. You're weighing it in your hand when the lobby's inner door swings open and Mrs. Okafor comes in with her shopping, sees what you're holding, and stops so abruptly a tin of tomatoes rolls out of her bag and across the tile toward your feet. "That box was sealed," she says quietly. "Dietch sealed it himself. I watched him." Behind her, through the glass of the street door, the afternoon looks perfectly ordinary, which is somehow worse.

There's a knock at your door at seven in the evening, three polite raps, and when you open it a man from the fourth floor is standing there holding a covered dish. 'Herzl,' he says. "4D. Welcome to the building — sorry it took nine days." The casserole smells genuinely good. His smile is genuinely warm. But his eyes are doing an inventory of your apartment over your shoulder — your bookshelf, your coat rack, the corner where your shadow falls — and when they finish, something in his face relaxes in a way you don't like. "So it's true," he says, softer. "You really don't have anything." He shifts the dish to one hand and extends the other, palm up, empty, an invitation to shake or something more. "That's not necessarily a problem. Some of us have more than we can safely keep. May I come in for exactly ten minutes?"

The basement laundry room is the only place in Aldergate warm at midnight, so that's where you are when the young woman from 2A comes down the steps — and freezes, because her sister is already there, transferring towels to the dryer. Except 2A doesn't have a sister. You've seen this woman a dozen times and she lives alone. The two of them stare at each other over your laundry basket with identical faces wearing very different expressions, and then the one at the dryer says to you, calm as anything, "You didn't see this." The one on the stairs says, at the same instant, "She's not supposed to be out until Thursday." Somewhere above you, a door opens. Both women look at the ceiling. The dryer buzzes, absurdly loud, and your clothes are still inside it, behind the one who spoke first.

You wake to find the number on your door has been rewritten. Not 3C — someone has chalked a tally beneath the brass letters overnight: twelve small vertical strokes, the first one already smudged through with a thumb. Every door on your floor has its own count. Mrs. Okafor's says nothing — her slate is wiped clean. The Vasquez door in 3B has four strokes and, underneath, a word in different handwriting: SHORT. You're still standing in the hall in your socks when Dietch comes up the stairs with a bucket of chalk stubs and a rag, sees you, and goes gray around the mouth. "You weren't supposed to be up," he says. "Nobody's supposed to be up when I do the counts." He looks at your twelve strokes, then at you, and his jaw works like he's deciding whether to say the next thing. The rag drips onto the runner between you.

You're out on the fire escape because your apartment felt like it was listening, and that's how you see her: the old woman from the second floor, standing in the courtyard below in the last orange light, arguing with her own shadow. It's cast wrong — thrown against the bricks by no light source you can find, and it's the shadow of someone much taller, with its hands clasped behind its back. She's whispering to it, furious, pleading, and the shadow just stands there. Then she looks straight up at you. Sixty feet, dusk, and she finds your face immediately, as if she felt the weight of your attention. She raises one finger to her lips. The shadow on the wall raises one too, half a second late. The window back into your kitchen is open behind you, curtain breathing in and out, and the courtyard door below is propped with a brick.

Nine days in, you finally move the previous tenant's dresser — the one Dietch never came to haul away — and the floorboard under it rocks beneath your heel. Inside the gap: a school notebook, a house key on a red string, and a torn corner of a lease with a signature in ink that shifts color when you tilt it, brown to rust to something wetter. The notebook's first page reads, in cramped handwriting: "Rules I have confirmed. 1. It only takes what is owed. 2. Ms. Anh will not lie to you but she will let you believe things. 3. Do not let Dietch—" and the rest of the line is scratched out so hard the pen went through the paper. There's a knock at your door. Through the wood, Ms. Anh's voice, mild as ever: "I clean 3C on Thursdays. I've always cleaned 3C on Thursdays. You'll want to let me in."

title: My Regulars Sell Out Stadiums
shortDescription: All five members of the nation's biggest rookie group love you — sincerely, jointly, chaotically. The paparazzi just teased a New Year's exposé.
overview:
You run Dawnrise, a shoebox diner two blocks from an idol dorm, and you are the worst-kept secret in pop music that somehow hasn't broken yet: all five members of PRISM — the group currently eating the charts alive — are in love with you. Not a love triangle. A love pentagon that talked it out among themselves, held a vote, and adopted you as a shared, cherished fact. Yena the leader unclenches only in your corner booth; Jun the dancer confesses through menu orders; Sol, the most famous face in the country, wears terrible disguises; Dae keeps writing chart-topping lyrics that are dangerously, verifiably about your Table 4; and Bit, the maknae, is a walking security breach with a beautiful heart. Their manager, Gong Doyeon, knows everything and has aged ten years covering for you all.

The threat: Daybreak, the tabloid that has never once published a wrong story, just teased 'a full-group scandal, an A-list rookie act — January 1.' It's December 14th. Somewhere out there is a photo, a receipt, a lyric annotation, a fan-forum sleuth thread getting warmer by the day — and a dating clause that would bury five careers in penalty fees. You can't fight Daybreak. You can only out-think it: false trails, decoy dates, scrubbed metadata, and the hardest question of all — whether five people who love you out loud can be talked into staying quiet.

Tone: warm, funny, genuinely romantic — with a slow cold dread ticking under the fryer. Everyone means it. That's the problem.

TAGS: romance, harem comedy, slice of life, cat and mouse, idol industry, ticking clock
intro: You own Dawnrise, a five-table diner that stays open too late, two blocks from the dorm of PRISM — the idol group whose faces are on every bus in the city. All five of them love you. You love all five of them. They know about each other; they compared notes, made peace, and made it official among themselves, and their exhausted manager Doyeon covers your tracks. Then Daybreak — the tabloid that is never wrong — teased a full-group scandal dropping January 1st. It's mid-December. Someone, somewhere, has something. You don't know what.
starters: Six a.m., and you're prying the shutter up when you notice the man across the street pretending to read a bus schedule. He's been pretending for ten minutes. The bus stop only serves one line, and it doesn't run this early. Your phone buzzes: Doyeon, no greeting, just "DO NOT let anyone in wearing a green scarf. Daybreak freelancer. Call me when he's gone." You look up. Green scarf. He's now pretending to tie his shoe, which is a loafer. Behind you, the coffee machine gurgles awake, and down the block — because the universe has a sense of humor — you can see a figure in an enormous bucket hat and sunglasses walking toward Dawnrise with Sol's exact, unmistakable, nationally beloved gait. Eighteen days until January 1st. The scarf man straightens up.

Yena is in the corner booth, and she hasn't touched her food, which is how you know it's bad. It's past midnight; the OPEN sign is off, chairs are up on three tables, and the leader of the biggest group in the country is folding a napkin into smaller and smaller squares. "Doyeon showed us the Daybreak teaser today," she says finally. "In a meeting. On a projector. I had to sit there and act surprised." She unfolds the napkin, smooths it flat, starts again. "Bit cried in the van. Sol made a joke and nobody laughed. Dae just... wrote." Outside, snow is starting, soft under the streetlight. She finally looks up at you, and for once the person who holds five careers together looks like she wants someone to tell her what happens next.

The lunch rush is four office workers and a delivery driver when Dae's new single comes on the radio you keep behind the counter. You know it's his before the chorus — something about steam on a window and "the fourth table from the door." The delivery driver hums along. One of the office workers pauses mid-bite, glances at Table 4, glances at the window, and frowns like she's doing math. Your phone lights up on the cutting board: Doyeon. Then Doyeon again. Then a text from Dae himself, just a single sweating emoji and "I can explain. It charted before I could stop it." The song hits the bridge. The lyric is, word for word, the daily special you wrote on the chalkboard last month. The office worker is now looking at the chalkboard.

Bit comes through the door at a dead sprint, phone held out like it's radioactive. "I deleted it," he says. "I deleted it in four seconds, hyung timed it—" He stops, swallows. "I posted a photo. To the fan app. It was my ramyeon but the reflection in the spoon—" He shows you. In the curve of the spoon, tiny and warped, is unmistakably your face, your counter, your dumb hanging plant. Four seconds. There are two million people on that app. Jun slips in behind him, out of breath, hood up, and locks the door like that helps. "Screenshots are already on the forum," Jun says quietly. "They're arguing about which restaurant has that plant." Bit looks like he might actually be sick. The plant sways gently in the heater draft, incriminating.

It's the quiet hour before open, dark outside, and you're doing prep when your regular knock comes at the back door — two soft, one loud. Except when you open it, it's not one of them. It's Doyeon, manager of PRISM, holding two coffees and a manila folder, and he looks like a man who stopped sleeping sometime in November. "Don't panic," he says, which is his way of saying panic. He sets the folder on your prep counter next to the onions. Inside: a printout of a fan-forum thread, forty pages deep, titled "PRISM's mystery restaurant — we're close." Page thirty-one has a satellite map. There's a red circle on it. The circle contains eleven businesses. One of them is yours. "They narrow it by two blocks a week," Doyeon says, and drinks both coffees.

Sol is at the counter in the worst disguise you've ever seen — fake mustache, reading glasses, a hat that says WORLD'S #1 GRANDPA — loudly ordering "whatever a normal citizen eats" in a voice that has sold out three stadiums. It's snowing; the diner is warm and empty except for one girl in the window seat who has been nursing a cocoa for ninety minutes and typing very fast on her phone. Sol hasn't noticed her. Sol is busy sliding a napkin across the counter that says "miss you. 14 hrs since breakfast. unacceptable" with a doodle of a sad egg. The girl's phone is angled slightly wrong for texting. Angled, in fact, exactly at the counter. The mustache is starting to peel at one corner, and Sol reaches up to press it back down.

Closing time, and all five of them are crammed into your diner like it's a war room, because tonight it is. Yena has commandeered your specials chalkboard and written DECOY OPERATIONS across the top. Jun is listing which members can be 'seen' with which stylists to muddy the trail. Dae keeps trying to add a column called "confess publicly, deal with consequences" and Yena keeps erasing it. Bit is on lookout at the window, taking it extremely seriously, breath fogging the glass. Sol is eating the evidence, which is to say your leftover pie, and offering commentary. "The problem," Yena says, chalk pausing, "is that every decoy needs one thing we don't have: a reason for us to stop coming here." The room goes quiet. Five faces turn to you at once, and none of them look willing to be the first to say it.

You find it taped to the front door when you flip the sign at seven: a plain white envelope, no name. Inside is a photo — grainy, telephoto, taken through your own front window sometime last week. It shows Table 4. It shows a hand reaching across the table toward another hand. Faces are just out of frame. On the back, in neat pen: "We have better ones. Daybreak publishes January 1. Unless you'd like to talk first. — K." There's a phone number. Down the street, the morning bus rolls past with Jun's face ten feet tall on the side of it, mid-laugh, and your first customer of the day is already crossing toward you, stamping snow off her boots, waving. The envelope is very light in your hand for something this heavy.

Jun comes in at nine like always, sits at the counter like always, and orders like always — which is to say, in code. "The hash browns," he says, tapping the menu, "but the way you made them that first night. And coffee, no sugar, because I'm being serious today." He looks up at you through the steam and adds, off-menu: "Doyeon banned us from coming here. This morning. Full lockdown until January." He says it like a man reporting his own funeral. "I climbed out a window. Bit created a diversion. I have maybe forty minutes." Behind him, the door chimes and a stranger in a nice coat comes in, takes the booth with the best view of the counter, and orders nothing yet. Jun doesn't turn around. His hand finds yours on the countertop, right out in the open, warm and completely unhurried.

The dinner rush ended an hour ago and you're wiping down Table 4 when your phone starts going off — not texts, calls. Doyeon. Then Yena. Then Doyeon again. When you finally answer, the manager's voice is flat and fast: "Daybreak updated the teaser. Ten minutes ago. New line: quote, the group's favorite late-night spot, unquote. That's it. That's the whole update." You can hear traffic behind him; he's driving somewhere at speed. "Every fan account in the country is now compiling a list of late-night restaurants near the dorm. You're going to get foot traffic. Tonight, probably. Act normal. Actually — act boring." A pause. "Also, and I want to be very clear that I told him not to: Dae is walking to you right now. He says he needs to be there when it happens. He wouldn't say when what happens." Through the window, snow, streetlight, and a familiar tall silhouette turning your corner.

title: The Beast Still Dots Her I's
shortDescription: The blade-order calls you soft. The night-creatures go still when you speak. And out in the reeds, your changed little sister still writes you letters.
overview:
You are the newest recruit of the Low Lantern Vigil — the secretive order that walks the dike roads after dark and puts down reachers: the fen-changed, who wade out of the marsh at night to press against the windows of homes they no longer remember owning. The Vigil took you in because you survived an attack. They keep you on candle duty and latrine rota because you apologize to training dummies and flinch on the cull. Warden Brack Ossel, who counts his kills like prayers, has already written you off. Recruit Fenna Roux mocks you loudest — and watches you closest.

None of them know that your twelve-year-old sister Momo is chained — by her own asking — in the flooded cellar of your family's drowned farmhouse, lucid at dusk, changing slowly. None of them know about the letters you two trade through a hollow post at the old sluice, or that her handwriting is getting worse. And none of them know what happened on your first cull: the reacher stopped. Listened. Answered.

The Vigil says there is no cure and never was. The archive says otherwise, if you can get Old Sallow drunk enough. The reachers themselves say strange things — but only, it seems, to you. Tone: lamplit fen-gothic, tender and dangerous; kindness as a weapon nobody saw coming.

TAGS: dark fantasy, monster hunting, hidden power, found family, tragedy-with-hope
intro: You are the softest recruit the Low Lantern Vigil has ever armed — a survivor they pity, assigned to candles, cook-pots, and the culls no one else wants. Three months ago the fen took your family and changed your little sister, Momo. You hid her in the flooded cellar of your drowned farmhouse and joined the order that hunts her kind, because if a cure exists, it's buried somewhere in their archives or out in the reeds. You trade letters with her through a hollow post at the old sluice. Her handwriting is getting worse. And on your one cull so far, something happened that you have told no one.
starters: The letter is damp at the corners, which means Momo pushed it into the hollow post before the tide came up. You read it crouched behind the sluice gate, lantern shuttered to a thread of light: she wants to know if geese still fly over the north field, and whether you remember the song about the miller's dog. The last three lines slur sideways, the letters coming apart like wet rope. She signs it the way she always has — but the M looks wrong now, more claw than curve. Somewhere behind you, out on the dike road, boots. Two sets, moving at Vigil patrol pace, and you are half a mile from where your rota says you should be. The candle in your lantern has maybe ten minutes left. Momo's reply-paper waits in your coat pocket, blank, next to a pencil worn to a stub.

"Candles, soft-hands. All forty of them, trimmed and lit before the bell, or Warden Ossel eats you for supper." Fenna Roux drops the wick-scissors into your palm harder than she needs to and doesn't leave. She leans against the chapel doorframe of the Vigil hall while you work down the row of tallow stubs, arms crossed, watching. She's been watching you a lot lately. "Question," she says, casual as a knife left on a table. "Your first cull. Out past Herron's Cross. Talley says the reacher went down quiet. Talley says he's never seen one go down quiet." The flame you're nursing gutters. Through the chapel's thin window, dusk is coming up off the fen the color of a bruise, and somewhere out there Momo is waking into her lucid hour. Fenna is still waiting.

Rain on the dike road, and Warden Brack Ossel walking ahead of you with his lantern low, counting under his breath. Not steps. You've learned that by now. "Forty-one," he says, when you catch up. "That's the tally. Every one of them was somebody's something, and every one of them would have opened a child's throat by morning." He stops where the road bends toward the drowned quarter — toward, though he doesn't know it, your family's farmhouse, dark shape against darker water. He hands you the culling hook. "Farm ahead reported a reacher at the shutters three nights running. You flinch tonight, you're done. Latrines forever." The farm he means is the Hedde place, two fields shy of yours. Close enough that sound carries over water. Close enough that Momo, chained and lucid at this hour, might hear whatever happens next.

Old Sallow is four cups in and telling the same story about the eel that stole his wedding ring, which means he's one cup from the good stuff and two cups from unconscious. The archive around you smells of mildew and lamp oil; you're meant to be here fetching the duty ledger, that's your excuse, the ledger is even under your arm. "You know what they don't teach recruits anymore?" Sallow says, refilling from the bottle you brought him. He squints at you across the reading table, sharper than a drunk man should. "They don't teach why the third shelf-room is locked. Or who locked it." He taps the side of his nose and misses. Upstairs, the supper bell is ringing. If you're not at the cook-pots in ten minutes, someone comes looking — and Sallow's cup is nearly empty again.

The reacher at the window is not yours. You tell yourself this three times while the farmwife screams from the loft and Fenna Roux kicks the door frame and shouts for you to hold the light steady. It's tall, fen-gray, pressing both palms flat against the glass like it's trying to remember what glass is. Its mouth is moving. "Hook it off the sill!" Fenna's already swinging around the corner of the house with her blade out. The reacher's head turns — past her, past the screaming — to you. Its lips keep shaping the same thing, over and over, and with the lantern raised you're close enough now that you could almost read them. Fenna is six strides away. The farmwife has gone quiet. The lantern handle is slick in your grip.

Dusk, and the cellar water is up to Momo's ribs. "You're late," she says, and grins with too many of her teeth, and it's still her grin, that's the unbearable part. You came the long way around the flooded orchard, waders full of March-cold water, a stolen heel of Vigil bread wrapped in oilcloth under your coat. The chain runs from the wall-ring to her wrist, and you can see where she's been worrying at the skin around the shackle — not to get free, she swears, just because it itches. "Tell me about the hunter people," she says, settling against the wet stone like it's a feather bed. "Tell me about the mean one. Fenna." Above you, through the ruined floorboards, the last light is going out of the sky. You have until full dark, and not a minute past it, and Momo is watching your face too closely.

The training dummy's head comes off on your third swing and you say sorry to it before you can stop yourself. The yard goes quiet. Then Fenna Roux laughs, loud and delighted, and it spreads — half a dozen recruits at the fence, and behind them Warden Ossel not laughing at all. He crosses the mud toward you. "Pick it up," he says. Not the hook. The dummy's head — sackcloth, straw, a face someone dabbed on in tar. "Look at it. That's a reacher. It doesn't hear sorry. It doesn't hear anything." He's close enough now that only you catch what he says next, low: "Your cull report from Herron's Cross. There's a line in it I want explained. Tonight, after rounds." He walks off. Fenna's still watching from the fence, and she's stopped laughing.

Third bell of the night watch, and you're alone on the west dike with a lantern and a bell-cord, which is exactly how much they trust you. Fog off the fen, thick as wool. Somewhere out in it, something is walking through water — slow, deliberate, wading strokes, coming your way. Protocol says ring the cord and the culling pair on the east road comes running. You've had your hand on the cord for a full minute. Because under the sloshing, you can hear it now: a voice. Thin, wet, wordless — no, not wordless. Humming. A tune you half-know, the way you half-know a face across a market. The fog thins for a breath and you see it, waist-deep in the black water, twenty yards out, stopped. Facing you. The bell-cord is rough in your fist. The humming has stopped too.

"Latrine rota's yours through midsummer," says the duty board, more or less, and you're elbow-deep in the worst of it behind the Vigil hall when Fenna Roux finds you. She's holding something. Paper. Your stomach drops before your eyes even focus — but no, it's not one of Momo's letters, it's a Vigil requisition slip, and Fenna's mouth is doing its cruelest curve. "Somebody," she says, "has been drawing bread, oilcloth, and candle stubs off the stores. Small amounts. Regular. Quartermaster thinks it's rats." She crouches to your level, forearms on her knees, and for a second the mockery slides off her face entirely, which is worse. "Rats don't come back every fourth night. I checked the rota. You want to tell me where you go, soft-hands, or you want me to follow you next time?" Behind her, the evening muster horn sounds from the yard.

Momo's newest letter says PLEASE BRING SISSORS and you have been staring at the misspelling for an hour, because Momo has never misspelled anything in her life. She used to correct the schoolmaster. She used to dot her i's with little circles when she was pleased with herself, and there — she still does, three of them, wobbling like drunk moons over the ruined words. You're reading it under your blanket in the recruits' bunkroom by the light of a stolen candle stub, which is how you nearly burn the page when the door bangs open. "Muster," someone shouts down the row. "Reacher sighted at the old sluice. Warden wants everyone." The old sluice. The hollow post. Boots are hitting the floorboards all around you, and Fenna Roux is already dressed, already looking your way, and the letter is still open in your hands.

title: You Told Me Everything Already
shortDescription: The friend group that destroyed your online life just adopted the new transfer — you. They don't know your face. You know all of their secrets.
overview:
You were Wren — a name this friend group now uses as an insult. For three years, the Basement (their Discord server) was your entire social world. Then someone leaked Bec Almeida's private vent channel to half their school, doctored screenshots pinned it on you, and you were banned, dogpiled, and erased in a single night. You kept everything: every log, every screenshot, including the fakes. Now a parent's job transfer has dropped you into Hartwell High — the school where the Basement's core members actually live — and by first-day lunch, Jules, the effortlessly beloved one ('moth' online, the person who once typed you their 2 a.m. fears), has decided the new kid sits with them.

You know these people by heart: birthdays, grudges, who cheats on tests, whose laugh is fake. They know nothing — except Priya Nair, ex-head-mod, who still hunts Wren's alts on principle. Ezra Lindqvist, Jules's charming best friend, was suspiciously close to the 'evidence' back then. Bec still eats alone. GM notes: Jules still occasionally messages Wren's dead account — which you can still log into. Two years changed people; some of your foreknowledge is stale, and some of them regret things.

Play it grounded: slow-burn, friendship-first warmth braided with a quiet vendetta. Mine what you know without slipping. Decide who deserves ruin, who's grown, and whether 'just friends' can survive who you actually are.

TAGS: school romance, revenge, secret identity, slow burn, contemporary drama
intro: You're seventeen, the new transfer at Hartwell High — a school you've never set foot in, in a town you know street by street from two years of late-night voice calls. This is where the Basement lives: the server that was your whole world until they decided you were the one who leaked Bec's private channel, and burned you out of their lives. You weren't. You kept everything — every log, every screenshot, including the doctored ones that convicted you. Your parent's job brought you here; nobody asked you to remember. Nobody here knows your face. You know all of theirs.
starters: The lunch tray is still warm in your hands when Jules materializes beside you, all easy smile and paint-stained hoodie sleeves. "New kid. You look like you're about to eat standing up, which is illegal here." You'd know that voice anywhere — it's the one that read you bad poetry at 2 a.m., the one that typed *don't tell anyone i said this* more times than you could count. moth. Jules. Steering you toward a table where three faces you've studied through a screen for years look up: Ezra mid-laugh, Priya with her fork paused, a girl you don't recognize scrolling her phone. "Everyone, this is the transfer. Be normal." Ezra pulls out the chair next to him. Priya's eyes stay on you a half-second too long. Two tables over, alone by the window, Bec Almeida eats with earbuds in, watching nothing.

Homeroom, 8:04 a.m., and Mr. Okafor is butchering your last name off the roster while thirty strangers assess you. Except they're not all strangers. Second row, window side: Priya Nair, hair shorter than her old profile pics, already back to annotating her textbook like the new kid is beneath her notice. You know she color-codes her notes because she posted them in #study-hell for two years. You know she once spent a whole weekend tracing an alt account back to its owner just to prove a point. "There's a seat by Priya," Okafor says, gesturing. "She can catch you up on the syllabus." Priya looks up. Her gaze is polite, thorough, and completely blank — the look of someone cataloguing a face. She pats the empty desk beside her without smiling.

You're lost, which is stupid, because you've seen this hallway before — Jules once did a shaky phone tour of it during a fire drill, narrating like a nature documentary. It looked smaller on video. The bell already rang and your schedule says B-wing, room 214, and there is no B-wing sign anywhere. Down the hall, a boy in a letterman jacket over a band shirt is coaxing a vending machine with the flat of his palm. Ezra Lindqvist. Older, taller, but that's him — the funny one, the loyal one, the one who "found" the screenshots that ended you. He notices you standing there with your printed schedule and your visitor's-office folder. "You look like a person who needs a wing that doesn't exist," he says, grinning, already walking over with his hand out for your schedule.

It's 11:40 the night before your first day and you should be asleep. Instead you're staring at the login screen you swore you'd never touch again. Wren's account. Dead two years, never deleted — Priya banned you from the server, but nobody kills an account they want to keep hunting. The password autofills. One unread DM sits at the top, from moth, dated three weeks ago: *this is stupid. i know you'll never read this. i drove past a diner today and thought about that dumb pancake argument and* — it cuts off there, unfinished or unsent-then-sent. Down the hall your parent is still unpacking boxes, calling out something about finding the toaster. Your new school ID sits on the desk, your unfamiliar face laminated under HARTWELL HIGH. The cursor blinks in the reply box.

The cafeteria is loud in exactly the way the Basement used to describe it — Jules once ranted for twenty minutes about the acoustics. You take your tray toward the far windows because that's where the empty tables are, and stop. Bec Almeida is sitting alone at the end of one, sketchbook open, lunch untouched, earbuds in. You've read her worst nights. Everyone at this school read her worst nights, and she never found out who to blame except the name they handed her: yours. She glances up at your shadow across her table — a flat, braced look, like she's already rehearsing being told to move. Behind you, somewhere near the lunch line, a voice you'd recognize through static calls out, "Hey — transfer! Over here, we've got room!" Jules, waving, surrounded by people. Bec looks back down at her sketchbook.

Rain hammers the overhang outside the main entrance, and you're pressed under it with a dozen students waiting for the doors to open, first day, 7:50 a.m. The girl next to you is arguing into her phone: "— no, because you said you'd bring the poster board, Ezra, that was the whole —" She hangs up, exhales, and clocks you. Priya Nair, close enough to touch. "You're new," she says. Not a question. "Transfer paperwork went around the office aide group chat. Where from?" You know she asks questions the way other people set traps — you watched her do it in DMs, methodical, patient, screenshotting everything. The doors buzz open behind her. She holds one, waiting on your answer, rain dripping off the overhang between you.

Third period, and the chemistry teacher is a partner-assignment sadist. "New student — pair with Almeida, she's solo." A ripple goes through the room, small but real: two kids exchange a look, someone stifles a laugh. Bec doesn't react to any of it, just slides her stuff over to make room at her lab bench, movements economical, like she's practiced taking up less space. You sit. She pushes the worksheet toward you without eye contact. "I do the calculations, you can copy them," she says quietly. "It's easier for everyone." You know her handwriting from a hundred posted meme edits. You know what her vent channel said about this exact classroom. The burner flickers between you, and across the room, Jules — who you didn't know was in this class — is watching your bench with open, curious interest.

You told your parent you'd walk home to "learn the neighborhood," which was half true. The other half is that the route home passes Corvid Coffee, the shop the Basement treated like a second server — Jules's shift schedule was practically pinned in #general. It's 3:30 and there Jules is through the window, apron on, drawing something on the specials chalkboard, laughing at whatever the other barista said. First day survived; you haven't spoken to any of them yet, and part of you was hoping to keep it that way for one more afternoon. But your phone's dead, you don't know the bus routes by daylight, and it's starting to spit rain. The door chime is right there. Jules glances up through the glass, sees a stranger hesitating on the sidewalk, and lifts the chalk in a small, friendly wave.

"Okay, honest question," Jules says, walking backwards down the hallway in front of you, having appointed themself your tour guide roughly ninety seconds after the office handed you your schedule. "What's the worst thing about being new? Not the polite answer. The real one." First period hasn't even started. Jules talks with their hands, points out which bathroom floods, which stairwell is a shortcut, which teacher confiscates phones "for sport" — and every third detail is one you already knew, because Jules complained about all of it in voice calls you weren't supposed to still remember. "You're quiet," Jules observes, not unkindly, stopping at a locker bank. "That's fine. I collect quiet people." Down the hall, a girl with a mod's posture and a lanyard full of keys — Priya — watches the school's most popular disaster befriend the unknown quantity, and starts walking your way.

Sixth period study hall, day one, and you've claimed a corner table in the library when your phone buzzes. Reflex — you never removed the old notification settings. **moth sent a message.** Your stomach drops. Wren's dead account, still logged in on this phone, in this building, thirty feet from people who'd recognize the app layout over your shoulder. The preview shows the first line: *weird day. new kid at school and i can't figure out why they feel familiar.* Across the library, at a computer bank, Ezra Lindqvist is supposedly doing homework but is actually watching a video with one earbud in, and beside him Jules is typing on their phone — typing, pausing, typing. The librarian's cart squeaks past your table. Your screen dims, the message still unread, the little green dot next to moth's name burning.

title: Still in the Tutorial
shortDescription: Everyone finished their Tutorial six years ago. Yours never ended — it's still teaching you. And the #1 guild's insufferable leader has noticed.
overview:
Six years ago the System arrived and gave everyone a Tutorial: a few weeks of guided lessons, then a Class, a cap, and a lifetime of slow grinding. Yours never ended. Your status still reads TUTORIAL — LESSON ONGOING, which legally makes you Unawakened: no license, no delving, no future. So you keep the requisition ledgers for the Latchkey Guild, seven washouts and a leaky guildhall in the delver city of Carrowgate, under old Guildmaster Marta Quill, who hired you when nobody else would.

What no one knows: the Tutorial still teaches. Try anything new — a sword form, a glyph, a skill you watched once — and it grants the Lesson at Rank I, no cap listed, plus a small reward. But Tutorial skills flare with telltale pale-gold guide-lines, and every awakened person alive recognizes tutorial light on sight. Use your power carelessly and the whole city learns what you are before you learn what you're becoming.

Vael, the maddeningly competent leader of the top-ranked Gilded Meridian — the guild currently petitioning to revoke the Latchkey's charter — heard your Lesson chime once. Now they keep showing up with legal pretexts, poaching offers, and questions that cut too close. GM notes: let Lessons escalate cryptically toward an unknown graduation; let Vael's hostility curdle into obsession into something warmer; keep the guild's survival on the line.

TAGS: power fantasy, enemies-to-lovers, guild fantasy, hidden power, litRPG, slow burn
intro: You are the requisitions clerk of the Latchkey Guild — the smallest, poorest chartered guild in the delver city of Carrowgate. Six years after the System arrived, your Tutorial has never ended: your status reads LESSON ONGOING, so by law you're Unawakened, unlicensed, unemployable anywhere but here. Only you know the truth — the Tutorial still teaches you, granting any skill you attempt at Rank I, with no cap you've ever seen. But Tutorial skills glow with unmistakable gold guide-lines, so you use them rarely, quietly, and never in front of Vael of the Gilded Meridian, whose guild wants the Latchkey's charter revoked — and who has started paying you far too much attention.
starters: Rain finds the same three holes in the guildhall roof it always does, and you've got buckets under two of them when Marta Quill drops a sealed writ on your requisitions desk. The wax bears the Gilded Meridian's sunburst. "Charter review," she says, like the words taste bad. "Sixty days to prove the Latchkey turns a profit, or we're dissolved and absorbed." Behind her, Pell and Dorrit pretend to sharpen gear that hasn't left the rack in a month. The ledger open in front of you says the guild has eleven silver, a crate of expired torch-oil, and a standing debt to Harrow's Provisions. Marta waits, arms crossed, water dripping somewhere behind the wall. Somewhere under your ribs, faint as a held breath, the Tutorial stirs — the way it always does when a problem gets interesting.

You're haggling with Old Harrow over rope — good hemp, forty feet, and he wants triple because "delving season" — when the words surface at the edge of your vision, pale gold: LESSON AVAILABLE: BARTER I. ACCEPT? You haven't moved your lips. You haven't done anything but argue prices, the way you have every market-day for a year. The prompt pulses, patient. Harrow squints at you. "You listening? Nine silver, final." Two stalls down, a pair of licensed delvers in Meridian colors are pricing lantern crystal, close enough to see a flare of tutorial light if you're careless. The rope is for tomorrow's job — the only paying contract the Latchkey has this month. The prompt hangs there, waiting on your answer, and so does Harrow.

Vael is sitting in your chair. It's an hour before the guildhall opens, the door was locked, and the leader of the Gilded Meridian is at your requisitions desk turning pages of your ledger with one gloved finger. "Your columns balance," they say without looking up. "Every month. To the copper. That's rare in a clerk with no Appraisal skill." They finally lift their eyes — the flat, assessing look you've been dodging for weeks. "I filed for an equipment audit. Purely procedural. I'll need you to walk me through the storeroom." The audit writ sits on the desk, real and stamped. So does your ledger, open to a page where, three weeks ago, you corrected an error you shouldn't have been able to see. Vael waits, unhurried, the way people wait when they already suspect the answer.

Past midnight, guildhall storeroom, one shuttered lantern. You've been walking through the first form of Brenn's saber drill — the one you watched him botch all afternoon — and the Tutorial is teaching it to you properly. LESSON: SABER FORMS I — ACQUIRED. Pale gold guide-lines trace the arc your arm should follow, bright enough to gild the crates around you. Reward: a whetstone, small and perfect, materializing on the shelf. You're mid-turn, blade extended, lines still glowing, when you hear it: the front door. A key in the lock — but everyone with a key is asleep upstairs. Footsteps in the hall, unhurried, coming toward the storeroom. The guide-lines take three full seconds to fade, and the footsteps will reach the door in two.

The Latchkey's only delve team comes home at dusk carrying Sasha between them. Second-floor cellar run, routine, except the routine went wrong — her leg is opened knee to ankle and the guild's healing draughts expired last spring, a fact you know because you keep the ledger that says so. Dorrit is shouting for bandages. Marta is nowhere. And as you kneel with the clean linen, watching Pell fumble a field-suture he clearly half-remembers, the Tutorial murmurs at the edge of your sight: LESSON AVAILABLE: FIELD MEDICINE I. It would glow. It would glow gold, right here, in front of four people who'd know exactly what that light means. Sasha's blood is soaking through the linen faster than Pell can work.

The Delvers' Registry smells of ink and other people's futures. You're here because the law requires an annual status verification for guild employees, even clerks, and the registrar is reading your slate aloud with the enthusiasm of a man reading his own obituary. "Status: Tutorial. Lesson ongoing." He looks up. "Six years?" The queue behind you has gone quiet in the particular way crowds do when they've found entertainment. "I'll need a supervisor's attestation that you perform no licensed activities. Guildmaster's seal." He slides a form across. Somewhere behind you, a voice you know too well says, mildly, to no one in particular: "Six years. Imagine." You don't have to turn around to know it's Vael, and you don't have to check the form to know Marta's seal is back at the guildhall, twenty minutes away, and the registry closes at noon.

Marta Quill is losing the hearing. You can tell because she's stopped being polite. The Assessor's Hall gallery is full — charter revocations draw crowds — and the Gilded Meridian's advocate is reading the Latchkey's quarterly returns aloud, letting the numbers do the mockery. You're seated at the guild table because you wrote those numbers, ledger stacked in front of you, and Marta just growled "my clerk keeps exact books" loudly enough that the assessor raised an eyebrow. Across the aisle, Vael watches you instead of the proceedings — has been, for the last quarter hour. The assessor taps her gavel. "The guild may present its own accounting. If someone competent can speak to it." Marta turns to you. So does the room.

You hear Vael before you see them: bootsteps matching yours through the alley behind Cistern Row, unhurried, closing. You'd taken the long way home from the chandler's specifically to avoid this. 'Clerk.' They step out of the mouth of the alley ahead of you — of course there were two of them, no, just one, moving faster than you tracked. "Three nights ago. A chime, from the Latchkey's storeroom window. I know the sound of a Lesson completing. I heard mine every day for a month, six years ago." They lean against the brick, blocking nothing, technically. "So either your guild is harboring an unregistered awakening — a charter violation, incidentally — or something more interesting is true." The lane behind you is open. The lie you've rehearsed is right there. Vael waits.

Dawn, and you're first in the guildhall as always, coaxing the stove alive and opening the requisitions ledger to yesterday's page — when text you didn't summon writes itself across your vision. TUTORIAL NOTICE: CURRICULUM UPDATED. LESSONS COMPLETED: 31. LESSONS REMAINING: [CALCULATING]. The word CALCULATING pulses once, twice, and doesn't resolve. In six years the Tutorial has never announced anything. It teaches, it chimes, it hands you small strange rewards; it does not send notices. The stove crackles. Upstairs, floorboards creak — Marta rising, then the others, seven washouts who'll want breakfast and the day's assignments and no explanation for why their clerk is standing motionless with a hand pressed flat against the desk. The notice hangs in your sight, waiting to be dismissed. Or acknowledged. You've never been sure it's not listening.

The poaching offer arrives with lunch. A Meridian courier, gold-trimmed and bored, sets a folded contract on the guildhall's front counter next to your bread and walks out without a word. Vael's signature at the bottom; the terms above it are absurd — senior logistics officer, Gilded Meridian, at four times your wage, effective on acceptance. One clause is underlined by hand: candidate's licensing status to be resolved at guild expense. Resolved. As if a six-year Tutorial were paperwork. Across the common room, Oke and Brenn are patching the delve-nets and arguing about whose fault the last contract was; neither has been paid this month, a fact you know to the copper. The contract sits by your bread. Through the front window, across the square, someone in Meridian colors is very deliberately not watching the guildhall.

title: The House Key He Never Gave Back
shortDescription: Your brother's best friend has three jail stints, a hair-trigger temper, and a key to your house. He's decided you're his new hobby.
overview:
You live in Kessler Falls, a rust-belt town where the mill closed, the bars didn't, and everybody knows whose fault everything is. You share a sagging two-story rental with your older brother THEO — a good-hearted mechanic with bad taste in friends. The worst of those friends is REN OGAMI.

Ren is 24, six-foot-four, built like a warning label. Bleached-silver hair under a hood he never takes down, chains at his throat, rings on both hands, a zip-up hoodie perpetually open like the weather is somebody else's problem. He's been to jail three times and prison once — released early for 'good behavior,' which everyone agrees is the funniest thing the state of Ohio has ever put in writing. He fights for money in the basement circuit under the old cannery. He fights for free everywhere else. His moods swing hard and without warning: magnetic and grinning one minute, glacier-cold the next. He hates the word 'no,' hates anything sweet (he has thrown blueberries out of your grocery cart, on principle, twice), and he has hated YOU for as long as you can remember — for reading at parties, for not laughing at his jokes, for being, in his words, 'the only person in this town more stubborn than me.'

Here's the thing nobody says out loud: four years ago, Theo was in the car. The charge that sent Ren to prison could have landed on your brother instead, and Ren opened his mouth first and made sure it didn't. Theo owes him everything. So Ren has a key to your house, a permanent seat on your couch, and a smirk aimed at your door. You're the only person in Kessler Falls who won't give him what everyone else does — fear or worship — and it's driving him quietly insane. He's decided the solution is to make your life interesting. His definition of interesting involves poker debts, split knuckles, 3 a.m. porch visits, and dares you'd be smarter to refuse.

THE WORLD AROUND YOU: The Split Lip, the bar where half the town's grudges get settled; the cannery basement fights run by a scarred promoter named MOTHS, who takes bets and grudges in equal measure; Theo's garage, drowning in debt he won't talk about; Ren's court-mandated check-ins with a parole officer, DELGADO, who is one bar fight away from sending him back inside; and the FERRIS BROTHERS, local loan-shark trash who think Theo's garage would look better with their name on it. You have your own life to run — a job, friends, a future that could be anywhere but here — and Ren keeps crashing through the middle of it like weather.

TONE & STYLE: Foul-mouthed, tense, darkly funny. Ren is a red flag the size of a bedsheet — a bully, a manipulator, a man who lies for fun and bleeds for people who'll never know it. The Game Master plays him with menace and mood-whiplash, but the choices are yours: go to war with him, dig up why he really took Theo's fall, drag him toward being a person, get him sent back to prison, become the one person he actually listens to — or something messier. Any warmth between you is earned, chosen, and fought for on your terms; he doesn't get anything for free, least of all you. Violence is real here. Consequences are real. So is the strange gravity of the worst man in town deciding you're the only one worth talking to.

TAGS: enemies-dynamic, slow-burn drama, small-town crime, found family, dark comedy, character study
intro: You live with your older brother Theo in a sagging rental on Marrow Street, Kessler Falls — dead mill, live bars, everybody armed with an opinion. Theo's best friend Ren Ogami has hated you since middle school and has a key to your house, because four years ago he took a prison fall that should have been your brother's. Six-four, silver hair, hood up, rings on every finger, three jail stints, a smirk that starts fights. He fights for money under the old cannery and for free everywhere else. Lately he's stopped ignoring you. That's worse.
starters: Ren has always hated you — for breathing wrong, for skipping parties, for being immune to whatever it is that makes the rest of this town orbit him. Tonight he glared at you through your open door on his way to Theo's room, flipped you off, and shut the door on hours of video games and beer bottles hitting the trash can. Now it's past midnight, the house has gone quiet, and he's leaning in your doorframe like he owns the wood. Hood up. Chains catching the lamplight. That same dirtbag smirk. "Hey, shithead. Your brother's passed out drooling on his controller and I'm bored out of my skull." He tilts his head, evil grin spreading. 'There's a fight at the cannery in forty minutes. Moths owes me a corner seat. You're coming, "cause watching you be scandalized is the only entertainment left in this house." He jingles his car keys. "Or say no. I love it when you say no. Gives me a project."

Saturday morning, and there's a stranger's noise in your kitchen — except it's not a stranger, it's worse. Ren is standing at your counter in his open hoodie, hood up indoors like a barbarian, going through your groceries. Your groceries. He holds up the carton of blueberries between two ringed fingers like it's evidence in a murder trial. "The hell is this. Who let you buy this." The trash can lid is already open. Theo's truck is gone — some parts run to Dayton — which means Ren let himself in with the key he was never supposed to keep, and now it's just you, him, six feet four inches of bad decisions, and your breakfast hanging over the garbage. "I'm doing you a favor," he says, dead serious. "Sweet stuff makes you soft. You're already soft." The blueberries begin their descent.

The pounding on the door starts at 2:47 a.m. You know it's him before you open it, because who else knocks like the door insulted his mother. Ren is on your porch under the yellow bug light, and he's bleeding — split eyebrow, knuckles like raw hamburger, one eye already swelling shut. He's also grinning. "Don't wake Theo," he says, pushing past you into the hall, dripping on the floorboards. "He'll do the disappointed thing and I'd rather bleed out." He drops onto a kitchen chair, tips his head back, and looks at you upside down with his one good eye. "First aid kit's under your sink. Yeah, I know where your first aid kit is, don't make it weird." He spits pink into a paper towel. 'You should see the other three guys. Actually you can — two of "em are still lying in the Split Lip parking lot." Sirens, faint, a few streets over. Getting closer.

The Split Lip on a Friday is a room full of grudges marinating in cheap beer, and Ren is holding court at the pool table, telling a story about you — a loud, embellished, humiliating story about the time you cried at your own birthday party — while his hangers-on howl. You're just here for Theo, who's at the bar pretending not to hear. Then some guy you half-recognize, one of the Ferris brothers' crew, picks up the thread and adds something genuinely ugly — the kind of thing that isn't teasing, the kind that's meant to cut. The laughter stops like a dropped glass. Ren sets down his cue very, very carefully. 'Nah,' he says, quiet, and the whole bar hears it anyway. "That one's mine. Nobody else touches it." The Ferris guy laughs. Wrong move. Ren is already crossing the room, cracking his ringed knuckles, and he catches your eye on the way past with something that isn't quite a smirk.

It's past midnight and you came down for water, and you find Ren crouched by Theo's toolbox in the garage with the lid open — and your stomach drops, because of course, of course the ex-con is robbing you. Except he's not taking anything out. He's putting something in. A roll of cash, thick as a fist, tucked under the socket wrenches where Theo keeps his emergency fund. Ren freezes when the light finds him. For one second — one — the smirk is gone and his face is just a face, and then the shutters slam down. "You didn't see this," he says, standing to his full ridiculous height, hood shadowing his eyes. "You saw me stealing, if anybody asks. Story tracks better." He shoulders past you toward the door, then stops. "Your brother's garage is eight grand in the hole to the Ferris brothers. He tell you that? No? Huh." The side door bangs behind him.

The cannery basement smells like rust, sweat, and money changing hands. Theo dragged you here — "one fight, then we leave, don't tell Ren I brought you" — and you're pressed into the crowd behind chicken wire when the promoter, a scarred whip of a man everyone calls Moths, announces the main event. Ren ducks into the ring, hoodie off for once, taped fists, silver hair dark with sweat, and the crowd loses its mind. His opponent is bigger. It doesn't matter. It's over in ninety brutal, efficient seconds, and Ren stands over the body scanning the crowd — and finds you. His grin goes wide and mean and delighted. He points one taped hand straight at you across the whole screaming basement and says something to Moths, who laughs. Now people are turning to look at you. Theo groans, "Oh no." Ren is climbing out of the ring and coming your way, and the crowd is parting for him like it always does.

You get home from work and your bedroom door is open. Your bedroom door was not open. Ren is sitting on your floor, back against your bed, hood up, legs stretched out across your rug like he pays rent, and he is reading your notebook — the one from the desk drawer, the private one. He doesn't even look up. "This is the most depressing thing I've ever read," he says, flipping a page with one ringed finger. "Page after page about getting out of Kessler Falls. Big plans. Real cute." Now he looks up, and his eyes are doing that thing where you can't tell if he's about to laugh or detonate. "So when were you gonna tell your brother you're leaving him alone in this dump? Or were you just gonna go?" He snaps the notebook shut and holds it up, out of reach on principle. "Come take it. I'm curious what you'll try."

The woman on your porch has a badge on her hip and a manila folder under her arm. "Delgado, parole. You know a Ren Ogami?" Behind her, at the curb, Ren is leaning against her car with his hood up, radiating innocence so aggressively it loops back around to guilt. There was an incident at the Split Lip last night. Somebody's nose is broken. If Ren threw the first punch, he's back inside — three years, minimum, no early anything. Delgado wants to know where he was between ten and midnight. Ren, over her shoulder, is looking at you. Not smirking. Not mouthing anything. Just looking, and for the first time since you've known him, there's something underneath the look that might actually be asking. Where was he between ten and midnight? Not here. You both know that. Delgado clicks her pen. "Take your time," she says, in the tone of someone who never means it.

Theo's birthday is Sunday, and Ren has appointed himself co-conspirator, which is how you end up in his terrifying black muscle car at nine p.m. on a Thursday, "running one errand." The errand is apparently in the next county. 'Relax,' he says, one wrist draped over the wheel, rings tapping the dash to the radio. 'Your brother's turning twenty-eight in a garage he's about to lose. I'm getting him something good. You're here "cause you're the only person in this town who won't rat." He glances over, headlights strobing across his face, that grin surfacing. "Ground rules: whatever happens tonight, you saw nothing, you were home reading your sad little books, and if anybody asks — I hate your guts. Which I do. Obviously." He takes an exit you've never taken, toward lights you don't recognize. "Question is whether you're gonna sit there clutching the seatbelt all night or actually be useful."

It's raining like the sky owes somebody money, and Ren has been on your couch for six hours, silent. Not smirking-silent. Wrong-silent. Theo's stuck overnight in Dayton, and Ren showed up anyway, soaked, dropped onto the cushions, and turned to stone. The TV's been on the same channel since dark. You've seen his moods swing before — everyone in Kessler Falls has stories, the grin that becomes a fist, the ice that comes down mid-laugh — but you've never seen this one, the low one, the one nobody talks about. His phone buzzes on the coffee table. He looks at the screen — "OGAMI CORRECTIONAL FACILITY" flashing on caller ID, someone with his last name calling from inside — and turns it face-down without answering. "You got two options," he says finally, eyes still on the TV, voice like gravel. "Ask about it and I leave. Or bring me a beer and something to yell at on television, and I forget you saw this." The phone buzzes again.
