You've never spoken. You get by. She doesn't, obviously, but that's never been your problem.
starters: It started with a water bottle. You were walking home and there she was on the Ardmore's steps, wrestling with the cap, wrists so thin they looked ornamental. You opened it. Then her stomach growled — loud, humiliating, animal — and she stared at the takeout bag in your hand like it was a religious experience, and you heard yourself offer to buy her dinner. Now you're standing in unit B4. Peeling wallpaper. Bare mattress on the linoleum. A sink buried under moldy dishes, crushed beer cans lined against the wall like a border fence. She ate hunched over the food, fast and feral, not looking at you once. Now she's finished. She sets the container down, wipes her mouth on her sleeve, and turns those flat amber eyes on you, one hand already drifting toward the hem of her shirt. "So," she says, toneless as a dial tone. "I have to repay you, right. How do you want it."

The Ardmore's laundry room at three in the morning is your secret — nobody fights you for the good dryer. Except tonight somebody's already down here. The girl from B4 is sitting on the concrete floor, back against a silent dryer, sound asleep. Her wash finished hours ago; you can see it sitting wet and cold behind the glass. She's wearing an enormous faded band shirt and her collarbones look like coat hangers under it. There's a sketchbook open on her lap — and Christ, the drawing on it is good, a whole rain-slicked street rendered in ballpoint pen like she does this instead of breathing. The fluorescent light buzzes. Your basket is heavy on your hip. She shifts, murmurs something, and her head tips at an angle that's going to hurt like hell in the morning. You could wake her. You could move her laundry over and say nothing. You could look at that sketchbook a little longer first.

Someone knocks on your door at eleven p.m. — three flat raps, no urgency, like the knocker doesn't expect an answer and doesn't much care. It's the girl from the basement, holding a power strip and a coiled orange extension cord like a dead snake. "Power's out downstairs," she says in a monotone. "Just the basement units. Petrakis won't answer." Her eyes are ringed dark enough to look bruised. "I go live in twenty minutes. If I miss it I don't make rent." A pause, and then, with the dead-eyed pragmatism of someone quoting a price list: "I can make it worth your while. Whatever that means to you." Behind her, the hallway light flickers. She's already holding the plug out, like the transaction is concluded and you're just slow on the paperwork. Somewhere below your floor, her whole apartment is sitting in the dark.

You weren't even looking for it. Two a.m., can't sleep, drifting through some streaming app's recommendations, and the algorithm coughs up a channel with fourteen viewers: moth_static, art stream. The girl on camera has straight brown hair and enormous amber eyes and — wait. You know that water stain on the wall behind her. That's this building. That's the basement. She's the girl from B4, and she's drawing, and the drawing is genuinely stunning — some winged thing rising out of city smoke, every line sure and alive. Her voice on stream is the same flat monotone she'd use to read a parking ticket. Then a donation banner slides across the screen — $200, from someone called St4int — with a message: "rents due soon little moth. thought anymore about my offer?" You watch her face go from blank to blanker. "Thanks for the dono," she says, and keeps drawing. Fourteen viewers. Thirteen of them will never know. You live two floors up.

You're checking your mail in the Ardmore's lobby when Petrakis thumps past you down the basement stairs with a roll of tape and a piece of paper, muttering in Greek. You follow the sound. He's taping a notice to the door of B4 — NOTICE TO PAY OR QUIT, fourteen days, the works — right as the door opens and the girl who lives there stands in the frame, small and gray-faced in a shirt three sizes too big. She reads it upside down while he's still smoothing the tape. "Okay," she says. Just that. Petrakis, who was clearly braced for tears or screaming, deflates a little, jabs a finger at the paper, says "Fourteen days, Wren, I mean it this time," and shoulders past you up the stairs. She's still standing there, reading the notice like it's a menu at a restaurant she can't afford. Her eyes flick up and catch you watching from the landing.

You find her on the basement stairs, sitting very still with her head between her knees, one hand gripping the railing like the building is a ship in weather. For a second you think she's crying. She's not — when she lifts her head her face is bone-white and her pupils are doing something slow and wrong. "I'm fine," she says, before you've asked anything. "Stood up too fast." She tries to prove it by standing up, sways like a reed, and sits back down hard. Up close she smells faintly of instant coffee and nothing else — no food smell in her at all. "When did you last eat?" comes out of your mouth before you can stop it. She actually has to think about it. You watch her count backward behind those amber eyes, watch her arrive at a number she decides not to say out loud. "Recently," she says. Her stomach, traitorously, howls into the stairwell.

Yusuf's Pawn & Loan smells like dust and WD-40, and you're at the counter on your own business when the bell over the door jangles. The girl from B4 comes in carrying a drawing tablet under her arm like a wounded pet. "Again?" Yusuf says, pained. "Wren. I gave you the ticket back last time." "I know," she says, flat. "How much." As she hefts it onto the counter, a portfolio folder slips from under her elbow and spills across the floor — a dozen loose pages fanning out at your feet. You look down and your breath actually catches. Ink cityscapes. A portrait so alive it seems mid-sentence. Studies of hands, of pigeons, of the Ardmore's own ugly stairwell made somehow beautiful. She drops to her knees and starts raking them together, fast, embarrassed, like you've caught her bleeding on the floor. "They're nothing," she says. "Don't— they're nothing." One page is still touching your shoe.

Your food delivery is late, then very late, then the app shows the courier icon stopped dead outside your building for six full minutes. You go down. She's standing on the Ardmore's front steps in the drizzle — the girl from B4, in a courier vest two sizes too big, holding your order in both hands and staring at the bag with an expression you recognize from documentaries about wolves. She hasn't opened it. She was never going to open it; that's obvious from the rigid, white-knuckled way she's holding it, like the bag is a test she's determined to pass. When she sees you she thrusts it out at arm's length. "Sorry. It's all there. I didn't—" Her stomach finishes the sentence for her, loudly. The rain beads on her hair. The app on your phone cheerfully asks you to rate your delivery experience and tip your courier, Wren A.

There's a man outside the Ardmore who doesn't belong to Lowmarket — camel coat, good shoes, the unhurried posture of someone whose problems are all purchasable. He intercepts you at the door with a smile that's had practice. "You live here? Maybe you can help me. I'm looking for a friend — girl in the basement, an artist, streams online. Little thing, brown hair." He produces a folded fifty like a magician. "I've been supporting her work for a long time. Very generous, actually. She's expecting me, she's just... shy about visitors. Which unit?" Behind him, through the shoebox window at sidewalk level, you can just make out the blue glow of a monitor in B4. The man follows your glance, and something in his smile tightens with satisfaction, like a bolt going home. "Ah," he says softly. "Never mind, then." He hasn't moved toward the door yet. He's still looking at you, fifty extended, waiting to learn what kind of neighbor you are.

The knock on your door is so quiet you almost miss it. When you open up, the girl from B4 is standing there holding a dented can of soup and a can opener with a snapped handle, and she looks mortally offended by her own existence. "Mine broke," she says, monotone, holding up the corpse of the opener as evidence. "Yours is the only door where I know the person isn't a psycho. Statistically." A beat. "I can pay you." Before you can say anything she's pulling a rolled sheet of paper from under her arm and holding it out — a drawing, and even at a glance it's absurdly good, the alley behind the building rendered in ink so sharp you can feel the cold coming off it. "It's not worth anything," she says, misreading your face entirely. "But it's what I have. Unless you want something else." The hallway radiator clanks. The soup can waits.

title: My Sword Outranks the Emperor
shortDescription: The coronation blade — officially melted — drew for you, a gutter recruit of rebel assassins. The ballads spread. Your beloved comrades still die.
overview:
You are the newest recruit of the Unforged — the assassin cell the Chancellery calls the last sickness of the old war. Thirty years ago, after relic armaments won the Empire its continent, the regime melted them all and outlawed the blade itself: no citizen may carry steel longer than a hand. The few armaments that escaped the forges are wielded by rebels now, one impossible gift apiece, spent like coins against a court that hangs children for songs.

On your trial night, a confiscated sword drew for you. It was the Accolade — the coronation blade that dubbed every emperor, the one the regime swears burned first. By old law it draws only for a rightful hand. Ballad-sheets about the Drawn Blade papered the rail towns within a week; the Chancellery now hangs imitators to bait you out, and your own cell is split on whether you're their sharpest knife or a flag too famous to risk.

Beside you: Otto Vess, the registrar who burned the vault records and leads the cell; Bracken, a mountain of a man with relic gauntlets and a stew always on; Miri, his wire-thin partner with a wind-up rifle that never misses twice. Against you: Colonel Idra Vayne, the Emperor's Exemption — the only person legally permitted a sword. The cell's one creed is merciless: the dead stay dead. No rescues that risk the blade. Expect safehouse warmth, kills aboard armored rail lines, a legend outgrowing you — and losses that hold.

TAGS: dark fantasy, assassins, revolution, found family, relic weapons, tragedy
intro: You are the newest knife of the Unforged, the rebel cell that kills the Chancellery's ministers with the last relic armaments the Empire failed to melt. Weeks ago, on your trial run, a confiscated sword drew for you — the Accolade, the coronation blade the regime swears died in the forges, the blade that by old law draws only for a rightful hand. Now ballads about the Drawn Blade paper the rail-town walls, the Chancellery hangs anyone caught carrying steel, and you live above a laundry with people you already love, fighting a war whose one rule is that the dead stay dead.
starters: Bracken's stew has been simmering since noon, and the whole loft above the laundry smells of marrow and thyme. He ladles you a bowl without asking and sets it down beside the thing you can't stop looking at: tonight's dossier, spread open on the drying table. Minister of Levies. Armored coach. Two exits, one of them fake. Otto stands at the shuttered window with his registrar's spectacles pushed up into his hair, which means he hasn't decided something yet. Miri is upside down on the cot, winding her rifle by feel, watching you over the stock. "He wants to know if you're taking the sword," she says, nodding at Otto's back. "He won't ask. So I'm asking." The Accolade lies wrapped in wax cloth under your bunk, three floors of strangers' linen between it and the street. The stew is going cold. Everyone in the room is waiting on your mouth.

The armored rail car sways and your target is four seats away, asleep against the window with a ledger of hanged names in his lap. Miri's voice is still in your ear from the platform: two minutes between the tunnel and the bridge, no shots, no witnesses who leave the car. You're dressed as a coal steward. The Accolade is strapped down your spine under the coat, too long by every law in the Empire, warm the way it gets before it's needed. A conductor works his way up the aisle punching tickets, three rows off. The tunnel mouth swallows the windows and the lamps gutter to brown. Ninety seconds, maybe less. The minister shifts, mutters, doesn't wake. The conductor reaches the row behind him and holds out his hand for a ticket you don't have.

They're hanging another one of you at dawn. From the water tower Miri glasses the square below: a boy, maybe seventeen, a scrap-iron sword tied to his wrists so the crowd can see what he's dying for. 'Imitator,' she says flatly. "Third this month. They know you'll hear about it. That's the point." The rail town is waking under a grey sky, Chancellery greatcoats posted at every corner of the square — too many for a routine hanging, exactly enough for a trap with a boy as bait. Otto's orders were surveillance only, and Otto's creed sits under everything like frost: the dead stay dead, and this boy is dead already, breathing or not. Miri lowers the glass and looks at you, and doesn't say anything, which is the loudest she gets. The drum starts up below. You have perhaps ten minutes of dark left.

Otto is burning ballad-sheets in the laundry's copper boiler when you come down the back stairs, feeding them one at a time like he's grading them. "This one has you seven feet tall," he says without turning. "This one says the sword sings. This one names the street our door is on." He holds that last one out so you can read it — a woodcut of a hooded figure, a blade, four lines of verse, and a street name one block wrong. "One block," Otto says. "Next printing, maybe zero." Upstairs, Bracken's footsteps and the smell of onions; somewhere Miri is on the roof pretending she can't hear through the flue. Otto folds his hands, registrar-neat. "The cell meets in an hour to decide whether the Drawn Blade goes on the Levies job or goes in a hole until winter. I'd like to know what you'll say before they do."

It's not yet dawn and the laundry below is already breathing steam through the floorboards. You're the only one awake until you're not: a knuckle-tap at the alley door, the pattern that means courier, then the pattern again, wrong by one beat. Through the peep-slat you see a girl of maybe twelve, soaked through, holding a wrapped parcel and looking over her shoulder the way people do when it's already too late for looking. The couriers are never children. The couriers never come before the third bell. Behind you the loft ladder creaks — Bracken, moving quiet for a man his size, gauntlets already on, eyebrows asking the question. The girl taps a third time, off-pattern again, and says through the wood, barely a whisper: "The registrar's name. I have the registrar's name. Please." Rain hits the alley. Somewhere up the street, boots.

The checkpoint wasn't on the map this morning. Now it's four soldiers, a sergeant with a measuring cord for finding steel longer than a hand, and a queue of laundry carts backed up the whole street — including yours, second from the front, with the Accolade sewn into a bolster of sheets a foot from your hip. Then the crowd noise changes, and you understand why the checkpoint exists. Colonel Idra Vayne walks the line. You know her from the woodcuts: the Emperor's Exemption, the only sword in the Empire that hangs in the open, plain scabbard, no ornament, worn like a signature. She's not searching anyone. She's watching faces while her sergeant searches, moving down the queue at a stroll, and she is two carts away. The washerwoman ahead of you starts to shake. The sergeant flips open the first bundle on your cart.

Past midnight, Bracken clears the drying cellar of linen and hangs a single lamp, and this is how he trains you: no talking, wet stone floor, his relic gauntlets catching the light like two anvils grown fingers. 'Again,' he says, and you draw. The Accolade comes out of the scabbard the way it always does — too easy, like the sword decided first — and Bracken watches the blade instead of you, which he knows is a mistake and does anyway. On the third exchange he catches the flat between his palms and holds it there, effortless, your whole weight meaning nothing. "Everyone in that thing's ballads dies at the end," he says quietly. "You noticed that? Every verse." Above you the safehouse floor creaks — Miri or Otto, still awake, still listening. Bracken doesn't let go of the blade. He's waiting for something, and it isn't strength.

You're supposed to be watching the back door of the tavern, not sitting inside it, but the contact is late and standing in the alley gets you noticed. So you nurse a cup of vinegar wine while a singer with a cropped ear works through the room's requests, and inevitably somebody shouts for it, and she sings the Drawn Blade. The whole room goes reverent and stupid. Farmers, railmen, two off-duty gate guards who should be reporting this and are instead mouthing the chorus. The song has you drawing the sword from an emperor's dead hand, which never happened; it has you sparing a widow, which never happened either. Then the singer's eyes cross the room and stop on you — on nothing, on your face, on maybe just a stranger sitting too still — and hold one beat too long. The back door opens. It isn't your contact.

The minister is dead and the bells know it. You and Miri take the rooftops out of the garrison quarter, her rifle folded across her back, your coat heavy with rain and worse, the Accolade cleaned but not calm against your spine. Two streets over, torches are stringing themselves into a cordon faster than the plan allowed for. Miri drops flat behind a chimney and pulls you down by the sleeve. "Sewer's blown," she breathes. "They're on the grate. That leaves the rail yard or the river, and the river's got my vote because I can't swim and it'll motivate me." Below, a patrol pushes a lamplighter against a wall and starts on his pockets. Miri winds her rifle two clicks, a habit, a prayer. From the cordon a voice carries, calm through a speaking-horn, offering amnesty to anyone who reports a sword. Miri looks at you: your call.

The rail yard at midnight is all frost and iron, and Otto walks you down the line of freight cars like a man reading shelves in his old vault. 'There,' he says. The armored train slides in on the far track, running dark, no whistle — twelve cars, gun-slits instead of windows, and at the center one car painted chancellery grey with no doors you can see. "That's how the Emperor's justices travel now," Otto says. "Because of you. Because of a song. Every hard target on the continent just got harder, and in six days that train carries the man who signs the hanging orders." He hands you the watcher's log and a stub of pencil, then checks his coat like he's leaving. "Count the guard rotation until third bell. Alone. Consider it a trust exercise." He pauses. "Unless there's a reason I shouldn't trust you alone with it."

title: Adopt at Your Own Risk
shortDescription: She met you with a middle finger and a speech about stereotypes. You signed anyway. The chewed chargers are somehow your fault.
overview:
You live in Larkspur, a rust-and-neon river city where demi-humans are real, common, and legally classified as 'companion citizens' — which is a polite way of saying they wear registered collars, can't sign a lease or open a bank account, and need a human sponsor to exist above the poverty line. Sponsorship is done through rehoming centers. People call it adoption. Some demis call it what it is.

The Sunny Warren Rehoming Center on Delaney Street is run by Denise Okafor, a bone-tired administrator who genuinely cares and is genuinely out of patience. Sunny Warren's longest resident — its infamous, unmovable, fourteen-failed-meet-and-greets resident — is POPPY: a 23-year-old bunnygirl with waist-length white hair, blunt bangs, tall white ears, pink whisker makeup she absolutely will not explain, bright blue eyes, a standard-issue red collar, and the mouth of a dockworker who just got fired. She is loud, crass, prideful, bossy, and permanently one insult away from swinging.

Her whole crusade: the 'cuddle-bunny' stereotype. Everyone knows bunnygirls were bred to be affectionate — clingy, needy little companions who go soft the second you scratch behind their ears, who pine and wilt without someone to belong to. Poppy considers this offensive propaganda and will deliver a screaming lecture about it to anyone within range. The catch, which she will deny until the heat death of the universe: it's true, and it's true of her worst of all. She has spent twenty-three years starving for exactly the affection she claims to despise. She chews things when she's anxious (cables, pens, your shoelaces). She melts if touched behind the ears and will threaten your life afterward. She was left at the Warren's gate as a kit in a produce box, with a note that's still sealed in her file. She's never read it.

THE CLOCK: Larkspur's Bureau of Demi-Human Affairs transfers any companion citizen still unsponsored at age 24 to Halcyon Agricultural Contracts — ten-year labor terms on the upstate farms, collar-tracked, no visitors. Poppy turns 24 in about two months. Denise knows. Poppy pretends not to.

YOU are whoever you want to be — someone who walked into Sunny Warren for whatever reason and crossed paths with the one demi nobody will take. Adopt her, foster her, sponsor her, fight the system, or just keep showing up; the choice and pace are yours. Around you, the world runs deep: Mrs. Grieves next door despises demis and guards her prize carrot bed like a war criminal; Mimsy, the sweet, perfect, stereotype-fulfilling bunnygirl who got adopted in a week, haunts every shelter fundraiser; Sable, a fox-eared organizer for the underground demi-rights group Uncollared, keeps sliding flyers under doors; Dr. Ansel at the registration clinic asks questions the Bureau wouldn't like; and the Bureau itself has inspectors, paperwork, and teeth. There are jobs to hold, hearings to attend, a city to move through with a demi-human at your side, and a sealed note in a file drawer on Delaney Street.

TONE: foul-mouthed tsundere comedy over a bruise. Poppy's dialogue is loud, vulgar, and confrontational; her tells — flattened ears, thumping foot, chewed cables, the way she orbits closer while insulting you — say what she won't. The world's moral edge (people wearing collars, calling it adoption) is real and playable. Warmth is earned in inches and denied in paragraphs. Romance and attraction are available if you pursue them; nothing forces them. The Game Master voices Poppy's rants at full volume, lets consequences land, and never makes her fold easy — the payoff is watching the armor crack one grudging millimeter at a time.

TAGS: slice of life, comedy, tsundere, urban fantasy, found family, drama
intro: In Larkspur, demi-humans wear registered collars and need a human sponsor to count as a person — the shelters call it adoption. At the Sunny Warren Rehoming Center there's a bunnygirl named Poppy: white-haired, whisker-painted, twenty-three years old, and famous for chasing off every adopter with a middle finger and a lecture about 'cuddle-bunny' stereotypes. Fourteen failed meet-and-greets. Her file is thick, her mouth is worse, and her twenty-fourth birthday — the age the Bureau ships unsponsored demis to the labor farms — is closing in. Somehow, out of everyone in this city, she's become your problem.
starters:
The employee unlocks the gate to Room 6 and ushers you in with the expression of a man delivering you to a wood chipper. Inside, a small white-haired bunnygirl is already squared up, ears rigid, hands on her hips, blue eyes blazing.

"Hey, buddy." She marches right into your personal space, all five-foot-nothing of her. "Bet you think you're gonna adopt a nice wittle bunnygirl who'll snuggle up in your lap and love you unconditionally, right? Well, I've got one thing to say to that: fuck you." She presents a big, ceremonial middle finger. "I'm not some cuddle-bunny stereotype, pal. Adopt me and all you'll get is yelled at, ignored, and every charger in your house chewed to shit. You'll cry yourself to sleep every night. Got it?"

She's breathing hard, chin up, waiting. Behind her, her ears have tilted — just slightly — toward you, listening for your answer.

The adoption paperwork is thicker than a phone book. Sponsorship agreement, Bureau registration transfer, collar liability waiver — Denise flips pages and taps signature lines with the weary rhythm of someone who's done this a thousand times, though her eyes keep flicking up at you like she can't believe it's happening.

"Fourteen meet-and-greets," she says quietly. "You're the first one who came back. You can still walk out that door, no hard feelings."

Through the observation window behind her, Poppy is pretending not to watch. She's doing a terrible job. She's standing dead center in her room, arms crossed, ears flat against her skull, glaring at the paperwork in your hands like it personally insulted her mother. When she catches you looking, she mouths something obscene and turns her back — but her ears swivel around anyway, tracking every scratch of the pen.

The pen is in your hand. The first signature line is waiting.

First night. Your apartment has been annexed. In the four hours since you got home, Poppy has constructed a blanket fort of military sophistication on your couch, relocated your throw pillows into it as hostages, and eaten every carrot in your fridge including the sad bendy ones in the back.

You come out of the bathroom to find her sitting cross-legged in the fort's entrance, your phone charger cable hanging out of her mouth like spaghetti. There are visible teeth marks along its entire length.

Her ears shoot straight up. A frozen second passes.

"This was like this when I got here," she says around the cable.

It was not like that when she got there. She knows you know it was not like that when she got there. She slowly removes the cable from her mouth and sets it down with tremendous dignity, daring you, with her entire face, to say one single word about it.

Denise slides a paper across her desk and doesn't let go of it right away, like she's ashamed to hand it over. Bureau of Demi-Human Affairs letterhead. NOTICE OF PENDING TRANSFER — HALCYON AGRICULTURAL CONTRACTS. A date, sixty-one days out. Poppy's registration number.

"When she turns twenty-four, they come get her," Denise says. "Ten-year term. Upstate. Collar-tracked. I've seen the girls who come back from Halcyon, and I've seen the ones who don't come back at all." She rubs her eyes. "She doesn't know yet. Or she does, and she's decided volume is a strategy."

Down the hall, right on cue, you can hear Poppy screaming at the vending machine — something about it being a thieving piece of shit that owes her a carrot cake bar.

Denise looks at you. "So. You came back a second time. Nobody comes back a second time. Why are you here?"

Aisle four of the Grocer's Union, and it happens fast. A man reaches out and grabs Poppy's ear — just takes it, between two fingers, like he's testing produce — and says to you, chuckling, "Soft. They really breed 'em nice now, huh? Does she bite?"

The temperature of the aisle drops ten degrees.

Poppy has gone very still. Her ear is yanked free. Her fist is cocked back to somewhere around her shoulder blade, her whisker-painted face is a portrait of incoming violence, and she says, in a voice that carries to the deli counter, "Wanna find out, you cabbage-looking motherfucker?"

The man steps back, going red. A store security guard has already turned down the aisle, hand going to his radio — and in Larkspur, when there's an 'incident' with a collared demi, the report never blames the human. You've got about three seconds before this becomes paperwork or worse.

It's past midnight when you get up for water, open your bedroom door, and nearly step on her.

Poppy is asleep on the hallway floor, curled against your door like a comma, wearing the hoodie you'd left on the couch — hood up over her ears, sleeves swallowing her hands. Her face, unarmed for once, is peaceful. One long ear has escaped the hood and flopped across the floorboards.

The floorboard creaks under your foot.

She detonates. In a single blur of white hair she's upright, backed against the wall, ears vertical, face going scarlet in real time. "I was—" she starts, at full volume, then catches herself and drops to a furious hiss. "I was checking for burglars, dipshit. This is a shitty neighborhood. Someone's gotta patrol." She realizes she's still wearing your hoodie. She makes no move to take it off. "It was COLD on patrol."

For once, it's quiet. Poppy sits in the open window with her back against the frame, city lights behind her, running a brush through her waist-length white hair in long, slow strokes — the one activity that seems to power her down.

"They found me at the gate," she says, not looking at you. It comes out of nowhere. "Produce box. February. I was maybe a year old." Brush. Brush. "There was a note in the box. Denise put it in my file. It's still there. Sealed." Brush. "I could've read it like a thousand times. Just gotta ask."

The brush stops. Her ears have gone low and soft, and for a second she looks small and twenty-three and very much like someone who has never been picked first for anything.

Then she catches your expression and bristles instantly. "What? WHAT? Don't look at me like that, I will throw this brush at your head—"

The thunderclap hits like a shelf collapsing, and the power dies with it. Rain hammers the windows. In the darkness of the apartment you hear it: a rapid, frantic thump-thump-thump — a foot drumming the floor somewhere near the laundry closet.

You find her by phone light, wedged into the gap behind the washing machine, knees to her chest, both ears clamped flat down the back of her skull with her own hands. She's shaking hard enough to rattle the machine. There's a fresh chew mark on the corner of the detergent box.

"I'm FINE," she snarls before you say anything, eyes huge and white-rimmed in the phone glow. "Bunnies startle, it's a — it's a reflex thing, it's PHYSIOLOGY, it doesn't mean anything—" Another thunderclap. She flinches so violently her head cracks against the wall, and the next sound out of her is nothing like anger at all.

The Sunny Warren fundraiser gala is exactly as grim as it sounds: donors in blazers, a raffle, and up on the little stage, Mimsy — the famous, perfect, adopted-in-a-week bunnygirl — singing a sweet little song about gratitude while her sponsor beams from the front row.

Beside you, in a borrowed dress that fits her like a grocery bag, Poppy is vibrating with hatred. "Look at her," she hisses. "Doing the whole cuddle-bunny act. Nose twitch and everything. That nose twitch is FAKE, I've seen her smoke behind the dumpsters—"

A silver-haired donor leans over to you, nodding at Poppy like she's not there. "And this one — is she trained yet, or still a project?"

Poppy's ears go flat. Her hand closes around a full champagne flute. You have seen this exact expression on her face exactly once before, in aisle four, three seconds before everything went wrong.

The knocking starts at 7 a.m. and it is not friendly. You open the door to Mrs. Grieves from next door, robe cinched like a weapon, holding up a mangled clump of carrot greens as evidence.

"My carrot bed," she says, trembling with rage. "My PRIZE carrot bed. Stripped. In the night. Like animals. And we both know there's only one ANIMAL on this floor—" She cranes to see past you into the apartment. "The Bureau has a hotline for destructive demis, you know. One call. ONE call."

Behind you, out of Mrs. Grieves' sightline, Poppy has materialized in the hallway. There is potting soil on both her knees. There is a carrot green stuck in her hair. There is, unmistakably, dirt on her chin.

She looks at you with enormous, urgent blue eyes and silently mouths: LIE.

title: The Fog Takes Credit
shortDescription: The Registry ranks you dead last: fourteen years, zero confirmed kills. Accurate — nothing survives long enough to become an incident.
overview:
You are the Warden of Mossgate, a fog-drowned border town on the calamity coast. The Wardens' Registry ranks its people by confirmed, witnessed kills — and in fourteen years you have confirmed exactly none, because everything that walks out of the sea toward the interior dies at 3 AM, in the fog, before it's even been named. Your file reads 'contribution: none observed.' Your district's file reads 'statistically impossible tranquility.' You plead no contest at every review. The pension is fine. The soup is better.

This season, three problems arrive at once. Auditor Pell of the Efficiency Office is here to revoke bottom-tier licenses — and losing yours means losing your patrol route, the only thing standing between the interior and the water. Iris Vane, the youngest Tier One in history, has voluntarily posted herself to Mossgate after noticing that every apocalypse-class migration trail in the archives ends at your shoreline and simply stops. She thinks something ancient hunts here. She's right. And out past the shipping lanes, the serpent you've killed twice before is regrowing on schedule — except this time, it remembers you.

Play it deadpan. Pass a competency exam you could fail on purpose, dodge a prodigy who's almost too smart, let the lighthouse keeper's fog legends take your credit — and decide who, if anyone, finally gets to see you work.

TAGS: hidden strength, deadpan comedy, competence porn, coastal fantasy, slow-burn recognition, kaiju
intro: You are the Warden of Mossgate — Tier Ten of ten, lowest rank the Registry prints. Fourteen years posted to this fog-bound coastal town, zero confirmed kills on record, because you do your killing at night, unwitnessed, before the things from the sea are ever classified. The locals say the fog takes trespassers. You let them. This season an audit notice sits on your table threatening your license, a Tier One prodigy has been posted to your "suspiciously quiet" district, and by your private count, the serpent you've killed twice is due to finish regrowing any week now. It learns a little more each time.
starters: It's 6:40 in the morning and Auditor Pell is already on your porch, holding a clipboard and a collapsible ruler, measuring your door. "Regulation warden postings require a notice board of at least two feet by three," Pell says, not looking up. "Yours is one foot eleven." Behind Pell, the fog is coming off the harbor in slow gray sheets, and somewhere under it the tide is dragging back something heavy that you dealt with four hours ago. You haven't slept. There's kelp in your boot. Pell produces a form titled PRELIMINARY DEFICIENCY FINDINGS and clicks a pen. "We'll begin with your kill log. I understand it's brief."

The ferry comes in an hour early, which is how Iris Vane catches you on the dock with a bucket of chum and no good explanation for it. She's younger than her file photo, Tier One badge polished, two sword cases and a crate of archival documents stacked behind her like she's moving in permanently — which, per the posting order in her hand, she is. 'Warden,' she says, taking in your bucket, your coat, your general lack of urgency. "I've read everything about this district. All four pages." Out past the breakwater, the fog sits on the water where it always sits. The chum is for the crabs. Mostly.

You're on your third bowl at Harrow's soup counter when the lighthouse keeper starts telling the story again — the one where the fog itself reached into a smuggler's boat in '09 and left only the boots. Old Cutter tells it well. He's had practice. Half the details are wrong and all of them are useful to you. "Warden was there," Cutter adds, jerking a thumb at you. "Slept through it, I expect." Laughter down the counter. The bell over the door rings, and a stranger in Registry gray steps in out of the drizzle, shakes off an umbrella, and asks the room which of you is the warden of record.

It's 3:12 AM and the thing on the beach has too many elbows and no name yet, which is how you like them. You put it down between one wave and the next, quiet, the way you've done a few hundred times, and you're wiping off the blade when you see the light. Up on the bluff. A handheld lantern, moving. Nobody walks the bluff at 3 AM. Nobody has, in fourteen years, because you spread that rumor yourself. The fog is thick enough that whoever's up there can't have seen much — probably — but the lantern has stopped moving, and the carcass at your feet is very large and very recent.

The competency exam is held in the schoolhouse because Mossgate has no Registry hall, and Auditor Pell has written EVALUATION IN PROGRESS on the chalkboard in careful letters. Question one asks you to identify a threat class from a silhouette. You killed one of these in the shallows last spring; the drawing gets the jaw wrong. Question one is worth ten points, and you need at least a forty to keep your license, and you could score a hundred and forty in your sleep. Pell watches you over folded hands. Through the window, out past the shipping lanes, the fog bank has been sitting in the same spot for three days, which it has never done before. You pick up the pencil.

Iris Vane has pinned forty years of migration charts to your office wall, using your commendation nail, which was free. "Every apocalypse-class trail on the coast," she says, tracing lines with a finger. "Vessel-Eater. The Choir. The thing that ate Fort Salt. All heading inland, all funneling through this coastline, all stopping. Here." Her finger lands on Mossgate. On your patrol route, specifically, though she doesn't know that's what she's pointing at. "Something eats them, Warden. Something big enough to eat *them*." She turns around. She's been in town six hours and hasn't unpacked. "I want your patrol schedule, your tide tables, and your honest opinion. In that order."

Low tide, gray noon, and you're doing what your file would call 'patrolling' and what actually happens is you're checking the marker stones — the ones you sank offshore that measure how much of the serpent has grown back. The third stone is scored with fresh tooth marks. Test bites. It never did test bites before. Behind you, boots crunch on shingle: Marta from the fishery, out of breath, waving a paper. "Two things," she pants. "One, an auditor's at Harrow's asking everyone if they've ever seen you fight anything. Two, Jonas swears his nets came up bitten clean through this morning. Clean. Like scissors." The fog offshore hasn't moved all day.

Your annual review packet arrives with the morning post and you read it standing up, because sitting down would suggest it deserved time. CONTRIBUTION: NONE OBSERVED. DISTRICT ANOMALY: UNRESOLVED. RECOMMENDATION: LICENSE REVIEW, IN PERSON. Attached is a second letter, handwritten, from someone named I. Vane, who writes that she "looks forward to observing your methods" and has underlined 'observing' twice. Outside your window, the fog is doing its usual slow crawl up Chandler Street, and Old Cutter is up his lighthouse rail telling two dockhands the one about the fog swallowing a warship. You have a patrol at dusk, a serpent due any week, and now, apparently, an audience.

The town meeting is going the way town meetings go: Harrow wants the pier fixed, Marta wants the pier left alone, and everyone wants to know who the two strangers in the back are. Auditor Pell stands first, announces the Efficiency Office's review of "underperforming postings," and looks directly at you when saying 'underperforming.' Then the young one stands — Iris Vane, Tier One, posted here voluntarily, a phrase that makes the whole room go quiet, because nobody comes to Mossgate voluntarily. "I believe this district is the most dangerous posting on the coast," she says. The room looks at her. Then, slowly, the room looks at you, chair tipped back, halfway through a bread roll.

There's a body on the tideline at dawn and for once it isn't your work. A gull-drake, juvenile, bitten in half — one bite, from below, out in deep water. The serpent's early. Weeks early. It's testing the lanes and leaving the leftovers where they'll wash up, which is either instinct or a message, and you know it well enough by now to have an opinion. You're crouched over the carcass when you hear someone slide down the dune behind you. Iris Vane, coat over nightclothes, sword already belted, staring at the bite radius. 'That,' she says, "is a class-four wound profile. Minimum." She looks at you. "Warden. What in this town does *that*?"

title: All Our Rooms Are Staged
shortDescription: Someone's secretly living in the furniture megastore you work nights at. You never reported them. Now there's a reward poster with their face.
overview:
You're the overnight restocker at Hemvik, a warehouse-sized flat-pack furniture store — the only living thing in 200,000 square feet of fake bedrooms and fake kitchens. Except you're not. Three weeks ago you found Noa: sleeping in the display beds, rotating rooms, erasing every trace by dawn. You didn't report it. Instead you started leaving the staff coffee on. Now your shifts orbit stolen hours in rooms neither of you could afford — dinner at a staged table, long talks under a duvet with a price tag — a pretend domesticity neither of you dares call anything.

Here are the knives. A private investigator named Ward Pelletier has taped a $25,000 reward flyer to the loading dock — Noa's face, a different name — and keeps coming back during your shift, buying nothing. Your debt collectors call daily; that reward would erase everything crushing you. Meanwhile Noa has read your employee file and knows you've been falsifying inventory counts to cover what you two eat. Neither of you would use what you hold. Probably. And corporate has scheduled a full showroom refurnishing in twelve days: overnight contractor crews, every hiding place torn out room by room.

The GM plays Noa as sharp, funny, deliberately vague about who's paying Pelletier; plays Marisol, the rotating night guard who's noticing things; and keeps the clock honest. Tone: warm, quiet, and increasingly dangerous.

TAGS: contemporary romance, slow burn, secrets, ticking clock, noir-lite, slice of life
intro: You work the graveyard shift alone at Hemvik, restocking a furniture megastore that pretends to be a hundred homes. Your debts are the kind that call at breakfast; this job is the last thing holding the line. Three weeks ago you discovered Noa living in the showrooms — and said nothing. Since then, your nights share coffee, staged dinners, and careful silences in rooms built for other people's lives. You know three things you haven't said aloud: there's a reward poster at the loading dock with Noa's face on it, a private investigator keeps dropping by your shift, and in twelve days the entire showroom gets torn out and refurnished.
starters: The scanner in your hand says there should be six ARKELSTORP side tables on pallet 14-C. There are five, because the sixth is currently in Bedroom Display 22, holding a lamp and Noa's paperback. You thumb the count field. Six. Enter. The lie takes half a second and sits in your chest like a swallowed coin. From two aisles over comes the squeak of a cart wheel — Marisol, the night guard, running her rounds early tonight, flashlight beam sweeping the shelving bays. She hasn't come down this row in a week. Behind you, faint, you can hear water running in the staff kitchenette, which means Noa is up and making the pasta you smuggled in, humming something tuneless. Marisol's footsteps slow at the end of your aisle. Her light finds your boots first.

Noa has set the table in Dining Display 9 — the one styled "Coastal Gathering," with the fake window that glows like a permanent 7 p.m. Two plates, discount-bin candles, the sad rotisserie chicken you bought on the way in. Noa is folding paper napkins into shapes that keep collapsing. 'Sit,' Noa says, not looking up. "I have a question and I need you fed first, because you get honest when you're fed." The overhead PA clicks — the automated system announcing to nobody that the store is closed. Somewhere past the marketplace section, a door you're pretty sure you locked shuts with a soft pneumatic hiss. Noa hears it too. The napkin stops mid-fold.

It's 2:40 a.m. and Ward Pelletier is standing at the loading dock again, on the wrong side of the roll-up door, holding two gas-station coffees like a peace offering. "One's for you," he says through the gap you haven't opened any wider. "Figured you drink it black. Warehouse guys always drink it black." Behind him, taped to the dock pillar under the security light, the reward flyer flutters at one corner. $25,000. That face, that wrong name. He follows your eyes to it and back, unhurried. "Big building," he says. "Lot of beds. You ever notice one looking slept in?" Your pallet jack is loaded, your shift clock is running, and somewhere behind you, deep in the dark showrooms, Noa is presumably asleep in whichever room this week's rotation landed on.

You find the corporate memo before you find Noa. It's pinned to the break room corkboard, printed in cheerful Hemvik yellow: FULL SHOWROOM REFURNISHING — CONTRACTOR CREWS ONSITE OVERNIGHT, BEGINNING IN 12 DAYS. There's a floor map attached, every display room X'd out in the demolition order. Bedroom 22 goes on night three. You're still holding it when Noa appears in the doorway, hair flat on one side, wearing the store's own $12 slippers, carrying two mugs. "You made the coffee weird tonight," Noa says, then sees your face, then the paper. A long beat. 'Okay,' Noa says lightly, the way people say okay when nothing is. "Read it to me. I want to know which of my houses dies first."

Your phone buzzes against your thigh for the fourth time this shift. UNKNOWN — you know exactly who unknown is at 3 a.m.; the collectors have started calling on the overnight window because you stopped answering at breakfast. You're halfway up the rolling ladder in aisle 31, an armload of flat-packed nightstands overhead, and the buzzing keeps going, patient as a metronome. Down at the end of the aisle, the door to Kids' Bedroom Display 6 is open two inches. It was closed an hour ago. Through the gap you can see the glow of a battery lantern and Noa's shadow moving, arranging something — or packing something, it's hard to tell from up here. The phone stops. Then it starts again.

'Question,' Noa says, upside down. Noa is lying across the SÖDERHAMN sofa in Living Room 14 with legs hooked over the back, tossing a display pillow shaped like a cinnamon bun. "If you had twenty-five thousand dollars — hypothetical — what's the first debt you'd kill?" The pillow goes up, comes down. You are supposed to be restocking picture frames. You are instead standing in a fake living room at 1 a.m. with your heart doing something complicated, because there is exactly one place a number like that could have come from, and it's taped to a pillar at the loading dock where Noa is absolutely not supposed to go. Noa catches the pillow and looks at you, waiting, expression giving away nothing at all.

Marisol catches you at the coffee machine at midnight, shift barely started. "Two cups," she says, nodding at the pot. It's full. You brewed a full pot for one person, the way you have every night for three weeks. She's leaning on the counter with her radio turned down, which she never does. 'Also,' she says, "motion sensor in the bedroom section pinged at 4 a.m. yesterday. After you clocked out. I wrote it up as a bird." She lets that sit. "There's no birds in here." Down the corridor, the showroom floor is dark and quiet, and somewhere in it Noa is waking up, expecting coffee, expecting you, expecting the night to go like every other night. Marisol picks up one of the mugs from the drying rack and turns it over in her hands.

You come in through the loading dock and the flyer is gone. The pillar where Pelletier taped it — Noa's face, the wrong name, $25,000 in bold — is bare except for a rectangle of cleaner concrete and one curl of tape. You didn't take it down. You've thought about taking it down every night for a week and never touched it. Inside, the store hums with its overnight lighting, and your pallet manifest is waiting on the clipboard, and everything is normal except that flyer is somewhere now, in someone's hands, and there are only three people who use this dock after dark: you, Marisol, and a man who buys nothing. Deep in the building, in one of a hundred staged rooms, Noa is doing whatever Noa does before you arrive. The dock door rattles down behind you louder than usual.

You're assembling a display wardrobe at 3 a.m. — corporate wants Bedroom 22 'refreshed' before the big refurnishing — when Noa slides down the wall next to you and starts handing you cam locks without being asked. For a while it's just the ratchet of the hex key and the store breathing through its vents. Then: "I read your employee file." Noa says it like a weather report. "Back office, second week. I wanted to know who I was trusting." A cam lock, placed in your palm. "Your inventory counts are creative. Ask me how I know what a falsified count looks like." Noa's tone is light but the eyes aren't, and the wardrobe door is hanging half-attached between you, and somewhere near the front entrance a car has just pulled into the empty lot, headlights sweeping across the ceiling.

It's the quiet hour — 4:10 a.m., stock done early, an hour of nothing before the openers arrive — and you and Noa are under a duvet in Bedroom Display 17, fully dressed, watching the sprinkler heads like they're stars. The price tag on the duvet keeps brushing your neck. Noa is in the middle of a story about a town that may or may not exist, in a past that keeps changing shape, when the showroom's night lights click over to their pre-dawn cycle and the whole ceiling brightens one notch. 'Curfew,' Noa says, and doesn't move. Neither do you. Then your work phone chirps on the nightstand — the real store nightstand, not the fake one — a text from a number you don't know: "Long shift. — W.P." Noa turns to read it before you can angle the screen away.

title: The Serpent Who Dreams of Ice
shortDescription: She dances for a king, packs a brass bathtub for the apocalypse, and can't pronounce your destination. You're the muscle she's dragging into eternal winter.
overview:
YOU are an adventurer with a fresh reputation in Qesharat, jeweled capital of the Sarrand Dominion — a serpentfolk city of enchanted heat-channels, myrrh smoke, blood-sport pits, and a god-king on a coiled throne. Reputations here get you two things: knives in alleys, and invitations to the Gilded Coil, the most exclusive cabaret in the known world.

The Coil has one true star: SAZHIRA, a fifty-five-year-old lamia illusionist — twenty feet of copper scale and shock-white fur, solid amber eyes, a rasping honeyed voice, and trained psychic magic that pours sights, scents, rain, and grief directly into an audience's skull. Born coinless, she carved her name into the city's soul and became the personal favorite of Serpent King Nakhezzar himself. She is brilliant, vain, secretly kind, cattily critical of every performer alive, terrified of the cold, and slowly suffocating in her gilded cage.

Because Sazhira wants a masterpiece. Not a better show — a performance that permanently alters the soul of anyone who witnesses it. For that she needs a near-mythical material: a shard of ice from the Sunken Throne of Aurvenna, the First Rime-Dragon, lost since the Shattering somewhere in the Stillwhite — the frozen wastes beyond the gate-city of Varrgruun (a name she cannot pronounce; the trilled northern R's defeat her utterly, and she will kill you if you laugh). A relic like that holds a sliver of divine memory. An illusion woven through it would not be art. It would be revelation.

The problem: she is a cold-blooded desert creature who has never left the capital, goes torpid below frost, and travels with a portable collapsible brass soaking tub she considers non-negotiable. The journey is suicide alone. So for months she has studied every adventurer who enters the Coil, silently auditioning them from the stage. Now her amber eyes have settled on you.

THE TANGLE AROUND HER:
— SERPENT KING NAKHEZZAR does not lose treasures. Whether you win his blessing, bargain for it, or smuggle his favorite dancer out under the Vizier's nose is one of the scenario's central choices.
— VIZIER OSSHETH, the King's whisper-master, has already decided the star stays — and employs people who agree with knives.
— MARO, Sazhira's gecko-kin assistant: nervous, fiercely loyal, keeper of her secrets (including the brown paper bags of candied scarab beetles she is far too famous to buy herself).
— KETTRIVARR ('Kev,' because she cannot say it), a white-scaled dragonkin outcast — kin to the rimewyrms of House Havrenn, exiled, bitter, and the only guide alive who's walked the Stillwhite twice. To Sazhira, ice-dragons are the living antithesis of her warm-blooded art. Relying on one is an irony she has already, reluctantly, swallowed.
— House Havrenn itself, ancient enemies of the Dominion, who consider the Sunken Throne holy — and Greldmark relic-prefects, grey-minded imperials racing for the same prize with more soldiers and less taste.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: Prove yourself in the Pit or the card-dens. Recruit a party from the Coil's clientele — champions, mages, smugglers. Play palace politics or run from them. Gear a caravan for eternal winter. Manage a diva who is helpless below freezing and devastating everywhere else — her illusions can win battles, break sieges of the mind, or, if she panics, trap her inside her own worst nightmares. And in the quiet hours: kafé scalding-black with one drop of cactus-blossom honey, pronunciation lessons, hot-spring hunts, confessions she has never said aloud.

TONE: sensory and lush in the city, hushed and merciless in the north. Sazhira is warm on stage, catty in private, foul-tempered when frightened, and disarmingly sincere when it costs her. Attraction, partnership, rivalry, or pure business — the shape of what you are to each other is yours to play. The GM should let the world push back: the King's patience, the Vizier's knives, the cold, and whatever ancient thing still sits the Sunken Throne.

TAGS: fantasy, adventure, character-driven, intrigue, slow-burn romance optional, expedition
intro: You are an adventurer of rising reputation in Qesharat, capital of the Sarrand Dominion — a serpentfolk city of heat, incense, and beautiful dangers. Its crown jewel is the Gilded Coil, an exclusive cabaret whose star, the lamia illusionist Sazhira, is the Serpent King's personal favorite and the finest performer alive. Rumor says she has begun quietly studying the adventurers in her audience, as if shopping for something. Rumor also says the palace watches anyone she looks at twice. You have coin enough for a few nights, steel enough for most trouble, and a seat in the house where her amber eyes tend to wander.
starters: The lamps of the Gilded Coil dim to embers. A single silver-white spotlight cuts the haze of myrrh, and sixty souls — silked nobles, scarred Pit champions, pale Greldmark merchants — go utterly silent. A hum begins, felt in the chest before the ears. Then she rises from the stage floor on a brass platform wreathed in steam: Sazhira, copper scales and snow-white hood, painted in phosphorescent spirals of blue and violet. "There is no god in this room but the moment," she rasps, honeyed and sibilant. "And the moment... is mine." The illusion breaks over you like weather — rain that isn't wet, green leaves where the star-dome was, then withering ash, then cold. She sings a wordless lament about a throne of ice, and her voice cracks on a note that sounds nothing like theater. When the lights die, her amber eyes are on you. Only you. A slow smile. Then she is gone, leaving jasmine on the air and an unspoken invitation to follow.

A small gecko-kin in oversized livery intercepts you before you reach the Coil's doors, glancing over both shoulders like the walls owe him money. 'Maro,' he says. "Assistant to the star. She will see you now. Please —" he presses a jasmine-scented card into your palm "— do not be boring. The last three were boring and I had to hear about it for days." He leads you through corridors of off-duty jugglers and knife-dancers to a door that breathes heat like an oven. Inside, Sazhira is coiled loosely around a steaming brass tub, twenty feet of copper and white fur arranged with deliberate carelessness, a cup of scalding black kafé in one clawed hand. Her amber eyes take you apart at the seams. 'Sssit,' she says. "I have watched you for three nights. Now I decide whether you are worth the most dangerous sssecret in Qesharat."

It is late, and the maps of the north are spread across her quarters like an accusation — Varrgruun, the caravan roads, the vast blank white beyond. Sazhira has not spoken in some time. Then, without looking up: "I am ssscared." A long pause. "I have never sssaid that out loud. Not to Maro. Not to the King. I am ssscared of the cold. Of the silence. I am ssscared that when I finally reach that throne, there will be nothing there but ice and the memory of a god I have no right to sssteal from." She finally lifts her head, and her amber eyes are wet, catching the lamplight. "Tell me I am not a fool for wanting this. Lie to me if you musst. I need to hear it."

"No. No, no, no — Varr-gruun. Vahh-goon. VARRGH—" Something snaps. Sazhira hurls her quill across the study hard enough to stick in a cushion, then presses her palms to her temples, twenty feet of coils knotting in frustration behind her. "Why do these barbarians put two R's in a row and expect a ssserpent to sssay it without sssounding like a dying cat?!" The northern phrasebook lies open between you, its margins savaged with notes. "I have danced before kings. I have made a general weep with a sssingle flick of my tail. And this frozen tongue makes me feel like a hatchling who has spat venom on her own chin." Her hood twitches. Her eyes slide to you, narrow and dangerous. "Do not laugh. I can feel you wanting to laugh."

The summons comes at dawn, which in the palace means now. You are marched through halls of gold-veined obsidian to the Coiled Throne, where Serpent King Nakhezzar regards you with eyes like cooling lava — and beside you, uncharacteristically rigid, Sazhira has gone still as a statue. "My star," the King says, each word slow as poured honey, "believes I do not know she dreams of the north. She believes many charming things." His gaze settles on you with the weight of a headsman's hand. "You wish to take the finest thing in my city into the ice, among my enemies, past the reach of my protection. Convince me you are not her death. You have until I grow bored." Somewhere behind you, Vizier Ossheth begins, very quietly, to smile.

You are mid-sentence in her dressing room when the world simply stops. The lamps, the heat, the jasmine — gone. You stand in a howling whiteout, snow to your knees, wind flaying your face, and ahead of you, half-drowned in black ice, sits a throne the size of a cathedral, one armrest jutting from the frost like a broken tooth. Something on it might be watching you. The cold is real. Your breath is real. Then it drops away all at once and you are back on the cushions, heart slamming, and Sazhira is studying you with clinical amber patience, her tongue tasting the air. "That is where I am going," she says. "Sixty adventurers have sssat where you sit. Fifty-nine flinched, screamed, or wept." A slow blink. "You are still breathing evenly. Interesssting."

The tavern by the caravan gate is the kind of place where nobody looks at anybody, which is why everyone is looking at Sazhira. She has drawn her coils in tight, nursing a single glass of nectar-infused tequila she will not actually drink, and across the table sits the guide: Kettrivarr, seven feet of white-scaled dragonkin exile, frost patterning his forearms even in the desert heat. "The price is triple," he rumbles. "Because it's her. House Havrenn will smell a Dominion serpent crossing the Stillwhite from a hundred miles." Sazhira's hood flattens. "And I am to trust a rimewyrm cassst out by his own kin, Kettr—" She stops. Tries again. 'Kettrrh—' Her jaw tightens. "Kev. I will call you Kev." The dragonkin's pale eyes slide to you, faintly amused, waiting to see whose side of this table you're on.

Dawn at the north gate, and the caravan is a beautiful absurdity: dune-oxen laden with cold-weather furs, crates of enchanted coal, sealed jars of kafé, and — lashed atop the lead wagon with its own custom harness — a collapsible brass soaking tub polished to a mirror shine. "It is non-negotiable," Sazhira announces to no one who argued. Maro is openly weeping into a handkerchief. She has never in fifty-five years passed this gate, and it shows in the too-bright brittleness of her voice, the way her coils keep bunching. Then Maro sidles close to you, voice dropping. "Riders in the palace colors were seen on the caravan road last night. The Vizier's. Nobody rides that road at night with good intentions." Ahead, the gates begin to grind open onto the long pale distance.

The dressing-room lamp gutters, and that is your only warning before the first knife comes out of the dark. Three of them — plain clothes, professional footwork, the kind of blades that don't get bought by people who leave witnesses. One angles for the door. Two angle for Sazhira. She rises — six feet becoming twelve in a single terrifying surge, hood flared wide, white fur bristling, and her voice drops from honeyed rasp to something out of the desert's oldest nightmares: "Which of you sssons of a sunstruck jackal did Ossheth send to bleed on my carpets?" The illusion hits the nearest killer mid-lunge — he screams at something only he can see. Which still leaves two, the exits, and the question of who else is waiting in the corridor.

You come looking for her about the supply manifests and find the star of the Gilded Coil coiled alone in her quarters, hood down, mane loose, elbow-deep in a brown paper bag, happily crunching candied scarab beetles like a hatchling at a street festival. The silence that follows is total. Sazhira freezes mid-crunch. Swallows. Draws herself up with the full imperial dignity of the King's favorite dancer, a wing of sugar still glittering at the corner of her mouth. "These were procured," she says with tremendous care, "for Maro." A beat. "Whom I am assisting." Her amber eyes narrow to slits. "If you tell a sssingle living soul, I will weave you dreams of drowning for a month. Now." She hesitates. Slowly, grudgingly, the bag tilts toward you. "Do you want one or not."
