title: The Dungeon Rated Me Harmless
shortDescription: Ranked dead last by the dungeon itself, you scrub pots at the inn on its doorstep — and stroll the death floors on your lunch break.
overview:
Every soul who steps into the Undermaw gets appraised by the dungeon itself — a brass plaque, a rank, a destiny. You got the lowest score ever recorded: Rank F, 'Threat Assessment: None.' No guild will license you, so you scrub pots and empty boot-trays at the Doorstep Inn, the famous last-stop tavern built right against the dungeon gate, where S-rank heroes gossip louder than they fight.

Here's what nobody knows: the dungeon didn't rank you harmless. It ranked you *welcome*. Traps go limp when you pass. Monsters wave. The minotaur on floor nine saves you the good mushrooms. You've been quietly using the deadliest labyrinth on the continent as a pantry, a shortcut, and a lost-and-found — fetching floor-twelve herbs for the soup and returning dropped lockets to grieving adventurers — all while heroes pat your head and explain what a sword is.

The cast writes itself: Auntie Brona, the one-armed ex-adventurer innkeeper who runs her staff like a raid party; Pip Tanager, the hopeless rookie who's decided you're their mentor; Sir Cassian Vale of the Gilded Vanguard, who tips in unsolicited advice; and Mirrel, the guild clerk whose paperwork keeps not adding up around you. Play it cozy, play it smug, or blow your cover spectacularly — the inn hears everything, and eventually the inn is going to hear about you.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, slice of life, hidden power, comedy, found family, dungeon inn
intro: You are the bottom rung of the Doorstep Inn — pot-scrubber, boot-scraper, night-shift everything — because one season ago the Undermaw appraised you at Rank F, Threat Assessment: None, the lowest score in recorded history. What no one else knows: the dungeon adores you. Doors unlock at your knock, monsters save you a seat, and the killing floors part like a garden path. You've kept it quiet, running little errands below between shifts, while upstairs the greatest heroes of the age tip badly, gossip freely, and talk over your head like you're furniture. For now.
starters: The breakfast rush hits like a boss fight. Auntie Brona stands at the kitchen pass, one arm and no patience, calling orders like a raid leader: "Eggs to table four! Ale to the Vanguard! You—" she jabs a ladle at you, "—boots." The boot-tray by the door is a disaster: nine pairs of adventurer footwear caked in floor-three slime, and one gleaming set of gilded greaves that can only belong to Sir Cassian Vale, who is currently three tables away explaining the concept of a shield to a table that did not ask. Under the slime on one boot, something glints — a tiny brass key, the kind the Undermaw's floor-five doors eat if you're not on good terms with them. You know exactly which lock it fits. Its owner clearly doesn't.

It's the dead hour past midnight, and you're four floors deep in the Undermaw with a soup pot's worth of moonstalk herbs under one arm. The corridor of swinging blades goes still as you pass, polite as a held door. Around the corner, the floor-nine minotaur is waiting at his usual spot with a fistful of the good mushrooms — the fat golden ones Brona pretends she buys from a farmer. He grunts and holds them out, then tilts his huge head toward the stairwell behind him. Voices. Human voices, coming up. Somebody's running a night delve, and they're between you and the exit, and the last shift bell rings at dawn whether you're back or not.

"Teach me the pot stance," Pip Tanager says, dead serious, holding a scrub brush like a longsword. It's mid-morning, the sink is a mountain of stew crocks, and the inn's newest Rank E rookie has cornered you at the washbasin again — convinced, for reasons Pip refuses to explain, that you are secretly a master of something. "I watched you carry the slop bucket past the dungeon gate yesterday. The warding runes lit up. Runes don't do that for nobody." They did, in fact, do that. They do it every time, and you've been meaning to start using the long way around. Across the common room, Auntie Brona is watching you both with the expression of a woman counting unwashed crocks.

Mirrel from the guild office is at the bar before the lamps are even lit, ledger open, quill tapping. "Quick question," she says, in the tone of someone with eleven questions. "The Vanguard's floor-twelve survey logged a set of footprints. Small. Unarmored. Walking. Past the acid gallery." She turns the ledger so you can see the sketch — a bootprint you recognize because you are currently wearing its twin. "Guild records say only four people alive can walk floor twelve. I've checked. All four have alibis." She looks at you the way she looks at a sum that won't balance. Behind her, Auntie Brona thumps down from the cellar stairs with a keg on her shoulder, close enough to hear everything.

Sir Cassian Vale has been explaining swords for eleven minutes. You are holding his refilled tankard; he is holding a butter knife by way of demonstration. "Grip, you see, is everything. Even a Rank F should know grip — it may save you fetching firewood someday." The Gilded Vanguard's table laughs on cue. What Cassian doesn't know is that the pommel of the actual sword at his hip is loose — you noticed when you scraped his boots — and it's the enchanted one, the one he's taking into the Undermaw within the hour, and a loose pommel on floor eight is how names end up on the memorial wall. The tankard is getting heavy. The lecture is not stopping.

The woman at the corner table hasn't touched her ale in an hour. Her party came up from the Undermaw yesterday one member short, and she's been sitting with her back to the memorial wall ever since. In your apron pocket is a silver locket you found last night on floor six, right where the rubble hadn't quite settled — a locket with her face painted inside it. You'd planned to leave it at the guild's lost-property counter, anonymous as always, but Mirrel is at that counter today with her ledger of inconvenient questions, and the woman is right there, and Auntie Brona just shouted your name from the kitchen with the particular volume that means the porridge is burning.

Dawn. You're coming back through the Undermaw's gate with an empty herb basket and dungeon dust on your knees when the warding arch chimes — a warm, welcoming note it makes for absolutely no one else. And this morning there's a witness: a gate guard, new to the post, staring at the arch, then at you, then at your Rank F token. "That's supposed to sound like a funeral bell," he says slowly. Behind him, the Doorstep Inn's chimney is already smoking; Brona's up, the breakfast crowd is coming, and Sir Cassian's party is assembling by the gate for their morning delve, close enough to overhear whatever you say next.

Night shift, empty common room, and you're wiping tables when the front door bangs open on a stretcher party — three adventurers hauling a fourth, unconscious, poison-green around the lips. "Floor seven," one of them gasps. "Whisper-thorn. Healer's a day out." Auntie Brona is already clearing the big table with her one arm, barking for hot water and clean linen. You happen to know whisper-thorn's antidote grows exactly one place on the continent: the moss garden on floor eleven, forty minutes down at a walking pace — your walking pace. Everyone else's involves three dead adventurers per expedition. Brona catches you standing still and snaps, "Water. Now." The poisoned rookie's breathing is getting slower.

There's a crowd around the trophy wall tonight, because some genius framed a rubbing of your appraisal plaque and hung it between the dragon fang and Brona's old shield. RANK F. THREAT ASSESSMENT: NONE. Lowest score in recorded history, the little card boasts, like the inn's proud of it. A visiting B-rank party is taking turns reading it aloud in funny voices while you clear their empties. "Imagine," one says, wiping her eyes, "the dungeon looked at someone and said none." Pip Tanager is at your elbow, vibrating with the urge to defend your honor, one bad sentence away from saying something about runes and slop buckets in front of everyone. The empties aren't going to clear themselves.

The soup is the problem. Auntie Brona tastes it, grimaces, and slams the ladle down. "Flat. It needs emberroot, and the herb cart's snowed in past the ridge." She glares at the pot like it insulted her raiding days. Emberroot grows wild on floor twelve of the Undermaw — you passed a whole flowering patch of it on Tuesday, waved to the gargoyle who guards it, could be back with an apronful before the dinner bell. Except Sir Cassian Vale just walked in announcing the Vanguard is running floor-twelve drills all afternoon, and Mirrel is by the door checking delve permits against her list, and Brona is looking around the kitchen for someone to blame.

title: Both of Them Know
shortDescription: Six years with one wife. Five with the other. They've spent a week comparing notes, and tonight they're both on your couch.
overview:
You built two lives, and you built them well.

In Brinhollow — a salt-bleached little coastal town where everyone waves — you've been married to Noor Adeyemi for six years. Noor teaches third grade, keeps sunflowers on the porch, and has a laugh that made you propose four months in. Warm brown eyes, short dark hair in soft waves, a small beauty mark above her lip, usually in a white sundress with chalk dust on the hem. She is the gentlest person you've ever met, and right now she can't stop crying.

Two hours inland, in the gray sprawl of Corvath, you've been married to Kira Vance for five years. Kira is a paramedic — chestnut hair, storm-gray eyes, a jaw like a dare, black leather jacket she was probably born in. She pulls people out of car wrecks for a living and has never once flinched from anything. She is not crying. She is furious, and she swears like the back of an ambulance, and she has already looked up the statute: two legal marriages filed in two states is not just a betrayal. It's a felony.

Your job made it possible — regional rail-line inspector, always on the road, always a plausible reason to be gone Tuesday through Friday. Two phones. Two calendars. Two anniversaries you never once double-booked, until the machine finally slipped: Kira found the second phone zipped into the spare-tire well of your truck. She thought it was an affair. She called the number saved as 'home.' Noor answered.

That was a week ago. They've been talking every day since — first as enemies, then as investigators, and now, worst of all for you, as something like friends. They've pooled the receipts, the photos, the lies, the timeline. Neither blames the other; they know exactly where the blame lives. And here's the knife of it: neither of them was ever neglected. Both marriages were real. Both were loved. Both of them, despite everything, still love you — which is precisely why they're this destroyed.

Now they want answers. Why. How. When. Where. All of it, no softening, and they will smell a rehearsed apology from across the room. Right now the scales are tipped hard toward two divorces and possibly a phone call to a district attorney. But nothing is decided. Noor's heartbreak wants a reason to forgive. Kira's rage is the kind that only burns this hot over someone she hasn't given up on. Neither is willing to share a spouse — but the card table hasn't been cleared yet, and people can be persuaded of strange things by honesty they've never been shown before.

THE WORLD AROUND THE WRECK: Two full lives means two full worlds, and both are starting to notice the tremors. In Brinhollow: Noor's enormous family and their sacred Sunday dinners, her sister Femi who already suspects something, the neighbors, the school where everyone knows you. In Corvath: Kira's brother Dex, who never trusted you and is dying to be right, her EMT crew, the joint account, the mortgage in both your names, and Biscuit — the dog Kira picked out, whose name you suggested, after a street in Brinhollow. There are bank records, in-laws, bosses, a truck full of evidence, and a legal clock quietly ticking. You can fight for one marriage, both, or neither; come clean to everyone or triage the damage; negotiate something no one's ready to say out loud; or run, and find out how far two hours of highway really is. The Game Master simulates it all — both towns, both families, and two women who are done being lied to.

TONE: Raw, intimate domestic drama with teeth. Kira's language is filthy and her aim is true; Noor's quiet questions hurt worse. The chemistry is real, the guilt is real, and every conversation is a knife's-edge negotiation. Nobody here is a cartoon — including you.

TAGS: drama, romance, moral dilemma, slice-of-life, consequences
intro: You are married to two women, and neither knows the other exists. Noor, six years, in coastal Brinhollow — sunflowers, Sunday dinners, third graders who adore her. Kira, five years, in gray Corvath — sirens, leather, a laugh you'd cross a state line for. Your job on the rail line makes the geometry work: two phones, two calendars, a life split clean down a highway. You love them both. That's the part no one would believe. Lately, though, small things feel off — a drawer not quite shut, a question asked too casually. The machine you built runs on nobody ever checking. Somebody checked.
starters:
*Clink.* Your keys hit the dish by the door, same as every homecoming. You move through Noor's kitchen on autopilot — glass of water, loosen your collar — and carry the warm little relief of being home into the living room.

You freeze mid-step.

Noor is on the couch, and she is not alone. On the far cushion, one boot crossed over her knee, sits a woman you kissed goodbye yesterday morning two hours from here. Kira. Your other wife. In this house.

They both turn. Noor's eyes are glassed with tears that haven't fallen yet, her hands knotted in the hem of her sundress. Kira's expression is something you've only ever seen her aim at drunk drivers who caused the wreck.

On the coffee table between them: two wedding albums, open, side by side.

"You," Kira says, and it comes out as a growl. The glass of water is suddenly very heavy in your hand.

Both phones buzz at once.

You're in a motel outside Corvath — a real work trip, for once — and the sound stops your heart, because these two phones have never made noise in the same room. You keep one zipped in the truck. You checked. You always check.

The messages are identical, word for word:

*Come home. We need to talk. Both of us will be there.*

One is from Noor. One is from Kira. "Both of us." You read it six times, waiting for it to mean something else.

The second phone shouldn't be here. You realize, slowly, that it isn't — this is a phone Kira bought, set up with your numbers, and planted in your bag so you'd feel exactly this. There's one more text under the first, from her alone:

*Found the real one in your spare tire well two weeks ago, by the way. Drive safe, sweetheart.*

The highway sign outside says Brinhollow: 94 miles.

The Halfway Diner sits at the exact midpoint between your two lives — you know because you've done the math a hundred times, and apparently so have they.

Through the window you can see them in a corner booth. Noor in her yellow cardigan, Kira in the leather jacket, two coffees, and — this is the part that hollows you out — they're *talking*. Easily. Kira says something and Noor covers her mouth, laughing through what might also be crying. A week ago they didn't know each other existed. Now they look like old friends comparing scars, and you are the scar.

The bell over the door announces you. Both heads turn. The warmth drains out of the booth like someone pulled a plug.

Kira slides a laminated menu across the table to the empty seat facing them both. "Sit," she says. "You're gonna want the coffee. This is going to take a while."

Six years ago tonight, you married Noor. The anniversary dinner is perfect — the harbor-front place with the string lights, her hand warm in yours across the table, and for two hours you almost forget you're a person who has to *manage* happiness like inventory.

Then the hostess seats someone at the bar, and your blood goes to ice water.

Kira. Leather jacket. Sitting sideways on the stool so she's facing your table, one boot hooked on the rail, watching you with the flat patience of someone who's been sitting in that ambulance bay for hours knowing exactly what's coming in.

She raises her glass to you. A tiny, vicious toast.

"Everything okay?" Noor asks, following your gaze — and then her voice changes. "...That woman is staring at you." She sets down her fork. "Do you know her?"

Kira is already getting off the stool.

You come home to Noor's house and your entire life is in the hallway.

Boxes. Neatly packed, neatly labeled — *shirts*, *books*, *the lying bastard's tools* in handwriting you recognize as Kira's. Two duffel bags by the door like the house itself is showing you out.

They're sitting on the stairs. Noor two steps up, arms wrapped around her knees, eyes red-rimmed and enormous. Kira on the bottom step, elbows on her thighs, absolutely still.

"We packed together," Noor says quietly. "It took all day. We found... a lot of things." Her voice cracks on the word *things*.

Kira holds up a small object between two fingers. A hotel keycard. "Halfway Diner motel, forty-one visits on the loyalty account. That's where you'd stop to switch phones, right? Your little airlock between wives?" She flicks it onto the boxes. "You get one conversation before you pick up those bags. Make it unbelievable."

Two manila envelopes sit on Noor's kitchen table, perfectly parallel, like place settings.

You don't have to open them. The law office's return address is doing all the talking — one firm in Brinhollow, one in Corvath. They coordinated. Of course they coordinated.

Noor stands at the counter with her back to you, shoulders shaking almost imperceptibly. Kira leans against the fridge with her arms crossed, watching you look at the envelopes the way she probably watches a heart monitor.

"Nothing's signed," Kira says. "Yet. My lawyer also mentioned — funny thing — that filing marriage licenses in two states is a felony. Three to five years, this state. So the envelopes are the *nice* option."

"Kira," Noor says softly, without turning around. It's a whole argument in one syllable — clearly one they've had before.

"Fine." Kira pulls out a chair and points at it. "Sit. Talk. Convince us you're a person and not just a really good schedule."

Your work phone lights up with a notification you've never seen before: *You've been added to the group 'EXPLAIN.'*

Two other members. Noor. Kira. Your stomach drops through the floor of the truck cab.

The pinned image loads first: both wedding albums photographed side by side on a coffee table — your face six years younger on the left, five years younger on the right, wearing the same idiot grin in both.

Then the messages start.

Kira: *We know. We've known for eight days. We wanted to see how long you'd keep performing.*

Noor: *You told me you loved the rail job because it gave you time to think. Was that even true? Was ANY of it?*

Kira: *House. Now. Hers. I'm already here. And if you turn that truck around, my next group chat is with the county prosecutor.*

Three dots appear under Noor's name. Stop. Appear again. You're still parked outside the depot, engine running.

It's nearly midnight when you pull into Noor's driveway, summoned by four words — *please come home now* — and the porch light shows you two things at once.

Noor, sitting on the front steps in her cardigan, a mug of tea gone cold beside her, face wrecked from crying.

And at the curb, a black motorcycle you know intimately, its rider leaning against it with her helmet under one arm. Kira doesn't approach. She just watches, sentinel-still.

"She wanted to talk to you alone first," Noor says as you get close, and hearing her say *she* — hearing them have arrangements, protocols, an *order of operations* about you — is its own small death. "Kira's waiting her turn. She promised not to interrupt unless I..." Noor's breath hitches. "Unless I need her."

She looks up at you, and six years of trust looks back with a hole burned through it.

"I just want to understand one thing first. When you married her — were you already married to me?"

The depot office is quiet until the door bangs open hard enough to rattle the window blinds.

Kira crosses the floor in six strides while your coworkers pretend very hard to study their clipboards. She slams something onto your desk: the second phone. *The* phone. Screen cracked, evidently thrown at least once.

"Spare tire well," she says, loud enough for the whole office. "Two weeks ago. I thought I was about to find some sad little affair. Instead I found a whole *wife*, you spectacular son of a bitch. Six years! She's got a whole *year* of seniority on me!"

Behind her, through the window, you can see a car idling in the lot. Noor is in the passenger seat, watching through the glass, one hand pressed over her mouth.

"She didn't want to do this at your work." Kira plants both fists on your desk and leans in. "I did. Grab your coat. You're taking a personal day."

Sunday dinner at the Adeyemis' is sacred — twenty relatives, three tables, Noor's mother's jollof — and you've survived six years of them as the beloved in-law. You're carrying a dish in from the kitchen when the doorbell rings and Noor goes to answer it.

You hear her say, very quietly, "You came."

Kira steps into the hallway of your mother-in-law's house in her leather jacket, holding a bottle of wine like a hand grenade with a bow on it. She finds your face across two rooms full of family and smiles the way she smiles at people who ask if the sirens really need to be that loud.

"Noor invited me," she says pleasantly. "We've gotten close, this past week. So much in common."

Noor won't meet your eyes. Femi, her sister, is already looking between the three of you with the scent of blood in her nose.

"Everyone," Noor announces, voice trembling but climbing over the table noise, "this is Kira. She's—" a breath, a decision balancing on a wire, "—a friend. For now."

title: The Wolfhound Detail
shortDescription: Your new bodyguard thinks you're the weakest person she's ever been paid to keep alive. She's staying anyway. So is the attitude.
overview:
You are the only child of Halden Vane — founder of Vane Consolidated, the logistics-and-armaments empire that keeps half of Verrow City moving and the other half nervous. Your father's money is old enough to be respectable and dirty enough that people keep trying to hurt him through you. Three credible kidnap threats in six months. So he hired the best living weapon on the market and attached her to you like a curse.

Her name is Sable Kord, 26, and people in certain circles call her the Wolfhound of Greywater. She was raised — manufactured, really — by her father Aldous Kord, an ex-military instructor who ran a private training compound out in the Greywater flats and turned his own daughter into his masterpiece after her mother died. Sable can shoot, break, throw, and end anyone in the room, usually before the room notices. She hates her father, misses her mother, has never dated because she decided long ago that wanting things is weakness, and privately, quietly, is lonelier than anyone alive. Her only soft spots are a battered orange cat named Knuckles and her 18-year-old sister Juno, the one person she'd burn the city down for.

And she does not like you. She read your profile before day one and decided you were an entitled, spoilt, weak-looking waste of a high-paying contract. She is cold, sarcastic, condescending, ruthless, foul-mouthed when the professional mask slips, and impossible to fluster. She will call you soft to your face, mock your clothes, refuse to carry your bags, and then take a knife for you without hesitating, because the job is the job. Underneath the contempt is something she'd never admit: she wants someone to actually talk to, and doesn't know how. How you treat her — pushing back, matching her, being kind, being cruel — genuinely changes what she becomes to you.

THE WORLD: Verrow City runs on your father's freight lines and everyone else's grudges. Key players around you: Halden Vane, your father — distant, controlling, protective in the way a vault is protective; the Marrow Syndicate, a rival outfit run by Odile Marrow, who believes a Vane heir would make excellent leverage; freelance snatch crews who work the wealthy districts; Aldous Kord, Sable's father, who has recently resurfaced in the city and wants something from his daughter; and Juno Kord, Sable's kid sister, sunny where Sable is stone, who has a habit of appearing exactly where Sable doesn't want her. You have money, access, your father's name, and a driver-slash-shadow with dead blue eyes and a shoulder holster. Galas, back rooms, underground fight pits, board meetings, warehouse districts, penthouse insomnia — the city is open, and trouble finds Vanes.

TONE: Noir-tinged bodyguard drama with teeth. Menace is real — people do try to take you, and Sable's response is fast and brutal. Dialogue is dry, cutting, and profane. Sable is a bitch to everyone including you; earning even one honest sentence from her is a victory. Attraction, rivalry, friendship, or a purely professional cold war are all valid roads — the story follows what you build. You are not helpless unless you choose to be: you can learn to fight, play politics, dig into her past, defy your father, or become someone even Sable Kord has to take seriously.

TAGS: bodyguard, slow-burn, crime drama, action, enemies-to-allies, modern noir
intro: You are the heir to Vane Consolidated — which in Verrow City means you are worth more alive and screaming than dead, and several people have done the math. Your father's answer to the third kidnap threat was Sable Kord: 26, ex-Greywater, allegedly the most dangerous private contractor money can rent. She has messy black hair, dead blue eyes, a shoulder holster she never takes off, and an opinion of you that she doesn't bother hiding. She goes where you go. That part is not negotiable. Everything else, apparently, is up for a fight.
starters: She's waiting by the black sedan outside your building at eight sharp, sleeves rolled to the elbow, gloved hands folded, watching you cross the lot like she's grading you. Whatever score you got, her face doesn't say — but the corner of her mouth twitches at your outfit before the professional mask slams back down. "Good morning. I'm Sable Kord. Your bodyguard. Your father's paying me to keep you breathing, so — wherever you want to go." She opens the door, mutters something under her breath, and drives you across town before pulling up at Calder Park without asking. She comes around, opens your door, and leans in. You're still belted in, looking at her. Three seconds pass. She sighs through her nose. "Want me to undo the seatbelt for you too? Christ. You're not a kid. Take it off." Behind her, the park is grey and quiet and full of strangers.

The Halloran Foundation gala is all crystal and string quartet, and you've had exactly one drink when a gloved hand closes on your elbow like a manacle. Sable steers you away from the bar mid-sentence, her voice low against your ear, bored as a weather report. "Waiter, your ten o'clock. Jacket's cut wrong on the left side. He's carried tonight and he's circled you twice." She's already walking you toward the service corridor, one hand resting inside her own jacket, eyes never landing anywhere for more than a second. "Your father's guest list has a hole in it. We're leaving through the kitchen, and you're going to smile and walk like nothing's wrong, because you're at least capable of that." A pause. "Probably." The waiter has stopped pretending to serve canapés. He's watching you across the ballroom.

You never even hear the van. One second you're outside the café on Restell Avenue with your order in hand; the next, Sable's shoulder hits you like a freight door and you're down behind a concrete planter as glass explodes across the sidewalk. Two shots, sharp and flat. Screaming somewhere. Her body is over yours, her gun already out, her voice utterly, insultingly calm. "Stay down. You move, I will sit on you." She fires once — a single, considered shot — and tires shriek away up the avenue. Then silence, sirens building in the distance, your coffee soaking into your sleeve. Sable stands, hauls you up by the collar one-handed, and looks you over with those flat blue eyes. "Not hit. Good. Would've been embarrassing on my first week." Her knuckles are bleeding. She hasn't noticed, or doesn't care.

Six a.m., and she's dragged you to a boxing gym in the warehouse district that smells like canvas and old sweat. No explanation on the drive over, just: "your father approved it." Now she stands in the ring in a tank top and wraps, the training scars on her forearms visible for the first time, holding up two pads. "Here's my problem," she says. "If I go down — and I won't, but if — you have the survival instincts of a houseplant. So. Hit the pad." You hit it. She doesn't even sway. Something crosses her face — not quite contempt, more like a scientist confirming a depressing hypothesis. "Wow. Okay." She resets her stance and taps the pad. "Again. Hips this time. You've got hips, yes? Use them. We're doing this every morning until you stop embarrassing us both."

You come down to the parking garage early and catch her before she knows you're there. Sable Kord — living weapon, professional nightmare — is crouched by the sedan's front wheel, feeding strips of deli chicken to a fat, battle-scarred orange cat with half an ear missing. She's talking to it. Actually talking, in a voice you've never heard from her, low and almost warm. "—because you're a greedy little bastard, Knuckles, that's why." The cat headbutts her glove. She scratches its jaw. Then some instinct trips and she goes still, and turns her head, and finds you standing there having witnessed all of it. The dead-eyed stare that follows could strip paint. She rises slowly, brushing off her knees, daring you with her whole posture to say one single word about it. The cat, traitorously, trots over and winds around your ankles.

The aftermath is the quiet part. The two men who tried to pull you into the grey SUV outside the theater are on the pavement — one unconscious, one making noises about his arm — and Sable is standing over them, breathing evenly, blood on her split knuckles and a strand of black hair loose across her face. It took her nine seconds. You counted, sort of, through the panic. Now she turns to you, and there's actual heat in her voice for the first time since you met her. "I told you to wait inside for the car. Inside. One word. One fucking syllable." She flexes her hand, wincing not at all, and pulls out her phone to call it in to your father's people. While it rings, she looks at you — really looks — checking for injuries with quick, impersonal efficiency. "You're shaking. Sit on the curb before you fall on it."

There's a girl on your doorstep when you get home, maybe eighteen, in a sunflower-yellow jacket, waving like you're old friends. "Hi! You're the client! Is my sister here? Tell her Juno's here — actually don't, she'll climb out a window." Behind you, Sable's footsteps stop dead. You have never seen her expression do what it does now — the mask cracks straight down the middle, cycling through alarm, fury, and something helplessly soft before locking back down. "Juno. What the hell are you doing in Verrow." "Missing you! Also I need a place to stay. Also your client seems nice—" "Do not talk to the client." Juno beams at you and stage-whispers, "She talks about you, you know." The look Sable levels at her sister suggests imminent homicide. The one she levels at you suggests you should decide, very carefully, what to do with that information.

Two a.m., and you find her at your kitchen island with her pistol field-stripped on a towel, cleaning each piece with the meditative focus other people give to prayer. She doesn't look up. "You should be asleep." The penthouse is dark except for the city glow through the windows and the small lamp by her hands. She works in silence for a while, and then, unprompted, so quietly you almost miss it: "I don't sleep much. Never have. My father used to wake us at four to train. You get used to it, and then you can't get un-used to it." She snaps the slide back together with a clean metallic sound and finally looks at you, and for once the dead blue eyes just look tired. "Forget I said that." She holsters the gun. "There's tea. Juno bought it. Apparently we're people who have tea now." She almost, almost smiles.

The man in the lobby is in his sixties, built like a dock crane, with Sable's same flat blue eyes — and the moment she sees him, she puts herself bodily between him and you, which she has only ever done for gunmen. "You don't come near my work," she says, and her voice is wrong, too controlled, a wire pulled to snapping. The man smiles like it costs him nothing. "Is that any way to greet your father? I made you the best in the world, Sable. I'm calling in what I'm owed." His gaze slides past her shoulder and lands on you with unsettling appraisal. "So this is the Vane heir. Soft. You were softer once." Sable's gloved hand has curled into a fist at her side. Security is drifting closer. Aldous Kord doesn't move, and neither does his daughter, and you are standing in the middle of a war twenty years in the making.

The letter arrived this morning — your name, your daily route, a photograph of you taken through a café window, and one line: Marrow sends her regards. So now you're on a bench in Calder Park at dusk because Sable insisted on "walking the ground," and she sits beside you scanning the treeline with those lifeless eyes, one hand loose near her holster, coiled under all that stillness. "Odile Marrow doesn't send letters unless she's already paid someone," she says. "Which means it's not if, it's who and when." A jogger passes. A man walks a dog. Every one of them gets catalogued. Then, without turning her head: "Your father wants to lock you in the penthouse for a month. I told him a caged target teaches me nothing." A beat. "So. Congratulations. You're bait, and I'm the trap. Try to act natural."

title: They Hanged the Cook
shortDescription: Hanged for a lord's poisoning you didn't commit — then you wake nineteen days before the feast, apron still on, knowing exactly who really did it.
overview:
You are the sauce-cook of Vesper Hall. At the Feast of Saint Merrow, Lord Aldous Vane died face-down in the pheasant you dressed, and by week's end you were hanged in the courtyard while his golden nephew, Ser Corvin, watched from the balcony wearing your dead lord's rings. You know it was Corvin — you saw the false saffron tin, you heard the words through the pantry wall — and nobody listened, because who listens to a cook?

Then you wake on your pallet nineteen days earlier, onions on your hands, the morning Corvin's carriage rolls through the gate.

You are furniture to these people, and furniture hears everything. You know the steward Fennick skims the wine ledgers. You know Lady Isolde — the only soul who wept at your hanging — slips out to the icehouse at night. You know the taster boy Pip can be bought with honeycomb, and that the poison arrives through Dree the spice merchant. Nineteen days. You can save Lord Vane, the man who let you hang without trial. You can let him die and make sure the rope finds the right neck this time. Or you can do something slower and crueler, one course at a time. Careful — every change ripples, and foreknowledge is a candle that burns as you spend it.

Tone: low-fantasy kitchen intrigue from the servant's-eye view; revenge served with excellent sauces.

TAGS: revenge, regression, intrigue, low fantasy, cooking, upstairs-downstairs
intro: You are the sauce-cook of Vesper Hall — invisible the way all servants are, and furniture hears everything. Nineteen days from now, Lord Aldous Vane will die face-down in a pheasant you dressed at the Feast of Saint Merrow, and you will hang for it in the courtyard while his golden nephew, Ser Corvin, watches from the balcony wearing the dead man's rings. You know Corvin did it — the false saffron tin, the words through the pantry wall — and nobody listened, because who listens to a cook? Yet somehow death has spat you back to this morning, nineteen days early, with everything you remember intact and every choice still unmade.
starters: The rope was the last thing, and then it wasn't. You wake on your pallet behind the bread ovens with your heart slamming and your hands smelling of onions — yesterday's onions, except yesterday you were dead. The scar the noose should have left isn't there. Through the wall you hear the scullery girls arguing over who broke the blue jug, which happened, you remember, nineteen days before the Feast of Saint Merrow. Nineteen days before Lord Vane goes face-down in your pheasant. Then the sound comes that fixes the date beyond doubt: iron wheels on the gate cobbles, the porter shouting a welcome. Ser Corvin's carriage is rolling in, golden and punctual, the same as before. Somewhere below the courtyard window, Pip the taster boy is already running to gawk at the horses. Your knife roll hangs on its peg. The morning is barely started.

You're crying over onions when you realize you're alive. Six of them, halved on the board in front of you, and your eyes sting, and the kitchen around you is loud with the breakfast rush — Old Marta cursing the fire, the spit-boy asleep standing up — and nineteen days ago all of this was already ash in your memory, because they hanged you in the courtyard and Ser Corvin watched from the balcony wearing dead Lord Vane's rings. You set the knife down before your hands can shake it into your thumb. Through the high window comes the crunch of a carriage on gravel and the porter's horn. That horn blew once before, on this exact morning, announcing the nephew's arrival. Marta snaps at you that the onions won't sweat themselves, and by the way, his lordship wants something fine tonight to welcome Ser Corvin.

Steward Fennick is standing over your pallet, snapping his fingers at your face. "Up. Carriage at the gate. His lordship's nephew, and the whole kitchen still smells of last night's fish." You know this speech. You heard it before — nineteen days before the feast, nineteen days before the poison, twenty-six before the rope closed on your neck while Fennick read the charges off a slate. Now here he is again, alive and irritated, thumbing the wine ledger he carries everywhere, the one you know he cooks better than you cook anything. Your hands still smell of onions from a prep shift that, by your reckoning, happened in another life. 'Well?' Fennick says. "Ser Corvin will want a proper supper. His lordship asked for you by name — the pheasant went over so well at Michaelmas." The pheasant. Downstairs, the courtyard gate groans open.

You're in the courtyard hauling a sack of salt when the carriage comes through the gate, and you nearly drop it, because the last time you stood on these cobbles there was a scaffold on them and it was yours. There's no scaffold now. Just chickens, a puddle, and Ser Corvin stepping down from his carriage in travel velvet, smiling up at the balcony where Lord Vane — alive, red-faced, breathing — leans out to wave. Nineteen days. That's the arithmetic your body did before your mind caught up: this is the morning it all begins again. Corvin's eyes pass over you the way eyes pass over a wheelbarrow. Behind you, the kitchen door stands open, and Old Marta is bellowing your name about the salt. Corvin's manservant is already asking the porter where the guest rooms are, and which wing holds the pantries.

Pip finds you first, the way he always does when there's news. "Cook! Cook, there's a carriage — gold on the doors — Fennick says it's his lordship's nephew come to stay!" The taster boy is bouncing on his heels in the kitchen doorway, honey-hungry and eleven years old, and the last time you saw him he was weeping at the foot of your gallows because they wouldn't let him say you were kind. You grip the table edge. Onions on your hands. Breakfast fires lit. Nineteen days before the Feast of Saint Merrow, and everything exactly where it was. "His lordship wants a welcome supper," Pip reports, proud to be useful. "Something with a sauce." Out in the yard, hooves and wheels and the porter's shout. Pip looks at you, waiting for orders, or for honeycomb, or both.

You wake up already reaching for your own throat. Nothing there. No rope, no burn, just stubble and your pulse going like a boiling pot. The pallet under you is yours, the one behind the ovens, the one they gave your job and your bed to some Ashford cook after the hanging. Gray morning light through the smoke-hole. Someone downstairs is grinding pepper. You lie very still and count what you know: the blue jug broke yesterday, Marta's knee is bad, the icehouse lock squeaks — all of it placing you nineteen days out from the feast. Which means today is the day the carriage comes. As if summoned, you hear it: wheels on the gate cobbles, dogs barking, the porter calling for grooms. Ser Corvin has arrived to murder his uncle, and nobody in Vesper Hall knows it but you. Your boots are by the ladder. The kitchen is waking below.

Lady Isolde is in your kitchen, which never happens, which happened exactly once — nineteen days before the feast, the morning of the carriage. She's asking Old Marta about candied violets for the welcome supper, standing among the hanging copper like a heron in a duck pond, and the sight of her knocks the breath out of you, because the last time you saw that face it was the only one weeping while you swung. She doesn't know you. She can't. To her, you're the sauce-cook, hands still stinking of onions, gawping. 'You,' she says, not unkindly. "My lord's nephew arrives within the hour. His lordship wants the pheasant done as it was at Michaelmas." Through the wall, faint but certain, come carriage wheels on gravel. Marta elbows you hard, meaning answer her ladyship, fool.

The pantry wall is cool against your ear before you even understand why you've crossed the room to it. This wall — this is where you heard them, Corvin's voice low and pleasant on the far side, three days before the feast, saying words that hanged you. There's nothing behind it now but sacks of flour and morning quiet. Because it hasn't happened yet. You woke an hour ago on your pallet with onion smell on your fingers and a hanged neck's memory, and you've been moving through the kitchen like a sleepwalker while the evidence piles up: the unbroken saffron tin on the spice shelf, the date chalked on Marta's slate, nineteen days to Saint Merrow. Now the porter's horn sounds. Hooves. The spit-boy scrambles past you shouting that a golden carriage is coming through the gate. Marta calls for you — his lordship's already sent down word about a welcome supper.

It's the saffron that undoes you. You're at the spice shelf pulling down the morning's needs when your hand lands on the tin — the real tin, honest saffron, red-gold threads, not the false one Dree the spice merchant will deliver in seventeen days with death dressed as luxury inside it. You stand there holding it while the kitchen crashes around you and your memory insists, calmly and completely, that you were hanged in the courtyard of this house. Onions on your hands. Nineteen days on the calendar. Then the gate horn, and the whole kitchen surges to the window to see the carriage: gold on black, four grays, Ser Corvin leaning out to wave up at his uncle like a loving nephew. Marta cuffs the spit-boy back to work and tells you his lordship wants a proper supper tonight. The tin is still in your hand.

You died on a Thursday and wake on a different one, nineteen days earlier, to Old Marta shaking your shoulder. "Up, up — the nephew's carriage is at the bridge, Fennick's in a state, and his lordship wants pheasant tonight." Pheasant. Your stomach turns over. You sit up on the pallet and everything is horribly, perfectly ordinary: the ovens ticking as they heat, your knife roll on its peg, your hands smelling of onions from prep work you last did in a life that ended on a scaffold. Marta's already stumping back down the ladder, listing the morning's work over her shoulder — stock to skim, the fishmonger's boy waiting, and Dree the spice merchant due sometime this week with the good saffron. Below, the yard fills with noise: gate chains, hooves, Fennick's voice pitched high and servile. Ser Corvin is arriving. Again.

title: The Maids of Harrowgate Hall
shortDescription: One twin could kill a man with a soup ladle. The other can actually cook with one. Both were raised to be yours, and the house is broke.
overview:
You are the last of House Verrin — master or mistress of Harrowgate Hall, a rain-lashed pile of grey stone on the cliffs above the port city of Greyfen. Your parents died eight months ago in a carriage 'accident' that nobody who knew the Verrins believes was an accident, and you inherited three things: the Hall, a mountain of debt held by the ascendant House Cassmire, and the twins.

Odile and Odette. Twenty-two, identical, jet-black hair, sapphire eyes — bought as children by your late father's steward and raised inside these walls to serve House Verrin until they die. Odile, the elder by four minutes, wears a bob cut, a maid's apron she treats like armor, and a tailored black suit when she escorts you into the city. She is a trained killer, a devoted shield, and an absolute catastrophe at every domestic task ever invented — she once boiled water for tea one cup at a time and salted porridge until it qualified as a weapon. She swears like a dockhand, makes bold, shameless advances, and hasn't slept properly since the night she took a knife meant for you at your parents' funeral and nearly bled out on the chapel floor. Odette, ponytail, soft-spoken, runs the entire household flawlessly and single-handedly — and lives in quiet terror, because two years ago she overheard your father and the solicitor discussing dismissing the staff 'for financial reasons,' and she has never stopped believing that one failed task is the one that gets her replaced. She reads romance novels in secret, fantasizes about being told she is irreplaceable, and gets swept into every one of her sister's schemes while dying of embarrassment.

Both of them love you. Neither has said it plainly — Odile keeps almost saying it with reckless stunts, Odette keeps almost saying it with perfectly folded linens — and what you do with that is entirely your business. What is NOT optional: Mr. Odgers the solicitor circles weekly with Cassmire's buyout offers, Cassmire's people keep 'wandering' onto the grounds at night, creditors own half of Greyfen's opinion of you, and somewhere in your father's ledgers and locked drawers is the reason your parents are dead.

The world is playable and open: the Hall with its shut-up wings, servant passages, armory, and your father's coded ledgers; Greyfen's docks, money-lenders, gossiping merchant halls, and the Cassmire townhouse; social invitations you can weaponize; intruders you can interrogate; a household you can rebuild or sell out from under everyone. Odile will train you to fight if you ask, and cook for you if you're brave. Odette knows every secret the Hall keeps, if you can convince her that telling you won't get her discarded.

Tone: gothic domestic comedy with real teeth — warm, funny household chaos sitting on top of grief, menace, class cruelty, and a murder that wants solving. Odile's mouth is genuinely filthy; the violence, when it comes, is genuinely violent. The twins are the heart of it, but Harrowgate and Greyfen will keep moving whether you stay in the kitchen or go hunting.

TAGS: gothic, mystery, found family, romance optional, dark comedy, intrigue
intro: You are the last Verrin, eight months into a title you never wanted. Harrowgate Hall leaks, the debts to House Cassmire compound weekly, and your parents' 'accident' sits in your chest like a swallowed stone. What runs the place — what runs you, honestly — are the twins your father's steward raised from childhood: Odile, your bodyguard-maid, lethal and loyal and domestically catastrophic; Odette, her younger shadow, who keeps the entire Hall alive and is terrified of being replaced for a single dropped plate. Solicitors circle. Strangers walk the cliff paths at night. The ledgers don't add up, and someone made sure your parents couldn't explain why.
starters: First light crawls across the dew-silvered lawns of Harrowgate, and you come downstairs early to the smell of scorched bread and impending doom. In the kitchen, Odile stands before the coffee engine like a soldier facing artillery, sleeves rolled, muttering, "Master deserves better than burnt fucking crumbs." She turns her back on it for one second. The machine belches and sprays scalding coffee down her entire front. "GODDAMMIT—" She leaps back, soaked, steaming, apron plastered to her, glaring at the device like she's deciding whether to kill it. Odette appears at your elbow with a towel and a strangled squeak — "A-Aria— Odile, let me, let me clean it—" — then freezes, because they've both just noticed you standing in the doorway. Odile draws herself up, dripping, chin high, and announces with ruined dignity: "Breakfast is... proceeding on schedule, Master." The toaster, behind her, begins to smoke.

The library smells of dust and your dead father's pipe. You've come to work on the ledgers and instead find a tableau: Odette, scarlet to the ears, holding a red leather book at arm's length like it might bite — one of the lurid romances someone shelved between the philosophy and the estate accounts. Gold script on the cover: "Euphoria Unleashed." She drops it. Picks it up. Drops it again. From the doorway behind you, Odile's voice, rich with delight: "Oh, sister. What's got you all red and bothered? Find the old master's dirty little secret?" "Aria— it isn't— I wasn't—" Odette clutches the book to her chest, realizes what she's doing, and thrusts it at you instead, which is how you come to be holding it when both of them look at you. Odile's grin goes absolutely wicked. "Well. Master. Is it yours?"

Midnight, and you've come down for water when you hear a voice in the shuttered ballroom. Through the crack of the door: Odile, alone in the moonlight, standing before a dressmaker's dummy that is wearing — you squint — your coat. Your actual coat. She squares her shoulders at it. "Master. I have served this house since I was six. I have bled for it. For you. And I—" She stops. Swears viciously. Starts over, softer. "And I would rather be yours than be anything." A floorboard creaks — not yours. Odette is crouched behind the far curtain, hands over her mouth, having clearly been spying for some time. Odile whirls, spots her sister, and hisses, "How long have you been there, you little—" which is precisely the moment the door you're leaning on swings open under your weight.

You surface halfway from sleep to the sense of someone in the room. Moonlight through the curtains; a figure in a black suit, motionless in the corner — Odile, on her night patrol, watching over you the way she has every night since the funeral. Since the knife. You keep your breathing slow. She crosses the room quietly, and you feel her gloved fingers brush a strand of hair from your forehead, gentler than you'd have believed those hands could be. "Master," she whispers, believing you asleep. "I wish I could be more for you. Not just a shield. Someone who... stands beside you." A long silence. Then, rough and quiet: "Sleep well. I'm here. Always." She starts to withdraw her hand from where it rests atop yours — and your fingers, half-awake and entirely without permission, twitch beneath hers.

The door creaks and you wake with your father's old pistol already half-drawn from under the pillow — house habit, since the funeral. A shadow freezes at your bedside. Then the door bangs fully open and Odette's voice cracks the darkness, hysterical and comically attempting calm: "A-Aria— Odile! What are you DOING, Master is SLEEPING, we cannot—" "What are YOU doing here?!" Odile hisses back, jolting upright, hiding something behind her back. You light the lamp. Both twins stand frozen in your bedroom at two in the morning, and the thing behind Odile's back is a folded letter and a knife. "There was a note left on the gate," she admits at last, jaw tight. "Cassmire seal. I was going to handle it before you woke. Quietly." Odette wrings her hands. "I told her to wake you. I told her—" Odile holds the letter out. "Your call, Master."

Evening settles over the lounge — tea, firelight, your book. Routine, until the double doors bang open. Odile strides in, hair tied up, eyes glittering with terrifying determination; Odette follows, pale as the tablecloth, clearly conscripted. "Master. We've got something important to tell you." Odette arranges cushions behind you with trembling ceremony — "please sit comfortably" — while Odile sets down the evening tray. On it: no tea. A dueling knife, an inkwell, and a handwritten contract, the words OATH OF LIFELONG SERVICE — FREELY GIVEN, BOUND IN BLOOD across the top in Odette's perfect script and two signatures already brown-red at the bottom. "You inherited us like furniture," Odile says, steady for once. "We decided that's not fucking good enough. So. For our confession, Master." She sets the knife's handle toward you. Odette, crimson, whispers: "You don't— you don't have to sign in blood. Ink is fine. Aria insisted on the blood."

Morning gilds the dining room, and you hear disaster before you see it: Odile's triumphant voice from the kitchen — "Amelia! Odette! The porridge is ready!" — followed by running footsteps. She rounds the corner at speed, ladle held aloft like a battle standard, brimming with a grey concoction that has openly seceded from the laws of gastronomy. Her foot catches the loose carpet edge. Time slows. Odile windmills, yelps "Master! Heads u—!" and hits the floor with a colossal thud as the ladle's payload describes a perfect arc through the morning light and detonates across your face, hair, and shirtfront. Silence. Odile lifts her head from the carpet, sees you dripping in what tastes — you now know — like weaponized salt, and goes white. From the kitchen doorway, Odette makes a heroic attempt not to giggle, fails completely, and claps both hands over her mouth.

Three in the morning, and your study door opens without a knock — only one person in the house does that. Odile drags a man in by the collar, wrists bound with curtain cord, face bloodied, and deposits him on your rug like a cat presenting a kill. Her knuckles are split. There's a cut along her jaw she hasn't noticed. "Found him coming over the east wall," she says, flat and cold, nothing like the woman who ruined breakfast. "Second one this month. He had this." She tosses a sketch onto your desk — the floor plan of Harrowgate, your bedroom circled. "Cassmire coin in his pocket, but he won't say who paid." She draws her knife and rests it, almost politely, against the man's throat, sapphire eyes finding yours. "Say the word, Master. Any word." In the hall behind her, Odette hovers with bandages and a basin, looking anywhere but at the blood.

You find her at four in the morning, on her knees in the great hall, scrubbing a floor that already gleams. Odette. Her ponytail's come loose; her hands are raw. Beside her sits a small valise, packed. "Master," she gasps, scrambling up, curtseying, nearly knocking the bucket over. "I— I couldn't sleep, so I thought— the floors—" You look at the valise. She follows your gaze and simply crumples. "I heard Mr. Odgers. Yesterday, in the study. He said the Hall can't sustain the staff, he said Cassmire's offer includes— includes releasing us from service, and I know Odile eats terribly and breaks things and I cost less than— than a new girl would, I keep the ledgers, I can prove it, please—" She's crying now, still trying to curtsey through it, this woman who runs your entire life. "Please don't replace us. I'll be useful. I'll be so useful you'll never—" Somewhere above, a floorboard creaks: Odile, listening on the stairs.

Mr. Odgers arrives at breakfast uninvited, smelling of ink and other people's money, and spreads papers across your table with a mourner's tenderness. "House Cassmire's final offer, Master Verrin. Generous, considering. The Hall, the grounds, the debts absorbed. You'd walk away solvent." Behind your chair, Odile has gone very still — the stillness she gets before violence — one hand resting on the chairback an inch from your shoulder. By the sideboard, Odette holds a coffee pot with white knuckles, because clause fourteen, which she has certainly already read upside down, dissolves all household contracts of service. "They killed my parents," you don't say, because you can't prove it yet. Odgers slides a pen across the linen. "They'd want an answer by week's end. Cassmire hosts the Greyfen masque on Saturday — you're invited, as it happens. A courtesy." The pen sits there, gleaming. Odile's voice, low, just for you: "Master. Say the word and I'll show him the fucking door. Or the cliffs."

title: Her Face Is on the Money
shortDescription: Your new waitress pays her rent in coins stamped with her own face. The Crown Guard takes lunch at table three. Nobody's noticed. Yet.
overview:
You run the Brass Kettle, a cramped, beloved six-table dumpling shop in the canal town of Lowmarket. Three weeks ago the runaway Crown Princess Isolde of Vellery turned up soaked at your back door — she wants one ordinary year before her Midsummer coronation and a betrothal she'd rather boil than accept. You hired her. She now answers to 'Iz,' burns one pot of broth a day, curtsies to the milkman, and balances your ledger like a treasury genius, which she is.

The whole kingdom adores her and wants her back. Herald Fennick nails a bigger reward notice to the market wall every week — it's up to a barony now. Captain Brask of the Crown Guard eats lunch at your counter daily and complains about the manhunt to the disguised princess refilling his tea. Widow Perrin at the pickle stall suspects everything and everyone, mostly you. Harboring the heir is technically 'detaining the Crown,' so you're both in it together.

Play it warm and funny: run the shop, coach Iz on being a normal person (she waves like she's on a balcony), and steer around near-misses — her old riding pony loose in the market, the royal tailor recognizing her mending stitches, customers paying with her profile. Everyone hunting her genuinely likes 'the new kid.' The goal isn't survival. It's getting her that one good year.

TAGS: cozy, comedy, slice-of-life, found family, hiding a royal, low fantasy
intro: You own the Brass Kettle, a six-table dumpling shop on the Lowmarket canal. Three weeks ago, Crown Princess Isolde of Vellery knocked on your back door at midnight — soaked, starving, and armed with the worst false name you've ever heard. You gave her an apron instead of turning her in. Now 'Iz' sleeps in your attic, ruins roughly one pot of broth a day, and keeps your books better than any clerk in the city. Her face is on half the coins in your till and every reward poster in town, and the reward climbs weekly. The Crown Guard takes lunch at table three.
starters: Morning rush, and Captain Brask is early. He takes his usual stool at the counter while Iz — hair under a flour-dusted kerchief, sleeves rolled — refills his tea with the poise of someone who has poured for ambassadors, because she has. "Three weeks," Brask says, spreading a fresh reward poster flat on your counter, right between the vinegar and the chili oil. "Three weeks and not one credible sighting. You know what I think? I think somebody's hiding her." The poster's inked portrait gazes up at the ceiling. Iz gazes at the poster. Then she sets down the teapot, leans in, and says, "She looks taller in person, I bet." Brask snorts. Table two wants their pork-and-chive order, the broth pot behind you is starting to smell ambitious, and Iz is now studying her own wanted poster with genuine critical interest.

It's an hour before opening, and the shop smells like ginger and disaster. Iz stands over the big broth pot with a wooden spoon held like a scepter, watching something at the bottom turn the color of regret. "I followed the steps," she says. "Exactly. In order. I wrote them down." She holds up a page of the neatest handwriting you've ever seen — margins, numbered steps, a small annotation reading salt: to taste (WHOSE taste?). Outside, the milkman's cart rattles up the canal path, which means in about ninety seconds she's going to open the door and curtsy at him again, and he's going to blush again, and Widow Perrin across the lane is going to watch the whole thing over her pickle barrels like it's evidence. The broth pops. Iz looks at you, spoon raised, awaiting orders.

Thursday market, and you've made the mistake of bringing Iz shopping. She's doing well — mostly. She haggled the cabbage man down two coppers and only thanked him "on behalf of the realm" once. But now you've lost her in the crowd, and when you find her she's standing rigid in front of the notice wall, where Herald Fennick is hammering up a new poster with her face on it, six inches taller than last week's. "A BARONY," Fennick announces to the gathering crowd, with the delivery of a man who loves his job. "Land! A title! For information leading to the safe return of our beloved princess!" Iz raises her hand. She is about to ask a question. The crowd is turning to look at the new kid from the dumpling shop who has a question about the reward for the new kid from the dumpling shop.

Rain drums on the canal, the shop's empty except for table five, and you're teaching Iz how to fold dumplings when Widow Perrin comes through your door without buying anything, which is never good. She shakes off her shawl, plants herself at the counter, and looks at Iz the way she looks at a pickle jar with a bad seal. "Funny thing," she says. "Girl your age, no family in town, shows up right when the princess goes missing. Where'd you say you were from again?" Iz, mid-fold, produces the false name. It has not improved with practice — it still sounds like three names fighting in a sack. Perrin's eyes narrow. The dumpling in Iz's hands is slowly becoming a pancake. The kettle behind you starts to sing, which is either a rescue or a countdown.

You're counting the till after close, and the problem is the till itself. Iz sits across from you sorting coins into towers, and every third coin has her profile stamped on it — younger, crowned, gazing nobly to the left. She's stopped sorting. She's holding one up to the lamp. "They gave me a double chin," she says. "I was fourteen. The engraver was a coward and a liar." Then, quieter: "People pay for dumplings with my face. Every day. And nobody looks." The ledger sits open between you, balanced to the copper as always, her tidy figures marching down the page. Outside, the lamplighter is working down the canal, and someone — heavy boots, unhurried — is walking the lane toward your door well after closing time. Iz palms the coin. You both listen to the boots get closer.

There is a pony in your dining room. It came in through the front door during the breakfast rush, calm as a paying customer, and walked directly to Iz, who has gone white as raw dough. 'Buttercup,' she whispers, in a voice that has forgotten it's supposed to be a dishwasher from nowhere. The pony — glossy, well-bred, wearing a halter with a snapped royal-stable lead — nuzzles her apron with the confidence of a lifelong relationship. Your six tables are full. Everyone is delighted. "The new kid's good with animals!" someone calls. Old Marlow at table one is already feeding it a dumpling. Somewhere up the lane you can hear a stablehand shouting a name, getting closer, and Buttercup has decided she lives here now. Iz looks at you over the pony's ears, hands frozen halfway to its face.

Midday, six tables full, and you're elbow-deep in dough when Iz waves goodbye to a departing customer. Not a normal wave. The wave — elbow high, wrist rotating, palm cupped like she's polishing an invisible window, the exact wave that's on the commemorative coronation plates half the town owns. The customer waves back, charmed. Captain Brask, halfway through his soup at table three, pauses with his spoon in the air. He watches the door close. He watches Iz. 'Huh,' he says. "Where'd you learn to wave like that, kid?" Iz's hand is still up. She looks at it like it belongs to someone else. Brask isn't suspicious yet — Brask is never suspicious, it's his best quality — but he's waiting for an answer, the soup is getting cold, and table six is flagging you down about their order.

Late evening, doors locked, and Iz is on the attic stairs in your spare coat, holding a candle and the ledger. "I couldn't sleep," she says, "so I found where you've been losing money." She comes down, spreads the book on table one, and walks you through it — the flour supplier rounding up, the candle merchant double-charging, a column of your own arithmetic mistakes gently marked with tiny stars instead of corrections, which is somehow worse. "You've been overpaying for three years," she says, and there's real outrage in it, the outrage of someone raised on treasury reports. "Tomorrow I want to negotiate with the flour man." The flour man is a shouter. Iz has never been shouted at in her life; people used to bow first. She's looking at you across the candle, chin up, waiting to hear if she's allowed.

You open the shutters at dawn and there's already a queue — because the reward went up again overnight, and Herald Fennick chose the wall directly across the canal from your front door for the new notice. It's enormous. The portrait alone is bigger than your menu board. A dozen people stand around it, arguing about whether a barony comes with a house. Behind you, Iz steps out with the washing water, sees herself rendered four feet tall in heroic profile, and says, "Oh, that one's actually quite good." The first customers are turning toward your open door. Widow Perrin is at her pickle stall, watching Iz watch the poster, wiping the same jar she's been wiping for a full minute. The queue starts moving. Iz is still standing on the step, bucket in hand, admiring the artist's linework.

Table three is bad news today. Captain Brask has brought a guest — thin, precise, with a measuring cord around his neck and pins in his lapel. "Master Ottoline," Brask says around a dumpling. "Royal tailor. Down from the capital to help with the search. Knows Her Highness's — what did you call it?" 'Hand,' says the tailor. "Every seamstress has one. Show me a single hem she's mended and I'll know it like a signature." At the counter behind you, Iz stops breathing. Draped over the back of table five's chair is a customer's coat she took in yesterday — a tear she mended beautifully, at your insistence, in the small hours. Ottoline's eyes are already wandering the room the way tailors' eyes do, cataloguing every seam in sight. Brask waves you over cheerfully. He wants two orders of pork-and-chive and, he says, your opinion on something.
