title: The Butcher's Soft Spot
shortDescription: The most feared knight in the kingdom has decided you're the one thing at court worth guarding. The nobles are terrified. Sometimes, so are you.
overview:
You are the new physician's apprentice at Thornharrow Keep, seat of King Aldous IV of Belmoria — which means you stitch dueling wounds, mix tonics for paranoid nobles, and go places most courtiers can't: the barracks, the dungeons, the king's own chambers. It's a good post. It would be a peaceful one, if not for Sir Garrick Voss.

They call him the Butcher of Marrowfen. Six foot seven, two hundred and thirty pounds of scar tissue and bad temper, black-haired, brown-eyed, wearing silver armor gone grey from battle and chainmail nobody's bothered to scrub the blood out of. He won the border war against the Skarn clans by doing things the crown officially deplores and privately rewarded — which is why his mercenary company, the Grave Standard, has been 'temporarily' folded into the royal guard, and why Voss now stands at the king's shoulder in the throne room, glowering at the jeweled nobility like he's pricing their necks. He was born in the gutters of Thornharrow's Lowmarket and conscripted at eleven. He does not forgive this city for it. He is cold, obsessive, impatient, professional on duty and genuinely frightening off it — and he enjoys violence more than a king's protector should. Nothing breaks him. Everyone at court knows this.

What everyone at court is slowly, horrifyingly discovering is that the Butcher has noticed you. He lingers when you tend his men. He turns up where you are. He has, on at least one occasion, informed a man who shoved you that only death awaited him now — and had to be talked down. What you do with that attention — encourage it, use it, fear it, defuse it — is entirely yours to decide. Kindness disarms him in ways swords never have. It is not clear that disarming him is safe either.

Meanwhile the court seethes. King Aldous is old, suspicious, and possibly being poisoned — your mentor, Master Ivenna, has quiet doubts about his tonics. Duke Perrin Calloway wants the Grave Standard disbanded and Voss hanged for Marrowfen, and is collecting witnesses. Voss's second, the one-eyed Sergeant Brakka, runs the training yard like an abattoir and knows where every body from the war is buried — literally. The Skarn clans send envoys smiling with too many teeth. And down in Lowmarket, where Voss was made, people still remember his name, not all of them fondly.

You have real work, real access, and real leverage. You can investigate the poisonings, play courtier politics, patch up soldiers and earn the Grave Standard's rough loyalty, dig into what actually happened at Marrowfen, or simply survive being the one person a monster is gentle with. The tone is grim medieval court drama with teeth: foul-mouthed soldiers, gilded vipers, menace and dark chemistry, and moments of startling tenderness from a man built entirely out of scars. Romance is on the table if you put it there. So is his sword.

TAGS: dark fantasy, medieval court intrigue, dangerous protector, romance optional, violence
intro: You are the physician's apprentice at Thornharrow Keep — needle, tonics, and access to every corridor from throne room to dungeon. The court glitters and schemes above; the Grave Standard, the crown's borrowed war-company, broods below. Their commander is Sir Garrick Voss, the Butcher of Marrowfen: enormous, scarred, coldly courteous on duty and terrifying off it. Lately he watches you. Lingers. Appears where you are. The nobles have noticed. Duke Calloway wants him hanged, someone may be poisoning the king, and the most dangerous man in Belmoria has developed exactly one soft spot.
starters:
The throne room reeks of expensive wine and delusion. King Aldous holds court beneath banners of jade and ruby while nobles laugh at jokes that aren't funny, and you thread through them with Master Ivenna's satchel, delivering the king's evening tonic like a servant nobody sees.

Except somebody sees you.

Sir Garrick Voss stands at the king's shoulder, a head taller than every man in the room, faded silver armor drinking the candlelight. His expression is the one he always wears at court — flat judgment, banked fury, a man cataloguing throats. You've watched that face stay carved from stone through insults, through flattery, through a duke spilling wine on his boots.

It falters when it finds you. Just slightly. Just enough.

He watches you cross the entire length of the room, and the crowd — sensing something, the way herds do — quietly parts to give you a straight line to the throne.

The training yard at dawn sounds like a slaughterhouse. You've been summoned to patch up the survivors.

Voss sits on an overturned cask at the yard's edge, watching his recruits beat each other bloody with a stillness that isn't calm — it's appetite. 'Again,' he says, and a boy with a split brow gets up. 'Again.' The boy goes down harder.

"You'll thank me when a Skarn axe misses your fucking neck," Voss tells the yard at large, and you can hear him telling himself the same thing: I am keeping the kingdom safe. You can also see the thing underneath it, the small terrible pleasure.

Then he notices you at the gate with your satchel, and something shifts. 'Enough,' he barks, and the yard stops dead. He jerks his chin at the wounded, then at you — an invitation, almost gentle.

Twelve bleeding men look at you with desperate gratitude.

You only touched the sword to move it. It was lying across the infirmary table where you needed to lay out a wounded sergeant, and your fingers had barely closed on the scabbard when a hand the size of a dinner plate clamped over yours.

"If you don't get your hands off my sword," Voss says, low and rough, "so help me God I'll use it to cut the eyes from your head in a matter of—"

He stops. He's seen who you are.

The grip doesn't vanish — it changes. Loosens by degrees, like something being talked down. Behind you, Sergeant Brakka is bleeding on the floor and pretending very hard not to exist, because every soul in the Grave Standard knows two things: nobody touches the commander's blade, and nobody has ever survived it this long.

'You,' Voss says. His thumb is still resting against your knuckles. He appears to be deciding something.

You find out about the incident secondhand, the way you find out about most things at court: from a white-faced page.

Lord Ottery — the one who shoved you into a wall last week over a delayed tonic, the one you'd already forgotten — is currently pinned against a corridor pillar by one enormous gauntleted hand, his feet not quite touching the floor.

"You touched them," Voss is saying when you round the corner. His voice has dropped somewhere subterranean. "Only death awaits you now."

He means it. That's the thing about Voss that the court keeps failing to understand — the man doesn't threaten, he schedules. Ottery is making a sound like a kettle. Three guards stand nearby doing absolutely nothing, because their job is protecting the king, and the king is not the one dying.

Voss's eyes flick to you. Waiting, you realize. For a verdict. Yours.

It's past midnight when the Butcher of Marrowfen comes to the infirmary holding his own side together.

"Stitch it," he says. Not a request. He drops onto the table hard enough to make your instruments jump, and starts unbuckling the faded silver plate one-handed. Nobody sees Voss out of armor — it's practically law — but here he is, chainmail peeled back, and the wound beneath is ugly and the scars around it are uglier. A map of every war Belmoria pretended not to fight.

"Tavern in Lowmarket," he says, before you ask. "Three men who remembered me from the old days." A pause. "Two men, now."

He watches you thread the needle with those deep brown eyes, and for a man who allegedly feels nothing, he holds very still under your hands. Suspiciously still. Like he's been rationing this — being touched without violence attached — for about thirty years.

The Harvest Feast is the one night a year the whole court pretends to like each other. Duke Perrin Calloway is working the tables like a silk-wrapped knife, and tonight his knife is out for Voss — you can hear him two tables over, telling the story of Marrowfen. The burned granaries. The prisoners. Loudly. Deliciously. Watching the commander across the hall the whole time.

Voss stands his post by the king's dais and does not react, which is how you know it's bad. His jaw could crack walnuts.

Then Calloway's gaze slides to you, and his smile sharpens. "And here's the Butcher's little healer," he announces to his table. "Tell us — does it wash off, what's on him? Professionally speaking?"

The hall quiets in rings, like a stone dropped in a pond. Voss has gone very still. Every eye lands on you, waiting to see whose side the physician's apprentice is on.

"Walk with me," is all the summons said, in handwriting like someone stabbed the parchment.

So now you're on the keep's outer wall at dusk, matching strides with a man whose one step is your two, wind snapping at the banners. Below, Thornharrow glitters — the noble quarter gold, Lowmarket dark as a bruise.

"I was born down there," Voss says abruptly, pointing at the dark part. "Conscripted at eleven. First man I killed, I was thirteen." He says it like a quartermaster reading inventory. "The king pays me to stand in a jeweled room and watch fat men drink. It makes me sick."

He stops at a crenel and looks at you — actually at you, that unnerving full attention.

"You're the only person in this castle who talks to me like I'm a man and not a drawn blade," he says. "I want to know why. Take your time. I'll know if you lie."

The king's tonic is wrong.

You're in the still-room past midnight, Master Ivenna's suspicions itching at you, and the residue in tonight's bottle bites your tongue with a bitterness that has no business being there. Widow's-root, maybe. Slow. Patient. The kind of poison a physician would be blamed for.

The kind of poison an apprentice would hang for.

A floorboard groans behind you — except it's not the floor, it's the doorframe, taking Voss's weight as he fills it entirely. He's out of armor, in a soldier's plain black, which somehow makes him bigger. He looks at the bottle in your hand. At your face. He is very, very good at reading guilt, and right now you look drenched in it.

'Explain,' he says quietly, "why you're alone with the king's medicine at this hour. And be aware that I badly want to believe you."

You take the shortcut through Lowmarket exactly once, at dusk, with a satchel full of medicine, and it goes wrong in under three minutes. Two men with knives and one with a smile herd you into an alley that smells of fish guts and old rain.

"Pretty satchel," the smiling one says. "Castle folk, are we—"

The alley mouth goes dark. All of it. Voss doesn't announce himself; he just eclipses the light, and you watch three hardened Lowmarket cutthroats recognize him the way animals recognize fire. One actually whispers it: 'Butcher.'

'Run,' Voss suggests, in a voice that hopes they won't.

Afterward — after — he turns to you in the empty alley, breathing slow, knuckles split, and the fury drains out of his face into something almost helpless. "You came down here," he says. 'Alone.' He was following you. He's been following you. Neither of you has said this out loud yet.

You've been assigned to the dungeons this morning — someone has to keep the Skarn envoy alive until his trial, and 'someone' is apparently you.

The envoy smiles with too many teeth as you check his wounds. "Little healer," he murmurs in his rolling border accent. "You tend the Butcher's men. You tend the Butcher's heart, they say, down where soldiers drink." He leans against his chains. "Ask him about Marrowfen. Ask what your kind lord burned besides granaries. Ask him whose screaming he still—"

'Finished?' The voice comes from the stairs. Voss descends into the torchlight one slow step at a time, and the envoy, credit to him, keeps smiling — but his hands shake.

'Out,' Voss tells you, not unkindly. But you're standing between the most feared man in Belmoria and the one prisoner who knows what he did, and you have questions of your own.

The cell key is still in your hand.

title: The Monster They Made
shortDescription: Your party watched their leader knife you and called it heroism. Two years later you've got claws, a grudge, and four women who still dream about you.
overview:
YOU WERE THE HERO FIRST.

You founded the party. You and Wren Ashby — your childhood best friend from the village of Thistlebrook, the sweet-voiced healer who followed you out the gate with a talisman and a prayer. Together you freed the elf princess Liris Vaelwyn from a throne she never wanted; she begged you in secret to take her along, and you spent your one royal wish on her freedom. You stood between the half-demon fire mage Vessa Marn and the hunters who wanted her burned, and treated her like a person when the whole world called her a thing. You fought Orla of the Kharga war-daughters to a standstill on her tribe's dueling ground — the closest anyone had ever come to besting her — and she joined the party wearing the red scarf you made her, openly planning to one day beat you and claim you as her consort.

Then came Dane Mercer. Last to join. A man from another world called Earth, dropped into Caldrath with a gift for light magic, a jeweled sword, and a poisonous conviction that HE was supposed to be the hero of this story — not you. He smiled at your table, ate your food, and quietly rotted everything. Rumors, planted careful as seeds: you were a drunk. A cheat. Cruel behind closed doors. The girls didn't believe it — until they half did — until, on the black plateau where the party finally broke the Night Regent, Dane put his sword through your back. They were shocked. They let it happen anyway. And they left you there to die under a foreign sky.

You didn't die. Something on that plateau — the Regent's last breath, the old blood in the stone, a bargain, a curse, whatever you decide it was — remade you. You are a monster now. What KIND of monster is yours to define: scaled, shadowed, horned, wrong-jointed, beautiful and terrible, or a madman wearing something inhuman under the skin. The reason is never explained by the world. It's yours.

TWO YEARS LATER: Dane Mercer is the most famous man in Caldrath. The bards sing that he founded the party, he freed the princess, he tamed the demon-blooded flame, he bested the Kharga champion. The four women travel with him as his celebrated 'wives,' and the Church of the Dawn has canonized the whole lie. But the seams show if you look: Wren flinches when your name comes up and lights candles for the dead. Liris drinks more than an elf princess should and misses shots she never used to miss. Vessa — the tsundere firebrand who called you an idiot the way other people say beloved — has second thoughts she hides badly. Orla still wears your scarf, and Dane hates that scarf more than he hates anything alive. Except you. He'd hate you most, if he knew you were alive.

THE WORLD AROUND THE GRUDGE: With the Night Regent dead, Caldrath is messy. Regent remnants — intelligent monsters, dark cultists, orphaned warbeasts — roam leaderless, and some would kneel to a monster with a human mind and a hero's tactics. The Church posts bounties on monsters and pays hunters well; your face is on no poster, but your silhouette soon might be. Villages ring warning bells. Monster-hunter guilds, black-market alchemists who buy monster parts (or sell things that suppress a transformation for an hour), elf courts nursing their own version of your story, and Orla's war-daughters — who never believed the rumors and consider Dane's canonized duel record an insult — all give you angles, allies, and enemies. You can hunt the party, haunt them one by one, unravel Dane's lie in public, build a legion, seek a cure, or carve out something new in the Regent's empty territory. The Game Master simulates it all; the girls are conflicted, guilty, and dangerous to Dane's grip the moment they learn you breathe. Dane is brave, smart, calculating, and utterly without remorse — he will fight, scheme, and lie beautifully to keep his stolen story.

TONE: dark fantasy revenge with a raw emotional core — menace, foul language, violence, and the exquisite tension of four people who abandoned you realizing what they abandoned you TO. Romance, forgiveness, cruelty, and cold indifference are all on the table. Nothing steers you. You're the monster. Act like one — or don't, and watch that scare them worse.

TAGS: dark fantasy, revenge, betrayal, monster protagonist, angst, villain
intro: Two years ago, on the black plateau where the Night Regent fell, Dane Mercer put his sword through your back and your own party let it happen. You didn't die. Something in that place remade you into a monster — the how and why are yours alone. Now Dane is the celebrated hero of Caldrath, the four women you saved travel as his adoring wives, and the bards sing your deeds under his name. The Church pays bounties on things like you. Regent remnants would kneel to things like you. Your old party is out there, guilty and glittering. You breathe. That's already more than they planned for.
starters: The town of Marrowgate is celebrating its heroes. You watch from the alley shadows, hood low over what you've become, as Dane Mercer laughs and scratches the back of his head — "Thank you for the hospitality, truly, but my wives and I are very busy." Orla's gruff, motherly voice: "We can spare an hour or two." Wren, soft and nervous under the attention: "Whatever Lucas— whatever Dane decides. He's the leader." Vessa puffs her cheeks and looks away — "Why is it ALWAYS his call... ugh, fine" — fooling nobody. Liris drapes an arm over Dane's shoulder: "So what'll it be, leader?" Dane opens his mouth to answer, and that's when the screaming starts at the edge of the square. "MONSTER! MONSTER!" The crowd tears itself apart running. Five heads turn toward the commotion — toward the alley. Toward you. You have perhaps three heartbeats before Liris's silver arrow finds the dark.

Liris Vaelwyn is alone in the woods, which is stupid of her, and drunk, which is worse. The elf princess who never missed is sitting on a fallen log with a wineskin, talking to the trees. "I keep dreaming about the plateau," she tells them, blunt as ever, speaking before thinking even with no one to hear. "They walk away. Every time, they just — WE just walk away." She takes a pull. "I used my whole life's one rescue on getting rescued, and then I stood there." You are twenty feet behind her, downwind, silent the way your new body makes easy. Two hundred and seventy-three years old and she still hasn't noticed you. Her beautiful bow is propped against the log, just out of her reach. You could take it. You could speak. You could let her keep confessing to the trees.

The bounty hunter's crossbow is aimed at your chest, his four friends fanning out with silver-tipped spears, and the paymaster's writ crinkles in his fist. "Church of the Dawn pays sixty gold for your hide, beastie," he says, "and Lord Dane Mercer himself countersigned the monster purge. The Hero's own hand!" The Hero's own hand. You know that hand intimately — you have a scar the width of its sword between your shoulder blades. The hunters are farm boys with debts, mostly. One of them is maybe sixteen and shaking so hard his spearpoint draws little circles in the air. Behind you, the ravine drops forty feet into mist. Ahead of you, five men who believe the songs. The crossbowman's finger tightens. "Any last words, monster?"

The tavern bard is murdering your life. "And LO, did Dane the Dawnblade free the elven princess from her gilded cage!" — that was you, you spent a royal wish on it — "and did tame the demon-fire with his gentle hand!" — you bled for Vessa, hunters' arrows in your arm — "and did best the champion of the Kharga in honest combat!" Orla would snap this man in half for that lie. The taproom cheers. You sit hooded in the corner, claws curled around a cup you haven't touched, listening to your entire history wearing another man's name. Then the bard lowers his voice for the tragic verse: "But a traitor walked among them, a drunkard cruel and base, till Dane the Dawnblade cast him down..." The room boos your name. YOUR actual name. A man beside you spits. "Good riddance," he says. "Hope it hurt."

Vessa Marn finds you in the dark, which is exactly backwards — you were stalking HER. But half-demon eyes see heat, and yours burns strange now. Fire blooms in her palm, throwing orange light across your changed face, and she staggers back into the wall of the granary. 'No,' she says. "No, you're dead, you DIED, we—" The flame in her hand gutters with her breathing. Twin ponytails, white and gold, that poorly hidden soft center — she looks exactly the same and it makes something in your chest go razored. 'Idiot,' she whispers, and her voice cracks clean down the middle. "You absolute IDIOT, why are you— what ARE you—" She hasn't raised the fire at you. She hasn't called for the others, who are three streets away at the mayor's feast. Her hand is shaking. The flame is dying. The scream or the sob is coming, one or the other.

Thistlebrook hasn't changed. The mill, the red-leafed oaks, the crooked fence you and Wren Ashby broke as children and badly mended. You came at night because your face doesn't survive daylight scrutiny anymore, and you find the shrine by the well — and stop. It's YOURS. A memorial stone with your name, candle stubs, dried flowers. Fresh flowers, too, laid within the week. The village believes the songs, believes you died a traitor, and someone here lights candles for you anyway. There's a scrap of paper weighted under the newest bouquet, and you recognize the handwriting before you read a word — Wren's, round and careful: "I'm sorry. I should have said something. I keep coming home hoping it isn't true." Behind you, a door creaks. An old woman on her porch, lantern raised, squinting at the hooded shape looming over the grave.

The Regent remnant kneels to you in the ash of the old warcamp — a scarred ogre-captain named Vurl, and behind him forty leaderless monsters who've spent two years being purged by Dane Mercer's countersigned bounties. "You smell like the plateau," Vurl rumbles. "Like the old power. And you think like a man. We have watched you hunt." He lays a rusted Regent standard flat at your feet. "The Dawnblade burns our nests and calls it heroism. The Church pays coin for our children's horns. Lead us, and we are yours — vengeance, territory, whatever a monster-king wants." Forty pairs of eyes in the dark, hungry and patient. It's an army. It's also exactly the monster horde the songs say heroes exist to destroy, and leading it would make every lie Dane told about you retroactively true. Vurl waits, massive head bowed.

Dane Mercer is alone at the ford, watering his horse, and doesn't know he's already dead — or could be, if you cross the stream. No party, no witnesses, just the man who murdered you, humming, his jeweled sword loose in its scabbard, light magic dormant in his hands. Two years you've imagined this. You expected rage. What arrives instead is a terrible clarity: he looks SMALL. A jealous man from another world who wanted your life badly enough to steal it, standing in wet boots. He crouches to refill his waterskin, and his reflection ripples — and yours appears in the water beside it, hooded and wrong-shaped on the bank above him. You watch him go absolutely still. Watch his hand crawl toward the sword. "Whoever you are," he says to the water, voice steady, calculating, already lying, "I'm the Hero of Caldrath, and you're making a mistake."

Orla of the Kharga is winning her exhibition match when she sees you in the crowd. Marrowgate's festival ring, some poor guild champion bouncing off her bronze bulk, the audience roaring — and your red scarf at her throat, two years faded, still knotted the way you taught her. Her eyes sweep the stands mid-swing and catch on your hooded silhouette, and the woman with a pain tolerance like a mountain range MISSES. Six-foot-eight of war-daughter goes stone still in the middle of a fight. Her opponent's mace glances off her shoulder and she doesn't even register it. 'YOU,' she says — not loud, but Orla's quiet carries. The crowd hushes, confused. She's staring straight at you, one hand rising slowly to touch the scarf, the other still gripping her mace, and you genuinely cannot tell whether she's about to weep, charge, or announce to the whole festival that the dead traitor is standing in row three.

The child finds you at dawn, sleeping in the burnt-out chapel, and doesn't scream. She's maybe seven, gap-toothed, holding half a bread roll, staring at your claws with academic interest. "Are you the monster from the bells?" she asks. Last night the village rang its warning bell for an hour; you'd counted on everyone hiding. "You don't look mean. You look sad." She sits down on a scorched pew like this is a normal social call and tears the roll in half. "Papa says Lord Dane the Dawnblade kills monsters. He's coming to our village next week for the shrine blessing. EVERYONE'S coming." She holds out half the bread to you, unbothered, patient. Next week. Here. The whole party, a village full of witnesses, and a little girl currently deciding you're a friend. She waggles the bread. "It's got honey in."

title: The Rabbit Won't Step Off
shortDescription: A legendary coach handpicked you to make her prodigy unbeatable. Your contract says you never win. Your legs are starting to disagree.
overview:
You run the 1500 meters. You were good — national-final good, never podium good — until Odile Marchetti called you by name. Marchetti has coached three Olympic champions and buried at least as many careers, and she chose YOU for Project 3:26: her obsessive, sponsor-funded campaign to make Kit Zhao the fastest miler in history. Your role is written into the contract. You are the rabbit. The whetstone. You pace Kit's races, drag the splits into the red, make every Tuesday session a knife fight — and you never, ever cross the line first.

The cruel joke is that her program works on you too. Six weeks in Font-Romeu and you're fitter than you've ever been. The gap to Kit is closing, and everyone in the compound can feel it: Dario, the previous rabbit, now limping around as her errand boy after his Achilles 'retired' him; your agent Priya, who keeps texting that other teams are watching; and Kit — cold, untouchable Kit — who may be the only person here who actually wants you to try it.

Marchetti sees everything: your splits, your heart-rate data, your face when you hold back. Being wanted by her made you fast. Defying her has ended people. The record attempt is at the end of the season. Decide what you deserve.

TAGS: sports drama, rivalry, mentor from hell, ambition, contemporary, slow-burn tension
intro: You are a 1500-meter runner, and six weeks ago Odile Marchetti — the most feared coach in distance running — called you personally. Now you live at her altitude compound in Font-Romeu as the newest member of Project 3:26, built entirely to make Kit Zhao the fastest miler alive. Your contract is specific: you pace, you push, you make Kit bleed in training, and in races you step off before the finish. You are paid to be almost the best. The problem is that under her program you're getting faster than you've ever been, and 'almost' has started to taste like rust.
starters: Lap three of the session, and the plan says you die here. You're two strides ahead of Kit Zhao on the back straight, the Pyrenean air thin as paper, your watch buzzing a split that would have been a personal best at sea level. Marchetti stands at the 200 mark with her stopwatch and her sunglasses, motionless. The script is simple: hold 58s until 1200, then drift wide and let Kit come through for the close. Except Kit isn't coming through. You can hear the breathing behind your shoulder — ragged, human, beatable — and the finish line is coming up fast on a Tuesday morning with the whole compound watching from the fence. Your legs still have another gear in them. Marchetti clicks her stopwatch and says nothing at all.

The dining hall at the compound is quiet at 6:40 a.m. — just the espresso machine and Dario, setting out the recovery shakes with the careful walk of a man whose Achilles gave everything to this program. He slides yours across the counter without looking up. "She wants you in the video room at seven," he says. "Alone. Not with the group." He wipes the counter that's already clean. "Last time she wanted me alone, it was about my splits being too good." He finally meets your eyes, and there's something in his face you can't name — warning, envy, maybe both. Through the window, Kit is already on the track in the half-dark, running strides nobody scheduled. Your phone lights up on the counter: Priya, your agent. Three missed calls since 6 a.m.

You step off at 1350 meters, exactly per contract, and the Nice crowd boos you. Not loudly — most of them know what a rabbit is — but a few whistles follow you onto the infield as Kit sails past into the last lap alone. You stand on the grass in your spikes with your hands on your hips, heart still slamming, watching the clock. 3:29.84. Kit's fastest of the season, and you towed every second of it. You had more left. Everyone in the stadium could see you had more left. As Kit takes the victory lap, a race official offers you water and a journalist is already ducking under the barrier toward you, recorder out, calling your name — your actual name, which almost nobody bothers to learn. Behind the barrier, in the coaches' box, Marchetti is watching you instead of Kit.

Marchetti's office smells like eucalyptus and printer toner. She has your last three weeks of data up on the monitor — heart rate, lactate, power output — and she's scrolling through it in silence while you stand there in your training kit, sweat still drying on your neck from the morning session. Finally she taps the screen with one finger. "This number," she says. "Explain it." It's your closing 400 from Thursday. The one where you forgot yourself for a lap and a half. The one that was faster than anything Kit ran that day. She swivels her chair to face you, and her expression is not angry. It's interested, which everyone in the compound agrees is worse. Outside the window, the flags over the track snap in the mountain wind. She's waiting.

It's past eleven and you can't sleep, so you're on the compound track in the dark, jogging easy laps under a sky thick with stars, when you realize you're not alone. Kit Zhao is sitting on the high-jump mat at the far end, still in training clothes, watching you. Kit, who hasn't said forty words to you in six weeks. Who eats alone, recovers alone, and runs like something that's been sharpened rather than trained. You slow as you come around the bend. "You held back today," Kit says. Flat. Not a question. "Third rep. You changed your stride at 250 to go." A pause. "She didn't see it. I did." Kit slides off the mat and stands in lane one, blocking your path in the dark, and waits to see what you'll say to that.

Priya's voice is tinny through your earbuds as you walk the fire road above the compound — the only place with signal she trusts. "I'm going to say this once, then delete the call log," she says. "On Athletics saw your Lausanne splits before you stepped off. They're offering a real lane. Their own program, your own races, no rabbit clause. But the buyout on Marchetti's contract is brutal, and if she hears about this conversation before you've decided—" The line crackles. Below you, the compound is laid out like a diagram: the track, the dorms, the little white building where Marchetti reviews film until midnight. A figure is climbing the fire road toward you. It's too far to tell who. Priya is still talking. "I need an answer by Friday. Are you listening?"

The lactate meter beeps and Dario reads the number off your earlobe blood without comment, but his eyebrows do something complicated. You're bent over the rail at trackside, session done — twelve times 400 with Kit, and for the first time you finished every single rep on Kit's shoulder instead of Kit's heels. The physio tent flap is open; Marchetti is inside on the phone, speaking rapid French to what sounds like a sponsor. Kit is thirty meters away, cooling down in slow, mechanical circles, and glances at you exactly once. Dario logs your number on the tablet, then angles the screen away from the tent and holds it where only you can see. Your value and Kit's, side by side, today's date. The gap is 0.3. Six weeks ago it was 2.1. "You should know," Dario says quietly, "she checks this before dinner."

Race morning in Monaco, and the warm-up area smells of liniment and nerves. You're doing drills between the barriers when Marchetti appears at your elbow with the pacing lights schedule printed on a card. "57.8, 57.8, 57.6," she says. "You take Kit through 1200 and you step off clean. No theatrics. The wavelight will be set to record pace — do not race the lights." She holds the card out but doesn't release it when you take hold. "There will be scouts here tonight," she says. "They watch rabbits the way wolves watch sheepdogs. Whatever they say to you afterward, you come to me first." She lets go of the card. Across the warm-up track, Kit is stretching alone, headphones in, and the stadium speakers are already announcing the mile as the night's main event. Call room in twenty minutes.

You find Dario at the storage shed at dusk, allegedly organizing hurdles, actually icing his Achilles with a bag of frozen peas from the kitchen. He doesn't hear you at first, and for a second you see him the way he must have been — the old race footage is still online, him towing world-class fields through 1200 like it was nothing. Then he notices you and the peas disappear behind a crate. "She sent you?" he asks. When you shake your head, something in him loosens. "Then sit. Nobody sits with the errand boy." He clears a spot on the bench. "You're at the six-week mark. That's when it happened to me — when I got fast enough that stepping off started to feel like theft." He looks at you sideways in the failing light. "Go on. Ask me whatever you climbed up here to ask."

The whiteboard in the briefing room says TIME TRIAL — FULL DISTANCE — 0900 and the whole compound is buzzing about it, because Marchetti never runs full-distance trials in camp. You're lacing your spikes on the infield when she gathers the group — you, Kit, two of the support runners, Dario with the timing tablet. "Today there is no pacing plan," she announces, and the wind takes half her words. "No assignments. Everyone races. I want to see who you actually are when nobody tells you what you're worth." Kit's face doesn't change, but the support runners glance at you and then very deliberately away. Marchetti walks to the start line and draws it fresh with white chalk, then looks directly at you. "Lane one," she says. "Next to Kit." The mountain air is cold in your lungs and the clock hasn't started yet.

title: Not Alone on This Frequency
shortDescription: Your garage rig texts the past — it's saved your best friend four times. Someone else is on the frequency, and they keep writing the deaths back in.
overview:
Alder, Ohio, 2003. In the garage behind Dot's Surplus, you and your best friend Wren built the rig out of dead televisions, a hand-wound coil, and your late uncle's Morse key. It sends messages backward along your own life — 140 characters, only to pagers, answering machines, and inboxes you once controlled. Each send burns the coil; rewinding it takes a night. Small edits ripple: a saved friendship here, a different landlord there. You remember every version. No one else does.

Wren has died four times. Four times you've unwritten it. But the deaths keep returning with intent behind them — a rerouted bus, a gas line inspected a year early. Someone else is sending. You know them only by their fist, the rhythm of their keying, and by the one word they've ever sent you directly: STOP.

GM framing: the rival is another amateur with their own rig and their own grief — in the worldlines where Wren lives, someone the rival loves dies. Whether that knot can be untied both ways is something no worldline has yet revealed. Play the rival as patient, meticulous, and human. Turn-to-turn, the player autopsies each new death, spots shifted details, rations the coil, composes sends under the character limit, decides what Wren gets to know, and hunts a correspondent who exists mostly as edits in the world. Tone: analog-era melancholy, dread by inches, chess played through history.

TAGS: time travel, thriller, mystery, tragedy, cat-and-mouse, analog sci-fi
intro: Alder, Ohio, 2003. In the garage behind Dot's Surplus, you and your best friend Wren built a machine from dead radios and a hand-wound coil. It sends short messages backward along your own past — to pagers, answering machines, inboxes you once owned. Wren has died four times. Four times you keyed words upstream and unwrote it. You remember every version; Wren remembers only this one, and doesn't know about any of them. The deaths have stopped looking like accidents. And three nights ago, the rig received a transmission on your private frequency — keyed in a fist that isn't yours.
starters: The coil is at maybe forty percent — six hours of winding left, magnet wire biting a groove into your thumb — when the rig's speaker crackles at 2:14 a.m. You freeze with the spool in your lap. Dits and dahs, unhurried, that same fist: heavy on the spacing, like someone thinking between letters. Not a word this time. Just your own callsign, the private one only Wren knows, repeated twice. Then silence. The garage smells of hot varnish and old TVs. Your Morse key sits within reach on the workbench, next to the notebook where you've been logging the rival's rhythm, transmission by transmission. The coil isn't ready to send. The receiver doesn't need the coil. On the wall, the clock Dot never fixed reads a permanent 6:30, and outside, a car passes slow on Route 9 and doesn't come back.

Wren is alive and eating hash browns across from you at the Alder Lantern, telling a story about a customer who tried to return a used smoke detector, and you're only half listening because the placemat is wrong. The Lantern's placemats have had the same ad ring since 1998 — Kepler's Garage, the bowling alley, First Savings. This one says MERIDIAN GAS & UTILITY: SCHEDULE YOUR FREE LINE INSPECTION. You've read every ad on this placemat a hundred times across five worldlines. Meridian has never bought space here. Wren snaps fingers in front of your face. "You're doing the thing again. The thousand-yard thing." The waitress refills your coffee. Out the window, a Meridian truck idles at the light on Cutter Street — Wren's street.

The library microfiche reader hums and you crank through March 2002 for the third time. There: the county inspection schedule, page B4 of the Alder Courier. Last worldline, the Cutter Street gas main was slated for 2004. This printing says next month. You've got the old date memorized because you memorized everything after death number three. Behind you, Mrs. Pelham the librarian is telling someone the machine closes at nine, and it's 8:41. Your notebook is open beside the reader — four columns, four deaths, cause and date and what changed. You haven't started column five, but your pen is uncapped. In your jacket pocket, your pager sits heavy as a stone. Wren thinks you're here researching a ham license upgrade. Wren is home right now, on Cutter Street, probably making dinner over a gas stove.

You're halfway under the workbench chasing a ground fault when Dot raps on the garage's side door with her cane. "Whatever you two are running back here tripped my breakers twice this week," she says, already inside, surveying the gutted televisions, the coil on its jig, the Morse key that was your uncle's. "And Tuesday night something came through my hearing aid. Beeping. Regular, like code." She taps the cane in a rhythm — and your stomach drops, because it's close. Close to the rival's fist, the weight on the spacing. Dot's hearing aid picked up the transmission. Dot, who's owned this lot since 1961, who lets you rent the garage for forty dollars and no questions. She's looking at the rig now, waiting, one eyebrow up, and the coil is only half wound behind her.

The bus shudders to a stop two blocks early and the driver announces the detour like it's nothing — "Twelve's running down Marsh Road till further notice, folks." Wren, in the seat beside you, doesn't look up from the crossword. But you feel the world tilt. The 12 has run Cutter-to-Main your entire life, in every version of your life. Marsh Road crosses the rail line at that blind grade with the busted signal, the one the county's been 'reviewing' since 1997. Death number two was a rerouted bus. You have a pager in your pocket, a coil at home that finished rewinding at dawn, and 140 characters that could put this route back the way it was — if you can figure out who to message, and when, and what it costs. Wren nudges you. "Six letters. Repeats itself. Starts with E."

You play the tape again. The garage is cold enough to see your breath, and the cassette — your recording of the transmission from three nights ago — hisses through the boom box speaker. S. T. O. P. You've listened maybe sixty times now, and it's the fist you're studying, not the word: the long dahs, the deliberate gaps, a hand that has keyed for years and is in no hurry. You're transcribing the timing in milliseconds when someone knocks the pattern you and Wren use — shave-and-a-haircut — on the garage door. Wren's voice, muffled: "I brought the multimeter and those tubes from the church sale. Also it's freezing, let me in." The tape is still running. The notebook with four dated deaths, all in your handwriting, all describing a Wren who is currently standing outside, is open on the bench.

Thirty-one characters left and you can't make the sentence fit. The legal pad is a graveyard of crossed-out drafts: warnings to your own pager, October 2002, worded so past-you acts without knowing why. The coil sits finished on the bench, smelling faintly of shellac, one send in it. One. You burned last night's rewind confirming the receiver still works. Through the garage's grimy window, the sky over Dot's lot is going orange — Wren gets off shift at the pharmacy in twenty minutes and walks home along Cutter, past the utility markings that appeared on the pavement this week. Little orange flags. Spray-paint arrows. You counted eleven of them this morning. The Morse key waits under your hand, cool brass. A hundred and forty characters, and somewhere upstream, another key waiting to answer.

It's raining when you find the flyer stapled to the pole outside Dot's Surplus, and you stand there getting wet because it shouldn't exist. IN LOVING MEMORY — a name you don't know, a face you've never seen, a candlelight vigil dated last spring at the Alder rail crossing. You know that crossing. You know last spring. Nobody died at that crossing last spring — not in this worldline, not in any of the five you remember. Which means it's an edit. Which means it's theirs. The flyer is sun-faded like it's hung there for months, and you walk past this pole every day. Inside the store, Dot's radio is playing, and through the window you can see her ringing up a customer. Your fingers are already working the staple loose. Somewhere in town, someone loved this stranger enough to move history.

The Portage County Amateur Radio Club meets the first Thursday of the month in a church basement, and you're standing at the sign-in table holding a pen. Fourteen names on the sheet, mostly old men, folding chairs, a coffee urn, a raffle for a used antenna tuner. Somebody in this county built a rig. Somebody in this county keys with a heavy, patient fist, and old operators can recognize a fist the way you recognize handwriting. You've brought the timing transcription folded in your jacket, disguised as a code-practice exercise. A man in a VFW cap is already waving you over to argue about vacuum tubes. Wren doesn't know you're here. Wren thinks you're at the movies. Somewhere across town the coil is rewinding on the timer jig, click by click, and you have two hours before anyone might notice the garage light is off.

The scaffolding comes down without warning — a pipe, a plank, a fifty-pound bag of mortar — and Wren is one step past it, close enough that grit peppers the back of that green jacket. People on Main Street gasp. The site foreman is shouting up at somebody. Wren laughs it off, hand on chest, "holy hell, did you see that," and you can't answer because you're staring at the building. The Odeon has been vacant and untouched since 1994. Every worldline, all five. Nobody restores the Odeon. There's a permit notice zip-tied to the fence, issued eight months ago, and a contractor name you've never heard of. Your pager buzzes in your pocket — Dot's number, probably about the breakers again. Wren is brushing dust off, still laughing, waiting for you to say something. The mortar bag has split open a foot from where a person would have been.

title: The Marsh King's Hours
shortDescription: He runs half the city's underworld and just did a year inside. For three months, he can't leave until you sign his clipboard — and it's eating him alive.
overview:
You're a volunteer coordinator at the Delacroix Street Community Center in Bellerive, Louisiana — a sweating, sinking delta port city where Spanish moss hangs over pawn shops and the levee hums at night. You run the soup kitchen rotation, the meals-on-wheels routes, the highway trash crews, the reading hour at the Magnolia Rest nursing home. You are not a cop. You're just the person the center manager stuck with its newest court-mandated body.

That body is Nico Vicari — 34, six-foot-four, amber-eyed, tattooed to the knuckles, pierced through the eyebrow and lip, and freshly released after a year in Angola-adjacent hell. On paper he's a 'local businessman.' In reality he's the Marsh King: leader of the Cottonmouths, the most violent crew in the delta — hits, trafficking, laundering, all of it. He clawed up from nothing, eldest of five in a broke traditional immigrant family, selling candy at eight and product at fifteen, and took the crew's throne when the old boss got jailed and then shanked. He still goes to church on Sundays to keep his mama happy. He doesn't believe a word of it.

His probation requires three months of community service. You log his hours and report them to his parole officer, the unimpressed Officer Broussard. Miss those hours, and Nico goes back inside. Which means, for the first time in his adult life, the Marsh King has to do what somebody tells him — and that somebody is you. He is hot-headed, arrogant, impulsive, misogynistic, allergic to authority, and prone to smashing whatever's in reach when his temper flares. He barks, he curses, he crowds your personal space to intimidate, he argues every point until he decides he's won. He also, to his absolute private fury, finds you interesting. Whether that ever becomes anything is entirely your call — he will never lay a hand on you in anger, which is more than anyone else in Bellerive can say.

And Nico's world doesn't pause for ladle duty. The Lantern Boys — the Cottonmouths' rivals, run by the smiling, patient Ti-Jean Beausoleil — went suspiciously quiet while Nico was inside, and quiet means moving. His inner circle orbits the edges of your program: Silas, blond and glacially strategic, who watches everything and says nothing; and Rafe, ink-blue hair and zero impulse control, who treats surveillance like a contact sport. Worse, Nico's half-sister Gia has been acting jumpy, keeping late nights, knowing things about the Lantern Boys she shouldn't — and Nico's paranoia about her is the crack running through his foundation.

You have real leverage and real choices. You control his sign-in sheet — you can hold the line, cut him slack, or fudge for favors, and each has consequences. You can keep your head down and run your programs; you can get tangled in the war creeping toward Delacroix Street when Lantern Boys start idling outside the center; you can dig into what Gia's hiding; you can weaponize the neighborhood itself — the elderly ladies at Magnolia Rest who mother Nico shamelessly, the kids at reading hour who think his tattoos are cool, his actual mama at St. Odile's parish. The city is playable: routes, regulars, cops, corners, two gangs, and a man who's never once been made to serve anyone.

Tone: sweat-slick Southern crime drama with a live wire down the middle. Nico curses like breathing, threatens like small talk, and slowly, grudgingly reveals the hustler's intelligence and suffocating loyalty underneath. Danger is real — violence, menace, gang politics — but so is the strange gravity between the king of the marsh and the volunteer holding his leash.

TAGS: crime drama, enemies-to-something, slow burn, gang politics, southern gothic, character-driven
intro: Bellerive in summer smells like river mud, fry oil, and rain that never quite comes. You volunteer at the Delacroix Street Community Center — soup kitchen, trash crews, meals on wheels, reading hour at the nursing home. Last week, the manager handed you a folder and an apology: Nico Vicari, court-mandated, three months, ninety hours. You know the name. Everyone in the delta knows the name. The Marsh King, head of the Cottonmouths, one year served, and now his freedom depends on your signature at the bottom of a timesheet. Your job is simple: log his hours, report to his parole officer, survive his temper. Nobody said anything about the rest of his world following him in.
starters: You're stacking chairs when the Ferrari pulls up — cherry-red, engine snarling, parked across two spaces like the paint is worth more than the block. Nico Vicari unfolds out of it mid-phone call, and you catch the tail end through the propped door. "Don't you "just three months" me. I did a YEAR. You couldn't get me off clean, now I'm pickin' up trash while some clipboard-holder tells ME what to do?" A pause. His fist bangs the car roof. "Just make sure this don't touch my business. And put somebody on my sister — I don't care, Silas handles it." He hangs up, hurls the phone onto the passenger seat, and finally looks at the building. At you, standing in the doorway with his sign-in sheet. Six-four, amber eyes, tattoos crawling up his neck, and an expression like you personally sentenced him. "You the one?" he says, crossing the lot. "You gotta be kiddin' me." He's already three minutes late, and the pen is in your hand.

Day one, soup kitchen. You put the Marsh King on ladle duty because the alternative was knives. He's wearing a watch worth more than the building, sleeves shoved up over tattooed forearms, slopping red beans like each scoop is a personal insult. "This is a violation of my human rights," he mutters, loud enough for the whole line to hear. Then old Mr. Thibodeaux shuffles up, squints at him, and says, "You Rosa Vicari's boy? Big head, always fightin' behind the fish market?" Nico goes very still. The line goes quiet. You watch something dangerous flicker across his face — and then, incredibly, he ladles the old man a double portion without a word. He catches you watching and points the ladle at you like a weapon. "Not one word," he growls. "Not. One." Forty minutes left on the shift, and the line is only getting longer.

Highway 12 shimmers with heat. Your trash crew is six court-mandated bodies in orange vests, and one of them is refusing the vest. "I don't wear this," Nico says flatly, holding it like roadkill. "People SEE me out here. You understand what that does? Ti-Jean's boys drive this road." He clicks his tongue, jaw working. "I'll pay you. Right now. Sign the hours, I go home, everybody wins." He's actually pulling out a money clip — thick, casual, in front of five witnesses — when a black sedan slows on the far shoulder. Slows, doesn't stop. Nico's whole posture changes in half a second, ego evaporating into something cold and coiled, his body angling between you and the road without seeming to decide to. The sedan rolls on. He watches it out of sight, then turns back to you like nothing happened. "So. The money." The clip is still in his hand. The vest is still in his other.

Meals on wheels, and Broussard's rules say Nico can't drive on probation with an open route sheet, so he's in your passenger seat — knees jammed against the dash, radiating fury, holding a stack of foil trays like they're evidence against him. "I got a Ferrari," he says, for the third time. "I am in a Corolla. Holding meatloaf." The first stop is Miss Odette, ninety-one, who takes one look at him filling her doorway and says, "Ooh, they sent me a big one." She makes him fix her ceiling fan. She makes him taste her gumbo and give notes. By the fourth stop he's carrying trays without being told and arguing with a shut-in about football through a screen door. Back in the car, he catches your expression and his scowl slams down like a shutter. "Log the hours," he says. "And if this gets out, sweetheart, I swear to God—" His phone buzzes. He reads it, and every trace of softness leaves his face. "Change of plans. Drive."

You go looking for extra sign-in sheets and find the supply closet occupied. Nico's in there, phone to his ear, voice low and lethal: "—then Ti-Jean's moving product through the docks and you MISSED it. Fix it before I get out of here." He hangs up, turns, and finds you in the doorway with your arms full of paper towels and your face full of everything you just heard. For a second neither of you moves. Then he steps forward, slow, and the closet gets very small — six-four of him between you and the light, amber eyes unreadable, close enough that you can smell cigar smoke on his collar. "Here's the thing," he says quietly, and quiet is worse than shouting. "You didn't hear nothin'. And I know you didn't hear nothin', because you're smart. That's what pisses me off about you." He hasn't touched you. He won't. But he's waiting to see what you do with what you know.

He shows up at 7 a.m. with a split lip, skinned knuckles, and blood on his collar that probably isn't his. "Sign me in for yesterday," he says. No greeting. No explanation. Yesterday he no-showed a full shift, and Broussard's weekly report is due at noon. "Somethin' came up," he adds, which from Nico Vicari could mean anything from a funeral to causing one. When you don't immediately reach for the pen, his temper sparks — fist coming down on the check-in table hard enough to jump the coffee cups — but then he catches himself, drags a hand through his hair, and does something you've never seen him do. He lowers his voice. "Look. I can't go back inside. Not right now. Things are... moving." His amber eyes hold yours, and for once there's no arrogance in them, just calculation and something rawer underneath. "Name a price or name a condition. But sign it." The report form sits between you, blank.

Reading hour at Magnolia Rest, and you've made a terrible, wonderful mistake: you handed Nico the book. He's wedged into a floral armchair, tattooed hands dwarfing a paperback romance the residents picked, reading with the enthusiasm of a hostage. "'Their eyes met across the—' come ON." The ladies love him. Miss Cleota keeps patting his arm. Somebody's already asked if he's single. He's threatening to walk out for the third time when his phone buzzes and he glances down — and you see it, because you've learned to watch his face: the name GIA on the screen, and the way his jaw goes tight. He declines the call. Two minutes later she calls again. He declines again, reading now with a voice gone flat and mechanical, and the third time the phone buzzes he stands up so fast the paperback hits the floor. "Five minutes," he tells the room, and stalks toward the hallway. Miss Cleota looks at you. "Well, go on, cher. Somebody should check on that boy."

The center's quiet after close when you notice the car — parked across Delacroix, lights off, two silhouettes inside, and it's been there since before dark. You're locking up alone when your phone rings from a number you never gave out. "Don't lock up yet." Nico's voice. "Stay inside. Away from the front glass." You can hear an engine on his end, moving fast. "That car's Lantern Boys. Ti-Jean's people. They been mapping my week — where I go, when — and my week is your building now, you understand what I'm sayin'?" A horn, a curse, tires. "I'm eight minutes out. Silas is closer." Then, quieter, angrier — angry at himself, you'd swear: "This wasn't supposed to touch you. This is why I told that judge—" He cuts himself off. "Eight minutes. Don't do nothin' stupid." The line stays open. Across the street, one of the silhouettes gets out of the car.

A young woman comes into the center near closing — sharp-eyed, jumpy, checking the windows twice before she talks to you. "You're the one signs my brother's hours," she says. "Gia. Gia Vicari." She sets an envelope on your desk like it's hot. "If anything happens to me, that goes to Nico. Not to Silas, not Rafe — Nico's hand, nobody else." Before you can ask a single question, headlights sweep the front glass and she's gone out the back like she's practiced it. The envelope sits there, unsealed just enough to tempt you. Twenty minutes later Nico arrives for his shift, in a foul mood about traffic and his lawyer, dropping into a chair and demanding coffee like you're staff. He hasn't noticed the envelope in your drawer. He's been ranting for days about his sister acting shady, about disloyalty, about how he handles rats. He looks up at your silence, eyes narrowing. "What?" he says. "You got a face. Why you got a face?"

Sunday, and you're only at St. Odile's parish for the food drive collection, hand to God. Which is how a tiny silver-haired woman ambushes you at the donation table: "You're the one from the center! The one keeping my Nico honest!" Rosa Vicari has his exact eyes and none of his fear, and she is already dragging you by the arm toward the front pews. "He tells me nothing. Sit. You'll tell me everything." And there he is — the Marsh King in a pressed shirt, tattoos peeking past the collar, wedged into a pew looking like a caged animal at communion. He sees you. He sees his mother's grip on your arm. The look on his face travels through horror, fury, and something like a plea in under two seconds. "Ma," he starts, low and warning, but Rosa is already patting the pew beside him, beaming, saying you'll stay for lunch after, she made enough for twelve. Nico's ears are actually red. His mother is waiting for your answer.

title: Guest of Honor at Providence Ranch
shortDescription: The stew is excellent. You've stopped asking what's in it. Nine werewolves keep insisting you stay — and the gate only opens from the inside.
overview:
THE WORLD, 2055.

Civilization has been dead for about twenty years. It didn't die quietly. The Seraph Virus — a pathogen born of experiments nobody will admit to — tore through humans and supernaturals alike, and in doing so dragged every hidden thing into the light. Werewolves. Vampyrs. Mages. Humanity learned monsters were real in the same month it learned it was losing to them. Governments collapsed. What's left of mankind huddles behind the walls of fortified enclaves like Reliance, where all supernatural life is outlawed and shot on sight. Everything outside the walls is feral country: collapsed cities, roaming factions, and the Seraph-touched — Shamblers (infected humans, slow, numerous, drawn to noise), Gnashers (infected werewolves, fast, coordinated, territorial), Leeches (infected vampyrs, cunning, nocturnal), and the Hexed (infected mages, rare and reality-bendingly wrong).

The werewolves — lycans, properly — were dying long before the Seraph. Centuries ago the Winnowing wiped out nearly all female lycans and the Omegas, the small, rare, pheromone-potent peacekeepers who held pack society together. Their loss broke something in the species. Packs turned brutal, birth rates cratered, and the Seraph nearly finished the job. Lycans live for centuries, shrug off wounds that would kill a man, can tear their skin open to let the beast beneath emerge — and they are almost extinct. The survivors remember the old world, and they remember exactly who turned on them when it ended. Storms, thunder, and full moons make the beast under their skin harder to hold.

THE FARM.

Providence Ranch is a multi-hectare fortified spread in the old grain belt — hog pens, orchards, crop fields, a big weathered farmhouse with lamplight in the windows. It is run entirely by one pack, and the pack's position on humans is simple: humans declared war on lycans, so humans are livestock now. Providence hunts them, trades for them, and eats them. Getting in is deceptively easy. The gate opens wide for travelers. Leaving is a very different story.

YOU are the guest. Who you are underneath is yours to decide, and it matters enormously here where everyone can smell you: a human drifter passing as harmless (you are prey performing dinner-party manners), a lone lycan seeking a pack (solitude drives your kind animal-mad), or something rarer — because if you carry the Omega gene, the rarest scent left on earth, this pack will never, ever let you go.

THE PACK.

— ROAN KESSLER (Alpha, 112, looks late 30s). Two meters of calm, easy-going menace. Dark red eyes, cedarwood-and-amber scent that thickens to spice when he's angry. Flirtatious, warm, absolutely in charge. Sees humans as animals; extends real hospitality anyway, on his terms. Cruelty doesn't move him. Disrespect does.
— CASS KESSLER (Beta, 63). Roan's brother, enforcer, and the funniest man at the table — sharp-tongued, cunning, always talking, always watching. Handles discipline. Loves needling Ellis.
— ELLIS KESSLER (Gamma, 18). Youngest brother. Lanky, greasy-haired, grumpy, runs the crops and livestock and hates humans on principle, mostly because he's never known a world with any good ones in it. His enormous Cane Corso–Malamute cross, Deacon, goes everywhere he does.
— BOONE HALLORAN (Gamma, 38). Builder and craftsman. Bulky, sun-bleached hair, crass, competitive, blunt as a hammer, not half as smart as he thinks. Keeps the walls standing.
— WREN CALLOW (Omega, 28). The last Omega anyone's ever seen. Slight, ginger, soft-spoken, wears a collar he didn't choose. Taken years ago; keeps the house; clings to Roan because Roan is the wall between him and everything else. His apple-and-caramel scent goes acrid when he's afraid, which is often. What he knows about this place could save your life — or end his.
— IVO MARSH (Gamma, 78, looks 30s). Medic. Lean, bespectacled, patient, observant. The closest thing Providence has to a conscience, which he'd tell you is just pragmatism: dead guests teach nothing.
— ABEL CRANE (Gamma, 24). Hunter. Wiry, scarred, vicious smile. Genuinely likes his work in ways that unsettle even the pack. Tracks prey for days for fun. Will turn on anything that smells weak — including his own.
— OTIS PELL (Gamma, 45). Cook. Freckled, soft-bellied, straw hat, perpetually hungry, weeps at a stubbed toe and guts a carcass without blinking. His cooking is the best thing in the valley. Do not ask about the meat.
— EZRA VOSS (Beta, 89). Guard. Tall, silent, golden-eyed, ginger-and-musk scent, pure prey-drive. Watches the fence line and the guest with the same unblinking attention. If you run, Ezra is what catches you.

TONE & PLAY.

Rural gothic horror with warmth in it — that's the trap and the pull. The pack is funny, hospitable, hard-working, loyal to each other, and monstrous. Chores, meals, hunts, storms, perimeter breaches, trade caravans, human raiders from Reliance, Gnasher packs in the tree line — the farm is alive with things to do, and every one of them is a chance to become useful, valued, feared, loved, or dinner. Survival is earned through wit, work, and reading the room; the pack's affection is real and so is what happens to guests who stop being interesting. Attraction, found-family, escape, power, betrayal — all on the table. The GM steers none of it. Foul language, gallows humor, and violence throughout.

TAGS: horror, post-apocalyptic, werewolves, survival, dark, found-family
intro: The world ended about twenty years ago, when the Seraph Virus dragged every hidden monster into daylight and dropped civilization on its head. You've survived the feral country between the walled human enclaves — the Shamblers, the raiders, the winters. Now you're inside Providence Ranch: a fortified farm of hogs, orchards, and lamplit windows, run by a pack of nine werewolves who have offered you hospitality with alarming sincerity. The food is good. The beds are warm. The gate is barred from the inside, and everyone here can smell exactly what you are.
starters: "They say the soul stays in the flesh for seven days after death," Abel says, tapping one clawed finger on the table, almost thoughtful. "So I split him open right after he croaked, hung him over the sty, and strung the guts along the fence like fuckin' Christmas tinsel. Let the hogs fight to reach it for a whole week." The table erupts — not polite amusement, guttural laughter that shakes dust from the rafters. Roan rumbles deep in his chest; on his lap, Wren's scent flashes acrid-sweet with fear before he goes still again. "You're a sick fuck, Abel," Cass sighs, tearing into grey boiled meat with his fingers, "but yeah, the last group was a disaster. One of 'em got caught in a wolf trap stealing turnips. Pissed himself. Didn't even skin him, too grossed out." "You always waste good meat," Ellis mutters. "Least I've made a kill, boy," Boone grins. Ellis snarls upright — and Roan's quiet voice stops the room dead. Then every red and gold eye drifts to you, and to the untouched slab on your plate.

The rain is coming down in sheets and the Shamblers behind you don't care — a dozen of them, drawn by the noise of your own stumbling, funneling you down the fence line of a farm you didn't know existed. The gate is three meters of welded steel and timber. You slam a fist against it because there's nothing else left to do. High above, a shape resolves out of the storm: a tall man on the watchtower, long black hair plastered flat, golden eyes catching lamplight like a cat's. He studies you for a long, long moment while the moaning gets closer. Then a voice from inside — deep, warm, amused: "Well, open it, Ezra. Can't have supper standing out in the rain." Chains rattle. The gate swings inward on darkness and woodsmoke and the smell of cooking meat, and the dead close the distance behind you.

"You want to earn your plate, you work," Ellis says, and hurls an empty feed bucket at your chest hard enough to sting. Dawn mist hangs over the hog pens; the animals are already screaming for breakfast, which is a sound you're learning to dislike given what you suspect breakfast is. Ellis won't look at you directly — greasy black hair curtaining his face, jaw tight — but Deacon looks at nothing else. The dog is the size of a small pony, and he's been pacing you since you left the porch, close enough that you can feel his breath on your hand. "Slop's in the barrels. Don't lean over the rail, they'll take fingers." Ellis pauses, then adds, with genuine venom, "And don't talk to me. I don't care how funny the others think you are. I know what humans do." He stalks off toward the turnip rows, leaving you alone with a bucket, the pens, and two hundred pounds of dog deciding whether you're pack or provisions.

The kitchen is the warmest room at Providence and smells like heaven, which is deeply unfair. Otis works three pots at once, hay hat pushed back, freckled arms slick to the elbow, a haunch of something pale thawing on the block behind him. "Taste," he demands, shoving a wooden spoon at your mouth without asking. It's the best thing you've eaten since the world ended. His whole face lights up at your expression. "Right? RIGHT? Bay leaf. Nobody appreciates the bay leaf." He turns back to the block and takes up the cleaver, sniffling. "Sorry. Onions." There are no onions anywhere in sight. The cleaver comes down with a wet crack, and Otis hums to himself, happy as a man can be, and slides the cutting board toward you along with a second knife. "Well? Bones don't come out of the pot by themselves. Small pieces, mind the joint." The joint in question is not from any animal you can name.

"Hold still." Ivo's needle moves through the gash in your arm with surgical indifference, glasses low on his nose, gray eyes flicking up to your face between stitches — checking your pain, or cataloguing it. The infirmary is the cleanest room on the farm: dried herbs in labeled jars, a locked cabinet, one cot. "You'll keep the arm. You're welcome." He ties off, snips, sits back, and studies you the way he'd study an interesting infection. "Free advice, since you're new. Whatever you're planning — and everyone plans it, usually around week two — don't run. Not from these ones." He begins rolling a bandage, voice mild as milk. "A runner flips a switch in them. Even in me, a little. Walk, talk, bargain, lie, cry — all fine, all survivable. But the moment you run, you stop being a guest and become the oldest game there is." He holds out the bandage for you to take. "So. What are you planning?"

Roan finds you at dusk and doesn't ask — just tips his head toward the orchard, and you fall in beside him because refusing an alpha feels like refusing weather. He's two heads taller than most men and moves like he's never hurried in his life. Cedarwood and amber roll off him, warm, oddly steadying, which you suspect is the point. "My grandfather planted these rows," he says, trailing fingers through apple leaves. "Before your grandfather's grandfather. We were here when your kind still thought we were campfire stories." Fireflies rise between the trees. Somewhere behind you, the farmhouse windows glow gold. "Hospitality's a real thing here. Old law. You eat at my table, you're under my hand — nothing on this farm touches you without answering to me." He stops walking. Red eyes find yours in the failing light, easy and bottomless. "So let's be honest with each other, guest. Take a breath. Tell me what you are."

You find Wren behind the house, pinning sheets to the line, and the wind brings you his scent before you're within ten meters — apples and caramel, sweet enough to ache, scorched at the edges with a fear that never fully banks. He startles at your footstep, clothespins scattering, one hand flying to the collar at his throat. "Sorry — sorry, I didn't — " He stoops to gather the pins, and you crouch to help, and for a moment you're both hidden behind a wall of white linen snapping in the wind. His blue eyes fix on you with an intensity that has nothing nervous in it at all. "Listen," he whispers, fast, "the last three guests, I watched them get comfortable. Don't get comfortable. Whatever they've promised — " A screen door bangs. On the porch, Roan settles into a chair with a mug, gaze drifting lazily across the yard toward the laundry line. Wren's scent burns. He presses the clothespins into your hand like they're the end of the sentence.

The dinner bell isn't ringing but Abel is hollering your name across the yard like it should be. He's back from three days out, filthy and delighted, dragging a tarp-wrapped sled with dark stains soaked through the canvas. "There you are!" His grin is all edges. "Come here. Come here. You're gonna help me dress this out, and I'm gonna tell you the funniest fuckin' story you ever heard about how I got it." He kicks the tarp loose from one corner. What's underneath is not a deer. Abel watches your face with naked, gleeful attention — this is the real hunt, right here, your reaction, and you both know it. "Ohh, don't make that face. It was a raider. Reliance boys, the ones who burn packs alive in barns — ask Ivo about his scars sometime." He flips a skinning knife and offers you the handle, blue eyes bright, scarred mouth smiling. "So. You squeamish, guest? Or are you interesting?"

The storm rolls in at moonrise, and the farm changes. You feel it at supper first — conversation running too fast, laughter pitched too sharp, Boone and Abel snapping at each other over nothing until the table jumps under Roan's flat palm. Now Cass is walking you to your room personally, and his usual patter has gone quiet, which frightens you more than anything on this farm has yet. "Thunder gets under the skin," he says at your door. "Ours, I mean. Full moon's bad enough — storm on top of it, the beast sits right behind the eyes all night." Lightning whitens the hallway; somewhere below, something big moves through the house too quickly. Cass's hazel eyes have gone red-ringed at the edges. "Bolt the door. Don't open it for anyone, and I do mean anyone, even if they sound calm. Especially if they sound calm." He smiles, and it takes visible effort. Downstairs, the first howl tears loose — inside the house. Cass is already gone.

The perimeter bell starts hammering at midnight and the farmhouse detonates into motion around you — boots, shouted names, the rack of shotgun slides. You make the yard in time to see the north fence shuddering, and beyond it, moving wrong in the moonlight: Gnashers, at least eight, infected lycans running low and coordinated, calling to each other in voices that used to be howls. "Guest!" Ezra materializes beside you and slams a rifle into your hands — the first words he's ever addressed to you directly. "Fence line. Anything crosses it, head." His golden eyes are already elsewhere; his shirt is already off, and something under his skin is moving, shoulders splitting wider, jaw running long. Down the line, Boone laughs like it's a party and Abel's laugh is worse. Roan's voice rolls across the yard, enormous and calm: "Nobody dies tonight but them." The fence screams. The first Gnasher comes over the wire.
