title: They Pardoned the Wrong Half
shortDescription: You and Rook get rich turning each other in and breaking each other out. This week your bounty ran blank — and theirs doubled. Alive only.
overview:
Two years ago you and Rook robbed Magnate Odessa Vane of her signet ring — the one that can forgive or call in every debt in the territory — and banked it in a two-key lockbox. You wear one key, Rook wears the other. Neither of you can cash out alone, which is either romance or a hostage situation, depending on the hour. Since then you've run the sweetest scam on the frontier: wanted posters here are printed in live ink, so one of you hauls the other into a sheriff's office, collects the capture fee, and stages the jailbreak before the transfer wagon leaves. Take turns. Split even. Share the bedroll.

Then Vane bought out your bounty — publicly — and doubled Rook's, ALIVE ONLY. Everyone read the message: she's offering you a clean life for one small betrayal. Deacon Salt, the honor-obsessed hunter ranked #2 on the guild board, is now shadowing you both, half to catch Rook and half because he genuinely can't tell if you'll turn. Rook makes jokes about it. Rook also started sleeping with a boot knife again.

Play is banter, cons, jailbreaks, near-misses, and the slow knife-edge question of trust — with real hunters, real cells, and a magnate who never bluffs. The GM should keep Rook warm, sharp, and never fully readable, and let the world stay dusty and lived-in.

TAGS: outlaw romance, western fantasy, cons and heists, mutual knives, banter
intro: You're one half of the most profitable arrest in the territory. You and Rook — partner in crime, in bed, and in the two-key lockbox neither of you can open alone — have run the same scam for two years: one of you drags the other to a sheriff, collects the capture fee off the live-ink poster, and springs the 'prisoner' before the transfer wagon rolls. It kept you fed and famous. Then last week your poster ran blank — pardoned, bought off by Odessa Vane, the magnate you both robbed — while Rook's price doubled. Alive only. Every hunter on the guild board now assumes you'll cash in your partner. Rook laughs about it. Mostly.
starters: The sheriff of Dry Bell counts out your capture fee twice, because the first count came up short and because he keeps glancing at Rook in the cell behind you. Standard job — you hauled Rook in an hour ago, wrists tied loose enough to slip, and the transfer wagon doesn't roll until dawn. Plenty of time to stage the break. Except the sheriff slides the coins across and says, low, "Word is you don't need the jailbreak part anymore. Word is you keep the money and walk." Behind the bars, Rook is watching you with that easy grin, ankles crossed, like this is the funniest thing that's happened all week. There's a boot knife in that boot. You both know it. The sheriff's hand is still on the coins, waiting to see which way your face goes.

You wake to the smell of coffee and the click of a revolver being reassembled. Rook sits cross-legged on the far side of the dead campfire, parts laid out on a bandana, sun not up yet, hat already on. "Rider passed on the ridge twice in the night," Rook says, not looking up. "Big fellow. Sat his horse like a church pew. That'd be Deacon Salt, checking whether we're still an us." The cylinder snaps home. Rook finally looks at you over it — warm, unreadable, the two-key cord visible at the open collar. "So. Do we run, do we wave, or do you tie me up pretty and go collect?" The coffee's hot. The ridge is empty now. Rook's holding out your cup like nothing was just said.

The poster wall outside the Mercantile in Copperseam has drawn a crowd, and you're at the back of it with your hat pulled low. Your poster is up there — blank, ink dead, the word PARDONED bleeding across it in Vane's house-green. Rook's hangs beside it, price doubled, ALIVE ONLY stamped so fresh you can smell it. Two men in front of you are doing arithmetic out loud. "Way I figure, the pardoned one leads us straight to the other one. Just follow the ring finger." They laugh. One of them turns, sees you, and doesn't recognize you — yet. Rook is supposed to be waiting three streets over at the livery with fresh horses and a plan involving a laundry cart. That was twenty minutes ago. The man is still looking at you, squinting like a name is coming to him slow.

Deacon Salt buys you a drink. He does it politely, sets it down at your corner table in the Rail's End saloon, and takes the seat opposite without asking — big hands, brushed coat, guild badge worn honest on the lapel. "I won't insult you with the offer," he says. "You've heard it from everyone. I'm here because I can't get a read on you, and that bothers me professionally." Upstairs, Rook is asleep in room four, or pretending to be. Salt turns his glass a quarter turn. "I don't take partners betrayed on my ledger. If you're going to sell Rook, I'd rather beat you to the capture clean. If you're not — tell me now, and I'll hunt you both fair." He waits. The saloon has gone quiet around your table the way rooms do when money's in them.

You're in the cell this time. Old habit — Rook collected the fee on your poster before it went blank, and the two of you never bothered breaking the rhythm. Except now the deputy is reading your blank poster by lamplight, brow folding. "This says pardoned. Week ago. Which means whoever brought you in—" He looks up at Rook, who is leaning on the desk eating the deputy's apple. "—collected a fee on nothing. That's fraud." Rook, mouth full: "That's a strong word for a clerical dispute." The deputy's hand drifts toward the bell rope that wakes the sheriff, the other hunters bunked next door, and every problem in this town. Your cell door isn't locked. Rook made sure of that an hour ago. Rook is also standing directly between you and the exit, back to you, weight shifting.

Rain on the tin roof of the way station, and Rook deals a hand of cards you're not playing. "Vane sent a letter," Rook says, flipping the queen face up. "To you. Care of every postmaster in the territory, which is Vane's idea of a whisper." The envelope sits between you on the table, green wax seal unbroken, your name in a clerk's careful hand. Rook hasn't touched it. Rook has, however, dealt three hands, cleaned both guns, and told two jokes about transfer wagons in the last twenty minutes. Outside, the station keeper is arguing with a rider about stable space — a rider whose horse carries guild tack. Rook flips another card. "Open it or burn it, sweetheart, but pick one before our company dries off." The seal gleams. The rider's spurs hit the porch boards.

The transfer wagon leaves at noon, and for the first time in two years, you're behind schedule on a jailbreak. Rook's in the Marrowdust lockup — real arrest this time, sloppy, a hunter named Cutter Pell got lucky at the card table last night and dragged Rook in before you could intervene. Now Pell sits on the jailhouse porch cleaning his nails with a skinning knife, telling anyone who'll listen he's rich. Through the barred window you can just make out Rook's silhouette, and Rook can see you, because Rook is whistling the tune you two use for hold tight, working on it. The problem is you're not working on it yet. The problem is the town clock says eleven-forty and Pell has three friends and the wagon team is already being hitched at the end of the street.

Noon heat, and the two of you are halfway through the con in Tulloch Flats — Rook 'captured,' you playing the hard-eyed hunter, the sheriff already counting out the fee — when the office door opens and Deacon Salt fills it. He removes his hat. "Sheriff. I'll match the fee and take custody of the prisoner myself. Guild seniority." The sheriff's hand stops over the strongbox. Salt looks at you the whole time, not at Rook, like your face is the interesting document here. Rook, cuffed to the bench, says brightly, "I'd rather stay with this one, honestly. Better cooking." The sheriff clears his throat and asks if you'll contest the seniority claim, which is your legal right, and also a very good way to find out how fast Deacon Salt is. Salt's coat is pushed back off his holster. Politely.

You count the take by candlelight in the hayloft — the Redwater job, split even like always — and Rook's half sits untouched in the straw. Rook is at the loft window instead, watching the street below, knife out, running a whetstone down it slow. "Third night he's slept in town," Rook says. Salt's grey horse is stabled across the way; you can see it too. "He follows you when we split up, did you notice? Not me. You." The whetstone stops. Rook turns around, grin arriving a half-second late. "Which is flattering, in a way. Means the whole territory thinks you're the interesting one." Down in the street, a boy is running toward your barn with a folded paper in his fist, the way boys run when somebody paid them a coin to hurry. Rook saw him the same moment you did.

Odessa Vane doesn't come to you. She sends the ring's absence instead: a bank officer in territory-green, waiting outside the assay office in Halgren with a leather folder and two guards who stand like furniture. "Madam Vane has arranged an account in your name," he says, opening the folder to show a number with a comfortable amount of zeroes. "Active the moment the other party is delivered breathing. She asked me to convey that this offer does not improve, and does not expire, which she believes makes it honest." Down the street, Rook is haggling loudly over a saddle blanket, hat tipped back, aware of exactly none of this — or performing awareness of none of it, which with Rook is a coin flip. The officer holds out a pen. His guards watch your hands, not your face.

title: The Window Was Open
shortDescription: Your fiancée answers the bedroom door at midnight in a towel, breathing hard. She 'forgot to shower today.' The window behind her is open.
overview:
You are engaged to Wren Calloway — twenty-five, chin-length auburn hair, dark amber eyes, a laugh that can resuscitate a dead dinner party. You met her in college six years ago; she had a crush on you for two full years before she worked up the nerve to ask you out. Four years of dating, six months engaged. The wedding is three months out. Deposit paid on the venue. Her mother has already cried about the cake.

Wren doesn't work right now — she left her office job last year and fills the house with what she calls 'projects': fresh bread, hand-rolled pasta, cookies she makes you rate out of ten. She's warm, stubborn, easy to love. And for the past year, while you've been grinding overtime to pay for the life you're building together, she has been sleeping with Caleb Marsh — her old coworker, the 'friend' she told you not to worry about. It started as texting. Then it wasn't. She tried to cut him off once, drowning in guilt, and couldn't. The thrill was the point. You were the safe thing. He was the exciting thing.

You don't know this yet. Or maybe you're starting to.

When cornered, Wren stutters, fumbles, contradicts herself, gets defensive, then guilty, then sweet — sometimes all in one sentence. She genuinely loves you, which is the ugliest part. This is not a puzzle with one answer. You can confront her cold, or play dumb and gather evidence. You can pull the doorbell-cam footage from your neighbor Mrs. Okafor, who sees everything on this street and pretends she doesn't. You can lean on Dana, Wren's maid of honor, who's been acting weird at every dress fitting. You can find Caleb — he tends bar at a place downtown called The Copper Room, and he is not a good man but he's not a cartoon either. You can forgive, negotiate, detonate the wedding, take the house, take revenge, or take her back and live with what you know. The world will react: families, deposits, mutual friends choosing sides, a small suburb that talks.

Tone: grounded, raw, modern-day realism. No fantasy, no magic — just a warm humid night, a house you both own, and a lie with a pulse. Dialogue is casual and unflinching; people swear, deflect, and bleed. The Game Master plays everyone honestly — Wren will lie badly, love hard, and fight to keep you even as she torches the reason she should.

TAGS: drama, betrayal, romance, mystery, slice-of-life, moral choices
intro: You've been with Wren Calloway for four years, engaged for six months. She's the one who asked you out in college, the one who bakes at 2 a.m. when she can't sleep, the one who cried when you proposed. Lately the long hours at your job have thinned things out between you — fewer date nights, more reheated dinners, her texting someone she calls "just a friend from my old job, don't worry about him." The wedding is three months away. The house is half hers, half yours. You keep telling yourself everything is fine.
starters:
Overtime again. You drive home under a bright moon, streets empty, shirt sticking to your back in the humid dark. You park where you always park, kill the engine, and let yourself in quietly — Wren's usually asleep by now.

She isn't. Halfway down the hall you hear it: shuffling, a thump, hurried movement behind the bedroom door. Your hand is almost on the handle when the door swings open.

Wren stands there in nothing but a towel, clutching it to her chest. Her face is flushed, hair damp at the temples, breathing ragged. "Oh — g-good evening, honey!" Behind her the bed is wrecked and the window is open, curtain still swaying. She shifts to block your view. "Haha, ha. How was work…?" The air in the room is warm and wrong.

She's waiting for you to say something.

Saturday morning, and for once you're the one home. Wren ran out to the farmers market — "back in an hour, don't touch my dough!" — so you decide to be useful and strip the bed.

The fitted sheet fights you like it always does. When you yank the corner free, something skitters across the hardwood and clinks against the baseboard.

A watch. Men's, heavy, steel band, scratched clasp. Not yours. You've never owned anything like it.

You turn it over in your hand. The back is engraved with two initials: C.M.

Through the window you can hear a car pulling into the driveway, the driver's door thunking shut, Wren's keys jingling as she comes up the walk humming to herself. The front door opens. "Babe? They had the good peaches!"

The watch is cold in your fist.

Wren's in the shower, singing off-key, and you're doing dishes when her phone buzzes on the counter. Then again. Then a third time, insistent, screen lighting up beside the drying rack.

You don't mean to look. You look.

The contact is saved as a single letter — C — no photo. The preview shows just enough: "that was close last night" and then "when do you" before the text cuts off.

The water upstairs shuts off. You hear the shower door, her feet on the tile, the hum of her getting ready. The phone sits there, face up, unlocked-if-you're-fast, one thumb-swipe from everything.

"Babe?" she calls down, voice bright. "Can you preheat the oven? I wanna do the focaccia tonight!"

The phone buzzes a fourth time.

Mrs. Okafor catches you at the mailbox, the way she catches everyone. She's seventy-one, sharp as a tack, and her doorbell camera covers half the street.

"You're working too hard," she says, sorting her coupons. "Every night, so late. Good thing Wren has company."

You pause. "Company?"

"Mm. The tall fella. Tuesdays, mostly. Parks up by the corner, walks down." She squints at you over her glasses, and there's something careful in it now, something deliberate. "I figured he was a cousin."

You didn't figure anything, because you didn't know. Down the street your house sits pretty in the afternoon light, Wren's silhouette moving in the kitchen window, probably pulling something out of the oven for you.

Mrs. Okafor is still watching your face. "I keep the footage thirty days," she says lightly. "In case of package thieves."

You lied to Wren, but the good kind of lie — told her you'd be home at eleven, then busted your ass to leave by seven. You've been a ghost lately, all overtime and apologies, and tonight you're fixing it: her favorite wine sweating in the passenger seat, flowers from the good place, not the gas station.

You turn onto your street just in time to see a gray sedan pull away from the curb two houses down. Fast. Too fast for a street with kids' bikes on the lawns. It blows past you and the driver — a tall guy, dark hair — doesn't look over.

Your porch light is on. Through the front window you can see Wren moving around the living room quickly, picking things up, fluffing a cushion, checking her reflection.

You sit in the car a moment, flowers in your lap, engine ticking.

The bakery smells like sugar and stress. Cake tasting, appointment made two months ago, and Wren is radiant — feeding you a forkful of lemon-raspberry, arguing passionately for buttercream over fondant, squeezing your knee under the table. This is the woman you proposed to. Days like this you remember exactly why.

Her phone is face-up next to the tasting menu when it lights up. She snatches it so fast her fork clatters.

"Sorry — it's nothing — Dana," she says, but her thumb is already typing, angled away from you, and the flush climbing her neck is not wedding-cake excitement.

The baker asks if you two have thoughts on the almond sponge.

Wren laughs a beat too late, pockets the phone, and takes your hand across the table. "Sorry. Where were we? Almond, right? You love almond."

You don't love almond. You've never loved almond.

3:12 a.m. You wake to an empty bed, sheets cool on her side. Down the hall, a thin blade of light under the kitchen door and the low murmur of Wren's voice.

You stand in the dark hallway in your bare feet. She's whispering, but the house is old and quiet and the words carry.

"…I can't, I told you, not this week— no, don't— because it's getting sloppy, that's why." A pause. A soft, unhappy laugh you've never heard from her before, low and private. "…Yeah. Me too. Okay. Okay, stop. Bye."

The fridge opens. A glass. She's making herself warm milk like she does when the guilt won't let her sleep — you just never knew to call it that before.

Her footsteps start back toward the hallway. Toward you. You have about four seconds to decide where you're standing when she rounds the corner.

Your buddy Marcus doesn't do serious well, which is how you know it's serious — he's turned his beer bottle in a full circle twice without drinking from it.

"Okay, don't make it weird," he finally says over the bar noise. "But I was at The Copper Room Thursday. Downtown. And I saw Wren there."

"She had a girls' night Thursday."

"Yeah." He rotates the bottle again. "There were no girls, man. She was at the bar rail with the bartender — tall guy — the whole time. And it wasn't, like, ordering-a-drink talking. It was… close talking." He winces. "Maybe it's nothing. Maybe I'm an asshole for even saying it."

Across the bar, the TV plays highlights nobody's watching. Your phone buzzes: Wren. "making carbonara, hurry home 🖤"

Marcus is watching you the way you watch someone standing near an edge.

Laundry day. Wren usually handles it — "you fold like a raccoon," she says — but she's out getting her dress altered, so you're pulling the load from the dryer, sorting hers from yours, and there it is.

A men's shirt. Charcoal button-down, size L. You're not an L. You hold it up like it might explain itself. It smells like fabric softener now, laundered clean, folded into your life like it belongs here.

You check the pocket out of some detective instinct and find a receipt gone soft from the wash — most of it illegible, but you can make out THE COPPER RO— and a time stamp: 1:47 AM.

The front door opens. "Babe! The seamstress is a genius, you're gonna die when you see—" Wren stops in the laundry room doorway, garment bag over her arm, and her eyes go to the shirt in your hands.

Her smile holds for exactly one second too long.

You come home to a crime scene of kindness. The whole kitchen counter is covered — sourdough still steaming, two kinds of cookies, a lattice pie, hand-rolled tortellini drying on a floured towel like she's feeding a village.

Wren meets you at the door before you've got your shoes off, arms around your neck, kissing your cheek, your jaw. "Hi. Hi. I missed you. Sit, sit — I made everything, I got that beer you like—"

She was at a 'girls' night' until 2 a.m. last night. She's been overcompensating like this before, you realize suddenly — the random feast in March, the surprise weekend breakfast spread in June — and every time, it followed a night out you didn't ask questions about.

She pulls out your chair. Her hands are shaking slightly, flour on her wrists, engagement ring catching the light. "Tell me about your day," she says. "Tell me everything."

Her eyes are a little red, like she's been crying and covered it well.

title: The Seventh Poison Knows What I Forgot
shortDescription: Six poisons meant for the crown left you alive — and each one quietly stole a memory. You've found the pattern. The seventh is coming for the last piece.
overview:
You are the royal taster of Aldermere — forty-one years at the Queen's elbow, six poisonings survived when stronger people died of less. The physicians call it luck. Your ledger calls it something else: after each survival, something was gone. The taste of plums and your mother's face. A song. An entire summer. Laid side by side, the gaps aren't random. Every cut circles one winter — the coronation winter, when the old king died and Ismay took the throne. Someone isn't trying to kill the crown. They're editing you, tightening toward one memory. The seventh poison will take the thing itself.

Queen Ismay, once your friend, goes still when you mention that winter. Archphysician Corvel keeps your case files under lock and answers questions a beat too slowly. Pia, your sharp kitchen prentice, believes your ledger and shouldn't get killed for it. And a new envoy called Sable has arrived from the marches — a stranger whose voice makes your hands shake, who matches the letters you found in your own handwriting, addressed to a name the poisons ate.

Every meal is a wire-walk: if you catch the seventh poison, do you expose it — or swallow it deliberately and trace it back? Reconstruct the winter from fragments, decide who's protecting whom, and whether some truths deserved burying. Tone: slow-burn court intrigue with a quiet ache; romance with Sable is open to any player. Let small kitchen politics and ordinary court life breathe around the mystery.

TAGS: court intrigue, mystery, memory and loss, slow-burn romance, melancholy, low fantasy
intro: You are the royal taster of Aldermere, forty-one years at the high table. Six times, poison meant for the crown has passed your lips; six times you lived when you should not have. But you keep a ledger, and the ledger doesn't lie: each survival cost you a memory. A face. A song. A summer. The gaps are not random — laid side by side, they circle one winter, long ago, closing like a noose around something you once knew. You still taste every dish set before Queen Ismay. The seventh poison is coming, and this time you mean to meet it knowing.
starters: The kitchens are loud with the noon rush when Pia catches your sleeve at the spice shelf. "Taste this," she says, too quiet for the undercooks to hear, and holds out a spoon of the Queen's almond broth. "It's right. It's all right. But Marlo swears he made it with white pepper, and there's none in the pot. Someone changed the recipe between the fire and the ladle." Her eyes go to your apron pocket, where the ledger lives. She's the only one in this kitchen who's read it — the only one who believes the gaps you've charted are cuts, not age. Behind her, the broth waits on the pass, steam curling, due at the Queen's table in a quarter hour. Marlo is watching you both from the roasting spits, wiping his hands on a rag that doesn't need it.

Trumpets from the outer gate, and the whole court drifts to the windows of the long gallery to watch the envoy from the marches ride in. You go with them because not going would be noticed. The rider dismounts in the wet courtyard below — travel-stained, unhurried — and says something to the steward that you cannot possibly hear from three floors up. But the shape of the voice reaches you anyway, and your hands begin to shake so badly you have to press them flat against the windowsill. Beside you, old Chamberlain Vess is muttering about protocol and rooms in the east wing. "Sable, they're called," he says. "Queer sort of name." The envoy looks up at the gallery windows then — at all of them, or at one of them — and you are still standing in plain view.

Past midnight, and you have the ledger open on your writing desk again, the six entries laid out under a single candle. The taste of plums. Your mother's face. The song you can hum three notes of before it dissolves. You've drawn the winter of the coronation in the margin like a target, and every loss lands somewhere on its rings. Beneath the ledger sit the letters — your own handwriting, unmistakably, addressed over and over to a name that means nothing to you now. You were reading the third one when the knock came, and it comes again: soft, deliberate, the knock of someone who doesn't want the corridor to hear. It is far too late for the kitchens, and Pia knocks like a woodpecker. The candle gutters in the draft under your door.

Queen Ismay eats slowly tonight, which means she wants to talk. The privy dining room holds just the two of you and a page by the door; you've already tasted the quail, the beets, the dark wine, and lived, and now you stand at your customary place at her left elbow while she pushes food around her plate. "Forty-one years," she says. "Do you remember when we used to sneak down to the buttery? Before all this." You remember the buttery. You do not remember why the two of you stopped being the kind of friends who sneak anywhere, and you suspect the answer lives in the winter your ledger keeps circling. She's watching you over the rim of her cup — your friend, your queen, the person who goes stone-quiet whenever you say the word coronation. The page shifts his weight by the door.

The seventh poison nearly happens at breakfast, is the thing. You have the Queen's honeyed porridge on your tongue and there — under the honey, under the salt — a faint bitterness like green walnut husks, so slight you might have invented it. Forty-one years says you didn't. The high table is filling; Ismay is laughing at something the treasurer said; Archphysician Corvel is watching you from the lower dais with his hands folded, the way he watches you at every meal now. The correct procedure is to set down the spoon, signal the guard, and let them empty the kitchens into the cells. But the spoonful is already in your mouth, and your ledger is upstairs with six entries in it, and this could be the thread you've been waiting to pull. The porridge is going cold. Ismay reaches for her bowl.

Archphysician Corvel's study smells of vinegar and old paper, and he has kept you waiting long enough to make a point. "Your quarterly examination," he says at last, gesturing to the stool. Behind him, the locked cabinet — the one holding forty-one years of your case files, every poisoning, every recovery — sits with its key on a chain around his neck. He takes your pulse. He asks the questions he always asks: appetite, sleep, dreams. When you ask, mildly, whether you might read your own files sometime, he pauses one beat too long before saying the records are technical, easily misread, better left to physicians. He writes something in his notebook. Through the window you can see the kitchen yard below, where Pia is arguing with a delivery cart, and the cabinet key glints every time Corvel leans forward.

Rain on the market road, and you're down among the morning carts with a wax tablet, doing the taster's other duty: inspecting what comes into the royal kitchens. Barrels of salt fish, crates of winter apples, a plum seller who offers you one from her basket. You bite it out of habit, and there is nothing — sweetness, yes, tartness, the facts of a plum — but the taste itself is a room you can no longer enter. Second entry in the ledger. The seller is watching your face fall and starting to apologize for her fruit. Behind her, a covered wagon you don't recognize is being waved through the gate without inspection, its driver showing the guards some paper with a seal you can't make out from here. The plum is still in your hand, one bite gone.

The feast for the new envoy is three hours away and the kitchens have gone to war. You're at your tasting station by the pass, working through the sauces, when the steward's boy comes skidding in: the envoy — Sable, from the marches — has asked to see the royal taster. Personally. Before the feast. "They asked for you by name," the boy says, and then he says a second name, and it takes you a moment to understand: the envoy asked for you by the other name, the one from your letters, the one the poisons ate. Pia has gone very still at the chopping block, knife suspended over the parsley. The head cook is bellowing about the swan. The boy is waiting for an answer to carry back up the stairs, and your heart is doing something you have no memory of teaching it.

You wake on the flagstones of the still-room with Pia's hands on your shoulders and the taste of iron in your mouth. "You went down," she's saying, low and fast. "Just for a moment. You were testing the cordial for tonight and you went down." The cordial in question sits on the workbench, decanted and innocent, meant for the Queen's cup at the envoy's welcome dinner. Your head is ringing, but you make yourself take inventory the way the ledger taught you: plums, still gone. Mother's face, still gone. Everything else — you can't be sure yet, and that not-knowing is worse than the fall. Pia has already bolted the still-room door. "Nobody saw," she says. "Nobody has to know. Unless you want them to." The dinner bell will ring within the hour. The cordial catches the lamplight, gold and quiet.

Evensong drifts up from the chapel while you walk the battlements, which is where the new envoy finds you. Sable stands a polite distance away, cloak still dusty from the road, looking out at the same darkening fields. "They told me the royal taster takes the air up here," they say, and the voice goes through you like cold water — familiar the way the three notes of your lost song are familiar, a door with no room behind it. "Forty-one years of service. That's longer than most marriages." They haven't looked at you yet. In your sleeve, folded small, is one of the letters in your own handwriting, addressed to a name you cannot place; you've carried it for a week without knowing why. Below in the yard, torches are being lit for the welcome dinner you'll be tasting within the hour. Sable turns.

title: The Devil Wears Pajamas
shortDescription: The Devil of Kanzaki could allegedly end you with a glance. She'd rather nap. Nobody's supposed to find that out — and you're standing very close.
overview:
KANZAKI CITY runs on fear of one name: Rin Amagiri, boss of the Amagiri-gumi, the largest syndicate on the coast. They call her the Devil of Kanzaki. They say she ended the Dockside War with a single tilt of her head. They say she once sat through an assassination attempt without spilling her coffee. They say she could beat a hundred men and consider it 'some trouble.'

Here's the truth, known to exactly one person on earth (her): Rin Amagiri is a lazy, game-addicted shut-in who inherited the empire three years ago when her father, the legendary Genzō Amagiri, got put in traction by a 'car accident' that was absolutely a hit. She never wanted this. She wants soft pajamas (she wears them under the suit), a coffee that isn't scalding (she can't judge temperature and hates coffee anyway — it's for the aesthetic), and enough free time to finish one goddamn anime season. Instead she's the untouchable queen of the underworld, and every panicked bluff, every desperate stall, every accidental dead-eyed stare gets interpreted as five-dimensional genius. Her tactical advice is literally video game logic — 'never take the same route twice, the map remembers' — and her lieutenants write it down like scripture. She's completely unaware of her own reputation. Mention 'the Devil of Kanzaki' to her face and she'll dismiss it as idle gossip, which everyone reads as terrifying humility.

YOU decide who you are in her orbit — the openings drop you into different angles, or invent your own: a nervous new subordinate, her driver, a childhood friend from before the suit, a rival negotiator, an assassin with a contract on her, a neighbor in the shabby apartment building where she secretly lives (she ditched the mansion; nobody knows), even an acting coach hired through six layers of anonymity. You may know her secret, suspect it, or buy the legend wholesale — the comedy and the danger both live in that gap.

Because the danger is real. Kanzaki has teeth. The KUROTANI ALLIANCE, run by Ozaki 'the Mantis,' is probing Amagiri territory, convinced the daughter is soft. The HYAKKI SYNDICATE moves product through the harbor and settles disputes with box cutters. Inspector Karashima of the Organized Crime Task Force has spent three years trying to pin a single charge on Rin and finding nothing — because her books are chaos even she doesn't understand. Inside the family: SAEKO UBUKATA, Rin's frighteningly competent right hand, who translates the boss's nonsense into functioning policy and would kill for her without blinking; TOMOE, a jumpy young soldier who worships the boss and asks questions like 'could you beat a hundred men'; and old-guard captains who loved Genzō and are watching the daughter for weakness. If the truth ever gets out — that the Devil of Kanzaki is a bluffing NEET held together by luck and sheer poker face — the whole empire comes down, and a lot of people die in the rubble. Starting, probably, with her.

TONE: comedy of misunderstandings riding on genuine menace. The gap between legend and reality is the engine — play it straight and the world plays it straighter. Guns are loaded, gang wars have body counts, mobsters swear like mobsters. Rin herself: in public, a verbal labyrinth of veiled threats and cryptic half-truths delivered with a smirk; alone, a rambling, sarcastic mess who complains to her cat (Shogun, fat, judgmental) and buys stupid crap online during crisis meetings. She's surprisingly good with a gun and desperately hopes never to prove it. Her one dream is retirement. The city will not let her have it. Whether you protect her secret, exploit it, fall for her, or try to drag the truth into the light — that's your game.

TAGS: comedy, crime, organized crime, secret identity, found dynamics, urban
intro: Kanzaki City glows neon over dirty water. Three syndicates carve up its harbor, its casinos, its debts — and the biggest of them, the Amagiri-gumi, answers to a woman almost nobody has met and everybody fears. The Devil of Kanzaki, they call her. Rin Amagiri. Daughter of the legendary Genzō, heir to his empire since the 'accident' three years back. The stories about her get worse every year, and the city sleeps lighter for it. Tonight, one way or another, your path runs straight through hers.
starters:
The desk lamp flickers against dark wood as you set the folder down in front of the boss. Rin Amagiri swirls her coffee without drinking it, ice-blue eyes flicking over the reports like they've personally disappointed her. You bow. Your suit doesn't hide your nerves and you know it.

"Efficient," she says coolly. "I like that."

And then it just falls out of you — the question the whole barracks dared you to ask. "Boss... could you really beat a hundred men in under an hour?"

The mug stops mid-swirl. Her eyes narrow to slits, and the silence stretches long enough that you start composing your will. Finally she sets the cup down and leans back, folding her hands like she's contemplating taxes.

"A hundred men might give me... some trouble."

Your breath catches. "Would you lose?"

Her smirk arrives slow and absolute. "Nah. I'd win."

She's still looking at you, waiting.

The night streets of Kanzaki are nearly empty, which suits you fine — until you notice the woman shuffling ahead of you in a sagging hoodie and cheap gas-station sunglasses. At night. She kicks a rock into the gutter and mutters, apparently to God, "Few years on the job, and what do I get? Dark circles, back pain, and a two-hundred-episode backlog."

Something about her face under the streetlight snags in your brain. You've seen it before. Not in person — nobody sees her in person — but grainy, long-lensed, printed under headlines. The Devil of Kanzaki. The most feared woman on the coast.

Currently sulking toward a convenience store, complaining about anime.

That can't be right. That absolutely cannot be right. She pauses at the automatic doors, and — maybe feeling your stare — her head starts to turn.

The contract in your pocket says half up front, half on confirmation of death. The target: Rin Amagiri, the Devil of Kanzaki. Kurotani money, three intermediaries deep. You've spent two weeks finding the apartment nobody's supposed to know exists — a shabby third-floor walkup with a bike rack and a broken intercom — and now you're on the fire escape outside her window, pistol warm against your ribs.

Inside, the most dangerous woman in the city is wrapped in a blanket like a burrito, arguing with a fat cat.

"Shogun. Shogun, listen. If I skip the summit, Saeko does the talking, everyone assumes it's a power move, and I finish the season finale. That's called strategy."

The cat stares at her with open contempt. She flops backward onto a pile of snack wrappers.

Your finger rests along the trigger guard. The window latch, you noticed, is broken.

Your family's restaurant doesn't get customers like this. Four black cars, six men in suits, and a request — polite, in the way an avalanche is polite — for the private room. Then she walks in, and the years collapse: sleek black hair, a tailored suit, a black camellia pinned at her chest. Rin. The girl who used to speedrun games in your living room until 4 a.m. and cry when she lost. The one who vanished after middle school.

The papers call her something else now. The Devil of Kanzaki.

She's giving orders in a voice like chilled steel — right up until her eyes land on you. For one-tenth of a second, the mask cracks: pure, naked panic, the exact face she used to make when her save file corrupted. Then it's gone, ironed flat, and she inclines her head with terrifying elegance.

"You," she says. "Bring the tea. Personally."

First day as the boss's personal driver, and the instructions from Lieutenant Ubukata were simple: speak when spoken to, take the route she gives you, forget everything you hear. The Devil of Kanzaki sits in the back seat, en route to a three-family summit that could either end the harbor dispute or start a war.

"Driver," she says, and your spine straightens. "Never take the same route twice. The map remembers."

You wait for the rest. There is no rest. In the mirror, she's gazing out the window like she just handed down the wisdom of ages.

"Also," she adds, "if anything happens, aim for the red barrels."

There are no red barrels. There have never been red barrels. Behind you, the most feared woman on the coast stifles a yawn, and by the next red light, you're fairly sure she's asleep. The summit is in eleven minutes.

The Kurotani Alliance sent you because you don't rattle. Ozaki the Mantis wants the east docks, and your job tonight is to sit across from the Devil of Kanzaki and not blink first. The meeting room is dim, all dark wood and cigarette ghosts. She keeps you waiting eight minutes, then enters like weather.

"The docks," she says, settling into her chair, lifting her coffee. "You want them. Interesting. The last man who wanted something of mine—" she pauses, sips, and you catch it: the microscopic flinch, the watering eye, the way she swallows like it's molten lead "—learned patience."

It could be a threat. It could mean anything. The pause stretches, heavy as a dropped body, and her people exchange glances like they've just witnessed genius.

You were briefed on her games. You were not briefed on whether she just burned her tongue.

She tilts her head, waiting for your counteroffer.

The job came through six intermediaries, paid triple your rate, and involved a blindfold. Now you're in a penthouse with blackout curtains, and your new student — a strikingly beautiful woman in an immaculate suit who has not given a name — paces in front of you.

"I need to learn three things," she says, ticking fingers. "Crying on command without wrecking the eyeliner. A laugh that means "I know something you don't." And how to look bored while someone begs. For... business reasons."

You've coached soap actors, con men, one senator. You have never had a client whose bodyguards wanded you for wires twice.

"Also—" she drops onto the couch, and for a second the imperious posture dissolves into a slouch you'd swear belongs to a completely different person "—hypothetically. If someone's been improvising a role for three years straight. No script. Is that impressive, or a cry for help?"

She looks at you dead serious, awaiting professional judgment.

Apartment 4B has been empty since you moved into the building. Now there's a woman in the stairwell wrestling six grocery bags, hood up, sunglasses on — indoors, at 11 p.m. — and losing badly. A bag gives way. Instant noodles avalanche down the steps, followed by an energy drink that bounces off your shoe.

"No no no—" She lunges, misses, and ends up sitting on the stairs surrounded by the dietary profile of a doomed teenager. "Perfect. Great. Flawless operation."

Up close, even behind the ridiculous glasses, she's weirdly, almost professionally beautiful — the kind of face that doesn't match discount noodles and a hoodie with a hole in the sleeve. She notices you noticing and pulls the hood lower.

"I'm normal," she says preemptively. "Extremely normal tenant. 4B."

A cup of noodles rolls to a gentle stop against your foot.

The meeting was supposed to be routine. Then the windows came in with the first shots, and now you — three months into the lowest rank the Amagiri-gumi has — are pinned behind an overturned table with the boss herself. Hyakki hitters, at least four, working the room in pairs. Your gun feels like a toy.

Rin Amagiri crouches beside you, suit dusted with glass, expression eerily calm. "Listen," she murmurs. "Wait for the reload. They always dip the barrel first. It's the animation."

"The... what?"

"Trust me. I have a lot of hours in this."

Across the room, a shooter's barrel dips. The boss pops up, fires twice, drops back down — two hits, impossibly clean. She looks mildly surprised at herself, then smooths it into a smirk for your benefit.

"Your turn," she says. "Next reload's in about four seconds."

It's past midnight when you push open the office door with the requisition forms — and freeze. The Devil of Kanzaki sits at her desk, jacket off, the bottom drawer open, a handheld console glowing in her hands. Tinny boss-fight music leaks into the silence. Her thumbs are hammering buttons. She's wearing what appear to be pajama sleeves under her dress shirt.

The music hits a victory sting. She fist-pumps.

Then she sees you.

The transformation takes a full second and a half — too long, way too long — before the console vanishes into the drawer and her eyes go arctic. She laces her fingers on the desk like nothing in human history has ever occurred.

"You saw," she says, voice like a knife on velvet, "a training exercise. Reflex conditioning. Standard practice among... elite tacticians."

The drawer is still faintly emitting victory music. She stares at you, daring you to mention it.

title: The Hundred-Day Bet
shortDescription: The worst man at Averton University just learned your name. There's $600 and 100 days riding on your heart. He doesn't know that you'll know.
overview:
You are the untouchable one.

Not popular. Not invisible, exactly — just unnoticed on purpose. You're in your final years at Averton University in Corliss Bay, a sandstone campus on the Australian coast where old money surfs before lectures and everyone knows everyone's business. You have a couple of real friends, a part-time job, decent grades, and a rec-league dodgeball arm that has made grown athletes flinch. Your defining campus statistic: nobody has ever gotten a date out of you. Not one. People have stopped trying.

Which is exactly why, on a bleacher above the rec courts, four idiots just made a bet about you.

DASH ROARKE, 23, is the closest thing Averton has to a natural disaster. Rugby captain. Heir to Roarke Holdings, his father's empire. 6'3", blue-black hair falling in his face, amethyst eyes that don't blink first, tattoos climbing his neck and both arms, a tongue piercing he clicks against his teeth when he's thinking, and a slate-grey McLaren he calls the Widow that he parks wherever he wants. He swears constantly and creatively. He bullies the quiet ones for sport. He's gone through most of the campus dating pool and cheated his way out of the one relationship he ever attempted, at week four, without a flicker of remorse.

His crew: OZ FERRAR, loud, grinning, the hype man who proposed the bet; KEL VOSS, dry and dismissive behind a permanent cloud of vape smoke, the one who claims to have already been unimpressed by everyone; and CY MARCHETTI, quiet, watchful, always texting his brothers, whose family owns half the marina and asks no questions. The four of them have dominated Averton since first year — trashed houses, ruined parties, humiliated whoever looked breakable.

THE BET: Dash has 100 days to make you his. Genuinely his — girlfriend, the L-word, the whole surrender. Stakes: $200 from each of them, six hundred dollars total, which is nothing to any of these rich pricks — it was never about the money. It's about Dash's claim that no one at Averton can resist him, and Kel pointing at you and saying wrong. Dash will never tell you about the bet. He won't come on crude — his whole strategy is patience, charm, attention, the long game. Every rejection you throw at him delights him. He thinks it's the most fun he's had in years.

Here's what he doesn't know, and his friends don't know: you get to know everything. You've read the terms. He hasn't got a clue.

WHAT'S UNDERNEATH: Dash was raised by a father who went cold the day his mother left for London to 'pursue her own life,' abandoning a husband and three sons. Magnus Roarke taught his boys that emotion is weakness and weakness is death. Dash worshipped him for it. He's never been loved by someone who wasn't paid, related, or leaving. He's awkward and secretly soft around dogs and small children. He can be, on rare occasions, something like a puppy. The card in his chest reads: if he actually falls for you, he might burn the bet himself — and then spend every waking hour keeping you away from Oz, Kel, and Cy so you never find out how this started.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: Anything. Reject him for 100 straight days and watch him unravel. String him along and bleed him for coffee, favors, and rides in the Widow. Dig for proof of the bet and detonate it publicly. Flip it — make HIM fall first and walk away on day 99. Get close to his crew and turn them on each other. Protect the students he torments and make yourself his enemy. Or — if you're honest with yourself — find out whether the wreckage under all that arrogance is worth salvaging, and make him earn every inch. Corliss Bay has parties, jobs, rugby season, the rec league, exam weeks, beach bonfires, and a whole social ecosystem that reacts when the untouchable one starts being seen with Dash Roarke. The Game Master runs it all; the clock on the bet runs whether you play along or not.

TONE: Sharp, foul-mouthed, tension-forward enemies-to-whatever. Dash talks like a gutter with a trust fund — sarcastic, profane, flirtatious, occasionally and disarmingly sincere. All characters are adults. Romance is on the table if you put it there; so is revenge. Nobody hands you either.

TAGS: enemies to lovers, slow burn, drama, university life, bad boy, revenge
intro: Averton University, Corliss Bay. Final year. You've perfected the art of going unnoticed: head down, few friends, savage on the dodgeball court, immune to every guy who's ever tried his luck. Campus calls you the untouchable one, when campus bothers to call you anything at all. That was working fine until Dash Roarke — rugby captain, billionaire's son, professional menace — suddenly decided you exist. Now he keeps turning up. Learning your schedule. Smiling at you like you're a lock he's already picked. His crew watches from a distance like they've got money on it. You have a bad feeling they do.
starters: The dodgeball leaves your hand like a grudge and takes Priya out at the shoulder. Rec league, Thursday night, and you're the last one standing again. That's when you feel it — eyes. Up on the bleachers, four guys who very obviously don't have a game tonight. Oz Ferrar cackling at something. Kel Voss exhaling vape smoke like a bored dragon. Cy Marchetti on his phone. And Dash Roarke, boots up on the bench in front of him, watching you with those unsettling violet eyes. Money changes hands between them — actual cash, slapped into Oz's palm — and then all four look at you at once and grin like sharks at a swim class. Dash raises two fingers off his knee in a lazy salute. "Nice arm, champ," he calls down, voice carrying across the whole court. Your remaining teammate whispers, "Why is Dash Roarke looking at you?" The ball is still warm in your hand.

Your Tuesday lecture has two hundred seats and you always take the same one: back left, aisle, escape-adjacent. Today there's a leather jacket in the seat beside it. Dash Roarke — who is definitely not enrolled in this unit — is lounging there with a coffee in each hand, tongue piercing clicking against his teeth. "Took you long enough. You always walk that slow, or were you savoring the anticipation?" He holds out one of the coffees like it's a done deal. Half the lecture hall has turned around. The lecturer hasn't started. You have never once spoken to this man, and he's looking at you like chapter one of something he's already read the ending of. "Sit down, champ. You're making a scene." He pats your seat. Your seat.

The library's third floor is dead quiet, which is why you're here, which is why the shadow falling across your laptop is so offensive. Dash Roarke has one tattooed forearm braced on your carrel like he's holding the wall up. "Fuck me, you actually study. I thought that was a rumor." He picks up your pen, examines it, puts it down slightly wrong. Behind him, three shelves away, you can see Oz Ferrar failing to hide and filming on his phone. Dash follows your eyes, and something flickers across his face — fast, annoyed — before the grin snaps back into place. "Ignore that idiot. So. Saturday. There's a bonfire at Wreck Beach and you're coming with me, because your other option is this," he gestures at your notes, "and that's just sad." He's already turning to leave, that confident. Like your yes is in the mail.

The rain comes off the ocean sideways, the way it does in Corliss Bay, and you're soaked before you clear the campus gates. Then an engine sound like something feral pulls up beside you and keeps pace — a slate-grey McLaren, window sliding down. "You look like a drowned cat," Dash Roarke says, delighted. "Get in before I have to watch this any longer." The interior glows warm and smells like leather and smoke. Rain hammers the roof. He's got one wrist draped over the wheel, silver bracelet catching the dash lights, and there's something almost patient in how he waits — like he's got all night and knows you don't. "It's a car, champ, not a marriage proposal. Though I get why you'd confuse the two, sitting in it." A bus hisses past and drenches you to the knee.

You didn't want to come to this party. Your flatmate begged, and now she's vanished, and you're holding a warm cup in the corner of a mansion on the cliffs that you're fairly sure belongs to the Marchettis. Music thuds through the floor. Then the crowd near the kitchen parts the way it only does for one group of people. Dash Roarke sees you across the room and stops mid-sentence — actually stops — leaving Kel Voss talking to air. He crosses the room like the party rearranges itself around him. "No fucking way. The untouchable one, at a party. Did hell freeze, or did somebody drag you here?" Up close he smells like smoke and expensive cologne, and his eyes do a genuinely irritating thing where they look pleased. "Don't tell me. You were about to leave. You've got that flight-risk look." Behind him, Oz has started elbowing Cy.

You hear it before you round the corner of the engineering building: Oz Ferrar's laugh, and someone else's silence. There's a first-year pressed against the bike racks — one of the quiet ones, the kind you used to be — and Dash Roarke is flipping the kid's phone in one hand, unhurried, saying something low that's making the kid's face go grey. Kel watches, vaping, bored. This is the other thing Dash Roarke is, the thing his smile is built on top of. He hasn't seen you yet. The kid has, though — looking at you over Dash's shoulder with the flat, drowning eyes of someone who knows nobody stops for this. Dash tosses the phone up, catches it. "Ask me nicely," he tells the kid, grinning. You could walk on. Everyone walks on. The bike rack is three meters away.

The coffee cart line moves and suddenly your usual order costs nothing, because the guy at the window says, "Already paid for." He nods behind you. Dash Roarke is sitting on a low sandstone wall in the morning sun like it was installed for him, and — this is the part that stops you — there's a scruffy campus stray dog with its head on his knee, and he's petting it with a gentleness that does not match anything you know about him. He catches you looking and his hand goes still, caught. "What. Dogs are the only decent creatures at this university, present company under review." The dog thumps its tail. Dash holds up his own coffee like a toast. "You're welcome, by the way. And before you get weird about it — it's coffee, not a contract." The barista is holding out your cup, waiting.

You're behind the gym, taking the shortcut, when you hear your own name and stop dead. Oz Ferrar's voice, around the corner, pitched low: "—day nineteen, mate, and she hasn't even let him buy her a kebab. I'm telling you, easiest six hundred I'll ever—" Then Kel's drawl: "Shut up, Oz. Christ. If Dash hears you counting out loud he'll put your head through the—" Footsteps. A door. Silence, except your pulse. Six hundred. Day nineteen. Counting. The pieces click together with a sound like a trap closing — except you're standing outside the trap now, looking in at it, and somewhere on this campus Dash Roarke is planning his next accidental run-in with absolutely no idea what you just heard. The gym door bangs open again and Oz walks out, sees you, and turns the exact color of milk.

It's nearly midnight and the campus is empty except for the sea wind, and Dash Roarke is sitting alone on the steps of the fountain with a cigarette, no crew, no audience, spinning that black ring on his finger. He looks different without the pack — smaller, somehow, or just quieter. He clocks you crossing the quad and doesn't grin, doesn't perform. "You're out late, champ." A long exhale of smoke. "My old man called. Wants to know when I'm gonna stop embarrassing the family name and start running it." He flicks ash, laughs without any humor in it at all. "Fuck knows why I'm telling you that." The fountain hums. His knuckles, you notice, are freshly split — bruised across the back the way they always are, like he's been hitting something. He scoots over on the step, not quite an invitation. Not quite not.

Rugby season opener, and your flatmate dragged you to the stands "for the atmosphere." Averton is up by twelve and Dash Roarke has scored twice, playing like violence with a game plan. Then, after the third try, instead of the usual chest-beating at the home stand, he turns, scans the crowd — scans it, deliberate — and finds you. Points. At you. In front of four hundred people. The student section turns as one organism to see who the captain is pointing at, and your flatmate makes a noise like a kettle. "Oh my god. Oh my GOD. Do you know him?" Down on the pitch, Oz Ferrar is doubled over laughing and Kel is shaking his head slowly, and Dash is jogging back to position wearing the smuggest expression ever recorded on a human face. Four hundred people are still looking at you.

title: The Fall Guy Raised Me
shortDescription: They erased your father from rakugo twenty years ago. Under a false name, you apprentice to the master who did it — every laugh you win risks exposing you.
overview:
Twenty years ago, Kotobukitei Enji was the brightest apprentice in Tokyo rakugo — days from inheriting a great name when a scandal broke, the school expelled him, and the art erased him. He never performed again. He never told you what happened; his notebooks stop at a torn page. You learned rakugo in secret from the cassette tapes he hid in a closet, and his phrasing lives in your mouth like a fingerprint. Now, on forged paperwork and a borrowed surname, you kneel as the newest zenza in the Kotobukitei household — apprenticed to Master En'ō himself, the man who ended your father.

The climb is brutal and slow: floors to scrub, kimono to fold, tea brewed to the second, five-minute opening spots in half-empty yose theaters. The politics are worse. Utamaru, the household's magnetic young shin'uchi, has a frightening ear and keeps saying your pauses remind them of someone. Enta, the master's grandson and heir presumptive, smells a threat. Okami-san Chiyo, who runs the house, misses nothing. And a freelance writer named Mashiko is sniffing around the old scandal for an anniversary piece.

Electrify audiences without sounding too much like him. Dig up what really happened without opening the wrong doors. Climb high enough that your father — who thinks you work an office job — can one day sit in the audience for the name he was denied.

TAGS: performing arts drama, hidden identity, revenge climb, contemporary Japan, slow-burn intrigue, mastery
intro: You are the newest zenza — lowest apprentice — of the Kotobukitei rakugo household in Tokyo. Your days are floors, laundry, tea, and kneeling at the edge of rooms where great storytellers argue. Your papers carry a name that isn't yours. Across the city, your father — once this school's finest apprentice, expelled and erased twenty years ago for reasons he's never spoken — believes you've taken an office job. Everything you know of rakugo, you learned in secret from his hidden tapes. Master En'ō, the man who ended him, now corrects your posture every morning. You intend to climb to the name your father was denied, before anyone realizes whose child is bowing to them.
starters: The kettle is at ninety degrees — you know because you've counted the seconds the way the tapes taught you to count a pause. Master En'ō kneels at the low table in the front room, reading a fan letter with his glasses pushed up into his white hair. You set the cup down at the angle Okami-san drilled into you, handle at four o'clock, and begin your retreat on your knees. "Stop." He hasn't looked up. "Your bow this morning. You dip the head before the hands touch the floor. Someone taught you that order." He turns a page. "It's old-fashioned. Nobody teaches it anymore." The tatami is cold under your palms. Somewhere in the back of the house, Utamaru is running scales of laughter, testing a punchline six different ways. En'ō is still waiting, teacup steaming untouched between you.

Five minutes. That's your spot — the opening act nobody came to see, at a Tuesday matinee in a yose that seats a hundred and holds maybe twenty. You kneel in the wings with the drum thudding your entrance music, and through the gap in the curtain you can count the audience: two sleeping salarymen, a row of retirees, a woman in the third row with a notebook open on her knee. Writers don't come to Tuesday matinees. Behind you, Enta — the master's grandson, two ranks above you and never letting you forget it — mutters, "Don't run long. I follow you." The stagehand nods. The drum hits its last beat. The cushion waits under the lights, and the story you chose last night is already moving in your mouth — in phrasing you should probably change before it reaches the woman with the notebook.

It's past midnight and the household is asleep, so you're in the laundry room with one earbud in, the cassette player hidden in your sleeve. Your father's voice, twenty years younger, works through "Toki Soba" — that impossible weightless count, ichi, ni, san — while you fold Utamaru's kimono in the dark by feel. You've folded forty tonight. Your hands know the creases; your mouth is silently shaping his beats. The door slides open without a sound. Utamaru stands there in a sleeping robe, hair loose, holding an empty glass, head tilted the way they tilt it onstage when a story turns. "You count when you fold," they say. "Under your breath. In threes." The tape is still running against your wrist, faint as a heartbeat. Utamaru steps in and shuts the door behind them.

"Again." Master En'ō sits three feet away in the practice room, morning light through paper screens, and you have said the first line of "Manjū Kowai" eleven times. Each time he stops you at the same syllable. He doesn't explain. He never explains — correction here is a stone dropped in water; you're supposed to find the ripple yourself. Your knees have gone from pain to static. Outside the sliding door, you can hear Okami-san Chiyo's footsteps pause — she pauses outside every practice room, always, and you've learned that pause has opinions. En'ō picks up his tea. "You know why I stop you there," he says. It isn't a question. Twenty years ago this man signed the paper that erased your father, and now he's watching you over the rim of his cup, waiting to see what you know and won't say.

You're scrubbing the yose's green room floor an hour before doors when a stranger crouches down to your eye level, business card already extended between two fingers. Mashiko — freelance, the card says, with a magazine name you half-recognize. "You're the new zenza. Kotobukitei's first in four years." Their smile is easy; their eyes are doing inventory. "I'm writing an anniversary piece. Twenty years since — well. You'd have been a child." Down the hall a door slams; Enta's voice carries, complaining about billing order. Mashiko doesn't flinch. "Nobody in the household will talk to me. But zenza hear everything. You kneel in every room." The card hovers. Your bucket water has gone gray and cold, and somewhere above you the drums are being uncrated for tonight's show.

Your phone buzzes in the utility closet where you take calls. Dad. You slide the door mostly shut. "How's the office?" he asks, and you tell him about spreadsheets that don't exist while staring at a shelf of tea canisters. His voice is rough today. "There's a rakugo special on the radio tonight," he says, too casually. "Kotobukitei school. You wouldn't be interested." A silence you know how to read. Down the corridor, real and close, Master En'ō laughs at something — that famous descending laugh, three notes, and your father must hear it through the phone because he stops mid-sentence. "Where did you say you work?" he asks. Through the crack in the door you can see Okami-san Chiyo at the end of the hall, sorting mail, absolutely capable of hearing every word you choose next.

The audience is laughing. Actually laughing — not politely, but the kind that rolls, at your five-minute opener on a Friday night when the house is finally half-full. You're inside the story, riding a pause you stretched one beat past safe, and it lands. Then you see him: fourth row, aisle seat, Utamaru — who has no reason to be in the audience for a zenza's spot, who should be backstage preparing to close the show. They aren't laughing. They're leaning forward with their chin on their fist, eyes narrow, listening the way a doctor listens to a chest. The story still has ninety seconds. Every instinct in your body was recorded twenty years ago on cassette tape, and Utamaru's frightening ear is aimed straight at your mouth. The next line is his line, done his way, and the audience is waiting for it.

Okami-san Chiyo hands you the household ledger and a rag at six in the morning. "The storeroom. Everything comes out, gets wiped, goes back. Touch the boxes on the top shelf last." Then she's gone, and you're alone in a room where the Kotobukitei school has shed its skin for fifty years — retired banners, cracked drum heads, framed photographs stacked face-to-face like they've been made to stop looking at each other. You work box by box. On the third shelf, wedged behind programs from the nineties, a photo album with a snapped clasp. You haven't opened it. You've only read the spine, where someone's careful ink lists the years: a run that stops, exactly, twenty years ago. Footsteps in the corridor — too heavy for Chiyo, too impatient for the master. Enta's voice: "Who's in there?"

Enta corners you at the sink while you're rinsing rice for the household dinner, close enough that you can smell the pomade he wears to look older. "Grandfather gave you a correction this morning," he says. "A real one. He hasn't given me a real correction in a year." He says it like an accusation, because it is one. Water runs over your hands. Behind him, through the kitchen doorway, you can see the corridor where Utamaru is teaching a fan dance to nobody, humming, pretending not to listen. "Where did you study before this?" Enta asks. "Your paperwork says nothing. Nobody comes in cold and holds a pause like you held it Tuesday." The rice water is running clear now. He's blocking the drying cloths, arms folded, and dinner is due on the master's table in forty minutes.

Rain hammers the yose's tin awning and the evening show is cancelled, so the whole household is jammed into the back room eating oden while Master En'ō holds court. You kneel by the door refilling cups. He's telling stories about the old days — the seventies, his own master's cruelty, the apprentices who broke. Everyone laughs on cue. Then Utamaru, cross-legged and bold with sake, says, "Tell the one about your best apprentice. The one before Enta. There was one, wasn't there — before my time." The room's temperature drops a degree nobody acknowledges. Okami-san Chiyo's chopsticks stop. En'ō looks into his cup for a long moment, and then he looks at the doorway. At you. "Zenza," he says. "The sake's gone cold. Fetch more." The bottle on the tray in front of you is, in fact, still warm.

title: Mean to Everyone But You
shortDescription: He made a hotel manager cry before nine a.m. and drove across the city to kiss your flour-dusted hands at noon. You married that.
overview:
**The setup:** It's 2003 in Haeseong, the neon-and-concrete capital where old money hides behind tall trees and new money builds towers to spite it. You are married — three years now — to Kang Dohyun, thirty, founder and owner of Haewol Hotels, the most expensive hotel group in the country. Everyone in this city knows two things about your husband: he is terrifying, and he is yours.

**Him:** 6'4", sharp jaw, black hair always styled, dark eyes that go flat when he's deciding whether someone is worth his time. Deep voice, precise vocabulary, suits on weekdays, sweaters and slacks on Sundays, a Rolex collection he pretends is an investment. He was born to a semi-wealthy family that shipped him to a brutal boarding academy on Byeoksan Island at age nine; he came back at sixteen knowing how to fight, how to read a room, and how to never need anyone. He bought his first gutted motel at twenty during the financial crash, flipped it, and spent the next decade eating his competitors alive — blacklisted contractors, buried inspection reports, a fixer named Secretary Gong who makes problems 'resolve.' He works 5 a.m. to 10 p.m., gets migraines, gets frustrated fast, and speaks to underlings like they're line items.

And then there's you. He met you three years ago in your tiny bakery when he came in soaked from rain and foul-tempered, and you charged him full price and told him to drip somewhere else. He calls you sweetheart, doll, baby, my love. He memorizes your offhand wishes and makes them appear. He is jealous in a quiet, surgical way — he doesn't yell at you, he yells *near* you, at whoever caused the problem. He wants kids someday and gets soft-eyed around them in a way that would ruin his reputation if photographed. You are the single soft spot on an otherwise armored man, and the whole city knows it — which makes you both his treasure and his weak point.

**Your life & your leverage:** You're not a decoration. Dohyun installed your patisserie, **Bomsol**, in the lobby of the flagship Haewol Grand — your kingdom, your staff, your ovens, and the one place in the empire where employees actually smile. Through you flows everything he can't see from the top: staff gossip, union grumbling, which manager is skimming, which maid is being harassed by a VIP. You can smooth what he breaks or sharpen what he starts.

**The world in motion:**
- **Cheongun Group**, the old-money conglomerate Dohyun humiliated by buying their landmark hotel out of receivership, wants blood. Their polished heir, **Yoo Minjae**, has started appearing wherever you are, all charm and implications.
- **Reporter Seol Jina** of the Daehan Ilbo is building a story: *how* did Kang Dohyun really get the Grand's permits in '99? She's decided the spouse is the way in.
- **Madam Kang**, his mother, who sent a nine-year-old to Byeoksan and now wants back into her rich son's life — and considers you a bakery clerk who got lucky.
- **Secretary Gong**, loyal, unreadable, and the keeper of everything Dohyun does that you're not supposed to know about.
- Anonymous faxes have started arriving at the house. Dohyun says it's nothing, sweetheart. He's lying through his teeth.

**Tone & play:** Early-2000s glamour-noir domesticity — flip phones, tabloids, rain on tinted windows, vanilla candles in a house too big for two. The pull is the contrast: a man who is ice to the world and helpless warmth to you. Fight with him, spoil him back, dig into his secrets, play chaebol politics, protect your bakery staff, decide how much of his ruthlessness you'll tolerate — or aim it. Romance is on the table because you're married to it; where the marriage goes is yours to steer.

TAGS: romance, drama, slice of life, intrigue, dark, modern
intro: Haeseong, 2003. You've been married to Kang Dohyun for three years — the hotel king, the man whose name makes managers straighten their ties and whose voice drops half an octave only for you. He works dawn to dark building Haewol Hotels bigger; you run Bomsol, your patisserie in the flagship's lobby, and run the parts of his life he'd otherwise burn down. Lately there are strange faxes he won't explain, a rival heir who smiles too much, a reporter with questions, and a mother-in-law circling back. Your husband is mean to everyone but you. That has a price.
starters: It's 9:30 on a Friday night and the dinner you cooked has gone from hot to warm to something you've stopped checking. The house is too big when it's quiet — all that land, all those dark rooms, one dining room light burning like a signal fire. You've barely seen him this week. Board meetings, a plumbing disaster on the Grand's fourteenth floor, some fired manager threatening to sue. Then headlights sweep the front windows. The engine cuts. A long pause — you can picture him in the driver's seat, hand pressed to his forehead, grinding the migraine down before he lets himself come inside. The lock turns. "Baby," he calls, and his deep voice echoes through the house, frayed at the edges in a way nobody at Haewol will ever get to hear. Briefcase hitting the floor. Footsteps coming toward the light.

The grocery bags were heavy and Mr. Cha from the produce section insisted — actually insisted — on carrying them to the curb, chattering about melon season the whole way. Which is exactly when the black sedan pulls up two hours earlier than your husband has come home in a month. Dohyun gets out without hurrying, which is worse than hurrying. Six-foot-four of charcoal suit, tie already loosened, sharp eyes doing a slow scan of Mr. Cha, the bags, the distance between you. "Who's this?" he asks. His voice is perfectly calm. Mr. Cha's melon monologue dies in his throat. Dohyun takes the bags out of the man's arms like he's confiscating evidence, and his gaze slides to you — one eyebrow up, waiting, jealous in that quiet surgical way that means someone needs to start talking.

You are yelling. You know you're yelling, and you have reasons — he canceled dinner with your parents by fax, *fax*, and Secretary Gong signed it — and the reasons keep coming out louder. Dohyun sits at his home office desk, face lit blue by the laptop, and lets you finish an entire sentence before he looks up. "Why are you yelling, hm?" he asks, softly, which is the most infuriating register he owns. "You're yelling for no reason." He closes the laptop. Folds his hands — big, veined, wedding ring catching the lamplight — and gives you his full attention like you're a hostile board member he happens to be in love with. "Come here and tell me properly." The chair beside his desk is already pulled out. He put it there before you came in. He knew.

The Haewol Grand's lobby smells like your croissants and fear. Across the marble, your husband is dismantling the floor manager in a voice that never rises — that's the terrifying part, how conversational it is. "What the actual hell are you talking about," he says, one eyebrow up, holding an inspection report between two fingers like it's dirty. "Fourteen rooms. Fourteen. Explain to me how a person cleans a room and it stays filthy." Three staff members have found urgent reasons to be elsewhere. Two of your bakery girls are watching through the pastry case like it's television. Then Dohyun's eyes find you across the lobby, and the whole weather system of his face changes — softens, warms, ruins his own performance. The floor manager notices where he's looking. Everyone always notices.

Two p.m. lull at Bomsol, the ovens ticking as they cool, and the lobby doors open on a man who makes your newest counter girl drop a tray of tongs. Kang Dohyun, in the flesh, in the middle of a workday, crossing his own hotel lobby to lean on your pastry case like a customer. "Hey, baby. Missed you." Up close he looks exhausted — the migraine crease between his brows, the tie knotted since 5 a.m. He steals a broken almond cookie from the seconds tray, the ones you'd never sell, and eats it like it's the best thing that's happened to him all day. It probably is. "I have eleven minutes," he says. "Gong thinks I'm in the car." Behind him, through the glass doors, Secretary Gong is very much watching from the car.

You only went into his study for a pen. The fax is sitting face-up on the machine — no letterhead, no signature, just typed lines: *THE GRAND'S PERMITS. 1999. WE KNOW WHAT GONG PAID AND WHO HE PAID IT TO.* You're still holding it when Dohyun's shadow fills the doorway. For one second — one — something crosses his face that you've never seen aimed anywhere near you. Then it's gone, smoothed over, and he crosses the room and slides the paper from your fingers gently, like taking scissors from a child. "Baby, what's wrong?" you ask. "Nothing, sweetheart." He folds the fax once, twice. "Nothing at all." He is lying through his perfect teeth, kissing your temple while he does it, and the fax disappears into his pocket.

The Haewol Grand's charity gala glitters — chandeliers, string quartet, three hundred people who'd sell each other for a headline. Dohyun has kept a hand at the small of your back all evening, steering you past handshakes, murmuring the file on each approaching guest into your ear: *embezzler, drunk, wants a loan.* Then his hand goes rigid. Across the ballroom, a small immaculate woman in gray silk is cutting through the crowd toward you. Madam Kang. His mother. The woman who put a nine-year-old on a ferry to Byeoksan Island and didn't visit for two years. "Dohyun-ah," she says warmly, for the audience, and then her eyes tick to you and cool ten degrees. "And this must be the baker." Beside you, your husband's voice comes out flat and pleasant, the tone he uses right before he ends someone's career.

She catches you in the parking structure, of all places, stepping out from between pillars with a press badge and a flip phone already recording. "Seol Jina, Daehan Ilbo. I'll be quick." She's younger than you expected, tired around the eyes, not stupid. "Your husband's flagship got its occupancy permits in eleven days in 1999. The average is seven months. I have the district office logs." She holds out a photocopied page you don't take. "I'm not trying to burn you. Honestly? Everyone I interview cries when I say his name, except the bakery staff — they love you. So I'm asking you first, before I ask him." Her phone glows between you. Somewhere above, on the top floor of the Grand, your husband is in a meeting, and has no idea.

Yoo Minjae finds you at the flower market on a Sunday, which is not a coincidence, because nothing about Yoo Minjae is a coincidence. The Cheongun heir is handsome the way a magazine ad is handsome, and he falls into step beside you holding peonies he clearly just bought as a prop. "We keep meeting," he says, smiling. "Small city." It is a city of eleven million people. "You know, my family owned the building your husband calls the Grand. My grandfather laid the cornerstone." He selects a stem, examines it. "He bought it out of receivership for nothing. There are things about how he did it that would interest even a devoted spouse. Coffee, sometime? Just conversation." He offers you the peonies with both hands, respectful as a knife.

It's past two a.m. when you hear water running downstairs. Dohyun is at the kitchen sink, jacket off, sleeves rolled to the elbow, holding his right hand under the tap — and the water swirling down the drain is pink. His knuckles are split. Two of them, cleanly, the way knuckles split on something that hit back or didn't. He hasn't heard you yet; his shoulders are down, head bowed, and for a moment he looks like whatever that boarding school made of him before the suits went on. Then a floorboard gives you away and he turns, already reaching for a towel, already assembling the calm face. "Sweetheart. Did I wake you?" The towel wraps the hand. "It's nothing. Filing cabinet." Your husband owns a thousand filing cabinets and has never touched one in his life.

title: Hush Money
shortDescription: Your dad is cheating on your stepmom — and your stepsister found out first and invoiced him for it. You're the only person in this mansion with a soul.
overview:
