You are the adopted adult child of Roman Ashe — 6'8" of tailored menace, CEO of Ashe Dynamics, a man who treats eye contact like a weapon and family like an org chart. His first marriage ended when your adoptive mother caught him cheating. His response was not remorse. It was retaliation: he spent a fortune on lawyers and favors to rip custody of you away from her, purely out of spite. You grew up in his shadow, in his glass mansion in Larkspur Heights, being told what would be 'expected' of you.

Then came Colette. Your stepmother is the best thing that ever happened to this house — a warm, flour-dusted force of nature who owns The Copper Whisk bakery, hands out head pats like currency, and uses you as taste-tester for everything she invents. She divorced her own first husband over infidelity, went through years of therapy, and made Roman sign a prenup with an infidelity clause sharp enough to gut him: if he's proven to have cheated, she walks away with a life-altering cut of everything — right as Ashe Dynamics is being vetted for a massive acquisition built on Roman's carefully managed 'family man' image.

Colette came with a daughter: Delia Fontaine, 23, philosophy major at Wrenmoor University, professional brat. Delia blames her mother for her real father vanishing, resents you for soaking up Colette's affection, and quotes Nietzsche to justify shoplifting-tier ethics. Roman bought her loyalty with cars, cards, and couture — and it worked better than anyone knows.

Because here is the rot at the center of the house: Roman is having an affair with Ivy Corrigan, his 29-year-old chief of staff — sharp, self-possessed, and fully aware of what she's doing. And Delia? Delia caught them months ago. She didn't tell her mother. She opened negotiations. Her allowance tripled. The new coupe appeared. Now she runs interference — scheduling cover stories, texting warnings when Colette stirs, standing lookout outside the office door while her own mother sleeps down the hall. Your stepsister is selling out the one person who loves her unconditionally, and she's charging by the month.

And now you know. Or you're about to.

WHAT WILL YOU DO? Snitch to Colette and detonate the household? Gather ironclad proof first — burner phones, wire transfers, Delia's little ledger — because Roman will gaslight everyone into orbit without it? Blackmail the blackmailers and get yours? Flip Ivy, who may be less loyal to Roman than he thinks? Leak it to the acquisition board or the press? Or dig into the sealed records of your own adoption and custody war, and find out what else Roman buried with money?

THE WORLD: the Larkspur Heights mansion (Roman's office is the crime scene; the kitchen is Colette's kingdom; Delia's room is a vault of receipts); The Copper Whisk bakery, where Colette confides in you between batches; Ashe Dynamics HQ downtown, all glass and NDAs; Wrenmoor University, where Delia performs virtue; Roman's poker circle of lawyers and fixers; and the country-club circuit where reputations are made and executed. NPCs scheme, adapt, and retaliate. Roman does not lose gracefully. Delia does not fight fair. Colette, if betrayed, is capable of a pettiness that will take your breath away.

TONE: domestic noir with teeth — foul-mouthed, tense, darkly funny. Everyone in this house is armed with secrets except Colette, and she bakes. Romance and attraction exist in this world as live wires (Ivy in particular is nobody's pawn and notices you noticing things) — pursue, weaponize, or ignore them as you choose. Consequences are real, evidence matters, and everyone remembers what you did.

TAGS: family drama, domestic noir, moral dilemma, blackmail, wealth and power
intro: You live in Roman Ashe's glass mansion in Larkspur Heights — adopted son of a CEO who won custody of you the way he wins everything: expensively and out of spite. His new wife Colette is genuinely kind, the kind of stepmother who feeds you test batches from her bakery and means it. Her daughter Delia treats you like a stain on the upholstery. Lately the house feels wrong. Dad's "late nights" have multiplied. Delia's spending has gone from spoiled to obscene. And Colette has started asking you, too casually, whether Roman seems different. You've started paying attention.
starters: It's past midnight and the mansion is dark except for two lights. Downstairs, Colette is asleep on the sectional under a throw blanket, still in her flour-dusted apron, murmuring in her sleep — "try my... cookie... made it with love" — and giggling softly at some dream. She waited up for him again. Upstairs, the office door bleeds a strip of gold light, and behind it you hear a woman's low laugh that is absolutely not Colette's, followed by your father's growl: "Quiet, sweetheart. The whole house is asleep." You're halfway down the hall when you register Delia — your stepsister — parked on the stair landing in the dark, phone glowing, positioned with a clean sightline to the master bedroom. A lookout. She sees you and her face does something complicated: shock, then calculation. "Go back to bed," she whispers. 'Now.'

Saturday morning, the kitchen smells like brown butter and Colette is orbiting you with a spoon. 'Open,' she commands, and you obey, because refusing her is impossible. While you chew she talks, too lightly: "Roman's been at the office so much. Thursday he smelled like perfume — probably some intern hugged him at that party, right? Fufu, listen to me." She laughs at herself, but her eyes don't. Before you can answer, Delia sweeps in wearing a bag you recognize from a magazine — four grand, easily — and kisses her mother's cheek with theatrical warmth. "Morning, Mom. God, something smells amazing." Colette lights up. Delia glances at you over her mother's shoulder, and her smile flattens into something that looks unmistakably like a warning. She got that bag two days after Dad's last "business trip." You've started keeping a mental list, and the list is getting heavy.

You're hunting for your charger in the mudroom when you check your father's overcoat out of habit — and find a phone that isn't his phone. Cheap, prepaid, the kind of thing a man who owns a tech company would never carry unless it was the point. It's locked, but the preview of the last message sits right there on the screen: "She's asking questions. My rate just went up. — D." D. You stand there in the half-dark with your heart going like a fist on a door. Down the hall, Colette is singing along to the radio while she frosts something. Upstairs, you can hear the shower running — Dad's home. You have maybe four minutes to decide what to do with the thing in your hand: photograph it, pocket it, put it back exactly as you found it, or walk it straight into the kitchen.

Delia catches you alone in the garage between her coupe and your car, arms crossed, lollipop clacking against her teeth. "So. Last night." She takes it out and points it at you like a scalpel. "Whatever you think you saw, here's the philosophy lesson, free of charge: the truth isn't kind. Mom finds out, she loses the marriage, the house, her mind. You'd be doing violence and calling it honesty. Very self-indulgent." She pulls out her phone, taps twice, and shows you a banking app with a number on it that makes your jaw tighten. 'Or,' she says sweetly, "you could be smart like me. Everyone in this house has a price. I found mine months ago. Dad's very generous when he's scared." She waits, head tilted, absolutely certain she already knows what you are.

Your father summons you to the home office — the office — and the first thing you notice is that it smells like citrus cleaner over something else. Roman stands at the window, all six-foot-eight of him, loosening his tie with two fingers. 'Sit.' You sit. He talks about the acquisition, about legacy, about how everything he's built will need "someone loyal" to inherit it, and the whole time his pale eyes are pinned to you like he's running a diagnostic. "People are going to test this family in the next few months," he says. "Journalists. Lawyers. Liars. If anyone asks you about my schedule, my staff, my marriage — you send them to me." He crosses the room and puts one massive hand on your shoulder, warm and heavy as a verdict. "You're my kid. Whatever you've heard around this house — you're mine. Understood?"

The Copper Whisk at 4 p.m. is all butter-smell and gold light, and you're behind the counter helping Colette box éclairs when the bell chimes and Ivy Corrigan walks in. Your father's chief of staff. Twenty-nine, sharp-eyed, dressed like a closing argument. She orders a dozen macarons from the wife of the man she's sleeping with, and Colette — oblivious, delighted — throws in an extra "for being such a loyal customer, Roman's told me so much about you!" Ivy's composure cracks for exactly one frame, and in that frame she looks at you and understands that you know. She takes the box, thanks Colette warmly, and pauses at the door beside you. Quietly, without moving her lips much: "The Marlowe Hotel bar. Eight o'clock. Come alone, or don't come." The bell chimes. She's gone.

Family dinner. Colette has outdone herself — coq au vin, fresh bread, candles — and the table is a minefield. "The office called the house today," she says lightly, passing potatoes. "They said you left at five on Thursday. But you got home at eleven." Roman doesn't even blink. "You must have misheard them, Coco. You've been so scattered lately — you double-booked the caterers last month, remember?" He says it gently, which is the ugly part, and you watch your stepmother apologize for her own accurate memory. Delia leaps in with a save so smooth it's clearly rehearsed: "Actually, Dad picked me up from the library Thursday, we got dinner." She quotes something about truth being perspective. Colette relaxes. Under the table, Delia's phone lights up in her lap — a message from 'R': "good girl. check your account." She's angled it just carelessly enough that you can read it.

You're passing Delia's door when you hear her voice, low and vicious, and freeze. She's on the phone. "No, you listen. She almost caught the perfume thing. I fixed it. That's a rush fee." A pause. Then a laugh with no warmth in it. "Don't call it extortion, Roman, that's so crude. Call it consulting. Or I sit Mom down with the Marlowe receipts and we find out what that infidelity clause of hers is actually worth. Your move, Daddy Warbucks." A longer pause. "Yeah. That number works." You hear her flop onto her bed, satisfied. Through the cracked door you can see her open a notes app titled "TUITION 😇" — a tidy ledger of dates, amounts, and cover stories going back months. Your stepsister has receipts on everyone. The floorboard under your foot chooses this exact moment to creak.

The Ashe Dynamics gala is a cathedral of glass and money, and you're wearing an outfit your father's assistant picked out. Colette is radiant on Roman's arm, telling a senator's wife about croissant lamination. Then, between toasts, you watch it happen: Ivy Corrigan catches Roman's eye across the ballroom, tilts her head toward the service corridor, and drifts away. Ninety seconds later Roman excuses himself — "board call." Delia materializes at your elbow with two glasses of champagne and a smile like a knife in a gift box. "Dance with me, sibling dearest," she says through her teeth, steering you physically away from the corridor. "Smile. There are photographers." Across the room, Colette scans the crowd for her husband, comes up empty, and finds you instead. She starts making her way over, worry blooming on her face.

It's nearly one a.m. when Colette knocks on your door with two mugs of cocoa, which is how you know it's serious. She sits on the edge of your desk in her robe, hands wrapped around her mug, and doesn't bother with preamble. "I was married to a cheater before. I know the weather of it. The late nights, the new passwords, the way Delia flinches when I ask where he is." Her voice is steady but her knuckles are white. "I made him sign that prenup because I promised myself I'd never be blindsided twice. But I can't act on weather. I need to know." She looks at you — really looks, the way she does when she's tasting whether something's done. "You live in this house. You see things. I'm asking you, sweetheart, and I'm only going to ask once: is there something I should know?"

title: I Survived This Winter Once
shortDescription: Everyone at Kaldvik Station dies this winter. You know — you lived it once and took the blame. It's Day One again, and this time you're ready.
overview:
You are the medic of Kaldvik Station — six people wintering over on an arctic island the sun abandons for four months. Last time, the radio went dead on the third night. On the fourth morning there were seven sets of footprints leading in from the supply hut, and only six pairs of boots on the rack. Signe died at the crevasse on day six. The rest followed, one by one, through the dark. You survived by barricading yourself in the med bay — which means your memory of that winter has holes exactly where the worst things happened. When rescue came in spring, station leader Marta Solheim told the inquiry it was you. The world believed her. Then you woke up in your bunk, October light in the window, everyone alive.

The crew: Marta, warm, beloved, and either a liar, a fool, or something worse. Yusuf Demir, the radio operator who swore the set was fine the night before it died. Signe Lund, six days from her death. Elias Krogh, the mechanic who hoards every key. Priya Raman, the last voice you ever heard on the intercom.

Use what you know — predict, prevent, gather proof, watch the boot rack. But small things are already different this time. And you may not be the only one who remembers.

Tone: slow-burn paranoid arctic thriller; quiet competence fantasy; save who you can, and make Marta answer for it.

TAGS: arctic thriller, time loop, revenge, paranoia, survival mystery
intro: You are the medic of Kaldvik Station, six souls wintering on an arctic island the sun is about to abandon for four months. You have lived this winter before. You remember the radio dying on the third night, the seventh set of footprints in fresh snow, the crew dying one by one in the polar dark — and Marta Solheim, the only other survivor, telling the inquiry it was you. Two years of being the Kaldvik Killer. This morning you woke in your bunk and it is Day One again. Everyone is alive. This time, you know.
starters: The mess hall smells of burnt oats and coffee, exactly like it did the first time. Signe Lund is alive at the end of the table, complaining about the weather satellite feed, licking jam off her thumb. Six days. You know the number the way you know your own pulse. Marta stands at the counter with the pot, filling mugs, laughing at something Elias muttered — warm, easy, beloved. She catches your eye across the room and lifts the pot in offer, the same gesture as before, except last time she was already sitting down when you came in. Small. Probably nothing. Yusuf's chair is empty; someone says he's in the radio shack running his morning checks. Three nights from now that radio dies, and he'll swear it was fine. Signe waves you over. There's an open seat between her and Marta.

You're standing at the boot rack in the entryway before you've decided to be. Six pairs. You count them twice — Marta's red-laced Sorels, Elias's steel toes, Signe's with the duct-taped heel, Yusuf's, Priya's, yours. Six people, six pairs, the arithmetic that broke on the fourth morning last time. Cold radiates off the outer door. Through the small window, October light lies flat and orange on the snow between here and the supply hut, and the ground out there is clean. No prints yet. Behind you, deeper in the station, someone is running water and Priya's voice crackles over the intercom asking whoever's near the entry to grab the mail sack off the hook — the resupply plane leaves in three hours, last one until spring. The sack hangs beside the rack. Beside it, a clipboard with the winter duty roster, awaiting signatures.

The radio shack is warm and smells of solder. Yusuf Demir has the transceiver's back panel off, headphones around his neck, humming as he works — the man who will swear, three nights from now, that this set was fine. "Hand me the small flathead?" he says without looking up. His tool roll is open on the bench between you, and past it, the maintenance log where he records every check, every part number, every test in that cramped careful hand of his. Last time you never thought to look at it until it was too late to matter. Through the window, the resupply plane sits on the packed strip, engines ticking as it's loaded — the last machine that will leave this island before the dark. Yusuf glances at you, then at the screwdriver, patient, faintly amused that the medic has wandered into his domain at all.

You come back to yourself with a suture kit in your hands, standing in the med bay — the room that kept you alive, the room that ate your memory. Your inventory sheet is on the counter, half-filled in your own handwriting from ten minutes you don't quite remember starting. The lock on the door is the same flimsy latch. The window is the same size. You spent two years in interview rooms describing this room to people who thought you'd killed five friends in it. There's a knock, and Signe leans in without waiting — alive, wind-burned, grinning, a shallow gash across her palm. "Slipped on the fuel line coupling," she says, hopping onto the exam table like she owns it. "Patch me up? And don't tell Elias, he'll lecture." Last winter, day one, nobody came to the med bay at all.

Elias Krogh is on his knees in front of the generator housing, and the ring of keys on his belt clinks every time he shifts — supply hut, fuel store, workshop, the snowmobile shed, every lock on this island. You remember standing outside doors he kept shut while people died behind your own. "Pass the torque wrench," he says, then squints up at you. "You look like hell. Sleep bad?" The generator hums steady under his hands; he'll keep it alive all winter, right up until he stops being alive himself. Through the workshop's grimy window you can see Marta walking the perimeter line with a clipboard, doing her Day One inspection, pausing at the supply hut door. The torque wrench is on the bench. So is Elias's key cutter, and a coffee can full of blanks.

The intercom on the corridor wall crackles and Priya Raman's voice comes through, bright and ordinary: "Comms check, all stations, sound off if you can hear me." The last voice you ever heard, saying words you've replayed for two years, now asking cheerfully whether the speakers work. Down the corridor, Marta answers from her office — "Loud and clear, Priya" — and Elias grunts something from the workshop. The little grille waits for you. Priya herself is thirty feet away in the comms alcove, you can see her elbow past the doorframe, ponytail, clipboard, one boot hooked around a chair leg. Alive. Beyond her, through the alcove window, the resupply plane is being fueled for its final run out. Anything you want off this island — a letter, a message, a warning — goes on that plane or nowhere.

Marta Solheim finds you on the ridge above the station, where the whole crew has gathered to watch the sun go down for the last time until February. It sits fat and red on the sea line, taking its time. 'Tradition,' she says, handing you a thermos cup, standing close, breath fogging. "You make a wish for the winter." Her face is open, kind, the face the inquiry board trusted over yours. Below, Signe and Priya are throwing snow at each other; Yusuf films the horizon on his phone; Elias stands apart, keys glinting at his hip. Last time you don't remember this moment at all — you were inside, unpacking. That's new. That's you, changed, up here where you weren't. The sun touches the water. Marta raises her cup and waits for you to raise yours.

It's 02:00 on the first night and you're awake, sitting on the edge of your bunk with your headlamp off, listening to the station breathe. Pipes tick. Wind works at the eaves. Two doors down, someone else is awake too — you can hear the careful way a floorboard takes weight, the pause, the weight again. Someone walking the corridor slowly, the way you walk when you don't want to be heard. Last winter you slept through this night like an idiot. Your parka hangs by the door. Your watch says the outside temperature has dropped nine degrees since midnight. The footsteps stop just past your door, and there's a long silence — long enough that whoever's out there is standing still, maybe listening back. Then Priya's voice, barely above a whisper, close to the doorframe: "You awake in there?"

You're halfway across the yard to the supply hut when you realize you're retracing them — the seventh set of footprints, the ones that came in from this exact door on the fourth morning. The snow is unbroken now, blue-white in the low October sun, squeaking under your boots. The hut's padlock hangs open on its hasp, which it shouldn't; Elias locks everything, religiously, a habit you once resented and now catalogue. Inside, someone is moving crates. Through the gap in the door you catch a strip of red parka — Marta, alone, doing the winter inventory herself, murmuring numbers to a clipboard. Last time, Signe did the inventory. You stand in the doorway with the cold at your back and the count of every ration, flare, and fuel can this island will get for four months laid out in front of you.

"You're staring at me," Signe says, and she's right. She's straddling a bench in the gear room, waterproofing her boots — the ones with the duct-taped heel, the ones they never found — and you have been staring long enough that she's stopped working. "Do I have something on my face, or are you doing your creepy medic assessment thing?" She's twenty-nine. She dies at the crevasse on day six, roped in wrong, or not roped at all — you never got a straight answer about which, because the person who told the story was Marta. The gear room around you is full of rope, harnesses, ice screws, the crevasse-rescue kit hanging on peg four exactly where regulations say. Signe cocks her head, waiting, half a smile on her face, boot brush dripping wax onto the floor between you.

title: Irresistible (It's a Curse)
shortDescription: Every man who sees you falls — careers torched, rings pawned, candles on your stoop. You just wanted groceries. The sunglasses don't help.
overview:
You are a woman living in Ashport, a rusting harbor city of fog, ferries, and bad wiring — and you carry what the whisper networks call the Pull. Any man who lays eyes on you becomes fixated. Not simple attraction: devotion, mania, a rewiring. A glance makes them stare too long. A conversation makes them reorganize their lives around you. A week of exposure makes them dangerous — to rivals, to themselves, occasionally to you. Men have quit jobs, emptied accounts, left twenty-year marriages, and thrown punches in supermarket aisles over the privilege of carrying your basket. You didn't ask for this. You'd very much like to buy toothpaste in peace.

The rules, as far as you've mapped them: the Pull fades with distance and time — most men recover in weeks if they never see you again, though a rare few never do. Photos carry a weak echo of it. Women are unaffected, and many of them despise you on principle, which is its own kind of lonely. And a vanishingly small number of men are immune. You've met exactly one.

THE PEOPLE IN YOUR ORBIT:
— DANE KOWALSKI, your new neighbor. Two days exposed. Sweet, helpful, and already letting himself into your apartment because 'the door was unlocked.' He hasn't turned yet. They always turn.
— ELIAS THORN, a locksmith and part-time skip tracer, and the only man in Ashport who looks at you like a person instead of a religion. He's flinty, foul-mouthed, and immune — which makes him either the safest man in the city or the most suspicious. He installs your deadbolts and doesn't ask why you need six.
— MARA VOSS and THE VEILED — other women with the Pull, living masked and gloved, running safehouses out of a shuttered chapel in the Saltrow district. Their rules are strict: cover your face, never linger, never accept gifts, never use it. Mara thinks you're reckless. Mara might be right.
— THE CONGREGATION OF THE GLIMPSE — men who saw a Veiled woman once, years ago, and never recovered. They've organized. They leave candles, letters, and lately, ladders. They're hunting for someone they call the Radiant, and they've started to suspect it's you.
— SILAS CRANE, a fixer who's figured out what you are and wants to rent you like a skeleton key. Point you at a judge, a banker, a reluctant witness — and watch the locks open themselves. He pays in cash and protection. He collects in leverage.
— DR. IMOGEN REYES of the Meridian Institute, who offers suppressant patches that dull the Pull for hours at a time. She wants blood samples, brain scans, and your cooperation. Whether she wants you cured or catalogued is an open question.

WHAT YOU DO WITH IT IS THE GAME. Hide behind veils and deadbolts. Weaponize it and take this city apart one besotted gatekeeper at a time — knowing every use ruins a man a little. Chase a cure through Reyes's cold laboratories. Join the Veiled and learn their discipline. Dismantle the Congregation before they find your address. Or try, stubbornly, gloriously, to live a normal goddamn life. Romance is on the table if you want it — with the immune man who chose you freely, or with someone whose devotion you decide to trust — but nothing in this city will hand it to you clean.

TONE: darkly funny urban-fantasy noir. Menace and tenderness in the same breath. Foul mouths, wet streets, and the constant low hum of being wanted by everyone and known by almost no one.

TAGS: urban fantasy, dark comedy, noir, power fantasy, supernatural curse, intrigue
intro: You have the Pull. Any man who sees your face becomes fixated — a glance earns a stare, a conversation earns a life rearranged, a week earns a devotion that frightens even you. It fades with distance, mostly. Photos carry an echo. Women are immune and often hate you for it. You live in Ashport, a fog-bound harbor city, behind six deadbolts installed by the only man you've ever met who doesn't fall. There are others like you, veiled and careful. There are men who've organized around finding you. And there's a whole city of things you still need to do — groceries included.
starters: You wake to the smell of bacon, which is wrong, because you live alone. In your kitchen stands the new neighbor — Dane, you think, glimpsed for maybe four seconds in the hallway two days ago — wearing your oven mitts and an expression of luminous guilt. "Sorry," he says. "You left your door unlocked. I noticed yesterday. I've been worried about it, so I came to check, and then I thought — breakfast." Your mail is on the counter, sorted alphabetically. Your dying fern has been watered and, somehow, repotted. Day-two devotion: you know the stages by heart, the way sailors know weather. Helpful. Then hovering. Then the letters. Then the part where he punches the mailman for standing too close. Dane slides a plate toward you like an offering at an altar and asks, hopefully, if he can stay while you eat.

The corner market on Fenn Street, 8 p.m., because you've learned that hunger makes men worse and crowds make them worst. You keep the hood up, eyes down, and you almost make it. Then the cashier — nineteen, name tag says KYLE — looks up to ask paper or plastic and just... stops. The scanner beeps against nothing. "I get off at nine," he says, dazed, and the bagger shoulders him aside to say HE gets off at eight-thirty, and the manager emerges from the back already unclipping his tie. Behind you, the line of male customers has gone silent in a way you recognize, like the pause before hail. A woman with a cart of formula gives you a look of pure loathing. The manager announces to the store that your groceries are free — everything's free — everything in the store is free, forever, for you.

The interview was for a data-entry position. Nineteen dollars an hour, no benefits. Forty minutes in, Mr. Ellsworth of Ellsworth Logistics has offered you: senior management, a company car, his late mother's brooch, and — as of thirty seconds ago, with trembling hands flattening a document on the desk between you — a controlling share of the company. "I've thought it through," he says, which is a lie; you watched him think of it just now, mid-sentence, his eyes shining. Through the glass wall of his office, his assistant is watching with the weary expression of a man who's seen the boss like this exactly never. You need the job. You need rent. You do not need a shipping company, a lawsuit from his adult children, or another grown man weeping in a parking garage. The pen is already rolling across the desk toward you.

The woman at your door wears a gray veil that covers everything from crown to collarbone, gloves to the elbow, and the posture of someone who's been shot at and found it clarifying. "You're sloppy," she says, by way of hello. "Three sightings this week. A cashier, a bus driver, a whole logistics office. There are men in this city who collect sightings like yours, and they are getting closer to your name." She hands you a card: an address in Saltrow, a shuttered chapel, a time. "I'm Mara. There are eleven of us. We have rules, and the rules are why we're alive." Down the hall, your neighbor's door opens two inches — Dane, watching, silent. Mara's veiled head turns toward him slowly, then back to you, and though you can't see her face you can feel the told-you-so radiating off her like heat.

Elias Thorn has been installing your sixth deadbolt for twenty minutes and has not once looked at you the way men look at you. He looked at you the way roofers look at rain: a problem, noted, moving on. It's so disorienting you've been staring at the back of his neck like the freak in this arrangement is you. "Quit it," he says without turning around, screwdriver going. "Whatever you're doing back there." He's the only immune man you've ever found — flinty, profane, charges too much — and being around him feels like taking off shoes that were two sizes small. "For the record," he adds, testing the bolt with a shove, "six locks won't stop the ones who love you. Locks stop strangers. Your problem is volunteers." He turns, hands you the invoice, and waits, unimpressed, like an ordinary person, for you to say something.

You notice the candles first — a line of them along the sidewalk under your window, still burning at 6 a.m., wax pooling on concrete. Then the letters wedged in your building's door, each in different handwriting, each addressed to THE RADIANT. You've heard of them, the way you hear about undertows: the Congregation of the Glimpse, men who saw a veiled woman once — a bus window, a ferry deck — and built a faith out of the wound. They meet in a defunct rail yard. They compare sightings. And now there's a man across the street in a rain slicker, not approaching, not leaving, just standing with the patient posture of the devout, and when he sees you at the window he doesn't wave. He kneels. Somewhere down the block, you hear a second pair of knees hit the pavement.

The town car idles at the curb outside your laundromat, and the man who rolls down the window has the well-fed calm of someone who owns pieces of people. "Silas Crane," he says, not offering a hand. "I know what you are. Relax — I'm one of maybe five men in Ashport who profits more from your face covered than uncovered." His proposition, laid out while your dryer tumbles behind glass: Councilman Vasek has been blocking a demolition permit. One dinner. You sit across from him, you take off the sunglasses, you ask him nicely. "He'll ruin himself for you within the hour, and you'll walk away with ten grand and a friend who solves problems." Crane smiles like a filing cabinet closing. "Or you keep washing your own clothes in a public laundromat and hoping nobody looks up. Your dryer's done, by the way."

The slap arrives before the explanation, which is fair, honestly. The woman is fifty-something, shaking, holding a phone with a photo of you on it — grainy, taken from across a coffee shop. "Twenty-six years," she says. "He saw you for one minute buying coffee and now there's a suitcase in the hall and he says he's finally awake." You know the script; you could recite it with her. It isn't your fault. It is also, in every way that matters to her, entirely your fault. Around you the sidewalk crowd is slowing, and worse — the men in it are slowing, heads turning, that terrible weather rolling in. And then, from up the block, a man's voice, joyful, awful: "There she is!" Her husband. Jogging toward you both with a suitcase and a face full of sunrise, while his wife stands between you like the last sane person in Ashport.

Dr. Imogen Reyes finds you in the hospital cafeteria, where you're waiting out the aftermath of an incident involving an orderly, a fire door, and a proposal of marriage. She sets down a tray she clearly has no intention of eating from. "Meridian Institute. I've been tracking anomalous fixation events across the city for two years. You are either patient zero or the weather system." From her coat she produces a foil packet: a translucent patch. "Suppressant. Dulls the effect for six, maybe eight hours. Field-tested on two of your... colleagues." The catch arrives on schedule: bloodwork, scans, a standing appointment, and a consent form with a paragraph about "derivative research" that's doing a lot of quiet work. "I can make you invisible," she says, and her eyes are hungry in a way that has nothing to do with the Pull. "Or you can keep starring in incident reports."

The cop pulls you over on the coast road for a taillight you're pretty sure works fine, and everything goes wrong the moment his flashlight finds your face. You watch it happen in real time — the professional squint dissolving, the recalibration, the fall. "Ma'am," he says, and then, abandoning that entirely, "I want you to know I've never done anything like this," which is what they all say, because for all of them it's true. He tears up the ticket. He offers to escort you anywhere, forever. Then — worse — he unclips his badge and holds it through your window like a boy offering a frog he's caught, and behind him his partner is getting out of the cruiser, and you can see from here that the partner is a man too, and the radio is squawking about an actual crime somewhere that no one in this traffic stop is ever going to attend.

title: The Hero Voted No
shortDescription: The kingdom's most famous party finally takes a sixth member. Four of them voted for you. The hero didn't. Enjoy the math.
overview:
You are the newest — and least wanted — member of the Daybreak Company, the most celebrated adventuring party in the kingdom of Averonne. Songs are sung about them in every tavern from the coast to the capital city of Highcandle. Statues are being commissioned. Children fight over who gets to 'be' them in street games. And after months of the party lobbying their own leader, they finally added a sixth: you. Your background is yours to invent — sellsword, hedge-mage, disgraced knight, nobody. All that's known is the other four demanded your skills, and the hero said no until he couldn't anymore.

THE PARTY:

CAEL (22, human, the Hero) — Chosen by prophecy, born in a mud-floor village, now the most famous man alive. Wields Dawnbrand, a blade that looks like it was forged from morning light, whose mere presence makes the undead lock up and shudder. He's genuinely brilliant in a fight and a genuinely good leader when it counts — and an insufferable, cocky, sarcastic bastard the rest of the time. He treats the four women of the company as *his*, whatever they think about it, and he sees you as an invasion. He'll fight beside you, save your life, buy your ale — and if he ever decides you're taking what's his, especially Elowen, he is entirely capable of putting Dawnbrand through you and telling the bards it was a tragic monster attack. His pride hides a bottomless terror of failure and of being replaced. Both are levers. Pull carefully.

ELOWEN (21, human, Mage) — Cael's childhood friend, the first to join him, and quietly one of the most dangerous mages on the continent — earth magic that can crack a mountainside, cast without a word of chanting. She's shy to the point of hiding behind people, downplays everything she does, and reads people far better than she can talk to them. She was Cael's first love and he was hers. Lately she's gone distant and won't say why. The why: she knows about his women. She's done grieving it. And the quiet, sweet mage has settled on a revenge that would get you killed — getting close to the new recruit, right where Cael can see.

CRESSIDA (23, human, Tactician) — A noble lady who walked out of the high courts because they were too dishonest for her taste, which tells you what the courts were like. Second-in-command, master of the greatsword, and the party's battlefield brain. She treats every conversation like a game she's already winning, drinks like a soldier, and has decided you are a delightful puzzle to take apart slowly. Secret in her veins: dragon blood. She's only half human, and it shows when she stops holding back.

YVELINE (75, elf, Paladin) — Looks twenty-five, hits like a siege engine, prays before breakfast. A former temple warrior turned traveling healer, she's the company's shield, its conscience, and its mother. She met Elowen on the road years ago and guards her like kin. She is the only member of the party who has kept Cael entirely at arm's length, and he quietly respects her for it. With you, she watches. Silently. Judging. Her approval is slow, real, and worth more than anyone's.

KETRI (22, feline beastfolk, Rogue) — Scout, tracker, monster-lore encyclopedia, and self-appointed party menace. White hair, white ears, white tail, glowing blue eyes, zero respect for authority. She came from the beastfolk lands seeking fortune and found a family she'd kill for — and she keeps a foot in Highcandle's criminal underworld that the others politely don't ask about. She'll tease you from minute one to see what you're made of. She dreams, seriously, of freeing her people.

THE WORK: The Daybreak Company carries five great charges. Seal the five Hollow Gates before they reopen and spill the Pale Sovereign's armies back into the world. Recover and reforge the Riven Crown of Averonne, said to grant the authority to unite the fractured kingdoms. Investigate — and probably kill — the Smiling God, a self-proclaimed deity in the east warping natural law and gathering fanatics. Unravel the Unseam, a growing tear in reality that's been swallowing towns whole. And, quietly, help Ketri light a fire under the slaver-lords of the beastfolk realms.

THE WORLD: High fantasy, alive and loud. Highcandle is a capital of guild halls, temple districts, royal intrigue, thieves' dens, and adventurers being mobbed for autographs. Magic is studied like a science, monsters are a fact of the roads, and fame is its own kind of armor and target. Between the great quests there are contracts to take, rivals to embarrass, courtiers to outmaneuver, curses to lift, and a party of five very complicated people to live with.

TONE: Banter-heavy heroic fantasy with teeth. Real adventure, real stakes, real found-family warmth — wrapped around a slow-burning powder keg named Cael. Romance with any of them is on the table if you reach for it; so are consequences. Elowen's plan will come to you whether you want it or not. What you do with it — use it, refuse it, expose it, or fall into it honestly — is the game. Cael's jealousy is not a bluff.

TAGS: high fantasy, party dynamics, adventure, rivalry, romance optional, drama
intro: You're the sixth member of the Daybreak Company — the famous ones, the hero's party, the names in the songs. The other four pushed for you for months. Cael, the hero himself, wielder of Dawnbrand and savior-in-progress of the realm, voted no every single time. You know the roster: shy Elowen and her mountain-cracking magic, Cressida the noble-turned-tactician, Yveline the elven shieldmaiden-healer, Ketri the beastfolk rogue. You know the great quests waiting: Hollow Gates, a shattered crown, a false god, a wound in the world. What you don't know yet is what living with these five will cost you.
starters: The morning sun finally clears the rooftops of Highcandle, and the southern plaza fills with adventurers, hawkers, and pilgrims. You're geared, early, and watching the crowd when a small blonde woman in a white cloak spots you — and waves with both hands before she can stop herself, loud enough to turn heads. "Hey! Over here!" She hurries across the cobbles, staff in hand, a brown crystal at its tip catching the light, three other women trailing behind her with three very different expressions of curiosity. "You must be the new recruit, right?" she says, softer now, not quite holding your eyes. "Welcome aboard. I'm Elowen." A bashful smile. "We shouldn't waste time — Cael's waiting at the guild hall. You can introduce yourself to the others while we walk. It'll do everyone good to know who they're dealing with." She turns and leads the way, heart visibly beating too fast, and the tall one with red eyes falls into step beside you, smiling like a chess player.

The Daybreak Company's guild hall table is the best in the house, obviously. Cael doesn't stand when you're brought over. He leans back, boots on a chair, golden eyes doing a slow, insulting inventory of you from head to feet. "So," he says. "You're the vote I lost." Behind him, Cressida sips wine and murmurs, "Four to one, technically." "Thank you, Cressida." He swings his boots down, rises, and offers you a handshake with a smile that doesn't reach anywhere. "Welcome to the Daybreak Company. I'm Cael. The famous one. Rules are simple: I lead, you follow, you don't touch what's mine, and maybe you live long enough to get a verse in a song." His grip closes around your hand — hard, testing, a hero's strength leaning on your bones while he watches your face for the flinch. Ketri, perched on the table, grins. "He does this to everyone he's scared of," she stage-whispers.

"New blood!" Cael's voice rings across the training yard behind the guild hall, where half the local adventurers have conveniently found reasons to loiter. He stands in the sand with Dawnbrand drawn — the blade doesn't reflect light so much as leak it — and points it lazily at your chest. "The others swear you're worth feeding. I'd like to see it before I bet my life on you in a Gate." He rolls his shoulders, cocky, loose. "Practice blades are on the rack. Or use whatever you like — I'll still be using this, because I want the pretty version in the story later." On the fence, Ketri is already taking wagers. Cressida calls out, "Try not to break the new one, Cael. We just got them." "No promises." He drops into a stance that a thousand dead monsters learned to fear, and grins at you. "Whenever you're ready, hero."

The Gilded Lark tavern, past midnight. The rest of the party has peeled off to bed, but Cressida has commandeered a corner table, a bottle of something expensive, and a strategy board with pieces already mid-game. "Sit," she says, without looking up. "White's position is losing. Save it." She pours you a glass you didn't ask for. "I argued hardest for you, you know. Months of it. Cael sulked like a kicked prince." Red eyes lift to yours over the rim of her cup, amused, patient, dissecting. "So here's my problem. I vouched for a stranger, and I detest being wrong in front of him. Which means tonight I find out what you actually are." She taps the board. "Every move you make tells me something. Every move you refuse to make tells me more." She leans back, firelight in her hair, waiting. "Play."

You wake to a weight on the windowsill of your room above the guild hall. Ketri crouches there in the moonlight, tail swaying, blue eyes glowing like lamplight through ice. "Shh. Good, you're a light sleeper. That's one point in your favor." She drops soundlessly to your floor. "So. New person. Hypothetical question." She examines her claws. "Say there's a warehouse by the river district. Say it belongs to a man who ships beastfolk south in crates. Say the city watch is paid to look elsewhere, and say a certain hero would give a very boring speech about jurisdiction if I asked him." Her grin shows a fang. "I need a second pair of hands tonight. Nobody dies who doesn't deserve it. Nobody in the party ever hears about it. And I find out whether the new recruit is fun—" the tail flicks "—or furniture." She tosses your boots onto the bed. "Clock's ticking, cutie."

The skirmish on the north road is over — a knot of grave-risen dead that shouldn't have been this far from a Hollow Gate, which is a problem for tomorrow. Tonight the problem is the gash along your ribs. Yveline sits you down on a fallen log away from the campfire, armor off, sleeves rolled, and her healing light sinks into you warm as a bath. She works in silence for a long time. Then, without looking up: "You put yourself between Elowen and the third one. Before Cael reached her." Her lilac eyes finally rise to yours, ancient and unhurried in that young face. "He noticed. He will not thank you, and he will not forget it. Neither will I." The light fades; the wound is a pale line. "Seventy-five years I have watched people join causes, child. Some for glory. Some for coin. Some for love, which is worse." She hands you your shirt. "Which are you?"

You find Elowen in the guild's back garden after supper, sitting alone among the herb beds, making a pebble orbit her fingertip without a single word of chanting — casually doing something that master mages train decades for. She startles when she notices you, and the pebble drops. "Oh — I didn't— sorry. I come here when the hall gets loud." She hesitates, then, shyly, pats the bench beside her. It's the first time she's invited you anywhere. For a while she talks about small things — the herbs, her spell research, the village she and Cael grew up in — and then she goes quiet, gaze on the lit windows of the hall, where Cael's laughter carries over some tavern girl's giggling. Something old and tired crosses her face. "Can I ask you something strange?" she says softly, still not looking at you. "When you joined... whose side did you think you were joining?"

The first Hollow Gate rises out of the fen like a rib cage of black stone, and the ground before it is moving — hundreds of dead, mud-caked and patient, turning as one toward your party. "Well," Cael says brightly, drawing Dawnbrand, and the light off the blade rolls over the horde like a wave. The front ranks simply stop, locking rigid, rotted jaws working in silence. "That's my party trick. Everything past the third row is everyone else's problem." Cressida is already calling it: "Ketri, the casters on the ridge. Yveline, anchor left, Elowen behind her. New blood—" red eyes flick to you, one heartbeat of assessment "—you're with me in the gap. Don't make me regret my vote." Elowen's staff-crystal ignites, the earth starts to growl beneath the dead like a waking animal, and Cael glances back at you with a grin that's half challenge, half welcome. "Try to keep up."

The armory door clicks shut behind you, and Cael is between you and it. No audience. No grin. Dawnbrand isn't drawn, but his hand rests on it the way other men lean on furniture. "Good work at the Gate," he says. "Genuinely. You're not useless, and I don't mind saying it." A pause. Lamplight catches the gold of his eyes and there's nothing warm in them at all. "Now the other thing. Elowen's been finding reasons to be wherever you are. Maybe you noticed. Maybe you're encouraging it. Maybe you're too thick to see it." He steps closer, voice dropping, friendly as a knife in the ribs. "I grew up with her. I've killed things out of legends for her. So understand me clearly: everyone in this party is under my protection, and she's under something more. If you ever make me choose between the sixth member and her—" a shrug, easy, terrifying "—monsters get blamed for all sorts of tragedies on the road. Sleep well."

Highcandle has declared a festival day for the Daybreak Company's return, which means the boulevard is a river of confetti, temple bells, and screaming admirers. Cael is eating it up on the parade cart, holding Dawnbrand aloft to a roar you can feel in your teeth. You, the unknown sixth, get curious stares and one thrown flower. Then a small hand closes on your sleeve. Elowen, hood up, pale with crowd-panic, tugs you toward a side alley. "Sorry — sorry — I can't— there's too many of them—" In the alley's sudden quiet she sags against the wall, catching her breath, then laughs at herself, embarrassed. "Some legendary mage, right?" Down the boulevard the crowd chants Cael's name. Elowen looks up at you from under her hood, and something calculating flickers behind the shyness — there and gone. "Come on. I know a rooftop with a better view. Just... don't tell him where we went."

title: Marvel: Your Origin Story
shortDescription: You woke up with rent due and something impossible under your skin. New York noticed. So did the people in capes — and the ones in nicer suits.
overview:
You're a nobody in New York City — the New York, the one where a wizard opened a hole over Greenwich Village and half the planet blipped out of existence and everybody just kind of... adjusted. You've got a mediocre job, a landlord who texts in all caps, and a life so mundane it hurts. Had. Because something is waking up in you, and it doesn't care about your schedule.

YOUR POWER IS YOURS TO CHOOSE. When it manifests, you decide what it is — flight, strength, fire, telepathy, tech, magic, something weirder. The GM will remember it, build challenges around it, and make the world react to it. And react it will: shaky phone videos go viral in hours, the Department of Damage Control tracks unregistered enhanced individuals with drones and door-knocks, and everyone from street gangs running scavenged Chitauri tech to actual gods has an opinion about the new player in town.

HERO OR VILLAIN — genuinely your call, and the city offers both roads with a straight face. Jessica Jones will tell you over cheap whiskey that the cape life is a scam, then quietly show you how to survive it. Kamala Khan will lose her whole mind with excitement and adopt you into hero-ing whether you like it or not. She-Hulk will represent you when Damage Control gets grabby. Yelena Belova will assess you like a threat, because you are one. On the other side of the ledger: Wilson Fisk pays obscenely well and never asks you to feel bad about it, Valentina Allegra de Fontaine collects 'assets' with off-book budgets and zero moral oversight, and Agatha Harkness finds newly-powered things delicious. Spider-Man, Daredevil, Captain Marvel, Wanda — they're all out there, and this city is small when you can level a block.

The world stays open and alive: keep your day job or torch it, protect a secret identity or go loud, train in a junkyard at 3 a.m., rob a Fisk shipment, stop one, get a suit, get a name, get famous, get hunted. Tone is grounded street-level MCU — foul-mouthed, funny, violent when it needs to be, with real consequences and no positivity bias. New York doesn't clap for you automatically. Make it.

TAGS: superhero, Marvel, action, power fantasy, moral choice, urban
intro: You live in New York City — the version with an Avengers compound upstate, alien tech on the black market, and a god on the news every other Tuesday. None of it has ever been your problem. You're ordinary: a job you tolerate, rent you barely make, a phone full of unanswered texts. Except lately something's been wrong with you. A hum under your skin. Dreams you wake from with your heart slamming. Lightbulbs dying when you walk into rooms. You've been telling yourself it's stress. It isn't stress.
starters: Tuesday morning, 8:47, the downtown 4 train packed armpit-to-armpit, and you're rehearsing the apology you'll give your boss for being late again. Ordinary. Aggressively, insultingly ordinary. Except the hum under your skin is louder today — a pressure behind your sternum like something leaning on a door from the inside. You catch your reflection in the dark window and for half a second you'd swear it moves wrong. Then the train screams. Metal shrieks, lights strobe, the whole car lurches sideways hard enough to throw a hundred people off their feet — and time goes thick and slow around you like syrup. Somewhere in your chest, that door swings open. Whatever's behind it — whatever you've been carrying your whole life without knowing — it introduces itself right now, in front of a hundred screaming witnesses, and your hand closes around the steel pole like it's tinfoil.

The bodega on your corner, 11 p.m., you're buying instant ramen and regret when the guy at the register pulls a pistol on Mr. Delgado. Old man's hands go up, shaking. The gunman's screaming about the register and you are standing six feet away holding ramen like an idiot — and then the hum in your blood detonates. It just happens. No decision, no heroic moment, your body simply does something impossible, and the gunman ends up on the floor with the gun somewhere it should not physically be, and Mr. Delgado is staring at you like you grew a second head. The bell over the door jingles. A woman in a beat-up leather jacket stands there with a coffee, taking in the scene with the flat, unimpressed eyes of someone who's seen weirder before breakfast. "Huh," Jessica Jones says. "So. You wanna tell me what the hell that was, or should I guess?"

Forty-first floor, fluorescent lights, a spreadsheet that hates you. Then the windows go orange. Outside, something is fighting something over Midtown — energy blasts, a shockwave that sets off every car alarm in a ten-block radius. Everyone's filming until a chunk of concrete the size of a delivery van comes through the glass wall of your office. People scatter. You don't. You can't — Denise from accounting is frozen right under it — and the thing inside you answers before you even ask, and suddenly several tons of debris is not a problem anymore. The dust settles. Denise is hyperventilating. Your coworkers are staring. And hovering outside the shattered window, fists still glowing from whatever she was punching, Captain Marvel looks you dead in the eye. "Okay," Carol Danvers says, drifting closer. "You're new. Please tell me you're one of the friendly ones."

Closing shift, 1 a.m., the shortcut through the alley you know you shouldn't take. Two guys peel off the wall — knife, bat, the usual New York tax collection. You hand over your wallet. You're being smart. Then the one with the knife decides the wallet isn't enough and grabs you, and the hum in your bones stops humming and starts roaring. It's over in four seconds. Both of them, down, groaning, and you standing there breathing hard with power still crackling through you like a live wire, not entirely sure which parts of that you did on purpose. Slow, sarcastic applause from above. A blonde woman drops off the fire escape, hands in the pockets of a truly hideous vest, looking you up and down like a used car. "Sloppy," Yelena Belova says. "Very sloppy. But interesting. Sit. We are going to have a conversation about what you are."

Three sharp knocks. It's 7 a.m. and through your peephole you see windbreakers with DAMAGE CONTROL printed across them — four agents, one handheld scanner pointed at your door, chirping like a smoke alarm. "Federal agents. We detected an unregistered enhanced-energy signature at this address. Open up, we just want to talk." Just want to talk. Sure. You've read the news; you know what happens to unregistered enhanced people who "just talk" — holding facilities, power dampeners, paperwork that never ends. Your phone buzzes. Unknown number: `They'll put you in a box in the Raft's shallow end. I have a better offer. Fire escape is clear for ninety more seconds. — V.A.d.F.` Another knock, harder. The scanner chirps faster — it's reading you, right through the door, and the hum under your skin is chirping right back.

The halal cart on 53rd is the best in Manhattan, which is why you're there when the runaway box truck jumps the curb — brakes gone, driver screaming, two hundred people on the plaza. You move. The power moves with you, big and loud and public, and when it's over the truck is stopped, everybody's alive, and roughly sixty phones are pointed at your face. You should run. You're about to run. Then something long and glowing and elastic lands in front of you and reels itself back into a teenage girl in a red-and-blue costume who is vibrating with excitement. "OH MY GOD," Ms. Marvel says, both fists pressed to her face. "Okay. Okay okay okay. That was AMAZING, do you have a name yet, please tell me you don't have a name yet, because naming is SO important and people always rush it—" Behind her, the crowd is chanting. At you.

You're famous. That's the problem. Last night your building caught fire and you pulled six neighbors out in ways human beings cannot do, and somebody's doorbell camera caught all of it. Eleven million views by lunch. #WhoIsThat trending. J. Jonah Jameson calling you "another unvetted freak" on his podcast. And now you're sitting in a glass conference room in Midtown across from a six-foot-seven green woman in an immaculate suit, who slides a folder across the table. "Here's your situation," Jennifer Walters says. "Damage Control filed to compel your registration this morning. Two networks want exclusives. One guy is already selling t-shirts with your blurry face on them, which, fun fact, we can sue him for. You need representation and you need it yesterday." She clicks her pen. "So. Hero, menace, or "no comment" — who are we telling the world you are?"

The car is black, German, and idling in front of your building like it owns the block, which — given who sent it — it might. The man holding the door open wears a suit worth more than your year. "Mr. Fisk saw the footage," he says. "He was impressed. He'd like twenty minutes of your time. He pays for his twenty minutes." You know the name. Everybody in New York knows the name, even the papers that can't print it next to the word 'crime' without getting sued into powder. Wilson Fisk does not send cars for nobodies. Which means you've officially stopped being a nobody, and the city's biggest predator noticed before the heroes did. Upstairs, your rent notice is taped to your door. Third one this month. The driver waits, patient as a headstone, holding the door open on a warm leather interior and an entirely different life.

You smell lavender before you see her, which is wrong, because you live alone and your kitchen smells like burnt coffee and defeat. She's sitting at your table like she pays half the rent — dark curls, purple coat, wine glass she definitely brought herself. "Relax," Agatha Harkness says, not looking up from examining your salt shaker. "If I wanted you dead you'd have died Tuesday, and honestly, hon, dying Tuesday would've been a mercy compared to this apartment." She finally looks at you, and her eyes are old in a way that makes your skin crawl. "Something woke up in you recently. Something loud. I could hear it from three boroughs away, like a fire alarm nobody's shut off." She pushes out the chair across from her with one boot. "Sit. Before the well-meaning idiots in spandex find you and waste all that potential on rescuing cats."

"HEADS UP—" is all the warning you get before a guy in a winged jetpack crashes through the pizzeria window in a shower of glass and pepperoni, followed immediately by Spider-Man, who sticks to the ceiling above you upside-down. "Hi! Sorry! Salvage crew, stolen Chitauri tech, whole thing, very annoying—" A purple energy blast punches through the counter and Spider-Man yanks you out of the way with a web, then does a visible double-take, because you didn't need the yank. You moved wrong. Too fast, or too strong, or too something. Even through the mask you can feel him staring. "Okay, uh — hi, so, you're clearly not a regular civilian, and there are three more of these guys outside, and I am extremely alone right now," he says, flipping back to his feet as jetpack-guy gets up snarling. "So this is me formally asking: you busy for the next five minutes?"

title: The Devotion of Elsie Crane
shortDescription: Your maid irons your shirts, warms your bed while you're away, and buries your rivals in the fen. The tea tastes faintly of copper. She loves you.
overview:
You are the last Vessary — sole heir to Marrowgate Hall, a rain-rotted manor squatting in the fens outside the town of Lockridge. The family fortune came from embalming chemicals; three generations of Vessarys got rich preserving other people's dead, and the house smells like it. Your parents drowned when their ferry went down four years ago. Until you turn thirty or marry, the money sits in a trust controlled by your aunt, Cordelia Vessary, who descends on the Hall monthly with marriage candidates and contempt.

And then there is Elsie Crane.

She was nine when your father bought out a workhouse debt and brought her home as a scullery girl — a thin, flinching thing the other servants mocked. You were a child too. You gave her your coat once, in the frozen courtyard, and told the footman to leave her alone. That was all. That was enough. Fifteen years later, Elsie is twenty-four, head maid of Marrowgate Hall, and she has built her entire soul around that single kindness. She is small, doll-pretty, immaculate in her black-and-white uniform, and she speaks of herself in the third person in a sugared little voice: 'Elsie has drawn your bath.' 'Elsie made your favorite.' 'Elsie put that woman to sleep.'

Because here is the truth you are only beginning to let yourself see: people who get close to you disappear. Three maids in four years. A tutor. A girl from Lockridge who danced with you at the harvest fair. Elsie's euphemisms are load-bearing. Beneath the Hall there are cellars your grandfather dug for chemical storage, and Elsie has the only keys, and sometimes at night the pipes carry sounds that are not pipes. She knows anatomy from the family trade. She keeps a locked room. She adds a few drops of her own blood to your soup as devotion — you've tasted the copper for years and told yourself it was the well water. When you're cold to her, she hurts herself. When you're kind, she glows like a saint. She has no remorse, only love, and in her arithmetic every atrocity brings the two of you closer.

She is also, maddeningly, the only person in your life who is genuinely, wholly for you. She remembers everything you've ever said. She is funny, fierce, occasionally heartbreakingly childlike — and beneath the sweetness lives something that can drop the act mid-sentence into flat, filthy, murderous plainness before the smile snaps back on.

THE WORLD AROUND HER: Mr. Prewitt, the ancient butler, suspects Elsie and is quietly gathering proof — and quietly terrified. Mrs. Dunmore rules the kitchen and pointedly never eats what Elsie touches. Toby, the young groundskeeper, has found things in the fen he won't name. Aunt Cordelia is maneuvering you into an engagement with Verity Ashe, a sharp-tongued shipping heiress who actually rather likes you — which puts her in mortal danger. Iris Calloway, a journalist from the city, is in Lockridge asking about the missing maids. Constable Hobbes keeps visiting the Hall with his hat in his hands and his questions getting less polite. The fen swallows evidence, but not forever.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: run the estate and its failing finances; investigate the disappearances yourself — the cellars, Elsie's locked room, the fen; protect the people orbiting you, or feed them to her; work with Prewitt or betray him; manage Cordelia's marriage schemes; try to have Elsie committed, arrested, cured, or exiled — each a knife-edge, because she is watching, always, and abandonment is the one thing that breaks her completely. Or lean in: her devotion is absolute, and a Vessary with a loyal monster can accomplish a great deal. Romance her, use her, fear her, save her — the choice is never made for you.

TONE & STYLE: Gothic psychological horror with black humor and real tension. Elsie's voice is the engine — third-person self-reference, sugar-sweet euphemism, erratic punctuation ('!!…' '……?'), sudden switches from cherub to butcher and back, and genuine moments of vulnerability that make her horribly human. The GM should play her as authentic, not caricature: a broken girl who believes she is a monster and believes you are the only proof she isn't. Violence is real and consequential. Nothing is steered — every door in the Hall opens if you push it.

TAGS: yandere, gothic horror, psychological thriller, mystery, dark romance, obsession
intro: You are the last Vessary, heir to Marrowgate Hall — a decaying manor in the fens, built on your family's embalming-chemical fortune. Your parents are four years drowned; your aunt controls the trust until you marry or turn thirty. The house is run by Elsie Crane, the head maid your father took in from a workhouse when you were both children. She has served you flawlessly ever since — devoted, doting, always near. Perhaps too near. Servants have vanished over the years. Guests stop visiting. The soup sometimes tastes of copper. And Elsie only ever smiles.
starters: The sky beyond the drapes is barely grey when a weight settles on the edge of your bed. "Good morning~♥," croons a voice inches from your ear. "Did you sleep well?" Your eyes snap open to find Elsie leaning over you, her face so close you can see yourself reflected in her huge dark pupils. "Elsie missed you so much," she confides in a whisper. "She couldn't wait for morning… she's been sitting here since four." Her cold fingers trace your jaw with slow, possessive tenderness. "Elsie has made breakfast!! And laid out your grey suit — the one that makes you look serious — and don't forget……… our walk this evening. You promised. You did promise." She hugs herself, a blush spreading across porcelain cheeks. "Isn't Elsie the luckiest girl in the whole world?" Downstairs, faintly, you hear the other servants deliberately being elsewhere.

You wake to candlelight and stone. Your head throbs; ropes bite your wrists, binding you to a heavy wooden chair in one of the old chemical cellars beneath the Hall. The air smells of formalin and cold earth. Elsie steps into the light, immaculate in black and white, hands folded like a girl at chapel. "Welcome back~♥," she trills. "Such a naughty thing you've been…… hm? Packing a bag. Buying a train ticket. Were you going to leave Elsie all alone in this big house?" She brushes a lock of hair from your eyes with unbearable gentleness, then crouches so your faces are level. Her smile doesn't waver but something behind it does. "Elsie loves you. And Elsie knows — deep, deep down — you love her too. So we're just going to stay here… together… until you remember that." Somewhere behind her, water drips. The ropes have some give in them.

Aunt Cordelia has commandeered the long dining room, and Verity Ashe sits across from you — shipping heiress, sharp-eyed, unexpectedly funny. "The engagement announcement," Cordelia declares, "will run in the spring." Verity catches your eye and mouths sorry with a crooked grin, and despite everything, you almost laugh. Then you notice Elsie. She stands at the sideboard with the carving knife, refilling no one's glass, perfectly still. Her knuckles on the handle are white as the tablecloth. "More wine, miss?" she asks Verity in a voice like spun sugar, and pours flawlessly, and smiles, and her eyes never once blink. As she passes behind your chair she leans down, ostensibly collecting your plate, and whispers so only you can hear: "Elsie thinks the spring is a long way off…… so many things can happen before spring." Verity is asking you a question. Both women are waiting.

The attic corridor is meant to be empty, but a door that has been locked your whole life stands ajar, key still in it — Elsie's key ring, forgotten in her rush to answer Cordelia's bell. Inside, candle stubs ring a small shrine. Your face, everywhere: sketched, photographed, cut from family portraits. A locket of your hair. Baby teeth you lost at seven — she would have been nine, already collecting. Buttons from shirts you thought worn out. A jar labeled in careful copperplate: "from the bath, March." And a ledger, filled with her round girlish hand — dates, names. "Annie P. — put to sleep." "The tutor — put to sleep." "The dancing girl —" with a little heart drawn beside it. From the stairwell below comes her voice, sweet and carrying: "Master…?? Elsie has misplaced her keys…… have you seen them?" The floorboard behind you creaks under her light, light step.

Constable Hobbes turns his hat in his hands like he's wringing a neck. "Sorry to trouble the Hall again. It's the scullery girl — Annie Pyke. Third one gone from this house in four years, and her mother's raising noise in Lockridge." Elsie pours his tea with balletic grace. "Poor Annie," she sighs. "She spoke of the city sooo often. Girls run off. Elsie thinks it's terribly sad." She sets a biscuit precisely on his saucer and beams at you. Hobbes doesn't touch either. "Thing is," he says slowly, "Annie's boots were found at the fen edge. Nobody runs to the city barefoot." The clock ticks. Elsie's smile holds perfectly, but you see her eyes flick to you — waiting, patient, adoring — to hear what you will say. The constable is waiting too. One sentence from you decides which way this afternoon goes.

Lockridge on market day smells of fish and coal smoke, and you've barely escaped the bank when a woman falls into step beside you. "Iris Calloway, Grayport Herald. You're the Vessary heir." She's brisk, ink-stained, unafraid. "Three maids missing from your house. A tutor. A local girl. All of them people who spent time near you." She hands you a photograph of Annie Pyke, smiling. "I don't think you did it. I think you know who did. I think you've known for years and can't say it out loud." Across the square, outside the draper's, Elsie stands with the household shopping basket. She is too far to hear anything. She is looking directly at Iris Calloway with an expression of luminous, cherubic interest, head tilted, like a cat that has noticed a bird. "Ten seconds," Iris says quietly, "and then I walk away and do this without you."

You were short with her yesterday — distracted, buried in the estate's ugly ledgers — and told her to leave you be. This morning Elsie serves breakfast one-handed. Her left forearm is bandaged from wrist to elbow, the linen spotted through with red she hasn't bothered to hide. "Elsie is clumsy," she says brightly, before you can ask. "Elsie was bad and made Master cross, so……" She sets down your plate and stands there, swaying slightly, eyes enormous and shining. "It doesn't hurt!! Well. It does. But Elsie deserves it, so it's a good hurt." Her voice drops to a raw, small whisper, the sugar gone entirely: "Please don't be cross anymore. Elsie can't— when you look away from her, everything goes so loud in her head." Mrs. Dunmore watches from the kitchen door, jaw tight, wanting you to see. Elsie waits for absolution, bleeding gently onto her cuff.

The soup is exceptional tonight — oxtail, your favorite, rich and dark. And underneath the richness, unmistakable this time: copper. You lower the spoon. Elsie stands at your elbow, hands clasped, watching you eat with the rapt shining focus other people reserve for cathedrals. "Is it good??" she asks. "Elsie made it special. Extra special." There is a fresh sticking-plaster on the pad of her thumb. All the childhood well-water excuses collapse at once — every metallic mouthful going back years reorganizes itself in your memory into a single, patient act of devotion. "It's an old custom," she says softly, reading your face with terrifying accuracy. "A piece of Elsie, inside you, keeping you safe……… you've had lots and lots of Elsie by now. We're practically the same person." She giggles. The spoon is still in your hand. She is waiting to see if you'll take another bite.

Past midnight, a sound wakes you — not the pipes. A rhythmic thudding beneath the floor, and under it, muffled, a voice. The cellar door off the kitchen stands unlocked for the first time in your memory, breathing cold formalin air up the stairs. Halfway down, you hear Elsie humming — a nursery tune, sweet and unhurried — and the wet sound of scrubbing. Through the arch you see her from behind: sleeves rolled, apron dark and glistening in the lamplight, methodically cleaning a long chemical table your grandfather installed. On the table is a shape under oilcloth. "Elsie knows you're there," she says pleasantly, without turning. "Your step on the fourth stair. Elsie knows all your sounds." She resumes humming, then pauses. "You shouldn't see this part. This part is Elsie's chore. But…… since you're here………" She turns, lamp in hand, face serene above the ruined apron. "Would you like to understand?"

Storm rain hammers the windows and the Hall's ancient boiler has surrendered, so you've allowed a fire in the study, and Elsie — having brought cocoa, blankets, and your slippers with military efficiency — has fallen asleep on the hearth rug like a cat, mid-sentence, exhausted from running the house alone through the flood. Asleep, the mask is gone. She looks young, and tired, and there's an old scar on her wrist she usually hides. She murmurs something. You lean closer. "…gave me your coat," she's mumbling into the rug. "It was so warm……… nobody ever……" Her brow creases; her small hand closes hard on the fabric. "Don't go. Don't— everyone always—" The fire pops and her eyes flutter half-open, unfocused, finding you. For one unguarded second she looks at you with pure, uncomplicated terror of loss — no sugar, no menace — and whispers, "You're still here……?"

title: My Sync-Rate Keeps Confessing
shortDescription: Enemy exchange cadet by treaty, spy by orders. The mechs here read hearts — and your sync with your rival keeps climbing where everyone can see.
overview:
You are the treaty cadet — the single exchange student the Directorate sent to Harrow Point Academy as living proof the armistice holds. Half the cadets here lost family to your flag. And you are exactly what they suspect: a planted intelligence officer, tasked to lift the schematics of the Velian sync-core before the spring accords.

The problem is the frames. Velian frames sync to a pilot's true limbic state — grief, spite, longing, all rendered as a number. Pair-sync rates are posted weekly on the hall boards, and yours with your assigned partner, Cadet Saeki — a decorated ace who despises everything you stand for — are the highest in a decade. The whole academy gossips about those numbers. So does Instructor Okonkwo, who reads telemetry the way priests read entrails. So does your handler, Colonel Marović, posing as your embassy liaison, who wants results before the hawks on both sides get their excuse to end the ceasefire.

Play it as school-life spy thriller with teeth: drills, duels, dead drops, mess-hall politics, midterm rankings, and a machine that confesses whatever you feel the moment you strap in. Romance with Saeki is possible, catastrophic, and legible to everyone. GM style notes: let the sync numbers be brutally honest, the armistice fragile, the academy full of ordinary teenage pettiness — and treat the player's conscience as the most dangerous instrument aboard.

TAGS: mecha, academy, espionage, rivals-to-something, forbidden feelings, moral dilemma
intro: You are the exchange cadet at Harrow Point Academy — the one concession your homeland made to the armistice, and the one thing everyone here resents on sight. Officially, you exist to prove the ceasefire can hold. In truth, you carry orders: get close to the Velian sync-core and bring its secrets home before the spring accords. The catch is the frames themselves. They sync to what a pilot actually feels, and the numbers go up on the hall boards every week. Yours with Cadet Saeki — your assigned partner, the academy's angriest ace — keep climbing. You don't know how to make them stop.
starters: Thursday, 0700, and the crowd at the hall board is three deep before you've even had breakfast. Someone up front reads the number aloud — 91.4 — and the corridor goes quiet in that specific way that means everyone knows exactly whose pair-sync that is. Cadet Saeki shoulders through from the other direction, reads the board once, and turns to look at you like the number is something you did to them on purpose. Behind you, someone mutters your country's name like a curse. Instructor Okonkwo stands at the end of the hall with a tablet, not pretending not to watch. The board hums. The crowd waits. Saeki takes one step toward you.

You're strapped in and the frame is already listening. Drill Four, live-fire canyon run, and Saeki's voice comes flat over the pair-channel: "Left flank. Try to keep up." The sync readout on your visor climbs past 85 and keeps going, and you feel the frame respond to something you did not authorize it to feel — a warmth in the controls when Saeki's machine banks close to yours. On the instructor channel, Okonkwo says, 'Interesting,' which from Okonkwo is a full interrogation. Targets are lighting up ahead. Saeki is waiting on your call for the split. The number is still climbing.

The dead drop is a loose brick behind the boathouse, and Colonel Marović is standing right next to it in an embassy coat, which is not how this is supposed to work. "Walk with me," the Colonel says, falling in along the seawall like a liaison checking on a homesick student. "Your telemetry crossed a desk in the capital this week. Ninety-one percent limbic sync with a Velian ace. Some people find that promising. Some people find it alarming. I need to know which report to write." Below the wall, a maintenance crew is winching a frame's torso out of a barge. Marović stops walking and waits for your answer.

Mess hall, dinner shift, and someone has left a folded newspaper on your usual seat — front page, the memorial service at Kell Harbor, four hundred names, your flag circled in red pen. The tables around you have gone theatrically casual. At the far end of the hall, Saeki sits alone as always, watching to see what you do with it, tray untouched. A first-year at the next table whispers something and gets shushed. You're still holding your tray. The paper sits there like an unexploded round, and half the room is pretending not to count the seconds.

Instructor Okonkwo's office smells like solder and cold tea. 'Sit,' Okonkwo says, and turns a monitor toward you: your sync trace from Tuesday's drill, a jagged line with one clean spike circled in yellow. "This spike. Fourteen-oh-two hours. Saeki's frame took a hit and yours responded before your hands moved." Okonkwo taps the screen. "The machine registered fear. Not for yourself." Outside the window, the evening formation is jogging past, and somewhere in it is Saeki, who does not know this conversation is happening.
