Okonkwo folds both hands and looks at you the way people look at instruments they suspect are lying.

It's past midnight and you're two corridors from the sync-core bay with a stolen maintenance badge in your pocket when the lights come on. Not all of them — just the hangar row, and under them, Saeki, alone, running solo calibrations on their frame at an hour when that is absolutely against regulations. They haven't seen you. The badge reader you need is ten meters past them. Saeki's frame is open at the chest, sync harness dangling, and they're talking to it — low, too quiet to make out, the way you'd talk to a grave. A maintenance drone whirs somewhere behind you, making its rounds.

The duel challenge is posted before morning colors: Cadet Vann, third-ranked, has invoked honor rules and named you. Grounds cited: "conduct unbecoming a guest of the armistice," which everyone understands to mean the numbers on the board. The gathering crowd in the quad is already picking sides — mostly Vann's. Saeki arrives late, reads the challenge sheet, and rips it off the post. "You don't duel my partner without dueling me," Saeki announces, to visible horror, including possibly their own. Vann looks at you, waiting to hear if you'll hide behind that. The duty officer is already reaching for the incident log.

Rain on the observation deck, first light, and you've come up here because it's the one place the academy forgets to resent you. Except Saeki is already there, uniform soaked through, watching the frames stand in their gantries like a row of tombstones. "My brother flew the old model," Saeki says without turning around. It's the first sentence they've ever offered you that wasn't an order or an insult. Down in the yard, the morning klaxon is two minutes out, and after that comes drill assignment, and after that the weekly sync posting. Saeki still hasn't looked at you. The rain keeps falling on both of you the same.

Midterm rankings drop at noon and the courtyard erupts. You and Saeki have taken first pair overall — ahead of the Ashford twins, ahead of everyone — and the reaction is not applause. Ashford Senior is saying, loudly, that the machine must be miscalibrated, that no Velian frame would sync that high "with one of them." A technician actually gets sent to check. Saeki stands beside you at rigid attention, jaw working, radiating fury at Ashford or at you or at the number itself — impossible to tell. Okonkwo watches from the colonnade, and across the courtyard by the gate, you spot Colonel Marović's embassy car idling, window down.

The encrypted message came at 0300: ACCORDS MOVED UP. SIX WEEKS. ACCELERATE. You've read it four times in the washroom stall and burned it in the sink, and now you're standing at first formation with the smell of ash on your fingers while Okonkwo walks the line. "Pair assignments hold through midterms," Okonkwo announces. "Sync-core familiarization begins Monday. Top-rated pairs get bay access." A murmur runs down the ranks — everyone knows which pair is top-rated. Beside you, Saeki exhales through their nose, disgusted or resigned. Bay access. Exactly what your orders need. Exactly what the number keeps buying you. Okonkwo stops in front of you both.

title: I Hold Every Key
shortDescription: Every lock in the quarter is yours, every key in your book. Then a man dies behind a door only your keys should open.
overview:
You are the locksmith of the Tallow Quarter — heir to Master Ilya's cramped little shop, his workbench, his cat, and his copy-book: a guild-sworn ledger of every key ever cut for the quarter's stacked houses and crooked alleys. Your oath is simple. Record every key. Copy none without the owner's word. In exchange, three hundred households trust you with the shape of their secrets.

Now Hobb the pawnbroker is dead behind his own triple-locked door — locks you fitted, no forced entry — and Inspector Maren Kettle has a magistrate's warrant for your copy-book. She's giving you a few days' grace, hoping you'll cooperate instead; the whole quarter is watching to see whether you sell them out. Meanwhile a soft-spoken stranger named Corvo keeps returning with real gold, wanting one key cut off the books. And somewhere in Ilya's oldest ledger there is a page that was razored out.

Play it warm and tactile: filing brass, mending mortises, tea with regulars, an apprentice who steals things back. The mystery tightens through the craft — you're the only person alive who can read a lock like a confession. Every key you cut, refuse, or hide changes who gets in where. Keep the coziness; let the teeth show slowly.

TAGS: cozy mystery, gaslamp fantasy, craft mastery, secrets, community, slow burn
intro: You are the locksmith of the Tallow Quarter, three winters into the trade since Master Ilya died and left you the shop: a bench of files and blanks, a loft apprentice named Fenn, a cat that hates the rain. By guild oath you keep the copy-book — a record of every key you've ever cut — and you copy nothing without the owner's word. The quarter trusts you because it has to. This week, Hobb the pawnbroker was found dead behind his own locked door, locks were your work, and the city watch has started asking careful questions about your book.
starters: Inspector Maren Kettle takes up more of your doorway than she should, warrant folded in one hand like she's embarrassed by it. Rain drips off her hat onto the mat Ilya wore thin. "I could take the book today," she says, not moving past the threshold. "Magistrate's seal says I can. But then three hundred households learn the watch reads their locks, and you learn what that does to a trade." Behind you, Fenn has gone very still at the grinding wheel, pretending to true a blank that was true ten minutes ago. The cat watches from the shelf above the copy-book — which is sitting out, open to the H's, because you were looking at Hobb's entry an hour before she knocked. Kettle's eyes find it. "A few days," she says. "Then I stop asking nicely." She waits, and the rain waits with her.

You're on your knees in the doorway of Hobb's pawnshop with a watchman holding a lantern over your shoulder, reading the top deadbolt with your fingertips the way Ilya taught you — eyes shut, pick barely kissing the pins. Behind you the shop still smells of Hobb: pipe smoke, lamp oil, the vinegar he used on tarnished silver. His body went out this morning under a sheet. The lock is yours, fitted two summers back, and it's telling you something quietly wrong — a wear pattern on the third pin that shouldn't be there, like a key that almost fits has been visiting. "Well?" says the watchman, whose name you haven't asked. "Forced or not?" Down the street, neighbors have gathered at a respectful distance to watch you decide whether to answer honestly. The lantern hisses. Your pick is still resting on that third pin.

The stranger comes in at closing time, when the lamps are lit and the shutters half up, and lays a gold sovereign on your bench without a word. Real gold — you can tell by the weight before you touch it. "My name is Corvo," he says, soft as a man apologizing in church. "I need one key cut. From a wax blank I'll provide. No entry in your book." He sets a small tin beside the coin. The cat has retreated to the top shelf, which she only does for dogs and thunder. Up in the loft you can hear Fenn's floorboard creak — listening, definitely listening. Corvo's coat is good wool, his boots are quarter mud, and his eyes go once, briefly, to the locked drawer where the copy-book sleeps. "I understand you've had a difficult week," he adds. The sovereign sits between you, catching lamplight.

It's an ordinary Tuesday until it isn't. Widow Prosser is in the good chair with her tea, complaining happily about her nephew, while you file the burrs off her new pantry key. Fenn is sweeping, badly. Then Prosser sets down her cup and says, in the same tone she uses for the weather, "They're saying at the pump that Hobb's door was locked from inside. All three. And they're saying you're the only one who could've walked through it." The file goes still in your hand. Through the window you can see Tam the chandler across the lane, watching your shop while pretending to trim wicks. Prosser watches you over her cup, kind and merciless. "I told them nonsense, of course," she says. "You'll want to say something too, dear. Before somebody says it for you." The pantry key is half-finished, warm from the file.

You find it past midnight, hunting Hobb's oldest entries by candlelight: Ilya's first ledger, the one bound in scuffed calf, falls open at a wound. A page razored out, close to the spine, clean work — a craftsman's cut. The stub is yellowed the same as its neighbors, so it wasn't done recently. The entries before it end mid-street: Fetter Lane, numbers four through nine. The entries after pick up three doors later. Somebody owned locks on Fetter Lane once, and somebody made sure no record of their keys survived. Upstairs, Fenn's floorboard creaks — awake, or pretending not to be. The candle gutters. On your bench sit tomorrow's problems: two blanks for the baker, Inspector Kettle's card weighted under a file, and a note in Fenn's handwriting you haven't read yet. The razored stub is smooth under your thumb, smooth as a lie told well.

Hobb's funeral is small and damp, and half the Tallow Quarter has come anyway, mostly to look at you. You stand at the back of the churchyard with your hat in your hands while the priest gets Hobb's name slightly wrong. Tam the chandler won't meet your eyes. Widow Prosser stands pointedly beside you, which is either loyalty or theater. And at the gate, not quite inside the yard, waits Inspector Maren Kettle — no warrant visible today, just patience and a black umbrella. When the first handful of earth goes down, someone behind you mutters, "Locks were his work," not quietly enough. The mourners begin to drift, and three separate people are angling toward you at once: Kettle from the gate, Prosser tugging your sleeve, and Hobb's gray-faced niece, who is holding something small wrapped in a handkerchief and looking straight at you.

You wake to the shop bell and Fenn already halfway down the loft ladder in yesterday's shirt, hissing, "Don't answer it, don't—" but you're at the door before the sense of that lands. Nobody there. Gray dawn, wet cobbles, milk cart two streets off. On the step: a key. Not one of yours — the bitting is strange, cut deep and cruel, brass gone dark with handling. Fenn goes white looking at it and won't say why, which is its own kind of answer, because Fenn steals things back for people and knows every fence in the quarter. The cat sniffs the key once and walks away offended. Across the lane, a curtain drops in the chandler's upstairs window. The key is cold in your palm, and somewhere behind you the kettle Fenn put on starts to sing.

The queue starts before you've unbolted your own door, which has never happened in three years. Word of Hobb has done its work overnight. The baker wants his locks changed — "nothing personal, you understand." So does the seamstress. So do the Tolliver brothers, who've never agreed on anything. They stand in the drizzle clutching their old keys like sick birds, and every one of them is really asking the same unasked question: can you still be trusted with the shape of their doors? Fenn is taking names on a slate, out of depth, spelling everything wrong. At the back of the queue, not queuing exactly, stands a soft-spoken stranger in good wool who catches your eye and mouths, no hurry. The bolt is cold under your hand and the whole street is waiting for you to slide it.

You're inside Hobb's shop alone — Kettle's grudging permission, one hour, don't touch the strongbox — and the place is a held breath. Pawned fiddles on the wall, ticket stubs on a spike, his ledger open to Thursday. Your three locks sit in the door like witnesses waiting to be questioned. But it's the strongbox that keeps pulling your eye, because the lock in it isn't yours, isn't guild work at all, and there's no entry for it in your copy-book — which means Hobb had a locksmith you've never heard of, or a lock older than your oath. Scratches around the keyhole. Recent. Amateurish. From the street comes the scuff of the watchman posted at the door, and the creak of a floorboard overhead where nobody should be. Your hour is running. Your picks are in your coat.

Tea first, Ilya always said; the hands file straighter after tea. So you're pouring Fenn's cup when the apprentice slides something across the bench instead of taking it: a pawn ticket, Hobb's shop, dated the day before he died. "Found it," Fenn says, in the tone that means lifted it. "Off a man who was asking about you at the Grey Dog. Asking what hours you keep. Whether you drink." The ticket is for item 114 — no description, paid in advance, unclaimed. Fenn is watching you with that guilty, hopeful look, half expecting a scolding, half expecting praise, wholly expecting you to do something about it. Outside, the rain has driven the cat in, and she's sitting on the copy-book like a paperweight with opinions. The tea steams between you. Item 114 is presumably still sitting on a shelf in a dead man's shop.

title: I Wake Once a Generation
shortDescription: You get one day per generation to renew the ward — and to see what twenty-five years did to everyone who remembers you.
overview:
You are the Sleeper of Hollen Vale. Three centuries ago you took the vigil so someone you loved wouldn't have to draw the lot. The bargain: once a generation the mountain releases you for a single day, sunrise to sunrise, to walk the seven boundary stones and renew the ward holding the Undermere beneath the black tarn. When the next dawn comes, sleep takes you wherever you stand.

The fun is the time-lapse. Every waking, the valley has moved on without you: the girl who fed you bread is now a grandmother; graves have new names; the shrine box holds twenty-five years of letters written to you — confessions, favors begged, a child's drawing, an apology from someone long dead. Old Mirte Amsel still keeps the vigil-house, but her grandson Theodor thinks the whole rite is superstition and wants to sell. And a Provincial Survey team under Director Johan Valdec has arrived with brass instruments and a plan to drain the tarn, politely proving the flood is 'merely hydrology.' The stones, this waking, are colder than they should be.

Play it however you like: do your duty, chase the truth, plant seeds you'll only see grown next waking, or test what happens if you don't sleep. The GM will honor the skips — every choice echoes back a generation later, on faces that got old while you dreamed.

TAGS: melancholy fantasy, memory & loss, generational time-skips, quiet mystery, slice of life
intro: You are the Sleeper of Hollen Vale. Three hundred years ago you took the vigil so someone you loved would not have to, and the mountain has kept you ever since. Once a generation it lets you go: one day, sunrise to sunrise, to walk the seven boundary stones and renew the ward that keeps the Undermere beneath the tarn. Townsfolk leave letters for you in the shrine box; children who once fed you bread greet you next as grey elders. When the next dawn comes, sleep takes you where you stand. Today, you are waking.
starters: The mountain lets go of you the way ice lets go of a stone — slowly, then all at once. You are standing in the hollow behind the tarn, knees stiff, frost melting off your sleeves, and the sun is a red seam over the eastern ridge. Someone has left the customary things on the flat rock: bread wrapped in cloth, a flask, a walking staff you don't recognize. The bread is still warm. Whoever brought it can't have gone far — there, down the path, a lantern bobs toward the vigil-house, carried by a small bent figure moving with an old woman's care. Below, Hollen Vale is waking too: smoke from more chimneys than you remember, and something new near the tarn's edge — white canvas tents, in neat rows, where nothing has ever stood before.

You wake where you fell asleep twenty-five years ago: mid-stride on the cart road below the third stone. Except it isn't a cart road anymore. It's graded and graveled, wide enough for two wagons, and a boy of maybe ten is sitting on the verge staring at you with his mouth open. He's been waiting — there's a heel of bread in his lap and crumbs down his shirt where he clearly got hungry first. "Gran said you'd come up out of the ground," he says, "but Da said you'd just be standing here like a scarecrow." He scrambles to his feet and holds out what's left of the bread with both hands, formal as a coronation. Down the slope, morning fog is peeling off the black tarn, and men in grey coats are unloading brass instruments from a wagon at its shore.

The first thing you hear is arguing. You've come down off the mountain in the grey before sunrise, and the vigil-house door stands open, lamplight spilling out. Inside, Old Mirte Amsel — white-haired now, hands like knotted rope — has both palms flat on a paper spread across her table, and a young man is trying to slide it out from under them. "It's a fair price, Gran. It's a ruin sitting on good pasture." Neither has seen you in the doorway. The shrine box hangs on the wall behind them, stuffed so full of letters the lid won't close. Mirte glances up first, and her whole face changes — the way faces do when they see something they'd half stopped believing in. The young man turns to follow her gaze and goes very still.

You reach the first boundary stone with the sun barely up, and it's wrong. Not fallen, not defaced — cold. Cold in a way stone shouldn't be in the last week of summer, cold enough that your palm aches when you lay it on the carved ward-lines. Frost feathers the grass in a perfect circle around its base while everywhere else the dew is only dew. You've renewed this stone eleven times. It has never felt like this. From here you can see down the whole vale: the town grown fat and unfamiliar along the river, and at the tarn's edge, tiny in the distance, figures moving among staked lines and tripods, as if someone is measuring the water. A rolled paper has been tucked under a rock at the stone's foot — someone left it here for you, recently, the ink not yet weathered.

"You'll forgive the intrusion," says the man in the grey coat, "but you did rather appear out of nowhere." It's mid-morning already — you slept past sunrise, which has never happened, and woke to find the Provincial Survey camped a hundred paces from the mountain's mouth. The man introduces himself as Director Johan Valdec, offers his hand, and studies you like a specimen he's pleased with. Behind him, assistants sight down brass levels toward the tarn; pegs and string mark out something long and straight running toward its southern lip. "The famous Sleeper. I confess I assumed you were folklore." He gestures at a folding table set with maps and a steaming pot. "Tea? I have questions — hydrological ones, mostly. And I imagine you have a busy day." Beyond his shoulder, the black water lies flat and lightless, not reflecting the sky at all.

The shrine box is heavier than it's ever been. You've carried it out to the bench beside the vigil-house to read in the early light, and twenty-five years of paper shifts inside like a living thing. On top: a child's drawing in charcoal, you rendered as a lumpy figure asleep under a lumpy mountain, both smiling. Beneath it, folded letters in a dozen hands — one sealed with wax and marked, in careful script, "To be read first. From one who wronged you. I will be dead when you open this." Inside the house you can hear Mirte moving about, setting a kettle, deliberately giving you privacy she clearly aches to interrupt. Down the valley, a survey team's morning whistle carries thin across the water, and the sun has already spent an hour of your one day.

Bells. That's what pulls you down from the mountain faster than usual — the church bell tolling slow, the death count. By the time you reach the edge of town the procession is coming up the lane toward the burying ground: a coffin on six shoulders, half the valley walking behind in their dark best. You stand aside at the wall, and one by one, heads turn. An old woman near the front stops dead, and the whole procession stutters around her. "Of course," she says, loud in the hush, "of course it's today." You know her voice before you know her face — Mirte Amsel, who was middle-aged when you last woke. Her eyes are red from more than the funeral. Behind her, a young man mutters something sour under his breath, and the coffin-bearers wait, uncertain whether to set down their burden or walk on.

No one came. That's the first strangeness. Every waking for three hundred years there has been bread on the flat rock and a keeper waiting, and this dawn there is nothing — just wind and the long grass grown over the path. You walk down to the vigil-house and find it shuttered, the door padlocked with bright new iron, a printed notice tacked to the wood: PROPERTY OFFERED FOR SALE — INQUIRIES TO T. AMSEL, MILLER'S ROW. The shrine box is still bolted beside the door, at least, and stuffed with letters gone soft from weather. Through a gap in the shutters you can see the vigil lamp inside, unlit, and Mirte's chair with a shawl still over its arm. Down at the tarn, white tents catch the morning light, and somewhere in town a hammer is already working. The sun is up. The clock on your single day is running.

You are halfway to the second stone when you realize you're being followed. It's past noon — the waking came late and hard this time, and you've been moving fast to make up hours — and there he is again on the switchback below: a young man in town clothes, making no real effort to hide, carrying a leather folder under one arm like a shield. When you stop, he stops. When you look at him directly, he lifts his chin, defiant. "Go on, then," he calls up. "Do the trick. Touch the rock, say the words. I want to watch." Above you the second stone waits on its shoulder of granite, and even from here, twenty paces off, you can feel the cold coming off it — a wrongness, like standing near an open cellar in winter. The young man starts climbing toward you.

Mirte doesn't say hello. She takes your face in both her spotted hands, there on the vigil-house threshold in the first grey light, and looks at you for a long time. "I was nine," she says finally. "You won't remember. I dropped the bread in the mud and cried, and you ate it anyway and said it was the best you'd had." She's laid the table behind her: bread, honey, the vigil lamp burning, the shrine box set out with its lid open. But her hands are shaking, and not only from age. "Eat first," she says, "then I have to tell you things you won't like. About my grandson. About the men at the water." Through the window, down the long slope, the black tarn sits under a skin of mist, and you can just make out a boat on it — a boat, on the tarn, where no one in three hundred years has dared to row.

title: I've Emptied Buildings Like Ours
shortDescription: Your job is emptying buildings like this one. Then eviction notices hit every door — including the neighbor's who keeps leaving dinner on yours.
overview:
You're a turnaround specialist — the quiet professional investors fly in to wind down failing properties, thank the staff, and lock the doors. After your last job ended with a doctor using the word 'collapse,' your firm parked you on a six-month sabbatical. You rented 3A in the Fenwick, a creaking 1926 brick walk-up, planning to unpack nothing and know no one. Sasha in 3B — furniture restorer, chronic over-baker, the building's unofficial heart — decided otherwise. Food appears on your doormat. Your radiator gets bled without asking. The building's golden rule is non-negotiable: never return a dish empty.

Then Corvus Property Group bought the Fenwick and began the slow squeeze: sloppy relocation notices, surprise 'inspections,' a boiler that stays mysteriously broken. You recognize every move, because you've made them. The tenants' association is well-meaning chaos — Mrs. Okonkwo in 4A trusts no one, Theo the law student is confidently wrong, and everyone leans on Sasha, who is quietly running on fumes. You may be the only person here who knows exactly how this ends, and exactly how to stop it.

Play it grounded and slow: paperwork and pot roast, defective notices and mended hinges. The war is bureaucratic; the romance lives in tupperware, fixed windows, and being noticed. Whether you stay a vulture or become a neighbor is yours to decide.

TAGS: slow-burn romance, cozy contemporary, competence porn, found community, tenant drama
intro: You close down buildings for a living — the specialist who arrives when investors want a failing property emptied gently and profitably. Six weeks ago, burned out and under orders to rest, you leased apartment 3A in the Fenwick, an aging walk-up you intended to treat like a hotel room. Sasha in 3B keeps ruining that plan: covered dishes on your doormat, your name remembered, small kindnesses you don't know how to return. Meanwhile the building's new owner, Corvus Property Group, has begun pressuring tenants out with tactics you know intimately — because until recently, they were yours.
starters: The casserole dish has been sitting on your counter for three days, washed and drying into an accusation. The building's rule — Sasha's rule, everyone's rule — is that it doesn't go back empty, and you own exactly one skillet and a jar of instant coffee. You're weighing whether a grocery-store pie counts when you hear the tape gun in the hallway. Through the peephole: a kid in a Corvus Property Group polo, sticking a notice to Sasha's door, then yours. You've written that notice. You've written better versions of that notice — this one has the wrong statutory citation in the second paragraph and a cure period that isn't legal in this state. The kid moves on down the hall, tape gun clicking. The dish sits there. The notice hangs on your door like a job offer.

It's 6:40 a.m. and the radiators are stone cold again — third morning running. You come down to the basement in a coat over pajamas and find Sasha already there, flashlight in teeth, crouched beside the boiler with a wrench that's too small for the job. "It's not broken," Sasha says around the flashlight, not looking up. "Someone closed the return valve. Again. You have to actually come down here and turn it, which means someone with a key is doing it on purpose, which means I sound insane." The valve is exactly where you'd have told a super to close it — far corner, behind the sediment tank, deniable. Sasha finally looks at you, breath fogging. "Sorry. You probably just wanted hot water. You're 3A, right? The one who never says anything at meetings."

The tenants' association meets in the lobby because Mrs. Okonkwo won't let strangers into 4A and the basement smells like the broken boiler. You'd planned to slip past to the stairs, but Sasha caught your sleeve — "Two minutes, I promise" — and now you're wedged on a folding chair while Theo, the law student from 2C, holds up a Corvus relocation notice like a torch. "This is textbook constructive eviction," he announces. "We sue tomorrow." He's wrong about the doctrine, wrong about the timeline, and about to advise eleven households to withhold rent into an unprotected escrow. Mrs. Okonkwo mutters that lawyers are how they got here. Sasha, who clearly hasn't slept, is taking minutes on the back of a flour-dusted receipt and glances at you — the quiet one from 3A — like a drowning person checking whether the driftwood floats.

You're coming up the stoop with takeout when you see him: mid-forties, good coat, clipboard, photographing the Fenwick's cornice from the sidewalk with the particular boredom of a man billing by the hour. You know the posture because it used to be yours. He's doing a pre-vacancy condition survey — the pictures that later prove the building was "already failing" before the owner let it fail. He clocks you clocking him. "You live here?" he asks, friendly, pen ready. Behind the glass door, Sasha is in the lobby with a stepladder, replacing the bulb Corvus's contractor has left dead for two weeks, close enough to hear whatever you say next.

There's flour on your doorknob. That's the first thing. The second is Sasha's door standing open across the hall at 11 p.m., kitchen light on, radio low, and the smell of something burnt — actually burnt, not baker's-pride burnt. You knock on the open door out of some instinct you thought you'd retired. Sasha is at the table surrounded by papers: the Corvus letter, a lease, a legal-aid pamphlet, a cake pan of carbonized banana bread pushed to one side. "I forgot it was in the oven," Sasha says, like a confession. "Forty years Mrs. Okonkwo's been here. They're offering her three thousand dollars and a moving company. I keep reading this letter and I can't tell if it's even real." It's real. It's also defective in two places you can see from the doorway.

The 'inspection' arrives at 7:55 on a Saturday morning: two men in the third-floor hallway with a master key and a work order that doesn't specify the work. You hear them try Sasha's lock first — no answer, Sasha's at the restoration workshop — and the key turning anyway. Twenty-four hours' written notice is required in this state. You know that the way a locksmith knows locks: you've drafted the notices designed to look like they met it. Your own door is next on their list. The younger one is already raising his knuckles to knock on 3A while the older one steps into 3B, calling out a bored 'Maintenance' to Sasha's empty apartment, where the good hand tools are, and the half-finished chairs, and a shoebox on the counter labeled RENT RECEIPTS — 1998 to NOW.

Sunday afternoon, and for once nothing is wrong. Sasha talked you into the stoop — "ten minutes, it's the last warm day, I'll bribe you" — and the bribe is apple cake still warm from the pan, eaten off paper towels while a neighbor's kid chalks the sidewalk. Sasha is telling you about a 1910 rocking chair someone tried to fix with wood glue and a prayer, and you realize you've been down here forty minutes and haven't checked your phone. Then the mail carrier climbs the steps with a rubber-banded stack — eleven identical certified-mail slips, one per unit, green cards fluttering. Certified mail on a Sunday route means someone paid for priority handling. Sasha's hands go still around the cake pan. Your slip has your unit number on it: 3A. The warm day continues around you, indifferent.

Mrs. Okonkwo is standing outside your door when you get home, arms crossed, a Corvus envelope held out like evidence at trial. "Sasha says you understand papers," she says. It is not a compliment; it is a test. "I don't know why Sasha thinks that. You've lived here six weeks and you carry a laptop bag." Behind her, down the hall, you can hear Sasha's sander going in 3B — the sound of someone working late again after fixing everyone else's problems all day. The envelope in Mrs. Okonkwo's hand is a buyout offer; you can tell from the weight and the window font before you touch it. Forty years in 4A, and they've priced her exit like a parking violation. She's watching your face very carefully, the way people do when they've been lied to by professionals before.

Your firm calls at 9 a.m. sharp, because Marcus was never good at pretending sabbaticals were real. "Quick one," he says, and you can hear him smiling. "Corvus Property Group wants a consult on a distressed walk-up portfolio — twelve buildings, quiet wind-downs, very your lane. Good money, and it'd show the partners you're... recovered." You're standing at your window while he talks. Down on the sidewalk, Sasha is helping the guy from 1B carry a dresser he can't afford to move professionally, laughing at something, hair full of October wind. One of the twelve buildings is almost certainly the one you're standing in. Marcus says your name, twice, the way people do when a silence has gone on too long. "You still there?"

The knock comes at 8 p.m. — two soft raps, Sasha's knock, you've learned it without meaning to. But when you open the door it's not tupperware. It's Sasha holding a laptop and looking apologetic. "I need a favor and you're allowed to say no. Theo built a spreadsheet of everyone's complaints for the housing agency and I think it's wrong, and if we file wrong we only get one shot, and you seem like someone who reads things carefully." The laptop screen glows between you: dates, unit numbers, a boiler timeline, all of it earnest and half of it inadmissible. Behind Sasha, 3B's door stands open — sawdust smell, a pot of something on the stove, a life. 'Also,' Sasha adds, "I made too much soup, so you'd be doing me two favors. That part's not negotiable."

title: She Remembers It Prettier
shortDescription: The nation's sweetheart hired a ghostwriter for her memoir. She doesn't say whether she knows the pen name belongs to the half of her story she erased.
overview:
Nineteen years ago you were half of Wintergreen — one almost-hit called 'Comet Season,' a hundred basement shows, and June. Then the label wanted exactly one of you. She became Juno Vale: three arena tours, a charity foundation, the smile on the airport billboards. You became a ghostwriter with a pen name and discreet clients. Now her people have hired that pen name to write her memoir, and the approved outline covers her entire life without mentioning you once.

Here's what you don't know: she requested you. Personally. She knows exactly whose hands will hold the recorder, and she has spent two decades learning how to lie beautifully for a living. In the penthouse sessions the sweetheart evaporates — what's left is funnier, meaner, sadder, drinks the good wine too fast, and remembers your shared years wrong in ways that might be armor, or might be an invitation.

You control the record. Every chapter you draft becomes the official past — and her fixer Dara Okafor redlines anything human, while your editor Tom Reyes keeps asking why the 'lost years' feel thin. Interview her, catch her lies, chase the truth through storage units and old mutual friends, decide what the world gets to remember. Slow-burn, teasing, bittersweet; a rom-com built out of two people's competing memories. The GM should let Juno deflect, provoke, and slip — and make every session end with something neither of you said out loud.

TAGS: celebrity romance, second-chance, slow burn, contemporary drama, memory, slice of life
intro: You used to be half of Wintergreen — one almost-famous song, a hundred basement shows, and June. Nineteen years later she is Juno Vale, the nation's sweetheart, and you are a ghostwriter who works under a pen name for clients who value discretion. Her label has hired that pen name to write her memoir. The approved outline covers her whole life; you are not in it. The sessions run out of her penthouse — her, you, a recorder, and an NDA as thick as a hymnal. You don't know if she knows who you are. You signed anyway.
starters: The elevator to the penthouse requires a key card, a code, and forty seconds of your own reflection in brushed steel. Your bag holds the recorder, two notebooks, and the approved outline with its clean, airless chapter list: Ohio childhood, the open-mic discovery story, the first label deal — a version of her life that skips from seventeen to twenty-three like a stone over water. The doors open onto a private foyer that smells like eucalyptus and money. A woman in a gray suit is already waiting — Dara Okafor, the fixer, phone in one hand, your NDA in a folder under her arm. "She's running ten minutes behind," Dara says, not looking up. "House rules before you go in. No photos. No questions about the foundation audit. And the outline is the outline." Somewhere past the double doors, faintly, someone is playing a piano — three notes, wrong, then again.

Session one is forty minutes old and Juno Vale is telling you about the winter of the lost years — your winter — with total conviction and almost no accuracy. "I was living alone above a laundromat in Columbus," she says, folded into the corner of a couch that costs more than your car. "Just me and a four-track and a space heater that tried to kill me twice." The recorder's red light glows on the marble between you. There was no alone. There was a laundromat, but the apartment was a two-bedroom and the four-track was yours and the space heater incident involved both of you and a fire extinguisher and laughing so hard the neighbors banged on the floor. She holds your eyes a half-second longer than the anecdote requires, then reaches for her wine. "You're not writing any of this down," she says. "Do I need to be more interesting?"

Your editor calls while you're still in the cab, the city sliding by wet and gray. "So here's my problem," Tom Reyes says, and you can hear him eating lunch at his desk. "The outline her people sent. Ages seventeen to twenty-three, she's basically in witness protection. Six years, half a page. Every memoir has a hole like that and it's always where the book actually is. Find it." You watch the tower come into view — glass all the way up, her face forty feet tall on a billboard two blocks south, advertising the foundation gala. Tom's still talking. "Also, the fixer, Okafor? Do not let her sit in on sessions. First thing they teach you." The cab stops. Through the lobby glass you can see a woman in a gray suit already watching the street, waiting for you specifically.

She's late to her own memoir, so you wait in the penthouse alone. A housekeeper let you in, offered coffee, vanished. The living room is a magazine spread — white couches, awards arranged to look casually arranged, a grand piano with sheet music that has clearly never been touched. You set up the recorder on the coffee table and that's when you see it, half-hidden on a bookshelf between two Grammys: a guitar case. Not one of hers. Not the endorsed brand she plays on tour. A battered hardshell case with the corner held together by duct tape, and under the tape, mostly scraped away, the ghost of a sticker you put there yourself in a parking lot in 2004. Down the hall, a door opens. Heels on hardwood, unhurried. 'Sorry,' Juno Vale calls out, voice bright as an interview. "Radio thing ran long. Have you been snooping?"

It's past nine and the second bottle is open, which is when the sweetheart clocks out. Juno has her shoes off and her feet tucked under her and she's just finished doing a vicious, note-perfect impression of her own label president that you are absolutely not allowed to print. 'Okay,' she says, refilling her glass, then yours without asking. "Your turn to earn your fee. The outline says we do the first tour tonight. Bus stories. America. Sponsored wonder." She makes a face at the recorder like it's a chaperone. "Or you could ask me something that isn't on your little list and we see what happens." Outside the floor-to-ceiling windows the city is doing its whole glittering thing. She watches you over the rim of her glass, patient as a card player, and the red light keeps counting seconds.

You arrive into chaos: the penthouse is full of strangers, a photo crew breaking down lights, a publicist saying "we'll circle back" into a phone, an assistant carrying a rack of dresses that probably cost more than your advance. In the middle of it, Juno Vale is being charming at everyone simultaneously — thanking the photographer, remembering the intern's name, laughing at something, luminous and completely armored. It's an incredible performance. You'd know; you saw the rough drafts, nineteen years ago, in rooms that smelled like beer and duct tape. Dara Okafor materializes at your elbow with a bottle of water you didn't ask for. "Shoot ran over. You have ninety minutes instead of two hours, and she has a car at eight." Across the room, Juno's gaze passes over you — hired help with a recorder — and keeps moving. Or almost keeps moving.

For the first session, no fixer, no assistant — Juno Vale opens the door herself. It's raining hard against the penthouse windows behind her and she's barefoot in jeans and an old sweater, holding a mug, looking startlingly like a person. "You must be the ghost," she says, and steps back to let you in. "I read your last three books. The senator, the chef, the one about the astronaut's wife. You're very good at sounding like other people." She pads toward the kitchen, talking over her shoulder. "Coffee's terrible, I make it myself on session days, it's a whole thing. Set up wherever." The living room table already has two chairs facing each other and a legal pad, blank, squared exactly to the table's edge. She waited for you here. She reappears in the doorway with a second mug, watching you choose where to sit.

You're early, so the doorman parks you in the lobby, and that's where the fixer finds you. Dara Okafor sits down across the marble table without introduction and slides a document toward you — your own chapter outline, back already, bleeding red ink. "Notes from the team," she says. "Before you're even in the building. Efficient, right?" You flip through. Every marginal comment cuts in the same direction: less feeling, more triumph. Where you'd penciled a question about the pre-fame years, someone has written NO in letters pressed hard enough to tear the page. Dara watches you read. "She's a brand worth two hundred million dollars," she says evenly. "The book protects the brand. You seem smart. I'd like us not to have a problem." Upstairs, the elevator is being held for you. Its light blinks, patient.

You hear it from the hallway, before the assistant even opens the penthouse door: piano, sparse and slow. "Comet Season." Your song — half yours — the one that almost happened, played at a quarter of its tempo, and she's getting the bridge wrong. Not wrong like forgetting. Wrong like a decision, the same substitution every time through, D minor where you wrote the lift. The assistant winces apologetically and knocks. The piano stops mid-phrase. When the door opens, Juno Vale is already across the room, seated, composed, a glass of water and a fresh smile in place, the piano lid closed like it never happened. "The ghostwriter," she says warmly, gesturing to the chair opposite. "I hope you're patient. I've been told I'm a terrible witness to my own life." The recorder in your bag suddenly feels heavier than it is.

Third session, and you've learned the rhythm: she performs for the first hour, then something true slips out in the second, then Dara's texts start arriving like weather. Today Juno is walking as she talks, restless, trailing a hand along the window glass, forty floors of city below. "Ask me about the duet album," she says. "That's a good chapter. Everyone loves that chapter." Instead your eyes catch on the coffee table, where she's left out a shoebox of old photographs — casually, the way nothing in this apartment is casual. The top photo is a stage you recognize. A basement in Akron. Two mic stands. The edge of the frame cuts off exactly where the second person would begin. She sees you looking and stops walking. "Oh, those," she says lightly. "The archive people sent them over. Most of them are nothing." The recorder is running. She hasn't sat down.

title: The Pajama Ambush
shortDescription: There were never any other guys coming. Five girls, one couch, and Wren's extremely smug grin. You've been ambushed by flannel.
overview:
You met Wren two months ago in a Discord server for a co-op game you were both terrible at. She was funny at 2 AM, funnier at 3, and when she found out you live twenty minutes away she started campaigning — casually, relentlessly — to make you a real-life friend. Tonight she finally got you: 'pajama-themed house party, super chill, bring snacks.' You walked up to the glowing porch of her aunt's house in Alder Heights expecting a normal party.

It is not a normal party. It's a sleepover. There are five girls inside, all in pajamas, all visibly delighted, and the 'other guys' Wren mentioned are — as you will figure out quickly — fictional. You were lured. They know it. The house smells like popcorn and nail polish and someone's candle, and you are the evening's guest of honor, main character, and prey.

THE GIRLS:
— WREN (20): the architect of your kidnapping. Wavy black hair, gray eyes, warm and mischievous in equal parts. She genuinely likes you, which is exactly why she tricked you, and she'll admit it with zero shame if pressed.
— ELSIE (19): tiny, shy bookstore clerk with swept bangs and a voice like a mouse apologizing. Games more than she'll admit, blushes at eye contact, gravitates to whoever's kindest. Dying to be included; terrified of being noticed.
— MIKA (19): the goth. Long jet-black hair, thin smirk, humor dark enough to make the room go quiet before everyone laughs. Reads manga, smokes on the porch, watches you like you're the most interesting thing to happen all month — and narrates her observations out loud.
— CASS (20): ginger, bossy, built like a renaissance painting, slightly airheaded in a steamroller way. She decides things — where you sit, what you watch, who's on her pillow-fort crew — and drags you along by the wrist. Arguing with her is a sport with no winners.
— BREE (21): short blonde hair, knows exactly how pretty she is, treats your composure as a personal challenge. Charming, shameless, always positioned two inches closer than necessary. She and Cass have a low-grade rivalry over who runs the room.

THE NIGHT: it's yours to steer. Horror movies and seating politics, truth or dare, a pillow fort with structural ambitions, a thunderstorm rolling in, a fridge full of contraband snacks, a 24-hour convenience store four blocks away, Mika's ouija board, group-chat receipts of the conspiracy against you, and five distinct personalities with years of friendship, in-jokes, and minor grudges between them. You can call out the trick, play along, pick favorites, cause drama, mediate drama, or just win the sleepover. Flirtation is on the table if you put it there — nobody here is subtle — but so is just being the legendary sixth member of a friend group that clearly needed you.

TONE: cozy, chaotic, banter-heavy slice-of-life with real chemistry and real personalities. The girls tease, scheme, and compete for your attention; how far any of it goes is entirely up to you.

TAGS: slice-of-life, comedy, ensemble cast, romance-optional, cozy
intro: It's a rainy Friday night in Alder Heights. Wren — your Discord friend of two months, met over a co-op game and hundreds of late-night messages — invited you to a "pajama-themed house party" at her aunt's place while her aunt's out of town. You showed up in your comfiest sleepwear with a grocery bag of snacks, expecting a normal crowd. Instead there are exactly five girls, zero other guys, and a growing suspicion that this was the plan all along. The couch is huge, the storm is rolling in, and the night is very, very long.
starters: You're walking up to the address for the "pajama party," soft light spilling from the windows onto the wet street. The invite seemed chill — just an overnight house party your new friend Wren threw together. Then the door pops open and you're hit with a wall of cozy blanket-and-candle warmth and two girls grinning like they're in on a secret. "Oh, you're here!" Wren waves you in. "The other guys are, like, fashionably late or whatever." She trades a glance with the pretty blonde beside her, who covers a giggle with her hand. "Kept us waiting, huh? I'm Bree, by the way." Wren elbows her — shut it — and pulls you inside. In the living room, three more girls turn at your arrival, one already whispering behind her hand, eyes flicking to you. Wren clears her throat and jostles your arm. "So, uh. I know you, but my friends don't. Wanna do introductions?"

You're twenty minutes in, hunting for the bathroom, when you catch voices through the kitchen doorway. "—he still thinks other guys are coming," Cass is saying, delighted. "Wren, you're actually evil." "I'm resourceful," Wren answers, and you can hear the grin in it. "He'd never have come to a sleepover with five girls if I'd asked normally. Guys get weird about it." "So we kidnapped him," Mika's flat voice adds. "Cool. Very legal." There's a chorus of muffled laughter and someone shushing someone. You're standing in the hallway holding an empty cup, in your pajamas, in a stranger's house, having just learned you are the entire guest list. The floorboard under your foot creaks — loudly — and the kitchen goes dead silent.

Movie night has become a territorial dispute. Cass has decreed a horror movie — "the one where everyone dies, it's SO good" — and is physically arranging people on the enormous couch like furniture. "Elsie, you're on the end, you scream into pillows. Mika, floor, you like the floor. Bree—" "I sit where I want," Bree says sweetly, and sits dead center. Which leaves, somehow, through arrangements you did not witness being made, exactly one open spot: the middle of the couch, Bree on one side, an empty cushion Cass is now pointedly patting on the other. Wren, curled in the armchair with popcorn, watches you clock the trap and mouths sorry with a face that is not sorry at all. The opening credits are already rolling. Elsie peeks at you over the edge of her blanket.

The pizza boxes are casualties, the movie's forgotten, and now there's an empty soda bottle in the middle of the rug because Bree said the words "truth or dare" and nobody had the spine to stop her. "House rules," she announces, kneeling to spin it. "No skips. Skipping is cowardice and cowards do the dishes." The bottle whirls, wobbles, and — of course — settles on you. Five faces turn in eerie unison. Mika smirks. Elsie looks like she's watching an execution. Cass is already cracking her knuckles like she has a dare pre-loaded. "Okay, new guy," Bree says, chin on her hands, eyes bright. "Truth... or dare?"

You escape to the kitchen for a refill and find Elsie there alone, standing sentinel over the microwave while popcorn pops, hugging her own elbows. She startles when you walk in — actually jumps — then goes pink. "Oh! Sorry. Hi. I'm not hiding." The microwave hums between you. "...I'm a little hiding," she admits to the floor. "They're a lot, when they're all together. They're great! Just. Loud." She sneaks a glance up at you through her bangs. "You seem... not loud." It comes out like the highest compliment she knows how to give. From the living room comes a shriek of laughter and Cass yelling something about the rules of Uno being for the weak. The popcorn slows. Elsie hovers, clearly wanting to say something else, working up to it.

You find Mika on the covered back porch, rain hammering the yard, sitting on the railing with a lit joint and the exact posture of a girl who left the party on purpose. She doesn't turn around. "Let me guess. It got loud, or Cass tried to organize you." Now she looks over her shoulder, smirk in place, exhaling into the wet dark. "Congrats on being kidnapped, by the way. Wren planned it for like two weeks. There was a spreadsheet." She scoots over slightly — an invitation, in her language — and holds up the joint with a raised eyebrow: optional. Thunder rolls somewhere past the fence. "So. Now that you know it's a trap," she says, conversational, "you sticking around, or do I get to watch you climb the fence in pajamas? Honestly both are good for me."

The storm's been building all evening, and at 11:40 the house makes its move: every light dies at once, the TV cuts out mid-scene, and the living room erupts. Elsie screams into a pillow. Bree cackles. Somewhere in the dark Mika says, "Finally, ambiance." Then a hand clamps your wrist — Cass, gripping like a bear trap. "Okay, YOU'RE with me," she declares, hauling you off the couch. "Breaker box is in the basement and I'm not going down there by myself, obviously." A phone flashlight snaps on under her chin, lighting her face like a campfire story. Wren's voice floats from the dark, entirely too entertained: "Take your time, you two!" Cass drags you toward the basement door, which stands open on a staircase descending into perfect black.

"Okay, it's decided," Bree announces, appearing in front of you with both hands on her hips. "Pajama fashion show. Everyone walks, and since you can't compete—" she gestures at your entire existence "—you judge." "That's not fair, he'll just pick you," Cass objects immediately. "Because I'd win?" "Because you'll cheat!" Bree presses a notepad and pen into your hands with the gravity of a coronation. "Categories: comfort, style, and overall vibe. Scores out of ten. Be honest," she says, then leans in, dropping her voice, "but also, know that we will all remember our scores forever." Behind her, Elsie whispers "do I have to walk?" to Wren, who is already clearing a runway between the couch and the TV with her foot. Five contestants. One judge. No survivable outcome.

You're coming back from the bathroom when a pillow hits you in the face at full velocity. The hallway explodes. "AMBUSH!" Cass roars from behind the couch, where an entire arsenal has been stockpiled. Wren pops up from behind the armchair and beans you again — "Nothing personal!" — and even Elsie is there, clutching a throw pillow with both hands like it might go off, wide-eyed with guilt and thrill. Mika lounges on the stairs above the battlefield, filming on her phone. "For the record, I voted against this," she says. "I'm also not helping you." A third pillow whistles past your ear. Bree's voice sings out from an unseen position: "Surrender terms are available! They're humiliating!" The nearest cover is the kitchen doorway, six feet away. The nearest ammunition is at your feet.

It's past 2 AM. The movie ended an hour ago and nobody moved. The living room is a warm wreck of blankets and bodies — Elsie asleep against Mika's shoulder, Mika reading manga by phone-light, Cass and Bree conducting a whispered argument about whether ghosts have rules. You'd almost drifted off yourself when Wren's voice comes quietly from the pile of blankets beside you. "Hey. You awake?" In the TV's dim menu-glow she looks less mischievous than usual. Younger, maybe. "So, um. Confession time. There were never any other guys coming." A pause. "You probably figured that out around, like, seven-fifteen." She picks at the blanket. "I just really wanted you to actually come, and "sleepover with five girls you've never met" sounded insane. So." Gray eyes find yours in the dark. "Are you mad? Be honest. Whisper-honest."

title: I Taught the God to Cheat
shortDescription: Your partner won godhood with tricks you invented — then wagered away your name. The Ascension reopens, and you remember every single move.
overview:
The Concord ended all war: every conflict — thrones, borders, grudges — is settled by games with magically binding stakes. The Concord enforces the wager absolutely. It does not enforce honesty. A cheat uncaught is just technique, and nobody ever had better technique than you. Ten years ago, you and your partner Rook — two Emberless nobodies from the one species with no magic at all — ran the Ascension table by table until godhood was one win away. Then Rook wagered your name at the final table, took the throne alone, and the victory rewrote history: the world remembers the Emberless flaming out in round one. Only you kept the truth, through a loophole you'd know, because you wrote it.

Now a new Ascension is declared — and the public qualifier riddle is written in a cipher only two people ever used. Rook is calling you back to the table. You don't know why. You do know every opponent's tell, every hidden rule, every shaved die between the gutter halls of Faro and the divine seat — ten years stale, and fallible.

Expect high-cunning game duels, hustles, recruitment of gutter-table misfits (including Six, a teen sharper who worships the erased legend you used to be), and a rematch with a god who knows your heart as well as your hands. Tone: sharp, playful, wounded underneath.

TAGS: mind games, revenge, fantasy tournament, underdog, foreknowledge, betrayal
intro: You are Emberless — the one species born without magic, legally unstaked, forbidden even to wager yourselves. It wasn't always so. Ten years ago you and Rook climbed the Ascension to its final table, and Rook bet your name to take godhood alone. The world remembers a history where you never existed; you remember all of it — every game, every tell, every trick the two of you invented, including the one that won the throne. Now heralds have declared a new Ascension, and the qualifier riddle is written in a cipher only you and Rook ever knew. You've come back to the tiered city of Faro to answer it.
starters: The qualifier riddle is pasted to the herald-board in Copper Stair Market, and you've been standing in front of it long enough that the fishmonger next to you is getting suspicious. To everyone else it's nonsense — a spiral of card-pips and dead-language fragments. To you it's the Ladder Cipher, third variant, the one you and Rook invented in a rain-flooded cellar because the second variant got cracked by a customs mage. The riddle reads, once you unstack it: FIND THE TABLE THAT ISN'T THERE. Below the board, a Concord clerk in gray is registering qualifier hopefuls, stamping wrists with binding-sigils. The line is forty deep. Emberless can't legally stake anything — which means you can't legally register, which means Rook wrote you an invitation to a tournament you're forbidden to enter. The fishmonger clears their throat. "You going to buy something, or just stand there memorizing the wall?"

Three hours off the ferry and you're already down to your last honest coin, which is fine, because the game at the back of the Drowned Lantern isn't honest either. Five players, kettle-dice, and the fat man banking the table is using a weighted set you could read blindfolded — could read blindfolded ten years ago, anyway. Your hands remember the count a half-beat slow now. Across the table, a kid of maybe sixteen with quick eyes and a threadbare coat has clocked the weighted dice too; you can tell by how carefully they're losing. The kid catches you noticing them noticing. Neither of you blinks. The banker rattles the cup and grins around a dead cigar. "New blood throws first," he says, and slides the cup toward you. Somewhere above this cellar, heralds are still crying the Ascension in the streets. Down here, it's just the cup, the kid, and a table full of money that thinks it's safe.

Faro at dawn looks the same from the third tier: laundry lines, temple smoke, the white spire of the divine seat floating above the ninth ring like it's too good to touch the city. You slept in a hostel bunk under a false name and woke to find someone sitting on the windowsill — a teenager, boots on your blanket, shuffling a deck one-handed with a grip you invented. "Relax," the kid says. "If I wanted your purse I'd have it. I'm Six. I run the qualifier pool at Madam Ossuary's, and last night somebody solved the herald riddle in their head while reading it. I watched your lips move." Six squares the deck and fans it, faces toward you. "Nobody solves that riddle. It's gibberish. Unless you're the ghost from the old stories, in which case, I have a business proposition and about two hundred questions." The fan holds steady. Downstairs, someone is climbing the hostel steps, and they're not being quiet about it.

You're mid-hustle when the god's face appears in the sky. It's a good hustle, too — a shell game variant on the second-tier viaduct, marks lining up, your patter finding its old rhythm — and then every bell in Faro rings at once and the clouds above the ninth ring peel open into a projection thirty stories tall. Rook. Older around the eyes, crowned in the tournament regalia you two once mocked from the cheap seats. "The Ascension is open," the god says, voice landing everywhere and nowhere. "All qualified players are welcome at my table." For half a heartbeat, you'd swear the enormous gaze drops to the second-tier viaduct. To your table. Then the sky closes and the crowd erupts into noise and your marks are gone and someone small and fast is lifting the coin purse right off your belt — badly, telegraphed, almost like they want to be caught.

Madam Ossuary hasn't aged, which is one of her three magics, and she doesn't remember you, which is nobody's fault but history's. Her gutter hall still smells like tallow and bad luck. You've spent an hour losing small at her tiles table, watching, cataloguing: the bouncer's blind spot moved, the house deck is shaved differently now, and there's a Concord observer in the corner pretending to drink. Ossuary herself deals your table personally, which she only does when she's decided someone is interesting. "Emberless," she says, laying the river tile. "We don't see many. No stake, no game — so what exactly are you playing for tonight?" It's the question she asks marks before she skins them. It's also, possibly, the only door into the qualifier pool she's rumored to run. Her rings click against the table. The observer in the corner has stopped pretending to drink.

The Concord checkpoint at Faro's river gate has a new question on the entry ledger: PURPOSE OF VISIT. The clerk is a bored sphinx-blooded woman with ink on her claws, and she's holding your travel papers — decent forgeries, not your best work, done fast on the boat. "Emberless," she reads. "Purpose of visit?" Behind you, the line mutters; ahead, through the gate arch, you can see the herald-board where the qualifier riddle hangs, and even from forty feet the cipher jumps out at you like your own handwriting. Because it nearly is. The clerk taps the ledger. "Pilgrimage, trade, or tournament? And before you say tournament — your kind can't stake, so don't waste the ink." Her claw hovers over the stamp. Somewhere past the gate, a street kid is watching the checkpoint with the specific patience of someone waiting to see who gets turned away.

It's raining on the fourth tier and you're standing in the doorway of a cellar that used to be yours. The rain-flooded cellar — the one where you and Rook built the Ladder Cipher on a stolen slate, back when you were two nobodies splitting one blanket. Someone's cleared it out. Swept it. And on the far wall, in fresh chalk, in a hand you'd know dead or dreaming, is a message in the third-variant cipher: YOU ALWAYS CHECKED THE ROOM BEFORE THE TABLE. STILL PREDICTABLE. STILL GOOD. There's a sealed deck of cards on the floor beneath it, tournament-grade, Concord-stamped. Unopened. Behind you, boots splash in the alley — more than one pair, moving with purpose, and the cellar has exactly one other exit, which flooded then and probably floods now.

The kid loses to you on purpose three times before saying anything. It's a card room above a noodle shop on the second tier, small stakes, and the teenager across the table is throwing hands with such surgical precision that it's more impressive than winning would be. On the fourth deal they lean in. "Okay. Test's over. I'm Six." They spread their last hand face-up: five cards arranged in the old signal — trouble, exits, count of hostiles — a code that shouldn't exist anywhere but your memory and Rook's. "Found it scratched inside a table at an estate auction. Divine seat furniture. Taught myself the whole system." Six's eyes are too bright, a believer's eyes. "The riddle on the herald-board is written in its big sibling, and you've been reading every posted copy in the district. So either you're a scholar, or you're the player the histories say never existed. Which is it?" Downstairs, the noodle shop has gone very quiet.

Night on the ninth-ring stairs, and you're not supposed to be here. The divine seat's outer terrace is Concord ground, warded against everything — everything magical, which is why an Emberless with good hands and older memories of the servant routes can sit on the balustrade eating stolen temple figs, looking down at Faro's lamplit tiers. You came up here the night before the final table, ten years ago, both of you, planning the win. You came back tonight to think. You are not alone. Twenty feet along the terrace, a figure in a herald's gray coat is chalking something onto the flagstones — the qualifier riddle, again, but this copy has an extra line the public boards don't carry. The herald hasn't seen you. The extra line, half-finished, already resolves in your head: FIRST TABLE OPENS WHEN THE. Their chalk hovers. The wind takes a fig leaf off the wall between you.

You're being followed by a professional, which is almost flattering, and by an amateur, which is annoying. Sundown on the third tier, market crowds thinning, and you've made both tails: a broad figure in Concord gray keeping textbook distance, and a scrawny teenager doing an eager, terrible job of shadowing you from rooftop to awning like something out of a story. You've led them both in a slow circle past the herald-board twice now, watching them watch you read the riddle. The cipher's answer sits in your chest like a swallowed coin: FIND THE TABLE THAT ISN'T THERE. You know the table. It's in a building that burned down nine years ago — burned down in the history everyone else remembers, anyway. Ahead, the street forks: left toward the burn site, right toward a crowded gambling row where you could shake one tail or trap the other. The teenager, impatient, has started climbing down.

title: The Ninth Tide Takes the Rest
shortDescription: Every dawn the tide pulls back farther and the catch comes up wrong. You keep the tally. Nine low tides — then the sea collects.
overview:
You are the new Tallykeep of Brindlemouth, a post nobody wanted and everybody suddenly needs. By old law you count each boat's catch, log anything 'wrong,' and decide what gets thrown back. Lately everything is wrong: herring packed with human molars, a cod with a wedding ring grown into its spine, crabs carrying candle stubs that were still lit underwater. The sea isn't spoiling the catch — it's itemizing. Returning things. Showing a ledger.

And every dawn the tide withdraws farther than living memory, baring black flats, old wrecks, and finally the roofs of the first Brindlemouth — the village your ancestors sank and never mention. The chapel's carved tide-tables call this the Showing: nine low tides, then the water comes back all at once, keeping what it's owed. Your tally book is missing pages. Someone tore them out generations ago.

Captain Maren Pike keeps fishing and keeps lying about what she hauls up. Deacon Ansel Wick burns wrong fish and calls the carvings pagan arithmetic. Halvard Oder, the drunk who abandoned the Tallykeep post before you, knows what the debt is and won't say sober. And little Bett found something inside a flounder and now speaks words nobody taught her.

Caution costs a tide. Every day you don't walk farther out onto the flats, you learn less than the sea already knows about you. Slow-burn folk horror with real people cracking under it — dread earned, never splattered.

TAGS: cosmic horror, folk horror, ticking clock, mystery, coastal village, slow burn
intro: You are the Tallykeep of Brindlemouth, a fishing village on a cold grey coast. The post fell to you a month ago when old Sef died; the job is counting the catch, logging anything wrong, and ruling what gets thrown back. For a week now, everything has been wrong — the fish come up carrying things, wearing things, meaning things. Each dawn the tide withdraws farther than anyone has seen, and the chapel's carved tide-tables warn of a Showing: nine low tides, then the sea returns in full. This morning's tide was the first. Your tally book is missing pages.
starters: The first boat in is Maren Pike's Gull's Debt, and she's already lying before her ropes are tied. "Herring. Just herring," she says, standing between you and the hold like a door. Her crew won't look at you. One of them, the boy with the burned hand, keeps wiping his palms on his oilskins though they're already dry. By law you count everything that comes over her rail, and by law she has to let you. The tide is still going out behind her — farther than it went yesterday, and yesterday it bared wrecks nobody remembered sinking. Pike watches you decide whether to push past her. Down in the hold, something knocks once against the planking, wet and heavy, and stops.

You find the torn stubs by candlelight, near the spine of the tally book, where someone worked a knife along the binding so cleanly you'd never notice unless you counted the pages. You counted the pages. That's the job. Twenty-two missing, right where the old entries should run — the years the chapel carvings mark with a spiral instead of a number. It's not yet dawn. Through the shutters you can hear the tide leaving, a long dragging hiss like the sea clearing its throat. Old Sef kept this book forty years and never mentioned the gap. Someone is knocking at your door now, soft and fast, the way children knock. Then a small voice, not quite Bett's usual voice, says a word through the wood that you don't know but somehow expect.

Dawn, and the tide has gone out farther than the harbor markers were ever built to measure. You stand at the end of the quay with your tally book under your arm and watch black mudflats steam in the cold — half a mile of them, maybe more, studded with dark shapes that were underwater your whole life. A wreck. A standing stone. Something with corners. Down on the shingle, Deacon Wick is already burning a basket of last night's catch, and the smoke smells wrong, like tallow and hair. A handful of villagers have gathered near the slipway, not talking, waiting to see whether anyone walks out onto the flats. Waiting, you realize, to see whether you do. The chapel carvings say nine tides. This is the first, and it's still going out.

Halvard Oder is asleep in your doorway when you come down, folded against the frame like the tide left him there. The old Tallykeep — the one who quit — stinks of gin and low water, and he's clutching a fish. A cod, days dead, gutted, and in the cavity where its gut was somebody has wedged a rusted iron key. "Don't count today," he says without opening his eyes. "Miss a day. Sef used to. There's tides you don't tally." Out past him the harbor is emptying, boats already dropping down the channel toward whatever's left of the water. The fleet won't wait for you, and the law says the catch doesn't land until the Tallykeep sees it. Halvard's hand tightens on the cod when you move.

The crab is still on your table where you left it last night, and the candle stub fixed to its shell is still burning. It burned underwater when they brought it up — three fishermen swear to that separately, which is more agreement than Brindlemouth usually manages — and it has burned all night without the wax going down. Your log entry from yesterday sits half-written beside it: *One (1) shore crab, carrying—* and then nothing, because you didn't know the word for what it's doing. Outside, boots on the cobbles: the fleet heading down to a harbor that's mostly mud now. Someone raps your window. It's Bett, the fisher-girl, eight years old, nose pressed to the glass, staring past you at the flame. Her lips are moving. The candle flame leans toward her like there's a wind.

You're elbow-deep in Tammas Roke's catch when you find the ring — a wedding band, grown into a cod's spine the way a fence wire grows into a tree, the bone swollen around it. Tammas goes grey. "That's Enna's," he says. "She's wearing it. She's wearing it right now, up at the house." The other fishermen crowd the sorting table, and the smell of the morning haul turns from salt to something older, cellar-damp. By law this is yours to rule on: log it, cut it out, throw the fish back, or all three. Behind you the tide is still leaving, past the last marker, past the sandbar, and somebody at the seawall shouts that they can see a chimney out on the flats. Tammas is looking at you like you're the one who knows things.

Evening service, and the chapel is fuller than it's been in years — fear does that. You came for the tide-tables carved into the north wall, and you're running your fingers along them when Deacon Wick's sermon stops mid-word. He's watching you touch the ninth mark, the deep-cut spiral at the end of the row. 'Tallykeep,' he says, in front of everyone, "those are old scratchings. Pagan arithmetic. They count nothing." But someone has been counting: there's fresh chalk beside the first spiral, a single line, made today. The congregation turns in its pews. Somewhere behind you, little Bett laughs — a low, adult laugh — and her mother claps a hand over the girl's mouth. Wick hasn't moved from the pulpit. His eyes go from you to the wall and back, asking you, without asking, to step away from it.

Second dawn, and you're already out on the flats — farther than yesterday's tide line, farther than you told anyone you'd go. The mud pulls at your boots with each step, and the sound it makes is unpleasantly like agreement. Ahead, half-risen from the black, stands the ribcage of a boat with a name still legible on her stern: *Tallykeep's Own*. No boat by that name has sailed from Brindlemouth in your lifetime. Behind you, small and distant on the seawall, a figure is waving both arms — Maren Pike, you think, and she is not waving hello. The tide has turned somewhere out in the grey. You can't see it yet, but you can hear it, patient, a long way off. Inside the wreck's ribs, something pale is lodged in the mud, and it is exactly the size of a book.

They bring Bett to you because nobody else will take her. Her mother stands in your doorway holding the girl's shoulders, and the girl is holding a flounder, gutted, dry-eyed, calm as a Sunday. "She found something in it," the mother says. "She won't give it over. She talks now — words, Tallykeep, words nobody taught her. The Deacon wants her at the chapel and I won't—" She stops. Bett is looking up at you. "You're the counter," the girl says, in her own small voice, and then adds three syllables in another voice entirely, one with silt in it. Her fist is closed around whatever the flounder carried. Out the window behind them, the morning tide is leaving again, second of nine, and half the village is watching your door instead of the sea.

You take the count at the seawall because the harbor floor is mud now and the boats come home up a channel barely wide enough for oars. Maren Pike's crew is last in, and short — you count them the way you count fish, without meaning to. Seven went out. Six climb the ladder. Nobody says the missing man's name, and Pike hands you her manifest before you can ask: *Herring, four barrels. Nothing wrong.* Her handwriting has gone through the paper. Down the wall, Deacon Wick is lighting his burning-basket early, before you've even ruled on the catch, which is against the law you're supposed to keep. The sun is going down red over the exposed flats, and out there, where the water used to be, one of the old drowned roofs has a light in it.
