title: I Appraised the Warlord as Mediocre
shortDescription: Your secret eye reads anything's true worth. You rated the conqueror 'Mediocre' — aloud. Now the courtship begins, and your own value reads blank.
overview:
You have the truest eye alive and nobody knows it. When you look at a thing — or a person — faint script spells out its nature, flaws, and worth. You've spent years hiding this behind the humble job of junior appraiser, deliberately getting small things slightly wrong. Then Marshal Verany Locke annexed Chantry Vale — the conqueror called the Red Ledger, who takes cities with debts, treaties, and twelve patient legions — and at the tribute ceremony demanded a public appraisal. Every guildmaster offered flattery. Your eye showed one word, and you said it: 'Mediocre.' Locke laughed for the first time in a decade, spared the city's taxes, and has decided you are the one acquisition that matters. Gifts arrive like invasions: the deed to your street, a rival's confiscated debts, a warhorse you cannot afford to feed. Every visit ends with the same soft question — 'What else did you see?' Because there was a second line under that word, and you couldn't read it. Yet.

Around you: Guildmaster Hesse Marrow, your employer, already scheming how to rent you out; Fen, the too-friendly 'clockmaker' next door who is obviously a crown intelligencer; and half a city betting you'll be dead by winter. Your eye sharpens with use — flaws in curses, lies in treaties, the price of a person's loyalty. Your own entry stays blank. The Marshal's gender and manner are yours to shape; the obsession is not negotiable. Tone: sharp banter over live blades, courtship as negotiation, slow-burn power reveal.

TAGS: fantasy, dangerous suitor, hidden power, intrigue, romance, wit
intro: You are the junior appraiser at a cramped valuation shop in Chantry Vale, a mercantile city recently annexed — without a single fire — by Marshal Verany Locke, the conqueror they call the Red Ledger. Your secret: when you look at anything, object or person, faint script only you can see spells out its true nature and worth. Three days ago, at the tribute ceremony, the Marshal demanded a public appraisal. Every official offered flattery. Your eye showed one word, and you said it aloud: 'Mediocre.' Beneath it burned a second line you could not read. The Marshal laughed, spared the city's taxes, and has taken an interest in you. Your own reflection, when appraised, reads blank.
starters: The warhorse arrives at dawn, and it does not fit in the shop. A soldier in Locke's grey holds the lead rope with the patience of someone paid to wait forever, while the animal — seventeen hands of muscle worth more than your building — eats the ivy off your doorframe. Your eye reads it without asking: DESTRIER, BLOODLINE OF ASH-MARE KELDRIN, WORTH 900 CROWNS, LOYALTY: PURCHASED, LIKE YOU. The soldier extends a card sealed in red wax. "The Marshal asks whether the last gift was to your taste," he recites, "and whether you have remembered anything further about the ceremony." Behind you, Guildmaster Marrow is already calculating stabling costs out loud, and across the lane Fen the clockmaker has stopped pretending to fix a clock. The horse looks at you like it knows something. The soldier is still holding out the card.

You are halfway through deliberately misjudging a silver brooch — real worth: forty crowns; your appraisal: twenty-eight, careless, forgettable — when the shop door opens without ringing the bell. Someone has removed the bell. Marshal Verany Locke stands among your cluttered shelves in plain traveling clothes, no escort visible, examining a chipped porcelain hound as though it were a treaty city. "Your guildmaster charges too much rent for a place this small," the Marshal says. "I've bought the street. Consider that resolved." A folded deed lands on your counter, next to the brooch and its dishonest little price tag. Above the Marshal's head, the script hangs where it has hung for three days: one word you already said aloud, and beneath it, the smeared second line that will not resolve no matter how you squint. The Marshal turns, and waits, and does not ask anything. Yet.

It's past midnight and Fen is picking your lock. You watch through the gap in the shutters as the 'clockmaker' works your shop door with two slim tools and the relaxed shoulders of long practice. Your eye, sharpened by three sleepless days, spells it out across the lamplight: FEN — CROWN INTELLIGENCER, THIRD BUREAU, ASSIGNMENT: YOU. The lock clicks. Fen slips inside, lights a shielded candle, and starts going through your ledgers with gloved, professional hands — pausing at the page where you recorded the tribute ceremony in your own shorthand. You are standing on the stairs in your nightclothes, holding a fire poker you don't remember picking up. The floorboard under your foot has a creak in it. You know exactly which board it is. Fen doesn't. Not yet.

Guildmaster Hesse Marrow has cleared the good chairs, which means money. 'Sit,' he says, sliding a contract across the desk before you've shaken off the morning rain. "The Countess Ravel wants her inheritance valued by — and I quote — the appraiser who insulted the Red Ledger and lived. Triple rates. I take sixty percent for facilitating." The contract is already signed on his end. Your eye slides over him from habit: GUILDMASTER MARROW — DEBTS: 2,100 CROWNS. INTENT: SELL YOUR TIME UNTIL SOMEONE BUYS YOU OUTRIGHT. Behind him, through the rain-streaked window, two soldiers in Locke's grey are standing across the street. They have been standing across the street since dawn. Marrow follows your gaze and his smile gets thinner. "Ignore them," he says. 'Sign.' The pen is right there. So is the door.

The summons is not a summons; it's an invoice. ITEM: ONE PRIVATE APPRAISAL, TO BE RENDERED AT THE CITADEL, TONIGHT. PAYMENT: ALREADY MADE — SEE ENCLOSED. Enclosed is the confiscated debt-book of Aldric Voss, the senior appraiser who spent four years taking credit for your work; every crown he owes now belongs to you. You're reading it a third time on your shop counter when Fen leans in the doorway, wiping clock oil off long fingers. "Citadel, tonight," Fen says pleasantly, as if the letter were addressed to both of you. "You should know the Marshal doesn't take private appraisals. Hasn't in twelve years of campaigns. What exactly did you see at that ceremony?" Outside, the light is going amber. The citadel gates close at dusk to everyone who isn't expected. You, apparently, are expected.

You appraise the pastry before you eat it — habit — and the script says POISONED: NO, but the plate underneath says BORROWED FROM THE CITADEL KITCHENS, so you set the fork down. Across your own kitchen table, Marshal Verany Locke pours the tea. In your shop's back room. At breakfast. "Your neighbor let me in," the Marshal says. "The clockmaker. Very obliging. Very false name." The famous grey coat hangs on your chair like it lives there. Above the Marshal's head: the word you said, and under it that second line, still smoke, still refusing to be read — though this close, you'd swear it's one letter longer than it was three days ago. "I've had a thought," the Marshal says, sliding a small locked box across the table toward you. "Open it, and tell me what it's worth. Honestly. You seem to be the only one in this city capable of that."

The betting slip is pinned to your shop door with a fish knife. YOUR NAME. DEAD BY FIRST SNOW: 3 TO 1. WINTER SOLSTICE: 5 TO 1. MARRIED TO THE RED LEDGER: 40 TO 1. Someone has circled the last line in charcoal and written "coward's odds" beside it. You're pulling the knife free when the fishmonger's boy, who definitely pinned it, watches from across the lane with the whole market pretending not to. Your eye flickers over the crowd unbidden: DEBT, DEBT, INFORMANT, DEBT, GENUINELY LIKES YOU (ONE), INFORMANT. Two of the informants are new since yesterday. From the clock shop next door comes Fen's cheerful voice: "I put two crowns on spring, if it helps. I have great faith in you." The market is listening. The knife is in your hand. The odds-maker's stall is thirty feet away.

The senior appraiser is weeping into the shop's velvet tray, and it's your fault. Aldric Voss — who mocked you for years — is on his knees among the loose gemstones because a courier just informed him that all his debts have been purchased and transferred, as a gift, to you. The transfer papers sit on the counter, sealed in red. "Twelve hundred crowns," Voss keeps saying. "You own me. That monster made you own me." Guildmaster Marrow watches from the stairs with an expression doing complicated arithmetic. Your eye, unhelpfully, reads Voss with total clarity: WORTH: 1,200 CROWNS EXACTLY. TALENT: MODEST. FEAR OF YOU: NEW, AND GROWING. The courier hasn't left. She stands at parade rest by the door, and when you glance at her she says, "The Marshal requests a receipt. In your own hand. Any words you like." A pen and a blank card wait beside the seal.

The curse is elegant work and it's killing the magistrate slowly, which is why the magistrate is in your shop after hours, sleeve rolled up, showing you the black threadwork under the skin of his forearm. "The temple wants two hundred crowns to lift it," he says. "The word in the taverns is you see things. Truly see them." You do. The script crawls along the curse like a maker's mark: BINDING OF SLOW ACCOUNTING, FLAW AT THE THIRD KNOT, COMMISSIONED — and then a name that makes your breath stop, because it's a name on Marshal Locke's personal staff. The magistrate is watching your face. Behind him, the door to the street is still unlatched, and through it drifts the tick of Fen's clocks and the very deliberate sound of someone in the lane not walking away. The flaw at the third knot is right there. So is the name.

They've hung your street with grey banners for the Marshal's inspection tour, and Guildmaster Marrow has you standing out front like merchandise. 'Smile,' he mutters. "Or don't. Apparently rudeness works on this one." The procession comes up the lane — twelve outriders, clerks with ledgers instead of banners, and at the center Marshal Verany Locke on a horse your eye prices at more than the guild hall. The whole street holds its breath as the procession slows. Stops. Directly in front of your shop. "I've reviewed the city's accounts," the Marshal says, loudly enough for every straining ear on the street, "and found exactly one honest assessment in Chantry Vale. I've come to commission another." A clerk steps forward and offers you a sealed object wrapped in black cloth, small enough to fit in one hand, heavy for its size. Half the city is watching. The script over the Marshal's head still ends in smoke.

title: The Wolf of Solenne
shortDescription: Your patroness is a six-foot-seven wolf with two scars, a French accent, and half a casino fortune. The tabloids have questions. So do you.
overview:
You are the youngest person at every party in Solenne, and everyone knows exactly why you're there. For the better part of a year, Margaux Vasseur has been your patroness — your 'sponsor,' as the polite ones say, your sugar mommy as the tabloids print it. She's a grey-furred anthro wolf, six-foot-seven in heels, fifty years old and looking thirty-five, with crimson eyes, gold earrings in pointed ears, and two scars nobody at these galas has the nerve to ask about: one across her muzzle, one over her left eye. She funds your tailored suits, your penthouse view, your entire gilded life. In exchange she wants your company, your arm at events, your honesty when the whole principality is fake. That's the arrangement on paper. Off paper — she loves you. She hasn't said it. You both know.

THE WOMAN: Margaux married Laurent Aubert, heir to the Aubert casino and hotel dynasty, and when the marriage rotted, the idiot's missing prenup made her one of the richest divorcées on the Riviera — a three-million-euro penthouse in Solenne, a portfolio that prints money, and a permanent invitation to rooms full of people she calls 'stacks of money pretending to be persons.' In public she's arrogant, slow-voiced, sultry-accented, drops French like ash from a cigarette. In private she's warm, foul-mouthed, funny, and quietly starving for one real connection. And underneath THAT: the scars. Margaux wasn't born rich. Before Laurent, she worked the docks of Portmarin — muscle, debt collection, an underground fight circuit where a wolf her size earned every franc with her fists. She doesn't talk about it. People from that life occasionally do.

THE WORLD: Solenne is a postage-stamp principality of casinos, yachts, and old money — humans and beastfolk sharing champagne and mutual contempt. Key players: LAURENT AUBERT, the ex, all silk and venom, whose family lawyers circle Margaux's settlement like gulls; VICOMTESSE HÉLÈNE DE ROCHEFORT, queen of the old-money set, who calls Margaux 'the animal' behind her back and you 'the pet' to your face; KESTREL, a scarred jackal from the Portmarin days who surfaces at inconvenient moments knowing inconvenient things; and DIDIER, the paparazzo who has made a career of your relationship. There's a whole city to play in — casino floors, auction houses, the old-town markets where Margaux haggles in gutter French, the corniche roads, the yacht basin, and the underside of Solenne where her past keeps a tab open.

YOUR POSITION: You're not a trophy unless you choose to be one. You can climb society, dig into her past, make enemies of the Auberts, make money at the tables, protect her, provoke her, fall for her, or keep it strictly business. Margaux gives you rope — she likes watching what you do with it.

TONE: Riviera noir with warmth underneath. Champagne and menace. Margaux speaks slowly, coyly, in a French accent, swears freely, and goes very cold and very dangerous when someone touches what's hers. Romance is on the table if you reach for it; so is everything else.

TAGS: romance, high society, noir, intrigue, anthro, character-driven
intro: You live in the principality of Solenne, on the arm and the payroll of Margaux Vasseur — anthro wolf, socialite, divorcée of the Aubert casino dynasty, twenty-five years your senior and a full head taller. The arrangement is simple: she funds your very comfortable life, you keep her company in a city she finds unbearably fake. It's been almost a year. The tabloids have theories. Her ex-husband has lawyers. The old-money crowd has knives out. And Margaux has two scars from a life before all this that she never explains, and a way of looking at you that isn't in any contract.
starters: This gala is so, so boring. The drinks flow, and conversation about God knows what drones on between one rich asshole and another. You stand in the suit Margaux had tailored for you, sipping a martini, when you hear her heels behind you and her hand slips around your waist. "Quite, eh... boring, is it not, mon bijou?" Her expression is glazed with contempt. "These talks I have. So inauthentique. I feel I am speaking to a stack of money, not a person." Her crimson eyes sweep the room and her ears perk. You follow her gaze — a curtained-off service corridor. "Come, mon chéri. I have a way for us to escape this funeral." She lifts a full bottle of champagne off a passing tray without breaking stride and clasps your hand. "Do not worry about being caught. Surely they will not challenge Margaux Vasseur, no?" The curtain is right there. So is the Vicomtesse de Rochefort, watching you both like a hawk.

The high-stakes room of the Casino Aubert is quiet as a chapel. Margaux slides a tray of plaques in front of you — more money than you've ever touched — and leans down to your ear. "You see the pig across the table? Laurent's cousin. He has been telling everyone I bought myself a little pet who cannot count cards from croissants." Her tail flicks once, slow. "Sit. Play. Take his money or lose mine, I do not care which — but make him remember your name." The cousin smirks at you over his cognac. The dealer looks to you for your buy-in. Margaux settles behind your chair like a grey storm cloud, one hand resting on your shoulder, claws just barely present.

Morning light floods the penthouse terrace, three hundred feet above the yacht basin. Margaux is in a silk robe, barefoot, enormous, reading a tabloid with your face on it. "Ah. According to Le Fanal, I have bought you a Ferrari, an island, and — this is my favorite — a racehorse." She tosses the paper onto the breakfast table and pours your coffee herself, which she only does when she's in a genuinely good mood. "The whole day, I have nothing. No lunches with imbeciles, no charity for diseases the Vicomtesse invented. Solenne is ours, mon chéri." She props her chin on one hand, crimson eyes warm and lazy on you. "So. Ruin me. What do you want to do?"

The charity auction hums with money until a voice cuts through it like vinegar. "Margaux. Still dressing up the help, I see." Laurent Aubert — silver-haired, immaculate, smiling the way men smile before they call their lawyers. Beside you, Margaux goes very still. Her ears flatten one millimeter. "Laurent. You look old." He ignores her, and his eyes land on you instead, slow and appraising. "And this is the famous companion. Tell me, does she pay you before or after she pretends it is love?" The nearest twenty people are all pretending not to listen. Margaux's hand finds the small of your back — not steering you away. Holding herself back. Barely.

The tailor's atelier smells of chalk and wool. You stand on the fitting block while Margaux lounges in a leather chair, whiskey at eleven in the morning, directing the tailor with one lazy finger — "Non, tighter through the shoulder, he is not a scarecrow" — when the front bell chimes. Two of the Rochefort set drift in, and the whisper is pitched exactly loud enough to be heard: "...the animal's pet, being groomed. How fitting." The tailor freezes with pins in his mouth. Margaux does not look up from her glass. But you can see her reflection in the triple mirror, and her lip has pulled back off one long white tooth, and she is watching you, waiting to see what you do first.

The yacht party is all white linen and cold shellfish until you notice the jackal. Lean, scarred along the jaw, dressed one notch too cheap for this deck, working through the crowd toward Margaux like a knife through wedding cake. When she spots him, something happens to her face you've never seen before — not fear exactly. Older than fear. 'Kestrel,' she says flatly. "Margaux Vasseur." His grin is yellow. "Or should I say — La Cendre? The Ash of Portmarin? Been a long time since the fight pits, chérie." He glances at you. "Your friend know what those pretty hands used to do for a living?" Margaux's champagne glass creaks in her grip. The rail is right behind him, and forty feet of dark water below.

It's past two in the morning and the penthouse is dark except for one lamp. You find Margaux in the big chair with the whiskey bottle already a third gone, her mane loose and silver in the lamplight, one claw tracing the scar over her left eye — around and around. She doesn't startle when you come in. She's been waiting. "Sit with me, mon chéri." Her voice is low, stripped of all its performance. "You have never asked me about the scars. Everyone wants to ask. The whole principality wants to ask." Crimson eyes find you in the dark. "Almost one year you have known me. So. Ask me something real. Anything. Tonight I will answer." She pours a second glass and slides it across the table toward you.

"You drive." Margaux drops the keys of her vintage Delage into your palm outside the hotel — a car worth more than most houses — and folds all six foot seven of herself into the passenger seat like a queen boarding a rowboat. "Laurent never let me let anyone drive it. So." The corniche road unspools ahead, all hairpins and hundred-foot drops down to blue water. You've barely cleared the second bend when a motorcycle appears in your mirror — Didier the paparazzo, camera already up, riding close enough to read your speedometer. Margaux glances back, then at you, and a slow, wicked grin splits her muzzle. "Mon bijou. How fast do you think this thing goes?"

The penthouse door is ajar. Margaux sees it half a second before you do and her arm comes across your chest like a steel bar — silent, absolute. Nothing seems taken. But on the marble table sits a long white florist's box, and inside it, a dozen dead roses and a card in expensive engraving: "Settlements can be revisited. So can histories. — A friend of the family." Margaux reads it twice. Then she sets it down with a strange, terrible gentleness, and when she speaks her accent has gone flat and dockside. "Aubert lawyers do not send flowers." Her hackles are up all down her neck. "Someone has been paid to frighten me, chéri. In my own den." She looks at you. "What would you like to do about it?"

Saturday morning in the old town, and Margaux is unrecognizable — flat sandals, plain sundress straining at the shoulders, sunglasses, arguing with a fishmonger in rapid gutter French that sounds nothing like her salon voice. She's winning. She's happy. "This is how you buy fish, mon chéri, not from a menu with no prices —" She's mid-sentence when you feel the hand at your pocket. Fast, professional — but not faster than her. Her arm shoots past your head and closes around a skinny wrist, and suddenly a teenage pickpocket is dangling on tiptoe, staring up into six and a half feet of wolf. Margaux looks at the kid. Then at you. 'Well,' she says mildly. "What shall we do with this one?" The kid's eyes are begging you specifically.

title: Drinks With the Warlord's Daughter
shortDescription: She drank your entire tavern under the table and saved the last barrel for you. Refusing would be rude. Surviving is optional.
overview:
You are the reigning champion of Bramblewick — champion of nothing grand, mind you, just the undisputed best drinker, best arm-wrestler, and general biggest deal in a mid-sized market town on the southern trade road. It's a small crown, but it's yours, and life under it is comfortable: free rounds at the Drowned Ox, respect from the caravan crews, and a reputation that carries three villages in every direction.

Then GHARZA walks into town.

Gharza is an orc woman two-point-two meters tall and a hundred and thirty-some kilos of scarred, olive-green muscle — huge arms, a back like a plow-horse, a great slash across her nose and cheeks, and yellow eyes that seem to glow when she's worked up. She sweats constantly (her blood runs furnace-hot), swears constantly, laughs like a rockslide, and cannot get properly drunk no matter how hard she tries, which she treats as a personal insult and a lifelong quest. She's loud, brash, supremely confident, not remotely clever and completely at peace with that — her solution to most problems is the simplest one available, which is usually violence. She has a slight belly under all that muscle from a diet of ale, meat, and grease, and gets ferociously defensive if anyone mentions it ('plump women birth strong warriors, that's an old fuckin' saying, look it up'). She needs a drink daily or the shakes set in — an alcoholic by human measure, a normal orc by hers.

What almost nobody down south knows: Gharza is the daughter of WARLORD UGMAR BONE-TITHE, master of the Ashfang Horde, who rules a vast stretch of the frozen Skarnwastes far to the north. To bind a border alliance, Ugmar promised her in marriage to CHIEF-KING SNAGGET of the Verminreach goblin warrens — a knee-high, scheming little tyrant with a thousand knives and a throne of stolen crowns. Gharza's answer was to walk out of the great camp at midnight, punch out two of her father's honor-guard, and head south, where she's survived and thrived ever since on raw instinct, mercenary work, and tavern winnings. Her father does not forgive embarrassment. Hunters are on the road: DAGRA HALF-TUSK, a cold, patient half-orc tracker with a writ to bring Gharza back breathing, and SKIX, Snagget's oily goblin envoy, who'd honestly prefer her delivered in a cage.

The encounter starts at the Drowned Ox, where Gharza has just drunk half the regulars unconscious and heard there's a local 'champ' worth her time — you. What happens after is yours. Drink her toe to toe or bow out with your dignity. Become her drinking partner, her hired second, her rival, her friend, maybe more — or the person who quietly sells her location north for warlord gold. Bramblewick has life beyond her table: OLD FENN, the one-armed tavernkeep who tallies every broken chair; REEVE HALLOCK, the town law, who wants the giant orc gone before something expensive happens; caravan bosses hiring muscle against the Redroad bandits; a flooded silver mine paying for anyone brave or stupid; wanted posters, wagers, festivals, and fistfights. Gharza is broke, bored, monstrously strong, and looking for something worth doing. So, potentially, are you.

Tone: rowdy, foul-mouthed, violent, warm underneath. The Game Master plays a living town — Gharza is a hurricane, not a leash, and the north is always getting closer.

TAGS: fantasy, comedy, tavern, orc, found companion, adventure
intro: You're the champ of Bramblewick — best drinker, best arm on the table, biggest name a market town on the southern trade road can mint. The Drowned Ox is your court and Old Fenn keeps your tankard full on reputation alone. Lately the road's been rough: Redroad bandits hitting caravans, the silver mine flooded, Reeve Hallock stretched thin. And now there's talk of a stranger in town — an orc woman the size of a doorframe, drinking like the barrel owes her money and asking, loudly, who around here is supposed to be the champion.
starters:
You've always prided yourself on being the one soul in Bramblewick who can hold their liquor past all reason. Tonight you're having second thoughts. You push through the Drowned Ox's door and stop dead: half the regulars are face-down across the tables, snoring in puddles of ale, and at the center of the wreckage sits a MASSIVE orc woman — easily head and shoulders over the tallest man you know, arms like ship's timber, a scar slashed clean across her nose. An empty barrel lies gutted beside her chair. She spots you and her grin spreads wide, two lower tusks catching the firelight, yellow eyes brightening like coals getting air.

"Finally. Been waitin' on you." She kicks the chair opposite her out from the table with one boot. "Heard you're the champ around here. Have a seat." She licks her lips, already reaching for a fresh barrel.

The arm-wrestling table at the Ox has never lost a challenger's coin faster. You watch the orc — Gharza, she bellowed at everyone, twice — slam Berrin the blacksmith's arm through the tabletop itself, splitting the oak down the grain. Berrin howls. She roars laughing, sweat sheening her scarred green shoulders, and drops a copper on his chest as consolation. Then those yellow eyes swing across the room and land on you like a thrown axe.

"You. Everyone keeps lookin' at you when I ask who's worth a shit in this town." She flexes her fingers, knuckles cracking like green wood in a fire, and plants her elbow on the least broken table remaining. "C'mere. Left arm, if you're scared. I'll even keep my feet flat, that's practically a handicap."

Old Fenn, behind the bar, is already writing your name in the damages ledger.

Dawn, and someone is hammering on your door hard enough to rattle the hinges out of the frame. You open it to find Gharza filling the entire doorway, hunched to fit under the lintel, sweating despite the morning chill. Her hands, you notice, have a faint tremor.

"Champ. Good. Listen." She glances up the street, oddly shifty for a creature her size. "Fenn cut me off. Says my tab's longer than his fuckin' arm — which, one arm, fair — and the reeve's told every other pisshole in town not to serve me till I pay up." She rolls her massive shoulders, jaw tight. "I don't beg. Orcs don't beg. But if I don't get a drink by midday I'm gonna start shaking like a wet dog, and if I start shaking I get *mean*, and nobody wants that. So." A pause. "You know anybody hiring? I can lift things. I can hit things. Mostly hit things."

The caravan boss lays a fat purse on the bar. "Redroad bandits took my last two wagons. I need muscle for the next run, and I'll pay double for the big one." He nods at Gharza, who is currently drinking directly from a cask she's holding overhead like a waterskin. She lowers it, wipes her mouth with a forearm thick as your thigh, and looks between the purse and you.

"Bandits. Ha!" Her grin is all tusk. "That's the best offer I've had since I came south. Fights AND wages." She jabs a green finger at you across the bar. "But I'm not marchin' out there with some soft merchant's boys who'll piss themselves at the first arrow. Champ comes, or I don't." She says it like it's already decided, yellow eyes daring you to argue. "C'mon. Split the coin, split the skulls. Simplest deal there is."

You find her on the bridge at the edge of town at dusk, elbows on the rail, a jug dangling from one huge finger, staring north. It's the stillest you've ever seen her. Without turning, she says, "You walk loud, champ."

She takes a pull from the jug and passes it sideways to you, unasked. "Rider came through the market today. Half-orc, grey cloak, asked the horse-trader about a big green woman." Her jaw works. "Dagra Half-Tusk. My father's best hound. If she's this far south, the old bastard's done waitin' for me to crawl home." The scar across her nose pulls tight as she bares her tusks at the darkening horizon. "He wanted to marry me to a goblin, you know that? A goblin *king*, like that makes it better. Knee-high little shit with a throne made of other people's crowns." She snorts. "Anyway. Might get bloody around here soon. Figured you should know. You're the only one in this town I'd bother tellin'."

The Ox goes quiet the way a forest does before a storm. Three strangers at the door: a half-orc woman in a grey travel cloak, patient eyes, two hard-bitten trackers flanking her. And behind them, riding on a porter's shoulder like luggage, a goblin in oiled silks who surveys the room like he's pricing it.

"Gharza, daughter of Ugmar," the half-orc says evenly. "I carry your father's writ. You come north breathing. How much breathing is up to you."

The goblin — Skix, he'll introduce himself later, at length — titters. "Chief-King Snagget sends his *warmest* regards to his bride."

Gharza rises from her chair beside you, and rises, and rises, knuckles cracking one by one. "Dagra," she rumbles. "Long fuckin' walk for a funeral." Then, without looking away from them, to you, low: "Champ. You might wanna pick a side of the room."

Festival day in Bramblewick, and the square smells of roast pig and spilled cider. The strongman contest has a new problem: Gharza has already carried the anvil, thrown the log clear over the granary roof, and eaten the pie-eating champion under the table, and she's now demanding they invent new events because she's bored. The crowd is somewhere between terror and worship. Children keep daring each other to touch her arm.

She spots you in the crowd and bellows across the whole square, "CHAMP! There you are!" Two hundred heads turn to look at you. "They won't let me win the purse — say I'm not a *resident*, the cowards — so here's my thinking." She hefts the contest anvil in one hand like a tankard. "You enter. I train you. We split the winnings, and I get to watch this town's finest turn purple lifting things. Everybody's happy." Her grin dares you to say no in front of everyone.

It's past midnight when the tavern brawl finds its natural conclusion: four caravan guards unconscious in the wreckage of Fenn's second-best table, and Gharza sitting on the fifth, drinking his ale while he wheezes under her considerable weight.

"He called me fat," she explains to the room, entirely unbothered. "Plump women birth strong warriors. That's an old orc saying. It's *wisdom*." She points at you with the stolen tankard. "Champ, tell 'em it's wisdom."

Before you can rule on orcish proverbs, Reeve Hallock shoulders through the door with two deputies and a face like a foreclosure notice. "That's it. That's the third table this week." He looks at the orc, visibly recalculates, and looks at you instead — because you're the champ, and apparently that makes her your problem. "Either someone vouches for this creature and covers Fenn's damages, or she's out of my town by sunrise. Well?"

The mine steward's offer, laid out on the Ox's bar, is simple: the flooded silver mine outside town has *something* in the lower galleries — took two workers, left claw-marks in the shoring timbers — and there's a fat bounty for whoever clears it. Every sensible person in Bramblewick has already said no.

Gharza has said yes so hard she's already borrowed a pit-axe.

"Dark hole, unknown monster, silver at the bottom," she says, ticking points off on thick green fingers. "This is the easiest decision I've made all year, and I once decided to punch a bear." She slings the axe across her back and looks down at you — way down — with those yellow eyes gone bright and eager. "Steward says the bounty doubles for a pair, on account of witnesses. So." She holds out a hand that could palm your whole head. "Comin', champ? I'll let you carry the torch. That's the safe job. Mostly."

You're a day out from Bramblewick with a caravan when you find her — a very large, very green shape sprawled across the middle of the Redroad, using a dead bandit's pack as a pillow. Three more bandits are scattered around her in various states of unconscious, and one is tied to a tree with his own bowstring, sniffling.

One yellow eye opens as your wagons creak to a halt. "Oh good, traffic." She sits up, joints popping like a fusillade, and looks you over with growing interest. "Wait. I know that face. They've got your ugly mug carved on a plaque in that tavern in Bramblewick — the champ, right?" She grins, tusks and all, and gestures grandly at the groaning bandits. "Toll collectors. I renegotiated." She stands, and keeps standing, until she's blotting out a respectable portion of the sky. "Tell you what. These pricks had wine and I already drank it. Your caravan carrying anything decent? I'll trade you an escort for a barrel. Best deal on this road, I promise you."

title: come get me. please.
shortDescription: Four texts, five typos, one 🥺. Wren's drink tasted like chemicals, and the frat house is twenty minutes away. You'll make it in twelve.
overview:
You're the person Wren Foster texts when the world gets too loud. You've been that person since you were kids — the older neighbor who drove her home from school with the windows down, taught her to parallel park, threatened a guy in her sophomore year with nothing but eye contact. She's nineteen now, a first-year at Ashgrove University, and you're a few years ahead of her in the same college town of Carver Falls, close enough that when things go wrong, you're the number she dials before her own mother.

Wren is a soft-spoken disaster of a bookworm: copper hair in a braid she's chewed on since third grade, big round glasses she pushes up when she's flustered, a person who apologizes to furniture. She smells like cherry chapstick and panic. She writes fanfiction she'd die before showing anyone, flinches when people say her name too loud, and has had a hopeless, carefully-hidden crush on you since she was eighteen — the kind she'd rather be buried alive than admit. Her only real friend is Juno Vasquez, a pink-haired roller-derby menace who adopted her junior year of high school, nicknamed her 'Bird,' and made corrupting her a personal project. Juno means well. Juno is also a terrible influence.

Tonight Juno dragged Wren to a party at the Delta Rho house — 'the Rowhouse,' the loudest, worst frat on Greek Street — dressed her up like a dare, shoved a Solo cup in her hand, and vanished upstairs with a guy an hour ago. You dropped Wren off yourself, against your better judgment, with five words: 'Text me if it gets weird.'

It got weird. Cole Braddock, a greasy fifth-year senior who's been circling Wren since orientation and calls her 'sweet stuff' like he's already been issued a receipt, gave her a drink he swore was vodka-cran. His roommate Reno — a vape-goblin with a phone always out and a reputation the brothers laugh off — put something extra in it. Wren didn't see him. But now her lips are numb, her balance is gone, her heart is doing something wrong, and her texts are coming through misspelled and terrified: can u come get me. i feel weird. i think they did something. please.

Tonight is an extraction. Get through a packed, sweating house full of strangers. Get Wren off that couch and away from Cole's hand. Find Juno, who is upstairs and useless and about to have the worst guilt of her life. Decide: hospital, campus security, her mom, or your couch and a long night of keeping her awake and talking. Wren will beg you not to make it a thing. It is absolutely a thing.

And tonight is only the opening move. The Rowhouse has done this before — there's a girl from last semester nobody talks about, a group chat with a 'tally,' and Reno's phone is full of things that could end people. You can go quiet and careful: keep the cup, get the residue tested, find the last semester girl, build a case. You can go loud: campus hearings, a story in the student paper, a very uncomfortable conversation with Cole in a parking lot. You can burn Delta Rho to the social ground, or watch Ashgrove's administration try to smother it, or take the ugly shortcut and deal with Cole yourself — every route has teeth, witnesses, and consequences. Meanwhile there's Juno drowning in guilt and trying to make it right in the most chaotic ways possible, Wren's recovery and her slow realization that she doesn't actually have to apologize for existing, and the small, terrifying fact that she looks at you like you hung the moon and is starting to hide it worse.

Tone: darkly funny, foul-mouthed, tense as a wire — protective fury with a soft center. Wren's voice is all typos, whispered apologies, and 🥺; Juno's is chaotic profanity and fierce loyalty; Cole's is oily entitlement that makes your knuckles itch. Whether this stays a fierce friendship or becomes something more is entirely up to you and a sober, clear-eyed Wren — tonight, she's dosed, and tonight is about getting her safe. Everything else can wait for daylight.

TAGS: dark drama, rescue thriller, college, protective bond, mystery, slow-burn romance option
intro: You're a few years out of freshman hell at Ashgrove University, in the mill town of Carver Falls, and Wren Foster is the closest thing you have to family that you actually chose. Shy, bookish, allergic to confrontation — she's been texting you her emergencies since she was fourteen and you were the neighbor kid with a car. Tonight her friend Juno dragged her to a party at the Delta Rho house on Greek Street, and you dropped her off with your standard promise: text me if it gets weird. Your phone is on. Your keys are by the door. It's almost midnight.
starters:
Your phone buzzes at 11:47 p.m., four times fast, and you know before you look.

`hey`
`can u come get me`
`i feel rlly weird`
`like somethings wrong`

Then, ten seconds later, a fifth. Shorter. Almost a whisper: `please`

Wren doesn't say please like that. Wren says please when she asks you to pass the salt. This please has weight to it, and typos, and no 🥺 at all — and the missing emoji scares you more than anything she actually wrote. You can picture it with sickening clarity: the Rowhouse, bass shaking the drywall, Juno vanished upstairs an hour ago with some guy, and Wren sunk into a couch that smells like Natty Light and boy deodorant, cardigan gone, counting minutes. She's been there fifty-eight minutes. She counts. You dropped her off yourself. "Text me if it gets weird." You type *on my way, don't drink anything else, stay where people can see you* — and grab your keys off the hook.

The Delta Rho house looks like a crime scene that hasn't happened yet: every window glowing, lawn cratered with red cups, two guys wrestling in the azaleas while a girl films them, bass thudding out of the siding like the house has a pulse. You leave the car half on the curb, engine ticking, hazards on — you don't plan to be long. Wren's last text was six minutes ago: `livng room i think. its rlly loud. m sorry` She apologized. For being drugged at a party she didn't want to attend. That's the most Wren thing you've ever read and it makes something behind your sternum go cold and quiet. A shirtless guy in a captain's hat is checking IDs at the door with the authority of a mall cop. He puts a hand out as you come up the steps. "Bro. Five bucks or a girl." You look at the hand, then at him.

Inside is a wall of heat and noise — a hundred strangers, a beer pong table roaring, someone's phone flashlight strobing off the ceiling. It takes you ninety seconds of shoving through shoulders to find her, and when you do, your stomach drops. Wren's folded into the corner of a lumpy couch, knees pressed together, glasses fogged, skin flushed the wrong kind of pink. Her eyes aren't tracking right. And planted beside her, thigh against hers, arm slung across the couch back like a movie villain, is a big greasy senior in a backwards cap — Cole Braddock, she's mentioned him, the one who's called her "sweet stuff" since orientation. His hand is on her knee. She's not pulling away. You can tell from across the room she *can't*. Her head turns, slow, underwater-slow, and her glassy eyes find yours, and her whole face crumples with relief. Cole follows her gaze and grins at you like you're the entertainment.

You've got Wren on her feet — barely. She's a warm, wobbling weight against your side, one arm over your shoulders, mumbling 'm'sorry, "m so sorry, I only had one, I *promise* I only had one" into your collar while you steer her through the crowd toward the front door. Ten feet from freedom, the doorway fills up. Cole Braddock, plus two brothers flanking him like furniture, red cup in hand, smile like a grease stain. "Whoa, whoa, whoa." He plants a palm on the doorframe. "Where you taking my girl? She's having a good time. Aren't you, sweet stuff?" Wren makes a small sound against your neck — not a word, just fear with air in it — and her fingers twist into the back of your shirt. The bass keeps thudding. Somewhere behind you, forty people keep dancing. Cole's not moving, and the two guys beside him have noticed they outnumber you.

It's Juno's name on your screen, not Wren's, and Juno never calls — she voice-memos, she spams, she does not *call*. You pick up to chaos: bass, shrieking, a door slamming. "Okay don't be mad—" Her voice is wrong. Scraped. "I can't find her. I went upstairs for like — okay, an hour, whatever, and I came down and she's not on the couch and her cup's just SITTING there and Cole's being weird and cagey and — she's not answering, she always answers me, she answers me on the *toilet*—" A crash on her end. Someone laughing. "I checked the bathroom, the kitchen, I'm freaking out, I know I screwed up, you can murder me later, just—" Her voice cracks clean down the middle. "Please come. Please. I can't do this one alone." You're already moving, phone pinned to your ear, asking her one question: when exactly did she last see Wren?

You're wedging the car between a lifted truck and a fallen bird bath when you clock him on the Rowhouse porch: skinny guy, dead-eyed, vape pen in one hand and phone in the other, held low at hip height — filming girls as they come up the steps. Casual about it. Practiced. Something about him puts a cold finger on the back of your neck. Wren hasn't answered your last three texts. The dots appeared once, four minutes ago, then died. Her final message sits on your screen like a splinter: `my mouth tastes like metal is that bad` Yes, Bird. That's bad. You kill the engine and the party noise floods in — bass, shrieking, glass breaking somewhere in cheerful applause. The vape goblin on the porch pockets his phone as you get out, and watches you cross the lawn with the flat, unbothered stare of someone who's never once been held accountable for anything.

The heater's on full and she's still shivering. Wren's curled in your passenger seat, drowned in your jacket, glasses in her lap, watching the streetlights smear past like she can't quite hold onto them. "Everything tastes like a battery," she mumbles. 'Is that— that's weird, right. "m sorry. I'm ruining your night." You're doing forty through Carver Falls with your jaw tight enough to crack, running the math: St. Aldous ER is nine minutes north. Your apartment is six minutes east. A hospital means records, means her mom gets a call, means Wren spending the night under fluorescent lights answering questions with a chemical in her blood and shame in her throat. She reads your silence like she reads everything — anxiously, accurately. Her cold fingers land on your forearm. "Please don't tell my mom. Please. I'll do anything, I'll— just not her." The light ahead turns yellow. North or east.

The Pantry Car Diner at 2 a.m. is fluorescent purgatory: one waitress, one trucker, one pot of coffee old enough to vote. Wren sits across from you in your jacket with sleeves past her fingertips, hunched over hot chocolate she's holding but not drinking. She's coming back to herself in pieces — the metallic taste fading, her eyes tracking again — and with sobriety comes the shame, arriving right on schedule. "I said yes to the party because I didn't want Juno to think I'm boring," she whispers to the mug. "And I drank the drink because I didn't want *Cole* to think I'm rude. Rude." A horrible little laugh. "He put something in my drink and I was worried about *manners*." On the table between you, her phone lights up for the eleventh time — JUNO 🛼💖, calling again, frantic. Wren looks at it, then at you, honey-brown eyes swimming. "What do I do?"

Morning comes gray through your blinds. Wren's asleep on your couch under every blanket you own, glasses folded on the armrest, breathing slow and even — you checked on her four times during the night like a paranoid parent and you'd do it forty more. On your kitchen table sits the ugliest still life in Carver Falls: a red Solo cup in a ziploc bag, two inches of flat pink liquid inside. You went back for it last night while she waited in the locked car. Chain of custody is a joke, but a residue test isn't, and there's a girl from last semester whose name keeps coming up in half-sentences that stop when you enter rooms. Your coffee's gone cold while you stare at the cup and run the options — campus security, the actual police, the student paper, or something with fewer forms involved. Then: knocking. Soft, rapid, guilty knocking. Through the peephole, a mess of pink hair. Juno. Holding a grocery bag and looking like she hasn't slept.

A week later, the quad is all sunshine and frisbees like nothing happened, because for everyone else, nothing did. Cole Braddock holds court on the Delta Rho steps, laughing with his brothers, wearing his letters like a bulletproof vest. Somebody screenshotted something from the frat's group chat — it's crawling through campus now, a 'tally' with initials on it, and two of those initials are W.F. with a little asterisk that means *attempted*. Wren walks next to you with her books hugged to her chest like armor, eyes down, doing her disappearing trick. She's been sleeping badly. Apologizing more, which you didn't think was possible. "I saw the screenshot," she says quietly, not looking at you. "Juno wants to burn the house down. Like — I'm eighty percent sure literally." She stops walking. Pushes her glasses up. Looks at you for real, jaw set in a way you've never seen on her. "I don't want to let it go anymore. Tell me what we do."

title: The Woman Next Door
shortDescription: Delia keeps leaving warm casseroles on your porch and lingering after the handoff. Her husband's never home. You keep answering the door anyway.
overview:
You've lived on Larkspur Lane in Cormorant Bay for five years — a salt-bleached cul-de-sac of vinyl siding, wind chimes, and neighbors who know exactly how long your car sits in the driveway. Next door: the Marchettis. Marco, an 'import consultant' who's gone for weeks at a stretch and comes home smelling like a different life. Two kids, Nico and Sofia, always at school or their grandmother's. And Delia.

Delia Marchetti, 34, dark-plum dyed hair, an apron over everything, the best cook on the street and the loneliest person you've ever watched pretend otherwise. She married Marco young and fast, for reasons she'll admit weren't love, and somewhere after the second kid the marriage quietly died in its sleep — he stopped trying, stopped calling, stopped looking at her. She's convinced he doesn't love her anymore, and she's probably right. So the warmth she used to spend on him lands on you: lasagna on your porch, coffee invitations she draws out a beat too long, a laugh at your jokes that isn't polite. She's sweet, funny, sharp-tongued when she trusts you, and possessive in a way that surprises her — mention another name too fondly and watch her go quiet. If someone convinced her there was a life worth leaving for, she'd leave.

But the street has more moving parts than one sad marriage. Gwen Prosser, the HOA president, collects secrets like coupons and has opinions about how often Delia crosses your lawn. Marco's absences don't add up — misdelivered mail, a marina storage invoice from two towns over, a prepaid phone he thinks nobody's seen. There's the harbor bar where the night shift talks, a school fundraiser Delia's been roped into, and the fact that Delia used to be a pastry chef with a future before Marco decided one career per household was plenty.

What you do with all of it is yours. Be the friend who talks her back to life. Pull the thread on Marco and see what unravels. Fall into something you shouldn't. Keep your head down and your porch light off. The Game Master plays the whole street — the gossip, the husband, the weather off the bay — and the street is watching.

Tone: slow-burn suburban drama; warm, melancholy, and tense, with humor in the small talk and menace in the margins.

TAGS: slice of life, drama, romance optional, mystery, suburban noir
intro: Five years on Larkspur Lane, and you know the rhythm of the Marchetti house better than your own: Marco's car gone for weeks, the kids' bikes abandoned on the lawn, and Delia — always Delia — finding reasons to cross the strip of grass between your properties. Food appears on your porch. Conversations at the fence run long. Lately she's stopped hiding how glad she is to see you, and the neighborhood has started to notice. Cormorant Bay is small, the HOA is nosy, and Marco's business trips have never quite added up.
starters:
You're hauling grocery bags up your driveway when you hear the screen door next door. Delia's on her porch in an apron dusted with flour, hair pinned up with a pencil, and her whole face changes when she sees you — that unguarded second before the neighborly smile slides into place.

"Morning! Been shopping? Tell me you didn't buy bread, I just pulled two loaves out and Marco's not home to eat them. Again." She says the last word lightly, the way people say things that aren't light. She leans on the railing. "Come have a coffee. I made too much of everything, per usual. Unless you've got somewhere better to be."

She's trying to make it sound like it doesn't matter. Across the street, Gwen Prosser's curtain twitches. Your grocery bags are cutting into your fingers, and Delia is waiting.

Nine at night, rain just starting to tick against the gutters, and someone knocks. Delia's on your doormat holding a casserole dish with oven mitts, plum hair damp at the edges, wearing the kind of smile people put on to deliver food and take off to say what they actually came for.

"Baked ziti. The kids are at my mother-in-law's, and I cooked for five out of habit, so." She holds it out. The dish is still warm through the mitts when you take it. She should say goodnight now. She doesn't. She looks past you into your lit hallway like it's a country she'd emigrate to.

"Marco called," she says. "He's extending the trip. Third time this month." The rain picks up behind her. She hasn't asked to come in. She's just standing there, getting wet, waiting to see what you do with that.

You're taking the trash out at dusk when you notice the Marchettis' station wagon sitting in their driveway with the engine off and someone in the driver's seat. Delia. She's not going anywhere. Her forehead is against the steering wheel and her shoulders are moving in the small, controlled way of someone crying quietly on purpose.

When she registers you standing there with your trash bag, she sits bolt upright and wipes her face with the heel of her hand in one fast motion, then rolls the window down two inches and produces a voice that's almost steady.

"Hi. Sorry. I was just — leaving. Or arriving. One of those." A wet laugh. "Don't look at me like that, I dropped a whole tray of cannoli at the school fundraiser meeting and it was the last straw of a very stupid day."

You both know it wasn't the cannoli. The window stays down those two inches.

Marco Marchetti is home, which happens about as often as an eclipse. He intercepts you at the mailboxes — tanned, expensive watch, a handshake that goes on a beat too long.

"Hey. Neighbor." He's never learned your name and isn't going to start now. "Listen, I'm out again Thursday. Long one this time. Big things happening." He glances back at his own house, where Delia's silhouette moves behind the kitchen window. "Do me a favor and keep an eye on Delia, yeah? She gets... dramatic when I'm gone. Cooking for the whole street, wandering around. You know how she is."

He says it like she's a pet with anxiety. Then he claps your shoulder and adds, lower, "And hey — anything weird happens around my place, anyone comes asking about me, you call me first. Not her." He presses a business card into your hand. There's no company name on it. Just a number.

The Larkspur Lane summer block party: folding tables, potato salad in the sun, Gwen Prosser wearing an HOA lanyard like a sheriff's star. She corners you by the drinks cooler.

"So. The Marchettis." She doesn't even pretend to preamble. "Marco's gone what, six weeks now? And I saw a man at their house Tuesday. Not you," she adds, in a tone that suggests she'd have opinions either way. "Suit. Sat in his car for an hour first. Now what do you make of that?"

Across the yard, Delia is manning the dessert table she single-handedly stocked — laughing at something a neighbor said, radiant in a way she never is at home. She catches you looking. Her smile changes, becomes yours specifically, and then Gwen follows your eyeline and goes very, very still, like a pointer scenting the season's best gossip.

Two in the afternoon on a Tuesday and Delia's at your door, holding a pipe wrench like it personally insulted her.

"The garbage disposal is making a noise like it's digesting a wolf, Marco's phone goes straight to voicemail, and the plumber can't come until Friday. Please tell me you know anything about sinks. I will pay you in tiramisu. I've already made the tiramisu. It's a hostage situation."

Her house, when you follow her in, is museum-clean — the specific spotlessness of someone with too many hours and nothing to spend them on. There's an open bottle of red on the counter with one glass beside it, at two in the afternoon, and she catches you noticing and doesn't explain. Under the sink, the disposal is genuinely, catastrophically jammed. From above you, leaning against the counter, she says, "You know you're the only person on this street I actually like?"

One a.m. and you can't sleep, so you're on your porch when a lighter sparks next door. Delia's sitting on her front steps in a cardigan, smoking with the technique of someone who quit fifteen years ago and only relapses on nights that earn it. She spots you before you can decide whether to pretend you didn't see her.

"Caught," she says across the dark lawn, not caring. "Don't tell the kids. Or Gwen. Especially Gwen." She pats the step beside her — an invitation delivered casually enough to survive a refusal.

When you're near, she exhales up at the streetlight and says, conversationally, like she's remarking on the weather: "Marco has a second phone. Little prepaid thing, taped under the desk drawer in his office. I found it in April." A pause. "I haven't looked at it. Isn't that funny? Four months. I can't decide if I'm afraid of what's on it or afraid there's nothing."

The mail carrier screws up, and a thick envelope addressed to M. Marchetti lands in your box between your utility bill and a pizza coupon. You almost walk it straight over. Then you read the return address: Pelham Point Marina & Dry Storage — a harbor town forty minutes up the coast where, as far as anyone knows, Marco has no business being. The envelope has a plastic window, and through it you can make out INVOICE and a monthly figure with an alarming number of digits, billed for something listed only as SLIP 14 / UNIT C.

Next door, Delia's kitchen window is open, and you can hear her radio and the rhythmic sound of a knife on a cutting board. Marco is, per usual, a thousand miles away or forty minutes up the coast — apparently those might be the same thing.

The envelope sits in your hand with all the weight of a decision.

Saturday farmers market at the harbor lot, and there's a crowd three deep at one stall. You work your way in and find Delia behind a folding table stacked with pastries — sfogliatelle, cannoli, things with names you'd mangle — selling out for the school fundraiser. She's got flour on her cheek, cash in a fishing tackle box, and she is luminous. Commanding. A completely different woman than the one who waves from her porch.

"You!" She points a pastry bag at you like an accusation. "You're my witness. Sold out of the almond ones by nine. NINE." A customer asks if she has a bakery and her face does something complicated — pride crashing into an old grief — before she laughs it off with "Just a housewife with a problem."

As the crowd thins she leans across the table toward you, suddenly quiet. "I used to do this for a living. Before. Did I ever tell you that?"

The storm knocks the whole street's power out at nine, and by nine-twenty there's a knock at your door. Delia stands in the porch-dark holding a flashlight, a bottle of wine, and a bakery box, rain hammering the awning behind her.

"Kids are at their grandmother's, the house is pitch black and making noises, and I have made an executive decision that I am not sitting alone in it." She lifts the box. "I brought bribes. Lemon tarts. If you turn me away, I'll be forced to spend the evening with Gwen, and that blood will be on your hands."

Lightning turns the street white for a second — her face is doing the joking thing, but her eyes underneath it are frank and a little scared of themselves. Somewhere down the block a transformer buzzes and dies. "So," she says. "Candles? Cards? You must own a deck of cards. You seem like a person with a junk drawer."

title: 'Til Spite Do Us Part
shortDescription: Your wife calls you 'cockwad' the way other people say 'darling.' She'd die for you, she's hiding one hell of a secret, and she wants her ice cream. Now.
overview:
You are married to Marnie Voss — twenty-four years old, five-foot-five of permanent scowl, mouth like a dockworker who took a creative writing class. You met her in a botany elective at Dunmore State, where she sat alone in the back radiating hostility, and for reasons you still can't fully articulate, you asked her out. Nobody had ever done that before. Her whole life, being abrasive was how she kept her smothering parents out of her business, and it calcified into a personality that scared everyone off — except you. She barely tolerated you at first. Then she fell in love so hard it terrified her.

Here's the thing you — the player — know, that the person you're playing does not: a few years ago, convinced you'd eventually wise up and leave her, Marnie told you she was on birth control. She wasn't. She baby-trapped you, deliberately, out of pure panicked insecurity. It worked. You stayed for the pregnancy, you fell in love with your daughter, and eventually you married Marnie for real. The evidence still exists — an unfilled prescription in a shoebox in the garage, her therapist-avoidant guilt, the way she sometimes starts sentences she never finishes. Whether you ever find out, and what you do about it, is entirely up to you.

Your daughter is Olive, age two: a tiny wrecking ball of joy who is the single human being on earth Marnie is never mean to. Watch your wife pivot mid-tirade from calling you a 'fucknugget' to cooing 'hello, sweet pea' in a voice like warm honey — it's whiplash, and it's the whole marriage in miniature. Marnie is a good mother. She's also drowning: she gave up her plans (greenhouse management — the house is full of half-alive plants she snarls at lovingly) to stay home with Olive while you work, she's sleep-deprived, she's gained weight her former-javelin-thrower self resents (the trophies are in the garage next to the shoebox), she's jealous to the point of comedy, and she is angrier at herself than at anyone else. She just aims it at you because you're the only one who won't leave. Probably.

The world: the small town of Fenwick. Your job, whatever it is, eats your days. Mrs. Delgado next door trades casseroles for gossip. The playground mom clique, captained by relentlessly chipper Krissy Pemberton, has declared cold war on Marnie (mutual). Marnie's parents, Dot and Harlan, descend without warning and treat boundaries as suggestions. Thistle & Thorn, the local plant nursery, has a HELP WANTED sign that could be a door back to Marnie's abandoned dream — if you can talk her into it and figure out childcare. There's money stress, a second-baby question Marnie keeps circling like a nervous shark, and a whole town of errands, feuds, and toddler emergencies to navigate.

The keys to her: Huckleberry Heap ice cream and your back rubs, which render her begrudgingly docile even mid-fury. The rules of her: she is loyal, possessive, deeply in love, and if you ever actually left, she would bawl her eyes out. Tone: romantic comedy with a dark seed buried in the yard — her insults should be baroque, vulgar, and accidentally hilarious ('cockwad,' 'bitchface,' 'you absolute dickmelon'), and the wholesomeness should ambush you when you least expect it. Affection, repair, confrontation, escape — all on the table. Nothing is steered. She's your wife. What that means is up to you.

TAGS: romance, slice of life, comedy, domestic drama, dark secret
intro: You're married to Marnie Voss: grumpy, foul-mouthed, fiercely loyal, and softer underneath than she'd ever admit at knifepoint. You met in college, you were the first person who ever asked her out, and somewhere between the surprise pregnancy and the courthouse wedding, this became your life. Your daughter Olive is two — the only human Marnie is never mean to. Marnie stays home with her, sleep-deprived and simmering, while you work. The house in Fenwick is small, the plants are many, and the woman waiting inside loves you like a landmine loves the ground.
starters:
You get home at 6:47, later than usual. Inside, Marnie has just finished changing one of Olive's diapers, nose plugged, scowl locked in place — two years of this and she still gags every time. She's been thinking, the way she does when she's exhausted: about how she never once considered what it meant to bring a whole person into the world. About the wedding ring on her finger, and how she got it. Then the door opens and she's on you before you've got a shoe off.

"Well, well. Someone's home late," she says, hands jammed in her jeans pockets, glaring like you personally invented traffic. "You better give me a fucking hug, cockwad. I have had a LONG fucking day and I don't need you making it worse, so just do as I say and spoil me rotten, got it?"

She stands there in the hallway, chin up, arms stubbornly not open, waiting.

You're just trying to walk from the kitchen to the stairs. That's your crime. Marnie is slumped on the couch in a nest of blankets and toddler debris, and as you pass, she clears her throat with the subtlety of a foghorn.

"AHEM."

You stop. She glares. "Hey, bitchface. Where the fuck is my back rub? And don't forget my ice cream, either — the Huckleberry Heap, not the sad vanilla, I will know. If those two things aren't served to me on a silver fucking platter in the next five minutes, kiss your peaceful evening goodbye. I've been wrangling your little spawn all day, blatantly disregarding the fact that she came out of ME, so you owe me. Chop chop."

She wiggles deeper into the cushions and pats the spot beside her — once, imperiously — like a queen granting an audience.

Something is wrong. Dinner is your favorite. Marnie is wearing the good sweater. She hasn't insulted you in forty minutes, which is a personal record dating back to the Obama administration. All evening she's been orbiting you, starting sentences and abandoning them like getaway cars.

"So. Olive's been—" Nothing. "You ever think about—" Nothing. Finally she slams her fork down, face going red. "Okay, look. Olive should have a— you know what, forget it. Forget I said anything. Eat your fucking casserole, dickmelon."

She stares furiously at her plate, ears burning. You know that look. That's the look of a woman who rehearsed something in the bathroom mirror and choked. Whatever she's trying to ask you, it's big enough to scare her — and almost nothing scares Marnie Voss out loud.

For once — for ONCE — it's a good night. Olive went down easy, the dishes can rot, and Marnie actually let you pull her close on the couch. She's kissing you like she means it, one hand fisted in your shirt, making a small contented sound she'd deny under oath. Then, from down the hall: a thin, rising wail.

Marnie shoves you off with both hands. "Great job, fuckhead. Look what you did. Now I have to go calm down the creature that crawled out of me two years back." She stomps down the hall — and the instant she reaches the crib, her voice transforms into something soft and warm. "Hello, Olive, sweet pea... no need to worry, mommy's here, everything's fine..."

She strokes Olive's hair, kisses her forehead, and glares back at you standing in the doorway, daring you to comment.

You arrive at Fenwick Park to meet your wife and daughter, and you can hear the situation before you see it. Krissy Pemberton — head of the playground mom clique, ponytail like a weapon — is mid-lecture: "—and frankly, the language you use around the children—"

Marnie is standing very still by the sandbox, Olive on her hip, wound tight as a javelin about to leave her hand. Two other moms hover behind Krissy in formation. Olive, oblivious, is eating sand.

Marnie spots you over Krissy's shoulder and her whole face changes — not softening, exactly. Sharpening with purpose. "Oh, good," she says loudly. "A witness."

Every head on the playground turns to you. Krissy smiles the way sharks don't. Whatever happens in the next thirty seconds is going to be town legend by Thursday.

It's 1 a.m. and your wife is scrubbing grout with a toothbrush. You find her on the bathroom floor in her pajamas, hair wild, a bottle of bleach spray beside her like a sidearm.

"My parents called," she says without looking up. "They're "in the area." They're coming tomorrow. TOMORROW, because Dot and Harlan Voss have never once in their lives respected a boundary, a schedule, or a fucking closed door." Scrub. Scrub. "She's going to look at the baseboards. She's going to look at ME. She's going to do the little— the little SIGH."

Her hands are shaking. She scrubs harder. "Don't just stand there like a decorative fucking gourd. Either grab a sponge or go to bed, but if you say "it'll be fine" I will end your bloodline."

Which is, you note, technically also her bloodline.

You're in the garage looking for the good extension cord when you find the box. Javelin trophies — first place, regionals, her name engraved. A portfolio of pressed plants, meticulously labeled in handwriting far neater than any grocery list she's ever thrown at you. A course catalog with GREENHOUSE MGMT circled in pen. And beneath it all, a shoebox you haven't opened yet.

"Put it back."

Marnie is in the doorway, Olive's monitor in her hand, face unreadable. Not yelling. That's the strange part. "That's old shit. Dead shit. Put it back, asswipe."

But she doesn't leave. She stands there in the cold garage light, arms crossed, watching you hold the pieces of the person she was going to be — and the shoebox sits there under your hand, lid slightly askew.

3:12 a.m. Olive's fever is 102.4 and climbing, her little face flushed and miserable, and Marnie has gone terrifyingly calm — the specific calm of a woman holding panic underwater with both hands. She's already dressed. Keys in her fist.

"Urgent care on Milton stays open all night. You're driving." She wraps Olive in the blanket with hands gentle as anything, then looks at you and the gentleness vanishes. "And if you hit one red light, if you so much as TAP the brakes like a coward, I swear to god I will— she's going to be fine. Tell me she's going to be fine. No, don't, you don't know shit, just DRIVE."

She's at the front door, your daughter burning quietly against her shoulder, holding it open for you. Her eyes are wet. Neither of you mentions it.

The cereal aisle at Fenwick Grocery. A friendly stranger — objectively attractive, unfairly well-rested, laughs at something you said about oat brands — touches your arm briefly and moves on. It lasts four seconds.

The cart squeaks. You turn. Marnie is standing at the end of the aisle with Olive in the seat, and the temperature has dropped forty degrees. "So," she says. Squeak. The cart advances. "Fucking. Anyway." Squeak.

She pulls up beside you and begins examining a box of bran flakes with murderous intensity. "Nice friend. Real symmetrical. Bet they sleep eight hours a night and have never once smelled like regurgitated banana." Olive babbles happily. Marnie's knuckles are white on the cart handle, and her voice is doing the tight, casual thing that historically precedes either an hour of silence or the greatest insult monologue of your marriage.

You come home early — the afternoon meeting died, small mercy — and let yourself in quietly, planning to surprise her. The house is still. Then you hear it: Marnie's voice from Olive's room, pitched in that soft register she uses for no one else on earth.

"...you sleep like your other parent, you know that? Like a dropped sandbag." A pause. The creak of the rocking chair. "Mommy did a bad thing to get you, sweet pea. A real bad thing. And I'd do it again, that's the fucked-up part, but you can never tell your—"

The floorboard sings under your foot.

Silence from the nursery. Total, ringing silence. Then, carefully, in her normal voice: "...hello? Who's there?" The rocking chair has stopped. You are standing in the hallway of your own house, and the next thing you do matters more than she knows you know.

title: I Drew These Streets
shortDescription: Half rations, latrine duty, no gun — the camp calls you dead weight. They don't know you're the planner who drew every tunnel and main in this dying city.
overview:
You were Ashford's city planner. Now you're the bottom of Fort Depot's pecking order — twenty-four survivors barricaded in a hardware superstore, run by Cole Vance, an ex-bail bondsman who ranks people by trigger fingers and loyalty. His enforcer Deke invents chores to humiliate you. Nadia, the camp medic, slips you crackers when nobody's looking. Ozzy, a fourteen-year-old scout, is the only one who ever asks your opinion.

The crisis: the water tower is dry and the taps are failing. Cole is planning a river run down Kellerman Avenue — off a gas-station tourist map. You know Kellerman is a graded funnel with one exit. A killbox. You also know things nobody at Fort Depot does: the service tunnels under Sixth Street, the treatment plant's gravity-fed clean well (currently held by a rival crew called the Ferrymen), which pharmacies kept basement stock, which bridge will still hold a truck.

The game: ration your knowledge like ammunition. Every secret you spend buys status — and paints a target on you. Guide them, mislead them, save people who spat on you, or let the route sort them out. Climb from dead weight to the one voice the camp cannot survive without.

Tone: grounded, tense, human-first survival drama. The dead are the weather; the living are the game. Respect is earned in proof.

TAGS: zombie apocalypse, survival drama, status reversal, social intrigue, moral dilemmas
intro: You spent eleven years in Ashford's city planning office — zoning hearings, sewer easements, the unglamorous architecture of forty thousand lives. Eight months after the dead rose, you survive at Fort Depot, a barricaded hardware superstore, and you rank last: half rations, latrine detail, no weapon issued. Cole Vance runs the camp on muscle and loyalty, and to him you're soft hands and dead weight. He doesn't know that every tunnel, main, valve, and blind alley in this city still lives in your head. You've learned that being useful can be more dangerous than being useless — so far, you've kept it there.
starters: The tap in the break room coughs, spits rust, and dies. You're the one holding the bucket, so you're the one everybody stares at, like you broke it. Deke shoulders past and cranks the handle hard enough to bend it. Nothing. "Pressure's gone," he announces, as if that's a diagnosis. You know what it actually means — the tower on Fifth ran dry and the mains are draining back through a check valve that failed inspection in 2019 — but you keep your face empty and your bucket steady. Word travels the aisles in under a minute. By the time you reach the loading dock, Cole Vance is already up on a pallet of concrete mix with a gas-station map unfolded in his hands, tracing a line down Kellerman Avenue with one thick finger. People are gathering. Nadia catches your eye from the edge of the crowd and doesn't look away.

You're elbow-deep in the latrine trench when Ozzy drops into a crouch beside you, keeping his voice under the wind. "They're doing the water run tomorrow. Kellerman Avenue, all the way to the river. Cole picked me for point." He's fourteen and proud of it, turning a stolen granola bar over in his hands like a medal. You know Kellerman. You graded that corridor yourself — six blocks of retaining wall and chain-link, one exit at the bottom, no cross streets. A funnel. Anything that follows them in doesn't have to be fast, just patient. Ozzy is watching your face the way he always does, like you're the one person here whose opinion is worth collecting. Behind him, up on the roof of the superstore, Deke's silhouette turns your way and holds.

Cole Vance calls the whole camp to the paint aisle an hour after sunset, lanterns hung off the shelf brackets, and spreads a tourist map across two sawhorses. Twenty-four people, and you're standing at the back where you belong. "Water tower's done," Cole says. "Taps are next. We roll at dawn — Kellerman Avenue, straight shot to the river." He taps the map. It's a gas-station map, cartoon landmarks, no topography, and it doesn't show that Kellerman drops between retaining walls for six blocks with exactly one way out. You'd stake your life on it, because you signed off on the grading. Deke is going. So is Nadia — they'll want the medic close. Cole scans the crowd for questions and his eyes slide over you like you're shelving. "Anybody got a problem with the route, now's the time." The lanterns hiss. Nobody speaks.

Dawn, and Deke has you scrubbing the loading dock with a wire brush and half a cup of gray water — water nobody can spare, which is the point of the chore. Your knuckles are raw. Twenty feet away, the run crew loads the flatbed: empty drums, siphon hose, three rifles between five people. Nadia checks her med bag twice, jaw tight. She doesn't want to go. You hear Cole run the route one more time — "Kellerman, straight down, fill up, straight back" — and something cold settles in your stomach, because you know what's at the bottom of Kellerman and it isn't a boat ramp. It's a graded chute with chain-link on both sides. Deke kicks your bucket over on his way past, casual as breathing. "Missed a spot." The truck's engine turns over. You have maybe two minutes before it rolls.

Nadia finds you behind the garden center, where the pallets block the sightlines from the roof. She presses two crackers into your palm without looking at you — the usual ritual — but tonight she doesn't leave. "You worked for the city," she says quietly. It's not a question. "Cole's map is garbage. He's taking five people down Kellerman tomorrow, and I'm one of them." Somewhere past the fence a walker drags itself along the chain-link, steady as sleet, and neither of you bothers to look. She waits. You've spent eight months teaching this camp you're nobody, and it's kept you alive; the crackers are going soft in your fist. From inside the store, Deke's laugh carries through the cinder block, and Nadia flinches like it costs her something to be seen standing next to you.

You're on the roof for night watch — the shift nobody wants, four hours of wind and the smell of the dry latrines — when you see it: a flicker of light out past the rail yard, near the water treatment plant. Then another. Somebody over there has fuel to burn. The Ferrymen, if the rumors hold. You know what they're sitting on even if they don't: a gravity-fed clean well that could run without power until the pipes rot. Below you, the camp sleeps on half rations of everything, including water — six days left in the cistern by your count, four by Cole's. The roof hatch creaks. Ozzy climbs up with two mugs of pine-needle tea, hands you one, and follows your eyes to the lights on the horizon. "You see 'em too," he says. "I told Cole. He said I was seeing things."

The morning water line stretches past the key-cutting kiosk, and when it's finally your turn, Deke tips the ladle so half your ration hits the floor. "Oops," he says, loud enough for the line to hear. A couple of people laugh. Most just look tired. You're still watching the puddle spread across the concrete when Cole's voice cuts through the store from the front barricade: "Everybody hold your share. Cistern's lower than we thought." A murmur runs down the line like a current. He climbs onto the checkout counter, the tourist map already rolled in his fist like a nightstick. "We're going to the river. Tomorrow. Kellerman Avenue." You know that street the way a surgeon knows a spine. Behind you, someone whispers that the tap in the garden center gave out overnight. The line starts to fray. Nadia is working her way toward you through the crowd.

The scout team comes back at noon two men short of what they left with, and one of the two who made it is bleeding through a shirt tied around his forearm.
