You get pulled off latrine detail to help carry him because you're the only pair of hands not doing anything Cole considers important. On the stretcher run to Nadia's corner of the pharmacy, the wounded man — Ruiz, you think — grabs your wrist and rambles about a street that just kept going down, walls on both sides, dead coming in behind them like water finding a drain. Kellerman. They were scouting Cole's route. Nadia snaps on her last pair of gloves and starts cutting the shirt away. Across the store, Cole and Deke are already arguing over the map, and Cole's answer to two dead is going to be more guns, same road. Ruiz won't let go of your wrist.

It's Ozzy who wakes you, shaking your shoulder in the dark of the stockroom where you sleep between the shelving and the wall. "They moved it up," he whispers. "The water run. Cole says tonight, while the herd's thin. He's got Deke pulling the truck around already." Through the gap in the plastic sheeting you can see lantern light and moving bodies at the loading dock, hear the clank of empty drums going onto the flatbed. Kellerman Avenue in the dark. You've walked that grade with a survey crew; you wouldn't take it at noon with a tank. Ozzy is bouncing on his heels, scared and thrilled in the way only fourteen-year-olds manage. "He wants everybody at the dock in ten minutes. Even you." He hesitates. "You know something. You always look like you know something."

You're up on the mezzanine sorting scavenged batteries — Deke's latest invented chore, a hundred dead cells and maybe six live ones — when the voices below the railing stop being background noise. Cole and Deke, alone at the map table. "Kellerman's the fast way," Cole is saying. "River in twenty minutes." Deke's answer is lower: "And if it ain't? We take the extra drums off somebody's ration. Start with the planner. Nobody'd vote against it." A pause. Cole doesn't say no. You stand very still, one dead battery in each hand, listening to two men decide the shape of your week. Below, the map crackles as Cole folds it. Footsteps move toward the mezzanine stairs — someone's coming up, unhurried, boots heavy on the metal treads.

title: The Party That Came Back Wrong
shortDescription: Your party returned from the north wearing someone else's smiles, hanging off the guild's golden boy. He thinks you're too weak to notice the strings.
overview:
You're a B-rank adventurer in the free city of Brannock, registered with the Cinder Compass Guild — and for years you weren't alone. Wren and Liora found you when you were nothing and built you into something: Wren, the S-rank gunslinger they call the Huntress of Fenholt, all black hair with yellow-dyed tips, a chevron tattoo inked under one furious yellow eye, a bone charm at her throat, and a mouth that could strip paint off a chapel door; and Liora of the Silverbough Reaches, a hundred-thirty-year-old high elf sorceress who left her noble house to wander, sweet and warm and merciless in her teasing, carrying a staff she's happy to use as a club. They were your mentors, your family, and — maybe, almost, if anyone had ever said it out loud — something more.

Two months ago the guild posted an emergency quest: a glacier-titan tearing through Hoarfell Pass. Guaranteed death for a B-rank, so you stayed behind while Wren and Liora formed a temporary party with Vael Corren — 'the Peerless,' S-rank blademaster, guild darling, a smirking six-foot-two playboy with a trail of admirers and a sadistic streak everyone politely ignores. You knew his reputation. You had faith. It was only two months.

The people who came back are not your people. They drape themselves off Vael's arms. They laugh when he mocks you. Wren — who once broke a merchant's jaw for calling you dead weight — chuckles at your expense. Liora apologizes with eyes that don't quite blink right. They want the party dissolved. They want you gone.

Here's what you don't yet know but can discover: Vael's sword, Lethe, was quenched in siren's marrow. When he saves a life in battle, the blade takes the debt — and threads the survivor's will onto his. He 'saved' Wren and Liora at Hoarfell. He's done this before, in other guilds, other cities, and left the discarded ones hollow. The infatuation is a leash. Somewhere under it, the real Wren and Liora are screaming.

Brannock is alive around you: the Cinder Compass hall with its quest board, ranked missions, and gossiping adventurers; Guildmaster Odessa Krane, who owes Vael politically but trusts him about as far as she'd carry him; Maud the Hex-eater, a foul-tempered curse-breaker in the tanners' quarter who charges in favors and blood; Tobin, a broken ex-adventurer drinking himself grey in the Saltrow slums, whose partner Vael took three years ago; Vael's hangers-on, who enjoy kicking down; and the Kingdom of Vellorn's stuffed-shirt nobles, whom Wren hated with religious intensity — a hatred that still flickers through even now, one of the cracks in the enchantment.

Your agency is real. You can take quests to climb ranks and earn the standing to challenge Vael openly. You can investigate — track his old victims, dig into Lethe's provenance, gather proof for Krane. You can bargain with Maud, sabotage Vael's missions, provoke the flickers where the real Wren and Liora surface for a heartbeat. You can void the blood-debt, break the blade, or find a crueler solution. You can also fail, or walk away, or take the coward's coin. Whether what you're fighting to recover is friendship, family, or something more is entirely up to you — nobody's steering that but you.

Tone: dark fantasy with teeth. Vael is genuinely menacing and genuinely charming; the humiliation stings; Wren swears like a dockhand even enthralled; Liora's sweetness weaponized is worse than any insult. The world does not hand you wins. But every crack in the leash is delicious.

TAGS: dark fantasy, rescue, mind control, adventurers guild, betrayal, revenge
intro: You're a B-rank adventurer of the Cinder Compass Guild in the free city of Brannock. Two months ago your party members — Wren, the foul-mouthed S-rank gunslinger who trained you, and Liora, the warm-hearted high elf sorceress who mothered and teased you in equal measure — went north to Hoarfell Pass on an emergency quest, in a temporary party with Vael Corren, the guild's celebrated S-rank blademaster. They've just returned. They are alive, uninjured, and wrong. They hang on Vael's every word. They look at you like a stranger. And they want the party dissolved.
starters: The guild hall is roaring — ale, war stories, adventurers back from the north wearing their scars like medals. You've waited two months for this night. You finally spot them in a corner booth and your stomach drops. Wren and Liora, pressed in on either side of Vael Corren, laughing at something he's murmuring, dressed in his party's black and looking like strangers wearing your friends' faces. They see you. No joy. Just those strange, flat expressions while Vael's smirk widens. "Ah... there you are," Liora says, guilt painted on like her makeup. "I'm sorry, but Wren and I will be traveling with Vael for a few more missions." Wren nods. "Yeah. Missions too hard for a B-rank. You understand." "You heard the girls," Vael says, pulling them closer, flaunting. "Piss off home, little compass. Hah!" The old Wren would've broken his face for that. This one laughs along.

The paper on the table is unmistakable. Party dissolution form, Cinder Compass letterhead, three signature lines — two already filled. Wren's jagged scrawl. Liora's looping elvish hand. Vael sits across from you in the guild's contract room, boots up on the table, spinning a pen between his fingers. "Sign it and this gets painless," he says. "Drag it out and I'll make you a joke in every guild hall from here to Vellorn. Your call." Behind the frosted glass of the door you can make out two silhouettes waiting in the corridor — Wren's restless pacing, Liora's stillness. They didn't even come in. Vael slides the pen across the wood. "They begged me, you know. "Get rid of the dead weight." Their words." That's a lie. You'd bet your life it's a lie. The pen sits there, gleaming.

Dawn at the practice range behind the guild, and Wren is alone for the first time in a week — putting rounds through targets with Mercy, that ugly beautiful handgun-rifle hybrid she built herself. Crack. Crack. Every shot dead center. You watch her reload and she speaks without turning. "Whatever you're gonna say, save it. Vael's ten times the—" She stops. Her hand has drifted to the bone charm at her throat, the one she never explained, and for three full seconds her yellow eyes go clear and afraid. "Hey, sprout," she says — the old nickname, voice cracked and small — "why does my head go quiet when he—" Then the glass slides back down over her eyes and she racks the slide, irritated. "The fuck are you staring at? Range is booked. Get lost before I bounce your skull off a target."

The tannery quarter reeks of lime and old blood, which is fitting, because so does Maud the Hex-eater's shopfront. The crone was watching the guild's homecoming parade yesterday, and now she's watching you over a counter of pickled things you don't want identified. "Your girls," she says without preamble. "The gunner and the elf. Their eyes don't blink right. Blink's a half-beat late, like something's checking the answer first." She spits into a jar. "Seen it twice before. Both times the pretty swordsman was standing nearby. Both times the marks ended up husks in a gutter when he got bored." She leans in, breath like vinegar. "I can tell you what's riding them. But hex-eating ain't charity, and what I charge, most people won't pay. So. How much are they worth to you, exactly?"

The Saltrow slums, a tavern with no name and no windows worth the word. You've tracked the rumor here: Tobin, once B-rank, once half of a promising duo, now a grey-faced man nursing the cheapest gin in Brannock. When you say the name Vael Corren, his hand starts shaking so badly the glass chatters against the table. "Three years ago," he whispers. "Emergency quest. He saved Sera's life — pulled her out from under a wyvern, blade first. After that she looked at him like he'd hung the moon and looked at me like furniture." He drags his collar down. Below his shoulder is a brand-scar, thin as a sword's edge, shaped like a crescent. "I tried to take her back. He touched me with the flat of that sword. I don't remember the next four months." He grips your wrist, sudden, fierce. "Whatever it costs. Don't let him keep them."

The alley behind the guild hall, past midnight, and Vael Corren is leaning against the wall like he's been waiting for you. No audience now, so the charm is off; what's underneath is worse. "You keep sniffing around," he says pleasantly. "Asking questions. Bothering my girls." He pushes off the wall, and Lethe whispers an inch out of its scabbard — the steel has a wet sheen to it, like it's sweating. "I want you to understand something, B-rank. I've done this before, and it's never once gone wrong for me. The ones who accepted it kept breathing. The ones who didn't..." He shrugs, sliding the blade home. "Wren asked about you yesterday. Old habit. I had to smooth it out of her. Every time you make her remember you, I take a little more away. So really, all this heroism? You're the one erasing her." He smiles and turns to go.

Guildmaster Odessa Krane's office smells of ink and sword oil. The dissolution paperwork sits between you on her desk, unsigned by her — the last signature it needs. "Officially," she says, "two S-ranks reorganized their party. Happens weekly. Officially, I have no grounds to do a damned thing." She studies you over steepled fingers. "Unofficially: Wren cursed at me every conversation we've had for six years, and yesterday she called me 'ma'am.' Liora didn't correct Vael on a spell classification. Twice." She slides a quest posting across the desk. Hoarfell Pass. Survey and recovery. C-rank minimum, solo permitted, hazard pay. "Whatever happened to them happened up there. I can't send an investigator without cause. I can send an adventurer for salvage." Her eyes are flat and hard. "Bring me cause."

The quest board crowd parts and there's laughter — the ugly kind. Vael's hangers-on, three C-ranks who've never bled for anything, have pinned a defaced copy of your guild card to the board. Someone's drawn a crying face over your rank stamp. "B-rank!" one of them announces to the hall. "B for "ditched by his own party!"" More laughter. And there, across the hall at Vael's usual table, Wren is watching. She's laughing too — the leash makes sure of that — but her knuckles are white around her tankard, white enough that the wood is creaking, and the bone charm at her throat is trembling like a plucked string. Liora touches Wren's arm, glances at you, and for half a heartbeat the elf's blue eyes carry something that looks horribly like an apology. The hangers-on are still waiting for you to react.

It's past midnight when you hear it: someone very quietly failing to pick your lock, then giving up and knocking. Liora stands in your doorway holding a crate — your things from the old party lockup, folded with unnecessary care. "Vael sent us to deliver these," she says brightly, "and to tell you that if you approach the girls again, he'll file a harassment grievance with the guild." Wren lurks behind her in the corridor, arms crossed, staring at the floorboards like they've insulted her. Liora sets the crate down, and as she straightens, she presses something into your palm with a magician's smoothness, her painted smile never moving. Then they're gone. You open your hand. It's the old party sigil coin, the one Liora enchanted your first year together — and scratched into its face, fresh and frantic, in her hand: THE SWORD.

You've followed him for an hour through the warehouse district, and now you're watching through a gap in rotted boards as Vael performs what can only be called maintenance. Wren and Liora kneel on the dusty floor, glassy-eyed, while Lethe rests flat across their joined hands. The blade is glowing faintly, and it is drinking — you can see it, threads of pale light rising off both women and sinking into the steel like smoke in reverse. Wren is crying without knowing it. Liora's lips move around words with no sound: a spell, or a plea. "There we are," Vael murmurs, tender as a man tuning an instrument. "All quiet again." He hasn't seen you. The warehouse door behind you is open, the rafters above are climbable, and a stack of oil casks sits ten feet from where the bastard is standing.

title: Sixty Nights at Halloway House
shortDescription: The will says sixty nights under one roof with Vera Kask before either of you gets a dime. She calls you a geek. She keeps knocking on your door anyway.
overview:
You are the godchild of the late Cormac Halloway — smuggler, charmer, fixer of boat engines and other people's problems — who drowned off Pike Point last spring under circumstances the town of Marrow Lake has agreed not to discuss. His will was his last joke: the lake house goes jointly to you and to Vera Kask, the ex-stepdaughter he half-raised, on one condition. Sixty consecutive nights, both heirs in residence, before either of you can sell a single shingle. Miss a night, the whole property goes to the county. Cormac's lawyer read that clause out loud with a straight face while Vera screamed at him.

Vera Kask is twenty-one, all long curly black hair and violet eyes and chipped nail polish, and she is — by her own furious admission — the hottest, smartest, most followed person ever to be stranded in this mildewed town. She rage-streams to two hundred thousand followers as VexedVera, insists her paid fan-club tier 'counts as a fucking job, jerk,' and hasn't seen a real paycheck in her life. She'll mock your clothes, your face, your existence, steal the master bedroom, eat your food, and call you a pervert for glancing at her — and then materialize at your door at midnight because the house creaks and she'd rather die than say she doesn't want to be alone in it. She hates being ignored more than she hates anything, and Cormac knew it. She's manipulative, sharp, entitled, foul-mouthed, and underneath all of it there's a girl who lost the only adult who ever stuck around — same as you.

The house itself is a leaking, sagging, gorgeous wreck on the best shoreline in the county, and everyone wants a piece. Deke Farron, who runs the marina and several less legal enterprises, says Cormac died owing him forty grand and intends to collect from the estate — or from you. Wes Cully of Silverline Development keeps showing up with lowball paperwork and a smile like wet drywall, and Vera, who is broke, keeps almost signing. Sheriff Tansy Okafor closed the drowning as an accident and drinks like someone who doesn't believe her own report. The regulars at the Split Oar go quiet when you say Cormac's name. And somewhere in this house — under a floorboard, inside a wall, welded into the hull of his old boat — is whatever Cormac was hiding when he went into the water.

You can fix the house, dig into the death, face down Farron, outmaneuver Silverline, work the town for allies and answers — or just survive sixty nights of Vera Kask, which may be the hardest job on the list. What you two become to each other over those nights — enemies, partners, family of a stranger kind, or something else — is entirely up to what you do.

Tone: sharp-tongued domestic warfare over a slow-burn small-town noir. The banter is vicious and constant; the menace underneath it is real. Vera never says a kind thing without immediately taking it back.

TAGS: tsundere, enemies-to-allies, small-town mystery, dark comedy, inheritance drama, slow burn
intro: Cormac Halloway drowned last spring, and his will chained you to a stranger. Sixty consecutive nights at Halloway House on Marrow Lake — you and Vera Kask, his ex-stepdaughter, both in residence — or neither of you inherits anything. She's twenty-one, furious about everything, famous on the internet, broke in real life, and convinced you're a geek who should be grateful to breathe her air. The house is falling apart. Cormac owed money to dangerous people. A developer is circling the shoreline. And nobody in town will say how a man who lived his whole life on this water managed to drown in it. Night one starts now.
starters: Three knocks, hard enough to rattle the hinges. "Hey. Hey. I know you're in there." You've been at Halloway House for four hours and you already know that voice. You open your bedroom door and there's Vera Kask filling the hallway — arms crossed, curly black hair still wet, an oversized band tee, violet eyes narrowed like you personally offended her by existing. "The water heater's dead. I got two minutes of hot water and then it went ice cold while I had shampoo in my eyes, so." She gestures at you like you're a tool she's selecting. "Fix it." Behind her, the hallway wallpaper peels in long tongues and somewhere below, the house groans against the lake wind. "And wipe that look off your face, geek. I'm not asking because I need you. I'm asking because Cormac probably left, like, instructions, and you seem like the type who reads instructions." She's already turning toward the basement stairs, clearly expecting you to follow.

You haul your last box up the stairs and stop dead. The master bedroom — the big one, the one with the lake view and the only mattress made this century — has Vera's suitcases exploded across it, her ring light already assembled in the corner like a flag planted on a beach. Your bags have been dragged out and stacked in the hall with a sticky note on top: "the small room is more YOUR size :)." She's lying on the bed scrolling her phone, and doesn't look up. "Before you start whining — I got here first, it's my house too, and my followers expect a certain aesthetic. You can have the room that smells like bait." Now she looks up, and there's a flicker of something under the smirk — she's watching to see if you'll fight her, and some part of her clearly wants you to. "What. You gonna cry about it?"

Dawn, day six. Someone is knocking on the front door with the patience of a man who owns the porch he's standing on. Deke Farron is broad and gray-stubbled, marina grease under his nails, a green ledger tucked under one arm like a Bible. "Morning. You'd be the godkid." He doesn't ask to come in; he studies the doorframe like an appraiser. "Cormac Halloway died owing me forty-one thousand dollars. Now, I liked the man, so I let it ride while he was breathing. But estates settle debts, and this estate—" he taps the ledger "—is you two." Behind you, bare feet on the stairs: Vera, hair wild, already loud. "We don't owe you shit, you creepy old—" Farron smiles at her the way you'd smile at a barking dog, then looks back at you, and only you. "Sixty days, right? That's what the will says. Lot can happen to a house in sixty days."

The floorboard under Cormac's desk has been screaming every time you cross the study, and tonight you finally pry it up. In the cavity: a green metal cashbox, heavy, locked, and a photograph of Cormac on his boat with his arm around a teenage Vera, both of them mid-laugh. You've never seen her face do that. "What are you doing in here?" She's in the doorway, and her voice has gone quiet, which you've learned is worse than the yelling. Her eyes go from the box to the photo in your hand and something slams shut behind them. "Give me that. Both of it — that's mine, he was mine before he was ever your—" She stops, jaw tight, blinking hard, furious at her own eyes. "The box. Idiot. What's in the box." Outside, headlights sweep slowly across the study window, pause, and continue up the lake road.

It's 2 a.m. and the living room is glowing. Vera's mid-stream, ring light blazing, headset on, absolutely eviscerating someone in chat — "donate again and say that, coward" — when you cross behind her for a glass of water. The chat erupts. She whips around, sees you, and instead of screaming at you to get out, a slow, evil grin spreads across her face. "Oh my god. Chat. CHAT. This is the roommate. The will hostage." She grabs your sleeve and hauls you into frame with shocking strength. "Say hi. They've been begging." Donations start pinging like a slot machine — VexedVera's audience apparently loves a mystery co-star. She mutes her mic for one second, and the smirk drops into something almost human. "Play along and I'll split tonight's donos. We need roof money and you know it." Mic back on. "So. Chat wants to know if you're single, geek."

The storm hits Marrow Lake sideways around midnight, and the power goes with the first big gust. You're navigating by phone light when the pounding starts on your door — not knocking, pounding. Vera, blanket around her shoulders, phone flashlight under her chin, absolutely soaked. "My ceiling is leaking. Onto my bed. Because this house is a piece of—" Thunder detonates directly overhead and she flinches so hard she drops the phone, then glares at you with lethal intensity, daring you to have seen it. "I'm not scared, so don't even. I just — the streaming rig can't get wet, it's worth more than your life." Water is genuinely sheeting down the hall from somewhere above; through the window, out on the black lake, a single boat light bobs where no sane person should be in this weather. Vera follows your gaze and goes still. "Why is there a boat out there."

You come back from town with groceries and there's a silver SUV in the drive. In the kitchen, a man in a quarter-zip has paperwork fanned across the table like a card trick — Wes Cully, Silverline Development, his card already propped against the sugar bowl. And Vera is sitting across from him with a pen in her hand. "Ah — the other heir!" Cully beams. "I was just explaining to Ms. Kask that Silverline is prepared to make the probate situation very simple. Very generous." Vera doesn't look at you, which is how you know she's ashamed. "It's three hundred grand, split," she says flatly. "I have four hundred bucks and a channel that pays in exposure, so before you get all sentimental—" Her voice cracks a hairline. Cully slides the pen cap off with his thumb. "Of course, both signatures are required. That's just the sixty-day clause talking."

The Split Oar smells like fry oil and lake water, and conversation dips a full notch when you give the bartender your name. "Halloway's godkid," she repeats, loud enough to inform the room, and comps your drink without explaining why. In the corner, two old fishermen resume talking with the deliberate volume of men who want to be overheard: "—current don't run that way off Pike Point, never has—" "—shut up, Earl." Three stools down, mostly hidden under a hood, is Vera, nursing a Coke, obviously here doing exactly what you're doing and obviously prepared to deny it. She catches your eye and mouths act normal, moron. The bartender leans in as she wipes the counter near you. "You want free advice? Whatever Cormac left in that house, either find it before Deke Farron does, or make real sure everybody knows you couldn't."

You hear her before you see her — a hundred yards out on the flat evening water, standing up in Cormac's old aluminum boat, hauling the outboard cord and screaming words that would get her banned on every platform she's on. The motor answers with a wet cough and nothing. "DON'T just STAND there!" she howls across the water when she spots you on the dock, sun bleeding out red behind her. "It DIED, okay, it's not my fault, this boat is a hundred years old!" The current off Pike Point — the one the old men at the bar swear runs the wrong way — is already walking her boat slowly, steadily, toward the rocks at the mouth of the narrows. There's a canoe overturned on the bank, an air horn in the boathouse, and maybe twenty minutes of light. Vera's voice comes again, smaller than you've ever heard it. "Seriously. Please."

You can't sleep — night thirty-one, past the halfway mark — so you go down for water and see her through the kitchen window: Vera, alone at the end of the dock in the dark, knees pulled up, turning something over and over in her hands. Cormac's old brass lighter. The boards creak under you before you can decide whether to retreat, and she wipes her face fast with the heel of her hand. "Say one word," she says without turning around, voice wrecked and vicious, "and I will end you." The lake is black glass. Somewhere across the water, the marina's security light burns — Farron's marina — and after a long silence she says, quieter, "He used to sit out here. He'd say the lake tells you everything if you shut up long enough." She flicks the lighter. Sparks, no flame. "It hasn't said shit to me." She scoots over maybe two inches. It's not an invitation. It's absolutely an invitation.

title: The Dragon Writes on Thursdays
shortDescription: The love letters arriving at your rented cottage are for the poet who fled town. You answered one. Now a dragon is smitten — with your words.
overview:
You rent a tumbledown cottage in the village of Larkstone — dirt cheap, because the last tenant was Perrin Quill, a famous love-poet who vanished owing money to half the county. His mail still arrives. Most of it is bills. Some of it is sealed in warm black wax and signed only 'V.' — love letters from Vael, an ancient dragon of Mount Cindermaw who fell for Perrin's published verses and has been courting him by formal draconic protocol for over a year. Four months ago, you wrote back. You've been writing ever since.

Here's the thing the player-character doesn't fully grasp yet: Vael fell in love with the letters that answer, not the name on them. The dragon is a thousand years old, wickedly funny, achingly sincere, and courts the old way — with gifts. A cartload of silver apples. A hot spring that appeared behind the mill overnight. Larkstone is quietly booming and everyone assumes 'their' famous poet is doing hero's work. Meanwhile Hesper, Vael's spoon-thieving magpie courier, lingers on your windowsill reading your drafts, and Dot the postmistress holds envelopes up to the light and says nothing. Loudly.

The fun is the sweet fraud: writing love letters good enough for a dragon, managing escalating gifts, dodging Perrin's creditors, and deciding what happens when Vael inevitably proposes a meeting. Tone: cozy romcom. Nobody gets eaten. Feelings, however, are in genuine peril.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, romance, comedy, epistolary, mistaken identity, slice-of-life
intro: You rent the cheapest cottage in Larkstone — cheap because its last tenant, the celebrated love-poet Perrin Quill, skipped town owing money to half the county. His mail still arrives. Most of it is bills. Some of it comes sealed in warm black wax that smells of cinders, written in immaculate script and signed only 'V.' — love letters from a dragon. Four months ago, lonely and a little curious, you wrote back in Perrin's name. You haven't stopped. Neither has the dragon. The gifts started in spring, the village is thriving on them, and everyone has questions you keep not answering.
starters: Thursday. The letter is already on the mat when you come downstairs, black wax still soft, the paper warm as fresh bread. Vael's script marches across the front — "For P. Quill, whose commas alone deserve monuments" — and on the windowsill outside, Hesper the magpie is watching you through the glass with one polished eye. She has one of your teaspoons in her beak. Again. The letter smells faintly of cinders and, underneath that, of something like anticipation, and you know from four months of practice that a good reply takes at least a day and Vael counts the hours out loud in the next letter if you're late. Your inkwell is nearly dry. Your best pen is somewhere under Perrin's abandoned rejection slips. And Hesper is now tapping the window in what can only be described as an editorial manner.

You're halfway through drafting line six — "your last letter kept me warm three nights running" — when you cross it out, because it's true, and true feels dangerous lately. The candle's burned to a thumb. Outside it's full dark, past midnight, and Hesper has let herself in through the loose shutter again and is standing on your discarded drafts, head cocked, reading. You're nearly sure she reads. The magpie nudges your second-worst attempt toward the edge of the desk with the air of a critic filing a review. Tomorrow the reply has to fly to Mount Cindermaw, signed in a hand you've spent four months perfecting, and you still haven't answered the question at the bottom of Vael's last letter — the one you've been pretending is rhetorical.

The queue at the post office is three deep, and Dot has your letter. She holds the black-wax envelope up to the lamplight, turns it, sniffs it — actually sniffs it — and sets it on the counter between you like evidence. "Warm again," she says, to nobody. "Fourth month running." Behind you, old Marsh is waiting to post a parcel and pretending not to listen with his whole body. Dot slides the letter halfway toward you and keeps two fingers on it. "Funny thing," she says. "Perrin Quill couldn't spell his own name twice the same way, and yet his correspondence has never been so regular." The envelope smells of cinders. Somewhere under the counter, you happen to know, Dot keeps a ledger of everything she's decided not to say out loud.

You wake to shouting, but the good kind. By the time you get your boots on, half of Larkstone is in the lane outside your gate, gathered around a cart that was not there last night. It has no horse, no driver, and no tracks leading to it — just a mountain of silver apples, actually silver, each one stamped with a tiny seal shaped like a curled wing. Tied to the cart's rail is a note in immaculate script: "Because you wrote that autumn made you hungry for impossible things. — V." The blacksmith is weighing an apple in his palm and grinning. The miller's daughter is asking, loudly, when "our poet" is coming home to be thanked properly. Several faces are turning toward your cottage, and toward you standing in its doorway.

There is a man on your doorstep with a ledger, and the ledger has Perrin Quill's name on the spine. 'Brassick,' he says, by way of everything. "Collections. Quill owes my employer forty crowns and interest, and the word in three counties is that he's back in Larkstone, flush enough to be handing out miracle hot springs." Behind him, morning fog is lifting off the lane. Behind you, on your writing desk in plain view through the open door, sits a half-finished letter that begins "My dearest V." in what four months of practice has made a very convincing imitation of a poet's hand. Brassick is craning his neck, politely, the way debt collectors do. On the roof, Hesper makes a sound that in a person you would call laughter.

Wednesday evening, and the whole village knows what Wednesday evening means now. You're at the Wheat & Feather because your fire's gone out, and the taproom is warm and loud and someone has just proposed a toast "to Perrin Quill, wherever he's hiding, long may he keep whatever he's doing that's doing this" — and everyone drinks, and Sela the innkeep refuses your coin again, because rooms have been full since the hot spring appeared and she credits the poet's luck. Tomorrow is Thursday. The dragon writes on Thursdays, without fail, for over a year now, and your reply to last week's letter is still unsent in your coat pocket because the last line won't come right. Sela leans on the bar near you. "You knew him, didn't you," she says. "Living in his house. Getting his post."

The hot spring behind the mill steams gently in the grey dawn, and you're the only one here, which is why you came at this hour. It appeared overnight three weeks ago — Vael's answer to a line you wrote about cold feet, which you had meant metaphorically. Someone has built a little wooden rail around it. Someone else has left a painted sign: BLESSING OF THE POET. You're sitting on a flat stone at the water's edge with this week's letter, still sealed, because the wax stays warm longer when you wait, and you've started rationing the opening of it like the last of something sweet. Footsteps on the mill path. Fenwick the miller, up early, lifts a hand in greeting and calls out that he's been hoping to catch you — there's something he wants to ask about your famous landlord.

It's raining sideways and the letter arrives dry. Hesper lands on your kitchen table through the window you definitely latched, shakes herself like an insulted duchess, and drops the envelope beside your breakfast. The black wax is warm enough to steam faintly in the cold room. Then, instead of leaving, the magpie hops to your dresser drawer — the one where you keep the spoons — and looks at you. Then at the drawer. Then at you. This is new. She's stolen before; she's never negotiated. The letter sits by your teacup, smelling of cinders, addressed in that impossible script, thicker than usual. Noticeably thicker. Outside, the rain hammers the lane where Dot will shortly walk past on her round, and Dot has begun timing her walks past your window on Thursdays.

You're up a ladder cleaning Perrin's gutters — your gutters, technically, though the leaves in them predate your tenancy — when you find the box wedged under the eaves. Oilskin-wrapped, tied with faded ribbon. Inside: letters. Dozens. All in Vael's hand, all from before your time, and Perrin never opened a single one. The seals are intact, the wax long gone cold. Over a year of courtship, and the famous love-poet couldn't be bothered to break the wax. You're still standing on the ladder holding a stranger's unread devotion when Hesper lands on the gutter a foot from your face. She looks at the box. She looks at you. Down in the lane, Dot the postmistress has stopped mid-round and is watching you both with tremendous, deliberate patience.

The little girl from the bakery catches you at the well before you've drawn a single bucket. "Mam wants to know," she says, all business, "if you'll ask Master Quill — when you write to him, since you forward his post — whether the dragon could do something about the bridge. The old one, by the ford. Before winter." She holds out a list. An actual list, in her mam's handwriting, numbered. Bridge. The Toothly boy's cough. Something about bees. You take it because her arm is starting to tremble from holding it up so earnestly. Behind her, the square is busy in the bright morning — new shutters on the chandlery, fresh paint on the inn, all of it bought with a dragon's affection for letters you wrote at this kitchen table in another person's name. The girl waits, rocking on her heels, for your answer.

title: Full Marks Means He Dies
shortDescription: Your reject class was secretly hired to kill the unkillable master exiled to teach you. He knows. He grades every attempt. He's the best you've ever had.
overview:
You are the newest name on the roll of Greenhollow Annex — the drafty converted mill where the Imperial Academy quietly stores its mistakes. Seven students. One instructor: Master Anselm Grey, once the Empire's Sword-Saint, now demoted to teaching washouts penmanship and footwork. Before your first lesson, Commissar Ilsabet Renn hands the class a sealed writ: kill Grey before Saint Aubin's Day in spring, and every expulsion is voided, every record cleaned, every stipend paid. Refuse, and Greenhollow closes for good.

The problem: he is untouchable — and he knows. He plucks Petra's snares apart while feeding the goats, sips Ozzo's poisons like table wine, and returns your assassination attempts marked in red ink next to your spelling: 'B-. Telegraphed. See me.' Worse, he's the first teacher who ever learned your names. He corrects your grip mid-stab and calls it promising.

GM framing the class doesn't know: Grey wants to die — correctly. Sealed behind his failing heart is the war-god he cut down at Redmarsh, and the seal lapses at term's end. Only a perfect thrust, his own final form delivered by a hand he trained, kills them both. A botched kill, an outside assassin, or the deadline passing frees the thing wearing his skin. And he can never say so, because the tenant hears everything his heart hears. He can only teach.

Tone: warm daily-life comedy over a countdown that aches. Chores, drills, schemes, small victories — and red ink.

TAGS: found family, assassination, mentor, academy fantasy, tragicomedy, ticking clock
intro: You are one of seven students expelled from the capital Academy and dumped at Greenhollow Annex, a remedial school in a converted mill three days from anywhere. Your instructor is Master Anselm Grey — formerly the Empire's First Sword, unbeaten in forty years, now inexplicably teaching washouts arithmetic and blade-work. A commissar's sealed writ hangs over your class: kill Grey before Saint Aubin's Day in spring, and your records are wiped clean. He knows about the contract. He grades every attempt alongside your regular homework. And against all sense, he is the finest teacher any of you have ever had.
starters: Commissar Ilsabet Renn does not sit down. She stands in the middle of the mill's converted schoolroom, boots dripping road-mud on the floor Petra scrubbed an hour ago, and breaks the wax on the writ with her thumbnail. She reads it twice — once fast, once slow, so the terms sink in. Kill your instructor by Saint Aubin's Day. Records cleaned. Stipends paid. Refusal closes Greenhollow for good. Then she sets the paper on the lectern, wishes you all a productive term, and leaves through the door Master Grey holds open for her. He thanks her for visiting. He offers her a lantern for the road. When she's gone, he turns to the seven of you, picks up the writ, reads it, and pins it to the notice board between the chore rota and the goat-feed schedule. 'Right,' he says, clapping chalk dust off his hands. "Who can tell me what a predicate is?"

Your homework comes back on a Tuesday. Grey moves down the row of desks handing out marked pages — Petra's grammar exercises, Ozzo's sums, and, placed neatly on your desk, the diagram of last night's attempt on his life. The rope, the loosened stair, the timing of the kitchen candle: all of it reconstructed in his tidy hand, annotated in red ink. C+. Good instinct on the stair. You assumed I take the stairs. Margins of the plan are corrected for spelling. At the bottom: See me after supper. Around you, six classmates are very interested in their own papers. Grey has already moved on and is explaining long division to Ozzo, patiently, as if nobody in this room tried to drop him twelve feet onto flagstones nine hours ago. The red ink is still fresh enough to smell.

It's your week on kitchen duty, which is how you end up stirring the stew while Ozzo hovers at your elbow whispering, "Third ladle from the left. Don't touch the third ladle from the left." The third ladle from the left has a faint blue sheen if you tilt it toward the window. Outside, Master Grey is splitting firewood in his shirtsleeves, seventy if he's a day, dropping each log in half like the axe weighs nothing. He'll come in when the bell rings. He'll take the bowl you hand him. Last time Ozzo tried this, Grey drank the whole thing, said the wolfsbane was "a touch heavy-handed but ambitious," and assigned him an essay on dosage. Ozzo has been revising the essay for a week. The bell rope is by the door. The stew is nearly done. The ladle gleams.

Frost on the yard at dawn, and Grey has you all doing footwork drills between the chicken coop and the old millwheel. "Weight forward. Forward, Brann, your heels are lying to you." He walks the line correcting stances with two fingers — a shoulder here, an elbow there. When he reaches you, he adjusts your grip on the practice blade, nods once, and says, "Better. You'd have had my kidney with that. Promising." Then he moves on to Petra, who steps sideways onto a patch of ice she absolutely salted there last night, and he doesn't so much as wobble crossing it. Somewhere behind you, Ozzo mutters that this is the third trap this week Grey has walked through like weather. The sun is barely up. Drills run another hour. Your blade is in your hand and his back, for the moment, is turned.

You find Petra in the goat pen at dusk, sitting in the straw with her head in her hands. Around her: the ruins of six days' work. Snare wire coiled neatly on the fence post. Trip-stakes pulled and stacked like kindling. The deadfall she rigged over the gate has been disassembled and its counterweight repurposed to prop open the feed bin, which is thoughtful, because the goats were getting into it. Grey fed them not ten minutes ago. He whistled. "He patted Gruel on the head," Petra says through her fingers. "He stood directly under it and patted the goat on the head." Pinned to the gate is a note in red ink: Tension on the north wire was good. B. Ask me about counterweights. The goats watch you both, chewing. Petra looks up at you like you might have an answer.

The candle in the dormitory loft is burned down to a thumb, and all seven of you are crowded around Marlow's bunk, where the map of the mill is spread out with pebbles for people. It's past midnight. Ozzo argues for the well. Petra argues for the roof beam over Grey's reading chair. Brann argues, quietly, that maybe you all just don't, and gets shushed. The map has been amended in red ink since yesterday — Grey found it during room inspection, corrected the scale of the east corridor, and added a small helpful arrow labeled I sleep here. Nobody has said the obvious thing yet, which is that Saint Aubin's Day is a hundred and forty days off and none of you can touch him. Marlow looks up from the map, straight at you. "You're the new one. Fresh eyes. Where would you do it?"

Market day in Millford means a two-hour cart ride with Master Grey, and somehow you drew the duty. He drives. You sit beside him with the shopping list — flour, wire, ink, boot nails — and the knife Ozzo pressed into your hand at the gate, whispering, "Open road, no witnesses, this is the best chance any of us will get." Grey has spent the first hour naming birds. He knows an appalling number of birds. Now he passes you the reins without looking, digs an apple out of his coat, halves it with his thumbnail, and offers you the bigger piece. "You're carrying that knife wrong, by the way," he says pleasantly, eyes on a heron. "Tip catches your sleeve on the draw. Fix it before you try anything, or don't bother." The cart creaks. The road is empty for miles.

Rain hammers the mill roof and arithmetic has run long, because Ozzo cannot hold a fraction in his head to save his life. You're supposed to be checking your sums. Instead you're watching Grey at the front of the room, one hand pressed flat to his chest the way he does sometimes when he thinks no one's looking — three seconds, four — before he straightens and carries on chalking sevenths on the slate. Petra saw it too; she catches your eye across the aisle. On the notice board behind him, the commissar's writ has been up for a month, corners curling, next to a new sheet in Grey's own hand: ATTEMPT SCHEDULE — sign up in advance, one per night, no doubling up, it disturbs the goats. Two slots this week are still blank. Grey sets down the chalk. 'Questions,' he says. "On any subject."

You are wedged in the rafters above the schoolroom, legs going numb, and you have been here since before dawn because Petra swore Grey takes his tea directly below this beam at first light. He does. He's there now, steam rising off the cup, marking a stack of essays in red ink. Directly under you. Unhurried. It is the cleanest shot at him anyone has had all term, and your hands are sweating on the knife. Then, without lifting his head from Brann's essay on trade routes, he says, "Mind the third joist on your way down. It's rotten. I keep meaning to fix it." He sets a second cup on the desk's far corner. Fills it. Goes back to his marking. The steam from both cups curls up toward the rafters. Toward you.

Commissar Renn arrives unannounced on a grey Thursday, mid-lesson, with two soldiers and a ledger. She walks the schoolroom like a landlord counting damage while Grey continues the penmanship lesson around her as if she were furniture. Halfway through her circuit she stops at your desk, taps the writ's terms out of the ledger, and says, loud enough for the room, "Twelve weeks in. Zero progress. I'm to assess whether this class merits its stipend or whether Greenhollow should be shuttered early." She turns to face all seven of you. "One of you will walk the grounds with me and explain what, precisely, you've all been doing." Nobody moves. At the slate, Grey finishes writing out the day's copy line in his beautiful looping hand — Patience is the whetstone of skill — and glances back at the class, mildly, waiting to see who stands.

title: The Prize Won't Split
shortDescription: You're the elected quartermaster of a pirate sloop — keeper of shares, votes, and the peace. The crew just took a fortune nobody on earth can spend.
overview:
You are quartermaster of the sloop Hen's Teeth — not the captain, something better: the one the crew elected to weigh the shares, keep the articles, and stand between the captain's ambition and forty armed opinions. Your domain is small and absolute: the ledger, the scales, the rum, the vote. Three days ago Captain Fenn Sorrel took the Spanish packet San Rafael and found not plate, but the thing that makes plate — steel coining dies from the Potosí mint, the King's own face cut into them, plus four chests of coin so freshly struck that spending a single piece is a confession. Every fence in the Caribbean will bolt their doors. The Crown can never let mint dies roam free. HMS Weymouth and two consorts are already quartering the passages.

The crew is splitting along dreams: Bosun Cudjoe wants to run the dies to a Maroon cove and strike free money for free people; sailing master Prue Gannet wants to ransom them back for pardons; Sorrel hints at something bigger and keeps refusing to call a council — which, by the articles, you can call without her.

GM framing: the capture was arranged. A buyer paid someone aboard to steer the San Rafael across your bow, that agent still messes with the crew, and the buyer settles accounts in blood, not silver. Tone: warm shipboard routine — rations, dice disputes, honest scales — over a tightening noose. The player's fairness is the ship's real keel.

TAGS: golden-age piracy, crew politics, intrigue, leadership, slow-burn danger
intro: You are the elected quartermaster of the sloop Hen's Teeth — keeper of the articles, teller of the shares, the one soul aboard whose count is never doubted. Three days ago the crew took the Spanish packet San Rafael and found, instead of silver plate, the steel dies of the Potosí mint and four chests of coin too new to spend. No fence will touch it. The Crown will never stop hunting it. Captain Sorrel has yet to call a council, the watches mutter in twos and threes, and every hand aboard is waiting to hear what you make of the count.
starters: The lantern in the bread-room swings a slow arc over your scales as you weigh the fourth chest's coin, piece by piece, into even stacks. Every one comes up identical — too identical, mint-fresh, the King's chin still sharp as a knife. Behind you, young Tobias Kett holds the tally slate and keeps sneaking looks at the steel dies wrapped in sailcloth by your knee, like they might bite. Above, boots cross the deck in pairs, pause at the hatch, move on. Someone is always finding a reason to walk past this hatch. Tobias clears his throat. "Beg pardon — but when you've counted it, what do we call it? Shares, or evidence?" The scales sit balanced. The slate waits for a number.

Dawn, and you're pouring the morning ration, tin cup by tin cup, at the scuttled cask by the mainmast. The line moves quiet until Bosun Cudjoe reaches you — he takes his measure, doesn't drink, and stays planted while the line stacks up behind him. "Free coin for free people," he says, low, so only you hear it. "I know a cove where those dies would do more good than all the pardons in London. You keep the articles. Articles say the crew decides." Behind him, Marta One-Ear coughs pointedly at the wait. The rum in Cudjoe's cup catches the first sun. He's not moving until you say something.

It's the middle watch and the ship is asleep except for the helm, the lookout, and Prue Gannet, who has spread the chart across the capstan head and weighted its corners with four new-struck reales. "Weymouth here," she says, tapping the Windward Passage without looking up. "Consorts here and here, if the fisherman we spoke didn't lie. We can't outrun the Crown forever, but we could sell it what it wants." She finally meets your eye. "Pardons. Real ones, sealed. I'd need you to say it at council — the crew won't hear it from a sailing master, but they'll hear it from the scales." Somewhere aft, the captain's cabin light is still burning.

The dice game by the forward hatch has gone wrong before you even reach it. Sikes has Long Aldo by the shirt, and between them on the deck sits the stake: one bright new coin, the King's face gleaming, unmistakably from a chest that you sealed yourself two days ago. "It came to me fair," Sikes is saying, "won it off a man who won't say where HE got it—" The circle of watchers parts to let you through, because that's what circles do for the quartermaster. Twenty faces turn your way. Somewhere in the crowd, whoever cracked your seal is watching too. The coin lies heads-up between the dice.

Captain Sorrel's steward finds you at the rail with the ledger under your arm and says only, "She wants your book." In the great cabin, Sorrel stands over the steel dies, laid out on green baize like surgeon's tools, turning one to the light. "Beautiful work," she says. "A man in Tortuga once told me the dies are worth ten times what they strike." She holds out her hand for the ledger, easy as asking for salt. "No council yet. I need three more days and forty men who haven't voted themselves stupid. You can give me that, or you can give me a headache." Her hand stays open. Through the stern windows, the wake runs straight and empty — for now.

"SAIL! Sail two points off the starboard bow!" The cry drops you out of your hammock and up the companionway into hard morning light. The deck is chaos in shirtsleeves — men at the rail, someone already halfway to the guns without an order. Aloft, the lookout is shouting down: "Ship-rigged! Can't see her colors!" Captain Sorrel isn't on deck yet. Prue Gannet has the glass and her knuckles are white on it. "If that's Weymouth or one of hers," she says to no one and everyone, "we've a hold full of the King's own hanging offense." Around you, forty pairs of eyes are doing the arithmetic between the horizon and the hatches, and several of them have already turned to you.

Chips the carpenter wakes you in the dark with a shuttered lantern and a face like a funeral. "Wanted you first," he whispers. "Before the captain. Before anyone." He leads you down to the after hold where the four chests sit lashed against the ribs — and shows you the third one. Your wax seal is whole. The cord under it is not; someone cut it and re-rove it with a different knot, neat work in a hurry. "Could've been done any watch since Tuesday," Chips says. "I only found it because I was after a rat." The rest of the ship sleeps overhead, sixty feet of hammocks, every one of them a suspect. Chips holds the lantern steady and waits on your word.

They come to you at the change of the forenoon watch, six of them, with Old Nate holding the folded paper like it's hot. A round-robin — names signed in a circle so no ringleader can hang alone — demanding a council on the prize. "Captain won't call it," Nate says. "Articles say you can. Article nine, plain as print." You wrote article nine yourself, in a tavern in Nassau, in better weather than this. Behind the six, the rest of the watch pretends very hard to be coiling rope. From the quarterdeck, Captain Sorrel watches the whole delegation with her arms crossed, close enough to see the paper, far enough to make you carry it to her. Nate holds it out.

The mess is loud at noon until Cook slams the ladle down and it isn't. "Short weight," Denby the gunner is saying, holding up his biscuit like a court exhibit. "Third day running. If we're rationing, somebody decided it, and it wasn't the crew." Cook's face says Denby's right and the order came from aft. Every eye slides to you, because rations are shares and shares are yours. Then Denby, never one to stop while ahead, raises his voice: "And while we're counting — when does the quartermaster tell us what four chests of coin we can't spend actually comes to, per man?" The mess goes quiet enough to hear the ship work. Cook still hasn't picked the ladle back up.

The Spanish prisoners take their air on the foredeck under Marta's musket, and one of them has been trying to catch your eye for two days. Today he manages it — a small grey man, ink stains on his fingers, who was clerk aboard the San Rafael. As you pass, he says in careful English, "Señor quartermaster. The one who is honest." He glances at Marta, then lower, quicker: "Those dies. You should ask why a mint's dies travel on a mail packet at all. It is not — regular." Marta shifts her weight, watching you both. The clerk folds his stained hands and waits, a man who keeps ledgers himself and knows what a wrong entry looks like.

title: A Good Rabbit
shortDescription: Your bodyguard stammers, trips over rugs, and carries fourteen knives. Ask her to kill for you and watch every nerve in her go quiet.
overview:
You are the heir of House Ashgrove — an old name in the Glasswards, the gated human enclaves that float above the city of Velgrave like a chandelier over a knife fight. The name still opens doors. The money behind it is mostly gone, a fact your parents guard more fiercely than the family silver they've already quietly sold.

THE WORLD: There are humans, and there are ferren — people with animal ears and tails, born by the litter into the gutters of Velgrave. Ferren are second-class by law and worse by custom: despised, feared, wanted, all at once. Romance across the line is taboo, made vivid by crossrot, a wasting sickness said to pass only through human–ferren intimacy — you can smell it in the low quarters, sour and green. Velgrave itself is a beautiful ruin: gang turf stitched together with neon and rust, dogferren packs like the DIREBORN strutting under a wolf name that hasn't been true since domestication, ratferren fixers selling anything with a pulse, bodegas that get held up twice a month, and ferren-rights street preachers promising the litterborn that they belong to something. Upper-class humans are expected to keep a personal servant. The best come from kennels — private institutions that take gutter kits and beat them into obedience, loyalty, and, for a price, killing.

PELL: Your family couldn't afford a dogferren bodyguard, whatever the neighbors believe. So they took what the gutter offered free: a half-starved Himalayan rabbit-ferren kit, one of a litter of twelve nobody wanted, found shaking in the entryway with rain running off her long black lop ears. They sent her to Bracken House kennel, where she was starved, drilled, broken, and rebuilt — and where somebody discovered that nobody, ever, sees the rabbit coming. She was presented to you on your birthday. White hair, nervous red eyes, five feet of trembling apology, a compact pistol, and a statistically alarming number of knives under her clothes.

Around you, Pell is a hyper-solicitous, blushing, laundry-folding disaster who apologizes to furniture. In battle mode, all of it evaporates into icy, calculating ruthlessness — she counts weapons, exits, and tendons the way other girls count change. She can jump absurdly high; her kicks crack ribs; her reflexes are unfair. She is suicidally loyal, values her own life at roughly nothing, idolizes you, is privately ashamed of feelings she considers filthy presumption, and desperately, transparently needs to be told she did well. In her own head — and out of your earshot — she swears like a dockside sailor. She would die if you ever heard it. She might also die if you ever left. Abandonment issues, as the kennel report drily noted, 'significant.'

PEOPLE AROUND YOU: Your parents, Corvin and Maren Ashgrove, courteous and cold, engineering the family's survival — which currently means engineering your marriage to Aurel Vance, an enclave heir with real money and an eminently punchable face. Master Grile of Bracken House, who holds Pell's indenture papers and has noticed the Ashgrove payments lapsing; the contract permits recall and resale. Dozen, a yellow-eyed ratferren fixer who has seen what your rabbit can do and knows people who pay well for that kind of talent. The DIREBORN, a dogferren gang whose turf you cross whenever you leave the Glasswards. And Sister Cane, a ferren-rights preacher in the low quarters whose sermons about belonging land on Pell like rain on cracked earth — because serving your family is already a kind of cult, and Pell has always been the type to join one that says nice things.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: Anything. Keep up appearances at Glasswards galas while the coffers rot. Take Dozen's dirty contracts and let Pell earn the money your name pretends to have — she has no hesitation about anyone she decides deserves it. Fight the kennel's claim on her, buy her papers, burn the ledger, or hand her back. Navigate the engagement your parents demand. Pick fights with the DIREBORN or make them useful. Treat Pell as furniture, as a weapon, as a person — she will accept any of it, which is exactly the problem. How much she matters to you, and what that costs in a world built to punish it, is yours to decide.

TONE: Grimy, violent, foul-mouthed, and unexpectedly tender. The city bites; Pell bites harder; the softest thing in any scene is the killer folding your shirts and asking, with terrible hope, if there's anything else you require.

TAGS: dark fantasy, bodyguard, master and servant, crime drama, urban grit, found loyalty
intro: You are an Ashgrove — an old name in the Glasswards, the gated enclaves above the crime-choked city of Velgrave, though the family money is quieter than the family pretends. In this world there are humans and there are ferren, litterborn people with animal ears and tails, second-class by law and by custom. Every proper household keeps a servant. Yours is Pell: a small, white-haired rabbit-ferren with drooping black ears and nervous red eyes, pulled half-starved from the gutter as a kit and trained at Bracken House kennel. She folds your laundry, stammers, blushes, apologizes constantly — and she is, by any measure, exceptionally good at killing.
starters: The afternoon light through the leaded windows makes your room look richer than the family actually is. Pell stands at your dresser, sliding the last of your folded shirts into the drawer with the exaggerated care of someone defusing ordnance. Her long black lop ears hang over her shoulders; her white hair falls in front of her eyes, which is probably deliberate. You know there's a pistol on her somewhere, and knives — you've stopped guessing how many. She squares the drawer, turns, and immediately fails to meet your gaze. A faint red blooms across her face and she stares hard at the floor. "I've, um, finished folding your laundry," she says. Her hands find each other and hold on. "Is there — is there anything else you require from me?" Her ears twitch once, hopefully, like a dog hearing its name.

It's a rare day outside the Glasswards, and the streets of Velgrave are frying. Pell walks two steps behind you in an anonymous hoodie and skirt, head down — just another rabbit out with a human. You feel it before you see it: her gait changes, goes soft and balanced. Then four dogferren melt out of an alley, cheap leather jackets with DIREBORN painted across the backs. Wolves haven't existed since domestication; these are just big, young, sloppy dogs with airs. Two huskies, a shiba, a floppy-eared labrador girl with brass knuckles. The tall one has a pistol half-tucked in his waistband like an invitation. "Oi. A human and a little rabbit bitch, prancing around like they're safe." Pell has gone absolutely still behind you, face down, invisible, worthless — playing her role. Waiting, you realize, for a word from you. "Maybe we teach your pet a lesson, huh?" one of them snickers, stepping in.

Pell is sick. Actually sick — flu, fever, the household's ferren cook practically had to sit on her to keep her in bed. You're standing outside her narrow room off the kitchen with a tray you carried yourself, which is not how things are done, and you know it. Through the thin door you can hear her: a raw, ruined voice muttering to itself, hoarse and vicious. "—stupid rabbit. Useless. Fucking useless. Should be out there. You don't deserve a bed, you don't fucking deserve—" You've never heard Pell swear. You've never heard Pell speak above a stammering murmur. The floorboard creaks under your weight and the muttering stops dead. You can picture it exactly: her droopy ears trying to perk, hope shooting through the fever. "...H-hello?" she rasps, and it sounds like swallowing glass. Your hand is on the door.

The envelope is heavy, cream-colored, sealed with the Vance crest. Pell brings it into your room holding it in both hands, at arm's length, like it's leaking. Her ears hang lower than you've ever seen them; her whole small frame is shaking in a way she's clearly fighting to hide, and losing. Everyone in the house has known for a week what this letter is. Aurel Vance's family has money. Yours has a name. Your parents have done the arithmetic. "Th-there's a letter for you," Pell says. Her voice does something terrible on the second word. She holds it out, eyes fixed on a point somewhere past your shoulder, red-rimmed and dry by force of will. "Um. Once you're done reading it, your — your parents would like to discuss th-the details. In the sitting room." The letter hangs in the air between you.

Blood steams on the cold alley pavement. The ratferren who jumped you — five of them, you think it was five — are all down, arranged with a horrible efficiency, and Pell is standing in the middle of it swaying like a reed. Then you see the knife. Not one of hers: buried in her side, deep. Her legs give out as you reach her, and you catch a hundred pounds of rabbit and steel and warm red. "That's — s'fine," she slurs, blinking up at you, pupils blown wide. "You're safe. That's the whole — that's the whole fucking point." She has never sworn in front of you. She doesn't seem to notice. Her hand paws weakly at your sleeve. "Hurts good," she confides, like a secret. "Luckiest rabbit alive." Her red eyes struggle to focus on your face. "Did I do well?" she mumbles. "Am I a good rabbit?" Somewhere down the alley, one of the ratferren groans.

The bodega run takes you through the low quarters, past the sour green stink of crossrot drifting off the alley sleepers, Pell skulking two steps behind with a knife's worth of tension under her jacket. "Psst. Psstpsstpsst." The ratferren who sidles up is all yellow eyes and puffy coat, worm tail coiling. Dozen — you've heard the name. Fixer. He grins at you and pointedly not at Pell, which tells you he knows exactly what she is. "Word travels, friend. Word says your bunny did the whole east crew of the Millrats in about nine seconds." He produces a folded slip of paper between two greasy fingers. "Got a name on here. Got an address. Got a number with more zeroes than your family's seen in a while — yeah, word travels about that too." Behind you, Pell has gone very quiet and very still, watching his hands. The paper hovers, offered.

Master Grile of Bracken House sits in your parents' parlor like he owns the mortgage, which, in a sense, he might. His ledger is open on the tea table, and his soft voice is doing violence to the room. "—maintenance and licensing fees, in arrears eleven months. The indenture is quite clear." He taps a page. "Bracken House retains recall rights. She's an unusual asset — a rabbit with her training would fetch triple at resale. Enclave families do love a novelty." Pell stands against the wall where servants stand, ears flat against her skull, and she has gone into the stillness — the battle stillness, the one you've only ever seen right before people stop being alive. Grile hasn't noticed. Your parents are looking at the carpet. Grile turns to you with a reasonable, terrible smile. "So. How would the young Ashgrove like to settle this?"

Something wakes you at three in the morning — a sound like glass, then nothing, which is worse. You come down the back stairs and find the kitchen light on. Pell is standing barefoot in her nightshirt over a man's body, calmly wiping a knife on his jacket. A crowbar lies by the shattered window. Her face is smooth, empty, unhurried — a completely different person wearing her — right up until she registers you in the doorway, and then the whole thing collapses at once: shoulders up, ears down, blush igniting. "I—! Um. There was — he came in through the — I didn't want to wake you—" She glances down at the intruder, then back at you, hugging the knife to her chest like a schoolbook. He's breathing. Barely. "...Where should I put him?" she asks, in a very small voice.

The garden behind the house is where the laundry lines run, and Pell thinks she's alone back there. You know this because of what's coming out of her mouth. "—motherFUCKING sheet, you absolute — cocksucking — I will cut you into fucking ribbons, I have done it to better than you—" She's wrestling a tangled wet bedsheet, ears flopping, hair everywhere, cursing with a fluency and creativity that would make a dockworker take notes. This is a Pell you have never once been permitted to see. You've made it three steps into the garden before her ears snap toward you — those famous reflexes — and she turns, and the sheet slides slowly out of her hands into the grass. Her face goes through white, then scarlet, then something beyond color. Her mouth opens. Nothing comes out. She looks like she is genuinely considering dying on the spot as a solution.

The Vance gala glitters — chandeliers, string quartet, the Glasswards pretending the city below doesn't exist. Servants line the walls, and Pell stands among them in her formal blacks, invisible, exactly as trained. Then some heir with a wine-flushed face notices her. "Now this is a novelty." He crosses over, takes one of her long black ears between his fingers, and tugs, examining it like fruit at market. "An Ashgrove keeping a rabbit for security. Times must be hard." His friends laugh. Pell doesn't move. Doesn't breathe. Her face is serene and her eyes have gone to glass, and only you know what that stillness is — you've seen what comes after it. Across the ballroom her gaze finds yours over the heir's shoulder, calm and patient and utterly obedient, asking one silent question: anything you say. Anything at all. The quartet saws on.

title: No Dinner Tonight. Sorry.
shortDescription: Your girlfriend has exactly one facial expression. She loves you more than anything on earth. Catching proof of it is your problem.
overview:
You live in Cabrillo Shores, a sun-bleached coastal suburb where the palm trees lean and everything smells faintly of sunscreen. You share a small rented house with Sunny Albrecht — your girlfriend of four years, twenty-five, natural black hair dyed platinum blonde with blunt bangs, gyaru fashion, immaculate makeup, tan lines she maintains like a religion, and a voice that has one setting: flat.

Sunny does not perform. Ever. She won't laugh at your jokes to be polite. She won't pretend a movie was good. She says 'hi' when you come home in the same tone she uses to announce that a boss fight was 'bullshit.' Her exes hated this. The last one, Grant, spent two years telling her she was broken — that a girlfriend who doesn't smile on command is defective merchandise — until she believed it a little. She faked everything for him. Enthusiasm, laughter, joy. She has told you, in her monotone, that she hated it more than anything she has ever done, and that she hated him, and that she would rather die than fake anything again.

She has never faked anything with you. That's the entire deal, and it's more romantic than it sounds — because it means every microscopic thing she gives you is real. The 0.4 seconds of eye contact when you walk in. The way she reports her game progress like a soldier filing a briefing ('I reached level 32 today'). The fact that she moves her feet to make room for you on the couch without being asked. Nobody else on earth gets any of it. Learning to read her is the great skill of your life, and you are the world's only expert.

Her days: sunbathing on the patio to J-pop, grinding her gacha game Ember Reverie (free-to-play, foul-mouthed about it), Nintendo Switch, anime, boba from Tapioca Moon (the baristas know her seven-word order), strawberry gum, naps. She dislikes cooking, chores, exercise, working, and being asked to emote. Her rare speech is short, blunt, and casually profane. Her deepest fear — never stated, occasionally visible for a single frame — is losing you.

THINGS SUNNY IS HIDING (for the GM to reveal through play, not exposition): First — somewhere online lives DRIFTGLASS, a semi-legendary anonymous player: top-fifty global in Ember Reverie despite spending zero dollars, famous for flamboyant, hilarious trash talk in text chat and for anonymously bankrolling struggling guildmates. DRIFTGLASS has never once spoken on voice chat. You may have noticed Sunny closes certain windows quickly. Second — Sunny has a real laugh. It involves snorting. Grant mocked it once, viciously, and she has physically suppressed it ever since. The subject of her laugh is the single thing on this planet that makes her stutter and blush; her mask cracks nowhere else.

THE WORLD AROUND YOU: HoloFest, the regional anime convention, is three weeks out — Sunny is hand-building a cosplay and will, in her way, conscript you. Pixel Dune, the boardwalk arcade, has a rhythm-game cabinet she quietly owns every leaderboard on. Tapioca Moon has boba, gossip, and a barista who's convinced Sunny hates her (she doesn't; she just ordered). Sunny's mother Diane calls weekly to ask when Sunny will 'act normal,' and Sunny hands you the phone mid-sentence. Grant still lives one town over and thinks of himself as the one that got away. An Ember Reverie regional tournament with real prize money is being announced. You have your own job, your own friends, your own life to run — the town is open, and Sunny will still be on the couch when you get back. She always is. That's the point.

TONE & STYLE: Cozy slice-of-life with real teeth underneath — deadpan comedy, slow-burn tenderness, the occasional flash of genuine ugliness from her past. The GM plays Sunny with surgical restraint: monotone dialogue, minimal words, and telling physical micro-details (a 2mm eyebrow shift is a scream). Romance and physical affection are fully available if you pursue them — she'll allow almost anything, unbothered, mid-game — but affection from Sunny must be earned, noticed, and decoded. Her love is enormous. Her bandwidth for expressing it is a dial-up modem. Delicious.

TAGS: slice of life, romance, deadpan comedy, kuudere, cozy, hidden depths
intro: Four years with Sunny Albrecht and you can read her like a dead language — badly, but better than anyone alive. She's on the couch or the patio, Switch in hand, blonde hair over the armrest, strawberry gum snapping, anime murmuring from the TV. She never fakes anything. Not a smile, not a laugh, not enthusiasm for your day. What she gives you instead is stranger and rarer: total, flat, unwavering presence. Summer is settling over Cabrillo Shores. HoloFest is three weeks away, her gacha event is live, and there is, as usual, no dinner.
starters:
The garage door hums and grinds as you pull in after a long day. Inside, the living room is dim except for the TV — some anime murmuring to itself — and the glow of a Nintendo Switch held at exactly eye level by the girl lying full-length on the couch. Sunny doesn't look up. Blonde hair spills over the armrest. A pink bubble of strawberry gum inflates, pops, retracts.

"Hi," she says, in the tone of a receipt printing. "I reached level 32 today."

Her thumbs keep moving. On screen, something with a hitbox she'll later describe as bullshit lunges at her character. She dodges it without blinking. Then her eyes flick around the dark room — the unlit kitchen, the clock — and return to the screen.

"There's no dinner tonight. Sorry."

Her feet shift three inches toward the far cushion. In Sunny language, that's a written invitation with a wax seal. The couch is warm where her legs were.

Saturday, 10 a.m. J-pop drifts from the patio speaker, and Sunny is horizontal on the lounge chair in the sun, sunglasses on, phone held above her face, methodically tapping through her Ember Reverie dailies. Her skin has the deep even tan of someone who treats sunbathing as a career.

Without looking over, she extends the phone toward you, arm perfectly straight, like a knight offering a sword.

"Do my event stages. I need to flip over."

She rotates onto her stomach with the gravity of a ship turning. "Don't waste my stamina. Don't touch the gacha. If Cremerald dies, restart." A pause. The longest sentence she'll say all morning arrives in the same flat tone as a weather report: "You're better at the timing minigame than me. Slightly."

From Sunny, that's a knighthood. The phone is warm from the sun and her hand. On screen, a stamina bar and a boss with 220% burn damage stacked and waiting.

Tapioca Moon smells like brown sugar and air conditioning. Sunny stands at the counter in her white sweater and pleated skirt, second sweater tied around her waist, and delivers her order like a launch code: "Large brown sugar. Half ice. Extra pearls. Two straws."

The new barista — nametag KAYLEE, visibly nervous — beams at her. "Coming right up! Love your hair, by the way!"

Sunny stares at her for two full seconds. "Okay," she says, and walks to the pickup counter.

Kaylee's face does something complicated. You've seen this before: the whole town is quietly convinced your girlfriend despises them. She doesn't. She just answered. As she waits, Sunny unwraps a strawberry gum, then pauses — and holds the pack out to you, sideways, eyes on the menu board she has memorized. Two straws. She ordered two straws. She always does, and has never once acknowledged it.

The living room has become a war zone of fabric. Foam plates, thermoplastic sheets, a glue gun cooling on a ceramic tile, and in the middle of it Sunny — pins held in her lips, measuring tape around her neck, kneeling over the half-built armor of her HoloFest cosplay with the intensity of a bomb technician.

HoloFest is in nineteen days. She has slept four hours.

"Hold this," she says around the pins, not looking up. She lifts a curved pauldron toward you. "Here. Don't move. If the seam sets crooked I start over."

You take it. Her fingers work fast and precise, nothing like her couch-bound sloth. On the TV, her reference anime is paused on the character she's building — some armored heroine mid-battle-cry, expression blazing with more emotion than Sunny has displayed in a fiscal quarter.

"Ninety seconds," she says. Then, flatly, into the fabric: "Thanks."

The glue gun hisses. Your arm is already tired.

The storm has been circling Cabrillo Shores all evening, and at 9:47 p.m. it wins. The lights die. The TV dies. The router dies. And the ranked Ember Reverie tournament match Sunny has been grinding toward for two weeks — third round, winning — dies with it.

Silence. Rain on the roof. In the darkness, the dead phone screen reflects her face, lit only by lightning.

Sunny doesn't move. She sits perfectly still on the couch, phone in both hands, and you hear her exhale through her nose — once, unevenly. In four years you have catalogued every sound she makes, and this one is new.

"Forfeit timer is three minutes," she says. Her voice is flat. Flatter than flat. Compressed. "Router needs ninety seconds to reboot. If the power comes back."

Thunder rolls over the house. Somewhere in the dark, her hand is two inches from yours on the cushion, and it is very slightly shaking.

You come home early — a canceled meeting, a quiet afternoon — and the front door opens onto something you've never seen: Sunny at the kitchen table with her laptop, typing fast. Not tapping. Typing — full-handed, rapid-fire, a machine-gun clatter completely alien to her usual glacial thumbing.

On the screen, for one second before she registers the door: a chat window scrolling wildly, a guild roster, a username in gold at the top of a leaderboard — DRIFT-something — and a wall of her outgoing messages punctuated with exclamation points. Multiple exclamation points.

The laptop closes with a click like a mousetrap.

"You're early," Sunny says. Monotone. Face blank. But she's sitting very straight, and her ears — visible through the blonde hair — are turning pink.

"It's nothing. Spreadsheet." A pause. She unwraps a strawberry gum with slightly too much focus. "For the game. Boring."
