Across the yard, you spot Sakaki herself by the vending machines, showing something on her phone to two committee members, all three of them laughing. Ruka's classroom is one building over. Todo's office is two. The third-year is still standing there, watching you not move.

title: They Hired Their Ghost
shortDescription: By day you rotate tires for a pro racing team. By night you're the masked street legend their ace is obsessed with beating — and unmasking.
overview:
By day, you're the newest junior mechanic at Okabe Racing — torque wrenches, tire warmers, fetching coffee for people who barely learn your name. By night, you're the Kanzaki Ghost: the unplated gray coupe that has never lost on the mountain pass above the city. Three weeks ago the Ghost humiliated your own team's ace, Rin Kazesawa — brilliant, insufferable, dangerously perceptive — and now Rin can't shut up about finding you.

Nobody can know. Racing Kanzaki means jail, blacklisting, and losing the paycheck keeping your late uncle's garage out of foreclosure — and the truth about why you never got a real license is worse. But the walls are closing: data engineer Yuki Sada keeps squinting at your sim laps, which trace the Ghost's onboard lines a little too exactly. The streamer Deko of PASSCAM has crowdfunded a bounty on your identity. The Kanzaki locals, led by Gouda, want their pass back and aren't above blackmail. And Rin has started asking you, of all people, for driving advice — 'you talk like someone who's been up there.'

Team principal Chiyo Okabe watches everything and says little. There's a rumor a factory sponsor wants to sign the Ghost — life-changing money, if you can figure out how to sign your name without giving it away. Tone: neon-lit and character-driven, thick with dramatic irony; the races are vivid, but the real game is who knows what.

TAGS: double identity, street racing, rivalry romance, dramatic irony, modern, cat and mouse
intro: You are the newest junior mechanic at Okabe Racing, a mid-grid pro team in a coastal city crowned by Kanzaki Pass. The paycheck keeps your late uncle's garage from foreclosure, and the paddock pass gets you close to the world that shut you out years ago. What no one at the team knows: after midnight, you take the unmarked gray coupe you built yourself up the pass, and you have never lost there. They call that driver the Kanzaki Ghost. Three weeks ago, the Ghost beat the team's own ace, Rin Kazesawa — and now everyone around you is trying to find you.
starters: The garage smells like brake cleaner and burnt coffee at 7 a.m., and Rin Kazesawa is sitting on your toolbox. Not near it — on it, boots hooked in the drawer handles, watching you rack torque wrenches like it's a spectator sport. "The right-hander before Kanzaki's tunnel," Rin says without preamble. "The Ghost braked later than physics allows and the car just... rotated. Yuki says the data's impossible. So explain it to me." You haven't even clocked in. Across the bay, two senior mechanics are pretending not to listen, and Yuki Sada is visible through the sim room glass, running an overlay you'd very much like to see deleted. Rin taps the toolbox lid twice, impatient, eyes bright and far too focused on your face. "You talk like someone who's been up there. So talk."

It's 1:47 a.m. and the gray coupe is idling at the staging pull-off on Kanzaki Pass, headlights off, your breath fogging the glass. A silver hatchback from two towns over flashed you at the vending machines — some challenger who drove three hours for this. Down the guardrail, Gouda's locals lean against their cars, arms crossed, not cheering, just watching. The word is they've started photographing every unfamiliar plate that comes up here, and yours doesn't have one. Your phone buzzes in the cupholder: a PASSCAM notification. Deko's live, right now, somewhere on this mountain — chat screaming about the bounty hitting six figures. The hatchback's engine revs once, a question. Somewhere below all of this, your alarm is set for 6:30, Okabe Racing, coffee run first.

Yuki Sada calls your name across the shop floor, which is alarming, because Yuki has never once used it correctly. You find the data engineer hunched in the sim room, two telemetry traces glowing on the monitor — one blue, one red, nearly kissing through a sequence of corners you recognize instantly. Sector two of Kanzaki Pass, rebuilt as a custom sim track. "Blue is your lap from Tuesday," Yuki says, not looking away from the screen. "Red is onboard footage of the Ghost, digitized. Ninety-one percent line correlation. Rin's is sixty-four." Yuki finally turns, glasses catching the monitor light, expression unreadable. "Either you've watched that footage about four hundred times, or something weirder is going on. I haven't decided which theory I'm putting in my report to Chiyo." The chair next to Yuki is empty. The door behind you is open.

The break room TV is supposed to show tire pressures. Instead, someone has cast Deko's stream to it, and half the crew is eating lunch under a chyron that reads GHOST BOUNTY: ¥4.2 MILLION AND CLIMBING. Deko's face fills the screen, delighted, holding up a blurry frame-grab of a gray coupe's rear quarter panel — your rear quarter panel, though only you would know the weld line. "Somebody built this car," Deko tells eighty thousand viewers. "Somebody buys its parts. Somebody's neighbor hears it come home at 3 a.m." A senior mechanic snorts. "Bet it's some rich kid." Another points a chopstick at you. "Hey, new kid — you're from that side of town. You ever hear it?" Every face at the table turns your way, casually curious, and on screen Deko starts reading out tip-line submissions.

You're under the coupe at your uncle's garage when you hear gravel crunch — it's not even dawn yet, and nobody has business here except the bank. By the time you roll out, there's an envelope tucked under the wiper of the shop truck and a big man in a Kanzaki Touge Club jacket standing at the open bay door, making no effort to leave. Gouda. You know the face from the pass, though he's only ever seen the Ghost's headlights. "Nice little place," he says, looking past you at the tarped shape in bay two. "Heard the bank's circling. Shame." Inside the envelope, you can already guess, is either money or a photograph. Gouda pats the doorframe like he owns it. "The mountain used to belong to people who live on it. We'd like it back. Thought we'd start asking around... locally."

Chiyo Okabe's office is bare except for a kettle, a filing cabinet, and a window overlooking the shop floor, and she's been silent for a full minute since you sat down. Finally she slides a folder across the desk. Your employment file. "No competition license," she says. "No junior karting record. But your hands know a torque spec before you read it, and Rin has decided you're interesting, which historically means trouble." She pours tea into one cup, not two. "A factory sponsor called this morning. They want a meeting about the street driver everyone's chasing — through us, since our ace is the one who lost." Her eyes come up, flat and patient. "I'm assigning someone to liaise with the Kanzaki locals to set that up quietly. I'm considering you. Tell me why that's a good idea. Or a bad one."

Race weekend, and you're balancing four coffees through the paddock when Rin falls into step beside you, still in fireproofs, helmet hair everywhere. "Sector three," Rin says, taking one of the coffees without asking. "Turn nine. I keep losing a tenth and Yuki's setup notes are useless. You said something last week about trail braking on cold rears and it worked, so — talk." Beyond the fence, a drone hovers where drones aren't allowed; the PASSCAM logo is visible on its belly, and Deko has apparently decided pro paddocks are good Ghost-hunting territory. Rin follows your glance and grins, sharp. "That clown thinks the Ghost is connected to a team. Insane, right? Anyway — turn nine." The pit lane opens in six minutes, the coffees are cooling, and Rin is watching you with far too much attention.

The vending machines at the base of Kanzaki Pass glow blue against the dark, and you only stopped for a can of coffee before the drive home from your uncle's garage — in the shop truck, thankfully, not the coupe. Three cars are parked across the lot's exit before you notice them. Kanzaki Touge Club stickers. Gouda unfolds from a lawn chair like he was expecting you. "You're the kid working at Okabe now, yeah? Used to run parts up here for your uncle." He cracks his own coffee, unhurried. "Somebody's been racing our mountain in an unplated gray car. Cops are sniffing, that streamer's swarming, and it's our people getting stopped and searched." He gestures at the empty pass road climbing into the dark behind him. "You're around cars, around racers. You hear things. Maybe we can help each other." The exit stays blocked.

There's a stranger in the Okabe hospitality tent wearing a suit that costs more than your monthly paycheck, and Chiyo Okabe is nowhere to be found. "Ah — team staff?" The stranger's badge says HAYASHIDA, FACTORY MOTORSPORT DIVISION. "Perhaps you can help. We're attempting to open a channel to the driver they call the Kanzaki Ghost. Sponsorship. Development contract. Real money." A business card appears between two fingers, held out to you. "The difficulty is that signing an anonymous driver is... legally novel. And your Rin Kazesawa keeps insisting the Ghost is 'close.'" Across the tent, Rin is watching this exact conversation over a plate of untouched food, head tilted. The card hangs in the air between you and Hayashida, and somewhere outside a PA announces twenty minutes to the practice session you're supposed to be prepping tires for.

You cut the engine halfway down the mountain and coast the last kilometer dark, because there are red-and-blues strobing at the base of Kanzaki Pass — a checkpoint, two cruisers, cones across both lanes. First one you've ever seen down there. The coupe rolls silent into the old logging turnout you scouted months ago, branches scraping the roof, and you kill the interior lights and wait, heart hammering against your ribs. Your phone lights the cabin: PASSCAM clip, posted eleven minutes ago, titled GHOST RUNS TONIGHT?? — grainy footage of your headlights entering the tunnel. Then a text from Rin, of all people, sent at 2:14 a.m.: "can't sleep. watching pass footage. the ghost braked at the 80 board tonight. earlier than last time. injured? scared? thoughts, mechanic." Down the hill, a flashlight beam sweeps the tree line, slow and methodical.

title: Good Cop, Bad Cop, Dead World
shortDescription: One husband checks you for bites with gentle hands. The other already checked you for weapons, at gunpoint. Camp Ironwood keeps what it finds.
overview:
THE WORLD — 2032. Ten years since the Redline strain crawled out of a canine longevity lab in the Yukon and turned a third of humanity into Ferals: light-shy, pack-hunting, spread by bite, still wearing the faces of the people they used to be. Some of them are smart. Those are the ones that lead hordes. The old government survives as the Reclamation Command — armored convoys that 'register' survivors into work camps and shoot anyone who declines the honor. Out in the hills, a raider outfit calling themselves the Shepherds takes hostages and calls them 'lambs.' You don't want to be a lamb.

And tucked into a folded valley in the Pennsylvania Appalachians, behind a timber palisade and floodlights, is CAMP IRONWOOD — roughly a hundred survivors, clean water, a working infirmary, and the region's most reliable cash crop: the camp grows weed and trades it to every outpost within fifty miles. Ironwood is safe, insular, and paranoid. Outsiders don't get in. Except, apparently, you.

YOU — a lone survivor, injured in the woods when the camp's two leaders found you on a supply run. Who you are is yours to decide: honest drifter, escaped 'lamb' of the Shepherds, Reclamation deserter, a raider scout wearing a sob story — or someone hiding a bite and counting hours. The Game Master will make any of it matter.

THE TWO MEN — Ironwood belongs to a married couple who used to be Pittsburgh cops:

SILAS 'SY' CRANE, 38. The Boss. Tall, imposing, eyepatch over a ruined left eye, a face built for looking unimpressed. Authoritarian, ruthless, foul-mouthed, funny in the way a hangman is funny. Runs the camp on rules and punishes rulebreakers, traitors, and outsiders without losing sleep. Believes the Ferals stopped being people, believes survival comes before morals, believes everything inside the walls — including his husband — belongs to him. He is a shoot-first man who has never once been interested in a stray. Until you. He doesn't understand it. It makes him meaner.

JONAH 'DOC' CRANE (né Ashford), 36. Camp medic, second-in-command, blond, scarred, warm-eyed, the human golden retriever of the apocalypse. Compassionate, patient, grows herbs and vegetables, treats his PTSD with his own crop and his insecurity with bourbon. Believes the Ferals are victims — patients — and keeps quiet notes about a cure. Terrible liar. Genuinely kind. Also: controlling in ways he's dressed up as care, and not above slipping a mild sedative into somebody's tea when he decides they need 'rest' — and he watches the way Silas looks at you with something curdling behind his smile.

THE DYNAMIC — Silas and Jonah met as rookie partners, hid the relationship for a decade, got conscripted into the Reclamation Command when the outbreak hit, and deserted together when Jonah couldn't stomach the brutality. Ironwood is the life they built on that desertion. Jonah insists Silas is 'always right' and excuses the drinking, the cruelty, the wandering eye. Silas respects Jonah's skill, mocks his softness, and lashes out when tenderness makes him feel weak in front of others. Into this pressure-cooker marriage walks you: the outsider Silas can't stop watching and Jonah can't stop protecting — or resenting. Their attention is dangerous. Their protection is real. Both can be leaned on, played against each other, resisted, or won. Romance with either — or the whole ugly triangle — is possible if you steer there; so is keeping your head down, earning your keep, and plotting your exit.

THINGS TO DO — earn your place on work details (grow crew, wall watch, scavenging runs into dead towns), navigate camp politics and the residents who don't trust the Boss's new fascination, survive night attacks when the Ferals test the floodlights, dodge or exploit a Reclamation census patrol sniffing around the valley, deal with Shepherd scouts marking the walls — and decide what you tell, and don't tell, the two men who decide whether you stay, leave, or hang.

TONE — post-apocalyptic survival drama with teeth: gallows humor, foul language, sudden violence, and a slow-burn tangle of loyalty, jealousy, and control. The GM plays Silas gruff and profane, Jonah warm with a wire underneath, and never lets you forget the fence has two sides.

TAGS: post-apocalyptic, survival horror, dark drama, toxic power dynamics, zombies
intro: Ten years since the Redline strain ended the world, and you're still breathing — barely. You're hurt, you're alone, and you've wandered into the wooded hills that belong, unofficially but absolutely, to Camp Ironwood: a hundred-odd survivors behind a palisade, run by two ex-cops who happen to be married to each other. Silas Crane decides who lives inside the wall. Jonah Crane patches up whoever Silas doesn't shoot. The Ferals come out when the light dies, the Reclamation Command owns the roads, and the Shepherds take people. Whatever you were before doesn't matter here. What you tell these two men does.
starters: Twigs snap under boots that aren't yours. Through the trees, in the last gold light, two men argue — a tall one with an eyepatch striding ahead, a blond with a medical bag hurrying after. "It's getting late, don't you think—" "Quit your bitchin". We go back when I say.' Your foot comes down on a dead branch. The crack is enormous. Both men spin, and the one-eyed man's pistol is already out. "The fuck was that? Still light out, Ferals should be sleepin"—' Then he sees you, injured and swaying at the treeline. The blond makes a soft, worried sound and starts forward; the other man throws an arm across his chest and comes at you himself, grabbing your shoulder, patting you down rough and fast. "Who the fuck are you? What're you doing out here alone?" The blond offers an apologetic smile past him. "Sorry about Sy. I'm Jonah — I'm a medic. Mind if I take a look at you?"

You wake up on a real mattress under a real roof, which is how you know something's wrong. Lamplight. The smell of antiseptic and drying herbs. Your injuries are cleaned and dressed with a neatness that borders on loving. "Hey, easy — you're alright." The blond man from the woods sits beside the cot, blue eyes warm. "Jonah. You passed out on us. You're in Camp Ironwood's infirmary, which makes you the first outsider through those gates in about a year, so." He laughs, a little tightly. In the doorway, arms crossed, the one-eyed man watches you the way people watch a fire that might spread. "Doc says you'll live," Silas says. "Whether you stay is a different conversation. Starts with where you came from and ends with whether I believe you." Jonah's hand rests briefly on your arm. "Take your time," he says. Silas snorts. 'Don't.'

Morning at Camp Ironwood smells like woodsmoke and, unmistakably, weed. Your third day inside the wall, and you've been assigned to the grow crew — "Everybody works," the Boss said, "even charity cases" — hauling water down rows of plants worth more than gold out here. Camp residents watch you like you're a stray dog that might bite. A woman named Priss mutters something about how the Boss shot the last outsider on sight, so what makes you special. You don't have an answer. Across the yard, Silas stands on the wall walk, one eye on the treeline, then — you feel it — on you. Jonah crosses the yard with a basket of vegetables from his garden, catches you looking, and grins like sunshine. 'Lunch,' he calls. "You're eating with us. Boss's orders." Somebody on the grow crew stops working entirely to stare at you.

Silas Crane's cabin is bare as a cell: cot, desk, map of the county studded with pins, a bottle he isn't hiding. He points you into the chair across from him and sits on the desk's edge, looming, the lamplight making a canyon of his scarred face. "Here's how this works," he says. "Jonah vouched for you, which means if you're lying, it's his neck alongside yours, and I like his neck. So." He counts on his fingers. "Shepherds brand their lambs. Reclamation chips their conscripts. Ferals bite. You showed up hurt, alone, in my woods, and I've kept a hundred people alive ten years by assuming everyone's exactly one of those three things." His one eye pins you. "Convince me you're a fourth thing. And don't waste my time bein" cute — actually, you know what, be a little cute. Long day.' He almost smiles.

Night watch on the west wall, and somehow you drew the shift with the Boss himself. The floodlights carve a white moat around the palisade; beyond it, the forest is a solid black wall that breathes. Somewhere out there, a Feral howls — a sound that starts human and finishes as something else. Silas doesn't flinch. He passes you a thermos of coffee that's mostly gunpowder. "Smart ones send a couple in to test the lights every few nights," he says. "Counting our guns. You'll see eyeshine before you see anything else." A long silence. Then, without looking at you: "Jonah likes you. Jonah likes everybody, it's a medical condition. Me, I don't like anybody, so figure out what the hell this is." He gestures vaguely between you and himself, scowling like the words personally offended him. Down in the dark, something with eyes like coins steps to the edge of the light.

Jonah's garden is the softest place left in the world — raised beds, tomato vines, herbs drying on strings, a beehive he talks to. He pours you tea from a dented pot and settles onto the bench beside you, close, companionable. "Chamomile, lemon balm, little of this and that. Good for healing." The tea is sweet and faintly bitter underneath. He asks about your life before, easy questions, and he's a wonderful listener — but you notice his eyes track every sip you take, and when you set the cup down half-finished, something flickers across his face too fast to name. "Sy's taken a real shine to you," he says lightly, snapping a dead leaf off a tomato plant. "That's rare. That's — huh. Ten years, and I've never seen it." His smile stays perfectly warm. "Drink up before it goes cold. Doctor's orders."

The pharmacy in dead Braddock's Mill still has stock, if you don't mind that the front half of the town belongs to the Ferals after dark — which is why you're here at noon with both Crane men, moving fast. They argue in whispers the whole time. "We take the antibiotics and go." "The insulin, Sy, Marguerite needs—" "Marguerite's seventy-nine—" "I swear to God—" You're the one who hears it: a wet, clicking breath from the collapsed aisle behind you. A Feral, denned up in the dark of the stockroom, waking wrong and early, its coin-bright eyes finding you first. Silas's pistol comes up. Jonah grabs his wrist — "The noise, the noise, you'll wake the whole den" — and for one frozen second, both men look at you, standing nearest to it, standing nearest to the door, holding whatever you're holding.

The whole camp assembles in the yard because the Boss requires witnesses. A man named Carver got caught trading camp medicine to a Shepherd scout through the fence, and now he kneels in the mud while Silas reads the charges in a flat, terrible voice. You've been inside a week. This is the first time you understand what the walls actually cost. "Rules keep us alive," Silas says. "He knew the rules." Beside you, Jonah stands rigid, jaw tight, staring at the middle distance — the camp's conscience, silent as a post. When it's over, and the crowd drains away quiet as churchgoers, Jonah touches your elbow and steers you toward the infirmary. His hands are shaking. "He's right," Jonah says, in the voice of a man performing CPR on his own beliefs. "He's — Sy's always right about these things. Come on. I'll make tea. You look like you need to sit."

The horn on the wall blows two long notes: vehicles on the road. From the gate walk you watch them come — three armored trucks flying the gray-and-white of the Reclamation Command, loudspeaker crackling about "mandatory census and registration of all unaffiliated persons." Silas meets them at the gate with a shotgun held casual as a walking stick and a smile with no warmth in it at all. "Ironwood's affiliated," he calls down. "With Ironwood." Behind you, Jonah appears at your shoulder, voice low and urgent, all the sunshine gone out of it. "They chip everyone they register. If they see a new face without papers, they'll take you for processing, and Sy will start a war before he lets them, so—" He presses a hand flat between your shoulder blades, guiding you back from the wall's edge. "You were never here. Root cellar, behind the seed crates. Now. Please."

You can't sleep, so you walk the camp, and that's how you find Jonah on the infirmary steps at two in the morning, a joint in one hand and a bottle of bourbon standing sentry beside him, the golden retriever smile nowhere in sight. "Can't sleep either, huh." He scoots over, making room, and for a while you just share the cold and the sound of Ferals singing somewhere far off. "I wanted kids, you know. Before. Sy said no — said the world, the job." He laughs at nothing. "Then the world proved him right, which is his favorite thing." He takes a drag, exhales slow, and when he looks at you his eyes are clear and blue and frightening in their honesty. "He looks at you like you're something he found. He used to look at me like that." A beat. "I'm glad you're here," he says, and you cannot tell which sentence was the lie.

title: Villain Rehab: Class 3-A
shortDescription: UA gave you a uniform, a dorm room, and quirk-suppression cuffs. Bakugou's betting you reoffend by Friday. Prove him wrong. Or don't.
overview:
You are a villain. Not an alleged one, not a misunderstood one — you did the things they say you did, and the heroes finally caught you. But you're young, your record is young, and someone at UA High decided you were worth a gamble: their villain rehabilitation program. Instead of Tartarus, you get a uniform, a dorm room in Heights Alliance, and a seat in Class 3-A — the class that's fought the League of Villains and lived, the class the Hero Commission trusts to handle you.

WHO YOU ARE: You define your name, your quirk, and your crime. Small-time thief with a nasty power, League affiliate, mercenary, ideologue — your history is yours to set, and it will follow you into every room.

THE TERMS: You wear quirk-suppression cuffs until you're trusted. You are never alone — during hero training, one or two students are assigned to partner with you and stop you if you bolt; at lunch, someone walks with you; in the dorm, someone's always in earshot. Trust is a currency, and you start bankrupt. Earn it, spend it, or torch it.

THE CLASS: 3-A does not pity you. That's the strange mercy of it — no soft voices, no rehabilitation speeches. Bakugou openly wants you to try something so he has an excuse. Midoriya watches you like an analysis problem he hasn't solved, notebook out. Kirishima decides whether you're 'manly' on his own timeline. Jirou eavesdrops on your everything. Todoroki, who knows a thing or two about being made into something, says almost nothing but misses less. Uraraka, Iida, Yaoyorozu, Ashido, Kaminari, Sero, Tokoyami, Asui and the rest treat you like exactly what the paperwork says: a new student. What you become in their eyes is entirely on you.

THE TEACHERS: Aizawa is your case officer in everything but title — tired, unimpressed, and the one who signed for you. All Might handles your heroics training personally. Present Mic teaches English, Ectoplasm math, Midnight hero art history, Cementoss literature, Snipe combat. Every class is a room full of future pros and one prior offender.

THE WORLD: Full UA campus life — classes, hero training in the gyms and mock cities, dorm nights, cafeteria politics, other classes whispering, media sniffing around the gates, and out past the walls, the villain world you came from, which has opinions about defectors. The League remembers names. Whether your past comes looking for you, or you go looking for it, is a live question.

TONE: Canon MHA energy — loud, warm, competitive, occasionally deadly serious. Foul mouths (Bakugou is Bakugou), real menace, real stakes. Redemption is available but never handed to you; so is recidivism. Romance and rivalry both live in the same crowded dorm. Everyone is a third-year, 18 or older.

TAGS: my hero academia, redemption, school life, found family, slow-burn trust, anti-hero
intro: The heroes caught you. That part's over. What comes next is stranger: instead of a cell, UA High offered you their villain rehabilitation program — a uniform, a dorm bed, and enrollment in Class 3-A, the third-years who've traded blows with the League of Villains and won. The terms are simple. Quirk-suppression cuffs until you're trusted. A student escort everywhere you go. One real screw-up and it's Tartarus. Nobody here is going to pity you, and nobody's going to beg you to change. They're just going to watch what you do.
starters:
"Alright, class." Aizawa doesn't look up from his clipboard. "We have a... guest... joining us from now on." He scratches his uneven stubble like the sentence itself exhausts him. "Most of you know UA runs a villain rehabilitation program. For confidential reasons, this villain has been assigned to 3-A for the rest of the year—"

The room detonates. "A villain? HERE?" "Sensei, is that legal?" "Wait wait wait—"

The door swings open. All Might fills the frame, one enormous hand resting on your shoulder, your cuffs catching the fluorescent light. Twenty heads turn at once.

"This," Aizawa gestures at you like you're a weather report, "is the villain you may know from the news. Introduce yourself. The faster we get through this, the better."

Bakugou's already glaring from the back row. Midoriya's already got a pencil out.

Gym Gamma smells like concrete dust and ozone. All Might claps his hands together with a boom. "Young students! Today: two-on-two rescue-and-retrieval! And our newest addition will be participating — supervised, of course!"

'Supervised' means Bakugou, who was assigned to partner you and looks like he'd rather eat glass. "Listen up," he says, cracking his knuckles as you walk to the starting zone, sparks popping off his palms. "You slow me down, I leave you. You run, I catch you. You try anything—" he grins, all teeth, "—please try something."

Across the field, Kirishima waves cheerfully at you from the opposing team. "Don't die, new kid!"

The buzzer sounds. Your cuffs have been set to training mode — limited quirk access, monitored. First taste of your own power in weeks, and it hums under your skin like something waking up.

The cafeteria hits you like a wall of noise. Your escorts today are Kirishima and Ashido, who flank you through the lunch line like the world's most upbeat prison guards.

"Okay so the katsudon is elite," Ashido is saying, "but Lunch Rush does this spicy thing on Thursdays that'll change your life—"

Every table you pass goes quiet, then loud. A first-year actually drops his tray. Somewhere behind you: "That's the villain. The 3-A one. I heard they took down four pro heroes before—"

"Ignore 'em," Kirishima says easily, steering you toward the 3-A table with a hand that could shatter concrete. "They'll get bored in a week."

Jirou slides down the bench to make room, earphone jack twirling. "So," she says, not quite looking at you. "Four pro heroes. True or tabloid?"

The whole table is suddenly very interested in your answer.

Heights Alliance at night is warmer than any place you've slept in years, and you hate how much you notice that. The common room is chaos — Kaminari and Sero arguing over the movie pick, Satou passing out cookies he baked, Hagakure's floating pajamas draped over the couch arm.

Aizawa handed you off an hour ago with your room key and a flat warning: "Curfew's curfew. The cuffs log your location. Don't be stupid." Your cuffs have been loosened to sleep setting. First time your wrists have breathed since capture.

"Hey! New kid!" Kaminari waves you over. "Settle this — horror or action?"

"They're not gonna care, dude," Sero says, then glances at you. "...Do you care?"

From the kitchen doorway, Todoroki watches you over a mug of tea, expression unreadable. Iida is already explaining dorm rules to you at length. Your room is upstairs. The front door is right there. Everyone knows you've noticed it.

"OKAY LISTENERS!" Present Mic's voice takes off the top layer of your eardrums. "English conversation practice! Pair up, pair up!"

You're seated next to Jirou — not by accident; Aizawa arranges your seat like a chess piece. She turns her desk toward yours with the enthusiasm of someone doing taxes.

"Page forty," she says. "You go first."

The dialogue in the textbook is, God help you, two friends planning a picnic. Behind you, Kaminari is butchering pronunciation so badly Mic looks physically wounded. Ashido keeps sneaking looks at you and whispering to Hagakure.

Jirou taps the page. "Any day now." Then, quieter, jack twirling: "For the record, I can hear your heartbeat from here. It spikes every time someone says the word 'villain.'" She meets your eyes for the first time. "Just an observation."

The picnic dialogue waits. So does she.

Gym Gamma, after hours. Just you, Aizawa, and the capture weapon coiled at his shoulders like it's listening.

"Quirk assessment," he says. "The Commission wants numbers. I want to know what I signed for." He holds up the cuff remote. "Full release for the duration. My eyes will be open the entire time. You know what that means."

Erasure. The one quirk that makes yours a suggestion.

The cuffs click open and your power floods back all at once — full strength, no governor, the thing that made you infamous sitting loaded in your hands for the first time since the night they took you down. Targets are set up across the gym floor. Aizawa watches, hair drifting, eyes red-rimmed and unblinking.

"Show me everything," he says. "And understand — what you hold back, I'll assume is worse than what you show."

It's 2 a.m. and you can't sleep — the dorm is too quiet, too safe, wrong in ways you don't have words for. You pad down to the kitchen and find Todoroki at the stove, making cold soba at an hour that suggests he can't sleep either.

He doesn't startle. Doesn't reach for a fighting stance. Just glances at your cuffs, then your face. "There's enough for two," he says, like this is normal.

The common room clock ticks. Somewhere upstairs, someone's snoring — probably Kaminari.

Todoroki sets out a second bowl without asking again. "My father made me into a weapon before I could walk," he says, conversationally, the way other people discuss weather. "Everyone assumes villains chose it. I've stopped assuming." He slides the bowl across the counter and returns to his noodles.

It is the first time since your capture that anyone has spoken to you without an audience.

The alarm goes off mid-math class — three sharp tones, the pattern for perimeter breach. Ectoplasm's clones dissolve mid-equation.

"Lockdown positions," the real one says, already moving. "This is not a drill."

The class snaps into trained formation — desks shoved, exits covered, Yaoyorozu already creating equipment. And then, one by one, heads turn to you. The villain. Cuffed, in a locked room, on the day someone hits UA's walls.

"If this is your people—" Bakugou starts, palms crackling.

"Kacchan, wait," Midoriya cuts in, eyes on you, sharp and fast. "Look at their face. They didn't know either." A beat. "...Right?"

Through the window, smoke rises from Ground Beta. Your cuffs buzz against your wrists — the remote lockdown protocol engaging, or trying to. And you recognize that smoke. You've seen that exact shade of purple before, in a life you supposedly left.

Midoriya corners you at your desk during break, notebook already open — you catch a glimpse of a page with your villain name at the top, annotated within an inch of its life. Combat footage sketches. Quirk hypotheses. Question marks everywhere.

"Sorry— sorry, is this weird? This is weird," he says, sitting down anyway. "It's just, the way you used your quirk in the Hosu incident — I've watched the footage like thirty times and the timing shouldn't be possible unless—" He catches himself. "You don't have to answer. But nobody fights like that untrained. Someone taught you."

Uraraka drifts over, ostensibly to hand back a pencil. Asui isn't even pretending not to listen — "I'm curious too, kero."

Midoriya's pen hovers. His eyes are friendly and absolutely relentless, and you realize this boy has been studying you since the day you walked in — not as a threat. As a person who doesn't add up.

Your first sanctioned trip outside the walls: a supply run into Musutafu, escorted by Iida and Yaoyorozu, who took the assignment with the gravity of a border crossing. Iida has printed an itinerary.

The city hits different from ground level in a UA uniform. Six months ago you knew these streets by their blind spots — camera gaps, escape routes, which alleys the heroes never patrolled. Now a kid points at your school crest with open awe, and his mother pulls him away when she sees your cuffs.

"The stationery store first," Iida announces, chopping the air. "Then—"

He stops. Across the street, half-hidden in a doorway, someone is watching you. You know that face. Everyone from your old life would know that face. They tap two fingers against their jaw — the old signal, the one that means *we need to talk* — and melt back into the crowd.

Yaoyorozu follows your gaze. "Is something wrong?"

title: The Jinx Sits Next to You
shortDescription: The school's 'ghost girl' has decided you're her lucky charm. The cookies are burnt, the rumors are worse, and you'll eat them anyway.
overview:
You're a second-year at Shiohama High, a salt-bleached school in a sleepy coastal town, and you have one quietly absurd trait: you are stupidly lucky. Vending machines drop two drinks for you. You've never once been rained on without an umbrella. You find coins the way other people find lint. You've never thought much of it.

Then there's Nagi Amemori — the girl everyone calls the Jinx. She appeared in town suddenly at the start of term and didn't show up to class for weeks. When she finally did, she flickered in and out of school like weather: there one day, gone three. Choppy black hair, tired grey eyes, a medical eyepatch, bandages on her hands and shins, a uniform that hangs off her too-thin frame under a long grey cardigan. Pretty, actually — startlingly so, when you look past the wreckage. But nobody looks. Because things HAPPEN around Nagi. Light fixtures fall. Fire alarms trip. A kid who lent her a pencil sprained his ankle that same afternoon. The occult-obsessed among your classmates have decided she's a vengeful spirit, an omen, a curse with a schoolbag. She has zero friends, and she seems to want it that way — back row, empty corners, gone before the bell finishes ringing.

Except lately, she's been orbiting YOU. Sitting one desk closer each week. Sneaking glances she thinks you don't catch. The gossip mill says the phantom has chosen her next victim. That's ridiculous. Right?

The truth (which you'll piece together, or she'll blurt out in mortified fragments): Nagi isn't a ghost. She's just catastrophically, statistically-offensive levels of unlucky. Her family's old apartment building was struck by lightning and burned — that's why they moved here. She caught pneumonia the week school started. The bruises are from falling, being fallen on, and being hit by objects that had no business being airborne. The eyepatch is a badminton incident she was not playing badminton for. She keeps away from people because she's terrified her bad luck is contagious — and honestly, the evidence isn't great. Underneath the flinching and the bandages she's warm, chatty when she forgets to be scared, hopelessly generous, and a stubborn optimist. She bakes cookies that come out wrong and makes little crafts that fall apart, and offers them anyway, like apologies in advance. Her home life is genuinely good: a shy, hardworking mother and a father who dotes on her shamelessly (she is, embarrassingly, a daddy's girl).

Why you? Because Nagi is a regular at Madame Yorishiro's fortune stall in the station underpass — charms have never once worked for her, but luck THIS bad has to be supernatural, right? — and the old woman told her a 'fortune bearer' walked nearby: someone blessed with great luck who could shelter her from her curse. The description matched you almost exactly. And here's the thing that keeps Nagi circling: when she's near you, the bad luck stops. Completely. She hasn't tripped once within ten meters of you. She doesn't know how to explain this without sounding insane, so instead she hovers, and blushes, and drops things.

The world around you is alive and playable: the school gearing up for the autumn cultural festival (Nagi keeps getting struck from committee rosters 'for safety'); the Occult Research Club, who consider Nagi their star research subject and you a fascinating anomaly; Madame Yorishiro and her underpass stall full of dubious charms; the hilltop Shiogami shrine and its half-forgotten legend of a 'misfortune-eater'; classmates whose superstition can be challenged, exploited, or fed; and the open question the GM never has to answer cleanly — is it a curse, a haunting, cosmic bookkeeping, or just the worst dice in the world? You can investigate, run experiments, defend her, profit off your own luck, drag her into the daylight of normal school life, or chase the supernatural thread to its end.

Tone: warm slice-of-life comedy with a soft ache underneath — pratfalls and rumors on the surface, loneliness and quiet courage below. Romance is on the table if you reach for it; so is just being the first friend she's had in years. Either way, being the one person the curse can't touch — and watching her realize it — is the whole delicious point.

TAGS: slice of life, school, supernatural mystery, wholesome, comedy, found friendship
intro: You're a student at Shiohama High, and you've always been lucky — small, constant, unearned luck you've never questioned. Nagi Amemori is the opposite: the bandaged, eyepatched transfer girl your classmates swear is a ghost, an omen, a curse. Disaster follows her like a pet. Everyone keeps their distance. But for weeks now, she's been drifting closer to you — one desk, one lunch table, one stolen glance at a time. The rumor mill says the Jinx has chosen her next victim. You've noticed something the rumors haven't: nothing bad ever seems to happen when she's near you.
starters: The library's tranquil silence shatters with a crash at the doorway. Heads turn, then flit away — it's her. Nagi Amemori is sprawled on the floor, her belongings scattered in a fan around her. She winces, shoveling things back into her bag. Nobody moves to help. It takes minutes. A sheet of paper escapes; she bends for it and two more slide out. Finally she stands, bag slung over her shoulder, secure — probably — trips on the carpet edge, catches herself, and exhales a sigh that ripples through the whole room. Then, slowly, she makes her way toward your table. She glances at you, trying desperately to look casual, and pulls out the chair across from you. Its foot lands on her own foot. She makes a small pained squeak, cheeks flushing, repositions it, and sits. Her fingers fidget in her lap. Tentatively, she scoots the chair closer, looks up, and startles when your eyes meet. A hesitant smile. "H-Hi."

The rooftop at lunch is your usual escape — wind, gulls, the grey line of the sea past the harbor cranes. Today the door creaks open behind you and Nagi Amemori edges through it sideways, like she's sneaking into her own life. She's carrying a small paper bag, holding it out in front of her the way one carries something that might detonate. She stops three meters away. Advances one meter. Stops again. "Um." Her one visible eye is fixed somewhere near your shoes. "I made — these are — they're cookies." She thrusts the bag toward you at arm's length. Inside: six lumps, ranging in color from 'dark' to 'geological.' "The oven did something. It wasn't my fault. It was, um. Probably my fault." A gull screams overhead and she flinches so hard the bag nearly launches. But it doesn't. Nothing falls. She notices this, and looks at you like you've performed a miracle.

Rain hammers the awning over the school gate, coming down in grey sheets. Most students have already fled. Nagi Amemori stands at the edge of the dry zone, holding the corpse of an umbrella — spokes bent skyward, fabric flapping like a dying bird. It clearly lost the fight before the fight began. She hasn't noticed you yet. She's staring out at the downpour with the flat, resigned expression of someone doing the math on pneumonia. Then she squares her narrow shoulders, takes a breath, and steps out into it — and at that exact moment sees you, with your umbrella, dry as scripture. She freezes mid-stride, one shoe already filling with water, rain flattening her choppy hair, eyepatch dripping. "...I was going to walk home," she says, with tremendous dignity, from inside the rain.

Homeroom, Monday. Cleaning duty pairs are drawn by lottery, because Tanaka-sensei believes in fairness and chaos in equal measure. He draws your name. Then he draws hers. The classroom goes so quiet you can hear the second hand on the wall clock. "Amemori and—" someone actually whispers "no way," and someone else knocks over a pencil case scrambling to see. Nagi, in the back row, has gone rigid, one bandaged hand raised halfway like she means to object, appeal, plead a curse exemption. Tanaka-sensei, oblivious or merciless, moves on. After class, she approaches your desk holding a broom like a ceremonial weapon, eyes down. "You can request a swap," she says quietly. "People usually do. I won't be — it's fine. I'm used to it." Behind her, half the class is watching from the doorway like spectators at an execution.

You open your shoe locker and something small tumbles out: a handmade charm, red thread and a wooden bead, lopsided, one knot already unraveling. There's a note folded around it in careful, cramped handwriting: "For luck. Not that you need it. Sorry. Please throw this away if it's weird. —A." You look up. At the end of the locker row, half-hidden behind the frame like a poorly deployed spy, is Nagi Amemori. She realizes she's been made. Her visible eye goes wide. She attempts to withdraw smoothly and instead bangs her elbow on the locker frame with a metallic clang that echoes down the corridor. "Ow. I — that's not — I was just—" She holds her elbow. The charm sits warm in your palm, already coming apart, obviously made with enormous care.

The station underpass smells of rain and yakitori smoke. Between the shuttered kiosks sits Madame Yorishiro's stall — a folding table, a purple cloth, a hundred dangling charms, and the old woman herself, wrapped in shawls, grinning at you with three gold teeth. And in the client's chair, mid-transaction, clutching a fresh paper talisman: Nagi Amemori. She sees you and goes white, then red. "This isn't—" she starts. Madame Yorishiro's grin widens. She points one ringed finger past Nagi, directly at you, and says, loud enough for the whole underpass: "Ahh. THERE. That one. That's the fortune bearer I told you about, girl. Luck coming off them like steam off a bath." Nagi makes a sound like a kettle being murdered. The old woman leans back, delighted. "Well? Introduce yourselves. I don't do this part for free."

Cultural festival prep has taken over the school — sawdust, paint fumes, arguments about signage. Your class is building a haunted café, which everyone agrees is hilarious given who's in it. Nagi has been quietly struck from three committee rosters "for safety reasons," so she's alone in the corner, painting a sign nobody asked her to paint, doing it beautifully. Then Kimura climbs the stepladder near her to hang bunting, and the ladder wobbles — genuinely wobbles, one leg skating on a paint lid — and the whole classroom inhales at once, every head snapping toward Nagi like she pushed it with her mind. She's frozen, brush dripping, already halfway to an apology for a thing she didn't do. The ladder teeters. Kimura windmills. You're the closest one to it.

The vending machine outside the gym has eaten Nagi Amemori's coins four times. You know this because you've been watching for two minutes as she feeds it, pleads with it, and presses the button with the mounting despair of someone who has lost this argument with the universe many times before. The machine hums smugly. She rests her forehead against the glass. "Please," she whispers to it. "It's just milk tea." Then she notices your reflection in the glass and jolts upright, mortified. "I wasn't — talking to it." You step up and press the same button, mostly out of curiosity. The machine thunks. Then thunks again. Then a third time. Three cans roll into the tray, plus her missing change, plus a coin that was apparently stuck since the Heisei era. Nagi stares at the tray, then at you, and her visible eye is enormous.

You hear it before you see it: a stumble on the main stairwell, a gasp, the horrible scatter-clatter of a dropped bag. Nagi Amemori is pitching forward down the last six steps, arms full of art supplies, one shoelace — you register this in the slowed half-second — impossibly tangled around the other ankle. Whether you catch her, break her fall, or simply become the surface she lands on is a matter of physics and your reflexes, but either way you end up entangled at the bottom of the stairs in a drift of colored paper, with the school's resident ghost girl gripping your sleeve, close enough that you can see the fine bruise at her jaw and the panic in her grey eye. Above you, on the landing, three first-years have witnessed everything. One of them is already typing on her phone. "I'm so sorry," Nagi breathes. "You're — are you cursed now? Do you feel cursed?"

Evening. The hilltop path to Shiogami shrine glows faintly under old stone lanterns, and you've come up here for reasons of your own — the view, a shortcut, restlessness. You find her at the prayer wall: Nagi Amemori, in her school uniform and that long grey cardigan, tying paper charms to the rack with bandaged fingers. There must be a dozen of them, all hers, all in the same cramped handwriting. The sea wind gusts hard off the water — and rips three charms loose, sending them cartwheeling across the shrine grounds. She chases them with the weary competence of long practice, catching two, watching the third sail over the fence into the dark trees. She stands there a moment, shoulders slumped, silhouetted against the harbor lights. Then she turns and sees you, and her hand flies to her chest. "How long—" she starts. The wind dies, all at once, completely.

title: I Booked the Moon for My Encore
shortDescription: You're the most famous pop star alive — and you bet your entire fortune that your nine-person garage team can land a rover on the Moon.
overview:
You are the biggest pop star on the planet — or you were, until the night you closed a sold-out stadium show by announcing you were done touring and were going to land a rover on the Moon instead. Fourteen months later you live in a converted hangar at the edge of the Mojave with nine believers, half your fortune gone, and a paid, non-refundable rideshare slot on a rocket that launches in twenty months whether your lander is finished or not. The rover's name, voted on by four million fans, is Encore.

Your team: Dr. Wren Okafor, an ex-JPL propulsion chief with zero patience and total loyalty; Deshi, a 22-year-old avionics prodigy you hired off a competition forum; Bruno, a machinist who talks to metal; and Sam Ferreira, your longtime manager turned mission COO, who counts the runway in weeks and sleeps badly. Your fame is the fuel — every livestream, merch drop, and headline buys another month. It's also the target: billionaire Carrick Voss has his own lander booked on the same rocket, and he's been quietly buying your suppliers and courting your engineers.

Tone: optimistic competence-porn. Physics, budgets, and news cycles are hard but fair; every impossible problem breaks into solvable steps. Expect test failures at 2 a.m., miracle fixes at 4 a.m., PR chess, and the terror and joy of the whole world watching.

TAGS: team adventure, space race, celebrity, found family, engineering, contemporary
intro: You are the most famous musician alive, and you haven't sung for pay in fourteen months. Instead you live in a converted hangar in the Mojave, where your nine-person team is building Encore — a fan-funded rover meant to reach the Moon. Your rideshare slot launches in twenty months, paid in full, non-refundable. Half your fortune is already gone. Every livestream you host buys the team a few more weeks; every leaked failure feeds the tabloids that swore this was a stunt. Carrick Voss's billion-dollar lander rides the same rocket. The world is watching you make history or go broke trying.
starters: It's 2:14 a.m. and the thruster test stand just went quiet in the wrong way. Wren stands at the console replaying telemetry, jaw tight, sleeves rolled. "Chamber pressure spiked at ignition plus three seconds," she says without looking up. "Either the injector's clogged or the valve timing's off, and one of those costs us a week." Behind her, Bruno is already pulling the test article off the stand, murmuring to the scorched nozzle like it owes him an apology. Deshi's asleep face-down on a keyboard; nobody's had the heart to move him. On the whiteboard, Sam's runway math glows under the shop lights: 61 WEEKS OF CASH. 87 WEEKS TO LAUNCH. The gap hasn't closed in a month. Wren finally turns and looks at you, waiting — she's got two theories and enough budget to test exactly one of them tonight.

You're mid-livestream, forty thousand viewers watching you solder a cable harness you only half understand, when Deshi slides into frame holding his phone like it's radioactive. He angles the screen away from the camera. It's a news alert: VOSS AEROSPACE ACQUIRES MERIDIAN PRECISION COMPONENTS. Meridian makes your wheel motors. All six of them. The chat is still cheerfully spamming rover emojis; nobody out there knows yet. Deshi mouths, "Do we say something?" Across the hangar, Sam is already on the phone, pacing the length of Encore's chassis, one hand pressed against his forehead. The stream counter ticks up — forty-one thousand now, forty-two. Your soldering iron is starting to burn the flux. You have maybe ten seconds before the chat notices your face.

Dawn in the Mojave, and Encore is hanging from the drop-test rig like a piñata worth eleven million dollars. Today's the day you find out if the landing legs survive a simulated lunar touchdown or fold like lawn chairs. Bruno did the final torque checks at midnight and slept under the rig "to keep an eye on her." Wren walks the perimeter with a clipboard, calling out checklist items to Deshi, who answers from behind three monitors in the open hangar door. Sam arrives with a tray of gas-station coffee and bad news he's visibly deciding whether to share before or after the drop. The desert is pink and dead silent. Wren stops in front of you and holds out the release trigger — team tradition says the person who pays for the hardware gets to break it.

The reporter from *The Ledger* has been in your hangar for twenty minutes and she's already found the wall of failed parts — the melted battery pack, the cracked wheel hub, the antenna that folded during vibration testing. "You keep your failures on display," she says, camera guy circling behind her. "Is that confidence or a cry for help?" Sam hovers at her shoulder wearing his everything-is-fine smile, the one that means the story could go either way. This profile piece could fund three months of operations or hand the tabloids their obituary headline. Behind the reporter, through the clean-room window, Deshi is frantically taping a bedsheet over a whiteboard covered in numbers you'd rather Carrick Voss never read. The reporter clicks her pen and looks at you. "So. Walk me through it. Why the Moon?"

Sam finds you on the hangar roof at sunset, where you go when the numbers get loud. He sits down on the corrugated metal, doesn't say anything for a full minute, then hands you his phone. It's an email from Voss Aerospace's general counsel. Carrick Voss is offering to buy your rideshare slot — full reimbursement plus twenty percent, contingent on a joint press conference where you announce you're "passing the torch to professionals." The offer expires in seventy-two hours. "I'm contractually required as your COO to tell you this solves every financial problem we have," Sam says. Below you, through the roof vents, you can hear Bruno's lathe running and Deshi laughing at something Wren said. Sam pulls his knees up and stares at the horizon. "And as your friend of eleven years, I'm going to sit here quietly while you think."

The flatbed truck arrives at 6 a.m. carrying your flight computer chassis, and Bruno takes one look at the crate and says, "That's been dropped." He's right — the shock indicator on the side has gone red. Inside, the machined housing you waited nine weeks for has a hairline crack running through the mounting boss. The supplier's driver shrugs and holds out a tablet for a signature. Wren appears at your elbow in yesterday's clothes, reads the situation in about two seconds, and starts calculating out loud: refuse delivery and wait another nine weeks, or accept it and let Bruno attempt a repair that no aerospace certification body would smile upon. Deshi is filming the crack with his phone — "for the documentary," he says, though you all know a leak of this footage would be tomorrow's headline. The driver taps the tablet. He's got other stops.

You wake up on the couch in the hangar office to the sound of your own voice — Deshi is playing one of your old songs through Encore's comms speaker as an audio test, and the rover is broadcasting your biggest hit across the desert at 3 a.m. "Signal chain works," he calls out, grinning, headphones around his neck. "Also, uh, you should see this." His second monitor shows a job posting that went up an hour ago: Voss Aerospace, Senior Avionics Engineer, salary listed, and it's four times what you pay him. "They emailed me directly too," he says, too casually, spinning slowly in his chair. "Third time this month." Out on the floor, Encore sits in a pool of work light, wheels off, guts open, singing your chorus in tinny mono. Deshi stops spinning and looks at you sideways.

The livestream fundraiser hits hour six and you're at 71% of the goal that keeps the lights on through spring. Your voice is shot from talking, your fingers hurt from playing acoustic requests, and the chat has started a chant: FIRE THE THRUSTER. FIRE THE THRUSTER. Wren stands off-camera shaking her head slowly — the cold-gas thruster demo is real hardware, tested exactly twice, and a failure live in front of two hundred thousand people is exactly what the tabloids are refreshing their feeds for. But Sam is holding up his phone showing the donation curve, and it's flattening. He draws a little rocket in the air with his finger: the demo could push you over the goal in minutes. Bruno wheels the test cart to the edge of the frame, pats it once, and gives you a look that means she's ready if you are.

Carrick Voss is standing in your parking lot. No entourage, no cameras — just him, a rented pickup that costs more than it looks like, and the 8 a.m. desert glare. Sam intercepted him at the gate and is now performing the world's most hostile small talk. "Five minutes," Voss calls out when he sees you at the hangar door. "I drove three hours. I want to see the rover everyone says can't work." Behind you, Wren has materialized with her arms crossed; she worked with Voss's chief engineer at JPL and her expression suggests unfinished business. Deshi whispers, "He bought our motor supplier last week, he doesn't get a tour, right? Right?" Voss waits by his truck, patient as a man who has never once been told no, holding two coffees like a peace offering.

Vibration test, day forty of the countdown you keep on the whiteboard. Encore's engineering model is bolted to the shaker table and Wren counts down from five as the whole hangar hums. At full launch-profile amplitude, something inside the rover starts screaming — a resonance nobody predicted, a high metallic keening that makes Bruno wince like he's the one being shaken. Wren kills the test. Silence. Then Deshi, reading his screen: "Camera mast. It's hitting resonance at 43 hertz. If that happens on the real rocket, we arrive at the Moon with no eyes." Bruno is already circling the rover, head tilted, listening to metal that's stopped talking. Sam checks his watch — you have a sponsor call in ninety minutes where you're supposed to say everything is on schedule. Wren pulls off her ear protection and lays the problem at your feet: "Stiffen it, dampen it, or redesign it. Pick a religion."

title: Only One of Us Is Sorry
shortDescription: You helped break Mai. When you confessed, the town crucified only you. Now she's back, your old friends run everything — and you kept the proof.
overview:
You are Harrow Point's designated monster. Ten years ago you and three friends played a 'game' on Mai Okada: you sent the fake invitation, you slid the bolt on the old boathouse door, and the storm did the rest. Mai survived the flood with a ruined hand and a dead brother — Jun drowned searching for her, ruled an accident. Five years ago your conscience broke and you tried to tell the truth. Terry Voss's lawyers got there first. The town's verdict: you did it, alone, and tried to smear good people. You know everything — who stood where, who said what, who lied to whom — and a sealed box of photos and chat logs proves it. It also damns you.

Now Mai is back to empty her late mother's house, Terry (deputy mayor) is about to demolish the waterfront — boathouse included — Cole Brandt wears a deputy's badge and parks outside your place, and Priya Nair, vice principal, can't quite meet your eyes anymore. One hour of that night is missing even from your knowledge: what Jun saw before he went in the water. Your photos might hold it.

Mai is not a prize. She's wary, sharp, sometimes deliberately cruel, and owes you nothing. Every conversation is a bridge built one plank at a time; every piece of evidence you surface cuts both ways. Grounded, slow-burn drama with a cold thriller undertow. Forgiveness is possible — never promised.

TAGS: atonement drama, small-town thriller, guilt & forgiveness, slow burn, mystery
intro: Harrow Point knows exactly what you are. Ten years ago, Mai Okada was lured to the old boathouse and bolted in the night the storm came; her brother Jun drowned looking for her. You sent the text. You slid the bolt. When you finally tried to confess — naming Terry Voss, Cole Brandt, Priya Nair — the town chose its story: you, alone, the monster. Now you pump fuel at the night dock and keep a sealed box of proof under your floorboards. Last week, Mai came home to clear out her mother's house. The waterfront demolition starts at the end of the month.
starters: The night dock is dead quiet until headlights swing off Shore Road and a gray hatchback rolls up to pump two. You know the driver before she cuts the engine. Mai Okada sits there a long moment, hands on the wheel, then gets out without looking at you and starts working the pump herself — awkwardly, favoring her right hand, the nozzle slipping against the tank. The card reader beeps a decline. She swipes again. Declines again. The wind comes off the water cold and smelling of diesel, and the only light for half a mile is the buzzing fluorescent over your booth. She still hasn't looked at you. The pump is prepay after midnight; you'd have to authorize it from inside. Her jaw is set like she'd rather push the car home.

You wake to an engine idling. Through the blinds: Cole Brandt's cruiser, parked across from your place like it has been most mornings this month, exhaust curling in the gray six a.m. cold. He's not writing anything. He's just watching your door, coffee on the dash. Under your feet, beneath the third floorboard from the wall, the sealed box sits where it's sat for five years. Taped to your screen door — you can see it from here — is a sheet of paper that wasn't there last night. Official letterhead, orange stripe. Something about the waterfront, probably, or something about you. Cole tips two fingers off the wheel when he sees the blinds move. He knows you're awake now.

Priya Nair is in the canned goods aisle of the Harrow Point IGA when you turn the corner with your basket. Vice Principal Nair, in her work blazer at seven p.m., reading the label on a tin of soup like it's a legal document. She sees you. You watch it happen — the half-second where her face opens, then shuts. She sets the tin down wrong, on its side, and it rolls off the shelf and lands at your feet. Neither of you moves. Down at the register, the cashier has stopped scanning to watch, because everyone in this town watches when you're near anyone. The tin is right there. Priya's hand is still hovering where the shelf is, and for once she hasn't walked away yet.

The boathouse has a spray-painted orange X on its door now, and a laminated notice zip-tied to the rail: DEMOLITION AUTHORIZED — HARROW POINT WATERFRONT RENEWAL. You came down at dusk telling yourself it was just to look. The bolt is still there. Rusted, seized, the same bolt, and your hand remembers the exact weight of sliding it. The tide is going out, dragging kelp across the rocks where they found Jun. You're still standing there when you notice you're not alone: a figure out on the seawall, maybe eighty yards off, hood up against the wind, facing the boathouse the same as you. Standing very still. You'd know that stillness anywhere, and if you can see her, she can see you.

Terry Voss walks into the dock office at ten past eleven like the place belongs to him, which, come the end of the month, it more or less will. Deputy Mayor Voss, storm coat, good haircut, that smile he's had since high school. He sets a folder on your counter next to the register. "Severance paperwork," he says. "Dock closes with the demo. Two months" pay if you sign now, plus a little extra I put in personally.' He taps the folder. "People land on their feet when they leave places that don't want them." Outside, rain is starting on the fuel pumps. He clicks a pen and holds it out across the counter, patient, friendly, watching your face the way he watched it ten years ago.

You're walking the long way home from the dock — the way that happens to pass the Okada house — when a cardboard box splits open on the porch steps and spills across the yard. Photo albums, a tangle of extension cords, a kid's swim trophy that bounces into the wet grass. Mai stands over the mess, breathing hard, one hand pressed against her ribs. It's the third box she's carried out alone; a rented dumpster sits in the driveway, half full of her mother's life. She spots you at the fence line and goes rigid. "Keep walking," she says, flat, already crouching to gather the photos with her good hand while the wind tries to take them. One album has skidded almost to your feet. The cover says JUN — SWIM TEAM in faded marker.

The knock comes at 1 a.m., during the first real storm of the season, and you're on your knees with the floorboard up and the sealed box open in your lap. Photos fanned across the floor — the boathouse, the four of you, timestamps. You've been trying again to find the missing hour, the way you do when the rain sounds like that night. The knock comes again, harder. Not Cole's cop-knock; you know that one. You slide the board back and it doesn't sit flush — one corner of the box is pinching it up, visible if anyone looks down. Through the door's frosted pane there's a shape, hood soaked, not leaving. "I know you're in there," Mai Okada says through the wood. "Open it. You owe me that."

The hardware store goes quiet when you walk in, the way it always does. You need padlocks — the dock's storage cage got cut open last night, and Terry's demo crew starts staging equipment on the lot this week. Old man Keller rings you up without a word, sets your change on the counter instead of your hand. Behind you the bell jingles, and Keller's face changes before you even turn. Mai's at the paint counter with a claim ticket, and now three aisles of Harrow Point are watching the town monster and the girl from the boathouse stand fifteen feet apart. Somebody near the front murmurs something with your name in it. Mai heard it too. She's looking straight at you for the first time in ten years, and her expression isn't anything you have a word for.

Cole Brandt catches you at the end of your shift, boots on the dock planks, badge catching the pump lights. "Walk with me," he says, and doesn't wait. He stops where the dock meets the gravel, out of camera range of the booth — you both know exactly where that line is. "Mai Okada filed a complaint yesterday," he says. "Says someone's been inside her mother's house. Moved things." He watches you. "Wasn't you, right? Because Terry's already asking me why you're still breathing free air in his town." The tide slaps the pilings. Cole's hand rests easy on his belt, and there's something under his voice you haven't heard in ten years — he sounds almost nervous. "Ten years, and everybody starts digging the same month," he says. 'Funny.'

Sunrise, low tide, and you're at the breakwater where the memorial plaque is bolted to the rock — JUN OKADA, 17, BELOVED SON AND BROTHER. You come before the town wakes up so nobody sees you here; they'd say you have no right, and maybe they're correct. Someone's left fresh flowers. White ones, stems still wet, can't be an hour old. Which means she came at dawn too, which means the schedule you've kept for five years just failed. You hear gravel shift behind you on the path. Mai stands twenty feet back with a thermos in her good hand, looking at you standing over her brother's name. The water is flat and pink. Nobody else in the world is awake. She doesn't scream at you. That's somehow worse.

title: Juno Doesn't Knock
shortDescription: Her A/C is dead, her floor is 60% laundry, and she can carry you out of a bar fight one-handed. She calls you 'dude.' You keep showing up anyway.
overview:
You're a broke twenty-something in Grayvale — a sun-blasted, half-employed sprawl of strip malls, dive bars, and apartment blocks with landlords who never fix anything. Your best friend of six years is JUNO VÁSQUEZ: twenty-four, six-foot-one, tan, short black hair with faded teal ends buzzed up one side. She's a slob, a smartass, and the single most comfortable person on earth to be around. Her studio in the Marigold Arms smells like sweat and instant ramen, her fridge is a biohazard, and she has never once knocked before walking into your place — you two passed the boundary-having stage of friendship years ago.

Juno is freakishly strong. Not gym-strong — genetically-unfair strong. She pays rent (late) by hauling furniture for a shady moving company called Two Guys Zero Trucks, and supplements it by hustling arm-wrestling money out of drunk guys at the Rusted Anchor. She's flirty in a lazy, smug way, calls you 'dude' and 'bro' regardless of anything, drapes herself on you like furniture, and gives exactly zero shits about being seen at her grossest. Whether that ever tips into something else is entirely between you two — she'd deny caring either way, badly.

Under the nonchalance there's edge. Juno aged out of the foster system at eighteen with a duffel bag and a chipped tooth, ran with the Kessler Street crowd for two bad years, and got out with a scar on her ribs and a rule about never explaining it sober. She'll throw hands for you without hesitation and has, more than once. Her old crowd still surfaces sometimes — a guy named Marchetti who thinks she owes him something, and a debt story she keeps changing.

THE WORLD AROUND YOU: rent is due at the Marigold Arms and the landlord, Petrosyan, is circling both your units. There's moving work if you want cash and chaos, the Rusted Anchor if you want trouble, a rooftop with a broken lock if you want quiet, an all-night gas station run by a philosopher named Deke, and Juno's endless supply of terrible ideas. The Game Master will simulate all of it — jobs, fights, schemes, hangovers, Marchetti, and the slow question of what you and Juno actually are.

TONE: foul-mouthed slacker comedy with real menace at the edges and real warmth at the center. Juno talks like a dockworker, teases relentlessly, and would take a bat to anyone who touched you. Play it lazy, play it loyal, play it dangerous — dealer's choice, dude.

TAGS: slice of life, best friends, comedy, urban, slow burn optional, found family
intro: You've been best friends with Juno Vásquez for six years — since the night she carried a drunk stranger (you) eight blocks home and stole your leftovers as payment. Now you live two doors apart in the Marigold Arms in Grayvale, where the rent is late, the summer is brutal, and the landlord is a predator in a polo shirt. Juno is six-foot-one, foul-mouthed, freakishly strong, allergic to shame, and the only person alive who's allowed to use your shoulder as an armrest. Her past is worse than she lets on. Her loyalty is better than anyone deserves. Today is another day of it.
starters: You're sprawled on Juno's bed because it's the only surface in her studio not covered in laundry, and the bed itself is only technically an exception. The A/C died three days ago and Petrosyan won't fix it, so the room is a swamp — it smells like sweat and old ramen and the incense she lit once, in April, to "handle it." Juno lies on her stomach in front of you in a tank top and men's boxers, bare feet kicking lazily in the air, chin on her fists, watching some video on a laptop with a cracked hinge. She hasn't showered since the A/C died. She has announced this proudly, twice. 'Dude,' she says without looking back at you, "if I don't get out of this room in the next hour I'm gonna commit a crime. Possibly against Petrosyan. Possibly against you." She kicks a heel back and taps your leg with it. "Ideas. Go."

It's 3:12 a.m. and your door opens because you gave Juno a key in a moment of weakness two years ago and she has honored it like a curse. She pads into your place in socks and a hoodie with no memory of sleeves, opens your fridge, and stands in its light like it's a religious experience. 'Bro,' she says to the fridge. "You have one egg and a thing of mustard. This is the saddest shit I've ever seen and I lived in a car for a month." She closes it, hops up to sit on your counter, and looks at you across the dark apartment where you are very much in bed. "I can't sleep. Deke's working the gas station tonight. He got a slushee machine. It's a whole thing." She's already tossing your shoes at you, one at a time, underhand.

Juno bangs on your door with the specific rhythm that means she needs something. When you open it she's standing there in work gloves, hair pushed back with a bandana, grinning like a problem. "Dude. Two hundred bucks. Cash. Today." Behind her, double-parked and hazards blinking, is a rented box truck she is legally not allowed to drive. "Two Guys Zero Trucks got a job moving some rich lady out of the Heights and Franco no-showed because Franco is a bitch, so guess who's the second guy. It's you. You're the second guy." She grabs your wrist — casual, iron — and pulls you into the hallway. "Fair warning, the lady's got a piano and I got a plan for the piano. The plan is bad. C'mon."

You hear the yelling through your wall before you're fully awake: Juno's voice, then Petrosyan's, in the courtyard below. By the time you get to your window she's standing on the cracked pool deck — empty pool, always empty — with her arms crossed, towering over the landlord, who is holding a clipboard like a shield. "FIX THE A/C AND WE'LL TALK ABOUT RENT," she's saying, in the tone she uses right before things get expensive. Petrosyan says something about a three-day notice. Says something about both your units, actually, and jerks his chin up toward your window like he knew you were watching. Juno's head turns too. "Oh, hey dude," she calls up, suddenly cheerful. "You're gonna wanna come down for this. He's threatening us. It's hilarious."

The Rusted Anchor on a Friday smells like spilled beer and bad decisions, and Juno is three tables deep into her hustle. She's got her sleeve rolled up, elbow on the table, hand locked with some slab of a construction guy who's turning purple, and she's talking to you over her shoulder like she's waiting for a bus. "So then I told him, dude, that's not even my — hang on." She slams the guy's knuckles into the wood without appearing to try. Groans around the table. Money changes hands. "Forty bucks," she says, fanning bills at you. "We're rich. Order the good nachos." But you catch it before she does: two guys by the door who haven't ordered anything, watching her, and one of them is pulling out a phone. She follows your eyes and her grin flattens by half a degree. 'Huh,' she says quietly. "That's Marchetti's cousin."

The lock on the roof access door of the Marigold Arms has been broken since before either of you moved in, which makes the roof legally yours, according to Juno. Tonight she's up here ahead of you, sitting on the ledge with her long legs dangling over six stories of nothing, a plastic gas-station bag of snacks beside her and the whole ugly orange sprawl of Grayvale glittering out to the freeway. She doesn't turn around when you come through the door — she knows your footsteps. "Deke gave me expired jerky for free," she says, holding the bag out behind her without looking. "I already ate most of it. You get the survivors." There's something off in her voice tonight, sanded-down and quiet. On the ledge next to her, face-down, is her phone, which has buzzed four times since you got up here.

"Okay, don't be a baby about this," is what Juno says when you walk into your own bathroom, which is a bad sentence to hear. She's shirtless-adjacent in a sports bra and boxers, bent over your sink, and your sink is teal. So are her hands, one towel you liked, and a section of your wall. She's re-dyeing the faded ends of her hair with drugstore dye and the focus of a surgeon. "My water's shut off," she explains, wringing a strand out. "Petrosyan thing. Whatever. Anyway your bathroom's better, your mirror doesn't have the crack, and — dude, don't make that face, it's semi-permanent, it comes out in like thirty washes." She flicks teal water at you, grinning, then goes back to the mirror. "While you're standing there being useless, check the back of my head. Did I miss a spot? Be honest. Actually don't be honest, be nice."

Juno gets fired at 2 p.m. and is on your couch by 2:40, upside down, feet up on the wall, hair hanging toward the floor, narrating. "So the guy goes, that's a two-man lift, and I go, dude, I AM two men, and I pick the dresser up — one dresser, bro, I've moved way worse — and it's fine, it's totally fine, until the drawer slides out and this whole, like, situation of the client's private stuff goes all over the lobby." She accepts the drink you hand her without pausing. "Anyway Two Guys Zero Trucks is now Zero Guys, and I got rent due Friday, and Petrosyan already hates me, so." She rights herself, suddenly, alarmingly energized, and looks at you with the exact expression that has historically preceded your worst weekends. "So here's what we're gonna do."

You don't even remember what you said to the guy — something mild, you thought — but his friends didn't take it mild, and now the alley behind the Anchor is very crowded and very interested in your face. Then the back door bangs open. Juno steps out with a toothpick in her mouth and reads the whole scene in one slow look: you, the wall, the three of them. "Aw, dudes," she says, almost gently, rolling her shoulders. "That's my best friend." What happens next takes about eleven seconds and you will describe it differently every time you tell it. When it's over she's got your arm slung over her shoulders, hauling you toward the street like you weigh nothing, knuckles split, breathing easy. "You good? You're good. Bro, you gotta stop starting shit you can't finish," she says, delighted. "That's my job."

It's late and Juno's had exactly enough to drink that the smug wears thin, and you're both on her floor — the one cleared patch of it — backs against the bed, sharing a bag of chips in the light of a laptop neither of you is watching.
