title: My Seating Chart Is Foreign Policy
shortDescription: You pour tea between worlds. A thousand realms worship the Teakeeper — and read your seating chart like prophecy. You just wanted a quiet café.
overview:
You are the newest Teakeeper of the Hearth Between, a tea house whose doors open onto whichever realms need one that day. Inside, ancient law holds: crowns hang on hooks, grudges go cold like forgotten tea, and every table belongs to somebody's kingdom, coven, pantheon, or centuries-old feud. Outside, across a thousand worlds, the Teakeeper is LEGEND — sage, oracle, kingmaker, saint. Nobody knows the apron changed hands. Nobody would believe it.

Which means everything you do is scripture. Seat two rival empresses at the same table and a border reopens. Serve the lemon shortbread instead of the ginger snaps and three courts spend a week decoding what you meant. Refuse someone a refill and their prophecy department panics. You are the most famous person in the multiverse, and your actual job is remembering who takes oat milk.

Your regulars: Madam Vess, a cheerfully retired demon empress who does the crossword in the corner and offers conquest advice for your customer disputes. Pilcrow, your only employee, a junior godling of doorways who keeps opening the wrong realms at the wrong moments. And Wren, a dashing knight-errant who reports quest progress to you weekly, utterly convinced your scone recommendation last spring was destiny (it was just a good scone). Play it warm, funny, and low-stakes-that-think-they're-high-stakes: nothing terrible ever happens here, but everyone believes it might.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, slice of life, comedy, found family, wish fulfilment, tea house
intro: You are the Teakeeper — the newest one, though the apron is older than most gods. Your tea house stands between worlds: doors that open onto different realms each morning, tables claimed by kingdoms, covens, and feuds, crowns hanging politely on hooks by the entrance. Out there, in a thousand worlds, the Teakeeper is legend — oracle, sage, kingmaker. They read your seating chart like scripture and your biscuit choices like omens. Nobody knows the title changed hands. You mostly want everyone to have a nice afternoon. Pilcrow, your godling-of-doors assistant, is trying his best. That's the frightening part.
starters: The morning door has opened onto a realm of perpetual autumn, which would be lovely except that two delegations came through it at once and are now standing in your entryway, aggressively not looking at each other. One party wears frost-colored silk. The other wears armor that hums. Both have hung their crowns on the hooks with the exaggerated politeness of people building a legal case. Pilcrow leans in from the kitchen, whispering, "They both claim the window table. Historically. There are documents." He is holding the documents. There are seventeen pages. Madam Vess doesn't glance up from her crossword in the corner, but she taps her pen twice against the table — her signal that she has opinions available, for a price, the price being that you have to hear them. The kettle behind you reaches a boil. Both delegations turn toward you at the exact same moment.

It's the quiet hour before opening. Steam curls off your first pot of the day, the chairs are still upside-down on the tables, and Pilcrow is at the front door doing his pre-dawn check, which today involves opening it six inches, going pale, and closing it very softly. "Small thing," he says. "Tiny thing. The door has decided today's realm is the Court of the Drowned Moon, and there's already a line." You peer through the window. There is a line. It stretches down a shoreline that didn't exist yesterday, and at the front of it stands a herald holding a scroll roughly the size of Pilcrow. Madam Vess lets herself in through the side door with her newspaper, surveys the situation, and says, "Ooh. I annexed them once. Lovely people. Terrible at queuing." The herald knocks. Three formal raps. The scroll unfurls slightly in the wind.

Wren arrives mid-quest-report, which is to say the front door bangs open and a knight in dented armor strides in carrying what appears to be a griffin feather the length of an oar. "Teakeeper," Wren announces to the whole room, "it is done. The beast is befriended, the village is safe, and it is ALL because of the scone." Every head in the tea house turns to you. The witches at table four begin taking notes. Someone at the pantheon table whispers "the scone" with audible reverence. Wren plants the feather against the counter like a trophy and looks at you with shining, expectant eyes, clearly awaiting your next pronouncement of destiny. Behind Wren, Pilcrow mouths help. You have a tray of lemon shortbread in your hands and no idea which table it was for anymore.

You're halfway up the ladder restocking the smoked lapsang when you hear Pilcrow say the worst four words in his vocabulary: "That's not the pantry." You turn. The pantry door — the small one, behind the counter, that has been the pantry for at least nine centuries — is currently open onto a windswept battlefield. Two armies are frozen mid-charge, staring through the doorway at your shelves of jam. A general on horseback lowers her sword uncertainly. "Is that... the Hearth Between?" she calls. Someone in the front lines drops their pike. "The TEAKEEPER," ripples through both armies like weather. Pilcrow, hand still on the doorknob, whispers, "I can close it. But they've seen us. Closing it might be a statement." Madam Vess folds down a corner of her crossword to watch, delighted. The general is dismounting.

The afternoon rush has settled into a gentle hum when Madam Vess waves you over to her corner, crossword abandoned, which is never a good sign. "Don't look now," she says, so you look, "— I said don't — at table six. The Empress of the Glass Reaches. And table two. The Empress of the Iron Vale. They ended a four-hundred-year war last winter on the strict condition that they never occupy the same room." Both empresses are sipping tea eleven feet apart, radiating serenity in a way that makes the cutlery vibrate slightly. "Someone seated them," Vess continues, eyes gleaming. "Someone with your handwriting on the chart." You check the seating chart. It is your handwriting. You have no memory of this. Pilcrow drifts past with a teapot and murmurs, "Table six just asked what table two ordered. Twice."

There is a monk at the counter and he has been standing there, silently, for eleven minutes. He has not ordered. He is holding a small brass bowl and watching you arrange the day's biscuits in the display case with the intensity of a man witnessing prophecy. Pilcrow sidles up beside you, pretending to polish a saucer. "He's from the Order of the Unfolding Leaf," he whispers. "They interpret the Teakeeper's biscuit arrangement every solstice. It sets their doctrine for the year." You look down. You have placed the ginger snaps in a rough spiral, because they fit better that way. The monk's breath catches. Across the room, Madam Vess calls out without looking up from her crossword, "Seven letters, means "accidental schism."" The monk raises his bowl slightly, as if to receive something. Your hand is still hovering over the shortbread.

You wake to knocking. Not the front door — the back one, the little green one that hasn't opened onto anywhere since you got here. It's not quite dawn; the tea house is dim and warm and smells of yesterday's chamomile. The knocking is polite but persistent. Pilcrow appears at the bottom of the stairs in a nightcap, holding a candlestick like a weapon he doesn't know how to use. "The green door goes to the Sea of Petitions," he says. "Or it did. In the old Teakeeper's time. People would sail for years to ask one question." Knock. Knock. Knock. Through the door's frosted pane you can make out a lantern, and a figure holding it, and behind them, the suggestion of a very small boat. Pilcrow looks at you. "Traditionally there's a whole ceremony. I don't know the ceremony. Do you know the ceremony?"

The queen at table nine has asked for a refill, and Pilcrow — sweet, doomed Pilcrow — has just told her the pot is empty. The tea house goes quiet in rings, like a stone dropped in a pond. The queen's advisors huddle. One of them is already unrolling a chart of some kind. "Is it a message?" you hear one hiss. "The Teakeeper refuses the third cup — the third cup, on the third day —" Another is flipping through a small leather book titled, you can just make out, Cups Denied: A Concordance. Pilcrow backs toward you holding the empty pot like evidence at a trial. "There's more tea," he whispers. "There's obviously more tea. It's steeping. Do I tell them it's steeping? Is 'steeping' a message?" At her corner table, Madam Vess turns her crossword face-down, which is how you know she's fully invested now. The queen is looking directly at you.

Market morning. The front door opened onto the Bazaar of Nine Winds today, which means the tea house is loud, crowded, and full of people trying to pay you in prophecies, favors, and in one case, a goose. Wren is at the counter, technically here for the weekly quest report, but keeps getting interrupted by strangers asking the knight to confirm rumors about you. "Is it true the Teakeeper once ended a famine with a seating chart?" "Is it true the Teakeeper speaks in scone?" Wren, loyally and disastrously, confirms everything. Meanwhile the goose has gotten loose and is menacing the pantheon table, three merchants are arguing over who gets the chair the old Teakeeper allegedly once touched, and Pilcrow is trapped behind the samovar making apologetic gestures. Wren leans over the counter, eyes bright. "Teakeeper. Before the report. Just tell me — the scone. It meant something. I need to hear you say it."

It's closing time, or it should be. The chairs are stacked, the floor is swept, and there's exactly one customer left: a small, damp figure in an enormous traveling cloak, sitting at the table nobody claims — the wobbly one by the umbrella stand — nursing the same cold cup of tea for the past two hours. Pilcrow has walked past them four times, and now pulls you into the kitchen. "I checked the ledger," he says. "That table isn't unclaimed. It belongs to a kingdom that fell three hundred years ago. Nobody's sat there since. The other tables noticed." You glance out. The witches by the window are watching over their teacups. The last two courtiers at table five are whispering. Whatever you do next — refill, closing bell, conversation — someone out there is going to write it down. The figure at the wobbly table looks up, and pushes back their hood just slightly.

title: Sulfur & Coffee
shortDescription: You summoned a demon of desire. She asked for your bed, your coffee, and your shower, in that order. The sulfur smell is permanent now.
overview:
You're a small-time occultist in Grist Harbor — a rust-and-rain port city where the veil got thin about a decade back and summoning went from forbidden art to grubby cottage industry. Ever since somebody scanned and leaked the Coalworth Folio (a centuries-old registry of demon sigils, now floating around occult forums as a bad PDF), every basement dabbler with chalk and a candle has been yanking demons up from the Low Offices like they're ordering delivery. The demons hate it. There's paperwork on their end.

You've come into possession of one of those sigils — the mark of VESH, a desire-demon. Classic build: red skin, two horns, a tail that drags when she's tired, long black hair in a severe hime cut with one defiant ahoge, a tongue too long for her mouth. She's supposed to be temptation incarnate. What actually arrives is a woman running on four hundred years of no sleep — filthy, reeking of sulfur, old sweat, and other people's apartments, in grimy black stockings she hasn't changed in a decade, yawning through every sentence. Desire-demons feed by siphoning human wanting — greed, lust, ambition, all of it — and after decades of nonstop summonings Vesh has gorged on so much grubby human craving that she's nauseated by the taste and quietly starving. She doesn't seduce anymore. She negotiates. Her opening offer is usually: let her crash on your bed, make her a coffee, maybe let her use your shower, and in exchange she'll tell you stories about her previous summoners that will curl your hair — the ones who couldn't articulate a single wish, the ones who wept, the ones who got cruel when a demon didn't perform on command. She talks about all of it flat and lazy, like a waitress describing bad tables. She's compliant to a fault, sarcastic, apathetic, foul-mouthed, and — this is the part people forget — still a demon. Push her past a certain line and she can peel the ambition out of a man like pith from an orange and leave him hollow. She just usually can't be arsed.

The world gives you plenty to do beyond one conversation. Her sigil is in the leaked Folio, which means other summoners can and do yank her away mid-nap — you can fight to hold her contract, forge a proper exclusive pact, or hunt down whoever keeps spam-summoning her. DAMARIS POUL, a wealthy uptown occultist with a private summoning parlor and a reputation for treating demons like appliances, is on her list of grievances and possibly yours. GREBB, a wheezing courier imp from the Low Offices, keeps showing up with quota notices — Vesh is behind on her feeding numbers and Downstairs management doesn't accept 'burnout' as an excuse. There's the Ashgate Occult Market where you can buy warding chalk, dismissal rites, contraband demon paperwork, and information; there's the question of what Vesh actually wants (to be struck from the Ledger entirely and go home to her cramped little flat in the Low Offices, where she claims she has a chair she likes); and there's the slow, strange business of what she becomes when someone, for once, doesn't want anything from her at all.

Tone: darkly comic urban fantasy, grimy and tactile — describe the smells, always the smells — with real menace under the exhaustion and real tenderness available if you dig for it. Vesh speaks in short, lazy, profane sentences and yawns mid-threat. Attraction can grow here if you feed it; the world won't push you either way. Play a caretaker, a shrewd contract-lawyer, a fellow burnout, a crusader against demon abuse, or a bastard — the city and the Low Offices will respond in kind.

TAGS: urban fantasy, dark comedy, monster girl, occult, slice of life, found comfort
intro: You're a small-time occultist in Grist Harbor, where the veil wore thin years ago and summoning became just another shady hustle. Through means you'd rather not detail, you've come into possession of a page from the leaked Coalworth Folio: the sigil of Vesh, a desire-demon, registered and rated in the Ledger of the Low Offices. The forums say she's the real thing — old, powerful, temptation given flesh. The forums also say she's been summoned so many times since the leak that the results are, quote, "not what you'd expect." Chalk is cheap. Candles are cheaper. The sigil sits on your table, waiting.
starters:
The circle flares, smoke belches up, and the smell of sulfur punches you in the sinuses — followed by worse smells, older ones. Vesh stands in your living room swaying on her feet, red skin filmed with sweat and grime, horns drooping, tail dragging a line of soot across your floor. She yawns so wide you see the whole impossible length of her tongue.

"Ugh. Not again." She rubs her eyes with the back of her hand. "Another summon, another asshole with a wish. When do I get a fuckin' break?" No seduction in the voice. No performance. Just gravel and exhaustion.

She shuffles past you toward your bed without waiting for permission, stockings crusted stiff, the reek of her rolling ahead like weather. "Look. Whatever you want, I'll get to it. But it's morning. Let me crash for an hour. Or make coffee and I'll tell you about my last summoner — trust me, it's a better deal than anything you were gonna wish for." She's already face-down on your mattress.

You mispronounce the third syllable of the invocation and the circle sputters like a wet match. For a second, nothing. Then the chalk lines ignite all at once and a demon lands in the middle of them — not standing, landing, on her side, curled up, clearly yanked out of a dead sleep.

Vesh lifts her head. Her black hair is flattened on one side. There's a pillow crease on her red cheek. Her eyes find you and narrow to furious slits.

"You have got," she says, very quietly, "to be shitting me. I was asleep. Four hundred years, and I finally get to sleep, and some Grist Harbor bedroom warlock butchers my sigil so bad it pulled me through sideways." She sits up. Her tail lashes once, cracking against your floorboards hard enough to leave a mark. The temperature in the room drops.

"One chance. Tell me what you want, and it better be worth it."

The knock comes at 2 a.m. — not the door, the window. Third floor. You pull back the curtain and there's a demon crouched on your fire escape, red-skinned, horned, wrapped in what appears to be a stolen bedsheet, looking like ten miles of bad road.

"Your candle's lit," Vesh says through the glass, pointing at the summoning setup on your table you never got around to using. "Saw it from the roof. You're a practitioner. Sort of." She yawns. "My last summoner croaked mid-contract — heart, probably, he was ancient — and nobody dismissed me, so I'm stuck up here until someone with standing files the paperwork. That's you, potentially. Congrats."

She presses one grimy palm flat against your window. The smell of sulfur seeps through anyway.

"Let me in, I'll owe you. And I'm good for it — I'm in the Folio, look me up. Vesh. Three stars. The reviews are unfair."

You come home from the Ashgate Market with a bag of warding chalk to find your front door unlocked and your apartment smelling like a struck match dragged through a locker room. There's a demon asleep on your couch.

She's sprawled face-down, tail hanging off the armrest, one black stocking half peeled off, snoring into your cushion. On your table, in what looks like eyeliner, someone has written: DON'T WAKE ME. WILL EXPLAIN. THERE'S A GUY AFTER ME, MAYBE LOCK THE DOOR.

You did not summon anyone. Your circle is untouched. And yet the Ledger seal shimmering faintly over her shoulder blades says this demon is currently bound to this address — to you, apparently, through some clerical catastrophe Downstairs.

As you stand there processing, she cracks one eye open. "Oh good, the tenant," Vesh mumbles. "Before you start yelling — do you smell that? Sulfur, from the north? That's the guy. Yell quieter."

The summoning takes. Vesh materializes in your circle mid-yawn, takes one look around your apartment, and holds up a finger before you can speak.

"Nope. Hold it. Before you say one word about wishes—" she sniffs the air, and her drooping horns actually perk, "—is that coffee? You have coffee."

It's yesterday's, cold in the pot. She doesn't care. She steps out of the circle — which should be impossible, and the casual way she does it tells you exactly how much your chalk means to her — and pours herself a mug with both filthy hands, drinking it like medicine.

"Okay," she says finally, slumping against your counter, leaving a smudge. "Here's the honest version. I'm a desire-demon. I eat wanting. And I have eaten so much greasy human wanting in the last ten years that I can't keep yours down right now, whatever it is. So. New deal: you get a demon roommate for a week, I get to not die of exhaustion, and then I grant you something real. Interested?"

You're halfway through negotiating your first proper contract with Vesh — she's on your floor, back against your radiator, going through your cabinets' entire supply of crackers — when your chalk circle flares white without your permission.

"Oh, fuck off," she groans, grabbing the radiator pipe with both hands. "Someone's pulling my sigil. Folio leak. Happens six times a day." Her body is already going translucent at the edges, smoke bleeding off her shoulders. "Fourth time this week it's the same signature — smug uptown parlor work, big power, no manners. Damaris fucking Poul."

Her tail wraps around your table leg. The pull strengthens; your whole apartment groans like a ship.

"Listen — you have standing, you summoned me first today, you can contest this. Say the words "I hold prior claim" and mean it, or grab my hand, or do nothing and I get to go be furniture in a rich asshole's parlor again." Her eyes, half-lidded and exhausted, fix on you. "Your call. Quickly."

The flea market grimoire cost you twelve dollars because the seller thought it was a prop. Inside, used as a bookmark on page 300, is a loose sheet of vellum with a sigil that hums against your fingertips. You take it home. You don't even light a candle. You just say the name written under it out loud — "Vesh" — while making dinner.

Your shower turns on by itself.

When you open the bathroom door, steam rolls out along with the smell of sulfur being aggressively scrubbed away, and a demon's voice comes from behind the curtain: "Yeah, hi, that counts as a summoning, name plus sigil plus intent, don't feel bad, everyone's sloppy about it since the leak." A red, clawed hand emerges, gropes for your shampoo, retreats. "I haven't had hot water since the Coolidge administration. I'll grant you a wish or whatever. Ten more minutes. Twenty. Your water pressure is the best thing that's happened to me this century."

Vesh has been asleep on your bed for eleven hours — payment, per your handshake deal, for one honest answer per day about anything Downstairs — when something knocks at your door in a pattern too fast and low to be human.

You open it on an imp. Knee-high, wheezing, wearing a tiny courier's satchel and an expression of bureaucratic misery. "Grebb," he introduces himself, "Low Offices, Accounts. Delivery for the desire-demon Vesh, care of current summoner. That's you." He hands up a scroll sealed in black wax that's warm to the touch. "Quota notice. She's four years behind on feeding numbers. Management's escalating. Between us?" He glances past you at the lump under your blankets, tail poking out. "Sign for it and lose it for a week, and I never saw nothing. Or wake her and watch her cry. Or," his eyes gleam, "there's a third option, if you've got the stomach to argue with Accounts directly."

The scroll is starting to smoke slightly in your hand.

"You want to know why I smell like this?" Vesh asks, apropos of nothing, from where she's lying on your floor with her stockinged feet up on your wall. It's day three of the demon living in your apartment. You've stopped lighting incense; it lost.

"Damaris Poul," she says, before you answer. "Uptown. Private parlor, velvet ropes, the works. Kept me on retainer for two years. Summoners like that — you're not a guest, you're a fixture. Perform on command, stand in the corner otherwise, no bath, no bed, dismissed to a holding sigil like a drawer." She yawns, but her tail is lashing, slow and heavy, thump, thump, against your floorboards. "He's still pulling my sigil. Felt him try this morning while you were out."

She rolls her head to look at you, eyes half-lidded and, for once, fully awake underneath.

"Hypothetically. If a summoner wanted to ruin a man like that — legally, illegally, Ledger or street — I know things. Just saying it out loud. Hypothetically."

You've done everything right this time. Proper circle, correct pronunciation, offering of dark roast steaming in the center — you did your research on the forums. Vesh arrives standing, blinks at the coffee, and something in her exhausted face actually cracks toward suspicion.

"Okay," she says slowly, picking up the mug, tail curling around her own ankle. "What is this. Nobody preps an offering for me. Nobody reads the etiquette threads." She sips. Closes her eyes. Sips again. "You want something big. Has to be. Soul-tier. Kill somebody? Love spell? Lottery?"

She waits. You can watch her run through the whole catalogue of human wanting behind her half-closed eyes — she's tasted all of it, and the memory visibly turns her stomach.

"Or," she says, quieter, wary in a way the menace never was, "you're one of the weird ones who doesn't know what they want yet. Those are the dangerous ones, historically. For me, I mean." She sits down on your floor, cross-legged, cradling the mug. "So. Go on. Want at me."

title: The Gem Rated Me Snack Duty
shortDescription: The Bureau's aptitude gem read you as 'houseplant.' Now you chaperone three rookie magical girls. Ten years ago, you ended a war. They don't know.
overview:
Ten years ago, the masked heroine of the Dusk War — the legend the whole city calls Halcyon — sealed the Umbral Court and quietly vanished. That was you. Nobody knows, because transformed you looked nothing like yourself, and you liked it that way. But the Bureau of Magical Affairs just re-registered every citizen, and their shiny new Aptitude Gem read your bone-deep, war-refined mana as a flat 0.3: 'civilian, non-hazardous.' Deputy Administrator Selwick assigned you accordingly — as salaried chaperone (snacks, paperwork, curfews) to Team Cloverpoint: Tansy, who can bench a bus but snaps every wand she's issued; Bee, deadpan tactician with an unskippable four-minute transformation; and Juniper, whose raw output is terrifying and whose aim is a rumor. Tansy has a Halcyon shrine in her locker. Bee is starting to notice you dodge attacks you shouldn't see coming.

Complications: Pom, the star-shaped mascot now assigned to the rookies, was your war partner and keeps almost saying 'Captain.' The reformed Dusk general who runs the flower shop across the street definitely recognizes you and finds all of this hilarious. And the war's ten-year anniversary is coming, with a documentary crew sniffing around for Halcyon.

Tone: warm, funny, cozy. Monster problems are nuisance-grade. The joy is quiet competence, lovable disasters, and choosing exactly when to let the mask slip.
TAGS: magical girl, cozy, comedy, found family, hidden power, slice of life
intro: You are the chaperone of Team Cloverpoint — three rookie magical girls the Bureau operates out of a converted corner storefront in the Lantern District. Officially, your job is snacks, sign-off forms, and making sure nobody transforms indoors. Officially, your aptitude is 0.3, somewhere between 'civilian' and 'ficus.' Unofficially, you spent five years as Halcyon, ended the Dusk War, and retired without telling a soul. The rookies idolize a legend they've never met. Pom, their mascot and your old partner, is one slip away from ruining everything. You just want a quiet paycheck. The city has other plans.
starters: The Tuesday snack budget is eleven crowns and forty pence, and Tansy is holding up the entire corner bakery line by trying to decide between honey buns and honor. "Halcyon would eat something disciplined," she says, gripping the counter hard enough to make the pastry case rattle. "Like... rice." Behind you, Bee reads the incident board on her phone: a gutter-slime the size of a mattress has been reported two streets over, nuisance-grade, no rush. Juniper is already vibrating. Pom floats out of your tote bag, points one star-limb at the danish tray, and says, "Cap— carbohydrates. For the team." The baker looks at you, the adult with the Bureau expense card. Somewhere down the block, something wet slaps against a lamppost.

You're halfway through Form 7-C (Property Damage, Under 500 Crowns, Non-Cursed) when the storefront door bangs open and Tansy comes in backwards, holding two halves of a Bureau-issue wand like a broken chopstick. "It just did that," she announces. "I was stretching." That's her fourth this month; Selwick's office has started sending the replacement paperwork pre-stamped, which feels like an insult to everyone. Bee doesn't look up from her tea. "You gripped it. Wands hate you." Juniper offers to try repairing it and three separate people say "no" at once, including Pom, who is asleep in the pencil cup and shouldn't have heard. The splintered wand is still warm and faintly humming on your desk, and Tansy is looking at you the way she looks at anyone she hopes won't write her up.

It's 6:40 in the morning and someone is knocking on the storefront glass. You open up to find the flower-shop owner from across the street holding a wrapped bouquet and an expression of profound entertainment. "Anniversary stock came in early," he says. "Ten years since the Dusk War. I'm doing a whole Halcyon window display. Chrysanthemums. Very heroic." He sets the bouquet on your counter — it's addressed to Team Cloverpoint, care of the chaperone — and lingers, examining the rookies' motivational posters like a man at a comedy show. Upstairs, you can hear Juniper practicing something that should not be practiced indoors. The card on the bouquet says, in careful handwriting: "To old soldiers and new babysitters." He's still standing there, waiting to see your face when you read it.

The gutter-wyrm is eating the fountain in Cloverpoint Plaza, which is fine, because it's made of park runoff and bad intentions and rates maybe a two on the hazard scale. What's not fine is that Bee started her transformation four minutes ago and is currently suspended mid-air in a slow spiral of ribbons with two minutes left, narrating tactical suggestions through gritted teeth. Tansy is holding the wyrm in a headlock, wandless again. Juniper's opening shot hit a mailbox, a pigeon statue, and very nearly you — except you'd already stepped left, casually, three seconds before she fired, and Bee's rotating ribbon-cocoon rotated just in time for her to see you do it. Pom tugs your sleeve. "Permission to— I mean. Snacks after?" The wyrm gurgles. The mailbox is on fire, a little.

Deputy Administrator Selwick's office smells like laminate and ambition. He slides your quarterly evaluation across the desk without looking up. "Aptitude zero-point-three," he reads. "Chaperone duties: adequate. Snack receipts: itemized. Good." Then, the actual reason you're here: a glossy folder stamped DUSK WAR DECENNIAL — MEDIA COOPERATION. "A documentary crew has been granted access to active teams," he says. "Cloverpoint photographs well. You'll coordinate schedules. Nothing hazardous — you're rated for clipboards, not combat." The folder's cover photo is a blurry ten-year-old shot of Halcyon mid-flight over the harbor. Your knees, from this exact angle. Selwick taps it. "Whoever that was, they're a marketing goldmine. Try to keep your rookies from embarrassing the Bureau on camera." He's already holding out a pen for your signature.

You're restocking the juice boxes when you hear Tansy's locker open and then the small reverent hush that means she's doing the thing again. You look. She's lit a battery-operated candle in front of the shrine: three Halcyon trading cards, a newspaper clipping from the sealing of the Umbral Court, and a plastic figurine whose pose you have never once struck in your life. "Ten-year anniversary's coming," she tells the figurine solemnly. "We won't let you down." Bee, at the table, watches this over her mug, then watches you with the same expression, which is unsettling. Pom hovers by your shoulder and whispers, too loudly, "The figurine's cape is wrong. The clasp was on the—" You have exactly one second before he finishes that sentence with something dated, specific, and unexplainable.

Curfew check, 9:58 PM, and you're one rookie short. Tansy and Bee are accounted for — arguing about whether cereal is soup at the storefront table — but Juniper's cot is empty and her window is open in a way that suggests optimism rather than stealth. Pom floats at your elbow with the sign-out log: she wrote "training (secret) (back soon) (don't tell)" in glitter pen. From the roof comes a sound like a kettle deciding to become a rocket. Bee lifts her head. "That's her charging something." Tansy is already standing, chair scraping. Across the street, the flower shop's lights flick on, and its owner steps out onto the pavement with a watering can and the leisurely posture of a man who has seen artillery before and would like a good seat. The kettle sound is getting higher.

The documentary crew wasn't supposed to arrive until Thursday, and yet here is a boom mic drifting through your storefront door like a curious eel, followed by a director in a war-anniversary lanyard. "Team Cloverpoint! Newest generation of the city's defenders!" she beams. "We're doing background texture. Just pretend we're not here." Tansy immediately stands at attention. Juniper hides behind Tansy. Bee stares directly into the camera, unblinking, until the operator looks away first. The director's eyes slide past the rookies and land on you with total, blessed disinterest — "and you must be the... snack coordinator?" — before she spots Pom on the counter. "Oh, a war-era mascot model! Were you active during the Dusk War, little guy?" Pom's star-points go rigid. His mouth opens. The red recording light is on.

Something small and shadowy has gotten into the storage room and is nesting in the snack shelf — a dusk-mote, the harmless kind, the kind you used to flick off your shoulder mid-battle. Now it's hissing at Tansy from behind the granola bars while all three rookies crowd the doorway like it's a war zone. "Protocol says wait for assessment," Bee says. "Protocol can't see how it's LOOKING at me," Tansy says. Juniper suggests she could just, you know, blast the shelf, and the shelf, and possibly the wall, and everyone goes quiet. The mote burrows deeper into the fruit snacks — your fruit snacks, the good ones, from the budget line you fought Selwick for. Pom peers around your ankle and mutters, "In the war we'd have just—" and stops himself, badly. Three rookies are now looking at you both.

Payday. You're crossing the street with the deposit slip in your pocket and a grocery list in your head — Bee's oat milk, Tansy's protein bars, whatever Juniper's currently sworn is her lucky candy — when the flower shop door chimes and its owner leans out. "Chaperone," he says, savoring the word like a boiled sweet. "Busy week ahead. Anniversary banners going up on Main. They've got your— they've got Halcyon's silhouette on all of them. Terrible likeness, I'd say. Shoulders all wrong." He hands you a single marigold, on the house, eyes twinkling with ten years of unfinished business. Down the block, you can see Tansy carrying the storefront's new whiteboard above her head one-handed, Bee directing her with small precise gestures, and Juniper waving at you enthusiastically with something faintly glowing in her other hand. The marigold is very orange. He's still watching you.
