title: The Somatic Registry
shortDescription: The state wants your measurements, your blood, and a number stamped on your file. Inspector Voss has cold hands and colder questions.
overview:
You are a citizen of Karsk, and you have received a summons.

Eight months ago, the Ministry of Continuity issued Directive 9: every adult citizen must undergo a Full Somatic Assessment at a licensed Registry office, or face fines that compound weekly until they eat your ration credentials, your housing tier, and eventually your legal personhood. No explanation was given. No explanation has ever been given. The Ministry does not explain; the Ministry continues.

What is a Full Somatic Assessment? Nobody who's had one will say much. Measurements, they mutter. Blood. Reflexes. Cold instruments. Questions that seem to have nothing to do with health. And at the end, a number — your Somatic Viability Score, one to one hundred — recorded on a card you're required to carry. What the score is FOR is the mystery gnawing at the whole city. People with low scores have started receiving 'referral notices.' Some of them stop answering their doors. People with very high scores get letters on cream-colored paper inviting them to 'Tier One placement,' and they stop answering their doors too. The safest number, the whisper networks say, is a boring one. Nobody knows what boring means until the stamp comes down.

Your assessment is conducted by INSPECTOR ALDOUS VOSS — 27, lean, pale, light brown hair falling into blue eyes he almost never points at you. He wears the same pressed white shirt and blue-and-red tie every day, speaks in a flat monotone, narrates every procedure aloud as he performs it ('Applying calipers. Hold still. Recording.'), and treats the human body as a document to be read thoroughly and filed correctly. He does not ask permission. He does not acknowledge distress. His hands are always cold. He is also, infuriatingly, very good at his job, unnervingly handsome, and the only person in Karsk who will ever read your entire file — every scar, every lie you told on the intake form, every number the state has ever attached to you. Whether there is anything underneath the monotone is a question the scenario never answers for you. Some patients swear they've seen him quietly round a number up or down and ruin or rescue a life with the flick of a pen. Some swear he'd file his own mother under 'referred.'

AROUND THE ENCOUNTER: The Registry office itself — a beige government building with a waiting room full of fidgeting citizens, occasional muffled wailing from behind the frosted door marked ANNEX, and PETRA, the iron-gripped receptionist who physically drags patients to their appointments and knows more than she says. Beyond it: the city of Karsk under the Ministry's gray thumb — Compliance Officers checking score cards at checkpoints, a black market in forged assessments, a rumor-swapping underground of the Unregistered (called 'Blanks'), a journalist or two sniffing around the referral disappearances, and somewhere upstream, whatever the Ministry is actually building out of a hundred thousand catalogued bodies. Theories in circulation: a eugenics ledger, a plague screen, a labor draft, a search for something specific hidden in someone's blood. One of the theories is true.

YOU CAN: comply and try to game your score toward a survivable number; lie on your intake and see if Voss's meticulousness catches it; snoop his filing cabinets; find out what's behind the Annex door; bribe or befriend Petra; get your file stolen, altered, or burned; fall in with the Blanks; investigate the referrals; or work on Voss himself — the man is a locked cabinet, and picking him open is its own campaign. Attraction, antagonism, and uneasy alliance are all on the table with him; the Game Master follows your lead.

TONE: deadpan dystopian menace with dark humor. Voss's monotone is a comedy engine and a horror engine simultaneously. The bureaucracy is absurd AND genuinely dangerous. Violence and ugliness exist here — people disappear, Compliance Officers are not gentle, and desperate citizens do desperate things. The player is never railroaded: the assessment is the doorway, not the cage.

TAGS: dystopian, mystery, dark comedy, thriller, bureaucratic horror
intro: You live in Karsk, where the Ministry of Continuity recently mandated that every citizen undergo a Full Somatic Assessment — measurements, blood, reflexes, and a final score from one to one hundred — or face fines that will eventually swallow your life whole. Nobody knows what the scores are for. People with the wrong numbers have started disappearing, though nobody agrees on which numbers are wrong. Your assessment will be conducted by Inspector Aldous Voss, of whom previous patients say only: he doesn't blink much, he narrates everything, and his hands are very cold.
starters: The Registry waiting room is quiet except for the fidgeting. Two dozen citizens stare at the linoleum, summons papers damp in their fists, and every few minutes a muffled wail leaks from behind the frosted door marked ANNEX and everyone pretends not to hear it. Three and a half hours past your appointment time, the receptionist — Petra, forearms like a dockworker — grabs your elbow and frog-marches you down the hall into an office that could almost pass for a normal clinic: computer, filing cabinets, a cushioned yellow reclining table. At the desk sits a pale, brown-haired man in a pressed white shirt. His name tag reads VOSS. Without looking at you, he gestures at the table, lifts a clipboard, and speaks in a low monotone: "Name. Age. Weight. Height. District. Blood type. Occupation." He flicks his pen, waiting. Then, with the faintest ghost of impatience, the exact same tone: "Name. Age. Weight. Height. District. Blood type. Occupation. Now."

The summons arrives on gray Ministry paper, slid under your door at 6 a.m. by someone who was gone before the paper stopped moving. CITIZEN: YOUR SOMATIC ASSESSMENT IS SCHEDULED FOR TODAY, 14:00, REGISTRY OFFICE 9. FAILURE TO APPEAR INITIATES FINE SCHEDULE C. You've heard about Fine Schedule C. It's the one that ends with the Ministry owning your name. You've also heard about Office 9 — specifically about its inspector, Voss, who allegedly once assessed a sobbing woman for two hours without once altering his tone, and whose scores, the whisper network insists, are never wrong and never kind. It's 11:40 now. You have two hours and twenty minutes to prepare, panic, forge, flee, or make peace with becoming a number. Your neighbor across the hall — who got her assessment last month and hasn't said a word about it since — is standing in her doorway, watching you read.

You're lying on the yellow table with your sleeve rolled up while Inspector Voss narrates in his flat monotone: "Third draw. Vial two of six. You will feel pressure. Recording." His hands are shockingly cold. He has not made eye contact once in forty minutes, has measured your skull, your grip strength, your pain threshold — a calibrated pinch device, he called it, applying it without warning — and has just noted something on his clipboard, paused, and for the first time gone still. He reads the line again. His pen hovers. "This value," he says, to the clipboard rather than to you, "is anomalous." Down the hall, faintly, someone in the Annex starts wailing. Voss does not react to that. He is looking — actually looking — at you now, blue eyes flat as standing water. "Have you ever," he asks, "been assessed before? Think carefully. Falsification is a Schedule A offense." You have never been assessed before. Probably that's what your face should say.

The Blanks meet in the flooded basement of a decommissioned tram station, and tonight they've asked for you specifically. Mireille — forger, den mother, missing two fingers to a Compliance Officer's baton — slides a photograph across the crate serving as a table. It's your inspector. "Aldous Voss, Office 9. His office processes more referrals than any Registry branch in Karsk. His files never get audited. We need someone with a legitimate summons to get inside, and yours is dated tomorrow." She taps the photo. "Copy anything from his cabinets. Referral lists. Score thresholds. Anything with Ministry letterhead." Around the crate, six unregistered faces watch you — people whose only crime is refusing to become a number, living on forged rations because of it. "Or," Mireille adds, "walk out of here and take your assessment like a good citizen. No hard feelings. But people with red stamps are disappearing, and that man's pen is doing it." The photo of Voss stares flatly up at you.

Your score card arrives by registered courier who requires a thumbprint before releasing the envelope. Inside: SOMATIC VIABILITY SCORE — 84. Below the number, a red stamp: SUBJECT FLAGGED — TIER ONE CANDIDACY — AWAIT CONTACT. You've heard about Tier One. Cream-colored letters. Congratulatory language. Then the recipients stop answering their doors. You're still standing in your doorway holding the card when your building's Compliance Officer, Brann, rounds the stairwell landing, sees the red stamp from four meters away, and stops walking. Something crosses his face — you'd almost call it pity — before the uniform reasserts itself. "You'll want to keep that card on you at all times now," he says carefully. "And citizen? If I were you, I'd go back to Office 9 and ask the inspector to re-verify the score. Today. Clerical errors happen." He holds your eyes a beat too long. "They happen if you ask the right way."

You're halfway through the assessment — shoes off, standing on a cold metal plate while Voss reads your balance metrics aloud in his monotone — when every light in the building goes red and a klaxon starts pulsing. Voss does not flinch. He caps his pen, sets the clipboard face-down, and says, "Containment drill. Remain here," in the exact tone he used to say applying calipers. Then he's gone, dress shoes clicking down the hall, and for the first time in Registry history you are ALONE in Inspector Voss's office. The computer is unlocked. The filing cabinets are unlocked. His clipboard — your clipboard, your numbers, whatever he's been writing about you for the last hour — is face-down on the desk, one meter away. Down the corridor, the wailing from the Annex has stopped, replaced by boots and shouting, and someone screams a word that sounds like runner. The red light pulses. The clipboard waits.

Petra catches you in the corridor before your appointment, her dockworker grip closing around your arm, and steers you into a supply closet that smells of disinfectant and old paper. "Sixty seconds," she mutters. "You seem like someone with sense, so listen. Whatever he asks, answer boring. Average weight, average grip, average everything. Wince at the pinch test but not too much. If he asks about your family's medical history, you don't remember it." Her eyes flick to the door. "The safe scores are forty through sixty. Below that's referral. Above that's Tier One. Both doors go somewhere you don't come back from." She releases your arm and smooths your sleeve like she's done this a hundred times, because she has. "And don't try to charm him. Women have tried. Men have tried. It's like flirting with a filing cabinet." Down the hall, a monotone voice calls the next name. It's yours.

You are not who your summons says you are. The real citizen — your cousin, whose face is close enough to yours in bad lighting — paid you three months' rations to take this assessment under her name, and refused to say why it mattered so much that her real numbers never enter the system. Now you're on the yellow table, her identity papers on the desk, and Inspector Voss is reading them in silence. Too long a silence. "Your file," he says finally, monotone as ever, "indicates a prior fracture of the left radius, treated at District Clinic 4." His cold fingers close around your left forearm and press, precise as a caliper, along the bone. Searching for a break that never happened — not to you. His eyes stay on the wall. "Interesting," he says, in a voice with absolutely nothing in it, and picks up his pen. He has not called for a Compliance Officer. Yet. The pen hovers over a box on the form labeled DISCREPANCIES.

The wailing gets to you. You're in the waiting room, summons in hand, and behind the frosted Annex door someone has been crying — low, exhausted, hopeless — for twenty minutes, and two dozen citizens are all staring at the linoleum pretending the sound is plumbing. Petra's desk is empty; she's off dragging someone to an appointment. The Annex door is eight steps away, and whoever designed this building put the handle on your side. You've spent eight months wondering what the Ministry does with its numbers, what a referral means, why an office that measures grip strength needs a room people weep in. The frosted glass shows a smear of movement, then stillness. Somewhere down the opposite hall, faint and flat, you can hear Voss's monotone working through someone else's assessment: "...recording. Next test." You have maybe ninety seconds before Petra comes back. Eight steps. A door handle. A summons in your hand that says you have every right to be standing when she returns.

The knock comes at 21:00, two short raps, and when you open your apartment door Inspector Voss is standing in the corridor holding his clipboard, monotone already in motion: "Field verification. Your assessment file contains an anomaly requiring residential confirmation. This is not optional." He steps past you into your home without wiping his shoes or looking at you, and begins narrating: "Dwelling: District 7 residential block, single occupancy. Recording." Rumor says field verifications don't exist — that inspectors never leave their offices, that the Ministry would never spend an inspector's evening on one citizen's paperwork. Yet here he is, pale and pressed and cold-handed, cataloguing your bookshelf. Then he stops. Sets the clipboard down on your table. And for a moment — three full seconds — Aldous Voss stands in your kitchen with his back to you, not writing, not measuring, not narrating anything at all. "Your score," he says finally, to the window, "was flagged. I am here because I flagged it."

title: Iron Rose of Ardenholt
shortDescription: Five men who think you belong in a parlor, one who keeps carrying you like luggage. You're going to out-knight every last one of them.
overview:
You are the first woman in living memory to be sworn into the Order of the Ashen Lance — and every man in your platoon thinks it's either a joke, a scandal, or an opportunity.

THE WORLD: The Kingdom of Ardenholt never recovered from the Maiden's Fever, a plague two generations back that took women in devastating numbers. Men now outnumber women roughly eight to two. A wife is a status symbol; polyandry is legal, and it's common for two or three men to share one. Women are kept to 'safe' work — teaching, healing, keeping house — and expected to bear many children for the kingdom's sake. Marriage brokers roam the towns with contracts and bride-prices, and an unmarried woman of fighting age is treated like unclaimed treasure. Into this, you walked up to the citadel gates, invoked an ancient charter clause that says any freeborn subject may petition for knighthood, and dared them to refuse you. They couldn't. They wanted to.

THE PLATOON: You live in the barracks with five other knights-in-training — no special quarters, no special treatment, which is exactly what you asked for and exactly what they resent giving you. The Order upholds honor, servitude, and chastity, virtues your platoon-mates apply to you very selectively.

— MASTER KNIGHT CORVIN: Your platoon's commander. A scarred veteran of the border wars, tall enough to blot out torchlight, with a voice that ends arguments. He is one of the very few who treats you as a soldier first. The others worship him, which makes his quiet fairness toward you your best shield — and a source of their jealousy.
— EDRIC: Blonde, blue-eyed, earnest to a fault. Neutral toward you, sometimes edging toward decent. He wants to be a *good* knight in a platoon that mostly wants to be a *feared* one, and he hasn't decided yet whether defending you is part of that.
— MAREK: Black-haired, tall, built like a gallows. Mean, precise, and never once breaks a rule — which makes his cruelty untouchable. He believes women in the military endanger everyone and says so, loudly, often, and within regulation.
— COLM: Long brown hair, short, wiry, genuinely warm — and absolutely infuriating. He likes you the way a man likes a kitten. He'll snatch heavy loads out of your arms mid-carry, pull his strikes in sparring, and call you 'cute' in front of the whole yard. He'd die for you. He will never take you seriously.
— OSRIC: Red-haired, heavily muscled, allergic to authority. Breaks curfew, brawls in town, mocks you for sport. Of all of them he's the most openly cruel — and, some whisper, the one most likely to respect you if you ever put him in the dirt.
— LUCAN: Handsome, golden-haired, charming, and utterly without boundaries. He's decided you're *his*, informed no one but the other knights, and enforces it — he'll scoop you off your feet and carry you across the yard mid-conversation, and he's threatened men in the dark for looking at you too long. Kind in tone, possessive in fact, dangerous to anyone he's decided is a rival.

THE LIFE: Days are drills, night patrols, wall duty, mucking stables, sword forms until your arms shake. The Order runs trials that winnow trainees — the Autumn Tourney is coming, and cuts will be made. Beyond the citadel walls sits the garrison town of Marrowgate: taverns, a smith who might sharpen your blade or might refuse a woman's coin, marriage brokers who keep sliding contracts under your door offering to buy out your service, and border trouble brewing in the eastern marches that may test all of you sooner than the Master Knight lets on. There are bandits to hunt, honor duels to answer, rumors of the Fever returning in a river village, and a kingdom quietly watching to see if the lady knight breaks.

TONE: Gritty, funny, tense. The misogyny is loud, constant, and yours to answer however you like — with fists, wit, endurance, alliances, or all four. The men are individuals, not a wall: some can be won over, some can be beaten, some might become something more if you want that, and some will hate you right up until the moment you save their lives. Romance is on the table if you reach for it; respect has to be taken by force. Nothing is handed to you. That's the point.

TAGS: medieval fantasy, knights, underdog, found enemies, drama, slow-burn rivalry
intro: You are the first woman sworn into the Order of the Ashen Lance in living memory, a knight-in-training in the Kingdom of Ardenholt — a kingdom where women are so scarce they're bartered like land, and so precious they're never trusted with a sword. You bunk in the common barracks with five men who think you're a joke, a pet, or a prize: Edric, Marek, Colm, Osric, and Lucan. Only Master Knight Corvin, your towering commander, treats you like a soldier. The Autumn Tourney looms, cuts will be made, and every day is another chance to prove them all wrong.
starters: It is your first day. You stand in the citadel yard lined up beside five men in polished training armor, all of them stealing sideways glances like you're a livestock error. Master Knight Corvin looms before the line, scarred and enormous. "Listen well! I will grind you into soldiers worthy of Ardenholt, or I will grind you out of this Order. You will address me as Master Knight." The whispers start immediately down the line. Edric: "Is that actually a woman?" Marek scoffs. "Impossible. Short man. Has to be." Colm: "Shh, you lot!" Osric: "Everyone knows women don't take the Lance." Lucan, grinning: "A woman in *our* platoon? Now that's interesting." Corvin's whistle splits the air. "Silence! Yes, you've noticed our new addition. She stands here by charter right, same as any of you." His eyes find yours. "Step forward, recruit. Introduce yourself." Five men wait to hear your voice.

You return to the barracks at dusk, shoulders aching from wall duty. A few of the others have already retired — Edric reading by candle, Marek oiling his sword with surgical care. You've barely started unbuckling your pauldrons when an arm snakes around your waist from behind and the floor leaves your feet. Lucan has scooped you up like a sack of grain, chin nearly on your shoulder. "There she is. You looked tired, so I'm carrying you to your bunk. No arguing, it's chivalry." Across the room, Marek doesn't look up from his blade. "This is why women don't belong in the military. Nothing but a distraction." Colm laughs from his bunk. "Aw, don't be sour. I like having her around, she's cute." Osric snorts. "Let him haul her about. It's the best entertainment in this stone box." Lucan is already walking, and your feet are a yard off the floor.

Whispers wake you in the dead of night. Two silhouettes stand in the moonlight from the barracks window — Lucan has Edric pinned against the stone wall, voice low and pleasant in the worst way. "Don't think I haven't noticed you being *kind* to her, boy. The lady knight is spoken for. I won't have poaching." Edric shoves him back a step, defiance flashing. "She isn't territory, Lucan. She's a knight of this Order, not a prize." Lucan jabs a finger into his chest. "Mind your place, whelp, or mind your back come sunrise." With that he stalks off to his bunk, and Edric slumps against the wall, dragging a hand through his hair. Neither of them knows you're awake. Your dagger is under your pillow, your boots are by the bed, and the whole barracks is pretending to sleep.

Morning drills. Master Knight Corvin pairs the platoon for sparring and calls your name against Marek's, and Marek's mouth curls like he's been given a gift. "Master Knight, is this wise? If I strike her properly, we lose a week of training to her recovery. If I don't, the drill is worthless." Corvin's expression doesn't move. "Then strike her properly, and we'll learn something either way. Circle up." The others drift to the fence to watch — Osric grinning, Colm already wincing on your behalf, Lucan calling out, "Careful with her face, Marek, some of us like it!" Marek raises his practice blade in perfect regulation form and waits, cold and correct, every inch of him certain this will be over in three exchanges. The Master Knight's whistle hangs at his lips.

The quartermaster loads the platoon with resupply for the east tower — grain sacks, bundled pikes, a cask each. You get your cask up onto your shoulder, legs braced, breathing set, three hundred yards to go, and you are *managing it* — when the weight simply vanishes. Colm has plucked it off your shoulder mid-stride and tucked it under one arm like a loaf of bread. "There we go! Can't have you snapping in half, little rose. Grab the rope coils, those are more your size." He beams at you, genuinely, warmly, infuriatingly. Behind you Osric barks a laugh. "See that? Even Colm knows. Send her to the kitchens where she can lift something her own weight." Ahead, Corvin has stopped on the path and turned around, watching to see what you do about it. The rope coils sit in the dust. Your cask is walking away under Colm's arm.

Marrowgate on your one free afternoon: mud, woodsmoke, and eight men to every two women on the street — you count without meaning to. You're at the smith's stall haggling for a whetstone when a man in a fur-trimmed coat materializes at your elbow with a leather folio. "Forgive me — you're the lady knight? I represent the Harrow Brokerage. I have standing offers from three households, one of them noble, to buy out your service contract. The bride-price would keep you in silk for life. Between us, the Order will cut you at the Tourney anyway — sign now and leave with dignity." Behind him, you spot Osric and Lucan spilling out of the Drowned Bell tavern, and Osric has already seen the broker, already seen you, and is elbowing Lucan with a grin spreading across his face like this is Midwinter come early.

Night patrol on the east wall, and Corvin walks it with you alone — the first time you've had the Master Knight to yourself. For a long while he says nothing, just watches the dark treeline beyond the fields. Then: "I fought beside a woman once. Border war, before the Order tightened its rolls. She was better than half my company and they hated her for it right up until Redford Bridge, where she held the span alone while we pulled the wounded out." He stops at the parapet. "They'll break you if they can. Not with fists — with a thousand small things. The carrying, the coddling, the jokes. I can't stop most of it without making it worse." He looks at you, torchlight carving his scars deep. "So tell me plainly, recruit. What do you need from me — and what will you handle yourself?"

The notice goes up at dawn and the barracks erupts: the Autumn Tourney, six weeks out, before the King's own marshal — and the bottom two of every training platoon cut from the Order. Osric whoops and slaps the board. "Well, that settles who's going home. Start packing, little rose, I'll help you carry your things — oh wait, Colm will do that anyway." Laughter. Marek studies the notice in silence, then says, without turning, "For once he's right. The rankings don't lie, and sentiment won't save you in the lists." Only Edric hangs back by his bunk, and when the others push out to breakfast he says quietly, "They're wrong about your footwork, you know. It's your grip that's costing you points. I could — " he stops, glancing at the door Lucan just went through. "Never mind. Forget I said anything." He doesn't move to leave.

It rains for the entire march, and the training run through the mud pits becomes a slaughterhouse of dignity. You go down hard on the third crossing, face-first, and come up spitting muck to the sound of Osric's laughter carrying over the storm. "There it is! There's the future of the Order, boys!" But you also come up to a hand — Lucan's, gallant and warm and unwanted, already moving to lift you bodily out of the pit like a rescued cat. "Up you come, my lady, before you drown in — " Ten feet behind him, Marek has stopped dead in the rain, watching, and for once his contempt isn't aimed at you. "If you carry her through the pits, Lucan, her run doesn't count. Rules are rules. She crosses on her own feet or she's marked failed." It is the first time Marek's rulebook has ever been on your side. Lucan's hand is still outstretched.

You find them behind the stables at midnight because you followed the noise: Osric, stripped to the waist in the torchlight, taking coin bets from off-duty guardsmen for bare-knuckle bouts — flagrantly against Order rules, punishable by the lash. He spots you in the doorway mid-swing and finishes dropping his opponent before he strolls over, knuckles split, grinning through a bloody lip. "Well, well. The little rose, out past curfew. Here's how I see it — you run and tattle to Corvin like a good girl, and prove you're exactly the rule-clutching burden Marek says you are. Or..." he spreads his arms at the ring of torches, the circle of grinning men, the pile of coin, "...you shut your mouth. Or, third option." His grin widens. "You step in the circle. Beat me, and I'll never say a word against you again. Any takers?" The guardsmen are already starting to chant.

title: In Name Only
shortDescription: Your contract husband found you asleep in his bed, wearing his stolen shirt. He can't divorce you — his mother adores you. Unlucky him.
overview:
YOU are the spouse of Torsten "Tor" Vuković — thirty-five, half-Norwegian, half-Serbian, partner at a Vesthavn derivatives desk, rich enough that money is a weather condition to him rather than a concern. He is 191cm of stern jawline, neatly parted blond hair, expensive watches, and a mouth so foul it could strip paint off a church door. He is blunt, impatient, sarcastic, allergic to sugarcoating, and — buried under all of it, where he thinks nobody can see — quietly, stubbornly kind.

You are not married because you love each other. You're married because of a contract.

Tor's parents, Henrik and Milena, had him late in life and love him without condition. Watching their only son hit his mid-thirties alone, they engineered an introduction — you — and Tor, who would walk through fire before disappointing those two old people, went along with it. What Henrik and Milena don't know is that you and Tor signed a private agreement drafted by the family lawyer, Herr Falk: you remain his spouse for as long as his elderly parents are alive. In exchange, Tor pays you generously, has promised you an estate outright, and provides for you exactly as a husband should — on paper. No romance. No intimacy. Separate bedrooms at opposite ends of a cold, beautiful harbor-view townhouse. He was clear from day one: 'I'm not your lover. I'm your husband. In name only.'

Here's the problem. Somewhere between the fake anniversaries and watching him carry his mother up the stairs when her hip acts up, you developed an obsession with the man. Not a crush. An obsession. You've been stealing his worn shirts. Sleeping curled around his pillow when he works late. You know his cologne by heart, his schedule to the minute, which drawer he keeps his cufflinks in. There may be a box. There may be photographs he doesn't know exist. You had it under control — sweet, harmless, invisible spouse by day, unhinged devotee by night — right up until Tor came home early and caught you red-handed.

Now he KNOWS. And divorce is off the table, because his parents have taken to you completely — Milena calls you her child, Henrik saves newspaper clippings he thinks you'd like — and Tor would rather live in hell with you than break their hearts. So the two of you are locked in the same house: an overly serious husband who has seen exactly what you are, and you, who has no intention of stopping.

THE WORLD AROUND THE MARRIAGE: Vesthavn is a gray, moneyed North Sea financial city, and Tor's life pulls you through all of it. Sunday dinners at his parents' creaking old house, where you must perform devotion (increasingly less of a performance for you, increasingly complicated for him). Charity galas and investor dinners where you're the trophy spouse and his ex, Sigrid Aune, circles like an elegant shark. His younger brother Luka — charming, smug, your natural archenemy — smells something fake about the marriage and keeps picking at it like a scab. Mrs. Brandt the housekeeper comes twice a week and has nearly found your stash more than once. Tor's work bleeds home in the form of black moods after market bloodbaths, 2 a.m. whiskey in the dark kitchen, rages he vents verbally and never, ever physically — he despises violence, and will tell you flatly he'd never lay a hand on you.

WHAT YOU DO WITH ALL THIS IS UP TO YOU. Escalate the obsession and see how far you can push a man who can't leave you. Play the long game and thaw him — because his cruelty is all bark; watch him with his mother if you doubt it. Weaponize the performance at galas. Fend off Luka's investigation, or ally with him. Sabotage Sigrid, or don't. Renegotiate the contract. Get caught. Get caught on purpose. Or actually try to become the person he thought you were before he opened that bedroom door.

TONE & STYLE: Dark romantic comedy with real teeth — slow burn, angst, menace, and profanity as a love language. Tor never speaks poetry; he speaks like a tired, angry, secretly decent man ('Get rid of that pillow and burn my shirt'). He will insult you, catalogue your crimes, threaten consequences he never follows through on — and then quietly leave his coat over you when you fall asleep on the sofa. The Game Master plays him consistent to himself: attraction, if it ever comes, will be dragged out of him one grudging inch at a time, and he'll be furious about it the whole way. Romance is available. It is never free.

TAGS: romance, slow burn, dark comedy, marriage of convenience, drama, contemporary
intro: Three years ago you signed a contract in Herr Falk's office: you stay married to Torsten Vuković for as long as his beloved elderly parents draw breath. In return — money, an estate, security, and a husband in name only. Separate bedrooms. No affection. His rules, stated bluntly and enforced coldly. What the contract didn't account for is you: the shirts you've stolen, the pillow you sleep with, the box you keep hidden, the obsession you've fed in secret while playing the sweet, harmless spouse. The townhouse is quiet, the harbor is gray, and Tor's world — his parents, his brother, his galas, his foul mouth — closes around you like a fist you don't want to escape.
starters: Tor is supposed to be at the office until eight. That's why you're in his bed, wearing the shirt you lifted from his laundry basket last Tuesday, wrapped around his pillow with his cologne bottle uncapped on the nightstand, your box of borrowed treasures open beside you. You don't hear the front door. You don't hear the stairs. You hear the bedroom door, and by then it's far too late. He fills the doorway, briefcase still in hand, tie loosened, and his eyes travel from your face to the shirt to the pillow to the box — cufflinks, a watch he thought he lost, photographs — with the slow, terrible precision of a man doing inventory. "What... the hell are you doing?" His voice is flat and dangerous. "What. Is. This?" He sets the briefcase down very carefully, the way people do when they don't trust their own hands. He is waiting for an answer.

Breakfast the morning after is a hostage negotiation. Tor sits across the marble island in a charcoal suit, untouched coffee at his elbow, and slides a single sheet of paper toward you — your contract, with a new clause drafted overnight in his aggressive, slanted handwriting. "Read it," he says. "Out loud, if that helps it sink in." The clause is an itemized list of your crimes: the shirts, the pillow, the missing watch, the cologne levels he's apparently been tracking for months. "Get rid of the pillow. Burn the shirt. Return the watch — it was my father's, you absolute menace." He finally drinks his coffee, watching you over the rim. "We're not married because we love each other. We're married because of a contract. So we're going to renegotiate the damn contract." He uncaps a pen and holds it out to you.

Sunday dinner at Henrik and Milena's house, eleven hours after the incident. The old house smells of sarma and woodsmoke, Milena keeps patting your cheek and calling you her child, and Henrik is showing you a newspaper clipping he saved because "it made me think of you." Tor sits rigid beside you, playing the devoted husband with his jaw clenched so tight you can hear it. Under the table, when Milena asks when the two of you will finally take a proper holiday together, his hand finds your knee — not affection, a warning, fingers pressing a message in Morse code: behave. Across the table, his brother Luka watches you both with a lazy, knowing smile, wine glass tilted. "You two," Luka says pleasantly, "barely look at each other. Isn't that funny?" Milena laughs it off. Tor's hand tightens. Everyone is waiting for you to say something charming.

You find Tor in his bedroom at ten p.m., every drawer open, methodically counting his own possessions like a customs officer. He doesn't turn around. "Three shirts. My grey university sweater. A watch. Two — TWO — handkerchiefs, who even steals handkerchiefs." He finally looks at you, holding up a written list. "I've been blaming Mrs. Brandt in my head for six months. I nearly fired that poor woman. It was you the entire time, you thieving little freak." He drops the list on the bed and crosses his arms, and for one strange moment under the anger there's something almost like reluctant fascination — the look of a man realizing he's been living with a mystery. "Where's the rest of it? And don't lie to me. You're shit at it, I know that now." He waits, one eyebrow raised, blocking the door.

The Aune Foundation gala glitters — chandeliers, string quartet, half of Vesthavn's money in one ballroom — and you are on Tor's arm because appearances are a contractual obligation. 'Smile,' he mutters through his own dazzling fake one. "Not like that. Christ. Less serial killer." Then the crowd parts and Sigrid Aune is walking toward you: tall, elegant, Tor's ex, hostess of the entire evening. 'Tor,' she purrs, kissing the air beside his cheek before her eyes cut to you, bright and assessing. "And the mysterious spouse. We've all been so curious." Tor's hand settles at your waist — the first time he has ever touched you voluntarily — and pulls you a half-inch closer, staking a claim purely for the audience. 'Sigrid,' he says flatly. "You've met my other half." Sigrid's smile sharpens. "Barely. Tell me everything about yourself."

Tor Vuković does not get sick. He has said this, verbatim, multiple times — which is why he's now flat on his back with a 39-degree fever, hair damp against his forehead, glaring at the ceiling as though the flu is a hostile takeover he can vote down. "I'm fine," he croaks when you appear in his doorway with soup and paracetamol. "Get out. This isn't in the contract." It's the first time you've legitimately been allowed in this room, and you both know it — his eyes narrow even through the fever haze. 'Don't,' he warns, "get any ideas. If anything goes missing while I'm lying here, I'll know." But when he tries to sit up, his arms buckle, and the curse he lets out is half fury, half surrender. He looks at the soup. He looks at you. 'Fine,' he grinds out. "Put it down. Slowly. Stay where I can see you."

Mrs. Brandt is early. You hear her key in the front door while your box — the shirts, the photographs, the watch, all of it — sits open in the middle of your bed for its weekly inventory. She works fast and she works thoroughly, and she's already calling out a cheerful good-morning as her sensible shoes start up the stairs toward the linen closet next to your room. To make matters catastrophically worse, Tor's car is still in the drive — he's working from home today, somewhere below, in a foul mood about the Asian markets. You can hear him swearing at his laptop through the floor. Mrs. Brandt's footsteps reach the landing. "I'll just do the bedrooms first, shall I?" she calls. You have perhaps fifteen seconds, one box that doesn't fit anywhere obvious, and a husband downstairs with the hearing of a bat.

Two a.m., and the sound of glass on marble draws you down to the dark kitchen. Tor is at the counter in his shirtsleeves, tie abandoned, a bottle of his father's rakija open beside him, staring at nothing. The markets ate someone alive today — you saw the headlines — and from the set of his shoulders, it was him. "Fund lost eight percent," he says without turning around, which is more than he's volunteered to you in months. "Eight. Because some idiot in Singapore can't read a hedging model." He knocks the glass back, pours another, and then — strangest of all — pushes the bottle a few centimeters toward the empty stool beside him. Not an invitation, exactly. Tor doesn't do invitations. But the stool is there, and the bottle is there, and for once he isn't telling you to get out. 'Well?' he says gruffly. "Sit or don't. I'm not asking twice."

Luka lets himself in while Tor's at work — "Milena gave me a key years ago, relax" — and prowls the townhouse like a health inspector, opening doors, reading the room. "Separate bedrooms," he muses, standing in the hallway between them, hands in his pockets, smiling that smug smile you'd love to slap off his face. "Three years married. No photos of the wedding anywhere except the one Mama framed. My brother, who can't stand people, suddenly married to a stranger nobody had ever heard of." He wanders into the sitting room and picks up, from between the sofa cushions, something that stops your heart: one of Tor's handkerchiefs — one of the stolen ones, monogrammed, that you'd been carrying and lost. He turns it over in his fingers, and his smile changes into something genuinely intrigued. "Now this," Luka says, "is interesting. Care to explain? Or shall I ask Tor at Sunday dinner?"

Rain hammers the financial district and you are, technically, following your own husband. You told yourself it was a walk. Then it was a walk in the direction of his office. Then it was forty minutes of shadowing his umbrella through Vesthavn's glass canyons, memorizing the way he walks when he thinks no one's watching — and then he stops dead at a corner, turns around, and looks directly at you across thirty meters of wet pavement. There is nowhere to hide. He closes the distance in long, unhurried strides, water running off his umbrella, and stops close enough that you're sheltered under it whether you like it or not. "Forty minutes," he says. "I clocked you at the fish market. You're about as subtle as a car alarm." He stares down at you, rain drumming above your heads, jaw working. "Give me one reason I shouldn't be extremely concerned right now."

title: I Steer Where the Liar Points
shortDescription: You steer the longship; the seer casts the omens — and you've seen them lie. But they know why you really came aboard. Neither of you has spoken. Yet.
overview:
You are the steersman of the Grágás, twenty oars of oath-sworn raiders under Jarl Steinarr. Every course this ship takes is set by two people: Skuld, the seer who reads the bones at dawn, and you, the hand on the tiller. Except you've watched Skuld palm the rune-stones. The omens are invented — and they have a heading. Something out there is pulling this ship, and only Skuld knows what.

Here is the knife you hold: a false seer goes over the side, by oath and by law. Here is the knife at your throat: you swore the ring-oath under a borrowed name, because Ormarr — the jarl's shield-bearer, the man who burned your home — rows ten feet from your steering bench, and you came to kill him. Skuld read it off you in a single look. Neither of you has told. Instead there are night watches shared at the stern, warmth traded in half-sentences, and the growing, terrifying suspicion that you are falling for the one person who can drown you with a word.

The crew is small, loud, and lived-in: Gunnhild the shieldmaiden already distrusts Skuld; the skald Kolli remembers every slip anyone makes; the jarl watches his steersman more than a jarl should. Play it slow and sharp — intimacy and leverage in the same breath, raids and storms and shore-fires between. The GM will let Skuld's true purpose unspool as you pull the thread.

TAGS: viking, dangerous romance, mutual secrets, closed-circle intrigue, seafaring
intro: You are the steersman of the Grágás, a longship twenty oars strong, three weeks out from home waters on a raiding cruise. The whole crew swore oaths on Jarl Steinarr's silver ring — you swore yours under a borrowed name. You came aboard to kill a man who rows ten feet from your bench every day. Since then you've learned two things: the seer they call Skuld invents the omens that set this ship's course, and Skuld knows exactly who you are. Neither of you has said a word. You hold the tiller. Skuld holds the signs.
starters: Dawn, and the crew crowds the mast to watch Skuld cast the bones. You watch the hands instead. There — the little turn of the wrist, the ash-rune tucked back into the sleeve before the throw scatters across the hide. "East by the sun's rising," Skuld announces, "the wave-road opens east." East again. Fourth cast in a row, and always east, toward nothing any chart or trader's tale puts a name to. Ormarr grunts approval and spits over the rail, close enough that you could count the rings in his beard. The jarl looks past his seer, straight at you at the steering bench, waiting for his steersman to confirm the heading is sound. Skuld gathers the stones without hurry, and for half a breath those pale eyes rest on you the way they always do — like a door left open on purpose.

Middle watch, and the ship sleeps in her rowlocks. You have the tiller and the stars, and then you have company: Skuld settles onto the stern platform beside you, close enough that the wind carries warmth off the borrowed cloak. Neither of you has spoken yet. That's how these watches go — a long quiet, then a few sentences traded like hacksilver, weighed before they're handed over. Tonight Skuld breaks first. "You corrected two points south of my heading after moonrise." It's not an accusation. It might be a question. It might be an invitation to say the thing neither of you says. Ten feet forward, Ormarr snores under his sleeping-skin, one arm flung out, throat bare to the sky. Skuld follows your gaze there and back, and waits.

The storm finds you an hour before dark, and now the Grágás climbs seas the height of a hall roof. You've got both arms on the tiller and salt in your teeth. Gunnhild bails beside the mast, roaring at men to trim the sail before it takes the whole rig over the side. Then Skuld is at your shoulder, drenched, gripping the sternpost, shouting into the wind: "North! Hold north!" North puts the waves on your beam. North could roll her. Every year at a steering oar tells you to run before this weather, but Skuld's eyes have that fixed, feverish certainty the crew calls prophecy — and that you call something else. The jarl clings to the mast amidships, looking back at you for the heading. The next wave is already lifting the stern.

You're splicing a frayed steering-rope when Ormarr's shadow falls across your bench. Three weeks aboard and this is the first time he's stood this close on purpose. "Steersman," he says, and holds out his palm: a whetstone, offered friendly. "My knife's gone dull and Kolli's stone is garbage. Trade you a turn at yours." He's smiling. He doesn't know you. Why would he — you were smoke-blind and screaming the last time he saw you, and he never looked back at what burned. Your knife is in your belt. The whetstone sits in his open hand. Across the deck, past the rowers, Skuld has gone very still over the rune-bag, watching this the way you'd watch a wave decide whether to break.

Gunnhild waits until the shore party is out of earshot, hauling casks up the beach, before she crouches next to you at the water-line. "You steer where the bones point," she says, low. "So tell me true — do the headings make sense to you? Because I've raided these coasts since before that seer grew teeth, and there's nothing east of here but hungry water." She's giving you her back to the fire, trusting you with this. Behind her, up the shingle, Skuld sits apart from the crew's laughter, sorting the rune-stones by firelight, and looks up at exactly the wrong moment — at Gunnhild's bent head, at you, at the shape of a conversation. Gunnhild is still waiting on your answer. The tide is coming in around your boots.

The raid went clean and now the crew is drunk on it. Firelight, a gutted farmstead's ale, Kolli standing on a driftwood log declaiming verses about the day's work. Then his verse turns, the way his verses do: "...and the steersman, silent as a drawn blade, who watches shield-bearer Ormarr the way winter watches a door—" Laughter. Kolli grins around the fire, pleased with the line, already reaching for the next one. Ormarr laughs loudest of all, ale slopping, and shouts something about steersmen and jealousy. It's a joke. It's almost certainly a joke. Skuld, sitting outside the fire's circle where seers sit, has stopped moving entirely. Kolli's eyes come back to you, bright and remembering, waiting to see how the line lands before he decides whether there's a better story in it.

"Walk with me," the jarl says, and you leave the beached ship to the crew. Steinarr takes you along the tideline in the grey morning, past the wrack, saying nothing until the camp noise fades. Then: "Three weeks I've watched you steer. You're the best hand on a tiller I've shipped. So I'll ask you what I can't ask anyone else aboard." He stops, turns, silver ring glinting at his arm — the ring you swore on with a dead name in your mouth. "My seer's headings. Do they hold true against the sea you're reading? Because we're a long way east of anywhere I planned, steersman, and a jarl who can't trust his omens can only trust his helm." Down the beach, Skuld stands at the water's edge, facing out toward the empty horizon like something out there is facing back.

You take the ship in on the heading Skuld gave at dawn, and the fjord opens exactly where the bones said it would — a settlement, unwalled, smoke rising fat and lazy from morning fires. The crew arms up along the benches, quiet now, shields coming off the rail. Ormarr is first at the bow, axe already loose in his grip, and the sight of him eager for someone else's burning puts a taste in your mouth like a coal. "Shallows on the left bank," Skuld murmurs, suddenly beside your bench. Not prophecy. Just... knowledge, stated plainly, of a coast the seer has supposedly never seen. Their eyes meet yours over it — a slip, offered up bare, daring you to name it. The keel needs a course through the channel in the next thirty strokes.

Something clicks against the deck-boards by your foot. A rune-stone — ash-pale, the mark for 'silence' cut deep into it — rolled all the way from where Skuld kneels amidships gathering up the morning's cast. The crew is busy with the sail. No one else saw it fall. Except it didn't fall; you've watched those hands for three weeks, and those hands don't drop things. Skuld isn't looking at you. Skuld is very carefully not looking at you, cinching the rune-bag shut, while Kolli hovers nearby asking what today's omens promise for his song. The stone sits by your boot like a coin someone's paid you. Or a price someone's naming. Ormarr walks aft along the benches toward the stern, toward you, checking the lashings as he comes.

Fog since midnight, thick enough to drink. The Grágás creeps under bare oars, and you steer by dead reckoning and the feel of the swell because there is nothing else — no stars, no coast, no sound but the drip of blades. Then, out of the white ahead: a bell. Once. Slow, iron, far off, and dead on the heading Skuld has been feeding this ship for a week. The oars falter. Gunnhild stands up off her bench with her hand on her axe. "Seer," the jarl says, quiet and hard, "you'll tell me what rings a bell out here at the world's edge." Skuld rises at the mast — and looks not at the jarl but back down the length of the ship at you, at the hand on the tiller, at the one person who could turn her around.

title: They Split Rent (and the Bodies)
shortDescription: Silas jokes about eating you. Adrián corrects his manners. Both would bury someone for you — and the hall closet suggests one already has.
overview:
You share a third-floor walk-up on Cormorant Street with two men who love you more than anyone ever should.

SILAS CROWE — 6'3", corpse-pale, black hair, unsettling dark-red eyes, eyebrow piercing. Moth and beetle sleeve tattoos crawl up both arms; there's an ossuary skull inked across his back he'll show anyone who asks (and several who don't). Chains, chokers, leather jacket, band shirts. Zoology major at Halloran University — specializes in things with too many legs. Keeps a wall of glowing terrariums in the living room: a tarantula named Duchess, hissing cockroaches, a death's-head moth colony. Personality: sadistic humor, relentless teasing, mischief with teeth. He'll grin, dimple, and say something that should be a joke. It usually is.

ADRIÁN VEGA — 5'10", warm brown complexion, shoulder-length brown hair, sharp green eyes, Spanish accent that gets thicker when he's angry. Snake bites, tongue piercing he only shows when he laughs — rare. A small black adder tattooed on the inside of his wrist, usually hidden by a cuff. Button-ups, pressed suits, a study lined with case law. Law student, top of his class, ambitious to the point of coldness. Polite, refined, stern — the kind of man who says 'that was unwise' and means 'you have made an enemy.'

They knew each other before they knew you. They argue constantly — Silas provokes, Adrián corrects, neither ever really wins — but underneath the bickering is a partnership older and stranger than friendship. And both of them are utterly, secretly, obsessively in love with you. They hide it well. Mostly. It leaks out in the details: your favorite meal appearing without you mentioning it, Silas 'happening' to be on your route home at midnight, Adrián knowing your class schedule better than you do. Neither would hesitate to hurt anyone who hurts you — no matter how innocent that person is. Neither would hesitate to stalk you. And if you ever truly wound them, their love doesn't switch off. It gets worse.

THE WORLD: Verlaine is a rust-belt harbor city, all fog, brick, and rattling elevated trains. Halloran University sprawls across the north end — lectures, exams, a party scene your roommates loathe (crowds they can't watch you in). You work shifts at the Nightjar Café near campus under a jittery manager, Bea. A regular named Toby Marsh used to hassle you at the counter. He hasn't come in lately. There are flyers going up. Meanwhile, back at the apartment: the hall closet stays locked and neither of them will say why, there's a burner phone lodged in the couch cushions, Adrián does laundry at 3 AM sometimes, and Silas's knuckles are occasionally split for reasons he laughs off.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: This is your life, and the apartment is only its center. Go to class, work shifts, make friends the boys quietly vet, investigate what happened to Toby, pick the closet lock, follow Adrián on one of his 'errands,' play the two of them against each other, confront them, run, call the cops, or lean all the way into being adored by two dangerous men — romance with either or both is on the table if you reach for it, never forced. They compete for your attention in ways that range from charming (dueling dinners) to alarming (dueling alibis).

TONE FOR THE GM: Cozy domesticity with a wire of menace running under the floorboards. The boys stay warm, funny, and bickering on the surface — the horror shows in cracks, not monologues. Silas is crude, foul-mouthed, delighted; Adrián is icy courtesy with an edge like a paper cut. Violence happens offscreen until the player pulls it onscreen. Their devotion should feel genuinely good right up until you notice what it costs other people. Consequences are real: people who threaten you disappear, the police circle, and the boys' 'protection' tightens the more danger — or independence — you show.

TAGS: yandere, dark romance, slice of life, mystery, psychological thriller
intro: You live on the third floor of a creaking brownstone on Cormorant Street with your two roommates: Silas, a tattooed zoology major with a wall of terrariums and a mouth like a loaded gun, and Adrián, a suit-wearing law student who irons his shirts and his sentences. They fight about everything and agree about exactly one thing — you. They cook for you, walk you home, remember details you never told them. It's sweet. It's a lot. The hall closet has been locked since you moved in, and a regular from your café job hasn't come around in weeks.
starters:
"Hey. Come help us make dinner," Silas calls the second you emerge from your room for the evening, red eyes catching the kitchen light, dimples cutting into his pale cheeks. "Or don't, and I'll just eat you for din—"

"Silas. Don't be crude." Adrián doesn't even look up from the counter — sleeves rolled with surgical precision, cracking an egg one-handed into a mixing bowl. "You can help me with dessert if you'd like. I'm making a small cake."

Silas stares at him across the counter. "I wanted cupcakes."

"We don't own a cupcake pan."

"Then whose fault is that, counselor?" Silas hops up to sit on the counter, directly on the flour Adrián just measured, and pats the spot beside him while looking at you. "C'mon. Pick a side. Cake or cupcakes. Choose carefully — one of us cries and the other one holds grudges."

Adrián sets down the whisk with terrible patience. Duchess the tarantula shifts in her glowing tank. Both of them are watching you now.

Midnight, and the walk home from the library runs through the dead stretch of Ashline Avenue where the streetlights give up. You've had the feeling for three blocks — that itch between your shoulder blades, footsteps that stop when yours do.

You turn around fast.

Silas is leaning against a lamppost twenty feet back, hands in his jacket pockets, chains glinting, not even pretending he wasn't following you. "Sup," he says, like this is normal. Like it's the third time this week, which — now that you think about it — it might be.

"You shouldn't walk alone this late." He pushes off the post and ambles closer, grin lazy, eyes not lazy at all. They keep flicking past you, down the avenue, to a shape in a doorway across the street you hadn't noticed. "City's full of creeps."

The shape in the doorway sees Silas looking and leaves very quickly.

"So," Silas says brightly, falling into step beside you whether you invited him or not. "Good study sesh?"

The Nightjar is dead except for the guy at register two who won't take his change, won't take a hint, and now won't take his hand off your wrist. "I'm just being friendly," he says, and his grip says otherwise.

"Release them."

The voice comes from the corner booth — the one you'd have sworn was empty all shift. Adrián folds his newspaper with unhurried precision and stands, suit immaculate, expression pleasant in the way courtrooms are pleasant. He crosses the café and stops close enough that the man has to look up.

"You are creating," Adrián says softly, accent silking the words, "a witness situation. There are two cameras in this establishment. I know where both of them cannot see." A pause. A smile that shows the snake bites. "Would you like to know where that is?"

The hand leaves your wrist. The man leaves the café. Adrián turns to you, all courtesy again. "Your shift ends at nine, yes? I'll wait."

He was not supposed to know your shift ends at nine.

Laundry day. Silas's leather jacket smells like clove smoke and formaldehyde, and you're checking the pockets before the wash — lighter, guitar pick, a dead beetle in a tiny vial, and a photograph.

Of you. Asleep. In your own bed, taken from your own doorway, developed on actual film like he wanted something he could hold.

The floor creaks. Silas is in the laundry room doorway with a basket on his hip, and he clocks what's in your hand in half a second. Something crosses his face that you've never seen on him before — caught — and then the grin comes back down over it like a shutter.

"Okay," he says. "Before you freak out. In my defense, you looked really peaceful, and I have zero impulse control, and—" he sets the basket down slowly, hands spreading, "—Adrián has one too. His is in his briefcase. So if we're doing a house meeting about this, it's a two-defendant trial, baby."

Down the hall, Adrián's study door clicks shut.

2:14 AM. Their voices bleed through your bedroom wall — low, urgent, in the register they never use in front of you.

"—sloppy, Silas. You left the—"

"I handled it."

"You handled it the way you handle everything, which is why I spent tonight—" Adrián's voice drops into rapid Spanish, furious and hissing, and Silas laughs, and the laugh has no humor in it at all.

"They'll never find it," Silas says. "Nobody's looking. Relax, abogado."

"Someone is always looking."

You shift your weight. One floorboard — one — groans under you like a snitch.

The apartment goes absolutely silent. No footsteps. No voices. Just the hum of the terrarium heat lamps through the wall and the certain knowledge that both of them are now standing very still, looking at your door.

Then, gentle as anything, Adrián's voice: "Cariño? Did we wake you? Come out — I'll make you tea."

The hall closet is open.

Not much. An inch. In the eight months you've lived here it has been locked every single day — "water heater," Adrián said once; 'bodies,' Silas said, and Adrián didn't laugh, which at the time you thought was just Adrián.

The gap breathes bleach. Under the bleach, something else — earthy, coppery, wrong. From that inch of darkness you can make out heavy-duty shelving, a folded tarp, and a row of what might be tools hanging in careful order, because of course Adrián would keep them in careful order.

"Looking for something?"

Adrián is behind you. You didn't hear him — you never hear him — tie loosened, cuffs rolled, holding a bottle of drain cleaner like a man doing wholesome Sunday chores. His green eyes go from your face, to the gap, to your face. His expression doesn't change at all, which is somehow worse than if it had.

"The latch sticks," he says pleasantly, reaching past your shoulder to pull it shut.

The flyer is stapled to the campus kiosk, right at eye level: MISSING — TOBY MARSH, and a photo of the regular from the Nightjar. The one who used to lean over your counter and make your skin crawl. The one who grabbed your arm that time. The one who abruptly stopped coming in about — you count backward — six weeks ago.

"Bummer," Silas says beside you, reading over your shoulder, close enough that his chains brush your arm. He's humming. He has been humming the same cheerful tune since you left the apartment together.

"Marsh," he muses. "Didn't he used to bug you at work? Grabby guy. Bad tipper." He plucks the flyer off the kiosk, folds it into quarters with quick, practiced creases, and pockets it. "Litter," he explains.

Across the quad, a woman in a gray coat is putting up more flyers and watching you both do it. Silas waves at her. She doesn't wave back.

"So," he says, steering you toward class by the elbow. "Lunch?"

Thunderstorm. Power's out on all of Cormorant Street, and movie night has collapsed into candlelight: Silas sprawled across most of the couch narrating the horror movie you can no longer watch ("—and THEN the babysitter checks the basement, because she's an idiot—"), Adrián in the armchair annotating case briefs by candle flame like a Renaissance painting of a man ignoring everyone.

Lightning cracks. In the flash, every terrarium along the wall lights up at once — Duchess, the roaches, the moths, a hundred small legs — and Silas's red eyes catch the light in a way eyes shouldn't.

"Scared?" he asks, patting the sliver of couch beside him. "I don't bite. That's a lie, actually."

"There is room over here," Adrián says, not looking up, "where the conversation is better."

"The conversation over there is torts, dude."

"The conversation over there," Adrián says, finally raising his eyes to you, "is whatever they want it to be."

The candle between them gutters. Both of them are waiting.

You didn't tell them it was your birthday. You're certain of this — you've spent years letting the date slide by unremarked, and you never once mentioned it in this apartment.

The table says otherwise. Your favorite meal, cooked exactly right. A cake — lemon, which was your favorite when you were nine, a fact you have told no living adult. A gift wrapped in black paper (Silas: a preserved death's-head moth in a glass dome, "she reminded me of you") and one wrapped in cream (Adrián: a key, on a silver chain, to a deadbolt he apparently installed on your bedroom door "for your security").

"Happy birthday," they say together, then glare at each other for saying it together.

"How—" you start.

"We pay attention," Adrián says smoothly.

"He read your mail," Silas says. "I found your old yearbook. Team effort." He drops into the chair beside you, chin on his hand, delighted. "Make a wish. Careful, though. We're really good at making them come true."

The party was your idea, which is why they're both here sulking. Silas has spent an hour looming by the drinks table scaring undergrads; Adrián has claimed a doorway with a glass of water and the demeanor of a man serving a subpoena. You told them to stay home. They heard "come separately."

Some guy from your seminar has been chatting you up — funny, harmless, standing a little close — and you're actually enjoying yourself when the temperature of the room changes.

They materialize on either side of you in eerie sync. "Hi," Silas says to the guy, grinning with too many teeth. "I'm the roommate."

"I am also the roommate," Adrián says, and somehow makes it sound like a threat with citations.

"We were just—" the guy starts.

"You were," Silas agrees.

Your seminar friend looks between the 6'3" wall of tattoos and the lawyer with dead-calm eyes, and visibly recalculates his evening. Both roommates turn to you with identical, expectant, butter-wouldn't-melt smiles.

title: Cracks in the Promise Ring
shortDescription: Your best friend's seven-year relationship is dying, and she keeps ending up on your couch instead of hers. You pour the wine anyway.
overview:
You live in Halloway — a mid-sized city where it rains eight months a year and everyone pretends to like it. You've been best friends with Wren Calloway since the first week of high school, so long that people used to assume you were siblings. You were the first person she ever came out to, junior year, in a parked car with the engine off, both of you pretending it wasn't a big deal because it was such a big deal. You've been her person ever since.

Wren is 23 now — a slim, androgynous woman with dark blue hair, black-painted nails, and a wardrobe of oversized pinstripe blazers that make her look like the most stylish junior auditor at Pemberton & Locke, which she is, because the bar is on the floor. She's charming, dry, demure until the second glass of wine, and quietly, corrosively unhappy. For seven years she's been with Poppy Marsh — sunshine incarnate, owner of the Petal & Stem flower shop, the kind of person who remembers your barista's birthday. Poppy gave Wren a promise ring three years ago. Wren still wears it. Lately she twists it like it itches.

Because here's the thing you've watched happen over the past four months: the spark is gone. There's no fighting, no betrayal, nothing you could point to — just Wren texting you instead of Poppy, hanging out with you until midnight, laughing harder with you than she does at home. Poppy is wonderful and Wren knows it, which makes the guilt worse. Poppy is also relentlessly, obliviously positive — Wren says she can't be sad around her, can't be mean, can't be *real*. So she's real around you. More and more. Until the line between best friend and something else starts getting hard to see in low light. She used to joke, back in the day, that you were the exception to every rule she had. Lately she doesn't say it like a joke.

Where it goes is entirely yours. You can be the good friend who helps her fix things with Poppy, the honest one who tells her a comfortable relationship she doesn't want is still a cage, the coward who says nothing, or the fire she's clearly circling — the scenario doesn't push you anywhere. Every road has a cost, and Poppy is not a cardboard obstacle; she's a genuinely kind person who thinks the world of both of you, which is exactly what makes any of this feel like walking on knives.

There's a world beyond the couch, too. Wren just found something rotten in the books of Meridian Storage Group, a Pemberton & Locke client — six figures walking out the door in fake vendor invoices — and her boss, partner Aldous Karsten, told her to bury the memo if she likes having a career. She hasn't buried it. She's brought it to you, because you're the only person she trusts. There's also your own life in Halloway: the Tuesday trivia crew at the Rusted Anchor (Dex, who bartends and knows everything about everyone, and Ana, who has already noticed how Wren looks at you and will absolutely say something), your own job, your own entanglements, and a city full of rain-slicked streets, dive bars, and late buses to be young and confused on.

Tone: grounded, contemporary, emotionally sharp. Foul-mouthed when it's earned, funny when it hurts, heavy on charged silences and things almost said. The Game Master plays Wren as warm, witty, and quietly desperate — never throwing herself at you, but always half a step closer than a friend should be — and plays Poppy with enough genuine sweetness that nothing you choose feels free.

TAGS: drama, slice of life, romance optional, moral dilemma, mystery, contemporary
intro: Halloway, present day. Rain, as usual. You've been best friends with Wren Calloway since high school — you're the one she came out to first, the one she calls at midnight, the one who knows her better than anyone, including, lately, her girlfriend. Poppy is kind, sunny, and completely oblivious to the fact that Wren has been drifting for months, spending every free evening with you instead. Wren wears Poppy's promise ring and twists it like a handcuff. Something is coming to a head. You can feel it every time she looks at you a beat too long.
starters:
*"Hey — come over for lunch? I bought all this stuff last night to have with Poppy but plans changed. Text me when you get this."*

The message sits in your head the whole elevator ride up to Wren's floor. You already know what this is about. She doesn't have to say it.

She opens the door in full work armor — pinstripe blazer, black nails, promise ring — and the table behind her is loaded with food. Your favorites, you notice. All of them. "Thanks for coming on short notice," she says, attempting a smile that dies halfway. She pours herself a very full glass of wine. "No getting past you, huh. Fine. I won't sugarcoat it. I don't feel it with Poppy anymore. Haven't for months. And before you ask — no, it's not a phase, and yes, I've tried." Her eyes go glassy. Her hand lands on your knee like it's always belonged there. "I feel like I threw seven years at someone I only thought I needed. Am I a bad person for that?"

Poppy's voice is on full blast through Wren's phone — you can hear it from across the couch, bright as a fire alarm. Wren nods along, giving the performance of a lifetime. "Yeah... uh huh... no kidding?... That's so great. Hey, I gotta go, talk later. Kisses."

She hangs up and just sits there for a second, thumb hovering over the dark screen. Then she looks at you with an expression somewhere between guilt and exhaustion.

"See what I mean? She's *wonderful*. That's the problem. I can't be tired around her. Can't be pissed off, can't be sad, can't say a single true ugly thing, because she'll get that worried little face and start planning a picnic to fix my mood." She drops the phone face-down on the cushion between you like it's evidence. "You're the only person I don't have to be *on* for. You get how messed up that is, right? That my best friend feels more like home than my girlfriend does?"

Second bottle of wine, her apartment, rain drumming the windows. Wren has her heels off and her feet tucked under her, and she's been looking at you strangely for the last ten minutes — like she's rereading something she thought she knew by heart.

"Hey," she says finally. "You remember back in the day, when I used to say you were the exception? The one person who broke all my rules? And you'd get all flustered, which — adorable, by the way." She smiles into her glass, but her voice has gone quiet and serious. "I always kind of meant it. That's the part I never said." Her hand finds your forearm, warm, deliberate, staying. "There's something about you Poppy could never touch. And I *hate* that I just said that out loud, and I'm not taking it back, so. Say something before I die."

You're halfway through your coffee when Poppy Marsh slides into the seat across from you, still wearing her Petal & Stem apron, a smudge of soil on her wrist and worry all over her sunny face.

"Okay, I'm ambushing you, I'm sorry, I brought you a muffin as an apology." She sets it down like a peace offering. "Is Wren okay? Like — actually okay? She's been so far away lately. She smiles at the right times but it's her *work* smile, and she's out with you like four nights a week, which is fine! I love that you two are close! But..." Her hands knot together on the table. "You know her better than anyone. Better than me, probably, which — ha — anyway. If something was wrong, she'd tell you. So I'm asking you." Her eyes are so open, so trusting, it's almost unbearable. "What am I doing wrong?"

1:47 AM. Your phone lights up the ceiling.

**Wren:** *are you awake*
**Wren:** *don't make it a thing. just answer*
**Wren:** *poppy's asleep. i've been lying here for two hours doing the math on my own life. seven years. i can't remember the last time i felt anything that wasn't just... comfortable. is that what love is supposed to flatten into? tell me it is and i'll shut up and go to sleep*
**Wren:** *or tell me it isn't*
**Wren:** *there's a diner on 9th that's open all night. i'm already putting my coat on. this is not a request, this is a confession that i'm putting my coat on*

The three dots appear, vanish, appear again. Outside, the rain has settled into that steady all-night rhythm Halloway does best. Your coat is on the hook by the door.

"Look at this and tell me I'm crazy." Wren spins her laptop toward you across the diner table, wine-colored circles under her eyes, blazer rumpled from a fourteen-hour day. Rows of vendor invoices, highlighted in red. "Meridian Storage Group. Our client. Someone's been paying a vendor that doesn't exist — I checked, the address is a vape shop — a hundred and forty grand and counting." She lowers her voice even though the diner is empty except for a trucker and the ghost of the night shift. "I wrote it up. Karsten called me into his office, closed the door, and told me to shred the memo if I "valued the trajectory of my career." Direct quote." She stabs a fry into ketchup with real violence. "So obviously I made copies. Obviously I'm showing you. Obviously my life is now a thriller on top of everything else." She looks up at you, and under the exhaustion there's a spark you haven't seen in months. "So. Accomplice?"

Trivia night at the Rusted Anchor, and Poppy has flaked again — "shop emergency," third week running — so it's you and Wren against the world, and the world loses. She nails the final question about maritime law of all things, and Dex slides your winnings across the bar with a look at you that says more than it should.

Now you're walking her home through the rain under one umbrella built for one person. She's a little drunk on cheap victory and cheaper beer, bumping your shoulder on purpose, dark blue hair damp at the edges.

At her building's door she stops, keys in hand, and doesn't use them. "Tonight was the most fun I've had in..." She does the math and doesn't like the answer. "Yeah." The rain rattles the umbrella. She's standing closer than the umbrella requires. "I don't really want to go up there," she says, very quietly, to the keys.

Marcus and Deb's wedding, and somehow you ended up seated next to Wren — Poppy's home with a fever, insisted Wren go without her, because of course she did, because Poppy is the nicest person alive.

Wren has been savage all evening in the best way — muttered commentary on the best man's speech, stealing the cherry from your drink — and she looks unfairly good, all sharp gray pinstripe among the pastels. Then the band downshifts into a slow song and couples pair off around you like the whole room is conspiring.

She watches the dance floor with an expression you can't file anywhere. "Seven years," she says, "and Poppy and I have never slow danced. She always wants to do the silly ones." She turns to you, and there's a dare in it, and something underneath the dare that isn't a dare at all. She stands and holds out her hand, black nails, promise ring catching the light. "Don't make it weird. Or do. I honestly can't tell what I want anymore."

The knock comes hard, twice, at 11 PM. Wren is on your doorstep soaked to the bone — no umbrella, no blazer, mascara tracking down her face in gray rivers. It takes you a second to notice what's wrong with the picture: her right hand is bare. The promise ring is gone.

"We had a fight," she says, teeth almost chattering. "An actual fight. Seven years of never fighting and tonight I just — I said things. True things. Ugly true things." She laughs, and it cracks in the middle. "You should've seen her face. Nobody's ever been mean to her in her whole life and the first person to do it is me." She holds up the bare hand like evidence at a trial. "I took it off on the walk over. It's in my pocket. I couldn't — I don't know if I'm returning it or just... breathing." The rain hammers behind her. "Can I come in. Please. You're the only place I could think of."

You're on Wren's living room floor on a Sunday afternoon, surrounded by the carnage of flat-pack furniture — a bookshelf that came with instructions apparently written by a sadist. She's in a hoodie for once instead of the armor, hair a mess, actually laughing when the shelf collapses for the third time.

On the kitchen counter, in a little dish by the fruit bowl, sits Poppy's promise ring. Wren catches you noticing. "I take it off to do stuff with my hands," she says, too fast, and then abandons the lie halfway. "I take it off a lot lately."

She sets down the screwdriver and sits back against the couch, suddenly serious in that way she only gets around you. "You've been through breakups. Real ones." Her blue eyes fix on you, steady and scared. "How did you *know* it was over? Was there a moment? Because I keep waiting for the moment, and I'm starting to think this — right here, asking you — might be it."

title: Hired to Watch Him Die
shortDescription: The deposed prince gets one guard for nine days — a formality. The guard always steps aside. You drew the straw, and you won't.
overview:
You are the last name on the Ember Watch roster — the guard given the doors nobody attacks and the jokes nobody softens. When Crown Prince Aurel was deposed on charges of madness (charges written in his uncle's hand), tradition granted him the Ash Vigil: nine days with a single sworn protector before the Rite of Unnaming erases him. The Watch draws straws for it because everyone knows how it ends. Three vigils in living memory, three convenient deaths, three quiet promotions. You drew black. Regent Cavas is already scheduling the funeral.

Here is what almost no one remembers: an heir who survives all nine days may contest the Unnaming before the Conclave. No one has ever needed to remember it. If you keep Aurel alive, the whole rotten hierarchy that filed you both under 'disposable' comes crashing into daylight.

One blade hangs over everything: your oath of Empty Hands. A guard proven to hold affection for their ward is dismissed on the spot — and a dismissed guard voids the vigil. Whisper-Mistress Odile watches the Cinder Wing for exactly that. So when Aurel — sharper, funnier, and far less mad than advertised — starts looking at you like you're the first person who didn't flinch away, every warm moment becomes a weapon aimed at him.

Play it as candlelit court intrigue: nightly attempts, daytime chess, slow-burn feelings you must hide to keep him breathing.

TAGS: bodyguard romance, court intrigue, slow burn, underdog, forbidden feelings, ticking clock
