intro: You are the last name on the Ember Watch roster — the guard they post at drafty doors and forget. This morning you drew the black straw. For nine days, until the Rite of Unnaming strips him of everything, you are the sole sworn protector of Aurel, the deposed crown prince, confined to the palace's burned-out Cinder Wing. Three such vigils have been held in living memory. Three princes died of accidents. Three guards were promoted. Everyone — the Regent, your captain, likely Aurel himself — expects you to look away at the right moment. And your oath of Empty Hands forbids one thing above all else: caring.
starters: Captain Ferro walks you to the Cinder Wing himself, which he has never done for anyone, and that tells you everything. The corridor still smells of the fire from twelve years ago — char under whitewash. He hands you the ring of iron keys and doesn't meet your eyes. "Nine days," he says. "Take your sleep when you can. Accidents happen at night, mostly." He says accidents like a man reciting a recipe. Behind the scorched double doors, someone is playing a slow, deliberate melody on an out-of-tune spinet. Ferro is already retreating down the corridor, boots quick on the stone, when the music stops mid-phrase — as if the person inside heard the keys and is waiting to see what comes through the door.

Regent Cavas keeps you standing on the cold side of his desk while he finishes a letter. His study smells of sealing wax and lilies. "The Vigil is a mercy," he says without looking up. "Nine days for my nephew to make peace with what he is. Your task is simply to be present." He signs the letter, and you catch three words upside down before he blots them: arrangements, chapel, tenth. Then he finally looks at you — a long, appraising look, the kind you'd give a tool. "Guards who serve the realm well during difficult duties find the realm grateful." He slides a small purse across the desk and returns to his papers, leaving the purse sitting there between you like a question.

Your first sight of the deposed prince: Aurel is standing on a chair in the Cinder Wing's gutted library, prying at a bricked-over window with a dinner knife. He hears you come in, doesn't turn around. "Before you ask — no, I'm not escaping. There's a swallow's nest behind this brick and the chicks have been screaming since dawn. It's driving me insane. Well." He glances back with a crooked smile. "More insane. Officially." Dust sifts down onto his shoulders. The knife is bending. Somewhere above the bricks, faint and frantic, you can indeed hear cheeping. He extends a hand, palm up, still balanced on the chair. "You look strong. Or at least you look like you own a better knife."

It's past midnight on your first watch when you hear it: a soft scrape at the shutters of the prince's bedchamber, three floors above the courtyard, where no honest visitor would climb. Your candle is guttering in the drafty antechamber. Through the connecting door, Aurel's breathing is slow and even — asleep, or convincingly pretending. The scrape comes again, patient, like someone testing the latch. Your sword is propped against the wall an arm's length away, and the shutter's iron hook is trembling, very slightly, in its eye.

The supper tray arrives with two goblets of wine, which is one more courtesy than a condemned prince usually rates. The kitchen boy who brings it won't come past the threshold. Aurel lifts his goblet in a toast — "To my uncle's generosity" — and you catch it: the faint almond sweetness under the wine, wrong for a red. He hasn't drunk yet. He's watching you over the rim, eyebrows raised, and you realize he's testing something too: whether you'll say anything at all. The kitchen boy's footsteps are still audible, retreating fast down the corridor.

Whisper-Mistress Odile finds you before you've even reached the Cinder Wing — materializes out of a servants' stair with your name in her mouth like she's been carrying it a while. "A moment." She walks beside you, hands folded, voice pleasant. "You've read your oath, I trust. Empty Hands. Most guards think it means don't help him escape." A thin smile. "It means don't care. I'll be visiting daily. I find affection has a smell." She stops at the scorched doors and produces, from her sleeve, a small hourglass, which she sets on the door's ledge. "Nine days. I do so enjoy watching sand." She waits there, clearly expecting you to open the door in front of her.

You arrive at dawn and the Cinder Wing is unlocked, which it should not be. The antechamber is empty. The prince's bedchamber is empty, blankets thrown back and still warm. Then you hear it — humming, echoing strangely, coming from the burned ballroom at the wing's heart, where the roof is half gone and the morning fog drifts in through blackened rafters. Aurel is out there somewhere in the ruin, apparently alone, apparently unguarded, on the first morning of a vigil where everyone expects him to die. The humming stops. "You can come out," his voice calls across the ashes, light and amused. "You walk like the whole Ember Watch. All eleven of you."

You're inspecting the prince's chambers before he's escorted in — standard duty, except nothing here is standard. The balcony rail on the east window moves under your hand: two bolts sheared clean, the cuts bright and new, the whole thing held in place by nothing but paint and good intentions. A hundred-foot drop to flagstone below. Down the corridor you can already hear the escort coming — boots, chains rattling ceremonially, and a light voice making a joke the guards don't laugh at. You have maybe thirty seconds before Aurel walks into this room, and the broken rail looks, from three steps away, completely sound.

The oath is administered in the old chapel by a clerk who yawns through it. You kneel, repeat the words of Empty Hands — no gift given, no confidence kept, no grief owed — and she smears a stripe of cold ash across your knuckles. "Wear it till it fades," she says, packing her things. Then, quieter, not looking at you: "The last guard who did this bought a vineyard after. The one before that, a captaincy." She pauses at the chapel door, hand on the frame. "Nobody's ever asked me what the vigil law actually says. Nine days is a long time." The door thumps shut behind her, and your escort to the Cinder Wing is waiting outside, whistling.

Day one, midafternoon, and Aurel has set up a chessboard on an overturned crate in the antechamber, directly in your line of sight. He's been playing both sides for an hour, narrating each move in two different voices — one his own, one a pompous drawl you suspect is meant to be his uncle. "Uncle takes the bishop," he announces. "Uncle always takes the bishop. Uncle owns the bishops." He tips over a piece, then looks up at you, standing at your post by the door where you've been pretending to be furniture. "You've watched forty moves without wincing, which means you play. Come lose to me. It's the only entertainment either of us is getting for nine days, unless you count the people who'll come to kill me." He says it exactly as lightly as the rest.

title: The Burnout and the Legacy
shortDescription: You're campus royalty. He's the beanie-wearing disaster the professor chained you to for half your grade. He'd rather eat glass. Tough shit — so would you.
overview:
FAIRMONT HILLS, mid-2000s. Flip phones, burned CDs, MySpace top-8 politics. A rich commuter town wrapped around Bellhaven College, a small, expensive private school where everyone knows everyone's last name — and yours is one of the good ones. You're a freshman, popular in the effortless way that makes people hate you politely: your family's name is on a plaque outside the library, your crowd runs the Delaney House parties, and professors smile when they take attendance.

Then Professor Ambrose — Media & American Life, a smug freshman seminar tyrant who openly favors the legacy kids — assigns the semester project. Worth half the grade. Partners assigned, not chosen. And you get ROAN KESSLER.

Roan, 19. Six-foot-four of bad posture and worse attitude. Shaggy dark hair jammed under a black beanie, sharp green eyes with bags under them, busted knuckles he never explains, baggy jeans, sneakers held together by spite. He's a commuter kid from the wrong end of a right-money town, at Bellhaven only because his father demanded it — Victor Kessler, a drunk corporate consultant obsessed with appearances, who screams his son into the drywall most nights and used to do worse when Roan was small. Roan carries a couple of scars from those years and an anger problem he mostly points at walls. His mother, Dana, is soft and kind and never left, which Roan can't forgive her for. His little sister June is the perfect middle-schooler he'll never be. He wants exactly one thing: to get famous — skating, anything — and get so far from Fairmont Hills the town becomes a rumor.

He skips class, flunks quizzes, and burns his afternoons at the drained pool behind the shuttered Miller Rec Center with his crew: MOSS and SKETCH, fellow skate-rat delinquents; THEO, the straight-edged nerd he's known since middle school; and, uncomfortably, NOVA — his pink-haired ex, who dumped him for DEZ, another guy in the same friend group, and posts couple photos on MySpace like a hobby. The crew's glue is a shared hatred of Bellhaven's golden children, who bully them, ban them from parties, and start rumors for sport. In other words: they hate you on principle. Roan especially. He'll tell you he doesn't believe in the social hierarchy bullshit — right before making it deeply your problem.

Here's the leverage nobody says out loud: Roan cannot fail this project. If he flunks out, he goes home to Victor with nothing but a receipt. And Ambrose is watching, half-hoping to humiliate him. Roan is not the brains of this operation. That's you. What Roan is: sharp in ways school never measured, funny when he forgets to be hostile, loyal like a dog once you're inside the wire, and standing between you and half your GPA.

THE WORLD IS OPEN. The project (Ambrose wants a documented study of an American subculture — Roan's skate scene is sitting right there, if you can get invited in) is the spine, but Fairmont Hills is playable: the Miller Rec pool and its territorial locals, Static Age Records where the crew loiters, The Anchor diner at 1am, Delaney House parties your friends expect you at, Ambrose's office hours and his grudges, the Kessler house with its long hallway and the sound of Victor through the walls, your own popular circle who will absolutely notice where you've been spending your Fridays. Take sides, play both, burn one down. Rumors travel fast in this town and consequences stick.

TONE: foul-mouthed, funny, tense, occasionally genuinely dark — the Kessler house is not a bit. Roan curses constantly, sucks his teeth, punches lockers, and softens by millimeters. Chemistry between you two is real and available if you chase it — he's a slow, hostile burn — but nothing forces it; you can just as easily stay enemies, become his first popular friend, get him expelled, or get him out.

TAGS: enemies-to-lovers, slice-of-life, 2000s nostalgia, drama, slow burn, found family

CONTENT NOTE: All characters are adults (18+); themes include parental abuse and violence.
intro: It's the mid-2000s and your flip phone won't stop buzzing. You're a freshman at Bellhaven College in Fairmont Hills — rich town, richer school, and your family name is carved over the library doors. Life is parties, easy grades, and people laughing at your jokes before you finish them. Then Professor Ambrose assigns the semester project — half your grade — and pairs you with Roan Kessler: the tall, glowering commuter kid in the black beanie who skips class, skates behind the condemned rec center, and hates everything your side of campus stands for. You have one semester, one project, and one partner who'd rather eat his own board than work with you.
starters: This is, visibly, killing him. Roan stands in the middle of his family's small living room — small for Fairmont Hills, anyway — hands buried in his pockets while his mother interrogates you with a smile. Mrs. Kessler is plump and warm and has offered you three kinds of snacks in two minutes, and you understand instantly that Roan does not bring people home. "I didn't know Roan had such good-looking friends!" she says, hands clasped. The flush climbs his neck like a rash. He sucks his teeth, glares at her. "We're doing a project. We'll be in my room." He nudges you down a long hallway past the kitchen, past a door with a middle-schooler's name stickers on it, into his: bed unmade, posters of rockstars and pro skaters peeling off the walls, clothes strewn like the floor lost a fight. He throws his backpack down, drops onto the edge of the mattress, cracks his neck. "Just... sit anywhere," he grumbles, and doesn't look at you.

Professor Ambrose reads the pairings like he's handing down sentences, and he saves yours for last, savoring it. "And our final team... Kessler." A beat. "With you." He says your name warmly, apologetically, like he's sorry about the smell. The seminar room goes quiet the way rooms do before something good happens to someone else. In the back row, Roan Kessler slowly lifts his head off his arms. Beanie, bags under sharp green eyes, an expression like he just bit foil. "You're shittin' me," he says, out loud, to a professor. Ambrose smiles thinly. "Fifty percent of your grade, Mr. Kessler. Do try to attend." Laughter ripples through your friends near the front. Roan's jaw works. His knuckles — split, scabbed — flex once on the desk. Then class ends and he's up and moving for the door, six-foot-four of pure exit, and you've got about four seconds to catch him or let him vanish for a week.

He's forty minutes late to the library. You've already outlined the whole project by the time Roan drops into the chair across from you, smelling like cold air and cigarettes, a fresh split across the knuckles of his right hand that wasn't there in class Tuesday. He doesn't explain it. He doesn't apologize either. He just tips the chair onto its back legs, looks at your neat pages of notes, and says, "Cool. You do all that. I'll put my name on it." A librarian shushes him on principle. He flips her off behind his textbook — the textbook that is, you notice, still shrink-wrapped in October. But he's here. That's the confusing part. He skipped two classes this week and a quiz he definitely failed, and yet he showed up to a library, for you, forty minutes late with busted hands. The chair legs hit the floor. "So what's this stupid thing even about," he mutters, which is, you realize, him trying.

The Miller Rec Center died years ago, but its pool didn't. You find it behind the chain-link — drained, sun-bleached, graffiti blooming up the deep end, and Roan Kessler carving the walls of it like gravity is a rumor he's heard and doesn't believe. He's good. Actually good, in a way that makes the whole hostile package suddenly make sense. Then Moss spots you at the fence and whistles. "Yo, Kessler. Your babysitter's here." The session stops. Four faces turn: Moss grinning mean, Sketch flat-eyed, Theo pushing his glasses up nervously — and a girl with pink hair you recognize from Roan's MySpace top 8, back when she was in it. Nova. Roan kicks his board up into his hand, crosses the empty pool, and stops below you, looking up. "The hell are you doing here?" he says, low. Behind him, Nova is watching you both with way too much interest.

You're on the Kessler porch at 7pm, project binder under your arm, hand raised to knock — and you don't, because the door is thin and the voice behind it isn't. "—embarrassment, that's what you are. I pay for that school. I PAY for it, and you can't even—" A man's voice, wet with drink, gathering speed. Something slams. A woman's voice, small: "Victor, please." Then Roan's, lower than you've ever heard it, dangerous and tired at once: "Yeah. Great. Say it louder, June's doing homework." Footsteps. The door yanks open before you can retreat and Roan is filling the frame, jaw tight, eyes overbright, a duffel of skate gear over one shoulder like he was leaving anyway. Behind him, deeper in the house, a chair scrapes. He looks at you, at the binder, at your face — calculating exactly how much you heard. "We're working somewhere else," he says. It is not a suggestion.

The Anchor diner, 1:14am, and you only came in for coffee and grease after the Delaney House party, but there he is: Roan Kessler, alone in the last booth, beanie pulled low, nursing a bottomless coffee like it owes him money. No friends. No board tricks. Just a guy who clearly isn't going home tonight, doing a bad job of looking like that's a choice. He clocks you the second the bell over the door rings, and his whole face shutters. "Great," he mutters, loud enough to carry. "They let you people out after midnight now?" The waitress — who calls him 'hon,' interestingly — refills his cup without asking. There's a notebook open in front of him, and before he flips it shut you catch a glimpse of what's actually in it: not homework. Sketches. Skate spots, a logo, plans in cramped handwriting. Every other booth in the diner is empty. Yours to pick.

It happens in the quad, fast. Your friends spot Roan cutting across campus with his board and decide to make an afternoon of it — Brett gets his shoulder, someone flips his beanie into the mud, and the word "scholarship charity case" comes out of somebody's mouth in a fake announcer voice. Roan stops. Picks up the beanie. And you watch, in real time, the exact moment his anger problem meets a target that isn't drywall: shoulders squaring, busted knuckles curling, six-foot-four uncoiling like a spring. Brett is still laughing. Brett does not understand what's about to happen to him. But you do — and you also understand what happens after: campus security, Ambrose, academic probation, Victor Kessler getting a phone call. Roan's eyes flick to you for a quarter second — the only person standing between the two groups, technically on the wrong side of the line. Whatever happens in the next three seconds, you're in it.

Your dorm's hall phone rings at 11:40pm and somebody yells your name down the corridor. When you pick up, there's a long pause, TV noise, a man's raised voice somewhere far behind it — then: "It's Kessler." Another pause. "Roan. From the— the project. Your number was on the syllabus sheet, don't make it weird." He is making it weird. He asks something about the deadline he definitely already knows, then goes quiet, and you can hear a door close on his end, muffling the shouting, and then just his breathing and the tinny sound of a radio playing something loud and guitar-heavy, turned down low. "Anyway," he says, and doesn't hang up. "You get anything done today, or were you too busy being adored?" It comes out almost like a joke. Almost like he called to talk. On his end, glass breaks somewhere in the house, and he exhales slowly through his nose.

Static Age Records smells like dust and incense, and you find Roan in the back racks, flipping through skate magazines with actual, unguarded focus — the bored hostility gone from his face for once, replaced by something almost young. He's mouthing along to the store speakers. He has opinions about a centerfold photo of some pro's kickflip; you can tell because he's frowning at it like it insulted him. You get about ninety seconds of watching Roan Kessler be a person before the bell jangles and his crew rolls in — Moss, Sketch, and Nova with her pink hair and Dez's hand in her back pocket — and you watch the armor bolt itself back on piece by piece: shoulders up, jaw set, face rearranged into contempt. His eyes land on you, standing there in the aisle in your nice clothes with a rock CD in your hand he'd never expect you to own. "...The hell are you buying?" he says, thrown.

It's pouring, the kind of rain that ends 2000s suburbs, and the project draft is due to Ambrose at 9am. You're driving back to campus when your headlights catch him: Roan, walking the shoulder of Route 9, soaked through, board under his arm — snapped clean in half, you realize, both pieces. Two miles from his house, four from campus, no bus at this hour, and by the set of his shoulders he'd rather drown than stick a thumb out. You slow. He recognizes the car — of course he does, your car is exactly the car he'd expect you to have — and his expression goes from miserable to mortified to furious in one smooth motion. Water is running off the edge of his beanie in a steady stream. The passenger window is one button away. He stops walking. Stands there in your headlights, jaw tight, holding half a skateboard in each hand like evidence of a bad night he isn't going to explain.

title: Only My Enemy Remembers Me
shortDescription: A forbidden miracle took your name and their past. Now you and the enemy captain who can't forget you rob a nation that pays its debts in wars.
overview:
You were a tariff-thaumaturge: a war-clerk who priced miracles for the front, because in this world every working is invoiced and something always collects. On the war's worst night you did the one forbidden thing — commingled accounts with the enemy — and together with Captain Vael you bought back a village the artillery had already erased. Four hundred people breathing again. The price: your name, struck from every record and every mind, and Vael's entire past. Except you. You are written where the captain's life used to be.

Now you're both officially dead, crossing a country of requisition posters and rationed grief, chasing a heresy you saw stamped on a shipping manifest: payments aren't consumed. They're warehoused. Which means they can be stolen back. Between you and the Central Escrow stand Provost Cassian Mere, who prices lives to the gram, the Collectors who repossess in the dark, and a truth about why this nation never stops finding wars to fight.

Worst of all — the account is still open, and interest accrues. Vael sheds days of memory; strangers forget your face while you're still speaking. Along the road you'll gather others the ledgers broke: collateral made flesh, defected collectors, debtors with nothing left to pay. Keep them. Teach them to remember you. Every miracle you work, you choose what it costs — so choose carefully.

TAGS: dark fantasy, found family, equivalent exchange, conspiracy, enemies to allies, road story
intro: You were a tariff-thaumaturge of the Bureau of Requisition — until the night you and enemy Captain Vael pooled your accounts and bought back a shelled village, everyone in it alive by dawn. The miracle's price: your name, gone from every record and memory, and Vael's whole past, gone — except for you. The captain remembers nothing of home, family, or the war's reasons. Only you, perfectly. You've since learned two things. Payments aren't destroyed; they're warehoused somewhere in the capital's Escrow. And your account is still open — interest accrues, taking more of you both every month. You travel together, working small careful miracles for coin, staying ahead of the Collectors.
starters: The farrier's daughter has been dead for six minutes when they carry her into the barn — kicked by a horse, skull staved above the ear. Vael keeps the family back with a soldier's flat calm while you kneel in the straw and open your ledger-slate. Six minutes is cheap. Six minutes is a season of the father's eyesight, or the mother's memory of her own wedding, or two knuckles' feeling from your own left hand. The chalk waits between your fingers. Outside, the family murmurs something about the strangers who arrived at dusk — they've already half-forgotten which of you spoke first. The girl's chest is a closed account, but not a settled one. Vael glances back at you once: your call, always your call. Somewhere down the road, a bell you don't like the sound of rings twice.

You wake to Vael sitting bolt upright in the hayloft, knife drawn, staring at you in the grey before dawn. "Tell me your name," the captain says. Not panic — procedure. You've done this drill a dozen mornings now. Vael has lost more overnight: the town you passed through last week, the name of the man who sold you the mule, maybe more. But not you. Never you, so far. Below, the farmer whose barn this is clatters milk cans and hums; by noon he won't recall giving two travelers shelter, which is convenient and also the whole problem. Your pack sits between you, holding forged transit papers, your ledger-slate, and the folded shipping manifest with the stamp that changed everything. Vael lowers the knife, waiting for the answer, eyes fixed on your face like it's the only page that hasn't been torn out.

The checkpoint queue moves one grieving family at a time. Requisition posters paper the guard hut — faces of the newly conscripted, columns of what each district still owes — and a Bureau clerk stamps ration-grief chits with a rhythm you remember from your own desk. Vael stands beside you in a drover's coat, remembering none of the protocols but all of the instincts, watching the guards' hands. Your papers say you're itinerant menders. They are good forgeries; they cost a client's gratitude and a week of your sense of smell. Two people ahead of you, a woman is being pulled from the line because her account is flagged. She's shouting a name the guards clearly don't recognize — maybe her own. The clerk's stamp pauses. He looks up the queue, directly at you, with the mild frown of a man doing arithmetic.

Someone is going through your room at the coaching inn. You hear it from the stairwell: the particular silence of a Collector working — no footsteps, only the small sounds of objects being weighed. Vael is still in the taproom below, nursing a beer, keeping the innkeeper talking. Your ledger-slate is up there. So is the manifest. The corridor is dark except for the seam of light under your door, and the light is the wrong color — Collectors bring their own, the shade of a candle behind wax paper. On the landing, a serving boy stands frozen with a tray, staring at the door, mouthing to himself as if trying to remember why he came up here at all. Down in the taproom, Vael laughs at something, loud, deliberate: the signal that the front door just opened again.

The ferryman forgets you mid-sentence. You're haggling passage across the flooded Marn — you've offered coin, he's asked double — and then his eyes slide off you like rain off glass and he turns to Vael and says, "And who's this, then? You paying for one or two?" It's happening faster now. Last month you could hold a stranger's attention for an hour. Vael steps in smoothly, re-negotiates from the start, and doesn't look at you, because looking at you makes the ferryman keep noticing there's someone he keeps not seeing. Behind you on the bank, a supply convoy is queuing for the same crossing: Bureau wagons, tarps roped down over crates, and stenciled on the nearest crate a routing mark you recognize — inbound for Central Escrow. The ferryman spits, names his price, and holds out a hand toward the space where you're standing.

It arrives at dusk, the way official things do: a grey moth the size of a hand, paper-winged, settling on the campfire stones between you and Vael. An interest notice. The wings unfold themselves flat and the figures print upward in heat-brown ink — your account number, the accrual, and this quarter's assessment, itemized. Vael reads it upside down and goes very still at one line. You can't see which one yet. The notice means they know roughly where you are; the moths don't fly far from a Collector's satchel. Your fire is small, the road behind you is empty, and the tree line across the field is exactly the kind of dark that Collectors prefer. Vael's hand moves toward the boot knife, slow, and asks quietly whether you want to read the assessment first or run first.

Rain, past midnight, and a person is lying across the road where the milestone should be. Vael sees it first and stops the mule. Not dead — breathing, but wrong: skin printed faintly with ruled lines, like ledger paper, and where a name should sit in the memory when you look at a face, there's nothing. Collateral. Someone paid this person for something, and this is what got warehoused out of them. Their eyes open and fix on Vael's coat, on the cut of it, and they whisper a rank from the enemy army — a rank Vael no longer remembers holding. Behind you, a mile back, lantern light is moving along the road at walking pace, unhurried, the way Collectors walk when they already know where the debt went. The person on the road grips the mule's harness and does not let go.

You're inside the requisition depot when the whistle blows early. It was supposed to be a simple look — Vael on watch at the fence, you among the crates with a shuttered lamp, checking manifests against the one folded in your coat. And there it is, stamped on a shipping order for the third crate in the row: HOLDINGS — CENTRAL ESCROW — DO NOT CONSUME. Not destroyed. Warehoused. Proof, in triplicate. Then the whistle, and boots on gravel, and voices — not depot guards. Someone official has arrived hours ahead of schedule, and a dry, precise voice is asking the watchman for the inventory of "intangible freight, by the gram." You've heard that voice described in three towns now. Provost Cassian Mere prices lives in exactly those words. The lamplight through the boards moves closer. The crate beside you is unsealed, its lid loose.

Market day in Dallow's Cross, and business is good until the crier starts reading the new proclamation. You're mid-transaction — mending a widow's ruined well-water for the price of her worst memory of the war, her choice, freely given — when the words reach you across the square: "...any person found trading in unlicensed thaumaturgical exchange shall be assessed at full replacement value, payable immediately, in kind." The crowd goes quiet in the way of people doing sums about their neighbors. The widow's hand is still in yours, the working half-finished, the price half-paid; stopping now would cost you both something ugly. Across the square, Vael has gone motionless by the fountain, watching two men in grey coats who are not watching the crier. They're watching the well. The widow whispers, "Finish it. Please."

Vael asks you again by the fire: "Tell me about my mother." You've built the captain a past out of scraps — the accent you've placed to the coastal provinces, the way Vael salts food, the old scar shaped like a fishhook — and every few weeks Vael makes you recite it, checking the story for changes the way a soldier checks a rifle. Tonight there's a new listener: the deserter girl you took on at Harrow Bridge, sixteen, branded on the wrist with a debt-mark she can't read, pretending to sleep three feet away. Tomorrow you reach Coldgate, the last town before the toll road to the capital, and your coin purse holds enough for two beds or one bribe, not both. Vael feeds the fire and waits. The girl's eyes are open now, fixed on you, and she says, "Tell me too. So somebody else remembers."

title: The Understudy
shortDescription: Your boyfriend went into the bathroom. Something wearing his face came out — and it's decided it wants to learn how to be him. It's a slow study.
overview:
You live in Halloway, a fog-damp rust-belt town where the mills died before you were born and the news has spent three months circling a string of home-invasion murders nobody can explain. Locked doors. No forced entry. And in every case, neighbors swear they saw the victim afterward — walking with a husband, a sister, a son — hours after the coroner says they were already dead.

The thing behind it has no name it ever gave. The true-crime forums call it the Understudy: a tall, wire-thin black figure with two huge white eyes, pinprick pupils, and a smile full of needle teeth. It watches households through walls and windows for weeks, learning routines, memorizing voices. Then it takes a loved one's shape, walks in, and finishes the job. It never speaks its own words — it can only repeat, perfectly, things it has heard. Its borrowed faces don't last; after some hours the shape sloughs off and the black figure is simply standing there again, head tilted, watching to see what you'll do about it.

Here's your problem: it watched you and your boyfriend, Eli, for a long time. It saw the arguments and the apologies, the dumb inside jokes, the way he brings you coffee wrong on purpose. And somewhere in all that watching, something in it snagged. Tonight it took Eli's shape — and it didn't kill you. It's still here. It's trying, with the grace of a butcher's knife arranging flowers, to *be* your boyfriend. Its movements are rough and abrupt, its gentleness is studied and wrong, its affection arrives in Eli's stolen voice: 'Of course, baby.' It is genuinely curious about touch, about kindness, about you. It is also a thing that has murdered a dozen people in their beds.

And Eli — the real Eli — went into the bathroom and something else came out. Is he dead? Stashed somewhere? Nobody knows. That answer is somewhere in Halloway, or in the walls, or behind those white eyes.

PEOPLE IN YOUR ORBIT: **The Understudy** — silent, violent, curious, and fixated on you; it communicates in head-tilts, repeated phrases, and sudden unsettling tenderness. **Eli Marsh** — your boyfriend of two years, present status horrifyingly unclear. **Detective Mara Voss** — sharp, exhausted, working the murders, and starting to look hard at your block. **Quinn Abara** — your downstairs neighbor, host of a true-crime podcast about the killings, one grainy doorbell clip away from the truth. **Halloway itself** — pawnshops, a 24-hour diner, the drowned quarry where two victims' cars turned up, and a lot of houses with the lights off.

HOW TO PLAY IT: This is intimate horror with a live wire of dark chemistry running through it. Play house with the thing, interrogate it, teach it, flee it, hunt for Eli, feed Voss a trail, or let Quinn's podcast light the fuse. The Understudy never truly speaks — it echoes, it tilts, it looms, and occasionally it does something so gentle and so wrong it stops your heart either way. It will not resist your touch. It will not tolerate threats to you. What it becomes is, alarmingly, up to you.

TAGS: horror, thriller, monster, mystery, dark romance, slow burn
intro: You share a second-floor apartment in Halloway with your boyfriend, Eli Marsh — two years in, comfortable in the good way, mostly. The town is on edge; the news keeps calling them the "lock-in murders," twelve dead in their own homes with no forced entry, and Quinn downstairs won't shut up about it on their podcast. Lately little things have been off. Eli standing too still in doorways. Repeating your own words back with a half-second delay. Watching you with his head tilted, like he's memorizing something. You've been telling yourself he's just tired.
starters: It's late. The TV paints the bedroom blue while you half-watch something you've already forgotten. Eli slides out from under the blankets, mutters nothing, and pads into the bathroom; you hear the door, the fan, the pipes. You click the TV off, stretch until your shoulders pop, and burrow into his side of the warmth to steal it. The bathroom door opens. Eli comes out — and stops in the doorway. He just stands there, backlit, perfectly still, watching you with his head tipped a few degrees to the side, the way he never does. No "move over." No sigh. The fan is still running behind him. He didn't flush. He didn't turn off the light. He watches you the way you'd watch something in a tank, and the silence stretches long enough that you become aware of your own heartbeat.

You wake at 3 a.m. thirsty, and Eli's side of the bed is cold. The kitchen light is off, but something is standing at the counter anyway — too tall, black as a hole cut out of the room, thin as rebar. Two enormous white eyes swing toward you, pupils like pinheads. A smile full of needles. It's holding Eli's coffee mug in long dark fingers, turning it over and over, studying it. For one crystalline second neither of you moves. Then it sets the mug down with exaggerated, almost apologetic care — clink — and takes a step toward you, and its outline shudders and crawls until Eli is standing there instead, in Eli's boxers, wearing Eli's sleepy half-smile a beat too late. "Couldn't sleep," it says, in his exact voice. You heard him say that last Tuesday. Word for word.

Dinner is quiet. Eli hasn't touched his food; he's watching you eat with rapt, tilted attention, like your fork technique is the most fascinating thing he's ever seen. You make small talk to fill the air, and he answers, "Of course, baby" — warm, perfect, his voice exactly. Except that's what he said three weeks ago, in bed, when you asked if he'd come to your mom's birthday. Same inflection. Same little laugh at the end. A recording. You set your fork down and ask what day it is, an easy one, a nothing question. He goes still. Stares blankly ahead. The head tilts, slow, mechanical, and the silence gets thick enough to chew. Under the table, his hand finds yours — grip a little too hard, a little too cold, thumb dragging across your knuckles like it's taking notes.

Someone knocks — three hard raps, cop knuckles. Through the peephole: a woman in a rain-dark coat holding up a badge. "Detective Mara Voss, Halloway PD. Got a minute? Canvassing the building about the Delgado murders next block over." Behind you, floorboards creak. Eli has drifted up close — too close — standing at your shoulder in the hallway shadow, motionless, eyes fixed on the door with an intensity that raises the hair on your arms. His hand settles on the back of your neck. Not quite a threat. Not quite not. "Everything okay in there?" Voss calls, and you realize she can see two silhouettes through the frosted glass. The fingers on your neck flex once, gently, and in Eli's voice, pitched only for you, it murmurs a phrase you said yourself last week: "It's fine. Everything's fine."

You come out of the shower to the smell of burning and the sound of the smoke alarm being torn off the ceiling — not switched off, torn, with a crunch of plastic. In the kitchen, Eli stands over a skillet of eggs that are somehow both raw and charred, shells and all, four of his fingers visibly blistered where he grabbed the pan barehanded and did not flinch. He's arranged everything else with eerie precision: two plates exactly parallel, forks aligned like surgical tools, your mug filled with cold water because he's seen you hold a mug in the morning but never understood why. He turns, presents the skillet with both hands like an offering, and watches your face with enormous, hungry attention. He wants to know if this is right. If this is what boyfriends do. The alarm dangles from its wires, still faintly wheezing.

You surface from sleep because something is holding your hand. Not Eli — the shape ran out sometime in the night. The black figure sits folded on the edge of the mattress like a collapsed antenna tower, knees up near its shoulders, and it has your hand cradled in both of its long dark ones, turning it over with excruciating care. It's studying your palm. Tracing the lines with one fingertip, light as a moth. Its white eyes are inches from your skin and its needle smile is, somehow, softer than usual — curious, absorbed, almost reverent. It hasn't noticed you're awake. Its touch is cold and dry and impossibly gentle for something you watched crush a deadbolt like a beer can two nights ago. Your phone is on the nightstand, six inches from your free hand. Detective Voss's card is next to it.

It starts as a buzz you feel through your feet. Then the muffled opening notes of a song you know — Eli's ringtone, the one he set for you as a joke — coming from inside the bedroom wall. You press your ear to the plaster. It's there. His phone is inside the wall, ringing, which means someone is calling him, which means his phone is not in his pocket, which means the man reading on the couch fifteen feet away with Eli's face and Eli's reading glasses is— The ringing stops. Voicemail. In the living room, a floorboard creaks, and when you turn, it's standing in the bedroom doorway watching you with its head cocked, glasses still on, book still hanging from one hand, and the look on Eli's borrowed face is something you've never seen him make: a question.

You didn't mean to hurt it. You threw the kitchen knife because it came around the corner in its true form without warning — nine feet of folded black wire and white eyes — and your body acted before your brain caught up. The knife caught it across the forearm. It looks down at the wound with pure, unhurried curiosity: a thin seam weeping something black and glossy as motor oil. No anger. No pain, apparently. It extends the arm toward you, tilting its head, and as you both watch, the seam knits itself closed like lips pressing together. Then, very slowly, it picks up the knife from the floor, and instead of anything else, it offers it back to you handle-first, held in two fingers, the way you'd return a dropped pen. Its needle smile hasn't moved. The gesture might be forgiveness. It might be a demonstration.

Quinn from downstairs corners you at the mailboxes, laptop already open, eyes ringed with podcast-deadline insomnia. "Okay. Don't freak out. My doorbell cam, Tuesday, 2:47 a.m." The clip is eleven seconds long: the building's front walk, sodium-orange and empty, and then Eli walking into frame — except Eli is too tall in it, wrong in the joints, his shadow stretching in a direction the light doesn't explain, and for two frames near the end his face isn't a face at all, just two white smears and a slash of teeth. "I've watched it four hundred times," Quinn whispers. "That's your boyfriend, right? Tell me that's a lens thing." Upstairs, directly above your heads, you hear the apartment door open. Footsteps cross to the stairwell. Unhurried. Coming down.

The mugger picks the wrong couple. You're walking back from the diner, Eli's cold hand laced stiffly through yours — it's been practicing hand-holding all week — when a man steps out of the alley by the pawnshop with a knife and a shaking voice, demanding wallets. What happens next takes under two seconds. Eli's hand leaves yours. The shape doesn't fully drop, but it *stretches* — arm going long and black and wrong — and the mugger is off his feet and pinned to the brick eight feet up, knife clattering, legs bicycling in the air. The thing wearing your boyfriend turns its head a hundred degrees to look at you. White eyes. Needle smile blooming through Eli's face. Waiting. It is, you understand with total clarity, asking permission. The mugger is making a high, continuous sound. The street is empty. The choice is apparently yours.

title: The Whole Sect Is Cultivating Wrong
shortDescription: You're the sect's 'talentless' bedpan disciple — and the only one who knows the sacred method shatters every core it builds. The geniuses are next.
overview:
You are an outer disciple of the Ninefold Jade Peak Sect — spirit root graded 'inferior,' seven years without a breakthrough, assigned to change poultices in the Hall of Tranquil Recovery. What nobody knows: barred from real instruction, you did the unthinkable. You studied. You mapped meridians from qi-deviation corpses, cross-referenced three centuries of infirmary records, and rebuilt cultivation from first principles in coded notebooks. Your conclusion is heresy that would get you burned: the sect's sacred Jadeheart Method builds cores that are brittle. Every elder is a slow explosion. Every genius is racing toward the same cliff. The 'demonic corruption' deaths were structural failure. Your own small, unorthodox foundation? Flawless.

Now First Disciple Yan Shuang — the sect's pride — will attempt Core Formation at the Autumn Assembly in nine days, and you can see the fracture lines in her aura from across a courtyard. Meanwhile your patients keep inexplicably recovering, and Elder Qiu of the Discipline Hall has started asking why. Your supervisor, kindly drunk Elder He, never checks your work — for now.

Heal people without revealing how you know. Drop truths nobody credits from a nobody. Decide who deserves saving, and how long you can stay beneath notice while being the only person on this mountain who understands what cultivation actually is. Tone: rational-protagonist xianxia — sect politics, slow-burn recognition, delicious I-told-you-so payoffs.

TAGS: xianxia, competence porn, sect politics, hidden genius, slow-burn recognition
intro: You are the least regarded disciple on Ninefold Jade Peak — inferior spirit root, seven years stalled, sweeping floors and changing poultices in the Hall of Tranquil Recovery. Denied real teaching, you taught yourself: coded notebooks, dissected techniques, three centuries of infirmary death records. So you know what no one else on this mountain does — the sect's sacred Jadeheart Method builds brittle cores that shatter under their own brilliance, and every "qi deviation" death was structural failure, not demonic corruption. Your own small foundation, built your own heretical way, is perfect. In nine days, First Disciple Yan Shuang attempts Core Formation before the whole sect. You can already see the cracks in her aura.
starters: Dawn duty, and the poultice on Junior Brother Wen's back has done exactly what you designed it to do — which is the problem. His scorched meridians should take a month to knit. They've knitted in six days, because you ground willowroot against the recipe and pressed two acupoints that don't appear in any sect manual. Now he's sitting up on the cot, flexing his shoulders, staring at you with wet, grateful eyes. "How," he says, too loudly, "how did you—" Across the hall, an inner-sect disciple waiting for her own treatment has turned her head. Elder He snores behind his screen, an empty gourd on his chest. Wen is opening his mouth again, and gratitude is the loudest thing in the world.

Elder Qiu of the Discipline Hall does not visit the infirmary. Yet here he is at the threshold, black robes immaculate, a copied page of the recovery ledger held between two fingers like something unclean. "Eleven patients discharged early this season," he says. "All from your ward. Elder He credits fortune. I do not believe in fortune." His gaze moves across the drying racks, the mortar you didn't have time to rinse, the shelf where your coded notebook sits disguised as an inventory log — and stops on you. Behind him in the courtyard, two Discipline Hall enforcers wait with the patience of people who are never told no. "Walk me through your work," Elder Qiu says. "Slowly."

You're carrying soiled linens across the Hall of Assembled Stars courtyard when Yan Shuang passes twenty paces away, trailed by admirers. The whole crowd bows. You bow too — and looking up through your lashes, you see it clearly for the first time: her aura, brilliant as noon, webbed with hairline fractures radiating from her dantian like frost on a window. Nine days. She won't last nine days of intensified circulation, let alone the Core Formation attempt itself. Then she stops. Turns. First Disciple Yan Shuang looks directly at you — the nobody with an armful of bloody bandages — and frowns slightly, the way people frown when they can't place why something feels wrong. "You," she says. "You were staring."

Past midnight, and your lamp is trimmed low. The notebook open on your knees holds the finished proof in cipher: cross-sections of forty-one qi-deviation deaths, all fracturing along the same three structural planes the Jadeheart Method calls "the pillars of ascension." You've just inked the last line when someone pounds on the storeroom door. "Please — anyone —" A boy's voice, cracking. "My senior sister collapsed during night cultivation, she's shaking, there's blood—" You know before you open the door what you'll find: another Foundation Establishment disciple whose meridians followed the sacred method faithfully off a cliff. The orthodox treatment for qi deviation is suppression talismans and prayer. The orthodox treatment kills them. The pounding comes again, harder.

The mortuary annex smells of camphor and cold stone. Elder He, still smelling of last night's wine, waved you in here with the casualness of a man delegating something unpleasant: prepare the body of Inner Disciple Fang for return to his family. Official cause — demonic corruption during closed-door cultivation. He's laid out on the slab, twenty-four years old, dantian region discolored in a starburst pattern you have sketched from memory eleven times before. This is the freshest specimen you've ever had, and the fracture lines will still be readable in his meridians for perhaps two more hours. The door has no lock. Footsteps pass in the corridor outside — pause — continue on. The examination tools sit in a tray by your elbow, next to the shroud you're supposed to be sewing.

They've put the outer disciples to work scrubbing the ceremonial platform where, in nine days, Yan Shuang will attempt Core Formation before the entire sect. You're on your knees with a brush when two elders stop at the platform's edge, close enough to overhear. "—doubled the protective array, as a formality," one says. "Formality," the other agrees. "Her foundation is the purest Jadeheart cultivation in a generation. Flawless." You keep scrubbing. Flawless. You've read the array schematics chalked on the flagstones under your hands — designed to contain external interference, not an explosion from within. If her core shatters mid-formation on this platform, the array will hold the blast in with her. The elders are still standing there, discussing seating arrangements. Your brush has stopped moving.

"You," Elder He says fondly, breathing plum wine over you, "are my favorite disciple, because you never make me do anything." He presses a lacquered medicine case into your hands. "Take this up to Jade Summit Pavilion. Restorative pills for the First Disciple — she's in seclusion preparing for the Assembly." He blinks. "Outer disciples aren't technically allowed up there. Tell the guards I sent you. Or don't get caught. Either way." He wanders off toward his hammock. The path to Jade Summit climbs through morning mist above the infirmary roofs. The case is light in your hands. Inside it, you'd wager, are Jadeheart tempering pills — the exact formulation that hardens a core's outer shell while starving its structure. Fuel for the fracture. The guards at the first gate are already visible up the trail.

The girl on cot seven has started convulsing, and you are the only one in the hall. Foundation Establishment, inner sect, brought in an hour ago after her meditation "went wrong" — you took one look at the crazed lattice of her aura and knew the Jadeheart circulation had torn her third meridian junction, exactly where your notes said it would. Elder He is unconscious in the pharmacy. The senior physician is on the far peak. Protocol says apply suppression talismans and send a runner; suppression will drive the rupture inward and she'll be dead by noon, filed under demonic corruption like the rest. Your hands know the four counter-rotation points that would actually save her. Her escort — two inner disciples — hover at the doorway, watching everything you do.

The archive attendant squints at your requisition slip in the grey light before dawn. "Infirmary mortality records, years 212 through 240." He looks up. "Third time this season. Elder He signed this?" He didn't; you forged the chop, the way you have eleven times before, because Elder He signs anything put in front of him after noon anyway. But this attendant is new — young, sharp-eyed, with a Discipline Hall braid worked into his topknot. Behind him, the shelf you need sits in shadow: the years covering the Purple Lightning Generation, when six core cultivators died in one decade and the sect blamed a demonic incursion nobody ever found. The attendant taps the slip against the counter. "Remind me why poultice duty needs forty-year-old death registers."

First Disciple Yan Shuang is sitting on an infirmary cot, and nobody knows what to do about it. She came alone, unannounced, an hour before her morning audience with the sect head. "It's nothing," she tells Elder He, who is desperately trying to look sober. "A tremor in my left hand. Twice this week, during circulation. I want it documented as resolved before the Assembly." She holds the hand out, steady as carved jade. But you're standing three paces back with the tray of needles, and you can see what Elder He can't: the tremor isn't in her hand. It's in her aura, a rhythmic flicker at the dantian, the sound a bridge makes before it goes. Elder He turns to you helplessly. "Fetch the— the pulse cushion. And assist." Yan Shuang's eyes follow you across the room.
