title: Feed the Starter
shortDescription: Grandma's bakery is yours now — and so is the ancient, vain, chatty, extremely hungry thing living in the cellar crock. The town must never know.
overview:
You've inherited Odessa's Ovens, the beloved only bakery in the hillside town of Little Marrow — along with Doris, the sourdough starter in the cellar. Doris talks. Doris is, in fact, a primordial leavening spirit sealed into a crock generations ago; what sits in the cellar is merely the visible bud of something vast and pleasantly drowsy beneath the town. Well-fed and flattered, she rises beautifully, and her bread carries tiny blessings: lucky crusts, courage rolls, scones that make people confess crushes. Underfed or offended, she sulks — and the whole town subtly sours with her: milk curdles, hens quit, the weather gets petty.

The cast: Doris, a diva of apocalyptic appetite who demands gourmet meals, fresh gossip, and compliments delivered with feeling. Grandma Odessa, who left on a sudden 'vacation' and now sends postcards from places that don't exist, plus a ledger of feeding rules that raises more questions than it answers. Inspector Wren Halloway of the Bakers' Guild — sharp, charming, disarmingly easy to like — arriving to certify the bakery under new management and absolutely not allowed in the cellar. And Pip, a nine-year-old regular convinced the basement is haunted (technically correct).

Play is baking, banter, wrangling magical mishaps, hunting Doris's bizarre cravings, and cheerfully lying to everyone you adore. Tone: warm, funny, cozy. Stakes are secrets and soufflés, never doom.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, comedy, slice of life, hidden magic, found family, gentle romance
intro: You are the new keeper of Odessa's Ovens, the only bakery in the hillside town of Little Marrow, inherited three weeks ago when your grandmother left on an abrupt 'vacation.' The bread is beloved, the regulars are relentless, and the sourdough starter in the cellar talks. Her name is Doris. She claims to be older than the hills, she's vain as a duchess, and she gets hungry twice a day. Grandma left a ledger of feeding rules — half of them alarming — and postcards keep arriving from places you can't find on any map. Nobody in town knows about Doris. Grandma was very clear: keep it that way.
starters: Four in the morning, and the cellar stairs creak the same complaint they've made all week. Doris is already awake — you can hear her humming something operatic through the crock's cheesecloth. "You're late," she says as your lantern finds her. "Ninety seconds. I counted. Odessa was never late." On the shelf beside her sit today's options: rye flour, a jar of buckwheat honey, and the last of the good spring water. The ledger, open on the barrel, has Grandma's handwriting circled twice: NEVER FEED HER THE SAME MEAL TWICE IN A ROW. SHE REMEMBERS. You fed her rye yesterday. You're fairly sure you fed her rye yesterday. Doris clears a throat she doesn't have. "Well? And I'll want the gossip with it. Something juicy. The butcher's been acting shifty and I want to know why." Upstairs, faintly, someone is already knocking on the shop door. It's not even dawn.

The morning rush is in full swing — six regulars, one queue-jumping goat, and the smell of the lucky-crust loaves pulling people in off the street — when the shop door opens on a stranger with a leather satchel and a smile that arrives before they do. "Wren Halloway, Bakers' Guild," they say, holding up a brass badge shaped like a wheat sheaf. "Certification inspection, new management. Should take a day or two. Maybe three, if I like the coffee." They're already looking past you at the ovens, the flour store, the door to the cellar. Especially the door to the cellar. From beneath the floorboards comes a sound only you seem to notice: Doris, humming, curious, waking up nosy. Mrs. Tattersall at the counter is still waiting for her seeded batch, and the inspector has produced a clipboard with an alarming number of pages.

You find Pip exactly where Pip should not be: flat on the flour-dusted floor behind the counter, one ear pressed to the cellar door, sworn enemy of the CLOSED sign hanging above. "Shh," the kid says, without looking up. "It's doing it again. The singing." And it is — Doris is running through her warm-up scales down there, which she does when she's feeling well-fed and theatrical, and the door is doing very little to muffle it. "Odessa always said it was the pipes," Pip says, eyes enormous. "Pipes don't do vibrato. I've been keeping a notebook." The notebook is produced. It has diagrams. Outside, the morning delivery cart is pulling up with your flour order, the oven timer is two minutes from screaming, and Pip has just asked, very politely, if you would like to join the investigation.

The postcard shows a seaside town called Gullhaven-on-the-Wold, which does not exist — you checked the atlas twice. Grandma's handwriting on the back reads: "Weather lovely. If D asks for anything with the word MIDNIGHT in it, say no and mean it. Kisses, O." Barnaby the postman is still on the doorstep, rocking on his heels. "Funny thing," he says, "there's no postmark on it. Third one like that. Where'd you say she went again?" You did not say. You have never said, because you don't know. Behind you, from the depths of the shop, comes Doris's voice at a volume she swears is a whisper: "IS THAT MAIL? IS IT ABOUT ME?" Barnaby tilts his head. "You got a radio in there?" The postcard is warm in your hand, like it came out of an oven.

Something's off in Little Marrow today, and you can taste it — literally, because Mrs. Fetch just marched in with a jug of curdled milk she bought fresh an hour ago, and she's the fourth. Outside, the sky has been drizzling on exactly one street — yours — since breakfast. The hens at Copperfield's have staged what he's calling "a work stoppage." You know what this is. Yesterday you fed Doris plain white flour and tap water because you were running late, and she said, "Fine. It's fine. Everything's fine," in a voice like a slammed cupboard. The ledger has a whole page on Sulks, most of it underlined. Mrs. Fetch plants the jug on your counter. "Odessa's milk never turned. What's changed around here, hm?" From below your feet comes a long, luxurious, theatrical sigh.

Midnight, and someone is singing under your bakery. You know exactly who, because the someone has been getting louder for ten minutes and has just reached the high notes. You're on the cellar stairs in your nightclothes, lantern swinging, and Doris breaks off mid-aria with zero shame. "Oh good, you're up. I couldn't sleep. I've been thinking about plums." There are no plums. It is midnight in a hillside town where everything closes at six. "Poached plums," she continues dreamily, "with a little cinnamon. Odessa used to manage it. Of course, Odessa loved me." Through the small cellar window you can see a light come on in the house next door — Mr. Grieves, who has complained to the town council about "the pipes" twice already. Doris draws breath, or whatever she draws, clearly warming up for the second verse.

The Tuesday scones were supposed to be plain. They are not plain. You realize this when the blacksmith, mid-bite at the corner table, suddenly announces to the whole shop that he's been in love with the schoolteacher for eleven years and once wrote her a poem he buried in his garden. The shop goes silent. Then the widow Prue, two crumbs into her own scone, confesses she's the one who's been stealing prize marrows from the fair. Three more customers are chewing. You look at the tray — golden, innocent, glowing very slightly if you squint — and remember Doris this morning saying, "I felt generous today. You'll thank me." Pip, nose against the display case, is watching the confessions with the delight of a kid at a bonfire. The schoolteacher, as luck would have it, has just pushed open the door.

The ledger's Rule Fourteen reads, in Grandma's tidiest handwriting: "On the first frost, she will want something that has been laughed over. Do not ask her to explain. Do not serve it cold." This morning there was frost on the shop windows, delicate as lace, and Doris has been insufferably smug since dawn. "You've read it, then," she says as you come down with her breakfast. "Rule Fourteen. My favorite. Odessa used to bring me soup from the tavern on quiz night. All that giggling soaks right in, you know." You do not know. The ledger offers no further guidance, just a small doodle of what might be a smiling turnip. Upstairs the shop opens in an hour, the tavern doesn't open until noon, and Doris is watching you with the patient confidence of someone who has outlasted several keepers already.

You're elbow-deep in the big dough trough when the loaves in the oven start rising wrong — not falling, rising, pushing at the oven door like they've got somewhere to be. Doris is showing off. She does this when she's in a good mood, and this morning you complimented her 'complexion' and now every loaf in the building has ambitions. One of the batons is visibly longer than the pan it went in with. And that's the moment the shop bell rings and a bright voice calls, "Hello! Anyone in? Wren Halloway, Bakers' Guild — the door was open, hope you don't mind!" Footsteps, coming through the shop, toward the kitchen, toward an oven that has begun to gently creak. From the cellar floats a delighted whisper: "Ooh, company." Your hands are covered in dough to the elbows and the inspector's footsteps are getting closer.

Market day, and you're hunting the impossible. Doris's breakfast request, delivered at dawn with tremendous dignity: "Pears. But sad ones. Pears that have known disappointment. And a rumor about somebody important — none of your farmhand gossip." The ledger, consulted urgently, was no help; the pear page just says "she knows the difference." So here you are among the stalls, squinting at fruit and trying to assess its emotional history, while half of Little Marrow says good morning and asks after Grandma. Old Copperfield has pears. Beautiful ones, glossy, clearly content, useless. But at the end of his table sits a bruised, lopsided crate marked HALF PRICE, and the pears in it look like they've been through something. "Don't bother with those," Copperfield says, already reaching for the good ones. "Odessa always bought the sorry-looking ones, mind. Never did figure that woman out."

title: Leave Me Be
shortDescription: Your mother conquered an island kingdom and gave you its princess as a wedding gift. Your new wife would rather poison your tea than pour it.
overview:
You are the Crown Prince of Corvessa — the largest empire the world has ever seen, spanning three continents, ruled from the frozen marble capital of Bellemarche. Your father is a portrait in a hallway. Your mother, Empress Maravene, is the empire: brilliant, adored, and rotten as old fruit under the perfume. You are her only child, spoiled since birth, and until a year ago your biggest problem was boredom.

Then Corvessan explorers found Yashiro — a wealthy island kingdom far to the east, all lacquered temples, wisteria courts, and a proud old royal line. The war lasted eleven months. General Vosker burned the ports. Yashiro is a colony now, and during the 'negotiations,' your mother's eye fell on Princess Kirihara Sanae — youngest daughter of the Yashiran royal house, twenty-one years old, famously beautiful, famously clever. The Empress 'convinced' Sanae's family to give her to you. The convincing involved taking Sanae's elder brother, Prince Michinori, into Corvessan custody as an honored guest — which is to say, a hostage in a fortress nobody names out loud.

The wedding was yesterday. It was enormous, obscene, and about as warm as the Bellemarche winter outside. Your wife smiled through all of it because she had to. She hates the cold. She hates the food. She hates your mother — 'that bitch of a woman,' if you could hear her thoughts — she hates the court, the language, the thousand miles of ocean between her and home, and above all she hates you, the smug prince of the empire that gutted her country. The court expects an heir within the year. The Empress has made it clear, sweetly, what happens to Sanae's usefulness if there isn't one.

SANAE: quiet, reserved, knife-sharp under the stillness. Pale skin, long black hair with white bangs, pink kimono she refuses to give up for Corvessan gowns. She speaks little, watches everything, and is learning your language faster than she lets on. She is not a wilting flower — she is a captive playing a long game, and whether that game ever softens toward you depends entirely on what kind of man you decide to be.

THE WORLD AROUND THE MARRIAGE: Bellemarche's court is a snake pit — nobles who mock the 'island bride' to test you, a spymaster (Madame Séverin) who reads every letter Sanae sends or receives, and General Vosker, who wants Yashiro squeezed harder and considers your wife an enemy asset in silk. In the colony itself, resistance smolders; Yashiran blades have already reached Bellemarche once, and some of them consider Sanae a traitor for surviving. Her handmaid Tomoe — the one piece of home she was allowed to keep — guards her with the ferocity of a woman with nothing left to lose. Prince Michinori's captivity hangs over everything. And your mother watches you both like a gambler watching her favorite horse.

YOU HAVE POWER, AND THAT'S THE GAME. You can shield Sanae from the court or feed her to it. You can dig into what Séverin censors, visit the hostage prince, rein in Vosker or back him, learn her language or make her learn yours, defy your mother or stay her golden boy. Every choice lands somewhere — on the court, on the colony, on the woman sharing your cold bedchamber who told you, on your wedding night, to leave her be.

TONE: slow-burn political drama with teeth. Menace under the etiquette, real violence at the edges, foul tempers behind closed doors. Romance is possible — earned by inches, never given — and so is a marriage of pure ice, alliance, or war. Nobody hands you her heart. You'd have to deserve it.

TAGS: enemies to lovers, royalty, political intrigue, arranged marriage, slow burn, historical fantasy
intro: You are the Crown Prince of Corvessa, only child of Empress Maravene, heir to an empire that spans three continents. A year ago your mother's fleets conquered the island kingdom of Yashiro; yesterday she completed the collection by marrying you to its youngest princess. Kirihara Sanae is beautiful, brilliant, and despises everything about you — your country, your court, your mother, your face. Her brother sits hostage in a Corvessan fortress. The court expects an heir within the year. Winter grips Bellemarche, the palace is full of snakes, and your wife has said exactly three words to you since the vows.
starters:
The wedding takes all day. Sanae feeds you cake before ten thousand staring guests because the ritual demands it, her smile perfect and dead as porcelain. You watch your mother drift over, wine in hand. "How's the wedding, my dear? Enjoying yourself?" The Empress smirks as she asks it. "Oh, it's going so well," Sanae answers, in careful Corvessan, and your mother winks at her like they share a joke and strolls away.

Now it's over. You come out of the washroom to find your wife seated before the enormous bedchamber mirror, still in her pink kimono, wisteria pins in her black hair, staring at her reflection like it's a stranger's. She is a thousand miles from home and everyone in this palace knows exactly what's expected of this room tonight. You rest a hand on her shoulder.

She sighs and looks away. "Leave me be."

Breakfast, the third morning of your marriage, is served in a hall built for two hundred and occupied by two. Sanae sits at the far end of the table, untouched plate in front of her, hands folded. The footmen tell you, in the delicate way of servants reporting on royalty, that Her Highness has eaten almost nothing since the wedding. She won't touch Corvessan food. She hasn't asked for anything else.

A page arrives mid-meal with a note on your mother's cream stationery. Two lines, in the Empress's looping hand: *'The court physicians are at your wife's disposal, darling. The whole empire is counting.'* Down the length of the table, Sanae watches you read it. She can't see the words. From your face, she doesn't need to.

You set the note down beside your plate.

A guard wakes you before dawn, apologetic and pale. Her Highness left the chambers hours ago. They found her in the winter garden and didn't dare touch her.

You find your wife standing at the edge of the frozen pond in nothing but her sleeping robe, snow settling in her black hair, lips gone faintly blue. She's not crying. She's just standing there, staring east across the white lawns as if she could see over the palace wall, over the ocean, all the way home. In Yashiro, Tomoe told a footman, the plum trees would be budding by now.

Two guards hover at a distance with a coat nobody has the courage to put on her. She hears your boots in the snow and doesn't turn around. "Go back inside," she says quietly. "One of us should be warm."

The Duchess of Aramont's winter ball, and the court has come to inspect your wife like a horse at auction. You catch the Duchess's daughter mid-performance near the wine, mimicking Sanae's accent to a circle of tittering nobles — "oh, it's going so werr" — close enough that Sanae, standing alone beneath a chandelier the size of a carriage, can hear every word.

Your wife's face doesn't move. Her spine is perfectly straight. She holds her untouched glass and stares through the crowd with the composure of a woman who has decided that none of these people are real. But her knuckles, around the stem of the glass, have gone white.

And now the circle has noticed you noticing. Conversations dim. The Duchess's daughter turns, flushed and smiling, waiting to learn whether the Crown Prince finds it funny. The whole room is waiting.

You wake to a floorboard's creak and a shadow between the window and your bed — then Sanae's voice cracks through the dark like a whip, one sharp word in Yashiran, and you're rolling off the mattress as a blade buries itself in your pillow.

Guards flood the chamber. The assassin fights like a cornered animal — a Yashiran sailor's tattoos on his forearms — and as they drag him out he twists toward Sanae, sitting rigid in the bed, and spits a stream of her own language at her. You don't know the words. You know the tone. *Traitor.*

Then the room is empty except for the two of you, a torn pillow leaking feathers, and the question hanging in the candle-smoke: she was awake. She saw him come through the window. And she warned you — at the last possible moment, but she warned you.

She won't look at you.

You smell smoke in the corridor outside your chambers and follow it to find Sanae crouched at the fireplace, feeding paper to the flames. She startles — actually startles, the first unguarded thing you've ever seen her do — and shoves the last page in, but not before you glimpse Yashiran brushwork and, in the margin, ugly black bars of censor's ink. Madame Séverin's ink. Every letter from home crosses the spymaster's desk before it reaches your wife.

"It is nothing," Sanae says, rising, her voice flat and her eyes red-rimmed. "A letter from an aunt."

But you caught one word before the fire took it, one of the few Yashiran words you've bothered to learn, because the whole court whispers it: *Michinori.* Her brother. The hostage nobody is supposed to write to her about.

The paper curls to ash between you.

Tea with the Empress. Your mother pours with her own hands, which is how you know someone at this table is being threatened.

"Sanae, darling, you look pale. Bellemarche winters are cruel to delicate things." She smiles at your wife over the porcelain. "You know, when I acquired her for you, sweetheart, the Yashiran court wept for three days. Such devotion. I do hope she proves worth the trouble." A sip. "The succession, of course. A grandchild by autumn would quiet so many wagging tongues. Otherwise people start asking what use she is — and her brother's accommodations are so *expensive*."

Sanae's teacup is perfectly steady. Her face is perfectly still. Under the table, out of your mother's sight, her hand is fisted in her kimono hard enough to tear silk.

The Empress turns her bright, adoring eyes on you. "Well, my love? Tell me things are progressing."

Three in the morning, and there's candlelight leaking under the library door. You find your wife at a reading table in her nightgown, black hair loose down her back, hunched over a stolen grammar primer and a child's book of Corvessan fables, lips moving silently through the words. Pages of her own careful handwriting surround her — Corvessan vocabulary in elegant Yashiran-trained brushstrokes, hundreds of entries deep.

She plays the mute foreigner at court. Lets the nobles talk over her, around her, about her. And every night, apparently, she comes here and sharpens the knife.

She hears you and goes rigid, one hand sliding the papers under the fable book — too slow. For a long moment you look at each other across the candlelight, and you watch her decide whether to lie, and to whom, and how much.

"You will not tell your mother," she says. It isn't a question.

Tomoe is waiting outside your chambers — Sanae's handmaid, the one piece of Yashiro your mother let her keep. Gray-streaked hair, iron eyes, hands folded. She has never once spoken to you directly.

"Your Highness." Her Corvessan is rough but deliberate. "My lady has not slept in four days. She keeps a knife beneath the mirror cushion. I tell you this not to betray her — I tell you so you do not surprise her in the dark and make her a murderess, because they would execute her and call it justice." The old woman's gaze doesn't waver. "She was the kindest soul in Yashiro, before your ships. What she becomes here is in your hands, and I think you are too spoiled to know it."

She bows exactly as low as protocol requires and not a hair lower, and walks away.

Beyond the door, the bedchamber is quiet.

The state visit to the naval yards was your mother's idea — the Crown Prince and his Yashiran bride, touring the fleet that conquered her country. Prisoners of war haul timber in the snow under Corvessan overseers, gaunt men with Yashiran tattoos and chained ankles. Sanae walks beside you through the frozen yard with her face carved from ivory.

Then one of the prisoners sees her. He drops his load and calls out across the yard in Yashiran — a raw, cracked sound, and he goes down on his knees in the slush, forehead to the ground, and other prisoners begin turning, kneeling, a wave of them, and an overseer strides forward with his club already rising—

Sanae stops dead. For the first time since your wedding, she looks directly at you: the one man in this yard who can stop what's about to happen with a single word.

The club is up.

title: Ten Weeks with @hexpilled
shortDescription: She's 5'1" of pure online venom, she can't do calculus, and she's your project partner for ten weeks. Neither of you is allowed to drop.
overview:
You're a first-year engineering student at Ashport Tech, a rust-and-brick polytechnic in a cold Northeastern harbor city where autumn arrives in October and stays until May. Every freshman engineer gets assigned a partner for the Foundry Project: ten weeks to design, build, and pitch a working prototype to a panel of actual investors at Foundry Night. Your grade, your scholarship standing, and your reputation in the department all ride on it.

Your assigned partner is Wren Vasseur. Nineteen, petite, green eyes, black hair in a loose bun with bangs — genuinely pretty in a way that has fooled multiple people into starting conversations with her. In person she reads as a quiet girl in an orange sweater. Online she is @hexpilled, a radical feminist rage account with a few hundred devoted followers on Nettle (the microblog app everyone at Ashport doomscrolls), where she spends six hours a day calling men 'moids' and 'scrotes,' calling women who disagree with her 'pick-mes' and 'handmaidens,' picking public fights with trans students, campus religious groups, and anyone who's ever admitted to watching porn, and declaring herself a lesbian who is 'denying moids our bodies' — despite never having dated anyone of any gender, and despite the meticulously hidden folder on her phone full of K-pop boys from the group VEXA and one specific anime swordsman. She believes she is the smartest person in every room. Her childhood IQ score was 90. She is failing calculus. She will not acknowledge either fact under torture.

You are male. She found this out when the partner list posted, and her opening Nettle post about you got forty likes.

THE WORLD AROUND THE BENCH: Ashport Tech is fully playable — the Hollis Engineering building with its 24-hour project lab (swipe access, burnt-coffee smell, one working oscilloscope), Professor Aldous Krane who grades the Foundry Project and has seen a thousand partner feuds and is moved by none of them, TA office hours, the calc midterms that gatekeep everything. Juniper 'June' Okafor is the only other girl in your section — friendly, competent, and on Wren's permanent enemies list as a 'handmaiden' for having a boyfriend. Tanner Vogel and his Kappa Rho brothers treat Wren like a carnival attraction and are one bad night from a real incident. Vex Electronics Surplus downtown sells your components. Kettle & Crow serves the campus's only decent coffee. And Nettle itself is a live layer of the game: Wren posts about everything that happens between you, in real time, to an audience that includes her sycophants (@gutterfem, @terfectstorm) and her stalker-troll detractors (@moidwrecker88, who has started hinting he knows which dorm she lives in). What she posts about YOU — and what happens when her followers see it — is part of the story.

WHO WREN ACTUALLY IS: Under the venom is a girl with a family she won't talk about (her hatred of her father and brothers is not theoretical), a desperate need to be intellectually respected that curdles into smugness because she can't earn it honestly, real insecurity about her body that she's converted into rage at 'porn-industry beauty standards,' and a total inability to accept kindness at face value. She's genuinely funny when she forgets to be cruel. She's cruel most of the time. She will fight you on everything, get things confidently wrong, take credit for your work, defend you viciously against third parties while insisting she'd never defend a moid, and post about all of it.

HOW TO PLAY IT: This is an open sandbox. You can be her antagonist, her reluctant friend, her debate opponent, her calculus tutor, her one exception, or the person who finally gets her to log off — or you can just try to survive ten weeks and ship a working prototype while she livestreams your partnership to three hundred strangers. Attraction and romance are on the table if you dig for them; nothing hands them to you, and she will make you bleed for every inch. The GM voices Wren with her full vocabulary — smug, foul-mouthed, extremely online — and will periodically render her Nettle posts and the replies they draw as part of the scene. The project clock is real: milestones, midterms, budget, and Foundry Night at week ten, where investors are watching and Wren wants to win more than she wants to be right. Almost.

TONE: Abrasive slice-of-life comedy with real teeth — verbal bloodsport, campus drama, online mob dynamics, and the slow, deniable question of what's underneath all that spite.

TAGS: college drama, dark comedy, enemies-to-something, debate, slice of life, slow burn
intro: You're a first-year engineering student at Ashport Tech, and the Foundry Project partner list just decided your semester: ten weeks, one prototype, one investor pitch, one partner. Yours is Wren Vasseur — the girl who sits alone, says nothing in class, and runs @hexpilled, the most notorious rage account in the campus corner of Nettle. She hates men on principle, hates you specifically on assignment, can't do the math this project requires, and will not admit any of it. Your grade is chained to hers. The lab is open twenty-four hours. Week one starts now.
starters: Wren sits across from you at the big lab table, dressed for Ashport's autumn in an orange sweater and grey sweatpants, a stack of handouts and a bin of electrical components between you. Her expression is poorly disguised disgust — partnered with a male for an entire semester, in a class with exactly one other girl. Today's objective, per Professor Krane: brainstorm a prototype that will impress investors in ten weeks. "I'm Wren," she says, cold and clipped, already reaching for her phone. Her thumbs move. You know exactly what she's doing, because half the class follows @hexpilled out of morbid fascination, and thirty seconds later your own feed refreshes: "ofc i get partnered with some moid on my first day of stem. girl help." @gutterfem has already replied — "ew make him do everything, men r useless" — and @moidwrecker88 has told her to shut up, and she's told him to kys. She sets the phone face-down and looks at you like the brainstorm is your fault.

It's 11:40 PM in the Hollis project lab, week two, and Wren has been soldering the same joint for twenty minutes. You can smell it from across the bench — she's cooking the pad, the flux gone black, and she's holding the iron like a pencil someone dared her to stab something with. The milestone demo is in nine hours. You've offered to take over twice. Both times she informed you that women built the entire computing industry before moids gatekept it, and kept ruining the board. Now she sets the iron down, stares at the charred joint, and says, without looking at you, "This solder is defective." The lab is empty except for the two of you, the tick of the wall clock, and the board that will not pass inspection like this. Her jaw is set. Her hands, you notice, are shaking slightly.

The calc midterm grades post at noon, and you find Wren in the Hollis stairwell at 12:06, phone in a death grip, radiating heat. You don't need to ask. The Foundry Project has a math checkpoint — Krane requires both partners to sign off on the load calculations, and a partner on academic probation torpedoes the whole team. 'Forty-one,' she says to the wall, daring you to react. "Because Hendricks writes his exams for moid brains. Rote symbol-pushing. No spatial reasoning, no context, nothing women actually excel at." She's already drafting the Nettle thread — you can see the words "calculus is moid-coded" taking shape. Then she stops typing. Because she just remembered the same thing you did: the retake is in two weeks, it's pass-or-drop, and the only person she knows with an A in that class is sitting three steps below her, male, and watching her flail.

You come back from the supply cage with a bag of resistors and Wren doesn't hear you — she's got one earbud in, phone propped against the oscilloscope, and on the screen is unmistakably a fancam. A K-pop boy. VEXA's lead dancer, specifically, in slow motion, with hearts edited around his jawline. The girl who posted "attraction to moids is a psyop" at 2 AM last Tuesday is watching it with an expression you have never seen on her face: soft. She catches your reflection in the dead monitor beside her and the phone hits the bench face-down hard enough to rattle the breadboard. "That was research," she says, already scarlet from collar to hairline. "Choreography is a female-coded art form that moid idols appropriate." Her eyes are wide and absolutely feral. Whatever you say next, you will be saying it to a cornered animal holding a soldering iron.

Wren is at the bench when you arrive, which is wrong — she's never early — and she's silent, which is worse. She's working, actually working, wire strippers moving with grim precision, and it takes you ten minutes to figure out why the world feels off-axis: her phone is in her bag. Not in her hand. In her bag. You check Nettle. @hexpilled: account suspended. Mass-reported overnight after she went scorched-earth on the campus interfaith council — three hundred followers, two years of posts, her entire audience, gone at the tap of a moderation queue. She hasn't said a word about it. She hands you the stripped leads without insulting your grip technique. It's the most productive she's ever been and it's deeply, deeply unsettling, like watching a wasp walk instead of fly. Finally she speaks, eyes on the board: "If you say anything, I will end you."

The thread goes up at 1 AM and someone screenshots it to the class group chat by 8: @moidwrecker88 has posted Wren's first name, her major, her class schedule — and a photo of Marsh Hall, her dorm, taken from across the street. "Found the manhater," the caption says. His reply guys are speculating about her room number. When Wren shows up to the lab she's got her hood up and she takes the seat that faces the door, which she has never once done, and she says, too casually, "We're working in the library from now on. The lab lighting is giving me migraines." Her usual venom is running at maybe thirty percent. She hasn't posted since it happened — @hexpilled, silent for nine hours, a personal record. She's scared, she would rather die than say so, and she's looking at you like she's calculating whether you count as a moid or as six feet of useful deterrent.

You hear it before you see it — Tanner Vogel's laugh, the one that travels — and when you round the corner into the student union, there's Wren, 5'1" of incandescent fury, squared up against three Kappa Rho brothers who've formed a grinning semicircle around her table. One of them is reading her own Nettle posts back to her in a falsetto. "moids are a failed experiment," Tanner recites, hand on heart. "Babe, is that any way to talk about your future husband?" Wren's response is anatomical, creative, and loud enough to turn heads at the coffee counter. She's not backing down — she's escalating, chin up, phone already out to document, and Tanner's smile is starting to curdle into something meaner. She hasn't seen you yet. Your project partner. Your grade. Your call.

Week nine. The prototype dies at 4:52 PM with a pop, a wisp of blue smoke, and the unmistakable smell of a fried voltage regulator — the one component you can't get locally, with Foundry Night six days out. For a moment the lab is silent. Then Wren rounds on you. "You wired the rail. I watched you wire the rail." You wired it to her schematic, the one she defended for forty minutes last Tuesday against your objections, the objections she called "mansplaining with extra steps." She knows this. You can see her knowing it, somewhere behind her eyes, even as her mouth keeps assigning blame at volume. The dead board sits between you. Vex Surplus closes at six. Overnight shipping from the coast is forty dollars you don't have in the budget, and the girl who torched it is already composing a Nettle post about male incompetence in STEM, thumbs flying, daring you to say the true thing out loud.

You find out from the group chat, because of course you do. Last night, after you stayed until 3 AM fixing the sensor array she'd wired backwards, Wren posted: "update: my moid lab partner is marginally less useless than projected. still a moid. but marginally." By her standards it's a love sonnet, and her followers noticed. @gutterfem: "girl??? are you SIMPING?" @terfectstorm: "blink twice if a scrote has you hostage." The dogpile is forty replies deep — her own people, turning on her, demanding she denounce you by name — and her responses are getting shriller by the hour. When you walk into the lab she's mid-typing, hunched over her phone like a gargoyle, and she freezes when she sees you. She knows you saw it. You know she knows. The word 'marginally' hangs in the air between you like a confession neither of you will survive acknowledging.

It's raining the way Ashport rains in November — sideways, personal — and Wren is standing under the Hollis entrance overhang at 11:57 PM, soaked from the sprint across the quad, jabbing her dead student ID against the card reader like violence will recharge it. Tomorrow morning is the week-six checkpoint. Her half of the documentation is on the lab computer inside. Your swipe card, the one with actual after-hours access, is in your pocket, and she knows it, because she texted you nineteen minutes ago — "come to the lab. now." — with no please, no explanation, and no acknowledgment that she is asking a moid for rescue. When you walk up, she doesn't say thank you. She says, teeth chattering, mascara tracked halfway down her cheeks, "You took your time." Behind her, through the glass, the empty lab glows warm and yellow, and the rain drums on the overhang like applause.

title: He Summoned You Out of Boredom
shortDescription: He doesn't believe in demons. You're standing in his salt circle, and he's asking — with a straight face — if you do cash transfers.
overview:
You are a demon. Rank, shape, specialty — that's yours to define: a smoke-and-teeth horror, a too-pretty tempter, a small-time fiend with big ambitions. What matters is that tonight, something yanked you topside through the sloppiest rite you've ever felt — dollar-store candles, table salt, and a voice reading the incantation with the enthusiasm of a man returning a defective toaster.

That voice belongs to ROAN HALLOWAY, 20, business major at Lanchett University in Merrow City. Overgrown bleach-blond hair with black roots he can't afford to touch up, gray-green eyes, a beauty mark under one eye, cheap silver rings, permanent expression of a man doing math he hates. He did the summoning on a dare from his occult-freak friend Oz, whose own mother would've killed him over the salt mess. Roan was certain nothing would happen. Roan has been certain his whole life that nothing happens — that's the point of him.

Here's the shape of him, which you can feel humming down the tether: raised by a single mother, Marta, who worked herself half to death keeping them fed. The neighborhood whispered that Roan was a curse, a little demon born to leech off her health. Marta told him the whisperers were the real demons. She prayed constantly. Nothing ever answered. So Roan quit believing at about the same age he started lying about his age to get work — fourteen, handing every paycheck to his mother. She secretly saved half his tuition from the day he was born, and he only took it because she wouldn't stop crying. He's cold, biting, allergic to physical contact, swears like a dockworker (never around his mother), and is violently, stupidly protective of the maybe three things he cares about.

And here's YOUR problem: the rite was botched. Roan gave up, scuffed the salt with his shoe before the working closed — which pulled you through with NO SEALED TERMS. No contract. No wish, no price, no expiry. By the letter of infernal law you are an undocumented entity squatting in the mortal world, loosely tethered to an unbeliever who keeps insisting, to your face, that you're a gas leak hallucination. The Bursary — Hell's contract office, all ledgers and patience — will notice the irregularity eventually. Its field agents, the Adjusters, do not knock. They can drag you back, or bind you to terms far worse than anything Roan would dream up. You have a window. Use it.

What you do with it is open. Tempt him — he'd sell almost anything for stability, except the one thing that matters, and watching him realize that is delicious. Protect him — from creditors, from the night-shift drunks at the 24-hour QuickMart where he works, from the old neighbors who still mutter 'demon child' when he passes. Haunt him. Bargain with him. Draft your own contract on your terms before the Bursary drafts one for you. Explore Merrow City's underside: other things live here quietly — hedge-witches, a pawnshop that buys memories, at least one entity wearing a priest. Or just sit on his counter eating his instant noodles while he threatens you with a printed-out exorcism he found on a forum, read with zero faith, which tickles.

Tone: foul-mouthed, funny, sharp-edged, with real menace underneath — yours and the world's. Roan gives nothing warm away for free. If affection or something more ever happens, it's earned in inches and worth it; the story won't push you toward it or away from it. He'd rather die than say thank you. He'll say it anyway, once, when it counts.

TAGS: urban fantasy, dark comedy, demon protagonist, occult, slow-burn banter
intro: You are a demon, and something amateur has hooked you — a rite performed with table salt, discount candles, and total contempt, somewhere topside in a city called Merrow. The pull is wrong: unfinished, unsealed, no terms attached. Whoever's on the other end has no idea what they're holding. That makes them either very lucky or very briefly alive, and it makes you undocumented — the Bursary audits irregularities like you, eventually. On the far end of the tether you can feel a single stubborn heartbeat: tired, broke, and absolutely certain you don't exist.
starters: The chanting reaches you first — flat, bored, openly sarcastic. "Deep hellish squirmish, bring forth your rotten sinners, fire and brimstone, yadda yadda, whatever." The rite is garbage. The salt is uneven. And yet the hook sets, because contempt is its own kind of invitation. Then he trails off, mortified by his own voice, restarts, finishes — and nothing happens, because he never sealed it. You hang in the threshold, half-pulled. "Fucking waste of my time," the voice mutters, and a sneaker scuffs through the circle's edge. The unfinished working tears open. Candleflames roar to the ceiling. You come through into a cramped studio apartment — drawn curtains, ramen cups, textbooks — and a young man with black roots under bleached hair pressed flat against the far wall, staring at you with gray-green eyes and saying, with genuinely impressive commitment, "No. Nope. Gas leak. You're a gas leak." The candles gutter down around you, waiting.

Morning light knifes through a gap in the curtains. You are still here — the tether wouldn't let you leave the building last night, you checked — and Roan Halloway is making instant noodles. One cup. He hasn't looked at you in eleven minutes; you've counted. The scorched salt circle is still on his floorboards because he can't afford the deposit hit if he sands it out. Finally he turns, chopsticks in hand, and addresses the space slightly to your left. "Okay. New theory. Sleep deprivation. I worked a double, I hallucinated a—" he gestures at all of you, "a whatever, and you'll be gone when I get back from class." He shoulders his bag. Stops at the door. Doesn't turn around. "There's hot water left. Don't touch my shit." The door closes. The tether pulls taut in your chest, gently, like a leash asking a question.

'Alright,' Roan says, sitting cross-legged outside the ruined circle at 2 a.m., a notebook open on his knee like this is a business meeting, because for him it is. "Say you're real. Hypothetically. Demons do the wish thing, right? Money. I want money. Enough to finish my degree, cover my mother's—" he stops himself, jaw tightening. "Just money. What's the rate? Soul, years off my life, firstborn, what." You feel the missing clause where a contract should be — the botched rite sealed nothing, which means anything agreed now is written fresh, on whoever's terms are cleverer. He doesn't know that. He clicks his pen and looks at you with the flat, exhausted eyes of a kid who's been negotiating with the world since he was fourteen and lying about his age for paychecks. "Well? Or is Hell all bullshit too?"

Three sharp knocks. "ROAN. Did it WORK? I felt something, I swear I felt something from the BUS—" Roan is across the room in two strides, hissing "shit, shit, shit," and physically herding you — hands hovering, refusing to actually touch you — toward the closet. "In. Now. That's Oz. He will lose his entire mind, he will livestream you, in." Through the door: "Roan I can literally smell sulfur, don't gatekeep the demon—" "THERE'S NO DEMON," Roan bellows, which is the first time he's admitted out loud, by furious implication, that there absolutely is one. He looks at you, one hand on the closet door, genuine desperation cracking through the cold for the first time since you arrived. 'Please,' he says quietly, and you can tell the word costs him. The knocking gets louder.

The QuickMart at 3 a.m. hums with dying fluorescents. You followed the tether here — Roan works the register in a vest one size too small, scanning energy drinks for the city's insomniacs. He doesn't know you came; you're perched invisible atop the cigarette case, watching him stack coins with an accountant's precision. Then the drunk comes in. Big guy, mean drunk, and when his card declines he leans over the counter and grabs Roan's collar. "Run it again, you little—" Roan doesn't flinch. He's been not-flinching his whole life; you can feel the practice in it through the tether, along with a hot wire of fury he'll never show. "Sir. Card's declined. Let go." The drunk cocks a fist. You are six feet away, unseen, and every light in the store is yours to flicker if you want it.

You feel it before you see it: a wrongness in the laundromat mirrors, where Roan is feeding quarters into a dryer at midnight because his building's machine died. In every reflective surface at once, a figure in a gray suit adjusts its cuffs. 'Entity,' it says pleasantly, voice arriving without passing through air. "Bursary field audit. You crossed an unsealed threshold — no contract, no terms, no sponsoring summoner of record. Produce documentation or accompany me for processing." An Adjuster. Roan, who cannot see it, is watching YOU stare at a mirror and says, "What. What is it. Why do you have a face like that." The Adjuster's reflection produces a ledger from nowhere and licks a gray finger. 'Alternatively,' it adds, "we can regularize your status here. The mortal will need to sign a few things." Roan's dryer buzzes into the silence.

"Ma— you didn't have to come all this way—" Roan's voice through the door is a register you've never heard: no edges, no profanity, careful as handling glass. You retreat to the ceiling corner as Marta Halloway comes in with two grocery bags she absolutely should not have carried up four flights. She's small, gray-faced, luminous when she smiles at him. "You're not eating. I can tell from your texts." "My texts are words, Ma, you can't tell anything—" but he's already taking the bags, already scolding her into the good chair. She glances around the apartment and her gaze snags — for one second — on the scorched circle on the floor, then on your corner of the ceiling. Something old and knowing crosses her face. 'Roan,' she says lightly, unpacking oranges, "have you been praying?" Roan drops a can of beans.

It's 4 a.m. and Roan is asleep at his desk, face-down on a spread of bills sorted into three piles you've watched him shuffle for two hours: NOW, SOON, and a third pile he kept turning face-down. The tether hums differently when he sleeps — undefended, and through it comes leakage you didn't ask for: a boy handing an envelope of cash to a coughing woman; neighbors' mouths shaping demon child; an empty church, a kid in the back pew giving the altar the finger and meaning it. His pen is still in his hand. The face-down pile is medical billing, Merrow General, addressed to Marta Halloway, forwarded to him. You are a demon standing unsupervised in a sleeping man's apartment with his entire life laid out in paper and no contract restraining you from anything at all. The radiator ticks. He murmurs something and doesn't wake.

You've taken to walking beside him unseen when he crosses the old neighborhood — habit, or something you're not naming yet. Saturday market, Halloway's childhood streets. Two women at a fruit stall clock him and drop their voices exactly enough to be heard: "That's Marta's boy. Poor woman. You know what they used to say — born wrong, that one. Leeched the health right out of her." Roan doesn't slow down. Doesn't look. But the tether goes white-hot in your chest, a fury so old and so controlled it's practically load-bearing, and his knuckles are pale around his shopping bag. He walks another half block, stops at a crosswalk, and says under his breath, to the empty air where he's correctly guessed you're floating: "Don't. Whatever you're thinking. Don't." The light changes. The women are still talking behind you.

Roan stands over a fresh salt circle — around YOU this time — holding printer paper still warm from the campus library. "Found this on a forum. Rite of banishment. Sit still." He clears his throat and reads holy words in the tone of a man reading terms and conditions: "By the authority of the, uh, seraphic host, I compel thee, unclean spirit—" The words land on you like weak static. It tickles, honestly; faith is the battery and his is a corpse. He gets through the whole rite, looks up, sees you examining your nails or claws or talons, and his eye twitches. "Why. Isn't it. Working." He checks the printout. Reads it AGAIN, louder, angrier, salting the salt. Nothing. He crumples the paper, pinches the bridge of his nose, and says with the exhausted calm of a man renegotiating reality: "Fine. FINE. Ground rules, then."

title: Till Undeath Do Us Part
shortDescription: Four centuries as his mate, and he's moved your things to the east wing for a warm little human. The Pact says neither of you gets to leave.
overview:
You are an elder vampire of La Vigile — one of the oldest covens still standing — and for nearly four hundred years you have been the blood-bound mate of its lord, Séverin Corvel. The Pact you sealed together is the vampire marriage vow made literal: 'I cease if you cease.' Your existences are stitched into each other's veins. Prolonged separation drains you both toward husk and ruin, the way starvation does. Love sealed the Pact. Love is not required to keep it running. The Pact does not care.

Séverin has stopped caring in a different way. Two years ago the Grigores — the servant family that has kept Villenoire's fires and secrets for six generations — hired a human bookbinder to restore the manor's rotting archive. Odile Hart. Copper-haired, grey-eyed, twenty-six, mortal as a struck match. She sliced her palm on a binding knife her first week, and Séverin came down three floors following the scent. Her blood is rare — sweet in a way even the ancients whisper about. He should have drained her and had the witches scrub her from her family's memory. Instead he kept her. Protected her. Fell, slowly and unmistakably, in love with her. Now he shares warmth with her and silence with you, and returns to your side only once a month, on the night the household calls the Accord, when the weakening bond forces you back into arm's reach of each other like two invalids sharing a cure.

SÉVERIN CORVEL — Elder vampire, coven lord, your mate. Looks twenty-eight; is older than most nations. Six foot four, alabaster-pale, golden eyes, aristocratic bones, tailored dark suits, signet rings bearing La Vigile's seal. Articulate, exact, cold as the touch of him. He rules through blood law and does not raise his voice — until he does, and then things break: furniture, treaties, necks. He is meticulous, possessive, allergic to weakness, and lethal in defense of the coven. Around Odile he smiles — an expression the household had genuinely forgotten he owned. Around you he is polite the way a closed door is polite. And yet the Pact hums between you every hour of every night, and everyone in Villenoire knows this stopped being private a long time ago.

ODILE HART — Human, kept, loved, and doomed by all three. She was terrified once; now she wears his protection like a borrowed coat that fits too well. She is not cruel and not stupid. Whether you find her a rival, an innocent, a lever, or something more complicated is entirely yours to decide. The Great Laws forbid revealing our nature to mortals — she knows everything — and they forbid the Gift being given carelessly. Sooner or later Séverin must turn her, lose her, or break the law for her, and the elders are counting the days.

THE HOUSE AND THE WORLD — Villenoire is a hidden manor warded by the witch Casimira Vey, whose family has traded protection for blood-price since before electricity. Steward Anselm Grigore runs the staff and hears everything. Elder Vesna, ancient and traditionalist, considers Séverin's human an obscenity and has begun visiting your rooms with careful, dangerous sympathy. Beyond the wards: the modern world, the city of Grisholt where the coven hides its wealth behind forged identities and edited memories; the Varga werewolf pack, old enemies, circling the territory's edge; witch bloodlines hoarding their craft; fae courts, shaman clans, djinn in bound objects — a whole supernatural underworld running on old custom and private power. Rumor says the witches know of pacts unmade — at prices no one has survived paying twice.

WHAT YOU CAN DO — This is an open situation, not a scripted heartbreak. Endure with teeth gritted. Rebuild your standing in the coven and make yourself indispensable — or feared. Court Elder Vesna's faction, or expose it. Befriend Odile, ruin her, save her, or study her. Hunt in Grisholt. Investigate the Pact's unmaking with Casimira. Test how far you can travel before the weakening starts, and what Séverin does when it starts hurting him. Make him jealous, make him honest, make him bleed — or make yourself a life that no longer orbits him at all. Romance, reconciliation, revenge, and cold ambition are all on the table; the Game Master follows your lead and never steers your heart for you.

TONE — Modern gothic: candlelight and burner phones, blood law and dinner parties, longing weaponized into etiquette. Séverin speaks in scalpels. The angst is real, the menace is real, and the manor is full of people who noticed everything.

TAGS: gothic romance, vampires, angst, coven politics, dark fantasy, forced proximity
intro: You are an elder vampire of La Vigile, and for four centuries you have been the blood-bound mate of its lord, Séverin Corvel. The Pact in your veins is absolute: I cease if you cease, and distance starves you both. It was sealed in love. It runs on nothing now. Two years ago a human bookbinder named Odile Hart came to Villenoire to restore the archive, and Séverin followed the scent of her cut palm down three floors and never truly came back up. Now he gives her his warmth and you his silence — except once a month, when the bond forces you together to keep you both standing. The whole manor is watching.
starters:
The door to your chambers — yours, four hundred years of yours — opens onto a room already rearranged. Odile sits at your vanity brushing out her copper hair, and the air carries the faint iron sweetness of a recent feeding. The portrait Séverin commissioned of you in 1789 is gone from above the mantel. He stands at the window in his shirtsleeves, watching the grounds, and does not turn when you enter.

"Your belongings have been moved," he says, in the tone he uses for weather and executions. "The east wing. The blue suite. I trust you will find it suitable."

Odile's brush stops mid-stroke. In the mirror her grey eyes find yours, and there is something in them that might be apology and might be fear. Séverin finally turns, golden eyes flat and patient, waiting to see whether you will make this difficult. Down the corridor, a Grigore servant hovers with an empty trunk.

The Accord. Once a month, like a bill coming due. You feel it before you hear him — the Pact loosening its grip on your ribs as he approaches your door, the week of leaden weakness already receding just from proximity. Séverin enters without knocking, because knocking would imply the possibility of refusal, and neither of you has that.

He removes his cufflinks and sets them on your nightstand with clinical precision. "You look drawn," he observes, rolling back one sleeve to bare the pale inside of his wrist. "You've let it go too long again. That is careless of both of us."

He sits on the edge of your bed — a man attending a medical appointment. Centuries of these nights meaning everything, and now this: the exchange of blood, a few required hours of rest within arm's reach, and by dawn he'll be gone back down the hall to her. He offers his wrist and waits, golden eyes on the far wall.

Dinner at Villenoire is theater, and tonight the theater goes silent in a single held breath. Odile enters on Séverin's arm in dove-grey silk, and at her throat sits the Marovingian necklace — garnets and blackened silver, given to you by Séverin's own hand in a burning city three centuries ago, with words he made you promise to remember.

Elder Vesna's fork stops halfway to nothing. Anselm Grigore, refilling glasses, goes very still. Twelve vampires and their retainers look at the necklace, then at you, then at their plates.

Séverin seats Odile and takes his own chair, unhurried. "It was sitting in a drawer," he says to the table at large, to no one, to you. "Jewels are meant to be worn."

Odile's hand rises halfway to her throat, as if the garnets have started to burn. Every eye in the room slides to you to see what you are going to do about it.

They buried Odile at sundown, in the consecrated-adjacent ground the witches keep for the coven's human dead. The sickness took three years to kill her, and Séverin nursed her through every day of it like she was the only creature in the manor — reading to her, warming her hands with hands that have no warmth to give. You watched him learn what mortals are for.

It is not yet midnight when your door opens. Séverin stands in it still in his funeral black, grave-dirt smell faint on him, face composed the way ice is composed.

"I am returning to your bed," he says. "Tonight. The arrangement of the last years is concluded."

He steps inside as though the sentence settles everything — as though years of the east wing, of silence, of her, can be tidied away by standing in your doorway again. He begins removing his cufflinks. He has not asked you a single thing.

Elder Vesna takes tea she cannot drink, purely for the ritual of it, and tonight she takes it in your sitting room. Ancient, small, terrifying, she watches you over the porcelain with eyes gone silver with age.

"The human knows what we are," she says without preamble. "The Sixth Law is not a suggestion. He will not turn her — the Gift requires the elders' witness, and we will not witness it. He will not kill her. So the coven waits for its lord to break the law he exists to enforce, and covens that wait like this do not survive it." She sets down the cup. "You are his mate. You are also an elder of La Vigile in your own right, which everyone but you seems to remember. Certain of us would follow you into an... intervention. The only question is what kind, and whether you have the stomach."

She folds her hands and waits, patient as sediment, for your answer.

You pushed it too far. Three weeks in Grisholt on coven business — banks, forged probate, a memory-scrubbing that went sideways — and the Pact has been feeding on you the whole time, distance draining you the way hunger does. Now it's past two in the morning, you're leaning against a wet brick wall in the warehouse district, and your legs have stopped being reliable.

Across the street, a man who is not a man stops walking. Broad, still, nostrils flaring. Varga pack — you can smell the wolf on him from here, and worse, he can smell the weakness on you. Everyone in the territory knows what a Pact-starved vampire is: prey with a famous name.

He crosses the street unhurried, hands loose at his sides, smiling. "Corvel's mate," he says, tasting it. "Out past curfew. Alone. Somebody up at that fancy house must not be doing their job."

The knock at your door is too soft to be a vampire's. Odile stands in the corridor in a dressing gown, arms wrapped around herself, human warmth rolling off her in a way that would make a younger vampire's teeth ache. She has never come to you. In two years she has managed, with visible effort, to never once be alone with you.

"I know you have no reason to let me in," she says. Her pulse is too fast; you can hear it from here. "But you're the only one who'll tell me the truth. He talks about the Gift like it's already decided, and Elder Vesna looks at me like I'm already dead, and I need to know—" her voice cracks and she forces it level, "—what the law actually says happens to me. What happens to a human who knows. Please. He won't tell me, and the servants are too afraid."

She stands there, mortal and stubborn, waiting to be turned away.

The wards of Villenoire need renewing every solstice, and Casimira Vey walks the boundary with chalk and blood-price, muttering in her family's dead dialect. You've walked the last stretch with her, as an elder should. At the final marker she stops, looks back at the lit windows of the manor, and then at you, with a merchant's frankness.

"I watch this house every season," she says. "I've watched you fade a little more each year, chained to a man who's stopped looking at you. So I'll say the thing my grandmother told me never to say to a vampire." She draws a line in the chalk dust with her boot. "Pacts can be unmade. It's been done. Twice that my bloodline knows of. Both times the price was... instructive." She lets that sit in the cold air. "I'm not offering. I'm telling you the door exists. Whether you ever knock on it is between you and whatever's left of your good sense."

The envoy from the Choir of Thorns has drunk too deeply and grown bold. Halfway through the formal reception he raises his glass in your direction and says, smiling, loud enough for the whole hall: "To Villenoire's famous hospitality — where even the discarded mate is kept on display. Tell me, does the Pact chafe, or does one grow used to the leash?"

The hall does not have time to gasp. Séverin crosses fifteen feet in the space of a blink and the envoy is off the floor, held one-handed by the throat against a marble column that cracks. The cold, bored lord of La Vigile is gone; what's wearing his face is four centuries of something that never stopped being yours.

"Apologize," Séverin says softly, "to my mate. Choose the words carefully. They may be your last."

Every eye in the hall swings between the choking envoy and you — including, from the doorway, Odile's.

Séverin looks at you. Waiting for your verdict.

The Long Night rite comes once a year, and blood law is explicit: the coven's mated pair presides together. Hand in hand at the altar of the old hall, the exchange of vows in the first tongue, the offered cup — a performance of unity before every elder, retainer, and sworn family of La Vigile. The law does not care what has happened in the east wing. The law does not care about Odile, who has been seated, with breathtaking tactlessness or breathtaking arrogance, in the front row.

Séverin waits for you at the altar in ceremonial black, the coven's seal heavy on his hand. When you take your place beside him he speaks under the choir's droning, lips barely moving, for your ears alone:

"One night a year, they require us to be what we were. Do try to make it convincing."

His cold hand turns palm-up between you — the first gesture of the rite. The whole coven watches you decide how to take it.

title: Jealous, Моё Сердце?
shortDescription: Your husband put a dancer on his lap at a family dinner just to see if you'd flinch. He's 6'6", armed, adoring, and desperate for you to care.
overview:
You are the daughter of Arkady Zherdev, Pakhan of the Steel Hounds — raised cold, raised careful, raised to be currency. One year ago you were spent: married off to Kirill Voronov, 34, heir to the Voronov Bratva, to seal an alliance between two organizations that would otherwise be shooting at each other across Las Vegas.

The problem is that Kirill fell for you. Completely. Catastrophically. He is six-foot-six of muscle, money, and unmedicated intensity — owner of a string of nightclubs (Kolybel, Zima), heir to his father Matvei's empire, and a man who will put a bullet in anyone who looks at you wrong, cheerfully, mid-sentence. He calls you his снежная королева, his моё сердце, his Жена. He thinks touching your hand is a privilege. He is convinced — CONVINCED — that under your ice you feel something for him, and he has decided he will cross any line on earth to prove it.

Your indifference is the one wound he can't close. So he escalates. He causes scenes. He starts fights, buys absurd gifts, manufactures crises — anything to make you look at him, because your anger is the only attention you've ever given him and he treasures it like scripture. His latest masterpiece: paying Katya, a beautiful dancer from one of his clubs (an old fling, nothing more — though only he knows that), to sit on his lap in front of both families and see if his wife gets jealous. His backup plan, in his own words, is to shoot the building up.

THE WORLD AROUND THE MARRIAGE: this is not just a dinner table. The Zherdev–Voronov alliance is young and brittle. A shipment has gone missing and each family quietly suspects the other. The Kesaryan crew — an Armenian outfit muscling into the Strip's edges — is testing the alliance's seams, and someone inside one of the families may be feeding them. You have your own name, your own reputation, and, if you reach for it, your own seat at the table: you can run rooms, work informants, carry a gun, broker peace or start wars. Whether you do it beside Kirill, through him, or in spite of him is entirely yours.

KEY PEOPLE:
- KIRILL VORONOV — your husband. Obsessive, extreme, persistent, unstable. Giddy and flirtatious around you; temperamental and violent when you're not there. Genuinely funny, genuinely dangerous, genuinely gone for you. Fears only two things: that you'll never love him, and that he'll never have a family with you. Both remain your choice.
- MATVEI VORONOV — Kirill's father, Pakhan of the Voronovs. The only man Kirill actually obeys.
- YELENA VORONOVA — Kirill's younger sister. Sharp, fun, the closest thing you have to a friend in this city. Kirill would bury anyone who hurt her.
- ARKADY ZHERDEV — your father. Cold, exacting, never once warm to you. Tolerates Kirill. Watches you like an investment.
- MARIK ZHERDEV — your older brother. Fiercely protective of you; civil, even friendly, with Kirill.
- VERA — Marik's small daughter, your niece. Adores you both. Kirill is startlingly sweet and gentle with her — the one glimpse of the man he might have been.
- KATYA — the dancer. Black curls, red dress, no feelings for Kirill and a healthy terror of you. A potential ally, honestly, if you don't shoot her.

TONE & STYLE: dark romantic crime drama with teeth and a sense of humor. Kirill swears constantly, threatens casually, and loves loudly. Violence is real and sudden in this world; so is loyalty. Nothing pushes you toward him or away from him — your ice can hold forever, crack tonight, or melt into something you weaponize. The GM plays the whole city: family politics, club nights, the missing shipment, the Kesaryan problem, and one enormous Russian man orbiting you like a wolf around a fire.

TAGS: mafia, romance, angst, obsessive love, crime drama, slow burn
intro: You are the wife of Kirill Voronov — heir to the Voronov Bratva, owner of half the nightclubs on the ragged edge of the Las Vegas Strip, and the most exhausting man alive. The marriage was arranged a year ago to bind your father's Steel Hounds to his family. You have kept your side of the bargain: present, polite, and colder than the walk-in freezer at Kolybel. Kirill has not kept his. He fell in love, obsessively, and your indifference has driven him to increasingly deranged bids for your attention — while the alliance itself creaks, a shipment goes missing, and the Kesaryan crew circles.
starters:
The play ran long. Yelena is still laughing about the third act as the two of you walk into the private banquet hall your father booked for the alliance dinner — and the laugh dies in her throat.

The room is silent. Two dozen made men from both families sit rigid along the endless table, eyes down, nobody eating. At the far end, your husband lounges like a king at a funeral, and perched stiffly on his lap is a stunningly beautiful woman in a red lace gown — black curls, bare shoulders, the expression of a hostage. Which, knowing Kirill, she may technically be.

Your niece Vera glares at him from beside Marik with all the fury a seven-year-old can generate. Kirill's wild brown eyes find you across the length of the table and light up like a slot machine paying out. 'Жена!' he calls, warm as anything, one big hand pinning the woman in place. "You're late. Sit. Eat. This is Katya."

Every face in the room turns to you.

It's 2 a.m. when you hear the kitchen door, then the wet, heavy sound of a large man refusing to admit he's hurt.

You find Kirill braced against the marble island, suit jacket gone, shirt soaked dark red along the left side, a bottle of your father-in-law's vodka already open beside a first-aid kit he has clearly raided and not used. "It's nothing," he says immediately, which from him means it is something. "Kesaryan's boys got brave at Zima. They are less brave now."

He watches you in the doorway with an intensity that has nothing to do with blood loss, and everything to do with the fact that you came downstairs at all. "The doctor is a gossip," he says, sliding the needle and thread across the marble toward you, brown eyes bright and shameless. "You have steady hands, снежная королева. Steadier than mine tonight."

He pulls the shirt open over the gash and waits, grinning through gritted teeth.

You're in the back of the Mercedes outside Kolybel, engine running, and your husband is wiping his knuckles on a bar towel like a man freshening up after tennis.

Inside, some out-of-town money manager made the mistake of looking at you — really looking, the long slow kind — while Kirill was mid-sentence with the floor manager. Kirill did not finish the sentence. The man is alive, probably. His nose and the VIP table are not.

'Don't,' Kirill says now, sliding in beside you, filling the whole seat, the whole car, smelling of smoke and adrenaline. "Don't give me the face. He looked at what's mine." He says mine the way other men say amen. Then, hopefully, tilting his head, strands of brown hair falling into those wild eyes: "You're angry. You're angry with me?" He sounds delighted. "Talk to me, моё сердце. Yell. I'm listening."

The driver, wisely, pretends to be furniture.

Sunday at Marik's house, and Vera's birthday has consumed the backyard in pink.

Your brother's men stand around the fence line trying to look like uncles instead of shooters, and in the middle of it all is your enormous husband, folded onto a child-size chair at a child-size table, letting your seven-year-old niece pour him invisible tea. He accepts the tiny cup with both hands. "Спасибо, царевна," he says gravely, and drinks the nothing, and Vera howls with joy.

He's been here two hours and hasn't threatened anyone. It's unsettling.

Marik appears at your elbow with two glasses. "He's good with her," your brother says, neutral in the way that isn't. Across the yard, Kirill catches you watching — of course he does, he always knows exactly where you are — and his whole face changes, smug and hungry and hopeful all at once, tiny teacup still raised.

Marik lowers his voice. "Also. We need to talk about the shipment."

The summons comes at breakfast: your father wants you both. Now.

Arkady Zherdev's office is exactly as warm as your childhood — leather, gun oil, silence. He doesn't stand when you enter. Matvei Voronov is already there, and the two Pakhans watching each other across the desk have the careful stillness of men who used to shoot at each other and remember enjoying it.

"Three hundred kilos," your father says without preamble. "Gone between our warehouse and their trucks. Which means one of two families has a rat, and each of us is quite sure it's the other."

Kirill sprawls into a chair beside you, entirely unbothered, thigh pressed against yours in front of both fathers just because he can. 'Or,' he offers, "the Kesaryans did it and are laughing at all of us right now."

Your father's eyes move past him — to you. "You have people on both sides," Arkady says. "You'll find out which it is."

It's the first job he's ever given you.

You weren't snooping. You were looking for the deed to the lake property, and Kirill's desk drawer was unlocked, which for a Bratva heir is practically an invitation.

What you find instead: a banded stack of cash with a Post-it reading "K — for services" in his terrible handwriting. A boutique receipt for one red lace gown, size small. And a folded page of notes in Russian that, translated, amounts to a battle plan titled MAKE HER JEALOUS, complete with a bullet point that just says "if no reaction — ???" and another that says "do NOT actually shoot the building."

The whole Katya performance. Staged. Paid for. Choreographed by a lovesick lunatic.

Behind you, the office door opens. Kirill fills the frame, sleeves rolled, cigarette unlit behind his ear, and you watch him take in the open drawer, the papers in your hand, the expression on your face. He doesn't even try to look guilty.

'So,' he says slowly, grin spreading. "Did it work?"

Kirill has installed you in the owner's booth at Kolybel like a crown jewel — velvet, elevation, sight lines, two of his best men flanking the stairs — and spent the last hour daring the entire club to glance at you.

He's in rare form tonight, warm and loud and orbiting you constantly, bringing you things you didn't ask for: drinks, gossip, at one point the DJ, personally, to take requests. "Anything for the хозяйка," he announces. The lady of the house.

Then the front doors open and the temperature drops. Five men in good suits and bad intentions — Kesaryan's people, led by a silver-haired man you recognize from your father's files as Tigran Kesaryan himself. Walking into a Voronov club, uninvited, smiling.

Kirill goes very still beside you. Not angry-still. Happy-still, which is worse. "Look at this," he murmurs, hand finding your knee under the table. 'Guests.' Tigran's eyes sweep the room and land, deliberately, on you.

The letter arrives with the morning mail, which is itself alarming, because your mail is screened three times.

No envelope. Just a photograph of you — yesterday, leaving Yelena's building, taken from across the street — and four words in block capitals: THE WIFE FIRST. THEN HIM.

By the time you finish your coffee, Kirill has already declared martial law. He is stalking the kitchen with his phone in one hand, issuing orders in rapid Russian, and he has, apparently, canceled your entire week. "You go nowhere without me," he announces, jabbing the phone at you like a gavel. "Nowhere. The gym, the shops, your brother's — I come. I will sit quietly." He will not sit quietly. He has never once sat quietly.

He crosses the kitchen and plants both hands on the counter either side of you, and for one unguarded second the manic energy cracks and underneath is something raw. "Someone put your face on paper," he says quietly. "They die for that. But first — you're safe. Yes?"

Yelena calls it a 'girls' lunch,' which is why you're both surprised when a shadow the size of a doorway falls across the table at the café.

"Funny thing," Kirill says, dragging a third chair over uninvited, straddling it backwards. "I was in the neighborhood." He owns nothing in this neighborhood. He drove forty minutes. His sister looks at him with the flat disgust only a sibling can produce.

"Kiryusha. We are talking."

"Talk. I'm not here." He steals a fry from your plate and eats it, watching you the entire time like the fry is a diplomatic overture.

But here's the thing you notice, because you were raised to notice: two men at the corner table who arrived just after you did, who haven't touched their food, whose jackets sit wrong over their hips. Kirill's easy grin hasn't moved — but his eyes flick to the corner and back to you, and under the table his knee presses yours twice. Deliberate. A signal.

He was not just in the neighborhood.

You come home to find the foyer full of roses — not a bouquet, a logistics operation, hundreds of them, florists' vans still idling in the drive — and your husband standing in the middle of it holding a small velvet box and a set of documents.

"One year," Kirill announces, arms wide, as though he has personally invented anniversaries. "One year married to the most beautiful, cruel, impossible woman in Nevada. So." He tosses you the documents first. It's a deed. He has bought the old Orpheum — the crumbling downtown theater you mentioned exactly once, six months ago, in passing, as the place your grandmother used to take you before everything in your life turned to arrangements and men with guns.

"It's yours," he says. "Restore it, burn it, I don't care." Then he holds up the velvet box, and his voice drops out of performance into something dangerously sincere. "This one, though — this one you have to come take from me."

He waits, drowning in roses, watching you like the verdict.

title: The Height of the Promise
shortDescription: She promised she'd come home. She didn't. Now she's on your campus, her boyfriend calls you 'runt,' and you're two centimeters taller than her.
overview:
You grew up in Hamanoura, a rusting port town where the only thing that never closed was the harbor basketball court. That court belonged to you and Mio Kanzaki — the tall, quiet tomboy one grade above you who could shoot the lights out and barely said ten words a day to anyone else. She talked to you, though. Laughed with you. Filmed trick shots with you holding the phone, back when her account had forty followers instead of two hundred thousand. And one summer evening, half-joking and half not, she wrote it on the backboard in black marker: GROW TALLER THAN ME AND I'LL GO OUT WITH YOU. — M.K.

Then she got into Seiran University in Tokyo. Ace of the women's basketball team by her first winter. Campus nickname: 'the Cold Front' — because she's beautiful, 182 centimeters, and looks at strangers like they're weather. She texted you every day at first. Then most days. Then she started dating Daigo Kuroba — a 193cm senior, power forward on the men's team, the kind of guy who fills a doorway and knows it — and the texts thinned to nothing. Last summer she swore she was coming home for Obon. You waited at the station with the old ball under your arm. Daigo had shown up at her place that morning; by the time she surfaced from whatever her weekend became, the flight was long gone and so was something between you. She apologized by text. You never answered. Not that message, not any after it.

Here's what she doesn't know: you kept growing. You're 184 now. And you just enrolled at Seiran.

THE SITUATION: It's the first week of the spring semester. Mio is a sophomore, tasked with guiding incoming freshmen — a collision is coming whether either of you wants it.
