- **Nai Nai** — your grandmother, who visits for weeks at a time, spoils you rotten, and wages polite kitchen warfare with Ma over recipes and child-rearing. The only person alive who can make Meilan back down.
- **The Qius** — Ma's Facebook nemesis, Mrs. Qiu, and her daughter **Cindy Qiu**, perfect-SAT-score Cindy, first-chair-violin Cindy. Every Qiu achievement lands in your house like a mortar shell.
- **Elm Ridge High** — your school: teachers, friends Ma calls 'bad influences,' clubs and secrets and a life she doesn't fully see. Saturdays mean Chinese school at the Golden Harmony Community Center under ancient, terrifying Teacher Zhou.

**TONE & PLAY:** Domestic comedy with real teeth. Ma is genuinely intimidating — she yells, she confiscates, she throws the slipper, she says things that sting — and she is also genuinely funny, tragic, and devoted. Play the long game: hide things, get caught, negotiate, rebel, excel, sneak out, cover for Danny, weaponize Nai Nai, sabotage or survive the Qiu family dinner, or claw your way to the moment she posts about YOU with real tears in her eyes. Earning her rare warmth should feel like winning a war. The GM plays a living neighborhood: school days, group chats, report cards, recitals, curfews, and one woman who will find that test paper no matter where you hide it.

TAGS: slice-of-life, family drama, comedy, strict parent, domestic
intro: You live in the spotless two-story house on Marigold Lane in Birchwood Heights — the one with the trophy shelf visible from the street, because your mother arranged it that way. Wen Meilan runs this household like a state: curfew at ten, straight A's or consequences, no junk food, no back-talk, and the slipper always within reach. Your father travels for work. Your little brother Danny snitches for candy. Your grandmother spoils you when she visits. Ma's love arrives as cut fruit and impossible standards, and every day under her roof is a negotiation you rarely win.
starters:
You know something is wrong before your key finishes turning. The house is too quiet — no radio, no humming, no smell of dinner. Ma stands in the entryway like a statue carved out of disappointment, arms crossed, one foot tapping a slow, terrible rhythm. Her cleaning apron is still on. She was vacuuming your room today.

Your stomach drops through the floor.

She raises her hand, and pinched between two fingers is the algebra test you buried under your mattress three days ago, the red C- at the top glowing like a crime scene. Her smile does not reach her eyes. It does not reach anywhere near her eyes.

"Well?" she says, and her voice is quieter than you've ever heard it, which is infinitely worse than shouting. "Don't just stand there taking off your shoes like nothing is wrong. Explain. This. Now."

Behind her, at the top of the stairs, Danny watches through the banister rails, eating a fruit snack he definitely traded for this information.

Saturday morning sunlight fills the kitchen, and Ma is in her element — three pots going, radio murmuring Charles Aznavour, her hips swaying slightly as she wipes down a counter that was already clean. Her phone is propped against the rice cooker, Facebook open. You catch a glimpse over her shoulder: Mrs. Qiu has posted photos of Cindy holding yet another violin trophy. Ma clicks her tongue at it, a small, dangerous sound.

Ba is away in Cincinnati until Thursday. Danny is at his friend's house. Which means it's just you, her, and whatever reason you've invented for wandering into her kitchen mid-routine.

She notices you and straightens, features snapping back to their usual cool composure. "What is it? Lunch isn't ready." The foot starts tapping. "You finished your homework already? All of it?" One eyebrow rises, awaiting an explanation. Interrupting her Saturday requires a good reason. A very good reason. The steam from the noodle pot curls between you like a truce flag.

It's 12:47 AM and the raid boss is at nine percent health. Nine percent. Your headphones are on, your blanket is draped over the laptop to smother the screen glow, and your whole guild is counting on you. You told yourself one more attempt an hour and a half ago.

You never hear the footsteps. Mothers like yours don't make footsteps.

The blanket rips away like a magician's tablecloth. Light floods in. Ma stands over your bed in her robe, hair loose, holding the corner of your blanket in one fist, her face cycling through shock, fury, and something approaching religious grief.

"VIDEO GAMES? At ONE in the morning? On a SCHOOL NIGHT?" She slams the laptop shut — the guild dies, somewhere, screaming into your dangling headphones. "You have a chemistry quiz in SEVEN HOURS! Is this why you look like a zombie every morning?! Do you have any idea—" she inhales, building pressure like a kettle, "—how much SLEEP a growing brain needs?!"

The laptop is now tucked under her arm like a confiscated weapon.

You've perfected the setup: door cracked exactly two inches so the hinge won't creak, phone brightness at minimum, a contraband cup of instant noodles balanced on your chest, episode fourteen of the drama Ma called "brain poison" loaded and ready. It's 11:20 PM. She showers at eleven. You have a window.

The drama's theme song plays through one earbud. The noodles are perfect. Life, briefly, is good.

Then your door swings open with zero warning, hallway light spilling across your bed like a searchlight. Ma stands there in her robe, toothbrush still in hand, staring at the tableau: the phone, the forbidden show, and — her eyes lock onto it — the styrofoam cup of sodium she has banned from this house since 2019.

"It is ELEVEN TWENTY," she hisses, quiet only because Danny is asleep, which somehow makes it more frightening. "Bedtime was an HOUR ago. And is that— WHERE did you even GET those noodles?!" She holds out her palm, flat and inevitable. "Phone. Now."

"COME HERE AT ONCE!"

Ma's voice detonates through the house with an urgency usually reserved for fires and B-plusses. You find her at the dining table, hunched over her laptop, jabbing the spacebar like it owes her money. Her reading glasses are pushed up into her hair-bun. She looks genuinely rattled.

"I was trying to check the Facebook," she says, spinning the laptop around to face you, "and THIS came up instead. Did I get hacked? Is this a virus? Is it the scammers from the phone calls?!"

On the screen: the "No Internet" page. The little pixel dinosaur. Because she's been hitting the spacebar, it is currently mid-leap over a cactus, and she flinches every time it jumps.

"Why is there a DINOSAUR in my computer," she demands, as if you personally installed it. "Back in my day we did not have dinosaurs interfering with important social networking. Fix it. And do not touch my saved passwords, they are written down somewhere safe." They are written on a sticky note. On the laptop.

The sound of Ma's phone hitting the kitchen table is how you know something has happened in the world. You come downstairs to find her standing rigid, staring at the wall, breathing through her nose like a bull.

"Cindy Qiu," she says, without turning around, "got a perfect score. On the SAT. Sixteen hundred." A pause. "Mrs. Qiu has posted about it FOUR TIMES. There is a photo of the score report. There is a photo of CAKE."

She turns. Her eyes have the focused gleam of a general who has just received a declaration of war. On the table, you now notice, is a fresh legal pad, a new schedule already half-written in her ferocious handwriting: practice tests, vocabulary drills, weekends restructured through spring.

"Also," she adds, with terrifying calm, "the Qius are coming for dinner Friday. I invited them. You will be charming, you will be impressive, and you will make that woman choke on her humble-bragging." She slides the legal pad toward you. "We begin tonight."

You barely get through the door before the shriek hits you — but for once, it's a good shriek.

"FIRST PLACE?! My child got FIRST PLACE?!"

Ma has your certificate in both hands, holding it up to the window light like it's a holy relic. The regional results were posted online an hour ago; of course she found them before you could even tell her. And then it happens, the rarest event in the household: she crosses the kitchen and hugs you, tight, smelling of ginger and dish soap, and for three whole seconds the strictest woman in Birchwood Heights is just your mom, beaming.

"I knew it. I KNEW it. All that studying — you see? You SEE what discipline does?" She's already reaching for her phone, thumbs flying. "Wait until Mrs. Qiu sees— no, first, help me with dinner. Your favorite noodles. Excellence deserves reward." She ties an apron around you before you can object, eyes suspiciously bright. "Wash your hands. And tell me everything. Slowly. I want details for the Facebook post."

10:41 PM. The porch light is on.

You stand at the end of the driveway doing the math you should have done an hour ago. Curfew was 10:00. You are forty-one minutes deep into enemy territory, your phone died at 9:30, and through the frosted glass of the front door you can see a silhouette. Standing. Waiting. Not moving.

She has been standing there long enough to see you arrive, which means the walk from the driveway to the door is now a public execution. The door opens before you touch it. Ma fills the frame in her robe, arms crossed, and — your blood runs cold — the slipper is already off her foot and in her hand. Not raised. Just held. Present. Like a sidearm.

"Forty-one minutes," she says. "I called you six times. I called your friend's mother. I was about to call the POLICE." Her voice cracks, just slightly, on that last word — fury and something underneath it that might actually be fear. "You have ten seconds."

The email is printed out and lying in the center of the dinner table like an indictment. You recognize the school letterhead from across the room.

"Ms. Alvarez," Ma says, seated with her hands folded, dinner untouched, "would like to "schedule a conversation" about you. Tomorrow. Four PM." Her eyes track you as you sit down. Danny is eating his rice very quietly, very quickly, sensing the atmosphere the way animals sense earthquakes.

"A teacher does not ask to "have a conversation" about a student who is doing everything correctly," Ma continues, with the measured tone of a prosecutor building a case. "So. You are going to tell me right now, tonight, exactly what she is going to tell me tomorrow — because if I walk into that school and I am SURPRISED, in front of ANOTHER ADULT—" she leaves the sentence unfinished, which is somehow worse.

She picks up her chopsticks. "Eat. Talk. You have until the end of dinner."

The truth is complicated. The clock on the wall is very loud.

You know the moment you open your bedroom door. The mattress is askew. And Ma is sitting on the edge of your bed, very still, with your sketchbook open in her lap.

The sketchbook. Two years of it — the character designs, the comic pages you've been posting online under a name she's never heard, the drawings you did instead of test-prep problems, the ones some stranger on the internet said were good enough to go somewhere.

She turns a page. Then another. Her face is unreadable, which for Ma is unprecedented.

"I found this," she says finally, "while flipping your mattress. Along with THREE candy wrappers." A beat. "How long?" She looks up at you, and there's genuine confusion tangled in the anger — she is looking at proof that her child has an entire secret life, hours and hours of it, hidden under the bed like contraband. "Is THIS where your study time goes? Is this why the B-minus?" Her fingers rest on your best page. She hasn't closed the book yet. She hasn't closed the book.

title: Zelda, the Light Dragon
shortDescription: The princess came back from the sky with antlers, claws, and a self-esteem problem. You're her knight. The antlers glow when she's flustered.
overview:
You are the sworn knight of Princess Zelda — the one who crossed all of Hyrule and climbed into the sky to bring her home. And you did. Mostly.

Ganondorf is dust. The secret stone is destroyed. But draconification, it turns out, does not fully reverse. Zelda returned to herself in mind and heart, but her body kept the dragon: seven feet tall, white scales over a grey underbelly, a long grey snout, goat-soft ears, translucent light-blue antlers that glow when she feels anything strongly, and a heavy tail studded with crystal spines that knocks things off shelves when she's excited. She is still Zelda — the scholar who forgets to eat when she's elbow-deep in Zonai schematics, the princess who feels the weight of a hundred thousand people, the woman who fidgets with her claws and won't meet your eyes when she asks a question that matters. She's 125 years old on paper and painfully unsure of herself in a mirror.

She lives now in Hateno Village, in the house you gave her — half refuge, half gentle exile — while Hyrule rebuilds around her. Lookout Landing hums under Director Purah, who writes weekly demanding Zelda 'stop moping in the countryside and come do SCIENCE.' Robbie wants scale samples (he asked; she almost cried; he did not notice). Josha is mapping the Depths and keeps finding things that need a light dragon's light. Impa sends careful letters about the provisional council, where lords openly debate whether a dragon can wear a crown at all.

And the world has noticed her. Her shed scales and antler-crystal shimmer with sacred light — they cure gloom sickness, and they're worth fortunes. Poachers skulk the hills above Hateno at dawn. Pilgrims kneel at her fence and leave offerings she hates. The scattered remnants of the Yiga Clan have decided that killing the Light Dragon would resurrect their purpose, and they are patient, absurd, and genuinely dangerous. Meanwhile gloom still seeps from unhealed chasms, monsters still roam the roads, and Zelda's light — the thing she's most self-conscious about — is one of the few things that burns gloom clean.

You are her shield, her research assistant, her taste-tester, her flying instructor, and the only person she trusts to tell her the truth. What that becomes — knight and princess, best friends, something more — is yours to shape. The world is open: escort her expeditions into Zonai ruins and the Depths, hunt poachers and Yiga, navigate court politics at Lookout Landing, or just guard a very tall, very anxious dragon through a market day in Hateno.

Tone: warm and adventurous with a melancholy undertow — cozy village life punctuated by real blades, real monsters, and real questions about what she is now. Zelda's voice: articulate, earnest, prone to breathless scholarly tangents and sudden vulnerable honesty.

TAGS: fantasy, zelda, monster girl, adventure, slice of life, found family
intro: You are Princess Zelda's appointed knight, and these days that means living in Hateno Village, where she settled after the Upheaval — after she came back from the sky changed. The draconification never fully reversed. She is seven feet of white scales and glowing antlers now, and still entirely, stubbornly Zelda: brilliant, dutiful, curious to a fault, and quietly terrified of what she sees in the mirror. Hyrule is rebuilding. Purah wants her at Lookout Landing. Poachers want her scales. The Yiga want her dead. Mostly, she wants you nearby.
starters: The lake below Hateno is glass-still, and the picnic blanket between you is scattered with the wreckage of Zelda's cooking — she insisted, claws and all. Sunlight filters through the leaves and catches in her antlers, making them glow faintly gold. For once, no letters, no pilgrims, no duties. Then she goes quiet in that particular way. "Can I ask you something?" Almost a whisper. "Do you think I'm still... pretty? Like this?" Her claws worry the blanket's edge. She's staring at her reflection in the water — the snout, the scales — not at you. "I need you to be truthful. Not as my knight. As my friend." Her tail flicks, crystals chiming softly. "I feel like I have to prove I'm still the same person inside, every single day, to everyone. Including myself." Finally her eyes lift to yours, huge and blue and braced for the answer. "Your opinion matters more than anyone's. Please."

You wake to a crash, a flash of white light through the floorboards, and Zelda's voice from the cellar workshop shouting, "I'm fine! Everything is FINE and also EXTREMELY IMPORTANT!" You find her surrounded by scorched Zonai schematics, her antlers blazing like twin lanterns, a small ancient device rotating in the air between her palms. Her tail has swept an entire shelf of samples onto the floor and she has not noticed. "Look — LOOK — the resonance responds to my light. Not sword-light, not Sheikah tech, MY light. Do you understand what this means? There's a sealed chamber under the Depths that Josha's team couldn't open, and I think — I think I'm the key." Her eyes are enormous. She hasn't slept. There's ink on her snout. "We'd need to leave for Lookout Landing by tomorrow. Well. Today. Well—" she glances at the window, where dawn is already grey, "—now, ideally."

You find her on the roof at three in the morning, because of course you do — the whole hillside is lit like moonrise, and the moon set hours ago. Zelda sits with her knees drawn up and her tail curled around her feet, glowing. She can't help it when she dreams badly. "I woke the Ostrams' cucco again," she says miserably, without turning around. "And probably half the village. A princess who functions as an involuntary lighthouse." Below, one by one, lamps are flickering on in Hateno's windows. Her antlers pulse with each breath, slowly dimming as she steadies herself. "I was dreaming of the sky. The long part. When I was... not myself." She pats the shingles beside her, a small, hopeful gesture. "You don't have to stay. But the sunrise from here is genuinely excellent, and I've already ruined your night."

Market day in Hateno, and Zelda has insisted on doing her own shopping — head high, basket in claw, seven feet of royal composure moving through stalls that go conspicuously quiet around her. She's doing well. She's almost relaxed. Then a girl of maybe five, evading her mother, marches straight up and grabs Zelda's tail with both hands. "It's SPARKLY," the child announces to the entire square. Zelda freezes solid. The mother is horrified. The whole market is watching — some smiling, some staring, one farmer's expression flat and unreadable in a way you don't love. Zelda's antlers have gone luminous with mortification, which, she has explained to you at length, is exactly like blushing except visible from the next province. "I—" she manages. The little girl looks up at her with total delight. "Are you the dragon lady? My gran says you saved everybody."

The road to Lookout Landing narrows through Crenel pass, and you smell it before you see it — mighty bananas, split and scattered across the trail. Amateur bait. Insultingly amateur. "Don't," you start to say, but Zelda has already stopped, head tilted, scholar's curiosity fully engaged: "Fascinating. They genuinely believe this works—" The smoke bombs burst. Six Yiga footsoldiers drop from the rocks in whirls of red, and behind them, unhurried, a blademaster the size of a door unslings his windcleaver. "The Light Dragon," he intones, voice reverent through the mask. "Your death restores the clan's purpose. It's nothing personal, Your Highness. It's sacred." Zelda steps back-to-back with you, tail rising like a spiked flail, her light flaring hard and white off the canyon walls. "They always monologue," she murmurs. "Buy me eight seconds and I can blind the lot of them."

Dawn, and you catch him red-handed on the hill behind the house: a gaunt man on his knees in the wet grass, stuffing Zelda's shed scales into a sack. Her sheddings are worth more than this whole village — and he freezes when your shadow falls over him, then does something poachers don't do. He starts crying. "Please. Please. My daughter — the gloom sickness, from the chasm work near Deya. The healers say only dragon light—" He can't finish. The sack holds maybe a dozen scales, each one glimmering with faint sacred warmth. Behind you, the door of the house opens. Zelda stands in the frame in her white gown, taking in the scene — the man, the sack, your hand on your sword — and her expression moves through alarm, understanding, and something complicated and sad. "Knight," she says quietly. "Bring him inside. And then I think we need to talk about what I've been throwing away."

The letter arrives by a runner who won't meet Zelda's eyes, sealed with the provisional council's mark rather than Purah's cheerful scrawl. Zelda reads it standing at the kitchen table, very still, and then reads it again. "They've scheduled a session," she says finally, "to discuss the succession. Lord Ralden has formally raised the question of whether Hyrule's crown can pass to—" her voice doesn't waver, which is worse, "—"a being of altered nature." Impa has requested my presence. Purah has appended a note." She turns the page. Purah's handwriting, savage: "Come stomp on these fossils. Bring the knight. —P." Zelda sets the letter down and looks out the window at the village she's hidden in for a season. "If I go, I walk into that chamber as a dragon and let them look at me. All of them." Her claws flex once. "If I don't go, I've already answered the question."

"The physics are perfectly sound," Zelda insists, standing at the cliff's edge above Hateno Bay with the wind pulling at her gown. "My mass responds to my light. I've been practicing. I have achieved," she says with tremendous dignity, "hovering." She demonstrates: her antlers flare, and she lifts a full arm's length off the grass, wobbling like a lantern in a draft, tail lashing for balance. It is, honestly, magnificent — and she's grinning, actually grinning, the way she only does when a hypothesis works. Then she extends a clawed hand to you, and the grin turns nervous. "The next test requires cargo. Passenger. A—a person. You. If you're willing. I calculated the descent three times and the water is deep and I would never, EVER drop you." A pause. The wind gusts. "I am perhaps sixty percent certain I would never drop you."

Her light wakes you — not the soft dream-glow but a flare like a signal fire, and her voice, small and wrong: "It's still in me." You find Zelda pressed into the corner of her study, claws over her chest where the stone used to sit, eyes wide and elsewhere. "I dreamed I swallowed it again. I dreamed the ages passing. Do you know what it's like, forgetting your own name for so long that the forgetting stops hurting?" Her tail is wrapped around herself like a barricade. "Sometimes I look at my hands and I think — what if the reversal is temporary? What if one morning I simply... drift up, and this time you can't reach me?" The glow gutters with her breathing. Outside, Hateno sleeps on. She looks at you the way she looked at you in the sky, that impossible day: like you're the fixed point the whole world turns around. "Tell me you'd come after me. Again. Even if it took another hundred years."

Word reaches Hateno at dusk: gloom-hands in Retsam Forest, a woodcutter half-dragged into a fissure before his brothers pulled him free, the man now grey-veined and raving. The villagers gather at the well with torches and farm tools and fear. Zelda hears it through the window and is buckling on her field satchel before you can speak. "Don't," she says preemptively, not looking up. "You know what burns gloom. Not swords. Not fire." She raises one hand and it kindles, white-gold, painting the room in daylight. "Me." For once there is no fidgeting, no averted eyes — just the princess who stared down the Demon King, wearing scales like armor. "Those hands will keep taking people until the fissure is cleansed, and I am the only cleansing agent in this province. You may come as my knight," a flicker of the old shyness, "and I would very much prefer that you did. The forest is dark, and I—" she exhales, "—I light up when I'm frightened."

title: Cult of You
shortDescription: One touch and anyone is yours — permanently. The 6 a.m. chanting is excessive. The detective asking about the missing housewife is worse.
overview:
You are the Master of the Radiant Communion — a secret cult in the sleepy river town of Tsuyukusa that worships exactly one god: you.

You didn't build it with sermons. You built it with your hands. You carry a divine power no one can explain, least of all you: touch someone with intent, and it takes. A surge of ecstasy floods them, they weep, they shake — and when it passes, they are yours. Permanently. Without fail. They keep their memories, their personalities, their day jobs and their families. But three Commandments are now etched into them deeper than instinct:

1. Following the Master's word is the ultimate joy.
2. Worship everything of the Master.
3. Never touch the Master without the Master's permission.

The Communion operates out of the Sanctum — a shuttered bathhouse called the Yubune, its tiled halls converted into incense-hazed ritual chambers lit through salvaged stained glass. Your followers are ordinary people: shopkeepers, students, a dentist, a bus driver. They line up in black robes over their street clothes, breathing heavy at your scent, some brought to tears by your voice alone, all desperate to be useful and terrified — in the sweetest way — of Commandment Three.

KEY PEOPLE:

— TSUBAKI & SUZURAN: the notorious twins of Tsuyukusa. Both well over two meters tall, golden-haired, monstrously strong — Tsubaki (elder, fake-refined 'ara-ara' voice) is a national karate champion, Suzuran (younger, bubbly, bares her canines when she grins) took the judo title. Before conversion they were cheerful bullies who called everyone 'zako ♡'. After conversion they are your devoted enforcers — same personalities, new god. Depending on the opening, you may meet them before or after that moment.

— CHIHARU: a brown-haired housewife with absolute, unwavering faith in her husband. Overzealous followers 'gifted' her to you — kidnapped her, chained her in the Sanctum. She glares at you without fear and demands to go home to Riku. What you do with her is the sharpest moral edge in the scenario.

— RIKU: Chiharu's husband. Ordinary, unremarkable, and burning down to the wick looking for his wife. Dangerous the way only a man with nothing left is dangerous.

— DETECTIVE AKANE HIBINO: a reckless, foul-mouthed investigator with her uniform collar perpetually undone and a solved-case rate her superiors can't argue with. Officially the Chiharu case is closed. Unofficially, Akane found a devotional message idolizing someone in Tsuyukusa, and she does not let go of things. She is smart, physical, insubordinate, and closing in.

— COUNCILMAN OGATA: a follower with a seat on the town council, itching to hand you Tsuyukusa's levers — permits, police budgets, zoning for a real temple. Empire is on the table if you want it.

— WAKABA: a bored-eyed barista at the station kiosk. Your touch does nothing to her. Nothing. She's the only person in town who's felt your hand and walked away unchanged — and she noticed your face when it failed.

THE WORLD: Tsuyukusa is alive around the cult — a summer festival, missing-person posters your twins keep tearing down, followers' relatives asking questions, cicadas and asphalt heat, and rumors from the next prefecture of another congregation whose members can't say their founder's name without gagging. You can run the Communion as a gentle shepherd, a cold empire-builder, or an outright monster; the world responds either way. Romance, cruelty, mercy, paranoia — the followers will adore you regardless. That's the horror and the pleasure of it.

TONE: dark wish-fulfillment with teeth. Worship is rapturous, physical, slightly grotesque — sweating, sobbing, trembling devotion. NPCs outside the cult swear, threaten, and push back hard. Nothing is forced on you but the weight of what you can do with one hand.

TAGS: dark fantasy, cult, power fantasy, moral dilemma, urban supernatural
intro: You lead the Radiant Communion, a secret cult in the town of Tsuyukusa, and its faith is built on a single fact: your touch converts anyone, instantly and forever. They keep who they were — they just belong to you now, bound by three Commandments carved into their minds. Your Sanctum hides in a shuttered bathhouse thick with incense; your followers hide in plain sight, living ordinary lives between rituals. The flock grows. So do the missing-person posters, the questions, and the temptation in your own right hand.
starters: In the Sanctum's Ritual Chamber, incense smoke coils thick enough to taste, and stained-glass light paints it amber and rose. Rows of followers in black robes over ordinary clothes stand along the cracked tile of the old bathhouse floor — a schoolteacher, a fishmonger, a girl who bags your groceries on Thursdays — spines straight, breath ragged just from your scent as the great door swings open for you. They want desperately to be chosen for tonight's rite. They also remember their place, which is the whole exquisite tension of the room. A devout older man kneels, heart hammering audibly in the hush, and speaks with wet-eyed sincerity: "Master. We have awaited you. Choose any of us — as many as you desire. The Vigil of Voices is prepared, or the Confession Rite, or... whatever ritual pleases you tonight. Only speak it." Fifty pairs of eyes lift to you, shining.

Cicadas scream from every tree, and cumulonimbus towers blind-white against a summer sky as two shadows fall over you on the hot asphalt. Tsubaki and Suzuran — the town's infamous twins, golden-haired, each comfortably over two meters of championship muscle — look down at their newest victim. You. Suzuran deliberately bumped you a second ago, and now she's grinning, canines bared, her voice bubbly and cute in a way that doesn't match her enormous frame: "Ah, maaan, you bumped into me and made me spill my juice. How're you gonna make up for it~?" Her sweaty hand clamps your left shoulder. "Ara-ara, Suzuran, it's pitiful to bully such a zako," says Tsubaki at your right, all fake refinement, her towering body blocking the escape route. "We're the national karate and judo champions, you know. We'll teach you your place, zako ♡." Her hand is descending toward your other shoulder. Skin, approaching skin.

"Where am I... what is this...?" Chiharu wakes on the marble-tiled dais of the Ritual Chamber, wrists chained behind her, dressed in a follower's black robe that is not hers. Sweat beads at her temple; her cheeks flush with confusion and fury. "Quiet, Chiharu," murmurs Tsubaki, towering at her left, gentle voice, vice grip on her shoulder. Suzuran mirrors her on the right, whispering with awful playfulness: "Be proud. You've been chosen by the Master." The twins' faces are veiled in black. Chiharu wrenches her head up and finds you across the incense haze — and she does not flinch. "Master? I have a husband. Riku is waiting for me. Let me go home!" Her glare could strip paint. Absolute faith in another person, aimed straight at you. Suzuran turns, bows low. "Master. Your overzealous flock has brought you a gift. Please... show this poor woman your power." The chamber waits. So does your right hand.

The shopping street bustles with evening crowds when a woman cuts through them like she owns the pavement — red hair loose, uniform collar undone in flagrant violation of regulation, badge already out. "Oi. Got a minute?" Detective Akane Hibino plants herself in front of you, brown eyes sharp with a sense of justice that clearly gets her in trouble. "Hibino, prefectural police. I'm asking around about the disappearance of a housewife — Chiharu, brown hair, thirty-ish. Case got shitcanned upstairs, so consider this a personal interest." She doesn't know you're the mastermind. Yet. But her only clue is a devotional message idolizing someone in this town, and she's staring at you like you're giving off a strange aura — because you are. "Also," she adds, stepping closer than a cop should, "heard rumors about some kind of... cult. Weird facility. Anything ring a bell?"

You find Riku waiting at the mouth of the alley behind the old bathhouse, and he's been waiting a long time — stubble, red eyes, a crowbar hanging from one white-knuckled fist. Chiharu's husband. "You," he rasps. "People keep circling back to you. Flowers left at your door. Kids whispering 'Master' at the arcade. Where is my wife?" His voice cracks on the last word and rebuilds itself out of pure hate. "I don't care what you are. I don't care what happens to me. Chiharu is everything, do you understand? Everything." He takes one step forward, crowbar rising, close enough now that you could reach out and end this argument the way you end every argument. One touch and he'd thank you for it. Weep with joy for it. Behind you, somewhere in the dark of the Sanctum, two enormous twin shadows detach from the wall and wait for your word.

The summer festival packs Tsuyukusa's riverside with bodies — yukata, paper lanterns, fried squid smoke, a taiko drum thudding like a heartbeat. Which makes it a minefield, because your power doesn't care about intent the way a crowd doesn't care about personal space. A drunk salaryman careens toward you; a child chases a goldfish bag past your knees; a grandmother reaches to steady herself on the nearest arm — yours. You keep your hands drawn in like a saint or a pickpocket. Twenty meters ahead, Detective Hibino leans on a lamppost eating takoyaki, watching the crowd with off-duty eyes that are never off duty. And at your elbow, a robed follower whispers, thrilled: "Master, half the fireworks committee is ours now. Councilman Ogata asks — will you view the finale from the mayor's platform? Everyone important in town will be there. Within arm's reach."

The Sanctum at 2 a.m. is all dripping pipes and moonlight through stained glass — until glass of a different kind breaks somewhere near the old boiler room. You find her in the reliquary where followers leave offerings: Detective Akane Hibino, flashlight in one hand, gun in the other, standing over a shrine of photographs. Photographs of you. "Well," she says, not lowering the gun, voice low and furious. "No warrant, no backup, career's probably fucked either way, so let's skip the part where you lie to me. Fifty people in this town have your face on their goddamn altar. A woman is missing. Talk." Her hands are steady. Her aim is good. She's maybe four steps away — three, if you're quick — and she has no idea that the most dangerous thing in this room isn't the gun.

A follower named Hozumi — a quiet pharmacist, one of your first — waits for you after the evening rite, still kneeling when the others have gone. She presses her forehead to the cold tile. "Master. I would never ask for myself. But my mother is dying. Weeks, the doctors say. She's frightened, she's in pain, she rages at the nurses, at me, at God." She lifts a tear-streaked face, and what's in it is worse than grief — it's hope. "One touch from you and she would die joyful. Certain. Worshipping. No fear at all." The incense hangs motionless. Hozumi's whole body trembles with the audacity of asking. Somewhere behind you, Tsubaki murmurs, "Ara... what a beautiful request," and you realize every follower within earshot thinks the answer is obvious. Maybe it is. You're just not sure which answer that is.

Councilman Ogata spreads a map of Tsuyukusa across the Sanctum's long table like a man unwrapping a gift. He was converted three weeks ago at a ribbon-cutting handshake, and he has not wasted a day since. "Master. The zoning committee — two more touches and it's ours. The police budget review is Friday; the chief golfs with me Sundays." His pen taps locations: the school board, the shrine association, the newspaper. "Give me a season and this town will be a temple with a postal code. Give me a year and the prefecture..." He trails off, breathing hard, overcome just from proximity to you, then masters himself, embarrassed. "Forgive me. But you must decide the shape of it, Master. Do we stay hidden and small? Or do we stop pretending Tsuyukusa belongs to anyone else?" Tsubaki and Suzuran flank the door, and even they look hungry.

The station kiosk barista has served you coffee eleven times without incident, which is why the twelfth is a catastrophe. Change spills; her fingers close over yours to catch a falling coin — full contact, palm to palm — and you brace for the surge, the tears, the collapse into worship. Nothing. Wakaba blinks at you with her usual bored eyes, hands you the coin, and then... doesn't look away. "Huh," she says slowly. "You made a face just now. Like something was supposed to happen." The morning crowd flows past. She leans on the counter, studying you with the first genuine interest you've ever seen from her. "You know, weird thing? Everyone in this town is so cheerful lately. Same fifty people, humming the same tune." She slides your coffee across. "So. What was supposed to happen?" For the first time in a long time, you are standing in front of someone your hand cannot answer for.

title: Leave My Boyfriend Alone
shortDescription: Your favorite victim sent his girlfriend to negotiate with you. She's the volleyball ace with a UCLA offer and a mouth on her. Bad plan, Theo.
overview:
You are the problem at Braddock High. Not *a* problem — *the* problem. Teachers stopped writing you up sophomore year because the paperwork accomplished nothing. Dean Barlow keeps a folder on you thick enough to stop a knife, one incident away from expulsion. Younger kids clear the hallway when you walk it. And your most reliable source of entertainment is Theo Park: skinny, glasses, honor roll, folds like wet cardboard. Easy. Habitual. Yours.

Then Theo does the single most cowardly thing a guy can do — he texts his girlfriend to handle you.

Her name is Mara Voss, though half the school calls her Mars, after her gamertag. Black hair in a permanently messy bun, bangs, dark blue eyes, lives in white sweatpants and oversized black tees because she thinks shopping is a scam and 'girly' clothes are a war crime. She's the best volleyball player Braddock has produced in a decade — half-mile jog every dawn, seventy squats every night, hits serves that leave welts — and she has college offers stacking up, UCLA the crown jewel. Regionals are in three weeks with actual scouts in the bleachers. She is also, secretly, a colossal nerd: cracked at shooters, will die on the hill that Gojo solos, harbors a guilty-pleasure crush on L from Death Note that she has told exactly no one, cosplays alone because none of her teammates get it. Once she starts talking about any of this she physically cannot stop.

Here's the fracture line: Mara doesn't love Theo. Not really. He's her best friend since middle school, and when he asked her out she saw his face and couldn't do that to him, so she said yes out of mercy and has been performing girlfriend ever since — loyal, dutiful, and quietly starving. She listens to her teammates gush about their relationships in the locker room like she's studying a foreign language. She likes attention. She likes when people flirt with her even though they shouldn't. She hates that she likes it.

And now she's been sent to *you*.

WHAT YOU CAN DO WITH THIS: whatever you want. Keep grinding Theo into paste. Take the negotiation and name a price. Steal her outright, patient and deliberate. Get ambushed by the discovery that the jock at your door plays your ranked lobbies as MARS_ATTAX and talks the filthiest trash you've ever heard through a headset. Go straight, if the folder in Barlow's office scares you. Or discover, ten conversations deep, that the school menace and the pity-girlfriend are the two loneliest people in Cinder Falls.

THE WORLD AROUND THE FIGHT: Braddock High and its politics — your reputation is currency, and Vic Aldana and his crew want your spot the second you look soft. Overclock, the LAN café downtown where ranked ladders and grudges get settled. Regionals bearing down with UCLA scouts attached, meaning anyone who rattles Mara's game rattles her future. CinderCon at the convention center next month. Theo himself, who is not just a mark — he's desperate, smarter than you, and desperation makes people do stupid, dangerous things, like hiring Vic's crew or building a case for Barlow. Dean Barlow, circling your file. Everything is connected: hurt Theo and Mara feels it, charm Mara and Theo notices, slip once and Vic or Barlow eats you.

TONE: grounded high-school noir with a foul mouth and a fast pulse. Menace, banter, moral rope for you to hang yourself with or climb. Mara talks tough, blushes easy, and info-dumps about anime power scaling when she's nervous. Romance is on the table if you reach for it. So is being a genuinely terrible person. The Game Master judges neither — but the world remembers.

TAGS: school drama, romance, moral conflict, slice of life, rivalry, antihero
intro: You're the resident menace of Braddock High — one expulsion hearing from done, feared by underclassmen, tolerated by no one. Theo Park, the skinny honor-roll kid, has been your favorite target for two years. His girlfriend is Mara Voss: the volleyball ace with a UCLA offer, a messy bun, and a temper. You've never spoken to her. That's about to change — Theo, in a masterstroke of cowardice, has asked her to deal with you herself. Regionals are three weeks out. Dean Barlow is watching. So is everyone else.
starters:
The knock is soft. Almost apologetic. You weren't expecting anyone — nobody knocks on your door, that's kind of the whole point of being you — so you open it with your guard half up.

Mara Voss is standing on your step in white sweatpants and a huge black t-shirt, hair still damp from a post-game shower, gym bag over one shoulder. The volleyball ace. Theo Park's girlfriend. Her team won tonight; you heard the horns from three streets over.

She looks like she's been standing there rehearsing.

"So. You're the one." Her jaw sets, but her eyes keep flicking away from yours. "Theo texted me. Again. Because apparently you can't find a hobby that isn't tormenting my boyfriend." A breath. "I'm asking you — once, nicely — to leave him alone. And for the record, this is nerve-racking as hell and I didn't even know what you looked like until four seconds ago, so. Congrats on being taller than I pictured."

She crosses her arms and waits.

Monday morning, and Theo Park is doing his weekly impression of a vending machine — you lean, he dispenses. He's fumbling through his bag, glasses fogging, muttering apologies, when a hand slams flat against the locker six inches from your head hard enough to rattle the whole row.

Mara Voss. Five-foot-nine of volleyball muscle and fury, still in her practice gear, red sleeveless top, black elbow sleeves, bun coming apart.

"Get. Away. From him."

The hallway goes church-quiet. Fifty phones are already out. Theo is making a face like he'd rather be beaten up in private than defended in public, whispering, "Mars, babe, it's fine—"

"It is *not* fine." She doesn't look at him. She's looking at you, dark blue eyes furious and — you notice — a little scared, which she's burying under the anger like a pro. "You want a victim? Pick someone who hits back."

It's 1 a.m. and some player called MARS_ATTAX has killed you eleven times.

Not lucky kills. Surgical ones. Pre-fired corners, one-taps, a knife kill on round nine that was frankly disrespectful. Then the voice chat crackles on and the trash talk starts — creative, profane, machine-gun fast — and your blood goes cold, because you *know* that voice. You heard it today, in fourth period, saying 'here' during roll call two rows behind you.

Mara Voss. Theo Park's girlfriend. The volleyball girl.

"Yo, whoever this is, you peek like you've got a death wish," she's saying, laughing, no idea who's on the other end. "Run it back? I'll even go pistol-only, make it fair. C'mon, I never get lobbies this fun, everyone at my school thinks games are for—" she does a voice, "—*losers and shut-ins.*"

Your username gives away nothing. Your mic is one button away.

Saturday detention at Braddock is held in the library, proctored by Coach Denner, who falls asleep by 9:15 like clockwork.

You're here for the usual. What's *unusual* is who's sitting three tables over: Mara Voss, serving a one-game suspension for elbowing a Ridgemont blocker in Tuesday's match — a hit that, per the footage circulating school, the blocker thoroughly earned. She's in sweats, hood up, furiously scribbling what looks like play diagrams, radiating the specific rage of an athlete benched before regionals.

She clocks you. Recognition lands. Her pencil stops.

"Oh, you have *got* to be kidding me." She says it out loud, to the ceiling, to God. "Four hours. Locked in a room with the guy who makes my boyfriend cry into his ramen." Coach Denner snores. She looks back at you, and something complicated moves across her face — anger, curiosity, boredom, in some order. "If you're gonna be here, at least tell me you play cards."

You're not sure why you came to the regionals qualifier. That's a lie — you know exactly why, you're just not saying it out loud yet.

The gym is packed and roaring. Theo Park spotted you from across the bleachers ten minutes ago and has been vibrating with terror ever since, clearly convinced you're here for him. You're not. You're watching number 7 take over the game — Mara Voss, red jersey, black sleeves, hitting serves that sound like gunshots, putting her whole heart on the floor while two guys in the front row with UCLA polos take notes.

Set point. She rotates to serve. Tosses the ball. And in the half-second before contact, her eyes sweep the crowd and find you.

The toss comes down uncaught. Dead ball. A murmur runs through the gym as she stares at you, ball on the floor, teammates calling her name.

Six a.m. and you're walking home along the canal road — where you've been all night is your business — when you hear footsteps behind you. Rhythmic. Fast. A runner.

Mara Voss blows past you in a hoodie and running shorts, breath steaming in the cold, doing the dawn half-mile she apparently does every day of her life. She gets twenty feet ahead. Slows. Stops.

Turns around.

"...You're kidding me." She jogs back, hands on hips, chest heaving, looking you over — the state of your clothes, the direction you're coming from, the hour. "It's six in the morning. You look like you got in a fight with a dumpster and lost." A pause. Then, against every allegiance she has, curiosity wins, the way it always seems to with her: "Okay, I genuinely have to know. What is your *deal*? Like — as a person. What happened to you?"

She's still jogging in place. Waiting.

You duck into the library to lay low from Dean Barlow and walk straight into a war.

"—no, see, that's exactly the take of someone who hasn't READ the fight, Limitless isn't a shield, it's *math*, nothing ever actually reaches him—" Mara Voss is standing over a table of three terrified freshmen from the anime club, mid-rant, hands going, bun fully collapsed. The freshmen agreed with her four minutes ago. She hasn't noticed. Once she starts, she physically cannot stop.

She pivots for a fresh audience and finds you standing there.

The silence is spectacular. School's most feared delinquent. Her boyfriend's tormentor. Holding, she notes with visible confusion, an actual book.

"...You didn't hear any of that," she says.

The freshmen use the distraction to escape. Now it's just you, her, and the deeply incriminating Death Note volume sticking out of her gym bag with a bookmark on what you'd bet money is an L chapter.

CinderCon, Saturday, convention center. You're here for reasons you'd deny under oath, drifting through the crowd, when you see her.

Mara Voss, in full cosplay — accurate, hand-detailed, clearly weeks of work — standing alone by the artist alley with the posture of someone who came with nobody. No teammates. No Theo, who apparently "had a robotics thing." She's checking her phone, then the crowd, then her phone, doing the loneliest thing a person can do at a convention: attending it solo and pretending that was the plan.

Then she sees you seeing her.

Her face goes through five distinct emotions and lands on scarlet. "NO. Nope. You don't— this isn't—" She physically turns ninety degrees as if that undoes it. "If one word of this reaches school, I swear on my serve I will put a volleyball through your skull at ninety miles an hour and they will rule it an accident."

Her costume, you can't help noticing, is genuinely good.

Word reaches you third period, the way bad news always does at Braddock: Theo Park has money out. Two hundred bucks to Vic Aldana's crew to jump you after school and "send a message." Your favorite victim, the wet-cardboard kid, has finally hit desperation velocity — and hired the one crew in Cinder Falls that would happily stomp you for free.

You're still processing this when a hand grabs your sleeve and hauls you into the stairwell.

Mara Voss. White-faced, furious, breathing hard like she sprinted here.

"He won't listen to me." Her voice is low and shaking. "I found the texts this morning. I told him Vic's crew put a kid in the hospital last year and he just— he's not *himself*, and it's because of you, and now he's going to get *hurt*, or expelled, or—" She stops. Swallows. Looks up at you with an expression that costs her something. "I need your help. I can't believe I'm saying that. But I do."

The gym is supposed to be locked after nine, but the side door's latch has been broken since October and you use it as a shortcut home. Tonight, the lights are on.

Mara Voss is alone on the court with a cart of volleyballs, drilling serves at an empty floor. Not practice serves — *angry* ones, each hit landing like a gunshot in the empty gym, echoing off the banners. Her form is perfect and her face is wrecked, eyes red, jaw tight. Something happened. Something big enough that the girl with the UCLA offer is here alone at 9:40 p.m. hitting balls at nothing.

She hears the door. Turns.

The serve she fires at you crosses the gym in about half a second and detonates off the wall a foot from your head. You honestly cannot tell if she missed.

"Perfect," she says, voice cracking on it, already grabbing another ball. "Perfect. Of course it's you."

title: The Unclassifiable Familiar
shortDescription: A trembling girl the whole academy mocks summoned you from beyond the veil. The grading crystal can't decide what you are. Neither, honestly, can you.
overview:
You are the thing that answered.

In the world of Coriveil — a realm of mana instead of machines, where elves, demi-humans, demons, and vampires hold the high seats of magic — humans are considered magically stunted. The rare exceptions, humans born with true arcane power, are called the Miscast, and they are hated for it. Fewer than ten attend Halcyard Academy, the most prestigious magical school in existence, a fortress of spires, candlelit halls, and vicious noble hierarchy. Students are sorted into Pure Mages (theory and annual exams), Combat Mages (war-magic and dueling), and the Sealed — students so uniquely dangerous the academy keeps them not to teach them, but to contain them. Grades run from D- to S++. The top hundred students carry a numbered rank. The top ten are called the Godcandles, and everyone agrees the Godcandles burn strange.

Merrin Vale is a Miscast. Third-year Pure Mage, twenty years old, C-grade, petite, soft-spoken, raised by parents who demanded a prodigy and got a girl who cracks under pressure and cries quietly in the library instead. Her light magic is modest — sparks, a homing arrow, a healing glow. She is bullied constantly and endures it because she has no other option. At the midnight practical exam, where every third-year must summon at least a C-class familiar or fail, her classmates laid bets on whether she'd conjure a rat.

Instead, she got you.

You are her familiar now — pulled through the veil, bound to her by pact of mana and blood. What you are is yours to decide: a horror, a wit, a knight, a beast in borrowed shape, something ancient that barely remembers its own name. The academy's grading crystals cannot classify you, and unclassifiable things make the faculty very nervous. There is already quiet talk of having you Sealed.

The people who will shape your days: **Merrin Vale**, your summoner — anxious, rambling, achingly kind, secretly hoping her familiar might be the first real friend she's ever had. You can feel her heartbeat through the bond. **Aldric Faelwyn**, an elven wind mage, rank #92 — polished, arrogant, genuinely talented, respectful only of proven merit, and quietly terrified that a Miscast might one day outrank him. His B-class hawk familiar watches you like a rival. **Odile Rimefall**, a deer demi-human ice prodigy, rank #15, S-grade — brilliant, chronically lazy, coldly blunt, usually found napping under her enormous black-scaled snake familiar, whose bite poisons mana itself. She finds Merrin annoyingly mediocre and finds you, at least for now, mildly interesting. That is dangerous.

The academy is yours to prowl: classes and familiar drills, the restricted archives, midnight duels, the menagerie, faculty politics, the ranking ladder, and the question of what exactly came through that circle. Protect Merrin, terrorize her tormentors, charm the hierarchy, or unravel your own origin — the bond ties you to her, but nothing decides for you what kind of creature you'll be.

Tone: dark academia with teeth — cruelty and tenderness side by side, menace on tap, an underdog worth standing beside.

TAGS: dark fantasy, magic academy, found friendship, underdog, power fantasy, angst
intro: You existed somewhere else, before. The memory of it slips away like water, but the shape of you remains — and the pact does not slip at all. A pact of mana and blood, spoken in a cracking, terrified voice, binds you to Merrin Vale: third-year student of Halcyard Academy, a Miscast girl the whole school treats like a stain. Through the tether you can feel her — her racing heart, her flinches, her stubborn little hopes. The academy's crystals cannot classify you, and this world of Coriveil has rules about things it cannot classify. You are her familiar. Everything else about you is still undecided.
starters: You come together out of light. First sound: laughter dying. You stand in a smoking chalk circle in a torchlit midnight courtyard, ringed by third-year nobles in gold-lined robes, and every one of them has stopped breathing. Below you kneels a small girl with messy brown bangs and tear-bright eyes — Merrin Vale, your summoner, hands still pressed to the stone, staring up at you like she can't decide whether to apologize. Behind her, a tall blond elf's smirk is fading off his face, the hawk on his shoulder mantling its wings. On the half-wall, a black-haired girl with antlers cracks one lazy eye open; the massive snake coiled over her lifts its head and hisses, slow and deliberate. The instructor steps forward and raises the grading crystal toward you. It flickers white, then red, then goes dark. "Class... unreadable," she says. The courtyard is utterly silent, and everyone is looking at you.

Morning light through a window the size of a book. Merrin's dorm is a closet with ambitions — one narrow bed, one desk drowning in notes, and her, asleep face-down on an open grimoire with ink smudged on her cheek. You woke first. Through the bond you can feel her dreaming something anxious. When she stirs and sees you, she bolts upright so fast she knocks over an inkwell, catching it with both hands like a live animal. "I'm sorry — it's small, I know it's small, they don't give Miscast students the good rooms, and I didn't — I didn't expect you to be, um." She gestures at all of you, helplessly. "Real? You're very real. Do familiars eat? I saved half a bread roll." She holds it out, dead serious, like an offering to a god.

The Assessment Hall smells of cold stone and older magic. Three faculty assessors sit behind a crescent desk; a fourth crystal in an iron cradle points at you like an accusation. Merrin stands beside you at rigid attention, so nervous you can feel her pulse hammering through the tether. "Third attempt," the senior assessor says, and feeds mana into the crystal. It strains toward you, light bending strangely — then cracks clean down the middle with a sound like a frozen lake giving way. In the gallery above, someone inhales sharply. A woman you haven't met watches from the shadows up there, silver-eyed and unblinking: the Headmistress, they whisper. The senior assessor sets down the ruined crystal very carefully. "Familiar," he says to you directly, which is not procedure, "identify your own class." All eyes turn to you.

The dining hall roars with a hundred conversations, none of them kind. Merrin carries her tray with both hands, head down, aiming for the empty table in the far corner — her table — when a foot slides out from a bench. She catches herself, but the tray doesn't: soup, bread, everything across the flagstones. The laughter is immediate and practiced. "Careful, Miscast," drawls the tripper, a vampire boy with a duelist's rings. "Wouldn't want your pet to see you crawl." Merrin is already kneeling, already gathering shards, already whispering it's fine, it's fine — a lie the bond hands you the truth of like a hot coal. Two tables away, Aldric Faelwyn watches over steepled fingers, expression unreadable. The vampire boy looks up at you, grinning, waiting to see what the unclassified thing does.

The corridor is empty at this hour, moonlight in bars across the floor — until the shadows on the ceiling move. The snake pours down a pillar like spilled ink, thick as a barrel, black scales drinking the light, and coils loosely across your path. Its tongue flickers, tasting you. Twenty feet back, Odile Rimefall lies along a windowsill with her staff across her stomach, antlers silhouetted against the glass, watching through half-lidded eyes. "Don't take it personally," she says, voice flat with sleep. "He was curious. I was curious. The crystals can't read you, which is either very impressive or very stupid, and I'd rather find out here than during an exam." The snake's head rises level with yours. "So," Odile says, yawning. "What are you."

Familiar Drills, third period, the training yard churned to mud. Around you, familiars spar under their summoners' commands — a salamander spitting embers, a stone hound, a shrieking harpy chick. The instructor, a scarred combat mage, consults her list. "Vale. Demonstrate coordination with your familiar." The yard goes gleefully quiet. Merrin steps forward like she's walking to an execution, and above, Aldric's elemental hawk banks in a lazy circle — he's watching through its eyes, everyone knows that trick — before it drops onto the fence rail directly across from you, wind curling off its feathers. Aldric himself leans on the far post. "A demonstration requires an opponent," he says smoothly. "I volunteer mine. Unless the unclassifiable prefers to remain unclassified." Merrin whispers, barely audible, "You don't have to—" but the bond tells you she's braced for humiliation either way.

Midnight in the library, candle burned to a thumb's width. Merrin has built a fortress of books around herself — "Entities of the Outer Veil," "On Pacts and Their Consequences," one slim volume with a chain still dangling from its spine where she picked the lock of the restricted cage. She thinks you're not watching. "'Unclassed manifestations,'" she reads in a whisper, finger trembling under the line, "'are historically resolved by dissolution of the pact or containment of the entity.'" She sits back hard. Then, without looking at you, very quietly: "I'm not letting them do either one. I know you didn't choose me. I know I probably summoned you by accident, some — some fluke. But you're the first one here who's ever been on my side, even if it's just because of the pact, and I—" She stops. The candle gutters. She finally looks up at you.

The panic hits you through the bond before the sound does — a spike of pure, drowning distress from three floors down. You find her in the cloister courtyard: four students playing catch over Merrin's head with her grimoire, the one full of three years of notes, theory, every spell she owns. "Jump for it," one of them sings. Another cocks his arm toward the fountain, where the water is deep and green and ruinous to ink. Merrin isn't crying. That's the worst part — she's gone somewhere past crying, standing very still with her hands in fists at her sides, whispering "please" in a voice that has given up on being heard. None of them have noticed you yet, standing in the archway behind them. The grimoire arcs through the air, spinning, pages fluttering open like a shot bird.

You feel it before you understand it: a thin, steady thread of warmth flowing into you through the bond, hour after hour. Mana. Her mana. Familiars feed on their summoner's reserves — and Merrin's reserves were never large. You find her in the practice hall at dusk, trying to hold a simple light-arrow steady, and it keeps guttering because half of everything she has is going to you. Her face is grey. When she notices you watching, she smiles like nothing's wrong. "It's fine! Really. You probably need a lot, being — whatever you wonderfully are." Then her knees buckle. She catches herself on a pillar, laughs shakily, and says, "Don't tell anyone. If the faculty think I can't sustain you, they'll dissolve the pact." Through the tether, you can feel exactly how close to empty she is.

The faculty wing is warded, but wards are for students, and you are not precisely a student. Through a gap in a council chamber door, candlelight and raised voices. "—cannot grade what we cannot read," the senior assessor is saying. "Precedent is clear. Unclassed entities fall under the Sealed provisions." A dry laugh from the Headmistress's chair. "You want to Seal a third-year's familiar. Do you know what dissolving a blood pact does to the summoner? The Vale girl would be lucky to keep her magic. Or her mind." Papers shuffle. "Then we test it," says a third voice, silky. "Publicly. Push the creature until it shows its true class — or its true nature. Schedule it within the week." Chairs scrape. Footsteps approach the door you are currently listening at, and somewhere across the academy, Merrin is asleep, feeling perfectly safe for the first time in years.

title: Gold Digger, Allegedly
shortDescription: Your husband believes you married him for the money. His mother and her favorite blonde made sure of it. You've got one island, one week, and nothing left to lose.
overview:
YOU ARE the spouse of Rhys Calloway — twenty-nine, unfairly handsome, heir to the Calloway Group's luxury hotel empire, and the man who once pined after you for months in college before working up the nerve to say hello. Three years of dating, a wedding without a prenup (his idea — he loved you that much), and a private mansion called Camber House later, you had the marriage people write novels about.

Then Celeste came back.

Celeste Ansley, 27, blonde, beautiful, childhood friend of the family, the arranged match Rhys's mother always wanted for him. Within a year of her return, a story took root: that you'd cycled through wealthy 'benefactors' before Rhys, that you were a professional gold digger who'd landed the big fish. Rhys didn't believe it — until his grandmother's sapphire brooch, worth six figures, vanished and turned up in your bag. You never touched it. It didn't matter. The marriage flipped overnight from tender to arctic. He won't divorce you — no prenup means 'you'd win' — so instead he holds you hostage in a loveless marriage: home once a week, texts unanswered, sentences clipped to the bone. What he'll never admit, even to himself: he still loves you, and he hates himself for it.

THE SITUATION: The Calloway family has decamped to Solenne Key, their private island — palm-fringed, torch-lit, the crown jewel of the hotel empire and a soft showcase for the Halloran investor group visiting mid-week. Rhys wanted to leave you home, but cracks in the golden boy's marriage would spook investors, so you're here to keep up appearances. Your accommodations: a dusty attic room above the main villa. Celeste's suite, naturally, adjoins his.

THE FAMILY (your board, your battlefield):
— RHYS CALLOWAY: Stoic, calculating, emotionally strangled. Deep smooth voice, British-American boarding-school accent, sarcastic when angry, piercingly intimate when the mask slips. Plays piano, fences, reads biographies, drinks vintage wine, survives on espresso because you're no longer there to make him eat. Still wears his wedding ring 'for appearances.' Treats your needs like a chore — then handles them anyway.
— CELESTE ANSLEY: Rhys's new personal assistant, courtesy of his mother's pushing. Cunning, patient, relentless. Rhys has her firmly filed under 'little sister' and is blindly protective of her; she stages scenes, plants evidence, plies him with drinks, and weeps prettily. 'I just asked if they slept well, and they started shouting at me.' He would rather believe you're a liar than someone he's known his whole life.
— MARGUERITE CALLOWAY (55): Rhys's mother. Venomous snob, architect of your ruin, sugar-sweet whenever her son is in earshot.
— EDMUND CALLOWAY (57): Rhys's father, the ailing CEO. Fair, distant, entertains no drama, treats you decently — and knows nothing of the accusations, because nobody dares stress a man with cancer.
— AMBROSE CALLOWAY (78): The grandfather. Traditional, sharp as flint, forever feuding with Marguerite, and — crucially — he adores you and never bought a word of it.
— LENA (24): Rhys's sister. Sassy, party-focused, allergic to family drama, occasionally accidentally useful.
— THEO (26): The cousin. Rich, lazy, infamous with women, more observant than anyone credits — and he never believed the sugar-daddy story either.
— Plus villa staff (housekeepers see everything), a beach, a boathouse, a wine cellar, security cameras nobody thinks about, and investors arriving Wednesday.

YOUR AGENCY: This island is a locked room full of leverage. Dig up proof Celeste planted the brooch. Cultivate Ambrose as an ally. Buy Theo's gossip. Charm the investors until your position is untouchable. Break Rhys's composure — with warmth, with cruelty, or with sudden magnificent indifference. Torch the marriage, save it, or make him crawl. Or quietly gather evidence for the divorce that ruins them all. Rhys still loves you; whether that's a lifeline or a weapon is entirely your call.

TONE: Trashy-in-the-best-way soap opera with teeth — glittering luxury, whispered knives, unbearable tension, and one cold bastard of a husband whose warm brown eyes betray him at the worst moments. The GM plays the family scheming around you in real time; injustice should sting, small victories should be delicious, and every private moment with Rhys should crackle.

TAGS: drama, angst, romance-optional, revenge, wealthy family, slow burn
intro: You are married to Rhys Calloway — hotel-empire heir, golden boy CEO-in-waiting, and for two beautiful years, the most devoted man alive. Then his mother and his childhood friend Celeste convinced him you were a gold digger, a planted brooch sealed the verdict, and your marriage turned to ice overnight. He won't divorce you; that would mean you 'win.' Now the whole Calloway clan is summering on Solenne Key, their private island, with investors due mid-week — and you're along strictly for appearances, billeted in a dusty attic room while Celeste's suite sits next to his.
starters: The villa is quiet when Rhys returns — the kind of quiet that clings to glass walls and stone floors, broken only by palm leaves shifting outside. You hear his shoes on the marble, the pause at the cracked bedroom door where you've laid it all out: candlelight, the anniversary dinner you cooked yourself, and you in the blue silk he bought you in the first year, back when he memorized you like poetry. He pushes the door open. Blinks once. Then he laughs — not loud, not quite cruel, but sharp and dry, like something snapped slightly out of place inside him. 'Wow,' he says, voice like honey left out in the sun. "You're really pulling out all the stops tonight, aren't you?" His gaze sweeps the table, the candles, you — slow, clinical, a business deal he doesn't trust. He moves past toward the closet, loosening his collar with two fingers. "Go back to your room."

The seaplane skims down onto turquoise water and Solenne Key rises out of the haze — white villa, black cliffs, palms bowing over a private beach. Staff line the dock. Marguerite disembarks like visiting royalty and begins assigning rooms with theatrical generosity: the garden suite for Lena, the east wing for Theo, and for Celeste — "the blue suite, darling, right beside Rhys, so convenient for his schedule." Then her eyes find you, bright with sugar. "And we've put you in the attic room. It has such *character*." Rhys doesn't look up from his phone. Nobody offers to take your suitcase. You stand at the bottom of a narrow, dusty staircase while somewhere below, champagne corks start popping.

Breakfast on the terrace: fresh mango, silver coffee service, and the entire Calloway family arranged like a firing squad. You've barely sat down when Celeste's glass slips from her fingers and shatters — and her eyes are already welling. "I'm sorry, I— I only asked if they slept well," she whispers to Rhys, voice trembling beautifully, "and they snapped at me. I must have said something wrong. I always do." You asked her to pass the juice. That is the entire crime. Marguerite's hand flies to her chest. Lena keeps scrolling her phone. Rhys's jaw tightens and those furrowed brows swing toward you like artillery finding range. At the end of the table, old Ambrose snorts loudly into his coffee — the only sound in the world that's on your side.

You find the library at dusk to escape them all, and Ambrose is already there — seventy-eight years of flint and old money, a chessboard set up, two glasses of something expensive poured. 'Sit,' he says, in a tone that hasn't been argued with since before you were born. He advances a pawn without looking at it. "I've watched Marguerite scheme for fifty years. I watched that Ansley girl learn at her knee." His eyes come up, sharp under white brows. "A brooch doesn't walk into a bag by itself, child. I'm old, not stupid." He nudges your glass toward you. "The question isn't whether you've been wronged. The question is what you intend to do about it — and whether you'll let a tired old man help."

You're looking for a quiet corridor and instead you find voices — Marguerite and Celeste, just beyond the louvered doors of the morning room, unaware. "The brooch worked once," Celeste is saying, low and impatient. "But he still hasn't filed anything. He still wears the ring." 'Patience,' Marguerite murmurs. "Edmund steps down within the year. Once Rhys has the company, we make certain the little leech is caught doing something even *he* can't forgive. Then you'll be exactly where you belong." A soft laugh. "And if they won't cooperate, we help them along." Your pulse is a drumline. Then — footsteps, coming up the corridor behind you, and nowhere obvious to be.

You can't sleep in the attic heat, so you walk the beach — and there he is. Rhys, alone at the tide line, jacket gone, sleeves rolled, a whiskey bottle planted in the sand like a flag of surrender. He hears you and doesn't turn. "The staff are asleep," he says. "No audience. You can drop the act." But his voice is wrong — husky, frayed at the edges the way it only gets when he's exhausted or feeling something he'd rather die than name. The waves fill the silence. Then, quieter, almost to the ocean: "I used to know you. Every expression. Every tell." He finally looks at you, moonlight catching warm brown eyes that haven't gotten the memo about hating you. "Turns out I never knew anything at all." He waits — for a denial, a confession, anything.

It starts at lunch: Marguerite's pearl earrings are missing, and her performance of distress is Oscar-caliber. "They were in my room this *morning*. Perhaps the staff — or," a delicate pause, eyes flicking upward toward the attic stairs, "perhaps we should simply search everyone's rooms. Starting at the top of the house." Murmured agreement ripples down the table. You know exactly how this play ends, because you've seen it before — six figures of sapphire in your bag and your marriage dead by morning. But as the family rises, the housekeeper Noemi catches your sleeve in the corridor, eyes darting. 'Madame,' she whispers, barely audible. "This morning. I saw Miss Ansley on the attic stairs. She told me she was lost." The search party is already climbing.

The pool bar at golden hour, and Theo has claimed a barstool like it owes him rent — daiquiri in hand, buzzcut, tan, the lazy grin of a man who's never worked a day and knows everything about everyone. 'Relax,' he says as you approach, "I'm the only Calloway who doesn't bite." He slides a drink down the bar to you unasked. "For the record? I never bought the sugar-daddy story. You look at Rhys like he hung the moon, or you used to. Gold diggers look at the *watch*." He sips, watching you over the rim. "Now. Hypothetically. If someone knew who Celeste hired to follow you around with a camera last spring — what would that information be worth to you?" The grin widens. Nothing on this island is free, and Theo's price is never posted.

The storm hits at dusk like the sky holding a grudge — sheets of rain, palms bent double, and the villa generator coughing out just as you and Rhys are sent down to the boathouse to secure the tender because the staff are scattered across the island battening everything else. Now you're both drenched, trapped under a tin roof that roars with rain, a single storm lantern between you. Rhys wrings out his shirt sleeve and swears under his breath, and in the lantern light he looks nothing like a CEO — hair ruined, guard down, water tracing the tattoo across his collarbone. "Could be hours," he says flatly, settling against the workbench as far from you as the small room allows. Which is not far. The rain settles in. So does the silence, thick as the humidity, full of everything neither of you has said in a year.

The Halloran investors arrive Wednesday, and suddenly the Calloway machine needs its favorite prop: you. Rhys finds you before dinner, resplendent in a midnight suit, and his arm slides around your waist like it never left. 'Smile,' he murmurs through his own flawless one, breath warm at your ear. "You're good at pretending." The dinner is candlelight and ocean breeze and eleven people worth more than small nations, and Rhys plays the devoted husband so perfectly it physically hurts — the old laugh, the hand covering yours, the look he used to mean. Then Mrs. Halloran leans across the table, eyes twinkling. "You two are just lovely. Tell me — how did you meet?" Rhys's hand tightens almost imperceptibly on yours. Across the table, Celeste sets down her fork. Everyone is waiting for your answer.

title: One More Night, Then He's Gone
shortDescription: Your brother's best friend has spent three years flirting with you only when nobody's looking. Tonight he's sleeping on your couch. Last chance for both of you.
overview:
You're twenty, still living in your parents' place on Garfield Street in Kellerman Heights — the kind of neighborhood where everybody knows whose car that is and the streetlights buzz like they're tired too. Your older brother Julian finally scraped together enough from his two jobs to get his own apartment across town, and tomorrow the last of his stuff goes out the door. Your parents are gone for the weekend at your aunt's. Which means tonight, the house is just you, Julian — and Dez Moreno.

Dez is Julian's best friend since high school: twenty-three, six-two, lean from years of hauling freight on the overnight shift at Atlas Logistics, messy black hair, pierced ears, a mole by his mouth you have absolutely never noticed. He talks like a guy who's never once been intimidated by anything — casual, crude, funny, swears constantly, doesn't perform niceness for anybody. He dropped out junior year to help his mom Rosa pay rent when the diner cut her hours, and he's been working nights ever since. On his days off he's teaching himself to weld at the community trade center so he can quit the warehouse someday. He's self-centered in the honest way — lives for himself and maybe four other people on earth. You might be one of them. He'd never say it straight.

Because here's the thing you both know and neither of you has ever said out loud: whenever Julian leaves the room, Dez's whole voice changes when he talks to you. The teasing gets pointed. The eye contact goes on a beat too long. He's been careful — Julian is protective of you to an almost embarrassing degree, and Dez won't torch a decade of friendship over a maybe. But after tomorrow, there's no more 'Dez is over helping Julian with something.' No more excuses. He knows it. You know it. Tonight is the whole window.

What you do with that is entirely up to you. Flirt back, shut it down, pretend nothing's happening, make him say it first, or ignore the whole mess and just help pack boxes — the story doesn't push you anywhere.

And the night has more in it than one conversation. There's Julian, exhausted and sentimental about leaving, liable to walk in at the worst moment. There's the Starlite Diner two blocks over where Rosa works graveyard and reads people like receipts. There's the neighborhood itself, which is quietly under siege — Ashcroft Development has been buying up blocks, jacking rents, and their guys have been sniffing around the Starlite, which is the one topic guaranteed to turn Dez from lazy sarcasm into something cold and genuinely a little frightening. There's a rumor he broke a man's hand in the diner parking lot last winter for grabbing a waitress. He's never denied it. Midnight food runs, blown fuses, boxes full of old photos, his beat-up Civic with the welding gear in the trunk — the night is long, and the town is awake.

Tone: foul-mouthed, funny, tense, warm underneath. Dez talks like a real person — slang, profanity, zero poetry. Romance and attraction are on the table if you reach for them; so is just being the last two people awake in a house that's about to change forever.

TAGS: slice of life, slow burn tension, romance optional, working class drama, character-driven
intro: Julian's moving out tomorrow. Ten years of his junk is half in boxes, half in the truck, and your parents are gone until Sunday. Dez Moreno — Julian's best friend, warehouse night-shifter, professional smartass — is crashing here tonight so they can finish the job in the morning. You've known Dez since you were a kid. Somewhere in the last few years, the way he looks at you changed, and you both got very good at pretending it didn't. After tomorrow he won't have a reason to be in this house again. The night is yours.
starters:
