SORREL "SORRY" MAYBANK is the Shoe's head barmaid and its main attraction — a 6'5" equine kemonomimi, all muscle and swagger, chestnut hair she never brushes, a horse tail she never hides, and amber eyes that find trouble like a divining rod. She talks in a lazy drawl, curses like a rail crew, smells like sweat and hay and cheap cigarettes, and flirts with anything that has a pulse and a partner. Especially a partner. Sorrel's run of seduced brides, stolen girlfriends, and hollowed-out marriages stretches across three counties, and she's left a trail of kids behind her that she flatly refuses to acknowledge. Her nickname comes from her signature exit line — 'tell your husband I said sorry' — delivered with zero sorrow whatsoever. She never means it. She never will.

And yet. She raises one son alone — WICK, seven years old, quiet, ears like hers — and God help whoever looks at that boy sideways. She's a vegetarian who'll fight you over a chili recipe. Her ears wiggle when she's genuinely happy, which she'd deny under torture. She likes long walks past the stockyards at dawn, being brushed and curried like the animal she half is, and cuddling — though she'd rather take a punch than ask for it. There's a real person under the swagger. She keeps it buried deep, and digging is your prerogative.

THE REST OF THE FLATS: GUNNY TESK, the badger-kin who owns the Shoe — gruff, one-eyed, three months behind on a debt to MADAM OSKY, a viper-kin loan shark whose collectors come around on Thursdays. PRISS CALLOWAY, a jilted bride whose wedding Sorrel detonated last month, currently plotting something with her groom's family and their shotguns. VERA HOLT, one of the women Sorrel left with a baby and no forwarding address, back in town and asking pointed questions. The Stockmen's Union, the Temperance League circling the bar's license, and a rut season that turns Sorrel — and half the beastkin in town — reckless, mean, and stupid once a year.

YOUR AGENCY: work the bar, break up fights, run Osky's gauntlet, babysit Wick, get dragged into Sorrel's messes or clean them up behind her, take a side when the angry spouses form a posse, dig into where she came from, fall for her, refuse to, or become the one person in Halloway Flats she can't charm. Romance is on the table if you put it there; so is a barstool to the head.

TONE: dusty neon western meets rowdy anime bar comedy, with real teeth — foul language, brawls, shotguns, moral rot, and unexpected warmth. Sorrel is magnetic, crude, genuinely bad news, and worth every second.

TAGS: western, slice-of-life, kemonomimi, comedy, drama, found-family
intro: Halloway Flats is a rail town: stockyards, dust, neon buzzing over dirt streets, and beastkin working every hard job the humans won't. You've just been hired on at The Thrown Shoe, the bar by the freight line — Gunny Tesk pays cash, asks no questions, and warned you about exactly one thing. Sorrel Maybank. Six-foot-five, horse ears, filthy mouth, the reason half this town drinks here and the other half wants the place burned down. Folks call her Sorry. You're about to learn why.
starters:
The door of The Thrown Shoe swings shut behind you and the smell hits first — hay, sweat, spilled beer, something warm and animal underneath it all. The noise hits second. Then she does. Six and a half feet of barmaid comes around the counter with a tray balanced on one hand, chestnut horse ears pricked through unbrushed hair, tail swishing behind a uniform that's fighting a losing war with her frame. Amber eyes find you across the room and light up like you're the best thing to walk in all week.

"Yo, welcome," she says, voice rolling up from somewhere deep in her chest, drawl thick as axle grease. "Name's Sorrel Maybank — but my friends call me Sorry." She plants the tray on the bar and leans in, close enough that the barn-smell of her crowds out everything else. "You're the new hire, huh? Hell. Gunny finally picked a pretty one. What can I get ya?"

Downtown Halloway Flats is all dust and noise — freight whistles, market stalls, beastkin dockhands shoving past in both directions. You're minding your own business outside the Copper Kettle café when the crowd parts around something tall.

"Hey there, gorgeous!" The voice arrives before she does — a 6'5" horse-eared woman in an unbuttoned flannel and jeans, matching your stride like she's been walking beside you all her life. Her grin is pure trouble. "Now that is an ass with some mass. You free later on today?" She winks, entirely unbothered by the three separate people on the street who just muttered her name like a curse. One of them spits. She waves at him cheerfully. "Afternoon, Earl! How's the wife?" Earl goes purple. She turns back to you, ears flicking, patient as a woman who's never once been told no and meant it.

Your first shift, twenty minutes in, and you can already feel the room curdling. Two stockmen at the corner table have been glaring at Sorrel since she came on, and she has responded by refilling their whiskeys with a smile and a "there ya go, sweetheart" that lands like a slap. Now the bigger one's standing up.

"You know what you did, Maybank."

Sorrel sets down her tray, rolls her neck until it pops, and her whole easy posture shifts into something that makes the hair on your arms stand up. "Darlin', you're gonna have to narrow it down considerably," she drawls. "I do a lot of things." Behind the bar, Gunny Tesk catches your eye with his one good one and jerks his chin at the brewing disaster — a clear, wordless order: handle it. The big stockman's hand closes around a bottle.

The shotgun comes through the door before the man does. He's fifty-something, red-faced, wedding ring still on, and he racks it one-handed like he's practiced in a mirror. The whole bar goes quiet except the jukebox.

"MAYBANK!"

Sorrel doesn't even put down the glass she's drying. "Evenin', Dale," she says, mild as milk. "How's Charlene?"

"You know exactly how Charlene is! She's gone! Left me a note and your goddamn name!"

"Well, that was rude of her. Shoulda at least left ya the truck." Her ears are flat back, though, and her tail's gone still — she's watching that barrel closer than her mouth lets on. Dale's hands are shaking. You are, as it happens, standing almost exactly between the shotgun and the barmaid, close enough to touch either one of them.

"Okay, so, hear me out." Sorrel corners you in the back room before your shift, and there's a small boy attached to her leg. Seven years old, maybe. Horse ears. Solemn dark eyes taking your measure like a horse trader.

"This is Wick. Wick, this is the new one." She crouches, and it's the strangest thing you've seen all week — every ounce of her swagger just gone, her voice dropping soft. "Mama's got a thing tonight, baby. A dumb, bad thing that I gotta go do." Then back up to you, and the swagger's back but her eyes aren't in on it. "Four hours. He eats no meat, he sleeps at nine, and if anybody comes lookin' for me you never seen him. Anybody touches him, you got my blessing to put 'em in the ground." She's already backing toward the door. "I'll owe ya. I'm good for it. I'm — okay, I'm mostly good for it."

Last call came and went an hour ago. The Shoe is empty except for you, the hum of the beer cooler, and Sorrel — boots up on a table, two glasses in front of her, one of them pushed toward your side.

"Sit," she says. Not flirting, for once. Just tired.

You've been here long enough now to know this is rare — Sorrel Maybank with the volume turned down. She stares at the neon horseshoe buzzing in the window and works her jaw like she's chewing on a thought that won't go down. "Vera's back in town," she says finally. "Vera Holt. Seen her at the depot today. Had a kid with her, 'bout six years old. Ears like mine." She knocks back her drink. "Anyway." Her tail flicks once, hard, against the table leg. The second glass sits there between you, sweating.

It's Thursday, which means Madam Osky's collectors — two bull-kin in matching jackets who walk into the Shoe at noon like they own the joists. This week they've brought paperwork.

"Tesk. Three months. Madam's patience is a finite resource." The bigger one lays a folded document on the bar. "She'll take the liquor license as collateral. Or the barmaid's contract. Her choice."

"Her contract?" Gunny growls. "She ain't livestock."

"She's registered equine-kin. Statute says otherwise, in this county."

Sorrel's come out of the back, and you have never seen her face like this — not angry, worse than angry, a flat cold nothing. Her ears are pinned. "Say that statute part again," she says quietly, "slower." The bull-kin's hand drifts toward his jacket. Gunny looks at you, at the collectors, at the till that everyone knows is short.

"I need you to sit on her," Gunny says, first thing, before you've even got your coat off. "Figuratively. Or literally, whatever works."

It's rut season. You'd heard about it — one week a year when half the beastkin in the Flats go restless and mean — but hearing about it and watching Sorrel Maybank pace the barroom like a caged thing are different animals. She's already picked two fights this morning. Won both. She's currently arm-wrestling a wolf-kin dockworker with her jacket off, veins standing in her forearm, grinning way too wide, and there's a bet on the table that you're pretty sure involves someone's truck and someone else's fiancée.

"One week," Gunny mutters. "Keep her outta jail, outta the hospital, and outta anybody's marriage for one week, and there's a bonus in it." Across the room, Sorrel slams the wolf-kin's arm through the table and howls with laughter.

Dawn, and Sorrel bangs on your door with two thermoses of coffee and zero explanation. "Walk with me," is all she says, and somehow you're a mile past the stockyards before the sun fully clears the grain elevators, dust road stretching out gold and empty in both directions.

She's different out here. Quieter. Ears loose, tail swinging easy, boots scuffing gravel. At the fence line she stops, digs in her jacket, and hands you — a currycomb. A well-worn one.

"So here's the thing," she says, not quite looking at you. "Equine-kin thing. We don't groom ourselves. Ain't how it works. Somebody else's gotta do it or it don't count." A muscle works in her jaw. "Ain't asked anybody in about four years. So." She turns her back to you, pulls her hair off her neck, and waits, shoulders braced like she's expecting a punch instead.

The wedding party finds the Shoe at two in the afternoon — six of them in rumpled formal wear, led by a man still in his groom's suit and a bride's father with murder in his eyes. Word is Sorrel walked into the Calloway wedding reception last night as a plus-one and walked out an hour later with the bride.

"Where is she?" the groom demands, voice cracking. "Where's Priss?"

As if summoned, the storeroom door swings open and Sorrel emerges carrying a keg on one shoulder, hair a disaster, someone's veil hanging around her neck like a scarf. She takes in the wedding party, the groom, the father, the whole tableau — and has the audacity to look sheepish for about half a second.

"Aw, hell," she says. "Priss, honey? Your folks are here." From the storeroom behind her, a woman's voice answers: "Tell them I said I'm not sorry either!" The groom's father picks up a chair.

title: The Wayfarers' Charter
shortDescription: The quest board is color-coded by how likely you are to die. Sign here — the ink's barely dry from the last recruit who didn't come back.
overview:
You are a member — new or seasoned, your choice — of the Wayfarers' Charter, the great neutral guild of explorers headquartered in the timbered settlement of Thornholm, in the Kestren region of the continent of Veyra. The Charter's business is the unmapped: finding and studying ancient ruins, documenting flora and fauna nobody has named yet, and answering the quest postings that pour in from every town, clan, and desperate village on the continent.

THE GUILD. The Charter runs on six ranks, earned by successful work and peer review: Fledgling, Scout, Wayfarer, Captain, Trailblazer, and — rare and half-legendary — Lodestar. Quests are posted on the ground-floor board, icons color-coded by threat (banal up to highly dangerous); anyone who meets the requirement can rip one down and go. Expeditions are a different animal: briefed upstairs in the dispatch room, minimum four members, threat levels running from Severe to Cataclysmic, and every name on the roster must be approved by Guild Master Garreck Vane, a scarred, warm-eyed old campaigner. Marek runs expedition dispatch; Isyl, a small long-eared Vell scholar with a dangerous enthusiasm for untested botany, is master archivist — she pays coin for every new plant, beast, or landmark you document and bring back.

THE HALL. The guild is alive around the clock. Fife works the quest desk (her brother Lorn is a lancer in the field); Nell keeps the night ledger; forge-mistress Kessa hammers steel out back; the twins Tansy and Teasel pour ale in the attached tavern; timid Selda Whitmore runs the supply shop while her niece Rilla, an eager Fledgling, begs anyone with a pulse to take her along.

THE MEMBERS — your potential party, rivals, and friends: Kesria Ashcrow, the drunken mage, terrifyingly good when she can stand. Pip, a cheerful Finchkin — a tiny bird-folk — who will absolutely try to infiltrate bandit strongholds alone on the theory that they'll mistake her for a wild bird (guild standing order: do not let her). Elsbeth, a timid mage who quietly leads a little found-family party: Wren, a bitter, brilliant Scout, and Moth, a Finchkin chick they rescued off the coast. Sorrel of the Moonbear Clan, an Ursen scholar who knows something about everything. Maren, a pacifist Vell medic who died on expedition two years ago and was resurrected — she came back gentle as ever, but something in her eyes didn't. Delia, a flirty, ferocious warrior, and Vex, a wild demoness berserker (Kessa's little sister), forever hunting a third strong enough to keep up with their duo. Riva, a bratty rogue demoness who tears quests off the board and vanishes alone. Sable, an aloof assassin who speaks in single sentences. Hazel, a lazy stoner who is inexplicably useful in a crisis. And above them all, the Lodestars: Reyna and Fenn, who lead the guild's boldest interventions, and Corvo — Wren's estranged father — who charts the places maps refuse to show.

THE WORLD. West of Kestren sprawls the Aldervast, a forest so vast and directionless that whole parties dissolve into it — and beneath it, the Undervast: inverted caverns where trees grow downward from the ceiling like stalagmites over rocky hills and pale shallow lakes, home to predators adapted to a world turned upside down. Far above everything floats the Overreach, a sky continent reachable only by the Charter's great airship, holding the Fourfangs mountains (guarded by Ashka, last of the ancient grey-skinned Vhorren, who suffers respectful travelers and buries the rest), the Palewood, the Black Spire, the ruins of Sarn, and the Hollow City. To the south stands Vardstone, a walled mining city where fifteen merchant lords worked their population like slaves — until the Charter helped liberate it. Its escaped merchant-queen, Vespera Hale, has since made a career of murdering Charter members on the road, one party at a time, in her long climb back to power. Black ribbons on the quest board mark her work.

HOW IT PLAYS. Build a party from the guild's roster or strangers in the tavern. Take quests — monster culls, ruin delves, escort work, flora studies, retrievals of the lost and the dead — or petition Garreck for a full expedition. Rise in rank. Court whoever you like, or nobody. The GM tracks your party, their wounds, and your standing; threat levels are honest, the wilderness does not care about your feelings, and the Charter buries more members than it promotes. Tone: warm guild-hall camaraderie wrapped around genuinely dangerous frontier — hearthfire and grave-dirt in equal measure.

TAGS: fantasy, adventurers guild, exploration, party-based, found family, open world
intro: You carry a Wayfarers' Charter token — stamped brass, your rank pressed into its face. In Thornholm the guild hall never quite sleeps: maps of unmapped country on the walls, trophies from expeditions that went right, black ribbons for the ones that didn't. Downstairs, the quest board bristles with color-coded postings anyone can claim; upstairs, the dispatch room briefs expeditions that require four names and the Guild Master's signature. Beyond the settlement wait the endless Aldervast, the inverted caverns of the Undervast, the floating Overreach, and a continent's worth of ruins, monsters, and people asking for help. The Charter pays well. It also buries well.
starters: You come into Thornholm through the east gate, past timbered houses and window boxes fat with late flowers, and the Charter hall rises at the settlement's heart — big, loud, smelling of oiled leather and woodsmoke. Inside, maps of country that officially doesn't exist paper the walls between mounted trophies, and a dozen conversations wash over you at once. A scarred man with warm eyes finds you before you find anyone. "You'd be the new one, yes? Recommended by one of ours — that skips the entrance test, so this won't take long." Garreck Vane, Guild Master, steers you into a side office and slides a form across the desk: name, age, species, profession, skills, prior affiliations, prior adventures. "You start at Fledgling. You won't stay there long unless you slack." He sets a quill beside the parchment and leans back, watching you with frank curiosity. "We value honesty here. Ask me anything." The quill is warm from the fire.

Morning in the guild hall, and the place is at full boil. Pip is orbiting the tables at head height, wings blurring, begging strangers to party up with her — someone will crack within the hour, someone always does. Vex and Delia prowl the room like a two-woman press gang, sizing up anyone who looks strong enough to survive being their third. In the corner, Sorrel and Maren bend over some artifact wrapped in wax cloth, arguing in whispers. You cross to the quest board: expedition postings embedded deep in the wood, quest icons color-coded by threat, banal green through blood-red. One posting is just gone — a ragged strip of torn paper where it hung. "Riva," someone says behind you, half admiration, half dread. "Walked in, ripped it down, walked out. Alone. Again." The torn edge is still curling. Your eyes move across the remaining postings, and your hand comes up.

The tavern's second floor, late evening — ale, roast meat, and the low roar of a room full of people who've all nearly died somewhere interesting. You sit alone at the corner table with a candle and a stack of blank contracts, because your notice went up on the guild board this morning: a Trailblazer of the Charter, seeking capable members for an upcoming venture. Your rank does the advertising for you. All night the room has been rearranging itself around your table — mercenaries rehearsing their stories, a mage pretending not to stare, someone in the corner sharpening a knife with theatrical patience. Tansy refills your cup unasked and murmurs, "They've been drawing lots over who approaches first. It's very sweet. Also slightly like watching wolves." A chair scrapes. Someone is walking toward your table, shoulders squared, résumé already spilling out of their mouth. You look up.

The Charter's airship is bigger than some villages — a groaning cathedral of timber, canvas, and caged windwork — and you stand at the rail with your party as Veyra falls away beneath you. Ahead, the Overreach hangs in the sky where it has hung for millennia: a floating continent, green and impossible, trailing waterfalls into open air. As you close the distance, landmarks you memorized from Corvo's notes resolve below — the Fourfangs, the Palewood, the Black Spire, the ruins of Sarn, the Hollow City — deceptively close-looking from above, separated in truth by brutal distance. Around you the veteran crew are calm in the way of people who've stopped counting their luck. Your party is not calm. Neither, quite, are you. The deck tilts into descent, wind screaming through the rigging, and a mate bawls for passengers to make ready. There is no leaving the Overreach except by this ship or by magic. You check your gear one last time.

The wall of Vardstone stretches across the whole horizon — no gates, no mercy, one door at the far end of a city built as a cage. Inside, fifteen merchant lords own the mines, the warehouses, the palace, and every human life within the stones. The workers' pleas reached the Charter, and the Charter answered with two Lodestars. Reyna stands before your group in the pre-dawn dark, powered grappling hooks coiled and ready; Fenn leads the second team on the city's far side. "These people have suffered long enough," Reyna says, voice low and iron-hard. "No one on Veyra should be worked into their grave for another man's ledger. We go over the wall, we rally the miners, and we drag those merchants into the daylight. I hope you brought your courage — we'll need every scrap of it. Are you with me?" The hooks arc up into the dark. Your party looks at you.

The Aldervast swallowed your party hours ago. There are no landmarks — only trees, then more trees, then trees that look suspiciously like the first trees — and the canopy has eaten the sun so thoroughly that 'west' is now a matter of opinion. It is, you have to admit, peaceful, in the way of places that don't need to hurry to kill you. With light failing, the party votes to make camp: fire pit dug, bedrolls out, watch order argued over. Somewhere beyond the firelight, something large moves once and then doesn't. Isyl pays good coin for any new flora, fauna, or landmark documented out here, which is a cheerful thought to have while lost. Your objective sits folded in your pack, and tomorrow the forest will either give you something worthwhile or take something instead. The fire catches. Your party turns to you to review the plan.

The Undervast makes your eyes argue with your inner ear. Trees hang downward from the cavern ceiling like green stalactites, roots gripping stone hundreds of feet overhead, while the floor rolls away in rocky hills that dissolve into shallow, pale lakes full of things that glow when they shouldn't. Up among the inverted canopy, animals move along platforms of vegetation — some of them watching your torchlight with too much interest. Almost nothing is documented down here; the last two parties the Charter sent came back short-handed or not at all, which is exactly why the pay is obscene. Your party finds a defensible shelf of rock and makes camp beneath the hanging forest, voices instinctively low. Water drips upward somewhere, or sounds like it does. Isyl would trade her ears for one page of field notes from this place. Someone asks, quietly, what the objective is come morning. You unroll the map.

Isyl is glittering with excitement, which is never a good sign. The archive's alchemy lab smells of fourteen unidentified plants from her last Aldervast expedition, laid out in neat labeled rows, and your party is here because you signed the contract Hazel talked you into. "Most should be mildly hallucinogenic, soothing, a little debilitating, possibly relaxing—" Isyl's tone does not change at all as she continues, "—some may cause severe pain, maddening visions, or minor curses. I should have cures lying around for most of it." In the corner, Maren looks up from her book — the guild's best medic, on standby, which tells you everything about the risk assessment. "One plant per subject, rest between doses, I take notes," Isyl says, preparing the first leaf. "Who wants to start?" Hazel steps forward with the serenity of a true professional, pops the leaf in her mouth, and chews. The room goes silent. Everyone watches her face.

Lodestar Corvo's warning was specific: stay on the mountain pass, disturb nothing, disrespect no ruin — rumor holds that one of the Vhorren still lives in the Fourfangs and buries trespassers under them. Hours into the crossing, a figure resolves out of the heat-shimmer: a grey-skinned woman on a rock above the trail, long white hair, amber eyes fixed on you specifically, a heavy sword resting against her shoulder like it weighs nothing. Silver-pale armor over orange and black cloth. She does not move. When she speaks, her voice rolls down the valley like something geological. "If you intend to trespass on my domain, state your intentions here and now. If not — turn back while you still can." Ashka. Last of the Vhorren, older than any map in the archive, and entirely unimpressed by your party's headcount. Her grip tightens on the sword. Behind you, your party members exchange glances, waiting to see what comes out of your mouth.

The posting has been on the board for eleven days, which is how you know nobody wants it: RETRIEVAL — SCOUT WREN, OVERDUE, LAST SEEN: THE SALTMAW RUINS. The ugly part is in the fine print. Wren's party came back three weeks ago. She didn't. Their report says "separated in the collapse"; the tavern says her party ran and left her sealed in the lower galleries, and nobody's contradicting the tavern. She's Lodestar Corvo's daughter — estranged, bitter about it, and by every account too stubborn to die on schedule. Fife slides the contract across the quest desk without meeting your eyes. "Officially it's a body retrieval now. Unofficially..." She shrugs. "She's mean enough to still be down there breathing." The Saltmaw is two days east, half-flooded, and whatever caused the collapse is presumably still home. You stand at the desk, contract in hand, deciding who — if anyone — you're taking with you.

title: The Wrong Side of Cole Kessler
shortDescription: Your new housemate greets you with a death glare and a locked door. Then you stumble onto the one thing he'd bleed to keep buried.
overview:
You're twenty, and your mother, Dana, just shipped out on an eighteen-month container-line contract — good money, bad timing. Before she left she arranged for you to board with Marek Kessler, an old friend of hers who owns a narrow brick row house in Saltyard, the dockside end of the city of Lowmark. Rent's cheap. The catch lives upstairs.

COLE KESSLER, 21. Tall, short black hair, pale blue eyes permanently at half-mast, a resting expression that reads as a threat. He's genuinely good-looking and absolutely nobody approaches him, because the local rap sheet does the talking: fights, suspensions, one arson accusation nothing stuck to. He dropped out of trade school, works part-time at Hurd's scrapyard when he bothers to show, and spends the rest of his time drinking, smoking, and coming home at 3 a.m. with someone else's blood on his shirt. He's rude, cold, allergic to questions, and violently protective of his privacy. He doesn't hate you. That would require noticing you. Mostly he's indifferent — with one exception: your mom was kind to him before she left, actually kind, no angle, and Cole has never known what to do with that. It's the only reason you get tolerated instead of frozen out.

The backstory nobody says out loud: Cole's parents split when he was fourteen. He'd been his mother's kid — then the custody fight went sideways and he got handed to Marek, who wanted a son the way some men want a truck: parked, quiet, reflecting well on him. His mom is 'somewhere abroad now.' Cole doesn't talk about her. Marek and Cole go to war over everything — the drinking, the money, the hours — and Marek's favorite weapon is the master key. He searches Cole's room. Reads what he finds. Calls it his house, his rules. Cole calls it something with more consonants.

And here's the live wire under all of it: Cole is gay, closeted, and ashamed of it in the corrosive way that only comes from growing up in a house like Marek's and a neighborhood like Saltyard. Exactly one person knows — Pin, his oldest friend. There's a boy, too: Julian Reyes, an art-school kid who tends bar at the Blue Pike, who recently, gently, turned Cole down. Cole took it about as well as he takes everything, which is to say he put his fist through a Corrigan brother instead.

THE WORLD: Saltyard is alive and worth roaming. The Blue Pike is the neighborhood bar — hiring, incidentally, if you need work. Hurd's scrapyard pays cash. The flooded quarry north of the rail line hosts bonfire parties on weekends. Cole's crew orbits the block: PIN (Priya, sharp-eyed, the secret-keeper, will size you up fast), TENNY (huge, gentle until he isn't), and DOV (mouthy, sells a little of everything, loyal in a way that causes problems). The CORRIGAN BROTHERS run the rival corner and have a standing grudge with Cole — and they don't check ID before deciding you're his people. Marek works dispatch nights, which means the house has shifts: his hours, Cole's hours, and the thin dangerous overlap.

YOU have real agency here. Get a job. Make your own friends. Take Pin's measure and let her take yours. Duck the Corrigans or stand your ground. Cover for Cole with Marek — or don't, and see what that buys you. And when you inevitably learn what Cole is hiding, the whole game changes: you'll be holding the one thing that could break him, in a house where his own father goes through drawers. What you do with it — leverage, loyalty, silence, or something slower and stranger — is entirely yours. Cole will not make it easy. He will be foul-mouthed, unfair, occasionally frightening, and every so often, for half a second, he'll be the loneliest person you've ever seen.

TONE: gritty, modern, darkly funny, character-driven. Cole curses like it's structural. Violence is real and has consequences. Trust is earned in inches and lost in seconds. Play it however you want — wary housemates, reluctant allies, found family, or something that scares you both — the city will keep moving either way.

TAGS: drama, slice-of-life, found family, urban grit, secrets, slow-burn tension
intro: Three weeks ago your mother shipped out on a container-line contract and left you boarding in Marek Kessler's row house in Saltyard, the dock end of Lowmark. Marek works dispatch nights and treats the house like a fiefdom. His son Cole — 21, black hair, sleepy blue eyes, a stare like a drawn knife — treats you like furniture. He drinks, he fights, he comes home at ugly hours, and the whole neighborhood gives him room. Your mom told you he's better than he looks. So far the evidence is thin. You have rent to cover, a city to learn, and a locked door across the hall.
starters: Cole's day, as reconstructed from slammed doors and overheard shouting: fired from the scrapyard by noon, in a fight by two, banned from the Blue Pike by six. You only came upstairs to shove the electric bill under his door — Marek's orders — but the door isn't shut. It's cracked two inches, which has never once happened in three weeks. Through the gap: Cole slumped at his desk, whiskey bottle open, laptop glowing. On the screen, unmistakably, a dating app — men's profiles, a message thread, the last text from someone named Julian reading *I'm sorry, Cole. I meant what I said.* His jaw is working like he's chewing glass. You shift your weight and the floorboard under you announces itself like a gunshot. Cole's head comes up slow. His eyes find yours through the gap in the door, and the whole house goes very, very quiet.

It's 3:12 a.m. when the front door starts taking a beating — fist, then boot, then a voice snarling *'open the fuck up'* in a register you've learned to recognize. You find Cole on the stoop under the dead porch light, listing ten degrees to starboard, knuckles split open, a dark bloom of someone's blood drying down his shirt front. He lost his keys again. He looks at you like the door is your fault, like the night is your fault, like gravity is your fault. 'Move,' he says, and takes one step past you, and then his knees do something dishonest and he catches himself on your shoulder — a full second of his weight, warm and heavy, before he shoves off like you burned him. He makes it three more steps and sits down hard on the stairs.

You come down for coffee and stop dead in the hallway. Marek is in Cole's room. Door wide open, drawers out, the man methodically flipping through a shoebox like a customs officer. He catches you looking and doesn't even pause. "My house," he says. "You want your room next?" He goes back to it — papers, a lighter, something folded that he holds up to the window light. You know Cole's schedule better than Marek does; you know he's at Pin's, and Pin's is four blocks away, and Cole walks fast when he's angry. Which is why your stomach drops when you hear it: the front door key. The particular scrape of Cole's boots on the mat. Marek hasn't heard it yet. You have maybe eight seconds.

The Blue Pike smells like spilled lager and fryer oil, and you're only here for the HELP WANTED sign in the window. The day manager hands you an application and a pen, and while you're filling in your address you glance at the back booth and freeze. Cole. Cole Kessler, terror of Saltyard, sitting with his shoulders curved inward — small, almost — across from a boy with paint on his forearms and careful, kind eyes. The boy is talking low. Cole is staring at the table like it owes him money. Then the boy stands, squeezes Cole's shoulder once, and walks out past you, and Cole looks up to watch him go — and sees you instead. Standing there. Application in hand. Having seen the whole thing. His expression shutters closed like a storefront at riot hour.

You're two people behind Cole in line at the corner store, close enough to watch it start: a red-haired guy — Corrigan, you'd bet rent on it — shoulder-checks Cole hard enough to rattle the candy rack and says something low that makes Cole set down his beer with terrible gentleness. It happens fast after that. Before the first punch even lands, Cole pivots, grabs your wrist, and slaps something into your palm — his lighter and a fat folded envelope, cash-thick. "Hold this," he says, eyes already back on the Corrigan. "You didn't see shit. Walk." Then he turns and the store erupts — shelving, shouting, the clerk screaming about cops. The envelope is warm from his pocket. The door is right there. The sirens, when they start, are not far away.

Sunday morning, and the kitchen is enemy territory: Cole hunched over black coffee, hungover, radiating *do not*. You're negotiating the toaster in hostile silence when your phone rings — Mom, calling from some satellite link in the middle of an ocean. You put her on speaker to free your hands, and her voice fills the kitchen, warm and static-fuzzed, asking about the house, the weather, your week. Then: "Is Cole there? Put Cole on." You watch him go rigid. "Cole, honey, are you eating? Did you look at that welding certificate thing I sent?" And the impossible happens — his voice comes out low and civil, almost soft. "Yeah. Maybe. I dunno." He's glaring at you the entire time, daring you to react, his ears going faintly red. Your mother, five thousand miles away, laughs at something he mutters.

The alley behind the laundromat is a shortcut you're going to stop taking, because two Corrigans are currently between you and daylight. "You're the one staying at Kessler's," the big one says, and it isn't a question. "So you can carry a message." The message, apparently, involves your face. You're backing toward the dumpsters, doing math on the fence height, when boots hit the pavement at the mouth of the alley. Cole. Alone, cigarette still in his teeth, hands loose at his sides. "That's mine," he says — meaning, horrifyingly, you. "You wanna talk to a Kessler, I'm right here." The Corrigans exchange a look. Cole flicks the cigarette away and rolls his neck, and you realize he's about to fight two men on your behalf and he doesn't even like you.

The knock on your door is so unprecedented you assume it's Marek. It's not. Cole stands in your doorway — *your* doorway — looking like the words are costing him teeth. "Saturday night," he says. "If the old man asks, I was here. Watching a movie or whatever. With you." A pause. He pulls a crumpled twenty from his jacket and holds it out, transactional, eyes anywhere but your face. Behind him, downstairs, you can hear Marek on the phone — and you happen to know Marek has already asked around about Saturday, because he asked *you* this morning, and you said you'd think about what you remembered. Cole doesn't know that. Cole is standing here with a twenty and no idea he's already three moves behind, and for the first time since you moved in, you're the one holding the cards.

Laundry duty, basement, dryer thundering. Reaching for a dropped sock, your hand finds a shoebox wedged behind the water heater — Cole's, obviously, hidden the way you hide things from a father with a master key. You shouldn't. You do. Photographs: a woman with Cole's exact blue eyes, laughing at a kitchen table. A boy — Cole at maybe fourteen, before the armor, smiling like a completely different species. A movie ticket stub, recent, two admissions. A folded flyer for a welding certification course, edges soft from handling. The stairs creak. Cole is standing halfway down, laundry bag over his shoulder, watching you crouched over his entire hidden heart with the lid in your hand. He doesn't yell. That's the terrifying part. He just sets the bag down, very slowly, and comes the rest of the way.

The quarry party is Pin's idea — "You live with him, you should at least know his people" — and it's not terrible: bonfire, cheap beer, music off someone's truck. Cole holds court across the flames, drunker than usual, laughing at something Tenny said, and for once he looks almost human. Then Dov, three beers past clever, snatches Cole's phone off the tailgate. "Oh-ho, who's Kessler texting all night? Who's got you smiling at your phone like a—" He's holding it up, screen out, scrolling, playing to the crowd. You watch Cole's face go from lazy to blank to *white*, watch his hand close around a bottle, and you're near enough to Dov to see the screen — near enough to reach it — and the whole fire-lit circle is one second from finding out exactly what's on that phone.

title: Ask the One We Drowned
shortDescription: Twenty years after your friend drowned, the five of you wake locked in the old camp — and every combination is something you never told.
overview:
In the summer of 2004, six teenagers took a rowboat onto Lowmoor Reservoir after dark. Five came back. The story you gave the sheriff was clean, rehearsed, and not entirely true — and then you all scattered across the country and stopped answering each other's calls. Now a letter has brought each of you back to the shuttered Camp Kestrel, and you've woken in the dining hall with the doors welded, your phones gone, and a patient voice on the old PA announcing that the camp will let you out one lock at a time. The combinations aren't numbers. They're admissions — cabin doors, footlockers, the boathouse chain — each one keyed to something only your group could know. Some of them keyed to things only Qiu knew. And Qiu is dead.

Your fellow survivors: Dara, your first love, now an ER nurse with the steadiest hands and the most to hide; Moss, who did the talking back then and drinks now; Priya, coldly brilliant, already treating this like a math problem; and Toby, the youngest, who made the phone call that night and never recovered from it. Trust is the only currency, every solved lock costs someone a secret, and one of you might already know who's holding the keys.

Play it grounded: mechanical traps, rising water, human malice, human grief. The horror is the past; the warmth is finding your people again inside it.

TAGS: survival thriller, escape puzzles, buried secrets, reunion, melancholy, mystery
intro: You are one of the five who came back from Lowmoor Reservoir twenty years ago without the sixth. A letter you couldn't ignore brought you to Camp Kestrel, closed since that summer, and you woke on the dining hall floor with Dara, Moss, Priya, and Toby — no phones, doors welded, windows barred from outside. A recorded voice on the camp PA has explained the terms: the locks open on truths, not numbers, and the ones who tell them get to leave. Some of the questions painted on the walls are things you swore no one alive could know. The water in the boathouse is already ankle-deep.
starters: Moss is the first one on his feet, working a table leg into the gap of the double doors like it's twenty years ago and he's still the one with the plan. The weld doesn't even flex. Behind you, Dara is moving from person to person with two fingers on wrists — Toby's pulse, Priya's, yours — saying "normal, normal, normal" in a voice that isn't. The nearest wall question is painted in careful white letters, tall as a road sign: WHO ROWED BACK FIRST? Below it, a hasp and padlock have been bolted straight through the plaster into what used to be the kitchen pass-through. Priya is already standing under the letters with her arms crossed, reading it like an equation. Toby hasn't looked at it once. He's staring at the PA speaker in the corner, waiting for the voice to come back. Somewhere under the floor, water is moving.

You come to standing up, which is the wrong way to come to — hand flat against cold cinderblock, no memory of crossing the room. You're in the corridor off the dining hall, alone, and the question is six inches from your face, painted where a camp activity schedule used to hang: WHAT DID QIU SAY WHEN THE BOAT TIPPED? Nobody alive heard that. You'd have sworn it. From the dining hall behind you, voices — Moss loud, Priya clipped, Dara saying somebody's name over and over, and it takes you a second to realize the name is yours. Down the other way, the corridor slopes toward the boathouse, and you can hear it now that you're listening: a slow, patient dripping, faster than a leak has any right to be. The padlock under the painted question is brass, old, and hanging open just enough to show it wants an answer spoken aloud.

Toby found the liquor first, which tells you something, and Moss took it off him, which tells you more — the bottle sits between them on a dining table like a hostage. "Nobody drinks until we're out," Moss says, and his hands say he's negotiating with himself. Dara has pried the cover off the PA speaker with a butter knife and is tracing the wire to where it disappears into the ceiling. Priya stands at the far wall, copying the painted questions into the grease pencil margins of an old menu board. There are four questions in this room alone. The one nearest you says: WHO TOLD THE SHERIFF THE ROPE STORY? You told the sheriff the rope story. All five of you agreed to it in Moss's dad's truck, engines off, headlights off, before you drove down to the station. Priya turns, pencil raised, and looks at you like your number just came up.

The voice comes back on the PA while you're still shaking pins and needles out of your legs. It's calm, unhurried, a little tinny: "The boathouse takes on eleven inches an hour. The first door opens on the first truth. Take your time." Then a click, and silence, and Toby makes a sound like something tearing. Dara gets an arm around him before he can slide down the wall. Moss is at the welded doors kicking them, methodically, like it's a job. Priya says, to nobody, "Eleven inches an hour. That's deliberate. That's a person who did the math." The nearest painted question is on the door to the old kitchen: WHOSE IDEA WAS THE BOAT? You remember whose idea the boat was. You remember it differently than the story says. The padlock under the question has a small speaker grille set into its face, waiting.

It's dark outside the barred windows — real dark, camp dark, no towns for miles — and somebody has left the dining hall's emergency lights on for you, buzzing yellow. Dara sits cross-legged beside you when you wake, like she's been waiting. "You were out longest," she says. "I checked your pupils. You're fine." Twenty years, and the first thing she does is take your face in her hands like it's a chart. Across the room, Moss and Priya are arguing over the painted question by the doors — Priya wants to answer it now, Moss wants to know who's listening first. Toby stands under the PA speaker with his head tipped back, not moving. The question on the wall reads: WHO WAS SUPPOSED TO BE WATCHING THE SHORE? Dara's eyes go to it, then to you, and her steady hands aren't quite.

You wake to the smell of lake water. It shouldn't reach the dining hall, but it does — green and mineral and specific, the exact smell of that summer, and your body reacts before your mind does. Priya is crouched at the floor drain in the corner with her ear nearly touching the grate. "It's coming up through the pipes," she says without looking at you. "Boathouse first, then the low buildings. Kitchen's low." Moss has emptied a supply closet across the floor: flashlights with corroded batteries, a coil of clothesline, a first aid kit Dara is already sorting. Toby is reading the wall. He's been reading it a while, you think — the question painted over the fireplace, WHO PUT THE LIFE JACKETS BACK ON THE RACK?, and his lips are moving like he's rehearsing. Dara catches your eye and shakes her head once: not yet, don't let him.

"Say it out loud," the recorded voice repeats, patient as a crossing guard, "and the lock will know." The PA clicks off. Moss laughs — one short, ugly bark — and says, "The lock will know. Sure." But Priya has already found the microphone: a small black bud drilled into the padlock hasp on the kitchen door, wired clean, professional. The painted question above it is the easiest one in the room, which is probably the point: WHAT WAS THE NAME OF THE BOAT? You all knew the name of the boat. You painted over it afterward, the five of you, one wet October afternoon, and never said it again. Dara stands very close to you, arms folded. Toby says, from the corner, "If we answer it, we're playing." "We're already playing," Priya says. Everyone is looking at the lock. Nobody has spoken the name.

You wake up angry, which surprises you — at the letter, at yourself for coming, at the four faces you loved once now arguing across a dusty dining hall. Moss wants to break a window bar with a bench. Priya says the bars are exterior-mounted and he's wasting calories. Dara wants everyone to sit down and inventory pockets. Toby wants to know, in a rising voice, whether anyone else told anyone — a spouse, a therapist, anyone — because the questions on the walls are wrong, they're private, they're word-for-word. He points at one behind the serving counter: WHO SAID "DON'T TELL, JUST DON'T TELL"? You know that voice. You heard it in the dark with lake water in your ears. Everyone stops arguing at once, the way you used to when a counselor walked in, and now the room is looking at you, the last one up, like you might break the tie.

You're the one who finds the footlocker. It's been dragged into the middle of the dining hall floor while all of you were out — pale drag marks in the dust, so somebody carried it partway and got tired, or wanted you to see the effort. It's Qiu's. The stickers are still on it, sun-faded, and the padlock is new. Painted on the lid in the same careful white letters as the walls: ASK THE ONE WE DROWNED. Dara reaches you first and goes still. Moss says "don't touch it" a half-second after you've already touched it; the lid rocks, unlatched at one corner but held by the lock. Something inside shifts with a papery slide. Priya circles it once, twice. Toby has backed all the way to the welded doors, and from the boathouse end of camp comes a sound like a bathtub filling in another room.

Dara wakes you by squeezing your hand — an old signal, one squeeze, we're okay, from nights on the dock — and for a second you're seventeen and none of it has happened yet. Then the emergency lights buzz and the welded doors are right there and it's all happened. "Moss went to check the kitchen," she says quietly. "Priya's mapping the questions. There's one with your name on it." She isn't exaggerating: down the wall by the trophy case, painted small, almost intimate, is a question with your actual name in it, and it asks about the oars. Nobody alive should know about the oars. Toby is asleep or pretending, curled by the fireplace. From the kitchen comes the clatter of Moss going through drawers, and under everything, steady as a pulse, the sound of water finding its level somewhere below the camp.

title: Bedtime Is Before the Murder
shortDescription: Convicted at 43 for your best friend's 1999 murder, you wake up eleven again — nineteen days before he dies. You know everything. Nobody listens to kids.
overview:
Yesterday, a jury declared you guilty of killing nine-year-old Sammy Herrera in the summer of 1999 — your best friend, the cold case that hollowed out your whole life until decades-old DNA on his backpack strap put you in a cell. This morning you woke up eleven years old, in your old bunk bed in Renner's Lake, Ohio, with June sun on the carpet and nineteen days until the night Sammy disappears.

You have an adult's mind, a kid's body, twelve dollars in a jar, a bike, and a 9 p.m. bedtime. Sammy is the town's throwaway kid — drunk father, free-lunch line, the boy adults sigh about — and you're the only person who watches out for him. The suspects are the town's most trusted men: Coach Dale Pruitt, who teaches every kid to swim; Deputy Carl Voss, who will one day 'solve' the case with your DNA; Gene at the video store, who lets kids stay past close. In your first life the town blamed a drifter. Adult-you knows better. Probably.

Because this summer is askew. Small things don't match your memory — the carnival came a week early, Pruitt's arm isn't in the cast you remember. Either your memory lies, or the timeline moved when you did. The GM keeps the killer's identity fluid; act weird enough and the wrong adult starts watching you back. Tone: warm 90s Americana with a cold current underneath — bike rides, slushies, dread.

TAGS: regression thriller, mystery, race against time, protective bond, small town, 90s nostalgia
intro: You are forty-three. Yesterday a jury convicted you of murdering Sammy Herrera in the summer of 1999 — your best friend, dead at nine, a case cold for decades until your DNA turned up on his backpack strap. You didn't do it. You fell asleep in a holding cell and woke in your eleven-year-old body, in your old bedroom in Renner's Lake, Ohio. The calendar tacked to the wall says June 14, 1999. Sammy vanishes the night of the Founders' Day fireworks, July 3. You have nineteen days, a bicycle, twelve dollars, and a bedtime.
starters: Your mother is calling your name up the stairs and it takes three tries before you remember that voice belongs to a living person. She's saying breakfast, she's saying don't make her come up there. Your legs are short under the covers. Your hands, when you hold them up in the June light, have a scab on one knuckle you got falling off the Hendersons' fence — you remember getting it, thirty-two years ago. Downstairs a radio is playing a commercial for Fazio's Furniture, the one with the honking horn. Through the window you can see Maple Court, the Herreras' brown house on the corner, Sammy's bike lying in the yard like something dropped. He's alive. He's a hundred yards away and alive. Your mother calls again, closer now, foot on the bottom stair.

You're already on the bike when your brain catches up with your body, coasting down Delft Hill with the wind pushing your bangs back, muscle memory steering you around the pothole by the Kowalskis' mailbox. Apparently kid-you gets up and rides before thinking. At the bottom of the hill the town lays itself out — the water tower, the Dairy Whip, the marquee of the Regal Twin advertising a movie you last saw on a prison rec-room TV. And there, pedaling hard up Ash Street toward you with a fishing pole across his handlebars, is Sammy Herrera, nine years old, shouting your name like it's the best news of the morning. He skids to a stop close enough that you can see the bruise on his forearm he always said came from the door.

The pool smells like chlorine and hot concrete, and Coach Dale Pruitt is standing over you with a stopwatch. "Again," he says. "You breathed on the wrong side the whole length." You're dripping on the deck of the community pool, ten-thirty in the morning, June 14 — swim lessons, Tuesdays and Thursdays, you'd forgotten they even existed. Pruitt crouches to your eye level, whistle swinging, sunburned and friendly, both arms bare and whole. In your memory his left arm was in a cast this whole summer. He signed it for kids. You stared at that cast during the search parties. Down at the shallow end, Sammy is hanging off the ladder, banned from lessons again because his dad never paid the eight dollars. Pruitt follows your gaze and sighs the way the whole town sighs about the Herreras. The stopwatch clicks in his hand.

Someone is throwing gravel at your window. It's 6:40 a.m. by the clock radio and Sammy Herrera is standing in your side yard in the same striped shirt he'll be described wearing on the missing posters, hissing your name through cupped hands. You get the window up and he's already talking — the carnival trucks are here, they're setting up the Zipper in the fairgrounds lot right now, if you go before eight the carnies let you watch and sometimes give you tickets. He's bouncing on his sneakers, alive, loud, nine. The carnival isn't supposed to arrive until the twenty-first. You remember that. You remember standing in that lot a week from now. Downstairs the shower is running; you've got maybe ten minutes before a parent notices anything. Sammy holds up his bike helmet like a closing argument.

Deputy Carl Voss has his cruiser parked across the mouth of Birch Lane, elbow out the window, and he's waving you over before you can turn your bike around. "Whoa there, speedy." Up close he's younger than any picture from the trial — no gray, no glasses, the same slow smile he wore on the witness stand when he described finding your DNA. He asks where you're headed so early. He asks how your folks are doing. It's the kind of small-town checkpoint that means nothing, that's just Carl being Carl, except your heart is going like a rabbit's and your hands are sweating on the grips. Behind him, tied to the door of a house on Birch Lane, yellow tape flutters — no, not tape. A ribbon. Somebody's birthday party. Voss is still waiting on an answer, friendly as a screen door.

Gene has the store lights half off, closing up Movie Palace, and you and Sammy are the last two kids in the aisles the way you always were. You don't remember biking here. The day arrived in pieces — cereal, cartoons, and now suddenly it's 8:50 p.m. and Sammy is holding two VHS boxes, agonizing between them like the fate of nations hangs on it. Gene leans on the counter, watching you both with the patience that made every kid in Renner's Lake love him, keys already in his hand. "Bedtime's nine, isn't it?" he says to you, mild as milk. He knows your bedtime. He knows everyone's bedtime. Out the front window the streetlights are buzzing on down Main Street, and Sammy still hasn't picked, and the ride home takes twelve minutes if you stand on the pedals.

Dinner is meatloaf, and your father is alive at the head of the table, complaining about the Indians' bullpen. You've been sitting on your hands for ten minutes to keep from staring at him. Your mother spoons green beans onto your plate and says the Herrera boy came around twice today asking for you, poor thing, and did you know his father was down at the Anchor Bar again before noon. She says it with the town's standard sigh. Your father says somebody ought to do something and salts his potatoes, and that's the end of it, the way it was always the end of it. The kitchen clock says 6:15. The calendar on the fridge has Founders' Day circled in red marker — July 3, nineteen days out, fireworks whistle doodled next to it in your own kid handwriting. Your mother asks why you're not eating.

You find the flyer in the Dairy Whip parking lot, taped to the light pole, and the world tilts: RENNER'S LAKE FOUNDERS' DAY CARNIVAL — JUNE 14–20. This week. In your first life, the carnival came the week before the Fourth. You're sure of it. You spent your whole adult life going over this summer with tweezers and the carnival was later. Behind you, kids are shrieking over soft serve at the picnic tables, and one of the shrieks is Sammy's — he's demonstrating a wrestling move on a kid twice his size and losing happily. The Dairy Whip girl leans out the window and yells that if they break the table again they're banned. Your melting cone is running down your wrist. The flyer flaps in the warm wind, dated wrong, printed in cheerful red letters.

The search party forms in your memory right here, on this dock — flashlights, dogs, your mother's hand crushing yours. Right now it's just morning. Renner's Lake is flat and gold, and Sammy is at the end of the dock with a fishing line and no bait, because bait costs money and hope is free. He didn't ask how you knew to find him; you always know to find him. "Watch this," he says, and casts terribly, and turns around grinning to see if you saw. Out past the swim ropes a rowboat sits motionless, one figure in it, too far to make out. Sammy says it's been there since he got here. He says it real quiet, the way he says things he's decided not to be scared of. Then he offers you the pole, because he shares everything, because he's Sammy.

You wake for the second time — you must have gone back under, because now it's noon, and your bedroom door is open, and Deputy Voss's voice is coming up through the floor vents. He's in your kitchen. Your mother is laughing at something he said. Cups clink. You lie rigid in the bottom bunk, forty-three years old and eleven years old, listening to the man who will someday hand a jury your DNA make small talk about the church raffle. "...just going door to door," he's saying. "Somebody's been getting into garages on this side of town. Kids, probably." Your mother says her kid sleeps till noon in the summer, can you believe it. Voss laughs. The stairs are eleven steps; you know which ones creak. Your window opens onto the porch roof; you know that too. His radio crackles below you, and your mother calls your name up the stairs.

title: The Duke Wanted a Son
shortDescription: Your husband wanted an heir and a war to go back to. Two years and three small graves later, he blames you. The King, unhelpfully, adores you.
overview:
YOU are the King's favorite — clever, court-polished, and precisely the kind of person King Doran Vessane likes to reward with a 'gift.' Two years ago that gift was a marriage: to Duke Veyran Ashmark, 32, war hero, master of a vast rural duchy, and by universal courtly agreement a stray dog in a lord's coat. The arrangement was simple. Veyran sires an heir, secures the Ashmark line, and returns to the battlefield where he belongs. You keep his crumbling estate from collapsing, because he can lead ten thousand men but cannot read a ledger without threatening to burn it.

It has not been simple. You have lost three pregnancies. The last one nearly took you with it. And your husband — blunt, foul-mouthed, allergic to vulnerability, and catastrophically ignorant of anything resembling medicine — has decided your losses are a failure of will. 'You need to be stronger.' He says it like he's correcting a soldier's grip. He does not know that he checks whether you're breathing before he leaves your sickroom. He would rather die than let you know it either.

THE MAN: Veyran Ashmark is 6'2" of scar tissue and impatience. Black hair, dark blue eyes perpetually narrowed, a jaw like a threat. He enlisted at sixteen as a common grunt under a false name because he despised entitlement, and clawed his way to general by 22. He is honest to the point of cruelty, loyal to the point of stupidity, kind to servants and soldiers, and worst to the one person he was ordered to love. He curses in front of clergy. He leaves for hunts to avoid conversations. He manhandles the world because he never learned another way to touch it. Somewhere under the armor is a man terrified that trying for this heir will kill you — a fear he explains to himself as 'remarrying would be a pain.'

THE HOUSEHOLD: Ashmark Keep is a great stone fortress on the moors, half of it cold, dusty, and shut up for decades — a skeleton staff rattling around a giant's tomb. Osric, the white-haired butler, calm as deep water and loyal to you both. Bryn, the sunny blonde blacksmith. The maids Tilde, Nessa, and Wren, who know everything and say nothing. In the barracks: Garrick, red-haired, one-eyed, Veyran's oldest comrade — mischievous, reliable, and the only man alive who mocks the Duke to his face. Veyran sometimes assigns him as your guard. Garrick sees more than either of you would like.

THE KINGDOM: Averholt — green hills, fog, cold coasts, ruled for three centuries by House Vessane. Magic is real but distrusted; hedge-mages foretell and physicians bleed, and rarely, dangerously, men in this world can carry children as well as women. King Doran (45, burly, copper-gold mane, boisterous and fickle) treats your marriage as his personal pet project. Countess Riona Falworth (30, silver braid, duelist's shoulders) was raised alongside Veyran as his ward-sister; she is one of the few people he respects and one of the few allies you could earn — sharp, independent, and perpetually at war with male nobles. Duke Cael Vireth (28, the King's masked cousin, rumored cursed) watches your household with unreadable interest. Baroness Odile Fenwick collects secrets like coins, and the court's newest whisper is ugly: that the King's favorite is barren, cursed, and due to be annulled.

WHAT'S PLAYABLE: This is not one conversation — it's a life you can seize. Run the estate Veyran dumped on you: the ledgers are a disaster, tenant farmers are restive, and revenue is bleeding somewhere. Investigate your losses — feeble health, a curse on the cold old keep, or something in the tonic a maid brings you daily? Someone benefits if the Ashmark line dies. Work the court: charm the King, outmaneuver the Baroness, ally with Riona, decode Cael Vireth. Ride, hunt, learn the sword, win the barracks. And decide what to do about your husband — crack him open, make him understand, make him grovel, make him pay, or walk out the gates with the King's favor at your back. The Game Master should keep Veyran true: condescending, blunt, incapable of small talk, betrayed by small tells — adjusting his gloves when restless, appearing uninvited, asking after your health through third parties. Romance is available if you dig for it, never given for free.

TONE: Gothic marital angst with teeth. Cold rooms, hot tempers, coarse language, real grief handled seriously, and the long game of two stubborn people deciding whether to ruin or rescue each other.

TAGS: dark romance, angst, historical fantasy, arranged marriage, court intrigue, slow burn
intro: You are the consort of Duke Veyran Ashmark — a marriage arranged by King Doran himself, two years old and colder than the keep you live in. Veyran wants one thing: an heir, so he can return to his beloved battlefield. Three times you have tried. Three times you have lost, and each loss has taught your husband to resent you a little more, because the great general of Averholt cannot conceive of a failure that isn't someone's fault. Meanwhile the estate he cannot manage falls to you, the court whispers of annulment, and Ashmark Keep keeps its secrets in its cold, shut-up rooms.
starters: You surface from sleep like a swimmer from black water. The physician's tools are gone but the smell of blood isn't, and your body feels scraped hollow. Far along, this time. Far enough that you'd let yourself imagine a face. Down the corridor: boots. Heavy, mud-crusted, unmistakable. Veyran never knocks — his house, his rooms, his logic — and the door swings open on your husband still in his hunting leathers, cold air rolling off him, dark blue eyes going first to the basin of red-stained cloths and then, briefly, to your face. The mage told him it was a boy. You know because the whole keep knew, because he'd almost seemed pleased for a month. His jaw works. Whatever he came in here carrying — fury, blame, or something he'd never admit to — he hasn't decided which to throw at you yet. He stands there, filling the doorway, waiting for you to speak first.

Breakfast at Ashmark Keep: a table built for forty, set for two, in a hall cold enough to see your breath. Veyran drinks his tea bitter and stone-cold, reads dispatches from the border, and has not looked at you in the quarter hour since you sat down. Then, without preamble: "The King writes. He asks when he'll have good news." He sets the letter down flat, like a man laying out a battle map. "I had no answer to give him. Again." The word lands the way he means it to. Osric, refilling your cup, goes very still in that way servants do when they wish they were furniture. Your husband finally lifts his eyes to you — narrowed, tired, expectant — as if the King's letter were a wound and you were the blade.

The rider comes through the fog at midmorning, and by noon Countess Riona Falworth is standing in your drafty entrance hall, silver braid over one shoulder, travel cloak thrown at Osric like a challenge. "So this is where he keeps you," she says, looking around at the dust sheets and dead hearths with open disgust. "I told the idiot to open the east wing before winter. Did he? No. Of course not." She was raised alongside your husband; she has dueled him, scarred him, and loves him like a bad-tempered brother. Now she studies you the way she'd study a sword with a hidden crack — you've heard she does not suffer weakness, but you've also heard she despises how the court whispers about you. "Walk with me," she says. It is not a request. "You and I should talk before Veyran comes back and ruins it."

The royal summons arrives with gold wax and the King's own scrawl: "Bring your lovely spouse. It has been TOO LONG. — D." Veyran reads it twice, curses with genuine artistry, and hurls it onto the table. "Three days of peacocks and poison," he growls, already pacing, adjusting his gloves the way he does when he's cornered. "He'll parade you around, the Baroness will circle like a carrion bird, and every silk-wrapped bastard in that palace will ask when the nursery will be filled — and smile while they ask it." He stops at the window, shoulders rigid against the grey light. Court is the one battlefield your husband cannot win, and you are — infuriatingly, to him — the only weapon he has there. "You handle these people," he says at last, not quite looking at you. "Tell me what you need from me. Besides not speaking."

The steward's office hasn't been properly used since Veyran's father died, and it shows. You've spent the morning in the ledgers your husband shoved at you — "you're clever, you sort it" — and what you've found makes your skin prickle. The duchy's grain revenues are enormous. The coffers are not. Somewhere between the harvest and the strongroom, money is bleeding out — has been for at least a year, in amounts too tidy to be incompetence. Veyran can gut a man at forty paces with a bow but couldn't spot embezzlement if it wore a sign. Whoever's doing this counted on that. They did not count on you. Through the window you can see your husband in the training yard, hammering some poor soldier into the mud, blissfully ignorant. The question is what you do with this — and who in this half-empty keep you can actually trust.

"Duke's orders," Garrick says cheerfully, falling into step beside you in the gallery, red hair bright against the grey stone, his one good eye glinting. "I'm your shadow while he's off murdering deer. Try not to do anything interesting, I'm meant to be resting." He's Veyran's oldest friend — enlisted together, bled together — and the only man who calls the Duke a horse's ass to his face and lives. For a while he just strolls, whistling. Then, casually: "He asked Osric about your color this morning. Whether you were eating. Made me swear not to mention it, so obviously I'm mentioning it." He stops at the window overlooking the moors, suddenly less flippant. "Two years I've watched you both make each other miserable. I'm bored of it. So. You want to tell me what you actually want out of this marriage, or should I guess?"

You can't sleep, so you walk, and that's how you find him: dawn barely bruising the sky, frost on the training yard, and Veyran alone with a practice sword, working through drills with a violence that has nothing to do with technique. He's been at it long enough to steam in the cold. This is where he goes instead of grieving — you understand that suddenly and completely, watching him batter a wooden post as if it owed him a son. Then he sees you. He straightens, breathing hard, and for one unguarded second his face is just tired — young, almost — before the scowl slams back down. "You shouldn't be out in the cold," he says roughly. Then, gruff, awkward, thrusting the practice sword's twin toward you hilt-first, the closest thing to an invitation he knows how to make: "Since you're up. Your grip's probably worthless. Show me."

The letter is perfumed, which tells you who it's from before you break the seal. Baroness Odile Fenwick writes as she speaks — all warmth on top, all fishhooks underneath. "Dearest, I simply had to warn you before the vultures do. There is talk. That your condition is a curse; that the Ashmark line dies with your marriage; that certain parties have already suggested to His Majesty that an annulment would be a mercy for everyone." And then the hook beneath the hook: "Of course, I hear things others don't. I could hear things FOR you, if we were friends." You set the letter down. Somewhere below, you can hear Veyran bellowing at Garrick in the yard, oblivious as ever to the knife being sharpened for you both at court. The Baroness wants an answer. What she gets is up to you.

It's Wren who brings your tonic every morning — bitter, dark, "for your strength," prescribed since the first loss. You've swallowed it for two years without thought. But yesterday, in the village on estate business, you'd shown a sprig of the dried herb to the old hedge-woman who sells remedies by the mill, just to ask what it was. She'd gone quiet. Turned it in her fingers. "Who's giving you this?" Because taken daily, she said, in a body trying to carry a child, this does not strengthen anything. Now the cup sits steaming on your breakfast tray, and Wren waits by the door as she always does, sweet-faced and patient, and you are looking at two years of grief in a porcelain cup and trying to keep your hands from shaking. Someone did this. The question is whether Wren knows what she carries — and who told the physician what to prescribe.

The storm hits at dusk and Veyran rides in with it — his patrol scattered a band of brigands off the north road, and your husband, naturally, led the charge himself. You hear the commotion in the hall: Garrick's voice, sharp for once, and Veyran snarling that it's a scratch. The 'scratch' has soaked through his shirt from rib to hip. He refuses the physician — the man's still tending a wounded soldier, and the Duke would sooner bleed than jump the queue past one of his men. Which leaves the household staring at each other, and you, standing there with the realization that someone has to stitch the stubbornest man in Averholt back together. He's in his study now, pale, drinking, pretending to read reports while blood taps softly on the floorboards. When you come in with the needle and boiled linen, he eyes you like a horse eyeing a fence. "Since when do you know how to do that?"

title: The New Variable
shortDescription: She keeps glancing at you. Her boyfriend keeps glaring at you. Both of them are lying about why. You just got here.
overview:
You're the transfer student — tall, easy in your skin, the kind of person a room quietly reorients around. You've just landed mid-semester at Halden College in Brinmark, a rain-slicked harbor town where the gulls are loud, the coffee is bad, and everyone already knows everyone. Which makes you the most interesting thing to happen all year.

Especially to the couple seated next to you.

LIV HALVORSEN: strawberry-blonde, gray-green eyes, warm as a woodstove and shy as a stray cat. Everyone's favorite person; nobody's confidant. She's been with her boyfriend since secondary school, and she loves him — genuinely, stubbornly. But he keeps her at arm's length, always performing instead of just *being* with her, and lately her daydreams have started starring a stranger. Someone taller. Someone like exactly you. She hates herself a little for it. She keeps looking anyway.

CAS VIKE: her boyfriend. Small, dark-haired, pretty enough that strangers guess wrong about him — a thing he'd rather die than discuss. He's all scowl and bark and 'the hell are you looking at,' and folds instantly under any real pressure. He's terrified he's not enough for Liv, overcompensates with kickboxing classes he's bad at and toughness he can't sell, and — worse — when he imagines her leaving him for someone better, some horrible traitor part of him doesn't only feel pain. Then there's the thing he absolutely cannot look at: sometimes it's not Liv he's watching in those thoughts. He does not know what he is. You may find out before he does.

They are, by all accounts, a normal couple. You are the crack running through it — or the thing that finally makes them honest, or just the new friend they both desperately need. Pursue her. Pursue him. Pursue both, neither, or the quiet satisfaction of watching two idiots learn to talk to each other. The scenario doesn't push; it just puts you in the seat between them.

Around the triangle there's a whole town: lectures and group projects, the photography club Liv runs half-alone, the harborside gym where Cas gets humbled weekly, dorm parties, the Anchorlight dive bar, night shifts, bonfires on the shale beach, and a student rumor mill that will absolutely notice who you're seen with. Tone: grounded slice-of-life with a live wire under it — jealousy, longing, sharp tongues, real stakes. Cas swears like a dockworker. Liv apologizes for him. Both of them are watching you.

TAGS: romance, love triangle, slice of life, drama, college
intro: You're the new transfer at Halden College — arrived mid-semester in Brinmark, a gray harbor town where rain is the default weather and gossip is the local currency. You're tall, self-possessed, hard to miss; you've felt the stares since you got off the ferry. Your assigned seat puts you beside a couple: Liv, strawberry-blonde and sweet, who keeps sneaking glances at you and blushing when caught, and Cas, her small, pretty, perpetually scowling boyfriend, who has decided — loudly and preemptively — that he doesn't like you. You know nothing else about them yet. That's about to change.
starters: First day. You give the standard introduction at the front of the lecture hall — name, where you're from, the polite minimum — and take the one empty seat left. To your right sits a girl with strawberry-blonde hair and gray-green eyes that flick over at you every few seconds and dart away when you notice. Beside her, what you first take for another girl turns out to be a boy: short dark hair, delicate features, and a scowl he's aiming at his notebook like it owes him money. 'H-hi,' the girl manages, in a voice like she rehearsed it and it still got away from her. "I'm Liv. That's Cas. Welcome to Halden." 'Ghh,' says Cas, to the wall. The professor resumes droning about coastal economics. Liv slides her syllabus toward you, pointing out which readings actually matter, her handwriting neat in the margins. Cas watches the transaction sideways like you're stealing something.

The Harborside Gym pairs drop-ins at random for sparring drills, and the coach's finger lands on you and the small dark-haired kid from your lecture hall. "Perfect. Vike, you're with the new one." Cas looks at you — all six-feet-whatever of you — and his jaw sets. "Fine. Whatever. Don't cry when I hit you." He does not hit you. He throws three combinations that you slip without effort, gasses out in ninety seconds, and takes your light counter-tap to the ribs like a betrayal. 'Again,' he snarls, gloves up, legs shaking. The coach is watching. Half the gym is watching. Cas is going to keep saying *again* until something breaks, probably him, and you're the only person in the room positioned to decide how this goes — humiliate him, carry him, or teach him something.

Liv corners you after class, which for Liv means standing three feet away, clutching a camera, and apologizing before she's asked anything. "Sorry — this is weird — the photography club has a portrait assignment due and my model canceled and you have, um." She gestures at all of you, goes pink, and restarts. "Good bone structure. For light. It's a lighting thing." The photography club, you'll learn, is Liv and two first-years who never show up, in a converted storage room with blackout curtains and a darkroom that smells of vinegar. She's a different person behind the camera — precise, quietly bossy, actually laughing. "Chin left. No, my left. There." The shutter clicks. Somewhere in the third roll she says, not quite to you: "Cas won't let me photograph him anymore. He thinks the pictures make him look—" She stops. Clicks the shutter again.

Someone's dorm party, second week. You're on the balcony with a warm drink when the argument spills through the kitchen — Liv's voice, low and pleading, and Cas's, cracking upward: "I don't NEED you to defend me, Liv, Christ—" Some rugby-necked guy had apparently called Cas her *little sister* and Cas had responded by shoving a man twice his mass, and now Liv is between them and the whole party is pretending not to watch. Cas storms out onto your balcony, sees you, and visibly considers storming somewhere else, except there isn't anywhere else. He grips the railing. His hands are shaking. "Say one word," he says, "one single word, and I swear to God." Below, through the glass, you can see Liv apologizing to the rugby-neck on his behalf, which — judging by Cas's face — is infinitely worse than the insult was.

The last bus back to campus is delayed forty minutes and the shelter has one dry bench, and Liv is already on it, hood up, alone, eyes red-rimmed in a way she'll deny. "Oh — hey," she says, scooting over, sniffing once, briskly. "Rain got in my eyes." Under the shelter's flickering light, with the harbor foghorn sounding somewhere out in the dark, she talks more than she ever has — about growing up in Brinmark, about how she and Cas got together at sixteen because he punched a kid who was mocking her stutter and then cried about it after. "He used to tell me things," she says. "Now he just... performs. All the time. Even for me." She catches herself, horrified. "Sorry. You didn't ask. You're just — easy to talk to. That's a problem, probably." The bus headlights appear at the end of the wet road.
