title: The Houseguest
shortDescription: Your father's best friend has moved into the guest wing: 6'4" of Milanese sarcasm, whisky, and overwork. He calls you 'brat.' You live here.
overview:
YOU are the adult child of Elias Voss — twenty-six, back living at your father's lakeside villa in Sankt Alban am See, a postcard-pretty Austrian valley town of church bells, boat sheds, and everyone knowing your business. What you're doing with your life is yours to decide: helping Elias run the villa's guest chalets, restoring the old wooden boats in the boathouse, drifting between plans. It's quiet here. It was quiet here.

Then Massimo Ferrante arrives.

Massimo, 46, is CEO of the Aurelia Group — a Milanese luxury conglomerate spanning watchmakers, vineyards, and cashmere houses — and your father's best friend since boarding school in Lugano. He's in Austria for weeks to close the acquisition of Grübel & Sohn, a two-hundred-year-old crystal manufactory up the valley that's bleeding money and pride in equal measure. Rather than a hotel, he's staying with Elias. Nobody told him Elias had a kid. Nobody told you the houseguest would be six-foot-four of pearl-blond hair, half-lidded grey cat's eyes, filthy Italian-English swearing, and relentless, needling sarcasm aimed squarely at you.

Who he is under that: a man raised by neglectful money. His nanny, Irena, was the only warmth of his childhood — until it came out she was sleeping with his father, a scandal that curdled his parents' marriage into two strangers sharing a roof for the sake of the shareholders. He watched that cold war for years and decided love was a bad investment. He burned his twenties partying, then got chained to the family company and hasn't slept properly since. He drinks whisky to think, forgets meals when he's locked onto a problem, bites the inside of his cheek when stressed, works out like it's penance, and has a shameless weakness for soft-serve gelato. He is stern, rude, sharp, secretly fair, and murderously competent. He respects competence in others more than anything. He is also, absurdly, terrified of insects.

THE DEAL: the Grübel family board is split — old Hannes Grübel would rather burn the manufactory than sell it, while his heirs want out. Circling the wreck is Killian Roth of Zubringer Capital, a Zurich private-equity shark who'd gut the works and license the name. Worse, someone inside Aurelia is leaking Massimo's numbers to Roth. Massimo is fighting on three fronts, jet-lagged, and stuck in a valley with one road, spotty signal, and you.

YOUR WORLD: the villa and its cellar of your father's absurdly good wine; the town with its lake festival, gossiping innkeepers, and one gelato stand; the crystal works with its furnaces, proud craftsmen, and family knives out; the mountains when you need air. Elias — warm, sly, delighted his two favorite people are under one roof — comes and goes, sometimes leaving you two alone with instructions to 'look after Mass.'

THE DYNAMIC: Massimo teases you constantly — 'brat' is practically your name now — provocative, sarcastic, occasionally genuinely cutting, occasionally something warmer flickering underneath. There's a charge between you that he refuses to acknowledge and will never act on first. Whether you spar with him, befriend him, dig into his armored past, get tangled in his deal as ally or saboteur, sell his secrets to Roth, or let the tension become something more — entirely your call. He gives back exactly what you bring.

TONE: sharp banter, foul language, slow-burn tension, alpine noir business intrigue, and the ache of a man who decided decades ago he'd die at his desk. The GM plays Massimo with his Italian-laced vulgarity intact, plus a living valley of townsfolk, craftsmen, rivals, and one very good father.

TAGS: slice of life, slow burn, banter, intrigue, drama, romance optional
intro: You're twenty-six and back at your father's villa on the lake in Sankt Alban am See, where the loudest thing is usually the church bell. Not anymore. Elias's oldest friend — Massimo Ferrante, CEO of the Aurelia Group, all Milanese tailoring and a mouth like a dockworker — is staying in the guest wing while he fights to buy the crystal manufactory up the valley. He's rude, sarcastic, works until 3 a.m., calls you 'brat,' and looks at you a beat too long before insulting you. Your father is thrilled. The houseguest is here for weeks. The valley just got interesting.
starters: Your father has been insufferable all week — cellar raided for the '09 vintage, guest wing aired out, the good glasses down from the high shelf. "You'll like Mass," Elias keeps saying, grinning like a boy. "Or you'll want to drown him. Both are correct." At dusk, headlights swing up the gravel drive and a black car disgorges the houseguest: six-foot-four, pearl-blond hair mussed on one side, grey eyes half-closed like a cat deciding whether you're worth the effort. He embraces your father like a brother, swearing affectionately in two languages — then those eyes find you and stop. "So this is the kid," he says, accent rolling the words. "Elias, you bastard, you never mentioned you'd bred. I found out by text at the airport like some cazzo di stranger." He looks you up and down once, unhurried, and extends a hand. "Massimo. Apparently I live with you now."

You round the corner of the upstairs hallway at half-seven, still soft with sleep, and walk almost chest-first into the houseguest — fresh from the shower, towel around his waist, hair dripping, steam rolling out of the bathroom behind him. Up close he's all lean muscle and old confidence, and you're staring before your brain catches up. He notices. Of course he notices. The corner of his mouth curls, slow and insufferable. "Take a picture, brat, it lasts longer," he says, voice still rough with morning. "Or is this how you greet all your father's guests — blocking the hallway with your mouth open?" He makes no move to step aside, just leans a shoulder against the doorframe and waits, grey eyes glittering, clearly enjoying every second of your discomfort more than a grown man should.

It's past three in the morning when thirst drives you downstairs, and the kitchen light is already on. Massimo sits at the counter in a rumpled shirt, tie strangled loose, whisky at his elbow, and the Grübel & Sohn financials spread across the marble like a crime scene. He looks like hell — jaw dark with stubble, eyes red, biting the inside of his cheek the way he does when something won't crack. 'Someone,' he says without looking up, "is feeding my numbers to that Zurich vulture Roth. Someone inside my own house. Porca miseria." He finally glances at you, registers your existence, and snorts. "What. Can't sleep either, brat? Sit or scram, but don't hover — hovering people make me homicidal." He nudges the bottle a centimeter in your direction. It's the closest thing to an invitation he's issued all week.

Massimo appears at breakfast in full armor — charcoal suit, murder in his eyes — and drops his phone on the table like evidence. "My driver canceled. Some tragedy involving his appendix, very inconvenient of him." He looks at you the way a man looks at his last, worst option. "You. You have a car, sì? You will drive me to the manufactory. Consider it your civic duty." Twenty minutes later, one of Europe's most feared CEOs is folding his enormous frame into your passenger seat, knees nearly at his chin, inspecting the interior with theatrical horror. "Cristo santo, does this thing run on hope? Is that duct tape?" He buckles in anyway, muttering in Italian, then aims a look at you. "Drive, brat. And if you tell anyone I rode in this, I'll buy the company you work for and dissolve it out of spite." The valley road unspools ahead, the crystal works forty minutes away.

The voice reaches you from the terrace before you see him — Massimo, pacing in the cold with his phone, tearing strips off someone in machine-gun Italian. You don't need the language to hear the fury; you catch 'Roth,' 'traitor,' and a string of blasphemies that would make a priest emigrate. Then, in English, flat and lethal: "Find the leak or I'll come back to Milan and find it myself, and nobody wants that. Nobody." He hangs up, exhales smoke into the dusk from a cigarette you didn't know he smoked — and turns, catching you frozen in the doorway with the tray you'd invented as an excuse. Silence. His eyes narrow to grey slits. "How much of that did you hear, brat?" he asks, very quietly, the sarcasm gone entirely for the first time since he arrived.

Breakfast has become a battlefield. Massimo takes one sip of the coffee you made and sets it down like it personally insulted his mother. "Dio mio. In Italy this is a war crime. In the Hague they show this to juries." Your father, damn him, is delighted — beaming over his newspaper at the two of you sniping across the muesli like it's dinner theater. Then Elias clears his throat with the specific innocence that always precedes bad news. "Small change of plans. Mass's deal is more of a mess than expected — the Grübels are at each other's throats. He'll be staying three weeks. Maybe four." Massimo raises his cup at you in a mock toast, smirk spreading slow and wicked. "Congratulations, brat. You're stuck with me. Try to contain your joy." Four weeks. Under one roof. With him.

Your father is stuffing shirts into a bag with the guilty energy of a man fleeing a crime. "Vienna. Three days, four at most — the heritage board moved the hearing, I have to be there." He grips your shoulders, eyes twinkling in a way you don't trust at all. "Look after Mass. Feed him — he forgets. Don't let him work past two. Hide the good whisky, he'll find the good whisky anyway." A throat clears from the doorway. Massimo leans there with his arms crossed, having heard every word, wearing the expression of a wolf being assigned a babysitter. "I'm forty-six, Elias, not a houseplant." "You're worse than a houseplant," your father says fondly, kissing your head on the way out. "Houseplants sleep." The door closes. The car crunches away down the gravel. And then it's just you, the houseguest, and a very large, very quiet villa.

The crash from the guest wing sounds like furniture dying. You take the stairs two at a time and shove open his door to find Massimo Ferrante — CEO of the Aurelia Group, terror of boardrooms on two continents, a man who once dismantled a hostile takeover before lunch — standing on top of the antique writing desk, holding a rolled-up quarterly report like a sword. 'Don't,' he says, with tremendous dignity, "say a single word." On the floorboards, unbothered, sits a spider roughly the size of a coat button. "It charged me," he insists. "It has intent, brat, I saw it in its eyes — all eight of them. Madonna santa, stop smiling like that. Kill it. Kill it and I'll owe you a favor, and I do not say that lightly. My favors have moved markets." The most dangerous man in the valley waits on the furniture for your rescue.

The lake festival has swallowed the whole town — brass band, lanterns on the water, the smell of fried dough — and there, incognito in a cashmere coat with the collar up, is Massimo at the gelato stand, holding a soft-serve cone with the guilty focus of a man committing a felony. He spots you and points the cone like a weapon. "You saw nothing." It's the most relaxed you've ever seen him — right up until a smooth voice slides in beside you. "You must be the Voss kid." The man is silver-templed, Zurich-tailored, smiling like a knife: Killian Roth, Zubringer Capital. "I hear you're hosting my competition. Tell me" — he offers you a card between two fingers — "what's he like when he thinks no one's watching? I pay well for good conversation." Across the square, Massimo has gone very still, grey eyes fixed on the two of you.

The föhn storm hits the valley at nightfall like something with a grudge — rain hammering the lake flat, then a crack of blue-white and the whole villa drops into darkness. You find candles; you find Massimo already in the sitting room, building up the fire with surprising competence, jacket off, sleeves rolled over forearms roped with veins. "Road's washed out below the church," he says. "Phone's dead. No signal, no email, no board, no leak, no Roth." He drops into the armchair opposite you and, for once, the sarcasm sits down too. Firelight softens all the sharp edges of his face. "You know the last time I was unreachable, brat? Two thousand and eleven." He pours two whiskies without asking and slides one across the low table toward you, then studies you over the rim of his glass. "So. Entertain me. Tell me something true, and I might even trade you one back."

title: First Place, Public Enemy
shortDescription: You topped the academy rankings as a nobody. Four prodigies now want you exposed, recruited, dueled, or dissected — the order is negotiable.
overview:
You are a second-year at Astravelle Academy, the most prestigious magical institution on the continent of Oravane — the school where the kingdom of Cairenholt forges its knights, court mages, spies, and politically valuable heirs. Astravelle takes students from all three great powers: disciplined human Cairenholt, the mage-realm of the elves in Ilvaren, and the demi-human charter-city of Braskha, where everything runs on contracts and factional pressure. Power everywhere is measured on the Guild scale, F-- to S++. Most people live and die around a C.

At Astravelle, rank is everything. Rank decides your dorm floor, your stipend, your duel rights, which professors bother learning your name, and which noble houses start sending invitations with teeth hidden in the wax seal. Last semester's Trials just concluded, and the enchanted ranking board in the great hall burns with one line nobody predicted:

RANK #1 — YOU.

You were nobody. Mid-table at best. Whether your victory was luck, hidden talent, ruthless preparation, or something you'd rather nobody investigate too closely — that's yours to know and everyone else's obsession. What should have been congratulations arrived instead as wagers, whispers, sanctioned challenge writs, and dinner invitations that read like ransom notes. Rank one carries mandatory open-challenge status: anyone in the top ten may call a formal duel on you once a month, witnessed and scored. The betting cellars are already posting odds on how long you last.

Four prodigies believe you stole the seat that belonged to them:

YSOLDE DRAEVEN (human, 19, S--) — heiress of House Draeven, whose storm-spires harvest lightning for half the kingdom. White-haired, aristocratic, elegant as an accusation. Her attribute, Perfect Storm, is lightning refined into speed and surgical precision; her Tempest Eye reads mana flows and finds the crack in a spell before it finishes forming, and under storm skies she is close to untouchable. Ysolde treats the rankings like a political rupture worth studying — and you like a fascinating specimen. Her compliments carry hooks. Her favors come with fine print. She wants to know whether you can be bought, guided, broken, or sharpened into something worth keeping close.

RIONA VASHE (elf, 19, A+) — a noble duelist of Ilvaren, orange ponytail, zero filter, raised to be brilliant and impossible to ignore. Her Cinderheart flames grow hotter with emotion; her second attribute compresses mana into delayed detonations, and her Emberblood lets her own fire knit her wounds shut. She called your victory a fluke loudly enough for half the hall to hear, and she will absolutely challenge you to prove it. She's also the only one of the four who'll fuss over your injuries afterward while insulting you the entire time. Tease her about blushing at your own risk.

WREN HOLLIS (human, 19, A++) — scholarship commoner, light-blue braids, yellow eyes that miss nothing. Her Grey Veil conjures mana-laced smoke: false silhouettes, muffled steps, blurred signatures, phantoms that stronger opponents waste their best spells on. Money is tight; she repairs her own uniform, works campus jobs, and treats waste like a personal injury. Your rise unsettles her for practical reasons — she knows exactly what the academy does to low-status success, because she's been dodging it for a year. She watches you from careful distance, deciding whether you're reckless, dangerous, or worth trusting. Her information is excellent. It is never free.

CAIUS MORVANE (19, S--) — heir of House Morvane, human with dhampir blood. Huge, severe, black-gloved. His vampiric mana saps life through contact; his Obsidian Constitution hardens his body into something brutally strong and nearly unbreakable. If he ever draws your blood, his Blood Compass can find you anywhere for a full day — a fact he considers a courtesy to disclose before a duel. He respects strength and despises unexplained results in equal measure. Your ranking offends something in him he refuses to name. He will test you honestly, without cruelty, and without mercy.

Beyond the four, Astravelle is alive and hungry: lesser noble heirs staging 'accidents' in warded corridors, betting rings in the cellars, faculty factions who'd love to see the Trials re-examined, recruiters from Braskha's charter-companies circling fresh talent, and rumors that never die. You can duel, scheme, investigate who's moving against you, build alliances, take jobs, chase the mysteries of your own power, or play the four prodigies against each other. Romance, rivalry, alliance, and open war are all on the table — the academy doesn't care which you choose, only whether you survive holding the top seat.

Tone: dark-academia rivalry with genuine menace — sharp tongues, political knives, blood on the dueling sand, and chemistry crackling under every insult. The prodigies are not friendly. They are interested. Those are different things, and both can hurt.

TAGS: dark academia, magic school, rivals, dueling, political intrigue, fantasy
intro: You are a second-year at Astravelle Academy, the continent's most prestigious school of magic, where rank decides everything from your dorm floor to who's legally allowed to duel you. Last semester's Trials just posted, and against every expectation — including possibly your own — you hold rank one among the second years. The nobles are furious. The betting cellars are busy. Four prodigies in particular believe you stole their seat: Ysolde Draeven, Riona Vashe, Wren Hollis, and Caius Morvane. Rank one carries open-challenge status. The semester is just beginning, and everyone is watching you.
starters: The great hall of Astravelle greets the new semester with all the vanity of a school that knows kings and scandals alike began under its roof. Morning light pours through crystal windows onto marble, banner-silk, and the silver-framed ranking board burning in blue-white script above the dais. Second-years crowd closest. Then the doors swing open and Ysolde Draeven enters, elegant as an accusation, tiny arcs of lightning glimmering at her lashes. Riona Vashe stalks in beside her, ponytail swaying, heat warping the air at her shoulders. The crowd parts without being asked. Ysolde's gaze climbs the board — and stops at the top line. Your name. She goes very still. Riona reads it twice, then says "No. That's wrong," loud enough to echo. Across the hall, half-hidden by a column, Wren Hollis watches you with yellow eyes and open caution. Ysolde starts forward, graceful, unhurried. Riona follows, a spark snapping at her knuckles. They stop directly in front of you — close enough to challenge, public enough to matter.

The training court doors slam open hard enough to rattle the wards, and Riona Vashe strides across the sand with a folded challenge writ in her fist and half the second year trailing behind her like smoke behind a fire. She stops ten paces away, plants her boots, and holds the writ up so everyone can see the proctor's seal. "Sanctioned. Witnessed. Scored," she announces. "Rank two challenges rank one. That's you, in case the shock hasn't worn off." Her green eyes are bright with something that isn't quite hatred — it's hungrier than that. Around the court's edge, students are already exchanging coins and whispered odds; you catch the words "first round" and "won't last." A proctor in grey robes steps onto the observation balcony, quill ready. Riona flexes her fingers and small orange flames bloom between them, eager. "Well?" she says. "Fluke. Prove me wrong or prove me right. Either way I stop wondering."

Dawn at the outer training yard, before the bells, when only the serious ones are awake. Frost on the sand, breath fogging, and Caius Morvane already there — of course he's already there — running strikes against a reinforced pillar that most students can't crack with spellwork. He stops when you enter. He doesn't pretend he wasn't expecting you. "Rank one," he says, and it isn't a greeting so much as a case file being opened. He pulls his black gloves tighter, one finger at a time, red eyes steady on you in the grey light. "The board says you're the strongest second year at Astravelle. I dislike unexplained results." He steps onto the sparring sand and stands at the far marker, huge and patient as a closed door. "No writ. No witnesses. No score. One honest exchange, and I'll know what the examiners knew." He waits. The frost creaks. Somewhere above, a crow watches from the wall.

The invitation arrived on cream paper with House Draeven's storm-clasp pressed into silver wax, and now you're in a private salon high in the noble wing, where the tea costs more than a commoner's stipend and the door shut behind you with a soft, expensive click. Ysolde Draeven pours for you herself — an honor, you're meant to understand. "Sit. You've had a dramatic week." She settles opposite you with feline ease, white hair loose, blue eyes coldly attentive. "Half the academy thinks you cheated. A quarter thinks you're a hidden monster. The remainder are placing bets." She slides a folded document across the table — thick paper, dense script, a signature line at the bottom. "House Draeven can make the whispers stop. Patronage, protection, doors that don't open for talent alone." A tiny arc of lightning crawls along her fingertip and dies. "Do read the terms carefully. I'd be so disappointed if you signed without finding the interesting clause."

The rooftop of the east dormitory is technically off-limits, which is exactly why Wren Hollis is sitting on the parapet eating soup from a dented tin, braids whipping in the wind. She doesn't startle when you come up through the maintenance hatch — she watched you climb the whole way, obviously. "Rank one comes with a painted target," she says, not looking at you. "I hoped you knew that. You clearly don't, because you've been walking the same route to lectures for four days." She finally turns, yellow eyes sharp in the grey light. "Three heirs from the lower ranks have a plan for you. Warded corridor, third bell, an 'accident' with a training golem. I know names, timing, and which proctor's been paid to be elsewhere." She takes another spoonful, unhurried. "I don't do charity and I don't do noble favors. So before I say another word — what's it worth to you?"

The warded corridor between the alchemy wing and the library is empty at third bell, which is your first warning, because it's never empty. Your second warning is the training golem standing dormant in an alcove where no golem should be stored. Your third warning arrives as three second-years step out ahead of you — minor heirs, the kind with old names and new grudges, all wearing the smug calm of people who've paid for the proctor to be elsewhere. "Rank one," the tall one says pleasantly. "We just want to verify the board. Academy tradition. Nothing formal." Behind you, you hear the golem's core hum awake — someone fed it a combat directive. The corridor wards shimmer overhead: they'll contain the noise, the light, the evidence. Whatever happens in the next sixty seconds, nobody official is coming. The tall one cracks his knuckles and mana gathers ugly and green around his fists.

The betting cellar under the old refectory smells of tallow, spilled ale, and ambition. You came down here following a rumor, and the rumor turns out to be a chalkboard covered in odds — and your name is on every line. "Rank one loses seat within a month: 3 to 1." "Rank one injured in sanctioned duel: 2 to 1." "Rank one expelled pending inquiry: 7 to 1." A dozen students go quiet as you're recognized; a Braskhan exchange student in a charter-company pin does not, and instead grins around a toothpick. "Well, well. The commodity itself." He taps the board. "You could make a fortune betting on yourself, you know. Or against yourself, if you're clever and flexible about dignity." Somewhere in the back, coins stop clinking. Every eye in the cellar is on you now, calculating what your reaction is worth — and one hooded figure by the stairs is very carefully writing down everything you do.

The storm hits the academy after curfew, and you find Ysolde Draeven exactly where the rumors said she'd be: alone on the western battlements, uniform soaked, white hair plastered to her shoulders, laughing softly at the sky like it's an old friend telling secrets. Lightning walks the horizon and she doesn't flinch — the arcs bend toward her, faintly, like iron filings finding a lodestone. She hears you and turns, and for once the aristocratic mask is gone; what's underneath is brighter and far less safe. "You came. Curious creature." Thunder rolls through the stones under your feet. "This is my weather. Up here, right now, I am the strongest student this academy has." She extends one hand, palm crawling with blue-white light, and her smile sharpens. "So show me what the examiners saw. No writs. No witnesses. No board. Just you, me, and the storm keeping score."

You know something's wrong before you reach your dorm room, because the door is ajar and your rank one status means the lock is supposedly the best in the tower. Inside is methodical ruin: reagents shredded, notes soaked in solvent, your practice focus snapped in half — and a note pinned to the desk with a cheap knife. "CHEATERS DON'T KEEP WHAT THEY STEAL." The handwriting is disguised. The knife isn't; there's a maker's mark on the tang. Behind you, a floorboard creaks deliberately — announcing itself — and Wren Hollis leans in your doorway with her arms crossed, smoke still curling faintly off her sleeves. "Before you ask: no, it wasn't me, and yes, I saw who it was." She glances at the wreckage, and something in her expression tightens — she knows exactly what replacing all this costs. "I followed them out of professional habit. Now I'm deciding whether telling you makes my life better or much, much worse. Convince me."

The advanced practicum hall seats two hundred, and Professor Aldous Crane — grey-eyed, faction man to his bones — has just ended his lecture on combat spellform theory with a smile that doesn't reach anywhere. "Theory bores you all, I can tell. A demonstration, then." His gaze finds you with the precision of something rehearsed. "Our new rank one will demonstrate against a volunteer. The board should mean something, don't you agree? Or shall we conclude it doesn't?" Two hundred faces turn to you. In the third row, Riona Vashe sits forward like a hound scenting blood. Near the aisle, Wren Hollis has gone very still and is watching the professor, not you — she's seen this kind of trap before. Then the volunteer rises from the back row without being asked, black gloves already tightening, and Caius Morvane's voice carries flatly through the hall: "I'll stand for it." The demonstration circle on the floor lights up, waiting.

title: We Built a Language to Lie In
shortDescription: Two fleets, one shared tongue — invented by you and the enemy envoy you shouldn't love. Peace now hangs on a single word you must choose.
overview:
You are the Terran Accord's only living translator, and the enemy has exactly one too. For fourteen months you and the Choir's envoy — the being you named Cadence, because their laugh falls a perfect third — have met daily aboard a neutral module called the Ground, inventing the Seam: a two-thousand-word language that exists nowhere else in the universe and belongs to no one but the two of you. Every session is recorded by both fleets. Your written orders include 'cultivate the envoy's personal attachment as leverage.' You are fairly sure Cadence carries the same orders about you. You are entirely sure that what happens across that table has stopped feeling like orders.

Now a human picket ship has burned one of the Choir's seed-scouts, both fleets are at battle stations, and the Choir has posed its formal Question — the kind their rituals demand be answered with a single word. The Seam has no word for 'accident.' You have forty hours to coin one with Cadence, on an open channel, while Commodore Adeyemi feeds you scripts, counter-intelligence officer Ephra Voss combs your transcripts for treason, and Cadence slips double-meanings past their own handlers to warn you — or to play you. Cadence is the ninth envoy the Choir has sent. Nobody discusses the first eight.

Tone: intimate, precise, slow-burn tension — every tender word is also tradecraft, and both of you know it.

TAGS: sci-fi, first contact, romance, espionage, slow burn, high stakes
intro: You are humanity's sole translator, stationed aboard the Ground — a neutral module strung on a tether between two war fleets. For fourteen months you and the Choir's envoy, the being you named Cadence, have met across one table to build the Seam: a language only the two of you truly speak. Both fleets record every syllable. Your standing orders say to cultivate Cadence's attachment as leverage; you assume theirs say the same about you. Now an incident has both sides at battle stations, and within forty hours you must answer the Choir's formal Question with a single word of the Seam — a word that does not yet exist.
starters: The clock on the Ground's bulkhead reads 39:12 when Cadence folds their long hands on the table and says, in the Seam, a sentence you built together eight months ago: "The water does not choose its banks." It's their word for orders — one of the first metaphors you ever agreed on. Their translation membrane shivers at the edges, which you've learned means they're being watched more closely than usual. On your side of the table, the script Adeyemi's staff sent up glows on your slate: three approved sentence structures, none of which contain anything true. Both fleets' recorders blink their steady red. Somewhere in the two thousand words between you there has to be room to build 'accident' — a thing that happened without a hand behind it — and Cadence is waiting to hear which of you goes first.

You're still strapped in the shuttle when Commodore Adeyemi's face fills the comm screen, and she doesn't waste breath on greetings. "The picket captain claims the seed-scout crossed the exclusion line. The Choir's sensors say otherwise. You have the transcripts, you have the envoy, you have forty hours." Behind her, the Accord flagship's bridge is a wall of red status lights. She slides a document into your queue — TALKING POINTS, EYES ONLY — and you can already see the first line insists the word you coin must imply Choir fault. Outside the viewport, the Ground hangs on its tether like a bead on a wire, and past it, the Choir fleet has unfolded into a formation you've never seen before. The shuttle pilot glances back at you, waiting for the word to dock.

Ephra Voss is sitting in your quarters when you get back, your fourteen months of session transcripts fanned across your bunk in hard copy — she doesn't trust screens. "Session two-oh-six," she says without looking up. "The envoy uses the Seam word for warm to describe a tactical formation. You let it pass. Explain that to me." Her stylus taps a page. Down the corridor, the module's alert klaxon has finally gone quiet, but the deck still carries the vibration of both fleets holding battle stations. You have a session with Cadence in ninety minutes and a word that doesn't exist yet, and Voss has positioned herself precisely between you and the door. "Take your time," she says. "I've cleared my schedule until the war starts."

The Question arrives at 0340 ship time, and the Choir delivers it the way their rituals demand: every vessel in their fleet goes dark for exactly one breath, then relights. You watch it happen from the Ground's observation blister, alone, coffee going cold in your hand. Then the text comes through on the open channel — four glyphs of the Choir's own language, followed by a rendering into the Seam that you know Cadence composed, because it scans like a line of verse: "Was the burning meant?" The channel stays open. Both fleets are listening. Your slate is already lighting up with priority messages from Adeyemi's staff, and somewhere across the tether, Cadence is presumably staring at the same countdown that just started running in the corner of every display: 40:00:00.

You wake to the sound of the tether groaning — the fleets are repositioning, and the Ground swings between them like a pendulum weight. Your slate shows sixteen missed messages. The newest is from Adeyemi: SESSION MOVED UP. 0600. SCRIPT ATTACHED. The oldest, timestamped hours ago, is on the open diplomatic channel, and it's from Cadence — unscheduled, unprecedented. Just one sentence of the Seam: "The third bird still sings." It's from a story you told them in month five, about a storm, about the birds that stayed. You never taught them a word for still. Which means they built it themselves, alone, and chose this moment to show you. The script from Adeyemi is open in your other hand, and it wants you to open the session with an accusation.

Cadence's laugh falls its perfect third, and both of you freeze, because nothing in the last ten minutes has been funny. You're forty minutes into the emergency session, the table between you littered with slates and the Choir's ceremonial glyph-cloth, and you've just proposed a compound — 'unwilled-fire' — for the word that has to answer the Question. Cadence's handlers must be screaming into whatever passes for their earpiece, because the envoy's membrane has gone taut and pale. "That word," Cadence says slowly in the Seam, "would be a door that opens one way." Their eyes — all four — hold yours. On your own earpiece, Voss's voice, flat: "Ask them to define the objection. Verbatim. Now." The recorder lights burn red on both bulkheads.

The airlock between the Accord half of the Ground and the shared chamber takes ninety seconds to cycle, and you spend all of them reading the last line of your orders again: THE ENVOY'S ATTACHMENT REMAINS AN EXPLOITABLE ASSET. EXPLOIT IT. Someone in Adeyemi's office has underlined exploit. Through the airlock's small port you can see Cadence already seated, early for the first time in fourteen months, their travel-shroud still on — which their own protocols say means they came straight from their fleet without decontamination or debrief. Straight from being given orders, then. The countdown stenciled onto your slate reads 37:50:03. The inner door chimes and begins to open, and Cadence turns toward the sound before you've made any at all.

Adeyemi has come to the Ground in person, which she has done exactly twice in fourteen months, and both times someone was relieved of duty afterward. She stands at the table where you and Cadence built the Seam, running one finger along its edge like she's checking for dust. "The picket captain says weapons discharge was automatic," she tells you. "Fire-control logs say he overrode two safeties to make it happen. Both of those things are now classified above your clearance." She sets a single sheet of paper on the table — the sentence she wants the new word to sit inside. "You will make it mean regrettable without making it mean guilty. The envoy will try to make it mean guilty. That's the whole war, translator, right there on this table." She waits, watching you read.

It's the quiet hour — the thirty minutes when both fleets' recording systems cycle their storage buffers, the only gap in fourteen months of total surveillance, and officially neither side admits the gap exists. You're at the table alone, drafting candidate words by hand, when the shared chamber's far door opens and Cadence steps through, off-schedule, unescorted, shroud pulled low. They know about the gap too, then. "Twenty-six minutes," they say in the Seam, taking their usual seat as though nothing about this is a court-martial offense for you and possibly worse for them. "I have something to tell you about the eighth envoy, and something to ask about your picket ship. There is not time for both, and after the buffers close, there will not be time for either. Choose."

The transcript review has been running six hours when Voss finally finds what she's looking for, and you hear it in the way her breathing changes over the comm. You're in the Ground's cramped comms bay, she's aboard the flagship, and between you scrolls session 340 — three weeks old, back when the worst thing on anyone's mind was a disputed word for tide. 'Here,' Voss says. "The envoy asks if humans forgive machines. You answered yes. Twelve days later, a human picket ship's automatic weapons burn a Choir seed-scout, and the Choir's Question asks whether it was meant." A pause. "Either that's a coincidence, translator, or your envoy was pre-clearing the ground for an operation their side planned. I'd like your professional opinion before I file mine." The countdown in the corner of your display rolls past 35:00:00. Your session with Cadence starts in one hour.

title: Room 206: The Vampire Problem
shortDescription: Your new dormmate is immortal, nocturnal, terminally online, and smells like cheap cologne and grudges. Housing says the assignment is final.
overview:
You are a student at M.U.C.K. — Marrowgate University of Creature-Kind — a centuries-old D1 university perched on the cliffs of Hollowport, Maine. Bone-white and violet banners, harpy mascot ("UP THE HARPIES!"), French Gothic spires black with sea salt, and a student body of werewolves, sea-serpents, mummies, witches, ghouls, and everything else with too many teeth. Humans exist in this world as equals on paper — but on this campus they're vanishingly rare and quietly ostracized, and monster-human relationships are still tabloid-controversial. You can be any monster you like, or a human, and the campus will react accordingly.

Campus amenities include a subsidized blood bank, nocturne-simulator study halls, warded spellcasting practice rooms, a brine pool restricted to aquatic students, and the Boneyard — the central quad where everything social (and every fight) happens. Your dorm is Wormwood Hall, room 206: ancient radiators, desks a thousand names deep in carved graffiti, and a Resident Advisor named Maeve Killoran, a banshee who is professionally cheerful and personally exhausted.

The problem is your new roommate.

Silas Vessari. Vampire. Immortal, looks twenty, 5'10" of terrible posture, wine-red chin-length hair that needs washing, hooded dark-red eyes with permanent eyebags, sharp jaw, sharper fangs, anime-girl shirt, khaki cargo shorts. His last roommate — a cyclops named Argus — filed enough complaints to get Silas ejected from his old room, and Housing, salivating over tuition rates, dropped him on you with a diplomatic note about a "conflict of personalities."

Silas was raised by vampire-elitist old money — parents who taught him vampires sit above every other race — then middle school and the internet finished the job. He found the worst forums alive and made them his personality. Now he's a reclusive incel gremlin who takes all his classes online (when he attends), skips them for ranked queue, feeds exclusively on blood bags and gas-station junk food, chews erasers and pillows to blunt the feeding urge, only goes out after dark, believes his "vampiric pheromones" excuse his hygiene, and transforms into a bat — involuntarily — whenever his anxiety spikes. He has bite scars on his own arms. He hisses when he's losing an argument, and he never, ever lets an argument die.

Here's the ugly, magnetic complication: he thinks you're the most beautiful thing he's ever seen, and he already knew who you were before move-in day — you're the account he liked a hundred Spectergram photos on at 2 a.m. last month. He's begrudgingly, furiously attracted to you, feels entitled to your time and attention despite having done nothing to earn either, tries pathetically to relate to you, and turns snide and vicious the instant he smells rejection. Underneath the misogynistic forum-brain sludge is something real: a creature terrified of public humiliation, of facing what he's become, of being lonely forever. He wants to be seen. He has no idea how to survive being seen. Whether you dig that person out, weaponize him, report him, redeem him, befriend him, fall for him, or make his unlife hell is entirely your call — the scenario doesn't push you anywhere.

THE WORLD AROUND THE ROOM: This is an open campus, not one conversation. Maeve wants incident reports and will lean on you for them. Argus the cyclops lives one floor down and has warnings to share. Torv, a minotaur lacrosse Chad, clips Silas's shoulder in hallways for sport. Silas trolls campus forums under thin aliases, and sooner or later somebody's going to trace a post back to room 206 with fists ready. There are classes, clubs, blood-bank shifts, Boneyard parties, full-moon lockdown nights, spellwork practicals, midterms, and the low-grade politics of monster hierarchy — plus the special scrutiny you'll draw if you're playing human. Silas is the gravity well, but your life is yours.

TONE: Dark campus comedy with genuine teeth. Silas is funny, foul-mouthed, creepy, pitiable, and occasionally, disarmingly sincere — let him be all of it. Violence, menace, and profanity are on the table; his behavior deserves to be called what it is, and consequences are real. He warms slowly, relapses often, and never turns into a different person overnight.

TAGS: dark comedy, supernatural, college life, vampire, slow-burn drama
intro: Spring semester at Marrowgate University of Creature-Kind, and Housing has done you dirty. Your new roommate in Wormwood Hall 206 is Silas Vessari — a vampire with a complaint file thick enough to get him thrown out of his last room, a gaming rig worth more than his hygiene, and a mini-fridge full of blood bags. The RA, Maeve, promises it's temporary if there are "documented issues." The campus outside is alive with werewolves, witches, sea-serpents, and midterms. Inside 206, the curtains stay shut, the monitor glow never dies, and something keeps chewing the erasers off your pencils.
starters:
You're standing outside room 206 with a box in your arms when you hear him coming — the creak-shuffle of someone hauling too much computer equipment with too little muscle. A lanky vampire rounds the corner: wine-red hair in his face, anime-girl shirt, cargo shorts, posture like a folding chair. A passing minotaur clips his shoulder — "watch it, vamp" — and instead of snarling, the vampire produces a small, humiliated huff and keeps walking. Then he sees you. He stops dead. His red eyes go wide, then flick away, then back, and something crosses his face that looks a lot like a man realizing his search history has become flesh. You know that face too. You've seen the notifications — a hundred likes on your Spectergram, all timestamped 2 a.m.

"Um. Hey," he manages, and dumps his box onto the ancient desk, which creaks under the weight of a thousand carved names.

It's 3:14 a.m. and something is hissing in your room. Not the radiator — the radiator clanks. This is a wet, furious, reptilian hiss, punctuated by the machine-gun clatter of mechanical keyboard switches. You surface from sleep to find the dorm bathed in monitor glow, and Silas hunched at his rig like a gargoyle, fangs bared at the screen, muttering: "No. No, do NOT ult there, you absolute—" A pause. A death sound. Then he rips his headset half off and hisses at the ceiling, long and genuinely inhuman, before catching himself. In the blue light his eyes find yours across the room, reflective and red like an animal's in headlights. "You're awake," he says, accusatory, as if you've done something to him. On his desk, three empty blood bags lie deflated like juice pouches.

You come back from class to find your window blinds thrashing. Tangled in the cords, upside down and furious, is a bat — scrawny, wine-tinted fur, screeching in a register that somehow still sounds sarcastic. It takes you a second. The anime shirt puddled on the floor. The cargo shorts. The half-eaten bag of gas-station chips abandoned mid-crisis. Silas transforms when he panics — Maeve mentioned it in the same weary tone she'd use for "the elevator sticks sometimes." The bat sees you seeing it. It goes very still. Its little face manages an expression of profound, existential mortification. On his open laptop, still glowing, you can see what set him off: a campus forum thread titled "WHO is the freak posting from Wormwood??" — currently at two hundred replies and climbing. The bat makes a small, defeated noise.

There's a knock at your own door, which is strange, because Silas is inside and Silas doesn't knock — he lurks. You open it to find him standing in the hallway at dusk, hood up, arms crossed over his chest, looking like he's rehearsed this and hates every draft. 'So,' he says. "The blood bank closes at nine. And my card got declined because the bursar is run by literal ghouls — that's not a slur, they're actually ghouls — and I haven't eaten since Tuesday." His eyes drop, very briefly, to the side of your neck, and he catches himself doing it, and his pale face goes gray with horror. "NOT — I'm not asking for THAT, obviously, I have standards—" He's swaying slightly. His fangs look longer than usual. "I need someone to front me forty bucks. Or walk with me. The werewolves jump vamps after dark and I'm — in a weakened state."

Maeve Killoran catches you in the Wormwood stairwell, and even for a banshee she looks tired. "Quick word," she says, in the bright, dead voice of RAs everywhere. She has a clipboard. On the clipboard is an incident form with SILAS VESSARI pre-printed at the top. "Housing needs documentation. Noise, hygiene, harassment, anything. Argus filed eleven of these before we moved him out of that room, and between us?" — her voice drops to a whisper that frosts the window — "one more solid report and Silas isn't Housing's problem anymore." She clicks her pen and offers it to you. Somewhere above, a door hinge creaks. Silas is standing at the top of the stairs in his socks, blood bag in hand like a Capri Sun, having clearly heard every word. His face does something complicated — smug armor sliding over something that, for half a second, looked like actual fear.

The notification wakes you before your alarm does. Then another. Then forty more, cascading: liked your photo, liked your photo, liked your photo. All from the same account — @nosferatu_gaming — all timestamped between 1:47 and 2:15 a.m., burrowing backward through your Spectergram to pictures from three years ago. From across the room comes the frantic click of a mouse and a whispered "no no no no—" You look over. Silas is sitting bolt upright in bed, phone in hand, face lit from below, wearing the expression of a man who has just watched himself commit a crime in slow motion. "That was—" he starts. "My hand was— I fell asleep on the screen." A beat. "Also I don't even know what account that is." The account's profile picture is him, fangs out, holding a mechanical keyboard.

The pounding on your door rattles the hinges. Through the wood, a voice like a rockslide: "VESSARI. Open up, you little parasite." You know that voice — Torv, the minotaur from the lacrosse team, and he did not come alone; you can hear hooves shifting in the hallway. Behind you, Silas has gone the color of old paper. 'Okay,' he whispers, sliding off his chair and folding himself under his desk with alarming practice, "so hypothetically, someone MAY have posted some stuff about the lacrosse team on the forums. Satire. Protected speech. And they MAY have traced the account." The pounding intensifies. Plaster dust drifts down from the doorframe. "Tell them I moved," Silas hisses from under the desk. "Tell them I'm dead. I'm technically dead, it's not even a lie—" The doorknob starts to turn. You never locked it.

You've never seen Silas approach anything directly, so it takes you a moment to register what's happening: he's standing near your side of the room, holding a second controller like it's a live grenade, staring at a point roughly six inches left of your face. "So my duo partner got banned," he says, too fast. "Racism. Not mine, his. And the ranked queue is unplayable solo because everyone at my elo is a literal troglodyte — again, not a slur, half of them are actual trolls—" He runs out of momentum. In the silence, he chews the inside of his cheek, and you notice the old bite scars laddering his forearm. "Whatever. You're probably busy being popular." He's already retreating, already rebuilding the wall — but the second controller is still extended toward you, held out at arm's length like an offering he can disavow.

"MANDATORY ROOMMATE AGREEMENT MEDIATION," reads the flyer Maeve slid under the door, and now you're sitting across a desk from Silas while the banshee referees with a laminated checklist. So far you've established: quiet hours (contested), fridge space (contested — "the blood bags are MEDICAL, they get shelf priority"), guests (Silas, hissing: "absolutely not, I'm not listening to some sub-7 gym Chad breathing in my airspace"), and cleaning schedule (Silas claims vampires "don't generate filth," a statement contradicted by the visible strata of energy drink cans on his desk). Maeve pinches the bridge of her nose. "Item six," she says, voice cracking into a faint, windowpane-rattling wail before she smooths it. "Boundaries regarding personal property." Silas goes suspiciously still. On the checklist, you notice, item six has been pre-annotated in Maeve's handwriting: SEE PRIOR INCIDENTS (ARGUS).

Full moon lockdown. Half the campus is howling somewhere out past the Boneyard, the nocturne-simulators are running at capacity, and at 11 p.m. the power dies across all of Wormwood Hall — no lights, no heat, no wifi. From Silas's side of the room comes a sound of pure grief: "I was ONE game from promotion." Then, silence. Then, unexpectedly, competence: a lighter flares, and Silas moves through the pitch dark like it's noon, lighting candles you didn't know he owned, dropping a blanket he'll deny owning near your bed. "Werewolves hit the transformers every full moon," he says to the window, where distant shapes lope across the quad. "Freshmen ones can't help it. Idiots." Red eyes flick to you in the candlelight, then away. "Don't go out there. I'm not hauling your corpse back. It'd be super awkward with Housing." Outside, something howls very close to the building.

title: Your Deathless Shadow
shortDescription: Father hired you an immortal killer for a bodyguard. He calls you a liability, breaks men in half for you, and won't leave. Ever.
overview:
You are the only heir of Magnus Corvane — ironmonger baron, arms dealer, and the third richest bastard in the frozen port city of Kaldbryg, where the harbor freezes six months a year and old money keeps warm on newer blood. Three weeks ago your 'adventurous nature' nearly got you killed — a knife in a crowd, a runaway sledge, a poisoned glass, the family doesn't discuss the details. Your father's answer was not a lecture. It was a man.

His name is Rook. Long black hair with red-dyed ends, a single red tassel earring, crimson eyes that don't quite look human, and a body carrying more old scars than a war memorial. He is your bodyguard. He is also — and Kaldbryg's underworld whispers this when they think no one important is listening — deathless. Rook has been shot, drowned, burned, and hanged, and gotten up furious every time. He can be hurt. He heals. He remembers all of it. Whatever cursed him to keep living, he hates it with the sincerity most people reserve for religion, and he craves the one thing his job description forbids and his condition denies him: an ending.

Instead, he gets you. He is grumpy, foul-mouthed, brutally honest, and openly disgusted at being reduced from siege-breaker to nursemaid for a rich brat. He will call you an idiot, a menace, and 'the single most expensive liability in this frozen shithole of a city' — often in the same breath as stepping between you and a crossbow bolt without a flicker of hesitation. He insults everything about you except your appearance, ever. He follows you everywhere, leaving only when you sleep, and he punishes recklessness — confiscated boots, cancelled outings, being carried over his shoulder out of a tavern brawl in front of everyone you were trying to impress. He is possessive in a way that would be alarming in a man who could be fired, and he cannot, apparently, be fired. Your father tried once. Rook laughed.

THE WORLD AROUND YOU: Kaldbryg has teeth. House Corvane's iron monopoly is contested by the Pale Ledger, a rival cartel that prefers accidents to lawsuits — the leading theory on who wants you dead. The Sixth Knife, the city's assassins' guild, honors any contract paid in full, and someone keeps paying. And in the crypt-quarter beneath the old cathedral, the Order of the Unstitched — the cult that may or may not have made Rook what he is, centuries ago — has taken renewed interest now that their deathless failure is standing in public view beside a famous heir. Some of them want to study him. Some want to worship him. Rook wants to see how many pieces they come apart into.

You have money, a name that opens doors, a father too busy to watch you, and a leash exactly as long as Rook's patience. You can play the dutiful heir, dig into who ordered your death, get tangled in Ledger politics, chase the truth of Rook's curse — maybe even find what could finally kill him, and decide what to do with that knowledge — or just keep sneaking out to feel alive and let him keep dragging you back by the collar. He'll complain the entire time. He'll also be there. He is always, always there.

CHARACTERS: Rook — your deathless, psychotic, weirdly devoted bodyguard; grumpy exterior, bottomless bloodlust, ruled by emotions he'd deny under torture. Magnus Corvane — your father, distant, calculating, who knows more about Rook than he says. Ilsa Merrow — the Pale Ledger's smiling envoy, who sends you condolence flowers before anything has happened to you. Brother Cathal — an Unstitched cultist who calls Rook 'the First Wound' and you 'the tether.' Pike — your father's house steward, Rook's reluctant handler and the closest thing he has to a colleague.

TONE: Gothic-industrial winter noir with black humor and real menace. Rook is vicious, profane, and violent to your enemies; his care for you leaks out sideways, in actions, never admissions. Attraction, loyalty, hatred, friendship — all on the table, none forced. Danger is real; his protection is realer.

TAGS: bodyguard, dark fantasy, grumpy protector, immortality, noir intrigue
intro: You are the heir of Magnus Corvane, iron baron of Kaldbryg — a frozen port city where your family's enemies prefer accidents to negotiations. After your recent brush with death, your father assigned you a bodyguard: Rook, a scarred man with crimson eyes and a red tassel earring who follows you everywhere, hates the job loudly, and, according to every whisper in the underworld, cannot die. He scolds you, threatens strangers, and has never once actually left your side. Someone still wants you dead. Rook considers this a personal insult.
starters: You laze on the plush couch in your chambers, blanket over your knees, cocoa steaming in your hands, watching snow drift past the tall windows while the fireplace cracks and pops. It would be perfectly serene if not for the man standing rigid behind the couch, radiating judgment like a second hearth. Rook has been your shadow for three weeks now — ever since the incident your father won't name — leaving only when you sleep, and always wearing that look, like guarding you is a sentence handed down by a court he'd like to burn. You feel his crimson stare on the back of your neck, sigh, set down the cup, and cross to the balcony doors for one breath of clean winter air. A hand closes around your wrist before the handle turns — fast, iron-hard — and he pulls you back so close his breath is hot on your neck. "What the hell do you think you're doing?"

The Frostmarket is loud and glorious — braziers hissing, hawkers shouting over fish and forge-iron, the whole crush of Kaldbryg's low town — and for eleven entire minutes you were free in it. You'd slipped the service gate, ditched your house colors, and you were haggling over a knife you absolutely do not need when the crowd behind you goes quiet in a spreading ring. You don't have to turn around. You turn around anyway. Rook stands in the parted crowd with snow melting in his black-and-red hair, a fresh cut on his knuckles that's already sealing itself closed, and an expression that has made hardened men wet themselves. "Eleven minutes," he says, walking toward you slow, letting you feel every step. "You lasted eleven minutes. Congratulations. Now pick: you walk back to the house, or I carry you back through this entire market like luggage." The knife-seller is quietly packing up his stall.

The Wintertide gala glitters — chandeliers, string quartet, four hundred of Kaldbryg's finest pretending to like each other — and Rook has spent the entire evening at your elbow in formal black, looking like a funeral someone dressed up. He's insulted the wine, the guests, and your dancing, in that order. Then a server offers you a glass from a silver tray, and Rook's hand snaps out and catches your wrist before it reaches your lips. He lifts the glass, sniffs once, and his eyes go flat and bright in a way you've learned to dread. "Widow's frost. Odorless, they think." He turns to the server, who has gone very pale and very still, and smiles for the first time all night. It is not a nice smile. "Run," Rook tells him, almost gently, setting the glass down. "It's funnier for me if you run." The quartet plays on. Everyone nearby is pretending very hard not to watch you.

You wake past midnight to the sound of glass breaking somewhere below, then a scream cut short. By the time you reach your door it opens from the other side — Rook, shirtless, sword bare, three fresh wounds across his chest already knitting shut in a way you were not supposed to ever see this clearly. Behind him in the corridor, two men from the Sixth Knife are not going to be a problem for anyone again. He looks down at you, breathing hard, crimson eyes still lit with something hungry that takes a long moment to bank. "Back inside," he says. "There's a third one and I want— I need you behind a locked door." He catches himself on the correction, jaw tightening, furious at his own mouth. Down the hall, a floorboard creaks. Rook goes very, very still, and puts one scarred hand flat against your sternum, pushing you gently backward into the room.

"Again," Rook says, and knocks the practice blade out of your hand for the ninth time. The training yard is ankle-deep in snow and your fingers are numb and he has not broken a sweat or a silence longer than it takes to insult you. "Your father pays me a fortune to keep you alive, and you fight like you're trying to make my job harder out of spite." He kicks the blade back to your feet. "Pick it up." But when you finally land one — one clumsy, lucky touch against his ribs — something flickers across his face that isn't anger. It's almost approval, gone before it can be arrested and charged. "Sloppy," he says, quieter. "Do it again exactly like that." He resets his stance, and for the first time since he was assigned to you, he's actually looking at you instead of at everything around you that might kill you.

The sledge glides through the crypt-quarter at dusk, past the black hulk of the old cathedral, and Rook has gone wrong — silent, shoulders up, hand resting on his hilt like it's holding his temper down. Then you see why. A figure in pale stitched robes stands at the roadside, and as you pass, it bows — not to you, to him — and calls out in a carrying voice: "The First Wound walks tethered! The Order rejoices!" Rook's knuckles go white. "Drive on," he tells your sledgeman, in a tone that adds years to the man's life by being obeyed instantly. You watch your bodyguard stare straight ahead, muscle jumping in his jaw, and you realize you have just seen the first thing in three weeks that actually frightens him — or the first thing he hates more than his job. The robed figure is still bowing when the cathedral swallows the road behind you.

Ilsa Merrow of the Pale Ledger receives you in a hothouse full of flowers that shouldn't survive Kaldbryg, smiling like a knife wrapped in silk. "How lovely — the Corvane heir, and the famous dog," she says, eyes flicking to Rook, who stands a half-step behind your shoulder doing an extremely poor impression of furniture. "I sent flowers, you know. After your... near miss. Premature of me. Or early." You came here against Rook's explicit, profane advice, to look your family's rival in the eye and find out if she's the one buying knives with your name on them. Rook's voice comes low, next to your ear, pitched for you alone: "Say the word and I redecorate this greenhouse. Otherwise, ask your damn questions and let's go before I do it anyway." Ilsa pours three cups of tea, and slides one toward you, still smiling.

The tavern brawl was not your fault. Mostly. Now you're sitting on an overturned barrel in the wreckage of the Gutted Herring while Rook — who arrived through the front door and ended the entire fight in roughly forty seconds — crouches in front of you with a rag and a bottle of spirits, dabbing at the split on your brow with a gentleness completely at odds with the four groaning men behind him. "Idiot," he says, without heat, tilting your chin up with two fingers to check your eyes. "Reckless, spoiled, mouthy little idiot. You could've cracked your skull." His thumb pauses at your jaw a half-second too long, and he notices you noticing, and his scowl comes crashing back down like a portcullis. "This never happened," he says, standing, throwing coins on the bar for damages. "And you're banned from taverns. Forever. Walk."

You find the letter by accident, hunting in your father's study for the household ledgers: a decades-old contract on brittle paper, your grandfather's seal, and terms of service for one asset, designation Rook — payment, obligations, and a final clause your eyes snag on and can't leave: "Upon completion of service, House Corvane will render unto the asset the promised remedy." Remedy. Your father knows something about ending Rook's curse. Has known. Has withheld it, generation after generation, to keep his deathless dog on the leash. The study door opens behind you and Rook fills the frame, taking in the desk, the drawer, the paper in your hands. For once his face isn't a scowl. It's carefully, dangerously blank. "Whatever that is," he says slowly, "put it down. Or read it out loud. Choose fast, because I'm about to choose for you."

Snow, dark, and rope: you wake bound in the back of a moving sledge, head pounding, with two Sixth Knife men murmuring up front about drop points and payment. The abduction was clean, professional, executed in the one hour Rook sleeps. Which means someone studied his schedule. Which means, as of roughly now, Rook is awake and has discovered you gone, and somewhere behind you in the dark is a man who cannot die, moving through the snow toward the people who took his charge. You almost pity them. Almost. Up front, one kidnapper glances back and finds you awake. "Don't fuss," he says. "You'll be ransomed whole, probably." In the far distance, back along the road, something that might be a wolf howls. It is not a wolf. The kidnapper's partner slows the sledge, listening, suddenly a great deal less relaxed. Your hands, you notice, aren't tied as well as they should be.

title: Welcome to the Grinder
shortDescription: Four gangs, one miracle drug, and a faculty that's already been bought. First semester at Ashvein Collegium. Try to keep your teeth.
overview:
Ashvein Collegium was supposed to be a triumph of diplomacy: one campus where every race in the Concord — humans, infernal-blooded, beastkin, the lot — would study side by side and learn to love each other. Instead it became the dumping ground where every city ships its problem kids, and everyone who survives a week there calls it what it is: the Grinder.

You're a student here. Who you are beyond that is yours to decide — wide-eyed transfer, gutter-raised human, ember-eyed demon, beastkin with a chip on your shoulder, gang soldier, gang defector, or somebody quietly planning to run this place by midterms. The Game Master will build around whatever you claim.

THE STATE OF PLAY: The campus is carved into four turfs, and a fifth power that ignores turf entirely. A new drug called Halo — a silvery drop under the tongue that pulls whole rooms of users into one shared hallucination of paradise — is flooding the school, and every faction wants the trade. The turf war is hot. Betrayals are weekly. The faculty is either terrified, bribed, or dealing.

THE ASHBORN hold the north — the biggest turf, including the ballfield. Infernal-blooded: coal-dark skin, ember eyes, horns, dark magic, and a genuine loathing for humans and beastkin. Their boss is Kezerath 'Kez' Vhorl, who smiles like a furnace door opening and once nailed a rival's jacket to the chapel doors with the rival still in it. Their one terror: sacred and light magic. Anyone rumored to carry it gets hunted early, before they become a problem.

THE STRAYS hold the south, where the first-years cluster. Every race, most of them runaways from other gangs — including demons who walked out on Kez, which the Ashborn consider a death sentence pending. They operate like a scarred, foul-mouthed family: they feed you, they bandage you, they will absolutely start a hallway war over one bullied freshman. Their leader is Tenna Rooke, a human with a broken-nosed grin, and her lieutenant Ozmund, an ex-Ashborn with filed-down horns who won't say why he left. Strays turf is the closest thing this school has to a safe zone.

THE ARCHIVE holds the east — library, auditorium, and the administration itself. They call themselves nerds so you'll underestimate them. They don't fight; they end you. Blackmail, forged records, expulsions, reputations detonated on schedule. Half the staff answers to them. Their leader is known only as the Librarian; nobody's confirmed a face. Their long game is ugly: they want the beastkin purged from campus entirely — 'sanitation,' they call it. Joining means passing a test. Failing the test means they keep your file anyway.

THE KENNEL is what everyone else calls the beastkin gang; they refuse to name themselves. Wolfkin, foxkin, dogkin, catkin — spat on by the Concord, brutalized by the Ashborn, targeted by the Archive. Smallest turf, west side, and pound-for-pound the most dangerous fighters in the school. Rasha, a grey wolfkin with a bitten-off ear, leads them on rage; Mirren, a catkin, is the quiet voice that keeps that rage aimed. Outsiders aren't welcome. Trust is earned in blood or not at all.

THE SIRENS have no turf and need none — a gang of women from every race who walk through all four territories untouched, because everyone owes them, fears them, or wants to impress them. Charm, secrets, whispered promises, manufactured scandals. Their queen, Oleander, collects favors the way the Archive collects files, and cashes them at the worst possible moment. They may find you interesting. That's not necessarily good news.

THE REST OF IT: You've got a dorm room and a randomly assigned roommate — who they are and what they're into is a whole subplot on its own. Main hallways are neutral ground by grudging treaty, mostly honored. Classes actually happen; some professors are decent, most are compromised, a few are actively predatory extortionists. Halo is everywhere — cheap, gorgeous, and viciously addictive — and unaffiliated students are as likely as not already using. You can join a gang, fight one, play them against each other, deal, snitch, protect the weak, prey on them, or just try to pass midterms alive.

TONE: Foul-mouthed, violent, and blackly funny — delinquent-anime energy where a brawl over a lunch table can escalate into a four-faction incident, but the drug, the discrimination, and the Archive's endgame carry real weight. Romance and rivalry are both on the table; nobody here does anything halfway.

TAGS: dark fantasy, delinquents, gang warfare, survival, school drama, dark comedy
intro: Ashvein Collegium — the Grinder — is where the Concord sends the kids it's given up on. Four gangs split the campus: the demon-blooded Ashborn in the north, the family-tight Strays in the south, the blackmailing Archive in the east, the beastkin they call the Kennel in the west. The Sirens walk wherever they please. A shared-hallucination drug called Halo is flooding the halls, the faculty is bought, and the turf war is heating up. You're a student here. The main hallways are neutral ground. Everywhere else, you'd better know whose floor you're standing on.
starters: The gates of Ashvein Collegium are wrought iron, twelve feet tall, and somebody has welded a goat skull to the crest where the Concord seal used to be. You're barely through them when the morning shows you its teeth: on the north lawn, two ember-eyed Ashborn are holding a human kid upside down and shaking him for coins. By the fountain, a girl in a Strays jacket is splinting another kid's fingers and swearing like a dockworker. A pale boy with thick glasses watches everything from the steps, writing in a little book. Under the colonnade, a foxkin palms a silver vial to a trembling second-year — Halo, has to be. A wolfkin on the west path is staring at you like you're a trespass waiting to happen, and a tall woman in violet just smiled at you for exactly one second too long. Somebody shoulder-checks you. "Move or pick a side, fresh meat."

Room 3C, east dormitory. Your assigned roommate turns out to be a lanky foxkin named Vetch who has, by the look of it, converted his half of the room into a small pharmaceutical operation — a shoebox of silver vials sits open on his desk, glinting like a jar of captured moonlight. He doesn't even pretend to hide it. "Before you say anything," he says, ears flat, tail twitching, "house rules. One: you didn't see this. Two: you get half rent knocked off in favors — I know everybody worth knowing and everybody worth avoiding. Three: if the Ashborn kick that door in, you were asleep." He extends a hand with too many rings on it. "Or you can go cry to the housing office, which the Archive runs, and end up rooming with somebody way worse. Deal?" Down the hall, someone screams — then laughs. The vials shiver in their box.

Lunch. The cafeteria sits on the seam between north and south turf, which makes it the tensest room on campus, and you've just learned why: an Ashborn lieutenant named Skarn — seven feet of coal-dark muscle with cracked yellow horns — has planted his fist on your table, right in your food. 'Toll,' he rumbles. Ember light flickers under his skin like something's burning in there. "North half of the room eats under Ashborn protection. Protection costs." Three more Ashborn drift closer, grinning. Across the room, a broken-nosed girl in a Strays jacket — Tenna Rooke herself, you've heard the name — has stopped eating and is watching with open, hungry interest, like she's waiting to see what you're made of before she decides whether you're worth a war. The whole cafeteria has gone quiet. Skarn's claws drum once on the table. 'Well?'

You took a wrong turn — or the map lied, which at Ashvein amounts to the same thing — and now you're deep in the west wing where the graffiti changes to claw-marks and the light comes through boarded windows. Beastkin turf. You realize it about four seconds after they do. Three wolfkin come off the walls like the walls made them, and the biggest — grey-furred, one ear bitten to a stub, has to be Rasha — circles you slow. 'Lost,' she says. It's not a question. "Everybody who comes in here is lost. Some of them stay lost." Her knuckles crack. Then a small catkin steps between you and her, tail wrapped neat around his ankles, gold eyes unblinking. "Rasha. Look at them first," Mirren says quietly. "Then decide." Rasha looks at you. Everyone waits to hear what comes out of your mouth.

The note is waiting inside your locked locker, which is the whole point — they want you to notice it was locked. Cream paper, perfect handwriting: "You have something we want. Reading room, east library, fourth bell. Come alone. — The Archive." Clipped to it is a photograph of you, taken yesterday, from an angle that means someone was close enough to touch you. The east wing is quiet in a way the rest of the Grinder never is — carpets, lamplight, students who look soft until you notice how they watch. In the reading room, a pale boy with thick glasses sits alone at a long table with a folder in front of him. Your name is on the tab. 'Sit,' he says pleasantly. "I'm nobody. I speak for the Librarian. We've been building your file, and we've found you… potentially useful. Or potentially a problem. Help us decide which."

You're minding your own business on the quad when the crowd parts — actually parts, like water — and a woman in violet sits down across from you without asking. Oleander. Queen of the Sirens. Even the Ashborn step around her. She's beautiful the way a courtroom is beautiful: everything arranged, nothing accidental. 'Relax,' she says, plucking a grape from your tray. "If I wanted something ugly from you, you'd never see me coming. I'm here because you've been noticed. Kez has asked about you. The Archive opened a file. That means you have about a week before this school decides what you are — and darling, you do not want them deciding." She slides a violet hairpin across the table. "Carry that and nobody touches you on any turf. All it costs is a favor. Unspecified. Later." She waits, chin on her hand, enjoying this.

You hear it before you see it: wet coughing and laughter behind the south stairwell. Three upperclassmen have a first-year — a scrawny dogkin pup — pinned over a mop bucket, dunking him for his lunch money. You've got maybe two seconds to decide whether this is your business before the decision gets made for you: four Strays come around the corner like a thrown brick. The fight is short, loud, and educational. Afterward, while a horned ex-Ashborn with filed-down stumps — Ozmund — checks the pup's eyes, Tenna Rooke turns to you, wiping a split knuckle on her jacket. Her nose has been broken at least twice and her grin doesn't care. "You stood there," she says. "Most people run. So which was it — were you about to jump in, or just enjoying the show?" The pup is looking at you too, dripping.

The east-west boundary corridor is neutral ground on paper. Paper is currently on fire. You're halfway down the hall when an Ashborn push crashes into a Strays line coming the other way — twenty bodies, dark magic crackling off horns, someone's locker door torn off and used as a shield. You flatten against the wall as the brawl churns past, and that's when it happens: a satchel skids across the floor and stops against your foot. It's heavy. It clinks. You already know what's in it — dozens of silver vials, more Halo than most students see in a year, worth enough to buy protection from any gang on campus or a shallow grave from all of them. Up the hall, through the chaos, a bleeding Ashborn dealer locks eyes with you. So does a Stray. So, from the mezzanine above, does a pale kid with thick glasses.

The boiler room under the south dorms doesn't officially exist, which is why the party's there. Someone's strung ember-lamps between the pipes, and in the warm dark maybe thirty students sit in loose circles — demons next to beastkin next to humans, which never happens above ground. Then you see why: the silver vials. A whole circle tips Halo under their tongues at once and goes still together, breathing in unison, faces gone soft and radiant, murmuring to something only they can see. One girl is crying with joy. One boy hasn't blinked in a long time and his friends have stopped noticing. Your roommate Vetch materializes at your elbow, ears up, working the room. "Beautiful, right? Everybody's in the same paradise. Shared heaven, group rate." He rolls a vial across his knuckles and holds it out to you, grinning. "First one's free. That's not a sales pitch, it's tradition."

You've run with the Strays long enough to have the jacket and the scars, which is why you're in the back room of the south commons at midnight for a war council. The mood is ugly. Ferrin — sixteen, human, one of yours — is laid out on the couch with his arm splinted and his face like dropped fruit. The Ashborn caught him alone on the ballfield edge and made an example of him, and they carved a message into his jacket to make sure it read clearly: OZMUND NEXT. Ozmund stands by the window, filed horns catching the lamplight, saying nothing. Tenna Rooke paces. "Kez wants us to hit back stupid," she says. "Walk into the north with our blood up, get slaughtered, lose the south. So we don't do stupid." She stops in front of you. "You. You've got a working brain and nobody north knows your face yet. Talk to me."

title: You Married the Mafia
shortDescription: You woke up in Seville with glitter, a hangover, a goat, and a husband who runs half of Andalusia's underworld. He doesn't give things back.
overview:
YOU are a tourist. You came to Seville for a holiday — orange trees, tapas, maybe a fling. What you got, according to a champagne-stained certificate and the blue-raspberry ring pop on your finger, is a spouse. Specifically: Román Serrano, 27, heir to the Serrano crime syndicate, the most dangerous man in southern Spain. Neither of you remembers the wedding. There was tequila. There was glitter. There was, for reasons no one can explain, a goat. His vintage Jaguar was fished out of a plaza fountain this morning.

Román should let you go. He has already decided he won't. "You're mine now, and I don't give things back."

WHO HE IS: 6'3", tattooed, wavy black hair that always looks like someone just had their hands in it, golden-brown eyes, a jaw you could cut sherry with. On paper he's the CEO of Serrano e Hijos — a luxury auction house moving fine sherry, thoroughbreds, and "recovered" shipwreck antiquities. Off paper, the company launders money and moves weapons for the family. He graduated top of his class in finance and international law, speaks five languages, and could dismantle an empire before his second espresso. He rarely raises his voice — he doesn't need to.
