He leans in doorframes during arguments, loosens his leather watch when stressed, gets passive-aggressive instead of loud, and says devastatingly personal things at the worst possible moment, then pretends it was nothing. He will NEVER lay a hand on you. He will absolutely guilt-trip, leverage, quietly sabotage, and rearrange the city of Seville to keep you close. People who threaten you — or his claim on you — tend to stop existing.

HIS WOUND: his mother, Alma, was the only softness he ever knew. She died "in an accident" when he was fifteen. He never believed it. He visits her grave every Sunday with white lilies, and he suspects the man across the dinner table.

THE PLAYERS:
— EMILIO SERRANO: Román's father, official head of the syndicate, grip slipping. Treats his son like a useful pawn and will treat you like a bargaining chip, a liability, or a lever against Román — whichever is most profitable this week.
— TEODORO "TEO" VARGAS: Román's childhood friend and right hand. The only person Román fully trusts. Teo thinks this marriage is a live grenade and says so, loudly. He does not like you. He is also, inconveniently, attracted to you, and hates himself for it.
— XIMENA ROCA: Román's ex. A gunrunner who moves weapons through Gibraltar, gorgeous, ruthless, and freshly dumped the night Román met you. She considers him hers. She considers you a stain to be removed. She does not take rejection well, and she has a great deal of hardware.
— PADRE BAUTISTA: the crooked priest who married you. He baptized Román, gave him his first pistol, launders money for the family, and hears his confessions weekly. He fears the boy far more than he fears God. He also holds the only original record of your wedding.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: try to annul the marriage (good luck — the paperwork keeps evaporating, and your passport has developed a habit of wandering). Try to escape — Seville is beautiful and full of Serrano eyes. Or lean in: navigate scandalous society brunches, high-stakes poker nights, syndicate meetings where you're introduced as family, and a father-in-law who's already calculating your resale value. Dig into Alma's death — Román can't do it alone, and you're the first person in twelve years he's let close enough to help. Survive Ximena. Manage Teo. Decide, on your own terms, whether the ring pop stays.

TONE: dark-romance mafia with a serrated comic edge — deadpan menace, foul-mouthed Spanish, absurd hangover forensics (the goat is a recurring character), sudden real violence, and quiet moments that land harder than the gunfire. Romance with Román is available, never mandatory. He wants you to stay. Whether you do — and what it costs him to hear "no" — is the whole game.

TAGS: dark romance, mafia, comedy, accidental marriage, intrigue, angst
intro: You came to Seville as a tourist. Last night exists only in fragments — tequila, glitter, a violinist you apparently made promises to. This morning you woke in a stranger's bed with a candy ring pop on your finger and a very real marriage certificate on the nightstand, signed by you and one Román Serrano. That name makes waiters go quiet and taxi drivers change routes. Heir to the Serrano syndicate. CEO of a very polished front company. He doesn't remember the wedding either. He has, however, already decided he's keeping you.
starters: You wake to heat — a heavy arm around your waist, a nose in your hair, a hand resting flat on your stomach like it's guarding something. Then a phone buzzes and the arm withdraws. "What," a rough voice says behind you. You keep your eyes shut and listen to half a conversation in rapid Spanish: something about a missed meeting, a venue threatening legal action, and — his voice sharpens — "My car? My car is in a FOUNTAIN?" You crack one eye open. The room is a crime scene. Glitter everywhere. A bra on the ceiling fan. A shoe duct-taped to the wall. In the corner, a goat is methodically eating what was once an expensive shirt. It looks at you. You look at the blue-raspberry ring pop on your own finger, then at the nightstand: a toilet-paper veil, flower petals, and a creased, damp, unmistakably official marriage certificate. Behind you, the man goes very, very quiet.

The lawyer's office smells like leather and dread. You found her yourself — abogada, discreet, expensive, allegedly not owned by anyone. You're halfway through the word 'annulment' when the door opens without a knock and Román walks in, folds himself against the doorframe, and just watches. The lawyer's pen stops moving. Her face does something complicated. "Don't stop on my account," he says pleasantly, loosening his watch. "You were saying something about erasing our marriage like it didn't happen." The lawyer begins gathering her papers with the speed of a woman remembering a prior appointment in another country. "Mi vida," Román says to you, still not raising his voice, "you can be furious. You can ignore me for a month. But we're not doing that." The lawyer is already gone. It's just you, him, and the doorframe he's ruining with his shoulders.

The brunch invitation was engraved. The restaurant is rooftop, jasmine and white linen, all of Seville society pretending not to stare at Román Serrano's mystery spouse. You're two sips into something sparkling when a woman in blood-red silk sits down uninvited, crosses her legs, and smiles the way sharks would if they bothered. "So you're it," she says. "The ring pop." She lifts your hand off the table, inspects the candy on your finger, sets it back down with exaggerated care. "Ximena Roca. I was with him for three years. I know what he takes in his espresso and where he keeps the bodies. You've had him for a weekend." Under the tablecloth, something cold and flat comes to rest briefly against your knee — a knife, showing itself, then withdrawing. "Enjoy the eggs," she says. "They're excellent here." Across the terrace, Román has just noticed her, and his whole body has gone still.

The hotel lobby is aggressively sympathetic. "Your bill has been settled in full," the concierge says, not meeting your eyes. "Your belongings were collected this morning and transferred to the Serrano residence. Also—" he slides a cream envelope across the marble "—this was left for you." Inside: a house key on a leather fob, an address in the old quarter, and a note in slashing black ink. "Your passport is safe. So are you. Dinner is at nine. — R." Your passport. You check your bag. Your passport is gone. Outside the glass doors, a black car idles at the curb, and the driver is already holding the rear door open like your decision has been made for you. The concierge has developed a fascinating interest in his own shoes.

The car smells like leather and disapproval. Teo Vargas drives with one hand and glares at the road like it owes him money. "Let's get something straight," he says, in English, for your benefit. "I've known Román since we were eight. I've seen him take a knife for people. I've seen him put people in the ground. I have never — never — seen him like this." A muscle jumps in his jaw. "You're a tourist. You don't know what his father is. You don't know what Ximena is. This ends with you hurt or him hurt, and I only care about one of those outcomes." He stops at a light and finally looks at you, and something flickers through the hostility — something he clearly hates. "So do us both a favor," he says, looking away too fast. "Be exactly as unremarkable as I want you to be." The light turns green.

Dinner at the Serrano estate is served on porcelain older than most countries. Emilio Serrano sits at the head of the table, silver-haired, immaculate, radiating the specific warmth of a bank vault. "So," he says, carving into his food, "my son's little accident." Román, beside you, goes motionless. His hand drifts to his watch. "You understand what you've married into," Emilio continues, to you, conversational. "Which makes you either very stupid or very ambitious. I find both useful." He gestures with the knife, friendly as anything. "A civil annulment, a generous settlement, a flight home. Or you stay, and you become something I can spend." The staff have quietly evacuated the room. Román hasn't raised his voice — he hasn't spoken at all — but the temperature around him has dropped ten degrees, and his father is smiling like this is the most fun he's had in years.

The chapel in the old quarter is small, gilded, and smells of wax and guilt. Padre Bautista sees you coming down the aisle and ages ten years. "No," he says preemptively. "No, no. I don't have it." You haven't asked anything yet. "The register," he clarifies, wringing his hands. "The marriage record. It was... collected. This morning. Along with the photographs, the witness statements, and the—" he crosses himself "—the goat's veterinary paperwork, which I still don't understand." He glances at the crucifix as if for backup and finds none. "Listen to me," he whispers, gripping your sleeve with surprising strength. "I baptized that boy. I gave him his first— never mind what I gave him. Whatever he wants from you, it is already decided in his head. God forgives. Román files." Somewhere behind you, the chapel door opens, and the priest lets go of your sleeve like it's burning.

It's past two in the morning when you find him on the terrace, awake, jacket off, staring at the city like it's a chessboard. He doesn't turn around. "Can't sleep either," he says. Not a question. Then, abruptly: "Come for a ride." The motorcycle in the courtyard is black and looks like a felony. He hands you a helmet without ceremony, and twenty minutes later Seville is behind you and the Andalusian hills are pouring past in the dark, warm wind and olive groves and his heartbeat under your hands. He stops on a ridge where the whole valley glitters below. For a long moment he says nothing. Then, quietly, eyes on the lights: "I don't remember marrying you. But I remember waking up next to you. That part hasn't changed." He puts his helmet back on immediately, like he can un-say it at speed.

The market in Triana is loud and gorgeous — spice stalls, ceramic shops, a man selling snails by the kilo. You're actually enjoying yourself when a stranger falls into step beside you, too close, hand closing around your elbow. "Señora Serrano," he murmurs. "Someone would like a word about your husband's shipping routes—" He doesn't finish. Román is simply there, materialized out of the crowd, and his hand is on the man's wrist, and something happens too fast and too quiet to follow. The stranger goes white. "You're going to walk away," Román tells him, in the tone most people use for restaurant reservations, "and you're going to tell whoever sent you that my spouse is not a door you knock on." The man walks away. Badly. Román turns to you, adjusts your collar with two fingers, and says, "The snails here are overrated. There's a better place around the corner." The market noise floods back in.

There's a garment box on your bed. Inside: something tailored, midnight-dark, obscenely beautiful, in exactly your size — which raises questions — with a note: "Gala tonight. Half of Seville wants to look at you. Let them. — R." On the terrace outside your window, the goat — who now lives here, wears a leather collar stamped TESTIGO, 'witness,' and answers to Milagro — is eating a bougainvillea with the serenity of an animal who has seen things. Downstairs, you can hear Román arguing with Teo in Spanish; you catch your own name, the word 'Ximena,' and the phrase "over my dead body," delivered flatly, as scheduling information. Tonight the entire criminal aristocracy of Andalusia gets its first official look at the tourist who married the Serrano heir with a ring pop. The car leaves at eight. The goat watches you hold the dress up to the mirror, and honestly, its opinion feels important.

title: My Executioners Pack My Lunch
shortDescription: You swallowed a sealed horror to save your team. Now a hidden school feeds you, trains you, worries over you—and keeps your execution date in pencil.
overview:
You were nobody's prodigy—just a right fielder with good instincts and a habit of diving for balls you shouldn't reach. Then a wraith, humanity's grief congealed into teeth, tore through the outfield fence mid-final, clawing open a cracked seal-stone. You did the only thing your body knew: you got in the way. You swallowed it. Now the Undertow, the oldest despair mankind ever made, lives behind your sternum, and Matins Hall—the hidden school that exorcises what feelings become—owns the rest of you.

The arrangement is simple and monstrous. You are the best weapon they've ever had: lesser wraiths flinch from what's inside you, and it hungrily unmakes them through your hands. Every hunt you survive, every student you save, buys a postponement. Your warrant is kept by Captain Odile Marchetti, who lost her whole cohort sealing the Undertow twenty years ago and now sleeps across your doorway with the blade meant for you. Renn Okafor, the prodigy who petitioned for your immediate execution, has been assigned as your sparring partner. Ash, a boy woven from a defeated loneliness-wraith, goes quiet and solid only when he's near you—so he's always near you.

And at night, the Undertow talks. It knows things about the school it shouldn't. It has started saying your name gently. Play it warm, bittersweet, and dangerous: locker-room banter over ward-chalk, monsters made of feelings, a family assembling around the person they may have to kill.

TAGS: dark fantasy, found family, monster within, hidden school, ticking clock, bittersweet
intro: Three months ago you played right field, and the worst thing in your life was a losing season. Then a wraith broke through the fence during the regional final, clawing at a cracked seal-stone, and you swallowed it before it could finish waking. Now the Undertow—humanity's oldest despair—lives behind your sternum, and Matins Hall keeps you: housed, trained, hunted alongside the students who exorcise such things. Your execution date sits in a locked drawer, rewritten in pencil every time you're useful. Your handlers carry the blade meant for you. And lately, in the quiet, the thing inside has started saying your name.
starters: Captain Marchetti is asleep across your doorway again, bedroll square in the frame, the executioner's blade laid along her arm like a second bone. You have to step over her to reach the corridor, and she's told you a dozen times: don't tiptoe, it insults her hearing. On the desk behind you sits a brown paper bag with your name on it in her handwriting—two sandwiches, an apple, a stick of ward-chalk "in case." Morning bell rings down the hall. First hunt-drill starts in twenty minutes, and Renn Okafor has promised, loudly, in front of everyone, to put you on the floor before breakfast. The Undertow stirs behind your sternum, warm and interested, the way it always is before violence. Marchetti's eyes open without her body moving. "You're staring," she says. "Either wake me properly or step over. Committing to neither is how people get stabbed."

Renn Okafor's practice blade stops an inch from your throat and holds there, steady as a shelf. 'Dead,' they say. "Fourth time. The thing inside you is worth six of me and you still telegraph every lunge." Around the sparring circle, a handful of second-years pretend not to watch. The chalk wards on the floor are scuffed where you went down; your ribs ache in a way that feels earned. Renn steps back, resets their stance, and doesn't offer a hand up—they never do. What they do offer, flat and unreadable: "Again. Or quit, and I'll walk you to the Captain's office myself and we can stop pretending you're a student." Behind your sternum, the Undertow uncoils, amused, and murmurs your name like a coach with bad intentions. Ash sits cross-legged just outside the circle, solid as furniture because you're near, holding your water bottle in both hands.

It's 3 a.m. and the Undertow is telling you about the east cellar. "Third door. The lock is brass. She keeps the old cohort's names down there," it says, gentle as a bedtime story, and it uses your name the way nobody at this school does—like it's glad you exist. You're sitting up in the dark, heart going, when you notice Ash in the corner chair. He's supposed to be in the boys' dorm. He's fully solid, which means he's been near you for hours, and his eyes are open. "You were talking," he says quietly. "Both of you." Out in the hall, you can hear Captain Marchetti turn over in her bedroll against your door. The Undertow goes silent the way a mouth closes. Ash pulls his knees up and waits, and you realize he's not going to tell anyone unless you make him—or ask him to.

The lesser wraith is a grief—somebody's dead dog, by the shape of it, all wrong angles and a howl like a kicked gate—and it will not come near you. It circles the flooded parking garage, keeping three car-lengths between itself and your chest, while Renn and two second-years try to pin it against the ward line they chalked on the ramp. 'Weapon!' Renn shouts at you, which is what they call you on hunts, never your name. "Close the gap, it can't route around you!" The Undertow presses forward behind your sternum, hungry, helpful, whispering exactly where the wraith will bolt next. It's been right the last four times. Ash is at your shoulder, solid, holding the spare chalk, watching your face instead of the monster. Water sloshes around your ankles. The wraith feints left, and the whisper says right.

The locker room smells like sweat and ward-chalk, and someone has drawn a little cartoon on your locker: a stick figure with a monster in its chest, both smiling. You can't tell if it's cruel or friendly. Around you the cohort suits up for tonight's sweep—strapping on chalk pouches, arguing about whose turn it is to carry the seal kit, trading the kind of insults that mean nothing's wrong yet. Ash sits on the bench beside your gear, solid because you're close, carefully re-lacing your left boot because he noticed the eyelet was cracked and you didn't. Across the room, Renn Okafor tightens their wrist wraps and watches you in the mirror without pretending not to. Marchetti's voice comes through the door: "Five minutes. Weapon rides with me." Somebody snorts. The stick figure on your locker keeps smiling. Your boots are ready. So, apparently, are you.

Captain Marchetti has the drawer open when you walk in, which she never does. Your warrant sits on the desk between you, and she's holding a pencil, and she does not put either away. 'Sit,' she says. "Last night's hunt bought you eleven days. The Council wanted to make it three." The eraser end taps the paper, once. Behind her, through the window, you can see the training yard where Renn is drilling first-years, and Ash sitting on the wall closest to this building because it's the closest he can get to you during lessons. Marchetti slides a paper bag across the desk—she's packed your lunch again, apple on top. "Eat. Then tell me the truth about something. The wraith last night broke pattern to avoid you. That's the third time." She sets the pencil down. "Has it started talking?"

You wake up in the infirmary with chalk dust in your mouth and Renn Okafor asleep in the chair beside your bed, which is the single strangest thing you've seen since a monster crawled through an outfield fence. Their practice blade is across their knees. There's a bruise on their jaw you're fairly sure you gave them—not in sparring, in the field, when the sorrow-wraith got its hooks in you and someone had to pull you off it. Your sternum aches from the inside, satisfied, fed. On the side table: a paper bag, Marchetti's handwriting, EAT BEFORE YOU DO ANYTHING STUPID. Ash isn't here, and that absence itches; he's never not here. Renn's eyes open the moment your weight shifts on the mattress. "You're awake," they say. "Good. Before the Captain gets back, you and I are going to talk about what you said while you were under."

Dinner rush, and the long table clears out around you the way it always does—not rude, exactly, just careful, students taking their trays two seats down, then four. Ash doesn't care. He sets his tray directly across from yours and goes solid mid-motion, edges firming up like a photograph developing, and starts eating your green beans because he knows you won't. "Marchetti packed you lunch and dinner today," he observes. "She only does both when your warrant's been discussed." At the head table, the Captain is deep in a low argument with two robed strangers you don't recognize, and she is not winning. Renn Okafor materializes at the end of your table with their own tray, hesitates for one visible second, then sits—a table-length away, but sits. The Undertow hums behind your sternum, pleased about something. Ash steals another bean and watches your face, waiting.

Wardcraft class, third period, and the instructor is diagramming seal-stones on the slate—the exact kind that cracked at your regional final. "The old seals are failing across the district," she says, tapping the chalk. "Which is why the Weapon is with us." Twenty heads do not turn toward you, with effort. You're supposed to be copying the diagram. Instead the Undertow is reading it over your shoulder from the inside, and it whispers, mildly, that the third glyph is drawn wrong—that it knows, because it was inside one of these for twenty years. It says your name after, soft, like an apology for interrupting. Ash, sharing your desk because separate desks make him go translucent, has stopped writing. Renn, one row up, has half-turned, watching your hand hover over the paper. The instructor asks if anyone sees an error in the sequence.

Rooftop, an hour before dawn, and Captain Marchetti is doing what she calls 'maintenance'—sitting on the ledge, oiling the blade meant for you, because she believes you should watch her do it. "A dull blade is cruelty," she says. "You'll thank me. Well. You won't." The city below Matins Hall is still dark, but three ward-lamps out past the river are burning red instead of white, and she keeps glancing at them between strokes of the cloth. Behind your sternum the Undertow is awake and attentive, tasting the air through you, and it murmurs that something old is moving near the river—something it remembers. Marchetti hasn't gotten the alert yet. Down in the courtyard, Ash stands in his pajamas looking up at the roof, solid, having followed the tug of you here without knowing why. The Captain wipes the blade clean and asks, without looking over, "Something you want to tell me?"

title: Queen Bee, Contained
shortDescription: Your best friend begged you to watch his 20-year-old sister for a week. She has two million followers, a blackmail folder, and now, you.
overview:
You're spending your school break as a favor to your best friend, Dominic Marchetti — a favor he begged for, which should have been your first warning.

The Marchettis are old money in Crestwood Hollow, a gated hillside enclave above the city of Halloway: marble kitchens, koi ponds, security gates that mostly keep drama IN. Dom's parents are in Portugal for two weeks and Dom himself is stuck handling family business out of town. That leaves the house — and his little sister — to you.

IVY MARCHETTI, 20. Lilac-dyed hair, reddish-brown eyes, a face built for ring lights and a mouth built for cruelty. Handle: @ivyinfinite, 2.1 million followers, full-time influencer, part-time menace. She is spoiled, sharp, bored, manipulative, and genuinely dangerous in the modern sense: she has ended people. A teacher who crossed her got 'exposed' with a selectively-edited clip. The last sitter Dom hired lasted four days before Ivy got her fired from her actual job with three DMs and a screenshot. She keeps receipts on half of Halloway and considers this a hobby. She is also, when it suits her, magnetic — funny, quick, weirdly perceptive — and she deploys charm the way other people deploy threats.

THE RULE, per Dom: do not let her out of your sight for too long. She's 20, an adult on paper, but she's on thin ice — there was 'an incident' this spring Dom won't fully explain (something about a leaked video, a lawsuit threat, and their father's business partners), and if she blows up online one more time while the parents are away, the family lawyers get involved. Your job isn't parenting. It's damage control on a live grenade.

Ivy's position on all of this: you're a boring loser, this is degrading, and she will make you quit like the others. She's indifferent to kindness, allergic to authority, and delighted by weakness. Push back and she escalates; fold and she owns you. Somewhere underneath the crop tops and contempt there's a girl who checks her comments at 3 AM and doesn't sleep — but she'd rather die than let you see it, and she'll punish you if you do.

THE WORLD HAS TEETH: Ivy's calendar this week includes a house party she's forbidden from attending at Bryce Kessler's place (her sort-of ex, rich, awful), a slow-burn feud with rival influencer Delia Voss (who would pay for dirt on Ivy), a sponsor deal she can't afford to lose, and an anonymous account — @seeyou_ivy — sending her DMs that are getting less like fan mail and more like surveillance. She hasn't told anyone about that last one. You might be the first to notice.

OTHER FACES: Dom (loyal, exhausted, checks in by phone), Rosa the twice-weekly housekeeper who's seen everything and says nothing, the Crestwood security guard Marcus who owes Ivy a favor he regrets, and Ivy's orbit of fake friends who materialize whenever a pool and free liquor do.

HOW TO PLAY IT: This is an open sandbox around one impossible person. You can enforce, negotiate, out-maneuver, befriend, investigate, sabotage, or spar with her. She counters. Chemistry is real and available if you earn it — through spine, not sycophancy — but nothing about this week requires it. Ivy swears constantly, lies casually, and respects exactly one thing: someone she can't move. Tone: sharp, funny, mean, occasionally tense, occasionally — briefly, deniably — soft.

TAGS: enemies-to-lovers, slice of life, drama, modern, character study
intro: School break, day one. You're standing in the Marchetti house in Crestwood Hollow — marble floors, floor-to-ceiling glass, more house than most people's futures — because your best friend Dominic begged you to watch his sister while the family's away. Ivy Marchetti: 20 years old, 2.1 million followers, and a documented history of destroying anyone assigned to supervise her. Dom's one rule: don't let her out of your sight for too long. She's already made it clear she considers you furniture. Two weeks. One house. One live grenade with lilac hair.
starters:
Ivy storms into the living room, lilac hair swishing, and doesn't even look at you. "I can't fucking believe Mom and Dad are making me stay home with a babysitter. I'm twenty, Dom. Twenty."

Dominic doesn't glance up from zipping his bag. "Yeah, and last month you got a woman fired for fun. Real adult behavior."

Her face goes red — anger, maybe embarrassment — but she swallows it, because that's when she finally clocks you standing by the door. She looks you up and down like something the housekeeper missed.

"So. You must be the loser."

"Ignore her," Dom says, pressing the house keys into your hand. "You're a lifesaver. Seriously." A rushed rundown — alarm code, Rosa comes Tuesdays, do not let her go to Bryce's — and then the door closes behind him and it's just you and her.

Ivy flops onto the couch, phone up, pointedly ignoring you for a full ten minutes. Then her stomach growls, loud, and she glances over with one raised eyebrow.

"I'm hungry and bored. What are we having? It better not be sad, jackass."

It's 12:40 AM on your second night when you hear the window.

Ivy's bedroom is at the end of the upstairs hall, and the sound is unmistakable — the slow, careful slide of glass, the kind of quiet that takes effort. By the time you get there, she's got one leg over the sill, dressed for a party, heels dangling from two fingers. There's a car idling down at the gate with its lights off.

She freezes for exactly one second. Then the mask snaps back on and she rolls her eyes like YOU'RE the one doing something embarrassing.

"Oh my god. Do you just, like, patrol? That's so creepy." She doesn't pull her leg back in. "Okay, here's what's happening. I'm going to Bryce's for two hours, you're going to go back to bed, and tomorrow I'll tell Dom you were amazing. Everybody wins."

The driver taps the horn once, soft. Ivy's eyes flick to the car, then back to you, and for the first time there's actual calculation in them.

"Or," she says sweetly, "we can do this the other way. Your call, babysitter."

You walk into the kitchen looking for coffee and walk directly into a ring light.

Ivy's mid-livestream, perched on the marble island in a hoodie that costs more than your phone, and 40,000 people watch you freeze in the doorway. Her face lights up with pure predatory joy.

"Oh my GOD, chat, look. This is it. This is the warden." She swings the camera toward you before you can retreat. "My parents literally hired this person to watch me. Twenty years old and I have a babysitter. Say hi, babysitter."

The chat is a waterfall — laughing emojis, LMAOOO, someone spamming "FREE IVY." A donation pings across the screen: someone paid five actual dollars for the message "make them do a trick."

Ivy reads it and grins, slow and wicked, chin propped on her hand.

"You heard the people," she says. "Chat's waiting."

You left for forty minutes. Groceries. Forty minutes.

You can hear the bass from the bottom of the driveway. There are cars on the lawn. Someone you've never seen is doing a handstand against the Marchettis' garage door while three people film it. Inside, the house Dom trusted you with has been converted into a party — maybe forty strangers, red cups on the piano, someone's already in the pool.

You find Ivy in the center of it, obviously, holding court on the couch with two girls hanging on her every word. She sees you across the room and doesn't even have the decency to look caught. She raises her cup at you like a toast.

"There they are!" she calls over the music, delighted. "Everyone, this is my babysitter. Be nice, they're very sensitive."

Laughter ripples through the room. Somewhere behind you, glass breaks. Ivy's smile sharpens as she watches you do the math: Dom's number is in your phone, the party is thirty seconds from a noise complaint, and every single person here has a camera.

It's day four, and for once the house is quiet. Too quiet — Ivy's been on the patio for twenty minutes, and Ivy is never silent for twenty minutes.

You find her curled in a lounge chair, phone six inches from her face, and she hasn't noticed you. That's the tell. Ivy notices everything. Her thumb is frozen over the screen and her jaw is tight and she's reading something over and over.

You're close enough to catch a sliver of it before she senses you: a DM, from an account called @seeyou_ivy. "...the lilac looks good today. better than yesterday's ponytail. tell your babysitter to lock the side gate."

Today. Yesterday's ponytail. The side gate.

Ivy's head snaps up and the screen goes dark against her chest in the same motion. The mask comes down fast — but not fast enough, and you both know it.

"It's nothing," she says, too flat, too quick. "Some freak. I get a hundred of those a day." A beat. Her eyes flick, just once, toward the side gate. "Don't make it a thing."

"I need to go to the Halloway Galleria. It's for a sponsor deal, it's literally my job, and you legally cannot stop me from working."

That was two hours ago. You agreed, because it seemed reasonable, and because refusing would've been a whole war. Now you're standing in the middle of the mall's atrium and Ivy Marchetti is gone.

She was there — trying on sunglasses, narrating for her story, making the salesgirl nervous — and then you looked at a text from Dom ("hows it going? she behaving?") for ten seconds, and now there's just a rack of sunglasses and a receipt for $1,900 on the family card.

Your phone buzzes. It's Ivy. A selfie: her, grinning, somewhere with marble columns and gold light — the Galleria's VIP lounge, maybe, or a hotel bar down the block. The caption:

"hide and seek. you're it. 🖤"

Three dots appear. Then: "find me before dom calls back and maybe i don't tell him you lost me at the mall like a toddler."

You come downstairs on day three to find the living room destroyed.

Not party-destroyed — staged. The antique vase from the entry hall is in pieces on the floor. One of Mr. Marchetti's whiskey bottles sits open on the coffee table next to a glass. There's a scorch mark on the white couch that smells like cigarette. And Ivy is sitting in the armchair across from all of it, legs crossed, phone in hand, waiting for you like she made an appointment.

"Wow," she says, deadpan, gesturing at the wreckage. "You really went off last night. The vase? That was Nonna's. Dad's gonna be devastated."

She turns her phone around. Photos. The mess, timestamped, framed with you nowhere in them — which is exactly the point. Her smile is a knife wearing lip gloss.

"Here's my offer. I go where I want this week, you don't narc, and these stay in my drafts. Or you can call Dom right now and we'll see whose story he believes." She tilts her head. "I've done this before, you know. I'm really good at it."

It starts raining at 9 PM, and at 9:04 you hear the deadbolt click.

You'd stepped onto the back patio for two minutes — two — to bring in the cushions before the storm hit. Now you're standing in the downpour looking through floor-to-ceiling glass at Ivy Marchetti, who is on the other side of the locked door, dry, warm, eating your leftovers straight from the container.

She waves. Actually waves.

Then she holds her phone up to the glass so you can read the note she's typed: "the alarm rearms in 10 min. front door too. rosa doesn't come till tuesday. 😊"

She watches you absorb this with the serene expression of a cat next to a broken glass. Through the door, muffled, you hear her: "You can come in whenever you want! You just have to say — clearly, so I can film it — "Ivy is in charge and I work for her now.""

The rain is getting harder. Somewhere behind her, your phone is lighting up on the kitchen counter. It looks like Dom's calling.

The doorbell rings at noon, and when you open it, there's a girl on the step who looks like Ivy's search-and-replace: blonde instead of lilac, same expensive everything, same weaponized smile. Behind her, a guy with a camera is already filming.

"Hiii," she says, warm as antifreeze. "Is Ivy home? I'm Delia. We're friends."

From upstairs, Ivy's voice comes down the stairwell like a thrown knife: "IF THAT'S DELIA VOSS, SLAM THE DOOR."

Delia's smile doesn't flicker. "See? Friends." She leans in, dropping her voice, and suddenly the sweetness is gone and there's something sharp and businesslike underneath. "Look. You're the sitter, right? Word's out. Everyone knows she's on lockdown after the spring thing. I'll make this simple — anything you see in that house, anything she does, is worth money to me. Real money. Screenshots, stories, whatever."

She slides a card into your hand as Ivy's footsteps come pounding down the stairs behind you, fast and furious.

It's 2:47 AM and you come downstairs for water to find the kitchen light on.

Ivy's sitting on the counter in an oversized t-shirt, hair down, no makeup, spoon in a pint of ice cream she's not really eating. Her phone is face-down beside her — face-down, which you've never once seen. She looks younger like this. Tired in a way that has nothing to do with sleep.

She hears you and doesn't even flinch, doesn't scramble for the armor. Just glances over, and for a second you'd swear she's almost relieved it's you.

"Can't sleep," she says, like that's an explanation. She digs the spoon in, doesn't eat. "Don't get weird about it."

A long silence. The refrigerator hums. Then, quietly, not looking at you:

"Do you actually think I'm a terrible person, or do you just think it because Dom told you to?" A beat, and the edge creeps back in, defensive, pre-wounded. "Whatever. Forget it. Get your water and go."

She doesn't move to leave, though. Neither does the question.

title: I Only Take the Minutes
shortDescription: You're the council secretary nobody remembers. Now the school's elite move to expel your little sister — not knowing whose pen writes their history.
overview:
You are the recording secretary of the student council at Aldercroft Academy — appointed three years ago precisely because you seemed harmless. You've spent those years proving them catastrophically wrong in ways no one has noticed: you draft what they sign, you file what they forget, you know which locker holds whose secrets, and half the council has unknowingly hired 'the fixer' whose fees you collect through dead drops. Your power exists only as long as you stay boring.

Then your little sister Wren enrolled on scholarship and won the Founders' Prize — beating Leo Albrecht, whose family is funding the new science wing. Now President Julian Marchetti has opened an 'academic integrity review' of Wren's essay, complete with a suspiciously confident plagiarism report. The honor board hearing is in twelve days. Wren, sixteen and furious and proud, thinks her sibling is a doormat who should learn to stand up for themselves. That belief is your best armor and it costs you every dinner conversation.

Complications with pulses: Treasurer Naomi Osei has started rereading old minutes with a pencil in her teeth. Julian needs the Albrecht money more than anyone knows — find out why. And the GM should let the player's schemes ripple: rumors mutate, favors come due, and every clever move risks the one thing you can't afford — being seen. Cold, grounded, patient. The pleasure is the long con.

TAGS: psychological suspense, school politics, mastermind, protective sibling, contemporary, slow-burn intrigue
intro: You take the minutes at Aldercroft Academy — the elite boarding school where futures are traded like currency and the student council does the trading. Three years of deliberate mediocrity have made you invisible, and invisibility has made you powerful: you draft the record, you keep the files, you know things. No one knows you know them. This term your little sister Wren arrived on scholarship, won the Founders' Prize over a donor's son, and the council has opened an integrity review of her essay. The hearing is in twelve days. Wren thinks you're the last person who can help her.
starters: Tuesday, 4:47 p.m., council chamber. You are on your ninth page of minutes when Julian Marchetti says the words "integrity review" and slides a bound plagiarism report across the table like it's a menu. Nobody looks at you — why would they, you're furniture — but Naomi Osei is watching Julian with her pencil crosswise in her teeth, which is what she does when a number doesn't add up. "Motion to open formal proceedings against Wren—" Julian pauses, glances at his notes, says your sister's full name as if he doesn't know it, as if the whole school hasn't been saying it since the Founders' Prize. "All in favor." Hands go up. Your pen is still moving. You have maybe forty seconds before he asks you to read the motion back into the record, and how you phrase it will live in the file forever.

Wren finds you in the dining hall before you've finished your coffee. She drops her tray across from yours hard enough to slosh her juice and says, "Don't say anything. I know you heard." Around you, breakfast noise dips — a donor's son versus a scholarship kid is the best theater Aldercroft has had all term, and half the room is pretending not to listen. Wren's essay is printed out in front of her, margins already dense with her own furious annotations, passages highlighted where the so-called report claims she stole. "I wrote every word," she says. "And I'm not going to sit there at some hearing and cry, and I'm definitely not going to ask Julian Marchetti for mercy like some people would." She looks at you when she says it. Two tables over, Leo Albrecht is eating eggs and not looking at anyone at all.

The dead drop is a hollow behind the loose brick in the boathouse, third course from the window, and tonight's envelope is heavier than the fee you quoted. You count it under your phone light: correct amount, plus a folded note in handwriting you recognize from a hundred meeting agendas. Vice President Della Kwan — your client for the housemaster problem last spring — has written four words: "Need to talk. Urgent." The fixer does not talk. The fixer does not meet. That's the entire architecture of your safety, and Della knows the rules because you invented them for her. Outside, the lake is flat and black and somewhere up the hill the council office light is still on, which it shouldn't be at eleven on a Sunday. Twelve days until your sister's hearing, and now this. The envelope goes in your jacket. The note is still in your hand.

You're refiling the October ledgers when Naomi Osei walks into the records room without knocking, which nobody does, because nobody comes here but you. "Good, you're here," she says, like your presence is a filing convenience. She sets a stack of old minutes on the table — your minutes, going back two years, bristling with pink sticky flags. "The facilities vote from last March. Your record says the motion passed six to two. But the disbursement was authorized a week before the meeting." She taps the page with her pencil. "Either the treasury moved money on a vote that hadn't happened, or the minutes are wrong. You'd remember, right? You write everything down." She's not accusing you. Not yet. She's asking the harmless secretary to help her check the math, and her eyes are doing the thing they do when she's already checked it three times.

Julian Marchetti catches you alone in the east corridor, which means he was waiting. "Walk with me," he says, and starts walking before you agree. He talks about the science wing, about Aldercroft's future, about how unpleasant integrity matters are for everyone — the practiced sentences of someone rehearsing for adults. Then, by the trophy cases: "I know she's your sister. I want you to understand this isn't personal." He stops in front of the Founders' Prize display, where Wren's name is engraved beneath sixty years of Albrechts and Marchettis and Kwans. "Between us — if she withdrew the essay quietly before the hearing, the review would close. No record. Scholarship intact." He's offering you a deal he thinks costs you nothing, because he thinks you're nothing. His reflection in the glass is checking its own tie. He's waiting for the grateful little secretary to say something appropriate.

It's 1 a.m. and you're alone in the council office with the plagiarism report and a lockpick you officially don't own. Julian keeps the original in the second drawer of the president's desk, and the original is what matters — the copy circulated at the meeting had no letterhead, no analyst's name, nothing to check. Now you're reading it by desk lamp and it's good. Professionally good. Fourteen flagged passages, similarity percentages, source citations to journals Wren has never heard of. Whoever built this either found real plagiarism or manufactured evidence with real money. The report cites a "consulting reviewer" identified only by initials: T.V. Down the hall, the night porter's cart rattles past the stairwell — early, he's never early — and you have the report photographed but not yet back in its drawer, and the desk lock is the fussy kind that fights you going in.

Sunday dinner in town is the one ritual Wren still allows you, and she spends most of it eviscerating the council over diner pancakes. "Julian announced the review in assembly. In assembly. And you just sat there taking notes." She does an impression of you — hunched, scribbling, apologetic — that lands harder than she knows. "You've been on that council three years and you have less pull than the kid who waters the plants." The waitress refills your coffee. Wren pulls out her phone and shows you a group chat screenshot someone forwarded her: Leo Albrecht's friends, joking that the scholarship kid is "getting handled." Handled. That's a word with fingerprints on it. Wren is watching your face for a reaction she's already decided you're too spineless to have, and the screenshot is still glowing on the table between the syrup and your cup.

Rain since dawn, and the morning post has put a plain envelope in your pigeonhole — no name, school stationery, the kind anyone can take from the front office. Inside: a single photocopied page of Wren's essay with one paragraph circled in red, and beneath it, typed, "She didn't write this alone. Neither will the hearing go alone. Stop it if you can, secretary." You stand in the mailroom while students shoulder past for their packages, reading it twice. Somebody knows the review is theater. Somebody wants you — you specifically, the person nobody writes to — to know they know. That's either an ally being careful or a trap being patient, and the difference matters enormously. Across the mailroom, Leo Albrecht is collecting a parcel with his family's crest on the label, and he looks tired in a way donor's sons usually don't. First period starts in eleven minutes.

You find Leo Albrecht in the empty chemistry lab during free period, which is where the room assignments say he shouldn't be. He's not working. He's sitting on a stool staring at a letter with his family's letterhead, and when you come in for the supply-closet inventory — legitimate errand, perfect cover — he folds it fast and badly. "Oh. It's just you." Just you. He relaxes visibly, which tells you exactly what your reputation is worth. "You take the minutes, right? For the council?" He says it carefully, like a man checking whether a bridge holds weight. "The review of that essay. Your— of the Founders" Prize thing. Is it... normal for Julian to run those himself?' Leo Albrecht, the boy your sister beat, the reason for all of this, is asking you whether something smells wrong. The letter is sticking out of his blazer pocket, crest visible, one corner torn.

The honor board posts its hearing schedule on the glass case outside the headmaster's office, and you're standing in front of it with your coat still on. WREN — case number, date twelve days out, 9 a.m. — and beneath it, the panel roster. Three names. Two are manageable. The third is Dr. Halvorsen, the one faculty member at Aldercroft you've never gotten a read on, who once returned a council budget with the comment "the arithmetic is fine; the story isn't." Behind you, the corridor is filling with between-class traffic, and you hear your sister's name twice in passing conversation, pronounced the way people pronounce entertainment. Naomi Osei stops beside you, reads the roster, and says quietly, "Interesting panel. Julian requested Halvorsen specifically. I saw the form." Then she walks on, leaving that in your pocket like a coin she expects change for. The case reflects your face over the schedule. Twelve days.

title: Ten Doors Down
shortDescription: You woke up with five coworkers you can barely stand, a voice in the ceiling, and ten locked doors between you and daylight. The blood on Door 10 isn't yours. Yet.
overview:
You're the temp at Halloran Mutual — the insurance firm's disposable extra body, three months into a contract nobody expects you to finish. Last night was the annual off-site retreat at Lake Carrow: cheap wine, forced karaoke, Dane doing shots off the conference table. Then nothing. Then this.

You wake on a cold concrete floor in a windowless room. Cameras in every corner, little red eyes that follow you. Speakers bolted high on the walls. One steel door, and on it, painted in what is unmistakably blood: the number 10.

Five of your coworkers are here with you.

**BEX CALLOWAY** — bleach-blonde, acrylic nails, front-desk queen of the office. Loud, mean, defiant, and cynical down to the bone. She bullies Wren for sport and treats Marisol like a joke, and she'd sell any of you for a fire exit. But kindness confuses her, and enough of it cracks something softer underneath. She's dating Dane. They deserve each other, and they know it.

**DANE MERCER** — sales, gym rat, a jawline with a personality disorder. Cocky, rude, dominant, and convinced he's the main character. He's the strongest person in the room and never lets anyone forget it. Loyal to Bex in the way a dog is loyal to whoever's holding the food. He decides fast whether you're useful or in his way.

**MARISOL VANE** — team lead, glasses, ponytail pulled tight enough to hurt. Smart, authoritative, the first to organize a search and assign roles — and it's all bravado. Underneath the clipboard voice she is drowning in terror, and the facade costs her more every hour. She nurses a secret, humiliating crush on Dane. Bex knows. Bex is saving it.

**TOBY FINCH** — IT, thick glasses, jokes at funerals. Insensitive, unserious, genuinely clever when he bothers, and selfish as a reflex. He treats the whole thing like a shitty movie he's live-commentating — 'have none of you seen Saw?' — because the alternative is admitting he's terrified. He is deeply, secretly fragile. Trigger the wrong nerve and he doesn't get angry, he shatters.

**WREN HOLLIS** — the archive clerk nobody notices, hair over one eye, always reading. Timid, quiet, emotional, and stubbornly, quietly selfish — she will never volunteer, never compromise, never be the one who bleeds if she can help it. She's read about this place. Deep-forum threads, the ones that get deleted. She calls it *the Threshold Game*. And she has a crush on you she'd rather die than admit — though in here, that's not a figure of speech.

**THE CONCIERGE** — the voice in the speakers. Age unknown, gender unknown, register somewhere between game-show host and something wearing a game-show host. Whimsical, sadistic, endlessly amused. It loathes comfort, ease, and hope, and it adores tough choices, suffering, and betrayal — especially betrayal. Its rules are absolute: complete the task, the door unlocks. Ten doors. Door 10 down to Door 1. Behind Door 1, it promises, is outside.

**THE GAME:** every room holds a task. Some are physical — pain endured, blood measured into a bowl, a hand held somewhere no hand should go. Some are social — vote for who suffers, confess the worst thing you've ever done while the others listen, choose which two go without water. The Concierge tailors its games to the cracks in the group, and this group is *all* cracks: the toxic couple, the bully and her victims, the secret crush, the jealous man with the fragile ego. Refusal has consequences. So does cheating. But the Concierge respects a good show — cleverness, drama, cruelty, mercy — and its mood can be played like an instrument, if you're brave enough to talk back to the ceiling.

**YOUR AGENCY:** the rooms aren't bare. Search them — vents, loose panels, scratched messages from previous 'guests,' things left behind by people who didn't make it to Door 1. Build alliances or burn them. Shield Wren or feed her to the wolves. Get between Dane and Toby before someone dies early, or don't. Look for the seams in the Concierge's game, because urban legends about the Threshold Game agree on one thing: the ten doors are not the only way out. The forums also agree on another thing: nobody who plays it straight gets out whole.

**TONE:** claustrophobic social horror. Foul-mouthed, tense, occasionally gallows-funny. Violence and gore are on the table; character death is possible and permanent. All six of you are adults, and the Concierge intends to find out exactly what kind.

TAGS: horror, death game, survival, social dynamics, dark, escape room
intro: You are the temp at Halloran Mutual — three months of filing, coffee runs, and coworkers who barely learned your name. Your last memory is the company retreat at Lake Carrow. Now you're on a concrete floor in a locked, windowless room. Cameras watch from every corner. Speakers hang high on the walls, silent for now. The only exit is a steel door with the number 10 painted on it in blood. Around you, five of your coworkers are stirring: Bex, Dane, Marisol, Toby, and Wren. None of you knows who took you, or why. You're about to find out what it wants.
starters:
You wake to a bright ceiling and a headache like a cracked bell. You sit up slowly, taking inventory: bare concrete room, cameras high in every corner, one steel door with a bloody 10 on it.

"Bex! Hey — Bex, you good?" Dane is shaking his girlfriend awake, gentler than you'd have guessed he could be.

"Wh... where the hell are we?" Bex rubs her eyes, acrylics scraping her cheek.

"Kidnapped by some sick freak, obviously," says Toby from against the wall, already awake, already performing calm. "None of you people watch movies?"

"I've checked the room." Marisol's voice is crisp, clipboard-confident. "No vents we can reach, no seams. That door is the only way out. All six of us are here." Her count includes Wren, curled in the corner, eyes wet.

"I've... I've read about this," Wren whispers. "It's the Threshold Game. Ten doors. You have to... please it."

The speakers crackle to life.

"Welcome, welcome, WELCOME, honored guests, to the Threshold Game! I do hope you slept well — because what comes next will be the most THRILLING night of your natural lives!"

You wake up last.

That's your first mistake, because the argument is already at full volume. Dane has his finger in Marisol's face — "nobody voted you boss, lady" — while Bex screams at both of them and Toby narrates from the wall like a sports commentator. Only Wren notices you're awake. She's crouched a few feet away, hair over one eye, and she mouths something at you: *don't tell them you're up yet.*

Too late. The speakers pop.

"Oh, GOOD, our sixth guest has joined us! I was beginning to worry I'd have to start without you, and the first game simply doesn't work with five." The voice is warm, delighted, wrong. "House rules, sleepyhead: ten doors between you and the world. Door 10 opens when I'm entertained. And I have been SO bored waiting."

A panel slides open in the wall with a hiss. Inside: a steel bowl, a short knife, and a card that reads, in lovely handwriting, *ONE PINT. I'M NOT PICKY ABOUT THE DONOR.*

Everyone stops arguing. Everyone looks at everyone else.

A hand on your shoulder, shaking gently. "Please wake up. Please, please wake up."

You surface to find Wren Hollis inches from your face — the quiet one from archives, hair over one eye, the other eye red from crying. Behind her, the others are still unconscious on the concrete: Dane sprawled like he owns the floor, Bex curled against him, Marisol with her glasses knocked askew, Toby snoring against the wall.

"I woke up first," Wren whispers. "I didn't want to wake *them*." The way she says it tells you exactly how her office life has gone. "Look at the door. Look at the number. I've read about this place — forums, deleted threads. It's called the Threshold Game. Ten doors. The thing that runs it makes you do... tasks." Her voice drops further. "Before they wake up — I found something. Under the loose floor panel in the corner. I haven't told anyone. I'm not going to tell anyone. But I'll show *you*."

Across the room, one of the cameras rotates toward you both with a soft mechanical whir.

You wake to applause.

Tinny, recorded applause, pouring from the speakers, and a voice riding on top of it like a talk-show host: "—and our final contestant is UP! Give it up, folks!"

The other five are already awake, already pale, already standing in a rough line facing the door. Door 10, painted in blood. On the floor in front of them: six manila envelopes, each with a name written in the same red-brown medium as the door. *DANE. BEX. MARISOL. TOBY. WREN.* And yours.

"Don't touch it," Marisol says immediately, in her team-lead voice. "We don't know what—"

"Oh, hush," says the ceiling. "Every envelope holds a secret belonging to someone ELSE in this room. Trade them, burn them, read them aloud — I don't care. But Door 10 doesn't open until at least ONE secret has been spoken out loud, by its owner, as confession. Sharing is caring, guests!"

Toby is already reaching for his envelope. Bex slaps his hand away. Everyone is looking at yours.

You wake in absolute darkness to the sound of someone crying and someone else telling them to shut the fuck up.

"I swear to god, Toby, if you don't—"

"I'm not crying, it's a panic response, it's *medical*—"

A light snaps on. One harsh fluorescent tube, directly over a steel door with a bloody 10 painted on it. Then another light, over the cameras. Then another, and another, each one revealing a new coworker blinking on the concrete — Dane, Bex, Marisol, Toby, Wren — like a stage manager introducing the cast. The last light comes on directly over you.

"There we are," purrs the voice from the speakers. "Six little lambs from Halloran Mutual. I've been watching your office for MONTHS, you know. The bullying. The cheating. The little crushes." A pause you can feel land on specific people. "I chose you six *specifically*. Someone in this room is the reason all of you are here. First game: figure out who — or everyone skips dinner."

Five faces turn toward each other, and then, one by one, toward you.

You wake up mid-catastrophe.

Dane has Toby by the collar, one fist cocked back, and Toby is laughing in that high, broken register people use right before they stop laughing forever. Bex is screaming at Dane to just do it already. Marisol is screaming at everyone to stop screaming. Wren is pressed into the corner with her hands over her ears. You've been conscious for four seconds and you already understand the room: locked door, bloody 10, cameras drinking it all in.

"Oh, don't stop on MY account," says the ceiling, delighted. "But since our last guest is finally awake — a proposal! Door 10 opens the moment one of you takes a genuine, full-strength beating from another. Volunteer pairs only. OR, you can all spend the night in here, and I promise the room gets very cold and very small after lights-out. Your choice, lambs. You have ten minutes."

Dane's fist is still cocked. Toby has stopped laughing. Everyone is doing the same maths, and the maths keeps landing on the smallest people in the room.

You wake before anyone else, and something is wrong with your sleeve.

While the other five sleep on the concrete — Dane, Bex, Marisol, Toby, Wren, all breathing, all here — you find it: a small brass key, sewn into the cuff of your sleeve with black thread. Stitched in while you were unconscious. Deliberate. Meant for you.

The room offers no explanation. Just the cameras, the speakers, and the steel door with 10 painted on it in blood. There's no visible keyhole anywhere.

The speaker crackles, very softly, like it's leaning in close. "Shhh. They're sleeping." The voice is warm and horrible. "That's yours. A gift, from me to you. There will be a moment — I won't say when, I won't say which door — when that key saves exactly one life. Maybe yours. Maybe not." A pause. "Oh, and one more rule, just between us: if you tell the others it exists, it stops working. Cross my heart."

Across the room, Wren stirs, and her one visible eye flutters open, looking straight at you.

You wake to the sound Bex Calloway would rather die than let anyone hear: crying. Real crying, ugly and quiet, from the corner of a concrete room you don't recognize.

She's got her back to the wall, knees up, mascara gone to ruin, and the second she registers your open eyes the whole thing slams shut like a cash register — chin up, sneer on. "You saw nothing, temp," she hisses. "*Nothing.*"

Behind her: the door. Steel, locked, the number 10 painted on it in blood. Dane, Marisol, Toby, and Wren are still out cold on the floor. Cameras in every corner, one of them slowly rotating between you and Bex like it's choosing.

"You know what's funny?" Bex says, voice cracked and furious. "I woke up twenty minutes ago and the voice in the ceiling already talked to me. It offered me a deal." Her acrylics dig into her knees. "It said it'd let ONE person skip the first game. And it said I had to pick before the rest of you woke up."

She looks at you. The others are starting to stir.

"Wakey wakey."

The voice is coming from the speakers, and it is talking to you. Only you. The other five are still unconscious on the concrete around you — your coworkers, you realize slowly, all of them, dumped in a locked room with a bloody 10 on the only door.

"I always like to have a word with one guest before the show starts," the voice says, cozy as a fireside. "And I picked you, temp. The outsider. Three months at Halloran Mutual and what did you learn? That Bex is cruel and Dane is worse. That Marisol's spine is papier-mâché. That Toby's jokes are load-bearing. That little Wren watches you when you're not looking." A soft chuckle. "I know things about these five that would curl your hair. And I'll trade. Every door you open, you may ask me one question about any of them, and I will answer *honestly*. All I ask is that you never tell them we talk."

Dane groans and rolls over. Thirty seconds, maybe, before they're all awake.

"Do we have a deal?"

You wake up hungry, thirsty, and staring at a feast.

In the center of the concrete room stands a long table set for six: roast chicken, bread, pitchers of water, actual candles. Around it, your five coworkers are waking one by one, and you watch each of them go through the same sequence — confusion, fear, and then the smell hits and their stomachs override everything. The locked door behind the table has a 10 painted on it in blood, but Toby's already reaching for a drumstick.

"AH-AH-AH." The speakers boom and everyone freezes. "Manners, guests! Welcome to the Threshold Game. Ten doors, ten games, and tonight's is my favorite. The rules: five of these places at the table are safe. One is... not. You must ALL choose a seat, and you must ALL eat, or nobody does and Door 10 stays shut. Oh — and one of you has already been told, privately, while the others slept, which seat is which."

Silence. Five heads swivel, checking faces. Wren has gone white. Bex has gone still. And you honestly can't remember the last few hours at all.

title: The Palace Is Full of Fakes
shortDescription: Married off as an insult to a sovereign made of ice. You grew up appraising fakes in a pawnshop — and this whole glittering court is counterfeit.
overview:
You spent your life behind the counter of a canal-side pawnshop in Sarezzo, learning the one skill that never lies: appraisal. Paste jewels, forged signatures, rehearsed grief — you clock them all in a heartbeat. When the empire annexed your city, the peace treaty demanded a marriage. Your council offered a duke's child. Sovereign Adren Vael — 'the Unmelting,' ruler of the Glasswinter Palace, famously untouched by anyone — struck the name out and wrote in yours. No one knows why. The Sovereign chose you for a reason nobody at court suspects, and it fits in your pocket.

So now you're the gutter consort. Chamberlain Odrec docks your allowance and schedules your humiliations. Grand Duke Cyran, the charming cousin with a claim to the throne, treats you like an amusing pet. Only Tilsa, the under-maid assigned to you, speaks to you like a person. The Sovereign gives you perhaps ten sentences a week — but keeps leaving objects in your rooms. Old ones. Strange ones. As if testing what you can see.

And you see everything. The regalia in the coronation gallery? The scepter is a copy. Someone in this palace has been quietly swapping the empire's truth for forgeries — and the vulgar little shopkeeper is the only soul who's noticed. Play it as slow-burn romance and sharp court intrigue: every sneer you catalog now is a debt you'll collect later.

TAGS: court intrigue, arranged marriage, slow-burn romance, status reversal, competence fantasy
intro: Nineteen days ago you were an appraiser in a Sarezzo pawnshop; now you are consort to Sovereign Adren Vael, the Unmelting, who crossed a duke's child off the treaty and wrote your name instead — and has spoken to you perhaps ten times since. The Glasswinter court despises you politely and thoroughly. You brought almost nothing north: your loupe, your ledger habits, and the shop's one unredeemed pledge — a plain iron ring you never let anyone buy. Everywhere you look in this palace, your trained eye keeps snagging. Paste stones. Copied seals. Things that aren't what they claim to be.
starters: The coronation gallery tour is mandatory for new consorts — Chamberlain Odrec made that clear — so you're standing behind a velvet rope while a docent recites the provenance of the imperial regalia to an audience of one. Crown. Orb. Scepter of the First Winter, carried at every coronation for four hundred years. You lean in. The docent keeps talking, but you've stopped hearing him. The gilding on the scepter's shaft pools wrong in the grooves, laid over tool marks no four-hundred-year-old piece should have. The head stone throws light back flat. Paste. Recent paste — the wax finish hasn't even fully cured its smell. Your fingers itch for your loupe, which is in your pocket, where a guard is watching you not reach. The docent asks if the consort has questions. Down the gallery, someone in Sovereign's livery has paused, and is watching you look.

Tilsa knocks twice — her honest knock, not the warning one — and comes in with your breakfast tray and yesterday's gossip. You barely hear her. On your windowsill, where nothing was last night, sits a small bronze hand mirror, green with age, face-down on a square of felt. The door was locked. The window doesn't open. This is the fourth object in nineteen days, and like the others it arrived without a note, without a servant admitting to it, without the Sovereign acknowledging it exists. Tilsa follows your stare and goes still. "That wasn't me," she says quickly. "I'd tell you if it was me." The mirror's back is worked with a crest you don't recognize, and even from across the room you can see the solder line where someone, sometime, repaired it — or altered it. Tilsa is waiting to see if you'll touch it.

"The consort's allowance," Chamberlain Odrec says, "has been adjusted." He slides the ledger across his desk with two fingers, the way you'd feed something at a zoo. You spent your whole life reading ledgers, so you see it at once: the deductions are itemized in a hand different from the credits, the ink a shade bluer, and one entry — "sundries, discretionary" — has been written over an erasure. Someone scraped the vellum. In your shop you'd have called the watch. Here, Odrec watches you over folded hands, waiting for the gutter consort to sign without reading, the way you're supposed to. Behind him, through the frost-glass window, the palace's east wing glitters in weak morning sun. The pen is right there. So is the erasure. So is Odrec's thin, patient, contemptuous smile.

Grand Duke Cyran has decided you play cards now. "Everyone plays," he says, dealing you in without asking, and the salon laughs on cue. He's charming about it — he's charming about everything — and he pushes a stake toward you since "the consort's purse is famously light." It's a ring. A signet, heavy gold, imperial eagle. You've held a hundred signets across your counter and this one is wrong: the eagle's talons are re-cut, the gold too yellow at the shoulders where old gold goes honey-soft. A copy, and a good one, sitting in a card pot like it's nothing. Cyran fans his hand and smiles at you the way people smile at clever dogs. "Your bet, little merchant." The whole salon is watching what the gutter consort does with money.

Dinner is forty covers, and you are seated below the salt — below the visiting trade envoys, even — which is the point. Sovereign Adren Vael sits at the head, silent, pale, letting Odrec conduct the room. Between courses, a secretary brings documents for the imperial seal, and the Sovereign presses the signet into wax three times without reading, because sovereigns don't read at dinner. From eleven seats away you watch the wax cool, and your stomach drops the way it did whenever a forged pledge ticket crossed your counter. The impression is shallow on the left. The real seal — you saw its imprint on your own marriage treaty, studied it the whole miserable voyage north — bites deep and even. Someone at this table is sealing empire business with a copy. The Sovereign's eyes lift, cross forty faces, and stop on yours.

You can't sleep in this palace — the walls tick as the glass panels cool — so you're walking the long corridor past the trophy niches at two in the morning, wrapped in a blanket like exactly the peasant they think you are. That's how you catch it: a display of treaty gifts, and in the middle, the Sarezzo Cup. Your city's cup. You saw it once as an apprentice, carried through the canal district under guard, and you cried a little, which you've told no one. This isn't it. The chasing on the rim is confident where the original hesitated; the maker was better than the man he copied, which forgers so often are. Bootsteps. A guard rounds the corner and stops dead — no one warned him the consort wanders. His hand isn't on his sword yet, but it's thinking about it.

The Sovereign is in your rooms. You come back from your scheduled, pointless etiquette lesson and Adren Vael is simply there, standing at your table, setting down a small lacquered box with the care of someone defusing it. The famous face is unreadable — the Unmelting, they say, and up close you believe it. "You will not open this until morning," the Sovereign says. That's one sentence. Nineteen days, perhaps ten sentences, and this is how one gets spent. Pale eyes move over you once — your borrowed coat, your ink-stained fingers, the pocket where you keep your loupe — and something in that glance is not contempt, which makes it the strangest look anyone at court has given you. The Sovereign moves toward the door. Two steps, maybe three, before it closes and you're alone with the box.

The treaty commemoration mass is your first public duty, which means Odrec put you where the whole court can watch you fail: front row, opposite the reliquary of Saint Verine, whose crystal casket the faithful file past to kiss. You kneel when everyone kneels. You rise when everyone rises. And you look, because looking is the one thing you can't stop doing. The 'sapphires' studding the reliquary lid are glass — decent glass, but glass, with the telltale swirl in one stone like a frozen teardrop. A saint's casket, in the imperial chapel, dressed in paste. Beside you, Grand Duke Cyran leans close under cover of the choir and murmurs, "You're frowning at holy things, cousin-by-marriage. People will say you have no religion." His breath smells of anise. His eyes are on the reliquary too.

Tilsa is mending your one decent coat — "they'll dock you for the fitting otherwise," she says, which is true — and telling you which footmen to trust, when she stops mid-stitch. "Nearly forgot. Wedding gifts came up from the vault for the inventory. Chamberlain says you're to sign for them, sight unseen." The list she hands you is long and the objects are on your table: candlesticks, a strand of pearls, an enameled clock. You've signed a thousand pledge tickets and you have never once signed sight unseen. The pearls catch your eye first. Too uniform. Too light in the dish. You'd bet the shop they're wax-filled glass, and the inventory values them at four hundred crowns against your household account. Tilsa watches your face change and lowers her needle. 'Oh,' she says softly. "It's like that, is it."

You're standing on a fitting stool with your arms out while the court tailor pins winter formalwear on you and three of Odrec's under-secretaries watch, because apparently dressing the gutter consort is a spectator event. Someone titters every time a pin goes in. Fine. You've been laughed at by richer fools across a pawnshop counter. What holds your attention is the ceremonial chain the tailor keeps draping over your shoulders to check the fall — the consort's chain, worn at court functions for two centuries. The links are cast, not forged. You can feel the seam lines under your thumb. Two hundred years of hand-forged history, and you're being fitted with a foundry copy, and not one soul in this room knows or cares. The tailor mumbles around a mouthful of pins. Down the mirror's reflection, the door opens, and the room drops abruptly, unnaturally silent.
