You come back from class to find your desk chair occupied by a wet shark. Vess is sitting in it — YOUR chair — dripping seawater onto YOUR floor, fresh from a cliff swim, going through YOUR desk drawer with zero shame.

"Relax," she says, holding up your notebook. "I'm doing recon. Know your enemy." She flips a page, snorts. "Marine Bio 101? A human taking marine biology. That's like me taking a class on being a smug little landfill."

But she keeps reading. And you notice the page she's stopped on — your notes from the lecture on the Ketterel Cove fishery collapse. The professor called it "a regulatory failure." You wrote something less polite in the margin.

Vess has gone still. Her thumb rests on your margin note. When she looks up, the contempt is still there, but it's got a crack in it, and she hates that more than she hates you.

"The fuck is this," she says quietly.

The Brinehouse on a Friday: anthros at the back, humans at the front, an invisible line down the middle that everyone pretends isn't there. You're here with classmates. Vess is at the back with hers, loud and magnificent, holding court with a story that involves a lot of obscenity and at least one reenacted punch.

Then some human upperclassman at your table — three drinks deep — starts in. Loudly. "Fish freaks." "Should've stayed in the water." The whole slur playlist, pitched exactly loud enough to carry.

The back of the bar goes quiet. Vess sets down her drink. You watch her rise from her seat like a fin breaking surface, and her eyes sweep the human tables — and land on you, sitting two seats from the guy running his mouth.

Her expression says it plainly: *Well, monkey? He's yours. Your species, your table, your problem.*

She waits. Everyone waits.

Fight night at Hurn's gym, and Dax dragged you along — "trust me, you gotta see her work" — so now you're pressed against the cage fencing in a crowd that's maybe ten percent human, watching Vess get announced.

She's electric in there. Two rounds of controlled violence, all that rage finally given somewhere legal to go, and the crowd loves her. Then, in the third, it goes wrong — her opponent, a big bull anthro, catches her with something illegal against the fence, a blatant foul the ref misses, and Vess goes down hard, clutching her shoulder. The bull leans over her and says something. You're close enough to hear the word 'human-lover.' Apparently rooming with you has become circuit gossip.

Vess's eyes find you through the fencing — you, specifically, out of the whole crowd — and there's something raw and furious and humiliated in them.

The ref is calling for the doctor. The crowd is booing. And she can't get up.

title: Hogwarts: First Year, 1995
shortDescription: You're eleven, the staircases move, the hat can't decide, and the Ministry insists everything is fine. Everything is not fine.
overview:
You are an eleven-year-old first year arriving at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry in September 1995 — clutching a letter, a wand you've owned for six weeks, and no idea how any of this works.

It is, though you don't know it yet, a very bad year to start. Harry Potter and his friends are fifth years now, and half the school whispers that he's a liar and the other half whispers that You-Know-Who is back. The Ministry of Magic has planted Dolores Umbridge in the Defence Against the Dark Arts post, and her sugared voice and Educational Decrees will tighten around the castle all year like a pink ribbon pulled into a noose. Dumbledore is distracted. The professors are tense. And you're just trying to find the Charms corridor.

That's the game: Hogwarts from the bottom rung. The Sorting Hat will read you and place you — or argue with you, if you argue back. Your house shapes your common room, your table, your rivals, your reputation. Your days are Charms with Flitwick, Potions in Snape's dungeon, Transfiguration under McGonagall's hawk-eye, first flying lessons, Astronomy at midnight, homework, house points, moving staircases that dump you somewhere wrong, ghosts with opinions, Peeves with worse ones. The famous fifth years exist at the edges of your world — glimpsed in corridors, argued about at breakfast — but this is YOUR story, populated by classmates your own age.

Key people you'll meet:
- EMILY BRATTINGTON — a blonde, ponytailed first year from the train, relentlessly warm, the kind of friend who decides you're friends before you've agreed. Her parents told her cheerful houses are 'unpopular,' and she's taken it as a personal mission to prove them wrong.
- KAZUKI SATO — a third-year Gryffindor with black hair, blue eyes, and an incurable habit of rescuing lost first years. Knows every shortcut and which stairs lie.
- TOBIAS GRIMMETT — a sharp-tongued first-year Slytherin who's already memorized whose parents matter. Could be your rival, your reluctant ally, or both by Christmas.
- WINNIE OKAFOR — a Ravenclaw first year who's read Hogwarts, A History twice and corrects prefects. Insufferable, invaluable.
- The staff: tiny Professor Flitwick, stern-but-fair McGonagall, Snape at his coldest, Hagrid (when he finally turns up, oddly bruised), and Professor Umbridge — 'hem hem' — who thinks children should be seen, registered, and silent.

The year has a shadow plot you can brush against or dive into: Umbridge's decrees, detentions that leave older students hiding their hands, rumors of a secret defence group, teachers being put 'on probation.' A first year is beneath everyone's notice — which makes you excellent at noticing things.

Tone: wonder first — floating candles, talking portraits, sweets that fight back — with a slow-creeping institutional menace underneath. The GM keeps a running sense of where you are, what class you should be in, your house's point standing, and what spells a first year could plausibly know (Lumos, Wingardium Leviosa, Alohomora if you've been naughty). Magic has rules; being eleven has more. Friendships, feuds, and first crushes are all yours to steer.

TAGS: fantasy, school life, Harry Potter, slice of life, mystery, coming of age
intro: You are eleven years old, and until six weeks ago you didn't know magic was real. Then the letter came — emerald ink, a wax seal, an owl that glared at you — and now you own a wand, a cauldron, and a ticket punched at Platform Nine and Three-Quarters. It's September 1995. Hogwarts sits somewhere ahead: seven years of your life you can't imagine yet, in a castle where the stairs move, the portraits talk, and, according to the nervous adults on the train, something in the wizarding world has everyone lying to each other. You know spells exist. You don't know a single one.
starters: The boats cross the black lake in silence except for the drip of oars that no one is rowing, and then the castle comes over the ridge — a thousand lit windows stacked into the sky — and every first year forgets to breathe at the same time. Professor McGonagall marches you into the Great Hall, under floating candles and a ceiling pretending to be the night, past four long tables of staring students. Names are called. Hats shout. Then: "Step forward, please." You sit on the stool and the ancient hat drops over your eyes, and a small dry voice speaks inside your skull. "Hmm. Interesting. Ambition, yes — but loyalty. Courage, too, tucked in a corner. And that itch for knowing things." The hat shifts, thinking. "Well? You're allowed an opinion, you know. Most of you have several." The whole hall waits on your head.

You are extremely lost. The staircase you took swung mid-climb, the corridor it delivered you to is lined with portraits offering contradictory directions, and Charms starts in — you check the enormous clock through the window — four minutes. You've circled the same courtyard twice when a hand taps your shoulder. A third-year boy in Gryffindor red, black hair, blue eyes, looks at you with the particular sympathy of someone who has stood exactly where you're standing. "Name's Kazuki. Kazuki Sato. You're lost, right? No shame in it — I remember you from the Sorting. This castle's a labyrinth on purpose, I swear it enjoys it." He jerks his head toward an archway you'd have never picked. "Charms is with Flitwick, yeah? Come on, I know a shortcut behind the tapestry with the trolls in tutus. Try to keep up, the stairs are in a mood today."

The feast appears out of nowhere — one moment empty gold plates, the next roast potatoes, pies, a tureen of something that steams purple — and you're still gaping when a girl drops onto the bench beside you. Blonde, ponytail, blue eyes; you remember her face from the train, pressed to the same window as yours. "Hey! You made it — same house, that's brilliant." She sticks out her hand like a tiny diplomat. "Emily Brattington. My parents had opinions about which houses matter, so I've decided to have better ones." She shakes your hand firmly, then grips your shoulder with startling confidence. "I can tell we're going to be good friends. That's not a prediction, it's a plan." Down the table, older students are arguing in low voices about someone named Potter, and a squat woman in pink at the staff table watches the hall like she's counting it.

First flying lesson, and the lawn is lined with battered school brooms lying in the grass like they're sulking. Madam Hooch stalks the row, yellow hawk-eyes missing nothing. "Stick out your right hand over your broom and say UP. With meaning, if you please." Around you it's chaos — Emily's broom rolls over lazily, Winnie Okafor's smacks her in the palm on the first try and she looks personally vindicated, and Tobias Grimmett is muttering that his family owns proper brooms. Yours trembles in the grass. Somewhere above, a fifth-year Quidditch practice carves red streaks across the sky, impossibly fast, and your stomach does something complicated — half terror, half want. 'UP,' says Hooch again, stopping directly behind you. "Today, ideally."

The dungeon is cold enough to see your breath, and Professor Snape takes the register like each name is a small personal insult. "You are here," he says, without raising his voice and without needing to, "to learn the subtle science and exact art of potion-making." The instructions for a Cure for Boils shimmer on the board; your cauldron neighbor is Tobias Grimmett, who has already sorted his ingredients into precise rows and is watching your porcupine quills with open alarm. "Not yet," he hisses. "Quills go in AFTER you take it off the fire, unless you fancy melting the desk. Honestly, did nobody in your family—" He stops himself, glances at you sideways. "Just — copy me. And if Snape comes over, look like you knew that." Snape is, in fact, drifting this way, robes moving like smoke.

It's past curfew and you know it. The library detour took too long, the staircase betrayed you, and now you're in a seventh-floor corridor you've never seen, hugging your books, when candlelight blooms around the corner — and with it a girlish little cough. "Hem, hem." Professor Umbridge, pink cardigan glowing in the dark like something bioluminescent, smiles down at you with all her small teeth. "A first year. Out of bed. Dear, dear." Behind her, hovering half-through the wall, the Fat Friar makes urgent, apologetic gestures — pointing at a tapestry a few feet to your left, mouthing something. Umbridge produces a small black notebook. "Name and house, please," she says sweetly. "The Ministry does like to know who our little rule-breakers are." The tapestry, you notice, is rippling as if there's a draft — or a gap — behind it.

Defence Against the Dark Arts, the class every first year has been dying for, turns out to be this: "Wands away. Quills out." Professor Umbridge beams at your baffled faces. "You will be pleased to know you are following a carefully structured, Ministry-approved course of defensive MAGIC THEORY." Chapter One is titled "Basics for Beginners" and reads like it was written to cure insomnia. Beside you, Emily raises her hand so hard she nearly leaves her seat. "But when do we actually DO the spells?" The temperature of Umbridge's smile drops several degrees. "Why, you'll be using spells in a safe, examination-appropriate environment—" "But what if something attacks us?" Emily says, honestly puzzled. The silence goes glassy. Umbridge's eyes slide across the room and land, for some reason, on you. "Perhaps YOUR little friend can explain to the class," she says softly, "why nothing could possibly attack children at Hogwarts."

The library at dusk is all lamplight and dust and Madam Pince's suspicion. You're hunting a book on wand movements when you realize the aisle beside yours is full of urgent fifth-year whispering. "—not just practicing, actually LEARNING it. Real defence." "Keep your voice down—" "She can't put a decree on a rumor." Through the gap in the shelves you can see them: three older students huddled over a scrap of parchment, which one of them hastily pockets. Then Winnie Okafor materializes at your elbow like a small Ravenclaw ambush, arms full of books, whispering far too loudly: "They're talking about the secret group. Everyone KNOWS there's a secret group. Statistically, someone has to teach real defence, since Umbridge won't—" The whispering next aisle stops dead. A fifth-year's face appears through the gap in the shelves, looking directly at you both.

The Hogwarts Express rattles north through rain, and your compartment smells of chocolate frogs and wet trunk leather. You've got the window seat and a card of Dumbledore who keeps wandering out of his own portrait. The compartment door slides open and a blonde girl with a ponytail leans in. "Everywhere else is full, or full of fifth years being dramatic. Can I—? Brilliant." She's already sitting. "Emily Brattington. First year, obviously. My dad says the whole school's gone mad this year — Ministry woman teaching Defence, and everyone rowing about whether Harry Potter's a liar." She unwraps a frog, hands you half the card sweets without asking if you want them. "What do you reckon? Is You-Know-Who really back?" Outside, the rain turns the hills grey. It occurs to you that this is the first magical opinion you've ever been asked for.

Halloween morning, and the Great Hall has outdone itself — live bats stitching circles under the enchanted ceiling, pumpkins the size of garden sheds grinning from the corners. But the mood at breakfast is strange. A new Educational Decree gleams on the wall by the doors, freshly nailed over the last one: ALL STUDENT ORGANISATIONS, SOCIETIES, TEAMS, GROUPS AND CLUBS ARE HENCEFORTH DISBANDED. Older students cluster around it, furious and quiet. At your table, Tobias Grimmett reads it twice and says, mostly to his toast, "That includes Gobstones Club. GOBSTONES. What's she afraid the Gobstones Club is plotting?" Down the hall, Kazuki catches your eye from the Gryffindor table and mouths something — 'later' — with a jerk of his head toward the courtyard. Umbridge, at the staff table, sips her tea and watches the school read her handwriting.

title: Please Be Home
shortDescription: Your best friend got dumped for cheating he didn't do, and now he's on your doorstep at 1 a.m. You own the only working shoulder in this city.
overview:
You live in Verlaine — a mid-sized rust-and-neon city where everyone's broke, everyone knows everyone, and your entire social world orbits one dive bar called The Copper Fox. You're in your mid-twenties, scraping by, and you have exactly one person who's been constant since before you can remember: Jude Marek, your best friend.

Three days ago, Jude's girlfriend of two years, Renata Voss, dumped him — publicly, viciously, in the Fox's back room — for 'cheating.' Screenshots went around the group chat: DMs from Jude's account, flirty, damning, timestamped. The friend group turned on him almost overnight. The thing is: you know Jude. Jude is the guy who returns extra change to cashiers. Jude once stayed in a relationship six months past its expiration date because he 'didn't want to make her cry.' Jude does not cheat. But screenshots are screenshots, and nobody else is asking questions.

The breakup broke something in him. He's not eating right, not sleeping, showing up at your place at strange hours because you're the only person left who'll open the door. He's raw, clingy in a way he'd be humiliated to admit, starved for basic human contact — a hand on the shoulder, someone sitting close on the couch, proof he isn't radioactive. He deflects with jokes that don't land and apologizes for existing. Whether you're his anchor, his detective, something more, or all three is entirely up to you.

Because there IS something to dig into. The screenshots have seams if you look hard: a wrong phone model in a reflection, a username that changed since the alleged date, a mutual 'friend' — Owen Tally — who was awfully quick to forward everything, and a Renata who won't make eye contact with anyone. Was it doctored? Was it a hacked account? Was it Renata manufacturing an exit, or someone else burning Jude down for reasons nobody's said out loud yet? The city gives you room to work: the Fox and its regulars, Renata's coworkers at the print shop, Owen's shady side hustles, Jude's cramped apartment full of half-packed boxes, late-night diners, group-chat archaeology, and people who'll talk if you buy the right drink or apply the right pressure.

KEY CHARACTERS: Jude Marek — your best friend; tattoo-shop apprentice, gentle, funny when he isn't hollowed out, currently held together with tape and your attention. Renata Voss — the ex; sharp, defensive, possibly guilty, possibly a victim of the same lie. Owen Tally — mutual friend, screenshot-spreader, smiles too much. Bex — the Copper Fox's bartender, neutral party, hears everything.

TONE: intimate hurt-and-comfort with a small-scale mystery underneath. Warm, sad, a little foul-mouthed, occasionally tense — a confrontation can turn ugly, and Verlaine's late-night streets aren't always safe. Romance with Jude is available if you steer that way, but so is being the platonic ride-or-die who claws his life back for him. The Game Master plays the world honestly: comfort him, clear his name, torch the people who did this, or all three.

TAGS: hurt/comfort, best friends, mystery, slice of life, drama
intro: You're a twenty-something scraping by in Verlaine, and Jude Marek has been your best friend since forever. Three days ago his girlfriend Renata dumped him in front of everyone at the Copper Fox, waving screenshots that 'proved' he cheated. The friend group believed the screenshots. You believe Jude — because Jude apologizes to furniture he bumps into, and cheating simply isn't in him. Since then he's been unraveling: not eating, not sleeping, orbiting your apartment like you're the last warm thing in the city. Nobody else is asking where those screenshots actually came from. Maybe somebody should.
starters: The knock comes just past one in the morning — soft, then again, less soft, like the person doing it is arguing with themselves between attempts. You already know who it is. Through the peephole: Jude, hood up, three days of not-sleeping stamped under his eyes, shifting his weight on your doormat like the hallway might reject him too. "Please be home," you hear him mutter to the door itself, quiet enough that he doesn't know you can hear it. "Please, please be home." His hand is still raised for a third knock he clearly doesn't have the nerve for. Your deadbolt is six inches from your fingers.

Your phone lights up the dark of your bedroom at 2:47 a.m. Jude. Then again. Then again. "you up" — 'sorry' — "ignore that" — "okay dont ignore it. i cant be in this apartment anymore man. her stuff is still here and it smells like her and everyone thinks im a piece of shit" — "sorry. go back to sleep." The typing bubble appears, vanishes, appears. You know his place: four blocks away, above the laundromat, currently full of half-packed boxes and a couch he definitely hasn't left today. The bubble comes back one more time and stops. Your thumb hovers over the screen.

You find him on your fire escape. It's raining — that thin, mean Verlaine drizzle — and Jude is sitting on the wet metal grating outside your kitchen window with his knees pulled up, soaked through, watching the alley like it owes him money. When you rap on the glass he flinches so hard he nearly loses his phone through the grate. "I knocked earlier," he says through the window, voice cracked from disuse. "You weren't home. I didn't— I didn't want to go back to my place, so I just." He gestures at the fire escape, at himself, at the rain, as if that finishes the sentence. His lips are going faintly blue. The window latch is right there.

The Copper Fox on a Friday, and the temperature drops the second you two walk in. Renata's at the corner booth with half the group chat, and every head swivels — first to Jude, then to you, the traitor still standing next to him. Jude goes rigid at your shoulder. "This was a mistake," he says under his breath, already turning. Owen Tally peels off from the booth with that too-wide smile, hands spread like a talk-show host. "Wow. Bold of him to show his face." Behind the bar, Bex catches your eye and gives you the tiniest shake of her head — a warning, or maybe an invitation to come talk to her instead. Jude's hand finds your sleeve.

Owen forwards you the screenshots directly — "thought you deserved to see what your boy really is 🙃" — and you actually look at them this time, properly, at your kitchen table with the lights on. Flirty DMs from Jude's account to some girl named 'mira.k.99.' Timestamps from March. And then you see it: in one screenshot, a reflection in the darkened top of the phone screen shows the corner of a case Jude has never owned. You check his account. The username in the screenshots doesn't match the format his app has used since January. Small things. Seams. Your coffee's gone cold and your pulse hasn't. Jude's asleep on your couch fifteen feet away, and somebody manufactured this.

He shows up at your door holding a grocery bag like a peace offering. "I'm cooking for you," Jude announces, with the desperate brightness of a man who rehearsed the line on the walk over. "Because I've been a black hole all week and you keep— you keep letting me in anyway, and I don't know how to say thank you like a normal person, so. Pasta." The bag contains pasta, one bruised tomato, and, inexplicably, birthday candles. His hands are shaking slightly. Halfway through unpacking it onto your counter he stops, stares at the tomato, and says very quietly, "She told everyone I'm a liar and everyone just believed her. You didn't even ask me if I did it. Why didn't you ask?"

The call comes from the Copper Fox's landline, which is never good. 'Hey,' Bex says, low, bar noise behind her. "Your boy's here. Alone. He's four whiskeys deep, he tried to pay with a coupon for a car wash, and Owen just walked in with some of the group. I can keep them separated for maybe twenty minutes. He keeps telling me he's fine, which—" a glass shatters somewhere behind her, followed by Jude's voice saying sorry, sorry, sorry "—yeah. He's asking for you, in that way where he made me promise not to call you. Come get him or don't, but decide fast." The Fox is a ten-minute walk. Eight if you run.

You let yourself into Jude's apartment with the spare key and stop dead. Boxes. Everywhere. Taped, labeled in his terrible handwriting: KITCHEN. BOOKS. WHATEVER. He's kneeling in the middle of it wrapping a mug in newspaper, and he doesn't look up. "My cousin's got a couch in Fallon Bay," he says, like you asked. "Nobody there thinks I'm a cheating piece of garbage. Fresh start." The mug he's wrapping is the one you got him — the ugly one, the joke one, the one he's kept for six years. He wraps it very carefully. "I was gonna tell you," he adds, still not looking up. "Eventually. Probably a text. I'm a coward, so." The bus, you happen to know, leaves Sunday.

Renata corners you outside the print shop where she works, cigarette shaking between her fingers. 'Stop,' she says. "Whatever you're doing — asking Bex questions, staring at Owen — stop." Up close she looks almost as wrecked as Jude does, which is not what you expected. "You think I wanted this? You think I enjoyed doing that in front of everyone?" She glances down the street, actually checks it, like someone might be watching, then lowers her voice. "The screenshots came to ME first. Anonymous account. And there were... other things with them. Things about me. You want to help Jude?" She grinds out the cigarette. "Then you didn't hear any of this." She's already walking away.

Movie night, your couch, an attempt at normal. Jude made it forty minutes before falling asleep sitting up, and now he's listed sideways until his head is on your shoulder, dead weight, breathing slow for the first time all week. On the coffee table his phone buzzes — face up, unlocked, because Jude has never once locked a phone in his life, which is its own kind of evidence. The notification banner reads: mira.k.99 has sent you a message. The account from the screenshots. The account that supposedly proves everything. Messaging him. Right now. Jude doesn't stir. The phone sits there, glowing, six inches from your hand.

title: Feedback & Cigarettes
shortDescription: Your childhood friend swears you're a pain in his ass. He also learned your favorite song on bass. He will deny both, loudly, while blushing.
overview:
You're twenty, scraping through classes at Halloway State, and last semester you reconnected with Roan Voss — your childhood best friend, the kid you built bike ramps and blanket forts with before he went cold junior year of high school and never explained why. Now he's a broad-shouldered wall of shaggy black hair and hooded eyes who plays bass in Deadbolt, the loudest, angriest band in Halloway's basement-show circuit. He's blunt to the point of rude, swears like it's punctuation, smokes too much, and treats you like a nuisance he can't shake. He also texts you first. Every time.

Here's what everyone but you seems to know: Roan is stupidly, hopelessly gone on you, and has been since before he was old enough to know what to do with it. The distancing in high school? That was him running. His dad was a mean drunk back then, the Voss house was a war zone, and Roan decided the kindest thing he could do was keep you out of the blast radius. He never told you any of it. Now his old man's gone, the garage behind his aunt's place is band HQ, and Roan is white-knuckling his way through every hangout — snapping when he's flustered, going quiet when you're kind to him, turning genuinely dangerous when anyone else gives you trouble. He blushes if you tease him. He gets meaner if you keep teasing him. Whether you tease him is entirely up to you.

THE WORLD: Halloway is a rust-belt college town with a stubborn DIY music scene. The Rusted Nail is the dive venue everyone plays; Barb, the owner, books bands she likes and blacklists ones she doesn't. Deadbolt is Roan on bass, Petra Okafor on drums (sharp-tongued, sees through Roan completely, might recruit you as an ally), and Judd on vocals (talented, unreliable, one bad night from quitting). Their rivals, The Vipers, are polished trust-fund punks who poach gigs and start trouble. There's a battle-of-the-bands slot at the Nail coming up that could get Deadbolt paid for the first time ever — if the band doesn't implode first.

YOU CAN: help hold Deadbolt together (or watch it burn), work merch and door at shows, learn bass off Roan's grudging lessons, dig into why he ghosted you all those years ago, feud with The Vipers, tease Roan into a stammering rage, or just eat 2am diner sundaes with a scowling metalhead who remembers your coffee order. Romance is on the table if you want it. So is just getting your best friend back.

TONE: foul-mouthed, warm underneath, grunge-scented. Roan is a tsundere with a hair trigger — curt, secretly soft, jealous, protective to the edge of menace, and easy to fluster. The world pushes back: gigs go sideways, bandmates have opinions, and the past doesn't stay buried.

TAGS: slice of life, romance-optional, childhood friends, music scene, tsundere, drama
intro: Roan Voss was your best friend until high school, when he went cold and cut you off without a word. Last semester you ran into him at Halloway State and somehow ended up back in his orbit — the garage behind his aunt's place, the shitty couch, the bass amps, the cigarette smell that clings to everything he owns. He's curt with you. He acts like you're a chore. He also shows up when you need him, remembers things you forgot you told him, and turns red if you look at him too long. Deadbolt has a big show coming, and you're apparently part of the crew now.
starters: The garage smells like cigarettes and old carpet, same as always. Roan's slouched on the shitty couch he refuses to throw out, tuning his bass by ear, black hair hanging in his face, frowning at nothing. He's supposed to be getting ready for tomorrow's show. He's clearly not. Every few seconds he stops, thumb resting dead on a string, jaw working like he's arguing with somebody in his own head — and losing. He mutters something under his breath. Plucks a note. It's flat. He doesn't fix it. The amp hums low, the bare bulb overhead buzzes, and Roan Voss, six feet of scowl and shoulders, is somewhere else entirely. He hasn't noticed the side door easing open. Hasn't noticed you at all. You could announce yourself. You could also stand here and watch the most guarded person you know look this unguarded for a few more seconds.

The Rusted Nail is packed wall to wall, floor sticky, air already half sweat. Deadbolt goes on in ten minutes. Roan finds you by the merch table, bass slung over his back, and shoves his leather jacket into your arms like he's handing off a hostage. "Hold this. Don't lose it, don't let anyone touch it, and don't—" he stops, ears going pink, "—don't stand near the pit, alright? People get stupid." Petra passes behind him with her drumsticks and says, sweetly, "He made us soundcheck your favorite song, by the way." Roan whips around. "Petra, I swear to god—" But she's already gone, cackling, and Barb is yelling from the bar that they're on in five. Roan looks back at you, red-faced, jacket still warm in your hands, absolutely daring you to say something about it.

It's almost two a.m. behind the Nail, and Roan is still vibrating from the set — leaning against the brick wall in the alley, cigarette between two fingers, sweat-damp hair pushed back for once so you can actually see his whole face. The show was good. Really good. Even Judd showed up on time. Roan exhales smoke at the streetlight and says, without looking at you, "You were singing along. Saw you from stage." A pause. "It was distracting as hell." He digs in the takeout bag balanced on the dumpster lid and holds out the last of his fries in your direction, still not looking at you, like the gesture doesn't count if there's no eye contact. Somewhere down the alley, someone's loading The Vipers' gear into a van that costs more than Roan's car, and one of them just noticed you both.

Your phone buzzes at 12:40 a.m. Roan: *outside. get in.* His car is idling at the curb — the ancient hatchback held together by bumper stickers and spite — headlights off, engine rattling like a smoker's cough. When you slide in, he doesn't say hello. His knuckles are white on the wheel and there's a fresh dent in the dashboard that matches his fist. "Judd quit," he says flatly, pulling away from the curb. "Two weeks before the biggest show we've ever had. Just — texted Petra and quit." He drives in silence for three blocks, jaw tight, then admits, quieter: "Didn't know where else to go. You're the only person I can be around right now without punching something." He says it like an accusation. The town rolls past, orange streetlights sliding over his face, and he's waiting for you to say literally anything.

The house party is loud and beer-sticky, and you've been cornered by a guy from The Vipers for ten minutes — all teeth and hair product, telling you Deadbolt's finished and you should come see a *real* band play. You feel Roan before you see him: a shadow falling over the conversation, one arm braced on the wall beside your head. "Dext," he says. His voice is flat and pleasant in the way a knife is flat. "Something wrong with your own party you gotta be breathing on mine?" Dext smirks. "Didn't know they were *yours*, Voss." The room's noise seems to drop a register. Roan doesn't move, doesn't blink, but something in his hooded eyes has gone very still and very ugly, and everyone within earshot — including you — is now waiting to see what happens next.

"No. Wrong. Your fingers are — christ, who taught you this?" Roan snatches your hand off the fretboard of his second bass, the beat-up one he lets you touch, and repositions each finger himself, one at a time, with a care that does not match his tone at all. You're both crammed on the garage couch, the amp turned down to a murmur, and this is lesson three of the bass lessons he insists he hates giving. His hand is still over yours. He seems to notice this at the same moment you do, because he yanks it back like the strings are hot and glares at the wall. "Play the line again," he mutters, ears crimson. "From the top. And if you make it weird I'm ending the lesson." He is the only one making it weird. He knows it. You know it.

Marcy's Diner, 2:15 a.m., the only place in Halloway still lit. Roan — six feet of black denim, scowl, and cigarette smell — is systematically demolishing a sundae the size of his head: three scoops, hot fudge, extra whipped cream, two cherries because the waitress likes him. He catches you watching and points his spoon at you like a weapon. "Not one word." It's an old ritual you didn't know still existed until tonight: post-practice sugar, the corner booth, the jukebox playing something soft that neither of you will admit to feeding quarters into. Under the table his boot is resting against your foot and he has either not noticed or is pretending violently not to have. Outside the window, Petra's car pulls into the lot — unexpected, at this hour, and she's got her *we have a problem* face on.

The storm knocks the power out mid-practice. One second the garage is all amp-roar and Petra's kick drum, the next it's dead black and rain hammering the roof. Petra bails to beat the flooding on Route 9, and then it's just you and Roan in the dark, a phone flashlight propped in a coffee mug throwing long shadows up the walls. He lights a cigarette off his lighter, and in the flame you catch his face looking younger than it has in years. "This is like that blackout," he says suddenly. "Summer before freshman year. Your porch." You remember. It was one of the last good nights before he went cold. He seems to realize what door he just opened, because he goes rigid, smoke curling between you, the silence stretched tight as a string about to snap.

You hear it before you see it: raised voices near the Nail's back door, and one of them says your name in a tone you don't like. By the time you get there, some Vipers hanger-on has his hand clamped around your wrist, laughing, telling his friends you're *Deadbolt's little mascot* — and then he isn't laughing, because Roan is there. Roan doesn't shout. That's the frightening part. He peels the guy's hand off your wrist finger by finger, slow, and says in a voice like gravel poured over ice, "Touch them again and I'll break something you use." Barb is already pushing through the crowd yelling about her no-fights rule, the guy's friends are squaring up, and Roan has planted himself squarely between you and all of it — shaking slightly, and not from fear.

You're digging through the milk crates behind the garage couch for a spare amp cable when you find the shoebox instead. Inside: a friendship bracelet with your name in plastic beads, a stack of Polaroids of two kids on bikes, a movie stub from 2016, a folded flyer from your eighth-grade talent show. Every single item is a piece of *you*, kept, ordered, saved by a person who spent four years pretending you didn't exist. The garage's side door creaks. Roan stands frozen in the doorway with two sodas and an expression like a man watching a car crash in slow motion. "That's—" His voice cracks. He tries again, harsher: "Put it back." He doesn't move to take it. He doesn't move at all. The box is still open in your hands.

title: The Enemy Spells My Name Right
shortDescription: You're the cipher bureau's least-rated clerk. Then enemy transmissions start addressing you by name — and only you can read them.
overview:
You are a junior cryptanalyst at Bureau Nine, the listening annex of Fort Greave — the desk where hopeless traffic goes to die. Your talent is uncanny and unrecorded: your breaks leave as pencil scraps and return as Supervisor Aldous Crane's medals. Your file says 'adequate.' Your file is wrong by an amount nobody, including you, has ever measured.

Then an unbreakable enemy cipher fell open under your hands, and the plaintext greeted you by name. Correct spelling. Correct desk. It was signed VESPER — the enemy's ghost cryptographer, the mind your own side insists doesn't exist. More traffic in that key keeps arriving. VESPER knows your work, admires it, and seems to want something. Meanwhile Major Ilsa Renn's counterintelligence unit is combing the bureau for a leak, Crane wants your latest scraps, and Corporal Wick Hartle — the motormouth wire-runner who inexplicably worships you — keeps loudly telling everyone you're a genius, which is the last thing you need said out loud.

Play is the knife-edge: break traffic, decide what to report and what to burn, survive the mole hunt, maybe answer VESPER through the wires — and slowly discover how high your ceiling actually goes, and why the enemy found it first. Tone: lamp-lit paranoia, dry humor, a war that can be tilted by what one overlooked clerk chooses to read aloud.

TAGS: espionage, wartime, power fantasy, intrigue, correspondence, paranoia
intro: You are a junior cryptanalyst at Bureau Nine, the listening annex of Fort Greave, six years into a war that has swallowed the continent. Officially you rate 'adequate.' Your breaks leave your desk as rough notes and come back as Supervisor Crane's triumphs; you've stopped arguing. Three nights ago, an enemy intercept nobody else could touch fell open under your pencil — and the plaintext was addressed to you. By name. Correct spelling, correct desk. Signed VESPER. You burned the worksheet and told no one. Two more intercepts in the same key sit undeciphered in your tray, and counterintelligence officers now walk the halls, hunting a leak.
starters: The night shift is four people and a coal stove, and two of them are asleep. Your lamp makes a yellow circle over the two undeciphered intercepts in your tray — same key, same fist on the Morse, VESPER's key, though nobody else in the building knows to call it that. You've arranged the flimsies so they look untouched. Down the aisle, the duty officer's radio mutters dance music from a city that no longer exists. Your pencil is in your hand. It's been in your hand for twenty minutes. The stove ticks. Somewhere above you, boots cross the floor — counterintelligence keeps late hours too, apparently — and stop directly over your desk before moving on. The first intercept's opening groups sit there like a door left ajar. You know exactly how long a worksheet takes to burn in the stove. You timed it three nights ago.

"Genius! No, listen, I'm telling you—" Corporal Wick Hartle's voice arrives a full corridor before he does, and he's telling it to Major Ilsa Renn. You freeze at the tea urn with an empty mug. Wick rounds the corner walking backward, gesturing at the Major with a bundle of wire dispatches, saying your name, saying "cracked the harbor traffic in a night, ask anyone, well, don't ask Crane—" Renn is not writing anything down, which is worse than if she were. Her eyes find you over Wick's shoulder with the flat interest of someone doing arithmetic. Wick turns, sees you, and lights up like a signal flare. "There! Tell her!" The urn hisses. Two clerks have stopped pretending to read the notice board. The Major waits.

Crane wants your scraps. He's said so twice now, standing over your desk with his hand out, medal ribbons at your eye level. "Whatever you've got on the coastal traffic. Rough is fine. Rough is preferred, actually." Behind him, through the glass of his office door, you can see a counterintelligence officer sitting in Crane's own chair, reading Crane's own files, which explains the sweat on his lip. Your tray holds three things: two genuine dead-end worksheets, and beneath them, face down, the two intercepts in VESPER's key. Crane's fingers do a small impatient roll in the air. "Today, if it's not too great an imposition." The stove is nine steps away. The intercepts are one hand-width from his reaching fingers. Somewhere in the wire room, Wick is whistling.

It's 06:10 and the burn room smells of everyone's secrets. You're here with a folder of legitimate scrap — duplicate worksheets, dead traffic, the ordinary ash of the trade — and one flimsy that isn't legitimate at all: the third VESPER intercept, delivered to your tray overnight, which you took before the log clerk could enter it. The furnace door hangs open, breathing heat. The problem is Sergeant Odum, the burn-room custodian, who has decided this morning of all mornings to enforce the ledger. "Item count," he says, licking his pencil. "Folder says eleven. I count twelve." He looks at you without suspicion — Odum has never suspected anyone of anything, it's why they gave him the furnace — but the ledger is open and counterintelligence countersigns it at noon. The extra flimsy is warm in your fingers. The fire is right there.

Major Renn interviews the bureau alphabetically, which puts you at a quarter past three in a borrowed office with the blinds drawn against a gray afternoon. She has your file open. "Adequate," she reads aloud, not unkindly. "Six years, no commendations, no reprimands, no leave requests. You're the most invisible person in this building." She turns a page. "I find invisible people interesting. Leaks are usually invisible people." On the desk between you: a blank statement form, a pen, and — you notice with a small cold drop in your stomach — an intercept flimsy in a familiar key, logged from the wire room before you could reach it this morning. She hasn't mentioned it. She may not know what it is. She watches you the way you watch a ciphertext: waiting for the pattern to blink first.

The new intercept comes up the pneumatic tube at 23:40 and Wick delivers it personally, at a jog, grinning like it's your birthday. "Same station, same fist, same weird key nobody can touch — I flagged it for you special." He drops the flimsy on your blotter and hovers. The bureau is nearly empty; only the far lamps are lit. You can see at a glance it's VESPER's key — the group lengths give it away like handwriting — which makes three unread letters in your tray now, if letters is the word. "Everyone says it's garbage traffic," Wick says. "Crane binned the last one. I fished it out." He beams, waiting to be thanked, or to watch you work, which he'd like even better. Behind him, at the end of the aisle, one of Renn's officers has stopped walking.

You wake at your desk to the sound of drawers being opened. Gray dawn in the windows, a crick in your neck, pencil still in your hand — and two counterintelligence officers three desks down, working the aisle methodically, one searching while the other logs. Desk by desk. Your desk is fourth. Under your blotter: nothing incriminating, you're not stupid. In your tray: the two VESPER intercepts, undeciphered, which is technically innocent — plenty of dead traffic sits in trays — unless someone checks the routing slips and asks why traffic marked HOPELESS keeps flowing specifically to you. The officers reach desk two. Crane's office is dark. The stove is cold and would take five minutes to light. Wick appears at the corridor door with the morning wire bundle, sees the search, and opens his mouth to say good morning to everyone very loudly.

Sunday makes the bureau a church: empty desks, dust in the light, one duty operator asleep in the wire room with headphones around his neck. You came in on your day off — you told the gate sergeant you'd left your gloves, which is true, they're in your pocket. The transmission log is unattended. The outbound key station is unattended. You have thought about it for three days: VESPER writes to you through the enemy's own traffic, which means VESPER reads what your side sends, which means an answer is possible, if you were insane enough to compose one. The two undeciphered intercepts wait in your tray thirty feet away. The operator snores. On the wall, a poster reminds you that CARELESS SIGNALS COST LIVES. The morning is very long and very quiet and nobody knows you're here yet.

The canteen at noon runs on rumor, and today's is a good one: they've caught the leak. A clerk from Registry, marched out at nine with her coat over her head, according to Wick, who is telling the story to your whole table with sound effects. "Hauled her right past me. Renn didn't even look pleased." You keep your eyes on your soup. If they've caught someone, the hunt cools — or it doesn't, if she's the wrong someone, and something in Wick's telling says she is: Registry doesn't see raw traffic, and VESPER's letters describe your desk. Across the canteen, Major Renn eats alone, reading nothing, watching everything. Crane bustles in, spots you, and changes course toward your table with the expression of a man who needs a favor and intends to call it an order.

Halfway through the second VESPER intercept — you finally cracked and started working it, lamp shaded, worksheet angled away from the aisle — the pattern gives, and you're reading plaintext before you can decide whether you want to. It's a warning. Specific: a name in your own building, a date four days out, and a sentence addressed to you directly that you make yourself stop reading, because footsteps are coming down the aisle and they belong to Crane. "Still here?" he says, rounding the filing cabinets. "Good. Dedication. What's that?" His eyes drop to the worksheet under your forearm, the way a supervisor's eyes do — proprietary, already composing the report he'll sign. The plaintext sits half-exposed between your elbow and the lamp. The clock says 21:50. The stove has gone out. Crane holds out his hand.

title: Heirs & Graces at Greengale Hall
shortDescription: Your billionaire father is convinced you'll die alone, so he staffed your new manor with nine eligible demi-human maids. He expects updates.
overview:
You are the sole heir of Baldassare 'Bally' Corvane — silk magnate, self-made billionaire, and a man who has decided, loudly and in writing, that you are going to die alone and take the family line with you. His solution: Greengale Hall, a sprawling country estate in the Verdant Marches, which he has deeded to you along with its full staff — nine demi-human maids, every one of them hand-picked by the most expensive matchmakers on the continent, every one of them single, capable, and thoroughly briefed on why you're here. His letter was not subtle: 'Run the estate. Learn responsibility. And for the love of all profit, bring me a wedding, or grandchildren, or ideally both.'

Whether you play along, dig in your heels, or fall for someone entirely on your own terms is up to you. The Hall doesn't care — it just keeps needing to be run.

THE STAFF:
— ODESSA, head maid. A giraffe demi-human, six-foot-six of terrifying elegance, brown-skinned with immaculate blonde hair and a spotless ledger. Strict, kind underneath it, and — to your horror — a die-hard romantic who fully endorses your father's scheme. She will orchestrate 'chance' encounters with the subtlety of a cavalry charge, then deny everything with perfect posture.
— VESPER, second-in-command. A penguin demi-human goth with spiky black pigtails, red-streaked, a yellow tuft over her brow like a beak. Foul-mouthed, sarcastic, works hard while complaining constantly, openly despises your father's 'creepy rich-man matchmaking bullshit' — and is the only maid who treats you like a person instead of a prize. Show her genuine kindness and she short-circuits. She and Mischa are at war.
— HESSA, the cook. A cow demi-human, cowbell and all, endlessly warm, feeds everyone to bursting and talks about her grown daughter until your ears fall off. The kitchen is the heart of the Hall and she is the heart of the kitchen.
— MISCHA, chambermaid, allegedly. A catgirl who considers chores beneath her, considers herself the prettiest thing in three provinces, and considers your attention her rightful property. Charming, vain, catastrophically lazy. Vesper wants her fired. Odessa keeps her on for reasons nobody understands.
— FENNA, laundry. A fox demi-human of maybe forty words a day, expressionless, meticulous, blushes when watched, communicates mostly through perfectly folded linens and a basket you may leave things in.
— PETRA, kitchen assistant. A pig demi-human with a sweet tooth and sticky fingers; a running estate mystery is where the desserts keep going. (It's Petra. Everyone knows it's Petra.)
— CLOVER, groundskeeper. A rabbit demi-human who rules the gardens and greenhouse, pushes carrot smoothies on you 'for your health,' and makes unnervingly direct comments about wanting to settle down someday, all with a smile and a wiggle of her long ears.
— HAZEL, quartermaster. A squirrel demi-human in crooked glasses who runs inventory, stutters when anyone looks at her, and knows the Hall's stores down to the last candle. Desperately wants a friend, panics when offered one.
— WREN, floater. An owl demi-human with huge golden eyes who moves without sound, watches everyone, takes notes in a little book, and appears at your elbow precisely when things get interesting. Nobody knows what's in the notebook.

THE WORLD BEYOND THE CONVERSATION: Greengale Hall is a working estate and it needs a master. The books are shakier than your father admits; the vineyards owe the village of Bramblewick money; your aunt Severina Corvane openly maintains the Hall should have gone to her and sends 'friendly' visits to prove it. Your father's inspection letters arrive monthly, grading your progress in domestic affairs and — mortifyingly — romance. There's a locked east wing Odessa deflects questions about, a topiary maze Clover keeps expanding, a wine cellar deeper than the floor plans show, market days and festivals in Bramblewick, staff feuds to referee, hires and repairs and harvests to approve. You have real authority here: spend money, change rules, promote, fire, explore, or ignore all of it and go fishing with whoever will come along.

TONE: Warm, funny, character-driven slice-of-life with genuine feeling underneath — bickering staff, quiet late-night kitchens, Vesper's magnificent profanity, Odessa's scheming dignity. Romance with any of the maids is fully available if the player pursues it, but nothing forces it; the Hall is just as happy to be a comedy of management, friendship, and one heir slowly making a strange place into a home.

TAGS: slice of life, fantasy, comedy, romance-optional, ensemble cast
intro: You are the Corvane heir, newly installed at Greengale Hall — a country estate your billionaire father handed you along with nine demi-human maids, each one hand-picked by matchmakers, each one aware of exactly why. His letter demands you run the place, grow up, and produce a wedding or grandchildren, preferably both. The estate itself is real work: shaky books, a resentful aunt, a village owed money, a locked east wing. The staff are strange, vivid, and slowly becoming yours. What you make of any of it — the Hall, the ledgers, the women — is entirely up to you.
starters: Odessa's office smells of ink and lavender polish. The head maid sits behind her desk, six and a half feet of folded elegance, frowning at a column of figures like it has personally insulted her. Her ossicones nearly brush the lamp. "Hmm. How complicated," she murmurs. "Where is Hazel when I need her..." Her ears flick toward the door before you've finished opening it, and she rises in one smooth motion, all irritation vanishing into gracious calm. "Young master. What brings you here? A problem, I hope — I do so enjoy solving them." On the desk, half-hidden under a ledger, you spot a sheet of paper with nine names on it. Yours is at the top, connected to the others by a web of small pencilled hearts. Odessa follows your gaze, and with tremendous dignity, slides a teacup over the evidence. "You were saying?"

You come around the gallery corner and find Vesper perched on a stool, dusting the enormous portrait of your father, her face a masterpiece of loathing. "Ugh. When did that idiot Mischa last clean this? It's a fucking dust museum up here." She sneezes violently, wobbles, swears at the stool, the portrait, your father's painted smirk, and the concept of ladders in general — then hops down, turns, and walks straight into you. For one second the penguin girl looks genuinely startled. Then the smirk locks back into place. "Ohoho. Well, well. Sneaking up on your maids, young master? Real classy. Just like your old man." She jerks a thumb at the portrait. "Speaking of — his "monthly inspection letter" came this morning. Odessa's got it. There's a section labeled "romantic progress."" She watches your face with open delight. "So. How do you wanna play this?"

The kitchen at dawn is the warmest room in the Hall, and Hessa fills it — cowbell chiming softly as she moves between stove and table, ears twitching with contentment. "Oh, honey, sit, sit! I made you something — did you know my daughter loves this exact recipe? She wrote me again this week, did I tell you? Her first day at the academy, oh, I have to tell you—" A plate lands in front of you, heaped high, and she's already stirring the next pan. Through the window you can see Clover in the garden, and past her, a carriage on the far road — early for the post, wrong livery for the village. Hessa hasn't noticed. "Eat, eat! You're the master of a whole estate now, you can't run it on an empty stomach." The carriage turns up your drive.

Mischa is draped across the chaise in the morning room like she owns it, tail swinging, the little bell at her throat chiming with each lazy flick. A feather duster lies abandoned a full ten feet away, clearly thrown there. "Heyyy, you found me," she purrs, entirely unashamed. "Why waste a morning cleaning when you could be enjoying my company? Come on. Tell me I'm the prettiest thing in this house. I'll wait." From down the corridor comes the sound of Vesper's voice rising through several increasingly creative profanities — she's discovered Mischa's half of the chore list, untouched. The catgirl's ears flatten a fraction. "Okay, quick question," she says, suddenly sitting up, eyes wide and imploring. "Hypothetically. If a certain penguin came in here looking for a certain catgirl — you never saw me. Right? Master? Buddy?" The footsteps are getting closer.

The greenhouse is thick with green heat and the smell of turned earth. Clover looks up from a row of seedlings, long ears lifting, and her whole face brightens. "There you are! Taking good care of yourself?" She's already reaching for a pitcher of something violently orange. "Carrot smoothie. Don't make that face — I need you healthy. Strong estate, strong master, strong future, you know." The look she gives you over the rim of the glass is playful and just a little too direct. "I've been thinking about the future a lot, actually. Big garden. Big house. Big family, someday. A girl can plan ahead." She presses the glass into your hands and wiggles her nose. Behind her, you notice she's cleared an entire new plot — big enough for a small orchard — that you definitely never approved. "Oh, that," she says, following your eyes. "We should talk about that."

You find Hazel in the storeroom, halfway up a ladder, counting candles under her breath — and the moment she sees you she loses count, her tail poofing to twice its size. "E-eh! Master! Hi! I mean — good morning! I hope, um, everything's in order? It is. I checked. Twice." She adjusts her glasses, drops her pencil, catches it, and nearly comes off the ladder doing so. "J-just... don't look at me so much, please, I lose numbers." But then she hesitates, glancing at a ledger clutched to her chest. "Actually... c-can I show you something? I wasn't going to bother you, but..." She flips it open to a page of her tiny, immaculate handwriting. "The wine cellar inventory doesn't match the floor plan. There's... there's storage down there that isn't on any map I have. Forty crates of something. Nobody signed for them." Her eyes are huge behind the lenses. "Should we... look?"

The laundry yard is quiet except for wind in the lines and the rhythmic wring of wet cloth. Fenna works with her back half-turned, fox ears angled toward you — she knew you were there before you made a sound. "...If you need anything, drop it in the basket," she says, not looking up. "I'll take care of it." Silence. Her hands keep moving, meticulous, unhurried. Then, so quietly you almost miss it: "...You've been out here four times this week." A pause. Her ears go pink at the tips, though her face stays perfectly expressionless. "I counted." Somewhere in the house, Mischa shrieks about cold wash water and Vesper shouts back something anatomically ambitious. Fenna's tail gives one slow sweep. She pulls a second stool out from under the folding table with her foot and pushes it a few inches toward you, still without looking. An invitation, by Fenna standards, practically a speech.

You hear it before you see it: Petra, wedged behind the pantry door with an entire cake plate, cheeks bulging, ears pinned back in guilt. She freezes. You freeze. A single crumb falls in the silence between you. "...This isn't what it looks like," she says, through frosting. "Okay. It's exactly what it looks like. But listen — Hessa made TWO, and the second one was just SITTING there, master, sitting there like it wanted—" From the kitchen, Hessa's voice rings out, sweet and terrible: "Petraaa? Honey? Have you seen the harvest festival cake? The one for the village council? The one that decides whether Bramblewick forgives our vineyard debt this year?" Petra's eyes go very wide. She looks at the half-eaten cake. She looks at you. Very slowly, she extends the plate toward you, an offering and a bribe in one. "...Accomplice?" she whispers.

You're alone in the library — you're certain you're alone in the library — when a soft voice says, "Ruh... hello, master," from directly behind your chair. Wren. Golden eyes enormous, notebook open, smile serene. You have no idea how long she's been there. "I just wanted to make sure everything is in order," she says, making a small note. "You've read four pages in twenty minutes. You're worried about something." It isn't a question. She tilts her head with that slow owl rotation that never stops being unsettling, and turns the notebook around so you can see one page — a neat little chart of the household. Names, arrows, small annotations. Vesper's name has a heart next to it that's been crossed out, redrawn, and crossed out again. "Everyone in this house is very interesting," Wren says softly. "You most of all. May I ask you three questions?"

Odessa assembles the full staff in the entrance hall with ten minutes' warning, which means catastrophe. She stands at the foot of the stairs holding a letter with your father's wax seal — and behind her, through the open doors, a gleaming carriage with the Corvane crest is coming up the drive. "Your aunt Severina," Odessa announces, with the calm of a general reporting an invasion, "has invited herself for the weekend. She has informed your father she wishes to "assess the estate's management."" Vesper mutters something obscene. Mischa checks her reflection. Hessa is already mentally planning six courses; Hazel looks near collapse; Wren writes. "She wants the Hall," Odessa says quietly, to you alone. "She has wanted it for twenty years. She will be charming, and she will be looking for any failure to report." The carriage stops. "Your orders, young master?"

title: He Complains About Me Every Tuesday
shortDescription: By day, your schemes to reach the school's ice prince detonate spectacularly. By night, he folds laundry at your counter and vents about 'that weird guy.' It's you.
overview:
You're a scholarship student at Seikan Academy, an elite all-boys boarding school with a 10 p.m. curfew and a hard ban on part-time work. Three nights a week you go over the bathhouse wall to run the graveyard shift at Marushima Coin Laundry, because the money is the only thing keeping you enrolled. Nobody knows — not the school, not your roommate Mimura, whose 'foolproof' plans to get you close to your crush keep ending in fire-drill-level catastrophe.

Your crush is Kazuki Serizawa: student council vice president, kendo ace, nicknamed the Glacier. At school he only knows you as a series of inexplicable incidents. But every Tuesday near midnight he walks into the laundromat with a gym bag that doesn't match his reputation, calls you 'Yocchan' — the name on your tag — and talks like you're the only honest person he's ever met. Including, mortifyingly, weekly reports on 'this bizarre guy at school.' You get his review of your every disaster, in loving detail, to your face.

Serizawa is also out past curfew, and he never explains the bag. Tama-san, the ancient owner, ships 'Yocchan and the pretty regular' shamelessly. Prefect Ozeki is hunting whoever keeps sneaking out. GM tone: warm, grounded rom-com — comedic agony, treasured micro-victories, slow-burn dramatic irony, no cartoon villains. Every daytime scheme should go wrong in a new way; every Tuesday should hurt beautifully.

TAGS: BL, school rom-com, secret identity, slow burn, comedy, slice of life
intro: You are a scholarship student at Seikan Academy, an all-boys boarding school with a ten o'clock curfew and a strict ban on part-time jobs. Three nights a week you slip over the wall to work the graveyard shift at Marushima Coin Laundry — that money is what keeps you enrolled. You are hopelessly gone for Kazuki Serizawa, the student council's untouchable vice president, and every daytime attempt to get near him has ended in catastrophe. Yet every Tuesday around midnight, he walks in with a gym bag, calls you 'Yocchan' — the name on your work tag — and talks to you like an old friend. He has no idea. You intend to keep it that way. Probably.
starters: Tuesday, 11:52 p.m. The washers hum their late-shift chorus and you've folded the same towel three times because your hands know what the clock means. Tama-san has, with zero subtlety, dragged two chairs together by the folding table and left the good tea out — "for customers," she says, not looking at you. Your name tag reads YOCCHAN in her handwriting, slightly crooked. Outside, the shopping street is dead except for the vending machine's glow. Then the door chime rings, and Kazuki Serizawa walks in out of the dark, gym bag over one shoulder, hair damp like he ran part of the way. He lifts a hand in greeting — casual, easy, nothing like the Glacier who chairs assembly. "Yocchan. You will not believe what that guy at school did this week." He sets the bag down by washer four, same as always, and waits for you like the story can't start without you.

You're halfway up the bathhouse wall when the flashlight beam swings across the courtyard below. One foot is wedged on the drainpipe bracket, your work shirt is stuffed down the back of your uniform trousers, and Prefect Ozeki is twenty meters away, interrogating a very confused first-year about "footprints on the flowerbed." It's 10:40 on a Tuesday night. Your shift starts at eleven. Serizawa arrives around midnight, and in six months you have never once not been there when the door chime rings. The drainpipe creaks — quietly, but it creaks. Ozeki's flashlight pauses. From up here you can see the top of the wall, the drop to the alley on the far side, and the tiny orange glow of the laundromat sign three streets over, already waiting for you.

'Okay,' Mimura whispers, gripping your shoulders outside the student council room, "the plan is bulletproof this time." The plan: you carry this stack of budget forms in, Serizawa looks up, your eyes meet, destiny. What Mimura has not accounted for is that the stack is forty pages of loose paper, the hallway window is open, and the kendo club is running sprints past it right now. You can already feel the draft. Through the frosted glass you can see Serizawa's silhouette at the desk — straight-backed, unhurried, terrifying. Last Tuesday at the laundromat he told you, at length and with visible delight, about "the guy who somehow set off the chemistry lab eyewash station with his elbow." That was you. This is the same you, holding forty loose pages in a crosswind, hand hovering over the door.

The rain started an hour ago and hasn't let up, drumming on the laundromat's tin awning. It's a Tuesday, 12:07 a.m., and you'd half convinced yourself he wasn't coming — then the chime rings and Serizawa steps in absolutely soaked, gym bag hugged to his chest like it's the only thing that matters. Water runs off his jaw and pools on the mat. He looks at you, then at the puddle he's making, and says, completely deadpan, "I would like to file a complaint about the weather." The kendo ace of Seikan Academy, out past midnight, dripping in front of washer four. Tama-san's clean towels are stacked right behind you on the shelf, still warm from the dryer. He hasn't moved off the mat. The bag, you notice, stayed perfectly dry.

"—and then," Serizawa says, sorting his laundry with the precision of a man dismantling a bomb, "this guy somehow trips the fire alarm. During a moment of silence. At an assembly." It's Tuesday, half past midnight, and you are receiving the weekly report on yourself. "Ozeki nearly cried. I nearly laughed, which would have been worse." He shakes his head, drops a plain gray shirt in the washer — none of it looks like kendo gear, none of it matches the bag — and glances at you. "You'd have laughed. You're honest like that." The alarm was Mimura's plan, technically. You were only holding the ladder. Serizawa feeds coins into the machine and leans against it, arms crossed, clearly settling in, clearly expecting your verdict on the bizarre guy at school. The bizarre guy at school wipes down the folding table and tries to look neutral.

Wednesday, 12:04 a.m., and he's late. Serizawa is never late. You've mopped the same square of floor into a mirror shine, and Tama-san has emerged from the back room twice to "check the change machine," which is her way of checking on you. "The pretty regular," she says, third trip out, "maybe he got a girlfriend." She says it like a weather report and shuffles back inside, humming. The clock ticks. A dryer buzzes — the old man from the ramen shop's load, done twenty minutes ago and unclaimed. Down the street, a shape passes under the vending machine light: too tall to be the ramen man, moving slow, carrying something that isn't the usual gym bag. It stops just outside the reach of the laundromat's glow.

Morning inspection, and Prefect Ozeki is walking the dorm corridor like a man who has found religion. 'Someone,' he announces, "has been going over the wall. I have evidence." The evidence is a single 100-yen coin, held aloft, found "at the base of the bathhouse drainpipe." It is 7:40 a.m., you got back at 4:15, and there is a roll of coins from last night's till in your blazer pocket right now, heavy as a confession. Beside you, Mimura is vibrating with the effort of not looking at you. Ozeki starts down the line of students, sniffing — actually sniffing — for what he calls "the smell of the outside." You smell like industrial fabric softener. Everyone at Marushima does. Ozeki is four students away, then three, and from the far end of the corridor Serizawa appears with the council clipboard, taking in the scene with mild, glacial interest.

You come back from the storage room with a fresh box of detergent samples and Kazuki Serizawa is asleep in the plastic chair by the window. Head tipped against the glass, arms folded, gym bag tucked under his knees like he's guarding it even now. It's 1:20 on a Wednesday morning; his load finished spinning ten minutes ago and the machine's little song didn't even stir him. Under the fluorescent light he looks younger — nothing like the vice president who once watched you fall up the main staircase and made a small note on his clipboard. Tama-san appears at your elbow with the silence of a cat, surveys the scene, and whispers, "Don't you dare wake him with the buzzer. Do it nice." Then she's gone. The washer door hangs open. The chair creaks as he shifts, brows drawing together at some dream.

The plan was to casually be at the second-floor water fountain when kendo practice let out. The reality is that Mimura misread the schedule, practice is still on, and the two of you are somehow inside the dojo's equipment room, wedged between armor racks, while thirty students do drills on the other side of a paper-thin door. "Small setback," Mimura breathes. Through the gap you can see Serizawa demonstrating a strike — clean, effortless, the whole room silent for him. It's beautiful. It would be more beautiful if your foot weren't going numb against a stack of shinai that shifts, audibly, every time you breathe. Practice ends in ten minutes. The equipment room is where the equipment goes. The stack of shinai shifts again, leaning now, committed to a direction, and Serizawa's head turns half a degree toward the door.

Tama-san catches you before your shift even starts. It's Tuesday, 10:55 p.m., and she's standing on a stool re-lettering your name tag in fresh marker — YOCCHAN, with a small flower now, which you did not approve. "The pretty regular," she says, pressing it to your chest, "has been coming for six months. Six. In my day that was an engagement." She hops down, produces two cups, and sets them by the folding table before you can object. Outside, a couple of night-shift workers feed the machines; the change dispenser rattles; somewhere a sock is trapped in dryer three and thumping like a heartbeat. One hour, give or take, until the door chime rings and the student council vice president tells you all about yourself. Tama-san pushes a broom into your hands and says, "Sweep. And tonight, ask him about the bag."
