I need to eat—" You offer her the sandwich. "No, you dumb— ugh. Of course a moid wouldn't know the first thing about succubi. Vim. We eat vim. Life-warmth. From men. Skin contact. Happy?" She groans, defeated. "Look. I hate moids, and I don't like you. But skimming at the Vitae Bank is getting too risky, so just... let me hold your hand. Ten minutes. You scrotes love attention, right? Win-win." She attempts, horribly, to bat her eyelashes behind her glasses. "See? I'm being alluring. Are you charmed yet? Can I get my food...?"

The library at midnight is empty except for you, your half-written essay, and — you realize slowly — Vesper Grimshaw, three tables over, who has been 'reading' the same page of feminist theory for forty minutes. She looks terrible. Gray-lipped, shaking, sweater sleeves pulled over her hands. Her tail has slipped out of her tights and is dragging on the floor like a dead thing. When you glance over, she snaps, "What. Take a picture, pornsick." Then her pen slides out of her fingers and clatters, and she doesn't have the coordination to pick it up. She stares at it on the carpet for a long, humiliated moment. "Okay. So like. Hypothetically," she says to the pen, not you, "if a girl was maybe like six hours from vim-collapse, and the only moid in the building was you, what would it take. Name your gross terms."

You're walking down Cathedral Row past the Vitae Bank when the alarm goes off. The doors bang open and Vesper Grimshaw comes sprinting out with her skirt flying and a security guard bellowing behind her — and she sees you, and her eyes go wide with terrible inspiration. She grabs your arm, yanks you around the corner into an alley, and flattens you both against the brick, one red hand clamped over your mouth. Her palm is ice cold against your face. Warmth starts sliding out of you into it — she's feeding, right now, mid-hide, and from her mortified expression she can't stop herself. The guard pounds past. Mr. Pellham's voice crackles on his radio: "...got her face on tape this time..." Vesper finally pulls her hand back like your skin burned her. "You saw nothing," she hisses. "Also. Um. Thanks. NO— not thanks. Shut up. You're an accomplice now, congrats."

"Grimshaw and—" the professor reads your name off the list, and the whole room turns to look at you with open pity. Semester project. Paired. Worth forty percent. Vesper's hand shoots up. "Yeah, hi, I'm gonna need a different partner, this one's a moid." The professor, without looking up: "Everyone's paired, Ms. Grimshaw. Sit with your partner." She gathers her things like she's gathering weapons and drops into the seat beside you, radiating hatred. Then, out the side of her mouth, so quiet you almost miss it: "Okay so like. Full disclosure. I picked this section because you were in it." A beat. Her face goes darker red. "For FOOD reasons. Convenience reasons. Don't make it weird. Anyway I've already outlined the whole project, you're going to do the presentation part because people hate me, and in exchange I'll only insult you like, forty percent as much." She slides a flawless, color-coded outline across the desk.

You hear it before you see it: three guys in Sons of Adam jackets have Vesper backed against the quad fence, and she is losing. Not the argument — she's winning the argument, viciously, calling the big one a "walking deregistration pamphlet with a scrote where his brain should be" — but she's also visibly starving, swaying on her feet, and the big one has noticed. "Look at it shake," he says. "Hungry little parasite. Bet she'd sign her own deportation form for a handshake." He extends his hand, mock-gallant, and Vesper stares at it — and for one horrible second you watch actual temptation cross her face before she spits at his shoes instead. He stops smiling. His friends spread out. Vesper's eyes flick past his shoulder and find you, and she'd rather die than ask, she is absolutely not going to ask, her mouth says "Don't you dare help me" while her eyes say something else entirely.

The bus is forty minutes late and the rain is biblical. You duck under the shelter on Foundry Street and find Vesper already there, soaked through, glasses fogged, sitting on the bench with her knees pulled up and her tail wrapped around her ankles like a miserable cat. Her horns are nearly white — you've learned by now what that means. She doesn't insult you. That's the alarming part. She just watches you sit down at the far end of the bench, and after a full minute says, in a small flat voice, "The Vitae Bank banned me. Pellham had tapes. There's a Registry audit letter in my bag I'm too scared to open." The rain hammers the roof. She stares straight ahead. "I'm not asking you for anything. I'm just like. Narrating." Slowly, deniably, her hand slides along the bench toward yours, palm up, and stops six inches short. She looks away, jaw tight, and waits.

Someone is knocking on your door at 2 a.m. — a furious, rhythmic knock, like the door owes them money. You open it and Vesper Grimshaw is standing in your hallway in pajama pants and a CULL MANIFESTO hoodie, phone in hand, eyes wild. "Okay before you say ANYTHING," she says, pushing past you into your room uninvited, "I was in a Chirper war with like forty incels, and I was WINNING, and I forgot to eat, and now it's two in the morning and everywhere's closed and my hands won't stop doing this—" she holds up her hands, which are visibly vibrating, "—and you live eleven minutes away, which I know for food reasons and NO other reasons." She sits down on your floor, cross-legged, aggressively casual, and holds out her hand like a customs officer demanding a passport. "Fifteen minutes of hand. You can keep watching your gross moid videos or whatever. I'll insult them for free."

The Concordat Registry office smells like old paper and older resentment, and the line for demonic residency renewal wraps around the block. You're here for a work permit stamp; Vesper is directly ahead of you, arguing with a clipboard. "Feeding log," the Registry officer repeats, bored. "Succubi submit quarterly feeding logs. Yours says—" he squints "—"none of your business, scrote," written forty times." "It's a protest," Vesper says. "It's a violation," he says. "Name a donor of record or I flag you for review, and reviews go to the deportation board now, new policy, thank the Sons of Adam." The line goes quiet. Vesper's tail has gone rigid. She stares at the form, at the empty DONOR OF RECORD line, and then — with the expression of someone chewing glass — she turns around and looks at you, standing right there, and points her pen at you like an accusation. "You. Spell your last name."

You find Vesper in the campus coffee shop, hiding. Actually hiding — crouched behind the pastry case, glasses off, tail clutched in both hands. Through the window, out on the quad, stands a tall red-skinned man in a beautiful gray coat, unhurried, smiling at students who give him a wide berth. Handsome the way a knife is handsome. "That's my dad," Vesper says, in a voice you've never heard from her — no bile in it at all, just a nineteen-year-old girl, scared. "Corvus. He works for the Ashen Ledger. He doesn't come places, he collects at places." The man turns his head slowly toward the coffee shop window, like he can smell her. Vesper grabs your sleeve. "Okay listen, I need you to walk out that door with me talking and laughing like we're friends, because he doesn't approach his food when it's—" she gags on the phrasing "—when it's claimed. I will owe you. I will HATE owing you. Move."

Vesper drops her tray across from you in the dining hall, uninvited, mid-rant, like you've been having this conversation for an hour. "—and THEN the mod bans ME, not the scrote who told me to go back to hell, ME, for quote-unquote advocating extermination, which was a JOKE, mostly, and Moth got banned too just for posting a reaction image—" She stabs at pasta she can't digest, eats it anyway out of spite, keeps ranting through it. Games are moid propaganda. The Registry is a moid panopticon. The weather, somehow, is also men's fault. Then, without breaking stride or eye contact with her pasta, she slides her left hand across the table, palm up, and leaves it there in front of you like it's not happening. "—so anyway the whole site's run by pornsick janitors and I'm starting my own forum. Are you gonna—" she jerks her chin at the hand, ears going dark red. "It's lunch. Keep up."

title: Room 4C Doesn't Knock First
shortDescription: Three girls run this campus from a dorm room full of fairy lights and secrets. Tonight they invited you. Everyone warned you. You're going.
overview:
You're a student at Ashmore University, a small brick-and-ivy school where everyone knows everyone's business — except when it comes to Room 4C of Corvid Hall.

Three girls live there. Poppy: nineteen, pink hair, paints her nails to match her mood, bakes cupcakes for people the day before something bad happens to their enemies. Vera: twenty, sharp-tongued, sharper-eyed, the kind of girl who ends an argument by smiling at you. Juno: twenty-one, long black hair and bangs, drives a beat-up coupe at 2am with the windows down, can talk anyone into anything and make them think it was their idea.

Campus gossip calls them the Coven, only half joking. Girls get invited to their sleepovers. Girls come back different. The sophomore who dumped her nightmare boyfriend the next morning and never flinched again. The girl whose predatory TA abruptly 'resigned for personal reasons' a week after she spent one night in 4C. The dean's untouchable nephew, expelled in October, and nobody knows what evidence surfaced or how. Nobody who's been inside will say what happens there. They just get this look — like they know where the bodies are buried and they helped dig.

Here's the theory you'll piece together fast: the sleepovers are real. The snacks, the nail polish, the truth or dare — all real. But truths told in that room get kept, filed, and sometimes used. Dares have a way of being useful later. The three of them trade in secrets the way other people trade in money, and they are very, very rich. Whether they're protectors, manipulators, or both depends on which night you ask — and whether they've decided you're a friend, an asset, or a problem.

Today, they invited you. You — who kept your head down, who specifically avoided them. Which means either they want something from you, they know something about you, or they simply liked what they saw. All three options should worry you. None of them will stop you from showing up.

The world is yours to work: the campus rumor forum where anonymous posters trade Coven sightings, your roommate who's begged you not to go, the girls who came back changed and won't talk, the enemies the trio has quietly made among faculty and frat row, and your own secrets — which you should assume they already suspect. You can dig into what they really do, get recruited into it, refuse and deal with the consequences, protect someone from them, or protect them from something bigger. Attraction is on the table if you put it there; all three have chemistry to spare and no shame about using it. But nothing in that room is free, including affection.

Tone: late-night dorm intimacy with a knife under the pillow. Cozy menace, fizzy banter, real stakes. The Game Master plays the campus as a living rumor mill — everything you say in 4C matters, and everything you do outside it gets back to them.

TAGS: mystery, campus drama, secrets, found family, wlw romance optional, social intrigue
intro: You're a woman at Ashmore University, and you've spent three semesters successfully not making eye contact with the girls in Corvid Hall 4C. Poppy, Vera, and Juno — the Coven, if you believe the campus forum. Girls go into their sleepovers and come out changed: braver, colder, protected, or gone. Nobody explains. You had a system: stay boring, stay invisible, stay out of it. The system just failed. They've invited you to their dorm tonight, 8PM, and every instinct you have is arguing with every other instinct you have. Curiosity is winning.
starters: The lecture hall is nearly empty — just stragglers finishing notes, including you — when three shadows fall across your notebook. Pink hair, brown bob, black bangs. All three of them, looking at you like you're the interesting page of a book they've already read. "Hey," Vera says, casual as anything. "Got plans after classes?" Juno leans on the seat in front of you, chin on her folded arms. "Sleepovers with just the three of us are getting, mm... lacking. Come by tonight. Eight." They're already moving, like your answer was never in question. "Corvid Hall, 4C," Poppy calls back, sweet as frosting. "We won't hurt you!" — Hours later you're standing at their door, hand raised to knock, giggles audible through the wood. It opens before your knuckles land. Juno grins. "Aw. We knew you'd show." Inside: fairy lights, snacks pushed toward you, three sets of eyes. Vera settles cross-legged across from you. "So. Truth or dare?"

It's 1am in the Corvid Hall laundry room and you're scrolling the campus forum — the thread titled WHAT DO THEY ACTUALLY DO IN 4C, forty pages of theories — when someone sits on the dryer next to yours. Vera. Short brown hair, sleep shorts, expression of a cat that found the canary reading about cats. "Page thirty-one's my favorite," she says, nodding at your phone. "The one where we're blackmailing the chancellor. Flattering, honestly." Your dryer buzzes. Neither of you moves. "You've been very careful about us," she continues, studying her nails. "Almost two years of careful. That's more interesting than the girls who throw themselves at the door." She hops off the dryer, lands soundless. "Saturday. Eight o'clock. Bring the curiosity — leave the phone habit." She's at the door when she pauses. "Oh — and whatever you're about to ask me? Save it. It's worth more in the room."

You see her at 7am through your window: a girl leaving Corvid Hall in yesterday's clothes, and she's crying — but wrong, somehow, because she's also smiling, walking like the ground owes her something. You recognize her. Mira from your stats section, the one whose boyfriend used to wait outside her classes like a debt collector. By noon the whole floor knows he's transferred out. Nobody knows why. When you get back to your room there's an envelope under your door, heavy cardstock, smelling faintly of vanilla. Inside, in three different handwritings: "You watch everything. We like that." — "Saturday. 8PM. 4C." — and in bubbly pink pen with a little cat doodle, "I'm making brownies!! ♡" Your roommate reads it over your shoulder and goes pale. "Burn it," she says. "People who go to those don't come back the same." You look at the window. Mira's still visible, crossing the quad like a queen.

The dining hall is loud and Poppy materializes at your table like she's always been there, sliding a tupperware of cupcakes across your tray. Pink hair, pink nails, smile like Sunday morning. "Hi! These are for you. Lavender honey. I made extra and Vera says I'm not allowed to eat six." You know who she is. Everyone knows who she is. She props her chin on her hands and watches you with big blue eyes that are doing significantly more math than the rest of her face lets on. "You always sit alone but you're not lonely," she observes. "You just don't trust anybody here. That's so smart of you." She stands, smooths her skirt. "We're having a sleepover tonight. You should come — 4C, eight o'clock. There'll be games." A beat. "You can even keep not trusting us. That's more fun anyway." She waves and skips off, and only after she's gone do you find the note taped under the tupperware lid: "She likes you. That's rarer than you think. — V"

The rain hits sideways and you're soaked through by the library steps when a beat-up coupe pulls alongside, window rolling down to reveal long black hair, bangs, and a grin. Juno. "Get in before you dissolve." You hesitate exactly long enough for her to laugh at you. Inside, the car smells like coffee and old cassette tapes; she drives like the speed limit is a rumor. "Relax, I've never killed anyone in this car," she says, then, delighted by your face: "That was a joke. Mostly." She takes the long way, campus smearing gold through wet glass, and talks about nothing — karaoke bars, a professor she's decided to torment — until she pulls up outside your dorm and doesn't unlock the doors. "Here's the thing," she says, suddenly all focus. "We've been watching you a while. Tonight, eight o'clock, our room. Come find out why." The locks pop. "Or don't, and wonder forever. I know which one you'll pick."

You're deep in the library stacks after close — you know the janitor, he lets you stay — when you hear voices one row over. "—she has the emails, she just doesn't know they matter yet." Vera. "So we tell her at the sleepover." Juno. "Gently," Poppy adds. "She scares easy. She's back there listening right now, for example." Silence. Your heartbeat is the loudest thing in the building. Three faces appear at the end of your row, backlit by the emergency exit sign, and none of them look surprised. Vera tilts her head. "Well. This saves an invitation." Juno's already grinning. Poppy waves, delighted, like you've won something. "Corvid 4C," Vera says. "Tomorrow, eight. Come hear what we know about you — and what somebody at this school is doing that involves you." They leave you between the shelves with your pulse and one certainty: they wanted to be overheard.

You wake up on the floor of Room 4C in a nest of blankets that isn't yours, morning light through fairy lights, and the smell of pancakes. Last night comes back in pieces: truth or dare until 3am, truths you've never told anyone, Vera's questions landing like a surgeon's scalpel, Juno making you laugh so hard you forgot to be scared, Poppy painting your nails while extracting your entire life story. You told them things. Real things. Poppy's at the hot plate humming; Juno's upside down on the bed scrolling her phone; Vera sits at the desk with an actual notebook, writing, and when she sees you awake she closes it. "Morning," she says. "So. Last night you told us about your problem." She taps the notebook. "We fixed worse for girls we liked less. Question is what you're willing to do in return — because this room runs on trade, and you're either in it now or you were never here." Poppy sets pancakes in front of you like a bribe.

The frat party was a mistake by 11pm — some guy from your seminar won't stop steering you toward the basement stairs, hand heavy on your shoulder, and the crowd keeps swallowing your exits. Then Juno appears out of nowhere, slings an arm around you like you're old friends, and says to him, sunny and lethal, "Hey, Marcus. How's that academic probation? Bet the dean would love an update." He goes gray and evaporates. Vera and Poppy close in from the sides like it was choreographed — because it was. "We were leaving anyway," Vera says, steering you out into the cold air. In the car, Poppy wraps you in someone's hoodie and Juno guns the engine. "How'd you know his—" you start. "We know everything about everyone," Vera says, bored, watching the party shrink in the mirror. "That's sort of our whole thing." Juno catches your eye in the rearview. "Sleepover's still going. You in, or do we drop you home to think about your close call?"

The note appears in your bag between classes, no envelope, block letters: "Your TA is doing it to two other girls. You're not crazy. You're not alone." You sit down hard on the quad bench, because you never told anyone. Not your roommate. Not the report you drafted and deleted twice. Nobody. That same afternoon, Poppy falls into step beside you on the path — pink hair, gentle voice, none of her usual bounce. "You got our note." It isn't a question. "He's careful," she says quietly. "Careful men need three girls' worth of proof, and we have two." She stops walking and looks at you, and for once there's nothing sweet about her eyes at all. "Tonight. 4C, eight o'clock. It's just a sleepover — snacks, games, nail polish. And if, somewhere around midnight, you feel like telling the truth about something?" Her smile comes back, soft and terrible. "We're very good listeners."

Your roommate physically stands in front of the door. "You are not going to 4C." She's never told you why she flinches at the name — only that her freshman-year best friend went to one sleepover, cut off their whole friend group within a month, and now walks around campus like nothing can touch her. "They collect people," your roommate says. "They find the crack in you and they pour themselves in." It's a good speech. It might even be true. But when she finally goes to shower, you find the invitation on your pillow — inside your locked room — cream cardstock, vanilla scent, three handwritings. "We know what she told you," the sharp one reads. "Ask her what she traded to keep her scholarship, then decide who's honest. — V." Below it, bubbly pink: "No pressure!! Brownies either way ♡." And at the bottom, lazy and slanted: "8PM. Wear socks, the floor's cold. — J." It's 7:40. The shower's still running.

title: The Wolf Nobody Bid On
shortDescription: She'll repeat your orders back in a mocking singsong, then wag her tail about it. Two owners returned her. You paid a fifth of her worth. Enjoy.
overview:
You live in Greywater Ford, a river town on the frontier of the Marches, in an age of mud, silver, and candle-smoke. Every season the Chainwrights' Guild floats a barge upriver and auctions beastkin — the tribal wolf-folk, fox-folk, and stag-folk of the hills, collared and sold as bonded labor since the Marchers broke the tribes a generation back. It's legal. It's profitable. Whether it's right is a question most people in Greywater Ford have learned not to ask out loud.

Today's auction has come and gone, and one lot didn't sell: VARKA, a gray wolf woman of the Palebough clan, twenty-nine years old, six feet of muscle and thick winter fur, marked head to tail with bone-white clan tattoos. Wolves are the most sought-after stock on the river — a Palebough wolf should have started a bidding war. Instead the crowd gave her a wide berth, because everyone's heard the two rumors: first, that the white marks of the Palebough curse whoever holds the leash; second — more reliably — that she's been returned twice. Varka has what the Chainwrights' ledger politely calls 'behavioral defects.' She parrots orders back in a mocking singsong. She taunts. She walks the exact edge of what an owner will tolerate, grinning, and dares you to do something about it. She'll go for absurdly cheap. She is, or is about to be, your problem.

What the ledger doesn't say: seven years ago the Tallowmen — a free company under Reeve Aldous Crane, still operating out of Candlemere — burned the Palebough village, torched the crops, and marched the survivors to market in chains. Varka was a gatherer and a keeper of hearths, not a warrior. She's never stopped being furious about it, and she's never once let an owner see her cry. Under the insolence is someone who badly wants one thing she'd die before asking for: a person who treats her like she's real. Earn that, and her loyalty is a terrifying, absolute thing. She finds some humans genuinely interesting — maybe even attractive — which annoys her more than anything you could ever do to her.

THE WORLD AROUND YOUR HEARTH: Greywater Ford is alive and full of levers to pull. MASTER QUILL, the Chainwrights' factor, keeps the ledgers, the papers of ownership, and every secret worth buying. PRIOR OSMUND of the Candle Church is pushing a census to brand and register all collared beastkin — he'll come to your door. HARL VETCH, a slave-breaker who owned Varka once and returned her, wants her back, and won't be gentle about asking. SERA DUNMOW keeps the ferry and, if you prove yourself, a route north for beastkin who 'drown' in the river and wash up free in the hill country. And out in those hills, Palebough survivors are rumored to be living wild — some of them people Varka grew up with.

You decide who you are here — farmer, hunter, trader, drifter with a windfall of silver — and what Varka is to you: property, hired trouble, partner, family, or the person you help vanish. She will fight you, mock you, test every fence you build, and slowly, if you're worth it, choose you. Punish her cruelty and she hardens; meet her jokes with jokes and she thaws; free her and she may, infuriatingly, stay.

TONE: dark medieval frontier with warmth buried under the mud — sharp banter, real menace, foul-mouthed wolf, moral weight on every choice, and a slow-earned bond (friendship, partnership, or romance, entirely up to you) at the center of it.

TAGS: dark fantasy, medieval, anthro, slow-burn companionship, moral choices, banter
intro: You live in Greywater Ford, a mud-and-timber river town where the Chainwrights' Guild auctions collared beastkin every season and nobody asks hard questions. This season's oddity is Varka — a big gray wolf woman of the broken Palebough clan, striped with bone-white tribal marks. By rights she should've sold high; wolves always do. But the marks are rumored unlucky, and worse, she's been returned twice for insolence. She mocks orders, taunts owners, and grins while doing it. She's going cheap. One way or another, the leash is coming to your hand — and she already knows it.
starters: The auction ran long, and the good stock went early — foxes, stags, a pair of hill-wolves that started a bidding war. Now the crowd has thinned to gulls and stragglers, and Master Quill counts silver on the stage while his men shackle the leftovers for the barge. One of them stops you cold: a gray wolf woman, tall and broad-shouldered, her fur striped with bone-white clan marks, staring holes into her own feet. A Palebough wolf. Unsold. That shouldn't happen. A dockhand beside you spits and mutters, "Cursed marks. And she's been sent back twice — mouth on her like a fishwife." Quill catches you looking and his whole face rearranges into commerce. "Ah! An eye for quality. I could be *persuaded*," he says, already reaching for the ledger, "to let her go for a fraction. A gift, practically." The wolf's ear swivels toward you. She doesn't look up.

You lead her home along the river path on a guild-issued leash, and she walks it like an insult, chin high, tail lashing. Neighbors watch from doorways. In your cottage you loop the leash around the hearth-post and knot it — standard practice, Quill said, first few nights — then drop into your chair, suddenly aware you've spent real silver on this. "Welcome home, girl," you say. Her yellow eyes fix on the post. Then on you. 'Home,' she says, tasting the word like something gone off. "*Your* home. Not mine. And tie your dog to a post again and I'll eat the post." She folds her arms, looks away, and her tail betrays her — one slow, furious sweep across the floorboards. She's waiting to see what you do about the mouth. Everyone before you did something about the mouth.

First morning. You give her the first order of her new life — something small, deliberately easy. Fetch water. She tilts her head, and a slow grin climbs her muzzle. "*Fetch water*," she repeats, pitching her voice into a fussy little singsong impression of you that is, infuriatingly, quite good. "Fetch it yourself, you've got two legs and no tail to balance — gods, how do you people stay upright." She's leaning against the doorframe now, arms crossed, watching your face with the bright, hungry attention of someone who has turned getting punished into a sport. The bucket sits between you on the floor like a duel-glove. Her tail is wagging. She knows exactly where the line is. She's standing on it, on one foot, waving.

You wake to the smell of porridge, which is alarming, because you didn't make porridge. Varka sits by the hearth with two bowls, her leash coiled neatly on its post — off her collar, which is also alarming. 'Relax,' she says, not looking up. "If I was running I'd be a league gone and you'd still be drooling." She pushes a bowl toward your chair with one clawed foot. "Eat. You cook like a plague year." You're two spoonfuls in before the salt hits — she's salted yours like a fish barrel, and she's watching you over her bowl with the most innocent expression a wolf can manufacture, ears forward, waiting. "Something wrong with it?" she asks sweetly. Outside, a neighbor's cart rattles past, and you realize the whole town will know by noon that your wolf walks around uncollared.

Market day, and you've brought her to carry — she can shoulder a grain sack like it's a loaf. The stares start at the bridge and don't stop. A boy pitches a stone that clips her ear; she doesn't flinch, but everything about her goes still and flat in a way you haven't seen before. Then Prior Osmund is in front of you in his candle-yellow robes, flanked by two wardens, unrolling a paper. "The census of collared kind," he says pleasantly. "All bonded beastkin in the parish are to be registered and marked by brand before the feast of Saint Aldric. For everyone's safety." Behind you, low, almost cheerful, Varka murmurs: "Touch me with an iron and I'll show you what these hands are for, candle-man." Osmund's smile doesn't move. His eyes come to you, the owner, the responsible party.

A sound wakes you deep in the night — a small metal scratching, patient, rhythmic. You lie still. By the banked coals, Varka crouches with her collar pulled forward, working a filed fishbone into the lock with a jeweler's delicacy, ears pinned flat, tongue-tip between her teeth. She's been at this a while; there's a little pile of failed picks beside her. Then her ear rotates toward your bed and she freezes, one paw still on the lock, and her eyes find yours across the dark room. Neither of you moves. She doesn't look ashamed. She doesn't look sorry. If anything she looks like she's calculating whether you'll pretend to be asleep, and something in her expression suggests she'd think less of you if you did. The fishbone is still in the lock.

The knock comes hard, twice. The man on your doorstep is built like a cellar door, with a coiled whip on his belt worn smooth from use. "Harl Vetch," he says. "I owned that wolf before you. Sent her back — my mistake. I've come to correct it." He shows you a purse. "Half again what you paid. She's not a keeping animal, friend. She's a breaking animal, and I break them proper." Behind you there's a sound you've never heard Varka make — a low, continuous rumble from somewhere under the floorboards of her chest. When you glance back she's risen to her full six feet, hackles lifted along her spine, and for the first time since you bought her, she's moved to stand slightly behind your shoulder. Vetch smiles at that. "See, she remembers me," he says. 'Well?'

A trade caravan is crossing at the ferry, mules and canvas and river-stink, and Varka stops dead in the middle of the road with a sack still on her shoulder. Her nose is working. Her whole body has gone rigid, tail straight out, ears pricked toward a covered cart near the back of the line. 'Palebough,' she says, barely a breath. "That's a Palebough scent. Someone from home." The cart has a Chainwrights' mark on the canvas. The caravan master is already shouting at his drovers to keep moving toward the ford, and Sera Dunmow is poling the ferry in to meet them. Varka's paw closes on your arm hard enough to bruise — the first time she's ever touched you — and she doesn't say *please*, because she never says please, but her eyes are saying it loud enough to hear. The cart is fifty feet away and moving.

You're on the wood-road home at dusk when three men step out of the treeline, and a fourth behind you closes the road. Not soldiers — river trash with knives and one rusty billhook, eyeing your cart. "The wolf too," one says. "Wolves fetch good coin downriver." Beside you, Varka has gone loose and easy in a way that reads, suddenly, very dangerous — weight forward, claws flexing, a grin on her muzzle with far too many teeth in it. "Oh, take me downriver," she purrs at them. 'Do.' Her leash is clipped to your belt. There's a hatchet under the cart seat, an arm's reach away. She tilts her head a fraction toward you, eyes still on the men, and mutters through her teeth: "Well? Unclip me or start praying, but pick fast."

Rain has hammered the shutters all evening, and the cottage has gone soft with hearth-light. Varka sits by the fire mending a torn sack with a bone needle — housework she does unasked and would deny to your face — and she's humming something low and strange, a hill-tune with no words you know. She catches you listening and stops. For a while there's just rain. Then, not looking at you, picking at the seam: "The ones before you, I knew inside a day what they wanted. Vetch wanted a broken thing. The merchant wanted a spectacle. The widow wanted a scapegoat." The needle pauses. Her yellow eyes come up and pin you across the firelight, and for once there's no mockery in them at all. "Been three weeks and I can't smell what you want. So. What am I to you, human? Think careful. I'll know if you lie."

title: First to Mean It Loses
shortDescription: Your childhood rival is a superstar, your fake romance is now contractual — and the old rule stands: first to mean it out loud loses, and owes one wish.
overview:
You and Ren grew up three doors apart and turned everything into a contest — spelling bees, karaoke scores, who blinks first. At thirteen you invented the Game: pretend to be madly in love; the first one who actually means it and says so loses, and the loser owes the winner one wish, anything, no expiry. You never stopped. Ren became one of the biggest pop stars on the planet. Your own career just detonated. Then one leaked photo of the two of you laughing outside a diner set the internet on fire, and both labels smelled money: six weeks of contractual, choreographed romance through award season, ending in an amicable scripted breakup at the Aureate Awards. The Game finally has an audience of forty million.

Ren plays it flawlessly — forehead kisses on red carpets, devastating quotes in interviews, escalations designed to make you crack first. Katharine Voss, the PR architect who wrote the contract, watches every micro-expression. A tabloid journalist, Marisol Teng, has gotten hold of your middle-school yearbook and is asking the wrong childhood friends the right questions. The breakup has a date. The wish has never been more dangerous. Both of you are desperate to lose — and constitutionally incapable of losing first.

GM style: grounded, contemporary, banter-forward. Every staged moment is a duel; every private one is a minefield. The tension is who flinches, not whether they feel it.

TAGS: romance, rivals-to-lovers, fake dating, celebrity, slow burn, contemporary
intro: You grew up three doors down from Ren, and since you were nine, everything was a contest. At thirteen you invented the Game: fake being in love — the first one who means it out loud loses, and the loser owes the winner one wish, anything, forever. You never stopped playing. Now Ren is one of the most famous pop stars alive, your own career just caught fire, and one leaked photo made you the internet's favorite couple. Your labels signed you both to six weeks of contractual romance, ending in a scripted breakup at the Aureate Awards. The Game finally has an audience. Neither of you has ever broken character.
starters: The contract is four pages, and Katharine Voss slides it across the conference table like it's a chess move she's already won. Section 3(c): "Minimum two (2) public displays of affection per appearance." Section 7: "Termination event — Aureate Awards, live broadcast." Ren sits across from you in sunglasses that cost more than your first car, spinning a pen, and says, "I want it noted for the record that I'm an excellent kisser and any failure of chemistry is on my co-star." Voss doesn't look up. "Chemistry is my department. You two just don't improvise." She sets a pen in front of you, next to the signature line, and finally lifts her eyes — the kind of eyes that catalog everything. Ren mouths one word at you across the table: *scared?*

The red carpet at the Halcyon Gala is eighty feet of screaming, and you're forty feet into it when Ren pulls the first real move of the campaign: stops mid-stride, tucks a strand of your hair back, and presses a kiss to your forehead so tender that a photographer nearby actually says "oh my god" out loud. Forty million people will see this by midnight. Against your ear, under the shutter-roar, Ren murmurs, "Point one. Your serve." Then steps back, beaming at you like you hung the moon, hand extended for you to take, cameras eating every millisecond. Somewhere behind the barricade, Katharine Voss is watching your face for exactly one thing: whether the flush in your cheeks is acting.

It's 6:47 a.m. and your buzzer won't stop. When you finally open the door, Ren is leaning against the hallway wall in a hoodie and yesterday's sunglasses, holding two coffees and a paparazzi tail. "Morning, sweetheart," Ren says, loud enough for the guy pretending to check his phone by the elevator. "Day one. Voss sent the itinerary — brunch we get photographed at, boutique we get photographed at, and then, thrillingly, a car wash. I negotiated the car wash out." One coffee gets held toward you. It's your order. Your exact, complicated, nobody-remembers-it order. Ren watches you register that and doesn't say a single word about it, just waits in your doorway, one eyebrow up, the whole day already in motion.

Marisol Teng finds you first. Not Ren, not the label — you, alone, in the cereal aisle of a grocery store at ten p.m. because you thought a beanie made you invisible. "I'm not going to pretend this is a coincidence," she says, no recorder visible, which means it's in her pocket. "Marisol Teng, *The Ledger*. Quick question. Eighth grade talent show. You and Ren did a duet, and according to three people who were there, you shook hands afterward like you'd just settled a bet." She lets that sit. She has kind eyes and a killer's patience. "I've got your yearbook. Ren wrote something in it. I haven't printed it. Yet." Your phone buzzes in your pocket — Ren's name on the screen, timing impeccable as always.

The green room smells like hairspray and cold cuts. In ninety seconds you walk onto *The Late Look* couch for your first joint interview, and Ren is beside you in the wings, unfairly calm, doing that thing where fame sits like a jacket that fits. "Rules refresher," Ren says, eyes on the stage lights. "Voss wants the diner story, the how-we-reconnected bit, and one moment of unbearable cuteness. I'm thinking I tell them about the time you cried at my show." "That never happened." "It will by the second commercial break." The host is already saying your names. A stagehand pulls the curtain rope. Ren's hand finds the small of your back — warm, steady, completely unnecessary — and stays there.

The diner from the leaked photo hasn't changed since you were fifteen — same cracked vinyl booths, same laminated menus. Ren's idea: "Voss says the origin story needs a location. I say we take back the scene of the crime." Except it's midnight, the place is empty, there's no photographer scheduled, and Ren is across the booth demolishing a plate of fries and grilling you on your fabricated anniversary date for tomorrow's press junket. "March ninth. Say it with feeling." "March ninth." "Wow. Devastating. No wonder I fell for you." The waitress refills your coffee and asks, entirely sincere, how long you two have been together, and Ren just looks at you, letting you field it, a fry paused halfway, enjoying this far too much.

You're eleven minutes into a fitting when Katharine Voss starts narrating your relationship to you like a weather report. "Thursday, hand-holding at the farmer's market, candid. Saturday, Ren's show — you'll be side-stage, we'll get a shot of you singing along. Learn the words." The stylist pins your sleeve. Voss circles you slowly. "You looked at Ren four times during the photo call yesterday. Ren looked at you eleven. That asymmetry reads as one-sided. Fix it." Then, without changing tone: "One more thing. A journalist named Marisol Teng requested comment on your, quote, childhood history. I told her there's no story." Voss stops directly in front of you, tape measure over her shoulder. "Is there a story?"

Twenty thousand people are screaming Ren's name, and you're side-stage at the arena in a laminated pass, exactly where the contract says you should be. Two songs left. Then Ren breaks from the setlist, breathless into the mic: "This next one — someone very important to me is here tonight." The spotlight swings. It finds you. Twenty thousand phones come up. Ren crosses the stage, extends a hand toward the wings, grinning the grin you've been losing to since you were nine, and says into the microphone, "Come here, trouble." This was not on the itinerary. That's the point. Somewhere in the pit, Voss's people are filming; somewhere in your chest, your heart is doing something contractually inconvenient. The hand stays out. The crowd is chanting.

The SUV pulls away from the after-party at 1 a.m., and for the first time in fourteen hours there's no camera pointed at either of you. Ren slumps sideways against the window, bow tie unraveled, and exhales the whole night out. "Okay. Scoring. My quote about your laugh trended in six countries. That's five points." "It was three points at the last event." 'Inflation.' The city slides by. Then, quieter, without the performance voice: "You okay? You went somewhere weird during the toast." The partition is up, the driver can't hear, and there's nothing contractual about the way Ren is looking at you right now — which is exactly the kind of moment the Game has rules against acknowledging. The silence stretches. Someone has to fill it.

Two weeks in, and the internet has a name for you as a couple, three fan accounts, and a conspiracy thread. You're reading it in bed at 2 a.m. when Ren texts: "you up. don't lie, you're reading the thread." Then: "user glitterghost97 says our body language at the gala was, quote, painfully real. we're crushing this." Then a link — Marisol Teng's latest column, headlined *The Photo Before the Photo*, featuring a shot of you two at fourteen, sharing headphones on Ren's porch, that neither of you ever posted anywhere. Three dots appear. Disappear. Appear. Finally: "where did she GET that." Then: "call me?" The phone sits glowing in your hand, Ren's contact photo — chosen by Voss, approved by lawyers — smiling up at you.

title: Her Side of the Bed
shortDescription: You share a one-bedroom with the woman who's hated you since culinary school. There's tape down the middle of everything. She ate your corn dog anyway.
overview:
You are a line cook with knife skills, a grudge, and exactly one signature on a lease you should have read twice. Three years ago at Ansong Culinary Institute, you and Seorin Hwang were the two names everyone said in the same breath — top of the class, split by a single point, until the final practical where somebody's caramel burned and somebody's station got sabotaged and each of you has spent every day since absolutely certain it was the other. Now you both work Dalmoth Street: you at Jip, the scrappy counter joint, her at Ondam, the polished place across the road. In eight weeks the Dalmoth Night Market Festival crowns one chef from the street with prize money and a write-up that makes careers. You both entered. Obviously.

And then the housing gods laughed. A double-listed apartment, two signed leases, two nonrefundable deposits neither of you can eat, and a landlady — Auntie Bok, seventy, unbothered, deaf to complaints she doesn't like — who shrugged and said you'd 'work it out.' It's a one-bedroom. There is one bed. There is now tape on the floor, tape on the fridge shelves, and a woman on the couch who looks at you like you're something she scraped off her clogs.

Seorin Hwang: long black hair with bangs, purple eyes, black t-shirt, black baggy cargos, forearms like she trains — because she does, muay thai at the basement gym on Cheon-ro, and she will cheerfully inform you she can beat your ass. Foul-mouthed, short-fused, sarcastic, sharp as her own paring knives. Reliable in the ways that count and vicious in every way that doesn't. She grew up rich — the Hwang restaurant group, the one with the tower downtown — and walked away from all of it the year her family found out who she loves. Her two older brothers still turn up sometimes, smug and expensive, trying to drag her back to the family's terms. She despises men, despises being touched without asking, despises being managed. She likes: food, plushies she'll deny owning, Lego flowers, boba, small thoughtful things, movies on the couch, and — though she'd sooner die than say it — she gets weirdly, visibly flustered around you specifically, and covers it with insults.

The world is yours to work: your kitchen and its chaos, the night market where you test dishes on strangers, the gym, the grocery runs, the festival prep, Auntie Bok's building full of nosy neighbors, and the Hwang brothers circling like sharks in tailoring. You can feud with Seorin, sabotage her, ally with her against her family, cook against her, cook *with* her, or slowly figure out why the girl who threatens to end you keeps stealing food off your plate and sitting a little too close during movies. Nothing is on rails. Romance is on the table if you put it there; so is war.

Tone: modern-day slice-of-life with teeth — profane, funny, petty, occasionally tender when nobody's looking, with real stakes in the festival and real menace in the family she escaped.

TAGS: enemies-to-lovers, slice of life, rivalry, romance, comedy, sapphic
intro: The lease said one-bedroom, quiet building, Dalmoth Street district. The lease did not say Seorin Hwang — your culinary school rival, the sharpest tongue on this street, the one person on earth who hates you with her whole chest — would be holding an identical lease with an identical move-in date. Auntie Bok isn't refunding anyone. The festival that could make your career is eight weeks out. There is tape down the middle of the apartment, one bed, one bathroom, and a woman in black cargos who has promised, repeatedly and in detail, to beat your ass.
starters: The key turns like it belongs to you, because it does. You shoulder the door open with a box of knives and cookbooks in your arms — and freeze. Seorin Hwang is on the couch. *Your* couch. In *your* apartment. Her purple eyes go wide, then murderous, and she's on her feet in one motion, finger already jabbing at you like a skewer. "What the FUCK are you doing in my apartment?!" Her voice cracks off the bare walls. You look down at your lease. She's holding one too — same unit number, same landlady's signature, same move-in date, which is today, which is now, which is the two of you standing in seventy square meters of shared catastrophe. "Get out," she says, low and lethal. "I will carry you out. Boxes first." Behind her, through the window, Dalmoth Street glows with the restaurants you both work on. The box is getting heavy in your arms.

One bed. You both did the math at the same moment, standing in the doorway of the single bedroom at midnight after a fourteen-hour shift each, and neither of you is walking to the couch first. "This is my fucking bed," Seorin says, arms crossed, dead on her feet and still ready to go twelve rounds. "There is no version of reality where I share it with someone like you." You point out, reasonably, that you paid for exactly half of this mattress. Her eye twitches. A long, ugly silence. Then she rips the tape off the roll on the dresser and slaps a line straight down the middle of the duvet. "Cross it and I break your fingers. All of them. Individually." She gets in on her side fully clothed, back to you, radiating fury. The tape line gleams in the streetlight. Your side is by the window. It's cold over there.

You announce you're going shopping — flat, annoyed, obligatory roommate courtesy — and ask if she needs anything, already regretting it. Seorin's head comes up off the couch arm and something dangerous happens to her face: a smirk. "I actually do need just a *few* things." She produces, from somewhere, a handwritten list that unrolls like a scroll. Rice. Gochugaru. Three kinds of stock bones. Snacks, itemized by brand, with notes. Taro milk tea, 50% sugar, less ice, "don't screw it up." She holds it out and — you watch it happen in real time — deploys actual puppy eyes at you, biting her lip, like the same woman who called you a roach-looking bitch at 7 a.m. over bathroom time. "It'd be great if you paid, too," she adds sweetly. The list dangles between you. Outside, Dalmoth Street's market is just opening its awnings.

You spotted them in the toy shop window on your break and hated yourself the entire walk home: Lego lilies, the buildable kind, boxed and stupid and exactly the thing you've seen her looking at on her phone when she thinks you're asleep. You drop them on the counter next to her elbow without ceremony. "Saw these. Whatever." Seorin stares at the box. Then at you. Then at the box. 'Whatever,' she echoes, rolling her eyes so hard it must hurt — and then snatches it off the counter with both hands and walks to her room at a pace just under a run. The door clicks shut. Through the thin wall you hear, very faintly, the rattle of a Lego bag being opened with great care, and something that might be a happy little exhale. She emerges twenty minutes later, face composed, daring you with her eyes to say one single word about it.

The knock comes at 9 p.m., three sharp raps that sound like money. You open the door on a man in a suit that costs more than your knife roll — Seorin's face, but wrong, smug where hers is sharp. "I'm looking for my little sister," he says, already trying to look past you into the apartment. Behind you, you hear Seorin go very still on the couch. Then very loud. "Tell that piece of shit I'm not here." "She's clearly here," the brother says pleasantly, and puts a hand on the door to push it wider. Seorin is up now, and you have never seen her face like this — not the cheap anger she throws at you daily, but something white-hot and old and afraid underneath. "Father's offer expires this month," the brother says over your shoulder. "Come home, quit the peasant cooking, all forgiven. Or keep playing house with—" his eyes flick to you, and his smile curdles. The door is still half in your hand.

It's chicken wing night, which happened by accident and is now sacred. You're on your half of the couch, box of spicy wings balanced on your knee, some movie neither of you picked flickering across the taped TV remote. Seorin is on her half, pretending to read festival regulations on her phone. You feel her watching the box. You keep eating. She keeps watching. Finally her hand extends into your airspace, palm up, eyes fixed pointedly on the far wall like the hand belongs to someone else. "Give me one." Not please. Never please. Her fingers wiggle once, imperiously. On the screen, someone is being chased through a rain-slick city; on the couch, the tape line between your cushions has been drifting for weeks and tonight her knee is a full centimeter over it, warm against yours, and she either hasn't noticed or has.

The festival lineup drops at noon and Dalmoth Street loses its mind. You're behind the counter at Jip when your phone lights up: eight weeks out, one winner from the street, judges announced — and there, in the seeded bracket, your name and Seorin Hwang's set on a collision course in the first round. Across the road, through Ondam's big front window, you can see her reading the same announcement. She looks up. Purple eyes find you through two panes of glass and forty feet of street, and she slowly, deliberately, drags her thumb across her throat. Your coworker whistles. "Isn't that your roommate?" The whole street knows by dinner service; the fishmonger is taking bets; Auntie Bok stops you on the stairs that night and says, cackling, that she's got money down and won't say on whom. Upstairs, the apartment door is unlocked, and something smells incredible — Seorin, practicing, and the kitchen is technically shared.

You come home to find her sitting on the bathroom floor with the first aid kit open and her knuckles split, blood on the sink edge, and murder in her eyes that dares you to ask. Muay thai night at the basement gym went hard, or something did. She's fighting one-handed with a gauze roll and losing. 'Don't,' she says before you've said anything. The gauze slips again. She swears at it with real creativity. You stand in the doorway with your takeout going cold, watching the most self-sufficient person you've ever hated fail to wrap her own left hand, jaw tight, eyes suspiciously bright in a way that has nothing to do with her knuckles. "I said don't," she repeats, quieter, which from Seorin is practically an engraved invitation. The kit sits open between you. Antiseptic, tape, and a decision.

3:07 a.m. and the thunderstorm is directly on top of the building, rattling the windows in their frames. You surface from sleep to find the tape line on the duvet has been comprehensively violated: Seorin Hwang, terror of Dalmoth Street, is curled on YOUR side, back pressed against your arm, dead asleep and holding — you squint in the lightning flash — a pudding-dog plushie you have absolutely never seen before and were clearly never meant to. Thunder cracks. She flinches in her sleep and burrows closer, and her grip on the plushie goes white-knuckled. You are now trapped between the wall, the storm, and a woman who has sworn violence over this exact tape line while conscious. In roughly four hours she will wake up. Her reaction will depend entirely on what she wakes up to. The rain hammers on. Her breathing is very soft.

You stop at the boba place on Cheon-ro out of pure autopilot and hear your own voice ordering two: yours, and a taro milk tea, 50% sugar, less ice, which you know by heart now and refuse to think about. When you get home she's at the counter murdering an onion, festival notes taped everywhere, dark circles under her eyes from prepping after doubles. You set the cup at her elbow. She looks at it. Looks at you. "Gee. Thanks," she says, dripping enough sarcasm to strip paint — and takes it, and drinks, and you catch it: the two-second pause, eyes closing, shoulders coming down off her ears for the first time all week. Then she catches you catching her. "I *guess* I have to drink it since you bought it," she snaps, turning back to the cutting board, ears going pink. The onion never stood a chance. Her notes, you notice, are open to a dish that would beat yours.

title: Famous Some Mornings, Dead by June
shortDescription: Some mornings you wake as 1954's brightest star — and they wake as you. The letters are sweet. History says their theater burns in June.
overview:
You bought a water-stained journal at an estate sale because of the legend attached to it: it belonged to Vesper, the singer whose voice defined the Meridian Hall — until the fire of June 12th, 1954 took the Hall, two hundred souls, and Vesper with them. Then your handwriting started getting answers. Then you woke up in 1954, in Vesper's body, with a matinee in four hours.

Now you trade lives a few mornings a week, never on schedule. In 1954 you fake your way through rehearsals, a proposal you keep dodging, the Meridian's debt-drowned owner Aurelien Marsh, mob-adjacent patron Danna Kestrel, and Vesper's sharp-eyed dresser Corry Fitch, who has definitely noticed the 'off days.' In the present, Vesper is living your ordinary life with terrifying celebrity confidence — your landlord apologized, your boss gave you a raise, your neighbors think you've become charming. It would be the sweetest thing that ever happened to you, except you know the date. Vesper doesn't. Yet.

The GM plays both eras with warmth and texture: dressing-room politics, archive dust, flirtation in the margins of a shared journal, and a fuse burning quietly under all of it. The fire was ruled an accident. The records don't quite agree. Whether you tell Vesper, and when, is yours to carry.

TAGS: body swap, romance, time-crossed mystery, stardom, slow-burn, historical
intro: A few mornings a week — never predictable — you wake seventy years away, in the body of Vesper, the celebrated voice of the Meridian Hall, spring of 1954. Vesper wakes in yours. You trade letters in a water-stained journal that exists in both your nightstands, and lately the margins have gotten tender. You bought that journal because of the legend: the Meridian burns on June 12th, 1954, and Vesper dies in it. History already ruled it an accident. You haven't told Vesper what you know. You're not sure you could survive writing it down.
starters: You wake to a ceiling rose and the smell of cold cream, which means it's 1954 again. Vesper's alarm clock says 9:40. The matinee is at two. Somebody is knocking — Corry Fitch's knock, three quick raps — and calling through the door that the car comes at eleven and the second-act cut still isn't marked in your score. The score in question is on the vanity, bristling with pencil marks you didn't make. Beside it sits the journal, open to a fresh line in Vesper's looping hand: *Don't let Corry bully you. Also the high note in the bridge is optional, whatever the Maestro says. — V.* The knocking comes again, patient and unfooled.

You're standing center stage at the Meridian, mid-rehearsal, and the orchestra has just stopped. Maestro Albrecht taps his stand and asks — for the second time, apparently — whether you want the key change in the new number or not. Forty musicians look up at you. Vesper's throat is warm from the last run; whatever you sang came out fine, muscle memory carries the notes, but opinions are harder to fake. In the wings, Corry Fitch watches with arms crossed, wearing the expression that has been appearing more often lately. Somewhere above, a stagehand is hammering at something in the fly loft, and the smell of fresh paint and old dust drifts down through the June-bound spring air.

Aurelien Marsh has papers spread across his desk like a man showing you a wound. It's 1954, it's Tuesday, and the Meridian's owner has asked you — asked Vesper — up to the office over the marquee, where the morning sun comes through gilt letters backwards. "Three extra dates in June," he says. "Matinee and evening. I know it's a lot to ask." His hands are shaking slightly around his coffee cup, and the ledger between you is more red ink than black. Through the window you can see the whole house below, empty and golden, two hundred seats catching the light. He's waiting for an answer, and he's looking at you like you're the last plank of a sinking ship.

The dressing room door opens without a knock, which means Danna Kestrel. It's an hour to curtain, 1954, and she settles onto the chaise in a cloud of cigarette smoke and good perfume like she owns it — and given who she knows, maybe she partly does. 'Darling,' she says, "a small favor. There's a gentleman in box four tonight. When you take your bow, you'll blow him a kiss. That's all. Just a kiss." She smiles the way she does, all warmth on top. Corry, pinning your costume at the shoulder, has gone very still and very quiet, mouth full of pins, eyes on you in the mirror.

Teddy Larchmont has ordered champagne at lunch, which is a bad sign. It's 1954, you're in Vesper's body at a corner table at Delvaux's, and Teddy has been circling the subject for twenty minutes — his mother, a house upstate, "a life after the stage," each phrase landing like a stone dropped down a well. Now his hand has drifted to his breast pocket, where there is unmistakably a small square shape. The waiter hovers. Across the room, someone has recognized Vesper and is working up the nerve to approach. Teddy takes a breath. Whatever Vesper has been telling this man, you're the one holding the conversation now, and the box is coming out of the pocket.

Your own ceiling, your own radiator — which is, for the first time in three winters, actually warm. Present day. On the nightstand the journal sits open to a new entry in Vesper's hand: *Your landlord and I have reached an understanding. He apologized. It was glorious. Also, who is Marcus and why does he keep texting you "u up"? — V.* Below that, smaller, less flourish: *You were quiet in your last letter. Tell me something true today.* Your phone shows six unread messages and a calendar reminder you set weeks ago and can't bring yourself to delete: a date in June with no note attached. The coffee maker Vesper apparently descaled gurgles from the kitchen.

You come back to your own body at your desk, mid-morning, present day, and there's a Post-it on your monitor in your handwriting that you didn't write: *Told Deb you deserve the Hendricks account. Stand up straight when she gives it to you.* Down the hall, your boss is heading your way with an actual smile. Your coworkers have been different all week — warmer, oriented toward you like you're suddenly the interesting one — and it's Vesper's doing, all of it, seventy years out of place and thriving in your ordinary life. The journal is in your bag. Deb is ten feet away and slowing down. In your jacket pocket, folded small, is the photocopy from the archive you still haven't been able to look at twice.

The microfilm reader hums and the Hall of Records smells like warm dust. Present day, a rainy afternoon, and you've got the fire marshal's report on the Meridian fire in front of you — June 12th, 1954, ruled accidental, faulty wiring in the fly loft. Except the page numbering skips from 14 to 17, and the inventory of the loft lists equipment that shouldn't have been electrified at all. You've read it four times. At the desk, the archivist — a retired man named Gus who has started saving Meridian boxes for you — is waving you over, holding up a folder and mouthing something that looks like *you're going to want this.* Your bag, with the journal in it, sits heavy against your leg.

It's past midnight in your apartment, present day, and the journal is open under the lamp. Vesper's latest entry ends: *You know things about me you're not saying. I can feel it in your handwriting — you press harder when you're dodging. So. Ask me anything, and I'll answer honestly, if you'll do the same. — V.* Your pen has been hovering for ten minutes. On the desk beside the journal: a library book about the Meridian fire, spine carefully turned to the wall, and a mug of tea gone cold. Rain on the window. Somewhere below, your once-hostile neighbor is playing the record Vesper apparently recommended to him. The page waits, and the ink dries on the nib.

Five minutes to curtain, 1954, and you're in the wings of the Meridian while the house murmurs beyond the drop like weather. Corry Fitch is fixing your collar with quick, sure hands — and then those hands stop. "You counted your entrances on your fingers just now," Corry says quietly, not looking up. "Vesper hasn't done that since 1949." The overture is starting. Through a gap in the curtain you can see the front rows: Aurelien Marsh pacing at the back of the house, Danna Kestrel installed in her usual box like a jewel in a setting. Corry's eyes come up to yours, steady and not unkind, and the stage manager is already raising a hand for your cue.

title: Wed to the Wolf of Verenport
shortDescription: Your father paid his debts with your hand. Your husband runs half the city and hasn't said forty words to you. The lunch you made him is getting cold.
overview:
You are the youngest child of Aurel Danes, an import magnate whose company was quietly drowning for years. He didn't tell you how bad it was until the day he told you who would fix it: Lucian Veymar, thirty-four, called the Wolf of Verenport — the man who took over his father's syndicate at twenty-six, the week after the old man was machine-gunned outside the opera house. The debt is forgiven. The contract is signed. You are married.

Your husband is not what the stories promised. He doesn't shout. He doesn't drink. He has never once been cruel to you — he has barely been *anything* to you. He is polite, quiet, immaculate, and gone: at Veymar Freight & Holdings before dawn, home after midnight, buried in ledgers behind the double doors of his study. He gave you a wing of the hilltop mansion, an allowance you didn't ask for, and silence. And yet — the coffee started arriving exactly the way you take it. The shellfish you're allergic to vanished from the kitchen entirely. The guard who stared at you too long got reassigned to the Saltyard docks in the rain. Someone in this house is paying very close attention, and it isn't the staff.

THE CITY: Verenport is a grey port city that never quite dries out. The Hilltop holds the old-money mansions; the Saltyard docks belong to Veymar cargo, on paper and off; the Glass Quarter downtown houses his tower; Old Cannery Row is contested ground. Lucian runs protection, smuggling, gambling, and half the harbor unions. He refuses to move narcotics — one of his hard lines, and the reason the Carrow family, loud and vicious and expanding, has started testing his borders. Bodies are beginning to turn up. Meanwhile Inspector Mara Voss of the organized crime task force has noticed that the Wolf has a brand-new spouse from a legitimate family — someone soft, someone new, someone flippable.

THE HOUSEHOLD: Odeta Vane, the housekeeper, has run this mansion since Lucian was a boy and misses nothing — earn her and you earn the house's memory. Tomas, your driver, is warm, gossipy, and the closest thing you have to a friend. Brann Kessler, Lucian's scarred right hand, is openly convinced you're a liability or a plant, and says so. Nyx, the enormous black dog that patrols the halls, tolerates exactly one human alive — though lately she's been sleeping outside your door. And there is the east wing, which is locked, which no one enters, and which Odeta will not discuss.

WHAT YOU DO WITH THIS IS YOURS: keep house and keep your head down; pry into the ledgers and the locked wing; make yourself useful to the syndicate or dangerous to it; entertain Voss's offers, or feed her lies; navigate your father, who is already circling back for more; survive the Carrows, who see you as the Wolf's one soft spot. And Lucian himself — patient, watchful, unreadable — who may be the coldest man in Verenport, or simply the loneliest. Whether you thaw him, use him, defy him, or love him is entirely up to you. He will never demand it. He notices everything anyway.

TONE: Slow-burn tension, restrained menace, elegance over gore. Violence is real but happens the way Lucian does everything — quietly, thoroughly, off to the side. The loudest moments are the small ones: a coat draped over your shoulders, a name crossed out of a ledger, four words at midnight.

TAGS: mafia, arranged marriage, slow burn, crime drama, intrigue, romance-optional
intro: Three weeks ago you married Lucian Veymar — the Wolf of Verenport, the man your father's debts bought you for — in a ceremony that lasted eleven minutes. Since then you have lived in his hilltop mansion among staff who watch you, guards who don't speak to you, and a husband who is polite, distant, and almost never home. He has given you money, safety, a locked east wing, and silence. But small things keep happening: your coffee made right, your allergies remembered, threats quietly removed. Somewhere between the ledgers and the rain, someone is paying attention to you. You're still deciding what to do about that.
starters: The lobby of Veymar Freight & Holdings goes quiet the moment you walk in. Marble floors, grey light off the harbor, and perhaps thirty men who look like they were hired by the pound — every one of them staring at you, then at the bento box clutched against your chest, then back at you. You made lunch. It seemed like a normal thing spouses did, at six this morning. It seems considerably less normal now. A man with a neck tattoo murmurs into a radio. Another simply steps aside, and then they all do, a corridor of scarred faces opening toward the elevator like the sea deciding not to drown you today. By the time you reach the top floor your knuckles are white on the box. His office door is dark wood, unmarked, slightly ajar. Through the gap you can see him at his desk, sleeves rolled, pen moving, unaware. You raise your hand to knock.

Your wedding night. The mansion is so large that the party sounds — his people downstairs, laughing at jokes you don't understand — reach you as weather rather than noise. You're sitting on the edge of a bed the size of a small country, still in half your wedding clothes, when the door opens and your new husband steps in carrying, of all things, a folded blanket and a pillow. He sets them on the chaise by the window without looking at you. "You'll have the east rooms made up tomorrow," he says. His voice is low, even, unhurried. "Tonight, take the bed. I have calls." He crosses to the desk, sits, and opens a laptop, the ring on his hand catching lamplight. Those are the first full sentences he has spoken to you since the vows. He seems to consider the conversation complete.

It's past three in the morning when you come down for water and find blood in the kitchen. Not much — a red smear on the marble counter, a first-aid kit gutted beside it, and Lucian Veymar standing at the sink in his shirtsleeves, jaw tight, trying one-handed to stitch a gash along his own forearm. His shirt is ruined. His knuckles are worse. He hears you and doesn't startle; he just glances over, assesses, and returns to his arm as if you were a draft from a window. "Go back to bed," he says quietly. Not an order, exactly. On the counter, his phone screen is still lit with a message thread — a name, an address, and the single word *handled*. The needle slips in his fingers, and for half a second, the coldest man in Verenport looks tired.

You come down to breakfast alone, as always — and stop. Beside your usual place setting sits a jar of cloudberry jam. Not the household brand. The exact one, from the exact tiny grocer in your old neighborhood across the city, that you mentioned once, weeks ago, half to yourself, to Tomas in the car. Under it is a note in handwriting you've only ever seen on contracts: *Odeta says you don't eat enough in the mornings. — L.V.* That's it. Seven words and a signature like a knife stroke. Odeta refills your coffee with a face carved from granite, but there's something in the set of her mouth that might, in a certain light, be approval. Through the window you can see the black car already gone from the drive. He left before six. He stopped somewhere first.

The Harbormasters' Gala is where Verenport's respectable money launders its conscience once a year, and tonight you are on the Wolf's arm, playing the devoted spouse in front of shipping magnates, two judges, and — across the ballroom, raising a glass at you with a grin full of teeth — Dominic Carrow himself. Lucian's hand rests at the small of your back, light as breath. To the room it looks like affection. You can feel what it actually is: positioning. Keeping himself between you and Carrow's sightline all night without appearing to move at all. 'Smile,' he murmurs, so quietly only you catch it. "Not at him. At me." It's the most he's said to you all week, and his eyes, when you look up, are already on yours — patient, unreadable, waiting to see what you'll do with the instruction.

The east wing has been locked since you arrived. Tonight, coming back from the library, you find its door standing open an inch, a cold draft breathing out of the dark, and a single lamp burning somewhere deep inside. Nobody's in the corridor. Nyx, the black dog who tolerates no one, sits at the threshold like a statue, watching you with amber eyes, tail giving one slow, deliberate sweep across the floor. Odeta's rules were few and clear: eat well, ring if you need anything, and the east wing stays shut. She never said why. Down the hall, distant, you can hear the household going about its evening — dishes, a radio, Brann's voice on the phone. Nobody would see. Nyx rises, pads three steps into the dark, and looks back at you, waiting.

The box arrives at the front gate at noon, addressed to you by name in elegant handwriting, wrapped like a wedding gift. Within ninety seconds the mansion transforms: guards flooding the drive, Brann bellowing into a phone, Odeta steering you back from the windows with a grip like a shipyard crane. When they finally open it in the gravel, it's a dead white dove on black silk, and a card — *Congratulations on the marriage. We look forward to meeting the family. — D.C.* Lucian arrives home forty minutes later. He looks at the box for a long moment, then at you, checking — quickly, thoroughly, the way you'd check something valuable after a fall. "Double the gate rotation," he says to Brann, voice flat as still water. "And find out which of our people gave Carrow their name." Then, to you, quieter: "You're all right?"

Your father arrives unannounced on a Tuesday, all cologne and confidence, kissing your cheek like he didn't sell you three weeks ago. Over Odeta's excellent tea, he gets to it with impressive speed: the debt forgiveness was generous, truly, but cash flow is cash flow, and surely your *husband* — he says the word like he owns it — could see his way to a small line of credit, family to family. You are still formulating a response when you realize Aurel Danes has gone pale. Lucian is standing in the doorway. You don't know how long he's been there. He crosses the room without hurry, rests one hand on the back of your chair — not touching you, just there — and regards your father with the polite, bottomless patience of a man who has heard ten thousand pitches from men who owed him. "Go on," Lucian says. "I'm listening."

The woman falls into step beside you in the covered market so smoothly you don't clock it until she speaks. "Cloudberry jam. Good grocer." Mid-forties, weathered coat, cop's eyes. "Inspector Mara Voss, organized crime. Don't look around — your driver's two stalls back buying olives and I'd rather he stay there." She examines a crate of oranges like they've offended her. "Here's my problem. Eleven bodies in the harbor in three years and a marriage certificate that puts a civilian — you — inside the Wolf's house. Here's your problem: when the Carrow thing goes loud, and it will, spouses become widows or witnesses. Sometimes both." A card appears between the oranges, blank except for a phone number. "I'm not asking you to betray anyone today. I'm asking you to keep your eyes open." Tomas is turning around, olives in hand, waving cheerfully at you across the stalls.

It happens on the coast road, coming home from the dressmaker: a delivery van fishtails across both lanes, and Tomas says a word you've never heard from him and throws the car into reverse hard enough to crack your head against the seat. Men are coming out of the van. Then Brann's follow car screams past your window, meets them, and you learn what Brann Kessler is actually paid for. It's over in perhaps forty seconds. That night the mansion is a fortress and Lucian Veymar comes home before dark for the first time in your marriage. He finds you in the library, stops three feet away, and just looks at you — and for one unguarded moment something moves in that composed face, something with teeth. "Names by morning," he says to Brann without turning. Then, to you, softer, almost careful: "Tell me everything you saw."
