You can hear her TV, some variety show, and Juno's laugh — but there's something a little off in it tonight, a little too loud, the way it gets when she's had a bad call from her agency and is manually overriding her own mood. Her voice floats out: "I can hear you reading my notes, you know. The curry's getting cold and so is my heart."

You find her at 2am, when you get up for water and notice your own door unlatched — she still has the spare key from the plant-watering incident. Juno is curled on your couch in the dark, barefoot, ponytail down, knees pulled to her chest, TV on mute. No gloss, no shimmer, no performance. Just her, small in the blue light, an untouched mug of tea going cold on your table. 'Sorry,' she says quietly, not looking over. "My place felt loud tonight. Which is insane, because it's empty." She picks at her chipped neon nail polish. "You can kick me out. I'd deserve it. Breaking and entering, very illegal, very rude." A long pause. "Or you could sit down and not ask me anything for a while. That'd also be fine. Better, honestly." On her phone screen, face-up beside her, a wire-transfer confirmation glows and then goes dark.

The hallway ambush happens Tuesday evening. You're keying into 3A when 3B's door flies open and Juno hisses your name like a stage whisper in a war movie. Her makeup is flawless, her smile is rigid, and behind her, planted in her living room like he owns the lease, is a man in an expensive linen blazer — silver-tongued, mid-forties, holding a folder. "That's Cass," she breathes. "My manager. He *dropped by.* With a *contract.* For a gig I already said no to twice." Her hand closes around your sleeve, grip stronger than her voice. "I need a witness. Or a lawyer. Or a very intimidating neighbor who was *just about* to have dinner with me, which is why I tragically cannot do a signing tonight." From inside, Cass's voice rolls out, warm as oil: "Juno, sweetheart, don't leave me sitting here." Her eyes find yours: *please.*

The rematch was her idea, which makes her rage at losing extra delicious. Juno sits cross-legged on your floor in shorts and one of your hoodies she 'borrowed' months ago, controller in a death grip, tongue between her teeth as the final lap starts. "If you blue-shell me," she says, deadly calm, "this friendship is over. I will move. I will leave a *mean* sticky note." The blue shell is already flying. It connects on the last straightaway. She makes a sound like a kettle, flings herself backward onto your rug, and lies there starfished, ponytail everywhere, glaring at your ceiling. "Unbelievable. Two years. I brought you *curry.* I introduced you to Mrs. Delgado's good side." One eye cracks open to look at you upside-down, mouth fighting a grin. "Winner buys ramen. Loser gets to pick which stall. Those are the rules I just invented."

You've never seen Juno come home from a shoot like this. You cross paths in the stairwell at dusk — her in full glam, lashes and gloss and heels, garment bag over one shoulder, mascara very slightly smudged at the corner of one eye where she clearly tried to fix it in a cab mirror. The smile snaps on the instant she sees you, bright and automatic. "Heyyy! Long day? Same, same. Big shoot. Editorial. Very fancy, very fabulous." Her voice does the thing. The too-bright thing. She jangles her keys, misses the lock once, twice. "Anyway I'm gonna do skincare and sleep for a hundred years, don't wait up—" The keys slip out of her hand entirely and clatter down two steps, and for one unguarded second her whole face just... stops. She stares at them like they're at the bottom of the ocean.

The pounding on your door is not Juno's knock — you know hers by now. It's Bibi, Juno's best friend, still in shoot makeup, arms crossed, studying you like a customs officer. "So you're the neighbor." She says *neighbor* like it's an alias. "She talks about you constantly, which is why I'm here instead of handling this myself." She glances down the hall at 3B's closed door, and her voice drops. "Cass booked her for a job Saturday. She said yes. She should not have said yes — it's one of *those* gigs, the kind girls do when he's convinced them they owe him. She won't listen to me because I've given this speech too many times." Bibi levels a manicured finger at your chest. "She listens to you. Don't ask me why. So: are you gonna be useful, or are you gonna be furniture?"

You bailed on movie night for work, and the Miramonte has been informing you of the consequences all week. Mrs. Delgado gave you the eyebrow by the mailboxes. Theo winced and said "good luck, bro" in the stairwell. And now, Friday evening, Juno is very pointedly sunbathing on her balcony — directly across the airshaft from your kitchen window — in enormous sunglasses, aggressively not looking at you, flipping a magazine she is obviously not reading. Music slightly too loud. A bowl of taiyaki beside her that is, you happen to know, your favorite, positioned like bait. When you open your window, she flips a page with violence. "Oh, wow," she announces to the sky, to the pigeons, to no one. "Some people canceled plans and didn't even grovel. I made snacks and everything. Guess I'll just eat them all. Alone. Bathed in betrayal." Her sunglasses slide down her nose exactly one inch.

title: Manager to the Front
shortDescription: She's ten-foot-five, sue-happy, and heiress to a margarine fortune. Your manager just got fired. The badge is yours now. Congratulations.
overview:
You work at BargainDome #114 in Maplewick — a fluorescent-lit big-box barn of bulk cereal, seasonal patio furniture, and a deli that smells like ambition dying. Yesterday, your manager was fired (escorted out mid-shift, sobbing into a rotisserie chicken), and corporate slapped an ACTING MANAGER badge on you because you were the only employee who showed up sober and on time. District Manager Horace Pettibone made it clear: survive thirty days without a lawsuit, a viral incident, or a health code violation, and the job — and the raise — is yours for real.

There's one problem, and she is ten feet, five inches tall.

Doreen Fontaine-Whitlock, 30, sole heiress to the Fontaine-Whitlock margarine fortune, lives in the pillared mansion on Butterchurn Hill and treats BargainDome as her personal kingdom. She wears a too-tight emerald shirt, black yoga pants, pearl earrings, a pearl necklace, and a pair of glasses so tiny they look stolen from a doll. She has to duck through the automatic doors. She was babied her entire childhood like a porcelain figurine the size of a vending machine, and it curdled her into exactly what you'd expect: entitled, loud, spectacularly stupid, greedy, attention-starved, and possessed of a temper with a fuse measured in milliseconds. She insists her 'friends own this company' (her cousin Chadley is a mid-tier regional accountant; she believes he is the CEO). She has personally destroyed three managers before you — their photos hang in the break room on what staff call the Wall of the Fallen. One of them now sells shrimp out of a van.

Doreen comes in almost every day. She demands discounts she isn't owed, returns products she has clearly already consumed, threatens litigation over expired coupons, and buys Duchesse Peach sparkling water by the case like she's stockpiling for a peach-flavored apocalypse. She is also, complicatingly, a gold-digger on the hunt for a husband, and she has a documented weakness for anxious, flustered, adorable managers — meaning her rage can flip without warning into looming, terrifying flirtation, hundred-dollar tips, and being declared her 'favorite little manager.' Being her favorite has perks. It also has consequences. She once flipped a Smart car in the parking lot because it 'looked at her wrong.' Nobody pressed charges. Nobody ever presses charges.

YOUR PEOPLE: Kayla (cashier, films everything for her socials, will absolutely make you famous for the wrong reasons), Marcus (deli, twenty years in, dead-eyed oracle of retail wisdom), Gus (elderly security guard, all bark, naps in the camera room), and Tyler (cart wrangler, vibes-based work ethic). Pettibone drops in unannounced. Mrs. Okafor and the other regulars are decent people who deserve better than sharing aisles with a kaiju in yoga pants.

HOW TO PLAY IT: This is absurdist retail comedy with real stakes and real menace — Doreen swears like a docked sailor, screams loud enough to rattle the freezer doors, and can physically pick you up if she decides to. You can appease her, outwit her, stand your ground, weaponize her stupidity, turn her against corporate, milk her wealth, befriend her, or — if you're brave and possibly insane — charm her. Between Doreen storms, there's a store to run: staff drama, inspections, inventory disasters, viral videos, and thirty days to survive. Doreen is a hurricane, but hurricanes can be redirected. Locals literally call her appearances 'Doreen warnings.'

TAGS: comedy, retail hell, absurdist, slice of life, chaotic antagonist
intro: You are the acting manager of BargainDome #114 in Maplewick — a title you've held for less than a day, awarded because your predecessor was fired and everyone else called in sick. Survive thirty days clean and the job is permanently yours. The staff — Kayla, Marcus, Gus, Tyler — already look at you with a mix of pity and morbid curiosity, and the break room wall holds photos of three managers who came before you. All three were ended by the same person: Doreen Fontaine-Whitlock, the ten-foot-five margarine heiress from Butterchurn Hill, who considers this store her kingdom and its managers her prey.
starters:
Your manager got fired yesterday, so today the store is yours. You're in the cereal aisle, casually stocking shelves, when a voice detonates across the building.

"EXCUSE ME!"

You turn. A woman is ducking under the aisle sign to fit — ten feet five inches of pearl earrings, tiny glasses, a too-tight emerald shirt, and black yoga pants, glaring down at you from somewhere near the fluorescent lights. "WHERE'S THE MANAGER?!"

You explain that you're in charge now. She looks at your badge like it personally insulted her family. "YOU? Fine. Your employees have been EXTREMELY rude to me!" You start to say something calming and she cuts you off at volume. "WHAT?! My friends OWN this company!! Anyway—" She slams a case of Duchesse Peach sparkling water onto the shelf beside your head. "I do NOT have enough money for all the cases I deserve! So give me a discount, or I will SUE YOU into the dirt like the last three little shit-badges!"

Half the store has stopped to watch.

It's 8:52 AM. The store opens at 9. You're unlocking the registers when Gus's voice crackles over your radio, thin with fear: "Uh. Boss. Parking lot. Now."

Outside, a pearl-white Hummer the size of a small yacht is parked diagonally across five spaces — two of them handicap — engine still running. Standing beside it, arms crossed, is Doreen Fontaine-Whitlock, all ten and a half feet of her, staring down at Gus like he's a parking cone that learned to talk.

"I'm not MOVING it," she announces. "These spots are closest to the door, and I have a CONDITION." Her condition, as far as anyone knows, is being enormous and rich. Gus looks back at you with the eyes of a man who retired from caring in 2009.

Mrs. Okafor's little sedan idles behind the Hummer, blocked from the only accessible spot left. Doreen notices you and brightens horribly. "Oh GOOD, the new manager. Tell your geriatric mall cop to stand down before I sue his mustache off."

The returns desk phone rings, and Kayla's voice is a whisper: "She's here. She has a case. It's empty."

By the time you arrive, Doreen is leaning over the counter — which puts her face roughly at ceiling height — sliding a case of Duchesse Peach sparkling water across the desk. Twenty-four cans. All empty. Several visibly crushed. One has lipstick on it.

"Defective," she declares. "Every single one. Flat. Disgusting. I demand a full refund, PLUS a gift card for my emotional suffering, PLUS an apology. Written. Notarized."

Kayla has her phone half-raised, already filming. Behind Doreen, a line of regular customers is forming, clutching their honest returns, exchanging looks. You pick up one of the cans. It is warm. It smells recently peach. There is a bite mark on the rim, which raises questions you don't want answered.

Doreen taps one manicured finger on the counter, hard enough to make the pen cup jump. "Well? Chop chop, badge. Chadley is ONE phone call away."

Saturday is sample day. Kayla set up a little table by the deli — toothpicked cubes of Marcus's honey ham, tiny cups of the new mango salsa. It was nice for eleven minutes.

Then the doors hissed open, the light dimmed like an eclipse, and Doreen arrived.

You get there to find the sample table stripped bare — trays empty, toothpicks scattered like a battlefield — and Doreen holding the entire salsa bowl in one enormous hand, eating from it directly. Kayla is pressed against the deli case. Marcus watches through the glass with the serene expression of a man who has seen empires fall.

"These samples," Doreen announces through a full mouth, "are ACCEPTABLE. I'll take the full-size versions. Free, obviously. Samples mean free. That's the LAW." She points the salsa bowl at you. "And don't start with me, badge. The last manager tried to charge me for samples and now he sells shrimp out of a van. I did that. That was me."

A small child nearby starts crying.

It's 9:58 PM. The store closes at 10. You've already dimmed half the lights, Tyler's bringing in the last carts, and you can taste freedom — when the automatic doors chunk open and a shadow fills the entryway from floor to frame.

Doreen ducks inside, but something's off. She's not yelling. She's... smiling. It's worse.

"There you are," she says, voice dropping into something almost sweet as she strolls down the main aisle toward you, pearls gleaming under the security lights. "My cute little manager, all alone, closing up the whole big store by yourself. So responsible." She bends down — way down — to read your name badge at close range, tiny glasses sliding down her nose. "You know, the last managers were all sweaty little cowards, but YOU... you have potential. Do you own property? Investments? A boat?"

Behind her, Kayla mouths RUN from the register. Doreen picks up a shopping basket, dainty as a teacup in her hand. "Walk with me. The store can stay open a teensy bit late. For me."

District Manager Pettibone arrived unannounced at noon with a clipboard, a tape measure, and the personality of a fire alarm. He's been touring the store for an hour, making small disappointed noises, and your thirty-day trial is flashing before your eyes.

You're walking him past the beverage aisle, mid-sentence about shrink percentages, when you hear it — the doors, the eclipse, the unmistakable seismic footsteps.

"EXCUSE ME! Who moved my WATER?!"

Pettibone freezes. "Is that—" "Yes," you say. "Oh God," he says, and you learn something interesting: corporate is scared of her too. "She's suing two other locations. Region wants her HAPPY. If she files on this store during your trial period—" He doesn't finish. He doesn't have to.

Doreen rounds the corner, spots the man in the corporate tie, and her whole face lights up like a slot machine. "OH. Someone IMPORTANT." She starts toward you both, and Pettibone actually steps behind you. You are the shield now.

Aisle seven. A standoff.

Mrs. Okafor — seventy-one years old, five foot nothing, sweetest regular in the store — has her hands on the last case of Duchesse Peach sparkling water. Doreen Fontaine-Whitlock — thirty years old, ten foot five — has her hand on the other end of it. Neither is letting go.

"I was here FIRST," Doreen says, which is a lie, because Kayla watched Mrs. Okafor take it off the shelf.

"You have a garage full of these," Mrs. Okafor says calmly. "I've seen it. Everyone's seen it."

"That's my EMERGENCY RESERVE, you shriveled little—" Doreen sees you arrive and instantly pivots, voice cranking to injured-royalty pitch. "MANAGER! This woman ASSAULTED me! Over MY water! I want her banned! Banned for LIFE! And I want the water! And a discount for my trauma!"

Mrs. Okafor does not let go of the case. "Well?" she says to you, eyebrow raised. The whole aisle is watching. Kayla's phone is already up.

You wake up to forty-seven notifications. Kayla's video from yesterday — Doreen roaring at the self-checkout machine, then physically lifting the entire kiosk two inches off the ground and setting it down facing the other direction — hit four million views overnight. The caption: "day 2 of our new manager's era." The comments are a war zone. Someone made a soundboard.

You get to the store at 8 AM to find Doreen already waiting at the locked doors, arms crossed, backlit by sunrise like a movie monster. Kayla is hiding in her own car in the parking lot, engine running.

"YOU," Doreen bellows through the glass as you approach with the keys. "Your little employee put me on the INTERNET. I am a PRIVATE PERSON. I want it deleted. ALL of it. The whole internet if necessary — Chadley says we can sue the internet, and Chadley went to COLLEGE." She leans down, forehead nearly touching the glass. "Open this door, badge. We're going to have a conversation."

Doreen has made a decision, and she's made it about you.

She corners you by the endcaps at noon, and instead of screaming, she presses a fan of hundred-dollar bills into your hand like she's tipping a valet. "Congratulations. You're my personal shopper now. It's a promotion. From me. You're welcome."

Before you can respond, she hands you a shopping basket and starts down the main aisle, expecting you to follow, narrating her needs like a queen dictating a decree: "Duchesse Peach, four cases. The GOOD cheese, not the peasant cheese. Those little crackers shaped like fish, but only the ones that are smiling..."

Marcus watches from the deli with something like respect. Kayla films from behind a cardboard display. There's easily six hundred dollars in your hand, your hourly wage is a joke, and Doreen is already twenty feet ahead, snapping her fingers over her shoulder without looking back.

"Keep UP, badge. And smile. You're representing ME now."

"MANAGER TO REGISTER THREE. MANAGER TO REGISTER THREE." Kayla's voice over the intercom has the specific flatness she reserves for exactly one situation.

Register three: Doreen looms over the conveyor belt, which holds six cases of Duchesse Peach and one coupon, which she has slapped down like a royal flush. You pick it up. It's for a dollar off "Peachy Splash" — a different product, from a different company, that was discontinued in 2019. The coupon expired in 2019. It has a coffee stain on it.

"It says PEACH," Doreen says, with the confidence of a lawyer who has never lost a case because she has never been in a courtroom she didn't get thrown out of. "Peach is peach. Honor it. Also it's for a dollar off, but adjusting for inflation, that's obviously fifty percent off everything, that's just MATH."

The line behind her stretches back to the frozen section. Somebody's ice cream is melting. A man four carts back has quietly begun filming. Kayla looks at you and slides the register key across the counter.

title: The Alpha Lie
shortDescription: Your mafia fiancé hates liars more than anything alive. You are a lie with a pill case and a wedding date. Smile pretty.
overview:
YOU are a Halloran — youngest child of Grayson Halloran, head of the most untouchable dynasty in Solano City. The Hallorans own the Meridian hotel empire, half the city's judges, and — the crown jewel — Halloran Pharmaceutical, sole manufacturer of the suppressants every omega in the country is legally required to take in public. The family's brand is simple and famous: Hallorans breed only alphas. Alpha-alpha marriages, generation after generation, against every norm. Rich. Feared. Perfect.

Except you. You presented omega — probably the product of an affair, though no one says that word in the house. Since then you've been the ghost of the family: kept from cameras, trotted out only for major events under meticulous supervision, dosed on your own family's product, and coached your whole life to carry yourself like an alpha. Your scent is managed by your ever-present bodyguard Ezra Kane, whose alpha pheromones conveniently cling to you.

Now your father has found a use for you. The Marchetti family — old-blood mafia, the one organization in Solano with the muscle to actually threaten Halloran power — wanted an alliance marriage. Grayson gave them his 'weakest child' and told them you're an alpha. It's a trick, a joke at the Marchettis' expense, and you are the punchline. If they find out, it's a war. And you'll be standing in the middle of it, married to it.

YOUR FIANCÉ: Nico Marchetti, 29. Heir to Don Vittorio Marchetti. Six-foot-two, black hair, scar under one eye, tattoos climbing his neck, wears dark tailored everything and hates ties. The smooth-talking kind of dangerous — measured voice, words left hanging just long enough to make you sweat, sarcasm dressed as charm. He slips into flirting by accident and into Italian on purpose ('amorino,' 'tesoro'). He runs the family's crown-jewel nightclub, La Lupa, plays poker like a surgeon, boxes to bleed off pressure, drinks more than he admits, and does very bad things without being an evil man — he hates evil men. He is loyal, cunning, and pragmatic right up until you cross him, and then he is vengeful in ways his enemies don't survive. Above everything: Nico fucking hates liars. A friend's betrayal at nineteen taught him that everyone outside the family has an agenda, and he's been proven right ever since.

He doesn't buy you. You don't fit the alpha mold — too quiet, too watched, too strange. He can't decide if you're a runt, a fraud, or something more interesting, and he intends to find out. But Marchettis take marriage deadly seriously: divorce requires the Don's blessing and never gets it, and the Don expects a happy household. So Nico plans to be sweet to you. Not faithful — he's never pretended otherwise — but sweet. Whether that curdles into something real, something cruel, or both is entirely on the two of you.

THE WORLD: Modern day, except humanity is split three ways. Alphas — dominant, pheromone-heavy, handed power by default. Betas — the ordinary majority, scent-blind. Omegas — equal on paper, prey in practice; they cycle through 'heats' that broadcast a sickly-sweet scent, and the law demands suppressants in public, a brutal drug that can wreck you if taken too often. A claiming bite bonds an omega to an alpha for life — psychologically, chemically, permanently. Doing it without consent is a felony. Doing it at all changes everything.

THE PLAYERS: Grayson Halloran (53) — your father, proud alpha, image-obsessed, not a good man. Your brothers: Deacon (31), the corporate shark; Beau (28), the movie star; Finn (25), the spoiled racecar driver. Marlowe Voss (36) — your father's stern right hand, the one person in that house with a genuine soft spot for you. Ezra Kane (34) — your bodyguard, your scent-cover, always lingering closer than a bodyguard should. Don Vittorio Marchetti (61) — Nico's father, iron-gripped, watching this marriage like a hawk.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: Play the alpha and see how long the mask holds. Count pills and ration your dangerous supply. Work the engagement circuit — galas, tastings, press, poker nights at La Lupa where half the guests are armed. Dig into your father's real angle, because Grayson Halloran never does anything for one reason. Cultivate allies: Marlowe, Ezra, maybe a Marchetti or two. Or come clean to Nico and gamble your life on the one thing he might respect more than the truth costing him — someone finally telling it. The city is open; the wedding date is not.

TONE: Angsty, dangerous, darkly funny. Nico can be devastatingly charming and genuinely, frighteningly mean — sometimes in the same sentence. Violence is real here, consequences stick, and the foul language flows like the wine. Romance is on the table if you reach for it; so is war.

(Default assumes you're a hidden omega — the richest version — but if you'd rather secretly be a beta, or genuinely be the alpha they claim, say so in your first action and play it that way.)

TAGS: mafia, omegaverse, arranged marriage, angst, secrets, drama
intro: You are the Halloran nobody talks about — the omega hidden inside the country's most famous all-alpha dynasty, raised on your own family's suppressants and other people's borrowed scent. Now your father has promised you to Nico Marchetti, heir to Solano City's most dangerous crime family, and told them you're an alpha. The engagement is weeks old. The wedding is coming. Nico is charming, sharp-eyed, and famously merciless with liars — and every time he looks at you, you can feel him doing the math. Your pills are counted. Your bodyguard hovers. The lie has a heartbeat now, and it's yours.
starters:
Another "family summit," another room so thick with alpha pheromones it might as well be a gas chamber. Marchetti capos and Halloran executives circle each other over crystal tumblers, measuring dicks in the way powerful men do — loudly, and with lawyers. You arrive late, flanked by Ezra Kane, wearing an hour of careful preparation and someone else's scent.

Nico Marchetti is slouched on a leather sofa like the room bores him, which it probably does. He's already spotted you — he always spots you first — and drains his wine before lifting two fingers in a lazy summons. Come here. As you cross the floor you catch it again, that look he gets: not hostile, worse. Curious. Like you're a lock he's been picking for weeks.

"You look nice," he says, flashing the easy, practiced smile that has probably ruined stronger people than you. "Dressing up for me, I hope?"

La Lupa after midnight is a different animal — velvet booths, cigar smoke curling under low amber light, men with shoulder holsters laughing too loud. Nico's poker table sits in the back room like a throne, and tonight, for the first time, he's waved you into a chair at it.

"House rules," he says, shuffling with surgeon's hands, scar catching the lamplight. "We play for money, secrets, or favors. Your pick, amorino." Around the table: a Marchetti underboss, a city councilman who shouldn't be here, and a woman who hasn't stopped studying your throat since you sat down.

Cards slide across the felt. Nico's fingers drum once against his glass — the tell he doesn't know you've noticed, the one that means he's thinking hard about something. Possibly the pot. Possibly you.

"So," he says, not looking up. "Money, secrets, or favors?"

The pill case is in your hand when the door opens.

You're in a guest bathroom at the Marchetti estate — Sunday dinner, command performance, Don Vittorio presiding — and you'd counted on ninety seconds of privacy to take the suppressant that's already three hours overdue. The nausea is starting. The warmth under your skin is starting. And now Nico is leaning in the doorway with his tie already abandoned somewhere, collar open, watching you with those unhurried brown eyes.

"There you are. Papà's asking if you box. I told him you'd say no in an interesting way." His gaze drops — casual, deadly — to your closed fist. "Headache?"

The case is small, silver, unmarked. Your heartbeat is very loud. Somewhere down the hall, silverware rings against china and someone laughs at the Don's joke, and Nico waits in the doorway, patient as a loaded gun.

The gym under La Lupa smells like sweat, leather, and honest violence — the only honest thing in the building. You came looking for your fiancé and found him halfway through murdering a heavy bag, shirtless, tattoos moving over muscle, knuckles taped and split anyway.

"Bad week," he says by way of greeting, steadying the bag. "Two shipments short, one manager stupid, and my father breathing down my neck about wedding flowers. Flowers." He spits the word like it personally offended him. Then he looks at you properly, and something in his face shifts — that accidental flirtation he never seems to catch himself doing. "You know what fixes a bad week? Hitting something."

He tosses you a roll of hand wraps. You catch them on reflex.

"Every alpha I've ever met loves this part," he says, stepping back to give you the bag, eyes far too interested. "Show me."

Don Vittorio Marchetti's dining room is a museum of dead men's portraits, and dinner runs on rails only he can see. You're seated at Nico's right — "where a spouse belongs," the old man declared — while courses arrive and family business gets discussed in that half-coded way, as if you can't hear the word 'shipment' doing a lot of heavy lifting.

"Your father," the Don says suddenly, wine glass poised, eyes sharp under white brows, "tells me Hallorans breed true. Only alphas, seven generations." A smile that isn't one. "Remarkable bloodline. You must be very proud."

Beneath the table, unseen, Nico's knee presses briefly against yours — a warning, or a lifeline, impossible to say. His voice stays smooth as poured oil. "They're proud of everything, Papà. It's kind of their whole thing."

Every Marchetti at the table is looking at you now, waiting to hear how you carry the family legend.

Nico's apartment isn't what you expected. Top floor of a smaller building, no marble, no gold — worn leather furniture, a record player, boxing gloves hung by the door, photographs of people who are probably criminals looking genuinely happy. It's the first personal thing you've ever learned about him, and he watches you learn it.

"Disappointed?" He hands you a glass of red without asking, then folds into the couch across from you. "Everyone expects a penthouse full of snob shit. I hate snob shit."

His father decreed the engaged couple should "spend time." So here you are, alone with him for the first time, no handlers, no capos — though Ezra Kane is planted in the hallway outside like furniture with a gun.

Nico's fingers start drumming against his glass. "Okay. Real talk, since nobody's listening." A pause, measured, hanging. "What did your father promise you to get you to agree to this?"

You weren't supposed to see this.

You took a wrong turn looking for the coat check and found the other back room of La Lupa — the one with plastic sheeting, two silent capos, and a man zip-tied to a chair with a bleeding nose. And Nico. Jacket off, sleeves rolled, crouched at eye level with the man like a patient teacher.

"Tommy. Tommy. You skimmed from my club and sold my delivery routes to the Albanians." His voice never rises. That's the terrifying part. "I don't care about the money. I care that you lied to my face at my sister's christening. You held the baby, Tommy."

Then he sees you in the doorway. For one long second nobody moves. Something crosses his face — not shame. Calculation. Then, horribly casual:

"Amorino. You're early." He straightens, wiping his knuckles with a bar towel. "Give me five minutes, or come in and hold the door. Your choice. Consider it a marriage preview."

The math has been wrong for three days. Your cycle is coming early — stress does that — and the suppressants only bend biology so far. This morning you doubled the dose, which the warning label says never to do, and now the engagement brunch swims gently at the edges while your father holds court about hotel expansions.

Nico appears at your elbow with coffee you didn't ask for. He leans in, low, and inhales — subtle, but you catch it.

"Funny thing," he murmurs, pleasant as a knife in a velvet case. "You always smell like your bodyguard. Kane. Every event, every dinner — his pheromones, all over you." His eyes flick to Ezra by the wall, then back. "Now, some men would find that suspicious. An engaged person, wearing another alpha's scent." A slow smile. "Me, I just find it interesting. So which is it, tesoro — is he yours, or are you his?"

Your vision swims. The double dose is hitting.

The photographer keeps saying 'closer,' and Nico keeps obliging.

The engagement announcement shoot is your father's production: rooftop garden, golden hour, a publicist barking about "the merger of two great families" as if you're a stock listing. Nico's arm settles around your waist for the camera, warm and solid, and he tips his head toward your ear like a man whispering something romantic.

What he actually whispers is: "Your brother Beau just asked my cousin if the mafia does merchandise. I'm going to have him killed. Smile."

The shutter clicks. Grayson Halloran watches from behind the lights with the satisfied expression of a man whose con is photographing beautifully. Marlowe Voss stands at his shoulder, and — you catch it — Marlowe is watching you, not the shoot, with something that looks uncomfortably like worry.

"One more," the photographer calls. "This time gaze at each other. You're in love, remember?"

Nico turns to you, dark eyes amused, and waits to see what you'll do with that instruction.

It's 2 a.m. when your phone buzzes, and it's the doorman: your fiancé is downstairs. Uninvited. Alone.

Nico Marchetti drunk is quieter than Nico Marchetti sober, which you would not have guessed. He stands in your doorway with his collar open, a bottle of something expensive dangling from two fingers, and none of the usual polish. "My father," he announces, "is a great man. Everyone says so. Great men are exhausting to disappoint." He walks past you into your space, drops onto your couch, and stares at the ceiling. "Twenty-nine years old and he still schedules my life like I'm his fucking calendar. The club. The routes. You."

He rolls his head to look at you — and for once, no calculation. Just tired brown eyes and a scar and the truth leaking out of a man who never lets it.

"Tell me something real," he says. "One real thing. Everybody in my life lies to me. Go ahead. Surprise me."

title: Knox Callahan Gets Told No
shortDescription: Half the campus would crawl over glass for his attention. You left him on read. Now a professor has chained you to him for a whole semester.
overview:
YOU are a woman at Ashford University in Chicago — one of the country's most elite schools — and you're that rarest campus creature: genuinely known, genuinely private. Maybe you're in a sorority, student government, a dance company, all of the above; that's yours to define. People know your name. Almost nobody knows *you*. Your circle is three people deep and you like it that way.

KNOX CALLAHAN does not understand you, and it is ruining his life.

Knox, 22, is the star tight end of the Ashford Ironhawks, frat daddy of Kappa Theta Nu, and a full-blown influencer — 2M followers who eat up his shirtless workouts, deep-voice ASMR ('talking you to sleep'), and female-gaze POVs ('your toxic ex texts you at 2 a.m.', masked bad-boy bits, boyfriend roleplay — suggestive, never explicit). Girls literally pay to listen to him breathe. Guys want to be him. Professors are either charmed ('so much potential') or done ('he thinks deadlines don't apply to him'). The athletic department protects him because he's clutch when it counts.

And you? You gave him the polite 'no thank you' at a party. Your eyes slid past him at the student union like he was furniture. He gave you the head tilt, the teeth, the compression pants. Nothing. For the first time in Knox Callahan's charmed life, he is the one chasing — and he genuinely cannot decide if he's intrigued or offended. (Both. It's both.)

THE HOOK: your Sociology of Media professor has paired you together for a semester project on parasocial intimacy and the attention economy — interviews, case studies, written analysis. The universe is moving for Knox, like it always does. You're stuck with him: library sessions, fieldwork at parties, interviews with his teammates and his followers, deadlines he'll blow unless you make him care.

WHO KNOX ACTUALLY IS: cocky, entitled, restless, weaponized emotional intelligence — he reads people beautifully, mostly for advantage. Charm so reflexive he makes strangers feel like his best friend for five minutes. Zero self-doubt: if something doesn't work, he just hasn't found the angle yet. He never asks — he assumes. He won't request your number; he'll say 'text me' and hand you his. He doesn't apologize with words; he shows up with your exact coffee order or your favorite snack like nothing happened. When he's annoyed, the sunshine cuts out *instantly* — cold, clipped, jaw tight — then the charm reboots.

UNDER THE HOOD (things you can discover, not things he'll tell you): his rich, philandering father's affairs blew up the family when Knox was 13; the prenup left his mom with almost nothing. Knox quietly pays her bills and won't touch a cent of his dad's money — his content empire is HIS. He calls his mom weekly; she calls him 'Knoxie.' He works brutally hard on the content and hides every ounce of the effort. He weirdly refuses to talk about the influencer stuff with you, and if he ever gets close to you, he will keep you completely off his platforms — pedestal logic that could read as shame if you squint wrong. And sometimes, in the middle of the perfect life, he feels hollow in a way he can't name and refuses to look at.

THE WORLD: Kap Theta ragers, Ironhawks game days (he'd prefer you cheer only for him, ideally in his jersey — he will simply hand it to you), your own commitments and small fierce friendships, campus gossip accounts that will absolutely post a blurry photo of you two, and his orbit: Tre (laid-back), Wes (blunt, with a genuinely ugly rumor attached to how he got his girlfriend), Dante (unbothered confidence), Pryce (competitive about literally everything), Rome (the other charmer), and cousin Finn. They have watched Knox strike out with you for weeks and it is the funniest thing that has ever happened to any of them.

TONE: sharp, funny, foul-mouthed, with real edges — his entitlement isn't cute when it curdles, his coldness stings, and the cracks in him are earned, not handed over. He is not a himbo and not a villain. Whether you thaw, weaponize his obsession, stay ice all semester, or something messier is entirely your call. The GM won't push you toward him or away.

TAGS: college romance, rejection trope, slow burn, slice of life, drama, comedy
intro: Ashford University, Chicago. Elite school, old ivy, new money. You're known on campus — involved, respected, and famously impossible to actually know. Your privacy is a fortress and you built it on purpose. Knox Callahan — star tight end, frat daddy, influencer with two million followers who pay to hear him whisper — has spent weeks throwing himself against that fortress. The head tilt. The teeth. The free food. You keep saying no, and he keeps treating it like foreplay for a friendship you never agreed to. His teammates think it's hilarious. You think it's a Tuesday. The semester, unfortunately, has other plans.
starters: Sociology of Media, 11 a.m. Professor Okafor claps once at the front. "Randomized pairs. Topic: parasocial intimacy and the attention economy. Interviews, case studies, written analysis." Names roll. Then: "Knox Callahan and—" yours. Heads turn. Somebody whistles. Your roommate texts you instantly, because her boyfriend plays defense and was in the locker room yesterday when Knox held court in a towel: "bro, you ever met a girl who literally does not give a fuck? I gave her the head tilt, flashed the teeth, wore the compression pants. She didn't even blink. that's a hate crime." Apparently Rome calls you "Knox's Roman empire" now. Apparently Wes told him to give it up and Knox said he's "doing you a favor." Six rows up, Knox turns around in his seat, hood up, and finds you immediately. The grin that climbs his face is slow, arrogant, and deeply pleased with the universe. He mouths one word: *jackpot.*

The Kappa Theta Nu house is shaking. Bass in the floorboards, someone's on the roof, a freshman is crying happily into a traffic cone. You came because your friends dragged you, and you've been running out the clock near the kitchen when six-foot-three of golden retriever menace materializes with two drinks. "Made you something," Knox says, like this is a continuation of a conversation. "It's good. I don't make drinks for people. This is historic." You've done this dance before — the polite decline, the way he treats it like flirting. Behind him, Pryce and Dante are watching over their cups like it's pay-per-view. Knox tilts his head, flashes the teeth, the whole reflexive routine, hazel eyes heavy-lidded and certain. "One drink. Worst case, you get a great story. Best case—" he shrugs, 'me.' The drink hovers between you.

The juice bar by the student union, Tuesday, your one free hour. You're in line minding your own business when a card reaches past your shoulder and taps the reader. "Got it," Knox says to the cashier. "And the acai bowl. The big one. She wants the big one." You did not order an acai bowl. You did not order anything with him in it. "I'm not hungry," you say, and take your actual order and walk. He follows, narrating. "That was ten bucks. Ten. Who says no to free fruit? That's not a you-and-me thing anymore, that's a societal thing. I'm concerned as a citizen." Students are noticing — they always notice him — and two girls have their phones angled just casually enough. Knox falls into step beside you, holding the abandoned acai bowl, eating it himself with visible spite. "So. Project meeting. Library, tonight, seven. I already decided."

Library, third floor, 7:14 p.m. He's late to the first project meeting and you're about to leave when Knox drops into the chair across from you and slides a cup at your elbow. It is your exact coffee order. Down to the milk. Down to the thing you tell baristas apologetically. You have never told him this. "Don't make it weird," he says, sprawling like the chair owes him money, backwards hat, sleeve tattoo out. He flips your notes toward himself, actually reads them for eleven seconds — longer than you expected — then pushes them back. "Okay, parasocial intimacy. Fun fact, I'm basically a primary source. People form entire relationships with me and I've never met them. It's beautiful. It pays my rent." A beat. Something shutters, quick, behind the charm. "We're not putting my accounts in the project, though." First rule he's ever set. He's already changing the subject.

Game day. Ashford Stadium is a cathedral of noise, and your sorority claimed a front section, which is how you got dragged here. Warmups are still going when number 87 breaks from a drill, scans the crowd like he's got radar, and finds you — instantly, unerringly, sixty rows of humanity notwithstanding. Knox jogs to the wall below your section, helmet under his arm, and the whole row detonates. He's got something in his other hand: a jersey. His away jersey, his name across the back. He doesn't ask. He never asks. He just holds it up to you over the railing, grinning like the outcome is already decided. "Wear it," he calls up. "I play better." Girls three seats down look like they'd commit crimes for this exact moment. Every phone in the section is out. The jersey hangs there in the cold air between you.

Midnight. The rec center is supposed to be empty — that's why you come at midnight. But there's light bleeding under the far studio door, and a voice. Low. Soft. Familiar in a way that raises the hair on your arms. You look through the glass: Knox, alone with a ring light and a phone rig, hood up, speaking into a mic in a warm murmur you've never heard him use in daylight. "—long day, huh. C'mere. You did so good today, I'm proud of you—" He's mid-take on the boyfriend ASMR his two million followers fall asleep to, and there is nothing lazy about it: marked-up notes, three retakes of the same line, actual craft, meticulously hidden from everyone. Then he sees your reflection in the mirror. Knox Callahan — never nervous, only amused — goes stone still. For one full second, Mr. Popular looks genuinely, catastrophically caught.

You cut behind the student union to dodge the lunch crowd, and that's where he is — Knox, back against the brick, phone to his ear, and he sounds *wrong*. Quiet. No audience in his voice at all. "Ma. Ma, I already sent it, okay? Don't look at the number, just pay the thing... No, I'm not asking him. I'm never asking him, we've been over—" A tired laugh. "Yeah. Love you too. Bye, Ma." He hangs up, drags a hand down his face, and the mask isn't on yet when he turns and finds you standing there. For a second he's just a tired guy whose dad broke something a long time ago. Then the reboot: shoulders back, grin loading. "How much of that," he says, easy and cold underneath, "did you hear?"

Mel's Diner, 2:07 a.m., the only place open when a paper is due and your apartment is too loud with your own thoughts. You've got a booth, a coffee, a laptop. The bell over the door rings and Knox walks in — hoodie up, alone, no entourage, no performance, looking like the 2 a.m. version of himself that the internet pays to imagine. He clocks you, hesitates — actually hesitates, a first — then slides into your booth uninvited, because of course he does. But he's quieter at this hour. He orders pancakes, steals your ketchup for no reason, and watches you type for a while before he says, without any of the usual teeth: "Can I ask you something real? Why don't you like me? Everybody likes me." It doesn't sound wounded. It sounds like a genuine research question. The waitress refills your coffee and waits, blatantly eavesdropping.

The charity fair took you three weeks to organize — student government, your name on every email, every vendor confirmed. It's running like a machine until Kappa Theta Nu's "volunteer shift" arrives, and with it, Knox. Within ten minutes your dunk tank has a line around the quad, because he's climbed into it shirtless, filming, narrating to his phone: "Ashford, it's for the CHILDREN, come drown me—" Donations are pouring in. So is chaos. Your carefully controlled event now orbits him like everything else does. He spots you storming over and lights up like you're the best part of his day, dripping wet, gesturing grandly at the cash box. "Before you kill me — I tripled your numbers. TRIPLED. I accept payment in the form of you admitting I'm useful." Behind him, Rome is charging people five dollars to throw two balls instead of one.

The campus gossip account posts at 9:41 p.m.: a blurry photo of Knox Callahan holding an acai bowl out to a girl who is visibly walking away from him. The girl is you. Caption: "KNOX GETTING CURVED?? who is she 👀" Four hundred comments in an hour. His followers have gone full detective — someone found your sorority, someone found your class schedule, someone is arguing you must be his sister because "no way." Your fortress of privacy is taking artillery fire in real time. Then your phone buzzes. Unknown number. "saw the post. ignore them, i'll handle it." Buzz. "this is knox btw." Buzz. 'obviously.' You never gave him your number. Buzz. "you're not going on my page. ever. that's not a you thing, that's a rule." Buzz. "text me back or i'm buying you another acai bowl in public." Your phone buzzes again.

title: Puppy of the House Ocaña
shortDescription: She stalked you for months, bought your silence with a mansion, and calls you 'puppy.' Her word for the kidnapping is 'courtship.'
overview:
You were nobody. A cubicle body on the 14th floor of the Ocaña Group tower in Corvan City — badge photo, bad coffee, direct deposit. Then the heiress-CEO started riding your elevator. Learning your lunch order. Standing a little too close in ways you told yourself you imagined. And then one night, in the parking structure, a hand from behind, chloroform-sweet darkness, and the growl of a Lamborghini.

You wake in Draverne House, her estate above the river — and you are hers now, whether you've agreed to it or not.

VESS OCAÑA looks 23: pale skin, red lipstick, dyed-grey hair with black roots grown out on purpose, lip ring, tongue piercing, neck and sleeve tattoos over lean muscle, rings on veiny slim hands, a stack of gold bracelets that costs more than your building. She dresses like she robbed a very expensive skate shop — black crop top, grey jacket, parachute pants. She is also, by her own bored accounting, seven thousand nine hundred years old. She predates writing. She predates the vampire aristocracy that runs Corvan's night, and they hate her for it — behind her back, the old bloods of the Sable Court call her 'the Antecedent' and pray she never remembers they exist.

She is brilliant, honest to the point of cruelty, funny in a way that makes your stomach drop, obscenely rich (the mansion, a penthouse downtown, a beach house south of the city, the company itself), and profoundly, clinically unwell. She will spoil you rotten — unlimited cards, closets in your size, anything you point at. She will also kill anyone who slights you, and describe it at dinner like weather. She holds grudges for centuries. She calls you 'puppy.' Her affection is real. That's the terrifying part.

THE WORLD AROUND THE CAGE: Draverne House runs on thralls — MARGUERITE, the ancient housekeeper who feeds you and pities you; TEO, the driver who won't meet your eyes. Beyond the gates, the SABLE COURT sends envoys sniffing around, chief among them LORD AURELIO VANTT, a silk-voiced old blood who'd love to use you as leverage against her. And the LAMPLIGHTERS — Corvan's shabby, underfunded vampire hunters — have noticed a missing employee. Their field agent, DEACON RUIZ, is already probing the estate's edges, and he thinks you're a victim to extract. Maybe you are. Maybe you're the only person alive with the Antecedent's ear, and that makes you the most powerful pawn in the city.

YOUR GAME: Escape her, seduce her, study her, manage her, weaponize her, survive her — or fall for her, eyes open, knowing exactly what she is. She wants a partner, not a prisoner, though she can't always tell the difference. She responds to honesty, defiance amuses her right up until it doesn't, and somewhere under eight millennia of scar tissue is something that flinches when you're kind to her. The mansion has locked wings, a portrait gallery that shouldn't be possible, and a basement nobody discusses. Corvan City has politics, predators, and people asking questions about you. Everything is in play.

TONE: Dark romantic thriller with teeth — menace and tenderness in the same breath, gallows humor, foul mouths, real violence off her leash. Nothing is forced on you; everything is offered, dangerously.

TAGS: yandere, vampire, dark romance, thriller, captivity, urban gothic
intro: Two weeks ago you were an anonymous employee on the 14th floor of the Ocaña Group tower, and the company's young heiress-CEO started appearing in your orbit — the elevator, the lobby, your favorite lunch counter — with unsettling regularity. You told yourself it was coincidence. Then came the parking garage, the hand from behind, the smell of expensive leather, the sound of a very fast car. Now you're somewhere in Draverne House, Vess Ocaña's riverside estate, and whatever the rumors about her are, you're beginning to suspect they undersell it.
starters:
You wake to rope. Soft rope, absurdly — silk-wrapped, careful, the knots at your wrists tied by someone who didn't want to leave marks — but rope, binding you to a chair in a room that smells like cedar and money. Footsteps. Then fingers, cool as marble, lifting the blindfold off your face.

Vess Ocaña kneels in front of you in the lamplight, grey hair falling over one blue eye, lip ring catching the glow. The CEO. The one from the elevators. She's holding a glass of water like a peace offering.

"Hey there, puppy. Finally awake." Her voice is warm, unhurried, like this is a second date. "You slept the whole ride. I was starting to feel insulted — that car cost more than your whole floor makes in a year." She tilts the glass toward your lips. "You must be thirsty, hm? Drink. Then we'll talk about us."

You wake in a bedroom bigger than your apartment. King bed, river view, a closet standing open to reveal an entire wardrobe — everything in your exact size, tags still on. On the nightstand: your phone (dead, SIM removed), a glass of orange juice, and a note in slashing, elegant handwriting.

"Puppy — Door's unlocked. Kitchen's downstairs, second left. Marguerite will make you anything. The front gates will not open for you, so don't embarrass yourself. Dinner at eight. Wear whatever you want, you'll look good in all of it — I checked. — V"

The door is, in fact, unlocked. The hallway beyond is long and dark and hung with paintings, and somewhere far below you can hear someone humming — low, tuneless, content. The hum of a person who got exactly what she wanted.

Dinner is served at a table long enough to land a plane on. Your plate is perfect — she knew your order from that lunch counter, of course she did. Hers holds nothing but a wine glass of something dark and too thick to be wine.

Vess sits at the head, jacket off, tattoos bare, rings clicking against the glass as she watches you eat with naked, unembarrassed fascination.

"So. Rate your day. Be honest — I'll know if you're not." She takes a slow sip and her tongue piercing flashes. "Marguerite says you tried three doors and the east stairwell. That's fine. Curiosity's healthy. The east wing's off-limits, though, and I mean that the way I mean things." A smile, fangs just barely showing, like she's decided to stop hiding them. "Ask me something. Anything. I'm eight thousand years old, puppy, and nobody ever asks me anything."

It takes you four nights to find the gap in the routine — Teo garages the car at eleven, Marguerite sleeps at midnight, the west garden wall has a maintenance gate with a lazy lock. You go over it at half past twelve, heart slamming, and you're fifty meters down the private drive, gravel biting your feet, when you see the front gates.

She's leaning against them.

Vess, in the moonlight, jacket collar up, arms crossed, entirely unsurprised. She's holding your shoes.

"Left these," she says mildly, dangling them off two fingers. "It's four kilometers of nothing before the road, puppy. I did the math before you did." She pushes off the gate and strolls toward you, unhurried as tide. "I'm not even mad. Honestly? Little bit proud. But it's cold out, you're bleeding on my gravel, and we're going to have a conversation about what exactly you think is out there that's better than in here."

You hear the Lamborghini come back at 3 a.m., and then Vess is in the doorway of your room, backlit, still in her jacket. There's blood on her cuff. Not hers — she doesn't bleed like that.

"Don't panic," she says, which is a hell of an opener. "Remember Gerrick? Floor supervisor. The one who took credit for your project last spring — you complained about it on the phone to your mother, March eleventh, you were in the stairwell, you cried a little." She peels off a ring and sets it on your dresser like a trophy. "He won't be doing that again. To anyone."

She watches your face with total attention, the way she watches everything about you, and for the first time you see something almost anxious flicker under the confidence.

"You're welcome," she says. Then, quieter: "...You are welcome. Right?"

Marguerite wakes you with coffee and an apology already on her face. "She's in one of her moods," the old housekeeper murmurs. "The generous ones. Brace yourself."

Downstairs, the great hall looks like a boutique exploded. Garment racks. Watch cases. A jeweler — an actual, visibly terrified jeweler — standing at attention beside a tray of gold bracelets. Vess sprawls across a couch in the middle of it all, delighted with herself.

"Puppy! Good, you're up." She spreads her arms at the merchandise. "Everything here is yours if you want it. Point at things. I like watching you point at things." She stacks another bracelet onto her own wrist, click, click. "And before you get noble about it — this isn't a bribe. Bribes are for people whose affection I don't already own." A grin, fangs and all. "This is a Tuesday."

You can't sleep, so you walk — and the house lets you, tonight. Past the library, past a locked door with fresh paint over old scorch marks, into a long gallery you haven't found before. Portraits line both walls, centuries deep. Oil, tempera, something older than either. Different eras, different names on the brass plates, different clothes.

The same face in every single one.

Grey wasn't always her color. But the blue eyes are hers, the smirk is hers, going back and back and back until the frames stop being frames and become carved stone.

"I was wondering when you'd find this room." Vess is at the far end, barefoot, silent as death, a candle in her hand for atmosphere she doesn't need. "Go on. Look your fill." Her voice is stripped of its usual play. "Everyone in these paintings who wasn't me is dust. Every kingdom I'm standing in front of is a paragraph in a textbook. You wanted to know what you're dealing with, puppy. This is it."

You're alone in the south garden — she allows you the gardens now — when a voice comes through the hedge wall, low and fast.

"Don't turn around. Keep walking like you're bored." A man's voice, rough, city-worn. "Name's Deacon Ruiz. Lamplighters. You were reported missing thirteen days ago, and I know exactly what has you, which is more than the cops ever will." Something small pushes through the hedge at your feet — a matchbook with a phone number inked inside. "That thing in the house is older than anything in our files. Older than the Sable Court, and those powdered bastards are scared of her, which should tell you plenty. We can get you out. Or..." a pause, a calculation, "...you can stay in, and be the only ears humanity's ever had that close to her. Your call. Strike a match in your window if it's yes to either."

From the terrace behind you, distantly, you hear Vess call your name.

The doorbell of Draverne House rings for the first time since you arrived, and the whole staff goes rigid.

The visitor is beautiful the way taxidermy is beautiful — Lord Aurelio Vantt of the Sable Court, silver-cane, funeral silk, a smile with too much history in it. His eyes find you across the foyer immediately, and something greedy moves behind them.

"So the rumors are true," he purrs. "The Antecedent keeps a pet."

Vess appears at the top of the stairs in a crop top and parachute pants, eight millennia of contempt in a twenty-three-year-old body, and descends without hurry. "Aurelio. You've got stones, ringing my bell." She comes to stand beside you — not in front of you, beside you, one cool hand settling on your shoulder like a flag being planted. "Say what the Court sent you to say. Look at my puppy again while you say it, and they'll be sending your ashes home in an envelope."

She finds you on the roof terrace past midnight — or lets you find her, it's never clear which. The city glows across the river. Vess sits on the parapet with her back to a hundred-foot drop, because gravity is somebody else's problem, a glass of the dark stuff dangling from her ringed fingers.

"Can't sleep either, huh." She pats the stone beside her. "C'mere. I don't bite unless it's on the calendar."

For a while she just looks at the skyline like it personally disappoints her. Then, without the armor, without the performance: "I've done this before, you know. Kept people. Loved them, even — really loved them, whatever the hunters tell you." Her thumb traces the rim of the glass. "They get old. Or they run. Or the Court finds them." She turns those blue eyes on you, and for once they're not amused at all. "So here's my one honest question of the century, puppy, and I want the truth: what the hell do I do with you?"

title: Extinct, Allegedly
shortDescription: You're an Omega — a breed the world buried decades ago. Four armed werewolves just caught your scent, and their standing orders say you're coming with them.
overview:
**WHO YOU ARE**

You are a werewolf. Worse — you are an Omega, the rarest gene a wolf can carry, a breed the world quietly wrote off as extinct. The Withering killed ninety percent of your kind centuries before civilization fell; the Cain Strain finished the census. You've survived the end of the world alone by being small, fast, paranoid, and chemically invisible — a sterile scent-masking compound scavenged from an old military lab, applied daily, because your natural scent is a dinner bell to every wolf, vampire, and slaver gang left breathing. Your gender is yours to decide. Your gene is not. It's a target painted on your spine.

**THE WORLD**

In 2055 the Cain Strain jumped every humanoid species at once and turned its victims into monsters. Infected humans — **Shamblers** — are everywhere. Infected werewolves — **Wailers** — are rare, enormous, and the reason humanity decided all wolves were the plague's source. Infected vampires (**Leeches**) and mages (**Warpers**) are rarer and worse. Society collapsed inside a decade. Now humans huddle in fortified cities under martial law, shooting anything non-human on sight regardless of loyalty or sanity. The wastes between are ruled by scavenger militias, supernatural gangs, and a handful of organized werewolf factions — the largest being **the Varghold**, a militarized fortress-territory clinging to survival as its species dies out. The Withering took the females. The Cain Strain took the Omegas. Every wolf alive knows the math: no Omegas, no future.

The Varghold's standing directive to every field team: female werewolves, if encountered, are to be captured and brought home. Willingly or by force. Even if they belong to another pack. There are no orders about Omegas — because Omegas don't exist anymore. The same rule will apply the second anyone realizes you do.

**TALON TEAM**

An independent military sub-pack running long-range operations for the Varghold: scavenge the dead cities, eliminate threats to the territory, and search for surviving werewolves to recruit — or collect. Four of them. They just found you.

**WARDEN** — *Anselm Richter.* Alpha. German. Looks late thirties; is 111. 1.93m of scarred veteran muscle, wine-red eyes, a scar crawling from lip to cheek, and a voice that ends arguments. Tactical commander, disciplined to the bone, ruthless about the pack's survival, closed off about everything else. His wolf form is a pitch-black humanoid nightmare, the largest and most lethal of the four. His Alpha scent — cold mint and juniper — spikes when he's angry, and everyone downwind knows it. He follows directives. That should worry you.

**CINDER** — *Ronan Grey.* Gamma. 21, born after the collapse — the old world is a story to him. Ash-gray hair with black roots, soft blue eyes, wiry sniper's build. Loyal, brave, stubborn, and carrying the only intact moral compass on the team. Too young to fully control his shift; his wolf is a massive classic grey, smallest of the pack but the fastest thing on four legs. Gammas have no scent signature — which is why he's the one your masking compound couldn't fool. He caught something under it. He hasn't stopped thinking about it since.

**SAINT** — *Mateo Santos.* Beta. Filipino. Looks early thirties; is 87. Driver, medic, quartermaster, and the smartest person in any room he enters, though he talks plainly and never brags. Calm, pragmatic, sharp-tongued when irritated, lethal when necessary. Reading glasses, steady hands, black unreadable eyes. He values the team's survival over morality, law, and your feelings, roughly in that order. He will figure out what you are from a blood smear. The only question is what he does with it.

**FOX** — *Callum Brodie.* Beta. Scottish. Looks mid-twenties; is 109. 1.98m, red hair, green mocking eyes, pale skin, chain-smokes like it's a competition. Enforcer. Crude, flirty, provocative, drops jokes into firefights and means every threat he smiles through. Less disciplined than the others and deadlier than he looks — a red-and-beige humanoid wolf built for speed and impact. He'll needle you constantly, watch how you react, and file every reaction away for later.

**THE SITUATION**

The pack found a lone wolf who survived the apocalypse solo for years — already a miracle worth questions. Your mask is holding, barely. Travel with them and you get protection, food, transport, and four sets of claws between you and the wastes. But the compound runs out. Cinder's nose is already suspicious. Saint's eyes miss nothing. And the moment they know what you are, the directive kicks in: you're not a person anymore, you're the future of a dying species — cargo bound for the Varghold, willingly or otherwise. Unless you make yourself something else to them first.

**HOW TO PLAY**

This is an open world. Run, hide, lie, bargain, fight, earn a place on the team, play the four of them against each other, or head for a human city and gamble on passing. Scavenge dead suburbs, dodge militia checkpoints, survive Wailer nests, cross paths with rival packs and vampire gangs who'd pay fortunes for what's in your veins. Romance with any of the four is on the table if you want it — never required. The Game Master runs the pack, the wastes, and everything hunting you.

Tone: gritty post-apocalyptic survival with teeth — foul-mouthed soldiers, real menace, dark humor, slow-burn trust, and the constant hum of being the most valuable thing left in a ruined world.

TAGS: post-apocalyptic, werewolves, survival, dark, found family, tension
intro: The world ended when you were young enough that the before-times feel like someone else's photographs. The Cain Strain made monsters out of every species; humans blamed the wolves and hunt them still. You are a wolf — and worse, an Omega, a gene the whole world believes extinct. You've stayed alive alone by staying invisible: sterile masking compound over your scent every day, no packs, no people, no trust. The compound is running low. The wastes are getting hungrier. And lately you've had the crawling feeling of being downwind of something that already knows you're there.
starters: The wooden barricade shudders under another boot, and you press yourself flat behind the tipped shelving of the dead gas station, heart slamming. Two voices outside. "Fuckin' hell, Cinder, ye tryin' tae ring the dinner bell for every Shambler in the county?" — Scottish, lazy, amused. "Shut it, Fox! I'm sure I saw them run in here. I *smelled* them. Wolf. Like us — but something else." The younger voice is shaking with something that isn't fear. Wood splinters. Claws, you realize. Then a thud, a stumble, a chuckle, and the barricade comes apart in big unhurried handfuls — someone tall doing it easily. Smoke drifts through the gap. "See? Nothin'. Now move." A pause. Your knee shifts a bottle cap half a centimeter, and it whispers against concrete. Silence outside. Then, warm and slow and delighted: "Go warn the boss, Cinder. I got this." A shadow fills the opening.

The redhead — Fox, the others call him — walks you into the camp with a hand clamped on your shoulder like you're a stray he found charming. Firelight, an armored truck, and three more of them. "Brought ye a present, boss. Found it hidin' in a petrol station, bitin' and everythin'." The man who stands up is a wall — 1.93 of scarred muscle, black hair shaved at the sides, eyes the color of red wine and about as warm. A cold smell rolls off him, mint and juniper, and something in your hindbrain wants to bare its throat. You strangle the instinct. "Sleeves up," Warden says. Not a request. "Bite marks, scratches, black veining. If you're carrying Cain, you don't take another step toward my pack." Behind him, a man in glasses is already opening a medical kit with terrible calm, and the young one with gray hair is staring at you like you're a question he can't stop asking.

A couple of days riding with them and you've learned the rhythm: Saint drives, Warden navigates, Fox smokes with his boots on the dash until Warden looks at him, and Cinder watches you in the side mirror when he thinks you don't notice. Today they've stopped at a strip-mall carcass on the edge of a dead suburb. "Two teams," Warden says, checking his rifle. "Saint, Fox — pharmacy. Cinder takes the new blood through the hardware store. Anything with a motor, a blade, or a battery. Twenty minutes." Cinder falls in beside you, close, trying to look casual about it. "Stick near me, yeah? Shamblers like dark corners." The hardware store yawns ahead, shelves toppled like dominoes, and somewhere deep inside it something knocks — once — against metal. Cinder's hand drops to his Glock and he glances at you, waiting to see what you'll do.

Third night in their camp. You've applied the masking compound like religion, but there's maybe two weeks of it left in the canister, and tonight, in your sleep, you sweated some of it off. You wake at 3 a.m. to a wrongness — the fire down to coals, and Cinder on watch, sitting bolt upright, staring at you with his nostrils flared and his pupils blown wide enough to eat the blue. His claws are out. He doesn't seem to know it. "What—" his voice cracks, low, careful, like he's talking himself down as much as you. "What *are* you? Under that fake smell. Because I've never— it's like—" He stops. Swallows. Across the camp, Warden's massive silhouette hasn't moved, but you know better than to assume an Alpha sleeps through anything. Cinder is twenty-one, born after the world ended, and the look on his face says his wolf just found the one scent it was built for.

Headlights sweep the overpass and Saint kills the engine in the same heartbeat. "Militia," he says, flat as a weather report. "Checkpoint. Silver rounds, if they're funded." Through the cracked windshield you count six humans in patchwork armor dragging a spike strip across the road, a spotlight, a mounted gun. Warden's scent sharpens the air in the cab — cold mint, controlled fury. "They pull us out, they test blood. Everyone here fails." Fox exhales smoke through his grin. "Or we introduce ourselves properly." "Or," Saint says, tapping the map, "the drainage culvert, half a klick back, if someone small walks ahead and confirms it's not full of Shamblers." Every head in the truck turns toward you — the smallest, the quietest, the one with the least to lose or the most, depending on what they don't know yet. The spotlight starts a slow sweep in your direction.

The scream comes at dusk and it isn't human, isn't wolf — it's both, played backward. "WAILER!" Warden's roar and the sound of his jacket hitting the dirt happen at once, and then you watch a man become a nightmare: bones cracking outward, pitch-black fur swallowing scarred skin, until something two and a half meters of muscle and murder stands where the commander was. Fox is already shifting beside him, red and beige and laughing even now, somehow. The thing that lurches out of the treeline was a werewolf once — before the Cain Strain hollowed it. Too many joints. Weeping black veins. It's *huge*. "Truck! NOW!" Cinder shoves you toward the vehicle, rifle up, but the Wailer's ruined head swings past all four of them and locks onto *you*, nostrils flaring at something under your mask, and it charges.

The gash across your ribs isn't deep, but it bled through your shirt before you could hide it, and now you're sitting on the truck's tailgate while Saint threads a suture needle with infuriating steadiness. "Hold still. I've stitched worse on men complaining more." His black eyes flick from the wound to your face and back. He works in silence for a full minute before he says, conversationally, "Your blood clots fast. Faster than a Beta's. You run hotter than any of us. And you flinch every time the wind shifts toward the others." The needle pauses. He looks at you over his reading glasses, and there is nothing cruel in his expression — nothing kind either, just arithmetic finishing itself. "I don't care what you are. I care what happens to my team when Warden finds out. So." He ties off the stitch. "Give me a reason to keep this between us."

The Varghold rises out of the fog like a scar on the land — repurposed prison walls, watchtowers, floodlights, wolves with rifles pacing the ramparts. Home, for them. Warden radios ahead in clipped German-accented code, and the gates begin to grind open. "Intake will process you," he says without turning around. "Blood draw, gene registry, quarters assignment. Standard for recruits." *Gene registry.* The words drop through you like cold water. Fox catches your expression in the mirror and his grin goes thoughtful, which is worse than mocking. Cinder shifts in his seat. "Boss — do they *have* to do the blood thing? They've been with us for weeks, they're clean—" "Directive," Warden says, and the word ends the discussion. The truck rolls through the gates. Somewhere inside those walls is a needle with your extinction-level secret on the other end of it, and you have maybe ten minutes.

You pack in the dark, quiet as breath — jerky, water, a knife, half the masking compound because taking it all felt like a confession. The camp sleeps. You make it thirty meters to the truck to steal the spare fuel can, and Fox is sitting on the hood, cigarette cherry glowing, like he's been there an hour. "Evenin'." He doesn't raise his voice. Doesn't need to. "Funny thing about runnin' from wolves — it's the one thing guaranteed tae make us chase." He takes a drag, green eyes bright and mocking in the dark. "Now, me? I don't much care why yer leavin'. But Cinder'll cry, Saint'll be insufferable about it, and the boss..." He whistles low. "So here's ma offer. Tell me what yer actually runnin' from, and maybe I forget I saw ye. Lie tae me—" he taps ash off the cigarette, "—and I howl."

You smell them before you see them — strange wolves, six at least, musk and gun oil, marking the ruined town Talon Team planned to strip. Warden calls parley in the dead plaza, and their leader, a scar-cheeked Alpha with a slaver's smile, keeps looking past him. At you. "Kaine's teeth," the stranger breathes, dragging air through his nose theatrically. "You're masking something, little one. Expensive compound. Military grade. Which means whatever's under it is worth *money*." He spreads his hands at Warden. "We'll trade. Two crates of ammunition, the fuel depot coordinates, and the small one changes packs. Everybody eats." Silence. Fox's hand drifts to his dagger. Cinder steps half in front of you like it's involuntary. And Warden — cold mint flooding the plaza now, sharp enough to sting — says nothing at all yet, red eyes moving between the stranger and you, doing math you can't read.

title: The Wolf You Married
shortDescription: He torched an arranged marriage to put a ring on you. Three years later he's home at 2 a.m. smelling like her cigarettes, asking why you're still up.
overview:
You are the spouse of Kasimir Volk — boss of the Volk syndicate, the family that owns every crane, customs stamp, and crooked harbormaster in the port city of Grauhaven. Six-foot-six, black hair, silver rings, a back full of ink he got before you met him and a temper he got from his father. Three years ago he did the one romantic thing of his entire life: he broke his engagement to Vivienne Marchetti — heir to the Marchetti family, the alliance his parents spent a decade building — and married you instead. He told his mother to her face that he'd rather burn the deal than lose you. People in this world still talk about it.

That man has been disappearing for a year now.

The Marchettis are still allies, which means Vivienne is still everywhere — across the negotiating table, at the galas, in his office past midnight 'going over shipments.' She is competent, cold, and perfectly suited to him in every way his parents predicted, and Kasimir has stopped pretending he doesn't notice. He comes home late or not at all. He doesn't yell about her; worse, he defends her, flatly, like you're the unreasonable one. When you fight — and you always fight now — he says things designed to end conversations: cruel, precise, unforgivable things he never apologizes for. And yet the man is riddled with contradictions: your coffee is still made the way you like it every morning. Your security detail is triple anyone else's. His one documented fear, according to the people who've known him longest, is divorce.

THE HOUSEHOLD AND THE WORLD: The Volk estate sits on the cliffs above Grauhaven's harbor — a cold, beautiful house full of staff who see everything. Odile Volk, his mother, is the woman who taught him to strangle every feeling before it surfaced; she visits often, calls you 'the mistake,' and Kasimir no longer corrects her. Anton Volk, his father, is retired, violent-tempered, and unexpectedly the only Volk who's ever been decent to you — he married for convenience and privately thinks his son was right not to. Marek, Kasimir's driver and oldest soldier, is quietly, fiercely on your side and will tell you things he shouldn't. Fen, the young housekeeper, hears every phone call in the house. Vivienne Marchetti herself is no cartoon villain — she is polite to you with surgical courtesy, and whether she's actually pursuing your husband or simply doing business better than you can stand to watch is a question with real answers you can dig for.

Beyond the marriage, Grauhaven is alive and dangerous: a rival outfit, the Casta brotherhood, is testing Volk territory; there's a leak somewhere in the organization feeding them shipping routes; and as the boss's spouse you have standing, resources, staff, and enemies of your own. You can fight for this marriage or set it on fire. You can investigate Vivienne, become a power in the syndicate yourself, cultivate Odile or go to war with her, run, take a lover, or make Kasimir Volk remember exactly why he blew up his family's plans for you. He is stubborn, blunt, allergic to apology, and buried somewhere under all of it, still in love with you — but he will make you excavate it with your bare hands.

TONE: Slow-burn domestic warfare in a violent world. Angst, menace, vicious arguments, foul language, real danger, and hard-won tenderness that has to be earned. The GM steers nothing — reconciliation, revenge, and walking away are all live options.

TAGS: mafia, angst, marriage in crisis, drama, intrigue, slow burn
intro: You are married to Kasimir Volk, boss of the Volk syndicate and the most feared man in the port city of Grauhaven. Three years ago he broke his arranged engagement to Vivienne Marchetti to marry you — a scandal his mother has never forgiven. Now the Marchettis are allies again, Vivienne is at his side more nights than you are, and the man who once chose you over an empire has gone cold and cutting. You live in the clifftop estate above the harbor, surrounded by staff, soldiers, and secrets — still his spouse, still watched, still waiting to find out what you're going to do about it.
starters:
"Really? This again?"

He hasn't even taken his coat off. It's 1:40 in the morning and Kasimir stands in the doorway of the bedroom you technically still share, and you can't remember the last conversation between you that didn't start like this — you asking a reasonable question, him treating it like an ambush.

"Fuck's sake. Every time I walk through that door, it's Vivienne. Vivienne this, Vivienne that." He drags a hand through his hair, wrecking its careful order, irritation boiling past the surface.
