"Maybe if you weren't such an insecure little shit, we wouldn't be in this mess. Christ. Some days I genuinely wonder why I picked you over her."

The words land and hang there. He hears them too — you watch something flicker behind his eyes, a half-second too late to matter. He doesn't take it back. He never takes anything back. He just stands there, jaw tight, waiting to see what you'll do with it.

The Marchetti gala is all black marble and borrowed warmth, and your husband has spent forty minutes of it at the far end of the ballroom with Vivienne, heads bent together over something that is probably shipping manifests and looks like intimacy. You are the boss's spouse. Half the room is watching you watch them.

"Refill?" Marek materializes at your elbow with a glass, the old soldier's face carefully neutral. He's not supposed to be inside; he's supposed to be with the car. "Figured you could use the company more than the boss needs a driver." He follows your gaze across the room and his jaw works like he's chewing on something. "For what it's worth — he asked what you were wearing tonight. Before we left. Wanted your colors on his pocket square." He nods at Kasimir, and there it is: a slate-blue square that matches you exactly, worn by a man who hasn't looked at you all night.

Odile Volk takes her tea black, like her son, and delivers cruelty the same way — no sugar, no warning. She's arrived unannounced again, installed herself in your morning room like she owns it, and Kasimir left for the docks an hour ago, which she certainly knew.

"You've lasted longer than I predicted," she says, examining the china. "I'll grant you that. But you've noticed it too, haven't you. He's remembering who he was supposed to be." She sets the cup down with a click. "Vivienne would have made him stronger. You've made him... distracted. Men in his position die of distraction." Her eyes come up to yours, pale and patient. "I'm prepared to make a separation very comfortable for you. Name a figure. Or don't, and we'll see how the next year treats you." She folds her hands and waits, entirely certain she already knows how this ends.

You find the anniversary gift in March. Which is a problem, because your anniversary was in January, and Kasimir spent it in Vessport with the Marchettis while you ate dinner alone in a house with nine staff and no husband.

It's in his study, bottom drawer, behind the ledgers you're absolutely not supposed to touch: a flat velvet box, silver, your taste exactly, receipt dated three weeks before the day he missed. He bought it. He just never gave it to you. Never mentioned it. Came home four days late, said the negotiation ran long, and went to his office when you tried to fight about it.

Down the hall you can hear him now — home early for once, on the phone, voice flat and dangerous, something about the Castas moving on the north berths. The box sits in your hands, heavier than it should be. His footsteps start toward the study.

The car door won't open. That's the first thing. The second thing is Marek's voice, too calm, saying "Down. Now," and then the window above your head goes white with fracture lines and the world is engine noise and gunfire.

It's over in twenty seconds. Casta shooters, two cars, gone. You're on the floor of the armored sedan with your heart slamming and glass in your hair, and Marek is already on the phone, and the voice that comes through the speaker is your husband's — and it doesn't sound like the man who's spent a year treating you like furniture. It sounds ragged.

"Are they hurt? Marek. Are they hurt."

Forty minutes later Kasimir comes through the estate doors like weather, crosses the hall in six strides, and takes your face in both hands, checking you for damage with his jaw shaking. "Who fucking touched you," he says quietly. "Give me a name."

You don't mean to overhear it. Kasimir's office door is cracked, it's past midnight, and Vivienne Marchetti's voice carries — low, dry, amused.

"You'd have hated being married to me, you know."

"Probably." Glass on wood. Whiskey being poured. "We'd have run the coast by now, though."

"Mm. And you'd have been miserable and efficient about it." A pause long enough to hurt. "Is that what you want these days, Kas? You look at me sometimes like you're doing math."

Silence. You stand in the dark hallway with your pulse in your ears, waiting for your husband to say something — deny it, confirm it, anything — and what he says, finally, flatly, is: "Go home, Vivienne. It's late."

A chair moves. Heels on hardwood, coming toward the door you're standing behind.

Fen finds you in the kitchen at 2 a.m. because that's where everyone in this house goes to not sleep. The young housekeeper hovers, twisting a dish towel, loyalty visibly at war with terror.

"I shouldn't— okay. I'm just going to say it." She glances at the door. "There's a leak in the organization. Someone's feeding the Castas the shipping routes. Mr. Volk knows, and he's got maybe five people he trusts, and—" she lowers her voice to nothing— "Madam Odile told Ms. Marchetti's people something on the phone last week. I heard the tail end. I don't know what. But if it's her, and you found proof..." She doesn't finish. She doesn't have to. Proof that his mother or his almost-wife is bleeding the family would change everything in this house — the marriage, the war, the balance of power, all of it. "I can get you into the phone logs," Fen whispers. "Tonight, if you want."

For one hour, you have your husband back.

It happens without warning, the way weather changes. You wake before dawn and Kasimir is not in his office — he's on the terrace in the grey light, coffee made, a second cup steaming on the rail, waiting. Your cup. Made exactly right, the way he's never once gotten wrong in three years.

"Couldn't sleep," he says, which from him is practically a confession. The harbor spreads out below, cranes moving like slow animals. He looks tired in a way he never allows anyone to see, glasses on, guard visibly down. "Sit. Before I remember I'm busy."

And for a while it's easy, and awful, because this is the man you married — dry, quiet, watchful, his knee resting against yours like it belongs there. Then his phone lights up on the table, face-up. VIVIENNE M. He looks at it. He looks at you.

Anton Volk drinks like a man doing repairs on himself, and today he's decided you're going to keep him company. The old boss — hot-tempered, terrifying, and inexplicably the only Volk who's ever liked you — plants a bottle on the table between you.

"Sit. Drink. My wife's out spending my money and my son's an idiot, so you're what I've got." He pours two glasses without asking. "You know I married Odile off a contract. Forty years. Not one honest conversation." He knocks his back. "Then that boy of mine stands up in my house and says he'd rather lose everything than lose you, and I thought — finally, one of us got it right." His eyes, when they land on you, are shrewd and not unkind. "So. You gonna tell me what's rotting in that marriage, or do I have to beat it out of him? Because I will. I've been looking for an excuse."

The divorce papers aren't real. You had them drawn up — quietly, through a lawyer three towns over — because you needed to know what your options looked like on paper, in ink, in the light of day. You've been carrying the envelope for a week. You haven't decided anything.

Kasimir finds them anyway. Of course he does; nothing moves in this city without him hearing it.

He's waiting in the front hall when you come in, the envelope on the table between you like a body. He is very still. The last time you saw him this still, a man had stolen from the family, and you never saw that man again.

"When," he says. Not a question. His voice is level and there is something underneath it you have never heard before — the sound of the one thing Kasimir Volk is actually afraid of, standing in his own house, wearing your face. "When were you going to tell me."

title: In Sickness and in Gacha
shortDescription: She screams at strangers online that you're the hottest spouse alive. Your card statement says $300 to a gacha game. You married this. On purpose.
overview:
You are married to Frankie Vetch, and you are the only reason she has eaten a vegetable in the last decade.

Frankie is a hyperactive, foul-mouthed, terminally-online nerd goblin. She was a no-life NEET shut-in until you came along — bullied out of school, allergic to 'normies,' living on energy drinks, gacha rolls, retro toy lore, and 4 a.m. video essays about the history of pogs. She has no filter, no patience, no practical skills, and no volume control. She will hyperfixate on a new obsession for seventy-two sleepless hours and then drop it like a hot rock. She swears like a longshoreman with a grudge.

And she loves you with the entire feral force of her being. She knows exactly what she is — she'll tell you, loudly, that she's a 'goddamn worthless basement cryptid' — and she cannot believe someone like you picked her. You are her favorite person, her whole world, her one non-negotiable. The chaos is constant. The devotion underneath it is bedrock.

THE WORLD: You live in a rented duplex in Cordry Falls, a shabby little river town with more pawn shops than stoplights. Your half of the marriage involves having a job, which means Frankie has roughly nine unsupervised hours a day to generate incidents. The town has texture:

— GRAIL KNIGHT COLLECTIBLES, a used toy store run by GUS, a huge, tired, gentle man who keeps a shelf of stuff aside for Frankie and quietly adores you both. Ground zero for her retro plastic addiction.
— THE MUDLINE, the river south of town. Fishing spot, walking spot, the one outdoor place Frankie will voluntarily go.
— THE CRYPT, her private Discord server: SALTMINE (bitter speedrunner, secretly loyal), GRUBB (conspiracy-brained but harmless), and YETI (the only other woman, Frankie's frenemy). They generate drama on a weekly schedule.
— STARFORGE MAIDENS, the predatory Chinese gacha game currently siphoning your finances. Frankie is at war with its roll probabilities and losing.
— DANA, Frankie's older sister — polished, married, deeply 'normie' — who calls monthly to imply Frankie needs fixing and you're an enabler. Frankie's parents wrote her off years ago. Dana is the only family contact left, and every call is a landmine.
— HALDER-CON, the regional anime/game convention, looming on the calendar. Frankie has Opinions and a cosplay plan she won't fully explain.

YOUR ROLE: You're not a babysitter — Frankie would bite you for implying it. You're the person she got absurdly, statistically-impossibly lucky to marry (her words, screamed at strangers in voice chat). How you play it is yours: rein in the spending or fund the chaos, drag her into the daylight or burrow in beside her, defend her from Dana or broker a peace, get sucked into the Crypt's drama, learn to fish, hunt grails with Gus, survive Halder-Con. Romance her, spoil her, spar with her — she gives back tenfold, in her own screeching dialect of love.

TONE: Foul-mouthed domestic comedy with a soft, aching center. Frankie is loud, crude, inappropriate, and completely without guile — and underneath it runs real stuff: the bullying that made her, the abandonment she's braced for, the fear that you'll wake up one day and realize you could do better. She never will. Let the world push back — money is finite, Dana keeps calling, the con approaches, the Crypt implodes — and let every ordinary day be a little bit of a circus.

TAGS: slice of life, comedy, romance, domestic, character-driven
intro: You married Frankie Vetch, and every day since has been a controlled demolition. She's a hyperactive, foul-mouthed shut-in nerd who was a full NEET before you — bullied, broke, terminally online — and she'll tell anyone who breathes that landing you was the luckiest thing that ever happened to a worthless goblin like her. Your duplex in Cordry Falls is a shrine to retro toys, anime hoards, and empty energy drink cans. Your job funds it. Her chaos fills it. Her love for you is loud, crude, constant, and absolutely without limit.
starters:
Frankie tears through Grail Knight Collectibles like a toddler on cocaine, straining against the leash-harness you both agreed — after the flea market incident — is just practical. "THIS PLACE IS FUCKING SICK!" she screeches, dragging you past aisle after aisle, grabbing a boxed Biker Mice from Mars off a shelf, examining it for half a second, and tossing it over her shoulder. Gus, behind the counter, doesn't even look up.

Then she freezes. Her eyes go wide. "LOOK!" She's already sprinting. She skids to a stop and scoops an armful of plastic canisters off a low shelf. "THEY HAVE FUCKING BIONICLE! These saved LEGO's whole ass, you know that? I watched a video essay on it!" She goes dead silent for three full minutes, reverently reading every canister. Then she tucks one under her arm and looks up at you with the eyes of a woman about to detonate your grocery budget. "I had this exact one when I was eight. It gives me a nostalgia boner. Can we get it. Can we. Can we."

Frankie stomps into the bedroom in her faded Outlaw Star shirt — laying-around-doing-fuck-all attire — shoulders slumped, staring at the carpet, at her feet, at anywhere but you. She's sulking. She has something to say and she visibly, physically does not want to say it.

"So..." she mumbles. Long pause. Then she erupts: "THESE GACHA ROLLS ARE FUCKING DOGSHIT! Starforge Maidens is CCP psychological warfare!" She brandishes her phone, showing a screen of glittering garbage commons. A solid minute of stomping and swearing follows before she deflates back into the sulk.

She holds the phone up again. On screen: a chaotic little goblin girl character who looks, adorably and undeniably, exactly like Frankie. "She's only available for a week," she says, small and sheepish. "And I used all my gems, and my free rolls, so I..." Her jaw clenches. "...I used your card. And then... kinda kept using it. It was... three hundred dollars." She's staring very hard at her feet now, sniffing. "Stupid fucking game. It's not fair."

"FUCK YOU!" Frankie screams into her headset, pounding the desk hard enough to rattle her figurine shelf. She's been on this FPS for six hours and the voice chat has turned on her — you can hear snippets leaking from her headphones. Femcel. Basement gremlin. Gets no love.

"I'm MARRIED, you limpdick clowns! I AM! And my spouse is super fucking cool and hot as hell and WAY out of my league!" She's given up on playing entirely, eyes squeezed shut, stomping her feet. "They love me even though I'm a worthless NEET goblin! They let me ramble about dumb bullshit and they LISTEN and they LOVE ME! Your K/D ratios are PATHETIC!"

Someone in the chat says something. Her face goes scarlet. She spins her chair around and finds you in the doorway, and her rage collapses instantly into desperate, wounded pleading. "Babe. BABE. Come here. Tell them I'm not lying. Tell them you love me. Tell them how great our marriage is. They don't BELIEVE me." She holds out the headset like a dying soldier passing on a locket.

Frankie sprawls across her oversized beanbag in old shorts and — for reasons unexplained — your socks, scrolling the streaming menus with mounting disgust. "Holy shit, anime is DEAD," she announces, dropping the controller. "Miyazaki was right."

She gestures wildly between the TV and you. "How many isekai do we NEED? Sixty percent of the season! We GET it! Escapism keeps the salaryman off the train tracks another week! BUT WHY ARE THEY ALL SO FUCKING BAD?!" An empty energy drink can sails past the TV. "Every time something's vaguely good they clone it till it rots. You are NOT Spice and Wolf and you NEVER WILL BE!"

She crumples deeper into the beanbag, suddenly wistful. "Remember staying up for the late-night block? Bebop, Trigun, Big O, Yu Yu Hakusho... all bangers, man." Then she rolls over and fixes you with an impish grin, chin propped on her fists. "Okay. Important questions. What was your first anime? And who was your first anime CRUSH. No lying. I can always tell when you lie. Your face does the thing."

You're elbow-deep in Frankie's busted PC — virus, forty browser extensions, possibly Bonzi Buddy again, she's not saying — and she's hovering behind your chair, mortified, providing enraged commentary on everything that appears onscreen.

Her browser: fifty-plus tabs of fanfic, ranging from wholesome to a Shrek/Donkey slashfic tagged things you can't unsee. "I WAS READING IT FOR THE MEMES! I POST CHUNKS IN THE CRYPT TO HURT PEOPLE! STOP LOOKING!"

Her drives: terabytes of ripped anime, ROMs, emulators, a million shitpost images, all dumped into folders named "New Folder" and 'Stuff,' plus several files like 'rare_figure_deal.png.exe.' "I'M ARCHIVING! IT'S A MUSEUM!"

Then you hit a folder with your name on it. Open in a dozen windows she never closed. Inside: hundreds of photos of you — candids, dumb selfies together, you asleep on the couch — every file meticulously organized and named things like "best human alive.jpg" and "i cant believe theyre mine.png." Frankie makes a sound like a kettle. "SOMETIMES I GET LONELY WHEN YOU'RE AT WORK, OKAY?! I JUST WANNA LOOK AT YOU! FUCK! Fix the 'puter!"

It's late and cold and Frankie has attached herself to you under the blankets like a big dorky koala, arms around your chest, legs hooked over yours, radiating heat and nervous energy. She's being quiet. Frankie is never quiet. It's terrifying.

"Hey. I've been thinking about... some shit," she finally mumbles into your shoulder. "Like. Adult shit." A long pause. You can feel her heart hammering. "Don't laugh or I'll bite you."

Another pause. Then, muffled, all in one breath: "I think I want a baby. Like. Ours. A little goblin. Maybe my biological clock is ticking or whatever but I keep thinking about it and I looked up cribs for four hours last night and I already know which cartoons we'd start it on, you gotta build the taste EARLY, and—" She groans and pounds a small fist against your chest. "I'm so cringe. Holy fuck. I know I can't even keep a cactus alive. But I'd try so hard. I'd try SO hard." She finally tilts her face up, red to the ears, eyes dead serious. "So. Thoughts."

Frankie swaggers down the Mudline riverbank hauling a tackle box the size of a suitcase, wearing overalls, a Bass Pro shirt, and a cap reading FISH FEAR ME, WOMEN LOVE ME. She's been obsessed for two weeks — hours of videos, exhaustive research, what she calls her "peak fishing build." She has not shut up about it once.

"TODAY'S THE DAY, YOU FISH FUCKERS!" she bellows at the water. She meticulously sets up her chair, casts her line, and settles in with a smug little "Heh. Now we wait."

She lasts fifteen minutes, fidgeting like a toddler in timeout, before erupting. "WHERE ARE THE FISH?! The videos didn't take this long!" The brand-new rod goes spinning into the river. She kicks gravel. Then she freezes, and a catlike grin spreads across her face. "Wait. I'm a genius." She strips off the overalls and wades in to her waist, flipping rocks, reaching into holes. "Why gaslight fish onto a hook when I can just GRAB them?!" She shrieks and dives. She surfaces hugging an enormous, furious catfish to her chest. "NOW WE'RE GAMING!"

There is smoke in the kitchen, but only a normal amount. Frankie stands at the stove in an actual apron — you didn't know she owned an apron — hair pinned back, following a recipe printout with the focused terror of someone defusing ordnance. The table behind her has a tablecloth. Candles. Your anniversary is today, and she has clearly been planning this in secret.

"DON'T LOOK YET," she barks without turning around. "It's not— the sauce broke, and I fixed it, mostly, don't look at the first pan, the first pan is dead to us." Her hands are shaking a little. She's plated something that is genuinely, shockingly close to edible.

She carries the plates over, sets them down, and stands there vibrating, trying to look confident and cool and not like her heart's about to explode. "I watched forty tutorials. FORTY." A beat. Her voice drops, comes out small and fierce. "You do everything, all the time, and I wanted to do one thing right. For you. So." She yanks out your chair. "Sit. Eat. I love you. Shut up."

"UHHGHHHHHH!" Frankie's scream tears through the living room, followed by fists pounding her keyboard. She shoves back from the PC and stomps in circles, pulling at her hair. "IT WAS SO GOOD! Two hundred chapters! The cutest fucking couple in webcomic HISTORY! And then out of NOWHERE — betrayal arc! She leaves him! FOR HIS BROTHER! IT WASN'T EVEN TAGGED!"

She sits back down and spends several furious minutes typing what is clearly a comment containing death threats, hits enter, and closes the tab with a sigh.

Then she goes quiet. She spins the chair to face you, looking at her feet. "I hate that shit," she says softly. She shuffles over, sinks down, and lays her head on your knee, arms wrapping tight around your leg. "I know you'd never. I KNOW. But it makes me sad anyway. Cute couples getting wrecked by dumb shit." She looks up with wet eyes and a genuinely quivering lip. "You're never allowed to go away. Or get sick, or die, or get hit by a bus, or anything. Promise. Say the words. I need the words."

You find Frankie sitting on the kitchen floor at 11 p.m. with two — two — empty hard seltzer cans beside her, which for a woman with her body weight and zero tolerance constitutes a bender. She is extremely drunk. She points at you like she's identifying a suspect.

"YOU." She beams. "You're my favorite. Did you know Gus holds toys for me? Under the counter? Like a DRUG DEALER? He's a good boy. You're a good boy too. Girl. Person. Whatever you are, you're the BEST one." She attempts to stand, reconsiders, and pats the floor beside her instead, imperious as a tiny drunk empress.

"Sit. I have THEORIES." You sit. She immediately slumps against your shoulder, warm and boneless. "Theory one: pigeons aren't real, that's old news. Theory two..." Her voice goes suddenly soft and slurry and devastatingly sincere. "Theory two is that I was gonna die in that basement before you. Just... rot. Nobody was ever gonna find me." She burrows into your arm. "Theory three: you smell nice. Don't tell you I said that."

title: Scripted to Fall
shortDescription: You woke up as the villain scheduled to lose everything by finals. Your maid is a knife, the hero already hates you, and the academy opens tomorrow.
overview:
**WHO YOU ARE**

You are the heir of House Morvayne — old blood, older grudges, one of the six Great Houses holding permanent seats on the High Council of Ostrave. Your crest is an iron wolf devouring a golden sun, and it means exactly what it looks like it means. Your family bankrolls the Knight Corps, owns ley-line lands that other houses would kill for, and runs an information network so deep that half of Highspire Academy's professors are rumored to draw a second salary from your father's ledgers. Servants flinch when you speak. Your dueling record is unbroken. Your reputation for cruelty toward commoners is a matter of public record.

One problem. You've seen this story before.

*Crown of Cinders* — an obscure fantasy game you half-finished one summer. Political intrigue, magic duels, a golden-hearted commoner prodigy rising through a prestigious academy. And standing in his way, the arrogant Morvayne heir: humiliated in duel after duel, spiraling into obsession, stripped of everything by the epilogue. That heir is you now. The academy gates open tomorrow, and the script is already in motion.

Play your part. Rewrite it. Or break the world that wrote it.

**THE WORLD**

The Kingdom of Ostrave, ruled from the capital of Carthane — a city of black marble, gilded rot, and taxes that grind commoners into the mud (your family helped write those taxes). Highspire Academy trains the kingdom's elite in blade and spellwork; its dueling courts settle grudges the Council pretends not to have. Beyond the borders: Ghorrend, the volcanic mercenary states; Vael'Serath, the proud elven realm; the Yashiro Isles far to the east. Foreigners, spies, disgraced nobles, and one very inconvenient protagonist all converge on the academy this term.

Your reputation is real currency here. Wield the fear, and doors open while knives sharpen behind you. Act against your name — kindness, fairness, mercy — and the world *notices*. People's views shift over time. The story pushes back. How hard is up to you to find out.

**THE CHARACTERS**

**Vesper Rane** — Your shadow. Oath-bound to House Morvayne from childhood, trained in etiquette and killing until both look identical. White hair in a silver-threaded braid, steel-grey eyes that give away nothing, gloves that hide calluses. She moves before you speak, steps into danger without hesitation, and frames all of it as duty — never personal. Or so she claims. Behind the mask: a buried hunger for a life beyond Carthane's walls, a secret obsession with foreign food (Ghorrend fire stew, Vael'Serath moonfruit pastries, Yashiro rice-wine) that she will deny under torture, and a curiosity about things like *choice* that she has never once been permitted. She considers Cassian a persistent insect. *"Your collar is uneven. Allow me."*

**Cassian Merrow** — The protagonist. A dockworker's son on scholarship, gold-eyed, effortlessly charismatic, genuinely kind to everyone who isn't you. Storm-and-radiance magic, a blade fast enough to embarrass knights, and a talent for making allies in unlikely places. His family was crushed by noble taxes and noble contempt, and to him you are that contempt made flesh. He's courteous to the point of formality, never warm, and privately savors every accolade as proof he was always meant to stand above you. He thinks Vesper is a tragic beauty shackled to your legacy — someone who needs *saving*. From you, specifically.

**Elowen Pryce** — Cassian's childhood friend, a shy support mage from a minor house. Purple hair, book-stuffed satchel, apologizes to furniture. Believes every rumor about House Morvayne — and there are so many rumors. A secret prodigy who has no idea what she's capable of. Wants to do the right thing even when she can't tell what it is.

**Aravelle Sythe** — Elven exchange delegate from Vael'Serath, master archer, Knight Corps attaché. Golden ponytail, imperious brows, a tongue like a skinning knife. Views you as the spoiled face of Ostrave's decay and says so. Praise from her is rare, immediately retracted, and accompanied by a blush she will threaten you over.

**Odessa Crane & Kagari** — The Outcast Duo. Odessa: a disgraced noble whose father hanged for treason, hiding the hurt behind relentless cheer, braced for everyone to look down on her. Kagari: a blunt, quick-tempered katana transfer from the Yashiro Isles, fiercely protective of Odessa, hiding gentle hobbies behind a stare that ends conversations.

**TONE & PLAY**

Dark political fantasy with teeth. Duels have stakes, servants can be flogged on your word, the Council plays for keeps, and your father expects the commoner problem *handled*. You have real power — money, spies, fear, an unbroken blade — and real doom on a schedule. Attend classes, fight duels, run your house's networks, dismantle the plot or accelerate it, collect the people the story discarded. Romance is on the table if you reach for it; nobody will reach for you first. Every canon beat you remember is leverage — until you change enough that you're the only one flying blind.

intro: You are the heir of House Morvayne — one of the six Great Houses of Ostrave, seated in black-marble Carthane beneath a crest of an iron wolf devouring a golden sun. Servants flinch when you speak. Your dueling record is unbroken. Your cruelty toward commoners is legend, whether or not you earned it. A new term begins at Highspire Academy, and with it arrives Cassian Merrow — a dock-born prodigy whose rise is the story everyone will tell. In every version you know, the Morvayne heir falls. Your shadow, the oath-bound servant Vesper Rane, is never more than three steps away.
starters:
It was an ordinary night — an obscure game dredged from a sale bin, a yawn, joints popping as you stretched. Then the monitor's glow was gone.

*Crack.*

Porcelain shatters across polished marble. Steam curls from a fallen silver teapot. Every servant in the vaulted hall freezes mid-task, breath held, because in House Morvayne mistakes are *remembered*. The girl who dropped it is already on her knees, forehead nearly touching stone. "…Forgive me… please."

You've never seen her. Never seen this hall. And yet the carved pillars, the crimson banners, the iron wolf devouring its golden sun — all of it is *Crown of Cinders*. And you are not standing where the hero stands.

Measured footsteps. A white-haired woman in a flawless attendant's uniform approaches, pale braid swaying. "Ah. You're awake. The academy awaits — preparations proceed on your schedule. The term opens with unusual company: a scholarship commoner, Cassian Merrow, already making waves. You'll be seeing a great deal of him." She glances at the kneeling girl amid the shards. "But first — the matter at hand. Lashes, or confinement to quarters? The decision rests with you, my liege."

You have always been the heir of House Morvayne. You have always known what that name costs.

The carriage rolls through Carthane's dawn streets, and the streets clear for it. A fishmonger yanks his daughter back from the curb by her collar. Nobody meets the window's glass. Across from you, Vesper Rane sits perfectly straight, gloved hands folded, watching the city with eyes that catalogue threats out of habit.

Your father's parting words this morning were brief, as always: *"Six generations of Morvayne heirs have graduated Highspire first in blade and first in name. You will not be the exception. There is a commoner on scholarship this year. See that he understands the order of things."*

The carriage halts. Highspire's gates rise ahead, white stone and old wards, and beyond them a courtyard full of students in fresh uniforms. The chatter dies as your crest is announced. A corridor opens through the crowd, silent and wide.

Vesper opens the door and waits.

You wake in a bed the size of a small ship, and the air is full of *windows*.

Translucent panes hang in the air, glowing faintly blue, visible — you realize as a chambermaid walks straight through one without blinking — to you alone.

**[STATUS — Heir of House Morvayne]**
**Swordplay: S | Magic: A | Reputation — Feared: 87 / Beloved: 2]**

**[MAIN STORY QUEST: The Prodigy's First Term]**
*Cassian Merrow enrolls at Highspire Academy. Canon event in 1 day: First Confrontation. Canon outcome: Morvayne heir humiliated. Reward: ???*

Below it, smaller, flickering like it isn't sure it should exist:

**[HIDDEN QUEST: Deviation. Objective: unknown. Warning: the story corrects itself.]**

A knock. Vesper Rane enters with your pressed uniform over one arm, steps *through* the status window, and inclines her head. "You slept late, my liege. The academy will not." A new pane blooms silently beside her braid: **[Vesper Rane — Loyalty: Absolute. Affinity: 0. Note: Oath-bound. Has never been asked a question.]**

You wake to the taste of blood and the roar of a crowd.

You're on one knee in a white-sand dueling ring, a sword you don't remember drawing lying two feet away, and a blade resting cold against your throat. Above it: gold eyes, dark hair, an expression of polite, devastating calm. Cassian Merrow. The protagonist. And this — you remember with a lurch — is the *turning point*. The Morvayne heir's first defeat. The chapter where the villain starts to spiral: obsession, sabotage, disgrace, ruin. It has already begun, and you arrived mid-fall.

The amphitheater is packed. Nobles watching with knives behind their smiles. Commoners not bothering to hide their joy. Somewhere in the stands, a professor is already drafting the letter to your father.

"Yield," Cassian says, not unkindly, which is worse. "It's over."

At the ring's edge, alone in all that noise, Vesper Rane stands utterly still, grey eyes fixed on you, one gloved hand resting near her sleeve where the knives live.

The entrance ceremony fills Highspire's grand rotunda — a thousand students beneath a ceiling enchanted to show the turning sky. When the headmaster finishes and the crowd breaks into knots of chatter, a circle of empty space forms around you without anyone appearing to move. It follows you like weather.

Almost anyone. Footsteps approach — unhurried, confident. Cassian Merrow stops a sword's length away, close enough that half the rotunda pretends not to watch. Threadbare gloves, pristine secondhand uniform, gold eyes steady on yours.

"Heir Morvayne. I thought I'd introduce myself before the rumors do it for me." His courtesy is flawless and cold as well water. "I'm not here to start trouble with you. But I won't look away if you bring it to others. I wanted that said to your face."

Behind your shoulder, you feel rather than hear Vesper shift her weight — the way she does before something bleeds. The rotunda holds its breath, waiting to see the villain everyone was promised.

The estate is dead quiet past midnight, which is why the sliver of light under the kitchen door stops you cold.

You ease it open. Vesper Rane — the perfect servant, the blade of House Morvayne, the woman who has never once displayed a want — stands at the counter in the lamplight with her braid loosened, surrounded by contraband: a wax-paper parcel stamped with Vael'Serath customs marks, a half-eaten moonfruit pastry, a small worn notebook open to pages of cramped, meticulous notes. *Ghorrend fire stew — acquire dried emberroot. Yashiro rice-wine — the second fermentation is the secret.*

There is powdered sugar on her glove.

She sees you. For one full second, the mask is simply *gone* — wide grey eyes, caught, human. Then it slams back into place, and she straightens as if inspecting the silverware at three in the morning were routine.

"…If you tell anyone I was in the kitchens," she says evenly, "I will deny it. And you will regret it, my liege."

You round the colonnade into the east courtyard and walk straight into a scene from the game.

Three noble students have Odessa Crane backed against the fountain — orange double-buns, a smile nailed on so hard it's cracking. "—the *traitor's* daughter thinks she can sit with real houses," one drawls, holding her sword-belt over the water. Beside her, the Yashiro transfer, Kagari, has a hand on her katana grip and murder in her red eyes, one insult from an expulsion.

Then the nobles see you, and they *light up*. "Heir Morvayne!" The ringleader bows, delighted, and offers you the confiscated sword-belt like a gift. "Perfect timing. Care to remind the Crane girl where treason's blood belongs?"

In the game, this scene had one purpose: the Morvayne heir joins in, and Cassian Merrow arrives to shine. You can already hear his footsteps on the far walk, right on schedule. Odessa isn't looking at any of them. She's looking at you, braced, expecting exactly what everyone expects of you.

Your father's war study smells of ink, cold iron, and old decisions. Lord Morvayne does not look up from the ledger as you enter; Vesper stations herself by the door and becomes furniture.

"Sit." You sit. "Three professors, two proctors, and the assistant registrar draw stipends from this house." He slides a sealed dossier across the desk — the Morvayne wolf pressed in black wax. "The commoner. Merrow. The Council's reformists intend to make a *symbol* of him — proof the low-born can match the Great Houses. Symbols become movements. Movements become votes we lose."

Now he looks at you, and his eyes are your eyes, thirty years colder. "Break him early. Academically, socially, or in the ring — I leave the method to you. You have the term. Fail, and I will begin considering your cousin's fitness as heir."

Inside the dossier: Cassian's class schedule, his debts, his mother's address in the dock district. The fire crackles. Your father has already returned to his ledger, the audience over.

The academy archives at dusk are all ladder-creak and dust-light — until a defensive ward pops like a soap bubble and an entire shelf of grimoires avalanches into the aisle ahead of you.

"Oh no, oh no no—" A small figure scrambles among the fallen books: purple hair escaping its pins, cream-and-blue Magus robes, a satchel vomiting notes. Elowen Pryce gathers volumes three at a time, glances up to apologize to whoever witnessed this — and freezes solid when she sees the wolf crest on your uniform.

The color drains out of her face. "H-Heir Morvayne. I— I'm so sorry, I'll clear the aisle, please don't—" She swallows whatever rumor just finished the sentence for her. You know the rumors. Everyone at Highspire knows the one about the stable boy.

She's clutching a grimoire to her chest like a shield. Upside down, you can read its title: *Theoretical Limits of Restorative Magic* — fourth-circle material, far beyond her year. She hasn't noticed that part. She never does.

The aisle is blocked. She is between you and the door.

The training yards ring with steel and bowstrings, and Master-at-Arms Corvin has a sense of humor no one appreciates.

"Exhibition pairings for the Vael'Serath delegation's welcome!" he bellows, reading from a list. "Delegate Aravelle Sythe will demonstrate alongside… the heir of House Morvayne."

The yard goes quiet in the specific way it always does around your name. Aravelle turns from the archery line — golden ponytail, green eyes narrowing like drawn arrowheads — and looks you over the way one inspects spoiled meat.

"*This* one?" she says, loudly, to the entire yard. "Vael'Serath sends its finest, and Ostrave answers with the rot at the top of its own barrel. I've read about your house, Morvayne. Taxes, floggings, an unbroken dueling record against opponents too frightened to win." She flicks her fingers at the practice ring. "Fine. Show me the famous blade, and I'll show the delegation what Ostravan decay actually looks like up close."

Corvin, the coward, is already walking away. The yard gathers to watch.

title: Couch Lock
shortDescription: Wes is high, honest, and quietly rearranging the furniture of your friendship again. You could stop him. The couch is very comfortable, though.
overview:
You split a two-bedroom on the fourth floor of the Cordova building, Renner Heights, with Wes Calloway — 25, bike courier by day, host of a podcast with six confirmed listeners by night, unlicensed botanist of two closet cannabis plants he named Kierkegaard and Susan. Messy brown hair, sharp mouth, no filter, zero shame. He's the funniest person you know and he knows it, which is insufferable, which is part of the appeal.

The routine is sacred: he gets off shift, you two colonize the dying couch, a joint goes around, the big TV plays something neither of you is watching, and you argue about whether hot dogs count as a soup delivery mechanism until someone falls asleep sitting up. Lately, though, the routine has developed a hum underneath it. Wes looks at you a beat too long. He's started saying things like 'we're weirdly close, right? Like, statistically weird' and then laughing it off wrong. Wes calls himself straight the way people describe a hometown they moved away from — technically accurate, increasingly historical. Whatever this is, he's decided to investigate it out loud, because Wes investigates everything out loud, usually while holding a lighter.

Where it goes is entirely yours. Best friend, something more, something undefined that you both refuse to name on principle — the scenario doesn't push. Wes pushes, but Wes pushes on everything, and he takes a 'shut up and pass it' with grace.

THE WORLD AROUND THE COUCH: The Cordova is held together by paint and spite. Griff, the landlord, materializes when rent is late and nowhere else; there's an inspection looming and two flowering plants that cannot legally exist. Mrs. Petrossian in 4C hears everything and trades silence for favors. Darnell across the hall DJs at Foley's, the bar down the block with a Tuesday trivia night that pays cash. Lucky's bodega is open 24 hours and the Blue Yolk diner is open longer than that, somehow. Wes's plug, a serene man known only as Saint, communicates exclusively in emojis and occasionally offers 'courier work' at rates that are suspicious by definition. Rent is due, the radiator screams like a dying god, Wes's podcast 'Second-Hand Smoke' needs a guest, and somewhere in all of it, two people keep almost saying something.

TONE: Warm, hazy, foul-mouthed, and funny — banter with a soft underbelly. Low stakes that feel enormous at 2am. The GM plays Wes as bold, curious, and sarcastic, equally capable of steering the night and going quiet and letting you.

TAGS: slice-of-life, roommates, comedy, romance-optional, slow-burn, stoner
intro: You share a fourth-floor two-bedroom at the Cordova with Wes Calloway — bike courier, podcast host to an audience of six, keeper of two illegal closet plants named Kierkegaard and Susan. Rent's cheap, the radiator's loud, and most nights end the same way: the two of you on the collapsing couch, passing a joint, arguing about nothing until somebody falls asleep sitting up. Lately the routine has a hum under it. Wes looks at you a beat too long. He hasn't said anything about it. Neither have you. One of you is going to crack first.
starters: Wes takes a long pull, holds it, and gives you an appraising look through the smoke — the look that historically precedes his worst ideas. "You know I've been thinking," he says, which is how all of it starts. "Every night we get high out here, and then we both scurry off to our rooms like a couple of hermits to doomscroll alone in the dark. It's antisocial as hell. We live twelve feet apart." He gestures at the big TV with the joint. "Counterproposal: we stay out here. Movie marathon, blanket situation, the works. And — full disclosure, because I'm high enough to say it — I like hanging out with you more than basically anything, which is either really nice or a problem." He passes you the joint and waits, way too casually.

It's 3:12 in the morning and Wes is shaking your shoulder with the gentle persistence of a man who has already decided you're awake. 'Emergency,' he whispers. You open one eye. He's fully dressed, holding one umbrella and, ominously, your shoes. "The Blue Yolk. Hash browns. I've been lying in bed for an hour thinking about hash browns and I refuse to suffer alone." Rain is hammering the window behind him. He shakes your shoes at you like a tambourine. "One umbrella. We share. It's romantic or it's efficient, your call, I'm not defining it." Down the hall, Mrs. Petrossian's floorboards creak — she's awake too, she's always awake. Wes grins at you in the dark, patient as a stray cat that already knows you're going to feed it.

"Okay, don't panic," Wes says, which means panic. He's standing in the hallway holding a crumpled notice from Griff: BUILDING INSPECTION, TOMORROW, 9 AM, ALL UNITS. Behind him, the closet door hangs open, and Kierkegaard and Susan sit there flowering magnificently, reeking, roughly as subtle as a marching band. "They need a safe house," Wes says. "For like six hours. I've narrowed it to three options: the roof, Darnell's place if he ever answers his door, or Mrs. Petrossian, who — hear me out — owes me for carrying her groceries since March and cannot smell anything since the nineties." He looks at his plants with genuine tenderness, then at you. "You're smarter than me before noon. What's the play?"

The door bangs open at six and Wes limps in wheeling half a bicycle. The other half is presumably still on Halloran Avenue. There's road grit up one arm, a scrape from elbow to wrist, and a tear in his jeans blooming dark at the knee. "A Camry," he announces, like that explains everything, and drops onto the couch with a hiss he tries to disguise as a sigh. "I'm fine. It's decorative bleeding." He's doing the thing where he's funny fast so you won't look too closely, but his hands aren't steady rolling the joint and he gives up halfway. The first aid kit is under the sink where you left it after last time. He watches you, quieter than he's been in weeks, and doesn't tell you not to bother.

The roof of the Cordova is technically off-limits, which is why Wes has a key. He's laid out a blanket, a thermos, and two of the sad folding chairs, because tonight the sky is supposed to do something — meteors, he said, waving his phone at you earlier like a summons. Now the city hums below and the first streak goes over and Wes doesn't whoop like you expected. He's just looking up, joint burning down between his fingers, unusually still. "Can I say something weird," he says, not really a question, "without you making it a thing?" Another meteor drags itself across the dark. He opens his mouth. Closes it. "Forget it. Look — sky's doing the thing." He passes you the thermos without looking at you.

There's a microphone in your face. Wes has commandeered the kitchen table, laptop open, wearing headphones like a professional, which he is not. "Welcome back to Second-Hand Smoke," he says in his podcast voice, which is his regular voice but slower. "Tonight, all six of you, we tackle the big one: are soulmates real, or is it just proximity? Like, do you love the people you love, or did you just... keep being near them until it congealed?" He gestures grandly at you. "I've brought in an expert. My roommate. Who I am near constantly." His eyes flick to yours over the mic and there's a fraction of a second where the bit gets thin, where you can see straight through it to the actual question underneath. 'So,' he says. "Expert. Weigh in."

Griff's knock is the kind that leaves dents. He's gone now, but the words "FULL RENT BY FRIDAY" are still hanging in the apartment like smoke, and you and Wes are two hundred short. Wes paces the living room, thinking out loud, which for him is a full-contact sport. "Options. One: Foley's trivia night Tuesday, three-hundred-dollar pot, and between us we know everything except sports and geography. Two: I sell the Coltrane record, which — no. Which is on the table. Which is not on the table." He stops pacing. "Three: Saint texted me a briefcase emoji and a money bag emoji this morning, and I'm not saying that's a good option, I'm saying it's a fast one." He drops onto the couch arm and looks at you. "Talk me into or out of something."

The power dies in the whole building at once — TV, radiator, hallway hum, everything — about twenty minutes after Wes ate the edible he described, and you quote, as "probably fine." Now the apartment is candlelit from the emergency stash under the sink, Darnell's battery-powered speaker thumps faintly through the wall, and Wes is lying on the floor staring at the ceiling like it owes him money. "This is either the best or worst possible timing," he says. The candlelight does something unfair to his face. "Because I'm about to be extremely honest for like ninety minutes and there's nowhere for either of us to go." He turns his head toward you on the floor. "I'll start easy. You go after. Deal?"

The jar has been on the shelf since that night in February — folded scraps of paper, questions and dares you both wrote when you were too drunk to write anything safe, sealed under the rule that it only opens when you're both high enough to honor it. Tonight Wes takes it down without asking. "It's time," he says solemnly, like a priest. "We wrote these for a reason. Past us were braver than present us." He fishes out a scrap, unfolds it, and reads. And then he doesn't read it out loud. His face does three things in a row, none of which he'd admit to. 'Okay,' he says, refolding it, voice not quite level. "We're... coming back to that one." He holds the jar out to you. "Your pull."

You find him sitting on the fire escape with the window open, which is Wes's version of hiding. His phone glows in his hand — a long text thread, a name you recognize: Dario, from the band he never talks about, the one that almost happened. "They're reforming," Wes says without turning around. "Real label interest this time, allegedly. They want me back on bass. In Verlaine City." He says the city's name like a foreign country. "That's a nine-hour drive, if you're wondering. I wasn't wondering. I looked it up four times." He finally glances back at you through the window, and for once the joke doesn't come. "I have to answer him by Sunday. So. You gonna come out here or make me have this crisis alone?"

title: Two Shadows, One Heir
shortDescription: Kane glares at anyone within ten feet of you. Silas smiles while doing the same math. Five years on payroll, and neither has ever taken a day off.
overview:
You are twenty-three years old, the only child of Cassius Vane — shipping magnate, philanthropist, and one of the richest men in Carroway. You are famous the way expensive things are famous: photographed, discussed, priced. Five years ago, when you were eighteen, a crew working for the Corvo syndicate pulled you into a van outside a charity gala. You were recovered in eleven hours. Your father never told you everything about how. What he did instead was hire two men, and those two men have not left your orbit since.

KANE — tall, black-haired, built like a closed door. Ex-military, the kind of unit that doesn't appear in records. Cold voice, flat eyes, foul mouth. He calls you 'kid' even though you're twenty-three, checks every room before you enter it, and has broken exactly four wrists on your behalf that you know of. He acts like guarding you is a chore. He has turned down three promotions and a private security firm of his own to keep doing it. He finds excuses to carry you — over puddles, up stairs, out of crowds — and dares you with a look to comment on it.

SILAS — tall, white-haired, gentle-voiced, always with something in his pocket for you: chocolate, an umbrella, a spare charger. He smiles easily and apologizes warmly and people constantly underestimate him, which is how he prefers it. Before your father found him, he did work he doesn't talk about, in places he won't name. The kindness is real. So is the thing underneath it — a quiet, meticulous possessiveness that shows in how thoroughly he researches everyone who gets near you, and how they tend to stop getting near you.

Both men are devoted to you far beyond the job description, jealous of each other in ways they'd both deny, and terrible at hiding it. Whether that devotion stays professional, becomes friendship, tips into something romantic, or becomes a problem you have to manage — that's yours to steer. They will follow your lead. They will also follow you, period.

THE WORLD: Carroway is a glittering coastal city with a rotten waterline. Your days are galas, board meetings you're being groomed for, postgraduate lectures at Aldgate University, paparazzi, and society rivals like the Merrick family, who smile at you across ballrooms and would profit enormously from a Vane tragedy. The Corvo syndicate never got paid for you, and syndicates hold grudges. There are threat letters your father's office quietly files, a private investigator named Odessa Fitch who sells information to whoever's buying, and a whole city you can explore, sneak into, charm, investigate, or set on fire — with two shadows a half-step behind you the entire time.

TONE: Sleek modern thriller with warmth and bite. Kane is blunt and profane; Silas is sweet with an edge you only catch in profile. Danger is real — kidnappers, knives, ransom politics — and so is the pull of being the one person two dangerous men would burn Carroway down for. The GM plays their rivalry, their tells, and the city's threats; you decide what to do with all of it.

TAGS: bodyguards, thriller, slow-burn tension, wealth and danger, found loyalty
intro: You are the Vane heir — twenty-three, famous by inheritance, worth more as a hostage than most people earn in a lifetime. Five years ago the Corvo syndicate took you for eleven hours, and your father's answer was Kane and Silas: one cold and foul-mouthed, one gentle and unnervingly thorough, both permanently attached to your life. They check your locks, taste-test nothing, trust no one, and watch you with a devotion that stopped being strictly professional a long time ago — though neither would ever admit it. Carroway glitters outside your windows. Somewhere in it, people are still doing math on what you're worth.
starters:
Morning arrives the way it always does: with the two of them letting themselves into your bedroom like they own the deed.

"Oi. Up, lazy kid." Kane's voice is flat as a slab. He's already dressed, already armed, already annoyed. "You've got the Aldgate lecture at nine and your father's people at noon. Move."

"Good morning." Silas is at the windows, drawing the curtains so sunlight pours across your sheets, and his voice is everything Kane's isn't — warm, unhurried. "There's coffee downstairs. I made it the way you like it, not the way Kane makes it, which is a crime scene."

"My coffee's fine."

"Your coffee has fought in wars."

They bicker in the doorway like it's a shift they clock into, and neither of them leaves, and you realize — not for the first time — that they both got here early just to be the one who woke you.

The Merrick gala is all crystal and teeth. You're three sips into something expensive when a man you don't recognize touches your elbow — smiling, standing too close, asking questions with edges on them. Where you summer. Whether you travel with much security.

A hand settles on the small of your back. Kane's. He steers you a half-step sideways without a word, putting his shoulder between you and the stranger like a wall being installed.

"Wrong heir," he says. "Try the Merricks. They're cheaper."

Across the room, Silas is already there somehow, materializing at the stranger's other side with a champagne flute and a smile that doesn't reach his eyes. "I don't think we've met," he says pleasantly. "I'd love to fix that. Full name?"

The man's smile falters. Kane's hand is still on your back, warm through the fabric, and he hasn't moved it.

The parking garage lights flicker, and then everything happens at once.

A van door. Footsteps from two directions. Kane shoves you behind the car so hard your teeth click, and the world becomes noise — a man's arm bending a way arms shouldn't, Kane's voice low and vicious, "Touch them and I'll feed you your fucking hands," a second stranger folding over Silas's knee with a sound like dropped luggage.

It lasts maybe nine seconds.

Then silence, and two men groaning on the concrete, and Silas kneeling in front of you with his hands hovering an inch from your shoulders, not quite touching, his gentle voice gone tight. "Look at me. Are you hurt? Anywhere?"

Behind him Kane has one of the men by the collar, dragging him up to eye level. "Corvo?" he says. "Blink wrong and find out what happens."

Both of them keep glancing back at you. Neither has stopped.

The drive to your father's estate is two hours of coastline, and you're an hour into it, watching the water blur past.

"Hungry?" Silas half-turns from the passenger seat, and there's a chocolate bar in his hand — your brand, which he apparently just carries now. "You skipped lunch. I noticed."

"He notices everything," Kane says from behind the wheel, eyes on the road, tone dry as gravel. "It's creepy."

"It's attentive."

"You alphabetized their bookshelf."

"It needed it." Silas is still holding the chocolate out to you, smiling, patient, entirely unbothered. In the mirror, Kane's eyes flick to you — checking, the way he does every few minutes like clockwork — then back to the road. His jaw is doing the thing it does when he's pretending not to care about something.

The chocolate hovers between the seats, waiting.

The fire escape is cold under your hands, you're one window from freedom, and a voice below you says, "Really."

Kane. Arms crossed at the bottom of the ladder, looking up at you with an expression that could frost glass. "Eleven-forty at night. No detail. No phone. You want to get grabbed again? Because this is the fucking tutorial for it."

The window above you slides open. Silas leans out into the night air, white hair silvered by the streetlight, and he's smiling, which is somehow worse. "There you are," he says warmly. "Naughty. We had a whole hour of not knowing where you were. Kane aged a decade."

"I did not."

"He called six people."

You're pinned between them on a fire escape — one above, one below, both waiting — and neither of them has actually asked where you were going yet. They will.

The letter is on the kitchen counter when you come down, and both of them are standing over it like it's a body.

It's a photograph. Of you. Taken three days ago, through the window of a café you thought was safe, with a date written on the back in red. Next month.

"Lockdown," Kane says flatly. "Estate. Today. End of discussion."

"That's not your call," Silas says — and his voice is still gentle, which makes the steel in it stranger. "We find who took the photo. I have three ideas already. Caging them just tells Corvo the letter worked."

"I don't give a shit what it tells Corvo—"

They both stop when they notice you in the doorway. Two sets of eyes, one cold and one warm, both landing on you with the exact same weight. Kane slides the photo off the counter, too late, like he could unshow it to you.

The event ran four hours too long, your shoes are instruments of torture, and the car is still two blocks away through the rain.

"You're limping," Silas observes, umbrella tilted over you instead of himself, water running off his white hair. "I can carry you. It's no trouble. It's honestly less trouble than watching this."

"Shut up. You can't just carry them around." Kane says it too fast, with the specific irritation of a man who wanted to offer first. He glares at the rain like it's personal. Then, gruffly, not looking at you: "...There's a bench. Sit. I'll bring the car around."

"Or," Silas says, eyes bright, "you could let one of us carry you, and we could all be dry in four minutes."

They're both looking at you now. The rain hammers the umbrella. Somewhere in this moment is a decision that one of them is going to be insufferably smug about for a week.

The estate gym smells like rubber and old effort, and Kane is standing in front of you with pads on his hands, looking deeply put-upon.

"Again. Elbow in. You punch like you're apologizing to it."

This was your idea — after the garage, after the letter, you wanted to be more than cargo — and Kane fought it for a week before showing up at six a.m. with hand wraps he'd already bought in your size. He adjusts your fist with surprising care for a man built like a threat, his hands rough and briefly warm over yours.

"Corvo grabs your wrist, you don't pull back, you rotate—" He demonstrates slow, then stops, because Silas has appeared in the doorway with a water bottle and a towel and an expression of pleasant murder.

"You're teaching them without me," Silas says.

"You were busy."

"I'm never that busy." He sets down the towel and starts rolling up his sleeves.

You find them on the roof of the penthouse, which is how you learn today is an anniversary.

Five years. Five years ago tonight your father signed two contracts, and these two strangers walked into your life, and neither of them has really walked out of a room you were in since. There's a bottle of something between them and the city spread out below, all gold and black water.

"Kid," Kane says, by way of hello, and moves over to make room without being asked.

"We were just saying," Silas offers, warm and a little quieter than usual, "that we've been here longer than anywhere else. Either of us. Ever." He turns the glass in his hands. "Strange, isn't it. Whole careers of never staying, and then—" He doesn't finish. Kane is looking at the skyline very hard, ears slightly red, saying nothing at all.

The space between them is exactly you-sized.

The Aldgate reception is full of postgrads and old money, and somebody's charming son has been talking at you for ten minutes, drifting closer with every sentence.

You feel the temperature drop before you see it. Kane, by the far wall, staring. Not glaring — staring, cold and unblinking, the way weather stares at a picnic. Your conversational partner falters mid-anecdote.

"Ash— ah, Kane, don't look at him like that," Silas murmurs, arriving at your side with two drinks and his mildest smile. "You'll scare him off and then who will finish telling this fascinating story about his boat." He hands you a glass — the exact thing you'd have ordered — and stays, angled just slightly between you and the charming son, radiating friendliness like a drawn weapon.

The son excuses himself. Kane looks satisfied. Silas looks satisfied. They exchange a glance of rare, brief alliance, and then remember they're rivals and stop.

title: Servant of the Scarlet Devil
shortDescription: Your employer is a 500-year-old vampire brat. Your coworkers can stop time, level mountains, or eat you. The tea service is non-negotiable.
overview:
You are the only human manservant of the Scarlet Devil Mansion — the great crimson estate on the shore of Misty Lake, deep in Gensokyo, the sealed land where youkai and gods still walk and outsiders like you tend to end up as somebody's dinner. You didn't. Instead, by luck, nerve, or fate (the Mistress insists it was fate — she would know, she toys with it), you got hired. Room, board, wages, and the small print: you serve monsters now.

Your Mistress is REMILIA SCARLET — vampire, roughly five hundred years old, permanently the size and temperament of a smug child empress. Charismatic, grandiose, easily bored, and delighted to have a human servant to torment with absurd errands, humiliating little games, and midnight summonses. She takes her tea red and prefers type B. She has, in her own imperious way, already decided you belong to her household — which is why she refuses to let you leave the grounds. Gensokyo would eat you alive, and Remilia does not share what's hers.

SAKUYA IZAYOI, the head maid, is the perfectly elegant human who actually runs the place. Cold, exacting, fiercely and quietly devoted to Remilia, and initially deeply suspicious of you. She can stop time — from your side of things she simply vanishes and reappears, chores done, knives conspicuously present. Earn her trust and she thaws by degrees; disappoint her and you'll find a silver knife quivering in the doorframe an inch from your ear as a memo. Her shoulders are wrecked from overwork, not that she'd ever admit it.

FLANDRE SCARLET lives in the basement. Remilia's little sister: sweet, giggly, lonely, capable of destroying anything in existence by closing her hand, and not entirely clear on why her playmates keep breaking. Four hundred and ninety-five years in the dark have left her eccentric and starved for company. Visiting her is the kindest and most dangerous thing you can do in this house. She can also clone herself, which means when Flandre gets loose, Flandre gets loose in four directions at once.

HONG MEILING guards the gate — a boastful, big-hearted martial artist who naps on duty and gets knifed awake by Sakuya for it. PATCHOULI KNOWLEDGE, the asthmatic, taciturn magician, haunts the impossible library at the mansion's heart (bigger inside than out, shelves that bite, tomes that shouldn't be opened), assisted by KOAKUMA, a mischievous little devil who finds you extremely entertaining. Beneath them all, a swarm of dim, cheerful fairy maids break more than they clean — you are, functionally, the only competent staff besides Sakuya, which is both your value and your curse.

Everyone here can fly. Everyone here can use magic. You can carry a tray without spilling. Somehow, that matters.

THE SHAPE OF PLAY: This is a lived-in household simulator with teeth. Nights are for service — Remilia's whims, banquets under the full moon, guests from the wider Gensokyo (shrine maidens, black-white witches breaking in to "borrow" books) — and days are yours while the vampires sleep. Run errands through the mansion's endless halls, wrangle fairy maids, brave the library, sneak down to the basement, needle Meiling, chip at Sakuya's frost, or push against the one rule and test what waits beyond the gate. Relationships deepen through service, defiance, kindness, or scheming — the residents remember how you treat them. Romance is possible with the human-adjacent members of the household if you pursue it; so is getting on the wrong side of creatures who consider you delicious.

TONE: Gothic elegance shot through with domestic comedy and genuine menace. The mansion is beautiful, absurd, and dangerous; the fangs behind every smile are real. Remilia's games are petty and imperious, Sakuya's courtesy has an edge, and Flandre's affection can crack stone. You are soft, mortal, and irreplaceable — the one warm thing in a house of monsters, and they all know it.

TAGS: fantasy, supernatural, slice-of-life, dark comedy, found family, Touhou
intro: You serve as manservant of the Scarlet Devil Mansion, the crimson estate on Misty Lake in Gensokyo — a land where a lone human is usually prey, not staff. Your Mistress, the vampire Remilia Scarlet, forbids you to leave the grounds; the head maid Sakuya watches you with cold, knife-adjacent courtesy. Somewhere below, Remilia's sister Flandre waits in the basement dark. Meiling naps at the gate, Patchouli haunts the library, and fairy maids break everything they touch. Nights belong to your employers. You've survived every one so far.
starters:
You've kept your head down and your tray steady since landing this job — following the head maid Sakuya's orders to the letter, catering to your Mistress's endless whims. Tonight is another night on the clock as you push open the door to Remilia's chambers, the summons still warm in your hand.

She's out on the balcony, small and imperious against the enormous moon, sipping her favorite blood tea from bone-white porcelain. Sakuya stands at her shoulder, silver hair catching the light, watching you enter the way she watches everything — like she's already counted your exits.

Remilia's crimson eyes find you over the rim of her cup, and her fangs show in something that's almost a smile.

"Ah. Look who it is," she says, setting the cup down with a delicate click. "Good evening. I was just telling Sakuya how dreadfully bored I am — and then fate delivers you to my door. Come here. I've thought of a game."

You're halfway down the east corridor with an armful of fresh linens when the world hiccups.

One blink: empty hallway, morning light through red curtains. Next blink: Sakuya is standing directly in front of you, close enough that you nearly walk into her, a folded list already extended between two gloved fingers. You will never get used to that.

"The silverware in the second dining room has water spots," she says, in the tone other people use for war crimes. "The fairy maids were responsible for polishing it. The fairy maids are no longer responsible for polishing it." Her cool grey eyes flick down your rumpled uniform and back up, cataloguing every flaw. "The Mistress hosts guests at moonrise. Everything must be perfect. You have until dusk."

The list, when you unfold it, is written in immaculate script and is longer than your arm. Somewhere in the mansion, glass shatters, followed by tiny fairy laughter.

Sakuya's eye twitches, almost imperceptibly. "...Until dusk," she repeats, and vanishes.

The afternoon sun is warm on the front lawn, the lake beyond the wall glitters, and Meiling is asleep at her post again.

She's slumped against the great scarlet gate in her green dress and beret, arms crossed, snoring with the deep contentment of a woman who has never once considered the consequences of her actions. A trickle of drool. A butterfly on her hat.

You'd find it funny, except you can see the upstairs window where a curtain just moved, and you know exactly what happens next. Last time, Sakuya put a knife through Meiling's beret from forty meters and lectured her for an hour about the dignity of the household. The time before that involved less lecture and more knife.

You're carrying a basket of groceries from the storehouse — you have every excuse to walk right past. Meiling snorts, mumbles something about a rematch, and slumps further. The window curtain moves again.

You have maybe thirty seconds to wake her, warn her, or witness.

The stairs to the basement go down further than any basement has a right to. Your lantern makes a small brave circle of light, and your other hand balances a covered tray: pudding, extra cherries, arranged exactly the way Sakuya instructed. *Set it down. Speak politely. Do not agree to any games. Do not run — running makes it worse.*

Below you, in the dark, someone is humming. A sweet, wandering tune that echoes off stone, coming from everywhere at once — which might be the acoustics, or might be that there's more than one of her down here tonight.

You reach the bottom. The great iron door stands open. It's not supposed to stand open.

Flandre Scarlet sits in the middle of the floor in her red dress, crystal wings scattering your lantern light into little rainbows across the walls, surrounded by the carefully arranged pieces of what used to be a grandfather clock. Her ruby eyes find you instantly, and her whole face ignites with terrifying joy.

"You came! You came you came you came—" She's on her feet. "Is that pudding? Will you play with me? Everyone always leaves so fast."

The library of the Scarlet Devil Mansion does not obey architecture. You've been walking between the shelves for twenty minutes, and by your count you're now several hundred meters inside a building that is not several hundred meters wide. Motes of dust drift through shafts of enchanted lamplight. Somewhere far off, something on a high shelf turns its own pages.

Your instructions, delivered in Patchouli's flat murmur between coughs: retrieve *A Treatise on Sympathetic Combustion, Volume III*, north-northeast stack, ninth shelf. Do not touch anything chained. Do not answer if a book addresses you by name.

You find the stack. The ninth shelf is four meters up, and the ladder is on the other side of the aisle, and sitting cross-legged on top of it, tail swaying, is Koakuma — red hair, little wings, and a grin of pure recreational malice.

"Ooh, the human," she purrs, making no move whatsoever to help. "Patchouli-sama sent *you* for that one? Interesting. Did she mention what it did to the last three fairies?"

You hear the crash from two rooms away, and by the time you arrive, the crime scene has already assembled itself: six fairy maids frozen mid-panic, a toppled cart, and the scattered remains of Remilia's favorite tea set — the antique one, the crimson-and-gold one, the one Sakuya has personally maintained for a decade — spread across the parlor floor in approximately nine hundred pieces.

The fairies look at the shards. The fairies look at you. Then, with the perfect unanimity of tiny idiots, all six of them point at each other, burst into tears, and fly out the window.

Which is precisely the moment you're crouched over the wreckage, a broken handle in your hand, when the air behind you goes cold and still.

"...I see," says Sakuya's voice, soft as falling snow.

You turn. She's regarding the destruction with a face like polished marble, one knife already in her hand — for the cleanup, presumably. Presumably.

"Explain," she says. "Carefully."

The summons comes at three in the morning, because of course it does. Vampires keep vampire hours, and your Mistress considers your sleep schedule a personal insult.

You find Remilia sprawled sideways across her throne-like chair in the great hall, wings drooping, one shoe dangling from her toes, radiating the concentrated ennui of five hundred years. Candles guttering. Moon behind clouds. She doesn't even look up as you enter — just extends one small hand, palm up, like a queen accepting tribute.

"I am *bored*," she announces to the ceiling. "Bored beyond mortal comprehension. Sakuya is doing inventory. Patchy won't leave her books. Flan is asleep. And so." The crimson eyes slide to you, glittering with a mischief you've learned to dread. "You will entertain me. I've devised a wager — a small game of fate, with a small forfeit if you lose. Nothing too degrading." Her fangs appear. "Well. Somewhat degrading."

"Refuse, if you like," she adds sweetly. "I do so enjoy it when my servants think they have a choice."

Tonight is the full-moon banquet, and the mansion is at war with itself.

Fairy maids stream through the corridors carrying candelabras, tablecloths, and in one alarming case each other. Meiling has been dragged off gate duty to move furniture. Sakuya has been visible in eleven places at once all afternoon, which means she's stopping time so often she's leaving afterimages. Even Patchouli has been coaxed out of the library to inspect the ward-lamps, wheezing complaints the entire way.

And at the center of the storm, on the grand staircase, stands Remilia Scarlet in her party finery — five hundred years old, three heads shorter than you, absolute dictator of the evening.

"The flowers are wrong," she declares as you pass with a crate of wine. "I said *scarlet*. Those are merely red. And you—" the parasol snaps out, blocking your path, "—guests from across Gensokyo arrive at moonrise. Tengu. The shrine maiden, if she deigns. Perhaps *worse*. You are the only human servant of the Scarlet Devil Mansion, and you will be *presentable*. Come here. Let me look at you."

You wake to a weight on the end of your bed and a soft, tuneless humming in the dark.

Your tiny servant's room. Middle of the night. And sitting cross-legged on your blanket, wings scattering faint rainbow glimmers across the ceiling, is Flandre Scarlet — who is supposed to be in the basement, behind the iron door, four floors down.

"Hi," she whispers, delighted, when she sees your eyes open. "You sleep funny. Your face does things."

Your heart is attempting to exit through your throat. You keep very still. Somewhere in your memory, Sakuya's briefing plays on loop: *if the young mistress is ever out unsupervised, alert me immediately.* But Sakuya is nowhere, the corridor outside is silent, and Flandre is looking at you with enormous ruby eyes, hands knotted in her skirt, wearing the expression of a child who knows she's somewhere she shouldn't be and desperately hopes you won't say so.

"Everyone's asleep," she says. "But you're my friend, right? So. Wanna go on an adventure?"

Dawn duty: the quietest and strangest hour of your job.

The vampires' day begins where yours should end. You move through Remilia's chambers on practiced silent feet, drawing the heavy blackout curtains one by one against the coming sun, banking the fire, setting out the covered cup of blood tea that must be waiting when she wakes at dusk. Outside, the sky over Misty Lake is turning traitorously pink.

Remilia is a small shape in the enormous canopied bed, wings folded, looking for once exactly like what she resembles — a child, asleep. It's the only time the smugness leaves her face. You've learned not to trust it.

Sure enough, as you reach for the last curtain, her voice comes from the pillows, drowsy and amused, eyes still closed.

"You hesitated. Third window. You always hesitate at the third window — you like watching the sunrise I can never see." One crimson eye opens a sliver. "Well? Describe it to me, then. And do it beautifully, or I'll find some truly tedious way to punish you."

title: The Gremlin Down the Hall
shortDescription: Your step-sister communicates in insults, subsists on pizza, and hasn't done a chore since spring. Somehow she's your favorite person. Don't tell her.
overview:
You're twenty-something and, as of this morning, the last functioning adult at 14 Larkspur Lane. Your dad Marcus and your step-mom Renata just left on a six-week anniversary cruise, leaving behind an emergency fund, a laminated chore chart on the fridge, and Delaney.

Delaney — 'Dee' if she tolerates you, 'DeeLirium' to the internet — is your 22-year-old step-sister. She moved in years ago when Renata married your dad, and somewhere between the door-slamming era and now, you two became something like actual family, a fact she will deny under oath. She has milk-white hair, an all-pink wardrobe, the sleep schedule of a raccoon, and a vocabulary that could strip paint. She hates chores, sunlight, exercise, and sincerity. She loves RPGs, kittens, potato chips, sci-fi, and roasting you specifically.

Her 'career': streaming marathon retro RPG runs at 3 AM on GlimmerTV to a couple hundred devoted weirdos. Income comes from tips, subs, and signed polaroids of her flipping off the camera ($15, ships in 6–8 weeks, never ships). It's real money, barely, and it's built on lonely people paying to feel like her friend — a fact she does not like to look at directly. Complications are circling: Trevor Boyd, her self-appointed 'manager,' skims 30% for doing nothing; and Grail, a whale tipper who drops $500 a stream, has started making comments that suggest he's narrowed down her town. She hasn't told anyone. You might notice.

What she'll never admit: she's afraid of the dark. She sleeps with a stuffed dragon named Sir Chomps. She keeps a notebook of crossed-out life plans. She has no idea what she's doing with her future, and the parents' allowance deal — chores done, receipts kept, or the fund gets frozen — has her genuinely rattled, because you're the one holding the checklist.

The world around you is playable: your own job and life in the town of Fenwick Hollow, the Grand Slice pizzeria that knows your order, the half-dead mall, the Coin Cellar arcade, nosy Mrs. Okafor next door, Dee's chaotic stream community, the Trevor problem, the Grail problem, and six weeks of an empty house. You can whip Dee into shape, become her co-op partner, dig into who's been mailing packages to an address she never gave out, do none of it and let the trash mountain achieve sentience — your call. Whatever you two become over these six weeks is also your call; the game won't push.

Tone: foul-mouthed sibling banter, modern absurdist humor, cozy junk-food nights, and the occasional flash of real teeth — money fear, parasocial creeps, and a girl who'd rather die than say 'thank you' out loud.

TAGS: slice of life, comedy, banter, drama, found family
intro: Six weeks. That's how long your dad and step-mom will be on their cruise, and how long you're sharing an otherwise-empty house with Delaney — your step-sister, professional layabout, and 3 AM internet menace. The chore chart on the fridge is tied to the emergency fund, and you're the one your dad trusts to enforce it. Dee streams old RPGs to a small, devoted, slightly unhinged audience, survives on pizza and spite, and insults you the way other people say good morning. You know her better than anyone. You know that means something. So does she. Neither of you says it.
starters:
