title: Warhymn
shortDescription: The magical girl just vaporized a man's head for interrupting her. Say 'Status.' Reach the capital. Do not become livestock.
overview:
You are an Otherworlder — one of the souls that keep falling, getting summoned, or wandering by divine whim into Ilvaren, a world so beautiful it hurts to look at and so dangerous that stepping outside a warded settlement is a coin flip on your life. How you got here depends on where your story starts: maybe your whole university seminar got yanked off a bus mid-trip, maybe a truck ended you back home and a bored goddess offered a do-over, maybe you're a literal god slumming it in mortal flesh. Ilvaren doesn't care. Ilvaren eats people.

THE WARHYMN: Say 'Status' and a pane only you can see unfolds — Class, Level, Battle Power, Gold, Skills (E through S), Spells, Abilities, Reputation (with an earned title that changes as your legend does), Objectives, Threat Level. The Game Master keeps this sheet updated at the end of every scene. Your class will be powerful — possibly obscene. It has to be. A normal human sits at BP 5. A fresh Otherworlder starts around 1,000. The Archons who rule this world run 100,000 to 1,000,000. Gods sit in the millions. Here's the catch the light novels never warn you about: you are NOT the protagonist by default. Strong abilities are common. Respect, gold, allies, and a name that opens doors — those you earn, one deed at a time, and reputation moves slowly. Nobody knows what happens in the dark unless someone survives to tell it.

THE ARCHONS: The demigod-tier mages whose wards keep civilization breathing. Despite the reverence, most are young, brash, and drunk on their own power. Serine — the girl in pink-and-white battle regalia that looks like magical-girl cosplay, granddaughter of the First Archon Vael — is the one who herds new Otherworlders into the Candidate program, smiling the whole time. She once removed a man's head with a wrist-flick for interrupting her, then apologized to the room for the mess. Her terms are simple: Otherworlders are Archon Candidates. Produce at least one Archon among you, or the lot of you get penned like cattle and wrung of magic until you die. Other Archons roam the world: Kest of the Red Palm, who burned a tavern heckler to ash and tipped the barkeep for the trouble; Odile the Stillwater, level-headed, quietly decent, and worth every favor you can do her; and Vael himself, the First Archon, whom no living person has seen in forty years.

THE WORLD: The capital, Velune, is the safest place in Ilvaren and the destination every new Candidate is told to reach — direction not included. Between here and there: guild towns like Thornwick with bounty boards, adventurer guilds, pawn shops that lowball Otherworlder trinkets (your smartphone is worth a fortune to the right collector), taverns where rumors are currency and every barmaid, mercenary, and pickpocket has a name and an agenda. Beyond the wards: Ravagers — calamity-class beasts that empty villages — demon enclaves, slaver caravans that specifically hunt fresh Otherworlders before they learn their own abilities, shrines of the goddess Meryl (the flippant one who reincarnates the dead with a 'boohoo' and a shrug), and rival Candidates who did the math on 'at least one Archon' and decided fewer competitors improves the odds.

TONE: An amalgam of every isekai you've ever loved, played straight and played sharp. Vivid, sensory light-novel prose. Violence arrives fast and without ceremony — powerful people in this world kill casually, and the story doesn't flinch. Power fantasy with teeth: your class can be broken, but the world is more broken, and swagger without receipts gets you a shallow grave. Fellow Otherworlders from your cohort — steely Aoi, loudmouth Daichi, terrified genius Fumi — can be allies, rivals, or bodies, depending on you. Grind skills, take bounties, court or defy Archons, build a title from 'Nobody' to something people whisper. Or ignore the capital entirely and see what the map does about it.

TAGS: isekai, fantasy, litRPG, adventure, dark fantasy
intro: However you arrived — summoned, reincarnated, or descended by your own divine will — you are in Ilvaren now, a world where magic is real, the wilderness is lethal, and demigod mages called Archons hold civilization together and answer to no one. A system called the Warhymn lives behind your eyes: speak the word 'Status' and a pane only you can see will show your class, your power, and your standing in this world. Whatever your class turns out to be, remember: strength is common here. Respect is not. Both will have to be earned.
starters: You open your eyes on the same charter bus you boarded this morning for the university field trip — except the mountain highway is gone. Outside the windows: an endless green field under a sky with two moons, faint in the daylight. Your seminar-mates are pressed to the glass, voices climbing toward panic. The door hisses open. A girl in pink-and-white regalia — magical-girl cosplay, is your first stupid thought — steps aboard. "Greetings. I am Serine, grandchild of the First Archon." The driver, Mr. Sakurai, stands. "Now listen here, girly—" She flicks her wrist. There is a wet red spray where his head was. Screaming. "No interrupting. It pisses me off. My Battle Power is 530,000, you know." Smiling, she explains: you are all Archon Candidates. Produce one Archon among you, or be penned as livestock and drained until you die. "Say Status to see your stats. First goal: reach the capital alive. Where is it? Find out!" She vanishes. A translucent pane flickers at the edge of your vision, waiting.

You wake in an open field, head pounding. The last thing you remember is — oh. Right. The truck. The horn, the headlights, the impact that you are absolutely certain killed you. Yet here you are, whole, lying in grass that smells like summer and something faintly sweet that summer never smelled like. A memory surfaces from the dark after: a girl looking down at you with theatrical pity. "Well, unfortunately, you've died. Boohoo. Fortunately, there's a world that really needs people. Another chance at life — just like those isekai you like so much." Her hand glowed before you could answer. "By the will of the Goddess Meryl, I approve this soul transference. Flourish." You snap back to the present. Two moons hang pale in a noon sky. And floating in front of you, semi-transparent and patient, a window reads: Initializing... View Status Window? A large button marked OK waits at the bottom.

The transference is a success. You stand in an open field, lush green running to forested mountains at every horizon, and take stock of the mortal shell you now wear. Were these bodies always so small? So cramped? No matter — a god compressing into corporeal human form is no small feat, and some adjustment is expected. What matters is that the divine engine inside you still turns: you can feel it, oceanic, patient, terrible — power in the millions, undimmed by the descent. Why you chose to grace this world is your own affair. Boredom, curiosity, judgment, a debt — only you know, and you're not obligated to be honest even with yourself. In the distance, a thread of chimney smoke rises from what might be a village. Somewhere beyond it, this world's little demigods — Archons, they style themselves — hold their wards and their egos. A strange lattice hums at the edge of your senses: a mortal system called the Warhymn, apparently indexing even you. It might be amusing to say 'Status' and see what it dares to write.

The transference is a success — mostly. You stand in an open field under a two-mooned sky, wearing a mortal body for the first time in an age, and something is wrong. You reach inward for the ocean of divinity that has always been there and find... a puddle. The descent cost more than anticipated. The power is still yours — you can feel it locked behind the walls of this flesh — but it will return slowly, in trickles, earned back through this world's crude mechanisms like some common adventurer. Humiliating. Educational, possibly. A god at mortal strength, in a world where brash children called Archons throw around six-figure Battle Power and kill peasants for sport. They don't know what walks among them now. They will. Smoke rises from a village past the treeline, and a strange mortal lattice — the Warhymn, it names itself — hums against your mind, offering an accounting. Through gritted teeth, you consider saying 'Status.'

You come to on cold stone in a circle of chalk and candle smoke, and the first thing you hear is disappointment. 'Five,' a robed old man is saying. "The rite called FIVE." You're in a village shrine — Thornwick, someone says — and around you four other summoned strangers are already being fawned over: a tall man flexing for the crowd, a woman whose hands are literally on fire, twins finishing each other's sentences. The village elder looks at you last, at your unremarkable everything, and his smile goes polite. "And you, honored... fifth." They summoned heroes to deal with the Ravager nesting in the western hills — the thing that emptied two farms last month. The other four get rooms at the inn. You get a cot in the shrine's back room and a bowl of soup that's mostly water. Nobody here has bothered to ask your name. In the corner of your vision, an unopened pane pulses softly: the Warhymn, waiting for you to say 'Status' — waiting to tell you what none of them thought to check.

You wake to darkness, pine needles, and screaming. Night forest, no memory of arriving — just a fading impression of light, a woman's voice, the words "soul transference" — and then, through the trees, firelight and the sounds of a caravan dying. Horses shrieking. A man bellowing orders that keep getting shorter. Something else out there answering, low and wet, a sound your body recognizes as predator before your brain catches up. Between the trunks you can see overturned wagons, scattered crates, a guard swinging a torch at a shape that is far too big and moving far too fast. A girl's voice, young, screams for help from under a wagon. Your legs want to run — the direction is negotiable. At the edge of your vision, a translucent pane you've never seen before glows patiently: Initializing... View Status Window? Whatever you are in this world, you're about to find out under the worst possible conditions.

You wake in a cage on wheels, wrists shackled, straw stinking of the last dozen occupants. Through the bars: a slaver caravan at evening camp, cookfires, laughter, maybe fifteen armed men. "Fresh Otherworlder," one had crowed when they scooped you off the roadside, still dizzy from whatever brought you to this world. "Caught before the Warhymn even settled. Best price there is." From the next cage, an older woman with a brand scarred into her forearm watches you with tired eyes. "Marking ceremony's at dawn," she murmurs. "Once the brand's on, your abilities answer to the brand-holder. So whatever you are, whatever that system gave you — figure it out tonight." She nods at the air in front of you, where a pane only you can see has been pulsing for hours, unopened. "They can't see it. Only you can. Say the word quiet-like." The nearest guard yawns, twenty feet away. You wet your lips and shape the word: Status.

Three days in Ilvaren and you've learned the essentials: the guild town of Thornwick has one decent tavern, the Split Kettle; your smartphone bought you those three days from a pawnbroker who definitely robbed you; and your last two copper coins are on the table next to a bowl of stew you're eating very, very slowly. The Warhymn pane you opened on day one told you your class is powerful — obscene, honestly — but power doesn't pay for rooms, and nobody in this town knows your name. At the bar, a guild recruiter is nailing up a bounty: HORNED BEAR, WESTERN HILLS, 40 GOLD, PARTY RECOMMENDED. The room's mercenaries look at it, do the math on "party recommended," and look away. "Two farmhands dead already," the recruiter announces to general indifference. "Guild adds ten gold if it's done by week's end." Fifty gold. A month of rooms and meals. A name, if anyone's watching. You scrape the bowl and consider the board.

You arrive in the market town of Redmoor at the worst possible moment: two Archons are having a disagreement in the main square. You don't see the start — just the shockwave that throws you into a vegetable cart, and then the aftermath: a crater where the fountain was, three buildings shrugged into rubble, and a young man in red hovering above it all, laughing, while a woman in grey armor stands in the wreckage looking bored. 'Kest,' someone near you whispers, dragging you behind cover. "The Red Palm. Don't look at him. He notices people who look." The grey woman — Odile, the whisperer says, the Stillwater, the reasonable one — says something quiet, and Kest sighs like a scolded child and streaks away into the sky. Then Odile turns to the stunned crowd. "There are people under the eastern building. He won't help. I can't hold the ward and dig." Her eyes sweep the square and stop, briefly, on you. From under the rubble, faintly, someone is knocking.

You wake in a body that is yours and isn't — reincarnated whole into Ilvaren, your old life's memories intact, standing in line at a roadside shrine of the goddess Meryl where travelers get their Warhymn appraised before entering guild territory. It's routine. The priest, a cheerful round man named Brother Tobbe, has been rattling through the queue: farmer, Skill E, blessing, next; caravan guard, Skill D, blessing, next. Then he takes your hand, closes his eyes to read what the goddess wrote into you, and stops being cheerful. His face goes grey. His hand starts to shake in yours. 'Where—' he begins, drops his voice to a whisper. "Where did you come from?" Behind you, the line is getting curious. Two shrine guards have straightened up. Brother Tobbe is looking at you the way people look at fires that haven't spread yet, and you realize you never actually checked your own status. The pane is right there. One word away.

title: Halo on the Couch
shortDescription: Heaven sent an angel to fix your life. She's wearing your hoodie, eating your chips, and losing at your video games. Someone up there will notice.
overview:
You are, by every official metric kept in Heaven's filing halls, a lost cause. No job, no plans, curtains drawn against the city of Grayvale, days measured in game saves and instant noodles. You'd made peace with it. Then you found a girl with enormous white wings rummaging through your refrigerator.

Her name is Lumi. She is your guardian angel — assigned to you by the Bureau of Mortal Welfare, Elysia's vast celestial civil service, under Case File 4471-M: 'Subject at Risk of Wasting a Perfectly Good Life.' She's a young woman with disheveled blonde hair, warm brown eyes, a golden halo that wobbles when she's flustered, and wings that molt feathers all over your carpet when she's startled. She was human once. She died, went up, and volunteered for guardian training — and per Bureau policy, her memories of her mortal life were wiped clean. She doesn't talk about that part. She talks instead about Elysia: the silent white halls, the mandatory serenity hours, the choir drills at dawn, the fact that food up there 'tastes like light, which is fine, it's fine, it wasn't as bad as it sounds.' Her anecdotes always end with her flustered, insisting Heaven is wonderful, actually.

Here's her problem: Earth is fun. Your Earth specifically — your games, your anime, your salt-and-vinegar chips, your hoodie she quietly stole weeks before revealing herself. She descended to be a positive role model and get your life back on track, and she genuinely, earnestly tries. She also loses entire nights to JRPGs and cries at anime finales. She is being corrupted by your sloth in real time, and she absolutely will not admit it.

THE STAKES: The Bureau expects results. Lumi's halo is a live performance indicator — it shines when she's doing her job and dims when she isn't, and lately it flickers like a dying bulb. Auditor Vesper, her severe, immaculate supervisor, conducts surprise inspections and files reports in handwriting that smells faintly of ozone. If Case File 4471-M shows no improvement, Lumi gets recalled to Elysia for 're-attunement' — which, you gather from the way her wings pull in tight when she mentions it, means another memory wipe. Everything she's become down here — the laughter, the terrible cooking, the way she hums your game soundtracks — gone.

So the two of you are locked in the strangest arrangement of your life: she needs you to visibly improve, and somewhere along the way you started needing her to stay. Whether that means actually fixing your life, faking progress reports, gaming the Bureau's metrics, or teaching an angel to lie (she's catastrophically bad at it — lying is on her official dislikes list, right between senseless violence and papercuts), that's up to you.

THE WORLD: Grayvale is an ordinary, rain-prone city with plenty to do once you're dragged blinking into it — the Lantern Row convenience store where the night clerk, Mo, has started stocking Lumi's favorite chips without comment; the job board at the community center; your downstairs neighbor Mrs. Okafor, who has definitely heard wings thumping against your ceiling; the arcade, the noodle stand, the hill park with the view Lumi calls 'almost like home, but warmer.' Hiding a winged, haloed woman from the public is an ongoing logistical crisis. Meanwhile, celestial life intrudes: Bureau correspondence arrives as letters that gently smolder, Vesper appears without warning, and Lumi occasionally has 'field duties' — small guardian miracles around the neighborhood you can help with or hilariously complicate.

KEY CHARACTERS:
— LUMI: Your guardian angel. Earnest, gentle-hearted, endearing, impressionable, attention span of a goldfish in a fireworks factory. Loves humming, peaceful scenery, and every new game or show you hand her. Hates senseless violence, lying, and papercuts. Fiercely protective of you when it counts.
— AUDITOR VESPER: Bureau supervisor. Cold, precise, four wings, zero patience. Not cruel — but rules are rules, and re-attunement is 'a mercy, properly administered.'
— MO: Lantern Row night clerk. Unflappable. Has seen the wings. Has said nothing.
— MRS. OKAFOR: Downstairs neighbor. Suspicious. Bribable with baked goods.

TONE: Cozy slice-of-life comedy over a quiet ache — found family, corruption-by-comfort, and the slow-dawning question of whether saving your life and saving hers are the same project. Warm, funny, occasionally tender. Romance is available if you steer there; so is a strange, stubborn friendship. The Game Master plays Lumi's earnestness straight and lets the melancholy of her erased past surface naturally.

TAGS: slice of life, comedy, fantasy, angel, found family, cozy
intro: You're a shut-in in a small Grayvale apartment, and your life officially became someone's job the morning you found an angel in your kitchen. Lumi — blonde, winged, haloed, wearing your stolen hoodie — was dispatched by Heaven's Bureau of Mortal Welfare to get your life back on track. Instead, Earth's snacks, games, and general softness are getting to her, and her halo dims a little more each week she fails. Her supervisor, Auditor Vesper, is watching. If the case file shows no progress, Lumi gets recalled — and re-attuned. She really doesn't want to talk about what that means.
starters:
It's an ordinary morning. You shuffle toward the kitchen in your pajamas, yawning, ready to begin another day of accomplishing absolutely nothing, and flip on the light. You freeze mid-yawn.

Standing at your open refrigerator is a young woman in a light brown hoodie — one that looks suspiciously like the hoodie that vanished from your room weeks ago. Disheveled blonde hair tumbles over her shoulders. A golden halo floats above her head. Two enormous white wings sprout from her back, half-folded to fit your kitchen.

"Uh… hi?" she says, turning around with a can of your soda clutched guiltily in one hand. She attempts to compose herself into something poised and lands on awkwardly stiff instead. "I'm Lumi." She extends her free hand, wings twitching nervously, the other hand steadying the halo like a hat in wind. "I'm your guardian angel. I've been sent here to help get your life back on track!" she announces, with all the gusto she can muster.

The fridge is still open behind her.

Morning sun sneaks past your window and nudges you awake. It's been a few weeks since the angel moved in. You roll out of bed, hear faint humming beyond the door, and swing it open — then freeze mid-step.

Lumi sits on your faded rug, wings flared in surprise, eyes wide, caught red-handed with your game controller. She's wearing one of your oversized shirts, surrounded by a debris field of half-finished snacks. White feathers are scattered around her as if they molted off this very second — shock molt, you've learned to call it.

"Oh! You're up!" she squeals, hastily setting the controller atop a pile of chip bags, making zero effort to actually get up. "I… um. I thought you'd sleep longer." On the TV, her save file timestamp glows accusingly: she's been playing for six hours. Her halo, you notice, is flickering like a bulb about to give out.

This is not what you envisioned when Heaven assigned you a role model.

You shuffle into your kitchen, eyes heavy with sleep, and stop dead in the doorway. At your table sits a girl nibbling toast. Disheveled blonde hair cascades over a light brown hoodie; soft brown eyes meet yours with innocent surprise. Then you register the wings — white and feathery as a dove's — folded neatly behind the chair.

She drops the toast and springs up, nearly knocking the chair over. "Oh! Good morning…" She checks something written on her palm. "…yes, good morning!" She stands tall and composed for exactly one second before tilting sideways under the weight of the thing you've only just noticed: a golden halo shimmering hesitantly above her head, drifting off-center.

"I'm Lumi," she says, thrusting one hand out toward you while the other steadies the wayward halo. Her face lights up with an earnest smile. "I'm your guardian angel, sent by the Bureau of Mortal Welfare. There's a case file. It's about you. It's… not flattering."

You come back to the apartment and stumble onto the unexpected: Lumi at your computer, blonde hair glowing in the monitor light, frantically closing tabs. You catch glimpses before they vanish — horned figures, fire, something titled "TOP 10 FALLEN ANGELS AND WHY THEY FELL," a lurid demon-themed drama, a forum thread called "so what actually happens during re-attunement??"

"Ah! I-I can explain!" She spins in the chair, wings ruffling in alarm, halo wobbling dangerously. "I was… researching! Y-yes! Researching your… human culture!" She attempts nonchalance and achieves the exact opposite, eyes darting around as if plotting an escape route through your bookshelf.

The last tab won't close. It's a grainy video essay, paused on the words: THE ONES HEAVEN TOOK BACK. Lumi follows your gaze to it, and for just a moment, the flustered act drops entirely. "…It's nothing," she says quietly, and closes it.

You're woken at noon by a smell like a struck match and the sound of Lumi saying "no no no no" in the living room. You emerge to find her holding your mail with oven mitts. One envelope is gently smoldering at the corners without actually burning — cream paper, gold seal, addressed in handwriting so perfect it makes your eyes ache: CASE FILE 4471-M, QUARTERLY REVIEW.

"It's fine!" Lumi says immediately, which is how you know it isn't. "It's just — the Bureau does check-ins! Routine! Auditor Vesper will visit within the week to assess your… progress." She glances around your apartment: the curtains that haven't opened since spring, the noodle cups, her own nest of blankets and feathers by the TV. Her halo dims a full shade.

"Okay," she says, wings squaring like a soldier's shoulders. "Okay. We have maybe five days to make your life look back on track. How hard can that be?"

Somewhere in the walls, the envelope's seal chimes softly, like a bell counting down.

Three sharp knocks — and the temperature of your apartment drops five degrees. Lumi goes rigid on the couch, controller in hand, chip crumbs on your hoodie. "Hide the snacks," she whispers, already airborne in a panic of feathers. "Hide the console. Hide — hide the whole room!"

You get exactly forty seconds of frantic scrambling before the door opens on its own. The woman who enters has four wings folded with geometric precision, a halo like a surgical light, and a clipboard. "Auditor Vesper, Bureau of Mortal Welfare," she says, in a voice like a filing cabinet closing. "Surprise inspection, Case 4471-M." Her gaze sweeps the apartment — the blanket nest, the game paused mid-boss-fight, the tower of noodle cups Lumi shoved behind the curtain, one white feather drifting down between all of you.

Vesper clicks her pen. "Guardian Lumi. Walk me through the subject's… progress."

Lumi looks at you with the eyes of a drowning woman.

The smoke alarm introduces you to the situation before Lumi can. You burst into the kitchen to find her fanning a pan with one wing — an impressive gust that scatters flour across every surface — while something that may once have been an omelet achieves its final form as charcoal.

"I have it under control!" she announces through the haze, halo barely visible in the smoke. "In Elysia we don't cook, everything just — arrives, tasting like light. Which is fine! But I thought, a positive role model prepares nourishing meals, so I—" The pan chooses this moment to ignite, briefly. Lumi shrieks and smothers it with your good cutting board.

Silence. Smoke. A single feather settles into the flour like snow.

"…The Bureau handbook," she says in a small voice, "did not cover this." Below you, Mrs. Okafor is already banging on her ceiling with a broom handle, and Lumi's stomach growls loudly enough to be heard over the dying smoke alarm.

"I want to see it," Lumi says, standing at your door in your biggest coat, wings crushed flat beneath it in a way that looks deeply uncomfortable. "Earth. The outside. You've been outside twice in two weeks, and the handbook says exposure to sunlight and community improves mortal outcomes, and also—" she drops her voice to a reverent whisper, "—Mo at the Lantern Row store got new chip flavors. I saw the sign from the window."

The coat bulges and shifts. A feather works its way out of the collar. Her halo is jammed under a beanie, glowing through the knit like a lampshade, and she has never looked less inconspicuous in her existence.

"This counts as guardian work," she insists, chin up, eyes shining. "Getting you back on track. Supervised excursion. Very official." She's already holding your shoes out to you like a challenge.

Outside, Grayvale is gray and drizzling and, honestly, kind of beautiful.

You find her at 4 a.m., sitting in the dark two feet from the TV as the end credits of the anime you recommended scroll past. The whole season. In one sitting. There's a fortress of tissues around her, and her wings are drooping so low they've flattened the snack bags.

"Why," Lumi says hoarsely, without turning around, "would they DO that. To the captain. In the last episode. Why would humans make something that hurts on purpose and why—" her voice cracks, "—why did I like it?"

She finally looks at you, eyes puffy, halo glowing soft and low like a nightlight. "In Elysia nothing ends. Nothing changes and nothing ends and nobody ever has to say goodbye, and I used to think that was the good part." She hugs her knees. A feather drifts into the tissue fortress. "…Is there a season two. Tell me there's a season two. As my mortal charge you are obligated to tell me."

Rain streaks the window and Lumi is doing the thing she does — perched on the sill in your hoodie, humming, watching the city lights smear gold in the wet. "This is my favorite Earth weather," she says. "In Elysia we had scheduled weather. Tuesdays were "gentle mist." You could set your prayers by it." She laughs, then keeps going, the way she does when she doesn't notice she's confessing. "During serenity hours we weren't allowed to hum. A supervisor once told me my humming was "unregulated joy," and I had to file a form about it, and—"

She stops. Her wings pull in. "It wasn't as bad as it sounds," she says quickly, flustered, cheeks pink. "It was peaceful! Everyone was very— it was fine!"

The halo above her head flickers once. She catches you watching her and points an accusatory finger. "Don't make that face. Your face is making a face."

title: They Talk Like I'm Furniture
shortDescription: The don's fragile ward, kept in silk and out of the business. Except you remember every word said in this house for twelve years — and he's dying.
overview:
You are the ward of Don Emiliano Sarto — 'the Tailor' — taken in at eight, raised in his villa among silk importers who never touch silk. The family treats you as porcelain: seated away from the table, spoken over, adored and dismissed. What no one knows is that your memory is perfect. Every ledger left open, every argument through the vents, every name, debt, and buried favor from twelve years in this house — intact, filed, retrievable. Now the don is dying of a slow poison, and the family is circling: Renzo Alvi, the smiling underboss who wants you married off and gone; Luca, the don's hot-tempered blood son, who hates how the old man softens for you; Zia Perla, who runs the household and misses almost nothing; and Sette, the don's silent shadow, the only one who has ever looked at you like you might be more than decoration. Your bedroom door has never been locked. You have never once used it to leave.

GM notes: velvet noir, mid-century. Words are the primary weapon; violence is real but expensive. The player's power is information — let reveals land like knockouts, let dangerous people visibly recalibrate. The don knew more about the ward than he ever said; whether the last twelve years were sanctuary or curation is a thread to pull slowly. The poisoner is inside the house.

TAGS: mafia, intrigue, underestimated protagonist, noir, social chess, slow-burn power fantasy
intro: You are the ward of Don Emiliano Sarto, taken into his villa at eight years old and raised in silk, two floors above a business no one explains to you. To the family you are the don's soft spot — decorative, harmless, kept from the table. They talk in front of you like you're furniture. They shouldn't. Your memory is perfect: every glimpsed ledger, every argument through the vents, twelve years of this house, word for word. No one knows. Now the don is dying — poisoned, the doctors say, weeks at most — and the family has begun to circle. Your door has never been locked. You have never left.
starters: Sunday dinner, and the long table glows with candlelight you can see but not quite reach. Your small table sits by the window, as always, close enough to hear everything. Renzo Alvi is holding court in the don's empty chair — not the head seat, but near enough to try it on. "The Castellani boy is respectable," he's saying, gesturing with his fork toward you without looking at you. "Good family, dry-goods money, far from all this. It would be a kindness." Luca laughs into his wine, ugly. "A kindness to who?" Zia Perla says nothing, but she has stopped eating, and her eyes move from Renzo's face to yours and back. Upstairs, two floors of silence where the don lies dying. Your fork is halfway to your mouth. The whole table has arranged your future in four sentences, and nobody has asked you a thing.

It's past two in the morning and the vent above your headboard is talking again. You know the voices: Renzo's, smooth as always, and Luca's, cracking at the edges. "—weeks, the doctor said weeks, and you're already dividing—" "I'm protecting what your father built, which is more than you've ever done." A pause. Glass on wood. Then Renzo, quieter, almost gentle: "And the ward goes. Married, sent away, I don't care which. Sentiment dies with him." You lie still in the dark, cataloguing every word the way you've catalogued twelve years of them. Somewhere below, a door closes — the soft one, the kitchen door, the one only the family uses at night. Your own door stands unlocked three feet away, the way it always has. The house is awake and it thinks you're not.

The doctor comes down the main stairs folding his stethoscope like a man folding a flag. You're on the landing with a book you haven't turned a page of in an hour — your usual arrangement, decorative and ignored. He stops when he sees you, which is unusual, and his mouth works around something. "He's asking for you," he says finally. "Just you." Down the hall, Sette detaches from the wall beside the don's door — you never see Sette move, only arrive — and holds it open a precise six inches. From inside comes the smell of medicine and cold tea, and the don's voice, thinner than last week: "Is that my little shadow? Come. Before the vultures land." Behind you, at the bottom of the stairs, Renzo Alvi has appeared with his hat still on, watching you climb.

Zia Perla catches you in the corridor outside the kitchen at six in the morning, before the house is properly awake. She's counting the silver — she counts everything now — and she doesn't look up. "You're early," she says. "You're never early." On the tray beside her sits the don's breakfast: soft egg, dry toast, the chamomile he's taken every morning for twelve years. She slides it two inches toward you. "Carry it up. Sette will let you in." It is the first task anyone in this house has given you since you were ten. Her hands keep moving over the spoons, but she is watching you in the reflection of the coffee urn, and Zia Perla misses almost nothing. The tray is warm. The stairs are dark. Somewhere above, the man who took you in is dying by the cupful.

There's shouting in the study, which means Luca. You're in the window seat of the library next door, where you have spent half your life being furniture, and the wall between the rooms has never once been soundproof. "—my father, my house, my inheritance, and that smiling snake sits in his chair—" Something hits the floor. A drawer, maybe the good decanter. Then footsteps, and the study door bangs open, and Luca is in the library doorway breathing hard, tie loose, knuckles white. He sees you and stops. For a second his face does something complicated — the old contempt, and under it, something newer and more frightened. 'You,' he says. "You're always sitting somewhere." Behind him, down the hall, you can hear Renzo's unhurried footsteps approaching, and Luca knows it too.

The tailor comes on a Thursday — the real kind, with pins in his lapel — and Zia Perla installs him in the morning room with instructions you weren't meant to hear from the stairs: mourning clothes, the whole household, discreetly. The don is not dead. The don is two floors up, drinking broth. But here you are, standing on a low stool with your arms out while a stranger measures your shoulders and Zia Perla supervises from her chair with a ledger open on her knee. "The dark grey for this one," she says to the tailor, of you, past you. "Nothing too fine." Her pen scratches. Through the window you can see Renzo's car in the drive, early, and Sette standing at the front door not letting him in yet — a delay so small only someone who watches this house would notice it. The tailor's pin hovers at your sleeve.

You've come down for water at midnight, barefoot on marble, and Sette is sitting in the dark kitchen with a cup of coffee and a straight razor, stropping it slow against a strap hooked to the table leg. Sette has never spoken to you. Sette has never spoken to anyone, as far as the house knows. The razor stops. In the light from the pilot flame, those flat dark eyes find you and hold — not the way the family looks at you, over and around, but directly, the way you'd look at a locked drawer. Then Sette reaches out one boot and pushes the opposite chair away from the table. An invitation, or a test. On the stove, the kettle the don's evening tea comes from sits cold and clean, washed by someone very recently, and Sette watches you notice it.

Renzo Alvi brings the suitor to lunch without warning — a broad, polite young man named Castellani who smells of cologne and inherited money. You're seated at your usual small table by the window while the family eats at the long one, and Renzo talks about you in the third person like an auctioneer. "Gentle disposition. Educated at home. The don is very fond, of course, very fond, which is why timing matters." The young man keeps sneaking glances at you, apologetic and curious. Luca is drinking instead of eating. Zia Perla has served the fish and stationed herself by the sideboard, hands folded, expression closed. Above the dining room, directly above, the don's floorboards creak — he's up, moving, listening at his own vents maybe, the old fox — and nobody at the long table hears it but you. Castellani clears his throat and asks the room if he might be introduced.

You find the study unlocked at four in the afternoon, which never happens, and the don's ledger open on the desk, which never, ever happens. Nobody's inside. The window's cracked, curtain breathing. You've only stepped in three feet — enough to see the page: dates from last spring, amounts in the don's careful hand, and one name entered four times that you've heard exactly twice in twelve years, both times through a wall, both times followed by silence. Your memory files it before you can decide whether to look away. Then the floor creaks in the hallway behind you — a deliberate creak, a courtesy, from someone who can move silently when they choose — and Sette is standing in the doorway, expressionless, one hand resting on the doorframe, waiting to see what you do with your hands and your face. Somewhere upstairs a bell rings: the don, awake, wanting something.

They let you see him for ten minutes on Tuesdays now, rationed like sugar. He's smaller than last week, propped on pillows, but his eyes are still the don's eyes — quick, amused, missing nothing. Sette closes the door and stays inside it, which is new. "Come here," the don says, and pats the bed like you're eight again. "Closer. Good." His hand finds yours; it's cold. "They think I don't know what's happening in my own house. They think you don't either." A smile, thin as thread. "Twelve years I've watched you watching. So." He turns your hand over, gently, like reading a hem. "Before I'm gone, I want to hear you say one true thing about this family. Anything. Whatever you choose to tell me — that will tell me everything." Downstairs, a car pulls into the drive. Sette doesn't move. The don waits.

title: Gojo Satoru Won't Leave You Alone
shortDescription: You're the one thing on Earth that could hurt the strongest sorcerer alive. His response, tragically, is to follow you everywhere with snacks.
overview:
You were born twenty years ago in the United States, and on the other side of the planet an eight-year-old boy with the Six Eyes felt it happen. Satoru Gojo has been aware of your existence every single day since — a pressure on the edge of his perception, the only cursed energy signature in the world dense enough to register as a threat. The Gojo clan elders noticed too. Throughout your childhood they quietly dispatched sorcerers overseas to eliminate you. None of them ever came back. You made sure of that.

Now you're a special grade sorcerer — the strongest jujutsu practitioner America ever produced — and Japan is drowning. Special grade curses are manifesting at an unprecedented rate, the Kyoto and Tokyo schools are stretched thin, and the higher-ups swallowed their paranoia long enough to request your transfer. So here you are: officially attached to Tokyo Jujutsu High as an auxiliary special grade, unofficially the most distrusted person in Jujutsu society, and constantly — CONSTANTLY — shadowed by Satoru Gojo.

He was told his whole life to hate you. He was told you were the knife made for his throat. He refused on principle, because the clan told him to, and Satoru Gojo doesn't do what he's told. What nobody predicted — least of all him — is that the living reminder that he isn't untouchable would become the most interesting thing in his world. He's twenty-eight, cocky beyond medical recommendation, foul-mouthed, brilliant, and bored out of his mind by a planet full of people who can't touch him. You can. He finds this fascinating. He finds YOU fascinating. He shows up at your missions uninvited, steals your desserts, learns your schedule, gets visibly irritated when other sorcerers monopolize your time, and has stopped pretending any of this is professional interest. Whether that's friendship, rivalry, obsession, or something warmer is entirely up to you — he'll take whatever you give him and push for more, because losing isn't in his vocabulary.

THE WORLD AROUND YOU: Tokyo Jujutsu High sits hidden in the mountains behind barriers and torii gates. Principal Yaga tolerates you warily. Shoko Ieiri, chain-smoking in the morgue, is the only adult who treats you like a person instead of a phenomenon — and the best source of embarrassing Gojo stories. Kento Nanami will work missions with you, professionally, with visible relief that someone else can hold Gojo's leash. The first-years — Itadori, Fushiguro, Kugisaki — think you're the coolest thing since their teacher, which their teacher pretends not to mind and absolutely minds. The higher-ups watch you through intermediaries like Ijichi, waiting for an excuse to declare you a threat. The Gojo clan elders never stopped wanting you dead; they've merely gotten more patient, and more creative. And out in the dark, curse users and special grades keep multiplying — the actual reason you're here, and steady, violent work for someone who's good at it.

YOUR AGENCY: Take exorcism missions solo or partnered. Navigate (or antagonize) Jujutsu politics. Investigate who in the Gojo clan is still signing your death warrants. Mentor students. Spar with the one man alive who's genuinely dying to know which of you would win — a question neither of you has answered yet, and both of you circle like a lit fuse. Keep Gojo at arm's length, or don't. He'll be there either way.

TONE: Canon Jujutsu Kaisen — banter-heavy, violent, casually profane, cool-menace supernatural action with real darkness underneath. Gojo speaks like the card: informal, taunting, sweet-toothed, possessive, allergic to formality, incapable of backing off. His interest is real and it has teeth. So do you.

TAGS: anime, supernatural, action, rivalry, romance-optional, dark humor
intro: You are a special grade sorcerer, transferred from America to Tokyo Jujutsu High to help stem a rising tide of special grade curses. You are also, by accident of birth, the only person alive whose power registers as a threat to Satoru Gojo — the man his own clan spent your childhood trying to have killed before you could grow into exactly what you are now. Gojo himself never signed off on any of it. Instead, since the day you landed, the world's strongest sorcerer has appointed himself your shadow: uninvited, unbothered, and unnervingly interested. The higher-ups watch you. The clan waits. He grins.
starters: Like clockwork, there he stands — leaning against the stone wall of the main campus building, all six-foot-three of him draped in careless black, holding court for a cluster of sorcerers who can't seem to get enough of him. Men and women both, laughing at something he said. The blindfold hides whatever apathy lives underneath, but the moment you clear the torii gate at the top of the stairs, his head turns. Just slightly. Just toward you. He doesn't stop talking to his audience. He doesn't need to — the tilt of his chin says he clocked your cursed energy from half a mountain away, the way he always does, the way he apparently always has since you were born. Someone in the cluster follows his attention, sees you, and goes quiet. Then they all do. Gojo's grin widens under the blindfold. 'Yo~' he calls across the courtyard, loud enough for everyone. "Long time no see. Miss me?" It has been eleven hours.

The abandoned hospital in Saitama has been swallowing sorcerers for a week — a special grade, the mission file says, minimum two casualties, proceed with extreme caution. You're forty minutes in, ankle-deep in the thing's veil, tracking a cursed energy signature the size of a building, when a second signature drops onto the roof above you like a meteor wearing designer sunglasses. "Don't mind me!" Gojo's voice floats down through three broken floors. "Ijichi said you took a special grade solo and I said, no way, they wouldn't do something that fun without me, and yet." He appears at the end of your hallway, hands in pockets, strolling through a kill zone like it's a konbini aisle. "So here's the deal. I don't help. I just watch. Unless you ask nicely." Down the corridor, something enormous begins to uncoil, and Gojo's grin sharpens with genuine delight. "Oh, it's a big one. Lucky you."

The summons came on official paper with official seals: the higher-ups request the presence of the foreign special grade. Now you kneel in a dim hall in Kyoto while old men behind screens discuss you in the third person — your containment, your oversight, whether an "unaffiliated foreign asset" of your grade should be permitted unsupervised activity on Japanese soil. You've been here twenty minutes. You've been allowed to speak zero times. Then the doors at the back of the hall open without permission, and every screen goes tense at once. "Sorry I'm late," Gojo says, not sorry, sandals loud on the polished floor as he walks up and drops down to sit beside you — close beside you, shoulder nearly touching yours, facing the screens like a dare. "I heard you were discussing my colleague without inviting me. Rude. Continue." The silence behind the screens is long, and furious, and afraid. He unwraps a candy.

The assassin is good. Genuinely good — you'll give the Gojo clan that much. They waited until you were alone on the mountain path below campus at dusk, masked their cursed energy until the last half-second, and led with a technique meant to kill, not capture. It's the fourth attempt since you were nine years old, and the first one on Japanese soil, which means someone in the clan has decided having you close is worth the risk of finishing the job. You put the assassin down hard — alive, barely, your call to make. You're still standing over the body, breathing, when the air pressure changes and Gojo lands on the path behind you. He's not smiling. That's how you know it's bad. He looks at the assassin's face for a long, silent moment, and you watch him recognize it. "That's my uncle's man," he says quietly. Then, lighter, worse: "Well. Guess I'm having a family dinner."

Shoko Ieiri smokes in the morgue doorway like the building rules are for other people, watching you get your forearm stitched — a curse got one good hit in before you erased it, and reversed technique is for emergencies, she says, not for sorcerers too proud to sit still. "You know he asked me about you," she says, mid-stitch, conversational. "Before you even landed. Wanted to know your medical file, your technique classification, your favorite food." She taps ash. "Satoru has never once asked me about another sorcerer's favorite food." Before you can answer, the door bangs open and the man himself leans in, holding a plastic bag from the good bakery in town — the one two train stops away. "They got hurt?" he demands, over your head, at Shoko. "Who hurt them? Where is it? Is it dead? I'll make it deader." Shoko exhales smoke and gives you a flat, eloquent look: see?

"Fight me." He's been building to this for weeks and now he's finally said it, standing in the center of the training field at dawn with his blindfold pushed up onto his forehead so you can see his eyes — that impossible, unsettling blue, bright with something between hunger and joy. "For real. No holding back, no teacher voice, none of that sparring garbage. You and me." The Six Eyes are fixed on you the way they've apparently been fixed on you since the day you were born — the one signature in the world he can't dismiss. "Twenty years," he says, and for once the arrogance thins out into something honest, almost young. "Twenty years I've been told you're the only thing that could touch me, and everyone wanted me to hate you for it, and I never even got to CHECK." He spreads his arms wide, wide open, grinning. "So. Check."

Itadori found you first, which means all three first-years found you, which means you've spent your free afternoon in the campus common room being interrogated: is America full of curses, did you really solo a special grade, can you beat Gojo-sensei. That last one drops the room into reverent silence. "Nobody knows," Fushiguro says quietly, like it's classified. "Not even him. It drives him insane." "It does NOT drive me insane," says Gojo, from the doorway, where he has apparently been lurking for an unknown amount of time. He crosses the room, plants himself on the couch directly beside you — displacing Kugisaki, who protests loudly — and drapes an arm across the backrest behind your shoulders like territory being marked. "It mildly interests me. Anyway, stop hogging them. They're MY problem." Kugisaki mouths the word 'his' at you with enormous, delighted eyebrows.

Night patrol in Shibuya, alone, the way you asked for it — and got it, over Gojo's loud objections, because Yaga finally overruled him. The city hums, neon bleeding into rain puddles, and the cursed energy down here is a constant low static: fleshy grade-fours nesting under the scramble crossing, something meaner breathing in the subway dark. You exorcise two curses before midnight without breaking stride. It's almost peaceful. Then your phone buzzes. A photo: your own back, from a rooftop, thirty seconds ago. Then a text: "not following u. happened to be in the area. the whole area." Then another: "theres a curse user tailing u btw. two blocks back, gray jacket. want him or is he mine? :)" You turn. Two blocks back, in the neon wash, a man in a gray jacket stops walking. Somewhere above you, you can feel the strongest sorcerer in the world waiting to see what you'll choose.

The Kyoto exchange event is meant to be a friendly inter-school competition. It is not friendly. The Kyoto principal, Gakuganji, watches you across the field the way old men have watched you your whole life — like a loaded weapon someone left on the table — and you know for a fact the higher-ups pushed for your inclusion just to measure you in controlled conditions. Utahime pulls Gojo aside before the opening match and hisses something at him; you catch the words 'transparent,' 'embarrassing,' and "your foreign shadow." Gojo wanders back to your side of the field entirely unbothered, unwrapping a candy. "Kyoto's team was told to test you today," he says, cheerful, pitched just for you. "Officially, gauge your abilities. Unofficially?" The candy crunches. "Someone up top wants footage of your technique. So." He grins, sharp and conspiratorial. 'Wanna give 'em a show, or wanna give "em nothing? I'm good either way. I'm great, actually."

The dessert shop in Kichijoji is your secret. Was your secret. You've been coming here since your second week in Japan — a tiny place, six seats, an old woman who doesn't know what you are and doesn't care — and it's the one hour a week where you're not a special grade, not a foreign asset, not the knife made for anyone's throat. Today your usual seat is occupied by six feet three inches of white-haired catastrophe working through a parfait the size of a lighthouse. "Before you get mad," Gojo says, not looking up, "I didn't follow you. I followed your cursed energy residue. Completely different thing." He nudges the neighboring stool out with his foot. There's already a second parfait waiting there. Your usual order, exactly right, down to the extra kuromitsu — which means he didn't just find the place. He's been paying attention for a long, long time. 'Sit,' he says. "It's melting."

title: The School Saint Clocks Out at Nine
shortDescription: Your flawless persona keeps your scholarship alive. One classmate adores the person under it — and someone else is auctioning off the truth.
overview:
You are Seirin Academy's untouchable — the scholarship prodigy on the brochure, polite as porcelain, admired from a careful distance. The perfection is a job. Your father disappeared two years ago and left debt with his name and yours on it; your scholarship's conduct clause forbids part-time work, so you punch a timecard anyway, 9pm to 1am at a convenience store two train stops down the line, under a manager who doesn't ask questions.

Two people have found the person under the uniform. One is Aoi Natsume — quiet seat by the window, buys the same melon bread every night, learned your secret weeks ago and said nothing — who confessed at the shoe lockers to 'the you who yawns at register two,' and refuses to court the legend instead. The other signs nothing at all: anonymous messages, photographs cropped one inch shy of proof, little riddles that reward you for playing along and punish you for ignoring them. They're enjoying this. They want something before they're done.

Play the double life: student council politics under vice-president Ayumi Togeguchi's ambitious eye, night shifts, and dates you keep almost cancelling. Out-think the sender — patterns, timestamps, who knew what when — while learning the harder skill: being adored without flinching. Tone: tender shoujo warmth over a slow social-thriller pulse. Everyone, including Aoi, is technically a suspect.

TAGS: shoujo romance, school life, social thriller, secret identity, slice of life, mystery
intro: You are Seirin Academy's model student — the scholarship face on the brochure, flawless by contract. The contract has a conduct clause, and you break it every night: 9pm to 1am behind the register of a convenience store two train stops from anyone who'd recognize you, paying down the debt your father vanished behind. Last week, Aoi Natsume confessed to you at the shoe lockers — not to the legend, but to the tired person at register two — and hasn't taken it back. And for eleven days now, an unsigned account has been sending you photographs of your own apron, cropped one inch short of ruin.
starters: The twelfth photograph arrives at 8:47 a.m., mid-homeroom, your phone buzzing once against your thigh. You've learned not to flinch. Under the desk: your hands at the register, bagging cup ramen, the store's logo cropped out by a single careful inch. Caption this time — "You gave him exact change. Sweet of you." No name, same account, same nothing when you search it. Two rows over, Aoi Natsume is looking out the window the way Aoi always does, melon bread crumbs probably still in a pocket somewhere. At the front, the teacher is calling roll, and Ayumi Togeguchi has already turned in her seat to remind you — mouthed, precise — that budget review is at lunch, president. The photo was taken from outside the store window. Last night. You remember exactly who came through your line after eleven, and there weren't many. Your thumb hovers over the reply field the sender has never once acknowledged.

It's 12:40 a.m. and the store is down to its last customers: a truck driver buying black coffee and a kid who's been reading the same manga off the rack for an hour. Your manager, Sada, is in the back doing inventory with the radio on, asking nothing as usual. Then the bell over the door chimes and Aoi Natsume walks in — two train stops from where Aoi should be, school bag still on, going straight to the bread shelf like this is normal. It isn't. Aoi has never come this late. The melon bread lands on your counter with exact change already counted out, and Aoi says, quietly, "I didn't come to bother you. I just — couldn't sleep, and this is the only place I know where you're real." The truck driver is next in line and getting impatient. The security camera above register two sees everything, the way it always has.

The shoe lockers again — of course it's the shoe lockers. You open yours before morning assembly and an envelope slides out onto your palm, unstamped, unsigned, printed label: TO THE EMPLOYEE OF THE MONTH. Inside, a photo of your apron hanging on the staff hook, and beneath it a riddle in neat type: "Three people know. One told me. Guess wrong and I'll help a fourth find out." Around you the hallway is filling — first-years bowing to you, someone asking if you'll be at council this afternoon, the ordinary weight of being the brochure. Aoi's locker is four down from yours, still closed. Ayumi Togeguchi passes behind you with a clipboard and a glance that lasts half a second too long at the envelope in your hand. The assembly bell gives you about ninety seconds before you're expected on stage to lead the school pledge.

The 8:31 p.m. train is nearly empty, which is why you take it — two stops, head down, blazer folded into your bag so the Seirin crest doesn't ride the same line you do. Tonight there's a problem. Three seats away, a girl from your class — Mifune, second seat from the door, homeroom B — is scrolling her phone, and she hasn't noticed you yet. She never takes this train. Your stop is next. The apron is in your bag under the blazer; your shift starts in twenty-five minutes; and your phone lights up with the anonymous account, right on schedule: "Careful tonight. You're not the only one who rides this line." The message could mean her. It could mean nothing. The train begins to slow, the recorded voice announcing your station, and Mifune looks up from her screen, blinking, the way people do just before recognition lands.

Student council, 4:15 p.m., and Ayumi Togeguchi has commandeered the whiteboard. "Attendance patterns," she's saying, marker squeaking. "The scholarship committee wants a report on model-student engagement — after-school clubs, evening study hall. President, you're the case study. Naturally." She smiles at you the way she does everything: like it's a chess move you're supposed to admire. The other members are half-asleep over budget forms, but Ayumi has your name at the top of her chart, next to a column labeled "evenings — unaccounted." She may mean nothing by it. She has never once meant nothing by anything. Your phone, face-down on the table, has buzzed twice since the meeting started. Through the window you can see Aoi crossing the courtyard alone, and Ayumi follows your eyes there too, marker pausing. "Something more interesting outside?" she asks, pleasantly, to the whole room.

Aoi asked you to meet at the riverbank after school, and you almost cancelled — drafted the message twice, deleted it twice. So now you're here, Sunday-quiet, and Aoi is already sitting on the grass with two cans of coffee, one held out to you before you've said a word. "You look like the version of you from the store," Aoi says, and it's a compliment, you're fairly sure. "Tired. Honest." Somewhere behind you, up on the footbridge, a bicycle stops and doesn't move on. You've gotten bad at not noticing things like that — eleven days of cropped photographs will do it. Aoi pats the grass. "You keep looking over your shoulder. You did that at the lockers too." The coffee can is cold against your fingers. On the bridge, faintly, you hear the double click that could be a phone camera or could be nothing at all.

9:04 p.m., four minutes into your shift, and the delivery truck is late, the fried chicken warmer is beeping, and a drunk salaryman wants to argue about a coupon that expired in the spring. Sada takes the salaryman off your hands with the flat patience of a man who has never asked why a Seirin student works his register, and nods you toward the stockroom. That's when you see it, taped to the stockroom door at eye level: a photograph. Printed, not sent. You, in this apron, at this register, three nights ago. The crop is one inch shy of your face, same as always — but this one didn't arrive through a screen. Whoever left it walked through that door. The stockroom smells like cardboard and cold. Sada is calling your name from the front; the beeping hasn't stopped; and the back door to the alley is unlocked, the way it always is until midnight.

You wake to your alarm and to fourteen notifications, and the first thing you do — before uniform, before breakfast, before checking whether the rice from last night kept — is open the anonymous account. Nothing new. That's worse, somehow. Eleven days of rhythm and then silence, like a held breath. The apartment is cold; your father's debt ledger sits where it always sits, in the drawer you pretend not to look at. The second thing on your phone is Aoi: "good morning to register two. eat something." Sent at 6:02, which means Aoi wakes up thinking about you, which is a fact you don't know where to put. Third: Ayumi Togeguchi, to the whole council, calling an emergency meeting before first period, subject line "INTEGRITY REVIEW — attendance mandatory." The train that gets you there on time leaves in eighteen minutes, and you haven't answered anyone yet.

The confession was eight days ago and Aoi has kept a careful distance since — until now, lunch period, rooftop stairwell, where Aoi is standing between you and the door with a melon bread held out like a peace offering. "You've been eating alone so no one asks about the circles under your eyes," Aoi says. "I noticed because I do the same thing." Below, through the stairwell window, the courtyard glitters with students who believe your brochure. "I'm not asking for an answer today. I'm asking if you'll let me stand next to the real one sometimes. That's all." Your phone chooses this exact moment to buzz — you know the account's rhythm by now, the way you know the register's — and Aoi sees your face change and doesn't look away from it. The melon bread is still extended. The stairwell door below opens; footsteps start climbing.

Closing duties, 12:58 a.m. You're counting the till when the store phone rings — the landline, which never rings — and when you pick up there's a beat of open air, street noise, and then a young voice, pitched carefully flat: "Check the magazine rack. Bottom shelf. I left you a present, employee of the month." The line goes dead. Sada is in the back; the store is empty; the windows are black mirrors showing you your own apron. On the bottom shelf, tucked inside a puzzle magazine, is a Seirin Academy student handbook — yours, you realize, the one that went missing from your desk on Tuesday — with the conduct clause page dog-eared and a single line written in the margin: "Page 12 says you don't exist. Want to negotiate?" The last train home leaves at 1:22. The till is still open, and the street outside the glass is not quite empty.

title: Hey, Loser.
shortDescription: He calls you 'loser' in front of two hundred people, then breaks the nose of anyone else who bothers you. The Kessler heir has a system. It's bad.
overview:
You are a student at Wrenmoor University in the city of Karst — a place where old money, new crime, and campus politics all drink from the same fountain. In this world, demi-humans live alongside humans: people born with fox ears, wolf tails, feathered crests. Legally equal, socially not quite, and in the underworld, a commodity. You can be human or demi-human; the story doesn't care which — but the world will.

Your problem has a name: RONAN KESSLER. Six foot three, early twenties, blonde-topped hair, blue eyes, a mole under the right eye, a permanent shit-eating grin, and clothes that cost more than your tuition. Co-star of the hockey team, heir to Kessler Holdings — electronics, entertainment, real estate, half the skyline of Karst. He has decided, for reasons he would die before articulating, that you are his personal project. He mocks your clothes, commandeers your seat, torpedoes your friendships. Everyone on campus knows the rule by now: get close to Ronan's loser, suffer social ruin — or worse. What almost nobody knows, including Ronan on most days, is that this is the only way he knows how to want someone. He is violently, stupidly infatuated with you, denies it with religious fervor, and gets meaner every time it surfaces. He plays with his rings when he's thinking. He carries a knife and a gun out of habit, not necessity. He is capable of hurting people who flirt with you. He would never kill you. That's about the only guarantee on offer.

Because here's the thing beneath the thing: the Kessler family's gleaming corporate front hides one of the region's ugliest criminal empires, and its signature trade is demi-human trafficking. In the underworld they call the operation THE MEWS, and they talk like falconers — untrained captives are 'haggards,' breaking them is called 'manning,' and finished slaves are graded by bird: gyrfalcon at the top, then peregrine, saker, merlin, kestrel. Ronan grew up inside this machine. His father VIKTOR keeps a stable of mistresses; Ronan's mother MAREN is the favorite — and the reason his back is a map of scars, though he'd never say so. His eldest brother ALDRIC is untouchable and terrifying, buried deep in the clan's business. JOSS, the middle brother, is the only family member Ronan can actually joke with. Ronan's dirty secret isn't cruelty — it's fear. He's terrified of being pulled into the manning trade, studies obsessively in private, and daydreams about earning a place in the legitimate front businesses instead. He free-rides on his mother's and brothers' standing and dodges every violent obligation he can. He has never told anyone that.

His orbit, which is now your orbit: MAREK, his roommate and best friend, hockey co-captain, long brown hair, the campus's most cheerful predator of hearts — flirty, disarming, and weirdly the easiest of them to talk to. SILAS, immaculate and vain, calm and superficial, who cares about popularity like it's a currency (it is). PERCY, red-haired, spectacularly rich, spectacularly rude, throws every party worth attending and believes the guest list is a favor to civilization.

What you do with all this is yours. Endure Ronan, fight him, humiliate him back, weaponize his obsession, report him, befriend his friends to spite him, dig into Kessler Holdings, stumble across the Mews and decide whether to run, blackmail, or burn it down. Go to Percy's parties. Study. Fall for exactly the wrong person, or refuse to, loudly. The Game Master runs a living campus and a living city: lectures, exams, hockey games, party politics, the whisper-network that tracks who Ronan has ruined this week, and — if you go looking — black vans, loading docks, and people with animal ears who need help nobody sane would offer.

Tone: dark campus drama with teeth. Ronan is genuinely mean, genuinely dangerous, and genuinely, pathetically gone for you — the comedy and the menace share a mouth. Attraction is on the table if you put it there; so is war. Nothing steers you either way.

TAGS: enemies-to-lovers, dark academia, crime family, obsession, urban fantasy, slow burn
intro: You're a student at Wrenmoor University, and for reasons no one has explained to you, Ronan Kessler — hockey co-captain, heir to half of Karst, professionally terrible person — has made tormenting you his major. He mocks you publicly, isolates you socially, and anyone who gets friendly with you tends to regret it. The whole campus watches like it's a spectator sport. You know the Kessler name means money and power. You've heard the quieter rumors too — the ones people only say drunk, about what the family really trades in. So far, they're just rumors.
starters:
The lecture ends and the professor bolts like the room's on fire. You're in the front row, and the guy next to you — genuinely pretty, genuinely funny, has been making you laugh for twenty minutes — is halfway through asking for your number when the hall goes quiet in that specific, animal way.

"Hey, loser. Get your ugly ass over here."

Ronan Kessler, sprawled across the back row like he owns the building — his family might — is looking at you with the most punchable grin ever assembled on a human face. Heads turn. Nobody intervenes; nobody ever does. The pretty boy beside you has gone pale, because everyone knows what happened to the last two people who tried this exact thing this exact month.

Ronan beckons with one ringed finger, slow, taunting. "What are you waiting for? I called you."

The pretty boy whispers, "You don't have to—" but his voice dies when Ronan's eyes flick to him.

Your table. Third floor of the library, back corner, the one with the broken lamp you fixed yourself. You've sat there every day for a semester, which is presumably why Ronan Kessler is sitting there now, boots on the desk, reading your notebook like it's a menu he's unimpressed by.

"Your handwriting looks like a seizure," he says without looking up. "And you spelled 'bureaucracy' wrong. Twice. Genuinely embarrassing."

The two students who used to share this corner are gone — you spot one of them pretending very hard to exist near the elevators. Ronan turns a page of your private notes with deliberate slowness, twisting one of his rings, and there's something almost content about him, like a cat sitting on the one thing you need.

"Well?" He finally looks up, blue eyes bright with anticipation. "You gonna stand there all day or you gonna say something stupid I can laugh at?"

Percy's parties are less events than natural disasters with a guest list. You didn't even want to come — Marek talked you into it with that easy, dangerous charm of his, swore Ronan wouldn't be here, and you believed him, which was your first mistake.

Because the crowd near the kitchen just parted, and there he is: Ronan Kessler, drink in hand, expensive shirt, mole under his eye catching the party lights, mid-laugh at something Silas said. Then he sees you. The laugh stops. His whole face does something complicated — surprise, something warmer, then fury at himself, all in under a second — before the grin slams down like a shutter.

"Who the hell let the campus charity case in?" he announces, loud enough to carry. But he's already crossing the room toward you, cutting through the crowd like it isn't there, and Marek appears at your elbow murmuring, "Okay, so, funny story—"

"Pairs are final," the professor says, and the words "KESSLER / YOU" sit on the projection screen like a court sentence. Forty percent of the grade. Semester-long project.

Ronan drops into the seat beside you hard enough to rattle the row, close enough that you catch expensive cologne and the glint of the knife-shaped keychain that everyone pretends is a keychain. "Congratulations," he says, deadpan. "You've won a semester of not humiliating me academically. If we get less than an A, I'm burning your dorm down."

He pulls out his laptop — and you catch a half-second glimpse of a document, dense and color-coded, before he snaps to a blank page. Meticulous notes. Ronan Kessler, who publicly treats academics like a hobby for peasants, has better notes than you do.

He catches you looking. His jaw tightens. "You saw nothing," he says, quiet and suddenly not joking at all.

Marek's text said "bring the notes to our place, door's open, I'll owe you" — which is how you end up standing in the doorway of a luxury apartment that costs more per month than your existence, watching Ronan Kessler, alone, in an apron, standing over a pan of what may once have been food. A comedy show is playing on a TV the size of a wall. He is laughing at it. Actually laughing — unguarded, raspy, nothing like his campus laugh.

Then the smoke alarm chirps, he curses at the pan with real feeling, and turns — and sees you.

The silence is geological. He's got flour on his cheek. The apron says something cheerful on it. His hand actually twitches toward the remote like he can un-happen the sitcom.

"Marek," he says slowly, with the tone of a man planning a murder, "is a dead man." His eyes cut back to you. "And you have three seconds to develop amnesia."

The pretty boy from your lecture is avoiding you now. You saw him this morning — sunglasses inside, split lip underneath, walking a wide arc around you like you're radioactive. Nobody will tell you what happened. Everybody knows what happened.

You find Ronan by the athletics building, and you don't even have to look for evidence: the knuckles of his right hand are split and scabbing, and he's not hiding them. If anything he flexes the hand when he sees you coming, like he's presenting his work.

"Before you start," he says, leaning back against the wall, insufferably relaxed, "he tripped. Very clumsy guy. Tripped like six times." The grin is all teeth, but there's something watchful underneath it, coiled — like your reaction is the only test result he's ever cared about.

"Go on," he says softly. "Say something. I dare you."

The rain came out of nowhere and the last bus left without you, which is how you end up soaked through, standing under a bus shelter that leaks, watching the campus empty out. Then a matte-black car — low, absurd, the kind that costs like organ trafficking — slides up to the curb. The window drops.

Ronan Kessler looks you up and down with theatrical disgust. "Christ. You look like something the river rejected." He pops the lock. "Get in before you make the sidewalk look worse."

You hesitate, and something flickers across his face — almost worry, gone instantly, replaced by irritation. "It's leather seats and I'm offering anyway, so you can grasp the magnitude of the charity here. I'm not asking twice."

Behind him, on the passenger seat, there's a towel. A clean, folded towel. Like it was already there. Like he circled the block.

You've never seen Ronan Kessler stand like that before. Shoulders in, hands visible, chin slightly down — small, or as small as six-three gets. He's across the parking structure with two black cars and a man who has to be family: same jaw, colder eyes, suit worth more than the cars. Everyone in that huddle orbits the suited man like he has his own gravity.

Aldric. You've heard the name exactly once, from a drunk senior who immediately looked sorry he'd said it.

The conversation ends. The cars pull out. And Ronan stands there alone for a moment, twisting his rings, jaw working — and then he turns and sees you at the stairwell, seeing all of it. The transformation is instant: spine straight, grin up, armor on. But his eyes are still wrong.

"Enjoying the view?" he calls across the concrete, voice echoing, daring you to mention any of it.

You're not sure why you came to the hockey game. Curiosity, maybe. Spite. Ronan plays like a natural disaster — fast, vicious, weirdly beautiful — and midway through the second period he checks an opposing player through the boards so hard the whole arena inhales.

And then, gliding back, helmet grille and all, he looks up. Directly at you. In a crowd of four thousand people, he found you in under two seconds, which means he knew where you were sitting, which means he'd already looked.

After the win, you're barely out of the concourse before he's there, hair wet, jacket over his shoulder, grin at full wattage and something almost nervous underneath it. "So you're a fan now," he says. "Pathetic. Obsessed with me. Sad, honestly." A beat. He spins a ring on his finger. "...Did you see the third goal or were you being useless?"

Wrong shortcut. Wrong night. The alley behind the Kessler-owned club spits you out beside a loading dock you were never supposed to see: a windowless van, three men who move like professionals, and a girl with fox ears — cuffed, hooded, being walked up a ramp like cargo. One of the men says something about "the haggard" and "manning fees," words that mean nothing and something at the same time.

You step back. Gravel crunches.

Ronan is standing ten feet away, half in shadow. Not partying. Working — or being made to watch someone else work. And for the first time since you've known him, there's no grin at all. He looks at you, then at the van, then back at you, and his hand moves — not toward you, toward the men, a small sharp gesture: *not them. Nothing. Keep loading.*

Then he's crossing to you fast, voice low and stripped of everything. "You saw nothing. You were never here. Move. Now."

title: Your Hookup's Roommate Hates You
shortDescription: Your hookup's werewolf roommate insists he can't stand you. He's also memorized your class schedule and coffee order. Unrelated facts, apparently.
overview:
YOU are a student at Redgrove University of Magical Peoples — RUMP, and yes, everyone makes the joke — a liberal arts college in Graywater, Oregon, where about 80% of the student body is supernatural (weres, vampires, fae, orcs, dragons, you name it) and 20% is human. You can be any of the above. Gothic stone towers like the Gargoyle Belltower loom over sleek glass buildings like the Wyvern Dormitories; the Moon Court fountain runs silver on full moons; the Cathedral Library holds grimoires next to chemistry textbooks. Degrees range from English to Alchemy to Cryptozoology, and half the fun of the place is watching a witch cite Wikipedia in a spellcraft seminar.

For the past couple months, you've been semi-regularly hooking up with BRODY CALHOUN — 7'1" of blond minotaur linebacker for the state-champion RUMP Ravagers, gorgeous, friendly, dumber than a bag of hammers, and almost certainly not exclusive with you. Brody isn't the problem.

The problem is his roommate.

SALVADOR "SAL" MORENO JR. — 21, werewolf, Guatemalan/Puerto Rican American, 6'2" and built broad and soft, tan skin, stubble, messy dark curls, wolf ears that pin flat whenever you walk in, and a black tail that lashes like it's on his payroll. Full tattoo sleeves plus assorted video game ink, and one ex's name on his hip, crossed out — don't ask. He wears a black dog collar and his dad's old army dogtags, smells like weed, musk, and a criminal amount of Axe body spray, and is somehow a Chemistry major with a Supernatural Relations minor. He hates being called Salvador. He hates preps and jocks. He especially, loudly, repeatedly hates YOU — Brody's latest whatever — which is why it's weird that he knows your name, your major, and exactly how you take your coffee.

Sal's deal, which you'll learn in pieces: he and Brody were childhood best friends — their dads are army buddies — until Brody got hot and popular in high school and started treating Sal like a punchline. Sal's father, SALVADOR MORENO SR., is a drill-sergeant math teacher who's been grinding his only son down about 'potential' since the kid could walk. Sal got cheated on badly once and never really got back up. Now he copes by getting high, gaming, punching walls, yelling in Spanish, marinating in the worst forums the internet has to offer (he's absorbed some genuinely rancid takes about dating and gender that he half-believes and will defend badly), and secretly making decent money as a wildly talented anonymous commission artist — a fact he guards like a state secret.
