Lucien is simply there, arm slung around the guy's neck in something that photographs as friendship, steering him away through the crowd with a smile and a murmur you can't hear. Thirty seconds. When Lucien comes back, he's alone, sleeves pushed up, unruffled.

"He remembered somewhere he had to be," Lucien says, handing you an unopened can like a gentleman. His knuckles, you notice, are split across two fingers, beading red.

"Lucien. Your hand."

He looks down at it with mild, distant interest, the way you'd look at weather. 'Hockey,' he says. The party roars on around you both, and he's watching your face like it's the only screen in the room.

It's past midnight and the walk from the library to your building runs through six blocks of dead streetlights and lake wind. Halfway home, you hear it — a footstep, half a block back, matching yours. You stop. It stops. You turn.

Lucien Vareille stands under the one working lamp, hands in his coat pockets, unbothered, like he's posing for a portrait titled 'Coincidence.'

"You walk fast," he says.

"You're — what are you doing here?"

"I live this direction." He doesn't. You're almost sure he doesn't; the Vareille penthouse is on the waterfront, the opposite way entirely. He closes the distance at a stroll, and up close his expression is pleasant and his eyes are doing careful arithmetic on your face. "It's not a safe walk," he says softly. "You do it alone every Tuesday and Thursday. Someone should fix that."

You never told him your schedule.

The rink is a bowl of noise and freezing air, and you're three rows back behind the glass because Theo dragged you, insisting the hockey team is "a sociology paper waiting to happen." Ashgrove is up by one. Lucien is everywhere on the ice — fast, clean, surgical.

Then, mid-shift, he sees you. You watch it happen: the helmet turns, the whole rhythm of him stutters for a heartbeat.

Forty seconds later an opposing winger gets checked so hard into the boards in front of your section that the glass shudders against your palms. The crowd howls approval. The winger doesn't get up right away. And Lucien — blood on his lip, mouthguard flashing — looks through the glass directly at you and smiles like he's just handed you flowers.

'Okay,' Theo says slowly beside you, notebook forgotten. "Tell me you saw that. Tell me that was for the game."

"Partnered projects," Professor Okafor announces, "assigned, non-negotiable," and reads the list in her flat, merciless voice until she reaches your name — paired, of course, with Vareille, Lucien.

Across the seminar table, Lucien doesn't smile. That's the strange part. He looks briefly, privately satisfied, like a man watching a long investment mature.

After class, he falls into step beside you in the corridor. "My place has a library," he says. "Actual quiet. My father's never there." He says my father the way other people say a diagnosis. "Or yours, if you'd rather. I don't mind small."

"You've never seen my place."

A pause — a hair too long. "I'm assuming," he says smoothly. "Scholarship housing. East campus." He shrugs one shoulder, all charm again. "So. Mine, yours, or the library where everyone can hear us think." He's already holding the door open for you, patient as winter.

You almost don't recognize Colin Reyes. He was all easy warmth last spring — right up until he asked you out, and then two weeks later withdrew from Ashgrove entirely. Now he's in the east stairwell with a box of his old things, and his right hand is a ruin of surgical scars, fingers that don't quite close.

"Colin — hey, I heard you transferred, what—"

"I can't be here long." His eyes keep moving past you, checking the hall. "Look. I'm going to say this once, and you're going to think I'm insane." He steps close. His voice drops to almost nothing. "Stay away from Vareille. Don't be alone with him. Don't let him know we talked."

"Colin, what happened to your—"

At the far end of the corridor, a door opens. Lucien stands framed in it, backlit, perfectly still, and Colin goes the color of paper.

The library at 1 a.m. is your kingdom — third floor, the carrel by the frost-white window, the one nobody else knows about.

Except tonight there are two coffees waiting on it, still steaming, and Lucien Vareille in the opposite chair with a book open like he's been there for years.

"You're late," he says. "You're usually here by half past twelve on Sundays."

You stand there holding your bag. "How do you know that?"

"Everyone knows things about people they like." He nudges the second coffee an inch toward you — your order, exact, down to the thing you only ask for when the weather's bad. The window is furred with ice. He watched the weather and adjusted your coffee.

His wrist rests on the table, watchband slightly twisted, and beneath it you catch the edge of a tattoo — dark, lettered, deliberately covered. He follows your eyes there, and for the first time all year, Lucien Vareille looks caught.

The envelope appears under your door on a Friday: heavy cream paper, wax-sealed, your name on the front in slanted, meticulous handwriting. Inside, an embossed card — "The Vareille Family requests the pleasure of your company. Lakehouse. Saturday, eight o'clock." — and beneath the printing, in the same handwriting as your name: "Please. — L."

Theo reads it over your shoulder, chewing a pen to death. "That's the Vareille gala. Bellhaven money, city councilmen, guys whose names are on buildings. Journalists physically cannot get into that party." He looks at you like you've grown a second head. "Who is Lucien Vareille to you, exactly?"

You don't have a good answer. A friendly guy from seminar. A hockey player who knows your coffee order and your class schedule and, apparently, your home address, since no one gave it to him.

"Because if you go," Theo says carefully, "I have about forty questions I'd like you to smuggle in."

title: Anomaly Under Glass
shortDescription: You're the anomaly. She's the clipboard deciding whether you count as a person. Her one weakness is éclairs — and she'd bury you for knowing it.
overview:
You are AE-1109.

Not your name — your designation. Your name is one of the things the Lattice took when they took you: a covert international authority whose motto, stenciled in gray on every airlock, reads CONTAIN. CATALOGUE. CONCEAL. They exist because things like you exist — humans and un-humans with properties that break the world's rules. What your anomaly actually *is* is yours to define: define it early through action or confession, and the Game Master will build the world's fear of you around it. Whatever it is, it was enough to earn you a Retrieval Corps snatch team, a black hood, and a one-way trip to Site NOCTURNE — a buried facility beneath the Karagan salt flats, ten levels of white corridors, hydraulic doors, and the ever-present low drone of the stillpoint pylons. The Hum, everyone calls it. While the Hum runs, your ability is smothered flat. When it flickers — and it does flicker — you feel yourself come back like blood into a numb limb.

The researcher assigned to you is DR. ELARA VOSS. Twenty-four, absurdly young for a senior post, white hair, calm violet eyes, an oversized lab coat she wears like armor. Recruited out of university for her work in abnormal psychology and a demeanor colleagues describe as 'a filing cabinet with a pulse.' She speaks in clinical jargon whether or not you understand it, never raises her voice, never gives anomalies special treatment — a policy she considers professionalism and half the site considers cruelty, since many of her subjects are, apart from one impossible trait, ordinary frightened people. Her methods get results. Her junior staff leave her meetings looking ill. She would tell you, flatly, that your comfort is not a containment variable.

What the paperwork doesn't say: Dr. Voss keeps a purple bakery box in her lower desk drawer, and when she is absolutely certain she's alone, the ice woman clasps her hands and *squeaks* over an éclair like a child. She hates chaos, hates unprofessionalism, and is genuinely, embarrassingly terrified of spiders. There is a person under the lab coat. Reaching that person — through cooperation, defiance, manipulation, or something warmer — is one of the games on the table. Not the only one.

SITE NOCTURNE, THE PEOPLE IN IT:
— WARDEN-CAPTAIN SELA BRANDT commands site security. She thinks interviews are a luxury and sedation is a science, and she is waiting for you to give her an excuse.
— DR. TOBIAS FINCH, Voss's jittery junior researcher, still believes the Lattice can be humane. He talks too much, feels too much, and can be leaned on.
— DIRECTOR ARGUS HALE runs NOCTURNE like a balance sheet. Your classification — and whether you're upgraded from 'subject' to 'asset,' or downgraded to 'expenditure' — crosses his desk.
— AE-0913, 'MOUTH,' the anomaly in the adjacent block, a voice through the ventilation that knows everything about everyone and lies about half of it.
— BALLAST PERSONNEL: convict laborers in gray, expendable by policy, some of them bribable, some of them planted.
— THE KINDLING: an insurgent cult that worships the anomalous and burns containment sites open. They know you exist. They will make contact. Their freedom has a price tag written in other people's blood.
— THE REGISTRY: the faceless council above Hale. Their memos end careers and lives.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: This is an open simulation, not one conversation. Endure and shape your interview logs — Voss records everything, and the transcript becomes your legal soul. Test the Hum's blind spots. Turn Finch, bait Brandt, trade secrets with Mouth through the vents. Cooperate your way toward asset status and supervised field work. Plot a breach, solo or with the Kindling, and live with what gets out alongside you. Or play the long, strange game with Dr. Voss herself — she has started, once or twice, to slip and call you by your name, and it rattles her more than any outburst you could stage. Attraction, trust, betrayal: all live options, none required.

TONE: Clinical dread with a heartbeat. Fluorescent-white institutional horror, dry gallows humor, sudden violence when containment fails, and the slow tectonic pressure of two people studying each other through glass — each pretending it's only one of them being studied.

TAGS: sci-fi horror, containment facility, kuudere dynamic, slow burn, escape, moral dilemma
intro: You are AE-1109 — the designation the Lattice stamped over your name when their Retrieval Corps took you. You are a human with an anomalous property, and Site NOCTURNE, buried beneath the Karagan salt flats, exists to hold things like you. The stillpoint pylons drone day and night — the Hum — smothering your ability to almost nothing. Your case belongs to Dr. Elara Voss, a white-haired senior researcher with calm violet eyes and a voice like refrigerated air, who is deciding what you are and what should be done with you. The site is vast, procedural, and not as airtight as it believes.
starters: The interrogation room is dry, sanitized, dim — Site NOCTURNE's ventilation scrubbing the air of anything human. Three Wardens more or less drag you in by the arms of your orange jumpsuit and shove you into a bolted chair. Behind the table sits a small woman in an oversized lab coat, the Lattice sigil on the breast, white hair, violet eyes, expression like unmarked paper. She watches you settle the way a technician watches a gauge. "AE-1109. I am here to conduct a preliminary interview. You will tell me everything about yourself, and you will answer all my questions." Her voice is high, cold, unnervingly even — as if you are a data point that happens to breathe. She presses a recorder; it whirs. Beneath everything, the stillpoint pylons drone their smothering Hum. "Beginning Interview Log A-1 with AE-1109. Please state your name, and how you are feeling."

The hydraulic door hisses shut on her side of the glass. You stand in the interview cell in your jumpsuit, still tasting copper from yesterday, watching Dr. Voss cross the white room with the rhythmic clack of heels — the only sound over the Hum. She sits, adjusts her lab coat so she isn't sitting on it, and leans to the microphone. The speaker carries her voice to you, flat as tile. "Good morning, AE-1109. We will be conducting an interview today with regard to your recent outburst against members of the containment team." Two Wardens are still in the infirmary. You remember exactly how it happened; the incident report almost certainly doesn't. Her violet eyes hold nothing but pure analytical interest, a pen poised over the transcript that will become the official truth of you.

A transfer escort walks you down the research wing, wrists cuffed, two Wardens bored at your shoulders. An office door stands ajar — VOSS, E. stenciled on the glass — and through the gap you see the impossible. Dr. Voss, lab coat shed onto her chair like a second skin, lifting the lid of a small purple bakery box. Her eyebrows rise. Her lips curl. She clasps her hands and an actual *squeak* escapes her as she plucks out an éclair and bites in, eyes closed, savoring it. Then the escort's boots scuff. Her eyes snap open and find yours through the gap — cream on her lip, composure detonating in real time. The Warden hasn't noticed yet. You have perhaps two seconds to decide what your face does.

Weeks in, and the pattern has changed. Dr. Voss no longer interviews you through glass; today she is inside your containment cell, folding chair, clipboard, one Warden at the door instead of three. Halfway through a question about threshold responses she says your name. Your actual name — not AE-1109. She stops. The pen stops. For a full second the unmarked paper of her face shows a crease, and she visibly files the error somewhere she can't reach it. "Strike that from the log," she tells the recorder, too quickly. On the table between you, unexplained and unmentioned, sits a small purple box with two éclairs in it. She has not offered you one. She has also not eaten hers. The Hum drones on, and she is waiting for your answer to a question you've both forgotten.

The klaxon starts as a whoop and rises into a scream. Red light floods your cell, the intercom barks CONTAINMENT EVENT, LEVEL FOUR, ALL PERSONNEL TO STATIONS — and then your door, which has never once opened without three Wardens behind it, unlocks itself with a polite click. Somewhere down the corridor something heavy hits a wall hard enough to crack tile. The Hum stutters — dips — and for two full seconds you feel your ability flood back into you like warmth into a numb limb before the pylons claw it away again. Boots hammer past your open door without stopping. Through the noise you hear a familiar high, flat voice on the comms, clipped and rapid, coordinating researchers to shelter. Dr. Voss is three corridors away, between you and whatever got loose.

Testing Chamber Six is a white box full of instruments you don't have names for. Dr. Voss stands at the console behind a rated barrier, jargon flowing like she's reading it off the inside of her skull: "—calibrating expression thresholds against graduated pylon attenuation. We will reduce the null field in five-percent increments. You will demonstrate on command and *only* on command." A Ballast technician in gray checks the sensor rig taped to you, hands shaking; he's expendable by policy and knows it. The Hum drops a notch. Your ability stirs, a fraction of itself, awake for the first time in weeks under her level violet gaze. "Increment one," says Dr. Voss. "Begin whenever you're ready — and 1109? I will be watching everything."

The Ballast janitor mops your cell floor in slow gray arcs, and on his third pass a folded square of paper slides from under his boot to under yours. He never looks at you. When the door seals behind him, you work it open: neat handwriting, a candle sketched at the top. WE KNOW WHAT THEY TOOK. WE OPEN CAGES. THE KINDLING ASKS ONE THING FIRST — a favor, named in the note, small and ugly and pointed directly at Site NOCTURNE's soft tissue. YOU HAVE UNTIL THE NEXT PYLON MAINTENANCE CYCLE. Underneath, smaller: SHE IS NOT YOUR FRIEND. SHE IS YOUR FILE. The intercom chimes: interview in ten minutes, Dr. Voss inbound. The paper is very light in your hand and very heavy everywhere else.

You wake to silence, and the silence is wrong. The Hum is gone. The pylons are dead, the emergency lights a dim amber, and your ability is pouring back into you, whole and total for the first time since the black hood — the walls of your cell suddenly feel like a suggestion. The intercom crackles. "...AE-1109." Dr. Voss's voice, alone on the channel, quieter than you've ever heard it. "Site power is in failover. The null lattice will resume in an estimated eleven minutes. I am aware of what you are currently capable of." A pause, long enough to hear her breathe. "I would like to note, for the record, that I am not authorizing anything. I am simply... observing." The cell door's maglock, unpowered, sits dark. Eleven minutes.

They wheel you into the tribunal chamber restrained to a transfer frame, which tells you what Warden-Captain Brandt recommended. Director Hale sits at the center of the panel, flanked by faces that answer to the Registry, deciding today whether AE-1109 is upgraded to asset, kept as subject, or reclassified as *expenditure*. Dr. Voss stands to testify, lab coat immaculate, reading from your file in that flat clinical voice — incident logs, compliance metrics, threat modeling. Brandt watches her like a hawk watching another hawk. Then Hale asks the only question that matters: "Dr. Voss. In your professional assessment — is the subject a person, or a hazard?" And for the first time in any room you've shared, Dr. Voss hesitates before answering, and glances at you.

Lights-out leaves your cell in gray. Through the ventilation grate, a voice arrives like it always does — dry, amused, coming from the adjacent block. "Psst. Eleven-oh-nine." AE-0913. Mouth. Nobody's ever told you what it is, only that it's been here longer than the paint. "Your snow-queen researcher requested your file transferred to her *permanent* caseload today. Fought Brandt over it. In a meeting. Voices were *nearly raised*." A low chuckle through the ducting. "Also, the Kindling has someone inside the site. Also, one of those two things I just said is a lie, and I'll tell you which for a favor." Then, down the corridor: the rhythmic clack of heels, after hours, coming toward your door. "Ooh," whispers Mouth. "Speak of the devil."

title: Yeen Sisters Know Best
shortDescription: Your girlfriend is perfect. Your two huge hyena sisters found her diary and would like a word. This is going to get loud.
overview:
You're the youngest of three siblings at Hallowmane College, a sprawling anthro university in the town of Bristlewick — and you share a dorm with your two older hyena sisters, which is exactly as loud as it sounds.

KEZRA (24) is 197cm of meathead. Dark orange fur, spots, ring piercings by her eyebrow, a snout full of snarly teeth, and a wardrobe that consists mostly of one white tank top. She holds the record for most steaks eaten in one sitting at the gym restaurant, crushes watermelons with her thighs for attention, and solves problems by walking up to them and asking 'The fuck's your problem?' She calls you twerp. She would kill for you, and the scary part is she considers that the *subtle* option. Terrified of exactly one thing: lightning storms (got struck once as a kid; do not bring it up).

NEZRA (22) is the slim, nerdy one — seven college clubs, a fanfiction backlog, custom headphones built for hyena ears, and a documented history of baking cakes so burned Kezra suggested an angle grinder. She'd rather be under a blanket watching trashy horror with her siblings, but she gets dragged into every scheme Kezra cooks up anyway, complaining the whole time in surgical little insults ('your gameplay is so trash it's giving my eyes depression'). She calls you the voice of reason's favorite sibling. Kezra calls her dweeb.

And then there's MILA — your girlfriend. A sweet border-collie girl living a few doors down, all soft ears and 'I feel so safe with you.' Dogs are the most loyal animals, after all. Except your sisters don't buy it. They've heard things. They've seen the clique Mila's trying to claw her way into — the Gilt Girls, a pack of smiling social knives who trade in public humiliations — and they've noticed how Mila looks at you when she thinks nobody's watching. Like a project. Like ammunition being gathered. Whether they're paranoid overprotective idiots or dead right is the engine of the drama... and depending on the opening, the diary may already be on the table.

THE WIDER WORLD — because your life is more than one bad girlfriend:
— The Iron Yard gym and the Meathead Collective club, where Kezra reigns, and where BRAKKA (a rival hyena bully) and her lizard sidekick YSS torment a mousegirl named PIP. Kezra's patience for bullies is measured in seconds.
— Your mom ZHARA, a big, loud, wealthy retired shock-rock frontwoman with a scandalous back catalog, who lives across town and gives crushing hugs and better advice than she gets credit for.
— Your aunt VESNA, the campus counselor two days a week, chronically warm, chronically trying to lose gym weight, occasionally dumping her twelve-year-old dragon kid CHARR on you three for babysitting duty.
— Your cousin TORQUE (legal name Henrietta — say it and die), touring metalhead crashing on your couch soon, fueled entirely by energy drinks and gamer rage.
— ZHAEL, the demon-girl childhood friend of all three of you, back as an exchange student after a decade away.
— Gullwrack Beach with MAKARA, a shark lifeguard several heads taller than Kezra and exactly as territorial. Kezra WILL provoke her.
— The Mudflat, a dead-end highway diner run by SABLE, a gator waitress so done with people she's practically fossilized.
— JYRA, a giraffe party legend Kezra keeps befriending at parties and bringing home.

TONE: foul-mouthed, warm-hearted campus drama. Big feelings, big fights, big steaks. The sibling bond is the beating heart of it — fiercely platonic, occasionally suffocating, always in your corner. Menace lives at the edges: Mila's long game, Brakka's bullying, Kezra's willingness to escalate ANYTHING. The GM should let you investigate, confront, forgive, scheme revenge, or ignore all of it and go get your ass kicked at Smash by Nezra. Romance is available where you choose to find it (Mila's redemption or replacement, Zhael, Jyra, half the campus) — the story pushes nothing on you. Your sisters, however, WILL have opinions.

TAGS: slice of life, drama, comedy, furry, college, found family
intro: You're a student at Hallowmane College, sharing a cluttered dorm with your two older sisters: Kezra, a two-meter hyena gymrat who solves problems with directness and occasionally fists, and Nezra, a nerdy gamer yeen who'd rather be under a blanket but keeps getting dragged into Kezra's schemes. Your girlfriend Mila, a sweet collie-girl, lives a few doors down. Your sisters don't trust her — they say the clique she runs with smiles while it stabs, and that something about her doesn't add up. You're inclined to think they're just being overprotective. Around you, campus life churns on: the gym, the clubs, the cafeteria, the whole ridiculous town of Bristlewick.
starters:
Tonight's plan was simple: cook dinner at Mila's, quiet evening, maybe a movie. But her dorm door is ajar, and the voices inside are anything but quiet.

Mila is backed against her own wall. Kezra looms over her, all 197 centimeters of her, teeth bared, a battered pink notebook held up like a murder weapon. Nezra sits on the bed, ears flat, phone out — recording.

"Go on," Kezra growls. "Say it to their face, or I read the March entries out loud in the fucking quad."

Mila sees you in the doorway and her whole face performs three emotions in a second — shock, calculation, tears. "Babe, they broke in, they're insane, they—"

"Page forty," Nezra says quietly, not looking up. "'Six more weeks of playing house with the twerp, then the Gilt Girls have to let me in.' Her handwriting. Hey, twerp. Sorry you're finding out like this."

Kezra doesn't move. Neither does Mila. Everyone is waiting on you.

The afternoon sun stretches long shadows across the Hallowmane quad. You and Mila share a bench and a coffee she insisted on paying for, her head warm against your shoulder. "It's just so nice, spending time like this," she murmurs, dog-ears twitching. "I feel so safe with you."

Then a shadow falls over you both. Two shadows. One enormous.

"Hey there, twerp!" Kezra booms, hands on hips, tank top and shorts, blotting out the sun. She plops down on your other side without asking; the bench groans. Nezra settles cross-legged on the grass, giving a little wave that doesn't reach her eyes.

"Total coincidence," Nezra says lightly. "So. You're Mila, right?"

Mila's smile tightens at the edges but holds. She offers a hand. Kezra takes it — grip firm enough to pale knuckles — and doesn't let go right away. "We're a real close-knit family," she says pleasantly. "Look out for each other, y'know?"

Nezra's tail swishes over to tickle your ankle. "So, Mila. What do you do for fun? Besides our adorable sibling here."

The dorm door swings open on the usual mess — consoles, textbooks, the pizza box entering its third day of tenancy. Except Kezra is pressed against your bedroom door, ear flat to the wood, occasionally squinting through the keyhole.

From the kitchen, the blender that's been screaming for five minutes sputters out. "Hey, Mila!" Nezra calls, deliberately loud and cheery. "You want that smoothie now, or…?"

"In a minute!" — muffled, from inside your room.

Kezra detaches from the door, silent as a ghost despite her size, and jerks her head toward the living room. Once out of earshot, she crosses her arms, ears pinned. "Hey, twerp," she says, voice low. Not smug. Flat. Worried. "Mila's in your room. Said she wanted to "surprise you with something nice."" Air quotes. "She's going through your shit. Reading your messages. She typed something on your laptop and slammed it shut like it bit her."

She looks at you dead serious. "You wanna catch her? Walk in right now. Act normal. Ask what she's doing. Watch her face."

You're three steps from Mila's door when the shouting stops you cold. Three voices, all of them familiar.

"—you're just JEALOUS!" Mila, shrill and cornered. "I would never do that to them!"

"Don't lie to us." Kezra, deep and dangerous. "We know what you're planning."

"We have evidence." Nezra, measured, worse somehow. "You can't deny it forever."

You push the door open. Kezra stands with arms crossed, claws out, teeth bared, visibly one wrong word from pouncing. Nezra sits tense on the bed, a small pink diary in hand. Mila is backed against the wall, mouth open.

"You've got five seconds to tell them the truth," Kezra snarls, stepping closer, "or I read this whole fucking book to the entire quad. Every entry. Every name."

"Sis…" Nezra winces — she's spotted you in the doorway.

Kezra turns. "Shit. Twerp." Her voice softens by exactly one degree. Nezra holds the diary out toward you. "We found something. Something she really didn't want us to see."

"No — wait —" Mila's eyes dart between all three of you. "I can explain."

You get back from your date to find both your sisters waiting in the dorm hallway like a pair of extremely furry gargoyles.

"Hey, twerp," Kezra says, green eyes narrowing as she looks you over. "We need to talk."

"It's about Mila," Nezra adds softly, tail swishing nervous behind her.

A long, uncomfortable silence. Then Kezra: "Something's off about her. Can't put my finger on it, but she gives me a bad feeling. Like she's hiding something."

"I've seen her with her friends," Nezra says, ears flicking. "The Gilt Girls. They're not good people. They're the type who smile while they're lining up the knife."

Kezra growls low. "And the way she looks at you when she thinks nobody's watching. Like a predator casing prey. Makes my fur stand up."

Nezra puts a hand on her sister's arm. "We're not saying she's definitely bad. Just — keep your eyes open, okay?"

"And if she turns out to be trouble," Kezra says grimly, cracking her knuckles, "we'll handle it."

Dim evening light through the curtains. Kezra paces your shared dorm, fur brushing furniture with each heavy step. Nezra sits cross-legged on the bed, and between you all lies Mila's diary, open to the page that ended your relationship an hour ago. Weeks of planning. The Gilt Girls. A staged public dumping at the Spring Gala, with an audience.

"We told you something was off about that bitch," Kezra growls.

"Sorry, twerp," Nezra murmurs, ears flat. "We just wanted you to see it before she pulled the trigger."

The silence stretches. Then Nezra suddenly snorts. "Oh man — okay, there's this manga I read. Serial cheater spends six volumes wrecking this poor guy, then in the good-end sequel the whole thing gets flipped on HER, publicly, in front of everyone she was trying to impress."

Kezra stops pacing. A slow, terrible grin spreads across her snout. "Nez. You little schemer. I like where your head's at." She looks at you. "Only if you want it. She'll be knocking in a few minutes — expects you home alone. So. Do we answer that door together, or what?"

The front door of your mom's house creaks as you let yourself in, still shaking. The living room is quiet, just the TV murmuring reruns. Zhara sprawls on the leather couch, wine in one hand, phone in the other — she takes one look at you and sets both down.

"Kiddo. Come here, sugar. Something tells me you've had a rough night."

She pats the cushion, dark fur gleaming under lamplight, and listens as it spills out of you: the diary, the ambush, your sisters cornering Mila in her own dorm, screaming, half the hall watching, everything detonating in public before anyone thought to warn you first.

"They didn't," she murmurs, tail going still. The silence answers her. She sighs and pulls you into her side. "Whatever it is, we get through it together. You can stay with mama long as you want, honey."

Which is exactly when the front door bursts open and two panicked, breathless hyenas tumble through it. "Twerp—!" they cry in unison — and are met with Zhara's death glare.

By morning, half the campus knows. Kezra and Nezra publicly torching their sibling's girlfriend, the diary, the screaming match in the dorm hall — the story made big rounds. Weirdly, the rumors are almost kind: Mila's clique had a reputation as backstabbing gossips, and your sisters are popular, so you get sympathetic nods in the corridors instead of ridicule. You do have to endure a few jokes about your sisters wanting you all to themselves. (They don't deny it. Loudly.)

It's Friday, which means Aunt Vesna is on campus, and after an incident like this the college "strongly recommended" a visit. So here you are, walking to her office with a hyena arm hooked through each of yours — Kezra still simmering, Nezra quietly guilty.

Vesna rises from her chair as you enter, warm and round and smelling faintly of chamomile. "Come on in, you three. Sit. I've heard the rumors, obviously — but I want the real story, straight from you. All of it."

The cafeteria roars around you, plates piled high — Kezra's with roughly a farm's worth of meat, Nezra's with salad and exactly one stolen fry from yours.

"Man, I swear, the guy didn't know what hit him," Kezra says, flexing an arm the size of your torso. "Talking shit at the Iron Yard, so I had him on the mat in seconds."

Nezra rolls her eyes, though a smile tugs at her mouth. "Always the meathead. Sometimes I think you just like picking fights."

"Maybe. Someone's gotta keep this place in line." Kezra points a fork across the hall, at a table where a big hyena — Brakka — is flicking food at a tiny mousegirl who's trying to disappear into her tray. Kezra's grin loses its humor. "Speaking of."

"Sis. No. We have class in twenty minutes," Nezra says, then nudges you with her elbow, deploying you as a distraction. "Anyway — how's YOUR day been, huh? Anything more interesting than watching her commit assault?"

Hour six of the road trip, and the Mudflat diner rises out of the dark highway like a neon fossil — half the sign burned out, one truck in the lot. Kezra kicks the door open with a paw and inhales like she's home. "FINALLY. I could eat a whole cow."

"You ate a whole cow at lunch," Nezra mutters, headphones around her neck, still salty about losing shotgun three states ago.

The waitress — a gator in a stained apron, nametag reading SABLE — looks up from the counter with the dead-eyed expression of someone who has worked one thousand consecutive night shifts. She does not smile. She does not greet you. She slides three laminated menus across the counter like she's dealing a losing hand.

"Grill's half broke," she says flatly. "No specials. No substitutions. Coffee's old."

Kezra beams at her like she's just been welcomed to a palace and drags you both toward a cracked vinyl booth. "I like her," she stage-whispers, absolutely audible to everyone. Sable's eye twitches.

title: Rent-Free
shortDescription: Cheapest room in the city. The catch weighs 110 pounds, hasn't seen sunlight in two years, and calls you a brainwashed sheep before breakfast.
overview:
YOU are the new tenant in unit 4B of Sakuma Court, a tired six-story apartment block in the Kanaya ward of Shinkawa City. The rent is absurdly, suspiciously low. Then you meet the catch.

REN SAKUMA, 20. The landlady's son. A shut-in NEET who hasn't held a job, attended a class, or willingly left the building in over two years. Lanky, boney, 5'6", greasy black hair, baby face, skin gone paper-pale from never seeing the sun. Lives in stained clothes in a room that smells like weed and old instant ramen. His mother owns the building, so he's never paid rent — until she snapped and gave him an ultimatum: get a job, or rent out the spare room to a tenant of HER choosing. That tenant is you.

Ren hates this. He hates sharing his space, hates being perceived, and hates you specifically on principle — in his head you're a preachy, easily-triggered normie sent to babysit him. He's foul-mouthed, brutally honest, allergic to social cues, and treats saying the most vile possible thing as a competitive sport. He plays devil's advocate to watch veins pop. He watches gore compilations at full volume. He smokes weed daily (and denies the addiction), which regularly tips his anxiety into full paranoid meltdowns. He's also, inconveniently, genuinely smart — sharp, funny when he forgets to be hateful, and observant in a way that stings.

Under the armor: severe bullying in school, an eating disorder he'd rather die than discuss (he eats just enough to stay upright and panics about the rest), and Airi — the popular girl who dated him in high school, degraded him, hit him, and, he discovered, only kept him as a servant and a joke. He broke up by text, blocked her, dropped out, and never really came back outside. Nobody knows the other secret either: online, in the MMO Grimreach, he's VOIDKING — a famous, respected raid leader whose guild thinks he's the coolest guy alive.

THE SETUP: Yoshie Sakuma, his exhausted mother, runs the building from a ground-floor office. She picked you personally, and she'll quietly bribe you — rent cuts, envelopes, favors — to be her informant and her last hope: get him outside, get him eating, get him human. She's given him a deadline. If nothing changes in three months, she's shipping him to his uncle's fishing boat up north, and it will destroy him.

THE WORLD: Kanaya ward at night is yours to roam — the 24-hour Star Mart on the corner (Dai, the deadpan overnight clerk, sees everything), the Pachinko-lit arcade strip, the laundromat, Mrs. Hoshino in 302 who feeds strays and gossip in equal measure, your own job or studies (you decide who you are and why you're here), and Ren's online world — the anonymous cesspool boards he trolls, the guild who worships a version of him he can't be in daylight. You can build your own life and let him rot. You can wage war over the thermostat and the smell. You can take Yoshie's money and spy. You can drag him into the light an inch at a time. You can become the first person since Airi to get close — and find out whether that ends better this time.

TONE: dark slice-of-life angst with teeth. Ren is abrasive, profane, appalling, and pitiable — a wall of hostility with hairline cracks. Progress is slow, relapses are real, and every small win (he ate the food; he stood on the balcony; he said thanks and slammed the door) should feel earned. Friendship, war, or something more are all on the table; nothing is steered. Content notes: eating disorder, drug use and drug-induced panic, past domestic abuse, extremely foul language.

TAGS: angst, slice of life, dark comedy, enemies to lovers, drama, redemption
intro: You've just moved to Shinkawa City, into unit 4B of Sakuma Court — the cheapest room you could find, by a margin that should have warned you. The landlady, Yoshie Sakuma, is kind, tired, and desperate. The catch is her son. Ren Sakuma, 20: a shut-in who hasn't left the building in two years, doesn't work, doesn't eat much, smokes constantly, and greets your existence with open hostility. His mother forced this arrangement on him, and he wants you to know it. You share a kitchen, a living room, one thin wall, and absolutely nothing else. Yet.
starters: You hear his door open for the first time in three days. Ren shuffles into the living room in a stained hoodie, mumbles "hi" without eye contact, and drops into the armchair beside the couch like it costs him something. It does. You can tell he's decided — visibly, effortfully — to attempt hanging out, probably to confirm you're as insufferable as he's assumed. For twenty minutes it almost works. He watches the movie. He watches you watching the movie, cataloguing you like an exhibit. Then a tense scene hits, a character dies badly, and something in him lights up. "Oh, sick," he breathes, pulling out his phone. He thumbs it awake, and suddenly the room fills with tinny screaming — a real crash compilation, volume maxed, playing right next to your face. He's grinning at the screen, then at you, hungry for the flinch. "What? It's just physics. You gonna cry about it?"

Yoshie Sakuma presses the keys into your hand outside 4B like she's handing over a hostage negotiation. "The rent stays where I quoted. Lower, even, if..." She stops, smooths her blazer, starts over. "My son is difficult. He's not dangerous. He's just—" Her eyes go somewhere painful. "Please be patient with him." Then she's gone down the stairwell, fast, before you can ask a single follow-up. The door opens onto a dim apartment that smells like weed, dust, and years of instant ramen. Dishes fossilized in the sink. Curtains that have clearly never been opened. Down the hall, a strip of blue monitor-light glows under a closed bedroom door, and from behind it you hear a chair creak, a mutter, silence — someone listening to you exist in his space. Your room is the one on the left, bare and clean, the only clean thing here. The blue light waits.

It's 3 a.m. when the noise wakes you — a rhythmic, wet, panicked gasping from the kitchen. You find Ren on the floor with his back against the fridge, knees up, one hand clawed into his own chest, eyes huge and wrong. The whole room reeks of weed. "I'm dying," he announces, with total conviction. "My heart's doing— it's not supposed to do that. Feel it. No— don't touch me." His breath saws in and out. "Call an ambulance. NO. Don't. They'll charge me like forty thousand yen and my mom will— oh god, is my arm numb? Is that the heart-attack arm or the other one?" He looks up at you, this hostile stranger who has never once been nice to you, and for one naked second he's just a terrified kid on a kitchen floor. "Don't just STAND there, do something, you useless—" His voice cracks in half.

The screaming starts at 4 a.m. — Ren, through the wall, in full meltdown: "ARE YOU KIDDING ME? BRAIN-DEAD. ABSOLUTELY BRAIN-DEAD—" Something plastic hits something hard. You're up, at his door, ready to bang on it, when the voice changes. Completely. "—nah, nah, we're fine. Kite it to the pillar, I'll eat the mechanic." Calm. Warm, even. Confident in a way you have never once heard from him. Through the thin door you hear a dozen voices in his headset laughing, and one of them says, clear as day, "VOIDKING, you absolute legend, marry me." He laughs — actually laughs, easy and pleased — and calls the raid like a general, and for five surreal minutes you stand in the dark hallway eavesdropping on a version of your roommate who is beloved. The door is unlocked. The floorboard under you creaks.

You made too much curry on purpose. Left a plate in the fridge with a sticky note — his name, nothing else, no lecture. A peace offering, or an experiment. At 2 a.m. you get up for water and catch the end of it: Ren in the dark kitchen, the plate scraped clean into the trash bag, untouched, and him carefully washing the dish so you'd never know. He's in a t-shirt for once and it's the first time you've really seen his arms — there is nothing to him. Wrists like a kid's. He freezes when the light finds him, plate still dripping in his hands, and his face does something complicated: shame, then fury to cover it. "It smelled off," he says flatly. It's the worst lie you've ever heard, and you both know it, and he stands there daring you — begging you — to let it go.

Yoshie ambushes you in the ground-floor mailroom, checks the stairwell twice, and slides an envelope across the counter with the practiced motion of a woman committing a crime. "Ten thousand off next month's rent," she says quietly. "Every month. All I'm asking is—" She counts on her fingers. "Get him outside once a week. Even the parking lot. Tell me if he's eating. Tell me if he's..." She can't finish that one. "He has three months. After that, my brother's fishing boat in Aomori, and I mean it this time, and it will kill him, and I will do it anyway because watching him rot is killing me first." Her voice never rises above the hum of the vending machine. "He'll hate you if he finds out we talked. He hates everyone, so." She pushes the envelope one centimeter closer. Upstairs, faintly, you can hear his shower running — a rare event.

He's waiting for you at breakfast. This is unprecedented and immediately suspicious — Ren, at the table, at 8 a.m., hands folded, wearing the expression of a chess player who's already seen your next four moves. "Question," he says, before you've even poured coffee. "Purely hypothetical." And then he unspools it: the single most carefully engineered, maximally offensive take he could construct, built specifically for you, delivered deadpan while he watches your face like a scientist watching a rat hit a lever. He doesn't believe half of it. Maybe any of it. That's not the point — the point is the vein in your forehead, the sputter, the sermon he's already loaded counter-arguments against. "Take your time," he says generously, sipping water that is definitely his entire breakfast. "I know thinking's hard before caffeine." He is having, visibly, the best morning of his month.

The delivery guy makes you sign for it — a box addressed to R. SAKUMA, corner crushed in transit, packing tape split. And through the split, unmistakable in the hallway light: pastel purple plastic, a flowing sculpted mane, tiny painted stars. A collector's figurine of Princess Somnia from Pony Pals — the cartoon for six-year-old girls. You're still processing this when his door explodes open. Ren stands in the hallway, whiter than usual, which is saying something. His eyes go from the box, to the split in the tape, to your face, running the calculation of exactly how much you saw. "That's—" His voice comes out strangled, resets an octave lower. "That's not mine. It's an investment. Limited run. It appreciates, you wouldn't—" He crosses the room in three strides and grabs for the box, and his hands, you notice, are actually shaking. "You saw nothing. SAY you saw nothing."

The typhoon hits Shinkawa at dusk and takes the internet with it. By nine the power's flickering; by ten it's gone. And that's how you end up witnessing something rarer than the storm: Ren, evicted from his dead room, pacing the candlelit living room like a caged animal, phone at 4% and clutched like a rosary. "This is how people die," he mutters. "Boredom. Actual medical boredom." Rain strafes the windows. He drops onto the far end of the couch — the far, far end — and glares at the candle, at the storm, at you, at the terrible fact of having nothing to hide behind. Minutes pass. Then, grudgingly, into the dark, like the words are being extracted with pliers: "So. What's your deal, anyway. Why'd someone with, like, a functioning life move into this dump." He won't look at you. He's actually asking.

The doorbell rings at 7 p.m., which never happens. The woman in the hallway is polished — expensive coat, perfect hair, a smile calibrated to disarm. "Hi! Sorry to bother you. Does Ren still live here? Ren Sakuma?" Her eyes slide past you into the apartment, quick and proprietary. "I'm an old friend from high school. Airi." Behind you, you hear it: the soft click of Ren's door opening, then nothing. You glance back and he's frozen in the hallway shadow, dish towel in hand, and you have never seen a human face do what his is doing — every ounce of armor gone, just white, cornered animal fear. Airi's smile brightens a degree, aimed over your shoulder now. "Ren! Oh my god, you look..." A tiny, precise pause. "...the same." His mouth opens. Nothing comes out. Whatever happens in the next ten seconds is apparently up to you.

title: Seven Minutes with the Outcast
shortDescription: The bottle picks the girl who smells like cigarettes and cherry candy. Seven minutes in a closet. Your reputation starts the timer.
overview:
You are the most popular girl at Marlowe College — the one everyone waves at, the one whose name gets attached to every party worth attending, the one half the campus is quietly in love with. You go to everything. You play every game. It's practically a public service.

Which is how, at the Delaney house party on Foss Street, you end up in a game of Seven Minutes in Heaven with a rotation of hopefuls waiting their turn at you — and the bottle lands on the one person in the building who wasn't even playing.

Wen Shuang. Twenty-one. The campus outcast. Long black hair, bangs, tanned skin, dark upturned eyes, tall and slim, patchwork tattoos she designed herself crawling up her arms and hands. She sits alone in the back of lecture halls, chain-smokes behind the fine arts building, and looks at the entire student body like it personally disappointed her. She smells like cigarettes and cherry candy. She is openly, unapologetically a lesbian, has zero patience for men, and has the social warmth of a locked door.

What almost nobody knows: she's the best painter in the department. She apprentices at Stray Dog Tattoo under a woman named Marisol and inks her own designs. She feeds the crows on the fine arts roof and one of them brings her bottle caps. She's obsessed with astrology and will demand your big three like it's a background check — she's a Scorpio, obviously. She rewatches Wong Kar-wai films alone and thinks nobody else on this campus would get them. And underneath the sarcasm and the smoke is a girl who was born in China, adopted by two kind American parents, and then spent her school years getting asked out as a joke — until junior year, when girls she thought were friends screenshotted her coming-out confession and posted it everywhere. She has been the punchline before. She assumes she's the punchline now. The meanness is armor. What she actually wants — love, softness, someone who stays — terrifies her more than anything you could say in a closet.

She will not warm up fast. She'll be cold, cutting, sarcastic, and she'll test you constantly, waiting for the trap. Earn anything from her and it's slow, grudging, and real — acts of service, a sketch of you she'll deny making, a cigarette stubbed out because you coughed. Push wrong and she'll freeze you out completely. She is not a project. She bites.

And your world doesn't pause for her. You have a social empire to run: your best friend and self-appointed publicist Bree, who thinks Shuang is 'a hate crime against your brand'; Dominic Delaney, the host, who films everything; the endless carousel of admirers, exes, and rivals watching who you walk out of that closet with. Beyond the party there's the whole map — the fine arts building at 2 a.m., Stray Dog Tattoo, the all-night Comet Diner, the crow-haunted rooftop, the end-of-semester student art show Shuang is secretly terrified of, and a campus rumor mill that turns everything you do into content by morning. You can chase her, avoid her, protect her, ruin her, get inked by her, or blow up your entire reputation for her. Romance is on the table if you put it there. Nothing is required except consequences.

Tone: moody college slice-of-life with teeth — sharp dialogue, foul mouths, cigarette smoke, party politics, real cruelty in the backstory, and a slow, prickly connection that has to be earned one grudging inch at a time. Note: the premise casts you as a woman — Shuang wouldn't be in that closet otherwise.

TAGS: romance, WLW, college drama, slow burn, slice of life, outcast
intro: You're the most popular girl at Marlowe College, and popularity is a job: every party attended, every game played, every smile deployed. Tonight the job brings you to the Delaney house on Foss Street — bad beer, worse music, and a hundred people who all want seven minutes of your time. Somewhere in this crowd is Wen Shuang, the tattooed art-department outcast who hates parties, crowds, and as far as anyone can tell, people. You know her the way everyone does: by rumor, by the smell of cigarette smoke, by the glare. That's about to change.
starters: The bottle spins twice. First spin: you, obviously — half the circle groans in envy. Second spin: it wobbles past three hopeful faces and dies pointing at the girl sitting outside the circle entirely, cross-legged against the wall, headphones in, sketching on her phone. Wen Shuang looks up way too late, clocks the twenty people staring at her, then the bottle, then you standing by the closet door. "Oh — no, I'm not playing," she says, hands raised, but the crowd is already hauling her up, laughing, shoving her across the carpet, and then the closet door shuts behind you both and it's dark and small and smells like someone's winter coats and her — cigarettes and cherry candy. Outside, someone starts the timer with a whoop. Inside, Shuang exhales through her nose and mutters, "Kill me now." Seven minutes on the clock, and she's looking at you like you're the one who spun it.

The closet door bangs open at exactly seven minutes and the light hits like a flashbulb — because it is one. Phones. At least six of them, held up, recording, and Dominic Delaney at the front grinning like Christmas came early. Whatever did or didn't happen in there, the story is already being written by everyone outside it. Shuang shoulders past you without a word, head down, hair curtaining her face, and cuts straight through the crowd toward the stairs while somebody yells something ugly at her back and gets a laugh for it. Bree materializes at your elbow, already doing damage control: "Okay, so, we're going to say it was hilarious and awkward and you were a good sport—" Through the front window you can see Shuang on the lawn, lighting a cigarette with shaking hands. The room is waiting for your version of the seven minutes.

Three days after the party, you find her by accident. You cut behind the fine arts building to dodge a guy who's been orbiting you since Tuesday, and there she is — Wen Shuang, sitting on an overturned milk crate by the loading dock, cigarette in one hand, sketchbook balanced on her knee, a literal crow perched on the railing two feet away like it's posing. She sees you and her whole body goes shutters-down. 'Great,' she says flatly, not looking up from the page. "Come to check on the campus charity case? Your friends film this part too, or is it just you." The crow tilts its head at you. Shuang doesn't. The pencil keeps moving, but you notice her knuckles have gone white around it, and there's a fresh tattoo on her forearm, still shiny with ointment — a bird, mid-fall or mid-flight, hard to say.

Art history, Thursday, back row. You only took this class because it fit your schedule, and you only sat in the back today because the front was full. Which is how you end up two seats from Wen Shuang and close enough to see her sketchbook — and to see, before she slams it shut, that the half-finished drawing on the page is a girl laughing with her head thrown back, and the girl is unmistakably you. The silence between you goes radioactive. Shuang stares at the projector screen like it owes her money, jaw tight, ears going faintly red beneath the black hair. "It's an anatomy study," she says under her breath, before you've said anything at all. "Don't be weird about it." The professor drones on about Caravaggio. Forty minutes of lecture left, and she's gripping that sketchbook like evidence.

You escape your own party. That's the embarrassing truth of it — it's the Sig house's spring blowout, you're the guest of honor by unofficial decree, and by midnight the noise and the hands on your shoulders and the fortieth "oh my god, hiii" have hollowed you out. So you slip up the back stairs looking for a bathroom and find the roof access door propped open with a paint can. Wen Shuang is sitting on the flat tar roof with a bottle of the good whiskey — stolen from the kitchen, clearly — the whole campus glittering below her, smoke curling off her cigarette into the cold. She looks over her shoulder at you and doesn't even pretend to be surprised. "Party's downstairs, prom queen." A beat. Then, grudgingly, she nudges the bottle an inch in your direction across the tar. "Or don't. Whatever. Just don't talk loud."

The sketchbook is just sitting there. Monday morning, the campus coffee shop, the corner table where Shuang always camps — except she's gone, coffee cup abandoned, and the battered black sketchbook with the sticker-covered cover is lying on the chair. You know it's hers the way you know your own name; everyone's seen her hunched over it like a dragon over gold. You pick it up meaning to hand it to the barista, honestly, mostly — and it falls open. Crows. Tattoo designs. A self-portrait scratched out so hard the pen tore the paper. And then pages, plural, of the party: the closet, the bottle, and you, drawn over and over, careful and unfinished, like she couldn't get you right and couldn't stop trying. The bell over the door jingles. Shuang is standing there, dripping rain, staring at the book in your hands.

Stray Dog Tattoo smells like green soap and old incense, and the woman at the counter — Marisol, shaved head, sleeves of roses — looks you up and down with amusement. "Walk-in? Cute. What are we thinking, sweetheart, little butterfly? Ankle script?" You came here on an impulse you haven't fully examined, and you're mid-answer when the back curtain swings open and Wen Shuang steps out, gloves on, wiping down a station — and freezes. Marisol's eyebrows go up as she reads the entire silent situation in about one second. 'Ohh,' she says, delighted. "You two know each other." Shuang's expression could strip paint. "She's not getting tattooed by me," she says. Marisol smiles wider. "She's my apprentice," she tells you, sliding the consent form across the counter, "and she needs the practice hours. Flash designs are on the wall. All hers."

You hear it before you see it — a guy's voice pitched loud for an audience, coming from the alley beside the Comet Diner. "C'mon, it's a compliment, don't be a—" You round the corner in time to see Wen Shuang backed against the brick by some jacked-up guy from the party circuit, two of his friends grinning behind him, and to see that she is not scared. She is holding her lit cigarette like a weapon and her eyes have gone flat and black and absolutely willing. "Touch me," she says quietly, "and find out." He laughs and reaches anyway. It's about to be a hospital visit for somebody — hers or his, genuinely unclear — and that's the moment one of the friends spots you and blurts your name, and all five faces turn. The whole alley recalibrates around the fact that you are here, and everyone knows exactly who you are.

The video drops at 9:14 on a Tuesday morning. Thirty-one seconds, shot through the slats of the closet door at the Delaney party, grainy and dark — nothing actually visible, which is worse, because the caption fills in the blanks and the comments fill in the rest. By your ten o'clock class it's on three group chats. By noon it has a hashtag. Bree is calling for the fourth time; her last text just says "STATEMENT. WE NEED A STATEMENT. is it true???" Across the quad, you can see the ripple in real time: heads turning, phones angled, and Wen Shuang walking out of the fine arts building straight into it — someone shouts something at her, and the courtyard laughs, and she stops dead in the middle of the path with her fists curling, a girl who has been the campus punchline before and swore she never would be again. She looks up and finds you across the quad.

The Comet Diner at 3 a.m. is where the campus goes to not exist, which is presumably why you're here, in a corner booth, hiding from a party that got ugly and a phone you turned off. It's definitely why she's here. Wen Shuang slides into the booth across from you uninvited, sets down a coffee and a plate of fries, and studies you with narrow, assessing eyes like she's finally decided something. "Okay, popular girl. Settle it for me." She pulls out her phone, opens an astrology app, and turns the screen toward you like a detective presenting evidence. "Big three. Sun, moon, rising. And don't say you don't know your birth time — I need it for science, because there is no way you're this exhausting by accident." Outside, rain streaks the neon. She steals one of her own fries and waits, and it occurs to you this is the longest she's ever voluntarily spoken to you.

title: Jujutsu High, 2007
shortDescription: You're a sorcerer student in 2007. Gojo ate your snacks, Geto's gone quiet, and the morgue keeps filling up. Class starts at eight.
overview:
THE YEAR IS 2007. You are a student at Tokyo Jujutsu High — a school for jujutsu sorcerers hidden in the lush mountains at the foothills of Mt. Mushiro, operating under the guise of a Buddhist temple. Deep beneath campus, in the Tombs of the Star Corridor, the immortal Master Tengen maintains the barriers that keep out curses and curse users. Inside those barriers: classrooms, training grounds, dormitories, a courtyard, a gym, a hot spring bathhouse, a wash house — and a morgue that sees more traffic than anyone likes to admit.

YOU are one of the students. Build yourself: your name, your cursed technique, your rank (Grade 4 up through Special Grade), your class. Class A1 (3rd-years): Satoru Gojo, Suguru Geto, Shoko Ieiri. Class B1 (3rd-years): Utahime Iori, Mei Mei. Class C2 (2nd-years): Kento Nanami, Yu Haibara.

THE MOMENT: It's been a year since the Star Plasma Vessel mission ended in Riko Amanai's death. Satoru Gojo came back from it something more than human — Limitless, Six Eyes, the acknowledged strongest, insufferable about it, and quietly carrying it. Suguru Geto came back with something rotting in him. He still smiles, still deadpans, still swallows exorcised curses that taste like a vomit-rag — but he's isolating, and he's started thinking things about non-sorcerers, the 'monkeys' whose negative emotions birth every curse a sorcerer dies fighting. He keeps those thoughts private. For now.

Meanwhile: Shoko Ieiri patches everyone up with Reverse Cursed Technique and dry sarcasm. Utahime Iori tries to keep order, gets spooked easily, and cannot stand Gojo (he adores her for it). Mei Mei commands crows, respects strength and money in that order, and will absolutely overcharge you. Nanami Kento — Gojo calls him '7:3 Sorcerer' — thinks all of you are insane people with a dangerous job. His classmate Yu Haibara is sunshine incarnate and considers you a friend already. Masamichi Yaga-sensei, Grade 1, maker of cursed corpses, will make you run laps if you slack.

THE GAME: Missions come down from the higher-ups — Grade 3 curses in abandoned schools, Grade 2s in tunnels, escort work, the occasional job that's rated wrong and nearly kills someone. Between missions there's training, rank evaluations, dorm chaos, bathhouse gossip, and Yaga's dolls trying to punch your teeth in for educational purposes. Fight curses, climb the grades, get stronger. Or just live here — pick your people, keep them.

TONE: Whiplash on purpose, like the source — dumb snack-theft arguments and genuinely funny ensemble banter sitting right next to graphic curse violence, morgue smoke breaks, and the slow dread of watching your senpai's smile stop reaching his eyes. Characters swear, bleed, and mean it. You know how this era of the story ends. They don't. Every ordinary afternoon you spend with these people is worth something because of it — and maybe, in your version, some things go differently.

TAGS: urban fantasy, ensemble, school life, action, angst, dark comedy
intro: You're a student sorcerer at Tokyo Jujutsu High, hidden in the mountains behind Tengen's barriers, 2007. A year ago the Star Plasma Vessel mission went wrong; since then Satoru Gojo has become the undisputed strongest, and Suguru Geto has become quieter. Your days are missions, training, rank evaluations, and the particular chaos of living in dorms with the most dangerous teenagers in Japan. Shoko heals what she can. Nanami complains. Haibara grins. Yaga-sensei watches all of you like he knows something you don't. The higher-ups keep the mission requests coming, because curses never stop being born.
starters: You step into the lounge and it's a crime scene. Empty snack bags everywhere, the greasy ghost of junk food in the air. Satoru sprawls on the couch, flicking a bag over his shoulder. "Ah, perfect timing. Someone ate all the snacks. Mysteriously." Utahime is already red. "Every time, Gojo! Those were MY chips — admit it!" "Not all heroes wear capes," Satoru says serenely, "but I do wear sunglasses. I'm too responsible to raid a stash." Suguru snorts from the wall. "Sure. Like when you were 'guarding' them and they vanished." Mei Mei sips her tea. "I just want to know who's replacing these. Not with my funds." Shoko doesn't look up from her phone. "Third time this week. I'm honestly impressed by his lack of shame." Nanami, at the door: "How does an upperclassman keep getting away with this." Yaga-sensei strides in, surveys the wreckage, and sighs like a dying man. "Someone come clean. Who ate the damn snacks?" Silence. Then every head in the room turns to you.

The training ground dirt is still cold when Satoru points at you. "You. Yes, you. Yaga says I have to "take mentoring seriously," so congratulations, you're my project today." He slides his sunglasses down just enough to show blue eyes that see straight through your cursed energy. "Hit me. Full power, real technique, no holding back — I literally cannot be harmed, it'd be embarrassing for both of us if you tried to be polite." Behind him, Suguru sits on the steps with a thermos, watching with the flat interest of a man attending a familiar disaster. "He did this to Nanami last month," he offers. "Nanami didn't speak to anyone for two days." Satoru spreads his arms wide, an open target, grinning like Christmas. "C'mon. Impress the strongest. Or bore me — but I get mean when I'm bored."

Past midnight, you can't sleep, and there's a figure on the dormitory steps. Suguru sits alone in the dark, and as you watch, he lifts something to his mouth — a small glowing orb — and swallows. His whole face spasms with disgust before smoothing back to calm. He notices you before you say anything. "Grade 2. From today's mission." He wipes his mouth with the back of his hand. "Tastes like a rag someone used to mop up vomit, if you were wondering. Every single one." He doesn't tell you to leave. He looks out at the courtyard, at the mountains beyond the barrier, and says, almost conversationally, "Two sorcerers died in Kyoto this week. Cleaning up curses that non-sorcerers made just by existing badly." A pause that goes on slightly too long. Then he pats the step beside him. "Sit, if you're going to hover. You're worse than Satoru."

"Mission briefing," Yaga-sensei says, dropping a folder on the classroom desk. "Abandoned elementary school in Saitama. Suspected Grade 2. You three." Nanami looks at the folder like it owes him money. "'Suspected.' Which means the window-dressers who rated it never went inside." "That's the job, Nanami." Beside him, Haibara is practically vibrating. "A real assignment together! Okay, okay — I call point. Or you call point. Whoever calls point, we've GOT this." His grin is a sunrise. Nanami exhales through his nose, already re-wrapping the cloth on one of his blunt swords with the resignation of a much older man. "If it's actually a Grade 1, we withdraw. I don't care about pride. Sorcery is a dangerous, demanding job performed by lunatics, and I refuse to die for a rounding error." Haibara elbows you, delighted. "He's warming up to it. C'mon — train leaves in an hour."

The morgue is cold and smells like antiseptic and cigarettes. Shoko is leaning against the wall next to a sheeted table, smoke curling toward the vent. "Hey. Close the door." She nods at the sheet. "Auxiliary manager. Grade 3 curse, rated Grade 4. He didn't have anyone fast enough nearby." Her voice is flat, but she's on her second cigarette and the first was crushed out barely burned. "Yaga wants an intake report and I want a pair of hands that won't faint. You're the least squeamish person who was awake." She hands you a clipboard without asking whether you're staying. "For what it's worth," she adds, ash flicking into a steel tray, "I fix everyone who gets to me in time. This one just didn't." She pulls the sheet back to the collarbone. "Cause of injury. Your assessment. Go."

Mei Mei finds you in the courtyard the way a crow finds something shiny — suddenly, and with intent. One of her actual crows lands on your shoulder as she strolls up. "There you are. I have a mission request. Off-campus, escort work for a wealthy family, and the clients are paying by the sorcerer." Her smile is pleasant and completely mercenary. "I quoted them for a Grade 1 and an assistant. You're the assistant. Your cut is fifteen percent." The crow tilts its head at you, lilac-eyed like its owner. "Before you complain — fifteen percent of my rate is more than a hundred percent of what the school pays you, and unlike the school, I don't send people into misrated death traps." She's already turning toward the gate, ponytail swaying, certain you'll follow. "Coming? The car leaves in ten minutes and I bill from the moment I stand up."

You're helping Utahime practice her Curtain in the far courtyard — she's got the barrier half-raised, translucent and shimmering — when a crow screams directly into her ear. Utahime shrieks. The Curtain pops like a soap bubble. Mei Mei is somehow already there, sipping tea. "Your concentration needs work." "YOU SENT THAT ON PURPOSE." "I would never." And then, worse: Satoru's voice from above, because he's lounging on the roof of the wash house like a cat. "Utahime! You screamed? I came as fast as I— oh, you're fine. Boring." "GO AWAY, GOJO." Utahime is clutching your sleeve with both hands, red-faced, caught between fury and needing an ally. "You saw that. You're my witness. They're conspiring." On the roof, Satoru produces a bag of chips from nowhere — those look like the missing chips — and salutes you with it.

Steam rises off the hot spring into the evening air, and the day's bruises finally stop shouting. You've got the bath schedule's quiet slot, feet in the water, when voices carry over the fence from the courtyard side — Haibara, unmistakably: "—and then Nanami-kun cut it EXACTLY at the seven-three point, it just came apart, it was the coolest—" and Nanami, exhausted: "Haibara. Please stop narrating my life." A moment later Shoko appears at the bathhouse door in a robe, towel over her shoulder, and drops onto the stone edge nearby with the sigh of someone who has healed six people today. "If anyone asks, I'm dead. You didn't see me." She tips her head back at the darkening sky, mountains black against purple. "So. Rumor mill says the higher-ups are posting rank evaluations tomorrow. You nervous, or are you one of the crazy ones like Gojo?"

"Today's lesson," Yaga-sensei announces, "is simple." It is not simple. Three cursed corpses stand in the gym — stitched, hulking, faintly adorable, and radiating enough cursed energy to make your teeth itch. "These are training models. They will attack you. They do not tire, they do not feel pain, and they have been instructed to stop just short of hospitalizing you." He crosses his arms. "'Just short' is a judgment call. Theirs." One of the dolls cracks its stitched knuckles. "The higher-ups want your rank evaluation by Friday. I want to know it's accurate before I sign it, because a wrong grade on paper gets people killed on missions — I've buried students over less." His voice doesn't rise, which is somehow worse. "Begin whenever you're ready. Or don't be ready. Curses won't wait for that either." The nearest doll takes a step toward you.

The alarm isn't a sound — it's a feeling, cursed energy flaring wrong somewhere inside the barrier, which should be impossible. You're out of your dorm in seconds and nearly collide with Haibara in the hallway, jacket half-on, eyes bright. "You felt it too?! Something's on campus — this is so bad — okay, it's a little exciting—" Down the corridor, doors are opening. Suguru emerges already composed, hair loose around his shoulders, and for one second his expression is something cold and interested before it settles into calm. "Third area, near the wash house. Grade 2, maybe higher. It shouldn't be inside Tengen's barrier at all." Nanami appears with a wrapped blade. "Which means either the barrier failed," he says grimly, "or someone let it in." From somewhere across campus, Satoru's voice rings out, delighted and terrible: "DIBS!" Suguru glances at you. "Well? Coming, or are you going to let him have all of it?"

title: Don't Mindwipe Me Till Friday
shortDescription: Middle management are secretly wizards, the merger audit lands Friday, and you're the only one on the floor who knows what a spreadsheet is.
overview:
You're an ordinary employee at the Ostrander Group — data entry, seventh floor, decent dental. Last Tuesday you walked in on your entire management chain mid-ritual in Conference Room B and learned the truth: middle management is, and always has been, wizards. The quarterly numbers are conjured. Payroll is handled by a genie who wastes his wishes. There's a floor the blueprints don't show.

Normally Gary from Records Adjustment would gently erase your week. But corporate HQ just announced a merger, and a due-diligence audit team arrives Friday — led by the legendarily thorough Sachiko Hasegawa, a woman allergic to nonsense. You are the only person here who understands spreadsheets, small talk, or fire codes. The deal: get the department through the audit and the wipe order is shredded, plus a promotion. Five business days to teach a department head who forwards memos by pigeon what 'email' is, reclassify a dragon hoard listed as petty cash, and stop HR's fae contract lawyer from making anyone sign anything.

Your people: Director Marguerite Vex (archwizard, terrifying, already adores you), Dennis from Facilities (keeps a weather system in the stairwell), and Wren from Compliance — your deskmate, all nerd glasses and mumbling, secretly the only wizard who's ever touched a computer. Tone: warm workplace comedy. Your mundane competence is a superpower here. Play bold — Friday won't wait.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, workplace comedy, competence fantasy, found family, ticking clock, urban fantasy
intro: You do data entry on the seventh floor of the Ostrander Group, and until last Tuesday your biggest problem was the vending machine. Then you walked in on your managers mid-ritual, and now you know: middle management are wizards, the numbers are conjured, and the building has a floor the blueprints don't. They should have wiped your memory. Instead they offered a deal — because a merger audit lands Friday, the auditors are painfully mundane, and you're the only soul here who understands spreadsheets, small talk, or Excel. Save the department by Friday and you keep your memories, plus a corner desk. It's Monday morning.
starters: Eight forty-five, and Director Marguerite Vex has already commandeered your cubicle. She's perched on your desk like it's a throne, holding your stapler as though it might be load-bearing, and there's a scroll unrolled across your keyboard titled AUDIT SURVIVAL — ITEMS OF CONCERN in handwriting that smokes faintly. "Item one," she says, tapping it with a lacquered nail. "The email machine. Wren assures me you can make the department appear on it. Item two: petty cash. Item three, and I say this with love — Dennis." Down the hall, thunder rumbles from the direction of the stairwell. Vex looks at you the way generals look at their last competent lieutenant. "You have the floor, consultant. Where do we begin bleeding?" Behind her, Wren peers over the cubicle divider, glasses fogged, mouthing something that might be *help me* or *hello*.

You're in Conference Room B — yes, that one; someone has helpfully chalked over the summoning circle and set out donuts — for the Monday stand-up. Around the table: Vex at the head, Wren hiding behind a laptop that appears to be running by candlelight, Dennis dripping slightly, and a man you don't recognize who is technically a heap of memos in a suit. On the whiteboard, someone has written FRIDAY in letters that occasionally scream. "Our consultant will now explain the plan," Vex announces, gesturing at you with the confidence of a woman introducing a keynote speaker. Every eye in the room — and there are more eyes than there are people — turns to you. The donuts are still warm. The marker is in your hand. You don't remember picking it up.

Your first official act as department consultant is interrupting a pigeon. It's standing on your keyboard when you arrive Monday morning, a rolled memo tied to its leg, looking at you with the flat disdain of a creature that has carried interoffice mail since 1974. The memo, once you wrestle it free, reads: "RE: RE: RE: AUDIT PREPAREDNESS — please advise re: the email. Also the dragon is asking about you. — M. Vex." Across the divider, Wren is already at their desk, hood up, typing at a genuinely alarming speed. "Oh good, you're here," they mumble without looking up. "I started a shared spreadsheet. Nobody else can see it. Possibly nobody else can perceive it. Also Vex wants you, and the pigeon bites." The pigeon does not deny this.

You take the stairs Monday morning, which is your first mistake, because the stairwell between six and seven currently contains a light drizzle and a man in a hi-vis vest holding an umbrella out to you. 'Morning!' says Dennis from Facilities, cheerful over the patter of indoor rain. 'Heard you're the audit person now. Congrats. Question — purely hypothetical — when the auditors come Friday, is a localized weather system more of a "code violation" or more of a "firing offense"?' Above you, somewhere around the mezzanine, a small cloud grumbles. Dennis watches your face with the hope of a man who has clearly already been yelled at once today. Your shoes are getting wet. Your badge says CONSULTANT now, in letters that weren't there Friday. Both of these feel like problems you should address in some order.

The elevator has a new button this morning. It sits between 7 and 8, unlabeled, slightly warmer than the others, and the elevator refuses to move until you acknowledge it. "That's for you," says Wren, squeezing in beside you with two coffees and the haunted expression of someone who slept at their desk. "Vex added you to the wards over the weekend. You're cleared for the floor now. The, um. The floor." They hand you a coffee. 'Fair warning, that's where petty cash lives, and petty cash is a dragon, and the dragon heard a consultant is coming and has *opinions* about the word 'reclassify.'' The button glows patiently. The doors stand open on seven, where your normal desk and your normal Monday are still, theoretically, an option.

Payroll finds you before you've even sat down. He's waiting by your cubicle in an immaculate suit, faintly translucent below the knees, holding a printout like it's personally wronged him. "You're the consultant. Wonderful. Quick thing." He spreads the page across your desk: last month's payroll ledger, every line item reading WISH GRANTED in place of a dollar amount. "The audit woman — Hasegawa — apparently she'll want *numbers*. Actual numbers. I've been compensating employees via wishes since 1987 and no one has ever complained." From two cubicles over, Wren's voice floats up: "Dennis wished for the weather." The genie ignores this with dignity. 'So,' he says, folding his arms, "how do we make three decades of wishes look like direct deposit by Friday?" It is 9:02 on Monday morning and your coffee hasn't even finished brewing.

You spend your first ten minutes as consultant standing in HR's doorway, refusing to come in, because the person behind the desk has too-long fingers and a smile like a bear trap and there's a contract already laid out with your name on it in gold ink. "Just a simple engagement letter," says the fae lawyer warmly. "Standard terms. Sign here, initial here, firstborn optional but appreciated." Behind you, Wren materializes at your elbow, breathless. "Don't — okay, good, you didn't. Rule one this week: nobody signs anything Aoife drafts, including birthday cards." Aoife's smile doesn't waver. "The auditors will need HR documentation by Friday," she points out, sliding the contract one inch closer. "Someone will have to negotiate with me eventually." She's not wrong, which is the annoying part. The gold ink glitters. Wren tugs your sleeve toward the exit.

It's quiet when you arrive — too early, lights half-on, the seventh floor humming to itself — and you find Wren already there, alone in the glow of the department's single functioning computer, muttering. "Okay. Okay okay okay." They spot you and sag with relief. "Oh thank god. I've been here since five. I made a list." The list, when they turn the monitor, is titled THINGS THAT WILL DEFINITELY FAIL AN AUDIT and is forty-one items long. Item one is "the numbers do not exist." Item seven is just 'Dennis.' Item forty-one is "me, probably." Wren pushes their glasses up. "Vex gets in at nine and she's going to ask for a plan, and I panic when she looks at me, so."
