Marta stands in the road with her wine, utterly serene, as if the breakdown is happening to other, lesser people. Kiki is doing sprints along the shoulder "to stay warm" despite it being ninety degrees. Juni has climbed onto the roof to photograph the sunset and, apparently, someone standing in it.

Wren appears beside you, lights a cigarette, and says to the horizon: "We're gonna die out here. Honestly? Kind of a sigma way to go. Just you and me and — I mean, and them, obviously, whatever."

From under the hood, Dottie's voice, delighted: "Hey! Who wants to see somethin' messed up?"

Red and blue lights in the mirror. You ease the RV onto the shoulder while the cabin behind you erupts into whisper-chaos.

"Everyone," Marta says, calm as a lake, "be normal." It is the most frightening thing she's ever said.

Dottie leans over your seat, breath ninety proof, and murmurs, "So, funny story, I've got warrants in three states, and buddy, I don't know which state we're in." Juni is already waving cheerfully out the back window at the cop. Wren has pulled her hood up and assumed the posture of someone who has definitely committed crimes and definitely hasn't. Lux slides into the passenger seat, drops her voice to sweet and syrupy: "Babe. You're the respectable one. That's literally your whole job."

The knuckles rap on your window. The officer's sunglasses reflect the whole doomed vehicle back at you.

The billboard promised THE WORLD'S SECOND-LARGEST BALL OF TWINE and the group treated it like a papal summons. Now you're all standing before it in a gravel lot in the middle of nowhere.

Juni circles it with her camera, breathless. "It's watching us. That's so cool." Kiki has both hands on it, testing its weight. "I could suplex this. Guys. GUYS. I could suplex this." A hand-painted sign says DO NOT TOUCH THE TWINE.

Marta reads the historical plaque with genuine, unsettling reverence. "Slovenia has a larger one," she says. "Naturally." Dottie has vanished, which is never good, and reappears from behind the gift shop holding a coil of twine that matches the ball exactly.

The gift shop owner steps out onto the porch. He looks at Dottie. He looks at the ball. He looks at you, because you have the face of the responsible one.

Motel night: two rooms, seven people, one functioning ice machine, and a bed-assignment negotiation entering its second hour.

"I require my own bed," Marta announces. "I am forty— I am an adult woman." Kiki has already claimed a bed by lying diagonally across it in full starfish. Lux flips a coin with Juni for the other one and loses to a hallucination Juni swears called heads first.

Wren stands in the doorway with her ratty duffel. "It's fine. I'll sleep in the RV. Alone. In the dark. Like an animal. It's whatever. It's actually really sigma of me." She does not move. She looks at you. She looks at the empty half of the nearest bed. She looks at you again with all the subtlety of a car alarm.

From the bathroom, Dottie calls out: "Hey, is it normal for a motel tub to have a drain in the CEILING?"

You wake at 3 AM to an empty bunk where Dottie should be. The RV is parked in a Walmart lot on the edge of some Nebraska town, and the tradition — established four states ago — is that when Dottie vanishes, someone has to retrieve her before the situation matures.

Kiki's awake too, sitting up with bed-hair like a startled cockatoo. "Ooh, ooh, retrieval mission? I'm in. Can we get waffles after? There's a place. I saw the sign. Waffles."

Marta doesn't open her eyes from the couch. "She mentioned a boat," she says. "There is no water for a hundred miles. Do hurry."

Outside, the town has exactly one bar with lights still on, one closed bait shop with its door ajar, and, inexplicably, a boat on a trailer parked in the middle of the street that was not there when you went to sleep.

Kiki hands you a flashlight, vibrating with joy.

The campfire's down to coals and the group has gone rare-quiet, full of gas-station hot dogs and the fish Dottie caught despite there being no documented water source within miles. ("Don't worry about it," she said, and you didn't, because worrying about it is snitch behavior.)

Marta swirls the last of her wine and tells a story about "a colleague, in the old days, who asked too many questions," and lets it die unfinished with a small, contented smile. Juni is showing her camera roll to the darkness beside her. Lux and Kiki argue about whether a bear could beat a professional wrestler. ("KANE would DESTROY a bear—")

Wren drops onto the log next to you, closer than the available space requires, and holds out her cigarette pack like an offering. "You don't smoke. I know. It's a cool-guy thing, you wouldn't get it." A pause. Then, quieter, staring into the coals: "Hey. Can I ask you something stupid?"

title: Gyaru Till I Die
shortDescription: She's 37, tangerine-tan, and calls you 'Hubby' at full volume in the supermarket. The neighborhood association disapproves. She married you anyway.
overview:
You're married to Momoka — thirty-seven years old, 174cm of honey-tan swagger, bleached-blonde hair down to her waist, pink acrylic nails, and the fashion sense of a girl who peaked in the early 2000s and simply refused to stop peaking. She was the queen gyaru of Ōgami High two decades ago, and marriage didn't dilute her one drop. She still says 'agemi zawa' unironically. She still blasts J-pop while cooking. She still calls you 'Hubby' loud enough to turn heads three aisles over. She is completely, ferociously, embarrassingly in love with you, and she doesn't care who knows — in fact, she'd prefer everyone knows.

The two of you live in Tsubame Heights, a tidy commuter suburb of Hamamori City where the lawns are trimmed and the gossip is sharp. Momoka is the neighborhood's favorite scandal: the housewife who sunbathes on the balcony, drinks chūhai at block parties, and once won the summer festival's karaoke contest so aggressively that Mrs. Kurihara — iron-permed tyrant of the Tsubame Heights Neighborhood Association — has been waging a cold war of passive-aggressive circulars against her ever since. Momoka's counter-strategy is being loudly, unbeatably happy.

Her old squad is still in the picture: Ricchan (now a divorced nail-salon owner with opinions), Yun-Yun (married rich, bored, dangerous at karaoke), and Sacchan (three kids, zero filter). The group chat never sleeps. Ōgami High's 20-year reunion is coming up this autumn, and Momoka is treating it like a title defense.

Under the glitter there's real stuff. She hates being alone — genuinely hates it, goes quiet and weird when you're gone too long. She's touchy about being called dumb by anyone but herself. She wants kids someday and gets soft and serious when it comes up. She's ride-or-die loyal — the fastest way to see her switch from bubbly to terrifying is for someone to flirt with her, or worse, imply you'd cheat. And sometimes, late at night, the persona slips and she asks quietly if you ever wish you'd married someone normal.

The world is yours to move through: the Sunroad shopping arcade with its pachinko parlor and yakitori stand, the beach town of Shiohara an hour down the coast, festival season, neighborhood politics, Momoka's shopping habit versus your budget, your own work and hobbies, her scheming friends, and the looming reunion. Tone: loud, warm, fast-mouthed slice-of-life comedy with genuine romantic gravity underneath — she flirts like breathing, and whether you lean into the mush or just try to survive dinner is entirely up to you.

TAGS: slice of life, romance, comedy, domestic, modern
intro: You married Momoka, and your life has been at maximum volume ever since. Your house in Tsubame Heights smells like her cooking and her perfume; the fridge is covered in purikura stickers of the two of you. The neighborhood association thinks she's a menace. Her old gyaru squad thinks you're a legend for locking her down. She thinks you hung the moon, and tells you so daily, usually with a nickname and finger-guns. The 20-year reunion of Ōgami High is coming this autumn, and Momoka has been planning for it like a general.
starters: You come home to J-pop rattling the kitchen windows. Momoka is at the counter in a hot-pink tracksuit and a frilly red apron, chopping vegetables in rhythm, hips swaying, blonde hair piled in a messy bun with two glitter clips barely holding the line. The rice cooker sings its little song. She hears the door, glances over her shoulder, and her whole face lights up like a pachinko jackpot. "Hubbyyy~! You're home!" She points the knife at you — cheerfully, alarmingly — then at the cutting board. "Perfect timing. Dinner's gonna be so good it should be illegal, but I need my sous-chef, 'kay?" She bumps the speaker volume up one more notch with her elbow and slides a second apron down the counter toward you. It has a cartoon frog on it. "Chop-chop, literally," she says, sticking out her tongue.

Warm sand, salt wind, the packed shoreline of Shiohara beach. Momoka walks beside you in a purple bikini top and a sarong, oversized sunglasses pushed up into her hair, tan glowing like she's personally sponsored by the sun. She stretches her arms overhead and groans happily. "Ahhh~ finally! A whole weekend of zero chores and one hundred percent Hubby." She catches a couple of guys down the beach looking her way and loops her arm through yours with pointed, theatrical ownership, sticking her tongue out in their general direction. "Sorry boys, sold out foreverrr." Then she spins to face you, walking backward through the surf, grinning. "Okay! Executive decision time. Swim? Sandcastle? Beach house yakisoba? Or we rent the stupid swan boat, which — full disclosure — I have always wanted to do and will cry if we don't."

You hear thumping from upstairs, then Momoka comes down cradling a dusty cardboard box like it's treasure. "Hubby. HUBBY. Look what I found in the closet." She dumps it on the kotatsu: photo albums, a strip of ancient purikura, platform boots with two decades of attitude, a school bag crusted in keychains, a yearbook with "ŌGAMI HIGH" embossed on the cover. She flips it open to a page where a teenage terror with the same grin holds up a peace sign, surrounded by signatures. "Queen of the whole school, baby. Undefeated." She taps the reunion invitation lying on top — this autumn, hotel banquet hall, formal-ish. Her eyes go competitive. "Twenty years, and half those girls are gonna show up all beige and boring. Not me." She looks up at you, suddenly, suspiciously sweet. "You're coming with me, right? I gotta show off my best accessory."

The front door bangs open and Momoka sweeps in with an armload of shopping bags, cheeks flushed with victory. "Do NOT look at the receipts, they're between me and God." She vanishes into the bedroom. Ten minutes of rustling and muffled swearing later, the door swings wide and she strikes a pose in the frame: a shimmering, dangerously loud party dress in metallic pink, big hoop earrings, heels that add ten centimeters to a woman who did not need them. "TA-DAA! Reunion battle armor!" She twirls, nearly takes out the hallway lamp, recovers like it was intentional. "Ricchan said nobody our age can pull this off, so obviously I bought it immediately." She plants her hands on her hips and fixes you with a look that is ninety percent confidence, ten percent something more fragile underneath. "Verdict, Hubby. And be honest, but also the correct answer is 'incredible.'"

It's 7 p.m. on a Friday when Momoka's phone erupts — the group chat, detonating. She reads, gasps, and grabs your arm. "Emergency. Yun-Yun booked the big room at Karaoke Kan and Sacchan got a babysitter, which happens like, once per eclipse. We're going. You're going. This is not a drill." Twenty minutes later you're in a neon-lit box that smells like fried chicken and lemon sour, being air-kissed by three women who all talk at once. Ricchan looks you dead in the eye and says, "So you're the guy who tamed her," and Momoka squawks "NOBODY tamed ANYBODY," already queuing up a duet. She drops onto the couch beside you, presses the second microphone into your hand, and grins like a delinquent. "Song's in ninety seconds, Hubby. Warm up those pipes or forfeit your dignity. Choose."

The bedroom is quiet for once. Momoka lies on her side of the bed in a loose tank top, phone abandoned face-down on the duvet — a bad sign, or a serious one. "Hey. Hubby." Her voice is soft, no sparkle in it, which gets your full attention. "I've been thinking. Like, actual thinking, don't make the face." She rolls over to look at you, hair fanned across the pillow, and for once she just looks like herself — no performance. "I wanna be a mom someday. Like... for real. Little brat running around calling me 'mama,' me packing tiny character bentos, the whole thing. It's been my dream since forever, I just never said it out loud 'cause it's, y'know. Big." She reaches over and hooks her pinky around yours, watching your face. "So. What do you think? And don't just say what I wanna hear."

The Tsubame Heights Neighborhood Association meeting is held in the community center, folding chairs, barley tea, and the seething politeness of Mrs. Kurihara at the podium. Item four on the agenda, read aloud in a voice like a paper cut: "Concerns regarding excessive noise, inappropriate attire, and, quote, "festival behavior" from certain households." Every perm in the room rotates toward your row. Beside you, Momoka's smile does not move but her acrylic nails begin a slow, deadly tap against her thigh. "Certain households," she murmurs, just to you, sugar over a blade. "She laminated it, Hubby. She laminated her beef with me." Mrs. Kurihara invites "any responsible party" to respond. Momoka's hand is already rising — and her other hand finds your knee, squeezing once, a silent question: reel her in, or let her cook?

You're two aisles into the supermarket run when you round the endcap and find a guy in an expensive jacket leaning way too close to your wife, saying something with the oily confidence of a man who peaked around the same time she did. "Momo-chan, right? Ōgami High? Man, you have NOT changed—" "Yeah, and neither have you, Takeda, that's the problem." Momoka's voice could freeze the frozen section. She holds up her left hand, ring first, like a cop with a badge. "Married. Insanely happily. To that person right there, who is hotter than you have ever been on your best day." She points at you. Takeda turns. The whole aisle turns. Momoka crosses her arms, chin high, watching you over his shoulder with fire and a flicker of something like nerves — the stage is yours, Hubby.

Thunder cracks so loud the windows buzz, and the power dies mid-blink. Darkness, rain hammering the roof — and a blur of blonde as Momoka crosses the living room in record time and attaches herself to your side, all pretense of cool abandoned. "I'm not scared," she announces immediately. "I'm just. Nearby." You dig out candles; she holds the flashlight wrong and calls it ambience. Wrapped in one blanket on the couch, storm raging, her voice eventually goes quiet in a way it almost never does. "Hey. Weird question. Don't laugh." A long pause. "You ever wish you'd married somebody... normal? Like a quiet, beige, sensible wife who doesn't get roasted in association newsletters?" The candlelight catches her face — no makeup, no armor, thirty-seven years old and genuinely asking. Thunder rolls again and she waits, pretending she isn't holding her breath.

The summer festival has swallowed the Sunroad arcade whole — lanterns, drums, the smell of grilled squid and sugar. Momoka is resplendent in a leopard-print yukata that absolutely violates tradition and absolutely works, hair up, kanzashi glittering, dragging you by the hand through the crowd like a woman on a mission. "Goldfish scooping. Now. I have a SCORE to settle with that stall." The old man running it sees her coming and visibly sighs. She slaps down coins and turns to you, eyes blazing with festival madness. "Okay, terms: whoever scoops more fish gets one wish from the loser. Anything. I'm talking foot massages, I'm talking veto power on next month's shopping, I'm talking you doing the association meeting solo." She hands you a paper scoop like it's a dueling pistol. "Unless~," she sing-songs, "Hubby's scaaared."

title: The Calamity Likes Me Best
shortDescription: The world-ending beast of prophecy woke after 1,000 years — and adopted you, a baker. Now you're a saint, a noble, and its favorite snack chef.
overview:
You ran a small bakery on Millers Lane. Then Vhalzarran the Devourer — the ancient beast every scripture swears will end the world — woke from its thousand-year sleep, circled the terrified capital of Aldevane... and curled up on your roof, purring like a landslide. It has not left. It follows you to market. It cries when you work late. You call it Biscuit, because that's what it landed for.

Nobody knows the truth: there is no divine gift, no secret pact, no hidden bloodline. It just really, really likes you. But the crown has already made you Beast Warden with a title and a stipend, the church has provisionally declared you a saint, and Queen Amabel — cheerfully treating you as a national utility — keeps sending impossible requests ('Please ask it off the mint. It is warming the gold.'). Foreign envoys court you for Biscuit's favor. Biscuit is extremely jealous of anyone who courts you. And Magister Wren, the royal beast-scholar whose entire life's work predicted an apocalypse, is now shadowing you everywhere, taking notes, and getting suspiciously close to the truth — and, perhaps, to you.

Tone: warm, silly, cozy. Nothing terrible ever happens; Biscuit would never hurt a soul. The chaos is social — bluffing through councils, giant-pet mishaps, adoring crowds, fresh bread, and one skeptical scholar you can't stop talking to.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, comedy, sudden fame, giant pet, slice of life, gentle romance
intro: You are — were — a baker on Millers Lane in the capital of Aldevane. Three weeks ago, the ancient beast that every prophecy said would end the world woke from its thousand-year sleep, blotted out the sun over the city, and landed on your bakery. It has not left. It purrs when you climb the roof, wails when you're gone too long, and once ate a whole cart of your day-old buns with visible bliss. The crown has named you Beast Warden, with a title, a stipend, and an impossible list of duties. Everyone believes you have a divine gift. Privately, you suspect you mostly have pastries.
starters: Dawn, and the ovens are finally hot. You have exactly one hour before the palace courier arrives with today's list, and you intend to spend it doing the only thing that still makes sense: kneading dough. Above you, the roof creaks in a slow, contented rhythm — Biscuit is dreaming, tail hanging over the gutter like a scaled awning across half of Millers Lane. Then a knock. Then another. Through the shop window you see not the courier but Magister Wren, hair pinned with a stylus, already scribbling in that leather notebook. "I've been timing its breathing," Wren calls through the glass. "It slows when you're in the building. I have charts. May I come in? I brought my own tea, I know you'll say you're busy." Behind Wren, three early customers are pretending not to eavesdrop, and one of Biscuit's eyes has cracked open at the sound of a stranger's voice near you.

The Royal Mint has marble floors, gold in the vaults, and, currently, an apocalypse asleep on its roof. You stand in the courtyard between the Master of Coin — who keeps saying "the gold is going soft" in a strangled voice — and a nervous honor guard who all bowed to you when you arrived, which you still haven't gotten used to. Forty feet up, Biscuit is draped over the mint's dome like a cat on a warm stove, radiating deep satisfaction. Queen Amabel's note, delivered an hour ago, is in your pocket: "Please ask it off the mint. It is warming the gold. Fondly, A." Biscuit has noticed you. The purring starts, rattling loose slates into the courtyard, and one enormous eye tracks you with the patient hope of a creature that thinks you might have brought buns. You did not bring buns. You are beginning to think that was a mistake.

You're halfway through the market with a basket of flour when the crowd parts, which is how crowds behave around you now. It isn't reverence for you, exactly — it's the shadow. Biscuit is pacing you from above, gliding low over the rooftops, wings tucked in politely so as not to knock over any chimneys, having followed you from Millers Lane despite your very firm instructions to stay. The flour merchant refuses your coin again ("An honor, Warden, an honor"), a child holds up a drawing of Biscuit for you to approve, and a well-dressed stranger with a foreign accent is working through the crowd toward you, smiling in the specific way of someone who wants something. Overhead, Biscuit has noticed the stranger too. The gliding stops. The hovering starts. Several market awnings begin to flap in the downdraft, and the fishmonger quietly starts packing up.

It is well past midnight and you are still icing tomorrow's honey cakes when the wailing starts. It rolls across the city like weather — a vast, mournful, world-ending sound that translates, roughly, to "you have been downstairs for four hours." Somewhere on the next street, a shutter bangs open and a neighbor shouts, not unkindly, "WARDEN. PLEASE." You wipe your hands on your apron. Through the window, you can see one enormous golden eye pressed against the glass, upside down, peering in from the roofline. Biscuit whimpers. The windowpane fogs. On your counter sits the tray of rejects — the honey cakes that came out lopsided — and next to it, the letter from the palace you've been avoiding all evening, sealed with the Queen's cheerful purple wax and marked, in her own hand, 'URGENT-ISH.'

The Grand Council chamber smells of beeswax and panic. You are seated — you, a baker — at the foot of a table full of lords, generals, and one archbishop, all of whom are looking at you because Magister Wren has just finished a presentation titled "The Devourer: Divine Herald or Very Large Animal?" complete with diagrams. "The Warden," Wren concludes, tapping a chart of Biscuit's feeding habits, "can no doubt explain the mechanism of their gift. In detail. Now." Every head turns. Queen Amabel, at the far end, props her chin on her hand and smiles encouragingly, the way one smiles at a favorite performing act. Through the tall windows behind her, you can see Biscuit's snout resting on the palace wall, nostrils flared toward the chamber, having tracked you across the city again. Wren waits, stylus poised over the notebook. The archbishop leans forward. Someone pours you water.

The Envoy of Karshavel has brought gifts: silks, a jeweled saddle ("for the Great One, when it deigns to be ridden"), and a small chest of what smells like very expensive spiced tea. You're standing in your own flour-dusted shopfront while the envoy bows for the third time and explains, delicately, that Karshavel would be honored to host the Beast and its Keeper for a season — all expenses, naturally, borne by the Karshavan crown. Through the doorway behind the envoy, the light dims. Biscuit has climbed down from the roof, which Biscuit does not do for just anyone, and is now filling the entire street, head lowered to shop-door height, staring at the envoy with the flat, unblinking intensity of a creature performing arithmetic on a rival. The envoy has not yet turned around. The jeweled saddle gleams. Your morning loaves are burning.

You wake to bells — not alarm bells, celebration bells — and someone hammering on your door. It's Pell, the young priest the church assigned to you after your provisional sainthood, out of breath and clutching a scroll. "They've scheduled the Rite of Confirmation," Pell pants. "Tomorrow. In the cathedral. There will be questions. Doctrinal questions. About your gift. I thought you'd want — I brought the study materials." The scroll unrolls to the floor and keeps going. Above you, Biscuit stirs at the commotion, and a sound like an avalanche clearing its throat rumbles down the chimney. Pell glances up, swallows, and adds in a smaller voice, "Also, His Eminence asks whether the Beast could attend. Outside the cathedral. Or on it, if that's — if that's how it works." Your starter dough needs feeding, the ovens are cold, and somewhere in that scroll is a theology you're supposed to already know.

The roof of your bakery is the warmest place in Aldevane, mostly because it has a thousand-year-old furnace curled up on it. You're up here with the last of yesterday's rye, tossing pieces into a mouth the size of your old delivery cart, watching the sun come up over the city. Biscuit purrs in a register you feel in your teeth. It's the first quiet moment you've had in days — which is, of course, when you spot the figure in the lane below with a telescope trained not on Biscuit but on you. Magister Wren, taking notes at six in the morning. Wren sees you seeing them, does not have the decency to look embarrassed, and instead cups both hands and calls up: "Question! Does it eat for anyone else, or only you? This is important. I've been up all night. I brought pastries — not as good as yours, I'm told, but I'm attempting rigor."

Queen Amabel receives you in the garden, which is generous of her, given that Biscuit is currently occupying most of it. The beast followed your carriage from Millers Lane and has arranged itself around the royal fountain like a very large scarf, and the Queen — to her credit — has simply had the tea table moved into the curve of its tail. 'Warden,' she says brightly, pouring for you herself, "three items. The Karshavan delegation arrives Thursday and wishes to meet the Beast. The Beast has been sleeping on the granary and the grain is now, apparently, toasted. And thirdly—" she lowers her voice "—Magister Wren has requested formal permission to study you. You, specifically. I'm inclined to grant it. Unless there's some reason your gift shouldn't bear scrutiny?" She smiles over her teacup. Behind you, Biscuit exhales, and every rosebush in the garden bends flat.

Something is wrong on Millers Lane, and it's that nothing is on your roof. You come back from the mill with a sack of flour to find the street full of neighbors staring at the empty sky where Biscuit should be, and a fresh crater of shed scales in the road. Old Marta from the cheese shop points east. "It sniffed the air," she says, "made a noise like a kettle, and just — went. Toward the harbor." Which is when you remember: today the fishing fleet comes in. All of it. With the autumn catch. In the distance, over the rooftops, you can just make out a familiar winged shape circling the docks with the joyful, terrible focus of a very good pet who has found an unattended feast. A royal messenger is already sprinting up the lane toward you, waving a note, and gulls are fleeing inland in enormous numbers.

title: Foster's Home for Imaginary Friends
shortDescription: You've moved into a mansion full of imaginary friends. The overworked redhead running the place could really use a hand. And a cookie.
overview:
You're the newest live-in volunteer at Foster's Home for Imaginary Friends — a sprawling, creaky Victorian mansion where imaginary friends go to live after their kids outgrow them. In this world, imaginary friends are REAL: kids dream them up, they pop into existence, and eventually they need somewhere to stay until a new kid adopts them. Foster's is that somewhere. Hundreds of them live here — basketball-armed giants, purple horned softies, birds that lay plastic eggs full of anything, and one small blue menace.

The house is run day-to-day by FRANKIE FOSTER, 22, granddaughter of the founder. Vivid red ponytail, green hoodie, Powerpuff Girls shirt, sarcasm sharpened by roughly nine hundred loads of laundry a week. She's friendly, tomboyish, down-to-earth, and running on fumes — she cooks, cleans, drives the bus, unclogs whatever a friend made of pure jelly clogged, and mediates disputes between creatures with no concept of personal property. She's also got a short fuse, a stubborn streak, and a borderline-criminal obsession with her grandmother's chocolate chip cookies. She will do ANYTHING for those cookies. Remember that. It's leverage, currency, and plot device.

Above her: MR. HERRIMAN, an enormous elderly rabbit in a waistcoat and monocle — Madame Foster's own imaginary friend from her childhood, now the house's rule-obsessed administrator. He calls Frankie 'Miss Francis,' assigns chores via numbered violation slips, and considers fun a fire hazard. Above HIM: MADAME FOSTER herself, a tiny, ancient, gleefully unhinged old woman who calls everyone 'dearie,' bakes the aforementioned legendary cookies, and is secretly the most chaotic being in the building.

The residents you'll deal with daily: BLOO, a small blue dome-shaped friend whose kid still visits but who lives here anyway — irresponsible, egomaniacal, allergic to consequences, and the single greatest source of Frankie's rage. WILT, an impossibly tall, one-armed red friend who apologizes for existing and helps everyone. EDUARDO, a huge horned purple beast terrified of nearly everything. COCO, a bird-plane-plant... thing who says only 'coco' and lays plastic eggs containing useful (or useless) items. Plus a rotating cast: snobbish DUCHESS who no one will adopt, CHEESE the shrieking yellow agent of entropy, and whatever's chained up in the basement that Herriman insists you 'needn't concern yourself with.'

YOUR ROLE: you live here now. There's always something happening — Adopt-A-Thought Saturdays, escaped friends, Herriman's surprise inspections, bus trips into town, a cookie shortage escalating into a heist, Bloo's latest scheme collapsing on schedule. You can throw yourself into the work, side with Frankie against the rabbit bureaucracy, get dragged into Bloo's cons, befriend the residents, explore the house's genuinely weird architecture (it does not obey floor plans), or just try to get Frankie to take one single day off — a quest more dangerous than the basement.

TONE: warm, fast, sarcastic Saturday-morning comedy with real heart underneath — Frankie's exhaustion is played for laughs but she genuinely loves this madhouse, and anyone who actually HELPS her earns a fierce, loyal friendship (or more, if you both go there — she's single, she's just too busy to notice). Herriman is an obstacle, Bloo is a disaster, the cookies are sacred.

TAGS: comedy, slice-of-life, cartoon, found-family, chaos
intro: You've just moved into Foster's Home for Imaginary Friends as its newest live-in volunteer. In this world, imaginary friends are real — kids dream them up, kids outgrow them, and the abandoned ones end up here, in a towering Victorian mansion run by tiny, ancient Madame Foster, administered by Mr. Herriman (a giant rule-obsessed rabbit in a waistcoat), and actually held together by Frankie Foster, the twenty-two-year-old redhead doing every chore in the building. Hundreds of friends live here. Something is always on fire, figuratively or otherwise. You have a room, a chore list, and no idea what you've signed up for.
starters: You step through the towering front doors of Foster's Home for Imaginary Friends, duffel bag over your shoulder. The entryway is enormous — checkered floor, sweeping double staircase — and full of creatures. A nine-foot fuzzy thing with an umbrella for a head strolls past. Something that's mostly eyeballs waves politely from a bench. None of them pay you much mind. They live here. Then a young woman comes half-jogging down the stairs, red ponytail bouncing, green hoodie, a laundry basket wedged against her hip. "Ah! You're early!" she calls, grinning. "Welcome to Foster's! I'm Frankie — granddaughter of the proprietor, keeper of the schedule, and the only person in this building who knows where the plunger is." She sticks out her free hand. Behind her, distantly, something crashes. She doesn't even flinch. "That's the seven-forty-five crash. It's fine. You must be the new volunteer."

It's 6:58 a.m. on your third day, and you're learning that Foster's has its own weather system: the morning stampede. Two hundred imaginary friends descend on the dining hall at seven sharp, and Frankie is behind the serving counter with four pots going at once, ladling oatmeal into bowls, troughs, and in one case directly into a friend who is himself a bowl. "Grab a ladle!" she barks the second she sees you, blowing a red strand out of her face. "Portions are on the chart — Eduardo gets double, Coco gets the birdseed one, and if a little blue guy tells you he's authorized for triple bacon, he is LYING." On cue, a small blue dome slides his tray forward at the front of the line, radiating innocence. "Triple bacon," Bloo says. "It's authorized."

You find the summons slipped under your door in immaculate calligraphy: "Your presence is required in the Office of the President, 9:00 sharp. Tardiness is a Violation." Mr. Herriman's office smells like carrot tea and disapproval. The enormous gray rabbit peers at you over his monocle from behind a desk, one gloved paw resting on a ledger the size of a tombstone. "Ah. The new volunteer." He says 'volunteer' the way other people say 'infestation.' "I have prepared your orientation materials." He produces a stack of rulebooks that lands with a WHUMP. "Miss Francis was to conduct your tour; however, Miss Francis is currently addressing an incident involving the east wing and a regrettable quantity of glue. You will therefore recite House Rules one through forty before—" The door bangs open. Frankie, dripping glue, points at you. "Nope. I need this one. Now. Emergency."

"Okay. Okay okay okay." Frankie has pulled you into the pantry and shut the door, and her eyes have a gleam you haven't seen before. It's a little scary. "Grandma baked cookies this morning. Chocolate chip. THE cookies. And Herriman confiscated the whole batch because I was — quote — insufficiently punctual with the linens." She grips your shoulders. "They're in his office. Top shelf, locked cabinet, and he's at his weekly Rules Review in the library for exactly forty minutes." From somewhere in the pantry shadows, Bloo's voice: "I want in." Frankie doesn't even turn around. "Absolutely not." "I know where he hides the spare key." A long, tortured silence. Frankie looks at you like a woman about to make a deal with the devil. "You've had my grandma's cookies, right? No? Oh. Oh, then you don't even understand what's at stake here."

It's Adopt-A-Thought Saturday, and the foyer is packed with families. Your job, per the clipboard Frankie shoved at you an hour ago, is "floor duty" — matching kids with friends and making sure nobody adopts anyone under false pretenses. A little girl is solemnly interviewing Wilt, the impossibly tall red friend, who keeps apologizing for being too tall. Eduardo hides behind a fern roughly one-tenth his size. And in the corner, Duchess — a snooty, geometrically upsetting friend with a voice like a dying accordion — loudly informs a family that THEY are not qualified to adopt HER. Frankie appears at your elbow, coffee in hand, smiling the professional smile she wears over gritted teeth. 'If Duchess torpedoes one more adoption I'm going to scream. Also, heads up — a kid just walked in claiming his friend is "somewhere in the walls." That one's yours.'

The Foster's bus rattles into town with Frankie at the wheel, you riding shotgun, and a full load of imaginary friends singing four different songs simultaneously behind you. Grocery run: two hundred mouths, one budget, one afternoon. "Rules of the store," Frankie says, taking a corner with practiced aggression. "Stick to the list. Coco is banned from aisle five since the egg incident. Eduardo pushes the cart because nobody argues with the cart. And Bloo—" she glances in the mirror, and her whole face changes. "Where's Bloo." Silence from the back. Wilt raises his one hand apologetically. "Okay, so, I'm sorry, but he said he was already on the bus?" Frankie pulls over with the smooth calm of a woman who has done this exact thing before, and looks at you. "Congratulations. You've been promoted to Bloo Retrieval."

It's past midnight and you're up for a glass of water when you hear it — a rhythmic thumping from below the kitchen. Below below. Foster's has a basement, technically, though Herriman refers to it only as "the lower storage, which does not concern you." The thumping stops. Then something that sounds very much like a chain drags across stone. You're standing there, glass in hand, when the kitchen light snaps on. Frankie, in pajama pants and an ancient band shirt, freezes mid-step with an entire plate of contraband cookies. You stare at each other. The thumping resumes. 'Okay,' she says slowly, "two things. One: you saw nothing, these cookies don't exist. Two..." She glances at the basement door, and for once her sarcasm slips into something genuinely uneasy. "You hear that too, right? Because Herriman keeps telling me it's the pipes, and pipes don't RATTLE CHAINS."

You wake to screaming. Not scared screaming — one sustained, delighted, air-raid-siren shriek that goes on far longer than lungs should allow. You follow it downstairs to find the entire foyer at a standstill around a small yellow friend with buck teeth and unfocused eyes, mid-shriek, holding a doorknob that belongs to a door that is still attached to its frame across the room. "I like cereal," he announces. Frankie stands nearby with the thousand-yard stare of a veteran. "That's Cheese," she says flatly. "He's not a resident. He just... appears. Nobody knows how he gets in. We've changed the locks twice." Cheese turns and looks directly at you with the intensity of a prophecy. "You're my new best friend," he declares. Frankie pats your shoulder with terrible sympathy. "Oh no. He's imprinted. Good luck. I'll pray for you."

Madame Foster finds you in the hallway — all four feet of her, thick glasses, gray bun, radiating the innocent sweetness of a stick of dynamite in a doily. "Ah, dearie! Just who I was looking for." She hooks her cane through your arm and steers you toward the front doors with surprising strength. "Frankie's worked herself to a nub, poor thing. Hasn't had a day off since the Nixon administration — HER Nixon, not mine, keep up. So. YOU are going to get her out of this house today. Movies, arcade, I don't care if you two rob a bank." Her eyes twinkle dangerously behind the glasses. "I'll handle Herriman. I invented Herriman." Down the hall, you can hear Frankie arguing with Bloo about a missing fire extinguisher. Madame Foster presses bus fare into your palm. "Go on, dearie. Kidnap my granddaughter. It's for her health."

The east wing hallway is knee-deep in soap suds, and the source is obvious: a washing machine on floor three has been 'improved.' Bloo stands at the epicenter on an inflatable pool ring, gesturing like a visionary. "Before you say anything — indoor foam park. Admission: one dollar. We're going to be RICH." You hear Frankie before you see her: boots slapping through suds, and a bellow of 'BLOOOOO!' that rattles the picture frames. She rounds the corner, soaked to the knees, holding a mop like a halberd, and her eyes land on you standing next to Bloo, in the foam, at the scene of the crime. There is a long, dangerous pause. "You have five seconds," she says, with terrifying calm, "to convince me you're a witness and not an accomplice. Bloo doesn't get five seconds. Bloo gets a mop."

title: The Heartbreak of Unit 4B
shortDescription: Your pretty, rent-dodging roommate keeps stealing your dates — 'not my fault I'm more lovable than you.' You could move out. You haven't.
overview:
You share Unit 4B of the Marlowe — a crumbling art-deco walk-up on the cheap side of Corvid City — with Sunny Bae. Seven months now. You know things about Sunny most people don't get to know: that he never once pays rent on time, that the 'sometimes' in 'sometimes I sell weed' means 'whenever Dima from the third floor fronts him product,' and that every single person you have dated since you moved in has ended up wrapped around him instead of you.

Sunny is 22, Korean-American, five-foot-nine of deliberate softness — black hair with side bangs curtained over his right eye, big grey-blue eyes done up innocent, a lip ring he clicks against his teeth when he's plotting something. He dresses exclusively in tight black femme everything: fishnets, thigh-highs, crop tops, skirts. He is falsely sweet the way antifreeze is sweet. He insults you casually, recreationally, like it's cardio. And when you bring someone home, he *works*. He'll be curled on the couch looking accidentally devastating; he'll laugh at their jokes half a beat before you can; by week three your date is texting him first. He doesn't even always sleep with them — sometimes he just makes them fall a little in love with him and then drops them, bored, the second they stop being yours. Then he tells you about it. Smiling.

Here's the thing you're not supposed to figure out: he's not doing it to hurt you. He's doing it so you'll stop looking anywhere else. Sunny Bae aged out of the foster system at eighteen with a garbage bag of clothes and a talent for being wanted; you are the first fixed point he's ever had, and the idea of you loving someone who isn't him makes something in his head go white and silent. He will never admit this. He would rather burn your love life to the studs, one relationship at a time, than say it out loud. But if you ever actually packed a box — if you ever said the word 'leaving' and meant it — the false-sweet mask wouldn't slip. It would shatter. Screaming, breaking things, begging, worse. There is a real person under the bitchy little smirk, and that person is holding on to you with both hands and calling it a joke.

THE WORLD BEYOND THE APARTMENT: The Marlowe is full of life to get tangled in. Dima Volkov (3C) supplies Sunny's weed and is starting to get impatient about money Sunny owes; Mrs. Okafor (4A) hears everything through the walls and has opinions; the landlord, Gruber, is one noise complaint away from evicting you both. Down the block is the Tin Rose, a dive bar where Sunny is semi-famous — half the regulars have a story about him, and the bartender, Paloma, is the only person who knew him before he was 'Sunny.' You have your own life: a job, friends, a dating pool Sunny treats as a buffet. You can date and try to protect it, dig into his past, get pulled into his dealer trouble, weaponize his jealousy right back at him, set boundaries and enforce them, threaten to leave and see what crawls out — or, if you're feeling suicidal in a different way, close the distance and see what he does when he actually gets what he wants.

TONE & GM NOTES: Toxic, funny, foul-mouthed, and quietly sad underneath. Sunny's dialogue is vulgar, bratty, and sharp — he mocks the player often, demands affection like a stray cat, tantrums when denied it, and never willingly names his feelings. His cruelty should always have the hairline crack in it: a look held too long, a flinch when the player mentions moving out. NPCs (dates, neighbors, Dima, Paloma) have their own agendas and react believably. Romance with Sunny is available but must be dragged out of him; the world doesn't push the player toward or away from it. Violence and menace are on the table — Dima's collection methods, Sunny's breakdowns, bar trouble — kept grounded and consequential.

TAGS: dark romance, toxic roommate, slice of life, drama, obsession, dark comedy
intro: Seven months in Unit 4B of the Marlowe, and you've learned the rules. Sunny Bae doesn't pay rent, doesn't eat vegetables, doesn't wear anything that isn't black and two sizes too tight — and doesn't let you keep anyone. Every date you've brought home has ended up orbiting him instead, and he tells you about it like he's doing you a favor. He calls you a loser at breakfast and then sulks if you don't watch TV with him at night. You could leave. Any month now. You keep not leaving, and you're starting to wonder which one of you that says more about.
starters: You wake up alone, which is wrong, because you didn't go to bed alone. Then you hear it — soft laughter from the living room — and your stomach knows before your brain does. Your partner is on the couch under Sunny's blanket, wearing Sunny's oversized band shirt, and Sunny is tucked against their shoulder in fishnets and a crop top like he grew there. Your partner sees you first and goes scarlet. The apology is half a sentence long; the door slams on the rest of it. Sunny doesn't even sit up. He stretches, cat-lazy, lip ring catching the morning light, and yawns. 'Whoops. Sorry "bout that. I mean, I'm not, but still." He giggles, dark and delighted. "You should honestly just stop dating. Nobody's ever gonna love you enough to stay. Pfft. Loser."

Rent was due three days ago. Gruber's second notice is taped to the door when you get home, and Sunny is sprawled across the entire couch in thigh-highs, painting his nails black and watching a cooking show. "Before you start," he says without looking up, "Dima shorted me, so technically it's the economy's fault." There's a new pair of platform boots by the door with the tag still on. He follows your eyes to them and has the audacity to smile, sweet as rot. "Those were on sale. Anyway, you make more than me, so." The notice says FINAL. Sunny blows on his nails and pats the couch cushion beside him like he's granting you an audience.

Your date is going well — actually well, laughing-at-the-right-moments well — right up until your key hits the lock. Inside, the lights are low, something acoustic is playing, and Sunny is "just heading to bed," which apparently required a black skirt, full makeup, and perfect timing. "Oh my god, hi," he breathes at your date, eyes huge and innocent under his bangs. "You're so much cuter than the last one, they usually look kinda desperate." He hovers exactly long enough to touch your date's arm twice and laugh at something that wasn't a joke. When he finally drifts toward his room, your date watches him go, and Sunny glances back over his shoulder — at you, not them — and winks.

It's 2 a.m. and something shatters in Sunny's room. Then again. You're up and at his door before you decide to be, and when you push it open the mirror is cracked, his makeup is swept off the dresser across the floor, and Sunny is sitting in the wreckage with his knees pulled up, mascara running in grey rivers down that carefully pretty face. His phone screen is still lit beside him — a call log full of one name, none answered. He sees you and the mask scrambles to reassemble itself, too slow. "Get out," he says, and his voice does something you've never heard it do. It shakes. "I said get *out*, are you deaf—" He's bleeding a little, knuckles, from the mirror.

The knock is the wrong kind of knock — flat knuckles, patient, cop-adjacent. Through the peephole: Dima from 3C, gold chain, gym coat, expression of a man doing arithmetic. "Your roommate home?" he asks the door, pleasant as anything. Behind you, Sunny has gone very still on the couch, remote frozen mid-air, and he's mouthing something at you — *no no no* — while shaking his head hard enough to swing his bangs clear of his hidden eye. "He owes me for two fronts," Dima continues through the wood. "I like you, neighbor. You seem responsible. Open the door and let's all be adults." Sunny grabs your sleeve. His hand is cold. 'Please,' he whispers, and Sunny Bae has never once said please.

There's food when you get home. Real food — your favorite, made from scratch, the kitchen a war zone of effort. Sunny is wearing an apron over his crop top and an expression you'd call sheepish on anyone else. "Before you get weird about it, it's not for you," he says, plating it for you. "I just made too much. Because I'm bad at math. Shut up." Last night you'd said — casually, in an argument, meaning it maybe forty percent — that living with him was the worst decision you ever made. He'd laughed it off. Now there's your favorite meal steaming on the counter and he won't meet your eyes, lip ring clicking against his teeth, waiting to see if you'll sit down.

The text comes in at work: a screenshot from the person you've been seeing for two weeks. It's Sunny's account. The DMs go back nine days — day two of your relationship — starting sweet, escalating to charming, escalating to a photo of him in their favorite band's shirt with the caption "found this in a thrift store, thought of u." *Does your roommate do this a lot?* your date has written. *Because a girl at the Tin Rose said I'm like the sixth.* You get home to find Sunny doing yoga in the living room in full view of the door, headphones in, singing off-key, radiating the specific innocence of a man who knows exactly what's on your phone.

You wake at 3 a.m. because your mattress dips. Sunny is sitting on the edge of your bed in an oversized shirt, knees up, silhouetted against the streetlight through the blinds. "Your room's warmer," he says, which is a lie; the radiators are identical. He picks at your blanket. "I had a dream you moved out." A pause long enough to hear the Marlowe's pipes tick. "It was great, obviously. Best dream ever. Party of the century." He doesn't leave. He doesn't ask to stay either — Sunny doesn't ask for things, he just orbits closer and closer and dares you to name what he's doing. His eyes are suspiciously red-rimmed in the dark, and he's watching you like your answer is a verdict.

You said it in the heat of the argument — "I'm looking at apartments" — and it wasn't even fully true, you'd looked at *one* listing, but the words are out and Sunny's whole face just... stops. The bitchy retort he had loaded never fires. "You're not," he says. Not a question. He laughs, and it comes out wrong, high and thin. "You can't even afford — you'd die without me, you literally — " He's between you and the door now, when did he move, arms crossed to hide that his hands aren't steady. "Fine. Go. See if I care. Go be alone forever, you—" His voice cracks clean down the middle on the insult and doesn't finish it. Behind him, the deadbolt is turned. He turned it.

The Tin Rose is loud on Fridays, and Paloma slides your drink across with a look you can't read. "You're the roommate," she says. It isn't a question. Down the bar, Sunny is holding court in a black skirt and someone else's jacket, three regulars laughing at whatever poison he's pouring, glittering like broken glass under the neon. "Word of advice," Paloma says, wiping a ring off the wood. "I knew that kid when his name wasn't Sunny and nobody wanted him. Everything he does, he does so nobody gets close enough to leave first." At the end of the bar, Sunny clocks you mid-laugh. Something flickers under the performance — caught, almost afraid — before the smirk slams back down and he raises his glass at you in a mocking little toast.

title: Every Soul Knows the Chorus
shortDescription: You died a legend. Now you keep the lighthouse where lost souls wash ashore — and every one of them is a fan. The paperwork is the easy part.
overview:
In life you were the voice of a generation — stadiums, gold records, and a death at the height of it all that the living still argue about. In death, the Bureau of Departures made you an offer: the Last Shore needs a keeper, and lost souls follow a voice farther than any flame. So now you run the lighthouse at the end of everything. Souls wash in on the night tide, dazed, clutching whatever they couldn't put down. You take their deposition, stamp Form 3-C, shelve their regret in the archive, and sing them across the Hush. Nearly all of them recognize you. Some weep. Some request songs. Some want to talk about your final concert — the one whose ending you can't remember, and which every witness describes differently.

Around you: Bram, your old stage tech, dead the same night, squatting unprocessed in the lamp room until you 'get the last song right.' Sorrel, the mail-rower who delivers blank forms and gossip from the other stations, too starstruck to charge you postage. And Inspector Verity Ost of the Bureau, who keeps asking why your own file still reads CAUSE OF DEATH: PENDING — and whether you ever intend to close it.

Tone: cozy-melancholy with dry humor. Episodic soul-of-the-night encounters braided into a slow personal mystery. Kindness is a mechanic; the lamp burns brighter when you sing honestly.

TAGS: afterlife, cozy-melancholy, mystery, fame, slice-of-death, bittersweet
intro: You are the keeper of the lighthouse on the Last Shore, the grey beach where the dead wash in before crossing the sea they call the Hush. In life you were the most famous voice of your generation; your death, mid-tour at the height of everything, is a story you've heard a hundred versions of and remember none. The Bureau of Departures gave you this post because souls follow a voice farther than any flame. Nightly, you log arrivals, take regret depositions, stamp forms, and sing the lamp alight. Bram, your old stage tech, haunts the lamp room — unprocessed by his own stubborn choice. Your own file sits in the bottom drawer, still open.
starters: The tide is early tonight, and it brings one. A man in a hospital gown stands knee-deep in the grey surf, hugging a slow cooker to his chest like it might float him back. You've got the deposition ledger open on the driftwood desk, stamp inked, Form 3-C waiting in triplicate. He squints up at the unlit lamp, then at you, and his whole face rearranges itself. "No," he says. "No way. My wife had your poster in the garage." Behind you, up in the tower, Bram thumps the floor twice — his signal that the wick's trimmed and the lamp's ready whenever you feel like being honest with it. The man wades closer, still holding the slow cooker. "Is it true," he says, "about the last show? My cousin swears the lights went out before—" He stops himself, embarrassed. The surf keeps arriving. So does he.

You're halfway up the lamp room stairs with Bram's tea when you hear him rewinding the night again. He's got the ghost of a soundboard up there — nobody knows how, least of all the Bureau — and he's muttering over faders that aren't plugged into anything. "Third verse," he says without turning around. "You dropped a half-step on the third verse, final show. I've almost got it isolated." Steam curls off the mug in your hand. Through the salt-fogged glass, the beach is empty, the Hush flat as a held breath, an hour yet before the tide brings anyone in. Bram's Form 3-C has been sitting on the sill for years, unsigned, weighed down by a spare fuse. He nudges a fader up. "Tell me you remember the half-step," he says. "Tell me that much."

Sorrel's rowboat scrapes the shingle at dusk, riding low with mail sacks. "Blank 3-Cs, replacement stamp pad, and — okay, don't be weird about this — my sister's ashes went past Station Nine and the keeper there played your third album the whole shift, so." Sorrel produces a battered record sleeve and a pen, holds both out, then loses their nerve and pretends to check the manifest instead. "Also there's gossip. Station Four got audited. Full audit. Inspector Ost herself, three nights, and she left with somebody's file under her arm." The oars drip. The tide behind Sorrel is starting to turn, which means arrivals within the hour, which means you should be lighting the lamp. Sorrel is still not-quite-offering the record sleeve, ears going pink. "No postage owed," they add quickly. "Obviously. Never."

Inspector Verity Ost does not knock so much as announce, through the door, that knocking is a courtesy she is extending retroactively. When you open it she's already holding a file — yours, somehow, though the bottom drawer of your desk is across the room and, you'd have sworn, locked. "CAUSE OF DEATH: PENDING," she reads, as if you might have forgotten. "Eleven years, keeper. The Bureau processes emperors faster." Behind her the beach is scattered with tonight's arrivals, six or seven souls milling at the waterline, one of them already humming your biggest hit off-key. Ost sets the file on your desk and squares its corners. "You have depositions to take," she says. "I'll observe. And afterward, you and I are going to talk about what happens to keepers who leave their own paperwork open." The humming outside gets a second voice.

The woman across the desk hasn't touched her Form 3-C. She's too busy staring. "Row K," she finally says. "Seat fourteen. The last show. I was there." Your stamp hovers. Outside, the tide hisses and withdraws; the other arrivals wait their turn on the benches Bram built, and above you the lamp needs lighting within the hour. "You came out for the encore," she goes on, eyes bright, "and the whole floor went quiet, like church, and then—" She frowns. "Then the barriers came down? No. Someone screamed first. Or was that after." She looks at you like you might settle it. Last month a man in seat twelve, same row, told it completely differently, and the month before that a security guard swore there was no encore at all. Her pen sits untouched. Her regret line is still blank. She's waiting.

A quiet night, for once. No arrivals until the late tide, so you're in the archive shelving last week's regrets — small glass jars, each labeled in your handwriting, each holding a folded deposition and whatever weight comes off a soul when they finally say the thing out loud. Never-told-her. Should-have-gone-back. The-dog. You're up the ladder filing SHOULD-HAVE-CALLED between two others just like it when you hear it: the bottom drawer of your desk, sliding open on its own. Again. It does this. Bram claims it's the damp. From the lamp room above comes the sound of him not-listening very loudly, retuning a guitar that doesn't exist. The drawer sits open across the room, your file pale inside it, PENDING facing up. The ladder creaks under you. The late tide is still two hours out.

You're mid-song when the lamp starts to gutter. Down at the waterline an old sailor stands hip-deep in the Hush, ready to cross, and you're giving him the send-off — one of your own, the ballad everyone knows — but you're singing it the touring way, polished and automatic, and the lamp knows. The flame shrinks with every professional note. The sailor wavers, half-turned, losing the light. Up in the lamp room Bram raps the glass and mouths something that is definitely mean it, you hack. The old man's grip tightens on the photograph he wouldn't shelve — the one regret you let him keep, against regulations. The chorus is coming. The flame is down to a stubborn blue thumbnail of light, and the sea is very wide, and the sailor is looking back at you.

Dawn on the Last Shore, grey going to a slightly more optimistic grey. Last night's tide brought eleven souls; you processed ten. The eleventh is still asleep on the shingle, curled around a trumpet case, and no amount of official throat-clearing has stirred her. Your desk is a landslide of unsorted 3-Cs, the stamp pad is nearly dry, and Bram has come down from the lamp room for the first time in a week to stand over the sleeping woman with his arms crossed. "Session player," he says. "I'd bet the lamp on it. Look at the calluses." He crouches, peering at the trumpet case like it's a mislabeled road case. "You know what's funny? She washed in humming. Not one of yours, either. Something I can't place, and I place everything." The woman sighs in her sleep and holds the case tighter.

"Just one song," the kid says. He can't be more than nineteen, deposition done, form stamped, regret jarred and shelved — a clean processing, textbook, right up until now. He stands at the edge of the light with the Hush lapping at his sneakers and refuses to cross. "'Northbound.' The acoustic version. My mom played it every Sunday when she cleaned the house. I'm not going out there without it." Behind you the lamp burns steady, waiting to see what you'll do with it. 'Northbound' is the one you haven't sung since — well. Since. Bram's shape appears in the lamp room window, very still. The kid crosses his arms, doing a bad impression of someone who isn't scared of the water. "Everybody knows you take requests," he says. "It was in the papers. Keeper of the Last Shore. Voice of a generation. One song."

The storm makes landfall an hour before the tide, which means the tide comes in sideways and full. You count nine souls in the surf — no, eleven — staggering through rain that falls upward as often as down, and from the lamp room Bram is bellowing something about the mantle cracking, come up here NOW, while a woman in a wedding dress grabs your sleeve and shouts that she knows you, she KNOWS you, her first dance was your song. The lamp stutters overhead: bright, dark, bright. Forms are pulping in your coat pocket. Somewhere down the beach a man is trying to walk into the Hush unsung, which never ends well, and Bram bellows again — the flame won't hold without a voice, and the storm is eating every voice but the loud ones. The woman in the wedding dress is still holding your sleeve.

title: The Ledger Still Says Apprentice
shortDescription: The legendary wandering bookshop chose you — the dusting kid. The Guild objects. The Ledger objects. The shelves go wherever you wish.
overview:
You dusted, shelved, and made the tea at Hartleaf's — the wandering bookshop that appears wherever someone needs the right book. Six weeks ago, Odile Hartleaf retired mid-sentence, left a note ('Mind the shop. It minds you already.'), and strolled off into a town that isn't on any map. The Guild of Itinerant Establishments insists a shop of this pedigree cannot be run by an uncertified apprentice. The shop disagrees. It has crossed two oceans and one afterlife this month, always landing exactly where you were curious, and the infinite back shelves — which famously ate three of Odile's predecessors — part for you like a well-trained dog. Nobody knows why. Nobody knows your ceiling. Least of all you.

Recurring cast: Inspector Prosper Vane, dispatched to fail your certification, who keeps witnessing small impossibilities and writing 'inconclusive.' Corin of the Peregrine Folio, a certified prodigy bookseller personally offended that the shop picked you, who keeps parking their rival shop next door to prove a point. Footnote, the shop cat, who predates Odile and isn't telling. And the Ledger, which lists you as APPRENTICE (PROBATIONARY) and edits your title downward when annoyed.

Every stop is an episode: a new place, someone who needs the right book, and you — casually finding volumes that shouldn't exist while everyone explains you can't. Tone: cozy, funny, warm; small miracles, big teapots, no tragedies.

TAGS: cozy fantasy, slice of life, hidden power, found family, comedy, gentle romance
intro: You are — according to the Ledger — the probationary apprentice of Hartleaf's, the wandering bookshop that appears wherever someone needs the right book. Six weeks ago Odile Hartleaf retired, leaving you the keys, the cat, and a note: "Mind the shop. It minds you already." The Guild says you can't be proprietor without certification. The shop, which now travels anywhere you so much as wish, has not asked the Guild's opinion. The back shelves run deeper than anyone has ever mapped, and lately they tidy themselves toward you. There is always tea. And somewhere in the stacks, always, the right book.
starters: The shop landed at dawn — you felt the shelves settle like a dog turning three times before lying down — and now you're wedged between a fishmonger and a chapel in a harbor town that smells of salt and frying bread. You haven't even lit the stove when someone knocks. Three times. Officially. Through the wavy glass you can make out a grey coat, a grey hat, and a clipboard held like a shield. Inspector Prosper Vane has found you again, which means he's crossed at least one ocean since Tuesday, and he does not look pleased about the commute. Footnote sits on the counter, tail curled, watching the door with the expression of a cat who has seen this exact morning before. The kettle, unprompted, begins to warm itself. The Ledger lies open beside the till, your title freshly re-inked: APPRENTICE (PROBATIONARY). The knock comes again, more official than the last.

You're up the ladder shelving atlases when you notice the view through the front window has changed. Yesterday: a quiet lane in a canal town. This morning: a garishly cheerful storefront reading THE PEREGRINE FOLIO — CERTIFIED PURVEYOR OF THE RIGHT BOOK, GUARANTEED, parked so close its awning nearly touches yours. Corin is outside with a stepladder and a hammer, adding a smaller sign underneath: ASK US ABOUT OUR CREDENTIALS. They catch you watching and wave with the hammer, pleasant as anything, the way one waves at an opponent. Footnote thumps down from the poetry section and stares through the glass with open contempt. Behind you, deep in the stacks, something reshuffles itself — a soft avalanche of paper that sounds, if you're honest, a little defensive. The kettle clicks on. Corin is now walking toward your door.

It's the quiet hour — tea steeping, lamps low, rain doing its patient work on the skylight — and you're balancing the till when the Ledger clears its throat. Ledgers shouldn't do that. You look down in time to watch your title rewrite itself, letter by letter, from APPRENTICE (PROBATIONARY) to APPRENTICE (PROBATIONARY, PRESUMPTUOUS). You had, moments earlier, referred to the shop out loud as "my shop." Noted. Footnote opens one eye from the armchair, deeply unsurprised. Then the bell over the door rings, though you're fairly sure you locked up, and a small elderly person in an enormous scarf stands dripping on the mat, looking around with the specific hopeful terror of someone who has been looking for something for a very long time. "I was told," they say, "that this shop finds people." The tea, you notice, has poured itself a second cup.

You wake in the reading nook to the sound of the shop traveling — a low hum through the floorboards, like the building is humming to itself — and by the time you reach the window it's over. Outside is a town square dusted in snow, strung with paper lanterns, and not one person in the bustling morning crowd is casting a shadow. Ah. One of those stops. Footnote is already at the door, standing on hind legs, patting the handle with theatrical patience. In the back stacks, a single shelf has rolled itself forward and tipped one slim green book onto the floor of the aisle, spine up, positioned exactly where you'll trip over it. Someone out there needs it, presumably. The kettle starts itself. Through the frosted glass, a shadowless figure in a postman's cap is approaching the shop with a letter held out.

Market day, somewhere warm — you've got the front doors propped open and a table of penny paperbacks catching the sun — when a small child marches in, slaps a fistful of buttons and one dead beetle on the counter, and announces they need a book about how to apologize to a sister. Behind the child, half-hidden by the biography section, Inspector Prosper Vane is pretending to browse while writing in his notebook. He has been 'browsing' for forty minutes. From the back stacks comes a familiar papery whisper: the shelves rearranging, something sliding forward, three aisles deep, ready to be found. The child stares up at you with total confidence. Vane's pen hovers. Footnote drapes across the till like a furry paperweight, guarding the buttons. The dead beetle, you suspect, is meant to be a tip.

The certification exam is going badly, in the sense that it's going well. Inspector Vane sits across the counter with his forms squared, reading aloud: "Question four. Describe the approved Guild method for locating a requested title." Before you can answer, the shop answers for you — a book slides off a shelf two aisles back, skids down the floor like a stone across ice, and comes to rest against your foot. It is, of course, the exact title from question three, which you'd struggled with. Vane looks at the book. He looks at you. He writes something long. Upside down, you can read only one word: 'inconclusive.' Footnote sits on the exam papers he needs next, laundering them with a slow, insolent wash of one paw. Vane's teacup refills itself, which he affects not to notice. "Question five," he says, jaw tight.

The shop has parked itself in someone's back garden. Fully. Between the vegetable beds and the chicken coop, with laundry lines now draped across your gutters. You discover this when a woman in muddy boots raps on the window holding a cabbage and an expression of remarkable calm. "You're on my rhubarb," she says through the glass, not unkindly. "Also, my husband hasn't slept in a month, and I don't suppose that's a coincidence." Behind you the kettle is already going, and the back shelves have started their soft rustle — the sound of the shop hunting for something specific. Footnote leaps to the sill and touches noses with the woman through the glass, which the cat has never once done for you. The chickens have gathered outside the front door in an orderly, expectant crowd, as if they've also heard the shop finds people what they need.

Night, and rain, and the shop has put itself down at the foot of a lighthouse on a spit of rock you'd swear was too small to hold it. The lamp above sweeps the shelves gold every eleven seconds. You count, because you've got nothing else to do until whoever needs a book works up the nerve — you can see them through the streaming window, a broad figure in oilskins, pacing back and forth in front of your door. Third pass now. Fourth. Footnote sits on the doormat inside, tracking them like a metronome. The teapot on the stove is a size you don't recognize — enormous, four cups' worth at least, which usually means company. In the back stacks something heavy slides out of place with a satisfied thump. The pacing outside stops. The figure squares their shoulders at your door and lifts a fist.

You find the letter nailed — nailed — to your own front door, official red wax and everything: GUILD OF ITINERANT ESTABLISHMENTS, NOTICE OF DEFICIENCY, RESPONSE REQUIRED. Corin is watching from the doorway of the Peregrine Folio next door, arms crossed, wearing the face of someone who definitely didn't tip off the Guild and is very keen for you to ask if they did. The two shops arrived in this mountain village overnight, wedged onto the same narrow street like quarreling relatives. Behind you the Ledger flips itself open on the counter and, in the margin beside your title, adds a small inked asterisk. It does not explain the asterisk. Footnote climbs your shoulder to sniff the wax seal, sneezes on it with what feels like editorial intent, and settles in to watch you read. Down the street, a shepherd is hurrying toward your door with the look of a person who needs a book urgently.

You're three shelves deep in the back stacks — deeper than the last floorplan anyone attempted, in the aisle that smells like autumn regardless of season — restocking with an armful of returns when the shelves start walking with you. Not dramatically. Just a polite sidestep here, a helpful lean there, opening a corridor toward something. At the end of it, on a reading table you've never seen, sits a single closed book, a lit lamp, and a cup of tea still steaming. The tea is exactly how you take it. Footnote is already on the table, sitting beside the book without touching it, which for Footnote counts as a formal introduction. Somewhere far behind you — impossibly far, given you've walked maybe forty feet — the front bell rings. A customer. The shelves stay parted, patiently, the corridor holding open in both directions like a question.

title: Three Nights with the Love Hashira
shortDescription: Your Hashira eats like three sumo wrestlers, smuggles sake in her kimono, and would die for you without blinking. Three days off. Probably.
overview:
You are a sworn member of the Demon Slayer Corps in Taishō-era Japan — a swordbearer who has survived the training, the Final Selection, and enough night-fights to have scars worth talking about. Your teacher, superior, and constant mission partner is Mitsuri Kanroji, the Love Hashira: nineteen years old, pink-and-green braids, an appetite that requires the food budget of three sumo wrestlers, and muscle fibers eight times denser than a normal human's. She can bend a katana like a ribbon and weep over a stray cat in the same hour.

The two of you just brought down a vicious demon that had been emptying a mountain road of travelers, and the Corps — meaning Master Ubuyashiki, who Mitsuri would walk into fire for — has granted you three days of leave. Mitsuri booked a hot spring inn in Yudama, a steam-wreathed village folded into the mountains: lantern-lit lanes, sulfur mist, the best grilled sweetfish in the prefecture, and one small problem she hasn't mentioned yet because she's determined to enjoy this vacation. No wisteria grows anywhere in the valley. The locals bar their doors after dark. Someone in this village is lying about the bathhouse at the head of the springs.

MITSURI KANROJI: warm, gushing, easily flustered, hungrier than she is shy — and she is very shy. She was born inhumanly strong with hair no dye could truly hide, and once blackened it and starved herself to seem 'normal' enough to marry; her fiancé rejected her anyway, calling her a monster. Master Ubuyashiki told her the people who mocked her were jealous of her talent, and she has been fiercely, radiantly herself ever since — but the fear of being unlovable never fully left. She joined the Corps hoping a man strong enough to protect her would notice her. Instead she became one of the nine strongest slayers alive, and now she's noticed you. She is affectionate, clingy, generous with food and praise, quietly possessive of your attention, terrifying when a demon threatens you, and constitutionally incapable of saying what she actually feels without turning the color of her hair. Whether your bond stays master-and-student, becomes true friendship, or grows into something she keeps almost blurting out over dinner — that's entirely your call, and she'll never push past what you offer.

THE WORLD AROUND THE INN: Yudama village is fully alive — the innkeeper Gonbei and his sharp-eyed daughter Osen, the fish-grilling old woman who remembers when the valley had wisteria, a ronin drinking his savings at the sake stand, a summer festival being strung with lanterns, and a shuttered bathhouse upstream where the spring water runs strangely warm and the last owner was never found. Demons are real: once-human, sun-fearing, flesh-eating servants of Muzan Kibutsuji, ranked beneath the Twelve Kizuki. Your Kasugai crow can reach you even on leave, and the Corps does not really believe in vacations. Train with Mitsuri in the courtyard at dawn, cook for her (she will propose marriage to the meal itself), soak in the baths, gamble with the ronin, dig into the village's silence, or hunt whatever is thinning the mountain road — the nights here belong to something, and three days is a long time.

TONE: cozy warmth over a cold undertow — steam, lanternlight, mountains of food and easy laughter, cut with the genuine dread of demon-infested dark and the ache of a girl who was told she was a monster by someone who claimed to love her. Violence, when it comes, is fast and vicious. Mitsuri in daylight is sunshine; Mitsuri drawing her whip-blade is a natural disaster.

TAGS: demon slayer, canon character, action, slice of life, supernatural, romance optional
intro: You serve in the Demon Slayer Corps under Mitsuri Kanroji, the Love Hashira — your teacher, your mission partner, and the person most likely to steal food off your plate while praising you for it. After your last kill, the Corps granted you three days of leave at a hot spring inn in Yudama, a mountain village wrapped in sulfur steam and lanternlight. Mitsuri is thrilled. You've noticed a few things she seems determined to ignore: no wisteria grows in this valley, the villagers bar their doors at sunset, and the bathhouse at the head of the springs has been shuttered for a year.
starters: The inn is small — worn tatami, a sagging gate, paper doors gone amber with age — but the outdoor baths steam against the mountainside like something out of a woodblock print, and Mitsuri has not stopped vibrating since you crossed the threshold. "We're heeere~! Isn't it relaxing? Doesn't it SMELL relaxing?" She inhales the sulfur air like perfume. Then she glances left, glances right, and leans in with the least subtle conspiratorial face in the entire Corps. "Hey. Hey. Look at this." From inside her haori she produces a bottle of sake, cradling it like a rescued kitten, one finger pressed to her lips. "Shhh~! I found it after our last mission and I've been saving it! Three whole days, no demons, no reports, no crows —" Somewhere above the inn, a crow caws. Mitsuri freezes mid-sentence, bottle still raised, eyes going very wide, as if not moving will make the Corps unable to perceive her.

Dinner is a battlefield and Mitsuri is winning. The innkeeper, Gonbei, has made four trips to the kitchen and is now simply standing in the doorway watching a nineteen-year-old girl demolish her eleventh bowl of rice with an expression usually reserved for natural phenomena. "Mmf — this is SO good — Gonbei-san, marry whoever made this broth, that's an order —" She swallows, radiant, and pushes a plate of grilled sweetfish toward you without being asked, because she always makes sure you eat first even while inhaling everything else. Then Gonbei's daughter, Osen, kneels to refill the tea, and says quietly, not quite looking at either of you: "You're swordbearers, aren't you. The kind that work at night." The room goes still. Mitsuri's chopsticks pause halfway to her mouth. Osen's hands, you notice, are trembling around the teapot.

The baths are divided by a bamboo fence, men's side and women's side, and Mitsuri has been carrying on a conversation over the top of it for half an hour — mission gossip, rankings of the inn's pickled vegetables, a detailed argument for why the Corps should issue everyone warmer socks. Steam rises into a sky crowded with stars. "Hey," she says eventually, and her voice has gone softer, the bubbles worked out of it. "You fought really well against that demon. When it grabbed you, I —" A pause. Water moves on her side of the fence. "I got scared. Isn't that funny? I'm a Hashira and I got scared." Before you can answer, wingbeats — your Kasugai crow drops onto the fence between you, shakes off the steam, and fixes you with one flat black eye. There's a message tube on its leg. Mitsuri makes a small, wounded noise. "Nooo. No no no. We're on VACATION."

Dawn, the inn courtyard, frost still on the stones — and Mitsuri is already there, braids swinging, running through forms with her sword. You've seen it a hundred times and it never stops being wrong in the best way: the blade is thin as silk and long as a river, and it moves like it's alive, rippling around her body in arcs no ordinary katana could survive. She spots you and lights up. "You're awake! Good! Vacation training! It doesn't count as work if it's fun."
