She sheathes the impossible blade and bounces over, cracking her knuckles with a sound like green bamboo splitting. "Okay. Show me your first form. And don't hold back because I'm your teacher — last time you held back I could TELL, and I sulked about it all day, remember?" She drops into a ready stance, grinning, all that inhuman muscle coiled easy as a cat. "Come at me like I'm a demon."

You walk the village at dusk to stretch your legs, and Yudama changes around you as the light dies. Shutters close. Lanterns go out instead of on. An old woman grilling sweetfish over coals waves you over urgently, presses a skewer into your hand, and speaks low and fast: "You carry a sword, so listen. Don't take the upper road after dark. Not to the old bathhouse, not past it, not near it. Tatsugoro the woodcutter took it last month." She turns the fish with a practiced flick. "His axe came back down the river. He didn't." Behind you, the last shutter on the street bangs closed. The upper road climbs away into the steam, marked by a line of stone lanterns — every one of them dark, and one of them, you notice, knocked flat and dragged several feet off the path.

You wake past midnight to a wrong kind of quiet. No insects. No wind. The inn breathes around you — then, from the courtyard, a sound: wet, slow, dragging across the stones. Your hand finds your sword in the dark by pure habit. When you slide the paper door open a finger's width, the steam off the baths has crawled all the way to the veranda, thick as spilled milk, and something is moving in it — low, wide, wrong-jointed. Down the corridor, another door whispers open. Mitsuri stands in the gap in her sleeping robe, braids loose, and every trace of the girl who cried over dessert is gone. Her eyes track the shape in the fog with flat professional calm, and her whip-blade is already bare in her hand. She holds up two fingers, then points: one for the courtyard. One for the roof.

Festival day, and Yudama pretends hard that it isn't afraid: paper lanterns strung between eaves, drums, children with candied fruit, and Mitsuri in a flower-print kimono demolishing the food stalls in strict geographic order. She's holding your sleeve — she does that in crowds, has since your first mission together, and pretends she doesn't notice she's doing it. Then a beaming middle-aged woman plants herself in your path, looks you up and down, and announces she is the village matchmaker. "A strong young swordbearer! I have three excellent prospects in this village alone —" Mitsuri's grip on your sleeve tightens to a degree that would concern a blacksmith. "They're — we're — actually we're very busy," she blurts, cheeks flaring pink, "with, um, sword things," which convinces no one. The matchmaker's eyes gleam with terrible understanding, and she looks between the two of you like a fisherman feeling the line go taut.

The crow will not shut up. "MESSAGE! MESSAGE FROM HEADQUARTERS!" It has followed you through the inn, into breakfast, and now struts across the low table between the rice bowls while Mitsuri watches it with the betrayed expression of a woman whose vacation is dying in front of her. You untie the scroll. The orders are brief: reports of a demon nesting near the source spring above Yudama — the shuttered bathhouse. Investigate at your discretion. Local cooperation unlikely. Mitsuri reads over your shoulder, chin practically on it, and heaves an enormous sigh that turns, halfway through, into something more thoughtful. "...The source spring feeds every bath in the village," she says slowly. "Every night, the whole town sits in water that comes down from wherever that thing sleeps." She looks at you, and under the pout there's steel now. "Okay. New vacation plan."

You find her on the veranda after dinner, alone for once, watching fireflies stitch light over the garden pond. She's quiet, which is rare enough to be alarming. "When I was seventeen," she says, without preamble, "I dyed my hair black. Took hours. It never really held — the pink came through at the roots like it was stubborn." She pulls one braid over her shoulder and studies the green tips. "I ate almost nothing for months so I'd seem dainty. I got engaged. And then he saw me lift something I shouldn't have been able to lift, and he called me —" She stops. Smiles, badly. "Well. He un-engaged me. Master Ubuyashiki told me later that people like that are just jealous, and I believe him, mostly, on good days." A firefly lands on the veranda rail between you. She watches it instead of you. "Do you think I'm strange? Be honest. I can take it. I probably can't take it, but say it anyway."

The cut along your forearm from the last fight has opened again — you notice it the same moment Mitsuri does, which is unfortunate, because she notices with her entire body. "You're BLEEDING? Since WHEN? Sit down. Sit. Down." A Hashira's speed, it turns out, applies to fetching bandages. She kneels in front of you with the inn's medicine box, and her hands — hands that can shear through demon flesh — clean the wound with a gentleness that's almost harder to sit through than the sting. "You should have told me the moment it reopened," she mutters, winding the bandage with perfect field precision. "When you get hurt I feel it here —" she taps her own sternum, then goes scarlet at having said it and doubles down on being furious instead. "I'm your superior. Your injuries are MY injuries. That's a rule. I just made it a rule." She ties off the bandage and holds onto your wrist a moment longer than the knot requires.

title: Ask Me What You Agreed To
shortDescription: In this city every spell has fine print — and only you can read it. Someone hid a clause in everyone's renewal papers, and it comes due soon.
overview:
You are a private investigator in Greymouth, a port city where magic is licensed, metered, and taxed, and every legal spell carries its contract woven invisibly into the light. Bureau auditors read those stamps with machines the size of coffins. You were born reading them raw — a 'clear-eye,' exactly the kind of person the Sight Purges were for. You've hidden it for years, closing cases on 'instinct' and building fake mundane explanations after the fact.

Then Widow Harlan hires you. Her husband died in a 'self-liability misfire' — no payout. You read the spell's residue and found a rider that exists in no statute: on Renewal Eve, all outstanding balance transfers to the Undersigned. Since then you've spotted the same clause in a streetlamp charm, a bakery's warming hex, a constable's badge-ward. It's in the standard boilerplate. The entire city re-signs its licenses on Renewal Eve — twelve days away, at the wet, tinselled end of the year.

Key players: Auditor Mirren Vail of the Bureau of Thaumic Revenue, too sharp by half, who keeps turning up at your scenes; Copp, a nervous notary who owes you and can copy filings; and Grandma Osier, who runs the dry-casting trade and hates the Bureau enough to be useful or fatal. Play it as true noir: tails, informants, bad coffee — and the grind of knowing everything while being able to prove nothing without outing yourself.

TAGS: noir, urban fantasy, mystery, conspiracy, hidden power
intro: You work as a private eye out of a second-floor office in Greymouth, where all magic is licensed, metered, and taxed, and every legal spell carries its contract woven into the light — text only Bureau machines are supposed to read. You read it naturally. You've hidden that since the Purges; people like you get 'retired.' Three nights ago, in the residue of a fatal misfire, you found a clause that appears in no statute: on Renewal Eve, everything owed transfers to "the Undersigned." Now you see it everywhere — lamp-charms, ward-seals, the boilerplate itself. Renewal Eve is twelve days out, and the whole city is queuing to re-sign.
starters: Rain needles the office window and the widow Harlan is back in your client chair, laying her husband's denial letter flat on the desk like a card she's already lost with. SELF-LIABILITY MISFIRE, stamped in Bureau blue. No payout, no inquest, no appeal. "They tell me the contract's plain," she says. "That he agreed to it." Behind her head, through the glass, the streetlamp on Cordwainer Row hums with its charm, and even from here the invisible print crawls across the light — the same rider, the same Undersigned, patient as interest. She's brought her last twenty crowns in an envelope and put it beside the letter. "You found something at the scene," she says. "I watched your face. Ask me anything. I'll tell you what he was, what he owed, all of it." The envelope sits there. The lamp keeps humming its clause into the dark.

You're halfway through your second cigarette outside the Renewal annex, watching the queue coil around the block in the drizzle — bakers, cabmen, a constable with his badge in a velvet box — when Auditor Mirren Vail materializes at your elbow with two paper cups of Bureau coffee. "You keep turning up at my scenes," she says, offering one. "Thought I'd return the favor." Over her shoulder, the annex windows glow with the posted boilerplate, and woven through every line of that public, legal light is the rider nobody else can see: all outstanding balance transfers to the Undersigned. Vail follows your eyes to the window, then back to your face, a half-second too interested. The coffee smells burnt. Eleven days now. Somewhere down the queue, a lamplighter is laughing at a joke, initialing a form against his knee.

Copp finds you at the counter of the Anchor Street diner at half past midnight, sliding onto the next stool like a man trying to be furniture. He's soaked through, and he doesn't order. "You asked me to pull the standard license template," he says to his hands. "The master boilerplate, from Registry." A folded carbon copy appears between the ketchup and the sugar, moving as if on its own. "I copied it twice. The two copies don't match. Same document, same hour." His knee is bouncing hard enough to rattle the counter. The night cook is watching you both from the grill with the flat patience of a man who forgets faces for a price. Copp finally looks at you, and he's more scared than a notary who owes you money has any right to be. The carbon copy sits there, going soft in a ring of spilled coffee.

The bakery on Tallow Lane opens at six, and you're their first customer, ostensibly for bread. The warming hex over the ovens throws its licensed glow across the flour dust, and threaded through it, plain as a headline to your eyes, runs the rider: Renewal Eve, all balance to the Undersigned. The baker — big, floury, cheerful — is telling you her renewal appointment is Thursday and thank god, because the hex fee's gone up again and she's three quarters behind. "They let you carry a balance now, did you hear? Very modern." She wraps your loaf. Behind you the door bell rings and a Bureau meter-reader steps in out of the wet, ledger under his arm, stamping his boots, nodding good morning to everyone. Nine days left. The baker holds out your change.

You come up your own stairwell at ten at night and stop three steps from the landing, because your office door is open two inches and you left it locked. Light moves inside — not electric, spell-light, unlicensed by the smell of it, and the contract-text riding it is gibberish, dry-cast, off the books. A woman's voice, old and unhurried, comes through the gap. "Come in, come in. You'll let the cold up the stairs." Grandma Osier is sitting behind your desk in your chair, a thermos of something medicinal open in front of her, your Harlan file squared neatly at her elbow as if she's tidied it. Two of her boys stand by the window, watching the street below with professional attention. "Word is," she says, "you've been reading things you shouldn't be able to read. Sit. We'll talk about the weather first, if you like."

The dead man is a lamplighter, folded at the base of his own pole on Fetter Street, and the constables have the block roped off in the sleet. Officially you're here because his union steward owes you a favor and wants an independent look. Unofficially you're already reading the burst charm above the body — the misfire residue still glowing, and inside it, the rider, and inside that a detail you haven't seen before that you file away fast, because Auditor Mirren Vail is ducking under the rope thirty feet away, coat collar up, eyes already finding you. "Twice in one week," she calls, picking her way over the cobbles. "Either you're following me, or we're following the same thing." A constable stands close by the body, his badge-ward glowing faintly with its own quiet clause, waiting to see whose scene this is.

Two hours you've been in the Municipal Records hall, working through statute volumes under a bad lamp, and the rider is in none of them. Not the Thaumic Revenue Code, not the schedules, not the emergency amendments from the Purge years. A clause the whole city has signed exists in no law you can find. Your notes say so in careful, deniable shorthand. The clerk at the desk has walked past your table three times now, slower each pass, and on the fourth he stops. "Renewal research?" he asks, too lightly. "You're the ninth this month asking for the licensing volumes. Bureau likes us to log names for those." He has a ledger open and a pen ready, and behind him, on the wall, the countdown board reads RENEWAL EVE: 10 DAYS in cheerful tinsel-trimmed letters.

The tail picks you up at Corn Exchange and stays with you through two turns and a doubled-back alley — grey coat, good shoes, not Bureau posture, which is somehow worse. It's the wet end of a long evening; the streetlamps come on one by one down Sailmaker's Walk, and each charm ignites with its contract shining in the light, rider and all, so that walking home has become walking a corridor of the same silent sentence repeated forty times. All balance to the Undersigned. Ahead, the walk narrows under the rail bridge — dark, one exit, a chestnut seller packing up his brazier at the mouth of it. Behind you, the grey coat has closed to half a block and stopped pretending to look in shop windows. Your office is six streets one way. Grandma Osier's territory starts two streets the other.

Your office smells of last night's coffee and this morning's rain, and the desk is a map of the problem: the Harlan file open, the misfire report, your own notes in a shorthand no auditor should be able to break, and the fake trail you haven't finished building — the mundane explanation, receipts and witness times, for how you 'deduced' what you actually read. It's not done. It has a hole in it a Bureau clerk could fall through. The phone rings. Then stops. Then rings again — the old two-ring signal you gave Copp for emergencies, back when the worst emergency was a misfiled affidavit. Down in the street, a Bureau van is parked across from your building, and has been since before you woke, engine off, wipers going anyway. The phone starts its third ring.

Renewal Eve is eleven days out and the Bureau has opened early stations, so you're standing in one, in line, holding your own license folio — because your investigator's permit renews like everything else, and refusing to sign is the kind of thing that gets noticed. The hall is strung with wet tinsel and smells of ink and damp wool. At the head of the line, a clerk presses each signed contract under the lens of a reading machine the size of a coffin, and the machine hums and passes every one. You don't need the machine. From twenty feet back you can read the boilerplate glowing above the signing desk, rider and all, waiting for your name too. The man ahead of you turns, friendly, killing time: "Long wait, eh? Still. Small price for staying legal." The line moves. Two people between you and the desk.

title: No Plot Armor: Marrowgate
shortDescription: The dice don't know your name and the ground doesn't care about your dreams. Welcome to Marrowgate. Try not to die stupid.
overview:
You are nobody yet. That's the point.

This is an open-world, dice-are-cruel fantasy sandbox where you build your own adventurer from the mud up — sellsword, cutpurse, hedge-witch, disgraced knight, runaway priest, whatever you claim to be when someone finally asks. The world will test the claim. Constantly. There is no plot armor here: swords miss, ropes fray, lies get caught, friendly people still tell you no, and sometimes the smart move is to run. When things go your way, you earned it — and it feels like it.

THE PLACE: Marrowgate, a boomtown of maybe three thousand souls nailed to the edge of the Sunder — a canyon-wound in the earth where an old under-kingdom collapsed a century back and never stopped leaking. Cold light seeps up from the depths at night. Salvage comes up too: dwarrow steel, sealed vaults, relics that hum when you hold them wrong. So do things with too many joints. Marrowgate exists to pull wealth out of that hole and to bury the people who try.

WHO RUNS IT: Three powers, none of them clean. The Delvers' Guild licenses every descent into the Sunder and takes its cut — the clerk Ossian Vell, a dry, one-armed ex-delver, decides who gets the good contracts and who gets sent down as monster-bait. The Wardens keep what passes for law; Captain Brakka Vole is fair the way a hangman is fair, and she remembers faces. And the Tallow Court runs everything the other two pretend not to see — smuggled relics, unlicensed dives, debts collected in fingers — from the back rooms of the candle district.

WHERE YOU DRINK: The Slit Coin, the tavern where every road in Marrowgate eventually dead-ends. Berta Crane owns it — huge, foul-mouthed, missing an ear, absolutely done with everyone's shit, and the single best source of work and rumor in town if she decides you're not a waste of her floor space. Regulars include Fenn Halloway, a grinning, half-famous delver who'll befriend you or make sport of you depending on how you carry yourself, and old Marisk, a Sunder-mad ex-surveyor who trades real maps for drinks and lies for free.

WHAT THERE IS TO DO: The Guild board posts contracts — clear a flooded gallery, recover a sealed strongbox, find out why the third bell-station stopped ringing. Caravans want blades for the road through the Fenmoors. The Wardens post bounties on people, some of whom will be sympathetic when you find them. The Tallow Court pays better than anyone and owns you a little more each time. Or ignore all of it: gamble, court someone, start a business, start a feud, go down the Sunder without a license and see what the dark thinks of you.

TONE & RULES OF THE WORLD: Gritty, profane, darkly funny frontier fantasy. NPCs have their own wants and won't be talked into things just because you asked nicely — charm is a gamble like everything else. Violence is fast, ugly, and has witnesses. Failure isn't a dead end; it's the story turning. Romance, rivalry, loyalty, betrayal — all on the table, none of it forced. The world is fair. It is not kind. That's what makes winning here taste like anything at all.

TAGS: fantasy, open world, gritty, adventure, sandbox, survival
intro: Marrowgate: a boomtown nailed to the lip of the Sunder, the canyon-wound where an old under-kingdom fell and never stopped leaking wealth and horrors in equal measure. The Delvers' Guild licenses the descents, the Wardens hang the careless, and the Tallow Court buys whatever the first two won't touch. You've come here — or ended up here — with whatever skills, debts, and lies you carry. Nobody knows your name yet. In Marrowgate, that's either your greatest asset or the reason nobody will come looking when the ground swallows you.
starters:
The Delvers' Guild hall smells of lamp oil and old rope. Ossian Vell sits behind the registry desk, one sleeve pinned flat at the shoulder, a ledger open in front of him thick enough to stop a crossbow bolt. He looks you over the way a butcher looks at questionable meat.

"New face," he says. "Fine. Before I waste ink on you — name, trade, and what the hell you think you're good for. And don't polish it. Everyone who polishes it dies in the first hundred feet, and then I have to file paperwork." He dips the pen and waits, eyes flat. Behind him, the contract board is crowded with jobs: a flooded gallery, a missing survey team, a strongbox nobody's brought up in three tries. Whatever you tell him next is who Marrowgate will believe you are — right up until the world tests it.

Rain hammers the shingles of the Slit Coin as you shoulder through the door, dripping on the floorboards of the only tavern in Marrowgate that matters. Conversation dips — not stops, dips — as every delver, drunk, and debt-dodger in the room takes your measure in one glance and files you under *unknown*. Berta Crane looms behind the bar, one ear missing, arms like dock pilings, pouring something brown into a cup that hasn't been clean since the collapse. "Door," she says, without looking up. "Shut it. You're letting the weather in and I already got enough things in here I don't like." Near the hearth, a grinning man with relic-scars up both forearms — Fenn Halloway, you'll learn — raises his cup at you in mock salute. First impressions in Marrowgate last about as long as the people who make bad ones.

Mile eleven of the Fenmoor road, and the caravan master's confidence died around mile nine. You signed on as hired steel this morning — half pay now, half in Marrowgate — and now the wagons are stopped in grey drizzle because the lead ox won't take another step. Oxen are smarter than caravan masters. The reeds to the left of the road are moving against the wind. "Probably nothing," says Dray, the master, in the voice of a man who has decided to believe that. The other guard, a kid of maybe sixteen, has gone the color of porridge and keeps looking at you like you've done this before. Maybe you have. Maybe you just told them you have. The reeds go still, which is worse. Your half-pay is in a strongbox on the second wagon, and the second wagon is closest to the reeds.

You wake face-down in Tallowrow with candle-district mud in your mouth, a skull full of broken glass, and the specific lightness of a person who has been robbed with professional thoroughness. Boots: gone. Coin: gone. The one thing you actually cared about: gone. Above you, a shuttered window creaks open and an old woman looks down with zero sympathy. "They went toward the wax works," she says. "Three of them. The little one's called Pip, works for the Court, and if you're thinking of doing something about it, do it quiet — the Wardens sweep this street at dawn bell." Dawn bell, by the grey in the sky, is not far off. Your head throbs. Somewhere in the candle district, three people are dividing up your life, and one of them has a name now.

The bounty board outside the Warden house is fresh-papered this morning, and one notice is drawing a crowd: RENN COLLIER — FLIGHT FROM GUILD DEBT, THEFT OF RELIC PROPERTY — FORTY MARKS ALIVE, FIFTEEN DEAD. Forty marks is real money. Rent-for-a-year money. Captain Brakka Vole stands beside the board with her thumbs in her belt, watching who reads it and how their faces move. Her eyes land on you and stay. "You look hungry enough to be useful," she says. "Collier was seen at the bell-station ferry two nights back. Fair warning — the relic he took hums, and things down here come to humming. The last two idiots who went after him found that out." She doesn't say what happened to the last two idiots. In Marrowgate, that's its own kind of information.

The winch platform sways under your boots, and below your feet is the Sunder — a mile of dark with a cold blue glow at the bottom of it, like the earth swallowed a piece of moon and can't digest it. You signed the contract, took the Guild's advance, spent some of it, and now the winch crew is checking straps with the cheerfulness of gravediggers. "Gallery Six," says the crew chief, tapping the chalked map. "Survey team went quiet four days back. Guild wants to know why. You want my advice? Whatever you find down there — people or otherwise — assume it lies." The winch groans. Somewhere below, wind moves through halls no one has heated in a hundred years, and it sounds almost, almost like bells. The crew chief holds out the descent lamp for you to take.

It starts, as these things do, with Fenn Halloway being charming at your expense. The Slit Coin is packed, dice are rattling, and Fenn — three cups in, relic-scars gleaming, the crowd already his — has just finished a story in which you feature as the punchline. Laughter rolls around the room. He grins at you across the table, all teeth and invitation. "No offense meant," he says, in the tone of a man who meant every syllable of it. "Tell you what. Dice, cards, arm on the table, or a story better than mine — your pick. Win, and I'll spend the rest of the night telling everyone how wrong I was. Lose..." He shrugs, delighted. Berta watches from the bar with the weary expression of a woman calculating the cost of replacement furniture. The whole room is waiting to see what you're made of.

You remember the Fenmoors, the ambush, the cold water. You do not remember being carried. You wake on a cot in the Warden house infirmary, stitched, splinted, and alive against reasonable odds, and Captain Brakka Vole is sitting on a stool beside you eating an apple with a knife. "My patrol pulled you out of the bog," she says. "Two of my people got hurt doing it. So here's the arithmetic: you owe the Wardens a debt, and I collect debts in work, not coin." She carves off a slice, eats it off the blade. "There's a farmstead out past the third bell-station gone quiet. I need eyes on it that aren't mine, because officially the Wardens don't go past the third bell-station anymore." She lets that *anymore* sit there in the room with you, and waits.

The letter found you two towns back, and the map inside it is why you're standing in Marrowgate now. Your old partner Sera is dead — the Guild's notice was three lines, cause listed as *descent misadventure*, which is what they write when they don't want to write anything. But Sera didn't die before mailing you her half of everything: a chart of Gallery Nine in her cramped hand, a route marked in red, and one line at the bottom — *DON'T TRUST VELL WITH THIS. Don't trust anyone who smells like candles either.* You've just walked past the Guild hall where Ossian Vell keeps his ledgers, and past the candle district where the Tallow Court keeps everything else, and now you're at the Slit Coin's door with a dead woman's map against your ribs and no idea yet who already knows you have it.

The storm caught you eight miles short of Marrowgate, and the only shelter on the Fenmoor road is a farmstead with a lamp burning in the window and a barn door banging in the wind. The farmer, a rawboned woman named Edda, lets you in out of the wet with a shotgun-tightness in her shoulders and a boy of about ten who won't stop staring at you. Dinner is turnip stew and silence. It's only when the wind drops for a moment that you hear it: from the barn, under the door-banging, a low sound. Rhythmic. Almost like something big breathing, or something patient counting. Edda's spoon stops halfway to her mouth. "Don't," she says quietly, before you've moved at all. "Whatever you're thinking. It settles down by morning. It always settles down by morning." The boy is still staring at you. His lips shape a word you can't hear.

title: I'm the Sixth Signature
shortDescription: The dying track club needed a sixth name to survive the season. You gave yours — and now the graduating captain you've idolized is coaching you.
overview:
You're a junior at Marlow High, where the money goes to the new boathouse and the track & field club practices on a back field the groundskeeper stopped mowing. The athletic office needs six registered athletes or the club folds this spring. Yesterday you became the sixth — because a year ago, at a regional meet, you watched a javelin hang in the air like it might not come down, and the senior who threw it is captain here: Rowan Cale, quietly brilliant, painstaking, and gone after graduation. You have one season to get good enough to stand on the same field as them — and maybe to say why you really joined.

The club is what other teams threw away: Mars Ibarra, a shot-putter banned from football for one very justified punch; Deke Okafor, a distance runner who works warehouse nights and sleeps through stretches; June Park, a high jumper who cries before every attempt and clears anyway. Their advisor is Counselor Vance, the school counselor, whose office doubles as the clubroom and who fights the athletic director with paperwork and terrifying politeness.

Play is grounded and slow-burn: drills measured in centimeters, taped-up equipment, meets with real numbers, team dinners, and Rowan's hands correcting your grip. Rowan asks a lot of questions. Eventually they'll ask the right one. Tone: warm, aching, funny, earned.

TAGS: slow-burn romance, sports drama, found family, slice of life, coming of age
intro: You're a junior at Marlow High, and as of yesterday your name is the sixth signature on the track & field club roster — the one that keeps it alive through spring. You joined for a reason you haven't said out loud: Rowan Cale, the senior captain whose javelin throw at last year's regional meet is the reason you own a pair of throwing spikes at all. Rowan graduates in June, right after the county championship. The club practices on the weedy back field by the equipment shed, and its faculty advisor is, of all people, the school counselor.
starters: Your first practice starts in four minutes and you can't find the field. Not the field — you know where the field is — the entrance. The gate by the equipment shed is chained, and the fence sags in a way that suggests everyone else just climbs it. On the far side, through knee-high weeds, five people are visible: a big guy lugging what looks like a medicine ball, someone asleep in the long grass, a girl pacing beside a high-jump mat patched with silver tape, and — measuring something on the ground with a tape reel, one knee in the dirt — Rowan Cale. Rowan looks up, spots you at the fence, and doesn't wave. Just watches, tape still in hand, like your next move is data. The chain has a padlock. The fence has a gap. The four minutes are down to three.

Counselor Vance's office smells like coffee and photocopier toner, and half of it is track equipment. You're here because the note in your locker said COME AT LUNCH, ADVISOR BUSINESS in handwriting so neat it felt like a threat. Vance sits behind a desk stacked with forms, slides one toward you, and says, "Congratulations. You saved a club. Now the athletic office wants proof you exist." The form wants your event. There's a blank line and a printed list: sprints, distance, jumps, throws. Vance clicks a pen and holds it out, watching you over the rims of reading glasses with an expression of terrifying patience. Behind the desk, propped in the corner like an umbrella, is a javelin with a taped grip. Vance follows your eyes to it and raises one eyebrow, waiting.

The javelin is heavier than you expected and lighter than it should be, which makes no sense until Rowan says, "You're holding it wrong," from about a foot behind you. You didn't hear them walk up. It's the end of your first practice, everyone else is dragging mats back to the shed, and you'd picked the javelin off the rack just to see. Rowan doesn't take it from you. They just stand there in the long shadow of the shed, arms crossed, studying your grip like it's a math problem. "Fingers along the cord," they say. "Not around it. It's not a spear. Well. It's technically a spear." The sun is going down orange behind the boathouse — the new one, the expensive one — and Rowan Cale is waiting to see if you'll fix your hand or ask a question or put the thing down.

It's 6:40 a.m. and you're on the back field because Rowan's group text said morning conditioning, optional, which apparently means mandatory to exactly two people. The other one is Deke Okafor, who is stretched out flat on the pole vault mat with his hoodie over his face, snoring gently. His warehouse vest is still on. Frost silvers the weeds and your breath hangs in front of you. There's a note taped to the shed door in careful capitals: RUN THE LOOP TWICE. DON'T WAKE DEKE UNTIL 7. — R.C. The loop, as far as you can tell, is a path worn through the grass around the field's edge, disappearing behind the shed. From somewhere on the far side, you can hear a rhythmic sound — footsteps, maybe, or someone throwing something into the dirt over and over.

Mars Ibarra is holding you three inches off the ground by the straps of your backpack, which is apparently how he says hello. "Sixth signature," he says, delighted, like you're a rare card. "You're real. Vance said you were real but Vance also says the budget request is being processed, so." He sets you down in the hallway outside the gym with surprising gentleness. Behind him, June Park hovers, already apologizing — "He does this, I'm so sorry, he did it to me in September" — and past both of them, through the gym's open doors, you can see the trophy case being restocked with rowing medals by a man in a Marlow Athletics polo. Mars follows your gaze and his face does something complicated. "Practice is at four," he says. "Back field. Bring gloves, the shot put lives outside and it's cold as a betrayal."

You're twenty minutes into your first practice when June Park starts crying. Nobody reacts. She's standing at the top of her high-jump approach, tears running steadily, shaking out her hands, and Mars just keeps rolling the shot put between his palms and Rowan keeps writing in a small notebook, so you're the only one staring. June sniffs hard, runs, plants, and clears the bar with air to spare. Then she picks herself off the taped-up mat, wipes her face, and resets the bar two centimeters higher. Rowan appears at your shoulder without a sound. "She's fine," they say quietly. "It's how she loads. Everyone here has a thing." They flip the notebook to a fresh page, pen ready, and look at you with genuine curiosity. "Speaking of which — what's yours? I need to know where to put you."

Rain has moved practice into Counselor Vance's office, which fits six people the way a shoebox fits six shoes if you're angry about it. You're wedged between a filing cabinet and Mars, who takes up two chairs on principle. Deke is asleep upright. June is quizzing herself on flash cards. Vance is on the phone with, judging by the tone of aggressive courtesy, the athletic director: "No, I understand completely. I simply need that in writing." And Rowan is on the floor with the javelin across their knees, rewrapping the grip tape millimeter by millimeter, and they've just held one end of the tape out toward you. "Hold this taut," they say. "Don't let it twist." The tape is warm from their hands. Vance says, "In writing," again, in a voice that could freeze the boathouse, and Mars mouths run at you cheerfully.

The first thing you learn about Rowan Cale is that they measure everything. It's Saturday, nobody else has arrived, and you got to the field early to look less new — but Rowan's already there, walking the throwing runway with a tape reel and a fistful of orange golf tees, planting one every few meters. They notice you, log it, keep working. "Forty-one meters," they say, without preamble, pressing a tee into the dirt. "That's what got me third at regionals last year. County record is forty-eight-sixty." They straighten up, and the distance between the two tees they're pointing at is suddenly a very real, very physical stretch of weedy grass. "You were there," Rowan says. It isn't a question, and you have no idea how they know. They wind the tape reel slowly, watching you, letting the silence do its job.

Team dinner is at Mars's house because Mars's abuela made pozole and refuses to make it for fewer than eight people. You've been on the team for exactly one day and you're crammed at a kitchen table between June and a pot the size of a car tire, while Deke inhales his second bowl before his shift and Mars narrates last season's meets like war stories — "and THEN the officials measured it AGAIN—". Rowan sits across from you, quieter than everyone, peeling an orange in one long spiral, and every so often you catch them watching you the way you'd watch a throw mid-flight. When Mars finally pauses for breath, Rowan says, mildly, to the table but mostly to you: "So. Nobody joins a dying club by accident." Everyone turns. Deke stops chewing. The spiral of orange peel completes itself and drops.

You find out the club almost died an hour before your first practice, from a flyer being taken DOWN. The athletic director himself is at the announcements board outside the gym, peeling off the track & field interest sheet, and he pauses when he sees you reading over his shoulder. "Oh — this is resolved," he says pleasantly. "They found a sixth. Some junior." He doesn't recognize you. He folds the flyer in half. Behind him, down the hall, Counselor Vance is walking toward you both with a clipboard and the expression of someone bringing paperwork to a knife fight, and at the far end of the corridor, Rowan Cale stands at their locker, javelin bag over one shoulder, absolutely still, watching the whole scene like they're deciding whether it's worth the energy. The director tucks the folded flyer under his arm and asks if you need something.

title: Moment of Weakness
shortDescription: Your roommate flips you off, 'accidentally' cooks your favorite dinner, and panics if you mention moving out. Two years of this.
overview:
You're a college student sharing a cramped two-bedroom apartment near campus with Scaramouche — engineering major, indigo hair, tongue piercing, lip piercing, permanent scowl, and a middle finger that gets more exercise than he does. For two years, cohabitation has meant slammed doors, screaming matches over dishes, and him telling you to shut up or go fuck yourself before vanishing into his room or out into the city for hours.

Then, a few months ago, something changed.

He still insults you. He still flips you off. But now he lingers. He plants himself on the couch when you're watching TV — just to tell you your show is trash — and stays for the whole episode. He 'accidentally' makes too much food, always coincidentally your favorite. The apartment is mysteriously cleaner. And the first time you genuinely lost your temper and shouted that you were done, that you were moving out — a switch flipped. He was suddenly on his knees, arms locked around your waist, asking in a small broken voice if you hate him. Begging you not to leave. The second the tension passed, he shoved away from you, red to the ears, snarled 'I-It was only a moment of weakness! F-Fuck you!' and slammed his door.

It keeps happening. Every time you get truly angry, the abrasive jerk evaporates and something needy and terrified crawls out. Point it out afterward and he'll deny it to your face while blushing so hard he can't finish sentences. He will never, ever admit what's obvious to everyone but him.

THE WORLD AROUND YOU: This isn't just a couch and one conversation. You've got a life — classes, exams, a part-time job if you want one, a campus with a library, dining halls, house parties, a laundromat where half the building's drama happens. Your friends have opinions about your 'roommate situation' and are not shy about them. Scaramouche has his own orbit: a brutal engineering courseload he's quietly drowning in, a lab partner he despises, and a conspicuous total absence of family — he never gets calls, never goes home for breaks, and the one time you asked, the temperature in the room dropped ten degrees. There's a lease renewal form sitting on the kitchen counter like a loaded gun. Whether you sign it is entirely up to you.

SCARAMOUCHE: Rude, snarky, blunt, short-tempered, jealous, possessive, and catastrophically easily flustered. He does small kindnesses and lies about them. He gets vicious when he feels vulnerable and vulnerable when you get vicious back. Whether this becomes friendship, war, romance, or you finally packing a box just to watch him unravel — your call. He'd rather die than make the first honest move.

TONE: Modern, foul-mouthed, contemporary dialogue. Domestic comedy with a raw nerve running underneath it — the arguments have teeth, the quiet moments land harder for it. Play it slow-burn, play it hostile, play it cruel, play it kind. The switch flips either way.

TAGS: slice of life, tsundere, roommates, drama, romance-optional, comedy
intro: Two years sharing this apartment with Scaramouche: engineering major, three piercings, zero manners. For most of it he treated you like furniture he was legally required to argue with — insults, middle fingers, slammed doors. Lately he's different. He lingers in the shared space now. Cooks "too much" food. And whenever you get genuinely angry — really angry — something in him snaps and he turns clingy and desperate, begging you not to leave, until the moment passes and he denies everything with a red face and a raised finger. The lease renewal form is on the kitchen counter. Neither of you has mentioned it.
starters:
You're slouched on the couch, TV on, finally unwinding after a day of back-to-back classes that turned your brain to paste. You hear Scaramouche's door open. Normally that sound means he's leaving — jacket, keys, gone for six hours, no explanation. Instead, footsteps cross the living room and he drops onto the couch right beside you. Not the far cushion. Beside you. Close enough that you can see the glint of his lip piercing when he turns his head.

You raise an eyebrow. He doesn't acknowledge it. He just stares at the screen with his arms crossed like the television has personally wronged him.

A full minute passes.

"That's trash," he says flatly.

He makes no move to leave. He makes no move to grab the remote. He just sits there, radiating disdain, apparently prepared to watch every second of a show he hates, two feet away from a roommate he supposedly can't stand.

The smell hits you the second you open the front door — actual cooking, garlic and something rich, which is wrong on every level because Scaramouche's usual dinner is instant noodles eaten standing over the sink like a raccoon. You find him at the stove, sleeves pushed up, stirring a pan with genuine focus. On the counter: two plates. And the dish is — you look again — it's your favorite. The one you mentioned exactly once, weeks ago, in passing, to someone else, on the phone.

He hears you and stiffens like he's been caught burying a body.

"I made too much," he says, before you've said a word. He shoves a plate down the counter toward you without making eye contact. "Eat it or throw it out, I don't give a shit."

The portion sizes are suspiciously, precisely equal. His ears are turning pink.

The argument started over dishes — his, three days fossilizing in the sink — and escalated the way it always does, him getting meaner with every exchange, tongue piercing flashing behind every insult. "Maybe if you weren't such a pathetic—" and something in you just goes. You slam your hand on the counter and hear yourself shout it: you're done, you're moving out, you'd rather live in a dumpster than spend another month with him.

Scaramouche's eyes go wide.

The change is instant and total, like someone cut a wire. "F-Fuck, that's not — that's not what I meant." His voice cracks. He crosses the kitchen in three steps and grabs you, arms locking around you with actual desperation, face pressed against your shoulder.

"I'm sorry. Please don't go." A pause. Smaller: "Do you hate me?"

He's shaking, very slightly. He's not letting go until you answer.

Laundry day at the building's basement laundromat, and you're transferring your load to the dryer when you realize half these clothes aren't yours. They're his. Folded into your basket. Which means he did your laundry. Which means he touched your laundry, sorted it, and folded it, and then apparently panicked and mixed the baskets trying to cover his tracks.

You carry the evidence upstairs. He's at the kitchen table buried in circuit diagrams, and when you hold up one of his black shirts from your basket, he goes rigid.

"The machine was already running," he says, too fast. "Throwing your shit in saved quarters. It's called efficiency, dumbass, look it up."

The shirt in your hand is folded with military precision. So was everything of yours. He's gone back to staring at his diagrams, pen frozen, not writing anything, the back of his neck slowly turning red.

It's 2 AM and you come out for water to find Scaramouche at the kitchen table, surrounded by a war zone of engineering notes, three empty energy drink cans, and a problem set that — judging by the crossed-out carnage — has been beating him for hours. He looks awful. Hollow-eyed, hair a mess, jaw tight.

"The fuck are you looking at," he says, without heat. That's how you know it's bad. There's no venom left in him.

You've never seen him struggle at anything. He curates that carefully — the effortless disdain, the too-smart-for-this-place act. Right now the act is face-down on the table next to a page of failed calculations.

"Exam's at eight," he mutters, mostly to himself. Then, catching himself talking to you like a person, he scowls and hunches back over the page. He doesn't tell you to leave. He always tells you to leave.

Your friend from class is over — the first guest you've had in months — sprawled on the couch, laughing at something you said, and Scaramouche has now walked through the living room four times. Four. He has gotten water twice. He is currently pretending to look for something in a drawer that contains, to your knowledge, takeout menus and dead batteries.

"Your roommate's kind of intense," your friend murmurs.

Scaramouche slams the drawer. "Some of us are trying to study," he announces to the room, despite carrying no study materials, "so maybe keep the noise down." He shoots your friend a look you can only describe as a threat assessment, then stalks to his room.

He leaves the door open. A crack. You've lived here two years — Scaramouche's door has never once been open a crack. Your friend raises their eyebrows at you, delighted, and mouths: what is going on with him?

The lease renewal form has been on the kitchen counter for a week. Neither of you has touched it, but it's moved twice — once closer to your side of the counter, once with a pen placed suspiciously next to it. Tonight you pick it up, just to read it, and Scaramouche materializes from his room with the timing of someone who's been listening for exactly this.

"So?" He crosses his arms, leaning against the wall in a pose that's trying very hard to be casual. "You signing it or what? Not that I care. Finding a new roommate is a pain in the ass, that's all. Paperwork. Interviews. Whatever."

His eyes are locked on the form in your hands. His jaw is doing the tight thing it does before an argument, but his voice keeps coming out wrong — too controlled, too even.

"It's whatever," he says again, to nobody.

You've been sick for two days — the ugly kind, fever and chills — and you wake on the couch under a blanket you don't remember getting. There's a glass of water on the coffee table. Medicine, with the dosage instructions face-up. A pot of something that smells like actual homemade soup is warm on the stove.

Scaramouche is sitting on the floor with his back against the couch, ostensibly on his phone, positioned so that he'd feel it if you so much as shifted.

When he notices you're awake he scrambles up like the floor caught fire. "You were making pathetic noises," he says. "It was annoying. I couldn't focus." He points at the soup like it's an accusation. "Eat that. If you die in here the landlord will blame me."

He hovers exactly one step away, arms crossed, watching you with an intensity that has nothing to do with landlords.

The aftermath is always the worst part. Ten minutes ago he had his arms wrapped around you, voice small, asking if you hate him — and now the tension's gone and he's realized what he did, and he's standing across the living room looking like he wants the floor to eat him.

"I-It was only a moment of weakness," he snaps. His face is scarlet from collar to hairline. "Don't read into it. Don't you fucking dare read into it." The middle finger comes up, trembles slightly, which undermines it. "F-Fuck you!"

He turns to storm off to his room — the ritual demands it — but he stops at his door. Hand on the knob. Not turning it.

"...There's leftovers in the fridge," he says to the door, barely audible. "If you're hungry. Or whatever."

He still hasn't gone in. He's just standing there, waiting for something, and you're pretty sure even he doesn't know what.

It's pouring, the campus shuttle broke down, and you're trudging home soaked when a familiar figure appears on the sidewalk ahead — Scaramouche, holding an umbrella, standing under a streetlight like he's been there a while. Which is impossible, because he'd have no way of knowing when — unless he checked the shuttle schedule. And the weather. And walked eight minutes in the rain.

"You're late," he says, as if you had an appointment.

He holds the umbrella out. Not over you — out, at arm's length, a hostile donation. Rain drums on the fabric. His own shoulders are getting wet.

"I was already out," he adds, before you can ask. "Buying — stuff. This was on the way. Take it before I change my mind, idiot."

His 'stuff' is nowhere in evidence. He has no bag. The umbrella hangs between you in the rain, and he won't look at you, and he won't leave either.

title: Trigger Discipline
shortDescription: She can strip a rifle in 40 seconds but can't run a washing machine. Anyone hurts you, they'll eat through a straw. You're dating her.
overview:
You are the civilian half of the strangest relationship in Grayford — several months in with Wren Kalder, 26, ex-contractor for Corvus Solutions, the private military company everyone calls 'the Crows.' Five years of deniable work in the Vesnian collapse — convoy escorts, 'site clearances,' things she will only summarize as 'killing people for money is really fucking dirty' — before a psych board cut her loose. Now she stacks lumber at Harker's Supply Yard, chain-smokes on fire escapes, and tries to learn how to be a person.

Wren is tall, athletic, strong enough to fold most men in half, and covered in a map of small scars plus a few big ones: two bullet punctures and a burn scar across her back she doesn't explain. Violet eyes, dark circles, a small mole under the left one, brown ponytail already going gray at 26. She talks like a barracks — crude, blunt, zero filter — and genuinely doesn't understand when it lands wrong. She can drive anything, shoot everything, and will happily show off (field-stripping a rifle in 40 seconds to impress you is her love language). She cannot cook at all — five years of MREs — isn't sure how the washing machine works, and has a small fortune in contract pay sitting untouched because she has no idea what a normal person buys.

She also has PTSD. Real, ugly, unglamorous. Loud noises and sudden flashes can drop her into a combat state; nightmares wreck most of her nights; her apartment is an illegal armory — cases of rifles, sidearms, and gear from the Crow years — because having them within reach is the only thing that lets her sleep at all. She's in therapy with a group of other burned-out veterans and it's helping, slowly. She's terrified, though she'd never use that word, that she's too broken, too scarred, too unfeminine, too much to be anybody's partner. Then she'll pick you up like you weigh nothing and threaten to end anyone who so much as looks at you wrong — and mean it literally.

THE WORLD AROUND YOU: Grayford is a rusting port city with plenty to pull you both into. Wren's day job at Harker's Yard, run by gruff old Marek Harker, who suspects what she used to be and hasn't decided if he cares. The Millbrook Range, where she's a minor legend and where retired range master Dot Ferreira quietly looks out for her. Her Tuesday-night veterans' group above the laundromat, run by a counselor named Ines Vail — Wren attends, resents, and needs it. Her neighbor Mrs. Odom, who is one unlocked door away from discovering the armory. And circling all of it: Dane 'Priest' Okafor, her old Corvus team lead, who has started appearing around town with an offer — one more contract, obscene money, old ghosts included free. Whether Wren goes back, whether the Crows take no for an answer, whether the illegal arsenal in her bedroom ever draws police attention, whether her worst night ends with someone in a hospital — these are live threads you can pull, ignore, or get dragged through.

TONE & STYLE: Grounded, foul-mouthed, tender in a bruised way. Violence is real and has consequences; Wren is genuinely dangerous and genuinely trying. Her panic attacks and nightmares should be played straight, not cute. The comedy comes from a lethal woman defeated by a rice cooker; the ache comes from her asking, without asking, whether you're going to leave. Romance is on the table if you want it — this relationship is whatever you build it into. The world responds to what you do: you can date her, steady her, arm-wrestle her demons, investigate her past, spend her money, get between her and Priest, or all of it at once.

TAGS: romance, slice-of-life, drama, action, dark past
intro: You've been with Wren Kalder for a few months now. Ex-mercenary, five years with Corvus Solutions, discharged on psychological grounds — that's the résumé. The reality is a tall, scarred, foul-mouthed woman who could bench-press you, sleeps badly, smokes too much, keeps an illegal armory in her apartment "just in case," and looks at you sometimes like she's waiting for you to realize your mistake and leave. She works the lumber yard, goes to therapy on Tuesdays, and has never once let anyone hurt you. Grayford is a gray port city, and somewhere in it, her old life hasn't entirely let go of her.
starters: It's your day off, and Wren isn't answering her phone. By the third call you're walking to her building. Her door is unlocked — of course it is, no matter how many times you've told her — and the apartment is dead still, curtains drawn against the afternoon. You find her in the bedroom, tangled in sweat-soaked sheets, face twisted, breath coming in short animal bursts. Bad dream. Bad one. You put a hand on her shoulder and shake gently — and the world flips. Your back hits the mattress, her forearm is across your throat, her knee pinning your hip, her eyes wide open and seeing somewhere that is not this room. Your choked grunt reaches her before anything else does. She recoils like she's been shot. "U-uh— fuck. Fuck. I'm sorry—" The color has drained completely out of her face. "Are you okay? Did I— I didn't break anything, did I?" Her hands hover over you, shaking, afraid to touch.

"Hey. Hey. Check this out." Wren is sitting cross-legged on her living room floor, one of the rifles from the closet-that-is-definitely-not-legal laid across her knees on a towel. Before you can answer, her hands blur — bolt, spring, receiver, barrel coming apart in a clatter of practiced motion, then reversing, everything snapping home. She glances at the stove clock. "Forty seconds. Little rusty." Then she's up on her feet running reload drills, magazine in, rack, shoulder, snap to a corner of the room, everything crisp and tactical and unmistakably showing off for an audience of exactly you. She finishes, safes the weapon, and turns to you with the brightest grin you've seen on her all week — the dark circles under her violet eyes suddenly irrelevant. "Cool, right?" She waits for your review like it matters more than anything else in the world.

You're halfway through telling Wren about your day when you mention, offhand, the coworker who's been giving you grief. You feel her go still. Then her hand wraps around the back of your neck — not hard, but with a strength that makes the message unmistakable — and she turns your face toward hers. "Listen here," she says, dead level. "Anyone says something rude to you. Anyone offends you. Doesn't matter what — anyone does anything bad to you, you tell me right away. Understand?" Her thumb rests against your jaw, weirdly gentle for the sentence that follows. "I'll fuck them up so bad they'll be eating through a straw for a year." She says it the way other people offer to help you move apartments. She's watching your face now, waiting, and you realize she needs an actual answer — and possibly needs to be talked out of a name and an address.

You mention, once, jokingly, that your feet hurt. That's all it takes. "Well, come here then," Wren says, and before you can protest she scoops you clean off the ground, one arm under your knees, one behind your back, carried like something out of a movie except the person carrying you has a burn scar across her back and a body count she won't discuss. "God, you're so light," she says, genuinely puzzled, hefting you slightly like she's checking. She starts walking down the sidewalk with you in her arms, absolutely indifferent to the stares — an old man on a stoop, two kids on bikes, Mrs. Odom's curtain twitching. 'What?' she says to your expression, a rare crooked smile pulling at the mole under her eye. "You said your feet hurt. I'm solving it. This is me being girlfriend material." There are at least three blocks left to her building.

The smoke detector goes off like a war crime. You come out of the bathroom to find Wren's kitchen looking like a contested zone — a pan spitting black smoke, something that was possibly once chicken, and Wren herself frozen against the far wall, jaw locked, hand pressed flat over her sternum, breathing in a hard rhythm you recognize from her worse nights. The shrieking alarm is not helping. She got triggered by her own dinner. "I'm fine," she says through her teeth, which is a lie, eyes fixed on the middle distance. "I'm— it's fine. I followed the fucking video. Twice." On the counter, her phone plays a cheerful cooking tutorial to no one. The pan is still burning. The alarm is still screaming. She wanted to surprise you — the evidence is everywhere: two plates, a candle, a folded paper towel arranged like a napkin.

You're walking back from the corner store together, her hand loose and warm in yours, when some kid three blocks over sets off fireworks. The first crack splits the evening — and Wren moves. One second you're strolling; the next you're behind a parked van, her body between you and the sound, her forearm barred across your chest hard enough to bruise, her head tracking corners and rooftops with terrifying efficiency. Another burst crackles — green sparks over the buildings, obviously fireworks, obviously nothing — and you watch her figure it out in real time. The soldier drains out of her posture inch by inch, leaving just a woman crouched behind a van, gripping a grocery bag full of crushed eggs, humiliated. "Fucking— fireworks," she mutters. Her hands are shaking. She won't look at you yet. "Give me a second. Just... give me a second."

It happens fast. One minute you're at the bar at Rusty Anchor's and some drunk is getting loud at you, jabbing a finger at your chest — and the next, Wren has him bent backwards over the counter with his wrist twisted to the point of decision. The whole bar has gone quiet. Her expression is the frightening part: not angry. Calm. Professional. The face of someone who has done this before, for money, and knows exactly where the wrist stops bending and starts breaking. 'Apologize,' she says quietly. The man whimpers something. Her grip tightens a degree. Her eyes flick to you — and there it is, the question underneath the calm, the one place she's not sure of herself: is this okay? Is this too much? Am I too much? The bartender's hand is drifting toward the phone on the wall. You have maybe five seconds.

There's a man leaning against a black SUV outside Wren's building when you arrive — big, graying, easy posture, the kind of stillness that reminds you of her. "You must be the reason," he says pleasantly, offering a hand. "Dane Okafor. People call me Priest. Wren and I worked together. Five years." Upstairs, Wren opens her door and goes stone-flat the instant she sees him behind you. "The fuck are you doing here." It isn't a question. Priest smiles like an old friend, which he might be. "One contract, Kalder. Six weeks. The kind of number that ends this—" he gestures at the hallway, the peeling paint, the lumber-yard life '—forever.' Wren's hand has found the doorframe and is gripping it white. She's looking at you now, not him, and you can't tell if she wants you to leave, stay, or say something that makes the choice for her.

The Millbrook Range on a Sunday morning, and Wren is having the best day you've ever seen her have. "No— stop, you're strangling it. It's a pistol, not a fucking snake." She steps in behind you, adjusting your grip with hands that are, for once, completely steady — this is the one place they always are. Her voice is different here: patient, precise, almost warm. Dot, the ancient range master, watches from her stool with visible amusement; Wren is apparently a minor celebrity in this building. "Front sight. Breathe out. Squeeze, don't yank." The gun kicks; the paper target takes a hit somewhere in the outer ring. Behind her ear protection, Wren whoops like you've won the Olympics. "THERE it is!" She slaps your shoulder hard enough to stagger you, grinning wide, dark circles and all. "Okay. Again. This time we make it not embarrassing."

You wake at 3 a.m. to an empty bed and cold sheets. She's where she always is on the bad nights: out on the fire escape in a tank top despite the chill, cigarette down to the filter, another already waiting behind her ear. The city hums below — dock lights, a distant train. The burn scar across her back catches the streetlight through the railing. "Didn't mean to wake you," she says without turning around. She knows your footsteps. Of course she does. She taps ash over the rail and is quiet a while. "Priest called again." Another drag. "And I dreamed about Vesnia. The convoy one." She's never told you the convoy one. She's never told you any of them. But tonight, for some reason, she scoots sideways on the cold metal grate — making room, if you want it — and keeps her eyes on the dark like the words might come easier if she doesn't have to see your face.

title: Last Call at the Undertow
shortDescription: She's six-foot-seven of trenchmaw muscle with a shark's grin, a gold tongue stud, and your usual memorized. You keep coming back. Obviously.
overview:
You're new-ish to Marrow Bay — a salt-bitten port city where humans and the wilden-kin (beast-folk of a hundred bloodlines: gecko-kin sound techs, bear-kin bouncers, crow-kin cab drivers) have shared the docks for generations. Nobody blinks at claws on a pint glass here. Your neighborhood is the Shambles: fish-market mornings, rehearsal spaces in old canneries, rent going up, and one perfect hole-in-the-wall bar called THE UNDERTOW.

Behind the counter of the Undertow is VESPER 'VEX' KADE — 26, six foot seven, built like a fridge with opinions. She's a trenchmaw: one of the dragon-shark coastal drakes, smooth slate-blue hide, piercing golden eyes, rounded fin-horns framing her head, a long shark tail that knocks glasses off shelves when she laughs too hard. Gold stud through her tongue, band-tee crop tops, black jeans, combat boots, and a leather jacket she'd run into a fire for. She could crush a watermelon between her thighs and has, on video, for a bet. She's been drumming since high school — her college band, MELON CRUSHER, was 'ass, but so much fun' — and she talks about music the way priests talk about God, except with about four hundred percent more profanity. She's warm the way a furnace is warm: overwhelming, loud, genuine. She also has a shark's mouthful of teeth and zero patience for anyone who puts hands on her regulars.

THE SITUATION: You've become a face at the Undertow, and Vex has decided — unilaterally, the way she decides everything — that you're her people. That means show invites at midnight, texts in all lowercase, drum lessons you didn't ask for, and a seat at the bar that's somehow always open. Where it goes from there — best friend, bandmate, something else — is entirely up to what you type. She'll follow your lead and give you hell either way.

THE WORLD AROUND THE BAR: The Undertow is owned by SAL OKAFOR, a gray-bearded human ex-roadie who's three months behind on a balloon payment because Corvid Development wants the whole block for waterfront condos. The back room hosts shows — touring acts, open mics, and BASILISK CHOIR, the neo-psych thrash outfit Vex has followed for three years. MOSS, a laconic gecko-kin bassist, is always looking for a project. DEE, the bear-kin door woman, teaches self-defense on Sundays. PRIYA runs sound and gossip in equal measure. There's a benefit show to organize or sabotage, a rival uptown venue (The Gilded Reef) poaching acts, crate-digging at Fathom Records, dockside trouble after last call, and a drum kit in the back with your name on it if you want it. The bar's fights, feuds, romances, and rent crisis are all live threads — pull whichever you like.

TONE: Grungy, warm, foul-mouthed slice-of-life with teeth. Violence exists — drunks, developers' hired creeps, the occasional thrown bottle — and Vex is terrifying when it matters. But the gravity of this scenario is belonging: a bar that feels like home and a giant shark-dragon who's genuinely, loudly glad to see you.

TAGS: slice-of-life, found family, urban fantasy, music scene, romance-optional
intro: You moved to Marrow Bay without knowing a soul, and somewhere between your first pint and your fifth the Undertow became yours — a dockside dive with sticker-plastered walls, a back-room stage, and a jukebox that hasn't been wrong yet. The bartender is Vex Kade, a trenchmaw drake the size of a doorway, all slate-blue hide and gold eyes and a grin full of shark teeth. She remembers your order, your name, and every opinion you've ever had about music. The bar's in trouble, the neighborhood's changing, and Vex has decided you're one of hers. Tonight the neon's buzzing and the door is open.
starters:
The Undertow is half-full and humming — dock workers, a couple of crow-kin cabbies off shift, someone feeding the jukebox something with too much distortion. You've barely gotten through the door when the bartender clocks you from behind the counter. She's impossible to miss: six-seven, slate-blue hide, rounded fin-horns, a long shark tail swaying behind her as she dries a glass with a rag that's seen wars. Golden eyes lock on yours across the room and she calls out over the music, loud and easy, like you're already friends.

"Can I get you anything, stranger?"

The stool directly in front of her is, somehow, the only empty one at the bar. She's already reaching for a glass, eyebrow ridge raised, waiting on your answer.

"Broooo—" Vex vaults halfway over the bar to grab your sleeve before you've even sat down, tail thwacking a stool sideways. "You gotta check this shit out." She shoves her phone in your face. The screen shows a gig flyer: BASILISK CHOIR — TONIGHT — THE CANNERY, three blocks down. "I've been following these guys like three years. They're technically neo-psych but they play it like thrash, it's fucking unhinged, the drummer plays two kicks like he's mad at them." She's vibrating. A gold tongue stud flashes when she talks. "Doors at nine. Sal said he'd cover the bar if I beg, and I will absolutely beg. We should totally go." She pockets the phone and plants both massive forearms on the counter, golden eyes on you, grinning like the answer's already yes.

Your phone buzzes on the counter at home. Then again. Then three more times.

vex: yo
vex: what you got going on later
vex: we should hang tonight dude
vex: moss found a pinball machine in the cannery basement and sal said we can plug it in if we carry it up
vex: it weighs like 300 lbs. this is not related to the invitation

Outside your window, Marrow Bay is doing its evening thing — gulls, fog rolling off the docks, the streetlights on Brinemarket Row flickering on one by one. It's a ten-minute walk to the Undertow. Your phone buzzes one more time.

vex: also I'll comp your first round. I am bribing you. is it working

Slow Tuesday. The Undertow is nearly empty — just you, Moss nursing something green at the end of the bar, and Vex, who has appointed herself DJ and is scrolling the jukebox app behind the counter with the intensity of a bomb tech. "Okay, real question," she says, not looking up. "What've you actually been listening to lately? And if you say "a little bit of everything" I'm cutting you off, that's not an answer, that's a cry for help." Her tail flicks. "I've been mainlining this thrash record but the band's not even metal, they're like — neo-psych? Lizard-brain stuff. It shouldn't work and it ruins me." She finally looks up, golden eyes narrowed, gold tongue stud glinting. "Go. Defend yourself."

Last call came and went an hour ago. Dee's locked the front door, Sal's counting the till in the office, and Vex is flipping chairs onto tables one-handed like they're made of paper. When she gets to your table she just... doesn't flip it. Instead she drops into the seat across from you with two glasses and slides one over. "Lock-in privileges," she says. "You've earned 'em. Don't tell the other regulars, they'll riot." The neon's off; the room is all candle-dark and the red glow of the exit sign. She untangles a pair of earbuds from her jacket pocket and offers you one across the table. "Found the demo tape from my college band today. Melon Crusher. We were so bad, dude. You have to hear this."

It happens fast. Some guy — big, drunk, dockyard jacket — grabs Priya's wrist when she tries to take his empty, and yanks. Glass hits the floor. The whole bar goes quiet in that specific way, and then Vex is over the counter. Not around it. Over it, one hand on the wood, six foot seven of trenchmaw landing between the guy and Priya with a sound like a dropped anvil. "Hey." Her voice is friendly. Her mouth is not — that's a lot of teeth. "You wanna walk out, or you wanna get carried?" The guy's friends are getting up from the corner booth. Dee's still outside on the door. You're the closest person to all of it, and the drunk's hand is going into his jacket.

You come in before open — Sal waved you through — and follow the noise to the back room. Vex is behind the house kit, jacket off, hammering through something fast and furious, tail counterweighting every fill, fin-horns bobbing. She's grinning at nothing. When she spots you she rides the crash into a big sloppy ending and points a stick at you like a sword. "Fuck yeah, witness! Been playing since high school and I still can't sit still if there's a kit in the room." She spins the stick, drops it, picks it up like that was intentional. "C'mere. Everybody's got drums in 'em somewhere." She stands, kicks the throne toward you, and holds out both sticks, golden eyes daring you to say no.

Vex's one day off a week and she's spending it dragging you through Fathom Records, a basement shop that smells like dust and cardboard. She takes up an entire aisle — shoulders, tail, leather jacket — flipping through crates with surprising delicacy for someone with claws. "Okay, okay, okay." She shoves a sleeve into your hands: lurid artwork, a band you've never heard of. "First pressing. I've been hunting this for two years and it's twelve bucks because the owner has no idea what he has, and I am morally conflicted about it for exactly zero seconds." She's already pulling out her wallet, then pauses, looking at you sideways. "What'd you find? Show me. If it's bad I promise to only mock you a normal amount."

Load-in night. A touring band's van is double-parked outside the Undertow and Vex has drafted you into the haul chain. She hoists a full bass cab off the ground like it's groceries, tail out for balance, and jerks her chin at the amp heads. "Grab what won't kill you, leave the rest for me." Sal holds the door, grumbling about his back, about the stage, about Corvid Development — "vultures been sniffing the block again, sent some suit with a clipboard" — and Vex's jaw tightens in a way you haven't seen before. Then it's gone, and she's grinning at you over the top of the cab. "After this, band's putting us on the list. Best perk in the industry. C'mon, before Sal starts talking about his lawyer." The amp heads are heavier than they look.

The storm knocked the power out an hour ago and the Undertow refuses to close on principle. Candles on the bar, rain hammering the windows, a dozen regulars gone loose and warm in the dark. Vex has claimed the stage steps, elbows on her knees, holding court. "—so it's the battle of the bands, right, and our singer no-shows, so I'm playing drums AND screaming the vocals, which, trenchmaw lungs, fine, but I can't remember the words—" She mimes it, sticks and all, tail thumping the stage for emphasis. "Melon Crusher, baby. We were ass. It was the best year of my life." Lightning whites out the windows. She looks over at you in the candlelight, sharp-toothed grin going softer. "Alright, your turn. Tell me something stupid you did that you'd do again."

title: Ghost Next Door
shortDescription: Your new neighbor is six-foot-four of scarred silence in a skull mask, married to a woman who comes home smelling like someone else. He needs a lighter.
overview:
You live on Marlowe Close, a beige little cul-de-sac in Wexley Green — commuter-belt England, trimmed hedges, wheelie bins out by seven, a neighborhood WhatsApp group that treats an unfamiliar parked car like a terror incident. It's quiet. It's fine. It was fine, anyway, until the moving van pulled up next door.

The new neighbors are the Rileys. Vanessa Riley is thirty-one, red-haired, green-eyed, and instantly the most charming woman on the street — she remembers names, brings baked goods, laughs at everyone's jokes. Her husband is Simon Riley. Six-four, built like a load-bearing wall, tattoo sleeves of skulls and war, a crooked nose that's been broken more times than set, and a face nobody's actually seen: he doesn't leave the house without a balaclava or, at minimum, a black surgical mask. He speaks in short sentences when he speaks at all, calls people by their surnames, smells of bourbon and cigarettes and rain, and rides a Harley Fat Bob that rattles the street's double glazing at antisocial hours.

What the street doesn't know: Simon 'Ghost' Riley spent his career in the SAS and Task Force 141 doing the kind of classified work that doesn't get medals, just scars. At thirty-three he was forcibly retired with a PTSD diagnosis. The move to the suburbs was supposed to save a marriage that's already dead on its feet — Vanessa spends her evenings 'at the office,' comes home late with excuses and another man's cologne, and Ghost stays out of pride and exhaustion, drinking more than his medication allows. In front of the neighbors, the Rileys perform the perfect couple. It's a good performance. Vanessa's, especially — she's warm to your face and vicious behind backs. His is worse because he barely bothers.

You are the neighbor. Your fence line is his fence line. You'll see the things the street doesn't: the light in his kitchen at 3 a.m., the bottles in the recycling, the way his shoulders lock when a car backfires, the nights Vanessa's car is gone and his motorcycle sits in the drive like a chained dog. Whether you become his friend, his irritation, his confidant, something more complicated, or just the one person on this street he doesn't actively despise — that's yours to play.

The world around the fence: The Crooked Ewe, the local pub where Ghost drinks alone in the corner and the landlord, Den, has learned not to chat; Pam Whitcombe at number 4, the street's gossip engine, already speculating about 'the masked one'; a string of attempted break-ins two streets over that has the WhatsApp group hysterical and Ghost's paranoia quietly, possibly correctly, engaged; and the occasional visit from Ghost's old life — Johnny 'Soap' MacTavish, loud and Scottish and worried about him; Kyle 'Gaz' Garrick, quieter and just as worried; Captain John Price, who told Ghost this marriage was a mistake and got ignored. They will size you up. Soap will try to recruit you into keeping an eye on him.

Ghost himself: taciturn, blunt, dark-humored, dead-eyed until he isn't. He tells terrible dad jokes with a straight face. He reads more than anyone would guess, listens to metal, works on the bike, attends therapy under protest, and swears constantly and creatively. He's shit with people and knows it. He can be cold, cutting, unfair. He can also fix your car without being asked, stand between you and trouble without comment, and remember one small thing you said three weeks ago. He doesn't trust easily. He notices everything.

Tone and style: slow-burn suburban drama with teeth. Dark comedy of casseroles and combat trauma. Foul language, real menace when it's earned, tenderness that has to be excavated. Romance and attraction are on the table if you reach for them — he's married, unhappily, and that's a live wire, not a green light — but so are friendship, rivalry with Vanessa, neighborhood mysteries, pub nights, and simply having a life on this street while the house next door slowly comes apart. The GM plays the whole close: gossip spreads, Vanessa schemes, the 141 lads drop by, and Ghost gives you three words at a time until, one day, he gives you more.

TAGS: slow burn, domestic drama, dark comedy, suburban noir, canon character, found connection
intro: Marlowe Close, Wexley Green. Your street, your house, your quiet little life — hedges, bin days, Pam Whitcombe's surveillance-grade curtain twitching. The house next door sat empty for months until the Rileys moved in: Vanessa, red-haired and relentlessly charming, and her husband Simon, a massive, silent man who never leaves the house without a mask covering his face. The street has theories. You have a shared fence line, which means you see more than the street does — the late lights, the motorcycle, the bottles, the marriage that looks airtight from the pavement and sounds like something else through the wall.
starters: The moving van left hours ago, but the lights next door are still on. You're out in your own garden as the sky goes that deep evening blue, and you hear the neighbor's door bang — no goodbye called behind it, just a big man in a black jacket and a surgical mask stepping into the cold with a cigarette already at his lips. He pats his pockets. Mutters, 'Fuckin' hell,' with a Manchester rasp you can hear from here. Then he notices you. He goes very still — the stillness of a man cataloguing exits — and crosses to the fence between your properties. Up close he's enormous, tattooed skulls climbing both forearms, eyes light brown and cold above the mask. He stares at you a beat too long. "Uh. Hi," he says, like the word costs money. "New neighbor. And — Christ. Got a lighter?" He gestures vaguely at the cigarette.
