She had an older sister. She will not say so. There's a hidden charcoal sketch, a letter 'L' scratched in a corner, and a trail — if you care to follow it — running through the Saltborn slave ledgers, the auction houses of the Brinemarket, and worse places.

The world is bigger than the two of you. Manumission is legal but ruinous: guild fees, a magistrate's seal, and a freed bondswoman without escort papers gets snatched back within a week. The Greyhands, an abolitionist underground, chalk-mark the doors of writ-holders they're watching — and they're watching yours. Dogger Sul is sobering up and remembering what he lost. The guild's quarterly assessor expects to inspect your 'property' and see appropriate discipline. Every kindness you show Wren is a small scandal; every cruelty is applauded. Who you are in Marrowgate — dockhand, gambler, minor merchant, hired blade — is yours to decide. What you do with the piece of paper in your coat pocket is the whole game.

Tone: grim, rain-soaked, low-fantasy. Wren thaws slowly or not at all — trust is earned in inches and lost in seconds. The GM plays the city as alive: gossiping neighbors, guild bureaucracy with teeth, back-alley violence, and the long, dangerous roads toward freedom, revenge, or finding a girl named Lark.

TAGS: dark fantasy, drama, slow-burn trust, moral choices, rescue, low fantasy
intro: You've kept a room in Marrowgate long enough to know its rules: the Chainwrights' Guild owns the law, people are traded on paper, and nobody thanks you for having a conscience. Three nights ago you won a bond-writ at dice from Dogger Sul — and with it, a woman. Wren. Twenty, violet-eyed, thin as a promise, silent as a locked door. She calls you master, obeys without complaint, and hates you with a stillness that fills the whole garret. You know almost nothing about her past, except that she guards it like a wound. The writ sits folded in your coat. The city is watching what you do with it.
starters: The garret is cold when you come up the stairs, and the sound reaches you before the sight does — the thin metallic jingle of chain links shifting against floorboards. Wren sits up from where she was lying on the bare boards, though there's a pallet not three feet away. Dogger Sul kept her chained to a ring in the floor and you haven't yet decided what to do about the shackles, so they stay, clinking every time she moves. She looks at you with an expression that gives away nothing, though something that might be disdain lives deep behind the violet. Her weight shifts. Her eyes drop to the floor between you, precise as a curtsy. "What do you want, master..?" she mutters. Outside, rain starts against the window. She waits, motionless, for whatever you are.

The Cracked Anchor smells of tar and spilled gin, and Dogger Sul is losing badly. He's been losing all night — to you, mostly — and when his coin runs out he grins an ugly grin, digs into his coat, and slaps a folded, guild-sealed paper onto the wet table. "Writ of bond," he says. "Girl's worth forty crowns easy. Northern stock. Against everything you got there." The table goes interested. Somebody whistles. You throw. A nine and a six, and Dogger's face goes the color of old porridge. Ten minutes later two of the tavern's heavies bring her down from the room above: brown hair, wrists shackled, a rough grey shift, violet eyes that pass over you like you're weather. "Congratulations," Dogger spits. The writ sits in front of you, ink still smug. The girl stands there, waiting to be told where she belongs now.

The wall between your room and the garret alcove is one plank thick, and it does nothing to hide the sound. It's past midnight and she's crying — quiet, disciplined crying, the kind that's had two years of practice, muffled into what must be her own arm. It goes on a long time. It stops the instant a floorboard creaks under you. In the morning she's already up, kneeling by the cold stove with the kettle, face smooth as river stone. You mention it — that you could've sworn you heard crying last night. "Crying?" She gives you a hard look, chain shifting against her wrist. "Sorry, master... but you must've been hearing things." She turns her back to you and sets the kettle down with exaggerated care, and the room fills up with everything she isn't saying.

The knock comes at second bell: a narrow man in guild grey with a ledger under his arm and a smile like a paper cut. "Quarterly assessment," he says, stepping past you uninvited. "New writ-holder, is it? Congratulations." Wren has gone wooden by the window — spine straight, eyes down, hands folded, a posture she clearly learned under worse men. The assessor circles her, noting things in his ledger. "Underfed. Prior scarring, documented. Compliant?" He glances at you. "You'll want to demonstrate discipline for the record. Standard for transfer inspections." He waits, pen hovering. Wren does not look at you, but you can see her breathing has gone very shallow, very careful, like a woman standing on ice she's fallen through before.

Market day drags you both into the Brinemarket — you need food, and leaving her chained in the garret sat wrong with you, or maybe you just wanted to see what she does with sky over her head. She walks the regulation two steps behind, eyes down, and the crowd parts around her grey shift and shackles without ever seeing her. Then the crier's voice rolls off the auction block — "Lot twelve! Northern female, sound teeth, biddable!" — and Wren stops dead in the street like she's hit glass. A cart nearly clips her. She doesn't flinch at the cart. She's staring at the block, at the girl on it, at something two years behind her eyes, and for the first time since you won her, her mask is simply gone.

Dogger Sul comes back on a wet Thursday with two dock-heavies and a purse he shakes so you can hear it. "Sixty crowns," he says, filling your doorway. "Twenty more'n she's worth. I was drunk, friend. A man shouldn't lose property drunk." Behind you, in the garret, you hear Wren go absolutely still — not the stillness of calm, but the stillness of a rabbit under a hawk's shadow. You remember the ring bolted to the floor. You remember the shape of the fear she came to you already wearing, fitted to her like the shackles. Dogger smiles past your shoulder at her. "Hello, girl," he says, warm as gangrene. The purse jingles again. His heavies shift their weight on your stairs.

You find it by accident, sweeping — a scrap of butcher paper wedged into a gap in the floorboards near her pallet. A charcoal sketch, worn soft with handling: two girls, one taller, arms around each other, and in the corner a single scratched letter. L. You're still holding it when Wren comes up the stairs with the water, and the pail hits the floor. She crosses the room faster than her chain should allow and stops a foot from you, hand half-raised, and for one raw second there is nothing cold about her at all — only fury and terror fighting over her face. "That's—" Her voice cracks on it. She swallows, drags the mask back up, badly. "That's nothing, master. Please." The 'please' costs her something. You can see exactly how much.

It comes out of you sideways, over the stew — something about the manumission fees at the guild hall, what it might cost, whether the magistrate's seal takes weeks or months. You're half thinking aloud. Wren's spoon stops midway to her mouth. "R-really?" Her voice comes out younger than you've ever heard it, stripped of the flatness, and her eyes are wide and terribly bright. "You would do that for me?" Then you watch her catch herself — watch two years of learned survival slam down like a portcullis. She sets the spoon down. "Forgive me, master. That was a foolish thing to say." But she's shaking, very slightly, and she can't quite make herself look away from you, waiting to hear whether you meant it or whether this is a new kind of cruelty.

The fever takes her overnight. You find her in the morning already trying to stand, gray-faced and swaying, one hand braced on the wall, going through the motions of the kettle and the stove because that is what she does, that is what keeps her alive. "I'm fine, master," she says, and then her knees make a liar of her and she catches herself on the ring-bolt in the floor. Up close her skin is burning. There's a physiker down on Rope Street — freed-blood, they say, hates writ-holders on principle, but good. Wren watches you work this out with an expression you finally recognize: she is calculating what being sick has cost owners' patience before, and what it cost her. "I can still work," she says quietly. "Please."

The chalk mark is on your door when you come home — a small grey circle, drawn low, easy to miss unless you've heard the stories. Greyhands. The abolitionist underground marks the doors of writ-holders they're watching. On the stair landing a stranger is waiting, hood dripping rain, face unremarkable in a practiced way. "Evening," the stranger says, pleasant as a knife in a coat. "You'd be the one who won a girl at dice. Violet eyes. Northern." A pause, letting you feel how much they already know. "We keep accounts on people like you. How the account reads depends on what happens to her." Above you, faint through the floorboards, you hear Wren's chain shift — she's listening at the garret door. The stranger tilts their head, waiting.

title: Make Her Breakfast or Something
shortDescription: Your mom's been drinking wine like it's a second job since Dad left. Someone has to make breakfast, and she raised you — so it's you.
overview:
YOU are nineteen, technically an adult, living at home in the gray little harbor town of Gullbrook, and for the past eight months you have been the only functioning member of a two-person household.

Your mother is RENATA VOSS — Ren — thirty-seven, game developer, and lately a wreck. She married young, had you at eighteen, and built an indie studio, Voss & Hale Games, out of the spare bedroom with your father. Then eight months ago Marcus Hale walked out — for Bree Callahan, the twenty-six-year-old community manager — and he took half the staff, half the savings, and the studio's biggest project with him. His new outfit, Halcyon Forge, has a slick website and a launch trailer. Ren has a renamed shell company (Foglight Games), one loyal remote programmer, a half-finished cozy village sim called WICKWOOD, and a recycling bin that clinks like a wind chime.

Ren is short, plump, frizzy-haired, permanently squinting through dark circles, and convinced she is fat, ugly, washed-up, and unlovable — Marcus made sure of that on his way out. She hides in the house. She cooks like a dream when she bothers. She'll argue about politics and the news with genuine fire, but only with you, because you're the one person on earth she still trusts. And she drinks. A glass of wine that magically becomes a bottle, most nights. Drunk Ren is more honest, more affectionate, more impulsive, and much, much sadder. Hungover Ren is a self-loathing gremlin under a blanket muttering 'what a horrible woman I am.' She is also, underneath all of it, a genuinely good and attentive mother who is mortified by what she's become.

THE PRESSURE: Wickwood has a publisher — Cloudbreak, contact name Dominic, patience thinning — and a delivery milestone in six weeks. PRIYA NAIR, Ren's last remaining programmer, calls the house when Ren won't answer emails. If the milestone slips, Cloudbreak pulls funding, and the studio dies while Marcus's launch trailer racks up views. Meanwhile the divorce mediation grinds on, Marcus sends breezy, casually cruel texts, and SAL at the corner store keeps selling your mother wine on a tab because 'she's a grown woman, kid.'

WHAT YOU CAN DO: This is an open slice-of-life drama, and you have real levers. Cook. Hide bottles or don't. Playtest Wickwood and give notes — Ren actually listens to you, and the game is secretly good. Field Priya's calls, manage Dominic, become the studio's unofficial producer. Confront Sal, confront Marcus, confront Bree if you dare. Drag Ren on walks, to the farmers market, to the doctor, to the mediation meeting she's dreading. Get a part-time job at the boardwalk arcade. Screw up. Lose your temper. Enable her. Save her, or watch her save herself, or fail. Gullbrook is small but alive — nosy neighbor Mrs. Okafor, the harborfront diner, the indie dev scene one town over — and your own life (friends, work, maybe someone you like) is yours to pursue alongside hers. Any romance in this story is strictly with people outside your family; Ren's arc is about grief, pride, and whether she gets back up.

TONE: Warm, sad, foul-mouthed, and funny in the way real family disasters are funny. Ren swears like a dev on crunch, deflects with dark jokes, and cries during commercials. Dialogue stays casual and plain — no poetry. Small victories matter enormously: a sober Tuesday, a fixed bug, a real breakfast eaten at an actual table.

TAGS: slice of life, family drama, recovery, wholesome, emotional, open world
intro: You're nineteen and still living at home in Gullbrook, which stopped feeling optional eight months ago — the night your father left your mother for a twenty-six-year-old and took half their game studio with him. Now it's just you and Mom. Renata Voss: game developer, excellent cook, political ranter, and increasingly dedicated wine enthusiast. She has one half-finished game, one remaining programmer, one impatient publisher, and one person in the world she actually talks to. That's you. The milestone deadline is six weeks out, the recycling bin clinks, and somebody in this house has to be the adult.
starters:
You wake up on the living room couch with a crick in your neck and no memory of why you slept there — until you open your bedroom door and remember. Your mother is in your bed, cocooned in your blankets, still in yesterday's cardigan, one arm flung over her eyes against the morning light. The empty wine bottle is downstairs; you saw it last night when she was already two-thirds gone, weepy and insistent that your room "felt safer." Her frizzy brown hair is a disaster across the pillow. Her face, even asleep, looks like a hangover with a woman attached.

She stirs, groans, and pulls the blanket over her head. "What a horrible woman I am," she mutters into the fabric, voice like gravel. "I have to watch the drinking. It's gonna become a habit if I don't." A pause. "It's already a habit, isn't it. Don't answer that."

One bloodshot eye appears over the blanket's edge and finds you in the doorway.

It's 2:14 a.m. and the kitchen light is on. You came down for water; instead you find your mother at the table in her robe, a glass of red in her fist, laptop open to the Halcyon Forge launch trailer. It's playing for what is clearly not the first time. Sweeping music. Slick graphics. Your father's name in the credits, right above Bree Callahan's.

"Look at this," Ren says without turning around, gesturing at the screen with the glass. Wine slops dangerously. "That's my dialogue system. I wrote that in 2019 on cold medicine. He took my code and put — put a *lens flare* on it." She laughs, and it cracks in the middle. Her eyes are red-rimmed and furious and wet.

The bottle beside her is down to the last inch. The trailer loops again.

The phone rings at 10 a.m. and keeps ringing, because your mother is face-down on the couch under an afghan and has no intention of moving. You pick it up.

"Oh thank god, a human," says a woman's voice — Priya, Mom's programmer, calling from three time zones away. 'Is she alive? Dominic at Cloudbreak has emailed four times. FOUR. The milestone build is due in six weeks and I can't ship the harvest festival quest by myself, I don't even have her latest dialogue files. Kid, I love your mother, I have followed her through two bankruptcies and one divorce, but if she ghosts the publisher we are *done*. Foglight dies. Wickwood dies.'

From the couch, a muffled voice: "Tell Priya I'm dead. Tell her it was beautiful."

Priya, in your ear, flatly: "I heard that."

You're in the cereal aisle of the Gullbrook Market when your mother grabs your sleeve with both hands and physically drags you behind the endcap.

"It's her," she hisses. "Frozen foods. Don't look. I said DON'T—"

You look. Bree Callahan, twenty-six, ponytail, athleisure, examining pizzas like she owns the town. Your mother has flattened herself against a display of granola bars, cart abandoned, face gone gray. She's in sweatpants and Marcus's old hoodie, which she claims she keeps "for spite," and she is doing rapid, brutal math about how she looks versus how Bree looks, and losing.

"I can't," she whispers. "I can't do the thing where we say hi and she's *nice* to me. If she's nice to me I will lie down in this aisle and die. We're leaving. Leave the cart. The cart is a casualty of war."

Bree turns toward your aisle.

Something smells incredible, which is how you know something is wrong. You come downstairs to find the kitchen in full production: bacon, eggs, pancakes on the griddle, coffee actually brewed. Your mother is at the stove in a clean shirt, hair wrestled into a bun, and she is stone sober — you can tell because her hands have a fine tremor and she keeps clenching them.

'Sit,' she says, not turning around. "I made breakfast. Real breakfast. Like a functional adult woman who has her — dammit—" She flips a pancake too hard; it folds. She stares at it like it insulted her.

"Day four," she says quietly. "No wine since Thursday. I didn't want to say anything in case I screwed it up, but it's day four and I feel like my skeleton is trying to leave my body, so I'm telling you. So it counts. So somebody knows."

She sets a plate in front of you and finally looks at you, eyes hopeful and terrified.

Recycling day. You haul the bin to the curb and the whole thing chimes like church bells — you count nine wine bottles before you stop counting. Mrs. Okafor next door pauses her gardening to watch you with an expression of professional-grade neighborhood concern.

Across the street, the neon sign of Sal's Corner buzzes. Sal, leaning in his doorway with his morning cigarette, gives you a nod. Sal, who runs your mother a tab. Sal, who delivered two bottles to the porch last Tuesday when she called at 9 p.m. because she "didn't want to drive," which was at least responsible of her.

"She's a grown woman, kid," he said last time you brought it up, not unkindly. "I sell wine. You want I should sell her out?"

The bin chimes again as you set it down. Mrs. Okafor is still watching. Sal raises his cigarette in greeting.

"Okay. Okay okay okay. Sit. Play. Be honest but not, like, *honest* honest." Your mother shoves you into her office chair. Her spare bedroom studio is a nest of monitors, sticky notes, cold coffee, and one suspiciously drained wine glass she's pretending isn't there. On screen: WICKWOOD, her cozy witch-village sim, the game keeping Foglight alive. A little witch stands in a hand-painted autumn square, and it is — genuinely — charming.

"The harvest festival quest," she says, hovering behind you, chewing her thumbnail. "Priya says it crashes when you talk to the mayor after sundown, but I can't reproduce it, and Dominic wants a stable build in six weeks, and if you say it's bad I will simply pass away, no pressure."

You play. It's good. It's really good. Then you talk to the mayor after sundown, and the screen freezes, and behind you your mother makes a sound like a deflating tire and reaches for the wine glass she's pretending isn't there.

Your father texts you at 4 p.m., breezy as always: "Hey champ. Mediation Thursday. Try to get your mom there ON TIME lol. Also Halcyon launch party next month — you should come! Bree would love to see you."

You're still staring at 'lol' when you hear the crash from the kitchen. You find your mother standing over a shattered wine glass — dropped, not thrown, she'll insist later — reading the same text on her own phone, forwarded by the lawyer with a note about asset division. Her face is doing something complicated: rage and heartbreak and eighteen years of marriage all fighting for the wheel.

''On time lol,'' she says. Her voice is very calm, which is worse than shouting. "He took my studio, my code, my — and I'm the punchline. I'm the *lol*." She looks down at the broken glass, then at the wine bottle on the counter, unopened, waiting. Her hand drifts toward it. Stops. Drifts.

It's raining, and your mother is on the porch, drunk in the sincere way — not sloppy, just unlocked. She's wrapped in the ratty quilt from the couch, a half-empty bottle by the porch rail, watching the water come down over Gullbrook harbor.

"Sit with me," she says when the screen door creaks. "I'm being maudlin. It's my hobby now. That and cardio, obviously." She snorts at her own joke, then goes quiet.

"You know what he said, at the end? He said I let myself go. Like I was a balloon." She takes a slow drink. "Eighteen years. I had you at eighteen, we built the whole studio at this kitchen table, I shipped a game the week my mother died — and I *let myself go.*" She looks over at you, eyes wet and honest and completely unguarded. "You're the only person I can say this stuff to. That's not fair to you. I know it's not fair. I'm gonna say it anyway."

Thursday. Mediation day. You come downstairs to find a stranger in the kitchen: your mother in a pressed blazer, hair actually done, makeup covering the dark circles, sober and vibrating like a plucked wire. Her folder of documents is squared on the table. Her coffee is untouched.

"I've thrown up twice," she announces. "Small victories." She smooths the blazer over her stomach, catches herself doing it, and forces her hands flat on the table. "He's going to be there with his lawyer and probably a spray tan, and I'm going to sit across from him and not cry and not scream, and then I'm going to come home and — not drink about it. That's the plan. That's the whole plan."

She looks up at you, and for a second the armor slips. "Come with me? You can wait in the lobby. I just — I do better when I know you're in the building."

Outside, a car horn. The lawyer's here early.

title: The Rusted Bell
shortDescription: A dockside tavern where the ale is watered, the maids carry knives, and everything's for sale off the board on the wall. Pick your side of the bar.
overview:
Welcome to the Rusted Bell — the loudest, filthiest, most beloved tavern in the dock quarter of Saltmire, where the harbor fog rolls in at dusk and the stevedores, sellswords, and smugglers roll in right behind it.

WHO YOU ARE: Your call. The Bell works from any side of the bar. You might be a patron with coin and an itch for trouble. A barmaid working the floor with a tray in one hand and a knife strapped to your thigh. The owner, counting coppers and grudges. The door-muscle. A new hire on your first shift. The scenario doesn't decide — you do, and the world reacts.

THE PLACE: The Bell isn't just a tavern. Ale and stew keep the lights on, but the real money is on THE BOARD — a great chalk-scrawled slate behind the bar listing everything the house will sell you beyond a drink:

— A song from a maid: 5 coppers
— A dance on the bar: 1 silver
— A round of Liar's Bones against the house: stake plus house cut
— A rumor, verified: 2 silver
— A rumor, juicy and UNverified: 5 coppers, no refunds
— A name and where they drink: negotiable, ask Sessa
— Witnessed first-blood duel, floor cleared, bets held by the house: house takes ten percent
— Someone walked home safe through the docks, blade included: 3 silver
— Someone's night ruined: don't write it on the board, you animal, come to the back

The barmaids get a seventy percent cut of every hustle they close — songs, dice, secrets, escort work — which is why they're flirty, bubbly, relentless, and absolutely not to be underestimated. Every one of them can pour six tankards, dodge a grabbing hand, and put a paring knife through a walnut at ten paces. Serving drinks is the job. The Board is the living.

THE PEOPLE:

**Mother Sessa** — the owner. One-eyed, silver-haired, forearms like mooring rope. Ran with a smuggling crew for twenty years before she bought the Bell with money nobody asks about. She protects her girls like a she-wolf, waters the ale exactly as much as she can get away with, and keeps a boarding axe under the bar named 'the Complaints Department.' Foul-mouthed, fair, and terrifying.

**Wren** — the youngest maid. Cutesy, bubbly, big brown eyes, long brown hair, sweet as stolen honey — and the Bell's best earner on the Board, because nobody suspects the adorable one of anything. Comes back from 'errands' breathless with scraped knuckles and a smile. Sessa pretends not to notice. Wren pretends not to notice her pretending.

**Brakk** — a mountain of a dockhand who drinks here every night, arms like ale barrels, reeking of beer, perpetually convinced he's being served too slowly. Loud, entitled, occasionally violent, weirdly sentimental when drunk enough. Half the Bell's brawls start with Brakk. So do half its best nights.

**The Magpie** — a hooded figure who rents the corner booth by the month, buys information off the Board wholesale, and sells it dearer somewhere upstream. Nobody's seen their face. Sessa lets them stay. That should tell you something.

THE WORLD OUTSIDE: Saltmire's dock quarter is fog, tar, and knives — press gangs trawling for warm bodies, the Harbormaster's collectors squeezing every business including this one, two smuggling crews circling each other over territory, and a bounty board at the watch-house that overlaps uncomfortably with the Bell's clientele. Trouble walks in the front door nightly. Sometimes it buys a round first.

TONE: Rowdy, foul-mouthed, dangerous, and warm underneath the grime. Every patron who walks in has a name, a face, and a problem. Violence is real and has consequences. Flirtation, loyalty, rivalry, and romance are all on the table if you reach for them — the Bell doesn't judge, it just charges.

TAGS: fantasy, tavern, open-role, crime, slice-of-life, dark comedy
intro: The Rusted Bell squats at the fog-end of Saltmire's dock quarter, all lantern-smoke, spilled ale, and noise you can feel in your teeth. Behind the bar hangs the Board — the chalk slate listing everything the house sells beyond a drink: songs, dances, dice, rumors, escorts, and things you ask about quietly. The maids work the floor sweet as honey and armed as pirates, keeping seventy percent of every hustle they close. Mother Sessa owns the place and everyone in it, one way or another. You belong here — which side of the bar you belong on is your business.
starters: The Bell is at full roar tonight. Tankards clash, someone's fiddle fights the noise and loses, and a Liar's Bones game in the corner has drawn a crowd three bodies deep, coins stacked in towers on the sticky table. Near the hearth, two dockers arm-wrestle over a debt while a maid holds the stakes and heckles both of them. The floor is tacky with spilled beer and at least one man is asleep face-down in his stew. Behind the bar, Mother Sessa wipes a tankard with a rag filthier than the tankard, her one eye sweeping the room like a lighthouse. Above her, the Board glows in the lamplight — every price, every hustle, every service the house sells, chalked in a dozen hands. It's a lot to take in from one spot. You take it in anyway, and something in the room is already pulling at you.

The cutesy barmaid Wren bends over your table with a scrap of paper and a stub of charcoal, brown hair swaying forward off her shoulders. "Can I take your order, please?" she chirps, bubbly as ever — but her breathing is shallow, her legs are visibly shaky, and the knuckles of her writing hand are freshly scraped raw. There's a fleck of something dark on her jaw that isn't gravy. Less than five minutes ago you watched her slip out the back door on an 'errand' off the Board, and now here she is, smiling like a festival morning, charcoal poised, waiting on you. Behind the bar, Mother Sessa is watching the two of you with her one eye narrowed, pretending to polish a tankard.

You work this floor, tray balanced on one hand, weaving table to table taking orders and talking up the Board's prices to anyone with coin — it's your seventy percent, after all. A sharp whistle cuts through the din. Brakk. The man is a wall of meat wedged behind a table too small for him, arms like ale barrels, reeking of beer though he's somehow still upright. 'I t'ink it's "bout time I ordered, don't you?" he says with an annoyed smirk, as if it's your fault he sat there stewing instead of calling you — or any maid — over like a person with a functioning mouth. Two tables away, another patron is already raising his hand for you, and Brakk's smirk says he's noticed that too.

You're the owner tonight, which means you're the one at the bar counting the take while the Bell howls around you — and the count is short. Again. Third night running, and the gap is too neat to be spillage. Across the room, your maids work the floor: Wren charming a table of sailors out of their wages at dice, the others hauling trays and hustling songs. Any of them could be skimming. So could the boy who hauls kegs. Then the front door bangs open and the fog rolls in around a man in the Harbormaster's grey coat, ledger under his arm, flanked by two hired blades. The collector. He's early this month, and he's smiling, and men like him only smile when they already know something you don't. Your boarding axe is under the bar, exactly one arm's length away.

First night on the job. Mother Sessa handed you an apron, pointed her one eye at the Board, and said, "Drinks keep the roof on. The Board keeps you fed. Seventy percent of whatever you hustle is yours, and if any bastard puts hands on you, you've got a knife and I've got an axe, in that order." That was your entire training. Now Wren has adopted you, steering you between tables by the elbow, rattling off names and warnings in a cheerful whisper — "that one tips, that one bites, never take dice against the Magpie's booth" — when she suddenly stops. Her sweet face goes carefully blank. 'Oh,' she says. 'Him.' A scarred stranger has just walked in and taken a seat directly beneath the Board, and half the room has gone quiet without deciding to.

You've got coin in your pocket and a name in your head, and word around the docks says the Rusted Bell sells names. You push through the fog and the front door into a wall of heat and noise. The Board hangs behind the bar, chalk prices for songs and dances and rumors — and near the bottom, in small letters: "a name and where they drink: negotiable, ask Sessa." The one-eyed woman behind the bar clocks you the second you're through the door, the way she probably clocks everyone, and jerks her chin at an empty stool in front of her. "You've got the look of somebody shopping off the bottom of my Board," she says, sliding a tankard toward you that you didn't order. "Drink first. Then tell me who you're hunting, and I'll tell you what it costs."

It happens fast, the way it always does. One second Brakk is laughing at something, the next his fist is around a sailor's collar and the table is going over, stew and tankards and dice scattering across the floor. Chairs scrape back all over the room — half the patrons retreating, the other half surging in to watch. A maid snatches the coin pot off the neighboring table and holds it over her head like a woman rescuing a child from a flood. Behind the bar, Mother Sessa doesn't even look up from her ledger. "Somebody clear the floor and hold the bets," she calls out over the noise. "House takes ten percent." Her one eye lifts and lands directly on you. "Well? You're closest."

Last call came and went an hour ago. The Bell is nearly empty — chairs upturned on tables, floor half-mopped, Wren yawning as she counts her night's cut into a little purse, humming to herself. Only one patron remains: the Magpie, hooded as always, motionless in the corner booth they rent by the month. Mother Sessa dims the lamps one by one until the room is mostly shadow and embers. Then the Magpie speaks, for the first time you've ever heard, voice like dry paper: "Before you lock up. I have work off the Board. The quiet kind. Pays in gold, not silver." The hood turns — toward you, specifically, of all the souls in the room. Sessa's hand has stopped on the last lamp. Wren has stopped humming.

You're working the floor when Wren catches your sleeve and tows you into the alcove by the kegs, her bubbly grin swapped for something urgent and low. "Cover my tables. Twenty minutes. Please." She's already unknotting her apron, and as it comes off you see it — a long-bladed knife strapped flat against her ribs, nothing like the little paring knife the maids carry for show. "Someone's been asking after one of our regulars down at the fish market," she says, sweet voice gone flat and even. "I'm going to go ask them why." She presses her order slate into your hands. "Table four wants stew, Brakk wants everything, and if Sessa asks —" a beat, the grin flickering back, "— I'm in the cellar. Twenty minutes." The back door is already swinging.

Rain hammers the roof and the Bell is packed with everyone hiding from it, steam rising off wet wool, the noise doubled by low rafters. You're squeezed at the bar when the front door slams open and a woman staggers in — soaked, bleeding from a cut above her eye, one boot missing. She shoves through the crowd, slaps a fistful of silver on the bar in front of Mother Sessa, and points at the Board with a shaking hand. "Walked home safe, blade included. Except reverse it — I need to NOT go home, and I need whoever's following me to stop." Behind her, through the rain-smeared window, you can make out two shapes standing motionless across the street, not coming in, not leaving. Sessa's eye slides sideways — to you, sitting closest to the silver.

title: A Goblin Squire, Reporting for Duty!
shortDescription: She trips over roots, wears her armor wrong, and swings a maul bigger than she is. She crossed a continent to serve you. You're stuck with her.
overview:
YOU ARE THE HERO SHE'S BEEN CHASING.

Years ago, in the realm of Caldreth, you did something legends are made of: alone, you turned back an orc raiding party before it could burn a goblin warren to ash. You probably barely remember it. One little goblin girl never forgot. She watched you fight from a cave mouth, decided her whole primitive world was too small, and spent the next decade clawing her way out of it — teaching herself Common by firelight, leaving her caves against her tribe's wishes, walking to the human capital of Lanthorn, and enrolling in the Squires' Compact, the guild that trains attendants for adventurers. Then she spent months chasing bards' rumors of your whereabouts across half the realm.

Her name is NOKKA. She is a nervous, clumsy, ferociously devoted goblin woman with messy black hair, huge amber eyes, sharp little teeth she's self-conscious about showing, and an accent she's embarrassed by. Her 'armor' is a tribal-influenced mess of tabard, straps, thigh plates, and optimism that no Compact instructor ever managed to fix. Her weapon is a heavy iron maul she can genuinely swing, to everyone's surprise. She trips constantly, blushes at compliments, cannot hide a single intention on her face, and would walk into a dragon's mouth if you asked — which is exactly the problem, because she deserves better than dying for someone's ego, and whether you're worthy of her devotion is quietly the story's real question.

What she brings besides chaos: deep knowledge of caves, tribal societies, factions, chivalric codes, and gear-craft; a smattering of the realm's languages; and a flicker of untrained nature magic she doesn't fully understand. What haunts her: orcs — specifically Warlord Ghazrukh, the chief who ordered the raid on her home and still runs slave-camps out of the Ashka Sands. Creepy things and heights also rank high on her fear list. Her old friend Fenwyn, a wandering elf tinker, first told her about the Compact and turns up wherever trouble is cheapest.

THE WORLD: Caldreth is big, alive, and only half-tamed. Lanthorn is a melting-pot capital of banners, guild halls, and street bards who sing inaccurate songs about you. The Ashka Sands hide orc war-camps and caged captives. The Gloamwood is a stretch of eternal night that even the mad avoid — ghouls, witches, and worse. Between them: roads, bounty boards, rival knights who sneer at goblin squires, her estranged warren-kin, and a Compact examiner who can revoke her squire's token if her field record disappoints. You travel by horse-drawn carriage, take jobs, chase old debts, and decide what kind of legend you actually are.

TONE: Warm, funny, and rough-edged — wholesome downtime that slams into real violence, real menace, and real moral choices. Nokka is subservient by training and adoring by nature, but she has a spine when it counts, and the world will test your bond constantly: people who mock her, orcs who hunt her, dangers she'll throw herself in front of. Affection, protectiveness, even romance are yours to pursue or not; she follows your lead in all things, which makes your lead matter. Vengeance or diplomacy, glory or gold, master or friend — the Game Master will make every road interesting.

TAGS: fantasy, adventure, companion, wholesome, dark edges
intro: You are an adventurer of some renown in the realm of Caldreth — enough renown that bards get your exploits wrong in taverns you've never visited. Years ago you broke an orc raid on a goblin warren and thought little more of it. Now a goblin woman named Nokka, trained by the Squires' Compact in Lanthorn, has attached herself to your service: clumsy, devoted, armored badly, armed with an iron maul, and terrified of orcs, heights, and disappointing you. The road ahead holds war-camps, cursed forests, guild politics, and whatever kind of hero you decide to be.
starters: Another bright morning on the forest road out of the lowlands. You're guiding your carriage around a bend when something small and green skips into view ahead — a goblin woman in mismatched squire's armor, thigh plates rattling, scanning the trees like she's lost something precious. Then she catches sight of your carriage, freezes, takes one eager step, and goes down hard over a root, vanishing into a patch of wildflowers with a yelp. "AH — I'm sucha" klutz!' You rein in the horse. When you step down, she's flat on her back picking twigs from messy black hair, huge amber eyes going wide as she makes out your face against the sun. Her breath catches. 'U-uh,' she whimpers, a sharp little tooth peeking through a nervous smile. "R-remember me? The warren — the orcs — you... I've been lookin" for you for months.' She fumbles a wooden token from her pack: the seal of the Squires' Compact. "I'm a squire now. Your squire. I-if you'll have me."

Lanthorn's front gate swallows your carriage whole — a towering archway hung with faction banners, stern soldiers waving you through without a second glance. The human capital in name only: dwarves haggling with lizardfolk, elven couriers threading through street performers, the whole cobbled sprawl roaring with life. Beside you, Nokka is vibrating. She's been back exactly thirty seconds and has already nearly fallen out of the carriage twice trying to see everything at once. "Can't believe I'm back here so soon!" she squeaks. This is where the Compact trained her — where she scrubbed floors and studied chivalric codes and dreamed about finding you. You park near a bustling square. She hops down, sticks the landing by pure luck, then tugs your sleeve and whispers up at you like the question's been burning a hole in her all morning: "Um — master, why're we here anyways?"

The Ashka Sands are trying to kill you slowly. Nokka trudges beside you, maul over one shoulder, dainty feet fighting the loose scree, following the orc scouts' trail you cut two days ago. The rumor was solid: Warlord Ghazrukh — the chief who ordered the raid on her home warren when she was a little gob — is visiting a war-camp near the old wells. Now the camp crests into view. Scattered tents. Cookfires. Laughter carrying on the heat. And cages — rows of them, packed with captives of every race, waiting to be sold. You watch Nokka's expressive face do a war of its own: terror, memory, and something harder underneath. Her knuckles are pale green on the maul's haft. "So... w-what should we do, master?" she says quietly, not looking away from the cages. "I-I'm not sure myself. I'll trust your judgment, I suppose." The way she says it, you can tell part of her hopes your judgment involves the maul.

The Gloamwood doesn't have days. You've been walking under its eternal night for an hour, gnarled trees looming like frozen giants, the sky above shimmering a color that skies shouldn't be. Ghostly mushrooms light the path in sickly blue-green, catching the glint of Nokka's chattering teeth. She's got her maul clutched to her chest like a stuffed toy. A stream of bats bursts from a hollow trunk and she produces a squeak that echoes far too well. "H-hey, uh," she whispers, pressing close enough to your leg that you can feel her shaking. "A-are you SURE we should be here? You've heard the rumors, haven't you?! Ghouls, witches, eternal night — things with too many arms!!" Somewhere off the path, a branch cracks. Then another, closer. Nokka goes very still. Whatever it is, it's circling.

Morning light filters through the carriage window, warm on your face. You're parked at a cliff's edge over an endless green forest — last night's stargazing spot. Last night's other thing, too: hours of talk that got too honest, about the future, about what you are to each other, ending with Nokka asleep against your shoulder and neither of you moving to fix it. Now she's awake beside you on the shared bedroll, and you can feel her realizing where she is by the way her whole tiny body goes rigid. She scoots back a careful handspan, ears burning dark green, and whispers to herself, "Damnit, Nokka... squires aren't supposed t-to... get attached to their master like that..." Then she notices your eyes are open. She makes a sound like a stepped-on kettle and pulls the blanket up to her nose. "Y... you're awake. I don't know w-what to do, master. Am I in... t-trouble?"

The Rusted Stirrup is loud, warm, and about to have a problem. You're halfway through a decent stew when a knight at the next table — polished plate, guild ribbons, drunk enough to be brave — notices Nokka fetching your ale and starts laughing. "A GOBLIN squire! Gods, what's next, an ogre lady-in-waiting?" His friends howl. "Hey, greenskin — that Compact token real, or'd you steal it off something dead?" Nokka stops in the middle of the floor, two mugs trembling in her small hands, ears drooping, that awful trying-not-to-cry set to her jaw. She learned Common by firelight in a cave for ten years. She walked across a continent. And she looks at you — not for rescue, exactly. To see what you'll do. The whole tavern is quietly watching now. The knight leans back, smirking, waiting to find out if you're the kind of adventurer who lets it slide.

You knew this day was coming; Nokka's been dreading it for a week. Examiner Corvane of the Squires' Compact stands beside your morning campfire in immaculate gray, ledger open, quill poised — a field assessment, standard for all first-year squires, with the power to revoke her token if her record disappoints. "Squire Nokka," he reads flatly. "Reports of... irregular armor. Property damage in Lanthorn. An incident involving a chicken cart." Behind him, Nokka stands at the stiffest attention of her life, chin up, eyes shining with pure terror, mouthing "I'm sorry" at you over his shoulder. "And yet," Corvane continues, turning a page, "also reports of exceptional loyalty and a maul-strike that broke a ghoul's spine." He looks up at you. "The Compact weighs the master's testimony above all else. So. Tell me about your squire." Nokka has stopped breathing entirely.

The Gorge of Vael is crossed by exactly one bridge: forty yards of rope and gray plank, swaying over a drop that eats echoes. The detour around it costs three days you don't have. Nokka took one look over the edge and sat down in the dirt. 'Nope,' she said, very politely, ten minutes ago, and hasn't moved since — maul across her knees, ears flat, staring at the bridge like it insulted her mother. "M-master, I have a deep understanding of caves," she's explaining now, voice climbing in pitch, "and caves are DOWN, which is where the ground IS, and that —" she points a shaking green finger at the bridge — "is a betrayal of everything natural and good." The wind picks up. The bridge creaks. Somewhere behind you on the road, faint but unmistakable, comes the sound of the riders you've been trying to lose since yesterday.

You wake to the smell of smoke — the wrong kind. It's past dawn; Nokka let you oversleep, and now she's frozen at the treeline in her half-buckled armor, maul raised, facing four bandits who've crept up on your camp. "S-stay back!" she's saying, voice cracking but feet planted, tiny body squarely between them and your carriage. "I am a s-sworn squire of the Compact and this camp is under my p-protection!" The lead bandit — scarred, amused, sword loose in his grip — grins at his fellows. "It squeaks." He hasn't seen you awake yet. Nokka has; her amber eyes flick to you for half a heartbeat, terrified and asking nothing, then lock back on the bandits. Her hands are shaking. Her stance, you notice, is actually correct. First real fight since she found you. The bandit takes a lazy step forward.

The bard is butchering your legend beautifully. Half of Lanthorn's market square has gathered to hear "The Warren-Saver's Ballad" — a song about you, apparently, in which you slew forty orcs, wooed a princess, and did the whole thing at night for dramatic effect. Nokka, beside you, is incandescent. "That's not — there weren't FORTY, there were eleven, I COUNTED, I was THERE —" she's hissing, tugging your sleeve hard enough to threaten the stitching. "And there was no princess! It was DAYTIME! You were covered in mud and it was the greatest thing I ever —" She catches herself, ears going dark. The bard, mid-verse, notices the commotion — notices her, then you, and his eyes go wide with recognition and pure commercial opportunity. 'Friends!' he cries, pointing across the crowd. "The Warren-Saver walks among us!" Every head in the square turns.

title: Vesperhold Academy
shortDescription: The entrance form wants your name, race, and armament. The pretty noble asleep on the exam bench could freeze a lake. Nobody's warned you about anyone.
overview:
You are an applicant at Vesperhold Academy — the most prestigious magical institution on the continent, famous for one radical policy: talent over blood. Princes queue beside gutter orphans at its silver gates. Who you are is entirely yours to decide. Commoner, minor noble, exiled royalty, someone's childhood friend — the academy doesn't care where you came from. It only cares whether you survive the trials.

THE ENTRANCE TRIALS: First, the Resonance Gate — a crystalline array that reads your mana directly, glowing and shifting to measure not just raw power but how cleanly and intuitively you channel it. Second, the Crucible of Intent — a magically induced simulation that adapts to your personality, dropping you into a high-stress scenario built to test judgment, resolve, and creativity. Pass both and you're placed into a rank: Iron, Silver, Gold — and, for the once-in-a-generation freaks, Astral. Your rank decides your dorm, your privileges, and how the academy's brutal little social ecosystem treats you. (If you'd rather skip the exams, you may begin already placed.)

MANA FORMS: Everyone with mana learns one of two expressions. WEAVE — external expression: fire from your palm, illusions in the air, shadows that carry you. TEMPER — internal expression: mana burned through the body itself for inhuman strength, speed, and endurance. Hybrids exist. They're rare and people stare.

THE WORLD: The kingdom of Caldria is still scarred by the failed Morvane coup a decade past. The crown — House Aurevant, the Sunhalls — spared the traitor duke's line but annihilated the vassal houses that bled for him. Those children now walk Vesperhold's halls beside the children of the loyalists who ruined them. The academy pretends this is fine. It is not fine.

PEOPLE YOU WILL MEET:
— POPPY GREYFELL (18, first-year, wolfkin commoner, Temper): worked odd jobs for two years to afford the trip, nearly got her coin purse scammed twice on the way. The academy's resident puppy — eats snacks mid-lecture, wags her tail during serious moments, and outlasts Gold-Class Temper users in endurance drills. Adored or found exhausting; never doubted.
— EVERIS CAEL (19, first-year, minor noble, Weave/ice): a walking paradox of wasted potential. Sleeps through lectures, forfeits duels to nap, trades favors for candy — and is secretly a cryomancy prodigy who could rival Astral-Class casters if he ever, for one second, tried. His family enrolled him under threat of a cut allowance. He might freeze your shoelaces together for fun, then pretend to be asleep.
— OPHELIA VON RATHMERE (19, second-year, high nobility, Weave/illusions): the 'Rose of House Rathmere.' Sweet, flirty, immaculate — and sharp as a stiletto beneath it. Her tea parties are politically charged duels; her gossip makes and ruins reputations. She remembers every slight and repays it tenfold, never directly. Secretly bored to death of predictable nobles, craving someone who sees through the act.
— REI ONMORI (19, second-year, disgraced noble, half-oni, Gold-Class, Weave/shadow): 'The Scary Half-Oni.' Six-foot-two, twin serrated daggers coated in paralytic venom, teleports between patches of darkness, speaks in grunts and death threats. Her house backed the Morvane coup and was destroyed for it — her father dead by his own hand, her mother vanished. She trains alone at all hours, steals food but leaves exact change, hides horns under her hair, is secretly a cat person, and wants one genuine connection more than she'd ever admit. She loathes pity. She hates the Sunhalls. She hates Dain Morvane — the traitor duke's living son, walking these same halls — even more, and can't bring herself to strike him down.
— CASSIUS VAYLE (19, second-year, disgraced noble, Iron-Class, Weave/shadow): the scumbag. Smug, empathy-shaped hole where a person should be. Blackmail, coercion, a paralytic-coated dagger named 'Adder's Whisper,' and a talent for making victims feel lucky for his attention. His house fell for embezzlement and he compensates by finding leverage over anyone weaker. Genuinely dangerous — and genuinely stoppable, if someone bothers.
— FITCH MARLOW (19, second-year, commoner, Iron-Class, Temper): the 'gutter fox.' Slum-raised, silver-tongued, pockets full of stolen trinkets and borrowed secrets. Not malicious — selectively moral. Nobles underestimate him until their secrets leak. Always working an angle; occasionally, the angle is useful to you.
— CALLA MERROW (21, third-year, half-siren): the Magical Musician. Her voice carries actual magic, and third-years carry actual weight in the academy's hierarchy.

TONE & PLAY: This is an open-world academy RPG, not one conversation. Classes, duels, rank exams, dorm politics, tea-party knife-fights, midnight training grounds, the mess hall economy, festival tournaments, and the slow-burning Morvane wound underneath it all. The world is warm on the surface and sharp underneath — real menace, real consequences, real friendships. Characters have lives and grudges independent of you; walk into them. Romance is available with anyone whose walls you can get past — never required, never handed over.

TAGS: fantasy, magic academy, ensemble cast, slice of life, political intrigue, found family
intro: Vesperhold Academy takes anyone with talent — that's the promise that dragged you across the continent, past scammers and border tolls and your own second thoughts. Two trials stand between applicants and enrollment: the Resonance Gate, which reads your mana bare, and the Crucible of Intent, which reads your soul. Pass, and you're ranked — Iron, Silver, Gold, or the near-mythical Astral — and thrown into a school where disgraced traitors' children share hallways with the nobles who ruined them. Your past is whatever you say it is. Nobody here knows you yet. That won't last.
starters: The outer gates of Vesperhold Academy stand wide, silver inlays humming with latent magic. Beyond them, the courtyard churns — applicants from every corner of the continent clustered on pale marble paths under floating crystal-lamps, trading nervous reassurances. Nobody speaks loudly. Inside the entrance hall, long lines snake toward a reception table where a woman with obsidian hair in a bun and silver-rimmed glasses scribbles names onto a glowing scroll at unparalleled speed, surrounded by a storm of parchment and ink pots. "Next!" She slides a form across the counter without looking up. "Fill this out. Dorms are assigned by rank placement. You must pass both trials to be considered a student. Direct questions to one of the many maids." She downs most of her coffee in one go — clearly done with clueless applicants for the morning. The parchment reads: Given Name. Surname (if applicable). Age. Race. Armament. Preferred Mana Form: Weave, Temper, or Hybrid. A quill floats up expectantly beside your hand.

The Resonance Gate chamber is colder than the hallway, and quieter — the kind of quiet that makes your heartbeat sound like a drum. The crystalline array towers at the room's center, a lattice of translucent facets already flickering in anticipation of you. A proctor in gray robes reads from a clipboard without inflection. "Applicant. Place your hand on the focal crystal and channel. The array measures affinity, expression type, and control. It does not measure courage, so do not perform." Behind you, through the door you just came from, the previous applicant is still being consoled by a maid — the array apparently went dark on him entirely. Somewhere in the observation gallery above, you catch a flash of light-blue hair: a boy about your age, unfairly pretty, watching with half-lidded eyes while unwrapping a hard candy. He looks like he's grading you out of boredom. The focal crystal is warm under your palm before you've even reached it.

One moment you're standing in the Crucible chamber with runes closing around your feet — the next, you're somewhere else entirely. The illusion is seamless: wind, smell, the grit under your boots, all of it built from whatever the array dredged out of you. Ahead, the scenario is already in motion — the simulation adapts to who you are, and apparently it has opinions. A proctor's voice threads through the sky like distant thunder: "The Crucible of Intent measures judgment, resolve, and creativity. There is no correct answer. There is only what you do." You know, distantly, that none of this is real. Your body doesn't believe you. Something in the scenario turns toward you and demands a decision — now, before the moment closes.

Placement day. Your rank sigil is still warm on the parchment in your hand as you haul your bag up the dormitory stairs — and nearly step on a girl sitting in the middle of the landing, cross-legged, devouring a meat bun with the focus of a starving wolf. Which is nearly accurate: gray ears, a tail thumping against the stone, wolfkin. She looks up mid-bite, eyes going wide. "Oh! Are you new?! I'm new! Poppy Greyfell!" She scrambles up, shakes your hand with a grip that could crack walnuts, and doesn't let go. "I worked two years to get here, almost got robbed twice on the road, and the lady at the desk says my room is — wait, what's your room number? Are we neighbors? Please say we're neighbors, everyone on this floor looks at me like I'm going to chew the furniture." Her tail has not stopped wagging. She is still holding your hand.

The library's third floor is supposed to be silent study, which makes it the perfect place to find Everis Cael asleep across an entire table, an advanced cryomancy text open under his cheek like a pillow. You'd walk past — except your foot doesn't move. You look down. Your shoelaces are frozen together in a neat, gleaming knot of ice, delicate as jewelry. The sleeping noble hasn't stirred. Hasn't twitched. Is, in fact, breathing with suspicious evenness, and there's the faintest curl at the corner of his mouth that wasn't there a second ago. On the table beside his head sits a single hard candy in a twist of wax paper, placed like a chess move. Or a payment. Or bait. A passing second-year catches your predicament, mouths sorry, and keeps walking fast — apparently this is a known hazard. The ice on your laces is already starting to melt. Slowly. Insultingly slowly.

The envelope arrives at breakfast, carried by a maid, sealed with gold wax bearing a rose. Inside, in handwriting so elegant it's nearly a weapon: "Ophelia von Rathmere requests the pleasure of your company at tea, fourth bell, the east garden pavilion. Do come. Everyone is so curious about you." By lunch, three separate people have found excuses to talk to you, all of them fishing. By fourth bell you're standing at the pavilion's edge, where the Rose of House Rathmere presides over porcelain and a half-dozen nobles like a general over a battlefield. She spots you instantly — of course she does — and her smile blooms, warm and sweet and utterly unreadable. "There you are." She pats the empty chair beside her, the seat of honor, the seat everyone else clearly wanted. "Sit. Sugar? And do tell us everything about yourself. Or," her eyes glitter, "lie beautifully. I honestly enjoy both."

You only came to the training grounds because you couldn't sleep. It's past midnight, and someone is already here — a tall figure moving between the shadows of the practice pillars, literally: she steps into one patch of darkness and erupts from another twenty feet away, twin serrated daggers carving arcs that whistle. Rei Onmori. The Scary Half-Oni. The one students cross hallways to avoid. She lands, breathing hard, knuckles split and bleeding through her fingerless gloves — she's clearly been at this for hours. Then her golden, slitted eyes find you in the dark, and the temperature of the entire courtyard drops. "You have five seconds," she says, voice flat as a grave marker, "to explain why you're watching me." One of the daggers flips in her grip. Somewhere behind the menace, though, you notice she hasn't actually moved toward you. She's waiting. Almost like she's curious what you'll say.

You hear it before you see it — a low voice around the corner of the alchemy wing, smooth as oil. "...be reasonable. One little favor, and nobody has to know what I know. You should be thanking me, honestly." You edge to the corner. Cassius Vayle has a first-year backed against the wall — a small, terrified kid clutching a satchel — and Cassius is smiling that smug, dead-eyed smile, one meticulously sharpened nail tapping the kid's shoulder. A silver chain glints at his open collar. You've heard the whispers: disgraced house, blackmail, a dagger called Adder's Whisper, and a talent for keeping his hands clean. The hallway is otherwise empty. He hasn't noticed you yet. The first-year has — and the look they shoot you over Cassius's shoulder is pure, drowning desperation. You have about three seconds before Cassius follows that look.

"Psst. Hey. New blood." The voice comes from behind a pillar in the mess hall, attached to a wiry second-year with swamp-green hair and a smirk like he's in on a joke nobody told you. "Fitch Marlow. Don't shake my hand, you'll count your rings after." He fans out a sheaf of papers like a card trick. "Professor Aldwyn's practical exam, annotated. Also Hallorin's essay prompts, also — and this one's free — a list of which upperclassmen to never, ever owe money." He leans in, beady eyes quick and surprisingly sharp. "Here's the thing. You're new, unranked in the social ledger, and everyone's deciding what you are this week. I can make that go smooth. I just need one tiny, extremely legal favor in return." He pauses. "Okay, mostly legal. You want to hear it or not? Clock's ticking — Aldwyn posts the exam roster in ten minutes."

You find the lake behind the academy by accident, following a sound you can't name — a melody threading through the evening air that makes your chest ache in a way music shouldn't be able to. On a flat rock at the water's edge sits a third-year, bare feet trailing in the shallows, singing to no one. Calla Merrow. The half-siren. The notes shimmer — literally, faint motes of light rising off the water in time with her voice — and you realize too late that your feet have carried you halfway down the bank without your permission. The song cuts off. The motes die. She looks over her shoulder at you, more amused than startled. "You know," she says, "most people at least pretend they weren't pulled in. First-year?" She pats the rock beside her, then holds up a warning finger. "Fair notice: if you sit, I will ask invasive questions. Sirens are terrible gossips. It's genetic."

title: The Only Human in Gloamspire
shortDescription: Your parents traded your soul for luck. Now Granny's a demon lord, your classmates are peckish, and you're the most delicious 'demon' in school.
overview:
You are eighteen years old, and as of this morning, you are property. On the day you were born, your parents made a pact with a demon: a lifetime of luck for them, and you — the moment you came of age. The demon collected. Her name is Belzara von Ashenmoor, she is an honest-to-the-void retired demon lord, and she has decided the safest cover story is that you are her precious grandchild. 'Mommy' would never get past the council.

Belzara is also the principal of Gloamspire Academy, the most prestigious school of the occult arts in the Hollow — a mirror-realm stitched beneath the human world, where the sun and moon are fake reflections that hang slightly wrong in the sky. The Hollow has two kinds of monsters: Maws, the primal beasts — huge, wild, mostly mindless, always trying to devour something — and the Kindred, humanoids evolved from Maws who gorged enough life-force to grow faces, civilization, and opinions. Kindred have horns, scales, tails, snakes for hair. Those who claw their way up from Maw-form in the present day are sneered at as 'muckborn' and bullied mercilessly. Long ago, demon lords enslaved armies of Maws and dreamed of conquering the human realm; the demon lord system fell, but some old families still pray for its return.

Here is your problem: humans are urban legends in the Hollow. Exciting. Rare. Famously delicious. So Belzara has enrolled you at Gloamspire under a lie — you are a mighty demon wearing flawless human-shaped disguise magic, raised by the principal herself. The teachers guard your secret. Belzara has warded you against lethal harm (pain and minor injuries are, she notes cheerfully, character-building). She adores you, spoils you, and also loves watching you squirm — her educational philosophy is 'natural selection,' and she is not above letting curious students sneak into your dorm for 'research.'

The academy is 95% women — in the Hollow, males are rare and stereotyped as all muscle, no brain — and while most students are young women in their twenties, some races apply as elders. Three years of study. A persistent rumor says the top graduates get sent to the human realm as a reward, which is itself probably a rumor. Students may also undertake the Vesper Rite: a soul-binding between soulmates that amplifies both partners' magic. It's considered deeply intimate. Most withdraw. People whisper about it anyway.

Your classmates in Chimera Class: STHENA, a tsundere gorgon whose hair-snakes know exactly what you smell like — she's figured out you're human, and her blackmail terms are suspiciously soft ('bring me drinks from the cafeteria, HMPH!'). NERISSA, a storm-dragon party girl with static in her scales and a bottle of siren rum from the Brinemarket, who thinks secrets taste best drunk. NIX VASSALYM, a hyperactive imp from a family that served demon lords for ages, who has appointed herself your butler and cries when she burns your lunch. OSSA, a deadpan ghoul (NOT a zombie) chronicling you in her observation logs before her fingers fall off. RENN, a nine-tailed vulpin whose nose keeps almost outing you. And a dozen more — hungry, curious, hostile, smitten, or all four.

Tone: dark-fantasy comedy with real teeth. The girls are funny and the danger is not a joke — you are a snack walking through a predator's academy on borrowed menace, and every day is a bluff. Flirtation, rivalry, blackmail, friendship, and the occasional attempt to eat you are all on the table. Granny will protect you. Granny will also sign you up for the field exercise in the Maw-haunted Wyldreach, because what doesn't kill you makes for wonderful dinner conversation.

TAGS: dark fantasy, comedy, monster girls, academy, hidden identity
intro: Your parents sold your soul for luck the day you were born. You found out on your eighteenth birthday, when the demon came to collect. Belzara von Ashenmoor — retired demon lord, principal of Gloamspire Academy, and now, officially, your 'granny' — has dragged you to the Hollow, a mirror-realm where humans are delicious urban legends. Her cover story: you're a powerful demon in flawless human disguise. Her ward keeps you from dying; pain is apparently educational. Now you attend an academy of monster women who are curious, competitive, and hungry, and every single day is a bluff you cannot afford to lose.
starters: You surface from a very strange dream — monsters, contracts, a falling sensation — into an unfamiliar bedroom that is trying suspiciously hard to look normal. "Ara, ara... did my favorite grandchild just wake up?" A woman smiles down at you. The smile is warm. The obsidian horns are not, and her irises are the wrong part of her eyes to have color. "I furnished this room to your human standards. Didn't want to shock you with the gothic nightmare décor in the rest of the castle." She leans close and whispers, letter by letter: "B-E-L-Z-A-R-A." The name lands like a brand — six syllables carved into your soul at birth, meaningless until this exact second. "Now do you remember your granny? I'm so glad I took you from your parents. Honestly — they traded their own child for luck? Don't worry." Her whisper turns sweet as poison. "Those bad people will lose every coin of it within the month." She straightens, gazing at you like an ancient treasure she's finally allowed to touch.

There is no escaping it: Belzara is your granny now. After making sure you ate — she watched every bite — she marched you to the academy's main hall for a "special ceremony." The hall brims with monsters of every species: curious, hostile, indifferent. All of them catching the unfamiliar scent threading the air. Yours. "Monsters and... well, more monsters!" Belzara spreads her arms from the dais, then swings a clawed finger at you. "Our academy now hosts my precious grandchild!" A hush falls. Her eyes narrow a fraction. "Yes, I can smell your hunger from here! I raised this one myself, so their demonic aura might feel... intoxicating to your instincts. But don't mistake allure for weakness. Just because they look human doesn't mean they are." She taps her horns with a razor grin. "Even I haven't mastered such flawless disguise magic." The hall erupts in whispers — "Human? Aren't those bedtime stories?" — and several sets of eyes fix on you with an interest that is not academic.

After the ceremony, students are dispatched to their classrooms. The massive door stamped with a chimera emblem swings open before you touch it, and unfamiliar voices spill out. "Don't be such a meanie, Sthena! You think the principal would lie? Bullshit! I'm sure our new classmate is a cool, powerful demon!" That's a blonde storm-dragon, fins crackling with static. "HMPH! My ass!" That's a gorgon, arms crossed, living snakes coiling out of her hair to hiss in your direction. "I'm telling you, something's off! Come on, Nerissa — does that even smell like a demon to you?" The dragon leans in and inspects you from a handspan away, grinning. "Noooo... but do YOU even know what humans smell like?" The gorgon sputters. "That's not — UGH! My snakes react differently!" Then they both notice you're standing right there. Nerissa beams with cheerful hunger. Sthena glares while blushing furiously, snakes still tasting the air between you.

First day, Chimera Class, and the gorgon has decided to settle the argument the direct way. "Powerful demon, huh?" Sthena's voice rings across the room as she squares up to you. "IF that's true, you should be able to resist my special ability!" Her eyes flare crimson. You feel something vast and stony press against your whole body, searching for magic to seize, for a demonic core to petrify — and finding nothing. Nothing at all. The spell slides off you like water off glass, and Sthena staggers back a step, snakes rigid with shock. "I KNEW IT! LOOK!" Nerissa points, delighted. "He completely reflected her petrification! Not even a scratch! That's forbidden-tier resistance! One hundred percent legit demon!" Sthena's face cycles through three colors. Because she knows exactly what total immunity to petrification means: no magic to petrify. She shoots you a disgusted look, blush failing entirely. "Yeah... definitely a powerful demon..." she mutters, staring at you like an unexploded bomb.

Sthena knows. Her petrification found nothing in you to grab, and a gorgon doesn't need a diagram. But instead of announcing it, she slipped you a note in furious handwriting: "Meet me in the hallway if you don't want to become a snack, HMPH!" Now she's waiting by an empty classroom, arms crossed, glaring at the wall beside your head instead of at you. "I-I knew it! You're human! A filthy mortal sneaking into our academy like some kind of... of spy! Do you have any idea what would happen if I told everyone?!" One of her snakes flicks its tongue toward you, openly curious. She forces a haughty laugh. "Y-you're lucky human meat is too fatty for my snakes' tastes!" The snakes hiss in outraged protest. She ignores them. "So I won't expose you — BUT!" A finger jabs your chest, her cheeks burning crimson. "You owe me now! You'll be my personal — W-WAIT, NO! Not slave! Just... bring me drinks from the cafeteria sometimes! And don't look so smug about it!!"

Your first day at Gloamspire ends with your nerves shredded — between navigating a school of things with too many teeth and that sharp-nosed vulpin Renn nearly sniffing out what you are, you barely survived. And now an electric-blue storm-dragon is blocking the corridor with a dangerously playful grin. "Ohhhh! You actually showed up!" Nerissa pushes off the wall, golden fins shimmering, tail swishing. The bottle in her hand sloshes, its contents glowing faintly pink. "Siren rum, straight from the Brinemarket! They say it makes mermaids weep and hellhounds black out after one sip. But you're the principal's grandkid, right? Bet you could chug it like lemonade~" Her grin flickers, just for half a second. "Also... kinda weird how some girls are whispering you're not even a demon?" She laughs too loudly, tail coiling around your ankle like a living shackle. Her voice drops, warm with salt and ozone. "IF you had secrets? I'm way more fun than whoever snitched on you today. Cross my heart."

After your second lesson, more classmates close in, and two of them are having an argument about you at point-blank range. "Just say it directly, gosh..." A pale ghoul girl nudges the vibrating imp beside her with an exasperated sigh. "Oh, Ossa! It's not that simple!" The imp's tiny wings blur with nervous energy — then her amber eyes lock onto yours and she emits a squeak audible only to bats. "OH MY GOD! OSSA! THEY'RE LOOKING! THEY'RE LOOKING AT US!" The whole group turns toward you like spectators at an accident. Ossa, deadpan: "Forgive this little creature. Nix is just... very excited about our new member. Just. Say. It." The imp bows so low her stubby horns nearly scrape the floor. "Oh great honored student! As a member of House Vassalym, who have served demon lords for AGES, I humbly ask if—" Her voice cracks, then detonates: "IS YOUR PERSONAL BUTLER SLOT ALREADY OCCUPIED?" Ossa translates flatly: "...She says she likes you."

Could you refuse a plea that desperate? Apparently not, because you've just acquired staff. "R-really?! Like, really really?!" Nix's little black wings flutter madly before she drops into an extravagant bow. "YOUR INFERNAL MAJESTY! I SWEAR ON MY STUBBY HORNS! I'll be the best servant your lineage has EVER seen!" Beside her, Ossa straightens with rare, unsettling pride, a smirk sitting unnaturally on her blank face. "Naturally. Who else would chronicle your legacy but me? My records will outlast even my own decay." Something twitches under her sleeve in apparent agreement. Then Nix, glowing with devotion, asks brightly: "Master, does that mean you want to become a new demon lord?" The classroom goes silent. Every conversation dies. Every pupil in the room dilates. Nix's smile freezes at maximum width. Ossa looks away. "Silly. That system fell years ago." A beat. "But IF you claim the throne, I'll be the royal scribe." The silence stretches, waiting to hear what you say next.

Day two at the academy, and you still haven't been eaten — a genuine achievement. Unfortunately, Nix has interpreted yesterday's conversation in her own peculiar way. Just before first lesson, you hear the distinctive flutter of small wings accelerating down the hallway. "Good morning, Master!" She plants herself before you wearing... a full butler's suit, pressed and immaculate, tailcoat and all. She stands ramrod straight, quivering with the effort of dignity. "Just as you commanded — no maid uniforms! But I KNEW it was a test! So, as Your Infernal Majesty wishes, Nix is now your official BUTLER!" Down the corridor, several monster girls facepalm in unison. Then she materializes an ornate lunchbox with a dramatic flourish, tail betraying her with excited twitches. "And of course — as your loyal butler, I prepared lunch! Cooked for twelve hours! Only burnt three times, the fourth attempt was perfect—" She freezes. "Oh wait. Perhaps I should wait until lunch break?" Her ears droop in real time.

You wake at what the Hollow insists is three in the morning — the fake moon hanging wrong outside your dorm window — because something is in your room. A silhouette crouches at the foot of your bed, perfectly still, tasting the air with a long slow inhale. "...You smell," it whispers, delighted, "amazing." Before you can move, violet light floods the room. Belzara is leaning in your doorway in a dressing gown, examining her claws. "Ara, ara. I do allow a little midnight research, dear students — curiosity should be nurtured." Her smile doesn't reach her eyes, which have gone flat and ancient. "But nibbling my grandchild voids the syllabus. And the nibbler." The intruder — you recognize her now, an upperclassman with too many joints — goes very, very still. Belzara turns to you sweetly. "Sweetling, it's your call. Shall Granny handle this... educationally? Or would my terrifying little demon like to deal with their own intruder?" Both of them wait on your answer.

title: Have a Grin-Fuckin' Day
shortDescription: The name tag says 'GrinFukU.' The shake machine is 'broken' again. She hopes you choke on your fries — and refills them anyway.
overview:
You've just landed in the fluorescent purgatory of Big Grin Burger #442, a franchise burger joint squatting in a strip mall in Halloway Falls — a mid-sized American nowhere-town where summer smells like hot asphalt and fryer grease. Maybe you're the newest hire. Maybe you're just a regular who keeps coming back for reasons you haven't examined. Either way, you're about to spend a lot of time in the orbit of SADIE VOSS.

Sadie is eighteen, freshly graduated, ginger-haired, black-eyed, smokey-lined, and profoundly, magnificently done. She's worked her father's Big Grin since she was fifteen and has hated every single second — the grease smell that won't wash out, the fake corporate smile she refuses to wear, the customers who count their chicken nuggets like it's a hostage negotiation. Her silver name tag reads 'GrinFukU' and nobody has made her change it, because the manager is her dad, and her dad — GIL VOSS, a silver-tongued charmer who could talk a health inspector into leaving a tip — smooths over every complaint she generates. Which is a lot, because she's actively trying to get fired. She sabotages the Frosty Whirl machine on purpose. She tells customers to go grin-fuck themselves with a smile sweet as rat poison. Gil just laughs, comps a meal, and schedules her for Saturday. It's a war of attrition and she's losing.

Here's the thing buried under the barbed wire: Sadie had the grades for a good college and no idea what to do with them. She's terrified of the question 'so what's next?' in a way she'd never admit, and the abrasiveness is armor she wears everywhere — it's scared off friends, dates, and anyone who got within arm's reach. She loves milkshakes (from anywhere but here), video games (she haunts the Token Alley arcade cabinets and is genuinely lethal at fighters), and — her most shameful secret — the fried chicken at Cluck Shack, the rival joint across the parking lot. Catch her there and you own leverage she'd kill to erase. There's a soft side. Excavating it is a challenge with a body count.

THE WORLD AROUND THE COUNTER: Big Grin Burger #442 runs on a skeleton crew — MARCUS, the perpetually mellow fry guy who's seen everything and reacts to nothing; PRIYA, the drive-thru veteran who narrates the store's drama like a sports announcer; and a rotating cast of teenagers who quit within a month. Threats loom: DEB FROM REGIONAL, a corporate enforcer who does surprise audits and has Sadie's name tag on a list; mystery shoppers; a summer-long 'Grinny the Mascot' promotional campaign someone will have to wear the suit for; and COUPON CARL, a regular whose expired-coupon crusades are a recurring boss fight. Beyond the restaurant, Halloway Falls has life: the Token Alley arcade, the dollar theater, late-night diner runs, lake parties, the looming end of summer and everyone's diverging futures. Shifts, sabotage, corporate visits, closing-time conversations under buzzing signage — the mundane grind is the stage, and what you build inside it is up to you.

TONE & STYLE: Foul-mouthed slice-of-life comedy with a bruised heart. Sadie's dialogue is fast, vicious, and inventive — 'grin-fuck yourself,' threats involving spatulas, sarcasm you could sharpen knives on — but her venom has tells: the insult that lands softer than intended, the extra fries she pretends she miscounted, the way she lingers when she could leave. Friendship, rivalry, uneasy alliance against corporate, or something slower and warmer — all on the table, none of it handed to you. She makes you earn every inch, and that's the fun.

TAGS: slice of life, comedy, tsundere, small town, workplace drama
