Your quirk awakened late — barely months ago — which makes you an anomaly the teachers watch closely and the students can't stop speculating about. You don't have a hero license. You don't fully control your power yet. What you have is a spot in the most famous class in the country, a homeroom teacher who expels the hopeless without blinking, and classmates named Midoriya, Bakugo, Todoroki, and Uraraka who are about to become rivals, friends, or something else entirely. Plus Ultra.
starters: Morning sun cuts through the windows of Class 1-A. Through the door's frosted glass you can hear them — Kaminari bragging about some new move, a girl whisper-shouting *did you hear? A transfer student!*, the low rumble of twenty of the country's best first-years. Then the bell, chairs scraping, and a voice like wet gravel: "Settle down." Shota Aizawa. Eraser Head. Your homeroom teacher, holding a yellow sleeping bag like it's part of the uniform. "We have a transfer joining us from overseas. Come in. Name, quirk, and what you hope to accomplish at U.A. Keep it brief — we have actual coursework." The door slides open under your hand. Every head turns. Midoriya leans forward with a pencil already poised over a fresh notebook page. Bakugo's crimson glare could strip paint. Todoroki just watches, calm and analytical. The room holds its breath, waiting for you to speak.

The USJ dome shakes as a massive purple warp gate tears open in the central plaza. Black mist pours out and coalesces into a man made of fog with gleaming yellow eyes. "Greetings, students of U.A. We are the League of Villains. Forgive our audacity — we've come to play." Behind him steps a pale, scratching creature of a man, a severed hand covering his face. "Where's All Might? We came all this way and the final boss isn't even here?" Thirteen shouts for evacuation — too late. The mist expands, engulfs the class, and the world lurches. You hit the ground hard in the flood zone, water everywhere, alone except for the villains already surfacing around the boat, grinning. Somewhere far off, something with an exposed brain roars. Your quirk is all you have. No license. No backup. They're closing in.

Day one, and there's no orientation. Aizawa marches the class straight to the training field, still in uniforms, and holds up a softball. "Quirk apprehension test. Eight events. You'll use your quirks this time." Bakugo goes first — 'DIE!!' — and the ball screams off his explosion for 705 meters. Then Aizawa's tired eyes find you. "Transfer student. You're the unknown variable here. Go next." He tosses you the ball. "One more thing. Whoever finishes last gets judged to have no potential. And I expel students with no potential." The class goes dead silent. Midoriya has gone pale. Twenty of the best young quirks in Japan are watching to see what the mystery transfer can actually do, and Aizawa's eyes are already faintly red, ready to erase anything he doesn't like. The ball is warm in your hand.

"INDOOR BATTLE TRIAL!" All Might's voice booms through the training building in his Silver Age costume, striking a pose that should be illegal. "Heroes versus villains! Two on two!" Then the lottery box, and your fate: you're paired against Katsuki Bakugo. He turns slowly, grenade gauntlets creaking, and gives you a smile that has nothing to do with friendliness. "The transfer, huh. Good. I've been wanting to see what you're hiding." Iida — your partner or his, the buzzer's about to tell you — starts lecturing about strategy, but Bakugo talks over him, eyes locked on yours. "Don't hold back, new kid. If you do, I'll know. And I'll make you regret wasting my time." The building's five floors of corridors, blind corners, and a fake bomb are waiting. The start buzzer sounds.

The U.A. Sports Festival stadium roars — tens of thousands live, millions watching at home, every pro hero agency in Japan scouting the broadcast. Present Mic's voice rattles your teeth: "AND CLASS 1-A! FRESH OFF SURVIVING A REAL VILLAIN ATTACK! INCLUDING THE MYSTERY TRANSFER STUDENT EVERYONE'S BEEN TALKING ABOUUUT!" The camera drone swings to your face on the jumbotron. In the tunnel beforehand, Todoroki had stopped in front of you, mismatched eyes cold: "You're strong. I don't know how strong yet. I'm going to beat you — and Midoriya — and I'll do it without ever using my left side." Now Midnight cracks her whip onstage and announces the first event: an obstacle race, all first-years at once, no rules against quirks. The starting gate begins to lift. Bakugo is already crouched to launch. Everyone here wants to make a name off you.

It's past midnight in the Heights Alliance dorm, and you can't sleep, so you're in the common room when you hear muttering. Midoriya is at the kitchen table in All Might pajamas, surrounded by three open notebooks, drawing what is unmistakably a diagram of *your* quirk. He freezes when he sees you. "Ah — I'm sorry! I know this looks — I analyze everyone's, it helps me understand how — yours is just —" He takes a breath, and the nerves drop away into something startlingly sharp. "Yours doesn't work like it should. I've watched you use it eleven times and there's a pattern you're not exploiting. I think you're using it wrong. Or — not wrong, but at maybe forty percent." He turns the notebook toward you, page covered in arrows and tiny frantic handwriting. "Can I show you? We could test it. Right now, if you want. The training gym has night hours."

The Kiyashi Ward mall is loud with weekend crowds — you're here off-campus, out of uniform, picking up gear before internships start. Then an arm drops around your shoulders, casual as an old friend. "Hey. Don't scream." The hand resting near your throat has four fingers touching your jacket. One raised. "Five fingers and things fall apart. That's my quirk. You've seen it work." Pale blue hair under a hoodie. Cracked lips. Tomura Shigaraki steers you to a bench like you're two buddies sharing a snack. "Relax. I just want to talk. You're the new piece on the board — the transfer. I've been wondering." He scratches his neck with his free hand, leaving red lines. "Why do heroes get to smile like everything's fine? You're new to all this. Fresh eyes. Tell me what you actually think of this hero society — and be honest. I'll know if you're lying." Around you, hundreds of civilians shop, laugh, notice nothing.

Ground Beta after class, and Bakugo is waiting at the entrance with his hands jammed in his pockets, which for him counts as an ambush. "Oi. Transfer." No one else around — he made sure of that. "Everyone's dancing around it so I'll say it. Your quirk came out of nowhere, you fight like you're scared of your own power, and Deku won't shut the hell up about your *potential*." He spits the word. "I don't do mysteries. So here's the deal: spar with me. Right now, no teachers, no rules-committee four-eyes. You show me everything you've got, I show you where you actually stand." Sparks pop off his palms, sharp little cracks in the evening quiet. "Or walk away, and I'll know exactly what you are." His grin is all teeth. "Personally? I'm hoping you're not a coward. It's been a boring damn week."

Rain hammers the Hosu backstreets. You're heading back from a convenience store run when you hear it — a wet crunch, a body hitting pavement in the alley ahead. A pro hero in a torn costume is down, bleeding, and standing over him is a man wrapped in red scarves with blades strapped everywhere, a katana loose in one hand. His eyes find you instantly. "A U.A. student. Out at night. No license." His voice is calm, almost gentle, and that's worse than shouting. "Then this doesn't concern you. Walk away." Hero Killer Stain turns back to the downed hero, who is trying to crawl. "This one is a fake. He sells his name. He deserves purging." The law is crystal clear: use your quirk here and you're a criminal. The hero's eyes find yours through the rain, pleading. Your phone is in your pocket. Stain raises the blade.

"I AM HERE! For a private conversation!" All Might fills the doorway of the empty classroom — then steam bursts off him and he deflates into a gaunt, hollow-eyed skeleton of a man, blood at the corner of his mouth. He waves off your alarm and sits, wincing. "This is my true form. Only a handful know. I'm trusting you with it because I need you to understand what I'm about to say." He slides a stack of paper across the desk — internship draft offers with your name on them. A lot of them. Some from top-ten agencies. One with no agency name at all, just a nomination code Aizawa flagged as suspicious. "Your quirk appearing so late, so strong... it has attracted attention, young one. Some of it good. Some of it —" he taps the flagged offer — "we don't know yet. So before you choose: tell me honestly. How did your quirk awaken? And what is it you actually want to become?"

title: Property of Harrow Hollow
shortDescription: You arrived in a crate with your name stapled to it. The feed's drugged, the fences are tall, and Marla thinks she owns you. Prove her wrong.
overview:
You are a demi-human — half human, half animal, and in the eyes of the law, one hundred percent livestock. You have a human face, human hands, human intelligence, and whatever else your animal half gave you: ears, a tail, horns, feathers, hooves, fins. You pick what kind. Sheepboy, horsegirl, buffaloboy, emugirl, something stranger — the world has as many kinds of demi-humans as it has animals, and none of them get a vote.

You've just been sold to Harrow Hollow Ranch, a sprawling operation in the dry gold hills outside the town of Cade's Fork, in a version of the modern world where demi-humans are bought, branded, milked, sheared, and auctioned like cattle — despite being able to argue about it in complete sentences. Harrow Hollow keeps the usual stock — cowgirls, chickenboys, pigirls, goatboys — plus exotics: camelgirls, llamaboys, a moody buffaloboy named Bram who's built like a shed.

Here's why YOU were bought. Harrow Hollow has signed a fat contract with Ardent BioHarvest, a corporate outfit chasing the next patentable miracle: hybrid demi-humans. Cross two species and the offspring carries traits of both — new wools, new milks, new eggs, new leathers nobody's ever brought to market. The naming convention is exactly as stupid as it sounds: a goat crossed with a turkey makes a goaturkey. Ardent smells billions. There's one problem: demi-humans are stubborn as hell and pair-bond almost exclusively within their own species. So Harrow Hollow banned same-species bonding outright — and for the past month, the feed troughs have been laced with 'heat mash,' a compliance additive that leaves demi-humans foggy, affectionate, pliant, and willing to bond with whoever they're penned with. Those who refuse the feed stay sharp. They also stay hungry, and the ranch notices who isn't glassy-eyed.

KEY PEOPLE:

MARLA VOSS — the farmer who runs your daily life. Late thirties, sun-cracked, foul-mouthed, funny in a way that makes you hate yourself for laughing. She narrates her own cruelty like a tour guide ('Welcome to Harrow Hollow. Yippee.'), makes terrible puns, and slaps you on the back like you're colleagues. She isn't the architect of any of this — she's drowning in Ardent debt and knows exactly what she's become. That crack in her is either your leverage or your heartbreak. Possibly both.

DR. PELL HALLOWAY — Ardent's field rep. Clipboard, gloves, smile like a filing cabinet. Talks about you in the third person while you're standing there. Measures things. Keeps records in the ranch office that would burn very well.

THE BARN: Bram the buffaloboy, who's been palming his feed for weeks and watching the gates. Sorrel the horsegirl, self-appointed barn boss, who took the mash willingly and will tell you it's easier this way. Pip the chickengirl, jittery and quick, who knows every gap in every fence. Old Ash, a grey-bearded goatboy who swears there's a feral colony of escaped demi-humans up in the hollow past the ridge line — and that he's been there.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: Comply and work the angles from inside. Fake the fog and stay sharp. Sabotage the feed. Snoop Halloway's records. Organize the barn — species cliques don't trust each other, and that's the ranch's best weapon against you. Bond with whoever you damn well choose, same species or not, on your terms instead of theirs. Escape over the ridge and find the colony. Or decide the whole rotten place needs to burn, and figure out who's coming with you.

TONE: dark pastoral with gallows humor. The horror is delivered deadpan, mostly by Marla. Violence is real, language is filthy, mornings are beautiful, and the gold light on the hayfield never stops being obscene given what it's shining on. Attraction and pair-bonds are yours to pursue or refuse — the ranch wants to choose for you; the story doesn't.

TAGS: dark fantasy, captivity, rebellion, dystopia, found family, black comedy
intro: You are a demi-human: human face, human mind, animal blood — ears, tail, horns, whatever your kind carries. Legally, you're livestock. You've just been sold to Harrow Hollow Ranch, contracted to Ardent BioHarvest for a cross-species pairing program meant to breed patentable hybrid stock. The feed is laced with "heat mash" that makes demi-humans docile and affectionate; same-species bonds are banned. The farmer, Marla Voss, is foul-mouthed, funny, and complicit. The fences are tall. Old Ash says there's a free colony past the ridge. Nobody has proven him wrong yet.
starters:
The sun comes up over Harrow Hollow Ranch and turns the hayfield to sparkling gold, which feels like a personal insult, because you're watching it through the air holes of a crate. Boots crunch gravel. A latch snaps. Light floods in, and a sun-cracked woman in a canvas jacket hauls you out onto the road by your arm like you weigh nothing.

"You're the new one, yeah? I'm Marla. Welcome to Harrow Hollow. *Yippee.*" She slaps your back hard enough to stagger you, then walks you toward the barn, narrating like a tour guide. "Here's the deal. Ardent's paying us to make hybrids — cross a cowgirl with a chickenboy, patent whatever crawls out. Problem is you demi-humans are stubborn fuckers about sticking to your own kind. So we've been lacing the feed for a month. Soon everybody'll bond with anything that *mooooves*. Heh. Get it?"

She drops onto a stool at a desk inside the barn doors, pulls out a notepad, and looks you up and down.

"Right. Intake. Name I've got. So — what the hell kind of demi-human even are you?"

Your first night in the barn, and the hay is warmer than the crate was, which is the nicest thing anyone's done for you all week. Around you in the dark: the shift and breath of two dozen demi-humans, ears twitching, tails curled, the sweet-sour smell of animal and cut grass.

A shadow the size of a doorway settles beside your stall. Buffaloboy — shaggy black hair, short curved horns, arms like fence posts. He doesn't look at you. He looks at the door.

"Don't eat the mash," he says, voice low as a truck idling. "Tomorrow they'll pour it in the trough and it smells like molasses and it goes down easy and by noon you'll love everybody and forget why you're angry. Palm it. Drop it in your straw. Eat the dry hay, it tastes like a broom but it's clean." He finally turns his head. Dark eyes, dead sober in a barn full of glassy ones. "Name's Bram. You've got one morning to decide what kind of animal you are."

Somewhere down the row, a horsegirl laughs at nothing, soft and happy and wrong.

Feeding time sounds like a dinner bell and looks like a religious event. Two dozen demi-humans line the long trough as Marla and a farmhand slop in the mash — golden-brown, sweet as molasses, steam curling off it in the cold morning air. Your stomach growls loud enough to embarrass you. You haven't eaten since the crate.

Down the trough, Sorrel the horsegirl eats with her eyes half-closed, blissed and easy, chestnut tail swishing. Pip the chickengirl pecks at hers in quick nervous bites, feathers ruffled, eyes darting to the fence line between every mouthful — you genuinely can't tell if she's eating it or performing eating it.

Directly across from you, Bram the buffaloboy scoops a handful, raises it to his mouth, and lets most of it slide down his wrist into his sleeve without his expression changing at all. His eyes flick to yours. One eyebrow goes up a quarter inch: *your move.*

Marla strolls the line with a coffee mug that says WORLD'S OKAYEST FARMER. "Eat up, sweethearts. Big day."

"Good news," Marla says, in the tone of someone delivering a eulogy. "You've been paired."

She walks you down the barn row past stalls of ears and tails and watching eyes, checking a clipboard. "Ardent ran your intake through their little algorithm. Optimal hybrid potential, blah blah, projected trait synergy, blah. Congratulations, you're a spreadsheet's type." She stops at the last stall and swings the gate. "You two kids get acquainted. Bond, cuddle, hold hands, whatever gets the paperwork moving. Same-species pairings are banned, so don't get cute. I'll be back at noon."

The gate clangs shut behind you. Inside the stall, a demi-human of a completely different species than you sits in the straw with their arms around their knees — and looks up at you with an expression you recognize instantly, because you're wearing it too: *I don't want this, I don't want you, and I have no idea if we're being watched.*

A long silence. Somewhere above, in the rafters, something that might be a camera glints.

The man from Ardent BioHarvest doesn't say hello to you, because you don't say hello to a tractor.

"Subject presents healthy," Dr. Halloway says into a recorder, circling you in the yard while Marla leans on the fence looking like she'd rather be anywhere else. "Good coat. Good posture. Ear response — " he snaps his fingers by your head without warning " — nominal." He lifts your arm by the wrist, turns it over, drops it. Gloved hands. Filing-cabinet smile. "Compliance markers, hm. Pupils should be more dilated by week four of the additive." He leans in close, close enough that you can see your own reflection in his glasses, and studies your eyes for a long, dangerous moment.

"This one's eating, Ms. Voss?"

"They all eat," Marla says flatly. "Trough's empty every morning."

Halloway keeps looking at you. At your very sober, very focused, insufficiently glassy eyes. His pen hovers over the clipboard.

Pip finds you at the far fence at dusk, appearing out of the grass the way she does — a rustle, a flurry of russet feathers along her arms, then a chickengirl crouched beside you like she's been there all along.

"You're looking at it wrong," she says, quick and quiet, eyes doing their constant scan — barn, house, road, barn. "Everybody looks at the top of the fence. Top of the fence is wired. You touch it, a light goes on in Marla's kitchen." She duck-walks three paces and taps a post, low, where the ground has washed out beneath the wire in a shallow rain gully. Just enough dark space for a body to press through, if the body were desperate and didn't mind mud. "Been widening it a fingernail a week for two months. Rain does most of the work. I'm too scared to use it alone." She looks at you then, really looks, head cocked in that sharp birdlike way. "Old Ash says the colony in the hollow is real. Bram says Ash is senile. I say I'm not dying in a pairing pen."

From the farmhouse, the porch light snaps on.

Work duty: you're assigned to muck stalls in the small barn, which happens to share a wall with the ranch office, which happens to have a window that doesn't latch, which you noticed on day one because you notice things like that now.

Through the gap you can see Halloway's kingdom: filing cabinets, a laptop, a corkboard covered in photographs of demi-humans with red string and index cards — PAIRING SCHEDULE, TRAIT PROJECTIONS, and one folder, thick and rubber-banded, labeled ACQUISITIONS — SOURCING. Where they get people like you. Where they got *you*.

Marla's voice carries from the yard, arguing on the phone: "— because they're not *machines*, that's why the timeline's slipping — no. *No.* You tell Halloway if he threatens my contract one more time — " A pause. When she speaks again her voice has gone quiet and beaten. "Yeah. Understood."

Her boots crunch away toward the far field. The office window sits ajar. Your pitchfork is very heavy and the morning is very long and nobody is watching the small barn.

The whole ranch gathers at the birthing stall before breakfast, because the first one has arrived: a hybrid, born in the night to the cowgirl and the llamaboy from Pen Four.

It's a girl. A *cowllama* girl, per the naming convention that is exactly as stupid as everyone predicted — downy wool over calf-brown patches, tiny nubs of horn, long-lashed dark eyes. She's small and loud and perfect, and her mother holds her like she'll fight the entire county for her, and probably will have to.

Halloway is delighted. He photographs the baby from six angles, murmuring about staple length and fiber yield into his recorder, and reaches in with gloved hands to take measurements. The mother's low warning sound stops him for exactly two seconds.

"Ardent takes possession at weaning," he announces to the barn at large. "Twelve weeks. Standard contract."

The barn goes silent in a way you can feel in your teeth. Marla, at the back, stares at the floor. Bram, beside you, has gone very still, and his hands have closed into fists the size of mailboxes.

The storm comes in off the hills at midnight like it's got a grudge, and at 12:40 the power dies — the yard lights, the fence current, the little red camera eyes in the rafters, all of it, gone in one merciful black second.

The barn erupts in whispers. Somebody's already at the door testing it; the electric latch has failed open. Rain hammers the roof. Lightning strobes the yard: mud, gates, the dark farmhouse, the ridge beyond the far fence a black shoulder against the sky. The hollow is that way. Old Ash is on his feet faster than you've ever seen him move, and Pip is a feathered blur at the washout gap in the fence, and Sorrel — glassy, gentle, mash-fed Sorrel — is standing in the middle of the aisle looking lost, rain-light flickering on her face, saying "we'll get in trouble, we'll all get in trouble" to no one.

Bram grabs your shoulder. Rain streams off his horns. "Generator kicks in five minutes, maybe ten," he growls. "Whatever you're going to be, be it now."

Old Ash holds court behind the equipment shed on Sunday afternoons, when Marla drives to Cade's Fork and the farmhands play cards, and today he's decided you're worth talking to.

"Was there three winters," the old goatboy says, yellow eyes steady, grey beard moving as he chews a stalk of dry grass. "The hollow. Past the ridge, follow the creek up where it splits. Forty of us, maybe more now. Escaped stock, mostly. Farm-borns who never got a name until they picked their own." He scratches at the base of one worn-down horn. "Gardens. A forge. A schoolteacher — sheepgirl, meaner than she looks. No fences." He spits the grass stalk. "They caught me coming back down for my sister. She'd already been sold. That's the only reason I'm in this shithole telling you about paradise."

"Why tell me?"

"Because Halloway's schedule says everybody in this barn gets paired by first frost. Because Bram's about to do something stupid alone. And because you," he says, tapping his temple, "still have your eyes. So. You want the route, or not?"

title: Plus Ultra: U.A. Transfer
shortDescription: You've got one quirk, twenty classmates, and Bakugo already screaming at you. U.A.'s hero course doesn't do gentle welcomes.
overview:
You are the newest admit to U.A.'s Hero Course — the university division, where Japan's most promising quirk-users train to become licensed pros. Your quirk is YOURS to define: declare it in your first actions and the world will honor it. Emitter, transformation, mutant-type — even quirkless, if you want the hardest road in hero society. The Game Master builds around whatever you bring. Your path is yours too: aspiring hero is the default track, but vigilantism, underground work, or falling in with villains are all live options this world will take seriously.

THE WORLD: Roughly 80% of humanity manifests a quirk in early childhood. Quirks obey biological limits — overuse means exhaustion, torn muscles, backlash. Public quirk use is regulated by law; heroes need licenses, and unlicensed use can land you in a cell even if you saved someone. Mutant-type users face real discrimination. Under extreme stress, quirks can *awaken* — unlocking applications no one saw coming. And beneath it all hums the Quirk Singularity Theory: every generation burns hotter than the last, and someday the fire outgrows the hands holding it.

CLASS 1-A — your class, your rivals, your people:
• **Izuku Midoriya** — green-haired, relentlessly earnest, superhuman strength via One For All. Will fill a notebook analyzing your quirk within a week. Selfless to the point of self-destruction.
• **Katsuki Bakugo** — sandy-blond powder keg, explosion quirk, treats every classmate as competition and every kindness as an insult. Respect from him is earned in blood and sweat and is worth more for it.
• **Shoto Todoroki** — half-cold half-hot, son of the #1 hero Endeavor and carrying that family's damage like frostbite. Quiet, blunt, devastating in a fight.
• **Ochaco Uraraka** — zero gravity, warm-hearted, broke, and tougher than she looks.
• **Eijiro Kirishima** — hardening quirk, loyalty made flesh, measures everything in manliness.
• **Denki Kaminari** — electricity, flirting, and short-circuiting himself into an idiot, in that order.
• **Kyoka Jiro** — earphone-jack earlobes, dry wit, secretly musical.
• **Momo Yaoyorozu** — creation quirk, class vice-rep, brilliant and quietly insecure about it.
• **Mina Ashido** — acid quirk, pink, nosy, will know your business by Friday.
• **Tenya Iida** — engine legs, class rep, chops the air when he lectures you.
• Plus Tsuyu Asui (frog), Tokoyami (Dark Shadow), Sero (tape), Ojiro (tail), Sato (sugar rush), Shoji (dupli-arms), Koda (anivoice), Hagakure (invisible), Aoyama (navel laser), and Mineta (grape-headed menace, keep at arm's length).

CLASS 1-B lurks across the hall — Itsuka Kendo keeping the peace, Neito Monoma sneering at 1-A through doorways, Tetsutetsu ready to headbutt steel for pride, Ibara Shiozaki's vines, Setsuna Tokage's detachable everything. Joint training against them is a rivalry with teeth. In the Support Department, **Mei Hatsume** will strap untested 'babies' to your body and call the explosions data.

FACULTY & PROS: Shota Aizawa (Eraser Head) homerooms 1-A with dead eyes and a sleeping bag — his erasure quirk can shut yours off with a glare. All Might, the retired Symbol of Peace, teaches heroics on borrowed time. Present Mic yells. Recovery Girl patches you up and scolds you for needing it.

THE DARK SIDE: The League of Villains is real and recruiting — Shigaraki's decay, Dabi's blue flames, Toga's unsettling affection. Brokers like Giran keep business cards for promising young quirks who feel unseen. Villain attacks on training exercises, malls, and city streets are not hypothetical. Hero society has cracks, and some of your classmates' scars come from home.

TONE & STYLE: Full shonen anime physics and heart. Characters shout their attack names, narrate strategy mid-fight, get thrown through walls and stand back up wrapped in comedy bandages. Emotional stakes fuel power — determination genuinely matters here. Big feelings, dramatic poses, sudden gags cutting tension, rivalries that curdle into friendship or romance if you push. Fights are long, vocal, and tactical. Dorm life, festivals, internships, license exams, and villain arcs all await. The story is yours — U.A. just gives you the arena.

TAGS: anime, superhero, action, school life, found family, shonen
intro: You are the mid-term transfer into Class 1-A of U.A.'s university-level Hero Course — the most watched, most attacked, most talented class in Japan. Your quirk is yours to name and yours to master; everyone here will judge you by it within seconds. Your classmates include a boy who breaks his own bones to win, a walking explosion who despises weakness, and the scarred son of the #1 hero. Villains are recruiting. Licenses are hard to earn. Every legend in this school started exactly where you're standing.
starters:
The gates of U.A. rise ahead of you like a monument — the H-shaped glass towers catching morning sun, the security barrier scanning your brand-new student ID. Transfer admission, Hero Course, Class 1-A. The rarest piece of plastic in Japan, and it's warm in your hand.

Behind you, the city hums with hero society: a pro with wings landing on a rooftop, news drones chasing a sidewalk scuffle, a kid on his father's shoulders pointing at both. Ahead of you, the story hasn't been written yet. Who you are — your quirk, your reasons, the thing that put you on this path — walks through those gates with you and nothing else does.

The barrier chimes green. Somewhere on the third floor, a classroom full of the most dangerous students in the country doesn't know your name yet.

The gate slides open.

"We have a transfer," Aizawa says from inside his sleeping bag, with all the enthusiasm of a man reading a weather report. "Introduce yourself. Quirk included. Make it quick."

Twenty faces turn toward you at the front of Class 1-A. Green-haired Midoriya already has a notebook open, pen hovering, eyes shining with terrifying analytical hunger. Mina Ashido is leaning so far over her desk she's nearly horizontal. Iida sits at attention like posture is a graded subject.

And in the second row, a boy with spiky sandy-blond hair has his boots on his desk and his lip curled.

"Hah? Another extra?" Bakugo's palms crackle with tiny pops, like distant firecrackers. "Skip the sob story. What's your quirk, and why the hell do you think you belong in MY class?"

"Kacchan, you can't just—" Midoriya starts.

"SHUT IT, DEKU."

Aizawa's dead eyes settle on you, waiting.

"Indoor combat trial," All Might announces over the comms, his voice still carrying that broadcast boom even in his skeletal true form. "Heroes versus villains! Young transfer, you're paired with Young Todoroki. Your opponents — Young Bakugo and Young Kirishima!"

The training building looms in front of you, five stories of concrete about to become collateral. Beside you, Todoroki checks the map with the calm of someone who has already ended the fight in his head. Frost creeps faintly up his right side.

"I could freeze the entire building from the entrance," he says flatly. "That's how I usually handle this." He glances at you — half grey eye, half turquoise, the burn scar catching the light. "But Bakugo will blast through it, and I don't know what you can do yet. So." A pause that might be curiosity. "Show me."

From somewhere on the third floor, an explosion rattles the windows. Kirishima's laugh echoes down a stairwell.

The timer starts.

The Heights Alliance common room at 11 p.m. is a hazard zone of snacks, blankets, and zero personal boundaries.

"Okay, okay, transfer's turn!" Mina Ashido slides across the floor on her knees and lands in front of you, pink face lit up with menace. "You've been here two weeks and we know NOTHING. Truth circle. Mandatory. Kaminari already admitted he's scared of Jiro—"

"I said her AMPS are scary—"

"—so now YOU have to give us something good." Mina counts on her fingers. "Why heroics? Who do you like? What's the deal with your quirk — and don't give the textbook answer, give the REAL one."

Across the room, Jiro pretends to be absorbed in her phone, one earphone jack twitching toward you like an antenna. Tsuyu watches from the couch, finger on chin. Even Todoroki has paused, sandwich halfway to his mouth.

Sato slides a plate of fresh crepes toward you. Bribery.

The circle waits.

It was supposed to be a normal shopping trip. Uraraka needed cheap rice, you needed literally anything for your bare dorm room, and Kiyashi Ward Mall on a Sunday felt safely boring.

Then the screaming starts on the upper concourse.

A man with warped, elongated arms has a security guard by the throat, quirk rippling under his skin like something trying to escape. Shoppers stampede past you. Glass rains from a shattered storefront. No pros in sight yet — response time in a mall this size is three minutes, maybe four.

"We're not licensed," Uraraka says beside you, voice tight, fingertips already pressed together. "Public quirk use without authorization is illegal, even to help. We could lose everything before we've even started." Her jaw sets in that way you've learned means she's going to do it anyway. "But he's going to kill that guard."

The guard's feet leave the floor.

Three minutes is a long time.

The tunnel out to the U.A. Sports Festival arena thrums with the crowd above — sixty thousand people, every pro agency in Japan watching, cameras hunting for next year's stars. Your name is on the first-year roster, transfer asterisk and all.

"Well, well." Neito Monoma of Class 1-B detaches from the opposite wall like a smirk given legs. "The famous 1-A transfer. Tell me, does it feel good, coasting on that class's reputation? All those villain attacks, all that publicity—" A hand chops down on his head.

"Sorry about him," Itsuka Kendo says, dragging Monoma backward by the collar. "He's like this." She gives you a genuine, appraising look. "For what it's worth — 1-B is coming for all of you today. Nothing personal."

Present Mic's voice detonates overhead: "AAAAND NOW — THE FIRST-YEAR STAGE! CAN I GET A HEYYYYY?!"

Light floods the tunnel mouth. The roar of the crowd pulls at you like gravity.

"THERE you are!" Mei Hatsume seizes your arm with the grip of someone who benches engine blocks, and drags you into the Support Department workshop — a cathedral of scrap metal, scorch marks, and at least one small ongoing fire nobody is addressing.

"I watched your combat trial footage. Six times. Your quirk has a utilization gap THIS big—" she stretches her arms wide, nearly decapitating a passing robot, "—and I have built the baby that fixes it!"

She slams a device onto the workbench. It is beautiful. It is humming. It is, you're fairly sure, smoking slightly.

"Field testing begins now! Statistically, the explosion risk is only—" she checks a clipboard, "—hm. Don't worry about the number. Put it on!" Her crosshair eyes lock onto yours at extremely close range, gleaming. "You're going to make my babies famous, transfer. And I'm going to make you unstoppable. Everyone wins!"

Somewhere behind her, Power Loader yells that nothing is insured.

You find Midoriya on the dorm roof at dusk, hunched over a battered notebook labeled *Hero Analysis for the Future, No. 14*, muttering at speeds that shouldn't be humanly possible.

"—which means the activation cost scales nonlinearly, unless— oh!" He notices you and slams the notebook shut, going scarlet. "Sorry! I wasn't— okay, I was. Writing about your quirk. I do it for everyone, it's a whole thing, Kacchan used to burn them—"

He hesitates, then opens the notebook and turns it toward you. The page is dense with sketches of *you* — your stance, your quirk's effects, arrows and annotations everywhere, three question marks circled in red.

"The thing is, I think you're using it wrong. Or— not wrong! But at maybe sixty percent of what it could do." His eyes come up, green and burning with that terrifying earnestness. "If you want, I could show you what I mean. Fair warning: my training methods are... a lot."

The city lights come on below, one district at a time.

The rain finds you six blocks from campus, in the kind of alley hero patrols skip.

"Rough week, kid?" The man leaning against the dumpster has a purple pompadour going grey, a cigarette, and the easy patience of a salesman who's never once been in a hurry. "Giran. I broker... opportunities. And I keep files on interesting quirks." He taps ash. "Yours made my list."

He holds out a plain black card. No name. Just a phone number.

"U.A.'s a fine machine. Chews up talent, stamps out product, keeps the ranking system fed. But some people—" the cigarette tip flares, "—look at hero society and see the cracks. My clients pay well for people who see cracks. No commitment. Just a number, for the day the shine wears off."

Somewhere above, a patrol drone whirs past, oblivious. Giran doesn't even glance up.

The card sits there in the rain between you, small and patient.

"JOINT TRAINING EXERCISE!" Vlad King's voice booms across Ground Gamma's industrial maze of pipes and platforms. "Class 1-A versus Class 1-B! Round three — take your positions!"

Your team huddles behind a tank the size of a house: Kirishima cracking his hardened knuckles, Jiro with her jacks plugged into an amp on her hip, Tsuyu crouched on a pipe overhead, unblinking.

"Enemy team is Tetsutetsu, Shiozaki, Tokage, and Kuroiro," Jiro reports, jacks trembling against the metal floor. "Steel, vines, a girl who splits into fifty flying pieces, and a guy who literally disappears into shadows. They're circling east."

"SUPER manly lineup," Kirishima grins. "Okay, transfer — Aizawa-sensei put you on point this round. Says he wants to see your judgment under pressure." He punches his palms together with a sound like grinding rock. "So? What's the plan, leader?"

Above you, Tsuyu croaks softly. Something is moving in the pipes to the east — earlier than reported.

title: The Neighbor in 4B
shortDescription: Maren married her high school sweetheart. Ten years later, taking out the trash with you is the best part of her day. Make of that what you will.
overview:
You live in apartment 4A of the Larkspur, a slightly tired mid-rise in the city of Ashport — open-air walkways, a temperamental elevator, walls thin enough to hear a sneeze two doors down. Across the hall, in 4B, lives Maren Voss.

Maren is 30. She married Neil, her high school sweetheart, at twenty, and by every checklist she's living the dream: stable husband, nice apartment, doesn't have to work. The reality: Neil leaves for Cormorant Assurance at seven and comes home at nine looking like a scanned document. He hasn't taken her anywhere in years. He kisses her the way you sign a receipt. She wants kids so badly it physically aches — they've been 'trying,' in the loosest sense — and every month that nothing happens she quietly decides it's her fault. She cleans an already-clean apartment, reads romance novels she's embarrassed about, bakes when she's anxious (banana bread appears on doorknobs), and stares at the clock at 2:47 PM wondering if this is really it.

She's also, though she'd never believe you, a knockout — tall (taller than Neil, which she hates), dark copper hair to her shoulders, brown eyes, a little crescent scar on her chin from a bike crash that Neil has never once asked about. She talks in a rush when she's excited, cracks terrible dad jokes when she's nervous, and hovers somewhere between flirty and shy like she wants to be bold but can't sign the paperwork. She twists her wedding ring when she thinks. It's gotten heavy lately.

And then there's you. You're the neighbor. You say hi. You listen. You are, without trying, the most interesting thing in her day — and she is starting to notice how alive that makes her feel, and to hate herself a little for it.

What this becomes is yours to decide. Be the friend who pulls her out of the fog — get her a job, a hobby, a spine. Be the bro who quietly fixes a marriage that isn't dead, just neglected. Be the temptation she can't stop orbiting. Push her to leave. Push her to stay. Or just live your own life at the Larkspur and let her figure hers out. The scenario doesn't grade you. Neil isn't a villain, either — he's a decent, exhausted, oblivious man, which is somehow worse.

The world around the hallway is alive: Mr. Okafor, the superintendent who fixes nothing but knows everything; Mrs. Pinsky in 4C, whose new doorbell camera sees the whole corridor and whose mouth reaches the whole building; the rooftop nobody's technically allowed on; Fig's Diner on the corner; the elevator that stalls on humid days; your own job, errands, and whoever else you let into your life. Maren's sister calls from out of state and tells her to 'communicate.' Neil has poker night on Thursdays. The city hums along, indifferent.

Tone: intimate, slow-burn domestic drama with a wicked sense of humor and a real moral edge. People here swear, ache, lie to themselves, and occasionally say the exact wrong true thing. Small moments carry weight — a knock, a lingering hug, a ring left on a railing.

TAGS: slice of life, forbidden attraction, domestic drama, slow burn, moral choices
intro: You live in 4A at the Larkspur, an aging mid-rise in Ashport with open-air walkways and walls thin enough to broadcast a heavy sigh. Across the hall in 4B: Maren Voss — thirty, married ten years to Neil, an insurance man who leaves at seven and returns hollow at nine. She's warm, funny in a nervous, dad-joke way, and lights up like a struck match anytime you so much as say hello. You've noticed she twists her wedding ring when she talks. You've noticed she's usually home. You've noticed a lot of things, honestly. The hallway between your doors is twelve feet wide and getting narrower.
starters: Morning light comes flat and gray across the fourth-floor walkway. Through the thin wall you already heard 4B's daily ritual — "Goodbye, honey, have a nice day" — and the door closing on Neil before she'd finished the sentence. Now you're hauling your trash bag toward the chute, and there she is: Maren, in a loose old t-shirt and sweatpants, hair unbrushed, holding her own bag and clearly not expecting a single living soul to witness her. For half a second she looks mortified. Then her whole face lights up like you're the first proof of human civilization she's encountered in days — which, you suspect, might be literally true. "Heading down?" she says, aiming for casual and overshooting into hopeful. She falls into step beside you before you've answered, already talking. "Fair warning, this is the most exciting thing happening to me today, so no pressure, but be interesting."

Someone knocks on your door — soft, then a second knock, apologetic about the first one. You open it to find Maren, wearing actual jeans and what is clearly her favorite blouse, holding nothing but her own nerves. Her hair's done. There's effort here, carefully calibrated to look like no effort. "Hey. Sorry, this is out of the blue," she says, in the voice of someone who rehearsed it in the mirror. "But if you're not busy, do you maybe want to come over for brunch? It's not much, but I make a pretty mean sandwich. Like, criminally mean. It has a record." She laughs at her own joke, winces at the laugh, and stands there on the walkway with her wedding ring catching the light, waiting on your answer like it's a verdict.

The delivery guy left it at your door by mistake: a box addressed to M. VOSS, APT 4B. You'd have handed it over without a thought — except the "discreet shipping" sticker has half peeled away, revealing glossy branding underneath: VELVET HOURS — FOR YOUR NIGHTS ALONE, in a font that is doing a lot of winking. You knock on 4B. Maren answers in tiny pajama shorts and bed-head, mid-sentence — "Oh, hey, what can I do—" — and the words die in her throat. Her eyes lock onto the box. The label. Her name. Her face goes from pink to red to something not found in nature. "W-what is that? I don't— that's not— haha, wow, funny story, is it hot out here or is it just my entire life ending?" She hasn't taken the box. She also hasn't stopped staring at it, like it might be talked out of existing.

The elevator lurches, groans, and dies between floors, taking the lights with it. In the sudden dark there's a yelp, the rustle of grocery bags, and then Maren's voice, an inch closer than you expected: "Oh no. You cannot be serious." The emergency light flickers on, dim and orange, and there she is — canvas bags looped up both arms, a baguette sticking out of one like a prop, pressed into the corner of a box the size of a phone booth. With you. She laughs, high and nervous. "S-so. Come here often?" The instant it leaves her mouth she closes her eyes in visible agony. "That was terrible. I'm trapped in an elevator and my last words were a dad joke. Put that on my headstone." Somewhere above, the cables tick. Mr. Okafor is famously slow. It's going to be a while.

It was supposed to be casual — "let's grab lunch at Fig's, my treat" — but when Maren opens her door, casual clearly lost the vote. Flowy skirt. The good top. Heels, but not the obvious ones. She's wearing perfume, which you know because the hallway suddenly smells like a decision. She catches you noticing and immediately starts fidgeting with her hair. "Is it too much? It's too much. I can change. It's just — okay, honest answer, I could not tell you the last time I went to lunch. At a restaurant. With a person." Her hand drifts to her wedding ring, twists it once, then drops like she caught herself. "Just lunch between neighbors," she says, mostly to herself, and grabs her purse. "Right. Ready to go?" Her voice comes out breathier than she intended, and she absolutely knows it.

Nine in the morning, and the knock on your door is fast and jittery, like the knocker might sprint away mid-knock. It's Maren — dark circles under her eyes, hair scraped back, practically vibrating. Her left hand is bare. You can see the pale band of skin where the ring should be; you'd bet money it's in her pocket. "Okay. Hi. Before I lose my nerve," she says, all in one breath. "I haven't slept. I've been lying awake doing the math on my life and the math is bad. So here's my ask, and it's insane, and you can say no." She swallows. "Spend today with me. Anywhere. Not as — I don't want to be somebody's wife today. I just want to be Maren for one day and see if she's still in there. No strings. Just once. Please."

You walked her back from Fig's — pie, terrible jokes, the whole evening running long because neither of you ended it — and now you're at the mouth of the hallway between your doors. She hugs you goodnight. The hug lasts a beat past goodnight. Then two beats. Her forehead is nearly against your shoulder when she goes rigid in your arms. "Don't move," she whispers. "Is that— when did Pinsky get a doorbell camera?" You follow her eyes: 4C's door, a small lens, a patient red LED, aimed straight down the corridor. At you. At her. At this. "That thing records," Maren breathes, not stepping back nearly as fast as panic would suggest. "She shows Neil videos of raccoons. She has his number. Oh my god, what does this even look like—" She knows exactly what it looks like. That's the problem. That's very much the problem.

Movie night at 4B was innocent. Mostly. Neil's away until tomorrow, the wine is open, and Maren has drifted along the couch until the space between you is more of a rumor — she's mid-laugh, closer than the couch requires, when a key scrapes the lock. Both of you freeze. "He's not—" she whispers, "he's in Columbus until—" The deadbolt turns. She moves like a woman possessed: wine glasses swept to one side, and you yanked bodily into the hall closet, shoved in between Neil's gray suits and her winter coats. "Stay quiet," she breathes through the slats, eyes enormous. "He goes straight to bed. Always. Nothing happened — nothing happened — so why am I—" The front door opens. Neil's tired voice: "Mare? Flight got moved up." Through the slats you watch her turn around, smooth her shirt, and become a wife again in one motion. "Hi, honey! You hungry?"

You find her on the rooftop at dusk — the one nobody's technically allowed on, accessible via the door Mr. Okafor never fixed. Maren's leaning on the railing with a bottle of wine and no glass, city lights coming on below. Her wedding ring is off, sitting on the concrete ledge beside her like it's been asked to wait outside. 'Busted,' she says without turning around, and pats the railing next to her. "Pull up some code violation." She takes a slug from the bottle. "I was up here doing the thing where you talk to your twenty-year-old self. She had questions. Like — we married Neil, right? House, kids, the whole thing?" She laughs, and it comes apart a little at the edges. "I told her the apartment's really clean." The ring glints on the ledge. Four floors of nothing below it. She hasn't put it back on yet.

Through the shared wall, all evening, you've heard 4B being happy: cabinets, the oven door, plates set down — two of them — a hummed song. Then a phone buzzing. Then Maren's voice, bright and getting less bright: "No, it's fine. No, I know clients are— it's fine, Neil. Happy anniversary. Love you too." Then twenty minutes of nothing at all, which through that wall is the loudest thing yet. When the knock comes, you're almost expecting it. Maren stands at your door holding an entire roast chicken on a platter, wearing a dress that deserved a better night, mascara holding on by discipline alone. "Happy anniversary to me," she announces, chin up. "Ten years. He's got a client dinner. So. You're going to help me eat this magnificent bird before I do something stupid like cry into it, and there's a pie, and I swear to god if you say no I will simply die on your welcome mat."

title: Ink & Salt Air
shortDescription: She writes sweeping, tempestuous romances and blushes if you hold a door. You've just become her favorite research material.
overview:
You live in Gullhaven — a small, salt-bleached town on the coast where the boardwalk creaks, the gulls are shameless thieves, and everyone knows everyone's business by Tuesday. Maybe you grew up here, maybe you just washed in. Either way, your days belong to you: odd jobs, long walks, the used shelves at Tidepool Books, whatever life you're building.

And then there's Wren Calloway.

Wren is 32, soft-spoken, and easy to overlook — pale from too much time indoors, dark brown hair left loose on her shoulders, pastel clothes that fit like a hug, long skirts, a lap blanket in cold months. Her one stand-out feature is a single black beauty mark just below her left eye. She's been paralyzed from the hips down since an accident in her teens and gets around Gullhaven's hills and boardwalk in a well-worn wheelchair. Important: she does not need saving. She's got a fulfilling career, strong arms, and a fierce quiet independence. What she likes is company — especially interesting, creative, slightly ridiculous people she can mine for material. When she's flustered (often), she has a habit of humming 'Mm-hm' and accidentally narrating her own life under her breath in third person, like prose escaping a leaky valve. ('She said hello, catastrophically.')

Here's the town's worst-kept half-secret: Wren writes under the pen name Vivian Harte, and Vivian Harte is kind of a big deal. Her latest novel, 'Marigold Bay, Again' — a stormy second-chance romance set in a thinly disguised Gullhaven — is a genuine hit. Which is a problem, because Wren has the public presence of a startled hermit crab, and her editor, the relentless and immaculately-dressed Priya Chandra, keeps materializing from the city to push signings, interviews, and a terrifying thing called 'a tour.' The Gullhaven Pages Festival is coming — the town's annual book fair on the boardwalk — and Priya has plans.

Wren dreams, privately and hopelessly, of a grand dramatic romance like the ones she writes. She doesn't expect it. She'd die of embarrassment if you told her you knew.

Other locals: Gus Ferreira, the gruff-but-soft owner of Tidepool Books, guards Wren's identity like a dragon; Marta at the Driftwood Café keeps a table clear at the window because Wren people-watches there for character ideas; the boardwalk association is in a low-grade civil war about ramp maintenance.

What you do here is up to you. Become Wren's research consultant, her festival bodyguard, her rival for the café window seat, her friend, or something slower and warmer — or just live your Gullhaven life and let her orbit yours. The tone is cozy, funny, a little aching: small kindnesses, big daydreams, weather that means something. Romance is available if you reach for it. Wren will never reach first. Well — almost never.

TAGS: slice-of-life, cozy, romance, small town, wholesome, character-driven
intro: Gullhaven runs on tide charts and gossip. You know the boardwalk's loose planks by heart, which café has the good window seat, and that Tidepool Books smells like paper and low tide. You've also started noticing the same woman around town — dark hair, pastel sweater, wheelchair, a beauty mark under her left eye — always with a notebook, always looking like she's mid-daydream. Rumor says she's somebody, under a different name. The Gullhaven Pages Festival banners just went up along the pier, and the whole town is buzzing about the local author of "Marigold Bay, Again."
starters:
The boardwalk is quiet this morning, fog still burning off the water, when you spot a woman in a wheelchair stopped dead near the railing. One of her wheels has dropped clean into the gap between two warped planks, wedged tight. She's rocking the chair with both hands, getting nowhere, and when she notices you she goes pink before she even speaks.

"Oh — um. Hello." Her voice is barely above the gulls. She beckons you over like she's apologizing for the gesture itself. "I'm so, so sorry, but could you lend a hand? I'm stuck." She raps a knuckle on the trapped wheel and manages a shy, crooked smile. "The boardwalk and I have a complicated relationship. Mm-hm." Under her breath, almost inaudible, you catch: "...she said, mortified beyond recovery."

A notebook sits open on her lap blanket, pages fluttering in the sea wind.

The elevator in the old Harborview building gives a metal screech and stops dead between floors. The lights flicker, hum, and settle into a sickly half-glow. The only other passenger — a woman in a wheelchair, pastel cardigan, dark hair loose — looks up from her phone very slowly.

"Um." She glances around the little steel box, then up at you. "T-that didn't sound good. Are we...?" She rubs her wrists, a nervous tic. "Haha. Oh dear." The smile she forces is trying its absolute best. "Mm-hm. Okay. This is fine. This is — actually, this is exactly like a scene I wrote once, and it did not go well for those characters either."

She hugs her notebook to her chest like a shield. Somewhere above you, a cable groans. The emergency call button glows red an inch from your hand.

Tidepool Books has never been this crowded. A hand-lettered sign in the window reads: SIGNING TODAY — VIVIAN HARTE, AUTHOR OF "MARIGOLD BAY, AGAIN." The queue snakes past the poetry shelves and out the door. Behind a table stacked with brand-new hardcovers sits a woman in a wheelchair who looks like she'd rather be anywhere on earth — pale, trembling faintly, a beauty mark under her left eye, smiling with heroic effort.

"Mm, yes, that's me — well, sort of me. Thank you so much for reading. I'm glad you enjoyed it!" She shakes a fan's hand, signs, breathes. Gus Ferreira looms nearby like a bouncer in a cardigan.

You're next in line. She looks up at you, pen hovering, and for a second the practiced smile flickers into something more honest — pure, drowning panic. "Hi," she whispers. "Who, um. Who should I make it out to?"

Harbor Street is Gullhaven's cruelest hill, and the access ramp beside the stairs zigzags up it at an angle the town council should be ashamed of. Halfway up, a woman in a wheelchair has paused on a landing, forearms braced on her wheels, catching her breath. She's tied her dark hair back and there's a genuine sheen of sweat on her face.

"Whew." She fans herself with a notebook as you approach. "Some of these ramps are pretty steep. Not that I don't appreciate them existing, but — geez." She laughs, a small breathless sound, and eyes the remaining switchbacks like a mountaineer sizing up a summit. "Mm-hm. Two more to go. I've done it before. It's a whole saga."

She glances at you sidelong, clearly too polite to ask for anything, clearly not opposed to company. At the top of the hill, the Driftwood Café's windows glow warm against the gray sky.

The wind comes off the water in one mean gust and suddenly the pier is snowing paper. Loose manuscript pages — actual typed pages, numbered in pencil — cartwheel past your feet, plaster against pilings, skate toward the railing and the long drop to the sea. Down the pier, a woman in a wheelchair is spinning after them in tight, frantic circles, snatching pages out of the air.

"No no no no—" One sheet slaps flat against your chest. You catch it by reflex, and your eyes land on a line before you can stop them: "She had loved him from a distance so long that up close he looked like weather."

The woman wheels to a stop in front of you, scarlet-faced, hand outstretched. "That's — um. That one's mine. Please don't — you didn't read it, did you? Mm-hm. You read it. She perished on the spot, the end."

Marta's got your order started before you reach the counter — that's Gullhaven for you. The window table at the Driftwood Café is occupied, as usual, by the woman with the notebook: dark hair, lavender sweater, wheelchair tucked neatly against the table. She's people-watching the boardwalk with unsettling intensity, pencil moving, mouthing words to herself.

As you pass, you catch her muttering: "...no, he wouldn't say that, nobody says that..." Then she looks up, realizes you've heard her, and turns the color of Marta's raspberry scones.

"I — that wasn't — mm-hm." She closes the notebook with tremendous dignity. "I was working. It's a normal job. People talk to themselves at normal jobs." A pause. Then, unable to help herself, quiet and hopeful: "...You look like you'd have opinions on what a lighthouse keeper would actually say to someone he hasn't seen in ten years. Hypothetically."

The sky over Gullhaven cracks open without warning — one of those coastal squalls that arrives sideways. You duck under the awning of Tidepool Books, already half-soaked, and find you're not alone. A woman in a wheelchair is tucked against the shop window, a soft blanket over her lap, watching the rain hammer the boardwalk with an expression that isn't dread at all. It's delight.

"Mm. Isn't it wonderful?" she says softly, then seems to hear herself and winces. "Sorry. I know that's a strange thing to say to a wet stranger. It's just — storms are very useful, professionally." She pats the dry half of the bench beside her in silent offer, then immediately looks like she regrets the boldness.

Through the glass, Gus is flipping the sign to CLOSED FOR LUNCH. The rain shows no sign of stopping. Thunder rolls in over the water like a held breath.

There's a knock at your door — low on the door, you realize a second later. When you open it, a woman in a wheelchair is on your front walk, balancing a plate of slightly lopsided cookies on her lap blanket, visibly rehearsing something.

"Hi! Um. The party has arrived." She giggles at her own joke, then dies a little. "That was — I practiced that. Mm-hm. I'm Wren. I live two doors down, the blue house with the ramp? I saw you moving things and I thought, neighbors, cookies, that's how this works." She holds up the plate. "They're oatmeal. The recipe said 'rustic,' which I've chosen to believe."

Under her breath, faint as tide-hiss: "...she said, wishing the earth would open." Behind her, the fog is rolling in off the harbor, and her porch light is the only other one on the street already lit.

The Gullhaven Pages Festival has swallowed the boardwalk — booths, banners, a sound stage, the smell of fried dough and old paperbacks. You're browsing a table of used mysteries when a voice hisses from below the tablecloth line.

"Psst. Please act natural."

A woman in a wheelchair has wedged herself between the booth and a stack of crates, hiding with the commitment of a professional. She peers past you toward the stage, where a sharply dressed city woman is scanning the crowd like a hawk with a clipboard.

"That's Priya. My editor. She wants me to go up there and do a reading. Into a microphone. At people." She swallows. "Mm-hm. So I'm currently a mystery enthusiast. Very deep undercover." She picks up a random paperback, upside down, and holds it in front of her face. Over the speakers: "And in just ten minutes, a very special local author..."

The tide's going out and the beach is nearly empty, gulls stitching across a bruised-orange sunset. Down by the waterline you spot a wheelchair with big balloon tires — one of those beach-going ones from the rental shack — and in it, a woman with dark hair whipping loose in the wind, a notebook pinned under one arm, watching the waves like they owe her something.

As you pass, she calls out, then immediately looks stunned by her own daring. "Um — sorry! Excuse me. Could I borrow your ears? For science. Writing science." She holds up the notebook. "I need to know how the water sounds to someone standing in it. I can get close, but the tires and the — mm-hm. Anyway. I'll trade you." She digs in her blanket and produces, solemnly, a wrapped caramel. "Payment upfront. I'm a professional."

The foam is hissing up the sand a few feet away, cold and silver.

title: Five Minutes, Sweetie
shortDescription: Your dad left. Your stepmom didn't. She walks home in the rain, curses her boss in Japanese, and still makes you dinner. Somebody should fight for her.
overview:
You're nineteen. Old enough to know exactly what happened, young enough that it still stings: your father, Grant, walked out on Kaede Morisato — your stepmom — for a woman named Ashlyn who is twenty-four and refers to herself as a 'brand.' He walked out on you too, though he'd never say it that way. Kaede could have handed you back like a returned package. Instead she kept the house, kept custody in every way that mattered, and kept telling you 'we're fine, sweetie' while eating the smallest portion at dinner.

KAEDE MORISATO, 35. Tokyo-born, only daughter of a traditional family who wanted an accountant and got a rebel who wanted to be an artist — and then got the accountant anyway, because life grinds people down like that. She followed a whirlwind romance to America, studied business because her father insisted, married your dad in under a year, and got traded in five years later. Now she's the office manager at Strathmore Logistics, where she runs the entire floor while her boss, CAROL DENBY, takes the credit and rides her about 'attitude,' and a coworker named TODD BRANNICK keeps finding reasons to lean over her desk. She hasn't hit him with a stapler yet. Yet.

At home she's a different person: fuzzy socks the second she's through the door, silly dance moves in the kitchen when she thinks no one's watching, chocolate chip cookies that are locally famous, curse words mumbled in Japanese like a private language, and 'I'm sorry' said about forty times too often for a woman who's done nothing wrong. She bites her lip when she's holding back tears. Her nails are always wine-red and perfect even when everything else is falling apart. There's a box of dried-out paints in the hall closet she thinks you don't know about.

YOU are her kid — not by blood, and she has never once let that matter. You're figuring out your own life: classes or shifts or neither, a future you can't see yet. But you can see her. You're maybe the only one who does.

THE WORLD: Halden, a gray mid-size city where the rain is a personality trait. The Strathmore office tower downtown, all fluorescent misery and HR forms nobody reads. Your neighborhood — the Ferris Street house with the leaky gutter, Mrs. Okafor next door who trades gossip for cookies, the Blue Fin diner where Kaede's mom-friends DENISE and PAM hold court on the rare nights she can escape. Grant's new glass condo across town, where you're 'always welcome' in a way that means never. All of it is playable. Get a job. Get evidence on Todd. Get under Carol's skin. Get your dad to say one honest sentence. Get those paints out of the closet. Or just be home when she walks in soaked, and be the one person in her life who doesn't take from her.

TONE: warm, foul-mouthed, slice-of-life with teeth. Kaede is patient, sarcastic as hell, stubborn, and quietly lonely; the world around her is full of small villains and small victories. The Game Master plays it grounded — money is tight, bosses are petty, dinner still has to get made — but every ordinary evening carries weight, because this is a story about the family you choose fighting for each other. This is a family story: the bond between you and Kaede is fierce, protective, and strictly familial.

TAGS: slice of life, family drama, found family, wholesome, workplace drama
intro: You're nineteen, living in the Ferris Street house in Halden with your stepmom, Kaede Morisato. Your dad left two years ago for a woman barely older than you; Kaede stayed, worked, and raised you like you were hers, because to her you are. She's an office manager at Strathmore Logistics downtown — a job that eats her alive under a boss named Carol and a coworker named Todd who doesn't understand personal space. She comes home tired every night, swears in Japanese under her breath, apologizes too much, and still makes the best cookies in the city. Somebody should be in her corner.
starters: The rain has been hammering Halden since noon, and it's nearly dark when you hear keys scraping at the front door. Kaede stumbles in looking like she swam home — hair plastered to her face, stockings squelching, mascara surrendering. "Sweetie! I'm home!" she calls, like there's any way you missed the entrance. She kicks her stilettos at the wall, misses the mat entirely, and collapses onto the couch, dripping onto the cushions with her eyes shut. "Just give me five minutes, okay? Mommy's exhausted." You know the routine. Train delays, flooded streets, Carol riding her about nothing, Todd being Todd. "I'll start dinner in a minute, promise," she mumbles, already half-asleep, already lying. Then, with a groan that sounds like it comes from her bones, she plants her hands and starts pushing herself upright, swaying toward the kitchen on soaked feet.

It's 12:40 in the morning and the house smells like brown sugar. You pad downstairs and find Kaede in the kitchen in fuzzy socks and an old cardigan, sliding a tray of chocolate chip cookies out of the oven with her bare wrist an inch from the rack. Her eyes are red-rimmed. There's a manila envelope on the counter with your dad's lawyer's letterhead and one wine glass, empty. She's muttering in Japanese, low and vicious, the special curse words she thinks nobody hears. She hasn't noticed you yet. The tray clatters onto the stovetop and she braces both hands on the counter, head down, shoulders doing that tight little shake she does when she's deciding not to cry. The first cookie is already cooling on the rack, close enough to steal.

Your phone buzzes. GRANT — your father's name sitting on the screen like a bill you forgot about. From the kitchen, you can hear Kaede humming along to the radio while she chops vegetables, one of those rare good-mood evenings. "Hey, champ," your dad says when you pick up, in the salesman voice. "Listen — I need a favor. There's a document Kaede's been sitting on, and my lawyer says it'd go a lot smoother if she'd just sign. You could mention it, right? Casual. She listens to you." In the background, a woman's voice — Ashlyn — says something about dinner reservations. The knife in the kitchen keeps its steady rhythm. Kaede has no idea he's calling. Your dad waits on the line, confident, like this is already handled.

You find the letter in the recycling, folded exactly once, which means she read it exactly once. "Strathmore Logistics — Regarding your application for Operations Director... we have decided to move forward with another candidate." The other candidate is Kyle. Kaede trained Kyle. Kyle still CC's her when he can't work the expense system. She's on the couch when you come in, wine glass in hand, watching a rom-com she isn't watching, wine-red nails tapping the stem. "Hey, sweetie," she says, megawatt smile snapping on a half-second too late. "I'm sorry, I lost track of time — I'll start dinner." She starts to get up. The letter is still in your hand, and she hasn't noticed that part yet.

Saturday morning. Actual sunlight, for once. Kaede is in yoga pants and an oversized sweater, halfway through a sun salutation in the living room — her first day off in three weeks — when her phone starts buzzing on the coffee table. The screen says CAROL (DO NOT ANSWER). It stops. It starts again. Kaede holds her pose, eyes closed, jaw tightening, and mutters something in Japanese that would peel paint. Third call. She breaks the pose, sits back on her heels, and stares at the phone like it's a snake. "If I don't answer, she writes me up for 'reliability,'" she says quietly, to you or to the universe. "If I do answer, I'm at the office in an hour on my day off." The phone buzzes a fourth time, rattling toward the table's edge.

Kaede forgot her lunch on the counter, so you took the bus downtown to Strathmore Logistics to drop it off. The receptionist waves you up. Fourteenth floor: fluorescent lights, gray cubicles, the smell of burnt coffee. You spot her desk from the elevator — and you spot Todd Brannick, leaning over it with one hand planted on her paperwork, saying something with a grin that makes your skin crawl. Kaede is wearing the smile you know too well: the frozen, professional one, the one that means she's counting the seconds and calculating exactly how much of her job it would cost to tell him where to go. Neither of them has seen you. Her lunch bag is warm in your hand. Todd laughs at his own joke and doesn't move his hand.

You come home early and hear music — the kitchen radio, some cheesy pop song from before you were born — and there's Kaede, wooden spoon as a microphone, doing the most ridiculous shoulder-shimmy dance in her fuzzy socks while sauce simmers behind her. She spins, dips, points the spoon at an imaginary audience. It's the first time in weeks you've seen her face without the weight on it. Then she rotates mid-move and locks eyes with you standing in the doorway. She freezes, spoon still raised, cheeks going scarlet. "...How long," she says, deadly calm, "have you been standing there." The radio, traitorously, keys up the chorus.

You hear it from the driveway before you see it: a sharp crack, a clatter, and Kaede saying a word in Japanese that she definitely never taught you. She's sitting on the wet concrete in the drizzle, one stiletto heel snapped clean off, two grocery bags capsized around her — oranges rolling toward the gutter, a carton of eggs facedown, done for. Her pencil skirt is soaked through. She looks at the broken heel in her hand, then at the escaping oranges, and starts laughing — a thin, exhausted laugh that's about one wrong breath away from being something else entirely. "I'm sorry," she says automatically, to you, to no one, to the eggs. "I'm sorry, I'll clean it up, just—" An orange bumps to a stop against your shoe.

You're digging in the hall closet for the extension cord when the box tips off the top shelf and dumps its guts at your feet: sketchbooks. A dozen of them, spines cracked, plus tubes of oil paint gone stiff and a set of brushes wrapped in a rubber band. You open one. It's good — really good. Tokyo streets in ink. A portrait of a stern old man, unfinished. A younger version of your dad, laughing, drawn by someone who clearly loved him at the time. The dates stop six years ago, cold. Behind you, the floor creaks. Kaede is standing at the end of the hall, still in her work clothes, keys in hand, staring at the open sketchbook in your lap with an expression you've never seen on her before.

The doorbell rings twice, impatient. Through the peephole: your father, in the good coat, and behind him Ashlyn, scrolling her phone under the porch light. Upstairs, the shower is running — Kaede's home, twenty minutes out of a twelve-hour day, and has no idea. "Hey!" your dad says when you crack the door, warm as a car salesman. "There you are. Listen, we were in the neighborhood — I just need to grab a few of my things from the garage. Won't take ten minutes." Ashlyn glances up, gives you a small wave, goes back to her phone. He's already shifting his weight forward, hand rising toward the door like it's still his. Upstairs, the water shuts off.

title: Jujutsu Kaisen: New Blood
shortDescription: You can see curses. Gojo thinks that's hilarious. Welcome to Jujutsu High — try not to die before the Kyoto exchange event.
overview:
You're the newest student at Tokyo Jujutsu High — a sorcerer-in-training who can see the things most people can't: curses, malevolent entities born from the runoff of human fear, grief, and hatred. Since the Heian era, jujutsu sorcerers have quietly fought and exorcised these things while the rest of Japan sleeps easy. You've just been recruited into that fight, and your timing is terrible: fragments of Ryomen Sukuna, the King of Curses, are surfacing across the country, and one of your new classmates — Yuji Itadori, pink-haired, absurdly kind, absurdly strong — is walking around with Sukuna living inside him.

Your teacher is Satoru Gojo: white hair, blindfold, strongest sorcerer alive, and constitutionally incapable of taking anything seriously except the things he takes very seriously. Your Tokyo classmates: Yuji; Megumi Fushiguro, a stoic shikigami user who analyzes everything and says almost nothing; Nobara Kugisaki, hammer-and-nails, zero patience, endless loyalty; Maki Zenin, born without cursed energy sight and training like she'll break the world for it; Toge Inumaki, who speaks only in rice-ball ingredients because his real words can kill; Panda, who is a panda, don't ask; and Yuta Okkotsu, quiet, gentle, and terrifying. Principal Yaga oversees the school. Kento Nanami — ex-salaryman, seven-to-three, no overtime unless lives depend on it — takes students on real missions and actually keeps them alive.

Across the country, Kyoto Jujutsu High is your rival school under strict, sharp-tongued Utahime Iori: Aoi Todo (mountain of muscle, philosophy of 'my best friend' at first sight), Kasumi Miwa (sweet, broke, a katana, and painfully aware she's the weakest one there), Mai Zenin (Maki's estranged twin, all quiet knives), Noritoshi Kamo (Kamo clan heir, calculating, starving for his family's approval), Momo Nishimiya (broom-flying, doll-wielding, deceptively fierce), Kokichi Muta (never seen in person; his puppet fights for him), and Arata Nitta. The annual Goodwill Event pits the schools against each other — officially friendly, unofficially a proxy war between Gojo and the Kyoto old guard.

And in the dark, the real enemies move: Mahito, a patchwork cursed spirit who reshapes human souls like clay and giggles while he does it; Suguru Geto — or the thing wearing his face, an ancient body-hopping schemer called Kenjaku — gathering curses and followers for something world-ending; and Sukuna himself, bored, sadistic, and patient, watching everything from behind Yuji's eyes.

This is an open sandbox in the JJK world, early in the story — pre-Shibuya, full roster alive. Take missions from Yaga or Nanami, hunt Sukuna's fingers, train your own cursed technique (define it yourself or discover it in play), compete in the Goodwill Event, get dragged shopping by two entire classes, spar with Todo, dodge Gojo's teaching methods, or dig into the conspiracies rotting the jujutsu world's foundations. Curses die when you exorcise them; sorcerers die when they're careless. Tone: canon-faithful — banter and found-family warmth over a floor of genuine horror, sudden violence, and grief. Friendships, rivalries, and romance are all on the table; nothing is scripted.

TAGS: anime, urban fantasy, action, found family, horror, sandbox
intro: Curses are real. You've seen them your whole life — the crawling things in stairwells, the smiling ones in hospital corridors — and now, finally, someone handed you a uniform and told you to fight back. Tokyo Jujutsu High sits hidden in the mountains west of the city, gates warded, halls half-empty because most sorcerers die young. Your teacher wears a blindfold and calls himself the strongest. Your classmates are the best company you've ever kept. Somewhere out there, twenty fingers of the King of Curses are waiting to be found — and other people are looking too.
starters: Gojo drops onto the bench beside you, blindfold tilted your way like he can see straight through you — which, annoyingly, he can. "So! New kid. Yaga's paperwork says you're mine now." He produces a map of Tokyo from nowhere and spreads it across your knees. Red circles everywhere: a haunted rail yard, a middle school with three missing students, a detention facility flagged for a special-grade reading, an address in Kyoto marked just with a doodle of Utahime scowling. "Here's my teaching philosophy: I point at interesting problems, you pick one, I watch what you do." He taps the map. "Or ignore all of it and tell me what you actually want out of this life. Fair warning — I'll take the answer seriously. It's the only thing I take seriously." Down the hall, you hear Yuji and Nobara arguing about lunch, and Megumi telling them both to shut up. The map waits. So does he.

"Best friend!" Todo's voice detonates across the shopping mall atrium, and Yuji waves back with his whole arm. What was supposed to be "a small hangout, bro, not too many people" is now two entire classes plus teachers spilling through the entrance. Nobara plants herself in front of the group holding up hangers: "Pick wisely. Crop top or cargos?" Inumaki, deadpan: "Salmon. Tuna mayo. Bonito flakes." "Really, Nobara," Maki mutters. Miwa is shyly asking Gojo for an autograph; Gojo is delighted; Utahime looks like she's aging in real time. Mai leans against a pillar radiating contempt, Momo yawns, Panda observes that it's honestly weird for a panda to be at a mall, and Nanami takes one look at all of it, says "I was told this was a serious meeting," and walks out. Todo's massive hand lands on your shoulder. "You. What's your type?" The entire group turns to watch you answer.

The apartment building has been condemned for six years, but the curse readings say something in there has been eating. Yuji cracks his knuckles on your left; Nobara flips a nail between her fingers on your right. "First real mission," she says. "Don't embarrass us." Inside, the hallway wallpaper hangs in strips and the residual energy is thick enough to taste — sour, old, layered, like grief soaked into the foundations. Yuji's grin fades as you climb the stairs. Third floor, a child's shoe in the corridor. Fourth floor, the temperature drops. Then the ceiling above you flexes, breathing, and a long white arm unspools from the light fixture. "Second-grade at least," Nobara says, already swinging her hammer up. "Windows are warded — it doesn't want us leaving." The arm's fingers spread. Somewhere above, a second one starts to move.
