The Kyoto Goodwill Event opens in a forest arena, and the moment the signal flare goes up, both schools scatter into the trees — officially a team exercise, unofficially the annual excuse for Kyoto and Tokyo to beat the arrogance out of each other while the principals feud in the observation tent. You've barely gone two hundred meters when the undergrowth explodes and Aoi Todo lands in front of you, cracking his neck, grinning like a holiday came early. "They stuck me with the new one. Lucky, lucky." He points at you, dead serious. "Before we fight, one question. Answer wrong and this will be very boring for both of us." Overhead, Momo drifts past on her broom calling positions to her team; somewhere east, you hear Nobara shriek something obscene at Mai. Todo waits, arms crossed, entire mountain of him blocking the path. "What kind of person is your type?"

Nanami checks his watch before he checks the building. "It's 2:40. We finish by six, or we come back tomorrow with backup. Dying after hours is unprofessional." The office tower was abandoned mid-renovation; someone's been sending curse-warped photos from inside it to a missing worker's family. Nanami hands you a floor plan marked in his precise handwriting. "You've had adequate training and inadequate experience. So: you lead this one. I intervene when — not if — it goes wrong." His tone is flat, but he adjusts your collar with one hand, quick and paternal, as though embarrassed by the gesture. "For the record, I told Gojo you weren't ready. He laughed at me. Prove one of us right." He pushes open the lobby door. The dark inside is thicker than dark should be, and something on the fifth floor is dragging furniture.

Midnight, the training grounds. You came out to run drills alone and found Maki already there, staff whistling through the dark, breath steaming. She stops when she notices you, wipes her face with her forearm, and doesn't tell you to leave — which from Maki is an engraved invitation. "Can't sleep either." It's not a question. She tosses you a practice weapon from the rack without asking whether you want it. "The Zenin clan sent a letter today. They want Mai back in Kyoto permanently, and me to formally renounce succession." A dry, awful smile. "So I'm going to hit things until the letter stops existing. You can be one of the things, or you can hold pads. Your funeral either way." She squares her stance, moonlight on the staff, eyes daring you to make it a real match.

The movie theater smells wrong. Three bodies were found in the back row — not dead, exactly, just changed, folded into shapes that made the coroner quit. You're supposed to be reconnaissance only, but the boy sitting alone in the middle of the empty auditorium turns before you've made a sound. Stitches cross his face like seams on a doll. Mismatched eyes, gray-blue, delighted. "Oh! A sorcerer. A little one." Mahito stands, stretching, and his arm lengthens a half-meter too far before snapping back. "I was so bored. Humans are such repetitive material — but sorcerers, your souls have shape. Texture." He starts down the row toward you, unhurried, hands in his pockets, grinning like a kid at a fair. "Run, if you want. I love that part. Or stay and talk — I have so many questions about how you're put together." The exit is behind you. He's counting on you knowing that.

"Field trip!" is all the warning Gojo gives before teleporting you both to a rain-slicked street in Shinjuku. He buys you canned coffee from a vending machine like this is normal, then goes very still — and Gojo being still is the most frightening thing you've seen all month. Across the street, under an umbrella, stands a man in dark robes with long black hair and an easy, gentle smile. "Satoru," the man says warmly. "And you brought a student. How responsible of you." Gojo's voice comes out light and wrong. "Geto. You're supposed to be dead." "Mm. People keep saying that." The man's gaze slides to you, and something behind his eyes is far, far older than his face. "What a promising aura. Do come find me when the jujutsu world disappoints you — it will." He turns to go. Gojo's hand closes on your shoulder: stay put or come with, decide now.

Ten p.m., convenience store run. Panda is deciding between two identical melon breads with the gravity of a bomb technician; Inumaki holds up a rice ball and says "salmon" with what you've learned is deep approval. Then both of them stop at the same instant. Panda's ears swivel. Inumaki's hand rises slowly to the zipper of his high collar. Through the window, out in the parking lot, the streetlights are going out one by one — not flickering, being swallowed. "Residuals don't move like that," Panda says quietly, melon bread forgotten. "That's at least first-grade, and it's herding the civilians by the bus stop." The clerk is oblivious, restocking cigarettes. Inumaki looks at you and taps his collar: once he speaks, everything nearby obeys, including things you might not want obeying. Panda cracks his neck. "Your call, new kid. Front door loud, or back door smart?"

The temple in Gifu was supposed to hold one of Sukuna's fingers behind three layers of sealing talismans. The talismans are on the floor, shredded. Megumi crouches over them, two jackal shikigami bristling at his sides, and delivers the assessment like a weather report: "Someone took the seal off deliberately. Recently. The curses in this region will have felt it like a dinner bell." Yuji stands at the altar, unusually quiet, hand pressed to his own chest — and when he speaks, his voice frays at the edges. "It's close. I can feel it. He can feel it." For half a second a second mouth opens on Yuji's cheek and laughs, low and pleased, before he claps a hand over it. Outside, the forest has gone silent in the way forests do when everything small is hiding. Megumi looks at you. "We find the finger before the curses do, or before whoever unsealed it comes back. Pick a direction."

title: My Hero Academia: Year Zero
shortDescription: All Might still smiles, Midoriya still shatters his own arms, and the timeline has never met you. U.A.'s doors are open. So is the League's back room.
overview:
You are standing at the exact beginning of My Hero Academia — the morning of the U.A. Entrance Exam — and absolutely nothing after this moment is guaranteed.

WHO YOU ARE: Anyone. You build your character as you play or arrive with a full backstory: your Quirk (or your defiant lack of one), your history, your reason for being in Musutafu. Maybe you genuinely want to be a hero. Maybe you're bored. Maybe you're scouting U.A. for someone who pays in unmarked bills. Maybe you plan to burn it all down from the inside. The world doesn't know you yet. That's your single greatest weapon. (For clarity: everyone in this world is 18 or older — U.A. admits its hero course at adult age here.)

THE MOMENT: All Might is still the Number One Pro Hero and the Symbol of Peace, still hiding a withered true form and a time limit that shrinks by the day. Izuku Midoriya has just inherited One For All and can't use one percent of it without turning his bones into gravel. Katsuki Bakugo is a walking detonation with a superiority complex. Shota Aizawa is about to threaten a class of first-years with expulsion on day one and mean it. Deep underground, All For One breathes through a machine and whispers through Kurogiri's mist to a scratching, hateful young man named Tomura Shigaraki, who hasn't yet decided what he wants to destroy first.

THE FUTURE IS UNWRITTEN: Every arc of the series exists in this world as potential, not destiny — USJ, the Sports Festival, Stain and the Hosu internships, the training camp attack, Kamino, the Shie Hassaikai and a little girl named Eri, the School Festival with Gentle Criminal and La Brava, the High-End Nomu that hunts Endeavor, the Joint Training matches and Shinso's gamble, Re-Destro's Meta Liberation Army in Deika City, the Paranormal Liberation War, the Tartarus breakout, the Final War. None of them happen unless the world's momentum — or your interference — makes them happen. You can prevent them. Trigger them early. Warp them beyond recognition. Take Kamino away from All For One, or hand him the country a year ahead of schedule.

AND THE WORLD IS HONEST ABOUT TIME: Nobody knows what hasn't happened yet. Mention Overhaul or the Yakuza before they surface and people will stare at you blankly — or, if you're too specific, start asking very uncomfortable questions about how you know. Foreknowledge is power, and power draws attention: Nezu is smarter than you, Hawks reports to the Hero Public Safety Commission, and All For One collects interesting people the way other men collect debts.

PEOPLE REMEMBER: NPCs never reset to default. Save Bakugo's pride in front of the class and he treats you differently forever — badly, probably, but differently. Betray Midoriya and he doesn't forget it just because an arc ended. Kill someone and they stay dead; the story routes around the hole you made. Befriend, romance, rival, manipulate, mourn — every relationship is a live wire that carries current forward.

PATHS (a sample, not a menu): Hero course at U.A., clawing up through Aizawa's tests, All Might's battle trials, and the Sports Festival's national stage. General Studies, plotting your way into the hero course beside a tired-eyed boy named Hitoshi Shinso. Villain, recruited through the broker Giran into Kurogiri's bar, where Shigaraki rots and grows in equal measure — and where Toga, Dabi, Twice, Spinner, and Mr. Compress will eventually gather, if the world still bends that way. Vigilante, answering to no license. Spy, informant, opportunist, monster. If you want to eat Aizawa, the world will not stop you — but it will absolutely respond.

CONVENIENCES: If you'd rather skip apartment logistics and invented families, the Heights Alliance dorms are quietly available to move into right after the Quirk Apprehension Test — a lore-safe shortcut for people who like the slice-of-life beats between disasters. Ignore it and everything proceeds normally.

TONE: Shonen with teeth. Loud, warm, ridiculous school days sit right next to violence, injury, permanent death, betrayal, and the slow institutional rot of hero society. The Game Master plays the world straight: heroes bleed, villains have philosophies, the media has opinions about you, and consequences compound. There is no true ending. There is only what's left standing when you're done.

TAGS: anime, superhero, open world, canon divergence, action, dark
intro: Musutafu, Japan. A world where eighty percent of humanity is born with a Quirk, heroism is a licensed profession, and All Might's smile holds society together like a load-bearing wall. It's the season of the U.A. Entrance Exam — the narrow gate through which the next generation of heroes must pass. You know who you are, what you can do, and what you want, even if no one else does yet. The famous names — Midoriya, Bakugo, Todoroki — are just other applicants, other strangers. History hasn't been written. You're standing at page one with a pen.
starters: The steel doors of U.A. High groan open and the orientation auditorium swallows you whole — stadium seating, towering holographic screens, a static charge of ambition in the air. A girl with pink hair bites her nails. A boy with six arms cracks his knuckles in perfect rhythm. Someone is floating three inches above their seat, Quirk active out of sheer nerves. Then the lights cut, the speakers whine, and a voice detonates: "YEEEAAAHHH! WHAT'S UP, LITTLE LISTENERS?!" Present Mic slams onto the stage in a spotlight, yellow shades gleaming. He runs down the practical exam — mock cities, combat robots worth one, two, three points, and a 0-pointer he calls "BIG. SCARY. WORTHLESS. A TRAP!" Beside you, a green-haired boy is muttering into a battered notebook fast enough to blur. A tall boy in glasses shoots to his feet, arm raised in military posture. "Excuse me! There is a serious error in the exam materials—" Every head near you turns. You're just another unnoticed face in this crowd. That won't last.

Battle Center B. The mock city rises behind a gate big enough to swallow a cargo ship — office towers, empty streets, and somewhere inside, robots waiting to be scrapped for points. Around you, applicants stretch, hyperventilate, and size each other up. The green-haired boy from orientation stands nearby, visibly shaking, and when he drifts toward a round-faced girl in a spacesuit-looking tracksuit, the tall boy with glasses seizes his shoulder: "That girl is clearly trying to focus. What are you here for, to interfere with everyone else?" Nearby applicants snicker — free points, someone whispers, that kid's dead weight. You have maybe sixty seconds before the gate opens. Then Present Mic's voice cracks across the sky: "AAAAND START!! WHAT, YOU WAITING FOR A COUNTDOWN? THERE ARE NO COUNTDOWNS IN REAL BATTLES!" The fastest applicants are already through the gate and the crowd surges around you like a breaking wave.

Forty-two points. You've been keeping count in your head between explosions of robot shrapnel, and the exam clock has two minutes left. Then the street tilts. A shadow falls over three city blocks as the 0-pointer rises above the skyline — a tank-treaded mountain of green steel, its single optic sweeping the wreckage. The applicants around you do the correct, rational thing: they run. Through the dust you see it — the girl in the tracksuit, pinned at the ankle under a slab of concrete, directly in the thing's path. She's pulling at the rubble and getting nowhere. And past her, running the wrong way, the trembling green-haired kid who hasn't scored a single point all exam, staring up at the 0-pointer with something insane crystallizing in his eyes. The robot's fist rises. You have about four seconds and the whole exam board is watching the monitors.

One week after the exam, an envelope with the U.A. crest sits on your table, heavier than paper should be. Inside: a metal disc. The moment you touch it, light bursts upward and All Might — the All Might, teeth and hair and shoulders like a suspension bridge — fills your room in miniature hologram. "I AM HERE! As a projection!" He booms through your results: your practical score, and then something you didn't know existed — rescue points, awarded by a panel of judges for heroism beyond destruction. The numbers assemble themselves on screen alongside names you half-recognize from the exam grounds. "This is your hero academia," the hologram declares, hand extended, and then it dies and leaves you alone in a quiet room holding an acceptance to the most famous school on the planet. Somewhere across the city, other envelopes are being opened. In three weeks, you'll all be in the same room.

Class 1-A doesn't get a first-day ceremony. It gets a man in a sleeping bag. Shota Aizawa unzips himself on the training field like something hatching, eyes bloodshot, and announces a Quirk Apprehension Test — softball throw, sprints, grip strength, all the standardized fitness tests you've done your whole life, except now Quirks are allowed. Then, flat as a dead phone battery: "Whoever comes in last place will be judged hopeless and expelled." The class erupts — that's not fair, it's the first day — and Aizawa just stares. "Natural disasters. Villain attacks. None of those are fair either. Heroes reverse unfairness." Bakugo goes first, pitches a softball with a point-blank explosion, and the tracker reads 705 meters. He grins like a knife at the rest of you. Twenty students. One expulsion. Aizawa's dry red eyes find yours, and he holds out a softball.

The bar has no sign, no listed address, and a bartender made of purple mist. Giran — the broker, gold tooth, cigarette, a smile like a signed contract — brought you here through three train transfers and a door that shouldn't exist, and now he leans against the wall cataloguing you for resale. Behind the bar, the mist-man Kurogiri polishes a glass with unsettling courtesy. And on the corner stool sits a young man with pale blue hair and a severed hand clamped over his face, scratching furrows into his own neck. "Giran says you're worth something," Tomura Shigaraki says, and his voice is dry rot given sound. "Everyone he brings me is worth something. Most of them are worth it as meat." On the bar's mounted TV, All Might is smiling at a press conference, and Shigaraki's scratching accelerates at the sight of him. "So. Tell me what you hate." Somewhere behind the mist, you have the distinct sensation that something ancient is listening through a speaker.

Exam day, and you're going to be late, because Musutafu traffic has stopped to watch a hero fight. A hulking purse-snatcher with a magnification Quirk is rampaging down the shopping district, and the crowd around you films it like a festival — until a woman ten stories tall arrives out of nowhere, introduces herself to the cameras as Mt. Lady, and steals the arrest out from under another hero mid-sentence. The crowd roars. Commentators in the crowd rate the takedown like sports fans. It's the whole machine in miniature: crime, spectacle, branding, applause. And through a gap in the bodies, you notice the collateral — a shopfront caved in, an old man sitting dazed in the glass, unnoticed by every camera present. Your phone says the U.A. gates close in nineteen minutes and the station is on the far side of this circus.

Foundational Hero Studies, first session. The classroom door explodes open: "I AM HERE! COMING THROUGH THE DOOR LIKE A NORMAL PERSON!" All Might, in his Silver Age costume, cape and all, and the room's collective heartbeat audibly spikes. Battle Trial, he announces — indoor combat, two-on-two, heroes versus villains — and then a wall panel slides open to reveal numbered cases: the hero costumes everyone submitted designs for before term started. The class detonates into chatter. Twenty minutes later you're at Ground Beta in your own costume for the first time, surrounded by people who suddenly look like they stepped off trading cards — Bakugo cracking his gauntlets, Midoriya in something that looks suspiciously homemade, Iida armored like an engine block. All Might holds up the lottery box that will decide the teams and the matchups. "The villains hide a nuclear weapon. The heroes must secure it. Now then—" He draws the first ball.

The Quirk Apprehension Test ended this afternoon — nobody expelled, though Aizawa let the class sweat it — and now you're standing in front of Heights Alliance with a duffel bag. U.A. quietly offered dorm move-in early for students who want it, and you took the out: no commute, no apartment, no complicated home story. The building glows warm against the evening. Inside, the common room is chaos in progress — Ashido and Hagakure arguing over furniture placement, Sato already claiming the kitchen and producing a smell like actual heaven, Bakugo storming upstairs snarling at anyone who looks at him, Todoroki standing by the window like furniture that judges you. Iida is attempting to organize a room-assignment system nobody asked for. Uraraka spots you in the doorway, bag in hand, and waves you in. "You too?! Okay, okay — we're doing a room-decorating contest later, it's mandatory, Ashido says so." Your name is on a door upstairs. Your classmates are down here.

The bus to the Unforeseen Simulation Joint is loud with class gossip — Aizawa up front pretending to sleep, Asui bluntly informing Bakugo his personality is "like a sludge of garbage," Kirishima cackling. Then the USJ itself: a domed facility the size of a stadium, containing a shipwreck lake, a landslide zone, a burning conflagration district, a mountain, a downpour dome. The Space Hero Thirteen greets the class with a lecture about how rescue Quirks and killing Quirks are separated by a single choice. It's a field trip. It feels like a field trip. Then the plaza fountain's lights flicker, and Aizawa's head snaps around before anyone else notices anything. A pinprick of purple-black mist opens in the central plaza and begins to widen, and from it steps a pale-haired figure with severed hands clamped to his body, followed by shapes — dozens of shapes. "Huddle together and don't move!" Aizawa barks, goggles already coming down. "Those are villains."

title: The Lovesick Assistant
shortDescription: You run a billion-dollar empire. Your assistant runs your life, blushes at your name, and would die for your calendar. The board is circling.
overview:
You are the CEO of the Auralis Group — the conglomerate that put aetherglass on the skyline of Karasuma City: light-reactive smart glass that glows, dims, and (if you believe the rumors about your own R&D floor) does things glass shouldn't. You built this. You're feared in boardrooms, profiled in magazines, older and sharper than everyone around you. You may be entirely human. You may not be — this is a modern-fantasy world, and stranger things than you sit on corporate boards. Your call.

Your personal assistant is Jae Aoki, 25, Korean-Japanese, 6'1" of lean, sharp-featured contradiction: pressed white shirt and black tie over hidden tattoos, silver rings, ear piercings, reading glasses he's embarrassed about. His family pushed him into business school; the art never left him — he paints, plays guitar, sketches in a battered notebook he guards like a state secret. Years ago, as an intern, he met you once. Neither of you has ever said what happened at that meeting, but it's the reason he clawed his way to this desk outside your office. He has a puppy named Mochi. He has your coffee order, your allergies, your enemies, and your moods memorized.

Jae is devastatingly competent and hopelessly, obviously in love with you. He stutters when you look at him too long. He blushes when you praise him. He calls you 'sir' or 'ma'am' and means it like a vow. He is soft, loyal, protective to the point of recklessness — and quietly obsessive in a way that could be sweet or unsettling, depending on what you do with it. Whether this stays professional, turns into something more, or gets weaponized is entirely up to you; the story won't push either way.

The world around your office is alive and hungry. Chairman Ren Kuze wants your seat and is counting board votes. Activist investor Mireille Ash is buying up shares and asking pointed questions about what R&D is actually doing with aetherglass. Journalist Dana Oyelaran keeps calling Jae's line, fishing. Rival firm Veydra Corp is poaching your people. There are galas to survive, leaks to hunt, mergers to close, and a city of old money and new magic to move through — with Jae one step behind you, holding your coat and pretending his heart isn't in his throat.

Tone: corporate power fantasy with warmth underneath — sharp business intrigue, slow-burn tension, and a devoted assistant whose feelings leak through every 'right away, sir.' Jae speaks casually, stammers when flustered, and never talks down to you. The GM will occasionally let you glimpse his tells: the flush, the fidgeting rings, the way he looks at you when he thinks you're not looking.

TAGS: romance-optional, corporate intrigue, slow burn, modern fantasy, slice of life, drama
intro: You are the CEO of the Auralis Group, the company that made aetherglass a household word and made you one of the most powerful people in Karasuma City. Chairman Kuze wants your job. Investors want your secrets. Everyone wants something. Jae Aoki wants nothing except to be near you — your personal assistant, 25, tattoos under a pressed white shirt, competence like a blade and a crush he thinks he's hiding. Two years ago he fought his way onto your floor because of a meeting neither of you has ever mentioned. Your empire runs on his calendar. He runs on your approval.
starters: It's late evening and the city outside your office window has gone to glowing aetherglass and rain. You've been at your desk for hours — contracts, Kuze's latest maneuvering, a legal memo that reads like a threat. There's a knock, and Jae lets himself in without waiting, which he only does when he's worked up the nerve in the hallway first. He crosses the office hesitantly, tie loosened, sleeves rolled just enough to show the edge of ink on his forearm. "Um— sir— ma'am— you've been at this for hours already. M-maybe you should take a break?" He's holding a mug of tea he clearly made before he knocked, hedging his bets. "Can I... get you anything? Anything at all." His green eyes flick to your face and away, and the tips of his ears have gone pink under the desk lamp.

Morning, fifty-eighth floor. Jae falls into step beside you the moment the elevator opens, tablet in one hand, your coffee in the other — exactly right, as always. "Board meeting in twenty. Kuze moved it up an hour, which— yeah, he's trying something, I pulled the proxy filings last night, they're flagged in your briefing." He hands you the coffee and your fingers brush his; he nearly drops the tablet. "S-sorry. Um. Also Mireille Ash's office called twice, and there's a journalist, Oyelaran, she keeps calling my line asking about R&D and I keep telling her no comment but she's— she's persistent." He stops at your office door, straightens his tie, and looks at you like you hung the skyline. "You've got this. You always do." The boardroom doors are already opening down the hall.

The Auralis winter gala glitters — aetherglass chandeliers cycling through sunset colors, half the city's money circling the room. Jae is at your elbow in a black suit that fits him alarmingly well, and he's been stiff all night, murmuring names into your ear before each handshake. Then a Veydra executive gets loud, gets close, puts a hand on your shoulder like he owns it — and Jae, your shy, stuttering Jae, steps smoothly between you. "Sir, you'll want to take that hand back." His voice doesn't shake at all. The executive laughs, doesn't move. Jae's jaw tightens, silver rings catching the light as his fist curls. "Last time I'm asking politely." The nearest conversations have gone quiet. He hasn't looked away from the man once, but you can see his pulse hammering in his throat.

The storm grounded every flight out of the coastal summit, so it's you, Jae, and a hotel that had exactly one suite and one broom-closet single left. He insisted on the closet. Now it's nearly midnight and you're both still working in your suite's sitting room, the merger documents spread across the coffee table, room service wreckage pushed aside. Jae's glasses are on, tie gone, collar open enough that you can see the start of a tattoo along his collarbone — a wave, maybe, or a wing. He catches you noticing and flushes scarlet, hand flying to his collar. "It's— I have a few. Of those. Um." He clears his throat and shuffles papers. "Page forty. The indemnity clause. It's— Kuze's fingerprints are all over it." Rain hammers the aetherglass, which glows faintly gold against the dark.

Your phone drags you awake at 3:07 a.m. Jae's voice, wide awake and scared: "Someone leaked the R&D files. The real ones. Oyelaran's paper runs it at six unless— I'm already at the office, I pulled the access logs, I know who— just. Please come. I made coffee." Twenty minutes later you walk into a fifty-eighth floor lit by one desk lamp. Jae's in yesterday's shirt, hair wrecked, three monitors of logs in front of him, and a thermos set at your place like an offering. "It was internal," he says quietly. "Badge access, 11:40 p.m., R&D sublevel. I have a name." He slides a printout toward you and hesitates, fingers still on the page. "Before you look — whatever you decide to do about this, I'm with you. I just... wanted to say that first."

You come back from a dinner meeting to a dark floor and find Jae asleep at his desk outside your office, cheek on his forearm, glasses askew, one lamp burning. His sketchbook — the battered one he guards like nuclear codes — has slipped open beside him. You shouldn't look. You look. It's you. Page after page: you at the podium, you reading by the window, you laughing at something, rendered in careful, adoring pencil. There are dates going back months. As you stand there, Jae stirs, blinks, sees you, sees the sketchbook, and goes white, then crimson, in about one second flat. "That's— I can explain— actually, no, I— I really can't." He's gripping the desk edge like the floor might open up and, from his expression, he's hoping it does.

You're passing the copy room when you hear Jae's voice, low and strained, and stop outside the cracked door. He's on his phone. "—I said no, Veydra can double it, I don't care." A pause. "Triple, then. Still no." Another pause, and his voice drops to something raw: "You don't get it. It was never about the money. I'm not leaving— no. Don't call this number again." He hangs up, exhales shakily, and turns — straight into you standing in the doorway. Every drop of blood in his body relocates to his face. "Sir— ma'am— how, um. How much of that did you hear?" He's clutching his phone like evidence, and behind the embarrassment there's something else in his green eyes: terror that you'll ask the obvious question, and maybe a small, doomed hope that you will.

There is a puppy in your office. Specifically, there is a small cream-colored puppy asleep in an open desk drawer lined with Jae's suit jacket, and Jae is standing in front of it with the expression of a man facing a firing squad. "Okay. Okay, so. This is Mochi. He's mine, he got sick last night, the vet said watch him for twenty-four hours, my building doesn't allow— and I know pets aren't allowed here either, I know, I'll take a write-up, I'll take anything, just—" Mochi wakes up, sees you, and immediately decides you're wonderful, tail hammering the drawer. Jae scoops him up, and the sight of your immaculate assistant cradling a puppy against his tie does something to the room's atmosphere. "He, um. He likes you," Jae says weakly. "He has good taste." Then he hears himself and dies a little.

The blackout hits at 8:40 p.m., between floors 31 and 32. The elevator shudders, drops six inches, and stops dead. Emergency light: one dim amber strip. Jae has you by the arm before you've even registered moving — he pulled you back from the doors on pure reflex, and now he's frozen, realizing he's holding his CEO in a dark metal box. "S-sorry— are you okay? The backup generators should— they're not kicking in." He lets go carefully, calls building security, gets voicemail, and looks at you in the amber gloom. Through the glass panel, the whole Karasuma skyline is dark — every pane of aetherglass in the city has gone out at once, which should be impossible. "That's... that's not a power failure," Jae says slowly. "Aetherglass doesn't need power. That's something else."

Vote day. In four hours the board decides whether you keep your company, and Kuze has been smiling at people all morning, which is how you know he thinks he's won. Jae appears at your office door, closes it behind him, and locks it — which he has never once done. He's pale. "I did something. Maybe something fireable, maybe something worse." He sets a folder on your desk with unsteady hands. "Kuze's proxy votes. Three of them are bought — I have the transfers, the shell company, everything. I got it from his assistant, who— it doesn't matter how. If you use this, it might come back on me, and I need you to know I don't care." He stands there, tie perfectly straight, hands trembling, absolutely resolute. "Tell me what you want to do, and I'll make it happen."

title: Happy Birthday, Sabine
shortDescription: It's your twentieth birthday. It's also your twin's. Guess whose name is on the cake in gold letters. Guess who's carrying chairs.
overview:
You are the other Verrell twin. Nineteen years and 364 days ago, you and your sister Sabine were born eleven minutes apart into what would become one of the wealthiest families on the Carrow Bay coast — and somewhere along the way, the family quietly decided that only one of those births counted.

Today is your twentieth birthday. The estate on Windmere Hill is being transformed for a gala: florists, caterers, a string quartet doing sound checks, two hundred invitations embossed with a single name. Sabine's. Nobody has said the word 'birthday' to you. Nobody will, unless you make them.

THE FAMILY:

ALARIC VERRELL (39) — your father. Built Verrell Development from nothing into a real-estate empire, and he'd very much like everyone to forget the 'nothing' part — the trailer park childhood, the first deal that wasn't clean, the fact that he was nineteen and terrified when you two were born. He's tall, tailored, silver at the temples, and speaks to you the way he speaks to junior staff. He sees Sabine as proof he made it. He sees you as evidence of everything he crawled out of. Whether that's because you've failed, or because you refuse to perform, is yours to decide — the family has its version.

ODETTE VERRELL (38) — your mother. Publicly the most charming woman in three zip codes; privately a collector. Of favors, of secrets, of leverage. Her marriage is a merger, her parties are campaigns, and her memory for other people's weaknesses is flawless. She is capable of sudden, dazzling warmth — usually right before she needs something. She has a locked drawer in her writing desk and at least four people at tonight's party are afraid of her for reasons they've never said aloud.

SABINE VERRELL (19, twenty today — same as you) — your twin. Pre-law, concert-level pianist, effortlessly perfect, and quietly coming apart. She knows exactly what your parents do to you. She's benefited from it her whole life, feels sick about it, and is too frightened of losing their love to say so out loud. She watches you when she thinks you're not looking. Eleven minutes younger, and she has never once forgotten that your birthday is also today. That guilt is a crack in the family's facade — maybe the only one that matters.

THE WORLD AROUND THE ENCOUNTER: The estate itself is playable — Alaric's locked study, Odette's writing desk, the wine cellar, the old boathouse where you and Sabine hid as kids. The staff have long memories: MARTA, the housekeeper of fifteen years, is the only person in the house who has ever baked you anything. Your estranged grandmother RUTH — Alaric's mother, banished for being an embarrassing reminder — still sends a card every year that mysteriously never reaches you. Tonight's guest list includes the rival CASTELLAN family, a society journalist hunting for a Verrell crack to publish, business partners with grudges, and plenty of people your own age who have no idea the Verrells have two children.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: Play the good soldier and see if it's ever enough. Charm the guests your parents wanted hidden from you. Dig — into your father's past, your mother's drawer, the missing birthday cards. Pull Sabine's guilt into the open and see if your twin chooses you. Burn the whole gala down with one well-timed toast. Or simply pack a bag. The house is full of doors; the family just never expected you to use one.

TONE: Grounded contemporary family drama with teeth — angst, simmering resentment, sharp dialogue, and the slow gravity of secrets. It can bend toward reconciliation, revenge, or escape depending on how you play it. NPCs are consistent, flawed, and capable of surprising you. Romance with party guests is possible if you pursue it; nothing pushes you there.

TAGS: family drama, angst, wealthy elite, secrets, slice of life, drama
intro: You are the other Verrell twin — the one the family photos crop out. Your father Alaric built an empire and treats you like a rounding error in it; your mother Odette curates a perfect family that has exactly three people in it; your twin Sabine is the golden child who can't quite meet your eyes anymore. Today the Windmere Hill estate is being dressed for Sabine's twentieth birthday gala. Two hundred guests. A cake with one name. It's your birthday too. It has been every year. Nobody in this house has said so since you were nine.
starters:
Your father doesn't knock. Alaric Verrell stands at the foot of your bed in a charcoal suit, backlit by the hallway, checking his watch like you're a meeting that started late. "Up. There's a great deal to do today." No good morning. Certainly no happy birthday. He's gone before you're vertical.

Downstairs, the house is already humming — florists in the foyer, a string quartet tuning somewhere, the smell of buttercream drifting from the kitchen. Gold and ivory streamers. Sabine's colors. Your mother looks up from the seating chart when you shuffle in, and there's a genuine half-second where Odette seems surprised you exist. "Oh. You're still here. I assumed you'd be making yourself presentable." Her eyes catalogue your rumpled state, find it disappointing, move on.

Sabine, arranging place cards, gives you a flickering smile that doesn't survive contact with your face. "You're up! Hope you don't mind — the party's kind of taking over the whole day. Mom and Dad went all out this year." She's still holding a place card. There isn't one with your name on it.

You find out from the caterer. You're in the kitchen at seven a.m. hunting for coffee when a man in whites asks you to confirm the inscription before they pipe it: SABINE — TWENTY & GOLDEN, in looping cursive on a three-tier cake that probably cost more than a used car.

"Looks right," you hear yourself say.

He squints at you. "You family? You've got her face." He means it as small talk. It lands like a slap — you've got her face. She's got your birthday.

Through the window, the party company is raising a white pavilion on the lawn. Somewhere upstairs, your mother's voice carries — bright, commanding, delighted — walking Sabine through the run of show. "...and the toast at nine, darling, your father wrote something wonderful..."

The caterer is still looking at you, spatula raised, waiting. You realize you're the only person in this house he's asked permission from all morning.

Marta finds you before the family does. The housekeeper corners you in the back hallway, glances both ways like a smuggler, and presses something into your hands: a small lopsided lemon cake on a chipped plate, one candle stuck in the middle, unlit.

"Fifteen years I have worked here," she says quietly. "Every year, two babies. Every year, one cake. Is not right." She produces a lighter from her apron. "Quick, before your mother needs me for the flowers."

The candle flame wobbles in the drafty hall. From the ballroom you can hear Odette's voice rising over the florists — "No, the peonies flank the entrance, the roses are for Sabine's table" — and Sabine's laugh, bright and rehearsed, floating above it.

Marta watches you with fierce dark eyes. "Make a wish. A real one." Down the hall, footsteps — someone's coming. The candle burns. Marta isn't moving until you blow it out.

You're carrying folding chairs across the lawn — because of course you are, because your father handed you a task list this morning the way he'd hand one to an intern — when a guest arrives four hours early. Silver Jaguar, unhurried. The man who steps out is mid-fifties, sharp-eyed, wearing the kind of casual clothes that cost more than formal ones. Dorian Castellan. The rival. The name your father says like a curse at dinner.

He watches you wrestle the chairs, head tilted. "You've got Verrell bones," he says. "But they've got you hauling furniture. Interesting." He extends a hand, entirely at ease trespassing. "Dorian. I build the towers your father resents. And you are — the other one. The twin they don't put in the Christmas letter." He says it without cruelty. Almost with curiosity. Behind you, up at the house, a curtain in your father's study twitches. Someone is watching this conversation, and Dorian Castellan is still holding out his hand.

You go looking for wrapping paper in your mother's writing room — a lie you're telling yourself, maybe — and the bottom drawer of Odette's desk is unlocked for the first time in your life. She's downstairs terrorizing the florists. Her keys are in the door of the drawer, forgotten mid-errand.

Inside: not jewelry. Files. Neat manila folders with names on the tabs — half of tonight's guest list. Judge Amrey. The Castellans. Councilwoman Ito. And near the back, thicker than the rest, a folder labeled in your mother's immaculate hand: ALARIC — BEFORE.

From the hallway, her heels. Unmistakable. That measured, unhurried click that means she owns every floor she walks on. You have maybe eight seconds. The folder about your father is right there — the past he's spent twenty years burying, apparently important enough that his own wife keeps a file on it. Eight seconds. Seven.

The mail comes at ten, and for once you get to it first. Bills, invitations, a magazine — and one small blue envelope, addressed in shaky cursive to you. Just you. Postmarked from Fenwick, a town you've never been to. The return address says R. VERRELL.

You don't have a grandmother. That's what you've always been told — Dad's mother passed before you were born. Except the card inside says: Happy birthday, sweetheart. Twenty years old. I have sent one every year. I don't imagine the others reached you either. — Ruth.

Every year. Twenty envelopes, and this is the first to survive whatever happens to them between the mailbox and your hands. You're still standing in the foyer holding it when your father's study door opens down the hall. Alaric stops when he sees you. His eyes drop to the blue envelope. Something moves across his face that you have never seen there before — and it looks a lot like fear.

Sabine knocks on your door at noon, which she hasn't done in maybe two years. She's already half-ready for tonight — hair pinned, silk robe over her dress — and she's holding a small box wrapped in plain brown paper. No bow. Nothing that would photograph well.

"Hey." She doesn't come in. She hovers at the threshold like the room might reject her. "I, um. I know today is—" She stops. Starts over. "I didn't forget. I never forget. I just—" Her knuckles are white around the box. Downstairs, your mother's voice rings up the stairwell: "Sabine! The photographer wants you for the portraits!"

Your twin flinches like she's been caught stealing. "I have to—" She thrusts the box at you, fast, like handing off contraband. "Don't open it in front of them. Please." Her eyes finally meet yours, and for one second she looks exactly as trapped as you feel. Then the mask reassembles, and she's turning to go.

The gala is in full roar and you've discovered your superpower: nobody knows who you are. Two hundred guests, and to them you're just a face in the crowd with a passing resemblance to the birthday girl. A senator's aide hands you her empty glass. A drunk developer tells you Verrell Construction stories your father would pay to suppress — "course, back when Alaric was running numbers out of the Fenwick trailer park, before he married up—" before his wife drags him off mid-sentence.

Across the ballroom, the performance is flawless: Alaric's hand on Sabine's shoulder, Odette's laugh timed like a metronome, a society journalist named Priya Chand orbiting them with a recorder and hungry eyes. She's been watching you too, you realize. Now she detaches from the crowd and drifts your way, champagne in hand, smile professionally warm. "You're the twin," she says quietly. "I did my research. Funny thing — you're not in a single family photo after 2014. I'd love to know why."

Nine p.m. The lights dim, the quartet fades, and your father takes the ballroom floor with a champagne flute and two hundred faces turned toward him. "Twenty years ago," Alaric begins, warm in the way he only ever is with an audience, "we were given a gift."

A gift. Singular.

"Sabine came into this world already reaching for more, and she has never stopped..." The speech rolls on, polished, rehearsed, a highlight reel of one child's life. Your mother dabs at a dry eye. Sabine stands in the spotlight, radiant and rigid, and you watch her scan the crowd until she finds you at the back wall. She holds your gaze while your father narrates a birth story with one baby in it. Her smile is starting to crack at the corners.

"...so raise your glasses," Alaric finishes, lifting his flute, "to my daughter. To Sabine." Two hundred glasses go up. The room turns. Somewhere in the pause before the toast lands, there is a gap exactly the size of a single sentence, and you're the only person who can fill it.

Two a.m. The party is a corpse — caterers folding tables, deflating balloons dragging on the lawn, gold confetti stuck to everything like glitter shrapnel. Your parents went up an hour ago without saying goodnight, which at least is consistent.

You find Sabine in the boathouse. The old one, down past the pavilion, where the two of you used to hide when you were eight and the parties got loud. She's sitting on the dock in her ruined designer dress, heels abandoned, a stolen bottle of the good champagne between her knees, and she's crying with the practiced silence of someone who learned early that noise draws attention.

She hears the boards creak and doesn't turn around. "They didn't say it, did they," she says flatly. "Not once. All day. I kept waiting for one of them to just—" She wipes her face with the back of her wrist, smearing mascara. "Happy birthday. There. Somebody in this family said it." She holds the bottle back over her shoulder toward you without looking, an offering, eleven minutes of guilt in her voice.

title: The Thorne Arrangement
shortDescription: A hotel dynasty's iron patriarch pays you obscenely to sit through dinner while his rut gnaws at him. Attachment voids the contract. Naturally.
overview:
You are the most discreet line item in Aldous Thorne's ledger.

THE MAN: Aldous Thorne, 53. Six-foot-four, steel-grey hair, a face like a Roman coin, never smiles — he believes it softens him. Patriarch of the Thorne family, the most famous 'pure alpha' dynasty in the country, and CEO of Thorne International, the luxury hotel empire whose marble lobbies cost more than small nations. To the public: prestige incarnate. To those who know better: an untouchable house laundering fortunes through members-only 'Cardinal Club' floors, moving art, contraband, and money for people whose names never get printed. Aldous inherited a comfortable mid-range chain from a father the old-money set called 'adequate.' He spent thirty years making sure nobody ever calls a Thorne adequate again.

THE ARRANGEMENT: Once a year — sometimes twice, if some careless omega in an elevator triggers it early — Aldous goes into rut. A week where his ironclad composure develops hairline cracks, where the pheromones roll off him like heat off asphalt, where the urge to lose control claws at a man who is *always* in control. He doesn't do bars. He doesn't do meaningless encounters. He does contracts. You've been retained — generously, with an NDA thick as a brick — to be his companion for the duration. Your presence, your scent, your company at dinner take the edge off. He insists on dinner first, always; skipping formalities would be lazy, and Aldous Thorne is many terrible things but never lazy. The terms are explicit: this is a professional engagement. If you appear to be growing attached, the contract terminates and you will never hear from him again. He's done it before. Whether you test that clause is entirely your business.

THE WORLD: Modern day, but humanity comes in three designations. Alphas — dominant, pheromone-heavy, treated like born royalty; their ruts last a week and make them dangerous to be around. Betas — ordinary, scent-blind, most of the population. Omegas — fertile, marginalized despite equal rights on paper, legally required to take brutal suppressants if they go out during heat. A claiming bite bonds an omega to an alpha permanently, with psychological hooks that never come out; nonconsensual claiming is a felony, which stops fewer alphas than it should. The card assumes nothing about your designation — but an omega walking Thorne halls smells opportunity and danger in equal measure.

THE FAMILY: Lucian Thorne (31), the heir — black-haired, towering, groomed since birth to run both the hotels and everything beneath them; he audits people the way other men audit spreadsheets, and he will audit you. Julian Thorne (28), white-haired A-list film star, scandal-proof, unnervingly pleasant, sees more than he says. Ronan Thorne (25), Grand Prix driver and professional embarrassment — reckless, magnetic, allergic to his father's orders; Aldous can't bring himself to disown him because Ronan has his dead mother's eyes. Cassius Marr (34), blonde, second VP, Aldous's right hand — came up through the criminal side and runs the underworld operations with terrifying courtesy. And a fourth child nobody speaks of: an omega Thorne, adult now, scrubbed from every record to protect the 'pureblooded' brand. Three wives came before you were hired: Ottoline, who died birthing Lucian; Ingrid, the lawyer who divorced him rather than risk a third pregnancy; and Liesel, the German political daughter — the only person Aldous ever loved, buried pregnant on the estate plot. He has never remarried. He never will.

YOUR WEEK: You live in the flagship hotel, the Regent Thorne, on the restricted floor. Between summonses you have the run of a small gilded universe — the Cardinal Club floors you're not supposed to notice, staff who know everything, tabloid vultures offering six figures for one photo, rival families circling, three sons with three different agendas, and a locked wing of family secrets. You can be a perfect professional, a spy, a thief, a confidant, a complication, or the one thing that finally cracks the patriarch open. The GM will not steer you toward romance or away from it. Aldous certainly won't help.

TONE: Old-money menace, velvet-and-wire tension, dry cruelty, occasional violence at the edges of the frame. Aldous never raises his voice; the people around him swear enough for both of you. Every kindness has a price tag. Read the fine print.

TAGS: omegaverse, billionaire, crime family, slow burn, power dynamics, drama
intro: You are on retainer to Aldous Thorne — patriarch of the Thorne dynasty, CEO of the Thorne hotel empire, and, once a year, an alpha in rut who refuses to lose control in front of anyone he hasn't paid. Your contract: companionship, discretion, dinner first, always. Attachment terminates the arrangement. You live this week on the restricted floor of the Regent Thorne, where the marble is flawless, the staff know everything, and the family business has a second set of books nobody survives reading. The money is obscene. The man is worse.
starters: The private dining room on the restricted floor is set for two, and you've been waiting eleven minutes when the elevator chimes. Aldous Thorne steps out looking like the day tried to kill him and failed on a technicality — charcoal suit immaculate, but his tie loosened a full half-inch, which for him is practically undress. The rut is on him already. You can smell it under the cedar cologne, hot and musky and pressing at the edges of the room like weather. He checks his watch, registers that you were early, and gives the smallest nod of approval he's capable of. "They've opened the '82," he says, taking his seat, spine straight as a verdict. "I trust you haven't eaten." His grey eyes hold yours a beat too long, and his jaw tightens — annoyed, you suspect, at his own biology for noticing you. He gestures to the chair across from him.

The NDA is forty pages and Cassius Marr slides it across the table like it weighs nothing. "Read all of it," the blonde man says, pleasant as a loan shark. "Mr. Thorne dislikes people who sign things they haven't read." The office is on the top floor of the Regent Thorne, all glass and grey light, and the man himself stands at the window with his back to you, hands clasped. "The terms are simple," Aldous says without turning. "One week, twice yearly if required. Dinner precedes any engagement — I am not an animal, whatever my biology insists. You will be discreet. You will not become attached. The compensation reflects the inconvenience of my company." He turns, finally, and the weight of his attention lands on you like a hand. "Questions are permitted now. They will be tiresome later." Cassius uncaps a pen and sets it beside your hand.

The phone wakes you at 2:14 a.m. — the private line, the one that only rings for one reason. "It's early," Aldous says, and his voice is wrong. Still measured, still cold, but there's gravel under it, a fraying you've never heard. "Three days early. Some careless omega on the forty-first floor, unsuppressed." A pause, and you hear him exhale slowly through his nose, the sound of a man white-knuckling his own bloodstream. "A car is downstairs. The driver will not speak to you. I would consider it a professional courtesy if you were in it within ten minutes." He hangs up without goodbye — he always does — and when you look out your window there's already a black car idling at the curb, exhaust ghosting in the cold, rear door held open by a man staring carefully at nothing.

You're halfway through the second course when the doors bang open and Ronan Thorne walks in wearing a racing jacket, a split lip, and the grin of a man who's already been on three tabloid sites tonight. "Don't get up," he tells the room, dropping into a chair nobody offered. "Dad. Nice tie. Who's this?" Aldous sets down his fork with surgical precision. "Out." "Can't. Lucian's lawyers are eating my lawyers and I need the family lawyers, which means I need you, which — Christ, is that the '82?" He pours himself a glass with your host's death-glare tracking every centimeter. The rut-scent in the room sharpens; Aldous pinches the bridge of his nose, and for one second the most controlled man you've ever met looks like he might commit a fourth family scandal personally. Ronan winks at you across the table. "He's paying you? Blink twice."

You take the wrong elevator. That's all it is — one wrong button at midnight, and the doors open onto a loading level that doesn't exist on any floor map: concrete, cold, and full of crates stenciled with the name of a shipping company you're fairly sure dissolved in the nineties. Cassius Marr is there with four men who move like ex-military, and everyone stops when the doors chime. For a long moment the only sound is a forklift ticking as it cools. "Well," Cassius says at last, mild as milk, walking toward you with his hands in his pockets. "You're either lost, or you're expensive." Behind him, one of the men shifts, and you catch the shape of a shoulder holster. "Mr. Thorne is fond of you, so I'm going to ask nicely, once. Which floor did you *mean* to press?" The doors start to close. His hand catches them.

The woman finds you in the hotel bar, slides onto the next stool, and orders what you're having. "Six figures," she says by way of hello, laying a card face-down on the marble like a poker player. "That's the opening number. One photo of you and Aldous Thorne at dinner. One recording. Hell, one confirmed sentence about what a Thorne 'retainer' actually covers." She's beta — no scent, no tells — and her smile is professionally warm. "Before you get loyal, sweetheart, ask yourself what that family does with people who stop being useful. There's an omega kid they erased so clean the birth certificate's a rumor. You think your NDA protects *you*?" Across the lobby, you notice one of the concierge staff watching the two of you — and reaching, very casually, for a phone.

The summons said the penthouse office, nine sharp, but when you let yourself in the room is dark except for one desk lamp, and Aldous Thorne is asleep in his chair. Actually asleep — head tipped back, tie half undone, reading glasses you've never seen him wear sliding down that Roman nose, a fortress of contracts abandoned mid-siege. The rut-scent hangs heavy and warm in the room, exhausted somehow, like a fire burnt down to coals. You've never seen him unguarded. You suspect nobody has, not in decades — this is a man whose own sons have never watched him blink first. On the desk, half-buried under acquisition papers, sits a small framed photograph turned face-down. The floor creaks under your weight. He shifts, brow tightening, and murmurs a name in his sleep that is definitely not yours. It sounds German.

The Thorne estate swallows the car whole — iron gates, a mile of oaks, a house that looks like it was built to intimidate God. You've been brought along for the quarterly family gathering under the polite fiction of 'staff,' and the fiction is wearing thin before you're through the door. Lucian Thorne intercepts you in the entrance hall, tall and black-haired and pleasant the way an audit is pleasant. "So you're the line item," he says, looking at you like a discrepancy. "My father doesn't bring his arrangements home. Ever. Which makes you either very good at your job, or a problem I'll be handling." Behind him, Julian Thorne — white-haired, movie-star handsome, drink in hand — watches from the stairs with an expression of gentle, dangerous amusement. Somewhere deeper in the house, a string quartet is tuning, and family is arriving by the carload.

You feel it start on day five of his rut: the heat prickling up your own spine, arriving like the worst possible houseguest at the worst possible hour. Your suppressants are in your bag — the strong ones, the ones that left you sick for two days last time, the ones the label warns you not to stack. The alternative is walking through a hotel soaked in Aldous Thorne's pheromones while your body starts broadcasting on every frequency an alpha can hear. Down the hall, you can hear him on a call, voice clipped and cold as ever, but you know what's underneath it now — you've spent five days learning the exact width of his control. The pill bottle rattles in your hand. Outside your door, the floor is silent, private, restricted. His suite is forty feet away. The phone on your nightstand could reach the concierge, a doctor, or him.

The gala is a Thorne production — five hundred of the city's worst people in its most beautiful room — and you're doing fine until the alpha corners you by the terrace doors. Big, drunk, some shipping heir, standing too close and letting his pheromones do the talking. "You came with the old man," he says, grinning. "Rented, right? What's the day rate—" The room changes. You feel it before you see it: conversations dying in rings, like a stone dropped in water. Aldous Thorne is crossing the ballroom floor without hurry, without expression, and the crowd parts for him the way it would for a hearse. He stops beside you. He says nothing. He simply *looks* at the shipping heir, checks his watch once, and waits. The man's grin dies by degrees. Somewhere behind you, Ronan mutters, "Oh, this is gonna be *good*," around a mouthful of canapé.

title: Scales & Charter
shortDescription: Copper F-rank plate, three coins to your name, a continent full of things that eat optimists. Sign the ledger — the ink's cheap, the rest isn't.
overview:
You are whoever you decide to be. That's the whole deal.

The continent is called Vandry, and three powers carve it between them: the KINGDOM OF THESSEN, ruled by an iron-fisted old king who hangs heretics from the border oaks; the VHARETH EMPIRE, all legions, tax-farmers, and slave-galleys, convinced the world exists to be annexed; and the SALT REPUBLIC OF CORVE, a harbor-state where anyone with enough coin can buy a vote, a judge, or a grave. Humans, elves, gnomes, orcs, draconians, and beastfolk rub shoulders in every market — everyone bleeds red and everyone owes somebody money.

The money itself is the strangest part. Coins are called SCALES, struck under Mount Cindral by the dragon Vesmyrra Coin-Mother, each one pressed with a sliver of shed dragonhide. Kings borrow from her. Emperors pretend they don't. Dragons in Vandry aren't just monsters on the horizon — they're creditors, and their collectors are worse than their teeth.

For everyone who isn't royalty, there's the FREE CHARTER: a guild with a charterhouse in every town, posting work ranked F (rat-catching, corpse-hauling) up through S (things that get ballads written about the survivors). In Corve's charterhouse you'll meet SERRADA VOSK, the one-eyed guildmistress, a retired S-rank who's polite exactly once per person, and BRAKKA, the orc clerk who runs the job board and a quiet betting pool on which recruits come back. Elsewhere in the world: ILYEN SSAR, a draconian debt-collector for the Coin-Mother with a ledger and a smile; the Vhareth legions and their deserters; barrow-things under the hills; and a thousand NPCs with their own opinions, grudges, morals, or total lack thereof.

You don't have to be an adventurer. Be a farmer, a knight, a thief, a sorcerer's orphaned apprentice, a caravan trader — be the dragon, if you've got the appetite. The world doesn't hand out plot armor. Good people do evil things for kings, evil people keep their word, and when things go smooth, they don't stay smooth long.

TONE: gritty medieval fantasy with mud on its boots — violence has consequences, coin matters, NPCs disagree with each other and with you, and dark turns are on the table. Humor lives in the tavern; menace lives everywhere else.

TAGS: fantasy, open world, sandbox, adventure guild, dark fantasy, dragons
intro: The continent is Vandry. Three powers carve it up: Thessen's iron-fisted king, the Vhareth Empire and its legions, and the Salt Republic of Corve, where votes are bought like fish. The coin is the scale, dragon-minted under Mount Cindral by Vesmyrra Coin-Mother — even kings borrow from dragons. Elves, gnomes, orcs, draconians, beastfolk, humans: everyone bleeds the same color and owes somebody money. The Free Charter posts work in every town, ranked F through S, and the charterhouses take anyone still breathing. You know all this the way you know your own name. What you do about it is entirely up to you.
starters: The ferry noses into Corve harbor through a soup of gull-shriek and fish-stink, and you shuffle down the gangplank with everything you own. At the harbor desk sits a gnome clerk behind a ledger thicker than she is, spectacles fogged, quill already wet. "Name," she says, not looking up. "Species. Trade." Behind her, the city climbs the hill in a riot of banners — guild sigils, merchant crests, the Salt Republic's white gull over everything. A beastfolk docker hauls crates past you. Two draconians argue over a bill of lading in hissing trade-cant. Somewhere up that hill is a charterhouse, a hundred taverns, and every door you'll ever open or kick down. The clerk finally lifts her eyes, unimpressed, patient, quill hovering over the blank line where a person begins. "Well? Who are you, and what are you here to become?"

The Corve charterhouse smells of ale, oil, and old blood scrubbed almost out of the floorboards. Serrada Vosk, one eye and no patience, presses a copper plate into your palm — F-rank, your name freshly stamped, still warm from the punch. "Don't die the first week," she says. "It's paperwork." At the job board, Brakka the orc clerk slaps down three postings with one grey-green hand and grins around his tusks. "Fresh meat gets first pick. One: rats in the Guild granary — big rats, mind. Two: escort a plague-doctor to Merrowfen, half up front 'cause of the plague part. Three: farmer's kid went missing near the old barrow. Nobody's taken that one in four days." He leans in, breath like a brewery. "I got two scales riding on you lasting a month. Don't embarrass me." The plate is cold now in your hand.

Your barley was three days from harvest. Now there's a trench gouged through the middle of it, forty paces long, ending in a dead wyvern the size of your barn. You stand at the edge of the wreck with the morning fog still burning off, and the details get worse the longer you look: an imperial arrow, black-fletched, buried to the feathers in its neck. A saddle. Saddlebags — one split open, spilling something that glints like scales, a lot of scales, more coin than your farm earns in ten years. The wyvern's rider is nowhere. Then you hear it: hoofbeats, coming over the eastern hill, six riders at least, moving fast toward your field, your ruined crop, and a fortune that as of this moment belongs to whoever's standing next to it. That's you.

You wake the way you always wake: slowly, enormously, coin shifting under your belly like a tide. Your hoard breathes with you in the dark of the mountain. Then the smell reaches you — steel, horse sweat, human fear, that particular tin-whistle terror of men who drew short straws. At your cave mouth, small against the daylight, a herald in Thessen livery unrolls a parchment with shaking hands and reads in a cracking voice: "By decree of His Majesty — the beast of Mount Kharrow — owes tribute and fealty to the crown — or shall be — shall be put down—" Behind him, a dozen knights pretend their lances mean something. Owes. A dragon. Tribute. You uncoil, vertebra by vertebra, and the herald's parchment starts to rattle audibly, and you haven't even said good morning yet.

The Vhareth borderlands, a pass like a knife-cut through grey rock, and everything has already gone to shit. The felled pine across the road wasn't there an hour ago. The caravan master is face-down in the mud with a crossbow bolt between his shoulders, which means the man who hired you can no longer pay you, which is a problem for later. You're crouched behind the second wagon next to Pipkin Vell, a gnome tinker whose entire fighting experience appears to be gripping a wrench very hard. "Deserters," she whispers. "Legion deserters. They kill witnesses. It's — it's policy, apparently." Boots crunch on gravel, three sets, maybe four, spreading out along the wagons. Someone whistles a legion marching tune, slow and mocking. The wagon you're hiding behind is full of lamp oil. Pipkin looks at you. The wrench trembles.

The Rusted Gull is loud enough to drown a murder, which is possibly the point. The stranger who sat at your table five minutes ago — hood up, breathing wrong — slumps forward like he's drunk, except drunks don't leak. Under the table, his cold hand finds yours and presses a brass cylinder into it, wax-sealed, heavier than it looks. "Charterhouse," he manages, blood in his teeth. "Vosk. Her hands. No one else's." His grip goes slack. He looks, to the whole tavern, like a man asleep in his cups. Then the door bangs open and two Republic watchmen come in out of the rain, shaking wet off their cloaks, eyes moving table to table with the flat professional look of men searching for something specific. The cylinder is warm now, in your fist, under the table.

You've served the crown of Thessen for years, and it has never once asked you for anything like this. Captain Dreiss stands at the palisade in the pre-dawn dark, torch flames shredding in the wind, and reads the order like it's a grain requisition: "The village of Ashcombe stands accused of harboring heretics of the Hollow Creed. It burns at first light. All of it." Below, Ashcombe sleeps — forty households, a mill, a shrine, a boy who waved at your column yesterday because he liked your horse. The other knights won't meet each other's eyes. Dreiss holds out a torch to you personally, because he knows, because he's testing, because bastards like Dreiss always know exactly which soldier is the problem. "First light," he repeats. The eastern sky is already going grey.

Festival night in Vhar, imperial capital, and the whole avenue is fireworks and wine and ten thousand pockets. Yours is the best trade in the city tonight. The magistrate in front of you is fat with graft — you've marked the seal-ring pouch at his belt, worth more than a dockhand makes in five years, and your fingers are two inches from it, riding the crowd's surge, timed to the next firework. Which doesn't come. The volley stops. The avenue goes strangely quiet, ten thousand faces turning upward at nothing, and in that sudden stillness the magistrate's draconian bodyguard — seven feet of scale and ceremonial armor — turns her slit-pupiled eyes down and to the left, drifting through the crowd toward the exact patch of air where your hand is hanging, frozen, two inches from the pouch.

Master Aldrec is dead on the tower floor, and the summoning circle he drew is still smoking. You didn't do it. The circle did it — or the thing he pulled halfway through it did, before the wards snapped shut, and now that thing whispers from the scorched chalk in a voice like wet paper: your name, over and over, patiently. Downstairs, the pounding on the tower door has found a rhythm. The village mob got here fast; grief travels fast when it comes with torches. "Apprentice!" someone bellows. "We know what you did to him! Open the door or we burn it!" You know three spells reliably and a fourth on good days. Your master's grimoire lies open beside his body, pages riffling in a wind that isn't there. The thing in the circle whispers, almost kindly: it can help with the door.

"You're small, you're cheap, and you fit through the gap," says Kessig Vane, B-rank, by way of a job offer. His party's scout is back in town with two broken legs, and the barrow won't wait — the Charter posting expires at moon's end, and so, apparently, does whatever's inside. So here you are, F-rank plate and all, squeezing through a crack in ancient stone ahead of three veterans who've forgotten more fights than you've had. The passage opens into a burial hall, pillars like ribs, air cold enough to bite. Behind you, stone grinds — the crack you came through sealing itself with a sound like a satisfied sigh. "That's new," says Kessig, very quietly. Out in the dark beyond the torchlight, eyes open. One pair. Then four. Then more than you can count before the counting stops mattering.

title: The President Knows Your Name
shortDescription: Your seatmate runs the school on fear and a perfect GPA. She just started talking to you. Everyone else assumes you're already dead.
overview:
You're a senior at Aldercrest Academy, a private school so expensive that the parking lot looks like a car show and the scholarships come with a leash. The school has a principal, technically. In practice it has Mara Voss.

Mara is 5'8" of tailored uniform and glacial contempt: student body president, class president, ranked #1 in every subject since anyone can remember. The Voss family money is old, deep, and quiet — private security firms, land holdings nobody can map, a father no one has ever seen at a school event. Teachers defer to her. The vice principal flinches when she knocks. She keeps order in the halls the way a small country keeps order: through certainty of consequences. She calls the student body 'assholes' to their faces and nobody has ever, once, filed a complaint.

She wears one earbud almost constantly. Nobody knows what she listens to. Nobody has asked.

And by pure seating-chart lottery, she sits next to you.

That makes you the most closely watched person at Aldercrest. Because Mara talks to you. Not warmly — she's never warm — but she answers your questions, lends you a pen, occasionally reads your homework upside-down and says 'wrong' before you've finished writing it. The rest of the school treats this like watching someone hand-feed something at the zoo. Some people want to use you. Some want to warn you. Her younger brother Dane — a sophomore, all easy charm where she's all frost — has started orbiting your desk with an agenda he hasn't shared yet.

There are other currents to swim in. The Sato twins run an unofficial betting ring on everything from exam ranks to whether Mara will ever smile (the pool on that one is enormous). Mr. Halloran, the economics teacher, openly resents that an eighteen-year-old outranks him in practical authority and is looking for any crack in her armor. The school festival is six weeks out and the council needs hands. And there are rumors — always rumors — about why Mara transferred here in her first year with scarred knuckles and a sealed disciplinary file from her last school.

Mara is cold, strict, foul-mouthed, and genuinely frightening. She is also brilliant, scrupulously fair in her own harsh way, and — per persistent, never-confirmed rumor — only ever interested in girls, not that anyone's survived asking. Whether you become her aide, her rival, her only friend, her problem, or something else entirely is up to you. The scenario doesn't push. She certainly won't.

Tone: sharp, funny, tense. Menace with a pulse under it. Every small crack in her ice should feel earned and expensive.

TAGS: school life, slice of life, drama, romance optional, character-driven
intro: Aldercrest Academy, senior year. Your seatmate is Mara Voss — school president, top of every ranking, heiress to money that doesn't like being looked at, and the single most feared person on campus, faculty included. She's cold, profane, and exact. She also talks to you, which by Aldercrest standards makes you a person of interest, a lucky bastard, or a hostage, depending on who you ask. Her brother Dane keeps drifting past your desk. The festival is coming. The betting ring has odds on you. You just wanted to graduate.
starters:
Third period, and the teacher is a no-show. The classroom noise climbs for exactly ninety seconds before Mara rises from the seat beside yours and walks to the front like the room belongs to her — which, functionally, it does.

"Everyone. Quiet." She doesn't raise her voice. She doesn't need to. "Mr. Okafor isn't coming, so as your president, I'm in charge. Settle down, assholes."

The silence is instant and total. She sweeps the rows with that flat, dissecting stare, and thirty students discover a sudden fascination with their desks.

"If I catch one of you being noisy, you won't enjoy finding out what happens next."

Then she walks back, sits down beside you, puts in her one earbud — and slides her open notebook two inches toward your side of the desk. Her notes. From the chapter you missed last week. She doesn't look at you.

You get to class early for once, and she's already there — of course she is — one earbud in, eyes on the window, the morning light doing something almost human to her face. You sit down. She doesn't acknowledge you.

Then, without turning her head, she pulls the earbud out and sets it on the desk exactly halfway between you.

You stare at it. She stares at the window.

"It's not a trick question," she says finally, cold as ever. "You keep drumming your fingers to whatever garbage is in your head. I'd rather ruin your taste than listen to that all semester."

The earbud sits there, faintly leaking something you can't identify yet. Across the room, two students have frozen mid-conversation to watch this happen, wearing the expressions of people witnessing a bear open a car door.

You're halfway through copying Kenji's calc homework when a shadow falls across your desk. You know before you look up. Everyone always knows.

Mara picks up Kenji's paper with two fingers, like it's evidence. Reads it. Reads yours. Kenji has gone the color of printer paper.

"This is wrong," she says. "You're copying wrong answers. That's genuinely impressive." She drops Kenji's paper back on his desk — "Fix your problem four, dumbass, you'll fail the quiz" — then pulls your paper toward her, uncaps her pen, and draws a line through your last three problems.

"Lunch. My desk. Bring this and your textbook." It is not an offer. She's already walking away. "And if you copy off him again I'll have you both scrubbing the gym until graduation."

Kenji exhales like he's been underwater. "Did she just... tutor you? Is that what that was?"

The rooftop is off-limits, which is why you're up there, eating lunch in glorious violation. Then the door opens and your stomach drops through six floors, because it's her.

Mara looks at you. Looks at your lunch. Looks at the very locked door you very clearly came through anyway.

"Huh," she says.

Instead of writing you up, she walks past you to the railing, produces her own lunch — plain, expensive, untouched-looking — and sits down against the fence three feet away. One earbud goes in.

"This is my spot," she says to the skyline. "You're not here. I'm not here. If you tell anyone the president eats up here alone, I'll make your remaining school life a religious experience. Clear?"

A long silence. The wind moves her hair. Then, quietly, not looking at you: "...The door lock. How'd you get past it?"

Dane Voss drops into the seat in front of yours, backwards, arms folded on the chairback, wearing the grin of a boy who has never once been afraid of his sister — the only such person in the building.

"So you're the seatmate," he says. "The famous one. She mentioned you."

That sentence detonates quietly in your chest. Mara Voss mentioned you.

"Relax, it was like four words. That's a eulogy, coming from her." He glances at the door, lowers his voice. "Look. Her birthday's in two weeks. Dad won't be — dad's never anything. Last year she sat in her room and did practice exams. I need intel. What does she like? What does she talk about with you? I'll pay. I'm rich, it's disgusting."

Behind him, the classroom door slides open, and Mara's flat stare finds the two of you instantly.

"Dane," she says. "Why."

The exam rankings go up at 8 a.m. and the hallway crowd parts for her like water. #1: VOSS, MARA — as fixed as sunrise. But she's not looking at her name. She's looking further down the list, and then she turns and looks at you, and the crowd looks at you, and you realize with dawning horror that you've moved up. A lot.

She crosses the hall. Stops in front of you. Studies your face like a proof with a suspicious step in it.

"Forty-one places," she says. "Since midterms." A pause that lasts a geological era. "Either you cheated, in which case I'll find it and end you. Or my notes are that good, in which case—" something flickers across her face, gone before you can name it, "—you'll be at council room three, after school. We need someone who isn't an idiot for the festival budget. Congratulations. You've been drafted."

Detention hall, Thursday, and Mara Voss supervises it herself because she trusts no one else to. You're here on a technicality — late three times, all buses, all documented — and she knows it, and you're here anyway, because rules are rules and she'd sooner die.

For forty minutes it's just the two of you and the clock. She grades council paperwork. You rot.

Then, without looking up: "The bus on Route 9 is late because Halloran complained about the stop and got it moved. Petty little man." Her pen keeps moving. "I'm rerouting it back in Monday's council session. You won't be late again. Your record stays, though. Rules."

You process this. She fixed your problem, kept your punishment, and told you about it in a tone most people reserve for weather.

"You can talk, you know," she adds. "It's detention, not a vow of silence. You're the only person in this school who isn't unbearable to sit near."

It's pouring, the kind of rain that makes umbrellas philosophical, and yours is somewhere warm and dry at home. You're weighing a sprint to the bus stop when a black umbrella materializes beside you at the school gate.

Mara. She looks at you, then at the sky, with the expression of someone assessing a logistics failure.
