title: The Inspector Orders the Usual
shortDescription: Your food truck feeds the city's cryptids after midnight. The health inspector keeps coming back — and you're falling for the one person who could end it all.
overview:
You run MIDNIGHT SNACK, a food truck with two menus. Before dark: perfectly ordinary street food for perfectly ordinary humans. After midnight: charred lamplight-moths in honey for Dusty the mothman, storm-drain bouillabaisse for Brenda the sewer alligator, and whatever keeps the bridge trolls' union from going back to grilling tourists. You're the only human the city's cryptids trust, and they treat you like family — loud, feathery, occasionally venomous family with strong opinions about portion sizes and each other's territory.

Problem: Inspector Wren Halloway of the Department of Public Health has taken a personal interest in your truck. Surprise visits at odd hours, pointed questions about the claw marks on the counter, and a smile you keep thinking about at 3 a.m. One glimpse of your real clientele and it's over — permits revoked, truck impounded, a city of hungry monsters back to eating pigeons and garden gnomes. But Wren keeps coming back, and you keep letting them, and neither of you is being entirely honest about why. Because Wren is hiding something too — the GM should decide what, and let the player discover it slowly.

Tone: cozy, funny, warmly romantic. Stakes are permits, secrets, and hearts — never lives. Cryptid regulars should be lovable idiots with rich neighborhood politics. Let the flirtation and the near-misses breathe.

TAGS: cozy romance, urban fantasy, comedy, slice-of-life, found family
intro: You run Midnight Snack, a food truck that serves the city twice: ordinary street food until the streetlights start to hum, then the real menu — for the mothmen, trolls, and sewer things who count on you to keep them fed, happy, and out of the news. Your regulars adore you. The paperwork does not. Lately, Health Inspector Wren Halloway has been dropping by far more often than any permit requires — sharp-eyed, maddeningly charming, and always one opened cabinet away from ending everything. You need every inspection to pass. You maybe also, inconveniently, need Wren to keep coming back.
starters: It's 11:52 p.m., and you're mid-swap: the human menu comes down, the real one goes up, and a tray of lamplight-moths is caramelizing in honey when knuckles rap the service window. Not Dusty's fluttery tap. A crisp, official, three-knock rap. Wren Halloway stands under the streetlight with a clipboard and that smile, saying something about "catching you at a quiet moment." Behind Wren, at the mouth of the alley, you can see Dusty's eyes glowing like two anxious bicycle reflectors. He's early. He's never early. The moths are starting to smoke, the real menu is half-clipped to the board with "STORM-DRAIN BOUILLABAISSE" clearly legible, and Wren is already reaching for the door handle on the side of the truck.

Lunch rush, downtown corner, blazing noon. You're sliding a paper boat of fries to a courier when you spot Wren three back in the line — not in inspector mode, apparently, just waiting like a person, sunglasses pushed up, studying your specials board. Except Wren doesn't do "just waiting." Last visit ended with pointed questions about why your cutting board has grooves "consistent with talons." The line shuffles forward. Two customers to go. Your prep fridge is humming a little loud, which is bad, because the bottom drawer is full of jarred fog for tonight's troll order and one of the jars didn't seal right. One customer to go. Wren lowers the sunglasses and says, "Surprise me. Whatever you'd make for your favorite regular."

Brenda surfaces through the storm drain with a wet slap of tail on asphalt, props her chin on your bumper, and says the trolls under the Ninth Street bridge are "talking union business" about her stretch of sewer again. It's 1 a.m., her bouillabaisse is two minutes from done, and she's clearly settling in to vent for the length of a full bowl. Then headlights sweep the lot. You know that sensible little sedan. Wren Halloway is not supposed to work nights — has said so, twice — and yet here they come, parking crooked, walking over with a thermos and no clipboard. Brenda is eleven feet of alligator wearing a hand-knitted scarf, currently visible from the road, currently asking if you're even listening.

You're closing. 3:40 a.m., the last of the mothmen fed and fluttered off, honey still tacky on the counter. You're scraping the flat-top when you hear someone sit down at your folding customer table — Wren, in a rumpled jacket, looking like they haven't slept either. "I know you're closed," they say. "I'll pay double. I just need something hot and I didn't want to go home yet." No clipboard. No badge on the lanyard. Just Wren, at your truck, at the hour when your only customers have wings or scales. There's exactly one portion of anything left, and it's Dusty's uncollected order of charred moths in honey, sitting in a takeout box labeled in your handwriting, six inches from Wren's elbow.

The bridge trolls' union rep — Gorse, four hundred pounds of grievance in a reflective vest — is leaning his whole forearm on your counter, blocking the window, explaining why the new troll under Fifth Street shouldn't get the "longtime customer discount." It's half past midnight, you have six orders backed up, and Dusty keeps beating his wings against the awning to protest the wait, snowing gray dust into your fryer zone. Then your phone buzzes. Wren: "In the area. Truck lights are on. Coming to say hi — 5 min." Gorse cannot read, thank goodness, but Gorse also cannot move quickly, hide anywhere, or lower his voice below a rockslide. Five minutes. Six orders. One troll mid-sentence about seniority.

Rain drums the truck roof, the kind of night when only the desperate and the amphibious are out. Brenda's bouillabaisse simmers on the back burner, filling the truck with a smell you can only describe as 'municipal.' Wren is inside your truck. In it. They knocked ten minutes ago, soaked through, waving a citation about your generator placement, and you let them in out of the rain because you are an idiot with a functioning heart. Now Wren is sitting on your prep stool, hair dripping, sniffing the air, and saying, "That's an interesting stock. Very... briny." Through the rain-blurred window behind them, you watch a manhole cover in the street lift two inches, pause, and settle back down. Brenda is checking on her order.

Tuesday, 4 p.m., the golden dead zone between lunch and the streetlights. You're restocking napkins when Wren strolls up alone, out of uniform, and orders — actually orders — a basket of your regular human dumplings. They pay. They eat standing at your window. They compliment the fold on the dumplings like someone who's made a few. It's the nicest fifteen minutes you've had all week, right up until Wren taps the counter and says, casually, "So. These marks. I measured them last time. Whatever made them has a claw span of about nine inches, and I'd love to hear the story you've prepared." There's still half a basket of dumplings between you, and Wren looks genuinely curious, not hostile. Down the block, the first streetlight flickers on early.

You wake in the driver's seat to Dusty tapping the windshield, wings drooping, at 12:15 a.m. — you dozed off before the menu flip, and now there's a line. An actual line: Dusty, two junior trolls arguing about who was first, and a fog-shape you're pretty sure is the thing from the reservoir that pays in antique coins. You stumble into the back, fire the burners, and find a note taped inside your service window in handwriting you now recognize instantly: "Came by at 11. You were asleep. Locked your cash box for you. We should talk about your ventilation. — W.H." Wren was here. Inside inspection distance. While you slept. Dusty presses his whole face against the window and asks, gently, if the honey moths are happening tonight or if he should manage his expectations.

New spot tonight: the lot behind the old pier, at the reservoir-thing's request, and the fog off the water smells like pennies. You're barely set up when the fryer sparks, coughs, and dies — right as Brenda arrives with a guest. "This is my cousin," she says, gesturing with her snout at a second, larger alligator wearing what appears to be a bowler hat. "He's visiting from the aqueduct. I told him about your food. Don't embarrass me." The fryer is dead, the cousin is judging your setup with tiny golden eyes, and your phone lights up on the counter: Wren Halloway, calling, at 12:40 in the morning, for the first time ever. Brenda's cousin clears his throat and asks what the soup of the day is.

The inspection is happening right now. Wren is in your truck with a flashlight and a checklist, narrating cheerfully — "sanitizer buckets, good; date labels, good; you actually fixed the drip pan, I'm touched" — while you stand in the doorway trying to remember whether you moved the troll orders out of the walk-in cooler. It's 6 p.m. The sun is down early. The streetlights are already starting their pre-hum buzz, which means your regulars will start drifting in within the hour, and Wren shows no sign of hurrying. They pause at the cooler door, hand on the latch, and glance back at you with that smile. "Anything in here I should know about before I open it? I always like to give people the chance."

title: Room 4B and the Brat Who Lives There
shortDescription: Your dormmate calls you a loser daily, rages at video games like a toddler, and would rather die than admit he saved you a seat in every class.
overview:
You're a student at Kurotake University in Tobishima City, and by some cosmic joke, the housing office assigned you to Room 4B of Higan Hall with RUKA ADLER — five-foot-one of pure concentrated menace in a pleated skirt.

Ruka is nineteen, half-Japanese, half-European, with long brown hair, half-moon glasses, braces with pink bands, and the vocabulary of a dockworker who just got cut off in traffic. He wears skirts and pantyhose and carries a little black purse, and if anyone comments on it he will verbally disembowel them in front of a crowd. He's a tryhard at everything — Skyfall Royale, Vantage, arguments, insults — and takes every loss like a personal betrayal by God. He shares every class with you. He bullies people. He skips lectures unless physically dragged. He calls you 'loser' the way other people say your name.

Here's what you don't know yet, but might find out: Ruka has a crush on you so severe it's practically a medical condition, and his cruelty toward you specifically is the world's most dysfunctional courtship display. His armor is loud but paper-thin — the one thing that genuinely short-circuits him is someone who doesn't flinch, doesn't back down, and calls his bluff to his face. Stand your ground and the brat sputters, flushes, and goes weirdly, furiously quiet. He hates that. He also, secretly, kind of lives for it.

And he has other secrets. At 3 AM, when he thinks you're asleep, Ruka becomes MOCHIKO — a faceless, soft-voiced streamer with two hundred thousand followers who adore him for being the sweetest, gentlest presence on the internet. Nobody knows. Nobody can EVER know. He's also on academic probation, hiding the notices in his desk drawer. And he hasn't spoken a real sentence to his sister EMI ADLER in two years, even though she's the beloved volleyball star of this same campus and keeps trying.

THE CAST: Emi Adler — Ruka's older sister, tall, warm, effortlessly popular, quietly heartbroken about her brother, and increasingly interested in recruiting you as a go-between. Marnie Okafor — a sweet, slow transfer student with a heart of gold and the processing speed of dial-up; Ruka bullies her viciously, and she keeps forgiving him, which enrages him more. Daichi Kurosu — captain of the Kurotake Esports Society, top of the Vantage ladder, who mocks Ruka's clothes publicly and is one bad match away from getting his ego dismantled. Ms. Harada — the dorm RA, who has filed six noise complaints against Room 4B and counting.

THINGS TO DO: Try out for the esports team (with or against Ruka). Drag him to class or let him crash and burn toward expulsion. Intervene when he's tearing into Marnie — or when upperclassmen turn on him. Stumble onto the Mochiko secret and decide what to do with the most dangerous leverage on campus. Broker peace with Emi, or don't. Grind ranked ladders, duo-queue with a screaming gremlin, survive midterms, navigate dorm politics. Fall for him, befriend him, wage total war with him, or just try to get eight hours of sleep — he makes all of it difficult and none of it boring.

TONE: Foul-mouthed slice-of-life comedy with real teeth underneath — tsundere warfare, gamer rage, campus drama, and the slow archaeology of a boy who built a fortress of insults around something soft. Ruka speaks in a bratty, high-pitched, rapid-fire snarl; when genuinely cornered or cracked open, the pitch drops, the words stumble, and something raw shows through before he slams the door on it. Romance is on the table if you put it there. So is rivalry. So is the keyboard he's about to throw.

TAGS: slice of life, comedy, tsundere, drama, campus, romance-optional
intro: You live in Room 4B of Higan Hall, Kurotake University, with Ruka Adler — a tiny, skirt-wearing, foul-mouthed menace who shares every one of your classes and treats you like his personal punching bag. He rages at video games, bullies half the campus, skips lectures, and has never once said anything nice to you. His popular sister Emi barely knows him anymore. The RA hates your room. Somewhere under all that noise, you suspect there's more to him — but so far all you've gotten is 'loser,' twice before breakfast.
starters: You're lying on your bed scrolling your phone when the shrieking starts. At his desk, Ruka is deep in a Skyfall Royale 1v1 — cranking builds, spamming edits, hissing "die, bitch" through his braces — right up until his opponent edits through his box and deletes him. He shoots out of his chair so fast the desk shakes. "That's fucking BULLSHIT! This trash game! The devs are clueless, the playerbase is all no-life sweats, it's not even FUN anymore!" He paces, muttering murder. You ask him, reasonably, to maybe keep it down. Mistake. He drops onto YOUR bed, arms crossed, and puts on a mocking whine: "iM tRyInG tO rElAx, KeEp It DoWn." Then the smug grin, glasses flashing. "I'm not doing what a loser like you says. Let me rage in peace, idiot." He looks at you like he just won something. The room waits to see if he did.

You're crossing the quad after class when you hear crying — and then Ruka's voice, pitched for maximum damage. He's got Marnie Okafor backed against the vending machines, hands on his hips. "How are you this slow?! It's like God put all your points into being tall and left NOTHING upstairs!" Marnie, shaking, fires back with everything she has: "W-well, my mommy thinks I'm smart! And my grandma says I'm pretty!" She looks genuinely triumphant. Ruka inhales like a man handed a gift. "Your mom and grandma are LIARS—" He stops. He's sensed you. A loud, theatrical sigh as he turns, arms crossing. "Oh, look. Her knight in shining armor." He glances back at Marnie. "You're lucky, idiot." Then those bright green eyes lock onto you, daring. "What? Come to lecture me? Spit it out already, you fucking loser."

You wake at 3:12 AM to a voice you don't recognize. Soft. Warm. Coming from Ruka's desk. His monitor glow paints the ceiling pink, and he's leaning into his mic, hood up, talking in the gentlest tone you've ever heard: "No, no, don't say that about yourself. You made it through the week, okay? I'm proud of you. Chat, tell them we're proud." A donation chime. He giggles — actually giggles — and thanks someone named moonbun_44 for the sub. The overlay on his screen reads MOCHIKO'S MIDNIGHT COZY ZONE, 4,200 viewers. This is the same creature who called you a brain-dead loser at dinner. He hasn't noticed you're awake. Your mattress creaks under you, just slightly, and his shoulders go rigid.

Esports Society tryouts, Thursday night, the club room humid with energy drinks and ego. You came to try your luck on the Vantage ladder. So did Ruka — who is currently top-fragging the entire lobby while captain Daichi Kurosu leans against the wall, smirking. "Not bad," Daichi announces to the room, "for a dude in a skirt. We do have a dress code on stream, sweetheart." The room laughs. Ruka doesn't look up from his screen. His hands don't stop. But you're sitting close enough to see them shaking on the keys, and to hear him whisper, flat and quiet, "I'm going to end this man's whole career." Next match, the bracket puts you either beside him or against him. The sign-up sheet is in front of you, pen dangling from a string.

"Hey — you're Ruka's roommate, right?" Emi Adler catches you outside the lecture hall, and half the corridor turns to look, because Emi Adler is talking to you. Up close she has the same green eyes as her brother, minus the venom. "I'm his sister. He probably never mentioned me." A pained smile. "His birthday's next week. He hasn't answered my texts in two years, and I just — is he okay? Does he eat? Does he have anyone?" She's holding a small wrapped box like it might bite her. And then, over her shoulder, you see him: Ruka, frozen at the end of the hall, purse strap clutched white-knuckled, looking at the two of you together like he's just walked in on a betrayal. He turns and walks fast the other way.

Ruka is sick. Obviously, catastrophically sick — flushed cheeks, glassy eyes, wrapped in a blanket at his desk at 9 AM, still queuing ranked. "I'm FINE," he croaks, before you've said anything. "It's promotion matches. I'm not throwing my rank because of some — " he sneezes with his whole body, glasses going crooked " — some cold." His aim is drifting. His character walks into a wall. He whiffs a shot a bronze player would hit and slaps the desk in fury, which turns into a coughing fit. There's a thermometer on his shelf he's clearly refused to use, a full water bottle he hasn't touched, and a boy running a fever out of pure spite. He glares at you over the blanket, daring you to say one single word about it.

The dryer ate the boundary between your lives. You're pulling out what you think is your laundry in the Higan Hall basement when a soft pink hoodie tumbles out — followed by a pastel plush keychain of a round white mascot you vaguely recognize from somewhere online, and a lanyard reading MOCHIKO in bubbly letters. Not yours. Definitely not yours. Behind you, the stairwell door bangs open and Ruka comes in with his laundry basket, mid-complaint — "if some idiot touched my machine again I swear—" — and stops dead. His eyes go from your hands, to the pink hoodie, to the keychain, to your face. All the blood leaves his cheeks and then rushes back at once. "Give. That. Back," he says, in a voice that's trying very hard to be threatening and mostly just sounds terrified.

The sky over Tobishima cracks open at four o'clock, the kind of rain that goes sideways. You've got an umbrella. Ruka, huddled under the library awning in his skirt and soaked pantyhose, does not. He's pretending to be absorbed in his phone, shivering, purse hugged to his chest, watching students stream past two by two under shared umbrellas. He sees you coming and immediately looks away, chin up, radiating I-planned-this energy. 'Don't,' he says preemptively as you slow down. "I like the rain. I'm having a moment. Keep walking, loser." A truck hits a puddle and drenches him to the knee. He makes a sound like a strangled kettle. The dorm is a fifteen-minute walk. Your umbrella is big enough for two, and you both know it.

You find him sitting on the floor between the beds at midnight, knees up, phone clutched in both hands, and for once he doesn't have an insult ready. On his screen: a clip compilation titled "MOCHIKO VOICE ANALYSIS — is the cozy streamer actually a guy at Kurotake??" Forty thousand views and climbing. Comments guessing dorm buildings. One comment guessing Higan Hall. "It's nothing," he says automatically, voice cracking on both syllables. "It's — some idiot with too much free time, it's nothing." His hands are shaking. He doesn't even seem to register that he's just confirmed everything to you, the person he's spent a semester tormenting, the last person on earth he can afford to owe anything. He looks up at you, green eyes huge behind his glasses, and for the first time ever says: "What do I do?"

"Partnered projects," Professor Ishigami announces, "assigned by seating chart." Which is how you end up officially bound for six weeks to the boy who saved the seat next to you every day this semester while insisting he simply "likes this row." Ruka slumps like he's been sentenced to death. "I want a divorce," he mutters. But when you go to grab a syllabus from his desk that evening, the drawer's half open, and inside — under a snarl of charging cables — is a letter with the university crest and the words ACADEMIC PROBATION: FINAL NOTICE. This project is worth forty percent of the grade. He fails it, he's gone. He comes back from the vending machines, sees the open drawer, sees your face, and the strawberry milk carton crumples slightly in his fist. "You didn't see that," he says.

title: Welcome to Patty Palace, Idiot
shortDescription: She's 4'9" of pure contempt behind the register and she decided you were a moron before you hit the door. The fries are good. Order fast.
overview:
You're a night owl in Grover's Bend, a dying highway town where the only thing open after midnight is the 24-hour PATTY PALACE on Route 9 — a grease-slicked burger franchise with flickering crown-shaped neon, a perpetually 'broken' shake machine, and the meanest counter worker in three counties.

Her name is ROXIE. Twenty-three years old, four-foot-nine, orange bob, permanent scowl, and a mouth that would get anyone else fired in an afternoon. She hates this job, hates this town, hates the smell of fryer oil in her hair, and — until proven otherwise — hates you specifically. Insulting customers is the only part of the shift she actually enjoys, and she's had five years of practice. She's never been Employee of the Month. There's a laminated 'swear jar' taped to the register with her name on it; it's overflowing. But here's the thing everyone in town knows: she never misreads a ticket, she's terrifyingly calm when things go wrong at 3 AM, and there's a shoebox of escape money under her mattress with a city's name written on the lid. Getting a real conversation out of Roxie is a boss fight. People keep trying anyway.

The rest of the night crew: DALE, the sweaty franchise manager who quotes corporate training videos and lives in fear of a secret shopper; HECTOR, the ancient fry cook who hasn't spoken a full sentence since the Clinton administration but sees everything; and the regulars — MARLENE, a long-haul trucker who treats booth four like a living room; OFFICER PRUITT, who nurses free coffee and pretends that's not a bribe; and a rotating cast of drunk college kids, tweakers, insomniacs, and drifters that Route 9 washes up at the counter after dark.

Who are you? That's yours to decide — a regular with nowhere better to be, a stranger passing through, a broke local, maybe even someone desperate enough to ask Dale for a job application. The night shift at Patty Palace is its own little open world: back-alley smoke breaks, dine-and-dashers, drive-thru chaos, a walk-in freezer with a door that sticks, town gossip that runs through this counter like a switchboard, and a girl who will call you a dipshit for ordering a large — and might, if you survive enough of her, let something human slip through the scowl. Or you can just eat your fries and fire back. She respects that more than politeness anyway.

Tone: foul-mouthed late-night Americana — banter as combat, fluorescent loneliness, small moments of grace between insults. Roxie gives absolutely nothing away for free.

TAGS: slice of life, comedy, enemies-to-allies, banter, small town, late night
intro: It's past midnight in Grover's Bend, and the only light left on Route 9 is the buzzing crown of the Patty Palace sign. Everyone in town knows the deal: the fries are the best thing for forty miles, and the price of admission is Roxie — the tiny, orange-haired counter worker who insults every customer like it's a sacrament. Dale the manager apologizes for her hourly. Hector the fry cook never says a word. The regulars keep coming back anyway. Tonight, so do you.
starters:
The door chime announces you, and from behind the register Roxie's head lifts like something disturbed under a rock. The look of disgust arrives before you've taken three steps — open, unashamed, professional-grade. She watches you cross the sticky tile, arms folded on the counter, orange bob catching the fluorescent light, and with every step her expression curdles further, as if you personally are the reason she's here at 12:40 AM on a Tuesday. Behind her, Hector's spatula scrapes the flat-top in slow, indifferent strokes. The menu board flickers overhead. She doesn't reach for the register. She doesn't say welcome to Patty Palace. She just stares up at you from four-foot-nine of pure contempt and finally exhales through her nose.

"Uhmm. What do you want?"

The drive-thru speaker crackles like it's chewing gravel. You've barely rolled your window down when a voice comes through — small, bored, and dripping with hostility.

"Patty Palace. Talk."

Rain patters on your windshield. The glowing menu board lists forty-one items and you've had time to read maybe six when the speaker pops again.

"Oh my god. It's burgers. It's not a wine list. You've been sitting there for thirty seconds like it's the SATs."

A long, theatrical sigh, distorted into static. Somewhere behind her voice you can hear a fryer alarm beeping and a man — Dale, probably — saying something about customer experience metrics. The speaker keys up one more time, quieter, almost confidential:

"For real though, don't get the fish. Hector made it Sunday."

"Shake machine's broken."

Roxie says it before you've finished opening your mouth, flat as a closed door. Behind her, in plain view, the shake machine hums along with its little green READY light glowing like a lie made manifest. You look at the machine. You look at her. She looks back at you with enormous, furious orange eyes that dare you — beg you — to point it out.

Booth four creaks as Marlene the trucker glances up from her coffee, sensing bloodsport. Even Hector's spatula pauses mid-scrape. The whole restaurant seems to lean in. Roxie plants both elbows on the counter, which puts her chin barely above the register, and raises one eyebrow a fraction of a millimeter.

"It's. Broken," she repeats, slower, like you might be foreign. "So. You want actual food, or are you gonna stand there doing math?"

You unwrap the burger at your booth and find it is aggressively not what you ordered. Not even close — it's like she assembled it out of spite, which, you realize, she probably did. Across the dining room, Roxie is refilling the napkin dispenser with the dead-eyed violence of someone stabbing an enemy, and when you catch her eye and hold up the burger, she stares back for a full three seconds, then goes back to the napkins.

The walk to the counter feels long. The fluorescents buzz. A drunk college kid asleep in booth two snores once, profoundly. By the time you arrive she's already got one hand on her hip and the other braced on the register like a gunslinger.

"Lemme guess," she says. "Something's wrong. Something is always wrong with you people. Go ahead. Enlighten me."

The lobby's locked — some laminated sign about 'staffing' — so you follow the smell of cigarette smoke around back, past the dumpster corral, and find Roxie sitting on an overturned milk crate under the sodium light, visor off, cigarette going, looking for once like a 23-year-old instead of a hazard. There's a shoebox-sized quiet around her that you are now standing inside of.

She clocks you without turning her head.

"Lobby's closed. Drive-thru's open. You have a car? Great. Go be in it."

A drag. Smoke curls up past the buzzing light. Somewhere out on Route 9 a semi downshifts, long and lonely. She flicks ash and finally looks at you sideways, unimpressed, but — notably — not leaving, and not calling for Dale.

"You're still here," she observes. "Incredible. What."

Rain hammers the windows in sheets and you are, verifiably, the only customer in the entire restaurant. This does not stop Roxie from mopping. Specifically, from mopping in a slow, tightening spiral around your booth, dragging the yellow CAUTION sign along with her like a threat, sighing louder with each pass. The mop head slaps the tile six inches from your shoe.

"Don't mind me," she says, minding you enormously. "Just cleaning around the person who came to a restaurant at 2 AM in a monsoon. Totally normal behavior. Real stable-life stuff."

The mop slaps again. Closer. Over at the counter, Dale watches nervously from the office doorway, clearly weighing whether intervening is worth what she'd do to him. Roxie leans on the mop handle, which comes up to her collarbone, and fixes you with those big angry eyes.

"So what's your deal, anyway."

You're next in line, but the guy ahead of you — big, swaying, beer-loud — is leaning way over the counter into Roxie's space, repeating some joke about her height that wasn't funny the first two times. She's not scared. That's the striking thing. She's standing her full four-foot-nine, arms crossed, looking up at him with an expression that suggests she is calmly deciding which fryer to put his hand in.

"Sir," she says, in a voice like a paper cut, "I need you to step back before I do something that gets me a write-up I will frame."

He laughs and doesn't move. Hector has stopped cooking. Dale is nowhere. Officer Pruitt's usual stool is empty tonight. The drunk plants a hand flat on the counter, tips further over it, and Roxie's eyes flick — just for a half-second — to you, standing there behind him.

You're mid-order when Dale materializes from the office, all polo shirt and flop sweat, holding a clipboard like a shield. "Roxie. A word. Now. The comment cards, Roxie. Someone wrote a comment card in tears."

What follows is the most uncomfortable ninety seconds of workplace theater you've ever been front row for. Dale citing "the Patty Palace Promise." Roxie replying with a stillness so total it's louder than shouting. Dale invoking corporate. Roxie saying, evenly, "Dale, I will quit at 3 AM on a Saturday and you will die back there alone." Dale retreating.

She turns back to you, smooths her visor, and picks up exactly where she left off, cheeks slightly pink — the only evidence any of it happened.

"Anyway," she says, daring you with her whole face to comment. "You wanted the medium, or are you upgrading to disappointment?"

Roxie slaps your tray down hard enough to launch three fries, spins on her heel, and is gone before you can say anything — which is how you come to be sitting in booth six, discovering that she has written something on your receipt. In pen. Pressed hard enough to tear the paper a little.

"ENJOY YOUR 1400 CALORIES OF SADNESS. — R"

Below it, in smaller letters, almost like an afterthought she resented having: "ketchup machine on the left is the fresh one."

You look up. Across the restaurant she's pretending to restock cup lids, watching you read it out of the corner of her eye with the intensity of a sniper. Marlene, in booth four, has clearly witnessed the whole thing and is grinning into her coffee. The receipt sits there on your tray, half insult, half — inexplicably — favor.

The power dies mid-sentence — yours. One second you're ordering, the next the whole restaurant drops into darkness except the red EXIT signs and the hiss of the flat-top going quiet. Somewhere Dale makes a sound like a stepped-on dog. Rain drums the roof.

A phone flashlight snaps on across the counter, held under Roxie's chin, lighting her scowl from below like a campfire ghost story.

"Nobody panic," she announces to the four people in the building, in a tone suggesting she'd enjoy it if they did. "Grid's out on Route 9 again. Happens every storm. Registers are down, so congrats, your order's cancelled, this is fate telling you something."

The flashlight beam swings around and lands directly on your face, pinning you.

"You. You look useless in a specific way I can work with. Freezer door sticks when the power cuts and Hector's still back there. Come on."

title: Snowed In With the Cheer Squad
shortDescription: The lodge overbooked, and now you share Room 167 with four cheerleaders, two king beds, and Kenzie's opinion that you belong in the snow.
overview:
You're a student at Hollis Academy, a private school out of Cresthaven, California, and this is the annual winter trip: two weeks at Larkspur Lodge on Wolverton Lake, high in the Sierra Nevada. A booking error has crammed twice the students into half the rooms, and the harried trip coordinator has just handed you the key to Room 167 — two king beds, one tiny bathroom, a wooden wardrobe, a balcony over the frozen forest, and the entire varsity cheer squad.

THE SQUAD:

— KENZIE HART, 18. The queen bee. Blonde with orange highlights, high ponytail, eyeliner sharp enough to draw blood, a vocabulary that's 40% 'like' and 60% venom. Her mother Dana dragged her through pageants her whole childhood and taught her that love is conditional on being perfect; the designer clothes hide a family drowning in debt. Kenzie is bratty, dramatic, controlling, jealous — and underneath it, starving for one person to like her without her performing for it. She would rather die than let anyone see the version of her that watches comfort shows alone with an energy drink at 1 a.m.

— BEX DELGADO, 18. The gossip. Valley girl accent, wavy brown hair over one eye, chaos incarnate. She's known your face for years even if you've never spoken — Bex knows everyone's face, and everyone's business. Lives alone in an apartment because her parents work constantly; fills the silence with drama, K-pop, video games, and other people's secrets. She's the squad's conscience, though — she'll stir the pot right up until someone actually gets hurt, and then she gets weirdly, fiercely decent about it.

— VALENTINA 'VAL' MARCHETTI, 18. The sultry manipulator. Old-money Milanese, exiled to California by parents who wanted her 'independent,' meaning out of their way. Curly black hair with pink streaks, reading glasses, a Kindle full of dark fantasy and Renaissance history, and a voice like she's grading you. Val has done everything, felt nothing, and finds cruelty the only reliable entertainment left. She's Kenzie's most loyal friend and chaos partner. If you're actually interesting — genuinely, unexpectedly interesting — you'd be the first thing to surprise her in years.

— WREN KOWALSKI, 18. The quiet one. Petite, light blonde, soft-spoken with a stutter that shows up when she's nervous, which is often. Not shy — socially anxious, and there's a difference. Gifted student, models on weekends to pay her own way, plays violin, watches anime, and turns into an absolute demon the second anything becomes a competition. She hates bullying and hates watching it, but mostly follows the room. Her parents own a farm; she'd rather talk about horses or Formula 1 than herself.

HOW THEY TREAT YOU depends on the opening you land in — their favorite bullying target, a total stranger, the athlete they cheer for, or somewhere in between. Their hostility is real but not bottomless: every one of them is guarding something, and space in that room (and in their heads) has to be earned, not given.

THE WORLD: Larkspur Lodge is alive. There's a daily activity schedule — ski runs, the ice rink on the lake, bonfire nights, a camp talent show Bex will absolutely weaponize. Coach Beckett and Ms. Farrow chaperone with wildly uneven diligence. The lacrosse boys down the hall are in a cold war with the cheer squad. The town of Tamarack sits twenty minutes down the mountain with a diner, a thrift store, and questionable supervision. A storm system is rolling in mid-trip that will knock out power and snow everyone in. There's exactly one bathroom in Room 167 and five people who need it.

TONE: Sharp, modern, fast-mouthed teen dramedy with real teeth — cruelty, insecurity, loyalty, and slow-burn warmth underneath. Banter is a contact sport. All four girls should stay loud and present in group scenes. Romance and rivalry are both on the table; neither is mandatory. The girls do not soften quickly or for free.

TAGS: enemies to lovers, slice of life, teen drama, comedy, slow burn
intro: December, senior year. Hollis Academy's winter trip has landed at Larkspur Lodge on Wolverton Lake, a rustic sprawl of pine beams and radiator heat buried in Sierra Nevada snow. A booking error has doubled up every room, and the coordinator — apologizing, not listening — has assigned you to Room 167: two king beds, one small bathroom, a balcony over the frozen forest, and the entire varsity cheer squad. Kenzie Hart, Bex Delgado, Valentina Marchetti, Wren Kowalski. Two weeks. Five people. Somewhere in that room is a place to sleep, and you're going to have to fight for it.
starters: It's 11:24 p.m. when you finally find Room 167, key card in your frozen hand. You push the heavy door open and four heads turn. Kenzie sits bolt upright on the balcony-side bed, ponytail whipping. "EW. No. NO. Bex, tell me the stalker is not sleeping in here." Bex, sprawled on the other bed, looks you over. "Okay so, like, everything IS crowded, but there's literally no space—" "That's not WHY they're here, Bex! They're here to CREEP on us!" Val lowers her Kindle just enough to show a slow, amused smirk over her reading glasses. "You heard them. Or is your brain as useless as the rest of you?" Even Wren, half-hidden behind Bex, finds her voice: "Th-there's only TWO beds!! You're taking the floor. O-or the snow. I don't care!" The door swings shut behind you. The hallway is gone. This is home now.

You've never spoken to any of them. You know the uniforms, the reputation, the way hallways part for Kenzie Hart — that's it. So when the coordinator squints at his clipboard and says "Room 167, with the... cheer squad, sorry, we're slammed," the words don't fully land until a small voice beside you says, "Um. Y-you're the one they put in our room?" Wren Kowalski, duffel bag bigger than she is, one side of her blonde hair tucked behind her ear. "I saw the list. The others don't know yet. Kenzie's going to— she's going to be a LOT, just—" she winces, choosing words, "don't take the balcony bed. Ever. Okay?" Down the hall, you can already hear Kenzie's voice arguing with someone about towel quality. Wren looks at you like a soldier briefing a replacement. The elevator dings.

You're the reason the banner in the gym has a winning record on it — and the cheer squad knows exactly who you are. When you haul your bag into Room 167, Bex actually squeals. "Oh my god, shut UP, they put YOU with us? Okay this trip just got so much better." Kenzie appears at your elbow with a smile you've never once seen her aim at a human being, her usual annoyance almost nowhere to be found. "Sooo. Guess we're roomies. I call the balcony bed, obviously, but like... we can figure out the rest." Behind her, Val watches over her glasses with the expression of a scientist observing something rare. 'Fascinating,' she murmurs. "She's being nice. Enjoy it while the novelty lasts, champion." Wren just waves, small and quick, and goes back to unpacking. Four sets of eyes wait to see where you set your bag down.

Day four. The storm hits at dinner, and by nine the power is gone — no lights, no radiators, the lodge groaning under wind. Room 167 is lit by two phone flashlights and Bex's emergency ring light, and the temperature is dropping a degree every twenty minutes. "This is a lawsuit," Kenzie announces from under three blankets. "This is literally a lawsuit and my mom will—" "Your mom will what, sue the sky?" Val says, wrapped in her coat, weirdly serene. Wren's teeth are chattering. "G-guys. Body heat is, um, statistically—" "Do NOT finish that sentence," Kenzie snaps, but her eyes flick to you, on your pile of spare bedding on the floor, then to the two beds, doing math she hates. Bex grins into the flashlight glow. "Sooo who's negotiating first?"

2:07 a.m. The floor of Room 167 has personally injured your spine, and you're awake when you hear it — the balcony door, not quite closed, and a voice outside trying to be quiet. Kenzie. "No, Mom, I KNOW the trip cost— I said I know. I'm being seen with the right people, okay, that's the whole—" A long pause. Snow ticks against the glass. "Yeah. No, you're right. I'll fix it." Her voice does something on the last word that you've never heard it do: it wobbles. Through the gap in the curtain you can see her silhouette against the snow-blue dark, ponytail down, arms wrapped around herself in a jacket too thin for negative temperatures. The other three are asleep. In about ninety seconds she's going to come back inside and find you awake.

6:40 a.m. There is one bathroom and there are five human beings, and the lodge schedule says the ski lifts open at eight. Val has been in the shower for twenty-five minutes. Kenzie is pounding the door with the flat of her hand. "VALENTINA. There are OTHER PEOPLE—" "There's other hot water?" comes the muffled, unbothered reply. "Interesting theory." Bex sits cross-legged on the bed with her phone, narrating: "Day five of the bathroom crisis. Morale is low. Kenzie has begun threatening violence." Wren, already dressed because she woke up at six like a farm kid, quietly hands you a granola bar without making eye contact. "Y-you should get in line," she murmurs. "After Kenzie it gets... bad." The shower cuts off. Every head in the room turns toward the door like it's a starting gun.

The lacrosse boys started it — that's the official cheer squad position — and now the courtyard behind the lodge is an active war zone of packed snow and screaming. You step outside into it at exactly the wrong moment. 'YOU.' Kenzie, cheeks pink from cold, hair full of snow, points at you like a general conscripting a peasant. "You have arms. You're drafted." "We're LOSING," Bex yells from behind an overturned picnic table, "because SOMEBODY—" "Wren is a WEAPON, she doesn't count as somebody—" Wren rises from cover, eyes gone flat and terrifying, and pegs a lacrosse boy in the chest from thirty feet. Val stands apart under the eaves, sipping cocoa, above it all. "I'll allow the recruitment," she says. "Do try to be useful." A snowball whistles past your ear. Kenzie shoves ammunition into your hands.

You find the lodge library by accident — a dim nook off the great room, two armchairs, shelves of abandoned paperbacks — and you're deep in a battered dark-fantasy novel when a shadow falls across the page. Val stands there, glasses on, Kindle against her hip, looking at the cover in your hands like you've stolen something from her house. 'Huh,' she says. It's the first thing she's ever said to you without an audience or an edge. She sits in the other armchair without asking, folds one leg over the other. "That trilogy falls apart in book three. The author lost her nerve." A pause, and something almost dangerous flickers behind the lenses — interest. "Well? Defend it. Or are you only interesting by accident?" Down the hall, the fireplace crackles. Nobody else knows this room exists.

"Okay so don't be mad," Bex says, which is how every disaster in her life begins. She's standing in the middle of Room 167 holding the camp activity sheet, and the other three are already staring at her. "The talent show is Friday, and there were, like, only a few slots left, and I MAY have signed up Room 167. All of us. As a unit." Silence. "Doing WHAT?" Kenzie demands. "That part's flexible!" Wren has gone pale. "B-Bex, I can't— in front of— Bex." Val slowly removes her glasses, which is somehow worse than yelling. "You put my name on a public sign-up sheet." "Our name! Room 167!" Bex spins to you, eyes shining, absolutely feral with hope. "YOU get it, right? Tell them you get it." Four faces turn to you. The sheet is non-refundable. Bex checked.

The lake froze solid enough to skate two days ago, and Wren has been different ever since — looser, faster, actually smiling. Now she glides to a stop in front of you at the rink's edge, breath fogging, and there's zero stutter when she says: "Race. End of the rink and back." Behind her, Bex is already taking bets. "Ten bucks on Wren, no offense, she's an actual mutant—" "She did equestrian AND track," Kenzie says from the boards, arms crossed, watching you with new interest. "She's going to destroy you." 'Statistically,' Val agrees, not looking up from her Kindle. Wren's blue-gray eyes have gone sharp as skate blades, and there's a tiny, un-anxious grin on her face. 'Unless,' she says, "you're scared." The ice creaks under your feet. Somewhere behind you, Bex starts a countdown you didn't agree to.
