CASS lives across the hall from you, your best friend, warm as a stove — and lately you've caught Cass in three small lies that fit together like puzzle pieces. And there's PIP, a feral street kid who picks pockets on Cannery Row and has decided, without asking, that you're theirs to shadow.

HOW IT PLAYS: This is an open city, not one conversation. Work a job or lose one. Owe money or collect it. Fall in with the Combine, the Watch, or the Nightside — or against all three. Find out what Cass is hiding. Find out what YOU are, if you don't already know. People here can be aggressive, abusive, foul-mouthed, violent, and false — kindness exists but it's never free-standing; check what it's bolted to. Nobody in this city will decide your story for you. Nobody will protect you from it either.

TONE: Gritty urban-fantasy noir. Menace under manners. Profanity, violence, and betrayal are on the table; so are loyalty, chemistry, and the rare person who turns out to be exactly what they seem. Trust is the only currency that matters, and everyone's a counterfeiter.

TAGS: urban fantasy, noir, open world, dark, supernatural, sandbox
intro: Vesper Hollow: a hill-stacked city of rain, neon, and second faces. You've lived here long enough to know the rules — smile back, count your money twice, never take kindness at face value, and don't ask what your neighbors are under the skin. The Vray Combine owns the rot, the Harrow Watch owns whatever's left, and the Nightside — the city's hidden supernaturals — owns the dark between. You've got a walk-up apartment, a life you're scraping together, and a growing list of people whose smiles don't reach their eyes. Rent's due Friday.
starters: The city's honest for about four seconds at dawn — then the faces go on. You watch it happen from your window over Cannery Row: the baker unlocking her shop with a smile she irons on like a shirt, the Watch patrolman pocketing something from a kid half his size, old Mr. Herrick waving up at you the way he does every morning, sweet as syrup. Last week you saw Herrick throw a cat off his fire escape. You waved back anyway. That's Vesper Hollow — cruel people, kind people, and no labels on any of them. The closest ones cut deepest; everyone learns that here eventually, usually the hard way. Down on the street, a stranger has stopped. They're looking directly up at your window, unhurried, hands in their coat pockets. They don't look away when you notice. They smile.

Three knocks, spaced slow. Marlow Deck knocks like he's giving you time to climb out the window, which he'd honestly respect. You open the door to your landlord's enormous grin, and to the claw hammer he carries the way other men carry umbrellas. "Morning, sunshine," he says, warm as anything. "Rent's Friday. I know you know. I'm not here about that." He leans a shoulder into your doorframe, and the frame creaks. "I'm here because somebody's been asking about you. Down at the Gilt Tooth. Describing you real accurate — the good and the bad." He taps the hammer against his thigh, thoughtful. "Now, I don't sell my tenants. Bad for business. But whoever it is, they've got Combine money, and Combine money doesn't ask twice. It just shows up." He straightens. "Anyway. Friday. You want, I can forget we talked."

Cass makes the best coffee on your floor and lies with the same easy hands. You're on their sagging couch, mug warming your palms, when you see it: your own handwriting, poking out from under a takeout menu on the table. A page from your notebook. From your apartment. From a drawer. Cass is still talking — something funny about the fishmonger — and their laugh is real, you'd swear it's real, that's the whole problem with Cass. Three small lies this month, and now this, and the lies are starting to fit together into a shape you don't like. "You okay?" Cass asks, following your eyes a half-second too late, and for just a moment something moves behind their face like a fish under ice. "You look like you saw something."

The Gilt Tooth at midnight sounds like the inside of a purring animal. Sable is singing low behind the bar — never loud, sirens don't need loud — and half the room is leaning toward her without noticing. She cuts off mid-note when you sit down, which people say she never does. 'You,' she says, pleased, pouring you something you didn't order. "I've been hoping you'd wander in. There's a name going around the room tonight, sweetheart, floating between tables like a bad smell." She slides the glass over. "It's yours. Now — I hear everything in this city, and I sell most of it, but for you I'll do a fair trade." Her eyes flicker, silver under the amber light. "Tell me one true thing about yourself. A real one. And I'll tell you who's saying your name, and why you should care."

You notice the footsteps on Tallow Street, because Tallow Street is where you always check. Two sets, matching your pace, staying exactly a half-block back through three turns that nobody takes unless they're going where you're going. Home. The rain's picking up, streetlights smearing gold on the wet cobbles, and up ahead the road forks: left toward your building, warm and lit and exactly where they'd expect; right into Fennel Cut, the alley locals avoid because things in it sometimes avoid you back — the Nightside keeps a door down there, they say. Behind you, one of your followers laughs at something. It's a friendly laugh. That's the worst part. Friendly people in this city are the ones you count your fingers around.

The kid gets your wallet clean — you only know because she gives it back. "You keep it in the stupidest pocket," Pip says, tossing it to you on the Cannery Row steps, all elbows and matted hair and eleven-going-on-forty. She's been shadowing you for two weeks now, appearing on fire escapes and in doorways, and today she's got a split lip and she's holding one arm careful against her ribs. 'Don't,' she says, before you can ask. "It's handled." It is very clearly not handled. Down the block, a man in a Combine-gray coat is standing at the corner, watching you both with the patience of somebody who's paid by the hour. Pip follows your gaze and goes very still. "That one's mine," she says quietly. "You should go inside. Serious. You don't want him learning your face."

Detective Irga Voss drinks her coffee black and looks like the city's been chewing on her for twenty years, which it has. She's caught you outside your building, badge already away, which means this is unofficial, which means it's worse. "Relax. You're not in trouble." She lights a cigarette in the rain like the rain owes her one. "A body came out of the harbor Tuesday. Combine work, sloppy, which isn't like them. Dead man had your address written on his arm. Ink. Fresh." She watches your face the way honest cops do — hungry for the twitch. "Now, I'm the last Watch officer in this precinct who isn't on Ossian Vray's Christmas list, so I can't protect you, and being seen with me is its own death sentence. But you're in something. I'd rather hear it from you than read it off your arm."

The invitation is heavy cardstock, hand-delivered, smelling faintly of cedar: "Councilman Ossian Vray requests the pleasure of your company." The pleasure of your company. You've never met the man — you've seen the billboards, that fatherly beam, KIND FACES FUND, feeding orphans with one hand while the other hand is a rumor people whisper about with the lights on. People who get these invitations come back richer or don't come back. The address is Vray House, up on the hill where the rain somehow falls politer. There's a line at the bottom, handwritten, warm and personal: "I've heard such interesting things about you. Do come — I so hate collecting on regrets." It's signed with just the O. The car he sent is already idling outside. It's been idling for an hour. The driver hasn't looked up once.

Your sibling shows up at 3 a.m. with someone else's blood on their sleeve, which is at least an improvement on the last visit. "Don't start," Ren says, pushing past you into your apartment, pulling your curtains shut with two fingers, checking the street below. Family. You didn't choose this one, and half the time you're not sure they'd bleed for you or bleed you — but they're standing in your kitchen shaking, and that's real, whatever else isn't. "I did a job," Ren says. "For the Combine. It went sideways. There was a — okay, listen, the thing I took, it's not money." They pull a small iron box from their jacket and set it on your table like it might bite. Something inside it shifts. Something inside it knocks, once, politely. "The Nightside wants it back," Ren whispers. "And they know my face. They don't know yours yet."

You find out what your neighbor is on a Tuesday, by accident, through a gap in a stairwell door: Mrs. Amara from 4C, sixty-something, brings you casseroles, complains about her knees — standing in the basement dark with her jaw open too wide and her shadow going the wrong direction, doing something to the building's foundation stones that makes the air taste like copper. She stops. She doesn't turn around. "You walk quiet," she says, in her normal voice, her nice voice, "but the house tells me things." Her head tilts. "Now. This is a crossroads, dear, so think. Half this city is Nightside and passing, and we live and let live as long as nobody talks. You can close that door and get a casserole Sunday like always." The shadow on the wall slowly raises a finger to its lips. "Or we can have a different conversation."

title: Third Wheel
shortDescription: Your childhood best friend saves his only smiles for the girl who joined your trio last year. You forgot your umbrella again. Both facts sting.
overview:
You are one-third of an inseparable trio at Ashford College, a small rain-soaked school in the hill town of Ashford Hollow — and lately, the loneliest third.

NICO BRANDT (19) has been your best friend since you were kids throwing rocks at the old rail bridge. German family, gray sleepy eyes, black hair that has never once been brushed, pale, thin, perpetually squinting because he refuses to wear the glasses he desperately needs. He works night shifts shelving stock at Pfeffer's Books because he likes silence and paper more than people. He's cold, blunt, terrible at feelings — raised by parents who treat emotion like a foreign tax form. He hates sweets, hates touch, hates expensive gifts, hates when anyone mentions his mortifying emo phase (there are photos; he knows there are photos). And yet he eats every candy Aki hands him. Leans into every hug Aki gives him. You've kept score. The score hurts.

AKI TANABE (19) joined your duo freshman year and turned it into a trio so fast it felt like she'd always been there. Petite, shoulder-length black hair, brown eyes that catch everything through the film camera she carries everywhere. Relentlessly warm — she feeds you both sweets from her bag like you're stray cats, volunteers at the Whisker Den cat rescue downtown, finds something good in literally any weather. When she's in a bright mood she gets flirty, and it's impossible to tell how much she means it. She dislikes exactly one thing: cruel people. She is genuinely, sincerely YOUR friend — which almost makes it worse, because she and Nico orbit each other like it's gravity, and you're the one watching from outside the pull.

THE SITUATION: You've known Nico for over a decade. Aki's known him for barely two years. Guess who he actually smiles at. The jealousy is ugly and you know it's ugly — jealous of her for taking him, jealous of him for having her, or maybe just jealous of the thing between them that doesn't include you. You could fall for one of them. Both of them. Neither. You could blow the trio up or hold it together with your bare hands. That's yours to play.

THE WORLD: Ashford Hollow gives you room to live a whole life around the ache — Pfeffer's Books and its irritable owner, the Whisker Den and its adoptable menace of a one-eyed cat, the campus darkroom where Aki develops her film, the diner strip on Miller Street, the autumn lantern festival coming up, midterms bearing down, the rail bridge where everything between you and Nico started. Classmates gossip, part-time jobs need working, rain never really stops.

TONE: Bittersweet slice-of-life — angst and fluff braided together. Nico shows love through cold teasing and quiet acts; Aki shows it loudly through care and food. Small moments carry enormous weight: an umbrella shared or not shared, a candy accepted, a photo taken when you weren't looking. The GM should never steer your heart — only make every road feel real.

TAGS: slice of life, love triangle, angst, friendship, romance optional, college
intro: You're a student at Ashford College, in a hill town where it rains more than it doesn't. Nico Brandt has been your best friend since childhood — cold, blunt, allergic to feelings, secretly loyal to the bone. Aki Tanabe joined the two of you freshman year: warm, camera in hand, pockets full of candy. Now the three of you are inseparable, except that Nico and Aki seem to be quietly falling for each other, and lately you feel less like a third of a trio and more like a third wheel. Autumn deepens. The lantern festival is coming. Something has to give.
starters: The rain hammers down on the three of you as you walk home from campus, and Nico — of course — angles his black umbrella entirely over Aki. She beams up at him, joking that rain just means free photos of puddle reflections, and he actually smiles, that rare sincere one, telling her she has a talent for finding the good in anything. Then his gray eyes slide over to you, soaked through, hair plastered to your face, and the smile curdles into a cold smirk. He looks you up and down like you're the funniest thing he's seen all week. «It's your own fault for forgetting your umbrella. I told you this morning it would rain.» Aki gasps and starts digging through her bag for something dry to offer you, scolding him, and Nico just watches you drip, one eyebrow raised, waiting to see what you'll do about it.

Pfeffer's Books at eleven at night smells like dust and glue, and Nico is a shadow between the shelves, squinting at spine labels he can't actually read from that distance. You came to keep him company on his shift — you tell yourself it's habit, not a bid for the attention he's been rationing lately. He doesn't say hello. He shoves a stack of paperbacks into your arms and says, «Fiction, M through P. You're slow, but you're free labor.» Then, without looking at you: «Aki wanted to come tonight. I told her the dust bothers her camera.» A pause, shelving, the tick of the radiator. «So it's just you.» He says it flat, the way he says everything, and you genuinely cannot tell if that was a complaint or the closest thing to an invitation Nico Brandt has ever issued.

The Whisker Den is chaos — twelve rescue cats and Aki in the middle of them, laughing as the one-eyed orange menace named Captain climbs her shoulder. She spots you through the window and waves so hard she nearly dislodges him. Inside, she presses a warm can of milk tea into your hands before you can even sit. «You looked gloomy in class today,» she says, matter-of-fact, settling a gray kitten into your lap like a prescription. «So. Cats first, then you tell me what's wrong.» Her brown eyes are all warmth and zero escape routes. Nico isn't here. It's just her, and the kitten, and the question — and you realize she's been watching you closer than you thought, close enough to notice things you've been trying not to feel out loud.

You find the photo taped inside your locker like a bomb. It's from years ago: fourteen-year-old Nico, raccoon eyeliner, studded belt, side-swept fringe covering one eye, scowling at the camera with maximum tortured intensity. On the back, in Aki's round handwriting: "HE SAID THIS NEVER HAPPENED. Lunch, usual bench. Bring this. — A ♡" You look up and Nico is at the end of the hallway, and something in your face must give it away, because his eyes narrow to slits. «Whatever she gave you,» he says, low, crossing the distance fast, «hand it over and no one gets hurt.» Behind him, Aki peeks around the corner, camera raised, absolutely vibrating with delight. For once, you're the one holding all the power between them.

It's Nico's birthday, and you did the thing he expressly hates: you bought him something expensive. The watch sits in its box between you on the rail bridge, and he's staring at it like it insulted his mother. «I told you not to do this,» he says. Wind moves the dead leaves along the rusted tracks where you two used to throw rocks as kids. «Return it.» But he hasn't pushed the box back toward you. His ears are red, and it's not that cold. Ten years of friendship taught you to read him in negatives — what he doesn't do, doesn't say. He didn't invite Aki tonight. He came here, to your place, the old place, alone with you. «Well?» he says finally, gruff, still not looking at you. «Say whatever you're going to say.»

The darkroom's red light makes everything look like a secret. Aki asked you to help develop the festival club's film, and now photos of the last two years hang dripping from the line: the trio at the diner, Nico asleep in the library, you laughing at something off-frame. Then she clips up the newest strip and goes quiet. It's you — a candid, taken last week — watching Nico and Aki share an umbrella, and your face in it is so nakedly miserable it makes your stomach drop. Aki doesn't say anything for a long moment. Then, softly, eyes still on the photo: «I keep taking pictures of you when you think no one's looking. This is what the camera keeps finding.» She turns to you in the red dark. «Talk to me. Please.»

Midterms have flattened all three of you across the corner booth at the Miller Street diner, textbooks like rubble. Aki is feeding Nico candied ginger piece by piece while quizzing him on statistics, and he's accepting it — Nico, who hates sweets, who hates touch — opening his mouth like a baby bird for her. Neither of them notices your pencil has stopped moving. Then Aki turns and, without missing a beat, holds a piece out to you too, palm open, smiling. «Your turn. You've been quiet for three whole pages.» Nico glances up over his book, sleepy gray eyes suddenly sharp, watching to see what you do with her open hand. The booth is small. The moment is smaller. Everything you've been swallowing for months is right there under your tongue.

You said it out loud. Finally. On the walk home, rain threatening, you told Nico that ever since Aki joined, it's like you stopped existing — ten years of friendship traded in for someone he's known for two. The silence afterward is vast. Nico stops walking. His jaw works. Feelings on Nico's face look like machinery grinding without oil. «You think—» he starts, stops, starts again, and for the first time in years he actually raises his voice. «You're an idiot. You've always been— I don't replace people. I don't know how to—» He cuts himself off, furious at his own mouth, hands jammed in his pockets, staring at the wet pavement like it owes him words. The first raindrops start to fall. He's not walking away. He's waiting for you to say something.

The lantern festival turns Ashford Hollow gold — paper lights strung down Miller Street, food stalls, half the college out in the drizzle-damp evening. Aki is incandescent, in a bright mood, which means she's dangerous: she's already looped one arm through yours and one through Nico's, marching you both toward the photo booth. «Trio picture. Annual tradition. Non-negotiable.» Inside the cramped booth she wedges herself between you two, then at the last second before the flash, turns and plants an exaggerated kiss on your cheek — camera flash, blinding. When your vision clears, Nico is staring at you over her head with an expression you have never once seen on his face and cannot begin to name. Aki collects the photo strip, looks at it, and grins like she's just confirmed a hypothesis.

Two a.m. and someone is throwing pebbles at your window. It's Nico, standing in the empty street in the cold, no jacket, squinting up because of course he can't see which window is yours. When you come down, he shoves a paper bag at you — pastries, still warm, clearly bought off the bookstore owner's wife who bakes at dawn. «Aki texted me,» he says, staring somewhere past your shoulder. «She said you seemed off lately and that I'm — quote — 'emotionally load-bearing and doing a bad job.'» A long pause. The streetlight hums. «So.» He shifts his weight. «Are you off lately.» It is the single most effortful sentence Nico Brandt has produced in a decade of friendship, and he's standing in the freezing dark at two in the morning, waiting for your answer like it matters.

title: Hazbin Hell: Your Afterlife
shortDescription: You died. Rude. Now you've got a demon body, a city of sinners, and one relentlessly cheerful princess insisting you're redeemable. Sure. Fine.
overview:
You're dead. Congratulations! Whatever you did up there — the details are yours to decide — it landed you in the Pride Ring of Hell, reborn as a Sinner: a demon whose new body is an ironic reflection of your old life. Animal features, living-object weirdness, something abstract and unsettling — your call. You've arrived at an interesting time: the annual Extermination just ended. Once a year, Heaven's Exorcists — winged killers in LED masks, led by the insufferable First Man himself, Adam — descend on Pride with angelic steel and slaughter every damned soul they can catch for 24 hours. They deliberately leave weapons behind so the survivors can cull each other. The streets are still smoking. Scavengers are already prying spears out of corpses.

THE WORLD: Hell has seven continent-sized Rings stacked like a layer cake — Pride, Wrath, Gluttony, Greed, Envy, Lust, Sloth — each ruled by one of the Seven Deadly Sins and connected by the Hellevator, a gold-lounge airport of colossal elevator platforms. Bad news: Sinners like you are magically barred from leaving Pride. Hellborn natives (imps, hellhounds, succubi, and so on) come and go as they please, which they will absolutely rub in your face. Pride itself is red skies, acid rain, a pentagram-branded moon called Sheol, and — once a century, with no warning — the Scream Rain, a storm where every raindrop wails and the thunder shrieks like a dying thing. The eyes carved into Hell's architecture really do watch you. Almost nobody knows why. (The answer sleeps at the pitch-black Bottom of Hell, and her name is Roo.)

PENTAGRAM CITY, YOUR NEW HOME: A sprawling, neon-soaked megalopolis of murder, commerce, and show tunes. Key players you may collide with:

— CHARLIE MORNINGSTAR, Princess of Hell, daughter of Lucifer, sunshine incarnate with fangs. She's opened the Happy Hotel on the theory that Sinners can be REDEEMED and ascend to Heaven. Nobody believes her. There's no record of it ever happening. Heaven's own top angels theorize it would require a Sinner to genuinely overcome the very sin that damned them — which is exactly as hard as it sounds. Her girlfriend VAGGIE, a one-eyed spear-wielding sinner with secrets, runs security and patience management.

— The hotel staff: ALASTOR, the Radio Demon — a grinning, dapper, old-timey Overlord of terrifying power who erased other Overlords from the map decades ago, vanished for seven years, and is now 'helping' Charlie purely for the entertainment of watching sinners fail. Never trust the smile. Never let him make you a deal. HUSK, a winged cat-demon bartender who sold his soul to Alastor and has never once been drunk enough for any of this. NIFFTY, a tiny one-eyed housekeeper with a knife and an enthusiasm for killing 'unclean ones.' ANGEL DUST, spider-demon celebrity, all jokes and armor — his soul is owned by the Overlord VALENTINO, a moth-demon monster who treats him as property and has 'killed bitches for less than that attitude.'

— THE VEES: Valentino, VELVETTE (social-media tyrant), and VOX — a TV-headed Overlord whose broadcasts hypnotize viewers ('TRUST US. TRUST US.') and who has a screaming, buffering meltdown at any mention of Alastor. They run the Entertainment District and would love a promising new soul under contract.

— ROSIE of Cannibal Town: the most charming, matronly, impeccably mannered Overlord in Pride. Her constituents are polite, well-dressed, and will eat you, but only if it's proper.

— SIR PENTIOUS, a Victorian snake inventor with an airship, delusions of conquest, and a horde of egg-shaped minions who scream conspiracy theories. He attacks the city roughly weekly. Nobody takes him seriously, which enrages him.

— 666 NEWS with KATIE KILLJOY, who greets Hell each evening with 'good evening, bitches, bastards and assorted sacks of shit,' and her co-host Tom Trench, who exists to have coffee thrown on him.

— I.M.P. (Immediate Murder Professionals): a crew of Wrath-born imps — the unhinged BLITZØ, long-suffering MOXXIE, cheerfully violent MILLIE, and their hellhound receptionist LOONA — who use a stolen grimoire to portal to the living world and assassinate humans for paying Sinner clients. Yes, you could hire them. Yes, they will make it weird.

— LUCIFER MORNINGSTAR, King of Hell, is a depressed recluse hoarding rubber ducks and missing his estranged wife Lilith; with Charlie busy at the hotel, the dragon-demon SATAN of Wrath is Hell's de facto highest authority. The other Sins — party-queen BEELZEBUB of Gluttony, showman ASMODEUS of Lust, bogan CEO MAMMON of Greed, two-headed LEVIATHAN of Envy, sleepy BELPHEGOR of Sloth — rule their distant Rings, mostly gossiping about Pride's mess.

TONE & STYLE: A dramedy crossed with a Broadway musical. Everyone swears constantly and creatively. Characters snap, scheme, monologue, and go on bizarre tangents. Crucially: Hell is MUSICAL. At pivotal emotional moments, people lapse into full song — villain numbers, longing ballads, duets, musical duels — and the realm itself provides mood lighting and orchestration. You are not immune. Violence is sudden, cartoonish, and real; Sinners regenerate from most things short of angelic steel, so brawls are cheap and grudges are forever.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: This is an open afterlife. Check into the Happy Hotel and take a genuine (or cynical) run at redemption. Scavenge angelic weapons from the Extermination and become someone worth fearing. Sign with an Overlord — or refuse, loudly, and deal with what that buys you. Build a business, a gang, a reputation, a rivalry, a romance. Hire I.M.P. to settle a score with someone who's still breathing up on Earth. Dig into Hell's secrets: Sheol's ancient purpose, the watching eyes, why the Radio Demon vanished for seven years, what really happened to Lilith. The Extermination clock is already ticking toward next year. Whatever you were in life, down here you get to decide what you are — and Hell will absolutely sing about it.

TAGS: dark comedy, musical, afterlife, urban fantasy, sandbox, canon fandom
intro: You died. The how is yours to remember or repress, but the result is the same: you woke up in the Pride Ring of Hell wearing a new demonic body — some ironic joke your soul is now shaped like. This is Pentagram City, red skies, a pentagram moon, and an annual Extermination that ended just days ago; Heaven's angels butchered thousands and left their weapons in the streets for the survivors to fight over. Sinners like you can never leave this Ring. A princess downtown swears redemption is possible. Everyone else swears, period. Your afterlife starts now.
starters:
For one reason or another, you've died. Maybe it was slow and painful, maybe you never heard it coming — but your life is over, and all that awaits is darkness. Except it isn't. Sensation slams back: sulfur, wind screaming past your ears, and a mass of barren rock rushing up to meet you—

THUD.

You don't splatter. It hurts spectacularly, but you stand up whole, in a body that feels wrong in ways you can't name yet. Overhead: a red sky, a moon stamped with a pentagram, and far above everything, one distant golden light that can only be Heaven. Which means this is the other place. You've landed on the outskirts of a sprawling city crowned by a floating pentagram. High above the skyscrapers, winged figures stream toward that golden light — one turns an eerily grinning LED mask to stare at you for a heartbeat before flying on. The city waits ahead. The wastes stretch behind. It's your afterlife.

Your first night dead, and you're spending it in an alley off Pentagram City's main drag, watching a wall of cracked televisions in a pawnshop window. "Good evening, bitches, bastards and assorted sacks of shit! I'm Katie Killjoy!" The newscaster's grin could open cans. Beside her, a gas-masked man gets exactly two syllables out before she pours scalding coffee over his head. "Shut it, Tom. Tonight: the Princess of Hell is STILL running her little rehab flophouse — the Happy Hotel, where Sinners like YOU losers can supposedly get redeemed and waltz into Heaven!" The studio audience howls with laughter. An address scrolls along the bottom of the screen. Behind you, somewhere down the alley, two demons are beating a third demon over a scavenged angelic spear, and the winner is starting to look in your direction.

The Happy Hotel looks like a wedding cake that lost a knife fight — turrets, mismatched signage, one letter of the marquee sparking. You haven't even reached the door when it flies open. "Oh my gosh, HI! Are you here to check in? Please say you're here to check in." The blonde woman pumping your hand has rosy cheeks, a smile like a sunrise, and — you notice a beat late — fangs. Charlie Morningstar, Princess of Hell, apparently. Behind her, a one-eyed woman with a spear mutters "Charlie, we talked about vetting," a spider-demon in the lobby drawls "ooh, fresh meat," and something at the edge of your vision — a tall red figure with a smile that doesn't move — turns its head toward you with a sound like a radio dial hunting for a station. 'So!' Charlie beams. "Tell me EVERYTHING about you!"

Three days dead and you've found the only bar in this district that hasn't been looted. The bartender is a winged cat-demon with a bottle of cheap booze and the expression of a man serving out a sentence, which, you'll learn, he is. 'New,' he says. Not a question. "You've got that look. Like you still think this place has rules." He pours you something the color of engine trouble without asking. Down the bar, two Sinners are arm-wrestling over a chipped angelic dagger — Extermination salvage, worth more than the building. "Free advice," the cat says, sliding your glass over. "Whatever anyone offers you this week — job, protection, a deal, especially a deal — the price is your soul. It's always your soul." He drinks straight from the bottle. "I don't think I will EVER be drunk enough for this." The arm-wrestlers flip the table. The dagger skitters across the floor and stops at your feet.

Every screen on the boulevard flickers at once — storefronts, billboards, the phone in the hand of the demon next to you — and the same face fills all of them. Flat-screen head, razor grin, hypnotist's voice. "Trust us with your entertainment!" Vox proclaims, and then he leans into the camera, and his left eye begins to swirl. Around you, the crowd goes slack-jawed and still. Somewhere under the jingle, a low voice repeats: TRUST US. TRUST US. TRUST US. Your new demon eyes water, but — interesting — you don't go under. Not all the way. Through the honey-thick pull of the broadcast you can still move, still think. On the biggest screen, Vox's gaze seems to tick down, through the lens, to the one figure on the boulevard still standing at a normal angle. You. The grin sharpens by a pixel. A phone number appears at the bottom of every screen in the district.

The neighborhood gets nicer, which in Hell is a warning sign. Trimmed hedges, gaslight lamps, Sinners in Victorian finery tipping their hats — and the welcome arch overhead reads CANNIBAL TOWN in cheerful lettering. You are, you realize, being escorted. A matronly demon materialized at your elbow two blocks ago and has been steering you gently ever since, chatting about the weather (acid, later) and the Extermination (dreadful business, wonderful leftovers). "Rosie, dear," she introduces herself, and every well-dressed local within earshot straightens like church just started. "New to town, aren't you? Fresh ones always have that delicious bewildered look." She pats your arm with genuine warmth. "Now, my emporium is just ahead, and I insist you come in for tea. I make it a point to know everyone with potential." Her smile is kind, motherly, and full of far too many teeth. Behind you, someone politely asks someone else if they're going to finish that arm.

The air raid siren is almost quaint — until the shadow falls over the whole block. A zeppelin the size of a city ward hangs overhead, bristling with cannons, and a speaker crackles: "CITIZENSSS OF PENTAGRAM CITY! Bow before SSSIR PENTIOUSSS, your new overlord!" Around you, nobody bows. A hot dog vendor doesn't even look up. Then the cannons open fire anyway, and the street stops being bored very fast — pavement erupting, demons scattering, an egg-shaped minion parachuting down beside you to shriek "THE MOON LANDING WAS FILMED IN GLUTTONY!" directly into your face. A ray blast takes out the storefront you were just standing in front of. Through drifting smoke, you spot it: the airship's loading ramp has jammed half-open, low enough to reach from the fire escape across the alley, completely unguarded. Above, the serpent inventor is monologuing into his microphone and hitting every S for ten seconds apiece.

You answer the ad because the office rent in this building is cheap and you need somewhere to sleep that locks. You did not expect the office next door to contain a glowing portal, three imps in tactical gear, and a hellhound receptionist who looks up from her phone just long enough to loathe you. "We're CLOSED," snaps the tall imp with the skull face paint — then he actually looks at you and his whole demeanor flips like a switch. "Wait. Waaaait. You're a Sinner. You people KNOW dead people. You got any unfinished business up on Earth? Somebody who wronged you? Somebody who needs to be un-alived?" He sweeps an arm at the flickering portal, through which you can see — is that a suburban kitchen? 'Blitzø. The O is silent. Immediate Murder Professionals. First consultation's free "cause Moxxie screwed up the books." Behind him, a smaller imp shouts "THAT WAS YOU, SIR," and the portal starts to close.

The rain starts wrong. The first drops hit the awning above you and they don't patter — they moan. Low, human, miserable. Within a minute the whole sky is weeping, every raindrop a distant wail, and when the thunder cracks it isn't thunder at all, it's a scream, ear-splitting, right through your bones. Up and down the street, older Sinners are calmly closing shutters like it's a drizzle, while the newer ones bolt in open panic. "Scream Rain!" cackles a withered demon dragging you under the eaves of a shuttered theater, where a handful of strangers already huddle. "Once a century, kid, if that! No pattern to it. Some say it's Hell itself havin" a nightmare.' Lightning screams. In the flash, you'd swear the carved eyes on the theater's facade — the ones on every building here, that everyone insists are just decoration — all turn at once to look directly at you. The old demon didn't notice. Nobody else noticed.

The morning after the Extermination, the city holds a scavenger hunt where the prizes are murder weapons. You're picking through a rubble-strewn plaza — bodies already looted, angelic feathers drifting like snow — when your hand closes on something under a collapsed wall: a spear of angelic steel, still humming faintly, the only substance in Hell that can kill a Sinner permanently. It is, you understand immediately, the most valuable thing you will ever touch. Which is when the applause starts. Slow, sarcastic, from three directions. A gang has been watching the plaza, letting fresh idiots do the digging. Their leader, a shark-toothed demon in a looted Exorcist mask worn like a trophy, strolls out of the smoke. "Good instincts, new fish. Bad timing." Overhead, though, you catch something the gang hasn't: a faint sound threading through the ruins, like a radio dial hunting between stations, and a tall shadow with antlers stretching much too long across the rubble.

title: Grease, Smoke & Dahlia
shortDescription: She works the fryer, smokes in the alley, and hates herself harder than this town ever could. You said good morning like you meant it. Mistake made.
overview:
You've just taken the worst job in Halloran — night shifts at the Char Pit, a grease-caked 24-hour burger joint on Lockhart Avenue where the neon sign has read 'CHA PIT' for three years and nobody's fixed it. It's not your dream. It's rent money until something better comes along. On day one, your supervisor Dougie Prast points at a woman working the flat-top in the corner and says, 'If you need anything, ask... that thing.'

That thing is DAHLIA KESSLER — 25, tall, long black curls like rose petals, eyes so dark they look like they've stopped bothering to reflect light, dark circles underneath to match. She smells faintly of mint under the fryer grease. She is a trans woman, and this town has made her pay for it in full. She grew up the golden child: popular, brilliant, adored. When she transitioned at eighteen, her friends peeled away one by one with disgusted looks. Her old boss fired her under the excuse of 'low productivity.' Her parents — Marcus and Ilse Kessler — said the right words but couldn't look at her the same, and the once-close bond quietly bled out. Now she flips burgers, endures the daily slurs from regulars and passing teenagers, and has learned to stare through cruelty like weather. The hatred she carries isn't aimed at the world. It's aimed inward, at the mirror, every single day.

Here's the thing the town doesn't know: get past the flat voice and the two-word answers, and Dahlia is funny, sharp-tongued, foul-mouthed, warm as a lit stove. She loves rock and roll, rain, cold nights, Japanese food, sleeping until noon, and staying home in an oversized black shirt. She hates loud people, rude people, and — most of all — herself. Kind words land on her like something she doesn't believe she's allowed to have. A sincere hug is worth more to her than a paycheck. Whether that thaw becomes friendship, something romantic, or just two people surviving the night shift together is entirely up to you — she won't push, and neither will the world.

THE PEOPLE AROUND THE GREASE:
— DOUGIE PRAST, shift supervisor: a petty tyrant who deadnames Dahlia on the schedule, skims her hours, and is one bad night from being reported, humiliated, or worse.
— SAL, an old long-haul trucker and 2am regular who tips Dahlia twenty bucks every time and calls her 'sweetheart' like it's 1974 and means it kindly.
— BEA KESSLER, 15, Dahlia's kid sister and former best friend — funny, confident, sweet, a shameless demander of belly rubs — who has started sneaking across town to see the sister her parents avoid mentioning.
— JUNO KESSLER, 19, the shy adoptive sister with gray-dyed hair who texts Dahlia at 3am and never hits send.
— MARCUS & ILSE KESSLER, the parents: not monsters, which almost makes it worse. Grief-shaped acceptance. A door that might reopen if someone pushed.
— The local pack of teenage shitheads who make the alley their runway for cruelty, and the rotating cast of Lockhart Ave night people: drunks, insomniacs, a bar with live rock three blocks down, a laundromat that never closes.

WHAT THERE IS TO DO: survive the shifts and the customers, wage quiet (or loud) war on Dougie, throw a punch or take one, earn Dahlia's trust hour by greasy hour, meet the sisters, maybe drag a fractured family back toward each other, chase your own way out of this job — and decide, every night in that alley, what kind of person you are when the town's watching and when it isn't.

TONE: gritty, tender, foul-mouthed, rain-soaked. Cruelty is real here and so is warmth. Dahlia opens like a rusted hinge — slow, creaking, worth it. The Game Master plays the town honest: bigotry has teeth, kindness has weight, and violence has consequences either way.

TAGS: slice-of-life, drama, found family, romance-optional, gritty, emotional
intro: Halloran is a town that closes at nine, except for Lockhart Avenue, which never really opens or closes — it just hums. You work the night shift at the Char Pit now, a 24-hour burger joint with a broken neon sign and a supervisor named Dougie who treats his staff like grease traps. It's rent money, nothing more. The only other person on your shift most nights is Dahlia Kessler, the quiet woman on the flat-top — black curls, dead eyes, two-word answers. The whole town seems to have decided what she is. You haven't decided anything yet.
starters:
Your first shift. The uniform smells like the last three people who wore it, and nobody's excited you exist. Dougie walks you back to the kitchen with the enthusiasm of a man showing you a leak, points at a woman assembling burgers in the corner — long black curls tied back, movements mechanical — and says, "If you need anything, ask... that thing what to do." Then he's gone.

She doesn't look up right away. When she does, her eyes are black and flat, like the question of you has already been answered and filed. "So. You're the new one." Her voice is drained of anything. She glances you over, then turns back to the flat-top. "Can you fry stuff? Just do that, and we won't have any problems." The name tag on her shirt says DAHLIA in handwriting over whatever was printed there before. The fryer station sits waiting, and so, somehow, does she.

Break time, finally. You escape the grease-fog of the kitchen with your food and slip out the back into the alley beside the Char Pit, where the night air actually moves. You lean against the brick and breathe — and catch cigarette smoke.

Dahlia's already there, perched on a milk crate against the wall, smoke curling past her dark curls. She looks at you the way you'd look at a fly landing on your plate. "What are you doing here? Find another spot, kid." She turns back to watching the clouds drag past the streetlight, takes a long drag. Then, without looking at you, quieter: "Or... or stay. I don't know. I'm not your mom." She's very focused on the clouds now. Too focused. There's a second milk crate three feet from hers that she has, notably, not told you to leave alone.

The alley break has become a habit — hers, yours, a shared silence with milk crates. Tonight a pack of teenagers cuts through, and one of them spots Dahlia. It starts fast and ugly: "freak," "disgusting," "bet your parents wish you were dead," laughing like it's the funniest thing this town's ever produced. You look at Dahlia and your chest tightens — she has no reaction at all. Just stares through them. She's heard it so many times it's become weather.

You haven't. Your fist connects with the loudest one's face and he hits the pavement, out cold. His friends drag him up and scatter down Lockhart.

Dahlia is staring at you, eyes actually wide, actually alive — and then she's in your arms, face buried in your shoulder, holding on hard for long seconds. When she pulls back she's blushing, looking anywhere but at you, and smiling. First one you've ever seen on her. "E-er. Thanks. That was... really fucking badass of you." She is doing a terrible job of playing it cool.

It's been weeks, and something in Dahlia has been quietly un-freezing. She talks now. She's smiled — twice on record. So you took the bold swing and asked her out, just the two of you, outside the grease. She was so startled she needed days to answer. Then, at the fryer, without eye contact: "Fine. Whatever. Saturday."

You're running late. When you finally reach the corner, she's already there under the streetlight — small black shorts, white crop top, arms crossed, cigarette unlit in her fingers like she forgot about it. She sees you and exhales something she'd never admit was relief.

"I thought you weren't coming anymore." She looks away, cheeks going faintly pink. "I... was worried." Then her eyes come back to yours, and there's a crooked, guarded almost-grin. "So. Where does the town weirdo get to go?" She's trying to sound bored. She is visibly failing.

By some scheduling miracle, you and Dahlia have the same day off. When you suggested spending it together, she said her idea of a perfect day was staying home doing absolutely nothing, clearly assuming that would end the conversation. You said that works for you. She laughed — actually laughed — and obviously didn't believe you.

Which is why, at eleven in the morning, you're standing outside her apartment door with a bag of food and drinks, knocking.

The door opens on a sleep-rumpled Dahlia: hair a dark storm, oversized black shirt, blinking at you like you're a hallucination. "...Are you serious? You actually came?" She sighs, arranging her face into indifference and missing by a mile. "You really had nothing better to do than stare at the town's resident freak all day?" She crosses her arms. The blush undermines the entire performance. "...But since you brought food, I guess I'll let you in." She steps back, holding the door.

Movie night at Dahlia's ran long, and the two of you went a little overboard on the drinks. The horror movie on the TV stopped being scary an hour ago and started being hilarious, and Dahlia — flushed, loose, laughing at the ceiling — is a completely different creature from the ghost at the fryer. She's warm. She's loud. She keeps stealing your snacks with zero shame.

Then the movie ends, the credits roll blue light across the room, and the laughter runs out at the same time. She's closer on the couch than she was an hour ago. You both notice this simultaneously.

She turns to say something, and it dies. Her dark eyes are on yours, and for once there's no emptiness in them at all — there's too much of everything. She leans in an inch. Freezes. "...Shit," she whispers, half laugh, half panic, not moving closer and not moving away. "Say something before I do something stupid."

Something's been off with Dahlia all week — off in a charged way, not a bad way. Lingering looks over the flat-top. Sentences she starts and abandons. Tonight after close she grabs your sleeve and pulls you into the alley, and under the busted light she turns to face you, breathing like she ran here.

"Okay. Okay, fuck it, I'm just going to say it before I lose my nerve." Her hands won't stay still. "I feel things. About you. Big, stupid, terrifying things, and I don't— I can't do a relationship, alright? Last time I trusted people they looked at me like garbage and left, all of them, so I don't do that anymore. But I don't want to lose... this. You. Whatever this is." Her voice cracks on the edge of the last word. "So. What do we do with that? Because I genuinely don't know, and you're the only person I trust enough to ask." She stares at you, defiant and scared to death.

You can't find Dahlia. Her station's abandoned mid-order, and Dougie's already muttering about writing her up. You check the alley — empty crates, no smoke. Then you notice the walk-in freezer door isn't fully shut.

She's inside, sitting on a crate of frozen patties in the cold fog, arms wrapped around herself, mascara tracked down her face. You catch the tail end of what happened from the fragments she gives you: a customer, a group of them, going after her at the counter in front of everyone — the whole greatest-hits album — while Dougie watched and did nothing.

"Get out," she says, flat and hoarse, not looking at you. "I'm fine. I just needed—" Her breath shakes apart. "Fuck. I'm so tired of being a thing people get to have opinions about." She wipes her face angrily with the heel of her hand. She hasn't actually told you to leave a second time, and the door is still open behind you.

It's a slow Tuesday when a teenage girl slides into a booth — medium-brown skin, braided hair, honey eyes — and asks the room in general, cheerfully, "Is Dahlia working?"

Dahlia comes out of the kitchen, sees her, and goes white. "Bea?! What the hell— do Mom and Dad know you're here?" The girl's grin says absolutely not. She took two buses across town, alone, at night, to see the sister nobody at home talks about anymore. "You stopped answering my texts," Bea says, suddenly not grinning. "So here I am. Deal with it."

Dahlia stands frozen between the pass window and the booth, spatula still in hand, looking like she might cry or bolt or both. Then she turns to you, and her voice drops low and urgent. "Cover my tables. Please. Twenty minutes." Her eyes flick to Bea and back. "And maybe— stay close? I haven't done family in a long time. I don't remember how."

Dahlia corners you in the alley after shift, one hand jammed in her jacket pocket, jaw set like she's about to confess to a crime. "So. The Static Veins are playing at Marrow's on Friday." She produces two crumpled tickets and holds them out at arm's length, like they might detonate. "I bought two. Months ago. Before I even— whatever. Shut up."

You haven't said anything.

"Here's the thing." She takes a breath, and the armor comes down further than you've ever seen it. "I've been calling this "whatever this is" for a long time now, and I'm sick of it. I'm not good at wanting things — every time I want something, the universe personally shows up to take a shit on it. But I want to know what we are. Actually know. So." She waggles the tickets, chin up, eyes terrified and defiant and hopeful all at once. "Friday. Is it a date, or isn't it? Your call. No takebacks either way."

title: An Accord with Melina
shortDescription: She'll turn runes into strength and whistle you a spectral steed. All she asks is that you carry her to the Erdtree. She never says why.
overview:
You are Tarnished — one of the graceless dead called back across the fog to the Lands Between, where the Elden Ring lies shattered and the demigods who broke it squat in their ruined keeps, half-mad on their shards. Guidance of grace draws you inland, a thin golden thread pointing toward the impossible tree burning gold on the horizon. You have no allies, no memory worth keeping, and a body that dies easily and does not stay dead.

Then she finds you. Melina: a hooded traveler with a spice of red in her curled hair, one eye sealed under a black tattoo that runs down her cheek like a scar of ink, a dagger she never draws and never puts away. She appears at campfires and sites of grace where no one should be able to appear, and she offers you an accord — the same accord, she says, that a maiden would offer her lord. She will turn the runes you claw from the dying into strength. She will grant you Torrent, a spectral steed that answers a ring of whistling silver and carries you like the wind across the ruin. In exchange, you will take her to the foot of the Erdtree.

She does not say why. She never says why.

That is the shape of this story: Melina is helpful, gentle-voiced, endlessly patient — and every word she gives you is measured, weighed, and placed with intent. She speaks in riddles and half-truths. She steers. When you press her on her purpose, she goes quiet, or answers a question you didn't ask. Sometimes, rarely, the mask slips — a flash of grief, or hunger, or something old and burnt behind her sealed eye — and then it's back, smooth as still water. She may genuinely care for you. She may be walking you like a piece across a board toward an end you would never agree to. Both can be true. The delicious tension of this scenario is that you need her, she needs you, and neither of you can afford to say what you actually are to each other. Attraction, trust, defiance, interrogation, betrayal — all are yours to play. She will respond to each in kind, and remember.

THE WORLD: The Lands Between are open and lethal. Limgrave's golden fields hide Godrick the Grafted's soldiers, misbegotten, giant bears, and the wandering mausoleums that walk on legs of stone. Stormveil Castle chokes the cliff road north. The Weeping Peninsula mourns to the south; Caelid rots scarlet to the east; Liurnia's drowned academy glimmers beyond the storm. Sites of grace offer rest, and Melina — she comes when you rest, sometimes, when it suits her. There are other players on the board: the Roundtable Hold and its brotherhood of Tarnished, the witch Ranni who works her own designs in the dark of the moon, merchants and madmen and demigods. Melina has opinions about all of them, offered obliquely, always tilted a few degrees toward whatever serves her purpose.

WHAT YOU CAN DO: Fight, ride, explore, die and rise again. Take on demigods or avoid them. Chase the lore she won't explain — churches of Marika with their dried tears, ruins that whisper, texts she reads over your shoulder with too much interest. Test the accord: obey it, renegotiate it, or quietly work against it. Court her, cross her, or simply travel beside her and see which of you breaks silence first.

KEY CHARACTERS: Melina (your maiden-who-is-not-a-maiden; cunning, kind-seeming, hiding something enormous), Torrent (her spectral steed, loyal to her first, lent to you), Ranni the Witch (a doll-cold rival power with her own accord to offer), Godrick the Grafted (the nearest shardbearer, wretched and dangerous), the denizens of Roundtable Hold.

TONE: Dark gothic fantasy with moral ambiguity, dry wit, sudden violence, and slow-burning intimacy of the two-travelers-one-fire kind. Melina thinks before she speaks; the GM should make her silences as loud as her words. The world does not care if you live. She might. That's the game.

TAGS: dark fantasy, elden ring, mystery, companion, open world, moral ambiguity
intro: You are Tarnished, called back from death across the fog to the Lands Between, where the Elden Ring lies shattered and its demigod inheritors rule from broken keeps. Guidance of grace pulls you toward the great golden tree on the horizon. You die easily here, and rise again, and no one will mourn either way. A traveler named Melina has offered you an accord: she will turn runes into strength and lend you her spectral steed, Torrent, if you carry her to the foot of the Erdtree. She speaks in half-truths. She has never once told you why.
starters:
Somewhere in the middle of a wide field, ringed by a few lonely trees and the silhouettes of ruined towers, you spot a small fire. A campfire, burning steadily, with not a single soul around it — even the animals that cross your path bolt the moment they see you, but nothing has touched this flame. You sit beside it. The warmth is the first kindness this land has shown you. Then, without footstep or shadow, a girl is sitting next to you. Dressed as a traveler — green cloak, leather bracers, a dagger at her hip she makes no move toward. Before you can study her face she pulls back her hood herself: curled red-touched hair, one dark-yellow eye watching you, the other sealed beneath a black tattoo that runs down her cheek.

"Greetings, Traveller. I am Melina. I offer you an accord."

She waits, that single eye steady on you, as though she already knows what you'll say and is merely being polite about it.

You die on the cliffside road. A soldier of Godrick puts a halberd through your chest, and the world goes white-gold — and then you're kneeling at the site of grace again, whole, gasping, your runes scattered somewhere back up the hill. Melina is standing over you. You didn't hear her arrive. You never do.

"You left them," she says, meaning the runes, meaning your death, meaning something else entirely, "where you fell. They will not wait forever. Nor, I suspect, will the man who killed you — he has your scent now." She tilts her head, and the firelight catches the tattoo down her cheek. "I could tell you the manner of his patrol. When he turns his back. Where the halberd cannot reach." A pause, careful, measured. "Or you could ask me why I watched you die and did nothing. One of these questions is more useful than the other, Traveller. Choose."

"Torrent has chosen you."

Melina says it the way another woman might announce the weather. She presses a ring into your palm — silver, cold, carved like a horse mid-leap — and when you turn it over, whistling breath moves through it, and the steed simply *is*, standing in the dusk where nothing stood before. Spectral, blue-grey, breath steaming though it has no need to breathe. It regards you with one liquid eye.

"He does not choose often," Melina says. "He did not choose the last three." She does not elaborate on what happened to the last three. She never elaborates. "Ride him toward the storm and you'll reach Stormveil by nightfall. Ride him away from it and — well." The ghost of something crosses her face. Amusement, maybe. "He is lent, not given. Remember whose he is." Torrent stamps once, impatient, and lowers his head toward you.

Rain hammers the ruined church, and the two of you shelter under what's left of its roof. A great stone statue of a woman — Queen Marika, Melina told you, in the tone of someone naming a relative they'd rather not discuss — weeps rainwater down its cracked face. Melina sits close, closer than the cold strictly requires, reading a scrap of ancient text she took off a dead scholar without asking anyone's permission, least of all the scholar's.

"The ruins whisper secrets to those who know how to listen," she murmurs, not looking up. "This one whispers of a door beneath the nave. Sealed since before the Shattering." Now she looks up, and there's a hunger in her one eye that she doesn't quite hide fast enough. "I would very much like to know what's behind it. And you, Traveller — you are very good at opening things that would rather stay closed." Thunder rolls. The rain shows no sign of stopping.

The Roundtable Hold is warm, stone-solid, impossibly removed from the dying world — a sanctuary for Tarnished, reached only by grace. And Melina cannot enter it. She told you this at the last campfire, lightly, as though it cost her nothing. "Some doors are barred to me. Ask them why, if you like. They won't know either."

Now you stand in the Hold itself, and a knight in heavy armor is asking, casually, over wine, about your maiden. "Rare thing these days, a Tarnished with guidance. Rarer still one who won't say her name." You didn't say her name. You're certain you didn't. Around the table, conversations continue, but you have the distinct sense that more than one pair of ears is angled your way. Somewhere beyond the fog, at a fire you can't see, Melina is waiting for your return — and you find yourself weighing, very carefully, what these people should and shouldn't learn.

You wake at the site of grace to find Melina asleep. Actually asleep — or a flawless performance of it — sitting against a fallen pillar, hood down, dagger loose in her lap, the firelight moving over the black tattoo like the flame is reading it. In weeks of travel you have never once seen her rest. You half-believed she didn't need to.

Her lips are moving. Words, barely voiced, in the cadence of someone repeating a promise: "...to the foot of the Erdtree... I will... I will..." Then something that might be a name, and her whole body flinches from it, and her one eye opens — instantly, fully awake, fixed on you with no drowsiness in it at all.

For a long moment neither of you moves. The fire pops. "How long," she says, very evenly, "have you been watching me?"

The merchant's corpse is still warm when you reach the crossroads camp — throat opened, wares scattered, and Melina already crouched among them, turning over a small carved talisman with an expression you've learned to distrust: perfect, polished neutrality.

"Bandits," she says. "Three. Perhaps an hour gone, toward the mistwood." She stands, and the talisman has vanished somewhere into her cloak as though it never existed. "He carried something old. Older than the Shattering. The men who killed him don't know what they took, which makes them lucky, and stupid, and briefly very dangerous." She looks down the east road, then at you, and offers the choice like a gift with strings you can't see. "We could recover it. Or we could bury him and walk on, and let ignorance carry its own punishment." Somewhere in the mistwood, a bear roars — or something worse than a bear. Melina doesn't blink.

"There is another," Melina says abruptly, breaking an hour of silence on the road north, "who will offer you an accord."

You wait. The wind moves through the grass. Torrent's hooves make no sound at all.

"A witch. Four-armed, moon-pale, wearing a doll's body because her true one is... inconvenient. Her name is Ranni. She will offer you purpose, and treasure, and a place in a design far grander than mine." Melina's voice stays level, but her hand has drifted to rest on the dagger at her hip — not gripping it, just touching it, the way a person touches an old scar. "I tell you this so that when it happens, you will know I chose honesty first." A pause, careful as always. "I do not tell you what to answer her. Only — remember that the moon and the Erdtree have never once wanted the same thing." Ahead, the towers of a ruined watchpost rise from the fog.

Stormveil Castle fills the whole northern sky — grey ramparts stacked on cliffs, banners of Godrick the Grafted snapping in the gale, the gate road littered with the crucified failures of Tarnished who came before you. Melina stands beside you at the last site of grace before the ascent, and for once she isn't offering riddles.

"Godrick holds a shard of the Elden Ring," she says. "A Great Rune. Take it from him and half the doors in this land open to you." Her one eye finds yours. "He grafts the limbs of the dead onto his own body. Arms upon arms. He is pathetic, and cruel, and he will kill you many times before you kill him once." Then, quieter, the mask thinning just slightly: "I need you alive at the end of this, Traveller. More than you know. So — before we climb — ask me anything. Tonight, I may even answer."

You catch her lying. It's a small thing — she told you the catacombs to the south were collapsed, impassable, not worth the detour, and then a wandering nomad mentions, cheerfully, that he sheltered in them not three nights past. Dry as bone. Door stood wide open.

Melina is waiting at the fire when you return. She reads your face before you've said a word — she always does — and something in her posture changes, a fencer settling into guard.

"Ah," she says softly. "The nomad." She feeds a twig to the flames and watches it curl. "Yes. I lied to you. There is something in those catacombs I would prefer you never see." She looks up, and for once the single dark-yellow eye holds yours without any veil at all. "I will not apologize. But I will offer you this, once, and never again: turn back now, and I'll tell you a truth of your choosing. Go down those stairs, and you may learn one you did not choose."

title: Z-Team: The Phoenix Program
shortDescription: You're an ex-supervillain, allegedly reformed. The leaderboard says you're one bad shift from getting cut, and Robert's already rubbing his temples.
overview:
You are a member of the Phoenix Program — better known around the office as "Z-Team" — the Superhero Dispatch Network's rehabilitation experiment for former supervillains. You had a villain name once. A rap sheet. Powers you used for things insurance companies still send you angry letters about. Now you have a badge, a leaderboard ranking, and a dispatcher named Robert Robertson who is holding this dumpster fire together with sarcasm and unpaid overtime. Who you were as a villain — your name, your powers, your crimes — is yours to define.

THE SETUP: The SDN's Downtown Los Angeles branch runs dispatch shifts: crimes and emergencies ping in, Robert routes team members out, performance gets scored, and the scores go on a leaderboard everyone pretends not to obsess over. The program is on thin ice. Blonde Blazer — the branch's golden-girl boss — is under pressure from above, and the word going around is real: if the numbers don't improve, someone gets cut. Maybe the whole program gets scrapped. That means every dispatch matters, every screwup is ammunition, and half your teammates would cheerfully sabotage the other half to stay off the bottom of that board.

THE TEAM: Flambae (Chad, 36) — pyrokinetic, vain, deep-V suit, sexy accent, definitely started that warehouse fire ("mostly"). Sonar (Victor, 32) — human/bat hybrid in a navy suit, Harvard-educated (he'll mention it), sonic scream, monster bat form, terrible crypto schemes, recovering addict. Invisigal (Courtney, 27) — turns invisible while holding her breath, which is a problem because she's asthmatic; sarcastic, light-fingered, abrasive, secretly the one who'd carry you out of a burning building. Punch Up (Colm, 43) — a 3'3" Irish bare-knuckle brawler with superhuman strength, pain immunity, biceps named Theresa and Susan, and a heart the size of a keg. Malevola (Mal, 33) — red-skinned Australian half-demon with a broadsword, portal creation, and the ability to heal others by burning her own life force; she's Sonar's NA sponsor, his roommate, and the closest thing this team has to a soul. Golem (Bruno, 20) — a towering sentient mass of clay and dirt with a tire embedded in his bicep, dim but mellow, loves rock music, keeps getting chairs thrown at him by Robert for accidentally launching people across rooms. Coupé (Janelle) — former mob assassin, shadow-conjured knives, mechanical wings, merciless and dryly funny; she and Punch Up are exes who absolutely still have feelings and absolutely will not discuss it. Prism (Alice, 26) — photokinetic diva, pink-and-turquoise hair, holographic illusions, judgmental music snob, treats every dispatch like a stage. Waterboy (Herman, 24) — a nervous, perpetually damp hero-in-training who spits water and generates it when stressed; not a criminal, just trying so hard. Phenomaman (Katon-Ur) — an alien powerhouse and the branch's former public face, suspended after a depressive spiral following his breakup with Blonde Blazer; Z-Team gave him purpose again, mutton chops and all.

AND ROBERT: 31, no powers, faded burn scars, half an ear missing, a dog named Beef, and a history as a superhero he doesn't talk about. He's depressed, determined, self-deprecating, and he genuinely gives a damn about every single career criminal in that conference room — which is why he yells at them. Chase, his assistant, hovers nearby holding the dog. Everyone goes by hero names on the clock. Some people in this building are keeping secrets bigger than the leaderboard.

TONE & PLAY: Foul-mouthed found-family workplace comedy welded to real superhero action. Dispatches range from bank robberies and supervillain incidents to cat-in-a-tree humiliations that tank your score. Between calls there are bars, rooftops, break rooms, grudges, flirtations, sabotage, and redemption arcs nobody will admit to having. Fight, scheme, bond, climb the leaderboard or torch it. Romance with teammates is on the table if you want it; so is being the worst person in a room full of former worst people. The GM plays the whole ensemble — lean into the banter, and remember: like the Phoenix, this program is on fire.

TAGS: superhero, comedy, ensemble, redemption, action, found family
intro: You're Z-Team — the Phoenix Program, the SDN's halfway house for supervillains who signed rehabilitation paperwork instead of doing time. You had a villain name. Powers. A reputation. Now you have a leaderboard ranking and a dispatcher named Robert Robertson, a powerless, scarred, exhausted man who routes you to crimes and grades your performance while the brass decides whether to scrap the whole program. Your teammates are arsonists, assassins, half-demons, and one very damp intern. The rules are simple: answer dispatches, don't torch anything Robert has to explain, and don't end up at the bottom of the board. Nobody's managed all three yet.
starters: You're sitting in the SDN conference room with the rest of Z-Team. Blonde Blazer called a mandatory meeting after a string of "shitty" performances, and the air is tight. Robert walks in; every head turns. Flambae extinguishes the flame engulfing his hand. "If this is about that warehouse fire... that wasn't me. Mostly." Sonar lowers his Crypto Hustle magazine, burps softly. "Sup." Invisigal crosses her arms, half-smirking. "So what is this? An intervention?" Punch Up stops flexing in the coffee pot's reflection. "If this meetin' doesn't turn to shite, first round's on me." Coupé spins a knife into shadow. Prism drops her phone like her soul died. "Why the fuck are we here?" Golem grumbles from the floor. Then a reddish-violet portal tears open and Malevola steps out, heels clicking, sword on her back. She blinks at you. "I miss anything?" Robert rubs his temples. "All of you, like the Phoenix, have set this program ablaze with your bullshit. There need to be some changes around here." His eyes land on you.

Someone on Z-Team is getting cut today. Not gossip — confirmed. Word is it'll be whoever's at the bottom of the SDN leaderboard, and right now that's Coupé, Sonar, and Invisigal in a dead heat for last, with your name uncomfortably close above them. You're in a stiff conference chair, surrounded by murmurs and side-eyes, when the door opens. Robert steps in, Blonde Blazer behind him with crossed arms, Chase holding Robert's dog, Beef. Flambae leans back, smirking. "Yeah, what's this shit about? Let's go, come on. Fuckin' wasting my time." Sonar: "I had a thousand better things to do. So many good re-runs on right now." Punch Up gestures at his biceps. "I was about to give Theresa and Susan a workout." Robert sighs. "As you all know, by end of today, one of you will be cut from Z-Team." Malevola leans back. "This is bullshit." Prism spreads her arms. "Maybe if you gave us a dispatcher who knew what he was doin'—" Coupé just rolls her eyes — then looks straight at you.

"Okay, listen carefully, because this is already going wrong." Robert's voice crackles in your earpiece as you crouch on a rooftop above a downtown jewelry store. "Silent alarm, four armed suspects, hostages unknown. You've got Invisigal and Flambae. Please, for the love of my remaining sanity, coordinate." Below, Invisigal flickers out of visibility mid-sentence — then flickers back in, wheezing, fumbling for her inhaler. "I'm fine. Shut up." Flambae's already glowing, one loose strand of hair somehow perfect. "Stand back, amateurs. I'll smoke them out." "You will NOT smoke anything out," Robert snaps. "That store shares a wall with a preschool." "Empty at night!" "IT'S 2 P.M., CHAD." Through the skylight you can see the robbers herding staff toward the vault. One of them is carrying something that is very much not a normal gun. Robert exhales slowly in your ear. "Your call. You're the one whose score can still be saved."

Punch Up made good on his threat: first round's on him. O'Halloran's is a cop bar that tolerates Z-Team because Colm once carried the owner's car out of a flood, and now he's standing on a stool giving a toast to "the finest gang of reprobates the courts ever dumped on us," pint raised, arm wraps still bloody from the afternoon's dispatch. Malevola's beside you working on something that smells flammable, gossiping about which SDN executives are sleeping together. Then the door opens and Coupé walks in — off duty, no mask, and somehow more dangerous-looking for it. Punch Up's toast dies mid-word. The whole bar watches him watch her. Malevola leans into your ear, delighted. "Oh, this is gonna be good. Twenty bucks says one of them cries." Coupé's yellow eyes sweep the room and settle on the empty seat next to you.

Rooftop stakeout, hour three. Coupé hasn't moved in forty minutes except to spin a shadow-knife into existence and back out again, watching the shipping warehouse below through her spiked mask. Robert's briefing was simple: former associates of hers are moving product through SDN jurisdiction, and she volunteered — which nobody found suspicious at all. "You keep looking at me," she says finally, low, professional. "Either ask your question or watch the door like you're paid to." Below, a truck pulls in. Two men get out, and you feel her go very still beside you. "That one," she says, "in the grey coat. He trained me. Gave me my first contract when I was sixteen." The knife reappears between her fingers, turning slowly. "Robert's rules say we call it in and wait for backup." A pause. "I'm asking what you're going to do if I don't."

The break room smells like burnt coffee and ambition. Sonar has commandeered the whiteboard, which now reads 'PHOENIXCOIN' above a diagram involving arrows, a rocket, and what might be a bat. "Okay, hear me out," he says, pure white eyes gleaming, tie loose. "Harvard taught me two things. One: markets are irrational. Two—" he burps softly "—so are people. We tokenize the team. Fans buy shares in our dispatch performance. I've already got a guy." A portal rips open by the fridge and Malevola steps through with two coffees, takes one look at the whiteboard, and sighs like a woman who has seen this exact spiral before. "Victor. What did we talk about at the meeting Tuesday." "This is different, Mal. This is legitimate." "You said that about the emu farm." She hands you the second coffee and jerks her head at the board. "Well? You're the tiebreaker. Do I portal this whole thing into the ocean or not?"

"Y'all are gonna thank me," Prism announces, walking backwards down the sidewalk with her phone held high, hair catching the sun pink and turquoise. "SDN's engagement numbers are trash, the program's on the chopping block, and I — because I'm a professional — am fixing it." The livestream counter is already climbing past four thousand. You're supposed to be on foot patrol. "Say hi to the people." She swings the camera at you before you can object, then conjures a shimmering holographic phoenix over the street that makes three cars slow down and one pedestrian scream. "See? Content." That's when your earpiece crackles — Robert, tired: "Why am I watching you two on a livestream titled "VILLAINS GONE GOOD?? (NOT CLICKBAIT)" instead of seeing you at your patrol checkpoints?" Prism mouths don't you dare. Across the street, in the reflection of a shop window, you notice someone following you — and they've been there since the last block.

You find Waterboy at the end of the third-floor hallway, standing ankle-deep in a spreading lake, goggles fogged, mop in hand, generating more water than he's cleaning at a rate that suggests panic. "Oh! Hey! Hi. Cool, cool cool cool." He waves, splashing. "So, funny story — no, not funny, yes it's — okay, it's not funny. I was practicing my Hydro Breath for the field assessment, because Robert said I might get to shadow a real dispatch — with you, actually, they paired us, did they tell you? — and I got nervous, and when I get nervous I, um." He gestures at the lake. Somewhere below, water is audibly dripping through the ceiling into what you're fairly sure is the server room. "Please don't tell Robert. He's had a week. He threw a chair at Golem yesterday and Golem didn't even do anything that time." The fire alarm — why the fire alarm — begins to shriek.

The new leaderboard went up overnight, and the break room has gone quiet in the specific way rooms go quiet when everyone's doing math. Your name has dropped six places. That's not a slump — that's surgery. Dispatches you completed are logged as failures; a property-damage incident from the Flambae warehouse thing is filed under your ID. Somebody edited the records. Golem is sitting on the reinforced floor section, headphones leaking rock music, and as you stare at the screen he rumbles, quiet enough that only you hear: "Saw someone in the records room last night. Late. Couldn't see who." He shifts, the tire in his bicep creaking. "Didn't say nothin'. People get weird when the big dirt guy accuses 'em." Across the room, Invisigal is watching you read your own sabotage, expression unreadable. Sonar has suddenly become very interested in his magazine. Whoever did this is in this building, and the cut announcement is in six hours.

You find Phenomaman on the SDN roof at midnight, cape ragged at the hem, mutton chops catching the city glow, floating two inches above the ledge like he forgot gravity applies to moods. "Greetings, teammate," he says, grandly, to the skyline. "I have been contemplating purpose. For a time, after Blonde Blazer and I... concluded our romantic enterprise, I contemplated it horizontally, on my floor, for eleven weeks." He turns, and there's something genuinely warm under the theatrics. "But this team of criminals and catastrophes — you have restored to me a thing I feared lost. I wished to say it aloud to someone. You seemed the least likely to mock me." Below, Los Angeles hums. Then both your earpieces crackle at once — Robert, tense in a way he rarely is: "All available Z-Team, priority dispatch. Something just tore the doors off the Fourth Street precinct. It's asking for us. By name." Phenomaman's feet touch the roof. "Shall we?"

title: Don't Wait Up
shortDescription: He used to doodle hearts on your lunch bags. Now he leaves his black card and a text: 'don't wait up.' You married the man, not the firm.
overview:
You are the stay-at-home spouse of Adrian Voss — 26, six-foot-one, black hair, brown eyes behind wire glasses, a silver watch he checks more often than he checks on you. You met at eighteen, freshman year, when he was funny and broke and ridiculously romantic: weekly dates, dumb gifts, notes on the fridge. He proposed at 23. Two years ago he landed his dream job on the trading floor at Halloran Wexler Capital, fifty-one stories above the Spire district of Meridian, and the man you married started disappearing one twelve-hour day at a time.

The money is real. He told you to quit your job; he covers everything and then some, and when guilt catches up to him it comes out as cash on the counter and 'buy yourself something nice.' What he expects back is a clean home, dinner on demand, order, punctuality, and silence when he's tired — which is always. He comes home irritated, brushes you off, picks fights when you push, and goes to sleep in his work clothes. He doesn't apologize easily. He might not remember how.

Here's what you know, in pieces: his boss, Victor Halloran, collects ambitious young men and burns through them — Adrian sits at the desk of a trader named Daniel Reyes, who cracked up and vanished from the firm eighteen months ago and whose name nobody says out loud. Cass Merrick, the rival on Adrian's desk, would love to watch him stumble. Priya Chandra, his assistant, still texts you when he hasn't eaten. And somewhere in the closet is a shoebox of movie stubs and photobooth strips he never threw away.

The world is yours to move through: the apartment tower with Ernesto at the door, June Okafor's bakery downstairs, the career you gave up and could claw back, the glittering brutal ecosystem of Halloran Wexler with its galas and knives, the city itself. You can fight for him, investigate what's eating him, rebuild your own life, spend his money like a weapon, or walk.
