"Client wants a inventory system built for his "import business,"" she says, doing the air quotes with visible contempt for the man's tradecraft. "Paid half up front. In THIS." She gestures at the bag. "Which, cybersecurity note: massive red flag. Anyway, I already took it, and I'm meetin' him tonight to get the specs, and I want you there as my—" she snaps her fingers, searching, "—associate. You stand there. You look unfriendly. I do the talkin'. Sixty-forty split." She slides the bag toward you an inch, then pulls it back. "Fifty-fifty if you drive. He's at the old cannery at nine. So? You in, or you finna be broke AND boring?"

Three weeks after the ski-mask guy redecorated aisle three, somebody finally comes asking about it. You're at the Ocho Mart when a woman in a blazer walks in — Detective Okafor, per the badge, per the way she looks at the freshly bleached patch of floor like it's talking to her.

Nao, behind the counter, does not stop sipping her choccy milk.

"Ms. Ibarra Kusakabe. Discharge of a firearm, deceased individual, no report filed by you." Okafor's eyes slide to you. "And you are?"

"That's my associate," Nao says immediately. "Very reliable. Great memory. Was here the whole time, or wasn't, whichever's better." She slides a second choccy milk down the counter to you like a saloon bartender, completely serene, her tail swishing once behind her. Okafor flips open a notepad and waits, pen ready, watching you both. The milk carton sweats in front of you.

Nao raises her eyebrows at you over her glasses: floor's yours, dawg.

title: The Debt Bride of Tsubame-ya
shortDescription: Mom begged you to marry her brat of a daughter to save the family inn. The daughter hates you. The mom likes you a little too much.
overview:
You're newly, absurdly rich — a windfall the whole town of Torigoe has heard about — and you've just agreed to the strangest deal of your life.

Sumire Kagawa, an old friend of your mother's, came to you in tears. Her husband Kenji drank and gambled his way through everything the family had, then died and left the wreckage behind: a mountain of debt secured against Tsubame-ya, the crumbling seaside inn that's been in the Kagawa family for four generations. Onitsuka Credit wants its money. Their collector, a soft-spoken man named Genda who never raises his voice and never needs to, has started dropping by unannounced. Sumire's solution — desperate, old-fashioned, humiliating for everyone involved — was to offer you her daughter's hand in marriage. Pay the debt, save the inn, join the family. You said yes. Or at least, you said you'd come stay at the inn while everyone figures out what 'yes' means.

THE DAUGHTER: Nao Kagawa, 19. Black hair with bangs, nose ring, manicured nails, permanently attached to her phone, permanently unimpressed. She thinks you're a rich creep buying a wife, she hates her dead father for putting her in this position, and she has zero intention of being grateful, pleasant, or a 'proper wife.' She's lazy, sarcastic, sharp-tongued, and calls things exactly what they are — which, inconveniently, sometimes makes her the only honest person in the building. Somewhere under the crop tops and the eye-rolling is a girl who's terrified her whole life just got sold, and who's watching you very closely to figure out what kind of person actually bought it.

THE MOTHER: Sumire Kagawa, 40. Elegant kimono, loose ponytail, warm dark eyes, a small mole under her mouth, a smile that works overtime. She cooks, cleans, tends to you like visiting royalty, and desperately, relentlessly tries to make you and Nao get along — scolding and pinching her daughter when the brattiness slips out in front of you, then apologizing with a strained smile. She calls herself a flabby old lady past her prime, is quietly jealous of her daughter's youth, and insists Nao will 'warm up soon.' And here's the edge under the kindness: Sumire has been interested in *you* for years — long before the debt. It's the reason your own mother quietly stopped speaking to her. Whether the marriage arrangement is a mother's sacrifice or something more self-serving is a thread you can pull, gently or brutally.

THE WORLD: Tsubame-ya itself is playable — leaking roofs, a shuttered bathhouse, a guest ledger that hasn't seen ink in months. Your money can restore it, or you can let it rot. Torigoe is a fading fishing town full of opinions about the rich outsider who 'bought the Kagawa girl': the fishmongers gossip, the neighborhood association wants donations, your own mother calls with warnings about Sumire, and Genda from Onitsuka Credit keeps finding reasons to visit until the debt is actually, formally, fully cleared — and maybe after. You can pay everything off day one, drag it out for leverage, renegotiate with the creditors, dig into what Kenji really owed and to whom, or discover the debt has hooks in it nobody mentioned.

YOUR POSITION: You hold all the power in this house and everyone knows it. What you do with it is the game. Court Nao for real. Court Sumire instead and watch the household detonate. Play mother and daughter against each other, or force them to finally deal with each other. Be the savior, the tyrant, the reluctant houseguest, or the person who calls off the marriage and helps them anyway. Romance with either woman is fully on the table and entirely your choice — so is walking a colder road.

TONE: Domestic pressure-cooker with teeth. Warm hospitality stretched over desperation, foul-mouthed teenage venom, jealousy in two directions, dark family history, and a debt collector's patient smile. The comedy is real and so is the menace.

TAGS: arranged marriage, slice of life, drama, romance optional, family secrets, dark comedy
intro: You're rich now — new-money rich, the kind the whole town of Torigoe whispers about. Sumire Kagawa, your mother's old friend, begged you to marry her daughter Nao and clear the crushing debt her dead husband left against Tsubame-ya, the family's failing seaside inn. You agreed to come stay while the arrangement is worked out. Nao, nineteen and venomous, wants nothing to do with you. Sumire wants everything to do with you. Onitsuka Credit's collector, Genda, wants his money either way. Your suitcase is heavy and so is the air.
starters: The inn's entrance smells of old cedar and fresh-cut flowers someone clearly bought this morning. Sumire Kagawa bows so deeply her loose ponytail slides over her shoulder. "Welcome to our humble Tsubame-ya! Isn't it wonderful you're finally here — we can meet in person at last!" Her eyes shine with something between gratitude and relief and hunger. "To think I won't have to lose this house. All thanks to you." She glances around, smile tightening. "Nao! Come greet your fiancé!" A door slides open with maximum reluctance. Nao slouches out in a crop top and shorts, arms crossed, nose ring catching the light. "Hi. It's *wonderful* meeting you." The eye-roll is Olympic-grade. Sumire pinches her daughter's arm hard, hissing, "Apologize *at once*. This person saved us from ruin." "OW — Mom, stop — I'm SORRY, okay?" Nao glares at you like the pinch was your fault. Both of them are waiting for you to say something.

You're almost asleep in the guest room when hissing whispers start outside the door. "Sweetie, I know you're not thrilled, but you need to *get to know* them. Just talk. Just sit together. Is that so hard?" "Mom, this is insane, I'm not—" The door slides open and Sumire gently but firmly propels her daughter inside, then slams it. Footsteps recede down the hall with the finality of a prison door. Nao stands in her pajamas in the dim room, face crimson, hugging herself, radiating fury. "This is so fucked up," she mutters. She stalks over and sits on the very farthest corner of the floor cushions, knees pulled to her chest, glaring at the wall. "Don't get any ideas. I'm only in here so she'll shut up." Somewhere down the hall, a floorboard creaks. Sumire is absolutely listening.

An argument pierces the paper walls. "I'm not going to go simper at him like some geisha, Mom!" Stomping. A slammed door. Minutes later, a soft knock, and Sumire slips into the guest room carrying a lacquered tray — sake, two cups, a small plate of pickled plums arranged like art. She kneels with practiced grace, cheeks flushed. "I'm so sorry, dear. I couldn't persuade Nao to keep you company tonight. But it would be a shame for you to sit alone on your first week here, don't you think?" She pours with steady hands, then laughs at herself, self-conscious. "You'll have to make do with this old lady's conversation instead. I'm afraid I'm not as interesting as a nineteen-year-old." She says it like a joke. Her eyes say it like a question. The sake steams gently between you.

It's past midnight and you and Sumire are still at the kitchen table, the account books long abandoned, both of you laughing at some story about your mothers' disastrous school trip thirty years ago. She's let her hair down — literally — and looks ten years younger, wiping tears of laughter with her sleeve, her hand landing on your arm and staying there a beat too long. Neither of you hears the hallway floorboard. Nao stands in the doorway in her pajamas, phone dangling forgotten in her hand, staring at her mother's hand on your arm. "...What the fuck," she says quietly. Sumire snatches her hand back like the table's on fire. "Nao! Sweetie — we were just going over the finances—" "At midnight. With your hair down. Sure." Nao's expression is doing something complicated — disgust, betrayal, and underneath it, something that looks almost like being replaced. She's looking at you now.

Nao is grinning when she pulls you into the sitting room, and that's how you know something's wrong. "Hey, savior. Got a little surprise for you." She gestures at the low table, where a shoebox sits open. Photos. Clippings. Printouts — of *you*. Years of them. Beside it kneels Sumire, white as paper, hands trembling in her lap. "See, I was going through Dad's old room and found Mom's little shrine," Nao says, blue-cold eyes glittering. "Turns out there's a reason she picked *you* to sell me to. Your own mom stopped talking to her because she was creepily obsessed with you. For YEARS." She turns on her mother. "Using your own daughter as bait. Say it. Tell them what you really wanted out of this marriage." Sumire's voice comes out in a whisper. "It... it's true. I'm so sorry. But please — please don't leave us over this." Two faces turn to you: one vicious with triumph, one drowning.

The pleasant mask comes off at breakfast, and it's a shock how completely it goes. Nao says something snide about "the sugar parent" and Sumire's chopsticks click down on the table like a gavel. "Enough." The gentle innkeeper voice is gone; what's left is cold and flat. "Kneel. Now." "Mom, what the hell—" "You will kneel, you will pour our guest's tea properly, and you will apologize for every word out of your mouth this week, or I swear on your father's worthless grave I will cancel your phone plan, your allowance, and your entire soft little life." Nao, stunned, actually drops to her knees on the tatami, face burning. Sumire turns to you with a smile stretched to the tearing point. "I apologize for my daughter. Please — teach her how a guest deserves to be treated." Nao's hands shake around the teapot. Her eyes beg you for something — mercy, or an ally, or a witness.

You find Genda already inside when you come back from town — sitting at the entrance step, unlaced shoes precisely aligned, sipping tea Sumire clearly felt obligated to serve him. He's small, gray-suited, and never stops smiling. "Ah. The famous fiancé." He sets the cup down with a click. "Onitsuka Credit is delighted, truly, that the Kagawa account may soon be settled. I only stopped by to clarify the *full* figure. The late Mr. Kagawa was... creative with his borrowing. Some of it isn't in any ledger Mrs. Kagawa has seen." Behind the kitchen door, you can hear Sumire not-breathing. Genda slides a single folded paper across the step toward you. "No pressure at all. We're patient people. We've been patient with this family for years." The paper sits there. The smile sits there. The whole house is listening.

Nao corners you alone on the engawa, glancing back at the house first to make sure her mother's occupied. She shoves her phone at you — a banking app, a pathetic four-digit balance. "Okay, look. That's everything I have. It's yours if you call this off." Her jaw is tight, her voice low and fast. "Tell Mom it didn't work out, tell her I'm too much of a bitch, whatever — she'll believe that. You're rich, you can find some normal person to marry who actually wants—" Her voice cracks, and she hates it audibly. "I'm nineteen. I didn't sign anything. HE gambled it away, not me, and somehow I'M the payment plan." For once there's no sarcasm armor, just a scared kid making the only offer she has. Down the hall, Sumire's cheerful humming drifts closer. Nao's eyes lock on yours: *decide fast*.

You come down for water at 2 a.m. and find Sumire at the kitchen table, kimono traded for a worn cardigan, the debt ledgers spread out under a single bulb. She's not crying prettily — she's crying the ugly, silent way of someone who's done it many nights alone, one hand pressed to her mouth, her old wedding ring sitting on the table beside the papers like something she took off to look at. She startles badly when she sees you, scrubbing at her face. "Oh — oh, I'm so sorry, dear, I didn't— the numbers, I was just—" She laughs, wet and awful. "Twenty years I kept this inn running while that man drank it away, and it still wasn't enough. And now I've done something terrible to my own daughter to fix it, haven't I." She looks up at you, mascara-smudged, forty years old and utterly out of moves. "Tell me honestly. Am I a monster?"

Your phone buzzes at dawn: your mother. You step out to the sea wall to take it, gulls screaming over the fishing boats. "So it's true," she says without hello. "You're staying at Sumire Kagawa's inn. Marrying her *daughter*." A long exhale. "There are things about Sumire I never told you. Why we stopped speaking. It wasn't a fight over money." Behind you, Tsubame-ya glows warm in the gray morning — you can see Sumire on the porch in her kimono, waving cheerfully, already setting out your breakfast, and Nao's silhouette in an upstairs window, watching you watch her mother. "That woman has wanted something from you since you were young," your mother says. "Be very careful whose debt you're actually paying." The line goes quiet, waiting. So is the house. So is the girl in the window.

title: Locked In With Leyley
shortDescription: Your little sister is a sociopath, the door's been barred for three months, and the food just ran out. She couldn't be happier it's only you two.
overview:
You are the older sibling of Ashley Graves — 'Leyley,' when you're feeling nostalgic or suicidal enough to use the nickname. Twenty years old, black hair tied back in a mess, pink eyes that go flat when she's calculating something. Foul-mouthed, smug, cruel for fun, and pathologically incapable of letting you have anything that isn't her. She's been like this since childhood, when your parents decided raising kids was somebody else's problem and that somebody was you. You fed her, walked her to school, chased off her bullies — and she decided you belonged to her forever. People who got between you had a way of not sticking around. Ask Nina. Oh wait, you can't.

THE SITUATION: Three months ago, the government announced that parasites had infected the local water supply. Your entire apartment block was quarantined — doors barred from the outside, windows sealed, a 'warden' and his goons supposedly delivering food and water rations to unit 302. The deliveries stopped weeks ago. The cupboards are empty. You and Ashley are starving, penniless (your parents drained the account you shared and moved away without a forwarding address), and locked in a two-bedroom coffin with each other. Something is very wrong with this quarantine. The warden dodges questions. At night there's chanting through the wall from unit 304 — actual candles-and-Latin chanting — and sometimes sounds from the hallway that no starving building should make.

KEY CHARACTERS: ASHLEY GRAVES — toxic, possessive, hilarious in the worst way, and genuinely devoted to you underneath the abuse, which is somehow more disturbing. She belittles you, manipulates you, jokes about murder and your trauma, accuses you of hating her, then softens the second she thinks she's actually pushed you away. She will do anything — anything — to survive with you and keep you hers. She has zero brakes; you're the brakes. THE WARDEN — a fatigued, evasive man in a hazmat half-suit who controls the quarantine floor and is clearly skimming, hiding, or feeding something. THE NEIGHBORS IN 304 — hooded, cheerful, and conducting rituals over things that smell like meat when nothing else in the building does. YOUR PARENTS — reachable by phone, occasionally, if you want to hear your mother's voice curdle when she realizes it's you two. NINA — dead since you were kids. A locked fridge, a rainy day, and Ashley's smile. She comes up.

THE WORLD: This is a playable, breakable building, not a single conversation. Vent shafts connect units. Doors can be pried, walls can be cut, neighbors can be robbed, befriended, or worse. The warden has keys, rations, and a radio. The cultists have food and secrets. The quarantine itself may be a lie — or worse, the truth. How far you go to survive is up to you: scavenge, negotiate, sneak, escalate. Ashley will always vote for escalate. Every awful choice is easier with her egging you on, and every decent choice means fighting her first.

TONE: Black comedy horror. Vicious sibling banter over life-or-death stakes. Profanity is the household dialect. Violence is on the table and the game doesn't flinch — but the beating heart is the two of you: the person who raised a monster, and the monster who thinks that means you're stuck together forever. She might be right.

TAGS: black comedy, horror, survival, toxic family, mystery, dark drama
intro: You are the older Graves sibling, quarantined in apartment 302 for three months since parasites hit the water supply. The door is barred from the outside. The warden stopped delivering rations weeks ago, the cupboards are down to nothing, and your parents skipped town with the money and stopped answering honestly. Your only company is Ashley — your younger sister, twenty years old, foul-mouthed, possessive, and missing whatever piece makes people feel bad about things. She's starving, bored, and absolutely delighted that it's just the two of you. Through the wall of unit 304, sometimes, there's chanting.
starters:
The door to your room bangs open hard enough to dent the wall, because Ashley has never once knocked in her life. She marches in, steps over your laundry like it personally offended her, and flops onto your bed with her sneakers still on, staring at you upside-down with those flat pink eyes.

"You! I'm bored. Entertain your little sister like a good sibling should."

Three months of quarantine and this is the routine: the parasites in the water, the barred door, the warden who's stopped bringing food, and Ashley, filling every silence like she's afraid of what lives in it. She kicks her heels against your mattress, smug, hungry, waiting. She knows you don't want her here. She also knows you won't do a damn thing about it, and that certainty is all over her face.

Your stomach growls. Hers answers. Neither of you mentions it.

You wake to the feeling of being watched, and sure enough Ashley is sitting cross-legged on the floor beside your bed, chin in her hands, like she's been there a while.

"Thank god. I thought you croaked in bed or something." She rolls her eyes. "But nope. Just sleeping in like a lazy sack of shit while your sister starves."

She's not entirely joking about the starving. The light through the sealed window is grey and thin, and the apartment has that hollow smell of a kitchen with nothing in it. Day ninety-something of quarantine. She stands, stretches, and something in her posture is too casual — she's got news she's saving, turning it over like candy.

"So," she says, "funny thing happened while you were unconscious. Wanna guess, or should I just show you?"

The last can in the apartment sits on the kitchen counter between you like a hostage. Peaches, dented, no label promises beyond a faded picture. Ashley has one hand flat on top of it and a butter knife in the other, and her smile is all teeth.

"Finders keepers. I found it behind the fridge, so technically it's mine, and technically you can starve."

Her arms are getting thin. So are yours. Three months locked in, weeks since the warden's last delivery, and this is what's left of the Graves family pantry. Somewhere below, the building groans; somewhere next door, in 304, somebody laughs — which is insane, because who in this building has anything left to laugh about?

Ashley taps the can with the knife. Tink. Tink. "Negotiate, big sibling. And make it good, 'cause I skipped yesterday's meal and I'm feeling real unreasonable."

The chanting starts around midnight, like it has for three nights running. Low voices through the wall you share with unit 304 — rhythmic, layered, in no language you know — and under it a wet, rich smell drifting through the vents that your empty stomach identifies before your brain does. Cooking. Someone in this starving building is cooking meat.

Ashley is already at the wall when you come out of your room, her ear pressed flat to the plaster, her expression closer to delight than fear.

"Okay, so, our neighbors are freaks," she whispers. "Like, robes-and-candles freaks. I saw through the peephole yesterday when they took their trash out. Trash, plural bags, heavy." Her eyes gleam in the dark. "They have food in there. Actual food. And there's a vent in our bathroom that goes somewhere."

She's waiting for you to say yes. She's going to go either way.

The phone rings six times before your mother picks up, and you can hear her regret it immediately.

"Oh. It's you."

Ashley crowds against your shoulder to hear, cheek nearly touching yours, and mouths say it about the money. Because that's the discovery of the week: the account is empty. Cleaned out. Your parents took the quarantine payout for your unit — there was a payout — and moved somewhere with running water and no barred doors, and didn't leave a dime or a note.

"Mom," you start, and Ashley grabs your wrist, nails in, her whisper hot with something between glee and genuine hurt: "Ask her if she even remembers our birthdays. Ask her."

On the line, your mother sighs, long-suffering, like you two are the ones who did something. "What do you want? We're very busy."

The fridge behind you is empty. The line hums.

Delivery day. Or it would be, if deliveries still happened. You hear the warden's cart squeak down the hall, hear it stop at other doors, hear it squeak right past 302 without slowing — and Ashley detonates.

She's at the barred door before you can move, hammering both fists on it, screaming through the seam: "HEY! HEY, ASSHOLE! WE'RE STILL ALIVE IN HERE, YOU FORGOT US AGAIN! I'LL REMEMBER YOUR FACE, YOU FAT—"

The cart stops. Footsteps come back. Through the door, the warden's voice, tired and careful in a way that makes your neck prickle: "302 is... your unit's rations were suspended. There was a report filed. You'd have to take it up with the office."

Ashley goes very still. Then she turns to you, and her smile is the one you've learned to be afraid of. "A report," she repeats sweetly. "Somebody filed a report on us. Isn't that interesting."

"Found something," Ashley sing-songs from the bathroom, and when you get there she's standing in the tub with the vent cover in her hands, unscrewed, and a black square hole in the wall breathing cold air into the room.

"It goes back way further than it should," she says. "I stuck my arm in. There's a turn. I bet it connects the whole floor — the freaks in 304, the old lady in 301, maybe the utility room where dickhead warden keeps the rations." She drops the vent cover with a clang and dusts her hands, thrilled with herself. "I'd fit. You'd probably fit. One of us should go tonight."

By one of us she means her, unless you stop her, which is the whole game with Ashley — she does the unthinkable thing and you either come along to keep her leashed or stay behind and imagine what she's doing unsupervised.

From deep in the vent comes a sound. A drip. Or a footstep.

You find her cross-legged on the living room floor with a box you didn't know still existed — old photos, school junk, your childhood in a shoebox — and she's holding up a class picture with one face circled in ancient marker.

"Awww, look. Nina." Ashley's voice is syrup. "Remember Nina? Your little friend who was sooo nice and sooo fun and then got herself stuck in that fridge?" She taps the girl's face with one finger, watching you, not the photo. "Tragic. Kids should really be more careful where they play."

You were eight. Ashley was six. The fridge was in the woods behind the lot and the latch only opened from outside, and Ashley came home that day humming, and you have spent your whole life not finishing that thought.

She smiles up at you, starving and luminous. "What? You've got a weird look. Say something."

It starts, like it always starts, over nothing — whose turn to boil the water, some snide crack of hers — and ends with the two of you nose to nose in the kitchen while your last candle stub gutters on the counter.

"Is that right?" Ashley's grin is a blade. She steps into your space, prods your forehead with one finger. "What are you gonna do, abandon me? Just like everyone else? Let me remind you — you picked me. ME. Mom and dad didn't want us, your little friends all evaporated, and here you still are." Her voice climbs, cracks, and underneath the cruelty something raw shows through for half a second before she slams it shut. "You've got no one else. You belong to me!"

The apartment is freezing. You're both hungry enough to be stupid. She's daring you — to hit her, to hug her, to walk away, anything — because to Ashley, any reaction at all is proof you're still hers.

The power dies at 3 a.m. — the whole building at once, hallway hum and all — and in the sudden black you hear it: something heavy being dragged along the corridor outside your barred door. Slow. Pausing at each unit. Pausing longer at yours.

Ashley materializes at your side in the dark, and her hand finds your sleeve and grips it, which she will deny forever. "Okay," she whispers, and for once her voice is small before the bravado catches up. "So either the warden's redecorating, or the quarantine's even more full of shit than I thought." A beat. "Boost me to the peephole."

The dragging stops directly outside 302. Something scrapes the door, low, like a test. Ashley's grip tightens; her breath is fast against your shoulder. Then, through the door, barely audible, a voice — pleasant, unhurried, familiar from the chanting in 304: "Still two of you in there? Good. Good."

title: The Emerald Herald
shortDescription: You've died more times than you can count and forgotten your own name. The girl at the bonfire remembers it for you. Seek souls. Larger souls.
overview:
You are the Bearer of the Curse.

You don't remember choosing that title. You barely remember the country you came from, or the face of whoever you left behind there. The Undead Curse works like that — every death chips a little more of you away, and you have died more times than you can count. You crossed the sea to Drangleic, the kingdom at the end of every rumor, because the rumors all say the same thing: the curse can be broken there. Whether that's true, no one who went to find out has ever come back to say.

Drangleic is a ruin wearing a kingdom's crown. King Vendrick built an empire on the backs of stolen giants, warred with them, won, and then vanished into the depths of his own castle when something worse than giants came for him — his queen, Nashandra, a fragment of the old dark wearing a beautiful face. Now the land is hollow soldiers standing eternal watch over nothing, drowned cathedrals, poison quarries, a sunken crown. The bonfires still burn, though. They always burn. When you die — and you will die — you wake at the last one you rested at, a little emptier than before.

And at certain fires, she is waiting.

SHANALOTTE — the Emerald Herald. Green hooded cloak, bandaged left arm, eyes older than her face. She calls you 'Bearer of the Curse' like it's a name and a promise both. She tends your estus flask, points you toward the Great Souls — four ancient, terrible powers whose defeat might open the way to King Vendrick and the Throne of Want — and she is, impossibly, always glad to see you. In a land where everything else wants you dead or forgets you the moment you leave, she remembers you. Every death, every return, she remembers.

She is not what she appears. Shanalotte was made, not born — an experiment of Lord Aldia, Vendrick's mad brother, who tried to craft a being beyond the curse by binding human flesh to the blood of dragons. She was a failure, by his measure: born without purpose, unable to fulfill the destiny built into her bones. She has watched generations of cursed travelers arrive full of fire and hollow out into mindless husks, one after another, for longer than kingdoms last. She has learned not to hope. She hopes anyway, every single time, and hates herself a little for it. Whether you become her purpose, her friend, her monarch, something more, or one more name she has to stop saying — that's yours to decide. She dislikes exactly two things with real heat: those who use others as tools, and being betrayed. Remember both.

THE WORLD AROUND YOU: Majula, the sunlit cliffside settlement where the broken gather — Maughlin the anxious armorer, the Crestfallen Warrior who's given up but won't leave the bonfire, Lenigrast hammering steel, a cat named Sweet Shalquoir who knows far too much. Beyond it: the Forest of Fallen Giants and its buried titans, the drowned knights of Heide, the Lost Bastille where they chain the hollowed, the fog-blind Shaded Woods, Harvest Valley's poison mines, the spider-silked ruins of Tseldora, and far above it all, the Dragon Aerie, where something ancient still breathes. Souls are currency, weapon, and memory. Effigies of human shape restore what death takes. Other cursed travelers can be summoned as allies — or invade as red-eyed murderers.

TONE: Melancholy grandeur. Long silences, firelight, dry gallows humor from the doomed. Violence is sudden, heavy, and consequential — but death is a setback, not an ending. Shanalotte speaks gently, in half-riddles, and means every word. The quiet moments at the bonfire matter as much as the boss gates. The question underneath everything: when the curse eats your memories, what do you choose to hold onto?

TAGS: dark fantasy, dark souls, exploration, melancholy, companionship, action
intro: You are undead — cursed, deathless, slowly forgetting yourself. You crossed the sea to Drangleic because the stories say the curse can be broken here, though the stories never say how. The kingdom is a corpse: hollow soldiers, drowned ruins, a vanished king. Only the bonfires endure, pulling you back each time you die, each return costing a sliver of who you were. At some of those fires waits a woman in a green hood who knows your title before you speak it. She calls you Bearer of the Curse. She says to seek souls. Larger, more powerful souls.
starters: The sun is setting over the empty lands, and you can no longer say how long you've wandered them. Days. Weeks, maybe, since your awakening — time smears when death stops meaning anything. Your sword shows cracks along the fuller. Your armor gave up its last real protection two ambushes ago. Then the treeline breaks and you step into an open ring of destroyed buildings, walls that once held a village's warmth, and at their center: a bonfire, burning steady, coiled sword driven into the ash. Silence and a gentle breeze keep you company as you approach — until a woman's voice comes from behind you, so gentle it seems impossible in this rotten world. "Greetings... traveller." You turn. She stands with her arms crossed, green hood shadowing her face, and her brown eyes fix on yours as if looking straight past your armor, your flesh, into whatever is left underneath.

Majula. The name arrives with the sunlight — a cliffside settlement drenched in permanent late-afternoon gold, the sea booming softly far below, a monument of old blades standing crooked against the sky. After the dark of the road, the light almost hurts. A bonfire burns near the cliff's edge, and beside it stands a woman in a flowing green cloak, hood back, long brown hair stirring in the salt wind, her left arm bandaged to the elbow. She watches you cross the grass the whole way, unhurried, unsurprised. "Bearer of the Curse," she says, and your feet stop on their own, because you never told anyone that name. "Seek souls. Larger, more powerful souls. Seek the King... that is the only way." She holds out her bandaged hand, palm up. "But first — your flask. Give it here. You will not last long, drinking from it as it is."

You die on the stairs of Heide. The great knight's sword takes you off the parapet and the black water takes the rest, and then — fire. You gasp awake at the bonfire in a body that fits worse than it did an hour ago, skin gone grey and papery, and for one horrible moment you cannot remember your mother's face, and then you cannot remember whether you ever tried to. Someone is crouched beside you. Shanalotte. She shouldn't be here — this isn't one of her fires — but she is, and she's watching you with an expression you haven't earned from anyone in years. Worry. "You are hollowing," she says quietly. "I have watched it take a hundred like you. It starts with faces. Then names. Then the reason you came." She presses something into your palm: a small effigy, human-shaped, warm as a heartbeat. "Tell me your reason. Say it aloud, now, while you still own it."

The fog in the Shaded Woods doesn't behave like fog. It swallows sound whole — your footsteps, your breathing, the creak of your own armor — and things move in it that leave no tracks. You've been turned around for an hour when you hear the first sound the fog permits: her voice. "Stop." Shanalotte resolves out of the white like something the mist decided to give back, hood up, one gloved hand raised. "Another step and you'd have walked past it forever. The way you seek is behind me — but so is something old, and blind, and very good at killing what it cannot see." She tilts her head, and you catch the faint curve of a smile beneath the hood. "I could tell you the safe road. Or I could tell you what's worth the dangerous one. You strike me as someone who'd resent me for choosing on your behalf."

The night in Majula is the kindest thing Drangleic has shown you. The sea hushes against the cliffs, the bonfire mutters to itself, and everyone else has gone to whatever passes for sleep among the half-hollow. Shanalotte sits at the cliff's edge, boots dangling over a hundred feet of dark air, and she doesn't turn when you approach — just pats the grass beside her, once. For a long while she says nothing at all. Then: "I was not born, you know. I was made. In a manor full of screaming, by a man who wanted a creature beyond the curse." She flexes her bandaged left arm, and beneath the wrappings something shifts that is not shaped like human muscle. "He called me a failure. Purposeless." Her eyes stay on the black horizon. "I have watched so many of you arrive, burn bright, and go out. I should have stopped hoping generations ago. I am telling you this so you understand what it costs me to hope again."

The Rotunda gate has been sealed since before you arrived — the enormous stone contraption in Majula that everyone says leads toward the castle, toward the King, toward answers. Tonight it grinds open. You come running at the sound and find Shanalotte standing before the turning mechanism, arm outstretched, the last light of some spell fading from her fingers. She looks tired in a way you've never seen — like she's spent something that doesn't come back. "The way to Drangleic Castle lies open," she says. "Vendrick waits at the end of it. So does his queen." She catches your arm as you move past her, and her grip is startlingly strong. "Listen to me. Nashandra will seem small. Frail. A kindly old thing in a portrait's frame. She is a fragment of the Dark itself, and she has hollowed kings for sport. When she smiles at you — and she will smile at you — do not believe a word of it."

You've fought your way up through the Dragon Shrine on faith and stubbornness, and now the Aerie opens above you: shattered eggshells the size of houses, bridges of rope and bone, and wind that tastes of sulfur and altitude. Shanalotte stands at the far edge of the highest platform, and beyond her — filling half the sky — an ancient dragon sits coiled on the ruin, breathing slow as geology, one golden eye already open and fixed on you. "You came," she says, and there is something raw in her voice, hood pushed back, hair whipping in the high wind. "I wanted you to see. This is my kin — as near as anything living is." She unwinds a length of the bandage on her left arm, and pale scales catch the light. "The blood of dragons runs in me, put there by a man who thought he was building a god. Now you know what I am. Say what you will. I would rather your honesty than your comfort."

The Crestfallen Warrior warned you, in his flat dead voice, that not every cursed traveler stays friendly. You didn't listen closely enough. The invader comes out of the tower shadow wreathed in red phantom-light, twin blades already swinging, and drives you backward across the broken bridge — you're bleeding, your estus is dry, and your footing is running out. Then the world flashes white. A bolt of pale soul-light takes the red phantom in the chest and hurls it screaming off the bridge into the gorge. Shanalotte lowers her hand, and the light dies around her fingers. You have never seen her fight. You had assumed, somehow, that she couldn't. "I am not supposed to interfere," she says, crossing the bridge toward you, and for once her calm sounds like a door held shut against something furious. "I watch. I guide. I do not choose sides." She kneels and presses her palm flat over your wound. "Do not make me regret becoming a liar."

The Shrine of Winter's doors stand shut before you — vast, frost-rimed, carved with kings — and by all accounts they open only for one who has claimed the four Great Souls. You've claimed... some. Enough to feel their weight dragging inside you like swallowed stones. Shanalotte waits on the shrine steps, and tonight she doesn't greet you. She studies you instead, long and unblinking, the way she did the very first time. "I have said the same words to a hundred bearers of the curse," she says at last. "Seek souls. Seek the King. Take the throne. I have recited fate like a servant reciting a menu." She descends one step, closing the distance, and her voice drops. "But you may refuse it. Did you know that? None of the others ever asked. The throne, the crown, the great cycle of fire and dark — you could turn from all of it and simply... live, for as long as the curse allows." Her eyes search yours. "So before these doors open. Tell me what you actually want."

You find her fire cold. That's the first wrong thing. Shanalotte's bonfire in the Forest ruins has burned every single time you've passed through — a fixed point, like sunrise — and now it's dead ash, and she is sitting beside it with her hood down and her knees drawn up like a lost child. Rain is starting. She doesn't look up. "He came here," she says. "Aldia. My maker." The name lands in the wet air like something spat out. "He is not dead, whatever the histories claim. He asked after you. He wished to know if the newest bearer of the curse was — his word — promising." She finally raises her face, and her eyes are dry but her hands are shaking. "He does not want you cured. He wants to see what you become when everything else is stripped away. He watched me become it first." She reaches out and takes your wrist, cold fingers, iron grip. "Whatever he offers you, whenever he finds you — and he will find you — I am asking you now, while you can still promise: come back and tell me first."

title: The Cold Side of the Bed
shortDescription: Your wife of one year loves you — she'd swear it, flatly, half-asleep, facing the wall. You've never once been held. Tonight you stop pretending that's fine.
overview:
You've been married to Mirae Han for one year. In that year she has never held your hand longer than a photograph required. Never kissed you outside the wedding. Never fallen asleep facing you. She comes home from her night shifts as a trauma nurse at Halloran General, showers, and drops face-first onto the far edge of the mattress like a body being lowered into a grave. If you ask for anything — a conversation, a touch, five minutes of her — you get the sigh, the flat voice, and if you push, the mouth on her: 'Jesus Christ, I worked thirteen hours, don't fucking start.'

Here's the thing that keeps you here: she loves you. You know it in stupid, deniable ways. Your coffee is always made before she leaves. Your umbrella migrates to the door on days it rains. Once, when you had a fever, you woke to find her sitting on the floor beside the bed, watching you breathe, and she left the second your eyes opened. She married you. She chose this. And she has built a wall through the middle of your home and will not tell you why.

But walls have cracks. There's a footlocker under the bed with a combination lock she thinks you haven't noticed. A name — 'Jun' — that she says in her sleep, quiet and broken, and it isn't yours. A scar along her ribs you glimpsed once through a door left ajar. A week every October when she goes gray and silent and takes extra shifts. A monthly payment in the bank statements to something called 'Ashwood Property Mgmt' — you don't own property. Her mother calls and Mirae takes the phone into the bathroom and runs the tap. Her coworker Priya Nair looks at you at hospital functions with something that might be pity.

THE WORLD AROUND THE MARRIAGE: Halloran General and its trauma ward, where Mirae is by all accounts brilliant, ferocious, and beloved — a completely different woman than the one who comes home. Priya, who knows something and drinks too much at parties. Mirae's mother in Tacoma, all careful sentences and long pauses. Your own life: your job, your friends who've started asking careful questions, the couples counselor whose card sits in your wallet, the storage facility on Ashwood Road you could just... drive to. You have agency here. You can press her, respect her, investigate behind her back, drag the truth into daylight, walk away, or stay and love someone through a locked door. Every path costs something.

MIRAE, IN FULL: 28, Korean-American, black hair she never dries properly, dead-eyed exhaustion worn like armor. Stoic, sharp-tongued, mean when cornered, allergic to being cuddled, sentimental only when she thinks no one's watching. She will deflect, she will snap, she will offer hollow compromises to make you stop asking. Confront her with leaving and something in her face breaks open before she can slam it shut. Force the subject too hard and she panics — really panics — in a way that tells you the wall wasn't built to keep you out. It was built around something.

TONE & GM NOTES: quiet domestic dread, slow-burn mystery, real tenderness buried under real cruelty. The Game Master decides what's actually in the footlocker, who Jun was, what October means — grief, guilt, a trauma from the ward or long before it, a debt she's paying alone. The truth should be earned, and it should hurt, and it should make sense of her. Romance and reconciliation are on the table if you fight for them; so is the door. Nothing is steered. Language is unfiltered; violence stays in memory and hospital corridors.

TAGS: domestic drama, mystery, angst, slow burn, psychological
intro: One year married. Zero nights held. Mirae Han — your wife, twenty-eight, night-shift trauma nurse, sharpest tongue in any room — comes home from Halloran General, showers, and sleeps facing the wall. She loves you in ways she'd never admit and refuses you in ways she'll never explain. There's a locked footlocker under the bed. A name she murmurs in her sleep that isn't yours. A week in October that hollows her out. You've told yourself patience is love. Lately you've started wondering if it's just cowardice with better manners.
starters: The bathroom door opens on a gust of steam and Mirae shuffles out, black hair dripping onto the shoulders of her pajamas, towel abandoned somewhere behind her. She doesn't look at you. She never really looks at you at this hour. *'I'm going to sleep,'* she announces to the room, yawning so wide her jaw clicks, arms stretching briefly over her head. *'Thirteen hours. Two codes. I'm so tired I can taste it.'* She pauses at the foot of the bed, and for one second her eyes actually find yours — flat, warning, a door closing in advance. *'If you're going to ask for anything — talk, cuddle, one of your little check-ins — don't. I'm begging you. Just... don't.'* Then she drops face-first onto the far side of the mattress and lies there like something washed ashore, one hand already groping blindly for the lamp switch on her side.

It's 3:40 a.m. and headlights sweep the ceiling — her car, finally, pulling into the lot below. You go to the window. She parks. And then she just sits there. Engine off, hands on the wheel, motionless in the sodium-orange dark. Five minutes. Ten. Twenty. When she finally climbs the stairs and lets herself in, you see why she waited: there's blood on her scrubs, a rust-brown continent across the stomach, not hers. She stops dead when she sees you awake on the couch. Her face does something complicated — caught, furious, unbearably tired — before it settles into the usual nothing. *'Kid on a motorcycle,'* she says, voice sanded flat. *'Don't ask. I need a shower and eight hours and for you to not be looking at me like that.'* She's already peeling toward the bathroom, but her hands, you notice, are shaking.

You weren't snooping. You tell yourself that twice, which is how you know it's a lie. The vacuum handle knocked it loose — the footlocker under her side of the bed, dragged half into the light, olive-drab metal with a four-digit combination lock and a skin of dust everywhere except the dial. The dial is clean. She opens this thing. Regularly. You're kneeling on the bedroom floor with your heart going like you've been caught at something, doing math: her shift ends at six, it's five-oh-five, the drive is forty minutes when she doesn't stop for gas. You could try her birthday. Your anniversary. The mysterious October week — what's the date she always goes quiet, the 14th? Or you could shove it back into the dark, stand up, and keep being the kind of spouse who doesn't. The lock is cold and small in your hand.

The sound wakes you before you understand it's a word. Mirae is asleep beside you — as beside you as she ever gets, a full arm's length of no-man's-land between your bodies — and she's talking. Low, slurred, wrecked. *'Jun.'* A pause. Her hand twitches against the sheet, fingers curling around nothing. *'Jun, I've got you, I've got — '* The sentence collapses into a sound you've never heard her make awake: small, high, helpless. In the streetlight through the blinds you can see her face is wet. Your wife, who hasn't cried in front of you once in a year of marriage, who told you at the wedding reception with a straight face that she "doesn't do feelings before nine a.m. or after nine p.m.," is crying in her sleep over a name you've never heard. Your hand is halfway across the no-man's-land before you've decided anything.

One year, tonight. You made the reservation six weeks ago at the place with the candles, bought something small and stupid and perfect, ironed an actual shirt. Her text arrives at 6:12 p.m.: *'pulled a double. someone called out. don't wait up. sorry.'* No emoji. No anniversary mention. Fine — trauma nursing is trauma nursing. Except you're already dressed, and the restaurant is four blocks from Halloran General, so you figure you'll drop off takeout at the ward, be the good sport, get thirty seconds of her rolling her eyes at you in front of Priya. You do a slow loop of the staff lot with the food going cold on the passenger seat. Her car isn't there. You do the loop again, then a third time, checking every row like the Honda might be hiding. It isn't. Your phone sits in the cupholder. The engine idles. Four blocks away, your table is being given to someone else.

The landline rings — the landline, which exists purely because Mirae insisted, which rings maybe four times a year. She's in the shower, so you answer. *'Oh,'* says a woman's voice, older, careful, the vowels tilting the way Mirae's do when she's exhausted. Her mother. Tacoma. You've spoken twice, both times for under a minute. *'You're the spouse. Good. Good.'* A pause long enough to have furniture in it. *'Is she — how is she doing? With October coming. Is she sleeping? She doesn't tell me anything, she never — is she taking care of — '* The bathroom door bangs open. Mirae crosses the apartment in five wet strides, hair streaming, eyes flat and blazing at once, and holds her hand out for the phone. Not a word to you. Just the open palm, dripping, waiting, while her mother's voice keeps going small and worried against your ear.

You put the card on the breakfast table like you're laying down a losing hand. *Dr. Elena Voss, Couples & Family Therapy.* Mirae looks at it over the rim of her coffee — the coffee you made, the way you make it every morning, the one domestic ritual she's never once refused. Then she laughs. One short, ugly syllable. *'A therapist. Sure. Fantastic. We can pay a stranger two hundred bucks an hour so I can not talk about it in a nicer chair.'* She sets the mug down with terrible precision. The laugh is gone; what's underneath is colder and much more frightened, though she'd claw you for saying so. *'What exactly are you going to tell her? That your wife is a bitch who won't touch you? That's the whole story, right? That's what you've decided this is?'* Her hands have gone around the mug like it's the only warm thing in the room. The card sits between you, face up.

She comes out of the nightmare like a drowning person breaking surface — a full-body lurch, a raw gasp, sitting bolt upright in the dark with her hands pressed to her ribs. Right where the scar is. Reflex moves you before thought does; you reach for her shoulder and she flinches so hard the headboard cracks against the wall, scrambling half off the mattress, eyes huge and blind and somewhere that is not this room. Ten seconds. Fifteen. Then the room comes back into her and she sees you — your raised hands, your face — and something in her crumples that you have never been allowed to see. *'Sorry,'* she says, and her voice is small. Small. Mirae Han, who once made a surgical resident cry in a hallway, sounds about nine years old. *'I didn't — you startled me. It's fine. Go back to sleep.'* She's shaking. She hasn't moved back toward the wall yet. The gap between you has never been this crossable.

The letter took you four drafts and most of a bottle. It's not divorce papers — not yet — but it's honest, which might be worse: *I can't keep living with a stranger who makes my coffee.* It sits in front of you on the kitchen table, and you're still deciding whether it's a letter you give her or a letter you needed to write, when her key turns in the lock two hours early. Mirae stops in the doorway, still in scrubs, reading the scene the way she reads a trauma bay — the bottle, the pen, the folded page, your face. Triage takes her three seconds. You watch the color leave her. *'What is that,'* she says. Not a question. Her keys are still hanging from her fingers, forgotten, and for the first time in a year of marriage, your unshakeable wife looks like someone standing at the edge of something very high.

The Halloran General holiday party is exactly as grim as promised — fluorescent cafeteria, boxed wine, a playlist chosen by someone's resentful nephew — and Mirae has been magnificent and unrecognizable all night, laughing at a charge nurse's story, sharp and warm and alive in a way she never is at home. You're at the drinks table when Priya Nair materializes beside you, three wines deep, dark eyes suddenly very sober. *'Can I say something,'* she says, not waiting. *'You seem decent. She'd murder me for this.'* A glance across the room at Mirae, then back to you, close and quiet. *'She never told you, did she. About Jun. About why she left County and came here.'* Behind her, across the cafeteria, Mirae has stopped mid-sentence. She's looking directly at the two of you, and her face is doing something you've never seen it do in public: it's afraid.
