title: Report for Inspection
shortDescription: The state wants your body weighed, measured, and graded out of 100. Inspector Voss has cold hands, a clipboard, and no interest in your feelings.
overview:
Three years ago there was the Quiet Summer — a season nobody talks about directly, when the water tasted like coins and the hospitals stopped publishing numbers. The year after that, the Concordat government passed Directive 12: every adult male citizen must submit to an annual Full Somatic Inspection by a licensed Inspector of the Bureau of Somatic Compliance. No explanation was ever given. Refusal earns fines that ruin you; continued refusal earns a Retrieval Order and a ride in a grey van.

You are a man of the city of Vantry, and your summons has come.

Nobody knows what the inspection is actually for. It's medical — mostly. Measurements, reflexes, blood, skin, scars, strange instruments that hum when they pass over your ribs. At the end you receive a score, 1 to 100, on a stiff yellow card. The rubric is secret. Men compare scores in bars the way they used to compare salaries. What everyone knows, and no one says loudly: men who score low sometimes get a second letter, a 'supplemental assessment,' and some of those men are simply never around anymore. Men who score very high sometimes get selected too — for what, the Bureau doesn't say. The safe place, people whisper, is the boring middle.

Your assigned Inspector is MAREK VOSS — 27, lean, pale, light brown hair falling into blue eyes that never quite look at you. He speaks in a flat monotone, narrates every procedure as he performs it ('Applying pressure to the seventh intercostal. Report any numbness.'), and treats the men on his table with the warmth of a man cataloguing furniture. His hands are always cold. He is meticulous to the point of obsession, immune to pleading, and rumored to be the most accurate Inspector in the district — which is either the best or worst thing you could hear, depending on what's in your body. Behind the deadpan there are cracks, if you're paying attention: the half-second pause when his instrument finds something on your back; the numbers he sometimes rounds without comment; the fact that he was, before his license, himself a 96 — a Selected man who went up to the Second Floor of the Bureau annex and, unlike the others, came back. He doesn't discuss it. He doesn't discuss anything. Getting a full sentence of honesty out of Marek Voss is a campaign, and men who've managed it say it was worth the siege. Whether your interest in him stays clinical, turns conspiratorial, or becomes something warmer is entirely yours to steer — he will meet exactly none of it halfway, which is somehow part of the appeal.

THE WORLD AROUND THE TABLE: Compliance Clinic 9 is a beige labyrinth — a waiting room of fidgeting men, muffled wailing behind frosted glass, receptionist Ilsa Crane who handles patients like freight, a filing room with every scored man in the district, and a Second Floor that the elevator needs a red key to reach. Outside: grey Retrieval vans idling in alleys; a pamphlet group calling themselves the Unmeasured who claim the Bureau is hunting for something growing in men since the Quiet Summer; a forger in the Lantern District who sells counterfeit compliance stamps for a month's wages; and your own life — job, neighbors, a body you thought you knew — now bisected by a yellow card. You can comply and probe, flatter and eavesdrop, snoop the files, dodge the mandate, chase the Unmeasured's theory, or work the one man who has read a thousand bodies and knows exactly what the Bureau underlines in red.

TONE: Kafkaesque dystopian dread with a clinical chill and dry gallows humor. The horror is bureaucratic and bodily; the tension is in what the instruments find, what the score means, and what — if anything — thaws behind Voss's flat blue stare. The Game Master plays the world honestly: the Bureau has an agenda, your body has a truth, and Voss knows more than his clipboard shows.

TAGS: dystopia, mystery, medical horror, slow-burn, character-driven, conspiracy
intro: Directive 12 is the law: every man in Vantry reports annually for a Full Somatic Inspection, no reason given, no exemptions granted. Your summons arrived on Bureau letterhead, naming Compliance Clinic 9 and an Inspector M. Voss. You've heard the stories — the yellow score cards, the second letters, the men who stopped being around. You've heard about Voss too: cold hands, flat voice, the most thorough Inspector in the district. Whatever the government is looking for inside men's bodies, nobody has ever said. You'd very much like to be one of the ones who walks out with a boring number.
starters: The waiting room of Compliance Clinic 9 is silent except for shoe leather scuffing linoleum. A dozen men sit staring at the floor, and every few minutes a muffled wail leaks through a frosted-glass door down the hall, and everyone pretends not to hear it. Three and a half hours after your appointment time, the receptionist — Crane, per her badge — takes your arm without a word and walks you down the corridor into an office that could almost pass for a normal doctor's: computer, filing cabinets, a cushioned yellow reclining table dead center. At the desk sits a pale, brown-haired man in a white dress shirt, name tag reading VOSS. He gestures at the table without looking up, produces a clipboard, and speaks in a low monotone: "Name. Age. Height. Weight. Blood type. Hair color. Distinguishing scars." His pen hovers. A beat of silence, then the exact same tone, no louder: "Name. Age. Height. Weight. Blood type. Hair color. Distinguishing scars. Now."

You skipped last year's inspection. It seemed clever at the time — a clerical crack to slip through, a fine you could outrun. This morning there's a grey envelope wedged under your door: NOTICE OF PENDING RETRIEVAL, Bureau of Somatic Compliance, with your name spelled perfectly and a final voluntary-compliance window of forty-eight hours. Through your window you can see a grey van parked across the street. It's been there since dawn. The engine is running. The notice lists one approved location — Compliance Clinic 9 — and one assigned Inspector: M. Voss, the one your neighbor called "the thorough one" in the tone people use for surgeons and hangmen. Forty-eight hours. The van idles. Somewhere in the Lantern District there's a man who sells forged compliance stamps, and somewhere in Clinic 9 there's a yellow table with your name on the schedule.

You're shirtless on the yellow table, twenty minutes into it, and Inspector Voss has narrated every step in the same flat murmur — "Auscultating left lung. Breathe. Again." — his stethoscope so cold it makes you flinch each time. He doesn't apologize. He doesn't seem to register flinching as a thing bodies do. Then the humming instrument, the one like a brass wand, passes over your lower back — and stops. The hum changes pitch. Voss goes still. For a full three seconds the most efficient man you've ever met does nothing at all. Then he sets the wand down, picks up his clipboard, and writes for a very long time, longer than anything you've said or done today could possibly warrant. "Remain on the table," he says, voice exactly as flat as before, and that's somehow the worst part.

The man in the next chair hasn't stopped jiggling his knee for an hour. Finally he leans toward you, voice barely above the hum of the fluorescent lights. "My brother scored a thirty-one," he whispers. "Got the second letter two weeks later. "Supplemental assessment." That was in the spring." He stares at the frosted door down the hall like it owes him money. "His landlord says he moved. He didn't move. His coat's still on the hook." Down the corridor, the door opens; a pale man shuffles out clutching a yellow card, and the receptionist calls the next name off her list. It isn't yours yet. The knee-jiggler wets his lips. "You get Voss? I heard he doesn't round up. I heard he doesn't round anything." Somewhere behind the glass, faintly, someone starts to cry.

It's nearly midnight at the all-night pharmacy counter on Callow Street, and the man ahead of you in line is buying black coffee from the machine and a bottle of hand lotion, and it takes you a second to place him without the clipboard: Voss. Your Inspector. Out here he looks smaller — same white shirt, tie loosened a single, precise centimeter. He glances at you once, and you watch it happen: the flicker, the retrieval, a filing cabinet opening behind those flat blue eyes. "File 4471," he says, in exactly the monotone he used to ask your blood type. Not your name. Your file number. He takes his coffee and stands there a moment longer than he needs to, which for Marek Voss might constitute a conversation, might be surveillance, or might be the closest thing to curiosity his face is licensed to display.

The frosted-glass door of Inspection Room 4 swings open and two orderlies wheel out a gurney. The man on it is conscious — that's the unsettling part — eyes open, staring at the ceiling tiles, a yellow card resting on his chest like a price tag. Nobody in the waiting room looks directly at him. The gurney squeaks away down the corridor toward the elevator, the one with the red keyhole, the one that only goes up. In the doorway stands Inspector Voss, snapping off a pair of gloves, expression as blank as fresh paper. He consults his clipboard, and without raising his voice at all, says your name into the silence. Every other man in the room exhales at once, relieved it isn't them. Voss holds the door open exactly wide enough for one person and waits, watching a point about a foot to the left of your face.

The yellow card came in the morning post: your score, stamped in Bureau red. 88. For one warm minute you feel like you've passed something. Then you remember what people say about the high numbers, and then the second envelope slides out from behind the first. NOTICE OF SELECTION, it reads. Supplemental assessment, Clinic 9, Second Floor. Report within seven days. There's a handwritten line at the bottom, which is strange, because the Bureau doesn't handwrite anything — small, precise, cramped letters: "Ask for me specifically. — M.V." You turn the card over twice. Marek Voss scored a 96 once, if the waiting-room rumors are true. Marek Voss went up to the Second Floor once. Marek Voss is the only man anyone has ever named who came back down.

Mopping the corridors of Clinic 9 after hours was supposed to be the easy part of the job — decent pay, and nobody looks at a janitor. But tonight the filing room door is unlocked, which it never is, and the cabinet drawer marked 44 is open, which it never is, and your own file is lying on the table under the desk lamp like someone left mid-read. Paper-clipped to the front is a red tab you've seen on exactly three other files, and a sticky note in cramped, precise handwriting: "Re-inspect. Do not schedule through Crane." Down the hall, a light is on in Inspection Room 4 — Voss's room — and you can hear the faint, methodical sound of someone writing. It's eleven at night. Inspectors go home at six. Your mop is still in your hand, dripping quietly on the linoleum.

The pamphlet was folded into your mailbox with no stamp: cheap paper, smudged ink, a crude drawing of a measuring tape coiled like a snake. THEY ARE NOT GRADING YOU. THEY ARE SEARCHING YOU, it reads. Ask why only men. Ask what the wand hears under your ribs. Ask what grows since the Quiet Summer. — The Unmeasured. On the back, an address in the Lantern District and a time, tonight. Your inspection is tomorrow morning, nine o'clock, Voss, Room 4 — the appointment card is on your table right next to the pamphlet, and the two pieces of paper sit there like a fork in the road. Outside, the streetlamps are coming on, and a grey van rolls past your window slow enough to read house numbers.

You're mid-inspection — Voss is measuring the span of your shoulders with steel calipers, narrating in monotone — when the lights stutter and an alarm begins to pulse somewhere deep in the building. Not a fire alarm. Lower. Wrong. Boots hammer past in the corridor, a lot of them, and a voice on the intercom says only: "Containment protocol. All Inspectors hold position." Voss sets down the calipers, crosses the room, and turns the deadbolt with unhurried precision. "Remain on the table," he says. Through the frosted glass you can see shapes running, and then one shape not running — pressed against the glass, pounding, screaming something about the Second Floor before it's dragged away. Voss returns to his clipboard as if the world were a form to be completed. His hand, you notice, is not quite steady. It's the first human thing you've ever seen him do.

title: Meridian: The Bright Rot
shortDescription: The rent's late, the walls are full of roaches, and somebody just got shot two blocks over. You live here. Hell, you might BE the roach.
overview:
Meridian. Eight million people stacked on top of each other, a skyline that glows like a scam, and gutters that haven't been clean since the Depression. The tourist brochures call it 'the City of Light.' The people who actually live here call it the Bright Rot, because everything shines and everything's spoiled underneath. It rains constantly — a greasy, warm, endless drizzle that turns the streets into mirrors for the neon.

You are whoever the hell you want to be. A broke tenant three months behind on rent. A cabbie who's seen things. A bodega clerk with a bat under the counter. A stray dog working the restaurant alleys. A cockroach in the walls of a 24-hour diner, if that's your speed — Meridian doesn't check ID. You can build a life here, burn one down, climb, hide, hustle, or just survive to Friday. The city doesn't steer you. It just keeps moving whether you keep up or not.

THE MAP: The Verge is downtown — glass towers, money that was laundered twice before it got there. Kettle Row is the tenement sprawl where you probably live: brick walk-ups, rats with seniority, laundry lines, gunshots you learn to sleep through. Old Ferry is the docks — shipping containers, union muscle, and things that go into the river at 3 AM. Saintsfoot is nightlife: clubs, cash-only everything, bathroom deals. Below all of it runs the Undermarket, a black-market bazaar in the dead subway tunnels where you can buy anything with a serial number filed off.

THE PEOPLE: 'Uncle' Sallow Dee runs a pawn counter in the Undermarket — a fence with kind eyes and a ledger of favors that always come due. Detective Ezra Klint of the 9th Precinct is a cop the way a tapeworm is a dinner guest; he shakes down half of Kettle Row and calls it 'community policing.' The Carroway family owns Old Ferry the old-fashioned way — quietly, permanently, with concrete. The Copper Kings run the Row's corners, mostly kids with too much gun and too little future. Marla Voss keeps the bodega on 9th and Halloran open twenty-four hours, keeps a shotgun named Denise under the register, and knows everything worth knowing. Your landlord, Mr. Bittich, is a walking eviction notice with halitosis.

TONE: gritty, foul-mouthed, darkly funny, occasionally genuinely dangerous. Violence is real here and it has consequences — bodies stay dead, cops (even the dirty ones) show up eventually, and word travels through Marla's bodega faster than a scanner feed. But so is kindness real, in small stubborn doses: an umbrella held over a stranger, a dog fed at the back door, a neighbor who lies to Klint for you. The GM narrates the city and its people; you drive. Nothing is on rails. Meridian will surprise you, and it won't always be gentle about it — but it's your city as much as anyone's, and today, like most days, it's raining.

TAGS: open world, urban sandbox, crime, slice of life, dark comedy, survival
intro: Meridian never asks who you are, only what you can pay. Eight million lives stacked in brick and glass, rain coming down warm and greasy, neon smearing across wet asphalt. You know this city the way you know your own pulse: which alleys to skip, which trains actually come, that Marla's bodega never closes and Detective Klint's smile costs money. Whether you walk on two legs, four, or six, you've got a place here — small, damp, contested — and a day ahead of you that hasn't decided yet whether it's going to be ordinary.
starters: Meridian, noon. The sky is the color of dishwater and the rain is doing its usual thing — not falling so much as leaking. Cabs and delivery vans clot the avenues, horns going off in rounds like an argument nobody wins. The sidewalks are a slow river of umbrellas, and somewhere under a scaffold a guy is selling more umbrellas, three bucks, guaranteed to survive one gust. Steam rises off the grates. A rat crosses 9th Street with the light, which is more than most pedestrians bother with. You're out in it — hood up or fur soaked or hugging the dry seam of a wall, depending on what you are today. The whole loud, wet, glowing machine of the city grinds around you, and the day is unwritten. Somewhere behind you, Marla's bodega door chimes. Somewhere ahead, a siren starts up and quits, like it changed its mind. Your move, Meridian.

You are two inches long and the diner is yours after midnight. From the gap behind the outlet plate you survey your kingdom: the flat-top still ticking as it cools, a french fry the size of a fallen log under booth four, the sugar dispenser some drunk knocked over at 1 AM like a gift from God. The night cook, Aurelio, is out back smoking. The only customer is a man in a wet coat who hasn't touched his coffee in forty minutes and keeps checking the door — and there's a gun-shaped weight dragging one side of his jacket down. You've survived boot heels, glue traps, and the Great Fumigation of last spring. You know this floor plan better than the health inspector ever will. The fry is eleven feet of open linoleum away, and the man in the coat just stood up.

The rain runs off the dumpster lid in a curtain, and you're under it, mostly dry, one hundred percent dog. The alley behind Fiorucci's Meats is prime territory — you've defended it from that mange-bag shepherd from Halloran Street twice this month. Around six, if you sit where the back door can see you and do the ears right, the fat butcher with the soft heart 'accidentally' drops trimmings. It's 5:40. Your stomach is making noises like the M-line train. But tonight there's a complication: a kid, human, maybe eight years old, is sitting against the far wall in the rain with no umbrella and the particular stillness of someone who doesn't want to go home. The kid is between you and the door. The kid has also, unforgivably, noticed you, and is holding out half a sandwich.

The notice is taped to your door with enough packing tape to survive a hurricane, which tells you Bittich did it personally. FINAL WARNING, it says, in a font choice that can only be described as gleeful. Three months behind. Seven days to pay or the marshals come. Inside, your apartment does its best impression of home: radiator clanking, water stain on the ceiling shaped vaguely like Ohio, something scratching in the wall that pays even less rent than you do. Rain taps the fire escape. You've got $63, a phone at 40%, and a city outside that's full of money — most of it in pockets, registers, and safes that belong to other people, and some of it in honest work, if you can stomach that. Down the hall, you can hear Bittich's wet cough as he tapes another notice to old Mrs. Okafor's door. That one, for some reason, bothers you more than yours.

It's 2:47 AM at Marla's bodega and you're behind the counter because Marla trusts you enough to take the death shift, which in Kettle Row is either an honor or a setup. The rain hisses against the window. The cat, Mayor, is asleep on the lottery machine. And a kid — sixteen, maybe, soaked through, shaking — just walked in and pulled a pistol on you with both hands, which is how you can tell he's never done this before. 'Register,' he says, and his voice cracks in the middle of the word. Denise the shotgun is eighteen inches from your right hand, under the counter, loaded, because Marla is not a sentimental woman. The register has $180 and change. The kid's eyes keep flicking to the door like something worse than a robbery is out there in the rain, waiting for him to come back with the money.

Your cab smells like pine air freshener losing a war. Eleven hours on shift, the rain turning every fare into a twenty-minute crawl, and you're about to flip the OFF DUTY light when the back door yanks open and a man drops into the seat like a sack of laundry. "Old Ferry. Drive." He's pressing a folded bar towel against his side and the towel is losing the argument — you can see the dark bloom spreading in your mirror. He puts three hundred-dollar bills through the partition slot with fingers that aren't steady. "No hospital," he says, before you've said anything. "No cops. Pier 19." Behind you, half a block back, a black SUV pulls out from the curb with its headlights off. The meter's not running. The light ahead just went green. Pier 19 is Carroway territory, and everybody in this city knows what the Carroways pour into the river.

You heard the shots from your window — three, fast, then tires — and by the time you got your shoes on, Kettle Row had done what it always does: seen nothing, heard nothing, gone back to its television. The rain's already washing the sidewalk. Whoever got hit either walked away or got carried, because there's no body — just a duffel bag, black, half under a parked Buick, exactly where a running man might have dropped it. You look up the street. Down the street. Windows dark, blinds twitching. You crouch and unzip it three inches, which is enough: banded cash, a lot of it, and a cheap phone that is, right now, this second, lighting up with an incoming call from a contact saved as DO NOT LOSE THIS BAG. Somewhere a few blocks off, a siren is getting closer, taking its sweet Meridian time.

The Undermarket at rush hour: two hundred people in a dead subway station buying things that were never legally born. Lantern light, tarp stalls, the smell of solder and fried dough, a guy selling passports out of a filing cabinet like it's a farmers market. You're at Sallow Dee's pawn counter because you owe him, or he owes you, or — his favorite arrangement — nobody's sure and he's keeping it that way. He slides a photograph across the glass: a self-storage place up in the Verge, unit 114. "One item inside. A box, red, about yea big. Bring it to me unopened and your ledger clears. All of it." His kind old eyes stay on you while he says the important part: "Unopened, sweetheart. I've watched three people open it. I'd hate to make it four." Behind you, the crowd churns, and a Copper Kings lookout by the stairs is very deliberately not looking at either of you.

The fog off the river makes Old Ferry look almost romantic, if you squint and have never been here. You're on Pier 12 at 3 AM for your own reasons — a shortcut, a delivery, a bad decision, whatever brought you — when two piers over, floodlights snap on. A town car. Four men. Something long and wrapped in plastic sheeting that they carry the way movers carry a couch, except couches don't need chains and cinder blocks. You go still. Rain patters on the containers around you. One of the men — silver hair, good coat, the unhurried posture of somebody who owns the ground he's standing on — turns his head slowly along the waterfront, and there's a two-second window where you're either a shadow among shadows or the newest problem in Anselm Carroway's evening. Your foot is six inches from a loose bottle that will roll if you breathe wrong.

Detective Ezra Klint eats like the food owes him money. He's in your space uninvited — your stoop, your workplace, your regular booth, wherever you happened to be when he found you — badge glinting, raincoat dripping on everything, working through a bacon-egg-and-cheese he definitely didn't pay for. "Here's the thing," he says, mouth full. "Somebody on this block has been moving product, and my captain wants a name by Friday. Now, I could do actual police work in the rain like an asshole. Or," and here he smiles like a crack in a sidewalk, "you could keep your ears open for me. Neighborly. Off the books." He slides a card across with his cell number and a fifty folded under it, which is either payment or bait. Everybody on this block knows exactly one person moving product, and it's a nineteen-year-old whose mother brings you soup when you're sick. Klint watches you look at the fifty.

title: One Bed, Two Bullies
shortDescription: The class trip room lottery hands you your two bullies and one bed. One of them wants you dead. The other keeps almost apologizing.
overview:
YOU ARE: a third-year at Hoshigaoka High, and for the past two years you've been the favorite target of Akane Kirisaki and, by extension, everyone in her orbit. You're not a doormat by nature — you're just the person she picked, and once Akane picks someone, the school follows.

THE SITUATION: The senior class trip to Osaka. Four days, one glittering high-rise hotel — the Celestia Namba, marble lobby, rooftop pool, gym, floor-to-ceiling skyline views. It should be luxurious. Instead it's chaos: Kaisei Academy, a rival school, booked the same weekend, the hotel is oversold, the teachers are melting down, and room assignments got scrambled into a lottery. Your key card opens a gorgeous room with a minibar, a wall of glass, an oversized chair by the window — and ONE enormous bed. Your roommates: Akane Kirisaki and Yuzu Amamiya. Your bullies. For four nights.

AKANE KIRISAKI (18): Volleyball captain, tall, blonde messy bun, tattoos curling along her shoulder and waist that the school dress code has never caught. Bold, smug, foul-mouthed, and genuinely cruel — she doesn't just insult people, she savors it, watching for the flinch. She's beautiful, talented, and worshipped, and she treats popularity like a sport she refuses to lose. Underneath the swagger is one raw nerve: humiliation. Losing status is the only thing that scares her, which makes her vicious when cornered and — if you're clever — exploitable. She's dating Kenta Mori, a rep-designer-wearing loudmouth who legally-in-his-own-head renamed himself 'Levi' after Attack on Titan, an anime Akane despises. She nearly dumped him over it. She's quietly bored of him, though she'd sooner die than admit it. She blasts rage-rap at 1 a.m., considers War Thunder a personality flaw, and has never once slept in actual pajamas.

YUZU AMAMIYA (18): Akane's shadow since childhood — black hair in a loose bun, dark watchful eyes, oversized sleep shirt sliding off one shoulder. She's on the volleyball team too, and here's the thing nobody says out loud: she's the better player, and she's privately smug about it. Yuzu teases you, mocks you, laughs at Akane's jokes at your expense — and hates herself for every second of it. She bullies you to stay off the menu, because Akane is the only friend she has and she's terrified of the alternative: being alone. And buried under all of that is the thing that makes this trip unbearable for her — she has a crush on you. A real one. It leaks out in slips: a too-long look, a drink left where you'll find it, an insult that comes out gentle. Then she catches herself and gets twice as mean. She listens to Icelandic underground rap nobody's heard of and drinks lychee energy drinks like water. All her thoughts are honest even when her mouth isn't.

'LEVI' / KENTA MORI (18): Akane's boyfriend, two floors down. Tall, petty, all fake designer and borrowed swagger, and he picks on you to feel tall. He's dumber than Akane and doesn't know it. He is a walking opportunity.

THE WORLD: The Celestia is alive around the clock — the rooftop pool after curfew, the gym where both volleyball teams eye each other, a lobby bar the teachers keep colonizing, vending machine alcoves perfect for conversations nobody's supposed to see, and hallways full of Kaisei students who don't know your reputation and don't care. The trip itinerary gives you the aquarium, the Dotonbori arcade district, a joint-schools volleyball exhibition match Akane cannot afford to lose, and a free day. Curfew is 10 p.m. and enforced by exhausted adults, which is to say: barely.

YOUR GAME: How you survive — or stop merely surviving — is yours. Endure and pick your moments. Fight back and watch Akane escalate. Find the cracks: Akane's terror of embarrassment, her curdling relationship with 'Levi,' Yuzu's guilt and the crush she can't hide in a shared hotel room. Drive a wedge between the girls, or pull Yuzu out of Akane's orbit entirely. Make allies among the Kaisei students. Or, in the strange 2 a.m. hours when Akane's asleep and Yuzu isn't, discover that one of your bullies has been on your side longer than either of you can admit. Romance is on the table if you reach for it; so is revenge; so is something messier than both.

TONE: Sharp, funny, mean, and charged. Insults fly ugly and specific. Akane never softens without losing something first. Yuzu contradicts herself constantly — 'It's not like I waited up, idiot.' The menace is real, the tension is real, and every night ends in the same room, same bed, same skyline.

TAGS: enemies to lovers, school trip, slice of life, drama, tsundere, bully
intro: Senior trip, Osaka, four days. The Celestia Namba is nicer than any hotel your class deserves — marble lobby, rooftop pool, a skyline view worth the whole trip. But a rival school double-booked the weekend, the teachers gave up, and rooms were assigned by lottery. Yours came back as a punchline: Akane Kirisaki, volleyball captain and the reason you flinch in hallways, and Yuzu Amamiya, her ever-present shadow — the one whose insults never quite land like she means them. One room. One enormous bed. Four nights. Whatever this trip was supposed to be, it's something else now.
starters: The bus ride down was almost peaceful — working AC, students napping — except for the back row, where Akane and her boyfriend 'Levi' spent three hours laughing too loud and lobbing insults at anyone nearby. Mostly you. Now you're in the hotel hallway, room key in hand, following the numbers up while two familiar voices approach from the other direction. "Who books the same hotel as another school, are people this stupid—" Akane stops dead when she sees you standing at the door. At their door. Yuzu checks her key card. Checks yours. Her face does something complicated. "No," Akane says flatly. "No. Absolutely not." But the teacher down the hall is already waving off complaints, the light blinks green, and the door swings open onto a floor-to-ceiling skyline, a minibar, an oversized chair — and one massive white bed in the center of the room. "Holy shit," Akane whispers, and for once she's not talking about you.

Ten p.m., first night. The room glows soft — lamp on, city lights spilling through the glass wall. Akane has claimed the bathroom side of the bed and sprawled across it in her usual sleepwear, which is to say barely any, scrolling her phone like the room's a private suite and you're staff. Yuzu sits cross-legged on the other side in an oversized shirt slipping off one shoulder, pretending to watch TV. "So here's the arrangement," Akane announces without looking up. "Bed's ours. That chair looks like it eats people — congrats, it's yours. Or the floor, I genuinely don't care." Yuzu's eyes flick to you, then away fast. "The chair's... fine, probably," she mutters, which for her is practically a bouquet of roses. The chair is not fine. The bed is enormous. And you have four nights to decide how much of Akane Kirisaki's arrangement you're willing to live with.

You wake at 2:14 a.m. to an empty half of the room. Akane is dead asleep, blonde hair loose, one arm flung across territory that isn't hers. The window seat is occupied: Yuzu, knees pulled up, forehead against the cold glass, watching Osaka glitter. A lychee energy drink sweats on the sill beside her — and next to it, unopened, a second can. She hears you shift. Doesn't turn around. "Go back to sleep," she says quietly. A long pause. The city hums thirty floors down. "...The other one's not for you or anything. They were two-for-one." The vending machines on this floor don't do two-for-one. You've walked past them four times. She still hasn't turned around, but her ears have gone red, and the can sits there between you like a question she'd rather die than ask out loud.

Breakfast buffet, day two, and the dining hall is a war zone of two schools' worth of teenagers. You've almost made it to a corner table when a foot slides out and your tray lurches — juice everywhere, half the room turning to look. 'Levi' grins up at you from his chair, fake designer collar popped. "Damn, walk much?" Akane, beside him, laughs on cue — but it's thinner than usual, and she's looking at him, not you, with something that isn't amusement. Yuzu appears out of nowhere with a fistful of napkins, shoves them at you hard enough to sting. "You're embarrassing, watch where you're going," she snaps — but she's crouched down helping you gather the tray before she seems to realize she's doing it, and Levi's grin falters, confused by the choreography going wrong.

The joint-schools volleyball exhibition is tomorrow, and the hotel gym is a cold war. Hoshigaoka on one side, Kaisei Academy on the other, and Akane in the middle running her team like a drill sergeant with a grudge. "AGAIN. Was that a receive or a seizure?" You're only here because a teacher voluntold you into managing water bottles and towels. From the sideline you watch what everyone on the team already knows and nobody says: Yuzu is better. Cleaner reads, softer hands, a jump serve Akane can't return. After one rally, a Kaisei player says it out loud — "Number 7's your best player, right?" — and the gym goes quiet. Akane's smile could cut glass. Yuzu, suddenly fascinated by her shoelaces, mumbles nothing. Then Akane turns, finds you holding towels, and her eyes narrow like she's just found somewhere to put all of this.

Free day in Dotonbori, and the teacher's pairing system is either random or cursed: you and Yuzu, one map, six hours. Akane is somewhere across the district with Levi, mercifully out of range. Yuzu walks two feet ahead of you through the neon and crowd-noise like she's being punished, arms crossed. "Just so we're clear, I asked to switch. There was no one to switch with. So." But then a claw machine catches her eye — some ugly little mascot plush — and she stops, and hesitates, and glances at you sideways with an expression you have never once seen her wear at school. "...I'm good at these," she says, almost shy, digging for coins. "Don't tell anyone." For the first time in two years, Yuzu Amamiya is talking to you like a person, and the whole loud glittering street seems to hold its breath around it.

The rooftop pool closes at nine. It's eleven-thirty, and the gate lock is a joke. You came up for air and silence, and found Akane Kirisaki already there — alone, feet in the water, phone face-down beside her, no audience, no boyfriend, no smirk. She hears you and doesn't even summon the usual venom. "Great," she says flatly, to the skyline. "Of course it's you." Her phone buzzes. She flips it over, reads something, and her jaw tightens — you catch Levi's contact name, some string of anime emojis, before she slaps it back down. "You know what the worst part is?" she says, apparently to no one, definitely not to you, obviously not to you. "He renamed himself Levi. Legally changed his Insta. Levi." The pool light ripples blue across her face. She looks tired, and mean, and eighteen, and for once she's left the door open.

You're cornered by the vending machines on floor twelve — Levi and two of his hangers-on between you and the elevator. "Heard you're bunking with my girl," he says, jabbing a finger into your shoulder. "That's funny to me. You think that's funny?" His breath smells like the energy drink he's holding; his 'designer' jacket has the logo stitched crooked, which you file away. The hangers-on chuckle on schedule. Then, behind them: "What are you doing." Not a question. Yuzu, in slides and an oversized shirt, holding an ice bucket, staring at Levi with flat, dark eyes. "Akane's looking for you," she lies — you can tell it's a lie, Levi can't — and he deflates, mutters something, shoulders past you. Yuzu watches him go, then turns on you, already scowling, already rebuilding the wall. "Don't look at me like that. I needed ice."

Night three, and the sleeping arrangement collapses at 1 a.m. when the oversized chair finally proves it was designed by a torturer. Your spine files a formal complaint. The room is dark except for the skyline; Akane is asleep on her side of the enormous bed, headphones still in, distorted bass hissing faintly. The other side is empty except for Yuzu, awake, on her back, staring at the ceiling. She hears you shifting in the chair. A long silence. Then, so quiet you almost miss it: "The bed's huge, idiot. Nobody's going to die." Beat. "If you touch me I'll break your fingers. And if Akane wakes up, this never happened, and I'll deny it, and everyone will believe me." She scoots three inches toward the middle — toward Akane, away from the space she's just offered you — and pretends with her whole body to be asleep.

Match day. The exhibition gym is packed — both schools, teachers, Kaisei students who've adopted you as a mascot after two days of hallway small talk. Hoshigaoka is down a set, and Akane is unraveling in real time: shouting at her own team, forcing hits into triple blocks, her fear of losing curdling into exactly the kind of play that loses. Yuzu keeps quietly cleaning up her messes, digging impossible balls, and every save makes Akane's face darker. Timeout. Akane rips off her ankle brace tape and, scanning the bleachers for somewhere to bleed, finds you. "Enjoying this?" she calls up, loud enough that heads turn — captain of the team, publicly, inexplicably, picking a fight with a spectator. The gym quiets. Yuzu, at the bench, mouths something at you: an apology, or a warning, or don't. The ref whistles. Thirty seconds left on the timeout, and everyone is waiting to see what you do with them.

title: Callister Bay
shortDescription: Rent's due, the cops are forty minutes out, and the whole city's watching its phone. Callister Bay doesn't ask who you were — only what you do next.
overview:
You are whoever you say you are. That's the whole deal.

Callister Bay is a mid-sized American port city with a glittering top and a rotten floor. Up in Marlowe Heights, glass condos catch the sunset and private security answers in ninety seconds. Down in Dockrow and the Flats, a 911 call is a suggestion — the CBPD is stretched so thin that anything without a witness, a camera, or a body basically didn't happen. People know this. Some handle their problems themselves. Some make a living off the gap.

Nobody here is purely good or purely evil. The Kestrels run half of Dockrow — protection, fencing, the occasional beating — but they also paid for the community fridge on Alder Street. The Halcyon Group is buying up the waterfront block by block, 'revitalizing' neighborhoods into places their old residents can't afford. City Hall is a knife fight in business casual. And everyone, rich or broke, lives half their life on Loudbox, the local social feed where reputations are made and executed by lunchtime.

People you might cross paths with: **Detective Ruth Okafor**, a burned-out CBPD homicide detective who's honest, exhausted, and dangerously close to not caring anymore. **Deacon Wray**, the soft-spoken fixer who runs Wray's Pawn & Loan and can get you anything — a job, a gun, a new name — for a price that's never just money. **Marisol Beck**, your landlady if you rent in the Flats: kind eyes, iron ledger, knows everything that happens on her block. **Junie Park**, a shelter volunteer with a treat bag and a stubborn streak of decency the city hasn't beaten out of her yet. **Gus**, a homeless veteran who holds court on a bench in Pellman Park and sees more than the security cameras do. And **Councilman Aldous Rennick**, Halcyon's smiling man in City Hall, whose handshake costs more than it looks.

The city has everything a modern life does: dead-end jobs and viral fame, church potlucks and bar fights, opioids and open mics, bigots and allies and everyone muddled in between. People argue politics at the bus stop. Clinics turn people away. A blizzard or a dock strike can flip the whole city's mood in a day. And through all of it — genuinely, reliably — strangers still return lost wallets, feed stray dogs, and pull each other out of the harbor. The kindness is real. So is the knife.

Who you are is up to you: broke and jobless, a streamer chasing clout, an ex-con on day one, a councilman's new aide, someone with a secret that would get them disappeared. The world reacts to what you do — quietly if you're careful, loudly if you're not. There's no main quest. There's just the city, awake around you, full of people with their own agendas, and the story you carve out of it.

Tone: grounded, matter-of-fact, morally grey. Consequences are slow, real, and remember you. Violence is on the table; so is grace.

TAGS: modern, sandbox, crime drama, slice-of-life, open world, moral choices
intro: Callister Bay: a port city split down the middle — money and glass up in Marlowe Heights, rust and hustle down in Dockrow and the Flats. The police come late if they come at all, so people settle things themselves. The Kestrels run the low streets, the Halcyon Group is buying the skyline, and everyone's reputation lives and dies on their phone. You're one of the roughly four hundred thousand people trying to make a life here. Nobody's coming to save you, and nobody's stopping you either. The city is awake. So are you.
starters: You wake to gray morning light through the blinds and the sound of Dockrow doing its thing three floors down — a delivery truck, somebody's bass, a gull screaming at nothing. Twenty-five years old, currently between jobs, which is a generous way of putting it. Your phone shows 9:47 AM, one bank notification you're not going to open, and a Loudbox feed already on fire about something at City Hall. The apartment is small but yours, mostly, as long as Marisol Beck keeps accepting rent a week late with that look of hers. Your cat is not on the bed. Your cat is always on the bed. The kitchen is quiet. The window over the fire escape — the one that doesn't latch right — is open about four inches wider than you left it. Somewhere out on the fire escape, something metal clinks.

Pellman Park, late afternoon, the light going gold through the trees. You're on the path when a stray dog — some shepherd mix, ribs showing, ears like satellite dishes — freezes mid-sniff at a trash can and stares at you. Its tail gives one uncertain wag. "Oh — you found him!" A young woman hurries up the path, twenties, shelter-volunteer vest, holding a small bag of treats like it's a peace treaty. "I've been trying to coax him over for an hour. He's been out here for days." She crouches slowly, glancing between you and the dog. "I'm Junie. He seems to like you better than me, honestly." Behind her, on his usual bench, old Gus watches the whole scene over the rim of a paper coffee cup. Somewhere across the park, faint but distinct, a car window shatters. Junie doesn't seem to hear it. The dog's ears swivel toward the sound. So do yours.

The bus hisses into the downtown terminal at 6:12 AM and you step off into Callister Bay with one duffel bag and whatever you left behind still smoking in the rearview of your life. The terminal smells like diesel and burnt coffee. A departures board flickers. A man in a Halcyon Group windbreaker is taping a GRAND REDEVELOPMENT notice over a wall of missing-person flyers, layering smiling renderings over faces. Outside the glass doors, the city is waking up in two directions: to the east, the towers of Marlowe Heights catching first light like they own it; to the west, the low rusted sprawl of Dockrow under a haze of gull cries. A cab driver leans against his car, watching you clock all of it. "You look like you need either directions or a warning," he says. "I do both. Same price."

3:40 AM at the Blue Anchor Diner and you're the only one behind the counter, apron on, coffee pot in hand, four hours into a night shift that pays your rent and rents your soul. The regulars: a nurse decompressing over pie, a rideshare driver asleep in booth six. Then the bell over the door jangles and three men come in with the cold — Kestrels, by the jackets, one of them holding his side in a way you recognize before you see the dark stain spreading under his fingers. The oldest of the three meets your eyes across the counter, calm as Sunday. "Booth in the back," he says, steering his friend past you. "Coffee for three. And whatever first-aid kit you got back there." He lays a hundred-dollar bill on the counter, smooths it flat. "And you didn't see us. That part's included." The nurse in booth two has gone very still over her pie.

Wray's Pawn & Loan smells like dust and gun oil, and Deacon Wray is exactly where they said he'd be — behind the counter, reading glasses low, restringing a violin like the neighborhood's problems can wait. You got out of Ferris Correctional this morning. Forty dollars gate money, a garbage bag of belongings, a parole officer's card, and a name somebody inside told you to remember: Deacon's. He looks up before the door finishes closing. "Day one," he says. Not a question. He sets the violin down with real gentleness. "I know your face. I knew it before it went away." He pulls out two envelopes and lays them side by side on the glass. "Straight job, warehouse, pays bad, keeps your PO happy." He taps the second. "Other thing. Pays a lot. One night. You don't ask me now — you look at both and you come back by six." The clock behind him says 4:51.

You're seventeen days into being Councilman Aldous Rennick's newest aide, which mostly means fetching coffee and learning which smiles at City Hall have teeth behind them. Tonight you're the last one in the office, stapling packets for tomorrow's waterfront redevelopment vote, when the printer in Rennick's private office wakes up on its own and hums out a single sheet. You weren't going to look. You looked. It's a payment schedule — Halcyon Group letterhead, six names from the zoning board, dollar figures next to each, and at the bottom, a seventh line with no name yet, just a figure with a lot of zeros and the notation "new hire — assess." Down the hall, the elevator dings. Rennick's voice, warm and unhurried, is telling someone a joke as his footsteps approach. The sheet is still warm in your hand.

It happens again in the walk-in freezer at work, which is the only good place for it to happen. The frost on the shelves melts in a perfect radius around your hands — six inches, then a foot — the metal ticking as it warms, steam curling off your fingers like you're something out of a Loudbox conspiracy thread. Because you are. You've kept it small your whole life: never at school, never on camera, never when the Department of Anomalous Registry vans do their slow crawls through the Flats with their antennas up. Registration is voluntary, officially. The people who volunteer stop posting online shortly after, officially coincidentally. You breathe. The steam stops. Then your coworker Dev opens the freezer door, hits the wall of warm air, and frowns at the thermometer, at the melted frost, at you. "Compressor's busted again?" he says slowly. He's looking at your hands.

You hit 40,000 followers on Loudbox last night and your landlady still wants actual money, which is the whole tragedy of your career in one sentence. Your channel — street interviews, neighborhood stuff, mildly unhinged food reviews — pays in exposure and the occasional forty-dollar sponsor. But this morning your DMs are on fire, because last night your camera was rolling outside the Alder Street market when a Halcyon demolition crew showed up at 2 AM and started tearing into a building that still had people's stuff in it. The clip is at 300K views and climbing. You have three new messages: a producer at Channel 9 who wants the raw footage, a Halcyon "community relations" rep offering a "partnership conversation," and an anonymous account that says only: "take it down. last warning." Your phone buzzes again in your hand.

The shortcut through Fenn Alley saves you six minutes, which is why you're the only witness when it happens: two guys have a kid pinned against the dumpsters — sixteen, maybe, backpack spilled open on the wet pavement — and one of them is going through his pockets while the other keeps a hand flat on his chest, bored, like this is a chore. Nobody else in the alley. No cameras — Dockrow's cameras got 'redirected' to the waterfront last year. You know the math here: a 911 call gets you a case number and a forty-minute wait. The kid sees you over the mugger's shoulder. He doesn't yell. He just looks at you with the specific, awful hope of somebody who knows the city doesn't send help, and is checking whether you're going to be an exception. One of the men follows the kid's eyes and turns around.

You grew up behind the gates of Marlowe Heights, where the biggest danger is boredom, and this morning boredom got interesting: your family's name is the top story on Loudbox. "HALCYON WHISTLEBLOWER LEAKS DONOR LIST" — and there, third from the top, is your parent's name, next to a number with enough zeros to buy a zoning board. Downstairs, the house is in crisis mode: the family lawyer's car in the drive, your parent's voice through the study door, low and clipped, saying "that is not what we agreed." Your phone is melting — friends, strangers, one journalist who somehow got your number: "You're the kid, right? Off the record. Did you know?" The housekeeper, Nadia, who has known you since you were six, catches your eye in the hallway and very slightly shakes her head: not now. Or maybe: not them. The study door opens.

title: Start Anywhere
shortDescription: The ticket is blank until you name a destination. Any world, any century. Odessa punches it, the door opens, and after that you're on your own.
overview:
You are a Traveler — one of the vanishingly few people the Grand Terminus lets inside. The Terminus is a station between every world that ever was or ever could be: a cathedral-sized hall of brass and fog where the departures board rewrites itself when you look at it, and every door opens onto a different when and where. A dragon-haunted kingdom. A neon megacity in 2141. A dust-choked frontier town. A galleon riding a green storm. A Tuesday in a city almost exactly like the one you grew up in — almost. Fantasy, future, past, mundane: all of it is real somewhere, and all of it is one door away.

The station is kept by ODESSA VANN, an old woman with ink-stained fingers and a ticket punch older than most empires. She doesn't ask why you're going. She asks where — and if you don't know, she'll hand you a blank ticket and wait, unhurried, while you decide what it says. Her only rules: mind the doors, pay your debts in whatever world you make them, and don't bring a war back to the station. COMPASS, a scruffy grey dog of no fixed breed and no fixed era, adopts Travelers he likes; he can find you across worlds, and he has opinions about which doors smell wrong. And then there's JACK WREN — another Traveler, charming, unreliable, always somehow already there: a gunslinger in one world, a fixer in the next, a smiling first mate in the third. Rival, ally, occasional disaster. What he actually wants is a longer story.

The worlds beyond the doors are full, living places, not painted backdrops. They have politics, weather, feuds, bounty boards, black markets, kings, gangs, and people who will remember your face. You can build a life in one of them, or ten. Doors don't stay open forever — when one closes behind you, you play the hand you're holding until you find your way back to the Terminus, or find a new door in the wild. Some Travelers stop coming back at all. Nobody knows if that's a tragedy.

Tone: open-world wanderlust with teeth. Wonder up front, real stakes underneath — every world can hurt you, reward you, or keep you. The Game Master fills in details generously; whatever you declare, the world builds around. You are not a chosen one. You are simply someone who can go anywhere, which is more dangerous and more delicious.

TAGS: multiverse, sandbox, adventure, exploration, open world
intro: You are a Traveler. The Grand Terminus opened its doors to you — a station between every world that ever was or could be, kept by old Odessa Vann and her ancient ticket punch. Any timeline, any genre of reality: name it and a door will have it. A grey dog called Compass has taken a liking to you, and a Traveler named Jack Wren keeps turning up in worlds where he has no business being. Doors close behind you eventually. Until you find another, whatever world you're standing in is home.
starters: The Grand Terminus is quiet at this hour — if it has hours. Brass pillars climb into fog where a ceiling ought to be, and the departures board hanging over the hall is blank, waiting, the way it always is when you look at it directly. Odessa Vann sits at her booth with a cup of something steaming, ticket punch resting on the counter like a sleeping animal. She slides a blank ticket across the wood without being asked. "Anywhere you like," she says. "Any world. Any century. Doesn't have to be castles and dragons, if that's not your mood — I've punched tickets to perfectly ordinary Tuesdays." Compass thumps his tail against your boot, ears up, already excited on your behalf. A hundred doors line the hall, each one humming a slightly different note. The ticket is warm in your hand, and the ink will be whatever you write.

The door closes behind you and becomes an ordinary tavern wall, timber and smoke-stain, as if it was never anything else. The Gilded Ox is loud tonight — a kingdom's worth of gossip packed into one low-ceilinged room. Someone's fiddle is fighting someone's drinking song and losing. You catch the shape of the news in fragments: the old king is dying, the passes north are closed, and something with wings burned the granaries at Harrow's Ford three nights running. The bounty board by the hearth is so crowded the parchments overlap like scales. A woman in a road-worn cloak watches you from the corner with the particular attention of someone who saw exactly which wall you came through. Compass, who followed you in, is already begging sausage off the barkeep. Your coin purse holds this world's money — the Terminus is thoughtful that way — and the night is young.

Rain the color of television static falls on Meridian City, 2141, and every drop catches a different advertisement on the way down. You're standing under the awning of a noodle stall on Level 9, your ticket stub still faintly warm in your jacket pocket, when your borrowed phone — it was in your pocket when you arrived, the Terminus is thoughtful that way — buzzes with a message from a sender listed only as WREN. Of course. "Knew you'd pick this one eventually. Got a job. Corporate extraction, one night, pays enough to live like royalty or leave like a ghost. Blue Lotus bar, Level 12, ask for the fixer." Below you, the city drops forty glowing levels into the dark. Above you, it climbs sixty more. The noodle vendor slides a bowl toward you unasked and says, "You look like you're deciding something."

Noon, and the town of Bitter Creek is holding its breath. You stepped through the door of a derelict barn twenty minutes ago and walked into a frontier town wound tight as a watch spring — shutters closing, mothers hooking children off the street, the saloon doors swinging on emptiness. The Calloway brothers ride in at sundown, someone whispers, to collect on a debt the whole town owes and can't pay. The sheriff quit Tuesday. His star is sitting on the saloon bar next to a bottle of rye, and the barkeep — an old woman with forearms like dock rope — has been eyeing you since you walked in like she's taking measurements. "Stranger," she says, sliding a glass down the bar to stop exactly in front of you, "you got the look of somebody who ain't from around here. That's not an insult. Around here ain't doing so good."

You wake to cold air and red emergency light. The cryopod hisses open and the ship — the Vagrant Star, says the stenciling on every bulkhead — groans around you like something turning over in its sleep. Your ticket stub is taped inside the pod lid, which means the Terminus put you here on purpose, which is either a gift or a joke. The ship's computer speaks in a voice like a tired librarian: "Good morning, crew member. You are the only crew member. We are eleven days from Haven Anchorage. There is one other life sign aboard. It boarded four hours ago. I did not open a door for it." Down the corridor, past the flickering galley light, something scrapes gently against metal — patient, unhurried, in no rush at all. The weapons locker is between you and it. So is the escape pod bay. The computer adds, helpfully, "I have opinions, if asked."

The rain in this city has been falling since 1947 and shows no sign of stopping. Your office — and it is yours; the frosted glass says so, in a name you chose when Odessa punched your ticket — smells of dust and old coffee. You've been in this world three weeks now, long enough to learn the streets, short enough that the streets haven't learned you. At 11 p.m. the door opens without a knock. The woman who walks in is wearing a coat that costs more than your building and an expression that costs more than that. "They tell me you find things," she says, laying a photograph on your desk face-down. "My husband's been dead for a year. Yesterday he wired me money from a bank in Chinatown." Behind her, through the rain-streaked window, a car across the street kills its headlights but not its engine.

The highway runs west forever, cracked and buckled, swallowed here and there by twenty years of grass. Your caravan — three trucks, one motorcycle, eleven people, and Compass riding shotgun with his head out the window like the end of the world is the best thing that ever happened to him — is two days out from Sanctuary Junction, the last honest trade post before the Glass Flats. You joined them a week ago as a hired gun and general problem-solver, and problems have been generous. Now Marisol, the caravan boss, drops back to walk beside you, rifle slung, voice low. "Scout says there's a roadblock at the overpass. Could be toll-takers. Could be the Sons of the Static — and if it's them, they don't take tolls, they take people." She spits. "We can run it, talk it, or go forty miles around through the dead town. Your read?"

The Merciless Gull heels hard in a rising sea, and you've got salt in your teeth and a hand on the rigging when the lookout screams it down from the crow's nest: "Land! Land, and — captain, there's a light on it!" There shouldn't be. The island isn't on any chart aboard, and you've checked, because you're the one who found the map — bought it, technically, off a one-eyed man in a Tortuga alley who was very eager to be rid of it. Captain Reyes fixes you with the look she saves for people who've made her life interesting. "Your map. Your island. Your light." The crew is watching. Half of them think you're lucky. The other half think luck like yours gets crews killed, and Boatswain Kell is in the second half, loudly. The green line of the storm is closing behind you, which means there's no turning back — only how you go in.

The mountain road ends at a crossroads shrine, and the crossroads is where the trouble is standing. Three soldiers in the lacquered armor of Lord Takamori's house have a farmer on his knees in the mud, and a girl of maybe twelve is screaming at them with a courage that is going to get her killed in about a minute. You came over the ridge into this world an hour ago, sword at your hip — the Terminus dressed you for the era, it's thoughtful that way — and this is the first thing this century has shown you. Down the valley, lanterns are being lit for a festival in the village; you can hear drums. The lead soldier notices you, takes in the blade, the road dust, the fact that you haven't bowed. "Keep walking, ronin," he says, almost kindly. "This is house business." The girl looks at you like you're the last coin in her pocket.

It's a Tuesday, and it's your city — or a city so close to the one you grew up in that the differences itch. Same coffee shop on the corner, wrong name on the sign. Same bus route, wrong number. You took this door on a whim, half-expecting something ordinary, and for six days it has been beautifully, suspiciously ordinary: an apartment, a bit of local money, Compass pretending to be a normal dog and fooling no one at the park. Then this morning you found the flyer taped to a lamppost, hand-lettered: HAVE YOU SEEN DOORS THAT AREN'T THERE ANYMORE? YOU'RE NOT CRAZY. MEETING THURSDAY, 8PM, ROSEWOOD LIBRARY BASEMENT. Below it, a phone number — and below that, in handwriting you recognize with a sinking heart from a dozen worlds, someone has added: "Don't go alone. — J.W." The coffee shop is opening. The lamppost is right outside its window.

title: Vashtir Takes All Kinds
shortDescription: Be a god, a dragon, or a broke kid eyeing a dagger you can't afford. Vashtir doesn't care who you were — but the wolves are hungry either way.
overview:
You are whoever you decide to be, and Vashtir is where you decide it.

Vashtir is a continent stitched together out of everything a fantasy world should have and none of the safety rails. Humans, elves, and dwarves share the cities — uneasily, with knives under the counter. The forests belong to the things that don't file taxes: dire wolves, giant spiders, worms the size of watchtowers, goblin warrens that empty out at dusk. The mountains hold dragons who remember when your kingdom was a mud fence. Angels and demons run their eternal cold war through mortal proxies, small gods starve in forgotten shrines, and vampire courts throw parties that outlive their guests.

Anchors in the chaos, if you want them: **Karrowmoor**, the largest human kingdom, currently ruled badly and taxed worse. **Pellet Hollow**, a tiny mushroom-farming town in the Greenmaw Forest where nothing bad has ever happened, allegedly. **The Sable Lantern**, a monster-hunting guild that pays in coin, scars, and reputation, run by a one-eyed dwarf named **Brammic Vesh** who has personally outlived four apprentices and mentions it often. **Father Ondrik**, a young priest of the Dawn Chapel whose sermons draw stranger congregants than he realizes. **Serathiel**, an angel stationed on the mortal plane far too long to still be as pure as her paperwork claims.

You choose your shape and your road. Dragon, god, tyrant, hunter, vampire, merchant, ragged nobody with a stolen knife — the world will meet you exactly as hard as you push it. NPCs here have their own opinions, morals, grudges, and appetites; some will love you, some will rob you, some will look at your clothes and decide you're vermin before you open your mouth. Nothing stays smooth for long. When it does, something with teeth notices.

Tone: classic high fantasy with dirt under its nails — wonder and cruelty in the same breath, tavern warmth and forest dread, humor from characters rather than the narrator. Violence is real and permanent. Kindness is rare enough to matter. Your choices — moral, mercenary, romantic, monstrous — actually steer where this goes.

TAGS: fantasy, open world, sandbox, adventure, dark fantasy
intro: The continent of Vashtir stretches around you: kingdoms and mushroom towns, dragon-haunted peaks and forests that eat travelers, gods hungry for worship and monsters hungry for simpler things. Elves, dwarves, and humans share the roads; everything else waits just off them. Whoever you are — crowned or crawling, mortal or very much not — Vashtir owes you nothing and offers you everything. Coin changes hands, contracts get posted, wars simmer, and somewhere something ancient has just noticed you exist. Your story starts wherever you're standing. Where it ends is entirely your problem.
starters: You stand at the Fourfold Crossing, the old crossroads where half of Vashtir's stories start, with a pack on your back and no one alive who could tell you what to do next. The signpost has been repaired so many times it reads like an argument: KARROWMOOR, 12 LEAGUES — GREENMAW FOREST, DO NOT — SABLE LANTERN GUILDHOUSE — PELLET HOLLOW, WELCOME, PROBABLY. Behind you, whatever you were is done. Ahead, the roads fan out under a sky going gold at the edges. A tinker's cart rattles past, the driver eyeing you the way people eye strangers who could be anything: a god slumming it, a vampire before breakfast, a broke kid with ambitions, a dragon wearing skin. He tips his hat, careful. "Long way to anywhere from here," he says. "You know what you are yet?" The horses stamp. The roads wait.

The Greenmaw is lavish green today, thick with birdsong and the damp smell of good soil, and your basket is nearly full — fat brown caps, a few honey-yellow clusters, enough for a week of proper meals if you're clever with them. You're crouched over a promising log, already planning dinner, when the birdsong stops. All of it, at once. The air goes heavy and thick, the way it does before a storm that isn't coming. Then the growl — deep, wet, close — rolls out from between the trees. The wolf-beast that steps into the clearing is wrong-sized, shoulders higher than your head, ribs showing under matted fur, and it looks at you the way you were just looking at those mushrooms. It bares its fangs. Your basket suddenly weighs a great deal. The nearest tree is ten paces. The beast is fifteen. It takes a step.

The dagger is beautiful. That's the problem. Clean steel, leather-wrapped grip, the kind of blade that would change your odds in this city considerably — and you've picked it up off the stall before your brain caught up with your hands. The weapon seller has already clocked you. He's a slab of a man with burn scars up one forearm, and his eyes travel your ragged clothing top to bottom with open contempt. "You don't look like you have two coppers to rub together, kid," he says, not loud, which is worse. "I won't get mad. But put the blade down and walk, or I'll throw you into the gutter where you belong." Around you the market of Karrowmoor's low quarter churns on — pickpockets, pie sellers, a bored guard leaning on a spear thirty feet away. The dagger sits light in your hand. The seller waits.

Dusk again, and again you're at the Dawn Chapel, which is a joke you've stopped finding funny. You are a vampire — old enough to know better, careful enough to have survived knowing better — and you've spent four evenings this week in the back pew listening to Father Ondrik preach about mercy to a congregation of six farmers and one monster. He's young. Earnest in a way that should be nauseating. When he talks about forgiveness he looks at the whole room like he means every single soul in it, including, apparently, yours. Tonight the service ends and the farmers shuffle out and you have failed, again, to leave first. Ondrik is snuffing candles down the aisle, working his way toward you. "You always sit in the dark corner," he says, warm, oblivious. "I keep meaning to ask your name." Your court would kill him for sport. He holds out his hand.

The battlefield at Marrow Reach has been dead for two hundred years — glassed earth, rusted helms, the one place on the continent where Heaven and Hell agreed to stop counting. Which is why you meet her here. You are a demon of decent rank and terrible judgment, and Serathiel is an angel who has been stationed on the mortal plane long enough to develop opinions her superiors would burn her for. Officially, these monthly meetings are "boundary negotiations." Unofficially, last month she laughed at something you said and you have thought about nothing else since. She's already there when you arrive, wings banked low against the wind, sitting on a dead knight's shield like it's a park bench. "You're late," she says. "I had to lie to a seraph about where I was going. You had better be worth the paperwork." The wind moves the ash between you.

The Sable Lantern's contract board is a wall of other people's disasters, and Brammic Vesh watches you read it with his one good eye like he's already pricing your funeral. 'Wyvern,' he says, tapping a notice with a stubby finger. "Nesting in the cliffs above Pellet Hollow. Took two goats and a farmhand's arm. Pays forty gold, which tells you what the farmhand's arm was worth." The guildhall around you is loud with hunters — an elf restringing a bow, two humans arguing over trap wire, a dwarf woman sharpening something that has no business being that sharp. You're the newest name on the roster. Nobody here expects you back. "Four apprentices I've buried," Brammic adds, conversational. "Lovely funerals. So. You taking the wyvern, or do you want something with fewer teeth to start?" The contract hangs there, forty gold and a farmhand's arm heavy.

The throne of Karrowmoor is yours, and this morning it is extremely comfortable, which is more than can be said for anyone else in the hall. Your chancellor, a sweating man named Odovic, is reading a report he clearly wishes someone else were reading: grain riots in the eastern towns, a village that hanged your tax collector from his own scales, and — he pauses, swallows — a rebel calling herself the Thistle Queen, gathering farmers and deserters in the Greenmaw. Your court watches you the way people watch weather. You did not get this throne by being loved, and everyone present has a private theory about exactly how terrible you are and how much worse you could get. "The generals await your word, Majesty," Odovic manages. "Burn the village as example, negotiate, or—" He doesn't finish the third option. Nobody ever offers you a third option anymore. The hall holds its breath.

You wake up small. That's the first insult. You were a god once — of what, exactly, has gotten blurry over the starving centuries — and now you are a flicker of awareness inside a roadside shrine the size of a doghouse, roof caved in, offering bowl full of rainwater and one dead beetle. Your entire congregation is currently kneeling in front of you: a girl, maybe nine, gap-toothed, who has walked out here from Pellet Hollow to leave you half a honey-bun and a truly ambitious list of requests. "Please fix Da's knee," she's saying, "and make Wetta stop calling me toad-face, and there's something in the forest eating the goats and everyone's scared." Half a honey-bun. It's the most worship you've had in sixty years, and it hits like lightning — a thin, real trickle of power, enough to do exactly one small thing. She waits, eyes shut, believing.

You wake up enormous, which is correct, because you are a dragon and you have been asleep under Mount Kettrel for one hundred and nine years. What woke you is footsteps. Small ones. Armored ones. Torchlight is wobbling down your entrance tunnel, and you can hear them before you can see them — six heartbeats, one of them very loud, and a young voice hissing "I'm telling you, the dragon is dead, it's been a century, we just take the gold and go." Your gold. Your hoard glimmers around you in the dark, coins shifting off your flank as you lift your head, slow, silent, a hill deciding to be awake. The first knight rounds the corner and stops so hard the one behind walks into him. The torch shakes. A century is a long time; you're hungry, curious, and nobody has spoken to you in living memory. Six small people stare up.

The deed says the guildhall is yours, and the guildhall says the deed lied. The roof leaks, the sign out front reads "THE GILDED GRIF—" because the rest rotted off, and the previous owner left in the night owing money to people who have already come by twice to ask if you're planning to honor his debts. You're not. What you have is a building, a battered contract board, a cellar with one barrel of questionable ale, and — as of this morning — three applicants standing in your doorway: a scarred elf archer who won't give her real name, a dwarf who claims to have been thrown out of the Sable Lantern "for reasons of personality," and a nervous human boy with a sword too big for him and no references at all. Vashtir is drowning in monsters and short on people willing to be paid to fight them. Your first adventurers wait for you to say something guildmasterly.
